shelves.title: Pegfilgrastim for alcohol-associated hepatitis: a negative phase II trial
shelves.question: Does adding pegfilgrastim (long-acting G-CSF) to standard care improve 90-day survival in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis?
shelves.balance: In the United States, adding pegfilgrastim to prednisolone did not improve 90-day survival — 73% vs 83% in a trial stopped early at 34 patients — and it moved nothing else either: kidney injury, encephalopathy, and infections were the same. That sits against a 2020 meta-analysis in which G-CSF looked life-saving in Asian trials (death OR 0.15) and possibly harmful in European ones (OR 1.89), with the authors refusing to recommend it anywhere. A negative trial, honestly reported, is still evidence — and this one is the developer's own.

cards.headline: Pegfilgrastim plus prednisolone: 90-day survival 73% vs 83% — no benefit, in a trial stopped early at 34 patients.
cards.summary: 90-day survival 0.83 vs 0.73 (standard of care vs pegfilgrastim), p>0.05 — 34 patients; the trial was terminated early due to COVID-19.
cards.type: Phase II, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial.
cards.people: 34 patients with clinical alcohol-associated hepatitis and Maddrey discriminant function ≥32, randomized Mar 2017–Mar 2020: 18 standard of care, 16 SOC + pegfilgrastim 0.6 mg SC Day 1 and Day 8 (second dose withheld if WBC >30,000/mm³). All received prednisolone 40 mg/day as SOC. NCT02776059.
cards.result: Terminated early due to COVID-19. 9 patients did not receive the second dose (WBC >30,000). Survival at 90 days: SOC 0.83 (0.57–0.94) vs pegfilgrastim 0.73 (0.44–0.89), p>0.05; CI for difference −0.18 to 0.38. AKI, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy, and infections similar in both arms; no serious adverse events attributed to pegfilgrastim.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, n=34, stopped early — wide confidence intervals; the trial cannot exclude a benefit or a harm. All patients got prednisolone; pentoxifylline was allowed but none received it.
cards.source: Tayek JA et al. EClinicalMedicine 2022;54:101689. PMID 36267499. PMCID PMC9576807. DOI 10.1016/j.eclinm.2022.101689. Funded by NIH/NIAAA U01-AA021886 and U01-AA021884.
cards.search: pegfilgrastim g-csf alcohol-associated hepatitis alcoholic hepatitis prednisolone tayek eclinicalmedicine 2022 phase ii randomized trial maddrey discriminant function nct02776059 pmid 36267499

cards.headline: Seven trials, 396 patients: G-CSF looks life-saving in Asia and possibly harmful in Europe.
cards.summary: 90-day death OR 0.28 overall — but Asia OR 0.15 vs Europe OR 1.89 , with heterogeneity I²=80% — 7 studies, 396 patients.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs.
cards.people: 7 studies, 396 patients (336 with AH); 197 G-CSF, 199 placebo or pentoxifylline. 5 studies in Asia, 2 in Europe.
cards.result: 90-day death OR 0.28 (0.09–0.88, p=0.03) overall — but heterogeneity I²=80%. Asia: OR 0.15 (0.08–0.28, p<0.001), I²=0%. Europe: OR 1.89 (0.90–3.98, p=0.09) — tended toward higher mortality, not significant. Infections: Asia OR 0.12 (0.06–0.23); Europe OR 0.92 (0.50–1.68), NS.
cards.watchOut: Published in 2020, before the Tayek trial — his trial is not in this pooled estimate. The authors' conclusion: G-CSF cannot currently be recommended, particularly in Europe; whether the split is ethnic differences or patient selection and severity is unclear.
cards.source: Marot A et al. JHEP Rep 2020;2(5):100139. PMCID PMC7396826.
cards.search: marot 2020 g-csf alcoholic hepatitis alcohol-associated hepatitis meta-analysis systematic review randomized trials jhep reports pmcid pmc7396826 asia europe 90-day mortality

shelves.title: Albumin in cirrhosis: five trials, one pattern
shelves.question: When does infusing albumin actually help patients with cirrhosis — and when is it just chasing a number?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Albumins · Aldosterone · Ascites · Bacterial Infections · Cefotaxime · Cephalosporins · Combined Modality Therapy · Diuretics · Double-Blind Method · Drainage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Furosemide · Hospitalization · Humans · Hyperkalemia · Hyponatremia · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Diseases · Length of Stay · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Midodrine · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Norepinephrine · Paracentesis · Peritonitis · Plasma Volume · Pulmonary Edema · Quality of Life · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Random Allocation · Renal Insufficiency · Renin · Serum Albumin · Shock · Survival Rate · Time Factors · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents
shelves.balance: The five trials sort cleanly by indication. Albumin works where there's a defined circulatory job: alongside antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (Sort: mortality cut by two-thirds), and covering large-volume paracentesis (Ginès 1988: no renal complications vs 11 without). It works given long-term to outpatients with ascites (ANSWER: survival 77% vs 66%). It fails as a short inpatient campaign to normalize the level (ATTIRE: null, more serious adverse events) and bundled with midodrine on the transplant waitlist (MACHT: null). The pattern: albumin is a drug for specific hemodynamic jobs, not a lab-value cosmetic.

cards.headline: ATTIRE 2021: targeted albumin infusions in hospitalized cirrhosis — primary outcome 29.7% vs 30.2%, null, with more serious adverse events.
cards.summary: Patients received a median 200 g of albumin (targeted arm) vs 20 g standard care. The primary composite (new infection, renal dysfunction, or death between days 3–15) occurred in 29.7% (113/380) vs 30.2% (120/397) (adjusted odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.71–1.33; P=0.87). More severe or life-threatening serious adverse events occurred in the albumin group.
cards.people: 777 hospitalized patients with decompensated cirrhosis and albumin <30 g/L (most alcohol-related)
cards.result: Patients received a median 200 g of albumin (targeted arm) vs 20 g standard care. The primary composite (new infection, renal dysfunction, or death between days 3–15) occurred in 29.7% (113/380) vs 30.2% (120/397) (adjusted odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.71–1.33; P=0.87). More severe or life-threatening serious adverse events occurred in the albumin group.
cards.watchOut: A tenfold dose difference that moved the level but not the outcome — the strongest trial evidence that the admission albumin number is a severity marker, not a lever. Short horizon, inpatient strategy; it does not test chronic supplementation (Reference 2).
cards.source: China L et al., N Engl J Med 2021 (PMID 33657293 · EudraCT 2014-002300-24)

cards.headline: ANSWER 2018: long-term weekly albumin in decompensated cirrhosis — 18-month survival 77% vs 66% (HR 0.62).
cards.summary: Overall 18-month survival was 77% with standard medical treatment plus long-term albumin vs 66% with standard treatment alone (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.40–0.95; P=0.028); deaths 38/218 vs 46/213. Grade 3–4 non-liver adverse events were similar (22% vs 22%).
cards.people: 440 patients with decompensated cirrhosis and uncomplicated ascites (431 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis)
cards.result: Overall 18-month survival was 77% with standard medical treatment plus long-term albumin vs 66% with standard treatment alone (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.40–0.95; P=0.028); deaths 38/218 vs 46/213. Grade 3–4 non-liver adverse events were similar (22% vs 22%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-country — the survival signal awaits a blinded replication. But against ATTIRE it makes the shelf's point: duration and setting, not dose intensity, separated success from failure.
cards.source: Caraceni P et al., Lancet 2018 (PMID 29861076 · NCT01288794)

cards.headline: Sort 1999: albumin with antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — in-hospital death 10% vs 29%; renal impairment 10% vs 33%.
cards.summary: Infection resolution was similar (98% with albumin vs 94% without; P=0.36) — but renal impairment developed in 10% vs 33% (P=0.002), in-hospital death was 10% vs 29% (P=0.01), and 3-month mortality 22% vs 41% (P=0.03). Dosing: 1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3.
cards.people: 126 patients with cirrhosis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, all on cefotaxime
cards.result: Infection resolution was similar (98% with albumin vs 94% without; P=0.36) — but renal impairment developed in 10% vs 33% (P=0.002), in-hospital death was 10% vs 29% (P=0.01), and 3-month mortality 22% vs 41% (P=0.03). Dosing: 1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3.
cards.watchOut: Single-center, unblinded, pre-registration era — the oldest design here carrying the largest effect. Its result has never been re-tested at scale because it became standard of care on this one trial; the shelf prints it as the field's foundation, with its age visible.
cards.source: Sort P et al., N Engl J Med 1999 (PMID 10432325 — no registry ID, pre-registration era)

cards.headline: Ginès 1988: albumin after large-volume paracentesis prevented the renal and electrolyte complications seen without it (11 patients vs none).
cards.summary: Renal impairment or severe hyponatremia developed in 11 patients treated without albumin and in none treated with it; albumin prevented the activation of endogenous vasoconstrictor systems that follows fluid removal.
cards.people: 105 patients with cirrhosis and tense ascites undergoing repeated 4–6 L paracentesis (52 with intravenous albumin, 53 without)
cards.result: Renal impairment or severe hyponatremia developed in 11 patients treated without albumin and in none treated with it; albumin prevented the activation of endogenous vasoconstrictor systems that follows fluid removal.
cards.watchOut: From 1988 — endpoints are complications and physiology, not survival, and modern post-paracentesis practice descends from this single trial. It earns its card as the origin of an indication, labeled as such.
cards.source: Ginès P et al., Gastroenterology 1988 (PMID 3360270 — no registry ID, pre-registration era)

cards.headline: MACHT 2018: a year of midodrine + albumin on the transplant waitlist — no fewer complications (P=0.40), no survival benefit (P=0.53).
cards.summary: The probability of developing complications of cirrhosis did not differ between midodrine-plus-albumin and placebo (P=0.402), nor did one-year mortality (P=0.527) — even though the treatment measurably suppressed plasma renin activity and aldosterone, its intended mechanism.
cards.people: Patients with decompensated cirrhosis awaiting liver transplantation
cards.result: The probability of developing complications of cirrhosis did not differ between midodrine-plus-albumin and placebo (P=0.402), nor did one-year mortality (P=0.527) — even though the treatment measurably suppressed plasma renin activity and aldosterone, its intended mechanism.
cards.watchOut: The albumin is bundled with midodrine, so this tests a package, not albumin alone — and the mechanism markers moved while outcomes didn't (the shelf's recurring lesson in miniature). It tempers ANSWER: setting, dose, and duration differ, and the waitlist population is sicker.
cards.source: Solà E et al., J Hepatol 2018 (PMID 30138685 · NCT00839358)

shelves.title: C. difficile: the cure is easy — preventing the comeback is the contest
shelves.question: For C. difficile infection, standard antibiotics tie on initial cure — which strategies prevent the recurrence that causes the real toll?
shelves.mesh: Bezlotoxumab · Clostridioides difficile · Fidaxomicin · Vancomycin
shelves.balance: Standard antibiotics cure roughly 87–89% of first episodes no matter which you pick (Louie, Cornely). The disease's real toll is the ~1-in-4 who relapse — and three randomized strategies cut that: a narrow-spectrum drug that spares the flora (recurrence 15% vs 25%), the same drug stretched into a pulse in older patients (sustained cure 70% vs 59%), and an antibody that disarms the toxin while the gut recovers (recurrence ~17% vs ~27%, twice). What doesn't differ anywhere on this shelf: the initial cure.

cards.headline: Louie 2011: fidaxomicin matched vancomycin on cure (88.2% vs 85.8%) and cut recurrence to 15.4% vs 25.3%.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority trial, North America
cards.people: 629 enrolled; mITT 287 fidaxomicin (200 mg PO BID × 10 d) vs 309 vancomycin (125 mg PO QID × 10 d)
cards.watchOut: In the NAP1/BI/027 subgroup the recurrence advantage disappeared. Industry-sponsored (Optimer).
cards.source: Louie TJ et al., N Engl J Med 2011 (PMID 21288078 · NCT00314951)
cards.search: louie 2011: fidaxomicin matched vancomycin on cure (88.2% vs 85.8%) and cut recurrence to 15.4% vs 25.3%. randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority trial, north america 629 enrolled; mitt 287 fidaxomicin (200 mg po bid × 10 d) vs 309 vancomycin (125 mg po qid × 10 d) clinical cure 88.2% (253/287) vs 85.8% (265/309) — non-inferior. recurrence 15.4% (39/253) vs 25.3% (67/265), p=0.005. global cure 74.6% vs 64.1%. in the nap1/bi/027 subgroup the recurrence advantage disappeared. industry-sponsored (optimer). louie tj et al., n engl j med 2011 (pmid 21288078 · nct00314951) pmid 21288078 nct00314951 icd a04.7 clostridioides difficile · fidaxomicin · vancomycin

cards.headline: Cornely 2012: the European twin trial replicated it — cure 87.7% vs 86.8%, recurrence 12.7% vs 26.9%, sustained response 76.6% vs 63.4%.
cards.people: 535 enrolled; mITT 252 fidaxomicin vs 257 vancomycin, same doses/duration as Card 1
cards.watchOut: Unlike Card 1, the recurrence benefit here held in the 027 ribotype subgroup (22.2% vs 38.0%). Two trials, one sponsor program — replication across continents, not across independent groups.
cards.source: Cornely OA et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2012 (PMID 22321770 · NCT00468728)

cards.headline: EXTEND 2018: stretching fidaxomicin into an extended pulse in patients over 60 — sustained cure 70% vs 59% on vancomycin (P=0.030).
cards.summary: Sustained clinical cure 30 days after treatment ended: 70% (124/177) with extended-pulsed fidaxomicin vs 59% (106/179) with vancomycin — difference 11 percentage points (95% CI 1.0–20.7; P=0.030; OR 1.62), with no difference in treatment-emergent adverse events.
cards.people: 364 patients aged 60+ with C. difficile infection (362 dosed)
cards.result: Sustained clinical cure 30 days after treatment ended: 70% (124/177) with extended-pulsed fidaxomicin vs 59% (106/179) with vancomycin — difference 11 percentage points (95% CI 1.0–20.7; P=0.030; OR 1.62), with no difference in treatment-emergent adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the regimen — not just the molecule — is the intervention: the same drug given longer and tapered, letting the gut flora recover between pulses. It supports the shelf's mechanism story (spare the microbiome, prevent the comeback) more than it crowns a product.
cards.source: Guery B et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2018 (PMID 29273269 · NCT02254967)

cards.headline: Bezlotoxumab 2017: an antibody against toxin B, added to ordinary antibiotics, cut recurrence from ~27% to ~17% — in two separate trials.
cards.summary: Recurrence was significantly lower with bezlotoxumab in both trials — MODIFY I: 17% (67/386) vs 28% (109/395), adjusted difference −10.1 points (P<0.001); MODIFY II: 16% (62/395) vs 26% (97/378), adjusted difference −9.9 points (P<0.001). The antibody treats nothing — it neutralizes toxin while the antibiotics and the recovering flora do the work.
cards.type: Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (MODIFY I and MODIFY II)
cards.people: Adults with primary or recurrent C. difficile infection on standard antibiotics, enriched for recurrence risk
cards.result: Recurrence was significantly lower with bezlotoxumab in both trials — MODIFY I: 17% (67/386) vs 28% (109/395), adjusted difference −10.1 points (P<0.001); MODIFY II: 16% (62/395) vs 26% (97/378), adjusted difference −9.9 points (P<0.001). The antibody treats nothing — it neutralizes toxin while the antibiotics and the recovering flora do the work.
cards.watchOut: Prevention only, in a selected higher-risk population, at monoclonal-antibody prices — and the manufacturer's companion antibody (actoxumab) added nothing. The two-trial replication is the strongest design on this shelf; the cost-effectiveness question is not answered by either trial.
cards.source: Wilcox MH et al., N Engl J Med 2017 (PMID 28121498 · NCT01241552 · NCT01513239)

shelves.title: Uncomplicated diverticulitis: leaving out the antibiotic.
shelves.question: In CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis, does treatment without antibiotics recover patients as safely as treatment with them?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Diverticulitis, Colonic · Amoxicillin-Potassium Clavulanate Combination · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials, 1,151 patients. Omitting antibiotics did not significantly slow recovery, raise complications (AVOD 1.9% vs 1.0%; DIABOLO 3.8% vs 2.6% — both non-significant, both numerically favoring antibiotics), or raise recurrence; DIABOLO’s no-antibiotic group left hospital a day sooner. The boundary is the exclusions: sepsis, peritonitis, CT-complicated disease, and immune suppression were kept out of both trials.

cards.headline: AVOD 2012: skipping antibiotics in uncomplicated diverticulitis — complications 1.9% vs 1.0%, recurrence 16% in both groups at one year.
cards.summary: Perforation or abscess 1.9% (6/309) vs 1.0% (3/314), P=0.302. Median hospital stay 3 days in both groups. Recurrent diverticulitis needing readmission at 1 year 16% in both groups (P=0.881).
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, multicenter trial (10 surgical departments in Sweden, 1 in Iceland)
cards.people: 623 patients with CT-verified acute uncomplicated left-sided diverticulitis; 314 antibiotics (broad-spectrum, at least 7 days) vs 309 IV fluids only
cards.result: Perforation or abscess 1.9% (6/309) vs 1.0% (3/314), P=0.302. Median hospital stay 3 days in both groups. Recurrent diverticulitis needing readmission at 1 year 16% in both groups (P=0.881).
cards.watchOut: The event counts are small (6 vs 3) — they rule out a large penalty for skipping antibiotics, not a small one. Every patient was admitted and observed in hospital; that observation is part of the safety net the trial tested.
cards.source: Chabok A et al., Br J Surg 2012 (PMID 22290281 · NCT01008488)

cards.headline: DIABOLO 2017: observation matched antibiotics on recovery — and sent patients home a day sooner.
cards.summary: Median time to recovery 14 vs 12 days (HR 0.91, P=0.151). Complicated diverticulitis 3.8% vs 2.6% (P=0.377); recurrent 3.4% vs 3.0% (P=0.494); sigmoid resection 3.8% vs 2.3% (P=0.323); readmission 17.6% vs 12.0% (P=0.148); mortality 1.1% vs 0.4% (P=0.432) — none significant. Hospital stay 2 vs 3 days (P=0.006).
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, pragmatic multicenter trial (22 Dutch hospitals)
cards.people: 528 patients with a FIRST episode of CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis; 262 observation vs 266 amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days
cards.result: Median time to recovery 14 vs 12 days (HR 0.91, P=0.151). Complicated diverticulitis 3.8% vs 2.6% (P=0.377); recurrent 3.4% vs 3.0% (P=0.494); sigmoid resection 3.8% vs 2.3% (P=0.323); readmission 17.6% vs 12.0% (P=0.148); mortality 1.1% vs 0.4% (P=0.432) — none significant. Hospital stay 2 vs 3 days (P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: Every secondary endpoint numerically leans toward antibiotics and none is significant — this is “no difference shown,” and the intervals cannot exclude small harms. The separately published 24-month follow-up stayed concordant (recurrence 15.4% vs 14.9%).
cards.source: Daniels L et al., Br J Surg 2017 (PMID 27686365 · NCT01111253)

shelves.title: Low-FODMAP diet for irritable bowel syndrome: better than a usual diet, not better than good advice
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does a low-FODMAP diet improve symptoms compared with a usual diet or with standard dietary advice?
shelves.balance: A low-FODMAP diet clearly beat a typical diet in a controlled feeding study, but in two pragmatic trials it did no better than competent standard dietary advice. Reasonable to try; not proven superior to good standard advice. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for symptom relief vs a usual diet · MAYBE (weak evidence) for superiority over standard dietary advice.

cards.headline: Halmos 2014: symptom scores roughly halved on low-FODMAP vs a typical diet — in a feeding study where every meal was provided
cards.summary: Global symptom scores on the low-FODMAP diet were roughly half those on a typical Australian diet (visual analogue score 22.8 vs 44.9 mm, P<.001).
cards.type: Single-blind crossover feeding trial; all food provided
cards.people: 30 patients with IBS (plus 8 healthy controls)

shelves.title: Probiotics to prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea in older inpatients: a small yes, a large no
shelves.question: In older inpatients receiving antibiotics, do probiotics prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea or Clostridioides difficile diarrhea?
shelves.balance: One small trial showed a large benefit; the large, definitive multicentre trial that followed found none. Routine probiotics for this purpose are not supported by the best evidence. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the small positive stands as the dissenting card; the shelf's weight rests on PLACIDE.

cards.headline: Hickson 2007: a probiotic drink cut antibiotic-associated diarrhea from 34% to 12% — in 135 patients
cards.summary: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea 12% vs 34% (P=0.007); C. difficile diarrhea 0% vs 17% (P=0.001). Number needed to treat ≈ 5.
cards.people: 135 older inpatients (mean age 74) receiving antibiotics; probiotic drink vs control
cards.result: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea 12% vs 34% (P=0.007); C. difficile diarrhea 0% vs 17% (P=0.001). Number needed to treat ≈ 5.
cards.watchOut: A strikingly large effect for a small trial — an NNT of about 5 is flagged as such here. It is exactly the kind of small-trial result the large trial on Card 2 was built to test, and it did not survive that test. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Eradicating H. pylori to prevent gastric cancer: the benefit is real where incidence is high — and unproven as a blanket policy where it is low
shelves.question: In people infected with Helicobacter pylori, does eradication treatment prevent gastric cancer — in healthy carriers, in those with a family history, and in stomachs that have already produced one cancer?
shelves.mesh: Helicobacter pylori · Helicobacter Infections · Stomach Neoplasms · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: The pooled randomized record (Ford, Cochrane 2020: 7 trials, 8,323 healthy infected adults, six of them Asian) says eradication prevents gastric cancer with a relative risk of 0.54 — labeled relative, as this library insists — with a number-needed-to-treat of 72, and gastric-cancer mortality at a relative risk of 0.61 (NNT 135), while all-cause mortality did not move (RR 0.97). The regional gradient is the shelf: the same relative effect buys an NNT of roughly 57 in East Asia and roughly 345 in North America, because the absolute risk underneath it differs six-fold. The targeted trials sharpen the point — in Koreans with an affected first-degree relative, eradication halved cancer incidence (1.2% vs 2.7%; HR 0.45), and after endoscopic resection of an early cancer it halved metachronous cancers (HR 0.50; the Ford neoplasia subgroup pooled at RR 0.49, NNT 21). Shandong's 22-year follow-up adds the timing lesson: benefit concentrates in stomachs treated before advanced precancerous change. Hence the split stamp: LIKELY where incidence is high or risk is individual and concrete; POSSIBLE as a blanket policy in low-incidence Western populations, where it has never been directly tested. Tier C — cancer-incidence claims; developer verdict given personally. Two cards on this shelf (Choi 2018; Shandong) are re-cards — their home is Shelf #219, and they are counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Ford 2020 (Cochrane): across 7 trials and 8,323 healthy carriers, eradication cut gastric cancer incidence by 46% relative (RR 0.54; NNT 72)
cards.summary: Gastric cancer incidence: relative risk 0.54 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.72) — a 46% relative reduction , NNT 72 ; gastric-cancer mortality RR 0.61 (0.40 to 0.92), NNT 135; all-cause mortality RR 0.97 (not significant); esophageal cancer RR 1.22 (not significant) — 7 randomized trials, 8,323 healthy H. pylori-positive adults, six trials in Asian populations.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 (also published in Gut 2020). A systematic review — no trial registry number applies.
cards.people: 7 randomized trials with 8,323 healthy asymptomatic H. pylori-positive adults, followed for at least two years (one trial now reported to 22 years); six trials were conducted in Asian populations and one in a Latin American population at high risk. (The review record does not print a single mean age or sex mix across trials.)
cards.result: Eradication reduced gastric cancer incidence with a relative risk of 0.54 (95% CI, 0.40 to 0.72) — a 46% relative reduction, with a number needed to treat of 72 — and gastric-cancer mortality with a relative risk of 0.61 (0.40 to 0.92; NNT 135). All-cause mortality was unchanged (RR 0.97; 0.85 to 1.12) and esophageal cancer incidence was not significantly increased (RR 1.22; 0.59 to 2.54). In trials with at least 10 years of follow-up, the incidence estimate was unchanged (RR 0.54) with an NNT of 45. In the subgroup who had already had endoscopic resection of gastric neoplasia (3 trials, 1,841 participants), metachronous cancer fell further: RR 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70), NNT 21.
cards.watchOut: The relative risk is portable; the NNT is not. Because baseline gastric-cancer risk differs roughly six-fold between East Asia and North America, the analysis's IARC-based gradient puts the NNT near 57 in East Asia and near 345 in North America — the arithmetic heart of this shelf's split stamp. Almost all the trial evidence is from high-incidence populations; the low-incidence blanket policy is an extrapolation, graded POSSIBLE here, not a finding.
cards.source: Ford AC et al. Helicobacter pylori eradication for the prevention of gastric neoplasia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;7:CD005583. PMID 32628791. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD005583.pub3 (companion report: Gut 2020)

cards.headline: Choi 2020: with a first-degree relative who had gastric cancer, eradication halved incidence — 1.2% vs 2.7% over 9.2 years (HR 0.45)
cards.summary: Gastric cancer: 1.2% (10/832) on eradication therapy vs 2.7% (23/844) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.94), a 55% relative reduction and an absolute difference of 1.5 percentage points; among participants whose infection was confirmed eradicated, incidence was 0.8% (HR 0.27 vs persistent infection) — 1,676 first-degree relatives in Korea.
cards.type: Single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, N Engl J Med 2020
cards.people: 1,676 participants in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (832 treatment, 844 placebo), drawn from 3,100 screened first-degree relatives of patients with gastric cancer in South Korea; median follow-up 9.2 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Gastric cancer developed in 10 participants (1.2%) in the treatment group and 23 (2.7%) in the placebo group — hazard ratio 0.45 (95% CI, 0.21 to 0.94; P=0.03). Five of the 10 cancers in the treatment group occurred in participants with persistent H. pylori infection. Cancer developed in 0.8% of participants (5 of 608) whose infection was eradicated versus 2.9% (28 of 979) with persistent infection (hazard ratio 0.27; 0.10 to 0.70). Adverse events were mild and more common on treatment (53.0% vs 19.1%).
cards.watchOut: A targeted trial in a genetically and environmentally enriched population — its 1.5-point absolute difference is what 'high-risk individual' means on this shelf, and it is several-fold larger than what a low-incidence general population would see. About a quarter of eradication attempts failed on the clarithromycin-based regimen used, and half the treatment-group cancers arose in those failures: eradication must be confirmed, not merely prescribed.
cards.source: Choi IJ et al. Family History of Gastric Cancer and Helicobacter pylori Treatment. N Engl J Med. 2020;382:427-436. PMID 31995688 · NCT01678027. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1909666

cards.headline: Choi 2018 (re-card; home: Shelf #219): after endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer, eradication halved metachronous cancers — 7.2% vs 13.4% (HR 0.50)
cards.summary: Metachronous gastric cancer over a median 5.9 years: 7.2% (14/194) on eradication therapy vs 13.4% (27/202) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.94), an absolute difference of 6.2 percentage points — 396 patients after endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer or high-grade adenoma in Korea. Re-card: this trial's home is Shelf #219; it is counted once, there.
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, N Engl J Med 2018. Re-card — home shelf #219.
cards.people: 470 patients who had undergone endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer or high-grade adenoma were randomized; 396 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (194 treatment, 202 placebo); median follow-up 5.9 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Metachronous gastric cancer developed in 14 patients (7.2%) in the treatment group and 27 (13.4%) in the placebo group — hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI, 0.26 to 0.94; P=0.03), an absolute difference of 6.2 percentage points. Improvement in gastric corpus glandular atrophy grade at 3 years was also more frequent on treatment (48.4% vs 15.0%; P<0.001). There were no serious adverse events; mild adverse events were more common on treatment (42.0% vs 10.2%).
cards.watchOut: The strongest absolute benefit on this shelf, in the highest-risk stomachs — consistent with the Ford neoplasia subgroup (RR 0.49, NNT 21) on Card 1. It is carded here for the eradication question and counted once, at its home on Shelf #219, where it sits beside the Shandong trial in the cancer-prevention frame.

cards.headline: Shandong, 22.3-year follow-up (Li 2019; re-card — home: Shelf #219): two weeks of treatment halved incidence (OR 0.48) — with the benefit concentrated in stomachs treated before advanced precancerous change
cards.summary: Over 22.3 years in Linqu County, China: gastric cancer incidence odds ratio 0.48 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.71) and gastric-cancer mortality hazard ratio 0.62 (0.39 to 0.99) for two weeks of H. pylori treatment given in 1995 — 3,365 residents of a high-incidence county (2,258 H. pylori-positive). Re-card: this trial's home is Shelf #219; it is counted once, there.
cards.type: Blinded, randomized, factorial trial with 22.3-year follow-up (Shandong Intervention Trial), BMJ 2019. Re-card — home shelf #219.
cards.people: 3,365 residents of Linqu County, Shandong, China — a county with among the world's highest gastric cancer rates; the 2,258 participants seropositive for H. pylori were assigned to two weeks of amoxicillin plus omeprazole or placebo in 1995, with vitamin and garlic supplementation arms in parallel. Over 22.3 years, 151 gastric cancers and 94 gastric-cancer deaths occurred.
cards.result: H. pylori treatment reduced gastric cancer incidence (odds ratio 0.48; 95% CI, 0.32 to 0.71) and gastric-cancer mortality (hazard ratio 0.62; 0.39 to 0.99) over 22.3 years. The trial's timing analyses — the reason it is carded on this shelf — found the prevention benefit concentrated in participants treated before advanced precancerous lesions were established (and in those treated younger), the 'point of no return' gradient: once intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia are advanced, eradication still treats the infection but buys less cancer prevention. (Vitamin supplementation in the same trial also reduced incidence and mortality; those arms are reported at the trial's home on Shelf #219.)
cards.watchOut: One county, one era, one two-week regimen that would not meet modern eradication standards — and still the longest randomized lens the field has on timing. The gradient it shows is biologically coherent with Cards 2–3 (treat the infected relative, treat the resected stomach) but the subgroup timing claims are secondary analyses of a single trial: they guide judgment, they do not grade above the shelf's split stamp.
cards.source: Li WQ et al. Effects of Helicobacter pylori treatment and vitamin and garlic supplementation on gastric cancer incidence and mortality: follow-up of a randomized intervention trial. BMJ. 2019;366:l5016. PMID 31511230 · NCT00339768. DOI 10.1136/bmj.l5016

shelves.title: Drugs for MASH: three positive biopsy trials, two accelerated approvals — and no outcomes trial yet
shelves.question: In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH) with liver fibrosis, do resmetirom, semaglutide, or tirzepatide improve liver histology — and what remains unproven?
shelves.mesh: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Liver Cirrhosis · Thyroid Hormone Receptors beta · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Tirzepatide · Humans
shelves.balance: Stamped LIKELY by the developer's explicit override (the evidence was proposed at POSSIBLE; the developer raised it Nov 6, 2026, and the stamp carries that decision openly). The record itself: resmetirom (MAESTRO-NASH) resolved steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis in 25.9–29.9% versus 9.7% on placebo and improved fibrosis in 24.2–25.9% versus 14.2% — the first drug FDA-approved for MASH (accelerated approval, March 2024, for F2–F3 fibrosis). Semaglutide (ESSENCE, part 1) posted the largest resolution figure yet, 62.9% versus 34.3%, with fibrosis improvement of 36.8% versus 22.4%, and received accelerated approval in August 2025. Tirzepatide (SYNERGY-NASH, phase 2, n=190) resolved MASH in 44%, 56%, and 62% at ascending doses versus 10% — and is NOT FDA-approved for MASH; that is printed on its card, not implied away. Every endpoint on this shelf is a biopsy surrogate at about a year; no trial has yet shown fewer cases of cirrhosis decompensation, transplant, or death, and the cautionary card (REGENERATE's obeticholic acid — a fibrosis endpoint met, approval refused) is the standing reminder of what surrogate success does not guarantee. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: MAESTRO-NASH (Harrison 2024): resmetirom resolved steatohepatitis in 25.9–29.9% vs 9.7% and improved fibrosis in 24.2–25.9% vs 14.2% at 52 weeks
cards.summary: MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis: 25.9% (80 mg) and 29.9% (100 mg) vs 9.7% placebo; fibrosis improvement by ≥1 stage without worsening activity: 24.2% and 25.9% vs 14.2% (all P<0.001); LDL cholesterol fell 13.6–16.3% vs 0.1% — 966 patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and F1B–F3 fibrosis. Resmetirom became the first FDA-approved MASH drug (accelerated approval, March 2024, for F2–F3).
cards.type: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (MAESTRO-NASH, ongoing outcomes phase), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 966 patients formed the primary analysis population (322 on 80 mg resmetirom, 323 on 100 mg, 321 on placebo) — adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stage F1B, F2, or F3. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At week 52, MASH resolution with no worsening of fibrosis occurred in 25.9% (80 mg) and 29.9% (100 mg) versus 9.7% on placebo (P<0.001 for both); fibrosis improvement by at least one stage with no worsening of the activity score occurred in 24.2% and 25.9% versus 14.2% (P<0.001 for both). LDL cholesterol changed by −13.6% and −16.3% versus +0.1% at week 24 (P<0.001). Diarrhea and nausea were more frequent with resmetirom; serious adverse events were similar (10.9%, 12.7%, and 11.5%).
cards.watchOut: Both primary endpoints are biopsy surrogates read at 52 weeks, and the approval is an accelerated one, conditioned on the trial's outcomes phase showing benefit on liver outcomes that have not yet been reported. The absolute resolution advantage over placebo is about 16–20 percentage points — real, and far from a cure; most treated patients did not reach either endpoint.
cards.source: Harrison SA et al. A Phase 3, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Resmetirom in NASH with Liver Fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2024;390:497-509. PMID 38324483 · NCT03900429. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2309000

cards.headline: ESSENCE part 1 (Sanyal 2025): semaglutide resolved steatohepatitis in 62.9% vs 34.3% and improved fibrosis in 36.8% vs 22.4% at 72 weeks
cards.summary: Resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis: 62.9% on weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg vs 34.3% on placebo (difference 28.7 points; P<0.001); fibrosis reduction without worsening steatohepatitis: 36.8% vs 22.4% (difference 14.4 points; P<0.001); weight change −10.5% vs −2.0% — planned interim analysis of the first 800 patients with MASH and F2–F3 fibrosis. Semaglutide received FDA accelerated approval for MASH in August 2025.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ESSENCE), planned interim analysis (part 1), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 1,197 patients with biopsy-defined MASH and fibrosis stage 2 or 3 were assigned 2:1 to semaglutide or placebo for 240 weeks; part 1 reports the first 800 patients (534 semaglutide, 266 placebo) at week 72. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 62.9% of the semaglutide group and 34.3% of the placebo group (estimated difference 28.7 percentage points; 95% CI, 21.1 to 36.2; P<0.001). A reduction in liver fibrosis without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 36.8% versus 22.4% (difference 14.4 points; 7.5 to 21.3; P<0.001); combined resolution plus fibrosis reduction, 32.7% versus 16.1%. Mean body weight changed by −10.5% with semaglutide and −2.0% with placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis of an ongoing 240-week trial: the outcomes that would settle the shelf — progression to cirrhosis, decompensation, death — read out in part 2, years from now. The placebo resolution rate (34.3%) is also the highest on this shelf and a reminder that biopsy sampling and lifestyle drift move these endpoints; the drug-placebo difference, not the raw percentage, is the finding. Approval on this evidence is accelerated, as with resmetirom.

cards.headline: SYNERGY-NASH (Loomba 2024): tirzepatide resolved MASH in 44% / 56% / 62% by dose vs 10% on placebo — phase 2, and NOT FDA-approved for MASH
cards.summary: Resolution of MASH without worsening fibrosis at 52 weeks: 44% (5 mg), 56% (10 mg), 62% (15 mg) on weekly tirzepatide vs 10% on placebo (differences 34, 46, and 53 points; all P<0.001); fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage: 55% / 51% / 51% vs 30% — phase 2 trial, 190 participants with biopsy-confirmed MASH and F2–F3 fibrosis. Tirzepatide is NOT FDA-approved for MASH — it is approved for diabetes and weight management; this card reports a trial result, not an indication.
cards.type: Phase 2, dose-finding, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (SYNERGY-NASH), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 190 participants with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage F2 or F3 fibrosis underwent randomization; 157 had evaluable week-52 biopsy results, with missing values imputed by a placebo-pattern assumption. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Resolution of MASH without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 10% on placebo versus 44% (5 mg; difference 34 points; 95% CI, 17 to 50), 56% (10 mg; difference 46 points; 29 to 62), and 62% (15 mg; difference 53 points; 37 to 69) on tirzepatide (P<0.001 for all). Improvement of at least one fibrosis stage without worsening of MASH occurred in 30% versus 55%, 51%, and 51% — a secondary endpoint not formally tested for multiplicity in this phase 2 design. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The largest resolution gradient on the shelf comes from the smallest and earliest-phase trial — 190 participants, a fifth without evaluable biopsies, and fibrosis analyses not formally multiplicity-tested. Tirzepatide is NOT FDA-approved for MASH: any use for this indication today is off-label extrapolation from a phase 2 biopsy trial, however striking the gradient. A phase 3 outcomes program is the missing step, exactly as the authors state.

cards.headline: REGENERATE (Younossi 2019) — the cautionary card: obeticholic acid met its fibrosis endpoint, missed resolution, and the FDA declined approval
cards.summary: At the month-18 interim analysis: fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage without worsening steatohepatitis in 23% (25 mg) vs 12% on placebo (P=0.0002) — one primary endpoint met; steatohepatitis resolution not met (12% vs 8%; P=0.13); pruritus in 51% on 25 mg vs 19% on placebo — 931 patients with F2–F3 in the primary analysis. The FDA subsequently declined accelerated approval (advisory committee voted against in 2023; the application was withdrawn).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (REGENERATE), prespecified interim analysis, Lancet 2019
cards.people: 1,968 patients with fibrosis stages F1–F3 received at least one dose; the primary analysis covered 931 with stage F2–F3 (311 placebo, 312 obeticholic acid 10 mg, 308 obeticholic acid 25 mg). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The fibrosis-improvement endpoint was achieved by 12% on placebo, 18% on 10 mg (P=0.045), and 23% on 25 mg (P=0.0002); the steatohepatitis-resolution endpoint was NOT met (8% placebo, 11% on 10 mg [P=0.18], 12% on 25 mg [P=0.13]). The most common adverse event was pruritus — 19% on placebo, 28% on 10 mg, and 51% on 25 mg. Serious adverse event rates were similar across groups at the interim analysis.
cards.watchOut: Carded as this shelf's standing warning. A statistically clean win on one biopsy surrogate, in a large phase 3 trial, was not enough: regulators weighed the missed second endpoint, the symptom burden (half the high-dose group itching), lipid signals, and rare liver injury, and declined accelerated approval. When Cards 1–3 are cited for resmetirom, semaglutide, or tirzepatide, this card is the discount rate to apply to surrogate-only enthusiasm — the developer's LIKELY override on this shelf was made with this card on it.

shelves.title: Early effective therapy in Crohn's disease: top-down beats step-up — decisively, in newly diagnosed disease
shelves.question: In Crohn's disease, does starting effective therapy early — combined immunosuppression or biomarker-guided tight control from diagnosis — produce better remission and endoscopic outcomes than the conventional step-up sequence?
shelves.mesh: Crohn Disease · Infliximab · Adalimumab · Azathioprine · Biomarkers · Humans
shelves.balance: PROFILE is the strongest strategy trial this field has produced: in 386 patients randomized within days of diagnosis, top-down infliximab plus immunomodulator produced sustained steroid-free, surgery-free remission in 79% versus 15% on accelerated step-up — a 64-point absolute difference, with endoscopic remission 67% versus 44% and FEWER serious adverse events in the top-down group (15 vs 42). Two honest footnotes travel with it: the biomarker that was supposed to select who needs top-down therapy (PredictSURE) failed outright (interaction P=0.944) — everyone benefited, so the test adds nothing — and 'accelerated step-up' in PROFILE was still faster than real-world care usually is. CALM supplies the complementary lesson: managing to biomarkers plus symptoms (tight control) beat managing to symptoms alone on endoscopic remission (46% vs 30%). D'Haens 2008 and REACT show the same direction at longer horizons, with REACT's 24-month composite of surgery, hospitalization, and complications lower under early combined immunosuppression (HR 0.73). The boundary is printed plainly: all of this evidence is Crohn's disease — it does not card ulcerative colitis by analogy. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PROFILE (Noor 2024): top-down therapy from diagnosis — sustained steroid-free, surgery-free remission 79% vs 15%; the biomarker meant to guide it failed (P=0.944)
cards.summary: Sustained steroid-free and surgery-free remission to week 48: 79% on top-down infliximab plus immunomodulator vs 15% on accelerated step-up (absolute difference ≈64 points); endoscopic remission 67% vs 44% ; serious adverse events 15 vs 42 , favoring top-down — 386 patients with newly diagnosed Crohn's disease (median 12 days from diagnosis). The PredictSURE biomarker showed no treatment interaction (P=0.944) — it cannot select patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, biomarker-stratified randomized controlled trial (PROFILE), Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2024
cards.people: 386 adults with newly diagnosed active Crohn's disease (Harvey-Bradshaw Index 7 or above, with raised CRP or faecal calprotectin and endoscopic inflammation), randomized a median of 12 days after diagnosis (193 per group); mean age 33.6 years (SD 13.2); 46% were women. Randomization was stratified by biomarker subgroup, endoscopic severity, and disease extent; biomarker status stayed blinded.
cards.result: Sustained steroid-free and surgery-free remission to week 48 occurred in 79% of the top-down group versus 15% of the accelerated step-up group — an absolute difference of about 64 percentage points — and endoscopic remission in 67% versus 44%. Serious adverse events numbered 15 in the top-down group versus 42 in the step-up group. There was NO biomarker-treatment interaction (absolute difference 1 point; 95% CI, −15 to 15; P=0.944): the PredictSURE-IBD biomarker did not identify a subgroup that could safely be spared top-down therapy. Longer-term follow-up reported by the investigators continued to favor the early strategy.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparator — 'accelerated step-up' — is a protocolized escalation faster than most real-world step-up, which makes the size of the win more striking, not less. The failed biomarker is part of the result, not an embarrassment to footnote: PROFILE's practical message is 'treat early, effectively, in everyone newly diagnosed,' not 'test, then treat.' Single trial for the strategy at this magnitude; CALM and the earlier trials on this shelf supply the concordance.
cards.source: Noor NM et al. A biomarker-stratified comparison of top-down versus accelerated step-up treatment strategies for patients with newly diagnosed Crohn's disease (PROFILE): a multicentre, open-label randomised controlled trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024;9:415-427. PMID 38402895 · ISRCTN11808228. DOI 10.1016/S2468-1253(24)00034-7

cards.headline: CALM (Colombel 2017): tight control — escalating on biomarkers, not symptoms alone — raised endoscopic remission to 46% vs 30%
cards.summary: Mucosal healing (endoscopic remission, CDEIS <4 with no deep ulcers) at 48 weeks: 46% under tight control (symptoms + faecal calprotectin + CRP driving adalimumab escalation) vs 30% under symptom-only clinical management (difference ≈16 points; P=0.010) — 244 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease in 22 countries.
cards.type: Open-label, randomized, controlled phase 3 trial (CALM), Lancet 2017
cards.people: 244 adults (aged 18–75) with active endoscopic Crohn's disease (CDEIS above 6 with ulcers), CDAI 150–450, and no previous immunomodulators or biologics, at 74 hospitals and clinics in 22 countries, randomized after prednisone induction. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint — mucosal healing (CDEIS below 4) with absence of deep ulcers 48 weeks after randomization — was achieved by 46% of the tight-control group versus 30% of the clinical-management group (difference about 16 percentage points; P=0.010). Both groups escalated through the same adalimumab-based ladder (with azathioprine added at the top step); only the trigger differed — calprotectin 250 µg/g or above, CRP 5 mg/L or above, CDAI 150 or above, or prednisone use, versus symptom criteria alone.
cards.watchOut: CALM is a monitoring trial, not a drug trial: it shows that looking at the bowel's inflammation — not waiting for the patient to feel it — changes outcomes. It pairs with PROFILE rather than competing with it: PROFILE says start effective therapy at diagnosis; CALM says steer it by objective markers thereafter. Open-label, with endoscopy readers aware of the design's intent — the endpoint itself (endoscopic score) is the guard against pure expectation effects.
cards.source: Colombel JF et al. Effect of tight control management on Crohn's disease (CALM): a multicentre, randomised, controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2017;390:2779-2789. PMID 29096949 · NCT01260468. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32641-7

cards.headline: D'Haens 2008: the first top-down trial — early combined immunosuppression beat conventional management at weeks 26 and 52
cards.summary: Remission without corticosteroids and without bowel resection: at week 26, 60.0% on early combined immunosuppression (infliximab ×3 + azathioprine) vs 35.9% on conventional management (difference 24.1 points; P=0.0062); at week 52, 61.5% vs 42.2% (difference 19.3 points; P=0.0278) — 133 patients with recently diagnosed Crohn's disease in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany.
cards.people: 133 patients with recently diagnosed active Crohn's disease at 18 centres in Belgium, Holland, and Germany (67 assigned early combined immunosuppression, 66 conventional management); 129 were treated per protocol and analyzed. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At week 26, 39 of 65 patients (60.0%) in the combined-immunosuppression group were in remission without corticosteroids and without surgical resection, versus 23 of 64 (35.9%) controls — an absolute difference of 24.1 percentage points (95% CI, 7.3 to 40.8; P=0.0062). At week 52 the rates were 61.5% versus 42.2% (difference 19.3 points; 2.4 to 36.3; P=0.0278). Serious adverse events were similar (30.8% vs 25.3% of those analyzed as reported at the trial level; P=1.0 in the abstract's comparison).
cards.watchOut: The 2008 proof of concept that PROFILE later confirmed at scale: three infliximab infusions plus azathioprine up front, versus steroids first and everything else in sequence. Small, open-label, and from the pre-biosimilar era — carded here as the lineage, with PROFILE carrying the shelf's weight.

cards.headline: REACT (Khanna 2015): in community practice, early combined immunosuppression did not raise 12-month remission — but cut the 24-month composite of surgery, admission, and complications (HR 0.73)
cards.summary: Practice-level corticosteroid-free remission at 12 months: 66.0% at early-combined-immunosuppression practices vs 61.9% at conventional practices (adjusted difference 2.5 points; P=0.52 — no difference). The 24-month patient-level composite of surgery, hospital admission, or serious complications was lower with early treatment (hazard ratio ≈ 0.73 ) — 41 community practices, 1,982 patients, in Belgium and Canada.
cards.people: 41 community gastroenterology practices in Belgium and Canada were randomized (22 early combined immunosuppression, 19 conventional); 1,982 patients with Crohn's disease aged 18 or older were assessed, with 921 of 1,084 patients at intervention practices and 806 of 898 at control practices completing 12 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Twelve-month practice-level remission rates were similar (66.0% [SD 14.0] vs 61.9% [16.9]; adjusted difference 2.5%; 95% CI, −5.2 to 10.2; P=0.52). The 24-month patient-level composite rate of major adverse outcomes — surgery, hospital admission, or serious disease-related complications — was lower at early-combined-immunosuppression practices (hazard ratio about 0.73, per the trial's full report).
cards.watchOut: The null primary is printed in this card's title deliberately: in unselected community practice, the algorithm did not move the remission rate at a year. What moved was the harder, later composite — the outcomes patients actually fear — which is the pattern expected when early therapy mainly prevents damage accrual rather than symptoms. Cluster design, open label, and a composite assembled after the primary's null all counsel reading REACT as supportive, not load-bearing; PROFILE carries that role.
cards.source: Khanna R et al. Early combined immunosuppression for the management of Crohn's disease (REACT): a cluster randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015;386:1825-1834. PMID 26342731 · NCT01030809. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(15)00068-9

shelves.title: Long-term PPI safety: the one large randomized trial acquits the class of nearly every accused harm — the real harms are smaller and specific
shelves.question: In people taking a proton pump inhibitor for years, which of the harms attributed to PPIs in observational studies — fractures, pneumonia, kidney disease, dementia, cancer, death — survive randomization, and which harms are real?
shelves.mesh: Proton Pump Inhibitors · Pantoprazole · Omeprazole · Clopidogrel · Drug Interactions · Humans
shelves.balance: COMPASS is the reassurance trial and this shelf's anchor: 17,598 patients randomized to pantoprazole or placebo for a median of three years, prespecifying the whole observational charge sheet — pneumonia, fracture, gastric atrophy, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, COPD, dementia, cardiovascular disease, cancer, hospitalization, death — and finding no significant difference in any of it. The single exception was enteric infections (1.4% vs 1.0%; OR 1.33), with C. difficile about twice as frequent on only 13 events, not significant. The observational edifice that COMPASS acquits deserves its own honest sentence: claims-database associations (for example, dementia hazard ratios around 1.44 in German claims data) repeatedly failed to replicate in prospective and randomized data — confounding by indication and frailty, not pharmacology. What IS real is smaller and specific, and it is carded: rebound acid hypersecretion producing symptoms on withdrawal (44% vs 15% in healthy volunteers — a dependency mechanism, demonstrated in a blinded trial), and the clopidogrel interaction scare, which COGENT's randomized test cleared for cardiovascular harm while confirming the GI protection. COMPASS is a re-card here — its home summary sits on Shelf #137 — counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: COMPASS (Moayyedi 2019; re-card — home summary: Shelf #137): 17,598 patients, 3 years of pantoprazole — none of the accused harms; enteric infections the lone exception (1.4% vs 1.0%)
cards.summary: In 17,598 patients with stable cardiovascular disease randomized to pantoprazole 40 mg or placebo (median follow-up 3.01 years; 53,152 patient-years): no statistically significant difference in pneumonia, C. difficile, fracture, gastric atrophy, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, COPD, dementia, cardiovascular disease, cancer, hospitalization, or all-cause mortality. The exception: enteric infections 1.4% vs 1.0% (OR 1.33 ; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.75); C. difficile was about twice as common on only 13 events (not significant). Re-card: the trial's home summary is Shelf #137; counted once, there.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COMPASS pantoprazole component, 3×2 partial factorial), Gastroenterology 2019. Re-card — home summary on Shelf #137.
cards.people: 17,598 participants with stable cardiovascular disease and peripheral artery disease (8,791 pantoprazole 40 mg daily, 8,807 placebo), also randomized among rivaroxaban-plus-aspirin, rivaroxaban alone, or aspirin alone; median follow-up 3.01 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Safety events were collected every 6 months across the full prespecified list. There was no statistically significant difference between pantoprazole and placebo for any outcome except enteric infections (1.4% vs 1.0%; odds ratio 1.33; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.75). C. difficile infection was approximately twice as common with pantoprazole, on only 13 total events, and was not statistically significant. The authors' conclusion: pantoprazole is not associated with any adverse event when used for 3 years, with the possible exception of enteric infections.
cards.watchOut: Three years is long for a trial and short for a lifetime prescription — COMPASS acquits PPIs of the accused harms over the horizon it measured, in a cardiovascular population, at one drug and dose. It does not measure decade-scale use, and its multiplicity is worth one sentence: with this many outcomes, the single positive (enteric infections, CI just clearing 1.0) could itself be partly chance — a caution that cuts in the reassuring direction here. The claim-by-claim grading of the observational accusations lives at this trial's home on Shelf #137.
cards.source: Moayyedi P et al. Safety of Proton Pump Inhibitors Based on a Large, Multi-Year, Randomized Trial of Patients Receiving Rivaroxaban or Aspirin. Gastroenterology. 2019;157:682-691.e2. PMID 31152740 · NCT01776424. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2019.05.056

cards.headline: Reimer 2009: the demonstrated harm is dependency — 8 weeks of a PPI gave healthy volunteers acid symptoms on withdrawal (44% vs 15%)
cards.summary: After 8 weeks of esomeprazole 40 mg (then 4 weeks of placebo) vs 12 weeks of placebo, 44% (26/59) of the PPI group reported a clinically relevant acid-related symptom in weeks 9–12 vs 15% (9/59) on placebo throughout (P<0.001) — rebound acid hypersecretion with symptoms, in people who had never had reflux — 120 healthy volunteers, blinded throughout.
cards.people: 120 healthy volunteers randomized to 12 weeks of placebo or to 8 weeks of esomeprazole 40 mg daily followed by 4 weeks of placebo (59 analyzed per group for the withdrawal period). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) Symptoms were scored weekly on the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale.
cards.result: Acid-related symptom scores were significantly higher in the PPI group at weeks 10, 11, and 12 — after the drug had been stopped and replaced by placebo. Forty-four percent (26/59) of those randomized to the PPI reported at least one clinically relevant acid-related symptom (heartburn, acid regurgitation, or dyspepsia) in weeks 9–12, versus 15% (9/59) of the placebo group (P<0.001); at week 12 the per-symptom rates were 21% versus 2% (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Small, short, and in healthy volunteers — and still the cleanest demonstration on this shelf of a harm that matters at population scale: a drug started for a short course can manufacture the symptom that justifies continuing it. Rebound is transient (weeks), which is exactly why it traps people: the symptoms feel like the disease returning. Deprescribing guidance — taper, warn, bridge — follows from this card.

cards.headline: COGENT (Bhatt 2010): the clopidogrel-PPI interaction scare, tested — omeprazole did not increase cardiovascular events (HR 0.99) and cut GI events (HR 0.34)
cards.summary: In patients on aspirin plus clopidogrel: gastrointestinal events 1.1% with omeprazole vs 2.9% with placebo at 180 days (HR 0.34 ; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.63); cardiovascular events 4.9% vs 5.7% (HR 0.99 ; 0.68 to 1.44; P=0.96) — no interaction harm — 3,873 randomized (trial stopped early when the sponsor lost financing).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COGENT), N Engl J Med 2010
cards.people: 3,873 patients with an indication for dual antiplatelet therapy were randomized (3,761 analyzed) to clopidogrel plus omeprazole or clopidogrel plus placebo, all on aspirin. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) The trial was terminated prematurely when the sponsor lost financing, short of its planned ~5,000.
cards.result: The primary gastrointestinal composite (overt or occult bleeding, symptomatic ulcers or erosions, obstruction, or perforation) occurred at a rate of 1.1% with omeprazole versus 2.9% with placebo at 180 days (hazard ratio 0.34; 95% CI, 0.18 to 0.63; P<0.001); overt upper GI bleeding was also reduced (HR 0.13; 0.03 to 0.56). The primary cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, revascularization, or stroke) occurred in 4.9% versus 5.7% (hazard ratio 0.99; 0.68 to 1.44; P=0.96), with no heterogeneity in high-risk subgroups. Diarrhea was more frequent with omeprazole.
cards.watchOut: The definitive randomized answer to a pharmacokinetic worry (omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, clopidogrel needs it) that had generated years of observational alarm: the platelet-level interaction does not translate into clinical cardiovascular harm at detectable size — though the early termination left the trial underpowered for small effects, a qualifier printed here rather than smoothed over. Together with COMPASS, this card closes the two loudest PPI safety scares on randomized evidence.

shelves.title: Antivirals in chronic hepatitis B: suppressing the virus prevents progression and liver cancer — proven once against placebo, extended by histology and cohorts
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis B, does long-term antiviral therapy prevent disease progression, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma — or only normalize blood tests?
shelves.mesh: Hepatitis B, Chronic · Lamivudine · Tenofovir · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular · Antiviral Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Liaw 2004 is the one placebo-controlled hard-outcome trial this question will ever have — it was stopped early because withholding treatment had become untenable: in 651 patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, lamivudine cut disease progression from 17.7% to 7.8% (hazard ratio 0.45, labeled relative, with the absolute rates printed beside it) and hepatocellular carcinoma from 7.4% to 3.9% (HR 0.49). Its weakness is also carded: YMDD resistance mutations in 49% of treated patients eroded the benefit — the reason lamivudine itself is now a historical agent and entecavir and tenofovir, with high resistance barriers, carry the practice. What those drugs add is shown, not placebo-proven: five years of tenofovir regressed fibrosis in 51% of biopsied patients and left 74% of cirrhotics no longer cirrhotic on biopsy (Marcellin — an uncontrolled roll-over, labeled as such), and the Hosaka cohort found 5-year HCC incidence of 3.7% on entecavir versus 13.7% untreated after propensity matching (adjusted HR 0.37 — observational, and above this library's 0.5 observational floor it is supportive rather than decisive). The residual-risk sentence belongs on the shelf: suppression reduces but does not abolish HCC, HBsAg loss runs at only about 1% per year, and surveillance continues on treatment. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Liaw 2004: lamivudine in advanced hepatitis B — disease progression 7.8% vs 17.7% (HR 0.45 relative), liver cancer 3.9% vs 7.4% (HR 0.49); stopped early
cards.summary: Disease progression (decompensation, liver cancer, bacterial peritonitis, variceal bleeding, or liver death): 7.8% on lamivudine vs 17.7% on placebo — hazard ratio 0.45 (P=0.001), a 55% relative reduction with an absolute difference of 9.9 points; hepatocellular carcinoma: 3.9% vs 7.4% (HR 0.49 ; P=0.047); Child-Pugh worsening 3.4% vs 8.8% (HR 0.45) — 651 patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis; the trial was stopped early at a median of 32.4 months. YMDD resistance developed in 49% on lamivudine.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2004
cards.people: 651 patients with chronic hepatitis B and histologically confirmed cirrhosis or advanced fibrosis, assigned 2:1 to lamivudine 100 mg daily (436) or placebo (215) for up to 5 years; 98% were Asian and 85% were men. (The abstract record does not print mean age.) The independent monitoring board stopped the study after a median treatment duration of 32.4 months because the difference in endpoints had become significant.
cards.result: Endpoints were reached by 7.8% of patients on lamivudine and 17.7% on placebo (hazard ratio for disease progression 0.45; P=0.001) — a 55% relative reduction and an absolute difference of 9.9 percentage points. The Child-Pugh score increased in 3.4% versus 8.8% (hazard ratio 0.45; P=0.02), and hepatocellular carcinoma occurred in 3.9% versus 7.4% (hazard ratio 0.49; P=0.047). Serious adverse events were reported by 12% on lamivudine and 18% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's foundation and its caution in one trial. Genotypic YMDD resistance developed in 49% of lamivudine-treated patients, and Child-Pugh worsening was significantly more likely in those with resistance — the benefit was real and the drug was fragile, which is why modern practice uses entecavir or tenofovir and why no second placebo trial exists: after Liaw, withholding antivirals in advanced disease was no longer ethical. The effect sizes here clear this library's hard-outcome bar comfortably; the extrapolation to today's agents rests on their superior resistance profiles, not on new placebo data.
cards.source: Liaw YF et al. Lamivudine for Patients with Chronic Hepatitis B and Advanced Liver Disease. N Engl J Med. 2004;351:1521-1531. PMID 15470215. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa033364 (Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists.)

cards.headline: Marcellin 2013: five years of tenofovir — fibrosis regressed in 51%, and 74% of patients cirrhotic at baseline no longer had cirrhosis on biopsy
cards.summary: Among 348 patients with paired biopsies at baseline and week 240: histological improvement in 87% ; regression of fibrosis (≥1 Ishak unit) in 51% ; of 96 patients with cirrhosis at baseline, 71 (74%) no longer had cirrhosis at year 5, while 3 of 252 without cirrhosis progressed to it — open-label roll-over of two randomized trials (641 patients), uncontrolled after week 48.
cards.type: Open-label 5-year follow-up study (roll-over of two randomized trials), Lancet 2013 — labeled uncontrolled
cards.people: 641 patients received randomized treatment (tenofovir DF vs adefovir) in the parent trials (NCT00117676 and NCT00116805); 585 (91%) entered the open-label tenofovir phase and 489 (76%) completed 240 weeks; 348 (54%) had biopsies at both baseline and week 240. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At week 240, 304 of 348 patients (87%) had histological improvement (at least a 2-point Knodell necroinflammatory reduction without worsening fibrosis) and 176 (51%) had regression of fibrosis (P<0.0001). Of the 96 patients (28%) with cirrhosis (Ishak 5–6) at baseline, 71 (74%) no longer had cirrhosis, whereas 3 of 252 patients without baseline cirrhosis progressed to cirrhosis. Virological breakthrough was infrequent and not due to tenofovir resistance. 16% had adverse events; nine patients had serious events judged related to the study drug.
cards.watchOut: There is no control group after week 48 — everyone rolled onto tenofovir — so the regression percentages are descriptive, vulnerable to biopsy sampling variation and to survivorship (only 54% had paired biopsies). Carded as the histology bridge between Liaw's placebo-proven progression benefit and modern agents: consistent with viral suppression reversing fibrosis, at an evidence grade plainly below Card 1, and labeled so.
cards.source: Marcellin P et al. Regression of cirrhosis during treatment with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for chronic hepatitis B: a 5-year open-label follow-up study. Lancet. 2013;381:468-475. PMID 23234725 · NCT00117676 · NCT00116805. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(12)61425-1

cards.headline: Hosaka 2013: the residual-risk cohort — 5-year liver cancer incidence 3.7% on entecavir vs 13.7% untreated (adjusted HR 0.37, observational); suppression reduces risk, it does not erase it
cards.summary: After propensity matching (316 per cohort): cumulative 5-year hepatocellular carcinoma incidence 3.7% on entecavir vs 13.7% in untreated controls (P<0.001); adjusted hazard ratio 0.37 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.91) — a retrospective Japanese cohort (472 entecavir-treated, 1,143 untreated), labeled observational ; entecavir resistance was 0.8%. Risk reduction was greatest in patients at highest baseline risk.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study with propensity-score matching, Hepatology 2013 — observational evidence, labeled as such
cards.people: 472 entecavir-treated patients and 1,143 untreated patients with chronic hepatitis B at a Japanese liver center; propensity matching on known HCC risk factors produced 316 patients per cohort. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) No trial registry number applies (retrospective cohort).
cards.result: Cumulative HCC incidence at 5 years was 3.7% in the entecavir group and 13.7% in the untreated control group (P<0.001); Cox regression adjusted for known HCC risk factors gave a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI, 0.15 to 0.91; P=0.030). Drug-resistance mutations occurred in 0.8% of entecavir-treated patients. The greatest absolute risk reduction occurred in patients with the highest baseline risk scores (the PAGE-B-style stratification of age, sex, cirrhosis, liver enzymes, viral load, albumin, and bilirubin). A matched comparison suggested a larger HCC suppression effect for entecavir than for non-rescued lamivudine in patients with cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: Observational — and it stays labeled that way on this shelf. The adjusted HR 0.37 clears this library's 0.5 observational floor, the direction agrees with Liaw's randomized result, and the untreated 13.7% five-year incidence in a matched cohort is the honest counterfactual anchor; but untreated patients in routine care differ from treated ones in ways matching cannot fully remove. The clinical residue matters more than the ratio: 3.7% still developed liver cancer on effective therapy, HBsAg loss on nucleos(t)ide therapy runs at roughly 1% per year, and HCC surveillance therefore continues for as long as treatment does.
cards.source: Hosaka T et al. Long-term entecavir treatment reduces hepatocellular carcinoma incidence in patients with hepatitis B virus infection. Hepatology. 2013;58:98-107. PMID 23213040. DOI 10.1002/hep.26180 (Retrospective cohort — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Low-FODMAP diet for IBS: real relief against a usual diet — unproven against good dietary advice
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does eating low in FODMAPs — fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols — improve symptoms, and at what cost?
shelves.mesh: Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Diet, Carbohydrate-Restricted · Fermentation · Disaccharides · Monosaccharides · Oligosaccharides · Humans
shelves.balance: The honest summary is a split result. Against a typical diet, the effect is large (Halmos: symptom scores 22.8 vs 44.9 in a feeding study). Against a sham diet in the one placebo-controlled trial, low-FODMAP won clearly on symptom severity (IBS-SSS 173 vs 224) but its adequate-relief endpoint reached significance only per-protocol (61% vs 39%; intention-to-treat 57% vs 38%, P=0.051). Against competent traditional advice it tied twice (Böhn responders 50% vs 46%; Eswaran adequate relief 52% vs 41%, not significant, though pain responders favoured low-FODMAP 51% vs 23%). The trials are small and short — four weeks in the pragmatic studies — and the positive ones were dietitian-delivered. The costs are carded, not footnoted: fecal bifidobacteria fall on the diet, diet quality dips, and the reintroduction phase has no sham-controlled evidence. Three of the five cards are re-cards homed on Shelf #202, which holds the same trials under its own verdict (POSSIBLE vs a usual diet); each is counted once, at its home shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Halmos 2014: symptom scores roughly halved on low-FODMAP vs a typical diet — in a feeding study where every meal was provided (re-card; home: Shelf #202)
cards.summary: Overall gastrointestinal symptom scores on a 0–100 scale: 22.8 on the low-FODMAP diet vs 44.9 on a typical Australian diet (P<0.001) — 30 patients with IBS in a 21-day crossover where almost all food was provided.
cards.type: Randomized, single-blind, crossover feeding trial, Gastroenterology 2014. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #202, asked here for this slate’s low-FODMAP question; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 30 patients with IBS and 8 healthy controls, matched for demographics and diet; 21 days on each diet with a washout of at least 21 days between. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: IBS patients had lower overall gastrointestinal symptom scores on the low-FODMAP diet (22.8; 95% CI 16.7–28.8 mm) than on the Australian diet (44.9; 95% CI 36.6–53.1 mm; P<0.001); bloating, pain, and passage of wind were also reduced. Controls had minimal symptoms on either diet. All IBS subtypes reported greater satisfaction with stool consistency on low-FODMAP.
cards.watchOut: A feeding study, not free-living eating: nearly every meal was provided, FODMAP intake was engineered below 0.5 g per meal, and the comparator was a typical diet — not competent IBS dietary advice. It shows the diet can work under controlled conditions; Cards 2–4 test it against sham diets and real advice.
cards.source: Halmos EP et al. A diet low in FODMAPs reduces symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID 24076059 · ACTRN12612001185853. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2013.09.046

cards.headline: Staudacher 2017: the sham-diet trial — low-FODMAP won on symptom severity (IBS-SSS 173 vs 224), adequate relief only per-protocol — and bifidobacteria fell
cards.summary: Total IBS Severity Scoring System score at 4 weeks: 173 on low-FODMAP vs 224 on a sham diet (P=0.001). Adequate relief: 57% vs 38% intention-to-treat (P=0.051, not significant); 61% vs 39% per-protocol (P=0.042) — 104 patients, 2×2 factorial with a probiotic arm.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled, 2×2 factorial trial (low-FODMAP vs sham diet × multistrain probiotic vs placebo), Gastroenterology 2017
cards.people: 104 patients with IBS (Rome III), aged 18–65, at two UK hospitals; dietitian counselling in all groups; the sham diet restricted a similar number of foods and was of similar difficulty. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: There was no interaction between diet and probiotic. IBS-SSS total score was significantly lower on low-FODMAP than sham (173 ± 95 vs 224 ± 89; P=0.001). Adequate relief favoured low-FODMAP but missed significance intention-to-treat (57% vs 38%; P=0.051), reaching it per-protocol (61% vs 39%; P=0.042). Fecal Bifidobacterium species were lower on low-FODMAP than sham (P=0.008) and higher with the probiotic than placebo (P=0.019); overall microbiota diversity was unchanged.
cards.watchOut: The strongest design on this shelf — a genuine sham diet — and its headline relief endpoint still missed significance in the primary analysis. Four weeks only. The bifidobacteria finding cuts both ways: restriction changed the microbiome it is theorised to help, and the trial’s own probiotic arm is the proposed patch — itself unproven for symptoms (probiotic vs placebo symptom scores did not differ, P=0.721).
cards.source: Staudacher HM et al. A Diet Low in FODMAPs Reduces Symptoms in Patients With Irritable Bowel Syndrome and A Probiotic Restores Bifidobacterium Species: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID 28625832 · ISRCTN02275221. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2017.06.010

cards.headline: Böhn 2015: both diets improved symptoms; no significant difference between low-FODMAP and traditional advice (re-card; home: Shelf #202)
cards.summary: Responders (IBS severity score down by 50 or more): 50% on low-FODMAP vs 46% on traditional dietary advice (P=0.72); symptoms fell significantly in both groups — 75 patients, 4 weeks.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel, single-blind randomized trial, Gastroenterology 2015. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #202; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 75 patients meeting Rome III criteria for IBS at gastroenterology outpatient clinics in Sweden (38 low-FODMAP, 37 traditional advice); 67 completed. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Severity of IBS symptoms was reduced in both groups during the 4-week intervention (P<0.0001 within each group), without a significant difference between groups (P=0.62). At 4 weeks, 19 patients (50%) in the low-FODMAP group and 17 (46%) in the traditional-advice group had reductions in IBS severity scores of 50 or more (P=0.72). Food diaries showed good adherence in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The traditional advice was competent care — regular meals, smaller meals, less fat, insoluble fibre, caffeine, and gas-producing foods — so this trial asks the harder question and returns a tie. Single-blind, 4 weeks, and conducted in specialist clinics with dietitian support.

cards.headline: Eswaran 2016: no significant difference in adequate relief vs a modified standard diet — though pain responders favoured low-FODMAP (re-card; home: Shelf #202)
cards.summary: Adequate relief of IBS-D symptoms: 52% on low-FODMAP vs 41% on a modified NICE-guidelines diet (P=0.31, not significant). Abdominal pain responders: 51% vs 23% (P=0.008) — 92 US adults with IBS-D, 4 weeks.
cards.type: Single-centre randomized controlled trial, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2016. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #202; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.people: 92 adults with IBS-D (Rome III) were randomized after a 2-week screening period (65 women; median age 42.6 years); 84 completed (45 low-FODMAP, 39 modified NICE).
cards.result: Fifty-two percent of the low-FODMAP group vs 41% of the modified-NICE group reported adequate relief (P=0.31). The composite pain-plus-stool-consistency endpoint did not differ significantly (P=0.13), but abdominal pain responders were more frequent on low-FODMAP (51% vs 23%; P=0.008), and pain, bloating, consistency, frequency, and urgency scores improved more from baseline on low-FODMAP.
cards.watchOut: The first US trial of the diet, and its primary endpoint was null — the pain signal is a secondary endpoint. IBS-D only, 4 weeks, single centre. The PubMed record does not print a registry number for this trial.
cards.source: Eswaran SL et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing the Low FODMAP Diet vs. Modified NICE Guidelines in US Adults with IBS-D. Am J Gastroenterol. 2016. PMID 27725652. DOI 10.1038/ajg.2016.434 (The PubMed record does not print a registry number.)
