cards.headline: The costs card (Staudacher 2020): diet quality dipped on low-FODMAP, most nutrient intakes held — under specialist dietitian delivery
cards.summary: Across 130 patients from two randomized trials: a 4-week low-FODMAP diet delivered by a specialist dietitian did not change intake of most nutrients or diet diversity, but overall diet-quality scores were lower than on a habitual diet (P<0.01). At baseline only 5% of patients met the 30 g/day fibre target.
cards.type: Secondary analysis of two randomized controlled trials, Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 2020
cards.people: 130 individuals with IBS referred to a tertiary centre in London (63 randomized to low-FODMAP advice; 67 to sham or habitual-diet controls), with 7-day food records at baseline and 4 weeks. (The record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Habitual fibre intake was low — only 6 of 130 (5%) achieved 30 g/day. After 4 weeks of low-FODMAP advice there was no difference in intake of most nutrients versus controls and no loss of diet diversity; starch intake was lower than on habitual diet (109 vs 128 g/day; P=0.030), vitamin B-12 intake was higher, and overall diet-quality scores were lower after low-FODMAP advice than on habitual diet (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: This is the best-case nutritional picture: short-term, dietitian-delivered, in trial volunteers. The shelf’s standing cautions ride on it — long-term restriction is not what was tested, the reintroduction phase that is supposed to liberalise the diet has no sham-controlled trial behind it, bifidobacteria fall on the diet (Reference 2), and restrictive eating carries its own risks in susceptible patients, including avoidant/restrictive patterns. Delivered without a dietitian, none of these numbers are promised.
cards.source: Staudacher HM et al. Nutrient Intake, Diet Quality, and Diet Diversity in Irritable Bowel Syndrome and the Impact of the Low FODMAP Diet. J Acad Nutr Diet. 2020. PMID 31029650. DOI 10.1016/j.jand.2019.01.017 (Secondary analysis — the record prints no separate registry number.)

shelves.title: Surgery versus PPI for GERD: a near-tie in ordinary reflux — surgery wins only the truly refractory, carefully selected case
shelves.question: In chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, how does laparoscopic antireflux surgery compare with long-term proton-pump inhibitor therapy — and in PPI-refractory heartburn, who actually benefits from an operation?
shelves.mesh: Gastroesophageal Reflux · Fundoplication · Laparoscopy · Esomeprazole · Omeprazole · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Humans
shelves.balance: Two trials, two different questions, one coherent answer. In ordinary PPI-responsive GERD (LOTUS, 554 patients), five-year remission was 92% on esomeprazole vs 85% after surgery (P=0.048) — and that slim medical edge disappeared under dropout modelling; what durably differed was the symptom trade: surgery nearly abolished regurgitation (2% vs 13%) at the cost of more dysphagia (11% vs 5%), bloating (40% vs 28%), and flatulence (57% vs 40%), with similar serious adverse events. In refractory heartburn (Spechler 2019), the fence must be printed with the result: of 366 referred veterans, 288 were excluded before randomization — 99 had functional heartburn, not reflux — and only among the 78 with proven reflux-related refractory heartburn did surgery win clearly (success 67% vs 28% active medical vs 12% control). Sweden’s unselected registry then prices durability: 17.7% recurrence by a median 5.6 years, most managed by restarting medication. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: LOTUS (Galmiche 2011): at 5 years, remission 92% on esomeprazole vs 85% after antireflux surgery (P=0.048) — a difference that did not survive dropout modelling
cards.summary: Estimated remission at 5 years: 92% (95% CI 89–96) on esomeprazole vs 85% (81–90) after laparoscopic antireflux surgery (log-rank P=0.048); after best-case modelling of dropouts the difference was no longer significant — 554 patients with PPI-responsive chronic GERD.
cards.people: 554 patients with well-established chronic GERD who initially responded to acid suppression, in academic hospitals in 11 European countries; 266 assigned to esomeprazole 20–40 mg/day and 288 to surgery, of whom 248 were actually operated on; 372 completed 5-year follow-up. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Remission at 5 years was 92% on esomeprazole and 85% after surgery (P=0.048), but the difference lost significance when dropouts were modelled best-case. Symptom trade-offs at 5 years: acid regurgitation 13% on esomeprazole vs 2% after surgery (P<0.001, favouring surgery); heartburn 16% vs 8% (P=0.14); dysphagia 5% vs 11% (P<0.001), bloating 28% vs 40% (P<0.001), and flatulence 40% vs 57% (P<0.001) — the last three favouring medicine. Serious adverse events were similar (24.1% vs 28.6%), and deaths were few and unattributed (4 vs 1).
cards.watchOut: Everyone enrolled had already responded to a PPI — LOTUS answers the ordinary, treatment-responsive case, not refractory heartburn (Reference 2). Open-label, a third of patients did not complete 5 years, and the headline P value sits exactly at the border the dropout analysis then crosses. Surgery’s remission definition (needing acid suppression again = failure) is asymmetric by construction, and is printed here so agents weight it correctly.

cards.headline: Spechler 2019: in truly refractory, reflux-related heartburn, surgery succeeded in 67% vs 28% on active medical therapy vs 12% on control — after 288 of 366 referrals were excluded
cards.summary: Treatment success at 1 year (GERD quality-of-life score down by half or more): 67% with fundoplication (18 of 27) vs 28% with active medical therapy (7 of 25; P=0.007) vs 12% with control medical therapy (3 of 26; P<0.001) — in the 78 of 366 referred patients whose heartburn proved truly reflux-related.
cards.type: Randomized trial with systematic prerandomization workup (VA Cooperative), New England Journal of Medicine 2019
cards.people: 366 patients referred to VA gastroenterology clinics for PPI-refractory heartburn were enrolled (mean age 48.5 years; 280 men). Prerandomization workup excluded 288: 42 responded to a 2-week omeprazole trial, 99 had functional heartburn, 23 had non-GERD oesophageal disorders, 70 did not complete procedures, and 54 were excluded for other reasons. The remaining 78 with reflux-related heartburn were randomized.
cards.result: Surgery (laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication) succeeded in 18 of 27 patients (67%), significantly more than active medical treatment — omeprazole plus baclofen, with desipramine added depending on symptoms — at 7 of 25 (28%; P=0.007), and control medical treatment (omeprazole plus placebo) at 3 of 26 (12%; P<0.001). Active vs control medical therapy did not differ significantly (difference 16 points; 95% CI −5 to 38; P=0.17).
cards.watchOut: The fence is the finding: this is among the most carefully selected surgical populations in the GERD literature — roughly one in five referred patients qualified, and most exclusions were people whose heartburn was never reflux at all. The result does not generalise to unworked-up ’refractory’ heartburn, and the population was veterans — predominantly men, in VA clinics. Small numbers (78 randomized) mean the percentages move fast: three patients is 11 points in the surgical arm.
cards.source: Spechler SJ et al. Randomized Trial of Medical versus Surgical Treatment for Refractory Heartburn. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID 31618539 · NCT01265550. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1811424

cards.headline: The long tail (Maret-Ouda 2017): in Sweden’s full surgical cohort, 17.7% had reflux recurrence by a median of 5.6 years — most were simply back on medication
cards.summary: Recurrence of reflux — defined as antireflux medication for over 6 months or a second operation — in 470 of 2,655 patients (17.7%): 393 (83.6%) were managed with long-term medication and 77 (16.4%) had repeat surgery.
cards.type: Nationwide population-based retrospective cohort study (Swedish registries), JAMA 2017
cards.people: All 2,655 adults who underwent primary laparoscopic antireflux surgery in Sweden, 2005–2014 (median age 51.0 years; 1,354 men, 51.0%), followed for a median of 5.6 years through national patient, drug, and death registries.
cards.result: Reflux recurred in 17.7% overall. Risk was higher in women (hazard ratio 1.57, relative; 22.0% of women vs 13.6% of men), in patients aged 61 or older (HR 1.41, relative, vs 45 or younger), and with comorbidity (Charlson index 1 or more: HR 1.36, relative). Hospital surgical volume was not associated with recurrence (HR 1.09; 95% CI 0.77–1.53).
cards.watchOut: A registry cohort, not a trial: recurrence is a prescribing-and-reoperation definition, so it blends true anatomic failure with cautious re-prescribing, and there is no medical-therapy comparison arm. Its job on this shelf is narrower — it prices the durability of the operation outside trial selection, and it says roughly one patient in six is back on treatment within about six years. No trial registration applies to a registry cohort.

shelves.title: Secretagogues for IBS-C and chronic constipation: about one patient in five responds durably — diarrhoea and nausea are the price
shelves.question: In chronic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, do the gut secretagogues (linaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostone) and the prokinetic prucalopride produce durable responders beyond placebo?
shelves.mesh: Constipation · Peptides · Natriuretic Peptides · Chloride Channel Agonists · Serotonin 5-HT4 Receptor Agonists · Humans
shelves.balance: The class pattern is consistent across four drugs and five trials: a durable-responder rate of roughly one in five on drug against roughly one in ten — or fewer — on placebo, a number needed to treat of about 6–8. Linaclotide’s two trials put durable responders at 16–21% vs 3–6%; plecanatide at 21.0%/19.5% vs 10.2%; prucalopride (a prokinetic shelved with the secretagogues because the clinic question groups them) reached three or more complete bowel movements weekly in 30.9%/28.4% vs 12.0%, with no cardiovascular signal in a trial that monitored for one. In IBS-C, linaclotide’s FDA composite responder rate was 33.7% vs 13.9% (NNT 5.1). Lubiprostone’s base is the thinnest — one 4-week trial — and its nausea rate (31.7%) is the class’s worst; the secretagogues’ tax is diarrhoea, stopping treatment in about 4–6%. Every pivotal trial ran 12 weeks (lubiprostone 4); durability beyond that rests on open-label extensions, and no trial compares these drugs head-to-head with polyethylene glycol. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Lembo 2011: linaclotide’s two trials — durable responders 16–21% on drug vs 3–6% on placebo; diarrhoea stopped treatment in 4.2%
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (3 or more complete spontaneous bowel movements a week, up at least 1 from baseline, in at least 9 of 12 weeks): Trial 303 — 21.2% (145 μg) and 19.4% (290 μg) vs 3.3% on placebo; Trial 01 — 16.0% and 21.3% vs 6.0% (all P<0.01) — 1,276 patients with chronic constipation.
cards.type: Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dual-dose trials (Trials 303 and 01), New England Journal of Medicine 2011
cards.people: 1,276 patients with chronic constipation across the two 12-week multicentre trials, receiving placebo or linaclotide 145 μg or 290 μg once daily. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint was reached in Trial 303 by 21.2% and 19.4% of patients on linaclotide 145 and 290 μg vs 3.3% on placebo, and in Trial 01 by 16.0% and 21.3% vs 6.0% (P<0.01 for every comparison). All secondary endpoints favoured linaclotide. Adverse-event incidence was otherwise similar across groups; diarrhoea led to discontinuation in 4.2% of linaclotide patients.
cards.watchOut: Twelve-week trials; the authors themselves state that longer studies are needed for long-term risks and benefits — durability claims for this class rest on open-label extensions, not on blinded data. No trial on this shelf compares a secretagogue head-to-head with cheap osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol; the placebo gap is what is proven. Industry-funded (Ironwood/Forest).
cards.source: Lembo AJ et al. Two randomized trials of linaclotide for chronic constipation. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID 21830967 · NCT00765882 · NCT00730015. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1010863

cards.headline: Miner 2017: plecanatide — durable responders 21.0% and 19.5% vs 10.2% on placebo; diarrhoea in about 6%
cards.summary: Durable overall complete-spontaneous-bowel-movement responders over 12 weeks: 21.0% on plecanatide 3 mg and 19.5% on 6 mg vs 10.2% on placebo (P<0.001 for both) — 1,394 patients with chronic idiopathic constipation.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2017
cards.people: 1,394 patients with chronic idiopathic constipation, randomized to plecanatide 3 mg, plecanatide 6 mg, or placebo once daily for 12 weeks, recording bowel habits in an electronic diary. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Both doses beat placebo on the primary endpoint (21.0% and 19.5% vs 10.2%; P<0.001) and on weekly complete spontaneous bowel movements (increases of 2.5 and 2.2 per week vs 1.2 on placebo; P<0.001) and spontaneous bowel movements. The commonest adverse event was diarrhoea: 1.3% on placebo, 5.9% on 3 mg, 5.7% on 6 mg.
cards.watchOut: Same class shape as linaclotide — a real but modest responder gap of about 10 points, bought with diarrhoea in roughly 1 in 17 patients — and the higher dose added nothing, which is why 3 mg is the marketed dose. Twelve weeks, placebo-controlled only; no active-comparator data against polyethylene glycol.
cards.source: Miner PB et al. A Randomized Phase III Clinical Trial of Plecanatide, a Uroguanylin Analog, in Patients With Chronic Idiopathic Constipation. Am J Gastroenterol. 2017. PMID 28169285 · NCT01982240. DOI 10.1038/ajg.2016.611

cards.headline: Johanson 2008: lubiprostone — more bowel movements within 24–48 hours, in the class’s thinnest trial; nausea in 31.7%
cards.summary: Spontaneous bowel movements at week 1: 5.69 per week on lubiprostone vs 3.46 on placebo (P=0.0001); 56.7% had a bowel movement within 24 hours of the first dose vs 36.9% on placebo — 242 patients, and only 4 weeks of treatment.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2008
cards.people: 242 adults with chronic constipation, randomized to lubiprostone 24 μg or placebo twice daily for 4 weeks. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Lubiprostone produced more spontaneous bowel movements at week 1 (5.69 vs 3.46; P=0.0001) and at weeks 2–4 (P≤0.002), with better stool consistency, less straining, and better global effectiveness ratings (P≤0.0003). Within 24 hours, 56.7% of lubiprostone patients had a bowel movement vs 36.9% on placebo (P=0.0024); by 48 hours, 80% vs 60.7%. The two commonest treatment-related adverse events were nausea (31.7%) and headache (11.7%); nausea caused discontinuation in 5%.
cards.watchOut: The thinnest evidence of the four drugs on this shelf: one small 4-week trial with a bowel-frequency endpoint, not the durable-responder endpoint the later class trials used — which is why this shelf grades the class on Cards 1, 2, and 4 and keeps lubiprostone as supporting evidence. Its nausea signature (nearly a third of patients) is the worst tolerability in the class. The PubMed record prints no registry number for this 2008 trial.
cards.source: Johanson JF et al. Multicenter, 4-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of lubiprostone in patients with chronic constipation. Am J Gastroenterol. 2008. PMID 17916109. DOI 10.1111/j.1572-0241.2007.01524.x (The record prints no registry number.)

cards.headline: Camilleri 2008: prucalopride — 30.9% reached three or more complete bowel movements a week vs 12.0% on placebo; no cardiovascular signal in the trial
cards.summary: Three or more spontaneous, complete bowel movements per week, averaged over 12 weeks: 30.9% on prucalopride 2 mg and 28.4% on 4 mg vs 12.0% on placebo (P<0.001 for both) — 620 patients with severe chronic constipation.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, placebo-controlled phase III trial, New England Journal of Medicine 2008
cards.people: 620 patients with severe chronic constipation (two or fewer spontaneous complete bowel movements per week), randomized to placebo or prucalopride 2 mg or 4 mg once daily for 12 weeks. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 30.9% (2 mg) and 28.4% (4 mg) vs 12.0% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). An average increase of at least one complete bowel movement per week was achieved by 47.3% and 46.6% vs 25.8% (P<0.001). Satisfaction, symptom severity, and quality-of-life endpoints all favoured prucalopride. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events were headache and abdominal pain; there were no significant cardiovascular effects of treatment, with electrocardiography monitored.
cards.watchOut: Prucalopride is a prokinetic, not a secretagogue — it is on this shelf because the clinic question (’the prescription constipation drugs’) groups them. The 5-HT4 family’s history is the caution: cisapride and tegaserod were withdrawn over cardiac and ischaemic concerns. This trial, designed with that history in view, found no cardiovascular effect — reassuring, but 620 patients for 12 weeks cannot exclude a rare harm; the pooled programme (responder rates of 27.8% vs 13.2% across the pivotal trials, as presented at the shelf’s verdict) points the same way. Headache and abdominal pain are its everyday costs.
cards.source: Camilleri M et al. A placebo-controlled trial of prucalopride for severe chronic constipation. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID 18509121 · NCT00483886. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0800670

cards.headline: The IBS-C card (Chey 2012): linaclotide’s FDA composite responder rate 33.7% vs 13.9% (NNT 5.1) over 26 weeks
cards.summary: FDA composite endpoint responders (pain down 30% or more and at least one extra complete bowel movement, same week, for at least 6 of the first 12 weeks): 33.7% on linaclotide 290 μg vs 13.9% on placebo (P<0.0001; number needed to treat 5.1) — 804 patients with IBS with constipation, followed for 26 weeks.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2012
cards.people: 804 patients with IBS-C (mean age 44 years; 90% women), randomized to linaclotide 290 μg or placebo once daily for 26 weeks.
cards.result: FDA endpoint responders: 33.7% vs 13.9% (NNT 5.1; 95% CI 3.9–7.1). The pain criterion alone was met by 48.9% vs 34.5% (NNT 7.0) and the bowel criterion by 47.6% vs 22.6% (NNT 4.0); all remaining primary and secondary endpoints favoured linaclotide (P<0.001), and the differences persisted over 26 weeks. Adverse events were otherwise similar; diarrhoea caused discontinuation in 4.5% on linaclotide vs 0.2% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The best responder numbers on this shelf come from the IBS-C population — where the drug treats pain as well as bowel habit — not from plain chronic constipation (Reference 1). Effects are real but leave two-thirds of patients short of the composite responder bar, and diarrhoea remains the tax. The PubMed record does not print a registry number for this trial.

shelves.title: NSAID gastroprotection: celecoxib protected the whole gut better than diclofenac plus omeprazole — in patients not taking aspirin
shelves.question: In patients who need long-term NSAIDs, which strategy best prevents serious gastrointestinal harm — a COX-2-selective drug, a nonselective NSAID plus a proton-pump inhibitor, or misoprostol — and where does the evidence stop?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Celecoxib · Diclofenac · Omeprazole · Misoprostol · Peptic Ulcer · Humans
shelves.balance: The strategies separate by where in the gut you look. For the whole gastrointestinal tract, CONDOR (4,484 arthritis patients) found fewer clinically significant events on celecoxib alone than on diclofenac plus omeprazole (0.9% vs 3.8%; hazard ratio 4.3, a relative measure) — and the shelf prints CONDOR’s fence in its title and on its card: the trial excluded aspirin users, so it does not answer the aspirin question. For the upper gut alone, the shields tie (Chan 2002: recurrent bleeding 4.9% vs 6.4% after a healed bleed), yet about 1 in 20 of those highest-risk patients rebled within 6 months anyway. Misoprostol is the historical control on complacency: MUCOSA proved a hard-endpoint benefit against placebo (serious complications 0.57% vs 0.95%, a 40% relative reduction) and was abandoned anyway, because a fifth of patients quit it within a month, mostly with diarrhoea. Both Chan trials screened out or eradicated H. pylori first — eradication timing is part of the strategy, not an afterthought. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CONDOR (Chan 2010): whole-gut events 0.9% on celecoxib vs 3.8% on diclofenac plus omeprazole (HR 4.3, relative) — in a trial that excluded aspirin users
cards.summary: Clinically significant upper or lower gastrointestinal events over 6 months: 20 of 2,238 patients (0.9%) on celecoxib vs 81 of 2,246 (3.8%) on diclofenac slow-release plus omeprazole (hazard ratio 4.3; 95% CI 2.6–7.0 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates; P<0.0001).
cards.people: 4,484 patients with osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis at increased gastrointestinal risk, at 196 centres in 32 countries; all tested negative for Helicobacter pylori, and were aged 60 or older, or 18 or older with previous gastroduodenal ulceration. Patients taking aspirin were excluded by the trial’s eligibility criteria. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint — clinically significant upper or lower gastrointestinal events, adjudicated blinded — occurred in 0.9% on celecoxib vs 3.8% on diclofenac plus omeprazole (HR 4.3, relative; P<0.0001). Withdrawals for gastrointestinal adverse events were also fewer on celecoxib (114 patients, 6%, vs 167, 8%; P=0.0006). The gap across the whole gut — not just the upper tract, where the two strategies had previously looked equivalent — is the trial’s contribution; much of the event burden in the comparator arm was lower-gut and occult-blood-loss events rather than frank upper-gut bleeding.
cards.watchOut: The fence, printed as the shelf requires: CONDOR excluded aspirin users, so it does not answer gastroprotection for the very large group who take an NSAID plus low-dose aspirin — extrapolating its result to them is the commonest misuse of this trial. All patients were also H. pylori-negative, and follow-up was 6 months. Funded by Pfizer, celecoxib’s maker.

cards.headline: MUCOSA (Silverstein 1995): misoprostol cut serious NSAID complications from 0.95% to 0.57% — a 40% relative reduction that tolerability then killed
cards.summary: Serious upper gastrointestinal complications (perforation, obstruction, or bleeding) over 6 months: 25 of 4,404 patients (0.57%) on misoprostol vs 42 of 4,439 (0.95%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.598; 95% CI 0.364–0.982; P=0.049) — a 40% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed beside it.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (MUCOSA), Annals of Internal Medicine 1995
cards.people: 8,843 men and women (mean age 68 years) with rheumatoid arthritis receiving continuous therapy with any of 10 specified NSAIDs, at 664 practices in the United States and Canada. (The record does not print the sex split.)
cards.result: Serious upper gastrointestinal complications were reduced by 40% in relative terms on misoprostol 200 μg four times daily (OR 0.598; P=0.049): 0.57% vs 0.95% in absolute terms — about 4 events prevented per 1,000 patients treated for 6 months. Risk factors for complications were increasing age, prior peptic ulcer or bleeding, and cardiovascular disease; patients with all of them faced about a 9% 6-month risk.
cards.watchOut: The benefit was real and the drug was unusable: in the first month, 20% of misoprostol patients vs 15% on placebo withdrew, primarily because of diarrhoea and related problems, on a four-times-daily regimen. MUCOSA is why the field moved to PPIs and COX-2 drugs despite misoprostol being, to this day, one of the few gastroprotectives with a hard-complication endpoint win against placebo. A pre-registration-era trial (1991–93) — no registry number exists.

cards.headline: Chan 2002: after an ulcer bleed, celecoxib and diclofenac-plus-omeprazole tied (recurrent bleeding 4.9% vs 6.4%) — and roughly 1 in 20 rebled anyway
cards.summary: Probability of recurrent ulcer bleeding over 6 months: 4.9% (95% CI 3.1–6.7) on celecoxib vs 6.4% (4.3–8.4) on diclofenac plus omeprazole (difference −1.5 points; 95% CI −6.8 to 3.8 — not significant) — 287 patients whose NSAID ulcers had already bled once.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind trial, New England Journal of Medicine 2002
cards.people: 287 patients who used NSAIDs for arthritis and presented with ulcer bleeding; after healing, those negative for H. pylori were randomized (144 celecoxib plus placebo; 143 diclofenac plus omeprazole) for 6 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Recurrent ulcer bleeding occurred in 7 patients on celecoxib and 9 on diclofenac plus omeprazole; the 6-month probabilities were 4.9% vs 6.4% (difference −1.5 points; CI −6.8 to 3.8). Renal adverse events — hypertension, peripheral oedema, renal failure — were common in both arms (24.3% vs 30.8%).
cards.watchOut: The strategy lesson of the shelf: in the upper gut, COX-2 alone and nonselective-NSAID-plus-PPI are equivalent shields (this trial), and the whole-gut difference in CONDOR (Reference 1) came from below the stomach. But neither shield sufficed here — about 1 patient in 20 rebled within 6 months despite protection — which is why the highest-risk tier gets both shields, why H. pylori was eradicated or excluded before randomization in both Chan trials, and why ’stop the NSAID’ remains the strongest gastroprotection of all. The record prints no registry number for this 2002 trial.

shelves.title: Probiotics for IBS: strain-specific, heterogeneous, small trials — which strain, for whom, remains unclear
shelves.question: In irritable bowel syndrome, do probiotics improve global symptoms — and can the evidence name the strain, the dose, and the patient?
shelves.mesh: Probiotics · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Gastrointestinal Microbiome · Bifidobacterium · Humans
shelves.balance: The pooled number looks friendly — Ford 2018: relative risk of symptoms persisting 0.79 across 53 trials and 5,545 patients, a number needed to treat of about 7 — and the shelf still takes the library’s weakest stamp, because everything underneath that number is soft: dozens of different organisms and doses pooled together, heterogeneity and publication bias, and an update (Goodoory 2023: 82 trials, 10,332 patients) that found only 24 trials at low risk of bias and GRADE certainty low to very low for nearly every strain and outcome. The best single-strain trial (Whorwell) worked at exactly one of three doses, in women, for 4 weeks. The guidelines read the same record and split the difference the same way: ACG suggests against routine use; the AGA calls IBS probiotics a knowledge gap best used inside trials; British practice allows a time-limited trial of a named product. Adverse events in the trials tracked placebo; the rare harms (invasive infection in susceptible hosts, D-lactate case reports) are carded on Card 5. Strain-specific, heterogeneous, small trials — the framing is the finding. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Ford 2018: pooled across 53 trials, probiotics’ relative risk of persistent symptoms was 0.79 — and the authors still called the question unresolved
cards.summary: 53 randomized trials of probiotics, 5,545 patients: the pooled relative risk of IBS symptoms persisting after treatment was 0.79 (relative) — a number needed to treat of about 7 in the paper’s analysis — with substantial heterogeneity between trials.
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analysis, Alimentary Pharmacology and Therapeutics 2018
cards.people: 53 eligible randomized trials of probiotics in adults with IBS, involving 5,545 patients, from searches to July 2017. (A pooled population — the record does not print a combined mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Particular combinations, species, and strains appeared to benefit global symptoms and abdominal pain, and the paper’s pooled estimate put the relative risk of symptoms persisting at 0.79 with probiotics — but the authors concluded it was not possible to draw definitive conclusions about efficacy for any specific product. Adverse events were no more common with probiotics than with placebo. (The same review found rifaximin, an antibiotic rather than a probiotic, modestly effective in non-constipated IBS: relative risk of persisting symptoms 0.84.)
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity and publication bias are the story behind the point estimate: dozens of different organisms, doses, and endpoints pooled into one number that describes no product a clinician can actually prescribe. An NNT of 7 computed from that pool inherits every one of those problems. This card is the ’best case’ for the class, and the shelf’s stamp is set by Cards 2–5, not by this one. A meta-analysis — no trial registry number applies.
cards.source: Ford AC et al. Systematic review with meta-analysis: the efficacy of prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics and antibiotics in irritable bowel syndrome. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2018. PMID 30294792. DOI 10.1111/apt.15001 (Meta-analysis — no registry number.)

cards.headline: Goodoory 2023: the update — 82 trials, 10,332 patients, only 24 at low risk of bias; certainty low to very low almost everywhere
cards.summary: 82 eligible randomized trials containing 10,332 patients; only 24 were at low risk of bias across all domains. GRADE certainty for benefit: moderate for Escherichia strains on global symptoms, low for Lactobacillus strains, and very low for most combinations and most outcomes.
cards.people: 82 randomized trials of probiotics vs placebo in adults with IBS, containing 10,332 patients, from searches to March 2023. (A pooled population — no combined age or sex mix is printed.)
cards.result: For global symptoms there was moderate certainty of benefit for Escherichia strains, low certainty for Lactobacillus strains and Lactobacillus plantarum 299V, and very low certainty for combination probiotics and Bacillus strains. For abdominal pain, certainty was low for Saccharomyces cerevisiae I-3856 and Bifidobacterium strains and very low for most others; for bloating, very low throughout. Across 55 trials with more than 7,000 patients, the relative risk of any adverse event was not significantly higher with probiotics.
cards.watchOut: Thirty more trials than Ford 2018 and the conclusion barely moved — the constraint is trial quality and product chaos, not sample size. ’Low to very low certainty almost everywhere’ is the authors’ GRADE language, and it is why this shelf carries the library’s weakest stamp despite a statistically friendly pooled estimate on Card 1. Safety, at least, is not the obstacle: adverse events tracked placebo. A meta-analysis — no trial registry number applies.
cards.source: Goodoory VC et al. Efficacy of Probiotics in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Gastroenterology. 2023. PMID 37541528. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2023.07.018 (Meta-analysis — no registry number.)

(a pooled population — no combined age or sex mix is printed.) for global symptoms there was moderate certainty of benefit for escherichia strains, low certainty for lactobacillus strains and lactobacillus plantarum 299v, and very low certainty for combination probiotics and bacillus strains. for abdominal pain, certainty was low for saccharomyces cerevisiae i-3856 and bifidobacterium strains and very low for most others; for bloating, very low throughout.

cards.headline: Whorwell 2006: Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 — of three doses tested, only the middle one (10⁸) beat placebo
cards.summary: In 362 women with IBS, B. infantis 35624 at 1×10⁸ cfu beat placebo on abdominal pain, the composite symptom score, bloating, bowel dysfunction, incomplete evacuation, straining, and gas at 4 weeks (global relief more than 20% above placebo; P<0.02). The 10⁶ and 10¹⁰ doses did not separate from placebo.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, American Journal of Gastroenterology 2006
cards.people: 362 primary-care patients with IBS of any bowel-habit subtype — all women — randomized after a 2-week baseline to placebo or encapsulated B. infantis 35624 at 10⁶, 10⁸, or 10¹⁰ cfu/mL for 4 weeks. (The record does not print mean age.)
cards.result: Only the 10⁸ dose was significantly superior to placebo and to both other doses on the primary pain outcome and the composite score; global symptom relief exceeded placebo by more than 20% (P<0.02). The 10¹⁰ dose — a hundred times stronger — was not different from placebo and had significant formulation problems. No significant adverse events were recorded.
cards.watchOut: The best single-strain card in the probiotic literature is also the clearest demonstration of the shelf’s problem: the effect lives at one dose of one strain in one formulation, in women only, over 4 weeks — and a hundred-fold higher dose of the same organism failed. Nothing here licenses ’probiotics’ as a class, other strains, other doses, or the same strain in a differently made capsule. A 2006 trial — the record prints no registry number.
cards.source: Whorwell PJ et al. Efficacy of an encapsulated probiotic Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 in women with irritable bowel syndrome. Am J Gastroenterol. 2006. PMID 16863564. DOI 10.1111/j.1572-0241.2006.00734.x (The record prints no registry number.)

cards.headline: The guideline split, part 1 (ACG 2021): against probiotics for global IBS symptoms — while recommending the low-FODMAP trial and the secretagogues
cards.summary: The American College of Gastroenterology’s first IBS guideline (25 GRADE-assessed questions) suggests against probiotics for global IBS symptoms (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence) — in the same document that recommends a limited trial of a low-FODMAP diet and recommends chloride-channel and guanylate-cyclase activators for IBS-C.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (GRADE methodology, modified Delphi consensus), American Journal of Gastroenterology 2021
cards.people: A guideline, not a trial: 25 clinically important questions (9 diagnostic, 16 therapeutic) assessed after a comprehensive literature search. No patient population or registry number applies.
cards.result: The guideline recommends a positive diagnostic strategy over exclusion, serologic testing to exclude coeliac disease in IBS with diarrhoea, and faecal calprotectin to exclude inflammatory bowel disease. On treatment it recommends a limited trial of a low-FODMAP diet for global symptoms, chloride-channel activators and guanylate cyclase activators for IBS with constipation, rifaximin for IBS with diarrhoea, and gut-directed psychotherapy — while suggesting against probiotics for global IBS symptoms, conditionally, on very low-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: Carded so agents do not mistake this shelf’s MAYBE (weak evidence) stamp for a lone opinion: the largest US gastroenterology guideline read the same trials and landed against routine use. ’Conditional, very low quality’ is not ’proven useless’ — it is ’the evidence cannot support a routine recommendation’, which is exactly the gap Cards 1–3 document. A guideline — no registry number applies. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: The guideline split, part 2 (AGA 2020): probiotics only in the context of a clinical trial for IBS — a knowledge-gap verdict
cards.summary: The American Gastroenterological Association’s probiotic guideline made only conditional, strain- and context-specific recommendations across gastrointestinal disorders, and for IBS identified the evidence as a knowledge gap — suggesting probiotic use only in the context of a clinical trial.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (systematic reviews with GRADE), Gastroenterology 2020. The PubMed record for this guideline carries no abstract; the card is written from the published guideline itself.
cards.people: A guideline, not a trial: condition-by-condition systematic reviews of probiotics in gastrointestinal disorders, with technical reviews and GRADE assessments. No patient population or registry number applies.
cards.result: For IBS, the AGA found the evidence too thin and too strain-specific to recommend any product for routine care, and suggested that probiotics be used only in the context of a clinical trial — the ’knowledge gap’ designation. Its recommendations elsewhere were narrow and conditional (specific strains, specific settings), and its harm review noted the class’s rare but real risks: invasive infection (fungaemia and bacteraemia) in susceptible hosts — central lines, severe illness, immune compromise — and case reports of D-lactic acidosis with heavy probiotic use.
cards.watchOut: Read with Card 4, the transatlantic picture is consistent: ACG against routine use, AGA trial-only, and British/NICE practice allowing at most a time-limited trial of a named product with a stop rule if it fails. None of these bodies found the trials fraudulent or the products dangerous for ordinary patients — they found the evidence ungradeable beyond weak, which is this shelf’s stamp in guideline language. Rare invasive infections are a hospital-population caution, not a reason for healthy people to fear yoghurt-adjacent products. A guideline — no registry number applies.

shelves.title: AI-assisted colonoscopy: adenomas found, reliably — cancers prevented, unproven
shelves.question: Does computer-aided detection during colonoscopy find more adenomas — and does finding them prevent colorectal cancer?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Artificial Intelligence · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms · Deep Learning · Early Detection of Cancer · Humans · Mass Screening
shelves.balance: The detection claim earns LIKELY: randomized trials on three continents agree that computer-aided detection raises the adenoma detection rate (54.8% vs 40.4% in the GI-Genius trial; pooled RR 1.24, relative, across 21 trials and 18,232 patients) and roughly halves the adenoma miss rate in tandem studies. The fence is equally consistent: the extra lesions are overwhelmingly diminutive, advanced adenoma detection did not increase in the pooled analysis, nonneoplastic polypectomies rose, and no trial has measured cancer incidence or cancer death. Buy the detection claim at LIKELY; the cancer claim is not on this shelf because no one has earned it yet. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: GI-Genius CADe trial (Repici 2020, Gastroenterology): adenoma detection rate 54.8% with AI vs 40.4% without (RR 1.30, relative)
cards.summary: 685 patients undergoing screening, surveillance, or FIT-positive colonoscopy at 3 Italian centers, randomized to computer-aided detection (GI-Genius) or standard high-definition colonoscopy. Adenoma detection rate: 54.8% vs 40.4% — RR 1.30 [1.14–1.45], relative . Adenomas per colonoscopy: 1.07 vs 0.71 . The gains included adenomas ≤5 mm (33.7% vs 26.5%) and 6–9 mm (10.6% vs 5.8%). Withdrawal time did not differ (417 vs 435 seconds), and resection of non-neoplastic lesions did not increase (26.0% vs 28.7%).
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial, Gastroenterology 2020. The registry number is printed in the record’s own abstract (ClinicalTrials.gov no. 04079478): NCT04079478.
cards.people: 685 subjects analyzed (mean age 61.3 years [SD 10.2]; 337 men), undergoing colonoscopy for colorectal cancer screening, post-polypectomy surveillance, or workup of a positive fecal immunochemical test or symptoms, at 3 centers in Italy.
cards.result: The adenoma detection rate was significantly higher in the CADe group (54.8%) than in the control group (40.4%) (relative risk, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.14 to 1.45). Adenomas detected per colonoscopy were significantly higher with CADe (mean 1.07 [SD 1.54]) than without (mean 0.71 [SD 1.20]) (incidence rate ratio, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.15 to 1.86). There was no significant difference in withdrawal time or in the proportion of subjects with resection of non-neoplastic lesions.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain — about 14 more patients with an adenoma found per 100 colonoscopies — is real and consistent across this shelf’s trials. What it is made of matters: small adenomas dominate the increment, and most small adenomas never become cancers. Detection is a surrogate; the cancer endpoint is addressed in Card 4’s fence.
cards.source: Repici A et al. Efficacy of Real-Time Computer-Aided Detection of Colorectal Neoplasia in a Randomized Trial. Gastroenterology. 2020;159(2):512–520.e7. PMID 32371116 · NCT04079478. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2020.04.062

cards.headline: First CADe randomized trial (Wang 2019, Gut): adenoma detection 29.1% vs 20.3% — the gain was diminutive adenomas, and hyperplastic polyps rose too
cards.summary: 1,058 patients at a Chinese center, prospectively randomized to colonoscopy with or without a real-time automatic polyp detection system (visual notice plus sound alarm). Adenoma detection rate: 29.1% vs 20.3% (P<0.001) ; adenomas per patient 0.53 vs 0.31 . The increase came from diminutive adenomas ( 185 vs 102 found ); larger adenomas did not differ significantly (77 vs 58, P=0.075). Hyperplastic polyps — not precancerous — also rose sharply (114 vs 52).
cards.type: Prospective randomized controlled study (open, non-blinded), Gut 2019. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: ChiCTR-DDD-17012221. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 1,058 patients undergoing diagnostic colonoscopy: 536 randomized to standard colonoscopy and 522 to colonoscopy with the computer-aided detection system, in a population with a low baseline adenoma detection rate.
cards.result: The AI system significantly increased the adenoma detection rate (29.1% vs 20.3%, P<0.001) and the mean number of adenomas per patient (0.53 vs 0.31, P<0.001). This was due to a higher number of diminutive adenomas found (185 vs 102; P<0.001), while there was no statistical difference in larger adenomas (77 vs 58, P=0.075). The number of hyperplastic polyps detected was also significantly increased (114 vs 52, P<0.001). The authors noted that the cost-benefit ratio of these effects remained to be determined.
cards.watchOut: Open and non-blinded — endoscopists knew when the machine was watching, which can change inspection behavior itself. And the lesion mix is the shelf’s recurring caution: the system is best at finding the lesions least likely to matter, and it also finds more lesions that never mattered at all (hyperplastic polyps), each of which still gets resected and sent to pathology.
cards.source: Wang P et al. Real-time automatic detection system increases colonoscopic polyp and adenoma detection rates: a prospective randomised controlled study. Gut. 2019;68(10):1813–1819. PMID 30814121 · ChiCTR-DDD-17012221. DOI 10.1136/gutjnl-2018-317500

cards.headline: Tandem-colonoscopy trial (Wallace 2022, Gastroenterology): AI first halved the adenoma miss rate — 15.5% vs 32.4%
cards.summary: 230 patients at 8 centers (Italy, UK, US), each undergoing two same-day back-to-back colonoscopies, randomized to AI-assisted first or standard first. Adenoma miss rate: 15.5% (38 of 246 lesions) when AI went first vs 32.4% (80 of 247) when standard colonoscopy went first — adjusted OR 0.38 [0.23–0.62], relative . The advantage was largest for ≤5 mm lesions (OR 0.34) and nonpolypoid lesions (OR 0.24). Patients with no lesion found at first pass but at least one at second: 6.8% vs 29.6% .
cards.type: Randomized tandem (back-to-back) colonoscopy trial, Gastroenterology 2022. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03954548. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 230 subjects undergoing colorectal cancer screening or surveillance colonoscopy at 8 centers in Italy, the UK, and the US (116 AI-first, 114 standard-first), each examined twice on the same day.
cards.result: The adenoma miss rate was 15.5% (38 of 246) in the AI-first arm and 32.4% (80 of 247) in the standard-first arm (adjusted odds ratio, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.23 to 0.62). Miss rates were lower with AI first for lesions ≤5 mm (15.9% vs 35.8%; OR 0.34) and nonpolypoid lesions (16.8% vs 45.8%; OR 0.24), and in both proximal and distal colon. The mean number of adenomas found at the second colonoscopy was lower after AI first (0.33 vs 0.70, P<.001). No difference in adverse events was found.
cards.watchOut: The tandem design is the honest way to measure misses — but note what a miss rate is: a fraction of lesions found across two passes, dominated numerically by tiny lesions. Halving the miss rate of diminutive adenomas is not the same as halving missed cancers, and this trial, like every trial on this shelf, was not designed or powered to count cancers.
cards.source: Wallace MB et al. Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Miss Rate of Colorectal Neoplasia. Gastroenterology. 2022;163(1):295–304.e5. PMID 35304117 · NCT03954548. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2022.03.007

cards.headline: All 21 randomized trials pooled (Hassan 2023, Annals of Internal Medicine): detection up (ADR RR 1.24, relative) — advanced adenomas not increased, nonneoplastic removals up, cancer outcomes explicitly unclear
cards.summary: 21 randomized trials, 18,232 patients. Adenoma detection rate: 44.0% with CADe vs 35.9% without — RR 1.24 [1.16–1.33], relative (low-certainty evidence by the reviewers’ GRADE assessment); adenoma miss rate lower with CADe (RR 0.45, moderate certainty). But: CADe did not increase detection of advanced adenomas, and it increased removal of nonneoplastic polyps ( +0.18 polypectomies per colonoscopy ). The reviewers state plainly that the effect on cancer incidence and cancer mortality — the outcomes patients care about — remains unclear .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials, Annals of Internal Medicine 2023 (PROSPERO CRD42022293181, as printed in the record). (A meta-analysis — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the analysis itself.)
cards.people: 21 randomized trials including 18,232 patients undergoing colonoscopy for polyp and cancer detection, comparing CADe-assisted with standard colonoscopy (literature to February 2023).
cards.result: The adenoma detection rate was higher in the CADe group (44.0% vs 35.9%; relative risk, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.16 to 1.33; low-certainty evidence), corresponding to a 55% relative reduction in adenoma miss rate (moderate-certainty evidence). More nonneoplastic polyps were removed in the CADe group (0.52 vs 0.34 per colonoscopy; mean difference 0.18). Mean inspection time increased marginally (mean difference 0.47 minutes). The reviewers concluded that CADe increases detection of adenomas but not advanced adenomas, increases unnecessary removal of nonneoplastic polyps, and that its effect on patient-important outcomes — cancer incidence and cancer-related mortality — remains unclear.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the shelf’s fence, in the reviewers’ own words. The detection benefit is consistent and real; the chain from ‘more diminutive adenomas resected’ to ‘fewer cancers’ runs through surveillance intervals, pathology costs, and polypectomy harms that these trials did not measure, and the one lesion class closest to cancer — advanced adenomas — did not move.
cards.source: Hassan C et al. Real-Time Computer-Aided Detection of Colorectal Neoplasia During Colonoscopy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Ann Intern Med. 2023;176(9):1209–1220. PMID 37639719. DOI 10.7326/M22-3678

shelves.title: Early TIPS for high-risk variceal bleeding
shelves.question: Does early covered TIPS (within 72 hours) improve survival in high-risk cirrhosis patients bleeding from varices?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/complications/mortality/surgery/therapy · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/complications/mortality/surgery/therapy · Hepatic Encephalopathy/complications · Hypertension, Portal/complications · Liver Cirrhosis/complications/mortality/surgery/therapy · Polytetrafluoroethylene
shelves.balance: Tier C — slow lane: this stamp is PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict, because the shelf carries a mortality claim. Two randomised trials agree on direction. García-Pagán 2010 (63 high-risk patients): 16 deaths in total — 12 of 31 on pharmacotherapy plus band ligation versus 4 of 32 on early TIPS (P=0.01); 1-year actuarial survival 61% versus 86% (an absolute difference of 25 percentage points). Lv 2019 (129 patients in the intention-to-treat population): 15 of 84 (18%) died on early TIPS versus 15 of 45 (33%) on standard treatment; transplantation-free survival hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.98; P=0.04), with 1-year transplantation-free survival 86% versus 73% (absolute difference 13 percentage points, 95% CI 2 to 28). All-cause mortality is stated on every card beside any relative measure. Both trials are small and enrolled selected high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C, or B with active bleeding), so LIKELY — not higher — is the honest ceiling, and it remains proposed until the developer rules. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: García-Pagán 2010: early TIPS cut treatment failure and 1-year mortality in high-risk variceal bleeding
cards.summary: García-Pagán 2010: failure to control bleeding or rebleeding in 14 patients vs 1 ; 1-year survival 86% vs 61% with early TIPS.
cards.people: 63 patients with cirrhosis and acute variceal bleeding at high risk of treatment failure (Child-Pugh class C, or class B with persistent bleeding at endoscopy), randomised within 24 hours of admission: 32 early TIPS, 31 pharmacotherapy plus endoscopic band ligation. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over a median follow-up of 16 months, rebleeding or failure to control bleeding occurred in 14 patients in the pharmacotherapy group versus 1 in the early-TIPS group (P=0.001); the 1-year actuarial probability of remaining free of this end point was 50% versus 97% (P<0.001). Sixteen patients died: 12 in the pharmacotherapy group and 4 in the early-TIPS group (P=0.01); 1-year actuarial survival was 61% versus 86% (P<0.001) — an absolute survival difference of 25 percentage points. Seven pharmacotherapy patients received rescue TIPS, of whom four died. Serious adverse events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 63 patients, and the population is narrowly selected high-risk bleeders; the mortality result, though large, rests on 16 deaths in total.
cards.source: García-Pagán JC et al. Early use of TIPS in patients with cirrhosis and variceal bleeding. N Engl J Med. 2010;362:2370-9. PMID: 20573925. Registry ID: ISRCTN58150114 (from the record's databank).

cards.headline: Lv 2019: early covered TIPS improved transplantation-free survival in advanced cirrhosis with variceal bleeding
cards.summary: Lv 2019: transplantation-free survival hazard ratio 0.50 [0.25 to 0.98]; deaths 18% vs 33%.
cards.people: 132 patients with advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class B or C) and acute variceal bleeding randomised 2:1 (86 early TIPS, 46 control); after exclusion of 3 ineligible patients, 129 were in the intention-to-treat population (84 early TIPS, 45 control). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Fifteen patients (18%) in the early-TIPS group and 15 (33%) in the control group died; 2 (2%) versus 1 (2%) underwent liver transplantation. Transplantation-free survival was higher with early TIPS (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.98; P=0.04). Transplantation-free survival at 6 weeks was 99% versus 84% (absolute difference 15 percentage points, 95% CI 5 to 48; P=0.02) and at 1 year 86% versus 73% (absolute difference 13 percentage points, 95% CI 2 to 28; P=0.046). Hepatic encephalopathy occurred in 35% versus 36% (P=1.00); other serious adverse events occurred in 12% versus 24% (P=0.07).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, open-label trial in one Chinese academic hospital; all-cause deaths were 15 versus 15 in absolute count — the survival advantage is in the time-to-event and transplantation-free composite, in a 2:1 randomised population.
cards.source: Lv Y et al. Early TIPS with covered stents versus standard treatment for acute variceal bleeding in patients with advanced cirrhosis: a randomised controlled trial. shelves.title: Ustekinumab for ulcerative colitis
shelves.question: Does ustekinumab induce and maintain remission in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Induction Chemotherapy · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Subcutaneous · Maintenance Chemotherapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The UNIFI programme — an 8-week induction trial and a 44-week maintenance trial reported in one paper — found clinical remission at week 8 in 15.6% (130 mg) and 15.5% (~6 mg/kg) on ustekinumab versus 5.3% on placebo (P<0.001 for both; absolute gains of about 10 percentage points), and at week 44 in 38.4% (every 12 weeks) and 43.8% (every 8 weeks) versus 24.0% on placebo (P=0.002 and P<0.001; absolute gains of 14–20 percentage points). Serious adverse-event incidence was similar to placebo. Remission rates are modest in absolute terms — most patients did not remit — but the direction is consistent across induction and maintenance.

cards.headline: UNIFI induction: ustekinumab roughly tripled week-8 remission versus placebo — 15.5% versus 5.3%
cards.summary: UNIFI induction: week-8 remission 15.6%/15.5% on ustekinumab vs 5.3% on placebo.
cards.people: 961 patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis randomised to intravenous ustekinumab 130 mg (320 patients), a weight-range-based dose approximating 6 mg/kg (322), or placebo (319). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 8 (total Mayo score ≤2 with no subscore >1) occurred in 15.6% of patients on ustekinumab 130 mg and 15.5% on the ~6 mg/kg dose, versus 5.3% on placebo (P<0.001 for both comparisons) — absolute gains of about 10 percentage points over placebo.
cards.watchOut: Even on the active drug, about 5 of 6 patients had not reached clinical remission by week 8; remission here is the strict Mayo definition used by the trial.
cards.source: Sands BE et al. Ustekinumab as Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis. N Engl J Med. 2019;381:1201-1214. PMID: 31553833. Registry ID: NCT02407236 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank).

cards.headline: UNIFI maintenance: remission at week 44 was 43.8% (every 8 weeks) and 38.4% (every 12 weeks) versus 24.0% on placebo
cards.summary: UNIFI maintenance: week-44 remission 38.4% (12-weekly) and 43.8% (8-weekly) vs 24.0% on placebo.
cards.people: Patients who had responded to ustekinumab induction were re-randomised to subcutaneous ustekinumab 90 mg every 12 weeks (172 patients), every 8 weeks (176), or placebo (175). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 44 occurred in 38.4% of patients on ustekinumab every 12 weeks and 43.8% on ustekinumab every 8 weeks, versus 24.0% on placebo (P=0.002 and P<0.001 respectively) — absolute gains of 14.4 and 19.8 percentage points. The incidence of serious adverse events with ustekinumab was similar to that with placebo.
cards.watchOut: The maintenance population is enriched: only induction responders were re-randomised, so week-44 rates do not apply to all patients starting ustekinumab. Through 52 weeks there were 2 deaths and 7 cases of cancer among 825 ustekinumab-exposed patients, versus no deaths and 1 case of cancer among 319 placebo patients, as reported in the abstract.

cards.summary: Ustekinumab induces and maintains remission in ulcerative colitis, with modest absolute remission rates — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 961 patients in UNIFI induction and 523 induction responders in UNIFI maintenance.
cards.result: Induction remission was 15.6%/15.5% on ustekinumab versus 5.3% on placebo, and maintenance remission at week 44 was 38.4%/43.8% versus 24.0%, all statistically significant with absolute gains printed on the cards. shelves.title: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C: cure rates and the outcome gap
shelves.question: Do direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C across genotypes — and what evidence links cure (SVR) to liver outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Genotype · Hepacivirus/genetics · Hepatitis C, Chronic/drug therapy/virology · Interferon-alpha/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Liver Cirrhosis/virology
shelves.balance: LIKELY for the surrogate only — and this shelf makes NO hard-outcome claim. The randomised trials prove sustained virologic response (SVR, the cure surrogate): 90% SVR with sofosbuvir plus peginterferon-ribavirin in NEUTRINO, 99% SVR with sofosbuvir-velpatasvir versus 0% on placebo in ASTRAL-1, and 95–99% SVR in ASTRAL-2/3. But no placebo-controlled trial of mortality, decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma or transplantation exists or could now ethically be run, so the link from SVR to liver outcomes rests on observational evidence outside these cards and is NOT stamped here. SVR percentages must never be read as proven reductions in liver death or cancer. Distinct from Shelf #326 (hepatitis B antivirals — different virus, drugs and evidence shape).

cards.headline: NEUTRINO and FISSION: sofosbuvir regimens achieved SVR in 90% (genotypes 1/4/5/6) and 67% (genotypes 2/3)
cards.summary: NEUTRINO: SVR in 90% (genotypes 1/4/5/6); FISSION: 67% in both sofosbuvir and comparator groups (genotypes 2/3).
cards.people: NEUTRINO: 327 previously untreated patients with HCV genotype 1, 4, 5 or 6 (98% genotype 1 or 4) given sofosbuvir plus peginterferon alfa-2a and ribavirin for 12 weeks. FISSION: 499 patients with genotype 2 or 3 randomised to sofosbuvir plus ribavirin for 12 weeks or peginterferon plus ribavirin for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In NEUTRINO, a sustained virologic response at 12 weeks after the end of therapy was reported in 90% of patients (95% CI 87 to 93). In FISSION, a sustained response was reported in 67% of patients in both treatment groups; within the sofosbuvir-ribavirin group, response was 56% in genotype 3 versus 97% in genotype 2. Adverse events including fatigue, headache, nausea and neutropenia were less common with sofosbuvir than with peginterferon.
cards.watchOut: SVR is a virologic surrogate. NEUTRINO had no control group, and neither study reports mortality, decompensation or liver-cancer outcomes.
cards.source: Lawitz E et al. Sofosbuvir for previously untreated chronic hepatitis C infection. N Engl J Med. 2013;368:1878-87. PMID: 23607594. Registry IDs: NCT01497366 and NCT01641640 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank).

cards.headline: ASTRAL-1: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir cured 99% versus 0% on placebo — a surrogate end point, placebo-controlled
cards.summary: ASTRAL-1: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir cured 99% vs 0% on placebo — a surrogate end point, and the card labels it as such.
cards.people: 624 patients treated with sofosbuvir-velpatasvir and 116 with placebo, with chronic HCV genotype 1, 2, 4, 5 or 6, including compensated cirrhosis; 19% had cirrhosis and 32% had been previously treated. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The rate of sustained virologic response at 12 weeks after the end of therapy was 99% (95% CI 98 to >99) with sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks; 2 patients, both with genotype 1, had a virologic relapse. None of the 116 placebo patients had a sustained virologic response. Serious adverse events were reported in 15 patients (2%) in the sofosbuvir-velpatasvir group and none in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: This is the one placebo-controlled card on the shelf, and its end point is still SVR — the trial proves cure of the virus, not prevention of liver outcomes; follow-up was 12 weeks after therapy.

cards.headline: ASTRAL-2 and ASTRAL-3: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir beat sofosbuvir-ribavirin in genotypes 2 (99% vs 94%) and 3 (95% vs 80%)
cards.summary: ASTRAL-2/3: SVR 99% vs 94% (genotype 2) and 95% vs 80% (genotype 3) vs sofosbuvir-ribavirin.
cards.people: Genotype 2 trial: 134 patients on sofosbuvir-velpatasvir and 132 on sofosbuvir plus ribavirin, for 12 weeks. Genotype 3 trial: 277 patients on sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks and 275 on sofosbuvir-ribavirin for 24 weeks. Both trials included previously treated patients and compensated cirrhosis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In genotype 2, sustained virologic response was 99% (95% CI 96 to 100) with sofosbuvir-velpatasvir versus 94% (95% CI 88 to 97) with sofosbuvir-ribavirin (P=0.02). cards.watchOut: Comparators are other active regimens, not placebo, and the end point remains SVR; genotype 3 was the hardest to cure in every programme on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the trials prove cure (SVR) across genotypes — no placebo-controlled mortality or liver-outcome trial exists
cards.summary: The trials prove cure (SVR) across genotypes; no placebo-controlled mortality or liver-outcome trial exists, and the stamp is confined to cure — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: NEUTRINO/FISSION, ASTRAL-1 and ASTRAL-2/3 — the foundational direct-acting antiviral programmes.
cards.result: Sustained virologic response rates were 90% in NEUTRINO, 99% versus 0% on placebo in ASTRAL-1, and 99% (genotype 2) and 95% (genotype 3) in ASTRAL-2/3. The shelf is stamped LIKELY for SVR cure across genotypes. It is deliberately NOT stamped for liver outcomes: no card here reports mortality, decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma or transplantation from a placebo-controlled trial, and none exists — any claim that cure prevents those outcomes rests on observational linkage, which this shelf states as a gap rather than grading as benefit.
cards.watchOut: Do not let a 99% SVR figure do the work of an outcome claim in downstream summaries; keep the surrogate and the outcome gap together whenever this shelf is cited.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the honest ceiling for a single pivotal trial. In Bass 2010 (299 patients in remission from recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, over 90% also on lactulose), a breakthrough episode occurred in 22.1% on rifaximin versus 45.9% on placebo over 6 months (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.64; P<0.001) — a 58% relative reduction in hazard, and an absolute difference of 23.8 percentage points. Hospitalisation involving hepatic encephalopathy occurred in 13.6% versus 22.6% (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87; P=0.01). Adverse events were similar to placebo. One trial, however well conducted, does not earn more than POSSIBLE on this library's scale.

cards.headline: Bass 2010: rifaximin cut breakthrough hepatic encephalopathy — 22.1% versus 45.9% over 6 months
cards.summary: Bass 2010: breakthrough encephalopathy 22.1% vs 45.9% (hazard ratio 0.42 — a 58% relative reduction; 23.8 points absolute) over 6 months.
cards.people: 299 patients in remission from recurrent hepatic encephalopathy resulting from chronic liver disease, randomised to rifaximin 550 mg twice daily (140 patients) or placebo (159) for 6 months; more than 90% received concomitant lactulose. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A breakthrough episode of hepatic encephalopathy occurred in 22.1% of patients in the rifaximin group versus 45.9% in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.64; P<0.001) — a 58% relative reduction in hazard, corresponding to an absolute difference of 23.8 percentage points over 6 months. The incidence of adverse events and of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Single pivotal trial with 6-month follow-up; nearly all patients were also on lactulose, so the result is for rifaximin added to lactulose, not rifaximin alone.

shelves.title: How much fluid in acute pancreatitis: aggressive vs moderate resuscitation
shelves.question: Does aggressive early fluid resuscitation improve outcomes in acute pancreatitis, or cause overload?
shelves.mesh: Acid-Base Imbalance/etiology/therapy · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects/methods · Pancreatitis/complications/therapy · Resuscitation/methods · Ringer's Lactate/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Water-Electrolyte Imbalance/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-trial ceiling, for harm from the aggressive strategy. WATERFALL (249 patients in the first interim analysis, of 744 planned) was halted early because aggressive resuscitation caused more fluid overload without improving outcomes: moderately severe or severe pancreatitis developed in 22.1% on aggressive versus 17.3% on moderate resuscitation (adjusted relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.18; P=0.32), while fluid overload developed in 20.5% versus 6.3% (adjusted relative risk 2.85, 95% CI 1.36 to 5.94; P=0.004) — an absolute overload excess of 14.2 percentage points. Early stopping and the single-trial base cap the stamp at POSSIBLE, but the direction is clear enough to retire routine aggressive resuscitation as the default.

cards.headline: WATERFALL: aggressive fluids did not reduce moderately severe or severe pancreatitis — 22.1% versus 17.3%
cards.summary: WATERFALL: moderately severe or severe pancreatitis in 22.1% vs 17.3% on aggressive fluids (adjusted relative risk 1.30) — no benefit.
cards.people: 249 patients presenting with acute pancreatitis at 18 centres, randomised to goal-directed aggressive resuscitation (bolus 20 mL/kg, then 3 mL/kg per hour) or moderate resuscitation (bolus 10 mL/kg if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg per hour) with lactated Ringer's solution; this was the first planned interim analysis of a trial planned for 744 patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — development of moderately severe or severe pancreatitis during hospitalisation — occurred in 22.1% of the aggressive-resuscitation group and 17.3% of the moderate-resuscitation group (adjusted relative risk 1.30; 95% CI 0.78 to 2.18; P=0.32). Median hospital stay was 6 days (IQR 4–8) versus 5 days (IQR 3–7). The trial was halted at the interim analysis because of the safety difference (fluid overload, on the companion card) without a significant efficacy difference.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early at one third of planned enrolment, so efficacy estimates are imprecise; the point estimate favours moderate resuscitation but its confidence interval includes benefit for aggressive fluids.
cards.source: de-Madaria E et al. Aggressive or Moderate Fluid Resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis. N Engl J Med. 2022;387:989-1000. PMID: 36103415. Registry ID: NCT04381169 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank).

shelves.title: Inguinal hernia repair: mesh vs sutured repair, and laparoscopic vs open mesh
shelves.question: Does mesh repair reduce recurrence versus sutured repair — and does laparoscopic repair beat open mesh on pain and recovery at any recurrence cost?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials as Topic · Hernia, Femoral/surgery · Hernia, Inguinal/surgery · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Secondary Prevention · Surgical Mesh · Laparoscopy/mortality,statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Open mesh repair reduces hernia recurrence compared with open non-mesh repair (Cochrane individual-patient-data review of 20 trials: Peto odds ratio 0.37, a relative figure), with quicker return to usual activities. For the approach question, the large VA trial found open mesh superior to laparoscopic mesh for primary hernias on recurrence (4.9% vs 10.1% at two years), while laparoscopy bought only modest early-pain and one-day-earlier-return advantages and more complications; for recurrent hernias the two approaches had similar recurrence. Mesh, placed open, is the evidence-backed default in this trial base.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Scott) 2002: open mesh repair roughly halved-to-quartered recurrence versus non-mesh repair across 20 trials
cards.summary: Cochrane (Scott) 2002: open mesh repair roughly halved-to-quartered recurrence vs non-mesh repair across 20 trials (odds ratio 0.37, relative).
cards.type: Systematic review with individual patient data from randomised trials
cards.people: Twenty randomised or quasi-randomised trials comparing open mesh with open non-mesh repair of groin (femoral and inguinal) hernia, plus two trials of flat mesh versus plug-and-mesh; most data came from individual patient data supplied by the trialists. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Fewer hernia recurrences were reported after mesh repair (Peto odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.51 — a relative figure; the review summarises the reduction in recurrence risk as between 50% and 75% relative). Open mesh operations took 7–10 minutes less than Shouldice repairs but 1–4 minutes longer than other non-mesh methods. There were no clear differences in haematomas, seromas or wound/superficial infections; three serious operative complications were reported in each group. Mesh patients had shorter hospital stay and quicker return to usual activities in most trials; persisting pain may have been less frequent after mesh, but that result depended on one trial and data were missing for 11 trials; there was no difference in persisting numbness. The two flat-mesh versus plug-and-mesh trials showed no clear differences.
cards.watchOut: Trials were heterogeneous and span an era of evolving mesh technique; the persisting-pain signal rests on a single trial with much missing data, and there were too few data for recurrent, bilateral or femoral subgroups.
cards.source: Scott NW et al. Open mesh versus non-mesh for repair of femoral and inguinal hernia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2001;(4):CD002197. PMID: 12519568. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Neumayer 2004 (VA trial): open mesh beat laparoscopic mesh on recurrence for primary hernias (4.9% vs 10.1% at 2 years)
cards.summary: Neumayer 2004 (VA trial): open mesh beat laparoscopic mesh on recurrence for primary hernias ( 4.9% vs 10.1% at 2 years).
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (14 US Veterans Affairs centres)
cards.people: 2164 men with inguinal hernias randomly assigned to open mesh or laparoscopic mesh repair; 1983 underwent an operation and 1696 (85.5%) completed two-year follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Recurrence at two years was more common after laparoscopic repair (87 of 862, 10.1%) than open repair (41 of 834, 4.9%; odds ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.5 to 3.2 — a relative figure). Complications were also higher with laparoscopy (39.0% vs 33.4%; adjusted odds ratio 1.3, 1.1 to 1.6). Laparoscopy gave less pain on the day of surgery (mean visual-analogue difference 10.2 mm, 4.8 to 15.6) and at two weeks (6.1 mm, 1.7 to 10.5) and return to normal activities one day earlier (adjusted hazard ratio 1.2, 1.1 to 1.3). In prespecified analyses the approach interacted with hernia type (P=0.012): recurrence after repair of primary hernias was 10.1% laparoscopic vs 4.0% open, while after repair of recurrent hernias rates were similar (10.0% vs 14.1%). The authors concluded the open technique is superior for mesh repair of primary hernias.
cards.watchOut: Men only, in VA centres, with the laparoscopic learning curve of its era; results for recurrent hernias rest on a subgroup, and 14.5% of operated patients lacked two-year follow-up.
cards.source: Neumayer L et al. Open mesh versus laparoscopic mesh repair of inguinal hernia. N Engl J Med. 2004;350(18):1819-1827. PMID: 15107485. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Synthesis: mesh is the recurrence answer; open placement beat laparoscopy for primary hernias in the one large head-to-head trial
cards.summary: Mesh is the recurrence answer; open placement beat laparoscopy for primary hernias in the one large head-to-head trial — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Cochrane IPD review (20 mesh-vs-non-mesh trials) and the VA trial (2164 men, open vs laparoscopic mesh).
cards.result: Two separate questions, two clear answers. Mesh versus sutures: recurrence odds ratio 0.37 (relative) favouring mesh, with faster return to activities and no clear excess of wound complications. Open versus laparoscopic mesh: the VA trial's absolute recurrence gap (4.9% vs 10.1% at two years) outweighs laparoscopy's transient pain advantage and one-day-earlier return, and laparoscopy carried more complications; only in recurrent hernias were the approaches comparable. Nothing in this shelf tests mesh against no repair, or either approach in women.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the VA recurrence gap as a verdict on modern laparoscopic practice in expert high-volume hands — it is a verdict on the trial as run, in men, in its era.
cards.source: Synthesis of Scott NW et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2001;(4):CD002197. PMID: 12519568; Neumayer L et al. N Engl J Med. 2004;350(18):1819-1827. PMID: 15107485. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Timing of cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis: early vs delayed
shelves.question: Is early (same-admission, within days) laparoscopic cholecystectomy safer than delayed interval surgery for acute cholecystitis?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/economics,therapeutic use · Aza Compounds/economics,therapeutic use · Cholecystectomy, Laparoscopic/economics,methods · Cholecystitis, Acute/drug therapy,economics,mortality,surgery · Combined Modality Therapy · Conversion to Open Surgery/statistics & numerical data · Cost-Benefit Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — within 24 hours of admission in ACDC, and on admission even after more than 72 hours of symptoms in the Roulin trial — produces substantially less overall morbidity than antibiotics-first delayed surgery (11.8% vs 34.4% in ACDC; 14% vs 39% in Roulin), with shorter total hospital stay and lower costs, and no significant difference in conversion to open surgery or mortality in ACDC. Two concordant randomised trials, one large and multicentre, support operating during the index admission in operable patients.

cards.headline: ACDC (Gutt) 2013: cholecystectomy within 24 hours cut 75-day morbidity to 11.8% vs 34.4% with delayed surgery
cards.summary: ACDC (Gutt) 2013: cholecystectomy within 24 hours cut 75-day morbidity to 11.8% vs 34.4% with delayed surgery.
cards.people: 618 patients with acute cholecystitis randomly assigned to immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24 hours of hospital admission (304) or initial antibiotic treatment (moxifloxacin for at least 48 hours in all patients) followed by delayed laparoscopic cholecystectomy at days 7 to 45 (314). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, predefined relevant morbidity within 75 days, was significantly lower with immediate surgery: 11.8% vs 34.4%. Conversion rate to open surgery and mortality did not differ significantly between groups. Mean length of hospital stay was 5.4 vs 10.0 days (P<0.001) and total hospital costs €2919 vs €4262 (P<0.001), both favouring immediate surgery. The authors concluded immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy should become the therapy of choice for acute cholecystitis in operable patients.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and conducted in operable patients; the morbidity composite is a predefined bundle, and the cost figures are German hospital costs of the trial era. The trial does not address patients unfit for surgery, in whom drainage strategies (a different comparison) apply.
cards.source: Gutt CN et al. Acute cholecystitis: early versus delayed cholecystectomy, a multicenter randomized trial (ACDC study). Ann Surg. 2013;258(3):385-393. PMID: 24022431. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00447304, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Roulin 2016: even after 72+ hours of symptoms, early cholecystectomy beat delayed — morbidity 14% vs 39%
cards.summary: Roulin 2016: even after 72+ hours of symptoms, early cholecystectomy beat delayed — morbidity 14% vs 39% .
cards.people: 86 patients with acute cholecystitis and more than 72 hours of symptoms, randomly assigned to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy on admission (42) or delayed cholecystectomy at least 6 weeks after initial antibiotic treatment (44). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Overall morbidity after initial diagnosis was lower with early surgery: 6 of 42 (14%) vs 17 of 44 (39%) patients (P=0.015). Median total length of stay was 4 vs 7 days (P<0.001), duration of antibiotic therapy 2 vs 10 days (P<0.001), and total hospital costs were lower in the early group. Operative time (91 vs 88 minutes) and postoperative complications (15% vs 17%) were similar. The authors concluded early cholecystectomy is safe and preferable even beyond 72 hours of symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Small (86 patients) and single-programme: it extends ACDC's answer to later presenters but cannot exclude uncommon harms; cost figures are in Swiss francs as printed in the record (the abstract's currency glyph is corrupted in the MEDLINE text, so no currency figure is quoted here).
cards.source: Roulin D et al. Early Versus Delayed Cholecystectomy for Acute Cholecystitis, Are the 72 hours Still the Rule?: A Randomized Trial. Ann Surg. 2016;264(5):717-722. PMID: 27741006. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01548339, from the record's databank fields.
