cards.headline: Synthesis: operate during the index admission — the morbidity gap is large and consistent from 24 hours to beyond 72 hours of symptoms
cards.summary: Operate during the index admission — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ACDC (618 patients, surgery within 24 hours) and Roulin 2016 (86 patients, symptoms >72 hours).
cards.result: Both trials point the same way with large absolute morbidity differences (11.8% vs 34.4%; 14% vs 39%), shorter stays and lower costs, and neither found a conversion or mortality penalty for early surgery. The delayed strategy's morbidity accrues largely while waiting — recurrent biliary events and a harder later operation are the mechanism the numbers imply. The shelf's answer is confined to patients fit for surgery; percutaneous drainage versus surgery in high-risk patients is a different randomised comparison (the CHOCOLATE trial) and is not carded here because it does not test timing.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded (impossible for timing), and both predate current enhanced-recovery practice; the direction and size of the morbidity gap, not the exact percentages, are the durable findings.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gutt CN et al. Ann Surg. 2013;258(3):385-393. PMID: 24022431; Roulin D et al. Ann Surg. 2016;264(5):717-722. PMID: 27741006. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TyVAC trials)
shelves.question: Does a single dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine protect children in endemic settings — efficacy in Nepal and four-year durability in Malawi?
shelves.mesh: Endemic Diseases/prevention & control · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Meningococcal Vaccines/adverse effects,immunology · Nepal/epidemiology · Salmonella typhi/isolation & purification · Typhoid Fever/diagnosis,epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large phase 3 trials in endemic settings agree on a single dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine. In Nepal (20,019 children vaccinated), blood-culture-confirmed typhoid occurred at 79 vs 428 cases per 100,000 person-years against a meningococcal control vaccine (efficacy 81.6%, 95% CI 58.8 to 91.8 — a relative figure, absolute incidence beside it). In Malawi (28,130 children), the final 4-year analysis found efficacy of 78.3% (66.3 to 86.1), with protection in every age band including children under 2 years (70.6%, with a wide interval) and 163 children needing vaccination to prevent one case. Serious adverse events were similar between groups in Nepal (132 events in 6 months; one vaccine-related, pyrexia). Two large trials, consistent efficacy, proven durability: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Shakya 2019 (Nepal): one dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine was 81.6% efficacious against blood-culture-confirmed typhoid
cards.summary: Shakya 2019 (Nepal): one dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine was 81.6% efficacious (relative) against blood-culture-confirmed typhoid (79 vs 428 cases per 100,000 person-years).
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised controlled trial (participants and observers blinded; control was a meningococcal conjugate vaccine)
cards.people: 20,019 children aged 9 months to 16 years in Lalitpur, Nepal, received typhoid conjugate vaccine (10,005) or capsular group A meningococcal conjugate vaccine (10,014) in a 1:1 ratio; the report presents the prespecified primary analysis while 2-year follow-up continued. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Blood-culture-confirmed typhoid fever (the primary outcome) occurred in 7 participants on typhoid conjugate vaccine (79 cases per 100,000 person-years) and 38 on control vaccine (428 per 100,000 person-years): vaccine efficacy 81.6% (95% CI 58.8 to 91.8; P<0.001 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). In the first 6 months there were 132 serious adverse events (61 vaccine, 71 control), of which one (pyrexia) was judged vaccine-related. Fever in the first week occurred in 5.0% (vaccine) vs 5.4% (control). Seroconversion (Vi IgG at least quadrupled at 28 days) was 99% in the vaccine group (677 of 683 in the immunogenicity subgroup) vs 2% in controls (8 of 380).
cards.watchOut: An active-control trial (meningococcal vaccine), so 'efficacy' is against a real vaccine's background, and the case count at this interim analysis was small (7 vs 38) — the Malawi trial's 134 cases over 4 years are the durability evidence, next card.
cards.source: Shakya M et al. Phase 3 Efficacy Analysis of a Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine Trial in Nepal. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(23):2209-2218. PMID: 31800986. Registry ID: ISRCTN43385161, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Malawi final analysis 2024: efficacy held at 78.3% over more than 4 years — 24 vs 110 cases; 163 children vaccinated to prevent one case
cards.summary: Malawi final analysis 2024: efficacy held at 78.3% over more than 4 years — 24 vs 110 cases; 163 children vaccinated to prevent one case.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised controlled efficacy trial (final analysis, median follow-up 4.3 years)
cards.people: 28,130 healthy children aged 9 months to 12 years in Blantyre, Malawi, vaccinated with a single dose of Vi polysaccharide–tetanus toxoid conjugate vaccine (14,069) or meningococcal capsular group A conjugate vaccine (14,061), recruited from government schools and health centres; participants, parents and the study team were masked (administering nurses were not).
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 4.3 years (interquartile range 4.2 to 4.5), a first episode of blood-culture-confirmed typhoid fever (the primary outcome) occurred in 24 children on Vi-TT (39.7 cases per 100,000 person-years) and 110 on control vaccine (182.7 per 100,000 person-years): intention-to-treat efficacy 78.3% (95% CI 66.3 to 86.1 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it), with 163 children (95% CI 129 to 222) needing vaccination to prevent one case. Efficacy by age: 70.6% (6.4 to 93.0) at 9 months to 2 years, 79.6% (45.8 to 93.9) at 2–4 years, and 79.3% (63.5 to 89.0) at 5–12 years.
cards.watchOut: The under-2 efficacy interval (6.4 to 93.0) is wide because cases in that band were few — the point estimate supports the WHO routine-introduction recommendation the authors cite, but precision in the youngest children is genuinely low.

cards.summary: One dose, ~80% relative efficacy, still working at four years — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Nepal (20,019 vaccinated children) and Malawi (28,130 vaccinated children, 4.3-year median follow-up).
cards.result: Short-term efficacy in Asia (81.6%, on rates of 79 vs 428 per 100,000 person-years) and durable efficacy in Africa (78.3% at 4 years, 39.7 vs 182.7 per 100,000 person-years, number-needed-to-vaccinate 163) from two independently run phase 3 trials is the strongest pattern a vaccine shelf can hold. shelves.title: Vedolizumab versus adalimumab in ulcerative colitis (VARSITY)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, is gut-selective vedolizumab superior to anti-TNF adalimumab on clinical remission — the first head-to-head biologic trial in UC?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Infusions, Intravenous
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single head-to-head biologic trial in ulcerative colitis (VARSITY, 769 patients), vedolizumab was superior to adalimumab on clinical remission at week 52 (31.3% vs 22.5%) and on endoscopic improvement (39.7% vs 27.7%), but NOT on corticosteroid-free clinical remission, which numerically favoured adalimumab (12.6% vs 21.8%). One trial, however rigorous, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the single-trial rule.

cards.headline: VARSITY 2019: vedolizumab beat adalimumab on remission (31.3% vs 22.5%) and endoscopic improvement, but not on steroid-free remission
cards.summary: VARSITY 2019: vedolizumab beat adalimumab on remission ( 31.3% vs 22.5% ) and endoscopic improvement, but not on steroid-free remission.
cards.type: Phase 3b, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised head-to-head trial
cards.people: 769 adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis at 245 centres in 34 countries, randomised to vedolizumab 300 mg infusions (383) or adalimumab subcutaneous injections (386); prior exposure to a TNF inhibitor other than adalimumab was allowed in up to 25% of patients. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 52, clinical remission (total Mayo score ≤2, no subscore >1) occurred in 31.3% of the vedolizumab group vs 22.5% of the adalimumab group (difference 8.8 percentage points, 95% CI 2.5 to 15.0; P=0.006), and endoscopic improvement in 39.7% vs 27.7% (difference 11.9 points, 5.3 to 18.5; P<0.001). Corticosteroid-free clinical remission went the other way: 12.6% vs 21.8% (difference −9.3 points, −18.9 to 0.4). Exposure-adjusted infection rates were 23.4 vs 34.6 events per 100 patient-years, and serious infection 1.6 vs 2.2 per 100 patient-years.
cards.watchOut: Single head-to-head trial, industry-funded (Takeda), with no dose escalation permitted in either arm — a design that may disadvantage adalimumab, whose real-world dosing is often escalated. The steroid-free remission result favours adalimumab and is part of the trial's own hierarchical outcome set.
cards.source: Sands BE et al. Vedolizumab versus Adalimumab for Moderate-to-Severe Ulcerative Colitis. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(13):1215-1226. PMID: 31553834. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02497469; EudraCT 2015-000939-33 (from the record's databank fields).

shelves.title: Crohn's disease head-to-heads: risankizumab versus ustekinumab (SEQUENCE)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, does risankizumab beat ustekinumab on endoscopic response (SEQUENCE) — and what did ustekinumab's own pivotal programme show (UNITI)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Crohn Disease/diagnosis,drug therapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Ustekinumab/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Risankizumab was noninferior to ustekinumab for clinical remission at week 24 (58.6% vs 39.5%) and superior for endoscopic remission at week 48 (31.8% vs 16.2%) in the SEQUENCE head-to-head trial in anti-TNF-experienced Crohn's disease, and ustekinumab's own UNITI/IM-UNITI programme independently establishes ustekinumab as an effective induction and maintenance therapy against placebo — so the comparator risankizumab beat is a proven drug, not a straw man.

cards.headline: SEQUENCE 2024: risankizumab noninferior on clinical remission at week 24 and superior on endoscopic remission at week 48 versus ustekinumab
cards.summary: SEQUENCE 2024: risankizumab noninferior on clinical remission at week 24 and superior on endoscopic remission at week 48 vs ustekinumab.
cards.type: Phase 3b, multicentre, open-label randomised controlled trial with blinded assessment of endpoints
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease who had had an inadequate response to anti-TNF therapy or unacceptable side effects; 255 were assigned to risankizumab and 265 to ustekinumab at standard doses for 48 weeks (230 [90.2%] and 193 [72.8%] completed all assigned treatments). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Both primary endpoints were met: risankizumab was noninferior to ustekinumab for clinical remission at week 24 (CDAI <150; 58.6% vs 39.5%; adjusted difference 18.4 percentage points, 95% CI 6.6 to 30.3; noninferiority margin 10 points, analysed in the first 50% of patients completing week 24) and superior for endoscopic remission at week 48 (31.8% vs 16.2%; adjusted difference 15.6 points, 8.4 to 22.9; P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events appeared similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (endpoints were blindly assessed) in a single head-to-head trial funded by AbbVie, the maker of risankizumab; completion of all assigned treatment was notably lower with ustekinumab (72.8% vs 90.2%), which can flatter the newer drug in endpoint analyses.
cards.source: Peyrin-Biroulet L et al. Risankizumab versus Ustekinumab for Moderate-to-Severe Crohn's Disease. N Engl J Med. 2024;391(3):213-223. PMID: 39018531. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04524611 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: UNITI 2016: ustekinumab beat placebo for induction response and maintained remission — the proven comparator
cards.summary: UNITI 2016: ustekinumab beat placebo for induction response and maintained remission — the proven comparator.
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled induction trials (UNITI-1, UNITI-2) plus a randomised maintenance trial (IM-UNITI)
cards.people: UNITI-1 enrolled 741 patients with primary or secondary nonresponse to TNF antagonists or unacceptable side effects; UNITI-2 enrolled 628 patients in whom conventional therapy had failed or caused unacceptable side effects; 397 induction responders entered IM-UNITI maintenance. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Week-6 clinical response (CDAI fall ≥100 points or CDAI <150) with intravenous ustekinumab 130 mg or ~6 mg/kg vs placebo: UNITI-1 34.3%, 33.7% and 21.5% respectively (P≤0.003 for both comparisons); UNITI-2 51.7%, 55.5% and 28.7% (P<0.001 for both doses). In IM-UNITI, remission at week 44 was 53.1% with ustekinumab 90 mg every 8 weeks and 48.8% every 12 weeks vs 35.9% with placebo (P=0.005 and P=0.04). Adverse-event rates were similar among treatment groups within each trial.
cards.watchOut: Placebo-controlled programme from 2016: it establishes ustekinumab's efficacy, not its standing against newer agents — that comparison is SEQUENCE's job, carded above. Ustekinumab for ulcerative colitis is a different question and lives on Shelf #592.

cards.headline: Synthesis: risankizumab ahead of a proven comparator on endoscopic remission — LIKELY
cards.summary: Risankizumab ahead of a proven comparator on endoscopic remission — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SEQUENCE (520 patients randomised) and the UNITI/IM-UNITI programme (741 + 628 induction patients; 397 in maintenance).

shelves.title: Diarrhoea-predominant IBS: rifaximin and eluxadoline
shelves.question: Do rifaximin (TARGET 1/2) and eluxadoline improve IBS-D symptoms versus placebo — and what harms (pancreatitis with eluxadoline) bound their use?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy,etiology · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/complications,drug therapy · Rifamycins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rifaximin · Abdominal Pain/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Both drugs beat placebo in twin phase 3 programmes — rifaximin for adequate relief of global IBS symptoms (40.7% vs 31.7% pooled across TARGET 1 and 2) and eluxadoline for its pain-plus-stool composite (up to 29.6% vs 16.2% over weeks 1–12) — with modest absolute gains of roughly 9–13 percentage points. Eluxadoline's use is bounded by pancreatitis (5 cases, 0.3%, in its trials) and the sphincter-of-Oddi concerns that followed; rifaximin's adverse-event rate matched placebo.

cards.headline: TARGET 1/2 2011: two weeks of rifaximin gave adequate relief of global IBS symptoms in 40.7% vs 31.7% on placebo
cards.summary: TARGET 1/2 2011: two weeks of rifaximin gave adequate relief of global IBS symptoms in 40.7% vs 31.7% on placebo.
cards.type: Two identically designed phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (TARGET 1 and TARGET 2)
cards.people: Patients with irritable bowel syndrome without constipation, randomised to rifaximin 550 mg or placebo three times daily for 2 weeks and followed for a further 10 weeks. The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Adequate relief of global IBS symptoms during the first 4 weeks after treatment: TARGET 1, 40.8% vs 31.2% (P=0.01); TARGET 2, 40.6% vs 32.2% (P=0.03); combined, 40.7% vs 31.7% (P<0.001). Adequate relief of bloating: 39.5% vs 28.7% (P=0.005), 41.0% vs 31.9% (P=0.02), and 40.2% vs 30.3% combined (P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A ~9-percentage-point absolute gain on a self-reported relief endpoint, after a 2-week course, in IBS without constipation (the trials predate the IBS-D label used for eluxadoline); retreatment data are not in this record's abstract and are not carded.

cards.headline: Eluxadoline 2016: composite pain-and-stool response up to 29.6% vs 16.2% on placebo; pancreatitis in 0.3%
cards.summary: Eluxadoline 2016: composite pain-and-stool response up to 29.6% vs 16.2% on placebo; pancreatitis in 0.3%.
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (IBS-3001, 52 weeks; IBS-3002, 26 weeks)
cards.people: 2,427 adults with irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea, randomised to eluxadoline 75 mg or 100 mg or placebo twice daily. The abstract does not state mean age; it reports the trials enrolled men and women.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (composite response on ≥50% of days, weeks 1–12): IBS-3001, 23.9% (75 mg) and 25.1% (100 mg) vs 17.1% placebo (P=0.01 and P=0.004); IBS-3002, 28.9% and 29.6% vs 16.2% (P<0.001 for both). Over weeks 1–26 the 100-mg dose held up in both trials (29.3% vs 19.0%, P<0.001; 32.7% vs 20.2%, P<0.001), while the 75-mg dose did not reach significance in IBS-3001 (23.4% vs 19.0%, P=0.11). Common adverse events vs placebo: nausea 8.1%/7.5% vs 5.1%, constipation 7.4%/8.6% vs 2.5%, abdominal pain 5.8%/7.2% vs 4.1%. Pancreatitis developed in 5 of 1,666 patients in the safety population (0.3%).

cards.summary: AspECT 2018: high-dose PPI beat low-dose on the death/cancer/dysplasia composite; aspirin alone was not significant; the combination was strongest. (Tier C — the composite includes all-cause mortality; ruled Tier C at insert under the death-in-composite rule, PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised 2×2 factorial trial, unblinded, with masked pathology reporting
cards.people: 2,557 patients with Barrett's oesophagus of 1 cm or more at 84 UK centres and one Canadian centre, randomised to high-dose (40 mg twice daily) or low-dose (20 mg once daily) esomeprazole, with or without aspirin (300 mg/day UK; 325 mg/day Canada), treated for at least 8 years; median follow-up 8.9 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 313 primary composite events (time to all-cause mortality, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, or high-grade dysplasia) occurred. High-dose PPI was superior to low-dose PPI (139 events in 1,270 patients vs 174 in 1,265; time ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.58, p=0.038). Aspirin was not significantly better than no aspirin (127 events in 1,138 vs 154 in 1,142; time ratio 1.24, 0.98 to 1.57, p=0.068), though censoring patients at first NSAID use made the aspirin comparison significant (1.29, 1.01 to 1.66, p=0.043). High-dose PPI plus aspirin vs low-dose PPI without aspirin had the strongest effect (time ratio 1.59, 1.14 to 2.23, p=0.0068). Numbers needed to treat were 34 for PPI and 43 for aspirin; 28 participants (1%) reported treatment-related serious adverse events. Time ratios are relative measures of time to the composite event.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded treatment, a composite in which deaths from any cause count alongside cancer and dysplasia, and an aspirin effect that crosses significance only in a censoring sensitivity analysis — hence POSSIBLE for the chemoprevention half of this shelf. shelves.balance: LIKELY: Swallowed budesonide induces remission in eosinophilic oesophagitis in two randomised placebo-controlled trials — the purpose-built orodispersible tablet achieved complete clinico-histological remission in 58% vs 0% on placebo at 6 weeks (histological remission 93% vs 0%), and an earlier viscous budesonide trial cut mean oesophageal eosinophils from 68.2 to 5.5 per high-power field vs no significant change on placebo. cards.headline: EOS-1 2019: budesonide orodispersible tablets gave complete remission in 58% vs 0% on placebo at 6 weeks
cards.summary: EOS-1 2019: budesonide orodispersible tablets gave complete remission in 58% vs 0% on placebo at 6 weeks.
cards.people: 88 adults with active eosinophilic oesophagitis in Europe, randomised to budesonide orodispersible tablets 1 mg twice daily (59) or placebo (29) for 6 weeks; non-remitters were offered 6 weeks of open-label budesonide. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 weeks, complete remission (clinical plus histological, including dysphagia/odynophagia severity ≤2 on 0–10 scales and peak eosinophil count <5 per high-power field) was achieved by 58% of the budesonide group vs no patients on placebo (P<0.0001); histological remission alone was 93% vs 0% (P<0.0001). Five per cent of budesonide patients developed symptomatic mild candida infection, treated with an oral antifungal.

shelves.title: Preventing pancreatitis after ERCP: rectal indomethacin and hydration

shelves.balance: LIKELY: A single dose of rectal indomethacin immediately after ERCP cut post-ERCP pancreatitis from 16.9% to 9.2% in 602 high-risk patients (Elmunzer 2012) — a relative risk of about 0.54, at the edge of the library's 0.5 caution band, with a 7.7-percentage-point absolute reduction beside it — and moderate-to-severe pancreatitis from 8.8% to 4.4%. cards.headline: Elmunzer 2012: rectal indomethacin after ERCP cut post-ERCP pancreatitis from 16.9% to 9.2% in high-risk patients
cards.summary: Elmunzer 2012: rectal indomethacin after ERCP cut post-ERCP pancreatitis from 16.9% to 9.2% in high-risk patients.
cards.people: 602 patients at elevated risk for post-ERCP pancreatitis (on validated patient- and procedure-related risk factors; 82% had clinical suspicion of sphincter of Oddi dysfunction), assigned to a single dose of rectal indomethacin (295) or placebo (307) immediately after ERCP, all completing follow-up. cards.result: Post-ERCP pancreatitis developed in 27 of 295 patients (9.2%) in the indomethacin group vs 52 of 307 (16.9%) in the placebo group (P=0.005) — a relative risk of about 0.54 and an absolute reduction of 7.7 percentage points. cards.watchOut: A high-risk population dominated by suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (82%) — the absolute benefit will be smaller in average-risk ERCP. The headline relative risk (~0.54) sits inside the library's 0.5–2.0 caution band's edge, so the absolute rates must travel with it.

shelves.title: Beta blockade to prevent decompensation in compensated cirrhosis (PREDESCI)
shelves.question: In compensated cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension, do beta blockers (propranolol in responders, carvedilol in non-responders) prevent first decompensation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage · Ascites/prevention & control · Carvedilol/administration & dosage · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Hepatic Encephalopathy/prevention & control · Hypertension, Portal/complications,drug therapy,mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY (Tier C — the PREDESCI composite includes death): In PREDESCI — the single randomised trial of this question — beta blockade titrated by hepatic venous pressure gradient response (propranolol for responders, carvedilol for non-responders) reduced the composite of decompensation or death vs placebo (16% vs 27%; hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.97), driven by less ascites (hazard ratio 0.44). The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of carvedilol (Villanueva 2022, Card 2) corroborates it across four randomised trials (352 patients): carvedilol lowered decompensation (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.506, 95% CI 0.289 to 0.887), ascites (0.491, 0.247 to 0.974) and death (0.417, 0.194 to 0.896) — relative measures, with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). Two independent randomised evidence bases pointing the same way carry the stamp to LIKELY; the strategy still requires HVPG measurement to replicate PREDESCI, and the meta-analysis tests carvedilol against mixed controls rather than the HVPG-guided strategy itself. Note the topic draft's shorthand: PREDESCI is a beta-blocker trial, not a carvedilol-only trial.

cards.people: 201 patients with compensated cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mm Hg) without high-risk varices, at eight hospitals in Spain; acute HVPG responders to intravenous propranolol were randomised to propranolol vs placebo and non-responders to carvedilol vs placebo (100 on beta blocker: 67 propranolol, 33 carvedilol; 101 on placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (decompensation — ascites, bleeding, or overt encephalopathy — or death) occurred in 16 of 100 patients (16%) on beta blockers vs 27 of 101 (27%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.97, p=0.041; hazard ratio is a relative measure, absolute rates 16% vs 27%). The difference was driven by a reduced incidence of ascites (hazard ratio 0.44, 0.20 to 0.97, p=0.0297). Overall adverse events were similar between groups; six patients (four on beta blockers) had severe adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, and the intervention is a response-guided strategy (propranolol or carvedilol by acute HVPG response), not one drug at one dose — it requires HVPG measurement to replicate. The confidence interval for the primary hazard ratio reaches 0.97.
cards.source: Villanueva C et al. β blockers to prevent decompensation of cirrhosis in patients with clinically significant portal hypertension (PREDESCI): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. Lancet. 2019;393(10181):1597-1608. PMID: 30910320. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01059396 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Villanueva 2022: carvedilol IPD meta-analysis — decompensation SHR 0.506, death SHR 0.417 across 4 RCTs (352 patients)
cards.summary: Villanueva (2022): in an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials, carvedilol lowered decompensation (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.506) and death (0.417) in compensated cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension.
cards.type: Competing-risk time-to-event individual-patient-data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, J Hepatol 2022
cards.people: 352 patients with compensated cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension, pooled from 4 randomised trials: 181 treated with carvedilol and 171 controls (79 endoscopic variceal ligation, 92 placebo); baseline characteristics were similar between groups and standardised differences were under 10% after weighting. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Decompensation was less frequent with carvedilol than control (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.506, 95% CI 0.289 to 0.887, p=0.017), mainly through less ascites (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.491, 0.247 to 0.974, p=0.042); death was also lower (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.417, 0.194 to 0.896, p=0.025). Heterogeneity was nil for each outcome (I² = 0.0%). Subdistribution hazard ratios are relative measures; the abstract reports no absolute event rates for the pooled outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The controls mix two different comparators — placebo and endoscopic variceal ligation — and the analysis tests carvedilol itself, not PREDESCI's HVPG-guided propranolol-or-carvedilol strategy; only 352 patients across four trials.
cards.source: Villanueva C et al. Carvedilol reduces the risk of decompensation and mortality in patients with compensated cirrhosis in a competing-risk meta-analysis. J Hepatol. 2022. cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PREDESCI (201 patients with compensated cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension) and the Villanueva 2022 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (4 randomised trials, 352 patients).
cards.result: PREDESCI randomised the strategy of lowering portal pressure with beta blockers in patients proven to have clinically significant portal hypertension, and the benefit concentrated in ascites prevention (hazard ratio 0.44) within a 16% vs 27% absolute composite difference. shelves.title: H. pylori eradication regimens: bismuth quadruple therapy and vonoprazan
shelves.question: Which eradication regimen clears H. pylori best in the clarithromycin-resistance era — bismuth quadruple therapy versus standard triple, and vonoprazan-based therapy (pHALCON-Hp)?
shelves.mesh: Amoxicillin/adverse effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Clarithromycin/adverse effects · Drug Therapy, Combination · Helicobacter Infections/diagnosis,drug therapy · Helicobacter pylori · Lansoprazole/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 randomised trials converge — bismuth quadruple therapy (single-capsule bismuth/metronidazole/tetracycline plus omeprazole, 10 days) eradicated H. pylori in 80% vs 55% with clarithromycin-based triple therapy (intention-to-treat), and vonoprazan-based regimens were superior to lansoprazole triple therapy overall (80.8% triple, 77.2% dual vs 68.5%) and decisively so in clarithromycin-resistant infection (65.8% and 69.6% vs 31.9%). Clarithromycin triple therapy is the era's weak comparator in both trials, which is precisely the shelf's point.

cards.headline: pHALCON-Hp 2022: vonoprazan triple and dual therapy beat lansoprazole triple overall (80.8% and 77.2% vs 68.5%) and in resistant strains (~66–70% vs 31.9%)
cards.summary: pHALCON-Hp 2022: vonoprazan triple and dual therapy beat lansoprazole triple overall (80.8% and 77.2% vs 68.5%) and in resistant strains.
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (open-label dual-therapy arm; double-blind triple-therapy comparison)
cards.people: 1,046 treatment-naïve adults with H. pylori infection in the United States and Europe, randomised 1:1:1 to vonoprazan dual therapy (vonoprazan 20 mg twice daily + amoxicillin 1 g three times daily), vonoprazan triple therapy, or lansoprazole triple therapy, for 14 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In patients without clarithromycin- and amoxicillin-resistant strains (primary outcome), eradication was 84.7% (vonoprazan triple), 78.5% (dual) and 78.8% (lansoprazole triple) — both vonoprazan regimens noninferior. In clarithromycin-resistant infections, eradication was 65.8% (triple) and 69.6% (dual) vs 31.9% (lansoprazole triple) — both superior (differences 33.9 and 37.7 percentage points; P<0.001). In all patients, vonoprazan triple and dual were superior to lansoprazole triple (80.8% and 77.2% vs 68.5%; differences 12.3 points, P<0.001, and 8.7 points, P=0.013). Treatment-emergent adverse event frequency was similar between vonoprazan and lansoprazole regimens.
cards.watchOut: The dual-therapy arm was open-label, and even the best regimen eradicated only ~70% of clarithromycin-resistant infections — superiority over a failing comparator is not the same as a solved problem.
cards.source: Chey WD et al. Vonoprazan Triple and Dual Therapy for Helicobacter pylori Infection in the United States and Europe: Randomized Clinical Trial. Gastroenterology. 2022;163(3):608-619. PMID: 35679950. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04167670 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Malfertheiner 2011: bismuth quadruple therapy eradicated 80% vs 55% with standard triple therapy (intention-to-treat)
cards.summary: Malfertheiner 2011: bismuth quadruple therapy eradicated 80% vs 55% with standard triple therapy (intention-to-treat).
cards.people: Adults with H. pylori infection at 39 sites in Europe, randomised to 10 days of omeprazole plus a single three-in-one capsule of bismuth subcitrate potassium, metronidazole and tetracycline, or 7 days of omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin; 440 patients in the intention-to-treat population (218 quadruple, 222 standard) and 339 per-protocol (101 excluded from per-protocol, 12 lost to follow-up). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Non-inferiority was established in the per-protocol population (lower confidence bound above the −10% margin; 95% CI for the difference 15.1 to 32.3; p<0.0001). In the intention-to-treat population, eradication was 80% (174 of 218) with quadruple therapy vs 55% (123 of 222) with standard therapy (p<0.0001). Safety profiles were similar; the main adverse events were gastrointestinal and CNS disorders.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparator ran only 7 days of triple therapy — shorter than the 14-day courses now standard — which may widen the gap; the trial predates vonoprazan entirely.
cards.source: Malfertheiner P et al. Helicobacter pylori eradication with a capsule containing bismuth subcitrate potassium, metronidazole, and tetracycline given with omeprazole versus clarithromycin-based triple therapy: a randomised, open-label, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2011;377(9769):905-913. PMID: 21345487. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00669955 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: pHALCON-Hp (1,046 treatment-naïve adults, US/Europe) and Malfertheiner 2011 (440 patients, Europe).

shelves.title: Microscopic colitis: budesonide induction
shelves.question: Does budesonide induce remission in collagenous and lymphocytic colitis versus placebo — and in the incomplete microscopic colitis subtype?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Budesonide/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Colitis, Lymphocytic/drug therapy,pathology · Drug Administration Schedule · Induction Chemotherapy · Mesalamine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — budesonide induction in lymphocytic colitis: one small double-blind trial (57 patients) found clinical remission at week 8 in 79% on budesonide 9 mg vs 42% on placebo, with histological remission 68% vs 21%. MAYBE (weak evidence) — incomplete microscopic colitis: the one trial stopped early for poor recruitment (44 patients) and missed its primary endpoint (71.4% vs 43.5% remission, p=0.058), though secondary endpoints favoured budesonide. The topic draft promised maintenance data; both carded trials are 8-week induction studies, so this shelf makes no maintenance claim.

cards.headline: Miehlke 2019: budesonide induced clinical remission in lymphocytic colitis in 79% vs 42% on placebo at 8 weeks
cards.summary: Miehlke 2019: budesonide induced clinical remission in lymphocytic colitis in 79% vs 42% on placebo at 8 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy induction trial (with a mesalazine arm)
cards.people: 57 patients with active lymphocytic colitis (19 per group: budesonide 9 mg once daily, mesalazine 3 g once daily, or placebo, for 8 weeks); 72% were female and mean age was 59 years.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 8 (≤21 stools including ≤6 watery stools in the prior 7 days) was significantly higher with budesonide than placebo (79% vs 42%, intention-to-treat; P=0.01). Mesalazine (63%) was not significantly better than placebo (P=0.09). Histological remission at week 8: budesonide 68% vs mesalazine 26% (P=0.02) and vs placebo 21% (P=0.008). Adverse events occurred in 47.4% of the budesonide group, 68.4% of the mesalazine group and 42.1% of the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients per arm: the 79% vs 42% difference rests on a handful of remissions either way, and 8 weeks of induction says nothing about relapse or maintenance.
cards.source: Miehlke S et al. Efficacy and Safety of Budesonide, vs Mesalazine or Placebo, as Induction Therapy for Lymphocytic Colitis. Gastroenterology. 2018;155(6):1795-1804.e3. PMID: 30195447. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01209208 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Münch 2021: budesonide in incomplete microscopic colitis missed its primary endpoint in an under-recruited trial (71.4% vs 43.5%, p=0.058)
cards.summary: Münch 2021: budesonide in incomplete microscopic colitis missed its primary endpoint in an under-recruited trial (71.4% vs 43.5%, p=0.058).
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre, double-blind induction trial, discontinued prematurely
cards.people: 44 patients with active incomplete microscopic colitis (21 budesonide 9 mg once daily, 23 placebo, for 8 weeks) in the intention-to-treat analysis; recruitment was insufficient and the trial was stopped early. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 8 (mean <3 stools/day and <1 watery stool/day in the prior 7 days) was obtained by 71.4% on budesonide vs 43.5% on placebo (p=0.0582) — the primary endpoint was not met, which the authors attribute to the low sample size (type 2 error). All clinical secondary endpoints favoured budesonide: budesonide significantly decreased soft or watery stools (16.3 vs 7.7 as reported, p=0.0186) and improved all four dimensions of health-related quality of life. Adverse events with suspected relation to study drug: one patient on budesonide, two on placebo; no serious or severe adverse events in the double-blind phase.
cards.watchOut: A stopped-early trial that missed its primary endpoint is hypothesis-grade evidence — this is why the incomplete-subtype half of the shelf prints as MAYBE (weak evidence), not as a smaller version of the lymphocytic result.
cards.source: Münch A et al. Budesonide as induction therapy for incomplete microscopic colitis: A randomised, placebo-controlled multicentre trial. United European Gastroenterol J. 2021;9(7):837-847. PMID: 34414678. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — no reason is stated in the record.

cards.summary: One small positive trial, one small near-miss — split POSSIBLE / MAYBE (weak evidence), induction only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Miehlke 2019 (57 patients, lymphocytic colitis) and Münch 2021 (44 patients, incomplete microscopic colitis).
cards.result: Budesonide 9 mg daily for 8 weeks beat placebo on remission in lymphocytic colitis (79% vs 42%, P=0.01) and pointed the same way without reaching significance in the incomplete subtype (71.4% vs 43.5%, p=0.058). shelves.title: Biosimilar switching: NOR-SWITCH and PLANETRA
shelves.question: Is switching from originator infliximab to its biosimilar (CT-P13) non-inferior to staying on originator — across immune-mediated diseases including IBD (NOR-SWITCH) and in rheumatoid arthritis (PLANETRA)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/economics,therapeutic use · Biosimilar Pharmaceuticals/economics · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Inflammatory Bowel Diseases/drug therapy · Infliximab/therapeutic use · Norway · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Switching from originator infliximab to biosimilar CT-P13 was non-inferior to continued originator treatment on disease worsening over 52 weeks in NOR-SWITCH (30% vs 26%; adjusted difference −4.4%, within the prespecified 15% margin), and CT-P13 was equivalent to originator on ACR20 response at week 30 in PLANETRA's rheumatoid arthritis population (60.9% vs 58.6%, confidence interval within ±15%), with near-identical immunogenicity (antidrug antibodies 48.4% vs 48.2%). NOR-SWITCH was not powered for non-inferiority within any single disease, including IBD — stated on its card.

cards.headline: NOR-SWITCH 2017: switching to CT-P13 was non-inferior to staying on originator infliximab (disease worsening 30% vs 26%)
cards.summary: NOR-SWITCH 2017: switching to CT-P13 was non-inferior to staying on originator infliximab (disease worsening 30% vs 26%).
cards.people: 482 adults on stable hospital-based originator infliximab for at least 6 months at 40 Norwegian centres, randomised to continued originator (241) or switch to CT-P13 (241); 408 in the per-protocol set. Diagnoses in the full analysis set: Crohn's disease 155 (32%), ulcerative colitis 93 (19%), spondyloarthritis 91 (19%), rheumatoid arthritis 77 (16%), psoriatic arthritis 30 (6%), chronic plaque psoriasis 35 (7%). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Disease worsening during 52 weeks occurred in 53 patients (26%) on originator vs 61 (30%) on CT-P13 in the per-protocol set (adjusted treatment difference −4.4%, 95% CI −12.7 to 3.9), within the prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin (394 per-protocol patients were needed, assuming 30% worsening in each group). Serious adverse events: 24 (10%) originator vs 21 (9%) CT-P13; overall adverse events 168 (70%) vs 164 (68%); discontinuations for adverse events 9 (4%) vs 8 (3%).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority was shown for the pooled population only — the trial was explicitly not powered to show non-inferiority in individual diseases, so the IBD subgroups (Crohn's 32%, ulcerative colitis 19%) ride on the pooled result. The 15% margin is wide.
cards.source: Jørgensen KK et al. Switching from originator infliximab to biosimilar CT-P13 compared with maintained treatment with originator infliximab (NOR-SWITCH): a 52-week, randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2017;389(10086):2304-2316. PMID: 28502609. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02148640 (from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: PLANETRA 2013: CT-P13 equivalent to originator infliximab on ACR20 in rheumatoid arthritis (60.9% vs 58.6%)
cards.summary: PLANETRA 2013: CT-P13 equivalent to originator infliximab on ACR20 in rheumatoid arthritis (60.9% vs 58.6%).
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, multicentre, multinational, parallel-group equivalence trial
cards.people: 606 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, randomised to CT-P13 3 mg/kg (302) or innovator infliximab (304), both with methotrexate and folic acid. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 30 was 60.9% with CT-P13 vs 58.6% with innovator infliximab (95% CI for the treatment difference −6% to 10%, intention-to-treat), within the ±15% equivalence margin. Good or moderate EULAR responses (CRP) were 85.8% vs 87.1%. Drug-related adverse events were 35.2% vs 35.9%, and antidrug antibodies were detected in 48.4% vs 48.2%.
cards.watchOut: A treatment-initiation equivalence trial in rheumatoid arthritis, not a switching trial, and a single-biosimilar result: it supports CT-P13's equivalence to its originator, not biosimilar switching as a universal class claim.
cards.source: Yoo DH et al. shelves.title: Colonoscopy versus FIT as the screening invitation
shelves.question: Is inviting a population to once-only colonoscopy non-inferior to biennial FIT on colorectal-cancer mortality at 10 years (COLONPREV) — and what did the Swedish and US VA comparisons show (SCREESCO; CONFIRM)?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/diagnosis · Colonoscopy/adverse effects · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Immunohistochemistry · Occult Blood · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: colorectal cancer mortality is the primary outcome). COLONPREV's 10-year report (53,051 people in the intention-to-screen population) found biennial FIT non-inferior to one-time colonoscopy for colorectal cancer mortality: 0.24% (60 deaths) vs 0.22% (55 deaths); risk difference -0.02 percentage points (95% CI -0.10 to 0.06), against a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.16 percentage points — with higher participation for FIT (39.9% vs 31.8%). A single trial's non-inferiority finding on a mortality endpoint caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. SCREESCO's diagnostic-phase report (278,280 people) compares each strategy with usual care, not with each other, and shows early-detection gains (more stage I-II cancers) with slightly higher first-year gastrointestinal and cardiovascular event rates. The US CONFIRM trial's outcome report could not be pinned at build (see the slate summary); it is not carded.

cards.headline: Quintero 2012 (COLONPREV baseline): FIT invitation drew more participants (34.2% vs 24.6%); cancers found were equal, adenomas favoured colonoscopy
cards.summary: Quintero 2012 (COLONPREV baseline): FIT invitation drew more participants (34.2% vs 24.6%); cancers found were equal, adenomas favoured colonoscopy.
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial (screening invitation; interim baseline report of COLONPREV)
cards.people: 53,302 asymptomatic adults 50 to 69 years of age randomised in Spain to one-time colonoscopy (26,703 subjects) or FIT every 2 years (26,599 subjects); outcomes analysed in intention-to-screen and as-screened populations; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The rate of participation was higher in the FIT group than in the colonoscopy group (34.2% vs 24.6%, P<0.001). Colorectal cancer was found in 30 subjects (0.1%) in the colonoscopy group and 33 subjects (0.1%) in the FIT group (odds ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.61 to 1.64; P=0.99). Advanced adenomas were detected in 514 subjects (1.9%) in the colonoscopy group and 231 subjects (0.9%) in the FIT group (odds ratio 2.30; 95% CI 1.97 to 2.69; P<0.001), and nonadvanced adenomas in 1,109 subjects (4.2%) and 119 subjects (0.4%) respectively (odds ratio 9.80; 8.10 to 11.85; P<0.001) — relative measures from the baseline screening round.
cards.watchOut: This is the 2012 baseline-round report: participation and detection only. The mortality answer from the same trial is the 2025 card below — do not quote baseline adenoma yields as outcome evidence.

cards.headline: Castells 2025 (COLONPREV at 10 years): FIT invitation was non-inferior to colonoscopy invitation for colorectal cancer mortality (0.24% vs 0.22%)
cards.summary: Castells 2025 (COLONPREV at 10 years, pinned at build): FIT invitation was non-inferior to colonoscopy invitation for colorectal cancer mortality ( 0.24% vs 0.22% ). (Tier C — CRC mortality is the primary outcome; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Pragmatic, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial (screening invitation, intention-to-screen analysis)
cards.people: 57,404 presumptively healthy individuals aged 50 to 69 years at 15 tertiary hospitals across eight regions of Spain, randomly assigned to invitation to one-time colonoscopy (28,708) or biennial faecal immunochemical test (28,696); the intention-to-screen population consisted of 26,332 individuals in the colonoscopy group and 26,719 in the FIT group; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Participation in any form of screening was 31.8% in the colonoscopy group and 39.9% in the FIT group (risk ratio 0.79 [95% CI 0.77 to 0.82] — a relative measure). cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority of INVITATIONS at roughly 32-40% participation: most invitees were not screened by the assigned method, so the trial compares programmes as offered, not tests as performed; absolute mortality was low (about 1 death per 450 invitees) in both arms.

cards.headline: Westerberg 2026 (SCREESCO, diagnostic phase): versus usual care, both colonoscopy and FIT arms showed more early-stage cancers and slightly more first-year adverse events
cards.summary: Westerberg 2026 (SCREESCO, diagnostic phase): vs usual care, both colonoscopy and FIT arms showed more early-stage cancers and slightly more first diagnoses.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (screening invitation vs usual care; diagnostic-phase report)
cards.people: 278,280 individuals aged 60 years in Sweden randomised to once-only colonoscopy, 2 rounds of two-stool FIT with a low cutoff (10 μg per g feces), or usual care (control); in the analysis, 31,113 individuals were in the primary colonoscopy arm, 60,267 in the FIT arm, and there were 186,671 primary colonoscopy controls, of whom 120,521 were also controls for the FIT comparison; median follow-up 4.8 years; the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence rate of colorectal cancer was 107.9 in the colonoscopy arm and 99.9 in controls per 100,000 person-years (incidence rate ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.91-1.28) and 96.0 in the FIT arm and 103.9 in controls (0.92, 0.81-1.05) — relative measures. Rates of stage I-II colorectal cancer were higher in the colonoscopy arm (IRR 1.38, 1.09-1.74) and in the FIT arm (1.19, 0.99-1.43) versus controls. Rates of cardiovascular and gastrointestinal events were slightly higher in the intervention arms during the first year and were subsequently more similar to controls.
cards.watchOut: This report covers the diagnostic phase only (median follow-up 4.8 years) and compares each strategy with no screening — it does not compare colonoscopy with FIT, and incidence is initially higher with screening because cancers are found earlier; mortality results are not in this report.

cards.summary: As invitations, FIT is non-inferior to colonoscopy for 10-year colorectal-cancer mortality — POSSIBLE, Tier C proposed. (The CONFIRM outcome report could not be pinned and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COLONPREV baseline and 10-year reports (one trial, counted once) and SCREESCO diagnostic phase (278,280 individuals).
cards.result: COLONPREV answers the head-to-head question at programme level: colorectal cancer mortality 0.24% (FIT invitation) vs 0.22% (colonoscopy invitation), non-inferior within a 0.16-percentage-point margin, with better participation for FIT (39.9% vs 31.8%). shelves.title: Laparoscopic versus open resection for colon cancer: COLOR, COST, and CLASICC
shelves.question: Is laparoscopic colectomy for colon cancer oncologically equivalent to open surgery — the COLOR long-term results and the COST/CLASICC programmes that settled the question?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/mortality,surgery · Colectomy/methods · Colonic Neoplasms/mortality,surgery · Disease-Free Survival · Laparoscopy · Laparotomy · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (oncological equivalence): Three randomised programmes converge. COST: 3-year recurrence 16% laparoscopically assisted versus 18% open (hazard ratio 0.86, relative, non-significant), 3-year survival 86% versus 85%. COLOR: 3-year disease-free survival 74.2% versus 76.2% and overall survival 81.8% versus 84.2% — COLOR could not formally rule out its 7% non-inferiority boundary (upper confidence limit 7.2%), and the card says so; the difference was small. CLASICC's short-term report showed similar margins, Dukes C2 proportions and in-hospital mortality (4% vs 5%). Equivalence with faster recovery (COST: hospital stay 5 vs 6 days) is the claim — no survival-benefit claim, so not Tier C.

cards.headline: COST Study Group 2004: recurrence at 3 years was 16% after laparoscopically assisted colectomy vs 18% after open — hazard ratio 0.86; survival 86% vs 85%; stay 5 vs 6 days
cards.summary: COST (2004): recurrence at 3 years was 16% after laparoscopic vs 18% after open colectomy (hazard ratio 0.86); survival 86% vs 85%.
cards.people: 872 patients with adenocarcinoma of the colon at 48 institutions, randomised to open or laparoscopically assisted colectomy by credentialed surgeons; median follow-up 4.4 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 3 years, recurrence rates were 16% in the laparoscopically assisted group and 18% in the open group (P=0.32; hazard ratio for recurrence 0.86; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.17) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates. Wound recurrences were under 1% in both groups. Overall survival at 3 years was 86% versus 85% (P=0.51; hazard ratio for death 0.91; 0.68 to 1.21). Recovery was faster laparoscopically: median hospital stay 5 versus 6 days (P<0.001), parenteral narcotics 3 versus 4 days, oral analgesics 1 versus 2 days. Intraoperative complications, 30-day mortality, complications, readmission and reoperation were very similar.
cards.watchOut: Pre-registration-era reporting in this record (no registry ID in its databank fields), and 'laparoscopically assisted' is not identical to the totally laparoscopic technique of later practice.
cards.source: Clinical Outcomes of Surgical Therapy Study Group. A comparison of laparoscopically assisted and open colectomy for colon cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2004;350(20):2050-9. PMID: 15141043. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (enrolment predates routine registration).

cards.headline: COLOR Study Group 2009: 3-year disease-free survival 74.2% (laparoscopic) vs 76.2% (open) and survival 81.8% vs 84.2% — small differences, boundary not formally ruled out
cards.summary: COLOR (2009): 3-year disease-free survival 74.2% (laparoscopic) vs 76.2% (open) ; survival 81.8% vs 84.2%.
cards.people: 1076 patients eligible for analysis (534 laparoscopic, 542 open) of 1248 randomised, with solitary right or left colon cancer and BMI up to 30, at 29 European hospitals; median follow-up 53 months.
cards.result: Combined 3-year disease-free survival was 74.2% (95% CI 70.4 to 78.0) in the laparoscopic group versus 76.2% (72.6 to 79.8) in the open group (difference 2.0%; 95% CI -3.2 to 7.2; hazard ratio for disease-free survival, open versus laparoscopic, 0.92; 0.74 to 1.15). Combined 3-year overall survival was 81.8% versus 84.2% (difference 2.4%; -2.1 to 7.0; hazard ratio 0.95; 0.74 to 1.22) — relative measures beside their absolute rates. Positive margins, lymph-node yield, morbidity and mortality were similar. The authors state the trial could not rule out a difference in favour of open surgery because the upper confidence limit (7.2%) just exceeded the predetermined 7% non-inferiority boundary, while judging the difference small and clinically acceptable.
cards.watchOut: This is the honest weak point of the shelf and it is printed on the card: COLOR alone did not formally meet its non-inferiority boundary. The shelf's LIKELY rests on three programmes converging, not on COLOR alone.

cards.headline: Guillou 2005 (CLASICC, short-term): margins, Dukes C2 proportions and in-hospital mortality (4% vs 5%) similar; 29% of laparoscopic cases converted
cards.summary: CLASICC (2005): margins, Dukes C2 proportions and in-hospital mortality (4% vs 5%) similar; 29% of laparoscopic cases converted .
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (short-term endpoints report)
cards.people: 794 patients with colorectal cancer at 27 UK centres, allocated to laparoscopic-assisted (526) or open (268) surgery; 484 actually received laparoscopic-assisted and 253 open treatment, with 143 (29%) conversions from laparoscopic to open.
cards.result: The proportion of Dukes C2 tumours did not differ (7% open vs 6% laparoscopic; difference -0.3%; 95% CI -3.9 to 3.4; p=0.89), nor did in-hospital mortality (5% vs 4%; difference -0.9%; -3.9 to 2.2; p=0.57). Apart from laparoscopic anterior resection for rectal cancer, positive resection-margin rates were similar between groups. Patients whose operation converted had raised complication rates.
cards.watchOut: Short-term endpoints only in this report, a mixed colon-and-rectum population, and the authors explicitly withheld endorsement of laparoscopic anterior resection for rectal cancer at this stage — the colon conclusion is the one this shelf draws.

cards.headline: Synthesis: laparoscopic colectomy for colon cancer is oncologically equivalent in the programmes that tested it — LIKELY
cards.summary: Laparoscopic colectomy for colon cancer is oncologically equivalent in the programmes that tested it — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COST (872 patients), COLOR (1076 analysed) and CLASICC (794 patients, short-term report) — three independent randomised programmes.
cards.result: Recurrence and survival track each other closely in COST (16% vs 18%; 86% vs 85% at 3 years) and COLOR (disease-free survival 74.2% vs 76.2%), margins and mortality are similar in CLASICC, and recovery is faster laparoscopically (COST). Rectal resection technique is a different question (Shelf #868) and neoadjuvant rectal strategy is Shelf #866; neither is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Era effect: these trials ran from 1996 to 2003 with conversion rates and techniques of their time — they settle oncological equivalence, not modern enhanced-recovery outcomes (Shelf #869).

shelves.title: Robotic versus laparoscopic rectal cancer resection (ROLARR and REAL)
shelves.question: Does robotic assistance lower conversion to open surgery or improve outcomes in rectal-cancer resection versus conventional laparoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Conversion to Open Surgery/statistics & numerical data · Digestive System Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,economics,methods · Direct Service Costs/statistics & numerical data · Laparoscopy/adverse effects · Laparotomy · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Rectal Neoplasms/mortality,surgery
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — no conversion advantage (ROLARR) · POSSIBLE — lower locoregional recurrence in middle/low rectal cancer (REAL). ROLARR (471 patients, international): conversion to open laparotomy 8.1% robotic versus 12.2% laparoscopic (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, relative, non-significant, P=.16), with no significant difference in margins, complications or dysfunction. REAL (1171 analysed, China, middle/low tumours only): 3-year locoregional recurrence 1.6% versus 4.0% (hazard ratio 0.45, relative) and disease-free survival 87.2% versus 83.4% (hazard ratio 0.74), with no significant difference in overall survival (94.7% vs 93.0%). Each half rests on a single trial, so each caps at POSSIBLE; overall survival did not differ in REAL, so no survival claim is made and the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Jayne 2017 (ROLARR): robotic assistance did not significantly reduce conversion — 8.1% vs 12.2% (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, P=.16)
cards.summary: ROLARR (2017): robotic assistance did not significantly reduce conversion — 8.1% vs 12.2% (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, P=.16).
cards.people: 471 patients with rectal adenocarcinoma suitable for curative resection at 29 sites in 10 countries (mean age 64.9 [SD 11.0] years; 320 [67.9%] men), randomised to robotic-assisted (237) or conventional laparoscopic (234) resection; 466 (98.9%) completed the study.
cards.result: Conversion to open laparotomy occurred in 19 of 236 patients (8.1%) in the robotic group and 28 of 230 (12.2%) in the conventional group (unadjusted risk difference 4.1%; 95% CI -1.4% to 9.6%; adjusted odds ratio 0.61; 0.31 to 1.21; P=.16) — a relative measure, non-significant, beside its absolute rates. Circumferential margin positivity was 5.1% versus 6.3% (adjusted odds ratio 0.78; P=.56). None of the other reported prespecified secondary endpoints — intraoperative and postoperative complications, plane of surgery, 30-day mortality, bladder or sexual dysfunction — differed significantly.
cards.watchOut: Surgeons had varying robotic experience, which the authors note; a null on conversion from a single trial caps at POSSIBLE under the library's single-trial rule.
cards.source: Jayne D et al. shelves.title: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathways in colorectal surgery
shelves.question: Do ERAS pathways — the bundled perioperative package of early feeding, opioid-sparing analgesia, and early mobilisation — shorten hospital stay and reduce complications after colorectal resection versus traditional care?
shelves.mesh: Colonic Diseases/surgery · Elective Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,mortality · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Perioperative Care/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (via synthesis — the certainty ceiling is stated on the shelf face): The randomised base is many small trials, not two large ones. Varadhan 2010 pooled six RCTs (452 patients, 4-12 ERAS elements per trial): hospital stay was 2.55 days shorter (weighted mean difference -2.55; 95% CI -3.24 to -1.85) and complications fewer (relative risk 0.53; 0.44 to 0.64 — a relative measure), with no significant difference in readmission or mortality. LAFA, a 400-patient factorial trial, found laparoscopy — not fast-track care — was the only independent factor reducing stay and morbidity in its regression, with the shortest stay (median total 5 days) in the laparoscopy-plus-fast-track group. That tension is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Perioperative fluid strategy alone is drafted Shelf #657 and perioperative drugs are Shelves #352/#353 — different interventions, not carded here.

There was no statistically significant difference in readmission or mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials in OPEN surgery from before 2010, with bundles ranging from 4 to 12 elements — 'ERAS' is not one intervention across these trials, which caps the shelf's certainty however tidy the pooled numbers look.

shelves.title: Microbiome therapy for recurrent C. difficile: donor faeces, then a defined product (SER-109)
shelves.question: Does restoring the gut microbiome stop recurrent C. difficile infection — by donor-faeces infusion, and by the defined oral spore product SER-109?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Clostridioides difficile · Combined Modality Therapy · Diarrhea/drug therapy,microbiology,therapy · Duodenum · Feces/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials, a decade and a technology apart, point the same way. Van Nood 2013 (43 randomised patients analysed): donor-faeces infusion resolved recurrent C. difficile diarrhoea in 81% after one infusion (15 of 16 ultimately, 94%, after a second donor infusion) vs 31% on vancomycin alone and 23% on vancomycin with lavage — but the trial was small, open-label and stopped early. ECOSPOR III 2022 (182 patients, double-blind): the defined spore product SER-109 cut recurrence by 8 weeks to 12% vs 40% on placebo (relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.58 — beyond the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid). Adverse events were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal in both programmes and similar to controls. Two trials, but one is small/open/stopped-early and the products differ, so the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. The drug contest for C. difficile (fidaxomicin, bezlotoxumab, vancomycin regimens) lives on Shelf #170 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Van Nood 2013: donor-faeces infusion resolved recurrent C. difficile in 81% after one infusion vs 31% on vancomycin alone — a small trial stopped early
cards.summary: Van Nood 2013: donor-faeces infusion resolved recurrent C. difficile in 81% after one infusion vs 31% on vancomycin alone.
cards.type: Open-label randomised controlled trial, stopped after an interim analysis
cards.people: Patients with recurrent C. difficile infection assigned to vancomycin followed by bowel lavage and duodenal infusion of donor faeces (16 analysed), standard vancomycin for 14 days (13), or vancomycin with bowel lavage (13). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Resolution of C. difficile-associated diarrhoea without relapse at 10 weeks occurred in 13 of 16 patients (81%) after a first donor-faeces infusion; the 3 remaining patients received a second infusion from a different donor, with resolution in 2 (15 of 16 overall). Resolution occurred in 4 of 13 (31%) on vancomycin alone and 3 of 13 (23%) on vancomycin with lavage (P<0.001 for both comparisons with infusion). Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups except mild diarrhoea and abdominal cramping on the infusion day. After infusion, faecal bacterial diversity rose toward healthy-donor profiles.
cards.watchOut: Tiny (42 analysed), unblinded, stopped early — the profile that exaggerates effects; its historical role is proof of concept for microbiome restoration, and the effect size should be read through ECOSPOR III's blinded estimate, not this one.
cards.source: Van Nood E et al. Duodenal infusion of donor feces for recurrent Clostridium difficile. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(5):407-15. PMID: 23323867. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states Netherlands Trial Register number NTR1177.

cards.headline: ECOSPOR III 2022: SER-109 cut C. difficile recurrence to 12% vs 40% on placebo (relative risk 0.32)
cards.summary: ECOSPOR III 2022: SER-109 cut recurrence to 12% vs 40% on placebo (relative risk 0.32).
cards.people: 182 patients who had had three or more episodes of C. difficile infection (including the qualifying episode), enrolled after standard-of-care antibiotic treatment, assigned to SER-109 (purified Firmicutes spores, four capsules daily for 3 days) or placebo; diagnosis by toxin testing at entry. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Recurrence of C. difficile infection by 8 weeks occurred in 12% of the SER-109 group and 40% of the placebo group (relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.58; P<0.001) — a relative measure with its absolute rates printed, and beyond the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid. The benefit held by age stratum (relative risk 0.24 under 65 years; 0.36 at 65 or older) and by antibiotic received (0.41 after vancomycin; 0.09 after fidaxomicin). Most adverse events were mild to moderate and gastrointestinal, in similar numbers in both groups. SER-109 dose species were detectable by week 1, with bile-acid profiles known to inhibit spore germination.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 3 trial of one defined product, with an 8-week horizon and recurrence ascertained after a qualifying third-or-later episode: it establishes SER-109 for multiply recurrent infection, not microbiome therapy for a first recurrence, where the newer FMT literature (fenced in the synthesis) is still moving.

cards.headline: Synthesis: microbiome restoration works for multiply recurrent C. difficile; the defined product carries the reliable estimate — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Microbiome restoration works for multiply recurrent C. difficile; the defined product carries the reliable estimate — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: van Nood 2013 (42 analysed patients, donor faeces) and ECOSPOR III (182 patients, SER-109).
cards.result: Direction and mechanism agree across a decade: restoring the microbiome after antibiotics prevents the next recurrence (81% resolution vs 31% with vancomycin alone in the small open trial; 12% vs 40% recurrence, relative risk 0.32, in the blinded phase 3). The stamp is POSSIBLE because the blinded evidence is one trial of one product in multiply recurrent disease. Newer microbiome trials found by the currency sweep (faecal filtrate vs stool, FMT for primary infection, other live products) test adjacent questions and are fenced here, not carded; the antibiotic/bezlotoxumab contest stays on Shelf #170.

shelves.title: Hepatitis E vaccine (HEV 239): efficacy and its long tail
shelves.question: Does the recombinant hepatitis E vaccine prevent hepatitis E in healthy adults in an endemic setting — in the phase 3 trial, and in long-term follow-up?
shelves.mesh: China · Hepatitis E/immunology,prevention & control · Hepatitis E virus/drug effects,immunology · Immunoglobulin G/blood · Vaccines, Synthetic/administration & dosage,immunology · Viral Hepatitis Vaccines/administration & dosage,immunology · Genotype
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One very large phase 3 trial in Jiangsu, China (112,604 randomised adults aged 16–65): after three doses, vaccine efficacy against hepatitis E in the 12 months from a month after the third dose was 100.0% (95% CI 72.1 to 100.0) — 15 cases in the placebo group, none in the vaccine group. In the extended, still double-blind follow-up of the same trial, 4.5-year efficacy was 86.8% (95% CI 71 to 94), with 7 cases on vaccine (0.3 per 10,000 person-years) vs 53 on the hepatitis-B-vaccine control (2.1 per 10,000 person-years), and 87% of baseline-seronegative three-dose recipients maintaining antibody at 4.5 years. Adverse events were few, mild and similar between groups. One trial programme (however large) in one endemic province, with hepatitis B vaccine as the control, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; durability beyond 4.5 years rests on immunogenicity, not case counts. Hepatitis B vaccine material (Shelf #450) is a different virus and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Zhu 2010 (phase 3): three doses of HEV 239 were 100.0% efficacious against hepatitis E in the year after vaccination — 15 cases on control, none on vaccine
cards.summary: Zhu 2010: three doses of HEV 239 were 100.0% efficacious against hepatitis E in the year after vaccination (15 control cases, none on vaccine).
cards.type: Large-scale, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (hepatitis B vaccine as control)
cards.people: Healthy adults aged 16–65 years in Jiangsu Province, China, randomised 1:1 to three doses of HEV 239 (56,302) or hepatitis B vaccine control (56,302) at 0, 1 and 6 months; 48,693 (86%) and 48,663 (86%) received all three doses and formed the primary per-protocol efficacy set; 47% of those tested were HEV-IgG-seropositive at baseline.
cards.result: During the 12 months from 31 days after the third dose, 15 per-protocol participants in the control group developed hepatitis E and none in the vaccine group: vaccine efficacy 100.0% (95% CI 72.1 to 100.0) — a relative measure built on 15 cases, with the absolute rates printed here. Adverse effects attributable to the vaccine were few and mild, and no vaccine-related serious adverse event was noted.
cards.watchOut: A perfect point estimate on 15 endpoint cases, in one province, against an active (hepatitis B vaccine) control rather than saline placebo: the precision comes from the enormous sample, the fragility from the small case count — which is what the long-term follow-up (card below) was for.
cards.source: Zhu FC et al. Efficacy and safety of a recombinant hepatitis E vaccine in healthy adults: a large-scale, randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9744):895-902. PMID: 20728932. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01014845, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Zhang 2015 (long-term follow-up): efficacy was 86.8% over 4.5 years — 7 cases on vaccine vs 53 on control
cards.summary: Zhang 2015: efficacy was 86.8% over 4.5 years (7 vs 53 cases) — the full long-term report, re-pinned at the gate after the printed anchor proved to be a letter.
cards.type: Extended double-blind follow-up of the same phase 3 randomised trial
cards.people: The same Jiangsu cohort (56,302 per group as randomised), with treatment assignments remaining double-blinded and efficacy, immunogenicity and safety follow-up continued for up to 4.5 years.
cards.result: Over the 4.5-year study period, 60 cases of hepatitis E were identified: 7 in the vaccine group (0.3 cases per 10,000 person-years) and 53 in the control group (2.1 per 10,000 person-years), a vaccine efficacy of 86.8% (95% CI 71 to 94) in the modified intention-to-treat analysis — a relative measure with its absolute rates printed. Among baseline-seronegative participants assessed for immunogenicity, 87% of three-dose vaccine recipients maintained anti-HEV antibodies for at least 4.5 years (antibodies developed in 9% of controls, reflecting natural exposure). Adverse-event rates were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The same trial at a longer horizon — durability evidence, not an independent confirmation; and 4.5 years is the case-based horizon on this shelf, whatever longer immunogenicity follow-ups exist elsewhere.

cards.summary: Near-complete early protection settling to 86.8% at 4.5 years, from a single giant trial — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 3 trial (112,604 randomised) and its 4.5-year extended follow-up, labelled as one programme.

shelves.title: Gluten restriction in self-reported non-coeliac gluten sensitivity (Biesiekierski)
shelves.question: In patients with IBS-type symptoms who believe gluten harms them, does gluten itself reproduce symptoms once fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) are controlled (Biesiekierski's double-blind crossover trial) — and how does that sit beside the same group's earlier positive challenge trial?
shelves.mesh: Cohort Studies · Cross-Over Studies · Diet, Gluten-Free · Disaccharides · Glutens/adverse effects · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/chemically induced,diet therapy · Monosaccharides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (gluten-specific effects not reproduced once FODMAPs are controlled): The 2011 trial (34 patients, symptoms controlled on a gluten-free diet, no FODMAP control) found gluten worsened symptoms — 13 of 19 (68%) on gluten reported inadequately controlled symptoms versus 6 of 15 (40%) on placebo. The same group's 2013 crossover trial (37 subjects) first put everyone on a reduced-FODMAP diet — symptoms improved consistently — and then challenged with high-gluten (16 g/day), low-gluten or whey-control diets: symptoms worsened to a similar degree on gluten and on whey, gluten-specific effects appeared in only 8% of participants, no biomarker changed, and a 3-day rechallenge in 22 participants reproduced no gluten-specific effect. One small positive trial superseded in design by one small rigorous negative trial from the same investigators: POSSIBLE that the culprit in most self-reported gluten sensitivity is not gluten itself. The low-FODMAP diet shelf itself is already built elsewhere; this shelf asks only the gluten-specific question and does not re-card it.

cards.headline: Biesiekierski 2013: after FODMAP reduction, gluten challenge was indistinguishable from whey — gluten-specific effects in only 8% of participants
cards.summary: Biesiekierski 2013: after FODMAP reduction, gluten challenge was indistinguishable from whey — gluten-specific effects in only 8% of participants.
cards.people: 37 subjects (aged 24–61 years, 6 men) with non-coeliac gluten sensitivity and irritable bowel syndrome (Rome III criteria), without coeliac disease, placed on a 2-week reduced-FODMAP diet, then randomised to high-gluten (16 g gluten/day), low-gluten (2 g gluten + 14 g whey protein/day) or control (16 g whey protein/day) diets for 1 week, with washout; 22 participants then underwent a 3-day rechallenge (gluten, whey, or control).
cards.result: Gastrointestinal symptoms consistently and significantly improved during reduced FODMAP intake, but significantly worsened to a similar degree when diets included gluten or whey protein. Gluten-specific effects were observed in only 8% of participants. There were no diet-specific changes in any serum or fecal marker of intestinal inflammation/injury or immune activation, or in fatigue indices. During the 3-day rechallenge, symptoms increased by similar levels among groups; gluten-specific effects were not reproduced. An order effect was observed.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven subjects and 1-week challenges: the trial can miss a small truly-gluten-sensitive subgroup (its own 8% figure leaves that door open), and the order effect shows how expectation-sensitive these symptom endpoints are. The result reframes the average patient, it does not prove no one is gluten-sensitive.
cards.source: Biesiekierski JR et al. No effects of gluten in patients with self-reported non-celiac gluten sensitivity after dietary reduction of fermentable, poorly absorbed, short-chain carbohydrates. Gastroenterology. 2013;145(2):320-328.e1-3. PMID: 23648697. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Biesiekierski 2011: without FODMAP control, gluten did worsen symptoms — 68% vs 40% reporting inadequate control
cards.summary: Biesiekierski 2011: without FODMAP control, gluten did worsen symptoms (68% vs 40% reporting inadequate control) — the same group's earlier design, whose gluten vehicle carried FODMAPs.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled rechallenge trial (up to 6 weeks)
cards.people: 34 patients with irritable bowel syndrome in whom coeliac disease was excluded and who were symptomatically controlled on a gluten-free diet (aged 29–59 years, 4 men; 56% carried HLA-DQ2 and/or HLA-DQ8), receiving gluten or placebo as two bread slices plus one muffin daily alongside a gluten-free diet; 34 completed the study per protocol. (The abstract's arm counts are printed as 19 in the gluten group and 15 on placebo in its results sentence.)
cards.result: Of the gluten group, 13 of 19 (68%) reported that symptoms were not adequately controlled, compared with 6 of 15 (40%) on placebo (P=0.0001 by generalized estimating equation). On a visual analogue scale, patients were significantly worse with gluten within 1 week for overall symptoms (P=0.047), pain (P=0.016), bloating (P=0.031), satisfaction with stool consistency (P=0.024) and tiredness (P=0.001). Anti-gliadin antibodies were not induced, and there were no significant changes in fecal lactoferrin, coeliac antibodies, highly sensitive C-reactive protein or intestinal permeability, and no differences by DQ2/DQ8 status.
cards.watchOut: The bread-and-muffin vehicle carried fermentable carbohydrates as well as gluten — the confound the 2013 trial was designed to remove. This card is the 'before' picture; it is not independent evidence against the 2013 result, because the same group ran both and designed the second to test the first.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Biesiekierski 2011 (34 patients) and Biesiekierski 2013 (37 subjects, 22 rechallenged).
