shelves.title: Terlipressin plus albumin for type 1 hepatorenal syndrome (CONFIRM)
shelves.question: In cirrhosis with type 1 hepatorenal syndrome, does terlipressin plus albumin reverse the syndrome versus albumin alone — and how does its respiratory-failure harm signal weigh against the renal benefit?
shelves.mesh: Albumins/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Hepatorenal Syndrome/drug therapy,etiology,mortality · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Liver Transplantation · Renal Replacement Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C at build: the trial carries a serious respiratory harm signal, and mortality is reported beside the renal outcome on the shelf face). In CONFIRM (300 patients), terlipressin plus albumin achieved verified reversal of hepatorenal syndrome in 32% versus 17% (P=0.006) — and death within 90 days due to respiratory disorders in 11% versus 2%, with overall 90-day death in 51% versus 45%. A real renal benefit bought with a respiratory harm signal, in a single trial: POSSIBLE, and the developer rules personally.

cards.headline: CONFIRM (Wong 2021): terlipressin reversed hepatorenal syndrome more often (32% vs 17%) but respiratory deaths ran 11% versus 2%
cards.summary: CONFIRM 2021: terlipressin reversed hepatorenal syndrome more often ( 32% vs 17% ) but deaths from respiratory disorders within 90 days ran 11% vs 2% , against overall 90-day mortality of 51% vs 45%.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (albumin recommended in both groups)
cards.people: 300 adults with cirrhosis and type 1 hepatorenal syndrome randomised 2:1 to terlipressin (199) or placebo (101) for up to 14 days, with concomitant albumin strongly recommended in both groups; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Verified reversal of hepatorenal syndrome (two consecutive creatinine measurements of 1.5 mg/dL or less at least 2 hours apart, with survival without renal-replacement therapy for at least 10 days after treatment) occurred in 63 patients (32%) in the terlipressin group and 17 (17%) in the placebo group (P=0.006). HRS reversal by day 14 on any creatinine of 1.5 or less occurred in 78 (39%) versus 18 (18%) (P<0.001). By day 90, liver transplantation had been performed in 46 patients (23%) versus 29 (29%), and death had occurred in 101 (51%) versus 45 (45%). More adverse events — including abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea and respiratory failure — occurred with terlipressin, and death within 90 days due to respiratory disorders occurred in 22 patients (11%) in the terlipressin group versus 2 (2%) in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: The primary end point is a renal-reversal definition, not survival: overall mortality was numerically higher on terlipressin (51% versus 45%) and respiratory deaths were fivefold-plus higher. Patient selection (excluding advanced respiratory compromise) is inseparable from using this drug.
cards.source: Wong F et al. Terlipressin plus Albumin for the Treatment of Type 1 Hepatorenal Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(9):818-828. PMID: 33657294. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02770716, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Prednisolone or pentoxifylline for severe alcoholic hepatitis (STOPAH)
shelves.question: In severe alcoholic hepatitis, does prednisolone, pentoxifylline, both, or neither improve short-term mortality — and what happened to the prednisolone signal by 90 days and one year?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hepatitis, Alcoholic/drug therapy,mortality · Infections/etiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Pentoxifylline/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the outcomes are 28-day, 90-day and 1-year mortality). POSSIBLE for a prednisolone effect at 28 days: mortality 17% (placebo–placebo) versus 14% (prednisolone–placebo) in raw terms, odds ratio 0.72 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.01; P=0.06 — a relative measure that did not reach significance in the journal report; the full HTA report's severity-adjusted analysis gave 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.91). LIKELY for the rest: at 90 days and 1 year there were no significant between-group differences for either drug, pentoxifylline's 28-day odds ratio was 1.07, and serious infections ran 13% on prednisolone versus 7% off it. One factorial trial reported twice (journal + HTA monograph) — counted once as evidence.

cards.headline: STOPAH (Thursz 2015, NEJM): prednisolone's 28-day mortality odds ratio was 0.72 (P=0.06, not significant); pentoxifylline 1.07; no benefit at 90 days or 1 year
cards.summary: STOPAH 2015: prednisolone's 28-day mortality odds ratio was 0.72 (P=0.06, not significant); pentoxifylline 1.07; no benefit at 90 days or 1 year.
cards.people: 1,103 patients with a clinical diagnosis of severe alcoholic hepatitis randomised to placebo–placebo (269 analysed), prednisolone–placebo (266), pentoxifylline–placebo (258) or both drugs (260); 1,053 patients contributed to the primary end-point analysis; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality at 28 days was 17% (45 of 269) in the placebo–placebo group, 14% (38 of 266) in the prednisolone–placebo group, 19% (50 of 258) in the pentoxifylline–placebo group and 13% (35 of 260) in the combined group. The odds ratio for 28-day mortality was 1.07 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.49; P=0.69) for pentoxifylline and 0.72 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.01; P=0.06) for prednisolone — relative measures, with the absolute group rates beside them. At 90 days and at 1 year there were no significant between-group differences. Serious infections occurred in 13% of patients treated with prednisolone versus 7% of those who did not receive it (P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Three same-title NEJM records (PMID 26176387–26176389) are correspondence about this trial, not the trial, and are not carded. The prednisolone 28-day figure is a borderline relative effect inside the trial's own primary analysis — it is not a demonstrated survival benefit.

cards.headline: STOPAH full report (Thursz 2015, HTA): the severity-adjusted 28-day prednisolone odds ratio was 0.61 — and the benefit was not sustained beyond 28 days
cards.summary: STOPAH full HTA report 2015: the severity-adjusted 28-day prednisolone odds ratio was 0.61 — and the benefit was not sustained beyond 28 days. (The same trial's full report, counted once.)
cards.type: Full trial report (HTA monograph) of the same 2×2 factorial trial — a companion report, not a second trial
cards.people: The same STOPAH population as the card above: 5,234 patients screened across 65 UK gastroenterology and hepatology units, 1,103 randomised, 1,053 available for the primary end-point analysis; patients had Maddrey's discriminant function of 32 or more; prednisolone 40 mg daily and pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily, each for 28 days.
cards.result: At 28 days, deaths by arm were 45 of 269 (16.7%) in arm A (placebo–placebo), 38 of 266 (14.3%) in arm B (prednisolone), 50 of 258 (19.4%) in arm C (pentoxifylline) and 35 of 260 (13.5%) in arm D (both). The odds ratio for 28-day mortality was 1.07 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.40; P=0.686) for pentoxifylline and 0.72 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.01; P=0.056) for prednisolone; in the logistic-regression analysis accounting for disease severity and prognosis, the prednisolone odds ratio was 0.61 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.91; P=0.015) — a relative, adjusted measure. At 90 days and 1 year there were no significant differences in mortality between treatment groups. Serious infections occurred in 13% of prednisolone-treated patients versus 7% of controls (P=0.002). The report concludes that prednisolone reduces the risk of mortality at 28 days, but that this benefit is not sustained beyond 28 days, and that pentoxifylline had no impact on survival.
cards.watchOut: This is the same single trial as the NEJM card, reported in full — the two records are one piece of evidence. The adjusted analysis strengthens the 28-day signal; it does not create a 90-day or 1-year benefit, and the infection excess is in both reports.
cards.source: Thursz MR et al. The clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of STeroids Or Pentoxifylline for Alcoholic Hepatitis (STOPAH): a randomised controlled trial. shelves.title: Second-line therapy for primary biliary cholangitis: elafibranor (ELATIVE) and seladelpar (RESPONSE)
shelves.question: In primary biliary cholangitis with an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid, do the PPAR agonists elafibranor and seladelpar improve the cholestasis biochemical response versus placebo — and what do their itch and safety profiles show?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Bilirubin/blood · Chalcones/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cholestasis/blood,drug therapy,etiology · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary/blood,complications,drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 double-blind trials of the same question with two PPAR agonists both hit their biochemical-response primary end point by wide margins — elafibranor 51% versus 4% (difference 47 percentage points) in ELATIVE, seladelpar 61.7% versus 20.0% (difference 41.7 points) in RESPONSE — with alkaline phosphatase normalisation in 15% and 25.0% versus 0% on placebo in both. Seladelpar also reduced pruritus significantly; elafibranor's itch end point did not differ significantly. The outcomes are biochemical (a validated-response surrogate), not transplant or survival — that is why the claim stays a biochemical one on this shelf.

cards.headline: ELATIVE (Kowdley 2024): elafibranor biochemical response 51% versus 4% on placebo; itch end point not significant
cards.summary: ELATIVE 2024: elafibranor biochemical response 51% vs 4% on placebo; its itch endpoint was not significant.
cards.type: Multinational, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial
cards.people: 161 patients with primary biliary cholangitis who had an inadequate response to, or unacceptable side effects with, ursodeoxycholic acid, randomised 2:1 to once-daily elafibranor 80 mg (108) or placebo (53); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A biochemical response (alkaline phosphatase below 1.67 times the upper limit of normal, with a reduction of at least 15% from baseline, and normal total bilirubin) at week 52 occurred in 51% of the elafibranor group (55 of 108) versus 4% (2 of 53) on placebo (difference 47 percentage points, 95% CI 32 to 57; P<0.001). Alkaline phosphatase normalised in 15% versus none (difference 15 points, 95% CI 6 to 23; P=0.002). Among patients with moderate-to-severe pruritus, the change in Worst Itch Numeric Rating Scale through week 52 did not differ significantly (−1.93 versus −1.15; difference −0.78, 95% CI −1.99 to 0.42; P=0.20). Adverse events more frequent with elafibranor included abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: Biochemical response is the regulatory surrogate for this disease; ELATIVE does not show fewer transplants or deaths, and its itch result is a null that should not be rounded into a symptom claim.

cards.summary: RESPONSE 2024: seladelpar biochemical response 61.7% vs 20.0% , with alkaline phosphatase normalisation 25.0% vs 0%.
cards.people: 193 patients who had an inadequate response to, or a history of unacceptable side effects with, ursodeoxycholic acid (93.8% received it as background therapy), randomised 2:1 to oral seladelpar 10 mg daily or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A biochemical response (alkaline phosphatase below 1.67 times the upper limit of normal, a decrease of at least 15% from baseline, and normal total bilirubin) at month 12 occurred in 61.7% of the seladelpar group versus 20.0% on placebo (difference 41.7 percentage points, 95% CI 27.7 to 53.4; P<0.001). Alkaline phosphatase normalised in 25.0% versus 0% (difference 25.0 points, 95% CI 18.3 to 33.2; P<0.001). Among patients with moderate-to-severe pruritus at baseline, seladelpar reduced the pruritus numerical rating score more than placebo (least-squares mean change −3.2 versus −1.7; difference −1.5, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.5; P=0.005). Adverse events were reported in 86.7% versus 84.6%, and serious adverse events in 7.0% versus 6.2%.
cards.watchOut: Same surrogate caveat as ELATIVE, and the placebo response rate (20.0%) was much higher than ELATIVE's (4%) — cross-trial percentage comparisons between the two drugs are not randomised comparisons and are not made on this shelf.
cards.source: Hirschfield GM et al. A Phase 3 Trial of Seladelpar in Primary Biliary Cholangitis. N Engl J Med. 2024;390(9):783-794. PMID: 38381664. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04620733 and EudraCT 2020-004348-27, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two drugs, one question, two concordant phase 3 wins on biochemistry — LIKELY
cards.summary: Two drugs, one question, two concordant phase 3 wins on biochemistry — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ELATIVE (161 patients) and RESPONSE (193 patients), both in primary biliary cholangitis with inadequate ursodeoxycholic-acid response.
cards.result: Two independent phase 3 trials, two different PPAR agonists, the same response definition and the same result pattern: response differences of 47 and 41.7 percentage points over placebo, with alkaline phosphatase normalisation at 15% and 25.0% against 0% twice. That is the double-trial standard for LIKELY — for the biochemical claim as stated, not for survival or transplant outcomes, which neither trial measured as its end point. The obeticholic-acid cautionary card lives on the MASH shelf #323 for a different disease and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Head-to-head elafibranor-versus-seladelpar claims have no randomised basis; the differing placebo rates (4% versus 20.0%) warn against naive cross-trial ranking.

shelves.title: Bulevirtide for chronic hepatitis D (MYR301 and MYR202)
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis D, does the entry inhibitor bulevirtide produce a combined virological and biochemical response versus delayed treatment or tenofovir alone — in the phase 3 MYR301 trial (48-week and final 144-week reports) and the phase 2 MYR202 trial — and what happens after treatment stops?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B virus/genetics · Hepatitis B, Chronic/drug therapy · Hepatitis D, Chronic/drug therapy · Hepatitis Delta Virus/genetics · RNA
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The phase 3 MYR301 trial (150 patients) found a combined virological-and-biochemical response at week 48 in 45% (2 mg) and 48% (10 mg) versus 2% on delayed treatment (P<0.001 for each dose versus control), and its final 144-week report found combined response in 54–57% at end of treatment, falling to 24% in all groups 96 weeks after stopping, with sustained undetectable HDV RNA in about a third of end-of-treatment responders. The phase 2 MYR202 trial found the virological component in 54–77% across bulevirtide doses versus 4% on tenofovir alone at week 24. The control in MYR301 was delayed treatment rather than placebo, the end points are virological/biochemical rather than clinical outcomes, and MYR202 was open-label — a strong but single-pivotal-trial programme: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: MYR301 (Wedemeyer 2023): combined response at week 48 in 45% (2 mg) and 48% (10 mg) versus 2% with delayed treatment
cards.summary: MYR301 2023: combined response at week 48 in 45% (2 mg) and 48% (10 mg) vs 2% with delayed treatment.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised trial against delayed treatment (ongoing at publication)
cards.people: 150 patients with chronic hepatitis D, with or without compensated cirrhosis, randomised 1:1:1 to bulevirtide 2 mg daily (49), bulevirtide 10 mg daily (50) for 144 weeks, or no treatment for 48 weeks followed by bulevirtide 10 mg (51, control group); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A primary end-point response (undetectable HDV RNA, or a decrease of at least 2 log10 IU/mL from baseline, plus normalisation of alanine aminotransferase) at week 48 occurred in 45% of the 2-mg group, 48% of the 10-mg group and 2% of the control group (P<0.001 for each dose versus control). HDV RNA was undetectable at week 48 in 12% (2 mg) and 20% (10 mg) (P=0.41 between doses). ALT normalised in 12% of controls, 51% of the 2-mg group (difference 39 percentage points, 95% CI 20 to 56) and 56% of the 10-mg group (difference 44 points, 95% CI 26 to 60). No loss of hepatitis B surface antigen occurred by week 48. Headache, pruritus, fatigue, eosinophilia and injection-site reactions were more common with bulevirtide; no treatment-related serious adverse events occurred; bile acid levels rose dose-dependently.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was delayed treatment, not placebo, and the trial was ongoing — 48-week virological/biochemical response is not yet a liver-outcome result. Suppression, not cure: surface-antigen loss did not occur.
cards.source: Wedemeyer H et al. A Phase 3, Randomized Trial of Bulevirtide in Chronic Hepatitis D. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(1):22-32. PMID: 37345876. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03852719, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: MYR202 (Bogomolov 2023): virological response at week 24 in 54% (2 mg), 50% (5 mg) and 77% (10 mg) versus 4% on tenofovir alone — with rebound after stopping
cards.summary: MYR202 2023: virological response at week 24 in 54–77% across bulevirtide doses vs 4% on tenofovir alone — with rebound after stopping.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, parallel-group, open-label phase 2 trial
cards.people: 120 adults (aged 18–65 years) with chronic hepatitis D (59 with cirrhosis), enrolled in Germany and Russia, randomised to bulevirtide 2 mg (28), 5 mg (32) or 10 mg (30) daily plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, or tenofovir alone (30; 28 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), for 24 weeks; the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, undetectable HDV RNA or a decline of at least 2 log10 IU/mL occurred in 15 of 28 patients (54%, 95% CI 34 to 73) on bulevirtide 2 mg, 16 of 32 (50%, 32 to 68) on 5 mg and 23 of 30 (77%, 58 to 90) on 10 mg, versus 1 of 28 (4%, 0.1 to 18) on tenofovir alone (P<0.0001 for each dose versus tenofovir alone). By week 48 — 24 weeks after bulevirtide stopped — HDV RNA had rebounded, with median increases from week 24 of about 1.7–2.0 log10 IU/mL across the dose groups. There were no deaths associated with treatment, as reported in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, tenofovir-controlled and 24 weeks: MYR202 is dose-finding support for MYR301, and its post-treatment rebound shows the drug suppresses while given rather than eradicating the virus.
cards.source: Bogomolov P et al. Safety and efficacy of bulevirtide in combination with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in patients with hepatitis B virus and hepatitis D virus coinfection (MYR202): a multicentre, randomised, parallel-group, open-label, phase 2 trial. cards.headline: MYR301 final report (Wedemeyer 2026): combined response 54–57% at end of treatment, falling to 24% in all groups 96 weeks after stopping; a third of end-of-treatment responders stayed undetectable
cards.summary: MYR301 final report 2026: combined response 54–57% at end of treatment, falling to 24% in all groups 96 weeks after stopping. (A third report of the same trial, counted once.)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised trial — final and post-treatment report of MYR301 (a companion report of the trial carded above, counted once as evidence)
cards.people: The same MYR301 population as the card above: 150 patients with chronic hepatitis D randomised to bulevirtide 2 mg/day (49) or 10 mg/day (50) for 144 weeks, or delayed treatment for 48 weeks followed by bulevirtide 10 mg/day for 96 weeks (51 randomised; 50 in the delayed-treatment arm as analysed), then 96 weeks of post-treatment follow-up; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At end of treatment, virological response (undetectable HDV RNA or a decline of at least 2 log10 IU/mL) was 73% (2 mg), 76% (10 mg) and 92% (delayed-treatment/10 mg); ALT normalisation was 59%, 60% and 58%; combined response was 57%, 54% and 56%; and HDV RNA was undetectable in 29%, 50% and 52%. At 96 weeks after treatment ended, virological response had fallen to 33%, 30% and 32%, combined response was 24% in all groups, and undetectability was 20%, 22% and 20%. Sustained undetectability through follow-up occurred in 23 of 64 patients (36%) who were undetectable at end of treatment, with weeks continuously undetectable at end of treatment the most important predictor. Post-treatment hepatic serious adverse events occurred in 20 of 142 patients (14%) and resolved in 17 of 20 (85%).
cards.watchOut: This is the same single trial as the 48-week card above, not independent confirmation — and its lesson cuts both ways: efficacy is maintained and undetectability deepens on treatment up to 144 weeks, but most responses decay after stopping. The delayed-treatment arm's higher end-of-treatment virological response (92%) reflects its different treatment duration and must not be read as a dose effect.
cards.source: Wedemeyer H et al. 144 Weeks of bulevirtide monotherapy for chronic hepatitis D: Final and post-treatment results from a phase III randomized trial. J Hepatol. 2026;85(3):493-503. PMID: 41966308. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03852719, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bulevirtide suppresses hepatitis D on treatment, in phase 2 and phase 3 — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Bulevirtide suppresses hepatitis D on treatment, in phase 2 and phase 3 — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MYR301 (150 patients, phase 3; 48-week and final 144-week reports — two reads of one trial, counted once) and MYR202 (120 patients, phase 2).
cards.result: Across both trials the pattern is consistent and large: combined response 45–48% versus 2% at week 48 (MYR301), 54–57% at end of treatment in the final 144-week report, and virological response 50–77% versus 4% (MYR202, week 24), with ALT normalisation tracking the virology. The final report adds the stopping rule: 96 weeks after treatment ended, combined response had fallen to 24% in every group, though 36% of patients undetectable at end of treatment stayed undetectable. The caps are structural: one pivotal trial with a delayed-treatment control, surrogate end points, and relapse on stopping. POSSIBLE. Hepatitis B antivirals are home on Shelf #326 — hepatitis D is a different virus riding on HBV, with its own drug and trials, and nothing from #326 is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not describe bulevirtide as curative: no surface-antigen loss occurred in MYR301 by week 48, and MYR202's rebound is the natural history of stopping it.

shelves.title: Teduglutide for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure (STEPS)
shelves.question: In adults with short bowel syndrome dependent on parenteral support, does the GLP-2 analogue teduglutide reduce parenteral volume requirements versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/blood · Citrulline/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Endpoint Determination · Injections, Subcutaneous · Intestinal Absorption/physiology · Intestinal Diseases/blood,drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pivotal trial (STEPS, 86 patients), teduglutide produced responders (a reduction of more than 20% in parenteral support volume at weeks 20 and 24) in 63% versus 30% on placebo (P=0.002), with a mean parenteral-volume reduction of 4.4 versus 2.3 L/week at week 24 and one or more days per week off parenteral support in 54% versus 23%. A clinically meaningful effect in a rare disease, from one small 24-week trial with a volume end point: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: STEPS (Jeppesen 2012): teduglutide responders 63% versus 30% on placebo; parenteral volume down 4.4 versus 2.3 L/week
cards.summary: STEPS 2012: teduglutide responders 63% vs 30% on placebo; parenteral volume down 4.4 vs 2.3 L/week.
cards.people: 86 patients with short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure, given subcutaneous teduglutide 0.05 mg/kg/day (43) or placebo (43) once daily for 24 weeks, with parenteral support reduced when 48-hour urine volumes exceeded baseline by at least 10%; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Responders (more than 20% reduction in parenteral support volume from baseline at weeks 20 and 24) numbered 27 of 43 (63%) in the teduglutide group versus 13 of 43 (30%) on placebo (P=0.002). At week 24 the mean reduction in parenteral support volume was 4.4 ± 3.8 L/week (baseline 12.9 ± 7.8) with teduglutide versus 2.3 ± 2.7 L/week (baseline 13.2 ± 7.4) with placebo (P<0.001). A reduction of one day or more in weekly parenteral support occurred in 21 of 39 patients (54%) versus 9 of 39 (23%) (P=0.005). Teduglutide increased plasma citrulline, a biomarker of mucosal mass. Treatment-emergent adverse events leading to discontinuation numbered 2 (teduglutide) and 3 (placebo).
cards.watchOut: 86 patients and 24 weeks in a rare disease: the end point is parenteral volume, not independence from parenteral support, survival or quality of life, and durability beyond 24 weeks is outside this trial.
cards.source: Jeppesen PB et al. Teduglutide reduces need for parenteral support among patients with short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure. Gastroenterology. 2012;143(6):1473-1481.e3. PMID: 22982184. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00798967, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Upadacitinib for moderately to severely active Crohn's disease (U-EXCEL, U-EXCEED, U-ENDURE)
shelves.question: Does upadacitinib induce and maintain clinical remission and endoscopic response in Crohn's disease versus placebo — across its two induction trials and one maintenance trial, reported together?
shelves.mesh: Crohn Disease/complications,drug therapy · Herpes Zoster/chemically induced,etiology · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Neutropenia/chemically induced,etiology · Induction Chemotherapy/adverse effects,methods · Maintenance Chemotherapy/adverse effects,methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three phase 3 trials in one report (U-EXCEL, 526 patients; U-EXCEED, 495; U-ENDURE, 502) all hit both coprimary end points — clinical remission and endoscopic response — at induction (remission 49.5% versus 29.1% and 38.9% versus 21.1%) and at 52-week maintenance (remission 37.3% on 15 mg and 47.6% on 30 mg versus 15.1%). The safety ledger is on the card: more herpes zoster at the higher doses, hepatic disorders and neutropenia at 30 mg, and gastrointestinal perforations in 6 upadacitinib-treated patients across the programme. Three concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: Loftus 2023 (U-EXCEL, U-EXCEED, U-ENDURE): upadacitinib beat placebo on remission and endoscopic response in induction and maintenance
cards.summary: Loftus 2023 (U-EXCEL, U-EXCEED, U-ENDURE): upadacitinib beat placebo on clinical remission and endoscopic response in induction and maintenance.
cards.type: Three phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease: 526 randomised in U-EXCEL and 495 in U-EXCEED to upadacitinib 45 mg or placebo (2:1) once daily for 12 weeks; responders to upadacitinib induction were re-randomised in U-ENDURE (502) to upadacitinib 15 mg, 30 mg or placebo (1:1:1) for 52 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission (Crohn's Disease Activity Index below 150) at week 12 occurred in 49.5% versus 29.1% (U-EXCEL) and 38.9% versus 21.1% (U-EXCEED), and endoscopic response in 45.5% versus 13.1% and 34.6% versus 3.5% respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). At week 52 in U-ENDURE, clinical remission occurred in 37.3% (15 mg) and 47.6% (30 mg) versus 15.1% on placebo, and endoscopic response in 27.6% and 40.1% versus 7.3% (P<0.001 for all). Herpes zoster infections occurred more frequently in the 45-mg and 30-mg groups than in their placebo groups; hepatic disorders and neutropenia were more frequent at 30 mg; gastrointestinal perforations developed in 4 patients on 45 mg and in 1 patient each on 30 mg and 15 mg.
cards.watchOut: One sponsor programme in one report: the three trials are independent randomisations but share a design family and funder. Maintenance results apply to induction responders only, by design.
cards.source: Loftus EV Jr et al. Upadacitinib Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Crohn's Disease. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(21):1966-1980. PMID: 37224198. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03345849 (U-EXCEL), NCT03345836 (U-EXCEED) and NCT03345823 (U-ENDURE), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials, both end points, induction and maintenance — LIKELY
cards.summary: Three trials, both endpoints, induction and maintenance — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: U-EXCEL (526), U-EXCEED (495) and U-ENDURE (502) — three separately randomised trials in one report.
cards.result: The programme clears the double-trial bar three times over on the same two end points, with absolute remission gaps of about 18–32 percentage points over placebo. LIKELY. Upadacitinib for ankylosing spondylitis is home on Shelf #680 and for atopic dermatitis on Shelf #820 — different trials, not re-carded here; the risankizumab–ustekinumab head-to-head (#771) and Crohn's treatment strategy (#324) ask different questions. A later full-population final report of U-ENDURE (673 patients; PMID: 40738276) is consistent with the primary analysis carded here — week-52 clinical remission 36.2% (15 mg) and 51.5% (30 mg) versus 15.2%, endoscopic response 27.3% and 40.7% versus 7.2% — and is fenced here as a further report of the same trial, not independent evidence.
cards.watchOut: The perforation count (6 across the programme) and zoster signal belong in any summary of this shelf; efficacy percentages quoted alone misrepresent a JAK inhibitor's balance.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: True North (645 patients in the blinded induction cohort; 457 in maintenance) found clinical remission higher on ozanimod than placebo at induction (18.4% versus 6.0%; P<0.001) and at maintenance week 52 (37.0% versus 18.5% among week-10 responders; P<0.001), with clinical response and all key secondary end points also favouring ozanimod. It is a single pivotal programme — induction plus randomised-withdrawal maintenance in one report — so the single-programme ceiling caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Etrasimod, a different S1P modulator with two independent trials, is home on Shelf #1068.

cards.headline: True North (Sandborn 2021): ozanimod remission 18.4% versus 6.0% at induction and 37.0% versus 18.5% at maintenance
cards.summary: True North 2021: ozanimod remission 18.4% vs 6.0% at induction and 37.0% vs 18.5% at maintenance.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (induction plus randomised-withdrawal maintenance)
cards.people: Patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis: 645 in the double-blind induction cohort 1 and 367 in the open-label cohort 2, receiving ozanimod hydrochloride 1 mg (equivalent to 0.92 mg ozanimod) or placebo once daily for 10 weeks; 457 patients with a clinical response to ozanimod were re-randomised to double-blind ozanimod or placebo for maintenance through week 52; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission (three-component Mayo score) was significantly higher with ozanimod than placebo during induction (18.4% versus 6.0%; P<0.001) and maintenance (37.0% versus 18.5% among patients with a response at week 10; P<0.001). Clinical response was also higher during induction (47.8% versus 25.9%; P<0.001) and maintenance (60.0% versus 41.0%; P<0.001), and all other key secondary clinical, endoscopic and histologic end points improved significantly in both periods. Infection incidence was similar to placebo during induction and higher during maintenance; serious infection occurred in under 2% of patients in each group over the 52-week trial; elevated liver aminotransferase levels were more common with ozanimod.
cards.watchOut: Maintenance percentages are conditional on having responded at week 10 — they are not remission rates for all comers. One programme, one report: no independent replication trial is carded anywhere.

shelves.title: Etrasimod for ulcerative colitis: the ELEVATE UC trials
shelves.question: Does etrasimod induce and maintain clinical remission in moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis — in the 52-week treat-through ELEVATE UC 52 trial and the 12-week ELEVATE UC 12 induction trial?
shelves.mesh: Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy,pathology · Acetates/therapeutic use · Indoles · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two independent phase 3 double-blind trials: ELEVATE UC 52 (433 randomised) found clinical remission in 27% versus 7% at week 12 and 32% versus 7% at week 52 (treat-through), and ELEVATE UC 12 (354 randomised) found 25% versus 15% at week 12 (P=0.026 — the smaller, weaker of the two reads, stated plainly on the card). No deaths or malignancies were reported in either trial. Two concordant independent trials carry LIKELY. Ozanimod, the other S1P modulator, is home on Shelf #1067.

cards.headline: ELEVATE UC 52 and UC 12 (Sandborn 2023): etrasimod remission 27% versus 7% and 32% versus 7% (UC 52, weeks 12 and 52); 25% versus 15% (UC 12, week 12)
cards.summary: ELEVATE UC 52 and UC 12 2023: etrasimod remission 27% vs 7% and 32% vs 7% (UC 52, weeks 12 and 52); 25% vs 15% (UC 12, week 12).
cards.type: Two independent randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported together
cards.people: Adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis and inadequate response, loss of response or intolerance to at least one approved therapy, randomised 2:1 to oral etrasimod 2 mg or placebo: ELEVATE UC 52 (433 randomised; full analysis set 289 etrasimod, 144 placebo; 315 centres in 40 countries) with a 12-week induction followed by a 40-week treat-through maintenance period, and ELEVATE UC 12 (354 randomised; 238 etrasimod, 116 placebo; 407 centres in 37 countries) assessing induction at week 12; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In ELEVATE UC 52, clinical remission was achieved by 74 of 274 patients (27%) on etrasimod versus 10 of 135 (7%) on placebo at week 12 (P<0.0001) and by 88 of 274 (32%) versus 9 of 135 (7%) at week 52 (P<0.0001). In ELEVATE UC 12, remission at week 12 occurred in 55 of 222 (25%) versus 17 of 112 (15%) (P=0.026). Adverse events were reported in 206 of 289 (71%) versus 81 of 144 (56%) in ELEVATE UC 52 and in 112 of 238 (47%) versus 54 of 116 (47%) in ELEVATE UC 12. No deaths or malignancies were reported in either trial.
cards.watchOut: ELEVATE UC 12's induction gap (25% versus 15%, P=0.026) is much narrower than UC 52's — the two trials are concordant in direction, not in size, and the shelf does not average them away. Adverse events ran higher on etrasimod in UC 52 (71% versus 56%).
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Etrasimod as induction and maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis (ELEVATE): two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2023;401(10383):1159-1171. PMID: 36871574. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03945188 (ELEVATE UC 52) and NCT03996369 (ELEVATE UC 12), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two independent trials, one direction — LIKELY
cards.summary: Two independent trials, one direction — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ELEVATE UC 52 (433 randomised) and ELEVATE UC 12 (354 randomised) — two independent trials in one report.
cards.result: Unlike a single programme with sequential phases, ELEVATE randomised two separate populations, and both trials favoured etrasimod on remission — strongly in the 52-week treat-through trial (32% versus 7% at week 52) and modestly in the 12-week induction trial (25% versus 15%). That meets the double-trial standard for LIKELY. Ozanimod (True North) is home on Shelf #1067 — a different S1P modulator with its own trial base, cross-referenced and not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Treat-through week-52 rates (32%) and randomised-withdrawal rates on neighbouring shelves are not comparable designs; compare each drug within its own design.

shelves.title: Mirikizumab as induction and maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis (LUCENT)
shelves.question: Does the anti-IL-23p19 antibody mirikizumab induce and maintain clinical remission in moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (LUCENT-1 induction and LUCENT-2 maintenance)?
shelves.mesh: Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Herpes Zoster/chemically induced,etiology · Induction Chemotherapy/adverse effects,methods · Maintenance Chemotherapy/adverse effects,methods · Opportunistic Infections/chemically induced,etiology · Remission Induction · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage,adverse effects,immunology,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two separately randomised phase 3 trials in one programme: LUCENT-1 (1,281 patients) found clinical remission at week 12 in 24.2% versus 13.3% (P<0.001), and LUCENT-2 (544 induction responders re-randomised) found remission at week 40 of maintenance in 49.9% versus 25.1% (P<0.001), with all major secondary end points met in both trials. The safety record includes opportunistic infections in 15 of 1,217 mirikizumab-treated patients and cancers in 8, stated on the card. Two randomised trials with concordant results carry LIKELY; the maintenance figure is conditional on induction response, as on all withdrawal-design shelves.

cards.headline: LUCENT-1 and LUCENT-2 (D'Haens 2023): mirikizumab remission 24.2% versus 13.3% at induction week 12 and 49.9% versus 25.1% at maintenance week 40
cards.summary: LUCENT-1 and LUCENT-2 2023: mirikizumab remission 24.2% vs 13.3% at induction week 12 and 49.9% vs 25.1% at maintenance week 40.
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (induction plus randomised-withdrawal maintenance)
cards.people: Adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis: 1,281 randomised in the induction trial to intravenous mirikizumab 300 mg or placebo (3:1) every 4 weeks for 12 weeks; 544 patients with a response to mirikizumab induction were re-randomised in the maintenance trial to subcutaneous mirikizumab 200 mg or placebo (2:1) every 4 weeks for 40 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical remission occurred in 24.2% on mirikizumab versus 13.3% on placebo at week 12 of induction (P<0.001) and in 49.9% versus 25.1% at week 40 of maintenance (52 weeks overall) (P<0.001); the criteria for all major secondary end points — clinical response, endoscopic remission and improvement in bowel-movement urgency — were met in both trials. Nasopharyngitis and arthralgia were reported more frequently with mirikizumab. Among 1,217 patients treated with mirikizumab across the controlled and uncontrolled periods, 15 had an opportunistic infection (including 6 with herpes zoster) and 8 had cancer (including 3 with colorectal cancer); among placebo patients in induction, 1 had herpes zoster and none had cancer.
cards.watchOut: The maintenance 49.9% is a responder-enriched figure (only induction responders were re-randomised), and the cancer/opportunistic-infection counts come from the pooled controlled-plus-uncontrolled exposure, not a randomised comparison — both are stated as such rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: D'Haens G et al. Mirikizumab as Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(26):2444-2455. PMID: 37379135. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03518086 (LUCENT-1) and NCT03524092 (LUCENT-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Induction and maintenance both positive in two randomised trials — LIKELY.

shelves.title: Speeding gastrointestinal recovery after bowel surgery: alvimopan, and chewing gum
shelves.question: Does the peripherally acting mu-opioid antagonist alvimopan accelerate gastrointestinal recovery and shorten stay after bowel resection (its phase III programme) — and does the cheapest intervention in surgery, chewing gum as sham feeding, do the same in its randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Defecation/physiology · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Hysterectomy · Ileus/drug therapy · Intestine, Large/surgery · Intestine, Small/surgery · Laparotomy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The carded evidence is one phase III randomised trial of alvimopan (510 randomised): time to recovery of gastrointestinal function was accelerated at both 6 mg (hazard ratio 1.28) and 12 mg (hazard ratio 1.54), a mean difference of 15 and 22 hours versus placebo, and the 12 mg dose also accelerated the hospital-discharge order by a mean of 20 hours (hazard ratio 1.42). A single carded trial report caps at POSSIBLE; the pooled analysis of the phase III programme (PMID 17435541) is background only under the anchor rules and is not carded. Chewing gum is fenced, not carded: the pinned post-resection randomised trials (for example PMID 27157953, n=60, and PMID 33186193) report faster flatus and defecation in their abstracts without extractable figures, so no gum figure is printed on this shelf — the honest summary is that gum's trials are small, unblindable and report direction without numbers at abstract level.

cards.headline: Wolff 2004: alvimopan accelerated gastrointestinal recovery by a mean of 15 hours (6 mg) and 22 hours (12 mg) versus placebo, and the 12 mg dose accelerated the discharge order by 20 hours
cards.summary: Wolff (2004): alvimopan accelerated gastrointestinal recovery by a mean of 15 hours (6 mg) and 22 hours (12 mg) vs placebo.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial
cards.people: 510 patients scheduled for bowel resection or radical hysterectomy by laparotomy, randomised to alvimopan 6 mg, alvimopan 12 mg or placebo orally at least 2 hours before surgery and then twice daily until discharge or up to 7 days; the modified intention-to-treat population numbered 469 (451 bowel resection, 18 radical hysterectomy). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Time to recovery of gastrointestinal function (the composite primary endpoint) was accelerated in the alvimopan 6 mg group (hazard ratio 1.28, p<0.05 — a relative measure) and the 12 mg group (hazard ratio 1.54, p<0.001), with mean differences of 15 and 22 hours compared with placebo. Time to hospital discharge order written was also accelerated at 12 mg (hazard ratio 1.42, p=0.003; mean difference 20 hours). The incidence of adverse events was similar among treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: A 2004 trial from the pre-ERAS era, run against the background opioid and feeding practices of its time: the absolute hours saved may not transfer to a modern enhanced-recovery pathway, and 'discharge order written' is a process milestone, not discharge itself.
cards.source: Wolff BG et al. Alvimopan, a novel, peripherally acting mu opioid antagonist: results of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III trial of major abdominal surgery and postoperative ileus. Ann Surg. 2004;240(4):728-734. PMID: 15383800. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2004).

shelves.title: Givosiran, silencing ALAS1, for acute hepatic porphyria (ENVISION)
shelves.question: Does monthly givosiran, RNA interference against ALAS1, reduce the annualised attack rate in acute intermittent porphyria, and at what cost in liver and kidney signals?
shelves.mesh: Acetylgalactosamine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Aminolevulinic Acid/urine · Fatigue/etiology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Least-Squares Analysis · Liver/drug effects · Nausea/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal phase 3 trial (ENVISION, 94 randomised patients with acute hepatic porphyria) found a mean annualised attack rate of 3.2 on givosiran vs 12.5 on placebo among patients with acute intermittent porphyria — a 74% lower rate, a relative measure with the absolute rates beside it — with hepatic and renal adverse-event signals that are reported on the card face. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Attack-rate outcome; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: ENVISION 2020: givosiran cut the annualised porphyria attack rate from 12.5 to 3.2 (74% lower, relative) in acute intermittent porphyria, with more liver and kidney adverse signals
cards.summary: ENVISION (2020): givosiran cut the annualised porphyria attack rate from 12.5 to 3.2 (74% lower, relative) in acute intermittent porphyria.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (monthly subcutaneous dosing, 6 months)
cards.people: 94 patients with symptomatic acute hepatic porphyria randomised to givosiran 2.5 mg/kg (48) or placebo (46) monthly; 89 had acute intermittent porphyria, the population for the primary endpoint. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Among patients with acute intermittent porphyria, the mean annualised rate of composite porphyria attacks (hospitalisation, urgent health-care visit, or home intravenous hemin) was 3.2 with givosiran vs 12.5 with placebo — a 74% lower rate (P<0.001), i.e. a relative reduction printed with the absolute rates (3.2 vs 12.5 attacks per year) beside it; results were similar across all 94 patients with acute hepatic porphyria. Givosiran also lowered urinary ALA and porphobilinogen, reduced hemin days, and improved daily worst-pain scores. Adverse events observed more frequently with givosiran were elevations in serum aminotransferases, changes in serum creatinine and estimated GFR, and injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: Six months, 94 patients, in a rare disease with highly variable attack rates: the placebo group's 12.5 attacks/year marks a severely affected enrolled population, and the hepatic/renal signals need the long-term follow-up to be judged.
cards.source: Balwani M et al. Phase 3 Trial of RNAi Therapeutic Givosiran for Acute Intermittent Porphyria. The New England journal of medicine. 2020;382(24):2289-2301. PMID: 32521132. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03338816, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind trials a decade apart support single-dose treatment. In Thailand, where Campylobacter predominated and half the isolates were levofloxacin-resistant, single-dose azithromycin cured 96% by 72 hours against 85% for 3-day azithromycin and 71% for 3-day levofloxacin, with the shortest time to last unformed stool. In TrEAT TD, single-dose azithromycin (500 mg) was non-inferior to single-dose levofloxacin for 24-hour clinical cure (78.3% vs 81.4%), with all three single-dose regimens reaching about 96% cure by 72 hours; rifaximin's non-inferiority could not be shown (P=0.07), so the single-dose claim is LIKELY for azithromycin and levofloxacin where susceptibility holds, and unproven for rifaximin. Prevention with rifaximin is a different question — Shelf #1214.

cards.headline: Tribble 2007: single-dose azithromycin cured 96% by 72 hours, against 71% for 3-day levofloxacin, in Campylobacter-heavy Thailand
cards.summary: Tribble (2007): single-dose azithromycin cured 96% by 72 hours, against 71% for 3-day levofloxacin, in Campylobacter-heavy Thailand.
cards.people: 156 patients with acute diarrhoea treated in military field clinics in Thailand, randomised to single-dose azithromycin 1 g, 3-day azithromycin (500 mg daily) or 3-day levofloxacin (500 mg daily); Campylobacter organisms predominated (64% of patients), with levofloxacin resistance in 50% of Campylobacter isolates and no azithromycin resistance; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Cure at 72 hours was 96% with single-dose azithromycin, 85% with 3-day azithromycin and 71% with levofloxacin (P=0.002). Single-dose azithromycin also had the shortest median time to last unformed stool (35 hours; P=0.03). Microbiological eradication was 96-100% on azithromycin regimens versus 38% on levofloxacin (P=0.001), though the authors note this correlated poorly with clinical outcome. Post-dose nausea within 30 minutes was more frequent after single-dose azithromycin (14% vs <6%; P=0.06), mild and self-limited.
cards.watchOut: A Thailand-specific microbiology result: where Campylobacter is uncommon and fluoroquinolone resistance low, the levofloxacin gap narrows — the authors themselves found levofloxacin equal where isolates were susceptible or no pathogen was identified.
cards.source: Tribble DR, Sanders JW, Pang LW et al. Traveler's diarrhea in Thailand: randomized, double-blind trial comparing single-dose and 3-day azithromycin-based regimens with a 3-day levofloxacin regimen. Clin Infect Dis. 2007;44(3):338-46. PMID: 17205438. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: TrEAT TD 2017: single-dose azithromycin was non-inferior to levofloxacin at 24 hours (78.3% vs 81.4%); rifaximin non-inferiority not shown
cards.summary: TrEAT TD (2017): single-dose azithromycin was non-inferior to levofloxacin at 24 hours ( 78.3% vs 81.4% ); rifaximin non-inferiority not shown.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind controlled trial (three single-dose regimens, all with loperamide)
cards.people: 324 US and UK service members with acute watery diarrhoea in Afghanistan, Djibouti, Kenya and Honduras (2012-2015), randomised to single-dose azithromycin 500 mg (106), levofloxacin 500 mg (111) or rifaximin 1,650 mg (107), each with loperamide; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical cure at 24 hours: levofloxacin 81.4%, azithromycin 78.3%, rifaximin 74.8%. Azithromycin was non-inferior to levofloxacin (P=0.01 for non-inferiority); non-inferiority could not be shown for rifaximin (P=0.07). By 48 and 72 hours efficacy was equivalent across regimens (about 91% and 96%). Median time to last unformed stool did not differ (azithromycin 3.8 h; levofloxacin 6.4 h; rifaximin 5.6 h). Treatment failures were uncommon (1.9-4.4%) and adverse events, including post-dose nausea and vomiting, did not differ between arms.
cards.watchOut: Deployed military patients with acute watery (non-dysenteric) diarrhoea, all given loperamide: the result does not cover bloody diarrhoea, febrile dysentery or civilian travellers with comorbidity, and rifaximin's single-dose role stays unproven on this trial.
cards.source: Riddle MS, Connor P, Fraser J et al. Trial Evaluating Ambulatory Therapy of Travelers' Diarrhea (TrEAT TD) Study: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing 3 Single-Dose Antibiotic Regimens With Loperamide. Clin Infect Dis. 2017;65(12):2008-2017. PMID: 29029033. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01618591, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one dose is enough for azithromycin — LIKELY; the resistance map decides the drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: one dose is enough for azithromycin — LIKELY; the resistance map decides the drug.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Tribble 2007 (156 patients, Thailand) and TrEAT TD 2017 (324 service members, four countries).
cards.result: Both trials land on the same practical answer: a single dose performs as well as multi-day courses, and azithromycin is the regimen that held up both against a 3-day course (Tribble) and in head-to-head non-inferiority against levofloxacin (TrEAT TD). Where fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter dominates, levofloxacin's cure rate fell to 71% (Tribble); where it does not, the drugs are comparable. Rifaximin single-dose treatment remains short of proven non-inferiority — its proven role in this library is prevention, Shelf #1214.
cards.watchOut: These are treatment trials in mostly young, healthy adults; they say nothing about prophylaxis, children, pregnancy, or diarrhoea with blood or high fever, which needs its own assessment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tribble DR et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2007;44(3):338-46. PMID: 17205438; Riddle MS et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2017;65(12):2008-2017. PMID: 29029033. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Myotomy strategies for achalasia: pneumatic dilation versus Heller, and POEM (European Achalasia Trial; Werner; Ponds)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive achalasia, how do pneumatic dilation and laparoscopic Heller myotomy compare on treatment success at two years — and does peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) beat pneumatic dilation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Catheterization · Chi-Square Distribution · Esophageal Achalasia · Esophageal Perforation · Esophageal Sphincter, Lower · Esophagus · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fundoplication · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Laparoscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Retreatment · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · (Werner record: Adult · Dilatation · Esophageal Achalasia · Esophagitis, Peptic · Female · Fundoplication · Heller Myotomy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myotomy · Natural Orifice Endoscopic Surgery · Postoperative Complications) · (Ponds record: Adult · Dilatation · Esophageal Achalasia · Esophageal Sphincter, Lower · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Humans · Male · Manometry · Middle Aged · Natural Orifice Endoscopic Surgery · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Sphincterotomy · Treatment Outcome)
shelves.balance: SPLIT. LIKELY that pneumatic dilation and laparoscopic Heller myotomy are equivalent at 2 years: the European Achalasia Trial found therapeutic success in 86% versus 90% (P=0.46), with different harms (perforation 4% with dilation; mucosal tears 12% with myotomy). LIKELY that POEM is non-inferior to Heller myotomy (Werner: success 83.0% versus 81.7%, meeting the non-inferiority margin) and superior to pneumatic dilation (Ponds: success 92% versus 54% at 2 years, and 81% versus 40% at 5 years) — at a consistent price: reflux oesophagitis in 41–57% after POEM versus 7–20% after the alternatives in the early assessments. Correction made at build: the topic file attributed the POEM-versus-dilation trial to 'Werner et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2019'; the record is Ponds et al., JAMA 2019 — Werner (N Engl J Med 2019) compared POEM with Heller myotomy, not with dilation.

cards.headline: European Achalasia Trial (Boeckxstaens 2011): pneumatic dilation matched Heller myotomy at 2 years (success 86% vs 90%)
cards.summary: European Achalasia Trial (Boeckxstaens 2011): pneumatic dilation matched Heller myotomy at 2 years (success 86% vs 90%)
cards.people: 201 patients with newly diagnosed achalasia, randomised to pneumatic dilation (95) or laparoscopic Heller myotomy with Dor's fundoplication (106); mean follow-up 43 months. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Therapeutic success (Eckardt score ≤3): pneumatic dilation 90% at 1 year and 86% at 2 years, versus Heller myotomy 93% and 90% (P=0.46) — no significant difference. Lower oesophageal sphincter pressure, oesophageal emptying, and quality of life also did not differ at 2 years. Harms differed in kind: oesophageal perforation occurred in 4% during pneumatic dilation, and mucosal tears in 12% during Heller myotomy. Abnormal oesophageal acid exposure was seen in 15% versus 23% (P=0.28).
cards.watchOut: Equivalence at 2 years is not equivalence for life: dilation's failures accumulate with retreatment over longer horizons, and this record's mean follow-up is 43 months. The trial compared a single dilation strategy against surgery with fundoplication — the reflux figures belong to those exact strategies.
cards.source: Boeckxstaens GE et al. Pneumatic dilation versus laparoscopic Heller's myotomy for idiopathic achalasia. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 21561346. Registry ID: ISRCTN56304564, from the record's databank fields (the abstract also cites Netherlands Trial Register NTR37). cards.headline: Werner 2019: POEM was non-inferior to Heller myotomy at 2 years (success 83.0% vs 81.7%), with more reflux
cards.summary: Werner 2019: POEM was non-inferior to Heller myotomy at 2 years (success 83.0% vs 81.7%), with more reflux
cards.people: 221 patients with symptomatic achalasia, randomised to POEM (112) or laparoscopic Heller myotomy plus Dor's fundoplication (109). The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clinical success at 2 years (Eckardt score ≤3 without additional treatment): 83.0% after POEM versus 81.7% after Heller myotomy — a difference of 1.4 percentage points (95% CI −8.7 to 11.4; P=0.007 for non-inferiority against a −12.5-point margin). Serious adverse events: 2.7% versus 7.3%. Reflux oesophagitis on endoscopy: 57% versus 20% at 3 months and 44% versus 29% at 24 months. Oesophageal function and quality-of-life improvements did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The fundoplication in the surgical arm is part of the comparison: POEM was tested against myotomy-plus-wrap, and its reflux excess is measured against that protected comparator. Non-inferiority on symptoms at 2 years says nothing about Barrett's oesophagus or other long-term reflux consequences.
cards.source: Werner YB et al. Endoscopic or Surgical Myotomy in Patients with Idiopathic Achalasia. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 31800987. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01601678, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Ponds 2019: POEM beat pneumatic dilation at 2 years (success 92% vs 54%), with reflux oesophagitis in 41% vs 7%
cards.summary: Ponds 2019: POEM beat pneumatic dilation at 2 years (success 92% vs 54%), with reflux oesophagitis in 41% vs 7%
cards.people: 133 treatment-naive patients with newly diagnosed achalasia and Eckardt score above 3, randomised to POEM (67) or pneumatic dilation with 30-mm and 35-mm balloons (66); 130 underwent treatment (mean age 48.6 years; 56% men) and 126 completed the 2-year study.
cards.result: Treatment success (Eckardt ≤3 without severe complications or retreatment) at 2 years: 58 of 63 (92%) after POEM versus 34 of 63 (54%) after pneumatic dilation — a difference of 38 percentage points (95% CI 22 to 52; P<0.001). Reflux oesophagitis occurred more often after POEM: 22 of 54 (41%) versus 2 of 29 (7%) (difference 34 points; P=0.002). Two serious adverse events occurred, including one perforation. The abstract text carries no registry ID and the record's databank fields are empty; the trial's Dutch Trial Register number (NTR3593) is taken from the follow-up report's record below.
cards.watchOut: The dilation protocol was a single series of 30–35 mm balloons, and any need for further dilation counted as failure — a definition that stacks long-term results against dilation relative to real-world practice, where repeat dilation is routine management rather than failure.
cards.source: Ponds FA et al. Effect of Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy vs Pneumatic Dilation on Symptom Severity and Treatment Outcomes Among Treatment-Naive Patients With Achalasia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31287522. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (see the follow-up card for the trial's register number). cards.headline: Ponds 5-year follow-up (Kuipers 2022): POEM's advantage over dilation persisted (success 81% vs 40%)
cards.summary: Ponds 5-year follow-up (Kuipers 2022): POEM's advantage over dilation persisted (success 81% vs 40%)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the Ponds randomised trial — the same patients, counted once
cards.people: The Ponds trial cohort (133 randomised); 5-year follow-up data were available for 62 patients in the POEM group and 63 in the pneumatic dilation group.
cards.result: Treatment success at 5 years: 50 of 62 (81%) after POEM versus 25 of 63 (40%) after pneumatic dilation — an adjusted absolute difference of 41 percentage points (95% CI 25 to 57; P<0.0001). Failures after dilation were dominated by no initial effect (12 patients versus 1 after POEM) and recurrent symptoms (11 further patients in the dilation group, per the record).
cards.watchOut: This is a follow-up report of the trial carded above, not a second trial; it is carded separately because the 5-year horizon is where dilation strategies are usually judged, and the trial's success definition (any retreatment = failure) continues to apply.
cards.source: Kuipers T et al. Peroral endoscopic myotomy versus pneumatic dilation in treatment-naive patients with achalasia: 5-year follow-up of a randomised controlled trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 36206786. Registry ID: Dutch Trial Register NTR3593, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials triangulate the achalasia choice — SPLIT as proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: three trials triangulate the achalasia choice — SPLIT as proposed
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: European Achalasia Trial (201 patients), Werner 2019 (221), Ponds 2019 with 5-year follow-up (133).
cards.result: Dilation and Heller myotomy tie at 2 years; POEM ties Heller and beats dilation, including at 5 years. The consistent trade is reflux: POEM leaves the sphincter open without a wrap, and endoscopic reflux follows in roughly two of five patients early on. The choice among three effective options is therefore about durability, retreatment burden, and reflux — not about which one 'works'.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are in treatment-naive patients; none of this evidence addresses POEM or dilation after failed Heller myotomy, or achalasia subtypes managed differently.
cards.source: Synthesis of Boeckxstaens GE et al. 2011 (PMID: 21561346), Werner YB et al. 2019 (PMID: 31800987), Ponds FA et al. 2019 (PMID: 31287522) and Kuipers T et al. 2022 (PMID: 36206786). Registry IDs as on the trial cards.

shelves.title: Vonoprazan for erosive oesophagitis (Laine; Ashida)
shelves.question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, is the potassium-competitive acid blocker vonoprazan non-inferior to lansoprazole for healing at eight weeks and for maintenance of healing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Lansoprazole · Pyrroles · Sulfonamides · Esophagitis · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Peptic Ulcer · Treatment Outcome · (Ashida record: Adult · Aged · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Double-Blind Method · Esophagitis · Female · Humans · Lansoprazole · Male · Middle Aged · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Pyrroles · Recurrence · Sulfonamides · Wound Healing)
shelves.balance: LIKELY. Two independent phase 3 programmes agree. In the US/European trial (Laine), healing by week 8 was 92.9% on vonoprazan versus 84.6% on lansoprazole — non-inferior in the primary analysis and higher on the exploratory analysis, with superiority concentrated in severe (LA grade C/D) disease — and maintenance of healing at 24 weeks was also non-inferior and higher on the secondary analysis (differences 8.7 and 7.2 points for the 20 mg and 10 mg doses). The Japanese programme (Ashida) verified non-inferiority for healing separately (99.0% versus 95.5%). Non-inferiority was the prespecified primary framework in both; the superiority findings ride on prespecified-if-non-inferior or exploratory analyses, and the balance says so. This shelf is vonoprazan for erosive oesophagitis; vonoprazan inside H. pylori regimens is Shelf #777.

cards.headline: Laine 2023: vonoprazan non-inferior for healing (92.9% vs 84.6%) and maintenance, with superiority in severe disease
cards.summary: Laine 2023: vonoprazan non-inferior for healing (92.9% vs 84.6%) and maintenance, with superiority in severe disease
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind non-inferiority trial (healing and maintenance phases)
cards.people: 1,024 adults with erosive oesophagitis randomised to vonoprazan 20 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg once daily for up to 8 weeks; 878 patients whose oesophagitis healed were re-randomised to vonoprazan 10 mg, vonoprazan 20 mg, or lansoprazole 15 mg for 24 weeks of maintenance. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Healing by week 8: 92.9% on vonoprazan versus 84.6% on lansoprazole (difference 8.3 percentage points; 95% CI 4.5 to 12.2) — non-inferior in the primary analysis (10% margin) and superior on the exploratory analysis; heartburn-free days were non-inferior (difference 2.7 points). In LA grade C/D disease, healing at week 2 was superior (difference 17.6 points; 95% CI 7.4 to 27.4). Maintenance of healing at week 24: non-inferior in the primary analysis and superior on the secondary analysis — differences of 8.7 points (20 mg) and 7.2 points (10 mg) versus lansoprazole, and 15.7 and 13.3 points in grade C/D disease.
cards.watchOut: Read the analysis hierarchy honestly: the trials were designed and powered as non-inferiority studies; the superiority language comes from an exploratory analysis (healing) and a secondary analysis (maintenance) conducted under a fixed-sequence procedure if non-inferiority was shown. The benefit is real but its centre of gravity is severe oesophagitis; in mild disease the drugs are close.
cards.source: Laine L et al. Vonoprazan Versus Lansoprazole for Healing and Maintenance of Healing of Erosive Esophagitis: A Randomized Trial. Gastroenterology. 2023. PMID: 36228734. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04124926, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Ashida 2016 (Japanese phase 3): vonoprazan non-inferior for healing (99.0% vs 95.5%)
cards.summary: Ashida 2016 (Japanese phase 3): vonoprazan non-inferior for healing (99.0% vs 95.5%)
cards.people: 409 patients with endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis (LA grades A–D) randomised to vonoprazan 20 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg once daily; 401 completed the comparison study, and 305 with healed oesophagitis entered a 52-week maintenance extension. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Healed oesophagitis by week 8: 99.0% (203 of 205) on vonoprazan versus 95.5% (190 of 199) on lansoprazole, verifying non-inferiority (P<0.0001). Vonoprazan was also effective in LA grade C/D disease and in CYP2C19 extensive metabolisers. In the maintenance extension, recurrences on vonoprazan 10 or 20 mg were few (under 10%, as the abstract states qualitatively). Vonoprazan was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The maintenance arm of this report is an uncontrolled extension after re-randomisation into vonoprazan doses — it carries no lansoprazole comparator, so only the healing comparison is carded as comparative evidence. The same programme's separate randomised maintenance comparison (Ashida 2018, World J Gastroenterol: recurrence 16.8% on lansoprazole 15 mg versus 5.1% and 2.0% on vonoprazan 10 and 20 mg at 24 weeks, non-inferiority verified) is fenced here by name and not carded, to avoid double-counting one programme. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID, and none is invented.

shelves.title: Low-dose amitriptyline as second-line therapy for IBS in primary care (ATLANTIS)
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome whose symptoms persist despite first-line measures, does titrated low-dose amitriptyline improve global symptoms (IBS-SSS) versus placebo at six months?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Amitriptyline · England · Double-Blind Method · Primary Health Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One large, well-conducted primary-care trial: in 463 patients with Rome IV IBS of any subtype and continuing symptoms despite first-line therapy, titrated low-dose amitriptyline (10–30 mg) improved the IBS Severity Scoring System at 6 months by 27.0 points more than placebo (95% CI −46.9 to −7.1 on the between-group difference; P=0.0079). That is a modest average improvement on a 500-point scale, from a single trial — the largest tricyclic trial in IBS, as the authors note, but still one trial. Correction made at build: the topic file cites this trial as Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology; the record's journal is The Lancet (2023;402:1773–1785), and the card follows the record.

cards.headline: ATLANTIS (Ford 2023): low-dose amitriptyline beat placebo by 27 IBS-SSS points at 6 months in primary care
cards.summary: ATLANTIS (Ford 2023): low-dose amitriptyline beat placebo by 27 IBS-SSS points at 6 months in primary care
cards.people: 463 participants (mean age 48.5 years; 68% female) aged 18 or older with Rome IV irritable bowel syndrome of any subtype and ongoing symptoms (IBS-SSS ≥75) despite dietary changes and first-line therapies, recruited at 55 general practices in England; randomised to amitriptyline 10 mg once daily (232) or placebo (231) for 6 months, with self-titration up to 30 mg over 3 weeks.
cards.result: The primary outcome — IBS-SSS at 6 months — favoured amitriptyline by −27.0 points (95% CI −46.9 to −7.10; P=0.0079) in the intention-to-treat analysis. Discontinuation before 6 months: 46 of 232 (20%) on amitriptyline (13% for adverse events) versus 59 of 231 (26%) on placebo (9% for adverse events). Five serious adverse reactions occurred (two on amitriptyline, three on placebo). The trial's registration (ISRCTN48075063) appears in the abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-seven points on a 0–500 symptom scale is a real but modest average effect, and a fifth to a quarter of participants stopped treatment. This is a second-line, any-subtype primary-care population — the result does not identify which IBS subtype benefits most, and older small tricyclic trials are supportive background, not corroborating trials of this question.

shelves.title: Telephone and web cognitive-behavioural therapy for refractory IBS (ACTIB)
shelves.question: In adults with refractory irritable bowel syndrome, does gut-specific CBT — delivered by telephone or web — improve symptom severity versus treatment as usual at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Internet · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Remote Consultation · Severity of Illness Index · Telephone · Treatment Outcome · (follow-up record: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · England · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Male · Middle Aged · Surveys and Questionnaires · Telemedicine · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult)
shelves.balance: SPLIT. One large trial (558 patients with refractory IBS) and its own 24-month follow-up, counted once. At 12 months both formats beat treatment as usual on the IBS Severity Scoring System: telephone CBT by 61.6 points and web CBT by 35.2 points, with parallel gains in work and social adjustment. At 24 months the telephone format's advantage persisted (−40.5 points; P=0.002) while the web format's had attenuated to non-significance (−12.9 points; P=0.33). Corrections made at build: the topic file cites the anchor as Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology — the record's journal is Gut (2019); the Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology paper is the 24-month follow-up. The file's summary ('both formats improved by ~70 points, sustained at 24 months') matches neither the 12-month figures nor the 24-month web-CBT result, and the cards follow the records.

cards.headline: ACTIB (Everitt 2019): telephone CBT improved IBS-SSS by 61.6 points and web CBT by 35.2 points versus usual care at 12 months
cards.summary: ACTIB (Everitt 2019): telephone CBT improved IBS-SSS by 61.6 points and web CBT by 35.2 points versus usual care at 12 months
cards.type: Three-arm, multicentre randomised controlled trial (participants and therapists unblinded; assessors blinded)
cards.people: 558 adults with refractory IBS — clinically significant symptoms for at least 12 months despite first-line therapies — recruited from 74 general practices and three gastroenterology centres in London and the south of England (76% female; 91% white; mean age 43 years); 70.1% completed 12-month follow-up. Interventions: telephone-delivered CBT, web-based CBT with minimal therapist support, or treatment as usual.
cards.result: Co-primary outcomes at 12 months. IBS-SSS (usual care 205.6): 61.6 points lower with telephone CBT (95% CI 33.8 to 89.5; P<0.001) and 35.2 points lower with web CBT (12.6 to 57.8; P=0.002). Work and Social Adjustment Scale (usual care 10.8): 3.5 points lower (P<0.001) and 3.0 points lower (P=0.001) respectively. All secondary outcomes also favoured both CBT formats (P≤0.002). There were no serious adverse reactions.
cards.watchOut: A behavioural intervention cannot be blinded to participants, and the comparator is usual care, not an attention control — expectancy and therapist contact are part of what was tested. Thirty per cent of randomised patients did not complete 12-month follow-up.
cards.source: Everitt HA et al. cards.type: Non-prespecified naturalistic follow-up of the ACTIB randomised trial — the same patients, counted once
cards.people: The ACTIB cohort (558 randomised); 24-month outcomes were obtained for 323 participants (58%) — 119 of 186 in the telephone-CBT group, 99 of 185 in the web-CBT group, and 105 of 187 in the usual-care group.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean IBS-SSS was 40.5 points lower in the telephone-CBT group than usual care (95% CI 15.0 to 66.0; P=0.002) and 12.9 points lower in the web-CBT group (−12.9 to 38.8; P=0.33 — not significant). Work and Social Adjustment scores remained lower in both CBT groups: 3.1 points (P<0.001) for telephone CBT and 1.9 points for web CBT, per the record.
cards.watchOut: This follow-up was not prespecified and retained only 58% of the cohort; attrition of that size can manufacture or erase differences. The divergence between formats at 24 months is a finding about durability of a lightly-supported web programme, not proof the web format never works — its 12-month result stands on the card above.

shelves.title: Tenapanor for IBS with constipation (T3MPO-1 and T3MPO-2)
shelves.question: In adults with IBS-C, does tenapanor 50 mg twice daily increase the proportion achieving a combined pain-and-stool responder endpoint versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adult · Constipation · Deprescriptions · Diarrhea · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Isoquinolines · Male · Middle Aged · Sodium-Hydrogen Exchanger 3 · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · (T3MPO-2 record: Abdominal Pain · Constipation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Isoquinolines · Male · Middle Aged · Sulfonamides)
shelves.balance: LIKELY. Two phase 3 trials, both positive on the same combined responder endpoint: 27.0% versus 18.7% in T3MPO-1 (12 weeks; P=0.020) and 36.5% versus 23.7% in T3MPO-2 (the 6-of-12-week responder over a 26-week trial; P<0.001). Absolute gains are 8–13 percentage points, and diarrhoea is the price (discontinuation for diarrhoea 6.5% versus 0.7% in both trials). Two concordant trials: LIKELY. This shelf is tenapanor for IBS-C; tenapanor for hyperphosphataemia in dialysis is Shelf #1057.

cards.headline: T3MPO-1 (Chey 2020): tenapanor's combined responder rate was 27.0% versus 18.7% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.summary: T3MPO-1 (Chey 2020): tenapanor's combined responder rate was 27.0% versus 18.7% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (with a 4-week randomised withdrawal period)
cards.people: 629 patients with IBS with constipation randomised to tenapanor 50 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks; the intention-to-treat set was 606 (307 tenapanor, 299 placebo), mean age 45 years, 81.4% women; 84.7% completed the treatment period.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — at least a 30% reduction in average weekly worst abdominal pain and an increase of at least one complete spontaneous bowel movement from baseline, in the same week, for at least 6 of the 12 weeks — was met by 27.0% on tenapanor versus 18.7% on placebo (P=0.020). Abdominal and global IBS symptoms also improved (P<0.05). Diarrhoea was the commonest adverse event and caused discontinuation in 6.5% on tenapanor versus 0.7% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The responder bar is a composite requiring simultaneous pain and stool response sustained over half the trial — a stringent definition that keeps absolute rates low in both arms; conversely, it means the 8-point separation is a difference in genuine combined response, not in a single symptom.
