shelves.title: Endoscopic versus surgical drainage for painful chronic pancreatitis (Cahen; ESCAPE)
shelves.question: In patients with painful chronic pancreatitis and an obstructed, dilated pancreatic duct, does surgical drainage relieve pain more durably than endoscopic drainage?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calculi · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde · Constriction, Pathologic · Drainage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lithotripsy · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Pain Management · Pancreatic Ducts · Pancreaticojejunostomy · Pancreatitis, Chronic · Sphincterotomy, Endoscopic · Stents · (ESCAPE record: Adult · Analgesics, Opioid · Area Under Curve · Calculi · Drainage · Endoscopy · Female · Humans · Lithotripsy · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Pancreatic Ducts · Pancreatitis, Chronic)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Two small, necessarily unblinded Dutch trials point the same way on pain scores. Cahen (39 patients): surgical drainage produced lower Izbicki pain scores over 24 months (25 versus 51; P<0.001) and more complete or partial pain relief at the end of follow-up (75% versus 32%; P=0.007), with a median of 3 procedures versus 8. ESCAPE (88 patients) compared timing strategies — early surgery versus an endoscopy-first step-up: the integrated 18-month Izbicki score was lower with early surgery (37 versus 49; P=0.02), though end-of-follow-up pain relief was not significantly different (58% versus 39%; P=0.10) and mortality was 0% in both groups. Subjective endpoints, no blinding, and small samples cap this at POSSIBLE; the two trials also ask related but distinct questions (modality in Cahen; timing/strategy in ESCAPE), and the cards keep them distinct.

cards.headline: Cahen 2007: surgical drainage beat endoscopic drainage on pain (Izbicki 25 vs 51; relief 75% vs 32% at 2 years)
cards.summary: Cahen 2007: surgical drainage beat endoscopic drainage on pain (Izbicki 25 vs 51; relief 75% vs 32% at 2 years)
cards.people: 39 symptomatic patients with chronic pancreatitis and a distal obstruction of the pancreatic duct without an inflammatory mass, randomised to endoscopic transampullary drainage (19; 16 with lithotripsy) or operative pancreaticojejunostomy (20), followed for 24 months. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — average Izbicki pain score over 2 years — was 25 after surgery versus 51 after endoscopic drainage (P<0.001). Complete or partial pain relief at the end of follow-up: 75% surgical versus 32% endoscopic (P=0.007). Physical health scores favoured surgery (P=0.003). Complications, hospital stay, and pancreatic-function changes were similar, but endoscopic patients required more procedures (median 8 versus 3; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine patients is a very small base for a surgical-versus-endoscopic verdict, and pain — the endpoint — is exactly the outcome most open to expectation effects in an unblinded trial. The result is influential because it was first and large in effect, not because it is precise.
cards.source: Cahen DL et al. Endoscopic versus surgical drainage of the pancreatic duct in chronic pancreatitis. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17301298. cards.summary: ESCAPE (Issa 2020): early surgery beat an endoscopy-first strategy on integrated pain (37 vs 49), not on end-of-study relief (58% vs 39%, P=0.10)
cards.people: 88 patients with painful chronic pancreatitis, a dilated main pancreatic duct, and only recent opioid use (strong opioids ≤2 months or weak opioids ≤6 months), randomised at 30 Dutch hospitals to early surgical drainage within 6 weeks (44) or an endoscopy-first approach — medical treatment, endoscopy with lithotripsy if needed, surgery if needed (44); mean age 52 years, 24% women; 85 (97%) completed the 18-month follow-up.
cards.result: The primary outcome — Izbicki pain score integrated over 18 months — was 37 with early surgery versus 49 with the endoscopy-first approach (between-group difference −12 points; 95% CI −22 to −2; P=0.02). Complete or partial pain relief at the end of follow-up: 58% (23 of 40) versus 39% (16 of 41) (P=0.10 — not significant). Total interventions: median 1 versus 3 (P<0.001). Treatment complications (27% versus 25%), hospital admissions, pancreatic function, quality of life, and mortality (0% in both groups) did not differ significantly. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID, and none is invented.
cards.watchOut: ESCAPE is a strategy trial: the endoscopy-first arm could and did cross to surgery, so it tests timing, not endoscopy's intrinsic effect — pooling it naively with Cahen would blur exactly the distinction that matters. Its headline pain-relief proportion at study end is a null result (P=0.10) even though the integrated score is positive; the card prints both.

shelves.title: Same-admission versus interval cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis (PONCHO)
shelves.question: In mild gallstone pancreatitis, does cholecystectomy during the same admission reduce gallstone-related complications or readmission versus interval cholecystectomy weeks later?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cholecystectomy · Female · Gallstones · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf 'Tier C: No', but PONCHO's primary endpoint is a composite of readmission for recurrent gallstone-related complications OR MORTALITY within 6 months — a composite embedding death — so it is ruled Tier C at build under the library's rule. No mortality claim is made or supported: the abstract does not print the mortality component separately, and the only deaths-adjacent statement in the record is that none of the four cholecystectomy-related serious adverse events led to death. On the composite itself, same-admission cholecystectomy clearly won: 5% (6 of 128) versus 17% (23 of 136); risk ratio 0.28 relative (95% CI 0.12 to 0.66; P=0.002), with one bile-duct leak and one postoperative bleed in each group. One trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PONCHO (da Costa 2015): same-admission cholecystectomy cut the primary composite to 5% versus 17% (RR 0.28)
cards.summary: PONCHO (da Costa 2015): same-admission cholecystectomy cut the primary composite to 5% versus 17% (RR 0.28)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised controlled superiority trial (assessor-masked; participants and investigators unmasked)
cards.people: 266 inpatients recovering from mild gallstone pancreatitis at 23 Dutch hospitals, randomised to cholecystectomy within 3 days of randomisation (129) or discharge with cholecystectomy 25–30 days later (137); the primary analysis included 128 and 136 patients. Eligibility required a C-reactive protein below 100 mg/L, no opioid need, and tolerance of a normal diet; the abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a composite of readmission for recurrent gallstone-related complications (pancreatitis, cholangitis, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis needing intervention, or gallstone colic) or mortality within 6 months — occurred in 6 of 128 patients (5%) after same-admission cholecystectomy versus 23 of 136 (17%) after interval cholecystectomy (risk ratio 0.28 relative; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.66; P=0.002). Safety events: one bile-duct leakage and one postoperative bleed in each group, all judged treatment-related, none leading to death.
cards.watchOut: Tier C note for the developer: mortality is a named component of the primary composite, but the record never decomposes the composite — the trial's verdict is about recurrent gallstone events, and the card does not convert it into any survival statement. The population is specifically mild pancreatitis in patients already recovering; the result does not extend to moderately severe or necrotising pancreatitis.
cards.source: da Costa DW et al. Same-admission versus interval cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis (PONCHO): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 26460661. Registry ID: ISRCTN72764151, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: operate during the index admission in mild gallstone pancreatitis — POSSIBLE (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.summary: Synthesis: operate during the index admission in mild gallstone pancreatitis — POSSIBLE (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: PONCHO (da Costa et al., Lancet 2015), 266 patients.
cards.result: Waiting 25–30 days for interval cholecystectomy exposed one patient in six to a recurrent gallstone complication or readmission; operating during the same admission reduced that to one in twenty without a detectable surgical-safety penalty. A single trial with a large, mechanistically unsurprising effect: POSSIBLE, and Tier C only because the composite's wording includes mortality.
cards.watchOut: Systems that cannot offer timely index-admission surgery face the trial's real-world question — how long an interval is too long — which PONCHO does not dose out.

shelves.title: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus percutaneous drainage in high-risk acute cholecystitis (CHOCOLATE)
shelves.question: In high-risk patients (APACHE II ≥7) with acute cholecystitis, does laparoscopic cholecystectomy reduce major complications versus percutaneous catheter drainage?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Aged · Cholecystectomy, Laparoscopic · Cholecystitis · Drainage · Female · Humans · Male · Netherlands · Postoperative Complications · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf 'Tier C: No', but the record states the trial's primary endpoints were death within one year AND major complications — a mortality-bearing primary endpoint — so it is ruled Tier C at build under the library's rule. On mortality itself the trial is neutral and says so: death within one year was 3% after cholecystectomy versus 9% after drainage (P=0.27), and no mortality claim is made or supported. The complications verdict is decisive: major complications in 12% (8 of 66) versus 65% (44 of 68) (risk ratio 0.19 relative; P<0.001), driven by reinterventions (12% versus 66%) and recurrent biliary disease (5% versus 53%). One trial, stopped early at a planned interim analysis: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CHOCOLATE (Loozen 2018): cholecystectomy cut major complications to 12% versus 65% after drainage; death did not differ (3% vs 9%)
cards.summary: CHOCOLATE (Loozen 2018): cholecystectomy cut major complications to 12% versus 65% after drainage; death did not differ (3% vs 9%)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised controlled superiority trial, concluded early after a planned interim analysis
cards.people: 142 high-risk patients (APACHE II score ≥7) with acute calculous cholecystitis at 11 Dutch hospitals, randomised to laparoscopic cholecystectomy (66 treated) or percutaneous catheter drainage (68 treated). The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoints were death within one year and major complications (infectious and cardiopulmonary complications within one month, reintervention within one year, or recurrent biliary disease within one year). Death did not differ: 3% after cholecystectomy versus 9% after drainage (P=0.27). Major complications occurred in 8 of 66 (12%) versus 44 of 68 (65%) (risk ratio 0.19 relative; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.37; P<0.001). Reintervention was required by 8 (12%) versus 45 (66%) patients (P<0.001); recurrent biliary disease in 5% versus 53% (P<0.001); median hospital stay 5 versus 9 days (P<0.001). The trial's registration (Dutch Trial Register NTR2666) appears in the abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping at an interim analysis inflates effect sizes on average, and a 65% major-complication rate in the drainage arm is doing heavy lifting — much of it is reintervention and recurrence, the known failure modes of a temporising strategy, rather than immediate harm. The mortality neutrality (3% versus 9%, P=0.27) is itself imprecise: 134 treated patients cannot exclude a real survival difference in either direction, and none is claimed.
cards.source: Loozen CS et al. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus percutaneous catheter drainage for acute cholecystitis in high risk patients (CHOCOLATE): multicentre randomised clinical trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2018. PMID: 30297544. Registry ID: Dutch Trial Register NTR2666, appearing in the abstract text only; the record's databank fields carry no registry ID. cards.headline: Synthesis: in high-risk cholecystitis, definitive surgery beats temporising drainage on complications — POSSIBLE (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in high-risk cholecystitis, definitive surgery beats temporising drainage on complications — POSSIBLE (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: CHOCOLATE (Loozen et al., BMJ 2018), 134 treated patients.
cards.result: CHOCOLATE reversed the presumption that the sickest cholecystitis patients are best served by the least invasive option: drainage mostly deferred the problem into reinterventions and recurrences, while cholecystectomy's upfront risk did not translate into more deaths. Tier C attaches because death within one year was a primary endpoint — on which the trial was neutral — not because any mortality benefit is claimed.
cards.watchOut: APACHE II ≥7 defines 'high-risk' here; patients too unstable for any anaesthesia were not the trial's population, and the result should not be stretched to them.

shelves.title: Ursodeoxycholic acid to prevent gallstones after bariatric surgery (UPGRADE)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing bariatric surgery, does six months of ursodeoxycholic acid reduce symptomatic gallstone disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bariatric Surgery · Case-Control Studies · Cholagogues and Choleretics · Cholelithiasis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrectomy · Gastric Bypass · Humans · Laparoscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Obesity, Morbid · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Placebos · Postoperative Complications · Safety · Treatment Outcome · Ursodeoxycholic Acid
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The primary analysis in all randomised patients was null: symptomatic gallstone disease within 24 months occurred in 6.5% on ursodeoxycholic acid versus 9.7% on placebo (relative risk 0.67 relative; 95% CI 0.43 to 1.04; P=0.071). A prespecified subgroup analysis, backed by a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction (P=0.046), separates the result: in patients without gallstones at baseline the relative risk was 0.47 (0.27 to 0.84; P=0.0081) — and 0.37 in the Roux-en-Y subgroup — while in patients with asymptomatic gallstones at baseline there was no effect (1.22; 0.61 to 2.47). Correction made at build: the topic file's headline figures (1.6% versus 4.4%) do not appear in the trial's record; the card prints the record's own rates (6.5% versus 9.7% overall) and attributes the benefit to the subgroup where the record puts it.

cards.headline: UPGRADE (Haal 2021): UDCA missed its primary endpoint overall (6.5% vs 9.7%; P=0.071) but worked in patients without baseline gallstones (RR 0.47)
cards.summary: UPGRADE (Haal 2021): UDCA missed its primary endpoint overall (6.5% vs 9.7%; P=0.071) but worked in patients without baseline gallstones (RR 0.47)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled superiority trial
cards.people: 985 patients with an intact gallbladder scheduled for laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy at three Dutch hospitals, randomised to ursodeoxycholic acid 900 mg daily for 6 months (492) or placebo (493); the modified intention-to-treat population was 967, of whom 959 had primary-endpoint data; 189 (20%) had asymptomatic gallstones at baseline and 78 (8%) had a sleeve gastrectomy. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Symptomatic gallstone disease within 24 months: 31 of 475 (6.5%) on ursodeoxycholic acid versus 47 of 484 (9.7%) on placebo (relative risk 0.67 relative; 95% CI 0.43 to 1.04; P=0.071 — not significant). The prespecified interaction between treatment and baseline gallstones was significant (P=0.046): without baseline gallstones, relative risk 0.47 (0.27 to 0.84; P=0.0081), and 0.37 (0.20 to 0.71; P=0.0016) in the Roux-en-Y subgroup; with baseline gallstones, relative risk 1.22 (0.61 to 2.47; P=0.57). Adverse events were rare. The trial's registration (Netherlands Trial Register NL5954) appears in the abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty.
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis governs the shelf's headline: UPGRADE did not significantly prevent symptomatic gallstone disease in the whole randomised population. The subgroup claim is stronger than most — prespecified stratification with a significant interaction — but it remains a subgroup of a null trial, and the sleeve-gastrectomy subgroup was too small to judge.
cards.source: Haal S et al. Ursodeoxycholic acid for the prevention of symptomatic gallstone disease after bariatric surgery (UPGRADE): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled superiority trial. The lancet. shelves.title: ZED1227, a transglutaminase-2 inhibitor, for coeliac disease
shelves.question: In adults with coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet, does oral ZED1227 prevent gluten-challenge-induced duodenal mucosal injury versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Celiac Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Duodenum · Female · GTP-Binding Proteins · Glutens · Humans · Imidazoles · Intestinal Mucosa · Lymphocyte Count · Male · Middle Aged · Proof of Concept Study · Protein Glutamine gamma Glutamyltransferase 2 · Pyridines · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Transglutaminases
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single phase 2 proof-of-concept trial on a surrogate endpoint, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. In 163 adults with well-controlled coeliac disease undergoing a daily gluten challenge for 6 weeks, ZED1227 attenuated mucosal injury at all three doses: the difference from placebo in the change in villus-height-to-crypt-depth ratio was 0.44 (10 mg; P=0.001), 0.49 (50 mg; P<0.001), and 0.48 (100 mg; P<0.001), with intraepithelial lymphocyte density reduced significantly only at 100 mg, and possible symptom and quality-of-life improvement at that dose in the authors' cautious wording. Histology after an artificial challenge is not a clinical outcome — no data here address symptoms on a real-world diet, serology, or long-term safety. One phase 2 trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ZED1227 trial (Schuppan 2021): the transglutaminase-2 inhibitor attenuated gluten-induced mucosal injury at all doses over 6 weeks
cards.summary: ZED1227 trial (Schuppan 2021): the transglutaminase-2 inhibitor attenuated gluten-induced mucosal injury at all doses over 6 weeks
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled proof-of-concept trial with gluten challenge
cards.people: 163 adults with well-controlled coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet, assigned to ZED1227 10 mg (41), 50 mg (41), or 100 mg (41) or placebo (40) daily during a 6-week daily gluten challenge; adequate duodenal biopsies for the primary endpoint were available in 35, 39, 38, and 30 patients respectively. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — attenuation of gluten-induced mucosal damage, measured by the change in the ratio of villus height to crypt depth — favoured ZED1227 at every dose: estimated differences from placebo of 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.73; P=0.001) at 10 mg, 0.49 (0.20 to 0.77; P<0.001) at 50 mg, and 0.48 (0.20 to 0.77; P<0.001) at 100 mg. Differences in intraepithelial lymphocyte density were −2.7 and −4.2 cells per 100 epithelial cells at 10 and 50 mg (intervals crossing zero) and −9.6 (−14.4 to −4.8) at 100 mg. The authors state the 100-mg dose 'may have improved' symptom and quality-of-life scores. Rash occurred in 3 of 40 patients (8%) at 100 mg; other common adverse events were similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: A challenge trial in volunteers with well-controlled disease is a pharmacology demonstration, not evidence that patients can relax a gluten-free diet — no such claim is in the record or on this shelf. The flat dose-response on the primary endpoint (0.44/0.49/0.48) also argues for reading the result as a threshold effect rather than a graded one.
cards.source: Schuppan D et al. A Randomized Trial of a Transglutaminase 2 Inhibitor for Celiac Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34192430. cards.headline: Synthesis: mechanism proven in humans, clinical value unproven — POSSIBLE, exception candidate
cards.summary: Synthesis: mechanism proven in humans, clinical value unproven — POSSIBLE, exception candidate
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: the ZED1227 proof-of-concept trial (Schuppan et al., N Engl J Med 2021), 163 patients.
cards.result: ZED1227 establishes that oral transglutaminase-2 inhibition protects the coeliac mucosa against a controlled gluten insult — the first drug class to do so in a randomised trial. Whether that becomes a therapy depends on trials with clinical endpoints in patients eating real diets, which do not yet exist in this record.

shelves.title: Tenofovir in pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child hepatitis B transmission (Pan; Jourdain)
shelves.question: In pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B and high viral load (HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL), does tenofovir disoproxil from weeks 30–32 of gestation reduce mother-to-child transmission versus no antiviral therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alanine Transaminase · Antiviral Agents · China · Congenital Abnormalities · Creatine Kinase · DNA, Viral · Female · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical · Intention to Treat Analysis · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Pregnancy Trimester, Third · Tenofovir · Viral Load · Young Adult · (Jourdain record: Adolescent · Adult · Alanine Transaminase · Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis B · Hepatitis B Vaccines · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical · Male · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Tenofovir · Viral Load · Young Adult)
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two trials differ in context, and the cards do not average them. Pan (China; HBeAg-positive mothers, HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL; tenofovir versus usual care without antiviral therapy): mother-to-child transmission at postpartum week 28 was 5% versus 18% by intention to treat (P=0.007) and 0% versus 7% per protocol. Jourdain (Thailand; double-blind, placebo-controlled; infants received hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine within a median of about 1.2–1.3 hours of birth): transmission was 0% (0 of 147) versus 2% (3 of 147) — not significant (P=0.12) — because transmission with vigorous immunoprophylaxis alone was already low. Both findings stand: tenofovir clearly reduces transmission where background transmission is high; its added value where immunoprophylaxis is prompt and complete is unproven on these numbers.

cards.headline: Pan 2016: tenofovir cut mother-to-child transmission to 5% versus 18% (intention to treat) and 0% versus 7% (per protocol)
cards.summary: Pan 2016: tenofovir cut mother-to-child transmission to 5% versus 18% (intention to treat) and 0% versus 7% (per protocol)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (open; usual-care control without antiviral therapy)
cards.people: 200 HBeAg-positive mothers in China with HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL, randomised 1:1 to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg daily from 30–32 weeks of gestation until postpartum week 4, or usual care without antiviral therapy; all infants received immunoprophylaxis; follow-up to postpartum week 28. The abstract does not print mean maternal age.
cards.result: At delivery, 68% of tenofovir mothers (66 of 97) versus 2% of controls (2 of 100) had HBV DNA below 200,000 IU/mL (P<0.001). Mother-to-child transmission at postpartum week 28: 5% (5 of 97) versus 18% (18 of 100) by intention to treat (P=0.007), and 0% versus 7% (6 of 88) per protocol (P=0.01). Birth-defect rates were similar (2% versus 1%; P=1.00); more tenofovir mothers had creatine kinase increases, and after tenofovir was stopped, alanine aminotransferase elevations were more frequent (45% versus 30%; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: The control arm received no antiviral and no placebo, and the trial was not blinded; the per-protocol 0% is a completer figure and the intention-to-treat 5% versus 18% is the primary reading. Post-treatment ALT flares (45%) are part of the bargain of stopping tenofovir after delivery and belong in counselling.

cards.summary: Jourdain 2018: with prompt HBIG and vaccine, adding tenofovir did not significantly reduce transmission (0% vs 2%; P=0.12)
cards.people: 331 HBeAg-positive pregnant women in Thailand with alanine aminotransferase of 60 IU/L or less, randomised to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (168) or placebo (163) from 28 weeks of gestation to 2 months postpartum; infants received hepatitis B immune globulin at birth (median 1.3 hours) and hepatitis B vaccine at birth and at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months (median first dose at 1.2 hours); the primary analysis included 147 infants per group.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — infant HBsAg positivity confirmed by HBV DNA at 6 months — occurred in 0 of 147 infants (0%; 95% CI 0 to 2) in the tenofovir group versus 3 of 147 (2%; 0 to 6) in the placebo group (P=0.12 — not significant). Note the population difference too: Jourdain required ALT ≤60 IU/L and did not restrict entry by the viral-load threshold in Pan.

cards.headline: Synthesis: context decides — tenofovir's benefit is proven where transmission risk is high — SPLIT as proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: context decides — tenofovir's benefit is proven where transmission risk is high — SPLIT as proposed
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Pan 2016 (200 mothers) and Jourdain 2018 (331 mothers).
cards.result: Read together, the pair support tenofovir for HBeAg-positive mothers with high viral load — Pan's population — while showing that where infants reliably receive HBIG and vaccine within hours, residual transmission is already around 2% and a further drug effect is hard to demonstrate. Policy turns on which of those two worlds a given maternity service inhabits.

shelves.title: Obeticholic acid for primary biliary cholangitis (POISE)
shelves.question: In primary biliary cholangitis with an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid, does obeticholic acid achieve the composite biochemical endpoint (alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin thresholds) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase · Bile Acids and Salts · Bone Density · Chenodeoxycholic Acid · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factors · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary · Male · Middle Aged · Pruritus
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One pivotal trial on a biochemical surrogate: in POISE (216 dosed patients), the composite endpoint — alkaline phosphatase below 1.67 times the upper limit of normal with at least a 15% reduction, and normal bilirubin — was reached by 46% (5–10 mg titration group) and 47% (10 mg) versus 10% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). The price was pruritus (56% and 68% versus 38%) and more serious adverse events (16% and 11% versus 4%). Non-invasive fibrosis measures did not differ at 12 months, and the trial says nothing about transplant-free survival. A single trial with a surrogate endpoint, in a rare disease — flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. This shelf is the POISE question; elafibranor and seladelpar as second-line PBC therapy are Shelf #1062.

cards.headline: POISE (Nevens 2016): obeticholic acid met the biochemical composite in 46–47% versus 10% on placebo, with more pruritus and serious adverse events
cards.summary: POISE (Nevens 2016): obeticholic acid met the biochemical composite in 46–47% versus 10% on placebo, with more pruritus and serious adverse events
cards.people: 217 patients with primary biliary cholangitis and an inadequate response to ursodiol, or who could not tolerate it, randomised to obeticholic acid 10 mg, obeticholic acid 5 mg with titration to 10 mg, or placebo for 12 months; 216 received at least one dose and 93% were on background ursodiol. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (alkaline phosphatase <1.67× the upper limit of normal with a reduction of at least 15% from baseline, and a normal total bilirubin) occurred in 46% of the 5–10-mg group and 47% of the 10-mg group versus 10% on placebo (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Alkaline phosphatase fell by least-squares mean −113 and −130 U/L versus −14 U/L; bilirubin changed by −0.02 and −0.05 mg/dL versus +0.12 mg/dL. Changes in non-invasive fibrosis measures did not differ significantly at 12 months. Pruritus occurred in 56% and 68% on obeticholic acid versus 38% on placebo; serious adverse events in 16%, 11%, and 4% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The composite is built from two laboratory thresholds that predict outcomes at cohort level; POISE itself measured no clinical outcome — no deaths, transplants, or decompensations are compared — and no such claim is made on this shelf. The serious-adverse-event gradient (up to fourfold placebo) sits in the same record as the benefit and should not be separated from it.

shelves.title: Budesonide versus prednisone for autoimmune hepatitis (Manns)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive autoimmune hepatitis without cirrhosis, does budesonide plus azathioprine induce biochemical remission with fewer steroid-specific side effects than prednisone plus azathioprine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Budesonide · Child · Double-Blind Method · Female · HLA-DR3 Antigen · Hepatitis, Autoimmune · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One randomised trial (203 patients, non-cirrhotic, treatment-naive): the primary endpoint — complete biochemical remission WITHOUT predefined steroid-specific side effects at 6 months — was achieved by 47.0% on budesonide versus 18.4% on prednisone (P<0.001). Its two components also each favoured budesonide: remission 60% versus 38.8%, and freedom from steroid-specific side effects 72.0% versus 46.6%. Correction made at build: the topic file presents '60% versus 38.8%' as the remission-without-side-effects result; the record shows those are the remission-only figures, and the composite primary is 47.0% versus 18.4% — the card leads with the composite. One trial in a selected non-cirrhotic population: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Manns 2010: budesonide beat prednisone on remission without steroid side effects (47.0% vs 18.4%) and on remission alone (60% vs 38.8%)
cards.summary: Manns 2010: budesonide beat prednisone on remission without steroid side effects (47.0% vs 18.4%) and on remission alone (60% vs 38.8%)
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled multicentre trial (6-month double-blind phase, then open-label budesonide)
cards.people: 203 patients with autoimmune hepatitis without evidence of cirrhosis, randomised to budesonide 3 mg three times daily (or twice daily) plus azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day (100 patients) or prednisone 40 mg/day tapered to 10 mg/day plus azathioprine (103). The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — complete biochemical remission (normal AST and ALT) without predefined steroid-specific side effects at 6 months — was achieved by 47 of 100 patients (47.0%) on budesonide versus 19 of 103 (18.4%) on prednisone (P<0.001). Complete biochemical remission alone: 60% versus 38.8% (P=0.001). Freedom from steroid-specific side effects: 72.0% versus 46.6% (P<0.001). Among the 87 prednisone patients switched to budesonide for the open-label phase, steroid-specific side effects fell from 44.8% to 26.4% at month 12 (P<0.002).
cards.watchOut: The population excludes cirrhosis — precisely the patients in whom budesonide's first-pass advantage is lost through portosystemic shunting — so the result cannot be extended to cirrhotic autoimmune hepatitis. Six months of double-blind follow-up in a lifelong disease is induction evidence, not maintenance evidence. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID (a 2010 trial), and none is invented.
cards.source: Manns MP et al. Budesonide induces remission more effectively than prednisone in a controlled trial of patients with autoimmune hepatitis. Gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 20600032. shelves.title: N-acetylcysteine in non-acetaminophen acute liver failure (Lee)
shelves.question: In early-stage non-acetaminophen acute liver failure, does intravenous N-acetylcysteine improve transplant-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Acetylcysteine · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Failure, Acute · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Rate · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: survival is the trial's primary outcome). Lee (173 patients): the primary outcome, overall survival at 3 weeks, did not significantly differ (70% versus 66%; one-sided P=0.283). Transplant-free survival — a secondary outcome — favoured N-acetylcysteine overall (40% versus 27%; one-sided P=0.043), driven entirely by patients with coma grades I–II (52% versus 30%; one-sided P=0.010); in coma grades III–IV the direction reversed numerically (9% versus 22%; one-sided P=0.912). Correction made at build: the topic file states transplant-free survival 'improved overall (52% vs 30%)' — those are the grade I–II subgroup figures; the overall transplant-free figures are 40% versus 27%, and the card leads with the primary outcome, as the record does. All of the trial's headline P values are one-sided, which the card states wherever they appear.

cards.headline: Lee 2009: NAC missed on overall survival (70% vs 66%) but improved transplant-free survival in early coma grades only (52% vs 30%)
cards.summary: Lee 2009: NAC missed on overall survival (70% vs 66%) but improved transplant-free survival in early coma grades only (52% vs 30%)
cards.people: 173 patients with acute liver failure without clinical or historical evidence of acetaminophen overdose, stratified by site and coma grade, randomised to intravenous N-acetylcysteine (81) or placebo (dextrose) infusion (92) for 72 hours. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Primary outcome — overall survival at 3 weeks: 70% on N-acetylcysteine versus 66% on placebo (one-sided P=0.283 — not significant). Transplant-free survival: 40% versus 27% (one-sided P=0.043). By coma grade: in the 114 patients with grades I–II, transplant-free survival was 52% on NAC versus 30% on placebo (one-sided P=0.010); in the 59 patients with grades III–IV, it was 9% versus 22% (one-sided P=0.912). The transplantation rate was lower on NAC but not significantly (32% versus 45%; P=0.093). Nausea and vomiting were more frequent on NAC (14% versus 4%; P=0.031).
cards.watchOut: Every supportive figure on this card is either a secondary outcome, a subgroup, or both, and every P value the record prints for them is one-sided — a two-sided convention would roughly double them. The grades III–IV reversal (9% versus 22%) is not significant either, but it forecloses any 'give it to everyone' reading: the record's benefit is early-stage only, exactly as the shelf's question specifies. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Glucocorticoids plus N-acetylcysteine in severe alcoholic hepatitis (Nguyen-Khac)
shelves.question: In severe alcoholic hepatitis, does adding intravenous N-acetylcysteine to prednisolone reduce mortality at six months versus prednisolone alone?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcysteine · Antioxidants · Bilirubin · Cause of Death · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids · Hepatitis, Alcoholic · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisolone · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is the primary outcome). One trial (174 patients): the primary outcome, 6-month mortality, was 27% with prednisolone plus N-acetylcysteine versus 38% with prednisolone alone — not significant (P=0.07). One-month mortality was significantly lower (8% versus 24%; P=0.006), as were deaths from hepatorenal syndrome at 6 months (9% versus 22%; P=0.02) and infections overall (P=0.001). A null primary with coherent early secondary signals earns POSSIBLE, no more. This shelf is the NAC add-on question; prednisolone versus pentoxifylline is Shelf #1061 (STOPAH).

cards.headline: Nguyen-Khac 2011: adding NAC to prednisolone missed the 6-month mortality endpoint (27% vs 38%; P=0.07) but cut 1-month mortality (8% vs 24%)
cards.summary: Nguyen-Khac 2011: adding NAC to prednisolone missed the 6-month mortality endpoint (27% vs 38%; P=0.07) but cut 1-month mortality (8% vs 24%)
cards.people: 174 patients with severe acute alcoholic hepatitis, randomised to prednisolone plus intravenous N-acetylcysteine (85) or prednisolone alone (89); all received 4 weeks of prednisolone, and the NAC group received NAC on days 1–5 (day 1: 150, 50, and 100 mg/kg in sequence; days 2–5: 100 mg/kg/day), while controls received glucose infusions. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality at 6 months (the primary outcome): 27% in the prednisolone–NAC group versus 38% in the prednisolone-only group (P=0.07 — not significant). Mortality at 1 month: 8% versus 24% (P=0.006); at 3 months: 22% versus 34% (P=0.06). Death due to hepatorenal syndrome at 6 months: 9% versus 22% (P=0.02). Infections were less frequent with NAC (P=0.001); other side effects were similar.
cards.watchOut: The pattern — early benefit washing out by 6 months — is the classic alcoholic-hepatitis trial shape, and the secondary outcomes here are numerous enough that multiplicity deserves weight: 1-month mortality, hepatorenal deaths, and infections all point the same way, but none was the primary endpoint. Multivariable analysis in the record attributes 6-month survival to age, prothrombin time, and bilirubin trajectory — not to randomised group. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nguyen-Khac E et al. Glucocorticoids plus N-acetylcysteine in severe alcoholic hepatitis. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 22070475. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00863785, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Norfloxacin primary prophylaxis in advanced cirrhosis (Fernández; NORFLOCIR)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh ≥9) and low ascitic protein, does long-term norfloxacin prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and improve survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Infective Agents · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatorenal Syndrome · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Norfloxacin · Peritonitis · Risk Factors · Survival Analysis · (NORFLOCIR record: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Ascites · Double-Blind Method · Female · France · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Norfloxacin · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome)
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both trials test survival). Fernández (68 patients meeting strict criteria — Child-Pugh ≥9 with bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL or renal dysfunction, ascitic protein <15 g/L): norfloxacin reduced the 1-year probability of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (7% versus 61%; P<0.001) and hepatorenal syndrome (28% versus 41%; P=0.02) and improved survival at 3 months (94% versus 62%; P=0.003) and 1 year (60% versus 48%; P=0.05). NORFLOCIR (291 patients with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, a broader population): the primary analysis — Kaplan–Meier 6-month mortality — was null (14.8% versus 19.7%; P=0.21); a competing-risk analysis favoured norfloxacin (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.59 relative), concentrated in patients with ascitic protein below 15 g/L (0.35) and absent above it (1.39). The small, narrow trial is positive; the large, broad trial's primary is null; the overlap between them is the low-ascitic-protein population. SPLIT, Tier C.

cards.headline: Fernández 2007: norfloxacin cut SBP (7% vs 61% at 1 year) and improved survival in strictly defined advanced cirrhosis
cards.summary: Fernández 2007: norfloxacin cut SBP (7% vs 61% at 1 year) and improved survival in strictly defined advanced cirrhosis
cards.people: 68 patients with cirrhosis and low ascitic protein (<15 g/L) plus advanced liver failure (Child-Pugh ≥9 with bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL) or impaired renal function (creatinine ≥1.2 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen ≥25 mg/dL, or sodium ≤130 mEq/L), randomised to norfloxacin (35) or placebo (33) as primary prophylaxis. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: One-year probability of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: 7% on norfloxacin versus 61% on placebo (P<0.001). Hepatorenal syndrome: 28% versus 41% (P=0.02). Probability of survival: 94% versus 62% at 3 months (P=0.003) and 60% versus 48% at 1 year (P=0.05). The record's databank fields carry no registry ID (a 2007 trial), and none is invented.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-eight patients, and the 1-year survival P value is 0.05 — on the boundary. This trial's population is a carefully fenced highest-risk subset; quoting its SBP effect (7% versus 61%) for unselected cirrhosis would be a category error, as NORFLOCIR's broader test shows.
cards.source: Fernández J et al. Primary prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis delays hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival in cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 17854593. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: NORFLOCIR (Moreau 2018): norfloxacin did not reduce 6-month mortality on the primary analysis (14.8% vs 19.7%; P=0.21)
cards.summary: NORFLOCIR (Moreau 2018): norfloxacin did not reduce 6-month mortality on the primary analysis (14.8% vs 19.7%; P=0.21)
cards.people: 291 patients with Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis and no recent fluoroquinolone therapy, at 18 French sites, randomised to norfloxacin 400 mg once daily (144) or placebo (147) for 6 months, with follow-up to 12 months. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — 6-month mortality by Kaplan–Meier, censoring spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, transplantation, or loss to follow-up — was 14.8% on norfloxacin versus 19.7% on placebo (P=0.21 — not significant). In a competing-risk analysis treating transplantation as a competing event, the cumulative incidence of death at 6 months was lower with norfloxacin (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.59 relative; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.99), with the effect confined to ascitic fluid protein below 15 g/L (0.35; 0.13 to 0.93) and absent at or above it (1.39; 0.42 to 4.57). Norfloxacin reduced any and Gram-negative bacterial infections without increasing Clostridium difficile or multiresistant-bacteria infections.
cards.watchOut: The trial's positive results live in a secondary analytic framework (competing risks) and a subgroup; the primary analysis is null and leads this card. The censoring rule in the primary analysis — censoring at SBP, the very event norfloxacin prevents — is itself contestable, which is why the competing-risk analysis exists; the shelf presents both and stamps the primary.
cards.source: Moreau R et al. Effects of Long-term Norfloxacin Therapy in Patients With Advanced Cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 30144431. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01037959, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis works where the risk is; the broad survival claim failed its primary test — SPLIT (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis works where the risk is; the broad survival claim failed its primary test — SPLIT (Tier C pending verdict)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Fernández 2007 (68 patients) and NORFLOCIR 2018 (291 patients).
cards.result: The infection-prevention effect of norfloxacin is consistent across both trials. The survival effect is proven only in Fernández's narrow, highest-risk definition — and NORFLOCIR's subgroup pattern (benefit below 15 g/L ascitic protein, none above) points back to the same fence. Prescribing to the broad Child-Pugh C population on a survival rationale goes beyond this record.
cards.watchOut: Long-term fluoroquinolone exposure in cirrhosis carries resistance and adverse-effect questions that neither trial's follow-up fully answers; NORFLOCIR's infection data are reassuring for 6 months of treatment, not for indefinite use.

shelves.title: Polyethylene glycol versus lactulose for overt hepatic encephalopathy (HELP)
shelves.question: In cirrhotic patients hospitalised with overt hepatic encephalopathy, does polyethylene glycol 3350 resolve encephalopathy faster than lactulose?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Lactulose · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols · Surface-Active Agents · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One small single-centre trial (50 patients): polyethylene glycol 3350–electrolyte solution produced at least a one-grade improvement in hepatic encephalopathy score at 24 hours in 91% of evaluated patients (21 of 23) versus 52% (13 of 25) on lactulose (P<0.01), and halved the median time to resolution (1 versus 2 days; P=0.01). A large effect in a small trial of a speed-of-resolution endpoint — no mortality or longer-term outcome is addressed — is POSSIBLE. This shelf is acute treatment of overt encephalopathy; rifaximin for preventing recurrence is Shelf #595.

cards.headline: HELP (Rahimi 2014): PEG improved encephalopathy grade at 24 hours in 91% versus 52% on lactulose (n=50)
cards.summary: HELP (Rahimi 2014): PEG improved encephalopathy grade at 24 hours in 91% versus 52% on lactulose (n=50)
cards.people: 50 patients with cirrhosis admitted to one academic tertiary hospital with overt hepatic encephalopathy (of 186 screened), block-randomised to a single 4-litre dose of polyethylene glycol 3350–electrolyte solution (25) or standard lactulose (25). The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — improvement of at least 1 grade on the Hepatic Encephalopathy Scoring Algorithm at 24 hours — was met by 21 of 23 evaluated patients on PEG (91%) versus 13 of 25 (52%) on lactulose (P<0.01); one PEG patient was discharged before final analysis and one refused participation, hence the denominator of 23. Mean HESA score at 24 hours fell from 2.3 to 0.9 on PEG versus 2.3 to 1.6 on lactulose (P=0.002). Median time to encephalopathy resolution: 1 day versus 2 days (P=0.01). Adverse events were uncommon and none was definitely study-related.
cards.watchOut: A 24-hour surrogate of speed, in 50 patients at one centre, with two of 25 PEG patients missing from the primary denominator. Faster catharsis resolving encephalopathy faster is mechanistically coherent, but the trial cannot speak to mortality, recurrence, or length-of-stay effects beyond its own small sample (length of stay was a secondary outcome and is not quantified in the abstract).
cards.source: Rahimi RS et al. Lactulose vs polyethylene glycol 3350--electrolyte solution for treatment of overt hepatic encephalopathy: the HELP randomized clinical trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2014. PMID: 25243839. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01283152, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Baclofen for alcohol dependence in cirrhosis (Addolorato)
shelves.question: In alcohol-dependent patients with liver cirrhosis, does baclofen maintain alcohol abstinence versus placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Alcoholism · Baclofen · Double-Blind Method · Female · GABA Agonists · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Safety · Temperance
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One small single-centre trial (84 randomised patients, Rome): baclofen maintained total alcohol abstinence over 12 weeks in 71% (30 of 42) versus 29% (12 of 42) on placebo (odds ratio 6.3 relative; P=0.0001), with about double the cumulative abstinence duration (62.8 versus 30.8 days) and no hepatic side effects recorded. The effect is large; the base is one centre and 84 patients, and later baclofen trials in non-cirrhotic populations — a different question, fenced here without figures — were mixed. Within its cirrhotic population and 12-week horizon: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Addolorato 2007: baclofen maintained abstinence in 71% versus 29% on placebo in cirrhotic alcohol dependence
cards.summary: Addolorato 2007: baclofen maintained abstinence in 71% versus 29% on placebo in cirrhotic alcohol dependence
cards.people: 84 alcohol-dependent patients with liver cirrhosis (of 148 referred to one Rome institute), randomised to oral baclofen (42) or placebo (42) for 12 weeks; the primary outcome was the proportion achieving and maintaining alcohol abstinence, assessed at outpatient visits, with relapse defined as more than four drinks per day or at least 14 drinks per week over at least 4 weeks; analysis was by intention to treat. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Abstinence was achieved and maintained by 30 of 42 patients (71%) on baclofen versus 12 of 42 (29%) on placebo (odds ratio 6.3 relative; 95% CI 2.4 to 16.1; P=0.0001). Cumulative abstinence duration was about twofold higher on baclofen (mean 62.8 versus 30.8 days; P=0.001). Dropouts did not differ significantly (14% versus 31%; P=0.12). No hepatic side effects were recorded.
cards.watchOut: The safety sentence deserves its weight: the historical barrier to anticraving drugs in cirrhosis is hepatotoxicity, and this trial's clean hepatic record in 42 exposed patients is reassuring but thin. Twelve weeks is a short window in addiction medicine, and a single-centre Italian cohort referred to a specialist institute is not the general cirrhotic population.
cards.source: Addolorato G et al. Effectiveness and safety of baclofen for maintenance of alcohol abstinence in alcohol-dependent patients with liver cirrhosis: randomised, double-blind controlled study. Lancet (London, England). 2007. PMID: 18068515. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00525252, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Simvastatin after variceal bleeding in cirrhosis (BLEPS)
shelves.question: In patients surviving a variceal bleed on standard secondary prophylaxis, does adding simvastatin reduce rebleeding or death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Ligation · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Recurrence · Rhabdomyolysis · Risk Factors · Simvastatin · Spain · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is a headline outcome). One trial (BLEPS): the primary endpoint — the composite of rebleeding and death — was NOT reduced (22 of 69 on simvastatin versus 30 of 78 on placebo; P=0.423), and rebleeding alone was unchanged (25% versus 28%; P=0.583). Death, a secondary endpoint, was lower: 6 of 69 (9%) versus 17 of 78 (22%) (hazard ratio 0.39 relative; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.99; P=0.030), with no survival benefit in Child-Pugh class C. The trial's own authors state that survival was not the primary endpoint and the result requires validation — the card adopts their caution verbatim in substance. A survival signal on a secondary endpoint of a single trial whose primary was null: POSSIBLE, Tier C.

cards.headline: BLEPS (Abraldes 2016): simvastatin did not reduce rebleeding or the primary composite (P=0.423) but was associated with fewer deaths (9% vs 22%)
cards.summary: BLEPS (Abraldes 2016): simvastatin did not reduce rebleeding or the primary composite (P=0.423) but was associated with fewer deaths (9% vs 22%)
cards.people: Patients with cirrhosis on standard secondary prophylaxis (a beta-blocker plus band ligation) within 10 days of a variceal bleed at Spanish centres, randomised to simvastatin 20 mg/day for 15 days then 40 mg/day (69 patients) or placebo (78), followed for up to 24 months; the record describes the trial as comprising 158 patients while the two randomised groups it prints sum to 147 — the figures are carded exactly as printed and the discrepancy is flagged here rather than reconciled. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — the composite of rebleeding and death — occurred in 22 of 69 patients on simvastatin versus 30 of 78 on placebo (P=0.423 — not significant). Rebleeding: 25% versus 28% (P=0.583). Death: 6 of 69 (9%) versus 17 of 78 (22%) (hazard ratio 0.39 relative; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.99; P=0.030). Simvastatin did not increase survival in Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis. Serious adverse events: 49% versus 53%; two patients on simvastatin, each with advanced liver disease, developed rhabdomyolysis.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own conclusion is the correct frame: 'Survival was not the primary end point of the study, so these results require validation.' A secondary-endpoint mortality difference with a confidence interval ending at 0.99, in a trial whose primary composite (which includes death) was null, is hypothesis-grade evidence. The rhabdomyolysis cases at the 40 mg dose in advanced liver disease are part of the same record.
cards.source: Abraldes JG et al. Addition of Simvastatin to Standard Therapy for the Prevention of Variceal Rebleeding Does Not Reduce Rebleeding but Increases Survival in Patients With Cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2016. PMID: 26774179. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01095185, from the record's databank fields (the abstract also cites EudraCT 2009-016500-24). shelves.title: Lanifibranor, a pan-PPAR agonist, in MASH (NATIVE)
shelves.question: In patients with active, non-cirrhotic MASH, does the pan-PPAR agonist lanifibranor reduce the SAF activity score without worsening fibrosis versus placebo at 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Benzothiazoles · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfonamides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single phase 2b trial on histological surrogate endpoints, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. In NATIVE (247 patients), the primary endpoint — a decrease of at least 2 points in the SAF activity score without worsening of fibrosis at 24 weeks — was met at the 1200 mg dose (55% versus 33% on placebo; P=0.007) but not at 800 mg (48% versus 33%; P=0.07). Secondary histology favoured both doses: MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening in 49% and 39% versus 22%, and fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without MASH worsening in 48% and 34% versus 29%. Diarrhoea, nausea, peripheral oedema, anaemia, and weight gain were more frequent on lanifibranor. Histology at 24 weeks is not a clinical outcome; the topic file notes a phase 3 trial in progress, whose results are not carded here. This shelf is lanifibranor; resmetirom, semaglutide and tirzepatide in MASH are Shelf #323.

cards.headline: NATIVE (Francque 2021): lanifibranor 1200 mg met the histological primary endpoint (55% vs 33%); 800 mg did not (48% vs 33%; P=0.07)
cards.summary: NATIVE (Francque 2021): lanifibranor 1200 mg met the histological primary endpoint (55% vs 33%); 800 mg did not (48% vs 33%; P=0.07)
cards.people: 247 patients with non-cirrhotic, highly active MASH (the record uses the term NASH), randomised 1:1:1 to lanifibranor 1200 mg, lanifibranor 800 mg, or placebo once daily for 24 weeks; 42% had type 2 diabetes and 76% had significant or advanced fibrosis. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a decrease of at least 2 points in the SAF activity score without worsening of fibrosis — occurred in 55% on lanifibranor 1200 mg versus 33% on placebo (P=0.007), and in 48% on 800 mg versus 33% (P=0.07 — not significant). Resolution of MASH without worsening of fibrosis: 49% and 39% versus 22%. Improvement in fibrosis stage of at least 1 without worsening of MASH: 48% and 34% versus 29%. Both endpoints combined: 35% and 25% versus 9%. Liver enzymes fell and most lipid, inflammatory, and fibrosis biomarkers improved on lanifibranor. Dropout for adverse events was under 5% and similar across groups; diarrhoea, nausea, peripheral oedema, anaemia, and weight gain occurred more often on lanifibranor.
cards.watchOut: The dose story matters: one dose met the primary endpoint, the other missed it — a pattern compatible with a threshold effect or with chance at the lower dose, and the record cannot distinguish. SAF activity and fibrosis stage on biopsy are surrogates with known sampling variability; no liver outcomes (decompensation, transplant, death) were or could be measured in 24 weeks.

shelves.title: Efruxifermin, an FGF21 analogue, in MASH (HARMONY)
shelves.question: In patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does once-weekly efruxifermin improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening MASH versus placebo at 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Inflammation · Liver Cirrhosis · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #323 covers resmetirom, semaglutide, and tirzepatide in MASH, and Shelf #1679 covers the pan-PPAR agonist lanifibranor; this shelf is the FGF21 analogue efruxifermin alone. (The carded record uses the era's term NASH for the same condition the question calls MASH.) In the single phase 2b trial (128 patients in the USA), fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis at 24 weeks occurred in 39% (15 of 38) on efruxifermin 28 mg and 41% (14 of 34) on 50 mg versus 20% (8 of 41) on placebo in the biopsy analysis set (risk ratios 2.3 and 2.2 relative; P=0.025 and P=0.036); in the full analysis set the 50 mg comparison was not significant (33% versus 19%; P=0.123). Diarrhoea (≈40% versus 19%) and nausea were the commonest drug-related events; no deaths occurred. An author overclaim is flagged on the card: the record's interpretation claims the drug 'resolved NASH', but the printed primary endpoint was fibrosis improvement without worsening — resolution was not the primary measure. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single phase 2 trial, surrogate histology) and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: HARMONY 2023: fibrosis improvement 39–41% versus 20% at 24 weeks — one phase 2b trial, surrogate endpoint
cards.summary: HARMONY 2023: fibrosis improvement 39–41% versus 20% at 24 weeks — one phase 2b trial, surrogate endpoint
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (single trial)
cards.people: 128 adults with biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis (activity score ≥4 with each component ≥1) and stage F2 or F3 fibrosis at 41 US clinics, randomised to placebo (43), efruxifermin 28 mg weekly (42; two randomised patients were not dosed because of an administrative error), or efruxifermin 50 mg weekly (43); mean age 54.7 years (SD 10.4); 79 (62%) female; 118 (92%) white. The liver-biopsy analysis set numbered 113.
cards.result: Improvement in fibrosis by at least one stage with no worsening of steatohepatitis at week 24 (biopsy analysis set) occurred in 15 of 38 (39%) on 28 mg (risk ratio 2.3 relative, 95% CI 1.1–4.8; P=0.025) and 14 of 34 (41%) on 50 mg (2.2, 1.0–5.0; P=0.036) versus 8 of 41 (20%) on placebo. In the full analysis set (missing biopsies counted as non-response), the rates were 36% (28 mg; P=0.033) and 33% (50 mg; P=0.123, not significant) versus 19%. Efruxifermin-related diarrhoea occurred in 40% at both doses versus 19% on placebo (all but one event grade 1–2), nausea in 28% and 42% versus 23%. Five patients discontinued for adverse events on efruxifermin; four serious adverse events occurred in the 50 mg group (one drug-related ulcerative oesophagitis in a patient with reflux history). No deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions are printed on this card. First, the authors' interpretation states the drug 'improved liver fibrosis and resolved NASH' — the record's primary endpoint was fibrosis improvement without worsening of steatohepatitis; NASH resolution was not the printed primary measure, and the claim is flagged as an overreach beyond the endpoint. Second, the headline analysis excludes 15 randomised patients without paired biopsies; when they are counted as non-responders, the higher dose loses significance. Histology at 24 weeks is a surrogate — no clinical outcomes were measured.

shelves.title: Obeticholic acid for MASH fibrosis (REGENERATE)
shelves.question: In patients with MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does obeticholic acid 25 mg improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening MASH versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Biomarkers · Biopsy · Chenodeoxycholic Acid · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the claim rests on a single phase 3 trial, carded in two reports of the same patients (counted once). At the planned 18-month interim analysis, fibrosis improvement with no worsening of NASH occurred in 23% on obeticholic acid 25 mg versus 12% on placebo (p=0.0002), while the NASH-resolution co-endpoint was not met (12% versus 8%; p=0.13). A 2023 consensus-panel re-read of the same biopsies confirmed the fibrosis result (22.4% versus 9.6%; p<0.0001) and again missed resolution (6.5% versus 3.5%; p=0.093). Histology is a surrogate: no clinical-outcomes benefit is shown in these records, pruritus affected about half of patients on 25 mg, and the drug was not ultimately approved for this indication. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped. Distinct from Shelf #1671 (obeticholic acid for primary biliary cholangitis, POISE) and adjacent to Shelf #1710 (efruxifermin) and Shelf #323 (other MASH drugs).

cards.headline: REGENERATE interim: fibrosis improved in 23% versus 12% on obeticholic acid 25 mg; the MASH-resolution endpoint was missed
cards.summary: REGENERATE interim: fibrosis improved in 23% versus 12% on obeticholic acid 25 mg; the MASH-resolution endpoint was missed
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (planned 18-month interim analysis)
cards.people: 1,968 patients with fibrosis stages F1–F3 received at least one dose; the primary analysis covered 931 patients with stage F2–F3 fibrosis (311 placebo, 312 obeticholic acid 10 mg, 308 obeticholic acid 25 mg). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The fibrosis-improvement endpoint (≥1 stage, no worsening of NASH) was achieved by 12% on placebo, 18% on 10 mg (p=0.045), and 23% on 25 mg (p=0.0002). The NASH-resolution endpoint was not met: 8% on placebo, 11% on 10 mg (p=0.18), 12% on 25 mg (p=0.13). Pruritus occurred in 19% (placebo), 28% (10 mg), and 51% (25 mg). Serious adverse events were similar across groups (11%, 11%, 14%).
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis of an ongoing trial, on a histological surrogate. The authors' statement that the result is 'reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit' is an interpretation, not an outcomes finding — no clinical-outcome rates are printed in this record.

shelves.title: Stopping nucleos(t)ide therapy in chronic hepatitis B (FINITE; Toronto STOP)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B who have long-term viral suppression on nucleos(t)ide analogues, does stopping therapy (with close monitoring and retreatment rules) lead to durable off-treatment response or HBsAg loss versus continuing therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aftercare · Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Drug Monitoring · Female · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Tenofovir · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised stop trials answer in different registers, and the cards do not average them. FINITE (n=42, HBeAg-negative patients suppressed on tenofovir for years) found 62% of stoppers still off therapy at 144 weeks, with 43% achieving HBsAg loss or HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL and 19% losing HBsAg outright — POSSIBLE for that tightly selected population. The Toronto STOP study (n=67, broader population and agents) found sustained disease remission in only 29% of stoppers versus 82% of continuers at 72 weeks, HBsAg loss in a single stopper, a third relapsing and 38% retreated, and its authors conclude the benefit of stopping is limited — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for any general expectation of durable remission. The shelf question was re-scoped from the topic file's tenofovir-only wording to nucleos(t)ide therapy generally, because the second trial tests the broader question; the correction is disclosed here. Stopping is a monitored strategy with flares, not a cure pathway, on either record.

cards.headline: FINITE: 62% of selected stoppers stayed off tenofovir at 144 weeks; 19% lost HBsAg
cards.summary: FINITE: 62% of selected stoppers stayed off tenofovir at 144 weeks; 19% lost HBsAg
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (stop versus continue tenofovir)
cards.people: 42 non-cirrhotic HBeAg-negative patients who had received tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for at least 4 years with suppressed HBV DNA for at least 3.5 years; 21 stopped and 21 continued, followed for 144 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Of patients who stopped, 62% (13 of 21) remained off therapy to week 144. Four patients (19%) achieved HBsAg loss, and 43% (9 of 21) had either HBsAg loss or HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL at week 144. Median HBsAg change was −0.59 log10 IU/mL in stoppers versus +0.21 in continuers. Stoppers had initial fluctuations in viral load and ALT; no unexpected safety issues were identified.
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=42) and confined to HBeAg-negative, non-cirrhotic, long-suppressed patients. The topic file's summary — 'about one in five achieved HBsAg loss or sustained response' — conflates two different figures in the record: 19% is HBsAg loss alone; 43% is loss-or-low-DNA. Both are printed separately on this card.

cards.headline: Toronto STOP: sustained remission in 29% of stoppers versus 82% of continuers; authors conclude limited benefit
cards.summary: Toronto STOP: sustained remission in 29% of stoppers versus 82% of continuers; authors conclude limited benefit
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, phase 4 trial (stop versus continue nucleos(t)ide therapy)
cards.people: 67 patients on nucleos(t)ide therapy for at least 1 year with virological suppression (HBeAg-positive patients required seroconversion plus undetectable DNA for ≥12 months; HBeAg-negative patients undetectable DNA for ≥36 months), randomised 2:1 to stop (45) or continue (22) for 72 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Sustained disease remission (HBeAg-negative, HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL, normal ALT) at 72 weeks occurred in 29% (13 of 45) of stoppers versus 82% (18 of 22) of continuers. HBsAg loss occurred in two patients, one in each group. Among stoppers, 33% had virological or biochemical relapse, 38% were retreated, 31% developed ALT above 10× the upper limit of normal, and 16% ALT above 5×; no patient decompensated or died. The authors conclude the findings suggest limited benefit of stopping therapy.
cards.watchOut: The remission definition and population differ from FINITE's — broader agents and mixed HBeAg status — so the two trials are not measuring identical things; retreatment was needed more often in pretreatment HBeAg-positive patients (61% versus 22%).

shelves.title: Tenofovir alafenamide versus tenofovir disoproxil for chronic hepatitis B
shelves.question: In HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B, is tenofovir alafenamide non-inferior to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for viral suppression at 48 weeks, with less bone and renal toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Adenine · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alanine · Antiviral Agents · Biomarkers · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Tenofovir · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two twin phase 3 non-inferiority trials, one in each HBeAg population, agree. In HBeAg-negative patients, HBV DNA below 29 IU/mL at week 48 occurred in 94% on tenofovir alafenamide versus 93% on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (difference 1.8%, 95% CI −3.6 to 7.2), inside the 10% non-inferiority margin. In HBeAg-positive patients, suppression was 64% versus 67% (adjusted difference −3.6%, −9.8 to 2.6), also non-inferior. In both trials, alafenamide caused significantly smaller declines in hip and spine bone mineral density and smaller worsening of renal measures. The separation is on viral suppression plus bone and renal safety markers at 48 weeks; no record here shows a difference in clinical outcomes such as cirrhosis or liver cancer.

cards.headline: HBeAg-negative trial: suppression 94% versus 93% — non-inferior, with smaller bone and renal declines
cards.summary: HBeAg-negative trial: suppression 94% versus 93% — non-inferior, with smaller bone and renal declines
cards.people: 426 patients with HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B randomised 2:1 (285 tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg, 141 tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg; 425 treated) at 105 centres in 17 countries. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: HBV DNA below 29 IU/mL at week 48: 94% on alafenamide versus 93% on disoproxil (difference 1.8% [95% CI −3.6 to 7.2]; p=0.47), demonstrating non-inferiority against the 10% margin. Bone mineral density fell less on alafenamide (hip −0.29% versus −2.16%; spine −0.88% versus −2.51%; both p<0.0001), and median eGFR change was smaller (−1.8 versus −4.8 mL/min; p=0.004). Serious adverse events occurred in 5% versus 6%; one death in the disoproxil group was judged unrelated to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Endpoints are viral suppression and safety markers at 48 weeks; whether the bone and renal marker advantages become clinical outcome advantages needs the longer follow-up the authors themselves call for.

shelves.title: Mycophenolate versus azathioprine as first-line therapy in autoimmune hepatitis (CAMARO)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive autoimmune hepatitis, does mycophenolate mofetil induce biochemical remission more often than azathioprine (each with prednisolone) at six months?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Azathioprine · Mycophenolic Acid · Hepatitis, Autoimmune · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Immunosuppressive Agents · Prednisolone · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial (n=70) with its own 3-year follow-up (same patients, counted once). At 24 weeks, biochemical remission was achieved by 56.4% on mycophenolate plus prednisolone versus 29.0% on azathioprine plus prednisolone (difference 27.4 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 46.7; p=0.022), with no serious adverse events on mycophenolate versus 12.9% on azathioprine and fewer discontinuations (5.1% versus 25.8%). At 3 years, time to biochemical response remained faster on mycophenolate (median 16 versus 64 weeks; adjusted HR 2.74 relative), but the difference in patients still on their assigned treatment with normalised ALT was no longer significant (76% versus 57%; p=0.099). Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single randomised trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. The topic file's pinned anchor (PMID 36514163) is the CAMARO protocol paper, not a results report; it is fenced by name and this shelf is built on the trial's primary report (PMID 38101756), pinned at build, with the 3-year follow-up (PMID 42880409) as the second card.

cards.headline: CAMARO primary report: biochemical remission at 24 weeks in 56.4% on mycophenolate versus 29.0% on azathioprine
cards.summary: CAMARO primary report: biochemical remission at 24 weeks in 56.4% on mycophenolate versus 29.0% on azathioprine
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre superiority trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 70 patients with treatment-naive autoimmune hepatitis (mean age 57.9 years [SD 14.0]; 72.9% female), randomised to mycophenolate mofetil plus prednisolone (39) or azathioprine plus prednisolone (31).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — biochemical remission (normalised ALT and IgG) at 24 weeks — was met by 56.4% on mycophenolate versus 29.0% on azathioprine (difference 27.4 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 46.7; p=0.022). Complete biochemical response at 6 months was 72.2% versus 32.3% (p=0.004). Serious adverse events occurred in 0% on mycophenolate versus 12.9% (four patients) on azathioprine (p=0.034); discontinuations for adverse events were 5.1% versus 25.8% (p=0.018).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and small (n=70), and the only randomised trial of this first-line question — the shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The trial's protocol paper (Snijders et al., Trials 2022, PMID 36514163, EudraCT 2016-001038-91 as printed in its abstract) is a design paper and is fenced, not carded.

cards.headline: CAMARO 3-year follow-up: faster response on mycophenolate; on-treatment remission gap no longer significant
cards.summary: CAMARO 3-year follow-up: faster response on mycophenolate; on-treatment remission gap no longer significant
cards.type: Retrospective long-term follow-up of the same randomised cohort — same trial, counted once
cards.people: 67 of the 70 CAMARO patients (96%) had 3-year follow-up data (30 azathioprine, 37 mycophenolate, as printed in the record).
cards.result: At 3 years, 57% (azathioprine) versus 76% (mycophenolate) remained on trial-assigned treatment with normalised ALT (p=0.099). shelves.title: Tofacitinib for ulcerative colitis (OCTAVE)
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does tofacitinib induce remission at eight weeks and maintain it at one year versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chi-Square Distribution · Colitis, Ulcerative · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy · Janus Kinases · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Pyrimidines · Pyrroles · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a coherent three-trial phase 3 programme in one report. Remission at week 8 was 18.5% versus 8.2% (OCTAVE Induction 1) and 16.6% versus 3.6% (Induction 2) on tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily versus placebo; at week 52, remission in OCTAVE Sustain was 34.3% (5 mg) and 40.6% (10 mg) versus 11.1% on placebo. Infection and herpes zoster rates were higher on tofacitinib, and across the three trials adjudicated non-melanoma skin cancer occurred in five tofacitinib patients versus one on placebo and adjudicated cardiovascular events in five versus none — safety observations inside an efficacy programme, printed on the Sustain card; the powered cardiovascular-safety question for this drug is a different shelf (Shelf #384, ORAL Surveillance in rheumatoid arthritis), and no cardiovascular claim is made here. Distinct from Shelf #384 by question and population.

cards.headline: OCTAVE Induction 1 and 2: remission at week 8 in 18.5% and 16.6% on tofacitinib versus 8.2% and 3.6% on placebo
cards.summary: OCTAVE Induction 1 and 2: remission at week 8 in 18.5% and 16.6% on tofacitinib versus 8.2% and 3.6% on placebo
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 induction trials (one report)
cards.people: 598 patients (Induction 1) and 541 patients (Induction 2) with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis despite previous conventional therapy or TNF-antagonist therapy, randomised to tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily or placebo for 8 weeks. cards.result: Remission at 8 weeks occurred in 18.5% on tofacitinib versus 8.2% on placebo in Induction 1 (P=0.007) and 16.6% versus 3.6% in Induction 2 (P<0.001). Rates of overall infection and serious infection were higher with tofacitinib than placebo in both induction trials (the abstract reports this qualitatively, without percentages).
cards.watchOut: Absolute remission rates are modest — roughly one in six on active drug — against a background of patients who had already failed conventional or anti-TNF therapy; the placebo rates differ twofold between the twin trials (8.2% versus 3.6%), which is why both are printed.
