shelves.title: Mirikizumab for Crohn's disease (VIVID-1)
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does mirikizumab achieve clinical remission and endoscopic response versus placebo at one year — and how does it compare with ustekinumab?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Crohn Disease · Double-Blind Method · Male · Female · Adult · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Severity of Illness Index · Interleukin-23 Subunit p19 · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one large phase 3 treat-through trial (1,065 patients in the efficacy population) met both composite co-primary endpoints against placebo: the endoscopic response composite in 38.0% on mirikizumab versus 9.0% on placebo, and the CDAI clinical remission composite in 45.4% versus 19.6% (both p<0.0001). Serious adverse events were less frequent on mirikizumab (10.3%) than placebo (17.1%). The record's abstract does not print the ustekinumab head-to-head figures, so the topic file's claim of non-inferiority to ustekinumab for clinical remission cannot be carded from this record and is not asserted on this shelf. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single pivotal trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct from Shelf #1069 (mirikizumab for ulcerative colitis, LUCENT). Journal correction: the record is The Lancet 2024, not Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology as the topic file states.

cards.headline: VIVID-1: both composite co-primary endpoints met — endoscopic composite 38.0% versus 9.0%, remission composite 45.4% versus 19.6%
cards.summary: VIVID-1: both composite co-primary endpoints met — endoscopic composite 38.0% versus 9.0%, remission composite 45.4% versus 19.6%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 treat-through trial
cards.people: 1,150 patients randomised and treated (safety population); 1,065 in the efficacy population received mirikizumab (579), ustekinumab (287), or placebo (199) — adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease and previous inadequate response, loss of response, or intolerance to biological or conventional therapy. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The endoscopic response composite (PRO clinical response at week 12 plus endoscopic response at week 52) was reached by 38.0% on mirikizumab versus 9.0% on placebo (p<0.0001); the CDAI clinical remission composite (PRO response at week 12 plus CDAI remission at week 52) by 45.4% versus 19.6% (p<0.0001). Serious adverse events: 10.3% on mirikizumab, 10.7% on ustekinumab, 17.1% on placebo. Three deaths occurred (one ustekinumab, two placebo — including a placebo non-responder switched to mirikizumab after week 12); none were considered drug-related.
cards.watchOut: The co-primaries are composites that embed a week-12 response requirement, so they are not simple week-52 remission rates. shelves.title: Guselkumab for Crohn's disease (GRAVITI; GALAXI)
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does guselkumab — subcutaneous induction in GRAVITI, intravenous induction in GALAXI 2 and 3 — achieve clinical remission and endoscopic response versus placebo, and versus ustekinumab?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — three phase 3 trials agree. GRAVITI (subcutaneous induction and maintenance): clinical remission at week 12 in 56.1% versus 21.4% on placebo and endoscopic response in 41.3% versus 21.4%, with week-48 remission of 60.0–66.1% versus 17.1%. GALAXI-2 and GALAXI-3 (intravenous induction, reported together): both guselkumab regimens beat placebo on both composite co-primary endpoints in both trials (remission composite 47–55% versus 12–13%; endoscopic composite 34–39% versus 5–6%). The GALAXI report's interpretation claims superiority over ustekinumab at week 48 across multiple endpoints, but the abstract does not print the ustekinumab arm's endpoint rates, so that comparison is noted as the authors' claim and not carded with figures. Journal correction: GRAVITI's record is Gastroenterology 2025, not Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology as the topic file states.

cards.result: All multiplicity-controlled endpoints were met. At week 12, clinical remission was 56.1% on guselkumab 400 mg versus 21.4% on placebo (Δ 34.9; P<.001) and endoscopic response 41.3% versus 21.4% (Δ 19.9; P<.001). shelves.title: Guselkumab for ulcerative colitis (QUASAR)
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does guselkumab induction followed by subcutaneous maintenance achieve clinical remission at week 44 versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Colitis, Ulcerative · Male · Female · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Adult · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Induction Chemotherapy · Severity of Illness Index · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a phase 3 programme whose parts agree, preceded by a concordant phase 2b induction study (same programme, same registry number). Phase 3 induction: clinical remission at week 12 in 23% on intravenous guselkumab versus 8% on placebo. Phase 3 maintenance: remission at week 44 in 50% (200 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks) and 45% (100 mg every 8 weeks) versus 19% on placebo (withdrawal). The phase 2b study had already shown week-12 clinical response in about 61% on either intravenous dose versus 27.6% on placebo. Safety was favourable and consistent across the programme, with adverse-event rates in induction identical between groups (49%). Journal correction: the phase 3 record is The Lancet 2025, not Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology as the topic file states.

cards.headline: QUASAR phase 3: induction remission 23% versus 8% at week 12; maintenance remission 50% and 45% versus 19% at week 44
cards.summary: QUASAR phase 3: induction remission 23% versus 8% at week 12; maintenance remission 50% and 45% versus 19% at week 44
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 studies (induction and maintenance, one report)
cards.people: Induction primary population 701 adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (421 guselkumab 200 mg intravenously, 280 placebo); maintenance primary population 568 guselkumab induction responders re-randomised to guselkumab 200 mg every 4 weeks (190), 100 mg every 8 weeks (188), or placebo withdrawal (190).
cards.result: Clinical remission at induction week 12: 23% on guselkumab versus 8% on placebo (adjusted difference 15%, 95% CI 10–20; p<0.0001). Clinical remission at maintenance week 44: 50% (200 mg every 4 weeks; adjusted difference 30%, 21–38) and 45% (100 mg every 8 weeks; adjusted difference 25%, 16–34) versus 19% on placebo (both p<0.0001). In induction, adverse events were reported by 49% in both groups and serious adverse events by 3% (guselkumab) versus 7% (placebo); no active tuberculosis, anaphylaxis, or clinically important hepatic disorders were reported in either study.
cards.watchOut: The maintenance comparison is against withdrawal to placebo in induction responders, not against continued treatment in all-comers — the design enriches for patients already shown to respond.

shelves.title: Lirentelimab for eosinophilic gastritis and duodenitis (ENIGMA)
shelves.question: In patients with eosinophilic gastritis or duodenitis, does the anti-Siglec-8 antibody lirentelimab reduce tissue eosinophils and total symptom scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antigens, CD · Antigens, Differentiation, B-Lymphocyte · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Duodenitis · Enteritis · Eosinophilia · Eosinophils · Female · Gastritis · Gastrointestinal Tract · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Lectins · Leukocyte Count · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single small phase 2 trial (n=65) with large effects on its endpoints: gastrointestinal eosinophil counts fell by a mean of 86% on lirentelimab versus a 9% rise on placebo, the composite treatment response occurred in 63% versus 5%, and total symptom scores fell by 48% versus 22%. Infusion-related reactions were more frequent on the drug (60% versus 23%), otherwise adverse events were similar. The shelf must also carry what the trial cannot: the follow-on phase 3 development programme was discontinued, so no confirmatory trial exists or is coming from this programme. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped.

cards.headline: ENIGMA: eosinophil counts −86% versus +9%; treatment response 63% versus 5%; symptoms −48% versus −22%

cards.people: 65 adults with symptomatic eosinophilic gastritis, eosinophilic duodenitis, or both, randomised 1:1:1 to low-dose lirentelimab (AK002), high-dose lirentelimab (43 patients across both dose groups), or placebo (22), as four monthly infusions.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — mean percentage change in gastrointestinal eosinophil count — was −86% in the combined lirentelimab group versus +9% on placebo (least-squares mean difference −98 percentage points, 95% CI −121 to −76; P<0.001). Treatment response (>30% symptom-score reduction plus >75% eosinophil reduction) occurred in 63% versus 5% (difference 58 points, 36 to 74; P<0.001). Mean total symptom score changed by −48% versus −22% (difference −26 points, −44 to −9; P=0.004). Adverse events were similar to placebo except mild-to-moderate infusion-related reactions (60% versus 23%).
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 with 65 patients and a 2-week post-treatment primary assessment; the two dose groups are pooled for the primary endpoint, so no dose-response can be read from this card. The record's background cites animal-model rationale for the drug — background only; no animal data are carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Low free-sugar diet in adolescents with fatty liver (Schwimmer)
shelves.question: In adolescent boys with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, does a diet low in free sugars reduce hepatic steatosis versus a usual diet over eight weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · Child · Diet, Carbohydrate-Restricted · Dietary Sugars · Hispanic or Latino · Humans · Lipids · Liver Function Tests · Male · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: Forty adolescent boys (aged 11–16) with histologically diagnosed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and active disease were randomised to eight weeks of a diet restricting free sugars to under 3% of daily calories — with individualised menu planning and study meals provided for the whole household — or to their usual diet. Liver fat fell from 25% to 17% on the low-sugar diet versus 21% to 20% on usual diet (adjusted difference −6.23 percentage points, 95% CI −9.45 to −3.02; P<.001), and alanine aminotransferase improved (adjusted ratio of geometric means 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.81; P<.001); adherence was high (18 of 20 hit the sugar target). A clear short-term surrogate result in one small, open-label trial whose intervention included feeding the entire household — promising, preliminary, and labelled as such by its own authors. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Schwimmer 2019: eight weeks of a low free-sugar diet cut liver fat from 25% to 17% versus 21% to 20% on usual diet
cards.summary: Schwimmer 2019: eight weeks of a low free-sugar diet cut liver fat from 25% to 17% versus 21% to 20% on usual diet
cards.people: 40 adolescent boys aged 11 to 16 years with histologically diagnosed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and active disease (hepatic steatosis >10% and alanine aminotransferase ≥45 U/L) at two US academic centres; 95% were Hispanic. The intervention group received individualised menu planning and provision of study meals for the entire household to restrict free sugar intake to less than 3% of daily calories for eight weeks, with twice-weekly adherence calls; controls ate their usual diet. The primary outcome was change in hepatic steatosis by MRI proton density fat fraction.
cards.result: The mean decrease in hepatic steatosis was significantly greater in the intervention group (25% to 17%) than the usual diet group (21% to 20%): adjusted week-8 mean difference −6.23% (95% CI −9.45% to −3.02%; P<.001), against a prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 4%. Alanine aminotransferase fell from 103 to 61 U/L in the intervention group versus 82 to 75 U/L in controls (adjusted ratio of geometric means 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.81; P<.001). Of 12 prespecified secondary outcomes, 7 were null and 5 significant. All 40 boys completed the trial and there were no study-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, eight weeks, 40 boys, and the treatment was not just advice — meals were provided to the whole household, an intensity ordinary clinics cannot reproduce. The endpoint is imaging fat fraction, not clinical liver outcomes, and the authors themselves call the findings preliminary.

shelves.title: Bepirovirsen for chronic hepatitis B (B-Clear): sustained HBsAg loss in about 1 in 10 (phase 2b)
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis B (on or off nucleos(t)ide therapy), does 24 weeks of the antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen 300 mg weekly produce sustained HBsAg and HBV DNA loss after treatment ends — a step toward functional cure?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Oligonucleotides, Antisense
shelves.balance: In the single phase 2b B-Clear trial (Yuen 2022), 457 people with chronic hepatitis B — about half on nucleos(t)ide therapy, half not — were randomised to several bepirovirsen regimens or a placebo-first control. The primary outcome (HBsAg and HBV DNA both undetectable, sustained for 24 weeks after treatment ended, with no new antiviral therapy) was met by 9% of participants on nucleos(t)ide therapy and 10% not on it who received bepirovirsen 300 mg weekly for 24 weeks — roughly 1 in 10, with very wide credible intervals (0 to 31 and 0 to 38 respectively) — versus 0% in the control groups. Shorter or dose-reduced regimens did less (1–9%). Injection-site reactions, fever, fatigue, and alanine aminotransferase rises were more common on bepirovirsen. This is a genuine step toward finite therapy, but it is one phase 2 trial (THIN) in which the endpoint was met by a minority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a benefit claim for a minority endpoint on a single phase 2b trial, with phase 3 confirmation still pending.

cards.headline: Yuen 2022 (B-Clear): sustained HBsAg and HBV DNA loss in 9–10% on bepirovirsen 300 mg for 24 weeks, versus 0% in controls
cards.summary: Yuen 2022 (B-Clear): sustained HBsAg and HBV DNA loss in 9–10% on bepirovirsen 300 mg for 24 weeks, versus 0% in controls
cards.people: 457 participants with chronic hepatitis B virus infection, 227 receiving nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy and 230 not, randomised (3:3:3:1) to weekly subcutaneous bepirovirsen 300 mg for 24 weeks (group 1), 300 mg for 12 weeks then 150 mg for 12 weeks (group 2), 300 mg for 12 weeks then placebo for 12 weeks (group 3), or placebo for 12 weeks then bepirovirsen 300 mg for 12 weeks (group 4). Primary outcome: HBsAg below detection and HBV DNA below quantification, maintained 24 weeks after the planned end of treatment without new antiviral medication.
cards.result: Among participants on nucleos(t)ide therapy, a primary-outcome event occurred in 6 (9%; 95% credible interval 0 to 31) in group 1, 6 (9%; 0 to 43) in group 2, 2 (3%; 0 to 16) in group 3, and 0 (0%; 0 to 8) in group 4. Among those not on nucleos(t)ide therapy: 7 (10%; 0 to 38), 4 (6%; 0 to 25), 1 (1%; 0 to 6), and 0 (0%; 0 to 8) respectively. During weeks 1–12, adverse events including injection-site reactions, pyrexia, fatigue, and increased alanine aminotransferase were more common with bepirovirsen than placebo.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2b, investigator-unblinded, industry-funded (GSK, per the record), with small event counts and very wide credible intervals — the 9–10% figures could shift substantially in phase 3. 'Sustained loss' here means 24 weeks off treatment; longer durability and which patients respond are not yet established. Note the naming rule exception does not apply: bepirovirsen is the generic name of the tested antisense oligonucleotide.

shelves.title: Pegozafermin for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis (ENLIVEN): fibrosis improvement in about 1 in 4 (phase 2b)
shelves.question: In biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does the FGF21 analogue pegozafermin improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis at 24 weeks, versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Fibroblast Growth Factors · Fibrosis · Humans · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: In the single phase 2b ENLIVEN trial (Loomba 2023), 222 adults with biopsy-proven noncirrhotic steatohepatitis and stage F2–F3 fibrosis received subcutaneous pegozafermin (15 mg or 30 mg weekly, or 44 mg every 2 weeks) or placebo for 24 weeks. Fibrosis improvement by at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 22%, 26%, and 27% on pegozafermin versus 7% on placebo — absolute differences of 14 percentage points (95% CI −9 to 38; not significant for the 15 mg dose), 19 points (5 to 32; P=0.009), and 20 points (5 to 35; P=0.008). Steatohepatitis resolution without worsening fibrosis occurred in 37%, 23%, and 26% versus 2% on placebo. Nausea and diarrhoea were the most common adverse events. Both primary end points are 24-week biopsy surrogates from one phase 2b trial (THIN), and the lowest dose's fibrosis result was not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a genuine phase 2b histology signal at the two higher regimens, awaiting phase 3 confirmation on longer, harder outcomes.

cards.headline: Loomba 2023 (ENLIVEN): fibrosis improvement 26–27% on higher-dose pegozafermin versus 7% on placebo at 24 weeks; resolution 23–26% versus 2%
cards.summary: Loomba 2023 (ENLIVEN): fibrosis improvement 26–27% on higher-dose pegozafermin versus 7% on placebo at 24 weeks; resolution 23–26% versus 2%
cards.people: 222 patients with biopsy-confirmed noncirrhotic steatohepatitis (termed NASH in the record) and stage F2 or F3 fibrosis randomised (219 treated) to subcutaneous pegozafermin 15 mg weekly, 30 mg weekly, or 44 mg every 2 weeks, or pooled placebo, for 24 weeks. Primary end points: fibrosis improvement by ≥1 stage with no worsening of steatohepatitis, and steatohepatitis resolution without worsening of fibrosis, at 24 weeks.
cards.result: Fibrosis improvement: 7% with pooled placebo, 22% with 15 mg (difference 14 percentage points; 95% CI −9 to 38), 26% with 30 mg (difference 19 points; 95% CI 5 to 32; P=0.009), and 27% with 44 mg (difference 20 points; 95% CI 5 to 35; P=0.008). Steatohepatitis resolution: 2% with placebo, 37% with 15 mg (difference 35 points; 95% CI 10 to 59), 23% with 30 mg (difference 21 points; 95% CI 9 to 33), and 26% with 44 mg (difference 24 points; 95% CI 10 to 37). The most common adverse events with pegozafermin were nausea and diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Single phase 2b trial with 24-week paired-biopsy surrogate end points; the 15 mg dose's fibrosis difference was not statistically significant, and biopsy sampling variability is a known problem at this size. Funded by the developer (89bio, per the record). The trial used the older NASH terminology; the population is the same disease now called MASH.
cards.source: Loomba R et al. Randomized, Controlled Trial of the FGF21 Analogue Pegozafermin in NASH. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37356033. Registry ID: NCT04929483, from the record. shelves.title: Peginterferon add-on or switch after entecavir suppression in hepatitis B: seroconversion benefit only in suppressed patients
shelves.question: In HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B suppressed on long-term entecavir, does adding on or switching to peginterferon improve HBeAg seroconversion and HBsAg decline versus continuing entecavir alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Guanine · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Polyethylene Glycols · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The answer depends on where the patient starts, and the two randomised trials genuinely diverge. In patients already suppressed on long-term entecavir (Hu 2022; 153 HBeAg-positive patients with low HBsAg and undetectable DNA), adding on or switching to peginterferon alfa-2b for 48 weeks gave HBeAg seroconversion in 18.0% and 19.2% versus 2.0% on continued entecavir (absolute gains of about 16–17 percentage points), with HBsAg below 100 IU/mL in 30.0% and 34.6% versus 0%. In treatment-naïve patients, however, adding peginterferon to entecavir made no difference to seroconversion (Yang 2020; HBsAg seroconversion 4.1% versus 1.8%, P=0.809; HBeAg conversion 11.0% versus 12.5%, P=0.787), though elastography values improved slightly more with the combination. Both trials are small, open-label, single-country (China), and use serological surrogates (THIN); interferon adverse effects are the price of the strategy. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for seroconversion benefit in entecavir-suppressed patients / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for seroconversion when peginterferon is added in treatment-naïve patients.

cards.headline: Hu 2022: in entecavir-suppressed patients, add-on or switch to peginterferon gave HBeAg seroconversion in 18–19% versus 2% on entecavir alone
cards.summary: Hu 2022: in entecavir-suppressed patients, add-on or switch to peginterferon gave HBeAg seroconversion in 18–19% versus 2% on entecavir alone
cards.people: 153 HBeAg-positive patients with chronic hepatitis B treated with entecavir for at least 2 years, with HBsAg below 3000 IU/mL, HBeAg below 200 S/CO, and HBV DNA below 50 IU/mL, randomised (1:1:1) to add-on peginterferon alfa-2b (n=50), switch to peginterferon alfa-2b (n=52), or continued entecavir monotherapy (n=51) for 48 weeks. Primary end point: HBeAg seroconversion at week 48.
cards.result: HBeAg seroconversion was 18.0% with add-on and 19.2% with switch versus 2.0% with monotherapy (P=0.007 and P=0.005). HBeAg loss was 24.0% and 23.1% versus 5.9% (P=0.010 and P=0.013). HBsAg below 100 IU/mL was reached by 30.0% and 34.6% versus 0% (P<0.001), and HBsAg fell by −0.90 and −0.92 versus −0.06 log10 IU/mL (P<0.001). Add-on and switch strategies did not differ from each other. Adverse events were mainly peginterferon-related but generally tolerable.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, and the population was pre-selected for low HBsAg and full viral suppression — the group most likely to respond to interferon. Seroconversion is a surrogate; HBsAg loss itself was not the reported headline outcome. Interferon tolerability limits who can take this path.

cards.headline: Yang 2020: in treatment-naïve patients, adding peginterferon to entecavir made no difference to HBsAg or HBeAg seroconversion
cards.summary: Yang 2020: in treatment-naïve patients, adding peginterferon to entecavir made no difference to HBsAg or HBeAg seroconversion
cards.people: 144 treatment-naïve patients with chronic hepatitis B randomised to entecavir monotherapy (n=70) or entecavir with peginterferon added from week 26 to 52 (n=74), followed for at least 2 years. Primary end point: HBsAg loss.
cards.result: At week 104, HBsAg seroconversion was 4.1% (3/73) with combination therapy versus 1.8% (1/56) with monotherapy (P=0.809), and HBeAg conversion 11.0% (8/73) versus 12.5% (7/56) (P=0.787); sustained virological response was 98.5% versus 93.2% (P=0.150). Liver function recovery was better with monotherapy, while transient elastography values were lower with combination therapy (6.6 versus 7.8 kPa; P=0.028) and histology scores improved more — a fibrosis signal without a serological one.
cards.watchOut: Different population from Hu 2022 (treatment-naïve, not suppressed) and a shorter interferon exposure (weeks 26–52) — the null here does not cancel Hu's result in suppressed patients, and vice versa. Denominators in the abstract's seroconversion analysis (56 and 73) are smaller than the randomised totals, reflecting the per-protocol analysis set.

cards.headline: Synthesis: peginterferon helps seroconversion only in already-suppressed patients — SPLIT by population
cards.summary: Synthesis: peginterferon helps seroconversion only in already-suppressed patients — SPLIT by population
cards.people: 153 entecavir-suppressed patients (Hu 2022) and 144 treatment-naïve patients (Yang 2020).

shelves.title: Peginterferon for hepatitis delta (HIDIT-I): HDV RNA clearance in about 1 in 4; adefovir ineffective
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis delta, does 48 weeks of peginterferon alfa-2a — alone or combined with adefovir — clear HDV RNA versus adefovir alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hepatitis D, Chronic · Humans · Interferon-alpha · Polyethylene Glycols · RNA, Viral
shelves.balance: HIDIT-I (Wedemeyer 2011) remains the anchor randomised trial in hepatitis delta, and it is small (90 patients, THIN). Forty-eight weeks of peginterferon alfa-2a cleared HDV RNA at week 48 in 23% of patients when combined with adefovir and 24% with peginterferon alone, versus 0% on adefovir alone (P=0.006 and P=0.004) — so adefovir added nothing virologically, and adefovir alone was ineffective. The combined primary end point (HDV RNA clearance plus ALT normalisation) was met by only 2 patients in each peginterferon arm and none on adefovir. Twenty-four weeks after treatment, 28% of peginterferon-treated patients remained HDV RNA-negative. The combination did produce more large HBsAg declines (>1 log10 in 10 patients versus 2 and 0). Ten-year follow-up of the same trial (Wranke 2020; follow-up data in 60 patients) found liver-related complications in 17 patients, concentrated in non-responders and those with baseline cirrhosis, consistent with — but not proof of — a long-term payoff from off-treatment response; 19 patients were retreated, which clouds attribution. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real but minority virological response to peginterferon on a single small trial, with adefovir's contribution null.

cards.headline: Wedemeyer 2011 (HIDIT-I): HDV RNA clearance 23–24% on peginterferon arms versus 0% on adefovir alone; adding adefovir made no difference
cards.summary: Wedemeyer 2011 (HIDIT-I): HDV RNA clearance 23–24% on peginterferon arms versus 0% on adefovir alone; adding adefovir made no difference
cards.people: 90 patients with hepatitis delta virus infection randomised to 48 weeks of peginterferon alfa-2a 180 µg weekly plus adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg daily (n=31), peginterferon alfa-2a plus placebo (n=29), or adefovir alone (n=30), with 24 weeks of post-treatment follow-up. Primary end point: normalisation of alanine aminotransferase plus clearance of HDV RNA at week 48.
cards.result: The primary end point was achieved by 2 patients in the combination group, 2 in the peginterferon-alone group, and none on adefovir alone. HDV RNA was negative at week 48 in 23% (combination), 24% (peginterferon alone), and 0% (adefovir alone) (P=0.006 and P=0.004 versus adefovir). At 24 weeks after treatment, 28% of patients in the peginterferon arms had negative HDV RNA tests versus none on adefovir. A decline in HBsAg of more than 1 log10 IU/mL by week 48 occurred in 10 patients on the combination, 2 on peginterferon alone, and none on adefovir (P<0.001 combination versus adefovir; P=0.01 combination versus peginterferon alone).
cards.watchOut: Only 90 patients and a combined primary end point met by 4 patients in total — the virological separation is clear but rests on small numbers. The record's abstract does not detail adverse events; peginterferon's tolerability burden is well known clinically. Written before bulevirtide existed as a comparator.
cards.source: Wedemeyer H et al. Peginterferon plus adefovir versus either drug alone for hepatitis delta. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 21268724. Registry ID: ISRCTN83587695, from the record. cards.headline: Wranke 2020 (HIDIT-I 10-year follow-up): liver complications clustered in non-responders and patients with cirrhosis
cards.summary: Wranke 2020 (HIDIT-I 10-year follow-up): liver complications clustered in non-responders and patients with cirrhosis
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (HIDIT-I)
cards.people: Retrospective long-term follow-up of the HIDIT-I randomised cohort: follow-up data (at least one visit beyond post-treatment week 24) available for 60 patients (19 combination, 20 peginterferon alone, 21 adefovir alone); mean follow-up 8.9 years (range 1.6–13.4). Liver-related complications: liver-related death, transplantation, liver cancer, or hepatic decompensation.
cards.result: Clinical complications occurred in 17 patients during follow-up and were associated with nonresponse to therapy and baseline cirrhosis. Annual event-free survival in patients with cirrhosis versus without was 70% versus 91% at year 5 and 35% versus 76% at year 10. Nineteen patients were retreated with interferon-based therapy (42% of those in the peginterferon arms and 58% in the adefovir arm). The authors conclude off-treatment HDV RNA response to peginterferon was associated with improved long-term clinical outcome.
cards.watchOut: This is follow-up of the same trial, not an independent replication: retrospective, only 60 of 90 patients with follow-up data, and retreatment in a third of patients confounds the link between the original assignment and late outcomes. The response–outcome association is observational within the cohort.
cards.source: Wranke A et al. Ten-year follow-up of a randomized controlled clinical trial in chronic hepatitis delta. J Viral Hepat. 2020. PMID: 32707605. shelves.title: Pioglitazone for MASH in prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: histology improves in two trials; weight gain is the trade-off
shelves.question: In adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), does pioglitazone 45 mg daily improve liver histology versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Pioglitazone · Prediabetic State · Thiazolidinediones
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from the same research group point the same way. Belfort 2006 (55 patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven steatohepatitis; 6 months of pioglitazone 45 mg plus diet versus diet plus placebo) improved steatosis, ballooning, and inflammation, with necroinflammation reduced in 85% versus 38%, though the fibrosis difference was not significant (P=0.08). Cusi 2016 (101 patients with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes; 18 months) met its primary histological outcome in 58% on pioglitazone — an absolute treatment difference of 41 percentage points (95% CI 23 to 59) — with steatohepatitis resolution in 51% (difference 32 points; 95% CI 13 to 51) and a modest fibrosis-score improvement (−0.5; P=0.039). The costs: weight gain 2.5 kg greater than placebo in Cusi 2016, plus the class cautions carried on the separate pioglitazone harms shelf (#290) — this shelf is the liver-histology question only, distinct from the vitamin E question on Shelf #26. Both trials are single-group, single-centre, biopsy-surrogate studies (THIN in breadth, consistent in direction). PROPOSED LIKELY — consistent histological benefit across two randomised trials in the diabetes/prediabetes population, with weight gain as the quantified trade-off.

cards.headline: Belfort 2006: pioglitazone improved steatosis, ballooning and inflammation over 6 months; fibrosis difference not significant (P=0.08)
cards.summary: Belfort 2006: pioglitazone improved steatosis, ballooning and inflammation over 6 months; fibrosis difference not significant (P=0.08)
cards.people: 55 patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes and liver-biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis randomised to a hypocaloric diet (500 kcal/day reduction) plus pioglitazone 45 mg daily or diet plus placebo for 6 months, with histology, magnetic resonance spectroscopy liver fat, and glucose turnover assessed before and after.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, pioglitazone improved glycaemic control and glucose tolerance (P<0.001), decreased aspartate aminotransferase by 40% versus 21% (relative percent decreases; P=0.04) and alanine aminotransferase by 58% versus 34% (P<0.001), decreased hepatic fat content by 54% versus 0% (relative change; P<0.001), and increased hepatic insulin sensitivity by 48% versus 14% (P=0.008). Histology improved for steatosis (P=0.003), ballooning necrosis (P=0.02), and inflammation (P=0.008); necroinflammation was reduced in 85% versus 38% (P=0.001), while the fibrosis reduction did not differ significantly (P=0.08). Fatigue and mild lower-extremity oedema occurred in one pioglitazone patient; no other adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: Small (55 patients), short (6 months), proof-of-concept, and both arms received a hypocaloric diet — the diet itself contributed. Enzyme and fat changes are reported as relative percent changes. Fibrosis, the outcome that matters most long-term, was not significantly improved here.
cards.source: Belfort R et al. A placebo-controlled trial of pioglitazone in subjects with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 17135584. Registry ID: NCT00227110, from the record. cards.headline: Cusi 2016: 18 months of pioglitazone met the primary histology outcome in 58% (difference 41 points) and resolved steatohepatitis in 51%
cards.summary: Cusi 2016: 18 months of pioglitazone met the primary histology outcome in 58% (difference 41 points) and resolved steatohepatitis in 51%
cards.people: 101 patients with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven steatohepatitis at a single university centre, all prescribed a hypocaloric diet (500 kcal/day deficit), randomised to pioglitazone 45 mg daily or placebo for 18 months, followed by an 18-month open-label pioglitazone phase. Primary outcome: reduction of at least 2 points in the fatty liver disease activity score across 2 histological categories without worsening of fibrosis.
cards.result: The primary outcome was achieved by 58% of pioglitazone patients (treatment difference 41 percentage points; 95% CI 23 to 59) and steatohepatitis resolved in 51% (treatment difference 32 percentage points; 95% CI 13 to 51) (P<0.001 for each). The fibrosis score improved modestly (treatment difference −0.5; 95% CI −0.9 to 0.0; P=0.039), hepatic triglyceride content fell from 19% to 7%, and insulin sensitivity improved in adipose tissue, liver, and muscle; improvements persisted over 36 months of therapy. Overall adverse-event rates did not differ between groups, but weight gain was greater with pioglitazone (2.5 kg versus placebo).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and single research group (the same group as Belfort 2006) — independent replication by other groups is lacking. Histology is a surrogate; no trial here is powered for cirrhosis or liver events. Weight gain (+2.5 kg) works against the metabolic goals of this population, and the wider pioglitazone harm profile is assessed on Shelf #290.
cards.source: Cusi K et al. Long-Term Pioglitazone Treatment for Patients With Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis and Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Randomized Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2016. PMID: 27322798. Registry ID: NCT00994682, from the record. shelves.title: Efinopegdutide versus semaglutide 1 mg for fatty liver: greater relative liver-fat reduction in one phase IIa trial
shelves.question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (fatty liver), does efinopegdutide (a GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist) 10 mg weekly reduce liver fat more than semaglutide 1 mg weekly over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Humans · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: In the single phase IIa trial (Romero-Gómez 2023), 145 adults with fatty liver disease and MRI liver fat of at least 10% were randomised open-label to efinopegdutide 10 mg weekly or semaglutide 1 mg weekly for 24 weeks. The primary end point — the relative reduction in liver fat content — was larger with efinopegdutide: a least-squares mean relative reduction of 72.7% (90% CI 66.8 to 78.7) versus 42.3% (90% CI 36.5 to 48.1) with semaglutide (P<0.001). Those are relative reductions in an imaging measure, not proportions of patients cured, and not histology. Weight loss was similar (8.5% versus 7.1% of body weight; P=0.085), and gastrointestinal adverse events were somewhat more frequent with efinopegdutide. The comparison is against semaglutide 1 mg — a low dose by current standards — in an open-label, industry-run phase IIa study with no biopsy or clinical outcomes (THIN). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clear imaging-surrogate win over a low-dose comparator in one small open-label trial; whether it means better liver outcomes is untested.

cards.headline: Romero-Gómez 2023: relative liver-fat reduction 72.7% on efinopegdutide versus 42.3% on semaglutide 1 mg at 24 weeks (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Romero-Gómez 2023: relative liver-fat reduction 72.7% on efinopegdutide versus 42.3% on semaglutide 1 mg at 24 weeks (P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase IIa randomised open-label active-comparator trial
cards.people: 145 participants with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and MRI-estimated proton density fat fraction (liver fat content) of at least 10% at screening, randomised 1:1 to efinopegdutide 10 mg (n=72) or semaglutide 1 mg (n=73), both subcutaneous once weekly for 24 weeks after an 8-week titration; 33.1% had type 2 diabetes; mean body mass index 34.3 kg/m² and mean liver fat content 20.3% at baseline. Primary end point: relative reduction from baseline in liver fat content at week 24.
cards.result: The least-squares mean relative reduction in liver fat content at week 24 was 72.7% (90% CI 66.8 to 78.7) with efinopegdutide versus 42.3% (90% CI 36.5 to 48.1) with semaglutide (P<0.001) — relative reductions in the imaging measure. Mean percent weight reduction was 8.5% versus 7.1% (P=0.085). Adverse events and drug-related adverse events were slightly more frequent with efinopegdutide, mainly gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial, imaging surrogate only — no biopsy, no steatohepatitis resolution, no fibrosis or clinical outcomes. The semaglutide comparator dose (1 mg weekly) is below the doses now used for weight and liver indications, so 'beats semaglutide' here means beats low-dose semaglutide. Run by the developer (Merck authors, per the record). The headline percentages are relative reductions in liver fat, not absolute cure rates.

shelves.title: Entecavir versus lamivudine prophylaxis during R-CHOP: hepatitis 0% versus 13.3% in one trial
shelves.question: In HBsAg-positive patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving R-CHOP chemotherapy, does entecavir prophylaxis prevent hepatitis B reactivation and HBV-related hepatitis better than lamivudine?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Guanine · Hepatitis B · Humans · Lamivudine · Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse
shelves.balance: In the single randomised trial (Huang 2014), 121 HBsAg-positive patients with untreated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, normal liver function, and HBV DNA below 10³ copies/mL received entecavir 0.5 mg daily or lamivudine 100 mg daily from 1 week before R-CHOP chemotherapy until 6 months after it ended. Entecavir was better on every efficacy outcome: HBV-related hepatitis (the primary end point) occurred in 0% versus 13.3% (absolute difference 13.3 percentage points; 95% CI 4.7 to 21.9; P=.003), HBV reactivation in 6.6% versus 30% (difference 23.4 points; 95% CI 10.2 to 36.6; P=.001), and chemotherapy disruption in 1.6% versus 18.3% (difference 16.7 points; 95% CI 6.4 to 27.0; P=.002). Treatment-related adverse events were similar (24.6% versus 30%; P=.50). The effects are large and internally consistent, but this is one open-label trial from 10 centres in a single country, in patients with low baseline viral load (THIN). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a strong single-trial result that guidelines have since broadly followed, held at POSSIBLE because the pack rests on that one trial.

cards.headline: Huang 2014: HBV-related hepatitis 0% on entecavir versus 13.3% on lamivudine during R-CHOP; reactivation 6.6% versus 30%
cards.summary: Huang 2014: HBV-related hepatitis 0% on entecavir versus 13.3% on lamivudine during R-CHOP; reactivation 6.6% versus 30%
cards.people: 121 patients seropositive for hepatitis B surface antigen with untreated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, normal liver function, serum HBV DNA below 10³ copies/mL, and no prior antiviral therapy, randomised at 10 centres in China (2008–2012) to entecavir 0.5 mg daily (n=61) or lamivudine 100 mg daily (n=60), starting 1 week before R-CHOP and continuing to 6 months after chemotherapy completion. Primary end point: incidence of HBV-related hepatitis.
cards.result: HBV-related hepatitis occurred in 0% of the entecavir group versus 13.3% of the lamivudine group (difference 13.3 percentage points; 95% CI 4.7 to 21.9; P=.003). HBV reactivation occurred in 6.6% versus 30% (difference 23.4 points; 95% CI 10.2 to 36.6; P=.001), and chemotherapy disruption in 1.6% versus 18.3% (difference 16.7 points; 95% CI 6.4 to 27.0; P=.002). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 15 of 61 patients (24.6%) on entecavir and 18 of 60 (30%) on lamivudine (difference 5.4 points; 95% CI −10.5 to 21.3; P=.50).
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) and a substudy of a parent R-CHOP scheduling trial. Participants had low HBV DNA and normal liver function — results may not transfer to high-viral-load or anti-HBc-positive/HBsAg-negative patients, and there is no tenofovir comparison. The authors themselves conditioned the conclusion on replication ('if replicated').

shelves.title: Elebsiran (VIR-2218) with or without peginterferon in chronic hepatitis B: deep HBsAg falls, seroclearance uncontrolled (phase 2)
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis B on nucleos(t)ide therapy, does the siRNA elebsiran (VIR-2218), with or without pegylated interferon-alfa-2a, lower HBsAg and produce HBsAg seroclearance?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Interferon-alpha · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This is early, uncontrolled evidence and the stamp says so. In an open-label phase 2 study (Yuen 2024), 84 adults with chronic hepatitis B on nucleos(t)ide therapy (HBV DNA below 90 IU/mL, no cirrhosis) were enrolled — not randomised — into six cohorts receiving the siRNA elebsiran (VIR-2218) 200 mg every 4 weeks, alone or with pegylated interferon-alfa-2a for varying durations. Elebsiran lowered HBsAg substantially in every cohort (mean maximum reductions of −1.7 to −3.0 log10 IU/mL). HBsAg seroclearance occurred in 11 participants, all in the longer interferon-combination cohorts, and 6 of them remained clear 24 weeks after treatment ended; no one on elebsiran alone (cohort 1) or the shortest combination (cohort 6) cleared HBsAg. Alanine aminotransferase elevations were common in the interferon cohorts (60–94%) but uncommon on elebsiran alone (13%), and most adverse events were grade 1–2. Without randomisation or a control arm there is no counterfactual: how many of these patients would have cleared HBsAg anyway, and how much is elebsiran versus interferon, cannot be separated (THIN). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — promising pharmacology and a minority seroclearance signal in longer combination cohorts, from a single uncontrolled phase 2 study.

cards.headline: Yuen 2024: elebsiran cut HBsAg by 1.7–3.0 log10; seroclearance in 11 of 84 — all in longer interferon-combination cohorts, none on elebsiran alone
cards.summary: Yuen 2024: elebsiran cut HBsAg by 1.7–3.0 log10; seroclearance in 11 of 84 — all in longer interferon-combination cohorts, none on elebsiran alone
cards.people: 84 adults (of 124 screened) with chronic hepatitis B virus infection without cirrhosis, HBsAg above 50 IU/mL and HBV DNA below 90 IU/mL on nucleos(t)ide therapy for at least 2 months, enrolled at 23 sites in six countries into six open-label cohorts: elebsiran (VIR-2218) 200 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks alone (cohort 1, n=15) or with pegylated interferon-alfa-2a 180 µg weekly for varying durations (cohorts 2–6, n=15, 18, 18, 13, and 5). Primary end points were safety outcomes; HBsAg change and seroclearance were secondary.
cards.result: Mean maximum HBsAg reduction was −2.0 log10 IU/mL (95% CI −2.1 to −1.8) in cohort 1, and −2.2, −2.5, −2.4, −3.0, and −1.7 log10 IU/mL in cohorts 2–6. Eleven participants receiving elebsiran plus pegylated interferon had HBsAg seroclearance at some point (1 in cohort 2, 1 in cohort 3, 5 in cohort 4, 4 in cohort 5); 10 of the 11 developed anti-HBs, and 6 (1, 3, and 2 in cohorts 2, 4, and 5) sustained seroclearance through 24 weeks after treatment ended. No participant on elebsiran alone or in the 12-week combination cohort (cohort 6) had seroclearance. Among 26 HBeAg-positive participants, 12 had HBeAg seroclearance or anti-HBe seroconversion. Alanine aminotransferase elevations occurred in 2 of 15 (13%) in cohort 1 versus 60–94% across the interferon cohorts; most treatment-emergent adverse events were grade 1–2.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised and no control or placebo arm — cohort comparisons are confounded by different interferon durations and small cohort sizes (cohort 6 had 5 people). Participants were already virally suppressed on nucleos(t)ide therapy and mostly HBeAg-negative; seroclearance in 11 of 84 cannot be attributed between elebsiran and interferon. Funded by the developer (Vir Biotechnology, per the record); the study was still ongoing at publication.
cards.source: Yuen MF et al. VIR-2218 (elebsiran) plus pegylated interferon-alfa-2a in participants with chronic hepatitis B virus infection: a phase 2 study. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024. PMID: 39389081. Registry ID: NCT03672188, from the record. shelves.title: Bariatric-metabolic surgery for MASH (BRAVES): resolution in 56–57% versus 16% with lifestyle care at 1 year
shelves.question: In adults with obesity and biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), does bariatric-metabolic surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy) resolve steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis at 1 year, compared with lifestyle intervention plus best medical care?
shelves.mesh: Bariatric Surgery · Gastric Bypass · Gastrectomy · Humans · Life Style · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: BRAVES (Verrastro 2023) is the first randomised trial of metabolic surgery for steatohepatitis. In 288 adults with obesity (body mass index 30–55 kg/m²) and biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis, with or without type 2 diabetes, histological resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis at 1 year occurred in 56% after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and 57% after sleeve gastrectomy, versus 16% with lifestyle modification plus best medical care (P<0.0001) — absolute gains of about 40 percentage points; expressed relatively, the probability of resolution was 3.60 times (95% CI 2.19 to 5.92) and 3.67 times (2.23 to 6.02) higher with surgery. Per-protocol rates were 70%, 70%, and 19%. There were no deaths or life-threatening complications; severe adverse events occurred in 10 surgical participants (6%) and were managed without re-operation. This remains a single, open-label trial from one city (Rome) with a 1-year histological endpoint (THIN for durability and hard outcomes). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a large, decisive effect on the histological endpoint in one trial, distinct from Shelf #288, which asks whether metabolic surgery induces diabetes remission; this shelf's question is liver histology. (For prediabetes material the standing wording is 'delay', not prevention; this trial enrolled established steatohepatitis, with or without diabetes.)

cards.headline: Verrastro 2023 (BRAVES): steatohepatitis resolution at 1 year in 56% (bypass) and 57% (sleeve) versus 16% (lifestyle plus medical care)
cards.summary: Verrastro 2023 (BRAVES): steatohepatitis resolution at 1 year in 56% (bypass) and 57% (sleeve) versus 16% (lifestyle plus medical care)
cards.people: 288 participants aged 25–70 years with obesity (body mass index 30–55 kg/m²), with or without type 2 diabetes, and histologically confirmed steatohepatitis (termed NASH in the record), randomised (1:1:1) at three hospitals in Rome, Italy, to lifestyle modification plus best medical care (n=96), Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (n=96), or sleeve gastrectomy (n=96). Primary end point: histological resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis at 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary end point was met by 54 participants (56%) in the bypass group and 55 (57%) in the sleeve group versus 15 (16%) in the lifestyle group (P<0.0001). The calculated probability of resolution was 3.60 times greater (relative measure; 95% CI 2.19 to 5.92; P<0.0001) with bypass and 3.67 times greater (2.23 to 6.02; P<0.0001) with sleeve, against the absolute rates of 56–57% versus 16%. In the per-protocol analysis (236 participants), rates were 70%, 70%, and 19% respectively (P<0.0001). No deaths or life-threatening complications were reported; severe adverse events occurred in 10 participants (6%) who had surgery, none requiring re-operation, and all resolved with medical or endoscopic management.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable for surgery), single-city, and the endpoint is 1-year biopsy histology — durability beyond a year, fibrosis regression, and liver-event prevention are not shown here. Participants had body mass index 30–55 kg/m² and were surgical candidates; the result does not extend to lean steatohepatitis. Distinct from Shelf #288 (metabolic surgery for diabetes remission).
cards.source: Verrastro O et al. Bariatric-metabolic surgery versus lifestyle intervention plus best medical care in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (BRAVES): a multicentre, open-label, randomised trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 37088093. Registry ID: NCT03524365, from the record. shelves.title: Tetrathiomolybdate versus trientine in neurological Wilson disease: less early deterioration in one small trial; drug never marketed
shelves.question: In patients presenting with neurological Wilson disease, does initial treatment with tetrathiomolybdate preserve neurological function better than trientine?
shelves.mesh: Chelating Agents · Copper · Hepatolenticular Degeneration · Humans · Molybdenum · Treatment Outcome · Trientine · Zinc
shelves.balance: One small double-blind trial is the whole randomised evidence base (Brewer 2006; 48 patients, THIN). In patients presenting with neurological Wilson disease, mostly newly diagnosed, initial treatment for 8 weeks with ammonium tetrathiomolybdate (the specific salt tested — named because tetrathiomolybdate is not a marketed, regulated product and preparations differ) caused less early neurological deterioration than trientine: 1 of 25 patients (4%) worsened on tetrathiomolybdate versus 6 of 23 (26%) on trientine (P<.05), an absolute difference of about 22 percentage points. Four trientine patients died during follow-up, 3 of whom had shown initial deterioration; no deaths were reported in the tetrathiomolybdate arm in the record. The trade-off was haematological and hepatic laboratory effects: anaemia and/or leukopenia in 3 tetrathiomolybdate patients and further transaminase elevations in 4, versus anaemia in 1 trientine patient. Neurological and speech recovery over 3 years was good in both arms. The access caveat is part of the answer: tetrathiomolybdate has never been marketed, so this is evidence about a drug most patients cannot obtain, from a single 48-patient trial run by its developer's group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — less early neurological worsening than trientine in one small trial, with more laboratory adverse effects and a major availability caveat.

cards.headline: Brewer 2006: neurological deterioration in 1 of 25 on tetrathiomolybdate versus 6 of 23 on trientine (P<.05) in neurological Wilson disease
cards.summary: Brewer 2006: neurological deterioration in 1 of 25 on tetrathiomolybdate versus 6 of 23 on trientine (P<.05) in neurological Wilson disease
cards.people: 48 patients with the neurological presentation of Wilson disease, primarily newly diagnosed and not treated for more than 4 weeks with an anticopper drug, randomised double-blind at a university referral centre to 8 weeks of inpatient treatment with trientine hydrochloride 500 mg twice daily (n=23 analysed) or ammonium tetrathiomolybdate 20 mg three times daily with meals plus 20 mg three times daily between meals (n=25); all patients also received zinc 50 mg twice daily during the 8 weeks and zinc three times daily after discharge, with annual follow-up. Outcomes: frequency of neurological worsening, adverse effects, and degree of neurological recovery on semiquantitative neurological and speech examinations.
cards.result: Neurological deterioration occurred in 6 of 23 patients (26%) in the trientine arm and 1 of 25 (4%) in the tetrathiomolybdate arm (P<.05). Three patients receiving tetrathiomolybdate had adverse effects of anaemia and/or leukopenia, and 4 had further transaminase elevations; 1 patient receiving trientine had anaemia. Four patients receiving trientine died during follow-up, 3 having shown initial neurological deterioration. Neurological and speech recovery during the 3-year follow-up period were quite good.
cards.watchOut: Only 48 patients from a single referral centre, run by the group that developed tetrathiomolybdate; the deterioration difference rests on 7 events. Both arms received zinc, so this compares the two add-on strategies, not the drugs in isolation. Crucially, ammonium tetrathiomolybdate was never marketed — availability, not efficacy, is the binding constraint in practice, and later bis-choline salt preparations are not what this trial tested.
cards.source: Brewer GJ et al. Treatment of Wilson disease with ammonium tetrathiomolybdate: IV. Comparison of tetrathiomolybdate and trientine in a double-blind study of treatment of the neurologic presentation of Wilson disease. Arch Neurol. 2006. PMID: 16606763. Registry ID: NCT00004339, from the record. shelves.title: Machine perfusion versus cold storage in liver transplantation (Nasralla 2018; DHOPE-DCD 2021)
shelves.question: In liver transplantation, does machine perfusion of the donor liver reduce graft injury and organ discard compared with conventional static cold storage?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Allografts · Bile Ducts · Female · Graft Survival · Humans · Length of Stay · Liver · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Preservation · Perfusion · Survival Analysis · Temperature · Tissue Donors · Tissue and Organ Harvesting · Treatment Outcome · Waiting Lists · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials, two perfusion strategies, one direction. In 220 liver transplantations, normothermic machine perfusion halved graft injury (a 50% relative reduction in hepatocellular enzyme release) and halved the organ discard rate versus static cold storage, while allowing 54% longer mean preservation — but it did not significantly change bile duct complications, graft survival, or patient survival. In livers donated after circulatory death, dual hypothermic oxygenated perfusion cut symptomatic nonanastomotic biliary strictures — a clinical endpoint, not a surrogate — from 18% to 6%, and also reduced postreperfusion syndrome and early allograft dysfunction. The normothermic trial's headline endpoints are injury markers and utilisation; the hypothermic trial supplies the patient-level outcome. Neither trial shows a survival difference, and the two machines are not interchangeable — but machine perfusion, in one form or another, beats the ice box on every endpoint actually measured. PROPOSED LIKELY — two independent randomised trials with concordant benefit, tempered by a surrogate primary endpoint in one and no demonstrated survival gain in either.

cards.headline: Nasralla 2018 (COPE): normothermic perfusion halved graft injury and organ discard versus cold storage
cards.summary: Nasralla 2018 (COPE): normothermic perfusion halved graft injury and organ discard versus cold storage
cards.people: 220 liver transplantations in the European COPE consortium trial, randomised to ex-vivo normothermic machine perfusion or conventional static cold storage of the donor liver. Primary endpoint: graft injury measured by hepatocellular enzyme release (peak transaminases) in the first days after transplant.
cards.result: Normothermic preservation was associated with a 50% lower level of graft injury (a relative reduction in hepatocellular enzyme release), a 50% lower rate of organ discard, and a 54% longer mean preservation time than cold storage. There was no significant difference in bile duct complications, graft survival, or patient survival.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a biochemical injury marker, not a patient outcome, and the trial was not powered for survival. The discard-rate benefit arises in an unblinded setting — teams knew which livers were perfused when deciding to use them — so part of the utilisation gain may reflect confidence in the technology rather than organ quality alone. No registry ID appeared in the fetched abstract, so none is printed.
cards.source: Nasralla D et al. A randomized trial of normothermic preservation in liver transplantation. Nature. 2018. PMID: 29670285. cards.headline: van Rijn 2021 (DHOPE-DCD): hypothermic oxygenated perfusion cut biliary strictures from 18% to 6% in DCD livers
cards.summary: van Rijn 2021 (DHOPE-DCD): hypothermic oxygenated perfusion cut biliary strictures from 18% to 6% in DCD livers
cards.people: 160 patients enrolled in the Dutch DHOPE-DCD trial; 78 received a liver preserved by dual hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion and 78 a conventionally cold-stored liver, all donated after circulatory death. Primary endpoint: symptomatic nonanastomotic biliary strictures within 6 months.
cards.result: Nonanastomotic biliary strictures occurred in 6% of the machine-perfusion group versus 18% of the cold-storage group (relative risk 0.36, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.94; P=0.03). Postreperfusion syndrome occurred in 12% versus 27% (RR 0.43, 0.20 to 0.91) and early allograft dysfunction in 26% versus 40% (RR 0.61, 0.39 to 0.96).
cards.watchOut: This is a different technology from the normothermic trial — cold, oxygenated perfusion applied to the highest-risk (DCD) grafts — so the stricture benefit should not be read across to normothermic perfusion or to standard brain-death donor livers. Event counts behind the percentages are small, and the confidence interval for the primary endpoint is wide.
cards.source: van Rijn R et al. Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion in liver transplantation (DHOPE-DCD). N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33626248. Registry ID: NCT02584283, from the record. shelves.title: Everolimus with reduced tacrolimus after liver transplantation (H2304)
shelves.question: In de novo liver transplant recipients, does introducing everolimus at day 30 with reduced-exposure (or eliminated) tacrolimus preserve renal function without losing efficacy (treated biopsy-proven rejection, graft loss, death) at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Confidence Intervals · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Everolimus · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Graft Rejection · Graft Survival · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney · Kidney Function Tests · Liver Failure · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Sirolimus · Survival Analysis · Tacrolimus · Time Factors · Transplantation Immunology · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One large trial, a split answer. In H2304, 719 de novo liver recipients were randomised a month after transplant to everolimus with reduced tacrolimus, standard tacrolimus, or tacrolimus elimination. Everolimus plus reduced tacrolimus was noninferior on the composite of treated rejection, graft loss, or death (6.7% vs 9.7%), with significantly less treated rejection (2.9% vs 7.0%) and a significantly better adjusted change in kidney function (a difference of 8.50 mL/min/1.73 m² in eGFR change). But the tacrolimus-elimination arm was stopped early for excess rejection, and the everolimus arm paid for its gains with more discontinuations for adverse events (25.7% vs 14.1%) and more serious infections. So the strategy works on paper at 12 months for patients who tolerate it — roughly one in four did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN), noninferiority on a composite, a renal-function surrogate rather than hard kidney outcomes, and a real tolerability cost.

cards.headline: De Simone 2012 (H2304): everolimus + reduced tacrolimus noninferior, kidneys better, tolerability worse; tacrolimus elimination failed
cards.summary: De Simone 2012 (H2304): everolimus + reduced tacrolimus noninferior, kidneys better, tolerability worse; tacrolimus elimination failed
cards.people: 719 de novo liver transplant recipients randomised at day 30 (±5) to everolimus with reduced-exposure tacrolimus (n=245), tacrolimus control (n=243), or tacrolimus elimination (n=231). Primary outcome at 12 months: composite of treated biopsy-proven acute rejection, graft loss, or death, with a 12% noninferiority margin; kidney function (eGFR change) was the key secondary outcome.
cards.result: The composite occurred in 6.7% on everolimus + reduced tacrolimus versus 9.7% on tacrolimus control (difference −3.0%, 95% CI −8.7 to 2.6; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Treated rejection was 2.9% versus 7.0% (P=0.035). Adjusted eGFR change favoured everolimus by 8.50 mL/min/1.73 m² (97.5% CI 3.74 to 13.27; P<0.001). Discontinuation for adverse events was 25.7% versus 14.1% (relative risk 1.82) and serious infections were more frequent (relative risk 1.76). The tacrolimus-elimination arm was stopped early because of excess treated rejection.
cards.watchOut: A generous 12% noninferiority margin, a 12-month horizon, and a renal endpoint that is a change in estimated GFR — not dialysis or kidney failure. The patients who benefit are those who stay on everolimus; a quarter stopped it for adverse events. No registry ID appeared in the fetched abstract, so none is printed.
cards.source: De Simone P et al. Everolimus with reduced tacrolimus improves renal function in de novo liver transplant recipients (H2304). Am J Transplant. 2012. PMID: 22882750. shelves.title: Bezafibrate for primary biliary cholangitis with incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid (BEZURSO)
shelves.question: In primary biliary cholangitis with an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid (Paris-2 criteria), does adding bezafibrate 400 mg/day achieve a complete biochemical response over 24 months compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bezafibrate · Bile Acids and Salts · Cholangitis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypolipidemic Agents · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Treatment Failure · Ursodeoxycholic Acid
shelves.balance: A small trial with a lopsided biochemical result. In BEZURSO, 100 patients with primary biliary cholangitis responding inadequately to ursodeoxycholic acid were randomised to add bezafibrate 400 mg/day or placebo for 24 months. A complete biochemical response occurred in 31% on bezafibrate versus 0% on placebo, and alkaline phosphatase normalised in 67% versus 2%. But the outcomes that matter most did not separate: end-stage liver complications occurred in 2 patients in each group, and the trial was far too small and short to detect differences in transplant or death. Bezafibrate also raised creatinine slightly (+5% vs −3%) and caused more myalgia (20% vs 10%). Biochemical response is the accepted working endpoint in PBC and correlates with prognosis in cohort data, but it is still a surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one trial of 100 patients (THIN), decisive on blood tests, silent on clinical outcomes. Shelf #1062 homes the other second-line PBC therapies; this shelf is the fibrate-specific trial.

cards.headline: Corpechot 2018 (BEZURSO): complete biochemical response 31% on bezafibrate vs 0% on placebo over 24 months
cards.summary: Corpechot 2018 (BEZURSO): complete biochemical response 31% on bezafibrate vs 0% on placebo over 24 months
cards.people: 100 patients with primary biliary cholangitis and an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid (Paris-2 criteria), randomised to bezafibrate 400 mg/day (n=50) or placebo (n=50) for 24 months. Primary outcome: complete biochemical response (normal bilirubin, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, transaminases, and prothrombin index).
cards.result: Complete biochemical response occurred in 31% of the bezafibrate group versus 0% of the placebo group (difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 10 to 50; P<0.001). Alkaline phosphatase normalised in 67% versus 2%. End-stage liver disease complications occurred in 2 patients in each group. Creatinine rose 5% on bezafibrate versus a 3% fall on placebo, and myalgia was reported by 20% versus 10%.
cards.watchOut: Every efficacy endpoint is biochemical; with 100 patients and 2 events per arm, the trial says nothing reliable about transplant, liver failure, or survival. The creatinine rise matters in a population often co-managed for kidney risk, and fibrates are not FDA-approved for this indication in the United States — bezafibrate itself is not marketed there.

shelves.title: Treating minimal hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose: cognition and quality of life (Prasad 2007)
shelves.question: In cirrhosis with minimal hepatic encephalopathy, does 3 months of lactulose improve cognitive function and health-related quality of life compared with no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Cognition · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Lactulose · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Neuropsychological Tests · Psychometrics · Psychomotor Performance · Quality of Life · Sickness Impact Profile
shelves.balance: One small, open trial. Of 90 patients with cirrhosis screened, 61 had minimal hepatic encephalopathy and were randomised to lactulose or no treatment for 3 months. On lactulose, the mean number of abnormal neuropsychological tests fell from 2.74 to 0.75, while the untreated group barely moved (2.47 to 2.55); total Sickness Impact Profile scores — a quality-of-life measure — improved from 10.39 to 3.77 on lactulose and did not change without it (10.36 to 10.39). The direction is consistent and the effect sizes are not trivial, but the trial is tiny, unblinded (patients and testers knew who was treated), and short; practice effects on repeated cognitive testing and expectation effects on quality-of-life scores can both imitate benefit in exactly this design. No outcomes like overt encephalopathy episodes, falls, driving safety, or hospitalisation were measured. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a plausible, cheap, low-risk intervention resting on one small nonblinded trial (THIN). One harm belongs on the record even though this trial did not show it: the AASLD/EASL guideline warns that overuse of lactulose can cause dehydration, hypernatraemia and electrolyte loss, and can itself precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy — the opposite of the intent. That is a dosing harm, and it matters most in exactly this population, where a slide from minimal to overt encephalopathy is the outcome everyone is trying to prevent. The dose must be titrated to soft stools, not pushed.

cards.headline: Prasad 2007: lactulose improved cognitive test scores and quality of life over 3 months in minimal hepatic encephalopathy
cards.summary: Prasad 2007: lactulose improved cognitive test scores and quality of life over 3 months in minimal hepatic encephalopathy
cards.people: 90 patients with cirrhosis screened; 61 found to have minimal hepatic encephalopathy and randomised to lactulose (n=31) or no treatment (n=30) for 3 months. Outcomes: number of abnormal neuropsychological tests and Sickness Impact Profile (quality of life) scores.
cards.result: The mean number of abnormal neuropsychological tests fell from 2.74 (95% CI 2.40 to 3.08) to 0.75 (0.36 to 1.16) on lactulose, versus 2.47 (2.19 to 2.74) to 2.55 (2.16 to 2.94) without treatment (MANOVA P=0.001). shelves.title: Which plasma expander after large-volume paracentesis: albumin versus dextran 70 or polygeline (Ginès 1996)
shelves.question: In cirrhotic ascites treated by total paracentesis, does albumin prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction better than synthetic expanders (dextran 70, polygeline)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Albumins · Ascites · Blood Circulation · Dextrans · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Paracentesis · Polygeline · Renin
shelves.balance: One randomised trial from 1996, and it favours albumin clearly on its chosen endpoint. In 289 patients undergoing total paracentesis, post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction — defined by a rise in plasma renin activity at day 6 — occurred in 18.5% with albumin, 34.4% with dextran 70 (P=0.018), and 37.8% with polygeline (P=0.004). Two cautions keep the stamp modest. First, circulatory dysfunction is a renin-based surrogate: patients who developed it did worse afterwards (shorter time to readmission and shorter survival), but the trial did not show that the choice of expander itself changed readmission or survival — those follow-up comparisons were between patients with and without dysfunction, not between treatment arms. Second, it is a single trial (THIN), and polygeline is no longer widely used. Albumin is the expander with the evidence; the synthetics are not equivalent substitutes on the surrogate that predicts trouble. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one trial, a surrogate endpoint, but a large and consistent separation. The separate 1988 question of expansion versus no expansion lives on Shelf #167.

cards.headline: Ginès 1996: circulatory dysfunction after total paracentesis in 18.5% with albumin vs 34.4% dextran 70 and 37.8% polygeline
cards.summary: Ginès 1996: circulatory dysfunction after total paracentesis in 18.5% with albumin vs 34.4% dextran 70 and 37.8% polygeline
cards.people: 289 patients with cirrhosis and tense ascites treated by total paracentesis, randomised to intravenous albumin (n=97), dextran 70 (n=93), or polygeline (n=99) as plasma expansion. Primary measure: post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, defined by a >50% rise in plasma renin activity to above 4 ng/mL/hour at day 6.
cards.result: Circulatory dysfunction occurred in 18.5% of the albumin group, 34.4% of the dextran 70 group (P=0.018 versus albumin), and 37.8% of the polygeline group (P=0.004 versus albumin). In follow-up, patients who developed circulatory dysfunction — regardless of which expander they received — had a shorter time to first readmission (1.3 vs 3.5 months, P=0.03) and shorter survival (9.3 vs 16.9 months, P=0.01) than those who did not.
cards.watchOut: The readmission and survival figures compare patients by dysfunction status, not by randomised expander — they show the surrogate matters prognostically, not that albumin prolongs life in this setting. The dysfunction endpoint is a laboratory definition (renin rise), the trial predates trial registration (no registry ID in the record, none printed), and polygeline has largely left practice.
cards.source: Ginès A et al. Randomized trial comparing albumin, dextran 70, and polygeline in cirrhotic patients with ascites treated by paracentesis. Gastroenterology. 1996. PMID: 8831595. shelves.title: Simvastatin plus rifaximin in decompensated cirrhosis (LIVERHOPE)
shelves.question: In decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C), does simvastatin 20 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day for 12 months prevent acute-on-chronic liver failure and other severe complications compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure · Aged · Ascites · Bacterial Infections · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Agents · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Intention to Treat Analysis · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Rifaximin · Severity of Illness Index · Simvastatin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A properly done phase 3 trial with a null answer. LIVERHOPE randomised 237 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C) in 14 European hospitals to simvastatin 20 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day or placebo for 12 months. Acute-on-chronic liver failure — the primary endpoint — developed in 17.9% on treatment versus 14.2% on placebo (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.34; P=.52); if anything the point estimate leans the wrong way. Transplant or death occurred in 18.8% versus 24.2% (HR 0.75, 0.43 to 1.32; P=.32) and overall cirrhosis complications in 42.7% versus 45.8% (HR 0.93; P=.70) — neither significant, and the confidence intervals are too wide to claim the combination was proven useless for those endpoints, only that no benefit was shown. Adverse events were evenly matched (426 vs 419 events), but 3 patients (2.6%) on simvastatin developed rhabdomyolysis — the known statin hazard in advanced liver disease, and the reason statin enthusiasm in decompensated cirrhosis needs this trial in view. Tier C: death is part of the headline outcomes, so this shelf goes to the developer personally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial (THIN) whose primary endpoint clearly failed, with secondary-endpoint intervals too wide for a stronger null stamp.

cards.headline: Pose 2025 (LIVERHOPE): no prevention of acute-on-chronic liver failure with simvastatin + rifaximin; 3 cases of rhabdomyolysis
cards.summary: Pose 2025 (LIVERHOPE): no prevention of acute-on-chronic liver failure with simvastatin + rifaximin; 3 cases of rhabdomyolysis
cards.people: 237 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B in 194, C in 43; 72% male, mean age 57) at 14 European hospitals, randomised to simvastatin 20 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day (n=117) or placebo (n=120) for 12 months. Primary endpoint: development of acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF).
cards.result: ACLF developed in 17.9% on treatment versus 14.2% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.34; P=.52). Transplant or death occurred in 18.8% versus 24.2% (HR 0.75, 0.43 to 1.32; P=.32); complications of cirrhosis in 42.7% versus 45.8% (HR 0.93, 0.63 to 1.36; P=.70). Adverse events numbered 426 versus 419; rhabdomyolysis occurred in 3 treatment-group patients (2.6%).
cards.watchOut: The transplant-or-death hazard ratio (0.75) comes with an interval spanning a 57% relative benefit to a 32% relative harm — the trial neither shows benefit nor excludes it for that endpoint; the firm null is on the primary ACLF endpoint. The rhabdomyolysis cases are a harm signal specific to statins in decompensated cirrhosis and should not be read onto compensated disease.
cards.source: Pose E et al. Simvastatin plus rifaximin in decompensated cirrhosis (LIVERHOPE). JAMA. 2025. PMID: 39908052. Registry ID: NCT03780673, from the record. shelves.title: Cilofexor in non-cirrhotic primary sclerosing cholangitis (PRIMIS)
shelves.question: In non-cirrhotic large-duct primary sclerosing cholangitis, does the FXR agonist cilofexor 100 mg daily improve liver fibrosis over 96 weeks compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cholangitis, Sclerosing · Male · Middle Aged · Female · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Aged · Disease Progression · Young Adult · Treatment Outcome · Liver Cirrhosis · Adolescent · Ursodeoxycholic Acid · Receptors, Cytoplasmic and Nuclear · Receptor, Farnesoid X-Activated
shelves.balance: The first phase 3 trial in primary sclerosing cholangitis, stopped early because it was going nowhere. PRIMIS randomised 419 adults with non-cirrhotic (F0–F3) large-duct PSC at 205 sites in 16 countries to cilofexor 100 mg daily or placebo for 96 weeks; 416 were analysed. A planned interim futility analysis put the probability of eventual success at 6.8% (futility boundary ≤10%), and the trial was terminated. In patients with paired biopsies, fibrosis progressed in 31% on cilofexor versus 33% on placebo (difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −15.2 to 12.3; P=0.42). Itching — the class side effect — was more common on cilofexor (49% vs 36%). The early stop and the wide interval mean a modest benefit is not formally excluded, but a futility-stopped trial with a point estimate of essentially zero is not a maybe in any practical sense: there is no current reason to give this drug for PSC. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial (THIN), stopped for futility, so the null carries the wider uncertainty of an incomplete trial.

cards.headline: Trauner 2026 (PRIMIS): cilofexor did not reduce fibrosis progression in PSC; trial stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Trauner 2026 (PRIMIS): cilofexor did not reduce fibrosis progression in PSC; trial stopped early for futility
cards.people: 419 adults (18–75 years) with non-cirrhotic large-duct primary sclerosing cholangitis (fibrosis stage F0–F3) at 205 sites in 16 countries, randomised 2:1 to cilofexor 100 mg daily (n=277) or placebo (n=139); 416 in the full analysis set. Primary endpoint: progression of liver fibrosis by at least one stage at week 96, in the 197 patients with paired biopsies (133 cilofexor, 64 placebo).
cards.result: The trial was terminated early after an interim futility analysis estimated a 6.8% probability of success (prespecified futility boundary ≤10%). Fibrosis progression occurred in 31% (41/133) on cilofexor versus 33% (21/64) on placebo (treatment difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −15.2 to 12.3; P=0.42). Pruritus occurred in 49% (136/277) on cilofexor versus 36% (50/139) on placebo, grade 3 or higher in 4% versus 1%.
cards.watchOut: Only 197 of 416 analysed patients had paired biopsies, and early termination truncates follow-up — the confidence interval still spans a 15-point benefit to a 12-point harm, so the stamp is a practical null, not a precise one. Results apply to non-cirrhotic large-duct PSC; cirrhotic and small-duct disease were not studied.
cards.source: Trauner M et al. Cilofexor in non-cirrhotic primary sclerosing cholangitis (PRIMIS): a randomised, double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
