shelves.title: Xalnesiran with or without an immunomodulator in chronic hepatitis B (Piranga): HBsAg loss in a minority, most often with peginterferon added
shelves.question: In nucleos(t)ide-suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does the siRNA xalnesiran — alone, with the TLR7 agonist ruzotolimod, or with pegylated interferon — produce HBsAg loss after treatment ends?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Immunomodulating Agents · Interferon-alpha · RNA, Small Interfering · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Early, promising, and small. In the phase 2 Piranga platform trial, 159 people with chronic hepatitis B who were virologically suppressed on a nucleos(t)ide analogue received 48 weeks of xalnesiran alone or with an immunomodulator. HBsAg loss 24 weeks after treatment ended occurred only in xalnesiran arms: 7% on xalnesiran 100 mg, 3% on 200 mg, 12% with the TLR7 agonist ruzotolimod added, 23% with pegylated interferon alfa-2a added, and 0% on nucleos(t)ide analogue alone. Every case of HBsAg loss was in a participant whose screening HBsAg was below 1000 IU/mL, and grade 3 or 4 adverse events were common — 50% in the peginterferon arm, mostly raised alanine aminotransferase. The arms held about 30 people each, the trial was open-label with no formal between-group comparison, and HBsAg loss is a surrogate for functional cure rather than a clinical outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real off-treatment HBsAg-loss signal from one small phase 2 platform trial, strongest when peginterferon is added, in a selected low-HBsAg population.

cards.headline: Piranga (Hou 2024): HBsAg loss 24 weeks after treatment ended in 23% with xalnesiran plus peginterferon, 12% with ruzotolimod, 3–7% on xalnesiran alone, 0% on nucleos(t)ide analogue alone
cards.summary: Piranga (Hou 2024): HBsAg loss 24 weeks after treatment ended in 23% with xalnesiran plus peginterferon, 12% with ruzotolimod, 3–7% on xalnesiran alone, 0% on nucleos(t)ide analogue alone
cards.people: 159 participants with chronic hepatitis B and virologic suppression on nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy, randomised in a phase 2, multicentre, adaptive, open-label platform trial to 48 weeks of: xalnesiran 100 mg (n=30), xalnesiran 200 mg (n=30), xalnesiran 200 mg plus ruzotolimod 150 mg (n=34), xalnesiran 200 mg plus pegylated interferon alfa-2a 180 μg (n=30), or NA alone (n=35). Primary end point: HBsAg loss (HBsAg <0.05 IU/mL) at 24 weeks after the end of treatment.
cards.result: HBsAg loss occurred in 7% (95% CI 1 to 22) in group 1, 3% (0 to 17) in group 2, 12% (3 to 28) in group 3, 23% (10 to 42) in group 4, and none (0 to 10) in group 5. HBsAg seroconversion at the same time point occurred in 3%, none, 3%, 20%, and none, respectively. HBsAg loss with or without seroconversion occurred only in participants with a screening HBsAg level below 1000 IU/mL. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 17%, 10%, 18%, 50%, and 6% of groups 1 through 5, the most frequent being an elevated alanine aminotransferase level.
cards.watchOut: About 30 participants per arm, open-label, and no immunomodulator-alone arms, so the added effect of ruzotolimod or peginterferon cannot be isolated formally. HBsAg loss is a surrogate end point; whether it translates into durable functional cure or fewer clinical events is unproven, and the benefit was confined to people who started with HBsAg below 1000 IU/mL. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events in half the peginterferon arm temper the best efficacy figure.
cards.source: Hou J et al. Xalnesiran with or without an Immunomodulator in Chronic Hepatitis B. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 39774313. Registry ID: NCT04225715, from the record. shelves.title: REEF-1: JNJ-3989 siRNA moved 16–19% to stopping criteria; adding bersacapavir made it worse, not better
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis B, does the siRNA JNJ-3989 (ARO-HBV) — with or without the capsid assembly modulator bersacapavir (JNJ-6379) — get patients to nucleos(t)ide-stopping criteria on a nucleos(t)ide backbone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Capsid · DNA, Viral · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · RNA, Small Interfering
shelves.balance: The components pull in opposite directions, so this stamp is split. REEF-1 randomised 470 patients with chronic hepatitis B across 108 sites in 19 countries, all on nucleos(t)ide analogues (NA), to NA plus placebo (control, n=45), bersacapavir (JNJ-6379) dual therapy (n=48), JNJ-3989 (ARO-HBV) dual therapy at 40 mg (n=93), 100 mg (n=93), or 200 mg (n=96), or triple therapy with bersacapavir plus JNJ-3989 100 mg (n=95). The siRNA alone worked dose-dependently: the primary end point — meeting NA-stopping criteria at week 48 — was reached by 19% (18 of 94) at 200 mg and 16% (15 of 92) at 100 mg versus 2% (1 of 45) on control, with mean HBsAg declines of 2.6 and 2.1 log10 IU/mL at end of treatment, and 3 patients achieved HBsAg seroclearance 24 weeks after end of treatment. The capsid inhibitor subtracted value: bersacapavir dual therapy met stopping criteria in 0% of patients, and the triple combination (9%, 8 of 94; HBsAg decline 1.8 log) did worse than the matched siRNA-alone arm. Serious adverse events occurred in 10 of 470 patients (2%), with no deaths. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE — the JNJ-3989 siRNA component moves patients toward finite therapy; the bersacapavir component contributed nothing and diluted the combination. Read as one stamp it would mislead in both directions.

cards.headline: Yuen 2023 (REEF-1): NA-stopping criteria met by 19% (JNJ-3989 200 mg) and 16% (100 mg) versus 2% control; bersacapavir-alone arm 0%; triple arm 9% — worse than siRNA alone
cards.summary: Yuen 2023 (REEF-1): NA-stopping criteria met by 19% (JNJ-3989 200 mg) and 16% (100 mg) versus 2% control; bersacapavir-alone arm 0%; triple arm 9% — worse than siRNA alone
cards.people: 470 patients with chronic hepatitis B at 108 sites in 19 countries, in a phase 2b, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial. All patients received nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy and were assigned to control (NA plus placebos, n=45), JNJ-6379 (bersacapavir) dual therapy (NA plus once-daily oral JNJ-6379 250 mg, n=48), JNJ-3989 dual therapy (NA plus subcutaneous JNJ-3989 40 mg [n=93], 100 mg [n=93], or 200 mg [n=96] every 4 weeks), or triple therapy (NA plus JNJ-6379 plus JNJ-3989 100 mg, n=95). Primary end point: the proportion meeting NA-stopping criteria at week 48.
cards.result: The primary end point was met by 5% (5 of 91) of patients in the JNJ-3989 40 mg group, 16% (15 of 92) in the 100 mg group, 19% (18 of 94) in the 200 mg group, 9% (8 of 94) in the triple-therapy group, 2% (1 of 45) in the control group, and no patients in the JNJ-6379 dual-therapy group. Mean HBsAg declines at end of treatment were 2.6 log10 IU/mL (JNJ-3989 200 mg), 2.1 log10 IU/mL (100 mg), and 1.8 log10 IU/mL (triple therapy). HBsAg seroclearance was seen in 3 patients (two in the 200 mg group, one in the 100 mg group) at 24 weeks after end of treatment, and in none in the triple-therapy arm. Serious adverse events were reported in 10 (2%) of 470 patients; there were no deaths. The authors concluded that JNJ-3989 plus NA produced the greatest HBsAg declines, and that JNJ-6379 added no benefit.
cards.watchOut: Meeting NA-stopping criteria is a protocol milestone, not functional cure — only 3 patients serocleared HBsAg, and whether patients who stopped NA stayed suppressed is a separate follow-up question. Bersacapavir is named as the specific tested product because it is an investigational capsid assembly modulator, not an approved drug. Compare REEF-2 (Shelf #2162), the follow-on combination study in NA-suppressed patients: 0 functional cures despite on-treatment antigen suppression.
cards.source: Yuen MF et al. Efficacy and safety of the siRNA JNJ-3989 and/or the capsid assembly modulator JNJ-6379 for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus infection (REEF-1): a phase 2b, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2023. PMID: 37442152. Registry ID: NCT03982186, from the record. shelves.title: REEF-2: siRNA plus capsid modulator with NUC cessation in suppressed chronic hepatitis B — no functional cure in anyone
shelves.question: In NUC-suppressed, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B, can 48 weeks of JNJ-3989 + bersacapavir + NUC lead to off-treatment functional cure after stopping all therapy?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Nucleosides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A cleanly negative answer on the question that matters. In REEF-2, 130 nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA)-suppressed, HBeAg-negative patients received 48 weeks of the siRNA JNJ-73763989 plus the capsid assembly modulator bersacapavir plus NA, or placebos plus NA, then stopped all treatment and were followed for 48 weeks. On treatment, HBsAg fell by a mean of 1.89 log10 IU/mL in the active arm versus 0.06 with control — but at follow-up week 24, no patient in either arm had achieved the primary end point of off-treatment HBsAg seroclearance (functional cure), and none had by week 48 either. The combination did soften what happened after stopping — fewer and less severe HBV DNA rises and alanine aminotransferase flares, and more patients kept HBV DNA suppressed off treatment — but softening relapse is not cure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the stamp grades the functional-cure claim, which a well-run double-blind phase 2b trial tested directly and found in zero patients; the secondary off-treatment signals are noted, not upgraded.

cards.headline: REEF-2 (Agarwal 2024): zero functional cures in either arm despite a 1.89 log10 on-treatment HBsAg fall
cards.summary: REEF-2 (Agarwal 2024): zero functional cures in either arm despite a 1.89 log10 on-treatment HBsAg fall
cards.people: 130 nucleos(t)ide analogue-suppressed, HBeAg-negative patients with chronic hepatitis B in a phase 2b, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised study: JNJ-73763989 (JNJ-3989) 200 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks plus bersacapavir (JNJ-56136379) 250 mg orally daily plus NA, or matching placebos plus NA, for 48 weeks, followed by 48 weeks of off-treatment follow-up. Primary end point: off-treatment HBsAg seroclearance (functional cure).
cards.result: At follow-up week 24, no patients achieved the primary end point of functional cure (off-treatment HBsAg seroclearance), and no patients achieved functional cure at follow-up week 48. On treatment, mean HBsAg fell from baseline by 1.89 log10 IU/mL in the active arm versus 0.06 log10 IU/mL in the control arm at week 48. After all therapy stopped, the active arm had fewer and less severe post-treatment HBV DNA increases and alanine aminotransferase flares, and a higher proportion of patients with off-treatment HBV DNA suppression, with or without HBsAg suppression — but did not result in functional cure.
cards.watchOut: The null is on functional cure, the end point patients care about; the favourable secondary findings (fewer flares, more off-treatment DNA suppression) come from the same single trial and do not rescue the primary claim. The developer programme was later discontinued, so this combination will not be the one to test the idea further. Cross-point: REEF-1, the on-treatment companion trial, is Shelf #2161.

shelves.title: GS-4774 therapeutic vaccine in suppressed chronic hepatitis B: well tolerated, no HBsAg decline at any dose
shelves.question: In virally suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does the yeast-based T-cell vaccine GS-4774 lower HBsAg versus continuing oral antivirals alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A well-tolerated vaccine that did not move its target. In this randomised phase 2 trial, 178 patients with chronic hepatitis B, no cirrhosis, and at least a year of viral suppression on an oral antiviral were assigned to continue the antiviral alone or to add GS-4774 — a heat-inactivated, yeast-based T-cell vaccine — at 2, 10, or 40 yeast units every 4 weeks until week 20. There were no significant differences between groups in mean HBsAg decline at week 24 or week 48, and no patient in any group lost serum HBsAg. The only favourable crumbs were five cases of HBeAg loss among GS-4774 recipients versus none on control, and three patients on the highest dose with HBsAg declines of at least 0.5 log10 IU/mL — far too few to grade as benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a direct, adequately sized phase 2 test of the vaccine's stated purpose, negative at every dose.

cards.headline: Lok 2016 (GS-4774): no significant HBsAg decline at any dose at week 24 or 48, and no HBsAg loss in any patient
cards.summary: Lok 2016 (GS-4774): no significant HBsAg decline at any dose at week 24 or 48, and no HBsAg loss in any patient
cards.people: 178 patients with chronic hepatitis B and no cirrhosis, virally suppressed on an oral antiviral (OAV) for at least 1 year, randomised (1:2:2:2) in a phase 2 study to continue OAV alone or receive OAV plus GS-4774 at 2, 10, or 40 yeast units (YU) subcutaneously every 4 weeks until week 20; OAV continued for the remainder of the study. Primary efficacy measure: decline in serum hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) from baseline to week 24. Baseline mean HBsAg was 2.5–3.1 log10 IU/mL and 24–26% were HBeAg-positive.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between groups in mean HBsAg declines from baseline to week 24 or 48. Five HBeAg-positive patients receiving GS-4774 experienced HBeAg loss versus none in the control group. Three GS-4774 40 YU-treated patients had HBsAg declines of at least 0.5 log10 IU/mL, but no patient experienced loss of serum HBsAg. No virologic breakthrough occurred. Injection site reactions were the most frequent adverse event, and there were no treatment discontinuations. The authors concluded that GS-4774 was well tolerated but did not provide significant reductions in serum HBsAg in virally suppressed patients with chronic hepatitis B.
cards.watchOut: The trial tested GS-4774 in already-suppressed patients; the authors note efficacy in treatment-naïve patients was not determined — but the vaccine's rationale was precisely to add immune control on top of suppression, and on that rationale it failed. HBeAg loss in five patients is a post-hoc crumb across three dose arms, not a graded benefit. Cross-point: a later therapeutic vaccine given after siRNA antigen lowering (BRII-179) is Shelf #2165.

shelves.title: Selgantolimod (TLR8 agonist) in suppressed chronic hepatitis B: primary end point met by one patient of 48
shelves.question: In virally suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does weekly oral selgantolimod (GS-9688) produce clinically meaningful HBsAg declines versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Toll-Like Receptor 8 · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Immune activation, yes; meaningful antigen decline, barely. In this randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, 48 virally suppressed patients with chronic hepatitis B (24 HBeAg-positive, 24 HBeAg-negative) received weekly oral selgantolimod 3 mg or 1.5 mg, or placebo, for 24 weeks while continuing oral antivirals. The primary end point — an HBsAg decline of at least 1 log10 IU/mL by week 24 — was reached by exactly one participant. Against placebo (n=9), only selgantolimod-treated patients (n=39) had HBsAg declines greater than 0.1 log10 IU/mL (18% at week 24, 26% at week 48), HBsAg loss (5%, 2 of 39 through week 48), or HBeAg loss (16%, 3 of 19) — real pharmacology at a scale far below clinical usefulness, in a trial too small to weigh two HBsAg losses. Nausea (46%) and vomiting (23%) were common. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a phase 2 signal of serologic movement in a handful of patients, with the pre-specified primary end point met by one person.

cards.headline: Gane 2023 (selgantolimod): primary end point met by 1 of 48 participants; HBsAg loss in 2 of 39 treated through week 48
cards.summary: Gane 2023 (selgantolimod): primary end point met by 1 of 48 participants; HBsAg loss in 2 of 39 treated through week 48
cards.people: Forty-eight patients with chronic hepatitis B under viral suppression on oral antiviral treatment, randomised into HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative cohorts (n=24 each) to receive oral selgantolimod 3 mg, 1.5 mg, or placebo (2:2:1) once weekly for 24 weeks while maintaining oral antivirals, then followed on antivirals for a further 24 weeks. Primary efficacy end point: the percentage of patients with a ≥1 log10 IU/mL decline in HBsAg from baseline to week 24.
cards.result: The primary end point was reached by one participant, who was HBeAg-negative and received selgantolimod 1.5 mg. In contrast with placebo-treated patients (n=9), only selgantolimod-treated patients (n=39 total) had HBsAg declines greater than 0.1 log10 IU/mL at weeks 24 (18%, 7/39) and 48 (26%, 10/39), HBsAg loss (5%, 2/39 through 48 weeks), or HBeAg loss (16%, 3/19 through 48 weeks). The most common adverse events in selgantolimod-treated groups were nausea (46%), upper respiratory tract infection (23%), and vomiting (23%); gastrointestinal disorders were mostly mild and transient. Selgantolimod induced transient dose-dependent increases in serum cytokines, including IL-12p40, IFN-γ, and IL-1RA. The authors concluded that selgantolimod was generally safe and well tolerated and led to serologic changes associated with progression to durable cure in two individuals by week 48.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight patients, a placebo arm of nine, and a primary end point met by a single participant: the two HBsAg losses are the kind of count that chance and selection can produce at this size. Note the draft for this topic named a different first author and journal — the record is Gane et al., Journal of Hepatology 2023, and this card follows the record. A companion trial in viremic patients (Janssen et al., JHEP Reports 2024; NCT03615066 — named, not carded) found the same pattern of immune activation without significant HBsAg suppression.
cards.source: Gane EJ et al. Safety and efficacy of the oral TLR8 agonist selgantolimod in individuals with chronic hepatitis B under viral suppression. J Hepatol. 2023. PMID: 38133554. Registry ID: NCT03491553, from the record. shelves.title: BRII-179 therapeutic vaccine after siRNA HBsAg lowering: immune responses restored on paper, HBsAg not cleared
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis B, does lowering HBsAg with the siRNA elebsiran (BRII-835) restore HBV-specific immunity, and does adding the therapeutic vaccine BRII-179 (± interferon) amplify it?
shelves.mesh: Hepatitis B Antibodies · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B Vaccines · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Immunity, Cellular · Immunity, Humoral · RNA, Small Interfering
shelves.balance: An immunology study with an immunology answer — and no clinical one. In this phase 2a study, 90 participants with chronic hepatitis B received nine 4-weekly doses of the siRNA elebsiran (BRII-835), alone (n=10) or with the virus-like-particle therapeutic vaccine BRII-179, co-administered with interferon alfa (n=39) or without it (n=41), and were analysed over 72 weeks. Lowering HBsAg with the siRNA alone produced minimal recovery of HBV-specific immunity; adding BRII-179 changed the immune picture — anti-HBs antibody production and an expansion of interleukin-2-producing helper T cells specific for the Pre-S1/Pre-S2 antigens — and anti-HBs antibodies persisted at ≥100 IU/L in about 40% of combination participants for at least 32 weeks. But there was no sustained HBsAg seroclearance and no notable difference in mean HBsAg reduction at group level. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — immune-response endpoints only, in a small phase 2a analysis; whether this immune 'restoration' ever converts into functional cure is exactly what it does not show. Distinct from topic #2117 (elebsiran plus peginterferon as antiviral therapy): this shelf is the vaccine-immunogenicity question.

cards.headline: Ji 2025: elebsiran plus BRII-179 induced anti-HBs antibodies (≥100 IU/L persisting in ~40%) and Pre-S1/Pre-S2-specific T cells — but no sustained HBsAg seroclearance
cards.summary: Ji 2025: elebsiran plus BRII-179 induced anti-HBs antibodies (≥100 IU/L persisting in ~40%) and Pre-S1/Pre-S2-specific T cells — but no sustained HBsAg seroclearance
cards.people: 90 participants with chronic hepatitis B in a phase 2a study, treated with nine 4-weekly doses of the HBV-targeted siRNA elebsiran (BRII-835), either alone (n=10) or in combination with the virus-like particle-based therapeutic vaccine BRII-179 (containing Pre-S1, Pre-S2, and S antigens), co-administered with interferon alfa (n=39) or without it (n=41). Virologic, clinical, and immunologic parameters — HBsAg, alanine aminotransferase, anti-HBs, neutralising activity, and HBV-specific T-cell responses — were analysed longitudinally for 72 weeks.
cards.result: Combination therapy with elebsiran and BRII-179 was well tolerated. Although no sustained HBsAg seroclearance or notable difference in mean HBsAg reduction at the group level was observed, immunologic responses differed markedly between groups: HBsAg reduction mediated by siRNA alone was associated with minimal HBV-specific immune response recovery, whereas combining elebsiran with BRII-179 induced anti-HBs antibody production and an expansion of interleukin-2-producing helper T cells specific for Pre-S1/Pre-S2 antigens only. Anti-HBs antibodies persisted at ≥100 IU/L in approximately 40% of the participants for at least 32 weeks after combined treatment. The authors conclude that siRNA-induced HBsAg reduction may contribute to the persistence and efficacy of the humoral arm of HBV-specific adaptive immunity in participants receiving BRII-179.
cards.watchOut: The end points are laboratory immune responses, not cure, symptoms, or liver outcomes — and the headline clinical measure (HBsAg seroclearance) was not achieved in sustained form. shelves.title: Bulevirtide plus pegylated interferon for hepatitis D (MYR204): 46% undetectable HDV RNA after treatment ended
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis D, does combining bulevirtide with pegylated interferon alfa-2a produce more durable off-treatment HDV RNA undetectability than peginterferon alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hepatitis D, Chronic · Hepatitis Delta Virus · Interferon-alpha · Lipopeptides · RNA, Viral · Viral Load
shelves.balance: The strongest off-treatment result yet for a finite hepatitis D regimen — from one open-label phase 2b trial. In MYR204, patients received peginterferon alfa-2a alone for 48 weeks, bulevirtide 2 mg or 10 mg plus peginterferon for 48 weeks followed by bulevirtide alone for 48 weeks, or bulevirtide 10 mg alone for 96 weeks. Twenty-four weeks after all treatment ended, HDV RNA was undetectable in 46% of the 10-mg combination group versus 17% on peginterferon alone and 12% on bulevirtide alone — a 34-percentage-point advantage over bulevirtide monotherapy (95% CI 15 to 50; P<0.001) for the primary comparison — and the 46% figure held at 48 weeks after treatment. The end point is virologic, not clinical; the trial was open-label; and the winning regimen still left most patients detectable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one phase 2b trial with a durable off-treatment virologic benefit for the 10-mg combination. Cross-point: bulevirtide monotherapy versus delayed treatment is Shelf #1063; this shelf is only the combination question.

cards.headline: MYR204 (Asselah 2024): undetectable HDV RNA 24 weeks after treatment ended in 46% on bulevirtide 10 mg plus peginterferon, versus 17% peginterferon alone and 12% bulevirtide alone
cards.summary: MYR204 (Asselah 2024): undetectable HDV RNA 24 weeks after treatment ended in 46% on bulevirtide 10 mg plus peginterferon, versus 17% peginterferon alone and 12% bulevirtide alone
cards.people: Patients with chronic hepatitis D randomly assigned in a phase 2b, open-label trial to: peginterferon alfa-2a 180 μg weekly alone for 48 weeks (n=24); bulevirtide 2 mg daily plus peginterferon alfa-2a for 48 weeks, then bulevirtide 2 mg alone for 48 weeks (n=50); bulevirtide 10 mg daily plus peginterferon alfa-2a for 48 weeks, then bulevirtide 10 mg alone for 48 weeks (n=50); or bulevirtide 10 mg daily alone for 96 weeks (n=50). Primary end point: undetectable HDV RNA at 24 weeks after the end of treatment.
cards.result: At 24 weeks after the end of treatment, HDV RNA was undetectable in 17% of the peginterferon alfa-2a group, 32% of the 2-mg bulevirtide plus peginterferon group, 46% of the 10-mg bulevirtide plus peginterferon group, and 12% of the 10-mg bulevirtide group. For the primary comparison (10-mg combination versus bulevirtide monotherapy), the between-group difference was 34 percentage points (95% CI 15 to 50; P<0.001). At 48 weeks after the end of treatment, HDV RNA was undetectable in 25%, 26%, 46%, and 12% of the four groups, respectively. The most frequent adverse events were leukopenia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia, and the majority of adverse events were grade 1 or 2 in severity.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, phase 2b, and the end point is HDV RNA undetectability — a virologic surrogate, not cirrhosis, liver failure, or survival. The peginterferon-alone arm was small (n=24). Interferon brings its familiar cytopenias and tolerability burden, and even the best arm left 54% of patients with detectable HDV RNA after treatment.

shelves.title: Tobevibart plus elebsiran for hepatitis D (SOLSTICE): the combined end point favoured the antibody alone, the deep virologic end points favoured the pair
shelves.question: In chronic hepatitis D, does monthly tobevibart (anti-HBsAg monoclonal antibody) plus elebsiran (siRNA) beat tobevibart alone on combined virologic-plus-ALT response at 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antiviral Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis D, Chronic · Hepatitis Delta Virus · RNA, Small Interfering · Viral Load
shelves.balance: A genuinely split result, and the split is the story. In the ongoing phase 2 SOLSTICE trial, 65 participants with chronic hepatitis D were randomised to tobevibart plus elebsiran every 4 weeks or tobevibart monotherapy every 2 weeks. On the pre-specified combined end point (virologic response plus alanine aminotransferase normalisation) at week 24, the combination did worse: 47% (15 of 32) versus 70% (23 of 33) on tobevibart alone. Yet on the deeper virologic measures the combination pulled ahead by week 48: undetectable HDV RNA in 66% (21 of 32) versus 48% (16 of 33), and HBsAg below 10 IU/mL in 91% (29 of 32) versus 21% (7 of 33), while combined response converged (56% versus 61%). With 32–33 people per arm, no pre-specified hypothesis test, and an ongoing trial, neither half of the split can carry a strong stamp. SPLIT PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — adding elebsiran improves the combined response (the week-24 primary comparison went the other way); POSSIBLE — adding elebsiran deepens HDV RNA undetectability and HBsAg decline by week 48.

cards.headline: SOLSTICE (Asselah 2026): combined response at week 24 was 47% with tobevibart plus elebsiran versus 70% with tobevibart alone — but undetectable HDV RNA at week 48 favoured the combination, 66% versus 48%
cards.summary: SOLSTICE (Asselah 2026): combined response at week 24 was 47% with tobevibart plus elebsiran versus 70% with tobevibart alone — but undetectable HDV RNA at week 48 favoured the combination, 66% versus 48%
cards.people: 65 participants with chronic hepatitis D in an ongoing, phase 2, open-label trial, randomly assigned to tobevibart plus elebsiran every 4 weeks (n=32) or tobevibart monotherapy every 2 weeks (n=33). Both agents target hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg): tobevibart is a monoclonal antibody and elebsiran a small interfering RNA. The combined response required a virologic response plus normalisation of the alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level.
cards.result: At week 24, a combined response was observed in 47% of participants (15 of 32) who received tobevibart plus elebsiran and in 70% (23 of 33) who received tobevibart monotherapy. At week 48, a combined response was observed in 56% (18 of 32) with the combination and 61% (20 of 33) with tobevibart alone; undetectable HDV RNA (target not detected) in 66% (21 of 32) and 48% (16 of 33), respectively; normalisation of the ALT level in 56% (18 of 32) and 61% (20 of 33); and an HBsAg level below 10 IU/mL in 91% (29 of 32) and 21% (7 of 33). The authors conclude that both regimens decreased HDV RNA and ALT levels through week 48, and that the combination was associated with a high incidence of undetectable HDV RNA and of a decrease in the HBsAg level.
cards.watchOut: The two arms differ in dosing interval as well as in the added drug (combination every 4 weeks; monotherapy every 2 weeks), so this is not a clean add-on comparison. The trial is small, open-label, ongoing, and reported without a pre-specified hypothesis test — the week-24 combined-endpoint gap and the week-48 virologic gap are both compatible with chance at this sample size. Note: this SOLSTICE (hepatitis D) is a different trial from the SOLSTICE cytomegalovirus trial carded on Shelf #722.
cards.source: Asselah T et al. A Phase 2 Trial of Tobevibart plus Elebsiran in Hepatitis D. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID: 41211943. Registry ID: NCT05461170, from the record. shelves.title: HERO: patient navigation versus modified DOT for hepatitis C in people who inject drugs — equal cures either way
shelves.question: For people who inject drugs with hepatitis C, does modified directly observed therapy (mDOT) beat patient navigation for achieving cure (SVR)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Substance Abuse, Intravenous · Drug Users · Antiviral Agents · Sofosbuvir · Hepatitis C · Hepacivirus
shelves.balance: Two good models, no winner. In the HERO study — a pragmatic randomised trial at eight US cities (eight opioid treatment programmes and 15 community health centres) — 755 people actively injecting drugs received 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and were randomised to peer patient navigation (n=379) or modified directly observed therapy, mDOT (n=376). Sustained virologic response in the modified intention-to-treat population was 74% (226 of 306) with mDOT versus 76% (236 of 317) with navigation (adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.42; p=0.35); intention-to-treat SVR was 60% versus 62%, and per-protocol SVR among those who completed treatment and assessment was 91% versus 93% — no significant difference in any analysis. Treatment initiation (81% versus 84%) and completion (82% versus 83%) were also similar; mean adherence was higher with mDOT (78% versus 73%; difference 4.7%; p=0.0010) without translating into more cures. There were 421 serious adverse events, reflecting this population's burden of illness rather than the antivirals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large pragmatic trial shows the delivery model is not the bottleneck: with either organised support model, about three in four treated patients who inject drugs are cured, and programmes can choose on cost and fit.

cards.headline: Litwin 2022 (HERO): SVR 74% with mDOT versus 76% with patient navigation (AOR 0.97) in 755 actively injecting people with HCV
cards.summary: Litwin 2022 (HERO): SVR 74% with mDOT versus 76% with patient navigation (AOR 0.97) in 755 actively injecting people with HCV
cards.people: 755 people who inject drugs, actively injecting within 90 days of study entry, at eight US cities (eight opioid treatment programmes and 15 community health centres), in a pragmatic randomised trial. All participants received a fixed-dose combination of sofosbuvir 400 mg plus velpatasvir 100 mg orally once daily for 12 weeks, and were randomly assigned to patient navigation (n=379) or modified directly observed therapy, mDOT (n=376). The primary outcome was sustained virologic response (SVR); analyses were done in the modified intention-to-treat, intention-to-treat, and per-protocol populations.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat population, 226 (74%) of 306 participants in the mDOT group and 236 (76%) of 317 in the patient navigation group had an SVR, with no significant difference between groups (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 0.97 [95% CI 0.66 to 1.42]; p=0.35). In the intention-to-treat analysis, 226 (60%) of 376 in the mDOT group and 236 (62%) of 379 in the patient navigation group had an SVR (AOR 0.92 [0.68 to 1.25]; p=0.61), and in the per-protocol analysis, 226 (91%) of 248 versus 235 (93%) of 253 (AOR 0.79 [0.41 to 1.55]; p=0.44). HCV treatment initiation (81% mDOT versus 84% navigation) and treatment completion (82% versus 83%) were similar; mean adherence was 78% versus 73% (difference 4.7%; p=0.0010). There were 421 serious adverse events across the study. The authors concluded that active people who inject drugs can reach high SVRs in diverse settings with either model.
cards.watchOut: There was no unsupported-treatment control arm, by design: the trial compares two support models, and both arms' high initiation and completion rates may themselves reflect trial-grade support. The gap between per-protocol SVR (91–93%) and intention-to-treat SVR (60–62%) is attrition and missing SVR assessment, not drug failure — the clinically important number for programmes. The named tested programme models are patient navigation and modified directly observed therapy as delivered in HERO.
cards.source: Litwin AH et al. Patient-centred models of hepatitis C treatment for people who inject drugs: a multicentre, pragmatic randomised trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2022. p=0.44). hcv treatment initiation (81% mdot versus 84% navigation) and treatment completion (82% versus 83%) were similar; mean adherence was 78% versus 73% (difference 4.7%; p=0.0010). there were 421 serious adverse events across the study. the authors concluded that active people who inject drugs can reach high svrs in diverse settings with either model. there was no unsupported-treatment control arm, by design: the trial compares two support models, and both arms' high initiation and completion rates may themselves reflect trial-grade support. the gap between per-protocol svr (91–93%) and intention-to-treat svr (60–62%) is attrition and missing svr assessment, not drug failure — the clinically important number for programmes. the named tested programme models are patient navigation and modified directly observed therapy as delivered in hero. litwin ah et al. patient-centred models of hepatitis c treatment for people who inject drugs: a multicentre, pragmatic randomised trial. lancet gastroenterol hepatol. 2022. pmid: 36370741. registry id: nct02824640, from the record. mesh: humans · substance abuse, intravenous · drug users · antiviral agents · sofosbuvir · hepatitis c · hepacivirus

shelves.title: Six weeks is too short for recently acquired hepatitis C (REACT): more relapses, non-inferiority not met, trial stopped early
shelves.question: In recently acquired hepatitis C, is 6 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir non-inferior to the standard 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents · Australia · Canada · Carbamates · Drug Combinations · Female · Germany · Hepatitis C · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · New Zealand · Sofosbuvir · Switzerland · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: The short course fell short, and the trial was stopped early because of it. REACT randomised 188 people with recently acquired hepatitis C (infection within the previous 12 months; 97% male, 69% HIV-positive) to sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 6 weeks (n=93) or 12 weeks (n=95); the data safety monitoring board advised stopping enrolment early after a higher relapse rate in the short arm. Intention-to-treat SVR12 was 81.7% (76 of 93; 95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) with 6 weeks versus 90.5% (86 of 95; 82.7 to 95.6) with 12 weeks — an absolute shortfall of about 9 fewer cures per 100 patients — and non-inferiority against the 12% margin was not established in either the ITT or per-protocol analysis (per-protocol SVR12 89.4% versus 97.7%; difference −8.3%; p=0.025). Relapses: 9 in the short arm versus 2 in the standard arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — for the 6-week strategy in recently acquired HCV: a randomised comparison shows materially more relapses and fewer cures, so the saving of six weeks of drug is bought with retreatment.

cards.headline: Matthews 2021 (REACT): 6-week sofosbuvir/velpatasvir SVR12 81.7% versus 90.5% for 12 weeks; non-inferiority not met; trial stopped early
cards.summary: Matthews 2021 (REACT): 6-week sofosbuvir/velpatasvir SVR12 81.7% versus 90.5% for 12 weeks; non-inferiority not met; trial stopped early
cards.type: Open-label phase IV randomised non-inferiority trial (REACT)
cards.people: 188 participants with recently acquired hepatitis C virus infection (duration of infection ≤12 months; 97% male, 69% HIV-positive) in an open-label, phase IV, randomised non-inferiority trial at multiple centres, assigned to sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 6 weeks (short course, n=93) or 12 weeks (standard course, n=95). The primary end point was SVR12 (HCV RNA below the lower limit of quantification 12 weeks after treatment end); the non-inferiority margin was 12%. Recruitment was stopped early on the advice of the data safety monitoring board because of a higher relapse rate in the short-course arm.
cards.result: SVR12 in the intention-to-treat population was 81.7% (76 of 93; 95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) in the short-course group and 90.5% (86 of 95; 95% CI 82.7 to 95.6) in the standard group; non-inferiority was not established. In the per-protocol population, SVR12 was 89.4% (76 of 85) versus 97.7% (86 of 88), a difference of −8.3% (p=0.025), and non-inferiority was again not demonstrated. Treatment failure was mostly relapse: 9 participants in the short-course group and 2 in the standard group relapsed. The authors concluded that the 6-week course was not non-inferior to 12 weeks in recently acquired HCV and that the shorter course was associated with a higher relapse rate.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping truncates the sample (188 of a larger planned enrolment), so the exact size of the shortfall is imprecise — but the direction is consistent across ITT and per-protocol analyses and was strong enough for the DSMB to halt the trial. The population was 97% male and 69% HIV-positive, drawn from recently acquired infection cohorts; extrapolation to women or to chronic infection is weaker. Note the draft named a different first author (Martinello, who is a co-author); the record is Matthews GV et al., and this card follows the record.
cards.source: Matthews GV et al. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 vs. 6 weeks for the treatment of recently acquired hepatitis C infection. J Hepatol. 2021. PMID: 34023350. shelves.title: Does Gas-X work? Simethicone for gas and bloating
shelves.question: Does simethicone (Gas-X) relieve intestinal gas and bloating — and what did the placebo-controlled trials actually find?
shelves.mesh: Simethicone · Antifoaming Agents · Flatulence · Colic · Lactulose · Loperamide · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Simethicone is a defoaming agent — it coalesces small gas bubbles into larger ones — that is not absorbed and does not reduce how much gas the gut produces. The clean placebo tests of simethicone alone are null: in a double-blind crossover challenge, 600 mg simethicone changed neither breath hydrogen nor symptom scores after a lactulose load (Friis 1991), and in the largest standalone test, a multicentre double-blind trial in infant colic, simethicone was no more effective than placebo, including in the subgroup whose parents reported gas-related symptoms (Metcalf 1994). In acute-diarrhoea trials, gas-related discomfort was relieved fastest by loperamide PLUS simethicone, beating either agent alone and placebo (Kaplan 1999; Hanauer 2007) — but neither abstract reports simethicone alone beating placebo on the gas endpoint. Simethicone's well-proven role is a different one — clearing bubbles so endoscopists and sonographers can see — fenced in the synthesis, not carded. For the enzyme that prevents bean-and-vegetable gas, see Shelf #2430 (draft). Drafted Nov 9, 2026 at the developer's request (practical over-the-counter questions series, with Shelf #2430).

cards.headline: Friis 1991: simethicone 600 mg changed nothing — breath hydrogen and symptoms after a lactulose load were identical to placebo
cards.summary: Friis 1991: simethicone 600 mg changed nothing — breath hydrogen and symptoms after a lactulose load were identical to placebo
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers given 30 g lactulose (a fermentable sugar load chosen to produce gas and symptoms) with 600 mg simethicone or placebo, with end-expiratory breath samples analysed for hydrogen and gastrointestinal symptoms registered.
cards.result: There were no differences in biochemical parameters or symptom score between simethicone and placebo. The authors note that, in contrast to previous studies, they used a sufficiently large dose of lactulose to produce gastrointestinal symptoms, a higher dose of simethicone, and placebo tablets containing the same additives as the simethicone tablets — and found no demonstrable effect of simethicone on symptoms or intestinal gas production caused by carbohydrate malabsorption.
cards.watchOut: Ten volunteers and an artificial sugar load: a small, clean mechanistic test — its null on breath hydrogen is exactly what a defoamer's pharmacology predicts, since simethicone cannot reduce gas production.
cards.source: Friis H, Bodé S, Rumessen JJ et al. Effect of simethicone on lactulose-induced H2 production and gastrointestinal symptoms. Digestion. 1991;49(4):227-30. PMID: 1797602. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. (A Danish-language report of the same study, PMID 8259628, is the same trial and is not separately carded.) cards.headline: Metcalf 1994: for infant colic, simethicone was no better than placebo — 28% responded only to simethicone, 37% only to placebo
cards.summary: Metcalf 1994: for infant colic, simethicone was no better than placebo — 28% responded only to simethicone, 37% only to placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre crossover trial
cards.people: 83 infants between 2 and 8 weeks of age with infant colic, at three general paediatric practices in distinct geographic regions, treated with simethicone and placebo in double-blind crossover fashion (166 treatment periods of 3 to 10 days evaluated).
cards.result: Compared with baseline, improvement was reported for 54% of treatment periods, worsening for 22% and no change for 24% — and the likelihood of each rating was the same whether the infant was receiving simethicone or placebo. Twenty-eight percent of infants responded only to simethicone, 37% only to placebo and 20% to both, with no statistically significant differences among these groups; no difference appeared even when infants with parent-reported gas-related symptoms were separated out. The authors conclude simethicone is no more effective than placebo in the treatment of infantile colic.
cards.watchOut: Babies, not adults — carded because it is the largest rigorous standalone placebo test of simethicone for a gas-attributed symptom, and because colic is the use parents most often ask about; its null does not by itself settle adult bloating, and the adult challenge trial above points the same way.
cards.source: Metcalf TJ, Irons TG, Sher LD et al. Simethicone in the treatment of infant colic: a randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial. Pediatrics. 1994;94(1):29-34. PMID: 8008533. cards.headline: Kaplan 1999: loperamide-simethicone beat simethicone alone and placebo for diarrhoea with gas discomfort — simethicone alone never separated from placebo in print
cards.summary: Kaplan 1999: loperamide-simethicone beat simethicone alone and placebo for diarrhoea with gas discomfort — simethicone alone never separated from placebo in print
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, four-arm trial (48 hours)
cards.people: 493 outpatients aged 18 to 63 years with acute nonspecific diarrhoea and at least moderately severe gas-related abdominal discomfort, at a primary-care ambulatory practice in Acapulco, Mexico, randomised to loperamide-simethicone chewable tablets (124), loperamide 2 mg alone (123), simethicone 125 mg alone (123) or placebo (123), for 48 hours.
cards.result: Patients who received loperamide-simethicone had significantly shorter time to last unformed stool and faster relief of gas-related abdominal discomfort (gas pain, cramps, gas pressure and bloating) than patients who received loperamide alone, simethicone alone or placebo (P<.001), and the combination was more effective than all three for every end-of-study patient-assessed outcome (P≤.01). No significant differences in adverse events were found among the groups. The abstract reports no comparison in which simethicone alone beat placebo.
cards.watchOut: An industry trial (authors from McNeil Consumer Healthcare) in acute diarrhoea, not ordinary gas: it shows the combination works, and that simethicone alone was not a driver anyone could point to.
cards.source: Kaplan MA, Prior MJ, Ash RR et al. Loperamide-simethicone vs loperamide alone, simethicone alone, and placebo in the treatment of acute diarrhea with gas-related abdominal discomfort. A randomized controlled trial. Arch Fam Med. 1999;8(3):243-8. PMID: 10333820. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Hanauer 2007: the combination relieved gas discomfort fastest (all P=0.0001); simethicone alone's time to last stool (26.0 h) sat beside placebo's (29.4 h)
cards.summary: Hanauer 2007: the combination relieved gas discomfort fastest (all P=0.0001); simethicone alone's time to last stool (26.0 h) sat beside placebo's (29.4 h)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre, four-arm trial (48 hours)
cards.people: 483 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis with acute nonspecific diarrhoea and gas-related abdominal discomfort, randomised to loperamide/simethicone 2 mg/125 mg (121), loperamide alone (120), simethicone 125 mg alone (123) or placebo (121), for 48 hours.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a harmless defoamer whose solo trial record is null — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a harmless defoamer whose solo trial record is null — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Friis 1991 (10 healthy volunteers, lactulose challenge), Metcalf 1994 (83 infants with colic), Kaplan 1999 (493 adults) and Hanauer 2007 (483 adults) — the last two in acute diarrhoea with simethicone-alone arms.
cards.result: Every rigorous standalone comparison is null: no effect on gas production or symptoms under a fermentable load, no effect beyond placebo in colic, and no printed solo win in two large four-arm diarrhoea trials where the loperamide combination took the honours. Simethicone is also genuinely benign — unabsorbed, with adverse-event rates at placebo levels in these trials — and it has one proven job, defoaming for endoscopy and ultrasound visibility, which this shelf fences rather than cards; a 2018 functional-bloating trial that used simethicone as the comparator arm, without a placebo group, is likewise fenced (PMID 30511026). The honest answer to 'does Gas-X work?' is that it may change how gas feels as bubbles coalesce, many people report relief, and the controlled evidence that simethicone alone relieves gas is weak — MAYBE (weak evidence). The preventive with actual trial support for bean-and-vegetable gas is the enzyme on Shelf #2430 (draft).
cards.watchOut: Absence of evidence here is close to evidence of absence for gas PRODUCTION, but symptom relief is subjective and these trials were not powered for small comfort effects; the stamp grades the evidence, not any individual's experience.

shelves.title: Lactase enzyme drops for lactose intolerance: one small 1992 crossover — less breath hydrogen, fewer symptoms
shelves.question: In adults with lactose malabsorption and intolerance, does adding lactase (beta-galactosidase) enzyme to milk reduce malabsorption and symptoms compared with placebo-treated milk?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aspergillus niger/enzymology · Breath Tests · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lactose/metabolism · Lactose Intolerance/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · beta-Galactosidase/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Lactase tablets and drops are a staple over-the-counter purchase for people who cannot digest milk sugar, and the randomised evidence behind them is remarkably thin: one small double-blind crossover from 1992. In 16 adults with lactose malabsorption and intolerance, milk pre-treated with beta-galactosidase from Aspergillus niger produced significantly lower breath-hydrogen measures (peak p<0.01; cumulative excretion p<0.005) and a significantly lower cumulative gastrointestinal intolerance index (p<0.005) than placebo-treated milk, using a 400 mL milk challenge. The direction is exactly what the enzyme's mechanism predicts, and the outcome combines a malabsorption marker with symptoms — but one 16-person crossover is the whole pinned record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Enzyme-treated milk cut breath hydrogen and intolerance scores vs placebo-treated milk in 16 lactose malabsorbers (crossover)
cards.summary: Enzyme-treated milk cut breath hydrogen and intolerance scores vs placebo-treated milk in 16 lactose malabsorbers (crossover)
cards.people: 16 adult patients with lactose malabsorption and intolerance, studied in a double-blind crossover: 400 mL of intact milk with Aspergillus niger beta-galactosidase added, versus placebo, with a 5-hour hydrogen breath test and a cumulative gastrointestinal intolerance index.
cards.result: Versus placebo, lactase-added milk significantly reduced maximum breath H2 concentration (p<0.01) and cumulative H2 excretion (p<0.005); the cumulative intolerance index was also significantly lower (p<0.005). The authors conclude enzyme replacement with this beta-galactosidase decreases lactose malabsorption and its consequent intolerance.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen patients, one milk dose, one enzyme source, 1992. Breath hydrogen is a malabsorption surrogate; the symptom index moved with it, which helps, but modern large trials of the products people actually buy do not exist in the record this shelf could pin. The enzyme tested was beta-galactosidase from Aspergillus niger; the publication names no commercial brand.
cards.source: Corazza GR et al.. beta-Galactosidase from Aspergillus niger in adult lactose malabsorption: a double-blind crossover study. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 1992. PMID: 1543816. shelves.title: Gut-directed hypnotherapy for IBS in adults: benefits in ordinary clinics as well as in the founding unit, sustained to one year
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome that has not responded to standard management, does gut-directed hypnotherapy improve bowel symptoms compared with supportive therapy, waiting list, or psychotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Hypnosis/methods · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/psychology, therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Gut-directed hypnotherapy is the best-known psychological treatment for IBS, and unusually for this slate it has both a founding trial and a pragmatic replication. Whorwell's 1984 Lancet trial randomised 30 patients with severe refractory IBS to hypnotherapy or psychotherapy-plus-placebo: the hypnotherapy group improved dramatically on all features — pain, distension, bowel habit and well-being — with no relapses over 3 months. Lindfors moved the question out of the specialist unit: 138 patients with refractory IBS were randomised in two studies (hypnotherapy in private psychology practices versus supportive therapy; hypnotherapy in a small county hospital versus waiting list). Symptoms improved significantly at 3 months in the hypnotherapy groups in both settings, significantly more than controls in the first study with a trend in the second (p=0.17), and the gains held at 1 year — though the authors note effectiveness is lower outside highly specialised centres. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged THIN on trial count: two randomised studies, concordant, in exactly the refractory population that asks about it. (Paediatric hypnotherapy is Shelf #1142's question and is not duplicated.)

cards.headline: Pragmatic trials: hypnotherapy improved IBS symptoms at 3 months in private practices and a county hospital; gains sustained at 1 year (n=138)
cards.summary: Pragmatic trials: hypnotherapy improved IBS symptoms at 3 months in private practices and a county hospital; gains sustained at 1 year (n=138)
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials in routine clinical settings (Lindfors 2012)
cards.people: 138 patients with IBS refractory to standard management in two randomised studies: study 1 (n=90) gut-directed hypnotherapy (12 one-hour weekly sessions) in psychology private practices versus supportive therapy; study 2 (n=48) hypnotherapy in a small county hospital versus waiting-list control. Outcomes gastrointestinal symptom severity and quality of life at 3 months and 1 year.
cards.result: In both studies, IBS symptoms improved at 3 months in the hypnotherapy groups (p<0.05) but not in the control groups. The between-group difference in symptom severity was significant in study 1 (p<0.05) and a trend in study 2 (p=0.17). Results at 3 months were sustained up to 1 year.
cards.watchOut: Blinding a talking therapy is impossible and waiting-list controls inflate contrasts; the supportive-therapy comparison in study 1 is the fairer test, and it is the one that reached significance. Effect sizes outside specialist centres were smaller — expectations should be set accordingly.
cards.source: Lindfors P et al.. Effects of gut-directed hypnotherapy on IBS in different clinical settings-results from two randomized, controlled trials. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 21971535. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. cards.headline: Whorwell 1984: hypnotherapy produced dramatic improvement in all IBS features vs psychotherapy plus placebo in 30 severe refractory patients
cards.summary: Whorwell 1984: hypnotherapy produced dramatic improvement in all IBS features vs psychotherapy plus placebo in 30 severe refractory patients
cards.people: 30 patients with severe refractory irritable bowel syndrome randomised to hypnotherapy or to psychotherapy plus placebo; outcomes abdominal pain, distension, bowel habit and general well-being, with 3-month follow-up.
cards.result: The psychotherapy group improved slightly but significantly on pain, distension and well-being, but not bowel habit. The hypnotherapy group improved dramatically on all features, the between-group difference being highly significant. No relapses were recorded in the hypnotherapy group during the 3-month follow-up, and no substitution symptoms were observed.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, 1984, from the treatment's founding unit, with a brief abstract by modern standards — carded as the origin trial it is; the stamp rests on its concordance with the later pragmatic replication, not on this trial alone.

shelves.title: Antispasmodics for IBS: pinaverium beat placebo clearly in a 427-patient trial; otilonium showed a dose-dependent effect in a small dose-ranging study
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, do antispasmodic drugs — pinaverium bromide or otilonium bromide — relieve abdominal pain and global symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Calcium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage, adverse effects · China · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology, pathology · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy, pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Placebos/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Antispasmodics are first-line IBS prescriptions in much of the world yet are often dismissed as untested; two placebo-controlled trials of the two most studied agents say otherwise, at different strengths. Pinaverium bromide 50 mg three times daily, in 427 Rome III IBS patients across four Chinese hospitals, met its primary endpoints (pain reduction and stool-score improvement) in significantly more patients than placebo — 77.5% met a primary endpoint by week 4 (p<0.001) — and 60% versus 34% rated their symptoms globally improved, with mild side effects (nausea 3.7%, dizziness 3.2%). Otilonium bromide's evidence is a 93-patient dose-ranging study: individual symptoms mostly did not separate from placebo, but evacuation frequency fell significantly at 80 mg (−41.9% vs −8.36%; p<0.01) and a global discomfort index improved dose-dependently, significantly at 40 mg (p=0.013) and 80 mg (p=0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one solid trial for pinaverium, a supportive small one for otilonium.

cards.headline: Pinaverium: 77.5% met a primary endpoint by week 4 vs placebo (p<0.001); global improvement 60% vs 34% (n=427)
cards.summary: Pinaverium: 77.5% met a primary endpoint by week 4 vs placebo (p<0.001); global improvement 60% vs 34% (n=427)
cards.people: 427 patients with Rome III irritable bowel syndrome at four hospitals in China, randomised to pinaverium bromide 50 mg three times daily (n=218) or placebo (n=209) for 4 weeks; primary endpoints reduction in abdominal pain and Bristol stool score.
cards.result: Significantly more pinaverium patients met a primary endpoint (50.0% at week 2, 77.5% at week 4) than placebo patients (p<0.001), and likewise for the secondary endpoints (91.7% by week 4). Global improvement was reported by 60% on pinaverium vs 34% on placebo (p<0.001). No severe adverse effects; common ones were nausea (3.7%), dizziness (3.2%), increased blood pressure (2.3%) and abdominal discomfort (2.3%).
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the pinaverium-arm endpoint rates and the significance of the contrast but not the placebo-arm endpoint rates; the global-improvement comparison (60% vs 34%) is the fully quantified one. A single-country trial of an agent not marketed everywhere.
cards.source: Zheng L et al.. Pinaverium Reduces Symptoms of Irritable Bowel Syndrome in a Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2015. PMID: 25632806. Registry ID: NCT01641224. cards.headline: Otilonium dose-ranging: global discomfort index improved significantly at 40 mg (p=0.013) and 80 mg (p=0.001); most individual symptoms did not separate (n=93)
cards.summary: Otilonium dose-ranging: global discomfort index improved significantly at 40 mg (p=0.013) and 80 mg (p=0.001); most individual symptoms did not separate (n=93)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging phase I/II study (Chmielewska-Wilkoń 2014)
cards.people: 93 patients with Rome II IBS randomised to otilonium bromide 20 mg, 40 mg or 80 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks; primary variables abdominal discomfort, intestinal habits, evacuation frequency and stool consistency.
cards.result: Individual intensity/frequency measures (pain, discomfort, bloating) fell on otilonium but did not differ significantly between groups. Evacuation frequency fell significantly more on 80 mg than placebo (−41.9% vs −8.36%; p<0.01); regular intestinal habits returned in more patients on 40 mg (p<0.01 vs placebo), and diarrhoea frequency fell dose-dependently (trend p<0.001). The composite global discomfort index significantly favoured 40 mg (p=0.013) and 80 mg (p=0.001). Adverse-event frequency did not differ from placebo.
cards.watchOut: A phase I/II dose-finder, not a confirmatory trial: its positive results live in a composite index and selected endpoints while the headline symptoms missed significance. Carded as supportive evidence beside pinaverium's trial, not as a second pillar of equal weight.
cards.source: Chmielewska-Wilkoń D et al.. Otilonium bromide in irritable bowel syndrome: a dose-ranging randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. World journal of gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 25232263. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. shelves.title: Colace doesn't soften much: docusate never beat placebo and lost to psyllium
shelves.question: In people with constipation, does docusate sodium — the 'stool softener' in Colace — soften stools or increase bowel movements compared with placebo or standard laxatives?
shelves.mesh: Dioctyl Sulfosuccinic Acid · Constipation · Laxatives · Psyllium · Senna Extract · Hospice Care · Humans
shelves.balance: Docusate sodium — the 'stool softener' sold as Colace — has never beaten placebo, because the only placebo-controlled test is an add-on trial and it was null: in 74 hospice patients, docusate plus sennosides produced no difference from placebo plus sennosides in stool frequency, volume, consistency, difficulty or completeness of evacuation over 10 days (Tarumi 2013). There is no clean trial of docusate alone versus placebo. Head-to-head, it lost to a fibre laxative on its own home ground: in 170 people with chronic constipation, stool water content rose 2.33% on psyllium versus 0.01% on docusate (P=.007), and bowel movements in week 2 were 3.5 versus 2.9 per week (P=.02) (McRorie 1998). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the one placebo-controlled test is null and the one head-to-head is a clear loss, though a solo placebo trial was never run.

cards.headline: Tarumi 2013: adding docusate to sennosides changed nothing in 74 hospice patients — no difference in stool frequency, volume, consistency, difficulty or completeness
cards.summary: Tarumi 2013: adding docusate to sennosides changed nothing in 74 hospice patients — no difference in stool frequency, volume, consistency, difficulty or completeness
cards.people: 74 hospice patients in Edmonton, Alberta (35 to docusate plus sennosides, 39 to placebo plus sennosides), aged 18 or older, able to take oral medication, without a gastrointestinal stoma and with a Palliative Performance Scale score of 20% or more, treated for 10 days.
cards.result: There were neither significant differences between the groups in stool frequency, volume or consistency, nor in difficulty or completeness of evacuation. On the Bristol Stool Form Scale, more patients in the placebo group had Type 4 (smooth and soft) and Type 5 (soft blobs) stool, whereas in the docusate group more had Type 3 (sausage like) and Type 6 (mushy) stool (P=0.01). The authors conclude there was no significant benefit of docusate plus sennosides compared with placebo plus sennosides.
cards.watchOut: This is an add-on design — docusate was tested on top of sennosides, a stimulant laxative, in hospice patients — because there is no clean trial of docusate alone versus placebo to card: this is the only placebo-controlled test of docusate, and adding it to a working laxative added nothing. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Tarumi Y et al.. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral docusate in the management of constipation in hospice patients. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2013. cards.headline: McRorie 1998: psyllium beat docusate head-to-head — stool water rose 2.33% on psyllium versus 0.01% on docusate (P=.007)
cards.summary: McRorie 1998: psyllium beat docusate head-to-head — stool water rose 2.33% on psyllium versus 0.01% on docusate (P=.007)
cards.people: 170 subjects with chronic idiopathic constipation at multiple sites, in a randomised, double-blind, parallel study: a 2-week baseline (placebo) phase, then 2 weeks of psyllium 5.1 g twice daily plus docusate placebo, or docusate sodium 100 mg twice daily plus psyllium placebo, with stools collected and assessed.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, psyllium increased stool water content versus docusate (2.33% versus 0.01%, P=0.007); psyllium also increased stool water weight (84.0 versus 71.4 g per bowel movement, P=0.04), total stool output (359.9 versus 271.9 g/week, P=0.005) and the combined objective constipation score (475.1 versus 403.9, P=0.002). Bowel movement frequency in treatment week 2 was 3.5 per week on psyllium versus 2.9 per week on docusate (P=0.02), with no significant difference in week 1 (3.3 versus 3.1 per week).
cards.watchOut: A head-to-head against a fibre laxative, not a placebo trial of docusate — it shows docusate loses to psyllium on the very outcome it is sold for (stool water), with a short 2-week treatment phase. Authors were linked to the psyllium manufacturer, so the margin may flatter psyllium; it cannot rescue docusate, whose stool-water change was 0.01%. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: McRorie JW et al.. Psyllium is superior to docusate sodium for treatment of chronic constipation. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1998. PMID: 9663731. cards.headline: Synthesis: docusate never beat placebo and lost to psyllium on stool water — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: docusate never beat placebo and lost to psyllium on stool water — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: People with constipation across one 74-patient placebo-controlled add-on trial in hospice care and one 170-patient head-to-head trial in chronic idiopathic constipation.
cards.result: Added to sennosides, docusate produced no difference in stool frequency, volume, consistency, difficulty or completeness of evacuation (Tarumi 2013); against psyllium, docusate's stool-water change was 0.01% versus 2.33% and it produced fewer bowel movements in week 2, 2.9 versus 3.5 per week (McRorie 1998). cards.watchOut: Absence of a docusate-alone placebo trial is itself the finding to be honest about: the stamp rests on a null add-on trial plus a lost head-to-head, not on a direct solo test. Nothing here judges stimulant or osmotic laxatives, which are different drugs with their own evidence.

shelves.title: Anal fissure: creams heal many, surgery heals more and lasts
shelves.question: In adults with chronic anal fissure, do glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment or botulinum toxin injection heal the fissure, and how do they compare with lateral internal sphincterotomy (surgery)?
shelves.mesh: Fissure in Ano · Nitroglycerin · Botulinum Toxins · Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy · Ointments · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: A chronic anal fissure can often be healed without surgery — but surgery heals more, and keeps it healed. Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) 0.2% ointment healed 26 of 38 fissures (68%) versus 3 of 39 (8%) on placebo over 8 weeks (Lund 1997), and botulinum toxin 20 U injected into the internal anal sphincter healed 11 of 15 versus 2 of 15 on saline at 2 months (Maria 1998). In the one head-to-head trial, lateral internal sphincterotomy beat GTN on pain relief at 6 months (93.6% versus 57.44%) and on healing (89.36% versus 68.08%), because GTN's gains were eroded by recurrence in 34.04% (Mustafa 2022). The trade-off runs the other way on continence and side-effects: transient flatus incontinence (8.51%) and liquid incontinence (6.4%) occurred only after surgery in that trial, while headache affected 61.7% on GTN. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two placebo-controlled wins establish that medical therapy heals most fissures short-term, with surgery the more durable option when it fails or recurs.

cards.headline: Lund 1997: GTN ointment healed 68% of chronic fissures versus 8% on placebo in 8 weeks
cards.summary: Lund 1997: GTN ointment healed 68% of chronic fissures versus 8% on placebo in 8 weeks
cards.people: 80 consecutive patients with chronic anal fissure, randomised to topical 0.2% glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment or placebo, applied to the lower anal canal twice daily, with review every 2 weeks and healing assessed after 8 weeks of treatment (26 of 38 GTN and 3 of 39 placebo patients healed).
cards.result: After 8 weeks, healing was observed in 26/38 (68%) patients treated with GTN and in 3/39 (8%) patients treated with placebo (p<0.0001). Pain scores fell significantly in both groups after 2 weeks, but the fall was maintained only in those treated with GTN. Maximum anal resting pressure fell from a mean of 115.9 to 75.9 cm H2O after GTN (p<0.001) with increased anodermal blood flow; neither changed after placebo.
cards.watchOut: Over two-thirds of patients treated this way avoided the surgery that would otherwise have been required, but the authors note that long-term follow-up is needed to assess the risk of recurrent fissure after GTN healing.
cards.source: Lund JN et al.. A randomised, prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of glyceryl trinitrate ointment in treatment of anal fissure. The Lancet. 1997. PMID: 8988115. cards.headline: Maria 1998: botulinum toxin healed 11 of 15 fissures versus 2 of 15 on saline at 2 months
cards.summary: Maria 1998: botulinum toxin healed 11 of 15 fissures versus 2 of 15 on saline at 2 months
cards.people: 30 consecutive symptomatic adults with chronic anal fissure, all given two injections (total volume 0.4 ml) into the internal anal sphincter: 20 U of botulinum toxin A (15 patients) or saline (15 patients), in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
cards.result: After two months, 11 patients in the treated group and 2 in the control group had healed fissures (p=0.003); 13 in the treated group and 4 in the control group had symptomatic relief (p=0.003). Resting anal pressure was reduced by 25 percent in the treated group but not in the control group, and maximal voluntary pressures were unchanged. No relapses occurred during an average of 16 months of follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A very small trial (30 patients). Several control patients later crossed over to botulinum toxin injections or sphincterotomy, so the clean randomised comparison is the 2-month result.
cards.source: Maria G et al.. A comparison of botulinum toxin and saline for the treatment of chronic anal fissure. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1998. PMID: 9435326. cards.headline: Mustafa 2022: sphincterotomy beat GTN at 6 months — pain relief 93.6% versus 57.4%, healing 89.4% versus 68.1%
cards.summary: Mustafa 2022: sphincterotomy beat GTN at 6 months — pain relief 93.6% versus 57.4%, healing 89.4% versus 68.1%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — lottery randomisation, open surgery-versus-ointment comparison (Mustafa 2022)
cards.people: 94 patients with chronic anal fissure in the Colorectal Surgery Unit at Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University, Bangladesh, randomised to 0.2% GTN ointment 12-hourly for 8 weeks (47 patients) or lateral internal sphincterotomy (47 patients), with post-procedural outcomes followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Pain relief at 6 months was 57.44% in the GTN group versus 93.6% in the sphincterotomy group, the fall in the GTN arm attributed to recurrence of fissure (recurrence 34.04% with GTN). Healing at 6 months was 42/47 (89.36%) with sphincterotomy versus 32/47 (68.08%) with GTN (p=0.004); at 6 weeks healing was 85.1% versus 55.3% (p<0.001). Headache was significantly higher with GTN (61.7%), while transient flatus incontinence (8.51%) and liquid incontinence (6.4%) occurred in the sphincterotomy group and in 0.0% of the GTN group.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-centre trial: patients were randomised by lottery following purposive sampling, and a surgery-versus-ointment comparison cannot be blinded, so the effect sizes are indicative rather than precise.
cards.source: Mustafa G et al.. Clinical Outcome of 0.2% Glyceryl Trinitrate Topical Ointment Compared to Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy in the Treatment of Patient with Chronic Anal Fissure: A Randomized Control Trial. Mymensingh Medical Journal. 2022. PMID: 36189549. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: creams and toxin heal roughly two-thirds short-term; surgery heals more and lasts, at a small continence price — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: creams and toxin heal roughly two-thirds short-term; surgery heals more and lasts, at a small continence price — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lund 1997 (80 patients, GTN ointment versus placebo), Maria 1998 (30 patients, botulinum toxin versus saline), and Mustafa 2022 (94 patients, GTN ointment versus lateral internal sphincterotomy).
cards.result: GTN ointment healed 68% of fissures versus 8% on placebo at 8 weeks, and botulinum toxin healed 11 of 15 versus 2 of 15 on saline at 2 months. Against surgery, GTN's 6-month healing (68.08%) and pain relief (57.44%) fell short of sphincterotomy (89.36% and 93.6%), with recurrence in 34.04% eroding the cream's gains; the trade-off is continence — transient flatus incontinence in 8.51% and liquid incontinence in 6.4% of surgical patients in Mustafa 2022, versus none on GTN — against the cream's own high headache rate (61.7%). shelves.title: Stimulant laxatives work: bisacodyl and picosulfate beat placebo clearly
shelves.question: In adults with chronic constipation, do stimulant laxatives — bisacodyl tablets or sodium picosulfate drops — increase complete spontaneous bowel movements compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Bisacodyl · Cathartics · Constipation · Picolines · Citrates · Senna Extract · Lactulose · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Yes — in two large, modern, placebo-controlled trials the stimulant laxatives clearly increased complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBMs). With bisacodyl 10 mg/day for 4 weeks in 368 adults with Rome III chronic constipation, CSBMs per week rose from 1.1 to 5.2 on bisacodyl versus 1.1 to 1.9 on placebo (p<.0001), with spontaneous bowel movements 7.9 versus 3.2 per week and concordant quality-of-life gains. With sodium picosulfate drops for 4 weeks in 367 patients, CSBMs per week rose from 0.9 to 3.4 versus 1.1 to 1.7 on placebo (p<.0001), and 51.1% versus 18.0% reached at least 3 CSBMs per week. An older, small trial in geriatric long-stay inpatients found a senna-plus-bulk combination (Agiolax) produced more bowel actions than lactulose, but it had no placebo arm. Both big trials lasted only 4 weeks and were manufacturer-funded, so they settle short-term efficacy, not long-term safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large concordant placebo-controlled trials with large absolute gains, held at POSSIBLE by short duration and manufacturer funding.

cards.headline: Kamm 2011: bisacodyl lifted complete spontaneous bowel movements from 1.1 to 5.2 a week versus 1.1 to 1.9 on placebo
cards.summary: Kamm 2011: bisacodyl lifted complete spontaneous bowel movements from 1.1 to 5.2 a week versus 1.1 to 1.9 on placebo
cards.people: 368 patients with chronic constipation defined by Rome III criteria, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study at 27 centres in the United Kingdom, randomised 2:1 to oral bisacodyl 10 mg (n=247) or placebo (n=121) once daily for 4 weeks after a 2-week baseline period, recording bowel information in a daily electronic diary.
cards.result: The mean number of complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBMs) per week during treatment increased from 1.1 in both groups to 5.2 in the bisacodyl group and 1.9 in the placebo group (P < .0001). All secondary end points differed significantly in favour of bisacodyl (P < .0001), and the overall Patient Assessment of Constipation quality of life (PAC-QOL) score and all subscales improved significantly versus placebo (P ≤ .0070). Treatment with bisacodyl was well-tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Manufacturer-funded trial, and only 4 weeks of treatment — it establishes short-term efficacy and tolerability, not what happens with years of daily use.
cards.source: Kamm MA et al.. Oral bisacodyl is effective and well-tolerated in patients with chronic constipation.. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2011. PMID: 21440672. cards.headline: Mueller-Lissner 2010: sodium picosulfate lifted complete spontaneous bowel movements from 0.9 to 3.4 a week versus 1.1 to 1.7 on placebo
cards.summary: Mueller-Lissner 2010: sodium picosulfate lifted complete spontaneous bowel movements from 0.9 to 3.4 a week versus 1.1 to 1.7 on placebo
cards.people: 367 patients with chronic (functional) constipation fulfilling the Rome III diagnostic criteria, randomised in 45 general practices in Germany to sodium picosulfate drops or matching placebo in a 2:1 ratio for 4 weeks after a 2-week baseline period, with dose titration permitted and a rescue bisacodyl suppository allowed after more than 72 hours without a bowel movement.
cards.result: The mean number of CSBMs per week increased from 0.9 to 3.4 in the sodium picosulfate group and from 1.1 to 1.7 in the placebo group (P<0.0001); the percentage reaching an increase of ≥1 CSBM per week was 65.5% vs. 32.3% (P<0.0001), and the percentage reaching a mean of at least three CSBMs per week was 51.1% in the sodium picosulfate group and 18.0% in the placebo group (P<0.0001). Quality of life (PAC-QOL) improved significantly versus placebo, and treatment was well tolerated; nearly 50% of patients titrated the dose down during the study.
cards.watchOut: Manufacturer-funded trial of 4 weeks; dose titration and rescue suppositories were built into the design, so the result is for a titrated, rescue-backed regimen rather than a fixed dose taken in isolation.
cards.source: Mueller-Lissner S et al.. Multicenter, 4-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of sodium picosulfate in patients with chronic constipation..
