cards.headline: Kinnunen 1993: in geriatric long-stay patients, senna-plus-bulk (Agiolax) gave 4.5 bowel actions a week versus 2.2–1.9 on lactulose
cards.summary: Kinnunen 1993: in geriatric long-stay patients, senna-plus-bulk (Agiolax) gave 4.5 bowel actions a week versus 2.2–1.9 on lactulose
cards.type: Comparative trial against an active reference treatment (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 30 geriatric long-stay patients aged 65–94 years (mean 81.8) with chronic constipation, treated with a bulk laxative plus senna combination — the tested product is named in the publication: Agiolax, daily doses 14.8 g — versus lactulose (daily doses 20.1 g) as the reference medicine.
cards.result: Bulk laxative plus senna produced more frequent bowel habits (p < 0.05) than lactulose: 4.5 versus 2.2–1.9 bowel actions per week. Both laxatives proved safe to use, and the authors concluded bulk laxative plus senna was more efficient in treating constipation in geriatric long-stay patients.
cards.watchOut: Old (1993), very small (n=30), and no placebo group — and the tested treatment is a senna-plus-bulk combination product (Agiolax), so the result cannot be credited to senna alone; the population was institutionalised geriatric patients, not community-dwelling adults.
cards.source: Kinnunen O et al.. Safety and efficacy of a bulk laxative containing senna versus lactulose in the treatment of chronic constipation in geriatric patients.. Pharmacology. 1993. PMID: 8234438. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. shelves.title: Loperamide shortens acute diarrhoea by about a day
shelves.question: In adults with acute (non-bloody) diarrhoea, does loperamide shorten the illness compared with placebo, and how does it compare with racecadotril and with antibiotics in travellers' diarrhoea?
shelves.mesh: Loperamide · Antidiarrheals · Diarrhea · Thiorphan · Neprilysin · Rifaximin · Rifamycins · Travel · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Loperamide shortens acute non-bloody diarrhoea by about a day in the placebo test: in Hughes 1995, a UK general-practice trial of loperamide oxide 1 mg, loperamide oxide 2 mg and loperamide 2 mg against placebo in acute non-dysenteric diarrhoea, every active preparation was significantly superior to placebo, cutting the time to complete relief to about 24 hours versus 45 hours on placebo. Against another antidiarrhoeal it has no edge: in Vetel 1999 (n=157), diarrhoea duration was 14.9 hours on racecadotril versus 13.7 hours on loperamide (not significant), with more rebound constipation on loperamide (18.7% versus 9.8%). And in travellers' diarrhoea (DuPont 2007, n=310), loperamide alone was the slowest arm — time to last unformed stool 69 hours, versus 32.5 hours on the antibiotic rifaximin and 27.3 hours on the combination — because it slows the gut without treating the infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, roughly one-day shortening against placebo in ordinary acute diarrhoea, with clear limits in infectious travellers' diarrhoea.

cards.headline: Hughes 1995: loperamide and loperamide oxide brought complete relief in about 24 hours versus 45 hours on placebo
cards.summary: Hughes 1995: loperamide and loperamide oxide brought complete relief in about 24 hours versus 45 hours on placebo
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in general practice
cards.people: Patients with acute, non-dysenteric diarrhoea in United Kingdom general practice, in a double-blind comparison by the UK Janssen Research Group of General Practitioners of loperamide oxide 1 mg, loperamide oxide 2 mg, loperamide 2 mg and placebo as first-line treatment. The abstract does not state how many patients were studied.
cards.result: All the drug preparations were significantly superior to placebo, in particular reducing the time to complete relief of symptoms to about 24 hours, as opposed to 45 hours on placebo treatment. Loperamide oxide 1 mg was preferred by the authors because it produced fewer constipation-like episodes after treatment.
cards.watchOut: An old trial (1995) reported in summary form: the abstract gives no sample size and no per-arm figures beyond the relief times, and two of the three active arms were loperamide oxide, a related compound, rather than loperamide itself.

cards.headline: Vetel 1999: racecadotril and loperamide were indistinguishable — duration 14.9 versus 13.7 hours — but rebound constipation was commoner on loperamide
cards.summary: Vetel 1999: racecadotril and loperamide were indistinguishable — duration 14.9 versus 13.7 hours — but rebound constipation was commoner on loperamide
cards.people: 157 adults with acute diarrhoea in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-placebo, parallel-group study, treated with racecadotril 100 mg three times daily or loperamide 2 mg after each diarrhoeic stool, for 7 days or until recovery if earlier.
cards.result: Both groups passed similar numbers of stools before recovery (3.5 ± 0.5 for racecadotril vs. 2.9 ± 0.4 for loperamide), and the duration of diarrhoea was similar in both groups (14.9 ± 2.0 h for racecadotril and 13.7 ± 2.2 h for loperamide) — neither difference significant. Both treatments reduced associated symptoms and signs and were similarly well tolerated, but more patients on loperamide reported rebound constipation during treatment (18.7% vs. 9.8% with racecadotril).
cards.watchOut: A head-to-head trial with no placebo arm, from 1999: it shows the two drugs perform alike, not how either compares with no treatment — that comparison is the Hughes 1995 card above.
cards.source: Vetel JM et al.. Comparison of racecadotril and loperamide in adults with acute diarrhoea.. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1999. PMID: 10646048. cards.headline: DuPont 2007: in travellers' diarrhoea loperamide alone was the slowest arm — 69 hours to last unformed stool versus 32.5 on rifaximin and 27.3 on the combination
cards.summary: DuPont 2007: in travellers' diarrhoea loperamide alone was the slowest arm — 69 hours to last unformed stool versus 32.5 on rifaximin and 27.3 on the combination
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, three-arm trial in travellers' diarrhoea
cards.people: 310 adults with travellers' diarrhoea (acute diarrhoea with at least 3 unformed stools in 24 hours and at least 1 symptom of enteric infection) in Mexico who completed treatment with rifaximin 200 mg three times daily for 3 days (n=102), loperamide 4 mg initially then 2 mg after each unformed stool (n=104), or the combination of both (n=104).
cards.result: Rifaximin and rifaximin-loperamide significantly reduced the median time until passage of the last unformed stool (32.5 h and 27.3 h, respectively) versus loperamide alone (69 h; P = .0019). The mean number of unformed stools passed during illness was lower with rifaximin-loperamide (3.99) compared with rifaximin (6.23; P = .004) or loperamide alone (6.72; P = .002). All treatments were well tolerated with a low incidence of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Context card, not a placebo test: travellers' diarrhoea is usually bacterial, so an antibiotic can cure the cause while loperamide only slows the gut — loperamide being slowest here does not contradict its placebo-controlled benefit in ordinary acute diarrhoea, and the combination arm performed best on stool counts.
cards.source: Dupont HL et al.. Treatment of travelers' diarrhea: randomized trial comparing rifaximin, rifaximin plus loperamide, and loperamide alone.. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2007. PMID: 17382603. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised, double-blind, three-arm trial in travellers' diarrhoea 310 adults with travellers' diarrhoea (acute diarrhoea with at least 3 unformed stools in 24 hours and at least 1 symptom of enteric infection) in mexico who completed treatment with rifaximin 200 mg three times daily for 3 days (n=102), loperamide 4 mg initially then 2 mg after each unformed stool (n=104), or the combination of both (n=104). rifaximin and rifaximin-loperamide significantly reduced the median time until passage of the last unformed stool (32.5 h and 27.3 h, respectively) versus loperamide alone (69 h; p = .0019). the mean number of unformed stools passed during illness was lower with rifaximin-loperamide (3.99) compared with rifaximin (6.23; p = .004) or loperamide alone (6.72; p = .002). all treatments were well tolerated with a low incidence of adverse events. context card, not a placebo test: travellers' diarrhoea is usually bacterial, so an antibiotic can cure the cause while loperamide only slows the gut — loperamide being slowest here does not contradict its placebo-controlled benefit in ordinary acute diarrhoea, and the combination arm performed best on stool counts. dupont hl et al.. treatment of travelers' diarrhea: randomized trial comparing rifaximin, rifaximin plus loperamide, and loperamide alone.. clinical gastroenterology and hepatology. 2007. pmid: 17382603. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · anti-infective agents/*therapeutic use · diarrhea/*drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · drug administration schedule · drug therapy, combination · female · follow-up studies · humans · loperamide/*therapeutic use · male · probability · reference values · rifamycins/*therapeutic use · rifaximin · risk assessment · *travel · treatment outcome

cards.people: Adults with acute diarrhoea across a UK general-practice placebo-controlled trial (Hughes 1995), a 157-patient head-to-head trial against racecadotril (Vetel 1999), and a 310-patient travellers' diarrhoea trial against rifaximin (DuPont 2007).
cards.result: Versus placebo, loperamide-family treatment cut time to complete relief to about 24 hours versus 45 hours. Versus racecadotril, duration was 13.7 versus 14.9 hours (not significant), with more rebound constipation on loperamide (18.7% vs. 9.8%). In travellers' diarrhoea, time to last unformed stool was 69 hours on loperamide alone versus 32.5 hours on rifaximin and 27.3 hours on the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The placebo evidence rests on one old, briefly reported trial whose abstract states no sample size; nothing here covers bloody diarrhoea (dysentery), children, or diarrhoea where slowing the gut could be unsafe — the shelf is about acute non-bloody diarrhoea in adults.

shelves.title: Long-term albumin infusions in decompensated cirrhosis (ANSWER)
shelves.question: In people with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites, does long-term regular albumin infusion improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albumins · Ascites · Diuretics · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Furosemide · Humans · Hyperkalemia · Hyponatremia · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Cirrhosis · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, Tier C — one open-label randomised trial (ANSWER, n = 440) found that long-term weekly outpatient albumin improved 18-month survival in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites (77% vs 66%; mortality hazard ratio 0.62 — a 38% relative reduction in the hazard of death). A mortality claim resting on a single unblinded trial is Tier C. Short inpatient albumin top-ups are a different question, answered — negatively — on Shelf #2522 (ATTIRE). Split from the combined ANSWER/ATTIRE shelf at the developer's direction, Nov 14, 2026.

cards.headline: Long-term weekly albumin improved 18-month survival: 77% vs 66% (ANSWER)
cards.summary: Long-term weekly albumin improved 18-month survival: 77% vs 66% (ANSWER)
cards.people: 440 patients with cirrhosis and uncomplicated ascites on diuretics (spironolactone ≥200 mg/day and furosemide ≥25 mg/day) in 33 Italian hospitals; standard treatment plus human albumin (40 g twice weekly for 2 weeks, then 40 g weekly) for up to 18 months vs standard treatment alone; open-label; 431 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis
cards.result: Deaths: 38 of 218 in the albumin group vs 46 of 213 on standard treatment. Overall 18-month survival: 77% vs 66% (P = 0.028); the mortality hazard ratio was 0.62 (95% CI 0.40–0.95) — a 38% relative reduction in the hazard of death. Grade 3–4 non-liver-related adverse events were identical at 22% in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label — everyone knew who was receiving albumin, which can subtly change other care. A single trial, and a survival claim of exactly the kind that needs replication.
cards.source: Caraceni P et al.. Long-term albumin administration in decompensated cirrhosis (ANSWER): an open-label randomised trial. Lancet. 2018. PMID: 29861076. Registry ID: NCT01288794 (also EudraCT 2008-000625-19). shelves.title: Polyethylene glycol (PEG 3350) for chronic constipation
shelves.question: Does polyethylene glycol (PEG 3350 / macrogol) work for chronic constipation in adults, and how does it compare with lactulose?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chronic Disease · Constipation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a 304-patient, six-month, double-blind trial found treatment success in 52.0% on PEG vs 11% on placebo (P < 0.001), and a randomised head-to-head trial found low-dose PEG superior to lactulose with less flatulence. Two different comparators, two positive randomised trials, and no safety signal over six months — LIKELY.

cards.headline: Over six months, PEG relieved constipation in 52% of patients vs 11% on placebo
cards.summary: Over six months, PEG relieved constipation in 52% of patients vs 11% on placebo
cards.people: 304 adults with chronic constipation at 50 US centres; PEG 3350 (MiraLAX) 17 g once daily or placebo for 6 months, double-blind
cards.result: Treatment success (relief of modified Rome criteria in at least half of a patient's treatment weeks): 52.0% on PEG vs 11% on placebo (P < 0.001); 61% of PEG treatment weeks vs 22% of placebo weeks were successful. Efficacy was similar in the subgroup of 75 elderly patients. Diarrhoea, flatulence and nausea were the commonest adverse events but none differed significantly from placebo, and monthly laboratory testing showed no significant differences.
cards.watchOut: A trial of one branded formulation; 'success' is a symptom-criteria definition, not a cure rate.
cards.source: Dipalma JA et al.. A randomized, multicenter, placebo-controlled trial of polyethylene glycol laxative for chronic treatment of chronic constipation. Am J Gastroenterol. 2007. PMID: 17403074. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Low-dose PEG beat lactulose over four weeks, with less flatulence
cards.summary: Low-dose PEG beat lactulose over four weeks, with less flatulence
cards.people: 115 adults with chronic constipation in a multicentre randomised comparison (99 completed); PEG 3350 electrolyte solution, two 13 g sachets daily adjustable to one or three, vs lactulose
cards.result: After four weeks the PEG group had a higher number of stools and a lower median daily straining score than the lactulose group, with greater overall improvement; flatus was less frequent on PEG, while liquid stools were commoner on PEG in the first two weeks only. There were no serious adverse events and no significant laboratory changes in either group; 61 patients continuing PEG openly for two further months kept the benefit without toxicity.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm, and the abstract does not describe blinding — symptom scores could be coloured by expectations. The comparison is against lactulose, not against nothing.
cards.source: Attar A et al.. Comparison of a low dose polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution with lactulose for treatment of chronic constipation. Gut. 1999. PMID: 9895382. cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: PEG 3350 is one of the best-evidenced constipation treatments: a large, long, placebo-controlled trial plus a head-to-head win over lactulose. It works in about half of chronic sufferers by strict criteria (vs about one in ten on placebo), and proved safe over at least six months — the reasonable first osmotic laxative. Stimulant laxatives are shelved separately at #2477.
cards.watchOut: Most trials run weeks to months; data beyond a year of continuous use are thinner, and PEG treats the symptom, not the cause.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.

shelves.title: Biofeedback for dyssynergic defecation
shelves.question: Does biofeedback training help people whose constipation is caused by dyssynergic defecation (the pelvic floor tightening instead of relaxing during straining)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Biofeedback, Psychology · Cathartics · Constipation · Female · Gastrointestinal Transit · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · Pelvic Floor · Adolescent · Aged · Ataxia
shelves.balance: LIKELY — three randomised trials with three different comparators (laxative, sham feedback, placebo/diazepam) all favour biofeedback by wide margins (major improvement 80% vs 22%; adequate relief 70% vs 38% on placebo), with objective physiological change tracking the symptoms and benefits sustained to two years.

cards.headline: Five biofeedback sessions beat daily PEG: 80% vs 22% reported major improvement
cards.summary: Five biofeedback sessions beat daily PEG: 80% vs 22% reported major improvement
cards.people: 109 adults with chronic severe pelvic floor dyssynergia who had already failed 20 g/day fibre plus enemas or suppositories; five weekly biofeedback sessions vs polyethylene glycol 14.6–29.2 g/day plus five weekly counselling sessions
cards.result: Major improvement at six months: 43 of 54 (80%) with biofeedback vs 12 of 55 (22%) with laxatives (P < 0.001), sustained at 12 and 24 months. Biofeedback also produced greater reductions in straining, sensations of incomplete evacuation and anorectal blockage, use of enemas and suppositories, and abdominal pain (all P < 0.01). Every biofeedback patient reporting major improvement could relax the pelvic floor and expel a 50-mL balloon at 6 and 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Patients cannot be blinded to biofeedback and 'major improvement' is self-reported — though the objective balloon-expulsion change tracked the symptoms.
cards.source: Chiarioni G et al.. Biofeedback is superior to laxatives for normal transit constipation due to pelvic floor dyssynergia. Gastroenterology. 2006. PMID: 16530506. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Biofeedback beat both sham feedback and standard care in a three-way randomised trial
cards.summary: Biofeedback beat both sham feedback and standard care in a three-way randomised trial
cards.people: 77 adults (69 women) with chronic constipation and dyssynergic defecation; biofeedback vs sham feedback vs standard therapy (diet, exercise, laxatives), outcomes at 3 months, intention-to-treat
cards.result: The biofeedback group was more likely to correct dyssynergia and improve the defecation index (both P < 0.0001) and to shorten balloon-expulsion time (P = 0.02) than the other groups. Complete spontaneous bowel movements increased on biofeedback (P < 0.02) and were more numerous than in the other groups (P < 0.05); use of digital manoeuvres decreased (P = 0.03); global bowel satisfaction was higher than with sham (P = 0.04). Colonic transit improved after biofeedback or standard care but not after sham.
cards.watchOut: The sham control is this trial's strength — it rules out attention and expectation as the whole explanation — but 77 patients from one specialist centre is still small.
cards.source: Rao SS et al.. Randomized controlled trial of biofeedback, sham feedback, and standard therapy for dyssynergic defecation. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2007. PMID: 17368232. cards.headline: Biofeedback gave adequate relief to 70%, vs 38% on placebo pills and 23% on diazepam
cards.summary: Biofeedback gave adequate relief to 70%, vs 38% on placebo pills and 23% on diazepam
cards.people: 84 adults still constipated after a four-week run-in of education and medical management; biofeedback with electromyography feedback (n = 30) vs diazepam (n = 30) vs placebo (n = 24), all groups taught pelvic-floor exercises over six biweekly sessions
cards.result: Adequate relief of constipation three months after treatment: 70% with biofeedback vs 23% with diazepam (P < 0.001) and 38% with placebo (P = 0.017), by intention-to-treat. Unassisted bowel movements at follow-up were significantly more frequent with biofeedback than placebo (P = 0.005), and biofeedback patients reduced pelvic-floor EMG activity during straining significantly more than diazepam patients (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Diazepam was an odd comparator and performed worse than placebo — a reminder that muscle-relaxant logic does not fix a coordination problem.
cards.source: Heymen S et al.. Randomized, controlled trial shows biofeedback to be superior to alternative treatments for patients with pelvic floor dyssynergia-type constipation. shelves.title: Targeted albumin infusions during hospital admission for decompensated cirrhosis (ATTIRE)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with decompensated cirrhosis and low serum albumin, do repeated albumin infusions to a target level improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Albumins · Ascites · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Edema · Serum Albumin · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — one large randomised trial (ATTIRE, n = 777) found targeted inpatient albumin no better than standard care on its composite of new infection, kidney dysfunction or death (29.7% vs 30.2%), with more severe or life-threatening serious adverse events in the albumin group. Tier C because the shelf rests on a single trial. Long-term outpatient albumin is a different question — Shelf #2515 (ANSWER). Split from the combined ANSWER/ATTIRE shelf at the developer's direction, Nov 14, 2026.

cards.headline: Targeted inpatient albumin to a level of 30 g/L changed nothing — with more serious harm events (ATTIRE)
cards.summary: Targeted inpatient albumin to a level of 30 g/L changed nothing — with more serious harm events (ATTIRE)
cards.people: 777 hospitalised patients with decompensated cirrhosis and serum albumin below 30 g/L in the UK; repeated infusions of 20% albumin to target ≥30 g/L for up to 14 days vs standard care; median total albumin given 200 g vs 20 g
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint — new infection, kidney dysfunction, or death between days 3 and 15 — occurred in 113 of 380 patients (29.7%) in the targeted-albumin group vs 120 of 397 (30.2%) on standard care (adjusted odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.71–1.33; P = 0.87). More severe or life-threatening serious adverse events occurred in the albumin group.
cards.watchOut: ATTIRE tested a different strategy from ANSWER — days of inpatient top-up to a blood-level target, not months of weekly treatment — so it refutes the top-up strategy, not necessarily the long-term one.

shelves.title: Prophylactic antibiotics in necrotising pancreatitis: decades of trials, no demonstrated benefit — the largest blinded trial leaned the wrong way
shelves.question: In severe acute (necrotising) pancreatitis, do prophylactic antibiotics prevent infected pancreatic necrosis and death?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Antibiotic Prophylaxis* · Bacterial Infections/mortality, prevention & control* · Humans · Necrosis/complications · Pancreas/pathology* · Pancreatitis/complications*, mortality · Pancreatitis, Acute Necrotizing/complications · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Superinfection/prevention & control*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the pooled point estimates lean slightly toward antibiotics, but nothing reaches significance and the best trial is flat. The Cochrane review (7 trials, 404 patients with CT-proven necrosis) found mortality 8.4% versus 14.4% and infected necrosis 19.7% versus 24.4%, neither significant; its one significant subgroup — imipenem alone for pancreatic infection (RR 0.34) — was never confirmed (Villatoro 2010, PMID: 20464721). The largest double-blind trial, meropenem versus placebo in 100 patients, found infection in 18% versus 12% and mortality 20% versus 18%, both numerically favouring placebo (Dellinger 2007, PMID: 17457158). A 14-trial meta-analysis (841 patients) found mortality RR 0.74 (0.50 to 1.07) and infected necrosis RR 0.78 (0.60 to 1.02) and concluded no evidence supports routine prophylaxis (Wittau 2011, PMID: 21067283). The stamp stops at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the syntheses' intervals still admit a modest benefit and the underlying trials are small and old. Tier C: the shelf turns on mortality in a lethal disease, so it is flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Probiotics in pancreatitis (PROPATRIA) are homed at shelf #98.

cards.headline: Villatoro 2010 (Cochrane): prophylactic antibiotics in necrotising pancreatitis — mortality 8.4% vs 14.4% and infected necrosis 19.7% vs 24.4%, neither significant
cards.summary: Villatoro 2010 (Cochrane): prophylactic antibiotics in necrotising pancreatitis — mortality 8.4% vs 14.4% and infected necrosis 19.7% vs 24.4%, neither significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 RCTs (Villatoro 2010, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo in acute pancreatitis with CT-proven pancreatic necrosis: 7 evaluable studies, 404 patients. Regimens included beta-lactams, quinolone plus imidazole, and imipenem alone.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant effect on mortality (8.4% with antibiotics versus 14.4% in controls) or on infected pancreatic necrosis (19.7% versus 24.4%); non-pancreatic infection, overall infection, operative rates and fungal infection also did not differ significantly. The single significant finding was a subgroup: imipenem alone reduced pancreatic infection (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.84; p = 0.02). The reviewers note none of the included studies was adequately powered.
cards.watchOut: The absolute differences lean toward antibiotics but the trials are small and old, regimens differ, and the one significant result is a single-regimen subgroup — the classic anatomy of a finding that the largest blinded trial then failed to confirm (Dellinger 2007, carded next). This shelf is about prophylaxis in necrosis, not about treating established infection, which is a different question.
cards.source: Villatoro E et al. Antibiotic therapy for prophylaxis against infection of pancreatic necrosis in acute pancreatitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20464721. cards.headline: Dellinger 2007: meropenem prophylaxis in severe necrotising pancreatitis — infection 18% vs 12% on placebo, mortality 20% vs 18%; no benefit
cards.summary: Dellinger 2007: meropenem prophylaxis in severe necrotising pancreatitis — infection 18% vs 12% on placebo, mortality 20% vs 18%; no benefit
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Dellinger 2007, Annals of Surgery)
cards.people: Multicentre, prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in 32 centres in North America and Europe: 100 patients with clinically severe, confirmed necrotising pancreatitis received meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours (50 patients) or placebo (50), started within 5 days of symptom onset for 7 to 21 days.
cards.result: Pancreatic or peripancreatic infection developed in 18% (9/50) on meropenem versus 12% (6/50) on placebo (P = 0.401); overall mortality was 20% (10/50) versus 18% (9/50) (P = 0.799); surgical intervention was required in 26% versus 20% (P = 0.476). The authors conclude the study did not support early prophylactic antimicrobial use in severe acute necrotising pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: One hundred patients cannot exclude a modest benefit, and meropenem is one regimen — but this is the largest double-blind test ever done, its point estimates lean the wrong way, and it directly contradicts the imipenem subgroup signal in the Cochrane review. Prophylaxis here also means 1–3 weeks of carbapenem exposure in patients who mostly never develop infected necrosis.
cards.source: Dellinger EP et al. Early antibiotic treatment for severe acute necrotizing pancreatitis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Annals of Surgery. 2007. PMID: 17457158. cards.headline: Wittau 2011: 14 trials, 841 patients — mortality RR 0.74 (0.50–1.07), infected necrosis RR 0.78 (0.60–1.02); 'no evidence supports routine prophylaxis'
cards.summary: Wittau 2011: 14 trials, 841 patients — mortality RR 0.74 (0.50–1.07), infected necrosis RR 0.78 (0.60–1.02); 'no evidence supports routine prophylaxis'
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of antibiotic prophylaxis in severe acute pancreatitis: 14 trials, 841 patients, pooling mortality, infected pancreatic necrosis, non-pancreatic infection and surgical intervention.
cards.result: Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in mortality (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.07), infected pancreatic necrosis (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.02), non-pancreatic infections (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.06) or surgical interventions (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.20). The authors conclude that to date there is no evidence supporting routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severe acute pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis includes open-label and older trials that the Cochrane review handled differently, which is why its point estimates sit slightly further from the null — yet its intervals still cross 1 on every outcome. Two syntheses and the largest blinded trial agree on the only claim that matters: no demonstrated benefit.

shelves.title: Bowel preparation plus oral antibiotics: the pooled record says infections halve; the largest modern trial found no difference — SPLIT
shelves.question: In elective colorectal surgery, does mechanical bowel preparation plus oral antibiotics reduce surgical site infection versus no preparation or mechanical preparation alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage* · Cathartics/administration & dosage · Cefuroxime/administration & dosage* · Colectomy/methods* · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole/administration & dosage* · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols/administration & dosage · Preoperative Care/methods* · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control*
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which evidence you weight. The pooled randomised record favours the combination: a network meta-analysis of 46 trials (12,690 patients) found mechanical preparation plus oral antibiotics roughly halved the odds of surgical site infection versus preparation alone (OR 0.55, 95% CrI 0.39 to 0.76) and versus no preparation (OR 0.52, 0.32 to 0.84) (Koo 2023, PMID: 37256453). The largest modern direct trial disagrees: in MOBILE, 396 patients having colon resection had infection rates of 7% with the full package (polyethylene glycol plus oral neomycin and metronidazole) versus 11% with no preparation — not significant (p = 0.17) — with identical 4% dehiscence rates (Koskenvuo 2019, PMID: 31402112). The likely reconciliation is era: older trials ran against higher baseline infection rates and less modern background care. The shelf presents both without forcing a verdict the record does not contain. Not Tier C: a surgical-site-infection claim with no mortality claim, resting on a large pooled record plus a direct modern trial.

cards.headline: Koskenvuo 2019 (MOBILE): mechanical prep plus oral antibiotics versus no prep — surgical site infection 7% vs 11% (p = 0.17); the treatment made no significant difference
cards.summary: Koskenvuo 2019 (MOBILE): mechanical prep plus oral antibiotics versus no prep — surgical site infection 7% vs 11% (p = 0.17); the treatment made no significant difference
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Koskenvuo 2019, Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology)
cards.people: Multicentre, parallel, single-blinded randomised trial (MOBILE) in four hospitals in Finland: 417 patients undergoing elective colon resection were randomised to mechanical and oral antibiotic bowel preparation (MOABP) or no bowel preparation (NBP); the modified intention-to-treat analysis included 396 (196 MOABP, 200 NBP). MOABP was 2 L polyethylene glycol plus 1 L clear fluid the day before surgery, with oral neomycin 2 g and metronidazole 2 g that evening. The primary outcome was surgical site infection within 30 days.
cards.result: Surgical site infection occurred in 13 of 196 patients (7%) with MOABP versus 21 of 200 (11%) with no preparation (odds ratio 1.65, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.40 for NBP versus MOABP; p = 0.17) — not statistically significant. Anastomotic dehiscence was 4% in both groups; reoperations 8% versus 7%; two patients died in the no-preparation group and none in the MOABP group within 30 days. The authors propose mechanical plus oral antibiotic preparation not be routine in colon surgery.
cards.watchOut: Four hundred patients cannot exclude the pooled effect the network meta-analysis reports (carded next) — MOBILE's interval is wide. But MOBILE is the modern, direct, pragmatic test of the full package against nothing, in the era of intravenous prophylaxis and enhanced recovery, and it found no significant benefit on any outcome.
cards.source: Koskenvuo L et al. Mechanical and oral antibiotic bowel preparation versus no bowel preparation for elective colectomy (MOBILE): a multicentre, randomised, parallel, single-blinded trial. Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2019. PMID: 31402112. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02652637 (the report also names EudraCT 2015-004559-38). p = 0.17) — not statistically significant. anastomotic dehiscence was 4% in both groups; reoperations 8% versus 7%; two patients died in the no-preparation group and none in the moabp group within 30 days. the authors propose mechanical plus oral antibiotic preparation not be routine in colon surgery. four hundred patients cannot exclude the pooled effect the network meta-analysis reports (carded next) — mobile's interval is wide. but mobile is the modern, direct, pragmatic test of the full package against nothing, in the era of intravenous prophylaxis and enhanced recovery, and it found no significant benefit on any outcome. koskenvuo l et al. mechanical and oral antibiotic bowel preparation versus no bowel preparation for elective colectomy (mobile): a multicentre, randomised, parallel, single-blinded trial. lancet gastroenterology & hepatology. 2019. pmid: 31402112. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct02652637 (the report also names eudract 2015-004559-38). mesh: administration, intravenous · aged · anti-bacterial agents/administration & dosage* · cathartics/administration & dosage · cefuroxime/administration & dosage* · colectomy/methods* · elective surgical procedures · female · humans · male · metronidazole/administration & dosage* · middle aged · polyethylene glycols/administration & dosage · preoperative care/methods* · prospective studies · single-blind method · surgical wound infection/prevention & control*

cards.headline: Koo 2023: network meta-analysis of 46 trials — adding oral antibiotics to mechanical prep halved the odds of surgical site infection (OR 0.55)
cards.summary: Koo 2023: network meta-analysis of 46 trials — adding oral antibiotics to mechanical prep halved the odds of surgical site infection (OR 0.55)
cards.type: Network meta-analysis, 46 RCTs (Koo 2023, International Journal of Colorectal Disease)
cards.people: Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised trials in elective colorectal surgery: 46 RCTs, 12,690 patients, comparing mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) plus oral antibiotics (OAB), MBP alone, OAB alone and no preparation, with surgical site infection as the outcome.
cards.result: MBP plus oral antibiotics reduced surgical site infection versus MBP alone (OR 0.55, 95% credible interval 0.39 to 0.76 — a 45% relative reduction in odds) and versus no preparation (OR 0.52, 95% CrI 0.32 to 0.84). The pooled record therefore favours the combination, driven substantially by older and smaller trials assembled indirectly through the network.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates inherit the era of their trials: many included studies predate modern intravenous prophylaxis, laparoscopy and enhanced-recovery care, when baseline infection rates — and the room for bowel preparation to help — were larger. Indirect comparisons also assume the trials are exchangeable, which surgical practice over three decades is not.
cards.source: Koo CH et al. Effect of preoperative oral antibiotics and mechanical bowel preparation on the prevention of surgical site infection in elective colorectal surgery, and does oral antibiotic regime matter? a bayesian network meta-analysis. International Journal of Colorectal Disease. 2023. PMID: 37256453. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the pooled trial record favours prep plus oral antibiotics; the largest modern direct trial found no difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the pooled trial record favours prep plus oral antibiotics; the largest modern direct trial found no difference
cards.people: One modern multicentre RCT of the full package versus nothing (MOBILE, 396 analysed) and one network meta-analysis of the whole randomised record (46 trials, 12,690 patients).
cards.result: Pooled: SSI odds roughly halved by adding oral antibiotics to mechanical prep (OR 0.55 vs prep alone; OR 0.52 vs no prep). Direct and modern: SSI 7% versus 11% with the full package versus no preparation, not significant (p = 0.17), with identical dehiscence rates. Both can be true if the benefit shrank as background care improved — which is precisely the question a surgeon faces today.
cards.watchOut: Neither source isolates oral antibiotics alone against modern intravenous prophylaxis at scale, and neither addresses the costs of preparation — patient burden, electrolyte disturbance, microbiome effects — that sit outside the SSI outcome. Rectal surgery, where baseline infection risk is higher, is underrepresented in MOBILE (colon resections).
cards.source: Synthesis of Koskenvuo L et al. Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2019 (PMID: 31402112); Koo CH et al. International Journal of Colorectal Disease. 2023 (PMID: 37256453).

shelves.title: Prophylactic mesh at laparotomy closure (PRIMA): hernias cut from 30% to 13% with onlay mesh in high-risk patients — one trial
shelves.question: In high-risk patients having elective midline laparotomy, does prophylactic mesh reinforcement reduce incisional hernia versus suture closure alone?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Wound Closure Techniques/instrumentation* · Aged · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal/complications, epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Incisional Hernia/epidemiology, etiology, prevention & control* · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/complications, epidemiology · Surgical Mesh* · Suture Techniques* · Sutures
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a large effect in a single trial, in the population that has most to gain. In PRIMA, 480 patients having elective midline laparotomy with an abdominal aortic aneurysm or BMI ≥27 were randomised to suture closure, onlay mesh or sublay mesh: incisional hernia at 2 years occurred in 30% with suture, 13% with onlay mesh (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.69) and 18% with sublay mesh (OR 0.55, 0.30 to 1.00), while seroma was more frequent with onlay mesh and wound infection did not differ (Jairam 2017, PMID: 28641875). Long-term follow-up found mesh explantation for complications in 3.1% of onlay and 0% of retrorectus patients among those with reoperation data — serious mesh-specific morbidity was uncommon (van den Berg 2026, PMID: 39239718). The absolute benefit (about 17 fewer hernias per 100 closures) is a high-risk-stratum number; it will be smaller where baseline hernia risk is lower. Tier C: benefit rests on a single randomised trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Jairam 2017 (PRIMA): prophylactic onlay mesh cut 2-year incisional hernia from 30% to 13%; sublay mesh 18% — in high-risk midline laparotomy
cards.summary: Jairam 2017 (PRIMA): prophylactic onlay mesh cut 2-year incisional hernia from 30% to 13%; sublay mesh 18% — in high-risk midline laparotomy
cards.people: Multicentre, double-blind randomised trial (PRIMA) at 11 hospitals in Austria, Germany and the Netherlands: 480 patients undergoing elective midline laparotomy who were at high risk of incisional hernia — abdominal aortic aneurysm or body-mass index 27 kg/m² or higher — were assigned to primary suture closure (107), onlay mesh reinforcement (188) or sublay mesh reinforcement (185). The primary endpoint was incisional hernia during 2 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Incisional hernia occurred in 30% (33/107) with suture alone, 13% (25/188) with onlay mesh (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.69; p = 0.0016 — a 57% relative reduction in risk) and 18% (34/185) with sublay mesh (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.00; p = 0.05). Seroma was more frequent with onlay mesh (34/188) than with suture (5/107) or sublay mesh (13/185); wound infection rates did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in a deliberately high-risk population (aneurysm or obesity): the absolute benefit — 17 fewer hernias per 100 onlay closures — belongs to that risk stratum and shrinks as baseline hernia risk falls. The sublay estimate sits exactly on the significance boundary, and onlay's hernia advantage is bought with more seromas.
cards.source: Jairam AP et al. Prevention of incisional hernia with prophylactic onlay and sublay mesh reinforcement versus primary suture only in midline laparotomies (PRIMA): 2-year follow-up of a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28641875. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00761475. cards.headline: van den Berg 2026 (PRIMA long-term): at reoperation, mesh removal for complications occurred in 3.1% after onlay mesh and 0% after retrorectus (sublay) mesh
cards.summary: van den Berg 2026 (PRIMA long-term): at reoperation, mesh removal for complications occurred in 3.1% after onlay mesh and 0% after retrorectus (sublay) mesh
cards.type: Long-term follow-up study of a randomised trial (van den Berg 2026, Annals of Surgery)
cards.people: Long-term follow-up of the PRIMA trial's mesh patients, analysed as-treated from centres that made reoperation notes available: 242 of the 373 patients randomised to prophylactic mesh were included (127 onlay, 115 retrorectus/sublay), with median follow-up of 27 months (IQR 12–78) for reoperation outcomes after the index closure.
cards.result: Thirty-four patients underwent reoperation for any reason (22/127, 17.3% after onlay; 12/115, 10.4% after retrorectus). Reoperation for complications requiring mesh explantation occurred in 4/127 (3.1%) after onlay mesh and 0/115 after retrorectus mesh; mesh-related ileus occurred in 0 onlay patients and 3/115 (2.6%) retrorectus patients. Overall the mesh was removed in 10/127 (7.9%) of onlay patients during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: An as-treated, records-availability subset of the trial — 242 of 373 mesh patients — so these are descriptive long-term rates, not randomised comparisons, and reoperations for unrelated diagnoses dominate the denominator. The reassurance is real but bounded: serious mesh-specific morbidity at reoperation was uncommon in both positions.
cards.source: van den Berg R et al. Prophylactic Mesh-related Reoperations and Mesh-related Problems During Subsequent Relaparotomies: Long-term Results From the PRIMA Trial. Annals of Surgery. 2026. PMID: 39239718. Registry ID: none in the record (long-term follow-up of the PRIMA trial, NCT00761475). cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial — onlay mesh prevents roughly one hernia in six high-risk closures, at the price of seromas and a small long-term mesh-removal rate — POSSIBLE
cards.people: The PRIMA randomised trial (480 high-risk patients, 2-year hernia endpoint) and its long-term reoperation follow-up (242 mesh patients).

Long-term, explantation for complications occurred in 3.1% of onlay and 0% of retrorectus patients with reoperation data; mesh-related ileus in 2.6% of retrorectus patients. shelves.title: H2 blockers genuinely work for reflux — famotidine healed about 7 in 10 patients by 12 weeks against 3 in 10 on placebo — but PPIs heal roughly twice as fast and far more completely
shelves.question: In adults with reflux symptoms or erosive oesophagitis, do H2-receptor blockers (such as famotidine) relieve heartburn and heal the oesophagus versus placebo — and how do they compare with proton-pump inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Ulcer Agents/therapeutic use · Esophagitis, Peptic/drug therapy · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy · Histamine H2 Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sucralfate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit versus placebo; LIKELY inferior to PPIs. The Cochrane review (Khan 2007, PMID: 17443524) pooled 134 trials with 35,978 oesophagitis patients: H2-receptor antagonists reduced the risk of remaining unhealed versus placebo (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.84 — a relative effect), while PPIs beat H2RA-based therapy clearly (RR 0.51, 0.44 to 0.59). The class-level meta-analysis (Chiba 1997, PMID: 9178669) puts average healing at 51.9% for H2 blockers against 83.6% for PPIs and 28.2% for placebo, with heartburn freedom at 47.6% versus 77.4%. The famotidine trials themselves agree: 40 mg twice daily healed 69% of erosive oesophagitis by 12 weeks versus 29% on placebo (Simon 1994, PMID: 8186349), and both famotidine regimens beat placebo on symptoms and healing in the 338-patient US multicentre trial (PMID: 1746996). So the answer is two-part: for healing and symptom relief, H2 blockers are a real treatment, not a placebo with branding — and they are not interchangeable with PPIs, healing about three-fifths as many patients at about half the speed. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo / LIKELY (less effective than proton-pump inhibitors) (not Tier C: multiple placebo-controlled trials plus two syntheses). Sucralfate, the other pre-PPI alternative, is at shelf #2656; vonoprazan versus lansoprazole at #1661.

cards.headline: Khan 2007 (Cochrane): across 134 trials and 35,978 patients, H2 blockers healed oesophagitis better than placebo (RR of non-healing 0.74) — and PPIs beat H2 blockers clearly (RR 0.51)
cards.summary: Khan 2007 (Cochrane): across 134 trials and 35,978 patients, H2 blockers healed oesophagitis better than placebo (RR of non-healing 0.74) — and PPIs beat H2 blockers clearly (RR 0.51)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 134 RCTs (Khan 2007, Cochrane)
cards.people: 134 randomised trials with 35,978 participants with reflux oesophagitis, comparing PPIs, H2-receptor antagonists, prokinetics, sucralfate and placebo over 2–12 weeks; healing of oesophagitis was the primary outcome. Ten trials (1,241 participants) compared H2RA with placebo; 26 trials (4,032 participants) compared PPI with H2RA-based regimens.
cards.result: H2RA versus placebo: risk of oesophagitis remaining unhealed RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.84) — about a quarter lower in relative terms. PPI versus placebo: RR 0.22 (0.15 to 0.31). PPI versus H2RA (or H2RA plus prokinetic): RR 0.51 (0.44 to 0.59) for non-healing. Prokinetics showed no significant benefit over placebo. The reviewers conclude PPI therapy is the most effective treatment for oesophagitis, with H2RA therapy also superior to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The RR is a relative effect on remaining unhealed, not a healing percentage; the absolute healing rates by class are in the Chiba card. The review's search closed in December 2004 — it predates potassium-competitive acid blockers (vonoprazan, shelf #1661) and says nothing about long-term maintenance or symptom-only (non-erosive) disease.
cards.source: Khan M et al. Medical treatments in the short term management of reflux oesophagitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2007. PMID: 17443524. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chiba 1997: pooled healing proportions — PPIs 83.6%, H2 blockers 51.9%, sucralfate 39.2%, placebo 28.2%; heartburn-free 77.4% on PPIs versus 47.6% on H2 blockers
cards.summary: Chiba 1997: pooled healing proportions — PPIs 83.6%, H2 blockers 51.9%, sucralfate 39.2%, placebo 28.2%; heartburn-free 77.4% on PPIs versus 47.6% on H2 blockers
cards.people: 43 single- or double-blind randomised studies (7,635 patients) in adults with endoscopically proven erosive or ulcerative oesophagitis (grade II–IV), published to July 1996; healing and heartburn relief expressed per week by linear regression.
cards.result: Mean overall healing proportion, irrespective of dose or duration up to 12 weeks: PPIs 83.6% (±11.4), H2RAs 51.9% (±17.1), sucralfate 39.2% (±22.4), placebo 28.2% (±15.6). Healing speed: PPIs 11.7% per week versus H2RAs 5.9% and placebo 2.9%. Heartburn-free proportion: PPIs 77.4% versus H2RAs 47.6%; heartburn relief speed 11.5% versus 6.4% per week.
cards.watchOut: A semiquantitative pooling across trials of different grades, doses and durations — the percentages are class averages, not a head-to-head trial result, and they describe erosive disease, not the milder symptom-only reflux most H2 blockers are bought for.

cards.headline: Simon 1994: famotidine 40 mg twice daily healed erosive oesophagitis in 48% at 6 weeks and 69% at 12 weeks, versus 18% and 29% on placebo
cards.summary: Simon 1994: famotidine 40 mg twice daily healed erosive oesophagitis in 48% at 6 weeks and 69% at 12 weeks, versus 18% and 29% on placebo
cards.people: 318 US patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and erosive oesophagitis: 66 placebo, 125 famotidine 20 mg twice daily, 127 famotidine 40 mg twice daily; symptom diaries and endoscopy at weeks 0, 6 and (if unhealed) 12.
cards.result: Healing at 6 and 12 weeks: famotidine 40 mg twice daily 48% and 69%; famotidine 20 mg twice daily 32% and 54%; placebo 18% and 29% (each famotidine rate P ≤ 0.01 versus placebo; 40 mg twice daily also beat 20 mg twice daily). Famotidine produced more frequent global symptom improvement and faster heartburn relief than placebo. Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Twice-daily dosing at up to double the usual over-the-counter dose — the trial does not show that a single 10–20 mg famotidine tablet taken for an episode of heartburn heals anything; it shows what sustained, high-dose acid suppression does to erosions over 6–12 weeks.

cards.headline: USA Merck GERD Study Group 1991: in 338 patients, famotidine 20 mg twice daily gave significantly more complete daytime-heartburn relief than placebo, and both famotidine regimens healed more erosions
cards.summary: USA Merck GERD Study Group 1991: in 338 patients, famotidine 20 mg twice daily gave significantly more complete daytime-heartburn relief than placebo, and both famotidine regimens healed more erosions
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (USA Merck Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Study Group, 1991)
cards.people: 338 patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and endoscopically documented oesophageal erosions or ulcerations, randomised in a US multicentre double-blind trial to famotidine 40 mg at bedtime (n = 135), famotidine 20 mg twice daily (n = 137) or placebo (n = 66).
cards.result: Famotidine 20 mg twice daily produced a significantly greater proportion of patients with complete relief of daytime heartburn than placebo, and both famotidine regimens beat placebo on global scores and successful outcome; antacid consumption fell significantly on the twice-daily regimen. Both regimens healed significantly more patients endoscopically than placebo, with twice-daily dosing numerically superior to 40 mg at bedtime. The abstract reports significance rather than healing percentages — the Simon 1994 card carries the numbers.
cards.watchOut: A manufacturer study-group trial from the pre-PPI era with a small placebo arm (n = 66) and abstract-level reporting; its role here is corroboration of the placebo-controlled benefit, not precise effect size.

cards.headline: Synthesis: H2 blockers are real but second-tier acid suppression — LIKELY benefit over placebo, LIKELY inferiority to PPIs
cards.summary: Synthesis: H2 blockers are real but second-tier acid suppression — LIKELY benefit over placebo, LIKELY inferiority to PPIs
cards.people: One Cochrane review (134 trials, 35,978 participants), one class-level meta-analysis (43 trials, 7,635 patients) and two placebo-controlled famotidine trials in erosive disease (n = 318 and 338).
cards.result: Versus placebo: non-healing RR 0.74 (0.66–0.84); famotidine 40 mg twice daily healed 69% by 12 weeks versus 29% on placebo. Class healing averages: H2RA 51.9%, placebo 28.2%, PPI 83.6%; heartburn-free 47.6% versus 77.4% (PPI). PPI versus H2RA non-healing RR 0.51 (0.44–0.59). The benefit is genuine and roughly half the PPI effect, delivered at roughly half the PPI speed.
cards.watchOut: Almost all of this evidence is in endoscopically erosive disease treated for weeks at prescription doses. It does not measure the single low-dose tablet taken for one evening's heartburn, and it predates vonoprazan (shelf #1661). Surgery versus long-term PPI for chronic GERD is a different question, homed at shelf #328.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khan M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2007 (PMID: 17443524); Chiba N et al. Gastroenterology. 1997 (PMID: 9178669); Simon TJ et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1994 (PMID: 8186349).

shelves.title: Alginate–antacid (the tested product is Gaviscon Double Action) beats placebo for reflux symptoms — about 48% responders versus 33% — but it does not beat acid suppression, and adding it to a PPI failed its confirmatory trial
shelves.question: In adults with heartburn and reflux symptoms, do alginate–antacid combinations relieve symptoms better than placebo, antacids alone, or acid suppression?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alginates/therapeutic use · Antacids/therapeutic use · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy · Glucuronic Acid/therapeutic use · Hexuronic Acids/therapeutic use · Histamine H2 Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Proton Pump Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a real but modest symptom benefit against placebo or antacid alone, unproven against or on top of acid suppression. The meta-analysis (Leiman 2017, PMID: 28375448) pooled 14 trials (2,095 patients): alginates increased the odds of GERD symptom resolution versus placebo or antacids (OR 4.42, 95% CI 2.45 to 7.97, a relative odds measure), and appeared less effective than PPIs or H2 blockers without reaching significance (OR 0.58, 0.27 to 1.22). The largest single trial, of the branded alginate–antacid Gaviscon Double Action (Reckitt Benckiser), found 47.8% responders versus 33.2% on placebo at 7 days (Wilkinson 2019, PMID: 30272584) — about 15 extra responders per 100 treated — with a concordant pilot (Thomas 2014, PMID: 24471505). But when the same product was added to a PPI for breakthrough symptoms, the 262-patient confirmatory trial found 51% versus 48% response (Coyle 2017, PMID: 28464343). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo/antacid; no proven added benefit on top of a PPI) (not Tier C: multiple randomised trials and a meta-analysis, all short-term and symptom-based).

cards.headline: Leiman 2017: alginates raised the odds of GERD symptom resolution versus placebo or antacids (OR 4.42), but trailed PPIs and H2 blockers (OR 0.58, not significant)
cards.summary: Leiman 2017: alginates raised the odds of GERD symptom resolution versus placebo or antacids (OR 4.42), but trailed PPIs and H2 blockers (OR 0.58, not significant)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (Leiman 2017)
cards.people: 14 randomised trials (2,095 subjects) comparing alginate-containing compounds with placebo, antacids, H2-receptor antagonists or PPIs for GERD symptoms, from searches to October 2015; adults only, English-language reports.
cards.result: Versus placebo or antacids, alginate-based therapy increased the odds of resolution of GERD symptoms: OR 4.42 (95% CI 2.45 to 7.97) — an odds ratio, with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 71%). Versus PPIs or H2RAs, alginates appeared less effective but the pooled estimate was not statistically significant: OR 0.58 (0.27 to 1.22). The authors conclude alginates are more effective than placebo or antacids for treating GERD symptoms.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 4.42 overstates the risk ratio when placebo response is common — the biggest placebo-controlled trial (Wilkinson 2019) found responder rates of 47.8% versus 33.2%, an absolute gain of about 15 percentage points. The pooled trials used several different alginate products and comparators, and most were short.
cards.source: Leiman DA et al. Alginate therapy is effective treatment for GERD symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2017. PMID: 28375448. cards.headline: Wilkinson 2019: 47.8% of patients on the alginate–antacid met the responder definition at 7 days versus 33.2% on placebo (OR 1.85)
cards.summary: Wilkinson 2019: 47.8% of patients on the alginate–antacid met the responder definition at 7 days versus 33.2% on placebo (OR 1.85)
cards.people: 424 adults with GERD symptoms in a multicentre trial, randomised to Gaviscon Double Action chewable tablets (the alginate–antacid product of Reckitt Benckiser) or matched placebo for 7 days. Primary endpoint: a clinically important fall of at least 1.5 points in the Reflux Disease Questionnaire GERD dimension (heartburn plus regurgitation).
cards.result: Primary endpoint met by 47.8% on the alginate–antacid versus 33.2% on placebo (P = 0.0031; OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.78) — an absolute difference of about 15 percentage points over one week. Heartburn, regurgitation and dyspepsia dimensions each improved significantly, and overall treatment evaluation favoured the product (3.2 versus 2.2). Adverse events did not differ notably between treatments.
cards.watchOut: Seven days of treatment in symptomatic (not endoscopically graded) GERD, in a manufacturer-supported trial with a subjective questionnaire endpoint and a one-in-three placebo response: this measures short-term symptom relief, not healing, and not benefit over months.
cards.source: Wilkinson J et al. cards.headline: Thomas 2014 (pilot): the alginate–antacid cut overall reflux-questionnaire scores more than placebo over 7 days (difference −0.55, P = 0.0033)
cards.summary: Thomas 2014 (pilot): the alginate–antacid cut overall reflux-questionnaire scores more than placebo over 7 days (difference −0.55, P = 0.0033)
cards.people: 110 patients with GERD symptoms randomised to Gaviscon Double Action (Reckitt Benckiser) or matched placebo tablets for 7 days; primary endpoint the change in overall Reflux Disease Questionnaire score (heartburn, regurgitation and dyspepsia combined).
cards.result: The overall RDQ score fell more on the alginate–antacid than placebo (least-squares mean difference −0.55; P = 0.0033), with each dimension individually favouring treatment; patients' overall treatment evaluation was higher on the product (mean 4.1 versus 1.9; P = 0.0005). Adverse events did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A 110-patient pilot from the manufacturer's research programme, designed to size the effect for the larger Wilkinson trial — its role is corroboration. The −0.55 difference is on a multi-point symptom scale, not a patient-count outcome.

cards.headline: Coyle 2017: adding the alginate–antacid to a PPI looked good in a 52-patient exploratory study, then failed in the 262-patient confirmatory trial (51% versus 48% responders)
cards.summary: Coyle 2017: adding the alginate–antacid to a PPI looked good in a 52-patient exploratory study, then failed in the 262-patient confirmatory trial (51% versus 48% responders)
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind trials — exploratory and confirmatory (Coyle 2017)
cards.people: Patients with breakthrough reflux symptoms despite standard-dose once-daily PPI: an exploratory study (n = 52) and a confirmatory study (n = 262), randomised to add-on Gaviscon Double Action (Reckitt Benckiser) 20 mL after meals and at bedtime or matched placebo. Response in the confirmatory study: at least 3 fewer 'bad' days (heartburn/regurgitation score > 0.70) than during run-in.
cards.result: Exploratory study: significantly greater symptom-score reduction with add-on alginate–antacid (difference −2.10, 95% CI −3.71 to −0.48; P = 0.012) and more responders (75% versus 36%). Confirmatory study: response 51% on add-on versus 48% on placebo (OR 1.15, 0.69 to 1.91; P = 0.59) — no significant difference. The authors suggest response may vary with whether breakthrough symptoms are functional in origin.
cards.watchOut: The classic exploratory-to-confirmatory fade: the shelf's add-on claim must rest on the 262-patient trial, which is null. Breakthrough symptoms on a PPI are a mixed bag — reflux, hypersensitivity and functional heartburn — and a raft-forming agent can only address the first.
cards.source: Coyle C et al. Randomised clinical trial: addition of alginate-antacid (Gaviscon Double Action) to proton pump inhibitor therapy in patients with breakthrough symptoms. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2017. PMID: 28464343. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, modest, short-term symptom benefit over placebo — POSSIBLE benefit; not a substitute for acid suppression and not a proven PPI add-on
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, modest, short-term symptom benefit over placebo — POSSIBLE benefit; not a substitute for acid suppression and not a proven PPI add-on
cards.people: One meta-analysis (14 RCTs, 2,095 patients), two placebo-controlled trials of the same branded product (n = 424 and n = 110) and two add-on-to-PPI trials (n = 52 and n = 262).
cards.result: Versus placebo/antacid: pooled OR 4.42 (2.45–7.97) for symptom resolution; in the largest trial, responders 47.8% versus 33.2% at 7 days. Versus PPI/H2RA: OR 0.58 (0.27–1.22), not significant. As a PPI add-on: confirmatory trial 51% versus 48% (OR 1.15, not significant). Harms in these short trials were no different from placebo.
cards.watchOut: Nearly all modern trial evidence is for one manufacturer's product (Gaviscon Double Action, Reckitt Benckiser); other alginate products and plain antacids cannot borrow its numbers automatically — formulations differ, and the tested product is named on the cards for exactly that reason. Nothing here tests healing of oesophagitis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leiman DA et al. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2017 (PMID: 28375448); Wilkinson J et al. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2019 (PMID: 30272584); Coyle C et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2017 (PMID: 28464343).

shelves.title: Sucralfate healed reflux oesophagitis about as often as cimetidine in three small pre-PPI trials — and matched it in duodenal ulcer (72% versus 71%, against 35% on placebo) — but the trials are tiny, old and mostly single-blind
shelves.question: In reflux oesophagitis and peptic ulcer, does sucralfate heal and relieve as well as H2-receptor blockade?
shelves.mesh: Cimetidine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Esophagitis, Peptic/drug therapy · Esophagoscopy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Sucralfate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — sucralfate looks like an H2 blocker, on H2-blocker-era evidence. In the only double-blind reflux trial, healing at 12 weeks was 62% on sucralfate versus 59% on cimetidine (Elsborg 1991, PMID: 2011701); the two single-blind trials found 31% versus 14% (Hameeteman 1987, PMID: 3655273) and 48% versus 55% (Ros 1991, PMID: 1882895) at 8 weeks, none significantly different. The placebo anchor comes from duodenal ulcer: healing 71.8% on sucralfate versus 71.4% on cimetidine and 35% on placebo at 4 weeks (Khanna 1989, PMID: 2695513). No trial compares sucralfate with a PPI, and the trials are small enough that 'no significant difference' cannot exclude a real gap in either direction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — comparable to H2 blockers in small pre-PPI trials; never tested against PPIs) (not Tier C: four randomised trials, though all small and old). H2 blockers themselves are at shelf #2654.

cards.headline: Elsborg 1991: sucralfate healed reflux oesophagitis in 62% at 12 weeks versus 59% on cimetidine — no significant difference, and about half of each group lost their symptoms
cards.summary: Elsborg 1991: sucralfate healed reflux oesophagitis in 62% at 12 weeks versus 59% on cimetidine — no significant difference, and about half of each group lost their symptoms
cards.people: 60 patients with endoscopically verified reflux oesophagitis, randomised double-blind to sucralfate granulate 1 g four times daily or cimetidine 400 mg twice daily; endoscopy and symptom review at 4, 8 and 12 weeks; healing defined as complete epithelialisation (Savary–Miller).
cards.result: Healing at the 12-week endpoint: 62% on sucralfate versus 59% on cimetidine (not significant). About half of the patients in each group were relieved of symptoms (not significant). No adverse effects were recorded in either group.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients cannot prove equivalence — the confidence interval around a 3-point difference is wide enough to hide a clinically important inferiority (or superiority). 'No significant difference' in 1991-sized trials is the recurring pattern of this whole shelf.
cards.source: Elsborg L et al. Sucralfate versus cimetidine in reflux oesophagitis. A double-blind clinical study. Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology. 1991. PMID: 2011701. cards.headline: Hameeteman 1987: endoscopic healing 31% on sucralfate versus 14% on cimetidine at 8 weeks, with improvement in 53% versus 67% — small, single-blind, and statistically fragile
cards.summary: Hameeteman 1987: endoscopic healing 31% on sucralfate versus 14% on cimetidine at 8 weeks, with improvement in 53% versus 67% — small, single-blind, and statistically fragile
cards.people: 42 patients with endoscopically documented reflux esophagitis in a single-blind randomised multicentre study: sucralfate suspension 1 g four times daily or cimetidine 400 mg four times daily for 8 weeks; 40 evaluated.
cards.result: Symptomatic improvement was good and comparable in both groups. Endoscopy after sucralfate showed improvement in 53% and complete healing in 31%; after cimetidine, improvement in 67% and healing in 14%. Side-effects occurred in three patients (two on sucralfate, one on cimetidine) and none required withdrawal; one cimetidine patient developed a stricture during treatment.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, 40 patients evaluated, and the healing and improvement patterns point in opposite directions for the two drugs — a coin-flip-sized dataset. It corroborates 'same ballpark as cimetidine', nothing more precise.
cards.source: Hameeteman W et al. Sucralfate versus cimetidine in reflux esophagitis. A single-blind multicenter study. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 1987. PMID: 3655273. cards.headline: Ros 1991: healing after 8 weeks was 48% on sucralfate versus 55% on cimetidine — and some patients who failed one drug healed on the other after crossover
cards.summary: Ros 1991: healing after 8 weeks was 48% on sucralfate versus 55% on cimetidine — and some patients who failed one drug healed on the other after crossover
cards.people: 48 patients with erosive reflux esophagitis allocated to sucralfate tablets 4 g/day or cimetidine 1.6 g/day for 8 weeks in a randomised, prospective, single-blind crossover trial; 41 completed. Pretreatment sphincter pressure and serum pepsinogen I were tested as predictors of response.
cards.result: Complete healing of erosions at 8 weeks: 48% on sucralfate versus 55% on cimetidine; improvement in a further 19% versus 20% — neither difference significant. Symptom improvement was similar in extent. Some patients refractory to one drug healed when crossed to the other. One patient in each group was removed because of side effects.
cards.watchOut: A crossover design in a condition that heals over time invites carry-over and period effects, and 41 completers is small; the predictor findings (sphincter pressure, pepsinogen I) are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Ros E et al. Healing of erosive esophagitis with sucralfate and cimetidine: influence of pretreatment lower esophageal sphincter pressure and serum pepsinogen I levels. The American Journal of Medicine. 1991. PMID: 1882895. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Khanna 1989 (duodenal ulcer): 4-week healing 71.8% on sucralfate versus 71.4% on cimetidine and 35% on placebo — the shelf's only placebo anchor
cards.summary: Khanna 1989 (duodenal ulcer): 4-week healing 71.8% on sucralfate versus 71.4% on cimetidine and 35% on placebo — the shelf's only placebo anchor
cards.people: 80 patients with endoscopically proven active duodenal ulcer treated for 4 weeks: sucralfate (n = 40), cimetidine (n = 20) or placebo (n = 20), double-blind, with antacids allowed as needed; 60 completed (32, 14 and 14).
cards.result: Complete ulcer healing at 4 weeks: 71.8% sucralfate, 71.4% cimetidine, 35% placebo — both active drugs superior to placebo (P < .05), with no significant difference between them. Non-pain symptom scores favoured cimetidine at week 1 but were level by week 4; daytime pain relief was better on both active drugs than placebo.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial with 25% dropout and small comparator arms, in duodenal ulcer rather than oesophagitis — it establishes that sucralfate is an active drug against placebo, which the reflux trials (none placebo-controlled) cannot do on their own.
cards.source: Khanna SS et al. Sucralfate in the short-term treatment of duodenal ulcer. A double-blind comparison with cimetidine and placebo. Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 1989. PMID: 2695513. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: sucralfate performs like an H2 blocker in the small old trials — POSSIBLE benefit; its absolute effect rests on one small placebo-controlled ulcer trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: sucralfate performs like an H2 blocker in the small old trials — POSSIBLE benefit; its absolute effect rests on one small placebo-controlled ulcer trial
cards.people: Three reflux-oesophagitis trials against cimetidine (n = 42, 60 and 48; two single-blind) and one placebo-controlled duodenal-ulcer trial (n = 80).
cards.result: Reflux healing: 62% versus 59% (12 weeks, double-blind), 31% versus 14% (8 weeks, single-blind), 48% versus 55% (8 weeks, single-blind) — sucralfate versus cimetidine, no significant differences. Duodenal ulcer healing at 4 weeks: 71.8% sucralfate, 71.4% cimetidine, 35% placebo. Symptoms improved similarly on both drugs throughout.
cards.watchOut: Everything here predates PPIs: there is no sucralfate-versus-PPI trial, and the class-level healing average for sucralfate in erosive disease (39.2%, Chiba 1997, carded at shelf #2654) sits below the H2-blocker average (51.9%). Four-times-daily dosing away from food is the practical price of the coating mechanism.

shelves.title: Baclofen measurably cuts reflux episodes, but symptom relief in PPI-refractory patients appeared only in the subgroup whose symptoms were proven to track reflux — and about 1 in 6 stopped it for side effects
shelves.question: In adults whose reflux symptoms persist despite a proton-pump inhibitor, does adding baclofen reduce reflux episodes and improve symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Baclofen/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Esophageal pH Monitoring · *Gastroesophageal Reflux/diagnosis/drug therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · *Proton Pump Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, narrowly. Baclofen reduces reflux events themselves — acid and non-acid — in every study that counts them: median combined episodes fell from 23 to 8 after a single dose in heartburn patients (Vela 2003, PMID: 12534409), and a meta-analysis of 9 trials (283 participants) found consistent short-term reductions in episodes and transient sphincter relaxations (Li 2014, PMID: 25389436). The symptom evidence is thinner. In the one trial of the actual clinical question — add-on therapy for symptoms persisting on twice-daily PPI — overall wellbeing only trended better (P = 0.06), and significant benefit was confined to the 25 patients whose symptoms were proven to associate with reflux events (Pauwels 2022, PMID: 35665521); in an earlier 2-week trial, no between-group difference reached significance (Cossentino 2012, PMID: 22428773). Five of 31 baclofen patients in the refractory trial stopped for side effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — in patients with a proven symptom–reflux association) (Tier C: small trials, a subgroup-dependent main result, and a physiology-led evidence base). Baclofen for alcohol dependence in cirrhosis is a different question, homed at shelf #1677.

cards.headline: Pauwels 2022: in PPI-refractory GERD, baclofen helped only the subgroup with a positive symptom–reflux association — and 5 of 31 stopped it for side effects
cards.summary: Pauwels 2022: in PPI-refractory GERD, baclofen helped only the subgroup with a positive symptom–reflux association — and 5 of 31 stopped it for side effects
cards.people: 60 patients (41 women, 19 men; mean age 47.5) with persisting typical GERD symptoms on twice-daily PPI, randomised to baclofen 10 mg three times daily (n = 31) or placebo for 4 weeks as add-on therapy; 24-hour impedance-pH monitoring on PPI before and after, with ReQuest symptom diaries.
cards.result: Overall wellbeing showed only a trend favouring baclofen (P = 0.06). Split by symptom association probability (SAP), the SAP-positive subgroup (n = 25) improved significantly on baclofen (corrected P = 0.02) and worsened on placebo (corrected P = 0.008); SAP-negative patients did not benefit. Total reflux events fell over time, mainly in the baclofen condition, and high-proximal-extent reflux events dropped significantly after baclofen (corrected P = 0.009) but not placebo. Five baclofen patients stopped treatment because of side effects, and one patient withdrew consent.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is a subgroup of 25 patients inside a 60-patient trial whose headline comparison was a trend — exactly the evidence shape that most often fails to replicate. The trial's own conclusion is that impedance-pH testing must come first: baclofen for unselected 'refractory heartburn' is not what was shown.
cards.source: Pauwels A et al. Clinical trial: a controlled trial of baclofen add-on therapy in PPI-refractory gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2022. PMID: 35665521. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cossentino 2012: baclofen improved reflux measures and belching within its own group, but no change differed significantly from placebo between groups
cards.summary: Cossentino 2012: baclofen improved reflux measures and belching within its own group, but no change differed significantly from placebo between groups
cards.people: 43 GERD patients with abnormal 24-hour pH studies, randomised double-blind to baclofen or placebo for 2 weeks; 34 completed. Manometry, 24-hour pH monitoring and symptom questionnaires before and after treatment.
cards.result: Within the baclofen group, 24-hour pH score, total time pH < 4, reflux episode counts and postprandial episodes all fell significantly, and belching, regurgitation and overall symptom score improved. But placebo patients also improved on several symptom scores, and — the comparison that matters — no change in reflux parameters or symptoms differed significantly between the baclofen and placebo groups. Drowsiness did not limit baclofen use in this short trial.
cards.watchOut: A 2-week, 34-completer trial reported largely as within-group before–after changes; read naively it looks positive, read properly (between-group) it is null. It is carded as the shelf's caution against the older literature's reporting style.

cards.headline: Vela 2003: a single 40 mg dose of baclofen cut post-meal reflux episodes from a median of 23 to 8 in heartburn patients (acid 15 to 6, non-acid 4 to 2)
cards.summary: Vela 2003: a single 40 mg dose of baclofen cut post-meal reflux episodes from a median of 23 to 8 in heartburn patients (acid 15 to 6, non-acid 4 to 2)
cards.people: Nine healthy volunteers and nine heartburn patients, each studied twice in random order after a refluxogenic meal in the right lateral position: once after placebo, once after a single 40 mg oral dose of baclofen; 2 hours of combined impedance-pH monitoring per study.
cards.result: In heartburn patients, baclofen reduced median episodes of acid reflux (15 to 6, P = 0.004), non-acid reflux (4 to 2, P = 0.003), re-reflux (2 to 0, P = 0.02) and all reflux combined (23 to 8, P = 0.004), and reduced acid-related symptoms (9 to 1, P = 0.008). Healthy volunteers showed the same pattern (all reflux 10 to 2, P = 0.006).
cards.watchOut: Eighteen subjects, one dose, two hours, a laboratory meal: this is the pharmacology proof (fewer transient sphincter relaxations, fewer reflux events of both kinds), not evidence that weeks of baclofen make patients feel better — and 40 mg at once is a larger single dose than the 10 mg three times daily used in the refractory trial.
