cards.headline: Li 2014: pooling 9 small trials (283 patients and volunteers), baclofen reduced reflux episodes and transient sphincter relaxations short-term, with no significant excess of adverse events over placebo
cards.summary: Li 2014: pooling 9 small trials (283 patients and volunteers), baclofen reduced reflux episodes and transient sphincter relaxations short-term, with no significant excess of adverse events over placebo
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials totalling 283 GERD patients and healthy subjects, published before November 2013, comparing baclofen with placebo on reflux episodes, episode duration, transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs) and adverse events.
cards.result: The pooled analysis supported a short-term decrease in reflux episodes per patient, average reflux-episode length and TLESR incidence on baclofen. No serious adverse events or deaths were reported, overall adverse events did not differ significantly from placebo, and reported side effects were mild to moderate. The abstract reports the pooled findings qualitatively, without a single headline effect size. The PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: Nine trials averaging about 30 participants each, mixing patients with healthy volunteers and single-dose physiology studies with short treatment trials: the meta-analysis confirms the mechanism more securely than the clinical benefit, and its own authors call for a larger, well-designed trial.
cards.source: Li S et al. The effects of baclofen for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Gastroenterology Research and Practice. 2014. PMID: 25389436. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: the physiology is consistent and the clinical payoff is narrow — POSSIBLE benefit, confined to proven reflux-linked symptoms
cards.summary: Synthesis: the physiology is consistent and the clinical payoff is narrow — POSSIBLE benefit, confined to proven reflux-linked symptoms
cards.people: One refractory-GERD add-on trial (n = 60), one 2-week GERD trial (n = 43), one single-dose crossover study (n = 18) and a meta-analysis of 9 trials (n = 283).
cards.result: Reflux events fall on baclofen in every design that measures them (23 to 8 median episodes post-meal in the crossover study). Symptoms: significant benefit only in the symptom-association-positive subgroup of the refractory trial; between-group symptom differences null in the 2-week trial. Tolerability: 5 of 31 stopped for side effects in the refractory trial; pooled short-term adverse events not significantly above placebo.
cards.watchOut: Baclofen is a sedating, dependence-forming drug borrowed from neurology, dosed three times a day, for a benefit demonstrated in a 25-patient subgroup. The evidence supports a monitored trial in impedance-proven, reflux-linked refractory symptoms — not empiric use for 'PPI failure', much of which is functional heartburn that baclofen cannot help.

Gastroenterology Research and Practice. 2014 (PMID: 25389436).

shelves.title: FMT for IBS splits by delivery route: donor stool by colonoscope or gastroscope beat placebo clearly in two trials, while FMT capsules were no better than placebo — and in one trial worse
shelves.question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) improve symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/etiology · Adult · Double-Blind Method · *Fecal Microbiota Transplantation/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/physiopathology/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/etiology · Proof of Concept Study · Vertigo/etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the route and donor seem to decide the answer. Donor FMT delivered endoscopically beat autologous placebo twice: 65% versus 43% response by colonoscope (Johnsen 2018, PMID: 29100842) and 76.9% (30 g) to 89.1% (60 g) versus 23.6% by gastroscope using one screened donor (El-Salhy 2020, PMID: 31852769). Capsule FMT failed twice: placebo produced significantly greater symptom improvement at 3 months in Halkjær 2018 (PMID: 29980607), and Aroniadis 2019 (PMID: 31326345) found no difference (IBS-SSS 221 versus 236) before stopping for futility. Placebo responses were large everywhere (24–43%), all trials were single-centre or small, and no trial compares routes directly. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for endoscopically delivered donor FMT / LIKELY (no benefit) for oral capsule FMT as tested (not Tier C: four randomised placebo-controlled trials). Other IBS treatments are homed separately (peppermint oil #118, low-FODMAP diet #202, probiotics #331, amitriptyline #1662, rifaximin and eluxadoline #772).

cards.headline: Johnsen 2018: response at 3 months in 65% after donor FMT by colonoscope versus 43% after the patient's own stool (P = 0.049)
cards.summary: Johnsen 2018: response at 3 months in 65% after donor FMT by colonoscope versus 43% after the patient's own stool (P = 0.049)
cards.people: 90 patients with moderate-to-severe IBS (diarrhoea-predominant or mixed; IBS severity score ≥ 175) in northern Norway, randomised 2:1 to donor faecal transplant (n = 60) or placebo transplant of their own faeces (n = 30), delivered by colonoscope to the caecum; 83 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Response: symptom relief of more than 75 IBS-SSS points at 3 months.
cards.result: Response in 36 of 55 (65%) on active FMT versus 12 of 28 (43%) on placebo (P = 0.049). No serious adverse events were attributed to FMT; one active-group patient had transient nausea and vertigo, and a few patients in both groups had self-limiting abdominal pain. Four randomised patients were excluded after pinch biopsies showed microscopic colitis.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial whose P value sits at 0.049 with a 43% placebo response — the autologous-stool 'placebo' may itself be biologically active, and fresh and frozen donor material were mixed within the active arm. The result is positive but fragile.
cards.source: Johnsen PH et al. Faecal microbiota transplantation versus placebo for moderate-to-severe irritable bowel syndrome: a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, single-centre trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2018. PMID: 29100842. Registry ID: NCT02154867 (ClinicalTrials.gov), as printed in the record. cards.headline: El-Salhy 2020: response in 76.9% (30 g) and 89.1% (60 g) after a single screened 'superdonor' transplant by gastroscope, versus 23.6% on placebo
cards.summary: El-Salhy 2020: response in 76.9% (30 g) and 89.1% (60 g) after a single screened 'superdonor' transplant by gastroscope, versus 23.6% on placebo
cards.people: 165 IBS patients randomised 1:1:1 to their own faeces (placebo), 30 g or 60 g of frozen donor FMT, all from one healthy, well-characterised donor, administered by gastroscope into the duodenum. Response: a fall of at least 50 points in total IBS symptom score at 3 months.
cards.result: Responses: 23.6% placebo, 76.9% on 30 g (P < 0.0001) and 89.1% on 60 g (P < 0.0001) — a clear dose gradient. Fatigue and quality of life improved significantly in the FMT groups, intestinal bacterial profiles changed significantly, and adverse events were mild, self-limiting gastrointestinal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The largest and most positive FMT-in-IBS trial rests on one exceptional donor — the authors themselves say a well-defined donor with a favourable microbial signature is essential. That makes the result a proof about this donor and protocol, not yet a generalisable treatment; independent replication with other donors is the missing step.
cards.source: El-Salhy M et al. Efficacy of faecal microbiota transplantation for patients with irritable bowel syndrome in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Gut. 2020. cards.headline: Halkjær 2018: FMT capsules changed the microbiota but placebo beat them — symptom improvement at 3 months significantly favoured placebo (P = 0.012)
cards.summary: Halkjær 2018: FMT capsules changed the microbiota but placebo beat them — symptom improvement at 3 months significantly favoured placebo (P = 0.012)
cards.people: 52 adults with moderate-to-severe IBS randomised to donor FMT capsules or placebo capsules for 12 days, followed for 6 months with IBS severity scores, IBS quality-of-life scores and faecal microbiome sampling.
cards.result: At 3 months, improvement in IBS severity score differed significantly between groups in favour of placebo (P = 0.012), as did quality of life (P = 0.003). Faecal microbial biodiversity increased in the FMT group but not the placebo group. The authors conclude that altering the gut microbiota is not, by itself, enough to obtain clinical improvement in IBS.
cards.watchOut: The mirror image of the positive trials: pooled-donor capsules, no endoscopic delivery, and a placebo group that improved more. Whether the difference from the Johnsen and El-Salhy trials is the route, the dose, the donors or chance is exactly what this literature has not yet resolved.

cards.headline: Aroniadis 2019: FMT capsules in IBS-D — IBS-SSS 221 versus 236 at 12 weeks (P = 0.65); the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Aroniadis 2019: FMT capsules in IBS-D — IBS-SSS 221 versus 236 at 12 weeks (P = 0.65); the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.people: 48 patients aged 18–65 with moderate-to-severe diarrhoea-predominant IBS (IBS-SSS > 175) at three US centres, randomised to 75 donor FMT capsules over 3 days followed by identical placebo capsules, or the reverse order, crossing over at 12 weeks. Primary outcome: IBS-SSS difference at 12 weeks.
cards.result: IBS-SSS did not differ between FMT and placebo at 12 weeks (mean 221 versus 236, adjusted P = 0.65), and an interim analysis led to termination for futility. Adverse events were similar (abdominal pain 10% while on FMT versus 8% on placebo; nausea 8% versus 4%); one serious event (acute cholecystitis) occurred on placebo and was unrelated to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: A crossover design in a fluctuating condition, stopped at 48 patients: it rules out a big capsule effect in IBS-D, not a small one. Together with Halkjær it makes two null-to-negative capsule trials against two positive endoscopic-delivery trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two positive endoscopic-delivery trials, two negative capsule trials — the answer depends on how the stool is given, and placebo response is large throughout
cards.summary: Synthesis: two positive endoscopic-delivery trials, two negative capsule trials — the answer depends on how the stool is given, and placebo response is large throughout
cards.people: Four double-blind placebo-controlled trials (n = 90, 165, 52 and 48) using the patient's own faeces or inert capsules as placebo, with response defined on IBS severity scores at about 3 months.
cards.result: Response on active versus placebo: 65% versus 43% (colonoscopic, P = 0.049); 76.9–89.1% versus 23.6% (gastroscopic single donor, dose-ordered); capsules: symptom scores significantly favouring placebo in one trial, and 221 versus 236 (P = 0.65, futility stop) in the other. Adverse events were mild and similar across all four trials.
cards.watchOut: No trial has compared routes head-to-head, donors differed (single screened 'superdonor' versus pooled donors), and IBS placebo responses of 24–43% mean small trials can flip sign by chance. FMT for recurrent C. difficile infection is a different, established question and is not covered here; FMT to clear multidrug-resistant gut carriage is at shelf #1695.

shelves.title: Sacral nerve stimulation cut incontinent episodes from 9.5 to 3.1 a week where optimal medical therapy changed nothing — with perfect continence in 47% of implanted patients — but only test responders are implanted, and the trial base is small
shelves.question: In adults with severe faecal incontinence that has not responded to conservative care, does sacral nerve stimulation improve continence versus continued conservative management?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · *Electric Stimulation Therapy · Fecal Incontinence/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lumbosacral Plexus/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a big effect, a small and selected evidence base. In the only randomised trial against conservative care, sacral nerve stimulation reduced incontinent episodes from 9.5 to 3.1 per week over 12 months while optimal medical therapy (pelvic floor exercises, bulking agents, diet) produced no significant improvement, and 47.2% of implanted patients achieved perfect continence (Tjandra 2008, PMID: 18278532; Cochrane mean difference −6.30 episodes/week, 95% CI −10.34 to −2.26). A pilot trial found marginally larger short-term effects than percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (Thin 2015, PMID: 25644291), and the Cochrane reviewers conclude there is limited evidence that SNS improves continence in a proportion of patients, with device adverse events — site pain, seroma, lead problems, occasional removal — throughout (Thaha 2015, PMID: 26299888). The caveats are structural: the trial was unblinded, and only patients who respond to a test phase (90% in Tjandra) receive implants, so the estimates describe the test-then-implant pathway rather than all-comers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: the comparison with conservative care rests on a single randomised trial).

cards.headline: Tjandra 2008: incontinent episodes fell from 9.5 to 3.1 per week on sacral nerve stimulation while optimal medical therapy produced no significant improvement; 47.2% achieved perfect continence
cards.summary: Tjandra 2008: incontinent episodes fell from 9.5 to 3.1 per week on sacral nerve stimulation while optimal medical therapy produced no significant improvement; 47.2% achieved perfect continence
cards.people: 120 patients aged 39–86 with severe faecal incontinence, randomised to sacral nerve stimulation (n = 60) or best supportive therapy (n = 60: pelvic floor exercises, bulking agents, dietary manipulation), followed for 12 months with bowel diaries, anorectal physiology and quality-of-life indices.
cards.result: Test-phase screening improved incontinent episodes by more than 50% in 54 of 60 patients (90%); 53 received a full implant. In the stimulation group, mean incontinent episodes per week fell from 9.5 to 3.1 (P < 0.0001) and incontinent days from 3.3 to 1 (P < 0.0001); perfect continence was achieved in 25 patients (47.2%), and quality of life improved significantly in all four domains. The control group showed no significant improvement in continence or quality of life. There were no septic complications. The Cochrane review expresses the 12-month between-group difference as −6.30 episodes per week (95% CI −10.34 to −2.26).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the implanted group is pre-selected by a successful test phase — the 47% perfect-continence figure describes responders who passed screening, not everyone referred. That is also how the therapy is used in practice, but it inflates any comparison with an unselected control group.
cards.source: Tjandra JJ et al. Sacral nerve stimulation is more effective than optimal medical therapy for severe fecal incontinence: a randomized, controlled study. Diseases of the Colon & Rectum. 2008. PMID: 18278532. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thin 2015: against percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sacral stimulation showed marginally larger effects — at least 50% improvement in 11 of 18 versus 7 of 15 patients at 6 months
cards.summary: Thin 2015: against percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sacral stimulation showed marginally larger effects — at least 50% improvement in 11 of 18 versus 7 of 15 patients at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial — sacral versus percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (Thin 2015)
cards.people: 40 patients (39 women, mean age 59) with faecal incontinence, randomised investigator-blind to sacral nerve stimulation (n = 23) or percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS, n = 17); 15 progressed to permanent SNS implants and 16 completed a full PTNS course.
cards.result: Faecal incontinence episodes per week: SNS 11.4 at baseline, 4.0 at 3 months, 4.9 at 6 months; PTNS 10.6, 5.8 and 6.3. At least 50% improvement at 6 months in 11 of 18 SNS patients versus 7 of 15 PTNS patients; effect estimates for permanently implanted SNS were larger (10 of 15 responders). Cleveland Clinic incontinence scores improved in both groups, quality of life improved with both, and patients rated both treatments acceptable. Three participants reported device- or test-related pain events.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient pilot not powered for the comparison — it shows the cheaper, less invasive PTNS is in the same neighbourhood short-term, not that the two are equivalent.
cards.source: Thin NN et al. Randomized clinical trial of sacral versus percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation in patients with faecal incontinence. British Journal of Surgery. 2015. PMID: 25644291. cards.headline: Thaha 2015 (Cochrane): 'limited evidence' that sacral stimulation improves continence in a proportion of patients — 6 small trials in faecal incontinence, with device adverse events in every reporting trial
cards.summary: Thaha 2015 (Cochrane): 'limited evidence' that sacral stimulation improves continence in a proportion of patients — 6 small trials in faecal incontinence, with device adverse events in every reporting trial
cards.type: Systematic review of 8 randomised trials (Thaha 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: Six crossover and two parallel-group randomised trials of implanted sacral nerve stimulation: six in faecal incontinence (including the Tjandra and Thin trials carded here) and two in constipation, with searches to February 2015.
cards.result: For faecal incontinence, the parallel trials favoured SNS (Tjandra: mean difference −6.30 episodes per week at 12 months, 95% CI −10.34 to −2.26; Thin: −3.20 versus PTNS at 12 months, interval crossing zero). In the largest crossover trial, 24 of 27 blinded patients chose their stimulation-on period as the one they preferred, and 4 of 27 had adverse events leading to device removal. Reported harms across trials included implant-site pain (6%), seroma (2%), excessive vaginal tingling (9%), haematoma and lead misplacement. For constipation, SNS did not improve symptoms in the 59-patient trial. The reviewers call the evidence limited and ask for rigorous trials.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials are tiny crossover on/off studies (some with 2 participants) in already-implanted patients — they test whether stimulation matters once implanted, not whether offering SNS beats conservative care; only Tjandra asks this shelf's question directly.
cards.source: Thaha MA et al. Sacral nerve stimulation for faecal incontinence and constipation in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26299888. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large effect in the one trial that asks the question, supported by small on/off studies — POSSIBLE benefit, with responder selection built into the therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large effect in the one trial that asks the question, supported by small on/off studies — POSSIBLE benefit, with responder selection built into the therapy
cards.people: One randomised trial versus optimal medical therapy (n = 120), one pilot against PTNS (n = 40), and a Cochrane review of 8 trials.
cards.result: Episodes per week: 9.5 to 3.1 on SNS versus no significant change on medical therapy (between-group −6.30, 95% CI −10.34 to −2.26 at 12 months); perfect continence in 47.2% of implanted patients. Against PTNS, SNS effects were marginally larger. Harms are those of an implanted device: site pain, seroma, lead problems, and removal in a minority (4 of 27 in the largest crossover trial).
cards.watchOut: Everyone in these results passed a test-stimulation phase (90% in Tjandra) — the numbers apply to the test-then-implant pathway, not to unselected incontinence. Long-term (beyond 12 months) randomised comparisons with conservative care do not exist. Sacral neuromodulation for urinary urgency incontinence is a different question (shelf #912).

shelves.title: Diosmectite shortens acute diarrhoea by roughly a day in children (about 24 hours in pooled trials) and by about 15 hours in the one adult trial — a modest adjunct to rehydration, not a substitute for it
shelves.question: In acute diarrhoea, does diosmectite (smectite) shorten the illness in children or adults, as an adjunct to rehydration?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Antidiarrheals/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Feces · Gastroenteritis/drug therapy · Humans · Infant · Patient Compliance · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Silicates/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, modest shortening of the illness. In children, the meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (1,238 participants) found diarrhoea shortened by about 24 hours (random-effects pooled difference −24.4 h, 95% CI −29.8 to −19.1) with more children cured by day 3 (RR 1.64, 1.36 to 1.98; NNT 4) and adverse effects similar to placebo (Szajewska 2006, PMID: 16393300). The largest paediatric trials confirm a real, if small, physiological effect — stool output 94.5 versus 104.1 g/kg (Dupont 2009, PMID: 19268266, two trials reported together). In adults, a single trial found median recovery at 53.8 versus 69.0 hours (Khediri 2011, PMID: 21760777). The paediatric trials have quality limitations their own reviewers flag, and no trial shows an effect on dehydration or hospitalisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (not Tier C: a multi-trial base, though the adult claim rests on one trial).

cards.headline: Szajewska 2006: smectite shortened children's diarrhoea by about 24 hours (random-effects −24.4 h) and raised day-3 cure (RR 1.64, NNT 4)
cards.summary: Szajewska 2006: smectite shortened children's diarrhoea by about 24 hours (random-effects −24.4 h) and raised day-3 cure (RR 1.64, NNT 4)
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials (1,238 participants) of dioctahedral smectite versus placebo or control for acute infectious diarrhoea in children; six trials contributed to the duration analysis.
cards.result: Diarrhoea duration fell by a pooled weighted mean of −22.7 hours (95% CI −24.8 to −20.6, fixed-effect) and −24.4 hours (−29.8 to −19.1, random-effects). The chance of cure by intervention day 3 was higher on smectite (RR 1.64, 1.36 to 1.98 — a relative measure; number needed to treat 4, 95% CI 3 to 5). Adverse effects were similar in both groups. The authors caution that most included studies had important limitations and call for cost-effectiveness analysis before routine pharmacological therapy is recommended.
cards.watchOut: Small, older paediatric trials of variable quality; the tidy fixed-effect confidence interval flatters the precision. The direction of effect is consistent, the exact number of hours is not secure.
cards.source: Szajewska H et al. Meta-analysis: Smectite in the treatment of acute infectious diarrhoea in children. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2006. PMID: 16393300. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dupont 2009: in two trials (Peru n = 300, Malaysia n = 302), diosmectite cut stool output (94.5 versus 104.1 g/kg) and shortened diarrhoea in children 1–36 months old
cards.summary: Dupont 2009: in two trials (Peru n = 300, Malaysia n = 302), diosmectite cut stool output (94.5 versus 104.1 g/kg) and shortened diarrhoea in children 1–36 months old
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind trials reported together (Dupont 2009)
cards.people: Two parallel double-blind placebo-controlled studies in children aged 1–36 months with acute watery diarrhoea (at least 3 watery stools daily for under 72 hours), all receiving WHO oral rehydration solution: Peru (n = 300) and Malaysia (n = 302). Diosmectite dose 6 g/day (ages 1–12 months) or 12 g/day (13–36 months) for at least 3 days. One publication reporting two trials, carded once.
cards.result: Stool output — the key outcome for paediatric antidiarrhoeal drugs — was significantly lower on diosmectite in both studies; pooled, mean output was 94.5 (±74.4) g/kg versus 104.1 (±94.2) g/kg on placebo (P = 0.002), with the largest effect in rotavirus-positive children (rotavirus in 22% in Peru, 12% in Malaysia). Diarrhoea duration was also reduced, and the drug was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The absolute stool-output difference is about 10 g/kg — statistically solid, clinically modest — and children needing intravenous rehydration, or with bloody stools or fever above 39°C, were excluded: this is mild-to-moderate watery diarrhoea only.
cards.source: Dupont C et al. Oral diosmectite reduces stool output and diarrhea duration in children with acute watery diarrhea. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2009. PMID: 19268266. cards.headline: Khediri 2011 (adults): median time to recovery 53.8 hours on diosmectite versus 69.0 hours on placebo — a 15.2-hour difference (P = 0.029)
cards.summary: Khediri 2011 (adults): median time to recovery 53.8 hours on diosmectite versus 69.0 hours on placebo — a 15.2-hour difference (P = 0.029)
cards.people: 346 adults with acute watery diarrhoea (at least 3 watery stools per day for under 48 hours), randomised to diosmectite 6 g three times daily or placebo for 4 days in a multicentre double-blind trial; primary endpoint time to diarrhoea recovery; 329 analysed intention-to-treat (166 diosmectite, 163 placebo).
cards.result: Median time to recovery was 53.8 hours (range 3.7–167.3) on diosmectite versus 69.0 hours (2.2–165.2) on placebo — a difference of 15.2 hours (P = 0.029). Diosmectite was well tolerated. The PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: The entire adult evidence for this question is this one trial: a real but single result, on a median-based endpoint with wide ranges in both arms. It supports 'probably a shorter illness in adults too', not a precise number.
cards.source: Khediri F et al. cards.people: One paediatric meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,238 children), two paediatric trials reported together (n = 602) and one adult trial (n = 346).

shelves.title: Naloxegol worked in both of its identical phase-3 trials — response in about 44% and 40% versus 29% on placebo at the 25 mg dose — with pain scores and opioid doses unchanged; the price is gastrointestinal side effects
shelves.question: In adults taking opioids for chronic non-cancer pain who have opioid-induced constipation, does naloxegol restore bowel function without reversing pain relief?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — the rare clean replication. Two identical phase-3 trials found naloxegol 25 mg beat placebo on a strict responder definition in both (44.4% versus 29.4% and 39.7% versus 29.3%; absolute gains of about 15 and 10 percentage points), with the same result in patients who had already failed laxatives; the 12.5 mg dose succeeded in only one of the two (Chey 2014, PMID: 24896818). The analgesia question is answered by the trials' own pain data: scores and opioid doses tracked placebo exactly (Webster 2018, PMID: 28898536 — a flagged secondary report of the same trials). Over 52 weeks against usual laxative care, naloxegol produced more gastrointestinal adverse events (abdominal pain 17.8% versus 3.3%; diarrhoea 12.9% versus 5.9%) but no withdrawal events and no bowel perforations (Webster 2014, PMID: 25112584). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: two large replicated randomised trials plus a 52-week safety study).

cards.headline: Chey 2014 (KODIAC-04/05): response at 25 mg was 44.4% versus 29.4% (study 04) and 39.7% versus 29.3% (study 05) — significant in both; the 12.5 mg dose succeeded in only one
cards.summary: Chey 2014 (KODIAC-04/05): response at 25 mg was 44.4% versus 29.4% (study 04) and 39.7% versus 29.3% (study 05) — significant in both; the 12.5 mg dose succeeded in only one
cards.type: Two identical randomised double-blind phase-3 trials reported together (Chey 2014, KODIAC-04 and KODIAC-05)
cards.people: Two identical 12-week double-blind trials in outpatients with non-cancer pain and opioid-induced constipation: study 04 (652 participants) and study 05 (700 participants), randomised to naloxegol 12.5 mg, naloxegol 25 mg or placebo once daily. Response: at least 3 spontaneous bowel movements per week with an increase of at least 1 over baseline, for at least 9 of 12 weeks and at least 3 of the final 4. One publication reporting two trials, carded once.
cards.result: Response on 25 mg versus placebo: 44.4% versus 29.4% (P = 0.001) in study 04 and 39.7% versus 29.3% (P = 0.02) in study 05 — absolute gains of about 15 and 10 percentage points. In patients with prior inadequate laxative response, 25 mg gave 48.7% versus 28.8% (P = 0.002) and 46.8% versus 31.4% (P = 0.01). The 12.5 mg dose beat placebo in study 04 (40.8% versus 29.4%, P = 0.02) but not significantly in study 05. Time to first spontaneous bowel movement was shorter and days per week with a movement higher on 25 mg in both studies (P < 0.001). Pain scores and daily opioid doses were similar across groups; adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal, were most frequent at 25 mg. Funded by AstraZeneca.
cards.watchOut: A responder definition built on bowel-movement counts, in manufacturer-run trials with a placebo response near 30%: the absolute gain (roughly one extra responder per 7–10 treated) is the honest size of the effect. The trials excluded cancer pain — the methylnaltrexone evidence in advanced illness is a different shelf (#1797).
cards.source: Chey WD et al. Naloxegol for opioid-induced constipation in patients with noncancer pain. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24896818. cards.headline: Webster 2018: across both KODIAC trials, pain scores and opioid doses moved identically on naloxegol and placebo — no sign of reversed analgesia
cards.summary: Webster 2018: across both KODIAC trials, pain scores and opioid doses moved identically on naloxegol and placebo — no sign of reversed analgesia
cards.type: Secondary report of the KODIAC-04/05 trials — pain and opioid-dose outcomes (Webster 2018). A repeat report of the two trials carded above, flagged as such
cards.people: The same KODIAC-04 (n = 652) and KODIAC-05 (n = 700) populations as the Chey 2014 card, analysed for daily pain scores (0–10 numeric rating scale; baseline means 4.5–4.8) and daily opioid dose in morphine-equivalent units (baseline means roughly 120–152 units/day) over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Changes in mean weekly pain scores were small and statistically indistinguishable between naloxegol 12.5 mg, 25 mg and placebo in both studies (all P ≥ 0.57 versus placebo), as were changes in opioid dose (all P ≥ 0.19). Few patients changed maintenance opioid dose, for similar reasons across groups. The authors conclude centrally mediated analgesia was maintained during naloxegol treatment.
cards.watchOut: This is a re-analysis of the same two trials, not independent confirmation — it answers the specific fear (that a peripherally acting antagonist might nonetheless reach the brain) rather than adding efficacy evidence. Twelve weeks is also short for judging analgesic stability in chronic pain.
cards.source: Webster L et al. Treatment with Naloxegol Versus Placebo: Pain Assessment in Patients with Noncancer Pain and Opioid-Induced Constipation. Pain Practice. 2018. PMID: 28898536. Registry ID: NCT01309841 and NCT01323790 (the KODIAC-04/05 registrations), as printed in the record. cards.headline: Webster 2014 (KODIAC-08): over 52 weeks, naloxegol 25 mg caused more gastrointestinal effects than usual laxative care (abdominal pain 17.8% versus 3.3%; diarrhoea 12.9% versus 5.9%) but no withdrawal events and no bowel perforations
cards.summary: Webster 2014 (KODIAC-08): over 52 weeks, naloxegol 25 mg caused more gastrointestinal effects than usual laxative care (abdominal pain 17.8% versus 3.3%; diarrhoea 12.9% versus 5.9%) but no withdrawal events and no bowel perforations
cards.people: 804 outpatients with non-cancer pain (30–1,000 morphine-equivalent units per day for at least 4 weeks) and opioid-induced constipation, randomised 2:1 to naloxegol 25 mg daily (n = 534) or usual care (investigator-chosen laxative regimen, n = 270) for up to 52 weeks; mean exposure 268 versus 297 days.
cards.result: Any adverse event: 81.8% on naloxegol versus 72.2% on usual care. Events more frequent on naloxegol: abdominal pain (17.8% versus 3.3%), diarrhoea (12.9% versus 5.9%), nausea (9.4% versus 4.1%), headache (9.0% versus 4.8%), flatulence (6.9% versus 1.1%) and upper abdominal pain (5.1% versus 1.1%). Most gastrointestinal events came early, were mild or moderate, and resolved during or after treatment; 11 patients discontinued for diarrhoea and 9 for abdominal pain. Pain scores and mean opioid doses remained stable, no opioid-withdrawal events were attributed to the drug, and there were no bowel perforations; two patients in each group had an adjudicated major cardiovascular event judged unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against a heterogeneous 'usual care' chosen by investigators — the adverse-event gap partly reflects comparing a new drug with familiar laxatives under no blinding. It establishes tolerability and the absence of common serious harm over a year, not comparative efficacy.
cards.source: Webster L et al. Randomised clinical trial: the long-term safety and tolerability of naloxegol in patients with pain and opioid-induced constipation. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2014. PMID: 25112584. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Mesalazine does not prevent recurrent diverticulitis: in two phase-3 trials the placebo groups did numerically best, and no dose of mesalamine beat placebo at two years
shelves.question: In adults who have had acute diverticulitis, does mesalazine (mesalamine) prevent recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Colectomy · Colonic Diseases/diagnosis/drug therapy/surgery · Diverticulitis/diagnosis/drug therapy/surgery · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Mesalamine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Secondary Prevention · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The two PREVENT trials randomised 1,182 patients with prior diverticulitis to mesalamine 1.2–4.8 g daily or placebo for two years: recurrence-free proportions were 53–63% on mesalamine versus 65% on placebo in PREVENT-1 and 59–69% versus 68% in PREVENT-2 — placebo numerically ahead at every dose (Raskin 2014, PMID: 25038431). The DIVA trial found no significant difference on its primary symptom score after an acute episode, with recurrence low and comparable across groups (Stollman 2013, PMID: 23426454), and the Cochrane review of 7 trials (1,805 patients) found no evidence of a preventive effect (Carter 2017, PMID: 28973845). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (not Tier C: two large phase-3 trials). Treating acute uncomplicated diverticulitis — antibiotics or not — is shelf #178.

cards.headline: Raskin 2014 (PREVENT-1/2): recurrence-free at 104 weeks — 53–63% across mesalamine doses versus 65% on placebo (trial 1); 59–69% versus 68% (trial 2). Placebo did numerically best
cards.summary: Raskin 2014 (PREVENT-1/2): recurrence-free at 104 weeks — 53–63% across mesalamine doses versus 65% on placebo (trial 1); 59–69% versus 68% (trial 2). Placebo did numerically best
cards.type: Two identical randomised double-blind phase-3 trials reported together (Raskin 2014, PREVENT-1 and PREVENT-2)
cards.people: Two identical phase-3 double-blind trials in adults with at least one episode of acute diverticulitis in the previous 24 months that resolved without surgery: PREVENT-1 (590 patients) and PREVENT-2 (592 patients), randomised to multimatrix mesalamine 1.2 g, 2.4 g or 4.8 g once daily or placebo for 104 weeks. Recurrence: CT-proven diverticulitis or surgical intervention for diverticular disease. One publication reporting two trials, carded once.
cards.result: Mesalamine did not reduce recurrence at week 104 at any dose in either trial: recurrence-free proportions were 53–63% on mesalamine versus 65% on placebo in PREVENT-1, and 59–69% versus 68% in PREVENT-2. Time to recurrence was not reduced, proportions requiring surgery were comparable, and no new adverse events were identified. The authors' conclusion is explicit: mesalamine was not superior to placebo and is not recommended for this indication.
cards.watchOut: The recurrence definition was broadened for a portion of the study (also requiring abdominal pain and raised white-cell count alongside CT changes) — a wrinkle that cuts both ways, but with placebo ahead numerically at every dose in both trials, no plausible re-analysis rescues a benefit.
cards.source: Raskin JB et al. Mesalamine did not prevent recurrent diverticulitis in phase 3 controlled trials. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 25038431. Registry ID: NCT00545740 (PREVENT-1) and NCT00545103 (PREVENT-2), ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record. cards.headline: Stollman 2013 (DIVA): after acute diverticulitis, mesalamine did not significantly beat placebo on the global symptom score; recurrence was low and comparable in all groups
cards.summary: Stollman 2013 (DIVA): after acute diverticulitis, mesalamine did not significantly beat placebo on the global symptom score; recurrence was low and comparable in all groups
cards.people: 117 patients with CT-confirmed acute diverticulitis, randomised to placebo (n = 41), mesalamine (n = 40) or mesalamine plus Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 probiotic (n = 36) for 12 weeks, then followed for 9 further months. Primary measure: a 10-symptom global symptom score (GSS); entry required GSS ≥ 12 with an abdominal pain score above 2.
cards.result: The global symptom score fell in all groups without a statistically significant difference between mesalamine and placebo, though scores were consistently lower on mesalamine; complete response (GSS = 0) was significantly more frequent on mesalamine at weeks 6 and 52 (P < 0.05), particularly for rectosigmoid symptoms. Recurrence of diverticulitis was low and comparable across groups. Adding the probiotic provided no additional efficacy.
cards.watchOut: DIVA was a symptom trial (n = 117), not powered for recurrence — its recurrence data are a footnote to this shelf. The significant 'complete response' findings are secondary endpoints in a small trial whose primary comparison was null; they justify further research, not treatment.

cards.headline: Carter 2017 (Cochrane): across 7 trials (1,805 patients) there was no evidence that 5-ASA prevents recurrent diverticulitis (recurrence 31.3% versus 29.8%; pooled RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.09 — very low-quality evidence)
cards.summary: Carter 2017 (Cochrane): across 7 trials (1,805 patients) there was no evidence that 5-ASA prevents recurrent diverticulitis (recurrence 31.3% versus 29.8%; pooled RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.09 — very low-quality evidence)
cards.type: Systematic review of 7 randomised trials (Carter 2017, Cochrane)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials (1,805 participants) comparing mesalamine (5-ASA) with placebo or another active treatment for prevention of recurrent diverticulitis, including the PREVENT and DIVA trials carded here; all seven judged at unclear or high risk of bias.
cards.result: Recurrence occurred in 31.3% on 5-ASA versus 29.8% on control; the pooled risk ratio was 0.69 (95% CI 0.43 to 1.09) — a wide interval the reviewers rate very low-quality evidence, concluding there is no evidence of an effect. Adverse events (mainly gastrointestinal symptoms) did not differ: 67.8% versus 64.6% (RR 0.98, 0.91 to 1.06). The reviewers call for rigorous randomised trials before any role is accepted.
cards.watchOut: The pooled RR of 0.69 sits oddly beside raw recurrence rates that are nearly identical (31.3% versus 29.8%) — an artefact of weighting across heterogeneous smaller trials; the large PREVENT trials, which dominate patient numbers, are unambiguously null. Read the Cochrane as 'no demonstrated effect', not as a hidden benefit.
cards.source: Carter F et al. Mesalamine (5-ASA) for the prevention of recurrent diverticulitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28973845. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials null at every dose, a symptom trial null on its primary endpoint, a Cochrane review finding no evidence of effect — LIKELY no difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials null at every dose, a symptom trial null on its primary endpoint, a Cochrane review finding no evidence of effect — LIKELY no difference
cards.people: Two phase-3 prevention trials (n = 590 and 592), one post-episode symptom trial (n = 117) and a Cochrane review of 7 trials (1,805 patients).
cards.result: Recurrence-free at 2 years: mesalamine arms 53–69% versus placebo 65–68% across PREVENT-1/2. DIVA: no significant difference on the primary symptom score; recurrence low and comparable. Cochrane pooled recurrence: 31.3% versus 29.8%, no evidence of effect; adverse events equal.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about preventing the next episode after recovery. Treating an acute episode — including the antibiotics question — is different and is homed at shelf #178; mesalamine for ongoing symptoms of diverticular disease without diverticulitis is a separate literature not pooled here.

shelves.title: Alosetron relieves IBS-D symptoms in women (adequate relief 41% versus 29% sustained over 3 months) — and carries a real, uncommon serious harm: ischaemic colitis in roughly 1 per 1,000 patient-years, the risk that withdrew it from the market
shelves.question: In women with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does alosetron relieve symptoms — and how large is the risk of ischaemic colitis and serious constipation complications?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Carbolines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Colonic Diseases, Functional/diagnosis/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Gastrointestinal Transit/drug effects · Humans · Middle Aged · Receptors, Serotonin/drug effects · Receptors, Serotonin, 5-HT3 · Serotonin Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a genuine benefit bought with a genuine, uncommon, serious harm. Efficacy is consistent: adequate relief sustained across 3 months in 41% versus 29% (Camilleri 2000, PMID: 10744088), urgency controlled on 73% versus 57% of days (Lembo 2001, PMID: 11569692), and pooled global improvement RR 1.60 across 8 trials (Rahimi 2008, PMID: 18555935) — relative measures sitting on an absolute gain of roughly 12 responders per 100 women. The everyday harm is constipation (30% versus 3%). The decisive harm is rare: ischaemic colitis in 0.15% of trial patients versus none on placebo, and about 1.1 per 1,000 patient-years post-marketing (Chang 2006, PMID: 16606352), running at 0.95 per 1,000 patient-years even under the restricted risk-management programme, though without deaths or surgeries in that series (Chang 2010, PMID: 20197759). That risk withdrew the drug in 2000; it returned in 2002 restricted to women with severe IBS-D who have failed conventional therapy. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for symptom relief / POSSIBLE (harm): ischaemic colitis and serious constipation complications (Tier C: the serious-harm quantification rests on post-marketing and observational data).

cards.headline: Camilleri 2000: adequate relief for all 3 months in 41% on alosetron versus 29% on placebo — and constipation in 30% versus 3%
cards.summary: Camilleri 2000: adequate relief for all 3 months in 41% on alosetron versus 29% on placebo — and constipation in 30% versus 3%
cards.people: 647 women with diarrhoea-predominant or alternating irritable bowel syndrome, randomised to alosetron 1 mg twice daily (n = 324) or placebo (n = 323) for 12 weeks with a 4-week post-treatment period; primary endpoint adequate relief of abdominal pain and discomfort; analysis by intention to treat.
cards.result: Adequate relief for all 3 months of treatment: 133 (41%) on alosetron versus 94 (29%) on placebo — a difference of 12 percentage points (95% CI 4.7 to 19.2), roughly one extra sustained responder per 8 women treated. Urgency and stool frequency fell and stool firmness rose significantly. Constipation occurred in 30% on alosetron versus 3% on placebo, and drove the higher dropout on alosetron (24% versus 16%).
cards.watchOut: A pre-withdrawal trial in broadly recruited IBS — not the severe, refractory population to which alosetron was later restricted — and 12 weeks says nothing about years of use. The 30% constipation rate is the everyday harm; ischaemic colitis is too rare to be sized by a trial of 647 (see the Chang cards).
cards.source: Camilleri M et al. Efficacy and safety of alosetron in women with irritable bowel syndrome: a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2000. PMID: 10744088. cards.headline: Lembo 2001: satisfactory control of bowel urgency on 73% of days on alosetron versus 57% on placebo; global-improvement responders 76% versus 44% at week 12
cards.summary: Lembo 2001: satisfactory control of bowel urgency on 73% of days on alosetron versus 57% on placebo; global-improvement responders 76% versus 44% at week 12
cards.people: 801 women with non-constipated IBS and unsatisfactory control of bowel urgency (98% classified diarrhoea-predominant), randomised 2:1 to alosetron 1 mg twice daily (n = 532) or placebo (n = 269) for 12 weeks plus 2 weeks of follow-up; primary endpoint the proportion of days with satisfactory control of bowel urgency.
cards.result: Days with satisfactory urgency control: 73% on alosetron versus 57% on placebo (P < 0.001). IBS Global Improvement responders at week 12: 76% versus 44% (P < 0.001). Stool frequency, stool consistency and days with incomplete evacuation also improved versus placebo. Constipation was the most commonly reported adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Responder and day-level endpoints in a symptom-diary trial are generous measures — the stricter 'adequate relief in all 3 months' endpoint of the Camilleri trial (41% versus 29%) is the more conservative read of the same drug. Enrichment for urgency as the entry complaint also selects the patients most likely to respond.

cards.headline: Rahimi 2008: across 8 trials (4,170 patients), global improvement RR 1.60 and adequate relief RR 1.31 favour alosetron — with constipation RR 4.35 and 4 cases of ischaemic colitis (0.16%), all on alosetron
cards.summary: Rahimi 2008: across 8 trials (4,170 patients), global improvement RR 1.60 and adequate relief RR 1.31 favour alosetron — with constipation RR 4.35 and 4 cases of ischaemic colitis (0.16%), all on alosetron
cards.people: Eight multicentre randomised placebo-controlled 12-week trials (4,170 IBS patients, 80% women; mostly diarrhoea-predominant, only 2.6% constipation-predominant) of alosetron versus placebo, in women and men.
cards.result: Global improvement in symptoms: RR 1.60 (95% CI 1.44 to 1.76) in 3 trials. Adequate relief of pain and discomfort: RR 1.31 (1.20 to 1.43) in 6 trials, significant in both sexes (women RR 1.34, 1.21 to 1.48; men RR 1.23, 1.02 to 1.47). Tolerability was worse on alosetron (RR 1.19, 1.07 to 1.31), driven by constipation (RR 4.35, 3.01 to 6.26 — relative measures). In the alosetron groups there were 4 cases of ischaemic colitis (0.16%) and 2 of serious complications of constipation (0.08%); neither occurred on placebo, and alosetron was not associated with any deaths.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks on common endpoints flatter the drug — the absolute adequate-relief gain is about 12 percentage points (Camilleri card). The ischaemic-colitis count (4 cases) is too small to size the risk; that requires the post-marketing data in the Chang cards. The male estimate rests on few men, and alosetron's approval is for women.

cards.headline: Chang 2006: ischaemic colitis in 0.15% of alosetron trial patients versus 0.0% on placebo; post-marketing, about 1.1 cases per 1,000 patient-years — all 19 adjudicated trial-era cases reversible
cards.summary: Chang 2006: ischaemic colitis in 0.15% of alosetron trial patients versus 0.0% on placebo; post-marketing, about 1.1 cases per 1,000 patient-years — all 19 adjudicated trial-era cases reversible
cards.type: Systematic review of trial and post-marketing safety data with blinded case adjudication (Chang 2006)
cards.people: Pooled clinical-trial data and FDA post-marketing surveillance for alosetron; every reported case of ischaemic colitis or serious complications of constipation was re-adjudicated against pre-specified criteria by experts blinded to whether the patient had used alosetron or placebo.
cards.result: In trials, ischaemic colitis was more frequent on alosetron than placebo (0.15% versus 0.0%, P = 0.03), with no significant difference in the rate of serious complications of constipation. All 19 alosetron-using patients with ischaemic colitis had reversible colitis without long-term sequelae. From post-marketing data, the post-adjudication incidence was 1.1 per 1,000 patient-years for ischaemic colitis and 0.66 per 1,000 patient-years for serious complications of constipation.
cards.watchOut: Post-marketing rates rest on spontaneous reports over estimated exposure — the true incidence could be higher (under-reporting), and the exposed population was the original, less restricted one. 'Reversible in all 19' is reassuring but is 19 patients; regulators weighing this same evidence withdrew the drug.

cards.headline: Chang 2010: under the restricted risk-management programme, ischaemic colitis ran at 0.95 and constipation complications at 0.36 per 1,000 patient-years — similar rates to before withdrawal, but with no deaths, surgeries or transfusions
cards.summary: Chang 2010: under the restricted risk-management programme, ischaemic colitis ran at 0.95 and constipation complications at 0.36 per 1,000 patient-years — similar rates to before withdrawal, but with no deaths, surgeries or transfusions
cards.type: Post-marketing surveillance study under the risk management plan (Chang 2010)
cards.people: US adverse-event reports from November 2002 to June 2008, covering 29,072 patients who received 203,939 alosetron prescriptions under the risk management plan (restricted to women with severe IBS-D who had failed conventional therapy); cases classified by FDA/sponsor criteria with medical documentation.
cards.result: Incidence: ischaemic colitis 0.95 per 1,000 patient-years and complications of constipation 0.36 per 1,000 patient-years — similar to pre-withdrawal rates, though absolute case numbers fell. In clinical trials conducted after reintroduction, ischaemic colitis occurred in 4 per 1,000 patients on alosetron versus 2 per 1,000 on placebo, and constipation complications in 2 versus 0 per 1,000. No mesenteric ischaemia, surgeries, transfusions or deaths occurred among ischaemic-colitis cases, and no constipation complication involved toxic megacolon, perforation, surgery, transfusion or death; cases were typically short and improved on stopping the drug.
cards.watchOut: The risk-management plan did not lower the incidence rate — it shrank the exposed population and, the authors argue, mitigated outcomes through earlier recognition. Spontaneous-report numerators over prescription-based denominators remain approximate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent symptom benefit of about 12 extra responders per 100 women — against constipation in nearly a third and ischaemic colitis in roughly 1 per 1,000 patient-years
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent symptom benefit of about 12 extra responders per 100 women — against constipation in nearly a third and ischaemic colitis in roughly 1 per 1,000 patient-years
cards.people: Two large placebo-controlled trials in women (n = 647 and 801), a meta-analysis of 8 trials (4,170 patients), and two adjudicated safety analyses of trial and post-marketing data (including 29,072 patients under the risk programme).
cards.result: Benefit: adequate relief sustained over 3 months 41% versus 29%; urgency control 73% versus 57% of days; pooled global-improvement RR 1.60 (relative). Common harm: constipation 30% versus 3% (pooled RR 4.35). Serious harm: ischaemic colitis 0.15% in trials versus 0.0%, and about 1.1 (pre-restriction) to 0.95 (under restriction) cases per 1,000 patient-years; serious constipation complications 0.66 to 0.36 per 1,000 patient-years; no deaths in the adjudicated series.
cards.watchOut: Alosetron was withdrawn in 2000 and reintroduced in 2002 restricted to women with severe IBS-D failing conventional therapy — the population in which regulators judged this benefit–harm balance acceptable. Rifaximin and eluxadoline for IBS-D, with their own harm profiles, are at shelf #772.

shelves.title: Eight weeks to cure hepatitis C: glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cleared the virus in 93–99% across genotypes 1–6, with or without compensated cirrhosis
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C, does an 8-week course of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cure infection across genotypes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aminoisobutyric Acids · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzimidazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carbamates · Cyclopropanes · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Female · Genotype · Hepacivirus/genetics · Hepatitis C, Chronic/drug therapy/virology · Humans · Imidazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lactams, Macrocyclic · Leucine/analogs & derivatives · Male · Middle Aged · Proline/analogs & derivatives · Pyrrolidines · Quinoxalines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · RNA, Viral/blood · Sofosbuvir/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sulfonamides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Valine/analogs & derivatives · Viral Load
shelves.balance: The phase 3 programme answers the question directly, genotype by genotype. In patients without cirrhosis, ENDURANCE-1 and ENDURANCE-3 (Zeuzem 2018, 1,208 treated) found sustained virological response 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12 — the accepted definition of cure) of 99.1% with 8 weeks versus 99.7% with 12 weeks in genotype 1, and 95% in genotype 3 on either duration (the 12-week genotype-3 arm matched sofosbuvir–daclatasvir's 97%) (PMID: 29365309). For genotypes 2, 4, 5 and 6 without cirrhosis, Asselah 2018 pooled three phase 3 trials: 8-week SVR12 was 98% in genotype 2 and 93% in genotypes 4/5/6, against 99.5% and 99% at 12 weeks, with virological failure under 1% (PMID: 28951228). Cirrhosis was initially a 12-week population — EXPEDITION-1 (Forns 2017) achieved 99% SVR12 (145 of 146) with 12 weeks in compensated cirrhosis (PMID: 28818546) — until EXPEDITION-8 (Brown 2020) showed 8 weeks did the same in treatment-naïve compensated cirrhosis: SVR12 97.7% by intention to treat (335 of 343) and 99.7% per protocol, with one relapse (PMID: 31682879). Tolerability was benign throughout: adverse events resembled placebo in the blinded trial, and discontinuations for adverse events were at most 1%. The soft spots are genotype 3 (95%, and its 8-week cohort was a non-randomised add-on), the single-arm design of the cirrhosis and rarer-genotype trials, and populations these trials did not enrol — decompensated cirrhosis and patients who had already failed an NS5A-containing regimen. The programme was manufacturer-funded (AbbVie), stated on the cards where the record states it. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: a multi-trial phase 3 programme with more than 2,000 patients across the carded studies).

cards.headline: Zeuzem 2018 (ENDURANCE-1 & -3): genotype 1 SVR12 99.1% on 8 weeks versus 99.7% on 12; genotype 3 95% on either duration
cards.summary: Zeuzem 2018 (ENDURANCE-1 & -3): genotype 1 SVR12 99.1% on 8 weeks versus 99.7% on 12; genotype 3 95% on either duration
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised trials, ENDURANCE-1 and ENDURANCE-3 (Zeuzem 2018)
cards.people: Two phase 3 randomised open-label multicentre trials in 1,208 treated patients without cirrhosis with hepatitis C genotype 1 or 3 infection. Genotype 1 patients were randomised 1:1 to glecaprevir–pibrentasvir (300 mg/120 mg once daily) for 8 or 12 weeks; genotype 3 patients were randomised 2:1 to 12 weeks of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir or sofosbuvir–daclatasvir, with a further genotype-3 cohort non-randomly assigned to 8 weeks. Primary endpoint: sustained virological response 12 weeks after the end of treatment (SVR12).
cards.result: In genotype 1, SVR12 was 99.1% (95% CI 98 to 100) with 8 weeks and 99.7% (99 to 100) with 12 weeks. In genotype 3, SVR12 was 95% (93 to 98; 222 of 233) with 12 weeks of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir and 97% (93 to 99.9; 111 of 115) with sofosbuvir–daclatasvir; 8 weeks of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir yielded 95% (91 to 98; 149 of 157). Adverse events led to discontinuation in no more than 1% of patients in any group. Funded by AbbVie.
cards.watchOut: Genotype 3 is the programme's soft spot: 95% rather than 99%, its 8-week figure comes from a non-randomised add-on cohort, and genotype-3 patients with cirrhosis or prior treatment failure were not the population studied here. 'Across genotypes' should not be read as 'identical in every genotype'.
cards.source: Zeuzem S et al. Glecaprevir-Pibrentasvir for 8 or 12 Weeks in HCV Genotype 1 or 3 Infection. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 29365309. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02604017 (ENDURANCE-1) and NCT02640157 (ENDURANCE-3). cards.headline: Asselah 2018: genotypes 2, 4, 5 and 6 without cirrhosis — 8-week SVR12 98% (genotype 2) and 93% (genotypes 4/5/6), virological failure under 1%
cards.summary: Asselah 2018: genotypes 2, 4, 5 and 6 without cirrhosis — 8-week SVR12 98% (genotype 2) and 93% (genotypes 4/5/6), virological failure under 1%
cards.type: Three phase 3 trials including one randomised placebo-controlled trial (Asselah 2018)
cards.people: Three phase 3 trials in patients with hepatitis C genotype 2, 4, 5 or 6 infection without cirrhosis, untreated or previously treated: ENDURANCE-2 (randomised double-blind placebo-controlled, genotype 2, 12 weeks, n = 202 on drug versus 100 on placebo), ENDURANCE-4 and SURVEYOR-II Part 4 (open-label single-arm, 12 or 8 weeks). Primary endpoint SVR12 in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Among patients receiving glecaprevir–pibrentasvir for 8 weeks, SVR12 rates were 98% (95% CI 94.1 to 99.3) in genotype 2 and 93% (83.6 to 97.3) in genotypes 4, 5 and 6. With 12 weeks, rates were 99.5% (98.5 to 100) in genotype 2 and 99% (97.6 to 100) in genotypes 4/5/6. No virological failures occurred in patients with genotype 4, 5 or 6 infection; overall virological failure on 8 weeks was under 1%. The frequency and severity of adverse events were similar to those in patients receiving placebo.
cards.watchOut: The 8-week arms for genotypes 4/5/6 were single-arm cohorts, and the 93% figure for those genotypes at 8 weeks (versus 99% at 12) is the widest duration gap in the programme — on small numbers, with a confidence interval running from 83.6% to 97.3%. Genotypes 5 and 6 remain rare in trial populations, so their estimates rest on few patients.
cards.source: Asselah T et al. Efficacy of Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir for 8 or 12 Weeks in Patients With Hepatitis C Virus Genotype 2, 4, 5, or 6 Infection Without Cirrhosis. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2018. PMID: 28951228. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02640482 (ENDURANCE-2), NCT02636595 (ENDURANCE-4), NCT02243293 (SURVEYOR-II). cards.headline: Forns 2017 (EXPEDITION-1): the 12-week cirrhosis benchmark — SVR12 99% (145 of 146) in compensated cirrhosis
cards.summary: Forns 2017 (EXPEDITION-1): the 12-week cirrhosis benchmark — SVR12 99% (145 of 146) in compensated cirrhosis
cards.people: Single-arm open-label phase 3 trial at 40 sites in 146 adults with hepatitis C genotype 1, 2, 4, 5 or 6 infection and compensated cirrhosis, treatment-naïve or previously treated with interferon-based or sofosbuvir-plus-ribavirin regimens, given glecaprevir–pibrentasvir once daily for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint SVR12, intention to treat.
cards.result: SVR12 was achieved by 145 of 146 patients (99%, 95% CI 98 to 100), with one relapse (1%) at post-treatment week 8. Adverse events occurred in 101 patients (69%), 65 of them mild; the most common were fatigue (19%) and headache (14%). Eleven patients (8%) had serious adverse events, none judged related to the study drugs; no patient had an alanine aminotransferase elevation and none discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Carded as the benchmark the 8-week cirrhosis trial had to match, not as 8-week evidence: this is 12 weeks, single-arm, and in compensated cirrhosis only. Genotype 3 with cirrhosis was not enrolled (genotypes 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 only).
cards.source: Forns X et al. Glecaprevir plus pibrentasvir for chronic hepatitis C virus genotype 1, 2, 4, 5, or 6 infection in adults with compensated cirrhosis (EXPEDITION-1): a single-arm, open-label, multicentre phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2017. PMID: 28818546. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02642432. cards.headline: Brown 2020 (EXPEDITION-8): 8 weeks in treatment-naïve compensated cirrhosis — SVR12 97.7% intention-to-treat, 99.7% per protocol, one relapse
cards.summary: Brown 2020 (EXPEDITION-8): 8 weeks in treatment-naïve compensated cirrhosis — SVR12 97.7% intention-to-treat, 99.7% per protocol, one relapse
cards.people: Single-arm multicentre phase 3b trial of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir once daily for 8 weeks in 343 treatment-naïve patients with chronic hepatitis C genotypes 1–6 and compensated cirrhosis (67% genotype 1). Primary analyses compared the SVR12 confidence-interval lower bound against pre-defined thresholds derived from historical 12-week results.
cards.result: SVR12 in genotypes 1–6 was 99.7% per protocol (334 of 335; 95% CI 98.3 to 99.9) and 97.7% by intention to treat (335 of 343; 96.1 to 99.3); all primary and key secondary efficacy thresholds were met. One patient (genotype 3a) relapsed (0.3%) at post-treatment week 4. Common adverse events were fatigue (9%), pruritus (8%), headache (8%) and nausea (6%); serious adverse events occurred in 2%, none drug-related, and no adverse event led to discontinuation. Clinically significant laboratory abnormalities were infrequent.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, judged against historical thresholds rather than a randomised 12-week comparator, and restricted to treatment-naïve patients with compensated cirrhosis. It does not license 8 weeks for decompensated cirrhosis, prior direct-acting-antiviral failure, or post-transplant recurrence — populations outside this programme.
cards.source: Brown RS Jr et al. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks in treatment-naïve patients with chronic HCV genotypes 1-6 and compensated cirrhosis: The EXPEDITION-8 trial. Journal of hepatology. 2020. PMID: 31682879. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03089944. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — 8 weeks cures the large majority across all six genotypes; the exceptions are written on the programme's edges, not in its centre
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — 8 weeks cures the large majority across all six genotypes; the exceptions are written on the programme's edges, not in its centre
cards.people: Four phase 3 publications covering seven trials and more than 2,000 treated patients: ENDURANCE-1/-2/-3/-4 and SURVEYOR-II (no cirrhosis), EXPEDITION-1 (12 weeks, compensated cirrhosis) and EXPEDITION-8 (8 weeks, compensated cirrhosis).
cards.result: SVR12 on 8 weeks: genotype 1, 99.1%; genotype 2, 98%; genotype 3, 95%; genotypes 4/5/6, 93%; treatment-naïve compensated cirrhosis (genotypes 1–6), 97.7% intention-to-treat. Virological failure was under 1% in the non-cirrhosis trials; adverse-event discontinuation was at most 1%; in the one placebo-controlled component, adverse events resembled placebo. Cure here means SVR12 — undetectable virus 12 weeks after treatment — the field's accepted surrogate for eradication.
cards.watchOut: The whole programme was manufacturer-run (AbbVie), and several components are single-arm — acceptable where the endpoint is an objective viral measurement with a near-ceiling effect, but the estimates for genotypes 5 and 6 and for genotype 3 at 8 weeks rest on small numbers. SVR12 is a virological endpoint: the further claim that curing hepatitis C prevents cirrhosis complications and liver cancer rests on cohort evidence outside this shelf.

shelves.title: Cold vs hot snare for small colorectal polyps: complete resection 98.2% vs 97.4% in CRESCENT, and the bleeding that needed treatment happened only with the hot snare
shelves.question: In adults with small (4–9 mm) colorectal polyps, does cold snare polypectomy achieve complete resection as often as hot snare polypectomy, with fewer adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Adenomatous Polyps/surgery · Adult · Aged · Colon/pathology · Colonic Polyps/pathology · Colonoscopy/adverse effects · Electrocoagulation/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for 4–9 mm adenomatous polyps the randomised record says cold snare removes the polyp completely about as often as hot snare, without the cautery-related bleeding seen in the hot arm. In CRESCENT (Kawamura T et al., PMID: 28970290) complete resection was 98.2% with cold snare versus 97.4% with hot snare (difference +0.8%, 90% CI −1.0 to 2.7; non-inferiority p<0.0001), and post-operative bleeding requiring endoscopic haemostasis occurred only with hot snare (0.5%, 2 of 402 polyps). A later meta-analysis of 19 trials (Cavassola PRP et al., PMID: 38511795) found a small edge in complete resection for hot snare (risk difference 0.02) offset by more delayed bleeding and longer procedure times with hot snare. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cold snare is a reasonable standard technique for these small polyps — completeness is essentially preserved and the cautery harm is avoided.

cards.headline: Kawamura 2018 (CRESCENT): complete resection 98.2% cold vs 97.4% hot — non-inferior — and the only bleeding requiring haemostasis was in the hot group
cards.summary: Kawamura 2018 (CRESCENT): complete resection 98.2% cold vs 97.4% hot — non-inferior — and the only bleeding requiring haemostasis was in the hot group
cards.people: Multicentre randomised non-inferiority trial in 12 Japanese endoscopy units: 796 eligible sessile adenomatous polyps 4–9 mm in 538 patients, randomised to cold snare polypectomy (CSP) or hot snare polypectomy (HSP); completeness was checked by biopsies of the resection margin.
cards.result: Complete resection was 98.2% for CSP versus 97.4% for HSP, a difference of +0.8% (90% CI −1.0 to 2.7), confirming non-inferiority (p<0.0001). Post-operative bleeding requiring endoscopic haemostasis occurred only in the HSP group (0.5%, 2 of 402 polyps). The authors conclude CSP can be one of the standard techniques for 4–9 mm colorectal polyps.
cards.watchOut: Margin biopsies are a surrogate for true complete resection — they do not measure later recurrence at surveillance. Japanese expert centres and sessile adenomas only; results may not transfer to pedunculated, depressed or serrated lesions, or to less experienced operators.
cards.source: Kawamura T et al. A comparison of the resection rate for cold and hot snare polypectomy for 4-9 mm colorectal polyps: a multicentre randomised controlled trial (CRESCENT study). Gut. 2018. PMID: 28970290. Registry ID: UMIN000018328. cards.headline: Cavassola 2024 meta-analysis: 19 RCTs, 17,588 polyps — hot snare had a 2-point higher complete resection rate but more delayed bleeding and longer procedures
cards.summary: Cavassola 2024 meta-analysis: 19 RCTs, 17,588 polyps — hot snare had a 2-point higher complete resection rate but more delayed bleeding and longer procedures
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials (8,720 patients, 17,588 polyps up to 10 mm) comparing hot versus cold snare polypectomy, with complete resection, en bloc resection, procedure times and bleeding as outcomes.
cards.result: Hot snare showed a higher complete resection rate (risk difference 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.04, p=0.03, I²=63%), but also higher delayed bleeding (risk difference 0.00, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.01, p=0.01) and severe delayed bleeding (p=0.04). Cold snare was faster: polypectomy time −46.89 seconds (95% CI −62.99 to −30.79) and total colonoscopy time −7.17 minutes (95% CI −9.10 to −5.25). No significant differences in en bloc resection or immediate bleeding.
cards.watchOut: The pooled complete-resection difference is small, heterogeneous (I²=63%), and expressed as a risk difference rounded to 0.02 — it sits uneasily beside CRESCENT's own non-inferiority result, and definitions of 'complete' varied across trials.
cards.source: Cavassola PRP et al. HOT VERSUS COLD SNARE FOR COLORECTAL POLYPECTOMIES SIZED UP TO 10MM: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS OF RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS. Arquivos de Gastroenterologia. 2024. PMID: 38511795. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: completeness is essentially a tie at this size; the difference that matters to patients is cautery bleeding, which only the hot technique produced

shelves.title: Underwater EMR for 10–20 mm sessile polyps: R0 resection 69% vs 50% and en bloc 89% vs 75% against conventional EMR, with no extra time or harm
shelves.question: In adults with intermediate-to-large sessile colorectal polyps, does underwater endoscopic mucosal resection achieve en-bloc and complete resection more often than conventional EMR?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Colon/diagnostic imaging · Endoscopic Mucosal Resection/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa/diagnostic imaging · Intestinal Polyps/diagnostic imaging · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · Operative Time · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Rectum/diagnostic imaging · Secondary Prevention/methods · Treatment Outcome · Water
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — underwater EMR removed intermediate-size sessile polyps in one piece with clear margins more often than conventional EMR, at no cost in time or safety. In the anchor RCT (Yamashina T et al., PMID: 30981791) R0 resection was 69% underwater versus 50% conventional (p=0.011) and en bloc resection 89% versus 75% (p=0.007), with adverse events 2.8% versus 2.0% and median procedure times 165 versus 175 seconds. A 2024 meta-analysis of nine studies (Wang X et al., PMID: 38451998) points the same way for en bloc, R0 and complete resection, with fewer recurrences after underwater resection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the technique advantage is consistent, but it rests on one randomised trial plus pooled mostly non-randomised comparisons, and recurrence — not margin status — is the outcome patients ultimately care about.

cards.headline: Yamashina 2019: R0 resection 69% underwater vs 50% conventional (p=0.011) and en bloc 89% vs 75% for 10–20 mm sessile polyps
cards.summary: Yamashina 2019: R0 resection 69% underwater vs 50% conventional (p=0.011) and en bloc 89% vs 75% for 10–20 mm sessile polyps
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial at five Japanese institutions: patients with endoscopically diagnosed intermediate-size (10–20 mm) sessile colorectal lesions, 108 lesions treated by underwater EMR (UEMR, lumen filled with water, no submucosal injection) and 102 by conventional EMR (CEMR, with submucosal injection); only the most proximal lesion per patient was registered.
cards.result: R0 resection (en bloc with histologically negative margins) was 69% (95% CI 59%–77%) with UEMR versus 50% (95% CI 40%–60%) with CEMR (p=0.011). En bloc resection was 89% (95% CI 81%–94%) versus 75% (95% CI 65%–83%) (p=0.007). Median procedure time did not differ significantly (165 vs 175 seconds), nor did adverse events (2.8% UEMR vs 2.0% CEMR).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, in Japanese expert centres, of sessile lesions only, with a margin-status primary endpoint — it does not report recurrence or cancer outcomes, and the most-proximal-lesion rule means many patients contributed a lesion that may not be typical of all their polyps.
cards.source: Yamashina T et al. Comparison of Underwater vs Conventional Endoscopic Mucosal Resection of Intermediate-Size Colorectal Polyps. Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 30981791. cards.headline: Wang 2024 meta-analysis: nine studies, 1,727 polyps — underwater EMR raised en bloc (OR 1.69), R0 (OR 1.52) and complete resection (OR 1.67), and halved the odds of recurrence
cards.summary: Wang 2024 meta-analysis: nine studies, 1,727 polyps — underwater EMR raised en bloc (OR 1.69), R0 (OR 1.52) and complete resection (OR 1.67), and halved the odds of recurrence
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nine studies comparing UEMR with CEMR for sessile or flat colorectal polyps ≥10 mm: 881 polyps removed underwater and 846 conventionally, with outcomes to February 2023.
cards.result: UEMR was associated with higher en bloc resection (odds ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.36–2.10, p<0.00001, I²=33%), R0 resection (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.14–2.03, p=0.004, I²=31%) and complete resection (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.06–2.62, p=0.03, I²=0%), shorter procedure time (mean difference −4.27, 95% CI −7.41 to −1.13, p=0.008, I²=90%) and lower recurrence (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33–0.83, p=0.006, I²=6%). Adverse event rates were comparable between techniques.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled studies were not randomised, so operator preference for one technique in easier lesions could inflate the underwater advantage; the procedure-time pooling is highly heterogeneous (I²=90%). The recurrence signal is encouraging but comes from the same non-randomised base.
cards.source: Wang X et al. Underwater versus conventional endoscopic mucosal resection for ≥10 mm sessile or flat colorectal polyps: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2024. cards.summary: Synthesis: two independent lines agree — underwater resection gets more of these polyps out in one piece with clear margins, and pooled data add a recurrence advantage

shelves.title: Water-exchange colonoscopy: adenoma detection relative risk 1.28, pain about 2 points lower and less sedation requested — for about 90 seconds more insertion time
shelves.question: In adults undergoing colonoscopy, does water-exchange insertion improve adenoma detection and reduce insertion pain versus standard air insufflation?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/prevention & control · Adenoma/diagnostic imaging · Air/standards · Cecum/anatomy & histology · Colonic Polyps/diagnostic imaging · Colonoscopy/methods · Female · Humans · Insufflation/methods · Intubation/methods · Male · Pain Measurement/methods · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Water/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — across 13 randomised trials and 7,056 patients, water-exchange colonoscopy found more adenomas and polyps, hurt less, and needed less sedation and fewer helping manoeuvres than air insufflation; its only cost was about a minute and a half more to reach the caecum. In the meta-analysis (Liu Y et al., PMID: 30226480) the adenoma detection rate was higher with water exchange (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 1.18–1.38 — a relative measure; the record does not print the pooled absolute rates beside it) and the polyp detection rate likewise (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.21–1.39), maximum pain was lower (weighted mean difference −1.99) and on-demand sedation was requested less often (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77). Caecal intubation success was the same (relative risk 1.01). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): this is a technique change with consistent randomised support on detection and comfort alike.

cards.headline: Liu 2018 meta-analysis: 13 RCTs, 7,056 patients — adenoma detection relative risk 1.28 and polyp detection 1.30 with water exchange, pain lower by about 2 points, at the cost of 1.56 minutes more intubation time
cards.summary: Liu 2018 meta-analysis: 13 RCTs, 7,056 patients — adenoma detection relative risk 1.28 and polyp detection 1.30 with water exchange, pain lower by about 2 points, at the cost of 1.56 minutes more intubation time
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 13 randomised controlled trials (7,056 patients) comparing water-exchange (WE) colonoscopy with conventional air-insufflation (AI) colonoscopy, pooling technical quality, screening efficacy and patient-acceptance outcomes.
cards.result: Caecal intubation rate was similar (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.99–1.02, p=0.37) but intubation took longer with WE (weighted mean difference 1.56 minutes, 95% CI 0.75–2.37, p=0.002). Adenoma detection rate was higher with WE (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 1.18–1.38, p<0.00001) and polyp detection rate likewise (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.21–1.39, p<0.00001) — both relative measures. Maximum pain score was lower (weighted mean difference −1.99, 95% CI −2.68 to −1.30), on-demand sedation was requested less (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77), as were abdominal compression (relative risk 0.62) and repositioning (relative risk 0.74), and willingness to repeat colonoscopy was greater (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 1.07–1.21).
cards.watchOut: Detection-rate gains are reported only as relative risks in this record — a relative risk of 1.28 means very different absolute gains in a low-detection unit and a high-detection unit. Endoscopists cannot be blinded to technique, and adenoma detection is operator-sensitive, so performance bias is a real concern across the pooled trials.
cards.source: Liu Y et al. Water exchange versus air insufflation for colonoscopy: A meta-analysis. Saudi Journal of Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 30226480. Registry ID: none in the record.
