shelves.title: CO2 instead of air at colonoscopy: pain 2.6 vs 3.4 during the procedure and still lower six hours later, less bloating — and identical detection, time and completion
shelves.question: In adults undergoing colonoscopy, does carbon dioxide insufflation reduce post-procedure pain and bloating versus room-air insufflation, without compromising performance indicators?
shelves.mesh: Air* · Carbon Dioxide/pharmacology · Colonoscopy*/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Insufflation* · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/etiology · Patient Comfort* · Publication Bias · Risk
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — carbon dioxide is absorbed from the bowel far faster than room air, and the pooled trial record shows the comfort benefit that physiology predicts, without any loss of colonoscopy quality. In the meta-analysis of 23 studies and 3,217 patients (Rogers AC et al., PMID: 31900583), pain scores were lower with CO2 during the procedure (visual analogue scale 2.6 vs 3.4 with air; mean difference −0.7) and remained lower at 30 minutes, 1–2 hours and 6 hours after it, with less distension, bloating and flatulence — while sedation required, procedure time, caecal intubation and polyp detection did not differ. The benefit is real but modest in size: fractions of a point on a pain scale, not a transformation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a low-risk comfort improvement with no performance penalty, limited mainly by the small absolute size of the pain difference.

cards.headline: Rogers 2020 meta-analysis: 23 studies, 3,217 patients — CO2 lowered pain during colonoscopy (VAS 2.6 vs 3.4) and at 30 min, 1–2 h and 6 h after, with less bloating and no difference in sedation, time, intubation or polyp detection
cards.summary: Rogers 2020 meta-analysis: 23 studies, 3,217 patients — CO2 lowered pain during colonoscopy (VAS 2.6 vs 3.4) and at 30 min, 1–2 h and 6 h after, with less bloating and no difference in sedation, time, intubation or polyp detection
cards.people: PRISMA meta-analysis of 23 randomised studies (from 3,586 citations, 2004–2019) and 3,217 patients undergoing colonoscopy with CO2 versus air insufflation, reporting pain on numerical or visual analogue scales plus key performance indicators.
cards.result: Patients insufflated with air had 30% higher intraprocedural pain scores than those receiving CO2 (VAS 3.4 versus 2.6; mean difference −0.7, 95% CI −1.4 to 0.0, p=0.05 — the 30% figure is the authors' relative comparison of the two scores). The CO2 advantage persisted at 30 minutes, 1–2 hours and 6 hours post-procedure (mean differences −0.8, −0.6 and −0.2 respectively, p<0.001 for all), with less distension, bloating and flatulence (p<0.01 for all). There were no differences in sedation required, procedure time, caecal intubation or polyp detection rates.
cards.watchOut: The intraprocedural difference just reaches significance (p=0.05, confidence interval touching 0.0) and the absolute differences are small — under one VAS point. Pain scales and sedation practice varied across trials, and the record itself flags publication bias among its MeSH terms.
cards.source: Rogers AC et al. A meta-analysis of carbon dioxide versus room air insufflation on patient comfort and key performance indicators at colonoscopy. International Journal of Colorectal Disease. 2020. PMID: 31900583. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Acotiamide for functional dyspepsia: global response 52.2% vs 34.8% — but the pooled benefit is all postprandial distress (RR 1.29), with epigastric pain at 0.92
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does acotiamide improve meal-related postprandial-distress symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzamides/therapeutic use · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia/drug therapy · Eating · Female · Humans · Male · Postprandial Period/drug effects · Thiazoles/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the benefit is confined to meal-related, postprandial-distress symptoms. In the phase III trial (Matsueda K et al., PMID: 22157329), 52.2% on acotiamide 100 mg three times daily were global responders versus 34.8% on placebo (p<0.001; number needed to treat 6), but complete elimination of all three meal-related symptoms was uncommon on either arm — 15.3% versus 9.0% (p=0.004; NNT 16). The earlier meta-analysis (Xiao G et al., PMID: 25197703) found overall improvement (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.19–1.40 — a relative measure) driven by postprandial distress syndrome (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.09–1.53), with no benefit in epigastric pain syndrome (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.11). PROPOSED SPLIT: worth considering where it is licensed for fullness, bloating and early satiation after meals; the record gives no reason to expect it to help epigastric pain or burning.

cards.headline: Matsueda 2012 phase III: global response 52.2% on acotiamide vs 34.8% on placebo (NNT 6), but all three meal symptoms eliminated in only 15.3% vs 9.0%
cards.summary: Matsueda 2012 phase III: global response 52.2% on acotiamide vs 34.8% on placebo (NNT 6), but all three meal symptoms eliminated in only 15.3% vs 9.0%
cards.people: Multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase III trial in patients with functional dyspepsia: acotiamide 100 mg or placebo three times daily for 4 weeks, with 4 weeks of post-treatment follow-up; primary endpoints were global overall treatment efficacy (OTE) and elimination of all three meal-related symptoms (postprandial fullness, upper abdominal bloating, early satiation) from daily diaries.
cards.result: Responders by global OTE assessment: 52.2% with acotiamide versus 34.8% with placebo (p<0.001), a number needed to treat of 6. Elimination of all three meal-related symptoms over 4 weeks: 15.3% versus 9.0% (p=0.004), NNT 16. Both benefits were maintained through the 4-week post-treatment follow-up, and all secondary endpoints including quality of life significantly favoured acotiamide. Adverse event incidence was similar between groups, with no significant cardiovascular effects.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short for a chronic relapsing condition, and the headline global response (NNT 6) flatters the drug next to its own stricter endpoint — full elimination of the three target symptoms in only about one patient in seven. The trial population was Japanese, and acotiamide is not licensed in many countries.
cards.source: Matsueda K et al. A placebo-controlled trial of acotiamide for meal-related symptoms of functional dyspepsia. Gut. 2012. PMID: 22157329. Registry ID: NCT00761358. cards.headline: Xiao 2014 meta-analysis: overall improvement relative risk 1.29 — but postprandial distress 1.29 and epigastric pain syndrome 0.92, a clean split by subtype
cards.summary: Xiao 2014 meta-analysis: overall improvement relative risk 1.29 — but postprandial distress 1.29 and epigastric pain syndrome 0.92, a clean split by subtype
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six publications comprising seven randomised trials of acotiamide versus placebo in functional dyspepsia, searched to November 2013, pooling overall improvement and the postprandial distress (PDS) and epigastric pain (EPS) subtypes.
cards.result: Overall improvement favoured acotiamide (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.19–1.40, p<0.00001, I²=15% — a relative measure). By subtype: PDS improved (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.09–1.53, p=0.003, I²=0%) while EPS did not (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.11, p=0.39, I²=0%). Acotiamide also significantly improved elimination of some individual symptoms, adverse events did not differ from placebo, and subgroup analysis supported 100 mg three times daily as the effective dose.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis predates and overlaps the phase III trial's programme, so the two cards on this shelf are not fully independent evidence. Seven small-to-moderate trials, largely from one country's development programme, leave the EPS null and the PDS benefit both in need of outside replication.
cards.source: Xiao G et al. Efficacy and safety of acotiamide for the treatment of functional dyspepsia: systematic review and meta-analysis. TheScientificWorldJournal. 2014. PMID: 25197703. cards.summary: Synthesis: acotiamide helps the meal-related half of functional dyspepsia and not the pain half — prescribe to the subtype, not to the label
cards.people: One phase III RCT plus a seven-trial meta-analysis, together covering global response, complete symptom elimination, and the PDS/EPS subtype split.
cards.result: Global response: 52.2% vs 34.8% (NNT 6) in the phase III trial; pooled relative risk 1.29 for overall improvement. Complete elimination of all three meal symptoms: 15.3% vs 9.0% (NNT 16). Subtype: PDS relative risk 1.29 (significant); EPS relative risk 0.92 (null). Safety: adverse events similar to placebo in both sources. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit in postprandial distress, no shown benefit in epigastric pain syndrome.
cards.watchOut: Functional dyspepsia trials carry large placebo responses (34.8% here), so uncontrolled clinical experience will over-credit this drug. Tier C is set because the evidence is one development programme, short in duration, and split by subtype.

shelves.title: Diet in eosinophilic oesophagitis: remission 90.8% elemental, 72.1% six-food elimination — and only 45.5% for the allergy-test-directed diets families expect to work best
shelves.question: In children and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, do food-elimination diets induce histologic remission, and how do empiric elimination diets compare with allergy-test-directed diets?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Child · Eosinophilic Esophagitis/diet therapy · Esophagus/immunology · Humans · Remission Induction · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dietary therapy does induce histologic remission in eosinophilic oesophagitis, and the more the diet removes, the higher the remission rate — at a steep cost in burden. In the systematic review and meta-analysis (Arias A et al., PMID: 24534634), covering 33 studies and 1,317 patients, elemental (amino-acid formula) diets achieved remission in 90.8% of cases, six-food elimination in 72.1%, and allergy-test-directed elimination in only 45.5% — test-directed diets, the intuitively attractive option, performed worst. Children and adults responded similarly (63.3% vs 67.2% overall). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): empiric elimination — six-food, or elemental where feasible — is a genuine drug-free route to remission; test-directed elimination is not supported by its own numbers, and every diet here demands dietitian support and repeat endoscopy to prove it worked.

cards.headline: Arias 2014: 33 studies, 1,317 patients — histologic remission 90.8% on elemental diets, 72.1% on six-food elimination, and only 45.5% on allergy-test-directed elimination
cards.summary: Arias 2014: 33 studies, 1,317 patients — histologic remission 90.8% on elemental diets, 72.1% on six-food elimination, and only 45.5% on allergy-test-directed elimination
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 studies of dietary intervention in eosinophilic oesophagitis (1,128 children and 189 adults), with remission defined as fewer than 15 eosinophils per high-power field in oesophageal biopsies, pooling elemental diets, six-food elimination diets (SFED) and allergy-test-directed elimination diets.
cards.result: Elemental diets were effective in 90.8% of cases (95% CI 84.7%–95.5%, I²=52.3%), SFED in 72.1% (95% CI 65.8%–78.1%, I²=0) and allergy-test-directed elimination in 45.5% (95% CI 35.4%–55.7%, I²=75.1%). Additional strategies (cow's-milk elimination, gluten-free diets, four-food elimination) were also evaluated. There was no significant difference in remission between adults and children (67.2% vs 63.3%). The authors conclude dietary interventions are effective for histologic remission, with elemental diets and SFED the most effective.
cards.watchOut: This is overwhelmingly observational evidence — case series pooled, not randomised comparisons — so the ranking of diets is vulnerable to selection (elemental diets may go to the most motivated or most severe patients) and the test-directed estimate is highly heterogeneous (I²=75.1%). Histologic remission is also not the same as symptom relief, and reintroduction endoscopies are part of the real-world price.

systematic review and meta-analysis, 33 studies (arias 2014) systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 studies of dietary intervention in eosinophilic oesophagitis (1,128 children and 189 adults), with remission defined as fewer than 15 eosinophils per high-power field in oesophageal biopsies, pooling elemental diets, six-food elimination diets (sfed) and allergy-test-directed elimination diets. elemental diets were effective in 90.8% of cases (95% ci 84.7%–95.5%, i²=52.3%), sfed in 72.1% (95% ci 65.8%–78.1%, i²=0) and allergy-test-directed elimination in 45.5% (95% ci 35.4%–55.7%, i²=75.1%). additional strategies (cow's-milk elimination, gluten-free diets, four-food elimination) were also evaluated. there was no significant difference in remission between adults and children (67.2% vs 63.3%). the authors conclude dietary interventions are effective for histologic remission, with elemental diets and sfed the most effective. this is overwhelmingly observational evidence — case series pooled, not randomised comparisons — so the ranking of diets is vulnerable to selection (elemental diets may go to the most motivated or most severe patients) and the test-directed estimate is highly heterogeneous (i²=75.1%). histologic remission is also not the same as symptom relief, and reintroduction endoscopies are part of the real-world price. arias a et al. efficacy of dietary interventions for inducing histologic remission in patients with eosinophilic esophagitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. gastroenterology. 2014. pmid: 24534634. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · age factors · child · eosinophilic esophagitis/diet therapy · esophagus/immunology · humans · remission induction · risk factors · treatment outcome

shelves.title: Gastric electrical stimulation: vomiting scores better ON than OFF in the big crossover trial — yet no quality-of-life or emptying gain, and the earlier controlled pool was null
shelves.question: In adults with refractory gastroparesis vomiting despite dietary and drug therapy, does gastric electrical stimulation reduce vomiting frequency versus sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Electric Stimulation Therapy/instrumentation · Electrodes, Implanted · Female · Gastric Emptying/physiology · Gastroparesis/complications · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/diagnosis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — gastric electrical stimulation reduced vomiting in the largest blinded trial, but it did not improve quality of life or speed gastric emptying, and the earlier controlled literature pooled to no symptom benefit at all. In the multicentre crossover RCT (Ducrotte P et al., PMID: 31647902), vomiting scores were better with the device ON than OFF (median 2 vs 1 on a 0–4 scale, p<0.001) in patients with and without diabetes and with delayed or normal emptying — yet quality of life did not increase and emptying was not accelerated. The earlier systematic review (Levinthal DJ et al., PMID: 27085627) found total symptom scores did not differ between ON and OFF periods across five controlled studies (difference 0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4), while open-label studies showed large apparent benefits the authors attribute substantially to regression to the mean. PROPOSED SPLIT: a vomiting-frequency benefit in the best single trial, against null pooled symptom, quality-of-life and emptying outcomes — an implanted device with surgical risk earns a cautious, outcome-specific reading.

cards.headline: Ducrotte 2020 crossover RCT: vomiting score median 2 with stimulation ON vs 1 OFF (p<0.001) in 172 patients with refractory vomiting — but no gain in quality of life and no faster gastric emptying
cards.summary: Ducrotte 2020 crossover RCT: vomiting score median 2 with stimulation ON vs 1 OFF (p<0.001) in 172 patients with refractory vomiting — but no gain in quality of life and no faster gastric emptying
cards.people: Large multicentre randomised double-blind crossover trial: 172 patients (66% women, mean age 45; 133 with gastroparesis) with chronic (>12 months) refractory vomiting — idiopathic, diabetic (type 1 or 2) or post-surgical — had a gastric electrical stimulation device implanted, then received 4 months of stimulation (14 Hz, 5 mA, 330 μs pulses) or no stimulation in random order; 149 crossed over for a second 4-month period.
cards.result: Vomiting scores (0 = daily vomiting, 4 = no vomiting) were higher with the device ON (median 2) than OFF (median 1) in both crossover phases (p<0.001), in diabetic and non-diabetic patients, and scores rose significantly with the device ON in patients with delayed (p<0.01) or normal (p=0.05) gastric emptying. Gastric emptying was not accelerated during ON versus OFF, and having the device on was not associated with increased quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Everyone received an implanted device, so the trial cannot weigh benefit against the surgical and device risks of implantation itself — it compares ON with OFF in people already implanted. A one-point median shift on a vomiting scale, without quality-of-life gain, is a modest return, and 23 of 172 patients did not complete the crossover.
cards.source: Ducrotte P et al. Gastric Electrical Stimulation Reduces Refractory Vomiting in a Randomized Crossover Trial. Gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 31647902. Registry ID: NCT00903799. cards.headline: Levinthal 2017 meta-analysis: across five controlled studies, symptom scores did not differ between stimulation ON and OFF (0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4) — the big benefits live only in open-label studies
cards.summary: Levinthal 2017 meta-analysis: across five controlled studies, symptom scores did not differ between stimulation ON and OFF (0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4) — the big benefits live only in open-label studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of gastric electrical stimulation for gastroparesis (English-language clinical trials, 1990–2014), separating the five studies that randomly allocated patients to periods with or without stimulation from sixteen open-label studies, with total symptom severity (TSS) scores as the common outcome.
cards.result: In the five controlled studies, TSS scores did not differ between ON and OFF periods (0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4, p=0.15). In sixteen open-label studies TSS fell substantially (2.68, 95% CI 2.04–3.32) — but medical therapy (1.97), placebo arms (1.52) and botulinum toxin (2.32) also 'improved' TSS in their own literatures, baseline severity differed significantly between study types, and meta-regression showed baseline severity significantly drove the apparent treatment effects, consistent with regression to the mean in refractory populations.
cards.watchOut: This review predates the Ducrotte trial, so its controlled pool is older and smaller studies; its warning about open-label inflation nonetheless applies to how device results are usually quoted. Its outcome was total symptom severity, not the vomiting-specific score Ducrotte used — part of why the two cards can both be right.
cards.source: Levinthal DJ et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis: Gastric electrical stimulation for gastroparesis. Autonomic Neuroscience: Basic & Clinical. 2017. PMID: 27085627. cards.headline: Synthesis: vomiting frequency may fall with stimulation ON; overall symptoms, quality of life and emptying have not been shown to improve — the evidence splits by outcome and by study design
cards.summary: Synthesis: vomiting frequency may fall with stimulation ON; overall symptoms, quality of life and emptying have not been shown to improve — the evidence splits by outcome and by study design
cards.people: One large blinded crossover RCT (172 implanted patients) plus a meta-analysis of five earlier controlled and sixteen open-label studies.
cards.result: Vomiting: median score 2 ON vs 1 OFF (p<0.001, Ducrotte). Total symptoms: no ON–OFF difference in the controlled meta-analysis (0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4). Quality of life: no increase (Ducrotte). Gastric emptying: not accelerated (Ducrotte). Open-label benefit: large but confounded by baseline severity and regression to the mean (Levinthal). PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit claimed for vomiting only, unproven for the outcomes around it.
cards.watchOut: Neither source can answer the question a patient actually faces — implant versus no implant — because the blinded trial implanted everyone. Tier C is set because the controlled record is one modern trial against an older null pool, with outcome-specific disagreement.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ducrotte P et al. Gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 31647902); Levinthal DJ et al. Autonomic Neuroscience: Basic & Clinical. 2017 (PMID: 27085627).

shelves.title: Prucalopride in gastroparesis: symptom index 1.65 vs 2.28 and emptying half-time 98 vs 143 minutes — one coherent but small 34-patient crossover trial
shelves.question: In adults with gastroparesis, does prucalopride accelerate gastric emptying and improve gastroparesis symptom scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzofurans/therapeutic use · Breath Tests · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastric Emptying/drug effects · Gastroparesis/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Quality of Life · Serotonin 5-HT4 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small crossover trial found prucalopride improved gastroparesis symptoms, quality of life and gastric emptying all at once, which is exactly the pattern a prokinetic should produce — but it is 34 patients, four weeks per period, and three patients dropped out with adverse events on the drug. In that trial (Carbone F et al., PMID: 31295161) the total Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index was 1.65 on prucalopride 2 mg daily versus 2.28 on placebo (p<0.0001), and gastric half-emptying time was 98 minutes versus 143 on placebo (p=0.005). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a promising, coherent single-trial result that needs a larger parallel-group trial before it can carry more weight — and a reminder that prucalopride's gastroparesis use sits outside its constipation licence in most places.

cards.headline: Carbone 2019 crossover: GCSI 1.65 on prucalopride vs 2.28 on placebo (p<0.0001) and gastric half-emptying 98 vs 143 minutes — in 34 patients, with 3 adverse-event dropouts on prucalopride
cards.summary: Carbone 2019 crossover: GCSI 1.65 on prucalopride vs 2.28 on placebo (p<0.0001) and gastric half-emptying 98 vs 143 minutes — in 34 patients, with 3 adverse-event dropouts on prucalopride
cards.people: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover study in 34 patients with gastroparesis (28 idiopathic; 7 men; mean age 42): 4-week treatment periods of prucalopride 2 mg once daily or placebo separated by 2 weeks of washout, with symptom scores (Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index, PAGI-SYM, PAGI-QOL, daily diaries) and gastric emptying by 13C-octanoic acid breath test.
cards.result: Three patients were lost to follow-up; one serious adverse event occurred (small bowel volvulus, in the prucalopride group) and 3 patients dropped out because of nausea and headache (all on prucalopride). Versus placebo, prucalopride significantly improved total GCSI (1.65 ± 0.19 vs 2.28 ± 0.20, p<0.0001) and the fullness/satiety, nausea/vomiting and bloating/distention subscales, overall PAGI-QOL (1.15 ± 0.16 vs 1.44 ± 0.16, p<0.05) including clothing and diet domains, and gastric half-emptying time (98 ± 10 vs 143 ± 11 minutes on placebo and 126 ± 13 at baseline; p=0.005 and <0.001). The improvements also held in the idiopathic subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-four patients, predominantly idiopathic gastroparesis — diabetic gastroparesis, the largest real-world group, is barely represented. Four-week periods cannot show durability, crossover designs assume no carry-over, and the adverse-event dropouts and the one serious event all fell on the drug side.
cards.source: Carbone F et al. Prucalopride in Gastroparesis: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Crossover Study. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 31295161. shelves.title: Elobixibat for chronic constipation: 6.4 vs 1.7 spontaneous bowel movements in week 1 — a large effect on two weeks of controlled evidence, with a year of open-label safety behind it
shelves.question: In adults with chronic constipation, does the ileal bile-acid transporter inhibitor elobixibat increase spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/chemically induced · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bile Acids and Salts/metabolism · Carrier Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Chronic Disease · Colon/metabolism · Constipation/drug therapy · Dipeptides/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Gastrointestinal Transit/drug effects · Humans · Male · Membrane Glycoproteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life · Thiazepines/adverse effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — elobixibat produced a large short-term increase in spontaneous bowel movements in its phase 3 placebo-controlled trial, with mostly mild gut side effects, and a year of open-label treatment did not surface a new safety problem. In the 2-week randomised trial (Nakajima A et al., PMID: 29805116), spontaneous bowel movements in week 1 were 6.4 per week on elobixibat 10 mg daily versus 1.7 on placebo (p<0.0001). In the 52-week open-label study of 341 patients, 48% had an adverse drug reaction, most commonly mild abdominal pain (24%) and diarrhoea (15%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the short-term efficacy signal is strong, but the controlled evidence is two weeks long, from one country, and the long-term data have no comparator — durability and comparative place among constipation drugs remain open.

cards.headline: Nakajima 2018 phase 3: spontaneous bowel movements 6.4 per week on elobixibat vs 1.7 on placebo in week 1 (p<0.0001); 52-week open-label safety mostly mild abdominal pain and diarrhoea
cards.summary: Nakajima 2018 phase 3: spontaneous bowel movements 6.4 per week on elobixibat vs 1.7 on placebo in week 1 (p<0.0001); 52-week open-label safety mostly mild abdominal pain and diarrhoea
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial plus open-label extension (Nakajima 2018)
cards.people: Two Japanese phase 3 studies in adults aged 20–80 with at least 6 months of chronic constipation meeting Rome III functional-constipation criteria (fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements per week): a 2-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (133 assigned; 70 elobixibat 10 mg daily, 63 placebo) and a 52-week open-label single-arm study (341 allocated, dose adjustable 5–15 mg).
cards.result: In the randomised trial, week-1 spontaneous bowel movements were greater with elobixibat (least-squares mean 6.4, 95% CI 5.3–7.6) than placebo (1.7, 95% CI 1.2–2.2; p<0.0001). In the 52-week trial, 163 of 340 patients (48%) had an adverse drug reaction, most commonly mild gastrointestinal disorders (135, 40%); one moderate inguinal hernia was reported. The commonest reactions in both trials were mild abdominal pain (19% on elobixibat vs 2% on placebo in the 2-week trial; 24% over 52 weeks) and diarrhoea (13% vs 0% in the 2-week trial; 15% over 52 weeks). The authors conclude elobixibat resolved constipation short-term and was well tolerated short- and long-term.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled portion lasted only 2 weeks — long enough to show the colon responds, not that patients stay better, keep taking it, or do better than on cheaper laxatives. All participants were Japanese, and the long-term arm had no control group, so its 48% reaction rate has no background rate to compare against.
cards.source: Nakajima A et al. Safety and efficacy of elobixibat for chronic constipation: results from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial and an open-label, single-arm, phase 3 trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2018. PMID: 29805116. Registry ID: JapicCTI-153061, JapicCTI-153062. cards.summary: Synthesis: a big week-1 bowel-movement effect and an acceptable one-year tolerability picture, resting on two weeks of controlled data
cards.people: One 2-week randomised trial (133 patients) and one 52-week open-label study (341 patients), both Japanese phase 3 studies of elobixibat 10 mg daily.
cards.result: Efficacy (week 1): spontaneous bowel movements 6.4 vs 1.7 per week (p<0.0001). Harms: abdominal pain 19% vs 2% and diarrhoea 13% vs 0% in the controlled trial; 48% any adverse drug reaction over 52 weeks open-label, mostly mild gastrointestinal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Ondansetron for IBS-D: stools firmer by 0.9 points, urgency and frequency down, relief relative risk 4.7 — with pain unchanged and constipation the class price
shelves.question: In adults with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does ondansetron improve stool consistency and global symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cross-Over Studies · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Feces · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Ondansetron/adverse effects · Serotonin Antagonists/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ondansetron, borrowed from antiemetic practice, firmed stools and cut urgency and frequency in a crossover trial in IBS-D, without improving pain — a pattern that fits its gut-slowing pharmacology. In that trial (Garsed K et al., PMID: 24334242), stool form improved versus placebo (mean difference −0.9, 95% CI −1.1 to −0.6), symptom severity fell further (83 vs 37 points), and 65% reported adequate relief on ondansetron but not placebo versus 14% the other way round (relative risk 4.7, 95% CI 2.6–8.5 — a relative measure). The class meta-analysis (Zheng Y et al., PMID: 28291778) supports 5-HT3 antagonists in IBS-D while flagging their price: constipation (pooled relative risk 3.71). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a useful off-label option for the stool-and-urgency burden of IBS-D, prescribed knowing pain is not its target and constipation is its trade-off.

cards.headline: Garsed 2014 crossover: stool form improved by 0.9 points vs placebo, urgency and frequency down, adequate relief 65% vs 14% the other way — but pain unchanged
cards.summary: Garsed 2014 crossover: stool form improved by 0.9 points vs placebo, urgency and frequency down, adequate relief 65% vs 14% the other way — but pain unchanged
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in 120 patients meeting Rome III criteria for IBS-D: 5 weeks of ondansetron 4 mg versus placebo, with dose titration allowed up to two tablets three times daily in the first 3 weeks, daily stool diaries (Bristol Stool Form) and gut-transit measurement in the last week of each period; the primary endpoint was average stool consistency in the last 2 weeks of treatment.
cards.result: Ondansetron improved stool consistency (mean difference in stool form −0.9, 95% CI −1.1 to −0.6, p<0.001). Versus placebo, patients on ondansetron had fewer days with urgency (p<0.001), lower urgency scores (p<0.001), reduced frequency of defaecation (p=0.002) and less bloating (p=0.002), although pain scores did not change significantly. IBS symptom severity fell more with ondansetron than placebo (83 ± 9.8 vs 37 ± 9.7, p=0.001). Adequate relief was reported on ondansetron but not placebo by 65%, versus 14% on placebo but not ondansetron (relative risk 4.7, 95% CI 2.6–8.5, p<0.001 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: A crossover in a fluctuating condition, with dose titration that makes the effective dose hard to state, and a null pain result that matters — patients whose IBS-D is pain-dominant should not expect this drug to answer their main complaint. Long-term safety in this off-label use is extrapolated from antiemetic practice, not measured here.
cards.source: Garsed K et al. A randomised trial of ondansetron for the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. Gut. 2014. PMID: 24334242. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zheng 2017 meta-analysis: 5-HT3 antagonists as a class improved global IBS symptoms (relative risk 1.56) and stool consistency (1.63) — and tripled constipation (3.71)
cards.summary: Zheng 2017 meta-analysis: 5-HT3 antagonists as a class improved global IBS symptoms (relative risk 1.56) and stool consistency (1.63) — and tripled constipation (3.71)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (alosetron, ramosetron, cilansetron, ondansetron) versus placebo or conventional treatment in adults with non-constipated or diarrhoea-predominant IBS; 16 trials were high quality (Jadad ≥4).
cards.result: Global IBS symptoms improved with 5-HT3 antagonists (pooled relative risk 1.56, 95% CI 1.43–1.71 — a relative measure), with similar effects for alosetron, ramosetron and cilansetron; abdominal pain relief also favoured the class (relative risk 1.33, 95% CI 1.26–1.39), as did abnormal bowel habits or stool consistency (relative risk 1.63, 95% CI 1.33–1.99). Adverse events were more frequent (relative risk 1.15, 95% CI 1.08–1.22), driven by constipation (relative risk 3.71, 95% CI 2.98–4.61; in IBS-D-only trials 3.24, 95% CI 2.54–4.12). The authors list ondansetron among the effective agents and report rare serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A class-level pool: most weight comes from alosetron and ramosetron, agents with their own regulatory histories, so the class numbers support ondansetron only indirectly. The class's pain benefit (relative risk 1.33) also sits awkwardly beside Garsed's null pain result for ondansetron itself — trust the drug-specific trial on that point.
cards.source: Zheng Y et al. Efficacy and safety of 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 receptor antagonists in irritable bowel syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: ondansetron answers the stool, urgency and frequency parts of IBS-D; pain is untouched in its own trial, and constipation is the class trade-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: ondansetron answers the stool, urgency and frequency parts of IBS-D; pain is untouched in its own trial, and constipation is the class trade-off
cards.people: One drug-specific crossover RCT (120 patients) plus a 21-trial class meta-analysis.
cards.result: Stool form: −0.9 points vs placebo (Garsed). Adequate relief: relative risk 4.7 in the crossover comparison. Class effects: global symptoms relative risk 1.56, stool consistency 1.63, constipation 3.71 (all relative measures, Zheng). Pain: no significant change on ondansetron (Garsed). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about ondansetron only; the rifaximin/eluxadoline IBS-D question lives on its own shelf. Tier C is set because the drug-specific evidence is a single crossover trial, with the rest borrowed from its drug class.

shelves.title: Colesevelam in bile-acid diarrhoea: every biomarker moved (p<0.001) and no blinded symptom did — mechanism proven, clinical benefit still waiting on a larger trial
shelves.question: In adults with bile-acid diarrhoea (including diarrhoea-predominant IBS with bile-acid malabsorption), does colesevelam improve stool consistency and bowel symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bile Acids and Salts* · Biomarkers · Colesevelam Hydrochloride · Colon · Diarrhea · Double-Blind Method · Gene Expression · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome* · Receptors, G-Protein-Coupled
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the biology moves exactly as predicted and the symptoms, in the one placebo-controlled trial, do not. In that trial (Vijayvargiya P et al., PMID: 32088296), colesevelam significantly changed sequestered faecal bile-acid excretion and the synthesis markers C4 and FGF19 (all p<0.001) in 30 patients with bile-acid diarrhoea in IBS-D — yet stool frequency and consistency, colonic transit and permeability did not differ significantly from placebo. An earlier open-label study (Camilleri M et al., PMID: 25594801) did see firmer stools on colesevelam, and a meta-analysis of bile-acid sequestrants as a class (Soares GAR et al., PMID: 39428959) found more diarrhoea cessation (relative risk 3.27) across seven small trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mechanism proven, clinical benefit unproven in the only blinded test of this drug — larger trials are needed, as that trial's own authors conclude.

cards.headline: Vijayvargiya 2020 RCT: colesevelam moved every bile-acid biomarker (p<0.001) — and stool frequency, consistency, transit and permeability did not differ from placebo
cards.summary: Vijayvargiya 2020 RCT: colesevelam moved every bile-acid biomarker (p<0.001) — and stool frequency, consistency, transit and permeability did not differ from placebo
cards.people: Double-blind, parallel-group randomised trial at a single centre (December 2017–December 2018): 30 adults with IBS-D and evidence of increased bile-acid synthesis or faecal excretion, randomised to colesevelam (3 × 625 mg tablets twice daily) or matching placebo for 4 weeks, with stool diaries, faecal bile acids, serum C4 and FGF19, scintigraphic colonic transit, permeability testing and rectosigmoid mucosal gene expression; primary endpoints were change in total faecal bile-acid concentration and stool consistency.
cards.result: Colesevelam was associated with significant changes in sequestered faecal total bile-acid excretion (p<0.001) and serum C4 and FGF19 (both p<0.001), and a mean increase in faecal deoxycholic acid (10%, p=0.07) versus placebo; colonic mucosal expression of NR1H4 and P2RY4 fell and GPBAR1 rose versus baseline. Stool frequency and consistency, colonic transit and permeability did not differ significantly between groups. Colesevelam was well tolerated, and the authors state larger studies are needed to determine effects on clinical responses.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients for four weeks cannot exclude a real but modest symptom effect — 'not significant' here is not 'no effect'. But it is the only blinded test, and its clinical endpoints were uniformly null while its biomarkers were uniformly positive, which is the classic signature of a mechanism that may not translate.
cards.source: Vijayvargiya P et al. Effects of Colesevelam on Bowel Symptoms, Biomarkers, and Colonic Mucosal Gene Expression in Patients With Bile Acid Diarrhea in a Randomized Trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 32088296. Registry ID: NCT03270085. cards.headline: Camilleri 2015 open-label: colesevelam for 10 days increased faecal bile-acid excretion and serum C4 and produced more solid stool consistency in IBS-D
cards.summary: Camilleri 2015 open-label: colesevelam for 10 days increased faecal bile-acid excretion and serum C4 and produced more solid stool consistency in IBS-D
cards.people: Single-centre, unblinded, single-dose (fixed-dose) trial of colesevelam 1,875 mg (3 × 625 mg tablets) twice daily for 10 days in patients with IBS-D, measuring 48-hour faecal bile-acid and fat excretion and fasting serum C4, with stool diaries for 8 days before and 8 days during treatment.
cards.result: Colesevelam was associated with significantly increased faecal total bile-acid excretion and deoxycholic acid excretion, increased serum C4, and more solid stool consistency. There was a significant inverse correlation between bowel movements per week and the total bile acid sequestered into stool in the last 48 hours of treatment. Random stool samples did not accurately reflect 48-hour total or individual faecal bile-acid excretion, and sequestration did not increase faecal fat (no steatorrhoea).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded and uncontrolled, in a condition whose symptoms swing week to week — the firmer stools here are hypothesis-generating only, and this study is the optimistic half of the shelf's split. Its durable contribution is practical: random stool samples cannot substitute for 48-hour collections when bile-acid diarrhoea is being assessed.
cards.source: Camilleri M et al. Effect of colesevelam on faecal bile acids and bowel functions in diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2015. cards.headline: Soares 2025 meta-analysis: bile-acid sequestrants as a class improved diarrhoea cessation (relative risk 3.27) across 7 RCTs and 311 patients — with more abdominal cramps (5.27)
cards.summary: Soares 2025 meta-analysis: bile-acid sequestrants as a class improved diarrhoea cessation (relative risk 3.27) across 7 RCTs and 311 patients — with more abdominal cramps (5.27)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of bile-acid sequestrants for bile-acid diarrhoea, searched to November 2023 and prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42023445444): seven RCTs, 311 patients, 168 randomised to a sequestrant — colesevelam in 101 (60.1%), chenodeoxycholate in 40, cholestyramine in 18 and colestid in 9.
cards.result: Sequestrants were associated with significant improvement in cessation of diarrhoea (relative risk 3.27, 95% CI 2.08–5.15 — a relative measure) and in liquid-to-normal faecal consistency (relative risk 2.69, 95% CI 1.56–4.65), and with increased abdominal cramps (relative risk 5.27, 95% CI 1.21–22.93). There were no differences in urgency, adverse events overall, or nausea. The authors conclude sequestrants are effective for bile-acid diarrhoea on these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A class pool in which colesevelam is only part of the weight and one included agent (chenodeoxycholate) is not a sequestrant in the usual sense; seven small trials totalling 311 patients is a thin base for a relative risk of 3.27, and the cramps signal (relative risk 5.27, very wide interval) deserves equal billing.

cards.people: One placebo-controlled RCT (30 patients), one open-label study, and one seven-trial class meta-analysis (311 patients).
cards.result: Biomarkers: faecal bile-acid sequestration and C4/FGF19 changes all p<0.001 on colesevelam (Vijayvargiya). Blinded clinical outcomes: stool frequency and consistency not significantly different from placebo (Vijayvargiya). Unblinded: more solid stool consistency (Camilleri). Class-pooled: diarrhoea cessation relative risk 3.27, cramps relative risk 5.27 (Soares). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Colesevelam's glycaemia shelf in type 2 diabetes is a different question and lends this one no support. Tier C is set because the only blinded drug-specific trial is small and clinically null despite its positive biomarkers.

shelves.title: CDED plus partial formula in children's Crohn's: tolerated by 97.5% vs 73.6% for all-formula feeding, and week-12 remission 75.6% vs 45.1%
shelves.question: In children with Crohn's disease, does the Crohn's disease exclusion diet plus partial enteral nutrition induce and sustain remission more often than exclusive enteral nutrition?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Combined Modality Therapy/methods · Crohn Disease/diagnosis · Diet Therapy/methods · Enteral Nutrition/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Remission Induction/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Crohn's disease exclusion diet plus partial enteral nutrition was far better tolerated than exclusive enteral nutrition and, by week 12, kept significantly more children in corticosteroid-free remission. In the randomised trial (Levine A et al., PMID: 31170412), tolerance was 97.5% with CDED plus partial enteral nutrition versus 73.6% with exclusive enteral nutrition (p=0.002), week-6 remission was similar (75% vs 59%, p=0.38), and week-12 sustained corticosteroid-free remission favoured the exclusion diet (75.6% vs 45.1%, p=0.01; odds ratio 3.77). A 2024 network meta-analysis (Ma J et al., PMID: 39686992) ranked partial enteral nutrition plus CDED first among dietary strategies for both remission and tolerance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a child with mild-to-moderate Crohn's, this is a real-food alternative to the all-formula diet with a randomised trial behind it — delivered, as in the trial, with formula providing half then a quarter of calories and dietitian supervision.

cards.headline: Levine 2019 RCT: CDED plus partial enteral nutrition tolerated by 97.5% vs 73.6% for exclusive enteral nutrition, and week-12 sustained remission 75.6% vs 45.1% (OR 3.77)
cards.summary: Levine 2019 RCT: CDED plus partial enteral nutrition tolerated by 97.5% vs 73.6% for exclusive enteral nutrition, and week-12 sustained remission 75.6% vs 45.1% (OR 3.77)
cards.people: 12-week prospective randomised trial in children with mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease: CDED plus 50% of calories from formula (Modulen, Nestlé — the specific formula named in the publication) for 6 weeks, then CDED with 25% partial enteral nutrition (PEN) weeks 7–12 (n=40), versus exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) for 6 weeks then free diet with 25% PEN weeks 7–12 (n=38); the primary endpoint was dietary tolerance, with intention-to-treat remission at week 6 and corticosteroid-free sustained remission at week 12 as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: Four patients withdrew for intolerance within 48 hours; 74 children (mean age 14.2 ± 2.7 years) were analysed for remission. Tolerance: 39 of 40 (97.5%) on CDED plus PEN versus 28 of 38 (73.6%) on EEN (p=0.002; odds ratio 13.92, 95% CI 1.68–115.14). Week-6 corticosteroid-free remission: 30 of 40 (75%) versus 20 of 34 (59%) (p=0.38). Week-12 corticosteroid-free sustained remission: 28 of 37 (75.6%) versus 14 of 31 (45.1%) (p=0.01; odds ratio 3.77, 95% CI 1.34–10.59). Remission on CDED plus PEN was accompanied by sustained falls in C-reactive protein and faecal calprotectin and in faecal Proteobacteria.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 78 children, mild-to-moderate disease only — it says nothing about severe, stricturing or perianal Crohn's, and the week-12 comparison is partly a comparison of maintenance strategies (continued exclusion diet versus free diet) rather than of induction alone. The tolerance odds ratio's interval (1.68–115.14) shows how few intolerance events drive it.
cards.source: Levine A et al. Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet Plus Partial Enteral Nutrition Induces Sustained Remission in a Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 31170412. Registry ID: NCT01728870. cards.headline: Ma 2024 network meta-analysis: 14 studies, 564 children — PEN plus CDED ranked first for clinical remission (SUCRA 90.5%) and tolerance (88.0%), with EEN last for tolerance
cards.summary: Ma 2024 network meta-analysis: 14 studies, 564 children — PEN plus CDED ranked first for clinical remission (SUCRA 90.5%) and tolerance (88.0%), with EEN last for tolerance
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 14 RCTs (Ma 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (564 participants) of dietary therapy strategies in active paediatric Crohn's disease, searched to August 2024, comparing clinical remission and tolerance and ranking strategies by surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).
cards.result: For clinical remission, PEN plus CDED (odds ratio 7.86, 95% CI 1.85–33.40) and EEN (odds ratio 3.74, 95% CI 1.30–10.76) were both significantly superior to PEN alone. Tolerance of PEN plus CDED was significantly higher than EEN (odds ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.01–0.61, for intolerance as reported). By SUCRA, PEN plus CDED ranked first for remission (90.5%) and first for tolerance (88.0%), while EEN ranked last for tolerance (16.3%). The authors conclude PEN plus CDED can be an alternative to EEN and is more suitable for long-term management in children.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean heavily on indirect comparisons across small trials — the Levine trial is the main direct evidence for CDED, so this card corroborates rather than independently confirms it. SUCRA ranks are not effect sizes and should never be quoted to families as percentages of benefit.
cards.source: Ma J et al. Efficacy of different dietary therapy strategies in active pediatric Crohn's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. PeerJ. 2024. PMID: 39686992. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: CDED plus partial formula matches EEN for induction, beats it for staying in remission at 12 weeks, and is far easier for children to stay on
cards.summary: Synthesis: CDED plus partial formula matches EEN for induction, beats it for staying in remission at 12 weeks, and is far easier for children to stay on
cards.people: One randomised trial (78 children) plus a 14-trial network meta-analysis (564 children) in paediatric Crohn's disease.
cards.result: Tolerance: 97.5% vs 73.6% (Levine); PEN+CDED ranked first for tolerance in the network. Induction (week 6): 75% vs 59%, not significant (Levine). Sustained remission (week 12): 75.6% vs 45.1%, odds ratio 3.77 (Levine); PEN+CDED ranked first for remission (Ma). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The specific formula used in the anchor trial was Modulen (Nestlé), named in the publication; other formulas were not tested in this design, and families should not assume any over-the-counter shake reproduces the protocol. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single trial in one severity band.

shelves.title: FMT for ulcerative colitis: remission 24% vs 5% in the first placebo-controlled trial and a pooled odds ratio of 2.65 across 15 trials — with one donor behind most early remissions
shelves.question: In adults with active ulcerative colitis, does faecal microbiota transplantation induce clinical remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biological Therapy/methods · Colitis, Ulcerative/physiopathology · Feces/microbiology · Female · Humans · Male · Microbiota* · Middle Aged · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faecal microbiota transplantation induced remission in active ulcerative colitis more often than placebo in its first rigorous trial, and the pooled randomised record since has kept the same direction. In that trial (Moayyedi P et al., PMID: 25857665), remission at week 7 was 24% with weekly donor-stool enemas versus 5% with water-enema placebo (risk difference 17%, 95% CI 2%–33%), with no difference in adverse events — though the trial was stopped early for futility at an interim look, and seven of the nine remitters had received stool from a single donor. A later meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (Doukas PG et al., PMID: 41078065) found clinical remission in 62% on FMT versus 50.5% in controls (odds ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.76–4.00) and endoscopic response in 42% versus 22% (odds ratio 2.00). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real effect, of uncertain size, whose donor-dependence and delivery variability keep it a trial-and-specialist treatment rather than a standard one.

cards.headline: Moayyedi 2015 RCT: remission 24% with donor FMT enemas vs 5% with placebo at week 7 (risk difference 17%) — in a trial stopped early for futility, with 7 of 9 remissions traced to one donor
cards.summary: Moayyedi 2015 RCT: remission 24% with donor FMT enemas vs 5% with placebo at week 7 (risk difference 17%) — in a trial stopped early for futility, with 7 of 9 remissions traced to one donor
cards.people: Parallel randomised placebo-controlled trial in patients with active ulcerative colitis without infectious diarrhoea: FMT (50 mL enema from healthy anonymous donors, n=38) or placebo (50 mL water enema, n=37) once weekly for 6 weeks, with patients, clinicians and investigators blinded; the primary outcome was remission (Mayo score ≤2 with endoscopic Mayo score 0) at week 7.
cards.result: The trial was stopped early for futility by the Data Monitoring and Safety Committee, though enrolled patients completed it; 70 patients finished (3 placebo and 2 FMT dropouts). Remission at 7 weeks: 9 of the FMT group (24%) versus 2 of the placebo group (5%), a statistically significant risk difference of 17% (95% CI 2%–33%). There was no significant difference in adverse events. Seven of the 9 FMT remitters had received material from a single donor, and remission was commoner in UC of ≤1 year's duration (3 of 4 patients) than in longer-standing disease (6 of 34; p=0.04). Stool microbial diversity rose more with FMT than placebo (p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A trial stopped for futility that then reached significance on completion is fragile evidence — small changes in a few patients would move it — and the single-donor concentration of remissions means the 'treatment' may really be 'one donor's stool'. Enema delivery, weekly for six weeks, is also only one of many FMT protocols in use.
cards.source: Moayyedi P et al. Fecal Microbiota Transplantation Induces Remission in Patients With Active Ulcerative Colitis in a Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 25857665. Registry ID: NCT01545908. cards.headline: Doukas 2026 meta-analysis: 15 RCTs — clinical remission 62% on FMT vs 50.5% in controls (OR 2.65) and endoscopic response 42% vs 22% (OR 2.00), with low heterogeneity
cards.summary: Doukas 2026 meta-analysis: 15 RCTs — clinical remission 62% on FMT vs 50.5% in controls (OR 2.65) and endoscopic response 42% vs 22% (OR 2.00), with low heterogeneity
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised clinical trials of FMT in ulcerative colitis, regardless of administration route or dose: 6,737 records screened, 15 trials meeting inclusion, pooling clinical and endoscopic remission as odds ratios.
cards.result: Clinical remission was 62% in patients receiving FMT versus 50.5% in controls (odds ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.76–4.00). Endoscopic response was 42% versus 22% (odds ratio 2.00, 95% CI 1.09–3.68). Heterogeneity was assessed as low by I² and τ². The authors conclude FMT significantly improves clinical and endoscopic remission and is a promising non-pharmacological option for patients unresponsive to conventional treatments, while calling for prospective work on formulation, dosing and safety.
cards.watchOut: Pooling trials with different donors, routes, doses and control treatments (some controls received autologous stool rather than inert placebo) treats unlike interventions as one; the high control-group remission (50.5%) also shows how much background therapy and trial participation contribute. Low statistical heterogeneity does not remove that clinical heterogeneity.
cards.source: Doukas PG et al. Effectiveness and Safety of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation for Ulcerative Colitis Treatment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Digestive Diseases. 2026. shelves.title: Probiotic maintenance in chronic pouchitis: relapse 15% on the tested VSL#3 preparation vs 100% on placebo — a dramatic result from one small trial of one specific product
shelves.question: In adults with chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis for ulcerative colitis, does oral multi-strain probiotic bacteriotherapy maintain remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Bifidobacterium · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Feces/microbiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intestines/microbiology · Lactobacillus* · Life Tables · Male · Pouchitis/therapy · Probiotics/administration & dosage · Recurrence · Streptococcus
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the only dedicated maintenance trial, the multi-strain probiotic preparation tested kept chronic pouchitis in remission in 85% of patients over nine months, while every patient on placebo relapsed. In that trial (Gionchetti P et al., PMID: 10930365), relapse was 15% (3 patients) on the preparation versus 100% (20 patients) on placebo (p<0.001). The Cochrane review of pouchitis treatment (Holubar SD et al., PMID: 20556748) reached the same conclusion for this preparation in maintaining remission of chronic pouchitis. Two cautions define the stamp: the trial is 40 patients from the year 2000, and the publication names the tested product as VSL#3 but gives no company name in the record — probiotic products sold under similar descriptions today are not necessarily the formulation tested, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a striking result for the specific tested preparation, in a single small trial, that should not be read across to probiotics generally.

cards.headline: Gionchetti 2000: relapse of chronic pouchitis 15% on the VSL#3 preparation vs 100% on placebo over 9 months (p<0.001) — 40 patients, in remission after antibiotics
cards.summary: Gionchetti 2000: relapse of chronic pouchitis 15% on the VSL#3 preparation vs 100% on placebo over 9 months (p<0.001) — 40 patients, in remission after antibiotics
cards.people: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 40 patients with chronic pouchitis in clinical and endoscopic remission after antibiotic treatment, following ileal pouch–anal anastomosis for ulcerative colitis, randomised to the probiotic preparation VSL#3 (6 g/day; described in the publication as containing 5 × 10^11 per gram of viable lyophilised bacteria — 4 lactobacillus strains, 3 bifidobacterium strains and 1 Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus strain; the record names the product but no company) or identical placebo for 9 months, with monthly clinical and 2-monthly endoscopic/histologic assessment.
cards.result: Three patients (15%) in the VSL#3 group relapsed within the 9-month follow-up, compared with 20 (100%) in the placebo group (p<0.001). Faecal concentrations of lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and S. thermophilus increased significantly from baseline only in the VSL#3 group (p<0.01). The authors conclude oral administration of this probiotic preparation is effective in preventing flare-ups of chronic pouchitis. Because the publication names no manufacturer in this record and probiotic formulations change over time and between makers, current products sold under similar names may differ in safety and effectiveness from the preparation tested.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, one centre's programme, and a placebo relapse rate of 100% that itself signals a highly selected, relapse-prone population — in less selected patients the absolute benefit would be smaller. The result belongs to this exact multi-strain, high-dose preparation and cannot be generalised to other probiotics, doses or strains.

cards.headline: Holubar 2010 Cochrane review: VSL#3 was more effective than placebo for maintaining remission of chronic pouchitis — one of very few positive findings across 11 pouchitis RCTs
cards.summary: Holubar 2010 Cochrane review: VSL#3 was more effective than placebo for maintaining remission of chronic pouchitis — one of very few positive findings across 11 pouchitis RCTs
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (1966–October 2009) of medical therapies for treatment and prevention of pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis for ulcerative colitis: 11 RCTs assessing 10 pharmacologic agents, covering acute treatment, chronic-pouchitis maintenance and prevention.
cards.result: For treatment and maintenance of remission of chronic pouchitis (4 RCTs, 4 agents), glutamine suppositories were not more effective than butyrate suppositories and bismuth carbomer foam enemas were not more effective than placebo, while VSL#3 was more effective than placebo in maintaining remission in patients who had achieved remission with antibiotics. For prevention, VSL#3 was more effective than placebo in one study and not more effective than no treatment in another. For acute pouchitis, ciprofloxacin was more effective than metronidazole. The reviewers conclude larger RCTs are needed to determine the optimal agents.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane conclusion for maintenance rests substantially on the same Gionchetti trial carded above — corroboration of interpretation, not an independent second trial. The prevention data for the same product were inconsistent between the two prevention studies, a warning against extending the maintenance result to patients who have never had pouchitis.
cards.source: Holubar SD et al. Treatment and prevention of pouchitis after ileal pouch-anal anastomosis for chronic ulcerative colitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20556748. shelves.title: Curcumin added to mesalamine in UC: remission 53.8% vs 0% in a 50-patient trial and pooled relative risk 2.33 — big numbers on a small, heterogeneous base, with no named tested product
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis on mesalamine, does adding curcumin induce clinical remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Curcumin/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Male · Mesalamine/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Placebos/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial produced remission numbers too large to take at face value, and the pooled literature since is positive but highly heterogeneous. In the anchor trial (Lang A et al., PMID: 25724700), clinical remission at 4 weeks was 53.8% with curcumin 3 g/day added to mesalamine versus 0% with placebo added (p=0.01; odds ratio 42, 95% CI 2.3–760 — an interval that itself announces how few patients drive the result). The updated meta-analysis (Peng Z et al., PMID: 39612780) pooled eight trials and 482 patients: clinical remission favoured adjunctive curcumin (relative risk 2.33, 95% CI 1.25–4.34 — a relative measure) with substantial heterogeneity (I²=80%), and endoscopic remission was not significant. The trial record names no brand or company for the curcumin capsules used — it says only curcumin capsules, 3 g/day — so no current product can be identified as the tested one, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): an inexpensive, apparently safe adjunct with a promising but fragile record, awaiting a large trial.

cards.headline: Lang 2015 RCT: clinical remission 53.8% with curcumin plus mesalamine vs 0% with placebo plus mesalamine at 4 weeks — in 50 patients, with an odds ratio of 42 and an interval running to 760
cards.summary: Lang 2015 RCT: clinical remission 53.8% with curcumin plus mesalamine vs 0% with placebo plus mesalamine at 4 weeks — in 50 patients, with an odds ratio of 42 and an interval running to 760
cards.people: Multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study of 50 mesalamine-treated patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis (Simple Clinical Colitis Activity Index) who had not responded to 2 further weeks of maximum-dose oral and topical mesalamine: curcumin capsules 3 g/day (n=26) or identical placebo (n=24) for 1 month, mesalamine continued; the primary outcome was clinical remission (SCCAI ≤2) at week 4. The publication, as captured in this record, names no brand or manufacturing company for the curcumin capsules.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, 14 patients (53.8%) on curcumin achieved clinical remission at week 4 versus none on placebo (p=0.01; odds ratio 42, 95% CI 2.3–760). Clinical response (≥3-point SCCAI fall) was achieved by 17 (65.3%) versus 3 (12.5%) (p<0.001; odds ratio 13.2, 95% CI 3.1–56.6). Endoscopic remission (partial Mayo ≤1) was seen in 8 of 22 evaluated on curcumin (38%) versus 0 of 16 on placebo (p=0.043; odds ratio 20.7, 95% CI 1.1–393). Adverse events were rare and comparable between groups. Because no branded product or company is named in the record, current curcumin products — which vary widely in content and bioavailability formulations — may differ in safety and effectiveness from what was tested.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients and a zero-event placebo arm manufacture enormous, unstable odds ratios — a handful of placebo remissions (the rate any UC trial expects) would collapse the headline. One month is induction only; this trial says nothing about maintaining remission, dose, or which curcumin formulation, and endoscopy was missing in 12 of 50 patients.
cards.source: Lang A et al. Curcumin in Combination With Mesalamine Induces Remission in Patients With Mild-to-Moderate Ulcerative Colitis in a Randomized Controlled Trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2015. PMID: 25724700. Registry ID: NCT01320436. cards.headline: Peng 2025 meta-analysis: 8 RCTs, 482 patients — clinical remission relative risk 2.33 with curcumin, but I²=80% and endoscopic remission not significant (4.17, CI 0.63–27.71)
cards.summary: Peng 2025 meta-analysis: 8 RCTs, 482 patients — clinical remission relative risk 2.33 with curcumin, but I²=80% and endoscopic remission not significant (4.17, CI 0.63–27.71)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of adjunctive curcumin in ulcerative colitis (searched to 18 August 2023): eight RCTs, 482 patients, with seven studies reporting clinical remission and three endoscopic remission, pooled with a random-effects model.
cards.result: Adjunctive curcumin significantly improved clinical remission (relative risk 2.33, 95% CI 1.25–4.34, p=0.008, I²=80% — a relative measure), clinical improvement (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.10–3.36, p=0.02, I²=56%) and endoscopic improvement (relative risk 1.76, 95% CI 1.12–2.77, p=0.01, I²=62%). Endoscopic remission showed an increasing trend but was not significant (relative risk 4.17, 95% CI 0.63–27.71, p=0.14, I²=80%). No serious adverse events were reported. Subgroup analysis suggested efficacy rose with dose, with no significant impact of administration method or follow-up duration. The authors call for large-scale RCTs given the limited studies and substantial heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity of 80% means the pooled relative risk is an average of disagreeing trials, not a stable estimate — doses and formulations differed across them, which for an unregulated supplement category is precisely the variable that matters. The included trials are the same small literature the anchor trial dominates.
cards.source: Peng Z et al. Safety and efficacy of curcumin in the treatment of ulcerative colitis: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Explore. 2025. shelves.title: Terlipressin versus noradrenaline in hepatorenal AKI: a clear terlipressin win in the one ACLF trial, a statistical dead heat in the pooled trials — which population is yours?
shelves.question: In patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure and hepatorenal-type acute kidney injury, is noradrenaline (norepinephrine) as effective as terlipressin for AKI reversal and survival?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/drug therapy, etiology · Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure/complications · Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Terlipressin/therapeutic use · Vasoconstrictor Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which population you mean, and the two records on this shelf genuinely disagree in emphasis. In the population the question names — acute-on-chronic liver failure with hepatorenal-type AKI — the one head-to-head randomised trial (Arora V et al., PMID: 30076614; 120 patients, open-label) found terlipressin clearly ahead: response by day 7 in 41.7% versus 20% on noradrenaline, HRS reversal 40% versus 16.7%, less renal replacement therapy (56.6% versus 80%), and better 28-day survival (48.3% versus 20%); noradrenaline carried a mortality hazard ratio of 2.08 (95% CI 1.32 to 3.30) against terlipressin. But the pooled record across the broader hepatorenal syndrome–AKI population (Olson JC et al., PMID: 38285703; 7 trials, 376 patients) shows only a non-significant numerical edge for terlipressin on reversal (OR 1.33, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.22) and short-term survival (OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.53), with more drug-limiting adverse events on terlipressin in the ACLF trial (23.3% versus 8.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: in ACLF the single trial says terlipressin is superior and noradrenaline is not 'as effective'; across HRS-AKI generally the pooled trials cannot separate the two. Terlipressin against albumin alone is a different question, at shelf #1060.

cards.headline: Arora 2020: in acute-on-chronic liver failure with hepatorenal AKI, terlipressin beat noradrenaline on response (41.7% vs 20% by day 7), reversal (40% vs 16.7%) and 28-day survival (48.3% vs 20%)
cards.summary: Arora 2020: in acute-on-chronic liver failure with hepatorenal AKI, terlipressin beat noradrenaline on response (41.7% vs 20% by day 7), reversal (40% vs 16.7%) and 28-day survival (48.3% vs 20%)
cards.people: 120 consecutive patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure diagnosed with hepatorenal syndrome–acute kidney injury, randomised open-label to albumin plus terlipressin infusion (2–12 mg/day, n = 60) or albumin plus noradrenaline infusion (0.5–3.0 mg/hour, n = 60); baseline AKI stage and sepsis-related HRS-AKI were comparable between groups.
cards.result: Response to treatment was greater with terlipressin at day 4 (26.1% versus 11.7%; P = 0.03) and day 7 (41.7% versus 20%; P = 0.01). Reversal of HRS was 40% with terlipressin versus 16.7% with noradrenaline (P = 0.004), renal replacement therapy was required less often (56.6% versus 80%; P = 0.006), and 28-day survival was higher (48.3% versus 20%; P = 0.001). Adverse events limiting drug use were more frequent with terlipressin (23.3% versus 8.3%; P = 0.02) but reversible. On multivariate analysis, noradrenaline (versus terlipressin) predicted nonresponse (OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.27 to 7.33) and higher mortality (HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.30).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-programme, 120 patients — and a survival gap (48.3% versus 20%) far larger than the pooled head-to-head literature shows, which is the classic signature of a small single-centre trial overestimating an effect. ACLF with sepsis-related HRS-AKI is also a sicker, more specific population than HRS-AKI in decompensated cirrhosis generally, so the result should not be read across to every hepatorenal patient.
cards.source: Arora V et al. Terlipressin Is Superior to Noradrenaline in the Management of Acute Kidney Injury in Acute on Chronic Liver Failure. Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 30076614. randomised controlled trial (arora 2020) 120 consecutive patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure diagnosed with hepatorenal syndrome–acute kidney injury, randomised open-label to albumin plus terlipressin infusion (2–12 mg/day, n = 60) or albumin plus noradrenaline infusion (0.5–3.0 mg/hour, n = 60); baseline aki stage and sepsis-related hrs-aki were comparable between groups. response to treatment was greater with terlipressin at day 4 (26.1% versus 11.7%; p = 0.03) and day 7 (41.7% versus 20%; p = 0.01). reversal of hrs was 40% with terlipressin versus 16.7% with noradrenaline (p = 0.004), renal replacement therapy was required less often (56.6% versus 80%; p = 0.006), and 28-day survival was higher (48.3% versus 20%; p = 0.001). adverse events limiting drug use were more frequent with terlipressin (23.3% versus 8.3%; p = 0.02) but reversible. on multivariate analysis, noradrenaline (versus terlipressin) predicted nonresponse (or 3.05, 95% ci 1.27 to 7.33) and higher mortality (hr 2.08, 95% ci 1.32 to 3.30). open-label, single-programme, 120 patients — and a survival gap (48.3% versus 20%) far larger than the pooled head-to-head literature shows, which is the classic signature of a small single-centre trial overestimating an effect. aclf with sepsis-related hrs-aki is also a sicker, more specific population than hrs-aki in decompensated cirrhosis generally, so the result should not be read across to every hepatorenal patient. arora v et al. terlipressin is superior to noradrenaline in the management of acute kidney injury in acute on chronic liver failure. hepatology. 2020. pmid: 30076614. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acute kidney injury/drug therapy, etiology · acute-on-chronic liver failure/complications · adult · female · humans · male · middle aged · norepinephrine/therapeutic use · prospective studies · terlipressin/therapeutic use · vasoconstrictor agents/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Olson 2024 meta-analysis: pooling 7 head-to-head trials (376 patients) in HRS-AKI, terlipressin's edge on reversal (OR 1.33) and survival (OR 1.50) was numerical only — neither reached significance
cards.summary: Olson 2024 meta-analysis: pooling 7 head-to-head trials (376 patients) in HRS-AKI, terlipressin's edge on reversal (OR 1.33) and survival (OR 1.50) was numerical only — neither reached significance
cards.people: Systematic review and pairwise meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (376 participants) published 2007–2023 comparing noradrenaline plus albumin with terlipressin plus albumin for hepatorenal syndrome–AKI (or type 1 HRS) in adults, all with HRS reversal as an endpoint.
cards.result: HRS reversal was numerically more frequent with terlipressin (OR 1.33, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.22; P = 0.22) and short-term survival numerically higher (OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.53; P = 0.26), but neither difference was statistically significant. Terlipressin's adverse events were mainly abdominal pain and diarrhoea; noradrenaline's were cardiovascular (chest pain, ischaemia). Discontinuation for serious adverse events was 5.3% with terlipressin versus 2.7% with noradrenaline. The authors note the small total sample and shifting HRS-AKI diagnostic criteria across trials as the key limitations.
cards.watchOut: 376 patients across seven small trials cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction — the confidence interval for reversal (0.80 to 2.22) covers both equivalence and a doubling of odds. The pooled population is HRS-AKI broadly, not the ACLF subgroup the anchor trial studied, so the two cards are answering related but not identical questions.

cards.headline: Synthesis: terlipressin ahead in the one ACLF trial by a wide margin; inseparable from noradrenaline in the pooled HRS-AKI trials — the population decides the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: terlipressin ahead in the one ACLF trial by a wide margin; inseparable from noradrenaline in the pooled HRS-AKI trials — the population decides the answer
cards.people: One open-label randomised trial in ACLF with HRS-AKI (120 patients, Arora 2020) and a meta-analysis of 7 head-to-head trials in HRS-AKI generally (376 patients, Olson 2024).
cards.result: ACLF population: day-7 response 41.7% versus 20%, HRS reversal 40% versus 16.7%, 28-day survival 48.3% versus 20%, all favouring terlipressin; drug-limiting adverse events 23.3% versus 8.3% against it. Pooled HRS-AKI: reversal OR 1.33 (95% CI 0.80 to 2.22) and survival OR 1.50 (95% CI 0.64 to 3.53), both non-significant. PROPOSED SPLIT — by population.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the Arora survival figures as settled: they come from one open-label trial and are much larger than anything the pooled literature supports. Equally, do not quote the meta-analysis as proving equivalence — it is underpowered to do so. What the record supports is: no proven difference in HRS-AKI overall, a strong but unreplicated terlipressin signal in ACLF, and a practical trade-off (noradrenaline needs central access and intensive monitoring; terlipressin carries more drug-limiting adverse events). Tier C is set because the head-to-head base is one ACLF trial plus small pooled trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Arora V et al. Hepatology. 2020 (PMID: 30076614); Olson JC et al. PLoS One. 2024 (PMID: 38285703).
