shelves.title: Covered-stent TIPS for recurrent ascites: 93% versus 52% alive without transplant at one year — one small trial carrying a big claim, with the bare-stent era's encephalopathy warning behind it
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and refractory ascites, does covered-stent TIPS improve transplant-free survival versus repeated large-volume paracentesis with albumin?
shelves.mesh: Albumins/therapeutic use · Ascites/etiology, therapy · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy/etiology · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Hypertension, Portal/etiology, surgery · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Paracentesis*/adverse effects · Polytetrafluoroethylene · Portasystemic Shunt, Transjugular Intrahepatic*/adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Severity of Illness Index · Stents*/adverse effects · Survival Rate · Ultrasonography, Doppler
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the modern covered-stent trial is small but its primary outcome is hard and the gap is wide. Bureau C et al. (PMID: 27663604) randomised 62 patients with cirrhosis and recurrent ascites (at least two large-volume paracenteses within three weeks) to polytetrafluoroethylene-covered TIPS or continued large-volume paracentesis with albumin: one-year transplant-free survival was 93% with TIPS versus 52% with paracentesis, hospital days were halved (17 versus 35), and portal-hypertension bleeding and hernia complications occurred only in the paracentesis group (18% each versus 0%) — while the one-year probability of remaining free of encephalopathy was identical at 65% in both groups. The older Cochrane synthesis (Saab S et al., PMID: 17054221; 5 trials, 330 patients, largely uncovered-stent era) found no mortality difference (24-month OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.56) and significantly more encephalopathy with TIPS (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.6), though ascites control was far better. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): covered-stent TIPS probably improves transplant-free survival in recurrent ascites, but the survival claim rests on one 62-patient trial and the bare-stent literature warns that encephalopathy is the price when stents fail or patients are poorly selected. Early TIPS for variceal bleeding is a different question, at shelf #591.

cards.headline: Bureau 2017: covered-stent TIPS gave 93% one-year transplant-free survival versus 52% with repeated paracentesis plus albumin in recurrent ascites
cards.summary: Bureau 2017: covered-stent TIPS gave 93% one-year transplant-free survival versus 52% with repeated paracentesis plus albumin in recurrent ascites
cards.people: 62 patients with cirrhosis and recurrent ascites — at least two large-volume paracenteses within a period of at least three weeks — at four French tertiary centres, randomised to polytetrafluoroethylene-covered TIPS (n = 29) or large-volume paracentesis plus albumin as necessary (n = 33); all maintained a low-salt diet and were followed for one year.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, survival without liver transplantation at one year, was met by 93% of the TIPS group versus 52% of the paracentesis group (P = 0.003). Total paracenteses numbered 32 in the TIPS group versus 320 in the paracentesis group. Portal hypertension–related bleeding (18% versus 0%; P = 0.01) and hernia-related complications (18% versus 0%; P = 0.01) occurred only with paracentesis. Hospitalisation was 17 days with TIPS versus 35 days with paracentesis (P = 0.04). The one-year probability of remaining free of encephalopathy was 65% in each group.
cards.watchOut: Only 62 patients, recruited over seven years (2005–2012), in patients selected to be good TIPS candidates — the survival gap is large enough that a few events either way would move it, and the enrolled population had recurrent rather than strictly diuretic-refractory ascites. Encephalopathy equality at one year is reassuring but the trial was not powered for it, and longer-term shunt surveillance matters: the covered stent is precisely what distinguishes this trial from the disappointing bare-stent era.
cards.source: Bureau C et al. Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunts With Covered Stents Increase Transplant-Free Survival of Patients With Cirrhosis and Recurrent Ascites. cards.headline: Saab 2006 (Cochrane): in the bare-stent era, TIPS controlled ascites far better than paracentesis but did not reduce mortality and significantly increased encephalopathy (OR 2.24)
cards.summary: Saab 2006 (Cochrane): in the bare-stent era, TIPS controlled ascites far better than paracentesis but did not reduce mortality and significantly increased encephalopathy (OR 2.24)
cards.people: Five randomised trials (330 patients) comparing TIPS with paracentesis (with or without volume expanders) for refractory ascites in cirrhosis, searched to January 2006 — predominantly uncovered-stent trials, the technology Bureau 2017 set out to improve on.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ between TIPS and paracentesis at 30 days (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.10 to 10.06) or 24 months (OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.56). TIPS markedly reduced ascites re-accumulation at 3 months (OR 0.07, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.18) and 12 months (OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.28). Hepatic encephalopathy occurred significantly more often with TIPS (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.6); gastrointestinal bleeding, infection and acute renal failure did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis answers the question for uncovered stents, whose dysfunction rates undermined the procedure; it should not be used to overrule the covered-stent trial, and the covered-stent trial should not be used to erase its encephalopathy warning. Only one included trial used blinded outcome assessment. The two cards together describe a technology transition, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Saab S et al. TIPS versus paracentesis for cirrhotic patients with refractory ascites. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2006. PMID: 17054221. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: covered TIPS probably extends transplant-free survival in recurrent ascites (93% vs 52% at one year); the older literature says ascites control was never the problem — encephalopathy and stent failure were
cards.summary: Synthesis: covered TIPS probably extends transplant-free survival in recurrent ascites (93% vs 52% at one year); the older literature says ascites control was never the problem — encephalopathy and stent failure were
cards.people: One covered-stent randomised trial (62 patients, Bureau 2017) set against a five-trial Cochrane synthesis of the uncovered-stent era (330 patients, Saab 2006).
cards.result: Transplant-free survival at one year: 93% versus 52% favouring covered TIPS (Bureau). Mortality with older stents: no difference at 24 months, OR 1.29 (95% CI 0.65 to 2.56) (Saab). Ascites re-accumulation: strongly reduced by TIPS in both eras. Encephalopathy: no difference at one year in the covered-stent trial (65% free in both groups); increased with older stents (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.6). Hospital days halved with covered TIPS (17 versus 35). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The survival claim would be LIKELY if it had been replicated; it has not — one 62-patient trial in selected candidates is the whole covered-stent randomised base for this indication. Patient selection (age, bilirubin, prior encephalopathy, cardiac function) is doing much of the work in practice and is invisible in the pooled numbers. Tier C is set for the single-small-trial base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bureau C et al. Gastroenterology. 2017 (PMID: 27663604); Saab S et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2006 (PMID: 17054221).

shelves.title: L-ornithine L-aspartate for hepatic encephalopathy: consistently favourable small trials, a doubled relative chance of reversing minimal HE — and quality caveats that cap the claim
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, does L-ornithine L-aspartate improve encephalopathy grade and recovery versus placebo or standard care?
shelves.mesh: Ammonia/blood · Dipeptides/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Hepatic Encephalopathy/drug therapy · Humans · Liver/metabolism · Liver Cirrhosis/drug therapy · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Secondary Prevention · Systematic Reviews as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction of the randomised record is consistently favourable, but its foundations are soft. The appraisal by Butterworth RF et al. (PMID: 30706425) reports that meta-analyses of randomised trials over two decades generally find benefit for L-ornithine L-aspartate across presentations — better mental-state grade in overt encephalopathy, better psychometric performance in minimal encephalopathy (oral formulation particularly), and lower fasting blood ammonia in every trial that measured it — while noting that one meta-analysis raised study-quality concerns; network meta-analyses place LOLA comparable or superior to non-absorbable disaccharides and probiotics. The one pooled analysis with hard numbers on this shelf (He Q et al., PMID: 38403493; 6 trials, 292 patients, minimal encephalopathy) found LOLA more than doubled the relative chance of reversing minimal encephalopathy (RR 2.264, 95% CI 1.528 to 3.352) and reduced progression to overt encephalopathy (RR 0.220, 95% CI 0.076 to 0.637), with no mortality or ammonia difference in that subset. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): LOLA probably improves encephalopathy measures and minimal-HE reversal, but small trials, quality concerns, and no demonstrated mortality effect keep it short of LIKELY. The established HE shelves — rifaximin #595, PEG versus lactulose #1676, lactulose for minimal HE #2126 — ask different questions.

cards.headline: Butterworth 2019 appraisal: two decades of randomised trials and meta-analyses generally favour LOLA for overt and minimal hepatic encephalopathy — with study-quality concerns flagged in one meta-analysis
cards.summary: Butterworth 2019 appraisal: two decades of randomised trials and meta-analyses generally favour LOLA for overt and minimal hepatic encephalopathy — with study-quality concerns flagged in one meta-analysis
cards.people: A structured appraisal of the randomised-trial and meta-analysis literature on L-ornithine L-aspartate for hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis, covering overt encephalopathy graded by West Haven criteria, minimal encephalopathy by psychometric testing, post-TIPS encephalopathy, and secondary prophylaxis.
cards.result: Meta-analyses of randomised trials generally reveal evidence of benefit: improvement in mental-state grade in overt hepatic encephalopathy, improvement in minimal encephalopathy on psychometric testing (the oral formulation determined to be particularly effective), and concomitant lowering of fasting blood ammonia reported in all trials using that endpoint. Network meta-analyses showed LOLA comparable (or superior) in efficacy to non-absorbable disaccharides or probiotics. Single trials additionally report efficacy for post-TIPS encephalopathy and for secondary prophylaxis. One meta-analysis raised concerns over the quality of the underlying studies.
cards.watchOut: This is a narrative appraisal, not a fresh meta-analysis: its abstract reports directions of effect, not pooled effect sizes, so no number on this card should be quoted as a pooled estimate. The underlying trials are mostly small and short, encephalopathy grading is partly subjective, and the quality caveat the authors themselves relay is the reason this shelf's stamp stops at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: He 2024 meta-analysis: in minimal hepatic encephalopathy, LOLA reversed the condition (relative risk 2.264) and cut progression to overt encephalopathy (RR 0.220) versus placebo or no treatment
cards.summary: He 2024 meta-analysis: in minimal hepatic encephalopathy, LOLA reversed the condition (relative risk 2.264) and cut progression to overt encephalopathy (RR 0.220) versus placebo or no treatment
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (292 patients) of L-ornithine L-aspartate versus placebo or no intervention for minimal hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis, searched to January 2023.
cards.result: LOLA was more effective in reversing minimal hepatic encephalopathy (RR 2.264, 95% CI 1.528 to 3.352; P < 0.001; I² = 0.0%) and in preventing progression to overt hepatic encephalopathy (RR 0.220, 95% CI 0.076 to 0.637; P = 0.005; I² = 0.0%). In subgroup analysis, oral LOLA reversed minimal encephalopathy (RR 2.648, 95% CI 1.593 to 4.402) while the intravenous subgroup estimate did not reach significance (RR 1.669, 95% CI 0.904 to 3.084; P = 0.102). LOLA showed no significant advantage for mortality (RR 0.422, 95% CI 0.064 to 2.768) or ammonia levels (SMD 0.044, 95% CI −0.290 to 0.379) in this population.
cards.watchOut: Only 292 patients, and 'reversal' of minimal encephalopathy is a psychometric-test outcome, not a patient-experienced one; the striking progression estimate (RR 0.220) rests on very few events, as its wide confidence interval shows. The null ammonia result in this subset also sits awkwardly beside the ammonia-lowering reported across the wider trial literature — measurement timing and population differ, but the inconsistency is worth naming.

cards.headline: Synthesis: LOLA improves encephalopathy measures across presentations and reverses minimal HE in pooled trials — benefit on symptoms and tests, none shown on survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: LOLA improves encephalopathy measures across presentations and reverses minimal HE in pooled trials — benefit on symptoms and tests, none shown on survival
cards.people: The randomised literature as appraised by Butterworth 2019 (overt and minimal encephalopathy, post-TIPS, prophylaxis) plus the 6-trial minimal-encephalopathy meta-analysis of He 2024 (292 patients).
cards.result: Minimal HE reversal: RR 2.264 (95% CI 1.528 to 3.352) favouring LOLA; progression to overt HE: RR 0.220 (95% CI 0.076 to 0.637) (He). Overt HE: mental-state grade improvement and ammonia lowering reported consistently across the meta-analyses appraised (Butterworth, qualitative). Mortality: no significant difference where measured (RR 0.422, 95% CI 0.064 to 2.768). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Almost everything here is small-trial evidence with subjective or psychometric endpoints, much of it from an era and literature with known quality problems — exactly the profile that inflates effects. LOLA's reasonable role is as an adjunct with a favourable signal, not as a proven substitute for lactulose or rifaximin, and no trial shows it keeps anyone alive. Tier C is not set for this shelf (miner flag), but the certainty language in the balance should be read as the operative caution.

shelves.title: High-dose ursodeoxycholic acid in PSC: the liver tests improved, the patients did worse — endpoints 39% versus 26%, serious adverse events 63% versus 37%
shelves.question: In adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis, does high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improve liver biochemistry, histology or survival — or cause harm — versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Aspartate Aminotransferases/blood · Bilirubin/blood · Cholagogues and Choleretics/therapeutic use · Cholangitis, Sclerosing/drug therapy, mortality · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Function Tests · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Ursodeoxycholic Acid/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — this is the shelf where better blood tests hid a worse outcome. Lindor KD et al. (PMID: 19585548) randomised 150 adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis to high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid (28–30 mg/kg/day) or placebo for up to six years: liver enzymes fell significantly more on UDCA, yet 39% of the UDCA group reached a clinical endpoint (cirrhosis, varices, cholangiocarcinoma, transplantation or death) versus 26% on placebo, the adjusted risk of a primary endpoint was 2.3 times higher on UDCA (P < 0.01), the risk of death, transplantation or minimal listing criteria was 2.1 times higher (P = 0.038), and serious adverse events were far commoner (63% versus 37%; P < 0.01); the trial was stopped for futility. The wider meta-analysis (Othman MO et al., PMID: 23122450; 7 trials, 553 patients) found UDCA at any dose did not reduce mortality (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.35) or transplantation (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.12) despite improving liver tests, and noted the increased mortality signal came from the high-dose trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): high-dose UDCA in PSC improves biochemistry while increasing serious adverse events and clinical endpoints — it should not be used at these doses, and no dose of UDCA has shown a survival benefit in PSC. Cilofexor for PSC is a different drug and question, at shelf #2129.

cards.headline: Lindor 2009: high-dose UDCA improved liver enzymes in PSC but doubled the adjusted risk of clinical endpoints (2.3×) and raised serious adverse events from 37% to 63% — trial stopped for futility
cards.summary: Lindor 2009: high-dose UDCA improved liver enzymes in PSC but doubled the adjusted risk of clinical endpoints (2.3×) and raised serious adverse events from 37% to 63% — trial stopped for futility
cards.people: 150 adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis in a long-term randomised double-blind trial of high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid (28–30 mg/kg/day; n = 76) versus placebo (n = 74), with liver biopsy and cholangiography before randomisation and after five years; groups were similar at entry in sex, age, disease duration, liver enzymes, histology and Mayo risk score. The study was terminated after six years due to futility.
cards.result: Aspartate aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase fell more in the UDCA group (P < 0.01), but the improvements were not associated with fewer endpoints: 30 UDCA patients (39%) versus 19 placebo patients (26%) reached a pre-established clinical endpoint (development of cirrhosis, varices, cholangiocarcinoma, liver transplantation, or death). Adjusted for baseline stratification, the risk of a primary endpoint was 2.3 times greater on UDCA (P < 0.01) and the risk of death, transplantation, or meeting minimal listing criteria was 2.1 times greater (P = 0.038). Serious adverse events occurred in 63% on UDCA versus 37% on placebo (P < 0.01). The authors conclude high-dose UDCA improves serum liver tests but does not improve survival and carries higher rates of serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint composite mixes hard outcomes (death, transplant, cancer) with softer ones (varices, cirrhosis on biopsy), and the trial was stopped early, which can exaggerate harm estimates. But the direction is consistent across the composite, its hardest components, and serious adverse events — and there is no offsetting benefit anywhere in the record. The dose is the story: 28–30 mg/kg/day is well above conventional UDCA dosing, so this verdict is about high-dose therapy, not about every milligram of UDCA.
cards.source: Lindor KD et al. High-dose ursodeoxycholic acid for the treatment of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Hepatology. 2009. PMID: 19585548. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Othman 2012 meta-analysis: across 7 trials and 553 patients, UDCA in PSC improved liver tests but not mortality (RR 1.04), transplantation (RR 1.22), symptoms or cancer incidence
cards.summary: Othman 2012 meta-analysis: across 7 trials and 553 patients, UDCA in PSC improved liver tests but not mortality (RR 1.04), transplantation (RR 1.22), symptoms or cancer incidence
cards.people: Meta-analysis and systematic review of 7 randomised trials (553 patients) of ursodeoxycholic acid versus placebo in primary sclerosing cholangitis — low-dose UDCA in four studies, high-dose (17–30 mg/kg) in three, including the Lindor trial carded above.
cards.result: UDCA did not decrease mortality versus placebo (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.35) or the need for liver transplantation (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.12), had no effect on clinical symptoms, and did not decrease the incidence of cholangiocarcinoma. Liver function tests were significantly improved in UDCA-treated patients. The authors conclude UDCA had no beneficial effect on survival, liver histology, prevention of cholangiocarcinoma or symptoms, and note that high-dose UDCA was associated with increased mortality in one of the large randomised trials included.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mortality confidence interval (0.46 to 2.35) is wide — PSC trials are small and events few — so the meta-analysis alone proves neither benefit nor harm; its value is showing that no dose stratum produced a survival signal while biochemistry reliably improved. Title misspells the drug ('Urosdeoxycholic') in the original record; the card title here uses the correct spelling.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in PSC, UDCA is a drug that makes the blood tests prettier and the patient no better — and at high dose, measurably worse
cards.summary: Synthesis: in PSC, UDCA is a drug that makes the blood tests prettier and the patient no better — and at high dose, measurably worse
cards.people: One long-term high-dose randomised trial (150 patients, Lindor 2009) and a 7-trial meta-analysis across doses (553 patients, Othman 2012).
cards.result: Biochemistry: significantly greater falls in AST and alkaline phosphatase on UDCA in both records. Clinical endpoints on high-dose UDCA: 39% versus 26% reached the composite; adjusted risk 2.3× for the primary endpoint and 2.1× for death/transplant/listing; serious adverse events 63% versus 37% (Lindor). Across all doses: mortality RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.46 to 2.35), transplantation RR 1.22 (95% CI 0.7 to 2.12), no symptom or cholangiocarcinoma benefit (Othman). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) for high-dose UDCA.
cards.watchOut: Keep the dose boundary explicit: the harm verdict attaches to high-dose UDCA (28–30 mg/kg/day). For standard doses the record shows futility, not proven harm — no survival, histology, symptom or cancer benefit — which is its own reason the drug cannot be recommended as disease-modifying therapy in PSC. Tier C is set because the harm case rests on one trial, albeit a long-term double-blind one stopped for futility with consistent internal signals.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lindor KD et al. Hepatology. 2009 (PMID: 19585548); Othman MO et al. Arab Journal of Gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 23122450).

shelves.title: Routine nasogastric tubes after abdominal surgery: bowel function returned later and pulmonary complications were commoner with a routine tube across 33 trials — the Cochrane verdict was to abandon routine use
shelves.question: In adults having abdominal surgery, does routine nasogastric decompression until bowel function returns speed recovery compared with no tube or early tube removal?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Adult · Flatulence/physiopathology · Gases* · Humans · Intubation, Gastrointestinal/adverse effects/methods · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for the routine policy, not for the tube itself. Across 33 randomised trials and 5,240 patients (Nelson R et al., PMID: 17636780), patients managed without a routine nasogastric tube had an earlier return of bowel function (p<0.00001) and fewer pulmonary complications (p=0.01) than patients kept on routine decompression. Anastomotic leak did not differ (p=0.70); wound infection (p=0.22) and ventral hernia (p=0.09) trended against the no-tube group without reaching significance. The one outcome favouring routine tubes was vomiting — bought with increased patient discomfort — and length of stay was shorter without a tube, though heterogeneity makes that estimate soft. The reviewers' conclusion was unusually blunt: routine nasogastric decompression does not accomplish any of its intended goals and should be abandoned in favour of selective use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): keeping a tube in every abdominal-surgery patient until the bowel wakes up delays the recovery it is meant to speed and adds pulmonary risk; a tube placed for a specific indication is a different question, and this shelf does not answer it.

cards.headline: Nelson 2007 (Cochrane): 33 trials, 5,240 patients — earlier bowel function (p<0.00001) and fewer pulmonary complications (p=0.01) without a routine tube; leak unchanged (p=0.70)
cards.summary: Nelson 2007 (Cochrane): 33 trials, 5,240 patients — earlier bowel function (p<0.00001) and fewer pulmonary complications (p=0.01) without a routine tube; leak unchanged (p=0.70)
cards.people: 5,240 patients having abdominal operations of any type, emergency or elective (laparoscopic surgery and gastrostomy decompression excluded), randomised before the end of the operation to a nasogastric tube kept in until bowel function returned (2,628 patients) versus no tube or early removal in theatre, recovery or within 24 hours (2,612 patients). Trials spanned 1966–2006.
cards.result: Patients without routine tube use had an earlier return of bowel function (p<0.00001) and a decrease in pulmonary complications (p=0.01). Wound infection showed a non-significant trend favouring routine tubes (p=0.22), as did ventral hernia (p=0.09); anastomotic leak was no different between groups (p=0.70). Vomiting seemed to favour routine tube use, but with increased patient discomfort. Length of stay was shorter when no tube was used, though heterogeneity makes rigorous conclusion on that outcome difficult. No adverse events specifically related to tube insertion were reported. The reviewers conclude that routine nasogastric decompression does not accomplish any of its intended goals and should be abandoned in favour of selective use of the nasogastric tube.
cards.watchOut: Most component trials are old and small, several outcomes are reported as p-values without pooled effect sizes in the record, and 'abdominal surgery' spans everything from appendicectomy to gastrectomy — selective-use judgement for high-risk operations (gastric surgery, established ileus, obstruction) is not tested here. The review also predates modern enhanced-recovery practice, which has only moved further from routine tubes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: every intended goal of the routine tube failed its test — faster bowel recovery and fewer chest complications belong to the no-tube policy
cards.summary: Synthesis: every intended goal of the routine tube failed its test — faster bowel recovery and fewer chest complications belong to the no-tube policy
cards.people: Thirty-three randomised trials, 5,240 abdominal-surgery patients, pooled in the Cochrane review — the evidence base for routine versus selective nasogastric decompression.
cards.result: Bowel function: earlier without a routine tube (p<0.00001). Pulmonary complications: fewer without a routine tube (p=0.01). Anastomotic leak: no difference (p=0.70). Wound infection and ventral hernia: non-significant trends the other way. Vomiting: less with a routine tube, at the cost of more discomfort. Length of stay: shorter without a tube, heterogeneity-limited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for the routine policy.
cards.watchOut: A verdict against routine use is not a verdict against nasogastric tubes: decompression for obstruction, ileus with vomiting, or gastric outlet problems is treatment, not prophylaxis, and none of these trials test it. Nor does the review cover laparoscopic surgery, which was excluded. Tier C is not set: the base is 33 trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nelson R et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2007 (PMID: 17636780).

shelves.title: Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty for class 1–2 obesity: 49% of excess weight lost versus 3% with lifestyle alone at one year in MERIT — one randomised trial, supported by observational series
shelves.question: In adults with class 1 or class 2 obesity, does endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty added to lifestyle modification produce more weight loss than lifestyle modification alone?
shelves.mesh: Gastroplasty*/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Obesity/etiology/surgery · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run randomised trial with a large effect, surrounded by uncontrolled series. In MERIT (Abu Dayyeh BK et al., PMID: 35908555), 209 adults with class 1–2 obesity gained 49.2% excess weight loss at 52 weeks with endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) plus lifestyle modification versus 3.2% with lifestyle alone (p<0.0001); total body weight loss was 13.6% versus 0.8%, and 77% of the ESG group versus 12% of controls reached at least 25% excess weight loss. Benefit persisted: 68% of followed ESG patients still held ≥25% excess weight loss at 104 weeks, and metabolic comorbidities improved in 80% of the ESG group versus 45% of controls. Serious ESG-related adverse events occurred in 2% (3 of 131 who underwent ESG, including crossovers), with no deaths and no need for intensive care or surgery. The supporting systematic review (Hedjoudje A et al., PMID: 31442601) pools only observational studies — 1,772 patients, total weight loss 15.1% at 6 months and 17.2% at 18–24 months, severe adverse events 2.2% — consistent with MERIT but incapable of confirming it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ESG produces substantial, two-year-durable weight loss against lifestyle care in the one randomised test; comparison with bariatric surgery and with modern obesity pharmacotherapy is not in this record. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single trial.

cards.headline: Abu Dayyeh 2022 (MERIT): excess weight loss 49.2% versus 3.2% at 52 weeks; total body weight loss 13.6% versus 0.8%; serious ESG adverse events 2%
cards.summary: Abu Dayyeh 2022 (MERIT): excess weight loss 49.2% versus 3.2% at 52 weeks; total body weight loss 13.6% versus 0.8%; serious ESG adverse events 2%
cards.people: 209 adults aged 21–65 with class 1 or class 2 obesity at nine US centres, randomised to ESG plus lifestyle modification (n=85) or lifestyle modification alone (n=124) — low-calorie diet and physical activity in both arms — with crossover or retightening offered at 52 weeks and ESG follow-up to 104 weeks.
cards.result: At 52 weeks, mean percentage excess weight loss was 49.2% (SD 32.0) in the ESG group versus 3.2% (18.6) in controls (p<0.0001), and mean total body weight loss was 13.6% (8.0) versus 0.8% (5.0) (p<0.0001). At least 25% excess weight loss was reached by 59 (77%) of 77 ESG participants versus 13 (12%) of 110 controls. One or more metabolic comorbidities improved in 41 (80%) of 51 ESG participants (6 [12%] worsened) versus 28 (45%) of 62 controls (31 [50%] worsened). At 104 weeks, 41 (68%) of 60 ESG participants maintained ≥25% excess weight loss. ESG-related serious adverse events occurred in 3 (2%) of 131 participants who underwent ESG, without mortality or need for intensive care or surgery.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by necessity, with substantial attrition by 104 weeks (60 of 85 ESG patients in the maintenance figure) and a lifestyle-only comparator that lost almost nothing — the trial measures ESG against weak usual care, not against bariatric surgery or drug therapy. Weight regain beyond two years and nutritional consequences are outside this record.
cards.source: Abu Dayyeh BK et al. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty for treatment of class 1 and 2 obesity (MERIT): a prospective, multicentre, randomised trial. The Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35908555. Registry ID: NCT03406975. MeSH: Gastroplasty*/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Obesity/etiology/surgery · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss

cards.headline: Hedjoudje 2020 (systematic review): 1,772 patients in 8 observational studies — total weight loss 15.1% at 6 months, 17.2% at 18–24 months; severe adverse events 2.2%
cards.summary: Hedjoudje 2020 (systematic review): 1,772 patients in 8 observational studies — total weight loss 15.1% at 6 months, 17.2% at 18–24 months; severe adverse events 2.2%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 8 observational studies (Hedjoudje 2020)
cards.people: Eight original studies published 2016–2019 including 1,772 adults treated with endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, pooled for percent total body weight loss (TBWL), BMI reduction, percent excess weight loss and adverse events; no randomised trials were available to this review.
cards.result: Mean TBWL was 15.1% (95% CI 14.3 to 16.0) at 6 months, 16.5% (15.2 to 17.8) at 12 months and 17.2% (14.6 to 19.7) at 18–24 months; mean BMI fell by 5.65 kg/m² (5.07 to 6.22) and mean excess weight loss was 57.7% (52.0 to 63.4) at 6 months. The pooled severe adverse event rate was 2.2% (1.6% to 3.1%), including pain or nausea requiring hospitalisation (18 patients, 1.08%), upper gastrointestinal bleeding (9, 0.56%) and peri-gastric leak or fluid collection (8, 0.48%). The authors conclude ESG appears effective while noting comparative and randomised studies were still needed.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is uncontrolled: patients who choose and complete an endoscopic procedure, in expert early-adopter centres, with publication bias unmeasurable. The pooled percentages describe what happened after ESG, not what ESG causes — that causal estimate comes only from MERIT.
cards.source: Hedjoudje A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 31442601. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Bariatric Surgery* · Gastroplasty* · Humans · Obesity/surgery · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss

cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial with a large, durable effect, echoed by uncontrolled series — benefit against lifestyle care is real; the ranking against surgery and drugs is unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial with a large, durable effect, echoed by uncontrolled series — benefit against lifestyle care is real; the ranking against surgery and drugs is unknown
cards.people: One 209-patient randomised trial against lifestyle modification (MERIT, to 104 weeks) and a systematic review of 8 observational series (1,772 patients) — the evidence base for endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty in class 1–2 obesity.
cards.result: Weight: excess weight loss 49.2% versus 3.2% at 52 weeks (randomised); total body weight loss 13.6% versus 0.8%; observational TBWL 15.1–17.2% out to 18–24 months. Metabolic comorbidities: improved in 80% versus 45% in MERIT. Harms: serious procedure-related adverse events 2% (randomised) and severe adverse events 2.2% (observational), no deaths in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the observational 17% figures as the treatment effect — the randomised effect is the 49.2% versus 3.2% excess-weight-loss contrast, in patients with class 1–2 obesity only. Nothing here compares ESG with laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy or with GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy, the two comparisons patients actually face. Tier C is set for the single-trial randomised base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abu Dayyeh BK et al. The Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35908555); Hedjoudje A et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2020 (PMID: 31442601).

shelves.title: G-POEM for severe refractory gastroparesis: treatment success 71% versus 22% after sham at 6 months — a 41-patient sham-controlled trial stopped early, strongest in diabetic gastroparesis (89% vs 17%)
shelves.question: In diabetic gastroparesis refractory to medical therapy, does gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM) improve symptoms versus a sham procedure?
shelves.mesh: Female · Gastric Emptying · Gastroparesis/etiology/surgery · Gastroscopy/methods · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Pyloromyotomy/adverse effects/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first sham-controlled test of G-POEM, positive and small in equal measure. In the trial (Martinek J et al., PMID: 35470243), 41 patients with severe gastroparesis (17 diabetic, 13 postsurgical, 11 idiopathic) were randomised to G-POEM or a sham endoscopic procedure. Treatment success at 6 months (≥50% fall in the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index) was 71% (95% CI 50 to 86) after G-POEM versus 22% (8 to 47) after sham (p=0.005). In the diabetic subgroup — the population of the candidate question — success was 89% (56 to 98) versus 17% (3 to 57); postsurgical and idiopathic results were weaker and, in the authors' words, 'not entirely conclusive'. Median 4-hour gastric retention fell from 22% to 12% after G-POEM and was unchanged after sham. Twelve sham patients crossed over to G-POEM, 9 (75%) successfully. Enrolment was stopped early at interim analysis, short of the planned 86 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real sham-controlled effect, from a single small trial stopped early — the classic recipe for an overestimated effect size; Tier C.

cards.headline: Martinek 2022: success 71% versus 22% at 6 months (p=0.005); diabetic subgroup 89% versus 17%; gastric retention 22%→12% versus unchanged; trial stopped early at n=41 of 86 planned
cards.summary: Martinek 2022: success 71% versus 22% at 6 months (p=0.005); diabetic subgroup 89% versus 17%; gastric retention 22%→12% versus unchanged; trial stopped early at n=41 of 86 planned
cards.people: 41 patients with severe, refractory gastroparesis — 17 diabetic, 13 postsurgical, 11 idiopathic; 46% male — randomised to gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (21) or sham procedure (20); primary outcome was treatment success (≥50% decrease in Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index) at 6 months. Sham non-responders were offered crossover G-POEM.
cards.result: Treatment success was 71% (95% CI 50 to 86) after G-POEM versus 22% (8 to 47) after sham (p=0.005). By aetiology, success after G-POEM versus sham was 89% (56 to 98) versus 17% (3 to 57) in diabetic, 50% (18 to 82) versus 29% (7 to 67) in postsurgical, and 67% (30 to 90) versus 20% (3 to 67) in idiopathic gastroparesis. Median gastric retention at 4 hours fell from 22% to 12% after G-POEM and did not change after sham (26% to 24%). Of 12 crossover patients, 9 (75%) achieved treatment success. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board stopped enrolment after interim analysis, before the planned 86 patients.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for benefit inflates effect sizes, the diabetic subgroup is 17 patients, and the symptom index is subjective even under sham control — though the objective gastric-emptying result moved the same way. The candidate question asks about diabetic gastroparesis specifically; the trial randomised all-cause severe gastroparesis, and its non-diabetic strata were inconclusive.
cards.source: Martinek J et al. Endoscopic pyloromyotomy for the treatment of severe and refractory gastroparesis: a pilot, randomised, sham-controlled trial. Gut. 2022. PMID: 35470243. Registry ID: NCT03356067. cards.headline: Synthesis: sham-controlled proof of concept — real effect, uncertain size, diabetic patients the best responders
cards.summary: Synthesis: sham-controlled proof of concept — real effect, uncertain size, diabetic patients the best responders
cards.people: One randomised sham-controlled trial, 41 patients with severe refractory gastroparesis (17 diabetic), 6-month primary endpoint.
cards.result: Success 71% vs 22% overall (p=0.005); 89% vs 17% in diabetic gastroparesis; gastric retention objectively improved; crossover success 75%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single small trial stopped early.
cards.watchOut: Durability beyond 6 months, reflux and dumping consequences of pyloromyotomy, and comparison against gastric electrical stimulation or surgery are all outside this record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Martinek J et al. Gut. 2022 (PMID: 35470243).

shelves.title: Risankizumab for ulcerative colitis: remission in 20.3% versus 6.2% at induction and about 40% versus 25% at one year in two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does risankizumab induce and maintain clinical remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Colitis, Ulcerative/diagnosis/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Induction Chemotherapy/adverse effects/methods · Interleukin-23 Subunit p19/antagonists & inhibitors · Maintenance Chemotherapy/adverse effects/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Colon/diagnostic imaging/drug effects · Colonoscopy · Intestinal Mucosa/diagnostic imaging/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large phase 3 trials, reported together, point the same way. In INSPIRE, intravenous risankizumab 1200 mg put 20.3% (132/650) of patients in clinical remission at week 12 versus 6.2% (20/325) on placebo (adjusted difference 14.0%, P<.001). In COMMAND, responders re-randomised to subcutaneous risankizumab stayed in remission at week 52 in 40.2% (180 mg) and 37.6% (360 mg) versus 25.1% on withdrawal to placebo. No new safety risks were detected in either trial. The absolute remission rates remain a minority of patients, and follow-up ends at 52 weeks. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): risankizumab induces and maintains remission in moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, with roughly one in five remitting on induction and two in five responders still in remission at a year.

cards.headline: INSPIRE (induction): clinical remission at week 12 in 20.3% on risankizumab 1200 mg versus 6.2% on placebo (P<.001)
cards.summary: INSPIRE (induction): clinical remission at week 12 in 20.3% on risankizumab 1200 mg versus 6.2% on placebo (P<.001)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (Louis 2024, INSPIRE, reported with COMMAND)
cards.people: 975 analysed patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis and intolerance or inadequate response to conventional or advanced therapies, at 261 centres in 41 countries, randomised 2:1 to intravenous risankizumab 1200 mg or placebo at weeks 0, 4 and 8.
cards.result: Clinical remission (stool frequency score ≤1 and not above baseline, rectal bleeding score 0, endoscopic subscore ≤1 without friability) at week 12 was 20.3% (132/650) on risankizumab versus 6.2% (20/325) on placebo — an adjusted between-group difference of 14.0% (95% CI 10.0–18.0), P<.001, with the absolute rates printed alongside.
cards.watchOut: Even on the winning arm, four of five patients did not reach remission by week 12; the endpoint is a strict composite, and the trial enrolled a treatment-experienced population, so rates in biologic-naive patients may differ.
cards.source: Louis E et al. Risankizumab for Ulcerative Colitis: Two Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 39037800. Registry ID: NCT03398148 · NCT03398135. cards.headline: COMMAND (maintenance): week-52 remission 40.2% on risankizumab 180 mg and 37.6% on 360 mg versus 25.1% after withdrawal to placebo
cards.summary: COMMAND (maintenance): week-52 remission 40.2% on risankizumab 180 mg and 37.6% on 360 mg versus 25.1% after withdrawal to placebo
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 withdrawal trial (Louis 2024, COMMAND, reported with INSPIRE)
cards.people: 548 analysed patients who had responded to intravenous risankizumab induction, at 238 centres in 37 countries, re-randomised 1:1:1 to subcutaneous risankizumab 180 mg or 360 mg or placebo (risankizumab withdrawal) every 8 weeks for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 52 was 40.2% (72/179) on 180 mg and 37.6% (70/186) on 360 mg versus 25.1% (46/183) on placebo — adjusted differences 16.3% (97.5% CI 6.1–26.6, P<.001) and 14.2% (97.5% CI 4.0–24.5, P=.002). No new safety risks were detected in the treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: A withdrawal design measures the value of continuing, not of starting: the placebo arm is patients taken off a drug that had already worked for them, and a quarter of them stayed in remission for a year without it. Benefit beyond 52 weeks is unstudied in this record.
cards.source: Louis E et al. Risankizumab for Ulcerative Colitis: Two Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 39037800. Registry ID: NCT03398148 · NCT03398135. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 trials — a real but minority remission benefit, induction and maintenance both positive
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 trials — a real but minority remission benefit, induction and maintenance both positive
cards.people: Two phase 3 randomised trials totalling 975 induction patients and 548 maintenance patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, reported in a single JAMA record.
cards.result: Induction remission at week 12: 20.3% versus 6.2%. Maintenance remission at week 52: 40.2% (180 mg) and 37.6% (360 mg) versus 25.1% on withdrawal. No new safety risks detected. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials sit in one publication from one development programme; independent replication and head-to-head data against other advanced therapies are not in this record, and neither dose separated from the other.

shelves.title: Upadacitinib for ulcerative colitis: remission in 26–34% versus 4–5% at 8 weeks and 42–52% versus 12% at a year across three phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does upadacitinib induce remission at 8 weeks and maintain it at 52 weeks versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Creatine Kinase · Double-Blind Method · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Humans · Nasopharyngitis · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three phase 3 trials in one programme agree. Upadacitinib 45 mg induced clinical remission at week 8 in 26% (U-ACHIEVE induction) and 34% (U-ACCOMPLISH) versus 5% and 4% on placebo. Among induction responders, maintenance remission at week 52 was 42% on 15 mg and 52% on 30 mg versus 12% on placebo. Serious adverse events were less frequent on upadacitinib than placebo in the induction studies; the adverse events that did cluster on the drug were acne, nasopharyngitis and creatine phosphokinase elevation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): upadacitinib is an effective oral induction and maintenance therapy for moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, with a JAK-inhibitor monitoring burden the trials' size cannot fully price.

cards.headline: U-ACHIEVE induction and U-ACCOMPLISH: remission at week 8 in 26% and 34% on upadacitinib 45 mg versus 5% and 4% on placebo (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: U-ACHIEVE induction and U-ACCOMPLISH: remission at week 8 in 26% and 34% on upadacitinib 45 mg versus 5% and 4% on placebo (p<0.0001)
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 induction trials (Danese 2022, UC1 and UC2)
cards.people: 474 patients (UC1) and 522 patients (UC2), aged 16–75 years with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (Adapted Mayo score 5–9, endoscopic subscore 2 or 3), randomised 2:1 to oral upadacitinib 45 mg once daily or placebo for 8 weeks, at about 200 centres per study.
cards.result: Clinical remission per Adapted Mayo score at week 8: 83/319 (26%) on upadacitinib versus 7/154 (5%) on placebo in UC1 (adjusted difference 21.6%, 95% CI 15.8–27.4) and 114/341 (34%) versus 7/174 (4%) in UC2 (adjusted difference 29.0%, 23.2–34.7); p<0.0001 in both. Serious adverse events were less frequent on upadacitinib (3% in both studies) than placebo (6% and 5%).
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is induction only; the commonest on-drug events (acne, creatine phosphokinase elevation, nasopharyngitis) are the visible part of JAK-inhibitor safety — rarer cardiovascular, malignancy and infection risks cannot be sized by trials of this duration.

cards.summary: U-ACHIEVE maintenance: week-52 remission 42% on upadacitinib 15 mg and 52% on 30 mg versus 12% on placebo (p<0.0001)
cards.people: 451 patients who had achieved clinical response after 8 weeks of upadacitinib 45 mg induction, re-randomised 1:1:1 to upadacitinib 15 mg, upadacitinib 30 mg, or placebo for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 52 was 63/148 (42%) on 15 mg and 80/154 (52%) on 30 mg versus 18/149 (12%) on placebo (adjusted differences 30.7% and 39.0%; p<0.0001 for both). cards.watchOut: Maintenance enrols only induction responders, so the 42–52% figures describe a pre-selected group, not all starters; the placebo arm is again a withdrawal arm, which inflates the contrast with continuing therapy.

shelves.title: Filgotinib 200 mg for ulcerative colitis: remission in 26.1% versus 15.3% (biologic-naive) and 11.5% versus 4.2% (biologic-experienced) at week 10, held at week 58 — the 100 mg dose mostly missed
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does filgotinib 200 mg induce and maintain clinical remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Janus Kinase Inhibitors · Male · Pyridines/administration & dosage · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2b/3 programme, positive at the 200 mg dose only. In SELECTION, filgotinib 200 mg induced clinical remission at week 10 in 26.1% versus 15.3% on placebo in biologic-naive patients (difference 10.8%, p=0.0157) and 11.5% versus 4.2% in biologic-experienced patients (difference 7.2%, p=0.0103); at week 58, remission was 37.2% versus 11.2% in the 200 mg maintenance comparison. The 100 mg dose did not separate from placebo at week 10 and reached significance only at week 58 (23.8% vs 13.5%). Serious adverse events were similar across groups (about 4–5% in induction). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): filgotinib 200 mg induces and maintains remission in ulcerative colitis; the effect is dose-specific and the absolute induction gain is modest, especially after biologics.

cards.headline: SELECTION induction: week-10 remission on filgotinib 200 mg 26.1% vs 15.3% (biologic-naive) and 11.5% vs 4.2% (biologic-experienced); 100 mg not significant
cards.summary: SELECTION induction: week-10 remission on filgotinib 200 mg 26.1% vs 15.3% (biologic-naive) and 11.5% vs 4.2% (biologic-experienced); 100 mg not significant
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b/3 trial programme (Feagan 2021, SELECTION induction studies A and B)
cards.people: 659 patients in induction study A (biologic-naive; inadequate response to corticosteroids or immunosuppressants) and 689 in study B (biologic-experienced; inadequate response to TNF antagonists or vedolizumab), aged 18–75 with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, randomised 2:2:1 to filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, or placebo daily for 11 weeks, in 341 centres in 40 countries.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 10 on filgotinib 200 mg was 26.1% versus 15.3% on placebo in study A (difference 10.8%, 95% CI 2.1–19.5, p=0.0157) and 11.5% versus 4.2% in study B (difference 7.2%, 1.6–12.8, p=0.0103). Filgotinib 100 mg did not differ significantly from placebo at week 10 in either study. Serious adverse events in induction: 5.0% (100 mg), 4.3% (200 mg), 4.7% (placebo).
cards.watchOut: The biologic-experienced induction gain is 7.2 percentage points on a 4.2% placebo rate — real, but small in absolute terms; and the programme's positive dose is the higher one, so the shelf's claim cannot be extended to 100 mg.

cards.headline: SELECTION maintenance: week-58 remission 37.2% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 11.2% on withdrawal to placebo (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: SELECTION maintenance: week-58 remission 37.2% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 11.2% on withdrawal to placebo (p<0.0001)
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b/3 maintenance trial (Feagan 2021, SELECTION maintenance)
cards.people: 664 patients who had achieved clinical remission or Mayo Clinic Score response at week 10 entered maintenance; those on induction filgotinib were re-randomised 2:1 to continue their dose or switch to placebo, followed to week 58.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 58 was 37.2% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 11.2% in its placebo (withdrawal) group (difference 26.0%, 95% CI 16.0–35.9, p<0.0001); for 100 mg, 23.8% versus 13.5% (difference 10.4%, 0.0–20.7, p=0.0420). Serious adverse events in maintenance were 4.5% (100 mg) and 4.5% (200 mg); two deaths occurred, neither judged treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: As with all withdrawal maintenance designs, the comparison is continuing versus stopping in responders; 263 patients discontinued during maintenance, which thins the week-58 denominators.

shelves.title: Vedolizumab for Crohn's disease: maintenance remission 39.0% versus 21.6% at a year — but induction is slow, and the week-6 remission endpoint failed outright after TNF failure
shelves.question: In moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does vedolizumab induce and maintain remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies/blood · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Induction Chemotherapy · Infusions, Intravenous/adverse effects · Integrins/antagonists & inhibitors/immunology · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: SPLIT — maintenance works, induction barely does. In GEMINI 2, week-6 clinical remission was 14.5% on vedolizumab versus 6.8% on placebo (P=0.02), but the CDAI-100 response endpoint was not significant (31.4% vs 25.7%, P=0.23); among induction responders, remission at week 52 was 39.0% (every 8 weeks) and 36.4% (every 4 weeks) versus 21.6% on placebo. In GEMINI 3, in patients whose TNF-antagonist treatment had failed, the week-6 remission endpoint was missed (15.2% vs 12.1%, P=0.433) and separation appeared only at week 10 (26.6% vs 12.1%). Serious adverse events were more common on vedolizumab in GEMINI 2 (24.4% vs 15.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: vedolizumab maintains remission in Crohn's disease and can induce it, but slowly — it is the wrong drug to judge at six weeks, especially after TNF failure.

cards.headline: GEMINI 2: week-6 remission 14.5% vs 6.8% (P=0.02) but CDAI-100 response not significant; week-52 remission in responders 39.0%/36.4% vs 21.6%
cards.summary: GEMINI 2: week-6 remission 14.5% vs 6.8% (P=0.02) but CDAI-100 response not significant; week-52 remission in responders 39.0%/36.4% vs 21.6%
cards.people: 368 patients randomised to intravenous vedolizumab 300 mg or placebo at weeks 0 and 2 in the induction cohort (a further 747 received open-label vedolizumab); 461 induction responders were re-randomised to vedolizumab every 8 or 4 weeks or placebo to week 52. Adults with active Crohn's disease.
cards.result: Clinical remission (CDAI ≤150) at week 6: 14.5% on vedolizumab versus 6.8% on placebo (P=0.02); CDAI-100 response 31.4% versus 25.7% (P=0.23, not significant). At week 52, remission was 39.0% (every-8-weeks) and 36.4% (every-4-weeks) versus 21.6% on placebo (P<0.001 and P=0.004). Serious adverse events 24.4% versus 15.3%; infections 44.1% versus 40.2%; serious infections 5.5% versus 3.0%.
cards.watchOut: The induction win rests on one of two co-primary endpoints, and the maintenance population is responders only. The higher serious-adverse-event rate on drug (24.4% vs 15.3%) sits awkwardly with vedolizumab's gut-selective reputation and is reported here as the trial printed it.

cards.headline: GEMINI 3: after TNF-antagonist failure, week-6 remission 15.2% vs 12.1% (P=0.433, endpoint missed) — remission separated only by week 10 (26.6% vs 12.1%)
cards.summary: GEMINI 3: after TNF-antagonist failure, week-6 remission 15.2% vs 12.1% (P=0.433, endpoint missed) — remission separated only by week 10 (26.6% vs 12.1%)
cards.people: 416 patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease (CDAI 220–400), of whom 315 had previously failed TNF-antagonist therapy, randomised to intravenous vedolizumab 300 mg or placebo at weeks 0, 2 and 6.
cards.result: In the prior-TNF-failure population, clinical remission at week 6 was 15.2% on vedolizumab versus 12.1% on placebo (P=0.433 — primary endpoint not met). At week 10, remission was 26.6% versus 12.1% (nominal P=0.001; relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.3–3.6), and CDAI-100 response at week 6 was 39.2% versus 22.3% (nominal P=0.001). Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The week-10 result is a secondary, nominally significant analysis after a missed primary endpoint — supportive, not confirmatory. It does, however, match the drug's slow pharmacology and GEMINI 2's pattern.

shelves.title: Acute severe ulcerative colitis after steroid failure: ciclosporin and infliximab are a dead heat in two randomised trials — treatment failure 60% versus 54%, colectomy 48% versus 41%
shelves.question: In acute severe ulcerative colitis that has failed intravenous steroids, is ciclosporin as effective as infliximab at avoiding colectomy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Cyclosporine/therapeutic use · Drug Resistance · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Infliximab · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Steroids/administration & dosage · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised head-to-head trials, a decade of practice apart in style, agree there is nothing between the drugs. In CYSIF, treatment failure occurred in 60% on ciclosporin versus 54% on infliximab (absolute difference 6%, 95% CI −7 to 19, p=0.52). In the pragmatic CONSTRUCT trial, quality-adjusted survival did not differ (p=0.603), nor did colectomy: 48% on ciclosporin versus 41% on infliximab (p=0.223). Deaths were few and serious adverse reactions similar in both trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis, ciclosporin and infliximab are equally effective rescue therapies — the choice turns on centre experience, prior drug exposure and patient factors, not on efficacy.

cards.headline: CYSIF: treatment failure 60% on ciclosporin versus 54% on infliximab (p=0.52) in steroid-refractory acute severe colitis
cards.summary: CYSIF: treatment failure 60% on ciclosporin versus 54% on infliximab (p=0.52) in steroid-refractory acute severe colitis
cards.people: 115 patients at 27 European centres with an acute severe flare of ulcerative colitis (Lichtiger score >10) refractory to high-dose intravenous steroids, none previously exposed to either drug, randomised to intravenous ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day for a week then oral ciclosporin to day 98, or infliximab 5 mg/kg on days 0, 14 and 42; responders in both groups started azathioprine at day 7.
cards.result: Treatment failure (no response at day 7, relapse by day 98, no steroid-free remission at day 98, severe adverse event stopping treatment, colectomy, or death) occurred in 35/58 (60%) on ciclosporin versus 31/57 (54%) on infliximab — absolute risk difference 6% (95% CI −7 to 19), p=0.52. Severe adverse events: 16% (9 patients) on ciclosporin versus 25% (14) on infliximab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the composite failure endpoint mixes efficacy with tolerability; the confidence interval (−7 to 19%) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful edge for either drug. Neither arm's failure rate is low — rescue therapy still failed over half of patients by day 98.
cards.source: Laharie D et al. Ciclosporin versus infliximab in patients with severe ulcerative colitis refractory to intravenous steroids: a parallel, open-label randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2012. PMID: 23063316. Registry ID: NCT00542152. cards.headline: CONSTRUCT: no difference in quality-adjusted survival (p=0.603) or colectomy (48% ciclosporin vs 41% infliximab, p=0.223) over 3 years
cards.summary: CONSTRUCT: no difference in quality-adjusted survival (p=0.603) or colectomy (48% ciclosporin vs 41% infliximab, p=0.223) over 3 years
cards.people: 270 patients admitted unscheduled to 52 UK hospitals with severe ulcerative colitis failing intravenous hydrocortisone, randomised 1:1 to infliximab 5 mg/kg at baseline, 2 and 6 weeks, or ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day by infusion then oral therapy for 12 weeks; follow-up to 3 years.
cards.result: Quality-adjusted survival (area under the CUCQ curve) was 564.0 on infliximab versus 587.0 on ciclosporin (adjusted difference 7.9, 95% CI −22.0 to 37.8, p=0.603). Colectomy occurred in 55/135 (41%) on infliximab versus 65/135 (48%) on ciclosporin (p=0.223). Serious adverse reactions and deaths (3 on infliximab, 0 on ciclosporin) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A pragmatic trial with a quality-of-life primary endpoint rather than a colectomy endpoint, run in routine NHS hospitals — its null is the more generalisable one, but it was not powered as a formal equivalence trial for colectomy.
cards.source: Williams JG et al. Infliximab versus ciclosporin for steroid-resistant acute severe ulcerative colitis (CONSTRUCT): a mixed methods, open-label, pragmatic randomised trial. cards.people: Two randomised open-label trials totalling 385 patients with steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis (CYSIF, European centres; CONSTRUCT, UK hospitals).

shelves.title: Stopping infliximab in Crohn's remission: about 4 in 10 relapse within a year — but retreatment recaptures remission in almost 9 in 10
shelves.question: In Crohn's disease in sustained remission on combination therapy, does stopping infliximab lead to relapse — and can it be recaptured on retreatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antimetabolites/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Belgium · Biomarkers/blood · Crohn Disease/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · France · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Infliximab · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — stopping infliximab in deep remission is usually followed by relapse, though relapse is usually reversible. In the prospective STORI cohort, the 1-year relapse rate after stopping infliximab was 43.9%, and retreatment was effective and well tolerated in 88% of those who relapsed. In the randomised SPARE trial, 2-year relapse was 36% after infliximab withdrawal versus 14% on continued combination therapy (hazard ratio 3.45, 95% CI 1.56–7.69), while stopping the immunosuppressant instead gave 10%; of relapsed patients retreated per protocol, 25 of 28 regained remission, including 22 of 23 after infliximab withdrawal. A low-risk minority exists: STORI patients with at most 2 of its risk factors had a 15% 1-year relapse risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): withdrawing infliximab roughly triples relapse over two years; the harm is bounded by high recapture on retreatment, which is why this is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: STORI: 1-year relapse rate 43.9% after infliximab was stopped in deep remission — retreatment effective in 88% of relapsers
cards.summary: STORI: 1-year relapse rate 43.9% after infliximab was stopped in deep remission — retreatment effective in 88% of relapsers
cards.people: 115 patients with Crohn's disease treated for at least 1 year with scheduled infliximab plus an antimetabolite and in corticosteroid-free remission for at least 6 months, in whom infliximab was stopped and the antimetabolite continued, followed for at least 1 year (median 28 months).
cards.result: 52 of 115 patients relapsed; the 1-year relapse rate was 43.9% ± 5.0%. Risk factors included male sex, no surgical resection, leukocyte count >6.0×10⁹/L, haemoglobin ≤145 g/L, C-reactive protein ≥5.0 mg/L and faecal calprotectin ≥300 µg/g; patients with no more than 2 risk factors (about 29% of the cohort) had a 15% 1-year relapse risk. Retreatment with infliximab was effective and well tolerated in 88% of relapsers.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised — everyone stopped, so the 43.9% has no internal comparator, and patients were selected for unusually deep, durable remission. The risk-factor model comes from the same cohort it describes.
cards.source: Louis E et al. Maintenance of remission among patients with Crohn's disease on antimetabolite therapy after infliximab therapy is stopped. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 21945953. cards.headline: SPARE: 2-year relapse 36% after infliximab withdrawal versus 14% on continued combination therapy (HR 3.45) — and 22 of 23 retreated relapsers regained remission
cards.summary: SPARE: 2-year relapse 36% after infliximab withdrawal versus 14% on continued combination therapy (HR 3.45) — and 22 of 23 retreated relapsers regained remission
cards.people: 207 analysed adults with Crohn's disease in steroid-free remission for over 6 months on infliximab plus immunosuppressant for at least 8 months, at 64 hospitals in Europe and Australia, randomised to continue combination therapy (n=67), stop infliximab (n=71), or stop the immunosuppressant (n=69), followed for 2 years.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 8/67 (12%) on continued combination, 25/71 (35%) after infliximab withdrawal and 6/69 (9%) after immunosuppressant withdrawal; 2-year relapse rates were 14%, 36% and 10% respectively (HR 3.45, 95% CI 1.56–7.69, p=0.003, for infliximab withdrawal vs combination). Mean time in remission over 2 years differed by only −14 days (95% CI −56 to 27) between withdrawal and continuation. Of 28 relapsers retreated or optimised per protocol, 25 regained remission — 22 of 23 in the infliximab-withdrawal group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and relapse triggered protocolised retreatment, so the trial measures a stop-and-restart strategy, not abandonment of therapy; time in remission — the patient-level bottom line — was nearly identical across arms because recapture worked.
cards.source: Louis E et al. cards.result: Relapse after stopping infliximab: 43.9% at 1 year (STORI); 36% vs 14% at 2 years (SPARE, HR 3.45). Recapture on retreatment: 88% (STORI) and 22/23 (SPARE). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for withdrawal, Tier C: a harm claim resting on one randomised trial plus a cohort.
cards.watchOut: Both studies continued the immunosuppressant when infliximab stopped; stopping everything is a different, untested question here. Neither study was powered for rare consequences of relapse such as surgery or strictures.

shelves.title: After Crohn's resection: colonoscopy at 6 months with step-up treatment cut endoscopic recurrence at 18 months to 49% versus 67% with standard care (POCER)
shelves.question: After ileocolonic resection for Crohn's disease, does colonoscopy-guided step-up treatment prevent endoscopic recurrence better than standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Colonoscopy · Crohn Disease/pathology/surgery/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Mercaptopurine/therapeutic use · Metronidazole/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run randomised trial. In POCER, patients managed with colonoscopy at 6 months and treatment step-up for endoscopic recurrence had recurrence at 18 months in 49% (60/122) versus 67% (35/52) on standard care (p=0.03), and complete mucosal normality was maintained in 22% versus 8% (p=0.03). Of patients who stepped up for 6-month recurrence, 38% were in remission 12 months later. Adverse events did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): risk-stratified drug therapy plus a 6-month colonoscopy with step-up prevents endoscopic recurrence after Crohn's resection better than drug therapy alone — a single-trial result, and an endoscopic rather than clinical endpoint.

cards.headline: POCER: endoscopic recurrence at 18 months 49% with active (colonoscopy-guided) care versus 67% with standard care (p=0.03)
cards.summary: POCER: endoscopic recurrence at 18 months 49% with active (colonoscopy-guided) care versus 67% with standard care (p=0.03)
cards.people: 174 patients at 17 centres in Australia and New Zealand undergoing intestinal resection of all macroscopic Crohn's disease with an endoscopically accessible anastomosis; all received 3 months of metronidazole, high-risk patients also received a thiopurine (or adalimumab if intolerant). Randomised 2:1 to colonoscopy at 6 months with step-up for recurrence (active care, n=122) or no colonoscopy (standard care, n=52); endoscopic reading was blinded centrally.
cards.result: Endoscopic recurrence (Rutgeerts ≥i2) at 18 months occurred in 60/122 (49%) in the active-care group versus 35/52 (67%) in standard care (p=0.03). Complete mucosal normality was maintained in 27/122 (22%) versus 4/52 (8%) (p=0.03). In the active arm, 47 patients (39%) stepped up treatment at 6 months, and 18 of those 47 (38%) were in remission 12 months later. Adverse and severe adverse events did not differ significantly (severe events 27% vs 35%, p=0.36).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is endoscopic recurrence, not symptoms, hospitalisation or re-operation; the trial was unblinded to patients and treating physicians, the standard-care arm is small (n=52), and even the winning strategy left half of patients with recurrence at 18 months.
cards.source: De Cruz P et al. Crohn's disease management after intestinal resection: a randomised trial. The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25542620. Registry ID: NCT00989560. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, one clear endoscopic win — active surveillance after resection beats set-and-forget drug therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, one clear endoscopic win — active surveillance after resection beats set-and-forget drug therapy
cards.people: One randomised trial (POCER) of 174 post-resection Crohn's patients, 83% at high risk of recurrence, all on risk-stratified prophylaxis.
cards.result: Endoscopic recurrence at 18 months: 49% with 6-month colonoscopy and step-up versus 67% with standard care (p=0.03); complete mucosal normality 22% versus 8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial carries the claim.
cards.watchOut: Whether preventing endoscopic recurrence at 18 months prevents surgery years later is beyond this record; smoking (OR 2.4 in the trial) remains a recurrence driver no surveillance schedule removes.

shelves.title: Budesonide in Crohn's disease: it induces remission (47% versus 22% on placebo) but does not maintain it — and it is weaker than conventional steroids for induction
shelves.question: In ileal or ileocolonic Crohn's disease, does budesonide induce and maintain remission versus placebo or mesalazine?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Budesonide/administration & dosage · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy/methods · Maintenance Chemotherapy/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: SPLIT — budesonide starts remission but cannot hold it. For induction, the Cochrane review found budesonide 9 mg superior to placebo at 8 weeks: remission in 47% (115/246) versus 22% (29/133) (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.37–2.73) — but inferior to conventional corticosteroids (52% vs 61% remission; relative risk 0.85, 0.75–0.97), and markedly inferior in severe disease (relative risk 0.52). For maintenance, budesonide 6 mg was no better than placebo at 3, 6 or 12 months (12-month remission 55% vs 48%; relative risk 1.13, 0.94–1.35), with only small gains in CDAI scores and about 60 extra days to relapse. PROPOSED SPLIT: a reasonable gentler induction option for ileal Crohn's, clearly weaker than systemic steroids, and not a maintenance drug.

cards.headline: Induction (Cochrane 2015): budesonide 9 mg beat placebo (remission 47% vs 22%, RR 1.93) but lost to conventional steroids (52% vs 61%, RR 0.85)
cards.summary: Induction (Cochrane 2015): budesonide 9 mg beat placebo (remission 47% vs 22%, RR 1.93) but lost to conventional steroids (52% vs 61%, RR 0.85)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (Rezaie 2015, budesonide for induction)
cards.people: 14 randomised trials, 1,805 patients with active Crohn's disease: 9 trials (779 patients) against conventional corticosteroids, 3 placebo-controlled (535 patients), 2 against mesalamine (491 patients); remission defined as CDAI <150 at 8–16 weeks.
cards.result: At 8 weeks, remission on budesonide 9 mg was 47% (115/246) versus 22% (29/133) on placebo (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.37–2.73; 3 studies, 379 patients; moderate-quality evidence). Against conventional steroids, remission was 52% on budesonide versus 61% (relative risk 0.85, 0.75–0.97; 8 studies, 750 patients), and in severe disease (CDAI >300) the deficit was larger (relative risk 0.52, 0.28–0.95).
cards.watchOut: The placebo comparison rests on only 3 trials and 144 events; budesonide's case is tolerability (less systemic steroid exposure), which these remission figures do not themselves capture.
cards.source: Rezaie A et al. Budesonide for induction of remission in Crohn's disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26039678. cards.headline: Maintenance (Cochrane 2014): budesonide 6 mg no better than placebo at 3, 6 or 12 months (12-month remission 55% vs 48%, RR 1.13, not significant)
cards.summary: Maintenance (Cochrane 2014): budesonide 6 mg no better than placebo at 3, 6 or 12 months (12-month remission 55% vs 48%, RR 1.13, not significant)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (Kuenzig 2014, budesonide for maintenance)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials, 1,273 patients with quiescent Crohn's disease: 8 against placebo, 1 each against 5-aminosalicylates, systemic corticosteroids and azathioprine, and 1 dose comparison; controlled ileal-release or pH-modified budesonide.
cards.result: Remission maintained on budesonide 6 mg versus placebo: 64% vs 52% at 3 months (relative risk 1.25, 95% CI 1.00–1.58), 61% vs 52% at 6 months (1.15, 0.95–1.39) and 55% vs 48% at 12 months (1.13, 0.94–1.35) — none significant. Budesonide did prolong mean time to relapse by about 60 days (mean difference 59.93 days, 19.02–100.84) and slightly improved CDAI scores, and was not significantly different from azathioprine at 12 months (relative risk 0.81, 0.61–1.08, one 77-patient trial). Adverse events were not more common than on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The 3-month confidence interval touches 1.00 and heterogeneity was moderate (I²=56%); a small early effect that fades is possible, but by 12 months — the horizon that matters for maintenance — the pooled result is null.
cards.source: Kuenzig ME et al. Budesonide for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25141071. cards.headline: Synthesis: two Cochrane reviews draw one clean line — budesonide is an induction drug, not a maintenance drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: two Cochrane reviews draw one clean line — budesonide is an induction drug, not a maintenance drug
cards.people: Two Cochrane reviews covering 26 randomised trials and about 3,000 patients with ileal or ileocolonic Crohn's disease (induction 1,805; maintenance 1,273).
cards.result: Induction vs placebo: relative risk 1.93 for remission. Induction vs conventional steroids: relative risk 0.85. Maintenance vs placebo at 12 months: relative risk 1.13, not significant. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit for induction, no benefit for maintenance.
cards.watchOut: Both reviews search to 2014; later formulations and combination strategies are outside them. The reviews compare budesonide with mesalazine only thinly (two induction trials, one small maintenance trial), so the mesalazine part of the question is the least certain part of this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rezaie A et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26039678); Kuenzig ME et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25141071).
