shelves.title: Methotrexate for refractory Crohn's disease: weekly intramuscular high-dose treatment worked in the one large trial (failure to remit 61% versus 81%) — low-dose oral treatment never beat placebo
shelves.question: In refractory Crohn's disease, does weekly methotrexate induce remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Induction Chemotherapy/methods · Infliximab · Mercaptopurine/therapeutic use · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Steroids/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by dose and route. The Cochrane review of 7 trials (495 patients) found the small low-dose oral methotrexate studies uniformly negative: failure to enter remission was 81% versus 77% on placebo at 12.5 mg/week (relative risk 1.05) and numerically worse than placebo at 15 mg/week (33% vs 11% failing; relative risk 3.00, very wide interval). The one large placebo-controlled trial, using high-dose intramuscular methotrexate, did show benefit: 61% failed to enter remission versus 81% on placebo (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.93; number needed to treat 5) — at a price: 17% withdrew for adverse events versus 2% on placebo (relative risk 8.00). PROPOSED SPLIT: intramuscular high-dose methotrexate can induce remission in refractory Crohn's; the oral low-dose regimens actually used for convenience have no supporting trial result.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2014: across 7 trials the only positive result is the large intramuscular trial — failure to remit 61% vs 81% (RR 0.75, NNT 5), withdrawals 17% vs 2%
cards.summary: Cochrane 2014: across 7 trials the only positive result is the large intramuscular trial — failure to remit 61% vs 81% (RR 0.75, NNT 5), withdrawals 17% vs 2%
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (McDonald 2014, methotrexate for induction in refractory Crohn's disease)
cards.people: 7 randomised trials, 495 patients with active refractory Crohn's disease, comparing methotrexate (oral, intramuscular, intravenous or subcutaneous, 12.5–25 mg/week) with placebo, 6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine, 5-ASA, or infliximab combinations; primary outcome failure to enter remission and withdraw from steroids.
cards.result: The large intramuscular high-dose trial: 61% on methotrexate failed to enter remission versus 81% on placebo (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.93; number needed to treat 5), but withdrawals for adverse events were 17% versus 2% (relative risk 8.00, 1.09–58.51). Low-dose oral trials were null or worse: at 12.5 mg/week, failure 81% vs 77% on placebo (relative risk 1.05, 0.79–1.39); at 15 mg/week, failure 33% (5/15) vs 11% (2/18) on placebo (relative risk 3.00, 0.68–13.31). Adding methotrexate to infliximab showed no advantage over infliximab alone in two trials. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; evidence quality was graded very low to low for most outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is a single trial from the pre-biologic era, and its regimen (weekly intramuscular injections) is the one least used today; the review could not pool its trials, so every number here is one small study's number.
cards.source: McDonald JW et al. Methotrexate for induction of remission in refractory Crohn's disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25099640. cards.headline: Synthesis: methotrexate's Crohn's reputation rests on one intramuscular trial — oral substitution was assumed, never shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: methotrexate's Crohn's reputation rests on one intramuscular trial — oral substitution was assumed, never shown
cards.people: One Cochrane review of 7 randomised trials totalling 495 patients with refractory Crohn's disease.
cards.result: Intramuscular high-dose: failure to remit 61% vs 81% (relative risk 0.75), adverse-event withdrawals 17% vs 2%. Oral low-dose: no significant benefit in any trial. Combination with infliximab: no added benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT by dose and route, Tier C: the benefit claim rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: These trials predate modern biologic sequencing, so methotrexate's current place is usually as combination cover against immunogenicity — a use this induction evidence does not address.

shelves.title: Infected necrotising pancreatitis: a minimally invasive step-up approach cut death or major complications to 40% versus 69% with open necrosectomy — and the advantage held at 7 years
shelves.question: In infected necrotising pancreatitis, does a minimally invasive step-up approach reduce death or major complications versus primary open necrosectomy?
shelves.mesh: Debridement · Drainage · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Multiple Organ Failure/prevention & control · Pancreas/surgery · Pancreatitis, Acute Necrotizing/mortality/surgery · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Quality Control · Video-Assisted Surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial and its own long-term follow-up, both strongly positive on the composite. In PANTER, death or major complications occurred in 40% (17/43) with the step-up approach (percutaneous drainage, then minimally invasive necrosectomy only if needed) versus 69% (31/45) with primary open necrosectomy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.87, p=0.006); 35% of step-up patients needed drainage only. Death alone did not differ (19% vs 16%, p=0.70), but new-onset multiple-organ failure did (12% vs 40%, p=0.002). At a mean of 86 months, death or major complications remained lower with step-up (44% vs 73%, p=0.005), with fewer incisional hernias and less pancreatic insufficiency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): step-up is the better strategy for infected necrotising pancreatitis; the win is in complications, not in mortality alone.

cards.headline: PANTER: primary endpoint (major complications or death) in 40% on step-up versus 69% on open necrosectomy (RR 0.57, p=0.006); 35% needed drainage only
cards.summary: PANTER: primary endpoint (major complications or death) in 40% on step-up versus 69% on open necrosectomy (RR 0.57, p=0.006); 35% needed drainage only
cards.people: 88 patients with necrotising pancreatitis and suspected or confirmed infected necrotic tissue, at Dutch multicentre sites, randomised to primary open necrosectomy (n=45) or a step-up approach (n=43): percutaneous drainage first, then, if no improvement, minimally invasive retroperitoneal necrosectomy.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint occurred in 17/43 (40%) on step-up versus 31/45 (69%) on open necrosectomy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.87, p=0.006). New-onset multiple-organ failure: 12% versus 40% (p=0.002). Death: 19% versus 16% (p=0.70, not significant). Incisional hernias 7% versus 24% (p=0.03) and new-onset diabetes 16% versus 38% (p=0.02) favoured step-up; 35% of step-up patients were treated with drainage alone.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 88 patients from one national study group, in expert centres; the composite is driven by complications, and the trial cannot show a mortality difference at this size. Patients with an abdominal catastrophe needing immediate open surgery were not the population studied.
cards.source: van Santvoort HC et al. A step-up approach or open necrosectomy for necrotizing pancreatitis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20410514. Registry ID: ISRCTN13975868. cards.headline: PANTER long-term follow-up (86 months): death or major complications 44% step-up versus 73% open (p=0.005), with less exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
cards.summary: PANTER long-term follow-up (86 months): death or major complications 44% step-up versus 73% open (p=0.005), with less exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Hollemans 2019, PANTER follow-up)
cards.people: All 73 surviving PANTER participants (of 88 randomised) re-evaluated at a mean of 86 months after the index admission, comparing the original step-up and open-necrosectomy groups on death or major complications, pancreatic insufficiency, reinterventions, pain, quality of life and costs.
cards.result: From index admission to long-term follow-up, death or major complications occurred in 44% of the step-up group versus 73% of the open group (p=0.005). Incisional hernias 23% versus 53% (p=0.004), exocrine insufficiency 29% versus 56% (p=0.03) and endocrine insufficiency 40% versus 64% (p=0.05) all favoured step-up. Additional drainage (11% vs 13%) and pancreatic surgery (11% vs 5%) did not differ, answering the concern that step-up merely defers interventions.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up of one small trial's survivors — the long-term comparison inherits the original randomisation but adds seven years of unrandomised life; it confirms durability rather than providing independent replication.

shelves.title: After ERCP in high-risk patients: adding a pancreatic stent to rectal indomethacin does help — pancreatitis 11.3% versus 14.9%, and indomethacin alone failed the non-inferiority test
shelves.question: In high-risk patients undergoing ERCP, does a prophylactic pancreatic stent reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis beyond rectal indomethacin?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Humans · Administration, Rectal · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde/adverse effects · Indomethacin/therapeutic use · Pancreatitis/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Risk Factors · Stents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the stent, from one large rigorous trial that answered the question the other way than its designers hoped. In 1,950 high-risk patients, post-ERCP pancreatitis occurred in 14.9% (145/975) on rectal indomethacin alone versus 11.3% (110/975) on indomethacin plus a prophylactic pancreatic stent (risk difference 3.6%, 95% CI 0.6–6.6); indomethacin alone failed non-inferiority (p=0.18 for non-inferiority) and a post-hoc analysis found it frankly inferior (p=0.011). Serious adverse events, ICU admission and hospital stay did not differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in high-risk ERCP, the stent adds real protection on top of indomethacin — about 3–4 fewer pancreatitis cases per 100 procedures — so the technically harder combined strategy remains the standard this trial set out to retire.

cards.headline: Elmunzer 2024: pancreatitis 11.3% (stent + indomethacin) versus 14.9% (indomethacin alone); non-inferiority of indomethacin alone rejected
cards.summary: Elmunzer 2024: pancreatitis 11.3% (stent + indomethacin) versus 14.9% (indomethacin alone); non-inferiority of indomethacin alone rejected
cards.people: 1,950 patients aged 18 or older at high risk for post-ERCP pancreatitis, at 20 referral centres in the USA and Canada, randomised 1:1 to rectal indomethacin alone or rectal indomethacin plus prophylactic pancreatic stent placement; patients, clinicians and outcome assessors were masked to allocation.
cards.result: Post-ERCP pancreatitis occurred in 145/975 (14.9%) on indomethacin alone versus 110/975 (11.3%) on the combination (risk difference 3.6%, 95% CI 0.6–6.6). The upper confidence bound exceeded the 5% non-inferiority margin, so non-inferiority was not declared (p=0.18 for non-inferiority); a post-hoc intention-to-treat analysis found indomethacin alone inferior (p=0.011). The stent's relative benefit was consistent across subgroups and larger in the highest-risk patients. Safety outcomes did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and its primary framework was non-inferiority — the superiority reading is post-hoc, though the confidence interval (0.6–6.6%) excludes no difference. All patients were high-risk at referral centres; the result does not speak to average-risk ERCP, where stents are not standard.
cards.source: Elmunzer BJ et al. Indomethacin with or without prophylactic pancreatic stent placement to prevent pancreatitis after ERCP: a randomised non-inferiority trial. The Lancet. 2024. shelves.title: Acute pancreatitis fluids: lactated Ringer's beat normal saline on inflammation in a small blinded trial, and a 4-trial meta-analysis found less moderately severe or severe disease (OR 0.49) — on only 248 patients in total
shelves.question: In acute pancreatitis, does lactated Ringer's solution reduce systemic inflammation and organ failure compared with normal saline?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction, very small evidence base. In the triple-blind de-Madaria trial (40 patients), C-reactive protein at 48 hours was 28 mg/L on lactated Ringer's versus 166 mg/L on normal saline (p=0.037), with a similar gap at 72 hours (25 vs 217 mg/L, p=0.043), though SIRS criteria counts did not differ significantly. Pooling all 4 randomised trials (248 patients), the meta-analysis found lactated Ringer's halved the odds of moderately severe or severe pancreatitis (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.97) and reduced ICU admission (odds ratio 0.33, 0.13–0.81) and local complications (odds ratio 0.42, 0.2–0.88) — but found no difference in SIRS at 24 or 48 hours or in organ failure, the outcomes in this shelf's question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lactated Ringer's probably causes less inflammation and less severe disease than saline in acute pancreatitis, on evidence far thinner than the confidence of current practice.

cards.headline: de-Madaria 2018: CRP at 48 hours 28 mg/L on lactated Ringer's versus 166 mg/L on saline (p=0.037) in a 40-patient triple-blind trial; SIRS counts not significantly different
cards.summary: de-Madaria 2018: CRP at 48 hours 28 mg/L on lactated Ringer's versus 166 mg/L on saline (p=0.037) in a 40-patient triple-blind trial; SIRS counts not significantly different
cards.people: 40 adults admitted with acute pancreatitis (19 lactated Ringer's, 21 normal saline), randomised to one fluid for resuscitation; primary outcomes were SIRS criteria at 24, 48 and 72 hours and CRP at 48 and 72 hours.
cards.result: Median CRP was 28 (IQR 3–124) mg/L on lactated Ringer's versus 166 (78–281) mg/L on saline at 48 hours (p=0.037) and 25 (3–169) versus 217 (59–323) mg/L at 72 hours (p=0.043). Median SIRS criteria at 48 hours were 1 (0–1) versus 1 (1–2) (p=0.060, not significant). In-vitro companion experiments suggested a direct anti-inflammatory effect of lactate on macrophage activation.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and a biomarker primary story: CRP separated dramatically while the clinical SIRS count did not reach significance, and the trial was not powered for organ failure, necrosis or death.
cards.source: de-Madaria E et al. Fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's solution vs normal saline in acute pancreatitis: A triple-blind, randomized, controlled trial. United European Gastroenterology Journal. 2018. PMID: 29435315. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2021 (4 RCTs, 248 patients): moderately severe/severe pancreatitis OR 0.49 and ICU admission OR 0.33 with Ringer's — but no difference in SIRS or organ failure
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2021 (4 RCTs, 248 patients): moderately severe/severe pancreatitis OR 0.49 and ICU admission OR 0.33 with Ringer's — but no difference in SIRS or organ failure
cards.people: 4 randomised trials comparing lactated Ringer's with normal saline in acute pancreatitis, totalling 122 patients resuscitated with Ringer's and 126 with saline, identified from 7,964 abstracts screened.
cards.result: Moderately severe or severe pancreatitis was less likely with lactated Ringer's (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.97), as were ICU admission (odds ratio 0.33, 0.13–0.81) and local complications (odds ratio 0.42, 0.2–0.88). There was no difference in SIRS at 24 or 48 hours or in organ failure, and the trend to shorter hospital stay was not significant (standardised mean difference −0.18, 99% CI −0.44 to 0.07).
cards.watchOut: The entire randomised literature on this everyday choice fitted into 248 patients when pooled; the severity odds ratio's confidence interval (0.25–0.97) nearly touches 1, and fluid volumes and rates varied across the component trials.
cards.source: Zhou S et al. Comprehensive meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of Lactated Ringer's versus Normal Saline for acute pancreatitis. Pancreatology. 2021. PMID: 34332907. shelves.title: Faecal microbiota transplant for recurrent hepatic encephalopathy: in a 20-man trial, no FMT patient developed another episode in 5 months versus 5 on standard care — a pilot, not a proof
shelves.question: In cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, does faecal microbiota transplant improve cognition and reduce encephalopathy episodes versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cognition · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy/therapy · Humans · Male · Metabolome · Microbiota · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result in a trial too small to trust on its own. In Bajaj's open-label randomised trial in men with cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, 5 standard-care patients developed further encephalopathy episodes over 5 months versus none after a single FMT enema (from one rationally selected donor, after antibiotic pretreatment) (P=0.03); serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 10 standard-care patients (11 events) versus 2 of 10 FMT patients, both unrelated to FMT (P=0.02), and cognition improved in the FMT group but not on standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): FMT looks safe and promising for recurrent hepatic encephalopathy in this single small pilot; the effect size is exactly the kind that small open-label trials overstate, so it is held at POSSIBLE and Tier C.

cards.headline: Bajaj 2017: further hepatic encephalopathy in 0 FMT patients versus 5 on standard care (P=0.03); serious adverse events in 2 vs 8 patients
cards.summary: Bajaj 2017: further hepatic encephalopathy in 0 FMT patients versus 5 on standard care (P=0.03); serious adverse events in 2 vs 8 patients
cards.people: 20 outpatient men with cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy on standard care (lactulose/rifaximin-era therapy), randomised 1:1 to standard care alone or to 5 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics followed by a single FMT enema from one rationally selected donor, followed for 5 months (to day 150).
cards.result: Five standard-care patients and no FMT patients developed further hepatic encephalopathy (P=0.03). Serious adverse events occurred in 8 (80%) standard-care participants (11 events) versus 2 (20%) FMT participants, both events unrelated to FMT (P=0.02). Cognition improved in the FMT group but not the standard-care group; MELD score worsened transiently after antibiotics and reverted after FMT, and FMT increased microbial diversity and beneficial taxa.
cards.watchOut: Twenty men, one donor, one centre, open-label, and the intervention bundles antibiotics plus FMT, so neither the FMT's isolated effect nor generalisability to women or other donors is tested. A zero-event arm in 10 patients is fragile: one episode changes the headline.
cards.source: Bajaj JS et al. Fecal microbiota transplant from a rational stool donor improves hepatic encephalopathy: A randomized clinical trial. Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 28586116. shelves.title: Peptic ulcer bleeding: scheduled second-look endoscopy does not reduce rebleeding — pooled rebleeding relative risk 0.78 (0.53–1.14) across 1,513 patients, and the one high-risk-selected trial was null too
shelves.question: In high-risk peptic ulcer bleeding after successful endoscopic haemostasis, does scheduled second-look endoscopy reduce rebleeding versus on-demand endoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Hemostasis, Endoscopic · Humans · Male · Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage/surgery · Recurrence · Stomach Ulcer/complications/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the routine second look is a ritual the trials do not support. The 2024 systematic review pooled 10 randomised trials (1,513 patients) and found no difference in rebleeding (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–1.14), surgery (0.58, 0.29–1.15), mortality (0.89, 0.46–1.71) or transfusion (−0.01 units) between scheduled second-look and single endoscopy, at moderate quality of evidence. The 2022 trial that selected patients predicted to be at high risk of rebleeding — the subgroup most likely to benefit — likewise found no significant difference: clinical bleeding within 30 days in 11.8% with second-look versus 18.2% with observation (absolute difference 6.4%, −5.0 to 17.8), though 30.4% of scoped patients received further endoscopic treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): scheduled second-look endoscopy does not demonstrably reduce rebleeding after successful haemostasis; on-demand re-endoscopy for suspected rebleeding remains the fallback.

cards.headline: Pittayanon 2022: in patients predicted high-risk, 30-day bleeding 11.8% with scheduled second-look versus 18.2% with observation — not significant, trial stopped at half its target
cards.summary: Pittayanon 2022: in patients predicted high-risk, 30-day bleeding 11.8% with scheduled second-look versus 18.2% with observation — not significant, trial stopped at half its target
cards.people: 157 patients (of 314 planned) with bleeding peptic ulcers treated endoscopically who scored ≥5 on a validated 9-point rebleeding risk score (derived in 939 patients, validated in 1,334), randomised to scheduled second-look endoscopy (n=78) or observation alone (n=79); primary outcome clinical bleeding within 30 days.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 9/78 (11.8%) with second-look versus 14/79 (18.2%) with observation (absolute difference 6.4%, 95% CI −5.0 to 17.8 — not significant). Of patients scoped, 21/69 (30.4%) needed further endoscopic treatment. No patient needed surgery for bleeding; 30-day deaths were 6 versus 3 (p=0.285); transfusion and hospitalisation did not differ.

cards.result: Rebleeding: relative risk 0.78 (95% CI 0.53–1.14, moderate quality of evidence). Surgery: 0.58 (0.29–1.15). Mortality: 0.89 (0.46–1.71). Blood transfused: mean difference −0.01 units (−0.3 to 0.28, low quality). Sensitivity analyses matched the main results.

shelves.title: Adding Lactobacillus to H. pylori therapy: eradication relative risk 1.063 across 26 trials — a few extra cures per hundred, with genuinely fewer antibiotic side effects
shelves.question: Does adding a probiotic to standard eradication therapy improve Helicobacter pylori eradication rates and reduce antibiotic side effects?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Helicobacter Infections/drug therapy/microbiology · Probiotics/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Lactobacillus · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Helicobacter pylori/drug effects · Treatment Outcome · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a real but very small eradication gain, and a clearer side-effect gain. Pooling 26 randomised trials, the 2024 meta-analysis found Lactobacillus supplementation raised eradication rates with a per-protocol relative risk of 1.063 (p<0.001) — roughly a 6% relative improvement, a few extra eradications per 100 patients treated — with the clearest subgroup result for adding Lactobacillus to triple therapy (relative risk 1.124). Gastrointestinal side effects fell more substantially: diarrhoea relative risk 0.324, abdominal pain 0.438, nausea/vomiting 0.566, with no significant effect on bloating (0.820). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the eradication effect is too small to change regimen choice, and this record's own reporting is internally inconsistent (its printed confidence intervals do not match its risk ratios), so the shelf claims only a modest adjunctive nudge, mostly on tolerability.

cards.headline: Mishra 2024 (26 RCTs): eradication RR 1.063 per-protocol; diarrhoea RR 0.324, abdominal pain RR 0.438, nausea/vomiting RR 0.566 versus therapy alone
cards.summary: Mishra 2024 (26 RCTs): eradication RR 1.063 per-protocol; diarrhoea RR 0.324, abdominal pain RR 0.438, nausea/vomiting RR 0.566 versus therapy alone
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mishra 2024, Lactobacillus in H. pylori eradication)
cards.people: 26 randomised trials of Lactobacillus species supplementation added to standard H. pylori eradication therapy versus the same therapy without supplementation, in adults and children; trial sequential analysis and GRADEpro assessments reported by the authors.
cards.result: Eradication was higher with Lactobacillus: per-protocol relative risk 1.063 (p=0.000 as printed); in adults 1.050 and in children 1.223. Added to triple therapy, the relative risk was 1.124. L. reuteri (1.049, p=0.055) looked better than Lactobacillus GG (0.980, p=0.595). Side effects fell: nausea/vomiting relative risk 0.566 (p=0.037), diarrhoea 0.324 (p=0.000), abdominal pain 0.438 (p=0.007); bloating 0.820 (p=0.498, not significant).
cards.watchOut: The abstract's printed 95% confidence intervals are garbled — intervals such as '−0.21 to 2.11' cannot belong to these risk ratios — so the precision of every estimate here is unverifiable from the record itself. A 6% relative eradication gain is also far inside the range where small-study and publication biases operate in probiotic literatures.
cards.source: Mishra V et al. Efficacy of Lactobacillus spp. Supplementation in Helicobacter pylori Eradication: A Systematic Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials With Trial Sequential Analysis. Helicobacter. 2024. shelves.title: Pancreatic enzyme replacement in chronic pancreatitis: fat absorption rose from about 67% to 83% of intake versus placebo across the trials — nutrition and pain improved, on heterogeneous small studies
shelves.question: In chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency, does pancreatic enzyme replacement improve fat absorption, nutrition and pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Fats/metabolism · Enzyme Therapy · Enzymes/administration & dosage · Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Feces/chemistry · Humans · Nutritional Status · Pancreas/enzymology · Pancreatitis, Chronic/blood/complications/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the physiology works in the trials, with wide scatter. The 2017 systematic review pooled 17 studies (511 patients with chronic pancreatitis and exocrine insufficiency): the coefficient of fat absorption on enzyme replacement was 83.2% versus 67.4% on placebo (p=0.0001), and 83.7% versus a 63.1% baseline without treatment (p<0.00001). Enzyme replacement also improved nitrogen absorption, reduced faecal fat, faecal weight and abdominal pain, and follow-up studies showed better nutritional parameters, symptoms and quality of life, without significant adverse events. Heterogeneity was very high (I²=86–89%), and high-dose or enteric-coated preparations trended better. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): enzyme replacement demonstrably corrects fat malabsorption in chronic pancreatitis; the size of the gain in any one patient varies far more than the pooled average suggests.

cards.headline: de la Iglesia-García 2017 (17 studies, 511 patients): fat absorption 83.2% on enzymes versus 67.4% on placebo (p=0.0001); pain and faecal fat also improved
cards.summary: de la Iglesia-García 2017 (17 studies, 511 patients): fat absorption 83.2% on enzymes versus 67.4% on placebo (p=0.0001); pain and faecal fat also improved
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (de la Iglesia-García 2017, PERT in chronic pancreatitis)
cards.people: 17 randomised studies (511 patients) of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency from chronic pancreatitis, 14 contributing quantitative data; primary outcome the coefficient of fat absorption; doses, formulations and schedules varied.
cards.result: Coefficient of fat absorption was 83.2±5.5% on enzyme replacement versus 67.4±7.0% on placebo (p=0.0001; I²=86%), and 83.7±6.0% versus 63.1±15.0% at untreated baseline (p<0.00001; I²=89%). Enzyme replacement also improved the coefficient of nitrogen absorption and reduced faecal fat excretion, faecal nitrogen, faecal weight and abdominal pain, without significant adverse events; follow-up studies showed improved serum nutritional parameters, gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Fat absorption is a laboratory surrogate measured over days in metabolic-ward conditions, and I² of 86–89% means the component trials disagree wildly about the size of the effect — sample size, diagnostic criteria, study design and dose all contributed. Long-term outcomes (weight trajectories, bone health, survival) are not in this record.
cards.source: de la Iglesia-García D et al. Efficacy of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy in chronic pancreatitis: systematic review and meta-analysis. Gut. 2017. PMID: 27941156. shelves.title: Vonoprazan for non-erosive reflux heartburn: 44.8% of days heartburn-free versus 27.7% on placebo over 4 weeks — no PPI comparison in the trial
shelves.question: In non-erosive reflux disease, does vonoprazan relieve heartburn versus placebo — and versus a proton pump inhibitor?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Pyrroles/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Sulfonamides/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Heartburn/drug therapy · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Adult · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy · Aged · Placebos/administration & dosage · United States · Young Adult · Double-Blind Method · Non-Erosive Reflux Disease
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — versus placebo, clearly; versus a PPI, this record says nothing. In the US randomised trial of 772 patients with non-erosive reflux disease, the percentage of 24-hour heartburn-free days over 4 weeks was 44.8% on vonoprazan 10 mg and 44.4% on 20 mg versus 27.7% on placebo (least-squares mean differences 17.1% and 16.7%, both P<.0001), with separation already on day 1 (8.3% and 11.6% more patients heartburn-free) and benefit persisting through the 20-week extension (61–63% heartburn-free days). The two doses were indistinguishable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vonoprazan relieves heartburn in non-erosive reflux disease against placebo in a single trial; the head-to-head against a PPI that the question also asks about was not tested here and remains open.

cards.headline: Laine 2024: heartburn-free days 44.8% (10 mg) and 44.4% (20 mg) versus 27.7% on placebo (P<.0001), benefit from day 1 and sustained to week 24
cards.summary: Laine 2024: heartburn-free days 44.8% (10 mg) and 44.4% (20 mg) versus 27.7% on placebo (P<.0001), benefit from day 1 and sustained to week 24
cards.type: Randomised trial (Laine 2024, vonoprazan in non-erosive reflux disease)
cards.people: 772 US adults with heartburn at least 4 days per week and no erosive oesophagitis on endoscopy, randomised to placebo, vonoprazan 10 mg or vonoprazan 20 mg daily for 4 weeks, followed by a 20-week active-treatment extension (placebo patients re-randomised to vonoprazan); symptoms recorded in twice-daily electronic diaries.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — percentage of 24-hour heartburn-free days over 4 weeks — was 27.7% on placebo versus 44.8% on vonoprazan 10 mg (least-squares mean difference 17.1%, P<.0001) and 44.4% on 20 mg (difference 16.7%, P<.0001). The excess of patients with a heartburn-free day was 8.3% (10 mg) and 11.6% (20 mg) on day 1 and 18.1% and 23.2% on day 2. Over the extension, heartburn-free days averaged 61–63% across arms.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-diary endpoint over 4 placebo-controlled weeks in a condition with a 27.7% placebo response; there is no PPI comparator arm, so the trial cannot place vonoprazan against the standard drug class, and the flat dose-response (10 mg = 20 mg) argues for the lower dose only.
cards.source: Laine L et al. Vonoprazan is Efficacious for Treatment of Heartburn in Non-erosive Reflux Disease: A Randomized Trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2024. PMID: 38750866. shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a pilot trial whose parts point in different directions. In 34 patients with functional dyspepsia and over 10% weight loss, mirtazapine 15 mg reduced dyspepsia symptom severity from baseline at weeks 4 and 8 (P=.003 and P=.017) while placebo did not — but the between-group difference in change, the comparison that matters, was only a trend at week 4 (P=.059) and not significant at week 8 (P=.55). Improvements from baseline were significantly larger on mirtazapine than placebo for early satiation, quality of life, gastrointestinal-specific anxiety, weight and nutrient tolerance, mostly with large effect sizes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): in this selected subgroup (weight loss without depression or anxiety), mirtazapine plausibly helps the early-satiation/weight cluster of symptoms; a 34-patient pilot with a missed primary-style comparison cannot carry more than MAYBE.

cards.headline: Tack 2016 (pilot, n=34): mirtazapine improved early satiation, weight, quality of life and nutrient tolerance versus placebo — overall symptom change between groups P=.059 at week 4, P=.55 at week 8
cards.summary: Tack 2016 (pilot, n=34): mirtazapine improved early satiation, weight, quality of life and nutrient tolerance versus placebo — overall symptom change between groups P=.059 at week 4, P=.55 at week 8
cards.type: Randomised double-blind pilot trial (Tack 2016, mirtazapine in functional dyspepsia with weight loss)
cards.people: 34 patients (29 women, mean age 35.9 years) with functional dyspepsia and weight loss over 10% of original body weight (mean loss 12.4 kg), without depression or anxiety, randomised to mirtazapine 15 mg daily (n=17) or placebo (n=17) for 8 weeks after a run-in period; 2 patients per group dropped out.
cards.result: Mirtazapine reduced mean dyspepsia symptom severity versus week 0 at weeks 4 and 8 (P=.003 and P=.017); placebo did not (P>.37). The between-group difference in change showed a trend at week 4 (P=.059, large effect size) and was not significant at week 8 (P=.55). Improvements from week 0 to weeks 4 and 8 were significantly larger on mirtazapine for early satiation, quality of life, gastrointestinal-specific anxiety, weight and nutrient tolerance.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 34 patients, many endpoints, and the most global symptom comparison missed significance — the positive secondary endpoints are hypothesis-generating. Patients with depression or anxiety were excluded, so the result cannot be read as an antidepressant effect, nor extended to dyspepsia without weight loss.
cards.source: Tack J et al. Efficacy of Mirtazapine in Patients With Functional Dyspepsia and Weight Loss. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2016. PMID: 26538208. Registry ID: NCT01240096. shelves.title: Variceal bleeding prophylaxis: a network meta-analysis ranks carvedilol first among beta blockers for survival — but the mortality claim is indirect, and the direct win is on portal-pressure response
shelves.question: For primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, is carvedilol as effective as propranolol or other non-selective beta blockers?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — carvedilol looks at least as good as the older beta blockers everywhere, and better on the measures that are indirect. The 2023 network meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials (3,188 patients with gastroesophageal varices) found, against placebo, variceal-bleeding relative risks of 0.25 for nadolol, 0.33 for carvedilol and 0.52 for propranolol. Carvedilol beat propranolol directly on achieving a hepatic venous pressure gradient response (relative risk 0.43, 95% credible interval 0.26–0.69 for failure to respond), and ranked first for all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.32, 0.17–0.57 versus placebo) — a ranking built largely on indirect comparisons across trials of mixed primary and secondary prophylaxis, which is why the mortality part cannot be stamped as proven. PROPOSED SPLIT: for preventing variceal bleeding, carvedilol is at least propranolol's equal with a better portal-pressure response; the claimed survival advantage rests on network geometry, not on a head-to-head trial, and awaits one.

cards.headline: Cheung 2023 network meta-analysis (33 RCTs, 3,188 patients): carvedilol ranked first for mortality (RR 0.32 vs placebo) and beat propranolol on HVPG response (RR 0.43)
cards.summary: Cheung 2023 network meta-analysis (33 RCTs, 3,188 patients): carvedilol ranked first for mortality (RR 0.32 vs placebo) and beat propranolol on HVPG response (RR 0.43)
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cheung 2023, carvedilol versus other non-selective beta blockers)
cards.people: 33 randomised trials including 3,188 patients with cirrhosis and gastroesophageal varices, comparing carvedilol, propranolol, nadolol and placebo across primary and secondary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding; Bayesian network meta-analysis with SUCRA rankings.
cards.result: Variceal bleeding versus placebo: nadolol relative risk 0.25 (95% credible interval 0.11–0.51), carvedilol 0.33 (0.11–0.88), propranolol 0.52 (0.37–0.75). Carvedilol was more effective than propranolol at achieving a hepatic venous pressure gradient decremental response (relative risk 0.43, 0.26–0.69). All-cause mortality versus placebo: carvedilol ranked first (relative risk 0.32, 0.17–0.57; SUCRA 0.963), ahead of nadolol (0.48) and propranolol (0.77, interval crossing 1). The authors also ranked carvedilol safest, though adverse-event estimates were extremely imprecise (carvedilol relative risk 4.38, credible interval 0.33–161.4).
cards.watchOut: Network rankings are not head-to-head evidence: the mortality relative risk of 0.32 for a beta blocker in cirrhosis is larger than any single trial has shown and is assembled from indirect paths across trials mixing primary and secondary prophylaxis. The question asked about primary prophylaxis specifically; this record pools both settings.
cards.source: Cheung KS et al. Carvedilol Versus Other Nonselective Beta Blockers for Variceal Bleeding Prophylaxis and Death: A Network Meta-analysis. Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology. 2023. PMID: 37577228. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Synthesis: prescribe carvedilol on the pressure data if you like — do not quote the survival ranking as a trial result

shelves.title: Vaptans in cirrhosis: sodium rose by 1.8 mmol/L and ascites eased slightly — mortality and every cirrhosis complication were unchanged, and adverse events were four times as common
shelves.question: In cirrhosis with hyponatraemia or ascites, do vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists (vaptans) raise serum sodium and improve outcomes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Ascites/drug therapy · Benzamides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzazepines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyponatremia/blood/drug therapy · Liver Cirrhosis/drug therapy · Morpholines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrroles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Receptors, Vasopressin/administration & dosage · Sodium/blood · Spiro Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Tolvaptan · Treatment Outcome · Benzodiazepines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — to the outcomes that matter, with the harm on the face. The 2012 meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (2,266 patients with cirrhosis and ascites or hyponatraemia) found vaptans raised serum sodium by a weighted mean of 1.8 mmol/L (95% CI 0.79–2.96) and modestly reduced weight and time to first paracentesis — but mortality was unchanged (relative risk 1.06, 0.90–1.26), as were variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome and renal failure. Adverse events were more frequent on vaptans (relative risk 3.97, 1.78–8.83), including excessive urine volume (relative risk 9.96). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): vaptans correct the number and mobilise some water in cirrhosis, but no trial evidence shows they keep anyone alive or out of the complications that define the disease — and they add adverse events.

cards.headline: Dahl 2012 (12 RCTs, 2,266 patients): mortality RR 1.06 (0.90–1.26) and no effect on any cirrhosis complication; sodium +1.8 mmol/L; adverse events RR 3.97
cards.summary: Dahl 2012 (12 RCTs, 2,266 patients): mortality RR 1.06 (0.90–1.26) and no effect on any cirrhosis complication; sodium +1.8 mmol/L; adverse events RR 3.97
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Dahl 2012, vaptans in cirrhosis)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials (2,266 patients) of vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan, satavaptan, lixivaptan) versus control in cirrhosis with ascites or hyponatraemia; 8 trials double-blind; randomisation adequate in all; primary outcome mortality.
cards.result: Mortality: relative risk 1.06 (95% CI 0.90–1.26, I²=0%). No clear differences in variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome or renal failure. Serum sodium rose by a weighted mean difference of 1.8 mmol/L (0.79–2.96); weight fell and time to first paracentesis lengthened. Adverse events were more common on vaptans (relative risk 3.97, 1.78–8.83), including excessive urine volume (relative risk 9.96, 1.38–71.68). The authors concluded the data do not support routine vaptan use in cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: The trials pool three different drugs and two different indications (ascites and hyponatraemia), mostly short-term; a 1.8 mmol/L average sodium rise also conceals the minority who overcorrect, a risk the pooled adverse-event figures only partly capture.
cards.source: Dahl E et al. Meta-analysis: the safety and efficacy of vaptans (tolvaptan, satavaptan and lixivaptan) in cirrhosis with ascites or hyponatraemia. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2012. PMID: 22908905. shelves.title: Probiotic prophylaxis in predicted severe acute pancreatitis (PROPATRIA): infections unmoved at 30% versus 28% — and mortality doubled, 16% versus 6%, with bowel ischaemia in 9 patients versus none
shelves.question: In predicted severe acute pancreatitis, does probiotic prophylaxis prevent infectious complications — or increase mortality?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Pancreatitis/complications/prevention & control* · Placebos · Probiotics/therapeutic use* · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the prophylaxis did not prevent infection, and more patients died. In PROPATRIA (Besselink MG et al., PMID: 18279948), 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis were randomised within 72 hours of symptom onset to a multispecies probiotic preparation (n=153) or placebo (n=145), given enterally twice daily for 28 days; after one incorrect diagnosis was excluded in each group, 152 and 144 patients were analysed. The primary endpoint — the composite of infectious complications (infected pancreatic necrosis, bacteraemia, pneumonia, urosepsis, or infected ascites) during admission and 90-day follow-up — occurred in 46 patients (30%) on probiotics versus 41 (28%) on placebo (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.75–1.51): no benefit. Mortality went the other way: 24 patients (16%) in the probiotics group died, compared with 9 (6%) in the placebo group (relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.22–5.25). Nine patients in the probiotics group developed bowel ischaemia (eight with fatal outcome), compared with none in the placebo group (p=0.004). The authors' conclusion was plain: probiotic prophylaxis with this combination of probiotic strains did not reduce infectious complications, was associated with an increased risk of mortality, and should therefore not be administered in this category of patients. The record describes the intervention only as a multispecies probiotic preparation and names no branded product or company, so the harm is pinned to this preparation, given enterally in this dose schedule, in predicted severe disease — not to probiotics in milder illness. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in predicted severe acute pancreatitis, probiotic prophylaxis with the PROPATRIA multispecies preparation gave no reduction in infectious complications and doubled mortality, with a bowel-ischaemia signal that supplies a mechanism.

cards.headline: Besselink 2008 (PROPATRIA): infectious complications 30% on probiotics versus 28% on placebo (relative risk 1.06) — but deaths 16% versus 6% (relative risk 2.53), and bowel ischaemia 9 versus 0
cards.summary: Besselink 2008 (PROPATRIA): infectious complications 30% on probiotics versus 28% on placebo (relative risk 1.06) — but deaths 16% versus 6% (relative risk 2.53), and bowel ischaemia 9 versus 0
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Besselink 2008, PROPATRIA)
cards.people: 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation [APACHE II] score ≥8, Imrie score ≥3, or C-reactive protein >150 mg/L), randomly assigned within 72 hours of onset of symptoms to a multispecies probiotic preparation (n=153) or placebo (n=145), administered enterally twice daily for 28 days. One person in each group was excluded from analyses because of an incorrect diagnosis of pancreatitis, so 152 individuals in the probiotics group and 144 in the placebo group were analysed; groups were much the same at baseline in patient characteristics and disease severity, and analyses were by intention to treat.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — the composite of infectious complications (infected pancreatic necrosis, bacteraemia, pneumonia, urosepsis, or infected ascites) during admission and 90-day follow-up — occurred in 46 patients (30%) in the probiotics group and 41 (28%) in the placebo group (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.75–1.51), the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effect. Mortality was higher on probiotics: 24 patients (16%) died, compared with 9 (6%) on placebo (relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.22–5.25). Nine patients in the probiotics group developed bowel ischaemia (eight with fatal outcome), compared with none in the placebo group (p=0.004). The authors concluded that probiotic prophylaxis with this combination of probiotic strains did not reduce the risk of infectious complications, was associated with an increased risk of mortality, and should therefore not be administered in this category of patients.
cards.watchOut: Mortality was not the primary endpoint — the primary composite of infectious complications was null — so the doubled mortality rests on one trial's secondary finding, albeit one with a visible mechanism (bowel ischaemia in 9 patients versus none, 8 of them fatal) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design. The harm also belongs to this preparation and this setting: a multispecies probiotic given enterally twice daily for 28 days to patients with predicted severe disease. The fetched record names no branded product or company for the preparation, so no commercial product is named on this shelf, and the result does not convict probiotics in milder illness.
cards.source: Besselink MG et al. Probiotic prophylaxis in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2008. PMID: 18279948. Registry ID: ISRCTN38327949. cards.headline: Synthesis: one definitive double-blind trial — no infection benefit, doubled mortality, and a bowel-ischaemia mechanism — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: one definitive double-blind trial — no infection benefit, doubled mortality, and a bowel-ischaemia mechanism — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis (PROPATRIA), testing a multispecies probiotic preparation given enterally twice daily for 28 days against placebo, with 152 and 144 patients analysed.
cards.result: Infectious complications: 46 patients (30%) on probiotics versus 41 (28%) on placebo (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.75–1.51) — no benefit on the primary endpoint. Mortality: 24 patients (16%) versus 9 (6%) (relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.22–5.25). Bowel ischaemia: 9 patients on probiotics (eight with fatal outcome) versus none on placebo (p=0.004). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: PROPATRIA (Besselink MG et al., PMID: 18279948) is also carded as a harm card on live shelf #98 (Feeding acute pancreatitis early), where it serves as the warning card inside a broader feeding-timing and feeding-route question. This shelf asks the standalone probiotics question — in predicted severe acute pancreatitis, does probiotic prophylaxis prevent infectious complications or increase mortality — a genuinely different question, built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH) and #3489 (CAROLINA): a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf and the claim is a mortality harm claim.

shelves.title: Predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis: urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy did not reduce death or major complications (38% versus 44%, p=0.37) — cholangitis was the only component that fell
shelves.question: In predicted severe acute gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis, does urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy improve outcomes versus conservative treatment?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde/methods · Combined Modality Therapy · Conservative Treatment/methods · Female · Gallstones/complications/etiology/therapy · Humans · Male · Pancreatitis/therapy · Sphincterotomy, Endoscopic/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one multicentre randomised trial, adequately sized for its composite, says wait. In APEC, the composite of mortality or major complications within 6 months occurred in 45/117 (38%) with urgent ERCP and sphincterotomy (within 24 hours) versus 50/113 (44%) with conservative treatment (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.64–1.18, p=0.37), with no relevant differences in any component except cholangitis itself (2% vs 10%; relative risk 0.18, 0.04–0.78). Adverse events were reported in 74% versus 80%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): without cholangitis or persistent cholestasis, urgent ERCP does not improve outcomes in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis — conservative care with ERCP reserved for cholangitis is the strategy the trial supports.

cards.headline: APEC: primary composite 38% urgent ERCP versus 44% conservative (RR 0.87, p=0.37); cholangitis 2% versus 10% (RR 0.18)
cards.summary: APEC: primary composite 38% urgent ERCP versus 44% conservative (RR 0.87, p=0.37); cholangitis 2% versus 10% (RR 0.18)
cards.people: 232 patients with predicted severe acute gallstone pancreatitis (APACHE II ≥8, Imrie ≥3, or CRP >150 mg/L) without cholangitis, at 26 Dutch hospitals, randomised to urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy within 24 hours of presentation (n=118) or conservative treatment (n=114), with ERCP in the conservative arm reserved for cholangitis or persistent cholestasis; primary endpoint a 6-month composite of mortality or major complications; outcome assessors masked.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 45/117 (38%) in the urgent-ERCP group versus 50/113 (44%) in the conservative group (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.64–1.18, p=0.37). No individual component differed relevantly except cholangitis: 2/117 (2%) versus 11/113 (10%) (relative risk 0.18, 0.04–0.78, p=0.010). Adverse events were reported in 87/118 (74%) versus 91/114 (80%).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its confidence interval (0.64–1.18) cannot exclude a moderate benefit; 'predicted severe' enrols a mix in whom many would never have developed complications, diluting any effect concentrated in truly obstructed patients — but cholangitis, the one clear signal, is exactly the group already carved out for ERCP.
cards.source: Schepers NJ et al. Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy versus conservative treatment in predicted severe acute gallstone pancreatitis (APEC): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 32682482. Registry ID: ISRCTN97372133. shelves.title: Gallstone dissolution: adding chenodeoxycholic acid to ursodeoxycholic acid gained nothing — complete dissolution at 2 years 30% versus 28% on ursodeoxycholic acid alone, in a trial with no placebo arm
shelves.question: In adults with cholesterol gallstones, does ursodeoxycholic acid — alone or with chenodeoxycholic acid — dissolve stones and prevent symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chenodeoxycholic Acid/administration & dosage · Cholelithiasis/drug therapy · Cholesterol/metabolism · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Solubility · Ursodeoxycholic Acid/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two regimens actually compared; the placebo question in this shelf's title was never put to a trial in this record. In the British-Italian Gallstone Study Group trial of 154 patients with radiolucent cholesterol stones up to 15 mm in functioning gallbladders, complete dissolution at 24 months was 28% on ursodeoxycholic acid alone (10 mg/kg/day) versus 30% on the combination with chenodeoxycholic acid (5 mg/kg/day each), with mean dissolution rates of 47% versus 44% at 6 months and 59% versus 59% at 12 months; biliary pain frequency fell on both regimens, with no significant difference in side effects or dropouts. Because there was no placebo or untreated arm, how much dissolution exceeds the natural history of small radiolucent stones cannot be read from this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): combination bile-acid therapy adds nothing to ursodeoxycholic acid alone for stone dissolution; the versus-placebo half of the question is flagged as untested by the anchor record.

cards.headline: British-Italian Gallstone Study (2001): complete dissolution 28% on UDCA alone versus 30% on UDCA + CDCA at 24 months; pain fell equally on both
cards.summary: British-Italian Gallstone Study (2001): complete dissolution 28% on UDCA alone versus 30% on UDCA + CDCA at 24 months; pain fell equally on both
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial (Petroni 2001, British-Italian Gallstone Study Group)
cards.people: 154 symptomatic patients at six centres in England and Italy with radiolucent cholesterol stones ≤15 mm in functioning gallbladders, randomised to ursodeoxycholic acid 10 mg/kg/day alone or ursodeoxycholic plus chenodeoxycholic acid 5 mg/kg/day each, with dissolution assessed by 6-monthly oral cholecystography and ultrasonography for up to 24 months.
cards.result: Complete gallstone dissolution (intention-to-treat) was 28% on ursodeoxycholic acid alone versus 30% on combination therapy at 24 months, with no significant difference at any time point. Mean dissolution rates were 47% versus 44% at 6 months and 59% versus 59% at 12 months. Both regimens reduced the frequency of biliary pain, with no significant difference between them in side effects or dropout rate.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or no-treatment arm: the 28–30% complete-dissolution figures cannot be separated from spontaneous changes in small radiolucent stones, and the enrolled population (small stones, functioning gallbladder, symptomatic) is the most favourable minority of gallstone patients. Recurrence after stopping therapy is outside this record.
cards.source: Petroni ML et al. Ursodeoxycholic acid alone or with chenodeoxycholic acid for dissolution of cholesterol gallstones: a randomized multicentre trial. The British-Italian Gallstone Study group. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2001. PMID: 11136285. shelves.title: Hepatitis C after direct-acting antiviral failure: sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir cured 96% versus 0% on placebo after NS5A-inhibitor failure, and 98% versus 90% against sofosbuvir–velpatasvir in POLARIS-4
shelves.question: In hepatitis C with prior direct-acting antiviral failure, does sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir achieve sustained virological response?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aminoisobutyric Acids · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carbamates/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cyclopropanes · Drug Combinations · Drug Resistance, Viral · Female · Genotype · Hepacivirus/drug effects/genetics · Hepatitis C/complications/drug therapy/virology · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Lactams, Macrocyclic · Leucine/analogs & derivatives · Liver Cirrhosis/etiology · Macrocyclic Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Proline/analogs & derivatives · Protease Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Quinoxalines · Sofosbuvir/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sulfonamides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Viral Nonstructural Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase · Benzimidazoles · Benzopyrans
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials in the hardest-to-cure population, with response rates near the ceiling. In POLARIS-1 (prior NS5A-inhibitor failure), sustained virological response was 96% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 0% on placebo. In POLARIS-4 (prior direct-acting antiviral failure without an NS5A inhibitor), response was 98% on the triple combination versus 90% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir. Across both trials 46% of actively treated patients had compensated cirrhosis, results spanned genotypes, and 1% or fewer discontinued for adverse events; the commonest events were headache, fatigue, diarrhoea and nausea. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): 12 weeks of sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir is a highly effective salvage regimen after direct-acting antiviral failure.

cards.headline: POLARIS-1: SVR 96% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 0% on placebo in patients who had failed an NS5A-inhibitor regimen
cards.summary: POLARIS-1: SVR 96% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 0% on placebo in patients who had failed an NS5A-inhibitor regimen
cards.people: Patients with chronic hepatitis C who had previously failed a regimen containing an NS5A inhibitor: genotype 1 patients randomised 1:1 to sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir (n=150) or placebo (n=150) once daily for 12 weeks; patients with other genotypes (n=114) enrolled directly into the triple-therapy group. 46% of actively treated patients across the programme had compensated cirrhosis.
cards.result: Sustained virological response was 96% with sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 0% with placebo. The most common adverse events were headache, fatigue, diarrhoea and nausea, and the proportion discontinuing for adverse events in the active-treatment groups was 1% or lower.
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparator in a population with no approved salvage option makes the contrast stark but uninformative about relative efficacy against other salvage strategies; sustained virological response is a validated surrogate for cure, not a directly measured clinical outcome in this trial.
cards.source: Bourlière M et al. Sofosbuvir, Velpatasvir, and Voxilaprevir for Previously Treated HCV Infection. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28564569. cards.summary: POLARIS-4: SVR 98% on the triple combination versus 90% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir after non-NS5A direct-acting antiviral failure
cards.people: Patients with hepatitis C genotypes 1, 2 or 3 who had failed a direct-acting antiviral regimen not containing an NS5A inhibitor, randomised to sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir (n=163) or sofosbuvir–velpatasvir (n=151) for 12 weeks; 19 additional genotype-4 patients received the triple combination.
cards.result: Sustained virological response was 98% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 90% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir. Adverse events mirrored POLARIS-1 (headache, fatigue, diarrhoea, nausea predominating), with discontinuation for adverse events at 1% or lower in the active-treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: The 8-point gap over an already potent two-drug regimen is the trial's real clinical content; subgroup numbers by genotype and resistance pattern are small, and patients with decompensated cirrhosis were not the population studied.

cards.headline: Synthesis: salvage therapy that succeeds in 96–98% — the post-failure problem is largely solved for compensated disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: salvage therapy that succeeds in 96–98% — the post-failure problem is largely solved for compensated disease
cards.people: Two phase 3 trials (POLARIS-1 and POLARIS-4) totalling over 700 previously treated patients, 46% with compensated cirrhosis, reported in a single record.
cards.result: Sustained virological response: 96% vs 0% (placebo, after NS5A failure) and 98% vs 90% (sofosbuvir–velpatasvir, after non-NS5A failure). Discontinuation for adverse events ≤1%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials are one sponsor's programme in one publication, and the population excludes decompensated cirrhosis — the group in whom salvage is hardest and protease inhibitors are problematic.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bourlière M et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28564569), reporting POLARIS-1 and POLARIS-4.

shelves.title: Gastroparesis drugs ranked: only oral dopamine antagonists and tachykinin-1 antagonists beat placebo in a 29-trial network meta-analysis — clebopride first, domperidone second, confidence low to moderate
shelves.question: In gastroparesis, do prokinetic and antiemetic drugs — including domperidone — improve symptoms versus placebo, and how do they rank?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Gastroparesis/drug therapy · Nausea/chemically induced/drug therapy · Dopamine Antagonists/therapeutic use · Tachykinins/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for two drug classes only, on low-to-moderate confidence evidence. In a network meta-analysis of 29 randomised trials (3,772 patients), clebopride ranked first for global gastroparesis symptoms (relative risk of not improving 0.30, 95% CI 0.16–0.57) and domperidone second (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.98); no other drug was superior to placebo. At class level, oral dopamine antagonists (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77) and tachykinin-1 antagonists (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52–0.93) were the only efficacious classes. Oral metoclopramide ranked first for nausea, fullness and bloating, but on only one small trial. Only prucalopride was more likely than placebo to cause adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dopamine antagonists (domperidone the best-evidenced familiar name) and tachykinin-1 antagonists improve global gastroparesis symptoms; most other tested drugs did not beat placebo.

cards.headline: Ingrosso 2023 network meta-analysis (29 RCTs, 3,772 patients): clebopride RR 0.30 and domperidone RR 0.68 for not improving; only dopamine-antagonist and tachykinin-1 classes efficacious
cards.summary: Ingrosso 2023 network meta-analysis (29 RCTs, 3,772 patients): clebopride RR 0.30 and domperidone RR 0.68 for not improving; only dopamine-antagonist and tachykinin-1 classes efficacious
cards.people: 29 randomised controlled trials totalling 3,772 patients with gastroparesis, testing prokinetic and antiemetic drugs against placebo or each other, searched to 7 September 2022; efficacy judged on global symptoms and on nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloating and fullness, analysed intention-to-treat with dropouts counted as treatment failures.
cards.result: For global symptoms, clebopride ranked first (relative risk of not improving 0.30, 95% CI 0.16–0.57; P-score 0.99), followed by domperidone (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.98; P-score 0.76); no other drug was superior to placebo. By class, oral dopamine antagonists (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77) and tachykinin-1 antagonists (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52–0.93) were the only efficacious classes. Oral metoclopramide ranked first for nausea (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.21–1.00), fullness (RR 0.67) and bloating (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30–0.93), based on only one small trial. Only prucalopride was more likely to be associated with adverse events than placebo.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis leans heavily on indirect comparisons, and the authors rate confidence in the evidence as low to moderate for most comparisons; the top-ranked drug, clebopride, is not widely available, and the metoclopramide symptom rankings rest on a single small trial.
cards.source: Ingrosso MR et al. Efficacy and Safety of Drugs for Gastroparesis: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. Gastroenterology. 2023. PMID: 36581089. cards.headline: Synthesis: a two-class answer — dopamine antagonists and tachykinin-1 antagonists work, the rest of the shelf did not beat placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: a two-class answer — dopamine antagonists and tachykinin-1 antagonists work, the rest of the shelf did not beat placebo
cards.people: One network meta-analysis of 29 randomised trials (3,772 patients) in gastroparesis, searched to September 2022.
cards.result: Global symptoms: clebopride RR of not improving 0.30 (95% CI 0.16–0.57), domperidone 0.68 (0.48–0.98); class effects — oral dopamine antagonists 0.58 (0.44–0.77), tachykinin-1 antagonists 0.69 (0.52–0.93). No other drug superior to placebo; only prucalopride carried more adverse events than placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), confidence low to moderate for most comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Rankings from indirect evidence can flatter little-studied drugs (clebopride's first place rests on far less data than domperidone's second). The honest clinical read is class-level: dopamine antagonists first, tachykinin-1 antagonists second, everything else unproven against placebo.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ingrosso MR et al. Gastroenterology. 2023 (PMID: 36581089).

shelves.title: Tegaserod in women under 65 with IBS-C and no cardiovascular disease: response 44.1% versus 36.5% on placebo across four pooled trials — a real but modest edge, in a drug once withdrawn over cardiac fears
shelves.question: In women under 65 with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and no cardiovascular disease, does tegaserod improve global IBS symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Constipation/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Indoles/therapeutic use · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Serotonin Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, and confined to the population the FDA re-approved it for. Pooling four 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trials of tegaserod 6 mg twice daily in IBS-C, the indicated population (women younger than 65 with no history of cardiovascular ischaemic events; 2,752 participants) responded at 44.1% on tegaserod versus 36.5% on placebo (pooled odds ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.18–1.61; p<0.001); the overall female population (2,939 participants) responded at 43.3% versus 35.9% (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.18–1.59). Adverse events were similar between groups, and no significant cardiovascular events related to tegaserod were observed in patients with at most one cardiac risk factor. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tegaserod lifts global IBS-C response by roughly 8 percentage points over placebo in women under 65 without cardiovascular disease.

cards.headline: Shah 2021 pooled analysis of 4 RCTs (2,939 women): response 43.3% vs 35.9% overall and 44.1% vs 36.5% in women <65 without cardiovascular ischaemic history (OR 1.38)
cards.summary: Shah 2021 pooled analysis of 4 RCTs (2,939 women): response 43.3% vs 35.9% overall and 44.1% vs 36.5% in women <65 without cardiovascular ischaemic history (OR 1.38)
cards.people: 2,939 women with IBS-C in four 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trials of tegaserod 6 mg twice daily (tegaserod n=1,478; placebo n=1,461), including the FDA-indicated subgroup of 2,752 women younger than 65 years without a history of cardiovascular ischaemic events (tegaserod n=1,386; placebo n=1,366). Primary endpoint: subjective global assessment of IBS-C symptom relief over the last 4 weeks.
cards.result: Clinical response during the last 4 weeks was 43.3% on tegaserod versus 35.9% on placebo in the overall population (pooled odds ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.18–1.59; p<0.001) and 44.1% versus 36.5% in the indicated population (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.18–1.61; p<0.001). Adverse events were similar between groups, and no significant cardiovascular events related to tegaserod were observed in patients with ≤1 cardiac risk factor.
cards.watchOut: The trials were performed almost 20 years before this pooled re-analysis, the responder definition is a subjective global rating, and the absolute gain is about 8 percentage points — roughly one extra responder per 13 women treated. The cardiovascular reassurance applies only to the low-risk indicated population, not to women with ischaemic history, who are excluded.
cards.source: Shah ED et al. Tegaserod for Irritable Bowel Syndrome With Constipation in Women Younger Than 65 Years Without Cardiovascular Disease: Pooled Analyses of 4 Controlled Trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: four concordant trials, one modest responder gain, eligibility is the whole story
cards.summary: Synthesis: four concordant trials, one modest responder gain, eligibility is the whole story
cards.people: Four 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trials pooled (2,939 women with IBS-C; 2,752 in the indicated under-65, no-cardiovascular-disease population).
cards.result: Response on tegaserod 6 mg twice daily versus placebo: 44.1% vs 36.5% (indicated population, OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.18–1.61) and 43.3% vs 35.9% (overall, OR 1.37). Adverse events similar to placebo within the low-cardiovascular-risk population studied. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tegaserod's history — market withdrawal over cardiovascular concern, then restricted re-approval — means the population restriction is not fine print but the finding's boundary: nothing here speaks to men, to women 65 or older, or to anyone with cardiovascular ischaemic history.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shah ED et al. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2021 (PMID: 34047303).

shelves.title: Norursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis: alkaline phosphatase fell 12–26% dose-dependently over 12 weeks versus a 1.2% rise on placebo — a blood test, in a disease with no proven therapy
shelves.question: In primary sclerosing cholangitis, does norursodeoxycholic acid improve cholestasis biochemistry versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Cholangitis, Sclerosing/drug therapy · Cholestasis/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ursodeoxycholic Acid/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cholestasis biochemistry only, from a single 12-week phase 2 trial. In 161 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), norursodeoxycholic acid (norUDCA) reduced ALP by −12.3%, −17.3% and −26.0% at 500, 1,000 and 1,500 mg/day (p=0.029, p=0.003 and p<0.0001 versus placebo), while placebo rose +1.2%; secondary enzymes (ALT, AST, γ-GT) moved the same dose-dependent way. Serious adverse events were scattered across arms (seven, five and two patients on ascending norUDCA doses, three on placebo) with no difference in pruritus. No clinical outcome — transplant, decompensation, death — was or could be tested in 12 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): norUDCA lowers ALP dose-dependently with a placebo-like safety profile; whether that buys liver outcomes is a phase 3 question.

cards.headline: Fickert 2017 phase 2 RCT (n=161): ALP −12.3%, −17.3%, −26.0% across norUDCA doses versus +1.2% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Fickert 2017 phase 2 RCT (n=161): ALP −12.3%, −17.3%, −26.0% across norUDCA doses versus +1.2% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.people: 161 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis without concomitant ursodeoxycholic acid therapy and with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, recruited at 38 centres in 12 European countries, randomised to oral norUDCA 500, 1,000 or 1,500 mg/day or placebo for 12 weeks plus 4 weeks' follow-up. Primary endpoint: mean relative change in ALP.
cards.result: ALP fell by −12.3% (500 mg/day, p=0.029), −17.3% (1,000 mg/day, p=0.003) and −26.0% (1,500 mg/day, p<0.0001) versus a +1.2% rise on placebo. Secondary endpoints — ALT, AST, γ-GT and the rate of patients reaching ALP <1.5× the upper limit of normal — showed similar dose-dependent results. Serious adverse events occurred in seven patients on 500 mg/day, five on 1,000 mg/day, two on 1,500 mg/day and three on placebo; reported pruritus did not differ between treatment and placebo.
cards.watchOut: ALP is a surrogate in PSC — a prognostic marker, but lowering it has never itself been shown to delay transplant or death — and 12 weeks in 161 patients cannot speak to fibrosis, cancer or survival. A single phase 2 trial carries this shelf, so it is Tier C.
cards.source: Fickert P et al. norUrsodeoxycholic acid improves cholestasis in primary sclerosing cholangitis. Journal of Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 28529147. Registry ID: NCT01755507. shelves.title: Maralixibat in childhood PFIC (MARCH-PFIC): itch scores fell 1.1 points more than placebo and serum bile acids by 187 µmol/L more — with diarrhoea in 57% versus 20%
shelves.question: In progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, does maralixibat reduce pruritus and serum bile acids versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Male · Female · Cholestasis, Intrahepatic/drug therapy/blood · Child · Adolescent · Child, Preschool · Infant · Pruritus/etiology/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · ATP Binding Cassette Transporter, Subfamily B, Member 11/genetics · ATP Binding Cassette Transporter, Subfamily B/deficiency
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial in a rare childhood disease, hitting both its symptom and its biomarker endpoint. In MARCH-PFIC (93 children aged 1–17 years with PFIC and persistent pruritus), maralixibat improved morning itch scores in the primary BSEP cohort by −1.7 points versus −0.6 on placebo (between-group difference −1.1, 95% CI −1.8 to −0.3; p=0.0063) and cut total serum bile acids by −176 µmol/L versus a rise of 11 µmol/L on placebo (difference −187 µmol/L, 95% CI −293 to −80; p=0.0013). The price was gastrointestinal: diarrhoea in 57% on maralixibat versus 20% on placebo, all mild or moderate and mostly transient; serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 11% versus 7%, with no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): maralixibat relieves PFIC pruritus and lowers bile acids over 26 weeks; longer-term liver outcomes rest on the bile-acid surrogate.

cards.headline: Miethke 2024 MARCH-PFIC (n=93): itch −1.7 vs −0.6 and bile acids −176 vs +11 µmol/L in the BSEP cohort — diarrhoea 57% vs 20%
cards.summary: Miethke 2024 MARCH-PFIC (n=93): itch −1.7 vs −0.6 and bile acids −176 vs +11 µmol/L in the BSEP cohort — diarrhoea 57% vs 20%
cards.people: 93 children aged 1–17 years (median 3.0 years; 55% female) with progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis and persistent pruritus, at 29 centres in 16 countries, randomised to oral maralixibat (starting 142.5 µg/kg, escalated to 570 µg/kg twice daily; n=47) or placebo (n=46) for 26 weeks. The primary BSEP cohort held 14 maralixibat and 17 placebo participants with non-truncated BSEP deficiency.
cards.result: In the BSEP cohort, least-squares mean change in morning ItchRO(Obs) itch score was −1.7 (95% CI −2.3 to −1.2) on maralixibat versus −0.6 (−1.1 to −0.1) on placebo — difference −1.1 (95% CI −1.8 to −0.3; p=0.0063). Total serum bile acids changed by −176 µmol/L (95% CI −257 to −94) versus +11 µmol/L (−58 to 80) — difference −187 µmol/L (95% CI −293 to −80; p=0.0013). Diarrhoea occurred in 27 of 47 (57%) on maralixibat versus 9 of 46 (20%) on placebo, all mild or moderate and mostly transient; serious treatment-emergent adverse events in five (11%) versus three (7%); no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: The primary cohort is small (31 children) because PFIC is rare and genotypically split; itch is observer-reported by caregivers, and the liver-survival claim rides on serum bile acids as a predictor, not on transplant-free survival measured in this 26-week trial. A single trial carries the shelf — Tier C.
