shelves.title: Naldemedine for opioid-induced constipation (COMPOSE-1 and COMPOSE-2): responders 47.6% and 52.5% versus 34.6% and 33.6% on placebo — pain relief untouched, gut side effects the cost
shelves.question: In opioid-induced constipation with chronic non-cancer pain, does naldemedine increase spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo without worsening pain?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Chronic Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Constipation/chemically induced/drug therapy · Defecation/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Receptors, Opioid, mu/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two identical phase 3 trials, one answer. In COMPOSE-1 (547 patients with chronic non-cancer pain and opioid-induced constipation), responders — at least three spontaneous bowel movements a week with an increase of at least one over baseline, sustained — were 47.6% on naldemedine 0.2 mg daily versus 34.6% on placebo (difference 13.0%, 95% CI 4.8–21.3; p=0.002); in COMPOSE-2 (553 patients), 52.5% versus 33.6% (difference 18.9%, 95% CI 10.8–27.0; p<0.0001). Overall adverse-event rates matched placebo (49–50% versus 45–48%); the excess was gastrointestinal — treatment-related gut events in 15–16% on naldemedine versus 7% on placebo. As a peripherally acting antagonist, naldemedine is designed not to reach the central receptors that carry analgesia, and the trials enrolled patients on stable opioid regimens. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): naldemedine converts roughly one in six to eight treated patients into responders over placebo, at the price of gut upset in about one in twelve.

cards.headline: Hale 2017 COMPOSE-1 (n=547): responders 47.6% on naldemedine vs 34.6% on placebo (difference 13.0%, p=0.002)
cards.summary: Hale 2017 COMPOSE-1 (n=547): responders 47.6% on naldemedine vs 34.6% on placebo (difference 13.0%, p=0.002)
cards.people: 547 adults aged 18–80 with chronic non-cancer pain on a stable opioid regimen (at least 30 mg morphine equivalents daily for at least a month), not using laxatives, at 68 outpatient sites in seven countries in Europe and the USA, randomised to oral naldemedine 0.2 mg or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. A responder had ≥3 spontaneous bowel movements per week and an increase of ≥1 per week over baseline for at least 9 of 12 weeks, including at least 3 of the last 4.
cards.result: Responders: 130 of 273 (47.6%) on naldemedine versus 94 of 272 (34.6%) on placebo — difference 13.0% (95% CI 4.8–21.3; p=0.002). Adverse events occurred in 132 of 271 (49%) on naldemedine versus 123 of 272 (45%) on placebo; treatment-related events in 59 (22%) versus 45 (17%), largely gastrointestinal disorders (40 [15%] versus 18 [7%]).
cards.watchOut: The responder definition is a constructed bowel-frequency threshold, not a patient-global outcome, and the enrolled patients were laxative-free by design — real-world opioid-induced constipation usually arrives after laxatives have already been tried. Industry-funded (Shionogi & Co, Ltd).

cards.people: Two randomised double-blind phase 3 trials totalling 1,100 adults with chronic non-cancer pain and opioid-induced constipation, naldemedine 0.2 mg daily versus placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Responders 47.6% vs 34.6% (COMPOSE-1) and 52.5% vs 33.6% (COMPOSE-2); overall adverse events matched placebo (49–50% vs 45–48%), with treatment-related gastrointestinal events at 15–16% vs 7%. shelves.title: Green kiwifruit, prunes or psyllium for chronic constipation: all three raised complete spontaneous bowel movements in one small 4-week trial — kiwifruit best tolerated, none proven better than another
shelves.question: In chronic constipation, how do green kiwifruit, psyllium and prunes compare for stool frequency and gastrointestinal comfort?
shelves.mesh: Actinidia · Adult · Chronic Disease · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Constipation/diet therapy · Female · Fruit · Humans · Male · Prunus · Psyllium/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — three familiar foods all helped in one small, short, unblinded trial, and none beat the others. In 79 US adults with chronic constipation randomised to green kiwifruit (2/day), prunes (100 g/day) or psyllium (12 g/day) for 4 weeks, the proportions meeting the primary responder endpoint (an increase of at least one complete spontaneous bowel movement per week for at least 2 of 4 weeks) were similar across groups, while weekly complete spontaneous bowel movement rates rose significantly with all three treatments (p≤0.003). Stool consistency improved with kiwifruit (p=0.01) and prunes (p=0.049); straining improved with all three. Adverse events were most common with psyllium and least with kiwifruit, and fewer kiwifruit patients were dissatisfied at the end of treatment (p=0.02). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): each of the three is a reasonable first food-based step for chronic constipation; superiority of any one is unproven.

cards.headline: Chey 2021 comparative-effectiveness trial (n=79): responder proportions similar across kiwifruit, prunes and psyllium; all three raised weekly CSBM rate (p≤0.003)
cards.summary: Chey 2021 comparative-effectiveness trial (n=79): responder proportions similar across kiwifruit, prunes and psyllium; all three raised weekly CSBM rate (p≤0.003)
cards.people: 79 adults with chronic constipation (≤3 complete spontaneous bowel movements per week; mean age 42.7 years, 87% female) at a US medical centre, partially randomised to green kiwifruit 2/day, prunes 100 g/day or psyllium 12 g/day for 4 weeks; complete data in 75 (kiwifruit 29, prunes 24, psyllium 22). Primary endpoint: increase of ≥1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM) per week over baseline for at least 2 of 4 treatment weeks.
cards.result: Proportions of CSBM responders were similar for the three treatments on the primary endpoint. Comparing treatment weeks 3–4 with baseline, weekly CSBM rate increased significantly with all three (p≤0.003); stool consistency improved significantly with kiwifruit (p=0.01) and prunes (p=0.049); straining improved with kiwifruit (p=0.003), prunes (p<0.001) and psyllium (p=0.04). Bloating scores improved significantly only in the kiwifruit group (p=0.02). Adverse events were most common with psyllium and least common with kiwifruit; a smaller proportion of kiwifruit patients were dissatisfied with treatment (p=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Exploratory, partially randomised, unblinded (foods cannot be blinded), 4 weeks long and powered for none of the between-food comparisons — 'similar' here means 'not shown to differ in 79 people', not equivalence. The abstract reports significance levels rather than the responder percentages, so effect sizes cannot be quoted from this record. Single small trial — Tier C.
cards.source: Chey SW et al. Exploratory Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Green Kiwifruit, Psyllium, or Prunes in US Patients With Chronic Constipation. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2021. PMID: 34074830. Registry ID: NCT03569527. shelves.title: Liraglutide in NASH without needing diabetes (LEAN): steatohepatitis resolved in 39% versus 9% on placebo — in 45 biopsied patients, with fibrosis progression in 9% versus 36%
shelves.question: In non-alcoholic steatohepatitis without diabetes, does liraglutide achieve resolution of steatohepatitis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incretins/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Injections, Subcutaneous · Liraglutide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/complications/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking relative effect on a very small base. In the LEAN trial, 52 overweight patients with clinical evidence of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (with or without diabetes) were randomised to liraglutide 1.8 mg daily or placebo for 48 weeks; among those with end-of-treatment biopsy, resolution of definite steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis occurred in 9 of 23 (39%) on liraglutide versus 2 of 22 (9%) on placebo (relative risk 4.3, 95% CI 1.0–17.7; p=0.019), and fibrosis progressed in 2 of 23 (9%) versus 8 of 22 (36%) (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1–1.0; p=0.04). Gastrointestinal disorders were commoner on liraglutide (81% versus 65% of patients), including diarrhoea in 38% versus 19%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): LEAN is a genuine proof of concept for GLP-1 therapy in steatohepatitis — and, at 45 biopsied patients, only a proof of concept.

cards.summary: Armstrong 2016 LEAN (n=52): NASH resolution 9/23 (39%) vs 2/22 (9%), RR 4.3 (p=0.019); fibrosis progression 9% vs 36%
cards.people: 52 overweight patients with clinical evidence of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis at four UK medical centres, randomised to subcutaneous liraglutide 1.8 mg daily (n=26) or placebo (n=26) for 48 weeks, stratified by centre and diabetes status; primary outcome — resolution of definite steatohepatitis with no worsening of fibrosis — assessed centrally by two pathologists in the 45 patients who underwent end-of-treatment biopsy.
cards.result: Resolution of definite steatohepatitis occurred in 9 of 23 (39%) on liraglutide versus 2 of 22 (9%) on placebo (relative risk 4.3, 95% CI 1.0–17.7; p=0.019). Fibrosis progressed in 2 of 23 (9%) versus 8 of 22 (36%) (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1–1.0; p=0.04). shelves.title: Preoperative biliary drainage before pancreatic head cancer surgery: serious complications 74% with drainage versus 39% with early surgery — the drainage itself caused complications in 46%
shelves.question: In pancreatic head cancer with obstructive jaundice, does preoperative biliary drainage improve outcomes versus surgery alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde/adverse effects · Drainage/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Jaundice, Obstructive/etiology/surgery · Length of Stay · Lymph Node Excision · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatic Neoplasms/complications/surgery · Pancreaticoduodenectomy/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Preoperative Care · Stents · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — routine drainage hurt, in the one large randomised trial and in the network evidence behind it. In van der Gaag's multicentre trial, 202 patients with pancreatic head cancer and obstructive jaundice (bilirubin 40–250 µmol/L) were randomised to preoperative biliary drainage for 4–6 weeks or surgery alone within a week: serious complications within 120 days struck 74% of the drainage group versus 39% of the early-surgery group (relative risk in the early-surgery group 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71; p<0.001), with drainage-related complications in 46% of drained patients; surgery-related complications (47% versus 37%), mortality and hospital stay did not differ significantly. A 2018 network meta-analysis of 32 studies likewise ranked no preoperative drainage as the best approach for postoperative complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine preoperative biliary drainage in resectable pancreatic head cancer adds complications without improving surgical outcomes — drainage keeps its place for cholangitis, delay or neoadjuvant plans, which this trial did not test.

cards.headline: van der Gaag 2010 RCT (n=202): serious complications 74% (drainage) vs 39% (early surgery), RR 0.54 for early surgery (p<0.001); drainage complications in 46%
cards.summary: van der Gaag 2010 RCT (n=202): serious complications 74% (drainage) vs 39% (early surgery), RR 0.54 for early surgery (p<0.001); drainage complications in 46%
cards.people: 202 patients with cancer of the pancreatic head and obstructive jaundice (bilirubin 40–250 µmol/L, 2.3–14.6 mg/dL) at Dutch multicentre sites, randomised to preoperative biliary drainage for 4–6 weeks (n=106; attempted primarily by endoscopic endoprosthesis) followed by surgery, or surgery alone within 1 week (n=96); six patients excluded from analysis. Primary outcome: serious complications within 120 days of randomisation.
cards.result: Serious complications occurred in 75 patients (74%) in the biliary-drainage group versus 37 (39%) in the early-surgery group (relative risk in the early-surgery group 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71; p<0.001). Drainage was successful in 96 patients (94%) after one or more attempts, with complications in 47 (46%). Surgery-related complications occurred in 48 (47%) versus 35 (37%) (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11; p=0.14); mortality and length of hospital stay did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The trial answers the routine-drainage question in patients who could go straight to surgery with moderate bilirubin levels; it does not cover cholangitis, severe pruritus, planned neoadjuvant therapy or unavoidable surgical delay — the situations where drainage is still chosen deliberately. A harm claim on a single trial: Tier C.

cards.headline: Lee 2018 network meta-analysis (32 studies): no preoperative drainage ranked best for postoperative complications
cards.summary: Lee 2018 network meta-analysis (32 studies): no preoperative drainage ranked best for postoperative complications
cards.people: 32 studies of preoperative management of jaundice in resectable pancreatic head cancer undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, comparing preoperative biliary drainage by plastic stent, metal stent or percutaneous transhepatic drain with no preoperative drainage; ten studies fed the network meta-analysis of postoperative complications, wound infection, intra-abdominal infection and bleeding.
cards.result: Calculated odds ratios and P-scores ranked no preoperative biliary drainage as the best approach for the outcomes analysed; among drainage modalities (plastic stent, metal stent, percutaneous drain) the evidence was insufficient to determine a best option.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were not randomised, so this card corroborates direction rather than adding independent randomised proof; rankings from sparse networks are fragile. It is concordant with, and secondary to, the van der Gaag trial above.

shelves.title: Single-stage laparoscopic duct exploration versus two-stage ERCP then cholecystectomy: mortality and overall morbidity equal — ERCP clears more ducts and leaks less, LCBDE avoids pancreatitis and shortens stay
shelves.question: In choledocholithiasis, does single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration achieve duct clearance and outcomes equal to two-stage ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
shelves.mesh: Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde/methods · Cholecystectomy/methods · Cholecystectomy, Laparoscopic/methods · Choledocholithiasis/surgery · Common Bile Duct/surgery · Gallstones/surgery · Humans
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two routes trade complications, and neither wins the outcomes that matter most. In Lyu's meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (1,545 patients), preoperative ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy achieved a significantly higher duct stone clearance rate and a significantly lower postoperative bile leakage rate than single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration plus cholecystectomy — but a significantly higher rate of pancreatitis; LCBDE shortened overall hospital stay, and morbidity and mortality did not differ. The Cochrane review (Dasari 2013; five trials, 580 participants for the laparoscopic comparison) likewise found no significant difference in mortality (0.7% versus 1%) or morbidity between laparoscopic clearance and preoperative ERCP. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose by local expertise and by which complication the patient can least afford — pancreatitis and a second procedure on the ERCP side, bile leak and a longer stay on the surgical side.

cards.headline: Lyu 2019 meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 1,545 patients): clearance and bile leak favour pre-ERCP+LC; pancreatitis favours LCBDE+LC; morbidity and mortality equal
cards.summary: Lyu 2019 meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 1,545 patients): clearance and bile leak favour pre-ERCP+LC; pancreatitis favours LCBDE+LC; morbidity and mortality equal
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials totalling 1,545 patients with gallbladder and common bile duct stones (cholecystocholedocholithiasis), comparing single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LCBDE+LC) with preoperative ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy (pre-ERCP+LC); in seven trials duct stones were confirmed preoperatively, in five they were not.
cards.result: Pre-ERCP+LC had a significantly higher common bile duct stone clearance rate and a significantly lower postoperative bile leakage rate than LCBDE+LC, in all 12 trials and in the confirmed-stone subgroup; pre-ERCP+LC had a significantly higher rate of postoperative pancreatitis in both analyses. LCBDE+LC was superior for overall hospital stay. No significant differences were found in morbidity or mortality.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports directions and significance, not the pooled rates themselves, so the sizes of the clearance and leak advantages cannot be quoted from this record; five of twelve trials enrolled patients whose duct stones were never confirmed, diluting both arms with patients who may have needed neither procedure.
cards.source: Lyu Y et al. Laparoscopic common bile duct exploration plus cholecystectomy versus endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholecystocholedocholithiasis: a meta-analysis. Surgical Endoscopy. 2019. PMID: 30511313. cards.headline: Dasari 2013 Cochrane review: laparoscopic clearance vs preoperative ERCP — mortality 0.7% vs 1%, morbidity not significantly different
cards.summary: Dasari 2013 Cochrane review: laparoscopic clearance vs preoperative ERCP — mortality 0.7% vs 1%, morbidity not significantly different
cards.people: 16 randomised trials (1,758 participants) of surgical versus endoscopic clearance of common bile duct stones; the laparoscopic comparison relevant here — laparoscopic cholecystectomy plus laparoscopic duct exploration versus preoperative ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy — comprised five trials with 621 participants (580 in the mortality analysis). All trials were at high risk of bias.
cards.result: For laparoscopic clearance versus preoperative ERCP, mortality was 2 of 285 (0.7%) versus 3 of 295 (1%) (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.12–4.33), and morbidity did not differ significantly between the groups. (In the review's separate open-surgery comparison, open clearance left significantly fewer retained stones than ERCP: 6% versus 16%, OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.21–0.62.)
cards.watchOut: Every trial in the Cochrane set carried a high risk of bias, and the event counts for mortality are tiny — 'no significant difference' here is a wide interval, not proven equality. The Cochrane search closed in 2013; the Lyu analysis above is the more current of the two.
cards.source: Dasari BV et al. Surgical versus endoscopic treatment of bile duct stones. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24338858. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal where it counts, different where it hurts — a genuine SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal where it counts, different where it hurts — a genuine SPLIT
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials (12 RCTs, 1,545 patients; Cochrane set of 16 RCTs, 1,758 participants) comparing single-stage laparoscopic duct exploration with two-stage ERCP-based clearance.
cards.result: Mortality (0.7% vs 1% in the Cochrane laparoscopic subset) and overall morbidity: no significant difference in either analysis. Clearance rate and bile leakage favour pre-ERCP+LC; pancreatitis and hospital stay favour LCBDE+LC. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Neither meta-analysis can settle the question for a given hospital: LCBDE results depend on surgical expertise and ERCP results on endoscopist volume, and trial populations with unconfirmed stones blur the comparison further.

shelves.title: Balloon dilation versus sphincterotomy for bile duct stones: overall clearance favours sphincterotomy — unless the balloon is large (≥10 mm), when clearance and pancreatitis match; bleeding is rarer with dilation throughout
shelves.question: For removal of common bile duct stones, does endoscopic papillary balloon dilation preserve sphincter function without losing clearance compared with endoscopic sphincterotomy?
shelves.mesh: Catheterization · Common Bile Duct · Dilatation · Endoscopy, Digestive System · Gallstones/surgery · Humans · Sphincterotomy, Endoscopic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by balloon size. In Tringali's cumulative meta-analysis of 25 randomised trials, endoscopic papillary balloon dilation (EPBD) matched sphincterotomy for stone removal at first attempt (odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.65–1.38) but was inferior for overall stone clearance in studies published since 2002 (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.43–0.99) — except with large balloons (≥10 mm), where clearance matched (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.72–2.62). Pancreatitis overall did not differ significantly (OR 1.35, 95% CI 0.90–2.03), but was commoner with EPBD when balloons were <10 mm (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.07–2.97) and not with large balloons (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46–1.53); EPBD had lower rates of bleeding and cholecystitis. The earlier Baron meta-analysis (8 trials) found the same shape: similar overall removal (94.3% versus 96.5%) and complications (10.5% versus 10.3%), less bleeding with EPBD (0% versus 2.0%), more pancreatitis (7.4% versus 4.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: small-balloon dilation loses on clearance and pancreatitis; large-balloon dilation matches sphincterotomy while sparing the sphincter and bleeding less.

cards.headline: Tringali 2019 cumulative meta-analysis (25 RCTs): first-attempt removal equal (OR 0.95), overall clearance favours EST (OR 0.65) except with ≥10 mm balloons (OR 1.37)
cards.summary: Tringali 2019 cumulative meta-analysis (25 RCTs): first-attempt removal equal (OR 0.95), overall clearance favours EST (OR 0.65) except with ≥10 mm balloons (OR 1.37)
cards.people: 25 randomised controlled trials comparing endoscopic papillary balloon dilation (EPBD) with endoscopic sphincterotomy for removal of common bile duct stones, searched to October 2017, with subgroup analyses by stone size, balloon diameter and dilation time.
cards.result: Stone removal at first attempt did not differ (odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.65–1.38). Overall stone clearance favoured sphincterotomy in studies published since 2002 (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.43–0.99), but not in studies using large (≥10 mm) balloons (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.72–2.62). Pancreatitis did not differ overall (OR 1.35, 95% CI 0.90–2.03); it was more common with EPBD using balloons <10 mm (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.07–2.97) and no different with large balloons (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46–1.53). EPBD had lower rates of bleeding and cholecystitis, and large-balloon EPBD matched sphincterotomy on the need for mechanical lithotripsy.
cards.watchOut: The 'since 2002' split is a cumulative-meta-analysis construct — era, technique and stone-size mix all changed together, so the balloon-diameter subgroup is the more actionable read. Sphincter *function* preservation, the question's premise, is a physiological claim these clearance-and-complication trials largely did not measure directly.

cumulative meta-analysis of randomised trials (tringali 2019) 25 randomised controlled trials comparing endoscopic papillary balloon dilation (epbd) with endoscopic sphincterotomy for removal of common bile duct stones, searched to october 2017, with subgroup analyses by stone size, balloon diameter and dilation time. stone removal at first attempt did not differ (odds ratio 0.95, 95% ci 0.65–1.38). overall stone clearance favoured sphincterotomy in studies published since 2002 (or 0.65, 95% ci 0.43–0.99), but not in studies using large (≥10 mm) balloons (or 1.37, 95% ci 0.72–2.62). pancreatitis did not differ overall (or 1.35, 95% ci 0.90–2.03); it was more common with epbd using balloons <10 mm (or 1.78, 95% ci 1.07–2.97) and no different with large balloons (or 0.84, 95% ci 0.46–1.53). epbd had lower rates of bleeding and cholecystitis, and large-balloon epbd matched sphincterotomy on the need for mechanical lithotripsy. the 'since 2002' split is a cumulative-meta-analysis construct — era, technique and stone-size mix all changed together, so the balloon-diameter subgroup is the more actionable read. sphincter *function* preservation, the question's premise, is a physiological claim these clearance-and-complication trials largely did not measure directly. tringali a et al. a cumulative meta-analysis of endoscopic papillary balloon dilation versus endoscopic sphincterotomy for removal of common bile duct stones. endoscopy. 2019. pmid: 30727009. mesh: catheterization · common bile duct · dilatation · endoscopy, digestive system · gallstones/surgery · humans · sphincterotomy, endoscopic

cards.headline: Baron 2004 meta-analysis (8 RCTs): overall removal 94.3% vs 96.5%, bleeding 0% vs 2.0%, pancreatitis 7.4% vs 4.3% with EPBD
cards.summary: Baron 2004 meta-analysis (8 RCTs): overall removal 94.3% vs 96.5%, bleeding 0% vs 2.0%, pancreatitis 7.4% vs 4.3% with EPBD
cards.people: Eight fully published prospective randomised trials in English comparing endoscopic balloon dilation of the papilla with endoscopic biliary sphincterotomy for removal of common bile duct stones.
cards.result: Overall successful stone removal was 94.3% with EPBD versus 96.5% with sphincterotomy, and overall complications 10.5% versus 10.3% — both similar. Bleeding occurred less frequently with EPBD (0% versus 2.0%, p=0.001); post-ERCP pancreatitis occurred more commonly with EPBD (7.4% versus 4.3%, p=0.05); perforation and infection rates did not differ significantly. Mechanical lithotripsy was needed more often after EPBD (20.9% versus 14.8%, p=0.014).
cards.watchOut: These trials predate routine large-balloon dilation, so their pancreatitis penalty largely reflects small-balloon technique — exactly the subgroup the 2019 cumulative analysis separates out. The authors' own conclusion was narrow: EPBD preferred in coagulopathy, not routinely recommended otherwise, on 2004 technique.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the balloon's diameter decides — small loses, large ties, bleeding always favours dilation
cards.summary: Synthesis: the balloon's diameter decides — small loses, large ties, bleeding always favours dilation
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials (25 RCTs in 2019; 8 RCTs in 2004) of balloon dilation versus sphincterotomy for bile duct stone removal.
cards.result: First-attempt removal equal (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.65–1.38); overall clearance favours sphincterotomy overall (OR 0.65) but not with ≥10 mm balloons (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.72–2.62); pancreatitis excess confined to <10 mm balloons (OR 1.78) and absent with large balloons (OR 0.84); bleeding lower with dilation in both analyses (0% vs 2.0% in 2004). PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Neither analysis directly measured long-term sphincter function or recurrent-stone rates years later — the very outcomes the sphincter-preservation argument is about. The shelf answers clearance and early complications, and says so.

shelves.title: Metal versus plastic stents for malignant biliary obstruction: metal stays patent far longer (hazard ratio 0.36), needs fewer re-interventions, and pooled survival favoured metal (HR 0.74) across 10 randomised trials
shelves.question: In malignant biliary obstruction, do self-expandable metal stents stay patent longer than plastic stents — and at what cost in complications?
shelves.mesh: Bile Duct Neoplasms/complications/mortality · Cholestasis/etiology/mortality/therapy · Drainage/instrumentation · Humans · Metals · Palliative Care · Plastics · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patency decisively, survival modestly, in trial populations. Hong's updated meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials found metal stents associated with significantly longer stent patency than plastic stents (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.47, I²=0%), fewer re-interventions (weighted mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.28–0.90) and longer patient survival (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.85, I²=16.0%); results held in sensitivity analyses, and no publication bias was observed. The one soft spot: in the hilar-obstruction subgroup, the re-intervention advantage did not reach significance. The record reports no pooled complication penalty against metal to set against these gains — but it also predates much of the covered-versus-uncovered metal stent refinement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for palliation of malignant biliary obstruction, metal stents outlast plastic, spare re-interventions and were associated with longer survival; Tier C because the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim.

cards.headline: Hong 2013 updated meta-analysis (10 RCTs): patency HR 0.36 (0.28–0.47), survival HR 0.74 (0.64–0.85), re-interventions fewer by WMD 0.59
cards.summary: Hong 2013 updated meta-analysis (10 RCTs): patency HR 0.36 (0.28–0.47), survival HR 0.74 (0.64–0.85), re-interventions fewer by WMD 0.59
cards.people: Ten randomised clinical trials comparing self-expandable metal stents with plastic stents for palliation of malignant biliary obstruction, with subgroup analysis by distal versus hilar obstruction; endpoints were stent patency, re-intervention rate and patient survival.
cards.result: Metal stents were associated with significantly longer stent patency (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.47; I²=0%), fewer re-interventions (weighted mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.28–0.90; I²=76.4%) and longer patient survival (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.85; I²=16.0%) than plastic stents. All results remained significant in sensitivity analysis except the pooled re-intervention difference in the hilar-obstruction studies. No publication bias was observed.
cards.watchOut: A survival advantage from a stent is biologically indirect — plausibly mediated by fewer occlusions, infections and re-interventions — and the re-intervention pooling is highly heterogeneous (I²=76.4%). The 2013 search also predates later covered-metal and hilar-drainage trials. Mortality benefit claim: Tier C by the standing rules.
cards.source: Hong WD et al. Metal versus plastic stents for malignant biliary obstruction: An update meta-analysis. Clinics and Research in Hepatology and Gastroenterology. 2013. PMID: 23333231. cards.headline: Synthesis: patency is the proven win; survival rides along in the pooled trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: patency is the proven win; survival rides along in the pooled trials
cards.people: One updated meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials of metal versus plastic stents for malignant biliary obstruction.
cards.result: Patency HR 0.36 (95% CI 0.28–0.47), re-interventions fewer (WMD 0.59, 95% CI 0.28–0.90), survival HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.64–0.85), all favouring metal stents; hilar re-intervention subgroup not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: Cost runs the other way — metal stents are far more expensive up front — and neither this record nor the shelf prices the trade; for patients with very short expected survival, the patency advantage may never be cashed in. That judgement stays with the treating team.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hong WD et al. Clinics and Research in Hepatology and Gastroenterology. 2013 (PMID: 23333231).

shelves.title: Tacrolimus versus ciclosporin after liver transplantation: deaths and graft loss lower at one year (RR 0.85 and 0.73), rejection down — de novo diabetes up (RR 1.38), across 16 randomised trials
shelves.question: After liver transplantation, does tacrolimus-based immunosuppression reduce rejection and graft loss compared with ciclosporin-based immunosuppression?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Cyclosporine/pharmacology · Follow-Up Studies · Graft Rejection/immunology · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/pharmacology · Liver Transplantation/adverse effects/immunology · Risk Factors · Tacrolimus/pharmacology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the calcineurin contest was settled by 16 randomised trials, with one named price. McAlister's meta-analysis found one-year mortality (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.99) and graft loss (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61–0.86) significantly reduced with tacrolimus versus ciclosporin, alongside less acute rejection (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75–0.88) and far less steroid-resistant rejection (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.47–0.74). In absolute terms, treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of ciclosporin would avoid graft loss in five and death in two, and rejection in nine — but four additional patients would develop de novo diabetes (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.01–1.86). More patients stopped ciclosporin than tacrolimus (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.49–0.66); lymphoproliferative disorder and dialysis rates did not differ. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tacrolimus is the better default foundation after liver transplantation; Tier C because the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim.

cards.headline: McAlister 2006 meta-analysis (16 RCTs, ~3,800 recipients): mortality RR 0.85, graft loss RR 0.73, steroid-resistant rejection RR 0.54 — diabetes RR 1.38
cards.summary: McAlister 2006 meta-analysis (16 RCTs, ~3,800 recipients): mortality RR 0.85, graft loss RR 0.73, steroid-resistant rejection RR 0.54 — diabetes RR 1.38
cards.people: 16 randomised clinical trials of tacrolimus versus cyclosporin (ciclosporin) as primary immunosuppression after liver transplantation (1,899 tacrolimus and 1,914 cyclosporin recipients in the companion Cochrane report of the same analysis), with outcomes at one year.
cards.result: Mortality (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.99) and graft loss (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61–0.86) at one year were significantly reduced with tacrolimus. Acute rejection fell (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75–0.88), as did steroid-resistant rejection (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.47–0.74). De novo diabetes was commoner with tacrolimus (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.01–1.86); lymphoproliferative disorder and dialysis rates were not different; more patients stopped cyclosporin than tacrolimus (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.49–0.66). Per 100 treated with tacrolimus instead of cyclosporin: nine fewer rejections, seven fewer steroid-resistant rejections, five fewer graft losses, two fewer deaths — and four additional cases of diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The trials are from the era when the comparison was live; ciclosporin formulations and monitoring in the older trials are not today's, and one-year horizons cannot price tacrolimus's longer-term renal and metabolic costs. The same author group's Cochrane review (PMID: 17054241) is a twin publication of this identical 16-trial analysis — it is one body of evidence, not two, and is deliberately not carded separately.
cards.source: McAlister VC et al. Cyclosporin versus tacrolimus as primary immunosuppressant after liver transplantation: a meta-analysis. American Journal of Transplantation. 2006. PMID: 16827858. shelves.title: Benralizumab in eosinophilic oesophagitis (MESSINA): tissue eosinophils cleared in 87.4% versus 6.5% — but swallowing symptoms did not improve (DSQ difference 3.0 points, p=0.18)
shelves.question: In eosinophilic oesophagitis, does benralizumab deplete tissue eosinophils and improve dysphagia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Deglutition Disorders/etiology/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Eosinophilic Esophagitis/drug therapy/immunology · Eosinophils · Interleukin-5 Receptor alpha Subunit/antagonists & inhibitors · Leukocyte Count
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the drug did exactly what it was built to do to the tissue, and the patient felt no better. In the phase 3 MESSINA trial (211 patients aged 12–65 with symptomatic, histologically active eosinophilic oesophagitis), benralizumab produced a histologic response (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) in 87.4% versus 6.5% on placebo at week 24 (difference 80.8 percentage points, 95% CI 72.9–88.8; p<0.001) — but the change in Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire score did not differ significantly (difference in least-squares means 3.0 points, 95% CI −1.4 to 7.4; p=0.18), and neither did the endoscopic reference score. Adverse events were reported in 64.1% on benralizumab and 61.7% on placebo, with no discontinuations for adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: benralizumab is a proven eosinophil-depleting drug and an unproven dysphagia treatment — in EoE, clearing eosinophils and relieving symptoms have come apart.

cards.headline: Rothenberg 2024 MESSINA (n=211): histologic response 87.4% vs 6.5% (p<0.001); DSQ dysphagia change difference 3.0 points (p=0.18) — co-primary endpoints split
cards.summary: Rothenberg 2024 MESSINA (n=211): histologic response 87.4% vs 6.5% (p<0.001); DSQ dysphagia change difference 3.0 points (p=0.18) — co-primary endpoints split
cards.people: 211 patients aged 12–65 years with symptomatic and histologically active eosinophilic esophagitis, randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous benralizumab 30 mg (n=104) or placebo (n=107) every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. Co-primary endpoints: histologic response (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) and change in Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ) score (range 0–84, higher = worse).
cards.result: Histologic response at week 24: 87.4% on benralizumab versus 6.5% on placebo (difference 80.8 percentage points, 95% CI 72.9–88.8; p<0.001). Change in DSQ score did not differ significantly (difference in least-squares means 3.0 points, 95% CI −1.4 to 7.4; p=0.18), and there was no substantial between-group difference in change in the Eosinophilic Esophagitis Endoscopic Reference Score. Adverse events were reported in 64.1% of the benralizumab group and 61.7% of the placebo group; no patients discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A trial can hardly isolate a mechanism better: near-total eosinophil depletion without symptom benefit challenges the assumption that the eosinophil count is the disease. Twenty-four weeks may be short for fibrotic dysphagia to reverse, but the symptom gap is the finding, not a footnote. Single trial — Tier C.
cards.source: Rothenberg ME et al. Eosinophil Depletion with Benralizumab for Eosinophilic Esophagitis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38924732. Registry ID: NCT04543409. cards.people: One randomised double-blind phase 3 trial, 211 patients aged 12–65 with eosinophilic oesophagitis, 24 weeks.
cards.result: Histologic response 87.4% vs 6.5% (difference 80.8 percentage points, p<0.001); dysphagia (DSQ) difference 3.0 points (95% CI −1.4 to 7.4; p=0.18); endoscopic score likewise not substantially different; adverse events 64.1% vs 61.7%. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped; Tier C — single trial.

shelves.title: Pure oats on a gluten-free diet in coeliac disease: no signal of mucosal relapse, symptoms or serology harm across 28 studies — but the evidence quality is low and every trial used uncontaminated oats
shelves.question: In coeliac disease, can pure oats be added safely to a gluten-free diet without causing mucosal relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Avena/adverse effects · Celiac Disease/blood/diet therapy/pathology · Child · Diet, Gluten-Free/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Non-Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Observational Studies as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — adding pure oats changed nothing measurable, in low-quality evidence. Pinto-Sánchez's systematic review and meta-analysis (28 eligible studies; eight controlled trials totalling 661 patients, the rest observational) found oat consumption for 12 months did not affect symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.22, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.13; p=0.22), histologic findings (relative risk 0.24, 95% CI 0.01–4.8; p=0.35) or serologic tests, with no adult-versus-child subgroup differences — but the overall quality of evidence was rated low. The landmark Janatuinen trial behind much of the data randomised 92 adults to gluten-free diets with or without 50–70 g/day of oats and found no differences in symptoms, nutrition or duodenal architecture over 6–12 months. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): pure, uncontaminated oats appear safe for most people with coeliac disease — the catch is 'pure', since commercial oats are commonly contaminated with wheat, and the trial evidence cannot vouch for those.

cards.headline: Pinto-Sánchez 2017 meta-analysis (28 studies; 661 patients in controlled trials): symptoms SMD −0.22 (p=0.22), histology RR 0.24 (p=0.35) — null throughout, GRADE quality low
cards.summary: Pinto-Sánchez 2017 meta-analysis (28 studies; 661 patients in controlled trials): symptoms SMD −0.22 (p=0.22), histology RR 0.24 (p=0.35) — null throughout, GRADE quality low
cards.people: 28 eligible studies of adding oats to a gluten-free diet in coeliac disease: six randomised and two non-randomised controlled trials comprising 661 patients, plus observational studies, reporting symptoms, serology and histology; all randomised trials used pure/uncontaminated oats. Quality assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Oat consumption for 12 months did not affect symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.22, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.13; p=0.22), histologic scores (relative risk for histologic findings 0.24, 95% CI 0.01–4.8; p=0.35), intraepithelial lymphocyte counts (SMD 0.21, 95% CI −1.44 to 1.86), or serologic test results. Subgroup analyses of adults versus children showed no differences. The overall quality of evidence was low.
cards.watchOut: The histology interval (0.01–4.8) is wide enough to hide real harm in a minority — a small avenin-sensitive subgroup would be invisible in averages like these — and the evidence base leans on observational studies and few endpoints. Tier C: the shelf rests substantially on observational evidence.
cards.source: Pinto-Sánchez MI et al. Safety of Adding Oats to a Gluten-Free Diet for Patients With Celiac Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Clinical and Observational Studies. cards.headline: Janatuinen 1995 RCT (n=92): oats 50–70 g/day for 6–12 months — no difference in symptoms, nutrition or duodenal villous architecture
cards.summary: Janatuinen 1995 RCT (n=92): oats 50–70 g/day for 6–12 months — no difference in symptoms, nutrition or duodenal villous architecture
cards.people: 92 adults with coeliac disease — 52 in remission followed for 6 months and 40 newly diagnosed followed for 12 months — randomised to a gluten-free diet without oats or with oats (goal 50–70 g/day from oat-containing flour, muesli and rolled-oat cereal); mean intake was 49.9 g/day (remission group, 6 months) and 46.6 g/day (newly diagnosed, 12 months). Duodenal biopsies at start and end.
cards.result: The oat and control groups did not differ significantly in nutritional status, symptoms or laboratory measures. Patients in remission had no worsening of duodenal villous architecture or increased mononuclear-cell infiltration on either diet; all newly diagnosed patients were in remission at one year except one in the control group. Six patients in the oat groups and five in the control group withdrew.
cards.watchOut: A 1995 single-country trial of carefully sourced oats, in 92 adults — it anchors the meta-analysis but cannot exclude harm in children, in avenin-sensitive individuals, or from the contaminated commercial oats most patients actually buy.
cards.source: Janatuinen EK et al. A comparison of diets with and without oats in adults with celiac disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7675045. shelves.title: Transoral incisionless fundoplication (TEMPO) at 5 years: troublesome regurgitation eliminated in 86% and daily PPI use down from 100% to 34% — but after the 6-month randomised phase everyone had the procedure, so the long term is uncontrolled
shelves.question: In gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with incomplete response to a proton pump inhibitor, does transoral incisionless fundoplication eliminate reflux symptoms versus sham or continued PPI?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cross-Over Studies · Female · Fundoplication/adverse effects/economics/methods/statistics & numerical data · Gastroesophageal Reflux/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Proton Pump Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable symptom relief in the patients followed, on evidence that stops being randomised at 6 months. TEMPO randomised 63 patients with troublesome reflux refractory to PPI therapy, hiatal hernia ≤2 cm and abnormal acid exposure to transoral incisionless fundoplication (TIF 2.0) or continued PPI; after the 6-month evaluation every PPI-group patient elected crossover to TIF, so all 63 underwent the procedure. At 5 years (44 patients available), troublesome regurgitation was eliminated in 86% and troublesome atypical symptoms resolved in 80%; daily PPI use had fallen from 100% at screening to 34%; GERD health-related quality-of-life score improved from 22.2 to 6.8 (p<0.001); there were three reoperations and no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): TIF gives sustained relief for most selected patients at 5 years — with the selection (small hernia, PPI-refractory but procedure-suitable) and the uncontrolled follow-up printed on the shelf, and no sham comparison anywhere in this record.

cards.headline: Trad 2018 TEMPO 5-year report (63 randomised, 44 at 5 years): regurgitation eliminated in 86%, atypical symptoms resolved in 80%, daily PPI 34% vs 100% at screening, 3 reoperations
cards.summary: Trad 2018 TEMPO 5-year report (63 randomised, 44 at 5 years): regurgitation eliminated in 86%, atypical symptoms resolved in 80%, daily PPI 34% vs 100% at screening, 3 reoperations
cards.type: Randomised trial with long-term follow-up (Trad 2018, TEMPO)
cards.people: 63 patients with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, troublesome symptoms refractory to proton pump inhibitor therapy, absent or ≤2 cm hiatal hernia and abnormal oesophageal acid exposure, randomised to transoral incisionless fundoplication (TIF 2.0 with the EsophyX2 device, as named in the publication) or PPI therapy; after the 6-month evaluation all PPI-group patients crossed over to TIF, so all 63 underwent TIF. Follow-up available in 60 patients at 1 year, 52 at 3 years and 44 at 5 years.
cards.result: Troublesome regurgitation was eliminated in 88% of patients at 1 year, 90% at 3 years and 86% at 5 years; troublesome atypical symptoms resolved in 82%, 88% and 80% respectively. At 5 years, 34% of patients were on daily PPI therapy, compared with 100% at screening. Total GERD health-related quality-of-life score improved from 22.2 to 6.8 at 5 years (p<0.001). No serious adverse events occurred; there were three reoperations by the end of 5-year follow-up.
cards.watchOut: There is no sham arm and, after crossover, no control arm at all: the 5-year figures are a case series of the 44 of 63 patients still available, in a population pre-selected for small hernias and procedure suitability. Regression to the mean, placebo effect of a procedure, and attrition all point the same flattering way. Single trial, uncontrolled long term — Tier C.
cards.source: Trad KS et al. The TEMPO Trial at 5 Years: Transoral Fundoplication (TIF 2.0) Is Safe, Durable, and Cost-effective. Surgical Innovation. 2018. PMID: 29405886. shelves.title: Testosterone in men with cirrhosis and low testosterone: appendicular lean mass +1.69 kg and total lean mass +4.74 kg over 12 months versus placebo — mortality 16% versus 25.5%, not significant
shelves.question: In men with cirrhosis, low testosterone and sarcopenia, does testosterone therapy increase muscle mass versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon · Australia · Body Composition · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Muscle, Skeletal · Testosterone/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for body composition, from the first and only randomised trial of its kind. Sinclair randomised 101 men with established cirrhosis and low testosterone to intramuscular testosterone undecanoate or placebo for 12 months: appendicular lean mass was higher on testosterone (mean adjusted difference +1.69 kg, 95% CI +0.40 to +2.97; p=0.021), as was total lean mass (+4.74 kg, 95% CI +1.75 to +7.74; p=0.008), while fat mass fell (−4.34 kg, 95% CI −6.65 to −2.04; p<0.001); bone mass, femoral-neck bone density, haemoglobin (+10.2 g/L) and HbA1c (−0.35%) also favoured testosterone. Mortality was 16% versus 25.5% — lower, but not significantly (p=0.352) — and adverse events were not increased. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): testosterone rebuilds muscle and bone in hypogonadal men with cirrhosis over a year; whether that converts into survival needs the larger trial the authors call for.

cards.headline: Sinclair 2016 RCT (n=101): appendicular lean mass +1.69 kg (p=0.021), total lean mass +4.74 kg (p=0.008), fat mass −4.34 kg (p<0.001) on testosterone vs placebo
cards.summary: Sinclair 2016 RCT (n=101): appendicular lean mass +1.69 kg (p=0.021), total lean mass +4.74 kg (p=0.008), fat mass −4.34 kg (p<0.001) on testosterone vs placebo
cards.people: 101 men with established cirrhosis and low serum testosterone (total <12 nmol/L or free <230 pmol/L) at a single tertiary centre, randomised to intramuscular testosterone undecanoate or placebo for 12 months, double-blind; body composition by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry at baseline, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: Appendicular lean mass was significantly higher on testosterone (mean adjusted difference +1.69 kg, 95% CI +0.40 to +2.97; p=0.021); total lean mass +4.74 kg (95% CI +1.75 to +7.74; p=0.008); fat mass −4.34 kg (95% CI −6.65 to −2.04; p<0.001). Total bone mass rose (+0.08 kg, p=0.009) as did femoral-neck bone mineral density (+0.287 points, p<0.001); haemoglobin was higher (+10.2 g/L, p=0.041) and HbA1c lower (−0.35%, p=0.028). Mortality was non-significantly lower on testosterone (16% versus 25.5%, p=0.352), with no increase in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Lean mass on a scan is a surrogate — the trial does not show the gained muscle works better (strength, falls, hospitalisations unreported in this record) — and 101 men at one centre over 12 months cannot settle the mortality question its own point estimate raises. Single trial: Tier C.
cards.source: Sinclair M et al. Testosterone therapy increases muscle mass in men with cirrhosis and low testosterone: A randomised controlled trial. Journal of Hepatology. 2016. PMID: 27312945. shelves.title: Sertraline versus rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus: itch improved on both, no difference between them (p=0.740) — in 36 patients over 4 weeks, with liver enzymes favouring sertraline
shelves.question: In cholestatic pruritus, is sertraline as effective as rifampicin for itch relief?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Cholestasis/complications · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pruritus/drug therapy/etiology · Rifampin/therapeutic use · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — between the two drugs, in one very small single-blind trial. Ataei randomised 36 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus to sertraline 100 mg/day or rifampin (rifampicin) 300 mg/day for 4 weeks: pruritus relieved in both groups with no significant difference between sertraline and rifampin (p=0.740), and total bilirubin likewise did not differ significantly (p=0.106), while ALT, AST and ALP levels differed significantly between groups (p<0.01) in sertraline's favour on hepatic safety. With 18 patients per arm and no placebo group, 'no difference found' is a long way from 'equally effective' — the trial could not have detected anything but a very large gap. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): sertraline is a plausible rifampicin alternative when rifampicin's interactions or hepatotoxicity loom, on evidence that is suggestive at best.

cards.headline: Ataei 2019 RCT (n=36): pruritus relieved in both groups, no significant sertraline–rifampin difference (p=0.740); ALT/AST/ALP differed significantly (p<0.01)
cards.summary: Ataei 2019 RCT (n=36): pruritus relieved in both groups, no significant sertraline–rifampin difference (p=0.740); ALT/AST/ALP differed significantly (p<0.01)
cards.people: 36 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus, in a single-blinded randomised trial, divided into two equal groups receiving sertraline 100 mg/day or rifampin 300 mg/day for 4 weeks. Pruritus severity recorded on a visual analog scale at baseline and 4 weeks; ALT, AST, ALP and total bilirubin measured at three time points.
cards.result: Pruritus was relieved over follow-up in both groups, with no significant difference between sertraline and rifampin in pruritus management (p=0.740) and no significant difference in total bilirubin (p=0.106). ALT, AST and ALP levels were significantly different between the two groups (p<0.01), which the authors read as sertraline being safer than rifampin for hepatobiliary enzymes.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients, single-blind, four weeks, no placebo arm, and the abstract reports p-values without the visual-analog scores themselves — neither equivalence nor the size of either drug's effect can be extracted from this record. A non-significant p in n=36 is absence of evidence, and the stamp says so. Tier C.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a draw neither side can cash — sertraline's case is safety and convenience, not proven equal efficacy
cards.summary: Synthesis: a draw neither side can cash — sertraline's case is safety and convenience, not proven equal efficacy
cards.people: One single-blind randomised trial, 36 patients with cholestatic pruritus from PSC or PBC, 4 weeks.
cards.result: Itch relief: no significant difference between sertraline 100 mg/day and rifampin 300 mg/day (p=0.740); bilirubin no significant difference (p=0.106); liver enzymes significantly different between groups (p<0.01), favouring sertraline's hepatic profile. cards.watchOut: Rifampicin's real-world problems — drug interactions and idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity — are the clinical reason this comparison matters, but a 4-week, 36-patient trial measures neither well. Anyone citing this shelf for 'sertraline works as well' is over-reading it; the shelf's wording is deliberate.

shelves.title: Soluble fibre (psyllium) for IBS in primary care: responders 57% versus 35% on placebo in month 1 and 59% versus 41% in month 2 — bran helped later and worsened symptoms early, dropping out more
shelves.question: In irritable bowel syndrome in primary care, does soluble fibre (psyllium) improve symptoms versus placebo or insoluble bran?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/etiology/prevention & control · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Dietary Fiber/administration & dosage · Family Practice · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/diet therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Plantago · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for psyllium, not for bran, in the one large primary-care trial, backed by the wider meta-analysis. Bijkerk randomised 275 patients aged 18–65 with IBS in general practice to 10 g/day psyllium (n=85), bran (n=97) or placebo (rice flour, n=93) for 12 weeks: responders were 57% versus 35% for psyllium versus placebo in month 1 (relative risk 1.60, 95% CI 1.13–2.26) and 59% versus 41% in month 2 (RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.02–2.06); bran beat placebo only in month 3 (57% versus 32%; RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.12–2.57), a result that lost significance in the worst-case analysis. Symptom severity fell 90 points on psyllium versus 49 on placebo (p=0.03); quality of life did not differ. Ford's meta-analysis of 12 fibre trials (591 patients) likewise found the fibre effect limited to ispaghula (psyllium): RR of persistent symptoms 0.78 (95% CI 0.63–0.96), versus 0.87 (0.76–1.00) for fibre overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): psyllium is the only fibre with a demonstrated IBS benefit in primary care — and the distinction between soluble and insoluble fibre is the point of the shelf.

cards.headline: Bijkerk 2009 RCT (n=275): psyllium responders 57% vs 35% month 1 (RR 1.60) and 59% vs 41% month 2 (RR 1.44); bran only in month 3, and not in worst-case analysis
cards.summary: Bijkerk 2009 RCT (n=275): psyllium responders 57% vs 35% month 1 (RR 1.60) and 59% vs 41% month 2 (RR 1.44); bran only in month 3, and not in worst-case analysis
cards.people: 275 patients aged 18–65 years with irritable bowel syndrome in general practice, randomised to 12 weeks of 10 g psyllium (n=85), 10 g bran (n=97) or 10 g placebo (rice flour) (n=93). Primary endpoint: adequate symptom relief during at least two weeks in the previous month, assessed at one, two and three months; secondary: IBS symptom severity score, abdominal pain, quality of life.
cards.result: Responders were significantly more frequent with psyllium than placebo in month 1 (57% versus 35%; relative risk 1.60, 95% CI 1.13–2.26) and month 2 (59% versus 41%; RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.02–2.06). Bran was more effective than placebo only in month 3 (57% versus 32%; RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.12–2.57), and not statistically significant in the worst-case analysis (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.97–2.16). After three months, symptom severity fell 90 points with psyllium versus 49 with placebo (p=0.03) and 58 with bran (p=0.61 versus placebo). No differences in quality of life. Treatment completion: 54 of 85 (64%) on psyllium, 54 of 97 (56%) on bran and 56 of 93 (60%) on placebo; early dropout was most common in the bran group, mainly because symptoms worsened.
cards.watchOut: The 12-week benefit is symptom relief, not cure; a third of patients stopped before three months, and the responder endpoint is a patient rating over a month, not a daily diary. General practice IBS is the right setting here — hospital-clinic IBS may respond differently.
cards.source: Bijkerk CJ et al. Soluble or insoluble fibre in irritable bowel syndrome in primary care? Randomised placebo controlled trial. BMJ. 2009. PMID: 19713235. Registry ID: NCT00189033. cards.headline: Ford 2008 meta-analysis (12 fibre trials, 591 patients): fibre's effect was limited to ispaghula (RR of persistent symptoms 0.78)
cards.summary: Ford 2008 meta-analysis (12 fibre trials, 591 patients): fibre's effect was limited to ispaghula (RR of persistent symptoms 0.78)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials comparing fibre with placebo or no treatment in 591 adults with irritable bowel syndrome (minimum one week of therapy), from a wider review of fibre, antispasmodics and peppermint oil.
cards.result: Fibre overall gave a relative risk of persistent symptoms of 0.87 (95% CI 0.76–1.00); the effect was limited to ispaghula (psyllium) (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63–0.96). By comparison, antispasmodics (22 trials, 1,778 patients) gave RR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57–0.81) and peppermint oil (4 trials, 392 patients) RR 0.43 (95% CI 0.32–0.59).
cards.watchOut: Pooled 2008 trials are small and old, and 'fibre' as a class blends soluble and insoluble forms — which is precisely why this card's ispaghula-only subgroup, not its overall estimate, is the one to quote.
cards.source: Ford AC et al. Effect of fibre, antispasmodics, and peppermint oil in the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2008. PMID: 19008265. shelves.title: Total (Nissen) versus posterior partial (Toupet) fundoplication: reflux recurrence equal (OR 0.69, p=0.31) but long-term dysphagia far commoner after Nissen (OR 2.92) across 8 randomised trials
shelves.question: In gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, does posterior partial fundoplication cause less dysphagia than total (Nissen) fundoplication without losing reflux control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Fundoplication/methods · Gastroesophageal Reflux/surgery · Treatment Outcome · Recurrence · Deglutition Disorders/etiology · Laparoscopy/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — posterior partial fundoplication keeps reflux control and spares swallowing, in pooled randomised evidence. Peristeri's systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomised trials (1,545 patients; 799 total [Nissen] and 746 posterior partial [Toupet]) found long-term recurrence of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease was not statistically different between the techniques (odds ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.34–1.41; p=0.31), while long-term dysphagia was statistically lower with posterior partial fundoplication (OR 2.92, 95% CI 1.49–5.72; p=0.002) with low between-study heterogeneity (I²=0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients without dysmotility disorders, posterior partial fundoplication is the better balance — equivalent reflux control with less dysphagia.

cards.headline: Peristeri 2024 meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,545 patients): GORD recurrence OR 0.69 (p=0.31, NS); long-term dysphagia OR 2.92 (p=0.002) favouring posterior partial fundoplication
cards.summary: Peristeri 2024 meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,545 patients): GORD recurrence OR 0.69 (p=0.31, NS); long-term dysphagia OR 2.92 (p=0.002) favouring posterior partial fundoplication
cards.people: Eight randomised controlled trials totalling 1,545 patients undergoing laparoscopic fundoplication for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease without subsequent dysmotility disorders: 799 in the total (Nissen) fundoplication group and 746 in the posterior partial (Toupet) group. Outcomes: long-term recurrence of GORD and long-term dysphagia, pooled with RevMan in a random-effects model.
cards.result: Long-term recurrence of GORD did not differ significantly between Nissen and Toupet cohorts (odds ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.34–1.41; z=1.01, p=0.31). Long-term dysphagia was statistically lower in the Toupet group (OR 2.92, 95% CI 1.49–5.72; z=3.13, p=0.002) with low between-study heterogeneity (I²=0%).
cards.watchOut: Recurrence and dysphagia are summated across trials that define 'long term' and grade dysphagia differently, and the abstract gives no absolute recurrence or dysphagia rates — so the number-needed-to-treat for avoiding dysphagia cannot be derived from this record. The finding explicitly excludes patients with dysmotility disorders.
cards.source: Peristeri DV et al. Long-term efficacy of total versus posterior partial fundoplication in patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England. 2024. PMID: 37843095. shelves.title: Outpatient diverticulitis without antibiotics (DINAMO): admissions 3.3% versus 5.8% with antibiotics — noninferior at 90 days, but read alongside the inpatient no-antibiotic trials on live shelf #178
shelves.question: In mild acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, is outpatient treatment without antibiotics as safe and effective as treatment with antibiotics?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ambulatory Care/methods · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Disease Management · Diverticulitis, Colonic/diagnosis/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outpatients · Prospective Studies · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outpatient setting specifically, in one open-label noninferiority trial. DINAMO randomised 480 patients with CT-diagnosed mild acute diverticulitis presenting to the emergency department to outpatient treatment without antibiotics (n=242) or with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (n=238), plus anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care: hospital admissions were 3.3% (8/242) without antibiotics versus 5.8% (14/238) with antibiotics (mean difference 2.58%, 95% CI −1.17 to 6.32), confirming noninferiority; emergency revisits were 7.0% versus 6.7% (mean difference −0.3, 95% CI −4.83 to 4.22), and poor pain control at 2 days was 2.3% versus 5.7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): mild diverticulitis can be managed at home without antibiotics; the shelf is deliberately distinct from — and cross-points to — live shelf #178, which asks the no-antibiotics question for CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis without the outpatient setting (the coordinator's one-home adjudication is requested on the face of the summary).

cards.headline: Mora-López 2021 DINAMO (n=480): hospital admission 3.3% without antibiotics vs 5.8% with antibiotics — noninferior; revisits 7.0% vs 6.7%
cards.summary: Mora-López 2021 DINAMO (n=480): hospital admission 3.3% without antibiotics vs 5.8% with antibiotics — noninferior; revisits 7.0% vs 6.7%
cards.people: 480 patients with mild acute diverticulitis diagnosed by CT, presenting to the emergency department at 15 hospitals, randomised to outpatient non-antibiotic treatment (anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care; n=242) or classical outpatient treatment with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 875/125 mg every 8 hours plus anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care (n=238). Clinical controls at 2, 7, 30 and 90 days. Primary endpoint: hospital admission; secondary: emergency department revisits, pain control, emergency surgery.
cards.result: Hospitalisation rates were 8 of 242 (3.3%) in the non-antibiotic group versus 14 of 238 (5.8%) in the antibiotic group (mean difference 2.58%, 95% CI −1.17 to 6.32), confirming noninferiority. Revisits: 17 of 242 (7.0%) versus 16 of 238 (6.7%) (mean difference −0.3, 95% CI −4.83 to 4.22). Poor pain control at 2 days' follow-up: 5 of 221 (2.3%) versus 13 of 230 (5.7%) (mean difference 3.39, 95% CI −0.18 to 6.96).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and noninferiority — the design assumes, not proves, that antibiotics add nothing — and 'mild' CT-proven disease in emergency-department patients who could be sent home is a narrow slice of diverticulitis. Complicated disease, abscess, immunocompromise and older frail patients sit outside this trial. Single trial: Tier C.

randomised noninferiority trial (mora-lópez 2021, dinamo) 480 patients with mild acute diverticulitis diagnosed by ct, presenting to the emergency department at 15 hospitals, randomised to outpatient non-antibiotic treatment (anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care; n=242) or classical outpatient treatment with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 875/125 mg every 8 hours plus anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care (n=238). clinical controls at 2, 7, 30 and 90 days. primary endpoint: hospital admission; secondary: emergency department revisits, pain control, emergency surgery. hospitalisation rates were 8 of 242 (3.3%) in the non-antibiotic group versus 14 of 238 (5.8%) in the antibiotic group (mean difference 2.58%, 95% ci −1.17 to 6.32), confirming noninferiority. revisits: 17 of 242 (7.0%) versus 16 of 238 (6.7%) (mean difference −0.3, 95% ci −4.83 to 4.22). poor pain control at 2 days' follow-up: 5 of 221 (2.3%) versus 13 of 230 (5.7%) (mean difference 3.39, 95% ci −0.18 to 6.96). open-label and noninferiority — the design assumes, not proves, that antibiotics add nothing — and 'mild' ct-proven disease in emergency-department patients who could be sent home is a narrow slice of diverticulitis. complicated disease, abscess, immunocompromise and older frail patients sit outside this trial. single trial: tier c. mora-lópez l et al. efficacy and safety of nonantibiotic outpatient treatment in mild acute diverticulitis (dinamo-study): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, noninferiority trial. annals of surgery. 2021. pmid: 34183510. registry id: nct02785549. mesh: acute disease · adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · ambulatory care/methods · anti-bacterial agents · disease management · diverticulitis, colonic/diagnosis/therapy · female · follow-up studies · humans · male · middle aged · outpatients · prospective studies · tomography, x-ray computed · young adult

shelves.title: Laparoscopic lavage versus sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis (LOLA, 3 years): no difference in morbidity (84% vs 72%) or mortality (16% vs 18%) — but fewer reoperations and fewer stomas alive at 3 years, at the price of sigmoidectomy in 45% of lavage patients
shelves.question: In perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis, does laparoscopic peritoneal lavage avoid stoma and match sigmoidectomy on outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Diverticulitis/surgery · Diverticulitis, Colonic/complications/surgery · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intestinal Perforation/complications/surgery · Laparoscopy/adverse effects · Peritoneal Lavage/adverse effects · Peritonitis/etiology/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for morbidity and mortality, with a real stoma benefit bought at a cost. In the LOLA arm of the LADIES trial, 88 patients with purulent perforated diverticulitis were randomised to laparoscopic lavage or sigmoidectomy: at 12 months the composite of major morbidity and mortality occurred in 67% after lavage versus 60% after sigmoidectomy (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.54–3.03; p=0.58), with four deaths after lavage and six after sigmoidectomy. By 36 months, in the 77 patients with long-term follow-up, cumulative morbidity was 84% versus 72% (p=0.272) and mortality 16% versus 18% (p=1.000); reoperations were significantly fewer after lavage (45% versus 69%, p=0.039), patients alive with a stoma were fewer (11% versus 17%, log-rank p=0.0268) — but 45% of lavage patients had eventually undergone sigmoidectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): lavage does not match sigmoidectomy's safety case at 12 months and leaves nearly half needing the operation it was meant to avoid — the stoma advantage is real but selective, and better patient selection is the open question.

cards.headline: Vennix 2015 LOLA (n=88): major morbidity/mortality at 12 months 67% after lavage vs 60% after sigmoidectomy (OR 1.28, p=0.58); trial stopped early for increased events in lavage
cards.summary: Vennix 2015 LOLA (n=88): major morbidity/mortality at 12 months 67% after lavage vs 60% after sigmoidectomy (OR 1.28, p=0.58); trial stopped early for increased events in lavage
cards.people: 90 patients with purulent perforated diverticulitis (faecal peritonitis, age >85, high-dose steroids and haemodynamic instability excluded) at 42 hospitals in Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands, randomised 2:1:1 to laparoscopic lavage, Hartmann's procedure or primary anastomosis; 88 analysed after two exclusions. The trial was terminated early by the data and safety monitoring board because of an increased event rate in the lavage group. Primary endpoint: composite major morbidity and mortality within 12 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 30 of 45 (67%) patients in the lavage group and 25 of 42 (60%) in the sigmoidectomy group (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.54–3.03; p=0.58). By 12 months, four patients had died after lavage and six after sigmoidectomy (p=0.43).
cards.watchOut: Stopped early, underpowered and with two-thirds of patients hitting the primary endpoint in both arms — the trial rules out superiority, not equivalence, and its event rate warns against offering lavage casually. The comparator here pools Hartmann's and primary-anastomosis sigmoidectomy.
cards.source: Vennix S et al. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage or sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis: a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, open-label trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 26209030. Registry ID: NCT01317485. cards.headline: Hoek 2022 LOLA 3-year follow-up (n=77): morbidity 84% vs 72% and mortality 16% vs 18% (NS); reoperations 45% vs 69% (p=0.039); stoma alive 11% vs 17%; 45% of lavage patients eventually had sigmoidectomy
cards.summary: Hoek 2022 LOLA 3-year follow-up (n=77): morbidity 84% vs 72% and mortality 16% vs 18% (NS); reoperations 45% vs 69% (p=0.039); stoma alive 11% vs 17%; 45% of lavage patients eventually had sigmoidectomy
cards.people: Long-term follow-up in 77 of the 88 LOLA patients (39 randomised to sigmoidectomy, 38 to laparoscopic lavage), outcomes collected to 36 months: cumulative morbidity and mortality (primary), reoperations (including stoma reversals), stoma rates and sigmoidectomy rates in the lavage group.
cards.result: At 36 months, cumulative morbidity was 28 of 39 (72%) after sigmoidectomy versus 32 of 38 (84%) after lavage (p=0.272) and mortality 7 of 39 (18%) versus 6 of 38 (16%) (p=1.000). Reoperations were significantly fewer after lavage (17 of 38, 45%, versus 27 of 39, 69%; p=0.039); patients alive with a stoma in situ were fewer after lavage (11% versus 17% by Kaplan–Meier, log-rank p=0.0268). Eventually 17 of 38 (45%) patients allocated to lavage underwent sigmoidectomy.
cards.watchOut: The stoma advantage is measured among survivors and shrinks if counted against the 45% who eventually needed the resection anyway; cumulative morbidity numerically favours sigmoidectomy at both time points, even if not significantly. Open-label, small, and with 11 of 88 patients lost to long-term follow-up.
cards.source: Hoek VT et al. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage versus sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis: three-year follow-up of the randomised LOLA trial. Surgical Endoscopy. 2022. PMID: 35606544. Registry ID: NCT01317485. cards.headline: Synthesis: lavage is not superior and not equivalent — it is a stoma-sparing gamble with a near-even chance of surgery later
cards.summary: Synthesis: lavage is not superior and not equivalent — it is a stoma-sparing gamble with a near-even chance of surgery later
cards.people: One randomised trial (88 patients) with 12-month and 36-month follow-up, perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis.
cards.result: Major morbidity/mortality 67% vs 60% at 12 months (OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.54–3.03); at 36 months cumulative morbidity 84% vs 72%, mortality 16% vs 18% (both NS); reoperations 45% vs 69% (p=0.039); alive with stoma 11% vs 17% (p=0.0268); 45% of lavage patients eventually had sigmoidectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — single trial.
cards.watchOut: Purulent peritonitis only — faecal peritonitis was excluded — so this shelf has nothing to say about the sickest perforations, where lavage is least defensible. Patient selection, as the 3-year authors themselves conclude, is the unresolved variable.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vennix S et al. Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 26209030); Hoek VT et al. Surgical Endoscopy. 2022 (PMID: 35606544).

shelves.title: Dapagliflozin for liver fat in type 2 diabetes with fatty liver: MRI liver fat fell significantly versus control at 24 weeks — but the absolute fat loss is unpublished in the abstract, and monotherapy did not beat placebo in the second trial
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with fatty liver, does dapagliflozin reduce liver fat content versus control treatment?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy · Interleukin-6 · Liver/diagnostic imaging · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/complications/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha · Benzhydryl Compounds/therapeutic use · Glucosides/therapeutic use · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Magnetic Resonance Imaging
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on MRI fat, in two small 12–24-week trials whose reporting leaves the effect size half-told. Shi randomised 84 patients with type 2 diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease to dapagliflozin or a control group: at week 24 liver fat content (p<0.001) and pancreatic fat content (p=0.033) were significantly reduced versus control, along with ALT (p<0.001), TNF-α (p=0.004) and IL-6 (p=0.001) — but the abstract prints no absolute liver-fat values, so the size of the reduction cannot be stated from this record. Eriksson's EFFECT-II (84 participants, 12 weeks, four arms) found dapagliflozin reduced liver PDFF by 13% relative to baseline, omega-3 carboxylic acids by 15% and the combination by 21% — yet only the combination reduced liver PDFF versus placebo (p=0.046; liver fat volume −24%, p=0.037), while dapagliflozin monotherapy reduced all measured hepatocyte injury biomarkers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dapagliflozin reduces liver fat, with the honest caveat that the placebo-controlled trial found monotherapy's fat reduction significant only against baseline, not against placebo.

cards.headline: Shi 2023 RCT (n=84): dapagliflozin significantly reduced liver fat (p<0.001) and pancreatic fat (p=0.033) vs control at 24 weeks — absolute fat values not printed in the abstract
cards.summary: Shi 2023 RCT (n=84): dapagliflozin significantly reduced liver fat (p<0.001) and pancreatic fat (p=0.033) vs control at 24 weeks — absolute fat values not printed in the abstract
cards.people: 84 patients with type 2 diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, randomly assigned to dapagliflozin (n=42) or a control group (n=42). Primary endpoint: changes in liver fat content and pancreatic fat content by MRI-estimated proton density fat fraction at week 24; secondary: liver fibrosis index, inflammatory cytokines and liver enzymes.
cards.result: At week 24, the dapagliflozin group significantly reduced liver fat content (p<0.001) and pancreatic fat content (p=0.033) compared with the control group. Serum tumour necrosis factor-α (p=0.004), interleukin-6 (p=0.001) and alanine aminotransferase (p<0.001) also differed significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Significance without magnitude: the abstract reports p-values and no absolute liver-fat change, so no effect size can be quoted from this record, and the 'control' arm's treatment is not described in the abstract — this may not be a placebo-controlled comparison. Small, single-centre, 24 weeks, surrogate endpoint. Tier C.
cards.source: Shi M et al. Effect of dapagliflozin on liver and pancreatic fat in patients with type 2 diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications. 2023.
