cards.headline: Eriksson 2018 EFFECT-II (n=84): dapagliflozin −13%, omega-3 −15%, combination −21% liver fat from baseline — only the combination beat placebo (p=0.046)
cards.summary: Eriksson 2018 EFFECT-II (n=84): dapagliflozin −13%, omega-3 −15%, combination −21% liver fat from baseline — only the combination beat placebo (p=0.046)
cards.people: 84 participants with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD (mean age 65.5 years, BMI 31.2 kg/m², liver PDFF 18%) at five Swedish university-hospital research centres, randomised 1:1:1:1 to dapagliflozin 10 mg (n=21), omega-3 (n-3) carboxylic acids 4 g (n=20), both (n=22) or placebo (n=21) for 12 weeks, double-blind. Primary endpoint: liver fat content by MRI proton density fat fraction.
cards.result: All active treatments significantly reduced liver PDFF from baseline — relative changes: omega-3 carboxylic acids −15%, dapagliflozin −13%, combination −21%. Only the combination reduced liver PDFF (p=0.046) and total liver fat volume (relative change −24%, p=0.037) compared with placebo. Dapagliflozin monotherapy, but not the combination, reduced hepatocyte injury biomarkers (ALT, AST, γ-GT, cytokeratin 18-M30 and M65, fibroblast growth factor 21). Dapagliflozin alone and in combination improved glucose control and reduced body weight and abdominal fat volumes; no new or unexpected adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and 21 patients per arm: the trial can detect large combined effects but not the moderate monotherapy effect it hints at, and the PNPLA3 interaction (p=0.03) in this sample is exploratory. The monotherapy-versus-placebo null for fat sits beside a monotherapy benefit for injury markers — the two endpoints do not move together.
cards.source: Eriksson JW et al. Effects of dapagliflozin and n-3 carboxylic acids on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in people with type 2 diabetes: a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled study. Diabetologia. 2018. cards.headline: Synthesis: liver fat falls on dapagliflozin — the question is by how much, and against what
cards.summary: Synthesis: liver fat falls on dapagliflozin — the question is by how much, and against what
cards.people: Two randomised trials of dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes with NAFLD (84 patients each; 24 weeks and 12 weeks), both using MRI liver fat.
cards.result: Shi: liver fat p<0.001 and pancreatic fat p=0.033 versus control at 24 weeks (no absolute values printed). EFFECT-II: dapagliflozin −13% liver PDFF from baseline, combination −21%; only the combination beat placebo (p=0.046). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — small trials, surrogate endpoint, incomplete reporting in one record.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measured steatohepatitis resolution on biopsy, fibrosis regression or clinical liver outcomes. A prescribing decision on fatty liver still rests on the drug's diabetes, kidney and heart indications, with the liver-fat effect as supporting — not leading — evidence.

shelves.title: Green-Mediterranean diet in fatty liver (DIRECT PLUS): intrahepatic fat fell 38.9% proportionally versus 19.6% on a standard Mediterranean diet and 12.2% on healthy guidelines — at the same weight loss as Mediterranean
shelves.question: In fatty liver disease, does a green-Mediterranean diet reduce intrahepatic fat more than other healthy diets?
shelves.mesh: Araceae · Diet, Mediterranean · Diet, Reducing · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/diet therapy · Polyphenols/administration & dosage · Tea
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, long dietary trial with imaging endpoints. In DIRECT PLUS, 294 participants with abdominal obesity or dyslipidaemia were randomised for 18 months to healthy dietary guidelines, a Mediterranean diet, or a green-Mediterranean diet (further restricted in red/processed meat, enriched with green tea, walnuts and the aquatic plant Mankai — Wolffia globosa, as named in the publication): intrahepatic fat fell by 38.9% proportionally on green-Mediterranean versus 19.6% on Mediterranean (p=0.035, weight-loss adjusted) and 12.2% on healthy guidelines (p<0.001), despite similar weight loss in the two Mediterranean groups. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease prevalence after 18 months was 31.5% on green-Mediterranean versus 47.9% on Mediterranean and 54.8% on guidelines (p=0.012 between groups). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the green-Mediterranean pattern roughly doubles intrahepatic fat loss over a standard Mediterranean diet at equal weight loss — a single-trial, surrogate-imaging result, Tier C.

cards.headline: Yaskolka Meir 2021 DIRECT PLUS (n=294): intrahepatic fat −38.9% green-MED vs −19.6% MED (p=0.035) and −12.2% guidelines (p<0.001); NAFLD prevalence 31.5% vs 47.9% vs 54.8%
cards.summary: Yaskolka Meir 2021 DIRECT PLUS (n=294): intrahepatic fat −38.9% green-MED vs −19.6% MED (p=0.035) and −12.2% guidelines (p<0.001); NAFLD prevalence 31.5% vs 47.9% vs 54.8%
cards.people: 294 participants with abdominal obesity or dyslipidaemia (age 51 years, 88% men, BMI 31.3 kg/m², median intrahepatic fat 6.6%, 62% with NAFLD) randomised to healthy dietary guidelines (HDG), Mediterranean (MED) or green-Mediterranean (green-MED) weight-loss diets for 18 months, all with physical activity. Both MED groups were isocaloric and ate 28 g/day walnuts; green-MED additionally restricted red/processed meat and added green tea (3–4 cups/day) and a Mankai (Wolffia globosa) green shake (100 g/day frozen cubes), raising polyphenol intake. Intrahepatic fat change measured by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy; 89.8% retained at 18 months, 78% with eligible follow-up spectroscopy.
cards.result: Intrahepatic fat fell by 38.9% proportionally on green-MED versus 19.6% on MED (p=0.035, weight-loss adjusted) and 12.2% on HDG (p<0.001), despite similar moderate weight loss in both MED groups. NAFLD prevalence declined to 31.5% (green-MED), 47.9% (MED) and 54.8% (HDG) (p=0.012 between groups). Greater intrahepatic fat loss was independently associated with increased Mankai and walnut intake, decreased red/processed meat consumption, improved folate and adipokine/lipid biomarkers, and microbiome changes.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one workplace-based Israeli cohort, 88% men, and a multi-component intervention — the design cannot say whether Mankai, green tea, meat restriction or polyphenols did the work, and Mankai is not a generally available food. Intrahepatic fat by spectroscopy is a surrogate; no biopsy or clinical liver outcomes. Single trial: Tier C.

shelves.title: Band ligation versus beta blockers to prevent first variceal bleeding: bleeding was lower with ligation only in trials with unclear bias control (RR 0.56) — in adequately controlled trials there was no difference (RR 0.86), and mortality never differed (116/573 vs 115/594)
shelves.question: For primary prevention of variceal bleeding, does endoscopic band ligation prevent first bleeding better than beta blockers — and does either reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/mortality/prevention & control · Humans · Ligation/methods · Primary Prevention · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for first bleeding only, and only on the weaker half of the evidence. Gluud's meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials of band ligation versus beta blockers for primary prophylaxis of oesophageal varices found no mortality difference in any analysis — 116 of 573 patients died on ligation versus 115 of 594 on beta blockers overall; relative risk 1.22 (95% CI 0.84–1.78) in trials with adequate bias control and 1.02 (0.75–1.39) in trials with unclear bias control. Bleeding told two stories: no significant difference in the adequately controlled trials (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55–1.35), but significantly less bleeding with ligation in the unclear-bias trials (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.41–0.77); metaregression showed ligation's estimated benefit grew the shorter the follow-up and when trials were published as abstracts. The best-known single trial (Sarin 1999) did favour ligation: actuarial bleeding probability at 18 months 15% versus 43% on propranolol (p=0.04), with five deaths in each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ligation probably prevents some first bleeds that beta blockers do not — the unbiased trials cannot confirm it — and neither strategy has ever been shown to save lives in this comparison; Tier C, because the benefit claim rests on bias-prone trials.

cards.headline: Gluud 2007 meta-analysis (16 RCTs): mortality RR 1.22 (adequate bias control) and 1.02 (unclear); bleeding RR 0.86 (NS) in adequate trials vs 0.56 in unclear-bias trials
cards.summary: Gluud 2007 meta-analysis (16 RCTs): mortality RR 1.22 (adequate bias control) and 1.02 (unclear); bleeding RR 0.86 (NS) in adequate trials vs 0.56 in unclear-bias trials
cards.people: 16 randomised trials of banding ligation versus beta blockers as primary prophylaxis in patients with oesophageal varices and no previous bleeding (15 trials in patients with high-risk varices); only three trials reported adequate bias control (allocation sequence generation and concealment). Mortality reported for all trials: 573 ligation and 594 beta-blocker patients.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ significantly in trials with adequate bias control (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.84–1.78) or unclear bias control (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.75–1.39); overall deaths were 116 of 573 on ligation and 115 of 594 on beta blockers. Bleeding: no significant difference in adequate-bias-control trials (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55–1.35), but ligation significantly reduced bleeding in unclear-bias trials (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.41–0.77). Both treatments were associated with adverse events. In metaregression, ligation's estimated effect was significantly more positive in trials published as abstracts and with shorter follow-up.
cards.watchOut: This is the rare meta-analysis whose own stratification dissolves its headline: the bleeding benefit lives exactly where bias control is unproven. Thirteen of sixteen trials had unclear bias control, and abstract-only publication inflated the ligation effect — the honest summary is 'unproven advantage', not 'proven'.
cards.source: Gluud LL et al. Banding ligation versus beta-blockers as primary prophylaxis in esophageal varices: systematic review of randomized trials. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 18042114. cards.headline: Sarin 1999 RCT (n=89): actuarial bleeding at 18 months 15% with ligation vs 43% with propranolol (p=0.04); deaths five in each group
cards.summary: Sarin 1999 RCT (n=89): actuarial bleeding at 18 months 15% with ligation vs 43% with propranolol (p=0.04); deaths five in each group
cards.people: 89 consecutive eligible patients with large varices (>5 mm) at high risk of bleeding (82 with cirrhosis), assigned to propranolol titrated to a 25% reduction in baseline heart rate (n=44) or endoscopic variceal ligation weekly until obliteration or near-obliteration (n=45; mean 3.2 sessions). Mean follow-up 14±9 and 13±10 months respectively.
cards.result: After 18 months, the actuarial probability of bleeding was 43% in the propranolol group versus 15% in the ligation group (p=0.04); twelve propranolol patients and four ligation patients bled (three of the four before their varices were obliterated). Nine ligation patients had recurrent varices, a mean of 3.7 months after initial treatment. Five patients in each group died; variceal bleeding caused four deaths on propranolol and three on ligation. There were no serious complications of ligation; propranolol was stopped for side effects in two patients.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1999 trial of 89 patients with actuarial estimates — exactly the profile the Gluud metaregression flags as inflating ligation's benefit — and propranolol titration by heart rate alone is not modern portal-pressure-guided dosing. It is carded as the strongest individual trial, not as the verdict.
cards.source: Sarin SK et al. Comparison of endoscopic ligation and propranolol for the primary prevention of variceal bleeding. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1999. PMID: 10099140. cards.people: One meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (1,167 patients) plus its best-known component trial (89 patients), primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.
cards.result: Mortality: 116/573 (ligation) vs 115/594 (beta blockers); RR 1.22 in adequate-bias trials, 1.02 in unclear-bias trials. Bleeding: RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.55–1.35) in adequate-bias trials versus RR 0.56 (0.41–0.77) in unclear-bias trials; Sarin's trial: 15% vs 43% actuarial bleeding at 18 months (p=0.04), five deaths per group. shelves.title: Spironolactone alone matched spironolactone plus furosemide for moderate ascites — 94% versus 98% responded, and the single drug needed half as many dose reductions
shelves.question: In moderate ascites in cirrhosis, is spironolactone alone as effective as spironolactone combined with furosemide?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Ascites · Diuretics · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Furosemide · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Spironolactone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for clearing moderate ascites, starting with two diuretics bought nothing over starting with one. In the one head-to-head randomised trial (Santos J et al., PMID: 12873814), ascites responded in 98% on spironolactone plus furosemide versus 94% on spironolactone alone, with similar speed of mobilisation and similar complication rates — but the combination group needed its dose reduced far more often (68% versus 34%, P=0.002), the practical price of starting with both. The older head-to-head that frames the question (Pérez-Ayuso RM et al., PMID: 6339312) found spironolactone alone answered in 18 of 19 patients (95%) against 11 of 21 (52%) on furosemide alone (p<0.01), and 9 of the 10 furosemide failures later responded to spironolactone — spironolactone is the load-bearing drug of the pair. Neither trial was powered for survival, kidney failure, or hospitalisation, and both predate modern ascites care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): spironolactone alone clears moderate ascites as reliably as the combination, with fewer dose adjustments; the combination remains the escalation step, not the starting step.

cards.headline: Santos 2003: response 98% on the combination versus 94% on spironolactone alone — but dose reductions in 68% versus 34% (P=0.002)
cards.summary: Santos 2003: response 98% on the combination versus 94% on spironolactone alone — but dose reductions in 68% versus 34% (P=0.002)
cards.people: 100 nonazotemic patients with cirrhosis and moderate ascites, randomised to spironolactone plus furosemide (50 patients) or spironolactone alone (50 patients); doses were titrated up to 400 mg/day spironolactone and 160 mg/day furosemide, furosemide was added for spironolactone non-responders, and doses were reduced for excessive response.
cards.result: The response rate was 98% in the combination group versus 94% on spironolactone alone; the rapidity of ascites mobilisation and the incidence of diuretic-induced complications were similar in both groups. The need to reduce the diuretic dosage was significantly higher on the combination (68% versus 34%; P=0.002). The authors concluded spironolactone alone seems as safe and effective as the combination and, needing less dose adjustment, would suit outpatient treatment better.
cards.watchOut: A single 100-patient trial from 2003, unblinded by design, powered for ascites response — not for death, kidney injury, or admission. 'As effective' here means a 4-point response gap in a small sample; the confidence interval around that gap is wide, and the trial's escalation design (furosemide added to failures) means the alone arm was never left failing.

cards.headline: Pérez-Ayuso 1983: spironolactone alone answered in 18 of 19 (95%) versus 11 of 21 (52%) on furosemide alone — and rescued 9 of 10 furosemide failures
cards.summary: Pérez-Ayuso 1983: spironolactone alone answered in 18 of 19 (95%) versus 11 of 21 (52%) on furosemide alone — and rescued 9 of 10 furosemide failures
cards.people: 40 nonazotemic patients with cirrhosis, ascites, and avid sodium retention, randomised to furosemide (21 patients; 80 mg/day rising to 160 mg/day) or spironolactone (19 patients; 150 mg/day rising to 300 mg/day); non-responders were later crossed to the other drug.
cards.result: 11 of 21 patients responded to furosemide, while 18 of 19 responded to spironolactone (p<0.01). Of the 10 furosemide non-responders, 9 responded later to spironolactone. Response tracked the activity of the renin–aldosterone system: patients with higher renin and aldosterone did not respond to furosemide and required 300 mg/day of spironolactone.
cards.watchOut: This 1983 trial compares the two single drugs, not the combination the shelf asks about — it is carded as the mechanistic support for why spironolactone alone can carry the regimen, not as a second test of the combination question. Doses and background care are of their era.
cards.source: Pérez-Ayuso RM et al. Randomized comparative study of efficacy of furosemide versus spironolactone in nonazotemic cirrhosis with ascites. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small head-to-head trial, one older single-drug comparison — equivalence on response, a clear handling advantage to starting with one drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small head-to-head trial, one older single-drug comparison — equivalence on response, a clear handling advantage to starting with one drug
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 140 nonazotemic patients with cirrhotic ascites: Santos 2003 (combination versus spironolactone alone, n=100) and Pérez-Ayuso 1983 (spironolactone versus furosemide alone, n=40).
cards.result: Ascites response: 98% (combination) versus 94% (spironolactone alone) in Santos 2003; 95% on spironolactone versus 52% on furosemide in Pérez-Ayuso 1983. Dose reductions: 68% versus 34% (P=0.002) favouring spironolactone alone. No trial measured survival or kidney failure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: the equivalence claim rests on one small trial, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled nonazotemic patients with moderate ascites; nothing here speaks to tense or refractory ascites, where combination and escalation strategies are a different question.

shelves.title: Larazotide in coeliac gluten challenge: the permeability endpoint failed in both trials — symptoms and antibody rises were blunted at the lowest dose instead
shelves.question: In coeliac disease undergoing gluten challenge, does larazotide acetate prevent gluten-induced mucosal injury and symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Autoantibodies · Celiac Disease · Diet, Gluten-Free · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Glutens · Humans · Lactulose · Male · Middle Aged · Oligopeptides · Severity of Illness Index · Tight Junctions · Transglutaminases · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the endpoint the drug was built for failed; the symptoms moved. Larazotide acetate, a tight-junction regulator peptide, did not significantly change the urinary lactulose-to-mannitol (LAMA) permeability ratio versus placebo in either gluten-challenge trial (Kelly CP et al., PMID: 23163616, n=184; Leffler DA et al., PMID: 22825365, n=86) — and neither trial measured mucosal histology, so 'mucosal injury prevented' was never directly tested. What did move were symptoms and immune reactivity at the lowest dose: in Kelly 2013, larazotide 1 mg limited gluten-induced symptoms (P=0.002 versus placebo), and the anti-tissue-transglutaminase IgA rise was a mean ratio of 19.0 over baseline on placebo versus 5.78, 3.88, and 7.72 on larazotide 1, 4, and 8 mg (P=0.010, 0.005, and 0.025). The 2022 meta-analysis of four randomised trials (626 patients; Hoilat GJ et al., PMID: 34339872) confirms the split: no LAMA difference in any analysis, significantly better symptom scores only in the gluten-challenge subgroup. Adverse event rates were similar to placebo in both trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: larazotide blunts gluten-induced symptoms and antibody response at low doses, but its permeability primary endpoint — the closest proxy these trials offer for mucosal protection — was null throughout.

cards.headline: Kelly 2013: LAMA ratio no different from placebo — but 1 mg limited symptoms (P=0.002) and all doses blunted the antibody rise (19.0 on placebo versus 3.88–7.72)
cards.summary: Kelly 2013: LAMA ratio no different from placebo — but 1 mg limited symptoms (P=0.002) and all doses blunted the antibody rise (19.0 on placebo versus 3.88–7.72)
cards.people: 184 patients with coeliac disease maintaining a gluten-free diet, randomised after a gluten-free run-in to larazotide acetate 1, 4, or 8 mg three times daily or placebo, with 2.7 g of gluten daily for 6 weeks.
cards.result: No significant differences in lactulose-to-mannitol (LAMA) ratios were observed between larazotide and placebo groups. Larazotide 1 mg limited gluten-induced symptoms on the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (P=0.002 versus placebo). The mean ratio of anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA over baseline was 19.0 in the placebo group compared with 5.78 (P=0.010), 3.88 (P=0.005), and 7.72 (P=0.025) in the 1, 4, and 8 mg groups. Adverse event rates were similar between larazotide and placebo.
cards.watchOut: An exploratory trial whose primary permeability endpoint was null; the symptom and antibody findings are secondary endpoints, the dose pattern is non-monotonic (the middle dose looked best on antibodies, the lowest on symptoms), and no biopsy endpoint was taken — mucosal protection is inferred, never shown.
cards.source: Kelly CP et al. Larazotide acetate in patients with coeliac disease undergoing a gluten challenge: a randomised placebo-controlled study. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2013. cards.headline: Leffler 2012: gluten challenge itself failed to move the LAMA ratio significantly — larazotide limited symptom worsening only at some lower doses
cards.summary: Leffler 2012: gluten challenge itself failed to move the LAMA ratio significantly — larazotide limited symptom worsening only at some lower doses
cards.people: 86 patients with diet-controlled coeliac disease, randomised to larazotide acetate 0.25, 1, 4, or 8 mg or placebo three times daily, with or without gluten challenge (2.4 g/day) for 14 days.
cards.result: LAMA measurements were highly variable in the outpatient setting; the increase in LAMA ratio with gluten challenge was not significantly greater than in the gluten-free control, and among challenged patients the larazotide–placebo difference in LAMA ratios was not statistically significant. Larazotide appeared to limit gluten-induced worsening of gastrointestinal symptom severity at some lower doses but not at the higher dose; symptoms did worsen significantly in the challenge-placebo arm versus the placebo-placebo arm. No serious adverse events were observed; the most common adverse events were headache and urinary tract infection.
cards.watchOut: The challenge model itself wobbled here — 2.4 g/day of gluten worsened symptoms but did not significantly move the permeability assay — so a null LAMA result in this trial is weak evidence about the drug in either direction. Fourteen days is also short for mucosal change.
cards.source: Leffler DA et al. A randomized, double-blind study of larazotide acetate to prevent the activation of celiac disease during gluten challenge. cards.headline: Hoilat 2022 meta-analysis (4 trials, 626 patients): LAMA null everywhere; symptom benefit confined to the gluten-challenge subgroup
cards.summary: Hoilat 2022 meta-analysis (4 trials, 626 patients): LAMA null everywhere; symptom benefit confined to the gluten-challenge subgroup
cards.people: Four randomised trials of larazotide acetate (AT-1001) in coeliac disease, 626 patients (465 larazotide, 161 placebo); three trials reported gluten-challenge outcomes (2.4–2.7 g gluten/day) and two reported gluten-free-diet outcomes (overlapping sets).
cards.result: Change in lactulose-to-mannitol ratio did not significantly differ between larazotide and placebo, irrespective of gluten status. In the gluten-challenge subgroup, larazotide significantly improved change in total Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale and coeliac-specific GSRS scores versus placebo; no significant difference was seen in patients on a gluten-free diet. Larazotide reduced gluten-related diarrhoea versus placebo in challenged patients; other adverse events were comparable.
cards.watchOut: The pooled symptom benefit rests on the same two small challenge trials carded above, analysed under a fixed-effects model; the meta-analysis adds patients (two further trials on a gluten-free diet) but no new challenge evidence, and still no histology anywhere in the programme.
cards.source: Hoilat GJ et al. Larazotide acetate for treatment of celiac disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Clinics and Research in Hepatology and Gastroenterology. 2022. PMID: 34339872. cards.headline: Synthesis: a symptom signal at low dose against a uniformly null permeability endpoint — and mucosal injury never directly measured
cards.summary: Synthesis: a symptom signal at low dose against a uniformly null permeability endpoint — and mucosal injury never directly measured
cards.people: Two randomised gluten-challenge trials (n=184 and n=86) and a four-trial meta-analysis (626 patients) of larazotide acetate in coeliac disease.
cards.result: Permeability (LAMA ratio): no significant benefit in either trial or in the pooled analysis. Symptoms: significantly limited at larazotide 1 mg in Kelly 2013 (P=0.002) and in the pooled challenge subgroup. Antibody rise (Kelly 2013): 19.0× baseline on placebo versus 5.78×, 3.88×, and 7.72× on 1, 4, and 8 mg. Safety: adverse events similar to placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the benefit half rests on secondary endpoints of exploratory trials, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: The candidate question asks about mucosal injury; the entire larazotide challenge programme used a permeability assay and symptom scores, not villous histology. A shelf that claimed mucosal protection would be claiming an endpoint no trial measured.

shelves.title: Survodutide in MASH with fibrosis: steatohepatitis improved without worsening fibrosis in 47%, 62% and 43% across the three doses versus 14% on placebo — one phase 2 trial, a biopsy surrogate, and a dose response that peaked in the middle
shelves.question: In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis with fibrosis, does survodutide improve steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Liver*/drug therapy/pathology · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Liver/pathology/drug effects · Liver Cirrhosis*/drug therapy/pathology · Receptors, Glucagon*/agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on liver histology at 48 weeks, in a single phase 2 trial. In Sanyal AJ et al. (PMID: 38847460), 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis stage F1 through F3 were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide 2.4 mg, 4.8 mg or 6.0 mg, or placebo, over 48 weeks (a 24-week rapid-dose-escalation phase followed by a 24-week maintenance phase). The primary end point — histologic improvement in MASH with no worsening of fibrosis — occurred in 47% of the 2.4-mg group, 62% of the 4.8-mg group and 43% of the 6.0-mg group, versus 14% on placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve as best-fitting model). Secondary end points moved the same way: a decrease in liver fat content by at least 30% occurred in 63%, 67% and 57% across the survodutide doses versus 14% on placebo, and improvement in fibrosis by at least one stage in 34%, 36% and 34% versus 22%. The price was gastrointestinal: nausea in 66% on survodutide versus 23% on placebo, diarrhoea in 49% versus 23%, and vomiting in 41% versus 4%; serious adverse events occurred in 8% with survodutide and 7% with placebo. The authors concluded that survodutide was superior to placebo for improvement in MASH without worsening of fibrosis, warranting further investigation in phase 3 trials. The catches are on the face of the record: the end point is a biopsy surrogate with no liver-outcome data, the dose response was non-monotonic (the highest dose did worse than the middle dose on the primary end point), and one phase 2 trial is the whole evidence base. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in MASH with fibrosis stage F1–F3, once-weekly survodutide improved steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis in roughly half to three-fifths of patients versus 14% on placebo at 48 weeks, with frequent gastrointestinal adverse events — a single-trial, surrogate-endpoint result awaiting phase 3 confirmation.

cards.headline: Sanyal 2024: MASH improvement with no worsening of fibrosis in 47% (2.4 mg), 62% (4.8 mg) and 43% (6.0 mg) on survodutide versus 14% on placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve) — nausea 66% versus 23%
cards.summary: Sanyal 2024: MASH improvement with no worsening of fibrosis in 47% (2.4 mg), 62% (4.8 mg) and 43% (6.0 mg) on survodutide versus 14% on placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve) — nausea 66% versus 23%
cards.people: 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis stage F1 through F3, randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to once-weekly subcutaneous injections of survodutide at a dose of 2.4, 4.8 or 6.0 mg or placebo, and who received at least one dose. The 48-week trial had two phases: a 24-week rapid-dose-escalation phase, followed by a 24-week maintenance phase. Survodutide is a dual agonist of the glucagon receptor and the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor. The trial was funded by Boehringer Ingelheim.
cards.result: The primary end point — histologic improvement (reduction) in MASH with no worsening of fibrosis — occurred in 47% of the participants in the survodutide 2.4-mg group, 62% of those in the 4.8-mg group and 43% of those in the 6.0-mg group, as compared with 14% of those in the placebo group (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve as best-fitting model), the absolute rates printed alongside. Secondary end points: a decrease in liver fat content by at least 30% occurred in 63% of the 2.4-mg group, 67% of the 4.8-mg group, 57% of the 6.0-mg group and 14% of the placebo group; improvement (reduction) in fibrosis by at least one stage occurred in 34%, 36%, 34% and 22%, respectively. Adverse events that were more frequent with survodutide than with placebo included nausea (66% vs. 23%), diarrhoea (49% vs. 23%) and vomiting (41% vs. 4%); serious adverse events occurred in 8% with survodutide and 7% with placebo. The authors concluded that survodutide was superior to placebo with respect to improvement in MASH without worsening of fibrosis, warranting further investigation in phase 3 trials.
cards.watchOut: Histology is a surrogate: no liver-outcome data (cirrhosis, liver failure, death) exist in this record, and the trial ran 48 weeks in biopsy-selected patients with fibrosis stage F1 through F3 — it says nothing about cirrhotic (F4) disease. The dose response was non-monotonic: the 6.0-mg dose did worse than the 4.8-mg dose on the primary end point (43% versus 62%), so more drug was not more benefit, and the usable dose is unsettled until phase 3. Gastrointestinal adverse events were frequent at every dose.
cards.source: Sanyal AJ et al. A Phase 2 Randomized Trial of Survodutide in MASH and Fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38847460. Registry ID: NCT04771273 (EudraCT 2020-002723-11). cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 2 trial — a clear histologic win over placebo at every dose, a middle-dose peak, and a gastrointestinal price — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2 trial — a clear histologic win over placebo at every dose, a middle-dose peak, and a gastrointestinal price — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised phase 2 trial of 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stage F1 through F3, testing once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide 2.4 mg, 4.8 mg or 6.0 mg against placebo over 48 weeks.
cards.result: Improvement in MASH with no worsening of fibrosis: 47% (2.4 mg), 62% (4.8 mg) and 43% (6.0 mg) versus 14% on placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve as best-fitting model). Liver fat decrease of at least 30%: 63%, 67% and 57% versus 14%. Fibrosis improvement by at least one stage: 34%, 36% and 34% versus 22%. Gastrointestinal adverse events: nausea 66% versus 23%, diarrhoea 49% versus 23%, vomiting 41% versus 4%; serious adverse events 8% versus 7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: this trial (Sanyal AJ et al., PMID: 38847460) is also carded as a companion card on live shelf #1094 (survodutide for obesity), where it serves as the molecule's companion-programme card inside a weight-loss question. shelves.title: Which lifestyle change cuts liver fat most? The Cochrane network meta-analysis of 59 trials could not rank them — the data were too sparse for any clinical outcome
shelves.question: In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which lifestyle modification — aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, diet, or combinations — reduces liver fat most?
shelves.mesh: Bayes Theorem · Bias · Caloric Restriction · Diet, Carbohydrate-Restricted · Diet, Mediterranean · Exercise · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Life Style · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Odds Ratio · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Resistance Training · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — not because lifestyle change was shown not to work, but because the comparative evidence cannot crown a winner. The Cochrane network meta-analysis built for exactly this question (Buzzetti E et al., PMID: 34114650) included 59 randomised trials with 3,631 participants and 33 different interventions, yet found the data too sparse for the clinical outcomes: only 28 trials (1,942 participants) reported any outcome of interest, follow-up ran from 1 month to 24 months, and clinical events — death, cirrhosis, decompensation, transplantation, liver cancer — were so sparse that the planned network rankings could not be estimated and only direct head-to-head comparisons were performed. All but two trials were at high risk of bias. The review's own conclusion is that there is considerable uncertainty about the effects of lifestyle interventions versus no additional intervention on any clinical outcome over this follow-up, and it proposes aerobic exercise plus dietary advice as the combination to test in long trials — a research agenda, not a ranking. No liver-fat effect sizes that would order aerobic against resistance against diet are reported in the record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): on current randomised evidence no lifestyle modality can be ranked above the others for fatty liver; the honest answer to 'which most' is that the trials have not been built to say.

cards.headline: Buzzetti 2021 (Cochrane): 59 trials, 3,631 participants, 33 interventions — and the network could not be estimated for clinical outcomes
cards.summary: Buzzetti 2021 (Cochrane): 59 trials, 3,631 participants, 33 interventions — and the network could not be estimated for clinical outcomes
cards.people: 59 randomised trials (3,631 participants) of lifestyle interventions in non-alcohol-related fatty liver disease, comparing 33 interventions — advice, supervised exercise, special diets, combinations, or no additional intervention; 28 trials (1,942 participants) reported outcomes of interest; follow-up 1 month to 24 months; all but two trials at high risk of bias.
cards.result: The data were too sparse for the clinical outcomes, so the planned Bayesian network meta-analysis rankings were not performed and only direct comparisons were run. Clinical events related to fatty liver (mortality, cirrhosis, decompensation, transplantation, hepatocellular carcinoma, liver-related mortality) were sparse over 2 to 24 months of follow-up. One participant in one trial had an adverse event; no other intervention-related adverse events were reported. The authors concluded there is considerable uncertainty about the effects of lifestyle interventions compared with no additional intervention on any clinical outcome after short follow-up, and proposed aerobic exercise and dietary advice as the test combination for future long trials.
cards.watchOut: This record answers at the level of clinical outcomes and comparative certainty; it does not print liver-fat effect sizes by modality, so it cannot support a claim that any one exercise type or diet reduces liver fat most. Trials of 1–24 months also cannot see outcomes that take 8–28 years to separate, as the review itself notes.
cards.source: Buzzetti E et al. Lifestyle modifications for nonalcohol-related fatty liver disease: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 34114650. cards.summary: Synthesis: the ranking question is currently unanswerable from randomised evidence — 57 of 59 trials at high risk of bias, a third reporting no usable outcome
cards.people: One Cochrane network meta-analysis (59 trials, 3,631 participants) is the entire verified evidence base for the head-to-head ranking question.
cards.result: Network rankings: not estimable for clinical outcomes. Direct comparisons: considerable uncertainty for every lifestyle intervention versus no additional intervention. Harms: essentially none reported (one adverse event in one trial). shelves.title: Branched-chain amino acids in hepatic encephalopathy: oral trials improve symptoms (Marchesini 1990: 80% vs 35% improved) — acute intravenous trials null, survival unchanged (RR 0.88)
shelves.question: In hepatic encephalopathy, do branched-chain amino acids improve symptoms or survival versus control diets?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Bias · Diarrhea · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Nausea · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — but the split runs by route and by outcome, and the oral limb is stronger than a bare SPLIT implies. ORAL BCAA for encephalopathy manifestations: the classic trials line up. Marchesini 1990 (PMID: 2204661; double-blind, casein-controlled, n=64) improved the portal-systemic encephalopathy index (40→21% vs 37→36%) with 80% vs 35% of patients improving on two or more measures (p<0.001); the double-blind crossovers Egberts 1985 (PMID: 3882509) and Plauth 1993 (PMID: 8315258) each found significant psychomotor gains in latent encephalopathy; and Horst 1984 (PMID: 6706302) showed oral BCAA lets protein-intolerant patients take protein-equivalent nitrogen with far fewer encephalopathy episodes (stage 2 or greater: 1 of 17 vs 7 of 20). Against that: Eriksson 1982 (PMID: 6749604) was null — in 7 patients — and the largest oral trial, Les 2011 (PMID: 21326220, n=116), missed its recurrence endpoint (47% vs 34% remaining episode-free, P=0.274) while still improving neuropsychological tests and muscle mass. The Cochrane pool (Gluud 2017, PMID: 28518283; 16 trials, 827 participants) puts failure to improve at RR 0.73 (0.61–0.88), graded high-quality evidence — a LIKELY-grade symptom benefit for the oral route. ACUTE INTRAVENOUS BCAA is a different story: Wahren 1983 (PMID: 6345330; improvement 14 of 25 vs 12 of 25), Vilstrup 1990 (PMID: 2195106; 17 woke in each group) and Michel 1985 (PMID: 4079669; improved 12 of 36 vs 10 of 34) are all null, Rossi-Fanelli 1982 (PMID: 6749458) was not significant against lactulose (complete recovery 70% vs 47%), and the single positive acute trial, Cerra 1985 (PMID: 3892073), beat neomycin — an active control — without printing event counts. SURVIVAL: no trial shows a mortality benefit; pooled mortality is RR 0.88 (0.69–1.11), not significant. Two large trials in broader cirrhosis populations (Marchesini 2003, PMID: 12806613; Muto 2005, PMID: 16206505) found fewer composite cirrhosis events on long-term oral BCAA — context for biological activity, not encephalopathy or mortality evidence. Against lactulose or neomycin directly, no significant symptom edge was shown (RR 0.66, 0.34–1.30), and gastrointestinal upset is the cost (nausea/vomiting RR 5.56 in the review's fixed-effect analysis). PROPOSED SPLIT: LIKELY benefit for encephalopathy symptoms with oral BCAA; no demonstrated benefit for acute intravenous use or for survival. EXPANSION (Nov 18, 2026 — 10 references added, developer's verdict pending): the Cochrane review has been updated (Aamann 2026, PMID: 41542879; 18 trials, 934 participants): encephalopathy non-improvement RR 0.79 (0.64–0.96) and mortality RR 0.89 (0.71–1.12), with certainty graded low and very low respectively — the point estimates confirm the 2017 pool while the certainty language softens. The intravenous limb gains a modern trial and its own meta-analysis: Mehtani 2023 (PMID: 37975059) found a 24-hour improvement that was not sustained in ACLF, and Yokobori 2025 (PMID: 39780295) pooled the acute intravenous trials to a null (consciousness RR 1.26, 0.96–1.66; mortality RR 0.90, 0.70–1.16). The oral limb gains one modern pilot (Vidot 2019, PMID: 31390762) whose BCAA-alone arm did not separate from placebo. Six nutritional-context references now support the surrounding limbs without changing the stamp: albumin (Konstantis 2022, PMID: 35500317, SMD 0.52 across 20 cirrhosis trials; Nakaya 2007, PMID: 17234504; Takeshita 2009, PMID: 19285598), muscle (Ismaiel 2022, PMID: 35155535 — indices up, grip unchanged), late evening snacks (Chen 2019, PMID: 30883904 — less ascites and encephalopathy with snacks of mixed composition) and Japanese granules (Kobayashi 2008, PMID: 18297438 — null in compensated cirrhosis). The stamp is unchanged by the expansion.

cards.headline: Gluud 2017 (Cochrane): failure to improve encephalopathy RR 0.73 (0.61–0.88) — mortality RR 0.88 (0.69–1.11), nausea and vomiting RR 5.56
cards.summary: Gluud 2017 (Cochrane): failure to improve encephalopathy RR 0.73 (0.61–0.88) — mortality RR 0.88 (0.69–1.11), nausea and vomiting RR 5.56
cards.people: 16 randomised trials, 827 participants with hepatic encephalopathy classed as overt (12 trials) or minimal (4 trials); 8 trials of oral BCAA and 7 of intravenous BCAA; controls were placebo or no intervention (2 trials), diets (10), lactulose (2), or neomycin (2); all participants in 15 trials had cirrhosis; 7 trials at low risk of bias, 9 at high risk.
cards.result: BCAA had a beneficial effect on hepatic encephalopathy manifestations: the risk ratio for no improvement was 0.73 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.88; 827 participants; high quality of evidence), confirmed in low-risk-of-bias trials (RR 0.71, 0.52 to 0.96) and by trial sequential analysis. Mortality did not differ (RR 0.88, 0.69 to 1.11; 760 participants, 15 trials; moderate quality), and the required information size for mortality was not reached. BCAA increased nausea and vomiting in the fixed-effect analysis (RR 5.56, 2.93 to 10.55) but not in the random-effects analysis, and showed no effect on quality of life or nutritional parameters. Versus lactulose or neomycin specifically, no significant difference was found (RR 0.66, 0.34 to 1.30).
cards.watchOut: The control in most trials was diet or nothing, not the standard encephalopathy treatments — so the pooled benefit is largely 'better than no specific therapy', and the head-to-head against lactulose is both small and null. Nine of 16 trials were at high risk of bias, mainly unblinded or industry-funded, though the low-bias sensitivity analysis held.
cards.source: Gluud LL et al. Branched-chain amino acids for people with hepatic encephalopathy. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28518283. cards.headline: Aamann 2026 (Cochrane update): 18 trials, 934 participants — encephalopathy still improved (RR 0.79 for no improvement), mortality RR 0.89, but certainty now graded low to very low
cards.summary: Aamann 2026 (Cochrane update): 18 trials, 934 participants — encephalopathy still improved (RR 0.79 for no improvement), mortality RR 0.89, but certainty now graded low to very low
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis, 2026 update (Aamann 2026)
cards.people: 18 randomised trials published 1984–2023, including 934 adults with overt (13 trials) or covert (5 trials) hepatic encephalopathy; 10 trials assessed oral BCAA and 8 intravenous BCAA; control groups received diets (11 trials), no intervention or placebo (2 trials), non-absorbable disaccharides, antibiotics or other interventions; searches ran to 12 December 2024; risk of bias was assessed with the RoB 2 tool and certainty with GRADE.
cards.result: BCAA may have little to no effect on all-cause mortality, but the evidence is very uncertain (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.12; 17 studies, 867 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence suggests BCAA reduces hepatic encephalopathy — fewer participants without improvement (risk ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.96; 18 studies, 934 participants; low-certainty evidence). Nausea and diarrhoea occurred in 58 of 477 (12%) participants on BCAA vs 16 of 538 (3%) on control interventions (risk ratio 2.05, 0.40 to 10.58; very low certainty). Effects on albumin concentration (mean difference 0.60, −0.90 to 2.09) and nitrogen balance were very uncertain, quality-of-life data could not be meta-analysed, and no trials in children were found.
cards.watchOut: The update adds two trials and modern GRADE methods and lands on more cautious certainty grades than the 2017 version (which called the symptom evidence high quality), while its point estimates barely move (mortality 0.88 → 0.89; non-improvement 0.73 → 0.79). Read the two Cochrane cards together: the effects are stable, the confidence attached to them has been revised down.
cards.source: Aamann L et al. Branched-chain amino acids for people with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2026. PMID: 41542879. cards.headline: Marchesini 1990: oral BCAA beat casein over 3 months — encephalopathy index 40→21 vs 37→36; 80% vs 35% improved on two or more measures (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Marchesini 1990: oral BCAA beat casein over 3 months — encephalopathy index 40→21 vs 37→36; 80% vs 35% improved on two or more measures (p<0.001)
cards.people: 64 patients with cirrhosis and chronic hepatic encephalopathy in a multicentre double-blind trial; after a 15-day controlled-diet run-in (45–65 g protein/day), 30 patients received oral BCAA 0.24 g/kg/day and 34 an equinitrogenous amount of casein, each added to diet for 3 months; patients who did not improve were then given the alternative treatment for 3 more months.
cards.result: The portal-systemic encephalopathy index improved significantly on BCAA (from 40 [SD 14]% to 21 [17]%) but not on casein (from 37 [13]% to 36 [12]%). Two or more index parameters improved in 24 of 30 BCAA patients (80%; confidence limits 61–92%) versus 12 of 34 on casein (35%; 20–54%; p<0.001). Casein non-responders switched to BCAA improved rapidly. Semiquantitative nitrogen balance became consistently positive on BCAA, with mild improvements in nutritional parameters and liver function tests.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was casein — an equinitrogenous protein control, not an encephalopathy drug — so the trial shows BCAA beating an equal amount of ordinary protein, not beating lactulose. The second-phase crossover involved non-responders only and is not part of the randomised comparison.
cards.source: Marchesini G et al. Long-term oral branched-chain amino acid treatment in chronic hepatic encephalopathy. A randomized double-blind casein-controlled trial. The Italian Multicenter Study Group. Journal of Hepatology. 1990. PMID: 2204661. cards.headline: Horst 1984: oral BCAA let protein-intolerant patients take protein-equivalent nitrogen — stage 2 encephalopathy in 1 of 17 vs 7 of 20 on dietary protein (p<0.05)
cards.summary: Horst 1984: oral BCAA let protein-intolerant patients take protein-equivalent nitrogen — stage 2 encephalopathy in 1 of 17 vs 7 of 20 on dietary protein (p<0.05)
cards.people: 37 hospitalised protein-intolerant cirrhotic patients at six cooperating hospitals; after 1 week at 20 g/day dietary protein, weekly 20 g increments of either dietary protein or an oral branched-chain-enriched amino acid supplement until 80 g/day protein equivalent or stage 2 encephalopathy.
cards.result: Encephalopathy of stage 2 or greater developed in 7 of 20 patients in the protein group and 1 of 17 in the BCAA group (p<0.05). Mental-status grade (p<0.01), asterixis (p<0.05) and the portal-systemic encephalopathy index (p<0.01) all favoured BCAA; number connection test, EEG and ammonia did not differ. Nitrogen balance improved from negative to positive equally in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A protein-tolerance trial: BCAA won as a nitrogen source that does not provoke encephalopathy, in patients pre-selected for protein intolerance — it is not a trial of BCAA reversing established encephalopathy in unselected patients.
cards.source: Horst D et al. Comparison of dietary protein with an oral, branched chain-enriched amino acid supplement in chronic portal-systemic encephalopathy: a randomized controlled trial. cards.headline: Egberts 1985: double-blind crossover in latent encephalopathy — BCAA significantly improved psychomotor function, attention and practical intelligence (22 patients)
cards.summary: Egberts 1985: double-blind crossover in latent encephalopathy — BCAA significantly improved psychomotor function, attention and practical intelligence (22 patients)
cards.people: 22 inpatients with liver cirrhosis and latent (subclinical) portal-systemic encephalopathy identified by an extensive psychometric test programme; defined diet (35 kcal/kg/day, 1 g/kg protein) plus BCAA or casein 0.25 g/kg/day, each for 1 week in crossover.
cards.result: Taking the crossover design into account, significant improvements attributable to BCAA were demonstrated in psychomotor functions (line tracing, tapping, steadiness, auditory reaction time), attention (digit table) and practical intelligence (digit symbol, number connection test). Ammonia tended to decrease on BCAA; semiquantitative nitrogen balance increased on both treatments, with a tendency to a larger increase on BCAA.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are psychometric surrogates over 1-week periods in latent — not overt — encephalopathy, and the abstract reports significance without effect sizes; the trial cannot speak to clinical episodes or survival.
cards.source: Egberts EH et al. Branched chain amino acids in the treatment of latent portosystemic encephalopathy. A double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study. Gastroenterology. 1985. PMID: 3882509. cards.headline: Plauth 1993: 8 weeks of oral BCAA improved psychomotor performance (p<0.01) and driving capacity (p<0.002) in latent encephalopathy
cards.summary: Plauth 1993: 8 weeks of oral BCAA improved psychomotor performance (p<0.01) and driving capacity (p<0.002) in latent encephalopathy
cards.people: 17 patients with stable cirrhosis and latent portosystemic encephalopathy — diagnosed by psychometric testing of automobile driving capacity — received BCAA or placebo for 8 weeks, then crossed over to the other regimen for 8 weeks, as an adjunct to conventional therapy.
cards.result: BCAA but not placebo significantly improved psychomotor disturbances (p<0.01) and driving capacity (p<0.002). No adverse reactions were observed.
cards.watchOut: Small crossover in latent encephalopathy with psychometric endpoints; like Egberts 1985 it supports a symptom effect in minimal/latent disease, not fewer overt episodes or deaths.

cards.headline: Eriksson 1982: 30 g/day oral BCAA no better than placebo in chronic encephalopathy — in only 7 patients over 14 days
cards.summary: Eriksson 1982: 30 g/day oral BCAA no better than placebo in chronic encephalopathy — in only 7 patients over 14 days
cards.people: 7 patients with manifest cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy of six months' duration or longer; 30 g/day oral BCAA or placebo during two 14-day periods in crossover, evaluated by clinical observation, psychometric tests and EEG.
cards.result: Neither clinical observations nor psychometric testing nor EEG showed a significant difference between BCAA and placebo, despite significantly increased plasma BCAA concentrations confirming absorption; four patients given BCAA for longer periods (5 to 22 weeks) also showed no psychometric change. No side effects were seen.
cards.watchOut: The one clearly null oral trial — but with 7 patients it had almost no power to detect the effect the larger oral trials later showed; it caps the oral claim rather than cancelling it.
cards.source: Eriksson LS et al. Branched-chain amino acids in the treatment of chronic hepatic encephalopathy. Gut. 1982. PMID: 6749604. cards.headline: Les 2011: a year of oral BCAA after an encephalopathy episode — recurrence-free 47% vs 34% (P=0.274, not significant); neuropsychological tests and muscle mass improved
cards.summary: Les 2011: a year of oral BCAA after an encephalopathy episode — recurrence-free 47% vs 34% (P=0.274, not significant); neuropsychological tests and muscle mass improved
cards.people: 116 patients with cirrhosis and a previous episode of hepatic encephalopathy at four tertiary hospitals; all received a standard diet (35 kcal/kg/day, 0.7 g protein/kg/day) plus a supplement of 30 g/day BCAA or maltodextrin for 56 weeks.
cards.result: The actuarial risk of remaining free of hepatic encephalopathy did not differ between groups (BCAA 47%, maltodextrin 34%; P=0.274). The BCAA group performed better on two neuropsychological tests and increased mid-arm muscle circumference. Recurrence was associated with low baseline plasma albumin and with falling sodium and rising creatinine during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The largest oral trial missed its primary endpoint — the honest ceiling on the oral claim. Its positive findings are secondary (neuropsychology, muscle mass), the same pattern as the latent-encephalopathy crossover trials.
cards.source: Les I et al. Effects of branched-chain amino acids supplementation in patients with cirrhosis and a previous episode of hepatic encephalopathy: a randomized study. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21326220. cards.headline: Vidot 2019: blinded placebo-controlled pilot — combined synbiotics + BCAA improved cognition; the BCAA-alone arm did not separate from placebo
cards.summary: Vidot 2019: blinded placebo-controlled pilot — combined synbiotics + BCAA improved cognition; the BCAA-alone arm did not separate from placebo
cards.people: 61 participants with overt hepatic encephalopathy enrolled, 49 included in the intention-to-treat analysis, randomised in a blinded study to synbiotics, BCAA, combined synbiotics + BCAA, or placebo for 8 weeks; cognition assessed with the Trail Making Test and the Inhibitory Control Test, alongside biochemical, nutritional and mood scores.
cards.result: Despite evidence of a placebo effect, participants receiving the combined synbiotics/BCAA treatment showed significant improvement in Trail Making Test B and Inhibitory Control Test weighted lures compared with placebo at study completion (p ≤ 0.05); cognitive improvement occurred without a significant change in ammonia levels. The BCAA-alone arm was not reported as significantly different from placebo.
cards.watchOut: A pilot whose positive arm is the combination: it supports oral BCAA only as part of a synbiotic combination, and the authors call for a larger study to confirm. It is the one post-2017 placebo-controlled oral trial added to this shelf, and its BCAA-alone result is a caution against reading the older oral trials as stronger than they are.
cards.source: Vidot H et al. Supplementation with Synbiotics and/or Branched Chain Amino Acids in Hepatic Encephalopathy: A Pilot Randomised Placebo-Controlled Clinical Study. Nutrients. 2019. PMID: 31390762. cards.headline: Wahren 1983: intravenous BCAA in acute encephalopathy — improvement 14 of 25 vs 12 of 25 on glucose, deaths 10 vs 5; no benefit
cards.summary: Wahren 1983: intravenous BCAA in acute encephalopathy — improvement 14 of 25 vs 12 of 25 on glucose, deaths 10 vs 5; no benefit
cards.people: 50 patients with liver cirrhosis and acute hepatic encephalopathy at five medical centres in France and Sweden; intravenous BCAA 40 g/day in 5% glucose or 5% glucose alone (placebo) for 5 days or until 'wake up', with nutritional support of equal carbohydrate and fat.
cards.result: Clinical improvement was seen in 14 of 25 BCAA-treated patients and 12 of 25 receiving placebo (not significant); EEG responses were similar. In the BCAA group 10 of 25 patients died during the study, compared with 5 of 25 on placebo (not significant); 6 versus 3 died from encephalopathy. Plasma aromatic amino acids and methionine fell 20–40% on BCAA (p<0.05 to 0.01) — the biochemistry moved, the brain did not.
cards.watchOut: The founding acute intravenous trial, and a clean null: it separates the plasma amino-acid rationale from clinical effect, and its mortality point estimate runs the wrong way (not significant, small numbers).
cards.source: Wahren J et al. Is intravenous administration of branched chain amino acids effective in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy? A multicenter study. Hepatology. 1983. PMID: 6345330. cards.headline: Vilstrup 1990: intravenous BCAA-enriched amino acids vs glucose in acute encephalopathy — 17 woke in each group; deaths 11 vs 10
cards.summary: Vilstrup 1990: intravenous BCAA-enriched amino acids vs glucose in acute encephalopathy — 17 woke in each group; deaths 11 vs 10
cards.people: 65 patients with cirrhosis and acute hepatic encephalopathy, randomly treated with 1 g/kg/day of an amino acid mixture with 40% branched-chain content (32 patients) or isocaloric glucose (33 patients) for a maximum of 16 days; both regimens included glucose to a total of 26.5 kcal/kg/day and lactulose.
cards.result: In each group 17 patients woke up. Eleven patients died in the amino acid group and ten in the glucose group; renal failure developed in 4 versus 3 patients. The negative nitrogen balance on entry reversed in the amino acid group but not in the glucose group.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received lactulose, so this tests BCAA as an add-on to standard therapy — and finds nothing on waking or survival, only on nitrogen homeostasis.
cards.source: Vilstrup H et al. Branched chain enriched amino acid versus glucose treatment of hepatic encephalopathy. A double-blind study of 65 patients with cirrhosis. Journal of Hepatology. 1990. PMID: 2195106. cards.headline: Michel 1985: BCAA-enriched vs conventional amino acid infusion in acute encephalopathy — improved 12 of 36 vs 10 of 34, died 7 vs 7
cards.summary: Michel 1985: BCAA-enriched vs conventional amino acid infusion in acute encephalopathy — improved 12 of 36 vs 10 of 34, died 7 vs 7
cards.people: 70 cirrhotic patients with acute hepatic encephalopathy (cirrhosis confirmed by needle biopsy; encephalopathy by clinical and EEG parameters), treated 1979–1984: 36 received a BCAA-enriched amino acid solution and 34 a conventional commercial amino acid mixture, with 1,600 kcal/day from glucose and lipid emulsion over 5 days.
cards.result: No significant difference in clinical evolution: on the conventional solution 10 improved, 14 were unchanged, 10 deteriorated and 7 died; on the BCAA-enriched solution 12 improved, 14 unchanged, 10 deteriorated and 7 died. EEG tracing evolved in parallel, even though the plasma aromatic-to-branched-chain ratio was corrected by the modified solution.
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not state the allocation method (the Cochrane review counts the trial among its randomised set); the comparator was another amino acid solution, so this tests BCAA enrichment, not amino acids versus none.
cards.source: Michel H et al. Treatment of acute hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhotics with a branched-chain amino acids enriched versus a conventional amino acids mixture. A controlled study of 70 patients. Liver. 1985. PMID: 4079669. cards.headline: Rossi-Fanelli 1982: intravenous BCAA vs lactulose in deep coma — complete mental recovery 70% vs 47%, not significant (20 per group)
cards.summary: Rossi-Fanelli 1982: intravenous BCAA vs lactulose in deep coma — complete mental recovery 70% vs 47%, not significant (20 per group)
cards.people: 40 patients with cirrhosis and deep hepatic coma, in two groups of 20: intravenous BCAA solutions in 20% glucose versus lactulose plus glucose in isocaloric amount, over a 10-day observation period; 3 drop-outs from each group.
cards.result: Complete mental recovery was obtained in 70% of patients on BCAA and 47% on lactulose; the difference was not significant. Ammonia and free tryptophan decreased significantly upon mental recovery under both treatments; other plasma amino acid changes did not correlate with the clinical course.
cards.watchOut: No placebo group and 20 patients per arm: the 23-point recovery gap is exactly the kind of underpowered difference that can carry no claim either way — and the later pooled head-to-head against lactulose was likewise null.
cards.source: Rossi-Fanelli F et al. Branched-chain amino acids vs lactulose in the treatment of hepatic coma: a controlled study. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 1982. PMID: 6749458. cards.headline: Cerra 1985 (F080): the one positive acute trial — BCAA-enriched infusion beat neomycin on encephalopathy improvement and on survival/discharge (75 randomised)
cards.summary: Cerra 1985 (F080): the one positive acute trial — BCAA-enriched infusion beat neomycin on encephalopathy improvement and on survival/discharge (75 randomised)
cards.people: 75 patients with acute hepatic decompensation superimposed on chronic alcoholic cirrhosis, prospectively randomised to enteral neomycin 4 g/day plus 25% dextrose, or a neomycin-matching placebo plus isocaloric dextrose with F080 — a modified amino acid mixture enriched with BCAA to 36% and deficient in aromatic amino acids and methionine; 30 patients in the F080 group and 29 in the control group completed the trial.
cards.result: The F080 group demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in encephalopathy compared with the neomycin group, while maintaining nitrogen equilibrium; survival and discharge from hospital were statistically greater in the F080 group. The record reports these as significance findings without printing the underlying event counts.
cards.watchOut: The outlier among the acute trials, and the hardest to weigh: the control was neomycin (an active drug with its own harms), 16 of 75 randomised patients did not complete the trial, and the abstract prints no event counts behind the survival claim. The placebo-controlled intravenous trials did not replicate it.
cards.source: Cerra FB et al. Disease-specific amino acid infusion (F080) in hepatic encephalopathy: a prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled trial. JPEN. Journal of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition. 1985. PMID: 3892073. cards.headline: Yokobori 2025 (meta-analysis of intravenous BCAA in acute encephalopathy): consciousness improvement RR 1.26 (0.96–1.66), mortality RR 0.90 (0.70–1.16) — neither significant
cards.summary: Yokobori 2025 (meta-analysis of intravenous BCAA in acute encephalopathy): consciousness improvement RR 1.26 (0.96–1.66), mortality RR 0.90 (0.70–1.16) — neither significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yokobori 2025)
cards.people: 4 randomised trials, 219 patients with acute hepatic encephalopathy treated during the acute phase after admission (109 received intravenous BCAA, 110 placebo); critical outcomes were all-cause mortality and improvement in disturbance of consciousness; searches covered MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register and the Japanese ICHUSHI database.
cards.result: Improvement in disturbance of consciousness and mortality were not significantly different between intravenous BCAA and placebo (risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.66; and risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.16, respectively); the absolute difference in consciousness improvement was 118 more per 1000 (95% CI 18 fewer to 300 more). No significant differences were observed in nausea or diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 trials and 219 patients — the interval for consciousness improvement still includes a worthwhile benefit, so this is 'unproven' rather than 'disproven'. But pooled with the individual null trials carded above (Wahren, Vilstrup, Michel), the acute intravenous limb has now been negative in every era, including the modern one.
cards.source: Yokobori S et al. Intravenous branched-chain amino acid administration for the acute treatment of hepatic encephalopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Intensive Care. 2025. PMID: 39780295. (MeSH not yet assigned in the PubMed record.)

cards.headline: Mehtani 2023: intravenous BCAA in ACLF encephalopathy — faster improvement at 24 hours (40% vs 17.1%) that was not sustained at days 3 or 7; 28-day survival not significantly different
cards.summary: Mehtani 2023: intravenous BCAA in ACLF encephalopathy — faster improvement at 24 hours (40% vs 17.1%) that was not sustained at days 3 or 7; 28-day survival not significantly different
cards.people: Patients with EASL-defined acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) and overt hepatic encephalopathy, randomised to intravenous BCAA 500 mL/day for 3 days plus lactulose (39 patients) or lactulose alone (37 patients); 6 patients who developed COVID-19 after randomisation were excluded, leaving 70 analysed (35 per arm); the primary outcome was improvement by at least 1 encephalopathy grade at 72 hours. Registry: NCT04238416.
cards.result: Improvement by at least 1 grade at 24 hours occurred in 14 patients (40%) in the BCAA arm and 6 (17.1%) in the control group (P=0.03), translating to a shorter ICU stay, but the difference was not sustained at days 3 or 7. Overall survival was 40% at 28 days (48.5% vs 31.4%; P=0.14), not significantly different. Ammonia levels did not correlate with the grade of encephalopathy. The authors concluded that intravenous BCAA does not lead to a sustained improvement in encephalopathy grade in ACLF.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with post-randomisation exclusions, in the sickest encephalopathy population there is (ACLF): the transient 24-hour signal is hypothesis-grade, and the trial is best read as the modern confirmation of the older intravenous nulls rather than as a near-miss.
cards.source: Mehtani R et al. Intravenous BCAA Infusion Does Not Lead to a Sustained Recovery From Overt HE in ACLF - An Open Label Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hepatology. 2023. PMID: 37975059. Registry: NCT04238416. (MeSH not yet assigned in the PubMed record.)

cards.headline: Marchesini 2003 (context): a year of oral BCAA in advanced cirrhosis — combined death/deterioration endpoint OR 0.43 (0.19–0.96) vs lactoalbumin; fewer hospital admissions
cards.summary: Marchesini 2003 (context): a year of oral BCAA in advanced cirrhosis — combined death/deterioration endpoint OR 0.43 (0.19–0.96) vs lactoalbumin; fewer hospital admissions
cards.people: 174 patients with advanced cirrhosis randomised to 1 year of nutritional supplementation with BCAA versus lactoalbumin or maltodextrins; primary outcomes were prevention of a combined endpoint (death and deterioration to exclusion criteria), need for hospital admission, and duration of hospital stay.
cards.result: BCAA significantly reduced the combined event rate compared with lactoalbumin (odds ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.96; P=0.039) and nonsignificantly compared with maltodextrins (OR 0.51, 0.23 to 1.17; P=0.108). Average hospital admission rates were lower on BCAA (P=0.006 and P=0.003 against the two controls). In patients remaining in the study, nutritional parameters and liver function tests were on average stable or improved on BCAA, the Child-Pugh score decreased (P=0.013), and anorexia and health-related quality of life improved. Long-term compliance was poor.
cards.watchOut: Carded as context alongside Muto 2005: a cirrhosis-progression trial, not an encephalopathy trial — its endpoints are death, deterioration and admission, with no encephalopathy outcome — so it supports biological activity of long-term oral BCAA in advanced cirrhosis, not this shelf's symptom claim.
cards.source: Marchesini G et al. Nutritional supplementation with branched-chain amino acids in advanced cirrhosis: a double-blind, randomized trial. Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 12806613. cards.headline: Muto 2005 (context): oral BCAA 12 g/day cut a cirrhosis-events composite (HR 0.67, 0.49–0.93) in 646 patients — death, cancer, variceal rupture, liver failure, not encephalopathy episodes
cards.summary: Muto 2005 (context): oral BCAA 12 g/day cut a cirrhosis-events composite (HR 0.67, 0.49–0.93) in 646 patients — death, cancer, variceal rupture, liver failure, not encephalopathy episodes
cards.people: 646 patients with decompensated cirrhosis in a multicentre Japanese trial, randomised to oral BCAA granules 12 g/day for 2 years or a defined diet therapy (1.0–1.4 g protein/kg/day, 25–35 kcal/kg/day); median observation 445 days.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (death from any cause, liver cancer, rupture of oesophageal varices, or progression of hepatic failure) occurred significantly less often on BCAA (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.93; P=0.015). Serum albumin rose significantly more on BCAA (P=0.018) and the general-health-perception domain of the SF-36 improved (P=0.003); adherence was favourable.
cards.watchOut: Carded as context only: this trial's composite contains no encephalopathy endpoint, so it cannot support the shelf's symptom claim — it shows the same supplement moving broader cirrhosis outcomes in a sicker population. It was nutrient-controlled rather than placebo-blinded.
cards.source: Muto Y et al. Effects of oral branched-chain amino acid granules on event-free survival in patients with liver cirrhosis. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2005. PMID: 16206505. cards.headline: Konstantis 2022 (context): across 20 cirrhosis trials, BCAA raised albumin (SMD 0.52) and muscle mass (SMD 0.21) and reduced serious complications — mortality not significantly affected
cards.summary: Konstantis 2022 (context): across 20 cirrhosis trials, BCAA raised albumin (SMD 0.52) and muscle mass (SMD 0.21) and reduced serious complications — mortality not significantly affected
cards.people: 20 randomised trials of BCAA supplementation against an active comparator, diet or placebo in patients with liver cirrhosis — not restricted to encephalopathy — from databases searched to October 2021.
cards.result: Relative to other interventions, BCAA showed a beneficial effect on muscle mass (standardised mean difference 0.21, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.40) and plasma albumin concentration (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.86), a reduction in serious cirrhotic complications (log odds ratio −0.46, 95% CI −0.78 to −0.13) and an increase in body mass index (weighted mean difference 0.24, 0.08 to 0.40); no significant effect was noted on mortality or fat mass.
cards.watchOut: Carded as context: a broader-cirrhosis pool than this shelf's encephalopathy question, and the albumin result is heterogeneous (I² 85%). Its mortality null agrees with both Cochrane versions; its albumin and muscle findings are the strongest pooled support for BCAA's nutritional effects.
cards.source: Konstantis G et al. Efficacy of branched chain amino acids supplementation in liver cirrhosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Nutrition. 2022. PMID: 35500317. MeSH: Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Dietary Supplements · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Serum Albumin

cards.headline: Ismaiel 2022 (context): BCAA improved skeletal muscle index and mid-arm muscle circumference in cirrhosis — handgrip strength and triceps fat did not improve
cards.summary: Ismaiel 2022 (context): BCAA improved skeletal muscle index and mid-arm muscle circumference in cirrhosis — handgrip strength and triceps fat did not improve
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of BCAA and sarcopenia parameters (Ismaiel 2022)
cards.people: 12 studies involving 1,225 subjects with liver cirrhosis in the qualitative synthesis and 5 in the quantitative synthesis, assessing skeletal muscle index, mid-arm muscle circumference, handgrip strength and triceps subcutaneous fat before and after BCAA supplementation and against controls.
cards.result: Following BCAA supplementation, skeletal muscle index and mid-arm muscle circumference improved significantly, while no improvements were reported in handgrip strength or triceps subcutaneous fat. The authors caution that results should be interpreted carefully because the methodological quality of the included studies was limited.
cards.watchOut: Muscle quantity improved on measurement while muscle function (grip) did not — the same dissociation between surrogates and clinical outcomes that runs through the encephalopathy trials on this shelf. Carded as context for BCAA's anabolic limb.
cards.source: Ismaiel A et al. Effects of Branched-Chain Amino Acids on Parameters Evaluating Sarcopenia in Liver Cirrhosis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2022. PMID: 35155535. (MeSH not assigned in the PubMed record.)

cards.headline: Nakaya 2007 (context): a BCAA-enriched late evening snack for 3 months improved serum albumin, nitrogen balance and respiratory quotient vs an ordinary-food snack
cards.summary: Nakaya 2007 (context): a BCAA-enriched late evening snack for 3 months improved serum albumin, nitrogen balance and respiratory quotient vs an ordinary-food snack
cards.people: 48 patients with hepatitis C virus-positive liver cirrhosis in a multicentre randomised study, receiving a late evening snack of a BCAA-enriched nutrient mixture or ordinary food (such as a rice ball or bread) for 3 months; both groups were instructed on energy and protein intake; blood biochemistry, nitrogen balance, respiratory quotient and Short Form 36 quality of life were measured at baseline and 3 months.
cards.result: Total and late-evening energy intakes were similar in the two groups at 3 months. Serum albumin level, nitrogen balance and respiratory quotient improved significantly with the BCAA mixture but not with ordinary food; Short Form 36 parameters did not improve significantly in either group. The authors concluded that long-term oral BCAA supplementation as a late evening snack improves serum albumin and energy metabolism in cirrhosis better than ordinary food.
cards.watchOut: A nutritional-state trial, not an encephalopathy or events trial: it demonstrates the metabolic rationale of Japanese late-evening BCAA practice (correcting the overnight catabolic state, raising albumin) without testing clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Nakaya Y et al. BCAA-enriched snack improves nutritional state of cirrhosis. Nutrition. 2007. PMID: 17234504. cards.headline: Takeshita 2009 (context): a BCAA late-evening snack around chemoembolisation prevented the fall in albumin and total protein — ammonia fell on BCAA and rose on control
cards.summary: Takeshita 2009 (context): a BCAA late-evening snack around chemoembolisation prevented the fall in albumin and total protein — ammonia fell on BCAA and rose on control
cards.people: 56 patients with liver cirrhosis undergoing trans-arterial chemoembolisation for hepatocellular carcinoma at Nagasaki University Hospital, randomly placed in a BCAA group (28) or a control group (28); the BCAA group consumed a BCAA-containing snack (50 g) once daily at 22:00 from the day before chemoembolisation until 2 weeks after.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, the control group showed greater decreases in total protein, albumin, cholinesterase, total cholesterol and red blood cell count than the BCAA group over the 2 weeks after chemoembolisation. Ammonia levels decreased in the BCAA group and increased in the control group. The authors concluded that an oral BCAA late evening snack prevents suppression of liver function by chemoembolisation during the peri-procedure period.
cards.watchOut: A 2-week peri-procedural albumin-preservation result in cancer care: supportive of the albumin limb, and of nothing beyond it — not evidence about encephalopathy treatment, ascites or survival.
cards.source: Takeshita S et al. A snack enriched with oral branched-chain amino acids prevents a fall in albumin in patients with liver cirrhosis undergoing chemoembolization for hepatocellular carcinoma. Nutrition Research. 2009. cards.headline: Chen 2019 (context): late evening snacks in cirrhosis — better albumin and ammonia and lower occurrence of ascites and encephalopathy in meta-analysis (snacks of mixed composition)
cards.summary: Chen 2019 (context): late evening snacks in cirrhosis — better albumin and ammonia and lower occurrence of ascites and encephalopathy in meta-analysis (snacks of mixed composition)
cards.people: 8 studies comprising 341 patients with liver cirrhosis (167 in late-evening-snack groups, 174 controls), pooling late evening snack interventions of varying composition — not all BCAA-based — against control diets; outcomes included serum albumin, bilirubin, liver enzymes, prothrombin time, complications of cirrhosis and blood glucose.
cards.result: Late evening snacks had significant effects on albumin (effect size 0.233), ammonia (−0.425) and prothrombin time (−0.589), and on aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (−0.320 and −0.284); studies of clinical signs showed lower occurrence rates of ascites and hepatic encephalopathy than in control groups. There was no significant effect on Child-Pugh score. The authors concluded that late evening snacks improve liver function reserve in cirrhosis, with or without hepatocellular carcinoma.
cards.watchOut: The snacks were of mixed composition, so this card supports the late-evening feeding strategy within which the BCAA snacks (Nakaya 2007; Takeshita 2009) sit — it is not BCAA-specific evidence. Its ascites finding is one of the threads behind the separate oral-BCAA-and-ascites shelf.
cards.source: Chen CJ et al. Significant effects of late evening snack on liver functions in patients with liver cirrhosis: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
