meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (chen 2019) 8 studies comprising 341 patients with liver cirrhosis (167 in late-evening-snack groups, 174 controls), pooling late evening snack interventions of varying composition — not all bcaa-based — against control diets; outcomes included serum albumin, bilirubin, liver enzymes, prothrombin time, complications of cirrhosis and blood glucose. late evening snacks had significant effects on albumin (effect size 0.233), ammonia (−0.425) and prothrombin time (−0.589), and on aspartate and alanine aminotransferases (−0.320 and −0.284); studies of clinical signs showed lower occurrence rates of ascites and hepatic encephalopathy than in control groups. there was no significant effect on child-pugh score. the authors concluded that late evening snacks improve liver function reserve in cirrhosis, with or without hepatocellular carcinoma. the snacks were of mixed composition, so this card supports the late-evening feeding strategy within which the bcaa snacks (nakaya 2007; takeshita 2009) sit — it is not bcaa-specific evidence. its ascites finding is one of the threads behind the separate oral-bcaa-and-ascites shelf. chen cj et al. significant effects of late evening snack on liver functions in patients with liver cirrhosis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2019. pmid: 30883904. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · female · humans · liver · liver cirrhosis · liver function tests · male · middle aged · nutritional status · nutritive value · protein-energy malnutrition · randomized controlled trials as topic · risk factors · sarcopenia · snacks · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Kobayashi 2008 (context): Japanese BCAA granules (TK-98) for 168 weeks in compensated cirrhosis — no decompensation in either group; liver cancer 15.8% vs 25.0%, not significant
cards.summary: Kobayashi 2008 (context): Japanese BCAA granules (TK-98) for 168 weeks in compensated cirrhosis — no decompensation in either group; liver cancer 15.8% vs 25.0%, not significant
cards.people: 39 patients with compensated cirrhosis due to hepatitis C virus and baseline serum albumin between 3.6 and 4.5 g/dL, assigned to BCAA granules for oral use (TK-98 — the Japanese granule formulation of the Livact type) or to a no-treatment control group, for 168 weeks.
cards.result: No symptoms indicating decompensated cirrhosis — including ascites, oedema and hepatic encephalopathy — were reported in either group during the observation period. Hepatocellular carcinoma was noted in 8 of the 39 patients (3 on BCAA, 15.8%; 5 untreated, 25.0%), and time-to-event analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the groups; in a subgroup with baseline serum albumin below 4.0 g/dL, the incidence of liver cancer appeared likely to be lower on BCAA.
cards.watchOut: A small, null phase II trial in compensated disease, carded so this shelf carries the Japanese granule evidence whole — including where it shows nothing — rather than only its positive trials (Marchesini 2003; Muto 2005). Its subgroup suggestion is hypothesis-grade only.
cards.source: Kobayashi M et al. Inhibitory effect of branched-chain amino acid granules on progression of compensated liver cirrhosis due to hepatitis C virus. Journal of Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18297438. cards.headline: Synthesis: the symptom benefit is oral and real; the acute intravenous trials and the survival outcome are null — and BCAA's nutritional effects (albumin, muscle) are now pooled separately
cards.summary: Synthesis: the symptom benefit is oral and real; the acute intravenous trials and the survival outcome are null — and BCAA's nutritional effects (albumin, muscle) are now pooled separately
cards.people: Two Cochrane versions (2017: 16 randomised trials, 827 participants; 2026 update: 18 trials, 934 participants); 13 individual randomised trials carded — 7 oral (Marchesini 1990, Horst 1984, Egberts 1985, Plauth 1993, Eriksson 1982, Les 2011, Vidot 2019) and 6 intravenous (Wahren 1983, Vilstrup 1990, Michel 1985, Rossi-Fanelli 1982, Cerra 1985, Mehtani 2023) — plus an intravenous meta-analysis (Yokobori 2025), 2 large cirrhosis-events trials (Marchesini 2003, n=174; Muto 2005, n=646) and 6 nutritional-context references (Konstantis 2022, Ismaiel 2022, Nakaya 2007, Takeshita 2009, Chen 2019, Kobayashi 2008).
cards.result: Oral BCAA and encephalopathy manifestations: concordant benefit — Marchesini 1990 (80% vs 35% improved on two or more measures, p<0.001), Egberts 1985 and Plauth 1993 (significant psychomotor gains in double-blind crossovers), Horst 1984 (stage 2 encephalopathy 1 of 17 vs 7 of 20); the one null oral trial enrolled 7 patients (Eriksson 1982), the largest oral trial (Les 2011) missed recurrence (P=0.274) while improving neuropsychological tests, and the one modern placebo-controlled pilot (Vidot 2019) separated from placebo only in its synbiotic-combination arm. Acute intravenous BCAA: Wahren 1983, Vilstrup 1990 and Michel 1985 null, Rossi-Fanelli 1982 not significant versus lactulose, Cerra 1985 positive only against neomycin without event counts, Mehtani 2023 transient at 24 hours and not sustained, and the pooled intravenous estimate null (Yokobori 2025). Pooled across Cochrane versions: non-improvement RR 0.73 (2017) and 0.79 (2026 update); mortality RR 0.88 and 0.89 respectively, not significant in either. Nutritional limbs added in the expansion: albumin rose in the broader cirrhosis pool (Konstantis 2022, SMD 0.52) and in late-evening-snack trials (Nakaya 2007; Takeshita 2009), muscle indices improved without a grip-strength gain (Ismaiel 2022), late evening snacks of mixed composition were associated with less ascites and encephalopathy (Chen 2019), and Japanese BCAA granules were null in compensated cirrhosis (Kobayashi 2008). PROPOSED SPLIT with a LIKELY oral limb: the symptom benefit is real and concentrated in oral treatment; neither acute intravenous use nor survival has supporting evidence.
cards.watchOut: The developer's leaning toward LIKELY is borne out for oral BCAA on symptoms only; extending it to the whole shelf would claim a survival benefit no trial shows and an acute intravenous benefit the trials consistently refute. Note also the grading shift between Cochrane versions: the 2017 review called the symptom evidence high quality, the 2026 update grades it low certainty (mortality very low) — the flagship's certainty language, not its point estimates, is what changed. Ratios quoted are risk ratios from randomised trials, so the developer's observational 0.5–2.0 floor does not apply.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gluud LL et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28518283) and Aamann L et al. shelves.title: Unable to belch (retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction): botulinum toxin into the cricopharyngeus restored belching in 92–100% across three series — with no randomised trial and no placebo arm anywhere
shelves.question: In people who have never been able to belch — 'I have trouble burping' — with retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction, does botulinum toxin injection into the cricopharyngeus muscle restore the ability to belch and relieve the associated symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Female · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Adult · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Manometry · Eructation/etiology/drug therapy/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Neuromuscular Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Aged · Feasibility Studies · Pharyngeal Muscles/physiopathology/drug effects · Esophageal Sphincter, Upper/physiopathology/drug effects · Injections · Botulinum Toxins/administration & dosage · Deglutition Disorders/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a dramatic, consistent effect in uncontrolled data, and nothing stronger exists. In the only controlled study, a prospective comparison of manometry-diagnosed patients (Sanagapalli S et al., PMID: 39589004), 92% of 52 patients given endoscopic cricopharyngeal botulinum toxin injection could belch at 3 months versus 0 of 7 untreated controls (p<0.001), with global symptom scores improving from 7.3 to 1.8 while controls were static. In the syndrome-defining series (Bastian RW et al., PMID: 31236539), all 51 patients achieved belching and symptom relief after injection. In a retrospective series of 72 patients given 100 units under general anaesthesia (Karagama Y, PMID: 33893849), all could burp within 4 weeks and the ability persisted beyond 3 months in 96%. The pattern — an all-or-nothing mechanical outcome, restored immediately and often durably after the toxin wears off — is biologically coherent for a muscle that fails to relax. But there is no randomised or placebo-controlled trial, samples are small and self-selected, and diagnosis in two series was partly confirmed by response to the treatment itself. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the signal is about as strong as uncontrolled evidence gets, and it is still uncontrolled — Tier C for the developer's personal review.

cards.headline: Sanagapalli 2024: 92% of injected patients could belch at 3 months versus 0% of untreated controls — symptom score 7.3 to 1.8 versus no change
cards.summary: Sanagapalli 2024: 92% of injected patients could belch at 3 months versus 0% of untreated controls — symptom score 7.3 to 1.8 versus no change
cards.people: 65 subjects: 52 patients with manometry-confirmed retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction treated with flexible endoscopic cricopharyngeal botulinum toxin injection, 7 patients who deferred or declined treatment as controls, and 6 asymptomatic volunteers for diagnostic validation. All patients had been unable to belch since childhood.
cards.result: At 3 months, 92% of the treatment group could belch compared with 0 controls (p<0.001). Global symptom score improved from 7.3 ± 1.7 to 1.8 ± 2.3 in the treated group while controls were static (7.5 ± 2.1 to 7.7 ± 1.8; p<0.0001 for the comparison). Quality of life improved significantly only in the treatment group (p=0.0002), and 43 of 51 treated patients (84%) reported being satisfied or very satisfied.
cards.watchOut: Controls were patients who declined or deferred treatment — only 7 of them — so motivation and severity may differ between groups, and neither patients nor assessors were blinded. The manometric signature was present in all patients and no volunteers, which supports the diagnosis, but the treatment comparison itself is small and non-randomised.
cards.source: Sanagapalli S et al. Prospective Controlled Study of Endoscopic Botulinum Toxin Injection for Retrograde Cricopharyngeus Dysfunction: The Inability to Belch Syndrome. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 39589004. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bastian 2019: the series that named the syndrome — all 51 patients belched after injection, most apparently permanently retrained
cards.summary: Bastian 2019: the series that named the syndrome — all 51 patients belched after injection, most apparently permanently retrained
cards.people: 51 consecutive patients at a single US voice institute presenting with inability to belch plus the proposed syndrome's associated symptoms (gurgling noises, chest and abdominal pain/distension, excessive flatulence), treated with botulinum toxin injection into the cricopharyngeus as a combined diagnostic and therapeutic procedure.
cards.result: All 51 patients achieved the ability to belch and relief of the associated symptoms, and the majority appeared to have 'retrained' the ability to belch on a potentially permanent basis, beyond the pharmacological duration of the toxin.
cards.watchOut: No control group, no blinding, and a circular element: relief after injection was itself used to validate the syndromic diagnosis, so non-responders would challenge the diagnosis rather than count against the treatment. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Karagama 2021: 72 patients, 100 units under general anaesthesia — all burping within 4 weeks, 96% still burping after the toxin wore off
cards.summary: Karagama 2021: 72 patients, 100 units under general anaesthesia — all burping within 4 weeks, 96% still burping after the toxin wore off
cards.people: 72 patients (50 male, 22 female; mean age 30 years, range 18–68) with inability to burp and the associated symptom complex, treated between 2016 and 2020 with 100 units of botulinum toxin A injected into the cricopharyngeus under general anaesthesia via suspension pharyngoscopy; mean follow-up 24 months (range 1–48).
cards.result: All patients were able to burp again within the first 4 weeks after injection, and the ability persisted beyond 3 months — after the toxin's expected duration of action — in 96% of cases.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-operator, no comparator and no standardised outcome scale; 'able to burp' is patient-reported. The durability claim (benefit outlasting the drug) is intriguing and consistent across series, but follow-up completeness in a retrospective series is exactly where such claims inflate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 175 patients, three countries, one direction — and a complete absence of randomised evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: 175 patients, three countries, one direction — and a complete absence of randomised evidence
cards.people: Three studies totalling 175 treated patients with inability to belch attributed to retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction: one small prospective controlled study (52 treated, 7 controls) and two case series (51 and 72 patients).
cards.result: Ability to belch after botulinum toxin injection: 92% (controlled study, vs 0% untreated), 100% and 100% (series), with symptom relief and durability beyond 3 months in 96% in the largest series. No randomised trial, no placebo injection, no blinded assessment exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: the outcome is objective enough (can or cannot belch) that the uncontrolled signal deserves a shelf, labelled at its true grade.
cards.watchOut: Publication bias is a real risk for a new, named syndrome with a satisfying treatment story; clinics seeing failures may not publish. Dose, route (endoscopic vs percutaneous vs open) and diagnostic criteria (manometry vs syndrome alone) all vary between series.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sanagapalli S et al. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2024 (PMID: 39589004); Bastian RW et al. OTO Open. 2019 (PMID: 31236539); Karagama Y. European Archives of Oto-Rhino-Laryngology. 2021 (PMID: 33893849).

shelves.title: Rice-based oral rehydration solution in cholera: first-24-hour stool output cut by 36% in adults and 32% in children versus glucose ORS (13-trial meta-analysis) — but only 18% in non-cholera diarrhoea
shelves.question: For severe dehydrating diarrhoea, does oral rehydration solution made with rice instead of glucose reduce stool losses compared with the standard glucose-based WHO solution — and does the answer differ between cholera and other diarrhoeas?
shelves.mesh: Bicarbonates/therapeutic use · Child · Cholera/complications · Dehydration/prevention & control/therapy · Diarrhea/etiology/therapy · Fluid Therapy · Glucose/therapeutic use · Humans · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Oryza · Potassium Chloride/therapeutic use · Rehydration Solutions/therapeutic use · Sodium Chloride/therapeutic use · Time Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for cholera, where the effect is large and consistent; much weaker elsewhere, and the shelf says so. The meta-analysis of the 13 randomised trials (Gore SM et al., PMID: 1531430; 1,367 patients — 668 standard WHO glucose solution, 699 rice-based) found the rice solution significantly reduced the rate of stool output during the first 24 hours by 36% (95% CI 28–44%) in adults with cholera and by 32% (19–45%) in children with cholera, but by only 18% (6–30%) in infants and children with acute non-cholera diarrhoea; the authors concluded the benefit in cholera is sufficiently great to warrant its use, while the smaller non-cholera benefit needed sharper definition. A four-arm randomised trial in 182 adults with cholera (Alam NH et al., PMID: 1582603) agreed qualitatively: a substantial and significant reduction in stool output in the rice-ORS groups irrespective of feeding, and food itself did not potentiate either solution (the record reports no arm-level volumes, so none are quoted). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): rice-based ORS reduces purging in cholera by about a third in the first day — a stool-output benefit, in trials run against the older standard-osmolarity glucose solution; the library's separate shelf on reduced-osmolarity ORS asks the neighbouring formulation question.

cards.headline: Gore 1992 meta-analysis (13 trials, 1,367 patients): stool output in the first 24 hours reduced 36% (28–44%) in adults with cholera, 32% (19–45%) in children with cholera, 18% (6–30%) in non-cholera diarrhoea
cards.summary: Gore 1992 meta-analysis (13 trials, 1,367 patients): stool output in the first 24 hours reduced 36% (28–44%) in adults with cholera, 32% (19–45%) in children with cholera, 18% (6–30%) in non-cholera diarrhoea
cards.people: 1,367 patients with cholera, severe cholera-like diarrhoea, or acute non-cholera diarrhoea in 13 randomised trials comparing rice-based oral rehydration solution with the standard glucose-based WHO solution — 668 received the standard solution and 699 the rice-based solution; each trial was re-reviewed for eligibility, randomisation and outcome timing, with stool output during the first 24 hours as the main measure.
cards.result: The rice solution significantly reduced the rate of stool output during the first 24 hours by 36% (95% CI 28% to 44%) in adults with cholera and by 32% (19% to 45%) in children with cholera. In infants and children with acute non-cholera diarrhoea, stool loss was reduced by only 18% (6% to 30%). The authors concluded that the benefit of rice oral rehydration solution for patients with cholera is sufficiently great to warrant its use in such patients, while the considerably smaller benefit in non-cholera diarrhoea should be more precisely defined before its practical value can be judged.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is stool volume in the first 24 hours — a physiological win that eases fluid management — not mortality, and the comparator is the older standard-osmolarity glucose ORS, not the reduced-osmolarity formulation examined on the library's neighbouring ORS shelf; rice ORS also has to be cooked and used fresh, which the trials handled and field programmes must too.
cards.source: Gore SM et al. Impact of rice based oral rehydration solution on stool output and duration of diarrhoea: meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. BMJ. 1992. PMID: 1531430. cards.headline: Alam 1992 (Bangladesh, 182 adults with cholera): rice-ORS groups had a substantial, significant reduction in stool output with or without food; feeding changed nothing for either solution
cards.summary: Alam 1992 (Bangladesh, 182 adults with cholera): rice-ORS groups had a substantial, significant reduction in stool output with or without food; feeding changed nothing for either solution
cards.people: 182 adults with cholera in Bangladesh who, after four hours of intravenous polyelectrolyte rehydration, were randomised to one of four therapies: glucose-based ORS with no food for 24 hours, glucose ORS plus food from the start, rice-based ORS with no food for 24 hours, or rice-based ORS plus food from the start; all received tetracycline after 72 hours.
cards.result: No significant differences in ORS intake, stool output, or duration of diarrhoea were noted between the two glucose groups (with versus without food) or between the two rice groups. A substantial and significant reduction in stool output was, however, shown in the groups who received rice-based ORS irrespective of feeding. The authors concluded that food does not potentiate the efficacy of either solution in adults with cholera, and that rice-based ORS compared with glucose ORS substantially reduces purging in cholera patients. The record reports no arm-level stool volumes, so none are quoted.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1992 trial reported qualitatively in its abstract — it corroborates the meta-analysis's direction without adding quotable numbers, and all patients had intravenous rehydration and antibiotics around the ORS comparison.
cards.source: Alam NH et al. Effects of food with two oral rehydration therapies: a randomised controlled clinical trial. Gut. 1992. PMID: 1582603. cards.headline: Synthesis: rice in the sachet buys about a third less purging on day one in cholera — a real, narrow, formulation-level benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: rice in the sachet buys about a third less purging on day one in cholera — a real, narrow, formulation-level benefit
cards.people: Thirteen randomised trials (1,367 patients) pooled, plus a 182-patient four-arm trial in adults with cholera.
cards.result: First-24-hour stool output: −36% (adults with cholera), −32% (children with cholera), −18% (children with non-cholera diarrhoea), rice-based versus glucose-based ORS. PROPOSED LIKELY for the cholera claim — many trials, one direction, a large relative effect on a directly measured output.
cards.watchOut: Rehydration itself — getting enough of any correct ORS in, early — saves the lives; formulation refinements are second-order. This shelf does not compare rice ORS with today's reduced-osmolarity glucose ORS head-to-head, because the randomised record carded here predates that comparison.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gore SM et al. BMJ. 1992 (PMID: 1531430); Alam NH et al. Gut. 1992 (PMID: 1582603).

shelves.title: Whipple's disease: ceftriaxone or meropenem induction, then trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — every patient in the randomised trial achieved remission (endpoint OR 0.95 between inductions), and a follow-on study found 3 months of oral therapy did the work of 12
shelves.question: In previously untreated Whipple's disease, which induction antibiotic — ceftriaxone or meropenem — followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cures the infection, and is 3 months of the oral phase enough instead of 12?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Biopsy · Ceftriaxone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Intestinal Mucosa/microbiology/pathology · Male · Meropenem · Middle Aged · Remission Induction · Thienamycins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Tropheryma · Whipple Disease/drug therapy/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two induction drugs, in a disease so rare that 40 patients is a landmark trial; the duration answer comes from a non-randomised extension and is labelled as such. The randomised trial (Feurle GE et al., PMID: 19879276) assigned 40 previously untreated central-European patients to daily ceftriaxone (2 g once daily, n=20) or meropenem (1 g three times daily, n=20) infusions for 14 days, both followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 12 months: all patients were followed for the entire period (median 89 months), all achieved clinical and laboratory remission, and remission was maintained in all except 2 who died of unrelated causes; the odds ratio for the endpoint (remission for at least 3 years) was 0.95 (95% CI 0.05–16.29; p=1.0). One patient with asymptomatic cerebrospinal-fluid infection resistant to both treatments responded to chloroquine and minocycline. The extension study (Feurle GE et al., PMID: 23291038) treated a further 40 patients identically except for 3 months of oral therapy: 12 months was not more effective than 3 months on clinical, laboratory (p=0.405, p=0.631) or histological (p=0.456) measures, and 36 of 37 surviving patients — including 14 with cerebrospinal infection — were in remission without recurrence after a median 80 months, with one arthritis recurrence at 63 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): either induction cures; the shorter oral course rests on a sequential, non-randomised comparison — Tier C for the single small trial at the shelf's core.

cards.headline: Feurle 2010 RCT (n=40): all patients achieved remission on either induction; 3-year remission OR 0.95 (0.05–16.29); 2 unrelated deaths; 1 dual-resistant CSF case rescued by chloroquine + minocycline
cards.summary: Feurle 2010 RCT (n=40): all patients achieved remission on either induction; 3-year remission OR 0.95 (0.05–16.29); 2 unrelated deaths; 1 dual-resistant CSF case rescued by chloroquine + minocycline
cards.people: 40 previously untreated patients with Whipple's disease from central Europe, randomly assigned to daily infusions of ceftriaxone 2 g once daily (n=20) or meropenem 1 g three times daily (n=20) for 14 days — both antibiotics chosen for blood-brain-barrier penetration and Tropheryma whipplei susceptibility — followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 12 months; primary outcome was maintenance of remission for 3 years by a composite of clinical, laboratory and histology data; median follow-up 89 months (range 71–128).
cards.result: All patients were observed for the entire follow-up period and all achieved clinical and laboratory remission. Remission was maintained in all patients during observation except 2 who died from unrelated causes. A single patient with asymptomatic cerebrospinal infection resistant to both treatments responded to chloroquine and minocycline. The odds ratio for the endpoint (remission for at least 3 years) was 0.95 (95% CI 0.05–16.29; p=1.0). The authors concluded this was a randomised trial showing that ceftriaxone or meropenem, followed by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cures Whipple's disease.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and an odds-ratio interval running from 0.05 to 16.29: the trial proves the regimen cures, not that the two inductions are precisely equal — and Whipple's is rare enough that no larger trial is coming. One dual-resistant cerebrospinal case is a standing warning that the central nervous system is the sanctuary to watch.
cards.source: Feurle GE et al. Efficacy of ceftriaxone or meropenem as initial therapies in Whipple's disease. Gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 19879276. cards.headline: Feurle 2013 extension (n=40, non-randomised): 3 months of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole matched 12 — 36 of 37 survivors in remission at a median 80 months, including 14 with cerebrospinal infection
cards.summary: Feurle 2013 extension (n=40, non-randomised): 3 months of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole matched 12 — 36 of 37 survivors in remission at a median 80 months, including 14 with cerebrospinal infection
cards.people: 40 further untreated patients from central Europe (July 2004–July 2008), treated with an essentially identical protocol to the randomised trial except that oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily ran for 3 months instead of 12 after 14 days of intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily; efficacy compared against the previous study.
cards.result: Twelve months of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was not more effective than 3 months on clinical findings, laboratory data (p=0.405 and p=0.631) or histological data (p=0.456). Thirty-six of 37 surviving patients, including 14 with cerebrospinal infection, were in remission without evidence of recurrence after a median follow-up of 80 months; in one patient, Tropheryma whipplei arthritis recurred 63 months after initial therapy. The authors concluded ceftriaxone followed by three months of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is highly efficacious in Whipple's disease. Intestinal biopsy histology proved a more useful eradication marker than PCR in gut tissue.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised — a sequential cohort compared with the earlier trial's patients, so era and selection effects are uncontrolled; and a recurrence at 63 months shows why follow-up in this disease is measured in years, whichever duration is chosen.
cards.source: Feurle GE et al. Intravenous ceftriaxone, followed by 12 or three months of oral treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, in Whipple's disease. The Journal of Infection. 2013. PMID: 23291038. Registry ID: ISRCTN45658456. cards.headline: Synthesis: the regimen cures — induction choice is a coin the trial cannot call, and the oral year may be nine months longer than needed
cards.summary: Synthesis: the regimen cures — induction choice is a coin the trial cannot call, and the oral year may be nine months longer than needed
cards.people: One randomised trial (40 patients, two inductions, 12-month oral phase, median 89 months' follow-up) and one sequential extension cohort (40 patients, 3-month oral phase, median 80 months).
cards.result: Remission: 40 of 40 randomised patients on either induction (OR 0.95, CI 0.05–16.29); 36 of 37 survivors in remission after the 3-month oral course. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — rare-disease evidence, honestly small.
cards.watchOut: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after effective therapy is a recognised Whipple's complication described in this group's cohort work; it is not carded here because it is observational — readers managing paradoxical worsening should know it exists and is not necessarily relapse.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feurle GE et al. Gastroenterology. 2010 (PMID: 19879276); Feurle GE et al. The Journal of Infection. 2013 (PMID: 23291038).

shelves.title: Pepto-Bismol before the trip: bismuth subsalicylate cut travellers' diarrhoea from 40% to 14% at the high dose — 65% protection in students in Mexico, confirmed in a volunteer challenge study
shelves.question: In travellers to high-risk regions, does taking bismuth subsalicylate prophylactically prevent travellers' diarrhoea compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bismuth · Diarrhea/microbiology/prevention & control · Humans · Mexico · Organometallic Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Probability · Random Allocation · Salicylates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Tablets · Travel
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — old but genuinely randomised evidence for prevention (treatment of established diarrhoea is a different question, housed with the acute-diarrhoea shelves). In DuPont HL et al. (PMID: 3820443), 182 US students in Mexico were randomised within 48 hours of arrival to two tablets (high dose, 2.1 g/day), one tablet (low dose) or placebo, each four times daily for three weeks: among completers, diarrhoea occurred in 14% (7/51) on high dose, 24% (15/63) on low dose and 40% (23/58) on placebo — protection rates of 65% relative and 40% relative respectively; diarrhoea caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli occurred in one high-dose student, no low-dose students and seven on placebo. In a volunteer challenge study (Graham DY et al., PMID: 6352386), 32 healthy volunteers were dosed with bismuth subsalicylate or placebo around an oral challenge with enterotoxigenic E. coli strain H10407: diarrhoea occurred in 13% (2/15) on bismuth versus 56% (9/16) on placebo (p<0.03), and the organism was recovered less often from the bismuth group. Bismuth was well tolerated in DuPont; the commonest effects were blackening of tongue and stools, with tinnitus reported at a low frequency of 1.2 days per 100 days of treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): four-times-daily tablets buy roughly two-thirds protection for trips of up to three weeks — a real effect that has to be weighed against the dosing burden and the salicylate load.

cards.headline: DuPont 1987: diarrhoea in 14% on high-dose bismuth, 24% on low dose, 40% on placebo — protection 65% relative and 40% relative over three weeks in Mexico
cards.summary: DuPont 1987: diarrhoea in 14% on high-dose bismuth, 24% on low dose, 40% on placebo — protection 65% relative and 40% relative over three weeks in Mexico
cards.people: 182 US students who, within 48 hours of arrival in Mexico, were randomly assigned to bismuth subsalicylate tablets (262 mg each) as two tablets four times daily (high dose, 2.1 g/day), one tablet four times daily (low dose), or placebo four times daily, for three weeks; diarrhoea was defined as at least four unformed stools in 24 hours, or three in eight hours, plus another symptom. Results are reported for those completing the trial (51 high-dose, 63 low-dose, 58 placebo).
cards.result: Diarrhoea occurred in 7/51 (14%) on high dose, 15/63 (24%) on low dose and 23/58 (40%) on placebo — protection rates of 65% relative (high dose) and 40% relative (low dose). Diarrhoea caused by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli was found in one student on high dose, none on low dose, and seven on placebo. Bismuth subsalicylate was well tolerated; the most common side effects were blackening of tongues and stools, and tinnitus occurred at 1.2 days per 100 days of treatment, described as low and clinically insignificant.
cards.watchOut: A 1987 trial in young US students at one destination, analysed on completers, testing a demanding four-times-daily regimen for three weeks; adherence on a real holiday will be worse, and protection with it. Bismuth subsalicylate is a salicylate — the record does not address people who must avoid salicylates or who take anticoagulants.
cards.source: DuPont HL et al. Prevention of travelers' diarrhea by the tablet formulation of bismuth subsalicylate. JAMA. 1987. PMID: 3820443. randomised controlled trial (dupont 1987) 182 us students who, within 48 hours of arrival in mexico, were randomly assigned to bismuth subsalicylate tablets (262 mg each) as two tablets four times daily (high dose, 2.1 g/day), one tablet four times daily (low dose), or placebo four times daily, for three weeks; diarrhoea was defined as at least four unformed stools in 24 hours, or three in eight hours, plus another symptom. results are reported for those completing the trial (51 high-dose, 63 low-dose, 58 placebo). diarrhoea occurred in 7/51 (14%) on high dose, 15/63 (24%) on low dose and 23/58 (40%) on placebo — protection rates of 65% relative (high dose) and 40% relative (low dose). diarrhoea caused by enterotoxigenic escherichia coli was found in one student on high dose, none on low dose, and seven on placebo. bismuth subsalicylate was well tolerated; the most common side effects were blackening of tongues and stools, and tinnitus occurred at 1.2 days per 100 days of treatment, described as low and clinically insignificant. a 1987 trial in young us students at one destination, analysed on completers, testing a demanding four-times-daily regimen for three weeks; adherence on a real holiday will be worse, and protection with it. bismuth subsalicylate is a salicylate — the record does not address people who must avoid salicylates or who take anticoagulants. dupont hl et al. prevention of travelers' diarrhea by the tablet formulation of bismuth subsalicylate. jama. 1987. pmid: 3820443. mesh: adult · bismuth · diarrhea/microbiology/prevention & control · humans · mexico · organometallic compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · probability · random allocation · salicylates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · tablets · travel

cards.headline: Graham 1983: volunteers deliberately infected with enterotoxigenic E. coli — diarrhoea in 13% on bismuth versus 56% on placebo (p<0.03)
cards.summary: Graham 1983: volunteers deliberately infected with enterotoxigenic E. coli — diarrhoea in 13% on bismuth versus 56% on placebo (p<0.03)
cards.people: 32 healthy hospitalised volunteers challenged orally with enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli strain H10407; 600 mg doses of bismuth subsalicylate or placebo began 8 hours before challenge (at 8 and 2 hours before, and 2 and 4 hours after) and continued four times daily for three more days, to a maximum prophylactic dose of 9.6 g. Volunteers who developed diarrhoea were re-randomised to treatment doses, but the record's abstract reports the prevention results numerically.
cards.result: Diarrhoea occurred in 2 of 15 (13%) subjects receiving bismuth subsalicylate versus 9 of 16 (56%) receiving placebo (p<0.03). Enterotoxigenic E. coli were recovered less frequently from those receiving bismuth, suggesting prevention works by reducing the number or multiplication of the organisms; in vitro, bismuth subsalicylate and its components were each bactericidal at concentrations possibly attained during the trial.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two volunteers, one laboratory strain, inpatient dosing — a proof-of-mechanism study, not a field trial; its role is to show the DuPont field result is biologically real rather than a fluke of one student cohort. Doses around challenge were intensive and short.
cards.source: Graham DY et al. Double-blind comparison of bismuth subsalicylate and placebo in the prevention and treatment of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli-induced diarrhea in volunteers. Gastroenterology. 1983. PMID: 6352386. cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised designs, one answer — bismuth prevents a large share of travellers' diarrhoea while you keep taking it
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised designs, one answer — bismuth prevents a large share of travellers' diarrhoea while you keep taking it
cards.people: A 182-student field trial over three weeks in Mexico and a 32-volunteer controlled E. coli challenge study, both randomised against placebo.
cards.result: Field: diarrhoea 14% (high dose) and 24% (low dose) versus 40% on placebo — 65% and 40% relative protection. Challenge: 13% versus 56% (p<0.03). Harms in the field trial: black tongue and stools commonly; tinnitus 1.2 days per 100 treatment days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for prevention during travel of up to three weeks.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are from the 1980s, both are short, and neither addresses children, pregnancy, salicylate sensitivity or drug interactions — all live issues for a salicylate taken four times a day. This shelf is prevention only; antibiotic treatment of travellers' diarrhoea is housed at live shelf #1213 and rifaximin prophylaxis at #1214. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry it.
cards.source: Synthesis of DuPont HL et al. JAMA. 1987 (PMID: 3820443); Graham DY et al. Gastroenterology. 1983 (PMID: 6352386).

shelves.title: Endocuff Vision at colonoscopy: adenoma detection rose from 36.2% to 40.9% in ADENOMA, driven by screening patients (61.7% vs 50.9%) — but the same device changed nothing at flexible sigmoidoscopy (13.3% vs 12.2%)
shelves.question: Does attaching the Endocuff Vision mucosal-exposure device to the endoscope increase adenoma detection — at colonoscopy, and at flexible sigmoidoscopy screening?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Colonoscopes · Colonoscopy/methods · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Diagnosis, Differential · England · Equipment Design · Female · Humans · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Middle Aged · Quality Improvement
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the device helped where baseline detection and lesion yield were high, and did nothing where they were low. In the ADENOMA colonoscopy trial (Ngu WS et al., PMID: 29363535), adenoma detection was 40.9% with Endocuff Vision versus 36.2% with standard colonoscopy (P=0.02), driven by a 10.8-point gain in faecal-occult-blood-positive screening patients (61.7% vs 50.9%, P<0.001), with more cancers found (4.1% vs 2.3%, P=0.02). In the B-ADENOMA flexible sigmoidoscopy trial (Rees CJ et al., PMID: 32245908), detection was 13.3% with the device versus 12.2% without (p=0.353), with no differences in polyp yield, procedure time or experience. PROPOSED SPLIT: Endocuff Vision is a detection aid with a real but context-dependent effect — worthwhile in screening colonoscopy on this record, unproven at one-off sigmoidoscopy — and detection remains a surrogate for cancer prevention in both trials.

cards.headline: ADENOMA (Ngu 2019): adenoma detection 40.9% vs 36.2% overall (P=0.02); 61.7% vs 50.9% in FOBt-positive screening patients; cancers 4.1% vs 2.3%
cards.summary: ADENOMA (Ngu 2019): adenoma detection 40.9% vs 36.2% overall (P=0.02); 61.7% vs 50.9% in FOBt-positive screening patients; cancers 4.1% vs 2.3%
cards.people: 1,772 patients (57% male, mean age 62 years; 45% recruited through the Bowel Cancer Screening Programme) referred for colonoscopy for symptoms, surveillance or a positive faecal occult blood test at seven English hospitals, randomised to Endocuff Vision-assisted or standard colonoscopy.
cards.result: Adenoma detection rate: 40.9% with Endocuff Vision versus 36.2% standard (P=0.02). The increase was driven by FOBt-positive screening patients: 61.7% versus 50.9% (a 10.8% increase, P<0.001). Endocuff patients also had higher mean adenomas per procedure and higher detection of sessile serrated polyps, left-sided, diminutive and small adenomas, and cancers (4.1% vs 2.3%, P=0.02). The device was removed in 4.1% of cases; median intubation was a minute quicker, with no difference in caecal intubation or withdrawal time and no significant device adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The headline gain is a subgroup-driven result in a high-prevalence screening population; in symptomatic and surveillance patients the separation was smaller, and adenoma detection — especially of diminutive lesions — is a surrogate whose conversion into fewer interval cancers is inferred, not measured, here.
cards.source: Ngu WS et al. Improved adenoma detection with Endocuff Vision: the ADENOMA randomised controlled trial. Gut. 2019. PMID: 29363535. Registry ID: NCT02552017; ISRCTN11821044. cards.headline: B-ADENOMA (Rees 2020): adenoma detection 13.3% with Endocuff vs 12.2% standard at flexible sigmoidoscopy (p=0.353) — no gain on any measure
cards.summary: B-ADENOMA (Rees 2020): adenoma detection 13.3% with Endocuff vs 12.2% standard at flexible sigmoidoscopy (p=0.353) — no gain on any measure
cards.people: 3,222 participants (53% male) in the English BowelScope one-off flexible sigmoidoscopy screening programme at age 55, randomised at 16 centres to Endocuff Vision-assisted (n=1,610) or standard (n=1,612) sigmoidoscopy.
cards.result: Adenoma detection rate: 13.3% with Endocuff Vision versus 12.2% standard (p=0.353). No statistically significant differences were found in polyp detection rate, mean adenomas per procedure, polyp characteristics or location, participant experience, complications or procedural characteristics. Adenoma detection in the standard arm was itself 3.1% higher than the national BowelScope rate.
cards.watchOut: A shorter examination of the left colon in an average-risk screening population with a low baseline detection rate is a different test from full colonoscopy in FOBt-positive patients; the null here bounds the device's value in low-yield settings rather than contradicting the colonoscopy result.
cards.source: Rees CJ et al. BowelScope: Accuracy of Detection Using Endocuff Optimisation of Mucosal Abnormalities (the B-ADENOMA Study): a multicentre, randomised controlled flexible sigmoidoscopy trial. Gut. 2020. cards.headline: Synthesis: same device, two procedures — a real colonoscopy gain concentrated in screening, a sigmoidoscopy null
cards.summary: Synthesis: same device, two procedures — a real colonoscopy gain concentrated in screening, a sigmoidoscopy null
cards.people: Two English multicentre randomised trials of Endocuff Vision: 1,772 colonoscopy patients (ADENOMA) and 3,222 flexible sigmoidoscopy screening participants (B-ADENOMA).
cards.result: Colonoscopy adenoma detection 40.9% versus 36.2% (screening subgroup 61.7% versus 50.9%; cancers 4.1% versus 2.3%). Sigmoidoscopy detection 13.3% versus 12.2% (not significant). PROPOSED SPLIT, as in the balance above.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measures interval cancers or mortality; both were conducted within one national screening system with trained operators, and device removal (4.1% in ADENOMA) and anal-intubation discomfort temper routine use. shelves.title: Buspirone for functional dyspepsia: overall symptom severity 7.5 versus 11.5 on placebo and gastric accommodation nearly doubled in one 17-patient crossover trial — promising physiology, tiny evidence base
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does buspirone — a fundus-relaxing 5-HT1A agonist — improve meal-related symptoms and gastric accommodation compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Buspirone/administration & dosage · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia/drug therapy/pathology/physiopathology · Female · Gastric Emptying/drug effects · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one very small crossover trial with a coherent mechanism and a clear symptom result, and nothing behind it. In that trial (Tack J et al., PMID: 22813445), 17 patients with functional dyspepsia took buspirone 10 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks each: overall dyspepsia severity was 7.5 ± 1.3 on buspirone versus 11.5 ± 1.2 on placebo (P<.005), with significant gains in postprandial fullness, early satiation and bloating, and gastric accommodation rose from 141 ± 32 mL on placebo to 229 ± 28 mL on buspirone (P<.05), while sensitivity to gastric distension and solid emptying were unchanged and adverse events were similar between treatments. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): buspirone is a physiologically plausible, apparently well-tolerated option for postprandial-distress dyspepsia whose entire clinical case rests on 17 patients — it needs a real trial before it needs a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: Tack 2012: symptom severity 7.5 vs 11.5 (P<.005); accommodation 229 vs 141 mL (P<.05); fullness, early satiation and bloating all improved
cards.summary: Tack 2012: symptom severity 7.5 vs 11.5 (P<.005); accommodation 229 vs 141 mL (P<.05); fullness, early satiation and bloating all improved
cards.people: 17 patients (13 women; mean age 38.5 years) with functional dyspepsia, given buspirone 10 mg three times daily or placebo 15 minutes before meals for two 4-week periods separated by a 2-week washout, with barostat and breath-test measures of gastric sensitivity, accommodation and emptying before and after each period.
cards.result: Overall dyspepsia symptom severity: 7.5 ± 1.3 on buspirone versus 11.5 ± 1.2 on placebo (P<.005); postprandial fullness, early satiation and upper abdominal bloating each improved significantly on buspirone while placebo had no significant effect. Gastric accommodation increased on buspirone versus placebo (229 ± 28 vs 141 ± 32 mL; P<.05). Buspirone did not alter sensitivity to gastric distension or gastric emptying of solids; adverse events were similar between treatments.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients, four weeks, one centre's physiology laboratory: the effect size is large precisely where small-study effects live, there is no replication, and the record's gastric-emptying-of-liquids sentence is internally inconsistent (it describes delayed emptying alongside a shorter printed half-life), so this shelf makes no emptying claim. Tier C is set — a single small trial.
cards.source: Tack J et al. Efficacy of buspirone, a fundus-relaxing drug, in patients with functional dyspepsia. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2012. PMID: 22813445. cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 17 patients with functional dyspepsia (Tack 2012).

shelves.title: STW 5 (Iberogast) for functional dyspepsia: complete relief in 43.3% versus 3.3% at 8 weeks in the STW 5-II trial, and a pooled odds ratio of 0.22 for the most bothersome symptom across the placebo trials
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does the herbal preparation STW 5 (Iberogast) — or its STW 5-II variant — improve dyspeptic symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an old, small but concordant placebo-controlled record for one named herbal mixture. In the multicentre double-blind trial of STW 5-II (Madisch A et al., PMID: 14755152), the gastrointestinal symptom score fell significantly more on active treatment than placebo in the first 4 weeks (p<0.001), and after 8 weeks 43.3% on active treatment versus 3.3% on placebo reported complete relief of symptoms (p<0.001). The meta-analysis of STW 5 itself (Melzer J et al., PMID: 15606389) re-pooled three placebo-controlled trials (138 on verum, 135 on placebo) and found STW 5 more effective for the severity of the most bothersome gastrointestinal symptom (P=0.001; odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.11–0.47), with adverse events similar to placebo and no serious adverse events. The tested products are the named preparations STW 5 (Iberogast) and STW 5-II as described in the publications; neither record names the manufacturer in its abstract, and other herbal mixtures cannot borrow this result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients who want a herbal option, this specific preparation has genuine placebo-controlled support — from trials run two decades ago, at modest size.

cards.headline: Madisch 2004 (STW 5-II): symptom score fell significantly more than placebo by week 4; complete relief at 8 weeks in 43.3% vs 3.3% (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Madisch 2004 (STW 5-II): symptom score fell significantly more than placebo by week 4; complete relief at 8 weeks in 43.3% vs 3.3% (p<0.001)
cards.people: 120 patients with functional dyspepsia in a multicentre trial, randomised to STW 5-II (a variant of the herbal preparation containing extracts of bitter candytuft, matricaria flower, peppermint leaves, caraway, licorice root and lemon balm) or placebo across three consecutive 4-week treatment blocks, with switching in the third block guided by symptom control; primary outcome was the standardised gastrointestinal symptom score (GIS). The publication names the preparation STW 5-II; it does not name a manufacturer in the record.
cards.result: During the first 4 weeks the GIS decreased significantly more on active treatment than placebo (p<0.001). During the second 4 weeks, symptoms improved further in patients who continued or switched to active treatment (p<0.001) and deteriorated in those switched to placebo. After 8 weeks, 43.3% on active treatment and 3.3% on placebo reported complete relief of symptoms (p<0.001 vs placebo).
cards.watchOut: The switch-by-response design after week 4 means the clean randomised contrast is the first block; the 8-week complete-relief figures come from a design in which non-responders changed treatment, and STW 5-II is a modified variant — its result supports, but is not identical to, evidence for STW 5 itself.

cards.headline: Melzer 2004 (meta-analysis of STW 5): pooled odds ratio 0.22 (95% CI 0.11–0.47) for the most bothersome symptom across three placebo trials (n=273)
cards.summary: Melzer 2004 (meta-analysis of STW 5): pooled odds ratio 0.22 (95% CI 0.11–0.47) for the most bothersome symptom across three placebo trials (n=273)
cards.people: Six randomised trials of the herbal preparation STW 5 (Iberogast — containing, among others, Iberis, peppermint and chamomile extracts, as described in the record) were identified with the producer's involvement; raw data from the three placebo-controlled trials meeting selection criteria (138 verum, 135 placebo) were re-pooled, with a fourth reference-controlled trial (STW 5 n=199, control n=198) informing safety. The record names the product STW 5 (Iberogast); no manufacturer is named in the record.
cards.result: Pooled data showed verum more effective than placebo for severity of the most bothersome gastrointestinal symptom (P=0.001; odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.11–0.47). A fourth trial found no significant difference between STW 5 and cisapride. Adverse events were similar between verum and placebo, and no serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The search was conducted with the producer's consultation and the pooled trials are small and old; an odds ratio on a 'most bothersome symptom' scale is harder to translate into everyday benefit than the complete-relief rates in the Madisch trial, and cisapride — the active comparator — was later withdrawn for cardiac harm, dating the comparison.
cards.source: Melzer J et al. Meta-analysis: phytotherapy of functional dyspepsia with the herbal drug preparation STW 5 (Iberogast). Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2004. PMID: 15606389. shelves.title: Eosinophilic oesophagitis diets: milk-only elimination matched six-food elimination (remission 34% vs 40%, difference 6%, p=0.58) — and a step-up strategy spared endoscopies while reaching 79% remission at its widest step
shelves.question: In eosinophilic oesophagitis, is eliminating animal milk alone (one-food elimination) as effective as six-food elimination for histological remission — and what does a step-up dietary strategy achieve?
shelves.mesh: United States · Animals · Humans · Female · Male · Eosinophilic Esophagitis/drug therapy/pathology · Elimination Diets · Quality of Life · Fluticasone
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two diets, that is: starting with milk alone performed statistically indistinguishably from starting with six foods. In the randomised trial (Kliewer KL et al., PMID: 36863390), histological remission at 6 weeks was 34% on one-food (milk) elimination versus 40% on six-food elimination (difference 6%, 95% CI −11 to 23; p=0.58), although complete remission (≤1 eosinophil per high-power field) favoured six foods (difference 13%, 95% CI 2 to 25; p=0.031); 43% of one-food non-responders then remitted on six foods, and 82% of six-food non-responders remitted on swallowed fluticasone. In the prospective step-up study (Molina-Infante J et al., PMID: 29074457), a two-food elimination (milk and gluten cereals) remitted 43%, rising to 60% at four foods and 79% at six foods, while cutting endoscopies and diagnostic time by 20% versus starting at six foods. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): milk-first is an acceptable, far less restrictive opening move — with escalation paths that recover most non-responders.

cards.headline: Kliewer 2023: remission 34% (1FED) vs 40% (6FED), difference 6% (−11 to 23), p=0.58; complete remission favoured 6FED (difference 13%, p=0.031); steroid rescue remitted 82% of 6FED non-responders
cards.summary: Kliewer 2023: remission 34% (1FED) vs 40% (6FED), difference 6% (−11 to 23), p=0.58; complete remission favoured 6FED (difference 13%, p=0.031); steroid rescue remitted 82% of 6FED non-responders
cards.people: 129 adults (mean age 37 years; 54% men) with active symptomatic eosinophilic oesophagitis at ten US consortium sites, randomised to one-food elimination (animal milk only, n=67) or six-food elimination (milk, wheat, egg, soy, fish/shellfish, peanut/tree nuts, n=62) for 6 weeks; primary endpoint was histological remission (peak count under 15 eosinophils per high-power field), with prespecified crossover steps for non-responders.
cards.result: Histological remission at 6 weeks: 23 of 67 (34%) on one-food versus 25 of 62 (40%) on six-food elimination (difference 6% [95% CI −11 to 23]; p=0.58). Complete remission (≤1 eos/hpf) was significantly higher on six foods (difference 13% [2 to 25]; p=0.031); stricter partial thresholds and histology, endoscopy, symptom and quality-of-life changes did not differ significantly. Among non-responders, 9 of 21 (43%) remitted after stepping up from one-food to six-food, and 9 of 11 (82%) remitted after switching from six-food to swallowed fluticasone propionate. No adverse event occurred in more than 5% of either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable for diets), 6 weeks, and the confidence interval (−11 to +23 points) is wide enough to hide a meaningful advantage for six foods at the main threshold — 'no significant difference' here is not proven equivalence; the complete-remission endpoint did separate the diets. Tier C is set: a single randomised trial anchors the comparison.
cards.source: Kliewer KL et al. One-food versus six-food elimination diet therapy for the treatment of eosinophilic oesophagitis: a multicentre, randomised, open-label trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2023. PMID: 36863390. Registry ID: NCT02778867. cards.headline: Molina-Infante 2018 (2-4-6 step-up): remission 43% on two foods, 60% on four, 79% on six — with 20% fewer endoscopies than starting at six
cards.summary: Molina-Infante 2018 (2-4-6 step-up): remission 43% on two foods, 60% on four, 79% on six — with 20% fewer endoscopies than starting at six
cards.people: 130 patients (25 of them children) with eosinophilic oesophagitis at 14 centres, treated prospectively with a 6-week two-food-group elimination diet (milk and gluten-containing cereals), stepping up to four food groups (adding egg and legumes) and then six (adding nuts and fish/seafood) for non-responders; remission required symptom improvement plus under 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
cards.result: The two-food diet achieved remission in 56 of 130 patients (43%), with milk the trigger in 52% of responders, gluten cereals in 16% and both in 28%. Remission rates rose to 60% with four food groups and 79% with six. Overall, 55 of 60 (91.6%) two-/four-food responders had only one or two food triggers, and the step-up strategy reduced endoscopic procedures and diagnostic-process time by 20% compared with starting at six foods.
cards.watchOut: A prospective cohort without a randomised comparator: its rising remission percentages partly reflect cumulative time and repeated endoscopy rather than diet breadth alone, and it mixes children with adults — it supports the step-up pathway's practicality, not the head-to-head diet verdict, which rests on the Kliewer trial.
cards.source: Molina-Infante J et al. Step-up empiric elimination diet for pediatric and adult eosinophilic esophagitis: The 2-4-6 study. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2018. PMID: 29074457. cards.headline: Synthesis: start narrow, escalate on biopsy — milk-first ties six-food at the standard threshold and the pathway recovers most non-responders
cards.summary: Synthesis: start narrow, escalate on biopsy — milk-first ties six-food at the standard threshold and the pathway recovers most non-responders
cards.people: One randomised trial of 129 adults comparing one-food with six-food elimination (Kliewer 2023) and one prospective 130-patient step-up cohort (Molina-Infante 2018).
cards.result: Remission at 6 weeks: 34% (milk only) versus 40% (six foods), difference 6% (−11 to 23). Step-up data: 43% remit on two foods, 79% by six foods; 43% of milk-first non-responders remit on six foods and 82% of six-food non-responders remit on swallowed fluticasone. shelves.title: RBX2660 microbiota enema for recurrent C. difficile: model-estimated success 70.6% versus 57.5% on placebo in phase 3 — after the phase 2b trial missed its own primary endpoint
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection who have completed standard antibiotics, does a single RBX2660 microbiota-based enema reduce recurrence within 8 weeks compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Clostridioides difficile · Bayes Theorem · Diarrhea/drug therapy/prevention & control · Clostridium Infections/drug therapy/prevention & control · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Recurrence · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest absolute gain, carried by a Bayesian phase 3 analysis after a conventionally negative phase 2b. In PUNCH CD3 (Khanna S et al., PMID: 36287379), model-estimated treatment success (no recurrence within 8 weeks) was 70.6% on RBX2660 versus 57.5% on placebo — an estimated 13.1-point difference with a posterior probability of superiority of 0.991 — and over 90% of successes in both groups stayed recurrence-free through 6 months. In the earlier PUNCH CD2 trial (Dubberke ER et al., PMID: 36544075), intention-to-treat success was 56.8% (one RBX2660 dose plus one placebo dose) and 55.6% (two RBX2660 doses) versus 43.2% on placebo — differences that were not significant (both p=0.2), so the phase 2b trial missed its predefined primary endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): RBX2660 — the standardised stool-derived microbiota product tested under that name in these records (the records do not name its manufacturer) — probably prevents roughly one recurrence in eight treated patients beyond placebo, with mostly mild gastrointestinal adverse effects.

cards.headline: PUNCH CD3 (Khanna 2022): model-estimated success 70.6% vs 57.5% (difference 13.1 points; posterior probability of superiority 0.991); over 90% of successes sustained to 6 months
cards.summary: PUNCH CD3 (Khanna 2022): model-estimated success 70.6% vs 57.5% (difference 13.1 points; posterior probability of superiority 0.991); over 90% of successes sustained to 6 months
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial with Bayesian primary analysis (Khanna 2022, PUNCH CD3)
cards.people: 289 adults with one or more recurrences of C. difficile infection and a positive stool assay, previously treated with standard-of-care antibiotics, randomised 2:1 to a single blinded enema of RBX2660 (a standardised live microbiota consortium prepared from human stool, as described in the record) or placebo; 267 received treatment (180 RBX2660, 87 placebo). Primary endpoint: absence of C. difficile diarrhoea within 8 weeks.
cards.result: After alignment of the analysis with the phase 2b data it borrowed from, model-estimated treatment success was 70.6% on RBX2660 versus 57.5% on placebo (estimated treatment effect 13.1%; posterior probability of superiority 0.991); the original model gave 70.4% versus 58.1%. More than 90% of participants successful at 8 weeks had a sustained response through 6 months in both groups. Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent on RBX2660, driven mostly by mild gastrointestinal events; no serious treatment-related side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline rates are model estimates from a Bayesian analysis that integrates the earlier phase 2b trial — not raw proportions — and the placebo success rate (57.5%) is high, reflecting post-antibiotic natural history; a single enema of a donor-derived product also carries manufacturing and screening dependencies that capsules or defined consortia may not share.
cards.source: Khanna S et al. cards.headline: PUNCH CD2 (Dubberke 2023): success 56.8% and 55.6% on RBX2660 regimens vs 43.2% placebo — both p=0.2; the trial missed its primary endpoint
cards.summary: PUNCH CD2 (Dubberke 2023): success 56.8% and 55.6% on RBX2660 regimens vs 43.2% placebo — both p=0.2; the trial missed its primary endpoint
cards.people: Adults with at least three episodes of C. difficile infection and at least two rounds of standard antibiotics (or at least two severe episodes with hospitalisation), randomised 1:1:1 to two doses of RBX2660, two doses of placebo, or one dose of each, given 7 ± 2 days apart; primary endpoint was absence of recurrence to 8 weeks after the second dose, with safety followed to 24 months.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat treatment success at 8 weeks: 56.8% (25/45) with one RBX2660 dose plus one placebo dose, 55.6% (25/45) with two RBX2660 doses, and 43.2% (19/44) with two placebo doses (both comparisons p=0.2 versus placebo) — the trial did not meet its predefined primary endpoint. In the per-protocol population, success was 87.5% (21/24) for the mixed regimen versus 58.1% (18/31) on placebo (p=0.017) and 75.0% (21/28) for two RBX2660 doses (p=0.17). Safety was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The per-protocol separation comes from a small, post-randomisation subset and cannot rescue the intention-to-treat miss; the mixed one-dose regimen performing as well as two doses is also what justified the single-dose phase 3 design, so this trial is best read as dose-finding with a favourable trend.
cards.source: Dubberke ER et al. shelves.title: Split-dose bowel preparation: satisfactory cleansing in roughly two-and-a-half times the odds of day-before regimens across 47 trials (OR 2.51) — and patients prefer repeating it
shelves.question: For colonoscopy, does splitting the bowel-preparation dose between the evening before and the morning of the procedure clean the colon better than taking the whole preparation the day before?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cathartics/administration & dosage · Citrates/administration & dosage · Colon/drug effects · Colonoscopy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Laxatives/administration & dosage · Male · Organometallic Compounds/administration & dosage · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Phosphates/administration & dosage · Picolines/administration & dosage · Therapeutic Irrigation/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials, seven years of literature apart, agree that splitting the dose cleans better. The larger analysis (Martel M et al., PMID: 25863216) pooled 47 trials with 13,487 patients: split-dose preparations beat day-before preparations for colon cleansing (odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.86–3.39), including against day-before polyethylene glycol specifically (OR 2.60, 1.46–4.63), and more patients were willing to repeat a split regimen (OR 1.90, 1.05–3.46). The earlier polyethylene-glycol-only analysis (Kilgore TW et al., PMID: 21628016) found the same direction with a larger estimate — satisfactory preparations OR 3.70 (2.79–4.91) across five trials (N=1,232) — plus fewer discontinuations (OR 0.53) and less nausea (OR 0.55). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): split dosing is the better default schedule for colonoscopy preparation; the remaining questions are about product and volume, not about whether to split.

cards.headline: Martel 2015: 47 trials, 13,487 patients — cleansing OR 2.51 (1.86–3.39) for split-dose vs day-before; willingness to repeat OR 1.90
cards.summary: Martel 2015: 47 trials, 13,487 patients — cleansing OR 2.51 (1.86–3.39) for split-dose vs day-before; willingness to repeat OR 1.90
cards.people: 47 randomised trials (n=13,487) comparing split-dose regimens (polyethylene glycol, sodium phosphate, picosulfate or oral sulfate preparations) with day-before regimens before colonoscopy in outpatients; studies of children, inpatients and inflammatory bowel disease were excluded; primary outcome was efficacy of bowel cleansing.
cards.result: Split-dose preparations provided significantly better colon cleansing than day-before preparations (odds ratio 2.51; 95% CI 1.86–3.39), and than day-before polyethylene glycol (OR 2.60; 1.46–4.63), sodium phosphate (OR 9.34; 2.12–41.11) and picosulfate (OR 3.54; 1.95–6.45) separately. Split-dose polyethylene glycol of 3 L or more beat lower-volume split regimens in intention-to-treat analysis (OR 1.89; 1.01–3.46). Willingness to repeat was higher for split-dose versus day-before (OR 1.90; 1.05–3.46) and for low-volume versus high-volume split preparations (OR 4.95; 2.21–11.10). Other secondary outcomes did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Cleansing scales and outcome definitions varied across the 47 trials, and odds ratios on 'adequate cleansing' overstate the absolute gain when baseline adequacy is already high; the sodium-phosphate contrast (OR 9.34) has a very wide interval and that product class has its own safety history outside this record.
cards.source: Martel M et al. Split-Dose Preparations Are Superior to Day-Before Bowel Cleansing Regimens: A Meta-analysis. Gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 25863216. cards.headline: Kilgore 2011: split-dose polyethylene glycol — satisfactory preparations OR 3.70 (2.79–4.91), discontinuations OR 0.53, nausea OR 0.55
cards.summary: Kilgore 2011: split-dose polyethylene glycol — satisfactory preparations OR 3.70 (2.79–4.91), discontinuations OR 0.53, nausea OR 0.55
cards.people: Five randomised trials (N=1,232) in adults comparing split-dose with full-dose polyethylene glycol bowel preparation before colonoscopy (literature searched to January 2011).
cards.result: Split-dose polyethylene glycol significantly increased satisfactory bowel preparations (OR 3.70; 95% CI 2.79–4.91; P<.01) and willingness to repeat the same preparation (OR 1.76; 1.06–2.91; P=.03), and decreased preparation discontinuations (OR 0.53; 0.28–0.98; P=.04) and nausea (OR 0.55; 0.38–0.79; P<.01) compared with full-dose preparation.
cards.watchOut: Only five trials and a 2011 search date — this is the smaller, earlier estimate, and its larger odds ratio likely reflects lower baseline cleansing rates in older full-dose regimens; its value here is directional confirmation plus the tolerability outcomes (nausea, discontinuation) that the later analysis did not separate as cleanly.
cards.source: Kilgore TW et al. Bowel preparation with split-dose polyethylene glycol before colonoscopy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2011. PMID: 21628016. cards.headline: Synthesis: split the dose — the most reproducible scheduling result in bowel preparation
cards.summary: Synthesis: split the dose — the most reproducible scheduling result in bowel preparation
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised colonoscopy-preparation trials: 47 trials / 13,487 patients across all products (Martel 2015) and 5 trials / 1,232 patients for polyethylene glycol (Kilgore 2011).
cards.result: Better cleansing with split dosing: OR 2.51 (1.86–3.39) overall and OR 3.70 (2.79–4.91) for polyethylene glycol; willingness to repeat higher (OR 1.76–1.90); nausea and discontinuations lower with split polyethylene glycol (OR 0.55 and 0.53). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Cleansing quality is an intermediate outcome — neither analysis pools adenoma detection or interval cancer by schedule — and very early-morning second doses carry sleep and travel burdens that trials measure only as 'willingness to repeat'. shelves.title: Propofol versus midazolam-based sedation for colonoscopy: satisfaction higher by half a standard deviation and recovery about 3 minutes shorter — with no difference in cardiorespiratory events across 9 trials
shelves.question: For colonoscopy sedation, does propofol give better patient satisfaction, recovery and safety than midazolam with or without a short-acting opioid?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid · Colonoscopy · Procedural Sedation · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Midazolam/therapeutic use · Patient Satisfaction · Personal Satisfaction · Propofol/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — propofol's advantages are real but marginal, and its safety record in these trials is a tie. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (Dossa F et al., PMID: 31926966; 1,427 patients) found no significant differences in hypotension, hypoxia or bradycardia between propofol and midazolam (with or without opioids); patient satisfaction favoured propofol (standardised mean difference 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.79, with considerable heterogeneity), and recovery was shorter (SMD 0.41, 0.08–0.74) — a median difference of just 3 minutes 6 seconds. In the inflammatory bowel disease trial of nurse-administered propofol sedation (Steenholdt C et al., PMID: 33371995), satisfaction scores were 60.1 on propofol versus 51.2 on midazolam–fentanyl (P<.001), with less pain and more willingness to repeat colonoscopy, and no safety signals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patients prefer propofol and wake marginally faster; nothing here shows it to be safer or more dangerous than midazolam-based sedation in trial populations.

cards.headline: Dossa 2020: 9 trials, 1,427 patients — satisfaction SMD 0.54 (0.30–0.79) for propofol; recovery SMD 0.41; hypotension, hypoxia and bradycardia not significantly different
cards.summary: Dossa 2020: 9 trials, 1,427 patients — satisfaction SMD 0.54 (0.30–0.79) for propofol; recovery SMD 0.41; hypotension, hypoxia and bradycardia not significantly different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Dossa 2020)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials (1,427 patients) of propofol versus midazolam with or without short-acting opioids for colonoscopy sedation (literature searched to July 2018); cardiorespiratory outcomes were pooled as odds ratios and satisfaction and efficiency outcomes as standardised mean differences.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in cardiorespiratory outcomes (hypotension, hypoxia, bradycardia) between groups. Patient satisfaction was high in both groups, and most patients in both would accept the same regimen again; pooled satisfaction was greater with propofol (SMD 0.54; 95% CI 0.30–0.79), with considerable heterogeneity. Procedure time was similar (SMD 0.15; 0.04–0.27); recovery time was shorter with propofol (SMD 0.41; 0.08–0.74), a median difference of 3 minutes 6 seconds. The authors characterise propofol's benefits as marginal: small improvements in satisfaction and recovery time.
cards.watchOut: Satisfaction pooling carries considerable heterogeneity and unblinded patients can usually tell deep from moderate sedation, which inflates preference outcomes; trial populations exclude the highest-risk patients in whom propofol's safety questions actually live, so 'no difference in events' applies to studied populations only.
cards.source: Dossa F et al. cards.headline: Steenholdt 2022: satisfaction 60.1 vs 51.2 (of 65) for nurse-administered propofol versus midazolam–fentanyl in IBD colonoscopy (P<.001); no safety signals
cards.summary: Steenholdt 2022: satisfaction 60.1 vs 51.2 (of 65) for nurse-administered propofol versus midazolam–fentanyl in IBD colonoscopy (P<.001); no safety signals
cards.people: 130 patients with ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or suspected inflammatory bowel disease undergoing colonoscopy, randomised to deep sedation with nurse-administered propofol (n=63) or moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl (n=67); primary endpoint was a 13-item satisfaction score (13–65 points) at discharge; 88% had had a previous colonoscopy.
cards.result: Satisfaction was significantly higher with propofol (mean 60.1, SD 3.4) than with midazolam–fentanyl (51.2, SD 8.4; P<.001), driven by less pain, more amnesia, sedation more to patients' liking, and a better experience than previous sedations. Propofol patients more often preferred the same sedation for a future colonoscopy and would accept more frequent colonoscopies. Assistance from another colonoscopist and procedure disruption due to pain were significantly more frequent in the moderate-sedation group. There were no safety signals with nurse-administered propofol sedation.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial in IBD surveillance patients comparing deep propofol sedation with moderate sedation — depth and drug are confounded, so it shows patients prefer being deeply asleep, not that propofol per se beats an equally deep alternative; satisfaction at discharge is also measured before any delayed effects could appear.

shelves.title: Flavonoid tablets (MPFF) for acute haemorrhoid bleeding: bleeding stopped by day 3 in 80% versus 38% on placebo in one trial — and the Cochrane class review found less bleeding (OR 0.12) across the phlebotonics
shelves.question: In adults with an acute episode of internal haemorrhoids, does micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF) stop bleeding and settle symptoms faster than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Ambulatory Care · Double-Blind Method · Female · Flavonoids/therapeutic use · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Hemorrhoids/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent short-term symptom control from two small double-blind trials and a supportive class review, all with wide error bars. In the largest single trial (Misra MC et al., PMID: 10931020), bleeding from acute internal haemorrhoids had stopped by day 3 in 40 of 50 patients (80%) on micronised purified flavonoid fraction versus 19 of 50 (38%) on placebo (P<0.01), bleeding duration was 2.1 days shorter (95% CI 1.2–2.9), and continued treatment prevented relapse in 30 of 47 versus 12 of 30 patients (P<0.05). The second trial (Jiang ZM et al., PMID: 16846547) found significantly better evolution of pain, oedema and bleeding over 7 days on MPFF (bleeding p=0.021 at day 4 and p=0.047 at day 7), with tolerability similar to placebo. The Cochrane review of the wider phlebotonic class (Perera N et al., PMID: 22895941) found significantly less bleeding versus control (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.04–0.37) and better overall symptom improvement across 20 controlled studies (2,344 participants), while noting methodological limitations. The publications name the product only as micronised purified flavonoid fraction; neither trial record names a manufacturer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MPFF probably shortens an acute bleeding episode by a couple of days — useful for deferring a procedure, not a substitute for one.

cards.headline: Misra 2000: bleeding ceased by day 3 in 80% (40/50) on MPFF vs 38% (19/50) on placebo (P<0.01); bleeding duration 2.1 days shorter; relapse prevented in 30/47 vs 12/30
cards.summary: Misra 2000: bleeding ceased by day 3 in 80% (40/50) on MPFF vs 38% (19/50) on placebo (P<0.01); bleeding duration 2.1 days shorter; relapse prevented in 30/47 vs 12/30
cards.people: 100 outpatients with acute bleeding (under 3 days' duration) from internal haemorrhoids, randomised to micronised purified flavonoid fraction or placebo for 90 days; primary endpoint was cessation of bleeding on day 3. The record names the product only as micronised purified flavonoid fraction and names no manufacturer.
cards.result: Acute bleeding ceased by day 3 in 40 of 50 patients (80%) on MPFF versus 19 of 50 (38%) on placebo (P<0.01). Mean duration of bleeding was 2.1 days shorter on MPFF (95% CI 1.2–2.9; P<0.01). Among patients whose bleeding had stopped, continued treatment prevented relapse in 30 of 47 on MPFF versus 12 of 30 on placebo (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, 100-patient trial from 2000 with a day-3 endpoint in self-limiting disease — placebo bleeding also stopped in over a third by day 3 — and the relapse comparison is conditioned on initial cessation, a post-randomisation subset; no comparison against banding or other office procedures was attempted.
