cards.headline: Jiang 2006: pain, oedema and bleeding all evolved significantly better on MPFF over 7 days (bleeding p=0.021 at day 4, p=0.047 at day 7); tolerability matched placebo
cards.summary: Jiang 2006: pain, oedema and bleeding all evolved significantly better on MPFF over 7 days (bleeding p=0.021 at day 4, p=0.047 at day 7); tolerability matched placebo
cards.people: 90 patients (49 MPFF, 41 placebo; mean age 43.2 years) with an acute haemorrhoidal episode of under 48 hours at two hospital centres in Beijing, treated with MPFF (six tablets daily for 4 days, then four daily for 3 days) or placebo, with blinded symptom and sign grading (4-point scales) at days 0, 4 and 7. The record names the product only as micronised purified flavonoid fraction and names no manufacturer.
cards.result: Over 7 days there was a significant difference favouring MPFF in the evolution of pain and oedema (p≤0.001 at day 7) and bleeding (p=0.021 at day 4; p=0.047 at day 7). Global efficacy ratings by patients (p=0.007) and investigators (p=0.006) also favoured MPFF. No patient stopped treatment for adverse events; one MPFF patient reported gastrointestinal discomfort, and blood pressure, heart rate and laboratory values were unchanged in both groups. Baseline oedema was, however, significantly more frequent and severe in the MPFF group (p=0.024).
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are graded severity scores rather than hard cessation counts, the baseline oedema imbalance favours regression to the mean in the MPFF arm, and 7 days in a first acute episode cannot speak to recurrent or prolapsing disease.
cards.source: Jiang ZM et al. The impact of micronized purified flavonoid fraction on the treatment of acute haemorrhoidal episodes. Current Medical Research and Opinion. 2006. PMID: 16846547. cards.headline: Perera 2012 (Cochrane): phlebotonics beat control on bleeding (OR 0.12, 0.04–0.37) and overall symptoms across 20 controlled studies (2,344 participants) — methods limited
cards.summary: Perera 2012 (Cochrane): phlebotonics beat control on bleeding (OR 0.12, 0.04–0.37) and overall symptoms across 20 controlled studies (2,344 participants) — methods limited
cards.people: 24 randomised studies of phlebotonics (plant flavonoids including MPFF-type preparations, and synthetic compounds such as calcium dobesilate) for haemorrhoidal disease, of which 20 studies (2,344 participants) compared a phlebotonic with a control intervention; the class is heterogeneous and the review pools it as a class.
cards.result: Phlebotonics showed statistically significant benefit versus control for pruritus (OR 0.23; 95% CI 0.07–0.79), bleeding (OR 0.12; 0.04–0.37), bleeding after haemorrhoidectomy (OR 0.18; 0.06–0.58), discharge and leakage (OR 0.12; 0.04–0.42) and overall symptom improvement (OR 15.99; 5.97–42.84), but not for pain (OR 0.11; 0.01–1.11; P=0.06). The reviewers conclude there is potential benefit with few safety concerns, alongside methodological limitations requiring more robust trials.
cards.watchOut: A class-level pool across different compounds, doses and comparators with very wide intervals (the symptom-improvement OR of 15.99 is implausibly large and signals small-study effects); it corroborates direction for MPFF but cannot certify any single product's effect size.
cards.source: Perera N et al. Phlebotonics for haemorrhoids. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22895941. cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of MPFF in acute internal haemorrhoids (100 and 90 patients; Misra 2000, Jiang 2006) and a Cochrane review of 24 phlebotonic trials (Perera 2012).
cards.result: Bleeding cessation by day 3: 80% versus 38% (Misra). Symptom evolution significantly favouring MPFF at days 4–7 (Jiang). Class-level bleeding OR 0.12 (0.04–0.37) versus control (Perera). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

Tier C is not set: two randomised trials plus a Cochrane review carry the claim, though all are small or class-level.

shelves.title: Diltiazem cream versus GTN ointment for chronic anal fissure: healing tied (24 of 31 vs 25 of 29) but headaches halved — side effects in 13 of 31 versus 21 of 29 patients
shelves.question: In adults with chronic anal fissure, is topical diltiazem as effective as glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment for healing — and does it cause fewer headaches and other side effects?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diltiazem/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fissure in Ano/drug therapy · Follow-Up Studies · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroglycerin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Ointments · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for tolerability, not healing: the one head-to-head trial found equal healing and clearly fewer headaches on diltiazem. In that double-blind trial (Kocher HM et al., PMID: 11952579), healing or improvement was achieved by 24 of 31 patients on 2% diltiazem cream versus 25 of 29 on 0.2% GTN ointment (no significant difference), while side effects occurred in 13 of 31 versus 21 of 29 (relative risk 1.84 for GTN, 95% CI 1.11–3.04; P=0.01) and headaches in 8 of 31 versus 17 of 29 (RR 2.06, 1.18–3.59; P=0.01). The Cochrane review of non-surgical fissure therapy (Nelson RL et al., PMID: 22336789) places both creams in context: GTN healed only marginally better than placebo (48.9% vs 35.5%), botulinum toxin and calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, nifedipine) were equivalent to GTN with fewer adverse events, late recurrence approached 50% of initial cures, and no medical therapy came close to surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): diltiazem is the reasonable first cream — same modest healing as GTN, about half the headaches — with surgery still the definitive option behind both.

cards.headline: Kocher 2002: healing 24/31 (diltiazem) vs 25/29 (GTN), no significant difference; side effects 13/31 vs 21/29 (RR 1.84, P=0.01); headaches 8/31 vs 17/29 (RR 2.06, P=0.01)
cards.summary: Kocher 2002: healing 24/31 (diltiazem) vs 25/29 (GTN), no significant difference; side effects 13/31 vs 21/29 (RR 1.84, P=0.01); headaches 8/31 vs 17/29 (RR 2.06, P=0.01)
cards.people: Patients with chronic anal fissure at two centres, randomised to 2% diltiazem cream or 0.2% glyceryl trinitrate ointment applied perianally twice daily for 6–8 weeks; the trial was powered on side-effect incidence (at least 26 patients per group required); primary endpoint was side effects, with healing and symptomatic improvement as secondary outcomes. Twelve patients violated the protocol, withdrew or were lost to follow-up.
cards.result: Side effects: 21 of 29 patients on GTN versus 13 of 31 on diltiazem (relative risk 1.84; 95% CI 1.11–3.04; P=0.01). Headaches: 17 of 29 versus 8 of 31 (RR 2.06; 1.18–3.59; P=0.01). Healing and symptomatic improvement did not differ significantly: 25 of 29 on GTN versus 24 of 31 on diltiazem. The authors suggest diltiazem may be the preferred first-line treatment for chronic anal fissure.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient analysed sample powered for side effects, not for healing equivalence — the healing comparison cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction, and 12 protocol violations or losses in a trial this size leave the tolerability gap as the only firm finding. Tier C is set: a single head-to-head trial.
cards.source: Kocher HM et al. Randomized clinical trial assessing the side-effects of glyceryl trinitrate and diltiazem hydrochloride in the treatment of chronic anal fissure. British Journal of Surgery. 2002. PMID: 11952579. cards.headline: Nelson 2012 (Cochrane, 75 trials, 5,031 participants): GTN healed 48.9% vs 35.5% on placebo; calcium-channel blockers equal to GTN with fewer adverse events; recurrence ~50%; nothing medical approached surgery
cards.summary: Nelson 2012 (Cochrane, 75 trials, 5,031 participants): GTN healed 48.9% vs 35.5% on placebo; calcium-channel blockers equal to GTN with fewer adverse events; recurrence ~50%; nothing medical approached surgery
cards.people: 75 randomised trials (5,031 participants) of 49 comparisons among 17 non-surgical treatments for anal fissure (including GTN, botulinum toxin, diltiazem and nifedipine, and surgical sphincterotomy), in acute and chronic fissure and in children; outcomes were non-healing (persistence or recurrence) and adverse events.
cards.result: GTN was marginally but significantly better than placebo at healing fissure (48.9% vs 35.5%, p<0.0009), but late recurrence was common — in the range of 50% of those initially cured. Botulinum toxin and calcium-channel blockers were equivalent to GTN in efficacy with fewer adverse events. No medical therapy came close to the efficacy of surgical sphincterotomy, and none of the medical therapies carried surgery's incontinence risk.
cards.watchOut: Most component trials are small and old, healing definitions vary, and the calcium-channel-blocker verdict pools diltiazem with nifedipine studies; the review's durable message is about the whole class's ceiling (roughly half heal, half of those recur) rather than precise per-cream rates.
cards.source: Nelson RL et al. Non surgical therapy for anal fissure. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22336789. shelves.title: Rifaximin shortens travellers' diarrhoea by about a day: time to last unformed stool 32–33 hours versus 60–66 hours on placebo in two double-blind trials — for non-invasive pathogens
shelves.question: In travellers with travellers' diarrhoea, does rifaximin shorten illness compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Infective Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bacterial Infections/complications/drug therapy · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy/microbiology/parasitology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Middle Aged · Rifamycins/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Rifaximin · Travel · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree. Taylor 2006 (PMID: 16760520, n=399) found a median time to last unformed stool of 32.0 hours on rifaximin 200 mg three times daily versus 65.5 hours on placebo (P=0.001), essentially matching ciprofloxacin (28.8 hours). Steffen 2003 (PMID: 12809830, n=380) found 32.5 and 32.9 hours on rifaximin 600 and 1200 mg/day versus 60.0 hours on placebo (p=0.0001). The catch is the pathogen: rifaximin was less effective than ciprofloxacin against invasive intestinal bacterial pathogens, so the benefit is for the non-invasive, non-bloody illness that makes up most travellers' diarrhoea. No relevant side effects were reported in Steffen; Taylor found rifaximin safe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): about a day less illness for non-invasive travellers' diarrhoea.

cards.headline: Taylor 2006: time to last unformed stool 32.0 hours on rifaximin versus 65.5 hours on placebo (P=0.001) — ciprofloxacin 28.8 hours
cards.summary: Taylor 2006: time to last unformed stool 32.0 hours on rifaximin versus 65.5 hours on placebo (P=0.001) — ciprofloxacin 28.8 hours
cards.people: 399 adult travellers consulting travel clinics in Mexico, Guatemala and India with travellers' diarrhoea, randomised to rifaximin 200 mg three times daily, ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily (with a placebo third dose), or placebo three times daily, each for 3 days, with stool diaries for 5 days and pre- and post-treatment stool microbiology.
cards.result: Median time to last unformed stool was 32.0 hours on rifaximin versus 65.5 hours on placebo (P=0.001; risk ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.2, as printed for the primary endpoint) and 28.8 hours on ciprofloxacin (P=0.0003 versus placebo; P=0.35 versus rifaximin). Rifaximin was less effective than ciprofloxacin for invasive intestinal bacterial pathogens. The authors concluded oral rifaximin is a safe and effective treatment for travellers' diarrhoea caused by noninvasive pathogens.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is time to last unformed stool from a patient diary — a real benefit travellers feel, but a symptom-duration measure, not prevention of complications. The invasive-pathogen weakness matters where dysentery (bloody stool, fever) is commoner than in these clinic populations.

randomised double-blind multicentre trial (taylor 2006) 399 adult travellers consulting travel clinics in mexico, guatemala and india with travellers' diarrhoea, randomised to rifaximin 200 mg three times daily, ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily (with a placebo third dose), or placebo three times daily, each for 3 days, with stool diaries for 5 days and pre- and post-treatment stool microbiology. median time to last unformed stool was 32.0 hours on rifaximin versus 65.5 hours on placebo (p=0.001; risk ratio 1.6, 95% ci 1.2 to 2.2, as printed for the primary endpoint) and 28.8 hours on ciprofloxacin (p=0.0003 versus placebo; p=0.35 versus rifaximin). rifaximin was less effective than ciprofloxacin for invasive intestinal bacterial pathogens. the authors concluded oral rifaximin is a safe and effective treatment for travellers' diarrhoea caused by noninvasive pathogens. the endpoint is time to last unformed stool from a patient diary — a real benefit travellers feel, but a symptom-duration measure, not prevention of complications. the invasive-pathogen weakness matters where dysentery (bloody stool, fever) is commoner than in these clinic populations. taylor dn et al. a randomized, double-blind, multicenter study of rifaximin compared with placebo and with ciprofloxacin in the treatment of travelers' diarrhea. the american journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 2006. pmid: 16760520. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · anti-infective agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · bacterial infections/complications/drug therapy · ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · diarrhea/drug therapy/microbiology/parasitology · double-blind method · female · gastrointestinal agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · humans · male · microbial sensitivity tests · middle aged · rifamycins/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · rifaximin · travel · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Steffen 2003: time to last unformed stool 32.5 and 32.9 hours on rifaximin 600 and 1200 mg/day versus 60.0 hours on placebo (p=0.0001)
cards.summary: Steffen 2003: time to last unformed stool 32.5 and 32.9 hours on rifaximin 600 and 1200 mg/day versus 60.0 hours on placebo (p=0.0001)
cards.people: 380 adult volunteers with acute travellers' diarrhoea recruited in Antigua (Guatemala), Guadalajara and Morelia (Mexico) and the Kenyan coast, randomised 1:1:1 to rifaximin 600 mg/day, rifaximin 1200 mg/day or placebo, three times daily for 3 days with 5 days of follow-up diary cards and pre- and post-treatment stool, blood and urine sampling.
cards.result: Median time to the last unformed stool was 32.5 hours on rifaximin 600 mg/day and 32.9 hours on 1200 mg/day, compared with 60.0 hours on placebo (p=0.0001). Secondary clinical outcome measures also favoured rifaximin, and no relevant side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: Two doses, one answer: doubling the dose bought nothing (32.5 versus 32.9 hours), so this trial supports the lower dose. As in Taylor, the population is ordinary watery travellers' diarrhoea — the result should not be extended to dysentery.
cards.source: Steffen R et al. Therapy of travelers' diarrhea with rifaximin on various continents. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 12809830. shelves.title: Probiotics in cirrhosis: fewer encephalopathy hospitalisations than placebo in the blinded VSL#3 trial, no better than lactulose in the pooled record, and no mortality benefit
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, do probiotics improve recovery, recurrence or hospitalisation compared with placebo or lactulose?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/blood · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy/diet therapy/microbiology/mortality · Hospital Mortality · Hospitalization · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis/diet therapy/microbiology/mortality · Male · Microbiota · Middle Aged · Probiotics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Severity of Illness Index · Tertiary Care Centers · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — probiotics beat placebo or no treatment on the softer outcomes and match lactulose, but no trial shows a mortality benefit. In the one double-blind trial, the named preparation VSL#3 (CD Pharma India Private Limited) did not significantly cut breakthrough encephalopathy (34.8% versus 51.6%; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.38–1.11; P=.12) yet did cut hospitalisation for encephalopathy (19.7% versus 42.2%; HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.87) and for any cirrhosis complication (24.2% versus 45.3%; HR 0.52) over 6 months (Dhiman RK et al., PMID: 25450083). An open-label primary-prophylaxis trial found overt encephalopathy in 7 of 86 on probiotics versus 14 of 74 controls (Lunia MK et al., PMID: 24246768). Pooling 14 randomised trials (1,152 patients), probiotics versus no treatment/placebo improved minimal encephalopathy (OR 3.91), progression to overt encephalopathy (OR 0.40) and hospitalisation (OR 0.53), but versus lactulose every one of those comparisons was null, and mortality was unchanged against either comparator (Saab S et al., PMID: 26561214). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) against placebo for progression and hospitalisation; no demonstrated advantage over lactulose and no mortality benefit.

cards.headline: Dhiman 2014 (VSL#3): breakthrough encephalopathy 34.8% versus 51.6% (HR 0.65; P=.12, not significant) — but hospitalisation for encephalopathy 19.7% versus 42.2% (HR 0.45; P=.02)
cards.summary: Dhiman 2014 (VSL#3): breakthrough encephalopathy 34.8% versus 51.6% (HR 0.65; P=.12, not significant) — but hospitalisation for encephalopathy 19.7% versus 42.2% (HR 0.45; P=.02)
cards.people: 130 patients with cirrhosis at a tertiary hospital in India who had recovered from an episode of hepatic encephalopathy within the previous month, randomised to the probiotic preparation VSL#3 (9 × 10(11) bacteria; CD Pharma India Private Limited, New Delhi, India — the exact tested product and company as published) (n=66) or placebo (n=64) daily for 6 months.
cards.result: Breakthrough encephalopathy occurred in 34.8% on VSL#3 versus 51.6% on placebo (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.38–1.11; P=.12) — a trend, not a significant result on the primary outcome. Hospitalisation for encephalopathy: 19.7% versus 42.2% (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.87; P=.02). Hospitalisation for complications of cirrhosis: 24.2% versus 45.3% (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.28–0.95; P=.034). Child-Turcotte-Pugh and MELD scores improved significantly in the probiotic group but not on placebo. No adverse events were related to VSL#3.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome missed significance; the wins are secondary hospitalisation outcomes in a single-centre trial of 130 patients. The tested product is a specific high-dose multi-strain preparation — the result cannot be read across to shop-bought probiotics of different strains and doses.
cards.source: Dhiman RK et al. Probiotic VSL#3 reduces liver disease severity and hospitalization in patients with cirrhosis: a randomized, controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 25450083. Registry ID: NCT01110447. cards.headline: Lunia 2014: primary prophylaxis — overt encephalopathy in 7 of 86 on probiotics versus 14 of 74 controls over about 39 weeks
cards.summary: Lunia 2014: primary prophylaxis — overt encephalopathy in 7 of 86 on probiotics versus 14 of 74 controls over about 39 weeks
cards.people: 160 patients with cirrhosis without overt encephalopathy (mean age 48.6 years; 25 Child-Turcotte-Pugh class A, 51 class B, 84 class C; 75 with minimal encephalopathy) at a tertiary centre in New Delhi, randomised to probiotics 1 × 10(8) colony-forming units three times daily (n=86) or no test article (n=74). The record does not name the probiotic product or its maker.
cards.result: After mean follow-up of 38.6 weeks (probiotics) and 40.3 weeks (controls), 7 probiotic patients and 14 controls developed overt encephalopathy (P<.05; hazard ratio for controls versus probiotic group 2.1, 95% CI 1.31–6.53). Six probiotic patients and 7 controls died (P=.81). Three months of probiotics significantly reduced arterial ammonia, small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and orocaecal transit time, and improved psychometric and critical-flicker-fusion measures versus baseline.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a no-treatment control, so expectation and co-intervention effects are uncontrolled; the preparation is unnamed in the record, so the trial cannot be reproduced or its product bought on this evidence. Deaths were equal.
cards.source: Lunia MK et al. Probiotics prevent hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis: a randomized controlled trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2014. PMID: 24246768. Registry ID: CTRI/2012/07/002807 (in the abstract text). cards.headline: Saab 2016 meta-analysis (14 trials, 1,152 patients): probiotics beat no treatment on minimal-encephalopathy improvement (OR 3.91), progression (OR 0.40) and hospitalisation (OR 0.53) — and matched lactulose on all three; mortality unchanged
cards.summary: Saab 2016 meta-analysis (14 trials, 1,152 patients): probiotics beat no treatment on minimal-encephalopathy improvement (OR 3.91), progression (OR 0.40) and hospitalisation (OR 0.53) — and matched lactulose on all three; mortality unchanged
cards.people: 14 randomised studies totalling 1,152 patients with cirrhosis and minimal or overt hepatic encephalopathy, comparing probiotics with no treatment/placebo and with lactulose.
cards.result: Versus no treatment/placebo: improvement in minimal encephalopathy OR 3.91 (95% CI 2.25–6.80), progression to overt encephalopathy OR 0.40 (0.26–0.60), hospitalisation OR 0.53 (0.33–0.86). Versus lactulose: minimal-encephalopathy improvement OR 0.81 (0.52–1.27), hospitalisation OR 1.02 (0.52–1.99), progression OR 1.24 (0.73–2.10) — all null. Mortality: OR 1.07 versus lactulose and OR 0.69 (0.42–1.14) versus no treatment/placebo — no significant difference either way.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, short and strain-heterogeneous, and the placebo comparisons rest heavily on open-label no-treatment controls; the lactulose comparisons — the clinically relevant ones, since lactulose is standard — show no added value.
cards.source: Saab S et al. Probiotics are helpful in hepatic encephalopathy: a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Liver International. 2016. PMID: 26561214. cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but second-tier benefit — better than doing nothing, not better than lactulose, and silent on survival

shelves.title: Antioxidants for chronic pancreatitis pain: one positive Indian trial in young, mostly idiopathic disease — the larger blinded UK trial in mostly alcoholic disease found nothing
shelves.question: In patients with chronic pancreatitis and pain, do pancreatic enzyme supplements or antioxidants reduce pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antioxidants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · England · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/diagnosis/etiology/prevention & control · Pain Measurement · Pancreatitis, Alcoholic/blood/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Pancreatitis, Chronic/blood/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two blinded trials point in opposite directions, in different populations. In India, antioxidant supplementation cut painful days per month by 7.4 versus 3.2 on placebo (P<.001) and left 32% pain-free versus 13% over 6 months, in patients averaging 30 years old of whom 92 of 127 had idiopathic disease (Bhardwaj P et al., PMID: 18952082). In the UK ANTICIPATE trial, the named preparation Antox version 1.2 (Pharma Nord, Morpeth, UK) moved clinic pain scores by −2.33 points versus −1.97 on placebo (difference −0.36, 95% CI −1.44 to 0.72; P=.509), with diary pain, quality of life, opiate use and admissions all similar, in predominantly alcoholic chronic pancreatitis (Siriwardena AK et al., PMID: 22683257). Blood antioxidant levels rose in both trials, so the split is not a delivery failure. The enzyme half of this question is not separately carded here: pancreatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency — fat absorption, nutrition and pain — is homed at Shelf #3591. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) in young, non-alcoholic disease on the Indian trial; the treatment made no difference in the larger, older, mostly alcoholic UK population.

cards.headline: Bhardwaj 2009: painful days per month fell by 7.4 on antioxidants versus 3.2 on placebo (P<.001); pain-free at 6 months in 32% versus 13%
cards.summary: Bhardwaj 2009: painful days per month fell by 7.4 on antioxidants versus 3.2 on placebo (P<.001); pain-free at 6 months in 32% versus 13%
cards.people: 127 consecutive patients with chronic pancreatitis at a New Delhi centre (mean age 30.5 years; 86 men; 35 alcoholic, 92 idiopathic), randomised to antioxidant supplementation (n=71) or placebo (n=56) for 6 months. The record describes the intervention as antioxidant supplementation and does not name a commercial product or maker.
cards.result: Reduction in painful days per month: 7.4 ± 6.8 on antioxidants versus 3.2 ± 4 on placebo (P<.001; 95% CI for the difference 2.07–6.23). Reduction in analgesic tablets per month: 10.5 ± 11.8 versus 4.4 ± 5.8 (P=.001). Pain-free at 6 months: 32% versus 13% (P=.009). Oxidative-stress markers (TBARS) fell and antioxidant status (FRAP) rose significantly more on antioxidants.
cards.watchOut: A young, predominantly idiopathic (non-alcoholic) population unlike most Western chronic pancreatitis clinics; a single centre; and the preparation is unnamed in the record, so the exact formulation cannot be verified or reproduced from this publication.
cards.source: Bhardwaj P et al. A randomized controlled trial of antioxidant supplementation for pain relief in patients with chronic pancreatitis. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 18952082. cards.headline: Siriwardena 2012 (ANTICIPATE): pain fell equally on Antox and placebo (clinic scores −2.33 versus −1.97; difference −0.36, P=.509) — quality of life, opiates and admissions also similar
cards.summary: Siriwardena 2012 (ANTICIPATE): pain fell equally on Antox and placebo (clinic scores −2.33 versus −1.97; difference −0.36, P=.509) — quality of life, opiates and admissions also similar
cards.people: 70 patients with chronic pancreatitis of predominantly alcoholic origin in Manchester, UK, randomised to antioxidant therapy (Antox version 1.2, Pharma Nord, Morpeth, UK — the exact tested product and company as published; 2 tablets three times daily) or matched placebo for 6 months after 1 month of baseline data.
cards.result: Baseline-adjusted clinic pain score at 6 months fell by 2.33 points on antioxidants and 1.97 on placebo (between-group difference −0.36, 95% CI −1.44 to 0.72; P=.509). Diary daily pain scores: 2.93 versus 3.05 (difference 0.11; P=.808). Quality-of-life measures, opiate use, hospital admissions and outpatient visits were similar between groups, although blood vitamin C and E, beta-carotene and selenium levels rose significantly on antioxidants.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than the Indian trial (70 versus 127 patients) but blinded with a named, reproducible preparation and a predominantly alcoholic population — the population in which the oxidative-stress rationale was most often invoked. A 6-month horizon cannot exclude slower effects.
cards.source: Siriwardena AK et al. Antioxidant therapy does not reduce pain in patients with chronic pancreatitis: the ANTICIPATE study. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22683257. shelves.title: Large-balloon dilation for big bile-duct stones: clearance matches sphincterotomy, but mechanical lithotripsy is needed far less often — about 16% versus 25%, and 30% versus 48% in the largest trial
shelves.question: In patients with large common bile duct stones, does endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation reduce the need for mechanical lithotripsy compared with sphincterotomy alone?
shelves.mesh: Chi-Square Distribution · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde · Choledocholithiasis/diagnosis/surgery · Dilatation · Endoscopy, Digestive System/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods · Humans · Odds Ratio · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Risk Factors · Sphincterotomy, Endoscopic/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the procedure, not for a disease outcome: large-balloon dilation clears large stones as reliably as sphincterotomy while sparing the lithotripter. Pooling five randomised trials (621 patients, stones ≥10 mm), complete clearance was 93.7% with dilation versus 92.5% with sphincterotomy, but mechanical lithotripsy was used in 15.5% versus 25.2% (P=.003), and in stones over 15 mm in 24.2% versus 40% (P=.001), with pancreatitis 4.0% versus 5.0% and overall adverse events 7.9% versus 10.7% (Jin PP et al., PMID: 24833886). The largest single trial (MARVELOUS, 171 patients) found single-session complete removal in 90.7% with dilation alone versus 78.8% with sphincterotomy (P=.04) and lithotripsy in 30.2% versus 48.2% (P=.02), with pancreatitis 4.7% versus 5.9% (Kogure H et al., PMID: 32299114). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): equal clearance, materially less lithotripsy, no safety penalty shown.

cards.headline: Jin 2014 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 621 patients): clearance 93.7% versus 92.5% — lithotripsy 15.5% versus 25.2% (P=.003); in stones >15 mm, 24.2% versus 40% (P=.001)
cards.summary: Jin 2014 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 621 patients): clearance 93.7% versus 92.5% — lithotripsy 15.5% versus 25.2% (P=.003); in stones >15 mm, 24.2% versus 40% (P=.001)
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials with 621 participants comparing endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation with endoscopic sphincterotomy for retrieval of common bile duct stones ≥10 mm.
cards.result: Complete stone removal: 93.7% (dilation) versus 92.5% (sphincterotomy), P=.54. Clearance in one session: 82.2% versus 77.7%, P=.17. Mechanical lithotripsy: 15.5% versus 25.2%, P=.003; in the subgroup with stones larger than 15 mm, 24.2% versus 40%, P=.001. Overall adverse events 7.9% versus 10.7% (P=.25); post-ERCP pancreatitis 4.0% versus 5.0% (P=.54); haemorrhage 1.7% versus 2.8%; perforation 0.3% versus 0.9%; cholangitis 1.3% versus 1.3%.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials with differing balloon diameters and stone sizes; the lithotripsy advantage is a process outcome — fewer crushing sessions — not a patient-outcome difference, and rare harms (perforation, severe pancreatitis) are too infrequent for 621 patients to settle.
cards.source: Jin PP et al. Endoscopic papillary large balloon dilation vs endoscopic sphincterotomy for retrieval of common bile duct stones: a meta-analysis. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24833886. cards.headline: Kogure 2020 (MARVELOUS): single-session complete removal 90.7% with dilation alone versus 78.8% with sphincterotomy (P=.04); lithotripsy 30.2% versus 48.2% (P=.02)
cards.summary: Kogure 2020 (MARVELOUS): single-session complete removal 90.7% with dilation alone versus 78.8% with sphincterotomy (P=.04); lithotripsy 30.2% versus 48.2% (P=.02)
cards.people: 171 patients with large (≥10 mm) common bile duct stones at 19 Japanese institutions, randomised to endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation without sphincterotomy or to endoscopic sphincterotomy.
cards.result: Complete stone removal in a single session: 90.7% (dilation) versus 78.8% (sphincterotomy), P=.04. Lithotripsy use: 30.2% versus 48.2%, P=.02. Early adverse events: overall 9.3% versus 9.4%; pancreatitis 4.7% versus 5.9%. Procedure costs $1442 versus $1661 (P=.12).
cards.watchOut: Dilation here was performed without a preceding sphincterotomy, whereas much Western practice combines a small sphincterotomy with large-balloon dilation; the trial's comparison is dilation-alone versus sphincterotomy-alone. Japanese centres with high ERCP volumes may not match all settings.
cards.source: Kogure H et al. Multicenter randomized trial of endoscopic papillary large balloon dilation without sphincterotomy versus endoscopic sphincterotomy for removal of bile duct stones: MARVELOUS trial. Endoscopy. 2020. PMID: 32299114. cards.headline: Synthesis: same clearance, less crushing — a procedural win with no demonstrated safety cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: same clearance, less crushing — a procedural win with no demonstrated safety cost

shelves.title: Wire-guided cannulation at ERCP: an early trial cut pancreatitis from 11.3% to 2% and the pooled odds ratio was 0.23 — but the largest multicentre trial found 6.1% versus 6.3%, no difference at all
shelves.question: In patients having ERCP, does wire-guided cannulation reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis compared with contrast-guided cannulation?
shelves.mesh: Bile Ducts · Catheterization/methods · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Pancreatitis/etiology/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which randomised record you weight. A single-centre Korean trial found post-ERCP pancreatitis in 3 of 150 (2%) with wire-guided cannulation versus 17 of 150 (11.3%) with contrast cannulation (P=.001) (Lee TH et al., PMID: 19007927), and a meta-analysis of five randomised trials pooled a pancreatitis odds ratio of 0.23 (95% CI 0.13–0.41) with higher primary cannulation success (85.3% versus 74.9%; OR 2.05) for the wire technique (Cennamo V et al., PMID: 19532133). But the largest, multicentre randomised trial — 322 patients across nine Japanese centres — found pancreatitis in 6.1% versus 6.3% (P=.95) and primary cannulation in 83% versus 87%, no difference on either outcome; its only independent pancreatitis predictors were accidental pancreatic-duct wire insertions and contrast injections (Kobayashi G et al., PMID: 23368891). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the early single-centre and pooled record; the treatment made no difference in the largest multicentre test.

cards.headline: Lee 2009: pancreatitis in 2% with wire-guided cannulation versus 11.3% with contrast cannulation (P=.001) in 300 patients
cards.summary: Lee 2009: pancreatitis in 2% with wire-guided cannulation versus 11.3% with contrast cannulation (P=.001) in 300 patients
cards.people: 300 consecutive patients with native papilla and pancreaticobiliary disease undergoing therapeutic ERCP at a Korean tertiary centre, randomised to wire-guided cannulation without contrast injection or conventional contrast cannulation.
cards.result: Post-ERCP pancreatitis: 3 patients (2%) in the wire-guided group versus 17 (11.3%) in the conventional group (P=.001). On multivariate analysis wire-guided cannulation was protective (OR 0.1, 95% CI 0.024–0.490; P=.004); female sex and suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction were risk factors. Two of the three wire-group pancreatitis cases had suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction with unintentional pancreatic-duct wire cannulation.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, low-risk cohort with an unusually high control-group pancreatitis rate (11.3%) — the absolute benefit available in lower-risk practice is smaller, and operator expertise at one expert centre may not transfer.
cards.source: Lee TH et al. Can wire-guided cannulation prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis? A prospective randomized trial. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2009. PMID: 19007927. cards.headline: Kobayashi 2013: pancreatitis 6.1% versus 6.3% (P=.95) and cannulation success 83% versus 87% — wire guidance changed neither in 322 patients
cards.summary: Kobayashi 2013: pancreatitis 6.1% versus 6.3% (P=.95) and cannulation success 83% versus 87% — wire guidance changed neither in 322 patients
cards.people: 322 patients requiring selective biliary cannulation at six tertiary referral centres and three university hospitals in Japan, randomised to wire-guided (n=163) or conventional contrast (n=159) cannulation, with cross-over allowed.
cards.result: Post-ERCP pancreatitis: 6.1% (wire-guided) versus 6.3% (conventional), P=.95. Primary successful biliary cannulation: 136 (83%) versus 138 (87%), P=.40. Mean time to primary success 7.4 versus 7.2 minutes. The only independent pancreatitis risk factors were accidental guidewire insertions and unintended contrast injections into the main pancreatic duct (RR 8.70, 95% CI 2.46–30.81).
cards.watchOut: Cross-over design dilutes technique differences — failed primary attempts crossed to the other method, so the trial tests a starting strategy more than a pure technique. Even so, it is the largest and most generalisable record here, and it is flatly null.
cards.source: Kobayashi G et al. Wire-guided biliary cannulation technique does not reduce the risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis: multicenter randomized controlled trial. Digestive Endoscopy. 2013. PMID: 23368891. cards.headline: Cennamo 2009 meta-analysis (5 RCTs): pancreatitis OR 0.23 (0.13–0.41) and primary cannulation 85.3% versus 74.9% (OR 2.05) favouring wire guidance
cards.summary: Cennamo 2009 meta-analysis (5 RCTs): pancreatitis OR 0.23 (0.13–0.41) and primary cannulation 85.3% versus 74.9% (OR 2.05) favouring wire guidance
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials (to March 2009) comparing primary wire-guided cannulation with the standard contrast-assisted method at ERCP.
cards.result: Primary cannulation rate: 85.3% (wire-guided) versus 74.9% (standard); pooled OR 2.05 (95% CI 1.27–3.31). Post-ERCP pancreatitis: pooled OR 0.23 (95% CI 0.13–0.41) favouring wire guidance — a 77% relative reduction in odds.
cards.watchOut: This pool predates and cannot include the large null multicentre trial of 2013; small early trials with high control event rates dominate it. A pooled estimate that the largest subsequent trial contradicts should be read as the early record, not the settled one.
cards.source: Cennamo V et al. Can a wire-guided cannulation technique increase bile duct cannulation rate and prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis?: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.people: Randomised record totalling over 900 patients across the carded trial reports and meta-analysis: Lee 2009 (n=300, single centre), Kobayashi 2013 (n=322, nine centres), Cennamo 2009 (5 RCTs pooled).
cards.result: Pancreatitis: 2% versus 11.3% (Lee); 6.1% versus 6.3% (Kobayashi); pooled OR 0.23 in the pre-2013 meta-analysis. Cannulation success favoured wire guidance only in the early pool (85.3% versus 74.9%), not in the multicentre trial (83% versus 87%). PROPOSED SPLIT, as on the face of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: What predicted pancreatitis in the null trial was pancreatic-duct instrumentation itself, whichever starting technique was used — a mechanistic hint that avoiding pancreatic entry matters more than the wire-versus-contrast label. Tier C: directly conflicting randomised records.

shelves.title: Perforated diverticulitis with peritonitis: primary anastomosis leaves 95% stoma-free at a year versus 72% after Hartmann's (LADIES) — mortality and morbidity the same in both randomised trials
shelves.question: In patients with complicated diverticulitis (Hinchey III/IV), does primary anastomosis beat Hartmann's procedure for stoma-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anastomosis, Surgical/adverse effects · Colon, Sigmoid/surgery · Colostomy · Diverticulitis, Colonic/complications/surgery · Female · Humans · Ileostomy · Intestinal Perforation/etiology/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Peritonitis/etiology · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Proctectomy/adverse effects · Rectum/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is living without a stoma, not living longer. In LADIES (DIVA arm), 12-month stoma-free survival was 94.6% after sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis versus 71.7% after Hartmann's procedure (HR 2.79, 95% CI 1.86–4.18; P<.0001), with index-operation morbidity 39% versus 44% and mortality 6% versus 3% — neither significantly different (Lambrichts DPV et al., PMID: 31178342). DIVERTI found the same pattern: 18-month mortality 4% with primary anastomosis (with diverting stoma) versus 7.7% with Hartmann's (P=.42), overall morbidity 44% versus 39%, but stoma reversal by 18 months in 96% versus 65% (P=.0001) (Bridoux V et al., PMID: 28943323). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in haemodynamically stable, immunocompetent patients under 85, primary anastomosis roughly triples the chance of being stoma-free at a year at no shown mortality or morbidity cost.

cards.headline: LADIES 2019 (DIVA arm): 12-month stoma-free survival 94.6% with primary anastomosis versus 71.7% with Hartmann's (HR 2.79; P<.0001); morbidity 39% versus 44%, mortality 6% versus 3%
cards.summary: LADIES 2019 (DIVA arm): 12-month stoma-free survival 94.6% with primary anastomosis versus 71.7% with Hartmann's (HR 2.79; P<.0001); morbidity 39% versus 44%, mortality 6% versus 3%
cards.people: 130 patients aged 18–85 with perforated diverticulitis and purulent or faecal peritonitis (93 Hinchey III, 40 Hinchey IV at randomisation) at 42 hospitals in Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands, allocated to Hartmann's procedure (n=66 analysed) or sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis, with or without defunctioning ileostomy (n=64 analysed); in 27% of the anastomosis group no stoma was constructed at all.
cards.result: 12-month stoma-free survival: 94.6% (95% CI 88.7–100) with primary anastomosis versus 71.7% (60.1–83.3) with Hartmann's (HR 2.79, 95% CI 1.86–4.18; log-rank P<.0001). Short-term morbidity after the index procedure: 39% (25/64) versus 44% (29/66), P=.60. Mortality: 6% (4/64) versus 3% (2/66), P=.44.
cards.watchOut: Open-label surgical trial in patients the authors specify as haemodynamically stable and immunocompetent — the result should not be extended to unstable or immunosuppressed patients, who were the historical Hartmann's population. The trial stopped at 133 randomised of a larger planned sample.
cards.source: Lambrichts DPV et al. Hartmann's procedure versus sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis for perforated diverticulitis with purulent or faecal peritonitis (LADIES): a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, open-label, superiority trial. cards.headline: DIVERTI 2017: mortality 4% (primary anastomosis) versus 7.7% (Hartmann's), P=.42 — but stoma reversal by 18 months in 96% versus 65% (P=.0001)
cards.summary: DIVERTI 2017: mortality 4% (primary anastomosis) versus 7.7% (Hartmann's), P=.42 — but stoma reversal by 18 months in 96% versus 65% (P=.0001)
cards.people: 102 patients with purulent or faecal diverticular peritonitis (Hinchey III–IV) at French tertiary and associated centres, randomised equally to primary anastomosis with a diverting stoma or Hartmann's procedure, followed for up to 18 months.
cards.result: Overall mortality at 18 months: 4% (primary anastomosis) versus 7.7% (Hartmann's), P=.4233. Morbidity across resection and reversal operations: 44% versus 39%, P=.4233. Stoma reversal by 18 months: 96% of the anastomosis group versus 65% of the Hartmann's group (P=.0001).
cards.watchOut: In DIVERTI every anastomosis patient received a diverting stoma by protocol, so its question is anastomosis-plus-diversion versus Hartmann's — the reversal advantage partly reflects how much harder Hartmann reversal surgery is, which is itself part of the clinical point. Small trial (102 patients); mortality confidence intervals are wide.
cards.source: Bridoux V et al. Hartmann's Procedure or Primary Anastomosis for Generalized Peritonitis due to Perforated Diverticulitis: A Prospective Multicenter Randomized Trial (DIVERTI). cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one message — anastomosis trades nothing measurable in safety for a large gain in stoma-free life
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one message — anastomosis trades nothing measurable in safety for a large gain in stoma-free life
cards.people: LADIES (n=130 analysed) and DIVERTI (n=102), both randomised trials in Hinchey III/IV perforated diverticulitis.
cards.result: Stoma-free survival at 12 months 94.6% versus 71.7% (LADIES); stoma reversal 96% versus 65% at 18 months (DIVERTI). Mortality 6% versus 3% (LADIES) and 4% versus 7.7% (DIVERTI) — opposite directions, both non-significant. Morbidity statistically indistinguishable in both. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Boundary with Shelf #3622: that shelf homes laparoscopic lavage versus sigmoidectomy for purulent peritonitis; this shelf is the resection-choice question (anastomosis versus Hartmann's) in purulent or faecal peritonitis. Both trials excluded the unstable patients in whom Hartmann's remains the default. Tier C.

shelves.title: Psyllium (Metamucil) for diarrhoea: it halves faecal incontinence episodes with loose stools (2.5 vs 5.5 per week on placebo) and matches loperamide in chronic diarrhoea — but it did not prevent tube-feeding diarrhoea, and it has never been trialled in acute infectious diarrhoea
shelves.question: In adults with diarrhoea, does psyllium (Metamucil) help — and for which kinds of diarrhoea (chronic diarrhoea, faecal incontinence, diarrhoea-predominant IBS as an adjunct) — and where does it not help (acute infectious diarrhoea)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidiarrheals/administration & dosage · Cathartics/administration & dosage · Chronic Disease · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Diarrhea/etiology · Diarrhea/prevention & control · Dietary Fiber/administration & dosage · Dietary Fiber/pharmacology · Enteral Nutrition/adverse effects · Fecal Incontinence/diet therapy · Fecal Incontinence/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Loperamide/administration & dosage · Loperamide/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Psyllium/administration & dosage · Psyllium/pharmacology · Psyllium/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the kind of diarrhoea. Faecal incontinence with loose or liquid stools is where psyllium has its clearest trial support: in the largest fibre trial (Bliss 2014, PMID: 25155992; 189 community-living adults, 16 g/day for 32 days), estimated incontinence episodes were 2.5 per week on psyllium versus 5.5 per week on placebo, and psyllium was the only fibre of the three tested that significantly reduced frequency (carboxymethylcellulose increased it); an earlier 39-person trial from the same group (Bliss 2001, PMID: 11480529) found the proportion of incontinent stools on psyllium or gum arabic was less than half that on placebo. Against an active drug, psyllium matched loperamide: in an 80-person double-blind crossover trial (Markland 2015, PMID: 26347971) there were no differences between psyllium and loperamide for incontinence episodes, severity or quality of life, both improved within-group, and constipation was less frequent on psyllium (10% versus 29%). In chronic diarrhoea proper, the one direct trial is small and old: ispaghula husk plus calcium halved stool frequency just as loperamide did in 19 completers, and was significantly better for urgency and stool consistency (Qvitzau 1988, PMID: 3074458). The mechanism is demonstrated experimentally — psyllium, unlike calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran, made stools firmer and increased faecal viscosity dose-dependently in phenolphthalein-induced secretory diarrhoea (Eherer 1993, PMID: 8385040) — but that study had only 9 subjects. Where psyllium does NOT help: in enteral tube feeding, the psyllium-specific randomised trials found no reduction in diarrhoea incidence (Lertpipopmetha 2019, PMID: 30561029: 42.9% versus 31.7% with at least one diarrhoea day, P=0.41; Belknap 1997, PMID: 9176691: no significant difference in incidence), even though fibre in enteral feeds overall reduced diarrhoea in a 16-trial meta-analysis (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.49–0.82) — an effect driven by mixed fibre and partially hydrolysed guar gum, with the psyllium subgroup itself unclear (Kaewdech 2022, PMID: 36505240). For acute infectious diarrhoea there is no trial evidence at all: explicit PubMed searches this session found no randomised trial of psyllium in acute infectious diarrhoea or gastroenteritis — the only 'acute' data are the experimental laxative-induced model above and in-vitro work — so psyllium cannot be recommended there on evidence; oral rehydration therapy is the treatment used for dehydration caused by diarrhoea (Fontaine 2000, PMID: 10796624). Boundaries: diarrhoea-predominant IBS as an adjunct is NOT re-carded here — psyllium in IBS overall, including the primary-care trial and the fibre meta-analysis, is homed on Shelf #3619, and no diarrhoea-subgroup-specific psyllium trial was found to card separately; psyllium for constipation is compared on Shelf #3606; and bile-acid diarrhoea has a different drug — colesevelam — on Shelf #2773, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. PROPOSED SPLIT: psyllium helps faecal incontinence with loose stools and probably chronic diarrhoea (small, old evidence); it made no difference to tube-feeding diarrhoea incidence; and it is untested in acute infectious diarrhoea.

cards.headline: Bliss 2014 (n=189, the largest fibre trial in faecal incontinence): psyllium cut episodes to an estimated 2.5 per week versus 5.5 on placebo — the only one of three fibres that helped; carboxymethylcellulose made it worse
cards.summary: Bliss 2014 (n=189, the largest fibre trial in faecal incontinence): psyllium cut episodes to an estimated 2.5 per week versus 5.5 on placebo — the only one of three fibres that helped; carboxymethylcellulose made it worse
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial of three fibres versus placebo (Bliss 2014)
cards.people: 189 community-living individuals incontinent of loose/liquid faeces; after a 14-day baseline they consumed placebo or 16 g total fibre/day as carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), gum arabic (GA) or psyllium for 32 days. Primary outcome: faecal incontinence frequency; secondary: amount and consistency, supplement intolerance, quality of life, and mechanisms.
cards.result: Faecal incontinence frequency significantly decreased after psyllium supplementation versus placebo, in both intent-to-treat and per-protocol mixed model analyses. CMC increased FI frequency. In intent-to-treat analysis, the estimated number of FI episodes per week after supplementation was 5.5 for placebo, 2.5 for psyllium, 4.3 for GA and 6.2 for CMC. Only psyllium consumption resulted in a gel in faeces. Supplement intolerance was low, and quality-of-life scores did not differ among groups. The authors concluded that formation of a gel in faeces appears to be a mechanism by which residual psyllium improved FI.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, 32 days, and the headline figures are model-estimated episodes per week, not raw counts — the direction and the psyllium-only signal are the findings, not a precise halving for any one patient. This is incontinence of loose stools, not diarrhoea frequency in people with intact continence, and quality of life did not move.
cards.source: Bliss DZ, Savik K, Jung HJ, Whitebird R, Lowry A, Sheng X. Dietary fiber supplementation for fecal incontinence: a randomized clinical trial. Research in Nursing & Health. 2014. cards.headline: Bliss 2001 (n=39): on psyllium or gum arabic the proportion of incontinent stools was less than half that on placebo, and the placebo group had the most loose or liquid stools
cards.summary: Bliss 2001 (n=39): on psyllium or gum arabic the proportion of incontinent stools was less than half that on placebo, and the placebo group had the most loose or liquid stools
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of fibre supplements in faecal incontinence (Bliss 2001)
cards.people: 39 persons with faecal incontinence of loose or liquid stools, community-living; they recorded diet intake and stool characteristics and collected stools for 8 days before and at the end of a 31-day supplementation period, ingesting psyllium, gum arabic or a placebo (pectin) by random assignment.
cards.result: In the baseline period the groups were comparable on all variables measured. In the supplementation period: (a) the proportion of incontinent stools in the groups ingesting the fibre supplements was less than half that of the group ingesting the placebo, (b) the placebo group had the greatest percentage of stools that were loose/unformed or liquid, and (c) the psyllium group had the highest water-holding capacity of water-insoluble solids and total water-holding capacity. The authors concluded that supplementation with dietary fibre from psyllium or gum arabic was associated with a decrease in the percentage of incontinent stools and an improvement of stool consistency.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine people split three ways, and the abstract reports the fibre groups' result jointly ('less than half') rather than a psyllium-only percentage — the psyllium-specific estimate comes from the 2014 trial above. The abstract also notes the supplements appeared completely fermented, so the water-holding finding, not unfermented fibre, is the proposed mechanism here.
cards.source: Bliss DZ, Jung HJ, Savik K, Lowry A, LeMoine M, Jensen L, Werner C, Schaffer K. Supplementation with dietary fiber improves fecal incontinence. Nursing Research. 2001. PMID: 11480529. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Markland 2015 FIRM trial (n=80, double-blind crossover): psyllium and loperamide did not differ on incontinence episodes, severity or quality of life — both improved — but constipation was 29% on loperamide versus 10% on psyllium
cards.summary: Markland 2015 FIRM trial (n=80, double-blind crossover): psyllium and loperamide did not differ on incontinence episodes, severity or quality of life — both improved — but constipation was 29% on loperamide versus 10% on psyllium
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, psyllium versus loperamide (Markland 2015)
cards.people: 80 community-dwelling adults with at least 1 faecal incontinent episode on a 7-day bowel diary, at a Veterans Affairs medical centre and university affiliate (mean age 60.7 ± 10.1 years; 68% men); daily loperamide (plus placebo psyllium powder) or psyllium powder (plus loperamide placebo) for 4 weeks, a 2-week washout, then 4 weeks of the alternate treatment. Primary outcome: number of faecal incontinence episodes from 7-day bowel diaries.
cards.result: After determining nonsignificant carryover effects, combined analyses showed no differences between the loperamide and psyllium groups for reducing faecal incontinent episodes, symptom severity, or quality of life. Within each group, both loperamide and psyllium reduced faecal incontinent episodes and improved symptom severity and quality of life. Constipation occurred in 29% of participants for loperamide versus 10% for psyllium. The authors concluded that both loperamide and psyllium improve faecal incontinence, and that loperamide was associated with more adverse effects, especially constipation.
cards.watchOut: A no-difference result against an active comparator is not a placebo-controlled proof of efficacy on its own — it gains its weight from sitting beside the placebo-controlled Bliss trials. The abstract prints no episode counts, so no size of improvement is claimed here; limitations named by the authors are the washout length and the dropout rate after crossover. Mostly men, from a VA population.
cards.source: Markland AD, Burgio KL, Whitehead WE, Richter HE, Wilcox CM, Redden DT, Beasley TM, Goode PS. Loperamide Versus Psyllium Fiber for Treatment of Fecal Incontinence: The Fecal Incontinence Prescription (Rx) Management (FIRM) Randomized Clinical Trial. Diseases of the Colon & Rectum. 2015. PMID: 26347971. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Menees 2022 pilot (n=43): responders (>50% fewer episodes) were 50% on psyllium 6 g/day versus 38.9% on a low-FODMAP diet — not significant (P=.33) — and the severity score improved on the diet but not on psyllium
cards.summary: Menees 2022 pilot (n=43): responders (>50% fewer episodes) were 50% on psyllium 6 g/day versus 38.9% on a low-FODMAP diet — not significant (P=.33) — and the severity score improved on the diet but not on psyllium
cards.type: Single-centre randomised pilot trial, psyllium versus dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet (Menees 2022)
cards.people: 43 adults with faecal incontinence (Rome III) and at least 1 weekly FI episode associated with loose stool, randomised from October 2014 to May 2019 to 4 weeks of a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet (LFD) or 6 g/day psyllium; 37 completed the study (19 LFD and 18 psyllium). Primary outcome: proportion of responders, defined as >50% reduction in FI episodes versus baseline.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of treatment responders for treatment weeks 1–4 (LFD 38.9%, psyllium 50%, P=.33). Compared with baseline, mean faecal incontinence severity index score significantly improved with LFD (39.4 vs 32.6, P=.02) but not with psyllium (35.4 vs 32.1, P=.29). The LFD group reported improvements in quality-of-life coping/behaviour, depression/self-perception and embarrassment subscales; the psyllium group reported improvement in the coping/behaviour subscale. The authors note the psyllium group reported a greater reduction in overall FI episodes, whereas the LFD group reported consistent improvements in severity and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A 43-person pilot with an active dietary comparator and no placebo arm: it cannot confirm or refute psyllium's effect, and its one significant within-group result (severity) favours the diet. Carded to show the newest FI trial is inconclusive on its own — the shelf's FI claim rests on Bliss 2014 and Markland 2015.
cards.source: Menees SB, Jackson K, Baker JR, Fenner DE, Eswaran S, Nojkov B, Saad R, Lee AA, Chey WD. cards.headline: Qvitzau 1988 (chronic diarrhoea, 19 completers): ispaghula husk plus calcium halved stool frequency just as loperamide did — and was significantly better for urgency and stool consistency
cards.summary: Qvitzau 1988 (chronic diarrhoea, 19 completers): ispaghula husk plus calcium halved stool frequency just as loperamide did — and was significantly better for urgency and stool consistency
cards.type: Open randomised crossover trial, loperamide versus ispaghula husk and calcium (Qvitzau 1988)
cards.people: 25 patients with chronic diarrhoea at Hvidovre Hospital, Copenhagen, in an open, randomised crossover trial comparing loperamide with ispaghula and calcium; 19 patients completed both treatments. Before treatment the median number of daily stools was 7 (range 4–13), stool consistency was loose in all, and urgency was present in 16 out of 19 patients.
cards.result: Both treatments halved stool frequency, but with regard to urgency and stool consistency ispaghula and calcium was significantly better. The authors concluded that a combination of ispaghula and calcium seems to be a cheap and effective alternative to conventional treatment of chronic diarrhoea, and that side effects were minimized.
cards.watchOut: The only direct chronic-diarrhoea trial on this shelf is from 1988, open-label, with 19 completers — and the treatment was ispaghula COMBINED with calcium, so the effect cannot be credited to psyllium alone. 'Halved' is the authors' summary from a median of 7 stools a day; no per-treatment stool counts or p-values are printed in the abstract, so none are claimed here. This card is the whole of the chronic-diarrhoea evidence: thin, and flagged as such in the stamp.
cards.source: Qvitzau S, Matzen P, Madsen P. Treatment of chronic diarrhoea: loperamide versus ispaghula husk and calcium. Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology. 1988. PMID: 3074458. cards.headline: Eherer 1993 (mechanism, 9 subjects): in experimentally induced secretory diarrhoea, psyllium — but not calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran — made stools firmer and increased faecal viscosity, near-linearly with dose (9, 18, 30 g/day)
cards.summary: Eherer 1993 (mechanism, 9 subjects): in experimentally induced secretory diarrhoea, psyllium — but not calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran — made stools firmer and increased faecal viscosity, near-linearly with dose (9, 18, 30 g/day)
cards.type: Randomised-sequence experimental study in phenolphthalein-induced secretory diarrhoea (Eherer 1993)
cards.people: 9 normal subjects with secretory diarrhoea induced by phenolphthalein, treated in random sequence with placebo, psyllium, calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran; a dose-response study in 6 further subjects tested 9, 18 and 30 g of psyllium per day.
cards.result: Calcium polycarbophil and wheat bran had no effect on faecal consistency or on faecal viscosity. By contrast, psyllium made stools firmer and increased faecal viscosity. In the dose-response study, doses of 9, 18 and 30 g of psyllium per day caused a near linear increase in faecal viscosity. The authors concluded that psyllium, but not calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran, improves faecal consistency and viscosity in subjects with experimentally induced secretory diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Nine subjects (six in the dose-response part) — below the developer's usual ~10-human floor for SourceMed, and carded ONLY as the mechanism demonstration (gel/viscosity), explicitly flagged here and in the build note for his verdict; it carries no clinical claim on this shelf. Phenolphthalein-induced diarrhoea in healthy volunteers is a model, not infectious diarrhoea and not a patient population; the abstract prints no viscosity numbers, so none are claimed.
cards.source: Eherer AJ, Santa Ana CA, Porter J, Fordtran JS. Effect of psyllium, calcium polycarbophil, and wheat bran on secretory diarrhea induced by phenolphthalein. Gastroenterology. 1993. PMID: 8385040. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era study). cards.headline: Lertpipopmetha 2019 (enteral feeding, n=83, double-blind): psyllium-added formula did not reduce diarrhoea — 42.9% versus 31.7% had at least one diarrhoea day (P=0.41)
cards.summary: Lertpipopmetha 2019 (enteral feeding, n=83, double-blind): psyllium-added formula did not reduce diarrhoea — 42.9% versus 31.7% had at least one diarrhoea day (P=0.41)
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind controlled trial of psyllium in enteral nutrition (Lertpipopmetha 2019)
cards.people: 83 general medical ward patients expected to receive enteral nutrition for at least 5 days (42 psyllium group, 41 control), excluding haemodynamic instability, known significant gastrointestinal problems and recent pancreatitis; psyllium-added formula (Mucilin SF 15.2 g/L in the standard formula — the tested product, named as the publication gives it) versus the same fibre-free formula, for 10 days or until discharge, oral intake or death; bowel movements monitored with the King's Stool Chart, diarrhoea defined as a King's stool score of 15 or more.
cards.result: The proportion of patients with at least 1 day of diarrhoea was comparable (42.9% vs 31.7%; P=0.41, in the psyllium and control groups respectively). There were no significant differences in the frequency of daily bowel movements or the median diarrhoea score between the groups (3 vs 2, P=0.06, and 3.8 vs 2.4, P=0.42, respectively). The authors concluded that supplementation with psyllium showed no beneficial effect on reducing the incidence of diarrhoea in general medical patients receiving enteral nutrition — (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The point estimates numerically favour the fibre-free formula, so this is a genuine null, not an underpowered near-miss on the primary outcome — though 83 patients cannot exclude a modest effect. One formula, one centre, medical-ward patients; it answers the tube-feeding question for psyllium specifically, which is why it outranks the mixed-fibre meta-analysis beside it for this shelf.
cards.source: Lertpipopmetha K, Kongkamol C, Sripongpun P. Effect of Psyllium Fiber Supplementation on Diarrhea Incidence in Enteral Tube-Fed Patients: A Prospective, Randomized, and Controlled Trial. JPEN Journal of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition. 2019. cards.headline: Belknap 1997 (enteral feeding pilot, n=60): no significant difference in diarrhoea incidence with psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid — fewer liquid and more normal stools, but a 12% rate of small-bore tube occlusion
cards.summary: Belknap 1997 (enteral feeding pilot, n=60): no significant difference in diarrhoea incidence with psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid — fewer liquid and more normal stools, but a 12% rate of small-bore tube occlusion
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial of psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid in newly tube-fed patients (Belknap 1997)
cards.people: 60 patients from medical-surgical and intensive care units at a VA medical centre who received newly initiated enteral feeding via feeding tube; psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid 7 g twice daily, added to continuous feeding or given as a bolus with intermittent feeding, versus no psyllium, for 7 days after initiation of enteral feeding. Diarrhoea was defined as 3 or more liquid stools per day, or 2 or more liquid stools on successive days.
cards.result: Fifteen subjects (25%) developed diarrhoea. There were no significant differences in incidence of diarrhoea or percentage of days of diarrhoea between subjects who did and did not receive psyllium — (the treatment made no difference) to incidence. However, subjects who received psyllium in their continuous feedings had a significantly higher number of gelatinous stools, and the combined psyllium groups had a significantly lower number of liquid stools and a higher number of normal stools than subjects who did not receive psyllium. For the combined psyllium groups there was a 12% incidence of small-bore feeding tube occlusion requiring replacement.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient pilot whose own authors call for a larger study: the consistency signal (fewer liquid stools) without an incidence effect mirrors the later Thai trial's pattern in reverse, and the 12% tube-occlusion rate is a practical harm specific to giving a gel-forming fibre through small-bore tubes — the reason psyllium in tube feeds needs dilution and monitoring, per the authors.
cards.source: Belknap D, Davidson LJ, Smith CR. The effects of psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid on diarrhea in enterally fed patients. Heart & Lung. 1997. PMID: 9176691. psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid 7 g twice daily, added to continuous feeding or given as a bolus with intermittent feeding, versus no psyllium, for 7 days after initiation of enteral feeding. diarrhoea was defined as 3 or more liquid stools per day, or 2 or more liquid stools on successive days. fifteen subjects (25%) developed diarrhoea. there were no significant differences in incidence of diarrhoea or percentage of days of diarrhoea between subjects who did and did not receive psyllium — (the treatment made no difference) to incidence. however, subjects who received psyllium in their continuous feedings had a significantly higher number of gelatinous stools, and the combined psyllium groups had a significantly lower number of liquid stools and a higher number of normal stools than subjects who did not receive psyllium. for the combined psyllium groups there was a 12% incidence of small-bore feeding tube occlusion requiring replacement. a 60-patient pilot whose own authors call for a larger study: the consistency signal (fewer liquid stools) without an incidence effect mirrors the later thai trial's pattern in reverse, and the 12% tube-occlusion rate is a practical harm specific to giving a gel-forming fibre through small-bore tubes — the reason psyllium in tube feeds needs dilution and monitoring, per the authors. belknap d, davidson lj, smith cr. the effects of psyllium hydrophilic mucilloid on diarrhea in enterally fed patients. heart & lung. 1997. pmid: 9176691. registry id: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · diarrhea/etiology · diarrhea/nursing · diarrhea/prevention & control · drug administration schedule · enteral nutrition/nursing · feasibility studies · female · humans · male · middle aged · pilot projects · psyllium/administration & dosage · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Kaewdech 2022 (meta-analysis, 16 enteral-feeding RCTs): fibre overall cut diarrhoea (relative risk 0.64) — but only mixed fibre and partially hydrolysed guar gum were significant by type; the psyllium subgroup was unclear
cards.summary: Kaewdech 2022 (meta-analysis, 16 enteral-feeding RCTs): fibre overall cut diarrhoea (relative risk 0.64) — but only mixed fibre and partially hydrolysed guar gum were significant by type; the psyllium subgroup was unclear
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials with GRADE assessment (Kaewdech 2022)
cards.people: 16 randomised controlled trials in hospitalised adult patients receiving enteral nutrition, from 4,469 titles screened (databases searched from inception to 1 September 2022); fibre types examined in sensitivity analysis were soy polysaccharides (4 trials), psyllium (3 trials), mixed soluble/insoluble fibre (3), pectin (2) and partially hydrolysed guar gum, PHGG (2). Protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021279971).
cards.result: Overall, compared with fibre-free formulas, fibre supplementation reduced the occurrence of diarrhoea in patients receiving enteral nutrition by 36% relative (pooled relative risk 0.64; 95% CI 0.49–0.82; p=0.005; I²=45%), with GRADE showing moderate certainty. Only mixed fibre and PHGG significantly decreased the incidence of diarrhoea in the sensitivity analyses by fibre type (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75, and relative risk 0.47, 95% CI 0.27–0.83, respectively). The results for the remaining fibre types — including psyllium — were unclear. The authors concluded that fibre supplements help lessen post-feeding diarrhoea, but not all fibre types produced successful outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The trap this card exists to prevent: quoting 'fibre reduces tube-feeding diarrhoea, RR 0.64' as if it were a psyllium result. It is not — the significant subgroups are mixed fibre and PHGG, the psyllium subgroup (3 trials) was unclear, and both psyllium-specific trials carded on this shelf found no incidence benefit. The PubMed record for this article carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Kaewdech A, Sripongpun P, Wetwittayakhlang P, Churuangsuk C. cards.headline: Synthesis: one fibre, four different diarrhoeas — it firms loose stools where continence is the problem, matches loperamide in the small chronic-diarrhoea trial, does nothing for tube-feeding diarrhoea incidence, and is simply untested in acute infection
cards.summary: Synthesis: one fibre, four different diarrhoeas — it firms loose stools where continence is the problem, matches loperamide in the small chronic-diarrhoea trial, does nothing for tube-feeding diarrhoea incidence, and is simply untested in acute infection
cards.people: Nine sources: four faecal-incontinence trials (Bliss 2014, 189 subjects; Bliss 2001, 39; Markland 2015, 80; Menees 2022, 43), one chronic-diarrhoea crossover trial (Qvitzau 1988, 19 completers), one experimental mechanism study (Eherer 1993, 9 subjects), two psyllium-specific enteral-feeding trials (Lertpipopmetha 2019, 83 patients; Belknap 1997, 60), and one 16-trial enteral fibre meta-analysis (Kaewdech 2022).
cards.result: Faecal incontinence with loose stools: estimated 2.5 versus 5.5 episodes per week for psyllium versus placebo (Bliss 2014); proportion of incontinent stools less than half on fibre versus placebo (Bliss 2001); no difference versus loperamide on episodes, severity or quality of life, with constipation 10% versus 29% (Markland 2015); pilot versus low-FODMAP diet inconclusive (Menees 2022). Chronic diarrhoea: ispaghula plus calcium and loperamide both halved stool frequency from a median of 7 per day, ispaghula plus calcium significantly better for urgency and consistency (Qvitzau 1988). Mechanism: psyllium alone among the fibres tested firmed stools and raised faecal viscosity dose-dependently in induced secretory diarrhoea (Eherer 1993). Enteral tube feeding: no difference in diarrhoea incidence in either psyllium-specific trial (42.9% versus 31.7%, P=0.41, Lertpipopmetha 2019; no significant difference, Belknap 1997), while fibre overall gave a relative risk of 0.64 driven by mixed fibre and PHGG, not psyllium (Kaewdech 2022). Acute infectious diarrhoea: no randomised trial found on explicit PubMed search — untested. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit where loose stool meets weak continence and probably in chronic diarrhoea; (the treatment made no difference) for tube-feeding diarrhoea incidence; no evidence in acute infectious diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Boundaries on the face: psyllium for IBS overall lives on Shelf #3619 (its primary-care RCT and fibre meta-analysis are not re-carded here, and no diarrhoea-subgroup-specific trial was found for the IBS-D adjunct question); psyllium for constipation is compared on Shelf #3606; bile-acid diarrhoea is a different treatment question — colesevelam, Shelf #2773. Two flags for the verdict: the chronic-diarrhoea card (Qvitzau 1988) tests ispaghula COMBINED with calcium in 19 completers, and the mechanism card (Eherer 1993) has 9 subjects, below the usual ~10-human floor — both are labelled as such on their faces. Nothing here supports psyllium as a treatment for acute infectious diarrhoea, where oral rehydration is the established therapy (Fontaine 2000, PMID: 10796624).
