shelves.title: Loperamide beyond a week in chronic diarrhoea: effective at about 4–6 mg a day over 4–13 weeks in small double-blind trials, with few side-effects at therapeutic doses — the life-threatening cardiac record belongs to supratherapeutic abuse doses (median 200 mg a day), not to labelled use
shelves.question: In adults with chronic diarrhoea, is loperamide effective and safe when taken for more than a week — including long-term daily use?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antidiarrheals/toxicity · Cardiotoxicity/etiology · Chronic Disease · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ileostomy · Loperamide/adverse effects · Loperamide/therapeutic use · Loperamide/toxicity · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: BOUNDARY: this shelf is chronic diarrhoea only. Acute diarrhoea is homed separately at Shelf #2478 (loperamide versus placebo, racecadotril and rifaximin in acute and travellers' diarrhoea) and its acute trials are not re-carded here; the azithromycin-plus-loperamide travellers' question at #4603 is an adjunct question, not this one. EFFICACY BEYOND A WEEK: in chronic diarrhoea of mixed causes, loperamide beat placebo in small double-blind trials at ordinary doses — Mainguet 1977 (PMID: 326642; 18 completers with ileocolic disease or resection, median 6 mg/day) found stool frequency and weight significantly decreased, stools more solid and transit prolonged, with gastrointestinal side-effects few and comparable to placebo; Tytgat 1976 (PMID: 779663) found 11 of 15 patients improved in an open phase (optimal dose 4–14 mg/day) and relapse on blinded placebo substitution was obvious enough that the investigator guessed the code in 10 of 11 cases, while ileostomy output fell by 22% relative on loperamide (P less than 0.001). Benefit was sustained over multi-week treatment: Palmer 1980 (PMID: 7002706; 30 patients, three randomised 4-week periods) found loperamide 4.6 mg/day matched codeine and beat diphenoxylate on stool solidity and urgency, with the fewest central side-effects of the three; Cann 1984 (PMID: 6365490; 28 patients with irritable bowel syndrome, 5 weeks per period) found further significant improvement over placebo in diarrhoea, urgency and stool frequency, and 15 of the 18 patients who preferred loperamide remained satisfied at follow-up; Lavö 1987 (PMID: 3306903; 13 weeks, the longest placebo-controlled test) found significant advantages for stool consistency (p less than 0.001), pain (p less than 0.02), urgency (p less than 0.05) and overall response (p less than 0.03). SAFETY — THE TWO RECORDS MUST NOT BE MERGED. At therapeutic doses the trial record is quiet: side-effects few and comparable to placebo (Mainguet), least with loperamide among the antidiarrhoeals compared (Palmer; its discontinuations were for abdominal pain and constipation), and a single nightly self-titrated dose was described as safe over 13 weeks (Lavö). The FDA states loperamide 'is a safe drug when used as directed' and 'safe at approved doses', with labelled maxima of 8 mg/day over-the-counter and 16 mg/day prescription. The serious cardiac record — QT interval prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, other ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, cardiac arrest and death — is a supratherapeutic record: the FDA's 2016 Drug Safety Communication (updated 30 January 2018) concerns 'much higher than the recommended doses', primarily intentional misuse or abuse, and the systematic review of supratherapeutic exposure (Bekka 2026, PMID: 41817965; 129 published cases) found a median daily dose of 200 mg, 57% with known or suspected substance use disorder, severe toxicity in 64% of reported cases and fatalities in 13% — with severity dose-dependent (adjusted OR 1.04 per 10 mg) and severe toxicity reported at doses as low as 20–40 mg/day, just above the labelled maximum. So: effective and apparently well tolerated for weeks at 4–6 mg/day in the trials; no controlled trial runs beyond 13 weeks, so truly long-term daily safety rests on the absence of a therapeutic-dose signal rather than on long controlled follow-up; and the dose must not creep — the toxicology literature begins just above the labelled ceiling. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) at therapeutic doses, Tier C.

cards.headline: Mainguet 1977: in chronic diarrhoea from ileocolic disease or resection, loperamide at a median 6 mg/day beat placebo — stool frequency and weight significantly down, stools more solid, side-effects few and comparable
cards.summary: Mainguet 1977: in chronic diarrhoea from ileocolic disease or resection, loperamide at a median 6 mg/day beat placebo — stool frequency and weight significantly down, stools more solid, side-effects few and comparable
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in chronic diarrhoea (Mainguet & Fiasse 1977)
cards.people: 21 patients with chronic diarrhoea caused by ileocolic disease or resection; 18 completed the double-blind crossover comparison of loperamide (R 18 553) against placebo, at a median daily dose of 6 mg.
cards.result: Loperamide was superior to placebo in controlling chronic diarrhoea: the frequency and weight of stools significantly decreased, the stools became more solid, and carmine transit time was prolonged during loperamide therapy. Loperamide was consistently preferred to placebo by the patients. Gastrointestinal side-effects were few and comparable during both treatment periods.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance and direction, not the stool numbers themselves, so no effect size is claimed here. Eighteen completers with one family of causes (ileocolic disease or resection) — the cleanest placebo test in this population, but small and from 1977, and the abstract does not state the length of each treatment period.
cards.source: Mainguet P, Fiasse R. Double-blind placebo-controlled study of loperamide (Imodium) in chronic diarrhoea caused by ileocolic disease or resection. Gut. 1977. PMID: 326642. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Tytgat 1976: 11 of 15 patients with chronic diarrhoea improved at an optimal dose of 4–14 mg/day, blinded placebo substitution was guessed correctly in 10 of 11 cases — and ileostomy output fell by 22% relative (P less than 0.001)
cards.summary: Tytgat 1976: 11 of 15 patients with chronic diarrhoea improved at an optimal dose of 4–14 mg/day, blinded placebo substitution was guessed correctly in 10 of 11 cases — and ileostomy output fell by 22% relative (P less than 0.001)
cards.type: Open dose-finding phase followed by a double-blind placebo-controlled phase, plus a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study in ileostomy patients (Tytgat, Huibregtse & Meuwissen 1976)
cards.people: Fifteen patients (20 to 66 years) with long-standing chronic diarrhoea of varying etiology in the open-then-blinded study, the optimal daily dose (2 mg capsules) ranging from two to seven capsules; and 20 ileostomy patients (ages 25 to 73 years) in the crossover study of small-intestinal peristalsis.
cards.result: In the open phase, 11 patients showed a significant improvement in stool consistency and stool frequency and a decrease of abdominal cramps; loperamide appeared ineffective in two patients with cholerrheic diarrhoea, one with laxative-induced diarrhoea and one with diarrhoea of unknown etiology. The 11 successfully treated patients then entered a double-blind placebo-controlled trial for ten days or until relapse, at the same individually optimal dose; the investigator was able to guess the code correctly in ten out of eleven cases. In the ileostomy crossover study, mean daily ileostomy output decreased by 22% (relative) in the loperamide period compared with the drug-free study phase (P less than 0.001); 16 of the 20 patients guessed their code correctly, and many noticed increased urinary production and improved ileostomy care. The authors concluded that, because of its effectiveness, low side-effect liability and lack of toxicity, loperamide is a promising drug in the symptomatic treatment of chronic diarrhoea and a reliable agent in ileostomy patients.
cards.watchOut: The blinded chronic-diarrhoea phase enrolled only the 11 open-phase responders, so it tests maintenance and relapse rather than initial response in an unselected group — an enriched design that flatters the drug. The ileostomy comparison was against a drug-free phase within a crossover, and correct guessing in 16 of 20 patients shows the effect was large enough to unblind itself.
cards.source: Tytgat GN, Huibregtse K, Meuwissen SG. Loperamide in chronic diarrhea and after ileostomy: a placebo-controlled double-blind cross-over study. Archivum Chirurgicum Neerlandicum. 1976. PMID: 779663. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Palmer 1980 (4 weeks per drug, 30 patients): loperamide 4.6 mg/day matched codeine and beat diphenoxylate on solid stools and urgency — and had the fewest side-effects, particularly central ones
cards.summary: Palmer 1980 (4 weeks per drug, 30 patients): loperamide 4.6 mg/day matched codeine and beat diphenoxylate on solid stools and urgency — and had the fewest side-effects, particularly central ones
cards.type: Double-blind crossover trial comparing loperamide, codeine and diphenoxylate in chronic diarrhoea (Palmer, Corbett & Holdsworth 1980)
cards.people: 30 individuals with chronic diarrhoea, each undergoing three randomised treatment periods of 4 weeks' duration, with the daily dose increased gradually until control was achieved or side-effects became intolerable; stool frequency, consistency, urgency and incontinence were compared at a stable dose.
cards.result: Though 2.3 capsules (4.6 mg) of loperamide, 2.3 capsules (103.5 mg) of codeine and 2.5 capsules (12.5 mg) of diphenoxylate all reduced stool frequency to the same extent, diphenoxylate was significantly less effective in producing a solid stool. Before treatment 95% of patients experienced urgency, sometimes with faecal incontinence, often as their major disability; loperamide and codeine were more effective in relieving this than diphenoxylate. Side-effects, particularly central nervous effects, were greatest with diphenoxylate and least with loperamide. Approximately equal numbers discontinued each preparation: poor control and central-nervous-system side-effects were the usual reasons for stopping diphenoxylate and codeine, and abdominal pain and constipation for stopping loperamide. The authors concluded that both loperamide and codeine phosphate are superior to diphenoxylate in the symptomatic treatment of chronic diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm — this card ranks loperamide against the other antidiarrhoeals of its era over 4-week periods, it does not re-prove the placebo effect (the Mainguet, Tytgat, Cann and Lavö cards carry that). Its safety contribution is comparative tolerability: the price of loperamide control was abdominal pain and constipation, not central effects.

cards.headline: Cann 1984 (5 weeks per period): loperamide beat placebo on diarrhoea, urgency and stool frequency, prolonged whole-gut transit to 56 versus 42 hours — and 15 of 18 patients who preferred it remained satisfied at follow-up
cards.summary: Cann 1984 (5 weeks per period): loperamide beat placebo on diarrhoea, urgency and stool frequency, prolonged whole-gut transit to 56 versus 42 hours — and 15 of 18 patients who preferred it remained satisfied at follow-up
cards.type: Double-blind crossover randomised trial with follow-up, in irritable bowel syndrome (Cann, Read, Holdsworth & Barends 1984)
cards.people: 28 patients with irritable bowel syndrome who had undergone comprehensive diagnostic investigations and had failed to respond to coarse wheat bran (10–30 g daily); symptom scores, stool data and transit of a standard solid meal were measured at baseline and after five weeks of treatment with placebo and with loperamide in a flexible dosage regime, in double-blind crossover order.
cards.result: Loperamide accelerated gastric emptying compared with placebo (1.2 ± 0.1 vs 1.5 ± 0.1 hr; P less than 0.001) and delayed both small bowel transit (6.2 ± 0.3 vs 4.3 ± 0.3 hr; P less than 0.001) and whole gut transit (56 ± 5 vs 42 ± 4 hr; P less than 0.01). Eighteen patients said they felt better taking loperamide compared with placebo and, at follow up, 15 of these patients remained satisfied with the effects of the drug. Most symptoms improved significantly on placebo compared with baseline, but three — diarrhoea (P less than 0.01), urgency (P less than 0.01) and borborygmi (P less than 0.05) — showed a further significant improvement on loperamide. Improvement in diarrhoea was not associated with any change in stool weight but was associated with reductions in stool frequency (P less than 0.001), passage of unformed stools (P less than 0.01), and incidence of urgency (P less than 0.001).
cards.watchOut: An irritable-bowel population with a flexible dose (the abstract does not print the dose), and the follow-up satisfaction figure is uncontrolled — patients who liked the drug kept taking it. What the card establishes is 5-week placebo-controlled benefit plus a hint of durability: most responders were still satisfied at follow-up, the closest any card on this shelf comes to long-term daily use.
cards.source: Cann PA, Read NW, Holdsworth CD, Barends D. Role of loperamide and placebo in management of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 1984. PMID: 6365490. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Lavö 1987 (13 weeks — the longest placebo-controlled test): significant advantages for stool consistency (p less than 0.001), pain (p less than 0.02), urgency (p less than 0.05) and overall response (p less than 0.03); nightly self-titration 'safe and efficient'
cards.summary: Lavö 1987 (13 weeks — the longest placebo-controlled test): significant advantages for stool consistency (p less than 0.001), pain (p less than 0.02), urgency (p less than 0.05) and overall response (p less than 0.03); nightly self-titration 'safe and efficient'
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial over 13 weeks in irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea (Lavö, Stenstam & Nielsen 1987)
cards.people: 25 patients with irritable bowel syndrome, all with diarrhoea as a main symptom; 21 completed the 13-week trial (11 in the loperamide group and 10 in the placebo group). Subjective overall response, stool consistency and six individual symptoms (urgency, pain, frequency, flatulence, borborygmi and painful propulsions) were studied; dose was self-titrated and given as a single nightly dose.
cards.result: A significant advantage for loperamide was found for stool consistency (p less than 0.001), pain (p less than 0.02) and urgency (p less than 0.05). Subjective overall response was also significantly better in the loperamide group (p less than 0.03). Self-titration of dose and administration in a single nightly dose was safe and efficient.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen weeks is the ceiling of the controlled evidence on this shelf — nothing carded here runs longer, so 'long-term daily use' beyond three months is extrapolation, not trial evidence. The abstract gives p-values without group means, and the population is irritable bowel syndrome rather than chronic diarrhoea of all causes; 'safe' is the authors' summary of a 21-completer trial, not a powered safety finding.
cards.source: Lavö B, Stenstam M, Nielsen AL. Loperamide in treatment of irritable bowel syndrome--a double-blind placebo controlled study. Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology. Supplement. 1987. PMID: 3306903. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: FDA 2016 (updated 2018): serious heart problems and deaths occur with 'much higher than the recommended doses', primarily in intentional misuse or abuse — maxima 8 mg/day over-the-counter and 16 mg/day prescription; 'safe at approved doses'
cards.summary: FDA 2016 (updated 2018): serious heart problems and deaths occur with 'much higher than the recommended doses', primarily in intentional misuse or abuse — maxima 8 mg/day over-the-counter and 16 mg/day prescription; 'safe at approved doses'
cards.type: Regulatory communication — FDA Drug Safety Communication (not a trial)
cards.people: United States Food and Drug Administration safety announcement of 7 June 2016 (FDA warns about serious heart problems with high doses of the antidiarrheal medicine loperamide (Imodium), including from abuse and misuse), updated 30 January 2018 with packaging limits to encourage safe use; addressed to patients, consumers and health care professionals.
cards.result: The FDA states that loperamide 'is a safe drug when used as directed' and 'is safe at approved doses', and gives the maximum approved daily dose for adults as 8 mg per day for over-the-counter use and 16 mg per day for prescription use. It warns that the agency continues to receive reports of serious heart problems and deaths with much higher than the recommended doses of loperamide, primarily among people who are intentionally misusing or abusing the product, and that using much higher than recommended doses, either intentionally or unintentionally, can result in serious cardiac adverse events, including QT interval prolongation, Torsades de Pointes or other ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, and cardiac arrest. In cases of abuse, individuals often use other drugs together with loperamide in attempts to increase its absorption and penetration across the blood-brain barrier, inhibit loperamide metabolism, and enhance its euphoric effects; some individuals take high doses of loperamide to treat symptoms of opioid withdrawal. The 2018 update works with manufacturers to use blister packs or other single-dose packaging and to limit the number of doses in a package.
cards.watchOut: A regulatory communication, not a trial: it reports the pattern of spontaneous reports (harm concentrated at much-higher-than-recommended doses, mainly intentional misuse or abuse) and states the labelled maxima — it does not estimate a risk at therapeutic doses, and its reassurance ('safe at approved doses') is the regulator's summary, quoted as such. Carded explicitly as a regulatory source per the shelf's rules.

cards.headline: Bekka 2026 (systematic review of supratherapeutic exposure, 129 cases): median dose 200 mg/day, syncope in 45%, severe cardiotoxicity in 64%, fatalities in 13% — dose-dependent, with severe toxicity reported from 20–40 mg/day
cards.summary: Bekka 2026 (systematic review of supratherapeutic exposure, 129 cases): median dose 200 mg/day, syncope in 45%, severe cardiotoxicity in 64%, fatalities in 13% — dose-dependent, with severe toxicity reported from 20–40 mg/day
cards.type: Systematic review and dose–response analysis of case reports and case series of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure (Bekka et al. 2026)
cards.people: 129 published cases of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure (defined as more than 16 mg per day), identified through Medline/PubMed, Embase and Scopus, citation and conference-abstract searches; median age 31 years (IQR 26–39), 66% (n = 85) male, 57% (n = 73) with known or suspected substance use disorder; 91% (n = 117) were chronic or subacute exposures.
cards.result: The median daily ingested dose was 200 mg (IQR 113–343, n = 112) and the median blood concentration was 87 µg/L (IQR 33–210, n = 39). Syncope was frequently reported (45%, n = 58). Severe cases (64%, n = 83) were mainly characterised by polymorphic (55%, n = 46) or sustained monomorphic (40%, n = 33) ventricular tachycardias. Typical signs of opioid toxicity were reported in only 12% (n = 16) of cases. Severity was dose-dependent (adjusted OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01–1.07, per 10 mg), with severe toxicity occurring at doses as low as 20–40 mg/day and a median severe toxicity dose (TD50) estimated at 85 mg (95% CI 12–230 mg). Fatalities were reported in 13% of the cases (n = 17) and mortality was positively associated with concentration (adjusted OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01–1.16, per 10 µg/L), with a median lethal concentration (LC50) estimated at 210 µg/L (95% CI 70–436 μg/L). Bradycardia was independently associated with severity (adjusted OR 4.96, 95% CI 1.83–15.45). Purposeful co-ingestion of substances to increase loperamide exposure was reported in 5% of cases (n = 6, all cimetidine). The authors conclude that patients presenting with supratherapeutic loperamide exposure appear to be at high risk for life-threatening dysrhythmias and that close cardiac monitoring should be broadly considered in this population.
cards.watchOut: A case-report literature, not a cohort: the percentages are proportions among published cases (which select for drama), not risks for a user — 13% fatalities among reported cases does not mean 13% of supratherapeutic users die. Its two lessons for this shelf are the dose geography — the typical case took about twelve times the prescription maximum, in a substance-use context — and the warning at its edge: severe toxicity has been reported from 20–40 mg/day, only just above the 16 mg/day ceiling, so dose creep in chronic daily use is not a safe direction.
cards.source: Bekka E, Martinez-De la Torre A, Haschke M, Liakoni E, Weiler S. Toxicity profile of supratherapeutic loperamide: a systematic review and dose-response analysis. Clinical Toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2026. PMID: 41817965. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review of published cases). cards.headline: Synthesis: effective for weeks at 4–6 mg/day with a quiet therapeutic-dose record — and a cardiac harm record that starts above the labelled ceiling, not at it
cards.summary: Synthesis: effective for weeks at 4–6 mg/day with a quiet therapeutic-dose record — and a cardiac harm record that starts above the labelled ceiling, not at it
cards.people: Seven sources: five double-blind trials in chronic diarrhoea and diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (Mainguet 1977, 18 completers; Tytgat 1976, 15 chronic-diarrhoea patients plus 20 ileostomy patients; Palmer 1980, 30 patients; Cann 1984, 28 patients; Lavö 1987, 21 completers), the FDA Drug Safety Communication of 2016 (updated 2018), and a systematic review of 129 supratherapeutic-exposure cases (Bekka 2026). Acute diarrhoea is not covered here — it is homed at Shelf #2478.
cards.result: Efficacy beyond a week: loperamide beat placebo on stool frequency, stool weight or consistency and urgency in every placebo-controlled card, at median or typical doses of about 4–6 mg/day (Mainguet 6 mg/day; Palmer 4.6 mg/day; Tytgat individually optimal 4–14 mg/day), over treatment periods of ten days (blinded maintenance, Tytgat), 4 weeks per drug (Palmer), 5 weeks (Cann) and 13 weeks (Lavö); ileostomy output fell by 22% relative (Tytgat). Safety at therapeutic doses: gastrointestinal side-effects few and comparable to placebo (Mainguet), fewest side-effects among the antidiarrhoeals compared (Palmer), nightly self-titration described as safe over 13 weeks (Lavö), and the FDA's position that the drug is safe at approved doses (maxima 8 mg/day over-the-counter, 16 mg/day prescription). Safety above the ceiling: QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, ventricular tachycardias, syncope, cardiac arrest and death in the abuse literature — median dose 200 mg/day, 57% with substance use disorder, severe cases 64% and fatalities 13% of 129 published cases, severity dose-dependent with severe toxicity reported from 20–40 mg/day (Bekka 2026; FDA 2016/2018). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) at therapeutic doses, Tier C — the benefit is consistent across five small old double-blind trials and sustained to 13 weeks; the long-term gap (no controlled data beyond 13 weeks) and the narrow margin above the labelled maximum are stated on the face.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Three cautions: (1) every efficacy trial is small (15–30 patients), old (1976–1987) and at most 13 weeks — 'long-term daily use' for months to years has no controlled trial behind it, only follow-up satisfaction (Cann) and the absence of a therapeutic-dose harm signal; (2) loperamide treats the symptom, not the cause — chronic diarrhoea still needs its cause investigated, and nothing here covers bloody diarrhoea, dysentery, or use where slowing the gut could be unsafe; (3) the therapeutic and supratherapeutic records must stay separate — the cardiac deaths belong to doses around twelve times the prescription maximum taken for opioid effects, but the margin is thin at the top: severe toxicity has been reported from 20–40 mg/day.

tytgat 1976, 15 chronic-diarrhoea patients plus 20 ileostomy patients; palmer 1980, 30 patients; cann 1984, 28 patients; lavö 1987, 21 completers), the fda drug safety communication of 2016 (updated 2018), and a systematic review of 129 supratherapeutic-exposure cases (bekka 2026). acute diarrhoea is not covered here — it is homed at shelf #2478. efficacy beyond a week: loperamide beat placebo on stool frequency, stool weight or consistency and urgency in every placebo-controlled card, at median or typical doses of about 4–6 mg/day (mainguet 6 mg/day; palmer 4.6 mg/day; tytgat individually optimal 4–14 mg/day), over treatment periods of ten days (blinded maintenance, tytgat), 4 weeks per drug (palmer), 5 weeks (cann) and 13 weeks (lavö); ileostomy output fell by 22% relative (tytgat). safety at therapeutic doses: gastrointestinal side-effects few and comparable to placebo (mainguet), fewest side-effects among the antidiarrhoeals compared (palmer), nightly self-titration described as safe over 13 weeks (lavö), and the fda's position that the drug is safe at approved doses (maxima 8 mg/day over-the-counter, 16 mg/day prescription). safety above the ceiling: qt prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardias, syncope, cardiac arrest and death in the abuse literature — median dose 200 mg/day, 57% with substance use disorder, severe cases 64% and fatalities 13% of 129 published cases, severity dose-dependent with severe toxicity reported from 20–40 mg/day (bekka 2026; shelves.title: Standby antibiotics for travellers' diarrhoea: carry one and reserve it for moderate-to-severe illness — azithromycin first (the only defensible default for South-East Asia and for dysentery), ciprofloxacin undermined by resistance (75% of Campylobacter isolates fluoroquinolone-nonsusceptible), rifaximin only for non-invasive illness — and every course taken raises resistant gut colonisation
shelves.question: Should travellers to high-risk regions carry a standby antibiotic to self-treat travellers' diarrhoea — and if so, which one: azithromycin, ciprofloxacin (or another fluoroquinolone), or rifaximin — given current fluoroquinolone-resistance patterns?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Campylobacter/drug effects · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage · Cross-Sectional Studies · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Diarrhea/microbiology · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Enterobacteriaceae/isolation & purification · Humans · Loperamide/administration & dosage · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Prospective Studies · Self Care · Travel
shelves.balance: LIKELY — yes, carry one, but the carrying is not the treatment decision: the graded expert-panel guideline (Riddle 2017, PMID: 28521004) advises that most if not all travellers be provided with loperamide and an antibiotic for self-treatment, then gates its use by severity — no antibiotic for mild diarrhoea, antibiotics may be used for moderate diarrhoea, and antibiotics should be used for severe diarrhoea, with azithromycin preferred in severe illness and single-dose regimens acceptable. The benefit being bought is time: in the fluoroquinolone-susceptible era a single carried 500 mg dose of ciprofloxacin cut mean diarrhoea duration from 50.4 hours on placebo to 20.9 hours (Salam 1994, PMID: 7983954). The drug choice has since been decided by resistance, not by preference. In Thailand, 51 of 57 Campylobacter isolates (89%) were ciprofloxacin-resistant while azithromycin resistance was 2% (Mason 2017, PMID: 28883983); fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter rose in Thailand from zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995 and has since spread to enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, Shigella and non-typhoidal Salmonella (Tribble 2017, PMID: 28520997); and in the current GeoSentinel series (859 cases, 2015–2022), fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility was 75% in Campylobacter, 32% in non-typhoidal Salmonella, 22% in Shigella and 18% in diarrhoeagenic E. coli, against macrolide nonsusceptibility of 12% in Campylobacter — though 35% in Shigella (Amatya 2025, PMID: 41591385). Hence the guideline's regional rule: azithromycin for South-East Asia; a fluoroquinolone, azithromycin or rifaximin elsewhere. Rifaximin is the narrowest choice, not a substitute: it is less effective against invasive pathogens, with failure to achieve wellness in up to 50% of treated subjects in the guideline's summary, invasive pathogens account for approximately 10–20% of cases, and it is not appropriate for dysentery at any severity — if rifaximin is the carried first-line agent, azithromycin should also be carried for dysentery or febrile diarrhoea (Riddle 2017). The counterweight is colonisation, and it is quantified: among 430 travellers, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae acquisition was 11% with neither diarrhoea nor antibiotic, 21% with diarrhoea alone and 37% with diarrhoea plus an antibiotic — reaching 80% in South Asia and 69% in South-East Asia when diarrhoea and an antibiotic combined (Kantele 2015, PMID: 25613287); and among 288 travellers with diarrhoea, colonisation was 21% with no medication, 20% with loperamide alone, 40% with an antimicrobial alone and 71% with the guideline-style combination of loperamide plus an antimicrobial (Kantele 2016, PMID: 26691898). So: carry azithromycin as the default standby (the only one of the three that covers dysentery and fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter), hold it for moderate-to-severe illness, and treat ciprofloxacin as a legacy choice whose susceptibility can no longer be assumed. The head-to-head treatment trials behind these choices are homed elsewhere and are not re-carded here: rifaximin treatment at Shelf #4602, azithromycin plus loperamide at Shelf #4603, the single-dose azithromycin Thailand trial and TrEAT TD at Shelf #1213; prophylaxis questions sit at Shelf #4216 (bismuth) and Shelf #1214 (rifaximin prophylaxis) — this shelf is the carry-and-self-treat decision and the drug choice only.

cards.headline: Riddle 2017 (graded expert-panel guideline): most if not all travellers should be provided with an antibiotic for self-treatment — none for mild diarrhoea, may for moderate, should for severe; azithromycin preferred in severe illness and prescribed for South-East Asia; rifaximin not for dysentery
cards.summary: Riddle 2017 (graded expert-panel guideline): most if not all travellers should be provided with an antibiotic for self-treatment — none for mild diarrhoea, may for moderate, should for severe; azithromycin preferred in severe illness and prescribed for South-East Asia; rifaximin not for dysentery
cards.type: Graded expert-panel clinical practice guideline — critical appraisal of the literature plus expert consensus, NOT a trial (Riddle et al. 2017, International Society of Travel Medicine panel)
cards.people: A 15-member voting expert panel convened by the International Society of Travel Medicine; the guideline covers travellers from industrialised regions to higher-risk regions and addresses prophylaxis, diagnosis, therapy and follow-up, including how travellers should be directed on expectant management, over-the-counter agents, antibiotic use and seeking care during travel.
cards.result: The panel developed new functional severity definitions (mild: tolerable, does not interfere with planned activities; moderate: distressing or interferes; severe: incapacitating, and all dysentery — passage of grossly bloody stools — is severe), 20 graded recommendations and three non-graded consensus statements. On antibiotics: treatment is NOT recommended for mild travellers' diarrhoea (strong recommendation, moderate level of evidence); antibiotics MAY be used for moderate diarrhoea (weak recommendation, moderate level of evidence), with azithromycin a strong recommendation on high-level evidence and fluoroquinolones and rifaximin also listed with qualifications; antibiotics SHOULD be used for severe diarrhoea (strong recommendation, high level of evidence), with azithromycin preferred (strong recommendation, moderate level of evidence); single-dose antibiotic regimens may be used for moderate or severe diarrhoea (strong recommendation, high level of evidence). The panel's take-home algorithm states that most if not all travellers should be provided with loperamide and an antibiotic for self-treatment; that if the traveller is going to South-East Asia, azithromycin should be prescribed, while a fluoroquinolone, azithromycin or rifaximin can be used in all other regions; and that if rifaximin is given as the first-line agent, azithromycin should also be given in case of dysentery or febrile diarrhoea. On rifaximin's limits, the guideline text states it has demonstrated comparable efficacy to fluoroquinolones in non-invasive diarrhoea caused by diarrhoeagenic E. coli, is less effective for invasive pathogens with failure to achieve wellness in up to 50% of treated subjects, that invasive pathogens such as Campylobacter, Salmonella and Shigella species may account for approximately 10–20% of cases, and that rifaximin therefore cannot be recommended for areas where these invasive pathogens are common and is not appropriate for treatment of dysentery irrespective of illness severity. Consensus statement 23 records an incrementally increasing association between travel, travellers' diarrhoea and antibiotic use and acquisition of multidrug-resistant bacteria, with pre-travel counselling to include that risk balanced against the benefits of antibiotic use. The abstract's conclusion: strong evidence supports antimicrobial therapy in most cases of moderate to severe travellers' diarrhoea, while fluids alone, loperamide or bismuth subsalicylate may suffice for most mild diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: This is a guideline/consensus document and is carded as one: its standby recommendation rests on the treatment-trial literature plus panel judgement, not on any randomised trial of carrying versus not carrying an antibiotic — no such trial is carded on this shelf because none was found. Its fluoroquinolone recommendations carry an explicit non-unanimous GRADE, with the panel citing emergence of resistance, dysbiosis and musculoskeletal harms as uncertainties. The treatment trials the guideline appraises are homed on their own shelves and are not re-carded here: rifaximin treatment at Shelf #4602, azithromycin plus loperamide at Shelf #4603, and the single-dose azithromycin Thailand trial and TrEAT TD at Shelf #1213.
cards.source: Riddle MS, Connor BA, Beeching NJ, DuPont HL, Hamer DH, Kozarsky P, Libman M, Steffen R, Taylor D, Tribble DR, Vila J, Zanger P, Ericsson CD. Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of travelers' diarrhea: a graded expert panel report. Journal of Travel Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28521004. Registry ID: none in the record (guideline; no trial registration). cards.headline: Diemert 2006 (self-treatment review): between 20% and 50% of travellers develop diarrhoea, and effective treatment — usually an antibiotic plus an antimotility agent — can be brought by the traveller and started as soon as symptoms develop
cards.summary: Diemert 2006 (self-treatment review): between 20% and 50% of travellers develop diarrhoea, and effective treatment — usually an antibiotic plus an antimotility agent — can be brought by the traveller and started as soon as symptoms develop
cards.type: Narrative review of prevention and self-treatment of travellers' diarrhoea (Diemert 2006)
cards.people: Review of the literature on travellers from the industrialised world to developing countries, covering food and water precautions, non-pharmacological and antimicrobial prophylaxis, and traveller-initiated treatment.
cards.result: Of the millions who travel from the industrialised world to developing countries every year, between 20% and 50% will develop at least one episode of diarrhoea, making it the most common medical ailment afflicting travellers; although usually a mild illness, it can result in significant morbidity and hardship overseas. If diarrhoea develops despite precautions, effective treatment — usually a combination of an antibiotic and an antimotility agent — can be brought by the traveller and initiated as soon as symptoms develop.
cards.watchOut: A 2006 review stating the classic carry-and-start-early position in its pre-resistance-surge form: it predates both the 2017 severity-gated guideline (carded above) and the ESBL colonisation data (carded below), so its 'as soon as symptoms develop' timing is broader than the current severity threshold — read it as the historical rationale for standby carriage, with Riddle 2017 supplying the modern gate. Prophylaxis evidence is a separate question, homed at Shelf #4216 (bismuth prophylaxis) and Shelf #1214 (rifaximin prophylaxis).
cards.source: Diemert DJ. Prevention and self-treatment of traveler's diarrhea. Clinical Microbiology Reviews. 2006. PMID: 16847088. Registry ID: none in the record (review). cards.headline: Salam 1994 (the susceptible-era proof): a single carried 500 mg dose of ciprofloxacin cut mean diarrhoea duration from 50.4 hours on placebo to 20.9 hours, and liquid stools from 11.4 to 5.0
cards.summary: Salam 1994 (the susceptible-era proof): a single carried 500 mg dose of ciprofloxacin cut mean diarrhoea duration from 50.4 hours on placebo to 20.9 hours, and liquid stools from 11.4 to 5.0
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of single-dose ciprofloxacin for travellers' diarrhoea (Salam, Katelaris, Leigh-Smith & Farthing 1994)
cards.people: 88 British troops within their first 8 weeks of deployment in Belize who presented within 24 hours of the onset of diarrhoea, randomised to a single 500 mg dose of ciprofloxacin or placebo; 83 were evaluable (45 ciprofloxacin, 38 placebo), each recording stool number and consistency and associated symptoms for 72 hours or until recovery.
cards.result: Mean (SE) duration of diarrhoea, as time to the last liquid stool and last unformed stool, was reduced from 50.4 (4.5) hours and 53.5 (4.4) hours respectively in the placebo group to 20.9 (3.4) hours and 24.8 (3.8) hours in the ciprofloxacin group (p < 0.0001). Mean number of liquid stools was reduced from 11.4 (1.2) on placebo to 5.0 (0.7) on ciprofloxacin (p < 0.0001). The cumulative percentages with no unformed stool after 24, 48 and 72 hours were 64%, 82% and 93% on ciprofloxacin versus 11%, 42% and 79% on placebo (p < 0.0001, p < 0.001, and not significant, respectively). The authors concluded that a single 500 mg dose was effective empirical treatment that should maximise compliance and reduce the cost and duration of therapy.
cards.watchOut: This is the benefit case for standby self-treatment in its cleanest form — one dose, taken early, roughly halving a two-day illness — but it is a 1994 Central America trial from before fluoroquinolone resistance reshaped the choice: it shows what a working standby antibiotic buys, not that ciprofloxacin still works where the traveller is going. The resistance cards below (Mason 2017; Tribble 2017; Amatya 2025) are why the drug in the bag has changed even though this trial's logic has not. Young male military population, presenting within 24 hours — civilian travellers who start later may gain less.
cards.source: Salam I, Katelaris P, Leigh-Smith S, Farthing MJ. Randomised trial of single-dose ciprofloxacin for travellers' diarrhoea. The Lancet. 1994. PMID: 7983954. cards.headline: Mason 2017 (Thailand isolates): 51 of 57 Campylobacter isolates (89%) were ciprofloxacin-resistant, while azithromycin resistance stayed at 2% — the local arithmetic behind choosing azithromycin for South-East Asia
cards.summary: Mason 2017 (Thailand isolates): 51 of 57 Campylobacter isolates (89%) were ciprofloxacin-resistant, while azithromycin resistance stayed at 2% — the local arithmetic behind choosing azithromycin for South-East Asia
cards.type: Case-control study with antimicrobial resistance description of diarrhoeal isolates, US military deployed to Thailand 2002–2004 (Mason et al. 2017)
cards.people: 217 deployed US military personnel in Thailand, 2002–2004: 155 who presented to a field medical unit with acute diarrhoea enrolled as cases, plus 62 diarrhoea-free colleagues as controls; pathogen isolation frequencies were compared and antibiotic resistance of isolates described.
cards.result: Of the 155 subjects with diarrhoea, Campylobacter species was the most commonly identified pathogen, found in 54 (35%), followed by non-typhoidal Salmonella species in 36 (23%). Of the 57 separate Campylobacter jejuni and Campylobacter coli isolates, 51 (89%) were resistant to ciprofloxacin by the disc diffusion method. Nearly one-third of the Campylobacter species were resistant to ampicillin and to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Resistance to azithromycin remained low at 2% (n = 1). The authors concluded that the significant morbidity and marked fluoroquinolone resistance associated with Campylobacter infections in Thailand are important considerations when counselling on appropriate antibacterial regimens for civilian and military travellers.
cards.watchOut: Isolates from one deployed military population in one country in 2002–2004 — the rate is a Thailand/South-East Asia figure, not a global one, and disc-diffusion resistance is a laboratory category rather than a measured clinical failure rate. Its role on this shelf is narrow and decisive: in the region where Campylobacter predominates, the fluoroquinolone in the standby bag was already inactive against roughly nine of ten isolates two decades ago, while the macrolide was not. The head-to-head Thailand treatment trial that tested this clinically is homed at Shelf #1213 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Mason CJ, Sornsakrin S, Seidman JC, Srijan A, Serichantalergs O, Thongsen N, Ellis MW, Ngauy V, Swierczewski BE, Bodhidatta L. pathogen isolation frequencies were compared and antibiotic resistance of isolates described. of the 155 subjects with diarrhoea, campylobacter species was the most commonly identified pathogen, found in 54 (35%), followed by non-typhoidal salmonella species in 36 (23%). of the 57 separate campylobacter jejuni and campylobacter coli isolates, 51 (89%) were resistant to ciprofloxacin by the disc diffusion method. nearly one-third of the campylobacter species were resistant to ampicillin and to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. resistance to azithromycin remained low at 2% (n = 1). the authors concluded that the significant morbidity and marked fluoroquinolone resistance associated with campylobacter infections in thailand are important considerations when counselling on appropriate antibacterial regimens for civilian and military travellers. isolates from one deployed military population in one country in 2002–2004 — the rate is a thailand/south-east asia figure, not a global one, and disc-diffusion resistance is a laboratory category rather than a measured clinical failure rate. its role on this shelf is narrow and decisive: in the region where campylobacter predominates, the fluoroquinolone in the standby bag was already inactive against roughly nine of ten isolates two decades ago, while the macrolide was not. the head-to-head thailand treatment trial that tested this clinically is homed at shelf #1213 and is not re-carded here. mason cj, sornsakrin s, seidman jc, srijan a, serichantalergs o, thongsen n, ellis mw, ngauy v, swierczewski be, bodhidatta l. antibiotic resistance in campylobacter and other diarrheal pathogens isolated from us military personnel deployed to thailand in 2002-2004: a case-control study. tropical diseases, travel medicine and vaccines. 2017. pmid: 28883983. registry id: none in the record. mesh: none in the record.

cards.headline: Tribble 2017 (resistance review): fluoroquinolone resistance grew out of 1990s South-East Asian Campylobacter — Thailand, zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995 — and has since spread to E. coli, Shigella and Salmonella, with treatment failures recovering at placebo-like rates
cards.summary: Tribble 2017 (resistance review): fluoroquinolone resistance grew out of 1990s South-East Asian Campylobacter — Thailand, zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995 — and has since spread to E. coli, Shigella and Salmonella, with treatment failures recovering at placebo-like rates
cards.type: Systematic narrative review of antimicrobial resistance among travellers' diarrhoea enteropathogens (Tribble 2017)
cards.people: Review of the traveller-population literature: the PubMed database was systematically searched for articles on antibiotic susceptibility and diarrhoeal pathogens, covering Campylobacter species, enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, Shigella and non-typhoidal Salmonella.
cards.result: Antibiotic resistance related to travellers' diarrhoea has increased in recent years: fluoroquinolone resistance has expanded from the Campylobacter-associated cases well documented in South-East Asia in the 1990s to widespread occurrence, with increases also among enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative E. coli, Shigella and non-typhoidal Salmonella, and multidrug resistance among enteropathogenic Enterobacteriaceae and Campylobacter species further challenging empirical therapy. The review's full text quantifies the Thai emergence: fluoroquinolone resistance among Campylobacter species increased from zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995; in a separate traveller analysis Campylobacter jejuni caused 41% of confirmed bacterial enteritis cases, 53% of its isolates were norfloxacin-resistant, and clinical failure occurred in 33% of patients prescribed fluoroquinolones. The abstract records that treatment failures requiring early use of alternative agents, and delayed recovery comparable to placebo rates, emphasise the impact of resistance on effective treatment; the authors conclude that increasing resistance and its adverse impact on clinical outcome require continued surveillance and reconsideration of practice guidelines.
cards.watchOut: A review, carded for the resistance trajectory and its clinical consequences rather than as primary data — the primary isolate numbers on this shelf are Mason 2017 (Thailand) and Amatya 2025 (GeoSentinel). Resistance percentages are assembled from heterogeneous sources, eras and breakpoints, so they frame a direction and an order of magnitude; they are not a destination-by-destination table, and none is offered here.

cards.headline: Amatya 2025 (GeoSentinel, 859 cases, current patterns): fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility 75% in Campylobacter, 32% in Salmonella, 22% in Shigella, 18% in E. coli — macrolide nonsusceptibility lower for Campylobacter (12%) but 35% in Shigella
cards.summary: Amatya 2025 (GeoSentinel, 859 cases, current patterns): fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility 75% in Campylobacter, 32% in Salmonella, 22% in Shigella, 18% in E. coli — macrolide nonsusceptibility lower for Campylobacter (12%) but 35% in Shigella
cards.type: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of antimicrobial susceptibility in culture-confirmed travellers' diarrhoea, GeoSentinel Surveillance Network 2015–2022 (Amatya et al. 2025)
cards.people: 859 international travellers with acute diarrhoea and culture-confirmed Campylobacter species, non-typhoidal Salmonella species, Shigella species or diarrhoeagenic Escherichia coli, reported from 14 April 2015 to 19 December 2022 at 58 of 71 GeoSentinel sites; median (IQR) age 30 (23–43) years, 440 (51%) male; intermediate and resistant results were grouped as nonsusceptible.
cards.result: Among Campylobacter isolates, nonsusceptibility to fluoroquinolones was found in 206 of 274 isolates (75%; 95% CI, 70%–80%) and nonsusceptibility to macrolides in 30 of 255 isolates (12%; 95% CI, 8%–16%); Campylobacter fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility was highest in travellers to South Central Asia (45 of 51 isolates; 88%; 95% CI, 76%–96%). Among non-typhoidal Salmonella species, 96 of 302 isolates (32%; 95% CI, 27%–37%) were nonsusceptible to fluoroquinolones, 18 of 111 (16%; 95% CI, 10%–24%) to macrolides and 15 of 273 (5%; 95% CI, 3%–9%) to third-generation cephalosporins. For Shigella species, 44 of 196 isolates (22%; 95% CI, 17%–29%) were nonsusceptible to fluoroquinolones and 36 of 103 (35%; 95% CI, 26%–45%) to macrolides; of note, 19 of 24 Shigella isolates (79%; 95% CI, 58%–93%) from travellers to South Central Asia were fluoroquinolone-nonsusceptible, and 29 of 37 Shigella isolates (78%; 95% CI, 62%–90%) from travellers to South America were macrolide-nonsusceptible. For E. coli, fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility was 18% (12 of 66 isolates; 95% CI, 10%–30%). The authors conclude there was marked variability in nonsusceptibility to the two major treatment classes across global regions, that culture susceptibility should be obtained when possible, and that the findings may inform strategies for self-treatment and clinician management of travellers' diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: A convenience sample of travellers ill enough to reach GeoSentinel clinics and have a positive culture — resistance among all diarrhoea episodes in all travellers will differ, and several regional cells are small (24 and 37 Shigella isolates), so the extreme regional percentages carry wide confidence intervals, printed beside them. Nonsusceptibility pools intermediate with resistant results. Even read cautiously, the ordering is the point for standby choice: fluoroquinolones now fail the commonest invasive pathogen (Campylobacter) three times in four, while azithromycin's weakness is concentrated in Shigella rather than spread across pathogens.

cards.headline: Kantele 2015 (the counterweight, 430 travellers): ESBL colonisation was 11% with neither diarrhoea nor antibiotic, 21% with diarrhoea alone, 37% with diarrhoea plus an antibiotic — and 80% in South Asia when both combined
cards.summary: Kantele 2015 (the counterweight, 430 travellers): ESBL colonisation was 11% with neither diarrhoea nor antibiotic, 21% with diarrhoea alone, 37% with diarrhoea plus an antibiotic — and 80% in South Asia when both combined
cards.type: Prospective traveller cohort with pre- and post-travel stool screening and multivariable analysis (Kantele et al. 2015)
cards.people: 430 Finns travelling outside Scandinavia, with stool samples collected before and after travel and analysed for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL-PE) and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE), and questionnaires on antimicrobial use and other risk factors.
cards.result: Twenty-one percent (90/430) of the travellers became colonised by ESBL-PE and none by CPE. Geographic region, occurrence of travellers' diarrhoea, age, and use of an antimicrobial for travellers' diarrhoea were independent risk factors for contracting ESBL-PE. Eleven percent of those with neither diarrhoea nor an antimicrobial, 21% of those with diarrhoea but no antimicrobial, and 37% of those with diarrhoea plus an antimicrobial acquired ESBL-PE. The risk was highest in South Asia (46% overall), where 23% became colonised with neither factor, 47% with diarrhoea alone, and 80% with diarrhoea plus an antimicrobial; in South-East Asia the corresponding rates were 14%, 37% and 69%. The authors concluded that travellers' diarrhoea and antimicrobials for it are independent risk factors, with up to 80% of the diarrhoea-plus-antibiotic group contracting ESBL-PE, and that in modern pre-travel counselling for high-risk regions travellers should be advised against taking antibiotics for mild or moderate travellers' diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Observational, not randomised: travellers who took an antibiotic had diarrhoea — usually worse diarrhoea — so part of the gradient is the illness and the destination, not the drug alone; the multivariable analysis is what separates the antimicrobial as an independent factor, and the authors' own advice (against antibiotics for mild or moderate illness) goes further than the 2017 guideline's 'may use' for moderate illness. Colonisation is carriage on return screening, not infection — most carriers never become ill from it — but it is the mechanism by which standby use exports resistance to households and hospitals, which is why this card disciplines how readily the carried antibiotic should be taken, not whether it should be carried.
cards.source: Kantele A, Lääveri T, Mero S, Vilkman K, Pakkanen SH, Ollgren J, Antikainen J, Kirveskari J. Antimicrobials increase travelers' risk of colonization by extended-spectrum betalactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2015. PMID: 25613287. cards.headline: Kantele 2016 (the combination warning): among 288 travellers with diarrhoea, ESBL colonisation was 21% with no medication, 20% with loperamide alone, 40% with an antimicrobial alone — and 71% with loperamide plus an antimicrobial
cards.summary: Kantele 2016 (the combination warning): among 288 travellers with diarrhoea, ESBL colonisation was 21% with no medication, 20% with loperamide alone, 40% with an antimicrobial alone — and 71% with loperamide plus an antimicrobial
cards.type: Analysis of travellers with diarrhoea within the prospective Finnish traveller cohort (Kantele, Mero, Kirveskari & Lääveri 2016)
cards.people: 288 travellers with travellers' diarrhoea drawn from the 430-traveller prospective Finnish cohort, grouped by what they took for the episode: no medication, loperamide only, antimicrobial drugs alone, or loperamide and antimicrobial drugs together; post-travel stool screening for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
cards.result: Antimicrobial treatment of travellers' diarrhoea is known to increase the risk of colonisation with ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae. Among the 288 travellers with travellers' diarrhoea, the colonisation rate was 21% without medications, 20% with loperamide only, 40% with antimicrobial drugs alone, and 71% with loperamide and antimicrobial drugs combined.
cards.watchOut: Small subgroups and an observational split — travellers who reached for both drugs plausibly had the most severe episodes and the heaviest pathogen exposure, so 71% is an association in the worst-affected stratum, not a randomised estimate of the combination's added harm. It still matters for standby instructions, because loperamide plus an antibiotic is exactly the pairing the guideline recommends for rapid relief: the fastest symptomatic route and the highest colonisation rate are the same route, which is an argument for reserving the pair for illness that is genuinely disrupting the trip. The parent cohort is carded above (Kantele 2015); the azithromycin-plus-loperamide treatment trial itself is homed at Shelf #4603 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Kantele A, Mero S, Kirveskari J, Lääveri T. Increased Risk for ESBL-Producing Bacteria from Co-administration of Loperamide and Antimicrobial Drugs for Travelers' Diarrhea. Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2016. PMID: 26691898. Registry ID: none in the record (observational analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: carry azithromycin, gate it by severity, and leave ciprofloxacin behind — the standby logic survived; the standby drug did not
cards.summary: Synthesis: carry azithromycin, gate it by severity, and leave ciprofloxacin behind — the standby logic survived; the standby drug did not
cards.people: Eight sources: the graded expert-panel guideline (Riddle 2017), a self-treatment review (Diemert 2006), one susceptible-era randomised trial of single-dose standby-style treatment (Salam 1994, 83 evaluable), two resistance datasets (Mason 2017, 57 Thailand Campylobacter isolates; Amatya 2025, 859 GeoSentinel cases), a resistance review (Tribble 2017), and two prospective colonisation analyses from one Finnish cohort (Kantele 2015, 430 travellers; Kantele 2016, 288 with diarrhoea).
cards.result: Carry or not: the guideline advises providing most if not all travellers with loperamide and an antibiotic for self-treatment (Riddle 2017), the self-treatment literature frames the antibiotic-plus-antimotility combination as brought by the traveller and started when symptoms develop (Diemert 2006), and the value of a working single dose taken early was a halving of illness duration — 20.9 versus 50.4 hours to the last liquid stool (Salam 1994). Gate: no antibiotic for mild diarrhoea, optional for moderate, recommended for severe, with counselling that antibiotic use is associated with multidrug-resistant colonisation (Riddle 2017). Which drug: azithromycin — preferred for severe illness, prescribed for South-East Asia, and the required companion whenever rifaximin is carried, because rifaximin fails against invasive pathogens in up to 50% and is not appropriate for dysentery (Riddle 2017); the resistance record explains why — Campylobacter ciprofloxacin resistance 89% with azithromycin resistance 2% in Thailand (Mason 2017), a Thai fluoroquinolone-resistance rise from zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995 with later spread to E. coli, Shigella and Salmonella (Tribble 2017), and current fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility of 75% (Campylobacter), 32% (Salmonella), 22% (Shigella) and 18% (E. coli) against 12% macrolide nonsusceptibility in Campylobacter (Amatya 2025). Ciprofloxacin remains a guideline-listed option outside South-East Asia, but no fetched source supports assuming its susceptibility anywhere Campylobacter matters. Price of use: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae colonisation in 37% after diarrhoea plus an antibiotic versus 11% with neither (80% in South Asia), and 71% when loperamide and an antimicrobial were combined versus 21% untreated (Kantele 2015; Kantele 2016). PROPOSED LIKELY — the carry-and-self-treat strategy is guideline-endorsed and its benefit is trial-anchored, the azithromycin-first choice follows consistently from every resistance dataset fetched, and the colonisation cost is the reason the antibiotic stays in the bag for mild illness rather than a reason to leave it at home.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. No randomised trial of the carry decision itself was found: the standby recommendation is expert-panel guidance built on treatment trials, and those trials are homed on their own shelves (rifaximin treatment #4602; azithromycin plus loperamide #4603; single-dose azithromycin Thailand trial and TrEAT TD #1213; rifaximin prophylaxis #1214; bismuth prophylaxis #4216) and deliberately not re-carded here. Nothing on this shelf covers children, pregnancy, immunocompromised travellers, cholera, or persistent diarrhoea beyond 14 days, each of which changes the advice. Fluoroquinolone adverse effects (tendon, nerve, aortic and metabolic warnings) were not carded — no fetched source on this shelf quantifies them — so the case against ciprofloxacin as printed here rests on resistance alone, which the panel judged sufficient.

shelves.title: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) safety in a day: 4 g/day — the labelled ceiling — pushed ALT past 3 times the upper limit of normal in 31–44% of healthy volunteers, while the liver-failure cohorts took a median of 24 g and staggered overdoses were stratified by the presenting AST
shelves.question: 'How much acetaminophen (paracetamol) is safe in a day?' — What does the evidence say about the 4 g/day ceiling: liver-enzyme effects at the ceiling in healthy adults and in newly abstinent alcoholics, and where liver injury actually concentrates in the repeated supratherapeutic-ingestion and acute-liver-failure cohorts?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Acetaminophen/poisoning · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Alcoholism/complications · Drug Overdose · Female · Humans · Liver Failure, Acute/chemically induced · Liver Failure, Acute/epidemiology · Liver Failure, Acute/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which side of the 4 g/day line the evidence sits. AT the ceiling: in the randomised trial of healthy adults taking exactly 4 g/day, the maximum recommended dose, 31–44% of acetaminophen recipients (including the acetaminophen-alone group) had a maximum ALT more than 3 times the upper limit of normal, versus none of 39 on placebo (Watkins 2006, PMID: 16820551) — a common laboratory signal, though no clinical liver injury was reported in that trial; and in newly abstinent alcoholic patients, 4 g/day for 3 days produced peak mean ALT values indistinguishable from placebo (57 ± 45 versus 55 ± 48 IU/L), with no transaminase increase attributed to the drug (Kuffner 2007, PMID: 17537264). ABOVE the ceiling is where the injury cohorts live: in the prospective poison-centre series of repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (>4 g/24 h), no patient whose presenting AST was below 50 IU/L went on to hepatotoxicity, while 15% of those presenting with AST 50–1,000 IU/L did and 16% of those above 1,000 IU/L died or were transplanted (Daly 2004, PMID: 15459622); and in the US acute liver failure registry, acetaminophen caused 42% of all cases, the median dose ingested was 24 g — six times the daily ceiling — and nearly half the cases (48%) were unintentional, often assembled from two or more acetaminophen products taken at once (Larson 2005, PMID: 16317692). PROPOSED SPLIT: at 4 g/day the demonstrated harm is a frequent, usually transient enzyme rise rather than liver failure; the catastrophic outcomes in the fetched record come from doses well above the ceiling or from staggered supratherapeutic use — which is why the practical safety question is less the single-product dose than the total from all products combined.

cards.headline: Watkins 2006: at exactly 4 g/day, 31–44% of healthy adults on acetaminophen had a maximum ALT over 3 times the upper limit of normal — versus 0 of 39 on placebo
cards.summary: Watkins 2006: at exactly 4 g/day, 31–44% of healthy adults on acetaminophen had a maximum ALT over 3 times the upper limit of normal — versus 0 of 39 on placebo
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled inpatient trial of 4 g/day acetaminophen in healthy adults (Watkins 2006)
cards.people: 145 healthy adults in 2 US inpatient clinical pharmacology units, randomised to placebo (n=39), one of three acetaminophen/opioid combinations (n=80), or acetaminophen alone (n=26); every active treatment delivered 4 g of acetaminophen daily, the maximum recommended daily dosage, with an intended duration of 14 days on a controlled diet.
cards.result: None of the 39 placebo participants had a maximum ALT of more than 3 times the upper limit of normal. In contrast, the incidence of maximum ALT more than 3 times the upper limit of normal was 31% to 44% across the four acetaminophen groups, including the group treated with acetaminophen alone. Median maximum ALT was markedly higher on acetaminophen than placebo (ratio of medians 2.78; 95% CI 1.47–4.09; P<.001). Trough acetaminophen concentrations never exceeded therapeutic limits in any participant. The authors concluded that starting recurrent daily intake of 4 g of acetaminophen in healthy adults is associated with ALT elevations, and that adding an opioid does not seem to increase the effect.
cards.watchOut: An enzyme signal is not liver failure: the abstract reports ALT elevations, not clinical hepatitis or liver failure, in healthy volunteers observed for at most 14 days. The trial answers 'does the ceiling dose stress the liver measurably?' (yes, in a third or more of people) — it does not show that 4 g/day causes liver failure, and it does not test doses above 4 g/day or months of use.
cards.source: Watkins PB, Kaplowitz N, Slattery JT, Colonese CR, Colucci SV, Stewart PW, Harris SC. Aminotransferase elevations in healthy adults receiving 4 grams of acetaminophen daily: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2006. PMID: 16820551. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kuffner 2007: in newly abstinent alcoholic patients, 4 g/day for 3 days looked no worse than placebo — peak mean ALT 57 ± 45 versus 55 ± 48 IU/L
cards.summary: Kuffner 2007: in newly abstinent alcoholic patients, 4 g/day for 3 days looked no worse than placebo — peak mean ALT 57 ± 45 versus 55 ± 48 IU/L
cards.type: Multicenter double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial in newly abstinent alcoholic patients (Kuffner 2007)
cards.people: 443 patients enrolled at 2 alcohol detoxification centres — 308 randomised to acetaminophen 4 g/day and 135 to placebo for 3 days; 258 acetaminophen and 114 placebo patients completed the study.
cards.result: Peak mean ALT was 57 ± 45 IU/L in the acetaminophen group and 55 ± 48 IU/L in the placebo group, and the investigators found no transaminase increases attributable to acetaminophen. Their conclusion: 3 days of acetaminophen at the maximum recommended dose appears to be safe in newly abstinent alcoholic patients.
cards.watchOut: Three days is the whole trial. It rebuts the specific fear that a few days at the ceiling dose is uniquely dangerous in people who have just stopped drinking; it says nothing about weeks of 4 g/day use, about people with established liver disease, or about doses above the ceiling.
cards.source: Kuffner EK, Green JL, Bogdan GM, Knox PC, Palmer RB, Heard K, Slattery JT, Dart RC. The effect of acetaminophen (four grams a day for three consecutive days) on hepatic tests in alcoholic patients — a multicenter randomized study. BMC Medicine. 2007. PMID: 17537264. cards.headline: Daly 2004 (staggered overdose): nobody presenting with AST below 50 IU/L developed hepatotoxicity — risk rose with the presenting AST, not just the reported dose
cards.summary: Daly 2004 (staggered overdose): nobody presenting with AST below 50 IU/L developed hepatotoxicity — risk rose with the presenting AST, not just the reported dose
cards.type: Prospective poison-centre case series of repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen ingestion (Daly 2004)
cards.people: Patients aged 12 years and older presenting after repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen ingestion (more than 4 g in 24 hours) and referred to a poison centre: 277 patients were eligible and 249 were enrolled and stratified by presenting AST.
cards.result: At presentation, AST was below 50 IU/L in 126 patients, 50–1,000 IU/L in 47, and above 1,000 IU/L in 37 (39 had no AST data). No patient with a presenting AST below 50 IU/L developed hepatotoxicity (defined as aminotransferases above 1,000 IU/L). Of the 47 with AST 50–1,000 IU/L, 7 (15%) developed hepatotoxicity and 1 died; of the 37 with AST above 1,000 IU/L, 6 (16%) died or underwent liver transplantation. Injury from repeated supratherapeutic ingestion was thus largely apparent at presentation and tracked the presenting enzyme level.
cards.watchOut: These are people who had already taken too much and come to hospital — a risk-stratification study of overdose presentations, not a study of ordinary users, and reported doses in such series are unreliable, which is exactly why the presenting AST carries the prognostic weight here. It does not define a safe daily dose; it shows where, among people who exceeded 4 g/day repeatedly, the danger actually declared itself.
cards.source: Daly FFS, O'Malley GF, Heard K, Bogdan GM, Dart RC. Prospective evaluation of repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen (paracetamol) ingestion. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15459622. Registry ID: none in the record (prospective observational series). cards.headline: Larson 2005 (acute liver failure registry): acetaminophen caused 42% of US acute liver failure — median dose 24 g, and 48% of cases unintentional, often from several products at once
cards.summary: Larson 2005 (acute liver failure registry): acetaminophen caused 42% of US acute liver failure — median dose 24 g, and 48% of cases unintentional, often from several products at once
cards.type: Prospective multicentre acute liver failure cohort, US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (Larson 2005)
cards.people: 662 consecutive patients with acute liver failure (coagulopathy and encephalopathy) gathered prospectively over 6 years at 22 US tertiary care centres; 275 (42%) were determined to result from acetaminophen liver injury.
cards.result: The acetaminophen share of acute liver failure rose from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2003. The median dose ingested was 24 g (equivalent to 48 extra-strength tablets). Unintentional overdoses accounted for 131 cases (48%), intentional for 122 (44%), and 22 (8%) were of unknown intent; in the unintentional group, 38% had taken two or more acetaminophen preparations simultaneously and 63% had used narcotic-containing compounds. Overall, 178 patients (65%) survived, 74 (27%) died without transplantation, and 23 (8%) underwent liver transplantation; 71% were alive at 3 weeks, and transplant-free survival was similar for intentional and unintentional cases.
cards.watchOut: A liver-failure registry sees only the catastrophic tip of acetaminophen use — it cannot say how often ordinary dosing leads here, and it would be wrong to read 42% as a risk of taking the drug. What it does fix is the anatomy of the catastrophe: a median dose six times the daily ceiling, and in the unintentional half, doses assembled unknowingly from multiple products — the pattern the 4 g/day ceiling is meant to prevent.
cards.source: Larson AM, Polson J, Fontana RJ, Davern TJ, Lalani E, Hynan LS, Reisch JS, Schiødt FV, Ostapowicz G, Shakil AO, Lee WM; Acute Liver Failure Study Group. Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure: results of a United States multicenter, prospective study. Hepatology. 2005. PMID: 16317692. cards.headline: Synthesis: the ceiling dose measurably stresses the liver in a third of healthy people, but the failure record belongs to doses far above it — total dose from all products is the operative risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ceiling dose measurably stresses the liver in a third of healthy people, but the failure record belongs to doses far above it — total dose from all products is the operative risk
cards.people: Four sources: a randomised trial of 4 g/day in 145 healthy adults (Watkins 2006), a randomised trial of 4 g/day for 3 days in 443 newly abstinent alcoholic patients (Kuffner 2007), a prospective series of 249 repeated-supratherapeutic-ingestion presentations (Daly 2004), and a prospective registry of 662 acute liver failure patients (Larson 2005).
cards.result: At 4 g/day: maximum ALT above 3 times the upper limit of normal in 31–44% of healthy recipients versus 0% on placebo (Watkins 2006), but no attributable transaminase increase over 3 days in newly abstinent alcoholics (peak mean ALT 57 versus 55 IU/L; Kuffner 2007), and no clinical liver injury reported in either trial. Above 4 g/day taken repeatedly: outcome was stratified by the presenting AST — 0% hepatotoxicity when AST was below 50 IU/L, 15% hepatotoxicity at 50–1,000 IU/L, 16% death or transplant above 1,000 IU/L (Daly 2004). At the catastrophic end: acetaminophen caused 42% of US acute liver failure at a median ingested dose of 24 g, with 48% of cases unintentional and 38% of those involving two or more acetaminophen products at once (Larson 2005). PROPOSED SPLIT — the 'is 4 g safe?' question has two true answers: as a single-product dose in trials it produces frequent enzyme rises without demonstrated clinical injury; as a real-world total assembled from several products and exceeded day after day, it is where the liver-failure record begins.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. This shelf does not set a personal dose for anyone: it does not cover children, pregnancy, established chronic liver disease, low body weight, or malnourished patients, none of which the fetched records isolate, and product labels and several regulators set lower ceilings (for example for chronic use or smaller adults) than the 4 g/day tested here. The trials at the ceiling were short (3–14 days); long-term daily use at 4 g/day has no fetched trial record on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Watkins PB et al. JAMA. 2006 (PMID: 16820551); Kuffner EK et al. BMC Medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17537264); Daly FFS et al. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15459622); Larson AM et al. Hepatology. 2005 (PMID: 16317692).

shelves.title: Bowel (faecal) incontinence: anal bulking injections beat sham (52% vs 31% halved their episodes), tibial nerve stimulation did not beat sham, injections matched biofeedback training, and sphincter repair helps but fades over years — a SPLIT record
shelves.question: How is bowel (faecal) incontinence treated? Beyond pads and diet, which treatments have actually been tested — injections, nerve stimulation, exercises, surgery — and which ones worked? Clinical question underneath: in adults with faecal incontinence that has not settled with conservative measures, how effective are anal bulking-agent injections, percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sphincter training with biofeedback, and overlapping sphincter repair? (Fibre/psyllium for loose-stool incontinence and sacral nerve stimulation are homed on their own shelves — see the boundary note.)
shelves.mesh: Biofeedback, Psychology · Dextrans/therapeutic use · Fecal Incontinence/surgery · Fecal Incontinence/therapy · Humans · Hyaluronic Acid/therapeutic use · Tibial Nerve/physiology · Transcutaneous Electric Nerve Stimulation/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the tested treatments genuinely divide. Anal bulking injections worked against sham: in the double-blind NASHA Dx trial (Graf 2011, PMID: 21420555; 206 randomised), 52% of injected patients versus 31% of sham patients at least halved their incontinence episodes (odds ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.24-4.47, p=0.0089), with 128 treatment-related adverse events including 2 serious abscesses. But the same injections were no better than sphincter training with biofeedback in a second randomised trial (Dehli 2013, PMID: 23298304; 126 patients), in which both groups improved similarly over 2 years. Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation failed its sham test: in CONFIDeNT (Knowles 2015, PMID: 26293315; 227 randomised), 38% versus 31% responded (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.72-2.28, p=0.396). Sphincter repair is uncontrolled evidence: in a 23-woman series with mean follow-up of 87 months (Lamblin 2014, PMID: 25185844), 85% were satisfied and 60% had good continence, but the proportion keeping their continence correction fell from 85% at 1 year to 48% at 84 months. BOUNDARIES: psyllium/fibre for loose-stool incontinence is homed on Shelf #5267, and sacral nerve stimulation is homed on Shelf #2659 — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive sham-controlled result (bulking injections), one large negative sham-controlled trial (tibial nerve stimulation), equivalence with exercises in a head-to-head trial, and surgical repair that helps many patients but wanes.

cards.headline: Graf 2011 (double-blind sham-controlled, n=206): dextranomer/hyaluronic acid anal injections — 52% vs 31% at least halved their incontinence episodes (OR 2.36, p=0.0089)
cards.summary: Graf 2011 (double-blind sham-controlled, n=206): dextranomer/hyaluronic acid anal injections — 52% vs 31% at least halved their incontinence episodes (OR 2.36, p=0.0089)
cards.people: 206 patients aged 18-75 years with faecal incontinence at centres in the USA and Europe, randomised 2:1 to transanal submucosal injections of dextranomer in stabilised hyaluronic acid (NASHA Dx, the bulking product tested; n=136) or sham injections (n=70). Patients and investigators were masked for 6 months; the primary endpoint was response, defined as a reduction of 50% or more in incontinence episodes on a 2-week diary. The trial was funded by Q-Med AB, the product's maker.
cards.result: 71 patients who received NASHA Dx (52%) had a 50% or greater reduction in incontinence episodes, compared with 22 who received sham (31%) — an absolute difference of about 21 percentage points (odds ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.24-4.47, p=0.0089). 128 treatment-related adverse events were recorded, of which two were serious (1 rectal abscess and 1 prostatic abscess).
cards.watchOut: The sham response was itself large (31%), so the injection's added value is the 21-point gap, not the 52% headline. The trial was funded by the manufacturer, follow-up for the sham comparison was 6 months, and the abstract does not report how many patients became fully continent — halving episodes is a partial win for most responders.
cards.source: Graf W et al. Efficacy of dextranomer in stabilised hyaluronic acid for treatment of faecal incontinence: a randomised, sham-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21420555. cards.headline: CONFIDeNT (Knowles 2015, double-blind, n=227): percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation did NOT beat sham — 38% vs 31% responders (adjusted OR 1.28, p=0.396)
cards.summary: CONFIDeNT (Knowles 2015, double-blind, n=227): percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation did NOT beat sham — 38% vs 31% responders (adjusted OR 1.28, p=0.396)
cards.people: 227 adults with substantial faecal incontinence for whom conservative treatments (such as dietary changes and pelvic floor exercises) had not worked, at 17 UK specialist hospital units, randomised to percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS, via the Urgent PC neuromodulation system, named in the paper; n=115) or sham electrical stimulation to the lateral forefoot (n=112), once weekly for 12 weeks. Primary outcome: 50% or greater reduction in weekly faecal incontinence episodes from bowel diaries.
cards.result: 39 of 103 patients with full diary data in the PTNS group (38%) achieved a 50% or greater reduction in weekly episodes, compared with 32 of 102 (31%) in the sham group (adjusted odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.72-2.28, p=0.396) — no significant benefit. No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported; seven mild related adverse events occurred in each group, mainly pain at the needle site. The authors concluded PTNS for 12 weeks did not confer significant clinical benefit over sham.
cards.watchOut: Earlier uncontrolled case series had suggested 50-80% of patients benefit from PTNS — this trial shows how much of that was the ritual, attention and natural variation captured by a sham arm. The trial tested a 12-week course; it does not rule out effects in subgroups (the authors mention urgency) or with longer treatment, but those remain unproven, not established.
cards.source: Knowles CH et al. Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation versus sham electrical stimulation for the treatment of faecal incontinence in adults (CONFIDeNT): a double-blind, multicentre, pragmatic, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial.
