cards.headline: Dehli 2013 (randomised, n=126): bulking injections and sphincter training with biofeedback improved incontinence scores by similar amounts over 2 years — no difference between them
cards.summary: Dehli 2013 (randomised, n=126): bulking injections and sphincter training with biofeedback improved incontinence scores by similar amounts over 2 years — no difference between them
cards.people: 126 adults with anal incontinence, randomised to transanal submucosal injection of dextranomer in hyaluronic acid (4 × 1 mL; n=64) or to sphincter training with biofeedback (n=62). Primary outcome was the St Mark's incontinence score (0 = continent, 24 = complete incontinence) at 2 years, analysed with mixed models.
cards.result: Mean St Mark's score improved from 12.9 (95% CI 11.8-14.0) at baseline to 8.3 (95% CI 6.7-9.8) in the injection group, and from 12.6 (95% CI 11.4-13.8) to 7.2 in the training group. Comparisons between the groups showed no differences in effect between the treatments; the authors concluded the efficacy of anal injections and biofeedback did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Both arms improved by roughly 5 points, but with no untreated or sham arm this trial cannot separate treatment effect from regression to the mean — read alongside Graf 2011, the fair summary is that injections beat sham while training achieves similar scores without a procedure. Evaluators were blinded; patients, necessarily, were not.

cards.headline: Lamblin 2014 (sphincter repair series, n=23 women, ~7 years' follow-up): 85% satisfied, 60% good continence — but continence correction fell from 85% at 1 year to 48% at 84 months
cards.summary: Lamblin 2014 (sphincter repair series, n=23 women, ~7 years' follow-up): 85% satisfied, 60% good continence — but continence correction fell from 85% at 1 year to 48% at 84 months
cards.people: 23 women who underwent overlapping anterior anal sphincteroplasty over 10 years (1999-2009) in a gynaecological surgery department, mostly for sphincter defects after initially undiagnosed obstetric trauma. Mean age 52 years; mean follow-up 87 months (median 91.5). Outcomes were pre- and postoperative Jorge and Wexner incontinence scores, satisfaction, quality of life, and Kaplan-Meier conservation of the continence correction.
cards.result: Mean postoperative Jorge and Wexner score was 7.5 out of 20. Of the women followed, 17 (85%) declared themselves satisfied with the repair and 12 (60%) showed good faecal continence. Faecal incontinence had a negative impact on quality of life for 15% and on sexuality for 50% of patients. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed conservation of the continence correction of 85% at 1 year, 74% at 48 months, 67% at 60 months and 48% at 84 months.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-centre, uncontrolled series in a selected group (women with a defined sphincter defect, mostly obstetric) — there is no comparison treatment, and satisfaction (85%) runs well ahead of measured continence (60% good; under half keeping the correction at 7 years). The honest reading is real early benefit that erodes with time, in the patients most likely to benefit.
cards.source: Lamblin G et al. Long-term outcome after overlapping anterior anal sphincter repair for fecal incontinence. International Journal of Colorectal Disease. 2014. PMID: 25185844. cards.headline: Synthesis: one treatment beat its sham, one did not, one matched exercises, and surgery's benefit fades — the answer depends on which treatment is meant
cards.summary: Synthesis: one treatment beat its sham, one did not, one matched exercises, and surgery's benefit fades — the answer depends on which treatment is meant
cards.people: Three randomised trials (206, 227 and 126 patients; Graf 2011, Knowles 2015, Dehli 2013) and one 23-woman surgical series with ~7-year follow-up (Lamblin 2014), all in adults with faecal incontinence, most after conservative measures had failed.
cards.result: Bulking injections vs sham: 52% vs 31% responders (OR 2.36, p=0.0089). Injections vs biofeedback training: no difference (St Mark's 12.9→8.3 vs 12.6→7.2). Tibial nerve stimulation vs sham: 38% vs 31% (p=0.396) — no benefit shown. Sphincter repair: 85% satisfaction but continence correction conserved in only 48% at 84 months. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Boundaries (one-home rule): psyllium/fibre treatment for loose-stool incontinence is homed on Shelf #5267, and sacral nerve stimulation — the implanted treatment with its own crossover-trial record — is homed on Shelf #2659; neither is re-carded here. This shelf also does not cover pads, constipating medicines or dietary management, which remain the background care in every trial carded. Tier C.

shelves.title: Oral branched-chain amino acids and ascites: fewer ascites events in pooled liver-cancer treatment trials (relative risk 0.55) and a positive composite endpoint after liver resection — but no trial in decompensated cirrhosis tests BCAA against ascites itself
shelves.question: 'Does oral branched-chain amino acid treatment reduce ascites in advanced liver disease?' — In adults with cirrhosis, does oral branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) supplementation reduce the occurrence or severity of ascites compared with control diets, placebo or no supplementation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Ascites · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular · Female · Hepatectomy · Humans · Liver Neoplasms · Male · Middle Aged · Pleural Effusion · Postoperative Complications · Preoperative Care · Serum Albumin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the population caveat printed on the face: every direct ascites signal comes from an adjacent setting, not from decompensated cirrhosis with ascites as the primary endpoint. In liver-cancer care, a meta-analysis of 11 studies (974 patients undergoing hepatocellular carcinoma interventions; Chen 2015, PMID: 26155840) found ascites occurred less often on oral BCAA (relative risk 0.545, 0.316–0.938) and oedema likewise (relative risk 0.494). Before major liver resection, the one randomised trial (Kikuchi 2016, PMID: 27338747; n=77) missed its primary endpoint — refractory ascites alone 5.1% vs 13.2%, p=0.263 — but the composite of refractory ascites and/or pleural effusion was significantly less frequent on BCAA (5.1% vs 21.1%, p=0.047). A systematic review of 40 reports (Ooi 2018, PMID: 30390892) concluded BCAA may improve ascites and oedema in adults, without a pooled estimate. Indirect support: the two large cirrhosis-events trials homed on shelf #3630 (Marchesini 2003; Muto 2005) counted aggravation of hepatic failure — including ascites — inside composite endpoints that BCAA reduced (Moriwaki 2008, PMID: 19125940), but neither published ascites counts separately, and the one randomised trial of a BCAA-containing nutrition bundle in refractory ascites is homed on the refractory-ascites nutrition shelf (Sorrentino 2012, PMID: 22142548). The intravenous route is a separate, null story and stays on shelf #3630: nothing here supports intravenous BCAA for ascites.

cards.headline: Chen 2015 (meta-analysis, liver-cancer interventions): ascites relative risk 0.545 (0.316–0.938) and oedema relative risk 0.494 on oral BCAA
cards.summary: Chen 2015 (meta-analysis, liver-cancer interventions): ascites relative risk 0.545 (0.316–0.938) and oedema relative risk 0.494 on oral BCAA
cards.type: Meta-analysis of oral BCAA in hepatocellular carcinoma interventions (Chen 2015)
cards.people: 11 eligible studies, 974 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (most with underlying cirrhosis) undergoing anti-cancer interventions, comparing oral BCAA supplementation with control.
cards.result: Oral BCAA was associated with higher serum albumin (standardised mean difference 0.234, 95% CI 0.033 to 0.435; P=0.022) and lower rates of ascites (relative risk 0.545, 95% CI 0.316 to 0.938; P=0.029) and oedema (relative risk 0.494, 95% CI 0.257 to 0.952; P=0.035) than control. A mortality advantage was suggested in Child-Pugh class B patients but not confirmed; no effect was found on cancer recurrence or liver enzymes. No serious adverse events were attributed to BCAA.
cards.watchOut: The population is patients being treated for liver cancer, not patients with established ascites from decompensated cirrhosis, and ascites was a secondary outcome in the source trials. The relative risks are pooled across small, mostly Japanese studies of variable quality.
cards.source: Chen L et al. Efficacy and safety of oral branched-chain amino acid supplementation in patients undergoing interventions for hepatocellular carcinoma: a meta-analysis. meta-analysis of oral bcaa in hepatocellular carcinoma interventions (chen 2015) 11 eligible studies, 974 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (most with underlying cirrhosis) undergoing anti-cancer interventions, comparing oral bcaa supplementation with control. oral bcaa was associated with higher serum albumin (standardised mean difference 0.234, 95% ci 0.033 to 0.435; p=0.022) and lower rates of ascites (relative risk 0.545, 95% ci 0.316 to 0.938; p=0.029) and oedema (relative risk 0.494, 95% ci 0.257 to 0.952; p=0.035) than control. a mortality advantage was suggested in child-pugh class b patients but not confirmed; no effect was found on cancer recurrence or liver enzymes. no serious adverse events were attributed to bcaa. the population is patients being treated for liver cancer, not patients with established ascites from decompensated cirrhosis, and ascites was a secondary outcome in the source trials. the relative risks are pooled across small, mostly japanese studies of variable quality. chen l et al. efficacy and safety of oral branched-chain amino acid supplementation in patients undergoing interventions for hepatocellular carcinoma: a meta-analysis. nutrition journal. 2015. pmid: 26155840. mesh: amino acids, branched-chain · carcinoma, hepatocellular · databases, factual · dietary supplements · drug evaluation, preclinical · humans · liver · liver neoplasms · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.headline: Kikuchi 2016 (randomised trial): preoperative oral BCAA — refractory ascites alone not significant (5.1% vs 13.2%), but refractory ascites and/or pleural effusion significantly reduced (5.1% vs 21.1%, p=0.047)
cards.summary: Kikuchi 2016 (randomised trial): preoperative oral BCAA — refractory ascites alone not significant (5.1% vs 13.2%), but refractory ascites and/or pleural effusion significantly reduced (5.1% vs 21.1%, p=0.047)
cards.people: 77 patients undergoing major liver resection for hepatocellular carcinoma, randomly allocated to oral BCAA started 3 weeks before resection (39 patients) or no BCAA (38 patients); the primary endpoint was development of postoperative ascites. Registry: UMIN000004244.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in refractory ascites considered alone (BCAA 5.1% vs non-BCAA 13.2%; p=0.263). The occurrence of refractory ascites and/or pleural effusion was significantly less frequent in the BCAA group (5.1%) than in the non-BCAA group (21.1%; p=0.047), and the postoperative serum concentration of reduced-state albumin was greater immediately after resection in the BCAA group.
cards.watchOut: A surgical prevention trial in mostly compensated patients: it shows BCAA can reduce new fluid accumulation after a major hepatic insult, which is not the same as shrinking established ascites in decompensated cirrhosis — and its own primary endpoint, refractory ascites alone, was not significant.
cards.source: Kikuchi Y et al. cards.headline: Ooi 2018 (systematic review, 40 reports): BCAA may improve ascites and oedema in adults with cirrhosis — qualitative conclusion, no pooled estimate
cards.summary: Ooi 2018 (systematic review, 40 reports): BCAA may improve ascites and oedema in adults with cirrhosis — qualitative conclusion, no pooled estimate
cards.people: 40 articles (1989–2017) on BCAA supplementation in adults and children with liver cirrhosis, covering body composition, muscle strength, liver biomarkers, hepatic complications including ascites and oedema, event-free survival and quality of life.
cards.result: The review concluded that BCAA supplementation may be beneficial in improving muscle strength, ascites and oedema in adult liver patients, with potential clinically significant improvements in hepatic encephalopathy; in children, limited data suggested favourable effects on weight, fat-free mass and serum albumin.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis: dose, duration, disease severity and outcome tools varied so much between studies that the authors state overall conclusions are limited. It supports the direction of the ascites signal but cannot size it.
cards.source: Ooi PH et al. Effects of branched chain amino acid supplementation on patient care outcomes in adults and children with liver cirrhosis: A systematic review. cards.headline: Synthesis: an ascites signal exists for oral BCAA, but it is borrowed from neighbouring populations — POSSIBLE, not proven, in decompensated cirrhosis
cards.summary: Synthesis: an ascites signal exists for oral BCAA, but it is borrowed from neighbouring populations — POSSIBLE, not proven, in decompensated cirrhosis
cards.people: One meta-analysis in liver-cancer interventions (11 studies, 974 patients), one randomised trial before liver resection (77 patients), and one systematic review of 40 reports; no randomised trial in decompensated cirrhosis has tested oral BCAA against an ascites primary endpoint.
cards.result: Ascites occurred less often on oral BCAA in pooled liver-cancer treatment studies (relative risk 0.545) and the ascites/effusion composite was significantly reduced by preoperative BCAA in the resection trial, whose ascites-only endpoint was not significant. The mechanism is plausible — BCAA raises albumin synthesis and serum albumin (see the albumin cards on shelf #3630) — and the large cirrhosis-events trials counted ascites within composites that BCAA reduced, without publishing ascites separately. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for oral BCAA reducing ascites occurrence, with the population gap stated on the face of the shelf; a trial in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites as the primary endpoint is the missing study.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as evidence that BCAA treats established or refractory ascites: for refractory ascites the controlled evidence is a bundled nutrition protocol (homed on the refractory-ascites nutrition shelf), and intravenous BCAA has no ascites evidence at all.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chen L et al. Nutrition Journal. 2015 (PMID: 26155840); Kikuchi Y et al. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2016 (PMID: 27338747); Ooi PH et al. shelves.title: Protein in hepatic encephalopathy: restriction does not improve encephalopathy and increases protein breakdown (Córdoba 2004); vegetable and dairy protein outperform meat in small crossover trials, and a vegetable-protein feeding trial reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71% vs 23%
shelves.question: 'Should people with hepatic encephalopathy eat less protein — and is vegetable or milk protein better than meat?' — In cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, does the amount of dietary protein (restricted vs normal/high) or its source (vegetable and dairy vs meat) change encephalopathy outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Animals · Databases, Factual · Diet, Vegetarian · Dietary Proteins · Fibrosis · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Meat · Plant Proteins, Dietary · Protein-Energy Malnutrition · Proteins · Quality of Life · Vegetarians
shelves.balance: SPLIT, by question. AMOUNT: the only randomised test of restriction (Córdoba 2004, PMID: 15246205; n=30, episodic encephalopathy) found the outcome of the episode was not significantly different on a normal-protein diet versus a low-protein diet — while protein breakdown was higher on the restricted diet. Restriction is a treatment that does not treat, at a metabolic cost; current guidance (ESPEN 2019, PMID: 30712783) advises against it. SOURCE: the classic crossover trials consistently favour vegetable (and dairy) protein over meat — better nitrogen balance (Bianchi 1993, PMID: 8068051, n=8), better number-connection and EEG results (Uribe 1982, PMID: 6756833, n=10; de Bruijn 1983, PMID: 6336714, n=8) — and the largest trial, Maharshi 2016 (PMID: 26453952; n=120, minimal encephalopathy), used 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day of vegetable protein within full nutritional therapy and reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71.1% vs 22.8% on usual diet, with overt encephalopathy in 10% vs 21.7%. An uncontrolled series of 153 patients (Gheorghe 2005, PMID: 16200232) improved on a casein-vegetable high-protein diet, showing dairy protein at 1.2 g/kg/day is compatible with recovery. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for protein restriction vs normal protein in episodic encephalopathy — with restriction metabolically harmful; POSSIBLE (benefit) for vegetable/dairy protein over meat protein, and for protein-adequate nutritional therapy in minimal encephalopathy.

cards.headline: Córdoba 2004: normal-protein diet vs protein restriction in episodic encephalopathy — outcome not significantly different; protein breakdown higher on the restricted diet
cards.summary: Córdoba 2004: normal-protein diet vs protein restriction in episodic encephalopathy — outcome not significantly different; protein breakdown higher on the restricted diet
cards.people: 30 patients with cirrhosis admitted with an episode of hepatic encephalopathy, randomised to a low-protein diet with progressive increments or a normal-protein diet for 14 days, in addition to standard encephalopathy treatment; protein synthesis and breakdown were measured with the glycine-15N infusion method on days 2 and 14.
cards.result: The outcome of hepatic encephalopathy was not significantly different between the two groups. Protein synthesis was similar on the two diets, but patients on the low-protein diet showed higher protein breakdown. The authors concluded that diets with a normal content of protein can be administered safely during episodic encephalopathy and that protein restriction has no beneficial effect.
cards.watchOut: Small (30 patients) and short (14 days), in hospitalised episodic encephalopathy: it cannot exclude modest effects, and it does not address chronic protein targets. Its metabolic finding — restriction accelerates the body's own protein breakdown — is the result that has held up in guidelines ever since.
cards.source: Córdoba J et al. Normal protein diet for episodic hepatic encephalopathy: results of a randomized study. Journal of Hepatology. 2004. PMID: 15246205. cards.headline: Maharshi 2016: vegetable-protein nutritional therapy reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71.1% vs 22.8% and halved progression to overt encephalopathy (10% vs 21.7%)
cards.summary: Maharshi 2016: vegetable-protein nutritional therapy reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71.1% vs 22.8% and halved progression to overt encephalopathy (10% vs 21.7%)
cards.people: 120 patients with cirrhosis and minimal hepatic encephalopathy at a tertiary centre in New Delhi, randomised to nutritional therapy (30–35 kcal/kg/day with 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day of vegetable protein; n=60) or no nutritional therapy (usual diet; n=60) for 6 months. Registry: CTRI/2013/07/003851.
cards.result: After 6 months, a higher proportion of the nutritional-therapy group had reversal of minimal encephalopathy (71.1% vs 22.8%; P=.001), with larger improvements in psychometric scores and health-related quality of life; overt hepatic encephalopathy developed in 10% of the nutritional-therapy group vs 21.7% of controls (P=.04).
cards.watchOut: The intervention is a package — calories plus vegetable protein versus no therapy — in an open dietary trial, so the benefit cannot be divided between energy, protein amount and protein source. It is nonetheless the largest randomised trial in this area and its protein was vegetable protein at full recommended amounts.
cards.source: Maharshi S et al. Efficacy of Nutritional Therapy for Patients With Cirrhosis and Minimal Hepatic Encephalopathy in a Randomized Trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2016. PMID: 26453952. Registry: CTRI/2013/07/003851. cards.headline: Bianchi 1993 (n=8, printed on the face): vegetable protein beat animal protein on nitrogen balance (+0.2 vs −1.7 g/day, P<0.01) with better psychometric tests
cards.summary: Bianchi 1993 (n=8, printed on the face): vegetable protein beat animal protein on nitrogen balance (+0.2 vs −1.7 g/day, P<0.01) with better psychometric tests
cards.people: 8 patients with cirrhosis and chronic permanent encephalopathy, all on optimum lactulose therapy, fed two equi-caloric, equi-nitrogenous diets for 7 days each (71 g total protein/day): one with 50 g of protein of animal origin, one with 50 g of vegetable protein, in randomised crossover order.
cards.result: Nitrogen balance in the last 3 days of each period was significantly better on the vegetable protein diet (+0.2 [SD 1.4] g vs −1.7 [2.4] g; P<0.01), entirely through reduced urinary nitrogen excretion; ammonia, insulin and plasma amino acids were lower on vegetable protein. The clinical grading of encephalopathy improved slightly and psychometric tests improved significantly on vegetable protein, though they remained grossly abnormal.
cards.watchOut: Eight patients and 7-day periods: a metabolic-ward result, not a clinical-outcomes trial. Its value is that the comparison was equi-nitrogenous and on top of lactulose — the difference is the protein source itself, not the amount.
cards.source: Bianchi GP et al. Vegetable versus animal protein diet in cirrhotic patients with chronic encephalopathy. A randomized cross-over comparison. Journal of Internal Medicine. 1993. PMID: 8068051. cards.headline: Uribe 1982: vegetable protein diets (40 g and 80 g) improved number-connection times vs meat protein plus neomycin; EEG improved on the 80 g vegetable diet
cards.summary: Uribe 1982: vegetable protein diets (40 g and 80 g) improved number-connection times vs meat protein plus neomycin; EEG improved on the 80 g vegetable diet
cards.people: 10 patients with cirrhosis and mild chronic portal-systemic encephalopathy, crossed over between a 40 g/day meat protein diet plus neomycin–milk of magnesia (control therapy) and vegetable protein diets of 40 g/day and 80 g/day; the 80 g vegetable diet was rich in branched-chain amino acids and fibre. Mental state, asterixis, number connection tests, EEG and blood ammonia were assessed serially.
cards.result: No patient developed deep coma on either vegetable diet or on the control therapy. Number connection test times improved significantly on both the 40 g (P<0.05) and 80 g (P<0.05) vegetable protein diets compared with the meat-protein–neomycin periods, and EEGs improved significantly on the 80 g vegetable diet (P<0.05). Bowel movements increased on the 80 g diet; two diabetic patients had hypoglycaemia on the 40 g vegetable diet.
cards.watchOut: The control period included neomycin — an active encephalopathy drug — so vegetable protein alone matching or beating meat protein plus a drug is a strong direction of effect, but the design cannot separate the fibre, the amino-acid pattern and the protein source. Ten patients, short periods.
cards.source: Uribe M et al. Treatment of chronic portal-systemic encephalopathy with vegetable and animal protein diets. A controlled crossover study. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 1982. PMID: 6756833. cards.headline: de Bruijn 1983 (n=8, printed on the face): EEG peak frequency higher on vegetable than animal protein (7.10 vs 6.58 Hz, p=0.01); clinical scores and ammonia unchanged
cards.summary: de Bruijn 1983 (n=8, printed on the face): EEG peak frequency higher on vegetable than animal protein (7.10 vs 6.58 Hz, p=0.01); clinical scores and ammonia unchanged
cards.people: 8 stable patients with cirrhosis and mild or subclinical portal-systemic encephalopathy after shunt surgery, off all anti-encephalopathy therapy, alternating equal amounts of mixed, animal and vegetable protein in a crossover protocol over five consecutive 1-week metabolic-ward periods.
cards.result: Peak frequencies of the computer-analysed EEG were lower during the animal protein diet (6.58 ± 0.42 Hz) than during the vegetable protein diet (7.10 ± 0.44 Hz; p=0.01). Neurological impairment scores and trailmaking tests did not change between diets (the trailmaking tests showed a learning effect), and neither arterial ammonia nor plasma amino-acid ratios changed; nitrogen balance tended to be more positive on vegetable protein. The authors concluded a vegetable protein diet, rather than overall protein restriction, should be considered in this disorder.
cards.watchOut: The positive endpoint is an EEG surrogate in 8 post-shunt patients; the clinical scores did not move. It agrees with Bianchi and Uribe on direction, at the same small scale.
cards.source: de Bruijn KM et al. Effect of dietary protein manipulation in subclinical portal-systemic encephalopathy. Gut. 1983. PMID: 6336714. cards.headline: Gheorghe 2005: on a casein-vegetable high-protein diet (1.2 g/kg/day), 79.7% of 153 patients with overt encephalopathy improved by at least one grade in 14 days — uncontrolled
cards.summary: Gheorghe 2005: on a casein-vegetable high-protein diet (1.2 g/kg/day), 79.7% of 153 patients with overt encephalopathy improved by at least one grade in 14 days — uncontrolled
cards.people: 153 consecutive patients with cirrhosis and overt hepatic encephalopathy given a modified high-calorie, high-protein diet (30 kcal/kg/day, 1.2 g protein/kg/day) based on vegetable and milk-derived (casein) proteins, eaten as 4 snack-meals plus a late evening meal; mental status (West Haven), asterixis, number connection test and blood ammonia assessed daily for 14 days.
cards.result: 122 patients (79.7%) improved by at least one encephalopathy grade within 14 days; blood ammonia fell significantly in all patients (p<0.0001) and number connection scores improved significantly (p<0.0001). Improvement of two grades was commoner in stage 3 encephalopathy with a precipitant (50% vs 18.9%) and in Child-Pugh B than C (61.7% vs 14%).
cards.watchOut: No control group: episodic encephalopathy usually improves as precipitants are treated, so this series cannot attribute the improvement to the diet. What it does establish is that full-dose dairy-and-vegetable protein feeding is compatible with recovery — the opposite of the old restriction practice.
cards.source: Gheorghe L et al. Improvement of hepatic encephalopathy using a modified high-calorie high-protein diet. Romanian Journal of Gastroenterology. 2005. PMID: 16200232. cards.headline: Keshavarzian 1984 (n=6, printed on the face): doubling protein with vegetable protein (80 g vs 40 g) was tolerated in chronic encephalopathy — minor improvement in 2 of 6, none worsened
cards.summary: Keshavarzian 1984 (n=6, printed on the face): doubling protein with vegetable protein (80 g vs 40 g) was tolerated in chronic encephalopathy — minor improvement in 2 of 6, none worsened
cards.people: 6 patients with chronic stable portal-systemic encephalopathy requiring dietary and lactulose therapy, each given in random order for 5 days in hospital a conventional 40 g protein diet (30 g animal, 10 g vegetable) and an 80 g vegetable-protein-supplemented diet (30 g animal, 50 g vegetable); EEG, clinical indices and plasma amino acids assessed at the end of each period.
cards.result: The increase in vegetable protein was associated with minor improvement in EEG and clinical performance in two patients and no change in the others; no patient deteriorated. Fasting plasma phenylalanine and tyrosine were higher and the branched-chain/aromatic amino-acid ratio lower on the supplemented diet, yet encephalopathy did not worsen.
cards.watchOut: Six patients, 5-day periods: a tolerance study. It answers the safety half of the question — more protein, from vegetable sources, did not provoke encephalopathy — and nothing more.
cards.source: Keshavarzian A et al. Dietary protein supplementation from vegetable sources in the management of chronic portal systemic encephalopathy. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 1984. cards.headline: Iqbal 2021 (review): recommended intake is now 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day; vegetable or milk-based protein diets decrease encephalopathy symptoms in small studies, but the evidence is limited
cards.summary: Iqbal 2021 (review): recommended intake is now 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day; vegetable or milk-based protein diets decrease encephalopathy symptoms in small studies, but the evidence is limited
cards.people: Review of the literature on protein amount and source in hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis, covering protein restriction, vegetarian vs meat-based diets, dairy protein and branched-chain amino acids.
cards.result: The review records that the old practice of protein restriction has been replaced by a recommended intake of 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day, that case series and small studies show a vegetarian protein diet decreases encephalopathy symptoms compared with a meat-based diet, and that vegetable or milk-based protein diets are good substitutes for patients averse to meat — while the evidence remains limited and larger randomised trials are required.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, not a pooled analysis: it is carded as the map of current practice against which the primary trials on this shelf can be read, not as independent evidence.
cards.source: Iqbal U et al. A Comprehensive Review Evaluating the Impact of Protein Source (Vegetarian vs. Meat Based) in Hepatic Encephalopathy. Nutrients. 2021. PMID: 33530344. cards.headline: Synthesis: do not restrict protein; if protein source is changed, vegetable and dairy are the better-tolerated sources — both limbs rest on small trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: do not restrict protein; if protein source is changed, vegetable and dairy are the better-tolerated sources — both limbs rest on small trials
cards.people: One randomised trial of protein amount (Córdoba 2004, n=30), one randomised trial of vegetable-protein nutritional therapy in minimal encephalopathy (Maharshi 2016, n=120), three small crossover trials of protein source (n=8, 10 and 8, numbers printed on their cards), one tolerance crossover (n=6, printed), one uncontrolled high-protein series (n=153) and one narrative review.
cards.result: Amount: normal protein and restricted protein produced indistinguishable encephalopathy outcomes in the only randomised test, and restriction increased protein breakdown — the restriction limb is a null with a metabolic cost. Source: every crossover comparison favours vegetable over animal (meat) protein on nitrogen balance, EEG or psychometrics, dairy (casein) protein performed as ordinary, well-tolerated protein in the large uncontrolled series, and the one adequately sized trial used vegetable protein at 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day and reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71.1% vs 22.8%. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for restriction vs normal protein; POSSIBLE (benefit) for vegetable/dairy over meat and for protein-adequate feeding in minimal encephalopathy.
cards.watchOut: The source limb's trials are from 1982–1993 with 6–10 patients each; Maharshi 2016 is the only modern, adequately sized trial and it tests a feeding package, not protein source in isolation. A large modern trial of protein source in overt encephalopathy does not exist.

shelves.title: Refractory ascites and feeding: in the only randomised trial (Sorrentino 2012, 120 patients), a protein-centred nutrition protocol reduced paracentesis requirements, and adding intravenous nutrition after each tap gave the lowest mortality
shelves.question: 'When ascites keeps coming back despite water pills, does intensive feeding — a protein-rich diet, an evening protein snack and intravenous nutrition after each tap — help?' — In cirrhotic patients with refractory ascites undergoing repeated large-volume paracentesis, does aggressive nutritional support improve nutritional status, paracentesis requirement, morbidity and mortality compared with a low-sodium diet alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Ascites · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Dietary Proteins · Energy Intake · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Hepatorenal Syndrome · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Status · Paracentesis · Parenteral Nutrition · Peritonitis · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single randomised trial. Sorrentino 2012 (PMID: 22142548) randomised 120 patients with refractory ascites on serial large-volume paracentesis to (A) post-paracentesis intravenous nutritional support plus a balanced oral diet and a late-evening protein snack, (B) the same oral protocol without parenteral support, or (C) a low-sodium diet alone, and followed them for 12 months. The nutrition groups preserved nutritional parameters with less deterioration of liver function than controls, had lower morbidity and mortality, needed fewer paracentesis taps — and mortality was significantly better in the parenteral-support group than in either other group. The stakes are set by the observational record: protein-calorie malnutrition marks the sickest ascites patients (Sam 2009, PMID: 19602136; ascites in 64.6% vs 47.8% of admissions, adjusted mortality odds ratio 1.76, a relative measure). What this shelf does NOT show: the trial's intervention is a bundle, so the benefit cannot be credited to protein, the evening snack or the intravenous component separately; and no published study tests parenteral nutrition reversing ascites in hepatorenal syndrome specifically — this trial, in refractory ascites, is the nearest controlled evidence to that question, not an answer to it.

cards.headline: Sorrentino 2012: in refractory ascites, nutritional support cut paracentesis requirements and morbidity/mortality — and the parenteral-support group had significantly the lowest mortality
cards.summary: Sorrentino 2012: in refractory ascites, nutritional support cut paracentesis requirements and morbidity/mortality — and the parenteral-support group had significantly the lowest mortality
cards.people: 120 patients with cirrhosis and refractory ascites undergoing serial large-volume paracentesis, randomised into three groups of 40: group A received post-paracentesis intravenous nutritional support in addition to a balanced oral diet and a late-evening protein snack; group B received the same oral nutritional protocol without parenteral support; group C (control) received a low-sodium or sodium-free diet. Clinical, anthropometric and laboratory nutritional parameters and liver and renal function were followed for 12 months.
cards.result: Patients on the nutritional protocol showed better preservation of clinical, anthropometric and laboratory nutritional parameters, associated with decreased deterioration of liver function, compared with the low-sodium diet group. Groups A and B had lower morbidity and mortality rates than the control group, and mortality was significantly better in the parenteral-support group (A) than in the other two groups. In patients on the nutritional protocol there was a reduction in the requirement for paracentesis taps for refractory ascites. The authors concluded that post-paracentesis parenteral nutritional support with a balanced oral diet and an evening protein snack appears to be the best care protocol for cirrhosis complicated by refractory ascites.
cards.watchOut: One single-centre, unblinded trial of a bundled intervention, and the abstract reports the mortality advantage as significant without printing the mortality rates — the size of the effect cannot be verified from the record. The parenteral arm's edge is the trial's most striking finding, but the design cannot separate intravenous nutrition from the diet and snack given with it, and hepatorenal syndrome patients were not separately studied.
cards.source: Sorrentino P et al. Preservation of nutritional-status in patients with refractory ascites due to hepatic cirrhosis who are undergoing repeated paracentesis. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2012. PMID: 22142548. cards.headline: Sam 2009 (observational context): protein-calorie malnutrition in cirrhosis with portal hypertension — ascites in 64.6% vs 47.8% of admissions, in-hospital mortality 14.1% vs 7.5% (adjusted odds ratio 1.76, relative)
cards.summary: Sam 2009 (observational context): protein-calorie malnutrition in cirrhosis with portal hypertension — ascites in 64.6% vs 47.8% of admissions, in-hospital mortality 14.1% vs 7.5% (adjusted odds ratio 1.76, relative)
cards.people: 114,703 admissions with cirrhosis and portal hypertension in the US Nationwide Inpatient Sample, 1998–2005, comparing admissions coded with protein-calorie malnutrition (PCM) against those without; mortality impact quantified by multiple logistic regression.
cards.result: PCM was substantially commoner in cirrhosis with portal hypertension than in general medical inpatients (6.1% vs 1.9%; adjusted odds ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.4 to 1.7, a relative measure). Admissions with PCM had more ascites (64.6% vs 47.8%) and more hepatorenal syndrome (5.1% vs 2.8%), and in-hospital mortality was two-fold higher (14.1% vs 7.5%), with an adjusted mortality odds ratio of 1.76 (95% CI 1.59 to 1.94). Length of stay and charges were also greater.
cards.watchOut: Administrative data: malnutrition coding is incomplete and PCM may simply mark the sickest patients rather than cause their outcomes. Carded as the stakes for the Sorrentino trial — why feeding this population might matter — not as treatment evidence.
cards.source: Sam J et al. Protein-calorie malnutrition as a prognostic indicator of mortality among patients hospitalized with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Liver International. 2009. PMID: 19602136. cards.headline: Synthesis: one bundled-intervention trial supports intensive nutritional support in refractory ascites — POSSIBLE; the hepatorenal-syndrome question remains untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: one bundled-intervention trial supports intensive nutritional support in refractory ascites — POSSIBLE; the hepatorenal-syndrome question remains untested
cards.people: One prospective randomised three-group trial (120 patients with refractory ascites on serial paracentesis, 12 months) and one nationwide observational analysis (114,703 admissions) as context.
cards.result: The randomised evidence says a protein-centred nutrition protocol — balanced oral diet, late-evening protein snack, and (in the best-performing arm) intravenous nutritional support after each paracentesis — preserved nutritional status and liver function, reduced the need for paracentesis taps, and was associated with lower morbidity and mortality than a low-sodium diet alone. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit). No published study isolates the intravenous component, and none tests nutritional support as a treatment to reverse ascites in hepatorenal syndrome; clinicians' bedside observations of ascites reversing with parenteral feeding in hepatorenal syndrome have no controlled published counterpart.
cards.watchOut: A single unreplicated trial carries this shelf. If its mortality result is a small-sample artefact, the shelf collapses to 'feeding is safe and preserves nutrition' — which the trial also shows, and which is not nothing in a population whose untreated course is deterioration.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sorrentino P et al. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2012 (PMID: 22142548) and Sam J et al. Liver International. 2009 (PMID: 19602136).

shelves.question: 'Does eating enough protein — or taking oral nutritional supplements — help people with cirrhosis live longer?' — In adults with cirrhosis, does oral or enteral nutritional supplementation, or higher dietary protein intake, reduce mortality compared with a standard diet or lower intake?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dietary Supplements · Enteral Nutrition · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Malnutrition · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), honestly hedged. The randomised pool is null at the top line: Ney 2013 (PMID: 23421379) meta-analysed 6 trials of oral or enteral nutritional supplementation (470 patients; BCAA and parenteral trials excluded) and found no overall mortality reduction (relative risk 0.75, 0.42–1.32) — but the oral-supplement subgroup showed a significant mortality reduction (relative risk 0.40, 0.18–0.90), in trials of low quality (median Jadad 2). The cohort evidence points the same way with a threshold shape: in 630 transplant-waitlist patients (Ney 2015, PMID: 25667232), protein intake below 0.8 g/kg/day independently predicted waitlist mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, 1.2–2.7, a relative measure) while only 24% of patients reached the recommended 1.2 g/kg/day; and in a 121-patient prospective cohort (Daftari 2023, PMID: 37400778), higher total and dairy protein intakes tracked with lower cirrhosis-related mortality (hazard ratio 0.38 for each, confidence intervals crossing 1.0) while higher animal protein tracked with higher mortality (hazard ratio 3.8). BCAA-specific survival is a different shelf (#3630: mortality not improved, relative risk 0.88–0.89 across Cochrane versions), and the refractory-ascites nutrition trial's mortality finding is homed on the refractory-ascites shelf. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — enough for 'do not let protein intake fall short' as practice, not enough to promise a survival effect from supplements.

cards.headline: Ney 2013 (meta-analysis): oral/enteral nutritional supplementation and mortality in cirrhosis — overall relative risk 0.75 (not significant); oral-supplement subgroup 0.40 (0.18–0.90)
cards.summary: Ney 2013 (meta-analysis): oral/enteral nutritional supplementation and mortality in cirrhosis — overall relative risk 0.75 (not significant); oral-supplement subgroup 0.40 (0.18–0.90)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ney 2013)
cards.people: 6 randomised trials (4 oral nutritional supplementation, 2 enteral) with 470 patients with cirrhosis, comparing supplementation against a standard non-supplemented diet; parenteral and branched-chain amino acid interventions were excluded, as were interventions of 7 days or less. Primary outcome: survival.
cards.result: Combining all studies, there was no reduction in mortality (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32; P=0.31). A subgroup analysis of 3 of the 4 oral-supplement studies did demonstrate a mortality reduction (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.90; P=0.03). Study quality was suboptimal (median Jadad score 2). The authors concluded there is insufficient evidence to state definitively that oro-enteral supplementation improves outcomes, while remaining cautiously optimistic about benefit without increased adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's positive randomised signal is a subgroup of small, low-quality trials sitting under a null headline result — the classic configuration for an over-read finding. It justifies POSSIBLE and a call for adequately powered trials, not a stronger stamp.
cards.source: Ney M et al. Meta-analysis: oral or enteral nutritional supplementation in cirrhosis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2013. PMID: 23421379. cards.headline: Ney 2015 (cohort, 630 waitlist patients): protein intake below 0.8 g/kg/day independently predicted transplant-waitlist mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, 1.2–2.7, relative)
cards.summary: Ney 2015 (cohort, 630 waitlist patients): protein intake below 0.8 g/kg/day independently predicted transplant-waitlist mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, 1.2–2.7, relative)
cards.people: 630 adults with cirrhosis activated on a liver transplant waiting list (2000–2009) with complete dietary records; protein intake estimated from dietary records (mean 1.0 ± 0.36 g/kg/day; only 24% met the recommended threshold of more than 1.2 g/kg/day). Multivariable logistic regression and competing-risk analysis were used.
cards.result: Very low protein intake (below 0.8 g/kg/day) was associated with worse liver disease severity and was an independent predictor both of malnutrition by subjective global assessment (adjusted odds ratio 2.0, 95% CI 1.3 to 3.0, a relative measure) and of transplant-waitlist mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.7, a relative measure). The authors note protein intake is potentially modifiable and call for prospective studies of targeted protein repletion.
cards.watchOut: Observational: patients with worse liver disease eat less, so low intake is partly a marker of severity. Adjustment reduces but cannot remove that confounding — this card supports the threshold hypothesis (avoid very low intake), not proof that feeding to target extends life.
cards.source: Ney M et al. Insufficient Protein Intake Is Associated With Increased Mortality in 630 Patients With Cirrhosis Awaiting Liver Transplantation. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2015. PMID: 25667232. cards.headline: Daftari 2023 (prospective cohort, 121 patients): higher total and dairy protein intakes tracked with lower cirrhosis mortality (hazard ratio 0.38 each, intervals crossing 1.0); higher animal protein with higher mortality (3.8)
cards.summary: Daftari 2023 (prospective cohort, 121 patients): higher total and dairy protein intakes tracked with lower cirrhosis mortality (hazard ratio 0.38 each, intervals crossing 1.0); higher animal protein with higher mortality (3.8)
cards.people: 121 ambulatory patients with cirrhosis of at least 6 months' duration, followed for 48 months; dietary intake assessed with a validated 168-item food-frequency questionnaire, with total protein classified as dairy, vegetable and animal protein; Cox proportional hazards models with multivariable adjustment.
cards.result: After full adjustment, higher total protein intake was associated with lower cirrhosis-related mortality (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.2 to 1.1; p for trend 0.045 — a 62% lower relative risk at the point estimate) and higher dairy protein intake likewise (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.1; p for trend 0.046). Higher vegetable protein intake was inversely but not significantly associated with mortality, while higher animal protein intake was associated with a 3.8-fold relative increase in mortality risk (hazard ratio 3.8, 95% CI 1.7 to 8.2; p for trend 0.035).
cards.watchOut: 121 patients from a single centre, with the total- and dairy-protein confidence intervals crossing 1.0 — trend-level evidence, and dietary questionnaires measure habitual intake imperfectly. The dairy signal is the only milk-specific survival datum on this shelf and it is hypothesis-grade, not proof.
cards.source: Daftari G et al. Dietary protein intake and mortality among survivors of liver cirrhosis: a prospective cohort study. BMC Gastroenterology. 2023. PMID: 37400778. MeSH: Animals · Humans · Cohort Studies · Prospective Studies · Dietary Proteins · Cardiovascular Diseases · Diet · Liver Cirrhosis · Survivors · Risk Factors

cards.headline: Synthesis: no adequately powered trial proves feeding extends life in cirrhosis — but the null is a weak null, and every strand points away from protein shortfall
cards.summary: Synthesis: no adequately powered trial proves feeding extends life in cirrhosis — but the null is a weak null, and every strand points away from protein shortfall
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 6 randomised supplementation trials (470 patients), one 630-patient transplant-waitlist cohort with dietary records, and one 121-patient prospective dietary cohort followed 48 months.
cards.result: Randomised: overall mortality relative risk 0.75 (0.42–1.32), not significant, with the oral-supplement subgroup at 0.40 (0.18–0.90) in low-quality trials. Observational: protein intake below 0.8 g/kg/day carried an adjusted mortality hazard ratio of 1.8 on the transplant waitlist, and higher total and dairy protein intakes tracked with lower mortality in the prospective cohort while animal protein tracked higher. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for protein-adequate oral nutritional support on survival — sufficient to treat very low protein intake as a risk factor to correct, not sufficient to promise patients a survival gain from supplements.
cards.watchOut: The two randomised limbs (this shelf's subgroup; the BCAA pool on shelf #3630) both stop short of a proven mortality effect, and the cohort limbs are confounded by severity. If a future adequately powered feeding trial is null, this shelf's stamp should fall; if it confirms the subgroup, the stamp should rise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ney M et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2013 (PMID: 23421379); Ney M et al. Nutrition in Clinical Practice. 2015 (PMID: 25667232); Daftari G et al. BMC Gastroenterology. 2023 (PMID: 37400778).

shelves.title: Exercise training in cirrhosis: supervised exercise raised peak oxygen uptake by 5.3 mL/kg/min and added about 49 m to the 6-minute walk
shelves.question: Does exercise training help people with liver cirrhosis - fitness, walking distance, muscle and quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Body Composition / physiology · Exercise / physiology · Liver Cirrhosis / physiopathology · Liver Cirrhosis / rehabilitation · Quality of Life · Resistance Training / methods · Humans
shelves.balance: BOUNDARY: specific liver diseases - hepatitis, cirrhosis complications, MASH, albumin and TIPS - are homed on their own shelves, and cirrhosis nutrition is homed on shelves #5367-#5370; this shelf covers only exercise training in cirrhosis. The evidence is small but consistent. Román 2014 (PMID 24599772; the PubMed record as fetched this session prints no registry ID, so the card says 'none in the record') was a randomised pilot in 17 outpatients with cirrhosis (exercise n=8, control n=9): supervised moderate exercise for 12 weeks, with all patients receiving oral leucine 10 g/day, improved the 6-minute walk test from 365 m (160-420) to 445 m (250-500) (p=0.01) and the 2-minute step test (p=0.02); lower thigh circumference rose from 41 cm (34-53) to 46 cm (36-56) (p=0.02), and SF-36 general health (p=0.03), vitality (p=0.01) and social function (p=0.04) improved; there were no cirrhosis complications in either group. Zenith 2014 (PMID 24768811; NCT01799785) randomised 19 stable patients with Child-Pugh A or B cirrhosis (n=9 exercise, n=10 usual care) to supervised cycle-ergometer exercise 3 days a week for 8 weeks at 60-80% of baseline peak VO2: at week 8, peak VO2 was 5.3 mL/kg/min higher in the exercise group than in controls (95% CI 2.9-7.8; P=.001), thigh circumference (P=.001), thigh muscle thickness (P=.01) and self-perceived health (P=.01) were higher, and fatigue subscores were lower (P=.01); no adverse events occurred. Rocha 2025 (PMID 40976129) pooled 6 randomised trials with 244 participants aged 53-63 years with Child-Pugh A, B or C cirrhosis, mostly men: quality of life with resistance training had a standardised mean difference of 0.36 (0.01-0.76, p=0.04), and the 6-minute walk test improved by a mean difference of 49.39 m (16.53-82.24, p=0.03) after resistance and aerobic training, with no difference for VO2peak, thigh circumference or BMI; GRADE certainty was very low to moderate. Two tiny pilots plus a small meta-analysis of small trials, with a leucine co-intervention in one: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Román 2014: 12 weeks of supervised exercise plus leucine raised the 6-minute walk from 365 m to 445 m in 17 patients with cirrhosis
cards.summary: Román 2014: 12 weeks of supervised exercise plus leucine raised the 6-minute walk from 365 m to 445 m in 17 patients with cirrhosis
cards.people: 17 outpatients with cirrhosis randomised to an exercise group (n=8) or a control group (n=9) in a pilot study; all patients received oral leucine 10 g/day
cards.result: In the exercise group the 6-minute walk test rose from 365 m (160-420) to 445 m (250-500) (p=0.01) and the 2-minute step test improved (p=0.02). Lower thigh circumference rose from 41 cm (34-53) to 46 cm (36-56) (p=0.02), and SF-36 general health (p=0.03), vitality (p=0.01) and social function (p=0.04) improved. In the control group no statistically significant changes were observed in any parameter. No cirrhosis complications were observed in either group.
cards.watchOut: Only 17 patients, and every patient - including controls - took leucine 10 g/day, so the exercise effect cannot be separated from leucine; the PubMed record as fetched prints no registry ID.
cards.source: Román E, Torrades MT, Nadal MJ, et al. Randomized pilot study: effects of an exercise programme and leucine supplementation in patients with cirrhosis. Dig Dis Sci. 2014. cards.headline: Zenith 2014: 8 weeks of supervised cycling raised peak oxygen uptake by 5.3 mL/kg/min in 19 patients with cirrhosis

cards.people: 19 stable patients with Child-Pugh A or B cirrhosis (79% male, mean age 57.6 years, mean MELD score 10), randomised to exercise training (n=9) or usual care (n=10)
cards.result: At week 8, peak VO2 was 5.3 mL/kg/min higher in the exercise group than in controls (95% CI 2.9-7.8; P=.001). cards.headline: Rocha 2025: across 6 trials with 244 patients, exercise improved the 6-minute walk by 49.39 m and quality of life modestly
cards.summary: Rocha 2025: across 6 trials with 244 patients, exercise improved the 6-minute walk by 49.39 m and quality of life modestly

cards.headline: Synthesis: supervised exercise in cirrhosis improves walking distance and fitness in small trials, with no safety signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: supervised exercise in cirrhosis improves walking distance and fitness in small trials, with no safety signal
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded studies: two pilot trials (17 and 19 patients) and one meta-analysis of 6 trials (244 participants)
cards.result: The 6-minute walk improved by 80 m in one pilot (Román 2014) and by 49.39 m pooled across trials (Rocha 2025); peak VO2 was 5.3 mL/kg/min higher after 8 weeks of cycling (Zenith 2014). Quality of life improved modestly (standardised mean difference 0.36, Rocha 2025). No cirrhosis complications or adverse events were reported in the pilot trials.
cards.watchOut: Small numbers, short follow-up and very-low-to-moderate certainty; the stamp is POSSIBLE, and no claim is made about survival or liver outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Román 2014 (PMID 24599772), Zenith 2014 (PMID 24768811) and Rocha 2025 (PMID 40976129).

shelves.title: Weight loss to reverse steatohepatitis: about 10% of body weight — 90% resolution at 10% or more, 58% at 5% or more, with 7% the randomised trial's separating goal
shelves.question: How much weight loss is needed to reverse steatohepatitis in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biopsy · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Fatty Liver · Female · Fibrosis · Humans · Life Style · Liver · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Factors · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, dose-dependent) — the answer the carded evidence supports is a gradient with a threshold at the top: about 10% of body weight is the amount that reliably reverses steatohepatitis. In the largest paired-biopsy cohort (Vilar-Gomez 2015, PMID: 25865049, N = 293), every patient who lost 10% or more of body weight had a reduced activity score, 90% had resolution of steatohepatitis and 45% had fibrosis regression; at 5% or more, 58% had resolution. The one randomised trial (Promrat 2010, PMID: 19827166, N = 31) set a 7–10% goal: the lifestyle group lost 9.3% versus 0.2% and participants reaching 7% or more improved significantly more on every histologic component. A meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (Koutoukidis 2019, PMID: 31260026, 2,588 participants) confirms weight-loss interventions reduce the presence of steatohepatitis (odds ratio 0.14, a relative measure) without a significant fibrosis effect. Below 5%, resolution was uncommon in the cohort. PROPOSED LIKELY: aim for 10% or more to reverse steatohepatitis; 7–10% helps most patients; 5% resolves it in a minority-to-half depending on the group studied.

cards.headline: Vilar-Gomez 2015: weight loss of 10% or more resolved steatohepatitis in 90% of patients and regressed fibrosis in 45%; at 5% or more, 58% resolved (N = 293, paired biopsies in 261)
cards.summary: Vilar-Gomez 2015: weight loss of 10% or more resolved steatohepatitis in 90% of patients and regressed fibrosis in 45%; at 5% or more, 58% resolved (N = 293, paired biopsies in 261)
cards.people: 293 patients with histologically proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis at a tertiary centre in Havana, Cuba, encouraged to adopt lifestyle changes to reduce weight over 52 weeks (June 2009–May 2013); paired liver biopsies at baseline and week 52 were available from 261 patients.
cards.result: Overall, 72 patients (25%) achieved resolution of steatohepatitis, 138 (47%) had reductions in NAFLD activity score (NAS), and 56 (19%) had regression of fibrosis. Eighty-eight subjects (30%) lost 5% or more of their weight; among them 51 of 88 (58%) had resolution and 72 of 88 (82%) had a 2-point NAS reduction, versus lower rates in those losing less than 5% (P < .001). All patients who lost 10% or more had NAS reductions, 90% had resolution of steatohepatitis, and 45% had regression of fibrosis. All patients losing 7–10% with few risk factors also had reduced NAS; in patients with risk features including fasting glucose above 5.5 mmol/L (99 mg/dL), NAS fell significantly only with reductions of 10% or more. Degree of weight loss was independently associated with improvement in all histologic parameters (odds ratios 1.1–2.0, relative measures; P < .01).
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: patients who lose 10% differ from those who cannot, so part of the gradient may be who succeeds rather than weight loss alone — the randomised trial card is the check on that.

cards.headline: Promrat 2010: the randomised test of a 7–10% weight-loss goal — the lifestyle group lost 9.3% versus 0.2%, and reaching 7% or more separated histologic responders from non-responders (N = 31)
cards.summary: Promrat 2010: the randomised test of a 7–10% weight-loss goal — the lifestyle group lost 9.3% versus 0.2%, and reaching 7% or more separated histologic responders from non-responders (N = 31)
cards.people: 31 overweight or obese adults (body mass index 25–40) with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, randomised 2:1 to intensive lifestyle intervention (diet, exercise and behaviour modification, goal 7–10% weight reduction) or structured education (control) for 48 weeks; primary outcome was change in NAFLD activity score (NAS).
cards.result: The lifestyle group lost an average of 9.3% of weight versus 0.2% in controls (P = 0.003). A reduction in NAS of at least 3 points, or a post-treatment NAS of 2 or less, occurred in 72% versus 30% (P = 0.03). Percent weight reduction correlated significantly with NAS improvement (r = 0.497, P = 0.007). Participants who achieved the goal of 7% or more, compared with those losing less, had significantly greater improvements in steatosis (−1.36 versus −0.41, P < 0.001), lobular inflammation (−0.82 versus −0.24, P = 0.03), ballooning (−1.27 versus −0.53, P = 0.03) and NAS (−3.45 versus −1.18, P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one patients in one centre: the trial proves lifestyle weight loss improves histology and that 7% is a meaningful cut-point inside it, but it is too small to fix the exact threshold by itself.
cards.source: Promrat K et al. Randomized controlled trial testing the effects of weight loss on nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Hepatology. 2010. PMID: 19827166. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Koutoukidis 2019: across 22 randomised trials (2,588 participants), weight-loss interventions reduced the presence of steatohepatitis (odds ratio 0.14, relative) but made no significant difference to fibrosis
cards.summary: Koutoukidis 2019: across 22 randomised trials (2,588 participants), weight-loss interventions reduced the presence of steatohepatitis (odds ratio 0.14, relative) but made no significant difference to fibrosis
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Koutoukidis 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials with 2,588 participants (mean age 45 years, about 66% male) with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, comparing interventions aiming to reduce weight (15 behavioural programmes, 6 pharmacotherapy, 1 surgical) with no or lower-intensity intervention; median intervention duration 6 months.
cards.result: More-intensive weight-loss interventions produced greater weight change (−3.61 kg; 95% CI −5.11 to −2.12) and were associated with improved alanine aminotransferase (−9.81 U/L), steatosis (standardised mean difference −1.48) and histologic NAFLD activity score (−0.92), and with lower presence of steatohepatitis (odds ratio 0.14; 95% CI 0.04–0.49 — a relative measure; the record gives no absolute rates). No statistically significant change in histologic liver fibrosis was found (−0.13; 95% CI −0.54 to 0.27 — the treatment made no difference on that outcome). Twelve studies were at high risk of bias in at least one domain.
cards.watchOut: The pooled interventions mostly achieved modest weight loss (mean difference −3.61 kg), so the meta-analysis supports the direction, not the 10% threshold — the threshold comes from the paired-biopsy cohort and the goal-based trial.
cards.source: Koutoukidis DA et al. Association of Weight Loss Interventions With Changes in Biomarkers of Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Intern Med. 2019. PMID: 31260026. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: reversal is a dose response — under 5% rarely reverses steatohepatitis, 5% or more resolves it in 58%, 7–10% improves histology broadly, and 10% or more resolves it in 90%
cards.summary: Synthesis: reversal is a dose response — under 5% rarely reverses steatohepatitis, 5% or more resolves it in 58%, 7–10% improves histology broadly, and 10% or more resolves it in 90%
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective paired-biopsy cohort (N = 293 enrolled, 261 paired biopsies), one randomised lifestyle trial (N = 31, goal 7–10%), and one meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (2,588 participants). Total carded participants exceed 2,900, so no small-N labelling applies; the threshold estimates rest mainly on the cohort, which is printed here.
cards.result: Vilar-Gomez 2015 supplies the gradient (58% resolution at ≥5% loss; 90% resolution and 45% fibrosis regression at ≥10%); Promrat 2010 confirms under randomisation that reaching ≥7% separates responders; Koutoukidis 2019 confirms across trials that weight-loss intervention reduces steatohepatitis presence (relative odds ratio 0.14) without a proven fibrosis effect. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, dose-dependent): about 10% of body weight is the amount needed to reliably reverse steatohepatitis.
cards.watchOut: These data are lifestyle weight loss in biopsy-proven steatohepatitis cohorts assembled before the MASLD renaming; drug- or surgery-induced loss of the same percentage is a separate question, and fibrosis reversal lags steatohepatitis resolution at every dose.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vilar-Gomez E et al. Gastroenterology. 2015 (PMID: 25865049); Promrat K et al. Hepatology. 2010 (PMID: 19827166); Koutoukidis DA et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2019 (PMID: 31260026).

shelves.title: Infliximab vs adalimumab in Crohn's disease (no head-to-head trial): indirect and real-world evidence leans modestly to infliximab for induction — clearest in perianal disease — with hard outcomes broadly equal
shelves.question: Is infliximab better than adalimumab for inducing remission in moderate to severe Crohn's disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Crohn Disease · Adalimumab · Infliximab · Biological Therapy · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — no head-to-head trial exists; the lean rests on indirect and observational evidence only, printed on the face. No randomised trial has ever compared infliximab with adalimumab directly in Crohn's disease. The indirect evidence leans modestly toward infliximab for induction: in a network meta-analysis of 25 induction trials (8,720 patients), infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first of all agents for induction of clinical remission in the overall population (relative risk of failure to achieve remission 0.67 versus placebo), although risankizumab ranked first in both the biologic-naive and biologic-exposed subgroups (Barberio 2023, PMID: 35907636). The direct observational comparisons are split by outcome type: a US Medicare cohort found persistence, surgery and hospitalisation statistically indistinguishable (Osterman 2014, PMID: 23811254); a single-centre electronic-record cohort found more symptomatic non-response with adalimumab (OR 1.62) but no difference in surgery, hospitalisation or steroid use (Ananthakrishnan 2016, PMID: 26933751); and in 13,222 UK BioResource patients the two anti-TNF agents were broadly similar first-line, with infliximab superior specifically in perianal Crohn's disease (Kapizioni 2024, PMID: 38041850). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — indirect and observational only: infliximab is probably at least as good and modestly better for inducing remission, most clearly in perianal disease, but the difference has never been tested head-to-head and hard outcomes look equal.

cards.headline: Barberio 2023: in a network meta-analysis of 25 induction trials (8,720 patients), infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first for induction of clinical remission overall — but risankizumab, not either anti-TNF, ranked first in biologic-naive and biologic-exposed subgroups
cards.summary: Barberio 2023: in a network meta-analysis of 25 induction trials (8,720 patients), infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first for induction of clinical remission overall — but risankizumab, not either anti-TNF, ranked first in biologic-naive and biologic-exposed subgroups
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials in luminal Crohn's disease searched to 1 July 2022: 25 induction-of-remission trials (8,720 patients) and 15 maintenance trials (4,016 patients), comparing biological therapies and small molecules against placebo and, indirectly, against each other.
cards.result: Based on failure to achieve clinical remission, infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first versus placebo (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.56–0.79, p-score 0.95), with risankizumab 600 mg second and upadacitinib 45 mg third. However, risankizumab 600 mg ranked first for clinical remission in biologic-naive patients (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52–0.85) and in biologic-exposed patients (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.67–0.82). The record reports rankings and each drug's relative effect versus placebo; it reports no direct infliximab-versus-adalimumab effect estimate, because no such trial exists in the network.
cards.watchOut: A network ranking is not a head-to-head result: infliximab's first place is inferred through placebo arms of different trials run in different eras and populations, and the same analysis puts a newer agent ahead of both anti-TNF drugs in the subgroups clinicians actually ask about.
cards.source: Barberio B et al. Efficacy of biological therapies and small molecules in induction and maintenance of remission in luminal Crohn's disease: systematic review and network meta-analysis. Gut. 2023. PMID: 35907636. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Crohn Disease · Adalimumab · Infliximab · Biological Therapy · Remission Induction

cards.headline: Osterman 2014: in 2,330 Medicare new users, infliximab and adalimumab were indistinguishable — 26-week persistence 49% vs 47% (OR 0.98), surgery HR 0.79 and hospitalisation HR 0.88, all non-significant (the treatments made no difference on these outcomes)
cards.summary: Osterman 2014: in 2,330 Medicare new users, infliximab and adalimumab were indistinguishable — 26-week persistence 49% vs 47% (OR 0.98), surgery HR 0.79 and hospitalisation HR 0.88, all non-significant (the treatments made no difference on these outcomes)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort using US Medicare data 2006–2010: patients with Crohn's disease who were new users of infliximab (n = 1,459) or adalimumab (n = 871) after 31 January 2007; patients over 85 and those with other anti-TNF indications were excluded. Outcomes were persistence on therapy at week 26, Crohn's surgery and Crohn's hospitalisation, with propensity-score adjustment.
cards.result: After 26 weeks, 49% of infliximab patients remained on drug versus 47% on adalimumab (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.81–1.19). Surgery was less frequent with infliximab but not significantly (5.5 vs 6.9 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.60–1.05), and hospitalisation rates did not differ (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.07). The authors conclude the two agents had similar effectiveness on all three clinically important outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Medicare claims capture persistence, surgery and hospitalisation — not remission, the outcome this shelf asks about — and channeling (sicker or perianal patients being steered to infliximab infusions) can hide inside propensity adjustment.
cards.source: Osterman MT et al. Comparative effectiveness of infliximab and adalimumab for Crohn's disease. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2014. PMID: 23811254. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ananthakrishnan 2016: adalimumab carried a higher likelihood of symptomatic non-response at 1 year than infliximab in Crohn's disease (OR 1.62) — yet surgery, hospitalisation and prednisone use did not differ
cards.summary: Ananthakrishnan 2016: adalimumab carried a higher likelihood of symptomatic non-response at 1 year than infliximab in Crohn's disease (OR 1.62) — yet surgery, hospitalisation and prednisone use did not differ
cards.people: Single-centre electronic-health-record cohort of new anti-TNF initiations 1998–2010: 1,060 infliximab initiations (68% for Crohn's disease) and 391 adalimumab initiations (79% for Crohn's disease). Non-response was scored from the frequency of narrative mentions of relevant symptoms in the record; surgery, hospitalisation and steroid use were coded outcomes at 1 year.
cards.result: In Crohn's disease, the likelihood of non-response was higher with adalimumab than infliximab (odds ratio 1.62, 95% CI 1.21–2.17), with similar differences favouring infliximab for the individual symptoms of diarrhoea, pain, bleeding and fatigue. There was no difference in inflammatory-bowel-disease-related surgery, hospitalisations or prednisone use within 1 year in Crohn's disease, and no difference on any outcome in ulcerative colitis.
cards.watchOut: The positive outcome here is a text-mined symptom score, not endoscopic or even formally scored clinical remission, and the same study's hard outcomes were equal — the two findings must travel together.
cards.source: Ananthakrishnan AN et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Infliximab and Adalimumab in Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis. Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. 2016. PMID: 26933751. cards.headline: Kapizioni 2024: in 13,222 UK IBD BioResource patients, first-line anti-TNF effectiveness was broadly similar — with infliximab superior to adalimumab specifically in perianal Crohn's disease
cards.summary: Kapizioni 2024: in 13,222 UK IBD BioResource patients, first-line anti-TNF effectiveness was broadly similar — with infliximab superior to adalimumab specifically in perianal Crohn's disease
cards.people: Real-world cohort of 13,222 evaluable patients in the UK IBD BioResource who received at least one biologic; effectiveness was persistence free of discontinuation or failure, analysed with Kaplan–Meier methods and inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting, over up to 10 years in Crohn's disease.
cards.result: In Crohn's disease there were significant differences between first-line treatments over 10 years (P = 0.045), with superior effectiveness of infliximab compared with adalimumab in perianal Crohn's disease; anti-TNF therapy otherwise showed similar effectiveness first-line. After first-line anti-TNF failure in Crohn's disease, non-anti-TNF biologics were superior to a second anti-TNF (P = 0.035). The record reports no single pooled infliximab-versus-adalimumab effect estimate for luminal disease.
cards.watchOut: Persistence-free-of-failure blends efficacy, tolerance, funding and patient preference, and the infliximab advantage is localised to perianal disease — it should not be read as a general luminal-disease verdict.
cards.source: Kapizioni C et al. Biologic Therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Real-World Comparative Effectiveness and Impact of Drug Sequencing in 13 222 Patients within the UK IBD BioResource. cards.headline: Synthesis: no head-to-head trial exists; indirect rankings and symptom outcomes lean modestly to infliximab, hard outcomes look equal, and perianal disease is where infliximab's edge is clearest
cards.summary: Synthesis: no head-to-head trial exists; indirect rankings and symptom outcomes lean modestly to infliximab, hard outcomes look equal, and perianal disease is where infliximab's edge is clearest
cards.people: The carded evidence: one network meta-analysis (25 induction trials, 8,720 patients; 15 maintenance trials, 4,016 patients), two US comparative cohorts (2,330 Medicare new users; 1,451 initiations) and one UK registry cohort (13,222 patients). Total carded participants exceed 25,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the absence of any direct randomised comparison.
cards.result: Infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first for induction of remission in the overall network (RR of failure to remit 0.67 versus placebo) while risankizumab ranked first in the naive and exposed subgroups (Barberio 2023). Symptomatic non-response favoured infliximab in one cohort (OR 1.62 for adalimumab; Ananthakrishnan 2016), while persistence, surgery and hospitalisation did not differ in either US cohort (Osterman 2014; Ananthakrishnan 2016), and the UK cohort found the agents broadly similar except in perianal disease (Kapizioni 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — indirect and observational only.
cards.watchOut: Route and setting differ as much as molecule (hospital infusion with weight-based dosing and easy escalation versus home injection), and drug-level-guided dosing — covered on its own shelf — may matter more than which anti-TNF is chosen.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barberio B et al. Gut. 2023 (PMID: 35907636); Osterman MT et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2014 (PMID: 23811254); Ananthakrishnan AN et al. shelves.title: Anti-TNF drug levels in Crohn's disease — SPLIT by phase: maintenance monitoring and correcting a low trough helped (NOR-DRUM B, TAXIT), while monitoring from induction and level-guided escalation did not (NOR-DRUM A, TAILORIX)
shelves.question: Should adults with Crohn's disease have drug levels checked to guide anti-TNF dosing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Algorithms · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Belgium · Colitis, Ulcerative · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Crohn Disease · Drug Costs · Drug Dosage Calculations · Drug Monitoring · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Infliximab · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Tertiary Care Centers · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised trials genuinely divide, and the split is by phase of treatment and by what the level is used for. Proactive monitoring during maintenance helped in the largest trial: in NOR-DRUM part B, 458 patients on maintenance infliximab (mixed immune-mediated diseases, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) had sustained disease control without worsening in 73.6% with therapeutic drug monitoring versus 55.9% without (adjusted difference 17.6%) (Syversen 2021, PMID: 34932077). TAXIT points the same way for one use — correcting a low level: dose escalation in patients with troughs under 3 µg/mL raised Crohn's remission from 65% to 88%, and after optimisation, concentration-based dosing produced fewer flares than clinically based dosing (7% vs 17%), although 1-year remission itself did not differ (69% vs 66%) (Vande Casteele 2015, PMID: 25724455). Against that, monitoring from the start did not improve remission in NOR-DRUM part A (50.5% vs 53.0% at week 30; the treatment made no difference) (Syversen 2021, PMID: 33944876), and in TAILORIX, escalating infliximab by symptoms plus biomarkers plus drug levels produced the primary remission endpoint in 27–33% versus 40% with symptom-based escalation alone (P = .50) (D'Haens 2018, PMID: 29317275). Two cautions travel with the positive trials: NOR-DRUM pooled six diseases and its record does not report the Crohn's subgroup separately, and TAXIT's maintenance phase was null on its primary endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT (maintenance monitoring and low-level correction: benefit in NOR-DRUM B and TAXIT; induction-phase and escalation-algorithm monitoring: no benefit in NOR-DRUM A and TAILORIX).

cards.headline: Vande Casteele 2015 (TAXIT): correcting a low infliximab trough raised Crohn's remission from 65% to 88%, and concentration-based maintenance dosing halved flares (7% vs 17%) — but 1-year remission itself did not differ (69% vs 66%)
cards.summary: Vande Casteele 2015 (TAXIT): correcting a low infliximab trough raised Crohn's remission from 65% to 88%, and concentration-based maintenance dosing halved flares (7% vs 17%) — but 1-year remission itself did not differ (69% vs 66%)
cards.people: One-year randomised controlled trial at a tertiary centre in 263 adults (178 with Crohn's disease, 85 with ulcerative colitis) with stable responses to maintenance infliximab. All patients first had doses escalated or reduced by algorithm to a target trough concentration of 3–7 µg/mL (optimisation phase), then were randomised to clinically based dosing (n = 123) or continued concentration-based dosing (n = 128) for the maintenance phase.
cards.result: Of 76 patients with troughs under 3 µg/mL, 69 (91%) reached 3–7 µg/mL after dose escalation, with a higher proportion of Crohn's patients in remission than before escalation (88% vs 65%; P = .020); dose reduction in patients above 7 µg/mL cut drug cost by 28% (P < .001). In the randomised maintenance phase, the primary endpoint of clinical and biochemical remission at 1 year was reached by 69% with concentration-based dosing and 66% with clinically based dosing (P = .686; the treatment made no difference), but disease relapsed in fewer concentration-based patients (9 of 128, 7%) than clinically based patients (21 of 123, 17%) (P = .018).
cards.watchOut: The remission gain from escalation is a before–after comparison inside the optimisation phase, not a randomised contrast — the trial's only randomised remission comparison was null, and its positive finding is on flares.
cards.source: Vande Casteele N et al. Trough concentrations of infliximab guide dosing for patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 25724455. Registry ID: EudraCT 2011-002061-38 (from the record).
