cards.headline: D'Haens 2018 (TAILORIX): escalating infliximab using symptoms plus biomarkers plus drug levels did not beat symptoms alone — the primary endpoint was reached by 33%, 27% and 40% across the three arms (P = .50; the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: D'Haens 2018 (TAILORIX): escalating infliximab using symptoms plus biomarkers plus drug levels did not beat symptoms alone — the primary endpoint was reached by 33%, 27% and 40% across the three arms (P = .50; the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Prospective double-blind randomised trial in 122 biologic-naive adults with active luminal Crohn's disease at 27 European centres, all receiving infliximab induction combined with an immunosuppressant. At week 14 patients were randomised (1:1:1) to dose intensification guided by symptoms, biomarkers and serum infliximab concentrations in 2.5 mg/kg steps (n = 45), the same criteria with escalation from 5 to 10 mg/kg (n = 37), or dose increase to 10 mg/kg based on clinical symptoms alone (n = 40), followed to week 54.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — sustained corticosteroid-free clinical remission from weeks 22 to 54 with no ulcers at week 54 — was reached by 15 of 45 patients (33%) in the stepwise level-guided group, 10 of 37 (27%) in the 5-to-10 mg/kg level-guided group and 16 of 40 (40%) in the symptoms-alone control group (P = .50). Adding biomarker and drug-level criteria to escalation decisions did not increase clinical, endoscopic or corticosteroid-free remission.
cards.watchOut: This was an exploratory, proof-of-concept-sized trial (122 patients) in patients already receiving combination therapy from induction — it tests one escalation algorithm in early disease, not level-checking in established maintenance care.
cards.source: D'Haens G et al. cards.headline: Syversen 2021 (NOR-DRUM B): proactive drug monitoring during maintenance infliximab sustained disease control without worsening in 73.6% versus 55.9% without monitoring (adjusted difference 17.6%, P < .001)
cards.summary: Syversen 2021 (NOR-DRUM B): proactive drug monitoring during maintenance infliximab sustained disease control without worsening in 73.6% versus 55.9% without monitoring (adjusted difference 17.6%, P < .001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Syversen 2021, NOR-DRUM part B)
cards.people: Randomised, parallel-group, open-label trial in 458 adults with rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or psoriasis on maintenance infliximab at 20 Norwegian hospitals (228 randomised to proactive therapeutic drug monitoring, 230 to standard therapy); 454 received their allocated intervention and were analysed. The record does not report the Crohn's disease subgroup separately.
cards.result: The primary outcome — sustained disease control without disease worsening over 52 weeks — was observed in 167 patients (73.6%) in the monitoring group and 127 (55.9%) in the standard-therapy group, an estimated adjusted difference of 17.6% (95% CI 9.0%–26.2%; P < .001) favouring monitoring. Adverse events were reported in 60% and 63% of the groups respectively.
cards.watchOut: Six diseases were pooled into one primary outcome, and 'disease worsening' partly meant a decision to change treatment — a judgement the unblinded monitoring itself can influence; the Crohn's-specific effect is not separable from this record.
cards.source: Syversen SW et al. Effect of Therapeutic Drug Monitoring vs Standard Therapy During Maintenance Infliximab Therapy on Disease Control in Patients With Immune-Mediated Inflammatory Diseases: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34932077. Registry ID: NCT03074656. cards.headline: Syversen 2021 (NOR-DRUM A): starting monitoring at infliximab induction did not improve remission — 50.5% versus 53.0% at week 30 (adjusted difference 1.5%, P = .78; the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Syversen 2021 (NOR-DRUM A): starting monitoring at infliximab induction did not improve remission — 50.5% versus 53.0% at week 30 (adjusted difference 1.5%, P = .78; the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Syversen 2021, NOR-DRUM part A)
cards.people: Randomised, parallel-group, open-label trial in 411 adults with the same six immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) initiating infliximab at 21 Norwegian hospitals (207 randomised to proactive therapeutic drug monitoring, 204 to standard therapy); 398 received their allocated intervention and were analysed. The record does not report the Crohn's disease subgroup separately.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 30 was achieved in 100 of 198 patients (50.5%) in the monitoring group and 106 of 200 (53.0%) in the standard-therapy group (adjusted difference 1.5%, 95% CI −8.2% to 11.1%; P = .78). Adverse events were reported in 68% and 70% respectively. The authors conclude the findings do not support routine monitoring during infliximab induction to improve remission rates.
cards.watchOut: As with part B, the diseases are pooled; a Crohn's-only induction effect, in either direction, cannot be extracted from this record — the null is a class-level null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: levels help when they correct maintenance dosing, not when they drive induction or escalation algorithms — two positive and two null randomised results, split by phase
cards.summary: Synthesis: levels help when they correct maintenance dosing, not when they drive induction or escalation algorithms — two positive and two null randomised results, split by phase
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials — TAXIT (263 patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis on maintenance infliximab), TAILORIX (122 biologic-naive patients with active Crohn's disease), and NOR-DRUM parts A and B (411 patients starting and 458 patients established on infliximab across six immune-mediated diseases, Crohn's subgroup not separately reported). Total carded participants exceed 1,200, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Maintenance-phase monitoring sustained disease control in NOR-DRUM B (73.6% vs 55.9%) and, in TAXIT, correcting troughs under 3 µg/mL was followed by remission rising from 65% to 88% in Crohn's disease, with fewer flares on continued concentration-based dosing (7% vs 17%) but no difference in 1-year remission (69% vs 66%). Induction-phase monitoring in NOR-DRUM A (50.5% vs 53.0%) and level-guided escalation in TAILORIX (27–33% vs 40%) both made no difference. PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit for maintenance monitoring and low-level correction; no benefit for induction-phase monitoring or escalation algorithms).
cards.watchOut: Almost everything carded here is infliximab: adalimumab level-guided dosing has no carded randomised trial on this shelf, and reactive testing at loss of response — the commonest real-world use — is a different question from the proactive strategies these trials tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vande Casteele N et al. Gastroenterology. 2015 (PMID: 25724455); D'Haens G et al. Gastroenterology. 2018 (PMID: 29317275); Syversen SW et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 34932077); Syversen SW et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 33944876).

shelves.title: Calprotectin monitoring vs symptoms alone in IBD — SPLIT: composite and subgroup outcomes favour monitoring in ulcerative colitis, but no carded trial won on its primary endpoint and Crohn's treat-to-target was null
shelves.question: Is fecal calprotectin monitoring better than symptom monitoring alone to prevent relapse in inflammatory bowel disease?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT — biomarker-guided management wins on some targets in some settings and makes no difference on others, and the strongest positive trial cannot be re-carded here. In ulcerative colitis in remission, monthly calprotectin with 5-aminosalicylate escalation above 300 µg/g did not significantly reduce relapse overall (35.3% vs 50.0%, P = 0.23), although among patients whose calprotectin actually rose, relapse was halved (28.6% vs 57.1%) (Lasson 2015, PMID: 25653861). In active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, calprotectin home monitoring missed its primary endoscopic endpoint (Mayo endoscopic subscore 0: 37.0% vs 33.4%, not significant) but achieved significantly more composite clinical-plus-endoscopic control (OPTIMISE; Danese 2024, PMID: 39274360). In Crohn's disease on ustekinumab, a treat-to-target strategy built on endoscopy, biomarkers and symptoms did not significantly improve endoscopic response at week 48 (38% vs 30%, P = 0.087) and produced less clinical response than symptom-driven care (STARDUST; Danese 2022, PMID: 35120656). The field's landmark positive trial, CALM (Colombel 2017, PMID: 29096949 — tight control 46% vs 30% endoscopic remission), is already carded as an evidence card on live shelf #324 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, under the one-home rule; it enrolled active Crohn's disease, not patients in remission being watched for relapse. PROPOSED SPLIT (calprotectin-guided escalation: benefit on composite control in active ulcerative colitis and in the calprotectin-risen subgroup in remission; no significant benefit on the primary endpoints of any carded trial, and no benefit for ustekinumab treat-to-target in Crohn's disease).

cards.headline: Lasson 2015: monthly calprotectin with dose escalation above 300 µg/g did not significantly cut relapse overall in ulcerative colitis in remission (35.3% vs 50.0%, P = 0.23) — but relapse was halved in patients whose calprotectin actually rose (28.6% vs 57.1%)
cards.summary: Lasson 2015: monthly calprotectin with dose escalation above 300 µg/g did not significantly cut relapse overall in ulcerative colitis in remission (35.3% vs 50.0%, P = 0.23) — but relapse was halved in patients whose calprotectin actually rose (28.6% vs 57.1%)
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled study of 91 adults with ulcerative colitis in remission, randomised to an intervention group (monthly faecal calprotectin for 18 months, with escalation of the oral 5-aminosalicylate dose when calprotectin exceeded 300 µg/g; 51 patients) or a control group managed without calprotectin guidance (40 patients). The primary endpoint was relapse by month 18.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 18 of 51 intervention patients (35.3%) and 20 of 40 control patients (50.0%) (P = 0.23; the treatment made no significant difference overall). A calprotectin above 300 µg/g occurred in 28 patients in each group; among those, 8 of 28 (28.6%) relapsed in the intervention group versus 16 of 28 (57.1%) in the control group (P < 0.05). The authors conclude calprotectin can identify patients at risk of a flare, in whom 5-aminosalicylate escalation is a therapeutic option.
cards.watchOut: The headline subgroup (patients whose calprotectin rose) is defined by a post-randomisation measurement, so its halved relapse rate is hypothesis-generating, not a randomised result — the trial's own primary comparison is null.

cards.headline: Danese 2024 (OPTIMISE): calprotectin home monitoring in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis missed its primary endoscopic endpoint (37.0% vs 33.4%, not significant) but significantly improved composite clinical-plus-endoscopic control (effect size 0.17–0.22)
cards.summary: Danese 2024 (OPTIMISE): calprotectin home monitoring in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis missed its primary endoscopic endpoint (37.0% vs 33.4%, not significant) but significantly improved composite clinical-plus-endoscopic control (effect size 0.17–0.22)
cards.people: Pragmatic randomised (1:1) controlled study of patients with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis (global Mayo score 2–6) treated with 2.4 g/day or less of 5-aminosalicylate, comparing treatment optimisation using faecal calprotectin home monitoring plus symptoms against symptoms (PRO-2) alone over 12 months; 193 patients completed the study (the record does not state the total number randomised).
cards.result: No significant difference was found for the primary endpoint (Mayo Endoscopic Subscore 0 at 12 months: 37.0% interventional vs 33.4% reference, after imputation for missing data). The composite endpoint of endoscopic subscore 0 with no rectal bleeding and stool frequency 1 or less was achieved at a significantly higher rate with calprotectin monitoring (effect size 0.17, 95% CI 0.02–0.32; P < 0.05), as was the corresponding subscore-1 composite (effect size 0.22, 95% CI 0.07–0.37; P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint with positive secondary composites is a weak form of win, the study was industry-funded (Ferring, per its record), and these were patients with active mild-to-moderate disease — not the in-remission relapse-prevention setting of this shelf's question.

cards.headline: Danese 2022 (STARDUST): treat-to-target management (early endoscopy, biomarker and symptom monitoring, dose intensification) did not significantly beat symptom-driven care on endoscopic response in Crohn's disease (38% vs 30%, P = 0.087)
cards.summary: Danese 2022 (STARDUST): treat-to-target management (early endoscopy, biomarker and symptom monitoring, dose intensification) did not significantly beat symptom-driven care on endoscopic response in Crohn's disease (38% vs 30%, P = 0.087)
cards.people: Open-label, multicentre, randomised phase 3b trial in adults with moderate-to-severe active Crohn's disease receiving ustekinumab: 498 patients received induction, and 440 week-16 responders were randomised to treat-to-target maintenance (n = 219) or standard-of-care, clinically driven maintenance (n = 221) through week 48. The treat-to-target arm escalated dosing when prespecified endoscopic, biomarker and clinical targets were missed.
cards.result: At week 48 there was no significant difference in endoscopic response (83 of 219, 38%, vs 66 of 221, 30%; P = 0.087), endoscopic remission (11% vs 15%), mucosal healing (14% vs 17%) or clinical remission (62% vs 70%); clinical response was significantly lower in the treat-to-target group (68% vs 78%; P = 0.020). The authors conclude timely escalation based on endoscopy, symptoms and biomarkers did not produce significantly better endoscopic outcomes than symptom-driven decisions alone.
cards.watchOut: The treat-to-target strategy here was anchored on early endoscopy with biomarkers as one input, in patients all receiving one specific drug — it tests a management package in active Crohn's disease, not calprotectin monitoring alone in remission.
cards.source: Danese S et al. Treat to target versus standard of care for patients with Crohn's disease treated with ustekinumab (STARDUST): an open-label, multicentre, randomised phase 3b trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2022. PMID: 35120656. Registry ID: NCT03107793. cards.headline: Synthesis: calprotectin monitoring has never won on a carded trial's primary endpoint, yet repeatedly wins on secondary and subgroup outcomes — and the one clearly positive strategy trial (CALM) is homed on live shelf #324
cards.summary: Synthesis: calprotectin monitoring has never won on a carded trial's primary endpoint, yet repeatedly wins on secondary and subgroup outcomes — and the one clearly positive strategy trial (CALM) is homed on live shelf #324
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised strategy trials — Lasson 2015 (91 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission), OPTIMISE 2024 (193 completers with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis) and STARDUST 2022 (440 randomised patients with Crohn's disease on ustekinumab). Total carded participants exceed 700, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. CALM (PMID: 29096949) is cross-pointed, not carded: it is an evidence card on live shelf #324.
cards.result: Primary endpoints: relapse 35.3% vs 50.0% (P = 0.23, Lasson), endoscopic subscore 0 in 37.0% vs 33.4% (not significant, OPTIMISE), endoscopic response 38% vs 30% (P = 0.087, STARDUST) — none significant. Secondary signals favoured monitoring in both ulcerative colitis trials (relapse 28.6% vs 57.1% in the calprotectin-risen subgroup; composite control effect sizes 0.17 and 0.22). PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit on composite/subgroup outcomes in ulcerative colitis; no significant benefit on any carded primary endpoint, and none for ustekinumab treat-to-target in Crohn's disease).
cards.watchOut: Monitoring only helps if an effective escalation exists for the patient in front of you: the ulcerative colitis trials escalated 5-aminosalicylates, a cheap, safe step — extrapolating the strategy to early biologic escalation carries different stakes and thinner proof.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lasson A et al. United European Gastroenterology Journal. 2015 (PMID: 25653861); Danese S et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39274360); Danese S et al. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2022 (PMID: 35120656). The CALM trial is carded on live shelf #324 and is cross-pointed in the balance and synthesis text only — it is not a card on this shelf.

shelves.title: Low-residue diet in an ulcerative colitis flare — untested, not disproven: no trial has ever randomised flaring patients to residue restriction, and the only fibre-feeding trial (in remission) found high fibre tolerated
shelves.question: Is a low-residue diet needed during an ulcerative colitis flare?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Calcium, Dietary · Cattle · Colitis, Ulcerative · Crohn Disease · Dietary Carbohydrates · Dietary Fiber · Food, Organic · Humans · Meat · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the practice has never been tested, not that it has been disproven. No carded record contains a randomised trial of a low-residue (low-fibre) diet during an ulcerative colitis flare. The Cochrane review of dietary interventions in inflammatory bowel disease (18 RCTs, 1,878 participants) found exactly one trial in active ulcerative colitis — a symptoms-guided diet in 21 participants, remission 36% vs 0%, relative risk 8.25 with a confidence interval running from 0.50 to 136.33, rated very low certainty — and concluded that the effects of dietary interventions are uncertain and no firm conclusions can be drawn (Limketkai 2019, PMID: 30736095). A systematic review of diet trials found low-residue/low-fibre diets were among the commonest interventions studied, but the few higher-quality trials showing significant symptom improvement tested exclusion or other specific diets, not residue restriction (Charlebois 2016, PMID: 25569442). The only carded trial that fed ulcerative colitis patients more fibre points the other way, in a different population: 17 patients in remission or with mild disease tolerated a catered low-fat, high-fibre diet for 4 weeks, all remained in remission, and quality of life and inflammatory markers improved (Fritsch 2021, PMID: 32445952) — reassuring about fibre, but not a flare trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a low-residue diet during a flare is an untested tradition; there is no trial evidence that it is needed, and no flare trial evidence that fibre is safe either — the gap itself is the finding.

cards.headline: Limketkai 2019 (Cochrane): across 18 diet RCTs (1,878 participants) there was only one trial in active ulcerative colitis — 21 participants, very low certainty — and no trial of a low-residue diet during a flare; the review concludes diet effects in IBD are uncertain
cards.summary: Limketkai 2019 (Cochrane): across 18 diet RCTs (1,878 participants) there was only one trial in active ulcerative colitis — 21 participants, very low certainty — and no trial of a low-residue diet during a flare; the review concludes diet effects in IBD are uncertain
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Limketkai 2019, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials comparing dietary manipulations with other diets in inflammatory bowel disease, searched to 31 January 2019: 18 RCTs with 1,878 participants — six in active Crohn's disease, seven in inactive Crohn's disease, one in active ulcerative colitis and four in inactive ulcerative colitis. Fourteen studies were rated high risk of bias, the rest unclear.
cards.result: The single active-ulcerative-colitis trial tested a symptoms-guided diet: at 6 weeks, remission in 36% (4 of 11) on the diet versus 0% (0 of 10) on usual diet (relative risk 8.25, 95% CI 0.50–136.33; 21 participants; very low certainty evidence). No included trial tested a low-residue or low-fibre diet during an ulcerative colitis flare. The authors conclude: the effects of dietary interventions on Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are uncertain, and no firm conclusions regarding benefits and harms can be drawn.
cards.watchOut: Absence of a trial is not evidence the diet fails — it is evidence the standard advice given to flaring patients rests on tradition; the one active-UC trial's confidence interval (0.50 to 136.33) is compatible with almost anything.
cards.source: Limketkai BN et al. Dietary interventions for induction and maintenance of remission in inflammatory bowel disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 30736095. cards.headline: Charlebois 2016: low-residue/low-fibre diets were among the commonest diet interventions trialled in IBD — but the few higher-quality trials with significant symptom improvement tested exclusion or other specific diets, not residue restriction
cards.summary: Charlebois 2016: low-residue/low-fibre diets were among the commonest diet interventions trialled in IBD — but the few higher-quality trials with significant symptom improvement tested exclusion or other specific diets, not residue restriction
cards.people: Systematic review of published clinical trials evaluating regular-diet interventions (dietary manipulation with ordinary foods) in adults with inflammatory bowel disease whose symptoms were objectively measured before and after the intervention; the interventions found fell into three categories: low-residue/low-fibre diets, exclusion diets, and other specific diets. The record reports no pooled effect size for low-residue diets.
cards.result: Of all included studies, the few that were of higher quality and observed a statistically significant improvement in symptoms in the diet group compared with the control group fell under the exclusion-diet or other-specific-diet categories. The review identifies exclusion diets and the low-FODMAP diet as the areas showing promise for therapeutic benefit in inflammatory bowel disease. No significant symptom benefit for low-residue/low-fibre diets is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: This review measured symptoms, not mucosal inflammation or flare resolution, and it pools Crohn's disease with ulcerative colitis — even its positive diet signals do not answer what a patient mid-flare should eat.
cards.source: Charlebois A et al. The Impact of Dietary Interventions on the Symptoms of Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review. Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition. 2016. cards.headline: Fritsch 2021: 17 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission or mild disease ate a catered low-fat, HIGH-fibre diet for 4 weeks — all remained in remission and quality of life improved (small N printed on the face; remission, not flare, population)
cards.summary: Fritsch 2021: 17 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission or mild disease ate a catered low-fat, HIGH-fibre diet for 4 weeks — all remained in remission and quality of life improved (small N printed on the face; remission, not flare, population)
cards.people: Parallel-group crossover study of 17 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission or with mild disease (with a flare within the past 18 months), randomised to a catered low-fat, high-fibre diet (10% of calories from fat) or an improved standard American diet (35%–40% of calories from fat) for 4 weeks, a 2-week washout, then the other diet; each participant served as their own control. Study N = 17.
cards.result: All patients remained in remission throughout the study. Both diets increased quality of life versus baseline (short IBD questionnaire 4.98 at baseline, 5.55 on the improved standard diet, 5.77 on the low-fat high-fibre diet; P = .02 and P = .001 respectively). Serum amyloid A fell on the high-fibre diet from 7.99 mg/L at baseline to 4.50 mg/L (P = .02); C-reactive protein fell numerically (3.23 to 2.51 mg/L, P = .07).
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients without active flares, fed catered meals for 4 weeks: this shows fibre was tolerated and did not provoke relapse in quiet disease — it cannot show fibre is safe or helpful during an actual flare, which is this shelf's question.
cards.source: Fritsch J et al. Low-Fat, High-Fiber Diet Reduces Markers of Inflammation and Dysbiosis and Improves Quality of Life in Patients With Ulcerative Colitis. cards.headline: Synthesis: the low-residue-during-flare rule is an untested tradition — no trial supports it, and the nearest fibre evidence (in remission) points the other way
cards.summary: Synthesis: the low-residue-during-flare rule is an untested tradition — no trial supports it, and the nearest fibre evidence (in remission) points the other way
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review (18 RCTs, 1,878 participants, only one 21-participant trial in active ulcerative colitis and none testing low-residue diet in a flare), one systematic review of regular-diet trials (no pooled low-residue effect reported in its record), and one 17-patient crossover trial of a high-fibre diet in remission or mild disease. The flare-specific evidence base is effectively empty, which is why the stamp is MAYBE rather than a verdict against the diet.
cards.result: No carded study randomised patients during an ulcerative colitis flare to low-residue versus ordinary diet. The Cochrane authors rate the whole diet literature in IBD as uncertain (Limketkai 2019); the symptom-focused review found its significant results in exclusion and other diets, not residue restriction (Charlebois 2016); and the only direct fibre-feeding trial found a high-fibre diet tolerated with improved quality of life in non-flaring patients (Fritsch 2021). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — needed-ness unproven either way.
cards.watchOut: Individual patients may still reasonably restrict residue for comfort during severe symptoms (pain, urgency, strictures elsewhere in IBD) — symptom comfort is a legitimate goal; what the evidence does not support is presenting restriction as treatment the flare requires.
cards.source: Synthesis of Limketkai BN et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019 (PMID: 30736095); Charlebois A et al. Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition. 2016 (PMID: 25569442); Fritsch J et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2021 (PMID: 32445952).

shelves.title: Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole for acute pouchitis — never tested against metronidazole alone: the one small head-to-head trial favours ciprofloxacin by itself, and the combination's evidence is uncontrolled, in refractory disease
shelves.question: Does ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole treat acute pouchitis better than metronidazole alone?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents · Ciprofloxacin · Colitis, Ulcerative · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole · Pouchitis · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the exact comparison in this shelf's question has never been randomised. A 2023 systematic review of all 20 randomised pouchitis trials (830 patients) found just one acute-pouchitis antibiotic comparison — ciprofloxacin alone versus metronidazole alone — and no trial of the combination against metronidazole alone (Alphonsus 2023, PMID: 37246609). That single trial was tiny (16 patients): ciprofloxacin produced a greater fall in the Pouchitis Disease Activity Index than metronidazole (6.9 vs 3.8 points, P = 0.002) with remission in 7 of 7 versus 6 of 9 (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 0.88–2.35, very low certainty in the meta-analysis), and no adverse effects versus 33% with metronidazole (Shen 2001, PMID: 11720319). The combination itself has only single-arm evidence, in a different population: 44 patients with recurrent or refractory pouchitis given ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole for 4 weeks, of whom 82% entered remission (Mimura 2002, PMID: 11966499) — with no comparator, that number cannot show the combination beats either drug alone, and refractory patients are not first-episode acute pouchitis. The indirect logic (ciprofloxacin alone at least as good as metronidazole alone; the pair rescues refractory cases) is why combinations are used, but it is logic, not a trial result. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): whether adding ciprofloxacin to metronidazole improves acute pouchitis outcomes is untested; the one head-to-head trial suggests ciprofloxacin alone, not the combination, is the better-supported first choice.

cards.headline: Shen 2001: the only randomised head-to-head — ciprofloxacin ALONE beat metronidazole alone on disease activity in 16 patients (PDAI fall 6.9 vs 3.8 points, P = 0.002), with no adverse effects versus 33% (small N printed on the face)
cards.summary: Shen 2001: the only randomised head-to-head — ciprofloxacin ALONE beat metronidazole alone on disease activity in 16 patients (PDAI fall 6.9 vs 3.8 points, P = 0.002), with no adverse effects versus 33% (small N printed on the face)
cards.people: Randomised clinical trial of 16 patients with acute pouchitis (Pouchitis Disease Activity Index score 7 or higher, symptom duration 4 weeks or less) after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis, assigned to a 2-week course of ciprofloxacin 1,000 mg/day (n = 7) or metronidazole 20 mg/kg/day (n = 9). Study N = 16.
cards.result: Both drugs significantly reduced the total PDAI and its symptom, endoscopy and histology subscores. Ciprofloxacin lowered the PDAI from 10.1 ± 2.3 to 3.3 ± 1.7 (P = 0.0001); metronidazole from 9.7 ± 2.3 to 5.8 ± 1.7 (P = 0.0002). The reduction was significantly greater with ciprofloxacin for total PDAI (6.9 ± 1.2 vs 3.8 ± 1.7; P = 0.002), symptom score (2.4 ± 0.9 vs 1.3 ± 0.9; P = 0.03) and endoscopic score (3.6 ± 1.3 vs 1.9 ± 1.5; P = 0.03). No ciprofloxacin patient had adverse effects; three metronidazole patients (33%) developed vomiting, dysgeusia or transient peripheral neuropathy.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen patients, one centre, two weeks: the direction is consistent but the trial is far too small to exclude chance or to detect uncommon harms — and it says nothing about the combination this shelf asks about.
cards.source: Shen B et al. A randomized clinical trial of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole to treat acute pouchitis. Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. 2001. PMID: 11720319. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mimura 2002: the combination itself — 82% of 44 patients with recurrent or refractory pouchitis entered remission on 4 weeks of ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole, in an open-label trial with no comparison group
cards.summary: Mimura 2002: the combination itself — 82% of 44 patients with recurrent or refractory pouchitis entered remission on 4 weeks of ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole, in an open-label trial with no comparison group
cards.people: Open-label single-arm trial of 44 patients (24 male, 20 female; median age 37.5 years) with active recurrent or refractory pouchitis (at least two episodes in the previous 12 months or persistent pouchitis requiring continual antibiotics, and a Pouchitis Disease Activity Index score of 7 or more), treated with metronidazole 400 or 500 mg twice daily plus ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 28 days.
cards.result: Thirty-six of 44 patients (82%) went into remission (PDAI clinical score 2 or less, endoscopic score 1 or less and total score 4 or less). Median PDAI fell from 12 (range 8–17) before therapy to 3 (range 1–10) after (P < 0.0001), and median Inflammatory Bowel Disease Questionnaire score improved from 96.5 to 175 (P < 0.0001). Even the eight non-remitters improved significantly. No serious side-effects were noted.
cards.watchOut: Without a control group, 82% remission mixes drug effect with natural fluctuation and regression to the mean — and these were refractory or relapsing patients, the group in whom clinicians reach for two drugs, not first-episode acute pouchitis.
cards.source: Mimura T et al. Four-week open-label trial of metronidazole and ciprofloxacin for the treatment of recurrent or refractory pouchitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2002. PMID: 11966499. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Alphonsus 2023: across all 20 randomised pouchitis trials (830 patients), the combination-versus-metronidazole trial does not exist — the single acute-pouchitis comparison gives remission 100% (7/7) on ciprofloxacin vs 67% (6/9) on metronidazole, relative risk 1.44, very low certainty
cards.summary: Alphonsus 2023: across all 20 randomised pouchitis trials (830 patients), the combination-versus-metronidazole trial does not exist — the single acute-pouchitis comparison gives remission 100% (7/7) on ciprofloxacin vs 67% (6/9) on metronidazole, relative risk 1.44, very low certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Alphonsus 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of medical therapy for the treatment and prevention of pouchitis in adults, searched to March 2022: 20 RCTs with 830 participants in total. Acute pouchitis contributed two comparisons: ciprofloxacin versus metronidazole (one study) and budesonide enemas versus oral metronidazole (one study).
cards.result: For acute pouchitis, ciprofloxacin achieved remission at 2 weeks in 100% (7 of 7) versus 67% (6 of 9) with metronidazole (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 0.88–2.35; very low certainty evidence — the confidence interval includes no difference). Budesonide enemas achieved remission in 50% (6 of 12) versus 43% (6 of 14) with oral metronidazole (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.51–2.67; low certainty). The authors conclude that, apart from vedolizumab and the De Simone formulation in chronic pouchitis, the effects of other medical interventions for pouchitis are uncertain. No included trial randomised the ciprofloxacin–metronidazole combination against metronidazole alone.
cards.watchOut: The review's 'very low certainty' grade for the one relevant trial is the shelf in miniature: pouchitis antibiotic practice, including combinations, rests on a handful of very small studies.
cards.source: Alphonsus L et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials: Medical therapies for the treatment and prevention of pouchitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2023. PMID: 37246609. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the combination has never been randomised against metronidazole alone — the evidence supports ciprofloxacin alone as at least metronidazole's equal, and the pair only as an uncontrolled rescue in refractory disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the combination has never been randomised against metronidazole alone — the evidence supports ciprofloxacin alone as at least metronidazole's equal, and the pair only as an uncontrolled rescue in refractory disease
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 16-patient randomised trial of the two single agents, one 44-patient single-arm combination study in refractory or recurrent pouchitis, and one systematic review of all 20 pouchitis RCTs (830 patients). The acute-pouchitis randomised evidence base totals 16 patients for the relevant drugs, so the small scale of the evidence is printed in the stamp reasoning and on the card faces.
cards.result: Ciprofloxacin alone reduced PDAI more than metronidazole alone (fall 6.9 vs 3.8 points, P = 0.002; remission 7/7 vs 6/9, RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.88–2.35) and was better tolerated (Shen 2001; Alphonsus 2023). The combination produced 82% remission without a comparator in refractory disease (Mimura 2002). No study isolates what adding ciprofloxacin to metronidazole contributes in acute pouchitis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Antibiotic choice in pouchitis is also a stewardship and tolerance question (metronidazole neuropathy, ciprofloxacin class warnings) that these tiny, short trials cannot weigh — another reason the honest stamp stays at MAYBE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shen B et al. Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. 2001 (PMID: 11720319); Mimura T et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2002 (PMID: 11966499); Alphonsus L et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2023 (PMID: 37246609).

shelves.title: Smoking cessation and ulcerative colitis — SPLIT, observational only: a small matched cohort found the disease worsened after quitting; a nationwide cohort found no difference at all
shelves.question: Does smoking cessation worsen ulcerative colitis symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cohort Studies · Colectomy · Colitis, Ulcerative · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Male · Smoking Cessation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face; the two best cohorts point in opposite directions. The older matched cohort found clear worsening after quitting: in 32 patients who stopped smoking after an ulcerative colitis diagnosis, the years after cessation (mean 7 years) brought significantly more years with active disease, hospitalisation and major medical therapy than their own smoking years, and their need for immunosuppression rose to the level of matched never-smokers and above continuing smokers — while colectomy risk did not change (Beaugerie 2001, PMID: 11467641). The much larger modern study found nothing of the kind: among 6,754 incident ulcerative colitis patients (878 smokers at diagnosis), those who quit within 2 years of diagnosis had rates of flares, thiopurine use, corticosteroid dependency, hospitalisation and colectomy that were not significantly different from persistent smokers (Blackwell 2019, PMID: 31389044). A narrative review of the wider literature describes the same inconsistency — some studies show a more benign course in smokers, others do not verify it, and colectomy does not seem determined by smoking status (Bastida 2011, PMID: 21734782). Both carded cohorts' authors, and the review, agree on the clinical bottom line that smoking's overall harms outweigh any colitis benefit and patients should be counselled to quit. PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only (worsening after cessation: the small matched cohort; no worsening: the nationwide cohort 200 times larger).

cards.headline: Beaugerie 2001: in 32 patients who quit smoking after diagnosis, ulcerative colitis worsened after cessation — significantly more years with active disease (P < 0.01), hospitalisation (P < 0.05) and major medical therapy (P < 0.01); colectomy risk unchanged
cards.summary: Beaugerie 2001: in 32 patients who quit smoking after diagnosis, ulcerative colitis worsened after cessation — significantly more years with active disease (P < 0.01), hospitalisation (P < 0.05) and major medical therapy (P < 0.01); colectomy risk unchanged
cards.people: Single-centre cohort of 32 patients with ulcerative colitis who stopped smoking after diagnosis, comparing each patient's course after cessation (mean follow-up 7 years) with their own course between disease onset and cessation (mean duration 9 years), and with 32 matched nonsmokers and 32 matched continuing smokers (matched for sex, age and age at onset). Severity was judged by flare-ups and the need for systemic steroids, immunosuppressive drugs and colectomy.
cards.result: After cessation, patients had an increased rate of years with active disease (P < 0.01), years with hospitalisation (P < 0.05) and years with major medical therapy — oral steroids, intravenous steroids and azathioprine (P < 0.01). The rate of years with immunosuppressive therapy after cessation was significantly greater in ex-smokers and nonsmokers than in continuing smokers (P < 0.01). The risk of colectomy in ex-smokers after cessation was similar to that of nonsmokers and continuing smokers. The record reports P values without pooled effect sizes for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two quitters, a before–after design inside the same patients (disease naturally evolves and treatment eras change over a 16-year span), and no adjustment for why each patient quit — quitting because of illness or hospitalisation would manufacture exactly this pattern.
cards.source: Beaugerie L et al. Impact of cessation of smoking on the course of ulcerative colitis. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2001. PMID: 11467641. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Blackwell 2019: in 6,754 incident ulcerative colitis patients, quitting smoking after diagnosis was NOT associated with a worse course — flares, thiopurine use, steroid dependency, hospitalisation and colectomy all non-significantly different from persistent smokers
cards.summary: Blackwell 2019: in 6,754 incident ulcerative colitis patients, quitting smoking after diagnosis was NOT associated with a worse course — flares, thiopurine use, steroid dependency, hospitalisation and colectomy all non-significantly different from persistent smokers
cards.people: Nationwide population-based study using a nationally representative UK clinical research database: 6,754 patients with incident ulcerative colitis during 2005–2016 with smoking status recorded in the 2 years before diagnosis, of whom 878 were smokers at diagnosis; subgroups of persistent smokers and smokers who quit within 2 years after diagnosis were compared on corticosteroid use and flares, steroid dependency, thiopurine use, hospitalisation and colectomy.
cards.result: Smokers at diagnosis had a similar risk to never-smokers of corticosteroid-requiring flares (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.92–1.25, as printed in the record), thiopurine use (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.62–1.14), corticosteroid dependency (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.60–1.11), hospitalisation (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.72–1.18) and colectomy (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.50–1.21). Rates of flares, thiopurine use, corticosteroid dependency, hospitalisation and colectomy were not significantly different between persistent smokers and those who quit smoking after diagnosis (the record reports this comparison without separate effect sizes). The authors conclude smoking cessation was not associated with a worse disease course.
cards.watchOut: Smoking status came from routine records (misclassification is likely, and dose and timing of quitting are coarse), and a database null cannot exclude a real but modest or short-lived post-cessation flare risk concentrated in the first months after quitting.
cards.source: Blackwell J et al. The impact of smoking and smoking cessation on disease outcomes in ulcerative colitis: a nationwide population-based study. cards.headline: Bastida 2011: reviewing the whole literature, some studies show a more benign course in smokers (fewer hospitalisations, flare-ups and oral steroids) but others do not verify it — and colectomy does not seem determined by smoking status
cards.summary: Bastida 2011: reviewing the whole literature, some studies show a more benign course in smokers (fewer hospitalisations, flare-ups and oral steroids) but others do not verify it — and colectomy does not seem determined by smoking status
cards.people: Narrative review of the evidence on smoking status and ulcerative colitis: the risk of developing the disease, effects on phenotype and disease course, nicotine as a therapeutic agent, and the effect of smoking cessation in patients with established disease. The record reports no pooled effect sizes; it is carded as a map of a divided literature, not as a measurement.
cards.result: Current smoking has a protective association with developing ulcerative colitis, and former smokers carry an increased risk of developing it. On disease course, the review finds the evidence inconsistent: some studies show lower hospitalisation rates, fewer flare-ups, lower oral steroid use and less proximal extension in smokers, while this is not verified by some other studies; the colectomy rate does not seem to be determined by smoking status. The review concludes that, given smoking is a major worldwide cause of death, physicians should advise, encourage and assist patients with ulcerative colitis who smoke to quit.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review cannot arbitrate between its own conflicting sources; its value here is documenting that the split predates and extends beyond the two carded cohorts.
cards.source: Bastida G et al. Ulcerative colitis in smokers, non-smokers and ex-smokers. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21734782. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the small matched cohort says quitting worsens colitis; the nationwide cohort 200 times larger says it does not — observational evidence, genuinely split
cards.summary: Synthesis: the small matched cohort says quitting worsens colitis; the nationwide cohort 200 times larger says it does not — observational evidence, genuinely split
cards.people: The carded evidence: one matched single-centre cohort (32 quitters, with 32 matched nonsmokers and 32 continuing smokers), one nationwide cohort (6,754 incident cases, 878 smokers at diagnosis) and one narrative review of the wider literature. Total carded participants exceed 6,800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that smoking cessation can never be randomised, so all evidence is observational.
cards.result: After cessation, the matched cohort recorded significantly more years with active disease, hospitalisation and major therapy (Beaugerie 2001). The nationwide cohort found no significant difference between quitters and persistent smokers on flares, thiopurine use, steroid dependency, hospitalisation or colectomy, and no significant differences between smokers and never-smokers either (Blackwell 2019). Both agree colectomy is unaffected. PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Whichever way the colitis question eventually resolves, every carded source agrees the systemic harms of smoking outweigh any possible colitis benefit — this shelf answers the narrow factual question and must never be read as a reason to keep smoking.
cards.source: Synthesis of Beaugerie L et al. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2001 (PMID: 11467641); Blackwell J et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2019 (PMID: 31389044); Bastida G et al. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2011 (PMID: 21734782).

shelves.title: Continuing biologics in pregnancy in IBD (observational only): no harm signal in large prospective registry data — active disease, not the biologic, is the demonstrated pregnancy risk
shelves.question: Should women with inflammatory bowel disease continue biologics during pregnancy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Azathioprine · Biological Products · Colitis, Ulcerative · Crohn Disease · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Intestinal Mucosa · Mercaptopurine · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Outcome · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects · Prospective Studies · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is and can be no randomised trial of continuing versus stopping biologics in pregnancy. The largest prospective registry analysis (PIANO; 1,490 completed pregnancies) found that exposure to biologics (642 pregnancies), thiopurines (242), both (227) or neither (379) made no difference to congenital malformations, spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or first-year infant infections — while higher disease activity itself was associated with spontaneous abortion (HR 3.41) and with preterm birth plus infant infection (OR 1.73), which is the risk continuation exists to prevent (Mahadevan 2021, PMID: 33227283). The registry's newer-biologic analysis points the same way for vedolizumab (66 exposed pregnancies) and ustekinumab (47), with no increased risk on any measured outcome and a recommendation to continue both throughout pregnancy (Chugh 2024, PMID: 37796648). The one discordant signal in the carded set is older and concerns thiopurines, not biologics: a 2015 meta-analysis found congenital abnormalities increased in thiopurine-exposed pregnancies versus unmedicated controls (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.03–8.43), while its anti-TNF cohort review found no increase in adverse outcomes (Mozaffari 2015, PMID: 25378092). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continuing biologics through pregnancy is not associated with worse maternal or infant outcomes in large prospective registry data, and uncontrolled disease is the demonstrated risk.

cards.headline: Mahadevan 2021 (PIANO): in 1,490 pregnancies, biologic exposure was not associated with malformations, spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or infant infections — but active disease was (spontaneous abortion HR 3.41)
cards.summary: Mahadevan 2021 (PIANO): in 1,490 pregnancies, biologic exposure was not associated with malformations, spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or infant infections — but active disease was (spontaneous abortion HR 3.41)
cards.people: Prospective, observational, multicentre US registry study (PIANO) enrolling pregnant women with inflammatory bowel disease between 2007 and 2019: 1,490 completed pregnancies with 1,431 live births and 1-year infant outcomes in 1,010. Exposure groups were thiopurines (n = 242), biologics (n = 642), both (n = 227) and unexposed (n = 379), with logistic regression adjusted for confounders.
cards.result: Drug exposure did not increase the rate of congenital malformations, spontaneous abortions, preterm birth, low birth weight, or infections during the first year of life, for biologics, thiopurines or the combination. Higher disease activity was associated with risk of spontaneous abortion (hazard ratio 3.41, 95% CI 1.51–7.69) and with preterm birth with increased infant infection (odds ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.19–2.51). The authors conclude these therapies can be continued throughout pregnancy to maintain disease control and reduce pregnancy-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Registry exposure is chosen, not randomised: women who continue biologics have more severe disease (which biases against the drugs) but also better-controlled disease by delivery (which biases for them) — the null on drug harm is reassuring, not proof of zero risk for rare outcomes like specific malformations.
cards.source: Mahadevan U et al. Pregnancy and Neonatal Outcomes After Fetal Exposure to Biologics and Thiopurines Among Women With Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Gastroenterology. 2021. PMID: 33227283. Registry ID: NCT00904878. cards.headline: Chugh 2024 (PIANO): vedolizumab (66 pregnancies) and ustekinumab (47) exposure showed no increased risk of abortion, growth restriction, malformations or NICU stay — continuation of both throughout pregnancy is recommended by the authors
cards.summary: Chugh 2024 (PIANO): vedolizumab (66 pregnancies) and ustekinumab (47) exposure showed no increased risk of abortion, growth restriction, malformations or NICU stay — continuation of both throughout pregnancy is recommended by the authors
cards.people: Multicentre prospective observational analysis from the same PIANO registry: 1,669 completed pregnancies with 1,610 live births (mean maternal age 32.1 years), with exposure cohorts of vedolizumab (66 exposed), ustekinumab (47), anti-TNF agents, immunomodulators, anti-TNF plus immunomodulator combination, and no exposure; outcomes were collected each trimester, at delivery and at 4, 9 and 12 months after birth.
cards.result: There was no increased risk of spontaneous abortion, small for gestational age, low birth weight, neonatal intensive care unit stay, congenital malformations or intrauterine growth restriction with in-utero vedolizumab or ustekinumab exposure. The preterm birth rate was lower in the ustekinumab cohort (0.0%) than in the vedolizumab (13.8%), anti-TNF (8.2%), combination (14.2%), immunomodulator (12.3%) and unexposed (9.7%) cohorts (P = 0.03). Serious infection rates at birth, 4 months and 12 months were comparable among all cohorts. The authors state continuation of ustekinumab and vedolizumab throughout pregnancy is recommended.
cards.watchOut: The exposed groups for the newer biologics are small (66 and 47 pregnancies) — large enough to exclude a big common harm, far too small to exclude rare malformations, and the 0% preterm rate in 47 ustekinumab pregnancies should be read as 'no signal', not as protection.
cards.source: Chugh R et al. Maternal and Neonatal Outcomes in Vedolizumab- and Ustekinumab-Exposed Pregnancies: Results From the PIANO Registry. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 37796648. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mozaffari 2015: the older literature's one warning signal is about thiopurines, not biologics — congenital abnormalities OR 2.95 versus unmedicated controls — while its anti-TNF cohort review found no increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes
cards.summary: Mozaffari 2015: the older literature's one warning signal is about thiopurines, not biologics — congenital abnormalities OR 2.95 versus unmedicated controls — while its anti-TNF cohort review found no increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analysis of pregnancy outcomes in inflammatory bowel disease: the meta-analysis compared 312 thiopurine-exposed pregnant women with 1,149 controls (women with IBD on no medication or on other drugs); cohorts evaluating anti-TNF drug safety in pregnancy up to July 2013 were reviewed systematically.
cards.result: Congenital abnormalities were significantly increased in the thiopurine-exposed group compared with the control group who received no IBD medication (summary odds ratio 2.95, 95% CI 1.03–8.43; P = 0.04); no significant differences were found for prematurity, low birth weight, spontaneous abortion or neonatal adverse outcomes. The anti-TNF cohorts demonstrated no increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes versus controls, except a significant decrease in gestational age in one trial. The authors conclude a benefit–risk ratio should be considered when prescribing or continuing therapy in pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: The thiopurine signal rests on a comparison against unmedicated women (who likely had milder disease) with a confidence interval that only just excludes 1.0, and the larger, later, prospective PIANO analysis found no malformation increase for thiopurines either — the signal is carded so it is visible, not because it outweighs PIANO.
cards.source: Mozaffari S et al. Pregnancy outcomes in women with inflammatory bowel disease following exposure to thiopurines and antitumor necrosis factor drugs: a systematic review with meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: large prospective registry data find no harm signal from continuing biologics — and identify active disease, the thing continuation prevents, as the real pregnancy risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: large prospective registry data find no harm signal from continuing biologics — and identify active disease, the thing continuation prevents, as the real pregnancy risk
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective analyses from the PIANO registry (1,490 pregnancies for anti-TNF/thiopurine exposures; 1,669 for vedolizumab/ustekinumab, with small exposed subgroups of 66 and 47) and one older systematic review (312 thiopurine-exposed pregnancies in its meta-analysis plus anti-TNF cohorts to 2013). Total carded pregnancies exceed 3,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies at shelf level; the newer-biologic subgroups are small and say so on their card.
cards.result: Biologic exposure was not associated with congenital malformations, spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or first-year infant infections (Mahadevan 2021), and the same held for vedolizumab and ustekinumab (Chugh 2024). Higher disease activity was associated with spontaneous abortion (HR 3.41) and preterm birth with infant infection (OR 1.73). The single contrary signal — thiopurine congenital abnormalities, OR 2.95 — is older, smaller and not about biologics (Mozaffari 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Registry follow-up here runs to 1 year of life; longer-term child outcomes (immune development, later infection, vaccine responses beyond infancy) are outside the carded records, and the newest agents have the thinnest exposure counts.

shelves.title: Vitamin D and Crohn's relapse — SPLIT by setting: small remission trials lean positive (pooled relative risk 0.47), but the largest trial, after surgery, found no benefit at all
shelves.question: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce relapse in adults with Crohn's disease?
shelves.mesh: Cholecalciferol · Crohn Disease · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome · Vitamins
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by setting, and the divide is named in the stamp. In medical remission, the signal favours vitamin D but rests on small trials: the first randomised trial (94 analysed patients) found relapse in 13% on 1,200 IU/day versus 29% on placebo, a difference that did not reach significance (P = 0.06) (Jorgensen 2010, PMID: 20491740), while a 2024 meta-analysis of the small randomised trials pooled a relative risk of clinical relapse of 0.64 overall and 0.47 in Crohn's patients in clinical remission (Valvano 2024, PMID: 36579768). In the postoperative setting, the largest and best-powered trial is plainly null: 25,000 IU weekly after ileocolonic resection did not reduce endoscopic recurrence (58% vs 66%, P = .37) or clinical recurrence (18.1% vs 18.3%) despite raising blood levels as intended (de Bruyn 2021, PMID: 32461138). A relative risk reduction quoted from the meta-analysis is a relative measure built from trials of a few dozen patients each; the absolute relapse rates in the one trial that reports them are 13% versus 29%. Correcting deficiency for bone health is a separate, uncontroversial reason to supplement; this shelf answers only the relapse question. PROPOSED SPLIT (medical remission: possible benefit in a meta-analysis of small trials, anchored on one non-significant trial; postoperative recurrence: no benefit in the largest trial).

cards.headline: Jorgensen 2010: vitamin D3 1,200 IU daily for 12 months — relapse 13% (6/46) versus 29% (14/48) on placebo, P = 0.06: a favourable difference that did not reach significance
cards.summary: Jorgensen 2010: vitamin D3 1,200 IU daily for 12 months — relapse 13% (6/46) versus 29% (14/48) on placebo, P = 0.06: a favourable difference that did not reach significance
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients with Crohn's disease in remission: 108 patients were included, of whom 14 were later excluded, leaving 46 randomised to oral vitamin D3 1,200 IU once daily and 48 to placebo for 12 months. The primary endpoint was clinical relapse.
cards.result: Vitamin D3 raised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D from a mean of 69 nmol/L (about 27.6 ng/mL) to 96 nmol/L (about 38.4 ng/mL) after 3 months (P < 0.001). The relapse rate was lower on vitamin D3 (6 of 46, 13%) than on placebo (14 of 48, 29%), but the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.06). The authors describe the reduction as insignificant and call for larger studies.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-four analysed patients and 20 relapses in total: the trial was powered to miss exactly the moderate benefit it hints at, so it supports neither 'works' nor 'does not work' on its own.

cards.search: jorgensen 2010: vitamin d3 1,200 iu daily for 12 months — relapse 13% (6/46) versus 29% (14/48) on placebo, p = 0.06: a favourable difference that did not reach significance jorgensen 2010: vitamin d3 1,200 iu daily for 12 months — relapse 13% (6/46) versus 29% (14/48) on placebo, p = 0.06: a favourable difference that did not reach significance does vitamin d supplementation reduce relapse in adults with crohn's disease? randomised controlled trial (jorgensen 2010) randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients with crohn's disease in remission: 108 patients were included, of whom 14 were later excluded, leaving 46 randomised to oral vitamin d3 1,200 iu once daily and 48 to placebo for 12 months. the primary endpoint was clinical relapse. vitamin d3 raised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin d from a mean of 69 nmol/l (about 27.6 ng/ml) to 96 nmol/l (about 38.4 ng/ml) after 3 months (p < 0.001). the relapse rate was lower on vitamin d3 (6 of 46, 13%) than on placebo (14 of 48, 29%), but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.06). the authors describe the reduction as insignificant and call for larger studies. ninety-four analysed patients and 20 relapses in total: the trial was powered to miss exactly the moderate benefit it hints at, so it supports neither 'works' nor 'does not work' on its own. jorgensen sp et al. clinical trial: vitamin d3 treatment in crohn's disease - a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study. alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2010. pmid: 20491740. registry id: nct00122184. mesh: cholecalciferol · crohn disease · double-blind method · humans · recurrence · treatment outcome · vitamins

cards.headline: de Bruyn 2021: high-dose vitamin D (25,000 IU weekly) after ileocolonic resection did NOT prevent recurrence — endoscopic recurrence 58% vs 66% (P = .37), clinical recurrence 18.1% vs 18.3% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: de Bruyn 2021: high-dose vitamin D (25,000 IU weekly) after ileocolonic resection did NOT prevent recurrence — endoscopic recurrence 58% vs 66% (P = .37), clinical recurrence 18.1% vs 18.3% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in 143 patients with Crohn's disease after ileocolonic resection with ileocolonic anastomosis at 17 hospitals in the Netherlands and Belgium, assigned to weekly oral vitamin D 25,000 IU (n = 72) or placebo (n = 71) for 26 weeks, with ileocolonoscopy at week 26 read by blinded readers. The primary endpoint was endoscopic recurrence (modified Rutgeerts score i2b or worse).
cards.result: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose in the vitamin D group from a median of 42 nmol/L (about 16.8 ng/mL) at baseline to 81 nmol/L (about 32.4 ng/mL) at week 26 (P < .00001), and stayed at 43 nmol/L (about 17.2 ng/mL) on placebo — the supplement did what it was supposed to do to blood levels. Endoscopic recurrence did not differ significantly (58% vitamin D vs 66% placebo; P = .37), nor did clinical recurrence (18.1% vs 18.3%; P = .91) or quality of life. Adverse events were few in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Postoperative recurrence is a specific, aggressive biology (recurrence at the anastomosis within 26 weeks) — this null does not directly refute a slower protective effect in medically maintained remission, which is why the shelf is SPLIT rather than negative.
cards.source: de Bruyn JR et al. High-Dose Vitamin D Does Not Prevent Postoperative Recurrence of Crohn's Disease in a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 32461138. Registry ID: NCT02010762. MeSH: Crohn Disease · Humans · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Quality of Life · Vitamin D · Vitamins

cards.headline: Valvano 2024: meta-analysis of the small randomised trials — pooled relative risk of clinical relapse 0.64 (95% CI 0.46–0.89), and 0.47 (0.27–0.82) in Crohn's patients in clinical remission
cards.summary: Valvano 2024: meta-analysis of the small randomised trials — pooled relative risk of clinical relapse 0.64 (95% CI 0.46–0.89), and 0.47 (0.27–0.82) in Crohn's patients in clinical remission
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials (Valvano 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022311184) of randomised clinical trials of vitamin D supplementation versus placebo in inflammatory bowel disease, searched to January 2022: 12 reports included; seven trials reported clinical relapse as a dichotomous outcome, totalling 458 patients with inflammatory bowel disease in the relapse analysis, of whom only 67 had ulcerative colitis (two studies).
cards.result: The pooled risk ratio for clinical relapse was 0.64 (95% CI 0.46–0.89; I² = 25%) — a 36% relative reduction in relapse risk. In Crohn's disease patients in clinical remission the pooled risk ratio was 0.47 (95% CI 0.27–0.82; I² = 0%), a 53% relative reduction. The authors note the ulcerative colitis subgroup was not significant and that well-powered studies are needed. Absolute relapse rates are not pooled in the record; in the largest contributing remission trial they were 13% versus 29%.
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative risk built from trials of a few dozen patients inherits their fragility — and the postoperative trial carded beside it (143 patients, null) is the size of several of these trials combined; whether it is inside this pooled estimate is not stated in the record.
cards.source: Valvano M et al. Effectiveness of Vitamin D Supplementation on Disease Course in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Patients: Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis. Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. 2024. PMID: 36579768. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: small remission trials lean positive (pooled relative risk 0.47 in remission), the largest trial — postoperative — is null; the split is by setting
cards.summary: Synthesis: small remission trials lean positive (pooled relative risk 0.47 in remission), the largest trial — postoperative — is null; the split is by setting
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials (94 analysed patients in medical remission; 143 patients after ileocolonic resection) and one meta-analysis of 12 randomised reports (458 patients in the relapse analysis). Total unique carded trial participants are in the hundreds, so no small-N stamp labelling applies at shelf level, but every individual trial is small and the card faces say so.
cards.result: In remission, relapse was 13% versus 29% in the anchor trial (P = 0.06; Jorgensen 2010) and the pooled relative risk across small trials was 0.64 overall and 0.47 in Crohn's remission (Valvano 2024). After surgery, high-dose vitamin D made no difference to endoscopic (58% vs 66%) or clinical (18.1% vs 18.3%) recurrence despite doubling blood levels (de Bruyn 2021). PROPOSED SPLIT (medical remission: possible benefit, small trials; postoperative: no benefit, largest trial).
cards.watchOut: Doses differed 20-fold between the positive-leaning remission trial (1,200 IU daily) and the null postoperative trial (25,000 IU weekly) — 'vitamin D' is not one intervention across these cards, and blood-level targets differed as well.

shelves.title: Testing for bile acid diarrhoea before rifaximin in IBS-D (diagnostic-yield evidence only): roughly one in four to one in three patients has bile acid malabsorption and a binder-responsive diagnosis rifaximin would miss
shelves.question: Should adults with irritable bowel syndrome be tested for bile acid diarrhea before starting rifaximin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anion Exchange Resins · Bile Acids and Salts · Cholestyramine Resin · Diarrhea · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Malabsorption Syndromes · Prevalence · Prospective Studies · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/diagnostic-yield evidence only, printed on the face; no trial has randomised a test-first strategy against rifaximin-first. What the evidence establishes is yield and consequence. Yield: roughly one in four to one in three patients meeting criteria for diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome has bile acid malabsorption on SeHCAT testing — a pooled rate of 28.1% (95% CI 22.6%–34%) across six studies and 908 individuals (Slattery 2015, PMID: 25913530), and 32% at the moderate threshold (7-day retention under 10%) across 18 studies and 1,223 patients, with 10% severe (Wedlake 2009, PMID: 19570102). Consequence: these patients have a specific, cheap, effective treatment that is not rifaximin — response to the bile acid binder colestyramine ran 96%, 80% and 70% by severity of malabsorption in the same review's pooled treatment data — so a positive test redirects therapy entirely, and a rifaximin course given first delays that redirect. The practical caveat is test availability: SeHCAT is unavailable in many countries including the United States, and the blood alternatives are imperfect — serum FGF19 at 145 pg/mL detected raised bile acid synthesis (C4 above 28 ng/mL) with only 58% sensitivity and 79% specificity in 258 patients with chronic diarrhoea (Pattni 2012, PMID: 23238290). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-yield evidence only: testing before rifaximin identifies a large, specifically treatable subgroup, but the test-first sequence itself is untested in a trial and the available tests miss cases.

cards.headline: Wedlake 2009: in 1,223 patients with IBS-D symptoms, 32% had moderate bile acid malabsorption on SeHCAT (retention under 10%) and 10% severe (under 5%) — and binder response rose with severity: 96%, 80%, 70%
cards.summary: Wedlake 2009: in 1,223 patients with IBS-D symptoms, 32% had moderate bile acid malabsorption on SeHCAT (retention under 10%) and 10% severe (under 5%) — and binder response rose with severity: 96%, 80%, 70%
cards.people: Systematic review of publications reporting patients presenting with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome symptoms who were tested for idiopathic bile acid malabsorption by SeHCAT scanning: 18 relevant studies (15 prospective) comprising 1,223 patients. Severity bands are 7-day SeHCAT retention under 5% (severe), under 10% (moderate) and under 15% (mild).
cards.result: Five studies (429 patients) found 10% (95% CI 7%–13%) had severe bile acid malabsorption (retention under 5%); 17 studies (1,073 patients) found 32% (95% CI 29%–35%) had moderate malabsorption (retention under 10%); seven studies (618 patients) found 26% (95% CI 23%–30%) had mild malabsorption (retention under 15%). Pooled data from 15 studies showed a dose–response to the bile acid binder colestyramine: response in 96% of patients with under 5% retention, 80% at under 10% and 70% at under 15%. The authors conclude idiopathic adult-onset bile acid malabsorption is not rare and IBS guidelines need revision so clinicians consider it.
cards.watchOut: These are prevalence figures in referred, tested populations — clinics that order SeHCAT may already suspect bile acid diarrhoea — and the binder response data are pooled observational treatment results, not a randomised comparison.
cards.source: Wedlake L et al. Systematic review: the prevalence of idiopathic bile acid malabsorption as diagnosed by SeHCAT scanning in patients with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19570102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Slattery 2015: meta-analysis of six SeHCAT studies (908 individuals) — pooled bile acid malabsorption rate in IBS-D of 28.1% (95% CI 22.6%–34%), with individual studies ranging from 16.9% to 35.3%
cards.summary: Slattery 2015: meta-analysis of six SeHCAT studies (908 individuals) — pooled bile acid malabsorption rate in IBS-D of 28.1% (95% CI 22.6%–34%), with individual studies ranging from 16.9% to 35.3%
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies recruiting adults meeting accepted criteria for diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (Manning, Kruis, or Rome I, II or III) who underwent SeHCAT testing, with bile acid malabsorption defined as 7-day SeHCAT retention under 10%: six relevant studies comprising 908 individuals, searched to March 2015, with study quality assessed by QUADAS-2.
cards.result: The rate of bile acid malabsorption ranged from 16.9% to 35.3% across studies; the pooled rate was 28.1% (95% CI 22.6%–34%), with significant heterogeneity (I² = 72.1%). Neither the diagnostic criteria used nor the study country significantly modified the rate. The authors conclude that in excess of one quarter of patients meeting accepted IBS-D criteria have bile acid malabsorption, with implications for interpreting previous IBS trials and for clinical practice.
cards.watchOut: Substantial heterogeneity (I² = 72%) means the true yield in any one clinic's population could sit well below the pooled figure — the honest statement is 'roughly a quarter to a third in tested series', not a precise 28%.
cards.source: Slattery SA et al. Systematic review with meta-analysis: the prevalence of bile acid malabsorption in the irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2015. PMID: 25913530. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Bile Acids and Salts · Diarrhea · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Malabsorption Syndromes · Prevalence

cards.headline: Pattni 2012: where SeHCAT is unavailable, the blood tests are imperfect — serum FGF19 at 145 pg/mL detected raised bile acid synthesis with 58% sensitivity and 79% specificity in 258 patients with chronic diarrhoea
cards.summary: Pattni 2012: where SeHCAT is unavailable, the blood tests are imperfect — serum FGF19 at 145 pg/mL detected raised bile acid synthesis with 58% sensitivity and 79% specificity in 258 patients with chronic diarrhoea
cards.people: Prospective diagnostic study of 258 patients undergoing routine investigation for chronic diarrhoea who provided fasting blood samples: 119 with normal serum 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (C4, 28 ng/mL or below, a measure of bile acid synthesis) and 139 with high C4 (above 28 ng/mL), including all causes of bile acid diarrhoea. Serum fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19) was measured in stored samples.
cards.result: FGF19 and C4 were significantly inversely related (r = −0.64, P < 0.001), and patients with raised C4 had significantly lower median FGF19. The sensitivity and specificity of FGF19 at 145 pg/mL for detecting a C4 above 28 ng/mL were 58% and 79% respectively; for C4 above 60 ng/mL they were 74% and 72%, with an area under the receiver-operating curve of 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.87). The authors note SeHCAT is not available in many countries and is underused in others, and propose FGF19 could be developed as a simple blood test to increase diagnostic rates.
cards.watchOut: FGF19 was validated against another blood marker (C4), not against SeHCAT or against treatment response — a 58% sensitivity means a negative blood test leaves bile acid diarrhoea very much on the table.
cards.source: Pattni SS et al. Fibroblast Growth Factor 19 and 7alpha-Hydroxy-4-Cholesten-3-one in the Diagnosis of Patients With Possible Bile Acid Diarrhea. Clinical and Translational Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 23238290. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: about one in four to one in three IBS-D patients has bile acid malabsorption and a binder-responsive diagnosis — testing first is high-yield, but the sequence itself has never been trialled and US-available tests are imperfect
cards.summary: Synthesis: about one in four to one in three IBS-D patients has bile acid malabsorption and a binder-responsive diagnosis — testing first is high-yield, but the sequence itself has never been trialled and US-available tests are imperfect
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews of SeHCAT prevalence in IBS-D (1,223 and 908 patients; overlapping primary studies) and one prospective diagnostic study of blood biomarkers (258 patients with chronic diarrhoea). Total carded participants exceed 2,300, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that all evidence is diagnostic and observational, with no strategy trial.
cards.result: Pooled bile acid malabsorption in IBS-D was 28.1% at the under-10% retention threshold (Slattery 2015) and 32% at the same threshold in the earlier review, with binder response of 70–96% by severity (Wedlake 2009). Serum FGF19, the proposed blood alternative where SeHCAT is unavailable, had 58% sensitivity and 79% specificity against raised C4 (Pattni 2012). No carded study compares outcomes of testing before rifaximin versus rifaximin first. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-yield evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Rifaximin non-response is itself a common trigger for bile acid testing in practice; this shelf's question is whether the order should be reversed, and on that ordering question the carded evidence is inference from yield, not a comparative result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wedlake L et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2009 (PMID: 19570102); Slattery SA et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2015 (PMID: 25913530); Pattni SS et al. Clinical and Translational Gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 23238290).
