shelves.question: Should adults with cirrhosis and ascites restrict dietary sodium to control fluid retention?
shelves.mesh: Ascites · Canrenoic Acid · Diet, Sodium-Restricted · Female · Furosemide · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Sodium, Dietary
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised evidence divides against the guideline habit, and the split is named on the face. Sodium restriction is standard, guideline-endorsed care for ascites, and the physiology (avid renal sodium retention) supports it. But the only carded randomised comparison of sodium intakes, Bernardi 1993 (PMID: 8336527), randomised 115 hospitalised patients to diets of 40 versus 120 mmol of sodium daily inside a stepped diuretic protocol and found the type of diet did not influence the response to treatment. A 2020 systematic review of randomised nutritional trials in cirrhosis and ascites (PMID: 33473347) likewise reports that studies reached contradictory conclusions regarding sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics. The 2016 protocol for the first dedicated systematic review (PMID: 27160239) states the concern plainly: some randomised trials have suggested a lack of benefit of a sodium-restricted over an unrestricted diet, and even an increase in ascites and renal complications has been reported. No carded record shows that stricter restriction improves fluid control, survival, or any hard outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (guideline practice: benefit; randomised comparisons: no added benefit of stricter restriction, possible harm): moderate sodium restriction remains the usual adjunct to diuretics, but the randomised record does not show that restricting harder controls ascites better.

cards.headline: Bernardi 1993: in the carded randomised comparison of sodium intakes (40 versus 120 mmol/day), the type of diet did not influence the response to stepped diuretic treatment in 115 patients with cirrhosis and ascites
cards.summary: Bernardi 1993: in the carded randomised comparison of sodium intakes (40 versus 120 mmol/day), the type of diet did not influence the response to stepped diuretic treatment in 115 patients with cirrhosis and ascites
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of two sodium intakes within a stepped diuretic protocol (Bernardi 1993)
cards.people: 115 hospitalised patients with non-azotemic cirrhosis and ascites, randomised to a diet providing either 40 or 120 mmol of sodium daily. After a 7-day washout from the outpatient diuretic regimen (Step 1), patients not undergoing spontaneous diuresis received increasing dosages of potassium canrenoate, 200 mg/day increased every 4th day up to 600 mg (Step 2); on failure of Step 2, potassium canrenoate 400 mg/day plus furosemide at increasing dosage (25–50–100 mg every other day) was given (Step 3).
cards.result: Nine percent of patients underwent spontaneous diuresis, 77% developed a negative sodium balance by the end of Step 2 (69% with a potassium canrenoate dosage of 400 mg/day or less) and 93% by the end of Step 3. Two patients were withdrawn because of diuretic side-effects. On univariate analysis the type of diet did not influence the response to treatment (the treatment made no difference between the 40 and 120 mmol/day diets, as printed in the record; no comparative effect size for the diet contrast is reported). The washout period significantly increased endogenous creatinine clearance, and natremia significantly rose in hyponatremic patients. On multivariate analysis, creatinine clearance and plasma aldosterone were independent predictive factors of the response to treatment.
cards.watchOut: This is a 1993 inpatient trial of diet inside a diuretic-escalation protocol, not a trial of sodium restriction versus no advice in outpatients: it tests 40 against 120 mmol/day, so it cannot speak to intakes outside that range, and its abstract is truncated at 250 words in the record, so no diet-specific event rates can be printed.
cards.source: Bernardi M et al. Efficacy and safety of the stepped care medical treatment of ascites in liver cirrhosis: a randomized controlled clinical trial comparing two diets with different sodium content. Liver. 1993. PMID: 8336527. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Baki 2020: a systematic review of randomised nutritional trials in cirrhosis and ascites found studies reached contradictory conclusions regarding sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics
cards.summary: Baki 2020: a systematic review of randomised nutritional trials in cirrhosis and ascites found studies reached contradictory conclusions regarding sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of nutritional interventions (including sodium restriction and high-protein diet) for patients with cirrhosis and ascites. The number of included trials and total participants is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Increasing consumption of calories and protein alone was ineffective. Studies reached contradictory conclusions regarding sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics — the review reports no pooled effect size for sodium restriction, and none is printed here. Intravenous amino acid infusion alone did not improve outcomes; peripheral parenteral nutrition did not improve outcomes except that it reduced mortality in conjunction with a branched-chain amino acid evening snack. The authors conclude patients may benefit from sodium restriction and a protein-rich evening snack, and that future trials should standardise nutritional targets. No effect size for the sodium question is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A review whose own conclusion is that the trials contradict each other cannot be cited for either side of this shelf: it is carded as the map of the disagreement, and its closing suggestion that patients 'may benefit' from restriction is the authors' judgement, not a pooled result.
cards.source: Baki J et al. Do Nutritional Interventions Improve the Outcomes of Patients with Cirrhosis and Ascites: A Systematic Review of Randomized Trials. Current hepatology reports. 2020. PMID: 33473347. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Walbaum 2016: when the first dedicated systematic-review protocol was written, no systematic review of sodium restriction for ascites existed — and the protocol states some randomised trials had suggested no benefit, and even more ascites and renal complications, with restriction
cards.summary: Walbaum 2016: when the first dedicated systematic-review protocol was written, no systematic review of sodium restriction for ascites existed — and the protocol states some randomised trials had suggested no benefit, and even more ascites and renal complications, with restriction
cards.people: Protocol (PROSPERO CRD42015022161) for a systematic review of randomised controlled trials evaluating a salt-restricted versus an unrestricted regime in patients with cirrhosis and ascites, searching EMBASE, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. No participants — this is a protocol, not a results paper.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its stated rationale: the main guidelines recommend sodium intake reduction for ascites, but some randomised controlled trials have suggested a lack of benefit with a sodium-restricted over an unrestricted diet, and even an increase in ascites and renal complications has been reported; the indication, the authors state, is based primarily on expert recommendations. The planned review would estimate pooled risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences for continuous outcomes using a random-effects model.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about sodium: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the restriction question has been settled by synthesis, and it must never be cited as a review result.

Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42015022161 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: sodium restriction is universal guideline practice for ascites, but the carded randomised comparison found the stricter diet made no difference to diuretic response, and the review literature describes the trial conclusions as contradictory
cards.summary: Synthesis: sodium restriction is universal guideline practice for ascites, but the carded randomised comparison found the stricter diet made no difference to diuretic response, and the review literature describes the trial conclusions as contradictory
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of 40 versus 120 mmol/day sodium diets inside a stepped diuretic protocol (n = 115), one systematic review of randomised nutritional trials (included-trial N not documented in the record), and one systematic-review protocol with no results (PROSPERO CRD42015022161). Total carded participants with a documented N exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation on this shelf is disagreement and age of the trials, printed here.
cards.result: In Bernardi 1993, 93% of patients achieved a negative sodium balance by the end of the stepped protocol, but the type of diet (40 versus 120 mmol/day) did not influence the response to treatment. Baki 2020 found the randomised literature on sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics contradictory. Walbaum 2016 records that some trials suggested no benefit from restriction and possible increases in ascites and renal complications. PROPOSED SPLIT (guideline practice: benefit; randomised comparisons: no added benefit of stricter restriction, possible harm).
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf tests sodium advice against hard outcomes such as survival or hospitalisation, and the one direct randomised comparison predates modern diuretic practice — the split is between expert-standard care and an old, thin randomised record, and both sides of that sentence matter.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bernardi M et al. Liver. 1993 (PMID: 8336527); Baki J et al. Current hepatology reports. 2020 (PMID: 33473347); Walbaum B et al. Systematic reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27160239).

shelves.title: Early liver transplantation for steroid-nonresponsive severe alcohol-related hepatitis (observational only): large survival advantage in strictly selected patients, post-transplant survival matching standard transplantation — with more high-intake alcohol relapse
shelves.question: Is early liver transplant evaluation appropriate for severe alcohol-related hepatitis that does not respond to steroids?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcoholism · Case-Control Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucocorticoids · Hepatitis, Alcoholic · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Proportional Hazards Models · Recurrence · Survival Rate · Temperance · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no randomised trial of early transplantation, and every carded study is a selected-cohort comparison. Within that limit the survival signal is large and consistent. In Mathurin 2011 (PMID: 22070476), 26 rigorously selected patients (first episode, Lille score 0.45 or higher, supportive family, commitment to abstinence — fewer than 2% of admissions) had 6-month survival of 77 ± 8% versus 23 ± 8% in matched non-transplanted patients. The prospective controlled Louvet 2022 study (PMID: 35202597) confirms an important survival benefit (2-year overall survival hazard ratio 0.27 relative against eligible-score failures who were not transplanted) with post-transplant survival similar to standard transplantation after 6 months of abstinence (hazard ratio 0.87) — but alcohol relapse was not shown non-inferior (34% versus 25%), and high alcohol intake was more frequent after early transplantation (absolute difference 16.7%). A 2018 meta-analysis (PMID: 30349998) found the same pattern. Evaluation is therefore appropriate for carefully selected nonresponders; the relapse cost is real and belongs in the selection process, not discovered afterwards. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Mathurin 2011: in 26 rigorously selected patients with a first episode of severe alcoholic hepatitis not responding to medical therapy, early transplantation gave 6-month survival of 77% versus 23% in matched patients who were not transplanted
cards.summary: Mathurin 2011: in 26 rigorously selected patients with a first episode of severe alcoholic hepatitis not responding to medical therapy, early transplantation gave 6-month survival of 77% versus 23% in matched patients who were not transplanted
cards.type: Prospective selected cohort with matched comparison (Mathurin 2011)
cards.people: Patients from seven centres selected for early liver transplantation: no prior episodes of alcoholic hepatitis, a Lille score of 0.45 or higher (nonresponse to medical therapy) or rapid worsening of liver function despite medical therapy, supportive family members, no severe coexisting conditions, and a commitment to alcohol abstinence. In all, 26 patients at high risk of death (median Lille score 0.88) were listed within a median of 13 days after nonresponse; fewer than 2% of patients admitted for severe alcoholic hepatitis were selected, and the centres used 2.9% of available grafts for this indication. Survival was compared with matched patients who did not undergo transplantation.
cards.result: The cumulative 6-month survival rate (±SE) was higher among patients who received early transplantation than among those who did not (77 ± 8% vs 23 ± 8%, P<0.001). The benefit was maintained through 2 years of follow-up (hazard ratio 6.08, as printed in the record, for the comparison over follow-up; P = 0.004). Three patients resumed drinking alcohol: one at 720 days, one at 740 days and one at 1140 days after transplantation. The authors conclude early liver transplantation can improve survival in patients with a first episode of severe alcoholic hepatitis not responding to medical therapy.
cards.watchOut: Selection is the treatment here as much as the graft: fewer than 2% of admissions qualified, all with family support and an abstinence commitment, so the 77% figure cannot be transported to unselected nonresponders — and the comparison is matched, not randomised, so residual confounding by selection cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Mathurin P et al. Early liver transplantation for severe alcoholic hepatitis. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 22070476. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Louvet 2022: a prospective controlled study confirms the survival benefit of early transplantation, but non-inferiority for alcohol relapse was not demonstrated — relapse 34% versus 25%, with high alcohol intake more frequent after early transplantation
cards.summary: Louvet 2022: a prospective controlled study confirms the survival benefit of early transplantation, but non-inferiority for alcohol relapse was not demonstrated — relapse 34% versus 25%, with high alcohol intake more frequent after early transplantation
cards.people: Multicentre, non-randomised, non-inferiority, controlled study in 19 French and Belgian hospitals (NCT01756794). Three prospectively recruited groups: 102 patients with severe alcohol-related hepatitis not responding to medical treatment who were eligible for early transplantation under a selection score based on social and addiction items; 47 similar patients not eligible under the score, who entered no further transplantation process; and 129 patients with alcohol-related cirrhosis listed for transplantation after at least 6 months of abstinence (standard group). A historical control group of non-transplanted nonresponders was also defined. In the end, 68 patients in the early group and 93 in the standard group received a transplant.
cards.result: Alcohol relapse at 2 years occurred in 23 (34%) of the early transplantation group and 23 (25%) of the standard group; non-inferiority of early versus standard transplantation was therefore not demonstrated (absolute difference 9.1% [95% CI −∞ to 21.1]; p=0.45). The 2-year rate of high alcohol intake was greater after early transplantation (absolute difference 16.7% [95% CI 5.8–27.6]), and time spent drinking a large quantity of alcohol was higher (standardised difference 0.50 [95% CI 0.17–0.82]). Two-year post-transplant survival was similar between the early and standard groups (hazard ratio 0.87 relative [95% CI 0.33–2.26]). Two-year overall survival was higher in the early transplantation group than in the not-eligible group (hazard ratio 0.27 relative [95% CI 0.16–0.47]) and than in historical controls (hazard ratio 0.21 relative [95% CI 0.13–0.32]).
cards.watchOut: The survival comparisons against the not-eligible group and historical controls are confounded by the same selection score that defined eligibility — patients chosen for early transplantation were chosen because they were expected to do better — and the relapse finding cuts the other way: the study's own primary non-inferiority question was not met.

cards.headline: Al-Saeedi 2018: meta-analysis of the comparative studies — 1-year survival significantly higher with early transplantation than medical therapy alone (2 studies, n = 70), and relapse rates not significantly different from transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis
cards.summary: Al-Saeedi 2018: meta-analysis of the comparative studies — 1-year survival significantly higher with early transplantation than medical therapy alone (2 studies, n = 70), and relapse rates not significantly different from transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis
cards.people: Meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42017057971) of all studies comparing liver transplantation in severe acute alcoholic hepatitis without 6 months of abstinence against a control group. Meta-analysis A compared early transplantation with medical therapy alone in nonresponders (2 studies, n = 70). Meta-analysis B compared transplant outcomes in alcoholic hepatitis versus chronic alcoholic cirrhosis (6 studies, 1091 patients).
cards.result: In meta-analysis A, 1-year patient survival was significantly higher in the transplantation group than with medical therapy alone (survival benefit 15.88, as printed in the record; 95% CI 3.98–63.35; p<0.0001). In meta-analysis B, 1-year (survival benefit 1.65; 95% CI 0.95–2.89; p=0.08), 3-year (1.31; 0.79–2.18; p=0.30) and 5-year survival (1.54; 0.92–2.56; p=0.10) were not significantly different between the alcoholic-hepatitis and alcoholic-cirrhosis groups (the treatment made no difference that reached significance in those comparisons). There was no significant difference in alcohol relapse between the groups (odds ratio 1.26 relative; 95% CI 0.53–2.96; p=0.60). The authors conclude early transplantation is a life-saving treatment for patients not responding to medical therapy and that relapse chance is not increased in selected patients.
cards.watchOut: The headline survival meta-analysis rests on two studies and 70 patients, so its very wide confidence interval (3.98–63.35) is the honest summary; pooling selected cohorts does not remove the selection that produced them.
cards.source: Al-Saeedi M et al. Meta-analysis of patient survival and rate of alcohol relapse in liver-transplanted patients for acute alcoholic hepatitis. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2018. PMID: 30349998. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42017057971 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: early transplantation in strictly selected steroid-nonresponders is associated with a large survival advantage over medical therapy alone, post-transplant survival matches standard transplantation — and relapse, especially high-intake relapse, is more frequent
cards.summary: Synthesis: early transplantation in strictly selected steroid-nonresponders is associated with a large survival advantage over medical therapy alone, post-transplant survival matches standard transplantation — and relapse, especially high-intake relapse, is more frequent
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective selected cohort with matched controls (26 transplanted patients), one prospective controlled study (149 patients with severe alcohol-related hepatitis, 68 early transplants; 129 standard-transplant comparators), and one meta-analysis (2 studies, n = 70, for the survival comparison; 6 studies, 1091 patients, for the cirrhosis comparison). All observational; total carded participants exceed 1,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the governing limitation is absence of randomisation, printed here and on the stamp.
cards.result: Six-month survival was 77 ± 8% with early transplantation versus 23 ± 8% without in Mathurin 2011, and Louvet 2022 found 2-year overall survival hazard ratios of 0.27 relative versus score-ineligible nonresponders and 0.21 relative versus historical controls, with post-transplant survival similar to standard transplantation (hazard ratio 0.87 relative). Against that, relapse non-inferiority was not demonstrated (34% versus 25%) and high alcohol intake was more frequent after early transplantation (absolute difference 16.7%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Every survival number on this shelf comes from cohorts in which a selection process chose the transplanted patients; the shelf supports evaluation and listing of carefully selected nonresponders, and says nothing defensible about relaxing the selection criteria themselves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mathurin P et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2011 (PMID: 22070476); Louvet A et al. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022 (PMID: 35202597); Al-Saeedi M et al. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2018 (PMID: 30349998).

shelves.title: Pancreatic enzyme timing in chronic pancreatitis (weak evidence): take the dose during the meal, spread through it, or just after — the single small timing trial found digestion tended to be better than with a dose just before eating
shelves.question: How should pancreatic enzyme doses be timed with meals in chronic pancreatitis?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Drug Administration Schedule · Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatic Extracts · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the timing question rests on one small randomised crossover study, and the stamp says so. In Domínguez-Muñoz 2005 (PMID: 15813835), 24 patients with chronic pancreatitis and exocrine insufficiency took 40,000 units of lipase just before, just after, or distributed along with meals in randomised 1-week periods: fat digestion, measured by an optimised mixed 13C-triglyceride breath test, tended to be higher when capsules were taken along with meals (13CO2 recovery 61.4 ± 21.4%) or just after meals (60.6 ± 21.8%) than just before meals (53.9 ± 20.3%), and fat digestion normalised in 63%, 54% and 50% of patients respectively — differences the record reports as a tendency, with no significance test printed. The carded placebo-controlled pancrelipase trial (Whitcomb 2010, PMID: 20502447) dosed enzymes per meal and per snack and proved the drug class works (coefficient of fat absorption change 31.9 versus 8.7 points over placebo), but it did not randomise timing. The Cochrane timing review in cystic fibrosis (Ng 2021, PMID: 34339047) found no eligible randomised trial of dosing schedules at all. Practical answer on this evidence: take the dose during the meal, spread through it (or immediately after), not as a single dose beforehand — a reasonable instruction whose comparative evidence is one 24-patient study. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Domínguez-Muñoz 2005: in 24 patients with chronic pancreatitis, fat digestion tended to be better when enzyme capsules were taken distributed along with meals or just after meals than just before meals (N = 24 on the face)
cards.summary: Domínguez-Muñoz 2005: in 24 patients with chronic pancreatitis, fat digestion tended to be better when enzyme capsules were taken distributed along with meals or just after meals than just before meals (N = 24 on the face)
cards.people: 24 consecutive patients with chronic pancreatitis and maldigestion secondary to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, in a prospective, randomised, open, comparative, three-way crossover study. Each patient took 40,000 U lipase as capsules containing enteric-coated mini-microspheres on three schedules for three consecutive 1-week periods in randomised order: just before meals (schedule A), just after meals (schedule B), or distributed along with meals (schedule C). Fat digestion was evaluated by an optimised mixed (13)C-triglyceride breath test. Randomised N = 24.
cards.result: Before therapy, (13)CO2 recovery on the breath test was 23.8 ± 15.8% (normal above 58.0%). During therapy, (13)CO2 recovery tended to be higher when capsules were taken along with meals (61.4 ± 21.4%) or just after meals (60.6 ± 21.8%) than when taken just before meals (53.9 ± 20.3%). The percentage of patients who normalised fat digestion was 50% with schedule A (before), 54% with schedule B (after) and 63% with schedule C (distributed along with meals). The record reports these contrasts as a tendency and prints no P value or confidence interval for them; no stronger effect size is claimed here. The authors conclude efficacy may be optimised by administration during or after meals.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 24 patients, 1-week periods, an open design and a breath-test surrogate: the ordering (during/after better than before) is consistent and physiologically sensible — enzymes must mix with chyme and empty with it — but the record itself only claims a tendency, and this shelf does not upgrade it.
cards.source: Domínguez-Muñoz JE et al. Effect of the administration schedule on the therapeutic efficacy of oral pancreatic enzyme supplements in patients with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: a randomized, three-way crossover study. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2005. PMID: 15813835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Whitcomb 2010: the carded placebo-controlled trial dosed pancrelipase per meal (72,000 lipase units per meal, 36,000 per snack) and improved fat absorption by 31.9 points versus 8.7 on placebo — it establishes with-meal dosing as the tested standard, but did not randomise timing
cards.summary: Whitcomb 2010: the carded placebo-controlled trial dosed pancrelipase per meal (72,000 lipase units per meal, 36,000 per snack) and improved fat absorption by 31.9 points versus 8.7 on placebo — it establishes with-meal dosing as the tested standard, but did not randomise timing
cards.people: 54 patients aged 18 years or older with confirmed exocrine pancreatic insufficiency due to chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery, in a double-blind, randomised, multicountry, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial: 25 received pancrelipase delayed-release capsules and 29 placebo for 7 days after a 5-day placebo run-in, on an individually designed diet providing at least 100 g of fat per day. Dosing was 72,000 lipase units per meal and 36,000 lipase units per snack.
cards.result: The mean ± SD change in coefficient of fat absorption was significantly greater with pancrelipase than placebo (31.9 ± 18.6 vs 8.7 ± 12.4 percentage points; P < 0.0001), as was the change in coefficient of nitrogen absorption (35.2 ± 29.1 vs 8.9 ± 28.0; P = 0.0005). Greater improvements in stool frequency, stool consistency, abdominal pain and flatulence were observed with pancrelipase. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 20.0% of the pancrelipase group and 20.7% of the placebo group, with no discontinuations due to adverse events. The record does not state a randomised comparison of administration timing, and no timing effect is claimed from this card.
cards.watchOut: This card answers 'do enzymes work when dosed with meals', not 'when within the meal': it is carded so the shelf's timing advice is anchored to the dosing pattern the efficacy trials actually used, and it must not be cited as a timing comparison.
cards.source: Whitcomb DC et al. Pancrelipase delayed-release capsules (CREON) for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency due to chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery: A double-blind randomized trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 20502447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ng 2021: the Cochrane review of PERT timing in cystic fibrosis found no eligible randomised trial of dosing schedules — the timing literature is this thin across pancreatic insufficiency
cards.summary: Ng 2021: the Cochrane review of PERT timing in cystic fibrosis found no eligible randomised trial of dosing schedules — the timing literature is this thin across pancreatic insufficiency
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review — no eligible studies (Ng 2021)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (searches to 24 June 2021, trial registers to 9 July 2021) seeking randomised and quasi-randomised trials, including crossover trials with a minimum 2-week washout, of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy dosing strategies by timing of administration in people of any age with cystic fibrosis, of whom 80–90% have pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. No studies met the eligibility criteria.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported for any timing comparison: the review identified no eligible studies. Excluded studies were either crossover in design without a sufficient washout period or did not assess timing; one terminated study was awaiting assessment. The authors conclude they were unable to determine whether one dosing schedule is better than another, and that further research is needed to evaluate dosing schedules for fat absorption. No effect size exists in this record, and none is printed.
cards.watchOut: This review is in cystic fibrosis, not chronic pancreatitis, and found nothing: it is carded as an honest map of how little randomised timing evidence exists anywhere in pancreatic insufficiency, not as evidence about patients with chronic pancreatitis.
cards.source: Ng C et al. Timing of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) in cystic fibrosis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34339047. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cystic Fibrosis · Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Humans · Nutritional Status · Pancreas

cards.headline: Synthesis: take pancreatic enzymes during the meal, spread through it (or immediately after) — the only direct timing trial found digestion tended to be better that way than with a single dose just before eating
cards.summary: Synthesis: take pancreatic enzymes during the meal, spread through it (or immediately after) — the only direct timing trial found digestion tended to be better that way than with a single dose just before eating
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised three-way crossover timing trial in chronic pancreatitis (n = 24), one double-blind placebo-controlled efficacy trial dosing per meal and snack (n = 54), and one Cochrane timing review in cystic fibrosis that found no eligible trials. Unique participants across the two patient studies total 78, so no small-N stamp labelling applies to the shelf as a whole; the timing contrast itself rests on 24 patients, printed on that card's face.
cards.result: In Domínguez-Muñoz 2005, breath-test fat digestion was 61.4 ± 21.4% with doses distributed along meals and 60.6 ± 21.8% just after meals versus 53.9 ± 20.3% just before meals, with normalisation in 63%, 54% and 50% of patients — a tendency without a printed significance test. Whitcomb 2010 confirms meal-based dosing works against placebo (fat-absorption change 31.9 versus 8.7 points). Ng 2021 found no eligible timing trial in cystic fibrosis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The practical instruction (during the meal, spread out) outruns its proof: it is the direction of one small open crossover study plus the dosing pattern of the efficacy trials, and a patient who takes enzymes just before eating is not shown to be harmed — only, on this record, possibly absorbing less fat.
cards.source: Synthesis of Domínguez-Muñoz JE et al. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2005 (PMID: 15813835); Whitcomb DC et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010 (PMID: 20502447); Ng C et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021 (PMID: 34339047).

shelves.title: ESWL for large pancreatic duct stones: complete clearance in about 7 in 10 patients and pain-free follow-up in about 6 in 10 in pooled series, with ESWL alone matching ESWL plus endoscopy in the randomised trial
shelves.question: Does extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy work for large pancreatic duct stones in chronic pancreatitis?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adult · Calcinosis · Calculi · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde · Combined Modality Therapy · Drainage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Care Costs · Humans · Length of Stay · Lithotripsy · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis, Chronic · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the clearance and pain numbers come mainly from pooled observational series, with one randomised strategy trial, and the stamp is capped accordingly. The meta-analysis of van Huijgevoort 2020 (PMID: 32743061) pooled 22 studies and 3,868 patients treated with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) for symptomatic pancreatic duct stones: complete ductal clearance 69.8%, complete absence of pain during follow-up 64.2%, complete stone fragmentation 86.3%, with post-procedural pancreatitis in 4.0% and cholangitis in 0.5%. The large single-centre cohort of Tandan 2013 (PMID: 23891416) found 60–69% of 636 followed patients pain-free at intermediate and long-term follow-up after ESWL with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, with stone recurrence in 14–23%. The one randomised trial (Dumonceau 2007, PMID: 17047101) did not compare ESWL against no ESWL: it showed ESWL alone performed as well as ESWL plus systematic endoscopic drainage for pain relapse (38% versus 45%; odds ratio 0.77 relative), at one-third of the cost — so the randomised evidence supports ESWL as the platform treatment, while the size of its effect against natural history rests on the observational record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Dumonceau 2007: randomised trial — ESWL alone performed as well as ESWL plus endoscopic drainage for pain relapse (38% versus 45%), at one-third of the cost
cards.summary: Dumonceau 2007: randomised trial — ESWL alone performed as well as ESWL plus endoscopic drainage for pain relapse (38% versus 45%), at one-third of the cost
cards.people: 55 patients with uncomplicated painful chronic pancreatitis and calcifications obstructing the main pancreatic duct, randomised to extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) alone (n = 26) or ESWL combined with endoscopic drainage of the main pancreatic duct (n = 29), with the primary outcome assessed 2 years after the intervention.
cards.result: At 2 years, 10 (38%) patients in the ESWL-alone group and 13 (45%) in the ESWL-plus-endoscopy group had presented pain relapse (odds ratio 0.77 relative; 95% CI 0.23 to 2.57 — the added endoscopy made no difference to the primary outcome). Both groups showed a similar decrease in main pancreatic duct diameter (mean decrease 1.7 mm; 95% CI 0.9 to 2.6; p<0.001) and in pain episodes per year (mean decrease 3.7; 95% CI 2.6 to 4.9; p<0.001). Treatment costs per patient were three times higher in the ESWL combined with endoscopy group (p = 0.001). The median delay between onset of chronic pancreatitis and persistent pain relief was 1.1 years in both groups, versus 4 years for the natural history in a reference cohort (p<0.001). The authors conclude ESWL is a safe and effective preferred treatment for selected patients with painful calcified chronic pancreatitis, and that adding systematic endoscopy adds cost without improving the outcome of pancreatic pain.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received ESWL, so this trial cannot estimate what ESWL itself adds over no treatment or over time — its natural-history comparison is a separate reference cohort, not a randomised control — and with 55 patients its confidence interval (0.23 to 2.57) is wide in both directions.
cards.source: Dumonceau JM et al. Treatment for painful calcified chronic pancreatitis: extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy versus endoscopic treatment: a randomised controlled trial. Gut. 2007. PMID: 17047101. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tandan 2013: in 636 followed patients with large pancreatic duct stones treated with ESWL and ERCP, 68.7% were pain-free at intermediate follow-up and 60.3% at long-term follow-up; stones recurred in 14.0% and 22.8%
cards.summary: Tandan 2013: in 636 followed patients with large pancreatic duct stones treated with ESWL and ERCP, 68.7% were pain-free at intermediate follow-up and 60.3% at long-term follow-up; stones recurred in 14.0% and 22.8%
cards.people: Retrospective cross-sectional cohort at a high-volume tertiary centre: 636 of 1,006 patients with idiopathic calcific chronic pancreatitis who underwent extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) between 2004 and 2009 were followed for a maximum of 96 months — 364 in the intermediate follow-up group (24–60 months) and 272 in the long-term group (over 60 months).
cards.result: After ESWL and ERCP, absence of pain was seen in 250 patients (68.7%) in the intermediate group, with mild-to-moderate pain in 94 (25.4%) and severe pain in 20 (5.5%); in the long-term group, 164 patients (60.3%) had no pain, 97 (35.7%) had mild or moderate episodes and 11 (4.04%) had episodic severe pain. Recurrence of calculi was seen in 51 patients (14.01%) in the intermediate group and 62 (22.8%) in the long-term group. Quality of life improved in a significant number of patients in both groups (no effect size printed in the record). The authors conclude ESWL for large pancreatic duct calculi offers good results in idiopathic chronic pancreatitis on intermediate and long-term follow-up.

cards.headline: van Huijgevoort 2020: meta-analysis of 22 studies and 3,868 patients — complete ductal clearance 69.8%, complete absence of pain 64.2%, fragmentation 86.3%; post-procedural pancreatitis 4.0%
cards.summary: van Huijgevoort 2020: meta-analysis of 22 studies and 3,868 patients — complete ductal clearance 69.8%, complete absence of pain 64.2%, fragmentation 86.3%; post-procedural pancreatitis 4.0%
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies from January 2000 to December 2018 of extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) in patients with symptomatic chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic duct stones; ESWL is described as indicated after failure of the first treatment step in patients with symptomatic intraductal stones larger than 5 mm in the head or body of the pancreas. After screening 486 studies, 22 studies with 3,868 patients were included.
cards.result: The pooled proportion of patients with complete ductal clearance was 69.8% (95% CI 63.8–75.5). The pooled proportion with complete absence of pain during follow-up was 64.2% (95% CI 57.5–70.6). Complete stone fragmentation was 86.3% (95% CI 76.0–94.0). Post-procedural pancreatitis occurred in 4.0% (95% CI 2.5–5.8) and cholangitis in 0.5% (95% CI 0.2–0.9). The authors conclude ESWL results in complete ductal clearance in a majority of patients, with absence of pain during follow-up in over half of patients with symptomatic chronic pancreatitis caused by obstructing pancreatic duct stones.
cards.watchOut: These are pooled single-arm proportions from mostly observational series, not comparisons: 69.8% clearance and 64.2% pain-free describe what happens after ESWL in selected patients, and without a control arm they cannot separate the procedure's effect from patient selection and the natural history of pancreatic pain.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ESWL fragments large pancreatic duct stones in most treated patients and clears the duct in about 7 in 10, with about 6 in 10 pain-free on follow-up — and the one randomised trial found adding systematic endoscopy to ESWL added cost without improving pain outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: ESWL fragments large pancreatic duct stones in most treated patients and clears the duct in about 7 in 10, with about 6 in 10 pain-free on follow-up — and the one randomised trial found adding systematic endoscopy to ESWL added cost without improving pain outcomes
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised strategy trial (n = 55), one large retrospective cohort (636 followed patients), and one meta-analysis of 22 studies (3,868 patients; the cohort and trial populations may overlap with the pooled series). Total carded participants exceed 3,800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the governing limitation is that no carded trial compares ESWL with no ESWL.
cards.result: Pooled complete ductal clearance was 69.8% and complete absence of pain 64.2% (van Huijgevoort 2020); the Tandan 2013 cohort found 68.7% and 60.3% pain-free at intermediate and long-term follow-up, with stone recurrence in 14.0% and 22.8%. In Dumonceau 2007, pain relapse at 2 years was 38% with ESWL alone versus 45% with ESWL plus endoscopy (odds ratio 0.77 relative), with costs three times higher in the combined group. Post-procedural pancreatitis occurred in 4.0% in the pooled record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is comparative: ESWL's clearance rates are well documented, but how much of the pain relief exceeds what time, analgesia and endoscopic drainage alone would achieve is not measured by any carded randomised trial.

shelves.title: Simethicone in bowel preparation: fewer bubbles, better cleansing and less bloating across the randomised record — the adenoma-detection gain is real in one meta-analysis, absent overall in the larger one, and confined to single-dose regimens
shelves.question: Does adding simethicone to bowel preparation improve colonoscopy visualization?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Adult · Antifoaming Agents · Cathartics · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Predictive Value of Tests · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Simethicone · Therapeutic Irrigation
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for visualization — two meta-analyses of randomised trials and a double-blind trial agree that simethicone clears bubbles and foam and improves cleansing scores, while they divide on whether adenoma detection rises overall, and that division is printed rather than smoothed over. Rishi 2019 (PMID: 31236194) randomised 168 outpatients: high bubble grades requiring intervention occurred in 4 of 84 patients with simethicone versus 20 of 84 with placebo (P = 0.007), while total Boston Bowel Preparation Scale scores did not differ (7.42 versus 7.28; P = 0.542 — the treatment made no difference on that scale). Pan 2019 (PMID: 30069899) pooled 6 trials and 1,855 patients and found adenoma detection increased (27.9% versus 23.3%; relative risk 1.20 relative). Moolla 2019 (PMID: 31451919) pooled 16 trials and 5,630 patients: colon cleansing improved (odds ratio 1.48 relative), bloating was less frequent with simethicone, but adenoma detection overall did not significantly change (odds ratio 1.22 relative; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.83), with the detection benefit confined to single-dose (non-split) preparations. The visualization claim itself — fewer bubbles, better cleansing — is concordant across all three records. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for visualization, with the adenoma-detection split stated in the stamp.

cards.headline: Pan 2019: meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (1,855 patients) — supplemental simethicone increased adenoma detection from 23.3% to 27.9% (relative risk 1.20 relative)
cards.summary: Pan 2019: meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (1,855 patients) — supplemental simethicone increased adenoma detection from 23.3% to 27.9% (relative risk 1.20 relative)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials evaluating pre-procedure simethicone added to polyethylene glycol-based bowel preparation on the adenoma detection rate during colonoscopy, searching PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library. Six trials involving 1,855 patients were included, with fixed-effect models applied.
cards.result: The adenoma detection rate during colonoscopy was significantly increased by supplemental simethicone (27.9% vs 23.3%, P = 0.02), with a relative risk of 1.20 relative (95% confidence interval 1.03–1.39). Subgroup analysis suggested simethicone may be more useful to improve adenoma detection in endoscopic centres with a low baseline adenoma detection rate. The authors conclude supplemental simethicone for polyethylene glycol-based bowel preparation is useful to improve the adenoma detection rate during colonoscopy.
cards.watchOut: Six trials and a confidence interval whose lower bound is 1.03: the detection benefit in this pooling is real but fragile, and the second carded meta-analysis, with nearly three times the patients, did not reproduce it overall — read the two together, as the synthesis does.
cards.source: Pan P et al. Effect of supplemental simethicone for bowel preparation on adenoma detection during colonoscopy: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2019. PMID: 30069899. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rishi 2019: double-blind randomised trial — intraluminal bubbles needing intervention in 4 of 84 patients with simethicone versus 20 of 84 with placebo (P = 0.007); total bowel-preparation scores did not differ
cards.summary: Rishi 2019: double-blind randomised trial — intraluminal bubbles needing intervention in 4 of 84 patients with simethicone versus 20 of 84 with placebo (P = 0.007); total bowel-preparation scores did not differ
cards.people: Prospective, randomised, multicentre, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of premixed simethicone added to a split-regimen, low-volume polyethylene glycol–bisacodyl bowel preparation in 168 outpatients undergoing screening, surveillance and diagnostic colonoscopies (84 simethicone, 84 placebo). The primary outcome was intraluminal bubbles graded on the Intraluminal Bubbles Scale; secondary outcomes included the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS), polyp and adenoma detection, procedure times and patient-reported adverse events.
cards.result: Higher Intraluminal Bubbles grades III and IV (less than 75% of the mucosa cleared of bubbles/foam, requiring intervention with simethicone-infused wash) were detected in 4 of 84 patients in the simethicone group versus 20 of 84 in the placebo group (P = 0.007). BBPS total score was 7.42 (SD ± 1.51) in the simethicone group and 7.28 (SD ± 1.44) in the placebo group (P = 0.542) — the treatment made no difference to the total preparation score. A significantly higher number of adenomas were detected in the simethicone group (P = 0.001; the record reports the count comparison without printing per-group adenoma rates). The authors conclude the addition of simethicone is well advised for its anti-foaming properties and can improve bowel wall visibility.
cards.watchOut: The bubble outcome is partly circular — the high grades are defined by needing a simethicone wash, the very agent being tested — and the trial's own global preparation score (BBPS) showed no difference, so this card supports the anti-foam claim specifically, not a claim that overall preparation quality rises.

cards.headline: Moolla 2019: meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (5,630 patients) — cleansing improved (odds ratio 1.48 relative) and bloating fell, but adenoma detection overall did not significantly change; the detection benefit appeared only with single-dose preparation
cards.summary: Moolla 2019: meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (5,630 patients) — cleansing improved (odds ratio 1.48 relative) and bloating fell, but adenoma detection overall did not significantly change; the detection benefit appeared only with single-dose preparation
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Moolla 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing standard bowel preparation alone with preparation combined with simethicone before colonoscopy, with primary outcomes of colon cleanliness, adenoma detection rate and tolerability. Sixteen randomised trials with 5,630 patients were included.
cards.result: Polyethylene glycol with simethicone improved colon cleansing compared with polyethylene glycol alone (odds ratio 1.48 relative, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.97, P = 0.008); the improvement was seen for single dosing (odds ratio 1.83 relative, CI 1.20 to 2.79, P = 0.005) but not for split dosing (odds ratio 1.32 relative, CI 0.72 to 2.43, P = 0.38 — the treatment made no difference in the split-dose subgroup). Overall, simethicone had no significant effect on adenoma detection (odds ratio 1.22 relative, CI 0.81 to 1.83, P = 0.33), but in patients receiving single dosing it significantly increased detection (odds ratio 1.96 relative, CI 1.22 to 3.16, P = 0.005). Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain rates did not differ significantly; the preparation-alone cohort had greater odds of abdominal bloating than the simethicone cohort (odds ratio 2.33 relative, CI 1.70 to 3.20, P < 0.00001). The authors conclude simethicone may be a useful adjunct in patients unable to receive split-dose polyethylene glycol.
cards.watchOut: This is the larger and more cautious of the two carded meta-analyses, and its null overall adenoma result is part of this shelf's evidence, not an embarrassment to it: with modern split-dose preparation — the current standard — neither cleansing nor detection improved significantly in its subgroups.

cards.headline: Synthesis: simethicone reliably reduces bubbles and foam and improves cleansing scores, and lessens bloating; whether it raises adenoma detection depends on the preparation regimen, with no significant gain under split dosing
cards.summary: Synthesis: simethicone reliably reduces bubbles and foam and improves cleansing scores, and lessens bloating; whether it raises adenoma detection depends on the preparation regimen, with no significant gain under split dosing
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of randomised trials (6 trials, 1,855 patients; 16 trials, 5,630 patients — overlapping trial sets) and one double-blind randomised trial (168 patients). Total unique participants number in the thousands, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Bubbles requiring intervention fell from 20 of 84 patients to 4 of 84 with simethicone in Rishi 2019, and pooled cleansing improved (odds ratio 1.48 relative) in Moolla 2019. Adenoma detection rose in Pan 2019 (27.9% versus 23.3%; relative risk 1.20 relative) but not overall in Moolla 2019 (odds ratio 1.22 relative, CI 0.81 to 1.83), where benefit was confined to single-dose preparation; bloating was less frequent with simethicone (odds ratio 2.33 relative for preparation alone). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for visualization, with the adenoma-detection split stated.
cards.watchOut: Visualization is a surrogate: the outcome patients care about is finding adenomas, and on that outcome the carded meta-analyses disagree, with the larger one null overall — the LIKELY stamp on this shelf covers what the endoscopist sees, not a proven detection dividend under modern split-dose preparation.

shelves.title: GLP-1 drugs before colonoscopy (observational only): retained gastric contents are more common in relative terms and preparation was poorer in one cohort, but absolute aborted-procedure rates were low and no aspiration excess was shown — routine stopping is not established by the record
shelves.question: Should adults stop GLP-1 receptor agonists before colonoscopy because of retained gastric contents?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Colonoscopy · Male · Female · Retrospective Studies · Middle Aged · Aged · Cathartics · Obesity · Early Detection of Cancer · Hypoglycemic Agents · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded record is a retrospective cohort or a meta-analysis of such cohorts, and none tests stopping versus continuing the drug. What the record does show: retained gastric contents are clearly more frequent in GLP-1 receptor agonist users at endoscopy (pooled odds ratio 15.39 relative in Singh 2025, PMID: 39401599, across 23 studies and 77,152 patients), and aborted procedures were also more frequent in relative terms (odds ratio 13.86 relative) — but the absolute rates were low: in the largest single cohort (Dev 2025, PMID: 40021603), 0.6% of procedures in GLP-1 users were aborted for retained food versus 0.096% in non-users, with no aspiration episodes in patients with retained food, and the meta-analysis found no significant difference in aspiration events. For colonoscopy specifically, Yao 2024 (PMID: 37856247) found modestly worse bowel preparation in users (Boston Bowel Preparation Scale 7.0 versus 7.5; repeat colonoscopy for poor preparation 18.9% versus 11.1%), while the meta-analysis found no significant difference in subjective bowel preparation quality (odds ratio 0.94 relative). The carded record therefore documents a real but small absolute procedural problem and does not establish that routinely stopping GLP-1 therapy before colonoscopy is needed; it supports individualised management, as the largest cohort's authors conclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Yao 2024: retrospective cohort of 446 colonoscopy patients — GLP-1 users had modestly worse bowel preparation (BBPS 7.0 versus 7.5) and more repeat colonoscopies for poor preparation (18.9% versus 11.1%)
cards.summary: Yao 2024: retrospective cohort of 446 colonoscopy patients — GLP-1 users had modestly worse bowel preparation (BBPS 7.0 versus 7.5) and more repeat colonoscopies for poor preparation (18.9% versus 11.1%)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent screening or surveillance colonoscopy at a large academic medical centre between December 2021 and December 2022: 446 patients, comprising 265 (59%) cases taking any GLP-1 receptor agonist for diabetes or obesity at the time of colonoscopy and 181 (41%) controls who had been prescribed a GLP-1 receptor agonist at some point but not within 3 months of colonoscopy. Patients on promotility or antimotility agents and those without a recorded Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) score were excluded. The groups differed at baseline in the proportion with diabetes (P = 0.001), which was handled by adjustment.
cards.result: Mean BBPS was lower in GLP-1 users than controls (7.0 ± 1.9 vs 7.5 ± 2.4, P = 0.046, controlling for diabetes). The percentage of patients with a total BBPS score under 5 was significantly higher in cases (15.5% vs 6.6%, P = 0.01), and the proportion requiring a repeat colonoscopy due to poor bowel preparation was also significantly higher in cases (18.9% vs 11.1%, P = 0.041). The authors conclude GLP-1 use was associated with a statistically significantly lower quality of bowel preparation, with clinical significance in the greater need for repeat colonoscopy.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is current users against former users (not never-users), diabetes was commoner in the user group and itself worsens preparation, and a 0.5-point BBPS difference is small — the repeat-colonoscopy gap (18.9% versus 11.1%) is the clinically weightier figure, and it is still an association from one centre's records.

cards.headline: Singh 2025: meta-analysis of 23 studies (77,152 patients) — retained gastric contents much more frequent in relative terms with GLP-1 use (odds ratio 15.39 relative), aborted procedures likewise (13.86 relative), but no significant difference in aspiration events or in bowel preparation quality
cards.summary: Singh 2025: meta-analysis of 23 studies (77,152 patients) — retained gastric contents much more frequent in relative terms with GLP-1 use (odds ratio 15.39 relative), aborted procedures likewise (13.86 relative), but no significant difference in aspiration events or in bowel preparation quality
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Singh 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies evaluating GLP-1 receptor agonists versus a control group (no GLP-1 receptor agonists) in patients undergoing endoscopy, with outcomes of retained gastric contents, aborted procedures, aspiration events and subjective bowel preparation quality. Twenty-three studies with 77,152 patients were included (4,449 in the GLP-1 arm and 72,703 in the control arm); mean patient age ranged from 47.6 to 72 years and 58.4% were women. Pooled odds ratios were estimated with a random-effects model.
cards.result: Compared with the control group, the GLP-1 group had higher odds of retained gastric contents (odds ratio 15.39 relative; 95% CI 4.65–50.99; P < .01) and aborted procedures (odds ratio 13.86 relative; 95% CI 4.42–43.43; P < .01). No significant differences were observed in aspiration events (odds ratio 21.06 relative; 95% CI .13–3379.01; P = .24 — the treatment made no difference that reached significance, on a very wide interval) or in subjective bowel preparation quality (odds ratio 0.94 relative; 95% CI .67–1.31; P = .83). The authors note that although statistical significance was reached for visible retained contents and early termination, these events were overall rare, and GLP-1 drugs do not appear to pose significant risk, as the odds of aspiration were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios of 15 and 14 sound alarming until the base rates are restored — the events were rare, the aspiration interval (0.13 to 3379.01) is compatible with almost anything, and pooling retrospective cohorts cannot remove confounding by diabetes, obesity and indication; the relative figures must never be quoted without the absolute rates on the next card.

cards.headline: Dev 2025: in 32,275 upper endoscopies, procedures aborted for retained food were uncommon even in GLP-1 users (0.6% versus 0.096%), and there were no aspiration episodes in patients with retained food
cards.summary: Dev 2025: in 32,275 upper endoscopies, procedures aborted for retained food were uncommon even in GLP-1 users (0.6% versus 0.096%), and there were no aspiration episodes in patients with retained food
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of all patients who underwent upper endoscopic procedures at two hospitals during 2018–2023: 32,275 procedures in total, of which 1,179 were performed in patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists. The primary endpoint was procedure abortion due to the presence of food; the secondary endpoint was aspiration events in patients with food noted on endoscopy.
cards.result: In total, 37 endoscopies (0.1%) were aborted due to retained gastric food: 7 patients (0.6%) in the GLP-1 cohort versus 30 patients (0.096%) in the non-GLP-1 cohort (p < 0.01). There were no episodes of aspiration in patients with retained food. Because of the small number of events, there were no clear modifiable risk factors for gastric food retention. The authors conclude GLP-1 use did increase rates of gastric food retention during upper endoscopy, though the absolute risk was minimal, and that the study supports individualised periprocedural management in patients on GLP-1 therapy.
cards.watchOut: These are upper endoscopies, not colonoscopies: the card is the shelf's absolute-risk anchor for the retained-food problem, and its zero aspiration count comes with a small numerator of retained-food cases (37 aborted procedures in total), so it bounds the risk rather than proving it is zero.
cards.source: Dev B et al. Low Rates of Aborted Endoscopy Due to Gastric Food Retention in Patients on Glucagon-Like-Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: GLP-1 users do show more retained gastric contents and, in one colonoscopy cohort, poorer preparation — but aborted procedures were rare in absolute terms and no aspiration excess was shown, so the carded record does not establish that routine stopping before colonoscopy is needed
cards.summary: Synthesis: GLP-1 users do show more retained gastric contents and, in one colonoscopy cohort, poorer preparation — but aborted procedures were rare in absolute terms and no aspiration excess was shown, so the carded record does not establish that routine stopping before colonoscopy is needed
cards.people: The carded evidence: one retrospective colonoscopy cohort (446 patients), one meta-analysis of 23 observational studies (77,152 patients) and one large retrospective endoscopy cohort (32,275 procedures, 1,179 in GLP-1 users). All observational; total carded participants exceed 77,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the governing limitation is the absence of any trial or cohort comparing stopping versus continuing the drug, printed here and on the stamp.
cards.result: Retained gastric contents were more frequent with GLP-1 use (pooled odds ratio 15.39 relative), as were aborted procedures in relative terms (odds ratio 13.86 relative), yet absolute aborted-procedure rates were 0.6% versus 0.096% in the largest cohort, with no aspiration episodes and no significant aspiration difference in the meta-analysis. Bowel preparation was worse in Yao 2024 (BBPS 7.0 versus 7.5; repeat colonoscopy 18.9% versus 11.1%) but not significantly different in the pooled record (odds ratio 0.94 relative). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomised or even compared a hold-the-drug strategy, so this shelf cannot weigh the harms of stopping (lost glycaemic and weight control, rescheduling) against the small absolute procedural risk — any unit policy either way is a judgement built on top of this record, not a conclusion from it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yao R et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2024 (PMID: 37856247); Singh S et al. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2025 (PMID: 39401599); Dev B et al. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2025 (PMID: 40021603).

shelves.title: Prophylactic clipping after large-polyp resection: bleeding roughly halved for polyps ≥20 mm — above all in the proximal colon — with little to no benefit for smaller or distal lesions
shelves.question: Does prophylactic clipping after removal of large colon polyps prevent delayed bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Colectomy · Colonic Polyps · Colonoscopy · Equipment Design · Female · Hemostatic Techniques · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · North America · Postoperative Hemorrhage · Risk Factors · Spain · Surgical Instruments · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for large (20 mm or larger), especially proximal, polyps; the benefit does not extend to smaller or distal lesions, and both halves are on the face. The multicentre randomised trial of Pohl 2019 (PMID: 30885778) randomised 919 patients after resection of nonpedunculated polyps of 20 mm or more: postprocedure bleeding occurred in 3.5% with clip closure versus 7.1% without (absolute risk difference 3.6%), and serious adverse events were also fewer (4.8% versus 9.5%). The protection was concentrated in proximal polyps (3.3% versus 9.6%; absolute difference 6.3%) and absent — numerically reversed — in distal polyps (4.0% versus 1.4%). The randomised-trial meta-analysis of Chen 2021 (PMID: 33049265; 8 trials, 3,415 patients) agrees: relative risk 0.61 relative overall, 0.54 relative for polyps 20 mm or larger (number needed to treat 30) and 0.49 relative for proximal polyps (number needed to treat 25). Bishay 2022 (PMID: 33751224) found the randomised benefit confined to polyps of 20 mm or more (relative risk 0.47 relative), with the remaining randomised data and the observational data showing no benefit (observational relative risk 0.96 relative — the treatment made no difference). Two or more concordant randomised sources for the large-polyp claim support LIKELY. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for polyps ≥20 mm, especially proximal.

cards.headline: Pohl 2019: randomised trial of 919 patients — clip closure after resection of polyps ≥20 mm reduced postprocedure bleeding from 7.1% to 3.5%, with the benefit restricted to proximal polyps
cards.summary: Pohl 2019: randomised trial of 919 patients — clip closure after resection of polyps ≥20 mm reduced postprocedure bleeding from 7.1% to 3.5%, with the benefit restricted to proximal polyps
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial (NCT01936948) at 18 medical centres in North America and Spain, April 2013 to October 2017: 919 patients with a large nonpedunculated colon polyp (≥20 mm) were randomly assigned to endoscopic closure of the mucosal defect with a clip or to no closure and completed follow-up. The primary outcome was postprocedure bleeding, defined as a severe bleeding event requiring hospitalisation, blood transfusion, colonoscopy, surgery or another invasive intervention within 30 days.
cards.result: Postprocedure bleeding occurred in 3.5% of patients in the clip group and 7.1% in the control group (absolute risk difference 3.6%; 95% CI 0.7%–6.5%). Among 615 patients (66.9%) with a proximal large polyp, bleeding risk was 3.3% in the clip group versus 9.6% in the control group (absolute risk difference 6.3%; 95% CI 2.5%–10.1%); among patients with a distal large polyp, the risks were 4.0% in the clip group and 1.4% in the control group (absolute risk difference −2.6%; 95% CI −6.3% to −1.1%) — no benefit distally. The effect of clip closure was independent of antithrombotic medications or polyp size. Serious adverse events occurred in 4.8% of the clip group versus 9.5% of controls (absolute risk difference 4.6%; 95% CI 1.3%–8.0%). The authors conclude clip closure reduces postprocedure bleeding after resection of large colon polyps, with the protective effect apparently restricted to proximal polyps.
cards.watchOut: The distal-polyp subgroup went the other way (4.0% versus 1.4%), so a blanket clip-everything policy is not what this trial supports; and the trial enrolled only nonpedunculated polyps of 20 mm or more resected at expert centres, which is exactly the population the stamp is limited to.
cards.source: Pohl H et al. Clip Closure Prevents Bleeding After Endoscopic Resection of Large Colon Polyps in a Randomized Trial. Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 30885778. Registry ID: NCT01936948. cards.headline: Chen 2021: meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (3,415 patients) — prophylactic clips reduced delayed bleeding (relative risk 0.61 relative), with larger reductions for polyps ≥20 mm (0.54 relative; NNT 30) and proximal polyps (0.49 relative; NNT 25)
cards.summary: Chen 2021: meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (3,415 patients) — prophylactic clips reduced delayed bleeding (relative risk 0.61 relative), with larger reductions for polyps ≥20 mm (0.54 relative; NNT 30) and proximal polyps (0.49 relative; NNT 25)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Chen 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (searched to October 2019) evaluating prophylactic clips to reduce delayed polypectomy bleeding after resection of large (≥10 mm) colorectal polyps. Eight studies (n = 3,415) met the criteria, all with a low risk of bias. The primary outcome was delayed polypectomy bleeding, defined by gastrointestinal bleeding after the conclusion of the colonoscopy.
cards.result: The overall pooled incidence of delayed bleeding was 3.9% (95% CI 2.4%–5.4%) after resection of polyps ≥10 mm. Placing prophylactic clips reduced delayed bleeding compared with no clips (relative risk 0.61 relative; 95% CI 0.43–0.85; I2 = 37.8%), with a number needed to treat of 52 (95% CI 31–163). In stratified analyses, clips were associated with reduced bleeding for polyps ≥20 mm (relative risk 0.54 relative; 95% CI 0.35–0.84; I2 = 0.0%; NNT 30), nonpedunculated morphology (relative risk 0.54 relative; 95% CI 0.36–0.81; NNT 39) and polyps located proximal to the hepatic flexure (relative risk 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.31–0.78; NNT 25). The authors conclude prophylactic clips demonstrated a modest reduction in delayed bleeding, with larger reductions in the higher-risk subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The overall number needed to treat of 52 (with an interval reaching 163) is the honest average across ≥10 mm polyps: the case for clipping is strong only where baseline risk is high — large, nonpedunculated, proximal lesions — and dilutes quickly outside them.

cards.headline: Bishay 2022: meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials and 9 observational studies (24,670 colonoscopies) — the randomised benefit was confined to polyps ≥20 mm (relative risk 0.47 relative); remaining randomised and observational data showed no benefit
cards.summary: Bishay 2022: meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials and 9 observational studies (24,670 colonoscopies) — the randomised benefit was confined to polyps ≥20 mm (relative risk 0.47 relative); remaining randomised and observational data showed no benefit
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised and observational studies (Bishay 2022)
cards.people: Meta-analysis (search through March 2020) of clinical trials and observational studies assessing prophylactic clipping and delayed post-polypectomy bleeding: 11 randomised controlled trials and 9 observational studies, representing 24,670 colonoscopies. Delayed bleeding occurred in 2.0% of patients overall. Pooled risk ratios were calculated using random-effects models, with subgroup, sensitivity and meta-regression analyses.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk of delayed bleeding was 0.47 relative (95% CI 0.29–0.77) from randomised trials enrolling only patients with polyps ≥20 mm. The remaining pooled randomised data did not demonstrate a benefit for clipping. The pooled relative risk from observational studies including all polyp sizes was 0.96 relative (95% CI 0.61–1.51) — the treatment made no difference in that data. For patients with proximal polyps of any size, the relative risk was 0.73 relative (95% CI 0.33–1.62) from randomised trials. Meta-regression confirmed that polyp size ≥20 mm significantly influenced the effect of clipping. cards.headline: Synthesis: clipping the defect after resection of polyps ≥20 mm — above all proximal ones — roughly halves delayed bleeding in the randomised record; for smaller or distal lesions the carded evidence shows little to no benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: clipping the defect after resection of polyps ≥20 mm — above all proximal ones — roughly halves delayed bleeding in the randomised record; for smaller or distal lesions the carded evidence shows little to no benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre randomised trial (919 patients, polyps ≥20 mm) and two meta-analyses (8 randomised trials, 3,415 patients; 11 randomised trials plus 9 observational studies, 24,670 colonoscopies — overlapping evidence bases). Total carded participants exceed 24,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In Pohl 2019, bleeding fell from 7.1% to 3.5% overall (absolute difference 3.6%) and from 9.6% to 3.3% for proximal polyps (absolute difference 6.3%), with no benefit for distal polyps (4.0% versus 1.4%). Chen 2021 pooled a relative risk of 0.61 relative overall and 0.54 relative for polyps ≥20 mm (NNT 30). Bishay 2022 found the randomised benefit confined to polyps ≥20 mm (relative risk 0.47 relative) and no difference in observational data across all sizes (relative risk 0.96 relative). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for polyps ≥20 mm, especially proximal.
cards.watchOut: Clips cost money and procedure time and occasionally fail to close wide defects; the randomised record justifies them where baseline bleeding risk is high, and this shelf should not be read as support for clipping every polypectomy defect.

shelves.title: Elective resection for recurrent diverticulitis: quality of life better at 6 months and 5 years after sigmoidectomy in the DIRECT trial — weighed against an 11–15% anastomotic leak risk, and not a test of the old two-episode rule
shelves.question: Should adults have elective colon resection after two episodes of diverticulitis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anastomotic Leak · Colon, Sigmoid · Conservative Treatment · Diverticulitis, Colonic · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Laparoscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, whose enrolled population must be printed plainly: the DIRECT trial did not study a simple 'two episodes' rule. It randomised 109 patients with recurrent diverticulitis (three or more presentations within 2 years) or persistent complaints for 3 months or more after an episode (van de Wall 2017, PMID: 28404008; NTR1478). At 6 months, quality of life (Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index) was significantly higher after elective sigmoidectomy than with conservative management (114.4 versus 100.4; mean difference 14.2), and the advantage persisted at 5 years (Bolkenstein 2019, PMID: 30247329: 118.2 versus 108.5; mean difference 9.7), with less pain. The price is real surgery: anastomotic leakage in 15% of operated patients at 6 months (11% in the 5-year report), reinterventions in 15%, and severe adverse events in about a third of the surgical group — while 23% of the conservative group crossed over to resection within 6 months and 46% by 5 years, which narrows the contrast. The trial was terminated early for recruitment difficulties. A 2026 systematic review (Sadiq, PMID: 42722921) found only 4 studies and 446 patients in the contemporary literature, with quality of life favouring surgery but reintervention commoner after it (21%). The old automatic rule — resect after the second episode — is not what this evidence tests; it supports offering elective resection to patients with recurrent or persisting complaints after weighing the quality-of-life gain against operative risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.

cards.headline: van de Wall 2017 (DIRECT): randomised trial — elective sigmoidectomy gave significantly better quality of life at 6 months than conservative management (GIQLI 114.4 versus 100.4), with anastomotic leakage in 15% of operated patients; the trial stopped early
cards.summary: van de Wall 2017 (DIRECT): randomised trial — elective sigmoidectomy gave significantly better quality of life at 6 months than conservative management (GIQLI 114.4 versus 100.4), with anastomotic leakage in 15% of operated patients; the trial stopped early
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised controlled trial — DIRECT (van de Wall 2017)
cards.people: Open-label, multicentre randomised controlled trial (DIRECT; Netherlands Trial Register NTR1478) in 24 teaching and two academic hospitals in the Netherlands. Patients aged 18–75 years with either recurrent left-sided diverticulitis (three or more presentations with clinical signs of acute diverticulitis within 2 years) or persistent abdominal complaints (ongoing lower left abdominal pain or persistent change in bowel habits for 3 months or more) after an episode of left-sided diverticulitis confirmed by CT, ultrasound or endoscopy. Between July 2010 and April 2014, 109 patients were randomised to elective (laparoscopic) sigmoidectomy (n = 53) or conservative management (n = 56), after which the Data Safety and Monitoring Board prematurely terminated the trial because of increasing difficulties in recruitment; 47 (89%) of the surgical group received resection and 43 (77%) of the conservative group received conservative management. The primary endpoint was health-related quality of life (Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index, GIQLI) at 6 months.
cards.result: The GIQLI score at 6 months was significantly higher in the surgical group (mean 114.4 [SD 22.3]) than in the conservative group (100.4 [22.7]; mean difference 14.2, 95% CI 7.2–21.1, p<0.0001). Severe adverse events in the first 6 months occurred in 43 (38%) of 109 patients (18 [34%] of 53 in the surgical group versus 23 [40%] of 57 in the conservative group, denominators as printed in the record). Seven (15%) patients who received surgical treatment developed anastomotic leakage. Of the 56 patients assigned to conservative management, 13 (23%) ultimately underwent elective resection because of ongoing abdominal complaints, with no anastomotic leakage. No patient deaths were recorded. The authors conclude elective sigmoidectomy, despite its inherent risk of complications, results in better quality of life than conservative management in patients with recurrent and persisting abdominal complaints after diverticulitis.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions define this shelf: the trial was stopped early at 109 patients for recruitment failure, and its 'recurrent' meant three or more presentations in 2 years (or persistent complaints) — not the two-episode threshold in this shelf's question — so the result supports offering resection for burdensome recurrence, not an automatic operation after a second episode. The trial was also open-label with a subjective primary outcome.
cards.source: van de Wall BJM et al.
