cards.headline: Bolkenstein 2019: at 5 years the DIRECT quality-of-life advantage persisted (GIQLI 118.2 versus 108.5), but 46% of the conservative group had ultimately required surgery, and 11% of operated patients had anastomotic leakage
cards.summary: Bolkenstein 2019: at 5 years the DIRECT quality-of-life advantage persisted (GIQLI 118.2 versus 108.5), but 46% of the conservative group had ultimately required surgery, and 11% of operated patients had anastomotic leakage
cards.type: Five-year follow-up of a randomised controlled trial — DIRECT (Bolkenstein 2019)
cards.people: Five-year follow-up of the DIRECT randomised trial: the same 109 patients randomised to elective sigmoidectomy (N = 53) or conservative management (N = 56) for recurring diverticulitis (more than 2 episodes within 2 years, as restated in this report) and/or ongoing complaints (more than 3 months) after an episode of diverticulitis. The primary outcome was quality of life (GIQLI) at 5-year follow-up; secondary outcomes included SF-36, visual analogue pain score, EQ-5D-3L, morbidity, mortality, perioperative complications and long-term operative outcome.
cards.result: At 5-year follow-up, mean GIQLI score was significantly higher in the operative group (118.2 [SD 21.0]) than the conservative group (108.5 [SD 20.0]; mean difference 9.7, 95% CI 1.7–17.7). All secondary quality-of-life measures favoured surgery: higher SF-36 physical (P = 0.030) and mental scores (P = 0.010), higher EQ-5D score (P = 0.016) and a lower visual analogue pain score (P = 0.011). Twenty-six (46%) patients in the conservative group ultimately required surgery because of severe ongoing complaints. Of the operatively treated patients, 8 (11%) had anastomotic leakage and reinterventions were required in 11 (15%). The authors conclude elective sigmoidectomy resulted in significantly increased quality of life at 5 years, and that surgeons should counsel patients weighing superior quality of life, less pain and lower recurrence risk against the complication risk of surgery.
cards.watchOut: With 46% of the conservative arm eventually resected, the 5-year comparison is no longer surgery versus no surgery but early surgery versus delayed-or-never surgery — which makes the persisting quality-of-life gap more interesting, not less, but also means the trial cannot say how a never-operate strategy would fare.
cards.source: Bolkenstein HE et al. cards.headline: Sadiq 2026: systematic review of the contemporary literature found only 4 studies and 446 patients — quality of life improved more with surgery, but reintervention was more common after surgery (21%)
cards.summary: Sadiq 2026: systematic review of the contemporary literature found only 4 studies and 446 patients — quality of life improved more with surgery, but reintervention was more common after surgery (21%)
cards.people: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42024600674, as printed in the record) of clinical trials and observational studies published in English over the past decade reporting outcomes for persistent or recurrent diverticulitis. From 189 references, three retrospective cohort studies and one randomised controlled trial were included, totalling 446 patients (42.1% male), with follow-up ranging from 17 to 190 months. Treatments included elective resection and nonoperative management.
cards.result: Recurrence rates were 5.6–21.1% across the included studies. Quality of life showed greater improvement with surgery, but reintervention was more common after surgery (21%) than with nonoperative management. Recurrent or persistent diverticulitis demonstrated a higher recurrence risk, with increased incidence of surgery and comparable incidence of ostomy. The authors conclude that although surgical intervention may enhance quality of life, it may also necessitate more reinterventions, that contemporary literature detailing long-term outcomes is limited, and that standardising definitions of recurrent diverticulitis would enable comparative analyses. No pooled effect size is reported in the record, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Four studies and 446 patients is the whole contemporary comparative literature this review could find — one of them the DIRECT trial already carded on this shelf — so this card maps the thinness of the evidence rather than adding an independent result.
cards.source: Sadiq KO et al. Long-term outcomes in recurrent diverticulitis: a systematic review of treatment strategies and recurrence rates. International journal of colorectal disease. 2026. shelves.title: Biofeedback for levator ani syndrome: adequate relief in 87% of tenderness-confirmed patients in the single randomised trial, ahead of electrogalvanic stimulation and massage — and no benefit shown without the examination sign
shelves.question: Should adults with chronic anal pain and levator ani syndrome try biofeedback?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anus Diseases · Biofeedback, Psychology · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Massage · Middle Aged · Pain Management · Pelvic Floor · Prospective Studies · Syndrome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, with a selection condition that governs the answer. In Chiarioni 2010 (PMID: 20044997), 157 patients with levator ani syndrome and weekly pain were randomised to 9 sessions of biofeedback, electrogalvanic stimulation or massage (all with psychological counselling). Among patients 'highly likely' to have the syndrome — those with tenderness on traction on the levator muscles — adequate relief was reported by 87% with biofeedback, 45% with electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% with massage; pain days per month fell from 14.7 at baseline to 3.3 after biofeedback (8.9 and 13.3 for the other treatments), pain intensity fell from 6.8 to 1.8 on a 0–10 scale, and improvements were maintained for 12 months. Patients with only a 'possible' diagnosis (no tenderness) did not benefit from any treatment — so the shelf's answer is yes for examination-confirmed levator ani syndrome, and the trial gives no reason to expect benefit without that sign. The group's systematic review (PMID: 22110274) and a 2020 update (PMID: 32519087) both record biofeedback as the only treatment for this syndrome proven effective in a randomised setting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, in patients with levator tenderness on examination.

cards.headline: Chiarioni 2010: randomised trial of 157 patients — among those with levator tenderness ('highly likely' levator ani syndrome), adequate relief in 87% with biofeedback versus 45% with electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% with massage; no treatment helped patients without tenderness
cards.summary: Chiarioni 2010: randomised trial of 157 patients — among those with levator tenderness ('highly likely' levator ani syndrome), adequate relief in 87% with biofeedback versus 45% with electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% with massage; no treatment helped patients without tenderness
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trial of 157 patients meeting Rome II symptom criteria for levator ani syndrome plus weekly pain. Patients were categorised as 'highly likely' to have levator ani syndrome if they reported tenderness with traction on the levator muscles, or 'possible' levator ani syndrome if they did not. All patients received 9 sessions including psychological counselling plus one of three treatments: biofeedback to teach pelvic floor relaxation, electrogalvanic stimulation (EGS), or massage of the levator muscles. Outcomes were reassessed at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: Among patients with 'highly likely' levator ani syndrome, adequate relief was reported by 87% for biofeedback, 45% for EGS and 22% for massage. Pain days per month decreased from 14.7 at baseline to 3.3 after biofeedback, 8.9 after EGS and 13.3 after massage. Pain intensity decreased from 6.8 (0–10 scale) at baseline to 1.8 after biofeedback, 4.7 after EGS and 6.0 after massage. Improvements were maintained for 12 months. Patients with only a 'possible' diagnosis did not benefit from any treatment (the treatments made no difference in that subgroup, as printed in the record). Biofeedback and EGS improved the syndrome by increasing the ability to relax pelvic floor muscles and evacuate a water-filled balloon and by reducing urge and pain thresholds. The authors conclude biofeedback is the most effective of these treatments and EGS is somewhat effective, and that only patients with tenderness on rectal examination benefit.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one research group, no sham-biofeedback arm, and a subjective 'adequate relief' outcome: the effect size is large and durable to 12 months, but it has never been independently replicated in the carded record — and the benefit is explicitly confined to the subgroup with levator tenderness on examination.

cards.headline: Chiarioni 2011: systematic review of chronic proctalgia — success rates of 85% for biofeedback when patients are selected by tenderness on traction on the levator ani muscle
cards.summary: Chiarioni 2011: systematic review of chronic proctalgia — success rates of 85% for biofeedback when patients are selected by tenderness on traction on the levator ani muscle
cards.people: Systematic review addressing the pathophysiology, diagnostic evaluation and treatment of chronic proctalgia, coccygodynia, pudendal neuralgia and chronic pelvic pain syndromes. The review notes chronic or recurrent pain in the anal canal, rectum or other pelvic organs occurs in 7% to 24% of the population and is associated with impaired quality of life and high health care costs. The number of included studies and total participants is not documented in the record.
cards.result: The review reports that the large randomised controlled trial by the authors' group comparing biofeedback, electrogalvanic stimulation and massage for chronic proctalgia showed success rates of 85% for biofeedback when patients are selected based on physical examination evidence of tenderness in response to traction on the levator ani muscle (the trial's own report, carded on this shelf, prints 87% for the same 'highly likely' subgroup; each card carries its own record's figure). The review proposes that excessive tension (spasm) in the striated muscles of the pelvic floor is common to most pelvic pain syndromes, suggesting similar diagnostic and treatment approaches may improve outcomes in other pelvic pain disorders. No pooled effect size is reported in the record, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: This review is by the trial's own investigators and its biofeedback figure is the same single trial restated — it adds interpretation (the pelvic-floor tension hypothesis), not independent evidence, and must not be counted as a second confirmation.
cards.source: Chiarioni G et al. Chronic proctalgia and chronic pelvic pain syndromes: new etiologic insights and treatment options. World journal of gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 22110274. cards.headline: Carrington 2020: update review — biofeedback has proven effectiveness in a randomised setting only for levator ani syndrome, with over 90% short-term effectiveness reported for improving defecation effort in chronic proctalgia
cards.summary: Carrington 2020: update review — biofeedback has proven effectiveness in a randomised setting only for levator ani syndrome, with over 90% short-term effectiveness reported for improving defecation effort in chronic proctalgia
cards.people: Narrative update review for practising gastroenterologists and coloproctologists on the diagnosis and management of functional anorectal pain syndromes under the Rome IV criteria: chronic proctalgia (levator ani syndrome and unspecified functional anorectal pain) and acute proctalgia (proctalgia fugax), distinguished by symptom duration and digital rectal examination findings. The number of included studies and total participants is not documented in the record.
cards.result: The review states that chronic proctalgia is thought to be secondary to paradoxical pelvic floor contraction in many patients, and that biofeedback to improve the defecation effort has proven effective for over 90% in the short term (figure as printed in the record). It states that a number of therapies to relax the pelvic floor may be employed in functional anorectal pain syndromes, but only biofeedback to improve defaecatory dynamics in patients with levator ani syndrome has proven effectiveness in a randomised setting. Management of proctalgia fugax remains challenging, with treatment outcomes modest at best. No pooled effect size is reported in the record, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: A narrative update, not a systematic review with pooled numbers: its 'over 90%' short-term figure is the field's summary of the same small literature anchored by the one carded trial, so it corroborates the trial's standing in practice without independently verifying it.
cards.source: Carrington EV et al. Proctalgia Syndromes: Update in Diagnosis and Management. Current gastroenterology reports. 2020. PMID: 32519087. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for levator ani syndrome confirmed by tenderness on rectal examination, biofeedback gave adequate relief to 87% of patients in the only randomised trial — clearly ahead of electrogalvanic stimulation (45%) and massage (22%), with gains maintained at 12 months
cards.summary: Synthesis: for levator ani syndrome confirmed by tenderness on rectal examination, biofeedback gave adequate relief to 87% of patients in the only randomised trial — clearly ahead of electrogalvanic stimulation (45%) and massage (22%), with gains maintained at 12 months
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective randomised trial (157 patients) and two reviews by or centred on the same research programme (included-study Ns not documented in the records). Total carded participants with a documented N are 157, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the governing limitations — a single unreplicated trial and a tenderness-selected subgroup — are printed here and in the stamp.
cards.result: In Chiarioni 2010, adequate relief among 'highly likely' levator ani syndrome patients was 87% with biofeedback versus 45% with electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% with massage; pain days fell from 14.7 to 3.3 per month and pain intensity from 6.8 to 1.8 (0–10) with biofeedback, maintained for 12 months, while patients with only a 'possible' diagnosis benefited from no treatment. Both carded reviews record biofeedback as the only treatment for this syndrome with randomised evidence of effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, in patients with levator tenderness on examination.
cards.watchOut: Trying biofeedback is low-risk, but the honest expectation-setting from this record is narrow: benefit was shown in weekly-pain patients with levator tenderness treated in a specialist programme of 9 sessions with counselling — not in undifferentiated chronic anal pain.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chiarioni G et al. Gastroenterology. 2010 (PMID: 20044997); Chiarioni G et al. World journal of gastroenterology. 2011 (PMID: 22110274); Carrington EV et al. Current gastroenterology reports. 2020 (PMID: 32519087).

shelves.title: Twice-daily PPI in childhood eosinophilic esophagitis (observational only): histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — 68.6% responded to 8 weeks of twice-daily esomeprazole, 50.5% in the pooled literature, and a third do not respond
shelves.question: Does twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy heal eosinophilic esophagitis in children?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Deglutition Disorders · Drug Administration Schedule · Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Esomeprazole · Esophagoscopy · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Prevalence · Prospective Studies · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no placebo-controlled trial of proton pump inhibitors in children with eosinophilic esophagitis in the carded evidence. What exists is consistent prospective cohort evidence that twice-daily high-dose esomeprazole (1 mg/kg per dose) produces a histological response in about two-thirds of children with esophageal eosinophilia: 68.6% responded in Gutiérrez-Junquera 2016 (47% complete, 21.6% partial), and among children who remitted on that 8-week twice-daily trial, 70.1% remained in histological remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year (Gutiérrez-Junquera 2018). The pooled literature (Lucendo 2016; 619 patients, 188 of them children) puts histologic remission on PPIs at 50.5% overall, with twice-daily dosing non-significantly ahead of once-daily (55.9% vs 49.7%) and no significant difference between children and adults — so 'heals' is true for roughly one-half to two-thirds of children, not all, and the twice-daily advantage over once-daily dosing is itself unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: twice-daily PPI induces histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts; a substantial minority do not respond, and no randomised trial in children establishes the effect against placebo.

cards.headline: Gutiérrez-Junquera 2016: twice-daily esomeprazole (1 mg/kg per dose for 8 weeks) produced a histological response in 68.6% of 51 children — 47% complete and 21.6% partial (small cohort N on the face)
cards.summary: Gutiérrez-Junquera 2016: twice-daily esomeprazole (1 mg/kg per dose for 8 weeks) produced a histological response in 68.6% of 51 children — 47% complete and 21.6% partial (small cohort N on the face)
cards.people: 51 children (74.5% boys) with esophageal symptoms and esophageal eosinophil counts of 15 or more per high-power field, prospectively enrolled and treated with esomeprazole 1 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 8 weeks, with repeat endoscopy. Complete response was 5 or fewer eosinophils/high-power field; partial response was over 5 and under 15. N = 51.
cards.result: A histological response was observed in 35 children (68.6%): 24 children (47%) had a complete response and 11 (21.6%) a partial response; only 16 children (31.4%) were diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis under the study's framework. There were no differences in atopy history, allergy tests, pH study results or endoscopic scores between responders and non-responders; food impaction was more frequent in the children diagnosed with EoE (56.2% vs 20%, P = 0.01) and their mean pretreatment peak eosinophil count was higher (74.8 vs 46.3, P = 0.007). Of 14 patients on a lower maintenance dose, 11 (78.6%) remained in clinicopathologic remission at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: No control group: some of the 68.6% response could reflect natural fluctuation, regression to the mean, or co-interventions, and the cohort was enrolled for esophageal eosinophilia — under the terminology of the time, responders were classified separately from 'EoE', so the response figure spans the broader eosinophilia population.
cards.source: Gutiérrez-Junquera C et al. High Prevalence of Response to Proton-pump Inhibitor Treatment in Children With Esophageal Eosinophilia. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2016. PMID: 26513622. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gutiérrez-Junquera 2018: of 57 children who remitted on the 8-week twice-daily trial, 70.1% stayed in histological remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year, and 86% remained asymptomatic
cards.summary: Gutiérrez-Junquera 2018: of 57 children who remitted on the 8-week twice-daily trial, 70.1% stayed in histological remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year, and 86% remained asymptomatic
cards.people: 57 children with eosinophilic esophagitis and histological remission after an 8-week twice-daily esomeprazole trial (1 mg/kg per dose), maintained on esomeprazole 1 mg/kg/day for 1 year with symptom and adverse-event monitoring and a follow-up endoscopy at 12 months; no concomitant dietary restrictions or topical steroids. Complete remission was 5 or fewer eosinophils/high-power field; partial was over 5 and under 15. N = 57.
cards.result: Histological remission on maintenance therapy was present in 40 children (70.1%, 95% CI 56.5 to 81.5). The long-term remission rate was higher in children with initial complete remission than in those with partial remission (81% vs 50%, P = 0.014). 49 children (86%) remained asymptomatic. Of 12 children receiving esomeprazole 0.5 mg/kg/day for 12 additional months, 11 (91.6%) remained in remission. Mild, transient side effects not requiring PPI avoidance were observed in 5 children.
cards.watchOut: This cohort is selected for children who had already remitted on twice-daily PPI — the 70.1% is a maintenance figure among responders, not a response rate for all children starting treatment, and the cohort comes from the same programme as the 2016 study, so the two Ns overlap and must not be added.
cards.source: Gutiérrez-Junquera C et al. Long-term Treatment With Proton Pump Inhibitors Is Effective in Children With Eosinophilic Esophagitis. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2018. PMID: 29509636. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lucendo 2016: across 33 studies (619 patients, 188 children), PPIs gave histologic remission in 50.5% — twice-daily 55.9% vs once-daily 49.7%, a non-significant difference, with no child–adult difference
cards.summary: Lucendo 2016: across 33 studies (619 patients, 188 children), PPIs gave histologic remission in 50.5% — twice-daily 55.9% vs once-daily 49.7%, a non-significant difference, with no child–adult difference
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 studies (11 prospective) comprising 619 patients with symptomatic esophageal eosinophilia (188 children and 431 adults) treated with proton pump inhibitors. Primary outcomes were clinical response and histologic remission (under 15 eosinophils/high-power field).
cards.result: PPI therapy led to a clinical response in 60.8% (95% CI 48.38% to 72.2%) and histologic remission in 50.5% (95% CI 42.2% to 58.7%) of patients. No differences were observed by study population (children vs adults), publication type or quality. PPIs were non-significantly more effective administered twice daily than once daily (55.9% vs 49.7% histologic remission) and in prospective studies (52.6% vs 39.1%), and with pathologic pH monitoring (65.4% vs 49.3%). The authors note poor-quality evidence, heterogeneity (I² 67.5% for remission) and a significant publication bias in favour of studies reporting histologic responses.
cards.watchOut: Mostly observational studies with publication bias favouring positive results, so 50.5% is likely an optimistic pooled figure; the twice-daily versus once-daily comparison is between studies, not within a randomised comparison, and was not significant.
cards.source: Lucendo AJ et al. Efficacy of Proton Pump Inhibitor Drugs for Inducing Clinical and Histologic Remission in Patients With Symptomatic Esophageal Eosinophilia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2016. PMID: 26247167. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: twice-daily PPI heals the esophagus in roughly one-half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — but every carded study is observational, and about a third of children do not respond
cards.summary: Synthesis: twice-daily PPI heals the esophagus in roughly one-half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — but every carded study is observational, and about a third of children do not respond
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective cohorts from one Spanish programme (51 children at induction; 57 remitters followed on maintenance — overlapping populations, not additive) and one meta-analysis of 33 studies (619 patients, 188 children). No randomised or placebo-controlled trial in children is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: Twice-daily esomeprazole 1 mg/kg per dose for 8 weeks produced a histological response in 68.6% of children (47% complete); 70.1% of remitters stayed in remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year. Pooled across all PPI studies, histologic remission was 50.5%, with twice-daily dosing at 55.9% versus 49.7% once daily (not significant) and no significant child–adult difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: twice-daily PPI induces histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts; a substantial minority do not respond, and no randomised trial in children establishes the effect against placebo.
cards.watchOut: Response is not cure: remission was defined histologically (under 15, or 5 or fewer, eosinophils/high-power field depending on the study), maintenance data come only from initial responders, and children who fail PPI need the other EoE therapies — none of which this shelf evaluates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gutiérrez-Junquera C et al. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2016 (PMID: 26513622); Gutiérrez-Junquera C et al. cards.search: synthesis: twice-daily ppi heals the esophagus in roughly one-half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — but every carded study is observational, and about a third of children do not respond synthesis: twice-daily ppi heals the esophagus in roughly one-half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — but every carded study is observational, and about a third of children do not respond does twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy heal eosinophilic esophagitis in children? synthesis the carded evidence: two prospective cohorts from one spanish programme (51 children at induction; 57 remitters followed on maintenance — overlapping populations, not additive) and one meta-analysis of 33 studies (619 patients, 188 children). no randomised or placebo-controlled trial in children is carded, because none was found in the records fetched. twice-daily esomeprazole 1 mg/kg per dose for 8 weeks produced a histological response in 68.6% of children (47% complete); 70.1% of remitters stayed in remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year. pooled across all ppi studies, histologic remission was 50.5%, with twice-daily dosing at 55.9% versus 49.7% once daily (not significant) and no significant child–adult difference. proposed possible (benefit) — observational only: twice-daily ppi induces histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts; a substantial minority do not respond, and no randomised trial in children establishes the effect against placebo. response is not cure: remission was defined histologically (under 15, or 5 or fewer, eosinophils/high-power field depending on the study), maintenance data come only from initial responders, and children who fail ppi need the other eoe therapies — none of which this shelf evaluates. synthesis of gutiérrez-junquera c et al. journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2016 (pmid: 26513622); gutiérrez-junquera c et al. journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2018 (pmid: 29509636); lucendo aj et al. clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the american gastroenterological association. 2016 (pmid: 26247167).

shelves.title: Pioglitazone in MASH (formerly NASH) — steatohepatitis activity and resolution on biopsy: consistent benefit in every placebo-controlled trial and synthesis (fibrosis and stiffness are asked separately on shelf #5865)
shelves.question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH — formerly nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, NASH), does pioglitazone improve steatohepatitis activity on biopsy — histologic improvement and resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis — versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adipokines/blood · Adult · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Fatty Liver/drug therapy,metabolism,pathology · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Insulin/blood · Liver/pathology · Liver Cirrhosis/drug therapy,metabolism,pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Dropouts · Pioglitazone · Placebos · Thiazolidinediones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This shelf asks the ACTIVITY question only: does pioglitazone improve steatohepatitis activity on biopsy — histologic improvement and resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis? The FIBROSIS and liver-stiffness questions are asked separately on the companion shelf #5865, which is where the record divides; nothing on this shelf claims a fibrosis benefit. Scope: live shelf #2114 holds pioglitazone in steatohepatitis with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes (Belfort 2006; Cusi 2016, primary outcome met in 58%, absolute difference 41 percentage points); this shelf holds the general steatohepatitis evidence anchored on the non-diabetic trial populations. THE ACTIVITY EVIDENCE — consistent benefit in every placebo-controlled trial: Aithal 2008 (74 non-diabetic patients, pioglitazone 30 mg/day, 12 months) improved hepatocellular injury (P = .005) and Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004) versus placebo. Huang 2021 (90 Asian patients, 24 weeks) achieved steatohepatitis improvement without worsening fibrosis in 46.7% versus 11.1% (absolute difference 35.6 percentage points; P = 0.002), with the activity score falling 4.27 to 2.53 on pioglitazone and not changing on placebo. PIVENS (247 non-diabetic adults; primary record carded on shelf #26 and cross-pointed here) missed its primary composite at its prespecified threshold — 34% versus 19% (P = 0.04 against a required P < 0.025) — but its activity endpoints were strongly positive: steatosis (P < 0.001), lobular inflammation (P = 0.004) and resolution of steatohepatitis in 47% versus 21%. The pilots agree (Promrat 2004: histological improvement in two-thirds; Sanyal 2004: combination-therapy histology gains over vitamin E alone). THE SYNTHESES AGREE: Musso 2017 resolution OR 3.22 (a relative odds measure); Boettcher 2012 activity endpoints all positive (ballooning OR 2.11, lobular inflammation OR 2.58, steatosis OR 3.39, combined necroinflammation OR 6.52 — all relative odds measures); Wang 2023: histologic response does not differ by diabetes status; Shi 2025: pioglitazone ranks first among common medications for resolving steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis (SUCRA 91.4%). THE ONE DISCORDANT NOTE is PIVENS' primary composite missing its strict prespecified alpha — a threshold miss on a composite, in the same trial whose individual activity endpoints were all strongly positive. THE COST is uniform: weight gain wherever it is measured (+2.77 kg versus −0.55 kg in Aithal 2008; +4.7 kg in PIVENS; +2.70% of body weight in Musso 2017), with oedema alongside. No carded study measures clinical liver outcomes. For fibrosis stage and liver stiffness (kPa), see the companion shelf #5865.

cards.headline: Huang 2021: in 90 Asian patients with steatohepatitis, 24 weeks of pioglitazone cut the activity score (NAS 4.27 → 2.53) while placebo did not change, and steatohepatitis improvement without worsening fibrosis was achieved by 46.7% versus 11.1%
cards.summary: Huang 2021: in 90 Asian patients with steatohepatitis, 24 weeks of pioglitazone cut the activity score (NAS 4.27 → 2.53) while placebo did not change, and steatohepatitis improvement without worsening fibrosis was achieved by 46.7% versus 11.1%
cards.people: 90 patients (66 men; mean age 44.1 years) with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in Taiwan randomised double-blind to pioglitazone 30 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks; 66 patients (30 pioglitazone, 36 placebo) completed paired liver biopsies and form the histology analysis; liver fat was also measured by magnetic resonance imaging proton-density fat fraction.
cards.result: Alanine aminotransferase fell significantly on pioglitazone (86.9 ± 34.3 to 45.7 ± 35.8 IU/L; P = 0.003). The NAFLD activity score fell from 4.27 ± 1.14 to 2.53 ± 1.63 on pioglitazone (P < 0.0001) and did not change on placebo (3.94 ± 1.41 to 3.94 ± 1.51; P = 1.0). Steatohepatitis improvement without worsening of fibrosis was achieved in 46.7% (14/30) on pioglitazone versus 11.1% (4/36) on placebo — an absolute difference of 35.6 percentage points (P = 0.002). Liver fat content fell on magnetic resonance imaging proton-density fat fraction (20.2 ± 9.0% to 14.3 ± 6.9%; P < 0.0001). No significant difference in adverse events occurred between groups. The authors conclude that 24 weeks of pioglitazone treatment was well tolerated and effective in improving liver histology and reducing liver steatosis in Asian patients with steatohepatitis.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is steatohepatitis improvement WITHOUT WORSENING fibrosis — this trial does not show fibrosis itself improving; that question lives on the companion shelf #5865. Treatment lasted only 24 weeks, 24 of 90 randomised patients have no paired biopsy, and the record does not break the population down by diabetes status.

cards.headline: Aithal 2008: in 74 non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis, 12 months of pioglitazone improved hepatocellular injury (P = .005) and Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004) versus placebo — and added 2.77 kg of weight
cards.summary: Aithal 2008: in 74 non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis, 12 months of pioglitazone improved hepatocellular injury (P = .005) and Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004) versus placebo — and added 2.77 kg of weight
cards.people: 74 non-diabetic patients (45 men; median age 54 years) with histologically proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis randomised to standard diet and exercise plus pioglitazone 30 mg/day or placebo for 12 months; 61 patients (30 placebo, 31 pioglitazone) had liver biopsies at both the beginning and the end of the study.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, pioglitazone was associated with weight gain (mean change +2.77 kg vs −0.55 kg; P = .04) and reductions in glucose (+0.4 vs −0.1 mmol/L [+7.2 vs −1.8 mg/dL]; P = .02, as printed with the pioglitazone arm second in the record's ordering), HbA1c, insulin C-peptide, alanine aminotransferase (−10.9 vs −36.2 U/L, placebo versus pioglitazone; P = .009), gamma-glutamyltransferase and ferritin. Histologic features including hepatocellular injury (P = .005), Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004), and fibrosis (P = .05) were reduced in pioglitazone-treated patients compared with placebo. The authors conclude pioglitazone improved metabolic and histologic parameters, most notably liver injury and fibrosis, and that larger extended trials are justified.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the trial's activity endpoints (injury, Mallory-Denk bodies); its fibrosis result (P = .05, borderline) is carded on the companion shelf #5865, where the fibrosis question is asked. Only 61 of 74 randomised patients had paired biopsies, and the population is non-diabetic steatohepatitis — the trial does not cover simple steatosis without hepatitis.
cards.source: Aithal GP et al. Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of pioglitazone in nondiabetic subjects with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18718471. cards.headline: Sanyal 2004 (N = 20): adding pioglitazone to vitamin E improved steatosis, ballooning and Mallory's hyaline from baseline — but beat vitamin E alone only on steatosis, and 1 of 10 exposed patients stopped for hepatotoxicity
cards.summary: Sanyal 2004 (N = 20): adding pioglitazone to vitamin E improved steatosis, ballooning and Mallory's hyaline from baseline — but beat vitamin E alone only on steatosis, and 1 of 10 exposed patients stopped for hepatotoxicity
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial, vitamin E comparator, no placebo arm (Sanyal 2004) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 20 nondiabetic, noncirrhotic patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis randomised to vitamin E 400 IU/day alone or vitamin E 400 IU/day plus pioglitazone 30 mg/day for 6 months, with paired liver biopsies and euglycaemic-clamp metabolic testing; 10 patients per arm — N printed on the face.
cards.result: Vitamin E alone significantly decreased steatosis (mean grade 2.2 to 1.4; P < .02). Compared with baseline, combination therapy significantly decreased steatosis (mean 2.3 to 1; P < .002), cytologic ballooning (1.3 to 0.2; P < .01), Mallory's hyaline (0.7 to 0.2; P < .04) and pericellular fibrosis (1.2 to 0.6; P < .03), and increased metabolic clearance of glucose while decreasing fasting free fatty acid and insulin levels; the decreases in fasting free fatty acids and insulin independently predicted improvement in steatosis and ballooning. Two patients on combination therapy discontinued — one because of pregnancy, the other because of hepatotoxicity. The authors conclude that a combination of vitamin E and pioglitazone produces a greater improvement in steatohepatitis histology than vitamin E alone.
cards.watchOut: A 20-patient pilot with no placebo arm: head-to-head, the combination beat vitamin E alone only on steatosis — the ballooning and Mallory's hyaline gains are within-group (before–after) changes, which steatohepatitis histology can show spontaneously; and the hepatotoxicity withdrawal (alanine aminotransferase above 400 IU/L in the published discussion) is an early liver-safety flag in 1 of 10 exposed patients.
cards.source: Sanyal AJ et al. A pilot study of vitamin E versus vitamin E and pioglitazone for the treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2004. cards.headline: Promrat 2004 (N = 18): 48 weeks of open-label pioglitazone normalised ALT in 72% and improved histology in two-thirds of non-diabetic steatohepatitis patients — with 4% average weight gain
cards.summary: Promrat 2004 (N = 18): 48 weeks of open-label pioglitazone normalised ALT in 72% and improved histology in two-thirds of non-diabetic steatohepatitis patients — with 4% average weight gain
cards.type: Open-label pilot study, no placebo arm (Promrat 2004) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 18 non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis treated prospectively with pioglitazone 30 mg daily for 48 weeks, with insulin-sensitivity testing, body composition, and liver biopsies before and at the end of treatment. N = 18, printed on the face; there was no placebo or control group.
cards.result: By 48 weeks, serum alanine aminotransferase had fallen to normal in 72% of patients; hepatic fat content and size by magnetic resonance imaging decreased, and insulin sensitivity improved uniformly. Histological features of steatosis, cellular injury, parenchymal inflammation, Mallory bodies, and fibrosis were significantly improved from baseline (all P < 0.05), and using strict criteria histological improvement occurred in two-thirds of patients. Pioglitazone was well tolerated; the main side effects were weight gain (averaging 4%) and increased total body adiposity.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled 18-patient pilot: before-after histology in steatohepatitis improves spontaneously in a substantial minority, so this card can only corroborate the randomised cards above — it is the historical first signal, and its N is printed on the face.
cards.source: Promrat K et al. A pilot study of pioglitazone treatment for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2004. PMID: 14752837. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Boettcher 2012: across 4 placebo-controlled trials, thiazolidinediones improved ballooning (OR 2.11), lobular inflammation (OR 2.58), steatosis (OR 3.39) and combined necroinflammation (OR 6.52) — every activity endpoint positive
cards.summary: Boettcher 2012: across 4 placebo-controlled trials, thiazolidinediones improved ballooning (OR 2.11), lobular inflammation (OR 2.58), steatosis (OR 3.39) and combined necroinflammation (OR 6.52) — every activity endpoint positive
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 4 randomised, placebo-controlled trials of thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone and rosiglitazone) in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis identified to September 2010: 169 patients on a thiazolidinedione versus 165 on placebo for the class analyses; the pioglitazone-only analysis covers 137 versus 134 patients.
cards.result: Thiazolidinediones were significantly better than placebo in improving ballooning degeneration (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.33 to 3.36), lobular inflammation (OR 2.58, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.97) and steatosis (OR 3.39, 95% CI 2.19 to 5.25), and combined necroinflammation (OR 6.52, 95% CI 3.03 to 14.06) — all relative (odds) measures — but improvement in fibrosis was not significant for the class as a whole. When pioglitazone was analysed alone, the improvement in fibrosis with pioglitazone versus placebo was statistically significant (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77). Total body fat increased markedly and highly significantly with thiazolidinedione treatment. The authors conclude thiazolidinediones significantly improve ballooning, lobular inflammation, steatosis and necroinflammation, that pioglitazone may improve fibrosis, and that larger trials are needed on the fibrosis question.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the synthesis's activity endpoints; its fibrosis findings (class pool not significant, pioglitazone-only OR 1.68) are carded on the companion shelf #5865. The class pool mixes in rosiglitazone trials, and the search closed in September 2010, so this synthesis predates Cusi 2016 and Huang 2021 — Musso 2017 and the network meta-analyses carded below carry the later pooling.
cards.source: Boettcher E et al. Meta-analysis: pioglitazone improves liver histology and fibrosis in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2012. cards.headline: Musso 2017: pooled thiazolidinedione trials (516 patients) — NASH resolution OR 3.22, with all effects accounted for by pioglitazone, including in patients without diabetes
cards.summary: Musso 2017: pooled thiazolidinedione trials (516 patients) — NASH resolution OR 3.22, with all effects accounted for by pioglitazone, including in patients without diabetes
cards.people: 516 patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in 8 randomised controlled trials of thiazolidinedione therapy (5 evaluating pioglitazone, 3 rosiglitazone) lasting 6 to 24 months; the primary outcome was improvement in advanced fibrosis (stage F3–F4 to F0–F2) on liver biopsy.
cards.result: Thiazolidinedione therapy was associated with improved advanced fibrosis (OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.25 to 7.93; P = .01), improvement in fibrosis of any stage (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.47; P = .01), and NASH resolution (OR 3.22, 95% CI 2.17 to 4.79; P < .001). Analyses restricted to trials enrolling patients without diabetes gave similar results (advanced fibrosis OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.04 to 10.90). All effects were accounted for by pioglitazone use. Weight gain and lower-limb oedema occurred more frequently with thiazolidinedione therapy (initial body weight +2.70%, 95% CI 1.96% to 4.34%).
cards.watchOut: This card carries the resolution endpoint (OR 3.22, a relative odds measure); the same analysis's fibrosis endpoints (advanced OR 3.15, any-stage OR 1.66) are carded on the companion shelf #5865. The pooled trials are small (516 patients across 8 trials), three of the eight tested rosiglitazone, and histology is a surrogate — whether it translates into improved clinical outcomes requires further study.
cards.source: Musso G et al. Thiazolidinediones and Advanced Liver Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis: A Meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28241279. cards.headline: Wang 2023: across 7 pioglitazone trials (614 patients), histologic benefit did not differ between NAFLD patients with and without type 2 diabetes — the general-population bridge for this shelf
cards.summary: Wang 2023: across 7 pioglitazone trials (614 patients), histologic benefit did not differ between NAFLD patients with and without type 2 diabetes — the general-population bridge for this shelf
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials by diabetes status (Wang 2023)
cards.people: 614 patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in seven randomised, placebo-controlled trials of pioglitazone, three of them in non-diabetic patients, analysed to compare pioglitazone's effects in patients with versus without type 2 diabetes/prediabetes on histology (fibrosis, ballooning, inflammation, steatosis), liver enzymes, lipids, glucose measures, weight, and adverse events.
cards.result: No difference was found between patients with and without type 2 diabetes in histology, liver enzymes, blood lipids, HOMA-IR, weight, body mass index, or fasting blood glucose responses to pioglitazone. The authors conclude pioglitazone exerts a certain effect on alleviating NAFLD — improving histopathology, liver enzymes and HOMA-IR and reducing blood lipids — consistently in non-diabetic and diabetic patients, with oedema more frequent on pioglitazone in the diabetes subgroup, while noting that large, well-designed trials are required to confirm these conclusions.
cards.watchOut: 'No difference between subgroups' in a 614-patient indirect comparison is weak proof of equal benefit — the confidence intervals are wide, and the analysis pools the same small trials as the other cards on this shelf.
cards.source: Wang Z et al. Response to pioglitazone in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease patients with vs. without type 2 diabetes: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Frontiers in Endocrinology. 2023. PMID: 37065735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shi 2025 (network meta-analysis, 37 trials, 7,673 patients): pioglitazone ranked the most effective common medication for resolving steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis (SUCRA 91.4%)
cards.summary: Shi 2025 (network meta-analysis, 37 trials, 7,673 patients): pioglitazone ranked the most effective common medication for resolving steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis (SUCRA 91.4%)
cards.type: Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Shi 2025)
cards.people: 37 randomised trials involving 7,673 adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease comparing common western medications with placebo or each other, analysed as a Bayesian network meta-analysis (registered PROSPERO CRD42024509176); outcomes included resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis and a reduction of at least 2 points in the NAFLD activity score.
cards.result: Pioglitazone demonstrated the most significant effects in resolving nonalcoholic steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis, increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, and achieving a ≥2-point reduction in NAFLD activity scores, with a SUCRA probability of 91.4%. Cluster analysis revealed that resmetirom and aldafermin were superior options for enhancing liver function markers, while pioglitazone emerged as the best treatment for the comprehensive improvement of fatty liver disease. The authors conclude that pioglitazone outperformed other western medicines in terms of overall efficacy when treating fatty liver disease.
cards.watchOut: SUCRA 91.4% is a probability of ranking first among the compared drugs, not a measure of how large pioglitazone's advantage is; the network's pioglitazone evidence still rests on the same handful of biopsy trials carded individually on this shelf, most of them small and none powered for clinical liver outcomes.
cards.source: Shi R et al. Clinical Assessment of Common Medications for Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis. Journal of Evidence-Based Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39963857. Registry ID: none in the record (PROSPERO CRD42024509176). cards.headline: Synthesis: pioglitazone improves steatohepatitis activity and resolution in every placebo-controlled trial and every pooled analysis — the activity answer is yes; fibrosis is a separate question, asked on the companion shelf #5865
cards.summary: Synthesis: pioglitazone improves steatohepatitis activity and resolution in every placebo-controlled trial and every pooled analysis — the activity answer is yes; fibrosis is a separate question, asked on the companion shelf #5865
cards.people: Carded on this shelf: two placebo-controlled trials with positive activity endpoints (Aithal 2008, N = 74; Huang 2021, N = 90), two pilots (Sanyal 2004, N = 20; Promrat 2004, N = 18), and four syntheses (Boettcher 2012; Musso 2017; Wang 2023; Shi 2025). Cross-pointed, not re-carded: PIVENS (N = 247, primary record on shelf #26) and the prediabetes/type 2 diabetes trials Belfort 2006 and Cusi 2016 (shelf #2114).
cards.result: ACTIVITY AND RESOLUTION — consistent benefit: Aithal 2008 hepatocellular injury P = .005, Mallory-Denk bodies P = .004; Huang 2021 steatohepatitis improvement without worsening fibrosis 46.7% vs 11.1% (absolute difference 35.6 percentage points; P = 0.002), activity score 4.27 → 2.53 with no change on placebo; PIVENS (cross-pointed) steatosis P < 0.001, lobular inflammation P = 0.004, steatohepatitis resolution 47% vs 21% — though PIVENS' primary composite missed its prespecified threshold (34% vs 19%; P = 0.04 against a required P < 0.025); Musso 2017 resolution OR 3.22 (relative odds); Boettcher 2012 activity ORs 2.11–6.52 (relative odds); Shi 2025 ranks pioglitazone first for resolution without worsening fibrosis (SUCRA 91.4%); Wang 2023 finds the histologic response does not differ by diabetes status. COST: weight gain in every long trial (+2.77 kg Aithal; +4.7 kg PIVENS; +2.70% of body weight Musso), with oedema alongside. NOT ANSWERED HERE: fibrosis stage and liver stiffness — the companion shelf #5865 asks that question, and there the record divides.
cards.watchOut: The carded trials enrolled biopsy-proven steatohepatitis (MASH), so this shelf answers the steatohepatitis-activity question, not simple steatosis; histology is a surrogate — no trial here is powered for cirrhosis, liver failure or death; and the largest trial's primary composite missed its prespecified significance threshold even though its individual activity endpoints were strongly positive.

shelves.title: Ursodiol prevents gallstone formation after bariatric surgery (LIKELY): formation fell from 22–32% on placebo to 2–8% on treatment in two placebo-controlled trials — a partial completion of shelf #1668
shelves.question: In adults after bariatric surgery, does ursodiol prevent gallstone formation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Cholelithiasis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastric Bypass · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Ursodeoxycholic Acid · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1668, which covers ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) against symptomatic gallstone disease after bariatric surgery (the UPGRADE trial); this shelf homes the upstream outcome UPGRADE was not powered around — gallstone formation itself on imaging — and UPGRADE is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Two placebo-controlled trials measured formation directly and agree. Sugerman 1995 (gastric bypass; 233 patients with postoperative sonograms) found 6-month formation of 32% on placebo versus 2% on ursodiol 600 mg/day and 6% on 1,200 mg/day. Miller 2003 (gastric restrictive procedures; 152 randomised) found formation of 3% versus 22% at 12 months and 8% versus 30% at 24 months, favouring UDCA 500 mg/day, with fewer cholecystectomies (4.7% vs. 12%). The 2022 meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (Mulliri) pools the same direction: gallstone formation odds ratio 0.25 relative, with symptomatic disease and cholecystectomy also reduced. Absolute differences in the two trials are large (roughly 20–30 percentage points), so the relative measures are not carrying the claim alone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): six months of ursodiol after bariatric surgery prevents gallstone formation versus placebo, on two concordant placebo-controlled trials and a concordant 11-trial meta-analysis.

cards.headline: Sugerman 1995: after gastric bypass, gallstones formed by 6 months in 32% of patients on placebo versus 2% on ursodiol 600 mg/day (and 6% on 1,200 mg/day) — a 30-percentage-point absolute difference at the 600 mg dose
cards.summary: Sugerman 1995: after gastric bypass, gallstones formed by 6 months in 32% of patients on placebo versus 2% on ursodiol 600 mg/day (and 6% on 1,200 mg/day) — a 30-percentage-point absolute difference at the 600 mg dose
cards.people: Patients with body mass index over 40 kg/m2 undergoing gastric bypass, all with normal intraoperative gallbladder sonography, in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ursodiol 300, 600 or 1,200 mg/day begun within 10 days of surgery for 6 months or until gallstone development; 233 patients had at least one postoperative sonogram (placebo n = 56, 300 mg n = 53, 600 mg n = 61, 1,200 mg n = 63). Sonography was repeated at 2, 4 and 6 months.
cards.result: Gallstone formation at 6 months occurred in 32% (placebo), 13% (300 mg), 2% (600 mg) and 6% (1,200 mg) of patients. Gallstones were significantly less frequent with ursodiol 600 and 1,200 mg than with placebo (P < 0.001). Preoperative age, sex, race, weight, body mass index and postoperative weight loss did not differ significantly between groups. The authors conclude a daily dose of 600 mg ursodiol is effective prophylaxis for gallstone formation following gastric-bypass-induced rapid weight loss.
cards.watchOut: A 1995 gastric-bypass population losing weight rapidly by the standards of that era; formation was counted in the 233 patients with at least one postoperative sonogram rather than all randomised, and the 300 mg dose's 13% sits between placebo and the higher doses without a stated significance test in the record.
cards.source: Sugerman HJ et al. A multicenter, placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, prospective trial of prophylactic ursodiol for the prevention of gallstone formation following gastric-bypass-induced rapid weight loss. American Journal of Surgery. 1995. PMID: 7818005. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Miller 2003: after gastric restrictive procedures, gallstone formation was 3% on ursodeoxycholic acid versus 22% on placebo at 12 months, and 8% versus 30% at 24 months, with cholecystectomy in 4.7% versus 12%
cards.summary: Miller 2003: after gastric restrictive procedures, gallstone formation was 3% on ursodeoxycholic acid versus 22% on placebo at 12 months, and 8% versus 30% at 24 months, with cholecystectomy in 4.7% versus 12%
cards.people: Patients with morbid obesity undergoing vertical banded gastroplasty or adjustable gastric banding, in a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg/day versus placebo begun within 3 days of surgery for 6 months or until gallstone development; 152 patients were randomised (76 per group) after exclusions for prior gallstone surgery or preoperative gallstones. Imaging was by sonography or computed tomography before surgery and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: Gallstone formation was significantly less frequent with ursodeoxycholic acid than placebo at 12 months (3% versus 22%, P = 0.0018, Fisher exact test) and at 24 months (8% versus 30%, P = 0.0022), and cholecystectomy was performed in 4.7% versus 12% respectively (P < 0.02). Preoperative age, sex, weight, body mass index and postoperative weight loss did not differ significantly between groups. The authors conclude 500 mg daily for 6 months is effective prophylaxis for gallstone formation following gastric restrictive procedures.
cards.watchOut: The operations (vertical banded gastroplasty, adjustable banding) are no longer the dominant bariatric procedures, and formation kept rising in both groups between 12 and 24 months after the 6-month course ended — the trial shows prevention during and after a 6-month course in its era's surgery, not lifetime protection after modern sleeve gastrectomy.
cards.source: Miller K et al. Gallstone formation prophylaxis after gastric restrictive procedures for weight loss: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Annals of Surgery. 2003. randomised controlled trial (miller 2003) patients with morbid obesity undergoing vertical banded gastroplasty or adjustable gastric banding, in a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg/day versus placebo begun within 3 days of surgery for 6 months or until gallstone development; 152 patients were randomised (76 per group) after exclusions for prior gallstone surgery or preoperative gallstones. imaging was by sonography or computed tomography before surgery and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months. gallstone formation was significantly less frequent with ursodeoxycholic acid than placebo at 12 months (3% versus 22%, p = 0.0018, fisher exact test) and at 24 months (8% versus 30%, p = 0.0022), and cholecystectomy was performed in 4.7% versus 12% respectively (p < 0.02). preoperative age, sex, weight, body mass index and postoperative weight loss did not differ significantly between groups. the authors conclude 500 mg daily for 6 months is effective prophylaxis for gallstone formation following gastric restrictive procedures. the operations (vertical banded gastroplasty, adjustable banding) are no longer the dominant bariatric procedures, and formation kept rising in both groups between 12 and 24 months after the 6-month course ended — the trial shows prevention during and after a 6-month course in its era's surgery, not lifetime protection after modern sleeve gastrectomy. miller k et al. gallstone formation prophylaxis after gastric restrictive procedures for weight loss: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. annals of surgery. 2003. pmid: 14578732. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · cholagogues and choleretics · cholecystolithiasis · double-blind method · female · gallstones · gastroplasty · humans · male · middle aged · obesity, morbid · postoperative complications · prospective studies · ursodeoxycholic acid

cards.headline: Mulliri 2022: across 11 randomised trials, prophylactic ursodeoxycholic acid after bariatric surgery was associated with markedly lower odds of gallstone formation (odds ratio 0.25 relative), symptomatic disease (odds ratio 0.29) and cholecystectomy (odds ratio 0.33)
cards.summary: Mulliri 2022: across 11 randomised trials, prophylactic ursodeoxycholic acid after bariatric surgery was associated with markedly lower odds of gallstone formation (odds ratio 0.25 relative), symptomatic disease (odds ratio 0.29) and cholecystectomy (odds ratio 0.33)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mulliri 2022)
cards.people: 11 randomised controlled trials comparing ursodeoxycholic acid with controls for prevention of gallstone formation after bariatric surgery (published to February 2022), with 2,363 patients randomised to UDCA and 2,217 analysed, versus 1,415 randomised to control and 1,257 analysed. Results were similar in intention-to-treat analysis, in the sleeve gastrectomy subgroup, and in placebo-only comparisons.
cards.result: Prophylactic UDCA was significantly associated with decreased gallstone formation (odds ratio = 0.25, 95% confidence interval = 0.21–0.31), symptomatic gallstone disease (odds ratio = 0.29, 95% confidence interval = 0.20–0.42) and cholecystectomy rate (odds ratio = 0.33, 95% confidence interval = 0.20–0.55). All three are relative (odds) measures; the absolute formation rates from the two trials carded on this shelf (32% on placebo falling to 2–3% on treatment) show the absolute scale behind them. The authors conclude prophylactic UDCA after bariatric surgery prevents gallstone formation and symptomatic disease and reduces cholecystectomy.
cards.watchOut: The 11 pooled trials span different operations, doses and follow-up lengths, and the pool includes trials whose primary framing was symptomatic disease (the outcome homed on shelf #1668) — the formation-specific estimate is nonetheless reported separately, which is why this meta-analysis can be carded here without re-carding UPGRADE itself.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ursodiol prevents gallstone formation after bariatric surgery — placebo formation rates of 22–32% fell to 2–8% on treatment in two placebo-controlled trials, with a pooled odds ratio of 0.25 across 11 trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: ursodiol prevents gallstone formation after bariatric surgery — placebo formation rates of 22–32% fell to 2–8% on treatment in two placebo-controlled trials, with a pooled odds ratio of 0.25 across 11 trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (233 patients with postoperative imaging after gastric bypass; 152 randomised after gastric restrictive procedures) and one meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (2,217 versus 1,257 patients analysed). The symptomatic-disease outcome and the UPGRADE trial are homed on live shelf #1668 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Formation at 6 months: 32% on placebo versus 2% on ursodiol 600 mg/day (Sugerman 1995). Formation at 12 months: 22% on placebo versus 3% on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg/day, and 30% versus 8% at 24 months (Miller 2003). Pooled formation odds ratio 0.25 relative across 11 trials (Mulliri 2022). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate the sleeve-gastrectomy era and used 6-month courses; the meta-analysis's sleeve subgroup was concordant, but a clinician should not read this shelf as settling dose or duration for today's procedures — it settles that formation itself is preventable, the slice shelf #1668's symptomatic outcome left open.

shelves.title: G-POEM versus botulinum toxin injection in gastroparesis (POSSIBLE): success favoured G-POEM 65% vs. 40% in the only randomised head-to-head, without statistical significance, and diabetic patients were a minority subset — a partial completion of shelf #3525
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic gastroparesis, does gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy improve symptoms versus botulinum toxin injection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Botulinum Toxins · Gastric Emptying · Gastroparesis · Gastroscopy · Injections · Pyloromyotomy · Pylorus · Quality of Life · Radionuclide Imaging · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3525, which covers gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM) versus sham in diabetic gastroparesis; this shelf homes the head-to-head against botulinum toxin injection (BTI), and the sham trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The direct evidence is one small double-blind randomised trial (Gonzalez 2024; 40 patients with refractory gastroparesis) in which clinical success favoured G-POEM numerically at 3 months (65% vs. 40%) and 1 year (60% vs. 40%) but neither difference was statistically significant (P = 0.10 at 3 months). Two limits define this shelf and are printed on the cards: the trial was mixed-etiology — only 11 of its 40 patients had diabetic gastroparesis, with no diabetic-subgroup results in the record — and the supporting comparison (Tran 2023) sets one centre's G-POEM series (28 analysed patients, of whom 4 were diabetic) against BTI results from the published literature rather than a randomised comparator. A 2026 cost-effectiveness model built on the randomised data found BTI more cost-effective at 3 months and G-POEM at 12 months once repeat injections were counted — a durability argument, not new efficacy data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): G-POEM probably improves symptoms at least as much as botulinum toxin injection and likely more durably, but the single head-to-head trial was too small to demonstrate superiority, and diabetic-specific comparative results have not been reported.

cards.headline: Gonzalez 2024: the only double-blind randomised head-to-head — G-POEM clinical success 65% vs. 40% for botulinum toxin at 3 months (P = 0.10, not significant) and 60% vs. 40% at 1 year; only 11 of the 40 patients had diabetic gastroparesis (subgroup N on the face)
cards.summary: Gonzalez 2024: the only double-blind randomised head-to-head — G-POEM clinical success 65% vs. 40% for botulinum toxin at 3 months (P = 0.10, not significant) and 60% vs. 40% at 1 year; only 11 of the 40 patients had diabetic gastroparesis (subgroup N on the face)
cards.people: 40 patients (22 women; mean age 48.1 years) with refractory gastroparesis — medically managed for over 6 months and confirmed by gastric emptying scintigraphy — randomised at two expert centres to G-POEM or pyloric botulinum toxin injection, with 1-year follow-up. Etiologies were idiopathic (n = 18), diabetes (n = 11), postoperative (n = 6) and mixed (n = 4); mean symptom duration was 5.8 years. The record reports no results for the diabetic subgroup separately.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, 3-month clinical efficacy (a decrease of more than 1 point in mean Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index score), was higher with G-POEM than botulinum toxin injection (65% vs. 40%; P = 0.10 — the difference was not statistically significant), as was 1-year clinical success on intention-to-treat analysis (60% vs. 40%). Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index scores decreased in both groups at 3 months and 1 year. Gastric emptying scintigraphy improvement was 72% with G-POEM versus 50% with botulinum toxin (non-significant). Only three minor adverse events occurred, all in the G-POEM group. The authors conclude G-POEM seems to have a higher clinically relevant success rate, but this was not statistically demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients cannot settle a 25-percentage-point question (the confidence around 65% vs. 40% is wide), and for this shelf's diabetic question the trial is indirect: diabetic patients were 11 of 40, pooled with idiopathic and postoperative disease, and no diabetic-only success rates appear in the record.
cards.source: Gonzalez JM et al. cards.headline: Tran 2023: one centre's G-POEM series improved gastric emptying (−23.5%) and symptom scores (−9.6) after the procedure, against smaller transient improvements reported for botulinum toxin in the literature (10.1% and 4.0) — an indirect comparison; only 4 of 28 analysed patients were diabetic (subgroup N on the face)
cards.summary: Tran 2023: one centre's G-POEM series improved gastric emptying (−23.5%) and symptom scores (−9.6) after the procedure, against smaller transient improvements reported for botulinum toxin in the literature (10.1% and 4.0) — an indirect comparison; only 4 of 28 analysed patients were diabetic (subgroup N on the face)
cards.type: Retrospective case series with systematic-review comparator (Tran 2023)
cards.people: 65 patients who underwent G-POEM for gastroparesis at one institution (September 2018–June 2022), of whom 28 (22 women, 6 men) had both preoperative and postoperative gastric emptying scintigraphy and Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index scores; etiologies in the analysed set were diabetic (n = 4), idiopathic (n = 18) and postsurgical (n = 6), and half had prior failed interventions including botulinum toxin injections (n = 6). The botulinum toxin comparator comes from a systematic review of published BTI series, not from randomised or matched patients.
cards.result: After G-POEM, gastric emptying percentages fell significantly (mean difference −23.5%, p < 0.001) and symptom scores fell significantly (mean difference −9.6, p = 0.02). In the systematic review of botulinum toxin injection, transient mean improvements of 10.1% (gastric emptying) and 4.0 (symptom scores) were reported. The authors conclude G-POEM leads to significant improvement and is superior to botulinum toxin results reported in the literature.
cards.watchOut: A before–after series compared with other centres' published botulinum toxin results is the weakest comparative design on this shelf: case mix, scoring versions and follow-up differ, the symptom-score scales are not shown to be identical across sources, and the diabetic subset is 4 patients — this card corroborates direction only.

cards.headline: Sonaiya 2026: modelled on the randomised data, botulinum toxin was the cost-effective strategy at 3 months, but G-POEM became cost-effective by 12 months once repeat botulinum toxin sessions were counted — a durability argument built on the same small trial, not new patient data
cards.summary: Sonaiya 2026: modelled on the randomised data, botulinum toxin was the cost-effective strategy at 3 months, but G-POEM became cost-effective by 12 months once repeat botulinum toxin sessions were counted — a durability argument built on the same small trial, not new patient data
cards.people: A decision-tree cost-effectiveness model from a US health care system perspective over 3- and 12-month horizons, informed by randomised trial data and modelled on a 48.1-year-old patient with refractory gastroparesis (persistent symptoms despite 6 months of medical therapy, Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index score over 2). No new patients were studied; procedural costs, adverse events and repeat botulinum toxin sessions were incorporated.
cards.result: At 3 months, G-POEM had higher costs and marginally greater effectiveness than botulinum toxin injection (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio $288,341 per quality-adjusted life-year), making botulinum toxin the cost-effective strategy short-term. At 12 months, incorporating repeat botulinum toxin sessions, G-POEM became the cost-effective option (botulinum toxin yielded an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $334,046 per quality-adjusted life-year relative to G-POEM). Sensitivity analyses identified clinical success rates and procedural costs as the primary drivers; at 12 months G-POEM was cost-effective in most simulations at lower willingness-to-pay thresholds. The record reports no new clinical efficacy results.
cards.watchOut: A model inherits every uncertainty of the 40-patient trial it is built on — its 12-month conclusion follows from assuming botulinum toxin needs repeating while G-POEM does not, which is plausible but is an input assumption informed by the same limited data, not an observed outcome.
cards.source: Sonaiya S et al. Gastric Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy Versus Botulinum Toxin Injection for the Treatment of Refractory Gastroparesis: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: G-POEM looks at least as good as botulinum toxin injection and probably more durable, but superiority is undemonstrated — the one randomised head-to-head was small and non-significant, and diabetic-specific comparative results do not exist in the carded records
cards.summary: Synthesis: G-POEM looks at least as good as botulinum toxin injection and probably more durable, but superiority is undemonstrated — the one randomised head-to-head was small and non-significant, and diabetic-specific comparative results do not exist in the carded records
cards.people: The carded evidence: one double-blind randomised trial (40 patients; 11 diabetic), one single-centre G-POEM series with a literature comparator (65 treated, 28 analysed; 4 diabetic), and one cost-effectiveness model built on the trial. Total directly studied patients across the clinical reports: 105 treated, with diabetic patients a minority in both. The G-POEM versus sham evidence is homed on live shelf #3525 and cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Clinical success at 3 months: 65% (G-POEM) vs. 40% (botulinum toxin), P = 0.10; at 1 year 60% vs. 40% (Gonzalez 2024). Before–after improvements after G-POEM exceeded those reported for botulinum toxin in the literature (Tran 2023). Cost-effectiveness flips from botulinum toxin at 3 months to G-POEM at 12 months when repeat injections are counted (Sonaiya 2026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: For a clinician treating diabetic gastroparesis specifically, the honest position is extrapolation: pylorus-directed therapy beat sham on shelf #3525 and beat botulinum toxin numerically here, but nobody has published a diabetic-only head-to-head — a larger or diabetic-enriched trial could move this stamp in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gonzalez JM et al. Endoscopy. 2024 (PMID: 38141620); Tran D et al. Surgical Endoscopy. 2023 (PMID: 37430121); Sonaiya S et al. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 2026 (PMID: 42287743).

shelves.balance: This shelf asks the FIBROSIS question, and its non-invasive counterpart: does pioglitazone improve liver fibrosis on biopsy (fibrosis stage or score), and what does the liver-stiffness (elastography, kPa) evidence show? The ACTIVITY and resolution question is asked separately on the companion shelf #5857, where the record is consistent and the answer is yes; nothing on this shelf borrows that consistency. Scope: live shelf #2114 holds pioglitazone in steatohepatitis with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes (Belfort 2006; Cusi 2016) and is cross-pointed here; PIVENS' primary record is carded on shelf #26 and cross-pointed here. FIBROSIS ON BIOPSY — the record divides by analysis, not by endpoint definition: Aithal 2008 (74 non-diabetic patients, pioglitazone 30 mg/day, 12 months) reduced fibrosis versus placebo at exactly P = .05. Boettcher 2012 found fibrosis improvement NOT significant for the thiazolidinedione class as a whole, but significant for pioglitazone alone (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77 — a relative odds measure whose interval only just excludes no effect). Musso 2017, the synthesis whose primary outcome was fibrosis, found advanced fibrosis OR 3.15 (95% CI 1.25 to 7.93) and any-stage fibrosis OR 1.66 (1.12 to 2.47), with similar results in patients without diabetes (advanced fibrosis OR 2.95) and all effects accounted for by pioglitazone. Luo 2022's network analysis ranks pioglitazone first among the compared drugs for reducing biopsy fibrosis score. AGAINST: PIVENS — the largest and longest trial (247 non-diabetic adults, 96 weeks; cross-pointed from shelf #26) — found fibrosis improvement in 44% on pioglitazone versus 31% on placebo (P = 0.12), not significant, and Boettcher's class pool was likewise null. Cusi 2016 (cross-pointed, shelf #2114) points with the smaller trials (fibrosis score treatment difference −0.5; P = 0.039). That is a genuine split — smaller trials and pioglitazone-only pooling positive, the largest trial negative — not mere absence of data. LIVER STIFFNESS (kPa) — the evidence is thin, and it comes late: Kamolvisit 2021, the only placebo-controlled elastography trial found (98 people with HIV and prediabetes and fatty liver; baseline stiffness 5.4 kPa — early disease), showed no stiffness difference at 24 weeks (+0.014 vs +0.403 kPa; P = 0.199) and a significant one at 48 weeks (−0.184 vs +0.554 kPa; P = 0.016), a between-arm difference of about 0.7 kPa; the fat measure (controlled attenuation parameter) improved earlier and larger. Pereira 2025 (65 Brazilian patients on pioglitazone 30–45 mg/day for up to 10 years, retrospective, no control group) found FibroScan-AST (FAST) scores improved in both duration groups and the attenuation parameter fell significantly only in the 4–10-year group, but liver stiffness reduction itself was not significant (the only stiffness signal in its regression was a non-significant dyslipidemia association, adjusted OR 1.92, 95% CI 0.58 to 6.45); the group's earlier conference report recorded median stiffness 8.1 → 7.2 kPa with attenuation in 63% of a smaller 12–24-month cohort. On the ELF blood fibrosis score, Luo 2022 ranks liraglutide, not pioglitazone, first. NO MR-elastography trial and NO FIB-4-endpoint trial of pioglitazone exists in the record — stated plainly, because stiffness is the endpoint clinicians most often reach for. THE COST is uniform: weight gain wherever it is measured (+2.77 kg versus −0.55 kg in Aithal 2008; +2.70% of body weight in Musso 2017; +4.7 kg in PIVENS), with oedema alongside. No carded study measures clinical liver outcomes. For steatohepatitis activity and resolution, see the companion shelf #5857.

cards.headline: Aithal 2008: in 74 non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis, 12 months of pioglitazone reduced fibrosis versus placebo — at exactly P = .05, the borderline of significance
cards.summary: Aithal 2008: in 74 non-diabetic patients with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis, 12 months of pioglitazone reduced fibrosis versus placebo — at exactly P = .05, the borderline of significance
cards.people: 74 non-diabetic patients (45 men; median age 54 years) with histologically proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis randomised to standard diet and exercise plus pioglitazone 30 mg/day or placebo for 12 months; 61 patients (30 placebo, 31 pioglitazone) had liver biopsies at both the beginning and the end of the study.
cards.result: Histologic features including hepatocellular injury (P = .005), Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004), and fibrosis (P = .05) were reduced in pioglitazone-treated patients compared with placebo. Pioglitazone was also associated with weight gain (mean change +2.77 kg vs −0.55 kg; P = .04) and improvements in glucose, HbA1c, insulin C-peptide, alanine aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyltransferase and ferritin. The authors conclude pioglitazone improved metabolic and histologic parameters, most notably liver injury and fibrosis, and that larger extended trials are justified.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the trial's fibrosis endpoint; its activity endpoints (hepatocellular injury P = .005, Mallory-Denk bodies P = .004) are carded on the companion shelf #5857. P = .05 sits exactly on the conventional significance threshold, only 61 of 74 randomised patients had paired biopsies, and the population is non-diabetic steatohepatitis.
cards.source: Aithal GP et al. Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of pioglitazone in nondiabetic subjects with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18718471. Registry ID: none in the record.
