cards.headline: Boettcher 2012: pooling all thiazolidinediones, fibrosis improvement was NOT significant — but pioglitazone alone improved fibrosis (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77)
cards.summary: Boettcher 2012: pooling all thiazolidinediones, fibrosis improvement was NOT significant — but pioglitazone alone improved fibrosis (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 4 randomised, placebo-controlled trials of thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone and rosiglitazone) in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis identified to September 2010: 169 patients on a thiazolidinedione versus 165 on placebo for the class analyses; the pioglitazone-only analysis covers 137 versus 134 patients.
cards.result: Thiazolidinediones were significantly better than placebo in improving ballooning degeneration, lobular inflammation, steatosis and combined necroinflammation, but improvement in fibrosis was not significant for the class as a whole. When pioglitazone was analysed alone, the improvement in fibrosis with pioglitazone versus placebo was statistically significant (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77) — a relative (odds) measure whose interval only just excludes no effect. The authors conclude that pioglitazone may improve fibrosis and that larger trials are needed on the fibrosis question.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the synthesis's fibrosis findings; its activity endpoints are carded on the companion shelf #5857. The class pool mixes in rosiglitazone trials, the pioglitazone-only interval (1.02 to 2.77) barely excludes 1, and the search closed in September 2010 — Musso 2017 and Luo 2022 carry the later pooling.
cards.source: Boettcher E et al. Meta-analysis: pioglitazone improves liver histology and fibrosis in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2012. cards.headline: Musso 2017: pooled thiazolidinedione trials (516 patients) — advanced fibrosis OR 3.15 and any-stage fibrosis OR 1.66, with all effects accounted for by pioglitazone
cards.summary: Musso 2017: pooled thiazolidinedione trials (516 patients) — advanced fibrosis OR 3.15 and any-stage fibrosis OR 1.66, with all effects accounted for by pioglitazone
cards.people: 516 patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in 8 randomised controlled trials of thiazolidinedione therapy (5 evaluating pioglitazone, 3 rosiglitazone) lasting 6 to 24 months; the primary outcome was improvement in advanced fibrosis (stage F3–F4 to F0–F2) on liver biopsy.
cards.result: Thiazolidinedione therapy was associated with improved advanced fibrosis (OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.25 to 7.93; P = .01), improvement in fibrosis of any stage (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.47; P = .01), and NASH resolution (OR 3.22, 95% CI 2.17 to 4.79; P < .001) — all relative (odds) measures. Analyses restricted to trials enrolling patients without diabetes gave similar results (advanced fibrosis OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.04 to 10.90; P = .02; any-stage OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.02 to 3.03). All effects were accounted for by pioglitazone use. Weight gain and lower-limb oedema occurred more frequently with thiazolidinedione therapy (initial body weight +2.70%, 95% CI 1.96% to 4.34%). The authors conclude pioglitazone use improves advanced fibrosis in NASH, even in patients without diabetes, while noting that whether this translates into improved clinical outcomes requires further study.
cards.watchOut: This card carries the analysis's fibrosis endpoints; its resolution endpoint (OR 3.22) is carded on the companion shelf #5857. The pooled trials are small (516 patients across 8 trials, three of them testing rosiglitazone), the advanced-fibrosis interval is wide (1.25 to 7.93), and histology is a surrogate — the largest single trial, PIVENS, did not itself find a significant fibrosis benefit.
cards.source: Musso G et al. Thiazolidinediones and Advanced Liver Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis: A Meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28241279. cards.headline: Luo 2022 (network meta-analysis, 27 trials, 3,416 patients): pioglitazone ranked first for reducing biopsy fibrosis score and liver fat — but liraglutide, not pioglitazone, ranked first for the ELF score
cards.summary: Luo 2022 (network meta-analysis, 27 trials, 3,416 patients): pioglitazone ranked first for reducing biopsy fibrosis score and liver fat — but liraglutide, not pioglitazone, ranked first for the ELF score
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Luo 2022)
cards.people: 27 randomised trials including 3,416 patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease comparing vitamin E, pioglitazone, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists with each other or placebo, analysed as a network meta-analysis of invasive tests (fibrosis score, resolution of steatohepatitis) and non-invasive tests (liver enzymes, controlled attenuation parameter, enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) score, liver fat content, keratin-18); registered PROSPERO CRD42021283129.
cards.result: Pioglitazone treatment had the highest SUCRA ranking in decreasing liver fat content and fibrosis scores. Liraglutide treatment had the highest SUCRA ranking in decreasing controlled attenuation parameter and ELF scores and in increasing the resolution of steatohepatitis. Pioglitazone was superior to vitamin E in increasing the resolution of steatohepatitis and induced significantly higher decreases in alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyltransferase and keratin-18 than placebo. The authors conclude the network meta-analysis provides evidence for the efficacy of all four drug classes in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and that more randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: A SUCRA ranking is a probability of ranking first among the compared drugs, not an effect size: 'ranked first for fibrosis score' does not say by how much, and the network's fibrosis data still rest on the same small biopsy trials carded individually on this shelf. The ELF result cuts the other way — on that blood fibrosis score pioglitazone did not lead.
cards.source: Luo Q et al. cards.headline: Kamolvisit 2021: in 98 people with HIV and prediabetes, pioglitazone did not change liver stiffness at 24 weeks but did at 48 weeks (−0.184 vs +0.554 kPa; P = 0.016) — from a low baseline of 5.4 kPa
cards.summary: Kamolvisit 2021: in 98 people with HIV and prediabetes, pioglitazone did not change liver stiffness at 24 weeks but did at 48 weeks (−0.184 vs +0.554 kPa; P = 0.016) — from a low baseline of 5.4 kPa
cards.people: 98 people living with HIV and prediabetes (49 per group; mean age 50.8 years; 66.3% men) with fatty liver by ultrasonography or controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) ≥ 238 dB/m, all on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable HIV RNA (mean CD4 count 463.2 cells/mm3), randomised to pioglitazone 30 mg/day or placebo and followed for 48 weeks at Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok; liver stiffness and CAP were measured by transient elastography.
cards.result: Mean baseline CAP was 285.7 dB/m and mean baseline liver stiffness 5.4 kPa. At 24 weeks, the mean change of liver stiffness was +0.014 kPa in the pioglitazone group and +0.403 kPa in the control group (P = 0.199 — no difference), while CAP had already separated (−25.7 vs −5.6 dB/m; P = 0.040). At 48 weeks, the mean change of liver stiffness was −0.184 kPa in the pioglitazone group and +0.554 kPa in the control group (P = 0.016) — a between-arm difference of about 0.7 kPa — and CAP changed by −23.5 versus +10.2 dB/m (P < 0.001). Fasting plasma glucose also fell more on pioglitazone; body mass index, lipid profiles and liver enzymes did not differ between groups, and no serious adverse effects were observed in either group. The authors conclude pioglitazone significantly reduces CAP, liver stiffness, and fasting plasma glucose in people living with HIV with prediabetes and metabolic-associated fatty liver disease.
cards.watchOut: The only placebo-controlled elastography trial found — but the population is HIV with prediabetes and fatty liver, not biopsy-proven steatohepatitis; baseline stiffness of 5.4 kPa is early disease with little room to fall; the 48-week between-arm difference is about 0.7 kPa; and the fat measure (CAP) improved earlier and by more than stiffness did.

cards.headline: Pereira 2025: in 65 Brazilian patients on pioglitazone for up to 10 years, FAST scores improved and CAP fell in the long-treatment group — but liver stiffness reduction itself was not significant
cards.summary: Pereira 2025: in 65 Brazilian patients on pioglitazone for up to 10 years, FAST scores improved and CAP fell in the long-treatment group — but liver stiffness reduction itself was not significant
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre cohort, no control group (Pereira 2025)
cards.people: 65 patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease from three Brazilian public hospitals treated with pioglitazone at doses of 30–45 mg/day for up to 10 years, analysed retrospectively and stratified by treatment duration (1–3 years and 4–10 years); vibration-controlled transient elastography (liver stiffness and controlled attenuation parameter) and the FibroScan-AST (FAST) score were evaluated before and after treatment. There was no untreated control group.
cards.result: Alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyltransferase fell significantly in both treatment groups. A significant decrease in CAP levels was observed only in the 4–10-year group (P = 0.002). Improvement in FAST scores was observed in both groups (1–3 years, P = 0.042; 4–10 years, P = 0.012). Liver stiffness reduction itself was not significant: in the paper's logistic regression, the only stiffness-related signal was dyslipidemia associated with a non-significant trend toward higher odds of liver stiffness reduction (adjusted OR = 1.92, 95% CI 0.58 to 6.45; P = 0.284). The same group's earlier conference report (56 patients treated 12–24 months; Annals of Hepatology 2024) recorded median liver stiffness falling from 8.1 to 7.2 kPa, with attenuation in 63% of cases — figures from that earlier, smaller report, not from this paper's analysis. The authors conclude long-term pioglitazone therapy shows metabolic and hepatic benefits and potential as a cost-effective, accessible treatment option, particularly where newer alternatives are unavailable.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled before–after series: stiffness can drift with weight, glycaemia and time, and patients who remain on a drug for up to 10 years are a selected group. The FAST improvement is driven substantially by its enzyme and CAP components; the stiffness component itself did not significantly fall, and the 8.1 → 7.2 kPa medians come from the group's earlier conference report on a different (56-patient, 12–24-month) cohort.
cards.source: Pereira IVA et al. Long-term pioglitazone use in MASLD patients: insights from a multicentric preliminary study. Clinics (Sao Paulo). 2025. PMID: 40845474. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pioglitazone and fibrosis divide by analysis — smaller trials and pioglitazone-only pooling positive, the largest trial negative; the stiffness evidence is thin, and later than the fat evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: pioglitazone and fibrosis divide by analysis — smaller trials and pioglitazone-only pooling positive, the largest trial negative; the stiffness evidence is thin, and later than the fat evidence
cards.people: Carded on this shelf: one placebo-controlled trial's fibrosis endpoint (Aithal 2008, N = 74), three syntheses (Boettcher 2012; Musso 2017; Luo 2022), one placebo-controlled elastography trial (Kamolvisit 2021, N = 98) and one retrospective series (Pereira 2025, N = 65). Cross-pointed, not re-carded: PIVENS (N = 247, primary record on shelf #26) and the prediabetes/type 2 diabetes trials Belfort 2006 and Cusi 2016 (shelf #2114).
cards.result: FIBROSIS ON BIOPSY — a genuine split: Aithal 2008 fibrosis P = .05 (borderline); Boettcher 2012 thiazolidinedione-class pool not significant, pioglitazone-only OR 1.68 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.77; relative odds); Musso 2017 advanced fibrosis OR 3.15, any-stage OR 1.66, non-diabetic advanced OR 2.95 (all relative odds; all effects accounted for by pioglitazone); Luo 2022 ranks pioglitazone first for reducing biopsy fibrosis score but not for the ELF blood score (liraglutide first); PIVENS (cross-pointed) fibrosis improvement 44% vs 31% (P = 0.12) — the largest and longest trial found no significant fibrosis benefit; Cusi 2016 (cross-pointed, shelf #2114) fibrosis score treatment difference −0.5 (P = 0.039) points with the smaller trials. LIVER STIFFNESS — thin: Kamolvisit 2021 no difference at 24 weeks, −0.184 vs +0.554 kPa at 48 weeks (P = 0.016; about 0.7 kPa between arms) from a 5.4 kPa baseline in HIV with prediabetes; Pereira 2025 FAST improved but stiffness reduction not significant (adjusted OR 1.92, 95% CI 0.58 to 6.45). No MR-elastography trial and no FIB-4-endpoint trial of pioglitazone exists in the record — stated plainly. COST: weight gain wherever measured (+2.77 kg Aithal; +2.70% of body weight Musso; +4.7 kg PIVENS). NOT ANSWERED HERE: steatohepatitis activity and resolution — the companion shelf #5857 asks that question, and there the answer is consistently yes.
cards.watchOut: Every fibrosis claim here is a biopsy surrogate from small trials pooled different ways — the answer changes with the pooling rule, which is exactly why the stamp is SPLIT; no trial is powered for cirrhosis, liver failure or death; and the stiffness record is two studies, neither in biopsy-proven steatohepatitis populations with advanced fibrosis.

shelves.title: Late-evening snack in cirrhosis: nutrition improves — body protein accretes with nighttime feeding (+0.53 kg over 12 months) and albumin rises in pooled trials — but hard outcomes are unproven
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and malnutrition, does a late-evening snack improve nitrogen balance and outcomes versus no snack?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Circadian Rhythm · Dietary Proteins · Energy Intake · Female · Growth Hormone · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3 · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Neutron Activation Analysis · Nutritional Status · Nutritional Support · Proteins · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #5369, where an evening protein snack appears only as one component of an intensive feeding bundle in refractory ascites; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the isolated late-evening snack in cirrhosis with malnutrition, and none of #5369's carded records is re-carded here. The best trial isolates timing: the same 710 kcal/day supplement given at night increased total body protein by 0.53 kg over 12 months while daytime feeding produced no significant change, at equal total intakes (Plank 2008, N = 103). Pooled snack trials show the metabolic side of the same picture — improved respiratory quotient and carbohydrate oxidation within weeks and higher serum albumin by 3–12 weeks (Guo 2018, 14 trials, 478 patients) — and a network meta-analysis found the snack better than no snack in direct randomised comparisons on nutritional indicators (Yu 2022). Nitrogen balance and nutritional status therefore improve; what does not exist in the carded records is a hard-outcome result — no mortality, ascites or encephalopathy effect size for the isolated snack is reported. (A further snack trial, Nakaya 2007, is homed on shelf #3630 and is cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a late-evening snack improves nitrogen balance and nutritional status in adults with cirrhosis and malnutrition; benefit on survival and complications is unproven.

cards.headline: Plank 2008: a nighttime (late-evening) supplement for 12 months increased total body protein by 0.53 kg versus no significant change with the same supplement given in daytime — protein accretion equivalent to about 2 kg of lean tissue
cards.summary: Plank 2008: a nighttime (late-evening) supplement for 12 months increased total body protein by 0.53 kg versus no significant change with the same supplement given in daytime — protein accretion equivalent to about 2 kg of lean tissue
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of supplement timing (Plank 2008)
cards.people: 103 patients with liver cirrhosis (68 men, 35 women; median age 51 years; Child-Pugh A 52, B 31, C 20; viral hepatitis 67, alcohol 15, cholestatic 6, other 15) randomised to receive 710 kcal/day of supplementary nutrition either in the daytime (0900–1900) or at nighttime (2100–0700) for 12 months; total body protein was measured by neutron activation analysis at baseline, 3, 6 and 12 months, and total daily energy and protein intakes were assessed by dietary recall.
cards.result: Total body protein at baseline was similar between groups (85 ± 2% of predicted in daytime, 84 ± 2% in nighttime). In the nighttime group, total body protein increased significantly at 3 months (+0.38 ± 0.10 kg, P = 0.0004), 6 months (+0.48 ± 0.13 kg, P = 0.0007) and 12 months (+0.53 ± 0.17 kg, P = 0.003); in the daytime group no significant changes were seen. Daily energy and protein intakes rose above baseline in both groups at 3 months (P < 0.0001) with no difference between groups, isolating timing — not total intake — as the differing exposure. The authors equate the gain to about 2 kg of lean tissue sustained over 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is nighttime versus daytime feeding, not snack versus no snack — it proves timing matters for body protein, and the endpoint is a body-composition measure: the record reports no mortality, ascites or hospitalisation outcome.
cards.source: Plank LD et al. Nocturnal nutritional supplementation improves total body protein status of patients with liver cirrhosis: a randomized 12-month trial. Hepatology. 2008. PMID: 18627001. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Guo 2018: across 14 trials (478 patients), a late-evening snack raised respiratory quotient and carbohydrate oxidation and increased serum albumin (mean difference 2.98 in the review's pooled analysis) at 3–12 weeks
cards.summary: Guo 2018: across 14 trials (478 patients), a late-evening snack raised respiratory quotient and carbohydrate oxidation and increased serum albumin (mean difference 2.98 in the review's pooled analysis) at 3–12 weeks
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 trials comprising 478 cases of patients with cirrhosis treated with a late-evening snack, examining energy metabolism (respiratory quotient, substrate oxidation) and liver-related blood measures; the record does not state the unit for the pooled albumin mean difference, and none is printed here.
cards.result: Respiratory quotient (mean difference 11.09 as printed in the record) and carbohydrate oxidation (mean difference 0.05) were significantly elevated with one to three weeks of late-evening snack (P < 0.05). Serum albumin (mean difference 2.98) and cholinesterase (standardised mean difference 1.09) were increased with three to twelve weeks of treatment (P < 0.05). There was no significant improvement in alanine aminotransferase (P = 0.53), aspartate aminotransferase (P = 0.96) or total bilirubin (P = 0.32).
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, short and heterogeneous in snack composition, and several effect sizes are printed in the record without clear units — this review supports a metabolic and albumin signal, not a clinical-outcome claim.
cards.source: Guo YJ et al. Effects of Late Evening Snack on Cirrhotic Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Gastroenterology Research and Practice. 2018. PMID: 29805447. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Yu 2022 (network meta-analysis): in direct comparisons within randomised trials, a late-evening snack was better than no snack, and enteral nutrition plus a late-evening snack was better than either alone — while indirect comparisons between regimens were not statistically significant
cards.summary: Yu 2022 (network meta-analysis): in direct comparisons within randomised trials, a late-evening snack was better than no snack, and enteral nutrition plus a late-evening snack was better than either alone — while indirect comparisons between regimens were not statistically significant
cards.people: Bayesian network meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials enrolling 1,148 patients with cirrhosis in total across all nutritional regimens compared (parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition with or without branched-chain amino acids, enteral nutrition plus probiotics, combined parenteral plus enteral nutrition, late-evening snack, enteral nutrition plus late-evening snack, and no late-evening snack), with outcomes including albumin, total protein, Child-Pugh and model for end-stage liver disease scores, bilirubin, transaminases and overall survival.
cards.result: The direct comparisons showed enteral nutrition plus a late-evening snack was better than the snack alone and enteral nutrition alone, and the late-evening snack was better than no late-evening snack, on the review's nutritional and liver-function indicators. The indirect comparisons between regimens were not statistically significant; the authors rank enteral nutrition plus intestinal probiotics highest overall, with the snack-containing regimens close behind. No pooled mortality effect size for snack versus no snack is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Six trials spread across eight regimens means each direct edge rests on very few patients, and 'better' here refers to the review's composite of nutritional indicators — the record gives no snack-versus-no-snack survival numbers, so none are claimed on this shelf.
cards.source: Yu B et al. The efficacy of parenteral nutrition (PN) and enteral nutrition (EN) supports in cirrhosis: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35060537. cards.headline: Synthesis: the isolated late-evening snack improves the nutritional state of cirrhosis — body protein accretes when the supplement is timed at night, albumin and energy metabolism improve in pooled trials — but no carded record shows it improves survival or other hard outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: the isolated late-evening snack improves the nutritional state of cirrhosis — body protein accretes when the supplement is timed at night, albumin and energy metabolism improve in pooled trials — but no carded record shows it improves survival or other hard outcomes
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 12-month randomised timing trial (N = 103), one meta-analysis of late-evening-snack trials (14 trials, 478 patients) and one network meta-analysis of nutritional regimens in cirrhosis (6 trials, 1,148 patients across all regimens). Total carded participants exceed 1,700, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Nighttime supplementation increased total body protein by 0.53 kg at 12 months where daytime supplementation did not (Plank 2008); pooled snack trials showed higher albumin and improved substrate oxidation (Guo 2018); and direct randomised comparisons favoured snack over no snack on nutritional indicators (Yu 2022). Nitrogen-balance improvement is part of this picture through the metabolic outcomes pooled in the reviews; no carded record reports a mortality benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a late-evening snack improves nitrogen balance and nutritional status in cirrhosis and malnutrition; effects on survival and complications are unproven.
cards.watchOut: The snack tested across these reports varies (a 710 kcal supplement, branched-chain-amino-acid mixtures, ordinary food) and the strongest trial compares timing rather than snack versus nothing — the shelf's claim is deliberately limited to nutrition and nitrogen balance, where the evidence converges.
cards.source: Synthesis of Plank LD et al. Hepatology. 2008 (PMID: 18627001); Guo YJ et al. Gastroenterology Research and Practice. 2018 (PMID: 29805447); Yu B et al. Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35060537).

shelves.title: Bedtime alginate add-on on a PPI: plausible but untested as a specific strategy — general add-on evidence is positive in one trial, while the homed bedtime trial's confirmatory study found no advantage over placebo add-on
shelves.question: Does adding an alginate at bedtime help adults with reflux who still have nighttime symptoms on a proton pump inhibitor?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alginates · Deglutition Disorders · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Gastrointestinal Agents · Glucuronic Acid · Heartburn · Hexuronic Acids · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Omeprazole · Prospective Studies · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2655, which covers alginate efficacy generally; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the bedtime add-on in patients still symptomatic on a proton pump inhibitor, and none of #2655's carded records is re-carded here. Flag for the developer: the one trial that dosed alginate-antacid after meals and at bedtime in PPI breakthrough patients (Coyle 2017) is already carded on #2655 — its exploratory study favoured the add-on but its confirmatory study found no significant difference versus placebo add-on (51% vs 48% response) — so it is cross-pointed here in prose only, its PMID kept out of the card source lines. The free evidence for the add-on in inadequate responders is thinner: adding alginate to omeprazole doubled complete heartburn resolution in nonerosive reflux (56.7% vs 25.7%; Manabe 2012), alginate add-on matched domperidone add-on in PPI partial responders with systemic sclerosis (Foocharoen 2017), and 54–71% of PPI failures responded on alginate combinations with no control arm (Tangvoraphonkchai 2025). No free record isolates a single bedtime dose or reports night-time symptoms separately. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a bedtime alginate add-on may help adults who still have night-time symptoms on a PPI, by extrapolation from the general add-on evidence — the specific bedtime strategy itself is untested in the free records, and the homed bedtime trial's confirmatory result was null.

cards.headline: Manabe 2012: adding sodium alginate to omeprazole doubled complete heartburn resolution in nonerosive reflux disease — 56.7% versus 25.7% on omeprazole alone at 4 weeks
cards.summary: Manabe 2012: adding sodium alginate to omeprazole doubled complete heartburn resolution in nonerosive reflux disease — 56.7% versus 25.7% on omeprazole alone at 4 weeks
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial of alginate add-on (Manabe 2012)
cards.people: 87 patients enrolled with heartburn on at least 2 days per week for the preceding month and no endoscopic mucosal breaks (nonerosive reflux disease); 76 were randomised to omeprazole 20 mg once daily plus sodium alginate 30 mL four times a day (n = 36) or omeprazole alone (n = 40) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Complete resolution of heartburn for at least 7 consecutive days by the end of treatment was significantly more common with the alginate combination (56.7%) than with omeprazole alone (25.7%) in the record. One patient in the combination group had mild drug-related diarrhoea that was not clinically serious. The record does not report a night-time-symptom subgroup or bedtime-specific dosing result.
cards.watchOut: These were nonerosive-reflux patients starting the combination, not proven PPI non-responders with night-time symptoms, and the alginate was dosed four times daily rather than as a single bedtime dose — the trial supports add-on alginate generally, not the bedtime strategy specifically.
cards.source: Manabe N et al. Efficacy of adding sodium alginate to omeprazole in patients with nonerosive reflux disease: a randomized clinical trial. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2012. PMID: 22050449. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Foocharoen 2017: in PPI partial responders, add-on alginic acid improved symptoms and quality of life from baseline but was no better than add-on domperidone — 21.6% did not respond to the alginate combination (the comparison made no difference)
cards.summary: Foocharoen 2017: in PPI partial responders, add-on alginic acid improved symptoms and quality of life from baseline but was no better than add-on domperidone — 21.6% did not respond to the alginate combination (the comparison made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised active-comparator add-on trial in PPI partial responders (Foocharoen 2017)
cards.people: Adults with systemic sclerosis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: 148 enrolled, of whom 88 had PPI partial-response reflux; 80 were randomised to omeprazole plus domperidone (n = 38) or omeprazole plus alginic acid (algycon) (n = 37) for 4 weeks, each with the other's placebo; most had diffuse systemic sclerosis.
cards.result: After treatment, symptom severity, symptom frequency scores and quality of life improved significantly from baseline in both groups, with no significant difference in symptom grading between groups at the end of the study. Non-response occurred in 5 of 38 (13.2%) domperidone patients and 8 of 37 (21.6%) alginate patients; about 17% overall were non-responsive. There was no PPI-only or placebo add-on arm, so the within-group improvements cannot be separated from time and placebo effects in this record.
cards.watchOut: The population is systemic-sclerosis reflux — a dysmotility-driven disease unlike ordinary reflux — and with no placebo add-on arm, 'improved from baseline' is weak evidence; the trial's firm finding is equivalence with domperidone, not superiority over staying on the PPI alone.
cards.source: Foocharoen C et al. Effectiveness of add-on therapy with domperidone vs alginic acid in proton pump inhibitor partial response gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in systemic sclerosis: randomized placebo-controlled trial. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2017. PMID: 27179107. Registry ID: NCT01878526. cards.headline: Tangvoraphonkchai 2025: in patients who had failed standard-dose PPI therapy, adding alginate four times daily for 28 days produced response rates of 54% (generic) and 71% (original formulation) — with no PPI-only control group
cards.summary: Tangvoraphonkchai 2025: in patients who had failed standard-dose PPI therapy, adding alginate four times daily for 28 days produced response rates of 54% (generic) and 71% (original formulation) — with no PPI-only control group
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial, formulation comparison in PPI failures (Tangvoraphonkchai 2025)
cards.people: 48 patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease who had failed standard-dose PPI treatment, randomised in a multicentre prospective non-inferiority trial to generic alginate or original alginate (both four times daily for 28 days, in combination with PPIs); response was measured with the Reflux Disease Questionnaire at days 7 and 28.
cards.result: Response rates at day 7 were identical (45.83% in both groups); by day 28 they were 54.17% for generic and 70.83% for original alginate (p = 0.23). Total questionnaire scores and symptom-free rates did not differ significantly between groups at either time point, and adverse-event rates were comparable (16.67% vs 8.33%, p = 0.66). Because every patient received alginate, the record contains no estimate of the add-on's effect versus continuing the PPI alone, and no bedtime-dose or night-time-symptom analysis.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a purchasing question (generic versus original alginate), not the add-on question: its response rates describe what happened on combined therapy in refractory patients, with regression to the mean and continued PPI effect unmeasured.
cards.source: Tangvoraphonkchai K et al. Comparable efficacy of generic and original alginate for symptom control in PPI-refractory GERD. Scientific Reports. 2025. PMID: 40760009. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: add-on alginate probably helps some PPI inadequate responders — one add-on trial doubled complete heartburn resolution — but the bedtime-dose, night-time-symptom version of the question has no dedicated trial among the free records, and the refractory-population data have no untreated comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: add-on alginate probably helps some PPI inadequate responders — one add-on trial doubled complete heartburn resolution — but the bedtime-dose, night-time-symptom version of the question has no dedicated trial among the free records, and the refractory-population data have no untreated comparator
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised add-on trial versus PPI alone in nonerosive reflux (76 randomised), one randomised add-on comparison against domperidone in PPI partial responders with systemic sclerosis (80 randomised), and one randomised formulation comparison in PPI failures (48 patients, all receiving alginate). Total carded participants are 204, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Complete heartburn resolution was 56.7% with alginate plus omeprazole versus 25.7% with omeprazole alone (Manabe 2012); alginate add-on matched domperidone add-on in partial responders, with 21.6% non-response (Foocharoen 2017); and 54–71% of PPI failures responded on combined therapy without a control arm (Tangvoraphonkchai 2025). No carded record isolates a bedtime dose or reports night-time symptoms separately. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a bedtime alginate add-on may help PPI non-responders with night-time symptoms, by extrapolation from the general add-on evidence — the specific strategy is untested.
cards.watchOut: The one trial that did dose alginate after meals and at bedtime in PPI breakthrough patients (Coyle 2017) is homed on shelf #2655 and is cross-pointed in the balance, not re-carded — its confirmatory study found no significant advantage over placebo add-on, which is a further reason this shelf's stamp stays at MAYBE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Manabe N et al. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2012 (PMID: 22050449); Foocharoen C et al. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2017 (PMID: 27179107); Tangvoraphonkchai K et al. Scientific Reports. 2025 (PMID: 40760009).

shelves.title: Aspirin plus PPI and Barrett's cancer risk alone (SPLIT): observational studies associate the drugs with less adenocarcinoma, but the bias-graded review and the trial's cancer-specific outcome show no significant association
shelves.question: Does aspirin plus a proton pump inhibitor reduce cancer risk in adults with Barrett's esophagus?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Barrett Esophagus · Case-Control Studies · Esophageal Neoplasms · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Proton Pump Inhibitors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #773, which covers the AspECT trial on its composite of death, adenocarcinoma and high-grade dysplasia; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — cancer risk alone. FLAG FOR THE DEVELOPER (one-home precedent b): the AspECT record itself (PMID: 30057104) is already carded on the home shelf, so it is NOT re-carded here; this pack is built entirely on three free reports that address the cancer-specific outcome. They split. In a Veterans Affairs nested case-control study where PPI use was almost universal (94–95%), filled aspirin/NSAID prescriptions were associated with a lower risk of adenocarcinoma (adjusted incidence density ratio 0.64) — effectively aspirin on a PPI background (Nguyen 2010). A second cohort found PPI use associated with reduced high-grade dysplasia/cancer while aspirin/NSAID showed only a nonsignificant trend (Nguyen 2009). But the 2025 systematic review with bias assessment found aspirin not significantly associated with progression in pooled observational data (adjusted OR 0.84), graded all observational evidence serious-to-critical risk of bias, and reported that the single randomised trial found no significant association for high-grade dysplasia/cancer — very low certainty overall (Ko 2025). PROPOSED SPLIT (observational studies: aspirin/PPI use is associated with less cancer; the randomised trial's cancer-specific outcome and the bias-adjusted review: no significant association) — the combination's effect on cancer alone is unproven.

cards.headline: Nguyen 2010: in Barrett's patients almost all taking a PPI, filled aspirin/NSAID prescriptions were associated with a 0.64 adjusted incidence density ratio for adenocarcinoma — the closest record to 'aspirin plus PPI, cancer alone'
cards.summary: Nguyen 2010: in Barrett's patients almost all taking a PPI, filled aspirin/NSAID prescriptions were associated with a 0.64 adjusted incidence density ratio for adenocarcinoma — the closest record to 'aspirin plus PPI, cancer alone'
cards.people: Nested case-control study within a national Veterans Affairs cohort of 11,823 patients with a first Barrett's esophagus diagnosis: 116 incident esophageal adenocarcinoma cases matched to 696 controls without cancer; 95% of cases and 94% of controls had at least one filled proton pump inhibitor prescription.
cards.result: In this setting of almost universal PPI use, filled NSAID/aspirin prescriptions were associated with a reduced risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (adjusted incidence density ratio, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.42–0.97) — a relative measure; the record gives no absolute cancer rates by aspirin use. Filled statin prescriptions were also associated with reduced risk (0.55; 95% CI, 0.36–0.86), and the authors caution that the strong inverse associations with even short periods of use raise concerns of uncontrolled confounding.
cards.watchOut: Prescription fills are not randomised exposure: patients who fill aspirin differ from those who do not, the aspirin and non-aspirin NSAID effects are pooled, and the authors themselves flag uncontrolled confounding as a live concern.
cards.source: Nguyen DM et al. Medications (NSAIDs, statins, proton pump inhibitors) and the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma in patients with Barrett's esophagus. Gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 20188100. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nguyen 2009: PPI prescriptions after Barrett's diagnosis were associated with a reduced risk of high-grade dysplasia or cancer, while aspirin/NSAID showed only a nonsignificant trend — and the record prints no effect size for either
cards.summary: Nguyen 2009: PPI prescriptions after Barrett's diagnosis were associated with a reduced risk of high-grade dysplasia or cancer, while aspirin/NSAID showed only a nonsignificant trend — and the record prints no effect size for either
cards.people: Retrospective observational study of 344 patients with documented Barrett's esophagus (mean age 61 years, 94.2% male), followed for 2,620 patient-years, during which high-grade dysplasia or esophageal adenocarcinoma developed in 33 patients; 67.2% were prescribed a PPI (mean 5.1 years) and 49.1% an NSAID (mean 3.6 years).
cards.result: PPI treatment after Barrett's diagnosis was associated with a reduced risk of high grade dysplasia or cancer, and this association persisted after adjustment for gender, age, and the length of Barrett's esophagus. NSAID and/or aspirin therapy were associated with a nonsignificant trend toward lower incidence of high grade dysplasia or esophageal cancer. The record reports no effect size (no hazard ratio or event rates by drug) for these associations — printed plainly, none is invented here.
cards.watchOut: Only 33 outcome events in a single-centre retrospective cohort, with the outcome combining high-grade dysplasia and cancer — it cannot isolate a cancer-only effect of the aspirin-plus-PPI combination, and confounding by indication applies to every drug studied.
cards.source: Nguyen DM et al. Medication usage and the risk of neoplasia in patients with Barrett's esophagus. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2009. PMID: 19523538. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ko 2025: across 16 observational studies aspirin was NOT significantly associated with Barrett's progression (adjusted OR 0.84), all observational evidence was at serious or critical risk of bias, and the one randomised trial found no significant high-grade dysplasia/cancer association
cards.summary: Ko 2025: across 16 observational studies aspirin was NOT significantly associated with Barrett's progression (adjusted OR 0.84), all observational evidence was at serious or critical risk of bias, and the one randomised trial found no significant high-grade dysplasia/cancer association
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of chemoprevention in Barrett's esophagus (prospectively registered, PROSPERO CRD42024532338): 16 observational studies and 1 randomised controlled trial, with a comprehensive risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE rating.
cards.result: PPIs and statins were associated with reduced odds of progression (adjusted OR 0.46; 95% CI, 0.25–0.86; and adjusted OR 0.53; 95% CI, 0.37–0.74 — relative measures), while aspirin use was not significantly associated (adjusted OR 0.84; 95% CI, 0.65–1.08; P = 0.17). Among observational studies, 6 were at critical and 10 at serious risk of bias. The only trial included was at low risk of bias and reported no significant associations for aspirin and PPI comparisons and high-grade dysplasia/esophageal adenocarcinoma. GRADE certainty was very low, and the authors conclude there is little rationale to recommend these medications for chemoprevention in Barrett's esophagus.
cards.watchOut: The review's trial statement concerns the high-grade dysplasia/cancer outcome, not the AspECT composite homed on shelf #773 — the two can both be true, and this shelf exists precisely because the cancer-only cut reads differently from the composite.
cards.source: Ko MT et al. Chemoprevention of Barrett's Esophagus: a Systematic Review and Comprehensive Assessment of Bias. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2025. PMID: 40794904. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: observational data link aspirin (on a PPI background) and PPI use to less Barrett's cancer, but the bias-adjusted review finds aspirin's association nonsignificant and the single trial's cancer-specific outcome null — the combination is unproven for cancer alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: observational data link aspirin (on a PPI background) and PPI use to less Barrett's cancer, but the bias-adjusted review finds aspirin's association nonsignificant and the single trial's cancer-specific outcome null — the combination is unproven for cancer alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: a nested case-control study in 11,823 Barrett's patients (116 cancer cases, 696 controls), a retrospective cohort of 344 patients with 33 neoplasia events, and a 2025 systematic review of 16 observational studies plus 1 randomised trial. The AspECT trial record itself is homed on live shelf #773 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Aspirin/NSAID fills were associated with an adjusted incidence density ratio of 0.64 for adenocarcinoma where PPI use was near-universal (Nguyen 2010); PPI use was associated with less high-grade dysplasia/cancer with only a nonsignificant aspirin trend in a smaller cohort (Nguyen 2009); pooled observational aspirin data were nonsignificant (adjusted OR 0.84) with serious-to-critical bias throughout, and the one trial showed no significant cancer-specific association (Ko 2025). PROPOSED SPLIT (observational: benefit; bias-adjusted review and trial cancer outcome: no significant association).
cards.watchOut: Every favourable number on this shelf is observational and prescription-based; the moment bias is graded formally, the aspirin signal loses significance — do not read this shelf as a reason to start aspirin for Barrett's chemoprevention.

shelves.title: Steroid versus diet in eosinophilic esophagitis (no head-to-head trial): indirect evidence puts histologic response in the same range for both — 68–77% for swallowed steroids, 69% for six-food elimination
shelves.question: Is a swallowed topical steroid better than dietary elimination for eosinophilic esophagitis in adults?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Humans · Steroids · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #774, which covers swallowed budesonide versus placebo; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the head-to-head against dietary elimination. No randomised trial has compared a swallowed topical steroid directly with dietary elimination in adults. The comparison exists only indirectly: a meta-regression of 51 articles found summary histologic response rates of the same order for fluticasone (68.3%), budesonide (76.8%) and six-food elimination diet (69.0%), with the authors stating plainly that heterogeneity prevents direct comparison of the modalities (Cotton 2017). A modelled cost-utility analysis built on the same literature found topical fluticasone about as effective as the elimination diet but more expensive over 5 years, with the diet more effective and less expensive in the base case (Cotton 2017). In adults, the comparative literature is otherwise about combining the two rather than choosing between them (Reed 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no head-to-head trial exists; indirect evidence puts steroid and diet response rates in the same range, so neither can be called better.

cards.headline: Cotton 2017: across 51 articles, histologic response was 68.3% for fluticasone, 76.8% for budesonide and 69.0% for six-food elimination diet — the same order of magnitude, with direct comparison explicitly not possible
cards.summary: Cotton 2017: across 51 articles, histologic response was 68.3% for fluticasone, 76.8% for budesonide and 69.0% for six-food elimination diet — the same order of magnitude, with direct comparison explicitly not possible
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-regression of published studies of topical fluticasone, topical budesonide and six-food elimination diet for eosinophilic esophagitis (51 articles meeting inclusion criteria; mixed adult and paediatric literature, with age examined in the meta-regression).
cards.result: Summary histologic response rates were 68.3% (95% prediction limits 16.2–96.0%) for fluticasone, 76.8% (36.1–95.1%) for budesonide, and 69.0% (31.9–91.4%) for six-food elimination diet. Symptom response rates were 82.3%, 87.9% and 87.3% respectively. The authors conclude the response rates are on the same order of magnitude but that heterogeneity of study designs prevents direct comparison of modalities — there is no head-to-head estimate in this record.
cards.watchOut: These are side-by-side summaries of separate small studies, not a comparison within patients: prediction limits are extremely wide (16–96%), and differences in baseline eosinophil counts and age — not the treatments — explained much of the variation.
cards.source: Cotton CC et al. Six-Food Elimination Diet and Topical Steroids are Effective for Eosinophilic Esophagitis: A Meta-Regression. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2017. PMID: 28608048. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Administration, Topical · Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Humans · Steroids · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Cotton 2017: in a modelled cost-utility comparison, topical fluticasone was about as effective as six-food elimination but cost more over 5 years ($9,261.58 vs $5,719.72 per person), and the diet dominated both steroids in the base case
cards.summary: Cotton 2017: in a modelled cost-utility comparison, topical fluticasone was about as effective as six-food elimination but cost more over 5 years ($9,261.58 vs $5,719.72 per person), and the diet dominated both steroids in the base case
cards.people: Cost-utility analysis from the payer perspective using a modified Markov model, with transition probabilities and histologic response estimates taken from the group's systematic review and meta-regression of topical corticosteroids versus six-food elimination diet as first-line eosinophilic esophagitis therapy.
cards.result: In the base-case scenario, topical fluticasone was about as effective as the six-food elimination diet but more expensive at a 5-year horizon ($9261.58 vs $5719.72 per person); the diet was more effective and less expensive than both topical fluticasone and topical budesonide in the base case. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis showed little uncertainty in relative treatment effectiveness and somewhat greater uncertainty in relative cost, with most simulations finding the diet less expensive. Patient-level costs and quality of life were not accounted for.
cards.watchOut: A model, not a trial: its 'more effective' verdict for diet is inherited from the same indirect meta-regression inputs as the first card, so the two cards are not independent confirmations — and it prices payer costs only, not the burden of living on an elimination diet.
cards.source: Cotton CC et al. Cost Utility Analysis of Topical Steroids Compared With Dietary Elimination for Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 27940272. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Reed 2019: in adults, the comparative cohort literature studies diet and steroids combined rather than against each other — and this record's abstract reports no effect size for the combination
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study, abstract without effect size (Reed 2019)
cards.people: Adults with eosinophilic esophagitis treated with combination therapy of elimination diet plus topical corticosteroids (budesonide or fluticasone), reported as a retrospective cohort in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology (Reed 2019).
cards.result: The record's abstract is a brief report introduction and reports no effect size — no response rates, eosinophil counts or comparative numbers are printed in the record, and none are invented here. Its indexed finding, per its title, is that combination therapy with elimination diet and corticosteroids is effective for adults with eosinophilic esophagitis; the quantitative results sit in the full text, not in the record fetched this session.
cards.watchOut: Carded for what it shows about the state of the adult literature — clinicians combine the modalities — not as comparative evidence: with no numbers in the record it cannot rank steroid against diet, and combination success says nothing about which single therapy is better.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no head-to-head trial exists in adults; indirect summaries put histologic response in the same range for steroids (68–77%) and elimination diet (69%), and the only direct-comparison exercise is a cost model that found them about as effective
cards.summary: Synthesis: no head-to-head trial exists in adults; indirect summaries put histologic response in the same range for steroids (68–77%) and elimination diet (69%), and the only direct-comparison exercise is a cost model that found them about as effective
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-regression of 51 published articles, a cost-utility model built on that same literature, and an adult retrospective cohort of combination therapy whose record reports no effect size. Participant totals for the review-level cards are not documented as a single N in the records, so no total-N figure is printed; the limitation here is indirectness, not a small patient count.
cards.result: Histologic response rates were 68.3% (fluticasone), 76.8% (budesonide) and 69.0% (six-food elimination diet), with the reviewers stating direct comparison was prevented by heterogeneity (Cotton 2017). The cost-utility model found fluticasone about as effective as the diet but more expensive over 5 years (Cotton 2017). No carded record randomises or directly compares the two strategies in adults. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — neither therapy can be called better on current evidence.
cards.watchOut: Anyone claiming steroids beat diet (or the reverse) in adults is going beyond the evidence: the field has placebo-controlled steroid trials and diet trials, but the deciding head-to-head trial has not been done.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cotton CC et al. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2017 (PMID: 28608048); Cotton CC et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2017 (PMID: 27940272); Reed CC et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2019 (PMID: 30885887).

shelves.title: Dupilumab after steroid failure in eosinophilic esophagitis (subgroup evidence): benefit held regardless of prior steroid inadequate response or intolerance, with 60.9% vs 0.0% histologic remission in the paediatric refractory subgroup
shelves.question: Is dupilumab effective for eosinophilic esophagitis that does not respond to topical steroids?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Deglutition Disorders · Double-Blind Method · Endoscopy · Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Glucocorticoids · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #396, the dupilumab eosinophilic esophagitis shelf without the steroid-refractory specification; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — patients whose disease has already failed, not tolerated, or cannot take swallowed topical corticosteroids (STC). The evidence is subgroup analysis of a single trial programme, so it caps at POSSIBLE. In the phase 3 LIBERTY EoE TREET programme, prespecified subgroup analysis found dupilumab 300 mg weekly improved histologic, symptomatic and endoscopic outcomes versus placebo at week 24, maintained at week 52, regardless of prior STC use or of inadequate response, intolerance or contraindication to STC — though the record prints no effect sizes for these subgroups (Bredenoord 2024). A second programme report reaches the same conclusion by prior budesonide/fluticasone use (Bredenoord 2025). The one subgroup report with numbers is paediatric: in EoE KIDS, children with prior inadequate response/intolerance/contraindication to STC achieved histologic remission in 60.9% on higher-exposure dupilumab versus 0.0% on placebo at week 16 (Chehade 2026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, subgroup evidence: dupilumab works in the steroid-refractory population about as it does in steroid-naive disease, but no trial has enrolled a steroid-refractory population as its primary population.

cards.headline: Bredenoord 2024: in LIBERTY EoE TREET, dupilumab improved histology, symptoms and endoscopy versus placebo regardless of prior swallowed steroid use or inadequate response/intolerance/contraindication to steroids — with no subgroup effect sizes printed in the record
cards.summary: Bredenoord 2024: in LIBERTY EoE TREET, dupilumab improved histology, symptoms and endoscopy versus placebo regardless of prior swallowed steroid use or inadequate response/intolerance/contraindication to steroids — with no subgroup effect sizes printed in the record
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial (Bredenoord 2024)
cards.people: Prespecified subgroup analysis of the phase 3 LIBERTY EoE TREET study (adolescents and adults), categorising patients by prior swallowed topical corticosteroid (STC) use and by inadequate response, intolerance or contraindication to STC; dupilumab 300 mg once weekly versus placebo for 24 weeks (parts A and B), with a further 28 weeks in part C.
cards.result: Regardless of prior STC use, dupilumab increased the proportion of patients achieving ≤6 eosinophils per high-power field and improved Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire score versus placebo at week 24, with improvements maintained or improved at week 52; outcomes after switching from placebo to dupilumab at week 24 were similar to those in the dupilumab group at week 24, in every subgroup including inadequate/intolerance/contraindication to STC. The record reports no effect size (no percentages or score changes) for any subgroup — printed plainly, none is invented here. The authors conclude dupilumab was efficacious and well tolerated regardless of prior STC status.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup analysis, not a refractory-population trial: patients were enrolled for active EoE, then split by steroid history, so the refractory subgroup is smaller than the trial and its estimates — not printed in this record — carry subgroup uncertainty.
cards.source: Bredenoord AJ et al. Dupilumab demonstrated efficacy and was well tolerated regardless of prior use of swallowed topical corticosteroids in adolescent and adult patients with eosinophilic oesophagitis: a subgroup analysis of the phase 3 LIBERTY EoE TREET study. Gut. 2024. PMID: 38050037. Registry ID: NCT03633617. cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial (Bredenoord 2025)

cards.summary: Chehade 2026: in children whose EoE had failed or not tolerated swallowed steroids, higher-exposure dupilumab produced histologic remission in 60.9% versus 0.0% on placebo at week 16 (N = 102; subgroup N on the face)
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial, paediatric (Chehade 2026)
cards.people: Subgroup analysis of the phase 3 EoE KIDS study: 102 children aged 1–11 years with EoE unresponsive to proton-pump inhibitors, randomised to weight-tiered higher- or lower-exposure dupilumab or placebo to week 16, then continued or switched to week 52; 82 (80%) had prior swallowed topical corticosteroid use and 59 (58%) had prior inadequate response, intolerance and/or contraindication (IRIC) to steroids.
cards.result: At week 16, higher-exposure dupilumab improved histologic remission rates versus placebo in patients with prior steroid use (60.7% vs 0.0%, nominal P < 0.0001) and in patients with prior IRIC to steroids (60.9% vs 0.0%, nominal P < 0.0001); secondary endoscopic and histologic outcomes were similar, responses were maintained at week 52, and results were similar or numerically lower with lower-exposure dupilumab. Safety was consistent with the known dupilumab profile.
cards.watchOut: Children aged 1–11, not adults, and a subgroup of 59 IRIC patients within a 102-child trial: it is the only carded record with refractory-subgroup numbers, and its rates should not be transplanted directly onto adult practice.

cards.headline: Synthesis: within one trial programme, dupilumab's benefit holds in patients with prior steroid failure or intolerance — quantified in children (60.9% vs 0.0% histologic remission) and reported qualitatively, without effect sizes, in adolescents and adults
cards.summary: Synthesis: within one trial programme, dupilumab's benefit holds in patients with prior steroid failure or intolerance — quantified in children (60.9% vs 0.0% histologic remission) and reported qualitatively, without effect sizes, in adolescents and adults
cards.people: The carded evidence: two subgroup reports from the phase 3 LIBERTY EoE TREET programme in adolescents and adults (NCT03633617), and one subgroup report from the phase 3 EoE KIDS trial in 102 children, of whom 59 had prior inadequate response, intolerance or contraindication to swallowed steroids. All cards come from a single drug programme, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.result: Dupilumab improved histologic, symptomatic and endoscopic outcomes versus placebo irrespective of prior swallowed steroid use or steroid inadequate response/intolerance/contraindication, maintained to week 52 (Bredenoord 2024; Bredenoord 2025 — no effect sizes in either record). In children with prior steroid IRIC, histologic remission was 60.9% versus 0.0% at week 16 on higher-exposure dupilumab (Chehade 2026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, subgroup evidence.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised a steroid-refractory population as its primary population: the refractory claim rests on subgroup consistency, and the adult records do not print the subgroup numbers — a dedicated refractory-population trial could still shift the estimate.

shelves.title: P-CAB versus PPI for severe erosive esophagitis with nighttime breakthrough (inferred, not trialled): better severe healing than lansoprazole and stronger night-time acid suppression in pH studies — in two separate evidence bases
shelves.question: Is potassium-competitive acid blocker therapy better than proton pump inhibitors for severe erosive esophagitis with nighttime breakthrough?
shelves.mesh: Lansoprazole · Humans · Sulfonamides · Pyrroles · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Severity of Illness Index · Esophagitis, Peptic · Esophagitis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1661, which covers vonoprazan versus lansoprazole for healing of erosive esophagitis overall; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — severe (LA grade C/D) disease together with nighttime breakthrough. The two halves of the slice rest on different evidence. For severe healing, a meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials (2,208 participants) found vonoprazan 20 mg superior to lansoprazole 30 mg for healing severe esophagitis at weeks 2, 4 and 8 (week 8 relative risk 1.175), but not for mild disease (Simadibrata 2024) — the home shelf's trials re-pooled by severity, not re-carded here. For the nighttime half, no trial enrols severe esophagitis patients with nighttime breakthrough: the evidence is pharmacodynamic — in healthy volunteers, night-time intragastric pH ≥4 was held 60.5% of the night on vonoprazan and 66.0% on tegoprazan versus 36.1% on esomeprazole (Yang 2022, N = 16), tegoprazan raised pH ≥4 within 2 hours versus 7 hours for dexlansoprazole (Han 2023, N = 24), and a 55-trial network meta-analysis ranked vonoprazan and tegoprazan best for nocturnal acid inhibition (Zou 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the class heals severe esophagitis better than lansoprazole and suppresses night-time acid more than PPIs in healthy volunteers — but the exact population in the question has never been trialled.

cards.headline: Simadibrata 2024: across 4 randomised trials (2,208 participants), vonoprazan beat lansoprazole for healing SEVERE erosive esophagitis at every time point (week 8 relative risk 1.175) but not mild disease
cards.summary: Simadibrata 2024: across 4 randomised trials (2,208 participants), vonoprazan beat lansoprazole for healing SEVERE erosive esophagitis at every time point (week 8 relative risk 1.175) but not mild disease
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials (Simadibrata 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing vonoprazan 20 mg daily with lansoprazole 30 mg daily for healing of erosive esophagitis, with subgroup analysis by severity (Los Angeles grade A/B mild versus C/D severe) and by study location; 4 trials, 2,208 participants, all at low risk of bias.
cards.result: Vonoprazan was superior to lansoprazole for healing severe erosive esophagitis at all weeks (week 2 RR 1.294, 95% CI 1.169–1.433; week 4 RR 1.160, 1.059–1.270; week 8 RR 1.175, 95% CI 1.107–1.247 — relative measures; the record gives no absolute healing rates for the severe subgroup), but healing was similar for mild esophagitis (P-interaction < 0.01). Any, serious, and drug-related treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: A severity re-pooling of the same trials homed on shelf #1661: it sharpens the severe-disease answer but adds no new patients, and without absolute severe-subgroup healing rates the size of the advantage in percentage points cannot be stated from this record.
cards.source: Simadibrata DM et al. Vonoprazan is superior to lansoprazole for healing of severe but not mild erosive esophagitis: A systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2024. PMID: 38353152. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yang 2022: in 16 healthy volunteers, night-time gastric pH stayed ≥4 for 66.0% of the night on tegoprazan and 60.5% on vonoprazan versus 36.1% on esomeprazole (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Yang 2022: in 16 healthy volunteers, night-time gastric pH stayed ≥4 for 66.0% of the night on tegoprazan and 60.5% on vonoprazan versus 36.1% on esomeprazole (small N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised crossover pharmacodynamic study in healthy volunteers (Yang 2022)
cards.people: Randomised, open-label, 3-period, 6-sequence crossover study in 16 healthy subjects (6 CYP2C19 extensive, 5 intermediate and 5 poor metabolisers), each receiving a single night-time dose of tegoprazan 50 mg, vonoprazan 20 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg with continuous intragastric pH monitoring. Randomised N = 16.
cards.result: After tegoprazan, intragastric pH rose above 4 within approximately 1 hour and was maintained stably at night; the percentage of night-time at pH ≥4 was 66.0% for tegoprazan, 60.5% for vonoprazan and 36.1% for esomeprazole. Tegoprazan's night-time suppression was slightly but not significantly longer than vonoprazan's and greater than esomeprazole's; acid suppression by both potassium-competitive acid blockers was independent of CYP2C19 phenotype, while esomeprazole's tended to be influenced by it.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen healthy volunteers, single doses, a pH surrogate: this shows the class controls night-time acid in a normal stomach — it does not show better healing or fewer night symptoms in patients with severe erosive esophagitis.
cards.source: Yang E et al. Night-time gastric acid suppression by tegoprazan compared to vonoprazan or esomeprazole. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2022. PMID: 35146797. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Han 2023: in 24 healthy men, tegoprazan reached mean gastric pH ≥4 within 2 hours of evening dosing versus 7 hours for dexlansoprazole (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Han 2023: in 24 healthy men, tegoprazan reached mean gastric pH ≥4 within 2 hours of evening dosing versus 7 hours for dexlansoprazole (small N on the face)
cards.type: Randomised crossover pharmacodynamic study in healthy volunteers (Han 2023)
cards.people: Randomised, open-label, single-dose crossover study in 24 healthy male volunteers receiving oral tegoprazan (50, 100 or 200 mg) or dexlansoprazole 60 mg in each of two periods separated by a 7- to 10-day washout, with gastric pH monitoring. Randomised N = 24.
cards.result: All tegoprazan groups reached mean pH ≥4 within 2 hours, whereas the dexlansoprazole group required 7 hours after drug administration; up to 12 hours after evening dosing, 50, 100 and 200 mg tegoprazan showed a stronger acid-suppressive effect than 60 mg dexlansoprazole, with dose-dependent increases in the time with gastric pH above 4 and above 6. From 12 hours after dosing, dexlansoprazole's effect was comparable to the tegoprazan groups.
cards.watchOut: Healthy men only, single doses, and the comparator is one PPI formulation: the early-night advantage is a pharmacodynamic onset effect, and by 12 hours the PPI had caught up — no patient outcomes were measured.
cards.source: Han S et al. Comparison of Pharmacodynamics between Tegoprazan and Dexlansoprazole Regarding Nocturnal Acid Breakthrough: A Randomized Crossover Study. Gut and Liver. 2023. PMID: 36317518. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Male · Dexlansoprazole · Cross-Over Studies · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Benzene Derivatives · Imidazoles

cards.headline: Zou 2024: across 55 randomised trials (2,015 participants), vonoprazan (SUCRA 91.0%) and tegoprazan (91.8%) ranked best of all acid-suppressive regimens for nocturnal acid inhibition, ahead of every PPI group
cards.summary: Zou 2024: across 55 randomised trials (2,015 participants), vonoprazan (SUCRA 91.0%) and tegoprazan (91.8%) ranked best of all acid-suppressive regimens for nocturnal acid inhibition, ahead of every PPI group
cards.people: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 55 randomised trials with 2,015 participants comparing acid-suppressive drugs (potassium-competitive acid blockers, PPIs, H2-receptor antagonists, bedtime H2-blocker add-on, and placebo) on nocturnal acid-inhibitory effect.
cards.result: For nocturnal acid inhibition, tegoprazan (SUCRA 91.8%) and vonoprazan (SUCRA 91.0%) performed best, followed by newer PPIs (76.6%), bedtime H2-blocker add-on (61.3%), isomer PPIs such as esomeprazole and dexlansoprazole (38.6%), traditional PPIs (32.6%), H2-blockers (23.1%) and placebo (0.3%). In subgroups including crossover trials, younger and healthy participants, and night-time administration, vonoprazan or tegoprazan remained better than most regimens. The record reports rankings, not absolute pH or clinical outcome rates.
cards.watchOut: SUCRA rankings summarise pH studies, mostly in healthy volunteers: being ranked first on night-time pH is not evidence of better healing, symptom relief or safety in severe esophagitis, and rankings carry no effect size.
cards.source: Zou S et al. Acid-suppressive drugs: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of their nocturnal acid-inhibitory effect. Pharmacotherapy. 2024. PMID: 38049205. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Bayes Theorem · Gastric Acid · Histamine H2 Antagonists · Gastroesophageal Reflux

cards.headline: Synthesis: the class advantage is real on both halves of the slice — better severe-esophagitis healing than lansoprazole (week 8 relative risk 1.175) and stronger night-time acid suppression than PPIs — but the two halves have never been tested together in the patients the question names
cards.summary: Synthesis: the class advantage is real on both halves of the slice — better severe-esophagitis healing than lansoprazole (week 8 relative risk 1.175) and stronger night-time acid suppression than PPIs — but the two halves have never been tested together in the patients the question names
cards.people: The carded evidence: a severity-stratified meta-analysis of 4 healing trials (2,208 participants), two small randomised crossover pH studies in healthy volunteers (N = 16 and N = 24, printed on their faces), and a network meta-analysis of 55 nocturnal-acid trials (2,015 participants). Total carded participants exceed 4,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small volunteer studies carry their Ns on their faces.
cards.result: Vonoprazan healed severe (LA C/D) erosive esophagitis more often than lansoprazole at weeks 2, 4 and 8, with no advantage in mild disease (Simadibrata 2024). At night, potassium-competitive acid blockers held intragastric pH ≥4 for 60.5–66.0% of the night versus 36.1% for esomeprazole (Yang 2022), reached pH ≥4 hours faster than dexlansoprazole (Han 2023), and ranked first for nocturnal inhibition across 55 trials (Zou 2024). No carded trial enrols severe esophagitis patients selected for nighttime breakthrough. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the halves into a stronger claim than either supports: healing superiority is shown against lansoprazole in trial patients, night-time superiority is shown on pH in healthy volunteers — the combined claim for severe disease with nighttime breakthrough is an inference, and this shelf labels it as such.
cards.source: Synthesis of Simadibrata DM et al. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2024 (PMID: 38353152); Yang E et al. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2022 (PMID: 35146797); Han S et al. Gut and Liver. 2023 (PMID: 36317518); Zou S et al. Pharmacotherapy. 2024 (PMID: 38049205).

shelves.title: Bismuth in H. pylori salvage after first failure (LIKELY benefit): 98.0% vs 69.2% eradication for bismuth quadruple versus standard triple salvage, concordant across two network meta-analyses
shelves.question: Does adding bismuth to salvage therapy improve Helicobacter pylori eradication after a first treatment fails?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bismuth · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Helicobacter Infections · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Levofloxacin · Male · Middle Aged · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Taiwan · Tetracycline · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #777, which covers bismuth quadruple therapy as a regimen in the clarithromycin-resistance era; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — salvage after a first eradication attempt has failed, and specifically whether the bismuth component improves the salvage result. The direct trial randomised post-failure patients to a bismuth-containing quadruple salvage (esomeprazole, bismuth, tetracycline, levofloxacin) versus the standard non-bismuth levofloxacin triple: eradication was 98.0% versus 69.2% by intention-to-treat, an absolute difference of 28.8 percentage points (Hsu 2017). Two network meta-analyses of the second-line literature point the same way: bismuth quadruple regimens of 10–14 days sit among the most effective salvage options (Chang 2020, 54 studies, 8,752 participants), and non-quinolone bismuth quadruple therapy for 10 days or more beat 7-day triple therapy (odds ratio 2.25), with quinolone-based bismuth quadruple ranked the optimum second-line approach (Yeo 2019, 26 trials, 3,628 participants). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): concordant randomised and pooled evidence says adding bismuth to salvage therapy raises eradication after first-line failure, with duration of at least 10 days part of the effect.

cards.headline: Hsu 2017: after first-line failure, bismuth quadruple salvage eradicated H. pylori in 98.0% versus 69.2% on standard levofloxacin triple therapy — an absolute difference of 28.8 percentage points (N = 102)
cards.summary: Hsu 2017: after first-line failure, bismuth quadruple salvage eradicated H. pylori in 98.0% versus 69.2% on standard levofloxacin triple therapy — an absolute difference of 28.8 percentage points (N = 102)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial of 102 consecutive H. pylori-infected patients after failure of first-line therapies, allocated to 10 days of esomeprazole-bismuth-tetracycline-levofloxacin quadruple therapy (n = 50) or esomeprazole-amoxicillin-levofloxacin triple therapy (n = 52); H. pylori status was assessed 6 weeks after treatment, and the study was stopped after an interim analysis.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat eradication was 98.0% (49/50) with the bismuth quadruple regimen versus 69.2% (36/52) with triple therapy (difference 28.8%; 95% CI, 15.7% to 41.9%; P < 0.001); per-protocol results were similar (97.8% vs 68.6%, P < 0.001). The bismuth regimen was superior after failure of standard triple therapy (100% vs 75.0%, P = 0.010) and after failure of non-bismuth quadruple therapy (95.0% vs 52.6%, P = 0.003). Overall adverse events were 22.0% versus 11.5%, and compliance 90.0% versus 98.1%.
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early at an interim analysis, which tends to inflate effect sizes, and it compares whole regimens — the bismuth arm also swapped amoxicillin for tetracycline, so the 28.8-point gap is the bismuth-containing regimen's advantage, not bismuth alone isolated.
cards.source: Hsu PI et al. Ten-Day Quadruple Therapy Comprising Proton Pump Inhibitor, Bismuth, Tetracycline, and Levofloxacin is More Effective than Standard Levofloxacin Triple Therapy in the Second-Line Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 28719592. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chang 2020: across 54 second-line studies (8,752 participants), bismuth quadruple therapy for 10–14 days and quinolone-based bismuth quadruple therapy were significantly superior salvage regimens, including after documented first-line triple failure
cards.summary: Chang 2020: across 54 second-line studies (8,752 participants), bismuth quadruple therapy for 10–14 days and quinolone-based bismuth quadruple therapy were significantly superior salvage regimens, including after documented first-line triple failure
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials (January 2000 to September 2018) of second-line H. pylori eradication regimens: 54 studies totalling 8,752 participants receiving 16 regimens, with subgroup analyses by clarithromycin and levofloxacin resistance and by documented failure of first-line triple therapy.
cards.result: Compared with 7-day bismuth quadruple therapy, the significantly superior regimens included quinolone-based bismuth quadruple therapy for 10–14 days and bismuth quadruple therapy for 10–14 days, alongside quinolone-based sequential and triple therapies and probiotic add-on strategies. Subgroup rankings were distributed similarly in high clarithromycin-resistance and high levofloxacin-resistance countries and in patients with documented failure of first-line triple therapy. The record reports the ranking and significance, not pooled eradication rates per regimen.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean on indirect comparisons across eras and resistance backgrounds: they support bismuth quadruple as a class choice for salvage, but the exact gain over any one named alternative depends on local resistance, which the pooled record cannot supply.
cards.source: Chang YL et al. Efficacy of second-line regimens for Helicobacter pylori eradication treatment: a systemic review and network meta-analysis. BMJ Open Gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 32883715. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yeo 2019: across 26 second-line trials (3,628 participants), non-quinolone bismuth quadruple therapy for 10+ days beat 7-day triple therapy (odds ratio 2.25), and quinolone-based bismuth quadruple ranked the optimum salvage regimen
cards.summary: Yeo 2019: across 26 second-line trials (3,628 participants), non-quinolone bismuth quadruple therapy for 10+ days beat 7-day triple therapy (odds ratio 2.25), and quinolone-based bismuth quadruple ranked the optimum salvage regimen
cards.people: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised trials (January 2005 to February 2018) of second-line H. pylori regimens in patients with persistent infection after first-line treatment: 26 trials with 3,628 participants; evidence quality appraised with GRADE.
cards.result: All regimens showed pooled eradication rates under 90%. Compared with 7-day triple therapy, quinolone-based therapy (OR 4.29, 95% credible interval 1.67–12.12; SUCRA 0.95 — a relative measure), non-quinolone-based bismuth-containing quadruple therapy for 10 days or more (OR 2.25, 95% CrI 1.10–4.62; SUCRA 0.78), and sequential therapy (OR 2.91) were significantly more effective. Longer regimens had higher eradication but more adverse events. The authors conclude quinolone-based bismuth-containing quadruple therapies for 10 days or more are the optimum second-line regimens.
cards.watchOut: Even the best salvage regimens pooled under 90% eradication, and the bismuth advantage is entangled with treatment duration (10+ days) — the record cannot separate how much is bismuth and how much is simply treating longer.
cards.source: Yeo YH et al. Systematic review and network meta-analysis: Comparative effectiveness of therapies for second-line Helicobacter pylori eradication. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2019. PMID: 30169908. Registry ID: none in the record.
