cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — bismuth-containing salvage outperforms non-bismuth salvage after first-line failure, by 28.8 absolute percentage points in the direct trial and consistently across two network meta-analyses totalling over 12,000 participants
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — bismuth-containing salvage outperforms non-bismuth salvage after first-line failure, by 28.8 absolute percentage points in the direct trial and consistently across two network meta-analyses totalling over 12,000 participants
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre randomised salvage trial (N = 102), and two network meta-analyses of the second-line randomised literature (54 studies, 8,752 participants; 26 trials, 3,628 participants). Total carded participants exceed 12,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Bismuth quadruple salvage eradicated 98.0% versus 69.2% for standard levofloxacin triple therapy by intention-to-treat (Hsu 2017). Bismuth quadruple regimens of 10–14 days ranked significantly superior among 16 second-line regimens, including after documented triple-therapy failure (Chang 2020), and bismuth-containing quadruple therapy for 10 days or more beat 7-day triple therapy (OR 2.25) in a second network analysis (Yeo 2019). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The direct trial was stopped early and changed two drugs at once, and pooled salvage eradication still sits under 90%: bismuth improves salvage, it does not make salvage certain — susceptibility-guided choices and local resistance still govern the individual patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hsu PI et al. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2017 (PMID: 28719592); Chang YL et al. BMJ Open Gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 32883715); Yeo YH et al. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2019 (PMID: 30169908).

shelves.title: Risankizumab induction in Crohn's disease (LIKELY benefit): remission 45% vs 25% and 42% vs 20% over placebo in ADVANCE and MOTIVATE, with endoscopic response to match
shelves.question: Does risankizumab induce remission in adults with moderate to severe Crohn's disease?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Biological Products · Crohn Disease · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #771, which covers the head-to-head SEQUENCE comparison of risankizumab versus ustekinumab; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the placebo-controlled induction evidence (ADVANCE and MOTIVATE). Both phase 3 induction trials met all coprimary endpoints at week 12 at both doses: in ADVANCE, CDAI clinical remission was 45% on risankizumab 600 mg versus 25% on placebo (adjusted difference 21 percentage points) and endoscopic response 40% versus 12%; in MOTIVATE, in biologic-experienced patients, remission was 42% versus 20% and endoscopic response 29% versus 11% (D'Haens 2022). An earlier phase 2 placebo-controlled trial pointed the same way (pooled remission 31% versus 15%; Feagan 2017), and a meta-analysis of the IL-23 class found a relative risk of 1.87 for inducing clinical remission versus placebo at high certainty (Vuyyuru 2023). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, supported by phase 2 and class-level pooling, establish that risankizumab induces clinical remission and endoscopic response in moderate to severe Crohn's disease.

cards.headline: D'Haens 2022 (ADVANCE and MOTIVATE): risankizumab 600 mg induced CDAI remission in 45% vs 25% (ADVANCE) and 42% vs 20% (MOTIVATE) over placebo at week 12, with endoscopic response 40% vs 12% and 29% vs 11% — all coprimary endpoints met in both trials
cards.summary: D'Haens 2022 (ADVANCE and MOTIVATE): risankizumab 600 mg induced CDAI remission in 45% vs 25% (ADVANCE) and 42% vs 20% (MOTIVATE) over placebo at week 12, with endoscopic response 40% vs 12% and 29% vs 11% — all coprimary endpoints met in both trials
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials reported in one paper (D'Haens 2022)
cards.people: Two randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase 3 induction trials in patients aged 16–80 years with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, given intravenous risankizumab (600 mg or 1200 mg) or placebo at weeks 0, 4 and 8. ADVANCE (intolerance or inadequate response to biologics or conventional therapy): 931 assigned (600 mg n = 373, 1200 mg n = 372, placebo n = 186), 850 in the primary analysis. MOTIVATE (prior intolerance or inadequate response to biologics): 618 assigned (600 mg n = 206, 1200 mg n = 205, placebo n = 207), 569 in the primary analysis.
cards.result: ADVANCE at week 12: CDAI clinical remission 45% (152/336) on 600 mg and 42% (141/339) on 1200 mg versus 25% (43/175) on placebo (adjusted differences 21%, 95% CI 12–29, and 17%, 8–25); stool-frequency/abdominal-pain remission 43% and 41% versus 22%; endoscopic response 40% (135/336) and 32% (109/339) versus 12% (21/175). MOTIVATE at week 12: CDAI remission 42% (80/191) on 600 mg and 40% (77/191) on 1200 mg versus 20% (37/187) on placebo (adjusted differences 22%, 95% CI 13–31, and 21%, 12–29); stool-frequency/abdominal-pain remission 35% and 40% versus 19%; endoscopic response 29% (55/191) and 34% (65/191) versus 11% (21/187). All coprimary endpoints were met at both doses in both trials (P ≤ 0.0001, as printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: The 1200 mg dose performed no better than 600 mg on remission, so more drug is not more benefit; MOTIVATE's patients had already failed biologics, so its placebo rate and gains should not be transplanted onto biologic-naive patients; and both trials enrolled from age 16, so a small adolescent fraction sits inside this adult-framed shelf.
cards.source: D'Haens G et al. Risankizumab as induction therapy for Crohn's disease: results from the phase 3 ADVANCE and MOTIVATE induction trials. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35644154. Registry ID: NCT03105128 (ADVANCE); NCT03104413 (MOTIVATE). MeSH: Abdominal Pain · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Biological Products · Crohn Disease · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy

cards.headline: Feagan 2017: the phase 2 placebo-controlled trial pointed the same way first — pooled risankizumab remission 31% versus 15% on placebo at week 12 (difference 15.0%, P = 0.0489; N = 121)
cards.summary: Feagan 2017: the phase 2 placebo-controlled trial pointed the same way first — pooled risankizumab remission 31% versus 15% on placebo at week 12 (difference 15.0%, P = 0.0489; N = 121)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 study at 36 referral sites in patients aged 18–75 years with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 220–450 with mucosal ulcers): 121 patients randomised to intravenous risankizumab 200 mg (n = 41), 600 mg (n = 41) or placebo (n = 39) at weeks 0, 4 and 8; 93% had previously been treated with at least one TNF antagonist.
cards.result: At week 12, clinical remission (CDAI < 150) was achieved by 25 (31%) of 82 pooled risankizumab patients versus 6 (15%) of 39 placebo patients (difference 15.0%, 95% CI 0.1 to 30.1; P = 0.0489); by dose, remission was 24% on 200 mg (P = 0.31) and 37% on 600 mg (difference 20.9%, 2.6 to 39.2; P = 0.0252). Adverse events occurred in 79% overall; the most common serious adverse event was worsening of the underlying Crohn's disease, and no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: A 121-patient phase 2 study whose pooled result just reaches significance (P = 0.0489) and whose low dose did not: it is supporting evidence for the phase 3 pair, not a stand-alone proof.
cards.source: Feagan BG et al. Induction therapy with the selective interleukin-23 inhibitor risankizumab in patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 study. cards.headline: Vuyyuru 2023: across 18 trials (5,561 patients), targeting IL-23 induced clinical remission with a relative risk of 1.87 versus placebo — high-certainty class evidence behind the risankizumab trials
cards.summary: Vuyyuru 2023: across 18 trials (5,561 patients), targeting IL-23 induced clinical remission with a relative risk of 1.87 versus placebo — high-certainty class evidence behind the risankizumab trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised placebo- or active-comparator-controlled induction and maintenance trials of selective IL-23p19 and IL-12/23p40 inhibitors in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (paediatric and adult): 18 trials, n = 5,561, most rated low risk of bias, with GRADE certainty assessed.
cards.result: Targeting IL-23 was superior to placebo for inducing clinical remission (risk ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.58–2.21 — a relative measure) and endoscopic remission (RR 3.20, 95% CI 2.17–4.70), and for maintaining clinical remission (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.10–1.77), at high GRADE certainty for all outcomes. Induction benefit held in biologic-naive (RR 2.20) and biologic-experienced (RR 1.82) subgroups. Targeting IL-23 was associated with a decreased risk of serious adverse events during induction versus placebo (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.44–0.73).
cards.watchOut: A class-level pool that mixes IL-23p19 agents with the IL-12/23p40 inhibitor ustekinumab and mixes induction with maintenance trials: it corroborates the mechanism, while the risankizumab-specific numbers live on the trial cards.
cards.source: Vuyyuru SK et al. Efficacy and Safety of IL-12/23 and IL-23 Inhibitors for Crohn's Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2023. PMID: 37378711. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, a concordant phase 2 trial and high-certainty class pooling all show risankizumab inducing remission and endoscopic response by week 12
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, a concordant phase 2 trial and high-certainty class pooling all show risankizumab inducing remission and endoscopic response by week 12
cards.people: The carded evidence: ADVANCE (931 assigned; conventional- or biologic-failure population) and MOTIVATE (618 assigned; biologic-failure population) reported in one paper, a phase 2 trial (121 randomised), and a meta-analysis of 18 IL-23 trials (5,561 patients). Unique risankizumab induction participants exceed 1,600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: CDAI remission at week 12 was 45% versus 25% (ADVANCE, 600 mg) and 42% versus 20% (MOTIVATE, 600 mg), with endoscopic response 40% versus 12% and 29% versus 11% respectively (D'Haens 2022). The phase 2 trial found pooled remission 31% versus 15% (Feagan 2017), and IL-23 targeting induced remission at a relative risk of 1.87 versus placebo across the class (Vuyyuru 2023). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Induction is not maintenance or comparative effectiveness: this shelf says nothing about how long remission lasts or how risankizumab compares with ustekinumab head-to-head — that comparison is homed on live shelf #771.
cards.source: Synthesis of D'Haens G et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35644154); Feagan BG et al. Lancet. 2017 (PMID: 28411872); Vuyyuru SK et al. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2023 (PMID: 37378711).

shelves.title: Methotrexate for Crohn's relapse prevention (POSSIBLE, intramuscular only): continuing weekly injections after methotrexate-induced remission kept 65% vs 39% in remission at 40 weeks
shelves.question: Does methotrexate prevent relapse in adults with Crohn's disease in remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Crohn Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Injections, Intramuscular · Male · Methotrexate · Prednisone · Recurrence · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3584, which covers methotrexate for inducing remission in refractory Crohn's disease; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — relapse prevention in patients already in remission. The pivotal trial took patients who had entered remission on intramuscular methotrexate and randomised them to continue low-dose intramuscular methotrexate or switch to placebo: at 40 weeks, 65% remained in remission on methotrexate versus 39% on placebo, an absolute reduction in relapse risk of 26.1 percentage points, and fewer methotrexate patients needed prednisone for relapse (28% vs 58%) (Feagan 2000). The Cochrane review of 5 studies (333 patients) confirms intramuscular methotrexate's superiority at 40 weeks (relative risk 1.67 for maintained remission) but finds the oral-route evidence thin and not statistically significant, and oral methotrexate no better than 6-mercaptopurine (Patel 2014). A small earlier oral trial showed only a nonsignificant trend to fewer flares (Arora 1999). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the maintenance benefit is proven for weekly intramuscular methotrexate after methotrexate-induced remission, in one 76-patient trial — the route, the induction history and the single-trial base all limit it.

cards.headline: Feagan 2000: after remission induced by methotrexate, continuing weekly intramuscular methotrexate kept 65% in remission at 40 weeks versus 39% on placebo — an absolute relapse-risk reduction of 26.1 points (N = 76)
cards.summary: Feagan 2000: after remission induced by methotrexate, continuing weekly intramuscular methotrexate kept 65% in remission at 40 weeks versus 39% on placebo — an absolute relapse-risk reduction of 26.1 points (N = 76)
cards.people: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre North American Crohn's Study Group trial: patients with chronically active Crohn's disease who had entered remission after 16–24 weeks of intramuscular methotrexate 25 mg weekly were randomised to methotrexate 15 mg intramuscularly once weekly (n = 40) or placebo (n = 36) for 40 weeks, with no other Crohn's treatments permitted; remission was a Crohn's Disease Activity Index score of 150 or less.
cards.result: At week 40, 26 patients (65%) were in remission in the methotrexate group compared with 14 (39%) in the placebo group (P = 0.04; absolute reduction in the risk of relapse, 26.1%; 95% CI, 4.4% to 47.8%). Fewer methotrexate patients required prednisone for relapse (11 of 40 [28%] vs 21 of 36 [58%], P = 0.01). No methotrexate patient had a severe adverse event; one withdrew because of nausea.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-six patients whose remission was itself methotrexate-induced: the trial answers 'should methotrexate responders keep taking it?', not 'should any patient in remission start methotrexate?' — and the confidence interval on the benefit is wide (4.4 to 47.8 points).
cards.source: Feagan BG et al. A comparison of methotrexate with placebo for the maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease. North American Crohn's Study Group Investigators. New England Journal of Medicine. 2000. PMID: 10833208. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Patel 2014 (Cochrane): across 5 maintenance studies (333 patients), intramuscular methotrexate beat placebo (relative risk 1.67 for maintained remission), but oral methotrexate evidence was sparse and not significant
cards.summary: Patel 2014 (Cochrane): across 5 maintenance studies (333 patients), intramuscular methotrexate beat placebo (relative risk 1.67 for maintained remission), but oral methotrexate evidence was sparse and not significant
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of methotrexate for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease, searching to 9 June 2014: 5 studies, n = 333 patients; 3 studies at low risk of bias and 2 at high risk of bias due to blinding.
cards.result: Intramuscular methotrexate was superior to placebo for maintenance of remission at 40 weeks: 65% of intramuscular methotrexate patients maintained remission versus 39% on placebo (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.67 — a relative measure; 76 patients), with a number needed to treat of 4 to prevent one relapse and moderate GRADE quality. There was no statistically significant difference at 36 weeks between oral methotrexate (12.5 mg/week) and placebo (22 patients; low GRADE quality). A pooled analysis of two small studies (n = 50) showed no statistically significant difference in continued remission between oral methotrexate and 6-mercaptopurine (77% vs 57%; RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.92 to 2.00).
cards.watchOut: The review's positive pooled result is the single Feagan trial re-counted: the remaining studies are small, partly unblinded, and concern the oral route — so the shelf's certainty rests on one trial programme, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Patel V et al. Methotrexate for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25157445. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arora 1999: oral methotrexate showed only a nonsignificant trend to fewer flares in steroid-dependent Crohn's — 46% versus 80% flared, P < 0.1 (small N = 33 on the face)
cards.summary: Arora 1999: oral methotrexate showed only a nonsignificant trend to fewer flares in steroid-dependent Crohn's — 46% versus 80% flared, P < 0.1 (small N = 33 on the face)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral methotrexate in 33 patients with steroid-dependent Crohn's disease, a third of whom had previously failed 6-mercaptopurine; methotrexate 15 mg/week (adjustable to 22.5 mg/week) or placebo for up to 1 year or until treatment failure, with 28 patients evaluable after 5 dropped out. Randomised N = 33.
cards.result: Fewer methotrexate-treated patients (6/13, 46%) had flares of Crohn's disease than placebo-treated patients (12/15, 80%), but this did not achieve statistical significance (P < 0.1, as printed in the record). There was a nonsignificant trend toward more significant side effects on methotrexate (3/13, 23%, vs 0/15, 0%; P < 0.2), and laboratory indices of inflammation did not differ between groups. The authors describe a trend toward fewer flares balanced by more side effects.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-three randomised and only 28 evaluable patients, in steroid-dependent active disease rather than stable remission: it is the oral-route cautionary card — underpowered, nonsignificant, and not the population in this shelf's question.
cards.source: Arora S et al. Methotrexate in Crohn's disease: results of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Hepato-Gastroenterology. 1999. PMID: 10430331. cards.headline: Synthesis: weekly intramuscular methotrexate prevents relapse after methotrexate-induced remission (65% vs 39% still in remission at 40 weeks); oral methotrexate for maintenance is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: weekly intramuscular methotrexate prevents relapse after methotrexate-induced remission (65% vs 39% still in remission at 40 weeks); oral methotrexate for maintenance is unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: one pivotal randomised maintenance trial (76 patients, all prior methotrexate responders), a Cochrane review of 5 studies (333 patients, overlapping the pivotal trial), and one small oral-route trial (33 randomised, 28 evaluable). Unique participants total roughly 380 with the overlap noted, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the single small trials carry their Ns on their faces.
cards.result: Continuing intramuscular methotrexate 15 mg weekly kept 65% in remission versus 39% on placebo at 40 weeks, with prednisone rescue needed by 28% versus 58% (Feagan 2000). Cochrane pooling confirms the intramuscular result (RR 1.67, relative) and finds oral methotrexate not significantly better than placebo or 6-mercaptopurine (Patel 2014); the small oral trial's flare difference was nonsignificant (Arora 1999). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pivotal trial, intramuscular route only.
cards.watchOut: Route and history are the whole story here: the proven regimen is weekly injections continued after methotrexate itself induced remission — extrapolating to oral methotrexate, or to patients whose remission came from another drug, goes beyond every card on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feagan BG et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2000 (PMID: 10833208); Patel V et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25157445); Arora S et al. Hepato-Gastroenterology. 1999 (PMID: 10430331).

shelves.title: Probiotics for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis: E coli Nissle 1917 and Lactobacillus GG matched mesalazine in trials, but placebo-controlled proof is lacking (PARTIAL completion of the pouchitis shelf #2776)
shelves.question: Do probiotics help maintain remission in adults with ulcerative colitis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy,pathology,therapy · Double-Blind Method · Escherichia coli · Female · Humans · Male · Mesalamine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Probiotics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Recurrence · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2776 covers probiotic maintenance of remission in chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch surgery for ulcerative colitis; the slice carded here is ulcerative colitis itself, in adults whose disease is in remission. The strongest evidence is active-comparator, not placebo: Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 matched mesalazine in two double-blind trials (Kruis 1997, 12 weeks, relapse 16.0% on E coli Nissle vs 11.3% on mesalazine, not significant; Kruis 2004, 12 months, per-protocol relapse 36.4% vs 33.9%, significant equivalence P = 0.003). Lactobacillus GG likewise showed no difference in relapse rate versus mesalazine at 12 months (Zocco 2006, P = 0.77), though relapse-free time was longer (P < 0.05). The one placebo-controlled trial carded was small and negative: Lactobacillus acidophilus La-5 plus Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 maintained remission in 25% vs 8% on placebo, not significant (Wildt 2011, N = 32 printed on the face). No carded trial shows a probiotic beating placebo or standard therapy for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis; the tested preparations are specific named strains/preparations, and results cannot be assumed for other probiotic products. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — specific tested preparations (E coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus GG) performed as well as mesalazine in maintenance trials, but placebo-controlled evidence is thin and the one small placebo trial made no significant difference.

cards.headline: Kruis 2004: over 12 months, E coli Nissle 1917 maintained ulcerative colitis remission as effectively as mesalazine — per-protocol relapse 36.4% vs 33.9%, with significant equivalence (P = 0.003)
cards.summary: Kruis 2004: over 12 months, E coli Nissle 1917 maintained ulcerative colitis remission as effectively as mesalazine — per-protocol relapse 36.4% vs 33.9%, with significant equivalence (P = 0.003)
cards.people: 327 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission, recruited for a double-blind, double-dummy trial of the probiotic preparation Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 200 mg once daily (n = 162) versus mesalazine 500 mg three times daily (n = 165), followed for 12 months with clinical and endoscopic activity indices and histology; the per-protocol relapse analysis included 110 and 112 patients respectively.
cards.result: Per-protocol relapses occurred in 40/110 (36.4%) patients in the E coli Nissle 1917 group and 38/112 (33.9%) in the mesalazine group (significant equivalence, P = 0.003). Subgroup analyses showed no differences by duration or localisation of disease or pretrial treatment. The safety profile and tolerability were very good for both groups and not different. The authors conclude the probiotic shows efficacy and safety in maintaining remission equivalent to mesalazine.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is mesalazine, not placebo: equivalence to an active maintenance drug does not by itself prove the probiotic beats no treatment, and the headline analysis is per-protocol (222 of 327 recruited).
cards.source: Kruis W et al. Maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis with the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 is as effective as with standard mesalazine. Gut. 2004. PMID: 15479682. randomised controlled trial (kruis 2004) 327 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission, recruited for a double-blind, double-dummy trial of the probiotic preparation escherichia coli nissle 1917 200 mg once daily (n = 162) versus mesalazine 500 mg three times daily (n = 165), followed for 12 months with clinical and endoscopic activity indices and histology; the per-protocol relapse analysis included 110 and 112 patients respectively. per-protocol relapses occurred in 40/110 (36.4%) patients in the e coli nissle 1917 group and 38/112 (33.9%) in the mesalazine group (significant equivalence, p = 0.003). subgroup analyses showed no differences by duration or localisation of disease or pretrial treatment. the safety profile and tolerability were very good for both groups and not different. the authors conclude the probiotic shows efficacy and safety in maintaining remission equivalent to mesalazine. the comparator is mesalazine, not placebo: equivalence to an active maintenance drug does not by itself prove the probiotic beats no treatment, and the headline analysis is per-protocol (222 of 327 recruited). kruis w et al. maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis with the probiotic escherichia coli nissle 1917 is as effective as with standard mesalazine. gut. 2004. pmid: 15479682. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · anti-inflammatory agents, non-steroidal/therapeutic use · colitis, ulcerative/drug therapy,pathology,therapy · double-blind method · escherichia coli · female · humans · male · mesalamine/therapeutic use · middle aged · probiotics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · recurrence · remission induction

cards.headline: Kruis 1997: in the earlier 12-week double-blind trial, relapse was 16.0% on E coli Nissle 1917 vs 11.3% on mesalazine — no significant difference (N = 120)
cards.summary: Kruis 1997: in the earlier 12-week double-blind trial, relapse was 16.0% on E coli Nissle 1917 vs 11.3% on mesalazine — no significant difference (N = 120)
cards.people: 120 patients with inactive ulcerative colitis in a double-blind, double-dummy study comparing mesalazine 500 mg three times daily with an oral preparation of viable E coli strain Nissle (serotype O6:K5:H1) for 12 weeks; outcomes were clinical activity index (CAI), relapse rates, relapse-free times and global assessment.
cards.result: Start and end CAI scores showed no significant difference between groups (P = 0.12). Relapse rates were 11.3% under mesalazine and 16.0% under E coli Nissle 1917 (not significant). Life-table relapse-free time was 103 ± 4 days for mesalazine and 106 ± 5 days for E coli Nissle 1917 (not significant). Global assessment was similar, tolerability was excellent in both groups, and no serious adverse events were reported. The authors describe probiotic treatment as another option for maintenance therapy, on a preliminary study.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is short for a maintenance question, and the point estimate for relapse numerically favoured mesalazine; this trial supports 'not clearly worse', not benefit.
cards.source: Kruis W et al. Double-blind comparison of an oral Escherichia coli preparation and mesalazine in maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1997. PMID: 9354192. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zocco 2006: Lactobacillus GG alone or with mesalazine showed no difference in relapse rate versus mesalazine at 12 months (P = 0.77), but relapse-free time was longer on Lactobacillus GG (P < 0.05)
cards.summary: Zocco 2006: Lactobacillus GG alone or with mesalazine showed no difference in relapse rate versus mesalazine at 12 months (P = 0.77), but relapse-free time was longer on Lactobacillus GG (P < 0.05)
cards.people: 187 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis randomised to Lactobacillus GG 18 × 10^9 viable bacteria/day (65 patients), mesalazine 2400 mg/day (60 patients), or Lactobacillus GG plus mesalazine (62 patients), with disease activity index, endoscopic and histological scores at 0, 6 and 12 months and at relapse; the primary endpoint was sustained remission.
cards.result: Overall analysis showed no difference in relapse rate at 6 months (P = 0.44) or 12 months (P = 0.77) among the three treatment groups. However, treatment with Lactobacillus GG seemed more effective than standard mesalazine in prolonging the relapse-free time (P < 0.05). The authors conclude Lactobacillus GG seems effective and safe for maintaining remission and could be an option for preventing relapse.
cards.watchOut: The positive finding is a secondary time-to-relapse signal in a trial whose primary relapse-rate comparison made no difference between groups (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome as analysed).
cards.source: Zocco MA et al. Efficacy of Lactobacillus GG in maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2006. PMID: 16696804. cards.headline: Wildt 2011: the carded placebo-controlled trial was small (N = 32, printed on the face) and negative — remission maintained in 25% on La-5/BB-12 vs 8% on placebo at 1 year (P = 0.37, the treatment made no significant difference)
cards.summary: Wildt 2011: the carded placebo-controlled trial was small (N = 32, printed on the face) and negative — remission maintained in 25% on La-5/BB-12 vs 8% on placebo at 1 year (P = 0.37, the treatment made no significant difference)
cards.people: 32 patients with left-sided ulcerative colitis in remission (including proctitis, with at least one relapse within the last year) randomised 2:1 in a double-blind placebo-controlled study to Probio-Tec AB-25 (Lactobacillus acidophilus La-5 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12; 20 patients) or placebo (12 patients) for 52 weeks; no other ulcerative colitis medication was allowed. Randomised N = 32.
cards.result: Five patients (25%) in the Probio-Tec AB-25 group and one patient (8%) in the placebo group maintained remission after 1 year (P = 0.37). Median time to relapse was 125.5 days (range 11–391) on probiotic and 104 days (range 28–369) on placebo (P = 0.683). Probio-Tec AB-25 was overall well tolerated. The authors conclude no significant clinical benefit could be demonstrated versus placebo in this small trial.
cards.watchOut: With 32 patients this trial can neither prove nor exclude a maintenance effect; it is carded because it is the placebo-controlled counterweight to the mesalazine-comparator trials, and its small N is printed on the face.
cards.source: Wildt S et al. A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with Lactobacillus acidophilus La-5 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 for maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis. Journal of Crohn's & Colitis. 2011. PMID: 21453880. Registry ID: NCT00268164. cards.headline: Synthesis: named probiotic preparations (E coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus GG) performed as well as mesalazine for maintaining ulcerative colitis remission, but no carded trial shows a probiotic beating placebo — the one small placebo trial was negative
cards.summary: Synthesis: named probiotic preparations (E coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus GG) performed as well as mesalazine for maintaining ulcerative colitis remission, but no carded trial shows a probiotic beating placebo — the one small placebo trial was negative
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind E coli Nissle 1917 versus mesalazine trials (N = 120 over 12 weeks; N = 327 recruited over 12 months), one three-arm Lactobacillus GG trial (N = 187), and one small placebo-controlled La-5/BB-12 trial (N = 32). Total carded participants = 666, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small placebo trial's N is printed on its face.
cards.result: Relapse on E coli Nissle 1917 was 16.0% vs 11.3% on mesalazine at 12 weeks (not significant) and 36.4% vs 33.9% per-protocol at 12 months (equivalence P = 0.003). Lactobacillus GG showed no difference in relapse rate versus mesalazine at 12 months (P = 0.77) with longer relapse-free time (P < 0.05). La-5/BB-12 maintained remission in 25% vs 8% on placebo (P = 0.37, not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — equivalence to mesalazine for the named tested preparations; superiority over placebo unproven.
cards.watchOut: Probiotic effects are preparation-specific: these results concern the exact strains named on the cards (E coli Nissle 1917; Lactobacillus GG; La-5/BB-12) and cannot be extended to other products, whose composition and quality may differ.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kruis W et al. Gut. 2004 (PMID: 15479682); Kruis W et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1997 (PMID: 9354192); Zocco MA et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2006 (PMID: 16696804); Wildt S et al. Journal of Crohn's & Colitis. 2011 (PMID: 21453880).

shelves.title: How long on strict low FODMAP before reintroducing? No duration trial exists — services restrict for weeks to 2 months, then reintroduce, and completing reintroduction tracks with long-term benefit (PARTIAL completion of the low-FODMAP efficacy shelf #202)
shelves.question: How long should adults stay on the strict low FODMAP diet before reintroducing foods for irritable bowel syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anthropometry · Diet, Carbohydrate-Restricted/methods,statistics & numerical data · Disaccharides/analysis · Electric Impedance · Female · Fermentation · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/diet therapy,physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Monosaccharides/analysis · Nutrition Assessment · Nutritional Status · Oligosaccharides/analysis · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Polymers/analysis · Quality of Life · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #202 covers whether the low FODMAP diet works for irritable bowel syndrome; the slice carded here is the timing question — how long the strict restriction phase should last before reintroduction. The honest headline is that no carded study randomised patients to different strict-phase durations, so there is no trial-derived number of weeks. What the fetched records do show is how the phased diet is actually run and what happens after reintroduction: in the Bellini 2020 service cohort, patients started the reintroduction phase after 2 months of restriction, and symptoms, quality of life and nutritional adequacy were maintained long term on an adapted diet. Completion of reintroduction as per protocol was itself associated with long-term symptom improvement in the Foulkes 2025 service evaluation (P = 0.049), satisfactory relief was 69% after restriction and 57% long term in O'Keeffe 2018, and a personalised post-reintroduction diet sustained adequate relief in 67% at 12 months in the small Staudacher 2022 follow-up (N = 18, printed on the face). The evidence therefore supports treating restriction as a short diagnostic phase — weeks to about two months in the services reported — followed by structured reintroduction, rather than staying strict indefinitely; it does not support any precise week count. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational/service evidence only: no duration trial exists, and the timing answer is descriptive, not tested.

cards.headline: Bellini 2020: in this service cohort the reintroduction phase began after 2 months of strict low FODMAP restriction — and benefit and nutritional adequacy persisted on the adapted diet at 6–24 months
cards.summary: Bellini 2020: in this service cohort the reintroduction phase began after 2 months of strict low FODMAP restriction — and benefit and nutritional adequacy persisted on the adapted diet at 6–24 months
cards.people: 73 patients with irritable bowel syndrome given a low FODMAP diet (T0); after 2 months (T1), 68 started the reintroduction phase; at the end of that period (T2), 59 were advised to continue an adapted low FODMAP diet, and 41 were evaluated again after a 6–24 month follow-up (T3). Questionnaires and bioelectrical impedance vector analysis were performed at each time point.
cards.result: The low FODMAP diet was effective in controlling digestive symptoms in the short and long term and improved quality of life, anxiety and depression; food-related quality of life improved without affecting nutritional adequacy. Acceptability problems were reported and adherence decreased in the long term. The perception of trigger foods at T2 differed quite from that at T0. The record gives a concrete service timing — 2 months of restriction before reintroduction began — but it did not compare different restriction durations.
cards.watchOut: An evaluation study of one service's pathway, not a duration trial: the 2-month figure describes what this service did, not a tested optimum, and 32 of 73 patients were not evaluated at the final follow-up.
cards.source: Bellini M et al. A Low-FODMAP Diet for Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Some Answers to the Doubts from a Long-Term Follow-Up. Nutrients. 2020. PMID: 32784614. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: O'Keeffe 2018: after dietitian-led restriction and reintroduction, satisfactory relief was 61% short term and 57% long term, and 82% of patients settled on an adapted (not strict) FODMAP diet
cards.summary: O'Keeffe 2018: after dietitian-led restriction and reintroduction, satisfactory relief was 61% short term and 57% long term, and 82% of patients settled on an adapted (not strict) FODMAP diet
cards.people: 103 patients with irritable bowel syndrome prospectively recruited to a questionnaire study after completing dietitian-led low FODMAP education; symptoms were measured at baseline and after FODMAP restriction (short term), and symptoms, dietary intake, acceptability, food-related quality of life and healthcare utilisation were assessed after FODMAP reintroduction (long term). The record does not state the number of weeks of restriction.
cards.result: Satisfactory relief of symptoms was reported by 12% at baseline, 61% at short-term follow-up and 57% at long-term follow-up. At long term, 84 patients (82%) continued an 'adapted FODMAP' diet (mean total FODMAP intake 20.6, SD 14.9 g/day) versus 19 (18%) on a 'habitual' diet (29.4, SD 22.9 g/day, P = .039). Nutritional adequacy was not compromised in either group; the adapted diet cost significantly more (P < .001) and affected social eating (P < .01), with no effect on food-related quality of life; healthcare utilisation was similar.
cards.watchOut: The record does not report how many weeks the restriction phase lasted, so this card supports the reintroduce-and-personalise sequence, not any specific duration — that gap is printed here rather than filled in.
cards.source: O'Keeffe M et al. Long-term impact of the low-FODMAP diet on gastrointestinal symptoms, dietary intake, patient acceptability, and healthcare utilization in irritable bowel syndrome. Neurogastroenterology and Motility. 2018. PMID: 28707437. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Foulkes 2025: completing FODMAP reintroduction as per protocol was associated with long-term symptom improvement (P = 0.049) — the reintroduction phase, not prolonged restriction, tracked with durable benefit
cards.summary: Foulkes 2025: completing FODMAP reintroduction as per protocol was associated with long-term symptom improvement (P = 0.049) — the reintroduction phase, not prolonged restriction, tracked with durable benefit
cards.people: 184 patients in an observational service evaluation of dietary management of irritable bowel syndrome, with questionnaire data at baseline, short term (following FODMAP restriction) and long term (following FODMAP reintroduction) collected during clinical dietetic appointments. The record does not state the number of weeks of restriction.
cards.result: Satisfactory relief from global symptoms was 14% at baseline, rising to 69% at short-term follow-up and 57% at long-term follow-up (P < 0.001). The largest long-term improvements were in abdominal bloating (72% at baseline to 48% long term, P < 0.001), abdominal pain (61% to 30%, P < 0.001) and flatulence (71% to 40%, P < 0.001). High adherence at short-term follow-up was not associated with long-term symptom improvement, but long-term adherence was associated with global symptom severity (P = 0.032), and completion of FODMAP reintroduction as per protocol was associated with long-term symptom improvement (P = 0.049). The authors call for randomised trials of cause and effect.
cards.watchOut: Associations in a service evaluation cannot show that reintroduction timing causes the long-term outcome — patients who complete reintroduction may differ from those who stay strict or drop out.
cards.source: Foulkes R et al. A service evaluation of FODMAP restriction, FODMAP reintroduction and long-term follow-up in the dietary management of irritable bowel syndrome. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. 2025. PMID: 39498596. Registry ID: none in the record. observational service evaluation (foulkes 2025) 184 patients in an observational service evaluation of dietary management of irritable bowel syndrome, with questionnaire data at baseline, short term (following fodmap restriction) and long term (following fodmap reintroduction) collected during clinical dietetic appointments. the record does not state the number of weeks of restriction. satisfactory relief from global symptoms was 14% at baseline, rising to 69% at short-term follow-up and 57% at long-term follow-up (p < 0.001). the largest long-term improvements were in abdominal bloating (72% at baseline to 48% long term, p < 0.001), abdominal pain (61% to 30%, p < 0.001) and flatulence (71% to 40%, p < 0.001). high adherence at short-term follow-up was not associated with long-term symptom improvement, but long-term adherence was associated with global symptom severity (p = 0.032), and completion of fodmap reintroduction as per protocol was associated with long-term symptom improvement (p = 0.049). the authors call for randomised trials of cause and effect. associations in a service evaluation cannot show that reintroduction timing causes the long-term outcome — patients who complete reintroduction may differ from those who stay strict or drop out. foulkes r et al. a service evaluation of fodmap restriction, fodmap reintroduction and long-term follow-up in the dietary management of irritable bowel syndrome. journal of human nutrition and dietetics. 2025. pmid: 39498596. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · irritable bowel syndrome/diet therapy · female · male · adult · oligosaccharides/administration & dosage · diet, carbohydrate-restricted/methods · monosaccharides/administration & dosage · middle aged · fermentation · disaccharides/administration & dosage · follow-up studies · surveys and questionnaires · polymers/administration & dosage · patient compliance · treatment outcome · aged · abdominal pain/diet therapy · young adult

cards.headline: Staudacher 2022: 12 months after structured restriction, reintroduction and personalisation, adequate relief was 67% vs 28% at baseline — in a small follow-up of 18 patients (N printed on the face)
cards.summary: Staudacher 2022: 12 months after structured restriction, reintroduction and personalisation, adequate relief was 67% vs 28% at baseline — in a small follow-up of 18 patients (N printed on the face)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a trial cohort (Staudacher 2022)
cards.people: 18 participants with irritable bowel syndrome who had been through structured FODMAP restriction, reintroduction and personalisation in a previous short-term clinical trial, invited to a single follow-up at 12 months; symptoms, stool output, dietary intake, quality of life, stool microbiota (qPCR) and short-chain fatty acids were recorded and compared with pre-intervention baseline. Follow-up N = 18.
cards.result: Adequate relief occurred in 5/18 (28%) at baseline and 12/18 (67%) after 12 months of personalised low FODMAP diet (P = 0.039); IBS symptom severity score fell from a median 227 (IQR 99) to 154 (89) (P < 0.001). Bifidobacteria abundance did not differ from baseline (median 9.29 vs 9.20 log10 rRNA genes/g, P = 0.766), although total short-chain fatty acids, acetate, propionate and butyrate were lower. The authors conclude reintroduction and personalisation may normalise some effects of short-term restriction.
cards.watchOut: Only 18 of the original trial participants were followed, with no parallel control group at 12 months; this shows a personalised diet can sustain benefit, not how long the strict phase should be.
cards.source: Staudacher HM et al. Long-term personalized low FODMAP diet improves symptoms and maintains luminal Bifidobacteria abundance in irritable bowel syndrome. Neurogastroenterology and Motility. 2022. PMID: 34431172. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no study has randomised strict-phase duration — services restrict for weeks to about 2 months, then reintroduce, and completing reintroduction (not staying strict) is what tracks with long-term benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: no study has randomised strict-phase duration — services restrict for weeks to about 2 months, then reintroduce, and completing reintroduction (not staying strict) is what tracks with long-term benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one service cohort with an explicit 2-month restriction before reintroduction (N = 73, 41 at final follow-up), two service/questionnaire cohorts following patients through restriction and reintroduction (N = 103; N = 184), and one 12-month personalised-diet follow-up (N = 18, printed on its face). Total carded participants = 378, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Satisfactory relief after restriction was 61–69% across the services and 57% long term after reintroduction in both larger cohorts; completing reintroduction as per protocol was associated with long-term improvement (P = 0.049), and a personalised diet sustained adequate relief in 67% at 12 months. No carded record compares 2 vs 4 vs 8 weeks of restriction, and two records do not even state the restriction length — both gaps are printed on the cards. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: restrict briefly (the reported service used 2 months), then reintroduce; the exact week count is untested.
cards.watchOut: Anyone quoting a precise number of weeks for the strict phase is quoting convention, not trial evidence: the duration question itself has never been randomised in the records fetched for this shelf.

shelves.title: Rifaximin after relapse in IBS-D: repeat treatment beat placebo modestly in TARGET 3 (38.1% vs 31.5% responders) — evidence covers relapse after response, not non-response (PARTIAL completion of the general IBS-D rifaximin shelf #772)
shelves.question: Is rifaximin effective for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea after other treatments fail?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy,etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/complications,drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Retreatment · Rifamycins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rifaximin
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #772 covers rifaximin for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea (IBS-D) in general; the slice carded here is the patient whose symptoms come back or persist after initial treatment — the retreatment question, answered almost entirely by one programme, TARGET 3. In TARGET 3 (Lembo 2016), patients who had responded to an open-label 2-week course of rifaximin 550 mg three times daily and then relapsed were randomised to repeat rifaximin or placebo: responders after the first repeat course were 38.1% vs 31.5% (P = .03) — a real but modest absolute gain of 6.6 percentage points, driven by abdominal pain (50.6% vs 42.2%, P = .018) rather than stool consistency (51.8% vs 50.0%, P = .42, the treatment made no difference on that component). A secondary analysis of the same programme (Cash 2017) found the minimally clinically important difference in quality of life in 38.6% on retreatment vs 29.6% on placebo (P = 0.009). Outside the programme, a retrospective tertiary-centre series (Pimentel 2011) found over 75% of initial responders responded again to retreatment, up to five courses, without shortening benefit. Because the randomised evidence is a single trial programme, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: repeat rifaximin helps a modest extra fraction of relapsing IBS-D responders, with low and similar adverse-event rates.

cards.headline: TARGET 3 (Lembo 2016): in IBS-D patients who responded to rifaximin then relapsed, repeat rifaximin beat placebo — responders 38.1% vs 31.5% (P = .03), an absolute gain of 6.6 points
cards.summary: TARGET 3 (Lembo 2016): in IBS-D patients who responded to rifaximin then relapsed, repeat rifaximin beat placebo — responders 38.1% vs 31.5% (P = .03), an absolute gain of 6.6 points
cards.people: Adults with IBS-D (mean abdominal pain and bloating scores of 3 or more, with loose stool) at 270 centres in the United States and Europe, 2012–2014. Patients first received open-label rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 2 weeks; of 1074 patients (44.1%) who responded, 382 (35.6%) did not relapse during an observation phase of up to 18 weeks and 692 (64.4%) did; 636 of the relapsers were randomised to repeat rifaximin (n = 328) or placebo (n = 308), each 550 mg/placebo three times daily for 2 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — percentage of responders after the first repeat treatment (≥30% decrease in abdominal pain and ≥50% decrease in frequency of loose stools, for 2 or more weeks during a 4-week post-treatment period) — was 38.1% with rifaximin vs 31.5% with placebo (P = .03). Abdominal-pain responders were 50.6% vs 42.2% (P = .018); stool-consistency responders were 51.8% vs 50.0% (P = .42 — the treatment made no difference on that component). Significant improvements were also noted for prevention of recurrence, durable response and bowel-movement urgency. Adverse event rates were low and similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: This is an enriched population: only initial rifaximin responders who relapsed were randomised, so the result says nothing about rifaximin in patients who never responded to a first course — and the absolute advantage over placebo is modest (6.6 percentage points).
cards.source: Lembo A et al. Repeat Treatment With Rifaximin Is Safe and Effective in Patients With Diarrhea-Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome. Gastroenterology. 2016. PMID: 27528177. Registry ID: NCT01543178. cards.headline: Cash 2017 (TARGET 3 secondary analysis): retreatment also improved quality of life — the minimally important difference was reached by 38.6% on rifaximin vs 29.6% on placebo (P = 0.009)
cards.summary: Cash 2017 (TARGET 3 secondary analysis): retreatment also improved quality of life — the minimally important difference was reached by 38.6% on rifaximin vs 29.6% on placebo (P = 0.009)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial (Cash 2017)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the TARGET 3 programme (NCT01543178): 2579 patients received open-label rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 2 weeks; 1074 of 2438 evaluable patients (44.1%) were responders, and among the 636 patients with relapse who entered double-blind retreatment, quality of life was measured with the validated 34-item IBS-QOL questionnaire across 8 domains.
cards.result: Open-label rifaximin produced a mean improvement from baseline in IBS-QOL overall score of 54.9%; responders improved significantly more than nonresponders on the overall score and all eight subdomains (P < 0.001 for all), and 52.2% of responders vs 21.0% of nonresponders achieved the minimally clinically important difference (≥14-point improvement; P < 0.0001). Among relapsed patients in the double-blind phase, the minimally important difference in overall IBS-QOL was achieved by 38.6% on rifaximin vs 29.6% on placebo (P = 0.009).
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same single programme as the Lembo 2016 card — it adds a quality-of-life outcome, not independent confirmation, which is why the shelf stamp stays capped at POSSIBLE for a single trial programme.
cards.source: Cash BD et al. Repeat treatment with rifaximin improves irritable bowel syndrome-related quality of life: a secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 28932270. Registry ID: NCT01543178. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Pimentel 2011: in real-world tertiary practice, over 75% of initial rifaximin responders responded again to retreatment — up to five courses, with no shortening of benefit (retrospective, N = 71 retreated)
cards.summary: Pimentel 2011: in real-world tertiary practice, over 75% of initial rifaximin responders responded again to retreatment — up to five courses, with no shortening of benefit (retrospective, N = 71 retreated)
cards.people: Retrospective chart review at a tertiary care centre, 2007–2011: 522 charts reviewed; 71 subjects with nonconstipated irritable bowel syndrome had received rifaximin and at least one retreatment — 48 had a second course, 22 a third, 7 a fourth and 4 a fifth. Retreated N = 71, printed on the face.
cards.result: More than 75% of subjects who initially responded to rifaximin also responded to any further retreatment, with no significant reduction in benefit for successive retreatments, and no change in the duration of benefit (median time between treatments) across successive courses. The authors conclude retreatment was successful up to five times without decrease in duration or effect in real-world practice.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, uncontrolled and from the programme's own tertiary centre: patients who return for retreatment are selected for having benefited before, so the >75% figure cannot be compared with the randomised TARGET 3 response rates.
cards.source: Pimentel M et al. Effects of rifaximin treatment and retreatment in nonconstipated IBS subjects. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2011. PMID: 21559740. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for the relapsing IBS-D responder, one repeat 2-week rifaximin course adds a modest benefit over placebo (38.1% vs 31.5% responders) — a single-programme answer, capped at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: for the relapsing IBS-D responder, one repeat 2-week rifaximin course adds a modest benefit over placebo (38.1% vs 31.5% responders) — a single-programme answer, capped at POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 retreatment programme (TARGET 3: 636 relapsed responders randomised; its quality-of-life secondary analysis covers the same patients) and one retrospective retreatment series (71 retreated patients). No carded randomised trial addresses rifaximin in patients who failed non-rifaximin treatments first — that gap is printed here.
cards.result: Repeat rifaximin beat placebo on the composite responder endpoint (38.1% vs 31.5%, P = .03) and on abdominal pain (50.6% vs 42.2%), but made no difference on stool consistency (51.8% vs 50.0%, P = .42); quality-of-life minimally important difference 38.6% vs 29.6% (P = 0.009); retrospective retreatment response exceeded 75% among prior responders. Adverse events in TARGET 3 were low and similar between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (TARGET 3, NCT01543178).
cards.watchOut: The slice this shelf cannot answer is the true non-responder: every randomised patient here had already responded to rifaximin once, so 'after other treatments fail' is answered for relapse-after-response, not for failure of other drug classes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lembo A et al. Gastroenterology. 2016 (PMID: 27528177); Cash BD et al. Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology. 2017 (PMID: 28932270); Pimentel M et al. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 2011 (PMID: 21559740).

shelves.title: Hypnotherapy for diet-refractory IBS: never trialled in diet non-responders — benefit is shown only indirectly, in refractory and referred IBS (PARTIAL completion of the refractory-IBS hypnotherapy shelf #2456)
shelves.question: Is gut-directed hypnotherapy effective for irritable bowel syndrome that does not respond to diet changes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Equivalence Trials as Topic · Female · Humans · Hypnosis/methods · Intention to Treat Analysis · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic · Psychotherapy, Group/methods
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2456 covers gut-directed hypnotherapy for irritable bowel syndrome refractory to standard management, carding the Lindfors trials and Whorwell 1984; the slice asked for here is narrower — irritable bowel syndrome that does not respond to diet changes specifically. That exact population has never been enrolled in a carded trial: no fetched record defines its patients by diet non-response. The evidence carded here is therefore indirect, from the neighbouring refractory/referred populations, and the stamp is discounted for that indirectness. In IMAGINE (Flik 2019), patients referred from primary and secondary care had adequate relief at 3 months in 40.8% (individual) and 33.2% (group) vs 16.7% on educational supportive therapy (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–7.4 for hypnotherapy vs control). In explicitly refractory patients, Moser 2013 found improvement in 60.8% vs 40.9% after treatment and 54.3% vs 25.0% over 15 months, while Dobbin 2013 found hypnotherapy improved symptom severity less than biofeedback at 12 weeks in refractory women, with the two equal by 24 weeks. A 2024 network meta-analysis found face-to-face gut-directed hypnotherapy efficacious for abdominal pain (relative risk of pain not improving 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.96), but detected no significant effect among trials recruiting only refractory patients for the therapies analysed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — indirect evidence only for the diet-nonresponder slice: benefit is shown in refractory and referred IBS, not in diet-defined non-responders.

cards.headline: IMAGINE (Flik 2019): in referred IBS patients, adequate relief at 3 months was 40.8% with individual and 33.2% with group hypnotherapy vs 16.7% with educational supportive therapy (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–7.4)
cards.summary: IMAGINE (Flik 2019): in referred IBS patients, adequate relief at 3 months was 40.8% with individual and 33.2% with group hypnotherapy vs 16.7% with educational supportive therapy (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–7.4)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial in 11 hospitals in the Netherlands: 354 patients with irritable bowel syndrome, aged 18–65, referred from primary or secondary care, randomised to six sessions of individual hypnotherapy (150), group hypnotherapy (150) or group educational supportive therapy (54); the intention-to-treat population was 342 (142 individual, 146 group, 54 control) after exclusions for ineligibility. The record does not define participants by non-response to diet changes.
cards.result: Adequate relief at 3 months: 40.8% (95% CI 31.7–50.5) individual hypnotherapy, 33.2% (24.3–43.5) group hypnotherapy, 16.7% (7.6–32.6) control. At 12 months: 40.8%, 49.5% and 22.6% respectively. Hypnotherapy was more effective than control at 3 months (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–7.4, P = .0240) and 12 months (2.8, 1.2–6.7, P = .0185). Group hypnotherapy was non-inferior to individual hypnotherapy per-protocol. Eight unexpected serious adverse reactions were reported, judged unrelated to therapy.

cards.headline: Moser 2013: in IBS explicitly refractory to usual treatment, gut-directed group hypnosis improved 60.8% vs 40.9% after treatment and 54.3% vs 25.0% over 15 months
cards.summary: Moser 2013: in IBS explicitly refractory to usual treatment, gut-directed group hypnosis improved 60.8% vs 40.9% after treatment and 54.3% vs 25.0% over 15 months
cards.people: 164 patients with irritable bowel syndrome (Rome III) screened; 100 refractory to usual treatment were randomised 1:1 to supportive talks with medical treatment (SMT) or SMT plus gut-directed hypnotherapy (10 weekly group sessions within 12 weeks); 90 received the allocated intervention and analysis was by intention to treat. 'Refractory to usual treatment' is the record's definition — diet non-response is not specified separately.
cards.result: After treatment, 28/46 (60.8%) hypnotherapy patients and 18/44 (40.9%) SMT patients had clinically important improvement (absolute difference 20.0%, 95% CI 0–40.2%, P = 0.046); over 15 months, 54.3% vs 25.0% improved (absolute difference 29.4%, 95% CI 10.1–48.6%, P = 0.004). Hypnotherapy improved physical and psychological well-being significantly more than SMT alone (P < 0.001); gender, age, disease duration and IBS type did not influence long-term success.
cards.watchOut: The closest population to this shelf's question — but 'refractory to usual treatment' bundles diet, drugs and reassurance together, so the diet-specific effect still cannot be separated out.

cards.headline: Dobbin 2013: in refractory IBS, brief hypnotherapy improved symptom severity less than biofeedback at 12 weeks (difference −58.8 points favouring biofeedback, P = 0.029), with the two equal by 24 weeks
cards.summary: Dobbin 2013: in refractory IBS, brief hypnotherapy improved symptom severity less than biofeedback at 12 weeks (difference −58.8 points favouring biofeedback, P = 0.029), with the two equal by 24 weeks
cards.people: Women referred by their GP with refractory irritable bowel syndrome symptoms: 128 consecutive patients were suitable, 97 were randomised to biofeedback or hypnotherapy (three one-hour sessions over 12 weeks), 76 attended therapy and 61 were assessed in the 24-week follow-up comparison. Randomised N = 97; completer N printed in the result.
cards.result: Mean (SD) change in IBS symptom severity score 12 weeks post-treatment was −116.8 (99.3) with biofeedback and −58.0 (101.1) with hypnotherapy — a statistically significant between-group difference of −58.8 (95% CI −111.6 to −6.1, P = 0.029) favouring biofeedback. In the 61 patients followed, biofeedback and hypnotherapy were equally effective at improving symptom severity, total non-gastrointestinal symptom scores and anxiety and depression ratings over 24 weeks. The authors suggest biofeedback may be more cost-effective as it requires less expertise.
cards.watchOut: Only three sessions, women only, and heavy attrition (97 randomised, 61 in the follow-up comparison): a brief-intervention result that tempers the larger refractory-trial findings rather than overturning them.
cards.source: Dobbin A et al. Randomised controlled trial of brief intervention with biofeedback and hypnotherapy in patients with refractory irritable bowel syndrome. cards.headline: Goodoory 2024 network meta-analysis: face-to-face gut-directed hypnotherapy improved abdominal pain (relative risk of pain not improving 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.96) — but in refractory-only trials, no therapy except group CBT separated from control
cards.summary: Goodoory 2024 network meta-analysis: face-to-face gut-directed hypnotherapy improved abdominal pain (relative risk of pain not improving 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.96) — but in refractory-only trials, no therapy except group CBT separated from control
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 42 randomised controlled trials of brain-gut behavioural treatments in 5220 adults with irritable bowel syndrome (literature searched to 16 December 2023), reporting pooled relative risks of abdominal pain not improving, with dropouts counted as treatment failures. The included trials overlap with the trials carded on this shelf and on home shelf #2456.
cards.result: The behavioural treatments with the largest evidence demonstrating efficacy for abdominal pain were self-guided/minimal-contact cognitive behavioural therapy (relative risk of pain not improving 0.71, 95% CI 0.54–0.95), face-to-face multicomponent behavioural therapy (0.72, 0.54–0.97) and face-to-face gut-directed hypnotherapy (0.77, 0.61–0.96). Among trials recruiting only patients with refractory global IBS symptoms, group CBT was more efficacious than routine care for abdominal pain, but no other significant differences were detected. No trials were low risk of bias across all domains, and there was evidence of funnel-plot asymmetry.
cards.watchOut: The refractory-only subgroup analysis — the analysis closest to this shelf's question — found no significant hypnotherapy effect on pain; the positive pooled estimate comes from the broader, mostly non-refractory trial set.
cards.source: Goodoory VC et al. Effect of Brain-Gut Behavioral Treatments on Abdominal Pain in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Gastroenterology. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: hypnotherapy works in refractory and referred IBS, but the diet-nonresponder population itself has never been trialled — so for this slice the evidence is indirect and the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: hypnotherapy works in refractory and referred IBS, but the diet-nonresponder population itself has never been trialled — so for this slice the evidence is indirect and the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large multicentre trial in referred patients (354 randomised), two smaller trials in explicitly refractory patients (100 and 97 randomised), and one network meta-analysis of 42 trials (5220 participants, overlapping with the carded trials). Total unique randomised participants across the three trials = 551, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Adequate relief favoured hypnotherapy over supportive/educational control in IMAGINE (odds ratio 2.9 at 3 months) and in refractory patients in Moser 2013 (54.3% vs 25.0% improved over 15 months); Dobbin 2013 found brief hypnotherapy inferior to biofeedback at 12 weeks and equal at 24 weeks; the 2024 network meta-analysis found a pain benefit overall (relative risk of pain not improving 0.77) but no significant hypnotherapy effect in refractory-only trials. No record defined patients by failure of diet changes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — indirect evidence only for diet-refractory IBS.
cards.watchOut: If a future trial enrols patients specifically after low FODMAP or other dietary failure, this shelf should be re-cut around it; until then the honest claim is 'refractory IBS evidence, applied indirectly'.

shelves.title: Standard Mediterranean diet and liver fat: beats a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in a 12-person crossover, but no better than a low-fat diet in larger trials — a comparator split (PARTIAL completion of the green-Mediterranean shelf #3624)
shelves.question: Does a Mediterranean diet reduce liver fat in adults with metabolic associated fatty liver disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Diet, Mediterranean · Fatty Liver/diet therapy,metabolism,pathology · Female · Glucose Clamp Technique · Humans · Insulin Resistance · Lipid Metabolism · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Obesity, Abdominal/diet therapy,metabolism,pathology · Pilot Projects
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3624 covers the green-Mediterranean variant in DIRECT PLUS; the slice carded here is the standard Mediterranean diet against control diets in fatty liver disease. The evidence splits by comparator, and the stamp names the split. Against a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in the smallest trial, the Mediterranean diet won clearly: relative reduction in hepatic steatosis 39 ± 4% vs 7 ± 3% (P = 0.012) in a 12-person crossover (Ryan 2013, N printed on the face). In the two larger head-to-head trials against low-fat diets, it did not: Properzi 2018 found relative steatosis reductions of 32.4% on Mediterranean vs 25.0% on low-fat (between-group P = 0.32 — the treatment made no difference between diets, both improved), and MEDINA (George 2022) found no between-group differences, with intrahepatic lipid improving significantly within the low-fat group (−17%, P = .02) but not within the Mediterranean group (−8%, P = .069). Against no-treatment control, Katsagoni 2018 found a Mediterranean diet improved liver stiffness versus control (P < 0.001 after adjustment), with ALT normalisation seen only in the Mediterranean-lifestyle arm. A 2023 meta-analysis of 10 trials (737 adults) found no significant effect on liver enzymes and a non-significant stiffness change. PROPOSED SPLIT (comparator split: Mediterranean diet reduces liver fat versus the low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in one small crossover and improves stiffness versus usual care, but shows no advantage over a low-fat diet in the two larger head-to-head trials).

cards.headline: Ryan 2013: in a 12-person crossover (N printed on the face), the Mediterranean diet cut hepatic steatosis by a relative 39 ± 4% vs 7 ± 3% on a low-fat/high-carbohydrate diet (P = 0.012)
cards.summary: Ryan 2013: in a 12-person crossover (N printed on the face), the Mediterranean diet cut hepatic steatosis by a relative 39 ± 4% vs 7 ± 3% on a low-fat/high-carbohydrate diet (P = 0.012)
cards.people: 12 non-diabetic subjects (6 female, 6 male) with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and abdominal obesity, in a randomised crossover 6-week dietary intervention: every subject undertook both the Mediterranean diet and the control low-fat/high-carbohydrate diet in random order, with a 6-week washout between. Crossover N = 12. Insulin sensitivity was measured by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp and steatosis by localised magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
cards.result: There was a significant relative reduction in hepatic steatosis after the Mediterranean diet compared with the low-fat/high-carbohydrate diet: 39 ± 4% versus 7 ± 3% (P = 0.012). Insulin sensitivity improved with the Mediterranean diet, whereas after the control diet there was no change (P = 0.03 between diets). Mean weight loss was not different between the two diets (P = 0.22). The authors conclude that even without weight loss, the Mediterranean diet reduces liver steatosis and improves insulin sensitivity in this population.
cards.watchOut: A pilot crossover of 12 people over 6 weeks per diet: the largest relative effect on this shelf comes from its smallest study, which is why the stamp is a split rather than a benefit verdict.
cards.source: Ryan MC et al. The Mediterranean diet improves hepatic steatosis and insulin sensitivity in individuals with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Journal of Hepatology. 2013. PMID: 23485520. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Properzi 2018: Mediterranean and low-fat diets reduced hepatic steatosis to a similar degree — relative reductions 32.4% vs 25.0%, between-group P = 0.32 (the Mediterranean diet made no difference versus low-fat)
cards.summary: Properzi 2018: Mediterranean and low-fat diets reduced hepatic steatosis to a similar degree — relative reductions 32.4% vs 25.0%, between-group P = 0.32 (the Mediterranean diet made no difference versus low-fat)
cards.people: Adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease randomised to a 12-week ad libitum isocaloric Mediterranean diet or low-fat diet, with hepatic steatosis measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy: 56 subjects enrolled, 49 completed the intervention and 48 were included in the analysis.
cards.result: At week 12, hepatic steatosis had reduced significantly in both groups (P < 0.01), with no difference in liver fat reduction between groups (P = 0.32): mean (SD) relative reductions were 25.0% (±25.3%) on low-fat and 32.4% (±25.5%) on Mediterranean. Liver enzymes also improved significantly in both groups. Weight loss was minimal and not different between groups (−1.6 ± 2.1 kg low-fat vs −2.1 ± 2.5 kg Mediterranean; P = 0.52). Within-group improvements in Framingham Risk Score, total cholesterol, triglycerides and HbA1c were observed on the Mediterranean diet (all P < 0.05) but not the low-fat diet; adherence was higher on Mediterranean (88% vs 64%; P = 0.048).
cards.watchOut: Both diets were ad libitum and isocaloric with minimal weight loss, so the trial compares dietary patterns fairly — and on liver fat the Mediterranean pattern's numerical edge (32.4% vs 25.0% relative) was well within chance.
cards.source: Properzi C et al. Ad Libitum Mediterranean and Low-Fat Diets Both Significantly Reduce Hepatic Steatosis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2018. PMID: 29729189. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MEDINA (George 2022): no between-group difference between Mediterranean and low-fat diets — intrahepatic lipid improved significantly within the low-fat group (−17%, P = .02) but not within the Mediterranean group (−8%, P = .069)
cards.summary: MEDINA (George 2022): no between-group difference between Mediterranean and low-fat diets — intrahepatic lipid improved significantly within the low-fat group (−17%, P = .02) but not within the Mediterranean group (−8%, P = .069)
cards.people: Multicentre parallel randomised trial in adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: 42 participants (25 female [60%], mean age 52.3 ± 12.6 years) randomised 1:1 to an ad libitum Mediterranean diet (19) or low-fat diet (23) for 12 weeks; 39 completed the study. Intrahepatic lipid was measured by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy; secondary outcomes included insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), visceral fat, liver stiffness and metabolic outcomes.
cards.result: Following 12 weeks there were no between-group differences. Intrahepatic lipid improved significantly within the low-fat group (−17% [log scale]; P = .02) but not within the Mediterranean group (−8%, P = .069). HOMA-IR reduced in the low-fat group (6.5 ± 5.6 to 5.5 ± 5.5, P < .01) but not the Mediterranean group (4.4 ± 3.2 to 3.9 ± 2.3, P = .07). No differences were found for liver stiffness. Visceral fat reduced significantly in both groups (low-fat −76% [log scale], P < .0005; Mediterranean −61%, P < .0005). The authors note that delivering dietary interventions to free-living adults with fatty liver disease is challenging.
cards.watchOut: The Mediterranean arm started with lower intrahepatic lipid and HOMA-IR than the low-fat arm, and only 42 patients were randomised — a small, imbalanced trial whose null between-group result still counts against any claimed Mediterranean advantage.

cards.headline: Katsagoni 2018: against a no-intervention control, a Mediterranean diet improved liver stiffness (P < 0.001 after adjustment); ALT improvement required the full Mediterranean lifestyle arm
cards.summary: Katsagoni 2018: against a no-intervention control, a Mediterranean diet improved liver stiffness (P < 0.001 after adjustment); ALT improvement required the full Mediterranean lifestyle arm
cards.people: 63 overweight/obese patients (mean age 50 ± 11 years, BMI 31.8 ± 4.5 kg/m2, 68% men) with ultrasonography-proven nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and elevated ALT and/or gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, randomised to control (written healthy-lifestyle information only), Mediterranean diet, or Mediterranean lifestyle (diet plus physical-activity and sleep guidance), with seven 60-minute group sessions over 6 months aiming at weight loss and Mediterranean adherence; 88.8% completed the study.
cards.result: Both Mediterranean groups showed greater weight reduction and higher Mediterranean adherence than control (all P < 0.05). The Mediterranean lifestyle group improved ALT levels (ALT under 40 U/l, P = 0.03; 50% reduction of ALT, P = 0.009) and liver stiffness (P = 0.004) versus control after adjusting for percentage weight loss and baseline values. The Mediterranean diet group improved only liver stiffness versus control (P < 0.001 after adjustment). The authors conclude small changes towards the Mediterranean lifestyle, along with weight loss, can be a treatment option.
cards.watchOut: The outcome here is liver stiffness and enzymes, not imaging-measured liver fat, and both Mediterranean arms also pursued weight loss — so this card supports benefit versus doing nothing, not superiority over another active diet.
cards.source: Katsagoni CN et al. Improvements in clinical characteristics of patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, after an intervention based on the Mediterranean lifestyle: a randomised controlled clinical trial. cards.headline: Del Bo' 2023 meta-analysis: across 10 Mediterranean-diet trials (737 adults), no significant effect on liver enzymes, and the liver-stiffness change was non-significant (−0.42 kPa, 95% CI −0.92 to 0.09, P = 0.10)
cards.summary: Del Bo' 2023 meta-analysis: across 10 Mediterranean-diet trials (737 adults), no significant effect on liver enzymes, and the liver-stiffness change was non-significant (−0.42 kPa, 95% CI −0.92 to 0.09, P = 0.10)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of Mediterranean diet interventions in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease over the last 10 years, with intervention durations from 6 weeks to 1 year and varied strategies (energy-restricted Mediterranean diets, low-fat Mediterranean variants, added exercise): 10 trials, 737 adults in total. The pooled trials overlap with the trials carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The Mediterranean diet significantly reduced total cholesterol by −0.46 mg/dL (95% CI −0.55 to −0.38, P = 0.001) — a very small absolute change as printed in the record. Liver stiffness decreased by −0.42 kPa (95% CI −0.92 to 0.09), which was not significant (P = 0.10), and no significant findings were documented for liver enzymes or waist circumference. The authors conclude the Mediterranean diet might reduce some outcomes linked with fatty-liver severity but that further randomised trials are necessary, noting variation across trials.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools heterogeneous Mediterranean interventions and reports enzymes and stiffness rather than a pooled liver-fat effect — it tempers, but does not directly re-test, the imaging results on the other cards.
cards.source: Del Bo' C et al. Does the Mediterranean Diet Have Any Effect on Lipid Profile, Central Obesity and Liver Enzymes in Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) Subjects?
