cards.headline: Synthesis: the Mediterranean diet reduces liver fat versus a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in one tiny crossover and improves stiffness versus usual care, but shows no liver-fat advantage over a low-fat diet in the two larger head-to-head trials — a comparator split
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Mediterranean diet reduces liver fat versus a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in one tiny crossover and improves stiffness versus usual care, but shows no liver-fat advantage over a low-fat diet in the two larger head-to-head trials — a comparator split
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials (crossover N = 12; parallel N = 48 analysed, N = 63, N = 42) and one meta-analysis of 10 trials (737 adults, overlapping with the carded trials). Total unique participants across the four trials = 165, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the 12-person crossover's N is printed on its face.
cards.result: Relative steatosis reduction was 39% vs 7% favouring Mediterranean over low-fat/high-carbohydrate in Ryan 2013 (P = 0.012); 32.4% vs 25.0% with no between-group difference in Properzi 2018 (P = 0.32); intrahepatic lipid −8% (not significant within group) vs −17% on low-fat in MEDINA with no between-group difference; liver stiffness improved versus no-intervention control in Katsagoni 2018 (P < 0.001 adjusted); the 2023 meta-analysis found no significant enzyme effect and a non-significant stiffness change. PROPOSED SPLIT (comparator split, named in the stamp).
cards.watchOut: All four trials are small and short (6 weeks to 6 months), and none enrolled patients under the MAFLD label itself — they are fatty-liver (NAFLD) populations, which is the population the MAFLD question inherits.

Liver International. 2022 (PMID: 35357066); Katsagoni CN et al. The British Journal of Nutrition. 2018 (PMID: 29947322); Del Bo' C et al. Nutrients. 2023 (PMID: 37242133).

shelves.title: Lactulose for covert hepatic encephalopathy: reverses the minimal form in about half to two-thirds of patients across four trials — LIKELY benefit, with grade 1 disease untested separately (PARTIAL completion of the minimal-HE shelf #2126)
shelves.question: Is lactulose effective for covert hepatic encephalopathy in adults with cirrhosis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognition/drug effects · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Gastrointestinal Microbiome/drug effects · Hepatic Encephalopathy/drug therapy,etiology,microbiology · Humans · Lactulose/therapeutic use · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2126 covers lactulose for minimal hepatic encephalopathy (MHE) on a single trial (Prasad 2007, cross-pointed here and not re-carded); the slice carded here is covert hepatic encephalopathy broadly — the term that groups minimal with grade 1 disease. The carded trial set is wider than the home shelf's and concordant: a multicentre randomised trial found MHE reversal at 60 days in 64.18% on lactulose vs 22.58% on no therapy (Wang 2019; number needed to treat 2.4 as printed); Mittal 2011 found recovery in 47.5% on lactulose vs 10% on no treatment (P = 0.006 for the treatment groups vs none); Sharma 2008 found psychometry normalisation in 54.8% on lactulose; and in Sidhu 2016 the lactulose arm reversed MHE in 69.1% (rifaximin 73.7%; rifaximin's non-inferiority was not established). A meta-analysis of 9 trials (434 patients) found lactulose reduced the relative risk of no improvement to 0.52 (95% CI 0.44–0.62) and of progression to overt encephalopathy to 0.17 (0.06–0.52), at the cost of more diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38). Two honest limits: every carded trial enrolled the minimal end of covert disease — no fetched trial isolated grade 1 covert encephalopathy — and most trials were open-label. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised trials and a meta-analysis show lactulose reverses covert (minimal) hepatic encephalopathy and reduces progression to overt disease; the grade 1 end of covert disease is untested separately.

cards.headline: Wang 2019: in a multicentre randomised trial, lactulose reversed minimal hepatic encephalopathy in 64.18% vs 22.58% on no therapy at 60 days (P = .0002; number needed to treat 2.4)
cards.summary: Wang 2019: in a multicentre randomised trial, lactulose reversed minimal hepatic encephalopathy in 64.18% vs 22.58% on no therapy at 60 days (P = .0002; number needed to treat 2.4)
cards.people: 98 patients with cirrhosis and minimal hepatic encephalopathy in a multicentre, open-label randomised controlled trial at 11 teaching hospitals in China, allocated 2:1 to lactulose (67 patients) or no therapy (31 patients) for 60 days; the primary endpoint was the MHE reversal rate, with quality of life and gut microbiota also assessed.
cards.result: At day 60, the MHE reversal rate was 64.18% in the lactulose group vs 22.58% in the no-therapy group (P = .0002), with a number needed to treat of 2.4 as printed in the record. Physical functioning improved significantly more with lactulose (change 4.62 ± 6.16 vs 1.50 ± 5.34, P = .0212). Proteobacteria abundance was significantly higher in MHE patients than in healthy volunteers (12.27% vs 4.65%, P < .05), and microbiota composition differed between lactulose responders and non-responders. The authors conclude lactulose significantly improves the MHE recovery rate.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a no-therapy control, so expectation and co-intervention effects are not excluded; the comparator also means the trial cannot separate lactulose's effect from the effect of being treated and retested.
cards.source: Wang JY et al. Lactulose improves cognition, quality of life, and gut microbiota in minimal hepatic encephalopathy: A multicenter, randomized controlled trial. Journal of Digestive Diseases. 2019. PMID: 31448533. Registry ID: ChiCTR-TRC-12002342 (from the record). cards.headline: Mittal 2011: minimal hepatic encephalopathy recovered in 47.5% on lactulose vs 10% on no treatment after 3 months (treatment groups vs none, P = 0.006), and overt encephalopathy developed in 2.5% vs 10%
cards.summary: Mittal 2011: minimal hepatic encephalopathy recovered in 47.5% on lactulose vs 10% on no treatment after 3 months (treatment groups vs none, P = 0.006), and overt encephalopathy developed in 2.5% vs 10%
cards.people: 322 consecutive patients with cirrhosis screened for minimal hepatic encephalopathy (diagnosed by two or more abnormal psychometric tests); 160 (49.69%) had MHE and were randomised to no treatment, lactulose 30–60 mL twice daily, probiotics, or L-ornithine L-aspartate for 3 months (about 40 patients per group, as the recovery percentages imply), with arterial ammonia and Sickness Impact Profile quality-of-life assessment at baseline and 3 months.
cards.result: After 3 months, MHE recovered in 4 patients (10%) on no treatment, 19 (47.5%) on lactulose, 14 (35%) on probiotics and 14 (35%) on L-ornithine L-aspartate; improvement was significant in all three treatment groups versus no treatment (P = 0.006). Overt hepatic encephalopathy developed in 9/160 patients (5.6%): 4 (10%) on no treatment, 1 (2.5%) on lactulose, 2 (5%) on probiotics and 2 (5%) on L-ornithine L-aspartate. Sickness Impact Profile score improved significantly more in all treatment groups than in no treatment (P < 0.001), and arterial ammonia fell significantly more in the treatment groups (lactulose −8.47 ± 5.8 µmol/L vs −0.52 ± 7.8 µmol/L, P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Four-arm trial with about 40 patients per arm and no placebo; the P = 0.006 reported is for the treatment groups against no treatment collectively, and overt-encephalopathy events were few (9 in total).
cards.source: Mittal VV et al. A randomized controlled trial comparing lactulose, probiotics, and L-ornithine L-aspartate in treatment of minimal hepatic encephalopathy. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2011. PMID: 21646910. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sharma 2008: lactulose normalised abnormal psychometry in 54.8% of minimal hepatic encephalopathy patients over 1 month — the same as probiotics (51.6%) and the combination (56.6%)
cards.summary: Sharma 2008: lactulose normalised abnormal psychometry in 54.8% of minimal hepatic encephalopathy patients over 1 month — the same as probiotics (51.6%) and the combination (56.6%)
cards.people: 190 patients with cirrhosis without overt encephalopathy (Child A 37.4%, B 37.9%, C 24.7%) evaluated by psychometry and P300 auditory event-related potentials; minimal hepatic encephalopathy was diagnosed in 105 (55.2%). The 105 were randomised to lactulose 30–60 mL/day (35), probiotics (35), or lactulose plus probiotics (35) for 1 month; response was normalisation of the abnormal test parameters.
cards.result: Significant improvement was seen in abnormal psychometry, P300 event-related potentials and venous ammonia in all three groups after treatment (lactulose group ammonia 102.3 ± 63.1 to 69.3 ± 33.3 µmol/L). Normalisation of abnormal psychometry and P300 was seen in 54.8% on lactulose, 51.6% on probiotics and 56.6% on the combination. The authors conclude lactulose, probiotics, or their combination are equally effective in treating minimal hepatic encephalopathy.
cards.watchOut: No untreated or placebo arm: 'equally effective' among three active treatments over 1 month cannot exclude spontaneous or practice-effect improvement on repeat psychometry, which the no-treatment arms on the other cards put at 10–23%.
cards.source: Sharma P et al. An open-label randomized controlled trial of lactulose and probiotics in the treatment of minimal hepatic encephalopathy. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2008. PMID: 18467909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sidhu 2016: the lactulose arm reversed minimal hepatic encephalopathy in 69.1% (38/55) at 3 months — close to rifaximin's 73.7%, whose non-inferiority to lactulose was not established
cards.summary: Sidhu 2016: the lactulose arm reversed minimal hepatic encephalopathy in 69.1% (38/55) at 3 months — close to rifaximin's 73.7%, whose non-inferiority to lactulose was not established
cards.people: Prospective, randomised, open-label non-inferiority trial at a tertiary institute in northern India: 527 patients with cirrhosis screened, 351 eligible and tested, 112 (31.9%) found to have minimal hepatic encephalopathy (two or more of five neuropsychometric tests positive) and randomised to lactulose 30–120 mL/day (55) or rifaximin 400 mg three times daily (57) for 3 months; health-related quality of life was assessed with the Sickness Impact Profile.
cards.result: By intention to treat, MHE reversal at 3 months was 73.7% (42/57) on rifaximin and 69.1% (38/55) on lactulose — a 4.6% difference (90% CI −9.3% to 18.4%); non-inferiority of rifaximin over lactulose could not be established because the pre-specified −5% margin lies within that interval. Quality of life improved significantly in both groups (P = 0.20 between groups). Flatulence (P = 0.004) and diarrhoea (P = 0.0002) were significantly more frequent on lactulose.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial without a no-treatment arm: the 69.1% lactulose reversal rate gains meaning only alongside the 10–23% spontaneous reversal rates in the controlled trials carded here.
cards.source: Sidhu SS et al. Rifaximin vs. lactulose in treatment of minimal hepatic encephalopathy. Liver International. 2016. PMID: 26201713. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Luo 2011 meta-analysis: lactulose halved the relative risk of no improvement (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.44–0.62) and cut progression to overt encephalopathy (relative risk 0.17, 0.06–0.52), with more diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38)
cards.summary: Luo 2011 meta-analysis: lactulose halved the relative risk of no improvement (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.44–0.62) and cut progression to overt encephalopathy (relative risk 0.17, 0.06–0.52), with more diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (January 1990 to July 2011) comparing lactulose with placebo or no intervention in minimal hepatic encephalopathy, restricted to studies with a Jadad score above 3: 9 studies with 434 patients. The pooled trials overlap with the trials carded on this shelf and with the home shelf's trial.
cards.result: Compared with placebo or no intervention, lactulose significantly reduced the relative risk of no improvement in neuropsychological tests (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.44–0.62, P < 0.00001), shortened number-connection test-A time (weighted mean difference −26.95, 95% CI −37.81 to −16.10), reduced the mean number of abnormal tests (−1.76, −1.96 to −1.56), prevented progression to overt hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.17, 0.06–0.52, P = 0.002), reduced blood ammonia (weighted mean difference −9.89 µmol/L, −11.01 to −8.77) and improved health-related quality of life (−6.05, −6.30 to −5.20). There was no significant difference in mortality (relative risk 0.75, 0.21–2.72, P = 0.66 — the treatment made no difference on mortality), and lactulose significantly increased diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38, 1.35–14.25, P = 0.01). All relative measures are labelled relative; the record does not give pooled absolute event rates for these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, mostly open-label, and ethnically mixed (the authors ran sensitivity analyses on ethnicity and quality); the striking progression relative risk of 0.17 rests on few overt-encephalopathy events.
cards.source: Luo M et al. Clinical efficacy and safety of lactulose for minimal hepatic encephalopathy: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2011. PMID: 21971378. cards.headline: Synthesis: across four randomised trials and a 9-trial meta-analysis, lactulose reverses covert (minimal) hepatic encephalopathy in roughly half to two-thirds of patients versus 10–23% untreated — LIKELY benefit for the minimal end; grade 1 covert disease untested separately
cards.summary: Synthesis: across four randomised trials and a 9-trial meta-analysis, lactulose reverses covert (minimal) hepatic encephalopathy in roughly half to two-thirds of patients versus 10–23% untreated — LIKELY benefit for the minimal end; grade 1 covert disease untested separately
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials enrolling patients with minimal hepatic encephalopathy (N = 98, 160, 105 and 112) and one meta-analysis of 9 trials (434 patients, overlapping with the carded trials). Total unique participants across the four trials = 475, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Reversal/recovery on lactulose was 64.18% vs 22.58% on no therapy (Wang 2019), 47.5% vs 10% on no treatment (Mittal 2011), 54.8% normalisation with no untreated arm (Sharma 2008), and 69.1% against rifaximin's 73.7% (Sidhu 2016). The meta-analysis gives a relative risk of no improvement of 0.52 and of progression to overt encephalopathy of 0.17, no mortality difference, and more diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — for covert hepatic encephalopathy as trialled, i.e. its minimal form.
cards.watchOut: Covert hepatic encephalopathy spans minimal and grade 1 disease; every carded trial enrolled minimal disease by psychometry, so the LIKELY stamp inherits that boundary — it should not be read as trial proof for grade 1 presentations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang JY et al. Journal of Digestive Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 31448533); Mittal VV et al. shelves.title: Beta-blockers vs no treatment for first variceal bleeding: pooled placebo-controlled trials favour the drug, but they enrolled large varices — medium varices were never isolated (PARTIAL completion of the band-ligation comparison shelf #3625)
shelves.question: Should nonselective beta-blockers be used to prevent first variceal bleeding in adults with cirrhosis and medium varices?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Ascites/complications · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/complications · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/mortality,prevention & control · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic/complications · Male · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Middle Aged · Nadolol/therapeutic use · Prognosis · Propranolol/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3625 covers primary-prevention beta-blockers versus band ligation, and live shelf #776 covers beta-blockers versus placebo for preventing decompensation in clinically significant portal hypertension (the PREDESCI programme, PMID 30910320 — already carded there and cross-pointed here, not re-carded). The slice carded here is the older, direct comparison the other shelves do not home: beta-blocker versus no treatment/placebo for first bleeding in patients with established varices. The pooled individual-patient analysis of the four placebo-controlled trials (Poynard 1991, 589 patients) found 78 ± 3% free of bleeding at 2 years on a beta-blocker vs 65 ± 3% on placebo (P = 0.002), with fatal bleeding also reduced (90 ± 2% vs 82 ± 3% free, P = 0.01) and overall survival not significantly different (71% vs 68%, P = 0.34). The individual trials split: Idéo 1988 found nadolol almost abolished first bleeding (1/30 vs 11/49 controls over a mean 24 months), while the Italian multicentre trial in large varices found no significant overall difference (74% vs 59% free of bleeding over 42 months), with benefit confined to patients without ascites. Two boundaries are printed plainly: the trials enrolled large varices, not medium varices as a defined stratum — no fetched trial isolated medium varices — and the modern placebo-controlled frontier has moved to small varices (the BOPPP protocol, 740 patients planned, no results in the record). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled placebo-controlled evidence favours beta-blockers for preventing first bleeding, but the medium-varices population itself was never trialled as such and the individual large-varices trials divide.

cards.headline: Poynard 1991: pooling individual data from the four placebo-controlled trials (589 patients), beta-blockers left 78% free of first bleeding at 2 years vs 65% on placebo (P = 0.002), and reduced fatal bleeding
cards.summary: Poynard 1991: pooling individual data from the four placebo-controlled trials (589 patients), beta-blockers left 78% free of first bleeding at 2 years vs 65% on placebo (P = 0.002), and reduced fatal bleeding
cards.people: Individual-patient analysis of four randomised controlled trials in patients with cirrhosis and oesophageal varices who had never bled: 589 patients, of whom 286 received a beta-adrenergic antagonist (propranolol in 203, nadolol in 83) and 303 received placebo. Outcomes at 2 years were freedom from upper gastrointestinal bleeding, fatal bleeding, and survival, with adjustment for age, severity of cirrhosis, ascites and variceal size.
cards.result: After 2 years, the mean (± SE) percentage with no upper gastrointestinal bleeding was 78 ± 3% in the beta-blocker group and 65 ± 3% in the control group (P = 0.002); freedom from fatal bleeding was 90 ± 2% vs 82 ± 3% (P = 0.01); survival was 71 ± 3% vs 68 ± 3% (P = 0.34 — the treatment made no significant difference to overall survival, though after adjustment for age and severity of cirrhosis survival was better on treatment, P = 0.09). Freedom from bleeding or death was 62 ± 3% vs 53 ± 3% (P = 0.04). Efficacy for preventing bleeding (P < 0.001) and fatal bleeding (P = 0.004) was the same after adjustment for cause and severity of cirrhosis, ascites, and size of varices. Both propranolol and nadolol prevented a first episode of bleeding.
cards.watchOut: A 1991 pooling of 1980s trials, before band ligation, carvedilol and modern cirrhosis care; it establishes the drug-versus-nothing effect, not the drug's place against today's alternatives — that comparison lives on shelf #3625.
cards.source: Poynard T et al. Beta-adrenergic-antagonist drugs in the prevention of gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with cirrhosis and esophageal varices. An analysis of data and prognostic factors in 589 patients from four randomized clinical trials. Franco-Italian Multicenter Study Group. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1991. PMID: 1674104. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Idéo 1988: nadolol almost abolished first bleeding — 1 of 30 patients bled vs 11 of 49 on placebo/ranitidine over a mean 24 months (freedom from bleeding at 2 years 94.4% vs 70.2%, P < 0.02)
cards.summary: Idéo 1988: nadolol almost abolished first bleeding — 1 of 30 patients bled vs 11 of 49 on placebo/ranitidine over a mean 24 months (freedom from bleeding at 2 years 94.4% vs 70.2%, P < 0.02)
cards.people: 79 consecutive patients with cirrhosis and large oesophageal varices on endoscopy who had never bled, randomised to placebo, ranitidine 300 mg/day, or nadolol 40–120 mg/day; because ranitidine and placebo did not differ significantly, they were combined as the control group (49 patients) against nadolol (30 patients), with a mean follow-up of 24 months.
cards.result: Only 1 of 30 patients in the nadolol group bled, while 11 of 49 control patients bled. The percentages not bleeding at 1 and 2 years were 100% and 94.4% for nadolol and 81.2% and 70.2% for controls (P < 0.02). There were no differences in the mortality rate. The authors conclude nadolol significantly protects against the first gastrointestinal bleeding episode in cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-centre, with the control group assembled post hoc from two arms; its near-total protection (1 bleed in 30) is the optimistic extreme of this shelf's evidence, not the pooled estimate.
cards.source: Idéo G et al. Nadolol can prevent the first gastrointestinal bleeding in cirrhotics: a prospective, randomized study. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1988. PMID: 3276591. cards.headline: Italian Multicenter Project 1989: in 174 patients with large varices, propranolol made no significant overall difference (74% vs 59% free of bleeding over 42 months) — benefit appeared only in patients without ascites (83% vs 61%, P = 0.028)
cards.summary: Italian Multicenter Project 1989: in 174 patients with large varices, propranolol made no significant overall difference (74% vs 59% free of bleeding over 42 months) — benefit appeared only in patients without ascites (83% vs 61%, P = 0.028)
cards.people: 174 consecutive patients with large oesophageal varices in a multicentre randomised single-blind trial, assigned to propranolol titrated to reduce resting heart rate by 25% (85 patients) or placebo (vitamin K; 89 patients); 3 were lost to follow-up and 26 were withdrawn from propranolol (23 for side effects, 3 for low compliance). The record carries no personal first author; the trial is reported under its group name, which the source line reproduces.
cards.result: Over 42 months, the cumulative proportion free of bleeding was 74% (95% CI 63–85%) on propranolol and 59% (95% CI 43–79%) on control, and survival was 51% (95% CI 39–63%) vs 59% (95% CI 43–75%): neither difference was significant (the treatment made no difference overall). In the retrospective subgroup without ascites at randomisation, freedom from bleeding was significantly higher on propranolol (83% vs 61%, P = 0.028; during the ascites-free period 94% vs 58%, P = 0.002). No differences were found in patients with ascites, and survival was not significantly affected by treatment in any subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Almost a third of the propranolol group left treatment (side effects or compliance), the positive ascites finding is a retrospective subgroup, and the trial's placebo was vitamin K — a 1980s design whose null overall result is the pessimistic counterweight on this shelf.
cards.source: Italian Multicenter Project for Propranolol in Prevention of Bleeding. Propranolol prevents first gastrointestinal bleeding in non-ascitic cirrhotic patients. Final report of a multicenter randomized trial. Journal of Hepatology. 1989. PMID: 2671121. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BOPPP protocol (Patel 2024): the current placebo-controlled trial targets small varices, not medium — 740 patients planned for carvedilol vs placebo over 36 months, with no results in the record
cards.summary: BOPPP protocol (Patel 2024): the current placebo-controlled trial targets small varices, not medium — 740 patients planned for carvedilol vs placebo over 36 months, with no results in the record
cards.people: Protocol for a pragmatic, multicentre, placebo-controlled, triple-blind randomised trial in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland: patients aged 18 or older with cirrhosis and small oesophageal varices that have never bled, randomised 1:1 to carvedilol 6.25 mg once or twice daily or matched placebo for 36 months; planned enrolment 740 patients across 55 hospitals. The primary outcome is time to first decompensating event (a composite including variceal haemorrhage, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, Child-Pugh/MELD progression and liver-related mortality).
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its stated premise is that it remains uncertain whether giving a nonselective beta-blocker at an earlier stage, when varices are small, can prevent variceal haemorrhage and reduce decompensation, and that clinical equipoise exists. The protocol is carded to mark the boundary of the evidence: the placebo-controlled question is being re-asked at the small-varices stage, while no trial in the records fetched isolates medium varices.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about beta-blockers: it must never be cited as a trial result, and its population (small varices) is adjacent to, not the same as, this shelf's medium-varices question.
cards.source: Patel VC et al. Beta-blockers or Placebo for Primary Prophylaxis (BOPPP) of oesophageal varices: study protocol for a randomised controlled trial. Trials. 2024. PMID: 38627804. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled placebo-controlled data favour beta-blockers for preventing first variceal bleeding (78% vs 65% free of bleeding at 2 years), but the trials enrolled large varices, split individually, and never isolated medium varices — POSSIBLE for the medium-varices slice
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled placebo-controlled data favour beta-blockers for preventing first variceal bleeding (78% vs 65% free of bleeding at 2 years), but the trials enrolled large varices, split individually, and never isolated medium varices — POSSIBLE for the medium-varices slice
cards.people: The carded evidence: one individual-patient meta-analysis of the four placebo-controlled trials (589 patients, which pools the trials represented by the Idéo and Italian cards), the two largest constituent trials reported separately (79 and 174 patients), and one ongoing-trial protocol in small varices (740 planned, no results). PREDESCI (PMID 30910320) is cross-pointed to its home on live shelf #776 and is not carded here.
cards.result: Freedom from first bleeding at 2 years was 78 ± 3% on beta-blocker vs 65 ± 3% on placebo in the pooled analysis (P = 0.002), with fatal bleeding reduced (freedom 90% vs 82%, P = 0.01) and overall survival not significantly different (71% vs 68%, P = 0.34). Individually, nadolol nearly abolished bleeding in one small trial (1/30 vs 11/49) while the largest trial found no significant overall effect (74% vs 59% free of bleeding). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for medium varices the claim rests on extrapolation from large-varices trials, adjusted for variceal size in the pooled analysis.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as a verdict on beta-blocker versus band ligation (shelf #3625) or on preventing decompensation in portal hypertension without variceal bleeding as the endpoint (shelf #776): it answers only drug versus no treatment for first bleeding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Poynard T et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1991 (PMID: 1674104); Idéo G et al. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1988 (PMID: 3276591); Italian Multicenter Project for Propranolol in Prevention of Bleeding. Journal of Hepatology. 1989 (PMID: 2671121); Patel VC et al. shelves.title: TMP-SMX for SBP prophylaxis: beat no prophylaxis in one small trial and matched norfloxacin head-to-head — a plausible alternative, not a proven equal (PARTIAL completion of the norfloxacin-only shelf #1675)
shelves.question: Should adults with cirrhosis take norfloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
shelves.mesh: Ascites/complications · Bacteremia/etiology,prevention & control · Bacterial Infections/etiology,prevention & control · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Peritonitis/etiology,prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination/administration & dosage,adverse effects,economics
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1675 covers norfloxacin prophylaxis alone in advanced cirrhosis; the slice carded here is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and the head-to-head comparison. TMP-SMX has one small placebo-controlled trial: Singh 1995 found spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or spontaneous bacteraemia in 3% (1/30) on TMP-SMX vs 27% (8/30) on no prophylaxis (P = 0.025), with deaths 7% vs 20% (P = 0.15, not significant). Against norfloxacin, two small randomised trials found no difference: Alvarez 2005, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis 16.0% on TMP-SMX vs 9.4% on norfloxacin, deaths 20.0% vs 21.9%; and Lontos 2014, infections 9 vs 10 episodes and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis 2 patients in each group over 12 months, with more definite/probable adverse events on TMP-SMX (22.5% vs 0%, P = 0.01). The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Komolafe 2020, 29 trials, 3896 participants) found no evidence of differences between any antibiotic and no intervention for mortality or serious adverse events, at low or very low certainty — clinically important differences could not be ruled out. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — TMP-SMX prevented spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in one small trial and matched norfloxacin in two head-to-head trials, so it is a plausible alternative where norfloxacin is unsuitable; the pooled certainty is low.

cards.headline: Singh 1995: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cut spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or bacteraemia to 3% (1/30) vs 27% (8/30) on no prophylaxis (P = 0.025) — in a single small trial (N = 60)
cards.summary: Singh 1995: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cut spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or bacteraemia to 3% (1/30) vs 27% (8/30) on no prophylaxis (P = 0.025) — in a single small trial (N = 60)
cards.people: 60 consecutive patients with cirrhosis and ascites at a university-affiliated Veterans Affairs medical centre, randomly assigned to no prophylaxis or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one double-strength tablet daily, five times a week (Monday to Friday); entry was stratified by serum bilirubin (over 51 µmol/L [over 3 mg/dL]), ascitic fluid protein (under 1 g/dL) and serum creatinine (over 177 µmol/L [over 2 mg/dL]) so high-risk patients were balanced. Median follow-up was 90 days. Trial N = 60, printed on the face.
cards.result: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or spontaneous bacteraemia developed in 27% (8/30) of patients without prophylaxis vs 3% (1/30) on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (P = 0.025). Overall infections developed in 30% (9/30) vs 3% (1/30) (P = 0.012). Death occurred in 20% (6/30) without prophylaxis and 7% (2/30) on the drug (P = 0.15 — not significant). Side effects, particularly haematologic toxicity, could not be attributed to the drug in any patient. The authors conclude trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was efficacious, safe and cost-effective for prevention in this trial.
cards.watchOut: One 60-patient, single-centre trial from 1995 with 90-day median follow-up: the entire placebo-controlled case for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole rests on 9 outcome events, and local resistance patterns have changed since.
cards.source: Singh N et al. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the prevention of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7887554. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Alvarez 2005: head-to-head, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurred in 16.0% on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs 9.4% on norfloxacin — no significant difference, and deaths were 20.0% vs 21.9% (N = 57)
cards.summary: Alvarez 2005: head-to-head, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurred in 16.0% on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs 9.4% on norfloxacin — no significant difference, and deaths were 20.0% vs 21.9% (N = 57)
cards.people: 57 patients with cirrhosis and ascites evaluated between March 1999 and March 2001, all with a previous episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or ascitic fluid protein at or below 1 g/dL and/or serum bilirubin at or above 2.5 mg/dL, randomly assigned to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 800/160 mg/day five days a week (25 patients) or norfloxacin 400 mg daily (32 patients); mean observation was 182 days on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 163 days on norfloxacin.
cards.result: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurred in 3 patients on norfloxacin (9.4%) and 4 on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (16.0%). Extraperitoneal infections occurred in 10 patients on norfloxacin (31.3%) and 6 on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (24.0%). Death occurred in 7 patients on norfloxacin (21.9%) and 5 on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (20.0%). Side effects occurred only in the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole group. The authors conclude the two drugs were equally effective for prophylaxis in this small sample, making trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole a valid alternative to norfloxacin. No P values for the between-group outcome comparisons are given in the record.
cards.watchOut: With 57 patients and 7 spontaneous bacterial peritonitis events in total, 'equally effective' means 'no difference detected', not proven equivalence — the point estimate for peritonitis numerically favoured norfloxacin.
cards.source: Alvarez RF et al. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole versus norfloxacin in the prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis. Arquivos de Gastroenterologia. 2005. PMID: 16444382. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lontos 2014: over 12 months, infections were 9 episodes on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs 10 on norfloxacin and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis was 2 patients in each group — but definite/probable adverse events were 22.5% vs 0% (P = 0.01)
cards.summary: Lontos 2014: over 12 months, infections were 9 episodes on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs 10 on norfloxacin and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis was 2 patients in each group — but definite/probable adverse events were 22.5% vs 0% (P = 0.01)
cards.people: 80 patients with cirrhosis at high risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (mean age 53.0 ± 9.3 years), assigned to norfloxacin 400 mg daily (40) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily (40) and followed for 12 months; Child-Pugh status, model for end-stage liver disease and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis risk factors were similar between groups. The primary endpoint was incidence of infection.
cards.result: There were 10 episodes of infection in the norfloxacin group and 9 in the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole group (P = 0.79). Two patients in each group developed spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (P = 0.60). Transplantation differed in favour of norfloxacin (P = 0.03) but death did not. Total adverse events were similar (7 vs 10, P = 0.59), but trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole carried an increased risk of a definite or probable adverse event (22.5% vs 0%, P = 0.01). The authors conclude the study failed to demonstrate a difference in preventing infection and that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can be considered an alternative first-line prophylaxis.
cards.watchOut: The transplantation difference (P = 0.03) is a secondary outcome in an 80-patient trial and is more likely allocation/listing chance than a drug effect; the robust signal here is the adverse-event difference against trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
cards.source: Lontos S et al. A randomized controlled study of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole versus norfloxacin for the prevention of infection in cirrhotic patients. Journal of Digestive Diseases. 2014. PMID: 24612987. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Komolafe 2020 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): across 29 trials (3896 patients) there was no evidence that any prophylactic antibiotic differed from no intervention on mortality or serious adverse events — certainty low or very low
cards.summary: Komolafe 2020 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): across 29 trials (3896 patients) there was no evidence that any prophylactic antibiotic differed from no intervention on mortality or serious adverse events — certainty low or very low
cards.people: Cochrane network meta-analysis of randomised trials of antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in adults with cirrhosis (searched to November 2018): 29 trials, 3896 participants, nine antibiotic regimens including norfloxacin and sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, and no active intervention; 23 trials (2587 participants) contributed to one or more outcomes. Participants had ascites with low protein or a previous history of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; follow-up ranged from 1 to 12 months. The pooled trials overlap with the trials carded on this shelf and on home shelf #1675.
cards.result: Approximately 10% of trial participants developed spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and 15% died. There was no evidence of differences between any of the antibiotics and no intervention in mortality (very low certainty) or number of serious adverse events (very low certainty); because of wide credible intervals, clinically important differences could not be ruled out. Many trials were at high risk of bias and overall certainty was low or very low. None of the trials reported health-related quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A network estimate dominated by small, old, high-bias-risk trials: 'no evidence of difference' at very low certainty is a statement about the evidence base, not proof that prophylaxis does nothing — the norfloxacin-specific randomised evidence lives on shelf #1675.
cards.source: Komolafe O et al. Antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in people with liver cirrhosis: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 31978256. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevented spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in one small trial (3% vs 27%) and matched norfloxacin in two head-to-head trials, with more drug-attributed adverse events — a plausible alternative, at low pooled certainty
cards.summary: Synthesis: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevented spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in one small trial (3% vs 27%) and matched norfloxacin in two head-to-head trials, with more drug-attributed adverse events — a plausible alternative, at low pooled certainty
cards.people: The carded evidence: one placebo-controlled trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole trial (N = 60), two norfloxacin head-to-head trials (N = 57 and N = 80), and one Cochrane network meta-analysis (29 trials, 3896 participants, overlapping with the carded trials). Total unique participants across the three trials = 197, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the 60-patient anchor trial's N is printed on its face.
cards.result: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis/bacteraemia was 3% on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs 27% on no prophylaxis (P = 0.025; Singh 1995), with mortality 7% vs 20% (not significant). Against norfloxacin, peritonitis rates were 16.0% vs 9.4% (Alvarez 2005) and 2 patients in each group (Lontos 2014), while definite/probable adverse events favoured norfloxacin (0% vs 22.5%, P = 0.01). The Cochrane network analysis found no demonstrable mortality difference for any antibiotic at low/very low certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as an alternative prophylactic where norfloxacin is unsuitable.
cards.watchOut: Antibiotic choice for prophylaxis also turns on local quinolone resistance and prior exposure, which none of these records measures; the shelf answers comparative efficacy in trials, not a local prescribing rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singh N et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 1995 (PMID: 7887554); Alvarez RF et al. Arquivos de Gastroenterologia. 2005 (PMID: 16444382); Lontos S et al. shelves.title: Baclofen or acamprosate in alcohol-related liver disease: baclofen's evidence splits between a positive cirrhosis trial and null larger data; acamprosate is unproven in advanced liver disease — SPLIT (PARTIAL completion of the baclofen-in-cirrhosis shelf #1677)
shelves.question: Do baclofen or acamprosate help maintain abstinence in adults with alcohol-related liver disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Alcoholism/complications · Alcohol Drinking/adverse effects · Acamprosate/therapeutic use · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic/drug therapy · Liver Cirrhosis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1677 covers baclofen in cirrhosis on its single positive trial (Addolorato 2007, cross-pointed here and not re-carded); the slice carded here is the broader alcohol-related liver disease population and, above all, acamprosate, which the home shelf does not cover. The evidence genuinely divides, drug by drug and study by study, and the stamp names the split. For baclofen beyond the homed trial: the largest free randomised trial, in 180 veterans with chronic hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder, found baclofen made no difference to percentage of days abstinent versus placebo (absolute difference 1.3%, P = 0.95; Hauser 2017), and a meta-analysis of baclofen in alcohol use disorder with liver disease found the pooled randomised comparison non-significant (relative risk of abstinence 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92; Duan 2023). Against that, a 2024 systematic review of medications for alcohol use disorder in alcohol-associated cirrhosis (8 studies, 794 patients) found treatment associated with a relative risk of alcohol consumption of 0.68 (95% CI 0.48–0.97) — but baclofen supplied 6 of its 8 studies, including the homed trial, and heterogeneity was high (I2 = 67%). For acamprosate, the cirrhosis evidence is one study inside that review plus a real-world matched analysis in cirrhosis/alcohol-associated hepatitis that found no difference in abstinence or mortality at 1 year and higher readmission in the acamprosate group (85% vs 57%, P < 0.001; Oldroyd 2024) — confounding by severity is the likely explanation, but benefit is unproven in advanced liver disease. Safety across the review was reassuring (5 of 165 serious adverse events possibly/probably drug-related). PROPOSED SPLIT (baclofen: positive homed cirrhosis trial and positive pooled cirrhosis review, but null in the largest free randomised trial and in the baclofen-specific pooled randomised comparison; acamprosate: no abstinence benefit shown in advanced liver disease).

cards.headline: Gratacós-Ginès 2024: in alcohol-associated cirrhosis, medications for alcohol use disorder reduced alcohol consumption (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.97) — but baclofen supplied 6 of the 8 studies and acamprosate only 1
cards.summary: Gratacós-Ginès 2024: in alcohol-associated cirrhosis, medications for alcohol use disorder reduced alcohol consumption (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.97) — but baclofen supplied 6 of the 8 studies and acamprosate only 1
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (searches to May 2022) of medications for alcohol use disorder in patients with cirrhosis: 8 studies of 4 treatments (baclofen 6 studies, metadoxine 1, acamprosate 1, faecal microbiota transplant 1) in 794 patients in total; 4 were cohort studies and 4 randomised trials, and only the randomised trials entered the meta-analysis. The primary outcome was alcohol abstinence; safety was secondary. The baclofen studies overlap with the trial homed on live shelf #1677.
cards.result: Medications for alcohol use disorder were associated with a reduced rate of alcohol consumption (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.97, P = 0.03) — expressed by the authors as increasing alcohol abstinence by 32% relative to placebo or standard treatment — despite high heterogeneity (I2 = 67%). Of 165 serious adverse events in treated patients, only 5 (3%) were possibly or probably related to the study medications. The authors conclude these medications are effective in promoting abstinence in cirrhosis with a good safety profile, while calling for larger studies, especially in advanced liver disease. The relative measure is labelled relative; the record does not give a single pooled pair of absolute abstinence rates.
cards.watchOut: The pooled positive result is mostly a baclofen result, and within baclofen it leans on the small homed cirrhosis trial; it provides almost no independent information about acamprosate (one study) in liver disease.
cards.source: Gratacós-Ginès J et al. Medications for alcohol use disorder promote abstinence in alcohol-associated cirrhosis: Results from a systematic review and meta-analysis. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2024. PMID: 37625154. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hauser 2017: the largest free baclofen trial was null — in 180 veterans with hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder, baclofen made no difference to days abstinent vs placebo (absolute difference 1.3%, P = 0.95)
cards.summary: Hauser 2017: the largest free baclofen trial was null — in 180 veterans with hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder, baclofen made no difference to days abstinent vs placebo (absolute difference 1.3%, P = 0.95)
cards.people: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in hepatology clinics at four US Veterans Affairs medical centres: 180 veterans over 18 with chronic hepatitis C, comorbid alcohol use disorder and current alcohol use, given baclofen 30 mg/day or placebo (0 mg) for 12 weeks with manual-guided counselling. The primary outcome was percentage of days abstinent by timeline follow-back.
cards.result: Baclofen did not improve the primary outcome: percentage of days abstinent rose in both groups from 37.0% at baseline to 68.6% at 12 weeks, with no significant between-group difference in change (absolute difference 1.3%, 95% CI −9.1 to 1.7 as printed in the record, P = 0.95 — the treatment made no difference). Complete abstinence among those completing 4 weeks was 7.6% (6/79) on baclofen vs 10.1% (9/89) on placebo (odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.24–2.15); no heavy drinking between weeks 4 and 12 was 25.3% vs 15.7% (odds ratio 1.82, 0.85–3.90). Craving, anxiety, depression and biomarkers showed no between-group differences. The authors conclude baclofen 30 mg/day does not appear superior to placebo in this population.
cards.watchOut: Hepatitis C liver disease in veterans is not the same population as alcohol-related cirrhosis, and the dose was fixed at 30 mg/day — but as the largest placebo-controlled baclofen trial in any liver population it is the strongest single counterweight to the homed positive trial.
cards.source: Hauser P et al. The safety and efficacy of baclofen to reduce alcohol use in veterans with chronic hepatitis C: a randomized controlled trial. Addiction (Abingdon, England). 2017. cards.headline: Duan 2023: pooling the baclofen randomised trials in liver disease, abstinence did not differ significantly from placebo (relative risk 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92) — the confidence interval is very wide
cards.summary: Duan 2023: pooling the baclofen randomised trials in liver disease, abstinence did not differ significantly from placebo (relative risk 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92) — the confidence interval is very wide
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of baclofen for maintaining abstinence in patients with alcohol use disorder and comorbid liver diseases (alcohol-related liver disease, hepatitis C, or cirrhosis): 5 studies, 322 patients in total. The total abstinence rate on baclofen was 53% (95% CI 0.23–0.84); in the alcohol-related liver disease and cirrhosis subgroups it was 63% and 55% respectively. Two included studies were randomised controlled trials and entered the placebo comparison.
cards.result: Analysing the two randomised controlled studies, there was no significant difference in abstinence rates between baclofen and placebo (relative risk 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92 — a relative measure, with no pooled absolute rates given in the record). One serious adverse event was reported across the included studies, and no cases of baclofen addiction were found. The authors conclude baclofen's efficacy for maintaining abstinence in this population still needs validation with further studies, noting baclofen is the only drug investigated in randomised studies for anti-craving effect in alcohol use disorder with liver disease.
cards.watchOut: Only two randomised trials and 322 patients across all five studies: the interval from 0.41 to 4.92 is compatible with substantial harm or substantial benefit, so this card says 'unproven', not 'disproven'.
cards.source: Duan F et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis: Efficacy and safety of baclofen in patients with alcohol use disorder co-morbid liver diseases. Journal of Psychiatric Research. 2023. PMID: 37441998. Registry ID: CRD42021284439 (PROSPERO, from the record). cards.headline: Oldroyd 2024: in real-world cirrhosis/alcohol-associated hepatitis care, acamprosate showed no difference in abstinence or mortality at 1 year — and readmission was higher in the acamprosate group (85% vs 57%, P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Oldroyd 2024: in real-world cirrhosis/alcohol-associated hepatitis care, acamprosate showed no difference in abstinence or mortality at 1 year — and readmission was higher in the acamprosate group (85% vs 57%, P < 0.001)
cards.people: Retrospective case-control study at a large UK tertiary centre: 451 patients admitted with alcohol-related cirrhosis and/or alcohol-associated hepatitis met inclusion criteria, of whom 55 were started on acamprosate during admission; after propensity matching on the factors that differed between groups (age, type of admission, psychiatric comorbidity, alcohol consumption, partner and employment status), 53 acamprosate patients were compared with 53 matched controls. The primary outcome was repeat hospitalisation; abstinence and mortality were assessed at 1 year.
cards.result: Before matching, acamprosate patients were younger (median 51 vs 57 years, P < 0.005), drank more (median 155 vs 80 units/week, P < 0.001) and had more psychiatric comorbidity (42% vs 20%, P < 0.001). After matching, at 1 year there was a significantly higher readmission rate in the acamprosate group (85% vs 57%, P < 0.001) and no statistically significant differences in abstinence rates or mortality. The authors suggest the readmission finding may reflect greater severity of alcohol use disorder in those prescribed acamprosate, or the limited ability of acamprosate to alter the disease course in this population.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confounded by indication — clinicians prescribe acamprosate to the heaviest drinkers — so the higher readmission rate cannot be read as acamprosate causing harm; what the study does show is the absence of any demonstrated abstinence benefit in advanced liver disease.
cards.source: Oldroyd C et al. Real-world analysis of acamprosate use in patients with cirrhosis and alcohol-associated hepatitis. BMJ Open Gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 39797662. cards.headline: Synthesis: baclofen's liver-disease evidence splits between the positive homed cirrhosis trial/pooled cirrhosis review and the null largest trial and pooled randomised comparison; acamprosate has no demonstrated abstinence benefit in advanced liver disease — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: baclofen's liver-disease evidence splits between the positive homed cirrhosis trial/pooled cirrhosis review and the null largest trial and pooled randomised comparison; acamprosate has no demonstrated abstinence benefit in advanced liver disease — SPLIT
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses (8 studies/794 patients in cirrhosis; 5 studies/322 patients for baclofen in liver disease — overlapping with each other and with the homed trial on shelf #1677), one randomised trial in hepatitis C (180 patients), and one matched real-world acamprosate analysis (53 vs 53 matched from 451 admissions). Total unique participants cannot be summed cleanly because the reviews pool the trials; no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Medications for alcohol use disorder in cirrhosis: relative risk of alcohol consumption 0.68 (0.48–0.97), driven by baclofen studies. Baclofen versus placebo in the pooled randomised comparison: relative risk of abstinence 1.42 (0.41–4.92), not significant; in the largest trial, days abstinent differed by 1.3% (P = 0.95, the treatment made no difference). Acamprosate in cirrhosis/alcohol-associated hepatitis: no significant abstinence or mortality difference at 1 year, with higher readmission (85% vs 57%) in a confounded observational comparison. Serious adverse events possibly/probably drug-related were 5 of 165 in the cirrhosis review. PROPOSED SPLIT (drug split and study split, both named in the stamp).
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf re-tests the homed Addolorato 2007 cirrhosis trial (shelf #1677); the split is between that trial's result and everything fetched since — a developer re-verdict on baclofen in cirrhosis may eventually need to reconcile the two shelves together.

shelves.title: BCAA for muscle mass in cirrhosis with sarcopenia (partial completion of #5367): SPLIT — small trials report gains, but the two larger controlled trials found BCAA added nothing to protein and exercise
shelves.question: Does branched-chain amino acid supplementation improve muscle mass in adults with cirrhosis and sarcopenia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amino Acids, Branched-Chain · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Sarcopenia · Standard of Care
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #5367 covers oral branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) for ascites and encephalopathy outcomes in advanced liver disease; this shelf answers only the outcome #5367 does not — muscle mass in cirrhosis with sarcopenia. Four randomised trials divide. Two small trials are positive: a 32-patient pilot found a significant within-group muscle-mass gain only in the BCAA arm (Hernández-Conde 2021), and a 54-patient frailty trial found skeletal muscle index rose within the BCAA group alongside frailty reversal (Siramolpiwat 2023). The two larger, placebo- or active-controlled trials are null: 60 patients given BCAA with exercise gained no more muscle than placebo (the treatment made no difference; Mohta 2022), and the largest trial, 150 patients over 12 months, found BCAA no better than whey protein for grip strength or lean mass (the treatment made no difference; Hey 2024). The positive trials are the smallest and lean on within-group change; the null trials include the only one big enough to be definitive and used an active protein control, which may itself build muscle. PROPOSED SPLIT — small early trials report muscle-mass gains with BCAA, but the two larger controlled trials (N=60 and N=150) found no advantage over placebo or whey protein: whether BCAA adds anything beyond adequate protein and exercise is unresolved.

cards.headline: Hernández-Conde 2021: in a 32-patient pilot (N on the face), only the BCAA group significantly improved muscle mass over 12 weeks (43.7 to 46 cm2/m2, P=0.023)
cards.summary: Hernández-Conde 2021: in a 32-patient pilot (N on the face), only the BCAA group significantly improved muscle mass over 12 weeks (43.7 to 46 cm2/m2, P=0.023)
cards.people: Pilot, prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 32 patients with cirrhosis and sarcopenia diagnosed by computed tomography, all receiving a nutritional and physical-activity intervention for 12 weeks; 17 received placebo and 15 received BCAA. Randomised N = 32.
cards.result: After treatment, only the BCAA group presented a significant improvement in muscle mass (43.7 vs 46 cm2/m2; P=0.023). Improvement in muscle mass occurred in 63% of patients overall and was more frequent in the BCAA group (83.3% vs 46.7%; P=0.056). Liver Frailty Index improved significantly in both groups (each P<0.001), so frailty gains cannot be credited to BCAA. The BCAA group had a higher increase in zinc levels (difference 12.3 vs 5.5; P=0.026) and a trend to greater albumin improvement (P=0.091). The authors conclude BCAA supplementation improves muscle mass in cirrhotic patients with sarcopenia.
cards.watchOut: A 32-patient pilot whose headline result is a within-group change (the between-group responder comparison was P=0.056, not significant): this is hypothesis-generating, and both arms received nutrition and activity co-interventions.
cards.source: Hernández-Conde M et al. Adding Branched-Chain Amino Acids to an Enhanced Standard-of-Care Treatment Improves Muscle Mass of Cirrhotic Patients With Sarcopenia: A Placebo-Controlled Trial. cards.headline: Mohta 2022: adding BCAA to exercise and dietary counselling made no difference to muscle mass at 6 months (the treatment made no difference) — adjusted difference +0.84, P=0.42
cards.summary: Mohta 2022: adding BCAA to exercise and dietary counselling made no difference to muscle mass at 6 months (the treatment made no difference) — adjusted difference +0.84, P=0.42
cards.people: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of 60 patients with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh score under 10) and sarcopenia by gender-specific CT skeletal muscle index cut-offs, randomised 1:1 to oral BCAA 12 g/day or placebo for 6 months, in addition to a home-based exercise programme (30 min/day), dietary counselling and standard medical therapy.
cards.result: After adjusting for baseline confounders (MELD score and calorie intake, both higher in the placebo arm), baseline skeletal muscle index and protein intake, the change in muscle mass at 6 months was similar in both groups (mean adjusted difference +0.84, CI -2.9 to +1.2, P=0.42) — the treatment made no difference. Secondary outcomes were also similar: handgrip strength (P=0.65), 6-m gait speed (P=0.20) and 6-min walk distance (P=0.39). Four patients in each arm had minor adverse events. The authors conclude that adding BCAA to exercise, dietary counselling and standard therapy did not improve muscle mass.
cards.watchOut: Both arms exercised and received dietary counselling, so this trial tests the BCAA increment over good standard care — a null here does not mean nutrition and exercise do not work, only that BCAA added nothing measurable in 60 patients.
cards.source: Mohta S et al. Randomised clinical trial: effect of adding branched chain amino acids to exercise and standard-of-care on muscle mass in cirrhotic patients with sarcopenia. cards.headline: Hey 2024: in the largest trial (150 patients, 12 months), BCAA was no better than whey protein for grip strength or lean mass (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Hey 2024: in the largest trial (150 patients, 12 months), BCAA was no better than whey protein for grip strength or lean mass (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 12-month double-blind randomised controlled trial of BCAA supplementation (30 g daily) versus an equicaloric, equi-nitrogenous whey protein control in 150 volunteers with cirrhosis and reduced muscle strength (74 BCAA, 76 control; median age 58 years, median MELD 14). Primary endpoint: increase in grip strength and upper-limb lean mass on DEXA.
cards.result: At 12 months, 57% in the BCAA arm and 61% in the control arm met the primary endpoint (P=0.80). There was no significant between-group difference in grip strength (mean-adjusted difference -0.15 kg, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.06, P=0.29) or upper-limb lean mass (1.7 kg, 95% CI -0.2 to 3.6, P=0.22) — the treatment made no difference. No significant differences were found in other body-composition parameters, physical performance, frailty, hospitalisation or mortality. Side effects were reported by 15% of volunteers, with distaste higher in the BCAA arm (P=0.045). The authors conclude BCAA did not improve muscle strength, mass, performance or frailty compared with whey protein.
cards.watchOut: The control was whey protein — itself a leucine-rich muscle-building supplement — so this trial shows BCAA is not superior to another protein source, not that protein supplementation is useless; it is nonetheless the largest and longest test of the BCAA-specific claim.
cards.source: Hey P et al. Branched-chain amino acid supplementation does not improve measures of sarcopenia in cirrhosis: results of a randomised controlled trial. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2024. PMID: 38404263. Registry ID: ACTRN12618000802202 (from the record). cards.headline: Siramolpiwat 2023: 16 weeks of BCAA improved the Liver Frailty Index more than control (-0.36 vs -0.15, P=0.01) and skeletal muscle index rose within the BCAA group, in 54 frail patients (N on the face)
cards.summary: Siramolpiwat 2023: 16 weeks of BCAA improved the Liver Frailty Index more than control (-0.36 vs -0.15, P=0.01) and skeletal muscle index rose within the BCAA group, in 54 frail patients (N on the face)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 54 patients with compensated cirrhosis and frailty (Liver Frailty Index 4.5 or above; mean age 65.5 years, Child-Pugh A/B 68.5%/31.5%), randomised after a 4-week dietary and exercise counselling run-in to twice-daily BCAA supplementation (210 kcal, protein 13.5 g, BCAA 2.03 g) or control for 16 weeks. Randomised N = 54.
cards.result: At week 16 the BCAA group had significantly greater improvement in Liver Frailty Index (-0.36 ± 0.3 vs -0.15 ± 0.28, P=0.01), BMI (+0.51 ± 1.19 vs -0.49 ± 1.89 kg/m2, P=0.03) and serum albumin (+0.26 ± 0.27 vs +0.06 ± 0.3 g/dL, P=0.01). Frailty reversion was significantly more frequent with BCAA (36% vs 0%, P<0.001). Compared with baseline, the BCAA group significantly increased skeletal muscle index (7.5 ± 1.6 to 7.8 ± 1.5 kg/m2, P=0.03) — a within-group comparison; the record does not report a between-group muscle-mass effect size. Only the BCAA group significantly improved all four physical-component domains of the SF-36.
cards.watchOut: The population was frail compensated cirrhosis (not selected for sarcopenia by imaging), the BCAA dose was small (about 4 g/day within a protein-containing supplement, so protein itself may explain gains), and the muscle-mass result is a within-group change without a reported between-group effect.
cards.source: Siramolpiwat S et al. Branched-chain amino acids supplementation improves liver frailty index in frail compensated cirrhotic patients: a randomized controlled trial. BMC gastroenterology. 2023. PMID: 37189033. Registry ID: TCTR20210928001 (from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: the muscle-mass evidence splits by trial size and control — small trials positive, the two larger controlled trials null
cards.summary: Synthesis: the muscle-mass evidence splits by trial size and control — small trials positive, the two larger controlled trials null
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials in cirrhosis with sarcopenia or frailty — 32 (pilot, placebo control), 60 (placebo control, with exercise), 150 (whey-protein active control, 12 months) and 54 (frailty population) participants; 296 unique randomised participants in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, though the two positive trials are the two smallest.
cards.result: Muscle mass improved significantly within the BCAA arm of the 32-patient pilot (43.7 to 46 cm2/m2, P=0.023; Hernández-Conde 2021) and skeletal muscle index rose within the BCAA arm of the 54-patient frailty trial (7.5 to 7.8 kg/m2, P=0.03; Siramolpiwat 2023). Against controls, BCAA made no difference to muscle-mass change in the 60-patient exercise trial (adjusted difference +0.84, P=0.42; Mohta 2022) or to grip strength and lean mass in the 150-patient whey-controlled trial (Hey 2024). PROPOSED SPLIT, as a partial completion of live shelf #5367 (which homes BCAA for ascites/encephalopathy, not muscle).
cards.watchOut: Do not average this split away: the fair reading is that BCAA has not beaten adequate protein plus exercise in any adequately sized trial, and the positive signals come from small trials and within-group changes.

shelves.title: Outpatient versus inpatient diverticulitis care (partial completion of #3621): in selected patients, home treatment is as safe as admission — pooled readmission 7%, emergency surgery 0.2% — at a third of the cost
shelves.question: Is outpatient management safe for adults with uncomplicated diverticulitis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Ambulatory Care · Diverticulitis, Colonic · Female · Health Care Costs · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Spain · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3621 homes an outpatient cohort whose randomised comparison is antibiotics versus no antibiotics (DINAMO); this shelf answers the different comparison #3621 does not — outpatient versus inpatient management itself. The only randomised trial of the setting question, DIVER (132 patients), found treatment failure in 4 inpatients and 3 outpatients with no difference between groups (P=0.619), no quality-of-life difference, and an episode cost three times lower as an outpatient (Biondo 2014). Two meta-analyses of the wider, mostly observational literature agree: pooled outpatient failure was 4.3% across 1,781 patients (Cirocchi 2019), and pooled readmission was 7% across 2,303 outpatients, with only 0.2% needing emergency surgery (van Dijk 2018). The catch is selection: the underlying studies predominantly excluded patients with comorbidity or immunosuppression, inability to tolerate oral intake, or no adequate social support — outpatient management is proven safe for selected patients, not for everyone who walks in. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in selected adults with CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis who can take oral treatment and have support at home, outpatient management is as safe as admission and much cheaper; the randomised base is a single 132-patient trial, which caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Biondo 2014 (DIVER): outpatient management failed no more often than hospitalisation (3 vs 4 failures, P=0.619) and cost a third as much per episode
cards.summary: Biondo 2014 (DIVER): outpatient management failed no more often than hospitalisation (3 vs 4 failures, P=0.619) and cost a third as much per episode
cards.people: Prospective multicentre randomised clinical trial (DIVER Trial) of 132 patients older than 18 years with acute uncomplicated left colonic diverticulitis, all confirmed by abdominal computed tomography. All patients received a first intravenous antibiotic dose in the emergency department; group 1 was then hospitalised and group 2 discharged for outpatient treatment. The primary endpoint was treatment failure of the outpatient protocol and need for hospital admission.
cards.result: Four patients in the hospitalisation group and three in the outpatient group presented treatment failure, without differences between the groups (P=0.619). No differences were observed in quality of life. The overall healthcare cost per episode was 3 times lower in the outpatient group, with savings of €1124.70 per patient. The authors conclude outpatient treatment is safe and effective in selected patients with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, with important cost savings and no negative influence on quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Only 132 patients and seven failure events in total: the trial can exclude a large harm of outpatient care but not a small one, and every patient was CT-confirmed, given an intravenous first dose, and judged fit for discharge — the selection is part of the intervention.
cards.source: Biondo S et al. Outpatient versus hospitalization management for uncomplicated diverticulitis: a prospective, multicenter randomized clinical trial (DIVER Trial). Annals of surgery. 2014. PMID: 23732265. Registry ID: EudraCT:2008-008452-17 (from the record). cards.headline: Cirocchi 2019: across 21 studies and 1,781 outpatients, pooled failure of outpatient management was 4.3% (95% CI 2.6%-6.3%), and almost no failures needed surgery (0.06%)
cards.summary: Cirocchi 2019: across 21 studies and 1,781 outpatients, pooled failure of outpatient management was 4.3% (95% CI 2.6%-6.3%), and almost no failures needed surgery (0.06%)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies (11 prospective, 9 retrospective, and only 1 randomised trial) including 1,781 patients managed as outpatients for uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, searched to September 2018. Failure was defined as any emergency hospital admission within 60 days of outpatient treatment.
cards.result: The pooled overall failure rate of outpatient management was 4.3% (95% CI 2.6%-6.3%). No subgroup factor significantly influenced failure: previous episodes (P=0.163), comorbidities (P=0.187), pericolic air (P=0.653), intra-abdominal abscess (P=0.326), registered protocol (P=0.078), follow-up type (P=0.700), antibiotic type (P=0.647) or diabetes (P=0.610); diverticulitis location was not a selection criterion (P=0.512). Among failures, most received prolonged antibiotics; percutaneous drainage was needed in 0.13% and surgical intervention for perforation in 0.06%. The authors caution that the data suggest safety with accurate patient selection (about 40% of patients) but rest on low-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: Only one of the 21 studies was randomised — the same DIVER trial carded above — so this review widens the patient count without adding independent randomised evidence, and its authors flag the low quality of the underlying data.

cards.headline: van Dijk 2018: pooled readmission after outpatient treatment was 7% (95% CI 6%-9%), emergency surgery 0.2%, and cost savings versus inpatient care ranged from 42% to 82%
cards.summary: van Dijk 2018: pooled readmission after outpatient treatment was 7% (95% CI 6%-9%), emergency surgery 0.2%, and cost savings versus inpatient care ranged from 42% to 82%
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies with 2,303 patients treated as outpatients for acute colonic diverticulitis confirmed by computed tomography or ultrasound. The included studies predominantly excluded patients with comorbidity or immunosuppression, inability to tolerate oral intake, or lack of an adequate social network.
cards.result: The pooled readmission rate for outpatient treatment was 7% (95% CI 6%-9%). Only 0.2% (2 of 1,288) of patients underwent emergency surgery and 0.2% (2 of 1,082) underwent percutaneous abscess drainage. In the two studies with comparable inpatient control groups, readmissions were 4.5% (3/66) and 6.3% (2/32) in outpatient groups versus 6.1% (4/66) and 0.0% (0/44) in inpatient groups (P=0.619 and P=0.174). Average healthcare cost savings for outpatient versus inpatient treatment ranged between 42% and 82%. The authors conclude outpatient treatment of uncomplicated diverticulitis seems a safe option for most patients.
cards.watchOut: 'Most patients' in the conclusion means most selected patients: the exclusion criteria in the primary studies (comorbidity, immunosuppression, poor oral intake, weak social support) define the population to which the 7% readmission figure applies.
cards.source: van Dijk ST et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of outpatient treatment for acute diverticulitis. International journal of colorectal disease. 2018. PMID: 29532202. cards.headline: Synthesis: for selected patients, outpatient care matches inpatient safety (failures 3 vs 4 in the only randomised trial; pooled readmission 7%) at a fraction of the cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: for selected patients, outpatient care matches inpatient safety (failures 3 vs 4 in the only randomised trial; pooled readmission 7%) at a fraction of the cost
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of the setting question (132 patients, DIVER) and two meta-analyses of the outpatient literature (21 studies/1,781 patients; 19 studies/2,303 patients — overlapping study sets that both include DIVER, so their Ns are not additive). Total unique randomised participants = 132, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite the reassuring pooled rates.
cards.result: Treatment failure did not differ between outpatient and hospital management in DIVER (3 vs 4 patients, P=0.619), with episode costs 3 times lower as an outpatient (Biondo 2014). Pooled outpatient failure was 4.3% (Cirocchi 2019) and pooled readmission 7%, with emergency surgery in 0.2% (van Dijk 2018). All evidence applies to selected patients — CT-confirmed uncomplicated disease, able to take oral treatment, with support at home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as a partial completion of live shelf #3621 (which homes the antibiotics-versus-none question in outpatients, not the setting question).
cards.watchOut: The safety claim is inseparable from triage: nothing here supports sending home a patient with peritonism, immunosuppression, vomiting, or no one at home, and the meta-analyses cannot repair that selection because the unselected patients were never studied as outpatients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Biondo S et al. Annals of surgery. 2014 (PMID: 23732265); Cirocchi R et al. Techniques in coloproctology. 2019 (PMID: 30684110); van Dijk ST et al. International journal of colorectal disease. 2018 (PMID: 29532202).

shelves.title: Botulinum toxin after topical failure in chronic anal fissure (partial completion of #2472): effective and sphincter-sparing, but less healing and more recurrence than sphincterotomy in treatment failures
shelves.question: Is botulinum toxin injection effective for chronic anal fissure that does not heal with topical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anal Canal · Botulinum Toxins, Type A · Chronic Disease · Female · Fissure in Ano · Humans · Injections · Male · Middle Aged · Neuromuscular Agents · Prospective Studies · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2472 covers chronic anal fissure treatment generally, including botulinum toxin against placebo and topical glyceryl trinitrate as first-line options; this shelf answers only the next step #2472 does not isolate — the patient whose fissure has already failed topical/conservative therapy, where the real choice is botulinum toxin injection versus lateral internal sphincterotomy (LIS). The one trial that explicitly enrolled conservative-treatment failures found surgery healed significantly more fissures than botulinum toxin, with significantly fewer recurrences, while botulinum toxin carried significantly less incontinence (Nasr 2010, 80 patients). A second randomised comparison found the same pattern over longer follow-up: healing equal by 3 months after an early surgical lead (88% vs 44% at 2 months), but higher recurrence after botulinum toxin and more early incontinence after surgery (Valizadeh 2012, 50 patients). A dose-ranging randomised study shows the injection itself, with retreatment of non-healers, heals most fissures by 2 months (89%-96%; Brisinda 2002, 150 patients) — so 'effective' is true in absolute terms, but in the topical-refractory patient it is the less durable of the two definitive options, bought with a lower continence risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): botulinum toxin heals a majority of topical-refractory fissures and avoids permanent sphincter damage, but heals fewer and recurs more than sphincterotomy — a reasonable step before, or instead of, surgery for patients who prioritise continence.

cards.headline: Nasr 2010: in 80 patients who had failed conservative treatment, sphincterotomy healed significantly more fissures than botulinum toxin and recurred less — but caused significantly more incontinence
cards.summary: Nasr 2010: in 80 patients who had failed conservative treatment, sphincterotomy healed significantly more fissures than botulinum toxin and recurred less — but caused significantly more incontinence
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trial of 80 consecutive patients with uncomplicated chronic anal fissure who had failed conservative treatment, randomised to intrasphincteric botulinum toxin injection or lateral internal sphincterotomy. Outcomes over 18 weeks of follow-up were pain relief, fissure healing, continence scores and fissure relapse.
cards.result: Healing was statistically significantly higher in the sphincterotomy group than the botulinum toxin group (P=0.0086; 95% CI for the difference 7.38%-45.69%). Sphincterotomy was also associated with a significantly higher rate of anal incontinence compared with botulinum toxin (P=0.0338; 95% CI -1.64%-27.53%), and the recurrence rate in the botulinum toxin group was significantly higher than in the sphincterotomy group (P=0.0111; 95% CI 6.68%-46.13%). The record reports these differences as confidence intervals and P values without printing each group's absolute healing percentage. The authors conclude sphincterotomy has a higher healing rate and lower recurrence, while botulinum toxin is a simple noninvasive technique that avoids the greater incontinence risk.
cards.watchOut: This is the only carded trial whose entry criterion is failed conservative treatment — the exact population of this shelf — but it is a single-centre 80-patient trial with only 18 weeks of follow-up, and its abstract reports differences without absolute group healing rates.
cards.source: Nasr M et al. Botulinum toxin injection versus lateral internal sphincterotomy in the treatment of chronic anal fissure: a randomized controlled trial. World journal of surgery. 2010. PMID: 20703472. Registry ID: none in the record.
