cards.headline: Valizadeh 2012: botulinum toxin caught up on healing by 3 months (from 44% vs 88% at 2 months) but recurred more by 6 months, while sphincterotomy caused more early incontinence
cards.summary: Valizadeh 2012: botulinum toxin caught up on healing by 3 months (from 44% vs 88% at 2 months) but recurred more by 6 months, while sphincterotomy caused more early incontinence
cards.people: Randomised prospective controlled trial of 50 consecutive adults with chronic anal fissure, randomly treated with lateral internal sphincterotomy or botulinum toxin injection (50 units into the internal sphincter). Complications, healing, recurrence and incontinence scores were assessed at 2, 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: At the 2-month visit, complete healing was found in 11 of the botulinum toxin group (44%) and 22 of the sphincterotomy group (88%) (P=0.001). By the 3-month visit there was no significant difference in healing between the groups. The overall recurrence rate after 6 months was higher in the botulinum toxin group than the sphincterotomy group (P<0.05). At 3 months the sphincterotomy group had a higher rate of anal incontinence (P<0.05); the final incontinence percentage was 4% in the sphincterotomy group (P>0.05). The authors conclude botulinum toxin has a higher recurrence rate, sphincterotomy provides rapid and permanent recovery but carries a higher incontinence risk, and treatment must be individualised.
cards.watchOut: A 50-patient trial in chronic fissure generally (not restricted to topical failures): its catch-up healing by 3 months may partly reflect slower botulinum-toxin action rather than equivalence, and 12 months is short for recurrence.
cards.source: Valizadeh N et al. Botulinum toxin injection versus lateral internal sphincterotomy for the treatment of chronic anal fissure: randomized prospective controlled trial. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2012. PMID: 22430300. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brisinda 2002: botulinum toxin healed 73%-87% of fissures by 1 month and 89%-96% by 2 months when non-healers were retreated — higher doses healed more
cards.summary: Brisinda 2002: botulinum toxin healed 73%-87% of fissures by 1 month and 89%-96% by 2 months when non-healers were retreated — higher doses healed more
cards.type: Randomised dose-comparison trial, all patients treated (Brisinda 2002)
cards.people: Randomised dose-comparison trial of 150 patients with posterior anal fissures, all treated with botulinum toxin injected into the internal anal sphincter on each side of the anterior midline. Group I received 20 units, retreated with 30 units if the fissure persisted; group II received 30 units, retreated with 50 units if the fissure persisted. Groups were comparable in age, sex, symptom duration and manometry pressures.
cards.result: One month after injection, complete healing was found in 55 patients (73%) in group I and 65 patients (87%) in group II (P=.04). At 2 months, a healing scar was found in 67 patients (89%) in group I and 72 patients (96%) in group II. Relapse occurred in 6 patients (8%) in group I who had healed at 1 month, and 2 other patients never healed; a persistent fissure was present in 3 patients in group II. Five patients in group II reported mild flatus incontinence lasting 2 weeks that disappeared spontaneously. Resting and maximum voluntary pressures did not differ between groups. The authors conclude botulinum toxin is effective in managing anal fissures while avoiding permanent complications, and higher doses give higher success with little increase in side effects.
cards.watchOut: Every patient received botulinum toxin — there is no placebo or surgery arm — so the 89%-96% healing includes spontaneous healing and the effect of retreatment, and follow-up was only 2 months, too short to capture the recurrence that dominates the head-to-head trials.
cards.source: Brisinda G et al. Effectiveness of higher doses of botulinum toxin to induce healing in patients with chronic anal fissures. Surgery. 2002. PMID: 11854696. cards.headline: Synthesis: botulinum toxin works in absolute terms (about 9 in 10 fissures healed by 2 months with retreatment) but in topical failures it is beaten on healing and recurrence by sphincterotomy, winning only on continence
cards.summary: Synthesis: botulinum toxin works in absolute terms (about 9 in 10 fissures healed by 2 months with retreatment) but in topical failures it is beaten on healing and recurrence by sphincterotomy, winning only on continence
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised botulinum-toxin-versus-sphincterotomy trials (80 patients enrolled after failed conservative treatment; 50 patients with chronic fissure) and one 150-patient randomised dose study of botulinum toxin with retreatment — 280 unique participants in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In conservative-treatment failures, sphincterotomy healed significantly more fissures (difference 95% CI 7.38%-45.69%) with significantly fewer recurrences and significantly more incontinence (Nasr 2010). Healing after botulinum toxin was slower (44% vs 88% at 2 months) but statistically indistinguishable by 3 months, with recurrence still higher at 6 months (Valizadeh 2012). With retreatment of non-healers, botulinum toxin alone healed 89%-96% by 2 months (Brisinda 2002). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as a partial completion of live shelf #2472 (which homes first-line fissure therapy, not the topical-refractory choice).
cards.watchOut: Only Nasr 2010 restricted entry to treatment failures; the other two cards enrol chronic fissure broadly, so the refractory-specific estimate rests mainly on one 80-patient trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nasr M et al. World journal of surgery. 2010 (PMID: 20703472); Valizadeh N et al. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2012 (PMID: 22430300); Brisinda G et al. Surgery. 2002 (PMID: 11854696).

shelves.title: Proton pump inhibitors and fractures with long use (PARTIAL, observational only): risk about 30% higher in relative terms and rising with duration — an association the randomised evidence on the home shelf did not confirm
shelves.question: Does taking a proton pump inhibitor increase the risk of bone fractures in adults who use it for more than a year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Ulcer Agents/adverse effects · Bone Density/drug effects · Canada/epidemiology · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects · Hip Fractures/epidemiology · Histamine H2 Antagonists/administration & dosage · Histamine H2 Antagonists/adverse effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Osteoporotic Fractures/epidemiology · Proton Pump Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Proton Pump Inhibitors/adverse effects · Research Design · Risk Factors · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #325. That shelf weighs fractures as one of several long-term PPI harms and cards the randomised pantoprazole evidence (no fracture difference over 3 years); this shelf covers the uncovered slice: fracture risk alone, with duration of use at its centre, from the observational literature the home does not card. Across 11 observational studies, PPI use was associated with hip fracture relative risk 1.30, spine 1.56 and any-site 1.16 (Yu 2011). An updated meta-analysis of 33 studies (2,714,502 individuals) found fracture incidence of 22.04% in users vs 15.57% in controls (pooled relative effect 1.28) with a duration gradient — odds ratio 1.29 for short use, 1.33 for medium and 1.62 for long use — but no bone-density difference (Nassar 2018). In the Nurses' Health Study, regular use for at least 2 years carried hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.35 (absolute risk 2.02 vs 1.51 per 1,000 person-years), rising with longer use and confined to ever-smokers (Khalili 2012). Every carded report here is observational, the relative effects sit in the confounding-prone range, and the randomised evidence on #325 found no fracture difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: long-term PPI use is associated with a modestly higher fracture risk, increasing with duration; causation is unproven.

cards.headline: Yu 2011: across 11 observational studies, proton pump inhibitor use was associated with modestly higher fracture risk — hip relative risk 1.30, spine 1.56, any site 1.16 (relative measures; observational only)
cards.summary: Yu 2011: across 11 observational studies, proton pump inhibitor use was associated with modestly higher fracture risk — hip relative risk 1.30, spine 1.56, any site 1.16 (relative measures; observational only)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 10 publications reporting 11 international studies, all observational case-control or cohort studies, primarily evaluating older adults, of proton pump inhibitor or histamine(2)-receptor antagonist use and fractures. The record does not print a pooled total participant number.
cards.result: The summary effect estimate for hip fracture was modestly increased among individuals taking proton pump inhibitors (relative risk 1.30; 95% CI 1.19 to 1.43 — a relative measure; the record prints no absolute fracture rates). There was also an increase in spine fractures (RR 1.56; 95% CI 1.31 to 1.85) and any-site fractures (RR 1.16; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.30) among proton pump inhibitor users, similar in men and women and after stratification by duration of use. Histamine(2)-receptor antagonist use was not significantly associated with hip fracture (RR 1.12; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.30). The authors state the possibility of residual confounding cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is observational: people prescribed PPIs for years differ from non-users in age, frailty, comorbidity and other drug use, and a relative risk of 1.30 sits inside the range such confounding can produce — this card shows association, not causation, and says so.

cards.headline: Nassar 2018: across 33 studies with 2,714,502 individuals, fracture incidence was 22.04% in PPI users vs 15.57% in controls (pooled effect 1.28) — and the association rose with duration, reaching odds ratio 1.62 for long use
cards.summary: Nassar 2018: across 33 studies with 2,714,502 individuals, fracture incidence was 22.04% in PPI users vs 15.57% in controls (pooled effect 1.28) — and the association rose with duration, reaching odds ratio 1.62 for long use
cards.type: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of epidemiological and cohort studies (Nassar 2018)
cards.people: 33 epidemiological and cohort studies providing data from 2,714,502 individuals (mean age 66.91 years; about one-third men and two-thirds women as printed), meta-analysing odds ratios, hazard ratios and risk ratios between proton pump inhibitor use and bone fracture incidence, and standardised mean differences in bone mineral density. Duration of use was categorised as short, medium and long in the included studies (the record does not print the year cut-points for each category).
cards.result: Overall, fracture incidence was 22.04% (95% CI 16.10 to 27.97) in proton pump inhibitor users and 15.57% (95% CI 12.28 to 18.86) in controls, with an overall pooled effect size of 1.28 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.35 — a relative measure, with the absolute incidences printed here). There was a trend towards increased fracture incidence with duration: short-duration use odds ratio 1.29 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.40), medium-duration use OR 1.33 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.55) and long-duration use OR 1.62 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.90). There was no significant difference between users and controls in cross-sectional bone mineral density values or in longitudinal bone-density change.
cards.watchOut: The duration gradient is the strongest causal-looking feature in this literature — but the underlying studies are observational, the duration categories are the included studies' own (not a uniform '>1 year' cut), and the same analysis finds no bone-density difference, which cuts against the simplest acid-suppression/calcium-absorption mechanism.
cards.source: Nassar Y et al. Proton-pump Inhibitor Use and Fracture Risk: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of bone metabolism. 2018. PMID: 30237993. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Khalili 2012: in 79,899 postmenopausal women, regular PPI use for at least 2 years carried a 35% relative higher hip-fracture risk (hazard ratio 1.35) — absolute risk 2.02 vs 1.51 fractures per 1,000 person-years — with risk rising with longer use, and no association in never-smokers
cards.summary: Khalili 2012: in 79,899 postmenopausal women, regular PPI use for at least 2 years carried a 35% relative higher hip-fracture risk (hazard ratio 1.35) — absolute risk 2.02 vs 1.51 fractures per 1,000 person-years — with risk rising with longer use, and no association in never-smokers
cards.type: Prospective cohort study, Nurses' Health Study (Khalili 2012)
cards.people: 79,899 postmenopausal women in the Nurses' Health Study who provided data on proton pump inhibitor use and other risk factors biennially since 2000 and were followed to 1 June 2008 (565,786 person-years); 893 incident hip fractures were documented.
cards.result: The absolute risk of hip fracture among regular users of proton pump inhibitors was 2.02 events per 1,000 person-years, compared with 1.51 events per 1,000 person-years among non-users. Compared with non-users, the risk among women who regularly used PPIs for at least two years was 35% higher in relative terms (age-adjusted hazard ratio 1.35; 95% CI 1.13 to 1.62), with longer use associated with increasing risk (P for trend < 0.01); adjustment for body mass index, physical activity and calcium intake did not materially alter the association (HR 1.36; 95% CI 1.13 to 1.63), nor did accounting for reasons for PPI use. The relation differed by smoking history (P for interaction = 0.03): among current and former smokers the multivariate hazard ratio was 1.51 (1.20 to 1.91), while among women who never smoked there was no association (HR 1.06; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.46). A meta-analysis of these results with 10 prior studies gave a pooled odds ratio of 1.30 (1.25 to 1.36).
cards.watchOut: One cohort of US nurses, all women: the smoking interaction means the headline association may not apply to never-smokers at all, and even in smokers the absolute excess is about half a fracture per 1,000 person-years — small for an individual, visible only at population scale.
cards.source: Khalili H et al. Use of proton pump inhibitors and risk of hip fracture in relation to dietary and lifestyle factors: a prospective cohort study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2012. PMID: 22294756. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: long-term PPI use is associated with a modestly higher fracture risk in observational data only — relative risks around 1.3, rising with duration — and the one large randomised test on the home shelf found no fracture difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: long-term PPI use is associated with a modestly higher fracture risk in observational data only — relative risks around 1.3, rising with duration — and the one large randomised test on the home shelf found no fracture difference
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of observational studies (11 studies; and 33 studies with 2,714,502 individuals) and one prospective cohort of 79,899 postmenopausal women. All carded evidence on this shelf is observational, which is printed in the stamp; total participants exceed 2.7 million, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Proton pump inhibitor users had higher fracture risk than non-users in every carded analysis: hip relative risk 1.30 and any-site 1.16 across 11 studies (Yu 2011); pooled effect 1.28 with fracture incidence 22.04% vs 15.57% and a duration gradient reaching odds ratio 1.62 for long use across 33 studies (Nassar 2018); and, for at least 2 years of regular use, hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.35 with absolute risks of 2.02 vs 1.51 per 1,000 person-years, confined to ever-smokers (Khalili 2012). Set against this, the randomised pantoprazole evidence carded on home shelf #325 (3 years, 17,598 patients) found no fracture difference — the observational association has not survived randomisation where it has been tested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: A relative risk near 1.3 from observational data, with no bone-density signal and a null randomised test, is exactly the profile of a confounded association; the honest reading is 'associated, unproven' — which is what the stamp says — not 'PPIs cause fractures' and not 'proven safe'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yu EW et al. The American journal of medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21605729); Nassar Y et al. Journal of bone metabolism. 2018 (PMID: 30237993); Khalili H et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2012 (PMID: 22294756).

shelves.title: Antivirals in chronic hepatitis B with normal liver enzymes (PARTIAL completion of #326): the evidence splits by how strictly the immune-tolerant subgroup is defined, and treatment is proven only to suppress virus in this group
shelves.question: Should adults with chronic hepatitis B and normal liver enzymes receive antiviral treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents/*therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/epidemiology/*etiology · Cohort Studies · DNA, Viral/blood · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hepatitis B e Antigens/blood · Hepatitis B virus/genetics · Hepatitis B, Chronic/*complications/drug therapy/mortality · Humans · Immune Tolerance · Incidence · Liver Neoplasms/epidemiology/*etiology · Liver Transplantation/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Republic of Korea/epidemiology · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #326 covers long-term antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B broadly (progression, cirrhosis and liver cancer) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #326 does not isolate: patients whose liver enzymes are normal, including the immune-tolerant phase. The observational evidence genuinely divides, and the split turns on how strictly the subgroup is defined. In a Korean cohort using normal ALT alone (Kim 2018), untreated immune-tolerant patients fared worse than treated immune-active patients (10-year liver cancer 12.7% vs 6.1%; hazard ratio 2.54 relative). But when the immune-tolerant phase is defined stringently — under 40 years old, very high viral load, ALT under 40 U/L (Lee 2021) — no liver cancer at all occurred in 194 untreated patients over a median 62 months, and a natural-history cohort (Lee 2020) found the risk concentrated in patients with intermediate viral loads, with zero cancers in the truly immune-tolerant subgroup. The one randomised trial in exactly this population (Chan 2014) shows treatment suppresses the virus (76% vs 55% suppressed at 192 weeks on combination versus single-agent therapy) but produced HBeAg seroconversion in only 5% and no surface-antigen loss, and no trial tests whether treating normal-enzyme patients prevents cancer or death. All hard-outcome evidence here is observational. PROPOSED SPLIT (observational only — risk definition decides: broadly defined normal-ALT cohorts show excess liver cancer when untreated, stringently defined immune-tolerant cohorts show negligible risk; whether treatment itself improves hard outcomes in this subgroup is untested in a trial).

cards.headline: Kim 2018: untreated immune-tolerant patients (normal ALT) had higher 10-year liver cancer (12.7% vs 6.1%) and death/transplant rates than treated immune-active patients — hazard ratio 2.54 relative for liver cancer
cards.summary: Kim 2018: untreated immune-tolerant patients (normal ALT) had higher 10-year liver cancer (12.7% vs 6.1%) and death/transplant rates than treated immune-active patients — hazard ratio 2.54 relative for liver cancer
cards.people: Historical cohort at a Korean tertiary hospital, 2000–2013: 413 untreated immune-tolerant-phase patients (hepatitis B e antigen-positive, HBV DNA ≥20,000 IU/mL, no cirrhosis, normal ALT defined as <19 IU/mL in females and <30 IU/mL in males) compared with 1,497 immune-active-phase patients (ALT ≥80 IU/mL) treated with nucleos(t)ide analogues. The immune-tolerant group was younger (mean age 38 vs 40 years).
cards.result: The 10-year estimated cumulative incidences of hepatocellular carcinoma (12.7% vs 6.1%; p = 0.001) and death/transplantation (9.7% vs 3.4%; p < 0.001) were significantly higher in the untreated immune-tolerant group than in the treated immune-active group. In multivariable analyses the immune-tolerant group had a higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (hazard ratio 2.54, 95% CI 1.54 to 4.18, relative measure) and death/transplantation (hazard ratio 3.38, 95% CI 1.85 to 6.16, relative measure), consistent through inverse-probability weighting, propensity matching and competing-risks analyses.
cards.watchOut: This is a cross-phase comparison — untreated immune-tolerant patients versus treated immune-active patients — not treated versus untreated patients within the normal-ALT subgroup, so it cannot by itself show that treating normal-ALT patients prevents cancer; phase, age and viral-load differences ride along with the treatment contrast.
cards.source: Kim GA et al. High risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and death in patients with immune-tolerant-phase chronic hepatitis B. Gut. 2018. PMID: 29055908. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lee 2021: with a stringent immune-tolerant definition (under 40, very high viral load, ALT <40 U/L), no liver cancer occurred in 194 untreated patients — the opposite answer from a tighter definition
cards.summary: Lee 2021: with a stringent immune-tolerant definition (under 40, very high viral load, ALT <40 U/L), no liver cancer occurred in 194 untreated patients — the opposite answer from a tighter definition
cards.people: Multicentre study of untreated immune-tolerant patients (n = 194) defined by American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases criteria — under 40 years of age, persistently hepatitis B e antigen-positive, serum HBV DNA >6 log10 IU/mL and ALT <40 U/L — compared with 454 treated hepatitis B e antigen-positive patients treated under practice and reimbursement guidelines. Patients with cirrhosis or liver cancer at baseline were excluded; median follow-up 62.1 months.
cards.result: Hepatocellular carcinoma did not develop in any patient in the untreated immune-tolerant group, whereas the cumulative probability of hepatocellular carcinoma in the treated group was 0.5%, 0.7% and 1.3% at 3, 5 and 9 years (p = 0.203). Ninety-seven of the untreated immune-tolerant patients entered the immune-active phase, of whom 86 (88.7%) started antiviral treatment; a high-normal ALT (20–39 U/L) was associated with an increased risk of phase change compared with ALT <20 U/L. After censoring at phase change, the cumulative liver cancer risk was also not significantly different between the groups (p = 0.258).
cards.watchOut: Half the untreated group left the immune-tolerant phase during follow-up and most then started treatment, so this cohort supports watchful waiting with monitoring in stringently defined patients — not a lifetime no-treatment conclusion for everyone with normal enzymes.
cards.source: Lee HW et al. Negligible HCC risk during stringently defined untreated immune-tolerant phase of chronic hepatitis B. European Journal of Internal Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33288393. cards.headline: Lee 2020: in untreated patients with high viral load but normal ALT, 9-year liver cancer risk was 1.9% and comparable to inactive carriers — and zero in the subgroup with viral load above 1,000,000 IU/mL
cards.summary: Lee 2020: in untreated patients with high viral load but normal ALT, 9-year liver cancer risk was 1.9% and comparable to inactive carriers — and zero in the subgroup with viral load above 1,000,000 IU/mL
cards.people: Cohort of untreated patients with persistently elevated HBV DNA (>20,000 IU/mL) but normal ALT (<40 IU/L) (n = 126) compared with inactive carriers (n = 621), enrolled 2006–2012; patients with cirrhosis or liver cancer at enrolment or prior nucleos(t)ide treatment were excluded.
cards.result: The cumulative hepatocellular carcinoma risks at 5 and 9 years in the untreated high-DNA/normal-ALT group were 1.1% and 1.9%, comparable with the inactive-carrier group (P = 0.549), with similar results after inverse-probability weighting and propensity matching. Within the untreated group there were no cases of hepatocellular carcinoma in the subgroup with serum HBV DNA >1,000,000 IU/mL (the immune-tolerant phase proper), significantly different (P = 0.002) from those with an intermediate HBV DNA level (20,000–1,000,000 IU/mL).
cards.watchOut: The untreated high-DNA group is small (126 patients) and mixes two different risks — the record itself separates the zero-event truly immune-tolerant subgroup from the intermediate-viral-load subgroup where the cancers arose, so the pooled 1.9% figure should not be quoted for either subgroup alone.
cards.source: Lee HW et al. Natural History of Untreated HBeAg-Positive Chronic HBV Infection With Persistently Elevated HBV DNA but Normal Alanine Aminotransferase. cards.headline: Chan 2014: the only randomised trial in normal-ALT, high-viral-load patients — combination therapy suppressed the virus more (76% vs 55% at 192 weeks) but seroconversion was 5% and no patient lost surface antigen
cards.summary: Chan 2014: the only randomised trial in normal-ALT, high-viral-load patients — combination therapy suppressed the virus more (76% vs 55% at 192 weeks) but seroconversion was 5% and no patient lost surface antigen
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial of 126 nucleos(t)ide-naive patients who were hepatitis B e antigen-positive with high HBV DNA and normal ALT, assigned to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus placebo (n = 64) or tenofovir plus emtricitabine (n = 62) for 192 weeks. Mean age 33 years; 89% Asian; mean baseline HBV DNA 8.41 log10 IU/mL.
cards.result: At week 192, 55% of patients (35 of 64) on tenofovir plus placebo and 76% (47 of 62) on tenofovir plus emtricitabine had HBV DNA <69 IU/mL (P = .016). HBeAg seroconversion occurred in 3 patients (5%), all in the tenofovir-alone group; no patient had loss of hepatitis B surface antigen, and no viral resistance was found. Both regimens were well tolerated. The trial measured viral suppression only — it reports no liver cancer, cirrhosis or mortality outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Suppression of viral load is a surrogate: this trial cannot say whether treating normal-enzyme patients prevents liver cancer or death, and its low seroconversion rate shows most treated immune-tolerant patients remain e antigen-positive on therapy.
cards.source: Chan HLY et al. Effects of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in hepatitis B e antigen-positive patients with normal levels of alanine aminotransferase and high levels of hepatitis B virus DNA. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24462735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the normal-enzyme subgroup splits by definition — broadly defined cohorts show untreated risk, stringently defined immune-tolerant cohorts show negligible risk, and treatment itself is trial-proven only to suppress virus
cards.summary: Synthesis: the normal-enzyme subgroup splits by definition — broadly defined cohorts show untreated risk, stringently defined immune-tolerant cohorts show negligible risk, and treatment itself is trial-proven only to suppress virus
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Korean cohort programmes reaching opposite conclusions under different subgroup definitions (413 untreated immune-tolerant vs 1,497 treated immune-active patients; 194 stringently defined untreated patients vs 454 treated; 126 untreated high-DNA/normal-ALT patients vs 621 inactive carriers) and one randomised trial in the exact population (126 patients). All hard-outcome evidence is observational.
cards.result: Untreated immune-tolerant patients defined by normal ALT alone had 10-year liver cancer incidence 12.7% vs 6.1% in treated immune-active patients (hazard ratio 2.54 relative) (Kim 2018); stringently defined untreated immune-tolerant patients developed no liver cancer at all over a median 62 months (Lee 2021), and untreated high-DNA/normal-ALT risk (1.9% at 9 years) was concentrated at intermediate viral loads, with zero events above 1,000,000 IU/mL (Lee 2020). Treatment suppresses HBV DNA (76% vs 55% at 192 weeks for combination vs single agent) with 5% seroconversion and no surface-antigen loss (Chan 2014). PROPOSED SPLIT (observational only), as stated in the balance.
cards.watchOut: Every hard-outcome number on this shelf is observational and the two directions come from different patient definitions and different comparators; the shelf must not be flattened into either 'treat everyone with normal enzymes' or 'never treat'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kim GA et al. Gut. 2018 (PMID: 29055908); Lee HW et al. European Journal of Internal Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33288393); Lee HW et al. Clinical and Translational Gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 32352711); Chan HLY et al. Gastroenterology. 2014 (PMID: 24462735).

shelves.title: Direct-acting antivirals in compensated cirrhosis (PARTIAL completion of #593): cure is nearly as high with compensated cirrhosis as without — about 98% vs 99% — with defined exceptions
shelves.question: In adults with hepatitis C, do direct-acting antivirals cure infection in people with compensated cirrhosis as well as in those without cirrhosis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Carbamates · Drug Therapy, Combination · Genotype · Hepacivirus/genetics · *Hepatitis C/drug therapy · *Hepatitis C, Chronic/drug therapy · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings · Humans · Ribavirin/therapeutic use · Sofosbuvir/therapeutic use · Sustained Virologic Response · Treatment Outcome · Benzimidazoles · Benzopyrans
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #593 covers direct-acting antiviral cure across genotypes and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #593 does not isolate: compensated cirrhosis versus no cirrhosis, head to head. The answer across three independent large datasets is that cure is nearly as high with compensated cirrhosis, with a small, consistent penalty. In the largest real-world analysis (Mangia 2020, 5,552 patients on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir), sustained virological response was 98.9% overall and 97.9% (1,055/1,078) in compensated cirrhosis — and cirrhosis was the only factor significantly associated with virological failure (P = .002), on only 55 virological failures in total. In the prospective HCV-TARGET cohort (Terrault 2016, 2,099 patients, 41% cirrhotic), overall cure was 95–97% by regimen duration and absence of cirrhosis was one of the factors predicting cure, though the record does not print a cirrhosis-specific percentage. The trial-side integrated analysis restricted to compensated cirrhosis (Jacobson 2017, 402 patients with Child-Pugh A cirrhosis across 6 trials of elbasvir/grazoprevir) found cure of 97.8% in treatment-naive patients on 12 weeks, with lower rates in treatment-experienced patients (88.9% on 12 weeks) and in genotype 1a with baseline resistance substitutions (73%) — the exceptions that define where 'as well' stops holding. Decompensated cirrhosis is a different question and is not covered here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C in compensated cirrhosis nearly as well as without cirrhosis (about 98% vs about 99%), with cure modestly lower in treatment-experienced patients and in genotype 1a with resistance substitutions.

cards.headline: Mangia 2020: in 5,552 real-world patients on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, cure was 98.9% overall and 97.9% (1,055/1,078) with compensated cirrhosis — cirrhosis was the only significant predictor of virological failure, on just 55 failures
cards.summary: Mangia 2020: in 5,552 real-world patients on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, cure was 98.9% overall and 97.9% (1,055/1,078) with compensated cirrhosis — cirrhosis was the only significant predictor of virological failure, on just 55 failures
cards.people: Analysis of 12 real-world cohorts worldwide: 5,552 adults treated with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 400/100 mg once daily for 12 weeks without ribavirin; 13.3% were treatment-experienced, 20.7% had compensated cirrhosis, and genotypes 1, 2, 3 and 4 made up 30.2%, 29.5%, 32.9% and 4.7%. Effectiveness was evaluated in 5,196 patients reaching week 12 or 24 after treatment.
cards.result: Overall, 98.9% of evaluated patients achieved sustained virological response (SVR12/24, i.e. cure). Rates were high in all genotypes including genotype 3 (98.3%; 1,649/1,677) and in compensated cirrhosis (97.9%; 1,055/1,078). Only 55 patients failed for virological reasons, and compensated cirrhosis was the only factor statistically significantly associated with increased risk of not achieving SVR (P = .002). A further 6% (332/5,552) did not achieve SVR for non-virological reasons, two-thirds of them lost to follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The non-cirrhosis cure rate is not printed separately in the record — the comparison is cirrhosis 97.9% against the 98.9% overall figure that includes the cirrhotic patients themselves, so the true cirrhosis penalty is about one percentage point, stated as approximate for that reason.
cards.source: Mangia A et al. Global real-world evidence of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir as simple, effective HCV treatment: Analysis of 5552 patients from 12 cohorts. Liver International. 2020. PMID: 32449966. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Terrault 2016 (HCV-TARGET): cure was 95–97% across ledipasvir/sofosbuvir durations in 2,099 prospectively followed patients, and absence of cirrhosis predicted cure — the record does not print a cirrhosis-specific rate
cards.summary: Terrault 2016 (HCV-TARGET): cure was 95–97% across ledipasvir/sofosbuvir durations in 2,099 prospectively followed patients, and absence of cirrhosis predicted cure — the record does not print a cirrhosis-specific rate
cards.people: Multicentre prospective observational study (HCV-TARGET): 2,099 participants with complete virological data (per-protocol population), of whom 1,788 received ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (282 for 8 weeks, 910 for 12 weeks, 510 for 24 weeks, 86 for other durations) and 311 received ledipasvir/sofosbuvir plus ribavirin. The population was 41% cirrhotic, 50% treatment-experienced and 66% genotype 1a.
cards.result: Sustained virological response at 12 weeks (SVR12) was achieved by 96% (95% CI 93%–98%) of patients on 8 weeks, 97% (95% CI 96%–98%) on 12 weeks and 95% (95% CI 93%–97%) on 24 weeks of ledipasvir/sofosbuvir; with ribavirin, 97% on 12 weeks and 95% on 24 weeks. Factors that predicted SVR12 were higher albumin (≥3.5 g/dL), lower total bilirubin, absence of cirrhosis, and absence of proton pump inhibitor use. The record does not print the SVR12 percentage for the cirrhotic subgroup separately.
cards.watchOut: A predictor statement ('absence of cirrhosis predicted SVR') without a printed subgroup rate supports direction, not size; this card corroborates the small cirrhosis penalty seen in the other two datasets rather than measuring it.
cards.source: Terrault NA et al. Effectiveness of Ledipasvir-Sofosbuvir Combination in Patients With Hepatitis C Virus Infection and Factors Associated With Sustained Virologic Response. Gastroenterology. 2016. PMID: 27565882. Registry ID: NCT01474811. cards.headline: Jacobson 2017: in 402 trial patients with compensated (Child-Pugh A) cirrhosis, elbasvir/grazoprevir cured 97.8% of treatment-naive patients on 12 weeks — but only 88.9% of treatment-experienced, and 73% in genotype 1a with resistance substitutions
cards.summary: Jacobson 2017: in 402 trial patients with compensated (Child-Pugh A) cirrhosis, elbasvir/grazoprevir cured 97.8% of treatment-naive patients on 12 weeks — but only 88.9% of treatment-experienced, and 73% in genotype 1a with resistance substitutions
cards.type: Integrated analysis of 6 clinical trials, cirrhosis only (Jacobson 2017)
cards.people: Integrated analysis of 6 clinical trials: 402 patients with hepatitis C virus genotype 1, 4 or 6 infection and Child-Pugh A compensated cirrhosis, all treated with elbasvir/grazoprevir 50 mg/100 mg once daily, with or without ribavirin, for 12–18 weeks. The endpoint was sustained virological response 12 weeks after treatment (HCV RNA <15 IU/mL).
cards.result: Among patients on 12 weeks of elbasvir/grazoprevir, SVR12 was 97.8% (135 of 138) in treatment-naive and 88.9% (48 of 54) in treatment-experienced patients. Adding ribavirin at 12 weeks did not increase response (treatment-naive 90.3%, 28 of 31). At 16–18 weeks, all treatment-experienced patients on ribavirin achieved SVR12 (49 of 49), as did 93.9% (46 of 49) without ribavirin. Virological failure was higher in genotype 1a than 1b or 4; in genotype 1a with baseline resistance-associated substitutions, SVR12 on 12 weeks was 73% (8 of 11) versus 98% (96 of 98) without substitutions. The record is restricted to cirrhotic patients and prints no non-cirrhosis comparator.
cards.watchOut: Cirrhosis-only by design: this card measures how high cure runs inside compensated cirrhosis and where it dips (treatment experience, genotype 1a resistance), while the cirrhosis-versus-no-cirrhosis contrast itself comes from the two cohort cards.
cards.source: Jacobson IM et al. Safety and Efficacy of Elbasvir/Grazoprevir in Patients With Hepatitis C Virus Infection and Compensated Cirrhosis: An Integrated Analysis. Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 28193518. Registry ID: NCT02105662 (one of six trial registrations in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: compensated cirrhosis costs about one percentage point of cure — roughly 98% versus 99% — with the real exceptions being prior treatment failure and genotype 1a resistance, not cirrhosis itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: compensated cirrhosis costs about one percentage point of cure — roughly 98% versus 99% — with the real exceptions being prior treatment failure and genotype 1a resistance, not cirrhosis itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 5,552-patient global real-world analysis with a printed cirrhosis-specific cure rate, a 2,099-patient prospective cohort in which absence of cirrhosis predicted cure, and a 402-patient integrated trial analysis restricted to compensated cirrhosis. The cross-genotype cure shelf is live #593, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Cure with compensated cirrhosis was 97.9% (1,055/1,078) against 98.9% overall on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, with cirrhosis the only significant predictor of virological failure on 55 failures (Mangia 2020). Overall cure was 95–97% by duration on ledipasvir/sofosbuvir with absence of cirrhosis predicting response (Terrault 2016). Within compensated cirrhosis on elbasvir/grazoprevir, cure was 97.8% in treatment-naive patients, 88.9% in treatment-experienced patients on 12 weeks, and 73% in genotype 1a with baseline resistance substitutions (Jacobson 2017). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), as stated in the balance.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf covers decompensated cirrhosis, where cure rates and the meaning of cure differ; and 'cure' throughout is sustained virological response, a surrogate whose link to liver outcomes is the separate question homed at #593.

shelves.title: Six-food elimination diet in adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis (PARTIAL completion of live #2768): about half to two-thirds reach histologic remission in three adult cohorts — all observational
shelves.question: Does the six-food elimination diet induce remission in adults with eosinophilic esophagitis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biopsy, Needle · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Eosinophils · Esophagus · Female · Food Hypersensitivity · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Skin Tests · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2768 homes elimination diets across children and adults together (Arias 2014 meta-analysis, PMID 24534634 — homed there, not re-carded here), reporting six-food remission of 72.1% in the mixed-age pool. This shelf asks about adults alone, from the three free adult-specific reports. In the original prospective adult series (Gonsalves 2012, 50 adults), 6 weeks of six-food elimination (milk, wheat, egg, soy, peanut/tree nuts, fish/shellfish) brought peak counts to ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field in 64% and to ≤10 in 70%, and systematic reintroduction brought the inflammation back — the closest thing to an internal control this literature has. The largest adult cohort (Zalewski 2022, 213 adults) found 54% below 15 eosinophils per high-power field after the diet, rising to 58% after an extended round. A UK–Italian series (Visaggi 2023, 58 adults) found a 56.9% response overall, but only 21.4% in pollen-sensitised patients assessed during pollen season versus 77.3% outside it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational: the diet induces remission in about half to two-thirds of adults who complete it; there is no randomised adult trial of the diet against no treatment, and the one randomised diet trial in this field (one-food versus six-food elimination) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Gonsalves 2012: after 6 weeks of six-food elimination, 64% of 50 adults reached ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field — and food reintroduction brought the disease back
cards.summary: Gonsalves 2012: after 6 weeks of six-food elimination, 64% of 50 adults reached ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field — and food reintroduction brought the disease back
cards.people: 50 adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis (dysphagia 96%, food impaction 74%, heartburn 94%) at a US academic centre, studied prospectively: endoscopy with biopsies and skin-prick testing for food and aeroallergens, then 6 weeks of six-food elimination diet, repeat endoscopy and biopsies, and systematic food reintroduction in histologic responders.
cards.result: Mean peak eosinophil counts fell from 34 to 8 per high-power field in the proximal oesophagus and from 44 to 13 distally (P<.0001). After the diet, 64% of patients had peak counts ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field and 70% had ≤10; symptom scores decreased in 94% (P<.0001). After food reintroduction, oesophageal eosinophil counts returned to pretreatment values (P<.0001). Based on reintroduction, the foods most often responsible were wheat (60% of cases) and milk (50%); skin-prick testing predicted only 13% of the foods identified.
cards.watchOut: No control group: spontaneous fluctuation, and the endoscopy-and-dietitian attention around the diet, cannot be separated from the diet's own effect — though relapse on reintroduction in the same patients is strong internal evidence that food was driving the disease.
cards.source: Gonsalves N et al. Elimination diet effectively treats eosinophilic esophagitis in adults; food reintroduction identifies causative factors. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22391333. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zalewski 2022: in the largest adult series (213 patients), 54% reached remission below 15 eosinophils per high-power field on the six-food diet, 58% after an extended round
cards.summary: Zalewski 2022: in the largest adult series (213 patients), 54% reached remission below 15 eosinophils per high-power field on the six-food diet, 58% after an extended round
cards.people: 213 adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis at a US academic centre who completed the six-food elimination diet (milk, wheat, soy, eggs, tree nuts/peanuts, fish/shellfish) as clinical care between 2006 and 2021, reviewed retrospectively; full responders were those below 15 eosinophils per high-power field after the diet, and most responders went on to structured food reintroduction.
cards.result: 115 of 213 patients (54%) responded to the initial six-food elimination, and 77% of responders had symptom improvement. After either the initial diet or one additional round of dietary elimination, 58% (123 patients) were below 15 eosinophils per high-power field, and the authors calculate that about 31% of initial non-responders may respond to a second attempt. Among patients who completed reintroduction, 69% had one food trigger identified, 24% had two and 4% had three; the commonest triggers were milk, wheat and soy.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-centre and without a comparison group; patients who complete a demanding diet and return for repeat endoscopy are a selected subset of all adults offered it, so 54% is a completer rate, not an intention-to-treat rate. (The record's own MeSH list includes 'Animals', an indexing artefact of the source record, copied as published.)

cards.headline: Visaggi 2023: overall response 56.9% — but in pollen-sensitised adults assessed during pollen season, response collapsed to 21.4% versus 77.3% outside the season
cards.summary: Visaggi 2023: overall response 56.9% — but in pollen-sensitised adults assessed during pollen season, response collapsed to 21.4% versus 77.3% outside the season
cards.people: 58 consecutive adults with active eosinophilic oesophagitis (≥15 eosinophils per high-power field before the diet) at UK and Italian centres who undertook the six-food elimination diet under dietitian supervision and had skin-prick testing for birch and grass pollen; 62.0% were pollen-sensitised. Response was compared according to whether the post-diet assessment fell during or outside the pollen season, using individual sensitisation and pollen-count data.
cards.result: Overall, the response to the diet was 56.9% (95% CI 44.1–68.8%). Among pollen-sensitised patients, response was significantly lower when assessed during pollen season than outside it (21.4% vs 77.3%; P=0.003); during pollen season, sensitised patients also responded far less than non-sensitised patients (21.4% vs 77.8%; P=0.01). The authors conclude that pollens may sustain oesophageal eosinophilia in sensitised adults despite avoidance of trigger foods.
cards.watchOut: Small (58 patients) and observational, with season assigned by assessment date rather than randomisation — but it identifies a concrete reason an adult may appear to fail the diet, and a reason to time the post-diet endoscopy outside pollen season.
cards.source: Visaggi P et al. Six-Food Elimination Diet Is Less Effective During Pollen Season in Adults With Eosinophilic Esophagitis Sensitized to Pollens. cards.headline: Synthesis: in adults, the six-food diet induces remission in roughly half to two-thirds of completers — on observational evidence alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: in adults, the six-food diet induces remission in roughly half to two-thirds of completers — on observational evidence alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: three adult observational reports (Gonsalves 50, Zalewski 213, Visaggi 58 adults; 321 in total), so no small-N stamp labelling applies. No randomised or untreated-control adult study of the six-food diet was free to card.
cards.result: Adult remission rates cluster around one-half to two-thirds: 64% to a strict ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field threshold (Gonsalves), 54% to below 15 (Zalewski) and 56.9% overall (Visaggi) — against 72.1% for the mixed child-and-adult pool homed on live shelf #2768. Relapse on food reintroduction (Gonsalves) and single-trigger identification in most responders (Zalewski) support a real dietary effect despite the absence of controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational: the six-food elimination diet induces histologic remission in roughly half to two-thirds of adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis who complete it.
cards.watchOut: Remission thresholds differ between cards (≤5, ≤10 and <15 eosinophils per high-power field), so the percentages are not strictly interchangeable; and every rate here is in diet completers with repeat endoscopy, not in all adults who start the diet.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gonsalves N et al. Gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 22391333); Zalewski A et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2022 (PMID: 35971213); Visaggi P et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2023 (PMID: 37307575).

shelves.title: Early versus delayed cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis in older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #650): no elderly randomised trial exists; observational data favour operating early in selected patients, and delay invites recurrence
shelves.question: Is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy better than delayed surgery for acute cholecystitis in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cholecystectomy, Laparoscopic/adverse effects,mortality · Cholecystitis, Acute/surgery · Conversion to Open Surgery · Humans · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the older-adult slice live shelf #650 leaves open (its ACDC and Roulin trials enrolled general adult populations). No randomised trial has tested timing in older adults specifically — the dedicated international study in patients 70 and over (GOLDENEYE) is still a protocol — so this shelf rests on elderly-specific observational evidence. Early cholecystectomy in patients aged 70 and over is feasible but not benign: across 8 series totalling 592 patients (mean age 81), conversion was 23%, perioperative morbidity 24% and mortality 3.5% (Loozen 2017). In 21,392 NSQIP patients, surgery delayed to day 3 or beyond carried significantly higher bleeding and mortality, and the authors report the delay penalty was most marked in the elderly subgroup (Daniel 2021). The one elderly head-to-head cohort found emergency surgery and medical treatment followed by elective surgery produced similar overall outcomes — with the emergency arm's 53% morbidity reflecting how much sicker its patients were (Sánchez Beorlegui 2009). And when older patients are drained first, waiting is expensive: in octogenarians, cholecystectomy delayed 6 weeks or more after drainage brought recurrent cholecystitis in 52.9% versus 4.9% with earlier surgery (Pan 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only: in selected older adults, operating early beats delaying — with selection, not age alone, doing the work.

cards.headline: Loozen 2017: early cholecystectomy in 592 patients aged 70 or over (mean age 81) — conversion 23%, perioperative morbidity 24%, mortality 3.5%
cards.summary: Loozen 2017: early cholecystectomy in 592 patients aged 70 or over (mean age 81) — conversion 23%, perioperative morbidity 24%, mortality 3.5%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of early cholecystectomy series in the elderly (Loozen 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies reporting early cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis in patients aged 70 years or older: 592 patients, mean age 81 years; 316 (53%) operated laparoscopically and 276 (47%) by open surgery; pooled rates calculated with a random-effects model.
cards.result: Early cholecystectomy in this elderly population was associated with a conversion rate of 23% (95% CI 18.6 to 28.3), perioperative morbidity of 24% (95% CI 20.5 to 27.5), and mortality of 3.5% (95% CI 2.3 to 5.4). The authors conclude early cholecystectomy seems feasible in elderly patients with acute cholecystitis, that patients who may benefit ought to be selected carefully to reduce morbidity, and that prospective studies comparing early surgery with alternative treatments are still needed.
cards.watchOut: This is a single-arm pool: it prices early surgery in the elderly (roughly 1 in 4 with a complication, 1 in 29 dead) but contains no delayed-surgery comparator, so by itself it cannot say early beats delayed — that comparison comes from the cohort cards that follow, with their confounding.
cards.source: Loozen CS et al. Early Cholecystectomy for Acute Cholecystitis in the Elderly Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Digestive surgery. 2017. PMID: 28095385. cards.headline: Daniel 2021: in 21,392 NSQIP cholecystectomy patients, surgery at day 3 or later carried significantly higher bleeding and mortality — a delay penalty the authors found most significant in the elderly
cards.summary: Daniel 2021: in 21,392 NSQIP cholecystectomy patients, surgery at day 3 or later carried significantly higher bleeding and mortality — a delay penalty the authors found most significant in the elderly
cards.people: 21,392 patients undergoing cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis in the US National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database, 2014–2016, divided by day of surgery (day 0, 1, 2, or 3 or later after admission) with adjustment for confounders; primary outcome short-term surgical morbidity and mortality, with subgroup analyses including the elderly and patients with diabetes.
cards.result: Compared with day 0, patients operated on day 1 or day 2 had lower composite morbidity, while patients operated at day 3 or later had a significantly higher bleeding and mortality rate. Subgroup analysis showed this delay trend to be more significant in the elderly and in diabetic patients who were delayed. The authors conclude that delaying cholecystectomy beyond 72 hours from admission is associated with a statistically significant increase in bleeding and mortality.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports the elderly subgroup finding qualitatively ('more significant in the elderly') without elderly-specific event rates, so this card cannot put a number on the older-patient penalty; and in database data, delay is partly a marker of patients who were sicker or harder to optimise, not purely a cause of their outcomes.
cards.source: Daniel FE et al. Timing of cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis impacts surgical morbidity and mortality: an NSQIP database analysis. Updates in surgery. 2021. PMID: 33475946. cards.headline: Sánchez Beorlegui 2009: in 147 patients aged 70 or over, emergency surgery (morbidity 53%, mortality 3.5%) and medical treatment followed by elective surgery (morbidity 9.6%, no deaths in the operated subgroup) gave similar overall outcomes
cards.summary: Sánchez Beorlegui 2009: in 147 patients aged 70 or over, emergency surgery (morbidity 53%, mortality 3.5%) and medical treatment followed by elective surgery (morbidity 9.6%, no deaths in the operated subgroup) gave similar overall outcomes
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study in patients aged 70 and over (Sánchez Beorlegui 2009)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 147 patients aged 70 years or older (mean age 80.6 years, maximum 101; 52% women) treated for 173 episodes of acute cholecystitis at a Spanish centre, 2003–2009: 103 episodes managed medically (of which 31 went on to elective surgery) and 85 patients treated with emergency surgery (78.5% laparoscopic).
cards.result: Elective surgery after medical treatment was performed laparoscopically in 100% of cases, with a 6.4% conversion rate, 9.6% morbidity and no mortality. Emergency surgery had a 19.7% conversion rate, 53% morbidity and 3.5% mortality. Taking all variables into account, the authors found emergency surgery and medical treatment followed by elective cholecystectomy achieved similar outcomes, with patients undergoing early laparoscopic cholecystectomy progressing best.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication dominates this comparison: the emergency arm took the patients too sick to wait (hence 53% morbidity), while the elective subgroup is the selected minority who settled on antibiotics and stayed well enough for a planned operation — and the medically managed patients who never reached elective surgery are not in its denominator. Read it as 'both pathways can end well in the right patients', not as a fair race.
cards.source: Sánchez Beorlegui J et al. [Treatment of acute cholecystitis in the elderly: urgent surgery versus medical therapy and surgery delay]. cards.headline: Pan 2023: in 152 octogenarians drained first for moderate-to-severe cholecystitis, delaying cholecystectomy 6 weeks or more brought recurrent cholecystitis in 52.9% versus 4.9% with earlier surgery
cards.summary: Pan 2023: in 152 octogenarians drained first for moderate-to-severe cholecystitis, delaying cholecystectomy 6 weeks or more brought recurrent cholecystitis in 52.9% versus 4.9% with earlier surgery
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study in octogenarians after gallbladder drainage (Pan 2023)
cards.people: 152 patients aged 80 years or older with moderate-to-severe acute cholecystitis who received percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage at a single centre, 2008–2021, and then underwent cholecystectomy either early (within 6 weeks of drainage; 82 patients) or delayed (6 weeks or later; 70 patients); retrospective comparison of operative and recurrence outcomes.
cards.result: Operative time, operation-related complications and mortality did not differ between early and delayed groups. Recurrent acute cholecystitis occurred in 4.9% of the early group versus 52.9% of the delayed group, and further biliary events in 8.5% versus 57.1% (both P<0.001). On multivariable analysis, delayed cholecystectomy was a significant risk factor for recurrent cholecystitis (odds ratio 19.42 relative, P<0.001) and further biliary events (odds ratio 15.95 relative, P<0.001). The authors recommend early cholecystectomy after drainage in this age group.
cards.watchOut: This population had already been selected twice — sick enough to need drainage, then fit enough to be offered surgery at all — and 'delayed' here means waiting after a drain, a different clock from the admission-timing question; the enormous recurrence odds ratio (19.42) comes from a single-centre retrospective analysis and should be read as direction, not precise size.
cards.source: Pan YL et al. Early cholecystectomy following percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage is effective for moderate to severe acute cholecystitis in the octogenarians. Archives of gerontology and geriatrics. 2023. PMID: 36470181. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in older adults the evidence is observational throughout — early surgery is feasible and delay is consistently punished, but no elderly randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: in older adults the evidence is observational throughout — early surgery is feasible and delay is consistently punished, but no elderly randomised trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one elderly systematic review of early-surgery series (Loozen 2017; 592 patients aged 70+), one 21,392-patient database timing study with an elderly subgroup signal (Daniel 2021), one elderly head-to-head cohort (Sánchez Beorlegui 2009; 147 patients aged 70+), and one octogenarian post-drainage timing cohort (Pan 2023; 152 patients aged 80+). Total carded participants exceed 22,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Early surgery at 70+: morbidity 24%, mortality 3.5% (pooled series). Delay beyond 72 hours: significantly higher bleeding and mortality, most marked in the elderly (NSQIP). Head-to-head in the elderly: similar overall outcomes for emergency versus delayed-elective pathways, under heavy confounding by indication. After drainage at 80+: recurrence 52.9% delayed versus 4.9% early. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the better default for older adults selected as fit for surgery; the general-adult randomised evidence stays homed on live shelf #650 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Every comparative card is confounded by the same mechanism — fitter older patients get earlier surgery — so the true causal advantage of 'early' in this age group is smaller than the raw gaps, and the shelf's honest headline is the absence of an elderly trial: the international GOLDENEYE study in patients 70 and over is still at protocol stage.
cards.source: Synthesis of Loozen CS et al. Digestive surgery. 2017 (PMID: 28095385); Daniel FE et al. Updates in surgery. 2021 (PMID: 33475946); Sánchez Beorlegui J et al. Revista de gastroenterologia del Peru : organo oficial de la Sociedad de Gastroenterologia del Peru. 2009 (PMID: 20066018); Pan YL et al. Archives of gerontology and geriatrics. 2023 (PMID: 36470181).

shelves.title: Percutaneous cholecystostomy in high-risk acute cholecystitis patients who cannot have surgery (PARTIAL completion of live #1667): symptoms resolve in about 9 of 10, but the one randomised trial found no mortality advantage over antibiotics and conservative care
shelves.question: Does percutaneous cholecystostomy improve outcomes in high-risk adults with acute cholecystitis who cannot have surgery?
shelves.mesh: Acalculous Cholecystitis/diagnostic imaging,surgery · Aged · Cholecystitis, Acute/diagnostic imaging,surgery · Cholecystostomy/adverse effects,methods · Female · Hospitals, University · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Republic of Korea · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: SPLIT (symptoms versus mortality) — for the non-surgical-candidate slice live shelf #1667 leaves open: CHOCOLATE compared drainage with surgery in high-risk patients who could still be randomised to an operation; this shelf asks what drainage achieves in patients who cannot have surgery at all. On symptoms, the series agree: drainage resolves the attack in 86–93% of patients (Hatzidakis 2002; Chung 2012), and in one grade-3 series 80% had no further attack after the drain was removed, with only 36% ever proceeding to cholecystectomy (Abdelsaid 2023) — drainage is often the definitive treatment, not just a bridge. On mortality, the one randomised trial is sobering: in 123 high-risk patients (APACHE II 12 or more), percutaneous cholecystostomy did NOT reduce 30-day mortality versus conservative treatment (17.5% versus 13%), and its authors suggest reserving drainage for patients not improving after 3 days of conservative care, ICU patients, or candidates for stone extraction (Hatzidakis 2002). Series mortality (90-day 9.3%, Aroori 2019; in-hospital 21% in acalculous disease, Chung 2012) tracks the underlying illness, not the drain. PROPOSED SPLIT: drainage reliably settles the gallbladder; it has never been shown to save lives compared with antibiotics and supportive care alone.

cards.headline: Hatzidakis 2002: the one randomised trial — in 123 high-risk patients, percutaneous cholecystostomy resolved symptoms in 86% but did not reduce 30-day mortality versus conservative treatment (17.5% vs 13%)
cards.summary: Hatzidakis 2002: the one randomised trial — in 123 high-risk patients, percutaneous cholecystostomy resolved symptoms in 86% but did not reduce 30-day mortality versus conservative treatment (17.5% vs 13%)
cards.people: 123 high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis (all with ultrasonographic criteria of acute inflammation and an APACHE II score of 12 or more) randomised to percutaneous cholecystostomy (63 patients; ultrasound- or CT-guided, technically successful in 60) or conservative treatment (60 patients).
cards.result: In the drainage group, symptoms resolved in 54 of 63 patients (86%); 11 patients (17.5%) died within 30 days — 6 of ongoing sepsis and 5 of severe underlying disease; 7 (11%) required surgery for persisting symptoms, catheter dislodgement or failed drainage; and 32 (51%) needed no further treatment. In the conservative group, 52 of 60 patients (87%) recovered fully and 8 (13%) died of ongoing sepsis within 30 days. The authors conclude percutaneous cholecystostomy did not decrease mortality relative to conservative treatment (the treatment made no difference to mortality), and suggest it for patients not improving after 3 days of conservative treatment, critically ill ICU patients, or candidates for percutaneous stone extraction.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial from 2002 with 123 patients: its mortality comparison (17.5% versus 13%) is imprecise and cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm, and conservative care has changed since — but it remains the only randomised evidence in genuinely non-surgical candidates, and its point estimate favours the conservative arm, which is why no mortality claim for drainage can be made.
cards.source: Hatzidakis AA et al. Acute cholecystitis in high-risk patients: percutaneous cholecystostomy vs conservative treatment. European radiology. 2002. PMID: 12111069. cards.headline: Chung 2012: in 57 patients with acute acalculous cholecystitis unfit for immediate surgery, drainage resolved symptoms within 4 days in 93%, and only 7% of non-operated survivors had a recurrence over a median 32 months
cards.summary: Chung 2012: in 57 patients with acute acalculous cholecystitis unfit for immediate surgery, drainage resolved symptoms within 4 days in 93%, and only 7% of non-operated survivors had a recurrence over a median 32 months
cards.people: 57 patients undergoing percutaneous cholecystostomy for acute acalculous cholecystitis at a single Korean university hospital, 1995–2010 — a population of seriously ill patients at high risk for cholecystectomy because of severe sepsis or underlying comorbidity; retrospective review with long-term follow-up of those managed without surgery.
cards.result: Drainage was technically successful in all 57 patients with no major procedure-related complications, and symptoms resolved within 4 days in 53 of 57 (93%). In-hospital mortality was 21% (11 of 57), reflecting the underlying illnesses. Elective cholecystectomy was later performed in 18 patients (31%); 28 patients were managed non-operatively with tube removal and, over a median follow-up of 32 months, recurrent cholecystitis occurred in only 2 (7%). The authors conclude drainage is an effective alternative for patients unfit for immediate surgery and that later cholecystectomy might not be needed after recovery.
cards.watchOut: Acalculous cholecystitis is the ICU form of the disease, driven by the underlying critical illness — the 21% in-hospital mortality is that illness speaking, and the low recurrence after recovery partly reflects that acalculous disease, unlike stone disease, has no gallstone left behind to re-obstruct; do not carry the 7% recurrence figure over to calculous patients.
cards.source: Chung YH et al. Can percutaneous cholecystostomy be a definitive management for acute acalculous cholecystitis?. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 21814147. cards.headline: Aroori 2019: in 53 patients drained because they were unfit or too unstable for surgery, 90-day mortality was 9.3% — concentrated in ASA grade 4–5 (18%) and acalculous disease (25%)
cards.summary: Aroori 2019: in 53 patients drained because they were unfit or too unstable for surgery, 90-day mortality was 9.3% — concentrated in ASA grade 4–5 (18%) and acalculous disease (25%)
cards.people: 53 patients (22 women; median age 74 years, range 27–95) undergoing percutaneous cholecystostomy for acute cholecystitis at a UK institution, 2005–2014, excluding malignancy; the stated indications were significant comorbidities in 28 patients (52.8%) and being too unstable for surgery in 21 (39.6%); 12 patients (22.6%) had acalculous cholecystitis.
cards.result: Median time from diagnosis to drainage was 3.6 days and median hospital stay 27 days. Overall 90-day mortality was 9.3%, with two further deaths by 12 months; mortality was significantly higher in ASA grade 4–5 patients (18% versus 0% in ASA 2–3; P=0.026) and in acalculous cholecystitis (25% versus 4.5%; P=0.035). The readmission rate was 18%, and 24 patients (45.2%) later underwent surgery. The authors conclude percutaneous cholecystostomy is a useful temporary or permanent procedure in patients unfit for surgery.
cards.watchOut: No comparator group: a 9.3% 90-day mortality in patients selected for being too sick to operate cannot be credited to or blamed on the drain. Nearly half the cohort later had surgery, so 'non-surgical candidate' was a temporary label for many — the purely definitive-drainage experience is the other half of this series.
cards.source: Aroori S et al. Percutaneous Cholecystostomy for Severe Acute Cholecystitis: A Useful Procedure in High-Risk Patients for Surgery. Scandinavian journal of surgery : SJS : official organ for the Finnish Surgical Society and the Scandinavian Surgical Society. 2019. PMID: 30227774. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Abdelsaid 2023: in 126 patients with grade-3 acute cholecystitis managed with drainage, 80% had no further attack after drain removal and only 36% ever proceeded to cholecystectomy
cards.summary: Abdelsaid 2023: in 126 patients with grade-3 acute cholecystitis managed with drainage, 80% had no further attack after drain removal and only 36% ever proceeded to cholecystectomy
cards.people: 126 patients (mean age 72 years, range 36–98; mean age-adjusted Charlson comorbidity score 3.72) presenting with Tokyo grade-3 (severe) acute cholecystitis at a UK general hospital and initially managed with percutaneous cholecystostomy — 52% after failed medical treatment; median drain duration 39.5 days; retrospective study of recurrence and of who went on to surgery.
cards.result: Eighty percent of patients developed no further attacks of acute cholecystitis after drain removal. Only 45 patients (36%) underwent later laparoscopic cholecystectomy; 9% were deemed unfit for surgery and 41 patients (33%) were managed conservatively after drain removal without a further attack or with only a mild antibiotic-treated one. Procedural complications occurred in 22% (blocked drain, pain, cellulitis around the tube). The 30-day mortality rate among patients who did not undergo cholecystectomy was 5%. The authors conclude drainage could be a definitive treatment in high-surgical-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and retrospective, in a journal without the record carrying MeSH indexing this session; 'no further attack' is counted from drain removal in survivors, so early deaths and the sickest patients sit outside that 80% — it describes the prognosis of patients who recover from the drained attack, not a treatment effect versus antibiotics alone.
cards.source: Abdelsaid K et al. Percutaneous Cholecystostomy in Severe Acute Cholecystitis: An Observational Study From a Single Institute. Cureus. 2023. PMID: 36743905. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: drainage settles the gallbladder in about 9 of 10 non-surgical patients and is often definitive — but a mortality benefit over conservative care has never been shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: drainage settles the gallbladder in about 9 of 10 non-surgical patients and is often definitive — but a mortality benefit over conservative care has never been shown
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial against conservative treatment (Hatzidakis 2002; 123 high-risk patients) and three retrospective series in patients unfit or too unstable for surgery (Chung 2012, 57; Aroori 2019, 53; Abdelsaid 2023, 126). Total carded participants are 359, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Symptom resolution: 86% (randomised trial) and 93% (acalculous series). Thirty-day mortality in the trial: 17.5% drainage versus 13% conservative — no benefit (the treatment made no difference to mortality). After recovery, recurrence without surgery was 7% in acalculous disease and 20% had any further attack in the grade-3 series; only about a third of drained patients ever proceeded to cholecystectomy. PROPOSED SPLIT (symptoms versus mortality): percutaneous cholecystostomy improves the local outcome — a settled gallbladder, often permanently — without demonstrated improvement in survival over antibiotics and supportive care. The drainage-versus-surgery comparison in operable high-risk patients stays homed on live shelf #1667 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The mortality neutrality comes from one small, old trial and the symptom success from uncontrolled series — the two halves of this split are not equally firm, and a patient failing to improve on antibiotics is exactly the subgroup the trial's authors picked out for drainage, a use the trial was not powered to test separately.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hatzidakis AA et al. European radiology. 2002 (PMID: 12111069); Chung YH et al. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 21814147); Aroori S et al. shelves.title: Terlipressin versus octreotide in acute variceal bleeding: equal control and survival in head-to-head trials — the difference is tolerability
shelves.question: In adults with acute variceal bleeding, is terlipressin as effective as octreotide for controlling bleeding and improving survival?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hemostasis · Humans · Lypressin · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide · Prospective Studies · Somatostatin · Terlipressin · Treatment Failure · Vasoconstrictor Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY (equivalence) — the head-to-head evidence says the two drugs control acute variceal bleeding equally, with no survival difference, and the only consistent separation is tolerability. The largest direct test, a 780-patient multicentre randomised noninferiority trial (Seo 2014), found 5-day treatment success of 86.2% on terlipressin versus 83.8% on octreotide, with mortality 8.0% versus 8.8% — both comfortably inside the prespecified 0.1 noninferiority margin. The double-blind adjuvant-to-banding trial (Abid 2009, 324 patients) agreed: bleeding control 92.6% versus 95.6%, in-hospital deaths 5.5% versus 4.3%. Pooling all 21 randomised trials of the two drug families (Huaringa-Marcelo 2021) gives a mortality relative risk of 1.01 (95% CI 0.83–1.22) — no difference (the treatment made no difference) — but significantly more adverse events with terlipressin/vasopressin than with octreotide/somatostatin (relative risk 2.39, 95% CI 1.58–3.63). PROPOSED LIKELY: terlipressin is as effective as octreotide for controlling bleeding and for survival; choose on adverse-effect profile, availability and local practice, not on expected efficacy. No shelf previously answered this head-to-head question (the terlipressin shelf in the library concerns hepatorenal syndrome, a different question).

cards.headline: Seo 2014: in 780 patients with acute variceal bleeding, 5-day treatment success was 86.2% on terlipressin versus 83.8% on octreotide, mortality 8.0% versus 8.8% — noninferior
cards.summary: Seo 2014: in 780 patients with acute variceal bleeding, 5-day treatment success was 86.2% on terlipressin versus 83.8% on octreotide, mortality 8.0% versus 8.8% — noninferior
cards.people: 780 patients with liver cirrhosis and acute gastroesophageal variceal bleeding in a prospective multicentre randomised noninferiority trial (noninferiority margin 0.1), assigned before endoscopy to terlipressin (n = 261), somatostatin (n = 259) or octreotide (n = 260), all followed by endoscopic treatment; patients with nonvariceal bleeding were excluded after endoscopy. Primary endpoint: 5-day treatment success — control of bleeding without rescue treatment, rebleeding, or death.
cards.result: Active bleeding at initial endoscopy was similar (43.7% terlipressin, 44.4% somatostatin, 43.5% octreotide). Treatment success by day 5: 86.2% terlipressin, 83.4% somatostatin, 83.8% octreotide (P = 0.636), with similar control of bleeding without rescue treatment (89.7%, 87.6%, 88.1%), rebleeding (3.4%, 4.8%, 4.4%) and mortality (8.0%, 8.9%, 8.8%; P = 0.929). The lower confidence bounds for terlipressin versus octreotide (0.090) lay within the 0.1 noninferiority margin — terlipressin was noninferior to octreotide, and haemostatic effects and safety did not differ significantly among the three drugs in this trial.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority design with a generous 0.1 margin: it excludes a large terlipressin disadvantage but cannot prove exact equality, and all patients received endoscopic therapy, so the comparison is of the drugs as adjuncts started before endoscopy — the setting guidelines actually recommend.
cards.source: Seo YS et al. Lack of difference among terlipressin, somatostatin, and octreotide in the control of acute gastroesophageal variceal hemorrhage. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2014. PMID: 24415445. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Abid 2009: double-blind, as an adjunct to band ligation, bleeding control was 92.6% on terlipressin versus 95.6% on octreotide, with deaths 5.5% versus 4.3% (324 patients)
cards.summary: Abid 2009: double-blind, as an adjunct to band ligation, bleeding control was 92.6% on terlipressin versus 95.6% on octreotide, with deaths 5.5% versus 4.3% (324 patients)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (double-blind, adjuvant to band ligation, Abid 2009)
cards.people: 324 cirrhotic patients with esophageal variceal bleeding randomised on admission, double-blind, to terlipressin (n = 163) or octreotide (n = 161), each with placebo in the other arm, as adjuvant therapy to endoscopic variceal band ligation; groups were comparable except more active bleeding at enrolment endoscopy in the octreotide group (25.5% vs 16%, P = 0.034).
cards.result: Control of variceal bleeding was achieved in 305 of 324 patients (94.1%): 151 of 163 (92.6%) on terlipressin versus 154 of 161 (95.6%) on octreotide. Sixteen patients died in hospital — 9 (5.5%) on terlipressin versus 7 (4.3%) on octreotide (P = 0.626) — the treatment made no difference to control or survival. Transfusion requirements were similar (3.7 ± 2.3 vs 3.9 ± 2.5 units, P = 0.273); hospital stay was shorter on terlipressin (108.4 ± 34.8 vs 126.4 ± 47.5 hours, P ≤ 0.001), a difference the authors themselves judged not clinically important. No cardiovascular side effects were observed in either group.
cards.watchOut: Single-country trial with an enrolment imbalance in active bleeding favouring terlipressin at baseline; its null result agrees with the larger Seo trial, which is why the pair can carry weight together.
cards.source: Abid S et al. Terlipressin vs. octreotide in bleeding esophageal varices as an adjuvant therapy with endoscopic band ligation: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19223890. Registry ID: none in the record.
