cards.headline: Huaringa-Marcelo 2021: across 21 randomised trials, mortality was identical between the terlipressin/vasopressin and octreotide/somatostatin families (relative risk 1.01) — but adverse events were more than twice as frequent with terlipressin/vasopressin (relative risk 2.39)
cards.summary: Huaringa-Marcelo 2021: across 21 randomised trials, mortality was identical between the terlipressin/vasopressin and octreotide/somatostatin families (relative risk 1.01) — but adverse events were more than twice as frequent with terlipressin/vasopressin (relative risk 2.39)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials (Huaringa-Marcelo 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomised controlled trials in cirrhotic patients with acute variceal bleeding, comparing terlipressin/vasopressin (T-V) against octreotide/somatostatin (O-S), each combined with endoscopic therapy; certainty of evidence rated moderate for the main outcomes by GRADE.
cards.result: Mortality: relative risk 1.01 (95% CI 0.83–1.22) — no difference. Bleeding control: RR 0.96 (95% CI 0.91–1.02); early rebleeding RR 0.91 (0.66–1.24); late rebleeding RR 0.94 (0.56–1.60); transfusion mean difference 0.04 units (−0.31 to 0.39); hospital stay mean difference −1.06 days (−2.80 to 0.69) — all similar. Adverse events, reported in 15 studies, were significantly higher with T-V than O-S: RR 2.39 (95% CI 1.58–3.63) — a relative measure; the review does not print a single pooled absolute adverse-event rate for the comparison.
cards.watchOut: The pooling groups drug families (terlipressin with the older, more toxic vasopressin; octreotide with somatostatin), so the adverse-event relative risk of 2.39 overstates what modern terlipressin alone would show against octreotide alone — the two direct trials carded here found no significant safety separation. Read the efficacy equivalence as drug-specific and the harm signal as family-level.
cards.source: Huaringa-Marcelo J et al. Vasoactive Agents for the Management of Acute Variceal Bleeding: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of gastrointestinal and liver diseases : JGLD. 2021. PMID: 33723542. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal control, equal survival, different side-effect reputations — the choice is tolerability and logistics, not efficacy
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal control, equal survival, different side-effect reputations — the choice is tolerability and logistics, not efficacy
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 780-patient three-arm noninferiority trial (Seo 2014), one 324-patient double-blind adjuvant trial (Abid 2009), and a 21-trial meta-analysis (Huaringa-Marcelo 2021). Total carded randomised patients exceed 1,100 in the direct trials alone, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Five-day treatment success 86.2% (terlipressin) versus 83.8% (octreotide) with mortality 8.0% versus 8.8% in the largest trial; bleeding control 92.6% versus 95.6% with deaths 5.5% versus 4.3% in the blinded trial; pooled mortality relative risk 1.01 (0.83–1.22). Every direct comparison is null on efficacy and survival — the treatments made no difference to each other — while family-level pooling shows more adverse events with terlipressin/vasopressin (relative risk 2.39). PROPOSED LIKELY (equivalence): terlipressin is as effective as octreotide for controlling acute variceal bleeding and for survival.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here is 'no demonstrated difference within noninferiority margins and pooled confidence intervals', not proof of identity; terlipressin's separate, proven role in hepatorenal syndrome is a different question homed elsewhere in the library and is not evidence for this comparison.

shelves.title: After a variceal bleed, ligation plus a beta-blocker beats ligation alone for rebleeding — survival benefit still unproven
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis who survive a variceal bleed, does combined band ligation plus a nonselective beta-blocker prevent rebleeding better than band ligation alone?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Adult · Aged · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Ligation · Male · Middle Aged · Nadolol · Prospective Studies · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY (rebleeding) — adding a nonselective beta-blocker to band ligation prevents variceal rebleeding better than ligation alone; a survival benefit is suggested but not proven. The direct multicentre trial (de la Peña 2005) found variceal rebleeding in 14% with ligation plus nadolol versus 38% with ligation alone (P = 0.006) over a median 16 months, with mortality statistically indistinguishable (11.6% versus 10.8% — the addition made no difference to survival in that trial). Pooling all five randomised comparisons of ligation with and without drug therapy (476 patients; Puente 2014) gives a rebleeding relative risk of 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.69) — a relative measure, with absolute rates of 14% versus 38% in the largest direct trial — and a mortality relative risk of 0.58 (0.33–1.03), a trend that does not reach significance. The asymmetry matters: adding ligation to drug therapy did not reduce rebleeding in the García-Pagán trial (1-year recurrence 26% versus 33%, P = 0.3) and added adverse events — the proven direction is drugs added to ligation, which is the comparison this shelf answers. The only neighbouring shelf, live #1678, asks whether simvastatin adds anything on top of combined standard prophylaxis; it does not answer this question. PROPOSED LIKELY for rebleeding prevention; mortality benefit unproven.

cards.headline: de la Peña 2005: variceal rebleeding was 14% with ligation plus nadolol versus 38% with ligation alone (P = 0.006); mortality was the same (80 patients)
cards.summary: de la Peña 2005: variceal rebleeding was 14% with ligation plus nadolol versus 38% with ligation alone (P = 0.006); mortality was the same (80 patients)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (multicentre, de la Peña 2005)
cards.people: 80 patients with cirrhosis (66% alcoholic; Child-Pugh A 15%, B 56%, C 29%) admitted with acute variceal bleeding, treated at emergency endoscopy with ligation or sclerotherapy plus 5 days of somatostatin, then randomised to endoscopic variceal ligation plus nadolol versus ligation alone, with ligation repeated every 10–12 days until eradication; median follow-up 16 months (range 1–24).
cards.result: Variceal bleeding recurrence was 14% in the ligation-plus-nadolol group versus 38% in the ligation-alone group (P = 0.006) — an absolute difference of 24 percentage points. Mortality did not differ: 5 patients (11.6%) died on combined therapy versus 4 (10.8%) on ligation alone. Sessions to eradicate varices were similar (3.2 ± 1.3 vs 3.5 ± 1.3), the 1-year actuarial probability of variceal recurrence was lower with combination therapy (54% vs 77%, P = 0.06), and nadolol adverse effects occurred in 11% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Only 80 patients and 9 deaths in total — the trial is powered for rebleeding, not survival, and its null mortality result is a precision problem as much as an answer. Nadolol was the beta-blocker; the class reading (any nonselective beta-blocker) comes from the pooled card, not from this trial alone.
cards.source: de la Peña J et al. Variceal ligation plus nadolol compared with ligation for prophylaxis of variceal rebleeding: a multicenter trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2005. PMID: 15726659. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Puente 2014: pooling five trials (476 patients), adding drug therapy to ligation cut rebleeding (relative risk 0.44) with a non-significant mortality trend (relative risk 0.58)
cards.summary: Puente 2014: pooling five trials (476 patients), adding drug therapy to ligation cut rebleeding (relative risk 0.44) with a non-significant mortality trend (relative risk 0.58)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in cirrhosis comparing combined endoscopic variceal ligation plus beta-blocker (with or without isosorbide mononitrate) against ligation alone (five studies, 476 patients) or against drug therapy alone (four trials, 409 patients), for prevention of variceal rebleeding; random-effects pooling.
cards.result: Against ligation alone, combination therapy reduced overall rebleeding (relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.28–0.69) and showed a trend towards lower mortality (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.33–1.03), without increasing complications. Against drug therapy alone (all trials used beta-blocker plus isosorbide mononitrate), adding ligation produced only a non-significant rebleeding trend (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.58–1.00) with no mortality effect (relative risk 1.24, 0.90–1.70) and more rebleeding from oesophageal ulcers. The review's conclusion: adding drug therapy to ligation improves ligation; adding ligation to full drug therapy does not clearly improve drugs.
cards.watchOut: The five ligation-comparison trials are small and span eras of endoscopic technique; the pooled relative risk of 0.44 is consistent with the largest direct trial's absolute rates (14% vs 38%) but the mortality relative risk's confidence interval still crosses 1 — survival remains a trend, and this card does not upgrade it.
cards.source: Puente A et al. Drugs plus ligation to prevent rebleeding in cirrhosis: an updated systematic review. cards.headline: García-Pagán 2009: adding band ligation to nadolol plus isosorbide did NOT reduce rebleeding (1-year 26% vs 33%, P = 0.3) and added adverse events — the reverse addition fails (158 patients)
cards.summary: García-Pagán 2009: adding band ligation to nadolol plus isosorbide did NOT reduce rebleeding (1-year 26% vs 33%, P = 0.3) and added adverse events — the reverse addition fails (158 patients)
cards.people: 158 patients with cirrhosis admitted with variceal bleeding, randomised in a multicentre trial to nadolol plus isosorbide-5-mononitrate alone (n = 78) or the same drugs combined with endoscopic band ligation (n = 80), with hepatic venous pressure gradient measured at randomisation and after 4–6 weeks; median follow-up 15 months.
cards.result: The 1-year probability of recurrent bleeding was similar (33% drugs alone vs 26% drugs plus ligation, P = 0.3) — adding ligation made no difference — with no significant differences in survival or need for rescue shunts, and significantly more overall and hospital-admission adverse events in the ligation group. Recurrent bleeding was significantly more frequent in hepatic venous pressure gradient non-responders than responders, and among non-responders rebleeding was similar with or without ligation.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers the mirror-image question (does ligation add to drugs?) against a two-drug regimen that included isosorbide mononitrate, which the de la Peña comparison did not use. It tempers any 'more is always better' reading without contradicting the drugs-added-to-ligation result carded above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: combined ligation plus beta-blocker beats ligation alone for rebleeding; survival benefit unproven; the benefit runs one way
cards.summary: Synthesis: combined ligation plus beta-blocker beats ligation alone for rebleeding; survival benefit unproven; the benefit runs one way
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct multicentre trial of ligation plus nadolol versus ligation alone (de la Peña 2005, 80 patients), a five-trial meta-analysis of the same comparison (Puente 2014, 476 patients), and one multicentre trial of the reverse addition (García-Pagán 2009, 158 patients).
cards.result: Rebleeding: 14% versus 38% in the direct trial (P = 0.006) and pooled relative risk 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.69). Mortality: 11.6% versus 10.8% in the direct trial and pooled relative risk 0.58 (0.33–1.03) — a trend, not a demonstrated benefit. Adding ligation to drug therapy, by contrast, made no difference to rebleeding (26% vs 33% at 1 year) and increased adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY (rebleeding prevention only): combined band ligation plus a nonselective beta-blocker prevents rebleeding better than band ligation alone after a variceal bleed.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is deliberately confined to rebleeding: quoting the mortality relative risk of 0.58 without its confidence interval (0.33–1.03) would overstate what this evidence shows.

shelves.title: Albumin in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: pooled halving of renal failure and death, resting on a small Sort-dominated base (Sort itself homed on #167)
shelves.question: In adults with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, does albumin plus antibiotics reduce kidney failure and death compared with antibiotics alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Albumins · Bacterial Infections · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peritonitis · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Renal Insufficiency · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three independent meta-analyses agree that albumin added to antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) roughly halves renal impairment and death, but the underlying randomised base is only four small trials (288 patients), and it is dominated by one trial — Sort 1999 — which is already homed, with its figures, on live shelf #167 ('When does infusing albumin actually help patients with cirrhosis?'). FLAG (precedent-b pattern): Sort's PMID is on the gate list and is NOT carded here and no figure from it is reproduced; this shelf answers the narrower SBP-specific question from the free pooled reports, each of which necessarily includes Sort among its trials — the reader should know the pooled estimates lean on that homed trial. Within those limits: Salerno 2013 pooled renal impairment of 8.3% with albumin versus 30.6% without (odds ratio 0.21 relative) and mortality of 16.0% versus 35.4% (odds ratio 0.34 relative); Leache 2023 found an SBP mortality relative risk of 0.49 (95% CI 0.32–0.75, low certainty); Bai 2022 found an SBP-subgroup mortality odds ratio of 0.36 (0.20–0.64). Direction and rough size are consistent everywhere, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE (weak evidence) — but a base this small and this dependent on one 1999 trial caps it below LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: albumin plus antibiotics probably reduces kidney failure and death in SBP compared with antibiotics alone; guideline practice already treats it as standard for high-risk patients.

cards.headline: Salerno 2013: pooling the four randomised trials (288 patients), albumin cut renal impairment from 30.6% to 8.3% and mortality from 35.4% to 16.0% in SBP
cards.summary: Salerno 2013: pooling the four randomised trials (288 patients), albumin cut renal impairment from 30.6% to 8.3% and mortality from 35.4% to 16.0% in SBP
cards.people: Meta-analysis of the four randomised controlled trials of albumin infusion in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (288 patients total); albumin was compared with no albumin in three trials and with an artificial colloid in one, and all patients received antibiotics. Fixed-effects pooling; no significant heterogeneity or publication bias detected.
cards.result: Renal impairment occurred in 12 of 144 patients (8.3%) given albumin versus 44 of 144 controls (30.6%) — pooled odds ratio 0.21 (95% CI 0.11–0.42), a relative measure, with individual-trial odds ratios ranging 0.19–0.30. Mortality was 23 of 144 (16.0%) with albumin versus 51 of 144 (35.4%) in controls — pooled odds ratio 0.34 (95% CI 0.19–0.60), relative, with individual-trial odds ratios ranging 0.16–0.55. Absolute differences: about 22 percentage points fewer renal impairments and 19 percentage points fewer deaths.
cards.watchOut: FLAG: the four pooled trials include the Sort 1999 trial, which is homed with its own figures on live shelf #167 and is deliberately not carded here; the pooled estimates therefore rest substantially on that homed trial plus three small ones. Four trials and 288 patients is a thin base for effects this large — large effects in small bases are exactly where later trials tend to shrink estimates.
cards.source: Salerno F et al. Albumin infusion improves outcomes of patients with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2013. PMID: 23178229. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Leache 2023: across 50 cirrhosis albumin trials, the SBP subgroup showed lower mortality with albumin (relative risk 0.49) — rated low certainty
cards.summary: Leache 2023: across 50 cirrhosis albumin trials, the SBP subgroup showed lower mortality with albumin (relative risk 0.49) — rated low certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, SBP subgroup (Leache 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 50 randomised trials of albumin in cirrhosis (5,118 participants) across all indications, with indication-specific mortality analyses; the spontaneous bacterial peritonitis comparison is albumin versus no albumin administration.
cards.result: In patients with SBP, albumin was associated with reduced mortality: relative risk 0.49 (95% CI 0.32–0.75), graded low certainty — a relative measure; this review does not print the SBP subgroup's absolute event rates. The same review found a mortality reduction in hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.53, 0.34–0.83) but no albumin mortality benefit in the other scenarios examined, and no benefit for liver transplantation or serious adverse events overall.
cards.watchOut: The SBP estimate inherits the same four-trial base (including the homed Sort trial, not carded here) — this is a re-pooling of substantially the same patients as the Salerno card, not independent confirmation; the agreement between the two reviews shows analytic robustness, not new data. Low certainty is the review's own GRADE rating.

cards.headline: Bai 2022: in 42 cirrhosis albumin trials, the SBP subgroup mortality odds ratio was 0.36 with albumin — while ascites and non-SBP infection subgroups showed no mortality benefit
cards.summary: Bai 2022: in 42 cirrhosis albumin trials, the SBP subgroup mortality odds ratio was 0.36 with albumin — while ascites and non-SBP infection subgroups showed no mortality benefit
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, SBP subgroup (Bai 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 42 randomised trials of human albumin infusion in cirrhosis, with prespecified subgroup analyses by target population (SBP, hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, non-SBP infections, large-volume paracentesis) and by treatment duration; odds ratios pooled with 95% confidence intervals.
cards.result: Overall, albumin decreased mortality (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.67–0.98). By subgroup, albumin significantly decreased mortality in SBP (odds ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.20–0.64, P = 0.0005) and in hepatic encephalopathy (odds ratio 0.43, 0.22–0.85), but not in ascites, non-SBP infections, or large-volume paracentesis — relative measures; the abstract does not print SBP-subgroup absolute rates. Albumin also decreased the incidence of renal impairment overall (odds ratio 0.63, 0.45–0.88).
cards.watchOut: Third re-pooling of substantially the same small SBP trial base (including the homed Sort trial, not carded here). The indication-specific pattern — benefit in SBP and encephalopathy, none in ascites or non-SBP infection — is the scientifically interesting part: it argues the SBP signal is not a generic 'albumin helps cirrhosis' artefact, but it cannot add patients the base does not contain.
cards.source: Bai Z et al. Use of human albumin infusion in cirrhotic patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Hepatology international. 2022. PMID: 36048318. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent halving of renal failure and death across three poolings — of one small, Sort-dominated base (POSSIBLE)
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent halving of renal failure and death across three poolings — of one small, Sort-dominated base (POSSIBLE)
cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses (Salerno 2013, 4 trials/288 patients with absolute rates; Leache 2023, 50 trials with an SBP subgroup; Bai 2022, 42 trials with an SBP subgroup). The Sort 1999 trial itself is homed on live shelf #167 and is not carded here — see the flag on the first card and in the balance.
cards.result: Renal impairment 8.3% versus 30.6% (odds ratio 0.21 relative) and mortality 16.0% versus 35.4% (odds ratio 0.34 relative) in the only pooling that prints absolutes; mortality relative risk 0.49 (0.32–0.75) and odds ratio 0.36 (0.20–0.64) in the two later re-poolings. Three analyses, one direction, similar size — but one shared, small denominator, which is why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: albumin plus antibiotics reduces kidney failure and death in SBP compared with antibiotics alone.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the three meta-analyses as three independent confirmations — they are three readings of substantially the same four trials. A modern, adequately powered SBP-specific trial remains the missing evidence, particularly for lower-risk SBP, where the absolute benefit must be smaller than the pooled 19-point mortality difference.

shelves.title: Carvedilol versus propranolol on portal pressure (PARTIAL of #3594): a greater mean HVPG fall in every direct trial, an inconsistent responder advantage, and a bigger pressure cost
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis, does carvedilol reduce portal pressure more than propranolol as measured by hepatic venous pressure gradient?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Antagonists · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Carbazoles · Carvedilol · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Heart Rate · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypertension, Portal · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Portal Pressure · Propanolamines · Propranolol · Vascular Resistance
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — read with pack #3594, which already homes the clinical-outcome question ('For primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, is carvedilol as effective as propranolol or other non-selective beta blockers?') through a network meta-analysis of bleeding and mortality. FLAG (precedent b): that network meta-analysis is the homed anchor for the wider question; its PMID is deliberately kept out of every card source line on this shelf, and none of its figures are used here. This shelf answers only the uncovered slice #3594 does not measure directly: the head-to-head hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) comparison in direct randomised trials. On the continuous measure the direction is unanimous: carvedilol lowers HVPG more — acutely −20.4% versus −12.7% (Bañares 1999), chronically −19% versus −12% (Bañares 2002), −19.3% versus −12.5% in the one trial where the difference was not significant (Hobolth 2012, P = 0.21), and a pooled mean advantage of −1.75 mmHg / −8.02 percentage points across six trials in the Cochrane analysis (Zacharias 2018). On the responder definition (≥20% fall or to ≤12 mmHg) the picture splits: Bañares found significantly more responders on carvedilol (64% vs 14% acute; 54% vs 23% chronic), but the largest trial (Kim 2016, 110 patients) found 49.1% versus 30.9% (P = 0.08, not significant) and the Cochrane responder pooling was likewise non-significant (relative risk 0.76 for failure to respond, 95% CI 0.57–1.02). The cost is systemic: carvedilol lowered mean arterial pressure more (−23.1% vs −11% acutely; −11% vs −5% chronically) and expanded plasma volume in the chronic trial. PROPOSED LIKELY for the question as asked — carvedilol reduces portal pressure more than propranolol on mean HVPG — with the responder-proportion inconsistency and the hypotension cost printed on the face.

cards.headline: Bañares 1999: acutely, carvedilol cut HVPG by 20.4% versus 12.7% for propranolol, with responders 64% versus 14% (35 patients)
cards.summary: Bañares 1999: acutely, carvedilol cut HVPG by 20.4% versus 12.7% for propranolol, with responders 64% versus 14% (35 patients)
cards.people: 35 patients with cirrhosis who had haemodynamic measurements before and after random administration of carvedilol (n = 14), propranolol (n = 14) or placebo (n = 7), in a multicentre randomised study of the acute portal-hypotensive effect.
cards.result: Carvedilol reduced HVPG from 19.5 ± 1.3 to 15.4 ± 1 mmHg (P < 0.0001), a fall of 20.4 ± 2% versus 12.7 ± 2% for propranolol (P < 0.05). A reduction of more than 20% of baseline or to ≤12 mmHg was achieved by 64% on carvedilol versus 14% on propranolol (P < 0.05). Both drugs similarly reduced hepatic and azygos blood flows, indicating carvedilol's greater effect came from reduced hepatic and portocollateral resistance; propranolol reduced heart rate and cardiac output more, while carvedilol reduced mean arterial pressure more (−23.1% vs −11%, P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: An acute, single-dose physiological study of 35 patients — it establishes the pharmacological gradient, not the chronic clinical effect; the larger mean arterial pressure fall is the finding that has shadowed carvedilol ever since.
cards.source: Bañares R et al. Carvedilol, a new nonselective beta-blocker with intrinsic anti- Alpha1-adrenergic activity, has a greater portal hypotensive effect than propranolol in patients with cirrhosis. randomised controlled trial (acute haemodynamics, bañares 1999) 35 patients with cirrhosis who had haemodynamic measurements before and after random administration of carvedilol (n = 14), propranolol (n = 14) or placebo (n = 7), in a multicentre randomised study of the acute portal-hypotensive effect. carvedilol reduced hvpg from 19.5 ± 1.3 to 15.4 ± 1 mmhg (p < 0.0001), a fall of 20.4 ± 2% versus 12.7 ± 2% for propranolol (p < 0.05). a reduction of more than 20% of baseline or to ≤12 mmhg was achieved by 64% on carvedilol versus 14% on propranolol (p < 0.05). both drugs similarly reduced hepatic and azygos blood flows, indicating carvedilol's greater effect came from reduced hepatic and portocollateral resistance; propranolol reduced heart rate and cardiac output more, while carvedilol reduced mean arterial pressure more (−23.1% vs −11%, p < 0.05). an acute, single-dose physiological study of 35 patients — it establishes the pharmacological gradient, not the chronic clinical effect; the larger mean arterial pressure fall is the finding that has shadowed carvedilol ever since. bañares r et al. carvedilol, a new nonselective beta-blocker with intrinsic anti- alpha1-adrenergic activity, has a greater portal hypotensive effect than propranolol in patients with cirrhosis. hepatology (baltimore, md.). 1999. pmid: 10385642. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adrenergic alpha-antagonists · adrenergic beta-antagonists · antihypertensive agents · blood pressure · carbazoles · carvedilol · esophageal and gastric varices · female · heart rate · hemodynamics · humans · hypertension, portal · liver cirrhosis · male · middle aged · placebos · portal pressure · propanolamines · propranolol · vascular resistance

cards.headline: Bañares 2002: over ~11 weeks, carvedilol lowered HVPG by 19% versus 12% for propranolol (P < 0.001), responders 54% versus 23% — but lowered arterial pressure more and expanded plasma volume (51 patients)
cards.summary: Bañares 2002: over ~11 weeks, carvedilol lowered HVPG by 19% versus 12% for propranolol (P < 0.001), responders 54% versus 23% — but lowered arterial pressure more and expanded plasma volume (51 patients)
cards.people: 51 patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension randomly assigned to long-term carvedilol (n = 26) or propranolol (n = 25), with haemodynamic measurements and renal function at baseline and after 11.1 ± 4.1 weeks.
cards.result: Carvedilol caused a greater HVPG decrease than propranolol (−19 ± 2% vs −12 ± 2%, P < 0.001), and more patients achieved a reduction of ≥20% or to ≤12 mmHg (54% vs 23%, P < 0.05). Carvedilol, but not propranolol, significantly decreased mean arterial pressure (−11 ± 1% vs −5 ± 3%, P = 0.05) and increased plasma volume and body weight (11 ± 5% and 2 ± 1%, P < 0.05); glomerular filtration rate was unchanged on either drug, diuretic doses were increased more often after carvedilol (27% vs 8%, P = 0.07), and adverse events requiring discontinuation occurred in 2 patients on carvedilol and 3 on propranolol.
cards.watchOut: The same group's second trial, so the two Bañares cards are a programme, not two independent programmes; 51 patients and 11 weeks cannot speak to decompensation risk from the arterial-pressure and plasma-volume effects, which the authors themselves flag as the limit on clinical applicability.
cards.source: Bañares R et al. Randomized comparison of long-term carvedilol and propranolol administration in the treatment of portal hypertension in cirrhosis. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2002. PMID: 12447861. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hobolth 2012: HVPG fell 19.3% on carvedilol versus 12.5% on propranolol — same direction, not significant (P = 0.21; 38 patients)
cards.summary: Hobolth 2012: HVPG fell 19.3% on carvedilol versus 12.5% on propranolol — same direction, not significant (P = 0.21; 38 patients)
cards.people: 38 patients with cirrhosis and HVPG ≥12 mmHg, double-blind randomised to carvedilol (n = 21) or propranolol (n = 17) for 90 days after a baseline HVPG measurement and an acute oral propranolol test dose, with HVPG repeated on treatment.
cards.result: HVPG decreased by 19.3 ± 16.1% on carvedilol and by 12.5 ± 16.7% on propranolol (each P < 0.01 within group), with no significant difference between the regimens (P = 0.21). The acute response to oral propranolol did not usefully predict the long-term response on either drug (the record's conclusion, reported qualitatively here).
cards.watchOut: The standard deviations (±16–17%) are nearly as large as the mean falls — with 38 patients the trial could not resolve a 7-point difference; its point estimates match Bañares almost exactly, so it is best read as an imprecise replication, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Hobolth L et al. Carvedilol or propranolol in portal hypertension? A randomized comparison. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22401315. Registry ID: NCT00493480. cards.headline: Kim 2016: the largest head-to-head trial (110 patients) found HVPG responders 49.1% on carvedilol versus 30.9% on propranolol — not significant overall (P = 0.08), significant only in advanced disease subgroups
cards.summary: Kim 2016: the largest head-to-head trial (110 patients) found HVPG responders 49.1% on carvedilol versus 30.9% on propranolol — not significant overall (P = 0.08), significant only in advanced disease subgroups
cards.people: 110 patients with liver cirrhosis and baseline HVPG >12 mmHg in a randomised multicentre open-label trial of carvedilol versus propranolol, with HVPG repeated after 6 weeks; primary endpoint a ≥20% fall in HVPG or to <12 mmHg (haemodynamic response), analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Response was 49.1% on carvedilol versus 30.9% on propranolol — a difference that did not reach statistical significance in the intention-to-treat analysis (P = 0.08). In post hoc subgroups carvedilol was significantly superior: MELD score ≥15 (58.3% [7/12] vs 0% [0/10], P = 0.005), Child-Pugh score ≥9 (46.2% vs 0%, P = 0.046), and in patients with ascites (51.5% vs 24.2%, P = 0.042); after adjustment for multiple comparisons only MELD ≥15 remained significant. Severe adverse events were higher in the carvedilol group, although drug-associated adverse events did not differ. The authors' conclusion: no clear overall advantage, possible greater effect in advanced cirrhosis, at a possible side-effect cost.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 6 weeks, and the significant findings are post hoc subgroups with tiny denominators (7/12 versus 0/10) — hypothesis-generating only. Its importance is the overall null on the responder endpoint at the largest sample size, which is why this shelf's stamp rests on the continuous HVPG measure, not the responder proportion.

cards.headline: Zacharias 2018 (Cochrane): carvedilol reduced HVPG more than traditional beta-blockers (mean difference −1.75 mmHg; −8.02 percentage points), but the responder advantage and all clinical outcomes were non-significant
cards.summary: Zacharias 2018 (Cochrane): carvedilol reduced HVPG more than traditional beta-blockers (mean difference −1.75 mmHg; −8.02 percentage points), but the responder advantage and all clinical outcomes were non-significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane, Zacharias 2018)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 11 randomised trials of carvedilol versus traditional non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol in nine trials, nadolol in one) in adults with cirrhosis and gastroesophageal varices; 10 trials (810 participants) contributed to the analyses, all classified at high risk of bias; haemodynamic pooling covered 6 trials and 368 participants.
cards.result: Carvedilol produced a greater HVPG reduction in absolute terms (mean difference −1.75 mmHg, 95% CI −2.60 to −0.89; I² = 0%) and in percentage terms (mean difference −8.02 percentage points, 95% CI −11.49 to −4.55; I² = 0%) — but no significant difference in failure to achieve a sufficient haemodynamic response (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.57–1.02) and no differences in mortality (relative risk 0.86, 0.48–1.53), upper gastrointestinal bleeding (relative risk 0.77, 0.43–1.37) or serious adverse events (relative risk 0.97, 0.67–1.42). Evidence quality was low to very low throughout.
cards.watchOut: One pooled trial used nadolol, not propranolol, as comparator, and every included trial was at high risk of bias — the review's own verdict is that the greater HVPG reduction is real on average but its clinical meaning is unproven. This card pools the direct trials; it does not use the network meta-analysis homed on pack #3594.
cards.source: Zacharias AP et al. Carvedilol versus traditional, non-selective beta-blockers for adults with cirrhosis and gastroesophageal varices. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30372514. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: on mean HVPG the answer is yes, consistently; on responder proportions and clinical outcomes it is unproven — and carvedilol costs more arterial pressure
cards.summary: Synthesis: on mean HVPG the answer is yes, consistently; on responder proportions and clinical outcomes it is unproven — and carvedilol costs more arterial pressure
cards.people: The carded evidence: four direct randomised head-to-head trials (Bañares 1999, n = 35; Bañares 2002, n = 51; Hobolth 2012, n = 38; Kim 2016, n = 110) and the Cochrane pooling of the direct-trial literature (Zacharias 2018; HVPG analysis 368 participants). The clinical-outcome network meta-analysis is homed on pack #3594 and is not carded here.
cards.result: Mean HVPG falls: −20.4% vs −12.7%, −19% vs −12%, −19.3% vs −12.5%, and a pooled advantage of −1.75 mmHg (−8.02 percentage points, I² = 0%) — carvedilol ahead in every dataset. Responder proportions: significantly ahead in both Bañares trials (64% vs 14%; 54% vs 23%), non-significant in the largest trial (49.1% vs 30.9%, P = 0.08) and in the Cochrane responder pooling (relative risk 0.76, 0.57–1.02). Mean arterial pressure fell more on carvedilol in both Bañares trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (mean HVPG reduction): carvedilol reduces portal pressure more than propranolol as measured by HVPG; whether that converts into fewer non-responders or better clinical outcomes is the part homed, and still open, on #3594.
cards.watchOut: HVPG is a surrogate: the stamp answers the pressure question as asked. Anyone quoting this shelf for bleeding or survival outcomes is quoting the wrong shelf — those live on #3594, where the survival claim is indirect and stamped SPLIT.

shelves.title: Albumin in acute-on-chronic liver failure (PARTIAL completion of pack #2522): setting-specific signals — paracentesis cover and a bundle study positive, resuscitation-fluid trial null on survival
shelves.question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does albumin infusion improve survival versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure · Albumins · Ascites · Ascitic Fluid · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Physiologic · Paracentesis · Plasma Substitutes · Shock · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, on ACLF-specific evidence only. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2522 already answers targeted albumin infusions in hospitalised decompensated cirrhosis broadly (the ATTIRE trial, homed there and NOT re-carded here — ATTIRE found no overall benefit in that broader population), and pack #2515 covers long-term outpatient albumin in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites. The uncovered slice is the ACLF population itself, and its direct evidence is thin and mixed. One small randomised trial in ACLF patients having a modest-volume paracentesis found albumin cover halved in-hospital mortality (27.5% vs 62.5%) alongside less circulatory dysfunction, kidney injury and encephalopathy. One prospective observational cohort of 230 ACLF patients found higher 28-day survival with a response-guided albumin-containing bundle (albumin–furosemide infusion ± a vasoconstrictor) than with standard medical therapy (75.7% vs 53.2%) — but the albumin cannot be separated from the bundle. The nearest randomised albumin-versus-other-fluid trial in critically ill cirrhosis (sepsis-induced hypotension, not enrolled by ACLF criteria) improved blood pressure faster with 20% albumin but made no difference to 28-day survival (58% vs 62%) and caused more pulmonary complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: albumin probably helps in specific ACLF settings (paracentesis cover; as part of volume/haemodynamic support), but a general survival benefit of albumin infusion in ACLF is not established, and the broad-population trial homed on #2522 was null.

cards.headline: Arora 2020: in 80 patients with ACLF having a modest-volume paracentesis, albumin cover cut paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (30% vs 70%) and in-hospital mortality (27.5% vs 62.5%)
cards.summary: Arora 2020: in 80 patients with ACLF having a modest-volume paracentesis, albumin cover cut paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (30% vs 70%) and in-hospital mortality (27.5% vs 62.5%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Arora 2020, albumin cover for paracentesis in ACLF)
cards.people: 80 patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure undergoing modest-volume (<5 L) paracentesis, randomised to albumin (8 g per dL of ascitic fluid removed, as reported; n = 40) or no albumin (n = 40), with serial monitoring for paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (PICD).
cards.result: PICD developed in 30% of the albumin group versus 70% of the no-albumin group (p = 0.001). The albumin group also had less hepatic encephalopathy (27.5% vs 50%; p = 0.04), less hyponatraemia (22.5% vs 67.5%; p < 0.001), less acute kidney injury (30% vs 62.5%; p = 0.001) and lower in-hospital mortality (27.5% vs 62.5%; p = 0.003). Albumin independently reduced the odds of PICD at day 6 (odds ratio 0.068, 95% CI 0.011–0.43).
cards.watchOut: This is albumin given for one defined indication — cover for a paracentesis of under 5 litres — in a single-centre trial of 80 patients; it does not test albumin as a general ACLF treatment, and the mortality gap is large for a trial of this size.

cards.headline: Pande 2022: in a prospective cohort of 230 patients with ACLF and ascites, a response-guided slow albumin–furosemide infusion bundle (± terlipressin) was followed by higher 28-day survival than standard medical therapy (75.7% vs 53.2%) — observational
cards.summary: Pande 2022: in a prospective cohort of 230 patients with ACLF and ascites, a response-guided slow albumin–furosemide infusion bundle (± terlipressin) was followed by higher 28-day survival than standard medical therapy (75.7% vs 53.2%) — observational
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort (Pande 2022, albumin-containing bundle vs standard care in ACLF)
cards.people: 230 patients with ACLF (CANONIC criteria), ascites grade II or worse and ACLF grade I or worse, in a prospective observational cohort: 136 received response-guided (urine sodium >80 mmol/day) slow albumin–furosemide infusion ± terlipressin (SAFI ± T) and 94 received standard medical therapy; a separate mechanistic cohort of 40 patients was also studied.
cards.result: Ascites was mobilised in 102 of 136 patients on the albumin-containing bundle versus 23 of 94 on standard therapy (p < 0.05). Twenty-eight-day survival was 75.7% (103/136) with the bundle versus 53.2% (50/94) with standard therapy (p < 0.001). Every patient who failed to reach the urine-sodium target died. Four patients in the bundle group developed scrotal gangrene. In the mechanistic cohort, 72% survived, with improvements in gut permeability, endotoxaemia, cytokines, neutrophil function and haemodynamics.
cards.watchOut: Observational and not randomised: sicker or less responsive patients may have sorted into the standard-therapy group, and the intervention is a bundle — albumin plus furosemide, often plus terlipressin — so the survival difference cannot be credited to albumin alone.
cards.source: Pande G et al. Response Guided Slow Infusion of Albumin, Vasoconstrictors and Furosemide Improves Ascites Mobilization and Survival in Acute on Chronic Liver Failure: A Proof-of-Concept Study. cards.headline: ALPS 2022: in 100 critically ill patients with cirrhosis and sepsis-induced hypotension, 20% albumin restored blood pressure faster than plasmalyte but made no difference to 28-day survival (58% vs 62%) and caused more pulmonary complications
cards.summary: ALPS 2022: in 100 critically ill patients with cirrhosis and sepsis-induced hypotension, 20% albumin restored blood pressure faster than plasmalyte but made no difference to 28-day survival (58% vs 62%) and caused more pulmonary complications
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (ALPS, Maiwall 2022 — adjacent population: critically ill cirrhosis with sepsis-induced hypotension, not ACLF-defined)
cards.people: 100 critically ill patients with cirrhosis and sepsis-induced hypotension, randomised open-label to 20% albumin (0.5–1.0 g/kg over 3 hours; n = 50) or plasmalyte (30 ml/kg over 3 hours; n = 50); mean SOFA score about 11 in both groups. This trial enrolled critically ill cirrhosis with sepsis, NOT patients defined by ACLF criteria — it is carded as the nearest randomised albumin-versus-other-fluid evidence and flagged as such.
cards.result: Albumin reached the primary endpoint (mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg at 3 hours) in 62% versus 22% with plasmalyte (p < 0.001), with faster lactate decline. But 28-day mortality was 58% with albumin versus 62% with plasmalyte (p = 0.57) — the treatment made no difference to survival. Treatment had to be stopped for adverse effects in 11 patients (22%) on albumin versus none on plasmalyte, mainly pulmonary complications.
cards.watchOut: Population flag: these patients were critically ill with cirrhosis and septic hypotension (mean SOFA ~11, so many would meet ACLF criteria), but the trial did not enrol or report by ACLF status — do not read its null survival result as a direct ACLF answer, and do not read its blood-pressure benefit as a survival benefit.
cards.source: Maiwall R et al. A randomized-controlled trial comparing 20% albumin to plasmalyte in patients with cirrhosis and sepsis-induced hypotension [ALPS trial]. Journal of hepatology. 2022. cards.headline: Synthesis: ACLF-specific albumin evidence is one small positive paracentesis trial, one positive observational bundle study, and one adjacent-population trial that improved blood pressure but not survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: ACLF-specific albumin evidence is one small positive paracentesis trial, one positive observational bundle study, and one adjacent-population trial that improved blood pressure but not survival
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of albumin cover for paracentesis in ACLF (80 patients), one prospective observational cohort of an albumin-containing bundle in ACLF (230 patients), and one randomised trial of albumin versus plasmalyte in critically ill cirrhosis with sepsis-induced hypotension (100 patients). Total carded participants 410, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Where albumin was compared with no albumin in ACLF itself, outcomes favoured albumin: less circulatory dysfunction and lower in-hospital mortality with paracentesis cover (27.5% vs 62.5%), and higher 28-day survival with a response-guided albumin–furosemide ± vasoconstrictor bundle (75.7% vs 53.2%, observational). Where albumin was compared with another resuscitation fluid in critically ill cirrhosis, haemodynamics improved faster but 28-day survival did not (58% vs 62%), and pulmonary complications were more frequent. The large broad-population trial of targeted albumin in hospitalised decompensated cirrhosis is homed on pack #2522 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a setting-specific benefit is plausible; a general survival benefit of albumin infusion in ACLF is unproven.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with #2522: that shelf's null result was in decompensated cirrhosis broadly, this shelf's positive signals are in narrower ACLF settings — the honest summary is that indication and setting, not the drug alone, seem to decide whether albumin helps.
cards.source: Synthesis of Arora V et al. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2020 (PMID: 31849085); Pande G et al. Journal of inflammation research. 2022 (PMID: 36072778); Maiwall R et al. Journal of hepatology. 2022 (PMID: 35460725).

shelves.title: Direct-acting antivirals in decompensated cirrhosis (PARTIAL completion of pack #2672): high cure rates even in Child-Pugh B/C, liver function improves after cure, survival benefit from programme comparisons
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C and decompensated cirrhosis, do direct-acting antivirals improve liver function and survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antiviral Agents · Carbamates · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Drug Resistance, Viral · Female · Genotype · Hepacivirus · Hepatitis C, Chronic · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Ribavirin · Sofosbuvir · Treatment Outcome · Viral Nonstructural Proteins · RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase · Benzimidazoles · Benzopyrans
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2672 covers 8-week glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cure in patients without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis, pack #5967 covers cure in compensated cirrhosis, and live #593 covers DAA cure rates generally. The uncovered slice is decompensated (Child-Pugh B/C) disease, and here the trials agree: sofosbuvir-based regimens cured roughly 83–94% of Child-Pugh B patients (ASTRAL-4) and 78–96% across the SOLAR-2 Child-Pugh B/C groups, with cure rates falling in Child-Pugh C (ALLY-1: 93% in Child-Pugh A/B vs 56% in class C). Cure was followed by better liver function: in the English expanded-access programme, MELD scores improved on treatment (−0.85) while they worsened in untreated patients (+0.75), and over 15 months serious decompensation events fell compared with untreated patients, though new liver cancers still occurred and some patients still died or needed transplant. No placebo-controlled survival trial exists or could now ethically be run, so the survival claim rests on these treated-versus-untreated programme comparisons. PROPOSED LIKELY: DAAs cure most patients with decompensated cirrhosis and improve liver function; a survival benefit is supported by cohort comparisons, not by a randomised survival trial.

cards.headline: ASTRAL-4 2015: in 267 patients with decompensated (Child-Pugh B) cirrhosis, sofosbuvir–velpatasvir cured 83% over 12 weeks, 94% with ribavirin added, and 86% over 24 weeks
cards.summary: ASTRAL-4 2015: in 267 patients with decompensated (Child-Pugh B) cirrhosis, sofosbuvir–velpatasvir cured 83% over 12 weeks, 94% with ribavirin added, and 86% over 24 weeks
cards.people: 267 treated patients with HCV genotypes 1–6 and decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh-Turcotte class B), randomised open-label in a phase 3 study to sofosbuvir–velpatasvir for 12 weeks, sofosbuvir–velpatasvir plus ribavirin for 12 weeks, or sofosbuvir–velpatasvir for 24 weeks; primary endpoint sustained virologic response 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12).
cards.result: SVR12 rates were 83% (95% CI 74–90) with 12 weeks of sofosbuvir–velpatasvir, 94% (95% CI 87–98) with ribavirin added, and 86% (95% CI 77–92) with 24 weeks; post hoc analysis found no significant differences between the three groups. Serious adverse events occurred in 16–19% across groups; the commonest events were fatigue (29%), nausea (23%) and headache (22%), with anaemia in 31% of ribavirin recipients.
cards.watchOut: ASTRAL-4 enrolled Child-Pugh B only — it does not answer how well treatment works in Child-Pugh C, where ALLY-1 (below) found much lower cure rates; and SVR is a viral endpoint, with the liver-function and survival evidence carried by the programme cohorts on the later cards.
cards.source: Curry MP et al. Sofosbuvir and Velpatasvir for HCV in Patients with Decompensated Cirrhosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26569658. Registry ID: NCT02201901. cards.headline: SOLAR-2 2016: in decompensated cirrhosis before transplant, ledipasvir–sofosbuvir plus ribavirin cured 87–96% of Child-Pugh B and 78–85% of Child-Pugh C genotype-1 patients
cards.summary: SOLAR-2 2016: in decompensated cirrhosis before transplant, ledipasvir–sofosbuvir plus ribavirin cured 87–96% of Child-Pugh B and 78–85% of Child-Pugh C genotype-1 patients
cards.people: 333 treated patients with HCV genotype 1 or 4 and advanced liver disease in an open-label randomised phase 2 study; cohort A (no transplant) had Child-Pugh B or C cirrhosis and was randomised to 12 or 24 weeks of ledipasvir–sofosbuvir plus ribavirin; cohort B was post-transplant. Figures here are cohort A, genotype 1.
cards.result: In cohort A, SVR12 in Child-Pugh B was 87% (20/23) with 12 weeks and 96% (22/23) with 24 weeks; in Child-Pugh C it was 85% (17/20) with 12 weeks and 78% (18/23) with 24 weeks. Across the whole study, 7 patients (2%) stopped treatment early for adverse events and 17 patients died, mainly from complications of hepatic decompensation — a reminder that curing the virus does not immediately reverse end-stage disease.
cards.watchOut: This was an exploratory phase 2 study not powered for formal comparisons between durations, and it mixes pre- and post-transplant cohorts in its safety totals; the decompensated pre-transplant figures quoted here are the cohort A genotype-1 results.
cards.source: Manns M et al. Ledipasvir and sofosbuvir plus ribavirin in patients with genotype 1 or 4 hepatitis C virus infection and advanced liver disease: a multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 2 trial. The Lancet. cards.headline: ALLY-1 2016: daclatasvir–sofosbuvir–ribavirin cured 82% of genotype-1 patients with advanced cirrhosis — but only 56% of Child-Pugh C patients, versus 93% in Child-Pugh A/B
cards.summary: ALLY-1 2016: daclatasvir–sofosbuvir–ribavirin cured 82% of genotype-1 patients with advanced cirrhosis — but only 56% of Child-Pugh C patients, versus 93% in Child-Pugh A/B
cards.people: 60 patients with chronic HCV of any genotype and advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A 20%, B 53%, C 27%) treated open-label with daclatasvir 60 mg plus sofosbuvir 400 mg plus ribavirin 600 mg daily for 12 weeks in the phase 3 ALLY-1 study (a separate post-transplant cohort of 53 patients is not counted here).
cards.result: In the cirrhosis cohort, SVR12 in genotype 1 was 82% (95% CI 67.9–92.0); rates for genotypes 2, 3 and 4 were 80%, 83% and 100%. The severity gradient was steep: SVR12 was 93% in Child-Pugh A or B but 56% in Child-Pugh C. There were no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The Child-Pugh C subgroup is small, so the 56% figure is imprecise; daclatasvir has also since been withdrawn from several markets — the card stands as evidence about treating decompensated disease, not as a regimen recommendation.
cards.source: Poordad F et al. Daclatasvir with sofosbuvir and ribavirin for hepatitis C virus infection with advanced cirrhosis or post-liver transplantation recurrence. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2016. PMID: 26754432. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Foster 2016: in the English expanded-access programme, treated patients' MELD scores improved (−0.85) while untreated decompensated patients worsened (+0.75)
cards.summary: Foster 2016: in the English expanded-access programme, treated patients' MELD scores improved (−0.85) while untreated decompensated patients worsened (+0.75)
cards.type: Prospective treatment programme with retrospective untreated comparison (Foster 2016, English expanded-access programme)
cards.people: 467 patients with HCV and decompensated cirrhosis (409) or risk of irreversible disease, treated in the 2014 English expanded-access programme with sofosbuvir-based regimens (ledipasvir or daclatasvir, with or without ribavirin) chosen by their clinicians; functional outcomes were compared with a retrospectively studied untreated decompensated cohort registered 6 months before treatment was available.
cards.result: Viral clearance was achieved in 81.6% overall — 90.5% (209/231) in genotype 1 and 68.8% (132/192) in genotype 3. Within 6 months, MELD scores improved in treated patients (mean change −0.85) but worsened in untreated patients (mean +0.75; p < 0.0001). Patients least likely to benefit had baseline albumin below 35 g/L (3.5 g/dL), age over 65, or low baseline serum sodium.
cards.watchOut: The untreated comparison group is retrospective and from an earlier period, so part of the MELD gap could reflect who was selected for treatment and when; this is programme evidence, not a randomised comparison.
cards.source: Foster GR et al. Impact of direct acting antiviral therapy in patients with chronic hepatitis C and decompensated cirrhosis. Journal of hepatology. 2016. PMID: 26829205. cards.headline: Cheung 2016: over 15 months after treatment, serious decompensations fell versus untreated patients — but 3% of those cured still died, 5% developed liver cancer and 12% were transplanted
cards.summary: Cheung 2016: over 15 months after treatment, serious decompensations fell versus untreated patients — but 3% of those cured still died, 5% developed liver cancer and 12% were transplanted
cards.type: Prospective programme cohort with untreated comparison (Cheung 2016, English Expanded Access Programme)
cards.people: 406 patients with decompensated cirrhosis treated prospectively with 12 weeks of all-oral DAAs in the English Expanded Access Programme and followed to 15 months from treatment start, with a retrospectively studied untreated cohort (n = 261) for comparison; 317 of 406 achieved SVR at 24 weeks post-treatment.
cards.result: Among those who achieved SVR24 there were, over 15 months, 9 deaths (3%), 17 new liver cancers (5%), 39 transplantations (12%) and 52 serious decompensation events (16%). Serious decompensations were less frequent in months 6–15 after treatment (7%) than in months 0–6 (18%) or in untreated patients over 6 months (28%). Liver cancer incidence did not differ significantly from untreated patients. The authors concluded treatment led to prolonged improvement in liver function with no paradoxical harm.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are reported mainly for patients who achieved SVR, which builds in a responder selection; and the untreated cohort is retrospective — the decompensation reduction is consistent with benefit but is not randomised proof of a survival effect.
cards.source: Cheung MCM et al. Outcomes after successful direct-acting antiviral therapy for patients with chronic hepatitis C and decompensated cirrhosis. Journal of hepatology. 2016. PMID: 27388925. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: DAAs cure most patients with decompensated cirrhosis — less reliably in Child-Pugh C — and liver function improves after cure, with fewer decompensations than in untreated patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: DAAs cure most patients with decompensated cirrhosis — less reliably in Child-Pugh C — and liver function improves after cure, with fewer decompensations than in untreated patients
cards.people: The carded evidence: three open-label trials in decompensated/advanced cirrhosis (ASTRAL-4, 267 patients; SOLAR-2 cohort A within 333 treated; ALLY-1 cirrhosis cohort, 60 patients) and two English expanded-access programme reports with untreated comparisons (467 and 406 treated patients). Total carded participants exceed 1,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cure (SVR12) rates were 83–94% in Child-Pugh B (ASTRAL-4), 87–96% in Child-Pugh B and 78–85% in Child-Pugh C (SOLAR-2), and 93% in Child-Pugh A/B versus 56% in Child-Pugh C (ALLY-1). After treatment, MELD improved in treated patients while worsening in untreated patients (−0.85 vs +0.75), and serious decompensations fell over 15 months relative to untreated patients, while liver cancer still occurred at a similar rate. PROPOSED LIKELY: DAAs improve liver function in decompensated cirrhosis and probably improve survival, on concordant trial cure rates plus programme comparisons — with no randomised survival trial behind the survival part of the claim.
cards.watchOut: Cure is not the same as recovery: a meaningful minority of cured patients still decompensate, develop liver cancer or need transplant within 15 months, so this shelf must not be read as 'treat and discharge' — surveillance continues after SVR in decompensated disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of Curry MP et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26569658); Manns M et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2016 (PMID: 26907736); Poordad F et al. shelves.title: Enzyme replacement after pancreatic surgery (PARTIAL completion of pack #3591): null as prescribed, positive as taken — the post-pancreatectomy slice
shelves.question: In adults with pancreatic exocrine insufficiency after pancreatic surgery, does enzyme replacement improve fat absorption and weight?
shelves.mesh: Enzyme Replacement Therapy · Humans · Nutrition Assessment · Pancreaticoduodenectomy · Quality of Life · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3591 covers enzyme replacement in chronic pancreatitis, and the mixed chronic-pancreatitis/pancreatic-surgery fat-absorption trial evidence is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here. The uncovered slice is the post-pancreatectomy population on its own, and its dedicated evidence is thinner and mixed. The one large placebo-controlled trial after pancreatoduodenectomy (304 patients, named product Norzyme) found no weight benefit in the intention-to-treat analysis — the treatment made no difference — but among patients who actually completed the protocol, the enzyme group gained 1.09 kg while placebo lost 2.28 kg, and poor compliance predicted weight loss. A small randomised trial found high-dose pancrelipase did not significantly reduce post-pancreatectomy fatty liver versus conventional enzyme supplementation (21% vs 39%; the treatment made no difference). A retrospective cohort of 469 cancer pancreatoduodenectomy patients found enzyme use independently associated with better survival (hazard ratio 0.72), an association, not proof. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: enzyme replacement plausibly improves nutrition and weight after pancreatic surgery when actually taken at adequate dose — the trial record does not show a benefit for simply prescribing it.

cards.headline: Kim 2020: after pancreatoduodenectomy, enzyme replacement made no difference to weight in the intention-to-treat analysis — but protocol completers gained 1.09 kg while placebo patients lost 2.28 kg
cards.summary: Kim 2020: after pancreatoduodenectomy, enzyme replacement made no difference to weight in the intention-to-treat analysis — but protocol completers gained 1.09 kg while placebo patients lost 2.28 kg
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Kim 2020, post-pancreatoduodenectomy PERT)
cards.people: 304 patients with pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (faecal elastase ≤200 μg/g) after pancreatoduodenectomy at 7 South Korean tertiary hospitals, randomised double-blind to pancreatic enzyme replacement — a single capsule of 40,000 IU pancreatin, Norzyme (40,000 IU, Pankreatan; Nordmark Arzneimittel GmbH & Co, Uetersen, Germany), 3 times daily with meals for 3 months (n = 151) — or placebo (n = 153). Only 71 enzyme-group and 93 placebo-group patients completed the protocol as defined.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis there was no significant difference in body weight between groups (the treatment made no difference). In the per-protocol analysis, the enzyme group gained a mean 1.09 kg and the placebo group lost 2.28 kg (between-group difference 3.37 kg; p < 0.001). Serum prealbumin rose more with enzymes (+10.9 mg/dL vs +7.8 mg/dL; p = 0.002). Poor compliance with enzyme replacement was a significant risk factor for weight loss (p < 0.001). Quality-of-life scores did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is per-protocol in a trial where fewer than half the enzyme group completed the protocol — patients who take enzymes reliably differ from those who do not, so the 3.37 kg gap overstates what prescribing alone achieves; the trial's own primary (intention-to-treat) answer was null.
cards.source: Kim H et al. Effects of Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy on Body Weight and Nutritional Assessments After Pancreatoduodenectomy in a Randomized Trial. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2020. PMID: 31520730. Registry ID: NCT02127021. cards.headline: Satoi 2016: high-dose pancrelipase did not significantly reduce fatty liver after pancreatoduodenectomy compared with conventional enzyme supplementation (21% vs 39%)
cards.summary: Satoi 2016: high-dose pancrelipase did not significantly reduce fatty liver after pancreatoduodenectomy compared with conventional enzyme supplementation (21% vs 39%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, active comparator (Satoi 2016, pancrelipase vs conventional enzymes after pancreatoduodenectomy)
cards.people: 57 patients with pancreatic cancer after pancreatoduodenectomy, randomised to pancrelipase delayed-release capsules (n = 29) or conventional pancreatic enzyme supplementation (n = 28); the outcome was new nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (liver-to-spleen attenuation ratio <0.9 on CT), a downstream consequence of fat malabsorption. The publication names the intervention only as pancrelipase delayed-release capsules — no brand or company is named in the record.
cards.result: Fatty liver developed in 6 of 29 patients (21%) on pancrelipase versus 11 of 28 (39%) on conventional supplementation — not a statistically significant difference (the treatment made no difference on this outcome). Of 10 control patients who crossed over to pancrelipase after a fatty-liver diagnosis, 5 improved. Advanced age and extended resection were independent risk factors for fatty liver.
cards.watchOut: Both groups received enzymes — this tests a high-dose pancrelipase strategy against ordinary supplementation, not enzymes against none — and with 57 patients it was too small to settle a 21% vs 39% difference; the fatty-liver endpoint is a proxy for malabsorption, not a direct fat-absorption measurement.
cards.source: Satoi S et al. Do pancrelipase delayed-release capsules have a protective role against nonalcoholic fatty liver disease after pancreatoduodenectomy in patients with pancreatic cancer? A randomized controlled trial. Journal of hepato-biliary-pancreatic sciences. 2016. PMID: 26748629. Registry ID: UMIN 000019817. cards.headline: Roberts 2017: in 469 patients after pancreatoduodenectomy for periampullary cancer, enzyme replacement use was independently associated with better survival (hazard ratio 0.72) — observational
cards.summary: Roberts 2017: in 469 patients after pancreatoduodenectomy for periampullary cancer, enzyme replacement use was independently associated with better survival (hazard ratio 0.72) — observational
cards.type: Retrospective cohort with propensity matching (Roberts 2017, PERT and survival after pancreatoduodenectomy)
cards.people: 469 patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy for periampullary malignancy at a single centre, reviewed retrospectively; 202 patients (43.1%) received pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and 267 did not, with multivariable and propensity-matched survival analyses adjusting for pathology variables and chemotherapy.
cards.result: Enzyme use was independently associated with improved overall survival on multivariable analysis (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.52–0.99; p = 0.044) and on propensity-matched analysis (p = 0.009). The association was concentrated in patients with a dilated pancreatic duct (≥3 mm) — the group most likely to have genuine exocrine insufficiency.
cards.watchOut: Observational: patients prescribed enzymes may differ in follow-up intensity, nutrition support and a dozen unmeasured ways, and the specific products and doses used are not standardised in the record — this card supports plausibility, not causation.
cards.source: Roberts KJ et al. Pancreas exocrine replacement therapy is associated with increased survival following pancreatoduodenectomy for periampullary malignancy. HPB : the official journal of the International Hepato Pancreato Biliary Association. 2017. PMID: 28711377. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: after pancreatic surgery the enzyme evidence is one large trial that was null as prescribed but positive as taken, one small null active-comparator trial, and one observational survival association
cards.summary: Synthesis: after pancreatic surgery the enzyme evidence is one large trial that was null as prescribed but positive as taken, one small null active-comparator trial, and one observational survival association
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised placebo-controlled trial after pancreatoduodenectomy (304 patients), one small randomised active-comparator trial (57 patients), and one retrospective cohort (469 patients). Total carded participants 830, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: As prescribed (intention-to-treat), enzyme replacement made no difference to weight after pancreatoduodenectomy; as actually taken (per-protocol), it was associated with a 3.37 kg weight advantage and better prealbumin. High-dose pancrelipase did not significantly beat conventional supplementation on fatty liver (21% vs 39%), and enzyme use was observationally associated with better survival after cancer surgery (hazard ratio 0.72). Direct fat-absorption (coefficient of fat absorption) proof in a purely post-surgical population is lacking on this shelf — the mixed-population absorption trials are carded with the chronic-pancreatitis shelf (#3591). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: benefit is plausible and compliance-dependent, not demonstrated for the prescription alone.
cards.watchOut: The compliance gap is the clinical story: fewer than half the trial's enzyme group took the protocol dose, so education, dose and follow-up — not the capsule alone — are what the evidence supports after pancreatic surgery.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kim H et al. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2020 (PMID: 31520730); Satoi S et al. Journal of hepato-biliary-pancreatic sciences. 2016 (PMID: 26748629); Roberts KJ et al. HPB : the official journal of the International Hepato Pancreato Biliary Association. 2017 (PMID: 28711377).

shelves.title: Combined oral and rectal mesalamine for ulcerative colitis induction: adding the enema raised remission from 43% to 64% in extensive disease
shelves.question: In adults with ulcerative colitis, is combined oral and rectal mesalamine more effective than oral mesalamine alone for inducing remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Administration, Rectal · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Colitis, Ulcerative · Double-Blind Method · Enema · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Mesalamine · Middle Aged · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. The direct trial is PINCE (127 patients with extensive mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis): adding a 1 g mesalamine enema nightly for the first 4 weeks to oral mesalamine 4 g/day raised remission at 8 weeks from 43% to 64% (p = 0.03), with improvement already separating at 4 weeks (89% vs 62%). Meta-analysis agrees: pooling the combined-versus-oral trials, combined therapy cut the risk of failing to achieve remission (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.47–0.91; number needed to treat 5), and a 40-trial network meta-analysis ranked combined oral + topical therapy first or second for induction, and first in trials dominated by left-sided or extensive disease — the population in whom the rectal component can reach the worst-affected bowel. The benefit is clearest in extensive disease; for disease confined to the rectum, topical therapy alone ranked highest. PROPOSED LIKELY: combined oral and rectal mesalamine induces remission more often than oral mesalamine alone in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, particularly extensive disease.

cards.headline: PINCE 2005: adding a mesalamine enema to oral mesalamine raised 8-week remission from 43% to 64% in extensive mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis
cards.summary: PINCE 2005: adding a mesalamine enema to oral mesalamine raised 8-week remission from 43% to 64% in extensive mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 127 ambulatory patients with extensive (beyond the splenic flexure) mild-to-moderate active ulcerative colitis in a randomised double-blind trial; all received oral mesalazine 4 g/day for 8 weeks, plus a bedtime enema for the first 4 weeks containing 1 g mesalazine or placebo. Remission and improvement were assessed with the ulcerative colitis disease activity index at 4 and 8 weeks.
cards.result: Remission at 4 weeks was 44% (95% CI 31–58) with the mesalazine enema versus 34% (95% CI 21–49) with placebo enema (p = 0.31), and at 8 weeks 64% (95% CI 50–76) versus 43% (95% CI 28–58; p = 0.03). Improvement at 4 weeks was 89% versus 62% (p = 0.0008) and at 8 weeks 86% versus 68% (p = 0.026). The combination was safe and well accepted.
cards.watchOut: One trial of 127 patients, all with extensive disease — the result should not be stretched to proctitis-only disease, where rectal therapy alone may suffice, and the enema was given for only the first 4 of the 8 weeks.
cards.source: Marteau P et al. Combined oral and enema treatment with Pentasa (mesalazine) is superior to oral therapy alone in patients with extensive mild/moderate active ulcerative colitis: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled study. Gut. 2005. PMID: 15951542. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (pince, marteau 2005) 127 ambulatory patients with extensive (beyond the splenic flexure) mild-to-moderate active ulcerative colitis in a randomised double-blind trial; all received oral mesalazine 4 g/day for 8 weeks, plus a bedtime enema for the first 4 weeks containing 1 g mesalazine or placebo. remission and improvement were assessed with the ulcerative colitis disease activity index at 4 and 8 weeks. remission at 4 weeks was 44% (95% ci 31–58) with the mesalazine enema versus 34% (95% ci 21–49) with placebo enema (p = 0.31), and at 8 weeks 64% (95% ci 50–76) versus 43% (95% ci 28–58; p = 0.03). improvement at 4 weeks was 89% versus 62% (p = 0.0008) and at 8 weeks 86% versus 68% (p = 0.026). the combination was safe and well accepted. one trial of 127 patients, all with extensive disease — the result should not be stretched to proctitis-only disease, where rectal therapy alone may suffice, and the enema was given for only the first 4 of the 8 weeks. marteau p et al. combined oral and enema treatment with pentasa (mesalazine) is superior to oral therapy alone in patients with extensive mild/moderate active ulcerative colitis: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled study. gut. 2005. pmid: 15951542. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, oral · administration, rectal · adolescent · adult · aged · anti-inflammatory agents, non-steroidal · colitis, ulcerative · double-blind method · enema · female · gastrointestinal hemorrhage · humans · male · mesalamine · middle aged · patient acceptance of health care · severity of illness index · survival analysis · treatment outcome

cards.headline: PINCE secondary analysis 2014: combination therapy also stopped rectal bleeding faster and improved symptoms within 2 weeks
cards.summary: PINCE secondary analysis 2014: combination therapy also stopped rectal bleeding faster and improved symptoms within 2 weeks
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Probert 2014, PINCE early-response analysis)
cards.people: The same 127 PINCE patients (extensive mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; oral mesalazine 4 g/day for 8 weeks plus 1 g mesalazine or placebo enema for the first 4 weeks), re-analysed for early response, mucosal healing, cessation of rectal bleeding, quality of life and acceptability. This is a secondary analysis of the trial on the previous card, not an independent population.
cards.result: Improvement in the abbreviated disease activity index (fall of ≥2 points) within 2 weeks was significantly more frequent with combination therapy (p = 0.032), and rectal bleeding ceased significantly faster (p = 0.003). More combination patients showed mucosal healing at week 4 (between-group p = 0.052). Quality of life improved in both groups, with a significant combination advantage at week 4 in several domains, and most patients found the enema treatment acceptable.
cards.watchOut: Secondary endpoints in the same 127 patients — supportive detail about speed of response, not independent confirmation of the remission result.
cards.source: Probert CS et al. Combined oral and rectal mesalazine for the treatment of mild-to-moderately active ulcerative colitis: rapid symptom resolution and improvements in quality of life. cards.headline: Ford 2012 meta-analysis: across the combined-versus-oral trials, combined 5-ASA cut failure to achieve remission (relative risk 0.65; number needed to treat 5)
cards.summary: Ford 2012 meta-analysis: across the combined-versus-oral trials, combined 5-ASA cut failure to achieve remission (relative risk 0.65; number needed to treat 5)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ford 2012)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials of oral versus topical versus combined 5-aminosalicylates in ulcerative colitis; the induction comparison of combined oral + topical therapy against oral therapy alone pooled 4 trials in mildly to moderately active disease.
cards.result: Combined therapy was superior to oral therapy alone for inducing remission: the relative risk of failing to achieve remission was 0.65 (95% CI 0.47–0.91), a relative measure, with a number needed to treat of 5. (For context within the same analysis, topical versus oral therapy alone did not significantly differ for induction, relative risk of no remission 0.82, 95% CI 0.52–1.28.)
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on PINCE-sized trials; the relative risk is a relative measure — the absolute gain in PINCE itself was 64% vs 43% remission at 8 weeks.

cards.headline: Barberio 2021 network meta-analysis: combined oral + topical mesalazine ranked first or second of all 5-ASA strategies for inducing remission across 40 trials
cards.summary: Barberio 2021 network meta-analysis: combined oral + topical mesalazine ranked first or second of all 5-ASA strategies for inducing remission across 40 trials
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 40 randomised trials of oral, topical and combined 5-aminosalicylates for induction of remission in ulcerative colitis (23 further trials addressed relapse prevention), with treatments ranked by P-score for combined clinical and endoscopic remission.
cards.result: Topical mesalazine ranked first (P-score 0.99) and combined oral + topical mesalazine second (P-score 0.87) for induction of clinical and endoscopic remission; in trials where at least half the patients had left-sided or extensive disease, combined therapy ranked first. High-dose oral mesalazine ranked third. For preventing relapse, combined therapy and high-dose oral mesalazine ranked first and second. All 5-ASA regimens were safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Rankings are model-based and mix direct and indirect comparisons across decades of trials with different remission definitions; the ranking agrees with, but does not replace, the direct PINCE comparison.
cards.source: Barberio B et al. Efficacy of Oral, Topical, or Combined Oral and Topical 5-Aminosalicylates, in Ulcerative Colitis: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: one direct trial, its secondary analysis, and two meta-analyses all point the same way — adding rectal mesalamine to oral mesalamine induces remission more often
cards.summary: Synthesis: one direct trial, its secondary analysis, and two meta-analyses all point the same way — adding rectal mesalamine to oral mesalamine induces remission more often
cards.people: The carded evidence: the PINCE randomised trial (127 patients) and its secondary analysis, a 12-trial systematic review (4 trials in the combined-versus-oral induction comparison), and a 40-trial network meta-analysis. Total directly randomised patients in the head-to-head trial: 127; pooled analyses cover several thousand trial participants.
cards.result: PINCE: 8-week remission 64% with combined therapy versus 43% with oral therapy alone, with faster bleeding cessation. Ford 2012: relative risk of failing to achieve remission 0.65 (95% CI 0.47–0.91), number needed to treat 5. Barberio 2021: combined therapy ranked first or second for induction, and first where disease was left-sided or extensive. PROPOSED LIKELY: combined oral and rectal mesalamine is more effective than oral mesalamine alone for inducing remission in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, with the clearest case in extensive disease.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is for adding a time-limited rectal course to oral therapy in active disease; it does not by itself answer how long rectal therapy should continue, which is a maintenance question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Marteau P et al. Gut. 2005 (PMID: 15951542); Probert CS et al. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2014 (PMID: 24012063); Ford AC et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 22108446); Barberio B et al. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2021 (PMID: 33433562).
