shelves.title: Mesalamine dose in ulcerative colitis (ASCEND I–III): 4.8 g/day helps in moderate disease, not in mild — a severity split
shelves.question: In adults with mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, is high-dose mesalamine more effective than standard-dose mesalamine for inducing remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Colitis, Ulcerative · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mesalamine · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Sigmoidoscopy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (severity) — printed on the face. The ASCEND programme asked the same question three times with the same answer pattern. In the whole mild-to-moderate population (ASCEND I, 301 patients), 4.8 g/day was not significantly better than 2.4 g/day (treatment success 56% vs 51%; the higher dose made no difference overall). In patients with moderate disease, the higher dose won each time: ASCEND I's prespecified moderate subgroup 72% vs 57% (p = 0.038), ASCEND II's moderate primary population 72% vs 59% (p = 0.036), and ASCEND III (772 patients, all moderate) met non-inferiority with a remission advantage for 4.8 g/day (43% vs 35%; p = 0.04), the advantage concentrated in patients previously treated with steroids or multiple ulcerative colitis medications. Tolerability was similar at both doses in all three trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (severity): high-dose mesalamine (4.8 g/day) is more effective than 2.4 g/day in moderately active ulcerative colitis; no advantage has been shown in mild disease.

cards.headline: ASCEND I 2005/2007: overall, 4.8 g/day was no better than 2.4 g/day (56% vs 51%) — but in the prespecified moderate subgroup it was (72% vs 57%)
cards.summary: ASCEND I 2005/2007: overall, 4.8 g/day was no better than 2.4 g/day (56% vs 51%) — but in the prespecified moderate subgroup it was (72% vs 57%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial (ASCEND I, Hanauer 2007)
cards.people: 301 adults with mildly to moderately active ulcerative colitis in a 6-week multicentre randomised double-blind trial of delayed-release oral mesalamine 2.4 g/day (400 mg tablets; n = 154) versus 4.8 g/day (800 mg tablets; n = 147); the primary endpoint was treatment success (complete remission or response) at week 6, with a prespecified subgroup analysis in moderate disease.
cards.result: Overall treatment success was 51% (77/150) on 2.4 g/day versus 56% (76/136) on 4.8 g/day (p = 0.441) — the higher dose made no difference in the whole population. In the moderate subgroup, success was 57% (53/93) on 2.4 g/day versus 72% (55/76) on 4.8 g/day (p = 0.0384). Both regimens were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The headline result is the null overall result; the moderate-subgroup advantage was prespecified, which strengthens it, but it is still a subgroup of a 301-patient trial — ASCEND II and III were designed to test exactly that subgroup.
cards.source: Hanauer SB et al. Delayed-release oral mesalamine 4.8 g/day (800 mg tablets) compared to 2.4 g/day (400 mg tablets) for the treatment of mildly to moderately active ulcerative colitis: The ASCEND I trial. Canadian journal of gastroenterology = Journal canadien de gastroenterologie. 2007. PMID: 18080055. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ASCEND II 2005: in moderately active ulcerative colitis, 4.8 g/day beat 2.4 g/day for treatment success (72% vs 59%)
cards.summary: ASCEND II 2005: in moderately active ulcerative colitis, 4.8 g/day beat 2.4 g/day for treatment success (72% vs 59%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial (ASCEND II, Hanauer 2005)
cards.people: 386 adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis randomised double-blind to delayed-release mesalamine 2.4 g/day or 4.8 g/day for 6 weeks; the primary efficacy population was the 268 patients with moderately active disease (139 on 2.4 g/day, 129 on 4.8 g/day). The primary endpoint was overall improvement (complete remission or clinical response) at week 6.
cards.result: In moderately active disease, treatment success was 72% (89/124) on 4.8 g/day versus 59% (77/130) on 2.4 g/day (p = 0.036). Adverse events and laboratory changes were similar between doses.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is 'treatment success' — remission or response — not remission alone; the stricter remission comparison comes from ASCEND III.

cards.headline: ASCEND III 2009: in 772 patients with moderately active ulcerative colitis, 4.8 g/day achieved clinical remission more often than 2.4 g/day (43% vs 35%)
cards.summary: ASCEND III 2009: in 772 patients with moderately active ulcerative colitis, 4.8 g/day achieved clinical remission more often than 2.4 g/day (43% vs 35%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial (ASCEND III, Sandborn 2009)
cards.people: 772 patients with moderately active ulcerative colitis in a multicentre randomised double-blind 6-week active-control non-inferiority study of delayed-release mesalamine 4.8 g/day (800 mg tablets) versus 2.4 g/day (400 mg tablets); the primary endpoint was treatment success (overall improvement in the Physician's Global Assessment with no worsening component) at week 6.
cards.result: Treatment success was 70% (273/389) on 4.8 g/day versus 66% (251/383) on 2.4 g/day, meeting the non-inferiority objective (95% CI for the difference, −11.2 to 1.9, for 2.4 minus 4.8 g/day). Clinical remission was achieved by 43% on 4.8 g/day versus 35% on 2.4 g/day (p = 0.04). The higher dose's advantage was clearest in patients previously treated with corticosteroids, oral mesalamine, rectal therapies or multiple ulcerative colitis medications. Both doses were well tolerated with similar adverse events.
cards.watchOut: ASCEND III was designed as a non-inferiority trial, so its remission difference (43% vs 35%) is a secondary-endpoint advantage, not the primary hypothesis — read it as consistent with ASCEND I and II rather than as standalone proof.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Delayed-release oral mesalamine 4.8 g/day (800-mg tablet) is effective for patients with moderately active ulcerative colitis. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19766640. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials, one pattern — the 4.8 g/day advantage appears in moderate disease and not in the overall mild-to-moderate population
cards.summary: Synthesis: three trials, one pattern — the 4.8 g/day advantage appears in moderate disease and not in the overall mild-to-moderate population
cards.people: The carded evidence: the three ASCEND randomised double-blind dose trials (301, 386 and 772 randomised patients; 1,459 in total), all comparing delayed-release mesalamine 4.8 g/day with 2.4 g/day over 6 weeks. Total carded participants exceed 1,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: ASCEND I (mild-to-moderate): success 56% vs 51% overall (no difference), 72% vs 57% in the moderate subgroup. ASCEND II (moderate primary population): success 72% vs 59%. ASCEND III (all moderate): success 70% vs 66%, remission 43% vs 35%. Safety was similar at both doses throughout. PROPOSED SPLIT (severity): high-dose mesalamine is more effective in moderately active ulcerative colitis; in mild disease the extra dose has not been shown to help.
cards.watchOut: All three trials tested one formulation family (delayed-release mesalamine in 400 mg vs 800 mg tablets) over 6 weeks; the dose conclusion is about induction in moderate disease, not about maintenance dosing or other formulations.

shelves.title: Once-daily versus twice-daily mesalamine for ulcerative colitis maintenance: equally effective in three trials and a meta-analysis
shelves.question: In adults with ulcerative colitis in remission, is once-daily mesalamine as effective as twice-daily mesalamine for maintaining remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Chemistry, Pharmaceutical · Colitis, Ulcerative · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa · Male · Mesalamine · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face, as an equivalence answer: once-daily mesalamine maintains remission as well as twice-daily dosing. The head-to-head trials agree. MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day given once or in two divided doses held clinical and endoscopic remission at 12 months in 64.4% vs 68.5% of patients (no significant difference). Prolonged-release mesalamine granules 2 g once daily actually outperformed 1 g twice daily at 1 year (70.9% vs 58.9% in remission; p = 0.024), with better self-reported adherence. A 6-month endoscopic-remission trial (826 patients) met its non-inferiority objective for once-daily MMX. Pooling 7 trials (2,745 patients), relapse risk did not differ between once-daily and conventional schedules (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.08), nor did adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: once-daily mesalamine is as effective as twice-daily mesalamine for maintaining remission — the point of the simpler schedule is adherence, and the trials show no efficacy price for it.

cards.headline: Kamm 2008: MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day once daily held remission as well as the same dose split twice daily over 12 months (64.4% vs 68.5%)
cards.summary: Kamm 2008: MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day once daily held remission as well as the same dose split twice daily over 12 months (64.4% vs 68.5%)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial (Kamm 2008, MMX mesalamine maintenance)
cards.people: Patients with ulcerative colitis in strictly defined clinical and endoscopic remission after a mild-to-moderate flare, randomised open-label to MMX mesalazine 2.4 g/day as a single dose (two 1.2 g tablets) or divided dose (1.2 g twice daily) for 12 months; safety population 459, efficacy population 451.
cards.result: At month 12, 64.4% of the once-daily group and 68.5% of the twice-daily group were in clinical and endoscopic remission (p = 0.351) — no significant difference (the dosing schedule made no difference). Clinical remission (relapse-free) was maintained by 88.9% once daily and 93.2% twice daily. Serious adverse events were similar (9 patients in each group).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and not powered as a formal non-inferiority trial — 'no significant difference' here is consistency evidence, which the meta-analysis on the last evidence card quantifies.

cards.headline: Dignass 2009: prolonged-release mesalamine 2 g once daily kept more patients in remission at 1 year than 1 g twice daily (70.9% vs 58.9%)
cards.summary: Dignass 2009: prolonged-release mesalamine 2 g once daily kept more patients in remission at 1 year than 1 g twice daily (70.9% vs 58.9%)
cards.type: Randomised single-blind non-inferiority trial (Dignass 2009, mesalamine granules maintenance)
cards.people: 362 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis in a multicentre randomised single-blind non-inferiority trial of oral prolonged-release mesalamine granules 2 g once daily versus 1 g twice daily (the same total daily dose) for 12 months; the primary objective was remission rate at 1 year by the ulcerative colitis disease activity index, using Kaplan–Meier methodology.
cards.result: At 1 year, 70.9% of the once-daily group remained in remission versus 58.9% of the twice-daily group (p = 0.024) — once daily was not only non-inferior but statistically superior on this endpoint. Self-reported adherence (visual analogue scale) was significantly greater with once-daily dosing at nearly all visits, though adherence measured by medication actually taken did not differ significantly. Overall adverse-event incidence did not differ (p = 0.23).
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, and the superiority signal rests on a Kaplan–Meier remission analysis while pill-count adherence did not differ — the safest reading is 'at least as effective', with any advantage plausibly mediated by how patients actually take a once-daily regimen.
cards.source: Dignass AU et al. Mesalamine once daily is more effective than twice daily in patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis. cards.headline: D'Haens 2012: once-daily MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day was non-inferior to twice-daily delayed-release mesalamine for maintaining endoscopic remission at 6 months
cards.summary: D'Haens 2012: once-daily MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day was non-inferior to twice-daily delayed-release mesalamine for maintaining endoscopic remission at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (D'Haens 2012, MMX vs delayed-release mesalamine maintenance)
cards.people: 826 patients with ulcerative colitis in endoscopic remission, randomised double-blind for 6 months to once-daily MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day or twice-daily delayed-release mesalamine at a total of 1.6 g/day; the primary endpoint was maintenance of endoscopic remission at month 6 in the per-protocol population. Note the total daily doses differ between arms (2.4 g vs 1.6 g).
cards.result: The non-inferiority objective was met: endoscopic remission at month 6 was maintained by 83.7% (per-protocol) and 77.8% (intention-to-treat) on once-daily MMX versus 81.5% (per-protocol) and 76.9% (intention-to-treat) on twice-daily delayed-release mesalamine (95% CI for the difference −3.9 to 8.1 per-protocol). Time to relapse did not differ (p = 0.51–0.55). Adverse events were similar (37.1% vs 36.0%).
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles two changes at once — schedule (once vs twice daily) and both formulation and total dose (MMX 2.4 g vs delayed-release 1.6 g) — so it shows the once-daily MMX regimen is not worse, without isolating schedule alone; the same-dose schedule test is the Kamm trial.
cards.source: D'Haens G et al. Once-daily MMX(®) mesalamine for endoscopic maintenance of remission of ulcerative colitis. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22565161. cards.headline: Ford 2011 meta-analysis: across 7 trials and 2,745 patients, relapse risk was the same with once-daily as with conventional mesalamine dosing (relative risk 0.94)
cards.summary: Ford 2011 meta-analysis: across 7 trials and 2,745 patients, relapse risk was the same with once-daily as with conventional mesalamine dosing (relative risk 0.94)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ford 2011)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (2,745 patients) in quiescent ulcerative colitis comparing once-daily 5-aminosalicylate dosing with a more frequent schedule of the identical total daily dose of the same drug, with at least 6 months of treatment; all trials used mesalamine. Outcomes were relapse of disease activity, non-compliance and adverse events.
cards.result: Relapse rates did not differ significantly between once-daily and conventional dosing (relative risk of relapse 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.08) — the dosing schedule made no difference to relapse. Non-compliance was not significantly less with once-daily dosing (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.46–1.66), and adverse events were similar (relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.97–1.20).
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.82–1.08) excludes a large penalty for once-daily dosing but not a small one, and the trials did not prove the expected adherence advantage — the case for once daily is equal efficacy with a simpler regimen, not proven better adherence.
cards.source: Ford AC et al. Once-daily dosing vs. conventional dosing schedule of mesalamine and relapse of quiescent ulcerative colitis: systematic review and meta-analysis. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21894226. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three head-to-head trials and a 7-trial meta-analysis agree — once-daily mesalamine maintains remission as well as twice-daily
cards.summary: Synthesis: three head-to-head trials and a 7-trial meta-analysis agree — once-daily mesalamine maintains remission as well as twice-daily
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised maintenance trials (451, 362 and 826 patients) and one meta-analysis of 7 trials (2,745 patients). Total carded participants exceed 4,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Remission at 12 months was 64.4% vs 68.5% for MMX once versus twice daily (no difference), and 70.9% vs 58.9% favouring once-daily granules; endoscopic remission at 6 months was non-inferior with once-daily MMX (83.7% vs 81.5% per-protocol). Pooled relapse risk: relative risk 0.94 (95% CI 0.82–1.08), with similar adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: once-daily mesalamine is as effective as twice-daily mesalamine for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here is about the maintenance schedule at an effective total dose — it does not license dropping the total daily dose, and none of these trials tested once-daily dosing for inducing remission in a flare.

shelves.title: Combined surgical closure plus anti-TNF for perianal fistulizing Crohn's (PISA programme): better MRI healing and fewer re-interventions, clinical closure not yet separated
shelves.question: In adults with perianal fistulizing Crohn's disease, does combined surgical drainage plus anti-TNF therapy heal fistulas better than anti-TNF therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Crohn Disease · Humans · Patient Preference · Quality of Life · Rectal Fistula · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitors · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. Confirm-first check (done at build): at least three free reports with ≥10 patients exist — the two PISA trials and the comparative systematic review carded here. Read the question precisely: in the PISA programme every patient first received seton drainage; the tested strategy was then surgical closure under a short course of anti-TNF versus continuing anti-TNF alone for a year. On that comparison, PISA-II (94 patients) found radiological (MRI) healing at 18 months in 32% with closure plus anti-TNF versus 9% with anti-TNF alone (p = 0.005), and far fewer re-interventions (13% vs 43%), though clinical closure did not differ significantly (68% vs 52%). The earlier PISA randomised trial (44 patients, stopped early for futility) likewise found fewest re-interventions in the surgical-closure-after-anti-TNF arm (3/14) versus anti-TNF alone (6/15) and seton drainage alone (10/15). A systematic review of seton and anti-TNF studies found the cohort studies that directly compared strategies favoured combined treatment in two of four. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: adding a surgical step (closure after drainage) to anti-TNF probably improves deep (MRI) healing and reduces re-interventions; the clinical-closure advantage is not yet significant, and no trial isolates drainage-plus-anti-TNF against anti-TNF with no surgical contact at all.

cards.headline: PISA-II 2022: surgical closure after seton drainage and short anti-TNF tripled MRI healing versus anti-TNF alone (32% vs 9%) and cut re-interventions (13% vs 43%)
cards.summary: PISA-II 2022: surgical closure after seton drainage and short anti-TNF tripled MRI healing versus anti-TNF alone (32% vs 9%) and cut re-interventions (13% vs 43%)
cards.people: 94 adults with Crohn's disease and an active high perianal fistula with a single internal opening in a multicentre patient-preference randomised trial (32 randomised, 62 chose their treatment); all had a seton inserted first. The surgical group (n = 38) received 4 months of anti-TNF therapy then surgical closure; the medical group (n = 56) received anti-TNF therapy for 1 year. The primary outcome was radiological healing on MRI at 18 months.
cards.result: Radiological healing at 18 months was significantly more common with surgical closure (12/38, 32%) than with anti-TNF alone (5/56, 9%; p = 0.005). Clinical closure did not differ significantly (68% vs 52%; p = 0.076). Fewer surgical-group patients needed a re-intervention (13% vs 43%; p = 0.005), perianal disease activity scores were lower at 18 months (p = 0.031), and recurrence after clinical closure was similar (14% vs 16%) and occurred only in patients without radiological healing. Adverse events were similar; 11% had anti-TNF side-effects.
cards.watchOut: Two-thirds of patients chose their own treatment rather than being randomised, so preference and anatomy (who was offered closure) can bias the comparison; and the surgical step tested is closure after drainage — not drainage alone — in fistulas with a single internal opening judged closable.
cards.source: Meima-van Praag EM et al. Short-term anti-TNF therapy with surgical closure versus anti-TNF therapy in the treatment of perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease (PISA-II): a patient preference randomised trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 35427495. Registry ID: Dutch Trial Registry NL7625; EudraCT 2018-002064-15. cards.headline: PISA 2020: in the stopped-early randomised trial, surgical closure after anti-TNF needed fewest re-interventions (3/14) versus anti-TNF alone (6/15) and seton drainage alone (10/15)
cards.summary: PISA 2020: in the stopped-early randomised trial, surgical closure after anti-TNF needed fewest re-interventions (3/14) versus anti-TNF alone (6/15) and seton drainage alone (10/15)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stopped early (PISA, Wasmann 2020)
cards.people: 44 patients with high perianal Crohn's fistulas with a single internal opening, randomised across 19 European centres to chronic seton drainage for 1 year, anti-TNF therapy for 1 year, or surgical closure after 2 months under a short course of anti-TNF; the primary outcome was fistula-related re-intervention by 1.5 years. A parallel prospective registry captured patients who declined randomisation. The trial planned 126 patients and was stopped by its data safety monitoring board for futility.
cards.result: Re-interventions were most frequent with seton drainage alone (10/15), intermediate with anti-TNF alone (6/15) and fewest with surgical closure (3/14; p = 0.02). Perianal disease activity and quality of life did not differ substantially between groups. In the parallel preference registry, seton drainage was not inferior on any outcome — a caution against over-reading the randomised result. The authors concluded chronic seton drainage should not be recommended as sole treatment.
cards.watchOut: Only 44 of 126 planned patients were randomised before the futility stop, so every arm is small and the re-intervention ranking is fragile; the registry cohort's different result underlines how much patient selection drives outcomes in this disease.
cards.source: Wasmann KA et al. Treatment of Perianal Fistulas in Crohn's Disease, Seton Versus Anti-TNF Versus Surgical Closure Following Anti-TNF [PISA]: A Randomised Controlled Trial. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2020. PMID: 31919501. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial, stopped early (pisa, wasmann 2020) 44 patients with high perianal crohn's fistulas with a single internal opening, randomised across 19 european centres to chronic seton drainage for 1 year, anti-tnf therapy for 1 year, or surgical closure after 2 months under a short course of anti-tnf; the primary outcome was fistula-related re-intervention by 1.5 years. a parallel prospective registry captured patients who declined randomisation. the trial planned 126 patients and was stopped by its data safety monitoring board for futility. re-interventions were most frequent with seton drainage alone (10/15), intermediate with anti-tnf alone (6/15) and fewest with surgical closure (3/14; p = 0.02). perianal disease activity and quality of life did not differ substantially between groups. in the parallel preference registry, seton drainage was not inferior on any outcome — a caution against over-reading the randomised result. the authors concluded chronic seton drainage should not be recommended as sole treatment. only 44 of 126 planned patients were randomised before the futility stop, so every arm is small and the re-intervention ranking is fragile; the registry cohort's different result underlines how much patient selection drives outcomes in this disease. wasmann ka et al. treatment of perianal fistulas in crohn's disease, seton versus anti-tnf versus surgical closure following anti-tnf [pisa]: a randomised controlled trial. journal of crohn's & colitis. 2020. pmid: 31919501. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adalimumab · adult · combined modality therapy · crohn disease · drainage · early termination of clinical trials · female · humans · infliximab · male · medical futility · outcome and process assessment, health care · patient acuity · quality of life · rectal fistula · reoperation · tumor necrosis factor inhibitors · wound closure techniques

cards.headline: de Groof 2016 systematic review: closure rates vary too widely to crown a strategy — but the cohort studies that compared them head-to-head favoured combined seton-plus-anti-TNF treatment
cards.summary: de Groof 2016 systematic review: closure rates vary too widely to crown a strategy — but the cohort studies that compared them head-to-head favoured combined seton-plus-anti-TNF treatment
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of seton drainage and anti-TNF treatment for Crohn's perianal fistula: 10 seton studies (305 patients), 34 anti-TNF studies (1,449 patients), 4 randomised trials of anti-TNF versus placebo (1,028 patients) and 4 cohort studies directly comparing combined treatment with a single strategy.
cards.result: Complete closure after seton drainage ranged from 13.6% to 100% across studies and after anti-TNF from 16.7% to 93%, with recurrence from 0–83.3% and 8.0–40.9% respectively — too heterogeneous to pool into a verdict. Of the four cohort studies making a direct comparison, two found a significant advantage for combined treatment (p = 0.001 and p = 0.014). The reviewers concluded that combination therapy with (temporary) seton drainage, immunomodulators and anti-TNF may be beneficial in achieving fistula closure.
cards.watchOut: The combined-treatment signal comes from non-randomised cohorts inside a review whose headline finding is heterogeneity; closure definitions and follow-up differ so much between studies that the percentages cannot be compared across cards.
cards.source: de Groof EJ et al. Treatment of perianal fistula in Crohn's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing seton drainage and anti-tumour necrosis factor treatment. Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland. 2016. PMID: 26921847. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: combined surgical-plus-anti-TNF care probably heals more fistulas deeply and needs fewer re-interventions — on one preference trial, one small stopped trial, and supportive cohorts
cards.summary: Synthesis: combined surgical-plus-anti-TNF care probably heals more fistulas deeply and needs fewer re-interventions — on one preference trial, one small stopped trial, and supportive cohorts
cards.people: The carded evidence: PISA-II (94 patients, patient-preference randomised), the PISA randomised trial (44 patients, stopped early), and a systematic review spanning 305 seton patients, 1,449 anti-TNF patients and 4 direct-comparison cohorts. Total carded participants exceed 1,800 across reports, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — though the randomised core is small.
cards.result: MRI healing at 18 months: 32% with surgical closure after drainage plus short anti-TNF versus 9% with anti-TNF alone (p = 0.005); clinical closure 68% vs 52% (not significant). Re-interventions favoured the combined/surgical strategy in both PISA trials (13% vs 43%; and 3/14 vs 6/15 arms). Two of four direct-comparison cohorts in the systematic review significantly favoured combined treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: combined surgical drainage/closure plus anti-TNF probably beats anti-TNF alone for deep healing and re-intervention, with the clinical-closure benefit not yet proven.
cards.watchOut: Every PISA patient had a seton placed first — there is no trial of anti-TNF with no surgical drainage at all in this population, so the shelf answers 'surgery added to anti-TNF' rather than 'any surgery versus none'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Meima-van Praag EM et al. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022 (PMID: 35427495); Wasmann KA et al. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2020 (PMID: 31919501); de Groof EJ et al. shelves.title: Balloon dilation for Crohn's strictures (observational evidence only — shelve with care): usually postpones surgery, repeat dilation the rule, no randomised comparison with surgery
shelves.question: In adults with Crohn's disease and a symptomatic stricture, does endoscopic balloon dilation delay or avoid surgery compared with surgery alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Balloon Enteroscopy · Constriction, Pathologic · Crohn Disease · Dilatation · Feasibility Studies · Female · Humans · Ileum · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — printed on the face, and this shelf should be shelved with care: there is NO randomised trial of balloon dilation against surgery for Crohn's strictures. Everything here is observational. What the series show: dilation usually works technically (89.1% of 3,213 procedures in a 1,463-patient pooled analysis) and relieves symptoms short-term (clinical efficacy 80.8%), with complications in 2.8% of procedures — but the benefit erodes: by 24 months, 73.5% of patients had been re-dilated and 42.9% had come to surgical resection, so dilation more often delays than permanently avoids surgery. Strictures of 5 cm or less fared best. The one direct comparison (79 patients, retrospective) found surgery more durable — re-intervention was more likely after dilation (odds ratio 5.62) — with similar major-complication rates (about 7.5% in both groups). A double-balloon dilation cohort kept 78.1% of patients surgery-free at 3 years, showing the delay can be long in selected patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): dilation is a reasonable first move for short, accessible strictures to postpone surgery, accepting that repeat dilation is the rule and a large minority still reach surgery within two years.

cards.headline: Bettenworth 2017 pooled analysis (observational): dilation succeeded technically in 89% and helped clinically in 81% — but by 24 months 73.5% had been re-dilated and 42.9% had needed surgery
cards.summary: Bettenworth 2017 pooled analysis (observational): dilation succeeded technically in 89% and helped clinically in 81% — but by 24 months 73.5% had been re-dilated and 42.9% had needed surgery
cards.type: Systematic review and pooled individual-participant analysis of observational series (Bettenworth 2017) — observational evidence
cards.people: Systematic review with individual-participant data pooling of endoscopic balloon dilation for stricturing Crohn's disease: 1,463 patients undergoing 3,213 dilation procedures across the published series, with a unique individual-patient database of 676 patients from 12 studies. Strictures were 98.6% ileal and 62% anastomotic (at a previous resection site). All data are from observational series — no randomised comparison exists.
cards.result: Technical success was 89.1% and short-term clinical efficacy 80.8%; complications occurred in 2.8% of procedures. After 24 months of follow-up, 73.5% of patients had undergone re-dilation and 42.9% surgical resection. In the 676-patient individual analysis, strictures of 5 cm or less were associated with a surgery-free outcome, and each additional centimetre of stricture length raised the hazard of surgery by 8% (p = 0.008). Stricture inflammation did not affect outcomes or complications.
cards.watchOut: Series patients are selected — endoscopists dilate strictures they judge reachable and safe — so these success rates describe chosen patients, not all strictures; and 'clinical efficacy' definitions varied between the pooled studies.
cards.source: Bettenworth D et al. A Pooled Analysis of Efficacy, Safety, and Long-term Outcome of Endoscopic Balloon Dilation Therapy for Patients with Stricturing Crohn's Disease. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2017. PMID: 28002130. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Greener 2015 (observational): the one direct comparison — surgery was more durable than dilation (re-intervention odds ratio 5.62), with similar major complications
cards.summary: Greener 2015 (observational): the one direct comparison — surgery was more durable than dilation (re-intervention odds ratio 5.62), with similar major complications
cards.type: Retrospective comparative cohort (Greener 2015, dilation vs surgery) — observational evidence
cards.people: Retrospective single-centre cohort of 79 patients with symptomatic stricturing Crohn's disease treated between 2006 and 2013: 39 referred for endoscopic balloon dilation and 40 for surgical resection. The primary outcome was the need for re-intervention (repeat dilation or surgery) during follow-up. This is the only carded report that compares dilation against surgery head-to-head, and it is not randomised.
cards.result: Re-intervention during follow-up was significantly more likely after dilation than after surgery (odds ratio 5.62, 95% CI 1.66–19.01; p = 0.005), as was later surgery or re-surgery (odds ratio 3.53, 95% CI 1.01–12.29; p = 0.047); re-intervention-free and surgery-free survival were both significantly shorter in the dilation group. Major complications were similar (7.6% dilation vs 7.5% surgery; p = 0.7).
cards.watchOut: Referral decided who got dilation and who got surgery — patients sent straight to surgery may have had longer, more complex or more symptomatic strictures — so the durability gap partly reflects case mix, in a cohort of only 79 patients.
cards.source: Greener T et al. Clinical Outcomes of Surgery Versus Endoscopic Balloon Dilation for Stricturing Crohn's Disease. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2015. PMID: 26544812. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sunada 2016 (observational): with double-balloon-assisted dilation of small-bowel strictures, 87.3% of patients were surgery-free at 1 year and 78.1% at 3 years
cards.summary: Sunada 2016 (observational): with double-balloon-assisted dilation of small-bowel strictures, 87.3% of patients were surgery-free at 1 year and 78.1% at 3 years
cards.type: Retrospective cohort (Sunada 2016, double-balloon dilation series) — observational evidence
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 85 consecutive patients with Crohn's small-intestinal strictures (97% de novo, not anastomotic) treated with double-balloon endoscopy-assisted balloon dilation between 2002 and 2014 — 321 sessions, 473 procedures — with a mean follow-up of 41.9 months. No surgical comparison group.
cards.result: The surgery-free rate after the first dilation was 87.3% at 1 year and 78.1% at 3 years. A coexisting fistula was strongly associated with eventually needing surgery (hazard ratio 5.50, 95% CI 2.16–14.0; p < 0.01), and the surgery-free interval was significantly shorter in patients with a fistula.
cards.watchOut: A single expert-centre series using double-balloon endoscopy, a technique not available everywhere; its better surgery-free figures than the pooled analysis may reflect technique, era, case selection — or all three.
cards.source: Sunada K et al. Long-term Outcomes in Patients with Small Intestinal Strictures Secondary to Crohn's Disease After Double-balloon Endoscopy-assisted Balloon Dilation. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2016. PMID: 26535767. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis (observational throughout): dilation usually postpones surgery and sometimes avoids it for years, but repeat dilation is the rule and the only direct comparison favours surgery for durability
cards.summary: Synthesis (observational throughout): dilation usually postpones surgery and sometimes avoids it for years, but repeat dilation is the rule and the only direct comparison favours surgery for durability
cards.people: The carded evidence: a pooled analysis of observational series (1,463 patients, 3,213 procedures), one retrospective dilation-versus-surgery comparison (79 patients), and one double-balloon dilation cohort (85 patients). There are no randomised trials on this shelf — every number is observational.
cards.result: Dilation is technically successful in about 9 of 10 attempts and relieves symptoms in about 8 of 10 patients, with complications in 2.8% of procedures. Durability is the weakness: 73.5% re-dilated and 42.9% resected by 24 months in the pooled series, and re-intervention was significantly more likely after dilation than after surgery in the direct comparison (odds ratio 5.62), while a specialist double-balloon cohort still had 78.1% surgery-free at 3 years. Short strictures (≤5 cm) do best; a fistula predicts failure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): dilation delays surgery for most suitable patients and avoids it for years in a substantial minority — it does not match surgery's durability, and this shelf is labelled observational and shelved with care.
cards.watchOut: Because no trial exists, the choice between dilation and surgery in the sources is driven by stricture length, site, fistula and patient preference — the shelf reports what happened to patients chosen for each route, not what would happen if the same patient took the other.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bettenworth D et al. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2017 (PMID: 28002130); Greener T et al. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2015 (PMID: 26544812); Sunada K et al. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2016 (PMID: 26535767).

shelves.title: Budesonide maintenance in microscopic colitis (PARTIAL completion of live #778): strong maintenance evidence — in collagenous colitis — with relapse after stopping
shelves.question: In adults with microscopic colitis, does low-dose budesonide maintain remission versus placebo after induction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Budesonide · Colitis, Collagenous · Drug Administration Schedule · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face, with a population flag: every maintenance trial was in collagenous colitis, one of the two microscopic-colitis subtypes; maintenance in lymphocytic colitis has not been trialled in these reports. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live #778 covers budesonide induction in microscopic colitis only. For maintenance after induction, two placebo-controlled trials agree strongly. Budesonide 6 mg/day for 24 weeks held remission in 76.5% versus 12% on placebo (Bonderup 2009). Low-dose budesonide (mean 4.5 mg/day) for 12 months held remission in 61.4% versus 16.7% (Münch 2016). A pooled analysis of the randomised programme found that not receiving maintenance therapy more than doubled relapse hazard (hazard ratio 2.71) and shortened median time to relapse from 207 to 56 days. The catch is what happens on stopping: relapse is the rule within weeks to months (82.1% relapsed during treatment-free follow-up in Münch), so maintenance works while it is taken rather than curing the tendency to relapse. PROPOSED LIKELY: low-dose budesonide maintains remission in collagenous colitis for as long as it is continued.

cards.headline: Bonderup 2009: budesonide 6 mg/day held remission in 76.5% of collagenous colitis patients versus 12% on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Bonderup 2009: budesonide 6 mg/day held remission in 76.5% of collagenous colitis patients versus 12% on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.people: 42 patients with histologically confirmed collagenous colitis and diarrhoea (>3 stools/day) entered 6 weeks of open-label budesonide 9 mg/day induction; the 34 patients in clinical remission were randomised double-blind to maintenance budesonide 6 mg/day (n = 17) or placebo (n = 17) for 24 weeks, followed by 24 weeks of blinded follow-up without treatment. Remission meant 3 or fewer stools per day.
cards.result: At the end of maintenance, 76.5% (13/17) of the budesonide group were in clinical remission versus 12% (2/17) on placebo (p < 0.001). After treatment stopped, the advantage washed out: at 48 weeks remission was 23.5% versus 12% (p = 0.6), and median time to relapse after stopping active treatment was similar (39 vs 38 days). Long-term budesonide was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Only the 34 of 42 patients who responded to induction were randomised, and each arm has just 17 patients — the effect is large but the trial is small, and its follow-up phase shows maintenance suppresses rather than cures.
cards.source: Bonderup OK et al. Long-term budesonide treatment of collagenous colitis: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Gut. 2009. PMID: 18669576. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Münch 2016: low-dose budesonide (mean 4.5 mg/day) held 1-year remission in 61.4% versus 16.7% on placebo — and 82.1% relapsed after it was stopped
cards.summary: Münch 2016: low-dose budesonide (mean 4.5 mg/day) held 1-year remission in 61.4% versus 16.7% on placebo — and 82.1% relapsed after it was stopped
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled maintenance trial (Münch 2016)
cards.people: Patients with histologically confirmed active collagenous colitis received open-label budesonide induction (9 mg/day tapered to 4.5 mg/day; product named in the publication: Budenofalk); the 92 patients in clinical remission were randomised double-blind to low-dose budesonide (mean dose 4.5 mg/day) or placebo for 12 months, with 6 months of treatment-free follow-up. The primary endpoint was clinical remission throughout the double-blind phase.
cards.result: Remission was achieved during open-label induction by 84.5% (93/110; median time to remission 10.5 days). Over the 12-month double-blind phase, remission was maintained by 61.4% (27/44) on low-dose budesonide versus 16.7% (8/48) on placebo (treatment difference 44.5%, 95% CI 26.9–62.7; p < 0.001). Quality of life was preserved on budesonide. During treatment-free follow-up, 82.1% (23/28) of former budesonide patients relapsed after stopping. Suspected adverse drug reactions were few (7/44) and all non-serious.
cards.watchOut: Again a responder-enriched design (only induction responders were randomised), and the near-universal relapse after stopping means the trial supports continuing low-dose therapy, not a fixed course with a durable after-effect.
cards.source: Münch A et al. Low-dose budesonide for maintenance of clinical remission in collagenous colitis: a randomised, placebo-controlled, 12-month trial. Gut. 2016. PMID: 25425655. Registry ID: NCT01278082; EudraCT 2007-001315-31. cards.headline: Miehlke 2013 pooled analysis: across the randomised programme, skipping maintenance more than doubled relapse hazard (hazard ratio 2.71) and shortened time to relapse from 207 to 56 days
cards.summary: Miehlke 2013 pooled analysis: across the randomised programme, skipping maintenance more than doubled relapse hazard (hazard ratio 2.71) and shortened time to relapse from 207 to 56 days
cards.people: Pooled analysis of 123 patients from 4 randomised controlled studies of collagenous colitis who had achieved clinical remission after short-term budesonide (9 mg/day); 40 patients received subsequent budesonide maintenance (6 mg/day for 6 months) and 83 received no active maintenance. Relapse risk factors were assessed by Cox regression.
cards.result: The overall symptom relapse rate was 61%. Absence of budesonide maintenance therapy was independently associated with relapse (hazard ratio 2.71, 95% CI 1.37–5.38), as were baseline stool frequency above 5 per day (hazard ratio 3.95) and diarrhoea duration over 12 months (hazard ratio 1.77). Maintenance delayed relapse: median time to relapse was 207 days with maintenance versus 56 days without (p = 0.005).
cards.watchOut: This pools patients across trials with different maintenance allocations, so it corroborates the two placebo-controlled trials rather than standing as a third independent trial.
cards.source: Miehlke S et al. Risk factors for symptom relapse in collagenous colitis after withdrawal of short-term budesonide therapy. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2013. PMID: 24216688. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials and a pooled analysis agree — low-dose budesonide holds remission in collagenous colitis while taken, and relapse follows stopping
cards.summary: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials and a pooled analysis agree — low-dose budesonide holds remission in collagenous colitis while taken, and relapse follows stopping
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled maintenance trials (34 and 92 randomised patients) and one pooled analysis of 123 randomised-programme patients. Total carded participants 249 across reports, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Maintenance remission: 76.5% vs 12% at 24 weeks on 6 mg/day, and 61.4% vs 16.7% at 12 months on a mean 4.5 mg/day — absolute gains of roughly 45–65 percentage points over placebo. Not maintaining therapy carried a relapse hazard ratio of 2.71, and after stopping, most patients relapsed (82.1% in treatment-free follow-up). PROPOSED LIKELY: low-dose budesonide maintains remission after induction in collagenous colitis; the evidence does not cover lymphocytic colitis maintenance or indefinite-duration safety.
cards.watchOut: The shelf question says microscopic colitis, but the maintenance trials enrolled collagenous colitis only — extrapolating the stamp to lymphocytic colitis is an assumption the face of this shelf flags, not a finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bonderup OK et al. Gut. 2009 (PMID: 18669576); Münch A et al. Gut. 2016 (PMID: 25425655); Miehlke S et al. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2013 (PMID: 24216688).

shelves.title: Methylnaltrexone in chronic non-cancer pain (PARTIAL completion of live #1797): prompt laxation by injection or tablet in two phase 3 programmes
shelves.question: In adults with opioid-induced constipation, does methylnaltrexone improve bowel function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid · Chi-Square Distribution · Constipation · Defecation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone · Narcotic Antagonists · Pain · Quaternary Ammonium Compounds · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live #1797 covers subcutaneous methylnaltrexone in advanced illness. The uncovered slice is chronic non-cancer pain, and it has its own two phase 3 placebo-controlled programmes. Subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 12 mg (daily or alternate-day) produced a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose in 34.2% of patients versus 9.9% on placebo (number needed to treat about 4; Michna 2011, 460 patients). Oral methylnaltrexone (300–450 mg daily) beat placebo on the same kind of endpoint, with responders at 49.3–51.5% versus 38.3% (Rauck 2017, 803 patients). A crossover analysis of the subcutaneous programme confirmed the effect within the same patients (9.7% responding on placebo versus 45.9% after crossing to methylnaltrexone). Pain scores and opioid doses did not worsen and withdrawal was not seen in these programmes — the drug acts peripherally — while abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhoea were the common adverse effects. PROPOSED LIKELY: methylnaltrexone improves bowel function versus placebo in opioid-induced constipation in chronic non-cancer pain, by either route.

cards.headline: Michna 2011: subcutaneous methylnaltrexone produced a bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose in 34.2% versus 9.9% on placebo (number needed to treat ≈ 4)
cards.summary: Michna 2011: subcutaneous methylnaltrexone produced a bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose in 34.2% versus 9.9% on placebo (number needed to treat ≈ 4)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Michna 2011, subcutaneous methylnaltrexone in non-cancer pain)
cards.people: 460 patients with opioid-induced constipation receiving opioids for chronic, nonmalignant pain, in a 4-week double-blind randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 study of subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 12 mg once daily or every other day (alternating with placebo injections) versus placebo.
cards.result: Within 4 hours of the first dose, 34.2% of patients in both methylnaltrexone groups had a rescue-free bowel movement versus 9.9% on placebo (p < 0.001); the estimated number needed to treat was about 4. Across all doses, about 29–30% of methylnaltrexone injections produced a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours versus about 9.4% of placebo injections (p < 0.001). Time to first bowel movement was shorter and weekly bowel movements increased more with methylnaltrexone (p < 0.05), with better stool form and less straining; constipation-specific quality of life improved significantly by week 4. Adverse events included abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea and hyperhidrosis.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week trial with a laxation endpoint — it shows the drug moves the bowel promptly in about a third of patients per dose, not that it normalises bowel habit long-term; patients were on stable opioids of at least 50 mg morphine equivalents in the companion oral programme's terms.
cards.source: Michna E et al. Subcutaneous methylnaltrexone for treatment of opioid-induced constipation in patients with chronic, nonmalignant pain: a randomized controlled study. The journal of pain. 2011. PMID: 21429809. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rauck 2017: oral methylnaltrexone 300–450 mg beat placebo — responders 49.3–51.5% versus 38.3% over 4 weeks
cards.summary: Rauck 2017: oral methylnaltrexone 300–450 mg beat placebo — responders 49.3–51.5% versus 38.3% over 4 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Rauck 2017, oral methylnaltrexone in non-cancer pain)
cards.people: 803 adults with chronic noncancer pain on at least 50 mg/day oral morphine equivalents with opioid-induced constipation, randomised double-blind in a phase 3 trial to oral methylnaltrexone 150, 300 or 450 mg or placebo once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 8 weeks of as-needed dosing. Responders had at least 3 rescue-free bowel movements per week with an increase of at least 1 per week over baseline for at least 3 of the 4 daily-dosing weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — mean percentage of dosing days producing a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours — was 24.6% on 300 mg (p = 0.002) and 27.4% on 450 mg (p < 0.0001) versus 18.2% on placebo. Responders were 49.3% (300 mg; p = 0.03) and 51.5% (450 mg; p = 0.005) versus 38.3% on placebo, and weekly rescue-free bowel movements rose by an extra 0.5 per week over placebo at both higher doses. The 150 mg dose did not separate as clearly. All doses were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The placebo responder rate (38.3%) is high, as is typical in constipation trials, so the drug's added value is the roughly 11–13 percentage-point responder gain and the faster within-4-hours laxation — not the headline percentages alone.
cards.source: Rauck R et al. Randomized, Double-Blind Trial of Oral Methylnaltrexone for the Treatment of Opioid-Induced Constipation in Patients with Chronic Noncancer Pain. Pain practice : the official journal of World Institute of Pain. 2017. PMID: 27860208. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Viscusi 2016: patients who had taken placebo crossed over to methylnaltrexone and their within-4-hour response jumped from 9.7% to 45.9%
cards.summary: Viscusi 2016: patients who had taken placebo crossed over to methylnaltrexone and their within-4-hour response jumped from 9.7% to 45.9%
cards.type: Placebo-crossover analysis of a phase 3 trial programme (Viscusi 2016) — supportive, open-label phase
cards.people: Placebo-crossover analysis of the subcutaneous methylnaltrexone phase 3 programme in chronic non-cancer pain: 134 patients who had received placebo for 4 weeks (median morphine equivalent dose 150 mg/day; mean 1.1 rescue-free bowel movements per week) then received open-label methylnaltrexone 12 mg as needed for 8 weeks, allowing a within-patient comparison.
cards.result: On placebo, 9.7% of patients had a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose and 9.0% of all placebo injections did so; after crossover to methylnaltrexone, the figures were 45.9% and 34.5%. The proportion achieving at least 3 rescue-free bowel movements per week with an increase of at least 1 rose from 35–40% during placebo weeks to over 70% at week 5 of methylnaltrexone and stayed there. Abdominal pain (9.7% vs 1.5% on placebo) and nausea (5.2% vs 6.7%) were the commonest adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The crossover phase was open-label, so expectation can inflate the contrast; its value is showing the same patients who did not respond on placebo responding on the drug, not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Viscusi ER et al. Efficacy and Safety of Methylnaltrexone for Opioid-Induced Constipation in Patients With Chronic Noncancer Pain: A Placebo Crossover Analysis. Regional anesthesia and pain medicine. 2016. PMID: 26650429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 programmes, two routes, one answer — methylnaltrexone produces prompt laxation in chronic non-cancer pain, in about a third of patients per dose
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 programmes, two routes, one answer — methylnaltrexone produces prompt laxation in chronic non-cancer pain, in about a third of patients per dose
cards.people: The carded evidence: the subcutaneous phase 3 trial (460 patients), the oral phase 3 trial (803 patients), and the crossover analysis of the subcutaneous programme (134 crossover patients). Total carded participants exceed 1,300, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Within-4-hour rescue-free bowel movements: 34.2% vs 9.9% (subcutaneous, first dose), 45.9% after crossover vs 9.7% on placebo within-patient, and responder rates of 49.3–51.5% vs 38.3% for oral dosing over 4 weeks. Effects were consistent across routes, with gastrointestinal adverse events the main cost and no signal of lost analgesia or withdrawal in these programmes. PROPOSED LIKELY: methylnaltrexone improves bowel function versus placebo in opioid-induced constipation in chronic non-cancer pain.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is the non-cancer-pain population only; the advanced-illness evidence (including the original Thomas trial) is homed on live #1797 and is not re-carded here, and neither shelf compares methylnaltrexone against the other peripherally acting opioid antagonists.
cards.source: Synthesis of Michna E et al. The journal of pain. 2011 (PMID: 21429809); Rauck R et al. Pain practice : the official journal of World Institute of Pain. 2017 (PMID: 27860208); Viscusi ER et al. Regional anesthesia and pain medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26650429).

shelves.title: Acute cholangitis: ERCP within 24 hours is associated with lower in-hospital mortality in observational timing studies — the only randomised trial tested drainage against surgery, not timing
shelves.question: In adults with acute cholangitis, does early ERCP drainage within 24 hours improve survival compared with delayed drainage?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bile · Cholangitis · Drainage · Emergencies · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Female · Gallstones · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Sphincterotomy, Endoscopic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence for the timing comparison) — every timing study behind the Tokyo Guidelines' early-drainage recommendation is observational. Pooled across 14 observational studies (84,063 patients), ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than later drainage (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90 — a relative measure; overall pooled in-hospital mortality was 1.9%), and a second meta-analysis of 7 non-randomised studies (88,562 patients) found the same direction for in-hospital mortality but no difference in 30-day mortality. The only randomised trial in the field (Lai 1992) did not test timing at all: it tested emergency endoscopic drainage against emergency surgery in severe cholangitis and found hospital mortality of 10% versus 32%. A large US inpatient cohort found mortality highest when ERCP was never performed or was delayed beyond 48 hours, with no mortality difference between ERCP within 24 hours and at 24–48 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): drainage within 24 hours is associated with lower in-hospital mortality, but the survival claim rests on observational timing data plus a randomised trial of drainage versus surgery — not on a randomised timing trial, which does not exist.

cards.headline: Lai 1992: in severe acute cholangitis, emergency endoscopic biliary drainage cut hospital mortality versus emergency surgery — 10% versus 32% — but the trial compared drainage with surgery, not early with delayed drainage
cards.summary: Lai 1992: in severe acute cholangitis, emergency endoscopic biliary drainage cut hospital mortality versus emergency surgery — 10% versus 32% — but the trial compared drainage with surgery, not early with delayed drainage
cards.people: 82 patients with severe acute cholangitis due to choledocholithiasis, randomly assigned to surgical decompression of the biliary tract (n = 41) or endoscopic biliary drainage (n = 41), each followed by definitive treatment.
cards.result: Hospital mortality was 10% (4 deaths) with endoscopic drainage versus 32% (13 deaths) with surgery (P < 0.03). Complications of decompression and definitive treatment developed in 14 patients treated endoscopically and 27 treated surgically (34% versus 66%). Time to normalisation of temperature and stabilisation of blood pressure was similar, but more surgical patients required ventilatory support. Concomitant medical problems, low platelet count, high serum urea nitrogen and low serum albumin before decompression were the other independent determinants of mortality.
cards.watchOut: This is the randomised anchor for urgent drainage itself, not for the 24-hour timing question: both arms were treated as emergencies, so the trial cannot say whether drainage at 24 hours beats drainage at 48 hours.
cards.source: Lai EC et al. Endoscopic biliary drainage for severe acute cholangitis. The New England journal of medicine. 1992. PMID: 1584258. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Du 2020: pooling 14 observational studies (84,063 patients), ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.81) — and the authors state a randomised timing trial is still needed
cards.summary: Du 2020: pooling 14 observational studies (84,063 patients), ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.81) — and the authors state a randomised timing trial is still needed
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Du 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies evaluating ERCP timing (<24, <48 and <72 hours from hospitalisation) in acute cholangitis; 14 studies including 84,063 patients (mean age 66 years) met the criteria.
cards.result: Overall pooled in-hospital mortality was 1.9% (95% CI 1.8%–7.6%), rising to 4.3% when administrative-database studies were excluded. In 9 studies, ERCP performed <24 hours versus ≥24 hours was associated with decreased in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90 — a relative measure); the corresponding odds ratios were 0.57 (95% CI 0.51–0.63) for <48 hours and 0.32 (95% CI 0.15–0.68) for <72 hours, all with I² = 0%. Hospital stay was shorter with earlier ERCP (mean difference 3.2 days for <24 hours, 95% CI 2.3–4.1). The authors conclude that a randomised trial of urgent ERCP is needed.
cards.watchOut: All included studies are observational: patients drained later may have been sicker, stabilised first, or drained late because they were deteriorating — confounding by indication can manufacture exactly this gradient, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational.
cards.source: Du L et al. Timing of Performing Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography and Inpatient Mortality in Acute Cholangitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clinical and translational gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 32352721. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lyu 2022: a second meta-analysis (7 non-randomised studies, 88,562 patients) found ERCP within 24 hours associated with lower in-hospital mortality and shorter stay, but no difference in 30-day mortality
cards.summary: Lyu 2022: a second meta-analysis (7 non-randomised studies, 88,562 patients) found ERCP within 24 hours associated with lower in-hospital mortality and shorter stay, but no difference in 30-day mortality
cards.people: Meta-analysis and systematic review of studies of ERCP timing in acute cholangitis; 7 non-randomised studies of 88,562 patients were included, comparing ERCP within 24 or 48 hours of admission with later ERCP.
cards.result: Compared with ERCP more than 24 hours after admission, ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (P < 0.0004) but no difference in 30-day mortality (P = 0.38). ERCP within 48 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (P < 0.00001) and lower 30-day mortality (P = 0.03) than ERCP after 48 hours, and ERCP within either window was associated with a shorter hospital stay (P < 0.00001 for both). The abstract reports P values without pooled effect sizes for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses draw on overlapping observational cohorts, so they are not independent confirmations; and the 24-hour advantage seen for in-hospital mortality disappears for 30-day mortality in this analysis.
cards.source: Lyu Y et al. Impact of the Timing of Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography for the Treatment of Acute Cholangitis: A Meta-analysis and Systematic Review. Surgical laparoscopy, endoscopy & percutaneous techniques. 2022. PMID: 36223305. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Parikh 2018: in 107,253 US inpatients with cholangitis from gallstones, mortality was highest with no ERCP or ERCP delayed beyond 48 hours — with no mortality difference between ERCP within 24 hours and at 24–48 hours
cards.summary: Parikh 2018: in 107,253 US inpatients with cholangitis from gallstones, mortality was highest with no ERCP or ERCP delayed beyond 48 hours — with no mortality difference between ERCP within 24 hours and at 24–48 hours
cards.people: Retrospective population-based study of the US National Inpatient Sample (1998–2012): 107,253 patients with a combined diagnosis of cholangitis and choledocholithiasis, of whom 77,323 underwent ERCP, grouped by ERCP timing — within 24 hours (urgent), 24–48 hours (early), after 48 hours (delayed), or none.
cards.result: The urgent group had the shortest length of stay and the delayed group significantly longer stays and the highest costs (P < 0.001). In-hospital mortality was highest in the no-ERCP group, followed by the delayed group (P < 0.001); there was no difference in mortality between urgent ERCP (within 24 hours) and early ERCP (24–48 hours). The authors conclude ERCP should not be delayed beyond 48 hours in acute cholangitis due to choledocholithiasis.
cards.watchOut: Administrative data cannot capture severity at presentation or why ERCP was delayed; the 'no ERCP' group's high mortality likely includes patients too ill or too well to scope, so this cohort supports 'do not delay beyond 48 hours' more firmly than 'within 24 hours saves lives'.
cards.source: Parikh MP et al. Outcomes Associated With Timing of ERCP in Acute Cholangitis Secondary to Choledocholithiasis. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29356786. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: earlier drainage is consistently associated with lower in-hospital mortality, but the timing evidence is entirely observational — the randomised trial answers a different question
cards.summary: Synthesis: earlier drainage is consistently associated with lower in-hospital mortality, but the timing evidence is entirely observational — the randomised trial answers a different question
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of endoscopic drainage versus surgery (Lai 1992, 82 patients), two meta-analyses of observational timing studies (Du 2020, 14 studies and 84,063 patients; Lyu 2022, 7 studies and 88,562 patients), and one national inpatient cohort (Parikh 2018, 107,253 patients).
cards.result: ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than later drainage in both meta-analyses (Du odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90, a relative measure), with no 30-day mortality difference in Lyu 2022, and the national cohort found the mortality penalty concentrated in the no-ERCP and beyond-48-hours groups rather than between the under-24 and 24–48 hour groups. Lai 1992 establishes that emergency endoscopic drainage itself beats emergency surgery (10% versus 32% hospital mortality). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence for timing): drain early — within 24 hours where feasible — but the survival advantage of the 24-hour line over 24–48 hours is an observational association, not a trialled fact.
cards.watchOut: Guideline language ('urgent drainage within 24 hours') is stronger than the underlying design mix; this shelf prints the association and its observational basis on the face so the recommendation is not mistaken for randomised evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lai EC et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1992 (PMID: 1584258); Du L et al. Clinical and translational gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 32352721); Lyu Y et al. Surgical laparoscopy, endoscopy & percutaneous techniques. 2022 (PMID: 36223305); Parikh MP et al. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2018 (PMID: 29356786).

shelves.title: Urgent colonoscopy for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding: finds the source sooner in one trial, improves no clinical outcome in any — elective timing is as good (LIKELY, the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In adults with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, does urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours improve outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Transfusion · Colonic Diseases · Colonoscopy · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Japan · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Time-to-Treatment · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree. Urgent colonoscopy found a definite bleeding source more often in Green 2005 (odds ratio 2.6 for the difference — a relative measure), but in no trial did it reduce further bleeding, transfusion, length of stay, surgery or death: Laine & Shah 2010 found further bleeding in 22% on urgent versus 14% on elective colonoscopy; Niikura 2020, the largest trial, found stigmata of recent haemorrhage in 21.5% versus 21.3% and 30-day rebleeding in 15.3% versus 6.7% (not significant); the meta-analysis of the 4 randomised trials (463 patients) found no significant difference in stay, transfusion, additional intervention or mortality. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in hospitalised acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, colonoscopy within 24 hours does not improve clinical outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy — timing can be set by stability, bowel preparation and local logistics rather than by the clock.

cards.headline: Green 2005: urgent colonoscopy found a definite bleeding source more often (odds ratio 2.6), but mortality, rebleeding, transfusion, stay and surgery were all the same as standard care (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Green 2005: urgent colonoscopy found a definite bleeding source more often (odds ratio 2.6), but mortality, rebleeding, transfusion, stay and surgery were all the same as standard care (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 100 consecutive patients presenting with lower gastrointestinal bleeding without an upper or anorectal source, randomised to urgent purge preparation followed immediately by colonoscopy (n = 50) or a standard-care algorithm based on angiographic intervention and expectant colonoscopy (n = 50).
cards.result: A definite bleeding source was found more often with urgent colonoscopy (diverticula 13, angioectasia 4, colitis 4) than with standard care (diverticula 8, colitis 3) — odds ratio 2.6 (95% CI 1.1–6.2), a relative measure. Endoscopic therapy was given to 17 urgent-group patients and angiographic haemostasis to 10 standard-care patients. Outcomes did not differ: mortality 2% versus 4%, hospital stay 5.8 versus 6.6 days, ICU stay 1.8 versus 2.4 days, transfusion 4.2 versus 5 units, early rebleeding 22% versus 30%, surgery 14% versus 12%, and late rebleeding 16% versus 14% over a mean follow-up of about 5 years — the treatment made no difference to any clinical outcome.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was a standard-care algorithm built around angiography and expectant colonoscopy, not a pure elective-colonoscopy arm, and a single centre's urgent-colonoscopy expertise may not transfer; the yield advantage also did not convert into therapy that changed outcomes.
cards.source: Green BT et al. Urgent colonoscopy for evaluation and management of acute lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage: a randomized controlled trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2005. PMID: 16279891. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laine & Shah 2010: urgent colonoscopy (within 12 hours) did not reduce further bleeding versus elective colonoscopy (36–60 hours) — 22% versus 14% — in patients hospitalised with serious haematochezia
cards.summary: Laine & Shah 2010: urgent colonoscopy (within 12 hours) did not reduce further bleeding versus elective colonoscopy (36–60 hours) — 22% versus 14% — in patients hospitalised with serious haematochezia
cards.people: Patients with haematochezia plus at least one severity marker (heart rate >100, systolic blood pressure <100, orthostatic change >20, haemoglobin drop ≥1.5 g/dL, or transfusion) had upper endoscopy within 6 hours; 85 were eligible, 13 (15%) had an upper gastrointestinal source, and the remaining 72 were randomised to urgent colonoscopy (n = 36, within 12 hours) or elective colonoscopy (n = 36, at 36–60 hours).
cards.result: Further bleeding occurred in 8 of 36 (22%) urgent versus 5 of 36 (14%) elective patients (difference 8%, 95% CI −9 to 26%). Units of blood transfused (1.5 versus 0.7), hospital days (5.2 versus 4.8), subsequent diagnostic or therapeutic interventions for bleeding (36% versus 33%) and hospital charges ($27,590 versus $26,633) were also not lower in the urgent group — the treatment made no difference. The authors note 15% of serious haematochezia had an upper source, supporting upper endoscopy first.
cards.watchOut: The trial was terminated before reaching its prespecified sample size, so it cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm; its confidence interval for further bleeding (−9 to +26 percentage points) is wide.
cards.source: Laine L et al. Randomized trial of urgent vs. elective colonoscopy in patients hospitalized with lower GI bleeding. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 20648004. cards.headline: Niikura 2020: in the largest trial (170 patients, 15 hospitals), colonoscopy within 24 hours identified stigmata of recent haemorrhage no more often than elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours (21.5% versus 21.3%) and did not reduce 30-day rebleeding
cards.summary: Niikura 2020: in the largest trial (170 patients, 15 hospitals), colonoscopy within 24 hours identified stigmata of recent haemorrhage no more often than elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours (21.5% versus 21.3%) and did not reduce 30-day rebleeding
cards.people: 170 patients with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding at 15 hospitals in Japan, randomly assigned to early colonoscopy within 24 hours of the initial visit (n = 79 analysed) or elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours after admission (n = 80 analysed); primary outcome was identification of stigmata of recent haemorrhage (SRH).
cards.result: SRH were identified in 21.5% (17/79) of the early group versus 21.3% (17/80) of the elective group (difference 0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −12.5 to 13.0; P = 0.967). Rebleeding within 30 days occurred in 15.3% of the early group and 6.7% of the elective group (difference 8.6, 95% CI −1.4 to 18.7) — not significant, and numerically favouring elective timing. There were no significant differences in successful endoscopic treatment, transfusion, length of stay, thrombotic events or death within 30 days; haemorrhagic shock during bowel preparation occurred in 2 elective-group patients (2.5%) and none in the early group.
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial in Japanese hospitals where diverticular bleeding predominates; the point estimate for rebleeding favoured the elective arm, so 'no benefit' is the supported reading — not proof that early colonoscopy is harmful.
cards.source: Niikura R et al. Efficacy and Safety of Early vs Elective Colonoscopy for Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding. Gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 31563627. cards.search: niikura 2020: in the largest trial (170 patients, 15 hospitals), colonoscopy within 24 hours identified stigmata of recent haemorrhage no more often than elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours (21.5% versus 21.3%) and did not reduce 30-day rebleeding niikura 2020: in the largest trial (170 patients, 15 hospitals), colonoscopy within 24 hours identified stigmata of recent haemorrhage no more often than elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours (21.5% versus 21.3%) and did not reduce 30-day rebleeding in adults with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, does urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours improve outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy? randomised controlled trial (niikura 2020) 170 patients with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding at 15 hospitals in japan, randomly assigned to early colonoscopy within 24 hours of the initial visit (n = 79 analysed) or elective colonoscopy at 24–96 hours after admission (n = 80 analysed); primary outcome was identification of stigmata of recent haemorrhage (srh). srh were identified in 21.5% (17/79) of the early group versus 21.3% (17/80) of the elective group (difference 0.3 percentage points, 95% ci −12.5 to 13.0; p = 0.967). rebleeding within 30 days occurred in 15.3% of the early group and 6.7% of the elective group (difference 8.6, 95% ci −1.4 to 18.7) — not significant, and numerically favouring elective timing. there were no significant differences in successful endoscopic treatment, transfusion, length of stay, thrombotic events or death within 30 days; haemorrhagic shock during bowel preparation occurred in 2 elective-group patients (2.5%) and none in the early group. an open-label trial in japanese hospitals where diverticular bleeding predominates; the point estimate for rebleeding favoured the elective arm, so 'no benefit' is the supported reading — not proof that early colonoscopy is harmful. niikura r et al. efficacy and safety of early vs elective colonoscopy for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding. gastroenterology. 2020. pmid: 31563627. registry id: nct03098173 (also umin000021129). mesh: acute disease · aged · aged, 80 and over · blood transfusion · colonic diseases · colonoscopy · elective surgical procedures · female · gastrointestinal hemorrhage · hospital mortality · humans · japan · length of stay · male · middle aged · recurrence · time-to-treatment · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Anvari 2020: meta-analysis of the 4 randomised trials (463 patients) found urgent colonoscopy did not differ from standard timing on stay, transfusion, intervention, mortality or rebleeding
cards.summary: Anvari 2020: meta-analysis of the 4 randomised trials (463 patients) found urgent colonoscopy did not differ from standard timing on stay, transfusion, intervention, mortality or rebleeding
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Anvari 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing urgent (<24 hours) with standard (>24 hours) colonoscopy in acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding (haematochezia); 4 randomised trials involving 463 patients met the criteria, with a separate analysis adding 9 non-randomised studies (n = 111,950).
cards.result: In the randomised trials, urgent colonoscopy did not differ significantly from standard timing in length of stay, units of blood transfused, rate of additional intervention required, or mortality, and colonoscopy-related outcomes — complications, rebleeding rates and diagnosis of a bleeding source — also did not differ. The analysis that added non-randomised studies showed higher mortality and surgery rates in the standard-timing group and shorter stay with urgent colonoscopy, the pattern expected when sicker patients are scoped later. GRADE certainty was low for the majority of outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The randomised and observational pools point in different directions — the observational signal is the one vulnerable to confounding by indication, so this shelf rests on the randomised pool; total randomised numbers remain small (463), which is why outcomes are stated as 'no demonstrated difference' rather than proof of exact equivalence.
cards.source: Anvari S et al. Urgent Versus Standard Colonoscopy for Management of Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 32091447. Registry ID: none in the record.
