cards.headline: Synthesis: across three randomised trials and their meta-analysis, scoping within 24 hours finds the source sooner but does not change what happens to the patient
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three randomised trials and their meta-analysis, scoping within 24 hours finds the source sooner but does not change what happens to the patient
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials (Green 2005, 100 patients; Laine & Shah 2010, 72 randomised patients; Niikura 2020, 170 patients) and one meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Anvari 2020, 4 trials, 463 patients).
cards.result: No trial found a significant advantage for urgent colonoscopy in further bleeding or rebleeding (22% versus 14% in Laine & Shah; 15.3% versus 6.7% at 30 days in Niikura), transfusion, length of stay, surgery or mortality; Green 2005 found a higher definite-source yield (odds ratio 2.6, a relative measure) that did not translate into better outcomes, and Niikura found no yield advantage at all (21.5% versus 21.3%). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours does not improve outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy in hospitalised acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.watchOut: These trials enrolled hospitalised patients stable enough to randomise; they do not address the unstable patient with ongoing massive bleeding, where urgent intervention follows resuscitation logic rather than this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Green BT et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2005 (PMID: 16279891); Laine L et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010 (PMID: 20648004); Niikura R et al. Gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 31563627); Anvari S et al. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2020 (PMID: 32091447).

shelves.title: Capsule endoscopy after negative bidirectional endoscopy in iron deficiency anaemia: finds a lesion in about half and a likely source in ~40% — a yield question, not an outcomes question
shelves.question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia and negative bidirectional endoscopy, does small bowel capsule endoscopy find a bleeding source?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Capsule Endoscopy · Humans · Intestinal Diseases · Intestine, Small
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence — this is a diagnostic-yield question, not a patient-outcome question) — capsule endoscopy finds something in about half of these patients. The 2012 systematic review (24 studies, 1,960 patients) pooled a diagnostic yield of 47% (95% CI 42%–52%), rising to 66.6% in studies enrolling only iron-deficiency-anaemia patients; the 2024 meta-analysis (12 studies, 1,703 patients without overt bleeding) found any small-bowel lesion in 61% but a lesion likely responsible for the anaemia in only 40%. In the one cohort matching this shelf's exact population — asymptomatic iron deficiency anaemia after negative bidirectional endoscopy (Kay 2025, 75 patients) — the yield was lower: 36% abnormal, only 8% actionable, angiodysplasia the commonest finding and no malignancies. Yield is not benefit: none of these studies shows that finding a source improves haemoglobin, transfusion or survival, and this shelf's stamp answers only the question asked — whether a source is found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational, yield only): expect a lesion in roughly half, a plausibly responsible lesion in about 40%, and an actionable finding in under 1 in 10 of the asymptomatic exact-population patients.

cards.headline: Koulaouzidis 2012: pooling 24 studies (1,960 patients), small-bowel capsule endoscopy had a diagnostic yield of 47% in iron-deficiency anaemia — 66.6% in studies enrolling only anaemia patients
cards.summary: Koulaouzidis 2012: pooling 24 studies (1,960 patients), small-bowel capsule endoscopy had a diagnostic yield of 47% in iron-deficiency anaemia — 66.6% in studies enrolling only anaemia patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic-yield studies (Koulaouzidis 2012)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies estimating the diagnostic yield of small-bowel capsule endoscopy in iron-deficiency anaemia; 24 studies enrolling 1,960 patients who underwent capsule endoscopy were included, with per-patient diagnostic yield as the outcome.
cards.result: The pooled diagnostic yield was 47% (95% CI 42%–52%), with significant heterogeneity (I² = 78.8%). In the 4 studies focused solely on iron-deficiency-anaemia patients the pooled yield was 66.6% (95% CI 61.0%–72.3%), versus 44% (95% CI 39%–48%) in the 20 studies not restricted to anaemia alone; vascular, inflammatory and mass/tumour lesions were all detected significantly more often in the anaemia-only studies (vascular 31% versus 22.6%; inflammatory 17.8% versus 11.3%; mass/tumour 7.95% versus 2.25%).
cards.watchOut: Yield here counts any positive finding judged relevant by the original studies, whose definitions varied; the included studies were largely retrospective with selection bias, and a 'yield' says nothing about whether acting on the finding helped the patient.
cards.source: Koulaouzidis A et al. Diagnostic yield of small-bowel capsule endoscopy in patients with iron-deficiency anemia: a systematic review. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2012. PMID: 23078923. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Capsule Endoscopy · Humans · Intestinal Diseases · Intestine, Small

cards.headline: Rossi 2024: in iron-deficiency anaemia without overt bleeding, capsule endoscopy found any small-bowel lesion in 61% — but a lesion likely responsible for the anaemia in only 40%
cards.summary: Rossi 2024: in iron-deficiency anaemia without overt bleeding, capsule endoscopy found any small-bowel lesion in 61% — but a lesion likely responsible for the anaemia in only 40%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic-yield studies (Rossi 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of videocapsule endoscopy in iron-deficiency anaemia without overt bleeding; 12 studies with 1,703 patients (47% male, age range 19–92 years) published to March 2023.
cards.result: The diagnostic yield for any small-bowel lesion was 61% (95% CI 44–77), and the yield for lesions likely responsible for the iron deficiency was 40% (95% CI 27–53). Heterogeneity was very high (I² = 97.7% for the overall-lesion analysis), so the pooled percentages are averages across widely differing study yields rather than a precise single figure.
cards.watchOut: The gap between 61% (any lesion) and 40% (likely responsible) is the honest core of this shelf: incidental small-bowel findings are common, and this analysis — like the others — measures detection, not downstream outcomes.
cards.source: Rossi RE et al. Diagnostic Yield of Small Bowel Videocapsule Endoscopy in Patients with Iron Deficiency Anemia. A Systematic Review and meta-analysis. Journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 38227849. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kay 2025: in the exact population — asymptomatic iron deficiency anaemia after negative bidirectional endoscopy — capsule endoscopy was abnormal in 36% and actionable in only 8%, with no malignancies found
cards.summary: Kay 2025: in the exact population — asymptomatic iron deficiency anaemia after negative bidirectional endoscopy — capsule endoscopy was abnormal in 36% and actionable in only 8%, with no malignancies found
cards.people: Retrospective review at a large US military gastroenterology programme of patients who underwent videocapsule endoscopy from January 2019 to April 2023 after negative bidirectional endoscopy for iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin <45 ng/mL); of 238 patients reviewed, 75 met the inclusion criteria for uncomplicated asymptomatic anaemia.
cards.result: Capsule endoscopy revealed abnormal findings in 36% of cases, with 8% having actionable findings necessitating repeat endoscopy; the most common abnormality was small-bowel angiodysplasia, and no small-bowel malignancies were detected. Patients over 65 had higher rates of abnormal and actionable findings. Referral delays beyond 180 days did not significantly affect outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre retrospective cohort of 75 selected patients in a military programme — younger and healthier than many anaemia populations — so its lower yield may reflect case mix as much as the test; it is carded because it is the only report matching the question's exact population.
cards.source: Kay C et al. The Diagnostic Yield of Video Capsule Endoscopy for Uncomplicated Asymptomatic Iron Deficiency Anemia With Negative Bidirectional Endoscopy in a Large Military Gastroenterology Program. Cureus. 2025. PMID: 40296971. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: capsule endoscopy finds a lesion in about half of these patients and a plausibly responsible one in about 40% — a detection answer, with outcome benefit untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: capsule endoscopy finds a lesion in about half of these patients and a plausibly responsible one in about 40% — a detection answer, with outcome benefit untested
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews of yield studies (Koulaouzidis 2012, 24 studies and 1,960 patients; Rossi 2024, 12 studies and 1,703 patients) and one exact-population retrospective cohort (Kay 2025, 75 patients). All of it is observational by design — a test-strategy question has no randomised comparison here.
cards.result: Pooled yields were 47% (Koulaouzidis) and 61% for any lesion / 40% for a likely-responsible lesion (Rossi); the exact-population cohort found 36% abnormal and 8% actionable findings, chiefly angiodysplasia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence, diagnostic yield only): yes — capsule endoscopy commonly finds a small-bowel source after negative bidirectional endoscopy, most often a vascular lesion; whether finding it improves patient outcomes is a separate question this evidence does not answer.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 61% figure without its pair: only ~40% of patients had a lesion likely responsible for the anaemia, and under 1 in 10 had an actionable finding in the exact-population cohort — the yield headline overstates clinical payoff if read alone.

shelves.title: Healed erosive oesophagitis: daily maintenance PPI beats on-demand therapy for staying in remission (81% versus 58%) — the erosive slice left open by pack #5661
shelves.question: In adults with erosive esophagitis, does maintenance proton pump inhibitor therapy prevent relapse better than on-demand therapy after healing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Esomeprazole · Esophagitis · Esophagoscopy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Remission Induction · Secondary Prevention · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5661, which answers on-demand versus daily proton pump inhibitor therapy in non-erosive reflux disease; this shelf covers the slice #5661 leaves open — patients whose erosive oesophagitis has healed. POSSIBLE — the one large head-to-head trial in exactly this population (Sjöstedt 2005, 477 patients randomised after healing) found 6-month remission in 81% on daily esomeprazole 20 mg versus 58% on on-demand treatment (P < 0.0001), with the gap wider in more severe baseline grades; overall symptomatic remission did not differ, though heartburn was more prevalent on demand. The systematic review of on-demand maintenance (Pace 2007, 17 studies, of which 2 enrolled erosive oesophagitis only) reached the matching conclusion: on-demand therapy is effective in non-erosive, mild and uninvestigated disease but not in (severe) erosive oesophagitis. In milder mixed disease (Bour 2005: non-erosive or grade 1–2 oesophagitis with frequent relapses), symptom relief at 6 months was 86.4% on continuous versus 74.6% on on-demand rabeprazole — not significant — at about a third of the drug use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: after healing of erosive oesophagitis, daily maintenance prevents endoscopic relapse better than on-demand therapy; the advantage is endoscopic first, symptomatic second, and smallest in mild grades.

cards.headline: Sjöstedt 2005: after healing of erosive oesophagitis, daily esomeprazole kept 81% in remission at 6 months versus 58% on on-demand treatment (P < 0.0001)
cards.summary: Sjöstedt 2005: after healing of erosive oesophagitis, daily esomeprazole kept 81% in remission at 6 months versus 58% on on-demand treatment (P < 0.0001)
cards.people: Patients with verified erosive reflux oesophagitis (Los Angeles grades A–D) were healed with esomeprazole 40 mg daily for 4–8 weeks; 494 of 539 enrolled patients (91%) healed, and 477 who were endoscopically healed with symptom control were randomised to 6 months of esomeprazole 20 mg either once daily (n = 243) or on demand (n = 234).
cards.result: After 6 months, 81% of the once-daily group remained in remission (endoscopic and symptomatic) compared with 58% of the on-demand group (P < 0.0001) — absolute rates printed alongside, so no relative-only claim is needed. The remission difference was present irrespective of baseline Los Angeles grade but was more pronounced for the more severe grades. There was no difference in overall symptomatic remission, although heartburn was significantly more prevalent in the on-demand group.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one drug, one dose (esomeprazole 20 mg): it anchors the endoscopic-relapse claim for healed erosive disease, but it does not test on-demand strategies with other proton pump inhibitors or in patients whose priority is symptom control alone — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.
cards.source: Sjöstedt S et al. Daily treatment with esomeprazole is superior to that taken on-demand for maintenance of healed erosive oesophagitis. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2005. PMID: 16091055. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pace 2007: across 17 on-demand maintenance studies, on-demand proton pump inhibitor therapy worked in non-erosive and mild disease but not in (severe) erosive oesophagitis
cards.summary: Pace 2007: across 17 on-demand maintenance studies, on-demand proton pump inhibitor therapy worked in non-erosive and mild disease but not in (severe) erosive oesophagitis
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials comparing on-demand proton pump inhibitor therapy with placebo, or on-demand with continuous therapy, for maintenance treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease; 17 studies met the criteria — 5 in non-erosive reflux disease only, 4 in non-erosive plus mild oesophagitis, 2 in erosive oesophagitis only, 2 in uninvestigated reflux symptoms, and 4 primarily pharmacoeconomic or quality-of-life studies.
cards.result: The review concludes that on-demand therapy with currently available proton pump inhibitors appears effective for long-term management of patients with non-erosive reflux disease or mild and uninvestigated forms of reflux disease, but not in patients with (severe) erosive oesophagitis — the population this shelf asks about. The abstract reports the review's conclusions without pooled effect sizes for the erosive subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Only 2 of the 17 studies enrolled erosive oesophagitis exclusively, and the review is qualitative for this subgroup — it corroborates Sjöstedt 2005's direction rather than independently quantifying the relapse difference.
cards.source: Pace F et al. Systematic review: maintenance treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with proton pump inhibitors taken 'on-demand'. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2007. cards.headline: Bour 2005: in mild-to-moderate reflux disease with frequent relapses (non-erosive or grade 1–2 oesophagitis), symptom relief at 6 months was 86.4% on continuous versus 74.6% on on-demand rabeprazole — not significant — using a third as much drug on demand
cards.summary: Bour 2005: in mild-to-moderate reflux disease with frequent relapses (non-erosive or grade 1–2 oesophagitis), symptom relief at 6 months was 86.4% on continuous versus 74.6% on on-demand rabeprazole — not significant — using a third as much drug on demand
cards.people: Randomised open-label study in patients with non-erosive reflux disease or Savary-Miller grade 1–2 oesophagitis and frequent symptomatic relapses; after a 4-week selection phase on rabeprazole 10 mg daily relieved symptoms in 88.6% of 176 enrolled patients, and 152 responders were randomised to rabeprazole 10 mg continuous (n = 81) or on-demand (n = 71) treatment for 6 months.
cards.result: At 6 months the symptom-relief rate was 86.4% on continuous treatment versus 74.6% on on-demand treatment — a difference that was not statistically significant (P = 0.065). Overall quality-of-life scores did not differ (86.25 versus 84.94). Mean daily rabeprazole consumption was significantly lower on demand (0.31 versus 0.96 tablets per day, P < 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: This trial measured symptoms, not endoscopic relapse, and two-thirds of its patients had non-erosive or grade 1 disease — it bounds the claim for mild disease and must not be read against Sjöstedt's endoscopic result in healed erosive oesophagitis of all grades.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for healed erosive oesophagitis, daily maintenance wins on endoscopic remission (81% versus 58%); the symptom gap is smaller and concentrated in more severe grades
cards.summary: Synthesis: for healed erosive oesophagitis, daily maintenance wins on endoscopic remission (81% versus 58%); the symptom gap is smaller and concentrated in more severe grades
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large randomised trial in healed erosive oesophagitis (Sjöstedt 2005, 477 randomised patients), one systematic review of on-demand maintenance across reflux disease (Pace 2007, 17 studies), and one randomised trial in milder mixed disease with a symptom endpoint (Bour 2005, 152 randomised patients). The non-erosive slice of this comparison is homed on pack #5661 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Daily esomeprazole 20 mg maintained remission in 81% versus 58% on demand at 6 months (Sjöstedt), the systematic review independently concluded on-demand therapy is not effective in (severe) erosive oesophagitis (Pace), and in mild disease symptom relief was statistically indistinguishable between strategies while on-demand used about a third of the drug (Bour). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: maintenance proton pump inhibitor therapy taken daily prevents relapse of healed erosive oesophagitis better than on-demand therapy, with the clearest benefit on endoscopic remission and in higher baseline grades.
cards.watchOut: Patients who value avoiding daily tablets and have mild healed disease may reasonably choose on-demand therapy accepting more heartburn — the evidence separates the endoscopic answer (daily wins) from the symptom-and-convenience trade-off (closer), and this shelf's question asks about relapse prevention.

shelves.title: Bedtime H2 blocker added to twice-daily PPI: better nighttime acid control on night one, gone by week one — the slice left open by live #2654
shelves.question: In adults with reflux symptoms that do not respond to twice-daily proton pump inhibitors, does adding a bedtime H2 blocker improve nighttime acid control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Circadian Rhythm · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastric Acid · Gastric Acidity Determination · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Male · Omeprazole · Ranitidine
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2654, which covers H2 blockers for reflux generally; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — a bedtime H2 blocker added to twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy. SPLIT (duration) — the small pH studies agree that the add-on works on the first nights and disagree with its own continuation. Peghini 1998 (12 healthy volunteers on twice-daily omeprazole) found bedtime ranitidine cut the percentage of the night with intragastric pH <4 from 48% (bedtime placebo) to 5–6%. Xue 2001 (105 patients with reflux disease on twice-daily proton pump inhibitors) found nocturnal acid breakthrough in 82% without versus 40% with a bedtime H2 blocker, and median overnight time with pH >4 of 51% versus 96%. But Fackler 2002 — the only study that kept measuring (43 subjects) — found the advantage present on day 1 of the H2 blocker and gone by day 7 and day 28: tolerance. Orr 2003 (19 patients) adds a second caution: gastric acidity fell, but oesophageal reflux measures did not change. No carded study enrolled documented twice-daily-PPI non-responders as such, and none measured symptom relief as the primary outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (duration): a bedtime H2 blocker improves nighttime gastric acid control acutely; sustained benefit beyond a week is not supported, and symptom benefit in true non-responders is untested.

cards.headline: Peghini 1998: in 12 healthy volunteers on twice-daily omeprazole, bedtime ranitidine cut overnight time with gastric pH <4 from 48% to 5–6% — better than a third omeprazole dose (31%)
cards.summary: Peghini 1998: in 12 healthy volunteers on twice-daily omeprazole, bedtime ranitidine cut overnight time with gastric pH <4 from 48% to 5–6% — better than a third omeprazole dose (31%)
cards.type: Randomised crossover controlled study in healthy volunteers (Peghini 1998)
cards.people: 12 healthy volunteers in a controlled crossover study: after 7 days of omeprazole 20 mg twice daily, overnight intragastric pH was monitored with four different bedtime supplements — placebo, additional omeprazole 20 mg, ranitidine 150 mg, or ranitidine 300 mg.
cards.result: Bedtime placebo left intragastric pH <4 for 48% of the night. Additional bedtime omeprazole reduced this to 31% (P < 0.005); bedtime ranitidine reduced it further, to 5% at 150 mg and 6% at 300 mg (P < 0.01 versus twice-daily omeprazole plus bedtime placebo). Acid breakthrough occurred in 11 subjects on bedtime placebo, 7 on bedtime omeprazole, 4 on ranitidine 150 mg and 3 on ranitidine 300 mg (P < 0.05, ranitidine versus placebo). Results for time with pH <3 were similar.
cards.watchOut: Twelve healthy volunteers, not patients with refractory reflux: this card establishes the pharmacology (bedtime histamine blockade covers the nocturnal gap) and cannot by itself support a symptom claim in twice-daily-PPI non-responders.
cards.source: Peghini PL et al. Ranitidine controls nocturnal gastric acid breakthrough on omeprazole: a controlled study in normal subjects. Gastroenterology. 1998. PMID: 9834259. cards.headline: Xue 2001: in reflux patients on twice-daily proton pump inhibitors, adding a bedtime H2 blocker raised median overnight time with gastric pH >4 from 51% to 96% and cut nocturnal acid breakthrough from 82% to 40%
cards.summary: Xue 2001: in reflux patients on twice-daily proton pump inhibitors, adding a bedtime H2 blocker raised median overnight time with gastric pH >4 from 51% to 96% and cut nocturnal acid breakthrough from 82% to 40%
cards.type: Clinical pH study in reflux patients (Xue 2001)
cards.people: Ambulatory pH studies in patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: group A, 60 patients on twice-daily proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole 20 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg); group B, 45 patients on the same twice-daily regimen plus a bedtime H2 blocker (ranitidine 300 mg, famotidine 40 mg or nizatidine 300 mg); 11 patients were studied on both regimens (group C).
cards.result: Median percentage of the night with intragastric pH >4 was 51% in group A versus 96% in group B (P < 0.0001); daytime values did not differ (73% versus 79.8%, P = 0.14). Nocturnal acid breakthrough occurred in 82% of group A and 40% of group B (P < 0.0001), and oesophageal acid exposure during breakthrough was shorter in group B (mean 18 versus 42 minutes, P = 0.04). In the 11 patients studied both ways, median overnight time with pH >4 rose from 54.6% without to 96.5% with the bedtime H2 blocker (P = 0.0013).
cards.watchOut: Groups A and B were different patients reviewed from pH-study records, not a randomised comparison — the 11-patient within-patient subset is the cleanest part; and the endpoint is gastric pH, a surrogate for the nighttime symptoms the clinical question cares about.
cards.source: Xue S et al. Bedtime H2 blockers improve nocturnal gastric acid control in GERD patients on proton pump inhibitors. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2001. PMID: 11552905. cards.headline: Fackler 2002: the bedtime-H2-blocker advantage was present on day 1 and gone by day 7 and day 28 — tolerance abolished the difference from twice-daily proton pump inhibitor alone
cards.summary: Fackler 2002: the bedtime-H2-blocker advantage was present on day 1 and gone by day 7 and day 28 — tolerance abolished the difference from twice-daily proton pump inhibitor alone
cards.people: 23 healthy volunteers and 20 patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease underwent ambulatory gastric and oesophageal pH monitoring at baseline and after 2 weeks of twice-daily omeprazole 20 mg, then received 28 days of twice-daily omeprazole plus bedtime ranitidine 300 mg with repeat pH testing on days 1, 7 and 28 of the combination; 18 controls and 16 reflux patients completed all five studies.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, all regimens decreased supine time with gastric pH <4 (P = 0.001). Twice-daily proton pump inhibitor plus one day of bedtime H2 blocker was the only regimen that significantly decreased supine gastric time with pH <4 compared with twice-daily proton pump inhibitor alone (P < 0.001). There was no difference between twice-daily proton pump inhibitor alone and the combination after 1 week or 1 month of combination therapy — the authors attribute the loss of effect to H2-blocker tolerance.
cards.watchOut: This is the only carded study that measured beyond the first nights, and it reverses the short-term story: any shelf or guideline quoting Peghini or Xue without Fackler overstates the durability of the strategy.
cards.source: Fackler WK et al. Long-term effect of H2RA therapy on nocturnal gastric acid breakthrough. Gastroenterology. 2002. PMID: 11874994. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Orr 2003: in 19 patients with symptomatic reflux disease, bedtime ranitidine 150 mg reduced gastric acidity on twice-daily omeprazole but did not significantly change oesophageal reflux or sleep-related reflux events
cards.summary: Orr 2003: in 19 patients with symptomatic reflux disease, bedtime ranitidine 150 mg reduced gastric acidity on twice-daily omeprazole but did not significantly change oesophageal reflux or sleep-related reflux events
cards.type: Controlled clinical pH and sleep study (Orr 2003)
cards.people: 19 individuals with symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, each studied on two occasions after 1 week of omeprazole 20 mg twice daily, with 24-hour oesophageal and gastric pH recording and polysomnography; participants received either ranitidine 150 mg at bedtime or placebo before a provocative meal.
cards.result: Ranitidine significantly reduced the percentage of time with intragastric pH <4 (P < 0.01). There was no significant difference in measures of gastro-oesophageal reflux, and reflux events did not occur significantly more often during periods of nocturnal acid breakthrough than during control intervals without breakthrough — the gastric pH improvement did not translate into measurably less oesophageal reflux in this small study.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients and a single-night comparison: underpowered for symptom or reflux-event outcomes, but it is the only carded study that looked past the stomach to the oesophagus — and found the surrogate and the target organ disagreeing.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bedtime H2 blockade fixes the gastric pH gap on night one; tolerance takes it back within a week, and no study shows symptom relief in documented non-responders
cards.summary: Synthesis: bedtime H2 blockade fixes the gastric pH gap on night one; tolerance takes it back within a week, and no study shows symptom relief in documented non-responders
cards.people: The carded evidence: four small physiologic pH studies — Peghini 1998 (12 healthy volunteers), Xue 2001 (105 reflux patients, 11 studied both ways), Fackler 2002 (43 subjects followed to day 28), and Orr 2003 (19 reflux patients). Total carded participants are under 200 and every study is small, though the total exceeds the small-N stamp threshold.
cards.result: Acutely, adding a bedtime H2 blocker to twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy markedly improves nocturnal gastric acid control (overnight pH <4 time 48% to 5–6% in Peghini; breakthrough 82% to 40% in Xue). With continued use the advantage disappeared by day 7–28 (Fackler), and the one study measuring oesophageal reflux found no significant change (Orr). PROPOSED SPLIT (duration): yes for nighttime acid control on the first nights; no demonstrated sustained acid-control benefit, and no direct evidence of symptom improvement in patients whose reflux symptoms persist on twice-daily proton pump inhibitors.
cards.watchOut: Intermittent (not nightly) bedtime use is the usual clinical workaround for tolerance, but no carded study tests that schedule — the shelf reports the tolerance finding and does not upgrade the workaround into evidence.

shelves.title: Grade II haemorrhoids: band ligation versus infrared coagulation — about equal efficacy, banding hurts more (the comparator live #1938 does not cover)
shelves.question: In adults with hemorrhoids, does rubber band ligation work better than infrared coagulation for grade II hemorrhoids?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhoids · Humans · Infrared Rays · Ligation · Light Coagulation · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1938, which compares haemorrhoidal artery ligation with rubber band ligation; this shelf covers the infrared-coagulation comparator #1938 does not. SPLIT (outcome) — the head-to-head trials find the two office procedures close on efficacy and consistently apart on pain. In the trial restricted to grade II bleeding piles (Gupta 2003, 100 patients), band ligation controlled symptoms better but hurt more, and coagulation patients returned to work sooner (2 versus 4 days) yet recurred or failed more often (P = 0.03 for both comparisons). Templeton 1983 (137 patients, grades I–II) found satisfactory outcomes in 92% after banding versus 85% after coagulation, with significantly more discomfort after banding (P < 0.001). Poen 2000 (133 patients) found 97% versus 92% symptom-free or improved, pain scores of 5.5 versus 3.3 (P = 0.018), and relapse of 18% versus 20% at about 19 months. The 2023 meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials found no significant difference in efficacy, prolapse, recurrence or urinary retention, with more postoperative pain after banding and less postoperative bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): banding is not clearly better — efficacy is about equal with a small durability edge in some trials, bought with more pain; coagulation is the gentler, more repeatable procedure.

cards.headline: Gupta 2003: in 100 patients with grade II bleeding piles, band ligation was more effective but more painful; infrared coagulation patients returned to work in 2 versus 4 days but recurred or failed more often
cards.summary: Gupta 2003: in 100 patients with grade II bleeding piles, band ligation was more effective but more painful; infrared coagulation patients returned to work in 2 versus 4 days but recurred or failed more often
cards.people: 100 patients with second-degree (grade II) bleeding haemorrhoids, randomised prospectively to rubber band ligation (n = 54) or infrared coagulation (n = 46); mean age 38 years, mean disease duration 17.5 months. Outcomes included postoperative pain and discomfort, time to return to work, relief of bleeding, and recurrence.
cards.result: Postoperative pain during the first week was more intense after band ligation (scores 2–5 versus 0–3 on a visual analogue scale), as were post-defecation pain and rectal tenesmus (P = 0.0059). Infrared coagulation patients resumed their duties earlier (2 versus 4 days, P = 0.03) but had a higher recurrence or failure rate (P = 0.03). The authors conclude band ligation is more effective in controlling symptoms and obliterating haemorrhoids but causes more pain and discomfort, while coagulation can be conveniently repeated if recurrence occurs.
cards.watchOut: The only carded trial restricted to grade II disease — the exact population of this shelf's question — but a single-centre study of 100 patients, and its abstract reports the recurrence difference by P value without the two recurrence rates.

cards.headline: Templeton 1983: in grades I–II haemorrhoids, satisfactory outcomes were 92% after band ligation versus 85% after infrared coagulation — with significantly more discomfort after banding (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Templeton 1983: in grades I–II haemorrhoids, satisfactory outcomes were 92% after band ligation versus 85% after infrared coagulation — with significantly more discomfort after banding (P < 0.001)
cards.people: 137 previously untreated outpatients with first- and second-degree haemorrhoids, allocated at random to infrared coagulation (n = 66) or rubber band ligation (n = 71); complete follow-up in 122 patients (60 coagulation, 62 banding) at 3 months to 1 year after treatment.
cards.result: Infrared coagulation produced a satisfactory outcome in 51 of 60 patients (85%: 34 asymptomatic, 17 improved); rubber band ligation in 57 of 62 (92%: 33 asymptomatic, 24 improved). Both methods were judged equally effective in first- and second-degree haemorrhoids. Side effects, particularly discomfort during and after treatment, were significantly more frequent after band ligation (P < 0.001), more banding patients lost more than 24 hours from work, the number of treatments needed did not differ, and coagulation was significantly faster to perform (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: A 1983 trial mixing grade I with grade II disease and using the devices and banding technique of its era; its efficacy percentages are 'satisfactory outcome' composites, not modern patient-reported outcomes.

cards.headline: Poen 2000: symptom relief was 97% after band ligation versus 92% after infrared coagulation, relapse at ~19 months was 18% versus 20% — and pain was higher after banding (visual analogue 5.5 versus 3.3, P = 0.018)
cards.summary: Poen 2000: symptom relief was 97% after band ligation versus 92% after infrared coagulation, relapse at ~19 months was 18% versus 20% — and pain was higher after banding (visual analogue 5.5 versus 3.3, P = 0.018)
cards.people: 133 consecutive patients with internal haemorrhoids and no concomitant anorectal disease at an academic hospital, randomised to rubber band ligation (n = 65) or infrared coagulation (n = 68), repeated at 4-week intervals until symptoms resolved (mean 1.6 sessions in both arms); outcomes assessed in 124 patients, with telephone follow-up for recurrence in 105 patients at a mean of 19.2 months.
cards.result: 58 of 60 banding patients (97%) and 59 of 64 coagulation patients (92%) were symptom-free or satisfactorily improved. Pain after treatment was more common and more severe after band ligation (visual analogue score 5.5 ± 3.7 versus 3.3 ± 3.3, P = 0.018). Symptomatic relapse to pre-treatment levels occurred in 9 of 50 banding patients (18%) and 11 of 55 coagulation patients (20%, P = 0.81). The authors judged the two equally effective and suggested coagulation first-line because of the pain difference.
cards.watchOut: Poen enrolled internal haemorrhoids of mixed grade (the grade III subgroup was tiny: 5 of 5 versus 2 of 4 symptom-free); the grade II reading comes from combining this trial with Gupta 2003 and Templeton 1983, not from a grade II stratum reported here.
cards.source: Poen AC et al. A randomized controlled trial of rubber band ligation versus infra-red coagulation in the treatment of internal haemorrhoids. cards.headline: Ding 2023: meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials found no significant difference between band ligation and coagulation in efficacy, prolapse, recurrence or urinary retention — banding caused more postoperative pain and less postoperative bleeding
cards.summary: Ding 2023: meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials found no significant difference between band ligation and coagulation in efficacy, prolapse, recurrence or urinary retention — banding caused more postoperative pain and less postoperative bleeding
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials comparing rubber band ligation with coagulation (infrared and non-infrared) for haemorrhoids, searching PubMed and Web of Science to April 2022; 9 trials met the inclusion criteria, all of moderate methodological quality.
cards.result: No significant difference was found between rubber band ligation and coagulation in efficacy rate, postoperative prolapse rate, recurrence rate or postoperative urinary retention. Patients undergoing band ligation had a higher postoperative pain rate and a lower postoperative bleeding rate than patients undergoing coagulation. Subgroup analysis found no significant difference between band ligation and infrared coagulation specifically in efficacy, postoperative bleeding or urinary retention, with banding again causing more postoperative pain.
cards.watchOut: The coagulation pool mixes infrared with other coagulation methods and the trials span decades of technique; the abstract reports significance without pooled effect sizes, so this card corroborates the pain–efficacy pattern rather than quantifying it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: banding and coagulation control grade II haemorrhoids about equally; banding's small durability edge in some trials is consistently paid for in pain
cards.summary: Synthesis: banding and coagulation control grade II haemorrhoids about equally; banding's small durability edge in some trials is consistently paid for in pain
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised head-to-head trials (Templeton 1983, 137 patients with grade I–II disease; Poen 2000, 133 patients; Gupta 2003, 100 patients with grade II disease) and one meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (Ding 2023). The artery-ligation comparison is homed on live shelf #1938 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Satisfactory outcomes were 85–92% for coagulation and 92–97% for banding across the trials; relapse was 18% versus 20% in Poen, while Gupta found significantly more recurrence or failure after coagulation (P = 0.03); the meta-analysis found no significant efficacy or recurrence difference. Every source agrees on the other half: banding hurts more (pain 5.5 versus 3.3 in Poen; significantly more discomfort in Templeton; more postoperative pain in Ding). PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): rubber band ligation does not work clearly better than infrared coagulation for grade II haemorrhoids — choose coagulation for comfort and repeatability, banding where durability matters most and pain is acceptable.
cards.watchOut: All of this evidence predates modern single-shot banding devices and contemporary patient-reported outcome measures; the direction (equal efficacy, more banding pain) has been stable across 40 years of trials, which is why the split — not a winner — is the honest stamp.

shelves.title: Wilson disease maintenance: trientine non-inferior to penicillamine for copper control in CHELATE — the head-to-head live #2119 does not cover
shelves.question: In adults with Wilson disease, is trientine as effective as penicillamine for maintaining copper control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Chelating Agents · Copper · Hepatolenticular Degeneration · Penicillamine · Trientine
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2119, which compares tetrathiomolybdate with trientine in newly presenting neurological Wilson disease; this shelf covers the maintenance head-to-head #2119 does not — trientine versus penicillamine in patients already stabilised. POSSIBLE — the one randomised head-to-head trial, CHELATE (2022), switched 53 patients who had been stable on penicillamine for at least a year to trientine tetrahydrochloride or kept them on penicillamine: non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper at 24 weeks differed by −9.1 μg/L (95% CI −24.2 to 6.1), inside the −50 μg/L non-inferiority margin, non-inferiority held at 48 weeks, and masked adjudication confirmed clinical stability in 100% of participants in both groups. The supporting cohorts are switch populations: 77 patients moved to trientine dihydrochloride after penicillamine withdrawal kept or improved hepatic symptoms in about 85% over a mean of 8 years with no progression to liver failure or transplant (Weiss 2022), and 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride prospectively were 98% responders at 12 months (Mohr 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: yes — for maintaining copper control in stable patients, trientine performed as well as penicillamine in the single non-inferiority trial, with long-term cohort experience consistent; the trial does not address initial decoppering of newly diagnosed patients.

cards.headline: CHELATE 2022: trientine tetrahydrochloride was non-inferior to penicillamine for maintaining copper control in stable Wilson disease (non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper difference −9.1 μg/L, inside the −50 μg/L margin)
cards.summary: CHELATE 2022: trientine tetrahydrochloride was non-inferior to penicillamine for maintaining copper control in stable Wilson disease (non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper difference −9.1 μg/L, inside the −50 μg/L margin)
cards.people: Randomised, open-label, non-inferiority phase 3 trial at centres in Brazil, Europe and the USA: patients aged 18–75 with stable Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for at least 1 year entered a 12-week stability run-in; 53 stable patients were randomised (27 to continue penicillamine, 26 to switch mg-for-mg to trientine tetrahydrochloride, TETA4), with the primary endpoint of serum non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper (NCC) by speciation assay 24 weeks after randomisation and a 24-week extension.
cards.result: At 24 weeks the mean difference in NCC by speciation assay between penicillamine and TETA4 was −9.1 μg/L (95% CI −24.2 to 6.1), with the lower confidence limit inside the −50 μg/L non-inferiority margin — non-inferiority met. At 48 weeks TETA4 remained non-inferior (mean difference −15.5 μg/L, 95% CI −34.5 to 3.6). Urinary copper excretion was lower with TETA4 at 24 weeks (mean difference 237.5 μg/24 h, 99% CI 115.6 to 359.4) but stayed in the expected range for well-treated patients in both groups and was not significantly different at 48 weeks. Masked adjudication by three independent clinicians confirmed clinical stability in 100% of participants at both 24 and 48 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 53 randomised patients, and a biochemical primary endpoint in patients pre-selected for stability on penicillamine: it answers maintenance switching, not which drug is better for initial treatment of newly diagnosed or unstable patients — and the trientine salt tested (tetrahydrochloride) differs from the dihydrochloride salt in the cohort cards below.
cards.source: Schilsky ML et al. Trientine tetrahydrochloride versus penicillamine for maintenance therapy in Wilson disease (CHELATE): a randomised, open-label, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 36183738. Registry ID: NCT03539952. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Chelating Agents · Copper · Hepatolenticular Degeneration · Penicillamine · Trientine

cards.headline: Weiss 2022: in 77 patients switched to trientine dihydrochloride after penicillamine withdrawal, hepatic symptoms improved in 49.4% and none progressed to liver failure or transplant over a mean of 8 years on trientine
cards.summary: Weiss 2022: in 77 patients switched to trientine dihydrochloride after penicillamine withdrawal, hepatic symptoms improved in 49.4% and none progressed to liver failure or transplant over a mean of 8 years on trientine
cards.people: Multicentre retrospective study of medical records of 77 patients with Wilson disease who started trientine dihydrochloride (TETA-2HCl) after withdrawal of D-penicillamine, with data collected for 48 months after the switch; mean duration of trientine treatment was 8 years (range 5 months to 32.5 years).
cards.result: Over trientine treatment, 35% of patients had no hepatic symptoms and hepatic symptoms improved in 49.4%, remained unchanged in 10.4% and worsened in 5.2%; no patient progressed to acute hepatic failure or needed a liver transplant. Neurologically, 46.7% had no symptoms, 14.3% improved, 36.4% remained stable and 2.6% worsened. Twelve patients discontinued trientine (8 switched to zinc, 2 for inadequate hepatic response, 1 for anaemia, 1 by patient decision), and treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 24.7%, most often gastrointestinal (9.1%) and nervous-system (5.2%) disorders.
cards.watchOut: A switch cohort with no continuing-penicillamine comparator: patients who had already failed or not tolerated penicillamine are exactly those expected to do relatively better after switching, so this card supports trientine's long-term adequacy, not its equivalence — equivalence rests on CHELATE.
cards.source: Weiss KH et al. cards.headline: Mohr 2025: prospectively, 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride for 12 months were 98% responders, with copper markers improved or stable and no treatment-related serious adverse events
cards.summary: Mohr 2025: prospectively, 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride for 12 months were 98% responders, with copper markers improved or stable and no treatment-related serious adverse events
cards.people: Prospective phase 2 study at one German centre: 51 patients with Wilson disease continued trientine dihydrochloride 300 mg (200 mg trientine base) for 12 months; primary outcomes were safety and efficacy, biomarkers of copper metabolism, and the course of hepatic and neurologic disease, including the Unified Wilson Disease Rating Scale (UWDRS).
cards.result: 50 of 51 patients (98.0%) were considered responders at the 12-month visit. UWDRS scores improved from a mean of 11.3 (SD 24.31) at baseline to 8.8 (22.86) at month 12, and biochemical liver parameters and copper markers (24-hour urinary copper, non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper) showed improved or stable disease throughout. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 5 patients (9.6%); no patient withdrew because of an adverse event and no serious adverse event was judged treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and single-centre: 'responder' status on continued treatment shows trientine maintenance holds copper control over a year, but with no penicillamine arm it cannot speak to the comparison this shelf asks about — it is context for CHELATE, not a second comparative test.

cards.search: mohr 2025: prospectively, 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride for 12 months were 98% responders, with copper markers improved or stable and no treatment-related serious adverse events mohr 2025: prospectively, 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride for 12 months were 98% responders, with copper markers improved or stable and no treatment-related serious adverse events in adults with wilson disease, is trientine as effective as penicillamine for maintaining copper control? prospective single-arm cohort study (mohr 2025) prospective phase 2 study at one german centre: 51 patients with wilson disease continued trientine dihydrochloride 300 mg (200 mg trientine base) for 12 months; primary outcomes were safety and efficacy, biomarkers of copper metabolism, and the course of hepatic and neurologic disease, including the unified wilson disease rating scale (uwdrs). 50 of 51 patients (98.0%) were considered responders at the 12-month visit. uwdrs scores improved from a mean of 11.3 (sd 24.31) at baseline to 8.8 (22.86) at month 12, and biochemical liver parameters and copper markers (24-hour urinary copper, non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper) showed improved or stable disease throughout. treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 5 patients (9.6%); no patient withdrew because of an adverse event and no serious adverse event was judged treatment-related. single-arm and single-centre: 'responder' status on continued treatment shows trientine maintenance holds copper control over a year, but with no penicillamine arm it cannot speak to the comparison this shelf asks about — it is context for chelate, not a second comparative test. mohr i et al. prospective study to assess long-term outcomes of chelator-based treatment with trientine dihydrochloride in patients with wilson disease. jgh open : an open access journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2025. pmid: 40104015. registry id: nct02426905. mesh: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: for maintenance in stable patients, trientine matched penicillamine on copper control in the one head-to-head trial, and switch cohorts stayed stable for years
cards.summary: Synthesis: for maintenance in stable patients, trientine matched penicillamine on copper control in the one head-to-head trial, and switch cohorts stayed stable for years
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised non-inferiority trial (CHELATE 2022, 53 randomised patients), one retrospective switch cohort (Weiss 2022, 77 patients), and one prospective single-arm maintenance cohort (Mohr 2025, 51 patients). The newly-presenting neurological comparison is homed on live shelf #2119 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: CHELATE found trientine tetrahydrochloride non-inferior to continued penicillamine on non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper at 24 weeks (−9.1 μg/L, 95% CI −24.2 to 6.1, against a −50 μg/L margin) and at 48 weeks, with 100% clinical stability in both groups; the cohorts show patients switched to or maintained on trientine dihydrochloride mostly improving or remaining stable over years, with about a quarter reporting treatment-emergent adverse events in the retrospective series. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: trientine is as effective as penicillamine for maintaining copper control in stable Wilson disease — a single-trial non-inferiority answer, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Salt forms differ across the evidence (tetrahydrochloride in CHELATE, dihydrochloride in the cohorts) and mg-for-mg switching was the trial's method; do not read CHELATE as covering de novo treatment, pregnancy, or patients unstable on penicillamine.

shelves.title: Zinc for hepatic encephalopathy: psychometric scores improve in small trials (zinc acetate; polaprezinc) — recurrence and survival benefit unproven
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, does zinc supplementation improve encephalopathy versus standard therapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Acetates · Acetic Acid · Administration, Oral · Blood Urea Nitrogen · Chronic Disease · Clinical Trials as Topic · Copper · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Male · Prospective Studies · Random Allocation · Trail Making Test · Zinc
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — zinc improves the psychometric tests by which mild encephalopathy is measured, in small trials, without a demonstrated effect on recurrence or survival. Reding 1984 randomised 22 patients with chronic encephalopathy to zinc acetate 600 mg/day or placebo for 7 days and found trail-making performance improved only in the supplemented group. Takuma 2010 randomised 79 patients to polaprezinc 225 mg/day added to standard therapy (protein-restricted diet including branched-chain amino acids, plus lactulose) or standard therapy alone for 6 months: encephalopathy grade, ammonia, Child-Pugh score and neuropsychological tests all improved significantly more with zinc, and physical quality of life improved while mental quality of life did not. Two meta-analyses pool the same small trial base: Chavez-Tapia 2013 (4 trials, 233 patients) found better number-connection-test performance (standardised mean difference −0.62) but no significant reduction in encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.59) and no mortality data; Shen 2019 (4 trials, 247 patients) found the number-connection benefit for zinc added to lactulose (standardised mean difference −0.97, moderate certainty) but no significant difference in digit-symbol performance or ammonia. A further preliminary placebo-controlled trial (Katayama 2014; 18 enrolled, 12 analysed, cirrhosis with hyperammonaemia and low zinc) found ammonia fell on zinc acetate 150 mg/day — described here in prose, not carded, because of its size and its hyperammonaemia (rather than overt encephalopathy) population. On preparations (the clarification exception for supplements): the publications name zinc acetate (Reding; Katayama) and polaprezinc, a zinc–carnosine compound (Takuma); the meta-analyses pooled 'any oral zinc supplementation' without a single tested product, so no one preparation carries the pooled claim, and currently sold zinc products may differ from those tested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: zinc supplementation improves psychometric encephalopathy measures versus standard therapy alone; benefit on recurrence, hospitalisation or death is unproven.

cards.headline: Reding 1984: in 22 patients with chronic hepatic encephalopathy, zinc acetate 600 mg/day for 7 days improved trail-making performance while placebo did not
cards.summary: Reding 1984: in 22 patients with chronic hepatic encephalopathy, zinc acetate 600 mg/day for 7 days improved trail-making performance while placebo did not
cards.people: 22 patients with cirrhosis and chronic encephalopathy in a double-blind randomised trial of oral zinc supplementation (zinc acetate 600 mg a day, as named in the publication) versus placebo for 7 days; encephalopathy was assessed by a trail-making test, and serum zinc and blood urea nitrogen were measured.
cards.result: By day 8, serum zinc had been restored to normal in the supplemented group. Hepatic encephalopathy, as assessed by the trail-making test, was improved in the supplemented group but not in the placebo group, and blood urea nitrogen increased significantly in the supplemented group — consistent with the authors' proposed mechanism, correction of the zinc deficiency that compromises conversion of ammonia to urea. The abstract does not report the between-group effect size for the trail-making result.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two patients and seven days of treatment: the founding trial of this literature is a short psychometric signal, and its abstract gives no effect size — it cannot support claims about recurrence, hospitalisation or survival.

cards.headline: Takuma 2010: adding polaprezinc 225 mg/day to standard therapy for 6 months improved encephalopathy grade, ammonia and neuropsychological tests versus standard therapy alone (79 patients)
cards.summary: Takuma 2010: adding polaprezinc 225 mg/day to standard therapy for 6 months improved encephalopathy grade, ammonia and neuropsychological tests versus standard therapy alone (79 patients)
cards.people: 79 patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, randomised to polaprezinc 225 mg daily (the zinc preparation named in the publication — a zinc–carnosine compound) in addition to standard therapies (a protein-restricted diet including branched-chain amino acid, and lactulose) or to standard therapies alone, for 6 months; outcomes included Short Form-36 quality of life, encephalopathy grade, laboratory parameters and neuropsychological tests.
cards.result: Zinc supplementation significantly decreased hepatic encephalopathy grade (P = 0.03) and blood ammonia (P = 0.01) and improved Child-Pugh score (P = 0.04) and neuropsychological tests (P = 0.02) compared with standard therapy. The physical component of quality of life improved significantly (P = 0.04) but the mental component did not (P = 0.95); in multivariate analysis zinc supplementation was independently associated with improvement in the physical component (P = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: The largest single trial is still only 79 patients, open in design as reported, and tests one specific preparation (polaprezinc) on top of a specific standard package including branched-chain amino acids — its result should not be transferred uncritically to other zinc salts or to zinc used alone.

cards.headline: Chavez-Tapia 2013: pooling 4 trials (233 patients), oral zinc improved number-connection-test performance (standardised mean difference −0.62) but did not significantly reduce encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64)
cards.summary: Chavez-Tapia 2013: pooling 4 trials (233 patients), oral zinc improved number-connection-test performance (standardised mean difference −0.62) but did not significantly reduce encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Chavez-Tapia 2013)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of any oral zinc supplementation versus no intervention, placebo or other interventions in adults with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy; 4 trials with a total of 233 patients were included.
cards.result: Oral zinc supplementation was associated with significantly improved performance on the number connection test (standardised mean difference −0.62, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.11; 3 trials, n = 189) but not with a significant reduction in encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.59 — a relative measure whose interval includes no effect; 2 trials, n = 169). Mortality, liver-related morbidity and other clinically significant outcomes were not reported in the included trials.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials used different zinc preparations and comparators, so the pooled estimate belongs to 'oral zinc' as a class, not to any product a reader can buy; heterogeneity and the tiny trial base cap this evidence at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Chavez-Tapia NC et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the use of oral zinc in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy. Nutrition journal. 2013. PMID: 23742732. cards.headline: Shen 2019: zinc added to lactulose improved the number connection test (standardised mean difference −0.97, moderate certainty) but not digit-symbol performance or ammonia, in 4 trials with 247 patients
cards.summary: Shen 2019: zinc added to lactulose improved the number connection test (standardised mean difference −0.97, moderate certainty) but not digit-symbol performance or ammonia, in 4 trials with 247 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Shen 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of zinc supplementation versus placebo or other treatment for hepatic encephalopathy in adults with cirrhosis, searching to December 2018; 4 trials with 247 patients were included, with risk-of-bias and GRADE certainty assessments; the analysed patients had mild encephalopathy (grade II or below).
cards.result: In patients with mild encephalopathy, zinc supplementation combined with lactulose over 3–6 months significantly improved number-connection-test performance versus lactulose alone (standardised mean difference −0.97, 95% CI −1.75 to −0.19; P = 0.01; moderate certainty; 3 trials, n = 227). There was no significant difference in the digit symbol test (standardised mean difference 0.44, 95% CI −0.12 to 1.00; very low certainty) or serum ammonia (mean difference −10.86, 95% CI −25.73 to 4.01; very low certainty), each in 2 trials with 137 patients. No included trial reported adverse events or hospitalisation effects.
cards.watchOut: Shen 2019 and Chavez-Tapia 2013 pool substantially the same handful of small trials, so the two meta-analyses are one evidence base read twice — and even read together they speak only to psychometric tests in mild encephalopathy.
cards.source: Shen YC et al. Zinc supplementation in patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrition journal. 2019. PMID: 31279342. cards.headline: Synthesis: zinc improves psychometric encephalopathy scores in small trials; recurrence and survival benefit are unproven, and the tested preparations differ
cards.summary: Synthesis: zinc improves psychometric encephalopathy scores in small trials; recurrence and survival benefit are unproven, and the tested preparations differ
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small randomised trials (Reding 1984, 22 patients, zinc acetate; Takuma 2010, 79 patients, polaprezinc) and two meta-analyses of substantially the same trial base (Chavez-Tapia 2013, 4 trials and 233 patients; Shen 2019, 4 trials and 247 patients). A third small trial (Katayama 2014) is described in the balance prose only.
cards.result: Every psychometric signal points the same way — number-connection and trail-making performance improve with zinc added to standard therapy (standardised mean differences −0.62 and −0.97) — and Takuma found parallel improvements in encephalopathy grade and ammonia. The harder outcomes do not follow: recurrence was not significantly reduced (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.59), ammonia pooling was not significant in Shen 2019, and no trial reported mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: zinc supplementation improves encephalopathy as measured by psychometric tests versus standard therapy alone; that is the whole of the demonstrated benefit.
cards.watchOut: Preparations are not interchangeable on this evidence: zinc acetate and polaprezinc are the named tested products, the meta-analyses pooled any oral zinc, and zinc excess itself causes copper deficiency — supplement enthusiasm should not outrun these small, old, psychometric-outcome trials.

shelves.title: Uncomplicated diverticulitis needing antibiotics: oral therapy matched intravenous therapy in three small randomised trials — the route question live #178 and DINAMO do not ask
shelves.question: In adults with uncomplicated diverticulitis who need antibiotics, is oral therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diverticulitis, Colonic · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Diverticulitis · Diverticulosis, Colonic · Pain · Acute Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three small randomised trials, all concordant, none large or blinded. This shelf asks the route question in patients who are receiving antibiotics; it is distinct from live shelf #178 and pack #3621 (DINAMO), which ask whether antibiotics can be omitted altogether, and neither of those is re-carded here. McClintock 2024 randomised 118 patients with CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis (modified Hinchey 0–1a) to oral or intravenous antibiotics — both delivered as outpatients through a Hospital-in-the-Home service — and found no significant difference in 30-day unplanned admissions, inflammatory markers, pain resolution or return to normal nutrition and bowel function, meeting its non-inferiority design. Ridgway 2009 randomised 79 patients with clinically diagnosed uncomplicated diverticulitis to oral or intravenous ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole: no oral patient needed conversion to intravenous therapy, symptoms resolved completely in both groups, and day-3 tenderness was equivalent. Ribas 2010 tested the step-down version — a short intravenous course of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid followed by oral therapy and early discharge versus 7 days of intravenous therapy in 50 patients — with no significant difference in treatment failure and a saving of €1,244 per patient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: in uncomplicated diverticulitis selected for antibiotic treatment, oral therapy performs as well as intravenous therapy; the trials are small, mostly unblinded, and enrolled patients well enough that route was genuinely in equipoise.

cards.headline: McClintock 2024: oral antibiotics were non-inferior to intravenous antibiotics in 118 outpatients with CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis — no significant difference in 30-day unplanned admissions or recovery measures
cards.summary: McClintock 2024: oral antibiotics were non-inferior to intravenous antibiotics in 118 outpatients with CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis — no significant difference in 30-day unplanned admissions or recovery measures
cards.people: Single-centre, unblinded, 1:1 non-inferiority randomised trial: 118 patients older than 18 with CT-proven acute uncomplicated colonic diverticulitis (modified Hinchey stage 0–1a) were allocated to intravenous (n = 58) or oral (n = 60) antibiotics, both groups treated in the outpatient setting through a Hospital-in-the-Home service. The primary outcome was the 30-day unplanned admission rate; secondary outcomes included C-reactive protein and white cell count, time to pain resolution, cessation of pain medication, and return to normal nutrition and bowel function.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the groups in 30-day unplanned admissions or inflammatory markers, and no significant difference in time to pain resolution, cessation of pain medication, return to normal nutrition or return to normal bowel function. The authors conclude outpatient management with oral antibiotics proved equally as safe and efficacious as intravenous treatment in this non-inferiority trial. The abstract reports the comparisons as non-significant without printing the two groups' event rates for the primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Both arms were outpatients under a Hospital-in-the-Home service with daily review — the trial shows route does not matter inside that safety net, not that oral therapy needs no monitoring; it was unblinded and single-centre.

cards.headline: Ridgway 2009: oral ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole was not inferior to the intravenous regimen in 79 patients with clinically diagnosed uncomplicated diverticulitis — no oral patient needed conversion to intravenous therapy
cards.summary: Ridgway 2009: oral ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole was not inferior to the intravenous regimen in 79 patients with clinically diagnosed uncomplicated diverticulitis — no oral patient needed conversion to intravenous therapy
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in two district general hospitals: 79 patients with clinically diagnosed acute uncomplicated diverticulitis were allocated to oral antibiotics and fluids (n = 41) or intravenous antibiotics and bowel rest (n = 38), both regimens using ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. Primary outcomes were surrogates for resolution (including tenderness on day 3 and length of stay) and failure of oral therapy.
cards.result: No patient in the oral group had to be converted to intravenous antibiotics, and there was complete resolution of symptoms in both groups. Tenderness was equivalent in both groups on day 3, and among secondary endpoints a serial decrease in C-reactive protein was the best serological predictor of resolution in both groups. The authors conclude oral antibiotics are not inferior to intravenous antibiotics in achieving resolution of clinically diagnosed diverticulitis.
cards.watchOut: Diagnosis was clinical, without a CT requirement — some enrolled patients may not have had diverticulitis at all, which biases a route comparison toward 'no difference'; its outcomes were resolution surrogates rather than complications or readmission.
cards.source: Ridgway PF et al. Randomized controlled trial of oral vs intravenous therapy for the clinically diagnosed acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. Colorectal disease. 2009. PMID: 19016815. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ribas 2010: a short intravenous course followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid matched 7 days of intravenous therapy in 50 patients — no significant difference in treatment failure, with €1,244 saved per patient
cards.summary: Ribas 2010: a short intravenous course followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid matched 7 days of intravenous therapy in 50 patients — no significant difference in treatment failure, with €1,244 saved per patient
cards.people: Prospective randomised trial in 50 patients with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis (25 per group): group 1 switched to oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid (1 g every 8 hours, the same drug by both routes) as soon as they improved and was discharged the day after; group 2 received intravenous therapy for 7 days; both groups received oral antibiotic at discharge. The endpoint was failure of treatment — inability to discharge on the expected day, emergency admission, or readmission.
cards.result: Most patients in both groups improved clearly between 24 and 48 hours after admission. There were no significant differences between the groups in failure of treatment. Treatment in group 1 represented a saving in hospitalisation costs of €1,244 per patient. The authors conclude most patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis can be managed safely with oral antibiotic after a short intravenous course, making a very short hospital stay a safe option.
cards.watchOut: This is a step-down trial — every patient started intravenously — so it supports early switch rather than oral-from-the-start; with 25 patients per group it can only exclude very large differences in failure.
cards.source: Ribas Y et al. Prospective randomized clinical trial assessing the efficacy of a short course of intravenously administered amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid followed by oral antibiotic in patients with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis. International journal of colorectal disease. 2010. PMID: 20526718. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in patients selected for antibiotics, oral therapy performed as well as intravenous therapy in all three small randomised trials — a consistent but thin evidence base
cards.summary: Synthesis: in patients selected for antibiotics, oral therapy performed as well as intravenous therapy in all three small randomised trials — a consistent but thin evidence base
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials (Ridgway 2009, 79 patients, oral versus intravenous from the start; Ribas 2010, 50 patients, early oral step-down versus 7-day intravenous; McClintock 2024, 118 patients, oral versus intravenous in outpatients). Total randomised participants: 247. The antibiotics-versus-none question is homed on live shelf #178 and pack #3621 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: No trial found a significant disadvantage for the oral route: no conversions from oral to intravenous (Ridgway), no significant difference in treatment failure with early switch (Ribas), and non-inferiority on 30-day unplanned admissions and recovery measures with both routes given at home (McClintock). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral antibiotic therapy is as effective as intravenous therapy for uncomplicated diverticulitis in patients judged to need antibiotics — supported by three concordant but small, mostly unblinded trials in selected, clinically stable patients.
cards.watchOut: None of these trials enrolled complicated diverticulitis, sepsis, vomiting or inability to absorb oral medication — the populations in which intravenous therapy is not a choice but a necessity; the shelf's answer applies only where route was genuinely optional.
cards.source: Synthesis of McClintock S et al. ANZ journal of surgery. 2024 (PMID: 37962086); Ridgway PF et al. Colorectal disease. 2009 (PMID: 19016815); Ribas Y et al. International journal of colorectal disease. 2010 (PMID: 20526718).

shelves.title: Standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PARTIAL completion of pack #2782): liver tests improve, transplant-free survival does not
shelves.question: In adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis, does standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improve transplant-free survival versus no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cholangitis, Sclerosing · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Time Factors · Treatment Failure · Ursodeoxycholic Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2782 already answers the high-dose question (high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improved biochemistry but caused harm); this shelf asks the separate standard-dose efficacy question #2782 leaves open, and no high-dose PMID is re-carded here. The one standard-dose placebo trial (Lindor 1997, 13–15 mg/kg/day, 105 patients) found no difference in time to treatment failure (relative risk 1.01) and no difference in time to liver transplantation, despite clear improvement in alkaline phosphatase, transaminases, bilirubin and albumin. Two meta-analyses of the randomised trials (Shi 2009, 465 patients; Triantos 2011, 567 patients across standard- and high-dose trials) agree: no significant effect on death, liver transplantation, or death and/or transplantation combined. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver blood tests in primary sclerosing cholangitis but has not been shown to improve transplant-free survival.

cards.headline: Lindor 1997: in 105 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, standard-dose ursodiol (13–15 mg/kg/day) made no difference to treatment failure or transplantation over a median 2.2 years
cards.summary: Lindor 1997: in 105 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, standard-dose ursodiol (13–15 mg/kg/day) made no difference to treatment failure or transplantation over a median 2.2 years
cards.people: 105 patients with well-documented primary sclerosing cholangitis randomised double-blind to ursodiol 13–15 mg/kg/day in divided doses or placebo (May 1989–July 1995); 102 patients (51 per group) had at least 3 months of follow-up and were analysed; median follow-up 2.2 years. The primary outcome was time to treatment failure — a composite of death, liver transplantation, histological progression, varices, ascites or encephalopathy, sustained quadrupling of bilirubin, marked worsening of fatigue or pruritus, intolerance, or withdrawal.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in time to treatment failure (relative risk of treatment failure with ursodiol 1.01, 95% CI 0.6–1.7) — the treatment made no difference. During the first two years, treatment was unsuccessful in 17 of 32 placebo patients (53%) and 16 of 31 ursodiol patients (52%), and there was no difference in time to liver transplantation or in patients with early-stage disease. Ursodiol, but not placebo, improved serum alkaline phosphatase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin and albumin at one and two years — the blood tests improved while the clinical outcome did not.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a broad composite dominated by soft components (symptom worsening, withdrawal, laboratory quadrupling), so the trial is most informative read alongside its own transplantation result — also null — and the meta-analyses below; it was not powered for death or transplantation alone.
cards.source: Lindor KD et al. Ursodiol for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Mayo Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis-Ursodeoxycholic Acid Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1997. PMID: 9041099. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shi 2009 meta-analysis: across 8 randomised trials (465 patients), ursodeoxycholic acid had no significant effect on death, liver transplantation, or the two combined
cards.summary: Shi 2009 meta-analysis: across 8 randomised trials (465 patients), ursodeoxycholic acid had no significant effect on death, liver transplantation, or the two combined
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials (465 patients) comparing ursodeoxycholic acid with placebo or no treatment in primary sclerosing cholangitis, searched to January 2009.
cards.result: Ursodeoxycholic acid significantly improved liver biochemistry but had no effect on pruritus or fatigue, and no significant effect on the incidence of death, liver transplantation, or death and/or liver transplantation — the treatment made no difference to transplant-free survival. A borderline difference favoured ursodeoxycholic acid for histological improvement (odds ratio 9.19, 95% CI 0.98–86.15, P = 0.05), with trends toward less histological deterioration and better cholangiographic appearances that the authors describe as trends, not established effects.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials mix standard and higher doses and are individually small; the very wide confidence interval on histological improvement (0.98–86.15) shows how little histology data exists — it should not be read as a survival signal.
cards.source: Shi J et al. Ursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Hepatology research : the official journal of the Japan Society of Hepatology. 2009. PMID: 19467021. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Triantos 2011 meta-analysis: across 8 randomised trials (567 patients), neither standard-dose nor high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improved mortality or transplantation outcomes
cards.summary: Triantos 2011 meta-analysis: across 8 randomised trials (567 patients), neither standard-dose nor high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improved mortality or transplantation outcomes
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 8 randomised clinical trials (567 patients) of standard-dose (>15 mg/kg/day defined as high dose in this review; five standard-dose and three high-dose trials) ursodeoxycholic acid versus placebo or no intervention in primary sclerosing cholangitis; endpoints were mortality or liver transplantation, pruritus, fatigue, cholangiocarcinoma and histological progression.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mortality (odds ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.4–1.4, as printed in the record), pruritus, fatigue, cholangiocarcinoma, or histology stage progression, and no differences were found in the dose subgroup analyses — the treatment made no difference at either dose range. The authors conclude that neither standard nor high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid influences the progression of primary sclerosing cholangitis favourably.
cards.watchOut: This review pools the high-dose trials whose harm is homed on pack #2782 with the standard-dose trials; its standard-dose subgroup is the part that answers this shelf's question, and it is null there too — the pooled null must not be used to imply standard-dose harm, which the high-dose trial alone established.
cards.source: Triantos CK et al. Meta-analysis: ursodeoxycholic acid for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2011. PMID: 21883323. Registry ID: none in the record.
