cards.headline: Synthesis: standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver blood tests in primary sclerosing cholangitis but has never been shown to improve transplant-free survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver blood tests in primary sclerosing cholangitis but has never been shown to improve transplant-free survival
cards.people: The carded evidence: one standard-dose placebo-controlled trial (Lindor 1997, 105 patients) and two meta-analyses of the randomised trials (Shi 2009, 465 patients; Triantos 2011, 567 patients, overlapping trial sets).
cards.result: Every clinical endpoint agrees: time to treatment failure relative risk 1.01 (Lindor), no significant effect on death, transplantation, or the combined outcome in either meta-analysis, while liver biochemistry consistently improves. The high-dose harm question is answered separately on pack #2782 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid does not improve transplant-free survival versus no treatment.
cards.watchOut: Absence of a survival benefit in small, short trials is not proof of a zero effect on rare late outcomes — but after three decades the burden of proof sits with benefit, and none has been shown at standard dose.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lindor KD et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1997 (PMID: 9041099); Shi J et al. Hepatology research : the official journal of the Japan Society of Hepatology. 2009 (PMID: 19467021); Triantos CK et al. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2011 (PMID: 21883323).

shelves.title: Endoscopic surveillance in gastric intestinal metaplasia (observational only): the cancer risk is real and quantified, but no study shows surveillance prevents gastric cancer death
shelves.question: In adults with gastric intestinal metaplasia, does endoscopic surveillance reduce gastric cancer death versus no surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Confidence Intervals · Disease Progression · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastric Mucosa · Gastritis, Atrophic · Humans · Incidence · Male · Metaplasia · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Odds Ratio · Population Surveillance · Precancerous Conditions · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Stomach Neoplasms · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — printed on the face, because this is a GAP-E question and the evidence is observational by design: there is no randomised comparison of surveillance versus no surveillance in gastric intestinal metaplasia, and no carded study compares gastric cancer death between surveyed and unsurveilled patients. What the cohorts do establish is the risk surveillance would have to act on: in the Dutch nationwide cohort (de Vries 2008), intestinal metaplasia carried an annual gastric cancer incidence of 0.25% within 5 years of diagnosis, yet only 28% of intestinal-metaplasia patients received any re-evaluation — surveillance practice was inconsistent with the risk. The Swedish population cohort (Song 2015) puts the annual incidence at 129 per 100,000 (standardised incidence ratio 3.4 versus the general population) and estimates about 1 in 39 people with intestinal metaplasia develops gastric cancer within 20 years. The only carded study that compares surveillance strategies (Zhang 2018, China) found that in extensive atrophic gastritis/intestinal metaplasia a 2–3-year surveillance interval was associated with earlier detection of gastric cancer — earlier detection, not shown lower mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): surveillance detects cancers in a genuinely at-risk group and may shift stage at detection, but a reduction in gastric cancer death versus no surveillance has never been demonstrated.

cards.headline: de Vries 2008: in a nationwide Dutch cohort, intestinal metaplasia carried a 0.25% annual gastric cancer incidence — yet only 28% of patients received any endoscopic re-evaluation
cards.summary: de Vries 2008: in a nationwide Dutch cohort, intestinal metaplasia carried a 0.25% annual gastric cancer incidence — yet only 28% of patients received any endoscopic re-evaluation
cards.people: All patients in the Dutch nationwide histopathology registry (PALGA) with a first diagnosis of a premalignant gastric lesion between 1991 and 2004, followed to December 2005: 22,365 with atrophic gastritis, 61,707 with intestinal metaplasia, 7,616 with mild-to-moderate dysplasia and 562 with severe dysplasia. Observational cohort; surveillance was whatever clinicians actually did, not an assigned strategy.
cards.result: The annual incidence of gastric cancer within 5 years of diagnosis was 0.1% for atrophic gastritis, 0.25% for intestinal metaplasia, 0.6% for mild-to-moderate dysplasia and 6% for severe dysplasia. Re-evaluation was received by only 26% of atrophic gastritis, 28% of intestinal metaplasia and 38% of mild-to-moderate dysplasia patients, versus 61% after severe dysplasia (P < .001). Risk rose with lesion severity (severe dysplasia hazard ratio 40.14, 95% CI 32.2–50.1), age and male sex (hazard ratio 1.50, 95% CI 1.3–1.7). The study quantifies risk and documents under-surveillance; it does not compare cancer death between surveyed and unsurveilled patients.
cards.watchOut: Registry follow-up captures cancers that occur, not cancers prevented: a cohort like this can justify asking the surveillance question but cannot answer it — lead-time and selection effects mean even a surveyed-versus-unsurveyed mortality split here would not be causal evidence.
cards.source: de Vries AC et al. Gastric cancer risk in patients with premalignant gastric lesions: a nationwide cohort study in the Netherlands. Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18395075. Registry ID: none in the record. it does not compare cancer death between surveyed and unsurveilled patients. registry follow-up captures cancers that occur, not cancers prevented: a cohort like this can justify asking the surveillance question but cannot answer it — lead-time and selection effects mean even a surveyed-versus-unsurveyed mortality split here would not be causal evidence. de vries ac et al. gastric cancer risk in patients with premalignant gastric lesions: a nationwide cohort study in the netherlands. gastroenterology. 2008. pmid: 18395075. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adenocarcinoma · adult · age factors · aged · aged, 80 and over · confidence intervals · disease progression · endoscopy, gastrointestinal · female · follow-up studies · gastric mucosa · gastritis, atrophic · humans · incidence · male · metaplasia · middle aged · netherlands · odds ratio · population surveillance · precancerous conditions · retrospective studies · risk factors · stomach neoplasms · time factors

cards.headline: Song 2015: in 405,172 Swedish patients, intestinal metaplasia carried an annual gastric cancer incidence of 129 per 100,000 — about 1 in 39 develop gastric cancer within 20 years
cards.summary: Song 2015: in 405,172 Swedish patients, intestinal metaplasia carried an annual gastric cancer incidence of 129 per 100,000 — about 1 in 39 develop gastric cancer within 20 years
cards.people: Population-based Swedish cohort of 405,172 patients who had gastric biopsies for non-malignant indications between 1979 and 2011, grouped by mucosal findings from normal mucosa through intestinal metaplasia to dysplasia; observational, with standardised incidence ratios against the general population and hazard ratios against the normal-mucosa group.
cards.result: After excluding the first two years of follow-up, 1,599 gastric cancers were identified. Annual crude incidence was 20 per 100,000 with normal mucosa (standardised incidence ratio 1.0), 100 per 100,000 for atrophic gastritis (2.8), 129 per 100,000 for intestinal metaplasia (3.4) and 263 per 100,000 for dysplasia (6.5); the dysplasia-versus-normal-mucosa hazard ratio was 10.9 (95% CI 7.7–15.4). The authors estimate that about 1 in 39 people with intestinal metaplasia will develop gastric cancer within 20 years, and state these numbers, with cost-benefit analyses, should guide surveillance policy — the study itself tests no surveillance strategy and reports no surveillance mortality effect.
cards.watchOut: Sweden is a low-incidence Western population and everyone in the cohort had a clinical reason for endoscopy; absolute risks — and therefore any plausible absolute benefit of surveillance — will differ in high-incidence East Asian populations, where most surveillance programmes operate.
cards.source: Song H et al. Incidence of gastric cancer among patients with gastric precancerous lesions: observational cohort study in a low risk Western population. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2015. PMID: 26215280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2018: in 332 Chinese patients with atrophic gastritis (with intestinal metaplasia), a 2–3-year surveillance interval in extensive disease was associated with earlier gastric cancer detection — not with a shown mortality difference
cards.summary: Zhang 2018: in 332 Chinese patients with atrophic gastritis (with intestinal metaplasia), a 2–3-year surveillance interval in extensive disease was associated with earlier gastric cancer detection — not with a shown mortality difference
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 332 patients with atrophic gastritis (location of atrophy and intestinal metaplasia recorded) first scoped between 2002 and 2005 in China, followed long-term; the analysis examined whether the endoscopic surveillance interval was associated with the stage at which gastric neoplasia was found. Observational — intervals were not randomised.
cards.result: Gastric neoplasia was diagnosed in 16 patients; annual incidence per person-year was 0.53% for total gastric neoplasia, 0.20% for early gastric cancer and 0.33% for advanced gastric cancer. Risk factors included atrophic gastritis and/or intestinal metaplasia involving both antrum and corpus (hazard ratio 2.898, P < .001) and Helicobacter pylori infection (hazard ratio 3.946, P = .018). In the extensive-disease group, a 2- to 3-year surveillance interval was associated with early detection of gastric cancer (P = .008, hazard ratio 0.015 as printed in the record). No mortality comparison between surveillance intervals or against no surveillance is reported.
cards.watchOut: Only 16 neoplasia events drive the interval analysis, the hazard ratio of 0.015 rests on very few early cancers, and patients who attend regular surveillance differ from those who do not — this is hypothesis-level support for surveillance intervals, not evidence that surveillance saves lives.
cards.source: Zhang L et al. Occurrence of gastric cancer in patients with atrophic gastritis during long-term follow-up. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29911441. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the risk that surveillance targets is well measured; whether surveillance itself reduces gastric cancer death is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: the risk that surveillance targets is well measured; whether surveillance itself reduces gastric cancer death is untested
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational: two nationwide Western cohorts (de Vries 2008, over 92,000 patients with premalignant lesions; Song 2015, 405,172 biopsied patients) and one Chinese surveillance-interval cohort (Zhang 2018, 332 patients). No randomised trial of surveillance versus no surveillance in gastric intestinal metaplasia exists in the carded record.
cards.result: Intestinal metaplasia carries an annual gastric cancer incidence of about 0.25% (de Vries) to 129 per 100,000 (Song), roughly 1 in 39 over 20 years; actual surveillance uptake in the Dutch cohort was only 28%, and the one interval comparison associates 2–3-yearly surveillance of extensive disease with earlier-stage detection. None of this demonstrates fewer gastric cancer deaths with surveillance than without it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): a mortality benefit is plausible and is the premise of MAPS-style guidance, but it remains unproven by any direct comparison.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the precision of the incidence numbers borrow certainty for the intervention: this shelf's honest answer is that the death benefit of surveillance in intestinal metaplasia is an inference from risk plus stage shift, not a measured outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of de Vries AC et al. Gastroenterology. 2008 (PMID: 18395075); Song H et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2015 (PMID: 26215280); Zhang L et al. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2018 (PMID: 29911441).

shelves.title: Pregabalin for chronic pancreatitis pain: one small positive placebo trial, a combination trial that cannot isolate the drug, and a mechanistic substudy of the same patients
shelves.question: In adults with chronic pancreatitis, does pregabalin reduce pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adult · Aged · Analgesics · Double-Blind Method · Female · Health Status · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Pancreatitis, Chronic · Pregabalin · Quality of Life · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, because the direct evidence is a single small short trial. Olesen 2011 randomised 64 patients with painful chronic pancreatitis to escalating pregabalin or placebo for 3 weeks as adjuvant therapy: pain relief was greater with pregabalin (36% vs 24%; mean difference 12%) and more pregabalin patients rated themselves much or very much improved (44% vs 21%). A mechanistic substudy of the same trial's patients (Bouwense 2015) found pregabalin responders — unlike placebo responders — showed anti-hyperalgesic changes and increased conditioned pain modulation, which supports a real central effect but adds no new patients. The only other randomised report (Sureshkumar 2021, 90 patients) tested pregabalin combined with antioxidants against placebo, so its positive result cannot be attributed to pregabalin alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: pregabalin probably reduces chronic pancreatitis pain modestly in the short term; there is no long-term or pregabalin-alone replication trial.

cards.headline: Olesen 2011: in 64 patients with painful chronic pancreatitis, 3 weeks of pregabalin relieved pain more than placebo (36% vs 24% relief; 44% vs 21% much or very much improved)
cards.summary: Olesen 2011: in 64 patients with painful chronic pancreatitis, 3 weeks of pregabalin relieved pain more than placebo (36% vs 24% relief; 44% vs 21% much or very much improved)
cards.people: 64 patients with pain from chronic pancreatitis randomised double-blind to increasing doses of pregabalin or placebo for 3 consecutive weeks as adjuvant analgesic therapy; the primary endpoint was pain relief on a visual analogue scale recorded in a pain diary, with Patients' Global Impression of Change, functional scales, quality of life and tolerability as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: Pregabalin produced more effective pain relief after 3 weeks than placebo (36% vs 24%; mean difference 12%, 95% CI 22%–2% as printed in the record, P = .02). The proportion rating their health status much or very much improved was higher with pregabalin (44% vs 21%, P = .048). Changes in physical and functional scales, pain character, quality of life and the number of serious adverse events were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: Three weeks is a very short horizon for a lifelong pain condition, the absolute advantage is modest (12 percentage points of relief), and pregabalin was an add-on to existing analgesia — the trial does not show what pregabalin does alone or beyond the first month.
cards.source: Olesen SS et al. Pregabalin reduces pain in patients with chronic pancreatitis in a randomized, controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21683078. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bouwense 2015: within the same trial's patients, pregabalin responders showed anti-hyperalgesic and pain-modulation changes that placebo responders did not
cards.summary: Bouwense 2015: within the same trial's patients, pregabalin responders showed anti-hyperalgesic and pain-modulation changes that placebo responders did not
cards.type: Mechanistic substudy of a randomised trial (Bouwense 2015)
cards.people: Post-hoc mechanistic analysis of 60 patients from the Olesen randomised trial of pregabalin versus placebo in chronic pancreatitis, grouped as responders (>30% pain reduction after 3 weeks) or non-responders to pregabalin (16 responders, 15 non-responders) or placebo (12 responders, 17 non-responders); pain sensitivity was measured with electric pain detection thresholds and conditioned pain modulation before and after treatment.
cards.result: Electric pain detection threshold change at dermatome C5 was greater in pregabalin responders than placebo responders (1.3 mA vs −0.1 mA, P = 0.015), and conditioned pain modulation increased more in pregabalin responders (9% vs −17%, P < 0.001), changing significantly from baseline only in pregabalin responders (P = 0.006). The authors call the study hypothesis-generating: pain relief with pregabalin was associated with anti-hyperalgesic effects and increased endogenous inhibitory modulation, unlike placebo response.
cards.watchOut: These are the same patients as the Olesen trial, re-analysed post hoc by responder status — this card adds mechanism, not independent confirmation, and responder-defined subgroups can manufacture apparent differences.
cards.source: Bouwense SA et al. Pregabalin and placebo responders show different effects on central pain processing in chronic pancreatitis patients. Journal of pain research. 2015. PMID: 26203273. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Sureshkumar 2021: pregabalin combined with antioxidants beat placebo over 8 weeks (90 patients) — but the combination design cannot isolate pregabalin's contribution
cards.summary: Sureshkumar 2021: pregabalin combined with antioxidants beat placebo over 8 weeks (90 patients) — but the combination design cannot isolate pregabalin's contribution
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of combination therapy (Sureshkumar 2021)
cards.people: 90 patients with chronic pancreatitis randomised double-blind to pregabalin plus antioxidant therapy or matched placebo for 8 weeks; primary outcomes were change in maximum pain intensity (visual analogue scale) and Izbicki pain score, with painful days, analgesic requirements, quality of life, hospital admissions and satisfaction as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: The combination group had a significant reduction in pain intensity versus placebo (visual analogue scale figures reported as 2 ± 0.8 vs 1.3 ± 0.9, P = 0.007, as printed in the record), fewer non-opioid analgesic requirement days (54.4 ± 2.9 vs 55.7 ± 1.5, P = 0.014) and fewer hospital admissions (0.2 ± 0.5 vs 0.6 ± 0.7, P = 0.002), with more patients satisfied (18% vs 11%, P = 0.03, as printed). The authors conclude the pregabalin–antioxidant combination significantly reduces pain in chronic pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: Antioxidants were given with pregabalin in the active arm and neither drug alone was tested, so this trial supports the combination only; some of its printed summary figures are internally hard to parse, and its effect sizes should be quoted only as the record gives them.
cards.source: Sureshkumar S et al. Efficacy of Pregabalin and Antioxidants Combination in Reducing Pain in Chronic Pancreatitis: A Double Blind Randomized Trial. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2021. PMID: 33206270. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/05/008492 (as given in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: pregabalin probably helps chronic pancreatitis pain modestly and briefly — one small direct trial carries the claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: pregabalin probably helps chronic pancreatitis pain modestly and briefly — one small direct trial carries the claim
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct placebo-controlled trial (Olesen 2011, 64 patients, 3 weeks), its mechanistic substudy in the same patients (Bouwense 2015, 60 analysed), and one combination-therapy trial (Sureshkumar 2021, 90 patients). Independent patients total about 154, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, but the direct-evidence base is a single trial.
cards.result: Pregabalin beat placebo on pain relief (36% vs 24%) and global improvement (44% vs 21%) in the only trial of pregabalin alone; mechanistic data from that trial are consistent with a central anti-hyperalgesic effect, and a pregabalin-plus-antioxidant combination also beat placebo without isolating pregabalin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a modest short-term benefit is likely real but rests on one small trial, with no long-term data.
cards.watchOut: Sedation, dizziness and misuse potential are class concerns for gabapentinoids in a population often already on opioids; none of the carded trials runs long enough to weigh those harms against continued benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Olesen SS et al. Gastroenterology. 2011 (PMID: 21683078); Bouwense SA et al. Journal of pain research. 2015 (PMID: 26203273); Sureshkumar S et al. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2021 (PMID: 33206270).

shelves.title: Itopride for functional dyspepsia: a positive phase II trial, two null phase III trials, and a modestly positive mixed-comparator meta-analysis — a split record
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does itopride improve symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Benzamides · Benzyl Compounds · Dopamine D2 Receptor Antagonists · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prolactin · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: SPLIT — printed on the face. The dyspepsia shelves elsewhere in the library cover tricyclics, buspirone and STW 5; itopride itself had no home, and its record genuinely divides. Holtmann 2006 (the phase IIb trial, 554 patients) found itopride 50–200 mg three times daily clearly beat placebo: 57%, 59% and 64% of patients were symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41% on placebo. The two phase III trials that followed (Talley 2008, about 1,170 patients) found global responder rates essentially identical to placebo in both trials (45.2% vs 45.6% and 37.8% vs 35.4% — the treatment made no difference on the co-primary global assessment), with only one of the two showing a Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire responder advantage. A 2012 meta-analysis of 9 trials (2,620 patients) pooling placebo, domperidone and mosapride controls found a modest itopride advantage (global assessment relative risk 1.11). PROPOSED SPLIT: itopride's benefit over placebo is unproven at phase III standard despite a positive early trial and a positive mixed-comparator meta-analysis.

cards.headline: Holtmann 2006: in 554 patients with functional dyspepsia, itopride beat placebo — 57–64% symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41%
cards.summary: Holtmann 2006: in 554 patients with functional dyspepsia, itopride beat placebo — 57–64% symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41%
cards.people: 554 patients with functional dyspepsia randomised to itopride 50, 100 or 200 mg three times daily or placebo for 8 weeks; 523 had outcome data. Primary endpoints were change in Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire symptom severity, patients' global assessment (proportion symptom-free or markedly improved), and pain/fullness severity.
cards.result: After 8 weeks, 41% of placebo patients were symptom-free or had marked improvement, versus 57%, 59% and 64% on itopride 50, 100 and 200 mg respectively (P < 0.05 for all comparisons). Symptom score improved most in the 100- and 200-mg groups (−6.24 and −6.27 vs −4.50 on placebo, P = 0.05), and the combined pain-and-fullness response favoured itopride (73% vs 63%, P = 0.04).
cards.watchOut: This was the phase IIb trial that justified the phase III programme — and phase II results in functional dyspepsia, a condition with very high placebo response (41% here), are exactly the results that most often fail to replicate, as the next card shows.

cards.search: holtmann 2006: in 554 patients with functional dyspepsia, itopride beat placebo — 57–64% symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41% holtmann 2006: in 554 patients with functional dyspepsia, itopride beat placebo — 57–64% symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41% in adults with functional dyspepsia, does itopride improve symptoms versus placebo? randomised controlled trial (holtmann 2006) 554 patients with functional dyspepsia randomised to itopride 50, 100 or 200 mg three times daily or placebo for 8 weeks; 523 had outcome data. primary endpoints were change in leeds dyspepsia questionnaire symptom severity, patients' global assessment (proportion symptom-free or markedly improved), and pain/fullness severity. after 8 weeks, 41% of placebo patients were symptom-free or had marked improvement, versus 57%, 59% and 64% on itopride 50, 100 and 200 mg respectively (p < 0.05 for all comparisons). symptom score improved most in the 100- and 200-mg groups (−6.24 and −6.27 vs −4.50 on placebo, p = 0.05), and the combined pain-and-fullness response favoured itopride (73% vs 63%, p = 0.04). this was the phase iib trial that justified the phase iii programme — and phase ii results in functional dyspepsia, a condition with very high placebo response (41% here), are exactly the results that most often fail to replicate, as the next card shows. holtmann g et al. a placebo-controlled trial of itopride in functional dyspepsia. the new england journal of medicine. 2006. pmid: 16495395. registry id: nct00272103. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · benzamides · benzyl compounds · dopamine d2 receptor antagonists · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · dyspepsia · female · humans · male · middle aged · prolactin · quality of life

cards.headline: Talley 2008: two phase III trials found itopride no better than placebo on global symptom response (45.2% vs 45.6% and 37.8% vs 35.4% — the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Talley 2008: two phase III trials found itopride no better than placebo on global symptom response (45.2% vs 45.6% and 37.8% vs 35.4% — the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials, phase III (Talley 2008)
cards.people: Two similar multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (International and North American) in men and women aged 18–65 with functional dyspepsia by Rome II criteria, negative endoscopy and Helicobacter pylori-negative, randomised to itopride 100 mg three times daily or placebo for 8 weeks (579 patients received itopride and 591 placebo across the programme, per the record's safety counts). Co-primary endpoints were global patient assessment of efficacy and the Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire.
cards.result: Global responder rates at week 8 were similar on itopride and placebo in both trials (45.2% vs 45.6% and 37.8% vs 35.4%, P = NS) — the treatment made no difference on the global co-primary endpoint. A Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire responder benefit appeared in the International trial (62% vs 52.7%, P = 0.04) but not the North American trial (46.9% vs 44.8%). Safety and tolerability were comparable with placebo except prolactin elevations, which occurred more often on itopride (18/579) than placebo (1/591). The authors conclude itopride did not show a difference in symptom response from placebo in this population.
cards.watchOut: These trials enrolled a narrower population (Helicobacter pylori-negative, heartburn almost excluded) than Holtmann's, so the split may partly reflect who was studied — but as the larger, confirmatory programme, its null global result is the one a prescriber must answer to.

cards.headline: Huang 2012 meta-analysis: across 9 trials (2,620 patients), itopride showed a modest advantage — global assessment relative risk 1.11 — against a mix of placebo and other prokinetics
cards.summary: Huang 2012 meta-analysis: across 9 trials (2,620 patients), itopride showed a modest advantage — global assessment relative risk 1.11 — against a mix of placebo and other prokinetics
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 9 randomised controlled trials enrolling 2,620 patients with functional dyspepsia (1,372 itopride, 1,248 controls), where control groups received placebo, domperidone or mosapride; outcomes were global patient assessment, postprandial fullness, early satiety and Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire score.
cards.result: Itopride was superior to the pooled controls for global patient assessment (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.19, P = 0.006), postprandial fullness (relative risk 1.21, 95% CI 1.03–1.44) and early satiety (relative risk 1.24, 95% CI 1.01–1.53), with a Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire weighted mean deviation of −1.38 (95% CI −1.75 to −1.01). Adverse-effect incidence was similar between groups and funnel plots showed no evidence of publication bias. These are relative measures; the record does not give the pooled absolute responder rates for the placebo-only subset.
cards.watchOut: Pooling placebo with active prokinetic comparators blurs exactly the question this shelf asks; the pooled advantage is driven substantially by the earlier positive trials, including Holtmann 2006, and does not overturn the phase III programme's placebo comparison.
cards.source: Huang X et al. Itopride therapy for functional dyspepsia: a meta-analysis. World journal of gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 23326147. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: itopride's evidence splits by trial generation — early promise, confirmatory failure, modest pooled signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: itopride's evidence splits by trial generation — early promise, confirmatory failure, modest pooled signal
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase IIb placebo-controlled trial (Holtmann 2006, 554 randomised), two phase III placebo-controlled trials (Talley 2008, about 1,170 patients), and one meta-analysis of 9 trials (Huang 2012, 2,620 patients, overlapping the trials).
cards.result: Holtmann found a 16–23 percentage-point responder advantage over placebo; Talley found none on global assessment in either of two trials; Huang's pooled relative risk of 1.11 for global assessment sits between them but mixes comparators. PROPOSED SPLIT: itopride cannot be stamped as effective versus placebo on the confirmatory evidence, nor as useless on the early evidence — the honest stamp names the split.
cards.watchOut: Itopride is not approved in the United States or much of Europe, so this shelf answers an evidence question for the many health systems where it is prescribed; prolactin elevation is its one consistent safety signal across the programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Holtmann G et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16495395); Talley NJ et al. Gut. 2008 (PMID: 17965059); Huang X et al. World journal of gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 23326147).

shelves.title: Direct-acting antivirals in people who inject drugs (PARTIAL completion of live #593): cure rates of 87–94% — close to general-population rates, with no randomised comparison against non-users
shelves.question: In adults with hepatitis C who inject drugs, do direct-acting antivirals achieve cure rates as high as in non-users?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antiviral Agents · Carbamates · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Packaging · Female · Genotype · Hepacivirus · Hepatitis C, Chronic · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Sofosbuvir · Substance Abuse, Intravenous · Sustained Virologic Response · Benzimidazoles · Benzopyrans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #593 answers direct-acting antiviral (DAA) cure rates generally (90–99% sustained virological response, SVR, in the registration trials); this shelf asks only about the people-who-inject-drugs population that #593 does not break out, and no #593 PMID is re-carded here. (The compensated- and decompensated-cirrhosis slices are homed elsewhere — wave-15 #5967 and wave-17 #6085 — and are not this population.) No trial randomises people who inject drugs against non-users, so the comparison is cross-study: SIMPLIFY (sofosbuvir-velpatasvir, 103 people with injection in the past 6 months) achieved 94% SVR12 with no virological failures; D3FEAT (a genotype-1 regimen, 87 people) achieved 91%; and the Hajarizadeh meta-analysis (38 studies, 3,634 participants) pooled SVR at 87.4% in people with recent injecting, 87.7% with recent drug use and 90.7% on opioid substitution therapy — a few points below registration-trial rates, with losses to follow-up, not virological failure, accounting for most of the gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence): cure rates in people who inject drugs are high and close to those in non-users, and ongoing drug use did not reduce cure in either prospective study.

cards.headline: SIMPLIFY 2018: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir cured 94% of 103 people with recent injection drug use — with zero virological failures
cards.summary: SIMPLIFY 2018: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir cured 94% of 103 people with recent injection drug use — with zero virological failures
cards.people: 103 participants with chronic hepatitis C (genotypes 1–6) and injection drug use in the past 6 months, recruited at 19 sites in seven countries, treated open-label with sofosbuvir 400 mg plus velpatasvir 100 mg once daily for 12 weeks in weekly electronic blister packs; 59% were receiving opioid substitution therapy, 74% had injected in the past month, 26% injected at least daily, and 9% had cirrhosis. Single-arm phase 4 trial — there was no non-user comparator group.
cards.result: 100 of 103 participants (97%) completed treatment; two were lost to follow-up and one died of overdose. There were no virological failures, and 97 of 103 (94%, 95% CI 88–98) achieved SVR12 (cure). The three participants with an end-of-treatment response who did not reach SVR12 were two losses to follow-up and one reinfection. Drug use before and during treatment did not affect SVR12. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 48 participants (47%, one grade 3, no grade 4); seven (7%) had a serious adverse event, one possibly treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm trial can show a regimen works in this population but cannot by itself prove equality with non-users — that comparison borrows the general-population rates from live #593, and SIMPLIFY's supported setting (weekly blister packs, study follow-up) may flatter completion versus routine care.
cards.source: Grebely J et al. Sofosbuvir and velpatasvir for hepatitis C virus infection in people with recent injection drug use (SIMPLIFY): an open-label, single-arm, phase 4, multicentre trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2018. PMID: 29310928. Registry ID: NCT02336139. cards.headline: D3FEAT 2018: a genotype-1 direct-acting regimen cured 91% of 87 people with recent injecting drug use or on opioid substitution therapy
cards.summary: D3FEAT 2018: a genotype-1 direct-acting regimen cured 91% of 87 people with recent injecting drug use or on opioid substitution therapy
cards.people: 87 treatment-naive participants with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1, recent injecting drug use (previous 6 months) and/or receiving opioid substitution therapy, recruited internationally; 71% were receiving opioid substitution therapy, 61% had injected in the previous six months, 45% in the previous month and 15% more than daily; 8% had cirrhosis. Treatment was paritaprevir/ritonavir, ombitasvir and dasabuvir with ribavirin (genotype 1a) or without (genotype 1b) for 12 weeks in weekly electronic blister packs. Open-label, single-arm.
cards.result: Treatment completion was 97% (84 of 87), with no virological breakthroughs. SVR12 was 91% (79 of 87, 95% CI 83%–96%). Of the five participants who completed treatment without SVR, one was lost to follow-up, one died, and three had virologic relapse. Drug use before and during treatment did not affect SVR12. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 46 participants (53%, six grade 3, no grade 4), and two cases of reinfection were observed.
cards.watchOut: The paritaprevir-based regimen is no longer a standard first-line choice and the study mixes recent injectors with people only on opioid substitution therapy; its value here is as an independent second programme showing the same pattern — high cure, losses driven by follow-up rather than drug failure.
cards.source: Grebely J et al. Paritaprevir, ritonavir, ombitasvir, and dasabuvir with and without ribavirin in people with HCV genotype 1 and recent injecting drug use or receiving opioid substitution therapy. The International journal on drug policy. 2018. PMID: 30384028. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hajarizadeh 2018 meta-analysis: pooling 38 studies (3,634 participants), cure was 87.4% in people with recent injecting drug use and 90.7% on opioid substitution therapy
cards.summary: Hajarizadeh 2018 meta-analysis: pooling 38 studies (3,634 participants), cure was 87.4% in people with recent injecting drug use and 90.7% on opioid substitution therapy
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 38 observational studies and clinical trials (3,634 participants) of direct-acting antiviral treatment in people with recent drug use and people receiving opioid substitution therapy; recent injecting drug use was assessed in 8 studies with 670 participants. Definitions of recent drug use varied, most commonly use in the past 6 months or at/during treatment.
cards.result: Among people with recent injecting drug use, treatment completion was 96.9% (95% CI 95.6–98.2) and SVR was 87.4% (95% CI 82.0–92.8). Among people with recent injecting or non-injecting drug use (21 studies, 1,408 participants), SVR was 87.7% (95% CI 84.2–91.3); among those receiving opioid substitution therapy (36 studies, 2,987 participants), SVR was 90.7% (95% CI 88.5–93.0). In meta-regression, clinical trials (versus observational studies) and older age were associated with higher SVR. The authors conclude responses were favourable in all groups, supporting broader treatment access.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 87–91% sits a few points below the 90–99% registration-trial rates on live #593, and the included studies are mostly observational with varying definitions of recent use — the gap is consistent with loss to follow-up in real-world cohorts rather than reduced drug potency, but this design cannot prove the two populations cure identically.
cards.source: Hajarizadeh B et al. Direct-acting antiviral treatment for hepatitis C among people who use or inject drugs: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2018. PMID: 30245064. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: people who inject drugs are cured at rates close to non-users — the shortfall is follow-up, not virology
cards.summary: Synthesis: people who inject drugs are cured at rates close to non-users — the shortfall is follow-up, not virology
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective single-arm treatment studies (SIMPLIFY, 103 participants; D3FEAT, 87 participants) and one meta-analysis of 38 studies (3,634 participants). No randomised or head-to-head comparison against non-users exists; the non-user benchmark (90–99% SVR) is homed on live shelf #593 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Cure (SVR12) was 94% in SIMPLIFY and 91% in D3FEAT, with no virological failures in SIMPLIFY and drug use during treatment not affecting cure in either study; pooled SVR was 87.4% for recent injecting and 90.7% on opioid substitution therapy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence): direct-acting antivirals achieve cure rates in people who inject drugs that approach those in non-users, and withholding treatment for ongoing use is not supported by these data.
cards.watchOut: Reinfection after cure is a real risk in this population (cases appear in both prospective studies) — high cure rates answer the treatment question, not the separate question of keeping people cured, which depends on harm-reduction and follow-up services.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grebely J et al. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2018 (PMID: 29310928); Grebely J et al. The International journal on drug policy. 2018 (PMID: 30384028); Hajarizadeh B et al. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2018 (PMID: 30245064).

shelves.title: Endoscopic combination therapy for bleeding peptic ulcer: adding a second method to epinephrine injection cuts rebleeding from about 19% to 10% and halves mortality
shelves.question: In adults with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulcer, does endoscopic combination therapy reduce rebleeding compared with epinephrine injection alone?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Epinephrine · Hemostasis, Endoscopic · Humans · Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Secondary Prevention · Vasoconstrictor Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. The index already homes second-look endoscopy (pack #3589) and endoscopy timing for ulcer bleeding; the combination-therapy question — whether epinephrine injection alone is enough — was not shelved. It is one of the most concordant answers in ulcer bleeding: the Cochrane review (Vergara 2007; 17 trials, 1,763 patients) found adding a second endoscopic method after epinephrine reduced further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4% (Peto odds ratio 0.51), emergency surgery from 10.8% to 7.1% and mortality from 5% to 2.5%. The earlier Calvet meta-analysis (16 trials, 1,673 patients) found near-identical absolute rates (rebleeding 18.4% to 10.6%; mortality 5.1% to 2.6%). The largest single trial carded (Chung 1997, adrenaline plus heat probe in actively bleeding ulcers) was neutral overall but showed the benefit concentrated where the meta-analyses predict it — spurting haemorrhage, where operative intervention fell from 29.6% to 6.5%. PROPOSED LIKELY: epinephrine injection should not be used alone for high-risk bleeding ulcers; a second method (thermal, clip or other injection) reduces rebleeding, surgery and death.

cards.headline: Vergara 2007 Cochrane review: across 17 trials (1,763 patients), adding a second endoscopic method to epinephrine cut further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4% and mortality from 5% to 2.5%
cards.summary: Vergara 2007 Cochrane review: across 17 trials (1,763 patients), adding a second endoscopic method to epinephrine cut further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4% and mortality from 5% to 2.5%
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 17 randomised studies (1,763 people) in adults with high-risk bleeding peptic ulcers (major Forrest stigmata, bleeding confirmed by endoscopy), comparing epinephrine injection alone with epinephrine plus a second haemostatic method (thermal, clip or other agent).
cards.result: Adding a second procedure reduced further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4% (Peto odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.39–0.66), emergency surgery from 10.8% to 7.1% (odds ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.45–0.89) and mortality from 5% to 2.5% (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.30–0.82). Subanalysis showed the further-bleeding risk fell regardless of which second procedure was applied and in all subgroups. The authors conclude additional endoscopic treatment after epinephrine injection reduces further bleeding, surgery and mortality.
cards.watchOut: The trials span eras and second methods (heat probe, clips, sclerosants), so the review establishes the class principle — never epinephrine alone — rather than crowning one second method; mortality events are few (about 5% baseline), so the mortality estimate is less precise than the rebleeding estimate.

cards.headline: Calvet 2004 meta-analysis: across 16 trials (1,673 patients), a second procedure after epinephrine reduced further bleeding from 18.4% to 10.6% and mortality from 5.1% to 2.6%
cards.summary: Calvet 2004 meta-analysis: across 16 trials (1,673 patients), a second procedure after epinephrine reduced further bleeding from 18.4% to 10.6% and mortality from 5.1% to 2.6%
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (1,673 patients) comparing epinephrine injection alone versus epinephrine plus a second endoscopic method in high-risk bleeding peptic ulcers, searched in MEDLINE, EMBASE and AGA congress abstracts 1990–2002.
cards.result: Adding a second procedure reduced the further bleeding rate from 18.4% to 10.6% (Peto odds ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.69), emergency surgery from 11.3% to 7.6% (odds ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.46–0.90) and mortality from 5.1% to 2.6% (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.31–0.84). The further-bleeding reduction held regardless of the second procedure used and across subgroups, and was more evident in high-risk patients and where no scheduled follow-up endoscopies were performed.
cards.watchOut: Calvet and the Cochrane review pool substantially overlapping trial sets, so they are two analyses of largely one evidence base, not two independent bases — the concordance strengthens confidence in the analysis, and the individual-trial card below shows where the effect concentrates.

cards.headline: Chung 1997: adrenaline plus heat probe versus adrenaline alone in 276 actively bleeding ulcers — no overall difference, but far fewer operations in spurting haemorrhage (6.5% vs 29.6%)
cards.summary: Chung 1997: adrenaline plus heat probe versus adrenaline alone in 276 actively bleeding ulcers — no overall difference, but far fewer operations in spurting haemorrhage (6.5% vs 29.6%)
cards.people: 276 patients with actively bleeding peptic ulcers found at endoscopy within 24 hours of admission at one university hospital, randomised prospectively to endoscopic adrenaline injection alone (136) or adrenaline injection plus heat probe treatment (140); outcomes were initial haemostasis, clinical rebleeding, operation, transfusion, hospital stay, ulcer healing at four weeks and in-hospital mortality.
cards.result: Initial haemostasis was achieved in 131 of 134 (98%) with adrenaline alone and 135 of 136 (99%) with dual treatment (P = 0.33). Overall outcomes did not differ significantly: clinical rebleeding 12 vs 5, emergency operation 14 vs 8, transfusion 2 vs 3 units, ulcer healing 79.1% vs 74%, in-hospital mortality 7 vs 8. But in the spurting-haemorrhage subgroup, 8 of 27 adrenaline-alone patients (29.6%) versus 2 of 31 dual-treatment patients (6.5%) required operative intervention (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.03–0.87), and hospital stay was shorter with dual treatment in that subgroup (4 vs 6 days, P = 0.01).
cards.watchOut: This trial enrolled only actively bleeding ulcers and was neutral on its overall comparisons — it is carded because it locates the benefit in the highest-risk (spurting) subgroup, not because it independently proves the pooled effect; subgroup findings in a single trial are hypothesis-level on their own.
cards.source: Chung SS et al. Randomised comparison between adrenaline injection alone and adrenaline injection plus heat probe treatment for actively bleeding ulcers. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1997. PMID: 9158465. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: epinephrine alone is not enough for high-risk bleeding ulcers — a second endoscopic method reduces rebleeding, surgery and death
cards.summary: Synthesis: epinephrine alone is not enough for high-risk bleeding ulcers — a second endoscopic method reduces rebleeding, surgery and death
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of substantially the same randomised trials (Calvet 2004, 16 trials, 1,673 patients; Cochrane/Vergara 2007, 17 trials, 1,763 patients) and one individual randomised trial of adrenaline plus heat probe (Chung 1997, 276 patients).
cards.result: Both poolings agree on absolute effects: further bleeding falls from about 18–19% to about 10–11% (a relative reduction of roughly half, odds ratio about 0.51–0.53), emergency surgery from about 11% to about 7%, and mortality from about 5% to about 2.5%. PROPOSED LIKELY: endoscopic combination therapy — epinephrine plus a second haemostatic method — reduces rebleeding compared with epinephrine injection alone in high-risk peptic ulcer bleeding.
cards.watchOut: These trials predate modern high-dose proton pump inhibitor co-therapy and widespread clip use; the comparison they settle is epinephrine-alone versus combination, and they do not rank today's second methods against each other.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vergara M et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2007 (PMID: 17443601); Calvet X et al. Gastroenterology. 2004 (PMID: 14762781); Chung SS et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1997 (PMID: 9158465).

shelves.title: Proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy for upper gastrointestinal bleeding: fewer bleeding stigmata and less endoscopic therapy — but no difference in death, rebleeding or surgery
shelves.question: In adults with nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does an intravenous proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy change outcomes versus after endoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Ulcer Agents · Blood Transfusion · Double-Blind Method · Endoscopy · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Omeprazole · Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage · Premedication · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes) — printed on the face. No pre-endoscopy proton pump inhibitor (PPI) home existed in the index. A precision first: the trials compare PPI started before endoscopy against placebo, an H2 blocker or no treatment before endoscopy — all patients could receive standard care, including PPI, after endoscopy — so they answer 'start before versus not before', which is the practical form of this shelf's question. The largest trial (Lau 2007, 638 patients, high-dose intravenous omeprazole) reduced the need for endoscopic therapy (19.1% vs 28.4%) and shortened stay, with no difference in transfusion, recurrent bleeding, emergency surgery or 30-day death. Both Cochrane versions (2010 and the 2022 update, the same 6 trials and 2,223 participants) agree: mortality odds ratio 1.12–1.14, rebleeding and surgery not significantly different, while the need for endoscopic haemostatic treatment fell (odds ratio 0.68). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes): pre-endoscopy PPI changes what the endoscopist finds and does, not whether the patient dies, rebleeds or needs surgery.

cards.headline: Lau 2007: omeprazole infusion before endoscopy cut the need for endoscopic therapy (19.1% vs 28.4%) but made no difference to death, rebleeding or surgery in 638 patients
cards.summary: Lau 2007: omeprazole infusion before endoscopy cut the need for endoscopic therapy (19.1% vs 28.4%) but made no difference to death, rebleeding or surgery in 638 patients
cards.people: 638 consecutive patients admitted with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, stabilised and randomised double-blind to omeprazole or placebo (each an 80-mg intravenous bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion) before endoscopy the next morning; 314 omeprazole and 317 placebo patients were included in the analysis.
cards.result: The need for endoscopic treatment was lower with omeprazole (60 of 314, 19.1%) than placebo (90 of 317, 28.4%; P = 0.007). There were no significant differences in mean blood transfused (1.54 vs 1.88 units, P = 0.12), recurrent bleeding (11 vs 8 patients, P = 0.49), emergency surgery (3 vs 4, P = 1.00) or death within 30 days (8 vs 7, P = 0.78) — the treatment made no difference to those outcomes. Hospital stay under 3 days was more common with omeprazole (60.5% vs 49.2%, P = 0.005); at endoscopy, fewer omeprazole patients had actively bleeding ulcers (12 of 187 vs 28 of 190, P = 0.01) and more had clean-based ulcers (120 vs 90, P = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Endoscopy was scheduled for the next morning, giving the infusion many hours to act; where endoscopy happens within a few hours of arrival the down-staging effect may be smaller — and down-staging is a process benefit, valuable for workflow and risk stratification, not a survival benefit.
cards.source: Lau JY et al. Omeprazole before endoscopy in patients with gastrointestinal bleeding. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17442905. Registry ID: NCT00164866. cards.headline: Sreedharan 2010 Cochrane review: across 6 trials (2,223 participants), pre-endoscopy PPI reduced stigmata and endoscopic therapy but not mortality (6.1% vs 5.5%), rebleeding or surgery
cards.summary: Sreedharan 2010 Cochrane review: across 6 trials (2,223 participants), pre-endoscopy PPI reduced stigmata and endoscopic therapy but not mortality (6.1% vs 5.5%), rebleeding or surgery
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 6 randomised trials (2,223 hospitalised participants) of proton pump inhibitor treatment (oral or intravenous) started before endoscopy for unselected upper gastrointestinal bleeding, versus placebo, histamine-2 receptor antagonist or no treatment; outcomes assessed at 30 days.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences in mortality (unweighted pooled rates 6.1% PPI vs 5.5% control; odds ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.72–1.73), rebleeding (13.9% vs 16.6%; odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.61–1.09) or surgery (9.9% vs 10.2%; odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.68–1.35) — the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes. PPI did reduce stigmata of recent haemorrhage at index endoscopy (37.2% vs 46.5%; odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.54–0.84), though this was not robust to sensitivity analysis, and reduced endoscopic therapy at index endoscopy (8.6% vs 11.7%; odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50–0.93).
cards.watchOut: Controls mix placebo, H2 blockers and no treatment, and routes mix oral and intravenous PPI, so the pooled null is a class-level answer; the stigmata result's fragility in sensitivity analysis is a further reason not to over-read the endoscopic findings.

PMID: 20614440. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kanno 2022 Cochrane update: the same 6 trials re-analysed — pre-endoscopy PPI likely reduces endoscopic treatment (odds ratio 0.68, moderate certainty) with no conclusion possible on mortality or rebleeding
cards.summary: Kanno 2022 Cochrane update: the same 6 trials re-analysed — pre-endoscopy PPI likely reduces endoscopic treatment (odds ratio 0.68, moderate certainty) with no conclusion possible on mortality or rebleeding
cards.people: 2022 update of the Cochrane review of proton pump inhibitor treatment initiated before endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding; the same 6 randomised trials (2,223 participants) were included — no new studies had been published since the 2008 search for the previous version — with GRADE certainty assessments added.
cards.result: Pre-endoscopic PPI may not reduce mortality (odds ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.76–1.70; 5 studies; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce rebleeding (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.62–1.06; 5 studies; low-certainty evidence), with no clear effect on surgery (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.65–1.26) or high-risk stigmata (odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.52–1.21). It likely reduces the need for endoscopic haemostatic treatment at index endoscopy (odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50–0.93; moderate-certainty evidence). The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to say whether pre-endoscopic PPI increases, reduces or has no effect on mortality, rebleeding or surgery.
cards.watchOut: An update that finds no new trials in over a decade is itself evidence about the field: the question has been left at low certainty, and this card is the same trial set as the 2010 card re-graded — not independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: starting a proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy tidies the endoscopy, not the outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: starting a proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy tidies the endoscopy, not the outcome
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large randomised trial (Lau 2007, 638 patients) and two versions of one Cochrane review (2010 and 2022; the same 6 trials, 2,223 participants).
cards.result: Consistently, pre-endoscopy PPI reduces actively bleeding stigmata and the need for endoscopic therapy (Lau: 19.1% vs 28.4%; pooled odds ratio 0.68 for endoscopic treatment) and may shorten stay, while mortality (pooled 6.1% vs 5.5%), rebleeding and surgery show no significant difference in any analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes): the before-versus-after timing of PPI in nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding changes endoscopic findings and workload, not survival.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against post-endoscopy high-dose PPI after endoscopic haemostasis of high-risk ulcers, a different question with its own evidence; this shelf is only about starting before the scope.

shelves.title: Empagliflozin and liver fat in steatotic liver disease: MRI trials show a modest fall, elastography trials show none — an imaging-surrogate split
shelves.question: In adults with metabolic steatotic liver disease, does empagliflozin reduce liver fat on imaging versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue · Adiposity · Adult · Alanine Transaminase · Aspartate Aminotransferases · Benzhydryl Compounds · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glucosides · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Liver · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate) — printed on the face, with the surrogate warning the question requires: every carded outcome is an imaging number, not liver histology, fibrosis progression or a clinical event. The library's other liver-fat shelves cover other agents (efinopegdutide on live #2115; dapagliflozin on pack #3623); empagliflozin itself had no home. The split runs along the measuring instrument. On MRI proton-density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF), empagliflozin won twice: E-LIFT (Kuchay 2018, 50 patients with type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin added to standard care versus standard care alone — not a placebo comparison) found a −4.0% between-group difference, and Cheung 2024 (98 patients without diabetes, genuinely placebo-controlled for 52 weeks) found a greater median reduction (−2.49% vs −1.43%). On transient-elastography controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), Taheri 2020 found no difference versus placebo, and the Tang 2022 meta-analysis of 3 trials (212 patients) found no improvement in CAP, steatosis or stiffness. PROPOSED SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate): empagliflozin probably lowers MRI-measured liver fat modestly; the elastography literature does not confirm it, and no carded study shows a histological or clinical benefit.

cards.headline: E-LIFT 2018: empagliflozin added to standard care reduced MRI liver fat more than standard care alone (between-group difference −4.0%) in 50 patients with type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: E-LIFT 2018: empagliflozin added to standard care reduced MRI liver fat more than standard care alone (between-group difference −4.0%) in 50 patients with type 2 diabetes
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, open comparator (E-LIFT, Kuchay 2018)
cards.people: 50 patients with type 2 diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease randomised to standard diabetes treatment plus empagliflozin 10 mg daily or standard treatment without empagliflozin for 20 weeks; liver fat was measured by MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF). This was an open comparison against standard care, not a placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Empagliflozin reduced liver fat significantly more than control (mean MRI-PDFF difference between groups −4.0%, P < 0.0001). Within groups, MRI-PDFF fell from 16.2% to 11.3% on empagliflozin (P < 0.0001) and from 16.4% to 15.5% on standard care alone (P = 0.057). The groups differed significantly for change in alanine aminotransferase (P = 0.005) but not aspartate aminotransferase (P = 0.212) or gamma-glutamyl transferase (P = 0.057).
cards.watchOut: Without a placebo or blinding, part of the −4.0% gap could reflect co-interventions and behaviour change in patients who knew they were on the new drug; and a 20-week imaging change in 50 patients is a surrogate signal, not evidence about steatohepatitis or fibrosis.
cards.source: Kuchay MS et al. Effect of Empagliflozin on Liver Fat in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial (E-LIFT Trial). Diabetes care. 2018. PMID: 29895557. Registry ID: NCT02686476. cards.headline: Cheung 2024: in 98 people with steatotic liver disease without diabetes, empagliflozin beat placebo on MRI liver fat over 52 weeks (−2.49% vs −1.43% median change)
cards.summary: Cheung 2024: in 98 people with steatotic liver disease without diabetes, empagliflozin beat placebo on MRI liver fat over 52 weeks (−2.49% vs −1.43% median change)
cards.people: 98 adults without diabetes (fasting plasma glucose < 7 mmol/L [< 126 mg/dL] and HbA1c < 6.5%) with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and MRI-PDFF ≥ 5%, randomised double-blind to empagliflozin 10 mg daily (49) or placebo (48 analysed with repeat imaging) for 52 weeks; the primary outcome was the between-group difference in MRI-PDFF change.
cards.result: The empagliflozin group had a greater reduction in median MRI-PDFF than placebo (−2.49% vs −1.43%, P = 0.025). Resolution of hepatic steatosis (MRI-PDFF < 5%) showed a nonsignificant trend (44.9% vs 28.6%, P = 0.094), and there was no significant difference in an alanine aminotransferase drop of ≥ 17 U/L (16.3% vs 12.2%), an MRI-PDFF drop of ≥ 30% (49.0% vs 40.8%) or the composite outcome (8.2% vs 8.2%). Empagliflozin produced greater drops in body weight (−2.7 vs −0.2 kg), waist circumference, fasting glucose and ferritin (all P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: This is the cleanest design carded and its headline effect is small — a 1.06 percentage-point greater median fat-fraction fall — with every categorical responder outcome nonsignificant; it supports a modest real effect on the MRI number, nothing more.
cards.source: Cheung KS et al. cards.headline: Taheri 2020: in 90 patients without diabetes, empagliflozin did not beat placebo on the elastography fat measure (controlled attenuation parameter, P = 0.396)
cards.summary: Taheri 2020: in 90 patients without diabetes, empagliflozin did not beat placebo on the elastography fat measure (controlled attenuation parameter, P = 0.396)
cards.people: 90 participants with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease without type 2 diabetes randomised double-blind to empagliflozin 10 mg/day (43) or placebo (47) for 24 weeks; hepatic steatosis and fibrosis were assessed by transient elastography (controlled attenuation parameter, CAP, and liver stiffness measurement), with change in CAP score at 24 weeks as the primary outcome.
cards.result: CAP score fell significantly in both groups with no significant difference between them (P = 0.396) — on the primary outcome the treatment made no difference. Liver stiffness fell in the empagliflozin group (6.03 ± 1.40 to 5.33 ± 1.08 kPa, P = 0.001) with no change on placebo, and in the subgroup with significant baseline steatosis (CAP ≥ 302 dB/m) steatosis improved more on empagliflozin (37.2% vs 17%, P = 0.035). Ultrasound fat grade, transaminases and fasting insulin fell within the empagliflozin group only.
cards.watchOut: CAP and MRI-PDFF do not measure fat with the same precision, so this null may be measurement insensitivity rather than absence of effect — which is precisely the split this shelf reports; the positive subgroup and within-group findings are secondary and should not be promoted over the null primary outcome.
cards.source: Taheri H et al. cards.headline: Tang 2022 meta-analysis: pooling 3 randomised trials (212 patients), empagliflozin showed no improvement in elastography fat, steatosis or stiffness versus control
cards.summary: Tang 2022 meta-analysis: pooling 3 randomised trials (212 patients), empagliflozin showed no improvement in elastography fat, steatosis or stiffness versus control
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 3 randomised controlled trials involving 212 patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, comparing empagliflozin with control (placebo or standard therapy) on controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) score, hepatic steatosis, liver stiffness measurement and liver enzymes and lipids.
cards.result: Compared with control, empagliflozin showed no improvement in CAP score, hepatic steatosis or liver stiffness score, nor in alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, low-density lipoprotein or triglycerides. The authors conclude empagliflozin may not be effective for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease on these measures — the treatment made no difference in this pooling.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are the elastography-based ones — this meta-analysis cannot see the MRI-PDFF trials' endpoint, so its null and the MRI trials' positives describe different instruments more than they contradict each other; with only 212 patients it is also too small to settle either.

cards.headline: Synthesis: empagliflozin lowers MRI-measured liver fat modestly; elastography studies do not confirm it, and liver fat is a surrogate either way
cards.summary: Synthesis: empagliflozin lowers MRI-measured liver fat modestly; elastography studies do not confirm it, and liver fat is a surrogate either way
cards.people: The carded evidence: two MRI-PDFF trials (E-LIFT, 50 patients with diabetes, open comparator; Cheung 2024, 98 patients without diabetes, placebo-controlled), one elastography trial (Taheri 2020, 90 patients, placebo-controlled) and one meta-analysis of the elastography trials (Tang 2022, 212 patients, overlapping).
cards.result: MRI-PDFF fell more on empagliflozin in both MRI trials (between-group −4.0% at 20 weeks; median −2.49% vs −1.43% at 52 weeks), while the CAP primary outcome in Taheri and the Tang pooling were null. PROPOSED SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate): a modest liver-fat reduction on MRI is the best-supported claim; no carded evidence addresses liver histology, fibrosis outcomes or clinical events.
cards.watchOut: Weight loss itself lowers liver fat and empagliflozin groups lost more weight (about 2.5 kg more in Cheung); these trials cannot separate a direct liver effect from the expected consequence of losing weight and improving glycaemia.

shelves.title: Gluten-free diet and mucosal healing in adult celiac disease: recovery in about two-thirds by 5 years, complete normalisation rare early — symptoms do not prove healing (observational cohorts)
shelves.question: In adults with celiac disease, does a gluten-free diet heal the small intestinal mucosa in adults diagnosed by biopsy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biopsy · Celiac Disease · Cohort Studies · Diet, Gluten-Free · Female · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — printed on the face: this shelf rests on follow-up-biopsy cohorts, not randomised trials, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The cohorts agree on the shape of the answer: a gluten-free diet heals the mucosa in many adults, slowly, and far from universally. In the Mayo Clinic cohort (Rubio-Tapia 2010, 241 adults with diagnostic and follow-up biopsies), confirmed mucosal recovery was 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years, even though 82% had a clinical response — symptoms were not a reliable marker of healing. In the largest adult series (Lanzini 2009, 465 adults), complete histological normalisation after a median 16 months on the diet was only 8%, with a further 65% in 'remission' with persistent intraepithelial lymphocytosis. In the Finnish cohort (Pekki 2015, 263 adults), incomplete recovery at 1 year was common and was predicted by more severe damage at diagnosis, while dietary adherence was excellent in both groups (97% vs 87%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): mucosal healing on a gluten-free diet is real but slow and incomplete in a substantial share of adults; a feeling of improvement does not prove the mucosa has healed.

cards.headline: Rubio-Tapia 2010: in 241 adults with biopsy-proven celiac disease, mucosal recovery on a gluten-free diet was 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years — while 82% felt clinically better
cards.summary: Rubio-Tapia 2010: in 241 adults with biopsy-proven celiac disease, mucosal recovery on a gluten-free diet was 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years — while 82% felt clinically better
cards.people: 241 adults (73% women) with biopsy-proven celiac disease at the Mayo Clinic, drawn from 381 adults, who had duodenal biopsies at diagnosis and at least one follow-up biopsy after starting a gluten-free diet; primary outcomes were mucosal recovery and all-cause mortality.
cards.result: The Kaplan-Meier rate of confirmed mucosal recovery was 34% (95% CI 27–40%) at 2 years and 66% (95% CI 58–74%) at 5 years after diagnosis. Most patients (82%) had some clinical response to the diet, but clinical response was not a reliable marker of mucosal recovery (P=0.7); serological response was associated with recovery (P=0.01). Poor compliance (P<0.01), severe disease with diarrhoea and weight loss (P<0.001), and total villous atrophy at diagnosis (P<0.001) predicted persistent damage. There was a trend toward lower mortality with recovery (adjusted hazard ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.02–1.06, P=0.06 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Only patients who actually received a follow-up biopsy are counted, so the cohort is selected; recovery rates in all diagnosed adults could differ. The mortality trend is borderline and observational — it does not prove that healing itself prolongs life.
cards.source: Rubio-Tapia A et al. Mucosal recovery and mortality in adults with celiac disease after treatment with a gluten-free diet. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010. cards.headline: Lanzini 2009: in 465 adults, complete normalisation of the duodenal mucosa on a gluten-free diet was exceptionally rare — 8% after a median 16 months
cards.summary: Lanzini 2009: in 465 adults, complete normalisation of the duodenal mucosa on a gluten-free diet was exceptionally rare — 8% after a median 16 months
cards.people: 465 consecutive adult coeliac patients studied before and during a gluten-free diet, with duodenal biopsies at diagnosis classified as Marsh I in 11, Marsh II in 25 and Marsh III in 429 cases; histological outcome was assessed after a median of 16 months on the diet.
cards.result: After a median 16 months on a gluten-free diet, 38 patients (8%) had histological 'normalisation', 300 (65%) had 'remission' with persistent intraepithelial lymphocytosis, 121 (26%) had 'no change' and 6 (1%) had 'deterioration'. Celiac serology was negative in 83% of patients with a Marsh III lesion during the diet. Male gender and adherence to the diet were independently associated with normalisation and remission. The authors conclude complete normalisation is exceptionally rare in adults despite adherence, symptom disappearance and negative serology.
cards.watchOut: 'Remission' here still includes persistent intraepithelial lymphocytosis, so this study's 8% complete-normalisation figure and Rubio-Tapia's 66% 5-year recovery figure use different definitions and follow-up lengths — they describe the same slow, often partial healing, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Lanzini A et al. Complete recovery of intestinal mucosa occurs very rarely in adult coeliac patients despite adherence to gluten-free diet. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19302264. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pekki 2015: in 263 adults, incomplete mucosal recovery after 1 year on a gluten-free diet was predicted by severe disease at diagnosis — and did not worsen symptoms, quality of life or long-term outcomes
cards.summary: Pekki 2015: in 263 adults, incomplete mucosal recovery after 1 year on a gluten-free diet was predicted by severe disease at diagnosis — and did not worsen symptoms, quality of life or long-term outcomes
cards.people: 263 biopsy-proven celiac patients in Finland divided into histological recovery versus incomplete recovery groups after 1 year on a gluten-free diet, with serology, laboratory values, bone mineral density, symptoms and quality of life measured at diagnosis and 1 year, plus long-term follow-up for mortality, malignancy and severe complications.
cards.result: The incomplete-recovery group had more severe mucosal damage (P=0.003), higher antibody values (P=0.017) and more signs of malabsorption (P<0.001) at diagnosis. At follow-up there was still a difference in antibodies (P=0.018) and femoral T-scores (P=0.024). Dietary adherence was better in the recovered group but excellent in both (97% vs 87%, P<0.001). There was no difference between groups in symptoms, quality of life or long-term outcomes.
cards.watchOut: One year is early in adult mucosal healing — Rubio-Tapia's cohort kept recovering out to 5 years — so 'incomplete at 1 year' should not be read as 'will never heal'; this study's reassuring long-term finding applies to adherent patients like these.
cards.source: Pekki H et al. Predictors and Significance of Incomplete Mucosal Recovery in Celiac Disease After 1 Year on a Gluten-Free Diet. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 26032154. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: on a gluten-free diet the adult celiac mucosa usually improves and often heals — but slowly, and complete healing is the exception in the first years
cards.summary: Synthesis: on a gluten-free diet the adult celiac mucosa usually improves and often heals — but slowly, and complete healing is the exception in the first years
cards.people: The carded evidence: three adult follow-up-biopsy cohorts — Rubio-Tapia 2010 (241 adults), Lanzini 2009 (465 adults) and Pekki 2015 (263 adults). Total carded participants exceed 900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. All evidence is observational.
cards.result: Recovery was 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years in the Mayo cohort; complete normalisation was only 8% at a median 16 months in the largest series, with most of the rest in partial remission; and incomplete recovery at 1 year was common in the Finnish cohort despite excellent adherence, predicted by severe disease at diagnosis. Clinical response (82% in the Mayo cohort) did not track mucosal recovery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): a gluten-free diet heals the small-intestinal mucosa in many adults, but healing is slow and frequently incomplete, and neither symptoms nor serology alone proves it.
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised trial of diet versus no diet in biopsy-diagnosed adults — nor could there ethically be one — so this answer rests on biopsy cohorts with differing recovery definitions and follow-up times; the consistent finding across them is partial, slow healing, not the exact percentage.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rubio-Tapia A et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2010 (PMID: 20145607); Lanzini A et al. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2009 (PMID: 19302264); Pekki H et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2015 (PMID: 26032154).
