shelves.title: Intravenous iron and quality of life in IBD anaemia (PARTIAL completion of pack #3231): quality of life improves on intravenous iron; the proven edge over oral iron is haemoglobin response, not a measured quality-of-life difference
shelves.question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron improve quality of life versus oral iron in inflammatory bowel disease?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency · Cohort Studies · Colitis, Ulcerative · Crohn Disease · Female · Ferric Compounds · Ferritins · Ferrous Compounds · Germany · Hemoglobinometry · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Maltose · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face, and narrowed on the face: quality of life clearly improves when intravenous iron corrects iron-deficiency anaemia in inflammatory bowel disease, but a quality-of-life advantage over oral iron specifically has not been directly demonstrated in the fetched records — the head-to-head evidence is about haemoglobin response. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3231 homes oral ferric maltol and haemoglobin in IBD anaemia and is not re-carded here; this shelf takes the intravenous-iron quality-of-life slice. In the one direct route comparison trial (Kulnigg 2008, 200 patients), intravenous ferric carboxymaltose was non-inferior to oral ferrous sulfate for haemoglobin rise (median 8.7 to 12.3 g/dL vs 9.1 to 12.1 g/dL) with faster early response. The Cochrane review (11 studies, 1,670 participants) pooled all intravenous versus all oral preparations and found more haemoglobin responders on intravenous iron (368/554 vs 205/373; relative risk 1.17, a relative measure; number needed to treat 11, low certainty), with fewer withdrawals for adverse events on intravenous iron. On quality of life itself: in FERGIcor (485 patients) both intravenous regimens improved quality-of-life scores by week 12, and in the PHOSPHARE-IBD analysis (97 patients) utility and SF-36 scores improved significantly after intravenous iron, driven by vitality — an improvement blunted when phosphate fell. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron improves quality of life as it corrects anaemia in IBD; the proven edge over oral iron is haemoglobin response and tolerability, not a measured quality-of-life difference.

cards.headline: Kulnigg 2008: intravenous ferric carboxymaltose was non-inferior to oral ferrous sulfate for haemoglobin in 200 IBD patients — median haemoglobin 8.7 to 12.3 g/dL vs 9.1 to 12.1 g/dL — with a faster early response
cards.summary: Kulnigg 2008: intravenous ferric carboxymaltose was non-inferior to oral ferrous sulfate for haemoglobin in 200 IBD patients — median haemoglobin 8.7 to 12.3 g/dL vs 9.1 to 12.1 g/dL — with a faster early response
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kulnigg 2008, ferric carboxymaltose vs oral ferrous sulfate)
cards.people: 200 patients with inflammatory bowel disease and iron-deficiency anaemia randomised 2:1 (137 ferric carboxymaltose : 63 oral ferrous sulfate) in a multicentre trial; intravenous ferric carboxymaltose up to 1,000 mg iron per infusion at 1-week intervals until the calculated iron deficit was replaced, versus ferrous sulfate 100 mg twice daily for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint was change in haemoglobin from baseline to week 12.
cards.result: Median haemoglobin improved from 8.7 to 12.3 g/dL on ferric carboxymaltose and from 9.1 to 12.1 g/dL on ferrous sulfate, demonstrating non-inferiority (P=0.6967). Response (haemoglobin increase >2.0 g/dL) was higher on ferric carboxymaltose at week 2 (P=0.0051) and week 4 (P=0.0346). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 28.5% (ferric carboxymaltose) and 22.2% (ferrous sulfate), with discontinuation for adverse events in 1.5% vs 7.9%. The record reports haemoglobin and safety outcomes; it does not report a quality-of-life comparison.
cards.watchOut: This is the direct intravenous-versus-oral trial behind the question, and its endpoint is haemoglobin, not quality of life — it shows the intravenous route corrects anaemia at least as well and faster, but it cannot by itself prove patients feel better than they would on oral iron.
cards.source: Kulnigg S et al. A novel intravenous iron formulation for treatment of anemia in inflammatory bowel disease: the ferric carboxymaltose (FERINJECT) randomized controlled trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18371137. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2021: pooling all intravenous versus all oral iron in IBD anaemia, intravenous iron produced more haemoglobin responders — 368/554 vs 205/373 (relative risk 1.17, number needed to treat 11, low certainty)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2021: pooling all intravenous versus all oral iron in IBD anaemia, intravenous iron produced more haemoglobin responders — 368/554 vs 205/373 (relative risk 1.17, number needed to treat 11, low certainty)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 11 randomised trials (Gordon 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review of 11 randomised studies (1,670 participants) of interventions for iron-deficiency anaemia in inflammatory bowel disease, including intravenous iron sucrose vs oral iron sulphate (2 studies), intravenous ferric carboxymaltose vs oral iron sulphate (1 study), intravenous iron isomaltoside vs oral iron sulphate (1 study), and the oral ferric maltol programme homed on pack #3231.
cards.result: An analysis of all intravenous preparations versus all oral preparations showed intravenous administration may lead to more responders (368/554 vs 205/373; relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 1.05–1.31 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome 11; low certainty due to risk of bias and inconsistency). Withdrawals due to adverse events may be greater with oral than intravenous iron (15/554 vs 31/373; relative risk 0.39, 95% CI 0.20–0.74, low certainty). The review notes quality of life is significantly affected by this anaemia, but the route comparisons rest on haemoglobin response; certainty was low or very low for all comparisons.
cards.watchOut: The pooled intravenous-versus-oral estimate mixes different preparations and mostly quiescent or mild-to-moderate disease; the reviewers rate certainty low, and the ferric maltol trial inside this review is homed on pack #3231 and not re-carded as evidence here.
cards.source: Gordon M et al. Interventions for treating iron deficiency anaemia in inflammatory bowel disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33471939. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FERGIcor 2011: in 485 IBD patients, both intravenous iron regimens improved quality-of-life scores by week 12 — ferric carboxymaltose beat iron sucrose on haemoglobin response, 65.8% vs 53.6%
cards.summary: FERGIcor 2011: in 485 IBD patients, both intravenous iron regimens improved quality-of-life scores by week 12 — ferric carboxymaltose beat iron sucrose on haemoglobin response, 65.8% vs 53.6%
cards.people: 485 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin <100 μg/L; haemoglobin 7–12 g/dL in women, 7–13 g/dL in men) and mild-to-moderate or quiescent inflammatory bowel disease at 88 centres in 14 countries, randomised open-label to ferric carboxymaltose (maximum 3 infusions of 1,000 or 500 mg iron) or individually Ganzoni-calculated iron sucrose doses (up to 11 infusions of 200 mg iron); 240 ferric carboxymaltose and 235 iron sucrose patients were analysed.
cards.result: More patients on ferric carboxymaltose than iron sucrose achieved haemoglobin response (increase ≥2 g/dL): 150 (65.8%) vs 118 (53.6%), a 12.2% difference (P=.004), or haemoglobin normalisation: 166 (72.8%) vs 136 (61.8%), an 11.0% difference (P=.015). Both treatments improved quality-of-life scores by week 12. Both study drugs were well tolerated, with drug-related adverse events in line with drug-specific experience.
cards.watchOut: FERGIcor compares two intravenous regimens, not intravenous versus oral iron — its quality-of-life finding shows intravenous treatment improves how patients feel as anaemia corrects, but the size of any quality-of-life edge over oral iron is not measured here.
cards.source: Evstatiev R et al. FERGIcor, a randomized controlled trial on ferric carboxymaltose for iron deficiency anemia in inflammatory bowel disease. Gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21699794. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PHOSPHARE-IBD analysis 2024: quality of life improved significantly after intravenous iron in 97 IBD patients, driven by vitality — and the gain was smaller when phosphate fell
cards.summary: PHOSPHARE-IBD analysis 2024: quality of life improved significantly after intravenous iron in 97 IBD patients, driven by vitality — and the gain was smaller when phosphate fell
cards.type: Randomised trial post-hoc quality-of-life analysis (PHOSPHARE-IBD, Bjorner 2024)
cards.people: 97 patients with inflammatory bowel disease and iron-deficiency anaemia enrolled in the randomised, double-blind PHOSPHARE-IBD trial across five European countries, allocated to ferric derisomaltose or ferric carboxymaltose, with SF-36v2 responses recorded at baseline and days 14, 35, 49 and 70.
cards.result: In both treatment arms, SF-6Dv2 utility values and all SF-36v2 scale scores except Bodily Pain improved significantly (P<0.0001), with no significant difference between the two intravenous preparations in utility improvement. The improvement in utility values was completely explained by improvement in Vitality scores; vitality improved significantly more with ferric derisomaltose than ferric carboxymaltose (P=0.026), and patients with the smallest decrease in phosphate had significantly larger vitality improvements at each time point (P<0.05) and overall (P=0.0006) — quality-of-life improvement is attenuated by hypophosphatemia.
cards.watchOut: This is a post-hoc analysis of 97 patients comparing two intravenous preparations, with no oral-iron arm; the phosphate finding is a caution about ferric carboxymaltose's phosphate effect eroding the very vitality gain the treatment is given for, not a comparison against oral iron.
cards.source: Bjorner JB et al. Hypophosphatemia attenuates improvements in vitality after intravenous iron treatment in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Quality of life research : an international journal of quality of life aspects of treatment, care and rehabilitation. 2024. PMID: 38874697. Registry ID: NCT03466983. cards.headline: Synthesis: intravenous iron improves quality of life as it corrects IBD anaemia — the demonstrated advantage over oral iron is haemoglobin response and fewer withdrawals, not a measured quality-of-life gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: intravenous iron improves quality of life as it corrects IBD anaemia — the demonstrated advantage over oral iron is haemoglobin response and fewer withdrawals, not a measured quality-of-life gap
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct intravenous-versus-oral randomised trial (Kulnigg 2008, 200 patients), one Cochrane review of 11 trials (1,670 participants), one intravenous-versus-intravenous randomised trial with quality-of-life outcomes (FERGIcor, 485 patients), and one randomised-trial quality-of-life analysis (PHOSPHARE-IBD, 97 patients). Total carded participants exceed 2,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Quality-of-life scores improved by week 12 on intravenous iron in FERGIcor and improved significantly across SF-36 domains after intravenous iron in PHOSPHARE-IBD, driven by vitality. Against oral iron, intravenous iron was non-inferior for haemoglobin in the direct trial and produced more responders pooled (relative risk 1.17; 368/554 vs 205/373; number needed to treat 11, low certainty), with fewer adverse-event withdrawals. No fetched record directly measures a quality-of-life difference between intravenous and oral iron. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron improves quality of life in IBD iron-deficiency anaemia; superiority over oral iron is shown for haemoglobin response, not directly for quality of life. The oral ferric maltol slice is homed on pack #3231.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this to a claim that intravenous iron beats oral iron on quality of life head-to-head: the trials that measured quality of life compared intravenous preparations with each other, and the trials that compared routes measured haemoglobin.

shelves.title: Avatrombopag before procedures in chronic liver disease (PARTIAL of pack #2819): transfusion avoided in up to 88% vs 38% on placebo
shelves.question: In adults with chronic liver disease and thrombocytopenia, does avatrombopag raise platelet counts and reduce platelet transfusion before a procedure versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Loss, Surgical/prevention & control · End Stage Liver Disease/complications/surgery · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Preoperative Care/methods · Surgical Procedures, Operative/adverse effects · Thiazoles/administration & dosage · Thiophenes/administration & dosage · Thrombocytopenia/complications/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of pack #2819 (avatrombopag in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, a null trial — a different population, not re-carded here). In chronic liver disease before a scheduled procedure, ADAPT-1 (n = 231) and ADAPT-2 (n = 204) both found avatrombopag roughly doubled-to-tripled avoidance of platelet transfusion or rescue procedures (65.6% and 88.1% vs 22.9% and 38.2% by cohort in ADAPT-1; 68.6% and 87.9% vs 34.9% and 33.3% in ADAPT-2; all P < .001), an earlier phase 2 trial (130 patients) showed platelet responses in about 48–49% vs 6–10% on placebo, and an integrated analysis of the 435 ADAPT patients confirmed consistency across subgroups. PROPOSED LIKELY: avatrombopag raises platelet counts and reduces platelet transfusion/rescue before procedures in chronic liver disease — a transfusion-avoidance benefit, not a demonstrated bleeding reduction.

cards.headline: ADAPT-1 and ADAPT-2 (2018): avatrombopag roughly doubled-to-tripled the share of patients avoiding platelet transfusion or rescue — e.g. 88.1% vs 38.2% and 65.6% vs 22.9% by baseline-count cohort (P < .001)
cards.summary: ADAPT-1 and ADAPT-2 (2018): avatrombopag roughly doubled-to-tripled the share of patients avoiding platelet transfusion or rescue — e.g. 88.1% vs 38.2% and 65.6% vs 22.9% by baseline-count cohort (P < .001)
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials reported together (ADAPT-1 and ADAPT-2, Terrault 2018)
cards.people: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in adults with thrombocytopenia and chronic liver disease undergoing scheduled procedures: ADAPT-1 (n = 231) and ADAPT-2 (n = 204). Within baseline platelet cohorts (<40 × 10⁹/L and 40 to <50 × 10⁹/L), patients were randomised 2:1 to 5 daily doses of avatrombopag (60 mg or 40 mg by cohort) or placebo. Registry IDs: NCT01972529 (ADAPT-1) and NCT01976104 (ADAPT-2).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — not requiring a platelet transfusion or rescue procedure for bleeding up to 7 days after the procedure — was met in ADAPT-1 by 65.6% (60 mg cohort) and 88.1% (40 mg cohort) on avatrombopag vs 22.9% and 38.2% on placebo (P < .0001 for both), and in ADAPT-2 by 68.6% and 87.9% vs 34.9% and 33.3% (P < .001 for both). Avatrombopag raised platelet counts and increased the share reaching ≥50 × 10⁹/L on procedure day. Adverse event incidence and severity were similar to placebo and consistent with the chronic liver disease population.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is transfusion avoidance and a platelet-count target, not bleeding itself: these trials were not powered to show fewer bleeding events, so the benefit should be stated as fewer transfusions/rescue procedures, not proven less bleeding.
cards.source: Terrault N et al. Avatrombopag Before Procedures Reduces Need for Platelet Transfusion in Patients With Chronic Liver Disease and Thrombocytopenia. Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29778606. Registry ID: NCT01972529, NCT01976104. cards.headline: Terrault 2014 phase 2: the platelet-response endpoint was reached by about 48–49% on avatrombopag vs 6–10% on placebo across two dosing cohorts (130 patients with cirrhosis)
cards.summary: Terrault 2014 phase 2: the platelet-response endpoint was reached by about 48–49% on avatrombopag vs 6–10% on placebo across two dosing cohorts (130 patients with cirrhosis)
cards.people: 130 adults with cirrhosis and platelet counts 10–58 × 10⁹/L randomised to avatrombopag or placebo in two sequential dosing cohorts (93 avatrombopag, 37 placebo) in the week before an elective procedure; primary endpoint a platelet rise of ≥20 × 10⁹/L to >50 × 10⁹/L at least once on days 4–8.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was achieved by 49.0% of avatrombopag patients in cohort A and 47.6% in cohort B, vs 6.3% and 9.5% on placebo, with a dose response; each regimen beat its cohort's placebo arm (P < .01) except the 100/40 mg regimen in cohort A (P = .17). Common adverse events were nausea, fatigue and headache. One avatrombopag patient (100/80 mg group), who had no Doppler assessment at screening, was diagnosed with portal vein thrombosis in post-treatment follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study with several regimens and two formulations, not the licensed 40/60 mg 5-day course tested in ADAPT; its role here is independent confirmation that the drug raises counts in this population, including the portal-vein-thrombosis caution that follows the class.
cards.source: Terrault NA et al. Phase II study of avatrombopag in thrombocytopenic patients with cirrhosis undergoing an elective procedure. Journal of hepatology. 2014. PMID: 25048952. cards.headline: Poordad 2020 integrated analysis: pooling both phase 3 trials (435 patients), avatrombopag's advantage on transfusion avoidance and procedure-day counts was consistent across subgroups
cards.summary: Poordad 2020 integrated analysis: pooling both phase 3 trials (435 patients), avatrombopag's advantage on transfusion avoidance and procedure-day counts was consistent across subgroups
cards.type: Integrated (pooled) analysis of two phase 3 trials (Poordad 2020)
cards.people: Integrated analysis of pooled data (N = 435) from the two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 ADAPT trials, re-examining the original endpoints plus subgroup, alternate baseline-count and additional platelet endpoints. Registry IDs: NCT01972529 and NCT01976104.
cards.result: Avatrombopag was superior to placebo on not requiring a platelet transfusion or rescue procedure, on achieving a platelet count ≥50 × 10⁹/L on procedure day, and on change in platelet count from baseline; the treatment effect was consistently positive across disease and baseline subgroups and alternate cohort definitions. Adverse event incidence and severity were similar to placebo, with a low risk of thromboembolic events and hepatotoxicity reported. The authors conclude the integrated analyses confirmed the phase 3 superiority findings.
cards.watchOut: This is a re-analysis of the same 435 ADAPT patients, not a third independent trial — it adds consistency checks, not new patients — and its record carried no MeSH terms, so its card uses the standard not-captured wording.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, a phase 2 trial and a pooled re-analysis all point the same way — avatrombopag raises counts and avoids transfusions before procedures in chronic liver disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, a phase 2 trial and a pooled re-analysis all point the same way — avatrombopag raises counts and avoids transfusions before procedures in chronic liver disease
cards.people: The carded evidence: ADAPT-1 and ADAPT-2 (435 patients together), one phase 2 trial (130 patients), and an integrated re-analysis of the ADAPT population. This shelf is a PARTIAL completion of pack #2819, which homes avatrombopag in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (a null trial); the chronic-liver-disease pre-procedure population is the uncovered slice built here, and no #2819 study is re-carded.
cards.result: In both ADAPT trials and in both baseline-count cohorts, avatrombopag roughly doubled-to-tripled the proportion of patients who avoided platelet transfusion or rescue procedures (range 65.6–88.1% vs 22.9–38.2%, all P < .001), and the phase 2 trial independently showed platelet responses in about 48–49% vs 6–10% on placebo. Adverse events were similar to placebo, with portal vein thrombosis the named caution from the phase 2 programme. PROPOSED LIKELY: avatrombopag raises platelet counts and reduces platelet transfusion/rescue before procedures in chronic liver disease — stated as transfusion avoidance, not proven bleeding reduction.
cards.watchOut: Transfusion avoidance is a surrogate-adjacent endpoint: whether avoiding transfusion at these thresholds reduces actual procedural bleeding was not demonstrated in these trials, and patients with counts ≥50 × 10⁹/L or with portal vein thrombosis risk were not the tested population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Terrault N et al. Gastroenterology. 2018 (PMID: 29778606); Terrault NA et al. Journal of hepatology. 2014 (PMID: 25048952); Poordad F et al. International journal of hepatology. 2020 (PMID: 32047671).

shelves.title: Ammonia traffic in cirrhosis: made in the gut, missed by the shunted liver, cleared by muscle — human interorgan catheter studies
shelves.question: In adults, how is ammonia produced in the gut and cleared by the liver and muscle in cirrhosis?
shelves.mesh: Amino Acids · Ammonia · Female · Humans · Hypertension, Portal · Kidney · Liver · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal · Portasystemic Shunt, Transjugular Intrahepatic · Splanchnic Circulation
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: standard physiology texts — Guyton & Hall and Ganong — for the urea cycle and glutamine handling; the interorgan measurements are the Olde Damink/Jalan human catheterisation programme). The textbook account: ammonia is produced mainly in the gut — small-intestinal glutaminase splitting glutamine, and colonic bacteria splitting urea and amino acids — travels in portal blood to the liver, and is cleared there by the urea cycle (with a periportal glutamine-scavenging back-up); skeletal muscle is the main extrahepatic sink, fixing ammonia into glutamine. In cirrhosis the liver's clearance fails and portosystemic shunting lets gut ammonia bypass it, so muscle and kidney handling decide the blood level. The carded human studies measured exactly this: across catheterised organs in 24 patients with cirrhosis and a TIPSS, the portal-drained viscera produced the most ammonia, skeletal muscle removed more ammonia than the cirrhotic liver did, and the kidneys produced as much ammonia as the whole hepatosplanchnic area (Olde Damink 2002). After a simulated gut bleed, renal ammonia production rose 6-fold while gut production did not change, and muscle was again the major removal site (Olde Damink 2003). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Olde Damink 2002: in 24 catheterised patients with cirrhosis, the gut produced the most ammonia, muscle removed more than the liver, and the kidneys matched the whole hepatosplanchnic area's production
cards.summary: Olde Damink 2002: in 24 catheterised patients with cirrhosis, the gut produced the most ammonia, muscle removed more than the liver, and the kidneys matched the whole hepatosplanchnic area's production
cards.type: Human physiology study (interorgan catheterisation, Olde Damink 2002)
cards.people: 24 metabolically stable, overnight-fasted patients with cirrhosis who had a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt (TIPSS), studied at TIPSS portography with blood sampling and flow measurement across the portal-drained viscera, leg, kidney and liver, and arteriovenous differences across spleen and mesenteric veins.
cards.result: The highest amount of ammonia was produced by the portal-drained viscera, which consumed glutamine and produced ammonia, alanine and citrulline. The kidneys also produced ammonia, in amounts equal to total hepatosplanchnic production. Skeletal muscle removed more ammonia than the cirrhotic liver, while releasing glutamine in excess of the ammonia nitrogen it took up. The authors conclude hyperammonaemia in these patients results from portosystemic shunting and renal ammonia production, and that urinary ammonia excretion and urea synthesis are the only routes that remove ammonia from the body.
cards.watchOut: All patients had a TIPSS, so shunting was anatomical and complete by design — the study quantifies the shunted state precisely, but gut and kidney production rates in cirrhosis without a shunt are inferred, not measured here.
cards.source: Olde Damink SW et al. Interorgan ammonia and amino acid metabolism in metabolically stable patients with cirrhosis and a TIPSS. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2002. PMID: 12395326. cards.headline: Olde Damink 2003: after a simulated gut bleed, renal ammonia production rose 6-fold while gut production did not change — muscle was the major removal site
cards.summary: Olde Damink 2003: after a simulated gut bleed, renal ammonia production rose 6-fold while gut production did not change — muscle was the major removal site
cards.type: Human physiology study (simulated and actual GI bleed, Olde Damink 2003) — N = 8 and N = 9
cards.people: Two studies in patients with cirrhosis and a TIPSS: study 1 simulated an upper gastrointestinal bleed by intragastric infusion of an amino-acid solution mimicking haemoglobin in 8 patients, with 4 hours of sampling from artery and femoral, renal, portal and hepatic veins; study 2 sampled 9 patients with an acute upper gastrointestinal bleed at TIPSS insertion.
cards.result: During the simulated bleed, arterial ammonia rose significantly (P=.002) with no change in ammonia production from the portal-drained viscera, while renal ammonia production increased 6-fold (P=.008) and muscle ammonia removal increased significantly; liver removal was unchanged. In the real-bleed study, ammonia was produced only by the kidneys (572 [184] nmol/kg body weight/min) and not by the splanchnic area (−121 [87] nmol/kg body weight/min).
cards.watchOut: Small studies (8 and 9 patients), printed on the face under the physiology labelling rule; the simulated bleed is an amino-acid load, not blood, though the concordant real-bleed arm is the check on that substitution.
cards.source: Olde Damink SW et al. The kidney plays a major role in the hyperammonemia seen after simulated or actual GI bleeding in patients with cirrhosis. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2003. cards.summary: Hayashi 1981: in 16 patients with decompensated cirrhosis, skeletal muscle took up ammonia, coupled to branched-chain amino acid use
cards.type: Human physiology study (femoral arteriovenous differences, Hayashi 1981)
cards.people: Femoral arteriovenous differences for free amino acids and plasma ammonia after an overnight fast in 16 patients with decompensated liver cirrhosis (with and without encephalopathy) and 8 control subjects.
cards.result: Ammonia was significantly taken up by skeletal muscle in the cirrhotic patients, and arterial ammonia level correlated positively with the arteriovenous differences of leucine, isoleucine and alanine. Releases of isoleucine, leucine and alanine from peripheral tissue were significantly reduced in decompensated cirrhosis, particularly with encephalopathy, while phenylalanine and tyrosine release rose — the pattern the authors read as muscle burning branched-chain amino acids to power ammonia detoxication into glutamine.
cards.watchOut: A 1981 single-region (leg) balance study: it shows muscle uptake and its amino-acid coupling, but whole-body muscle clearance is extrapolated from the leg, and glutamine production itself was inferred rather than traced.
cards.source: Hayashi M et al. Augmented utilization of branched-chain amino acids by skeletal muscle in decompensated liver cirrhosis in special relation to ammonia detoxication. Gastroenterologia Japonica. 1981. PMID: 7227760. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: gut makes it, the failing and bypassed liver misses it, muscle mops it up as glutamine, and the kidney can become a second source
cards.summary: Synthesis: gut makes it, the failing and bypassed liver misses it, muscle mops it up as glutamine, and the kidney can become a second source
cards.people: The carded evidence: interorgan catheterisation in 24 patients with cirrhosis and a TIPSS (Olde Damink 2002), simulated and actual gastrointestinal bleeding studies in 8 and 9 patients (Olde Damink 2003), and leg arteriovenous balance in 16 patients with decompensated cirrhosis and 8 controls (Hayashi 1981). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong.
cards.result: Production is intestinal first (portal-drained viscera highest, consuming glutamine), hepatic urea-cycle clearance is what cirrhosis and shunting remove, skeletal muscle removed more ammonia than the cirrhotic liver in the fasted state and was the major removal site during bleeding, and the kidney switched from background production equal to the hepatosplanchnic area to a 6-fold rise after a bleed — in real bleeds the only net producer measured (572 nmol/kg/min). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Every carded cohort had advanced cirrhosis, most with a TIPSS; the healthy-state version of this traffic (portal ammonia fully cleared on first pass) is the textbook account, supported here by the controls and by what changes when the liver is bypassed, not by catheter studies in healthy volunteers.

shelves.title: The enterohepatic circulation: a gram-sized bile acid pool recycled many times a day, topped up by a few hundred milligrams of synthesis
shelves.question: In adults, how does the enterohepatic circulation recycle bile acids and how many times a day does the bile acid pool circulate?
shelves.mesh: Bile · Bile Acids and Salts · Carbon Isotopes · Chenodeoxycholic Acid · Cholic Acid · Cholic Acids · Deoxycholic Acid · Deuterium · Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry · Humans · Indicator Dilution Techniques · Kinetics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: the liver makes primary bile acids from cholesterol, conjugates them, and secretes them into bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals; after a meal the bile acids do their detergent work in the small intestine and are then actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (about 95% per pass), return in portal blood, and are re-secreted — the enterohepatic circulation. The textbooks put the pool at roughly 2–3 g, cycling about 4–12 times a day (the figure varies by source and by how cycling is counted), with the small faecal loss replaced by new synthesis of a few hundred milligrams a day. The carded human isotope studies measured the components of that account: cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid pools of 0.84 g and 0.64 g with fractional turnover rates of 0.28 and 0.17 per day and matching synthesis rates (Everson 1987); a cholic acid fractional turnover of 0.46 per day by a microscale stable-isotope method whose human values agreed with the classic literature (Hulzebos 2001); and the feedback limb — feeding one bile acid suppressed synthesis of the others by 38–67% and shrank their pools by about half (Tauber 1996), which is how the returning pool tells the liver to stop making more. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Everson 1987: in 5 healthy adults, the cholic acid pool was 0.84 g and the chenodeoxycholic acid pool 0.64 g, turning over at 0.28 and 0.17 per day
cards.summary: Everson 1987: in 5 healthy adults, the cholic acid pool was 0.84 g and the chenodeoxycholic acid pool 0.64 g, turning over at 0.28 and 0.17 per day
cards.type: Human physiology study (stable-isotope bile acid kinetics, Everson 1987) — N = 5
cards.people: Five healthy subjects given 50 mg each of [24-13C]chenodeoxycholic acid and [24-13C]cholic acid, with steady-state kinetics measured from serum and from bile by stable-isotope gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; a further 10 subjects were studied for the serum dual-isotope technique.
cards.result: Serum and bile measurements agreed: chenodeoxycholic acid fractional turnover rate 0.17 ± 0.03 per day, pool 0.64 ± 0.1 g, synthesis 0.12 ± 0.03 g/day; cholic acid fractional turnover rate 0.28 ± 0.05 per day, pool 0.84 ± 0.29 g, synthesis 0.24 ± 0.10 g/day. Synthesis equals loss at steady state, so these are also the daily faecal loss rates the liver must replace — a few hundred milligrams against gram-sized pools.
cards.watchOut: N = 5, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. Fractional turnover per day is not the same as cycles per day: turnover counts the fraction of the pool lost and replaced daily, while cycling counts how often the pool passes through the intestine, most of it returning each time.
cards.source: Everson GT et al. Steady-state kinetics of serum bile acids in healthy human subjects: single and dual isotope techniques using stable isotopes and mass spectrometry. Journal of lipid research. 1987. PMID: 3553403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tauber 1996: feeding one bile acid suppressed synthesis of the others by up to 65% and shrank their pools by about half — the feedback limb of the circulation, in healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Tauber 1996: feeding one bile acid suppressed synthesis of the others by up to 65% and shrank their pools by about half — the feedback limb of the circulation, in healthy volunteers
cards.type: Human physiology study (bile acid feeding and synthesis feedback, Tauber 1996)
cards.people: Healthy volunteers given 500 mg/day for 4 weeks of cholic acid (n=6), chenodeoxycholic acid (n=6) or deoxycholic acid (n=5), or the non-absorbable antibiotic paromomycin (n=6) for 2 weeks, with pool size, synthesis rate and fractional turnover of the three main bile acids measured simultaneously by stable-isotope labelling before and during intake.
cards.result: Chenodeoxycholic acid feeding inhibited cholic acid synthesis by 65% and deoxycholic acid input by 67%. Deoxycholic acid feeding suppressed cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid synthesis by 53%, reducing their pool sizes by 64% and 57%. Cholic acid feeding nearly doubled deoxycholic acid input and pool, while inhibiting chenodeoxycholic acid synthesis by 38% and halving its pool. The returning bile acid load, in other words, throttles new synthesis — the feedback that keeps the pool constant while it cycles.
cards.watchOut: These are pharmacological oral loads of single bile acids in small volunteer groups (n=5–6 per arm), not meal physiology; they demonstrate the feedback mechanism and its size, not its minute-to-minute operation after food.
cards.source: Tauber G et al. Feedback regulation of bile acid synthesis measured by stable isotope kinetics in humans. European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology. 1996. PMID: 8900905. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hulzebos 2001: a microscale stable-isotope method measured the human cholic acid pool at 2.4 µmol per 100 g body weight with fractional turnover 0.46 per day — agreeing with the classic isotope literature
cards.summary: Hulzebos 2001: a microscale stable-isotope method measured the human cholic acid pool at 2.4 µmol per 100 g body weight with fractional turnover 0.46 per day — agreeing with the classic isotope literature
cards.type: Human physiology study (microscale stable-isotope cholic acid kinetics, Hulzebos 2001)
cards.people: Human volunteers (with parallel rodent work) given [2,2,4,4-2H4]cholic acid, with enrichment decay measured in 50 µl plasma samples; the human sample size is not printed in the record — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Human cholic acid pool size was 2.4 ± 0.7 µmol/100 g body weight, fractional turnover rate 0.46 ± 0.14 per day, and synthesis rate 1.0 ± 0.2 µmol/100 g body weight per day. The authors state the human data agreed well with literature values from conventional isotope dilution — an independent method landing on the same pool and turnover as the classic studies.
cards.watchOut: A methods paper spanning three species; only its human arm is used here, its human N is not printed in the record, and its per-100 g pool figure needs body-weight scaling before it can be compared with whole-pool gram figures.
cards.source: Hulzebos CV et al. Measurement of parameters of cholic acid kinetics in plasma using a microscale stable isotope dilution technique: application to rodents and humans. Journal of lipid research. 2001. PMID: 11714862. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a gram-sized pool, secreted and reclaimed repeatedly, with synthesis replacing only the small daily loss
cards.summary: Synthesis: a gram-sized pool, secreted and reclaimed repeatedly, with synthesis replacing only the small daily loss
cards.people: The carded evidence: stable-isotope kinetics in 5 healthy adults (Everson 1987), bile-acid feeding studies in 23 healthy volunteers across four arms (Tauber 1996), and an independent microscale isotope method in human volunteers (Hulzebos 2001, N not documented in the record). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep; Guyton & Hall.
cards.result: Measured pools for the two primary bile acids sum to about 1.5 g (0.84 g cholic + 0.64 g chenodeoxycholic), with synthesis of roughly 0.1–0.25 g/day per acid balancing faecal loss, and feedback suppression of synthesis by returning bile acids demonstrated directly (up to 65%). The Boron / Guyton & Hall account — a total pool of roughly 2–3 g secreted into the intestine and reabsorbed in the ileum repeatedly through the day (textbook figures run about 4–12 cycles daily), with only the small lost fraction replaced — is consistent with every measured component; the cycles-per-day figure itself is the textbook's, since the human studies measure pool, turnover and synthesis rather than counting cycles. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Do not confuse the three rates: cycles per day (textbook, ~4–12) counts intestinal passages; fractional turnover per day (~0.2–0.5) counts the share of the pool lost and replaced; synthesis (a few hundred mg/day) is the replacement itself. Quoting one as another is the classic error on this topic.
cards.source: Synthesis of Everson GT et al. Journal of lipid research. 1987 (PMID: 3553403); Tauber G et al. European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology. 1996 (PMID: 8900905); Hulzebos CV et al. Journal of lipid research. 2001 (PMID: 11714862). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology; Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Bilirubin's path from haem to bile — and why reduced conjugation raises the unconjugated form: human kinetics and the Gilbert natural experiment
shelves.question: In adults, how is bilirubin made, conjugated in the liver, and excreted into bile, and why does the unconjugated form rise when conjugation is reduced?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bile · Bilirubin · Carbon Isotopes · Computers · Erythrocyte Aging · Feces · Female · Humans · Kinetics · Liver · Male · Metabolic Clearance Rate
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: bilirubin is the end-product of haem breakdown — senescent red cells are dismantled in macrophages, haem oxygenase opens the haem ring to biliverdin (releasing iron and carbon monoxide), and biliverdin reductase yields unconjugated bilirubin, which is water-insoluble, travels to the liver bound to albumin, is taken up by hepatocytes, and is conjugated by UDP-glucuronyl transferase to mono- and diglucuronides; the water-soluble conjugates are secreted into bile and leave in the stool. Because plasma bilirubin is almost all unconjugated and its level is set by production against hepatic clearance, anything that cuts conjugation — Gilbert syndrome's reduced transferase activity is the human model — backs up the unconjugated form specifically. The carded human studies measured each step: production of 3.8 mg/kg/day and hepatic clearance of 47 ml/min in healthy adults (Berk 1969); bile from Gilbert patients carrying far less diglucuronide (68% vs 88%) and more monoglucuronide (23% vs 7%), localising the defect to adding the second glucuronic acid (Goresky 1978); and caloric restriction raising unconjugated bilirubin precisely in people with reduced transferase activity, not in haemolysis with normal enzyme (Felsher 1975). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Berk 1969: in 13 healthy adults, bilirubin production was 3.8 mg/kg per day and hepatic clearance 47 ml/min — the production-versus-clearance balance that sets the plasma level
cards.summary: Berk 1969: in 13 healthy adults, bilirubin production was 3.8 mg/kg per day and hepatic clearance 47 ml/min — the production-versus-clearance balance that sets the plasma level
cards.type: Human physiology study (isotope bilirubin kinetics, Berk 1969) — N = 13
cards.people: 13 healthy young adults given an intravenous tracer dose of unconjugated bilirubin-14C, with plasma isotope content followed for 24–30 hours and faecal and urinary radioactivity measured for 7 days (cumulative recovery averaged 96% of the dose).
cards.result: Hepatic bilirubin clearance was 47 ± 10 ml/min (mean ± SD), the bilirubin production rate 3.8 ± 0.6 mg/kg per day, and mean red cell life span 101 ± 13 days. Plasma disappearance needed three exponentials (half-times 18, 81 and 578 minutes), modelled as plasma unconjugated bilirubin exchanging with extrahepatic and intrahepatic pools and eliminated via the intrahepatic pool — production in, liver out, with the plasma unconjugated level as the balance point.
cards.watchOut: Tracer kinetics in 13 young healthy adults define the normal reference; the production figure is whole-body (mostly red-cell haem, with a minority from other haem proteins and ineffective erythropoiesis) and is not broken down by source in this study.
cards.source: Berk PD et al. Studies of bilirubin kinetics in normal adults. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1969. PMID: 5824077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Goresky 1978: Gilbert patients' bile carried 68% diglucuronide vs 88% in normals — the conjugation defect sits at adding the second glucuronic acid
cards.summary: Goresky 1978: Gilbert patients' bile carried 68% diglucuronide vs 88% in normals — the conjugation defect sits at adding the second glucuronic acid
cards.type: Human physiology study (bilirubin loads and biliary conjugates, Goresky 1978)
cards.people: Normal subjects and patients with Gilbert syndrome given intravenous bilirubin loads (3.4 µmol/kg, with 3-fold and 6-fold doses in normals), with plasma disappearance followed and bilirubin conjugates measured in bile-containing duodenal aspirates (group sizes are not printed in the record — N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Both groups cleared an identical initial proportion of the load, but Gilbert patients later showed reduced clearance with sustained plasma elevation and no reflux of conjugated bilirubin into plasma; tripling or sextupling the dose in normals did not reproduce the Gilbert pattern, excluding a simple uptake defect. In bile, bilirubin diglucuronide averaged 68% in Gilbert patients versus 88% in normals, and monoglucuronide 23% versus 7% (both P<0.001). Two days of caloric restriction (1,569 kJ/day) raised Gilbert patients' serum bilirubin without changing the biliary pattern; phenobarbital normalised plasma bilirubin and reverted the pattern toward normal.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record — the abstract reports no group sizes, so none is printed here. Duodenal aspirates sample bile indirectly, and the study predates UGT1A1 genotyping: it localises the functional defect, which later genetics assigned to reduced UGT1A1 expression.
cards.source: Goresky CA et al. Definition of a conjugation of dysfunction in Gilbert's syndrome: studies of the handling of bilirubin loads and of the pattern of bilirubin conjugates secreted in bile. Clinical science and molecular medicine. 1978. PMID: 668269. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Felsher 1975: cutting calories raised unconjugated bilirubin most in people with reduced glucuronyl transferase activity — not in haemolysis with a normal enzyme
cards.summary: Felsher 1975: cutting calories raised unconjugated bilirubin most in people with reduced glucuronyl transferase activity — not in haemolysis with a normal enzyme
cards.type: Human physiology study (caloric restriction and transferase activity, Felsher 1975)
cards.people: Patients with Gilbert syndrome and partial hepatic bilirubin UDP-glucuronyl transferase dysfunction, patients with haemolytic unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and normal subjects, studied for serum bilirubin response to reduced caloric intake, with hepatic transferase activity measured (group sizes are not printed in the record — N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Reduction in caloric intake produced a greater absolute rise in serum bilirubin in Gilbert/partial-dysfunction patients than in haemolytic patients or normals. Two patients with overt haemolysis but an exaggerated fasting response proved to have reduced transferase activities comparable to Gilbert syndrome; the other haemolytic patients had normal activities. Fasting plus the transferase inhibitor novobiocin in 2 normal subjects raised bilirubin more than either alone. The authors conclude the underlying transferase dysfunction, not the starting bilirubin level, drives diet-induced unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record. Transferase activity was assayed in liver tissue in an era before genotyping, and fasting also changes hepatic bilirubin uptake and haemodynamics — the study's internal contrast (haemolysis with and without low enzyme activity) is what isolates conjugation as the decisive step.
cards.source: Felsher BF et al. Caloric intake and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Gastroenterology. 1975. PMID: 807500. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: production is fixed by haem turnover, so the plasma unconjugated level is a clearance reading — cut conjugation and unconjugated bilirubin is what accumulates
cards.summary: Synthesis: production is fixed by haem turnover, so the plasma unconjugated level is a clearance reading — cut conjugation and unconjugated bilirubin is what accumulates
cards.people: The carded evidence: isotope kinetics in 13 healthy adults (Berk 1969), bilirubin-load and bile-conjugate studies in normals and Gilbert patients (Goresky 1978, N not documented in the record), and caloric-restriction studies across Gilbert, haemolytic and normal groups (Felsher 1975, N not documented in the record). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall.
cards.result: Healthy production runs at 3.8 mg/kg/day against a hepatic clearance of 47 ml/min, so plasma unconjugated bilirubin sits where production meets clearance. When conjugation is reduced, the product that backs up is the unconjugated substrate: Gilbert bile shows the conjugation shortfall directly (diglucuronide 68% vs 88%), plasma clearance of loads slows late (the conjugation phase), and fasting unmasks the defect only in low-transferase livers. The conjugated form does not accumulate in plasma in this setting — there is no conjugated reflux — because what little is conjugated is still secreted into bile normally. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers reduced conjugation with intact uptake and canalicular secretion (the Gilbert model). Where secretion itself fails or bile flow is obstructed, it is the conjugated form that refluxes into plasma — the opposite pattern, and a different mechanism, not a contradiction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Berk PD et al. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1969 (PMID: 5824077); Goresky CA et al. Clinical science and molecular medicine. 1978 (PMID: 668269); Felsher BF et al. Gastroenterology. 1975 (PMID: 807500). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: From meal fat to blood: why long-chain fat takes the lymph in chylomicrons and medium-chain fat takes the portal vein
shelves.question: In adults, what happens to dietary fat between ingestion and absorption, and why do medium-chain triglycerides reach the liver directly through the portal vein?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Blood Chemical Analysis · Body Mass Index · Cholesterol · Cross-Over Studies · Diet · Dietary Fats, Unsaturated · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Lipids · Lipoproteins · Male · Postprandial Period · Rats · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: dietary triglyceride is emulsified, hydrolysed by pancreatic lipase to 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids, solubilised in bile-salt micelles, taken up by enterocytes, re-esterified, and exported in chylomicrons into lymph — reaching the blood via the thoracic duct and the liver only later, as remnants. Medium-chain triglycerides break every step of that chain: their fatty acids (C8–C10) are hydrolysed faster, are water-soluble enough to leave the enterocyte without re-esterification or chylomicron packaging, bind albumin, and drain straight into the portal vein to the liver. The carded human studies show the route difference in people. A single MCT dose produced a much smaller serum and chylomicron triglyceride response than the same dose of long-chain fat in healthy men (Kasai 2003) — the signature of fat that mostly bypassed chylomicrons. Position-labelled decanoic acid confirmed the main route is portal while showing a minority does enter chylomicron triglyceride (Yli-Jokipii 2004). And in patients with fat malabsorption, an MCT formula measurably increased fat absorption where a long-chain formula did not (Craig 1997) — the clinical consequence of a route that needs less lipolysis, no micellar packaging and no lymph. The index's MCT weight-loss shelf (pack #5280) asks a different question and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Kasai 2003: in 25 healthy men, a 10 g MCT dose produced a far smaller chylomicron triglyceride response than 10 g of long-chain fat — fat that mostly never entered chylomicrons
cards.summary: Kasai 2003: in 25 healthy men, a 10 g MCT dose produced a far smaller chylomicron triglyceride response than 10 g of long-chain fat — fat that mostly never entered chylomicrons
cards.type: Human physiology study (single-dose MCT vs LCT crossover, Kasai 2003)
cards.people: 25 healthy male volunteers in a double-blind crossover comparison of a single test dose of 10 g medium-chain triglycerides or 10 g long-chain triglycerides, with blood sampled for 6 hours and results analysed by body mass index (below vs at or above 23 kg/m²). (The record's MeSH also lists a rat experiment reported alongside; only the human arm is carded here.)
cards.result: The long-chain diet produced significantly greater areas under the curve for serum and chylomicron triglyceride in the higher-BMI group than in the lower-BMI group. After the MCT dose, the higher-BMI group's response was significantly lower than its response to long-chain fat. A blunted chylomicron excursion after MCT is what the portal route predicts: medium-chain fatty acids leave the gut in portal blood on albumin rather than in chylomicrons through lymph.
cards.watchOut: A chylomicron-triglyceride curve is an indirect route marker — portal blood cannot be sampled in healthy volunteers — and the clearest separation was in the higher-BMI subgroup; the study shows the traffic pattern, and the textbook supplies the anatomy.
cards.source: Kasai M et al. Effect of medium-chain triglycerides on the postprandial triglyceride concentration in healthy men. Bioscience, biotechnology, and biochemistry. 2003. PMID: 12619672. cards.headline: Yli-Jokipii 2004: medium-chain fatty acids are mainly portal, but some do appear in chylomicrons — and where the fatty acid sits on the glycerol changes how much
cards.summary: Yli-Jokipii 2004: medium-chain fatty acids are mainly portal, but some do appear in chylomicrons — and where the fatty acid sits on the glycerol changes how much
cards.type: Human physiology study (position-labelled MCT fat loads, Yli-Jokipii 2004) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy normal-weight volunteers in a randomised double-blind crossover trial eating two fat loads containing decanoic acid (10:0) placed predominantly at the sn-1(3),2 positions (MML) or the sn-1,3 positions (MLM) of triglyceride, with chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride structures analysed by mass spectrometry.
cards.result: The authors' framing, tested by their measurements: medium-chain fatty acids are mainly absorbed via the portal venous system, yet are also incorporated into chylomicron triglyceride. The position of decanoic acid in chylomicron triglyceride reflected its position in the fat eaten, and chylomicron triglyceride species differed significantly between the loads (more 30:0 and 38:1 species after MML, P<0.05), while the overall magnitude of postprandial lipaemia did not differ between the two MCT structures.
cards.watchOut: N = 10, at the floor and printed on the face. This card is the corrective to an oversimplified 'MCT never enters chylomicrons' claim: mainly portal is the accurate statement, and the split depends on the triglyceride's structure.
cards.source: Yli-Jokipii KM et al. Positional distribution of decanoic acid: effect on chylomicron and VLDL TAG structures and postprandial lipemia. Lipids. 2004. PMID: 15357025. cards.headline: Craig 1997: in 24 patients with AIDS and fat malabsorption, an MCT-based formula increased fat absorption while a long-chain formula did not
cards.summary: Craig 1997: in 24 patients with AIDS and fat malabsorption, an MCT-based formula increased fat absorption while a long-chain formula did not
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (MCT vs LCT formula in malabsorption, Craig 1997)
cards.people: 24 patients (23 men, 1 woman) with AIDS and documented fat malabsorption in a double-blind randomised 15-day trial: after 3 days on a controlled solid diet (100 g fat/day) documenting malabsorption, 12 days on a liquid formula with 35% of energy as fat — 85% medium-chain triglycerides in one group, 100% long-chain triglycerides in the other — with stool fat and nitrogen measured.
cards.result: On the MCT formula, stool fat and stool nitrogen fell significantly (P=.01 and P=.03) and fat absorption increased significantly (P=.03) from the initial to the final period; the long-chain group showed no such improvement, and the between-group difference in fat-absorption change was significant (P=.04). The MCT group also tended to fewer bowel movements and abdominal symptoms, and body weight was maintained in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A malabsorption population, not healthy digestion: it shows the portal route rescuing absorption when the lipase–micelle–lymph pathway is failing, which is evidence about the route's independence from that pathway rather than about normal meal handling.
cards.source: Craig GB et al. Decreased fat and nitrogen losses in patients with AIDS receiving medium-chain-triglyceride-enriched formula vs those receiving long-chain-triglyceride-containing formula. Journal of the American Dietetic Association. 1997. PMID: 9183320. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: long-chain fat rides micelles into chylomicrons and lymph; medium-chain fatty acids skip the packaging and take the portal vein
cards.summary: Synthesis: long-chain fat rides micelles into chylomicrons and lymph; medium-chain fatty acids skip the packaging and take the portal vein
cards.people: The carded evidence: single-dose crossover physiology in 25 healthy men (Kasai 2003), position-labelled fat loads in 10 healthy volunteers (Yli-Jokipii 2004), and a randomised formula trial in 24 patients with fat malabsorption (Craig 1997). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep.
cards.result: The Boron & Boulpaep sequence — lipase hydrolysis, micellar solubilisation, enterocyte re-esterification, chylomicron export into lymph — is the long-chain pathway, and its postprandial chylomicron surge is measurable in healthy men. Medium-chain fatty acids, being shorter and more water-soluble, are absorbed mainly into portal blood (hence the blunted chylomicron response and the improved absorption when the conventional pathway fails), with a minority incorporated into chylomicrons depending on triglyceride structure. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Chain length is a gradient, not a switch: C12 (lauric acid) behaves partly like a long-chain fat, and even C8–C10 appear in chylomicrons to a degree — 'mainly portal' is the defensible wording, and it is the wording used throughout this shelf.

shelves.title: Secretin and CCK after a meal: the alkaline river and the enzymes it carries — human infusion and blockade studies
shelves.question: In adults, how do secretin and cholecystokinin coordinate pancreatic enzyme and bicarbonate secretion after a meal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amylases · Analysis of Variance · Benzodiazepinones · Bicarbonates · Bilirubin · Cholecystokinin · Devazepide · Double-Blind Method · Duodenum · Gallbladder · Gastric Juice · Humans · Intestinal Secretions · Male · Pancreas · Radioimmunoassay · Secretin · Stimulation, Chemical · Trypsin
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook division of labour: acid entering the duodenum releases secretin from S cells, and secretin drives the duct cells to secrete a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises the acid; fat and protein products release cholecystokinin (CCK) from I cells, and CCK drives the acinar cells to secrete enzymes (and contracts the gallbladder), with the vagus nerve setting the gain on both — secretin's fluid also flushes CCK's enzymes down the duct. The carded human infusion studies show the coordination directly. On a background secretin infusion holding plasma secretin at postprandial levels (~5 pM), a physiological CCK-8 infusion (~9 pM, the postprandial range) stimulated trypsin, amylase and bicarbonate output, and blocking the CCK receptor cut those responses by about three quarters and virtually abolished gallbladder contraction (Cantor 1991). Meal-stimulated enzyme secretion was almost completely blocked by atropine and 60% blocked by a CCK antagonist (Adler 1991) — CCK is the hormonal driver, cholinergic tone the permissive amplifier. And combined secretin–CCK testing in healthy volunteers produced peak duodenal bicarbonate of 108 mmol/L, the neutralising fluid in action (Law 2012). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Cantor 1991: on a postprandial-level secretin background, physiological CCK drove enzyme and bicarbonate output — and a CCK antagonist cut the responses by 74–98%
cards.summary: Cantor 1991: on a postprandial-level secretin background, physiological CCK drove enzyme and bicarbonate output — and a CCK antagonist cut the responses by 74–98%
cards.type: Human physiology study (secretin/CCK infusion with CCK blockade, Cantor 1991) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 normal subjects in a randomised crossover study receiving oral MK-329 (a CCK receptor antagonist) or placebo before a background intravenous secretin infusion (5 pmol/kg/h) and two 1-hour CCK-8 doses (about 15 and 40 pmol/kg/h), with gastric and duodenal juice aspirated separately using a duodenal recovery marker. N = 6, printed on the face under the physiology labelling rule.
cards.result: The secretin infusion produced maximum plasma secretin concentrations similar to postprandial values (~5 pM). The low CCK-8 dose raised plasma CCK from 1.8 ± 0.2 pM to 9.2 ± 1.3 pM (postprandial range) and the high dose to 23.4 ± 3.2 pM; CCK stimulated pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction, raising trypsin, amylase, bicarbonate and bilirubin output. MK-329 did not reduce basal secretion but inhibited the integrated responses to the low (physiological) CCK dose by 74% for trypsin (p<0.01), 89% for amylase and 75% for bicarbonate (p<0.05), and reduced the bilirubin (gallbladder) response by 98% (p<0.01).
cards.watchOut: N = 6, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. The design infuses both hormones rather than feeding a meal, so it isolates the hormonal limbs cleanly at the price of the cephalic and gastric phases.
cards.source: Cantor P et al. Inhibition of cholecystokinin-stimulated pancreaticobiliary output in man by the cholecystokinin receptor antagonist MK-329. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1991. PMID: 1713709. Registry ID: none in the record. human physiology study (secretin/cck infusion with cck blockade, cantor 1991) — n = 6 6 normal subjects in a randomised crossover study receiving oral mk-329 (a cck receptor antagonist) or placebo before a background intravenous secretin infusion (5 pmol/kg/h) and two 1-hour cck-8 doses (about 15 and 40 pmol/kg/h), with gastric and duodenal juice aspirated separately using a duodenal recovery marker. n = 6, printed on the face under the physiology labelling rule. the secretin infusion produced maximum plasma secretin concentrations similar to postprandial values (~5 pm). the low cck-8 dose raised plasma cck from 1.8 ± 0.2 pm to 9.2 ± 1.3 pm (postprandial range) and the high dose to 23.4 ± 3.2 pm; cck stimulated pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction, raising trypsin, amylase, bicarbonate and bilirubin output. mk-329 did not reduce basal secretion but inhibited the integrated responses to the low (physiological) cck dose by 74% for trypsin (p<0.01), 89% for amylase and 75% for bicarbonate (p<0.05), and reduced the bilirubin (gallbladder) response by 98% (p<0.01). n = 6, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. the design infuses both hormones rather than feeding a meal, so it isolates the hormonal limbs cleanly at the price of the cephalic and gastric phases. cantor p et al. inhibition of cholecystokinin-stimulated pancreaticobiliary output in man by the cholecystokinin receptor antagonist mk-329. scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1991. pmid: 1713709. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · amylases · analysis of variance · benzodiazepinones · bicarbonates · bilirubin · cholecystokinin · devazepide · double-blind method · duodenum · gallbladder · gastric juice · humans · intestinal secretions · male · pancreas · radioimmunoassay · secretin · stimulation, chemical · trypsin

cards.headline: Adler 1991: atropine almost completely blocked meal-stimulated pancreatic enzyme secretion and a CCK antagonist blocked 60% — CCK drives, the vagus amplifies
cards.summary: Adler 1991: atropine almost completely blocked meal-stimulated pancreatic enzyme secretion and a CCK antagonist blocked 60% — CCK drives, the vagus amplifies
cards.type: Human physiology study (meal and CCK stimulation with blockade, Adler 1991)
cards.people: Adult men studied with duodenal perfusion of graded caloric loads and intravenous infusion of increasing doses of caerulein (a CCK analogue), with pancreatic enzyme output measured before and during the cholinergic antagonist atropine and the CCK antagonist loxiglumide (subject number is not printed in the record — N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Graded duodenal caloric loads and graded caerulein doses each stimulated pancreatic enzyme output dose-dependently. Prestimulated secretion was inhibited by both atropine and loxiglumide; atropine almost completely blocked meal-stimulated secretion, whereas loxiglumide caused 60% inhibition. The enzyme response to exogenous CCK was significantly inhibited by both agents, plasma CCK was unchanged by atropine and rose with loxiglumide. The authors conclude enzyme secretion is predominantly dependent on cholinergic tone, with CCK modulating the response.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record. Caerulein is a CCK analogue rather than CCK itself, and 'almost complete' atropine blockade partly reflects atropine's effects on gastric emptying and duodenal delivery of the stimulus, not only on the pancreas.
cards.source: Adler G et al. Interaction of the cholinergic system and cholecystokinin in the regulation of endogenous and exogenous stimulation of pancreatic secretion in humans. Gastroenterology. 1991. PMID: 1702077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Law 2012: combined secretin–CCK stimulation in 20 healthy volunteers produced peak duodenal bicarbonate of 108 mmol/L — the neutralising secretion, measured
cards.summary: Law 2012: combined secretin–CCK stimulation in 20 healthy volunteers produced peak duodenal bicarbonate of 108 mmol/L — the neutralising secretion, measured
cards.type: Human physiology study (combined secretin–CCK function test, Law 2012)
cards.people: 20 healthy volunteers and 69 patients evaluated for chronic pancreatitis, all undergoing a combined secretin–CCK endoscopic pancreatic function test with duodenal fluid bicarbonate, lipase and amylase measured after stimulation; patients also had endoscopic ultrasound scored for pancreatitis features.
cards.result: Healthy subjects reached a peak bicarbonate concentration of 108 mmol/L, against 90 mmol/L in patients with fewer than 5 ultrasound features of chronic pancreatitis and 72 mmol/L in those with 5 or more (P<.001). Peak amylase, lipase and fluid volume did not separate the groups as well: bicarbonate had the best discrimination for chronic pancreatitis (area under the curve 0.738 vs 0.677 for amylase and 0.627 for lipase), and adding enzyme measurement to bicarbonate did not improve it.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic-accuracy study, carded for its healthy-volunteer physiology: it measures what the two hormones together elicit (a bicarbonate peak above 100 mmol/L) rather than separating secretin's share from CCK's — that separation is the Cantor card's job.
cards.source: Law R et al. Endoscopic pancreatic function test using combined secretin and cholecystokinin stimulation for the evaluation of chronic pancreatitis. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2012. PMID: 22281107. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: secretin supplies the alkaline river, CCK supplies the enzymes it carries, and cholinergic tone sets the gain on both
cards.summary: Synthesis: secretin supplies the alkaline river, CCK supplies the enzymes it carries, and cholinergic tone sets the gain on both
cards.people: The carded evidence: secretin/CCK infusion with receptor blockade in 6 normal subjects (Cantor 1991), meal and CCK-analogue stimulation with cholinergic and CCK blockade (Adler 1991, N not documented in the record), and combined-hormone function testing in 20 healthy volunteers (Law 2012). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall.
cards.result: At postprandial plasma levels (secretin ~5 pM background; CCK ~9 pM), CCK drove trypsin, amylase and bicarbonate output and gallbladder contraction, with CCK blockade removing 74–98% of the responses; meal-stimulated enzyme secretion depended on cholinergic tone (near-total atropine blockade) with a 60% CCK-antagonist-sensitive share; and the combined stimulus produced peak bicarbonate of 108 mmol/L in health. That is the Guyton & Hall coordination: duodenal acid → secretin → bicarbonate-rich ductal fluid; fat and protein products → CCK → acinar enzymes and gallbladder contraction; vagal tone amplifying both. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Infused-hormone studies reproduce the intestinal phase in isolation; a real meal adds cephalic and gastric phases and other peptides (for example peptide YY braking secretion later), so the percentages here describe the secretin/CCK core of the response, not the whole postprandial programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cantor P et al. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1991 (PMID: 1713709); Adler G et al. Gastroenterology. 1991 (PMID: 1702077); Law R et al. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2012 (PMID: 22281107). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: What sets gastric emptying: meal form sets the pace (liquid half-time 44 minutes vs solid 162), and duodenal fat and acid apply the brake — pyloric pressure, cholecystokinin and tonic duodenal occlusion in human studies
shelves.question: In adults, what sets the rate of gastric emptying of a meal, and how do fat and acid in the duodenum slow it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cholecystokinin/blood,metabolism · Duodenum · Female · Gastric Emptying · Gastrointestinal Motility · Humans · Hydrochloric Acid/pharmacology · Male · Oleic Acids/pharmacology · Osmolar Concentration · Radionuclide Imaging · Stomach/diagnostic imaging,physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (named here as framing, not as an evidence card): the stomach empties at a rate set by meal volume, physical state and caloric/osmotic content, gated by duodenal feedback — the enterogastric brake. The human record fetched for this shelf shows each element directly. Meal form sets the baseline rate: in 73 healthy volunteers given a standard scintigraphic test meal, the liquid component emptied with a median half-time of 44 minutes and the solid component with a median half-time of 162 minutes (Parker 2017). Duodenal contents, not gastric contents, carry the brake: emptying was fastest when duodenal contents were isotonic, and non-isotonic duodenal contents slowed it, while non-isotonic solutions in stomach or jejunum did not slow emptying so long as the duodenum stayed isotonic (Meeroff 1975). Fat is a brake signal: intraduodenal fat inhibited gastric emptying in humans (Valenzuela 1981, whose title also names secretin and the cholecystokinin octapeptide), and intraduodenal lipid at 2 kcal/min stimulated isolated pyloric pressure waves and basal pyloric pressure, suppressed antral and duodenal pressure waves, and raised plasma cholecystokinin versus saline in 8 healthy men (Vozzo 2002). Acid is a brake signal with a mechanical face: in 8 volunteers studied by synchronised videofluoroscopy and manometry, duodenal HCl induced frequent large-amplitude contractions and prolonged tonic occlusion of the duodenum within 15–30 seconds, whereas oleate or bile increased duodenal diameter and reduced contractility — the duodenum restricting outflow either by tonic resistance or by delaying clearance (Rao 1996). Several of these classic studies are small (n = 8) or report no number in the fetched record (printed as N not documented on the card face); the physiology is established because the findings converge, not because any one study is large.

cards.headline: Parker 2017: in 73 healthy volunteers, a standard scintigraphic meal's liquid component emptied with a median half-time of 44 minutes and its solid component in 162 minutes — meal form sets the baseline rate
cards.summary: Parker 2017: in 73 healthy volunteers, a standard scintigraphic meal's liquid component emptied with a median half-time of 44 minutes and its solid component in 162 minutes — meal form sets the baseline rate
cards.people: 73 healthy volunteers (34 men; mean age 45 ± 20 years in the liquid-emptying analysis) given the Nottingham test meal — 400 mL liquid nutrient (0.75 kcal/mL) with an optional solid component of 12 solid agar beads (0 kcal) — studied by gamma scintigraphy. N = 73.
cards.result: Gastric emptying half-time was a median 44 minutes (95% reference interval 28–78) for the liquid component and 162 minutes (144–193) for the solid component. The meal produced normal postprandial fullness (visual analogue scale ≥30 in 41 of 74 subjects) and dyspeptic symptoms were rare (≥30 in 2 of 74). No consistent effect of anthropometric measures on gastric-emptying parameters was present.
cards.watchOut: These are reference intervals in healthy volunteers for one standardised meal, not a universal emptying rate: a different meal's volume, calories and solid content move the half-time, which is the point of the question this shelf answers.
cards.source: Parker HL et al. Clinical assessment of gastric emptying and sensory function utilizing gamma scintigraphy: Establishment of reference intervals for the liquid and solid components of the Nottingham test meal in healthy subjects. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2017. PMID: 28589661. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meeroff 1975: gastric emptying was fastest when duodenal contents were isotonic — non-isotonic duodenal contents slowed it, but non-isotonic stomach or jejunum contents did not
cards.summary: Meeroff 1975: gastric emptying was fastest when duodenal contents were isotonic — non-isotonic duodenal contents slowed it, but non-isotonic stomach or jejunum contents did not
cards.people: Human volunteers studied with duodenal perfusion and recovery of non-absorbable markers (polyethylene glycol 4000 and phenol red) to quantify the rate at which liquid test meals left the stomach. N not documented in the fetched record — printed here as the record gives it.
cards.result: Gastric emptying was fastest when duodenal contents were isotonic; non-isotonic duodenal contents slowed emptying whether achieved by non-isotonic duodenal perfusates or by emptying of a non-isotonic test meal. Non-isotonic solutions in the stomach and in the jejunum did not slow gastric emptying so long as duodenal contents were isotonic. The authors located the osmoreceptors that slow gastric emptying in the duodenum, not in the jejunum or stomach.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record, and the study used liquid test meals and marker recovery, not a modern mixed solid meal — it establishes where the osmotic brake sits, not a clinical emptying rate.
cards.source: Meeroff JC et al. Control of gastric emptying by osmolality of duodenal contents in man. Gastroenterology. 1975. PMID: 1126594. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rao 1996: in 8 volunteers, duodenal acid produced tonic duodenal occlusion within 15–30 seconds, while oleate and bile widened the duodenum and quieted it — two mechanical routes to the same brake
cards.summary: Rao 1996: in 8 volunteers, duodenal acid produced tonic duodenal occlusion within 15–30 seconds, while oleate and bile widened the duodenum and quieted it — two mechanical routes to the same brake
cards.people: 8 healthy volunteers (5 men, 3 women) studied by synchronised videofluoroscopy and manometry during duodenal infusion of 0.9% saline, hydrochloric acid, 5% saline, bile, and sodium oleate, each mixed with 20% barium sulfate. N = 8 — a classic small physiology study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Within 15–30 seconds of infusion, hydrochloric acid and 5% saline induced frequent large-amplitude contractions greater than those induced by 0.9% saline, with rapid dispersion of acid followed by prolonged tonic occlusion of the duodenum and a decreased duodenal diameter compared with saline or oleate. After oleate or bile, duodenal diameter increased and there were fewer, smaller-amplitude, non-propagating contractions with prolonged retention. The authors concluded the duodenum serves as an immediate brake to gastric outflow either by delaying clearance (lipid/bile) or by offering rapid tonic resistance (acid).
cards.watchOut: Sub-10 study (n = 8), labelled plainly: it shows mechanism and timing in volunteers receiving duodenal infusions, not the size of the effect after an ordinary meal.
cards.source: Rao SS et al. Duodenum as a immediate brake to gastric outflow: a videofluoroscopic and manometric assessment. Gastroenterology. 1996. PMID: 8608883. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Vozzo 2002: in 8 healthy men, intraduodenal lipid at 2 kcal/min raised pyloric pressure, suppressed antral and duodenal waves, and raised plasma cholecystokinin versus saline
cards.type: Randomised human intraduodenal-infusion physiology study, n = 8 (Vozzo 2002)
cards.people: 8 healthy male volunteers aged 18–34 years receiving randomised single-blind intraduodenal infusions of 10% Intralipid at 2 kcal/min (continuous or pulsatile) or 0.9% saline, each at 1.8 mL/min for 3 hours, with antropyloroduodenal pressures recorded by a 16-lumen manometric assembly with a pyloric sleeve sensor and plasma cholecystokinin measured. N = 8 — a classic small physiology study, labelled plainly. Intralipid is named as the tested lipid preparation given in the publication.
cards.result: Both lipid infusions stimulated isolated pyloric pressure waves (P < 0.001) and basal pyloric pressure (P < 0.01) and suppressed antral (P < 0.05) and duodenal (P < 0.05) pressure waves compared with saline, with no difference between continuous and pulsatile delivery. Lipid significantly increased plasma cholecystokinin concentrations (P < 0.05) versus saline, decreased hunger, increased fullness, and reduced energy intake at a buffet meal (all P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Sub-10 study (n = 8), labelled plainly, in young healthy men receiving lipid by tube at a fixed caloric rate — it isolates the fat signal and its pyloric mechanism; it does not measure emptying of a self-eaten fatty meal.
cards.source: Vozzo R et al. Antropyloroduodenal, cholecystokinin and feeding responses to pulsatile and non-pulsatile intraduodenal lipid infusion. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2002. PMID: 11874551. Registry ID: none in the record.
