cards.headline: Synthesis: meal form and volume set the pace; duodenal fat, acid and osmolality apply the brake — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: meal form and volume set the pace; duodenal fat, acid and osmolality apply the brake — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: The carded human evidence: one scintigraphic reference-interval study in 73 healthy volunteers (Parker 2017), one classic duodenal-perfusion study with N not documented (Meeroff 1975), one classic intraduodenal-fat study with N not documented and no abstract captured (Valenzuela 1981), and two sub-10 volunteer infusion studies (Rao 1996, n = 8; Vozzo 2002, n = 8), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: Liquids empty far faster than solids (median half-times 44 vs 162 minutes for a standard meal's components). Emptying is fastest when duodenal contents are isotonic, and duodenal — not gastric or jejunal — osmolality slows it. Intraduodenal fat inhibits emptying, raising cholecystokinin, increasing pyloric pressure and suppressing antral waves; duodenal acid slows outflow within seconds by tonic duodenal occlusion, while lipid and bile slow it by widening and quieting the duodenum. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The small classic studies are carded with their Ns (or N not documented) on the face, as physiology rules require; the established stamp rests on convergence across five decades of human studies plus the textbook frame, not on any single study's size.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parker HL et al. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2017 (PMID: 28589661); Meeroff JC et al. Gastroenterology. 1975 (PMID: 1126594); Valenzuela JE et al. Gastroenterology. 1981 (PMID: 6269946); Rao SS et al. Gastroenterology. 1996 (PMID: 8608883); Vozzo R et al. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2002 (PMID: 11874551). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Hepatitis B screening linked to treatment: recommended by the USPSTF (grade B), but the liver-outcome evidence is indirect — no screening trial exists and treatment-outcome data are inconsistent
shelves.question: In adults at increased risk, does hepatitis B screening linked to antiviral treatment improve liver outcomes (the USPSTF test-and-treat strategy)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Emigrants and Immigrants · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens/blood · Hepatitis B Vaccines · Hepatitis B virus/immunology · Hepatitis B, Chronic/diagnosis · Humans · Mass Screening/adverse effects,standards · Risk Factors · United States
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — grade with care; the indirectness is the finding. USPSTF 2020 (Krist) recommends screening adolescents and adults at increased risk (B recommendation; moderate certainty of moderate net benefit), noting up to 60% of infected people are unaware of their infection. Its evidence report (Chou 2020; 30 trials, 20 cohorts, 94,168 participants) states plainly that no study directly evaluated screening versus no screening on mortality, hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis; antiviral therapy improved intermediate outcomes (numbers needed to treat 2.6 to 17) and might improve clinical outcomes on sparse, imprecise data. An independent review of the treatment link (Thiele 2013) found randomised trials showed no effect of antiviral therapy on hepatocellular carcinoma or mortality, with observational designs disagreeing in opposite directions. Antiviral shelves for diagnosed chronic hepatitis B are different questions; this shelf is the screening-strategy question.

cards.headline: USPSTF 2020: screening for hepatitis B in adolescents and adults at increased risk carries moderate net benefit (B recommendation) — with up to 60% of infected persons unaware of their infection
cards.summary: USPSTF 2020: screening for hepatitis B in adolescents and adults at increased risk carries moderate net benefit (B recommendation) — with up to 60% of infected persons unaware of their infection
cards.people: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement applying to asymptomatic, nonpregnant adolescents and adults at increased risk of hepatitis B virus infection. An estimated 862,000 people in the US live with chronic HBV infection; increased-risk groups include people born in regions with HBV prevalence of 2% or more (accounting for up to 95% of newly reported chronic US infections), people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, people with HIV, and sex partners, needle-sharing contacts and household contacts of infected persons.
cards.result: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that screening for HBV infection in adolescents and adults at increased risk has moderate net benefit, and recommends screening in this group (B recommendation). The statement notes that up to 60% of HBV-infected persons are unaware of their infection and many remain asymptomatic until cirrhosis or end-stage liver disease develops. The recommendation rests on an evidence chain — screening accuracy and yield, plus treatment effects in diagnosed disease — not on a trial of screening itself, as the next cards show.
cards.watchOut: A recommendation statement is a judgement over an indirect chain, not a study: its 'moderate certainty' is the Task Force's, and this shelf prints the chain's weak links on the following cards rather than borrowing the B grade as if it were trial evidence.
cards.source: Krist AH et al. Screening for Hepatitis B Virus Infection in Adolescents and Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33320230. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: USPSTF evidence report (Chou 2020): no study directly evaluated screening versus no screening on mortality, hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis — the chain is indirect; antiviral therapy improved intermediate outcomes (numbers needed to treat 2.6 to 17) and might improve clinical outcomes, on sparse and imprecise data
cards.summary: USPSTF evidence report (Chou 2020): no study directly evaluated screening versus no screening on mortality, hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis — the chain is indirect; antiviral therapy improved intermediate outcomes (numbers needed to treat 2.6 to 17) and might improve clinical outcomes, on sparse and imprecise data
cards.type: Systematic review and evidence report for the USPSTF (Chou 2020) — 30 trials, 20 cohort studies, 94,168 participants
cards.people: Updated systematic review for the USPSTF (literature 2014 to August 2019, surveillance to July 2020): 30 trials and 20 cohort studies, 94,168 participants in total, covering screening strategies and accuracy, antiviral therapy effects on intermediate and clinical outcomes, and cohort links between achieving intermediate outcomes and later clinical outcomes.
cards.result: No study directly evaluated the effects of screening versus no screening on clinical outcomes such as mortality, hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis — the indirectness is explicit in the record. Risk-factor-based screening strategies would identify nearly all infections, though screening only immigrants from high-prevalence countries missed about two-thirds of infections in one study (n = 21,008). Across 18 trials (n = 2,972), antiviral therapy versus placebo or no treatment increased achievement of intermediate outcomes (virologic suppression, HBeAg or HBsAg loss or seroconversion; numbers needed to treat from 2.6 to 17). Across 16 trials (n = 4,809), antiviral therapy might be associated with improved clinical outcomes, but data were sparse and imprecise; 9 cohort studies (n = 3,893) linked achieving an intermediate outcome to better clinical outcomes with hazard ratios ranging widely, from 0.07 to 0.87. Antiviral therapy also increased withdrawal due to adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The middle link of the chain — treatment improving the outcomes screening exists to prevent — is the weak one: intermediate outcomes (viral suppression, seroconversion) are surrogates, and the clinical-outcome trial data are described by the reviewers themselves as sparse and imprecise.
cards.source: Chou R et al. Screening for Hepatitis B Virus Infection in Nonpregnant Adolescents and Adults: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33320229. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thiele 2013 (systematic review of treatment trials): randomised trials found no effect of antiviral therapy on hepatocellular carcinoma or mortality in chronic hepatitis B, while observational designs disagreed with each other — the treatment link in the screening chain is itself unsettled
cards.summary: Thiele 2013 (systematic review of treatment trials): randomised trials found no effect of antiviral therapy on hepatocellular carcinoma or mortality in chronic hepatitis B, while observational designs disagreed with each other — the treatment link in the screening chain is itself unsettled
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Thiele 2013) — 35 studies; 8,058 patients. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of antiviral therapy (interferon and/or nucleos(t)ide analogues) versus placebo or no intervention for prevention of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and mortality in chronic hepatitis B: 8 randomised trials, 8 prospective cohort studies and 19 case-control studies, with 3,433 patients allocated to antiviral therapy and 4,625 controls, and follow-up to 23 years.
cards.result: Randomised trials found no effect of antiviral therapy on HCC or mortality. Cohort studies found antiviral therapy associated with an increased HCC risk (risk ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.95, a relative figure), while case-control studies found a decreased risk (risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.88, a relative figure); the difference between randomised and observational results was statistically significant (P < .001). Antiviral therapy did not affect mortality in cohort studies but reduced it in case-control studies (relative risk 0.71). The authors conclude the effect of antiviral therapy on clinical outcomes remains to be established and does not allow extrapolation to clinical practice. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.
cards.watchOut: This review predates wider use of the modern first-line antivirals and pools interferon-era trials, so its randomised null may understate current therapy; equally, its design-dependence warning (results flip with study design) is exactly the caution a screening-chain shelf must carry.
cards.source: Thiele M et al. Antiviral therapy for prevention of hepatocellular carcinoma and mortality in chronic hepatitis B: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ open. 2013. PMID: 23945731. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: the screening strategy is recommended (USPSTF grade B) but the outcome evidence is indirect at every link — no screening trial exists, and treatment effects on liver outcomes are inconsistent across designs; graded MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the screening strategy is recommended (USPSTF grade B) but the outcome evidence is indirect at every link — no screening trial exists, and treatment effects on liver outcomes are inconsistent across designs; graded MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: the USPSTF recommendation statement (Krist 2020), its commissioned evidence report (Chou 2020; 94,168 participants across the chain), and an independent systematic review of the treatment link (Thiele 2013). Antiviral shelves for diagnosed chronic hepatitis B elsewhere in the library answer treatment questions in known disease — a different question from whether finding and treating infection earlier improves liver outcomes.
cards.result: The chain runs: risk-based screening finds nearly all infections (one study: immigrant-only screening missed two-thirds); antiviral therapy reliably improves intermediate outcomes (numbers needed to treat 2.6–17 for suppression or seroconversion); cohorts link those intermediate gains to better clinical outcomes (hazard ratios 0.07–0.87, heterogeneous); but no trial has tested screening itself against liver outcomes, trial evidence that treatment improves clinical outcomes is sparse and imprecise (Chou), and randomised trials in an earlier treatment era found no HCC or mortality effect at all (Thiele). The strategy is reasonable and officially recommended; the claim that it improves liver outcomes is, on the carded evidence, an inference — stated as such on this shelf's face.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade on the strength of the B recommendation: a guideline grade over an indirect chain is not outcome evidence, and the two systematic reviews carded here disagree about how strong the treatment link is.
cards.source: Synthesis of Krist AH et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 33320230); Chou R et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 33320229); Thiele M et al. BMJ open. 2013 (PMID: 23945731). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ribavirin for chronic hepatitis E in transplant recipients: sustained clearance in about 4 of 5 — observational evidence only
shelves.question: In immunosuppressed or transplant recipients with chronic hepatitis E, does ribavirin achieve sustained viral clearance, and what predicts relapse? (Observational evidence.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hepatitis E/drug therapy · Hepatitis E virus/isolation & purification,physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Transplantation · Retrospective Studies · Ribavirin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Viral Load · Virus Replication/drug effects · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Hepatitis E virus/genetics · Organ Transplantation/adverse effects · RNA, Viral · Ribavirin/therapeutic use · Genotype · Hepatitis E/blood,drug therapy,virology · Hepatitis E virus/drug effects,physiology · Hepatitis, Chronic/drug therapy,virology · Immunocompromised Host · Kinetics · Plasma · RNA, Viral/analysis · Sustained Virologic Response · Transplant Recipients · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OBSERVATIONAL EVIDENCE ONLY, labelled as such on every card: no randomised trial of ribavirin for chronic hepatitis E exists. Two retrospective multicentre cohorts from the same research network agree closely: in 59 solid-organ transplant recipients, a median 3-month course of ribavirin (median 600 mg/day) cleared the virus in 95% by end of therapy and produced a sustained virologic response in 78%, with recurrence in 10 patients after stopping; in the larger European cohort of 255 recipients, sustained response was 81.2% after one course and 89.8% after a second course in some patients. The relapse predictors are consistent across both: a higher lymphocyte count at treatment start predicts sustained response, while anaemia severe enough to force dose reduction (28–29%) or transfusion is associated with more relapse. Viral-kinetic data add an early marker: a flat-partial plasma response pattern was associated with treatment failure, and every patient whose plasma HEV fell by more than 15% by day 7 achieved sustained response in that 41-patient cohort. Anaemia is the main harm throughout.

cards.headline: Kamar 2014 (observational): ribavirin cleared chronic hepatitis E in 95% of 59 transplant recipients by end of therapy; sustained response 78%, with recurrence in 10 after stopping — a retrospective case series, no control group
cards.summary: Kamar 2014 (observational): ribavirin cleared chronic hepatitis E in 95% of 59 transplant recipients by end of therapy; sustained response 78%, with recurrence in 10 after stopping — a retrospective case series, no control group
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre case series (observational), N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 59 solid-organ transplant recipients with prolonged hepatitis E viraemia (37 kidney, 10 liver, 5 heart, 5 kidney–pancreas, 2 lung), treated retrospectively at multiple centres; all 54 patients genotyped had genotype 3. Ribavirin began a median of 9 months after diagnosis, at a median dose of 600 mg/day for a median of 3 months (66% treated for 3 months or less).
cards.result: HEV clearance was observed in 95% of patients at end of therapy. Recurrence of HEV replication occurred in 10 patients after ribavirin was stopped. A sustained virologic response (undetectable serum HEV RNA at least 6 months after stopping) occurred in 46 of 59 patients (78%), and in 4 further patients who recurred and were re-treated for longer. A higher lymphocyte count when ribavirin was started was associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response. Anaemia was the main side effect, requiring dose reduction in 29%, erythropoietin in 54% and transfusion in 12%. The authors conclude ribavirin monotherapy may be effective and that a 3-month course seemed appropriate for most patients.
cards.watchOut: Observational with no untreated comparison group: spontaneous clearance and concurrent immunosuppression changes cannot be separated from the drug effect in this design, which is why the shelf stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational.
cards.source: Kamar N et al. Ribavirin for chronic hepatitis E virus infection in transplant recipients. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24645943. Registry ID: none in the record. (observational evidence.) retrospective multicentre case series (observational), n engl j med 2014 59 solid-organ transplant recipients with prolonged hepatitis e viraemia (37 kidney, 10 liver, 5 heart, 5 kidney–pancreas, 2 lung), treated retrospectively at multiple centres; all 54 patients genotyped had genotype 3. ribavirin began a median of 9 months after diagnosis, at a median dose of 600 mg/day for a median of 3 months (66% treated for 3 months or less). hev clearance was observed in 95% of patients at end of therapy. recurrence of hev replication occurred in 10 patients after ribavirin was stopped. a sustained virologic response (undetectable serum hev rna at least 6 months after stopping) occurred in 46 of 59 patients (78%), and in 4 further patients who recurred and were re-treated for longer. a higher lymphocyte count when ribavirin was started was associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response. anaemia was the main side effect, requiring dose reduction in 29%, erythropoietin in 54% and transfusion in 12%. the authors conclude ribavirin monotherapy may be effective and that a 3-month course seemed appropriate for most patients. observational with no untreated comparison group: spontaneous clearance and concurrent immunosuppression changes cannot be separated from the drug effect in this design, which is why the shelf stamp is capped at possible and labelled observational. kamar n et al. ribavirin for chronic hepatitis e virus infection in transplant recipients. the new england journal of medicine. 2014. pmid: 24645943. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · antiviral agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · chronic disease · drug administration schedule · female · hepatitis e/drug therapy · hepatitis e virus/isolation & purification,physiology · humans · male · middle aged · organ transplantation · retrospective studies · ribavirin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · viral load · virus replication/drug effects

cards.headline: Kamar 2020 (observational): in 255 European transplant recipients, sustained response to ribavirin was 81.2% after one course and 89.8% after retreatment — higher starting lymphocyte count predicted success; dose reduction and transfusion predicted relapse
cards.summary: Kamar 2020 (observational): in 255 European transplant recipients, sustained response to ribavirin was 81.2% after one course and 89.8% after retreatment — higher starting lymphocyte count predicted success; dose reduction and transfusion predicted relapse
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre cohort study (observational), Clin Infect Dis 2020
cards.people: 255 solid-organ transplant recipients with chronic hepatitis E treated with ribavirin monotherapy at 30 European centres, analysed retrospectively. Ribavirin was given at a median dose of 600 mg/day (mean 8.6 mg/kg/day) for a median of 3 months.
cards.result: The sustained virologic response rate was 81.2% after a first course of ribavirin, rising to 89.8% when some patients received a second course. An increased lymphocyte count at initiation was a predictive factor for sustained response, while poor haematological tolerance requiring dose reduction (28%) and blood transfusion (15.7%) was associated with more relapse after stopping. Pretreatment and on-treatment HEV polymerase mutations did not have a negative impact on clearance. Anaemia was the main adverse event. The authors conclude ribavirin is highly efficient for chronic HEV in transplant recipients.
cards.watchOut: Observational: the predictor findings (lymphocyte count, dose reduction, transfusion) are associations within a treated cohort — dose reduction may mark sicker patients rather than cause relapse. Overlap of centres and possibly patients with the 2014 series cannot be excluded from the records, so the two cohorts are not fully independent confirmations.
cards.source: Kamar N et al. Ribavirin for Hepatitis E Virus Infection After Organ Transplantation: A Large European Retrospective Multicenter Study. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2020. PMID: 31793638. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lhomme 2019 (observational): plasma hepatitis E kinetics on ribavirin — a flat-partial response pattern was associated with treatment failure, and every patient with a >15% fall in plasma HEV by day 7 achieved sustained response
cards.summary: Lhomme 2019 (observational): plasma hepatitis E kinetics on ribavirin — a flat-partial response pattern was associated with treatment failure, and every patient with a >15% fall in plasma HEV by day 7 achieved sustained response
cards.people: 41 solid-organ transplant patients with chronic hepatitis E whose plasma HEV kinetics were characterised during ribavirin therapy in a prospective observational study; sustained response was assessed 24 weeks after completing therapy.
cards.result: Plasma HEV fell from a median baseline of 6.12 log copies/mL in four patterns — monophasic (n=18), biphasic (n=13), triphasic (n=8) and flat-partial response (n=2) — with an estimated plasma HEV half-life of 2.0 days. Twenty-five patients (61%) achieved a sustained virological response 24 weeks after therapy. Patterns (i)–(iii) were not associated with baseline characteristics or outcome; a flat-partial response was associated with treatment failure. All patients with a day-7 plasma HEV decrease of more than 15% from baseline achieved sustained response.
cards.watchOut: Observational and small (41 patients; the flat-partial group is 2 patients), and its 61% sustained-response rate is lower than the larger cohorts' — a reminder that response rates vary by cohort and follow-up definition. The day-7 marker is a candidate predictor, not a validated rule.
cards.source: Lhomme S et al. Plasma Hepatitis E Virus Kinetics in Solid Organ Transplant Patients Receiving Ribavirin. Viruses. 2019. PMID: 31323954. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ribavirin probably clears chronic hepatitis E in most transplant recipients — consistent observational cohorts, no randomised trial, and relapse tracks with low lymphocytes and anaemia-forced dose cuts
cards.summary: Synthesis: ribavirin probably clears chronic hepatitis E in most transplant recipients — consistent observational cohorts, no randomised trial, and relapse tracks with low lymphocytes and anaemia-forced dose cuts
cards.people: Synthesis of the observational record carded above: retrospective series of 59 and 255 solid-organ transplant recipients and a 41-patient viral-kinetics cohort — 355 patients in total, with possible overlap between the two Kamar cohorts.
cards.result: Every cohort points the same way: about 4 in 5 treated transplant recipients achieve sustained viral clearance after a median 3-month ribavirin course, rising toward 9 in 10 with retreatment, against a background condition that rarely clears while immunosuppression continues. The relapse story is also consistent: recurrence after stopping occurred in 10 of 59 in the first series; higher lymphocyte count at initiation predicts sustained response in both large cohorts; anaemia-driven dose reduction and transfusion mark higher relapse risk; viral mutations did not predict failure; and a flat early kinetic response flags likely failure. Because all of this is observational — no randomised or untreated-controlled evidence exists — the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the evidence is labelled observational on the face of the shelf, as its GAP-E slate row requires.
cards.watchOut: Without a control arm, the true drug-attributable clearance rate is unknown; immunosuppression reduction — the other standard lever in chronic HEV — is entangled with ribavirin use in all of these cohorts and is not separable from the records carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kamar N et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24645943); Kamar N et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2020 (PMID: 31793638); Lhomme S et al. Viruses. 2019 (PMID: 31323954). Registry IDs: none in the records, as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: GALAD score for early HCC detection: better accuracy than AFP alone (phase 3 AUC 0.78 vs 0.66; sensitivity 62% vs 41% at matched specificity) — but never tested head-to-head against ultrasound surveillance in a randomised design
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis under hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, does the GALAD score (gender, age, AFP-L3, AFP, DCP) detect early HCC better than ultrasound with or without AFP? (Test-accuracy question.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/blood,diagnosis,etiology,epidemiology · Liver Neoplasms/blood,diagnosis,etiology,epidemiology · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Liver Cirrhosis/complications,blood,diagnosis · alpha-Fetoproteins/analysis,metabolism · Prospective Studies · Aged · Prothrombin · Biomarkers, Tumor/blood · Protein Precursors/blood · Predictive Value of Tests · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Reproducibility of Results · Adult · Sensitivity and Specificity · United States · Biomarkers
shelves.balance: ACCURACY VERDICT (this is a test-accuracy shelf, stamped as such). The strongest design is the phase 3 biomarker validation (Marsh 2025): in 1,558 patients with cirrhosis followed prospectively, GALAD measured within 12 months before HCC diagnosis had an AUC of 0.78 versus 0.66 for AFP alone (p<.001), and at a matched 82% specificity its sensitivity was 62% versus 41% for AFP (p=.001). Pooled across 10 diagnostic studies (Lu 2024), GALAD's sensitivity and specificity were 0.86 and 0.90 for all-stage HCC (AUC 0.94) and 0.83 and 0.81 for early-stage HCC (AUC 0.90) — but most pooled studies are case-control designs, which flatter accuracy. The original model (Johnson 2014) reported AUC values above 0.88 across stages in case-control data. The honest limit: no carded study randomises patients to GALAD-based versus ultrasound-based surveillance or compares GALAD directly against ultrasound ± AFP in the same prospective cohort — the phase 3 comparator was AFP alone, with ultrasound remaining the surveillance backbone in that study. So GALAD is a better blood test than AFP; whether it detects more early HCC than, or adds enough to, ultrasound surveillance is not established by the carded record.

cards.headline: Johnson 2014 (model derivation, 670 patients): the GALAD model (gender, age, AFP-L3, AFP, des-carboxy-prothrombin) discriminated HCC from chronic liver disease with AUC values above 0.88 at every disease stage
cards.summary: Johnson 2014 (model derivation, 670 patients): the GALAD model (gender, age, AFP-L3, AFP, des-carboxy-prothrombin) discriminated HCC from chronic liver disease with AUC values above 0.88 at every disease stage
cards.type: Diagnostic model derivation and validation, case-control (Johnson 2014) — 670 patients, test accuracy
cards.people: Case-control study at a single UK centre: 670 patients with chronic liver disease alone or hepatocellular carcinoma, sera collected prospectively for the study. The logistic-regression model was built in a discovery dataset and validated in independent datasets from the same and an external institution.
cards.result: The final model — gender, age, AFP-L3, AFP and des-carboxy-prothrombin ('GALAD') — when optimised for sensitivity and specificity gave AUC values of more than 0.88 irrespective of disease stage. The authors state the model now requires prospective testing in routine practice to determine whether it may replace or, more likely, enhance radiological approaches.
cards.watchOut: Case-control accuracy is an upper bound: cases are known cancers and controls are clinic patients, a spectrum far easier to separate than the small, early tumours surveillance must find. This card establishes the model, not its surveillance performance.
cards.source: Johnson PJ et al. The detection of hepatocellular carcinoma using a prospectively developed and validated model based on serological biomarkers. Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev. 2014. PMID: 24220911. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Marsh 2025 phase 3 validation (1,558 patients with cirrhosis, 109 HCC): GALAD beat AFP alone — AUC 0.78 versus 0.66 within 12 months before diagnosis, and sensitivity 62% versus 41% at a matched 82% specificity
cards.summary: Marsh 2025 phase 3 validation (1,558 patients with cirrhosis, 109 HCC): GALAD beat AFP alone — AUC 0.78 versus 0.66 within 12 months before diagnosis, and sensitivity 62% versus 41% at a matched 82% specificity
cards.type: Phase 3 biomarker validation, prospective cohort (Marsh 2025) — 1,558 patients, test accuracy
cards.people: Prospective cohort at 7 US centres: 1,558 patients with cirrhosis under 6-monthly surveillance (diagnosis per AASLD guidelines), followed a median of 2.2 years; 109 developed HCC (76 very early or early stage; annual incidence 2.4%). Biomarkers (AFP, AFP-L3, des-gamma carboxyprothrombin) were measured blinded on stored samples and GALAD performance was evaluated retrospectively within 12 months before clinical diagnosis.
cards.result: Areas under the curve within 12 months before HCC diagnosis were 0.78 for GALAD and 0.66 for AFP (p<.001). At a GALAD cutoff of −1.36 (specificity 82%), sensitivity at 12 months before diagnosis was 62%; AFP at the same 82% specificity had a sensitivity of 41% (p=.001) — an absolute sensitivity advantage of about 21 percentage points for GALAD over AFP alone.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is AFP alone, not ultrasound and not ultrasound + AFP — patients were under ultrasound-based surveillance throughout. A sensitivity of 62% at 12 months before diagnosis also means roughly 4 in 10 cancers were still missed by GALAD at that specificity; this is an adjunct-grade performance, not a replacement-grade one, on the study's own numbers.
cards.source: Marsh TL et al. A Phase 3 Biomarker Validation of GALAD for the Detection of Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 39293548. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lu 2024 meta-analysis (10 diagnostic studies): pooled GALAD sensitivity 0.86 and specificity 0.90 for all-stage HCC (AUC 0.94); for early-stage HCC, sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.81 (AUC 0.90)
cards.summary: Lu 2024 meta-analysis (10 diagnostic studies): pooled GALAD sensitivity 0.86 and specificity 0.90 for all-stage HCC (AUC 0.94); for early-stage HCC, sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.81 (AUC 0.90)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies (Lu 2024) — 10 studies, test accuracy
cards.people: Meta-analysis of diagnostic-accuracy studies of the GALAD model for primary hepatocellular carcinoma, searched across PubMed, Embase, Medline, Web of Science, Cochrane and Chinese databases, with QUADAS-2 quality assessment; 10 studies included.
cards.result: For all-stage HCC the pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% CI 0.82–0.90), specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.87–0.92) and AUC 0.94. For early-stage HCC the pooled sensitivity was 0.83 (95% CI 0.78–0.87), specificity 0.81 (95% CI 0.78–0.83) and AUC 0.90. The authors conclude GALAD maintains high sensitivity and specificity in early-stage disease.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are mostly case-control, the design that most inflates diagnostic accuracy; the pooled early-stage sensitivity (0.83) sits well above the prospective phase 3 figure (0.62 at matched specificity). Trust the prospective number for surveillance planning and treat the pooled number as a best case.
cards.source: Lu JL et al. Meta-analysis of the GALAD model for diagnosing primary hepatocellular carcinoma. Technol Health Care. 2024. PMID: 38759033. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vo 2025 cirrhosis cohort (196 patients): GALAD AUC 0.91 for HCC detection, higher than any single biomarker, with sensitivity 87.25% and specificity 82.98% at a cutoff of −0.518
cards.summary: Vo 2025 cirrhosis cohort (196 patients): GALAD AUC 0.91 for HCC detection, higher than any single biomarker, with sensitivity 87.25% and specificity 82.98% at a cutoff of −0.518
cards.type: Diagnostic accuracy cohort (Vo 2025) — 196 patients, test accuracy
cards.people: Prospective and retrospective cohort of 196 adults with cirrhosis at a single centre (102 with HCC, 94 without), comparing GALAD against single biomarkers; GALAD score correlated moderately with tumour size (r=0.44; p<0.001) and was higher with multiple tumours.
cards.result: GALAD scores were 2.5 in cirrhosis with HCC versus −2.46 without (p<0.001). The AUC was 0.91, higher than all single biomarkers (all p<0.001). At the optimal cutoff of −0.518, sensitivity was 87.25%, specificity 82.98%, positive predictive value 84.62% and negative predictive value 84.78%.
cards.watchOut: A case-enriched single-centre cohort (52% had HCC) cannot estimate surveillance performance in a real cirrhosis population with ~2% annual incidence — predictive values especially do not transfer. Its cutoff (−0.518) also differs from the phase 3 cutoff (−1.36), a reminder that GALAD thresholds are not yet standardised.
cards.source: Vo TD et al. Evaluating the GALAD Score for Detection of Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Patients With Cirrhosis. J Clin Gastroenterol. 2025. PMID: 39815729. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis (accuracy verdict): GALAD is a better blood test than AFP — the open question is ultrasound, and no carded study answers it
cards.summary: Synthesis (accuracy verdict): GALAD is a better blood test than AFP — the open question is ultrasound, and no carded study answers it
cards.people: The carded evidence: the derivation study (Johnson 2014, 670 patients), a prospective phase 3 validation cohort (Marsh 2025, 1,558 patients with cirrhosis, 109 HCC), a 10-study diagnostic meta-analysis (Lu 2024), and a single-centre cirrhosis cohort (Vo 2025, 196 patients).
cards.result: Against AFP alone the verdict is consistent: AUC 0.78 versus 0.66 prospectively, with about 21 percentage points more sensitivity at matched specificity in the year before diagnosis. Against ultrasound ± AFP — the comparison the question asks — there is no direct prospective or randomised evidence on the carded record; ultrasound remained the surveillance backbone in the phase 3 study. Pooled case-control accuracy (AUC 0.90–0.94) overstates surveillance performance relative to the prospective estimate. Practical reading: GALAD is supported as an adjunct to, or a blood-test upgrade within, surveillance — not as a proven replacement for ultrasound.
cards.watchOut: Cutoffs differ between studies (−1.36 phase 3; −0.518 single-centre) and AFP-L3/DCP assays are not available in every health system; a score that cannot be run locally, or run at a validated cutoff, does not deliver the carded accuracy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Johnson PJ et al. Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev. 2014 (PMID: 24220911); Marsh TL et al. Gastroenterology. 2025 (PMID: 39293548); Lu JL et al. Technol Health Care. 2024 (PMID: 38759033); Vo TD et al. J Clin Gastroenterol. 2025 (PMID: 39815729).

shelves.title: Acute gastric variceal bleeding: cyanoacrylate does not beat BRTO — a randomised trial and a cohort both show less rebleeding with BRTO and no mortality difference; the TIPS comparison is indirect only
shelves.question: In adults with acute gastric variceal bleeding, does endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection reduce rebleeding and mortality compared with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO)?
shelves.mesh: Balloon Occlusion/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Catheterization, Peripheral/adverse effects,instrumentation,methods · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Cyanoacrylates/administration & dosage · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/etiology,therapy · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/etiology,mortality,prevention & control,therapy · Hemostasis, Endoscopic/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Hemostatics/administration & dosage · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Recurrence · Survival Analysis · Tissue Adhesives/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: The premise of the question — that cyanoacrylate might be the better treatment — is not supported for rebleeding: the comparative evidence runs the other way, and mortality does not differ. In the one randomised head-to-head trial (Luo 2021, 64 patients after primary haemostasis), freedom from all-cause rebleeding at 1 and 2 years was 77% and 65.2% with cyanoacrylate versus 96.3% and 92.6% with BRTO (p=0.004), with similar survival and complications. A retrospective cohort with extended follow-up (Stein 2019, 161 patients treated for bleeding cardiofundal varices) found the same pattern: 1-year rebleeding 22.0% with cyanoacrylate versus 3.5% with BRTO (Cox HR 0.25 for BRTO), 6-week mortality 14.4% versus 13.1% and no long-term mortality difference (HR 0.89). A network meta-analysis of 9 secondary-prophylaxis RCTs (647 patients; Osman 2022) ranked BRTO best for rebleeding (versus cyanoacrylate: relative rate 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.77; low certainty) and found no intervention with a proven mortality advantage; its TIPS comparisons are indirect. No carded randomised trial compares cyanoacrylate directly with TIPS for gastric varices — that half of the question is unanswered by direct evidence, and this shelf says so rather than borrowing oesophageal-varix TIPS data. Cyanoacrylate versus band ligation for acute control is a different comparison and is not the question here.

cards.headline: Luo 2021 randomised trial (64 patients): BRTO prevented rebleeding better than cyanoacrylate — freedom from all-cause rebleeding at 2 years 92.6% versus 65.2% (p=0.004) — with similar survival and complications
cards.summary: Luo 2021 randomised trial (64 patients): BRTO prevented rebleeding better than cyanoacrylate — freedom from all-cause rebleeding at 2 years 92.6% versus 65.2% (p=0.004) — with similar survival and complications
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in patients with cirrhosis and a history of bleeding from gastroesophageal varices type 2 or isolated gastric varices type 1, after primary haemostasis: endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection (n=32) versus balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (n=32). Mean follow-up 27.1 versus 27.6 months. Primary outcomes: gastric variceal rebleeding and all-cause rebleeding.
cards.result: The probability of gastric variceal rebleeding was higher with cyanoacrylate than with BRTO (p=0.024). Freedom from all-cause rebleeding at 1 and 2 years was 77% and 65.2% with cyanoacrylate versus 96.3% and 92.6% with BRTO (p=0.004) — absolute differences of about 19 and 27 percentage points against cyanoacrylate. Survival rates, complication frequency and worsening of oesophageal varices were similar in both groups (the treatments made no difference to mortality). BRTO also resulted in fewer hospitalisations, shorter inpatient stays and lower medical costs in this trial.
cards.watchOut: This is secondary prophylaxis after haemostasis, not treatment of the acute bleed itself, and 64 patients at (per the record) a single programme is a small base for a practice ranking. BRTO also requires a suitable gastrorenal shunt and interventional-radiology capacity that many centres lack — the trial compares efficacy where both are available.
cards.source: Luo X et al. Endoscopic Cyanoacrylate Injection Versus Balloon-Occluded Retrograde Transvenous Obliteration for Prevention of Gastric Variceal Bleeding: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 33445218. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stein 2019 cohort (161 patients with bleeding cardiofundal gastric varices): rebleeding at 1 year 22.0% with cyanoacrylate versus 3.5% with BRTO (Cox HR 0.25), but mortality did not differ (6-week 14.4% vs 13.1%; long-term HR 0.89)
cards.summary: Stein 2019 cohort (161 patients with bleeding cardiofundal gastric varices): rebleeding at 1 year 22.0% with cyanoacrylate versus 3.5% with BRTO (Cox HR 0.25), but mortality did not differ (6-week 14.4% vs 13.1%; long-term HR 0.89)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort comparison (1997–2015) of 90 patients treated with endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection and 71 with BRTO (sodium tetradecyl sulfate sclerosis with balloon occlusion) for endoscopically confirmed bleeding cardiofundal gastric varices with portal hypertension; 89% had cirrhosis; mean MELD 14.4 (cyanoacrylate) and 13.4 (BRTO). Sixteen of 71 BRTO patients also had a simultaneous TIPS.
cards.result: Six-week rebleeding was similar (5.1% cyanoacrylate vs 3.5% BRTO; p=.62), but by 1 year 22.0% of cyanoacrylate patients versus 3.5% of BRTO patients had rebled (p<.01); long-term rebleeding was lower with BRTO (Cox HR 0.25; p=.03). Mortality at 6 weeks was 14.4% versus 13.1% (p=.85) and long-term mortality did not differ (Cox HR 0.89; p=.64) — the treatments made no difference to survival. One death in the cyanoacrylate group and five in the BRTO group were judged procedurally related (p=.088).
cards.watchOut: Eighteen years of practice (1997–2015) span major changes in both techniques, and 16 BRTO patients also received TIPS, contaminating the comparison in BRTO's favour for rebleeding. Treatment choice was by clinician and anatomy, not randomisation — concordance with the randomised trial is what gives this card its weight.
cards.source: Stein DJ et al. Balloon Retrograde Transvenous Obliteration Versus Endoscopic Cyanoacrylate in Bleeding Gastric Varices: Comparison of Rebleeding and Mortality with Extended Follow-up. J Vasc Interv Radiol. 2019. PMID: 30717949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Osman 2022 network meta-analysis (9 RCTs, 647 patients): BRTO ranked best for preventing rebleeding (versus cyanoacrylate relative rate 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.77; low certainty); no intervention showed a mortality advantage, and TIPS comparisons are indirect
cards.summary: Osman 2022 network meta-analysis (9 RCTs, 647 patients): BRTO ranked best for preventing rebleeding (versus cyanoacrylate relative rate 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.77; low certainty); no intervention showed a mortality advantage, and TIPS comparisons are indirect
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (Osman 2022) — 647 patients
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of secondary prophylaxis of gastric variceal bleeding in cirrhosis (searched to 23 March 2021): 9 RCTs, 647 patients with prior gastric variceal bleeding and follow-up beyond 6 weeks; 9 interventions compared, including BRTO, cyanoacrylate injection, TIPS and beta-blockers. Certainty rated by GRADE.
cards.result: BRTO was associated with lower rebleeding than beta-blockers (relative rate 0.04, 95% CI 0.01–0.26) and than cyanoacrylate injection (relative rate 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.77), both low-certainty. Beta-blockers carried a higher rebleeding risk than most interventions and higher mortality than cyanoacrylate (relative rate 4.12, 1.50–11.36) and cyanoacrylate plus non-selective beta-blockers (5.61, 1.91–16.43). The authors conclude indirect comparisons suggest BRTO may be best for preventing rebleeding while head-to-head RCTs are still needed; no mortality ranking is established.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates lean on indirect paths through small old trials, and the authors grade the key comparisons low-certainty. Crucially for this shelf's question, the network contains no direct cyanoacrylate-versus-TIPS randomised edge — any TIPS statement drawn from it is indirect and is not promoted to a verdict here.
cards.source: Osman KT et al. Secondary Prophylaxis of Gastric Variceal Bleeding: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Liver Transpl. 2022. PMID: 34860458. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for rebleeding, the ranking runs BRTO ahead of cyanoacrylate; for mortality, nothing separates them; for TIPS, the direct evidence does not exist
cards.summary: Synthesis: for rebleeding, the ranking runs BRTO ahead of cyanoacrylate; for mortality, nothing separates them; for TIPS, the direct evidence does not exist
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised cyanoacrylate-versus-BRTO trial (Luo 2021, 64 patients), one large retrospective comparison (Stein 2019, 161 patients), and a 9-trial network meta-analysis of secondary prophylaxis (Osman 2022, 647 patients).
cards.result: Rebleeding consistently favours BRTO: randomised absolute advantage of about 27 percentage points in 2-year freedom from rebleeding, cohort 1-year rebleeding 3.5% versus 22.0%, network relative rate 0.18 versus cyanoacrylate. Mortality shows no difference in the trial, the cohort, or the network. Against TIPS there is no direct randomised comparison in gastric varices on the carded record — the honest answer to that half of the question is 'not directly tested', not an extrapolation from oesophageal-varix trials. The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than higher because the randomised base is a single 64-patient trial.
cards.watchOut: All three sources address prevention of rebleeding after the index bleed is controlled; none shows any treatment changing the high early mortality of the acute bleed itself. Availability decides much of real practice: BRTO needs a gastrorenal shunt and specialist radiology, TIPS needs portal access and carries encephalopathy risk, and cyanoacrylate is the option most centres can deliver at the index endoscopy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Luo X et al. Hepatology. 2021 (PMID: 33445218); Stein DJ et al. J Vasc Interv Radiol. 2019 (PMID: 30717949); Osman KT et al. Liver Transpl. 2022 (PMID: 34860458).

shelves.title: Anticoagulation for portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis: recanalisation up, bleeding not up — on observational evidence, plus one prevention trial
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis, does anticoagulation improve recanalisation and survival without increasing bleeding compared with no anticoagulation?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/epidemiology,etiology · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/epidemiology,etiology · Humans · Incidence · Liver Cirrhosis/complications,drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Portal Vein · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis/complications,drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the treatment evidence is observational and is labelled as such. Two meta-analyses of mostly observational studies agree that anticoagulation roughly doubles recanalisation in relative terms (relative risk 2.61 in the 33-study analysis) and lowers thrombus progression, with no excess overall bleeding (11% in both groups in the 2017 analysis); the 2021 analysis also found a small relative survival advantage (relative risk 1.11). A large single-centre cohort found the same pattern (recanalisation in 56.8% treated vs 25.7% untreated; bleeding 19.7% vs 21.8%). Separately, the one randomised trial is a prevention trial: in 70 patients with advanced cirrhosis and patent portal veins, enoxaparin prevented portal vein thrombosis entirely (0% vs 16.6% at 48 weeks) with no haemorrhagic events reported. No randomised trial has tested anticoagulation as treatment for established portal vein thrombosis, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Villa 2012 (prevention randomised trial): enoxaparin prevented portal vein thrombosis in advanced cirrhosis — 0% vs 16.6% at 48 weeks — with no haemorrhagic events reported
cards.summary: Villa 2012 (prevention randomised trial): enoxaparin prevented portal vein thrombosis in advanced cirrhosis — 0% vs 16.6% at 48 weeks — with no haemorrhagic events reported
cards.type: Single-centre, nonblinded, randomised controlled trial (prevention), Gastroenterology 2012
cards.people: 70 outpatients with advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B7–C10), patent portal veins and no hepatocellular carcinoma, randomised at a single centre to enoxaparin 4000 IU/day subcutaneously for 48 weeks (n=34) or no treatment (n=36); outcome assessors were blinded, patients were not. This is a prevention trial in patients without thrombosis, not a treatment trial.
cards.result: At 48 weeks, no enoxaparin patient had developed portal vein thrombosis, compared with 6 of 36 controls (16.6%; P=.025); at 96 weeks the control figure was 10 of 36 (27.7%; P=.001). Liver decompensation was less frequent on enoxaparin (11.7% vs 59.4%; P<.0001), 8 enoxaparin patients and 13 controls died, and the actuarial probability of survival was higher on enoxaparin (P=.020). No relevant side effects or haemorrhagic events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Prevention, not treatment: these patients had patent portal veins at entry, so this trial does not show that anticoagulation recanalises an established thrombus. Small (n=70), single-centre and nonblinded, with surprisingly large decompensation and survival differences that no second prevention trial has confirmed.
cards.source: Villa E et al. Enoxaparin prevents portal vein thrombosis and liver decompensation in patients with advanced cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22819864. cards.headline: Loffredo 2017 meta-analysis (8 studies, 353 patients): anticoagulation raised recanalisation to 71% vs 42% and cut progression to 9% vs 33%, with bleeding 11% in both groups
cards.summary: Loffredo 2017 meta-analysis (8 studies, 353 patients): anticoagulation raised recanalisation to 71% vs 42% and cut progression to 9% vs 33%, with bleeding 11% in both groups
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, Gastroenterology 2017
cards.people: 353 patients with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis in 8 studies comparing anticoagulant therapy (low-molecular-weight heparin or warfarin) with no treatment; the underlying studies were not randomised treatment trials.
cards.result: Recanalisation occurred in 71% of anticoagulated patients vs 42% of untreated patients (P<.0001); complete recanalisation 53% vs 33% (6 studies, 217 patients; P=.002); thrombosis progression 9% vs 33% (6 studies, 225 patients; P<.0001). Any major or minor bleeding was 11% in both groups (6 studies, 257 patients), and spontaneous variceal bleeding occurred in a significantly lower proportion of anticoagulated patients (P=.04; the abstract does not print the two rates).
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence: clinicians chose who was anticoagulated, so treated and untreated patients differ in ways adjustment cannot fully remove. Labelled observational — this caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Loffredo L et al. Effects of Anticoagulants in Patients With Cirrhosis and Portal Vein Thrombosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 28479379. cards.headline: Wang 2021 meta-analysis (33 studies, 1,696 patients): anticoagulation increased recanalisation (relative RR 2.61) and overall survival (relative RR 1.11), with no significant difference in overall bleeding (relative RR 0.78)
cards.summary: Wang 2021 meta-analysis (33 studies, 1,696 patients): anticoagulation increased recanalisation (relative RR 2.61) and overall survival (relative RR 1.11), with no significant difference in overall bleeding (relative RR 0.78)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of observational studies, Advances in Therapy 2021
cards.people: 1,696 patients with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis in 33 studies comparing anticoagulation with no anticoagulation, including asymptomatic and non-transplant-candidate patients.
cards.result: Anticoagulation significantly increased portal vein recanalisation (relative risk ratio 2.61, 95% CI 1.99 to 3.43; P<0.00001) and overall survival (relative risk ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.21; P=0.01), and decreased thrombus progression (relative risk ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.49; P<0.0001). Overall bleeding did not differ significantly (relative risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.30; P=0.34). Early initiation increased recanalisation (relative risk ratio 1.58); Child-Pugh B/C and higher MELD predicted less recanalisation. All risk ratios here are relative measures; the abstract does not print pooled absolute recanalisation or survival rates for this analysis.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence, and it overlaps the 2017 meta-analysis and the primary cohorts in this pack — the studies are not independent, so their patient counts must not be added together. The survival signal is a small relative effect (relative RR 1.11) from non-randomised comparisons and is the weakest link in the pack.

cards.headline: Pettinari 2019 cohort (182 patients): thrombus shrank by over half in 56.8% on anticoagulation vs 25.7% untreated, bleeding was no more common on treatment (19.7% vs 21.8%), and 36% of recanalisers re-thrombosed after stopping
cards.summary: Pettinari 2019 cohort (182 patients): thrombus shrank by over half in 56.8% on anticoagulation vs 25.7% untreated, bleeding was no more common on treatment (19.7% vs 21.8%), and 36% of recanalisers re-thrombosed after stopping
cards.type: Single-centre retrospective cohort, Am J Gastroenterol 2019
cards.people: 182 patients with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis at a single centre (2008–2016) with at least 3 months of follow-up; 81 received anticoagulants and 101 were untreated, by physician discretion — not randomised.
cards.result: Thrombus extension decreased by more than 50% in 46 of 81 treated patients (56.8%, with complete recanalisation in 31 of those 46) vs 26 of 101 untreated (25.7%). Survival was higher in the treated group (Kaplan-Meier P=0.010), and anticoagulation was independently associated with longer survival in multivariable analysis (hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.91). Bleeding occurred in 16 treated (19.7%) and 22 untreated (21.8%) patients, was judged treatment-related in only 4 cases, and caused no deaths. Of the 46 patients who recanalised, 17 (36%) had recurrent thrombosis after anticoagulation was stopped.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was the physician's choice, so the survival association (hazard ratio 0.30) is vulnerable to confounding by indication — patients well enough to anticoagulate may have been destined to do better. Labelled observational.
cards.source: Pettinari I et al. Clinical Impact and Safety of Anticoagulants for Portal Vein Thrombosis in Cirrhosis. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 30538290. cards.headline: Synthesis: anticoagulation recanalises the portal vein and does not measurably increase bleeding — on observational treatment evidence, graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: anticoagulation recanalises the portal vein and does not measurably increase bleeding — on observational treatment evidence, graded POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one small prevention randomised trial (70 patients without thrombosis), two overlapping meta-analyses of observational treatment studies (353 and 1,696 patients) and one 182-patient cohort.
cards.result: Every treatment comparison points the same way: recanalisation roughly doubles in relative terms, thrombus progression falls, and bleeding rates on anticoagulation are the same as without it (11% vs 11%; 19.7% vs 21.8%) — while a third of recanalisers re-thrombose after treatment stops. The survival advantage rests entirely on observational comparisons and a small relative effect, so it is stated as an association, not a proven benefit. The only randomised evidence is for prevention (Villa 2012), a different question from treating established thrombosis. Because the treatment evidence is observational, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit) and labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analyses share primary studies with each other and with the cohort carded here, so the pack's patient counts overlap and must never be summed. Cross-point: no randomised treatment trial of anticoagulation for established portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis was found in this session's PubMed searches.
cards.source: Synthesis of Villa E et al., Gastroenterology 2012 (PMID: 22819864); Loffredo L et al., Gastroenterology 2017 (PMID: 28479379); Wang L et al., Advances in Therapy 2021 (PMID: 33155180); Pettinari I et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2019 (PMID: 30538290). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: High-volume plasma exchange in acute liver failure: transplant-free survival up in the one randomised trial (Larsen 2016 — no 'FULMAR' acronym in the record)
shelves.question: In adults with acute liver failure, does high-volume plasma exchange improve transplant-free survival compared with standard medical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cytokines/biosynthesis · Female · Humans · Liver Failure, Acute/immunology,mortality,therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Plasma Exchange · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial caps the stamp. In the Larsen 2016 open multicentre randomised trial (182 adults with acute liver failure), high-volume plasma exchange plus standard medical therapy raised overall hospital survival to 58.7% vs 47.8% on standard therapy alone (relative hazard ratio 0.56, stratified for liver transplantation), on a primary endpoint of transplant-free survival; severe adverse events were similar. A 2024 meta-analysis of 8 studies (2 randomised, 6 cohorts) found the same direction for plasma exchange overall (mortality relative risk 0.64 at ≤60 days). The newest aetiology-specific cohort (amatoxin poisoning, retrospective) found no overall difference on its primary outcome, with benefit only in a sicker subgroup. Premise correction: the slate called this trial 'FULMAR' — the published record carries no such acronym; it is an open randomised controlled trial, reported simply as Larsen et al., J Hepatol 2016, NCT00950508.

cards.headline: Larsen 2016 (open randomised trial): high-volume plasma exchange raised hospital survival to 58.7% vs 47.8% with standard therapy alone (relative HR 0.56) in acute liver failure
cards.summary: Larsen 2016 (open randomised trial): high-volume plasma exchange raised hospital survival to 58.7% vs 47.8% with standard therapy alone (relative HR 0.56) in acute liver failure
cards.type: Open, multicentre, randomised controlled trial, J Hepatol 2016
cards.people: 182 patients with acute liver failure randomised across centres to standard medical therapy alone (n=90) or standard therapy plus high-volume plasma exchange — exchange of 8–12 litres or 15% of ideal body weight with fresh frozen plasma — for three days (n=92). The trial was open (not blinded). The slate's name for this trial, 'FULMAR', does not appear in the published record; the record describes an open randomised controlled trial with no acronym.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was liver transplantation-free survival during hospital stay. Overall hospital survival was 58.7% with high-volume plasma exchange vs 47.8% with standard therapy (relative hazard ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.86; P=0.0083, stratified for liver transplantation). High-volume exchange before transplantation did not improve survival compared with standard therapy alone in the transplanted comparison (reported CI 0.37 to 3.98; P=0.75). Severe adverse events were similar in the two groups, and inflammatory (SIRS) and organ-failure (SOFA) scores fell more in the treated group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: One trial, open-label, and its survival advantage did not appear in patients who went on to transplantation — the benefit sits in transplant-free survival. No second randomised trial of high-volume exchange in adult acute liver failure was found this session, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Larsen FS et al. High-volume plasma exchange in patients with acute liver failure: An open randomised controlled trial. Journal of hepatology. 2016. PMID: 26325537. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00950508, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Sithamparapillai 2024 meta-analysis (8 studies): plasma exchange lowered mortality vs standard therapy — relative RR 0.64 at ≤60 days and 0.67 at 90 days
cards.summary: Sithamparapillai 2024 meta-analysis (8 studies): plasma exchange lowered mortality vs standard therapy — relative RR 0.64 at ≤60 days and 0.67 at 90 days
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2 randomised trials, 6 cohorts), Indian J Gastroenterol 2024
cards.people: 8 studies comparing plasma exchange with standard medical therapy in acute liver failure across all age groups — 2 randomised trials and 6 comparative cohorts, with 284 patients in the pooled plasma-exchange arms; single-aetiology studies (Wilson disease, rodenticide hepatotoxicity, acute fatty liver of pregnancy) were analysed separately.
cards.result: Plasma exchange was associated with lower mortality at ≤60 days (relative risk ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.80; P<0.001) and at 90 days (relative risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.90; P=0.008) than standard therapy; on subgroup analysis the benefit appeared irrespective of the volume exchanged. In the three single-aetiology studies the ≤90-day mortality reduction was larger (relative risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.74). Studies reported no major side effects attributable to plasma exchange. All risk ratios are relative measures; the abstract does not print pooled absolute mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: Mostly observational cohorts, all age groups (not adults only), any exchange volume (not specifically high-volume), and the Larsen trial carded above is one of its randomised trials — the counts overlap and must not be added to the trial's.
cards.source: Sithamparapillai K et al. Plasma exchange improves survival in acute liver failure - An updated systematic review and meta-analysis focussed on comparing within single etiology. Indian journal of gastroenterology : official journal of the Indian Society of Gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 38691239. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amanita-PEX 2025 (retrospective, 111 patients with amatoxin acute liver failure): 28-day transplant-free survival did not differ overall with plasma exchange — benefit appeared only in the encephalopathy grade ≥2 subgroup (36.4% vs 19.1%)
cards.summary: Amanita-PEX 2025 (retrospective, 111 patients with amatoxin acute liver failure): 28-day transplant-free survival did not differ overall with plasma exchange — benefit appeared only in the encephalopathy grade ≥2 subgroup (36.4% vs 19.1%)
cards.people: 111 patients with amatoxin-related acute liver failure at 25 centres (2013–2024), analysed retrospectively: 82 received standard care and 29 received at least one plasma-exchange session (standard therapeutic exchange, not the high-volume regimen of the Larsen trial). The exchange group was sicker at baseline (hepatic encephalopathy grade ≥2 in 76% vs 58%).
cards.result: The primary outcome, 28-day transplant-free survival, was not different between groups in all patients (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome). In the subgroup with maximal encephalopathy grade ≥2, transplant-free survival was 36.4% (8 of 22) with exchange vs 19.1% (8 of 42) with standard care, and exchange was independently associated with a lower risk of death or transplantation in that subgroup (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.73). After propensity matching, transplant-free survival was 52% with exchange vs 28% with standard care.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, one poisoning aetiology, standard-volume exchange, and the positive result is a subgroup finding after a null primary outcome — hypothesis-generating only. It neither confirms nor refutes the high-volume randomised result.
cards.source: Stahl K et al. Therapeutic plasma exchange in amatoxin associated acute liver failure-results from the multi-center Amanita-PEX study. Critical care (London, England). 2025. PMID: 41163058. Registry ID: none in the record. multicentre retrospective cohort (amanita-pex), critical care 2025 111 patients with amatoxin-related acute liver failure at 25 centres (2013–2024), analysed retrospectively: 82 received standard care and 29 received at least one plasma-exchange session (standard therapeutic exchange, not the high-volume regimen of the larsen trial). the exchange group was sicker at baseline (hepatic encephalopathy grade ≥2 in 76% vs 58%). the primary outcome, 28-day transplant-free survival, was not different between groups in all patients (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome). in the subgroup with maximal encephalopathy grade ≥2, transplant-free survival was 36.4% (8 of 22) with exchange vs 19.1% (8 of 42) with standard care, and exchange was independently associated with a lower risk of death or transplantation in that subgroup (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% ci 0.19 to 0.73). after propensity matching, transplant-free survival was 52% with exchange vs 28% with standard care. retrospective, one poisoning aetiology, standard-volume exchange, and the positive result is a subgroup finding after a null primary outcome — hypothesis-generating only. it neither confirms nor refutes the high-volume randomised result. stahl k et al. therapeutic plasma exchange in amatoxin associated acute liver failure-results from the multi-center amanita-pex study. critical care (london, england). 2025. pmid: 41163058. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · male · female · plasma exchange/methods,standards,statistics & numerical data · liver failure, acute/therapy,mortality · middle aged · retrospective studies · amanitins/adverse effects · adult · amanita · mushroom poisoning/complications · aged

cards.headline: Synthesis: high-volume plasma exchange probably improves transplant-free survival in acute liver failure — one randomised trial, graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: high-volume plasma exchange probably improves transplant-free survival in acute liver failure — one randomised trial, graded POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Larsen 2016 randomised trial (182 adults), a 2024 meta-analysis of 8 studies, and a 111-patient retrospective amatoxin cohort.
cards.result: The randomised evidence says high-volume plasma exchange plus standard care beats standard care alone on transplant-free survival (hospital survival 58.7% vs 47.8%; relative HR 0.56), with similar severe adverse events — but the advantage was not seen in patients who proceeded to transplantation. The broader plasma-exchange literature (any volume, all ages, mostly cohorts) points the same way on mortality, and the one modern aetiology-specific cohort is null overall with a sicker-subgroup signal. A single open randomised trial, supported but not independently confirmed, earns POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Premise correction carried on the face: the published Larsen record carries no 'FULMAR' acronym and describes an open randomised controlled trial — the pack uses the record's own description. The meta-analysis includes the Larsen trial, so evidence counts overlap across cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Larsen FS et al., J Hepatol 2016 (PMID: 26325537); Sithamparapillai K et al., Indian J Gastroenterol 2024 (PMID: 38691239); Stahl K et al., Critical Care 2025 (PMID: 41163058). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Hepatic extraction ratio: high-extraction drugs are flow-limited and lost to first pass, low-extraction drugs are capacity-limited — shown in humans by what a portacaval shunt does to each kind
shelves.question: What is the hepatic extraction ratio, how does it determine the first-pass effect and the difference between high- and low-extraction drugs, and how do liver blood flow versus intrinsic clearance each limit hepatic clearance?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aminopyrine · Biological Availability · Breath Tests · Cytochrome P-450 CYP3A · Female · Humans · Indocyanine Green/metabolism · Lidocaine/metabolism · Liver/blood supply · Liver Cirrhosis/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Midazolam/pharmacokinetics · Portacaval Shunt, Surgical
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: the extraction ratio E is the fraction of drug removed in one pass through the liver; hepatic clearance equals liver blood flow times E; oral bioavailability falls toward 1 − E, which is the first-pass effect. For a high-extraction drug E approaches 1, clearance tracks blood flow, and most of an oral dose never reaches the systemic circulation; for a low-extraction drug clearance tracks intrinsic clearance — enzyme capacity and unbound fraction — and barely notices flow. The carded human studies demonstrate each pole in people. A surgical portacaval shunt that cut hepatic blood flow by 65% halved the systemic clearance of high-extraction indocyanine green and lidocaine in milder cirrhosis while leaving intrinsic clearance unchanged and driving oral bioavailability to 1, and left the low-extraction aminopyrine breath test untouched in both severity groups (Pomier-Layrargues 1986, n=35). In 99 healthy volunteers, apparent oral clearance of the CYP3A probes midazolam and alfentanil ran roughly 4-fold and 2.5-fold above their systemic clearances — first pass measured, not theorised (Kharasch 2007). And the classic paediatric disposition study found the same high-extraction, large-first-pass behaviour for propranolol in children, with wide individual variability (Wilson 1976).

cards.headline: Pomier-Layrargues 1986: a portacaval shunt cutting liver blood flow 65% halved clearance of high-extraction drugs in milder cirrhosis, left intrinsic clearance unchanged, and did not touch the low-extraction aminopyrine test
cards.summary: Pomier-Layrargues 1986: a portacaval shunt cutting liver blood flow 65% halved clearance of high-extraction drugs in milder cirrhosis, left intrinsic clearance unchanged, and did not touch the low-extraction aminopyrine test
cards.type: Human physiological study (pre/post portacaval shunt drug-disposition study in cirrhosis), Gastroenterology 1986
cards.people: 35 patients with cirrhosis studied before and 18 months after portacaval shunt surgery — 14 with slight liver dysfunction (indocyanine green extraction ratio above 0.25, group 1) and 21 with severe disease (extraction ratio below 0.25, group 2) — with lidocaine clearance and bioavailability, indocyanine green clearance, aminopyrine breath test and hepatic blood flow measured.
cards.result: Hepatic blood flow fell by about 65% in both groups after shunt. In group 1, indocyanine green systemic clearance fell from 9.10 ± 0.68 to 4.40 ± 0.34 mL/min/kg (P < 0.05) while its intrinsic clearance was unchanged; lidocaine systemic clearance fell from 7.93 ± 0.93 to 5.09 ± 0.33 mL/min/kg (P < 0.05), intrinsic clearance again unchanged, and lidocaine bioavailability rose from 0.601 ± 0.076 to 1 — first pass abolished when blood bypassed the liver. In group 2 (severe disease), flow reduction had only minimal effects: indocyanine green systemic clearance fell slightly (3.90 to 2.28 mL/min/kg) and lidocaine clearance was unchanged. The aminopyrine breath test — a low-extraction, capacity-limited probe — was not affected by surgery in either group. The authors concluded flow reduction notably reduces clearance of high-extraction drugs when liver function is relatively preserved, and matters little once disease is severe.
cards.watchOut: A surgical-shunt experiment in cirrhosis, not healthy liver: it isolates the flow-versus-capacity contrast precisely because the shunt changes flow and bypass at once, but extraction behaviour in non-cirrhotic liver is inferred from the group-1 pattern rather than measured in health.
cards.source: Pomier-Layrargues G et al. Effect of portacaval shunt on drug disposition in patients with cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 1986. PMID: 3710065. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kharasch 2007: in 99 healthy volunteers, apparent oral clearance of midazolam ran about 4.5-fold its systemic clearance — first-pass extraction quantified in humans
cards.summary: Kharasch 2007: in 99 healthy volunteers, apparent oral clearance of midazolam ran about 4.5-fold its systemic clearance — first-pass extraction quantified in humans
cards.type: Human pharmacokinetic study (intravenous and oral probe-drug clearances), Clin Pharmacol Ther 2007
cards.people: 99 healthy volunteers (58 men, 41 women) genotyped for CYP3A5, given intravenous then oral midazolam and alfentanil (CYP3A probe drugs) on successive days, with plasma concentrations by mass spectrometry and pupil diameter as the pharmacodynamic readout.
cards.result: Systemic clearances were about 7.8 mL/kg/min for midazolam and 4.6 mL/kg/min for alfentanil (in the common CYP3A5*3/*3 genotype), while apparent oral clearances were about 35.2 and 11.8 mL/kg/min respectively — the several-fold gap between oral and systemic clearance is the first-pass effect expressed as a number: most of an oral dose of a well-extracted CYP3A substrate is cleared before or during its first circuit. The record reports consistent concordance between the two probes in clearances and extraction ratios, and no CYP3A5 genotype effect on systemic or oral clearance despite the genotype's effect in liver microsomes.
cards.watchOut: Midazolam and alfentanil are intermediate-extraction probes and part of their first pass is intestinal as well as hepatic CYP3A; the oral-to-systemic clearance ratio therefore measures combined gut-plus-liver first pass, not the hepatic extraction ratio in isolation.
cards.source: Kharasch ED et al. Influence of CYP3A5 genotype on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the cytochrome P4503A probes alfentanil and midazolam. Clinical pharmacology and therapeutics. 2007. PMID: 17554244. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wilson 1976: propranolol and propoxyphene in children showed the high-extraction pattern — a large presystemic (first-pass) effect and marked interindividual variability
cards.summary: Wilson 1976: propranolol and propoxyphene in children showed the high-extraction pattern — a large presystemic (first-pass) effect and marked interindividual variability
cards.type: Human pharmacokinetic study (sparse-sampling disposition study in children), Clin Pharmacol Ther 1976
cards.people: Children given single oral doses of propoxyphene, and children on chronic oral propranolol as tablets or solution, studied with sparse-sampling protocols designed to minimise blood draws; plasma concentration data pooled across children to construct disposition curves. The record does not print a single total N for the propranolol arm, so N is not documented on this card.
cards.result: Propoxyphene's average half-life in children was 3.5 hours. No clear bioavailability difference appeared between propranolol tablets and solution at the end of a dosing interval during chronic oral administration. Both drugs showed marked interindividual differences in plasma concentrations after oral dosing — findings the authors state are consistent with the high hepatic extraction ratio and large presystemic (first-pass) effect previously described in adults, and which led them to support plasma-level monitoring.
cards.watchOut: A 1976 sparse-sampling design in children: it documents the high-extraction pattern qualitatively (variability, first pass) rather than measuring an extraction ratio, and propoxyphene is no longer a drug in clinical use — the card stands for the physiology, not the agents.
cards.source: Wilson JT et al. Disposition of propoxyphene and propranolol in children. Clinical pharmacology and therapeutics. 1976. PMID: 1261164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one equation, two regimes — clearance equals flow times extraction, so flow governs high-extraction drugs and enzyme capacity governs low-extraction ones, and oral dosing exposes the difference as first pass
cards.summary: Synthesis: one equation, two regimes — clearance equals flow times extraction, so flow governs high-extraction drugs and enzyme capacity governs low-extraction ones, and oral dosing exposes the difference as first pass
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies (Pomier-Layrargues 1986; Kharasch 2007; Wilson 1976), framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep as textbook accounts.
cards.result: The human evidence lines up with the textbook model at every testable point. Cut flow and bypass the liver, and high-extraction clearance falls in proportion while intrinsic clearance and the low-extraction probe do not move (Pomier-Layrargues). Give a well-extracted drug by mouth to healthy people and its apparent clearance multiplies several-fold over its systemic clearance — the arithmetic of bioavailability near 1 − E (Kharasch). Choose the classic high-extraction drug propranolol and the signature is large first pass with wide between-person variability, present already in children (Wilson). Practical consequences the physiology dictates: dose changes in liver disease cannot be read off one rule — flow, shunting and severity move high-extraction drugs, enzyme capacity and binding move low-extraction drugs, and the same cirrhotic liver can leave one drug's clearance untouched while halving another's.
cards.watchOut: Direct hepatic-vein catheter measurement of extraction ratios across a drug panel in healthy humans is ethically constrained and largely historical; the modern human record demonstrates the model's consequences (flow changes, oral–systemic gaps) rather than tabulating E drug by drug, and the synthesis keeps that distinction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pomier-Layrargues G et al., Gastroenterology 1986 (PMID: 3710065); Kharasch ED et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 2007 (PMID: 17554244); Wilson JT et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 1976 (PMID: 1261164). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
