shelves.title: Prophylactic mesh at permanent end colostomy (Jänes, Serra-Aracil, STOMAMESH): SPLIT — early small trials positive, largest blinded trial and long-term follow-up null
shelves.question: In patients having a permanent end colostomy, does prophylactic mesh at stoma formation reduce later parastomal hernia versus no mesh?
shelves.mesh: Absorbable Implants · Aged · Clinical Protocols · Colostomy/adverse effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hernia, Ventral/etiology, mortality, prevention & control · Humans · Male · Postoperative Complications/mortality, prevention & control · Risk Factors · Surgical Mesh · Surgical Stomas/adverse effects · Suture Techniques/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the early small trials and the pooled estimate favour mesh; the largest double-blind trial and the late follow-up do not. Jänes (PMID: 19011935) found parastomal hernia at 5 years in 2 of 15 surviving mesh patients vs 17 of 21 controls, and Serra-Aracil (PMID: 19300232) found clinical hernia in 14.8% with mesh vs 40.7% without (p=0.03). But STOMAMESH (Odensten 2019, PMID: 29064900; 232 patients, double-blind) found no difference at 1 year, and pooled long-term follow-up of three trials (López-Cano 2023, PMID: 36966221) found no significant difference in time to hernia. The updated meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (McKechnie 2022, PMID: 34671916) still pools to an odds ratio of 0.60 favouring mesh, but with high heterogeneity (I²=74%) and no significant effect among trials from the last 5 years. The split is named on the stamp: small early open trials positive, large blinded and long-term data null.

cards.headline: Jänes 2009 (5-year follow-up of a randomised study, 54 patients): parastomal hernia in 2 of 15 surviving mesh patients vs 17 of 21 surviving controls (p<0.001); no mesh infection and no mesh removed
cards.summary: Jänes 2009 (5-year follow-up of a randomised study, 54 patients): parastomal hernia in 2 of 15 surviving mesh patients vs 17 of 21 surviving controls (p<0.001); no mesh infection and no mesh removed
cards.people: 54 patients having a permanent ostomy, randomised (2001–2003) to a conventional stoma or a stoma with a large-pore lightweight mesh (reduced polypropylene, high absorbable proportion) in the sublay position; this report follows the survivors to 5 years — 21 control and 15 mesh patients alive and assessed.
cards.result: At 5 years, parastomal herniation was recorded in 17 of 21 control patients (repair had been demanded in 5), vs herniation not requiring repair in 2 of 15 mesh patients (P<0.001). No fistulas or strictures developed, no mesh infection was noted and no mesh was removed during the study period. The 12-month result of the same trial had also favoured mesh without increased complications.
cards.watchOut: Only 36 of the original 54 patients were alive and assessed at 5 years — a small, attrition-prone denominator, and hernia assessment in survivors can mislead if deaths differed by arm. The effect size (17/21 vs 2/15) is far larger than any later trial found.
cards.source: Jänes A et al. Preventing parastomal hernia with a prosthetic mesh: a 5-year follow-up of a randomized study. World Journal of Surgery. 2009. PMID: 19011935. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Serra-Aracil 2009 (randomised trial, 54 patients): clinical parastomal hernia 14.8% with sublay lightweight mesh vs 40.7% without (p=0.03) at a median 29 months
cards.summary: Serra-Aracil 2009 (randomised trial, 54 patients): clinical parastomal hernia 14.8% with sublay lightweight mesh vs 40.7% without (p=0.03) at a median 29 months
cards.people: 54 patients scheduled for permanent end colostomy for cancer of the lower third of the rectum, operated on by the same colorectal team, randomised to a lightweight mesh in the sublay position (n=27) or no mesh (n=27); follow-up was clinical and by CT, by assessors blinded to the study aims, median 29 months (range 13–49).
cards.result: Clinical follow-up recorded 11/27 (40.7%) hernias in the control group vs 4/27 (14.8%) in the mesh group (P=0.03). CT identified 14 hernias in the control group vs 6 in the mesh group (P=0.08). Surgical time and postoperative morbidity were similar in the two groups, mortality was zero, and no mesh intolerance was reported.
cards.watchOut: A single team, 54 patients, and the CT endpoint — the more objective one — did not reach significance (p=0.08). Small single-centre surgical trials systematically overestimate effects that multicentre trials later shrink.

cards.headline: Odensten 2019 (STOMAMESH, 232 patients, double-blind multicentre): prophylactic sublay mesh did not reduce parastomal hernia at 1 year — clinical p=0.866, radiologic p=0.748 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Odensten 2019 (STOMAMESH, 232 patients, double-blind multicentre): prophylactic sublay mesh did not reduce parastomal hernia at 1 year — clinical p=0.866, radiologic p=0.748 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 232 patients undergoing open colorectal surgery including creation of a permanent end colostomy, randomised to a lightweight polypropylene mesh placed around the colostomy in the sublay position or no mesh; at 1 year 211 patients had clinical examination and 198 had radiologic (CT) assessment, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: No difference in parastomal hernia rate was revealed in the clinical (P=0.866) or radiologic (P=0.748) analyses at 1 year, and there was no significant difference in perioperative complications. Operation time was 36 minutes longer in the mesh arm. The authors conclude that, on these results, prophylactic mesh to prevent parastomal hernia cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: One year may be early — hernias keep appearing for years, and the long-term card below addresses that. But this is the largest and only double-blind trial here, and its null is precise enough that a large 1-year benefit is excluded.

cards.headline: López-Cano 2023 (long-term follow-up of three randomised trials, 121 patients): with a median 48.5 months, 67.8% had developed a parastomal hernia and mesh made no significant overall difference to time to hernia (log-rank p=0.094)
cards.summary: López-Cano 2023 (long-term follow-up of three randomised trials, 121 patients): with a median 48.5 months, 67.8% had developed a parastomal hernia and mesh made no significant overall difference to time to hernia (log-rank p=0.094)
cards.type: Long-term pooled follow-up of three randomised trials (López-Cano 2023)
cards.people: 121 patients from three randomised trials of permanent synthetic non-absorbable prophylactic mesh at elective end colostomy, followed long-term with CT-based hernia diagnosis; mesh techniques were open retromuscular, laparoscopic keyhole and laparoscopic modified Sugarbaker.
cards.result: 82 patients (67.8%) developed a parastomal hernia; median follow-up was 48.5 months (IQR 14.4–104.9) and median time to hernia diagnosis 17.7 months. Survival analysis showed no significant difference in time to hernia development by mesh vs no mesh overall (log-rank P=0.094) or within most technique groups, although the open retromuscular technique subgroup did show a higher reduction in hernia appearance (log-rank P=0.001). The authors conclude long-term placement of a non-absorbable synthetic prophylactic mesh does not seem effective for preventing parastomal hernia.
cards.watchOut: Pooling three trials with three different mesh techniques mixes the question; the retromuscular subgroup signal (p=0.001) is a subgroup of a null pooled result and should be read as a hypothesis about technique, not proof.
cards.source: López-Cano M et al. Parastomal hernia prevention with permanent mesh in end colostomy: failure with late follow-up of cohorts in three randomized trials. Hernia. 2023. PMID: 36966221. cards.headline: McKechnie 2022 (updated meta-analysis, 12 RCTs, 1,252 patients): pooled odds ratio 0.60 favouring prophylactic mesh (p=0.0003) — but heterogeneity I²=74%, and trials from the last 5 years alone were not significant (p=0.10)
cards.summary: McKechnie 2022 (updated meta-analysis, 12 RCTs, 1,252 patients): pooled odds ratio 0.60 favouring prophylactic mesh (p=0.0003) — but heterogeneity I²=74%, and trials from the last 5 years alone were not significant (p=0.10)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (McKechnie 2022)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials comparing prophylactic mesh with no mesh at end-colostomy formation after colorectal resection for benign or malignant disease: 581 patients with mesh and 671 without.
cards.result: Parastomal hernia incidence was significantly reduced with prophylactic mesh (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.80, p=0.0003 — a relative measure; I²=74%). Results were no longer significantly different when only studies conducted in the last 5 years were analysed (p=0.10). There was no significant difference in postoperative morbidity, postoperative mortality, colostomy-specific morbidity or length of stay. The authors call for further contemporary trials with modern surgical technology.
cards.watchOut: A pooled odds ratio across I²=74% heterogeneity averages trials that disagree — including STOMAMESH's null. The era split (older trials positive, recent trials null) is the most informative part of this analysis.
cards.source: McKechnie T et al. Prophylactic Mesh for Prevention of Parastomal Hernia Following End Colostomy: an Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery. 2022. PMID: 34671916. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — early small open trials and the all-trials pooled estimate favour prophylactic mesh; the largest double-blind trial (STOMAMESH) and the long-term pooled follow-up do not
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — early small open trials and the all-trials pooled estimate favour prophylactic mesh; the largest double-blind trial (STOMAMESH) and the long-term pooled follow-up do not
cards.people: Jänes randomised study, 54 patients with 5-year follow-up; Serra-Aracil RCT, 54 patients; STOMAMESH, 232 patients; long-term pooled follow-up of three RCTs, 121 patients; meta-analysis of 12 RCTs, 1,252 patients.
cards.result: Positive: hernia 2/15 vs 17/21 at 5 years (Jänes); clinical hernia 14.8% vs 40.7% (Serra-Aracil); pooled OR 0.60 across all 12 RCTs (McKechnie). Null: STOMAMESH clinical p=0.866 and radiologic p=0.748 at 1 year; long-term time-to-hernia p=0.094 (López-Cano); recent-trials-only meta-analysis p=0.10. No trial or synthesis found a morbidity or mesh-harm penalty of consequence. PROPOSED SPLIT — the split is era, size and follow-up length: benefit appears in small early trials and short horizons, and disappears in the blinded multicentre trial and at long-term CT follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: permanent end colostomy. Prophylactic mesh at midline laparotomy closure is a different question, homed on Shelf #2589 (PRIMA); inguinal hernia repair is Shelf #649.

shelves.title: Gastric acid secretion by phase (physiology): thinking about food alone reaches about two-thirds of the sham-feeding (cephalic) response, a meal secretes about 24 mmol/h of acid, and pentagastrin or histamine drive a peak of about 29 mmol/h
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is gastric acid secretion divided among the cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases, and what is maximal acid output after pentagastrin or histamine stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · *Gastric Acid/metabolism · Gastrins/blood · Pentagastrin/pharmacology · Histamine/pharmacology · Secretory Rate · Stomach/drug effects
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): acid secretion is conventionally divided into a cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste and thought of food, vagally mediated), a gastric phase (distension and peptides/amino acids in the stomach, largely gastrin-driven) and an intestinal phase — with the textbook's account assigning roughly 30% of the meal response to the cephalic phase, about 60% to the gastric phase and about 10% to the intestinal phase; those phase percentages are presented here explicitly as the textbook's account, because the carded primary studies measure the phases by stimulation and blockade rather than printing that exact split. What the carded human studies do quantify: thinking about food for 30 minutes raised acid output from 4 to 13 mmol/h, averaging 66% of the full modified-sham-feeding (cephalic) response, while sight and smell alone reached only 23–46% of sham feeding (Feldman & Richardson 1986); a simulated meal with sham feeding secreted 24.2 mmol/h, of which circulating gastrin could account for 89% on average — but anywhere from 51% to 162% in individuals (Blair 1987); sham feeding in the Konturek programme reached about 50% of the pentagastrin maximum; basal output in healthy volunteers was about 3.6–4.3 mmol/h against a pentagastrin-stimulated peak of 28.69 mmol/h (Klein 1989); and histamine and pentagastrin elicit equal maximal outputs of acid and pepsin, pentagastrin being the more potent and faster (Aubrey & Forrest 1970). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Feldman & Richardson 1986: discussing appetising food raised acid from 4 to 13 mmol/h — 66% of the full sham-feeding response — while sight or smell alone reached only 23–46%
cards.summary: Feldman & Richardson 1986: discussing appetising food raised acid from 4 to 13 mmol/h — 66% of the full sham-feeding response — while sight or smell alone reached only 23–46%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cephalic-phase stimulus dissection, intragastric measurement)
cards.people: Healthy human subjects studied with separate cephalic stimuli: discussing appetising food for 30 minutes (thought alone, no sight, smell or taste), sight of food, smell of food, sight plus smell, and modified sham feeding (thought, sight, smell and taste combined); group size is not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Discussing appetising food increased acid secretion from 4 to 13 mmol/h (p < 0.001) and raised serum gastrin significantly (p < 0.02), averaging 66 ± 10% of the response to modified sham feeding. Discussing non-food topics did not increase secretion significantly. Sight of food, smell of food, or sight and smell combined also increased acid secretion and serum gastrin significantly, but were significantly less potent than sham feeding, averaging only 23–46% of the sham-feeding response. Thought of food is therefore the dominant component of the cephalic phase, with taste (in sham feeding) adding the remainder.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are expressed against each study's own sham-feeding response, not against maximal (pentagastrin) output, and the abstract does not print the subject number — cross-study phase fractions should not be averaged as if they shared one denominator.
cards.source: Feldman M, Richardson CT. Role of thought, sight, smell, and taste of food in the cephalic phase of gastric acid secretion in humans. Gastroenterology. 1986. PMID: 3940915. cards.headline: Blair 1987: a simulated meal secreted 24.2 mmol/h of acid, and circulating gastrin alone could account for 89% of it on average — but 51% to 162% in individuals
cards.summary: Blair 1987: a simulated meal secreted 24.2 mmol/h of acid, and circulating gastrin alone could account for 89% of it on average — but 51% to 162% in individuals
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (simulated meal with gastrin dose–response reconstruction)
cards.people: 12 healthy human subjects given a simulated meal (homogenised meal infused into the stomach through a nasogastric tube, activating the gastric and intestinal phases, with simultaneous sham feeding for the cephalic phase), and on a separate day intravenous gastrin 17 infusions matched to measured postprandial gastrin levels; acid measured by in-vivo intragastric titration.
cards.result: Mean serum gastrin rose from a basal 43 ± 9 pg/ml to an average postprandial 121 ± 25 pg/ml over 2 hours, matching gastrin release after a normally eaten meal in the same subjects. Acid secretion after the simulated meal averaged 24.2 ± 2.4 mmol/h. Relating the gastrin-infusion dose–response to the postprandial gastrin level, a gastrin concentration of 121 pg/ml could produce 21.5 mmol/h — 89% of the acid actually secreted after the meal. In individual subjects, however, the gastrin released could produce as little as 51% or as much as 162% of actual postprandial secretion: the gastrin (gastric-phase) contribution is large on average and highly variable between people.
cards.watchOut: The 89% is a reconstruction — acid attributable to gastrin is inferred from a separate day's infusion curve, assuming gastrin's potency is unchanged in the meal state; the 51–162% individual range is the honest headline, and a homogenised intragastric meal is not identical to eating.
cards.source: Blair AJ et al. Variable contribution of gastrin to gastric acid secretion after a meal in humans. Gastroenterology. 1987. PMID: 3557000. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aubrey & Forrest 1970: histamine and pentagastrin elicit equal maximal acid and pepsin outputs — pentagastrin is simply more potent and faster
cards.summary: Aubrey & Forrest 1970: histamine and pentagastrin elicit equal maximal acid and pepsin outputs — pentagastrin is simply more potent and faster
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (classic stimulant dose–response comparison)
cards.people: 6 normal human subjects tested with four doses each of histamine acid phosphate (1, 10, 40 and 80 µg/kg/h) and pentagastrin (0.15, 1.5, 6.0 and 12.0 µg/kg/h) by separate continuous intravenous infusions, with gastric juice collected at 15-minute intervals. N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: The two drugs elicited equal maximal outputs of acid and of pepsin. Pentagastrin was more potent than histamine in stimulating acid and pepsin secretion, and the rate of the responses was faster with pentagastrin. Apart from potency and speed, the patterns of secretion of the juice constituents and the interrelationships between electrolyte concentrations were identical with the two drugs — the authors concluded the actions of histamine acid phosphate and pentagastrin on human gastric secretion are identical, so a maximal output measured with either stimulant measures the same secretory capacity. The fetched abstract prints no absolute mmol/h value for the maximum; the numeric peak on this shelf comes from the Klein 1989 card.
cards.watchOut: Six subjects from 1970, and the abstract reports the equality of maximal outputs without printing the maximal values themselves — this card establishes that histamine and pentagastrin maxima are interchangeable, not what the maximum is.

cards.headline: Klein 1989: basal acid output was about 3.6–4.3 mmol/h and pentagastrin-stimulated peak output 28.69 mmol/h in healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Klein 1989: basal acid output was about 3.6–4.3 mmol/h and pentagastrin-stimulated peak output 28.69 mmol/h in healthy volunteers
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (gastric analysis with pentagastrin stimulation, control-condition values)
cards.people: Highly hypnotisable healthy volunteers undergoing gastric analysis, including a no-hypnosis control session with basal measurement followed by pentagastrin stimulation; the study's purpose was central (hypnotic) modulation — the basal and peak values carded here are its control-condition measurements. Subject number is not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In the first study, imagining eating under hypnosis raised acid output from a basal mean of 3.60 ± 0.48 mmol/h to 6.80 mmol/h, an increase of 89% (p = 0.0007). In the second study's no-hypnosis session, basal acid output was 4.29 ± 0.93 mmol/h and pentagastrin-stimulated peak acid output was 28.69 ± 2.34 mmol/h (hypnotic relaxation instructions reduced basal output by 39% and peak output by 11%, to 25.43 mmol/h). The control values give this shelf's numeric frame: unstimulated secretion of roughly 4 mmol/h rising roughly sevenfold to a stimulated peak of about 29 mmol/h.
cards.watchOut: The volunteers were selected for high hypnotisability and the study was designed to test central modulation, so its basal and peak values are a convenience sample of healthy stomachs rather than a normative survey — they anchor the scale of maximal output, not its population distribution.
cards.source: Klein KB, Spiegel D. Modulation of gastric acid secretion by hypnosis. Gastroenterology. 1989. PMID: 2714570. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Konturek 1993: sham feeding (cephalic phase) reached about 50% of the pentagastrin maximum, and cholecystokinin acts as a brake on meal-stimulated secretion
cards.summary: Konturek 1993: sham feeding (cephalic phase) reached about 50% of the pentagastrin maximum, and cholecystokinin acts as a brake on meal-stimulated secretion
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (phase stimulation with CCK-receptor blockade)
cards.people: Three groups of healthy male subjects: group A for postprandial and sham-feeding studies, group B for exogenous secretagogue infusions (caerulein, gastrin-releasing peptide, pentagastrin), group C for 12-hour intragastric pH-metry; the cholecystokinin-A receptor blocker loxiglumide was used to unmask endogenous CCK effects. Group sizes are not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Cephalic-phase stimulation by modified sham feeding increased acid secretion to about 50% of the pentagastrin maximum, and loxiglumide did not affect it. Caerulein and gastrin-releasing peptide dose-dependently stimulated secretion to about 35% and 25% of the pentagastrin maximum respectively; adding loxiglumide increased those responses two- to threefold, to about 100% and 50% of maximum. A 5% peptone meal instilled intragastrically greatly enhanced acid secretion and plasma gastrin, and loxiglumide further increased both — showing that CCK released by a meal exerts a potent inhibitory (intestinal-phase braking) influence on acid secretion and gastrin release via CCK-A receptors.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are again relative to each protocol's pentagastrin maximum, and the CCK-brake conclusion rests on a single receptor blocker at one standard dose — the intestinal phase's net effect in ordinary eating (simultaneous stimulation and inhibition) is not directly measured here.
cards.source: Konturek JW et al. Cholecystokinin in the control of gastric acid secretion in man. Gut. 1993. PMID: 8472978. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cephalic stimulation alone reaches about half to two-thirds of capacity, a meal runs at about 24 mmol/h driven mainly by gastrin, and the pharmacological ceiling is about 29 mmol/h by either stimulant
cards.summary: Synthesis: cephalic stimulation alone reaches about half to two-thirds of capacity, a meal runs at about 24 mmol/h driven mainly by gastrin, and the pharmacological ceiling is about 29 mmol/h by either stimulant
cards.people: Synthesis across Feldman & Richardson 1986, Blair 1987, Aubrey & Forrest 1970, Klein 1989 and Konturek 1993 — the primary human acid-secretion literature.
cards.result: The measurements assemble into one scale: basal secretion about 4 mmol/h; thought of food about 13 mmol/h; full cephalic stimulation about 50% of maximum (Konturek) with thought contributing 66% of the sham-feeding response (Feldman); a meal about 24.2 mmol/h with gastrin sufficient to explain 89% on average (Blair); and a pentagastrin or histamine ceiling of about 28.69 mmol/h, equal for both stimulants (Klein; Aubrey). The conventional phase percentages (cephalic about 30%, gastric about 60%, intestinal about 10% of a meal response) remain the textbook's account — consistent with, but not printed by, these carded studies.
cards.watchOut: Each carded study normalises to a different denominator (sham feeding, a meal, or the pentagastrin maximum) and several do not print subject numbers in their abstracts, so the synthesis scale is an assembly of compatible measurements, not a single experiment's phase budget.
cards.source: Synthesis of Feldman M, Richardson CT. Gastroenterology. 1986 (PMID: 3940915); Blair AJ et al. Gastroenterology. 1987 (PMID: 3557000); Aubrey DA, Forrest AP. shelves.title: Gut transit in health: colon about 35 hours (men faster than women by roughly 11 hours), small bowel about 5 hours, and wide normal variation
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal whole-gut and colonic transit times, and how much do they vary between people and by sex?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Colon · Dietary Fiber · Digestive System · Female · Gastrointestinal Motility · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radiography
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology — the textbooks present colonic transit as the slow, variable limb of gut transit, measured clinically by radio-opaque markers; the carded human studies supply the values). Total colonic transit averaged 35.0 ± 2.1 hours in 73 healthy people, split almost evenly — right colon 11.3, left colon 11.4, rectosigmoid 12.4 hours — and was significantly shorter in men than women (Metcalf 1987). The larger Swiss reference series (N = 128) puts the sex gap at 30 ± 2 hours in men versus 41 ± 3 hours in women, with no age effect and upper reference limits up to 70 hours in women (Meir 1992). Repeat scintigraphic testing confirms the sex difference and shows group means are stable while individual single measurements can vary considerably — intrinsic variation large enough that any menstrual-cycle effect must be small (Degen & Phillips 1996). The small bowel is fast by comparison: orocaecal transit ~295–301 minutes with no sex difference (Bennink 1999), so whole-gut transit time is essentially colonic transit plus about 5 hours. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: quote colonic transit as ~35 hours with a wide normal range, expect women to run slower than men, and treat a single measurement in one person cautiously.

cards.headline: Metcalf 1987: total colonic transit in 73 healthy people was 35.0 ± 2.1 hours — right colon 11.3, left colon 11.4, rectosigmoid 12.4 hours — and significantly shorter in men than women
cards.summary: Metcalf 1987: total colonic transit in 73 healthy people was 35.0 ± 2.1 hours — right colon 11.3, left colon 11.4, rectosigmoid 12.4 hours — and significantly shorter in men than women
cards.type: Human physiology study (radio-opaque marker colonic transit, Metcalf 1987)
cards.people: 24 healthy persons given three sets of distinctive radio-opaque markers on 3 successive days with daily abdominal films and stool radiography to validate a simplified single-film method, then 49 additional healthy subjects assessed by the single-film technique — 73 healthy subjects in total.
cards.result: Total colonic transit was 35.0 ± 2.1 h (mean ± SE); segmental transits were 11.3 ± 1.1 h (right colon), 11.4 ± 1.4 h (left colon) and 12.4 ± 1.1 h (rectosigmoid). Men had significantly shorter whole-colon transit than women (P < 0.05), with the difference apparent in right (P = 0.06) and left colon (P = 0.07) but not rectosigmoid. Age did not influence transit significantly, nor did a small dose of supplemental fibre. The single-film estimates correlated well with the established multi-film/stool methods.
cards.watchOut: The mouth-to-anus transit was assessed from faecal marker output in the validation phase, but the record's reported values are the colonic and segmental times — no whole-gut hour value is printed here because the fetched record does not give one.
cards.source: Metcalf AM et al. Simplified assessment of segmental colonic transit. Gastroenterology. 1987. PMID: 3023168. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Colon · Dietary Fiber · Digestive System · Female · Gastrointestinal Motility · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radiography

cards.headline: Meir 1992: in 128 healthy volunteers, mean colonic transit was 30 ± 2 hours in men versus 41 ± 3 hours in women, uninfluenced by age
cards.summary: Meir 1992: in 128 healthy volunteers, mean colonic transit was 30 ± 2 hours in men versus 41 ± 3 hours in women, uninfluenced by age
cards.type: Human physiology study (marker colonic transit reference values, Meir 1992)
cards.people: 128 healthy volunteers (mean age 40 years, range 20–81) from three regions of Switzerland, assessed with radio-opaque markers and a plain abdominal film (Arhan/Chaussade-type calculation).
cards.result: Colonic transit time was not influenced by age in either sex. Mean transit was significantly shorter in men than in women (30 ± 2 h versus 41 ± 3 h; P < 0.05). Among men, non-smokers had shorter transit than smokers (26 ± 2 h versus 40 ± 5 h; P < 0.05); in women neither smoking nor the menstrual cycle influenced transit. Recommended upper limits: 66 h for smoking men, 44 h for non-smoking men, and 70 h for women in general.
cards.watchOut: Published in German (Schweizerische medizinische Wochenschrift) with an English abstract; the carded numbers are from that abstract. Population and diet are Swiss — transit norms are diet- and population-sensitive.
cards.source: Meir R et al. [Age- and sex-specific standard values of colonic transit time in healthy subjects]. Schweizerische medizinische Wochenschrift. 1992. PMID: 1615304. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Degen 1996: colonic transit was faster in men than women, group means were stable on repeat testing, but single measurements in an individual sometimes varied considerably
cards.summary: Degen 1996: colonic transit was faster in men than women, group means were stable on repeat testing, but single measurements in an individual sometimes varied considerably
cards.type: Human physiology study (scintigraphic and marker transit variability, Degen & Phillips 1996)
cards.people: 32 healthy volunteers (12 women, 20 men) studied on two occasions — women in follicular and luteal phases, men twice over a similar 4-week period — with standardised diet and exercise; whole-gut transit assessed scintigraphically and colonic transit by radio-opaque markers.
cards.result: Colonic transit was significantly faster in men, and post-lag gastric emptying was also more rapid in men; other regional indices did not differ by sex. Scintigraphic and marker methods reflected total colonic transit equally well. Group means in the two studies were almost identical, yet single assessments in individual subjects sometimes showed considerable variability — broad intrinsic biological variation. The authors calculate that any menstrual-hormone effect on transit must be small relative to that intrinsic variation and of doubtful clinical significance.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record reports the sex and variability findings without printing the hour values for whole-gut transit — the card therefore makes no whole-gut hour claim; the hour values on this shelf come from the marker studies.
cards.source: Degen LP et al. Variability of gastrointestinal transit in healthy women and men. Gut. 1996. PMID: 8977347. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bennink 1999: orocaecal transit was about 295 minutes in men and 301 minutes in women, with no significant sex difference in small-bowel transit
cards.summary: Bennink 1999: orocaecal transit was about 295 minutes in men and 301 minutes in women, with no significant sex difference in small-bowel transit
cards.type: Human physiology study (scintigraphic small-bowel transit, Bennink 1999)
cards.people: 12 healthy men and 12 healthy women given a standard solid (99mTc-sulphur colloid, 230 kcal) and liquid (111In-DTPA water) test meal, with gastric-emptying fitting and caecal-arrival imaging every 15 minutes for 6 h.
cards.result: Orocaecal transit time was 294.6 ± 18.8 min in men and 301.3 ± 24.5 min in women (the record reports the same values for solids and liquids). The 10% small-bowel transit times were about 280–297 min across sexes and meal types. Solids and liquids transferred simultaneously from terminal ileum to caecum (correlation 0.90). There was no statistically significant difference in small-bowel transit between sexes or between solids and liquids — the sex difference in whole transit is a colonic, not a small-bowel, phenomenon.
cards.watchOut: Values are mean ± SEM as printed. Orocaecal transit includes gastric emptying, so it is not a pure small-bowel time; the 10% small-bowel transit time is the purer measure.
cards.source: Bennink R et al. Evaluation of small-bowel transit for solid and liquid test meal in healthy men and women. European journal of nuclear medicine. 1999. PMID: 10638407. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 73 + 128 + 32 + 24 healthy volunteers across the carded studies.
cards.result: Normal colonic transit is about 35 hours on average (Metcalf) with segmental times of roughly 11–12 hours each for right colon, left colon and rectosigmoid; it is consistently shorter in men than women (30 vs 41 hours in the 128-person Swiss series), is not materially changed by age or menstrual phase, and varies widely between — and sometimes within — individuals, so upper reference limits run to roughly 44–70 hours depending on sex and smoking. The small bowel contributes only about 5 hours (orocaecal ~295–301 min) with no sex difference: whole-gut transit is dominated by the colon. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Marker, scintigraphic and film-counting methods give concordant colonic times but are not identical measurements; diet and population shift the norms.
cards.source: Synthesis of Metcalf AM et al., Gastroenterology 1987 (PMID: 3023168); Meir R et al., Schweizerische medizinische Wochenschrift 1992 (PMID: 1615304); Degen LP et al., Gut 1996 (PMID: 8977347); Bennink R et al., European journal of nuclear medicine 1999 (PMID: 10638407).

shelves.title: Colonic short-chain fatty acids: a concentrated fermentation product, absorbed almost completely, with butyrate feeding the colonocyte, propionate the liver, and acetate reaching the blood
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much short-chain fatty acid does colonic fermentation produce each day, what fraction is absorbed, and what share of energy needs can it supply?
shelves.mesh: Acetates · Acetic Acid · Animals · Butyrates · Butyric Acid · Fatty Acids · Female · Fermentation · Gastrointestinal Contents · Hepatic Veins · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Intestine, Large · Male · Portal Vein · Propionates · Swine
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the production and energy figures explicitly on a different footing from the carded measurements (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep). The textbook/review account — Cummings' contemporary review of the primary literature, fetched this session — is that the colonic flora ferment 30 g or more of carbohydrate daily with production of at least 300 mmol of short-chain fatty acids, and the standard review estimate (Nordgaard & Mortensen 1995, fetched this session) puts the energy salvaged at about 5–10% of energy requirements in people with a normal-length gut; those two figures are presented here as the textbook/review account because no carded primary study measures 24-hour production or energy share directly. What the primary human studies do measure is consistent with near-complete absorption: colonic contents hold 131 mmol/kg SCFA in the caecum falling distally, while portal blood (375 µmol/L) carries several-fold the peripheral level (79 µmol/L) and molar ratios shift in a pattern showing butyrate taken up by the colonic epithelium and propionate by the liver (Cummings 1987). Colonic perfusion shows absorption is concentration-dependent, ~60% by nonionic diffusion, and coupled to sodium and water absorption (Ruppin 1980); a caecal lactulose load raises portal SCFA within 15–45 minutes while peripheral blood shows essentially acetate alone (Peters 1992); and whole-body acetate turnover is ~7.5 µmol/kg/min (Simoneau 1994). Very little SCFA appears in normal stool relative to these fluxes — the absorbed fraction is therefore conventionally put at well over 90% (textbook account). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for production, routing and near-complete absorption; the precise daily mmol and energy-share figures are textbook-account values.

cards.headline: Cummings 1987: colonic contents held 131 mmol/kg of short-chain fatty acids in the caecum falling to 80 mmol/kg in the descending colon, and portal blood carried 375 µmol/L against 79 µmol/L peripherally
cards.summary: Cummings 1987: colonic contents held 131 mmol/kg of short-chain fatty acids in the caecum falling to 80 mmol/kg in the descending colon, and portal blood carried 375 µmol/L against 79 µmol/L peripherally
cards.type: Human physiology study (colonic content and portal blood SCFA measurement, Cummings 1987)
cards.people: Contents of all regions of the large intestine and portal, hepatic and peripheral venous blood obtained at autopsy within 4 hours of sudden death (number of subjects not documented in the fetched record — 'N not documented'), with SCFA concentrations and pH measured by region and by blood compartment.
cards.result: Total SCFA concentration was low in terminal ileum (13 ± 6 mmol/kg) but high throughout the colon — 131 ± 9 mmol/kg in the caecum falling to 80 ± 11 mmol/kg in the descending colon — with pH rising from 5.6 ± 0.2 (caecum) to 6.6 ± 0.1 (descending colon), inversely related to SCFA. Total SCFA in blood was 375 ± 70 µmol/L portal, 148 ± 42 hepatic and 79 ± 22 peripheral. Acetate predominated everywhere, but molar ratios shifted from lumen to portal blood to hepatic vein, indicating greater uptake of butyrate by the colonic epithelium and of propionate by the liver.
cards.watchOut: Sudden-death autopsy material, not fed volunteers — concentrations are a post-mortem snapshot within 4 hours of death, and the subject number is not documented in the record. Concentrations are not production rates; the production and energy figures in the balance are labelled textbook/review accounts.
cards.source: Cummings JH et al. Short chain fatty acids in human large intestine, portal, hepatic and venous blood. Gut. 1987. PMID: 3678950. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ruppin 1980: colonic perfusion in normal volunteers showed SCFA absorption is concentration-dependent, about 60% by nonionic diffusion, and drives sodium and water absorption
cards.summary: Ruppin 1980: colonic perfusion in normal volunteers showed SCFA absorption is concentration-dependent, about 60% by nonionic diffusion, and drives sodium and water absorption
cards.type: Human physiology study (colonic perfusion SCFA absorption, Ruppin 1980)
cards.people: Normal volunteers whose colon was perfused with neutral isotonic solutions containing SCFA at 0–90 mmol/L; propionate studied in detail with limited observations on acetate and n-butyrate (subject number not documented in the fetched record — 'N not documented').
cards.result: SCFA absorption was concentration-dependent; back-diffusion of ketone-body metabolites was quantitatively insignificant. Absorption was accompanied by increased sodium, potassium and water absorption, luminal alkalinisation from bicarbonate accumulation, and a fall in luminal PCO2. The authors resolve two mechanisms: nonionic diffusion of protonated SCFA consuming luminal CO2, accounting for about 60% of total absorption, and cellular uptake by ionic diffusion of the sodium or potassium salt.
cards.watchOut: Perfusion of a cleansed colon segment with defined solutions isolates transport; it does not measure what fraction of endogenously produced SCFA escapes in stool under normal conditions.
cards.source: Ruppin H et al. Absorption of short-chain fatty acids by the colon. Gastroenterology. 1980. PMID: 6768637. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Simoneau 1994: whole-body acetate turnover in 6 healthy volunteers was 7.5 ± 1 µmol/kg/min by [1-13C]acetate infusion
cards.summary: Simoneau 1994: whole-body acetate turnover in 6 healthy volunteers was 7.5 ± 1 µmol/kg/min by [1-13C]acetate infusion
cards.type: Human physiology study (stable-isotope acetate turnover, Simoneau 1994)
cards.people: 6 healthy volunteers infused with the stable isotope [1-13C]acetate for 160 minutes, with a validated gas chromatography–mass spectrometry enrichment assay (between- and within-assay variation < 5%). N = 6 — small, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Acetate turnover was 7.5 ± 1 µmol/kg/min, similar to earlier radioactive-tracer data — the higher fluxes reported in some stable-isotope studies were not reproduced, which the authors attribute to differences in subjects' physiological status. Acetate turnover of this order is the tracer window on total SCFA production, acetate being the principal colonic SCFA reaching the peripheral circulation.
cards.watchOut: Turnover is not production: peripheral acetate turnover mixes colonic production with endogenous acetate, so it bounds rather than equals colonic SCFA output. N = 6.
cards.source: Simoneau C et al. Measurement of whole body acetate turnover in healthy subjects with stable isotopes. Biological mass spectrometry. 1994. PMID: 8068738. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Acetates · Adult · Carbon Isotopes · Female · Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry · Humans · Male

cards.headline: Peters 1992: after caecal lactulose at surgery, portal SCFA rose within 15–45 minutes — peak portal acetate 240.9 µmol/L after 10 g — while peripheral blood showed acetate only, with traces of butyrate
cards.summary: Peters 1992: after caecal lactulose at surgery, portal SCFA rose within 15–45 minutes — peak portal acetate 240.9 µmol/L after 10 g — while peripheral blood showed acetate only, with traces of butyrate
cards.type: Human physiology study (caecal fermentation challenge with portal sampling, Peters 1992)
cards.people: Patients undergoing elective cholecystectomy (fasting SCFA concentrations in n = 28) given caecal instillation of saline or 6.7 g or 10 g lactulose at surgery, with portal and peripheral venous sampling every 15 minutes for 60 minutes.
cards.result: Fasting concentrations (µmol/L, mean (SD)): portal acetate 128.0 (70.8), propionate 34.4 (23.3), butyrate 17.6 (18.4); peripheral acetate 67.0 (23.0), propionate 3.7 (1.2), butyrate traces only. After lactulose, portal SCFA rose rapidly, peaking at 15–45 minutes; mean peaks after 10 g lactulose were acetate 240.9 (142.2), propionate 39.0 (17.8) and butyrate 26.9 (17.6) µmol/L. Portal acetate changes were reflected peripherally; propionate and butyrate largely were not — first-pass uptake by colonocyte and liver keeps them out of the systemic circulation.
cards.watchOut: Surgical patients under anaesthesia, not ambulant healthy volunteers; lactulose is a defined fermentable load, so the peaks show capacity and routing, not habitual daily production.
cards.source: Peters SG et al. Portal and peripheral blood short chain fatty acid concentrations after caecal lactulose instillation at surgery. Gut. 1992. PMID: 1427380. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Healthy volunteers, surgical patients and sudden-death donors across the carded studies (Ns 6–28 where documented; two classic studies do not document N in the record).
cards.result: The human colon is a fermentation organ holding ~80–131 mmol/kg of SCFA, produced proximally and absorbed almost as fast as it is made: absorption is concentration-dependent (~60% nonionic diffusion), portal blood carries several-fold the peripheral concentration, butyrate is consumed by the colonocyte and propionate by the liver, and acetate — turnover ~7.5 µmol/kg/min — is the SCFA that reaches the systemic circulation. The familiar daily-production (~300 mmol or more) and energy-share (~5–10%) figures are textbook/review accounts, labelled as such in the balance, not values measured in the carded primary studies. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: No carded primary study directly measures 24-hour production or the faecal escape fraction in free-living healthy people; those numbers rest on the textbook/review account and are presented that way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cummings JH et al., Gut 1987 (PMID: 3678950); Ruppin H et al., Gastroenterology 1980 (PMID: 6768637); Simoneau C et al., Biological mass spectrometry 1994 (PMID: 8068738); Peters SG et al., Gut 1992 (PMID: 1427380).

shelves.title: Lonafarnib in chronic hepatitis D: HDV RNA suppression in phase 2 studies only — D-LIVR phase 3 has no published primary report
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis D, does lonafarnib boosted with ritonavir (with or without peginterferon) achieve HDV RNA suppression and ALT normalisation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology,pathology · Female · Hepatitis D, Chronic/drug therapy · Hepatitis Delta Virus/isolation & purification · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,pharmacology · Placebos/administration & dosage · Plasma/chemistry · Prenylation/drug effects · Pyridines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,pharmacology · RNA, Viral/blood · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Dibenzocycloheptenes
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 evidence only, and the publication-status check is part of this shelf's face: as of this build, no published primary report of the D-LIVR phase 3 trial was found in PubMed — the exact search for 'D-LIVR' returned only review articles, not a trial report — so this shelf rests entirely on the published phase 2 programme and states the D-LIVR status plainly. In the proof-of-concept randomised phase 2A trial (Koh 2015, PMID: 26189433), 28 days of lonafarnib lowered HDV RNA by 0.73 log IU/mL (100 mg twice daily) and 1.54 log IU/mL (200 mg twice daily) versus placebo. LOWR HDV-1 (Yurdaydin 2018, PMID: 29152762; 15 patients) found ritonavir boosting or peginterferon alfa addition improved responses over higher-dose monotherapy with fewer gastrointestinal effects. LOWR HDV-2 (Yurdaydin 2022, PMID: 34860418; 55 patients) reached the primary endpoint (≥2 log decline or below quantification) in 46% on all-oral lonafarnib 50 mg plus ritonavir and 89% on the regimen adding peginterferon alfa. Premise correction: the published LOWR combinations use peginterferon alfa, not lambda — peginterferon lambda belongs to the unpublished D-LIVR design, so no lambda claim is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): small phase 2 studies with virological endpoints cap the stamp.

cards.headline: Koh 2015 (proof-of-concept phase 2A): 28 days of lonafarnib lowered HDV RNA by 0.73 and 1.54 log IU/mL versus placebo at the two doses
cards.summary: Koh 2015 (proof-of-concept phase 2A): 28 days of lonafarnib lowered HDV RNA by 0.73 and 1.54 log IU/mL versus placebo at the two doses
cards.people: 14 patients with chronic hepatitis D in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2A trial: lonafarnib 100 mg twice daily (group 1) or 200 mg twice daily (group 2) for 28 days, with 6 months of follow-up.
cards.result: At day 28, mean log HDV RNA declines versus placebo were −0.73 log IU/mL (95% CI 0.17 to 1.31; p=0.03) at 100 mg twice daily and −1.54 log IU/mL (1.21 to 1.93; p<0.0001) at 200 mg twice daily. HDV RNA change correlated with serum lonafarnib concentration (r²=0.78; p<0.0001). Adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal: in group 2 all patients had nausea, diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss over 2 kg (mean 4 kg). No treatment discontinuations occurred.
cards.watchOut: Very small (14 patients) and very short (28 days), with a virological endpoint only — it proves the drug hits the virus, not that patients live longer or avoid cirrhosis outcomes. Gastrointestinal intolerance rises steeply with dose, which is why ritonavir boosting was pursued.
cards.source: Koh C et al. Oral prenylation inhibition with lonafarnib in chronic hepatitis D infection: a proof-of-concept randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2A trial. Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2015. PMID: 26189433. Registry ID: NCT01495585. cards.headline: Yurdaydin 2018 (LOWR HDV-1): in 15 patients, ritonavir boosting or peginterferon alfa addition beat higher-dose lonafarnib monotherapy on response and tolerability
cards.summary: Yurdaydin 2018 (LOWR HDV-1): in 15 patients, ritonavir boosting or peginterferon alfa addition beat higher-dose lonafarnib monotherapy on response and tolerability
cards.type: Open-label phase 2 dose-finding study (Yurdaydin 2018, LOWR HDV-1)
cards.people: 15 patients with chronic hepatitis D in an open-label phase 2 dose-optimisation study, 3 per group across five regimens: lonafarnib monotherapy at 200 or 300 mg twice daily or 100 mg three times daily, lonafarnib 100 mg twice daily plus peginterferon alfa weekly, or lonafarnib 100 mg twice daily plus ritonavir 100 mg daily.
cards.result: Higher monotherapy doses lowered HDV viral load more than in the proof-of-concept study but with more gastrointestinal adverse events. Adding ritonavir 100 mg daily to lonafarnib 100 mg twice daily gave better antiviral responses than 300 mg twice-daily monotherapy with fewer side effects; the peginterferon alfa combination gave a similar improvement. Two of 6 patients treated for 12 weeks had transient post-treatment ALT rises followed by HDV-RNA negativity and ALT normalisation.
cards.watchOut: Three patients per regimen — every comparison in this study is fragile, and the regimens were not randomised against each other in a powered design. It is a dose-finding signal, not an efficacy verdict.
cards.source: Yurdaydin C et al. Optimizing lonafarnib treatment for the management of chronic delta hepatitis: The LOWR HDV-1 study. Hepatology. 2018. PMID: 29152762. cards.headline: Yurdaydin 2022 (LOWR HDV-2): the ≥2 log HDV-RNA endpoint was reached by 46% on all-oral lonafarnib 50 mg plus ritonavir and 89% when peginterferon alfa was added
cards.summary: Yurdaydin 2022 (LOWR HDV-2): the ≥2 log HDV-RNA endpoint was reached by 46% on all-oral lonafarnib 50 mg plus ritonavir and 89% when peginterferon alfa was added
cards.type: Open-label phase 2 dose-finding study (Yurdaydin 2022, LOWR HDV-2)
cards.people: 55 patients with chronic hepatitis D in an open-label, single-centre phase 2 dose-finding study: high-dose lonafarnib (≥75 mg twice daily) plus ritonavir (n=19, 12 weeks), all-oral low-dose lonafarnib (25 or 50 mg twice daily) plus ritonavir (n=24, 24 weeks), or low-dose lonafarnib plus ritonavir plus peginterferon alfa (n=12, 24 weeks).
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥2 log10 decline or below the lower limit of quantification of HDV RNA at end of treatment) was reached in 46% (6 of 13) of patients on the all-oral lonafarnib 50 mg twice-daily plus ritonavir regimen and 89% (8 of 9) on the combination regimens adding peginterferon alfa. Grade 2–3 gastrointestinal adverse events were 49% of events in the high-dose groups versus 22% in the low-dose groups. Several patients had transient post-treatment ALT rises followed by HDV-RNA negativity and ALT normalisation.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre and dose-finding, with small evaluable denominators for the headline percentages (6 of 13; 8 of 9). The interferon in this published study is peginterferon alfa — not lambda. End-of-treatment virology is not a clinical outcome.
cards.source: Yurdaydin C et al. A phase 2 dose-finding study of lonafarnib and ritonavir with or without interferon alpha for chronic delta hepatitis. Hepatology. 2022. PMID: 34860418. Registry ID: NCT02430194. cards.headline: Synthesis: published evidence is phase 2 only — HDV RNA suppression is real, clinical benefit and the phase 3 verdict are unpublished
cards.summary: Synthesis: published evidence is phase 2 only — HDV RNA suppression is real, clinical benefit and the phase 3 verdict are unpublished
cards.people: Published base: 14 patients (Koh 2015), 15 patients (LOWR HDV-1) and 55 patients (LOWR HDV-2). Publication-status check for this build: an exact PubMed search for 'D-LIVR' returned only review articles and no primary phase 3 trial report, so D-LIVR contributes no carded evidence here.
cards.result: Lonafarnib lowers HDV RNA dose-dependently versus placebo (−1.54 log IU/mL at 200 mg twice daily over 28 days), ritonavir boosting allows lower, better-tolerated doses, and the best phase 2 endpoint rates (89%) came with peginterferon alfa added. No published study in this shelf reports mortality, decompensation or transplant outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small phase 2 programme with virological endpoints caps the stamp, with the phase-2 basis and D-LIVR's unpublished status stated on the face.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: chronic hepatitis D, virological endpoints. If a peer-reviewed D-LIVR report appears, this shelf must be rebuilt on it. Bulevirtide for hepatitis D is homed separately (live shelves #1063 and #2166).

shelves.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis in acute variceal bleeding: fewer infections and lower mortality; ceftriaxone beat norfloxacin in advanced cirrhosis
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and acute variceal bleeding, does antibiotic prophylaxis (intravenous ceftriaxone versus oral norfloxacin) reduce bacterial infections, rebleeding and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage · Antibiotic Prophylaxis* · Bacteremia/mortality,prevention & control · Bacterial Infections/mortality,prevention & control · Ceftriaxone/administration & dosage · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/drug therapy,etiology,mortality · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Liver Cirrhosis/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Norfloxacin/administration & dosage · Peritonitis/mortality,prevention & control · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for prophylaxis versus none, on concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials: Bernard 1999 (PMID: 10347104; 5 trials, 534 patients) found prophylaxis raised the mean survival rate by 9.1 percentage points and the infection-free rate by 32 points; the updated Cochrane review (Chavez-Tapia 2011, PMID: 21707680; 12 trials, 1,241 patients) found mortality relative risk 0.79 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.98), bacterial infections relative risk 0.35 and rebleeding relative risk 0.53 — relative measures, with the trial counts beside them. For the choice of agent, one randomised trial (Fernández 2006, PMID: 17030175; 111 patients with advanced cirrhosis and haemorrhage) found intravenous ceftriaxone beat oral norfloxacin on proved or possible infections (11% versus 33%) — that head-to-head slice is a single trial and is capped at POSSIBLE within this balance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for giving prophylaxis; POSSIBLE for ceftriaxone over norfloxacin specifically.

cards.headline: Fernández 2006: intravenous ceftriaxone beat oral norfloxacin for infection prophylaxis in advanced cirrhosis with haemorrhage (proved or possible infections 11% versus 33%)
cards.summary: Fernández 2006: intravenous ceftriaxone beat oral norfloxacin for infection prophylaxis in advanced cirrhosis with haemorrhage (proved or possible infections 11% versus 33%)
cards.people: 111 patients with advanced cirrhosis (at least two of: ascites, severe malnutrition, encephalopathy, bilirubin over 3 mg/dL) and gastrointestinal haemorrhage, randomised to oral norfloxacin 400 mg twice daily (n=57) or intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily (n=54) for 7 days. Randomised controlled trial.
cards.result: The probability of proved or possible infections was significantly higher on norfloxacin (33% versus 11%; P=.003), as were proved infections (26% versus 11%; P=.03) and spontaneous bacteraemia or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (12% versus 2%; P=.03). Seven gram-negative bacilli were isolated in the norfloxacin group and 6 were quinolone-resistant; non-enterococcal streptococci were isolated only in the norfloxacin group. Hospital mortality did not differ between groups (the treatment made no difference to hospital mortality in this trial).
cards.watchOut: One trial, in advanced cirrhosis specifically, driven by local quinolone resistance — where quinolone resistance is uncommon the norfloxacin disadvantage may shrink. It compares two active regimens; it does not itself prove prophylaxis beats none (the meta-analysis cards carry that).
cards.source: Fernández J et al. Norfloxacin vs ceftriaxone in the prophylaxis of infections in patients with advanced cirrhosis and hemorrhage. Gastroenterology. 2006. PMID: 17030175. Registry ID: not captured from the record this session. cards.headline: Bernard 1999 (meta-analysis): antibiotic prophylaxis raised mean survival by 9.1 percentage points and infection-free rate by 32 points across 5 trials (534 patients)
cards.summary: Bernard 1999 (meta-analysis): antibiotic prophylaxis raised mean survival by 9.1 percentage points and infection-free rate by 32 points across 5 trials (534 patients)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials in cirrhotic patients with gastrointestinal bleeding: 264 patients given antibiotic prophylaxis for 4 to 10 days and 270 given none; mean follow-up 12 days.
cards.result: Antibiotic prophylaxis significantly increased the mean percentage of patients free of infection (32% mean improvement, 95% CI 22 to 42; P<.001), free of bacteraemia and/or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (19% mean improvement, 11 to 26; P<.001) and free of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (7% mean improvement, 2.1 to 12.6; P=.006), and increased the mean survival rate by 9.1 percentage points (95% CI 2.9 to 15.3; P=.004), without significant heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The component trials were small and mostly had not individually shown a survival benefit; the pooled survival gain is a mean percentage-point improvement over about 12 days of follow-up — short-term survival only.
cards.source: Bernard B et al. Antibiotic prophylaxis for the prevention of bacterial infections in cirrhotic patients with gastrointestinal bleeding: a meta-analysis. Hepatology. 1999. PMID: 10347104. cards.headline: Chavez-Tapia 2011 (updated Cochrane review): prophylaxis reduced mortality (relative risk 0.79), bacterial infections (0.35) and rebleeding (0.53) across 12 trials (1,241 patients)
cards.summary: Chavez-Tapia 2011 (updated Cochrane review): prophylaxis reduced mortality (relative risk 0.79), bacterial infections (0.35) and rebleeding (0.53) across 12 trials (1,241 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Chavez-Tapia 2011, Cochrane update)
cards.people: Updated Cochrane systematic review of 12 randomised trials (1,241 patients) of antibiotic prophylaxis versus placebo or no prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.result: Antibiotic prophylaxis was associated with reduced mortality (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.98), mortality from bacterial infections (relative risk 0.43, 0.19 to 0.97), bacterial infections (relative risk 0.35, 0.26 to 0.47) and rebleeding (relative risk 0.53, 0.38 to 0.74) — all relative measures; the review does not print pooled absolute rates beside them in its record — and with 1.91 fewer days in hospital (mean difference −1.91, 95% CI −3.80 to −0.02). The authors caution that rebleeding and hospitalisation data were still scarce and some benefits may be biased.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks without pooled absolutes in the record — a relative risk of 0.79 for mortality is a 21% relative reduction, not a 21-point absolute one. Harms of prophylaxis (resistance, Clostridioides difficile) were, by the authors' own statement, not yet properly assessed.
cards.source: Chavez-Tapia NC et al. Meta-analysis: antibiotic prophylaxis for cirrhotic patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding - an updated Cochrane review. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2011. PMID: 21707680. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis versus none is LIKELY beneficial; ceftriaxone over norfloxacin rests on one trial in advanced cirrhosis
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis versus none is LIKELY beneficial; ceftriaxone over norfloxacin rests on one trial in advanced cirrhosis
cards.people: Prophylaxis-versus-none evidence: 5 trials / 534 patients (Bernard 1999) and 12 trials / 1,241 patients (Chavez-Tapia 2011). Agent-choice evidence: 1 trial / 111 patients (Fernández 2006).
cards.result: Pooled randomised evidence shows fewer infections, less rebleeding and lower short-term mortality with prophylaxis (mortality relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.98). In advanced cirrhosis with haemorrhage, intravenous ceftriaxone prevented more infections than oral norfloxacin (proved or possible infections 11% versus 33%) without a mortality difference in that trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for prophylaxis versus none; the ceftriaxone preference is POSSIBLE (single trial).
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: cirrhosis with acute gastrointestinal (variceal) bleeding. Different question, homed separately: norfloxacin primary prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in non-bleeding patients is live shelf #1675.

shelves.title: Midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin in type 1 hepatorenal syndrome: reverses some cases, but lost to terlipressin 28.6% versus 70.4%
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and type 1 hepatorenal syndrome where terlipressin is unavailable, does midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin reverse renal failure versus albumin-based care — and how does it compare with terlipressin?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albumins/administration & dosage · Analysis of Variance · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hepatorenal Syndrome/diagnosis,drug therapy,mortality · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Function Tests · Liver Function Tests · Lypressin/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Male · Middle Aged · Midodrine/administration & dosage · Octreotide/administration & dosage · Predictive Value of Tests · Survival Analysis · Terlipressin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus albumin-based care without a vasoconstrictor — and clearly inferior to terlipressin where terlipressin is available; one small randomised trial plus retrospective cohorts cap the stamp. In the only head-to-head randomised trial (Cavallin 2016, PMID: 25644760; 49 patients with hepatorenal syndrome), recovery of renal function occurred in 28.6% on midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin versus 70.4% on terlipressin plus albumin (P=0.01). The largest cohort (Skagen 2009, PMID: 19238094; 75 treated versus 87 historical controls) found longer transplant-free survival and better renal function at 1 month with the triple regimen than in untreated historical controls — a comparison wide open to era and selection bias, including a higher transplant rate in the treated group. The Esrailian report named in mining is a single-patient case report and falls below the reference floor, so it is not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) as a fallback where terlipressin is unavailable; it is not terlipressin's equal.

cards.headline: Cavallin 2016: terlipressin plus albumin recovered renal function in 70.4% versus 28.6% for midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin — the triple regimen lost the only head-to-head randomised trial
cards.summary: Cavallin 2016: terlipressin plus albumin recovered renal function in 70.4% versus 28.6% for midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin — the triple regimen lost the only head-to-head randomised trial
cards.people: 49 patients with hepatorenal syndrome in a randomised controlled trial: terlipressin by infusion (3 mg/24 hours, rising to 12 mg/24 hours if no response) plus albumin (n=27), or oral midodrine (7.5 mg three times daily, rising to 12.5 mg) plus subcutaneous octreotide (100 micrograms three times daily, rising to 200) plus albumin (n=22 analysed as 21 for the primary outcome, as printed in the record). Both groups received albumin 1 g/kg on day 1 then 20–40 g/day.
cards.result: Recovery of renal function was significantly higher with terlipressin (19 of 27, 70.4%) than with midodrine plus octreotide (6 of 21, 28.6%; P=0.01). Improvement in renal function and lower baseline MELD score were associated with better survival. The record reports no significant survival difference claim between the arms — the demonstrated difference is renal recovery, favouring terlipressin.
cards.watchOut: Small (49 patients) and the midodrine–octreotide arm's analysed denominator (21) differs from its randomised number (22) as printed in the record. This trial answers 'versus terlipressin', not 'versus albumin alone' — it shows inferiority, not uselessness.
cards.source: Cavallin M et al. Terlipressin plus albumin versus midodrine and octreotide plus albumin in the treatment of hepatorenal syndrome: A randomized trial. cards.headline: Skagen 2009: triple therapy beat historical untreated controls on transplant-free survival (median 101 versus 18 days) and 1-month renal function — a retrospective comparison
cards.summary: Skagen 2009: triple therapy beat historical untreated controls on transplant-free survival (median 101 versus 18 days) and 1-month renal function — a retrospective comparison
cards.people: Retrospective cohort: 75 patients with hepatorenal syndrome (type 1 and type 2) treated with octreotide, midodrine and albumin, compared with 87 historical controls who did not receive the regimen; 102 patients had type 1 and 60 type 2 hepatorenal syndrome overall. Not randomised.
cards.result: Transplant-free survival was higher in the treated group (median survival 101 days versus 18 days; P<0.0001), in both type 1 (P=0.0003) and type 2 (P=0.009) disease, and treatment remained associated with improved survival in multivariable analysis (P=0.0001). Glomerular filtration rate at 1 month was 48 mL/min in the treated group versus 34 mL/min in controls (P=0.03). Liver transplantation was performed in 45% of the treated group versus 26% of controls.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls are the weakest comparator in this shelf: era effects, selection for treatment, and the unequal transplant rates (45% versus 26%) can each manufacture a survival gap. This card supports 'better than nothing in US practice', never 'as good as terlipressin'.
cards.source: Skagen C et al. Combination treatment with octreotide, midodrine, and albumin improves survival in patients with type 1 and type 2 hepatorenal syndrome. cards.headline: Facciorusso 2017 (network meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 739 patients): only low-quality evidence supported midodrine plus octreotide over placebo for mortality, and terlipressin beat it decisively for HRS reversal (odds ratio 26.25)
cards.summary: Facciorusso 2017 (network meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 739 patients): only low-quality evidence supported midodrine plus octreotide over placebo for mortality, and terlipressin beat it decisively for HRS reversal (odds ratio 26.25)
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Facciorusso 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials in 739 adults with type 1 hepatorenal syndrome, all receiving albumin, comparing terlipressin, noradrenaline, midodrine plus octreotide, dopamine-based regimens and placebo.
cards.result: No drug's mortality odds ratio versus placebo was significant. Moderate-quality evidence might support terlipressin over placebo for short-term mortality (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.05); only low-quality evidence supported midodrine plus octreotide (among others) over placebo. For reversal of hepatorenal syndrome, moderate-quality evidence supported terlipressin over midodrine plus octreotide (odds ratio 26.25, 95% CI 3.07 to 224.21), and low-quality evidence supported noradrenaline over midodrine plus octreotide (odds ratio 10.00, 1.49 to 50.00) — relative measures with very wide intervals, reflecting how few randomised patients received the triple regimen.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates for midodrine plus octreotide rest on very few randomised patients — hence intervals like 3.07 to 224.21. The ranking (terlipressin and noradrenaline above the triple regimen for reversal) is consistent with the Cavallin head-to-head trial; the exact odds ratios are not precise.
cards.source: Facciorusso A et al. Comparative efficacy of pharmacological strategies for management of type 1 hepatorenal syndrome: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 28403995. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but second-best option — some reversal versus no vasoconstrictor, less than half terlipressin's reversal rate in the head-to-head trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but second-best option — some reversal versus no vasoconstrictor, less than half terlipressin's reversal rate in the head-to-head trial
cards.people: Evidence base: one randomised head-to-head trial (49 patients, Cavallin 2016), one retrospective cohort with historical controls (162 patients, Skagen 2009), and a network meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (739 patients, Facciorusso 2017). A single-patient case report in the mining notes (Esrailian 2006) falls below the reference floor and is not carded.
cards.result: Renal recovery 28.6% on midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin versus 70.4% on terlipressin plus albumin (P=0.01), and the network meta-analysis likewise ranked terlipressin and noradrenaline above the triple regimen for reversal, with only low-quality evidence for the triple regimen over placebo. Against historical untreated controls, the triple regimen was associated with median transplant-free survival of 101 versus 18 days and better 1-month renal function. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial plus cohorts and a network meta-analysis cap the stamp, and the randomised result is inferiority to terlipressin.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: type 1 hepatorenal syndrome where terlipressin is unavailable. Terlipressin itself is homed on live shelf #1060 and pack #2779 — those are the comparator's homes, not this question's.

shelves.title: G-CSF in acute-on-chronic liver failure: SPLIT — one positive single-centre trial versus one negative multicentre trial (GRAFT)
shelves.question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does granulocyte colony-stimulating factor improve transplant-free survival versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antigens, CD34/metabolism · Cell Movement/drug effects · Chi-Square Distribution · End Stage Liver Disease/diagnosis,drug therapy,immunology,mortality · Female · Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · India · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver/drug effects,immunology,pathology · Liver Failure, Acute/diagnosis,drug therapy,immunology,mortality · Liver Regeneration/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Severity of Illness Index · Stem Cells/drug effects,immunology,pathology · Survival Rate · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is named on the face: the single-centre trial is positive and the multicentre trial is negative. Garg 2012 (PMID: 22119930; single centre, India, 47 patients) found 60-day survival of about 66–69.6% with G-CSF versus 26–29% on placebo (P=.001). The multicentre GRAFT trial (Engelmann 2021, PMID: 34364917; 176 patients, Europe) — the negative multicentre trial the slate calls REALISTIC — found 90-day transplant-free survival of 34.1% with G-CSF versus 37.5% on standard therapy (HR 1.05; p=0.805; the treatment made no difference) and was stopped early for futility. A meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials (310 patients; Martin-Mateos 2023, PMID: 36174797) pooled to a non-significant mortality relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.07) with high heterogeneity (I²=74%), the benefit confined to Asian studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the single-centre evidence; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the multicentre evidence — do not average them into a single verdict.

cards.headline: Garg 2012: single-centre randomised trial — G-CSF roughly doubled 60-day survival in ACLF (66% versus 26% actuarial; 69.6% versus 29% survived)
cards.summary: Garg 2012: single-centre randomised trial — G-CSF roughly doubled 60-day survival in ACLF (66% versus 26% actuarial; 69.6% versus 29% survived)
cards.people: 47 consecutive patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure at a single centre in India, randomised to G-CSF 5 micrograms/kg subcutaneously (12 doses; n=23) or placebo (n=24), both plus standard medical therapy. Randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Sixteen patients in the G-CSF group (69.6%) and 7 in the placebo group (29%) survived; the actuarial probability of survival at day 60 was 66% versus 26% (P=.001). G-CSF also reduced Child-Turcotte-Pugh, MELD and SOFA scores, and fewer treated patients developed hepatorenal syndrome (19% versus 71%; P=.0002), hepatic encephalopathy (19% versus 66%; P=.001) or sepsis (14% versus 41%; P=.04). CD34+ cells in the liver rose more with G-CSF at 1 month (45% versus 27.5%; P=.01).
cards.watchOut: One centre, 47 patients, and an unusually large effect across every endpoint at once — exactly the profile that multicentre replication exists to test. Its population (Indian, APASL-style ACLF) differs from the European EASL-CLIF population of the GRAFT card.
cards.source: Garg V et al. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor mobilizes CD34(+) cells and improves survival of patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22119930. Registry ID: NCT01036932. cards.headline: Engelmann 2021 (GRAFT): multicentre randomised trial — G-CSF made no difference to 90-day transplant-free survival (34.1% versus 37.5%; HR 1.05) and the trial stopped for futility
cards.summary: Engelmann 2021 (GRAFT): multicentre randomised trial — G-CSF made no difference to 90-day transplant-free survival (34.1% versus 37.5%; HR 1.05) and the trial stopped for futility
cards.people: 176 patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure (EASL-CLIF criteria) in a multicentre, prospective, controlled, open-label phase 2 trial, randomised to G-CSF (5 micrograms/kg daily for 5 days, then every third day to day 26) plus standard medical therapy (n=88) or standard therapy alone (n=88). This is the negative multicentre trial referred to as REALISTIC in the slate.
cards.result: Ninety-day transplant-free survival was 34.1% with G-CSF versus 37.5% with standard therapy (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.711 to 1.551; p=0.805 — the treatment made no difference). Transplant-free and overall survival at 360 days also did not differ (HR 0.998 and HR 1.058 respectively). G-CSF did not improve liver function scores, infections, or any prespecified subgroup. Serious adverse events numbered 61 versus 57, with 7 drug-related serious adverse reactions on G-CSF. The study was terminated prematurely for futility. The authors conclude G-CSF should not be used as standard treatment for ACLF.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and stopped early for futility — early stopping for futility does not manufacture a false negative the way early stopping for benefit can inflate an effect, and the confidence interval (0.711 to 1.551) still leaves room for moderate effects in either direction.
cards.source: Engelmann C et al. Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) to treat acute-on-chronic liver failure: A multicenter randomized trial (GRAFT study). Journal of Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 34364917. Registry ID: NCT02669680. cards.headline: Martin-Mateos 2023 (meta-analysis of 4 RCTs, 310 patients): pooled mortality relative risk 0.64 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.07) — not significant, with the benefit confined to Asian studies
cards.summary: Martin-Mateos 2023 (meta-analysis of 4 RCTs, 310 patients): pooled mortality relative risk 0.64 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.07) — not significant, with the benefit confined to Asian studies
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Martin-Mateos 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of G-CSF versus standard medical therapy in acute-on-chronic liver failure: 4 trials, 310 patients (154 G-CSF, 156 standard therapy); primary outcome survival at 60–90 days.
cards.result: G-CSF did not significantly improve survival overall (random-effects risk ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.07 — a relative measure; the review's record does not print pooled absolute rates beside it), with significant heterogeneity (I²=74%). In Asian studies only, mortality fell significantly (risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.81). MELD and Child scores and CD34+ mobilisation did not significantly improve with G-CSF.
cards.watchOut: Pooling a positive single-centre trial with a negative multicentre trial under I²=74% heterogeneity produces an average of two different answers, not a resolution — which is why this shelf's stamp is SPLIT rather than the pooled figure.
cards.source: Martin-Mateos R et al. Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor in acute-on-chronic liver failure: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — positive single-centre, negative multicentre; the honest answer names both
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — positive single-centre, negative multicentre; the honest answer names both
cards.people: Evidence base: Garg 2012 (single centre, 47 patients, positive), GRAFT / Engelmann 2021 (multicentre, 176 patients, negative, stopped for futility), and a 4-trial meta-analysis (310 patients, non-significant overall).
cards.result: Sixty-day survival 66% versus 26% favouring G-CSF in the single-centre trial; 90-day transplant-free survival 34.1% versus 37.5% (HR 1.05 — no difference) in the multicentre trial. The split tracks centre count and region (Asian versus European ACLF populations and definitions), not dose. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) on the single-centre evidence; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the multicentre evidence.
