shelves.title: Albumin dialysis (MARS) and Prometheus in ACLF: no survival difference in RELIEF or HELIOS despite biochemical clearance
shelves.question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does extracorporeal albumin dialysis (MARS) — or fractionated plasma separation (Prometheus) — improve survival versus standard medical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · End Stage Liver Disease/mortality,therapy · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis/mortality,therapy · Liver Failure, Acute/mortality,therapy · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Organ Failure/mortality,therapy · Multivariate Analysis · Peritonitis/mortality,therapy · Prospective Studies · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects,methods · Serum Albumin/metabolism · Sorption Detoxification/adverse effects,methods,mortality · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) to survival at the doses tested, in two concordant randomised trials. RELIEF (Bañares 2013, PMID: 23213075; 189 patients with ACLF) found 28-day survival of 60.7% on MARS albumin dialysis versus 58.9% on standard therapy, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.87 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.72). HELIOS (Kribben 2012, PMID: 22248661; 145 patients) found 28-day survival of 66% on Prometheus fractionated plasma separation and adsorption versus 63% on standard therapy (P=.70) and 90-day survival of 47% versus 38% (P=.35). Both devices cleared bilirubin and creatinine and MARS improved encephalopathy more often, without a survival gain. An individual-patient meta-analysis (Bañares 2019, PMID: 31632458) found no survival benefit overall, with a benefit only in the subgroup receiving more than 4 MARS sessions — a subgroup hypothesis, not a trial result. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for survival as tested.

cards.headline: Bañares 2013 (RELIEF): MARS albumin dialysis made no difference to 28-day survival in ACLF (60.7% versus 58.9%; adjusted OR 0.87)
cards.summary: Bañares 2013 (RELIEF): MARS albumin dialysis made no difference to 28-day survival in ACLF (60.7% versus 58.9%; adjusted OR 0.87)
cards.people: 189 patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure randomised to MARS extracorporeal albumin dialysis (n=95; up to ten 6–8-hour sessions) or standard medical therapy (n=94); 10 patients were excluded for protocol violations. Multicentre randomised trial.
cards.result: Twenty-eight-day survival was similar in the two groups in both intention-to-treat (60.7% versus 58.9%) and per-protocol (60% versus 59.2%) populations — the treatment made no difference to survival. After adjustment, no beneficial effect was observed (odds ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.72). At day 4, creatinine and bilirubin fell more and hepatic encephalopathy improved more often on MARS (62.5% versus 38.2% improving from grade II–IV to 0–I; P=0.07). Severe adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: The MARS arm was somewhat sicker at entry (more MELD over 20 and more spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as the precipitant, both near-significant) — adjustment did not rescue a benefit. Biochemical clearance and encephalopathy gains did not convert into survival.
cards.source: Bañares R et al. Extracorporeal albumin dialysis with the molecular adsorbent recirculating system in acute-on-chronic liver failure: the RELIEF trial. Hepatology. 2013. PMID: 23213075. cards.headline: Kribben 2012 (HELIOS): Prometheus fractionated plasma separation made no difference to survival in ACLF (28-day 66% versus 63%; 90-day 47% versus 38%, both non-significant)
cards.summary: Kribben 2012 (HELIOS): Prometheus fractionated plasma separation made no difference to survival in ACLF (28-day 66% versus 63%; 90-day 47% versus 38%, both non-significant)
cards.people: 145 patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure randomised to fractionated plasma separation and adsorption (Prometheus system; 8 to 11 sessions of at least 4 hours over 3 weeks) plus standard therapy (n=77) or standard therapy alone (n=68). Multicentre randomised trial.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat survival probabilities were 66% on Prometheus versus 63% on standard therapy at day 28 (P=.70) and 47% versus 38% at day 90 (P=.35) — the treatment made no difference to survival at either time point. Serum bilirubin fell significantly in the Prometheus group but not in controls. Side-effect incidence did not differ between groups. The authors state that further studies would be needed to test specific patient subsets.
cards.watchOut: The 90-day point estimate favours Prometheus by 9 points but with P=.35 in 145 patients it is compatible with chance — it is a hypothesis about subsets, not a demonstrated benefit.
cards.source: Kribben A et al. Effects of fractionated plasma separation and adsorption on survival in patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22248661. cards.headline: Bañares 2019 (individual-patient meta-analysis): MARS overall made no difference to survival; only the subgroup receiving more than 4 sessions did better
cards.summary: Bañares 2019 (individual-patient meta-analysis): MARS overall made no difference to survival; only the subgroup receiving more than 4 sessions did better
cards.people: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials of MARS albumin dialysis (285 patients in total, 165 with acute-on-chronic liver failure), comparing standard care alone or with up to 4 MARS sessions (low intensity) against standard care with more than 4 sessions (high intensity).
cards.result: Standard care plus MARS, irrespective of session number, did not improve survival versus standard care alone, in the whole population or in the ACLF subgroup — the treatment made no difference overall. In the high-intensity subgroup, survival was higher at 10 days (98.6% versus 82.8%; p=0.001) and 30 days (73.9% versus 64.3%; p=0.032), with a similar pattern within ACLF patients (30-day 73.3% versus 58.5%; p=0.041). Independent predictors of survival included age, MELD, ACLF grade and number of MARS sessions.
cards.watchOut: Session count is not randomised: patients who live longer and stay stable receive more sessions, so the high-intensity 'benefit' may be survivorship in disguise. It justifies a trial of intensive schedules, not a change in the verdict for therapy as tested.
cards.source: Bañares R et al. Meta-analysis of individual patient data of albumin dialysis in acute-on-chronic liver failure: focus on treatment intensity. Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 31632458. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: POINTER: postponed drainage in infected necrotising pancreatitis — no difference in complications or death, but fewer interventions
shelves.question: In adults with infected necrotising pancreatitis, does postponing catheter drainage until collections are walled off reduce complications and interventions versus immediate drainage?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Drainage* · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreas/pathology,surgery · Pancreatitis, Acute Necrotizing/drug therapy,pathology,surgery,therapy · Time-to-Treatment*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) to complications and death — with a real reduction in interventions, which is the reason to postpone. In POINTER (Boxhoorn 2021, PMID: 34614330; 104 patients with infected necrotising pancreatitis), the Comprehensive Complication Index over 6 months was 57 with immediate drainage versus 58 with postponed drainage (mean difference −1, 95% CI −12 to 10; P=0.90), and mortality was 13% versus 10% (relative risk 1.25, 95% CI 0.42 to 3.68) — postponing made no difference to complications or death. But the postponed group needed fewer interventions (mean 2.6 versus 4.4), and 39% of postponed patients were treated with antibiotics alone and never needed drainage. Long-term follow-up (Van Veldhuisen 2024, PMID: 37450701; 88 patients re-evaluated at a median 51 months) confirmed no difference in death or major complications after 6 months and fewer total interventions with postponement (median 1 versus 4). A meta-analysis of 7 mostly non-randomised timing studies (742 patients; Gao 2022, PMID: 35488104) pointed the same way: early intervention brought more gastrointestinal fistula or perforation and longer hospital stay, with a non-significant mortality odds ratio of 1.65. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the complication question — a single trial caps the stamp — with fewer interventions as the practical gain.

cards.headline: Boxhoorn 2021 (POINTER): postponed drainage made no difference to complications (Complication Index 58 versus 57) or mortality (10% versus 13%), but needed fewer interventions (2.6 versus 4.4)
cards.summary: Boxhoorn 2021 (POINTER): postponed drainage made no difference to complications (Complication Index 58 versus 57) or mortality (10% versus 13%), but needed fewer interventions (2.6 versus 4.4)
cards.people: 104 patients with infected necrotising pancreatitis in a multicentre randomised superiority trial: immediate catheter drainage within 24 hours of randomisation (n=55) versus drainage postponed until collections became walled off (n=49), both within a step-up approach.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, the Comprehensive Complication Index over 6 months (0 to 100, higher is worse), was 57 in the immediate group and 58 in the postponed group (mean difference −1, 95% CI −12 to 10; P=0.90) — the postponement strategy made no difference to complications. Mortality was 13% versus 10% (relative risk 1.25, 95% CI 0.42 to 3.68 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). The mean number of interventions was 4.4 with immediate versus 2.6 with postponed drainage (mean difference 1.8, 95% CI 0.6 to 3.0). In the postponed group, 19 patients (39%) were treated conservatively with antibiotics and never required drainage; 17 of them survived. Adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial that found no superiority either way on complications — its confidence interval (−12 to +10 on a 100-point index) excludes a large complication benefit from immediacy but is not a formal equivalence proof. The intervention-count difference is the robust practical finding.
cards.source: Boxhoorn L et al. Immediate versus Postponed Intervention for Infected Necrotizing Pancreatitis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34614330. Registry ID: ISRCTN33682933. cards.headline: Van Veldhuisen 2024 (POINTER long-term): at a median 51 months, death or major complications still did not differ (17% postponed versus 15% immediate), and total interventions stayed lower with postponement (median 1 versus 4)
cards.summary: Van Veldhuisen 2024 (POINTER long-term): at a median 51 months, death or major complications still did not differ (17% postponed versus 15% immediate), and total interventions stayed lower with postponement (median 1 versus 4)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Van Veldhuisen 2024, POINTER)
cards.people: 88 of the 104 POINTER patients who were alive after the initial 6-month follow-up, re-evaluated at a median follow-up of 51 months (immediate drainage n=47; postponed drainage n=41). Long-term follow-up of the same randomised trial, not a new trial.
cards.result: After the initial 6 months, the composite of death and major complications occurred in 7 of 47 patients (15%) in the immediate group and 7 of 41 (17%) in the postponed group (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.28; P=0.78 — the postponement strategy made no difference). Additional drainage procedures were performed in 15% versus 7% (relative risk 2.03, 95% CI 0.56 to 7.37). Over total follow-up the median number of interventions was 4 with immediate versus 1 with postponed drainage (P=0.001). Of patients successfully treated with antibiotics alone in the first 6 months, 93% (14 of 15) remained intervention-free. Pancreatic function and quality of life were similar.
cards.watchOut: Only survivors of the first 6 months were re-evaluated (88 of 104), so the long-term comparison is among survivors by construction. It confirms durability of the intervention saving, not a new survival verdict.
cards.source: Van Veldhuisen CL et al. Long-Term Outcome of Immediate Versus Postponed Intervention in Patients With Infected Necrotizing Pancreatitis (POINTER): Multicenter Randomized Trial. Annals of Surgery. 2024. PMID: 37450701. cards.headline: Gao 2022 (meta-analysis of timing studies): early minimally invasive intervention did not significantly raise hospital mortality (odds ratio 1.65, 95% CI 0.97 to 2.81) but prolonged hospital stay and increased gastrointestinal fistula or perforation versus delayed intervention
cards.summary: Gao 2022 (meta-analysis of timing studies): early minimally invasive intervention did not significantly raise hospital mortality (odds ratio 1.65, 95% CI 0.97 to 2.81) but prolonged hospital stay and increased gastrointestinal fistula or perforation versus delayed intervention
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of timing studies (Gao 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 clinical studies (742 patients with infected pancreatic necrosis requiring intervention): 321 received early minimally invasive intervention and 421 delayed intervention. The component studies were mostly non-randomised — this card is the pre-POINTER observational timing literature, pooled.
cards.result: Early intervention did not significantly increase hospital mortality (odds ratio 1.65, 95% CI 0.97 to 2.81; p=0.06) but was associated with a remarkably prolonged hospital stay and an increased incidence of gastrointestinal fistula or perforation compared with delayed intervention. The authors state that no firm conclusion can be drawn because of the quality of the available studies, and that timing ought to be investigated in prospective studies — the role POINTER then filled.
cards.watchOut: Pooled mostly non-randomised studies: sicker patients get intervened on earlier, which biases early intervention to look worse (confounding by indication). Its value here is direction and consistency with POINTER, not a causal estimate.
cards.source: Gao L et al. The clinical outcome from early versus delayed minimally invasive intervention for infected pancreatic necrosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Gastroenterology. 2022. PMID: 35488104. MeSH: Drainage/methods · Fistula/complications* · Humans · Length of Stay · Pancreatitis, Acute Necrotizing/surgery* · Prospective Studies

cards.headline: Synthesis: postpone — not because outcomes improve, but because they do not worsen while a third of patients avoid drainage entirely
cards.summary: Synthesis: postpone — not because outcomes improve, but because they do not worsen while a third of patients avoid drainage entirely
cards.people: One randomised trial: POINTER, 104 patients (Boxhoorn 2021), with long-term follow-up of 88 survivors (Van Veldhuisen 2024), plus a meta-analysis of 7 mostly non-randomised timing studies (742 patients; Gao 2022).
cards.result: Complications (Complication Index 57 versus 58) and mortality (13% versus 10%) did not differ between immediate and postponed drainage, at 6 months or at a median 51 months. Interventions did: mean 4.4 versus 2.6 initially, median 4 versus 1 over total follow-up, and 39% of the postponed group never needed drainage. The pooled observational timing literature pointed the same way (more fistula or perforation and longer stay with early intervention; mortality odds ratio 1.65, not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) to complications and death — a single randomised trial caps the stamp — with fewer interventions as the demonstrated gain of postponing.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: infected necrotising pancreatitis suitable for a step-up approach. Different question, homed separately: step-up versus open necrosectomy (PANTER) is pack #3585.
cards.source: Synthesis of Boxhoorn L et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34614330); Van Veldhuisen CL et al. Annals of Surgery. 2024 (PMID: 37450701); Gao L et al. Journal of Gastroenterology. 2022 (PMID: 35488104).

shelves.title: Prophylactic antibiotics in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: infected necrosis 12% vs 9% and mortality 5% vs 7% in the double-blind trial — no benefit
shelves.question: In adults with predicted severe or necrotising acute pancreatitis, do prophylactic antibiotics prevent infected necrosis or death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis, Acute Necrotizing/drug therapy/prevention & control · Placebos
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the only double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Isenmann 2004, n=114) found infected pancreatic necrosis in 12% on ciprofloxacin–metronidazole versus 9% on placebo and mortality of 5% versus 7% (the treatment made no difference). Meta-analyses agree on the endpoints that matter: Ding 2020 (11 RCTs, 747 participants) found no significant difference in infected pancreatic necrosis (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50–1.09) or mortality (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.44–1.15), and trial sequential analysis (Poropat 2022, 21 trials, 1,383 patients) likewise showed no significant reduction in infected necrosis (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04) or mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–1.10), although extra-pancreatic infections were fewer. The one positive trial (Pederzoli 1993, imipenem) was open-label against no treatment and predates modern care; the large meropenem trial (Dellinger 2007) is homed elsewhere in the library and is not carded here. This is why AGA/ACG guidance recommends against prophylactic antibiotics in severe or necrotising pancreatitis: antibiotics are for documented or strongly suspected infection, not prevention.

cards.headline: Isenmann 2004 (n=114, double-blind): infected necrosis 12% on ciprofloxacin–metronidazole vs 9% on placebo; mortality 5% vs 7%
cards.summary: Isenmann 2004 (n=114, double-blind): infected necrosis 12% on ciprofloxacin–metronidazole vs 9% on placebo; mortality 5% vs 7%
cards.people: 114 patients with acute pancreatitis plus C-reactive protein above 150 mg/L and/or necrosis on contrast-enhanced CT, randomised to intravenous ciprofloxacin 400 mg twice daily plus metronidazole 500 mg twice daily (n=58) or placebo (n=56); recruitment stopped after a planned interim analysis at half the calculated sample size.
cards.result: Infected pancreatic necrosis developed in 12% of the antibiotic group versus 9% of the placebo group (P=0.585); mortality was 5% versus 7%. Open antibiotic treatment was required by 28% on prophylaxis versus 46% on placebo. In the 76 patients with CT-confirmed necrosis there were no differences in infected necrosis, systemic complications or mortality. The authors concluded the study detected no benefit of antibiotic prophylaxis for infected pancreatic necrosis.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped at interim analysis with 114 of a planned 200 patients, so it is underpowered for small effects — but its point estimates favour placebo on the primary endpoint, and the meta-analyses below close the remaining gap.
cards.source: Isenmann R et al. Prophylactic antibiotic treatment in patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis: a placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Gastroenterology. 2004. PMID: 15057739. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Pederzoli 1993 (n=74, open-label): pancreatic sepsis 12.2% on imipenem vs 30.3% with no antibiotic — the positive outlier
cards.summary: Pederzoli 1993 (n=74, open-label): pancreatic sepsis 12.2% on imipenem vs 30.3% with no antibiotic — the positive outlier
cards.people: 74 patients with CT-demonstrated necrotising pancreatitis within 72 hours of onset, randomised to prophylactic imipenem 0.5 g intravenously every 8 hours for 2 weeks or to no antibiotic treatment; pancreatic sepsis was confirmed by culture of aspirated or operative samples. First author Pederzoli; Bassi C is a co-author of this report.
cards.result: Pancreatic sepsis occurred in 12.2% of imipenem-treated patients versus 30.3% of untreated patients (p<0.01), and the authors recommended prophylactic imipenem in acute necrotising pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: No placebo and no blinding, a no-treatment comparator, and 1993-era supportive care: this is the trial the prophylaxis practice was built on, and the later double-blind trial and pooled analyses did not reproduce its result on infected necrosis or mortality.
cards.source: Pederzoli P et al. A randomized multicenter clinical trial of antibiotic prophylaxis of septic complications in acute necrotizing pancreatitis with imipenem. Surgery, Gynecology & Obstetrics. 1993. PMID: 8480272. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Ding 2020 meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 747 participants): infected necrosis OR 0.74 and mortality OR 0.71 — neither significant
cards.summary: Ding 2020 meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 747 participants): infected necrosis OR 0.74 and mortality OR 0.71 — neither significant
cards.people: 11 randomised trials with 747 participants with acute pancreatitis, 376 receiving prophylactic antibiotics and 371 controls, pooled from Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library and Web of Science.
cards.result: No significant differences for infected pancreatic necrosis (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50–1.09; P=0.13), surgical intervention (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.62–1.38; P=0.70) or mortality (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.44–1.15; P=0.16). Prophylactic antibiotics did reduce non-pancreatic infection (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42–0.84; P=0.004) — an extra-pancreatic benefit that does not change the necrosis or survival answer.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios are relative measures; with confidence intervals crossing 1.0 for both infected necrosis and mortality, the pooled randomised record does not support prophylaxis for the outcomes the question asks about.
cards.source: Ding N et al. Assessment of prophylactic antibiotics administration for acute pancreatitis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Chinese Medical Journal. 2020. PMID: 31929369. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Odds Ratio · Pancreatitis/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.headline: Poropat 2022 trial sequential analysis (21 trials, 1,383 patients): infections fewer overall, but infected necrosis RR 0.81 and mortality RR 0.85 — both non-significant
cards.summary: Poropat 2022 trial sequential analysis (21 trials, 1,383 patients): infections fewer overall, but infected necrosis RR 0.81 and mortality RR 0.85 — both non-significant
cards.type: Systematic review with trial sequential analysis (Poropat 2022)
cards.people: 21 randomised trials with 1,383 patients with acute pancreatitis (703 prophylactic antibiotics, 680 controls), searched in Medline, Scopus and Web of Science.
cards.result: Mortality was similar (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–1.10) and infected pancreatic necrosis was not significantly reduced (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04). All infections were reduced (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.74), driven by sepsis (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.25–0.73) and urinary tract infections (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.25–0.86); hospital stay was 6.65 days shorter. Trial sequential analysis judged the extra-pancreatic infection finding firm, while infected necrosis and mortality still need firmer evidence.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks are relative measures. The firm finding is fewer extra-pancreatic infections; on infected necrosis and death — the reasons prophylaxis is given — the cumulative randomised evidence remains null.
cards.source: Poropat G et al. Systematic Review with Trial Sequential Analysis of Prophylactic Antibiotics for Acute Pancreatitis. Antibiotics (Basel). 2022. PMID: 36139970. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis does not prevent infected necrosis or death — treat infection when it is there, do not pre-treat the necrosis
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis does not prevent infected necrosis or death — treat infection when it is there, do not pre-treat the necrosis
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=114), one open-label positive outlier (n=74), and two meta-analyses covering 747–1,383 randomised patients.
cards.result: Across the randomised record, prophylactic antibiotics made no difference to infected pancreatic necrosis (12% vs 9% in the blinded trial; pooled OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50–1.09) or mortality (5% vs 7%; pooled OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.44–1.15; RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–1.10). Fewer extra-pancreatic infections are the only consistent gain. The stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the necrosis and mortality claims, matching guideline recommendations against routine prophylaxis.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers prophylaxis only. Antibiotics remain essential for documented infected necrosis and extra-pancreatic infection, and the large meropenem prophylaxis trial (Dellinger 2007) is homed on another shelf and was not re-carded here under the one-home rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Over-the-scope clip vs standard endoscopic therapy in high-risk upper GI bleeding: further bleeding 15.2% vs 57.6% in recurrent ulcer bleeding (STING), but an intention-to-treat null in large ulcers
shelves.question: In adults with high-risk non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, is an over-the-scope clip more effective than standard endoscopic therapy (clips/thermal) as first-line treatment for initial haemostasis and rebleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Hemostasis, Endoscopic/instrumentation/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage/therapy · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Surgical Instruments · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised record is positive but split by setting. In STING (Schmidt 2018), which enrolled recurrent peptic ulcer bleeding after initially successful haemostasis — not first presentation — further bleeding occurred in 15.2% with the over-the-scope clip (OTSC; the tested Ovesco OTSC system may be named under the product-clarification exception) versus 57.6% with standard therapy (absolute difference 42.4 percentage points). In first-line high-risk bleeding, STING-2 (Meier 2022) found clinical success in 91.7% versus 73.1%. But in large ulcers (≥1.5 cm), Chan 2023 found no intention-to-treat difference in 30-day rebleeding (10% vs 18%; p=0.23). A 2025 meta-analysis (14 studies, 7,211 patients, only five randomised) reports 30-day rebleeding RR 0.44 in relative terms. One consistent, unselected first-line trial is still missing, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: STING — Schmidt 2018 (n=66, recurrent ulcer bleeding): further bleeding 15.2% with OTSC vs 57.6% with standard therapy
cards.summary: STING — Schmidt 2018 (n=66, recurrent ulcer bleeding): further bleeding 15.2% with OTSC vs 57.6% with standard therapy
cards.people: 66 adults with recurrent peptic ulcer bleeding after initially successful endoscopic haemostasis, at nine academic referral centres in Germany, Switzerland and Hong Kong, randomised to haemostasis with an over-the-scope clip or standard therapy (through-the-scope clips in 31, or thermal therapy plus diluted adrenaline injection in 2). This is a recurrent-bleeding population, not first-line treatment of a first bleed.
cards.result: Further bleeding (persistent bleeding despite protocol therapy, or rebleeding within 7 days) occurred in 5 of 33 patients (15.2%) with OTSC versus 19 of 33 (57.6%) with standard therapy — absolute difference 42.4 percentage points (95% CI 21.6–63.2; P=0.001). Persistent bleeding after protocol haemostasis was 6.0% versus 42.4% (P=0.001); 7-day rebleeding was 9.1% versus 16.1% (P=0.468). Mortality at 30 days did not differ (12.1% vs 6.3%; P=0.672), and one patient in each group needed surgery.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-question trial in the hardest subgroup — patients already rebleeding once. Its large absolute benefit does not automatically transfer to first-line treatment of all high-risk bleeders, which is what STING-2 and the Chan trial below test.
cards.source: Schmidt A et al. Over-the-Scope Clips Are More Effective Than Standard Endoscopic Therapy for Patients With Recurrent Bleeding of Peptic Ulcers. Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29803838. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov number as printed in the record, NCT1836900 (STING study). cards.headline: STING-2 — Meier 2022 (n=100, first-line, Rockall ≥7): clinical success 91.7% with OTSC vs 73.1% with standard therapy
cards.summary: STING-2 — Meier 2022 (n=100, first-line, Rockall ≥7): clinical success 91.7% with OTSC vs 73.1% with standard therapy
cards.people: 100 patients (mean age 78 years; 70% men) with acute non-variceal upper GI bleeding and high rebleeding risk (complete Rockall score ≥7), randomised to first-line OTSC (n=48) or standard endoscopic treatment (n=52), in which all but one patient received conventional through-the-scope clips.
cards.result: Clinical success (successful haemostasis without recurrent bleeding) was 91.7% (44/48) with OTSC versus 73.1% (38/52) with standard treatment (p=0.019). Persistent bleeding occurred in 0 versus 6 patients (p=0.027) — all six were rescued successfully with OTSC. Recurrent bleeding was 8.3% versus 15.4% (p=0.362).
cards.watchOut: Only 100 of 246 screened patients were randomised (about five cases per centre per year), treatment was by trained OTSC operators, and the rebleeding component alone was not significant — a selected, expert-centre result.
cards.source: Meier B et al. Over-the-scope-clips versus standard treatment in high-risk patients with acute non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding: a randomised controlled trial (STING-2). Gut. 2022. PMID: 35321938. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03331224, from the record. cards.headline: Chan 2023 (n=100, ulcers ≥1.5 cm): 30-day rebleeding 10% OTSC vs 18% standard on intention-to-treat — no significant difference
cards.summary: Chan 2023 (n=100, ulcers ≥1.5 cm): 30-day rebleeding 10% OTSC vs 18% standard on intention-to-treat — no significant difference
cards.people: 100 patients with peptic ulcers of at least 1.5 cm and Forrest IIa or higher stigmata, in a multicentre international trial (July 2017–October 2020), randomised to OTSC (n=50) or conventional endoscopic therapy (n=50) as primary haemostasis. Large ulcers are only about 2.5% of all upper GI bleeders.
cards.result: Primary haemostasis was achieved in 92% (46/50) with OTSC and 96% (48/50) with conventional therapy. Among those, 30-day rebleeding was 4.35% (2/46) versus 18.75% (9/48) (p=0.03), but on intention-to-treat analysis there was no difference in 30-day rebleeding (10% vs 18%; p=0.23) or all-cause mortality (4% vs 8%; p=0.68), nor in transfusion, hospital stay, ICU admission or further interventions.
cards.watchOut: The per-protocol rebleeding signal disappears on intention-to-treat analysis because OTSC failed primary haemostasis more often — deployment failure is part of the treatment's real-world effect, especially on large fibrotic ulcers.
cards.source: Chan S et al. Use of over-the-scope clip (OTSC) versus standard therapy for the prevention of rebleeding in large peptic ulcers (size ≥1.5 cm): an open-labelled, multicentre international randomised controlled trial. Gut. 2023. PMID: 36307177. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03160911, from the record. cards.headline: Koh 2025 meta-analysis (14 studies, 7,211 patients; 5 RCTs): 30-day rebleeding RR 0.44 and mortality RR 0.47 in relative terms, favouring OTSC
cards.summary: Koh 2025 meta-analysis (14 studies, 7,211 patients; 5 RCTs): 30-day rebleeding RR 0.44 and mortality RR 0.47 in relative terms, favouring OTSC
cards.people: 14 studies (five randomised) with 7,211 patients comparing first-line OTSC with standard endoscopic treatment for acute non-variceal upper GI bleeding, searched to October 2024 under a PROSPERO-registered protocol with GRADE assessment.
cards.result: OTSC was associated with lower 30-day rebleeding (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.32–0.61), 7-day rebleeding (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.71) and 30-day mortality (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.33–0.67), higher overall clinical success (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09–1.24) and shorter procedure time (mean difference −6.80 minutes, 95% CI −12.53 to −1.07). All risk ratios are relative measures; the authors call for further large randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Nine of 14 studies are not randomised, so the pooled relative benefits are larger and more precise than the randomised record alone supports — the three RCTs carded above disagree with each other by setting.

cards.headline: Synthesis: OTSC wins where standard therapy has already failed or risk is extreme — routine first-line use is not yet proven
cards.summary: Synthesis: OTSC wins where standard therapy has already failed or risk is extreme — routine first-line use is not yet proven
cards.people: Three randomised trials (n=66 recurrent bleeding; n=100 first-line high-risk; n=100 large ulcers) plus a 14-study meta-analysis dominated by non-randomised data.
cards.result: Further bleeding 15.2% vs 57.6% (STING, recurrent bleeding), clinical success 91.7% vs 73.1% (STING-2, first-line high-risk), and an intention-to-treat null on 30-day rebleeding in large ulcers (10% vs 18%; p=0.23). The pattern supports OTSC as rescue and for selected high-risk lesions, with first-line benefit plausible but unconfirmed at scale — POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Device trials depend on operator training and lesion selection; none of the three trials was powered for mortality, and the pooled mortality claim rests mostly on observational studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Retatrutide and liver fat (phase 2 substudy, n=98): liver fat fell 82.4% in relative terms on 12 mg vs +0.3% on placebo at 24 weeks — a surrogate, phase-2 result
shelves.question: In adults with obesity (the MASH-risk population), does retatrutide reduce liver fat content versus placebo, and how does the reduction track with weight loss?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Fatty Liver/drug therapy · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Receptors, Glucagon/agonists · Liver/drug effects/metabolism · Obesity/drug therapy/complications · Aged · Fatty Acids · Peptides · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped, because the entire liver-fat evidence base is one phase 2 MRI-PDFF substudy (Sanyal 2024, n=98) of the phase 2 obesity trial, and liver fat content is a surrogate outcome: no MASH-resolution, fibrosis or clinical liver outcome has been reported for retatrutide. Within that substudy the effect is large and dose-ordered: mean relative change in liver fat at 24 weeks was −42.9% (1 mg), −57.0% (4 mg), −81.4% (8 mg) and −82.4% (12 mg) versus +0.3% on placebo (all P<0.001), and liver fat normalised (<5%) in up to 86% on 12 mg versus 0% on placebo. Reductions tracked weight and abdominal-fat loss. The parent trial's weight and glycaemia results are homed on live shelf #1090 and are not re-carded here; this shelf covers only the liver-fat slice. Phase 3 and histology data will decide whether the surrogate converts into liver benefit.

cards.headline: Sanyal 2024 substudy (n=98): relative liver-fat change at 24 weeks −81.4% (8 mg) and −82.4% (12 mg) vs +0.3% on placebo
cards.summary: Sanyal 2024 substudy (n=98): relative liver-fat change at 24 weeks −81.4% (8 mg) and −82.4% (12 mg) vs +0.3% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 substudy with MRI-PDFF liver-fat measurement (Sanyal 2024)
cards.people: 98 participants from the 48-week phase 2 obesity trial who had metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease with at least 10% liver fat, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide 1 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg or 12 mg, or placebo, for 48 weeks; the primary substudy endpoint was mean relative change in liver fat at 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean relative change in liver fat at 24 weeks was −42.9% (1 mg), −57.0% (4 mg), −81.4% (8 mg) and −82.4% (12 mg) versus +0.3% with placebo (all P<0.001 versus placebo). These are relative percentage changes in MRI-measured liver fat, not percentage-point changes and not histological outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A substudy of 98 people within a dose-finding obesity trial, on an imaging surrogate. There is no liver biopsy, no MASH-resolution or fibrosis endpoint, and no clinical liver outcome in this report — the phase-2/substudy basis is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Sanyal AJ et al. Triple hormone receptor agonist retatrutide for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: a randomized phase 2a trial. Nature Medicine. 2024. cards.headline: Sanyal 2024, same substudy: liver-fat reductions tracked weight loss, abdominal-fat loss and insulin-sensitivity measures
cards.summary: Sanyal 2024, same substudy: liver-fat reductions tracked weight loss, abdominal-fat loss and insulin-sensitivity measures
cards.type: Prespecified correlational slice of the same phase 2 substudy (Sanyal 2024) — not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 98 substudy participants; the parent phase 2 obesity trial (homed on live shelf #1090) reported weight reductions of 22.8% (8 mg) and 24.2% (12 mg) at 48 weeks, as summarised in this substudy report.
cards.result: The substudy reports that liver-fat reductions were significantly related to changes in body weight, abdominal fat, and metabolic measures associated with improved insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism — i.e. the liver-fat effect moved with overall fat loss rather than appearing as an isolated hepatic signal.
cards.watchOut: Correlation within one small substudy cannot separate a direct hepatic (glucagon-receptor) effect from the effect of losing roughly a quarter of body weight; mediation claims would need a dedicated design.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a very large surrogate effect in one small substudy — POSSIBLE, pending histology and phase 3
cards.summary: Synthesis: a very large surrogate effect in one small substudy — POSSIBLE, pending histology and phase 3
cards.people: One phase 2 MRI-PDFF substudy, 98 participants with MASLD and at least 10% liver fat, 24-week primary endpoint within a 48-week trial.
cards.result: Relative liver-fat reductions of 81–82% at the top doses versus +0.3% on placebo, steatosis resolution (<5% liver fat) in up to 86% versus 0%, tracking weight loss. No other published report measures retatrutide's liver-fat effect, and none measures MASH histology or clinical outcomes — so the honest stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) with the phase-2 substudy and surrogate basis printed on its face. Live shelf #1090 homes the parent programme's weight and glycaemia evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as evidence that retatrutide treats MASH: steatohepatitis resolution and fibrosis regression are unreported for this drug, and the substudy population was selected from an obesity trial, not a biopsy-proven MASH cohort.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Linerixibat for cholestatic pruritus in PBC: phase 3 GLISTEN itch difference −0.72 points vs placebo, with diarrhoea in 61% vs 18%
shelves.question: In adults with primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus, does linerixibat (an IBAT inhibitor) reduce itch severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antipruritics/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Cholestasis/drug therapy/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary/complications/drug therapy · Pruritus/drug therapy/etiology · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Thiazepines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GLISTEN, the phase 3 trial, IS now published in full (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology; 238 patients): linerixibat 40 mg twice daily improved worst-itch scores by −2.86 points versus −2.15 on placebo over 24 weeks (adjusted difference −0.72 points, 95% CI −1.15 to −0.28; p=0.0013) — statistically solid but a modest average gain on a 0–10 scale, bought with diarrhoea in 61% versus 18% and gastrointestinal discontinuations in 7% versus under 1%. The phase 2b GLIMMER trial missed its primary intention-to-treat endpoint (dose groups showed ≥2-point mean itch reductions but differences from placebo were not significant; significance appeared only in post-hoc monthly-itch and per-protocol analyses), and a modelling study links the itch gain to bile-acid lowering (correlation r=0.52). One positive phase 3 with a modest effect size and a missed phase 2 primary caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: GLISTEN — Hirschfield 2026 (phase 3, n=238): worst-itch change −2.86 on linerixibat vs −2.15 on placebo (difference −0.72; p=0.0013); diarrhoea 61% vs 18%
cards.summary: GLISTEN — Hirschfield 2026 (phase 3, n=238): worst-itch change −2.86 on linerixibat vs −2.15 on placebo (difference −0.72; p=0.0013); diarrhoea 61% vs 18%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Hirschfield 2026, GLISTEN)
cards.people: 238 patients with primary biliary cholangitis and moderate-to-severe pruritus (Worst Itch Numerical Rating Scale ≥4) at 115 centres in 19 countries, randomised to oral linerixibat 40 mg twice daily (n=119) or placebo (n=119) for 24 weeks; the primary endpoint was change in worst-itch score (0–10) over 24 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in worst itch was −2.86 (95% CI −3.23 to −2.50) on linerixibat versus −2.15 (−2.51 to −1.78) on placebo — adjusted mean difference −0.72 (95% CI −1.15 to −0.28; p=0.0013). Diarrhoea occurred in 61% (72/119) versus 18% (21/118) and abdominal pain in 18% versus 3%; discontinuations for gastrointestinal events were 7% versus under 1%; serious adverse events 12% versus 3%; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group also improved by more than 2 points, so the drug-attributable gain is the −0.72-point difference — real, but below the 2-point change patients typically call clearly noticeable, and diarrhoea affected three in five treated patients.
cards.source: Hirschfield GM et al. Linerixibat in patients with primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus (GLISTEN): a randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: GLIMMER — Levy 2023 (phase 2b, n=147): primary itch endpoint NOT significantly different from placebo; dose-response only in post-hoc analyses
cards.summary: GLIMMER — Levy 2023 (phase 2b, n=147): primary itch endpoint NOT significantly different from placebo; dose-response only in post-hoc analyses
cards.people: 147 adults with PBC and moderate-to-severe pruritus (≥4 on a 0–10 scale) who still scored ≥3 after a 4-week single-blind placebo run-in, randomised 3:1 to 12 weeks of double-blind linerixibat (20, 90 or 180 mg once daily; 40 or 90 mg twice daily) or placebo (n=36).
cards.result: All linerixibat groups showed mean worst-daily-itch reductions of at least 2 points at week 16, but differences from placebo were not significant on the primary intention-to-treat analysis. Post-hoc analysis of monthly itch score (the phase 3 endpoint) favoured 180 mg once daily (P=0.0424), 40 mg twice daily (P=0.0105) and 90 mg twice daily (P=0.0370), with a dose–response in the per-protocol population. Diarrhoea was the most frequent adverse event and rose with dose.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint rescued by post-hoc and per-protocol analyses is hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory — GLIMMER's role is dose selection for GLISTEN, and this shelf's stamp rests on GLISTEN alone.
cards.source: Levy C et al. GLIMMER: A Randomized Phase 2b Dose-Ranging Trial of Linerixibat in Primary Biliary Cholangitis Patients With Pruritus. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2023. cards.headline: Karatza 2024 (GLIMMER pharmacodynamic model): fall in bile-acid exposure correlated with itch improvement (r=0.52); 60% of strong bile-acid responders were itch responders
cards.summary: Karatza 2024 (GLIMMER pharmacodynamic model): fall in bile-acid exposure correlated with itch improvement (r=0.52); 60% of strong bile-acid responders were itch responders
cards.type: Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic modelling study of trial data (Karatza 2024)
cards.people: Participants in the phase 1/2 linerixibat programme and GLIMMER, modelled to relate linerixibat dose, total serum bile-acid exposure (AUC over 24 hours) and itch scores on a 0–10 scale.
cards.result: Linerixibat reduced bile-acid exposure dose-dependently, reaching steady state after 5 days. Baseline bile-acid levels did not predict itch response, but change in bile-acid AUC correlated with improvement in weekly itch score over 12 weeks (r=0.52, p<0.0001); among participants with at least a 30% fall in bile-acid exposure, 60% were pruritus responders (≥2-point itch improvement).
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc model of the same trial data — it supports the mechanism (less bile-acid reabsorption, less itch) but is not independent efficacy evidence and cannot substitute for the clinical endpoint.
cards.source: Karatza E et al. Serum bile acid change correlates with improvement in pruritus in patients with primary biliary cholangitis receiving linerixibat. Liver International. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest itch benefit, proven once at phase 3, at a high diarrhoea price
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest itch benefit, proven once at phase 3, at a high diarrhoea price
cards.people: One phase 3 trial (n=238, positive), one phase 2b trial (n=147, primary endpoint missed), and a bile-acid pharmacodynamic model of the same programme.
cards.result: GLISTEN's −0.72-point adjusted itch difference (95% CI −1.15 to −0.28) over 24 weeks, with diarrhoea in 61% vs 18%, is the whole confirmatory case; GLIMMER supplies dose rationale, not confirmation. GLISTEN's publication status — the open question at slate time — is settled: it is published in full and is carded here. Stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No data here on liver outcomes, transplant or survival — this is a symptom drug. Patients with mild itch, or who cannot tolerate diarrhoea, sit outside the population in which the benefit was shown (baseline worst itch ≥4).
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Vibrating capsule (Vibrant) in chronic constipation: ≥1 extra complete spontaneous bowel movement per week in 39.3% vs 22.1% on sham in the phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic idiopathic constipation refractory to laxatives, does a vibrating capsule increase complete spontaneous bowel movements versus a sham capsule?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Quality of Life · Constipation/diagnosis/drug therapy · Defecation · Treatment Outcome · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial of the tested product (the Vibrant vibrating capsule, named under the product-clarification exception) met both primary endpoints: in Rao 2023 (n=312), responders gaining at least 1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM) per week numbered 39.3% versus 22.1% on placebo capsule (P=0.001), and those gaining at least 2 numbered 22.7% versus 11.4% (P=0.008), over 8 weeks. A second randomised trial (VICONS, n=107) used a different, smartphone-controlled vibrating capsule in functional constipation and also favoured the device (responder rate 64.2% vs 35.8%). But the pooled meta-analysis is more equivocal — across four trials (705 patients) the CSBM change did not reach significance (mean difference 0.153, 95% CI −0.218 to 0.523) while spontaneous bowel movements did — and the phase 3 population was chronic constipation broadly, not a strictly laxative-refractory cohort. Single-product phase 3 plus mixed pooling caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Rao 2023 phase 3 (n=312, Vibrant capsule): CSBM+1 responders 39.3% vs 22.1% (P=0.001); CSBM+2 responders 22.7% vs 11.4% (P=0.008)
cards.summary: Rao 2023 phase 3 (n=312, Vibrant capsule): CSBM+1 responders 39.3% vs 22.1% (P=0.001); CSBM+2 responders 22.7% vs 11.4% (P=0.008)
cards.people: 312 adults with chronic constipation (904 screened), randomised to the vibrating capsule (Vibrant) or an identical placebo capsule, taken once daily, 5 days a week, for 8 weeks. Primary endpoints were gaining at least 1 (CSBM1) or at least 2 (CSBM2) complete spontaneous bowel movements per week over baseline during at least 6 of the 8 weeks.
cards.result: CSBM1 responders: 39.3% on vibrating capsule versus 22.1% on placebo (P=0.001); CSBM2 responders: 22.7% versus 11.4% (P=0.008). Straining, stool consistency and quality-of-life measures also improved significantly. Adverse events were mild and gastrointestinal, similar between groups, except a mild vibrating sensation reported by 11% of the active group; no one withdrew for it.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks only, a responder definition rather than a cure, and the enrolled population was chronic constipation as such — the record does not restrict entry to patients who had failed laxatives, so the laxative-refractory framing of the question is only partly matched by this trial.
cards.source: Rao SSC et al. Randomized Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Trial of Vibrating Capsule for Chronic Constipation. Gastroenterology. 2023. PMID: 36822371. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03879239, from the record. MeSH: Humans · Quality of Life · Constipation/diagnosis/drug therapy · Defecation · Treatment Outcome · Double-Blind Method

cards.headline: VICONS — Zhu 2022 (n=107, different smartphone-controlled capsule): responder rate 64.2% vs 35.8% on placebo (difference 27.7 percentage points)
cards.summary: VICONS — Zhu 2022 (n=107, different smartphone-controlled capsule): responder rate 64.2% vs 35.8% on placebo (difference 27.7 percentage points)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Zhu 2022, VICONS)
cards.people: 107 patients aged 18–74 with functional constipation at six hospitals in China, randomised to a smartphone-controlled vibrating capsule (n=53) or placebo capsule (n=54), two capsules per week for 6 weeks after a 2-week baseline period; the primary outcome was gaining at least one CSBM per week over baseline.
cards.result: Responder rate was 64.2% with the vibrating capsule versus 35.8% with placebo (difference 27.7 percentage points, 95% CI 10.4–45.1; P=0.005), with benefits persisting into follow-up. The most common device-related adverse event was abdominal discomfort (3.7%).
cards.watchOut: A different manufacturer's capsule, a different dosing schedule (twice weekly), and functional rather than idiopathic constipation — supportive of the device class, not a replication of the Vibrant phase 3 result.
cards.source: Zhu JH et al. Efficacy and safety of vibrating capsule for functional constipation (VICONS): A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2022. cards.headline: Haghbin 2024 meta-analysis (4 trials, 705 patients): CSBM change NOT significant (MD 0.153; P=0.42); spontaneous bowel movements improved (MD 0.159; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Haghbin 2024 meta-analysis (4 trials, 705 patients): CSBM change NOT significant (MD 0.153; P=0.42); spontaneous bowel movements improved (MD 0.159; P<0.001)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Haghbin 2024)
cards.people: Four randomised trials with 705 patients comparing vibrating capsule with placebo or sham in chronic idiopathic constipation, searched to June 2023 across Embase, Medline, Cochrane Central, Web of Science and other databases.
cards.result: Pooled complete spontaneous bowel movements did not improve significantly (mean difference 0.153, 95% CI −0.218 to 0.523; P=0.422), while spontaneous bowel movements did (mean difference 0.159, 95% CI 0.095–0.223; P<0.001). Pooled adverse events were not increased (OR 1.431, 95% CI 0.702–2.916; P=0.324) — an odds ratio, a relative measure. The authors conclude larger trials and real-world data are still needed.
cards.watchOut: The pooled CSBM null is the honest counterweight to the single positive phase 3: small earlier sham-controlled studies (including a colonic-transit study with no significant transit effect) dilute the phase 3 signal, and devices and schedules differ across the pooled trials.
cards.source: Haghbin H et al. Efficacy and safety of vibrating capsule in treatment of chronic idiopathic constipation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Translational Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2024. PMID: 38317751. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one good phase 3 for the named product, a supportive foreign trial of a different capsule, and a mixed pooled picture
cards.summary: Synthesis: one good phase 3 for the named product, a supportive foreign trial of a different capsule, and a mixed pooled picture
cards.people: Phase 3 Vibrant trial (n=312), VICONS trial of a different vibrating capsule (n=107), and a four-trial meta-analysis (705 patients).
cards.result: Responder gains of about 17 percentage points (CSBM+1) in the phase 3 trial and 27.7 points in VICONS, against a non-significant pooled CSBM effect — enough for POSSIBLE (benefit) for the Vibrant capsule over 8 weeks in chronic constipation, not enough for more, and not yet evidence in a strictly laxative-refractory population or beyond 8 weeks.
cards.watchOut: No comparison against standard laxatives or secretagogues exists in these reports; the question the trials answer is device versus sham, not device versus drug therapy.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: PHASE 2 ONLY — tulisokibart (anti-TL1A) in ulcerative colitis (ARTEMIS-UC): clinical remission 26% vs 1% on placebo at week 12
shelves.question: In adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does tulisokibart (anti-TL1A antibody) induce clinical remission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Colitis, Ulcerative/diagnosis/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Infusions, Intravenous · Remission Induction/methods · Tumor Necrosis Factor Ligand Superfamily Member 15/antagonists & inhibitors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2 ONLY, and the stamp is capped for that reason: the whole case is one 12-week phase 2 trial (ARTEMIS-UC, Sands 2024). In cohort 1 (135 patients, enrolled regardless of biomarker status), clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 26% on intravenous tulisokibart versus 1% on placebo (difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 14–37; P<0.001). Among patients positive on the trial's genetic likelihood-of-response test (75 patients across both cohorts), remission was 32% versus 11% (difference 21 points, 95% CI 2–38; P=0.02). Adverse events were similar between groups and mostly mild to moderate. There is no phase 3, no maintenance data and no endoscopic-outcome confirmation at scale yet; a class meta-analysis pools the same early trials and adds no independent patients. Phase 3 will decide whether this becomes a treatment or another phase 2 promise.

cards.headline: ARTEMIS-UC cohort 1 — Sands 2024 (phase 2, n=135): clinical remission 26% on tulisokibart vs 1% on placebo at week 12 (difference 25 points)
cards.summary: ARTEMIS-UC cohort 1 — Sands 2024 (phase 2, n=135): clinical remission 26% on tulisokibart vs 1% on placebo at week 12 (difference 25 points)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Sands 2024, ARTEMIS-UC)
cards.people: 135 patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis and glucocorticoid dependence or failure of conventional or advanced therapies, randomised regardless of genetic-test status to intravenous tulisokibart (1000 mg on day 1, then 500 mg at weeks 2, 6 and 10) or placebo; the primary endpoint was clinical remission at week 12.
cards.result: Clinical remission occurred in 26% of the tulisokibart group versus 1% of the placebo group (difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 14–37; P<0.001). Among all enrolled patients, adverse-event incidence was similar between groups and most events were mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2, 12 weeks, induction only, and a placebo remission rate of 1% that flatters the contrast — ulcerative colitis trials with less refractory populations usually show higher placebo remission. No maintenance, endoscopic or safety-at-scale data exist yet.

cards.headline: ARTEMIS-UC biomarker-positive analysis (n=75 across cohorts 1–2): remission 32% vs 11% (difference 21 points; P=0.02)
cards.summary: ARTEMIS-UC biomarker-positive analysis (n=75 across cohorts 1–2): remission 32% vs 11% (difference 21 points; P=0.02)
cards.type: Prespecified combined analysis of the same phase 2 trial (Sands 2024, ARTEMIS-UC) — not an independent trial
cards.people: 75 patients with a positive genetic-based diagnostic test for likelihood of response, pooled prespecified from cohort 1 and cohort 2 (cohort 2 randomised 43 test-positive patients only), treated with the same tulisokibart regimen or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Among test-positive patients, clinical remission occurred in 32% on tulisokibart versus 11% on placebo (difference 21 percentage points, 95% CI 2–38; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval nearly reaches zero (2–38 points), the analysis reuses cohort 1 patients, and the companion diagnostic is itself unvalidated outside this programme — the biomarker story is a hypothesis the phase 3 programme must prove, not a result to select patients by today.

cards.headline: Paudel 2026 class meta-analysis: anti-TL1A clinical remission OR 3.75 in relative terms — pooling the same early-phase trials
cards.summary: Paudel 2026 class meta-analysis: anti-TL1A clinical remission OR 3.75 in relative terms — pooling the same early-phase trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of anti-TL1A trials (Paudel 2026)
cards.people: 12 studies of TL1A antagonists in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease (searched to October 2025); pooled clinical response in ulcerative colitis was 67% on treatment, with adverse events in 48.3% of ulcerative colitis patients and serious adverse events in 3.9%.
cards.result: Anti-TL1A therapy was associated with clinical remission at OR 3.75 (95% CI 2.04–6.89) and clinical response in ulcerative colitis at OR 4.07 (95% CI 1.55–10.70) — odds ratios, which are relative measures. Endoscopic improvement in ulcerative colitis was pooled at 41% (95% CI 36–46%) and endoscopic remission at 13% (95% CI 10–17%).
cards.watchOut: The pool is the same small set of phase 2 trials (including ARTEMIS-UC itself and Crohn's studies of other TL1A agents), so it summarises rather than strengthens the evidence; it cannot lift a phase-2-only stamp.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a striking phase 2 induction result that remains, for now, a phase 2 result
cards.summary: Synthesis: a striking phase 2 induction result that remains, for now, a phase 2 result
cards.people: One phase 2 trial (178 patients randomised across two cohorts; 135 in the primary cohort), 12 weeks, plus a class meta-analysis of the same early trials.
cards.result: Remission 26% vs 1% in the primary cohort and 32% vs 11% in test-positive patients, with short-term tolerability similar to placebo. The effect size justifies phase 3; the evidence stage caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit) with PHASE 2 ONLY on the face, exactly as this shelf's title, balance and stamp carry it.
cards.watchOut: Anti-TL1A is a class with several agents in development; results for tulisokibart in ulcerative colitis should not be read across to other TL1A antibodies or to Crohn's disease, which has its own separate phase 2 record.

shelves.title: Faecal microbiota transplantation in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis: pilot and retrospective series only — 3-month survival 75% with FMT vs 38% on steroids in one small comparative series
shelves.question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis not responding to or ineligible for steroids, does faecal microbiota transplantation improve 90-day survival versus standard care/pentoxifylline?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation · Feces/microbiology · Female · Gastrointestinal Microbiome · Hepatitis, Alcoholic/microbiology/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nutrition Therapy · Pentoxifylline/therapeutic use · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — everything here is pilot-scale and non-randomised: there is no completed randomised trial of faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis in the published record fetched for this shelf. The Philips group's comparative series (2018) reported 3-month survival of 75% in 16 FMT patients versus 38% on corticosteroids, 29% on nutritional support and 30% on pentoxifylline — groups of 8–17 patients, not randomised. Their later single-centre retrospective series (2022) found 6-month survival of 83.0% in 47 FMT patients versus 56.0% in 25 matched pentoxifylline patients (P=0.012), with fewer infections, ascites and encephalopathy. A 2025 meta-analysis (8 studies, 444 patients) found higher 28- and 90-day survival with FMT in relative terms (RR 2.30 and 2.53 — relative measures) but no significant benefit at 6 or 12 months, and the benefit was restricted to the retrospective studies on subgroup analysis. The signal is consistent and the biology plausible, but confounding by patient selection is exactly what these designs cannot exclude — hence MAYBE, with the small numbers printed on the stamp.

cards.headline: Philips 2018 comparative pilot series (FMT n=16): 3-month survival 75% with FMT vs 38% steroids, 29% nutrition, 30% pentoxifylline (p=0.036)
cards.summary: Philips 2018 comparative pilot series (FMT n=16): 3-month survival 75% with FMT vs 38% steroids, 29% nutrition, 30% pentoxifylline (p=0.036)
cards.people: 51 men with severe alcoholic hepatitis treated at one centre: corticosteroids (n=8), nutritional support only (n=17), pentoxifylline (n=10) or healthy donor FMT (n=16); survival was compared at 1 and 3 months, with stool microbiota analysis in FMT recipients. This is the pilot comparative report of the Philips FMT programme (the group's earlier 2017 pilot study and case report are not carded — the 2017 pilot's record carries no abstract figures).
cards.result: Survival at 1 month was 63% (steroids), 47% (nutrition), 40% (pentoxifylline) and 75% (FMT) (p=0.179); at 3 months it was 38%, 29%, 30% and 75% respectively (p=0.036). Relative risk and hazard ratios for death were higher in every non-FMT group than with FMT, and FMT was followed by measurable shifts in stool microbial communities.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen FMT patients, treatment chosen clinically rather than randomly, all-male single-centre cohort: fitter patients may simply have been selected for FMT. Numbers this small can produce a 75%-versus-38% gap by selection alone.
cards.source: Philips CA et al. Corticosteroids, nutrition, pentoxifylline, or fecal microbiota transplantation for severe alcoholic hepatitis. Indian Journal of Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29931479. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Philips 2022 retrospective series (FMT n=47 vs pentoxifylline n=25): 6-month survival 83.0% vs 56.0% (P=0.012); infections 14.9% vs 52.0%
cards.summary: Philips 2022 retrospective series (FMT n=47 vs pentoxifylline n=25): 6-month survival 83.0% vs 56.0% (P=0.012); infections 14.9% vs 52.0%
cards.people: 72 men with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis at a single Kerala centre (January 2019–February 2021): 47 received healthy donor FMT (100 mL daily via nasoduodenal tube for 7 days) and 25 matched patients received pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily for 28 days; the primary endpoint was 6-month survival.
cards.result: Six-month survival was 83.0% with FMT versus 56.0% with pentoxifylline (P=0.012). Clinically significant ascites (25.5% vs 56.0%; P=0.011), hepatic encephalopathy (10.6% vs 40.0%; P=0.003) and critical infections (14.9% vs 52.0%; P<0.001) were all less frequent after FMT, alongside favourable gut microbiota shifts (Bifidobacterium abundance at 3 and 6 months).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised despite matching, all-male, one centre, and pentoxifylline is itself a weak comparator that guidelines do not recommend — beating pentoxifylline is a lower bar than beating best standard care.

cards.headline: Pakuwal 2025 meta-analysis (8 studies, 444 patients): 90-day survival RR 2.53 in relative terms — but no significant benefit at 6 or 12 months, and benefit confined to retrospective studies
cards.summary: Pakuwal 2025 meta-analysis (8 studies, 444 patients): 90-day survival RR 2.53 in relative terms — but no significant benefit at 6 or 12 months, and benefit confined to retrospective studies
cards.people: Eight studies with 444 patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (218 FMT, 226 standard care), searched to December 2023; survival ranges were 75–100% (FMT) versus 48–80% (standard care) at 28 days and 53–87% versus 25–56% at 90 days.
cards.result: Survival was higher with FMT at 28 days (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.24–4.28; P=0.01) and 90 days (RR 2.53, 95% CI 1.34–4.77; P<0.001) — risk ratios, which are relative measures — but not at 6 months (RR 1.89, 95% CI 0.89–4.05; P=0.10) or 12 months (RR 1.86, 95% CI 0.68–5.08; P=0.23). Subgroup analysis restricted the benefit to retrospective studies, and no serious treatment-related adverse events were reported. The authors call for an adequately powered multicentre randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: When the apparent benefit lives only in retrospective studies and fades at 6–12 months, selection bias and survivor effects are the leading explanations to exclude — the meta-analysis pools the same Philips-centre data carded above, so it is not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Pakuwal E et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of fecal microbiome transplantation in patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis. European Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2025. PMID: 40359297. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a promising pilot signal that only a randomised trial can settle
cards.summary: Synthesis: a promising pilot signal that only a randomised trial can settle
cards.people: Two non-randomised Philips-centre series (FMT n=16 and n=47; total FMT N = 63) and an eight-study meta-analysis (444 patients) dominated by the same data.
cards.result: Short-term survival consistently favours FMT (75% vs 38% at 3 months in the comparative pilot; 83.0% vs 56.0% at 6 months against pentoxifylline), but pooled 6- and 12-month benefits are non-significant and the effect is confined to retrospective designs. MAYBE (weak evidence) is the honest stamp for pilot data of this size, with the total N printed on its face.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses donor screening, infection transmission risk in immunocompromised cirrhotic patients, or which FMT route/dose/duration is right — all unresolved, and all reasons this belongs in trials rather than routine care for now.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: SPLIT — tenofovir vs entecavir and liver cancer risk in chronic hepatitis B: Korean nationwide cohort says tenofovir lower (HR 0.61); US veterans and an international consortium say no difference
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B on long-term therapy, is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate associated with a lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma than entecavir?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/diagnosis/mortality/prevention & control/virology · Cause of Death · Databases, Factual · Female · Guanine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Hepatitis B, Chronic/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality/virology · Humans · Incidence · Liver Neoplasms/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Protective Factors · Republic of Korea/epidemiology · Risk Factors · Tenofovir/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (observational only) — the cohorts directly conflict, and there is no randomised comparison, so no winner can be declared. Choi 2019 (Korean nationwide cohort, 24,156 patients) found hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) incidence of 0.64 per 100 person-years on tenofovir disoproxil versus 1.06 on entecavir (adjusted HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54–0.70), with the same direction in matched and hospital-cohort analyses. Against that: Su 2021 (US Veterans Affairs, 3,287 patients) found no difference at all (adjusted HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.76–1.32), and Hsu 2020 (international consortium, 5,537 patients) found the crude tenofovir advantage (SHR 0.45) disappeared after adjustment (SHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.42–1.56) and in propensity matching (adjusted SHR 0.89, 95% CI 0.41–1.92). All hazard ratios are relative measures from retrospective data, where who gets which drug is not random. Both drugs remain guideline first-line therapy; this shelf records the disagreement rather than resolving it, and the stamp can never be LIKELY on this evidence type.

cards.headline: Choi 2019 Korean nationwide cohort (n=24,156): HCC 0.64 vs 1.06 per 100 person-years; adjusted HR 0.61 favouring tenofovir
cards.summary: Choi 2019 Korean nationwide cohort (n=24,156): HCC 0.64 vs 1.06 per 100 person-years; adjusted HR 0.61 favouring tenofovir
cards.people: 24,156 treatment-naive adults with chronic hepatitis B in the Korean National Health Insurance Service database who started entecavir (n=11,464) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (n=12,692) in 2012–2014 (mean age 48.9 years; 62.6% men), plus a validation hospital cohort of 2,701 patients.
cards.result: Annual HCC incidence was 0.64 per 100 person-years on tenofovir versus 1.06 on entecavir; multivariable-adjusted HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.54–0.70) for HCC and HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.65–0.92) for death or transplant, favouring tenofovir. Propensity-matched analyses agreed (population cohort HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.54–0.70; hospital cohort HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.46–0.99). Hazard ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Nationwide size cannot remove confounding by indication: Korean prescribing patterns, calendar period and patient mix differed between the drugs, and later Korean hospital cohorts (cited within subsequent papers) did not reproduce a significant difference.
cards.source: Choi J et al. Risk of Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Patients Treated With Entecavir vs Tenofovir for Chronic Hepatitis B: A Korean Nationwide Cohort Study. JAMA Oncology. 2019. PMID: 30267080. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Su 2021 US Veterans cohort (n=3,287): HCC adjusted HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.76–1.32) — no difference between entecavir and tenofovir
cards.summary: Su 2021 US Veterans cohort (n=3,287): HCC adjusted HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.76–1.32) — no difference between entecavir and tenofovir
cards.people: 3,287 US Veterans Affairs patients with chronic hepatitis B who initiated entecavir (n=2,193) or tenofovir (n=1,094) from each drug's FDA approval to January 2017, followed for a mean of 5.4 years, analysed with multivariable Cox models, propensity adjustment and competing-risks analysis.
cards.result: No difference in HCC risk between entecavir- and tenofovir-treated patients (adjusted HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.76–1.32), and no difference in death or liver transplantation (adjusted HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.98–1.39). cards.watchOut: A mostly male veteran population with different HCC background risk and prescribing patterns from the Korean cohort — the conflict may be about populations and confounding structures, not about one study being simply wrong.

cards.headline: Hsu 2020 international consortium (n=5,537): crude SHR 0.45 favouring tenofovir became 0.81 (non-significant) after adjustment; matched analysis 0.89
cards.summary: Hsu 2020 international consortium (n=5,537): crude SHR 0.45 favouring tenofovir became 0.81 (non-significant) after adjustment; matched analysis 0.89
cards.people: 5,537 previously untreated patients with chronic hepatitis B at 19 centres in six countries/regions, treated with entecavir (n=4,837) or tenofovir (n=700) monotherapy and followed for HCC to December 2018; analysed with competing-risk regression and 1:1 propensity matching (1,040 patients).
cards.result: Before matching, the tenofovir cohort was younger with less advanced disease; unadjusted HCC risk favoured tenofovir (SHR 0.45, 95% CI 0.26–0.79; P=0.005), but after adjustment for age, sex, country, albumin, platelet count, alpha-fetoprotein, cirrhosis and diabetes the association disappeared (SHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.42–1.56; P=0.52), and the matched analysis found no association (adjusted SHR 0.89, 95% CI 0.41–1.92; P=0.77). Subdistribution hazard ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Only 700 tenofovir patients against 4,837 on entecavir, with wide confidence intervals — this study shows the Choi signal is fragile to adjustment, but it is not powered to prove exact equivalence either.

retrospective international consortium cohort (hsu 2020) 5,537 previously untreated patients with chronic hepatitis b at 19 centres in six countries/regions, treated with entecavir (n=4,837) or tenofovir (n=700) monotherapy and followed for hcc to december 2018; analysed with competing-risk regression and 1:1 propensity matching (1,040 patients). before matching, the tenofovir cohort was younger with less advanced disease; unadjusted hcc risk favoured tenofovir (shr 0.45, 95% ci 0.26–0.79; p=0.005), but after adjustment for age, sex, country, albumin, platelet count, alpha-fetoprotein, cirrhosis and diabetes the association disappeared (shr 0.81, 95% ci 0.42–1.56; p=0.52), and the matched analysis found no association (adjusted shr 0.89, 95% ci 0.41–1.92; p=0.77). subdistribution hazard ratios are relative measures. only 700 tenofovir patients against 4,837 on entecavir, with wide confidence intervals — this study shows the choi signal is fragile to adjustment, but it is not powered to prove exact equivalence either. hsu yc et al. tenofovir versus entecavir for hepatocellular carcinoma prevention in an international consortium of chronic hepatitis b. the american journal of gastroenterology. 2020. pmid: 31634265. registry id: none in the record (observational study). mesh: adult · antiviral agents/therapeutic use · carcinoma, hepatocellular/etiology/prevention & control · china · cohort studies · disease progression · female · guanine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · hepatitis b, chronic/complications/drug therapy · hong kong · humans · international cooperation · japan · liver neoplasms/etiology/prevention & control · male · middle aged · proportional hazards models · republic of korea · retrospective studies · taiwan · tenofovir/therapeutic use · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the largest cohort favours tenofovir; adjusted Western and multinational cohorts find nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the largest cohort favours tenofovir; adjusted Western and multinational cohorts find nothing
cards.people: Three retrospective cohorts totalling about 33,000 patients (24,156 Korean nationwide; 3,287 US veterans; 5,537 international consortium), no randomised trials.
cards.result: Direction 1: adjusted HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.54–0.70) for HCC favouring tenofovir (Choi). Direction 2: adjusted HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.76–1.32) (Su) and adjusted SHR 0.81–0.89, non-significant (Hsu). Both directions are presented because the evidence genuinely runs both ways; residual confounding is the most likely explanation for the discrepancy, and drug choice in chronic hepatitis B should rest on renal, bone, resistance and patient factors rather than on a proven HCC difference.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf is observational and relative. A randomised trial powered for HCC would need many thousands of patients followed for years and does not exist; treat any single-cohort claim of superiority with the suspicion this split record warrants.
