shelves.title: Odevixibat in Alagille syndrome (ASSERT phase 3, n=52): scratching score fell 0.9 points more than placebo and bile acids by 113 µmol/L more — diarrhoea 29% vs 6%
shelves.question: In children and adults with Alagille syndrome and cholestatic pruritus, does odevixibat reduce itch and serum bile acids versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Alagille Syndrome/drug therapy/complications · Male · Female · Child · Adolescent · Pruritus/drug therapy/etiology · Treatment Outcome · Bile Acids and Salts/blood · Adult · Child, Preschool · Young Adult · Carrier Proteins · Membrane Glycoproteins · Methylamines · Thiazepines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial in a rare disease (ASSERT, Ovchinsky 2024; 52 patients, median age 5.5 years): odevixibat 120 µg/kg daily improved caregiver-reported scratching by a least-squares mean of −1.7 points versus −0.8 on placebo over 24 weeks (difference −0.9, 95% CI −1.4 to −0.3; p=0.0024) and lowered serum bile acids by 90 µmol/L against a 22 µmol/L rise on placebo (difference −113 µmol/L, 95% CI −179 to −47; p=0.0012). Diarrhoea occurred in 29% versus 6%; no patient discontinued and there were no deaths. A 2026 systematic review of IBAT inhibitors confirms that for odevixibat in Alagille syndrome only this single dose (120 µg/kg/day) has reported outcomes, so there is no dose-ranging or replication. Note the acronym: this ASSERT is the Alagille odevixibat trial, verified by content (NCT04674761) — the same acronym is used by unrelated trials. The neighbouring maralixibat shelf (pack #3604) covers a different drug in a different disease (PFIC). A single small trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ASSERT — Ovchinsky 2024 (phase 3, n=52): scratching change −1.7 on odevixibat vs −0.8 on placebo (difference −0.9; p=0.0024)
cards.summary: ASSERT — Ovchinsky 2024 (phase 3, n=52): scratching change −1.7 on odevixibat vs −0.8 on placebo (difference −0.9; p=0.0024)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Ovchinsky 2024, ASSERT)
cards.people: 52 patients with genetically confirmed Alagille syndrome, significant pruritus and elevated serum bile acids, at 21 centres in ten countries, randomised 2:1 to oral odevixibat 120 µg/kg once daily (n=35) or placebo (n=17) for 24 weeks; median age 5.5 years (IQR 3.2–8.9), 52% male. The primary endpoint was change in caregiver-reported scratching score (PRUCISION instrument, range 0–4) from baseline to weeks 21–24.
cards.result: Scratching scores at weeks 21–24 averaged 1.1 on odevixibat versus 2.2 on placebo, from baselines of 2.8 and 3.0 — least-squares mean change −1.7 (95% CI −2.0 to −1.3) versus −0.8 (−1.3 to −0.3), a difference of −0.9 (95% CI −1.4 to −0.3; p=0.0024). The most common adverse events were diarrhoea (29% vs 6%) and pyrexia (23% vs 24%); serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 14% versus 12%; no patient discontinued and there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-two patients in a genotypically defined rare disease, a caregiver-reported symptom score, and 24 weeks of follow-up: the trial shows itch relief, not prevention of transplant or liver progression, which rest on the bile-acid surrogate and the ongoing open-label extension.
cards.source: Ovchinsky N et al. Efficacy and safety of odevixibat in patients with Alagille syndrome (ASSERT): a phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2024. PMID: 38670135. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04674761 and EudraCT 2020-004011-28, from the record. cards.headline: ASSERT, key secondary endpoint: serum bile acids fell 90 µmol/L on odevixibat vs a 22 µmol/L rise on placebo (difference −113 µmol/L; p=0.0012)
cards.summary: ASSERT, key secondary endpoint: serum bile acids fell 90 µmol/L on odevixibat vs a 22 µmol/L rise on placebo (difference −113 µmol/L; p=0.0012)
cards.type: Prespecified key secondary endpoint of the same phase 3 trial (Ovchinsky 2024, ASSERT) — not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 52 ASSERT patients; serum bile acids averaged 237 µmol/L (odevixibat) and 246 µmol/L (placebo) at baseline, with the endpoint taken as change to the average of weeks 20 and 24.
cards.result: Serum bile acids fell to a mean of 149 µmol/L on odevixibat versus 271 µmol/L on placebo — least-squares mean change −90 µmol/L (95% CI −133 to −48) versus +22 µmol/L (−35 to 80), a difference of −113 µmol/L (95% CI −179 to −47; p=0.0012), moving in the same direction as the scratching score.
cards.watchOut: Serum bile acids are a biomarker, not a clinical outcome: whether a 113 µmol/L greater fall translates into fewer transplants or better growth is being tested in the open-label ASSERT-EXT extension, not in this trial.

cards.headline: de Groot 2026 systematic review: for odevixibat in Alagille syndrome, outcomes exist for one dose only (120 µg/kg/day) and no consistent IBAT dose–response was found
cards.summary: de Groot 2026 systematic review: for odevixibat in Alagille syndrome, outcomes exist for one dose only (120 µg/kg/day) and no consistent IBAT dose–response was found
cards.type: Systematic review of IBAT inhibitors in Alagille syndrome and PFIC (de Groot 2026)
cards.people: 75 records (68 reporting serum bile acids, 63 reporting pruritus) covering the ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors maralixibat and odevixibat in Alagille syndrome and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, searched to July 2024 across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, including conference reports.
cards.result: No evident dose–response relationship was observed for either drug in either disease; for odevixibat in Alagille syndrome, outcome measures have been reported only at 120 µg/kg/day — the ASSERT dose. The authors conclude that dosing may need personalisation, including dose reduction in responders.
cards.watchOut: A review built largely on the same single ASSERT trial plus conference material: it confirms the thinness of the evidence base rather than adding independent patients, and it pools a second drug and disease (maralixibat in PFIC) that this shelf does not cover.

shelves.title: Pasireotide after pancreaticoduodenectomy: SPLIT — the NEJM trial halved severe fistula, leak or abscess, but later prospective series and the meta-analysis found no fistula reduction
shelves.question: In adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, does perioperative pasireotide reduce clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Abscess/epidemiology, prevention & control* · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatectomy · Pancreatic Ducts/surgery · Pancreatic Fistula/epidemiology, etiology, prevention & control* · Pancreaticoduodenectomy · Perioperative Period · Postoperative Complications/mortality, prevention & control* · Somatostatin/adverse effects, analogs & derivatives*, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — determined after reading the follow-up literature first, as commissioned. The Allen NEJM trial (300 patients, single centre, Novartis-funded, NCT00994110) found grade ≥3 fistula, leak or abscess in 9% on pasireotide versus 21% on placebo (relative risk 0.44; pancreaticoduodenectomy subgroup 10% vs 21%, relative risk 0.49). The later reports conflict: Elliott's prospective series (111 treated vs 168 historical controls) found fistula in 17.1% versus 15.5% with 38% dose-limiting nausea; the Washington University prospective evaluation (459 pancreaticoduodenectomies, 112 propensity-matched pairs) found identical severe fistula rates of 7.1% versus 7.1%; and the Liu meta-analysis (4 studies, 919 patients) pooled an OR of 0.78 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.24) for clinically relevant fistula — no reduction. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive single-centre RCT has not been reproduced, and no multicentre randomised trial has yet settled it.

cards.headline: Allen 2014 (NEJM RCT, 300 patients): pasireotide cut grade ≥3 fistula/leak/abscess to 9% versus 21% on placebo (relative risk 0.44); in the pancreaticoduodenectomy subgroup, 10% versus 21%
cards.summary: Allen 2014 (NEJM RCT, 300 patients): pasireotide cut grade ≥3 fistula/leak/abscess to 9% versus 21% on placebo (relative risk 0.44); in the pancreaticoduodenectomy subgroup, 10% versus 21%
cards.people: 300 patients at a single centre randomised double-blind to subcutaneous pasireotide 900 μg twice daily (n = 152) or placebo (n = 148), starting the morning of operation and continuing 7 days, stratified by resection type and duct dilation; 220 underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy and 80 distal pancreatectomy. Primary endpoint was pancreatic fistula, leak or abscess of grade 3 or higher. Funded by Novartis Pharmaceuticals; registered as NCT00994110.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 45 of 300 patients (15%). Grade ≥3 fistula, leak or abscess was significantly lower with pasireotide than placebo: 9% versus 21% (relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78; P = 0.006) — a 56% relative risk reduction, 12 percentage points absolute. The finding was consistent in pancreaticoduodenectomy (10% vs 21%; relative risk 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.95), distal pancreatectomy (7% vs 23%; relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.99), dilated duct (2% vs 15%; relative risk 0.11) and nondilated duct (15% vs 27%; relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.01).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, industry-funded, and the endpoint is a composite (fistula, leak or abscess grade ≥3) rather than clinically relevant fistula alone; the trial mixed pancreaticoduodenectomy with distal pancreatectomy, so the PD-specific numbers are the subgroup figures (10% vs 21%). A single centre's result is exactly what later reports then failed to reproduce.
cards.source: Allen PJ et al. Pasireotide for postoperative pancreatic fistula. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24849084. Registry ID: NCT00994110 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank list). cards.headline: Elliott 2018 (prospective single-arm study, 111 treated versus 168 historical controls): pasireotide did not reduce fistula — 17.1% versus 15.5% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Elliott 2018 (prospective single-arm study, 111 treated versus 168 historical controls): pasireotide did not reduce fistula — 17.1% versus 15.5% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 111 consecutive patients undergoing pancreatic resection (April 2015–October 2016) at a single institution, all receiving pasireotide 900 μg subcutaneously twice daily for up to 7 days starting immediately before surgery, compared with 168 historical controls (July 2013–March 2015); primary outcome was grade B/C fistula by International Study Group criteria. Groups did not differ in demographics, comorbidities, operation type, malignancy, gland texture or duct size.
cards.result: Pasireotide did not reduce fistula rate: 15.5% in historical controls versus 17.1% with pasireotide (p = 0.72). Subgroup analyses of pancreaticoduodenectomy, distal pancreatectomy, and soft gland texture and/or small duct size also showed no decrease in fistulas. Thirty-nine patients (38%) experienced dose-limiting nausea. The authors conclude pasireotide was not validated as a preventive measure for pancreatic fistula in this appropriately powered prospective study.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls invite era bias, and a single-arm design cannot match a randomised comparison — but the direction is the opposite of the NEJM trial, the sample is adequately sized, and a 38% dose-limiting nausea rate is a real cost of the regimen that the efficacy debate should not hide.
cards.source: Elliott IA et al. Pasireotide does not prevent postoperative pancreatic fistula: a prospective study. prospective study with historical controls (elliott 2018) 111 consecutive patients undergoing pancreatic resection (april 2015–october 2016) at a single institution, all receiving pasireotide 900 μg subcutaneously twice daily for up to 7 days starting immediately before surgery, compared with 168 historical controls (july 2013–march 2015); primary outcome was grade b/c fistula by international study group criteria. groups did not differ in demographics, comorbidities, operation type, malignancy, gland texture or duct size. pasireotide did not reduce fistula rate: 15.5% in historical controls versus 17.1% with pasireotide (p = 0.72). subgroup analyses of pancreaticoduodenectomy, distal pancreatectomy, and soft gland texture and/or small duct size also showed no decrease in fistulas. thirty-nine patients (38%) experienced dose-limiting nausea. the authors conclude pasireotide was not validated as a preventive measure for pancreatic fistula in this appropriately powered prospective study. historical controls invite era bias, and a single-arm design cannot match a randomised comparison — but the direction is the opposite of the nejm trial, the sample is adequately sized, and a 38% dose-limiting nausea rate is a real cost of the regimen that the efficacy debate should not hide. elliott ia et al. pasireotide does not prevent postoperative pancreatic fistula: a prospective study. hpb : the official journal of the international hepato pancreato biliary association. 2018. pmid: 29398424. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · case-control studies · drug administration schedule · female · humans · injections, subcutaneous · male · middle aged · pancreatectomy/adverse effects* · pancreatic fistula/diagnostic imaging, etiology, prevention & control* · pancreaticoduodenectomy/adverse effects* · prospective studies · risk factors · somatostatin/administration & dosage, adverse effects, analogs & derivatives* · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Dominguez-Rosado 2018 (prospective evaluation, 459 pancreaticoduodenectomies, 127 pasireotide): no difference in fistula, overall complications, readmission or mortality; identical severe fistula rates (7.1% vs 7.1%) in 112 matched pairs
cards.summary: Dominguez-Rosado 2018 (prospective evaluation, 459 pancreaticoduodenectomies, 127 pasireotide): no difference in fistula, overall complications, readmission or mortality; identical severe fistula rates (7.1% vs 7.1%) in 112 matched pairs
cards.people: All 459 patients undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy at a high-volume centre (April 2011–January 2017) followed prospectively in an institutional complications database; for 18 months, five surgeons used pasireotide routinely (127 patients, 28%), and pasireotide patients were propensity score-matched to non-pasireotide patients (112 pairs). Complications graded by the Modified Accordion Grading System.
cards.result: Patients receiving pasireotide had no difference in pancreatic fistula, overall complications, 90-day readmission or 90-day mortality. Among the 112 propensity-matched pairs, fistula rates did not differ significantly and severe (grades 3–6) pancreatic fistula rates were identical (7.1% vs 7.1%, p = 1.00). Pasireotide patients did have significantly less postoperative bleeding/anemia (8.7% vs 16.9%, p = 0.03 unmatched; 9.8% vs 19.6%, p = 0.04 matched). The authors conclude a multicentre randomised trial is needed to define pasireotide's role.
cards.watchOut: Pasireotide patients were more likely to have dilated ducts and a drain left in place — channeling that matching can only partly remove. The bleeding/anemia signal is a secondary finding in a study whose primary question (fistula) was null; it should not be promoted into a reason to use the drug without its own trial.
cards.source: Dominguez-Rosado I et al. Prospective Evaluation of Pasireotide in Patients Undergoing Pancreaticoduodenectomy: The Washington University Experience. cards.headline: Liu 2020 (meta-analysis, 4 studies, 919 patients): pasireotide reduced neither clinically relevant fistula (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.24) nor overall fistula — only readmission was lower
cards.summary: Liu 2020 (meta-analysis, 4 studies, 919 patients): pasireotide reduced neither clinically relevant fistula (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.24) nor overall fistula — only readmission was lower
cards.people: Four clinical studies totalling 919 patients (418 pasireotide, 501 controls) of pasireotide for prevention of postoperative pancreatic fistula after pancreatic surgery, identified through PubMed, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library; protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42018112334, as reported in the record).
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed pasireotide could reduce neither the clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula rate (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.24; P = 0.29) nor the overall fistula rate (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.48; P = 0.80). There were no significant differences in delayed gastric emptying, mortality or hospital stay; readmission was lower with pasireotide (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.85; P = 0.004). Subgroup analyses found no reduction in clinically relevant fistula after pancreaticoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy. The authors conclude pasireotide may not reduce clinically relevant fistula and call for investigator-initiated high-quality trials.
cards.watchOut: Four studies is a thin pool, and it mixes the one positive RCT with null prospective series — the pooled null is driven by the non-randomised reports. That is precisely the split this shelf exists to show: the answer depends on which design you trust.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — one positive single-centre RCT against two null prospective series and a null meta-analysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — one positive single-centre RCT against two null prospective series and a null meta-analysis
cards.people: One single-centre industry-funded RCT (300 patients, mixed resections), two prospective single-centre series (111 treated vs 168 historical controls; 459 pancreaticoduodenectomies with 112 matched pairs) and a 4-study meta-analysis (919 patients).
cards.result: Positive: grade ≥3 fistula/leak/abscess 9% vs 21% (relative risk 0.44) in the Allen trial. Null: 17.1% vs 15.5% (Elliott), identical 7.1% severe fistula rates in matched pairs (Dominguez-Rosado), and a pooled OR of 0.78 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.24) for clinically relevant fistula (Liu). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the NEJM relative risk without the follow-up literature, and do not quote the meta-analysis as proof of no effect — it pools one positive RCT with null observational series. A multicentre randomised trial, which both null series call for, is what would settle this.
cards.source: Synthesis of Allen PJ et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24849084); Elliott IA et al. HPB. 2018 (PMID: 29398424); Dominguez-Rosado I et al. Journal of the American College of Surgeons. 2018 (PMID: 29133263); Liu X et al. Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery. 2020 (PMID: 32207077).

shelves.title: Drains after pancreaticoduodenectomy: SPLIT — PANDRA found omission safe and fistula-reducing, the Van Buren trial was stopped early for higher mortality without drains; early removal in low-risk patients is the agreed part
shelves.question: In adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, does omitting a prophylactic intra-abdominal drain (or removing it very early) increase or decrease complications versus routine drainage?
shelves.mesh: Drainage* · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Operative Time · Pancreas/surgery* · Pancreatic Fistula/etiology · Pancreaticoduodenectomy · Postoperative Complications · Reoperation · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT on omission, concordant on early removal. PANDRA (Witzigmann 2016, 395 analysed, ISRCTN04937707) found drain omission noninferior for reintervention (16.6% no-drain vs 21.3% drain) with less clinically relevant fistula (5.7% vs 11.9%) and identical mortality (3.1% vs 3.0%). The Van Buren multicentre trial (137 patients, NCT01441492) reached the opposite conclusion and was stopped early by its DSMB because mortality rose from 3% to 12% without drains, with more and more severe complications. Early removal is the settled half: Bassi's RCT in low-risk patients (day-1 drain amylase ≤5000 U/L) found fewer fistulas and complications with day-3 removal, and the 2025 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (2,796 patients) supports a selective early-removal policy in pancreaticoduodenectomy — while its no-drain verdict applies to left pancreatectomy, not the Whipple. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Witzigmann 2016 (PANDRA RCT, 395 analysed): omitting drains was noninferior for reintervention (16.6% vs 21.3%) and halved clinically relevant fistula (5.7% vs 11.9%)
cards.summary: Witzigmann 2016 (PANDRA RCT, 395 analysed): omitting drains was noninferior for reintervention (16.6% vs 21.3%) and halved clinically relevant fistula (5.7% vs 11.9%)
cards.people: 438 patients undergoing pancreatic head resection with pancreaticojejunal anastomosis at two centres, randomised to intra-abdominal drainage (n = 202 analysed) or no drainage (n = 193 analysed) after 43 exclusions for no pancreatic anastomosis performed; dual-centre randomised noninferiority trial (ISRCTN04937707, named in the published title). Primary endpoint was overall reintervention rate (relaparotomy or radiologic intervention).
cards.result: Reintervention rates were not inferior in the no-drain group (drain 21.3%, no-drain 16.6%; P = 0.0004 for noninferiority). Overall in-hospital mortality was the same (3.0% vs 3.1%; P = 0.936) and overall surgical morbidity comparable (41.8% overall; P = 0.741). Clinically relevant pancreatic fistula (grade B/C) was significantly lower without drains (drain 11.9%, no-drain 5.7%; P = 0.030), as were fistula-associated complications (26.4% vs 13.0%; P = 0.0008). Operation time, haemorrhage, abscess, biliary leak, delayed gastric emptying, wound infection and hospital stay did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Planned sample size was 188 per group and the analysed 395 patients meet it, but 43 randomised patients (9.8%) were excluded after randomisation because no anastomosis was performed — a post-randomisation exclusion that noninferiority conclusions are sensitive to. Two centres, one anastomosis type (pancreaticojejunal).
cards.source: Witzigmann H et al. No Need for Routine Drainage After Pancreatic Head Resection: The Dual-Center, Randomized, Controlled PANDRA Trial (ISRCTN04937707). Annals of surgery. 2016. PMID: 27513157. Registry ID: ISRCTN04937707 (from the published title in the record). cards.headline: Van Buren 2014 (multicentre RCT, 137 patients): stopped early — mortality rose from 3% to 12% without drains, with more and more severe complications (the opposite result)
cards.summary: Van Buren 2014 (multicentre RCT, 137 patients): stopped early — mortality rose from 3% to 12% without drains, with more and more severe complications (the opposite result)
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial, stopped early (Van Buren 2014)
cards.people: 137 patients randomised at multiple centres to pancreaticoduodenectomy with routine intraperitoneal drainage (n = 68) or without (n = 69); groups did not differ in demographics, comorbidities, pathology, duct size, pancreas texture, baseline quality of life or operative technique. Registered as NCT01441492.
cards.result: Pancreaticoduodenectomy without drainage was associated with more complications per patient (median 2 [IQR 1–4] vs 1 [0–2]; P = 0.029), more patients with at least one grade ≥2 complication (47/69, 68% vs 35/68, 52%; P = 0.047), and higher average complication severity (P = 0.027). The no-drain group had more gastroparesis, intra-abdominal fluid collections, intra-abdominal abscess (25% vs 10%; P = 0.027), severe diarrhoea, need for postoperative percutaneous drain, and longer stay. The Data Safety Monitoring Board stopped the study early because mortality increased from 3% to 12% in patients without drainage.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for harm exaggerates the harm estimate — a trial stopped at a random high point for mortality (12% vs 3% on 137 patients is a handful of deaths) gives an unstable number. But a DSMB stop for mortality cannot be waved away either; this is the core of the split.
cards.source: Van Buren G et al. A randomized prospective multicenter trial of pancreaticoduodenectomy with and without routine intraperitoneal drainage. Annals of surgery. 2014. PMID: 24374513. Registry ID: NCT01441492 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank list). cards.headline: Bassi 2010 (RCT, 114 low-risk patients): removing the drain on day 3 instead of day 5 or later reduced fistula, abdominal and pulmonary complications and shortened stay
cards.summary: Bassi 2010 (RCT, 114 low-risk patients): removing the drain on day 3 instead of day 5 or later reduced fistula, abdominal and pulmonary complications and shortened stay
cards.type: Randomised trial of early versus late drain removal (Bassi 2010)
cards.people: 114 eligible patients who underwent standard pancreatic resections and were at low risk of postoperative pancreatic fistula by the institutional protocol (drain amylase ≤5000 U/L on postoperative day 1), randomised on day 3 to early drain removal (day 3) or standard removal (day 5 or beyond). Registered as NCT00931554. The population includes pancreaticoduodenectomy and other standard resections.
cards.result: Early drain removal was associated with a decreased rate of pancreatic fistula (P = 0.0001), abdominal complications (P = 0.002) and pulmonary complications (P = 0.007); median in-hospital stay was shorter (P = 0.018) and hospital costs decreased (P = 0.02). Mortality was nil. On multivariate analysis, timing of drain removal (P = 0.0003) and unintentional preoperative weight loss (P = 0.02) were independent risk factors for fistula. The record reports P values without the group fistula percentages, so no absolute rates are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: Only low-risk patients (day-1 drain amylase ≤5000 U/L) were randomised — the result licenses early removal in selected low-risk patients, not early removal for everyone, and the abstract's P-values without absolute rates limit how much weight the size of the benefit can carry.
cards.source: Bassi C et al. Early versus late drain removal after standard pancreatic resections: results of a prospective randomized trial. Annals of surgery. 2010. PMID: 20622661. cards.headline: Pietrogiovanna 2025 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 2,796 patients): level 1a evidence for selective early drain removal in pancreaticoduodenectomy — and for a no-drain policy in left pancreatectomy, not in pancreaticoduodenectomy
cards.summary: Pietrogiovanna 2025 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 2,796 patients): level 1a evidence for selective early drain removal in pancreaticoduodenectomy — and for a no-drain policy in left pancreatectomy, not in pancreaticoduodenectomy
cards.people: Thirteen randomised trials with 2,796 patients on routine prophylactic abdominal drainage in pancreatic surgery (10 trials in partial pancreatoduodenectomy, 1,744 patients; 7 in left pancreatectomy, 1,052 patients), covering four interventions: drainage versus no drainage, irrigation-suction versus passive drainage, closed-suction versus passive drainage, and early versus late removal; searched to 1 May 2025, with Cochrane risk-of-bias and GRADE assessment.
cards.result: Only two of eight stratified line-ups had sufficient data to meta-analyse. Early drain removal in partial pancreatoduodenectomy, following the trials' inclusion criteria, was safe and significantly reduced chyle leak (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.59; P < 0.01). Omission of routine drainage in left pancreatectomy was safe, with fewer postoperative pancreatic fistulas (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.77; P < 0.01) and a shorter hospital stay (mean difference −0.48 days, 95% CI −0.61 to −0.35; P < 0.01). The authors describe level 1a evidence for a selective early-removal policy in pancreaticoduodenectomy and a no-drain policy in left pancreatectomy.
cards.watchOut: Note what the meta-analysis does not say: for pancreaticoduodenectomy — this shelf's operation — the drain-omission line-up did not provide sufficient data for a pooled verdict, so PANDRA versus Van Buren remains unresolved at pooled level. The left-pancreatectomy no-drain result must not be imported into Whipple practice.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT on omission for pancreaticoduodenectomy; concordant on selective early removal in low-risk patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT on omission for pancreaticoduodenectomy; concordant on selective early removal in low-risk patients
cards.people: Two randomised trials of drain omission in pancreatic head resection reaching opposite conclusions (PANDRA, 395 analysed; Van Buren, 137, stopped early), one randomised trial of early removal in low-risk patients (114), and a 13-RCT meta-analysis (2,796 patients).
cards.result: Omission: noninferior reintervention and less fistula in PANDRA (16.6% vs 21.3%; fistula 5.7% vs 11.9%) versus more complications and a mortality-driven early stop in Van Buren (mortality 3% to 12% without drains). Early removal: fewer complications in low-risk patients (Bassi) and a safe selective early-removal policy at meta-analysis level. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: The two halves of this question have opposite evidence states: 'no drain at all after a Whipple' is genuinely contested between two RCTs, while 'take the drain out early in a low-risk patient' is supported at every level. A shelf that merged them into one verdict would misstate both.

shelves.title: Transient sphincter relaxations: the stomach-distension reflex that carries four of five healthy reflux episodes — and fires no more often in reflux disease
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are transient lower-oesophageal sphincter relaxations — how often do they occur after a meal, what triggers them (gastric distension), and what fraction of physiological and reflux-disease acid reflux episodes do they account for on manometry/pH-impedance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Atropine · Deglutition · Diagnostic Techniques, Digestive System · Electromyography · Esophagogastric Junction · Esophageal Sphincter, Lower · Esophagus · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Male · Manometry · Middle Aged · Muscle Relaxation · Pharynx · Physical Exertion · Postprandial Period · Stomach · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL slice, verified against its home: pack #2657 asks whether adding baclofen helps PPI-refractory reflux and cards transient lower-oesophageal sphincter relaxation (TLESR) counts only as that drug trial's outcome. This shelf asks the physiology itself — frequency, trigger, and share of reflux episodes — and none of #2657's carded studies is used here (its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's source lines; the home is cross-pointed in this prose only). Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: TLESRs are vagally mediated, swallow-independent relaxations of the sphincter (with crural-diaphragm inhibition), triggered mainly by gastric distension, occurring chiefly after meals, and forming the main route by which gastric contents reflux in health. The fetched human records quantify it. In ambulant healthy subjects recorded for 24 hours, 66% of reflux episodes fell in the 3 hours after food, transient LES relaxation was the mechanism in 82% of episodes regardless of activity or position, swallow-related relaxation accounted for 13%, and straining for only 20% (Schoeman 1995, N = 10). Postprandially, TLESR frequency was 3.5 ± 0.5 per 30 minutes in normal subjects in the atropine study's control period, with TLESR the major mechanism even when basal sphincter pressure was pharmacologically lowered (Mittal, Holloway & Dent 1995, N = 13). The trigger experiment: insufflating the stomach with 300–900 mL of CO2 produced intermittent TLESR episodes, and pharyngeal micro-stimulation produced graded sphincter relaxation — gastric distension is a sufficient trigger in humans (Mittal 1997, N = 8–10 per limb). Frequency in disease is not higher: after a standard meal, TLESR rate was 5.0/hour in reflux disease versus 4.5/hour in matched controls, and what differed was how often refluxate reached the proximal oesophagus during a TLESR (48.1% vs 10.9% at 7 cm above the sphincter), not the relaxations themselves (Iwakiri 2005, N = 10 + 10).

cards.headline: The share: transient relaxations caused 82% of reflux episodes in ambulant healthy people over 24 hours — swallow-related relaxation 13%, straining a factor in only 20%
cards.summary: The share: transient relaxations caused 82% of reflux episodes in ambulant healthy people over 24 hours — swallow-related relaxation 13%, straining a factor in only 20%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour ambulatory sleeve-sensor manometry/pH) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy subjects recorded ambulatorily for 24 hours with a perfused sleeve sensor on the lower oesophageal sphincter, intraluminal pressure transducers in stomach, oesophagus and pharynx, and pH 5 cm above the sphincter, including meals, moderate activity, standardised exercise, rest and sleep. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Most reflux episodes (81 of 123; 66%) occurred in the 3 hours after food intake; only 2 episodes occurred during exercise. Sphincter pressure was ≤3 cm H2O in 79% of reflux episodes. Transient LES relaxation was the mechanism of reflux in 82% of episodes, irrespective of activity or body position; swallow-related LES relaxations accounted for 13% and persistently absent LES pressure for 1%. Straining occurred in only 20% of episodes — in ambulant healthy subjects, reflux usually occurs during transient LES relaxations, and straining is not a major factor.
cards.watchOut: Ten healthy volunteers: the 82% share is the healthy-physiology figure this shelf exists to state; shares in hiatus hernia or severe oesophagitis populations are a different measurement and are not claimed here.
cards.source: Schoeman MN et al. Mechanisms of gastroesophageal reflux in ambulant healthy human subjects. Gastroenterology. 1995. PMID: 7806066. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Postprandial frequency: 3.5 transient relaxations per 30 minutes in normal subjects — and TLESR stayed the major reflux mechanism even when basal sphincter pressure was halved (N = 13)
cards.summary: Postprandial frequency: 3.5 transient relaxations per 30 minutes in normal subjects — and TLESR stayed the major reflux mechanism even when basal sphincter pressure was halved (N = 13)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (postprandial manometry/pH with atropine probe) — N = 13
cards.people: 13 normal subjects studied postprandially with simultaneous LES pressure, oesophageal pressures, oesophageal pH and crural-diaphragm electromyography for 30 minutes before and two 30-minute periods after atropine injection.
cards.result: Atropine reduced basal LES pressure from 16.4 ± 3 to 8.7 ± 2 mmHg. Reflux frequency fell from 3.5 ± 0.5 episodes in the control period to 0.4 ± 0.2 and 0.8 ± 0.3 in the two post-atropine periods (P < 0.05), and transient LES relaxation frequency fell in parallel from 3.5 ± 0.5 to 0.4 ± 0.2 and 1.5 ± 0.4 (P < 0.05). Transient LES relaxation with associated crural-diaphragm inhibition was the major mechanism of reflux under the low-LES-pressure conditions, and atropine-induced low basal pressure did not itself predispose to reflux — the relaxations, not the resting pressure, gate the episodes.
cards.watchOut: An atropine-probe study: its physiology payload is the control-period frequency and the mechanism attribution (TLESR with crural inhibition); the drug effect itself belongs to pharmacology, and the baclofen version of this probe is homed at pack #2657, not here.
cards.source: Mittal RK et al. Effect of atropine on the frequency of reflux and transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation in normal subjects. Gastroenterology. 1995. PMID: 7557138. cards.headline: The trigger shown directly: gastric distension with 300–900 mL of CO2 evoked transient relaxations in healthy volunteers; pharyngeal micro-volumes evoked graded sphincter relaxation (N = 8–10 per limb)
cards.summary: The trigger shown directly: gastric distension with 300–900 mL of CO2 evoked transient relaxations in healthy volunteers; pharyngeal micro-volumes evoked graded sphincter relaxation (N = 8–10 per limb)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (gastric-distension and pharyngeal-stimulation trigger experiments) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers studied postprandially on two days (atropine versus placebo) with oesophageal manometry and pH; the gastric-distension limb insufflated the stomach with 300, 600 and 900 mL of CO2 in 8 subjects, and the pharyngeal limb injected 0.05–0.4 mL water boluses into the pharynx in 9 subjects.
cards.result: Gastric distension resulted in intermittent episodes of transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation, and the frequency of distension-induced TLOSR was significantly decreased by atropine. Pharyngeal stimulation produced bolus-volume-dependent LOS relaxation, whose frequency and amplitude atropine decreased at bolus volumes of 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 mL. Atropine also reduced spontaneous postprandial reflux and TLOSR frequency versus placebo (P < 0.05). Together the limbs identify gastric distension as a sufficient human trigger for the reflex (with a pharyngeal afferent route also demonstrated) and the reflex arc as cholinergically mediated.
cards.watchOut: CO2 insufflation is an artificial, rapidly delivered distension: it proves sufficiency of the distension trigger, while the meal studies (References 1–2) establish that ordinary postprandial distension is the everyday route.
cards.source: Mittal RK et al. Atropine inhibits gastric distension and pharyngeal receptor mediated lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. Gut. 1997. PMID: 9378379. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Disease does not mean more relaxations: postprandial TLESR rate was 5.0/hour in reflux disease vs 4.5/hour in controls — what differed was proximal refluxate spread during a TLESR (N = 10 + 10)
cards.summary: Disease does not mean more relaxations: postprandial TLESR rate was 5.0/hour in reflux disease vs 4.5/hour in controls — what differed was proximal refluxate spread during a TLESR (N = 10 + 10)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (postprandial manometry/pH, patients vs matched controls) — N = 10 + 10
cards.people: 10 patients with reflux disease and 10 age-matched healthy controls, studied sitting with concurrent oesophageal manometry and pH monitoring for 3 hours after a standard meal, with acid reflux assessed 2 cm and 7 cm above the sphincter.
cards.result: The rate of TLESRs in reflux disease (5.0/hr [3.3–6.7]; median [IQR]) was similar to controls (4.5/hr [3.7–5.7]). Acid reflux 2 cm above the LES during TLESRs did not differ (75.0% vs 74.3% of TLESRs), but at 7 cm above the LES the incidence during TLESRs was significantly higher in patients (48.1% [27.2–71.4%]) than controls (10.9% [0.0–18.8%]). The authors conclude TLESR rate and the incidence of acid reflux during TLESRs are not increased in reflux disease — the disease relates more to the proximal extent of the refluxate than to the relaxations themselves.
cards.watchOut: Small matched groups and a sitting postprandial protocol: the equality of TLESR rates is the finding, but it is one laboratory's measurement — other protocols (recumbent, hernia subgroups) can differ, and this shelf does not claim TLESR frequency is never raised in any reflux subgroup.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a distension-triggered, meal-clustered reflex that carries ~4 out of 5 healthy reflux episodes — and is not itself the lesion in reflux disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: a distension-triggered, meal-clustered reflex that carries ~4 out of 5 healthy reflux episodes — and is not itself the lesion in reflux disease
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Transient lower-oesophageal sphincter relaxations in humans, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) frame them and the fetched records quantify: they cluster after meals (66% of episodes within 3 hours of food), run at roughly 3.5 per 30 postprandial minutes in laboratory recordings and ~4.5/hour over a 3-hour post-meal window in controls, are triggered sufficiently by gastric distension, and account for 82% of reflux episodes in ambulant health — with resting sphincter pressure and straining playing minor roles. Reflux disease does not raise their rate (5.0 vs 4.5/hr); it raises the proximal spread of what comes through them. The drug question that uses TLESR counts as an outcome (baclofen in PPI-refractory reflux) is homed at pack #2657 and is not duplicated here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Frequency figures are protocol-bound (meal size, posture, recording window differ across the four studies); the robust cross-study claims are the trigger, the postprandial clustering, the dominant share of episodes, and the health-versus-disease rate equality.

shelves.title: Colonic motor patterns: a quiet fasting colon, ~60 gentle propagated waves a day, and a handful of 110 mmHg mass-movement contractions after waking and meals
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the colon's motor patterns — the migrating motor complex in the fasting state and high-amplitude propagated contractions around waking and meals — how often do they occur, and how do they relate to mass movement and defecation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Circadian Rhythm · Colon · Colon, Sigmoid · Constipation · Defecation · Eating · Female · Gastrointestinal Motility · Gastrointestinal Transit · Humans · Male · Manometry · Middle Aged · Muscle Contraction · Peristalsis · Postprandial Period · Pressure · Reference Values
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account, with one correction this shelf states plainly: the human colon does not show the small bowel's orderly fasting migrating motor complex as its dominant pattern. The fetched 24-hour human manometry records instead show long quiescent stretches — activity low before meals and minimal during sleep — punctuated by two propagated patterns: rare, forceful high-amplitude propagated contractions (HAPCs), the manometric equivalent of mass movements, clustered after morning awakening and meals; and frequent low-amplitude propagated waves that do most of the everyday propulsion. In 14 healthy volunteers recorded for 24 hours, most activity was low-amplitude contractions in no recognisable pattern, while isolated high-amplitude contractions (up to 200 mmHg) propagating at ~1 cm/s occurred at a mean of 4.4 per subject per 24 h, mostly after awakening and in the late postprandial period, often felt as an urge to defecate or preceding defecation (Narducci 1987). The dedicated HAPC study put the rate at 6.1 ± 0.9 per 24 h with mean amplitude 110 mmHg, duration 14 s and velocity 1.11 cm/s, maximal after meals and awakening and minimal in the late afternoon and at night (Bassotti & Gaburri 1988, N = 20). Low-amplitude propagated waves (<50 mmHg, mean ~20 mmHg) were constant in all 16 volunteers at about 61 events per subject per day, over 80% by day, rising after meals and awakening (Bassotti 2001). Pancolonic spatiotemporal mapping in 8 healthy women confirmed propagating sequences as the organising pattern across the whole colon, with normal nocturnal suppression — the baseline against which severe constipation showed mid-colon paucity and disorganisation (Dinning 2010). So the fasting colon is mostly quiet rather than cycling through a migrating complex; waking and eating are the great organisers, and defecation is typically preceded by the high-amplitude pattern.

cards.headline: The 24-hour picture: activity minimal in sleep, low before meals, surging after meals and at awakening — with 4.4 mass-movement contractions a day, often felt as urge (N = 14)
cards.summary: The 24-hour picture: activity minimal in sleep, low before meals, surging after meals and at awakening — with 4.4 mass-movement contractions a day, often felt as urge (N = 14)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour colonic manometry in health) — N = 14
cards.people: 14 healthy volunteers with a colonoscope-positioned catheter recording transverse, descending and sigmoid colon for 24 hours, eating two 1,000 kcal mixed meals and a continental breakfast.
cards.result: Colonic motor activity was low before meals and minimal during sleep; the motility index increased significantly after meals and at morning awakening. Most activity was low-amplitude contractions, singly or in bursts, showing no recognisable pattern. All but two subjects also showed isolated high-amplitude (up to 200 mmHg) contractions that propagated peristaltically over long distances at approximately 1 cm/sec, at a mean of 4.4 per subject per 24 h; most occurred after morning awakening and some in the late postprandial period. These peristaltic contractions were often felt as an urge to defecate or preceded defecation, and could represent the manometric equivalent of mass movements.
cards.watchOut: Catheter coverage was transverse-to-sigmoid colon after colonoscopic placement and bowel preparation: the fasting-quiet conclusion is for the prepared, instrumented colon, and no small-bowel-style migrating motor complex was seen — the absence is reported here as the record states it, not smoothed into the textbook phrase.
cards.source: Narducci F et al. Twenty four hour manometric recording of colonic motor activity in healthy man. Gut. 1987. PMID: 3817580. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The high-amplitude pattern characterised: 6.1 ± 0.9 HAPCs per 24 hours at ~110 mmHg for ~14 seconds, propagating at ~1.1 cm/s — maximal after meals and awakening, minimal at night (N = 20)
cards.summary: The high-amplitude pattern characterised: 6.1 ± 0.9 HAPCs per 24 hours at ~110 mmHg for ~14 seconds, propagating at ~1.1 cm/s — maximal after meals and awakening, minimal at night (N = 20)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour HAPC characterisation) — N = 20
cards.people: 20 healthy volunteers studied with a colonoscopically positioned manometric probe and low-compliance infusion system recording segments proximal to the rectosigmoid junction; 110 HAPCs analysed from ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon.
cards.result: Mean HAPC frequency was 6.1 ± 0.9 (SE) per subject per 24 h, mean amplitude 110.37 ± 6.3 mmHg, mean duration 14.15 ± 0.8 s, and mean propagation velocity 1.11 ± 0.1 cm/s, with no significant differences among colonic segments. Diurnal variation was marked: maximum frequency after meals and after awakening in the morning, minimum in the late afternoon and during the night. The authors identify these HAPCs as the likely manometric equivalent of mass movements.
cards.watchOut: HAPC counts depend on the amplitude threshold and recording span used (compare Reference 1's 4.4/day at a higher observed amplitude range); the stable claims are the order of magnitude (a handful per day), the ~110 mmHg amplitude, and the waking/meal clustering.
cards.source: Bassotti G, Gaburri M. Manometric investigation of high-amplitude propagated contractile activity of the human colon. The American journal of physiology. 1988. PMID: 3189553. cards.headline: The everyday pattern: low-amplitude propagated waves were constant in everyone — about 61 per day at ~20 mmHg, over 80% by day, rising after meals and awakening (N = 16)
cards.summary: The everyday pattern: low-amplitude propagated waves were constant in everyone — about 61 per day at ~20 mmHg, over 80% by day, rising after meals and awakening (N = 16)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour propagated-wave analysis) — N = 16
cards.people: 16 healthy volunteers of both sexes studied for 24 hours with a colonoscopically positioned manometric catheter, eating two standard 1,000 kcal mixed meals and a 450 kcal breakfast; waves counted if <50 mmHg and propagated over at least three consecutive recording ports.
cards.result: Low-amplitude propagated contractile waves were constantly present in all tracings, averaging about 61 events per subject per day at a mean amplitude of about 20 mmHg. More than 80% of events appeared during the day, with a significant (P < 0.05) increase after meals and after morning awakening; in 25% of subjects the waves were accompanied by emission of flatus. The authors identify low-amplitude propagated waves — not only the rare high-amplitude contractions — as a constant physiological propulsive pattern of the human colon, related to sleep–wake cycles and meal ingestion.
cards.watchOut: A ≥3-port propagation rule defines the count: shorter propagated events are excluded by design, so 61/day is the rate of clearly propagated low-amplitude waves, not of all colonic contractions, most of which remain non-propagated segmental activity.
cards.source: Bassotti G et al. Low-amplitude propagated contractile waves: a relevant propulsive mechanism of human colon. Digestive and liver disease : official journal of the Italian Society of Gastroenterology and the Italian Association for the Study of the Liver. 2001. PMID: 11303973. cards.headline: Whole-colon mapping: propagating sequences organise the entire colon in health, with normal nocturnal suppression — the baseline that severe constipation loses (healthy controls N = 8)
cards.summary: Whole-colon mapping: propagating sequences organise the entire colon in health, with normal nocturnal suppression — the baseline that severe constipation loses (healthy controls N = 8)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour pancolonic spatiotemporal mapping; healthy control arm) — N = 8 controls
cards.people: 8 healthy female controls (with 14 female patients with scintigraphically confirmed slow-transit constipation for contrast) studied with a colonoscopically positioned silicone catheter with 16 recording sites spanning the colon at 7.5 cm intervals, tip clipped to the caecum, recording for 24 hours with spatiotemporal mapping.
cards.result: In health, pancolonic spatiotemporal mapping showed propagating sequences (PS) distributed across the colon with normal nocturnal suppression of PS. Against that baseline, slow-transit constipation showed a marked paucity of propagating pressure waves in the mid-colon (P = 0.01) from decreased extent of propagation of proximally originating PS (P < 0.0001), increased frequency of retrograde PS in the proximal colon, significantly reduced spatiotemporal organisation among PS (P < 0.001), and absence of the normal nocturnal suppression. The control arm is what this shelf cards: whole-colon propagated sequences, regionally organised and sleep-suppressed, are the healthy organising pattern.
cards.watchOut: The healthy arm is 8 women in a study designed around constipation: it contributes the whole-colon organisation and nocturnal-suppression baseline, while the frequency/amplitude numbers on this shelf come from References 1–3.
cards.source: Dinning PG et al. Pancolonic spatiotemporal mapping reveals regional deficiencies in, and disorganization of colonic propagating pressure waves in severe constipation. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2010. PMID: 20879994. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a mostly quiet fasting colon, organised by waking and meals into ~60 gentle propagated waves a day plus a handful of mass-movement contractions
cards.summary: Synthesis: a mostly quiet fasting colon, organised by waking and meals into ~60 gentle propagated waves a day plus a handful of mass-movement contractions
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human manometry studies above.
cards.result: Human colonic motor patterns, as the fetched 24-hour records show them: fasting and sleep are quiet (no dominant migrating motor complex of the small-bowel type — the honest correction to the textbook shorthand); morning awakening and meals are the organising stimuli; low-amplitude propagated waves (~61/day, ~20 mmHg) provide constant everyday propulsion; and high-amplitude propagated contractions (4.4–6.1/day, ~110 mmHg, ~1.1 cm/s) cluster after waking and meals, are felt as urge, precede defecation, and stand as the manometric equivalent of mass movements — all organised as propagating sequences across the whole colon with nocturnal suppression. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the migrating-motor-complex wording corrected on the face: in the human colon the pattern is quiescence-and-bursts, not a cycling fasting complex.
cards.watchOut: All four studies instrument a prepared colon with a catheter; absolute event counts vary with thresholds and sensor spacing, so this shelf's durable claims are the pattern (quiet fasting/sleep, waking/meal surges, two propagated wave classes, urge/defecation link), not any single count.

Digestive and liver disease. 2001 (PMID: 11303973); Dinning PG et al. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2010 (PMID: 20879994). shelves.title: Anorectal continence: tonic sphincter pressure, a sampling reflex with a guard contraction, and a sensation ladder from first filling to urge
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how is continence maintained and defecation controlled — resting anal sphincter pressure, squeeze pressure, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex and rectal sampling, and rectal sensation thresholds measured by manometry and balloon distension?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aging · Anal Canal · Defecation · Female · Healthy Volunteers · Humans · Male · Manometry · Mechanoreceptors · Middle Aged · Pressure · Rectum · Reference Values · Reflex · Sensation · Women's Health
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: continence rests on the internal anal sphincter's tonic resting pressure (the larger share), voluntary external-sphincter squeeze, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) — rectal distension transiently relaxing the internal sphincter so the sensitive anal canal can 'sample' rectal contents and discriminate gas from stool — and rectal sensation thresholds that trigger protective external-sphincter contraction and, at higher volumes, the urge to defecate. The fetched human records supply the numbers. High-resolution manometry in 62 asymptomatic women gave mean resting pressure of 88 mmHg under age 50 and 63 mmHg at 50 and over (age association r = −0.47), with squeeze pressure not age-related (Noelting & Bharucha 2012). The expanded normative set (163 asymptomatic participants; 96 women and 47 men with normal balloon expulsion used for reference values) confirms age lowers resting pressure in both sexes, squeeze increment and duration are higher in men, and fewer than 15% of asymptomatic people have a balloon expulsion time over 60 seconds (Oblizajek & Bharucha 2019). Sensation is rate-dependent physiology, not a fixed volume: in 12 normal men, first perception arrived with the initial steep pressure rise on rectal distension, the sensation of wind during the plateau, and desire to defecate at the final rapid pressure ascent — at lower volumes when filling was slow, implicating slowly adapting mechanoreceptors in parallel with the rectal wall (Sun & Read 1990). Anal relaxation (the RAIR) was always evoked by rapid intermittent distension and almost always accompanied by rectal sensation and a rise in external-sphincter activity — sampling with its guard reflex attached (Sun & Read 1990); RAIR parameters (latencies, inhibition amplitude and slope, recovery time and area under the inhibitory curve) are quantifiable at each sphincter level in healthy volunteers, with recovery proceeding from distal to proximal sphincter (Zbar 1998). Duthie-era sphincter studies anchor the classic account historically; their PubMed records were not carded where abstracts are absent, and the values above come from the fetched normative records.

cards.headline: Normative pressures: resting anal pressure averaged 88 mmHg under 50 years and 63 mmHg at 50+ in healthy women; squeeze pressure did not fall with age (N = 62)
cards.summary: Normative pressures: resting anal pressure averaged 88 mmHg under 50 years and 63 mmHg at 50+ in healthy women; squeeze pressure did not fall with age (N = 62)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative high-resolution anorectal manometry cohort) — N = 62
cards.people: 62 asymptomatic women aged 21–80 years (median 44; 30 under 50) without risk factors for anorectal trauma, undergoing high-resolution anorectal manometry, rectal sensation testing and balloon expulsion testing (Noelting, Bharucha et al. 2012).
cards.result: Age was associated with lower anal resting pressure (r = −0.47, P < 0.01): 88 (3) mmHg (mean (s.e.m.)) in women under 50 versus 63 (5) mmHg at 50 and over — but not with squeeze pressure. Older women had higher rectal pressure and rectoanal gradient during simulated evacuation (r = 0.3, P < 0.05) and a shorter balloon expulsion time (17 (9) s at ≥50 vs 31 (10) s under 50; r = −0.4, P < 0.01). Notably, 52 of 62 healthy women had higher anal than rectal pressure (a negative gradient) during simulated evacuation, so a negative rectoanal gradient alone cannot diagnose a defecatory disorder.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one catheter system: the resting-pressure values are reference values for high-resolution manometry in women, not universal cut-offs, and the study's own caution — most healthy women show a 'negative' evacuation gradient — is part of the physiology, not a footnote.
cards.source: Noelting J et al. Normal values for high-resolution anorectal manometry in healthy women: effects of age and significance of rectoanal gradient. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22986439. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The expanded reference set: 163 healthy people — age lowers resting pressure in both sexes, men squeeze harder and longer, and <15% of healthy people exceed 60 s balloon expulsion
cards.summary: The expanded reference set: 163 healthy people — age lowers resting pressure in both sexes, men squeeze harder and longer, and <15% of healthy people exceed 60 s balloon expulsion
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative manometry cohort, both sexes) — N = 163
cards.people: 163 asymptomatic healthy participants undergoing high-resolution anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion testing; the 96 women and 47 men with normal balloon expulsion time formed the reference-value set (Oblizajek, Bharucha et al. 2019).
cards.result: Age is associated with lower resting pressure, higher rectal pressure during evacuation, and a higher rectoanal gradient during evacuation in both women and men. In women, balloon expulsion time is inversely correlated with age, and BMI correlates with a higher threshold volume for discomfort and a longer expulsion time. The anal squeeze pressure increment, squeeze duration and high-pressure-zone length are higher in men than women. Less than 15% of asymptomatic people have a balloon expulsion time over 60 seconds, and prolonged expulsion is associated with manometric features of impaired evacuation even without symptoms — the reference frame for what 'normal' continence machinery looks like by modern manometry.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports associations and the expulsion-time distribution rather than a full percentile table of pressures; exact 5th–95th percentile values live in the full text, so this card claims the directions, sex differences and the <15% figure that the record states.
cards.source: Oblizajek NR et al. Anorectal pressures measured with high-resolution manometry in healthy people-Normal values and asymptomatic pelvic floor dysfunction. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2019. PMID: 30957382. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sensation thresholds are a sequence, not a volume: first perception at the first pressure rise, wind at the plateau, urge at the final ascent — and slow filling lowers every threshold (N = 12)
cards.summary: Sensation thresholds are a sequence, not a volume: first perception at the first pressure rise, wind at the plateau, urge at the final ascent — and slow filling lowers every threshold (N = 12)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled rectal distension: sensation and sphincter responses) — N = 12
cards.people: 12 normal male subjects undergoing rectal distension with water and air at randomised ramp rates of 10, 20, 50 and 100 mL/min and intermittent rapid distension with air, with anorectal motor activity and rectal sensation recorded (Sun, Read et al. 1990). Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Ramp distension produced sigmoid pressure–volume profiles with sensations at specific points: initial perception during the initial steep pressure increase, sensation of wind during the plateau phase, and desire to defecate at the onset of the final rapid ascent. Sensations occurred at lower volumes at low infusion rates, suggesting the triggering receptor is a slowly adapting mechanoreceptor lying parallel to the circular muscle, not a simple volume or pressure receptor. Anal relaxation was always evoked by intermittent rectal distension and was almost always associated with a rectal sensation and an increase in external anal sphincter activity; during slow ramp filling, anal relaxation could be absent or delayed — the internal sphincter can maintain continence for a long period while the rectum slowly fills. Under all circumstances, onset of rectal sensation was associated with increased external sphincter electrical activity.
cards.watchOut: Twelve men and laboratory balloons: the durable claims are the ordered sensation sequence, its rate dependence, and the coupling of sensation to external-sphincter contraction — absolute threshold volumes vary with distension method, which is precisely the study's warning about comparing laboratories.
cards.source: Sun WM et al. Sensory and motor responses to rectal distention vary according to rate and pattern of balloon inflation. Gastroenterology. 1990. PMID: 2394323. cards.headline: The sampling reflex quantified: rectoanal inhibitory reflex parameters (latencies, inhibition slope, recovery) are measurable at each sphincter level in healthy volunteers, recovering distal-to-proximal
cards.summary: The sampling reflex quantified: rectoanal inhibitory reflex parameters (latencies, inhibition slope, recovery) are measurable at each sphincter level in healthy volunteers, recovering distal-to-proximal
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (RAIR parameterisation in volunteers and patient groups)
cards.people: Healthy volunteers together with patients with idiopathic faecal incontinence and chronic constipation (42 patients in the clinical groups), with the rectoanal inhibitory reflex recorded at reproducible threshold volumes at multiple sphincter levels (Zbar et al. 1998).
cards.result: The rectoanal inhibitory reflex — internal anal sphincter relaxation in response to rectal distension, reflecting the anal sampling mechanism of rectal discrimination — was characterised by excitatory and inhibitory latencies, maximum excitatory and inhibitory pressures, amplitude and slope of inhibition, slope and time of pressure recovery, and area under the inhibitory curve. Significant linear trends were found for most parameters at each sphincter level; recovery time and area under the inhibitory curve differed between sphincter levels and patient groups, with the most rapid recovery in the distal sphincter of incontinent patients (P < 0.001). The authors infer a coordinated internal-sphincter response to rectal distension with recovery of anal pressure from the distal to the proximal sphincter — the sampling window opens and then closes in sequence.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives the healthy-volunteer N only within the combined study description (42 refers to the patient groups), so no volunteer N is printed on this card; the card is used for the reflex's parameter structure and distal-to-proximal recovery, not for a normative mean.
cards.source: Zbar AP et al. Parameters of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex in patients with idiopathic fecal incontinence and chronic constipation. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 1998. cards.headline: Synthesis: tonic internal-sphincter pressure, a sampling reflex with its guard contraction, and an ordered sensation ladder hold continence — and resting pressure falls with age
cards.summary: Synthesis: tonic internal-sphincter pressure, a sampling reflex with its guard contraction, and an ordered sensation ladder hold continence — and resting pressure falls with age
cards.people: Synthesis of the two normative manometry cohorts and the two distension/reflex studies above.
cards.result: Continence physiology in healthy humans, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) frame it and the fetched records measure: resting anal pressure (internal-sphincter tone) averages ~88 mmHg in younger women and ~63 mmHg after 50, falling with age in both sexes, while voluntary squeeze (higher increment and duration in men) does not show the same age fall; rectal distension triggers the rectoanal inhibitory reflex — a quantifiable, level-by-level internal-sphincter relaxation that lets the anal canal sample contents — coupled to a protective external-sphincter contraction; and sensation climbs an ordered ladder (first perception, wind, urge to defecate) at thresholds that depend on filling rate, not volume alone. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Manometry values are system-dependent (high-resolution solid-state catheters here); the cross-study durable claims are the component structure, the age/sex patterns, the reflex–sensation coupling and the rate dependence of thresholds.
cards.source: Synthesis of Noelting J et al. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2012 (PMID: 22986439); Oblizajek NR et al. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2019 (PMID: 30957382); Sun WM et al. Gastroenterology. 1990 (PMID: 2394323); Zbar AP et al. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 1998 (PMID: 9556245). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Gallbladder emptying and refilling: a biphasic, meal-paced contraction with immediate tracer-level refilling — and a 38% ejection-fraction floor for the standard CCK infusion
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how completely and how fast does the gallbladder empty after a fatty meal or cholecystokinin infusion (ejection fraction by serial ultrasound), and how does it refill between meals?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Bile · Breath Tests · Cholelithiasis · Digestive System Physiological Phenomena · Eating · Fasting · Feeding Behavior · Female · Food · Gallbladder · Gallbladder Emptying · Gastric Emptying · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatic Polypeptide · Radionuclide Imaging · Reference Values · Sincalide · Time Factors · Ultrasonography · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: fat and protein products in the duodenum release cholecystokinin (CCK), the gallbladder contracts and empties into the duodenum while the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, and between meals the gallbladder refills and concentrates hepatic bile. The fetched human records quantify the cycle. After a standard breakfast (40% fat), gallbladder emptying by serial ultrasound was biphasic — initially 0.015 ± 0.003/min, later 0.005 ± 0.001/min — the slower tonic contraction lasting while the stomach was still emptying solids; the gallbladder stayed small until refilling began at 249 ± 67 minutes, and refilling was 70% complete by 335 ± 57 minutes (Lawson & Everson 1983, N = 12). Refilling is not only a late event: with simultaneous scintigraphy and ultrasound, refilling begins immediately postprandially, and in healthy controls the gallbladder handles up to six times its basal volume within 90 minutes of a meal — emptying and refilling overlap as turnover, not sequence (Jazrawi 1995, 11 controls). The fatty-meal ultrasound study adds the resting side: healthy controls had smaller fasting volumes and greater fractional emptying than gallstone patients, whose abnormalities stemmed from a high resting volume (Kishk & Dodds 1987). For the CCK-infusion version, the multicentre normal-values study (60 healthy volunteers) fixed the standard: with sincalide 0.02 µg/kg infused over 60 minutes, the gallbladder ejection fraction at 60 minutes has the least variability (coefficient of variation 19%) and a lower limit of normal of 38% (Ziessman 2010). Meal ejection fractions by ultrasound vary with meal and method — which is why this shelf reports the meal studies as rates and timing, and reserves a single threshold number for the standardised infusion protocol that was designed to produce one.

cards.headline: After a fatty breakfast: biphasic emptying (0.015/min, then 0.005/min), tonic contraction while the stomach empties, refilling starting at ~249 minutes and 70% complete by ~335 minutes (N = 12)
cards.summary: After a fatty breakfast: biphasic emptying (0.015/min, then 0.005/min), tonic contraction while the stomach empties, refilling starting at ~249 minutes and 70% complete by ~335 minutes (N = 12)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (serial ultrasound gallbladder volumes after a fatty meal) — N = 12
cards.people: 12 healthy men and women eating a standard breakfast (40% fat); gallbladder volume, emptying and refilling by real-time ultrasonography, gastric emptying of solids by scintigraphy (99mTc-sulphur-colloid egg), transit by breath hydrogen, and pancreatic polypeptide by radioimmunoassay. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Gallbladder emptying was biphasic, initially 0.015 ± 0.003/min and later 0.005 ± 0.001/min, and gallbladder volume remained small until refilling began at 249 ± 67 min; refilling was 70% complete at 335 ± 57 min. The slower rate of emptying and tonic gallbladder contraction occurred during gastric emptying of solids, and refilling began when approximately 13% of solids remained in the stomach. Pancreatic polypeptide showed the expected biphasic meal response and returned to basal levels at about the time refilling began, but did not appear responsible for refilling. The authors conclude that gastric emptying of the solid, fat-containing portion maintains tonic gallbladder contraction through continued humoral mediator release, and when gastric emptying nears completion the stimulation ceases and the gallbladder refills.
cards.watchOut: Rates are fractional volume change per minute from ultrasound ellipsoid volumes in 12 subjects after one defined breakfast: they describe this meal's kinetics, and the refilling times carry wide standard errors (±67 and ±57 min) — the biphasic shape and the gastric-emptying linkage are the durable findings.
cards.source: Lawson M et al. Coordination of gastric and gallbladder emptying after ingestion of a regular meal. Gastroenterology. 1983. PMID: 6884711. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Emptying and refilling overlap: with dual scintigraphy/ultrasound, refilling begins immediately after a meal and the healthy gallbladder turns over up to six times its basal volume in 90 minutes (11 controls)
cards.summary: Emptying and refilling overlap: with dual scintigraphy/ultrasound, refilling begins immediately after a meal and the healthy gallbladder turns over up to six times its basal volume in 90 minutes (11 controls)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (simultaneous scintigraphy + ultrasound turnover measurement) — 11 healthy controls
cards.people: 11 healthy controls (with 14 patients with gallstones for contrast) studied fasting and at 10-minute intervals for 90 minutes after a standard meal with simultaneous scintigraphy and ultrasonography, allowing postprandial refilling and bile turnover to be calculated separately from net volume change.
cards.result: Ultrasonography and scintigraphy provided different gallbladder emptying patterns — because ultrasound net volume is influenced by postprandial refilling and scintigraphy is not. Simultaneous measurement showed refilling begins immediately postprandially. In healthy controls the gallbladder postprandially handles up to six times its basal volume within 90 minutes. In gallstone patients, emptying was impaired by both methods (scintigraphy P < 0.0001; ultrasonography P < 0.01), refilling and turnover were reduced between 60 and 90 minutes (P < 0.05), and the turnover index was markedly reduced (1.8 vs 3.5; P < 0.001) — the control arm establishes that 'emptying' after a meal is really continuous turnover, not a single contraction to a residual volume.
cards.watchOut: The six-times-basal-volume figure is a calculated turnover over 90 minutes from combined tracers, not a directly observed volume; it corrects, rather than replaces, the simpler ultrasound emptying curves of Reference 1.
cards.source: Jazrawi RP et al. Postprandial gallbladder motor function: refilling and turnover of bile in health and in cholelithiasis. Gastroenterology. 1995. PMID: 7615209. cards.headline: The resting side: healthy controls had smaller fasting volumes and greater fractional emptying after a fatty meal than gallstone patients — whose defect tracked a high resting volume (Dodds group, 1987)
cards.summary: The resting side: healthy controls had smaller fasting volumes and greater fractional emptying after a fatty meal than gallstone patients — whose defect tracked a high resting volume (Dodds group, 1987)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (sonographic fasting volume and fatty-meal emptying; control arm)
cards.people: 20 patients with asymptomatic gallstones and healthy control subjects without gallstones, with fasting gallbladder volume and postprandial emptying in response to a fatty meal measured sonographically (Kishk, Dodds et al. 1987). The fetched abstract does not state the control-group number — N not documented in the record for controls.
cards.result: Compared with control subjects without gallstones, the majority of patients with gallstones exhibited a higher resting gallbladder volume, less fractional emptying after a fatty meal, and a higher postmeal residual volume. These abnormalities all appeared to stem from the abnormally high resting gallbladder volume. Whether the increased volume and decreased fractional emptying in gallstone patients is a primary or secondary abnormality was undetermined; the authors suggest decreased gallbladder contractility may contribute to gallstone development or proliferation in some patients. The healthy-control arm is what this shelf cards: the normal pattern is a modest fasting volume with brisk fractional emptying after a fatty meal.
cards.watchOut: This record is qualitative for the controls — it prints no control ejection-fraction percentage — so no meal ejection-fraction number is taken from it; the quantified meal kinetics on this shelf come from References 1–2 and the infusion threshold from Reference 4.
cards.source: Kishk SM et al. Sonographic evaluation of resting gallbladder volume and postprandial emptying in patients with gallstones. AJR. American journal of roentgenology. 1987. PMID: 3554918. cards.headline: The CCK-infusion standard: 60 healthy volunteers set the ejection-fraction lower limit of normal at 38% — for sincalide 0.02 µg/kg infused over 60 minutes, measured at 60 minutes
cards.summary: The CCK-infusion standard: 60 healthy volunteers set the ejection-fraction lower limit of normal at 38% — for sincalide 0.02 µg/kg infused over 60 minutes, measured at 60 minutes
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre normative ejection-fraction study) — N = 60
cards.people: 60 healthy volunteers at 4 medical centres undergoing sincalide-stimulated cholescintigraphy with 99mTc-mebrofenin; each received 0.02 µg/kg sincalide (the CCK analogue) at three infusion durations (15, 30 and 60 minutes) on separate days, with ejection fraction variability and normal values calculated per protocol.
cards.result: The coefficient of variation was smallest for the 60-minute infusion measured at 60 minutes (19%; 95% CI 16–23%), versus 35% for the 30-minute infusion and 52% for the 15-minute infusion (all significantly different, P < 0.0007). For the 60-minute infusion at 60 minutes, the lower limit of normal for gallbladder ejection fraction was 38% (first percentile). The authors recommend this infusion method as the standard for routine clinical use because it minimises variability in measured ejection fractions.
cards.watchOut: The 38% threshold is protocol-bound — sincalide dose, 60-minute infusion, scintigraphic measurement at 60 minutes; it must not be applied to fatty-meal ultrasound ejection fractions, which use different stimuli and geometry and were never assigned this cut-off.
cards.source: Ziessman HA et al. Sincalide-stimulated cholescintigraphy: a multicenter investigation to determine optimal infusion methodology and gallbladder ejection fraction normal values. Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20080900. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: contraction is biphasic and meal-paced, refilling overlaps emptying as turnover, and the one hard threshold (38%) belongs to the standard CCK infusion only
cards.summary: Synthesis: contraction is biphasic and meal-paced, refilling overlaps emptying as turnover, and the one hard threshold (38%) belongs to the standard CCK infusion only
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Gallbladder motor physiology in healthy humans, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) frame it and the fetched records measure: a fatty meal produces biphasic emptying — a faster early phase (0.015/min) then a slow tonic phase (0.005/min) sustained while fat-containing solids are still leaving the stomach — with net refilling from about 4 hours and 70% refilling by about 5.5 hours (Lawson & Everson 1983, N = 12); at the tracer level, refilling in fact begins immediately and the organ turns over up to six times its basal volume in 90 minutes (Jazrawi 1995). Healthy fasting volumes are modest with brisk fractional emptying (Kishk & Dodds 1987), and under the standardised CCK-analogue infusion the ejection fraction's lower limit of normal is 38% (Ziessman 2010, N = 60). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
