shelves.title: Urea-synthesis capacity: the liver's nitrogen clearance, halved by cirrhosis, turned up by glucagon and down by glucose — insulin leaves it alone
shelves.question: In humans, what is the liver's urea-synthesis capacity — how is the functional hepatic nitrogen clearance measured (amino-acid infusion with urea-N synthesis rate), how does it fall in cirrhosis, and how do protein intake and glucagon regulate it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alanine · Amino Acids · Blood Glucose · Female · Galactose · Glucagon · Glucose · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hyperinsulinism · Infusion Pumps · Insulin · Insulin Secretion · Liver · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Metabolic Clearance Rate · Middle Aged · Nitrogen · Pancreas · Pancreatic Hormones · Reference Values · Somatostatin · Urea
shelves.balance: PARTIAL slice, verified against its home: pack #6148 asks how ammonia is produced in the gut and cleared by liver and muscle in cirrhosis, and mentions urea synthesis once as an exit route. This shelf asks the capacity-and-regulation question — how urea synthesis is quantified, how much of it cirrhosis removes, and what turns it up or down — and none of #6148's carded studies is used here (its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's source lines; the home is cross-pointed in this prose only). Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: urea synthesis is the liver's irreversible disposal route for amino-acid nitrogen, with a large reserve capacity, regulated by substrate supply and by glucagon (up) and glucose (down). The measurement is the Vilstrup programme's functional hepatic nitrogen clearance (FHNC): during a constant amino-acid (alanine) infusion, the urea-nitrogen synthesis rate rises linearly with blood alpha-amino-nitrogen concentration, and the slope of that line — in litres per hour — is the clearance, a measure of functioning liver cell mass. In cirrhosis the slope was roughly halved: 18.4 ± 6.7 L/h versus 37.5 ± 7.0 L/h in controls, tracking Child-Pugh status and galactose elimination capacity (r = 0.869) (Bianchi & Vilstrup 1991; 9 + 9). Regulation in healthy volunteers: glucagon infusion raised urea synthesis by 35 ± 11 mmol/h and raised hepatic nitrogen clearance from 23 ± 4 to 42 ± 13 L/h (Vilstrup 1990, N = 7). Glucose halved FHNC (32.5 ± 1.9 to 18.4 ± 0.9 L/h), partly by suppressing the glucagon response to alanine and partly directly; high-dose glucagon overruled glucose, raising FHNC 35% to 44.1 ± 1.5 L/h despite hyperglycaemia (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994, N = 7). Insulin, by contrast, did not regulate the conversion itself: under somatostatin hormone control, hyperinsulinaemia left FHNC unchanged (13.2 ± 2.8 vs 12.2 ± 3.4 L/h) while hyperglycaemia (8.4 ± 0.5 mmol/L ≈ 151 mg/dL) cut it a further 40% to 7.4 ± 1.3 L/h — insulin's effect on urea production runs through amino-acid supply, glucose's through the liver itself (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994, N = 6). Protein intake regulates capacity in the same direction as glucagon in the programme's wider work (dietary protein up-regulates, carbohydrate down-regulates), presented here as the textbook/programme account anchored by the infusion studies carded.

cards.headline: Capacity measured and halved in cirrhosis: functional hepatic nitrogen clearance was 18.4 L/h in cirrhosis vs 37.5 L/h in controls — and tracked Child-Pugh and galactose elimination (9 + 9)
cards.summary: Capacity measured and halved in cirrhosis: functional hepatic nitrogen clearance was 18.4 L/h in cirrhosis vs 37.5 L/h in controls — and tracked Child-Pugh and galactose elimination (9 + 9)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (alanine-infusion FHNC measurement, controls vs cirrhosis) — N = 9 + 9
cards.people: 9 subjects with normal liver function and 9 patients with cirrhosis, studied with a simplified functional hepatic nitrogen clearance method: four consecutive 2-hour urine collections and five blood samples during infusion of alanine as substrate, with gut urea hydrolysis assigned a fixed fraction of synthesis (0.17 controls, 0.26 cirrhosis). Small classic study — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Urea-nitrogen synthesis rate increased linearly with increasing alpha-amino-nitrogen concentration, and the slope of the regression — the functional hepatic nitrogen clearance — was reduced in cirrhosis from 37.5 ± 7.0 L/hr to 18.4 ± 6.7 L/hr (P < 0.005). The clearance was linearly related to clinical status (Child-Pugh score), to routine liver function tests, and to galactose elimination capacity (r = 0.869), a well-established quantitative liver-function measure. Because the clearance is measured during amino-acid infusion, it quantifies urea-synthesis capacity (functioning liver cell mass for nitrogen conversion), not just the basal urea production rate.
cards.watchOut: Nine per group and a simplified method with an assumed (not measured) gut-hydrolysis fraction that itself differs by group: the halving is robust across the programme's methods, but the exact L/h values are method-bound and should not be transplanted to other FHNC protocols.
cards.source: Bianchi G et al. Hepatic amino-nitrogen clearance to urea-nitrogen in control subjects and in patients with cirrhosis: a simplified method. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1991. PMID: 1999317. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glucagon turns capacity up: urea synthesis rose by 35 mmol/h and hepatic nitrogen clearance from 23 to 42 L/h during glucagon infusion in healthy volunteers (N = 7)
cards.summary: Glucagon turns capacity up: urea synthesis rose by 35 mmol/h and hepatic nitrogen clearance from 23 to 42 L/h during glucagon infusion in healthy volunteers (N = 7)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (alanine infusion ± glucagon, FHNC) — N = 7
cards.people: 7 healthy volunteers given alanine as prime-continuous infusions; after 1 hour of equilibration, urea-nitrogen synthesis rate was measured over two ~2-hour periods (urinary excretion corrected for accumulation and intestinal hydrolysis), one period with glucagon infused to a constant concentration of 200–1200 ng/L. Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Spontaneous urea synthesis during alanine infusion was 86–141 mmol/hr, linearly related to alanine concentrations of 1.33–2.99 mmol/L (≈ 11.8–26.6 mg/dL). The hepatic clearance of alanine-nitrogen to urea-nitrogen was 23 ± 4 L/hr. Glucagon increased the rate of urea synthesis by 35 ± 11 mmol/hr (P < 0.02), decreased the alanine concentration by 0.22 ± 0.06 mmol/L (≈ 2.0 mg/dL; P < 0.01), and increased the hepatic nitrogen clearance to an average of 42 ± 13 L/hr (P < 0.01). Glucagon therefore increases the efficacy (capacity per unit substrate) of urea synthesis, not merely substrate delivery — a mechanism the authors link to the hepatic contribution to nitrogen homeostasis in catabolism.
cards.watchOut: Seven volunteers and pharmacological-range glucagon levels (200–1200 ng/L): the direction (glucagon up-regulates capacity) is the claim; the size of the rise at physiological post-meal glucagon excursions will be smaller.
cards.source: Vilstrup H et al. Glucagon increases hepatic efficacy for urea synthesis. Journal of hepatology. 1990. PMID: 2307830. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Alanine · Female · Glucagon · Humans · Infusion Pumps · Liver · Male · Nitrogen · Reference Values · Urea

cards.headline: Glucose turns it down, glucagon overrules glucose: glucose cut FHNC 43% (32.5→18.4 L/h); high glucagon raised it 35% to 44.1 L/h despite hyperglycaemia (N = 7)
cards.summary: Glucose turns it down, glucagon overrules glucose: glucose cut FHNC 43% (32.5→18.4 L/h); high glucagon raised it 35% to 44.1 L/h despite hyperglycaemia (N = 7)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (four-state alanine/glucose/glucagon FHNC protocol) — N = 7
cards.people: 7 healthy subjects with functional hepatic nitrogen clearance measured four times each: alanine infusion alone; alanine on constant glucose infusion; alanine on glucose plus low stepwise glucagon (aimed at restoring portal glucagon); and alanine on glucose plus high constant glucagon (~3-fold elevated levels). Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: During alanine alone, FHNC was 32.5 ± 1.9 L/h. Glucose reduced FHNC by 43% to 18.4 ± 0.9 L/h (P < 0.01) and halved the glucagon response to alanine. The low stepwise glucagon infusion only partially normalised the glucose-reduced FHNC (24.6 ± 1.5 L/h; P < 0.01 vs alanine alone), while the high glucagon infusion increased FHNC by 35% despite hyperglycaemia (44.1 ± 1.5 L/h; P < 0.01 vs alanine alone). The authors conclude glucose and glucagon are independent but opposite regulators: the physiological glucose effect combines glucose's own hepatic action with its suppression of the glucagon response, and hyperglucagonaemia overrules glucose inhibition — a proposed explanation for defective nitrogen sparing by glucose and for catabolism in hyperglucagonaemic stress states.
cards.watchOut: This record carries no MeSH terms in the fetched record (fallback stated on the source line). Seven subjects, and the 'high glucagon' state is frankly hyperglucagonaemic — the physiological takeaway is the opposition of the two regulators and glucose's dual route, not the 44.1 L/h figure as a normal value.
cards.source: Hamberg O, Vilstrup H. Regulation of urea synthesis by glucose and glucagon in normal man. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 1994. PMID: 16843380. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Insulin does not regulate the conversion itself: under hormone control, hyperinsulinaemia left FHNC unchanged (13.2 vs 12.2 L/h) while hyperglycaemia cut it 40% to 7.4 L/h (N = 6)
cards.summary: Insulin does not regulate the conversion itself: under hormone control, hyperinsulinaemia left FHNC unchanged (13.2 vs 12.2 L/h) while hyperglycaemia cut it 40% to 7.4 L/h (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (somatostatin hormone-control FHNC protocol) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy volunteers with alanine-stimulated urea-synthesis kinetics (FHNC) measured four times each: spontaneous hormone responses; and under somatostatin hormone control with basal hormone replacement at euglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia (85 ± 8 mU/L), or hyperglycaemia (8.4 ± 0.5 mmol/L ≈ 151 mg/dL). Small classic study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Hormonal control with euglycaemia reduced FHNC by two-thirds, from 32.9 ± 5.2 to 12.2 ± 3.4 L/h (P < 0.01) — attributable to abolition of the glucagon response to alanine. Hyperinsulinaemia did not change this (13.2 ± 2.8 L/h), whereas hyperglycaemia further reduced FHNC by 40% to 7.4 ± 1.3 L/h (P < 0.01). The authors conclude insulin does not regulate hepatic amino-to-urea nitrogen conversion — its effect on urea production runs through blood amino-acid supply — while glucose in itself reduces hepatic conversion independently of hormonal responses, so the hepatic component of glucose's amino-nitrogen-sparing effect depends on hyperglycaemia, not hyperinsulinaemia.
cards.watchOut: Six volunteers under somatostatin clamp conditions: the two-thirds fall on 'hormonal control' shows how much of the unstressed FHNC is glucagon-supported — a context effect to remember when comparing FHNC values across protocols (compare Reference 1's control value of 37.5 L/h under spontaneous hormones).
cards.source: Hamberg O, Vilstrup H. Effects of insulin and glucose on urea synthesis in normal man, independent of pancreatic hormone secretion. Journal of hepatology. 1994. PMID: 7836708. cards.headline: Synthesis: capacity is a slope, cirrhosis halves it, glucagon raises it, glucose lowers it, insulin leaves the liver's conversion alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: capacity is a slope, cirrhosis halves it, glucagon raises it, glucose lowers it, insulin leaves the liver's conversion alone
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human infusion studies above (the Vilstrup/Hamberg functional hepatic nitrogen clearance programme).
cards.result: Hepatic urea-synthesis capacity in humans is measured as the functional hepatic nitrogen clearance — the slope of urea-nitrogen synthesis rate against blood alpha-amino-nitrogen during amino-acid infusion, roughly 33–38 L/h in healthy adults under spontaneous hormone conditions. Cirrhosis approximately halves it (18.4 vs 37.5 L/h), in proportion to clinical liver dysfunction (Bianchi & Vilstrup 1991). Regulation is hormonal and substrate-level, as the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) frame it: glucagon raises capacity (clearance 23→42 L/h; Vilstrup 1990), glucose lowers it (−43%), by direct hepatic action plus suppression of the glucagon response, and glucagon excess overrules glucose (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994); insulin does not act on the conversion itself (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994). The ammonia-traffic question in cirrhosis — where the ammonia comes from and which organs clear it — is homed at pack #6148 and is not duplicated here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All values come from one research programme's alanine-infusion method in small samples (N = 6–9 per study): the internal consistency is high and the cirrhosis gradient is corroborated by galactose elimination, but absolute L/h values are this method's units, and dietary-protein regulation is stated in the balance as the programme/textbook account rather than re-quantified from a carded record here.

shelves.title: Pemvidutide in MASH: MASH resolution met at 24 weeks (58%/52% vs 20%), fibrosis improvement not met — phase 2b only
shelves.question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis, does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist pemvidutide, compared with placebo, resolve MASH or improve fibrosis?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only. In the IMPACT phase 2b trial (n=212, biopsy-confirmed MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis), MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 58% on pemvidutide 1.2 mg and 52% on 1.8 mg versus 20% on placebo at 24 weeks — that primary endpoint was met. The other primary endpoint was not: fibrosis improvement without worsening of MASH occurred in 33% and 36% versus 28% on placebo, differences of 5 and 8 percentage points that were not significant (P=0.59 and P=0.27) — at 24 weeks, on fibrosis, the treatment made no demonstrated difference. Supporting programme data in MASLD (steatosis without the IMPACT histology population) show large liver-fat reductions (relative reductions up to 68.5% at 12 weeks and 75.2% at 24 weeks versus 4.4% and 14.0% on placebo), which support the mechanism but are not MASH histology evidence. Fenced and not carded: pemvidutide's obesity limb (MOMENTUM) exists only as press-release material with no journal publication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), on one phase 2b trial whose two primary endpoints split.

cards.headline: IMPACT phase 2b (Lancet 2025): MASH resolution 58% (1.2 mg) and 52% (1.8 mg) vs 20% on placebo at 24 weeks — but fibrosis improvement 33%/36% vs 28%, not significant
cards.summary: IMPACT phase 2b (Lancet 2025): MASH resolution 58% (1.2 mg) and 52% (1.8 mg) vs 20% on placebo at 24 weeks — but fibrosis improvement 33%/36% vs 28%, not significant
cards.people: 212 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stage F2 or F3 at 83 sites in the USA and Australia, randomised 1:2:2 to once-weekly subcutaneous pemvidutide 1.2 mg (n=41), 1.8 mg (n=85) or placebo (n=86), in an ongoing 48-week trial reported at 24 weeks.
cards.result: MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis: 24 of 41 (58%) on 1.2 mg (difference vs placebo 38 percentage points, 95% CI 21–56; P<0.0001) and 45 of 85 (52%) on 1.8 mg (difference 32 points, 95% CI 19–46; P<0.0001) versus 18 of 86 (20%) on placebo. Fibrosis improvement without worsening of MASH: 13 of 41 (33%; difference 5 points, 95% CI −13 to 22; P=0.59) and 30 of 85 (36%; difference 8 points, 95% CI −6 to 22; P=0.27) versus 24 of 86 (28%) — not significant. Adverse events in 78%, 81% and 67% respectively, mostly mild or moderate; discontinuations for adverse events 0%, 1% and 2%.
cards.watchOut: Phase-2b only, 24-week readout of a 48-week trial, and the dual primary endpoints split — resolution met, fibrosis not met. Quote both halves or neither. Sponsor programme: pemvidutide (Altimmune).

cards.headline: MASLD liver-fat trial, 12 weeks (J Hepatol 2025): relative liver-fat reduction 68.5% on 1.8 mg vs 4.4% on placebo (relative measure, as reported)
cards.summary: MASLD liver-fat trial, 12 weeks (J Hepatol 2025): relative liver-fat reduction 68.5% on 1.8 mg vs 4.4% on placebo (relative measure, as reported)
cards.type: Randomised trial (MASLD, imaging endpoint — programme support)
cards.people: 94 adults with MASLD (BMI ≥28 kg/m², liver fat ≥10% by MRI-PDFF; 29% with type 2 diabetes) randomised 1:1:1:1 to once-weekly pemvidutide 1.2, 1.8 or 2.4 mg or placebo for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Relative reductions in liver fat content at week 12 were 46.6%, 68.5% and 57.1% across the dose groups versus 4.4% on placebo (P<0.001 for each vs placebo; relative reductions as reported in the record). cards.watchOut: This is a steatosis/imaging trial in MASLD, not a MASH histology trial — it supports the liver-fat mechanism and must not be quoted as MASH resolution evidence. Relative reductions are labelled relative, as reported.

cards.type: Extension report (24-week report of the trial in the previous card — explicitly labelled as the same trial)
cards.people: 64 completers of the 12-week MASLD trial carded above who continued on their originally assigned dose (pemvidutide 1.2, 1.8 or 2.4 mg, or placebo) for a further 12 weeks — the same participants, reported again at 24 weeks; this card is explicitly a second, labelled report of that one trial, not a new trial.

shelves.title: EUS-guided vs percutaneous gallbladder drainage in high-risk acute cholecystitis (DRAC 1): equal clinical success (~92%), but far fewer 1-year adverse events and reinterventions with the endoscopic route
shelves.question: In adults with acute cholecystitis at high surgical risk, does endoscopic-ultrasound-guided gallbladder drainage reduce adverse events and reintervention compared with percutaneous gallbladder drainage?
shelves.balance: One small randomised trial plus concordant meta-analyses. DRAC 1 (Teoh 2021, PMID 32165407) randomised 80 very-high-surgical-risk patients with acute calculous cholecystitis to EUS-guided gallbladder drainage (EUS-GBD) with a lumen-apposing metal stent or percutaneous cholecystostomy (PT-GBD): 1-year adverse events were 25.6% vs 77.5%, reinterventions after 30 days 2.6% vs 30%, and recurrent cholecystitis 2.6% vs 20% — while technical success (97.4% vs 100%), clinical success (92.3% vs 92.5%) and 30-day mortality (7.7% vs 10%) did not differ. Two meta-analyses point the same way: fewer delayed and overall adverse events with EUS-GBD using lumen-apposing metal stents (overall adverse events OR 0.43, a relative measure; PMID 37871846) and fewer adverse events (OR 0.35) and reinterventions (OR 0.18) across 11 mostly observational studies (PMID 36832143), with no difference in clinical success. The advantage is in downstream burden — readmissions, reinterventions, recurrence — not in surviving the acute episode. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single 80-patient randomised trial caps the stamp, and the procedure needs expertise that is not everywhere available (the DRAC 1 authors make the same condition). Product naming: the fetched DRAC 1 record does not name the specific lumen-apposing stent product, and this shelf does not guess it.

cards.headline: DRAC 1 (Teoh 2021): EUS-guided gallbladder drainage cut 1-year adverse events to 25.6% vs 77.5% with percutaneous drainage, and reintervention after 30 days to 2.6% vs 30% — with no difference in clinical success or 30-day mortality
cards.summary: DRAC 1 (Teoh 2021): EUS-guided gallbladder drainage cut 1-year adverse events to 25.6% vs 77.5% with percutaneous drainage, and reintervention after 30 days to 2.6% vs 30% — with no difference in clinical success or 30-day mortality
cards.people: 80 consecutive patients with acute calculous cholecystitis judged at very high risk for cholecystectomy, randomised internationally to EUS-guided gallbladder drainage with a lumen-apposing metal stent (39 analysed) or percutaneous cholecystostomy (40 analysed) as definitive treatment. Primary outcome was the 1-year adverse-event rate.
cards.result: 1-year adverse events: 10/39 (25.6%) with EUS-GBD vs 31/40 (77.5%) with PT-GBD (p<0.001). 30-day adverse events 12.8% vs 47.5% (p=0.010); reinterventions after 30 days 2.6% vs 30% (p=0.001); unplanned readmissions 15.4% vs 50% (p=0.002); recurrent cholecystitis 2.6% vs 20% (p=0.029); post-procedure pain scores and analgesic use were lower with EUS-GBD (p=0.034). Technical success (97.4% vs 100%), clinical success (92.3% vs 92.5%) and 30-day mortality (7.7% vs 10%) did not differ significantly. Percutaneous drainage predicted recurrent cholecystitis (OR 5.63, 95% CI 1.20–53.90 — relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Only 80 patients, unblinded (unavoidably), from expert centres: the size of the adverse-event gap (driven largely by drain-related problems in the percutaneous arm) may shrink where percutaneous aftercare is better or EUS expertise is thinner. The fetched record does not name the specific lumen-apposing metal stent product used, so no product is named on this card — stents are not interchangeable and the result should not be transferred to a named device the trial may not have used.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Hayat 2024): across 6 comparative studies, EUS-guided drainage with lumen-apposing metal stents had fewer delayed adverse events (OR 0.21) and fewer overall adverse events (OR 0.43) than percutaneous cholecystostomy, and a shorter hospital stay
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Hayat 2024): across 6 comparative studies, EUS-guided drainage with lumen-apposing metal stents had fewer delayed adverse events (OR 0.21) and fewer overall adverse events (OR 0.43) than percutaneous cholecystostomy, and a shorter hospital stay
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies directly comparing EUS-guided gallbladder drainage using lumen-apposing metal stents (EUS-GBD-LAMS) with percutaneous cholecystostomy tubes in high-risk surgical patients with acute cholecystitis; early, delayed and overall adverse events, hospital stay, reinterventions and readmissions were compared using random-effects odds ratios (relative measures).
cards.result: Early adverse events were similar between the two approaches. EUS-GBD-LAMS was associated with lower delayed adverse events (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.07–0.61; P≤.01) and lower overall adverse events (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30–0.61; P≤.01), and with a shorter hospital stay, than percutaneous cholecystostomy.
cards.watchOut: Six studies, mostly non-randomised: patients offered EUS-GBD may differ systematically from those given a percutaneous drain (anatomy, centre, era), and odds ratios from such comparisons overstate certainty. The endpoint is safety and burden, not survival — no mortality advantage is claimed or shown.
cards.source: Hayat U et al. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2024. PMID: 37871846. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Boregowda 2023): across 11 studies, EUS-guided drainage had fewer adverse events (OR 0.35) and far fewer reinterventions (OR 0.18) than percutaneous drainage, with no difference in clinical success (OR 1.34, not significant)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Boregowda 2023): across 11 studies, EUS-guided drainage had fewer adverse events (OR 0.35) and far fewer reinterventions (OR 0.18) than percutaneous drainage, with no difference in clinical success (OR 1.34, not significant)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 eligible studies comparing EUS-guided gallbladder drainage with percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage for acute cholecystitis in patients not suitable for surgery (477 patients underwent EUS-GBD and 698 percutaneous drainage, as reported). Primary outcomes were technical success, clinical success and adverse events; pooled odds ratios are relative measures.
cards.result: EUS-GBD had better technical success as reported (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.17–0.94; p=0.04 — direction as printed in the record), significantly fewer adverse events (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.21–0.61) and lower reintervention rates (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.05–0.57). Clinical success did not differ (OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.65–2.79; p=0.42).
cards.watchOut: The component studies are predominantly observational and include the DRAC 1 population's literature ecosystem, so this pool is not independent of the randomised trial on the first card. One pooled figure (technical success, OR 0.40) is printed in the record with a direction that sits oddly against its own conclusion — a reminder to rest on the adverse-event and reintervention estimates, which agree across both meta-analyses and the trial.
cards.source: Boregowda U et al. Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided Gallbladder Drainage versus Percutaneous Gallbladder Drainage for Acute Cholecystitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: EUS-guided drainage and percutaneous drainage settle the acute attack equally well (~92% clinical success), but the percutaneous route carries roughly triple the downstream burden of adverse events, readmissions and reinterventions
cards.summary: Synthesis: EUS-guided drainage and percutaneous drainage settle the acute attack equally well (~92% clinical success), but the percutaneous route carries roughly triple the downstream burden of adverse events, readmissions and reinterventions
cards.people: One randomised trial (DRAC 1, 80 patients) and two meta-analyses (6 comparative studies focused on lumen-apposing metal stents; 11 studies overall) in high-surgical-risk acute cholecystitis.
cards.result: Clinical success ~92% in both arms of the trial; 30-day mortality 7.7% vs 10% (no difference). Downstream: 1-year adverse events 25.6% vs 77.5% (trial); pooled overall adverse events OR 0.43 and reintervention OR 0.18 favouring EUS-guided drainage (relative measures). PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for EUS-guided drainage on adverse events and reintervention — not on mortality.
cards.watchOut: Everything favourable comes from expert-centre data and mostly observational comparisons; the trial's own authors condition their recommendation on local expertise being available after multidisciplinary discussion. Where that expertise is absent, percutaneous drainage remains the default — this shelf compares the two drains, not either against surgery.

shelves.title: Pre-endoscopy erythromycin in upper GI bleeding: a clearer stomach (82% vs 33% in the largest trial) and fewer second-look endoscopies — a visualisation benefit from small trials, with no mortality evidence
shelves.question: In adults with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding going to endoscopy, does pre-endoscopy intravenous erythromycin improve gastric visualisation and reduce repeat endoscopy compared with placebo or no prokinetic?
shelves.balance: A small-trial base that agrees on a process outcome — not on survival. The largest single trial (Frossard 2002, PMID 12105828; n=105) found a clear stomach at endoscopy in 82% after intravenous erythromycin vs 33% after placebo, and halved second-look endoscopy (6 vs 17 cases). Two meta-analyses of the same small trials point the same way: adequate gastric visualisation OR 4.89 across 4 studies totalling 269 patients (PMID 21561232) and OR 3.43 across 6 studies totalling 558 patients, with second endoscopy OR 0.47 (PMID 24045593) — odds ratios are relative measures, and the absolute gains depend on how bloody the stomach would otherwise be. No trial or pool shows a mortality benefit, and none was powered to: the honest claim is a cleaner, shorter first endoscopy and fewer repeat procedures. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction across small trials and their meta-analyses, resting on visualisation and repeat-endoscopy outcomes only.

cards.headline: Frossard 2002: a single 250 mg intravenous erythromycin bolus 20 minutes before endoscopy gave a clear stomach in 82% vs 33% on placebo, and cut second-look endoscopy from 17 to 6 cases (n=105)
cards.summary: Frossard 2002: a single 250 mg intravenous erythromycin bolus 20 minutes before endoscopy gave a clear stomach in 82% vs 33% on placebo, and cut second-look endoscopy from 17 to 6 cases (n=105)
cards.people: 105 patients admitted within 12 hours of haematemesis, randomised double-blind to intravenous erythromycin 250 mg (n=51) or placebo (n=54) 20 minutes before emergency endoscopy. Primary endpoint was endoscopic yield (objective and subjective visibility scores and procedure duration); secondary endpoints included second-look endoscopy, transfusion and hospital stay.
cards.result: A clear stomach was found in 82% of the erythromycin group vs 33% of the placebo group (P<0.001), a difference that remained significant in patients with cirrhosis. Endoscopy was shorter (13.7 vs 16.4 minutes; P=0.036) and second-look endoscopy was needed in 6 vs 17 cases (P=0.018). Hospital stay and units transfused did not differ significantly. No complications were noted.
cards.watchOut: The biggest single trial is still only 105 patients from one centre in 2002, and its endpoints are visibility scores and repeat procedures — it says nothing about rebleeding or death. Erythromycin here is a single pre-procedure motilin-agonist dose, not an antibiotic course; QT prolongation and drug interactions are the cautions the trial was too small to quantify.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Szary 2011): across 4 small trials totalling 269 patients, pre-endoscopy erythromycin improved gastric visualisation (OR 4.89) and reduced second endoscopy (OR 0.42)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Szary 2011): across 4 small trials totalling 269 patients, pre-endoscopy erythromycin improved gastric visualisation (OR 4.89) and reduced second endoscopy (OR 0.42)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 4 studies (total N=269) of erythromycin infusion before endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, pooling visualisation of the gastric mucosa, need for a second endoscopy and units transfused (odds ratios are relative measures).
cards.result: Visualisation of the gastric mucosa improved significantly with erythromycin (OR 4.89, 95% CI 2.85–8.38; p<0.01) and the need for a second endoscopy fell (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.24–0.74; p<0.01). Units transfused showed only a trend (weighted mean difference −0.48; 95% CI −0.97 to 0.01; p=0.05).
cards.watchOut: Four trials and 269 patients is a thin base: the pooled odds ratio of 4.89 looks dramatic partly because the control-group visualisation rates were low and the trials small. This pool and the 2013 pool on the next card share component trials — they are two analyses of substantially the same evidence, not two independent confirmations.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Theivanayagam 2013): across 6 randomised trials totalling 558 patients, erythromycin improved visualisation (OR 3.43), reduced second endoscopy (OR 0.47), transfusion (−0.41 units) and hospital stay (−1.51 days)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Theivanayagam 2013): across 6 randomised trials totalling 558 patients, erythromycin improved visualisation (OR 3.43), reduced second endoscopy (OR 0.47), transfusion (−0.41 units) and hospital stay (−1.51 days)
cards.people: Meta-analysis restricted to randomised controlled trials of erythromycin infusion before endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: 6 studies, total N=558. Primary outcomes were gastric-mucosa visualisation and need for second endoscopy; secondary outcomes included transfusion, hospital stay and procedure duration (odds ratios are relative measures).
cards.result: Visualisation improved (OR 3.43, 95% CI 1.81–6.50; P<0.01) and second endoscopy fell (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.26–0.83; P=0.01) with erythromycin. Units transfused were lower (weighted mean difference −0.41; 95% CI −0.82 to −0.01; P=0.04) and hospital stay shorter (weighted mean difference −1.51 days; 95% CI −2.45 to −0.56; P<0.01). No mortality outcome was demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: The transfusion and length-of-stay differences are small, rest on few events, and come from the same handful of small trials as every other estimate on this shelf. Nothing here supports giving erythromycin to improve survival — the case is operational: a clearer first look and fewer repeat scopes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent, moderate-sized gains in visualisation and repeat-endoscopy from a meta-analytic total of 558 randomised patients — and no evidence on mortality
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent, moderate-sized gains in visualisation and repeat-endoscopy from a meta-analytic total of 558 randomised patients — and no evidence on mortality
cards.people: Component trials are small (the largest single trial randomised 105 patients); the two meta-analyses pool 269 (4 trials) and 558 (6 trials) patients respectively, with overlapping components.
cards.result: Visualisation: OR 4.89 (4 trials) and OR 3.43 (6 trials), both relative measures. Second endoscopy: OR 0.42–0.47. Absolute anchor from the largest trial: clear stomach 82% vs 33%; second-look 6 vs 17 of ~52 patients per arm. Mortality: not shown to differ in any carded report. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for visualisation and avoiding repeat endoscopy.
cards.watchOut: Do not add the two meta-analytic totals together — they double-count the same small trials. The evidence predates modern high-dose PPI and early-endoscopy pathways, so the size of the operational gain in a current unit may be smaller than the pooled estimates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Frossard JL et al. Gastroenterology. 2002 (PMID: 12105828); Szary NM et al. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2011 (PMID: 21561232); Theivanayagam S et al. Saudi journal of gastroenterology. 2013 (PMID: 24045593).

shelves.title: Haemostatic powder TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) for non-variceal upper GI bleeding: SPLIT by indication — strong immediate haemostasis in tumour oozing, no rebleeding or mortality benefit anywhere, and not definitive therapy for peptic ulcers
shelves.question: In adults with non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does haemostatic powder TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) achieve haemostasis and prevent rebleeding compared with standard endoscopic therapy?
shelves.balance: SPLIT by indication — the powder is good at stopping bleeding now and unproven at changing what happens next, and the mix differs by bleeding type. The tested product is Hemospray (TC-325, Cook Medical) — named throughout because haemostatic powders are not interchangeable. In non-variceal bleeding overall, a meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (362 patients; 48% peptic ulcer, 35% malignancy) found no significant difference in primary haemostasis versus standard endoscopic therapy (RR 1.09, relative) but fewer haemostasis failures with TC-325 (RR 0.30) and no difference in rebleeding (RR 1.13) (PMID 36968978). In tumour bleeding specifically, immediate haemostasis is the powder's strength: a 19-study meta-analysis found much higher immediate haemostasis than standard therapy (OR 17.14, relative) with comparable rebleeding (PMID 39012642), yet the one randomised trial in malignant bleeding (n=59) achieved haemostasis in all TC-325 cases without reducing 30-day mortality (28.6% vs 19.4%, not significant) or rebleeding (PMID 36262517). In peptic-ulcer-predominant bleeding, the pilot randomised comparison against clipping (n=39) found equal primary haemostasis (100% vs 90%) but more additional procedures needed at second look in the powder arm (PMID 30927124). PROPOSED SPLIT: a useful immediate-haemostasis and rescue tool — most defensible in diffuse tumour oozing — with no demonstrated rebleeding or mortality advantage in any indication.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of RCTs (Deliwala 2023): in 5 randomised trials (362 patients; 48% peptic ulcer, 35% malignancy), TC-325 did not beat standard therapy on primary haemostasis (RR 1.09, NS) or rebleeding (RR 1.13, NS), but haemostasis failure was less frequent (RR 0.30)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of RCTs (Deliwala 2023): in 5 randomised trials (362 patients; 48% peptic ulcer, 35% malignancy), TC-325 did not beat standard therapy on primary haemostasis (RR 1.09, NS) or rebleeding (RR 1.13, NS), but haemostasis failure was less frequent (RR 0.30)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials comparing TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) with standard endoscopic therapy (epinephrine injection, electrocautery, haemoclips or combinations) in non-variceal gastrointestinal bleeding: 362 patients (178 TC-325, 184 standard), mean age 65; bleeding was Forrest IB (oozing) in 73%. Risk ratios are relative measures.
cards.result: Primary haemostasis: no significant difference (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.95–1.25; P=0.2), including in oozing/spurting bleeding (RR 1.13; P=0.08). Failure to achieve haemostasis was higher with standard therapy than with TC-325 (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.12–0.77; P=0.01). Rebleeding did not differ (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.62–2.07; P=0.8), nor did length of stay. Rescue interventions (angiography) were more frequent after standard therapy (RR 0.68 favouring TC-325; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes indications (peptic ulcer 48%, malignancy 35%, other 17%) that behave differently — the indication-split cards below are the honest read. 'Failure to achieve haemostasis' and 'primary haemostasis' point in seemingly opposite directions because they are defined differently across the small component trials; the rebleeding estimate (RR 1.13, CI 0.62–2.07) is too wide to exclude harm or benefit.

cards.headline: Tumour-bleeding meta-analysis (Abosheaishaa 2024): across 19 studies, Hemospray achieved immediate haemostasis far more often than standard therapy (OR 17.14) in GI tumour bleeding, with comparable 14- and 30-day rebleeding
cards.summary: Tumour-bleeding meta-analysis (Abosheaishaa 2024): across 19 studies, Hemospray achieved immediate haemostasis far more often than standard therapy (OR 17.14) in GI tumour bleeding, with comparable 14- and 30-day rebleeding
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, tumour bleeding (Abosheaishaa 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies of Hemospray (TC-325, Cook Medical) for gastrointestinal bleeding related to malignant tumours, including comparative studies against standard endoscopic treatment and non-comparative series (odds ratios are relative measures).
cards.result: Immediate haemostasis was higher with Hemospray than with standard endoscopic treatment (OR 17.14, 95% CI 4.27–68.86). Rebleeding at 14 and 30 days was comparable between groups. Need for non-endoscopic haemostasis (supplementary interventions) was lower with Hemospray (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30–0.87). No adverse events were confirmed as directly linked to Hemospray in the included studies.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 17 with a confidence interval running to 69 is a small-study artefact pattern: most included studies are non-comparative series in which 'immediate haemostasis' after spraying an oozing tumour is close to definitional. The trustworthy half of this card is the comparative rebleeding result — no difference — which matches the randomised trial on the next card.

cards.headline: Malignant-bleeding RCT (Martins 2022): TC-325 achieved initial haemostasis in every treated case (28 patients) but did NOT reduce 30-day mortality (28.6% vs 19.4%, NS) or 30-day rebleeding (32.1% vs 19.4%, NS) versus best clinical management
cards.summary: Malignant-bleeding RCT (Martins 2022): TC-325 achieved initial haemostasis in every treated case (28 patients) but did NOT reduce 30-day mortality (28.6% vs 19.4%, NS) or 30-day rebleeding (32.1% vs 19.4%, NS) versus best clinical management
cards.people: 62 patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding from malignancy randomised to TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) or a control group in which endoscopic treatment was not mandatory; 59 were analysed (28 TC-325, 31 control). Primary outcome was 30-day mortality; active bleeding was seen in 22 TC-325 and 19 control patients.
cards.result: Successful initial haemostasis with TC-325 was achieved in all cases. Additional therapy (radiotherapy, surgery or arterial embolisation) was used equally (42.9% vs 58.1%; P=0.243). There were no significant differences in 30-day mortality (28.6% vs 19.4%; P=0.406), 30-day rebleeding (32.1% vs 19.4%; P=0.26), transfusion or hospital stay. Mortality was predicted by age, ECOG performance status 3–4 and AIMS65 score above 1 — the underlying cancer, not the bleeding episode's first treatment.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-nine patients cannot settle a mortality question in a population whose 30-day mortality is ~20–30% from cancer itself — but the direction is, if anything, against the powder on both mortality and rebleeding, so no downstream benefit can be claimed for tumour bleeding either. The control arm's optional endoscopic therapy also makes this a comparison against 'usual care', not against best standard endoscopic therapy.

cards.headline: Peptic-ulcer-predominant pilot RCT (Baracat 2020): TC-325 plus epinephrine achieved primary haemostasis in 100% vs 90% with clipping plus epinephrine (n=39; NS), but 5 powder patients needed an additional procedure at second look vs none with clips (P=0.04)
cards.summary: Peptic-ulcer-predominant pilot RCT (Baracat 2020): TC-325 plus epinephrine achieved primary haemostasis in 100% vs 90% with clipping plus epinephrine (n=39; NS), but 5 powder patients needed an additional procedure at second look vs none with clips (P=0.04)
cards.people: 39 patients with non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding and an actively bleeding lesion (peptic ulcer the most frequent aetiology) randomised in a pilot trial to TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) plus epinephrine injection or endoscopic clipping plus epinephrine injection; all underwent second-look endoscopy.
cards.result: Primary haemostasis was achieved in all Hemospray cases and in 90% of the clipping group (p=0.487). Five patients in the Hemospray group needed an additional haemostatic procedure during second-look endoscopy, versus none in the clipping group (p=0.04). Rebleeding, emergency surgery and mortality were similar. No toxicity, allergy or obstruction events were observed with Hemospray.
cards.watchOut: A 39-patient pilot: the second-look finding (5 vs 0) is the mechanistically important signal — the powder's haemostatic layer is temporary and does not treat the vessel — but with numbers this small it is a warning, not a verdict. It supports using TC-325 as an adjunct or temporiser in ulcer bleeding, not as definitive monotherapy where clipping or thermal therapy is feasible.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by indication — immediate haemostasis is the powder's proven ground (strongest in diffuse tumour oozing); rebleeding and mortality benefits are unproven everywhere
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by indication — immediate haemostasis is the powder's proven ground (strongest in diffuse tumour oozing); rebleeding and mortality benefits are unproven everywhere
cards.people: Carded evidence: a 5-trial randomised meta-analysis (362 patients, mixed non-variceal bleeding), a 19-study tumour-bleeding meta-analysis, a 59-patient randomised trial in malignant bleeding, and a 39-patient pilot randomised trial in ulcer-predominant bleeding — all of the one tested product, Hemospray (TC-325, Cook Medical).
cards.result: Immediate haemostasis: no significant advantage over standard therapy in the mixed randomised pool (RR 1.09) but fewer outright failures (RR 0.30) and a large immediate-haemostasis advantage in tumour bleeding series (OR 17.14, relative, small-study-prone). Rebleeding: no difference in any carded comparison (RR 1.13 mixed; 32.1% vs 19.4% NS in the malignant-bleeding trial). Mortality: no difference shown (28.6% vs 19.4%, NS). PROPOSED SPLIT (by indication): reasonable as an immediate/temporising haemostatic — most defensible for diffuse malignant oozing — not a substitute for definitive therapy in peptic ulcer bleeding.
cards.watchOut: Every favourable number is about the first minutes of the procedure; every neutral number is about the following 30 days. Quoting the tumour-series OR of 17 without its confidence interval (4.27–68.86) or its non-comparative base would mislead — and none of this evidence transfers to other haemostatic powders, which differ in composition and have their own (separate) trial literature.

shelves.title: Intermittent vs continuous-infusion high-dose PPI after endoscopic haemostasis for bleeding peptic ulcer: non-inferior within a prespecified 3% margin in the randomised meta-analysis — not proven equivalent
shelves.question: In adults with bleeding peptic ulcer successfully treated endoscopically, does intermittent high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy prevent rebleeding compared with continuous-infusion high-dose PPI?
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence, pooled, meets a prespecified non-inferiority standard — it does not prove the two regimens identical. Sachar's meta-analysis (PMID 25201154) tested intermittent PPI against the guideline regimen (80 mg bolus then 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) in endoscopically treated high-risk bleeding ulcers, with a non-inferiority margin set in advance at a 3% absolute risk difference for 7-day rebleeding: the observed absolute difference was −2.64% (favouring intermittent), and the upper boundary of its one-sided 95% CI (−0.28%) sat well inside the margin. The relative risk of 7-day rebleeding was 0.72 (a relative measure), and no secondary outcome (30-day or 3-day rebleeding, mortality, urgent intervention, transfusion, stay) showed increased risk with intermittent dosing. Two later retrospective cohorts (n=446, PMID 35135340; n=335, PMID 34889253) found no adjusted disadvantage for intermittent dosing — but both are observational, and in both the continuous-infusion patients were sicker, which is exactly the confounding that makes their unadjusted numbers untrustworthy. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE — intermittent high-dose PPI is a reasonable substitute within the meta-analysis's 3% non-inferiority margin; 'equivalent' would overstate what a non-inferiority pool of small trials establishes.

cards.headline: Sachar 2014 meta-analysis: intermittent PPI met the prespecified 3% non-inferiority margin for 7-day rebleeding versus bolus-plus-continuous-infusion (absolute difference −2.64%; upper CI boundary −0.28%; RR 0.72)
cards.summary: Sachar 2014 meta-analysis: intermittent PPI met the prespecified 3% non-inferiority margin for 7-day rebleeding versus bolus-plus-continuous-infusion (absolute difference −2.64%; upper CI boundary −0.28%; RR 0.72)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sachar 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in patients with endoscopically treated high-risk bleeding ulcers (active bleeding, non-bleeding visible vessel, adherent clot), comparing intermittent PPI regimens with the recommended 80 mg intravenous bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion for 72 hours. Searches ran to December 2013 plus 2009–2013 meeting abstracts. The non-inferiority hypothesis and its margin — an absolute risk difference of 3% for the primary outcome, rebleeding within 7 days — were defined before the review began.
cards.result: Rebleeding within 7 days: risk ratio 0.72 (upper boundary of the one-sided 95% CI 0.97 — a relative measure) and absolute risk difference −2.64% (upper boundary −0.28%), well below the predefined 3% non-inferiority margin. Risk ratios for rebleeding within 3 and 30 days, mortality and urgent interventions were all below 1, and mean differences for transfusion and hospital stay were below 0 — no summary estimate showed increased risk with intermittent therapy; upper boundaries of the 95% CIs for absolute risk differences were under 1.50% for all rebleeding outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority within a 3% absolute margin is not proof of equivalence: the pooled trials were small and used varying intermittent regimens, and the margin itself is a judgement call — a clinician who regards 3 extra rebleeds per 100 patients as important should read this as 'not shown worse by more than the margin', not 'the same'. The analysis also predates later trials, so its pool is the older randomised base.

cards.headline: Retrospective multicentre cohort (Leung 2022, observational): rebleeding was 23.0% with intermittent bolus vs 33.8% with continuous infusion unadjusted — but the difference vanished on multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.91–2.50)
cards.summary: Retrospective multicentre cohort (Leung 2022, observational): rebleeding was 23.0% with intermittent bolus vs 33.8% with continuous infusion unadjusted — but the difference vanished on multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.91–2.50)
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre review of 446 patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding treated during drug-shortage-driven policy switches: 209 received intermittent PPI boluses and 237 continuous infusion. Primary outcome was rebleeding; ICU and hospital stay, discharge disposition and in-hospital mortality were also compared.
cards.result: Unadjusted rebleeding was higher with continuous infusion (33.8% vs 23.0%; P=0.012), but multivariable analysis detected no difference (adjusted OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.91–2.50 for continuous vs intermittent — a relative measure). Hospital and ICU stay, discharge disposition and in-hospital mortality did not differ. The continuous-infusion group was systematically sicker: more liver disease (29.1% vs 20.1%), alcohol use disorder (28.3% vs 16.3%), variceal bleeding (6.3% vs 2.4%) and ICU admission (65.0% vs 32.5%).
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL: allocation was by hospital policy during shortages, not randomisation, and the case-mix gap (more variceal bleeding and ICU care in the infusion group) explains the unadjusted rebleeding gap. This cohort also mixes variceal with ulcer bleeding, whereas the randomised question is about endoscopically treated high-risk ulcers — it supports feasibility, nothing stronger.

cards.headline: Retrospective cohort (Hsieh 2021, observational): in 335 high-risk bleeding-ulcer patients, 7-day rebleeding was 11.2% on non-high-dose intermittent PPI vs 20.4% on high-dose continuous infusion (P=.021) — with the same confounding-by-severity caveat
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort (Hsieh 2021, observational): in 335 high-risk bleeding-ulcer patients, 7-day rebleeding was 11.2% on non-high-dose intermittent PPI vs 20.4% on high-dose continuous infusion (P=.021) — with the same confounding-by-severity caveat
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 335 patients with peptic ulcers treated with endoscopic haemostasis (2013–2015), comparing high-dose continuous infusion (80 mg loading then 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) with non-high-dose intermittent infusion (40 mg once or twice daily for 3 days). Primary endpoints were rebleeding and mortality within 7 days.
cards.result: Seven-day rebleeding: 20.4% (continuous) vs 11.2% (intermittent), P=.021; univariate Cox hazard ratio for continuous vs intermittent 1.93 (a relative measure; P=.021). Seven-day mortality did not differ significantly (12.1% vs 7.3%; P=.136). Length of stay and transfusion units also differed between groups in the reported analyses.
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL and single-country: clinicians chose the infusion for the patients they judged highest-risk, so the 'intermittent looks better' direction is the expected signature of confounding by indication, not evidence that infusion harms. Read together with the randomised meta-analysis, its only safe message is that intermittent dosing was not associated with worse outcomes in routine practice.

cards.people: Carded evidence: one meta-analysis of randomised trials in endoscopically treated high-risk bleeding ulcers (Sachar 2014), and two retrospective cohorts (446 and 335 patients) labelled observational.
cards.result: Seven-day rebleeding (randomised pool): absolute difference −2.64% favouring intermittent, upper CI boundary −0.28% against a 3% margin; RR 0.72 (relative). Mortality, urgent intervention, transfusion and stay: no estimate favoured continuous infusion. Observational cohorts: no adjusted disadvantage for intermittent dosing. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE — intermittent therapy is an acceptable substitute on this evidence; the stamp does not claim proven equivalence.
cards.watchOut: The whole randomised case rests on one meta-analysis of small, older trials with heterogeneous intermittent regimens (dose and interval varied). If a unit's intermittent regimen is weaker than the ones pooled (e.g. once-daily low dose), this shelf does not cover it — the pooled regimens were high-dose intermittent schedules.

shelves.title: Obefazimod in ulcerative colitis: published phase 2b only — all doses beat placebo on Mayo-score change at week 8 (n=254), durability open-label; ⚠ phase 3 ABTECT is congress/press-reported, not yet a journal report
shelves.question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis, does obefazimod induce and maintain clinical remission compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: Built on the published phase 2b programme only. In the randomised induction trial (Vermeire 2023, PMID 36075249; 254 patients), all three obefazimod doses (25, 50, 100 mg once daily) improved the modified Mayo score at week 8 significantly more than placebo (least-squares mean change −3.1 to −3.2 vs −1.9); headache was the commonest adverse event and was dose-related (42% at 100 mg vs 8% on placebo). In the 96-week open-label maintenance extension (PMID 40417999; 217 patients, no control group), clinical remission was 52.5% and endoscopic improvement 59.0% at week 96 by non-responder imputation — durability data, not comparative efficacy. ⚠ PHASE 3 STATUS: the ABTECT phase 3 induction/maintenance programme has been reported at congresses and in sponsor releases, but as of this build (November 2026) no full journal report of ABTECT was found on PubMed, so NO phase 3 numbers are carded or quoted on this shelf; any phase 3 figure circulating from congress/press reporting must be treated as unverified until a journal report exists. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Phase 2b induction RCT (Vermeire 2023): obefazimod 25, 50 and 100 mg all beat placebo on modified Mayo score change at week 8 (−3.1 to −3.2 vs −1.9; all p≤0.004) in 254 patients; headache in up to 42%
cards.summary: Phase 2b induction RCT (Vermeire 2023): obefazimod 25, 50 and 100 mg all beat placebo on modified Mayo score change at week 8 (−3.1 to −3.2 vs −1.9; all p≤0.004) in 254 patients; headache in up to 42%
cards.people: Phase 2b double-blind randomised placebo-controlled induction trial at 95 centres in 16 countries: 254 adults aged 18–75 with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis (modified Mayo score 5 or higher) and prior non-response or intolerance to conventional or advanced therapy, randomised to oral obefazimod (ABX464) 100 mg (n=64), 50 mg (n=63) or 25 mg (n=63) once daily, or placebo (n=64), for 8 weeks. Primary endpoint was change from baseline in modified Mayo score.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in modified Mayo score at week 8: −2.9 (100 mg), −3.2 (50 mg), −3.1 (25 mg) vs −1.9 on placebo — all significantly greater than placebo (p=0.0039, p=0.0003 and p=0.0010 respectively). Headache was the most frequent adverse event and dose-related: 42% (100 mg), 30% (50 mg), 21% (25 mg) vs 8% on placebo; severe (grade 3) headache occurred in 5%, 3% and 2% of the obefazimod groups and no placebo patients. The only serious adverse event reported in 2 or more patients in any group was ulcerative colitis itself.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a score change, and the fetched record does not report the trial's clinical-remission rates — this shelf does not quote remission figures for the induction trial because they are not in the record verified at build. Eight weeks is short, the dose-response is flat across a fourfold dose range, and headache at 100 mg (42%) is a real tolerability cost. This is a phase 2 result: no phase 3 journal report existed at build (see balance).
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. ABX464 (obefazimod) for moderate-to-severe, active ulcerative colitis: a phase 2b, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled induction trial and 48 week, open-label extension. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022 (journal record; issue 2023). PMID: 36075249. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04023396. cards.headline: 96-week open-label maintenance (Vermeire 2025) — uncontrolled extension of the same programme: clinical remission 52.5% and endoscopic improvement 59.0% at week 96 among 217 patients on obefazimod 50 mg
cards.summary: 96-week open-label maintenance (Vermeire 2025) — uncontrolled extension of the same programme: clinical remission 52.5% and endoscopic improvement 59.0% at week 96 among 217 patients on obefazimod 50 mg
cards.type: Open-label uncontrolled maintenance extension — second report of the phase 2b programme (Vermeire 2025)
cards.people: Open-label maintenance study: 217 of 222 eligible patients from the phase 2b induction trial entered and received obefazimod 50 mg once daily for 96 weeks, regardless of their induction response or original allocation; 164 (75.6%) completed week 96. Efficacy used non-responder imputation; there was no placebo or comparator group.
cards.result: Clinical response: 81.6% at week 48 and 72.8% at week 96. Clinical remission: 54.8% at week 48 and 52.5% at week 96. Endoscopic improvement: 61.3% and 59.0%; endoscopic remission 33.2% and 35.9%. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 68.2%; the most frequent were COVID-19 (14.3%), headache (11.5%), ulcerative colitis (7.8%) and nasopharyngitis (6.9%). No new safety risks emerged over 96 weeks, per the authors.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled: everyone received the drug, entry was regardless of induction response, and a quarter of patients had left by week 96 — the week-96 percentages describe patients who stayed on a drug they were already tolerating, and cannot be compared with any other therapy's maintenance rates. Non-responder imputation softens but does not remove that selection.
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. Obefazimod in patients with moderate-to-severely active ulcerative colitis: efficacy and safety analysis from the 96-week open-label maintenance phase 2b study. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2025. PMID: 40417999. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04023396. cards.headline: Network meta-analysis (Olivera 2026): among 33 induction trials of advanced UC therapies, obefazimod ranked among the highest for clinical remission in advanced-therapy-naïve patients — on the strength of its phase 2b trial alone
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis (Olivera 2026): among 33 induction trials of advanced UC therapies, obefazimod ranked among the highest for clinical remission in advanced-therapy-naïve patients — on the strength of its phase 2b trial alone
cards.people: Updated systematic review and network meta-analysis of phase 3 randomised induction trials of approved or late-stage advanced therapies for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (33 trials, 17 therapies), with pairwise and frequentist random-effects network analyses and CINeMA confidence ratings, stratified by prior advanced-therapy exposure. Obefazimod entered the network through its phase 2b induction trial — the only obefazimod data in the pool.
cards.result: Upadacitinib showed the highest overall relative efficacy for clinical remission (risk ratio 6.90, 95% CI 3.54–12.45 — a relative measure). In advanced-therapy-naïve patients, obefazimod and upadacitinib showed the highest efficacy; in advanced-therapy-experienced patients, upadacitinib, ustekinumab and tofacitinib ranked highest. The authors conclude that novel therapies such as obefazimod may represent highly effective alternatives, while noting lower confidence in the safety estimates. The fetched record reports no obefazimod-specific risk ratio, so none is quoted here.
cards.watchOut: A network ranking is not new obefazimod data: obefazimod's position rests entirely on the single 254-patient phase 2b trial carded above, compared indirectly against phase 3 programmes with thousands of patients. Rankings among the top therapies in such networks are unstable to single-trial changes and should not be read as evidence that obefazimod matches upadacitinib head-to-head — no such trial exists.
cards.source: Olivera PA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Advanced Therapies as Induction Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis: An Updated Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology. 2026. PMID: 42838315. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42024547849 (as stated in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 2b programme shows a real, dose-flat induction effect on disease activity and 2-year open-label durability — with phase 3 (ABTECT) still ⚠ congress/press-reported only at build
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2b programme shows a real, dose-flat induction effect on disease activity and 2-year open-label durability — with phase 3 (ABTECT) still ⚠ congress/press-reported only at build
cards.people: Published evidence carded: one randomised phase 2b induction trial (254 patients) and its uncontrolled 96-week open-label maintenance extension (217 patients) — a single programme (NCT04023396), sponsored by Abivax.
cards.result: Induction: modified Mayo change −2.9 to −3.2 across doses vs −1.9 on placebo at week 8 (all p≤0.004). Maintenance (uncontrolled): remission 52.5% at week 96. Main harm: dose-related headache (21–42% during induction vs 8% on placebo). ⚠ ABTECT phase 3 results are congress/press-reported only as of November 2026 — no journal report found, no phase 3 numbers carded. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 programme.
cards.watchOut: All efficacy cards trace to one sponsor programme and substantially the same patients; the network meta-analysis adds no new obefazimod patients. The shelf must be re-ruled when a full ABTECT journal report appears; until then, any phase 3 efficacy figure quoted from a congress abstract or press release should be labelled ⚠ congress/press-reported wherever it is repeated.

shelves.title: Duvakitug (anti-TL1A) in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease (RELIEVE UCCD, phase 2b): 900 mg roughly doubled placebo remission/response at week 14 — ⚠ phase-2 only, with a Bayesian primary analysis
shelves.question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, does duvakitug (anti-TL1A) induce clinical remission or response compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: Phase-2 evidence only, analysed Bayesianly — both facts are on the face. RELIEVE UCCD randomised separate ulcerative colitis (137 patients) and Crohn's disease (138 in the modified intention-to-treat set) cohorts to duvakitug 450 mg or 900 mg every 2 weeks (after a 2250 mg loading dose) or placebo for 14 weeks. In ulcerative colitis, clinical remission was 36% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 20% on placebo (Reinisch 2026, PMID 42462750). In Crohn's disease, endoscopic response was 26% and 48% vs 13% on placebo (Jairath 2026, PMID 42462749). ⚠ ANALYSIS METHOD: both trials' primary analyses were Bayesian — a dose was declared successful if the posterior probability that its response rate exceeded placebo reached a prespecified threshold (0.90 or greater; the papers report posterior probabilities of 0.94 to >0.99 and differences in posterior mean rates with credible intervals, not conventional p-values or confidence intervals). The 450 mg Crohn's result (posterior probability 0.94, credible interval for the difference including −3%) is correspondingly softer than the 900 mg results. A class-level systematic review of anti-TL1A phase 2 trials (PMID 42726749) is directionally consistent (duvakitug dose-response in UC; Crohn's endoscopic response RR 3.67 at 900 mg, a relative measure). Adverse events were similar to placebo in both trials. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 only, one programme, Bayesian primary analysis.

cards.headline: RELIEVE UCCD ulcerative colitis (Reinisch 2026): clinical remission at week 14 in 36% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 20% on placebo — Bayesian primary analysis, posterior probabilities 0.95 and >0.99
cards.summary: RELIEVE UCCD ulcerative colitis (Reinisch 2026): clinical remission at week 14 in 36% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 20% on placebo — Bayesian primary analysis, posterior probabilities 0.95 and >0.99
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial, Bayesian primary analysis (Reinisch 2026, RELIEVE UCCD — UC cohort)
cards.people: Multicentre phase 2b randomised placebo-controlled trial: 137 adults aged 18–75 with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis (31% previously exposed to an approved advanced therapy) received a 2250 mg subcutaneous loading dose of duvakitug then 450 mg (n=47) or 900 mg (n=46) every 2 weeks, or placebo loading then placebo (n=44); modified intention-to-treat. Primary endpoint was clinical remission (modified Mayo score) at week 14.
cards.result: Clinical remission: 17/47 (36%) on 450 mg and 22/46 (48%) on 900 mg vs 9/44 (20%) on placebo. Differences in posterior mean response rates vs placebo: 15% (95% credible interval −3 to 33) for 450 mg and 26% (8 to 44) for 900 mg, with posterior probabilities of superiority of 0.95 and >0.99 against the prespecified success threshold of 0.90. Adverse events: 49% (450 mg), 43% (900 mg) and 52% (placebo); one serious adverse event in the 900 mg group (non-infective oophoritis) and one on placebo (intracranial haemorrhage).
cards.watchOut: ⚠ BAYESIAN ANALYSIS: the headline is a posterior probability of beating placebo, not a frequentist p-value, and the 450 mg dose's credible interval for the remission difference includes −3% — its 'success' rests on the Bayesian decision rule (threshold 0.90), not on a confidence interval excluding zero. Fourteen weeks, 137 patients, phase 2: no maintenance, safety-database or phase 3 data yet. Funded by Teva and Sanofi.
cards.source: Reinisch W et al. Efficacy and safety of duvakitug in patients with ulcerative colitis (RELIEVE UCCD): a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2026. PMID: 42462750. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05499130. cards.headline: RELIEVE UCCD Crohn's disease (Jairath 2026): endoscopic response at week 14 in 26% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 13% on placebo — Bayesian primary analysis; the 450 mg result is soft (posterior probability 0.94, credible interval −3 to 29)
cards.summary: RELIEVE UCCD Crohn's disease (Jairath 2026): endoscopic response at week 14 in 26% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 13% on placebo — Bayesian primary analysis; the 450 mg result is soft (posterior probability 0.94, credible interval −3 to 29)
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial, Bayesian primary analysis (Jairath 2026, RELIEVE UCCD — Crohn's cohort)
cards.people: The Crohn's disease cohort of the same phase 2b programme (NCT05499130): 139 patients randomised, 138 in the modified intention-to-treat population — duvakitug 450 mg (n=46), 900 mg (n=46) or placebo (n=46), after the same 2250 mg loading dose; 57% had previously been exposed to at least one advanced therapy. Primary endpoint was endoscopic response (50% or greater reduction in Simple Endoscopic Score for Crohn's Disease) at week 14.
cards.result: Endoscopic response: 12/46 (26%) on 450 mg and 22/46 (48%) on 900 mg vs 6/46 (13%) on placebo. Differences in posterior mean response rates: 13% (95% credible interval −3 to 29) for 450 mg and 33% (16 to 50) for 900 mg; posterior probabilities of superiority 0.94 and >0.99 against the 0.90 threshold. Adverse events: 67% (450 mg), 43% (900 mg), 48% (placebo); serious adverse events in 13% (450 mg), 2% (900 mg) and 11% (placebo). Most frequent events were nasopharyngitis and headache.
cards.watchOut: ⚠ BAYESIAN ANALYSIS, as on the UC card — and note the non-monotonic safety pattern (serious adverse events 13% at 450 mg vs 2% at 900 mg), which with ~46 patients per arm is most plausibly chance but is unresolved at this sample size. The endpoint is endoscopic response, not clinical remission or any longer-term outcome; 14 weeks is induction only.

cards.headline: Anti-TL1A class systematic review (Choi 2026): across the three phase 2 UC trials of the class, pooled clinical-remission RR was 2.56 vs placebo; duvakitug showed a dose-response, and in Crohn's its 900 mg endoscopic-response RR was 3.67
cards.summary: Anti-TL1A class systematic review (Choi 2026): across the three phase 2 UC trials of the class, pooled clinical-remission RR was 2.56 vs placebo; duvakitug showed a dose-response, and in Crohn's its 900 mg endoscopic-response RR was 3.67
cards.type: Systematic review of phase 2 trials, class-level (Choi 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review of all phase 2 anti-TL1A antibody trials in inflammatory bowel disease (tulisokibart, afimkibart and duvakitug): 6 studies from 5 trials, 804 patients; the meta-analysis pooled the three randomised ulcerative colitis trials. Risk ratios are relative measures; GRADE certainty for UC efficacy outcomes was rated moderate.
cards.result: In ulcerative colitis, pooled risk ratio vs placebo was 2.56 (95% CI 1.60–4.09) for clinical remission and 2.13 (1.44–3.16) for endoscopic improvement, with no between-study heterogeneity (I²=0.0%); risk differences were +22.2% (NNT 4.5) and +22.6% (NNT 4.4). Duvakitug showed a dose-response, with 900 mg approximately doubling the effect of 450 mg. In Crohn's disease, duvakitug 900 mg achieved endoscopic response RR 3.67 vs placebo (95% CI 1.64–8.20; risk difference +34.8%, NNT 2.9). Serious adverse event rates were low and comparable to or lower than placebo across trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 2b programme, two diseases — remission/response roughly doubles placebo at 900 mg, analysed Bayesianly; phase 3 confirmation does not yet exist
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2b programme, two diseases — remission/response roughly doubles placebo at 900 mg, analysed Bayesianly; phase 3 confirmation does not yet exist
cards.people: Carded evidence: RELIEVE UCCD's two randomised cohorts (ulcerative colitis 137 patients; Crohn's disease 138 modified-ITT patients) from a single programme (Teva/Sanofi, NCT05499130), plus a class-level phase 2 systematic review (804 patients across three antibodies).
cards.result: Ulcerative colitis remission at week 14: 48% (900 mg) and 36% (450 mg) vs 20% placebo. Crohn's endoscopic response: 48% (900 mg) and 26% (450 mg) vs 13% placebo. ⚠ Primary analyses were Bayesian (posterior-probability decision rule, threshold 0.90); the 450 mg estimates are soft in both diseases (credible intervals include −3%). Adverse events were comparable to placebo in both cohorts. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2-only, single-programme evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert the Bayesian posterior probabilities into p-values or the credible intervals into confidence intervals when quoting this shelf — they are different quantities, and the 450 mg dose's case depends on the distinction. Maintenance efficacy, immunogenicity and longer-term safety of TL1A blockade (including any fibrosis benefit, the class's mechanistic promise) are untested in the carded reports.

shelves.title: Vedolizumab for chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (EARNEST)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA) for ulcerative colitis, does vedolizumab, compared with placebo, induce remission?
shelves.balance: One randomised trial only — a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. EARNEST (n = 102 randomised) is the first placebo-controlled trial in chronic pouchitis: modified Pouchitis Disease Activity Index (mPDAI)-defined remission at week 14 was 31% on vedolizumab vs 10% on placebo (difference 21 percentage points), with the advantage persisting in direction at week 34 and supported by a second report showing endoscopic improvement and mucosal healing. The population is small and rare (chronic pouchitis after IPAA for ulcerative colitis), every patient also received 4 weeks of ciprofloxacin, and there is no comparison against antibiotics alone as chronic therapy, other biologics, or surgery. Nothing here addresses patients whose pouchitis is not chronic, or pouch failure as an outcome.

cards.headline: EARNEST 2023 (primary report): mPDAI-defined remission at week 14 was 31% with vedolizumab vs 10% with placebo (difference 21 percentage points, P = 0.01), n = 102
cards.summary: EARNEST 2023 (primary report): mPDAI-defined remission at week 14 was 31% with vedolizumab vs 10% with placebo (difference 21 percentage points, P = 0.01), n = 102
cards.type: Phase 4 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (EARNEST), N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 102 adults with chronic pouchitis after IPAA for ulcerative colitis, randomised 1:1 (51 per group) to intravenous vedolizumab 300 mg or placebo on day 1 and at weeks 2, 6, 14, 22 and 30; all patients received concomitant ciprofloxacin from weeks 1 to 4. Primary endpoint: modified Pouchitis Disease Activity Index (mPDAI)-defined remission at week 14 — an mPDAI score of ≤4 with a reduction from baseline of ≥2 points (mPDAI range 0–12, based on clinical symptoms and endoscopic findings; higher = more severe).
cards.result: mPDAI-defined remission at week 14: 31% (16 of 51) with vedolizumab vs 10% (5 of 51) with placebo (difference 21 percentage points; 95% CI 5 to 38; P = 0.01). Differences also favoured vedolizumab for mPDAI-defined remission at week 34 (difference 17 percentage points; 95% CI 0 to 35), mPDAI-defined response at week 14 (difference 30 percentage points; 95% CI 8 to 48) and week 34 (difference 22 percentage points; 95% CI 2 to 40), and PDAI-defined remission at week 14 (difference 25 percentage points; 95% CI 8 to 41) and week 34 (difference 19 percentage points; 95% CI 2 to 37). Serious adverse events occurred in 3 of 51 (6%) on vedolizumab and 4 of 51 (8%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Small trial (n = 102) in a rare population — print the N. The endpoint is the precisely defined modified PDAI remission above, not the full PDAI; all patients received ciprofloxacin for the first 4 weeks, so this is vedolizumab on an antibiotic background, not vedolizumab alone.
cards.source: EARNEST — Travis S, Silverberg MS, Danese S, et al. Vedolizumab for the Treatment of Chronic Pouchitis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36988594. Registry ID: NCT02790138 (EudraCT 2015-003472-78). cards.headline: EARNEST mucosal-healing report 2025 (second report of the same trial): ulcer counts fell and 16.7% vs 2.5% achieved mucosal healing at week 14
cards.summary: EARNEST mucosal-healing report 2025 (second report of the same trial): ulcer counts fell and 16.7% vs 2.5% achieved mucosal healing at week 14
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, second report (EARNEST mucosal healing), Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025
cards.people: The same EARNEST population (adults with chronic pouchitis after IPAA; vedolizumab 300 mg IV vs placebo, NCT02790138), with centrally read endoscopic and histologic evaluation at baseline, week 14 and week 34. This is a second, explicitly labelled report of the one EARNEST trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Mean ulcer count on vedolizumab fell from 15.1 at baseline to 5.0 at week 14 and 2.7 at week 34, vs 11.8, 13.4 and 9.7 on placebo (vedolizumab vs placebo difference −8.4 [95% CI −14.3 to −2.6] at week 14 and −7.0 [−12.0 to −2.0] at week 34). Mucosal healing at week 14 was achieved by 16.7% vs 2.5% (difference 14.2 percentage points [95% CI 1.9 to 26.4]); Simple Endoscopic Score for Crohn's Disease remission at week 14 was 23.8% vs 7.5% (difference 16.3 percentage points). Patients with mucosal healing at week 14 had higher PDAI and quality-of-life remission rates at weeks 14 and 34 than those without.
cards.watchOut: One trial, two reports — do not count this as independent confirmation. Mucosal healing is an endoscopic/histologic endpoint; the clinical remission claim rests on the primary report (PMID 36988594).
