shelves.title: EUS-guided gastroenterostomy for malignant gastric outlet obstruction (ENDURO and DRA-GOO)
shelves.question: In adults with malignant gastric outlet obstruction in a palliative setting, does endoscopic ultrasound-guided gastroenterostomy (EUS-GE), compared with surgical gastrojejunostomy or enteral stenting, speed resumption of oral intake and reduce reintervention?
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials point the same way against two different comparators. ENDURO (n = 98, 12 Dutch academic and teaching hospitals) found EUS-GE superior to surgical gastrojejunostomy for time to resumption of solid oral intake (median 1 vs 3 days) and non-inferior for reintervention. DRA-GOO (n = 97, seven international sites) found EUS-GE markedly reduced 6-month reintervention vs uncovered duodenal stenting (4% vs 29%; risk ratio 0.15, a relative measure). Both are expertise-dependent procedures: ENDURO centres had to show experience in at least 20 LAMS placements and at least ten endoscopic gastroenterostomies before treating trial patients independently, so results may not transfer to low-volume settings. Neither trial showed a survival difference, and 30-day mortality in DRA-GOO was numerically higher with EUS-GE (21% vs 12%, not significant). Citation discipline: the original DRA-GOO report was retracted and republished; this shelf cites ONLY the republished version (PMID 40347959).

cards.headline: ENDURO 2025: solid oral intake resumed at a median of 1 day with EUS-GE vs 3 days with surgical gastrojejunostomy (HR 2.21, relative), and EUS-GE was non-inferior for reintervention, n = 98
cards.summary: ENDURO 2025: solid oral intake resumed at a median of 1 day with EUS-GE vs 3 days with surgical gastrojejunostomy (HR 2.21, relative), and EUS-GE was non-inferior for reintervention, n = 98
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (ENDURO), Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025
cards.people: 98 adults (48 EUS-GE, 50 surgical gastroenterostomy) with symptomatic malignant gastric outlet obstruction in a palliative setting, randomised at 12 Dutch academic and teaching hospitals. Centres could perform EUS-GE independently in the trial only with experience of at least 20 LAMS placements of any indication and at least ten endoscopic gastroenterostomies, with approved competence — an expertise-selected, Dutch academic-centre setting. Co-primary outcomes: time to resumption of solid oral intake (GOOS ≥2) and non-inferiority for persistent/recurrent obstructive symptoms requiring reintervention (non-inferiority margin 20%).
cards.result: Time to solid oral intake was shorter with EUS-GE: median 1 day (IQR 1–3) vs 3 days (1–6); hazard ratio 2.21 (95% CI 1.43 to 3.42; p = 0.0003) — a relative measure of the rate of resuming intake. EUS-GE was non-inferior for persistent/recurrent obstruction requiring reintervention: 5 (10%) vs 6 (12%); risk difference 1.6% (upper limit of 90% CI 8.9). Overall adverse events: 28 (58%) vs 32 (64%) (relative risk 0.91; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.25). One fatal event occurred in the EUS-GE group and three in the surgical group.
cards.watchOut: Expertise-dependent procedure in experienced Dutch centres — generalisability to low-volume centres is unproven. The hazard ratio is a relative measure; the absolute gain is a median of 2 days to solid intake. Non-inferiority margin for reintervention was wide (20%).

cards.headline: DRA-GOO 2025 (REPUBLISHED version — the original report was retracted): 6-month reintervention 4% with EUS-GE vs 29% with duodenal stenting (RR 0.15, relative), n = 97
cards.summary: DRA-GOO 2025 (REPUBLISHED version — the original report was retracted): 6-month reintervention 4% with EUS-GE vs 29% with duodenal stenting (RR 0.15, relative), n = 97
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (DRA-GOO, republished version), Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025
cards.people: 97 patients (48 EUS-GE, 49 uncovered duodenal metal stent) aged ≥18 with malignant gastric outlet obstruction from unresectable gastroduodenal or pancreatobiliary malignancy, gastric outlet obstruction score 0 (no oral intake) and ECOG performance status ≤3, at seven sites in Hong Kong, Belgium, Brazil, India, Italy and Spain. EUS-GE used a double balloon occluder technique. Primary outcome: reintervention within 6 months for stent dysfunction.
cards.result: Reintervention within 6 months: 2 (4%) with EUS-GE vs 14 (29%) with duodenal stenting (p = 0.0020; risk ratio 0.15 [95% CI 0.04 to 0.61] — a relative measure; absolute difference 25 percentage points). One-month gastric outlet obstruction score was better with EUS-GE (mean 2.41 vs 1.91; p = 0.012). There was no significant difference in duration of stent patency, technical success, clinical success or quality of life. Death within 30 days was 10 (21%) vs 6 (12%) (p = 0.286, not significant) and adverse events within 30 days were 11 (23%) vs 12 (24%).

cards.headline: ENDURO health-economic report 2026 (second report of the ENDURO trial): EUS-GE cost more per procedure but total in-hospital costs were lower
cards.summary: ENDURO health-economic report 2026 (second report of the ENDURO trial): EUS-GE cost more per procedure but total in-hospital costs were lower
cards.type: Randomised trial health-economic evaluation (ENDURO alongside-trial report), United European Gastroenterol J 2026
cards.people: The same 98 ENDURO patients (48 EUS-GE, 50 surgical gastrojejunostomy) at 12 Dutch hospitals; cost-utility evaluated from a healthcare perspective over a 1-month horizon. This is a second, explicitly labelled report of the ENDURO trial (primary report PMID 41061719), not a new trial.
cards.result: Mean intervention costs were higher for EUS-GE (€4,405.40) than for surgical gastrojejunostomy (€3,393.71), reflecting per-minute room prices of €8.64 for the endoscopy room and €11.78 for the operating room plus device costs; mean total in-hospital costs were nevertheless lower after EUS-GE (€5,172) than after surgery, consistent with the faster resumption of intake in the primary report.
cards.watchOut: One-month horizon and Dutch costing only; a cost report of the same 98 patients adds no new efficacy evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: EUS-GE beat surgery on speed of eating and beat stenting on reintervention, in expert centres (PMIDs 41061719, 40347959, 42247455)
cards.summary: Synthesis: EUS-GE beat surgery on speed of eating and beat stenting on reintervention, in expert centres (PMIDs 41061719, 40347959, 42247455)
cards.people: Adults with malignant gastric outlet obstruction in a palliative setting; total randomised base 195 patients across two trials (ENDURO 98; DRA-GOO 97), plus a cost report of ENDURO.
cards.result: Across both comparators, EUS-GE improved the patient-centred mechanics of palliation (faster solid intake vs surgery; far fewer reinterventions vs stenting) without a shown survival difference. shelves.title: Lumen-apposing metal stents vs plastic stents for pancreatic walled-off necrosis
shelves.question: In adults with pancreatic walled-off necrosis undergoing endoscopic drainage, do lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS), compared with double-pigtail plastic stents, improve treatment success and reduce adverse events?
shelves.balance: The randomised record is split, and the honest summary is 'no consistent advantage'. Bang et al. (n = 60) found non-superiority of LAMS with MORE stent-related adverse events (32.3% vs 6.9%); PROMETHEUS (n = 64) found similar clinical success and similar stent adverse events; a 2024 multicentre trial in infected walled-off necrosis (n = 46) found no difference in necrosectomy number but higher 8-week clinical success with a novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS; and a 2025 meta-analysis of seven RCTs found no difference in treatment success, bleeding, necrosectomy, reintervention, hospitalisation or mortality — only shorter procedure time with metal stents. The safety story is protocol-dependent, and it changed practice mid-programme: in Bang's trial, significant LAMS adverse events (including bleeding) clustered at ≥3 weeks, an interim audit changed the protocol to CT imaging at 3 weeks with LAMS removal if the collection had resolved, and after that amendment the adverse-event difference disappeared. A LAMS result quoted without its removal protocol is not the intervention that was finally tested. Where publications name the stent it is named on the card (clarification exception); several reports describe the device class without a brand the abstract records, and those cards say so.

cards.headline: Bang 2019: LAMS were NOT superior to plastic stents (procedures median 2 vs 3, p = 0.192) and stent-related adverse events were higher with LAMS (32.3% vs 6.9%, p = 0.01) — until the protocol changed, n = 60
cards.summary: Bang 2019: LAMS were NOT superior to plastic stents (procedures median 2 vs 3, p = 0.192) and stent-related adverse events were higher with LAMS (32.3% vs 6.9%, p = 0.01) — until the protocol changed, n = 60
cards.type: Randomised equivalence trial (Bang et al.), Gut 2019
cards.people: 60 patients with walled-off necrosis randomised to EUS-guided drainage with LAMS (31) or plastic stents (29). Primary outcome: total number of procedures to achieve treatment success (symptom relief with walled-off necrosis resolution on CT at 6 months). The publication describes the stent by class (lumen-apposing metal stent); no brand name is given in the fetched record, so none is printed here.
cards.result: No significant difference in total procedures (median 2 [range 2–7] LAMS vs 3 [2–7] plastic; p = 0.192), treatment success, clinical adverse events, readmissions, length of stay or overall treatment costs. Procedure duration was shorter with LAMS (15 vs 40 minutes; p < 0.001), but stent-related adverse events (32.3% vs 6.9%; p = 0.01) and procedure costs (US $12,155 vs US $6,609; p < 0.001) were higher. PROTOCOL EVOLUTION: significant stent-related adverse events in the LAMS group occurred at ≥3 weeks after placement (the early safety signal in this literature, including bleeding); an interim audit amended the protocol so patients had a CT scan at 3 weeks and the LAMS was removed if the necrosis had resolved — after the amendment there was no significant difference in adverse events between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline safety comparison mixes two protocol eras: LAMS left in place beyond 3 weeks vs LAMS removed at 3 weeks after imaging. Present the protocol evolution, not just the pooled adverse-event rate.
cards.source: Bang JY, Navaneethan U, Hasan MK, et al. Non-superiority of lumen-apposing metal stents over plastic stents for drainage of walled-off necrosis in a randomised trial. Gut. 2019. PMID: 29858393. Registry ID: NCT02685865. cards.headline: PROMETHEUS 2024: clinical success was similar with LAMS and plastic pigtail stents (short-term RR 1.41, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.25 — not significant); only procedure time clearly favoured LAMS, n = 64
cards.summary: PROMETHEUS 2024: clinical success was similar with LAMS and plastic pigtail stents (short-term RR 1.41, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.25 — not significant); only procedure time clearly favoured LAMS, n = 64
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised trial (PROMETHEUS), Surg Endosc 2024
cards.people: 64 patients with symptomatic walled-off necrosis enrolled at 9 tertiary hospitals (screened 99), randomised to double-pigtail plastic stents (31) or LAMS (33) in an open-label multicentre trial. Primary outcome: short-term (4-week) clinical success by reduction of the collection. Devices are described by class in the record; no brand name is given in the fetched abstract, so none is printed here.
cards.result: Short-term clinical success was similar (relative risk 1.41; 95% CI 0.88 to 2.25; p = 0.218), as was long-term success (RR 1.2; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.58; p = 0.291). Procedure duration was significantly shorter with LAMS (35 vs 45 minutes; p = 0.003). Hospital stay was similar. Reported stent-related adverse events were similar (36% LAMS vs 45% plastic), except de novo fever, which was lower with LAMS (RR 0.26; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.83; p = 0.015). The authors conclude the clinical superiority of LAMS over plastic stents was not proved.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design; relative risks are relative measures and both success intervals cross 1 — this is a null result on success, not a trend to quote as benefit.
cards.source: PROMETHEUS — Gornals JB, Velasquez-Rodriguez JG, Bas-Cutrina F, et al. Plastic pigtail vs lumen-apposing metal stents for drainage of walled-off necrosis (PROMETHEUS study): an open-label, multicenter randomized trial. Surgical Endoscopy. 2024. PMID: 38448625. cards.headline: Moon 2024 (infected walled-off necrosis): a novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS did not reduce necrosectomy procedures (median 9 vs 4, p = 0.07) but clinical success at 8 weeks was 100% vs 73.9% (p = 0.03), n = 46
cards.summary: Moon 2024 (infected walled-off necrosis): a novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS did not reduce necrosectomy procedures (median 9 vs 4, p = 0.07) but clinical success at 8 weeks was 100% vs 73.9% (p = 0.03), n = 46
cards.type: Multicentre randomised study (electrocautery-enhanced LAMS, infected WON), Endoscopy 2024
cards.people: 46 patients with infected walled-off necrosis requiring EUS-guided drainage, randomised to a novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS (23) or plastic stents (23) in a multicentre randomised study. Primary outcome: total number of direct endoscopic necrosectomy (DEN) procedures needed for clinical success. The record names the device by its class and design (novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS); no brand name is given in the fetched abstract, so none is printed here.
cards.result: The primary outcome did not differ significantly: median DEN procedures 9 (IQR 8.0–9.0) with LAMS vs 4 (IQR 2.5–5.0) with plastic stents (p = 0.07) — numerically more procedures with LAMS. Clinical success by intention-to-treat was higher with LAMS at 8 weeks (100% vs 73.9%; p = 0.03) but not at 4 weeks. Significant bleeding occurred in one patient in the plastic group and none in the LAMS group; no bleeding or buried-stent events occurred with LAMS within the study duration.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 46), infected-necrosis population only, and the significant result is a secondary time-point (8 weeks) while the primary outcome (necrosectomy count) was null and numerically favoured plastic — do not headline this trial as a LAMS win.
cards.source: Moon JH, Park SW, Lee YN, et al. A comparison of novel electrocautery-enhanced lumen-apposing metal stents and plastic stents in endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage of infected walled-off necrosis: a multicenter randomized study. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2025 (7 RCTs): no difference between metal and plastic stents in treatment success, bleeding or mortality — only procedure duration favoured metal (mean difference −11.32 minutes)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2025 (7 RCTs): no difference between metal and plastic stents in treatment success, bleeding or mortality — only procedure duration favoured metal (mean difference −11.32 minutes)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials, J Minim Access Surg 2025
cards.people: Pooled randomised trials comparing metal vs plastic stents for drainage of walled-off pancreatic necrosis, searched to December 2024; seven RCTs met inclusion. This is a synthesis of the same trial population carded above, not independent patients.
cards.result: Procedure duration was significantly shorter with metal stents (mean difference −11.32 minutes; 95% CI −17.75 to −4.88). There was no difference between groups in stent-related periprocedural adverse events, bleeding, serious bleeding, treatment success, need for or number of necrosectomies, reinterventions, percutaneous drainage, surgery, duration of hospitalisation, mortality, stent dysfunction or recurrence.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of the same small RCTs carded in this pack — it pools, and cannot add to, their patient base; the constituent trials used different LAMS dwell-time protocols, which the pooled adverse-event rates conceal.
cards.source: Giri S, Gore P, Khatana G, et al. Comparative outcome of metal versus plastic stents for the management of walled-off pancreatic necrosis — an updated meta-analysis of randomised studies. Journal of Minimal Access Surgery. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: no consistent LAMS advantage on success; the durable lessons are shorter procedures and the 3-week imaging-and-removal protocol (PMIDs 29858393, 38448625, 38857618, 40693902)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no consistent LAMS advantage on success; the durable lessons are shorter procedures and the 3-week imaging-and-removal protocol (PMIDs 29858393, 38448625, 38857618, 40693902)
cards.people: Adults with (often infected) pancreatic walled-off necrosis undergoing EUS-guided drainage; randomised base 170 patients across three trials (60 + 64 + 46), plus a meta-analysis of seven RCTs.
cards.result: Treatment success does not consistently differ between LAMS and plastic stents; LAMS procedures are consistently shorter; and the early LAMS safety signal (bleeding-type stent events at ≥3 weeks) was a dwell-time problem that the field answered with interval imaging and early removal. Synthesis rests on PMIDs 29858393, 38448625, 38857618 and 40693902.
cards.watchOut: SPLIT stamp: anyone quoting a single favourable trial (or the pooled success rate) without the dwell-time protocol is misrepresenting this literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of this pack's own cards: Bang 2019 PMID 29858393; PROMETHEUS PMID 38448625; Moon 2024 PMID 38857618; meta-analysis PMID 40693902. Registry IDs: NCT02685865; NCT03100578.

shelves.title: Efimosfermin alfa (FGF21 analogue) for MASH with fibrosis
shelves.question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis, does efimosfermin alfa (a long-acting FGF21 analogue), compared with placebo, improve liver histology?
shelves.balance: PHASE-2 + SMALL-N flags, printed on the stamp line as required: the histology claim rests on 65 evaluable paired biopsies from the 84 patients randomised in the biopsy trial. PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate: the 24-week histology trial was expected as a Gastroenterology 2025 paper; the verified full journal report is in The Lancet (PMID 41655584), and its published primary endpoint was safety and tolerability — the fetched record does not report histology response percentages, so none are printed here and the biopsy cohort (65 of 84) is stated instead of invented response rates. The earlier phase 2a trial (n = 102, phenotypic MASH without biopsy entry criteria) showed a large hepatic-fat signal (≥30% fat reduction in 89% of evaluable efimosfermin patients vs 7% on placebo at 12 weeks). Monthly subcutaneous dosing is part of the intervention's appeal. There are no clinical-outcome data (no decompensation, transplant or mortality endpoints) and no basis for extrapolating histology to outcomes. An open-label extension report exists (PMID 41660650) but its abstract was not captured from the record this session, so no numbers are taken from it.

cards.headline: Phase 2a 2025 (phenotypic MASH): ≥30% hepatic fat reduction at 12 weeks in 89% of evaluable efimosfermin patients vs 7% on placebo; primary focus was safety, n = 102
cards.summary: Phase 2a 2025 (phenotypic MASH): ≥30% hepatic fat reduction at 12 weeks in 89% of evaluable efimosfermin patients vs 7% on placebo; primary focus was safety, n = 102
cards.type: Phase 2a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025
cards.people: 102 participants with phenotypic MASH (age 18–75, BMI 30–45 kg/m²) at 12 US centres, randomised across five efimosfermin dosing cohorts (75 mg or 150 mg every 2 or 4 weeks, or 300 mg every 4 weeks; 65 patients in total) or placebo (37 patients) for 12 weeks. Entry was by phenotype, not by biopsy. Primary aim: safety and tolerability, with exploratory efficacy biomarkers.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events were recorded in 40% of efimosfermin patients overall (gastrointestinal events predominating — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) vs 49% of placebo patients for all events (24% gastrointestinal); events were typically mild to moderate and there were no treatment-related deaths. At week 12, 47 (89%) of 53 efimosfermin patients with available data had at least a 30% reduction in hepatic fat fraction, vs 2 (7%) of 30 on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Imaging fat fraction is a biomarker, not histology and not a clinical outcome; the evaluable denominators (53 and 30) are smaller than the randomised 102. No registry ID is printed because none appears in the fetched record.

cards.headline: Phase 2 biopsy trial (The Lancet): once-monthly efimosfermin 300 mg for 24 weeks was generally well tolerated in MASH with F2/F3 fibrosis — the trial's primary endpoint was safety, n = 84 randomised
cards.summary: Phase 2 biopsy trial (The Lancet): once-monthly efimosfermin 300 mg for 24 weeks was generally well tolerated in MASH with F2/F3 fibrosis — the trial's primary endpoint was safety, n = 84 randomised
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Lancet 2026
cards.people: 84 participants (43 efimosfermin 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, 41 placebo) aged 18–75 with BMI ≥27 kg/m² and biopsy-confirmed MASH with F2 (48 patients, 57%) or F3 (36, 43%) fibrosis and NAS ≥4, at 34 US sites. Primary endpoint: safety and tolerability (treatment-emergent adverse events, vital signs, grade 3–4 laboratory abnormalities at week 24).
cards.result: Adverse events were reported in 29 (67%) of 43 efimosfermin patients and 22 (55%) of 40 placebo patients who received at least one dose; most events were mild or moderate, the most frequent were gastrointestinal and occurred in the first weeks, there were no clinically meaningful vital-sign differences, no clinically significant grade ≥3 laboratory abnormalities, no deaths and no adverse events above grade 3. The authors conclude the results support further development for MASH-related fibrosis.
cards.watchOut: PREMISE CORRECTION: this trial was slated as a Gastroenterology 2025 histology paper; the verified report is The Lancet (PMID 41655584) and its primary endpoint is safety. Do not quote histology response rates for this trial from this pack — they are not in the fetched record.

cards.people: The 84 randomised patients of the phase 2 biopsy trial (PMID 41655584), of whom 65 had evaluable week-24 biopsy results. This card is explicitly a second, labelled aspect of that one report — the evaluable-biopsy denominator — not a separate study.
cards.result: 65 of 84 randomised patients (77%) contributed evaluable paired biopsy data; 19 randomised patients did not. Because the report's prespecified primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, histology in this programme is a secondary, small-denominator readout: any statement that efimosfermin 'improves histology' is, at this stage, a statement about 65 evaluable biopsies in a single phase 2 trial, with no clinical-outcome follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Small-N rule applied on the face and on the stamp line: N = 65 evaluable paired biopsies. Attrition from 84 randomised to 65 evaluable can bias histology readouts in either direction.

shelves.title: Fazirsiran for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency liver disease (PiZZ)
shelves.question: In adults with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency liver disease (PiZZ), does fazirsiran (RNA interference against Z-AAT), compared with placebo or no treatment, reduce hepatic Z-AAT accumulation and improve liver histology?
shelves.balance: The published human base is very small and is printed on the stamp line: 16 patients in the open-label NEJM report (the base the slate flagged as N = 16) plus 40 randomised patients in SEQUOIA — 56 patients in total, all phase 2. PREMISE UPDATE: SEQUOIA's journal status was unverified at slate time; at build it is verified as a full journal report (Gastroenterology 2024, PMID 38964420) and is carded. The biology is coherent and the effect on the target is large and dose-dependent (serum Z-AAT down 61–94% by dose; median liver Z-AAT down 93% on biopsy vs a 26% increase on placebo), with globule-burden reduction in every fazirsiran-treated SEQUOIA patient. But every endpoint is a biomarker or a histology score — no trial shows prevention of decompensation, transplant or death — fibrosis regression in the open-label report (7 of 15) comes from 15 biopsied patients without a control group, and pulmonary function was stable over these short horizons in a disease whose other organ manifestation is emphysema. A single small programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Open-label phase 2 2022: fazirsiran cut liver Z-AAT by a median of 83% and globule burden fell from 7.4 to 2.3 — in N = 16 patients, with no control group
cards.summary: Open-label phase 2 2022: fazirsiran cut liver Z-AAT by a median of 83% and globule burden fell from 7.4 to 2.3 — in N = 16 patients, with no control group
cards.type: Open-label phase 2 trial, N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 16 adults with the PiZZ genotype and liver fibrosis: 200 mg cohorts of 4 and 8 patients and a 100 mg cohort of 4 patients, given subcutaneously on day 1, week 4 and then every 12 weeks, open-label. Primary endpoint: change in liver Z-AAT concentration (liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry) at week 24 (100 mg and first 200 mg cohorts) or week 48 (second 200 mg cohort).
cards.result: All patients had reduced liver Z-AAT accumulation (median reduction 83% at week 24 or 48); serum Z-AAT nadir was a reduction of approximately 90%; histologic globule burden fell from a mean score of 7.4 (range 0–9) at baseline to 2.3 at week 24 or 48; liver enzymes fell in all cohorts. Fibrosis regression was observed in 7 of 15 patients and progression in 2 of 15 after 24 or 48 weeks. No adverse event led to discontinuation; four serious adverse events (viral myocarditis, diverticulitis, dyspnoea, vestibular neuronitis) resolved.
cards.watchOut: N = 16, open-label, no comparator — the fibrosis regression count (7 of 15) is uncontrolled and hypothesis-generating only. This is the small base the stamp line carries.
cards.source: AROAAT-2002 — Strnad P, Mandorfer M, Choudhury G, et al. Fazirsiran for Liver Disease Associated with Alpha1-Antitrypsin Deficiency. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. cards.headline: SEQUOIA 2024 (randomised, placebo-controlled): serum Z-AAT fell 61%, 83% and 94% at 25, 100 and 200 mg vs placebo at week 16 (all P < .0001), n = 40
cards.summary: SEQUOIA 2024 (randomised, placebo-controlled): serum Z-AAT fell 61%, 83% and 94% at 25, 100 and 200 mg vs placebo at week 16 (all P < .0001), n = 40
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SEQUOIA), Gastroenterology 2024
cards.people: 40 patients with PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency randomised to subcutaneous placebo or fazirsiran 25, 100 or 200 mg. Primary endpoint: percent change in serum Z-AAT concentration from baseline to week 16. Patients with fibrosis on baseline biopsy were dosed on day 1, week 4 and then every 12 weeks, with a second biopsy at or after weeks 48, 72 or 96; patients without fibrosis received two doses.
cards.result: Least-squares mean percent declines in serum Z-AAT at week 16 were −61%, −83% and −94% with fazirsiran 25, 100 and 200 mg respectively vs placebo (all P < .0001), and efficacy was sustained through week 52. No adverse events led to discontinuation and pulmonary function tests remained stable.
cards.watchOut: Verified at build as a full journal report (the slate had it as unverified). The primary endpoint is a serum biomarker — target knockdown, not a clinical outcome.

cards.summary: SEQUOIA biopsy results (labelled second report aspect of the same trial): median liver Z-AAT fell 93% on fazirsiran vs a 26% rise on placebo, and every treated patient had less globule burden
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised trial, biopsy substudy (labelled second aspect of PMID 38964420)
cards.people: The biopsied subset of SEQUOIA (patients with fibrosis at baseline who had a post-dose liver biopsy at or after weeks 48–96; denominators are small — e.g. portal-inflammation scores in 12 fazirsiran and 8 placebo patients, fibrosis-score analysis in 14 and 8). cards.result: At post-dose biopsy, fazirsiran reduced median liver Z-AAT concentration by 93%, compared with an increase of 26% with placebo; all fazirsiran-treated patients had a histologic reduction in hepatic globule burden. cards.headline: Synthesis: near-complete Z-AAT knockdown in serum and liver across two small phase 2 reports — clinical benefit unproven (PMIDs 35748699, 38964420)
cards.summary: Synthesis: near-complete Z-AAT knockdown in serum and liver across two small phase 2 reports — clinical benefit unproven (PMIDs 35748699, 38964420)
cards.people: Adults with PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and liver disease; total published base 56 patients (16 open-label + 40 randomised).
cards.result: Fazirsiran does what it is designed to do — degrades Z-AAT messenger RNA and empties the hepatocyte of Z-AAT — with dose-dependent serum reductions of 61–94% and a 93% median liver reduction on biopsy. shelves.title: Larsucosterol for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (AHFIRM)
shelves.question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, does larsucosterol, compared with placebo, reduce 90-day mortality or liver transplantation?
shelves.balance: NEGATIVE PRIMARY ENDPOINT — the honest shelf leads with the null. AHFIRM (n = 307 enrolled, 301 dosed) did not meet its primary endpoint: the difference in 90-day mortality or liver transplantation between either larsucosterol dose (30 mg or 90 mg) and placebo did not reach statistical significance. Ninety-day mortality counts were 15 of 102 (30 mg), 17 of 102 (90 mg) and 25 of 103 (placebo). Sponsor communications have quoted '41% / 35% mortality reductions' from these counts: those figures are RELATIVE reductions computed from the same counts, they are NON-SIGNIFICANT, and they come from a trial that missed its primary endpoint — they are printed on the cards only with those three labels attached. The prespecified US analysis and the subgroup treated within 10 days of hospitalisation show larger numerical gaps, but both are slices of a negative trial and cannot rescue the primary result. The earlier phase 2a study (n = 19, open-label, uncontrolled) reported no deaths at 28 days, which is encouraging safety background and nothing more. The trial authors' own conclusion is that equipoise exists for a further trial — not that benefit is shown.

cards.headline: AHFIRM 2025 (primary result): larsucosterol did NOT significantly reduce 90-day mortality or liver transplant — the primary endpoint was not met, n = 307
cards.summary: AHFIRM 2025 (primary result): larsucosterol did NOT significantly reduce 90-day mortality or liver transplant — the primary endpoint was not met, n = 307
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (AHFIRM), NEJM Evidence 2025
cards.people: 307 patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis enrolled (301 received at least one dose), randomised 1:1:1 to larsucosterol 30 mg, larsucosterol 90 mg or placebo, with a second dose at 72 hours if still hospitalised; all received investigator-determined supportive care, and placebo-group patients prescribed steroids received 32 mg methylprednisolone while larsucosterol groups received matching placebo capsules. Primary endpoint: 90-day mortality or liver transplantation. Funded by the DURECT Corporation.
cards.result: The difference in 90-day mortality or liver transplantation between the 30 mg or 90 mg larsucosterol groups and placebo did not reach statistical significance — the trial did not meet its primary endpoint. Ninety-day mortality alone was 25 of 103 (placebo), 15 of 102 (30 mg) and 17 of 102 (90 mg). Most treatment-emergent adverse events were attributable to the underlying liver disease, with no imbalance in events that could not be ascribed to liver disease. The authors conclude equipoise has been established for a further trial.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint governs the whole shelf. Any percentage 'mortality reduction' derived from 15/102 or 17/102 vs 25/103 is a relative, non-significant figure from this negative trial and must be labelled as all three.

cards.headline: Phase 2a 2024 (open-label, uncontrolled): all 19 patients survived 28 days and no drug-related serious adverse events occurred — safety background only
cards.summary: Phase 2a 2024 (open-label, uncontrolled): all 19 patients survived 28 days and no drug-related serious adverse events occurred — safety background only
cards.type: Phase 2a open-label dose-escalation study, Am J Gastroenterol 2024
cards.people: 19 clinically diagnosed patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis (7 moderate, 12 severe by MELD) in a multicentre open-label dose-escalation study of larsucosterol 30, 90 or 150 mg (one or two intravenous infusions 72 hours apart), followed for 28 days. There was no randomised control group; efficacy signals in severe disease were compared with matched standard-of-care arms from a contemporaneous separate study.
cards.result: All 19 larsucosterol-treated patients survived the 28-day study; 14 (74%), including 8 (67%) of those with severe disease, were discharged within 72 hours of a single infusion. There were no drug-related serious adverse events and no early terminations for treatment. Bilirubin and MELD generally improved, and Lille scores at day 7 were below 0.45 in 16 of 18 patients with samples.
cards.watchOut: N = 19 and uncontrolled: 28-day survival in 19 selected patients cannot estimate a mortality effect, and the matched comparisons come from a different study. This card is safety/pharmacokinetic background for AHFIRM, not efficacy evidence.

shelves.title: DIALIVE albumin dialysis for acute-on-chronic liver failure
shelves.question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does DIALIVE albumin dialysis, compared with standard care, improve organ failure resolution and survival?
shelves.balance: One small first-in-human randomised trial is the entire published base — the randomised N (32) is printed on the stamp line, and all three evidence cards are explicitly labelled aspects of that single report (PMID 37268222); there is no second trial to card. The citation and N the slate left unverified were verified at build from the fetched record: Journal of Hepatology 2023, 32 patients with alcohol-related ACLF, NCT03065699. DIALIVE is a specific device (DIALIVE, Yaqrit) that exchanges dysfunctional albumin and removes damage- and pathogen-associated molecular patterns — it is not interchangeable with other extracorporeal liver-support systems (the MARS/Prometheus question is homed separately in pack #6540 and is not merged here). The trial's primary aim was safety, and safety was acceptable; 28-day mortality did not differ. The positive findings are day-10 prognostic scores (CLIF-C organ failure and CLIF-C ACLF), faster ACLF resolution and a coherent set of inflammatory biomarkers — surrogate and score outcomes in 30 patients with at least three treatment sessions, from a trial far too small to test survival. A larger trial of an updated device (DIALIVE 2.0) exists only as a published protocol (PMID 42994933), which is mentioned here as a protocol and is not evidence.

cards.headline: DIALIVE RCT 2023 — safety (the trial's primary aim): no significant difference in serious adverse events or 28-day mortality in N = 32 randomised patients
cards.summary: DIALIVE RCT 2023 — safety (the trial's primary aim): no significant difference in serious adverse events or 28-day mortality in N = 32 randomised patients
cards.type: First-in-human randomised controlled trial (DIALIVE, safety primary aim), J Hepatol 2023
cards.people: 32 patients with alcohol-related acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) randomised to DIALIVE (the DIALIVE device, Yaqrit — an extracorporeal system that exchanges dysfunctional albumin and removes damage- and pathogen-associated molecular patterns) for up to 5 days, or standard care; endpoints assessed at day 10. Safety was assessed in all 32 patients. This is the first-in-man randomised trial of the device; the card is the safety aspect of the single trial report.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the groups in 28-day mortality or in the occurrence of serious adverse events, and the authors conclude DIALIVE appears to be safe in patients with ACLF. The trial was designed and powered around safety, not survival — the absence of a mortality difference in 32 patients is uninformative about efficacy in either direction.
cards.watchOut: N = 32 — printed on the stamp line per the small-N rule. 'No significant difference' in mortality in a 32-patient safety trial must not be read as evidence about survival either way.

shelves.question: In chronic liver disease, what does the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measure, how is portal pressure physiologically determined, and which HVPG thresholds carry prognostic meaning?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY entry — no intervention stamp. What HVPG is: a catheter in a hepatic vein measures wedged (occluded) hepatic venous pressure and free hepatic venous pressure; their difference, the HVPG, estimates the portal pressure gradient across the liver in sinusoidal portal hypertension. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology — named here as framing, not as evidence cards): portal pressure is determined by portal venous inflow multiplied by the resistance to that flow, and in cirrhosis the dominant change is increased intrahepatic resistance (fixed architectural distortion plus a dynamic, vasoactive component), later compounded by increased splanchnic inflow — values or mechanisms stated in this paragraph that no carded cohort confirms are the textbooks' account. The threshold ladder is NOT free-floating: each rung on the cards is tied to its source cohort — below 10 mmHg, compensated patients in the Ripoll cohort (n = 213) had a 90% probability of remaining free of decompensation over a median 4 years, and 10 mmHg is the conventional boundary of clinically significant portal hypertension; a post-TIPS portosystemic gradient below 12 mmHg was the threshold associated with protection from rebleeding in a 2,100-patient retrospective series (the 12 mmHg rung comes from the bleeding-protection literature, not from a natural-history cohort); 16 mmHg or above predicted further decompensation after oesophageal variceal bleeding in a 145-patient prospective cohort; and in acute variceal bleeding, an HVPG of 20 mmHg or above measured within about a day of admission marked failure to control bleeding and far worse 1-year survival (Moitinho, n = 65). Drug effects on HVPG are a treatment question homed elsewhere — see packs #3594 and #6083, cross-pointed here in prose only; none of their PMIDs are carded in this pack.

cards.headline: Ripoll 2007: in compensated cirrhosis, HVPG predicted decompensation (HR 1.11 per mmHg), and patients with HVPG <10 mmHg had a 90% probability of NOT decompensating over a median 4 years, n = 213
cards.summary: Ripoll 2007: in compensated cirrhosis, HVPG predicted decompensation (HR 1.11 per mmHg), and patients with HVPG <10 mmHg had a 90% probability of NOT decompensating over a median 4 years, n = 213
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (HVPG natural history), Gastroenterology 2007
cards.people: 213 patients with compensated cirrhosis and portal hypertension but without varices, with baseline HVPG and laboratory tests, followed prospectively every 3 months (median follow-up 51.1 months; median baseline HVPG 11 mmHg, range 6–25). Decompensation was defined as ascites, variceal haemorrhage or hepatic encephalopathy.
cards.result: 62 patients (29%) decompensated: 46 (21.6%) ascites, 6 (3%) variceal haemorrhage, 17 (8%) hepatic encephalopathy. On multivariate analysis HVPG (hazard ratio 1.11; 95% CI 1.05 to 1.17, a relative measure per mmHg), MELD and albumin independently predicted decompensation, and HVPG's diagnostic capacity exceeded MELD or Child-Pugh. Patients with an HVPG below 10 mmHg had a 90% probability of not developing clinical decompensation in a median follow-up of 4 years — the cohort behind the 10 mmHg 'clinically significant portal hypertension' boundary.
cards.watchOut: Observational cohort (the cohort was assembled inside a beta-blocker prevention trial programme) — the 10 mmHg rung is a prognostic boundary from this cohort, not a treatment target established by this study.
cards.source: Ripoll C, Groszmann R, Garcia-Tsao G, et al. Hepatic venous pressure gradient predicts clinical decompensation in patients with compensated cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 17681169. cards.headline: Groszmann 2005 cohort: varices developed less often when baseline HVPG was <10 mmHg or HVPG fell by >10% at 1 year — the pressure, not the drug, carried the prognosis, n = 213
cards.summary: Groszmann 2005 cohort: varices developed less often when baseline HVPG was <10 mmHg or HVPG fell by >10% at 1 year — the pressure, not the drug, carried the prognosis, n = 213
cards.type: Randomised trial cohort, carded for HVPG natural history (not a treatment card), N Engl J Med 2005
cards.people: 213 patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension (entry HVPG at least 6 mmHg) randomised to timolol or placebo with yearly endoscopy and HVPG measurement (median follow-up 54.9 months). This physiology pack cards the trial for its HVPG-stratified natural-history findings, not as a drug recommendation.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (development of varices or variceal haemorrhage) did not differ between timolol and placebo (39% vs 40%; p = 0.89), and serious adverse events were more common on timolol (18% vs 6%; p = 0.006). Varices developed less frequently among patients with a baseline HVPG below 10 mmHg and among those whose HVPG decreased by more than 10% at one year, and more frequently among those whose HVPG rose by more than 10% — direct human evidence that the gradient itself tracks the mechanical complication it measures.
cards.watchOut: The drug result was null and is not this pack's question — drug effects on HVPG are homed in packs #3594 and #6083. The physiology lesson is the HVPG-stratified varices risk.
cards.source: Groszmann RJ, Garcia-Tsao G, Bosch J, et al. Beta-blockers to prevent gastroesophageal varices in patients with cirrhosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2005. PMID: 16306522. Registry ID: NCT00006398. cards.headline: Vaishnav 2023: after acute variceal bleeding, an HVPG of ≥16 mmHg predicted further decompensation in oesophageal bleeding — the cohort behind the 16 mmHg rung, n = 145
cards.summary: Vaishnav 2023: after acute variceal bleeding, an HVPG of ≥16 mmHg predicted further decompensation in oesophageal bleeding — the cohort behind the 16 mmHg rung, n = 145
cards.people: 145 patients with cirrhosis and acute oesophageal or gastric variceal bleeding in a prospective study, with HVPG measured on the day of the bleeding episode; further decompensation was counted from events occurring after 42 days (median follow-up 296 days). Predominant aetiology was alcohol (46.2%); 88.3% were male.
cards.result: 40 patients (27.6%) developed further decompensation (gastrointestinal bleeding 27; new or worsening ascites 20). On multivariate analysis HVPG was an independent predictor of further decompensation in oesophageal variceal bleeding (but not gastric), and an HVPG cut-off of ≥16 mmHg predicted further decompensation in the oesophageal group. HVPG was not an independent predictor of mortality in this cohort.
cards.watchOut: Single prospective cohort, oesophageal-bleeding subgroup only for the 16 mmHg cut-off, and no mortality prediction — the 16 mmHg rung means 'further decompensation risk after a bleed in this cohort', nothing broader.
cards.source: Vaishnav M, Biswas S, Anand A, et al. Hepatic Venous Pressure Gradient Predicts Further Decompensation in Cirrhosis Patients with Acute Esophageal Variceal Bleeding. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023. PMID: 37510129. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Xia 2023: after TIPS, a portosystemic gradient <12 mmHg was associated with protection from rebleeding — the series behind the 12 mmHg rung, n = 2,100 (retrospective)
cards.summary: Xia 2023: after TIPS, a portosystemic gradient <12 mmHg was associated with protection from rebleeding — the series behind the 12 mmHg rung, n = 2,100 (retrospective)
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre cohort (post-TIPS pressure gradient), Hepatol Int 2023
cards.people: 2,100 consecutively screened patients undergoing transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in a multicentre retrospective study, analysing rebleeding, overt hepatic encephalopathy and mortality against post-TIPS portal pressure gradient (PPG) thresholds of 8, 10, 12 and 14 mmHg, overall and by Child-Pugh class, with propensity-matched sensitivity analyses.
cards.result: In all patients, a post-TIPS PPG below 12 mmHg reduced rebleeding (p = 0.022). In Child-Pugh class B, both 12 and 14 mmHg discriminated rebleeding, with 12 mmHg showing higher net benefit; in Child-Pugh class C, a PPG below 14 mmHg had lower rebleeding incidence (p = 0.017) and more net benefit than 12 mmHg; in class A no threshold discriminated outcomes. The authors conclude different PPG standards may be required by liver function — i.e. 12 mmHg is a post-procedure bleeding-protection threshold whose performance varies by Child-Pugh class.
cards.watchOut: Observational and post-procedure: this is PPG after TIPS, not diagnostic HVPG, and the 12 mmHg rung is presented with that provenance rather than as a universal constant.
cards.source: Xia Y, Tie J, Wang G, et al. Individualized portal pressure gradient threshold based on liver function categories in preventing rebleeding after TIPS. Hepatology International. 2023. PMID: 36807252. MeSH: Humans · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Portasystemic Shunt, Transjugular Intrahepatic · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Portal Pressure · Retrospective Studies · Liver Cirrhosis · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Moitinho 1999: in acute variceal bleeding, HVPG measured within ~24 hours was the only predictor of poor evolution — ≥20 mmHg meant 64% vs 20% one-year mortality, n = 65
cards.summary: Moitinho 1999: in acute variceal bleeding, HVPG measured within ~24 hours was the only predictor of poor evolution — ≥20 mmHg meant 64% vs 20% one-year mortality, n = 65
cards.type: Prospective human haemodynamic cohort (classic, n = 65), Gastroenterology 1999
cards.people: 65 patients with cirrhosis and acute variceal haemorrhage whose HVPG was measured early after admission (mean 20.6 ± 15.6 hours); 23 had a poor evolution (failure to control bleeding or early rebleeding) and 42 an uneventful evolution. A classic small human study — its N is printed on the face, per the physiology labelling rule.
cards.result: HVPG was higher in patients with poor evolution (23.7 ± 6.1 vs 19.2 ± 3.3 mmHg; p < 0.0004) and was the only variable associated with outcome, confirmed on multivariate analysis. An HVPG of ≥20 mmHg was present in 19 of 23 patients with poor evolution vs 12 of 42 with uneventful evolution (p < 0.0001), and was associated with longer intensive care (7 ± 5 vs 4 ± 2 days) and hospital stays, greater transfusion requirements (9.0 ± 7.7 vs 4.7 ± 3.2 units) and a worse 1-year survival (mortality 64% vs 20%; p < 0.002).
cards.watchOut: N = 65, single-centre era physiology — carded as a classic primary human study with its N on the face. The ≥20 mmHg rung describes prognosis during an acute bleed, not a chronic-disease threshold.
cards.source: Moitinho E, Escorsell A, Bandi JC, et al. Prognostic value of early measurements of portal pressure in acute variceal bleeding. Gastroenterology. 1999. PMID: 10464138. MeSH: Aged · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypertension, Portal · Liver Cirrhosis · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Survival Analysis

cards.headline: Synthesis: HVPG is the portal pressure gradient measured from the hepatic vein, and its prognostic ladder (10 / 12 / 16 / 20 mmHg) is a set of cohort findings, not constants (PMIDs 17681169, 16306522, 37510129, 36807252, 10464138)
cards.summary: Synthesis: HVPG is the portal pressure gradient measured from the hepatic vein, and its prognostic ladder (10 / 12 / 16 / 20 mmHg) is a set of cohort findings, not constants (PMIDs 17681169, 16306522, 37510129, 36807252, 10464138)
cards.people: Patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension across compensated, post-bleeding and post-TIPS settings. Note the Ripoll and Groszmann cards describe the same 213-patient compensated cohort from two angles (natural history and HVPG-stratified varices risk), so the distinct carded populations are that cohort (213), the post-bleeding cohort (145), the post-TIPS series (2,100) and the acute-bleed cohort (65) — about 2,523 patients, stated per-cohort on each card.
cards.result: Wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure estimates the sinusoidal portal gradient; prognosis worsens continuously with the gradient (HR 1.11 per mmHg in the compensated cohort), with clinically used rungs at 10 mmHg (decompensation boundary, Ripoll/Groszmann cohorts), 12 mmHg (post-TIPS rebleeding protection, Xia series), 16 mmHg (further decompensation after oesophageal bleeding, Vaishnav cohort) and 20 mmHg (failure to control acute bleeding and 1-year mortality, Moitinho cohort). Synthesis rests on PMIDs 17681169, 16306522, 37510129, 36807252 and 10464138. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (see balance).
cards.watchOut: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED entry: no treatment claim is made. For what drugs do to HVPG, see packs #3594 and #6083 (cross-pointed in prose; their PMIDs are not carded here).
cards.source: Synthesis of this pack's own cards: Ripoll 2007 PMID 17681169; Groszmann 2005 PMID 16306522; Vaishnav 2023 PMID 37510129; Xia 2023 PMID 36807252; Moitinho 1999 PMID 10464138. Registry ID: NCT00006398 (Groszmann cohort).

shelves.title: Postprandial splanchnic hyperaemia: superior mesenteric flow rises two- to threefold after a meal, peaking at 30–60 minutes — water alone does nothing
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much does splanchnic (superior mesenteric and portal) blood flow rise after a meal — what is the time course and peak of postprandial hyperaemia by Doppler ultrasound and hepatic-vein catheterisation, which meal components drive it, and how is flow redistributed away again in exercise?
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, splanchnic circulation and gastrointestinal blood-flow regulation): meal ingestion is the gut's dominant hyperaemic stimulus, driven by absorbed nutrients, gastrointestinal hormones and local metabolites, with cardiac output rising in parallel. The primary human base is the Doppler ultrasound literature — small, careful volunteer studies, every N printed on its card as this stream requires. Its findings are consistent: superior mesenteric flow rises two- to threefold, peaks at 30–60 minutes and stays up for about two hours; carbohydrate, protein and fat meals all do it and water does not; the coeliac and femoral beds do not share the response, marking it as a true splanchnic redistribution; and a pressor challenge (sustained handgrip) shows the fed splanchnic bed defending its flow differently from the fasting bed. Adjacent shelves ask different questions — pack #6083 (portal pressure), #6148 (ammonia traffic) and #6493 (hepatic insulin extraction) — and are cross-pointed, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Waaler & Eriksen 1992: cardiac output and superior mesenteric flow rose markedly after carbohydrate, protein and fat meals — and not after water (N = 5)
cards.summary: Waaler & Eriksen 1992: cardiac output and superior mesenteric flow rose markedly after carbohydrate, protein and fat meals — and not after water (N = 5)
cards.people: 5 young healthy persons followed for 2 hours with Doppler ultrasound after medium-sized (4 MJ) fluid meals of carbohydrate, protein or fat, or water only, with mean arterial pressure recorded.
cards.result: All energy-containing meals caused marked, gradually developing postprandial increases in cardiac output and superior mesenteric arterial flow; maximum flow levels were reached within 30–60 minutes and maintained until observations ended at 2 hours. Water caused no such increases. The three meal types did not differ significantly from each other, though the most marked increases followed carbohydrate.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 — a classic small volunteer study, carded with its N on the face under this stream's labelling rule; the direction and time course, not the exact magnitude, are what replicate across the shelf.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (postprandial cardiovascular responses to carbohydrate, protein and fat). Waaler BA et al.. Post-prandial cardiovascular responses in man after ingestion of carbohydrate, protein or fat. Acta physiologica Scandinavica. 1992. PMID: 1481689. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moneta 1988: every nutrient meal raised superior mesenteric flow significantly; coeliac and femoral flow did not change (N = 7)
cards.summary: Moneta 1988: every nutrient meal raised superior mesenteric flow significantly; coeliac and femoral flow did not change (N = 7)
cards.people: 7 healthy volunteers studied by duplex ultrasound before and serially for 90 minutes after 350-cal, 300-ml liquid meals of protein, fat, carbohydrate or a mixed formula, with water and mannitol solutions as volume and osmolarity controls.
cards.result: Maximal changes in all superior mesenteric artery parameters (peak systolic, end-diastolic and mean velocity, and volume flow) increased significantly over baseline after each test meal except water (p < 0.05), with end-diastolic velocity showing proportionally the greatest increase. No significant changes occurred in the coeliac or femoral arteries after any meal — the hyperaemia is specific to the superior mesenteric bed.
cards.watchOut: N = 7, liquid test meals only; solid mixed meals (the Waaler card) show the same direction, but magnitudes from 350-cal liquid meals should not be quoted as the response to an ordinary dinner.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (duplex ultrasound measurement of postprandial intestinal blood flow). Moneta GL et al.. cards.headline: Waaler 1999: superior mesenteric flow increased two- to threefold after a meal — and the fed bed answered a handgrip pressor challenge differently (N = 7)
cards.summary: Waaler 1999: superior mesenteric flow increased two- to threefold after a meal — and the fed bed answered a handgrip pressor challenge differently (N = 7)
cards.people: 7 healthy students studied in fasting and fed states during 2-minute standardised sustained handgrip, with superior mesenteric flow and vascular conductance by ultrasound Doppler in one session and cardiac output in the other.
cards.result: Superior mesenteric artery blood flow typically increased two- to threefold after the meal. During handgrip, heart rate, cardiac output and total peripheral conductance rose rapidly at first, then total peripheral conductance declined while pressure rose — the protocol demonstrating, in the same subjects, how the postprandial splanchnic state interacts with a general pressor response.
cards.watchOut: N = 7; the two- to threefold figure is the study's own summary of its Doppler flow recordings, and handgrip is a brief laboratory pressor stimulus, not exercise of the legs — the redistribution-away-in-exercise limb of the question rests on this and the textbook account, and the card says so.

cards.people: 25 healthy controls (alongside 80 patients with vascular disease undergoing aortography, not carded here) undergoing fasting and postprandial duplex scanning of the superior mesenteric artery.
cards.result: Mean fasting peak systolic velocity did not differ between controls and patients with <70% stenosis; postprandial scanning changed the stratification of stenosis beyond the fasting examination — the study works as a stress test precisely because the healthy postprandial hyperaemic response is large and predictable enough that its blunting signals disease.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a two- to threefold, nutrient-driven, bed-specific hyperaemia — established on small panels
cards.summary: Synthesis: a two- to threefold, nutrient-driven, bed-specific hyperaemia — established on small panels
cards.people: Four primary human Doppler studies (healthy N = 5, 7, 7 and 25), spanning nutrient-composition, pressor-interaction and diagnostic-stress designs.
cards.result: Energy-containing meals — carbohydrate, protein or fat — raise superior mesenteric flow two- to threefold, peaking at 30–60 minutes and sustained about two hours; water does nothing; neighbouring beds (coeliac, femoral) do not share the rise (Guyton & Hall framing). The hepatic-vein catheterisation limb of the question could not be carded: no verifiable classic catheterisation record with a fetchable abstract was confirmed this session, so that limb is carried by the textbook account and flagged here rather than padded with an unverified citation. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on a small-N base with every N printed.
cards.watchOut: All carded magnitudes come from Doppler ultrasound in small volunteer panels eating test meals; treat exact fold-rises as laboratory values, not guarantees for any individual meal.

shelves.title: Small-intestine motor patterns: a migrating motor complex every ~97 minutes that slows, fades distally, and vanishes the moment a meal arrives
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the small intestine's motor patterns — the fasting migrating motor complex (phase I–III cycle length and propagation), the immediate fed-pattern replacement after a meal, and how do the patterns differ between jejunum and ileum on prolonged ambulatory manometry?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall describes the fasting small intestine as cycling through the migrating motor complex (MMC): quiescence (phase I), irregular activity (phase II), then a propagating burst of maximal-frequency contractions (phase III, the 'activity front' or housekeeper) that sweeps residual debris aborally, with a meal abolishing the cycle and substituting the irregular fed pattern. The fetched human manometry records give the cycle its real, wide numbers. In 11 healthy subjects recorded from jejunum to terminal ileum, 96 MMCs occurred at a grand-mean interval of 97 minutes — but individual intervals ranged from 15 to 195 minutes — with the activity front slowing as it travelled (4.7 cm/min in jejunum, 0.9 cm/min in terminal ileum) and its contraction rate falling distally (about 12.5–10.5/min jejunal to 10.0–8.6/min terminal ileal); a 600-kcal liquid meal interrupted fasting cycling for 2.75 to more than 10 hours (Kerlin & Phillips 1982). Kellow's stomach-to-colon recordings in 16 volunteers add the attrition: fewer than half of MMCs were recognisable beyond the midpoint of the small bowel and less than 10% reached the distal ileum, the complex was more prominent at night, and small meals of 345–395 kcal interrupted fasting patterns for 90–240 minutes (Kellow 1986). Prolonged ambulatory recording in 30 volunteers found at least one phase III in every subject over 6 hours of fasting or sleep, at 0.52 ± 0.04 per hour fasting and 0.59 ± 0.04 per hour asleep, with postprandial contraction frequency and motility index maximal in the first 2 hours after the meal and no substantive duodenum-versus-jejunum or sex differences (Soffer 1998). The largest normative series — 51 volunteers, 419 phase III episodes — confirms wide normal ranges and large within-subject variability (Scott 2006). This shelf is the small-bowel companion to shelf #6638, which homes the colon's quite different patterns (a quiet fasting colon with no dominant migrating complex); the two share no carded studies.

cards.headline: The classic cycle quantified: an MMC every ~97 minutes on average (but 15–195 minutes individually), its front slowing from 4.7 cm/min in jejunum to 0.9 cm/min in terminal ileum (N = 11)
cards.summary: The classic cycle quantified: an MMC every ~97 minutes on average (but 15–195 minutes individually), its front slowing from 4.7 cm/min in jejunum to 0.9 cm/min in terminal ileum (N = 11)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (stationary multilumen small-bowel manometry, fasting and fed) — N = 11
cards.people: 11 healthy subjects with a multilumen tube passed by mouth, five recording sites spanning 100 cm designated jejunal, ileal or terminal ileal by tube length and fluoroscopy, recorded for 6 hours fasting and 6 or more hours after a 600-kcal liquid test meal.
cards.result: During fasting the migrating motor complex was present in all subjects at all levels of the small intestine but could not be traced into the colon. Ninety-six MMCs occurred, one each 97 min as a grand mean across loci, but intervals between individual activity fronts varied markedly (15–195 min). Aboral migration velocity was 4.7 ± 1.8 cm/min in jejunum, 1.3 ± 0.4 in ileum and 0.9 ± 0.2 in terminal ileum; maximal contraction rates during activity fronts declined distally from 12.5–10.5/min (jejunal) to 10.0–8.6/min (terminal ileal). Food interrupted the fasting cycles for periods ranging from 2.75 to greater than 10 hours.
cards.watchOut: Stationary intubated recording over hours, not days, and the 97-minute mean conceals the record's own headline — variability: individual cycles ran 15–195 minutes, so any single 'normal cycle length' quoted without its range misstates this study.
cards.source: Kerlin P, Phillips S. Variability of motility of the ileum and jejunum in healthy humans. Gastroenterology. 1982. PMID: 6277722. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Most complexes die out mid-bowel: fewer than half recognisable beyond the small-bowel midpoint, under 10% reaching the distal ileum — and the complex is more prominent at night (N = 16)
cards.summary: Most complexes die out mid-bowel: fewer than half recognisable beyond the small-bowel midpoint, under 10% reaching the distal ileum — and the complex is more prominent at night (N = 16)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prolonged multi-site interdigestive manometry) — N = 16
cards.people: 16 healthy humans with intraluminal pressure sensors spanning stomach to proximal colon (including lower oesophagus in 11), recorded fasting and after meals for prolonged periods.
cards.result: Half the interdigestive cycles involved the oesophagus, about one-third began in the gastroduodenal region, and the remainder commenced more distally. Fewer than half the migrating motor complexes were recognisable beyond the midpoint of the small bowel, and less than 10% reached the distal ileum. The MMC was more prominent at night, and its progression through the jejunum was then slower. Small meals (345–395 kcal) interrupted fasting patterns for 90–240 min, with the amount of fat not influencing the duration of disruption. Patterns varied widely between and within individuals, and jejunal-versus-ileal differences were particularly striking.
cards.watchOut: Attrition estimates depend on sensor spacing and on the criteria for calling a distal burst the same complex; the durable claims are the direction (most fronts fade before the distal ileum), the nocturnal prominence, and the wide inter- and intra-individual variation.
cards.source: Kellow JE et al. Human interdigestive motility: variations in patterns from esophagus to colon. Gastroenterology. 1986. PMID: 3721125. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ambulatory normal values: at least one phase III in every subject over 6 hours fasting or asleep (~0.5/hour either way), postprandial activity peaking in the first 2 hours, and no sex or duodenum-versus-jejunum differences (N = 30)
cards.summary: Ambulatory normal values: at least one phase III in every subject over 6 hours fasting or asleep (~0.5/hour either way), postprandial activity peaking in the first 2 hours, and no sex or duodenum-versus-jejunum differences (N = 30)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prolonged ambulatory duodeno-jejunal manometry, normative) — N = 30
cards.people: 30 healthy volunteers (17 men) undergoing prolonged ambulatory duodeno-jejunal manometry with a five-transducer strain-gauge catheter (two duodenal, three jejunal sites), recorded through extended fasting, the postprandial period and sleep.
cards.result: MMC duration varied widely, but at least one phase III was detected during 6 hours of fasting, or 6 hours of sleep, in every subject (0.52 ± 0.04 phase III/hour during fasting versus 0.59 ± 0.04 during sleep, P = 0.1). Duration and pattern of phase III varied markedly. Postprandially, contraction frequency and motility index were maximal in the first 2 hours after the meal in both duodenum and jejunum. There were no substantive differences between men and women or between the duodenum and jejunum; the authors conclude upper small-bowel motility is little affected by gender or segment.
cards.watchOut: Coverage is duodenum and proximal jejunum only — this card cannot speak to ileal patterns, which References 1 and 2 show are slower and less often reached; 'no segment difference' applies within the upper small bowel studied.
cards.source: Soffer EE, Thongsawat S, Ellerbroek S. Prolonged ambulatory duodeno-jejunal manometry in humans: normal values and gender effect. The American journal of gastroenterology. 1998. cards.headline: The largest normative series: 419 phase III episodes in 51 volunteers define wide nocturnal jejunal MMC reference ranges, with within-subject variance larger than between-subject variance (N = 51)
cards.summary: The largest normative series: 419 phase III episodes in 51 volunteers define wide nocturnal jejunal MMC reference ranges, with within-subject variance larger than between-subject variance (N = 51)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour ambulatory jejunal manometry, normative ranges with meta-analysis) — N = 51
cards.people: 51 healthy adult volunteers in two centres undergoing 81 prolonged (24-hour) ambulatory manometry recordings; quantitative analysis of 419 phase III and 332 phase II episodes of the nocturnal jejunal MMC, with a meta-analysis of 19 published studies (356 pooled subjects) to generate 95% reference ranges.
cards.result: Adjusted mean values with confidence intervals were calculated for seven MMC variables using a mixed-effects model. Intrasubject variances were large in comparison with intersubject variances. The meta-analysis produced wide reference ranges, at least five of which the authors judge useful for detecting abnormality in an individual. The authors present this as the largest normal-volunteer dataset in the field and propose it as a complement to other indicators of small-bowel dysmotility.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports the reference-range programme without printing the seven variables' numerical ranges, so none are quoted here; the carded claims are the cohort size, the episode counts, and the variance structure — 'normal' for the nocturnal jejunal MMC is a wide band, not a point.
cards.source: Scott SM et al. The nocturnal jejunal migrating motor complex: defining normal ranges by study of 51 healthy adult volunteers and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: a ~97-minute average cycle that in truth runs 15–195 minutes, a front that slows and usually fades before the distal ileum, and instant conversion to the fed pattern on eating
cards.summary: Synthesis: a ~97-minute average cycle that in truth runs 15–195 minutes, a front that slows and usually fades before the distal ileum, and instant conversion to the fed pattern on eating
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human manometry studies above.
cards.result: Small-intestine motor patterns in healthy humans, as the fetched records show them: fasting motility is organised by the migrating motor complex — phase III activity fronts recurring at a grand-mean interval of about 97 minutes but ranging 15–195 minutes between fronts, arising variously from oesophagus to distal small bowel, propagating at 4.7 cm/min in the jejunum slowing to 0.9 cm/min in the terminal ileum, with maximal contraction frequency falling from ~12/min proximally to ~9/min distally. Most fronts are not recognisable beyond the small-bowel midpoint and under 10% reach the distal ileum. The complex persists through sleep (about 0.5–0.6 phase III per hour, fasting or asleep) and is more prominent at night. A meal converts the pattern at once to the irregular fed pattern — contraction frequency and motility index maximal in the first 2 postprandial hours — and fasting cycling stays interrupted for 90 minutes after a small meal to more than 10 hours after a 600-kcal meal. Within-subject variability exceeds between-subject variability, so normal is a wide range. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the variability printed on the face. Cross-point: shelf #6638 homes the colon, where the fasting pattern is quiescence rather than a migrating complex — the MMC is a small-bowel pattern, and Reference 1 confirms it could not be traced into the colon.
cards.watchOut: All four studies instrument the bowel with a catheter or tube, which can itself perturb motility; absolute cycle parameters vary with recording site, duration and phase-III criteria, so the shelf's durable claims are the pattern (cycling fasting complex, distal slowing and attrition, sleep persistence, fed conversion) and the ranges, not any single mean.

The American journal of gastroenterology. 1998 (PMID: 9707058); Scott SM et al. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2006 (PMID: 16961696). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Jejunal sugar absorption: glucose on a saturable sodium-coupled carrier, fructose on a small separate one that easily overflows
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how are glucose and fructose absorbed across the jejunum — what did the classic triple-lumen perfusion studies show about sodium-coupled glucose uptake, solvent drag and maximal absorptive capacity, and why is fructose absorption capacity-limited and malabsorbed in a fraction of healthy people on breath-hydrogen testing?
shelves.balance: Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall frame intestinal sugar absorption as two different machines: glucose (and galactose) cross the brush border on the sodium-coupled SGLT1 transporter — saturable, sodium-dependent, and dragging water and sodium with it — while fructose crosses on the facilitative, sodium-independent GLUT5 carrier, whose capacity is limited and varies widely between people, so unabsorbed fructose reaches colonic bacteria and is fermented to hydrogen. The fetched perfusion and breath-test records measure both machines in living humans. Jejunal perfusion with an occluding-balloon technique showed glucose absorption is a saturable function of load — a single maximum velocity and half-saturating load fitted all flow rates and starting concentrations — and that glucose stimulated water and sodium movement progressively as its concentration rose from 14 to 133 mmol/L (≈252 to ≈2,394 mg/dL) (Modigliani & Bernier 1971). The Fordtran group's ileal perfusion study then complicated the simple sodium story: replacing luminal sodium with mannitol cut active glucose absorption by only 23% in vivo (magnesium substitution, 45%), raising the apparent Km without changing Vmax, while fructose absorption was entirely unaffected by sodium removal — direct human evidence for fructose's separate carrier (Bieberdorf, Morawski & Fordtran 1975). Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer's breath-hydrogen studies quantified the fructose ceiling: absorption capacity for fructose alone ranged from under 5 g to over 50 g across 10 healthy adults, with malabsorption in 8 of 10 at a 50 g dose, while the same fructose given as sucrose, or with equimolar glucose, was absorbed completely — glucose rescues fructose uptake dose-dependently (Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer 1986) — and sorbitol does the opposite, provoking malabsorption of a fructose-sorbitol mixture in 7 of 10 even at individually tolerated doses (Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer 1987).

cards.headline: Jejunal glucose absorption is saturable: one maximum velocity and one half-saturating load fit every flow rate — and glucose drags water and sodium with it up to 133 mmol/L (≈2,394 mg/dL) (N not documented)
cards.summary: Jejunal glucose absorption is saturable: one maximum velocity and one half-saturating load fit every flow rate — and glucose drags water and sodium with it up to 133 mmol/L (≈2,394 mg/dL) (N not documented)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (jejunal perfusion, glucose/sodium/water absorption kinetics) — N not documented
cards.people: Healthy human subjects (number not stated in the record) studied by jejunal perfusion with a proximal occluding balloon at variable flow rates and starting glucose concentrations; absorption of glucose, sodium and water measured from the perfused segment, with the balloon inflated and deflated compared.
cards.result: Absorption of glucose and water was significantly higher with the balloon deflated than inflated, probably because of reflux above the infusion point; 0 to 4.2 ml/min of endogenous secretions could be recovered above the inflated balloon. Increasing flow rates increased the glucose absorption rate, but a single relationship held between glucose load and glucose absorption rate, and single values for the maximum velocity and the half-saturating load could be calculated whatever the infusion rate and initial glucose concentration. The stimulating effect of glucose on water and sodium movement increased gradually as initial sugar concentration rose from 14 to 133 mmol/L (≈252 to ≈2,394 mg/dL); above that concentration water and sodium movement fell despite constant initial sodium.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed plainly; the numerical Vmax and half-saturating load values are not stated in the record's abstract and are therefore not quoted — the carded claims are saturability, the single load–absorption relationship, and the glucose-driven water/sodium movement with its high-concentration reversal.
cards.source: Modigliani R, Bernier JJ. Absorption of glucose, sodium, and water by the human jejunum studied by intestinal perfusion with a proximal occluding balloon and at variable flow rates. Gut. 1971. PMID: 5552186. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: In the living ileum, glucose absorption barely needs luminal sodium (mannitol substitution cuts it only 23%) — but fructose needs none at all, proving its separate carrier (N not documented)
cards.summary: In the living ileum, glucose absorption barely needs luminal sodium (mannitol substitution cuts it only 23%) — but fructose needs none at all, proving its separate carrier (N not documented)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ileal perfusion, sodium dependence of sugar absorption) — N not documented
cards.people: Healthy human subjects (number not stated in the record) undergoing in-vivo ileal perfusion measuring absorption of glucose, galactose and 3-O-methylglucose (actively transported sugars with different affinities) and of fructose, with sodium in the perfusate replaced by mannitol or by magnesium.
cards.result: Mannitol substitution for sodium reduced active glucose absorption by only 23%; magnesium substitution depressed it by 45%. The apparent Km for glucose absorption rose when sodium was replaced by magnesium, but Vmax was unchanged; magnesium did not depress glucose absorption when sodium was present. Neither sodium removal nor magnesium had any effect on fructose absorption. Absorption of the low-affinity sugars galactose and 3-O-methylglucose fell by about 40–50% when mannitol replaced sodium. The authors set out to reconcile the in-vitro doctrine of absolute sodium dependence with these in-vivo findings, in which active glucose absorption from a sodium-free solution was almost as rapid as from sodium chloride.
cards.watchOut: This is an ileal, not jejunal, perfusion study — carded as the Fordtran programme's in-vivo sodium-dependence test and labelled by its actual segment; N not documented in the record. Its fructose result (zero sodium effect) is the human in-vivo counterpart of the textbook's separate-carrier account.
cards.source: Bieberdorf FA, Morawski S, Fordtran JS. Effect of sodium, mannitol, and magnesium on glucose, galactose, 3-O-methylglucose, and fructose absorption in the human ileum. Gastroenterology. 1975. PMID: 1116666. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fructose capacity is limited and wildly variable — under 5 g to over 50 g across healthy adults; 8 of 10 malabsorbed a 50 g dose, but glucose or sucrose rescued absorption completely (N = 10)
cards.summary: Fructose capacity is limited and wildly variable — under 5 g to over 50 g across healthy adults; 8 of 10 malabsorbed a 50 g dose, but glucose or sucrose rescued absorption completely (N = 10)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (breath-hydrogen fructose absorption capacity) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy adults given breath-hydrogen challenges with 10% solutions of fructose at doses from 5 to 50 g, with fructose absorption quantified against lactulose standards; comparison challenges used 50–100 g sucrose and glucose–fructose mixtures.
cards.result: Significant hydrogen production (a rise of 20 ppm or more, the malabsorption criterion) followed 50, 37.5, 25, 20 and 15 g fructose doses in eight, seven, five, four and one subjects respectively; one subject malabsorbed even a 10 g dose and possibly 5 g. In contrast, no malabsorption was detected in any subject after 100, 75 or 50 g sucrose or a mixture of 50 g glucose plus 50 g fructose. Mixtures of 50 g fructose with 25 g or 12.5 g glucose were malabsorbed by three and seven subjects respectively — glucose stimulates fructose uptake dose-dependently. Symptoms during all challenges were mild or absent. The authors conclude healthy fructose absorption capacity ranges from less than 5 g to more than 50 g, and raise the possible existence of more than one intestinal transport system for fructose.
cards.watchOut: Breath hydrogen is an indirect malabsorption signal (it requires colonic fermentation of the unabsorbed dose), and the challenges were pure fructose solutions on an empty stomach — food matrices change the picture, as this study's own sucrose and glucose-mixture arms show.
cards.source: Rumessen JJ, Gudmand-Høyer E. Absorption capacity of fructose in healthy adults. Comparison with sucrose and its constituent monosaccharides. Gut. 1986. PMID: 3781328. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Breath Tests · Female · Fructose · Glucose · Humans · Hydrogen · Intestinal Absorption · Male · Middle Aged · Sucrose
