cards.headline: Sorbitol sabotages fructose: a mixture at individually tolerated doses was malabsorbed by 7 of 10 healthy adults and caused distress in 5 — while the same fructose as sucrose was absorbed cleanly (N = 10)
cards.summary: Sorbitol sabotages fructose: a mixture at individually tolerated doses was malabsorbed by 7 of 10 healthy adults and caused distress in 5 — while the same fructose as sucrose was absorbed cleanly (N = 10)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (breath-hydrogen fructose–sorbitol interaction) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy adults given breath-hydrogen tests after a fructose–sorbitol mixture dosed at amounts corresponding to each subject's individually measured absorption capacities, with the carbohydrates also given separately, and a sucrose-plus-sorbitol comparison mixture in four of the seven malabsorbers.
cards.result: Significant malabsorption of the fructose–sorbitol mixture was evident in 7 of 10 subjects, and the mixture caused mild to severe gastrointestinal distress in five; when the carbohydrates were given separately, symptoms were absent. Individual absorption capacities for fructose and sorbitol were significantly correlated. When four of the seven malabsorbers took a mixture with a similar amount of fructose given as sucrose plus a similar amount of sorbitol, malabsorption failed to appear and symptoms were absent. The authors conclude that in healthy adults sorbitol interferes with fructose absorption and/or vice versa.
cards.watchOut: Doses were titrated to each subject's own absorption capacity, so the 7-of-10 figure describes behaviour at the edge of capacity, not at ordinary dietary intakes; the durable claim is the interaction itself (sorbitol worsens, glucose and sucrose rescue fructose absorption).
cards.source: Rumessen JJ, Gudmand-Høyer E. Malabsorption of fructose-sorbitol mixtures. Interactions causing abdominal distress. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1987. PMID: 3602922. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: glucose rides a saturable sodium-coupled carrier that drags water with it; fructose rides a separate, sodium-independent, capacity-limited carrier that glucose rescues and sorbitol sabotages
cards.summary: Synthesis: glucose rides a saturable sodium-coupled carrier that drags water with it; fructose rides a separate, sodium-independent, capacity-limited carrier that glucose rescues and sorbitol sabotages
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human perfusion and breath-test studies above.
cards.result: Jejunal and ileal sugar absorption in healthy humans, as the fetched records show them: glucose absorption is a saturable function of luminal load — one maximum velocity and one half-saturating load describe it across flow rates — and absorbed glucose stimulates coupled water and sodium movement, rising with concentration to 133 mmol/L (≈2,394 mg/dL) and reversing above it. In vivo the sodium coupling is looser than the in-vitro doctrine: removing luminal sodium cuts glucose absorption by only about a quarter (mannitol) to a half (magnesium), through a Km effect with Vmax preserved. Fructose is handled by a separate, sodium-independent carrier whose capacity in health ranges from under 5 g to over 50 g; doses above capacity spill to colonic fermentation (breath hydrogen) with usually mild symptoms. Co-ingested glucose raises fructose uptake dose-dependently and sucrose is absorbed completely, while sorbitol interferes with fructose absorption. REFUSAL NOTED: the Holdsworth & Dawson 1965 fructose-absorption record (PMID: 14254528) has an empty abstract and its content could not be verified this session, so it is not carded; the perfusion-era claims rest on Modigliani & Bernier and the Fordtran group instead. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the two-carrier account and the fructose capacity limit are concordant across perfusion and breath-test methods.
cards.watchOut: The two perfusion studies do not document their subject numbers in the fetched records (printed on their faces), and breath-hydrogen malabsorption is a fermentation signal, not a direct mucosal measurement; transporter names (SGLT1, GLUT5, GLUT2) are the textbooks' molecular framing, assigned after these classic studies were done.

shelves.title: Saliva production: a circadian, sex-patterned resting flow — with stimulated gland capacity that survives healthy ageing
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much saliva is produced — unstimulated and stimulated whole-saliva flow rates, the glands' relative contributions at rest versus stimulation, and the circadian rhythm of flow and composition?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall and Ganong give the textbook account of salivary secretion: roughly 1,000–1,500 ml of saliva a day, produced at a low unstimulated whole-saliva flow of a few tenths of a ml/min at rest — dominated by the submandibular glands — and rising severalfold on stimulation, when the parotid glands' share grows; those specific figures are the textbooks' account, since the fetched primary records below mostly report rhythms and comparisons rather than printing the canonical rates. What the primary human records do establish is the rhythm and the modifiers. Dawes showed that unstimulated whole-saliva flow and its sodium and chloride concentrations follow a significant circadian rhythm, as does the composition of parotid saliva stimulated at a clamped flow of 1.0 ml/min (Dawes 1972, N = 8), and that unstimulated submandibular flow likewise cycles across the day (Dawes 1975, N = 9) — so a 'normal' flow value is meaningless without its clock time. The large cross-sectional records fix the person-level modifiers: in 629 adults, resting and stimulated whole-saliva secretion rates were significantly lower in women than men, and women's resting rate fell with age (Heintze 1983); in 116 unmedicated healthy people, unstimulated whole-saliva flow fell significantly with age (P < 0.001) while stimulated parotid flow did not differ across age groups from 20 to over 80 years (Percival 1994); and gland-specific measurement found no diminution at all in submandibular output, resting or stimulated, across ages 26–93 (Tylenda 1988, N = 90). The reconciled picture: resting whole-mouth flow ebbs with age and time of day, but the glands' stimulated secretory capacity is largely preserved in healthy ageing — the dry mouth of old age is more often medication and disease than gland failure, a conclusion Dawes' framework anticipates in noting that the sensation of dry mouth appears when unstimulated flow falls by roughly 40–50%.

cards.headline: Flow itself keeps time: unstimulated whole-saliva flow rate and its sodium/chloride concentrations follow a significant circadian rhythm (N = 8)
cards.summary: Flow itself keeps time: unstimulated whole-saliva flow rate and its sodium/chloride concentrations follow a significant circadian rhythm (N = 8)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (circadian cosinor analysis of whole and parotid saliva) — N = 8
cards.people: 8 subjects from whom unstimulated whole saliva and parotid saliva stimulated at a constant flow rate of 1.0 ml/min were collected at about 07.00, 11.00, 14.00, 17.00 and 22.00 h, with oral temperature recorded several times daily over spans of 4 to 26 days; least-squares cosine (cosinor) analysis tested for rhythms.
cards.result: Unstimulated whole saliva showed significant circadian rhythms in flow rate and in the concentrations of sodium and chloride, but not in protein, potassium, calcium, phosphate or urea. Stimulated parotid saliva — collected at a clamped flow — showed significant circadian rhythms in the concentrations of protein, sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride, but not phosphate or urea. Oral temperature also showed a circadian rhythm, and all rhythms had a 24.0 h periodicity.
cards.watchOut: N = 8, printed plainly, sampled repeatedly over many days — the design suits rhythm detection, and the record reports rhythm significance rather than printing the mean flow values, so no absolute ml/min figure is quoted from this card.
cards.source: Dawes C. Circadian rhythms in human salivary flow rate and composition. The Journal of physiology. 1972. PMID: 5016036. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The submandibular gland cycles too: its unstimulated flow rate shows a group-significant circadian rhythm across the waking day (N = 9)
cards.summary: The submandibular gland cycles too: its unstimulated flow rate shows a group-significant circadian rhythm across the waking day (N = 9)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (circadian cosinor analysis of submandibular saliva) — N = 9
cards.people: 9 subjects who recorded oral temperature and collected unstimulated submandibular saliva and submandibular saliva stimulated by sour lemon drops at a constant flow rate of 1 ml/min, at about 07.00, 11.00, 14.00, 17.00 and 22.00 h daily for about 11 days.
cards.result: Unstimulated submandibular saliva showed circadian rhythms, significant for the group as a whole, in flow rate and in the concentrations of sodium, potassium, magnesium, chloride and inorganic phosphate, but not in protein or calcium. Stimulated submandibular saliva showed group-significant rhythms in sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and inorganic phosphate, but not protein. The author warns that because of the high amplitude of many of these rhythms, they must be taken into account when establishing the normal range of salivary values.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, printed plainly; gland saliva was collected by cannulation/catheter methods of the era, and as with Reference 1 the carded claim is the rhythm's existence and its implication for reference ranges, not an absolute flow figure.

cards.headline: The big normative sample: resting and stimulated whole-saliva secretion rates are significantly lower in women than men, and women's resting rate falls with age (N = 629)
cards.summary: The big normative sample: resting and stimulated whole-saliva secretion rates are significantly lower in women than men, and women's resting rate falls with age (N = 629)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cross-sectional normative secretion-rate survey) — N = 629
cards.people: 629 adults (286 men, 343 females) in four age groups, each giving duplicate determinations of secretion rate and buffer effect of resting and chewing-stimulated (paraffin) whole saliva within an interval of 1–2 weeks.
cards.result: For all variables, duplicate tests correlated highly significantly — the measurements are reproducible. The secretion rate of resting as well as stimulated saliva was significantly lower for females than for males. For females, the resting secretion rate was negatively correlated with age. The buffer effect was also significantly lower in females for both resting and stimulated saliva, though for females it rose with age, tending to catch up with males. Irrespective of sex, resting secretion rate correlated highly with stimulated secretion rate.
cards.watchOut: A cross-sectional survey: the female age correlation mixes cohort with ageing, and the record's abstract reports significance and direction rather than the group mean rates, so no ml/min values are quoted from this card.
cards.source: Heintze U, Birkhed D, Björn H. Secretion rate and buffer effect of resting and stimulated whole saliva as a function of age and sex. Swedish dental journal. 1983. PMID: 6583873. cards.headline: Ageing ebbs resting flow but not the stimulated response: unstimulated whole saliva falls significantly with age (P < 0.001) while stimulated parotid flow is flat from age 20 to 80+ (N = 116)
cards.summary: Ageing ebbs resting flow but not the stimulated response: unstimulated whole saliva falls significantly with age (P < 0.001) while stimulated parotid flow is flat from age 20 to 80+ (N = 116)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age- and sex-stratified resting whole and stimulated parotid flow) — N = 116
cards.people: 116 unmedicated, healthy individuals in four age groups (20–39, 40–59, 60–79, and 80 years and over), in whom unstimulated (resting) whole saliva and stimulated parotid saliva flow rates were measured.
cards.result: A significant decrease in unstimulated whole-saliva secretion rates with age was observed (P < 0.001), but stimulated parotid flow rates were not significantly different across the four age groups. Females had significantly lower mean flow rates than males for both unstimulated whole saliva (P < 0.005) and stimulated parotid saliva (P < 0.05). The authors conclude that elderly subjects have no impairment in their ability to respond to sialogogues, but resting rates are significantly lower than in younger people and may contribute to the oral mucosal diseases of old age.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional and restricted to unmedicated healthy people — precisely the group in whom gland function should be best preserved; the card supports 'healthy ageing spares stimulated parotid capacity', not 'old mouths are never dry'.
cards.source: Percival RS, Challacombe SJ, Marsh PD. Flow rates of resting whole and stimulated parotid saliva in relation to age and gender. Journal of dental research. 1994. PMID: 8083437. cards.headline: Gland-specific ageing check: submandibular output, resting and citrate-stimulated, does not diminish at all between ages 26 and 93 (N = 90)
cards.summary: Gland-specific ageing check: submandibular output, resting and citrate-stimulated, does not diminish at all between ages 26 and 93 (N = 90)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (submandibular flow across the adult age span) — N = 90
cards.people: 90 male and female adults aged 26–93 years, none taking prescription medications for systemic disease, in whom unstimulated and citrate-stimulated submandibular saliva production was measured.
cards.result: There was no diminution in submandibular gland fluid output, at rest or during stimulation, with increasing age; similar findings previously reported for the parotid glands were also confirmed. The authors conclude that major-gland fluid secretion capacity is maintained in healthy older individuals.
cards.watchOut: Read alongside Reference 4 rather than against it: whole-mouth resting flow can fall with age (minor glands, mucosal and collection contributions included) while the named major glands' measured output is preserved; the two records measure different things and both are carded as reported.
cards.source: Tylenda CA et al. Evaluation of submandibular salivary flow rate in different age groups. Journal of dental research. 1988. PMID: 3166006. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: saliva flow is rhythmic, sex- and age-patterned at rest, but the glands' stimulated capacity survives healthy ageing
cards.summary: Synthesis: saliva flow is rhythmic, sex- and age-patterned at rest, but the glands' stimulated capacity survives healthy ageing
cards.people: Synthesis of the five primary human studies above.
cards.result: Saliva production in healthy humans, as the fetched records show it: unstimulated whole-saliva flow and submandibular flow both follow significant circadian rhythms, and composition (sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, phosphate) cycles even when parotid flow is clamped at 1.0 ml/min — so reference values are clock-dependent. Women secrete at significantly lower resting and stimulated whole-saliva rates than men (N = 629). Resting whole-saliva flow declines with age in cross-section, yet stimulated parotid flow does not differ from age 20 to over 80 and submandibular output is undiminished from 26 to 93 in unmedicated healthy people: the machinery's capacity is preserved, and resting-flow ebb is not gland failure. The textbooks' canonical quantities — on the order of 1,000–1,500 ml/day in total, a few tenths of a ml/min unstimulated whole-saliva flow, severalfold higher stimulated flow, submandibular dominance at rest giving way to a larger parotid share on stimulation (Guyton & Hall; Ganong) — are presented here explicitly as the textbook's account: the fetched primary records establish the rhythm, sex and age patterns but do not print those absolute rates. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the rhythm and the resting-versus-stimulated age dissociation, which are concordant across five independent records.
cards.watchOut: Absolute flow rates (ml/min) and daily volumes are carried as the textbooks' account because the carded records report rhythms, directions and significance rather than the canonical numbers; any future card printing an absolute rate should come from a record that states it.

shelves.title: Exocrine pancreatic response: a brisk, saturable secretin response and a gland that only a mixed meal switches from cycling to feeding
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does the exocrine pancreas respond to a meal and to secretin/CCK stimulation — what are enzyme and bicarbonate outputs in the classic duodenal-aspiration and secretin-test studies, and how is the cephalic versus intestinal phase divided?
shelves.balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep divide pancreatic secretion into a small cephalic phase (vagal, anticipatory), a gastric phase, and the dominant intestinal phase, in which acid-driven secretin releases a bicarbonate-rich fluid from the duct cells while fat- and protein-driven cholecystokinin (CCK) releases enzyme-rich secretion from the acini; between meals the gland cycles with the interdigestive migrating motor complex instead of secreting steadily. The fetched human aspiration and cannulation records measure those responses directly. Pure pancreatic juice collected by endoscopic duct cannulation from 20 normal subjects responded briskly even to small secretin doses (1 and 4 clinical units), with peak bicarbonate concentration after the 4-unit stimulus and the greatest volumes and bicarbonate and protein outputs after 70 units; protein and amylase concentrations were highest in the first specimens and fell after stimulation, and all indices plateaued 10–20 minutes into combined secretin–pancreozymin infusion (Denyer & Cotton 1979). An extended function test adding a second secretin–pancreozymin bolus showed the standard test already exhausts the discriminatory signal — repeat bolus stimulation cannot wring more diagnostic separation from the gland (Gilinsky 1983). The Lundh test meal gives the endogenous version: volume secretion rises immediately and identically in health and pancreatic insufficiency, while enzyme secretion is what fails in disease, with lipase and trypsin outputs tracking the secretin–cerulein test (Bozkurt 1990). And the phase logic was proven by duodenal perfusion in 6 healthy men: only a mixed meal converted the cyclical interdigestive secretory pattern into the sustained fed pattern — glucose, fat or protein alone, each releasing less or no CCK, left the cycle intact (Katschinski 1992). A modern endoscopic secretin test in 16 healthy volunteers confirms the textbook kinetics with contemporary methods: juice flow peaks early, bicarbonate concentration peaks late, and chloride and bicarbonate vary reciprocally at constant sodium and potassium (Conwell 2005).

cards.headline: Pure pancreatic juice in normals: brisk bicarbonate response even to 1–4 units of secretin, maximal outputs at 70 units, and a plateau 10–20 minutes into combined stimulation (N = 20 normal subjects)
cards.summary: Pure pancreatic juice in normals: brisk bicarbonate response even to 1–4 units of secretin, maximal outputs at 70 units, and a plateau 10–20 minutes into combined stimulation (N = 20 normal subjects)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (endoscopic pure pancreatic juice collection, secretin dose–response) — N = 20 normal subjects
cards.people: 20 normal subjects within a series of 54 patients whose pure pancreatic juice was obtained from within the pancreatic duct after endoscopic cannulation of the papilla of Vater, with intravenous GIH secretin given in small (1 and 4 clinical units) and large (70 units) doses and secretin–pancreozymin infusions; patients with chronic pancreatitis formed the comparison group.
cards.result: In all 20 normal subjects there was a brisk response to intravenous secretin in small dosage (1 and 4 CU). Peak bicarbonate concentrations occurred after the 4 CU stimulus, whereas volumes and bicarbonate and protein outputs were greatest after 70 CU. Total protein and amylase concentrations were highest in the first specimens collected and fell rapidly after stimulation. Plateau levels for all indices were achieved 10–20 minutes after starting infusions of secretin and pancreozymin. The authors also note that endoscopic cannulation cannot guarantee complete recovery of secretions, so volume and output measurements may be inaccurate.
cards.watchOut: The normal arm is 20 subjects inside a 54-patient clinical series, and collection was admittedly incomplete — the carded claims are the dose–response shape (small-dose briskness, concentration-versus-output dissociation, plateau timing), not absolute output volumes.
cards.source: Denyer ME, Cotton PB. Pure pancreatic juice studies in normal subjects and patients with chronic pancreatitis. Gut. 1979. PMID: 428831. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Bicarbonates · Chronic Disease · Humans · Pancreatic Juice · Pancreatitis · Proteins · Secretin · Time Factors

cards.headline: One bolus is enough: a second secretin–pancreozymin injection adds nothing to the standard pancreatic function test's discrimination (N not documented)
cards.summary: One bolus is enough: a second secretin–pancreozymin injection adds nothing to the standard pancreatic function test's discrimination (N not documented)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (extended secretin–pancreozymin function test, controls and patients) — N not documented
cards.people: Patients with varying degrees of pancreatic damage and control subjects (numbers not stated in the record) studied with an extended pancreatic function test in which a second injection of secretin and pancreozymin was given after completion of the standard test.
cards.result: The discriminatory value of the standard pancreatic function test with regard to bicarbonate and enzyme output was not enhanced by a second bolus dose of hormones. The authors conclude that the secretory potential of damaged exocrine tissue cannot be exhausted by prolonged stimulation employing repeat bolus stimulation — the standard single-stimulus test already captures the gland's responsive capacity.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed plainly, and the abstract reports no absolute bicarbonate or enzyme values; the card contributes the saturation point of the dose–response — repeat bolus stimulation adds no information — rather than normative outputs.
cards.source: Gilinsky NH, Mee AS, Marks IN. Evaluation of an extended pancreatic function test in normal subjects and in patients with chronic pancreatitis. South African medical journal = Suid-Afrikaanse tydskrif vir geneeskunde. 1983. PMID: 6849175. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The meal response (Lundh test): volume rises immediately and identically in health and insufficiency — it is enzyme output that separates them (N not documented)
cards.summary: The meal response (Lundh test): volume rises immediately and identically in health and insufficiency — it is enzyme output that separates them (N not documented)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Lundh test-meal pancreatic volume and enzyme kinetics) — N not documented
cards.people: Healthy subjects and patients with pancreatic insufficiency (numbers not stated in the record) studied by duodenal aspiration after the Lundh test meal, with prestimulatory and postprandial volume and enzyme kinetics measured, oral cimetidine pretreatment tested, and results compared against the secretin–cerulein test.
cards.result: Prestimulatory volume rates did not differentiate normal from pathological pancreatic function. After the test meal, the immediate increase in volume secretion was identical in healthy subjects and patients with pancreatic insufficiency, whereas the latter showed a drastic reduction of prestimulatory and postprandial enzyme secretion. Cimetidine taken 12 and 2 hours before the study had no effect on volume or enzyme secretion or on endogenous CCK release. Lipase and trypsin estimation correlated significantly between the Lundh test and the secretin–cerulein test, and the authors judge endogenous stimulation by the Lundh meal a reliable test for routine and scientific purposes.

cards.headline: Only the mixed meal flips the switch: intraduodenal glucose, fat or protein alone leave the cyclical interdigestive pattern intact, while the mixed meal — the strongest CCK releaser — converts it to the fed pattern (N = 6)
cards.summary: Only the mixed meal flips the switch: intraduodenal glucose, fat or protein alone leave the cyclical interdigestive pattern intact, while the mixed meal — the strongest CCK releaser — converts it to the fed pattern (N = 6)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (intraduodenal nutrient perfusion, pancreatic pattern conversion and CCK release) — N = 6
cards.people: 6 healthy male volunteers studied on 4 separate days, each receiving 180 minutes of intraduodenal perfusion (2 ml/min) of a mixed liquid meal (0.9 kcal/min) or isocaloric solutions of glucose, fractionated soya oil or casein hydrolysate/albumin (0.36 kcal/min), with duodenal aspirates for pancreatic enzyme outputs and blood for CCK and neurotensin.
cards.result: The mixed meal converted the cyclical interdigestive secretory pattern into the non-cyclical fed pattern, whereas none of the three individual nutrients abolished the interdigestive pattern. Lipid and protein perfusion, like the mixed meal, consistently stimulated CCK release — integrated incremental CCK release was 32.3 ± 9.9 pg/ml × 180 min with the mixed meal, 23.2 ± 6.5 with lipid (P < 0.05 versus mixed meal) and 13.4 ± 3.8 with protein (P < 0.05 versus mixed meal) — while the carbohydrate solution did not significantly release CCK. No perfusate raised neurotensin levels. The authors frame the study as assessing CCK's and neurotensin's roles in the interdigestive-to-fed conversion.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, printed plainly, and the individual-nutrient perfusions delivered a lower caloric load (0.36 versus 0.9 kcal/min), so 'only the mixed meal converts' is confounded by dose as well as composition; the CCK gradient across perfusates is the cleaner carded result.
cards.source: Katschinski M et al. Induction of the fed pattern of human exocrine pancreatic secretion by nutrients: role of cholecystokinin and neurotensin. The Clinical investigator. 1992. cards.headline: Modern confirmation by endoscopic secretin test: juice flow peaks early, bicarbonate concentration peaks late, and chloride and bicarbonate move reciprocally at constant sodium and potassium (N = 16)
cards.summary: Modern confirmation by endoscopic secretin test: juice flow peaks early, bicarbonate concentration peaks late, and chloride and bicarbonate move reciprocally at constant sodium and potassium (N = 16)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (secretin-stimulated endoscopic pancreatic function test in healthy volunteers) — N = 16
cards.people: 16 healthy volunteers completing a prospective randomised crossover study (17 enrolled) of the synthetic porcine secretin-stimulated endoscopic pancreatic function test, with and without standardised moderate sedation (meperidine/midazolam), duodenal fluid aspirated every 5 minutes for 1 hour for electrolyte measurement.
cards.result: Maximum pancreatic juice flow occurred during the early phase of secretion and maximum bicarbonate concentration during the late phase. Sodium and potassium concentrations stayed constant over the hour, while chloride and bicarbonate exhibited the reciprocal relationship seen in traditional gastroduodenal tube collection studies. Moderate sedation made no statistical difference to the secretory measures. The healthy-volunteer secretin response characterised here is the carded content; the study's purpose was to test whether sedation distorts the endoscopic function test.
cards.watchOut: The record names the stimulant product as published — synthetic porcine secretin (ChiRhoClin, Inc., Burtonsville, Maryland) — named here for clarification of what was tested, not as promotion. Absolute peak bicarbonate values are not stated in the fetched record and are not quoted; the carded claims are the phase timing and the reciprocal anion pattern.
cards.source: Conwell DL et al. The effect of moderate sedation on exocrine pancreas function in normal healthy subjects: a prospective, randomized, cross-over trial using the synthetic porcine secretin stimulated Endoscopic Pancreatic Function Test (ePFT). The American journal of gastroenterology. 2005. PMID: 15842594. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: secretin drives an early fluid wave whose bicarbonate concentration peaks late; meals work through CCK, and only a mixed meal switches the gland from its interdigestive cycle to the fed pattern
cards.summary: Synthesis: secretin drives an early fluid wave whose bicarbonate concentration peaks late; meals work through CCK, and only a mixed meal switches the gland from its interdigestive cycle to the fed pattern
cards.people: Synthesis of the five primary human studies above.
cards.result: The exocrine pancreatic response in healthy humans, as the fetched records show it: the gland answers even small secretin doses briskly, with peak bicarbonate concentration at a low dose (4 CU) but maximal volume and bicarbonate/protein outputs at high dose (70 CU), protein and amylase concentrations highest in the first juice and falling after stimulation, and a plateau 10–20 minutes into combined secretin–pancreozymin stimulation; a second hormone bolus adds no further information, marking the response as saturable at the standard test. To a meal (Lundh), volume rises immediately while enzyme output is the variable that carries the signal; the underlying pattern logic is cyclical between meals and converts to the sustained fed pattern only under a mixed meal, paralleling its superior CCK release (32.3 versus 23.2 lipid, 13.4 protein pg/ml × 180 min integrated increments; carbohydrate not significant). Contemporary endoscopic testing reproduces the classic kinetics: flow early, bicarbonate concentration late, chloride and bicarbonate reciprocal at constant cations. The cephalic-versus-intestinal phase division (a small vagal cephalic contribution against the dominant intestinal phase) is carried as the textbooks' account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep), since no carded record here partitions the phases numerically. AGE FLAG, per the slate: much of this primary base is 1979–1992 aspiration and cannulation methodology — methods and the two undocumented Ns are printed on the faces. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: dose–response shape, meal pattern conversion and electrolyte kinetics are concordant across four decades of methods.
cards.watchOut: Two of five records do not document subject numbers in their fetched abstracts (printed on their faces), aspiration methods incompletely recover secretion, and absolute normative output values (ml/hour, enzyme units) are not quoted anywhere on this shelf because no fetched record states them — the shelf's claims are kinetic and qualitative-quantitative (dose, timing, pattern), not a normative output table.

shelves.title: Normal oesophageal peristalsis on high-resolution manometry: latency ~6.0 s, posture- and population-dependent DCI/IRP norms, and ~7% ineffective swallows in health
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal oesophageal peristalsis and bolus transit on high-resolution manometry — distal contractile integral, distal latency and integrated relaxation pressure distributions in healthy volunteers, and what fraction of swallows are ineffective or failed in health?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). The Chicago-classification volunteer programme defines the metrics: distal latency median 6.0 s to the contractile deceleration point (Roman, PMID 20978487) and supine normative IRP/DCI that fall significantly when sitting (Xiao, PMID 22897486) — two labelled companion reports from the same 75-volunteer Northwestern cohort. An independent impedance-manometry cohort (Shi, PMID 23730912, N = 42) adds bolus-transit methodology and the base rate of imperfection in health: 6.3% weak and 0.7% failed liquid swallows, with a higher local IRP ceiling (20.5 mmHg). Pack #6637 covers transient lower-oesophageal-sphincter relaxations and reflux — a different question, cross-pointed, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Roman 2011: distal latency in 75 healthy volunteers — median 6.0 seconds to the contractile deceleration point, the timing metric the Chicago classification is built on
cards.summary: Roman 2011: distal latency in 75 healthy volunteers — median 6.0 seconds to the contractile deceleration point, the timing metric the Chicago classification is built on
cards.people: 75 healthy volunteers whose high-resolution oesophageal pressure topography studies were merged in a computer simulation, normalising oesophageal length on a 100 × 200 pixel grid over 20 seconds per swallow to derive composite normative morphology and latency.
cards.result: Stereotyped landmarks isolated the distal segment: pressure troughs proximally and distally, and the contractile deceleration point marking where peristalsis terminates in the distal oesophagus. Distal contractile latency timed to the deceleration point was median 6.0 s (95% CI 4.8–7.6 s); timed to lower oesophageal sphincter contraction it was 9.2 s (95% CI 6.5–11.5 s). Short latency identifies rapidly conducted (premature) contractions — the basis of the distal-latency criterion for spasm in the Chicago classification. (Same Northwestern 75-volunteer programme as the Xiao card — a companion report, labelled as such.)
cards.watchOut: A methods-defining re-analysis of volunteer studies: it establishes how latency should be measured and its normal median, not a per-swallow failure rate — that comes from the Shi card.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Roman S et al. Distal contraction latency: a measure of propagation velocity optimized for esophageal pressure topography studies. Am J Gastroenterol. 2011. PMID: 20978487. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Xiao 2012: posture moves the norms — in the same 75 healthy volunteers, sitting IRP, DCI and CFV were all significantly lower than supine (IRP threshold 15 → 11 mmHg, DCI upper limit 8000 → 2500)
cards.summary: Xiao 2012: posture moves the norms — in the same 75 healthy volunteers, sitting IRP, DCI and CFV were all significantly lower than supine (IRP threshold 15 → 11 mmHg, DCI upper limit 8000 → 2500)
cards.people: 75 healthy volunteers and 120 patients whose oesophageal pressure topography studies included test swallows in both supine and sitting positions, with integrated relaxation pressure (IRP), distal contractile integral (DCI), contractile front velocity (CFV) and distal latency measured in each posture.
cards.result: In healthy volunteers, normative values of IRP, DCI and CFV all decreased significantly in the sitting posture. Applying sitting norms (a 27% reduction in the IRP threshold, 15 to 11 mmHg; a 69% reduction in the DCI upper limit, 8000 to 2500 mmHg·s·cm) to the patient studies reclassified 11% as abnormal oesophagogastric-junction relaxation and 22% as hypercontractile, while 3 patients with abnormal supine IRP normalised sitting (vascular artefact removed). The authors recommend studying both postures but keeping Chicago classification diagnoses on supine swallows with supine norms until outcome data exist. (Companion report to the Roman card, same 75-volunteer cohort.)
cards.watchOut: Normative ranges are posture-specific: quoting a DCI or IRP without its posture mixes two distributions. The patient reclassification percentages describe threshold sensitivity, not disease prevalence.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Xiao Y et al. cards.headline: Shi 2013: in 42 healthy Chinese volunteers on high-resolution impedance manometry, 6.3% of liquid swallows were weak and 0.7% failed — ineffective swallows occur in health
cards.summary: Shi 2013: in 42 healthy Chinese volunteers on high-resolution impedance manometry, 6.3% of liquid swallows were weak and 0.7% failed — ineffective swallows occur in health
cards.people: 42 healthy fasted volunteers studied supine with high-resolution impedance manometry: 411 liquid and 398 viscous swallows analysed for IRP, DCI, CFV and distal latency, with impedance bolus-transit assessment.
cards.result: The 95th-percentile values for liquid swallows were IRP 20.5 mmHg and DCI 3195 mmHg·s·cm — a higher IRP ceiling than the Northwestern supine norm, showing population/system variation in the 'normal' range. By Chicago criteria, 6.3% (26/411) of liquid swallows were weak peristalsis and 0.7% (3/411) failed peristalsis in these healthy people; at the person level, 28.6% met criteria for oesophagogastric-junction outflow obstruction and 4.7% for weak peristalsis on liquid swallows — normal people can cross diagnostic thresholds. Viscous swallows lowered IRP and CFV versus liquid (both P = 0.000) with DCI unchanged (P = 0.211).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre Chinese cohort on an impedance system: its higher IRP 95th percentile (20.5 versus the Chicago 15 mmHg) warns against treating any one laboratory's ceiling as universal; per-person 'diagnoses' in volunteers show threshold behaviour, not disease.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Shi Y et al. Normative data of high-resolution impedance manometry in the Chinese population. J Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2013. PMID: 23730912. cards.headline: Synthesis: Normal oesophageal peristalsis on high-resolution manometry: latency ~6.0 s, posture- and population-dependent DCI/IRP norms, and ~7% ineffective swallows in health
cards.summary: Synthesis: Normal oesophageal peristalsis on high-resolution manometry: latency ~6.0 s, posture- and population-dependent DCI/IRP norms, and ~7% ineffective swallows in health
cards.people: Synthesis of Roman 2011, Xiao 2012 and Shi 2013, framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence cards). Pack #6637 (transient LOS relaxations) is cross-pointed, not duplicated.
cards.result: Normal peristalsis on high-resolution manometry is a propagated distal contraction arriving ~6 seconds after the swallow (median distal latency 6.0 s, 95% CI 4.8–7.6), with vigour (DCI) and junction relaxation (IRP) distributed widely enough that the Chicago thresholds are statistical ceilings, not physiological absolutes. Those ceilings are conditional: they fall substantially from supine to sitting (IRP 15 → 11 mmHg; DCI upper limit 8000 → 2500 mmHg·s·cm), and an independent Chinese impedance cohort found a higher supine IRP ceiling (95th percentile 20.5 mmHg). Health is not perfection — about 7% of liquid swallows in healthy volunteers are weak (6.3%) or failed (0.7%), and over a quarter of healthy volunteers can cross a person-level diagnostic threshold on one protocol. Normal HRM is therefore a posture-, system- and population-labelled distribution, and single abnormal metrics in asymptomatic people are expected base-rate events.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: the two Northwestern cards are companion reports of one 75-volunteer cohort (labelled on their faces), so the independent replication in this pack is the Shi cohort; bolus-transit completeness percentages by impedance were not printed in the fetched Shi abstract and are not quoted.

shelves.title: Cenicriviroc (CCR2/CCR5 antagonist) for MASH (NASH) with fibrosis — a failed programme
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and fibrosis, does the CCR2/CCR5 antagonist cenicriviroc, compared with placebo, improve fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis?
shelves.balance: This is a failed programme, and the shelf's value is the negative answer. Phase 2b CENTAUR (n=289) missed its primary endpoint (≥2-point NAS improvement: 16% on cenicriviroc versus 19% on placebo — the treatment made no difference) but met a secondary fibrosis endpoint at year 1 (≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening steatohepatitis: 20% versus 10%), and its year-2 final analysis showed that most year-1 fibrosis responders on cenicriviroc maintained their response. The phase 3 AURORA trial (n=1,778 randomised; part 1 n=1,293) then tested exactly that fibrosis claim and did not confirm it: 22.3% on cenicriviroc versus 25.5% on placebo achieved ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening steatohepatitis at month 12 (the treatment made no difference), and steatohepatitis resolution was likewise no better than placebo. Safety and tolerability were comparable to placebo throughout — the drug failed on efficacy, not on safety. There are no clinical-outcome data (decompensation, transplant, death) for cenicriviroc in MASH, and development for this indication did not proceed after AURORA.

cards.headline: CENTAUR phase 2b, year 1 (2018): primary NAS endpoint missed (the treatment made no difference), but the secondary fibrosis endpoint favoured cenicriviroc 20% vs 10%, n = 289
cards.summary: CENTAUR phase 2b, year 1 (2018): primary NAS endpoint missed (the treatment made no difference), but the secondary fibrosis endpoint favoured cenicriviroc 20% vs 10%, n = 289
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CENTAUR year 1), Hepatology 2018
cards.people: 289 adults with NASH, NAFLD activity score (NAS) ≥4 and fibrosis stages 1–3 (NASH Clinical Research Network) at 81 clinical sites, randomised to cenicriviroc 150 mg daily (n=145) or placebo (n=144) for 1 year.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — ≥2-point NAS improvement with no worsening of fibrosis — was achieved by a similar proportion on cenicriviroc and placebo (16% vs 19%, P = 0.52), as was resolution of steatohepatitis (8% vs 6%, P = 0.49): on activity, the treatment made no difference. The key secondary fibrosis endpoint — ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement with no worsening of steatohepatitis — was met by significantly more patients on cenicriviroc (20% vs 10%, P = 0.02), with greater benefits in those with higher baseline disease activity and fibrosis stage. Biomarkers of systemic inflammation fell on cenicriviroc, and safety and tolerability were comparable to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A positive secondary endpoint after a missed primary endpoint is hypothesis-generating, not proof — exactly the pattern AURORA later failed to confirm. Biopsy endpoints at a single year are also subject to sampling and reader variability.
cards.source: Friedman SL, Ratziu V, Harrison SA, et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of cenicriviroc for treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis with fibrosis. Hepatology. 2018;67(5):1754-1767. PMID: 28833331. No registry ID appears in the fetched record. cards.headline: CENTAUR final analysis, year 2 (2020): most year-1 fibrosis responders on cenicriviroc maintained benefit (60% vs 30%), but the overall 2-year fibrosis comparison was no better than placebo
cards.summary: CENTAUR final analysis, year 2 (2020): most year-1 fibrosis responders on cenicriviroc maintained benefit (60% vs 30%), but the overall 2-year fibrosis comparison was no better than placebo
cards.type: Phase 2b final (year 2) analysis of CENTAUR, Hepatology 2020
cards.people: The same CENTAUR cohort: of 289 randomised participants, 242 entered year 2. Arms A and C continued cenicriviroc 150 mg or placebo respectively for 2 years; arm B took placebo in year 1 and switched to cenicriviroc in year 2. Biopsies at baseline, year 1 and year 2.
cards.result: Over 2 years, a similar proportion on continuous cenicriviroc and on placebo achieved ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement with no worsening of NASH (15% arm A versus 17% arm C — the treatment made no difference overall). Among those who had responded at year 1, twice the proportion on cenicriviroc maintained the benefit at year 2 (60% arm A versus 30% arm C), including 86% of those with stage 3 fibrosis at baseline; patients who switched from placebo to cenicriviroc achieved the fibrosis endpoint in 24% versus 17% on continued placebo (P = 0.37). The safety profile was comparable across groups.
cards.watchOut: Year-2 analyses were exploratory, the switch design blurs the placebo comparison, and the maintained-response figure is a subgroup of year-1 responders. This card reports the same trial as the previous card at a later time point, not an independent trial.

cards.headline: AURORA phase 3 (2024): cenicriviroc made no difference on the primary fibrosis endpoint — 22.3% versus 25.5% on placebo, n = 1,778 randomised
cards.summary: AURORA phase 3 (2024): cenicriviroc made no difference on the primary fibrosis endpoint — 22.3% versus 25.5% on placebo, n = 1,778 randomised
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (AURORA), Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2024
cards.people: 1,778 adults aged 18–75 with NASH and stage 2/3 liver fibrosis, randomised to cenicriviroc 150 mg or placebo once daily in a 2-part phase 3 study (part 1: n=1,293, 12 months; part 2: n=485, planned 60 months); the study was discontinued. Biopsies at screening, month 12, and early discontinuation or termination.
cards.result: In part 1 at month 12, a similar proportion on cenicriviroc and placebo achieved the primary endpoint of ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening of steatohepatitis (22.3% vs 25.5%; odds ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.63–1.10; P = 0.21 — the treatment made no difference), and complete resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis was also similar (23.0% vs 27.2%, P = 0.21). The safety profile was generally comparable across treatment groups, and the authors conclude the study did not demonstrate efficacy for treating liver fibrosis in NASH, while cenicriviroc was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: AURORA enrolled stage 2/3 fibrosis (CENTAUR had included stage 1), and the study's discontinuation truncated part 2, so no long-term or outcome data exist. The 'Child' MeSH term in the record is a record artefact; the trial enrolled adults aged 18–75.
cards.source: Anstee QM, Neuschwander-Tetri BA, Wai-Sun Wong V, et al. Cenicriviroc Lacked Efficacy to Treat Liver Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis: AURORA Phase III Randomized Study. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024;22(1):124-134.e1. PMID: 37061109. Registry ID: NCT03028740. cards.headline: Synthesis: a phase 2 fibrosis signal that the phase 3 trial, designed to test it, did not confirm
cards.summary: Synthesis: a phase 2 fibrosis signal that the phase 3 trial, designed to test it, did not confirm
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CENTAUR (289 randomised; 242 into year 2) and AURORA (1,778 randomised) — the complete randomised programme for cenicriviroc in MASH with fibrosis.
cards.result: The sequence is the classic one this library exists to record: a missed primary endpoint with a positive secondary fibrosis signal in phase 2 (20% vs 10%), followed by a large phase 3 that found the treatment made no difference on that very endpoint (22.3% vs 25.5%, numerically favouring placebo). Cenicriviroc was consistently well tolerated, so the failure is an efficacy failure. The answer to the question asked is no — UNLIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: CENTAUR's two cards are one trial at two time points; the independent evidence is two trials, and the larger, later one governs the verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above (PMIDs 28833331, 31943293, 37061109). No additional source.

shelves.title: Firsocostat-based combinations (with cilofexor, and with semaglutide) for MASH with advanced fibrosis
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and advanced fibrosis (F3–F4), do firsocostat-based combinations (with the FXR agonist cilofexor, and with semaglutide), compared with placebo or semaglutide alone, improve fibrosis or steatohepatitis activity?
shelves.balance: Phase-2-only evidence, and it must lead with the negative: in ATLAS (n=392, bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis, F3–F4), the primary endpoint — ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH at 48 weeks — was not met by any regimen (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint): cilofexor/firsocostat 21% versus 11% on placebo, P = 0.17, and the other combinations and monotherapies were further from significance. What ATLAS did show for cilofexor/firsocostat was significant improvement on exploratory measures — a machine-learning fibrosis score, ≥2-point NAS reduction, steatosis, inflammation and ballooning components, liver enzymes and non-invasive fibrosis markers — plus pruritus in 20–29% on cilofexor-containing regimens versus 15% on placebo. The semaglutide-combination trial (n=108, F2–F3) was open-label with a safety primary endpoint: combinations with cilofexor and/or firsocostat improved liver fat (MRI-PDFF) and biochemistry more than semaglutide alone on exploratory analyses, despite similar weight loss. The monotherapy card explains the combination rationale: firsocostat (GS-0976) alone reduced hepatic fat (≥30% MRI-PDFF response in 48% on 20 mg versus 15% on placebo) but raised serum triglycerides (median relative increases of 11–13%) — the liability the FXR-agonist pairing was meant to offset. No trial shows a confirmed histological fibrosis benefit, and there are no clinical-outcome data.

cards.headline: ATLAS phase 2b (2021): primary fibrosis endpoint NOT met by any regimen (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint); cilofexor/firsocostat 21% vs 11% placebo, P = 0.17, n = 392
cards.summary: ATLAS phase 2b (2021): primary fibrosis endpoint NOT met by any regimen (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint); cilofexor/firsocostat 21% vs 11% placebo, P = 0.17, n = 392
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised placebo-controlled combination trial (ATLAS), Hepatology 2021
cards.people: 392 patients with bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis attributable to NASH (F3–F4; 56% had cirrhosis, 83% had NAS ≥5), randomised to placebo, selonsertib 18 mg, cilofexor 30 mg or firsocostat 20 mg, alone or in two-drug combinations, once daily for 48 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH at week 48) was achieved in 11% on placebo versus 21% on cilofexor/firsocostat (P = 0.17), 19% on cilofexor/selonsertib (P = 0.26), 15% on firsocostat/selonsertib (P = 0.62), 12% on firsocostat alone (P = 0.94) and 12% on cilofexor alone (P = 0.96) — no regimen separated from placebo. On exploratory endpoints, cilofexor/firsocostat significantly decreased the machine-learning NASH CRN fibrosis score (P = 0.040), produced ≥2-point NAS reductions and improvements in steatosis, lobular inflammation, ballooning, ALT, AST, bilirubin, ELF score and liver stiffness versus placebo (all P ≤ 0.05). Pruritus occurred in 20–29% on cilofexor regimens versus 15% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: ATLAS also contained selonsertib arms, a third drug whose programme is separate; only the firsocostat-containing regimens answer this shelf's question. Exploratory machine-learning and biomarker wins after a missed primary endpoint are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Loomba R, Noureddin M, Kowdley KV, et al. Combination Therapies Including Cilofexor and Firsocostat for Bridging Fibrosis and Cirrhosis Attributable to NASH. Hepatology. 2021;73(2):625-643. PMID: 33169409. Registry ID: NCT03449446. cards.headline: Semaglutide-combination phase 2 (2022): adding cilofexor and/or firsocostat improved liver fat and biochemistry over semaglutide alone on exploratory endpoints; safety was the primary endpoint, n = 108
cards.summary: Semaglutide-combination phase 2 (2022): adding cilofexor and/or firsocostat improved liver fat and biochemistry over semaglutide alone on exploratory endpoints; safety was the primary endpoint, n = 108
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised open-label proof-of-concept trial, Journal of Hepatology 2022
cards.people: 108 patients with NASH and F2–F3 fibrosis on biopsy (or MRI-PDFF ≥10% with liver stiffness ≥7 kPa), randomised to 24 weeks of semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly alone (n=21) or combined with once-daily cilofexor 30 mg (n=22), cilofexor 100 mg (n=22), firsocostat 20 mg (n=22), or semaglutide plus cilofexor 30 mg plus firsocostat (n=21), in an open-label proof-of-concept trial.
cards.result: Treatments were well tolerated; adverse-event incidence was similar across groups (73–90%) and most events were gastrointestinal. Despite similar weight loss (7–10%), combinations produced greater improvements than semaglutide alone in liver steatosis by MRI-PDFF (least-squares mean absolute changes −9.8 to −11.0% versus −8.0%), liver biochemistry and non-invasive fibrosis tests — all exploratory efficacy endpoints, the trial's primary endpoint being safety. The authors state that double-blind placebo-controlled trials with adequate numbers are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, about 21–22 patients per arm, no placebo group and no biopsy efficacy endpoint: the steatosis and biochemistry differences are exploratory and cannot establish a fibrosis benefit. The record's MeSH includes 'Double-Blind Method' although the paper itself is open-label — the paper's own description governs.
cards.source: Alkhouri N, Herring R, Kabler H, et al. Safety and efficacy of combination therapy with semaglutide, cilofexor and firsocostat in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis: A randomised, open-label phase II trial. cards.headline: Firsocostat (GS-0976) monotherapy phase 2 (2018): ≥30% liver-fat response in 48% on 20 mg versus 15% on placebo — with triglyceride increases of 11–13%, n = 126
cards.summary: Firsocostat (GS-0976) monotherapy phase 2 (2018): ≥30% liver-fat response in 48% on 20 mg versus 15% on placebo — with triglyceride increases of 11–13%, n = 126
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Gastroenterology 2018
cards.people: 126 patients with NASH (hepatic steatosis ≥8% by MRI-PDFF and liver stiffness ≥2.5 kPa by magnetic resonance elastography, or historical biopsy consistent with NASH and F1–F3 fibrosis), randomised 2:2:1 to firsocostat (GS-0976) 20 mg, 5 mg, or placebo daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: A ≥30% relative decrease in MRI-PDFF occurred in 48% on firsocostat 20 mg (P = 0.004 versus placebo), 23% on 5 mg (P = 0.43) and 15% on placebo; median relative MRI-PDFF decrease was 29% on 20 mg versus 8% on placebo (P = 0.002). Stiffness by elastography did not differ among groups, though the fibrosis marker TIMP-1 fell dose-dependently on 20 mg. The safety liability: median relative increases of 11% and 13% in serum triglycerides on firsocostat — the effect that motivated pairing the drug with an FXR agonist in the combination trials.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, imaging and biomarker endpoints only (no biopsy efficacy claim), and a less advanced population (F1–F3) than ATLAS. Monotherapy is carded as the combination rationale and the source of the triglyceride warning, not as evidence the combinations work.
cards.source: Loomba R, Kayali Z, Noureddin M, et al. GS-0976 Reduces Hepatic Steatosis and Fibrosis Markers in Patients With Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease. cards.headline: Synthesis: combinations improve fat and biomarkers in phase 2, but the one trial powered on fibrosis missed its endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: combinations improve fat and biomarkers in phase 2, but the one trial powered on fibrosis missed its endpoint
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATLAS (392, F3–F4), the semaglutide-combination trial (108, F2–F3) and the firsocostat monotherapy trial (126, F1–F3).
cards.result: The pattern is consistent and consistently short of proof: firsocostat reduces liver fat, cilofexor/firsocostat improves NASH activity measures and non-invasive markers, and adding the pair to semaglutide improves fat and biochemistry beyond semaglutide alone — yet the only trial with a histological fibrosis primary endpoint, ATLAS, found the treatment made no difference on that endpoint for every regimen tested. That is MAYBE (weak evidence): a biologically coherent phase 2 signal awaiting a positive biopsy-endpoint trial that has not been published.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade exploratory or machine-learning endpoints over a missed primary endpoint. Pruritus (cilofexor) and triglyceride elevation (firsocostat) are the combination's standing costs.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above (PMIDs 33169409, 35439567, 30059671). No additional source.

shelves.title: Darvadstrocel for complex perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease (ADMIRE-CD programme) — SPLIT
shelves.question: In adults with Crohn's disease and complex perianal fistulas refractory to conventional or biologic therapy, does a single local injection of darvadstrocel (expanded allogeneic adipose-derived stem cells) versus placebo achieve combined clinical and radiological remission?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue · Adult · Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Crohn Disease/complications · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Evidence-Based Medicine · Female · Humans · Israel · Male · Mesenchymal Stem Cell Transplantation · Mesenchymal Stem Cells · Middle Aged · Rectal Fistula/etiology/pathology/surgery/therapy · Transplantation, Homologous · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the split is the story. In ADMIRE-CD (212 patients, Europe and Israel), a single intralesional injection of 120 million darvadstrocel cells (the manufactured cell product Alofisel, Takeda — named under the clarification exception for manufactured cell products) beat saline placebo on combined remission at week 24 (50% versus 34% in the intention-to-treat population; difference 15.2 percentage points) and at week 52 (56.3% versus 38.6%). The much larger replication, ADMIRE-CD II (568 patients, Europe, Israel and North America), found combined remission of 48.8% versus 46.3% (difference 2.4 percentage points; p=0.571) — the treatment made no difference — with a notably higher placebo remission rate than in the first trial. A retrospective chart review of ADMIRE-CD participants (INSPECT, 89 patients) found remission was often sustained to 156 weeks in both arms, with no significant between-group difference in relapse. Safety was similar between arms in both trials. No regulatory status is asserted on this shelf: the record set carded here does not establish the product's current approval status in any jurisdiction, and that must be verified separately before any clinical use is contemplated. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: ADMIRE-CD: combined remission at week 24 in 50% on darvadstrocel versus 34% on placebo (difference 15.2 percentage points, p=0.024)
cards.summary: ADMIRE-CD: combined remission at week 24 in 50% on darvadstrocel versus 34% on placebo (difference 15.2 percentage points, p=0.024)
cards.people: 212 adults with Crohn's disease and treatment-refractory, draining complex perianal fistulas at 49 hospitals in seven European countries and Israel, randomised to a single intralesional injection of 120 million expanded allogeneic adipose-derived stem cells (Cx601, later named darvadstrocel) or 24 mL saline placebo, on top of standard surgical preparation.
cards.result: Combined remission at week 24 (closure of all treated external openings draining at baseline, plus absence of collections >2 cm on masked central MRI) was achieved by 53 of 107 (50%) on stem cells versus 36 of 105 (34%) on placebo in the intention-to-treat population (difference 15.2%, 97.5% CI 0.2–30.3; p=0.024); modified intention-to-treat results were 51% versus 36% (p=0.021). Treatment-related adverse events were less frequent on stem cells (17% versus 29%), most commonly anal abscess and proctalgia in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a confidence interval whose lower bound (0.2 percentage points) sits almost on no-effect; the result needed replication — and the replication (next cards) did not confirm it.
cards.source: Panés J et al. Expanded allogeneic adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (Cx601) for complex perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease: a phase 3 randomised, double-blind controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27477896. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01541579, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ADMIRE-CD at week 52: combined remission 56.3% on darvadstrocel versus 38.6% on placebo (difference 17.7 percentage points, p=0.010)
cards.summary: ADMIRE-CD at week 52: combined remission 56.3% on darvadstrocel versus 38.6% on placebo (difference 17.7 percentage points, p=0.010)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial, preplanned long-term (week 52) report of ADMIRE-CD
cards.people: The same 212-patient ADMIRE-CD population (modified intention-to-treat: patients randomised, treated, and with at least one post-baseline efficacy assessment), followed to week 52 after the single injection.
cards.result: At week 52, combined remission was 56.3% with stem cells versus 38.6% with placebo (difference 17.7 percentage points, 95% CI 4.2–31.2; p=0.010), and clinical remission (absence of draining fistulas) was 59.2% versus 41.6% (difference 17.6 percentage points; p=0.013). Adverse events occurred in 76.7% of the stem-cell group and 72.5% of controls over 52 weeks.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same single trial, not an independent replication — the shelf's positive limb rests on one randomised population of 212 patients.
cards.source: Panés J et al. Long-term Efficacy and Safety of Stem Cell Therapy (Cx601) for Complex Perianal Fistulas in Patients With Crohn's Disease. Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29277560. cards.headline: ADMIRE-CD II: combined remission 48.8% on darvadstrocel versus 46.3% on placebo (difference 2.4 percentage points, p=0.571) — the replication trial was null (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: ADMIRE-CD II: combined remission 48.8% on darvadstrocel versus 46.3% on placebo (difference 2.4 percentage points, p=0.571) — the replication trial was null (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ADMIRE-CD II)
cards.people: 568 adults with Crohn's disease and complex perianal fistulas (at most 2 internal and 3 external openings) with inadequate response to immunosuppressive agents or biologics, in Europe, Israel and North America, randomised to darvadstrocel (120 million cells; n=283) or placebo (n=285); both groups underwent curettage and closure of the internal opening.
cards.result: Combined remission at week 24 was achieved by 138 of 283 (48.8%) on darvadstrocel versus 132 of 285 (46.3%) on placebo (estimated treatment difference 2.4%, 95% CI −5.8 to 10.6; p=0.571 — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). Key secondary endpoints (clinical remission at week 24, time to clinical remission) also did not differ significantly. Treatment-emergent adverse events: 73.0% versus 73.4%, with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-arm remission rate (46.3%) was far higher than in ADMIRE-CD (34–38.6%), which may reflect the standardised surgical preparation both arms received; whatever the explanation, the larger and more geographically diverse trial is the one that failed, and it outweighs the first trial in any honest balance.
cards.source: Colombel JF et al. Darvadstrocel in Patients With Crohn's Disease With Complex Perianal Fistulas: The ADMIRE CD II Phase 3 Randomized Trial. Gastroenterology. 2026. PMID: 41790076. cards.headline: INSPECT: in ADMIRE-CD participants followed retrospectively, clinical remission was sustained to 156 weeks in both arms, with no significant difference in relapse
cards.summary: INSPECT: in ADMIRE-CD participants followed retrospectively, clinical remission was sustained to 156 weeks in both arms, with no significant difference in relapse
cards.type: Retrospective chart-review follow-up study (observational — labelled as such)
cards.people: 89 patients who had completed at least 52 weeks in ADMIRE-CD (43 darvadstrocel, 46 control), with outcomes collected retrospectively at 104 and 156 weeks and adverse events of special interest to 208 weeks.
cards.result: Clinical remission was observed in 67.4%, 53.5% and 53.5% of darvadstrocel patients at 52, 104 and 156 weeks, versus 52.2%, 43.5% and 45.7% of controls. Among patients in remission at week 52, remission was sustained at 156 weeks in 55.2% (darvadstrocel) and 54.2% (control). Time to fistula relapse and relapse incidence did not differ significantly between groups. No ectopic tissue formation was reported; one tumour event (malignant epidermoid carcinoma) occurred in a control patient.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, unblinded chart review of a selected trial-completer subset (89 of the original 212) — it can describe durability but cannot estimate a treatment effect, and its between-group comparisons are observational and underpowered.
cards.source: Panés J et al. INSPECT: A Retrospective Study to Evaluate Long-term Effectiveness and Safety of Darvadstrocel in Patients With Perianal Fistulizing Crohn's Disease Treated in the ADMIRE-CD Trial. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2022. PMID: 35099555. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.balance: SPLIT, trial by trial — this programme must not be averaged into a single verdict. Ulcerative colitis induction: HIBISCUS I met its endpoint (remission at week 10, 19.4% versus 6.9% on placebo; p=0.017) and its identical twin HIBISCUS II missed (18.2% versus 11.1%; p=0.17); etrolizumab was not superior to adalimumab in the pooled head-to-head analyses. In anti-TNF-experienced UC (HICKORY), induction was met (18.5% versus 6.3% at week 14; p=0.0033) but maintenance was missed (24.1% versus 20.2% at week 66; p=0.50 — the treatment made no difference). UC maintenance in LAUREL was also missed (29.6% versus 20.6% at week 62; p=0.19). Crohn's disease (BERGAMOT) inverted the pattern: induction missed on both co-primary endpoints, but maintenance was met (clinical remission 35% versus 24% and endoscopic improvement 24% versus 12% at week 66). Safety was unremarkable throughout, with adverse-event rates close to placebo. Development was stopped by the sponsor after this programme; etrolizumab is not an available therapy. This is a completeness shelf for a guideline-era question whose honest answer is: inconsistent induction, mostly failed maintenance, one positive Crohn's maintenance limb. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: HIBISCUS I and II: identical induction trials disagreed — remission at week 10 was 19.4% versus 6.9% (p=0.017) in HIBISCUS I, but 18.2% versus 11.1% (p=0.17, no difference) in HIBISCUS II
cards.summary: HIBISCUS I and II: identical induction trials disagreed — remission at week 10 was 19.4% versus 6.9% (p=0.017) in HIBISCUS I, but 18.2% versus 11.1% (p=0.17, no difference) in HIBISCUS II
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled induction trials (HIBISCUS I and II)
cards.people: Adults (18–80 years) with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis (Mayo Clinic score 6–12, endoscopic subscore ≥2) who were naive to TNF inhibitors: 358 patients randomised in each study (etrolizumab 105 mg every 4 weeks n=144/143, adalimumab n=142/143, placebo n=72/72).
cards.result: Remission at week 10 (Mayo Clinic score ≤2, all subscores ≤1, rectal bleeding subscore 0): HIBISCUS I — 28 of 144 (19.4%) on etrolizumab versus 5 of 72 (6.9%) on placebo (adjusted difference 12.3%, 95% CI 1.6–20.6; p=0.017). HIBISCUS II — 26 of 143 (18.2%) versus 8 of 72 (11.1%) (adjusted difference 7.2%, 95% CI −3.8 to 16.1; p=0.17 — the treatment made no difference). In pooled analyses etrolizumab was not superior to adalimumab on remission, endoscopic improvement, clinical response, histological remission or endoscopic remission, with similar numerical results. Serious adverse events in the pooled population: 5% etrolizumab, 5% placebo, 2% adalimumab; two deaths in the etrolizumab group were judged unrelated to treatment.
cards.watchOut: Two identically designed trials reaching opposite statistical conclusions on near-identical point estimates is the signature of a small true effect (or none) measured with noise — the placebo remission rate, not the drug rate, is what moved between the twins (6.9% versus 11.1%).
cards.source: Rubin DT et al. Etrolizumab versus adalimumab or placebo as induction therapy for moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (HIBISCUS): two phase 3 randomised, controlled trials. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 34798036. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02163759 (HIBISCUS I) and NCT02171429 (HIBISCUS II), from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: HICKORY (anti-TNF-experienced UC): induction remission met at week 14 (18.5% versus 6.3%, p=0.0033), but maintenance remission at week 66 was missed (24.1% versus 20.2%, p=0.50 — the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: HICKORY (anti-TNF-experienced UC): induction remission met at week 14 (18.5% versus 6.3%, p=0.0033), but maintenance remission at week 66 was missed (24.1% versus 20.2%, p=0.50 — the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled induction and maintenance trial (HICKORY)
cards.people: Adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis previously treated with TNF inhibitors, at 184 centres in 24 countries: 479 patients randomised in the blinded induction cohort (etrolizumab n=384, placebo n=95), plus a 130-patient open-label induction cohort; 232 induction responders were re-randomised to maintenance etrolizumab or placebo to week 66.
cards.result: Induction: remission at week 14 in 71 of 384 (18.5%) on etrolizumab versus 6 of 95 (6.3%) on placebo (p=0.0033). Maintenance: remission at week 66 among week-14 responders in 27 of 112 (24.1%) continuing etrolizumab versus 23 of 114 (20.2%) switched to placebo (p=0.50 — the treatment made no difference). Adverse-event proportions were similar between groups in both phases (induction 66% versus 66%); the most common adverse event was ulcerative colitis flare.
cards.watchOut: The maintenance comparison is among induction responders only, and continuing versus withdrawing a drug that induced the response is the comparison most favourable to the drug — it still did not separate.
cards.source: Peyrin-Biroulet L et al. Etrolizumab as induction and maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis in patients previously treated with tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (HICKORY): a phase 3, randomised, controlled trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 34798039. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02100696, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: LAUREL (UC maintenance): remission at week 62 in 29.6% on etrolizumab versus 20.6% on placebo (p=0.19 — the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: LAUREL (UC maintenance): remission at week 62 in 29.6% on etrolizumab versus 20.6% on placebo (p=0.19 — the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind maintenance study (LAUREL)
cards.people: 359 patients with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis enrolled into open-label etrolizumab induction; the 214 (60%) with a clinical response at week 10 were randomised to maintenance etrolizumab 105 mg every 4 weeks (n=108) or placebo (n=106) to week 62.
cards.result: Remission at week 62 among week-10 responders: 32 of 108 (29.6%) on etrolizumab versus 21 of 102 (20.6%) on placebo (adjusted difference 7.7%, 95% CI −4.2 to 19.2; p=0.19 — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). One or more adverse events: 65% on etrolizumab versus 80% on placebo (most commonly ulcerative colitis itself); serious adverse events 9% versus 8%; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: As in HICKORY, a responder-enriched maintenance population is the easiest setting in which to show a maintenance effect; LAUREL still missed, which is why the UC maintenance claim cannot be rescued by pooling.
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. Etrolizumab for maintenance therapy in patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (LAUREL): a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, phase 3 study. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 34798037. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02165215, from the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: BERGAMOT (Crohn's disease): induction missed on both co-primary endpoints at week 14, but maintenance was met at week 66 (clinical remission 35% versus 24%; endoscopic improvement 24% versus 12%)
cards.summary: BERGAMOT (Crohn's disease): induction missed on both co-primary endpoints at week 14, but maintenance was met at week 66 (clinical remission 35% versus 24%; endoscopic improvement 24% versus 12%)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind induction and maintenance trial (BERGAMOT)
cards.people: Patients with moderately-to-severely active Crohn's disease: 385 patients in the randomised induction cohort 3 (placebo n=97, etrolizumab 105 mg n=143, etrolizumab 210 mg n=145); 434 etrolizumab responders across induction cohorts were re-randomised to maintenance etrolizumab 105 mg (n=217) or placebo (n=217) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Induction at week 14 (210 mg versus placebo): clinical remission 33% versus 29% (adjusted difference 3.8%, 95% CI −8.3 to 15.3; p=0.52 — the treatment made no difference) and endoscopic improvement 27% versus 22% (p=0.32 — the treatment made no difference). Maintenance at week 66: clinical remission 76 of 217 (35%) on etrolizumab versus 52 of 217 (24%) on placebo (adjusted difference 11.3%, 95% CI 2.7–19.7; p=0.0088) and endoscopic improvement 51 (24%) versus 26 (12%) (difference 11.5%; p=0.0026). Adverse-event rates were similar across groups in both phases.
cards.watchOut: The one clearly positive limb of the whole programme sits downstream of a failed induction: maintenance randomisation enrolled only patients who had already responded to etrolizumab, so the result cannot support starting the drug in unselected Crohn's patients.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Etrolizumab as induction and maintenance therapy in patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease (BERGAMOT): a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, phase 3 trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2023. PMID: 36240801. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02394028, from the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: a split programme — induction inconsistent, UC maintenance failed twice, Crohn's maintenance positive after failed induction — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split programme — induction inconsistent, UC maintenance failed twice, Crohn's maintenance positive after failed induction — SPLIT
cards.people: Over 2,500 randomised patients across the four carded phase 3 reports (HIBISCUS I/II 716, HICKORY 609 in induction cohorts, LAUREL 214 in maintenance, BERGAMOT 385 in the main induction cohort plus 434 in maintenance).
cards.result: Met endpoints: HIBISCUS I induction, HICKORY induction, BERGAMOT maintenance (both co-primaries). Missed endpoints: HIBISCUS II induction, HICKORY maintenance, LAUREL maintenance, BERGAMOT induction (both co-primaries). No endpoint family was met consistently. PROPOSED SPLIT. Etrolizumab development was stopped and the drug is not marketed; this shelf exists so the library answers the question honestly rather than leaving a guideline-era gap.
cards.watchOut: Do not pool these trials into a single remission estimate: the populations (TNF-naive, TNF-experienced, responder-enriched maintenance) and the direction of results differ by design, and pooling would manufacture a verdict none of the trials supports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rubin DT et al. 2022 (PMID: 34798036), Peyrin-Biroulet L et al. 2022 (PMID: 34798039), Vermeire S et al. 2022 (PMID: 34798037) and Sandborn WJ et al. 2023 (PMID: 36240801), all carded above.
