shelves.title: Cendakimab in eosinophilic oesophagitis
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, does cendakimab (anti-interleukin-13 monoclonal antibody) versus placebo improve dysphagia days and histological response?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Eosinophilic Esophagitis/drug therapy · Male · Adult · Female · Adolescent · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Aged · Young Adult · Child · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Deglutition Disorders/etiology
shelves.balance: One programme, internally consistent. The phase 3 trial (430 patients aged 12–75) met both co-primary endpoints at week 24: dysphagia days fell more on weekly cendakimab than placebo (least-squares mean change −6.1 versus −4.2 days; p<0.001) and histological response (peak oesophageal eosinophil count ≤6 per high-power field) was achieved by 28.6% versus 2.2% (p<0.001), with endoscopic severity also improved and efficacy maintained at week 48. The earlier phase 2 HEROES trial of the same antibody (then called RPC4046; 99 adults) showed large reductions in oesophageal eosinophil counts and endoscopic and histological scores at week 16, though its dysphagia-diary difference was only numerical (p=0.0733). A gene-expression substudy of HEROES showed cendakimab normalised the oesophageal transcript profile in line with the histological changes. Symptom and tissue endpoints are kept separate on this shelf: the histological separation is dramatic, the symptom separation (about 2 extra dysphagia-free days) is modest. Adverse events were more frequent on cendakimab in phase 3 (about 84% versus 73% through week 48) but were not dose-limiting. No long-term-extension report was found in PubMed this session, so none is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme, however concordant, caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phase 3: both co-primary endpoints met at week 24 — dysphagia days −6.1 versus −4.2 (p<0.001) and histological response 28.6% versus 2.2% (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Phase 3: both co-primary endpoints met at week 24 — dysphagia days −6.1 versus −4.2 (p<0.001) and histological response 28.6% versus 2.2% (p<0.001)
cards.people: 430 patients aged 12–75 years with eosinophilic oesophagitis, randomised to cendakimab 360 mg once weekly for 48 weeks (n=143), cendakimab weekly for 24 weeks then every other week (n=143), or placebo for 48 weeks (n=144); the two cendakimab arms were analysed as a single weekly group to week 24.
cards.result: Change in dysphagia days at week 24 (validated modified Daily Symptom Diary): least-squares mean −6.1 (SE 0.3) days on cendakimab versus −4.2 (0.4) on placebo (p<0.001). Histological response (peak oesophageal eosinophil count ≤6 per high-power field): 28.6% versus 2.2% (p<0.001). Endoscopic severity improved more on cendakimab (least-squares mean change −5.2 versus −1.2 points). Efficacy was maintained at week 48. Adverse events through week 48 occurred in 83.8% (weekly/weekly) and 84.6% (weekly/every-other-week) of cendakimab patients versus 73.4% on placebo; the profile was not dose-limiting.
cards.watchOut: The two co-primaries tell different-sized stories: histology separates dramatically (28.6% versus 2.2%) while the symptom benefit is about 1.9 additional dysphagia-free days against a large placebo improvement (−4.2 days) — patients should be counselled on the symptom number, not the biopsy number.
cards.source: Dellon ES et al. Cendakimab in Adults and Adolescents with Eosinophilic Esophagitis. NEJM evidence. 2025. PMID: 40985784. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04753697, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Phase 2 (HEROES): oesophageal eosinophil counts fell by about 95–100 per high-power field on RPC4046 (cendakimab) versus 4.4 on placebo (p<0.0001); the dysphagia-diary difference was numerical only (p=0.0733)
cards.summary: Phase 2 (HEROES): oesophageal eosinophil counts fell by about 95–100 per high-power field on RPC4046 (cendakimab) versus 4.4 on placebo (p<0.0001); the dysphagia-diary difference was numerical only (p=0.0733)
cards.people: 99 adults with active eosinophilic oesophagitis (a steroid-refractory population), randomised to RPC4046 — the same anti-IL-13 antibody later named cendakimab — 180 mg or 360 mg once weekly, or placebo, for 16 weeks.
cards.result: Mean change in oesophageal eosinophil count per high-power field at week 16: −94.8 (SD 67.3) on 180 mg and −99.9 (79.5) on 360 mg versus −4.4 (59.9) on placebo (both p<0.0001). The 360 mg group also showed significant reductions in endoscopic severity score (p<0.0001), histological grade and stage scores (both p<0.0001) and clinician's global assessment (p=0.0352), with a numerical — not significant — reduction in dysphagia symptom diary scores (p=0.0733). The most common adverse events were headache and upper respiratory tract infection.
cards.watchOut: The phase 2 symptom endpoint missed significance even as every tissue endpoint separated — the same symptom–histology gap seen in phase 3, in miniature. cards.headline: HEROES gene-expression substudy: cendakimab reversed the eosinophilic oesophagitis transcript profile, and the changes tracked histological and endoscopic response
cards.summary: HEROES gene-expression substudy: cendakimab reversed the eosinophilic oesophagitis transcript profile, and the changes tracked histological and endoscopic response
cards.type: Mechanistic substudy of the phase 2 HEROES randomised trial (biopsy transcriptomics)
cards.people: Biopsy samples from HEROES participants (the 99-patient phase 2 population carded above) collected at baseline and after 16 weekly injections of cendakimab 180 mg or 360 mg or placebo; the record does not print a separate substudy N.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, cendakimab at both doses reversed expression of cardinal EoE genes and pathways, including IL-13 signalling (CCL26), mast-cell genes (CPA3, TPSB2/TPSAB1), epithelial differentiation (DSG1) and remodelling (POSTN). cards.watchOut: A substudy of an already-carded trial, not independent efficacy evidence: it strengthens the mechanism claim (IL-13 blockade reverses the disease transcriptome) but adds no new patients and no new clinical endpoint. N not documented separately in the record.

shelves.title: Carotegrast methyl (AJM300) in ulcerative colitis
shelves.question: In adults with moderately active ulcerative colitis, does oral carotegrast methyl (α4-integrin antagonist) versus placebo induce clinical response?
shelves.mesh: Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy/methods · Integrin alpha4/antagonists & inhibitors · Mesalamine/adverse effects · Nasopharyngitis · Phenylalanine/analogs & derivatives · Quinazolinones · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from one country, both positive on induction. The phase 3 trial (203 patients in Japan with moderately active UC and an inadequate response or intolerance to mesalazine) found clinical response at week 8 in 45% on carotegrast methyl 960 mg three times daily versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 3.30, 95% CI 1.73–6.29 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). The earlier phase 2 trial (102 patients) found response in 62.7% versus 25.5% (OR 5.35 — relative), remission in 23.5% versus 3.9%, and mucosal healing in 58.8% versus 29.4%. Adverse events were similar to placebo in both trials (about 38–39% in phase 3), with nasopharyngitis most common and no progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy observed — though trials of 8 weeks and a few hundred patients cannot exclude a rare class risk of α4-integrin blockade. A retrospective re-analysis of the phase 3 population (ASPECT) found lower baseline disease activity and lower anti-integrin αvβ6 antibody titres predicted remission, with symptom improvement detectable from week 2. Product naming (clarification exception): carotegrast methyl is marketed in Japan as CAROGRA tablets (EA Pharma / Kissei Pharmaceutical), approved in Japan in March 2022 per the approval report carded in the literature; it is not FDA-approved, and all evidence is Japanese. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phase 3: clinical response at week 8 in 45% on carotegrast methyl versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 3.30)
cards.summary: Phase 3: clinical response at week 8 in 45% on carotegrast methyl versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 3.30)
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study (Japan)
cards.people: 203 adults with moderately active ulcerative colitis (Mayo Clinic score 6–10, endoscopic subscore ≥2, rectal bleeding subscore ≥1) and an inadequate response or intolerance to mesalazine, at 82 hospitals and clinics in Japan, randomised to carotegrast methyl (AJM300) 960 mg orally three times daily (n=102) or placebo (n=101) for 8 weeks, with extension treatment to 24 weeks if remission was not achieved.
cards.result: Clinical response at week 8 (Mayo reduction ≥30% and ≥3 points, rectal bleeding improvement, and endoscopic subscore ≤1): 46 of 102 (45%) on carotegrast versus 21 of 101 (21%) on placebo (odds ratio 3.30, 95% CI 1.73–6.29; p=0.00028 — the odds ratio is a relative measure; the absolute difference is 24 percentage points). Adverse events occurred in 38% on carotegrast and 39% on placebo across the treatment and extension periods; nasopharyngitis was most common in both groups (10% versus 11%). One serious adverse event (anal abscess) in the carotegrast group was judged unrelated; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Induction only: the trial was not designed to show maintenance of remission, and the stringent response definition (which requires an endoscopic subscore ≤1) is stricter than the response definitions used in many UC trials, so cross-trial comparisons of the 45% figure mislead.
cards.source: Matsuoka K et al. cards.headline: Phase 2: clinical response 62.7% versus 25.5% (odds ratio 5.35), remission 23.5% versus 3.9%, mucosal healing 58.8% versus 29.4% at week 8
cards.summary: Phase 2: clinical response 62.7% versus 25.5% (odds ratio 5.35), remission 23.5% versus 3.9%, mucosal healing 58.8% versus 29.4% at week 8
cards.people: 102 patients with moderately active ulcerative colitis (Mayo Clinic scores 6–10, endoscopic subscores ≥2, rectal bleeding subscores ≥1) who had an inadequate response or intolerance to mesalamine or corticosteroids, randomised to AJM300 960 mg or placebo three times daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Clinical response at week 8: 62.7% on AJM300 versus 25.5% on placebo (odds ratio 5.35, 95% CI 2.23–12.82; p=0.0002 — a relative measure, beside the absolute rates). Clinical remission: 23.5% versus 3.9% (OR 7.81, 95% CI 1.64–37.24; p=0.0099). Mucosal healing (endoscopic subscore 0 or 1): 58.8% versus 29.4% (OR 4.65, 95% CI 1.81–11.90; p=0.0014). No serious adverse event, including progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, was observed.
cards.watchOut: The phase 2 response rate (62.7%) is higher than phase 3 (45%) under a less stringent response definition — the two percentages are not comparable and neither should be quoted without its definition. Eight weeks in 102 patients cannot characterise the safety of chronic α4-integrin blockade.

cards.headline: ASPECT (retrospective re-analysis of the phase 3 population): lower baseline activity and anti-integrin αvβ6 titres below 44.6 U/mL predicted remission; symptom improvement was detectable from week 2
cards.summary: ASPECT (retrospective re-analysis of the phase 3 population): lower baseline activity and anti-integrin αvβ6 titres below 44.6 U/mL predicted remission; symptom improvement was detectable from week 2
cards.type: Retrospective secondary analysis of the phase 3 trial population (labelled as such — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 186 patients from the phase 3 trial population (96 carotegrast methyl, 90 placebo) with biomarker and symptom-diary data.
cards.result: Low disease activity at baseline (partial Mayo score ≤5) was associated with higher remission rates (56.1% versus 33.3%). Baseline anti-integrin αvβ6 antibody titres below 44.6 U/mL predicted higher clinical remission (49.1% versus 26.8%). Symptom improvement was detectable from week 2. Faecal calprotectin correlated with the end-of-treatment endoscopic subscore (ρ=0.566), and a level below 387.5 µg/g predicted an endoscopic subscore of 0/1. The 1-year maintenance rate, mostly on oral 5-aminosalicylic acid alone after induction, was 56.5%.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, retrospective and derived from the same patients as the phase 3 card: the biomarker cut-offs (44.6 U/mL; 387.5 µg/g) are data-derived thresholds from a single dataset and will shrink or shift on external validation; they are profiling hypotheses, not prescribing rules.
cards.source: Matsuoka K et al. Optimising carotegrast methyl use in ulcerative colitis: patient profiling, predictive biomarkers, and timing of efficacy evaluation (ASPECT study). shelves.title: Appendicectomy for ulcerative colitis (ACCURE and COSTA)
shelves.question: In adults with ulcerative colitis, does appendicectomy added to standard therapy (versus standard therapy alone, or versus switching advanced therapy) reduce relapse and maintain remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Appendectomy/methods · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy/surgery/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Laparoscopy · Maintenance Chemotherapy/methods · Mesalamine/therapeutic use · Netherlands · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two studies at two different disease moments, pointing the same way, with different evidentiary weight. ACCURE, the randomised trial, enrolled 201 patients with UC in remission but treated for a relapse within the previous 12 months: laparoscopic appendicectomy plus continued maintenance therapy cut the 1-year relapse rate to 36% versus 56% on medical therapy alone (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.47–0.89 — a relative measure, beside the absolute rates; p=0.005). COSTA asked the harder question — active UC after biologic failure — but as a patient-preference cohort, not a randomised trial: patients who chose appendicectomy (continuing their existing advanced therapy) reached clinical remission without therapy failure at 12 months more often than patients who chose to switch to a JAK inhibitor (32.8% versus 12.2%; adjusted difference 22.9 percentage points), while therapy-failure and colectomy rates were similar. A histopathology report from ACCURE's Dutch appendicectomy arm found active appendiceal inflammation in 55.4% of specimens from patients whose colitis was quiescent — a plausible substrate, not proof of mechanism. Surgery's harms were modest in both studies (ACCURE serious adverse events 2% versus 0%; two incidental low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms were found in resected specimens). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: one open-label randomised trial plus one preference cohort does not make a surgical standard.

cards.headline: ACCURE: 1-year relapse in 36% after appendicectomy plus medical therapy versus 56% on medical therapy alone (relative risk 0.65, p=0.005)
cards.summary: ACCURE: 1-year relapse in 36% after appendicectomy plus medical therapy versus 56% on medical therapy alone (relative risk 0.65, p=0.005)
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, international, randomised controlled trial (ACCURE)
cards.people: 201 adults with established ulcerative colitis who were in remission but had been treated for a disease relapse within the preceding 12 months, at 22 centres in the Netherlands, Ireland and the UK, randomised to laparoscopic appendicectomy plus continued maintenance medical therapy (n=101) or maintenance medical therapy alone (n=100); 197 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis after eligibility exclusions.
cards.result: Relapse within 1 year (total Mayo score ≥5 with endoscopic subscore 2–3, or committee-adjudicated exacerbation criteria): 36 of 99 (36%) in the appendicectomy group versus 55 of 98 (56%) in the control group (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.47–0.89; p=0.005; adjusted p=0.002 — the relative risk is a relative measure; the absolute difference is 20 percentage points). Adverse events: 11% versus 10%. Serious adverse events: two (2%) in the appendicectomy group, none in controls. Two (2%) incidental low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms were found in resected specimens. No deaths.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: patients and physicians knew who had surgery, and part of the relapse definition rests on symptoms and treatment intensification, which knowledge of allocation can influence. The population is relapse-prone remission, not newly diagnosed or severely active disease — the result should not be generalised beyond it.
cards.source: ACCURE Trial Investigators. Appendicectomy plus standard medical therapy versus standard medical therapy alone for maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis (ACCURE): a pragmatic, open-label, international, randomised trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2025. PMID: 40228513. Registry IDs: ISRCTN60945764 and Netherlands Trial Register NTR2883, from the record's abstract (no databank fields in the record). cards.headline: COSTA: in active UC after biologic failure, patients who chose appendicectomy reached remission without therapy failure more often than patients who chose a JAK-inhibitor switch (32.8% versus 12.2%) — a patient-preference cohort, not a randomised trial
cards.summary: COSTA: in active UC after biologic failure, patients who chose appendicectomy reached remission without therapy failure more often than patients who chose a JAK-inhibitor switch (32.8% versus 12.2%) — a patient-preference cohort, not a randomised trial
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, patient-preference interventional cohort study (observational comparison — labelled as such)
cards.people: 116 patients with active ulcerative colitis (total Mayo score 5–12, endoscopic subscore ≥2) despite previous advanced therapy, at five hospitals in the Netherlands, included in the comparative analysis: 67 chose laparoscopic appendicectomy while continuing their existing advanced therapy at a stable dose, and 49 chose to switch to a JAK inhibitor.
cards.result: Clinical remission without therapy failure at 12 months: 22 of 67 (32.8%) after appendicectomy versus 6 of 49 (12.2%) after JAK-inhibitor switch (unadjusted difference 20.6 percentage points, 95% CI 6.1–35.1; p=0.010; adjusted difference 22.9 percentage points, 95% CI 6.1–39.8; p=0.016). Corticosteroid-free remission showed the same split; clinical response was 73.1% versus 53.1% and endoscopic response 48.4% versus 25.6%. Therapy failure (58.2% versus 57.1%) and colectomy (9.0% versus 8.2%) did not differ. Adverse events: 56.5% versus 60.0%; appendicectomy complications in three patients (4.3%), all Clavien-Dindo grade II or lower.
cards.watchOut: Patients chose their own treatment, so the groups differ by preference, prognosis and clinician advice in ways adjustment cannot fully remove — this is hypothesis-strengthening observational evidence, and the shelf grades it as such. The disease moment also differs from ACCURE (active, biologic-exposed disease versus remission maintenance), so the two studies corroborate a direction, not a single pooled effect.
cards.source: Visser E et al. Appendicectomy versus switching to a JAK inhibitor in inducing remission in patients with active ulcerative colitis after biologic therapy failure (COSTA): 1-year results of a multicentre, prospective, cohort study. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2026. PMID: 41512889. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03912714, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ACCURE histopathology: active appendiceal inflammation was present in 55.4% of appendix specimens from patients whose ulcerative colitis was quiescent
cards.summary: ACCURE histopathology: active appendiceal inflammation was present in 55.4% of appendix specimens from patients whose ulcerative colitis was quiescent
cards.type: Histopathology substudy of the ACCURE randomised trial (Dutch appendicectomy arm)
cards.people: 65 Dutch ACCURE participants who underwent appendicectomy while their ulcerative colitis was quiescent; specimens were re-scored centrally by a blinded gastrointestinal pathologist using the Robarts Histopathology Index (RHI, range 0–33), with active inflammation defined as RHI >3.
cards.result: Of the 65 patients, 49 (75.4%) maintained remission and 16 (24.6%) relapsed within one year. Active appendiceal inflammation was present in 36 of 65 specimens (55.4%). Inter-observer agreement between local and central scoring was moderate (κ=0.47). Inflammation was greater in patients with a peri-appendiceal red patch (RHI 15.5 versus 5.0; p=0.005); extensive epithelial neutrophil involvement (>5% of crypts) was associated with higher relapse rates (44.4% versus 18.0%; p=0.05), and relapsing patients had larger appendiceal diameters (median 9 versus 7 mm; p=0.03).
cards.watchOut: A within-arm pathology correlation: it shows the removed organ is often inflamed in quiescent UC, but because every patient in this analysis had the appendix removed, it cannot show that the inflammation caused relapses or that removing it caused the ACCURE benefit.
cards.source: Visser E et al. Histopathological Findings of Appendix Specimens in Quiescent Ulcerative Colitis: Correlations With Clinical Outcomes in the ACCURE Trial. United European gastroenterology journal. 2026. PMID: 41653087. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised relapse-prevention result and one preference-cohort remission result, at different disease moments — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised relapse-prevention result and one preference-cohort remission result, at different disease moments — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 201 randomised patients (ACCURE) and 116 patients in the preference cohort (COSTA), plus 65 appendix specimens in the histopathology substudy.
cards.result: ACCURE: relapse 36% versus 56% at 1 year (relative risk 0.65). COSTA: remission without therapy failure 32.8% versus 12.2% against a JAK-inhibitor switch, with no difference in therapy failure or colectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the randomised limb is a single open-label trial and the second limb is observational by design, so the claim stays at POSSIBLE with both designs labelled on the face.
cards.watchOut: Appendicectomy is irreversible and its benefit, if real, accrues over a year; neither study informs patients with a first presentation, fulminant colitis, or dysplasia, and neither compares appendicectomy against modern treat-to-target escalation in a randomised design — that trial does not yet exist in this record set.
cards.source: Synthesis of ACCURE Trial Investigators 2025 (PMID: 40228513), Visser E et al. 2026 (PMID: 41512889) and Visser E et al. 2026 (PMID: 41653087), all carded above.

shelves.title: Neostigmine for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
shelves.question: In adults with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction without mechanical obstruction or perforation, does intravenous neostigmine versus placebo or conservative care achieve prompt colonic decompression?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/chemically induced · Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neostigmine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence
shelves.balance: The effect is dramatic and the evidence base is tiny — both facts belong on the face. In the landmark Ponec trial (21 patients with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, caecal diameter at least 10 cm, unresponsive to at least 24 hours of conservative treatment), a single 2.0 mg intravenous dose of neostigmine produced prompt decompression in 10 of 11 patients versus 0 of 10 on saline (p<0.001), with a median time to response of 4 minutes. A second small randomised infusion study reported the same immediate pattern (10 of 11 versus 0 of 10) with less complete sustained response at 3 hours. The meta-analysis of all four randomised trials (127 patients in total) found single-dose resolution in 89.2% versus 14.65% (p<0.001). Harms are cholinergic and predictable: crampy abdominal pain, salivation and vomiting are common, and symptomatic bradycardia requiring atropine occurred in two patients in each of the small trials — cardiac monitoring and atropine at hand are part of the treatment, not an afterthought. Patients with bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, perforation or mechanical obstruction were excluded from these trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — based on a very small N = 127: the stamp carries the N because four small trials, however lopsided, are still four small trials.

cards.headline: Ponec 1999: prompt decompression in 10 of 11 patients after a single 2.0 mg IV dose of neostigmine versus 0 of 10 on saline (p<0.001), median time to response 4 minutes — N = 21
cards.summary: Ponec 1999: prompt decompression in 10 of 11 patients after a single 2.0 mg IV dose of neostigmine versus 0 of 10 on saline (p<0.001), median time to response 4 minutes — N = 21
cards.people: 21 patients with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (abdominal distension, radiographic colonic dilation, caecal diameter at least 10 cm) who had not responded to at least 24 hours of conservative treatment, randomised to neostigmine 2.0 mg intravenously (n=11) or intravenous saline (n=10); non-responders could receive open-label neostigmine 3 hours later.
cards.result: Clinical response (prompt evacuation of flatus or stool with reduced abdominal distension, assessed by a blinded physician): 10 of 11 on neostigmine versus 0 of 10 on placebo (p<0.001); median time to response 4 minutes (range 3–30). All eight patients who later received open-label neostigmine (seven placebo patients and the one neostigmine non-responder) decompressed. Two initial responders later required colonoscopic decompression for recurrence, and one eventually underwent subtotal colectomy. Side effects included abdominal pain, excess salivation and vomiting; symptomatic bradycardia developed in two patients and was treated with atropine.
cards.watchOut: N = 21, printed plainly: a 10-of-11 versus 0-of-10 split is about as strong as a 21-patient trial can look, and it is still a 21-patient trial from 1999 that has never been replicated at scale.
cards.source: Ponec RJ et al. Neostigmine for the treatment of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction. The New England journal of medicine. 1999. PMID: 10403850. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amaro 2000: immediate response in 10 of 11 on neostigmine versus 0 of 10 on placebo, but sustained improvement at 3 hours was incomplete in both groups — N = 21 by arm counts
cards.summary: Amaro 2000: immediate response in 10 of 11 on neostigmine versus 0 of 10 on placebo, but sustained improvement at 3 hours was incomplete in both groups — N = 21 by arm counts
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study — small N
cards.people: Patients with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (caecal diameter at least 10 cm, no mechanical obstruction) who had failed 24 hours of conventional management; the record's text says twenty patients were included while its arm counts are 11 (neostigmine 2.0 mg IV over 3–5 minutes, with ECG monitoring) and 10 (placebo) — the discrepancy is in the record itself and is flagged here rather than silently resolved. Patients with bradycardia, hypotension, active bronchospasm, perforation, prior partial colonic resection, active gastrointestinal bleeding, pregnancy or creatinine above 3 mg/dL were excluded.
cards.result: Immediate clinical response (passage of flatus or stool with decreased distension within 30 minutes): 10 of 11 on neostigmine (median time 4 minutes) versus 0 of 10 on placebo (p<0.001). Sustained response at 3 hours failed in 3 of 11 (27%) on neostigmine versus 8 of 10 (80%) on placebo (p=0.04). Of 18 patients treated with neostigmine across the blinded and open-label phases, 17 (94%) had an immediate response and 16 (89%) had no recurrent dilation. Crampy abdominal pain was the most common side effect (13 patients, usually mild); symptomatic bradycardia requiring atropine occurred in two patients. Two deaths in the neostigmine group were judged unrelated to the pseudo-obstruction or its treatment.
cards.watchOut: Small N with an internal count discrepancy in the record (twenty stated, 21 by arms). The sustained-response numbers are the honest corrective to the immediate-response headline: about a quarter of initial responders were not sustained at 3 hours.
cards.source: Amaro R et al. Neostigmine infusion: new standard of care for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction? The American journal of gastroenterology. 2000. PMID: 10638606. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of all randomised trials: single-dose resolution 89.2% on neostigmine versus 14.65% on control — across only 4 trials and 127 patients in total
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of all randomised trials: single-dose resolution 89.2% on neostigmine versus 14.65% on control — across only 4 trials and 127 patients in total
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (4 RCTs, total N = 127)
cards.people: 127 patients across the four published randomised trials of neostigmine for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (65 treatment, 62 control), including the two small trials carded above.
cards.result: Resolution of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction with a single dose: 89.2% on neostigmine versus 14.65% on control (p<0.001; number needed to treat 1, 95% CI 1–2, as reported). The authors conclude neostigmine is a safe and effective option for patients who have failed conservative management.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis cannot manufacture patients: the pooled N is 127, the component trials are the same small studies carded on this shelf (so this card corroborates, it does not independently replicate), and a number needed to treat of 1 from 127 patients should be read as 'very large effect in very small trials', not as precision.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a very large, very fast effect on a very small evidence base — POSSIBLE, N = 127
cards.summary: Synthesis: a very large, very fast effect on a very small evidence base — POSSIBLE, N = 127
cards.people: 127 randomised patients in total across all trials (treatment 65, control 62), from four small trials conducted around 1999–2013.
cards.result: Immediate or single-dose decompression: about 89–91% on neostigmine versus 0–15% on placebo across the carded reports; median time to response 4 minutes. Bradycardia requiring atropine occurred in a small but consistent minority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — based on a very small N = 127, with the N printed in the stamp per the library's small-N labelling rule.
cards.watchOut: Nothing in this evidence base addresses patients the trials excluded — mechanical obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, bradycardia, hypotension or bronchospasm — and colonoscopic decompression remains the fallback when neostigmine fails or is contraindicated; the trials predate modern supportive care, which cuts both ways and cannot be resolved from these records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ponec RJ et al. 1999 (PMID: 10403850), Amaro R et al. 2000 (PMID: 10638606) and Valle RG et al. 2014 (PMID: 25568788), all carded above.

shelves.title: Treatment of autoimmune pancreatitis: steroid induction, maintenance, and relapse therapy
shelves.question: In adults with autoimmune pancreatitis, do corticosteroid induction with long-term maintenance (versus cessation after remission), and immunomodulator or rituximab strategies for relapse, reduce relapse rates?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Autoimmune Diseases/drug therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis/drug therapy · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Recurrence · Time Factors · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf, because almost everything here is observational. Induction is not in serious doubt: in the Japanese standard-treatment survey (563 patients), remission was 98% with steroids versus 74% without, and in the international cohort (1,064 patients) 99% of treated type 1 and 92% of type 2 patients remitted on steroids. Relapse is the real problem — 31% in type 1 disease internationally, and 56% of relapses arrive within a year in the Japanese data. On maintenance, the single randomised trial (Masamune, 49 patients) found relapse over 3 years in 23.3% with continued low-dose prednisolone versus 57.9% after cessation at 26 weeks (p=0.011); the Japanese survey points the same way observationally (relapse 23% on maintenance versus 34% after stopping; p=0.048). For established relapse, the Mayo experience (116 type 1 patients) found relapse-free survival was similar whether relapse was treated with steroids alone or steroids plus an immunomodulator, nearly half of immunomodulator-treated patients failed or could not tolerate the drug, and rituximab produced complete remission in 10 of 12 steroid- or immunomodulator-resistant or intolerant patients. Relapse definitions vary across these cohorts and are not pooled on this shelf. Cross-point: inebilizumab in IgG4-related disease as a whole (MITIGATE) is Shelf #1818 — a disease-wide flare question, not this pancreas-specific treatment question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, with the observational basis stated on the face.

cards.headline: Masamune RCT: relapse over 3 years in 23.3% with maintenance prednisolone versus 57.9% after cessation at 26 weeks (p=0.011) — the only randomised trial, N = 49
cards.summary: Masamune RCT: relapse over 3 years in 23.3% with maintenance prednisolone versus 57.9% after cessation at 26 weeks (p=0.011) — the only randomised trial, N = 49
cards.people: 49 patients with autoimmune pancreatitis who had achieved remission with initial oral prednisolone, randomised to maintenance prednisolone 5–7.5 mg/day continued for 3 years (n=30) or withdrawn at 26 weeks (n=19), in Japanese tertiary centres; analyses were intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Relapses within 3 years: 7 of 30 (23.3%) in the maintenance group versus 11 of 19 (57.9%) in the cessation group (p=0.011); relapse-free survival was significantly longer with maintenance (p=0.007). No serious corticosteroid-related complications requiring discontinuation of prednisolone were observed.
cards.watchOut: N = 49 with an unequal 30/19 split: the absolute difference is large, but a handful of events moving arms would change the p-value, and 3 years of even low-dose steroid carries bone, glucose and infection costs this small trial was not powered to tally (it reports only complications serious enough to stop the drug).
cards.source: Masamune A et al. Randomised controlled trial of long-term maintenance corticosteroid therapy in patients with autoimmune pancreatitis. Gut. 2017. PMID: 27543430. cards.headline: Kamisawa 2009 (Japanese standard-treatment survey): remission 98% with steroids versus 74% without; relapse 23% on maintenance versus 34% after stopping — retrospective, labelled as such
cards.summary: Kamisawa 2009 (Japanese standard-treatment survey): remission 98% with steroids versus 74% without; relapse 23% on maintenance versus 34% after stopping — retrospective, labelled as such
cards.type: Retrospective multicentre survey (observational — labelled as such)
cards.people: 563 patients with autoimmune pancreatitis treated at 17 centres in Japan, of whom 459 (82%) received steroid treatment; maintenance treatment was given to 377 of the 459, and outcomes were compared between those maintained and the 104 who stopped.
cards.result: Remission: 98% in steroid-treated patients versus 74% (77 of 104) in patients not treated with steroids (p<0.001). Time to remission did not depend on the initial prednisolone dose (30 versus 40 mg/day). Relapse: 23% (63 of 273) in patients on maintenance treatment versus 34% (35 of 104) in patients who stopped (p=0.048). Of patients who relapsed, 56% did so within 1 year and 92% within 3 years of starting steroids; steroid re-treatment of relapse was effective in 97% of the 83 patients re-treated. The authors recommend an initial prednisolone dose of 0.6 mg/kg/day, tapered to a low maintenance dose over 3–6 months.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: patients who stopped steroids differ from those maintained (milder disease, side effects, clinician judgement), so the 23% versus 34% contrast corroborates the Masamune trial's direction but cannot estimate the maintenance effect on its own.
cards.source: Kamisawa T et al. Standard steroid treatment for autoimmune pancreatitis. Gut. 2009. PMID: 19398440. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hart 2013 (Mayo Clinic): relapse-free survival was similar for steroids alone versus steroids plus an immunomodulator; immunomodulators failed or were not tolerated in 45%; rituximab induced complete remission in 10 of 12 resistant or intolerant patients — observational
cards.summary: Hart 2013 (Mayo Clinic): relapse-free survival was similar for steroids alone versus steroids plus an immunomodulator; immunomodulators failed or were not tolerated in 45%; rituximab induced complete remission in 10 of 12 resistant or intolerant patients — observational
cards.type: Single-centre retrospective cohort (observational — labelled as such)
cards.people: 116 patients with type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis followed at the Mayo Clinic (median follow-up 47 months), of whom 52 experienced 76 relapse episodes; 38 received an immunomodulator for more than 2 months, and 12 with steroid or immunomodulator intolerance or resistance received rituximab.
cards.result: First relapses were treated with steroids alone (24 patients) or steroids plus an immunomodulator (27 patients), with similar subsequent relapse-free survival (p=0.23). Among 38 patients on immunomodulators for over 2 months, failure or intolerance occurred in 17 (45%). Of 12 patients treated with rituximab, 10 (83%) experienced complete remission and had no relapses while on maintenance therapy; treatment-limiting rituximab side effects were uncommon.
cards.watchOut: A 12-patient rituximab subgroup, selected precisely because other treatments had failed or were not tolerated, with no comparator: 10 of 12 is a signal to test, not an effect estimate. All comparisons in this cohort are vulnerable to confounding by indication.
cards.source: Hart PA et al. Treatment of relapsing autoimmune pancreatitis with immunomodulators and rituximab: the Mayo Clinic experience. Gut. 2013. PMID: 22936672. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hart 2013 (international cohort, 1,064 patients): steroid remission in 99% of type 1 and 92% of type 2 disease; relapse in 31% of type 1 versus 9% of type 2 — observational
cards.summary: Hart 2013 (international cohort, 1,064 patients): steroid remission in 99% of type 1 and 92% of type 2 disease; relapse in 31% of type 1 versus 9% of type 2 — observational
cards.type: Multicentre international retrospective cohort (observational — labelled as such)
cards.people: 1,064 patients meeting International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for autoimmune pancreatitis (978 type 1, 86 type 2) at 23 institutions in 10 countries, with data on organs involved, treatments, relapses and sequelae.
cards.result: Among treated patients, clinical remission on steroids occurred in 99% of type 1 and 92% of type 2 disease. Most patients with jaundice required biliary stent placement (71% of type 1, 77% of type 2). Relapses were more common in type 1 (31%) than type 2 (9%; p<0.001), and especially in type 1 patients with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis (56% versus 26%; p<0.001); relapses typically occurred in the pancreas or biliary tree. Re-treatment with steroids remained effective, with or without alternatives such as azathioprine. Pancreatic duct stones and cancer were uncommon sequelae in type 1 disease and did not occur in type 2 during the study period.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective registry data across 23 centres with differing diagnostic and treatment habits and differing relapse definitions — the type 1/type 2 contrast is robust at this size, but no treatment comparison in this cohort is randomised, and follow-up duration varies by centre.
cards.source: Hart PA et al. Long-term outcomes of autoimmune pancreatitis: a multicentre, international analysis. Gut. 2013. PMID: 23232048. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: steroids induce remission almost universally; maintenance halves relapse in the one small RCT; relapse therapy beyond steroids is observational — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroids induce remission almost universally; maintenance halves relapse in the one small RCT; relapse therapy beyond steroids is observational — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 49 randomised patients (maintenance question) set against 563 (Japanese survey), 116 (Mayo cohort) and 1,064 (international cohort) observational patients.
cards.result: Induction remission: 98–99% (type 1) on steroids across cohorts. Maintenance: relapse 23.3% versus 57.9% over 3 years in the RCT; 23% versus 34% observationally. Relapse therapy: immunomodulator failure or intolerance 45%; rituximab complete remission 10 of 12 in a selected subgroup. shelves.title: Treatment of chronic radiation proctopathy: hyperbaric oxygen helps refractory proctitis in one trial but not broader bowel dysfunction; sucralfate enemas rest on small trials
shelves.question: In adults with chronic radiation proctopathy (rectal bleeding after pelvic radiotherapy), how do hyperbaric oxygen therapy, sucralfate enemas, formalin application and argon plasma coagulation compare for bleeding control?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyperbaric Oxygenation · Male · Pelvis · Proctitis · Quality of Life · Radiation Injuries · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the split is by population and intervention, not noise. For endoscopy-defined refractory radiation proctitis, the Clarke double-blind crossover RCT (150 entered, 120 evaluable) found responders in 88.9% on hyperbaric oxygen vs 62.5% on sham air — an absolute risk reduction of 32%, NNT 3. For the broader HOT2 population (chronic bowel dysfunction after pelvic radiotherapy, 84 randomised), hyperbaric oxygen made no difference (the treatment made no difference) to bowel scores (p=0.50) or rectal bleeding scores (p=0.092). Sucralfate enemas were clinically superior to oral sulfasalazine plus rectal prednisolone in a 37-patient double-blind RCT, with durable responses in a 26-patient uncontrolled series (92.3% good response by 16 weeks, labelled observational). Formalin application and argon plasma coagulation are widely used but no randomised report for them is carded here, so this shelf makes no comparative claim for them. RICH-ART, sometimes cited in this area, is a radiation cystitis trial and is not evidence for proctopathy. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Clarke 2008 HBOT RCT: responders 88.9% vs 62.5% on sham air, absolute risk reduction 32%, NNT 3 — in refractory radiation proctitis, N = 150 entered / 120 evaluable
cards.summary: Clarke 2008 HBOT RCT: responders 88.9% vs 62.5% on sham air, absolute risk reduction 32%, NNT 3 — in refractory radiation proctitis, N = 150 entered / 120 evaluable
cards.people: 150 patients with chronic refractory radiation proctitis entered a randomised, double-blind crossover trial (120 evaluable); hyperbaric oxygen at 2.0 atmospheres absolute versus air at 1.1 atmospheres as sham, with sham patients crossed over to hyperbaric oxygen afterwards and follow-up to 5 years.
cards.result: After initial allocation the mean SOMA-LENT score improved in both groups, but improvement was nearly twice as great with hyperbaric oxygen (5.00 vs 2.61, p=0.0019) and responders by clinical assessment were 88.9% vs 62.5% (p=0.0009); the authors report an absolute risk reduction of 32% (number needed to treat 3). Bowel-specific quality of life was better with hyperbaric oxygen; differences were abolished after crossover, as expected in that design.
cards.watchOut: Crossover design: the long-term comparison is lost once sham patients cross to active treatment, and 30 of 150 entered patients were not evaluable. This was refractory proctitis specifically — not all post-radiation bowel symptoms (see the HOT2 card).
cards.source: Clarke RE et al. Hyperbaric oxygen treatment of chronic refractory radiation proctitis: a randomized and controlled double-blind crossover trial with long-term follow-up. International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics. 2008. PMID: 18342453. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: HOT2 2016: hyperbaric oxygen made no difference (the treatment made no difference) to bowel scores or rectal bleeding in broader chronic bowel dysfunction after pelvic radiotherapy, N = 84
cards.summary: HOT2 2016: hyperbaric oxygen made no difference (the treatment made no difference) to bowel scores or rectal bleeding in broader chronic bowel dysfunction after pelvic radiotherapy, N = 84
cards.people: 84 adults with chronic gastrointestinal symptoms for 12 months or more after pelvic radiotherapy, persisting despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy, randomised 2:1 to hyperbaric oxygen (100% oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres, 40 exposures over 8 weeks) or sham (21% oxygen at 1.3 atmospheres) in a double-blind phase 3 trial.
cards.result: No significant difference in change in the bowel component of the modified IBDQ score at 12 months (median change 4 vs 4; p=0.50, analysis n=69), and no significant difference in the rectal bleeding score among those bleeding at baseline (median change 3 vs 1; p=0.092, analysis n=40). Eye refractive changes, fatigue and ear pain were common in both arms.
cards.watchOut: HOT2 enrolled bowel dysfunction broadly, not endoscopy-defined refractory proctitis, and its bleeding-score analysis rested on only 40 patients — it tempers, but does not erase, the Clarke proctitis result; the two trials asked related but different questions.
cards.source: Glover M et al. Hyperbaric oxygen for patients with chronic bowel dysfunction after pelvic radiotherapy (HOT2): a randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Kochhar 1991 RCT: rectal sucralfate enemas beat oral sulfasalazine plus rectal steroids on clinical response at 4 weeks in radiation proctosigmoiditis, N = 37
cards.summary: Kochhar 1991 RCT: rectal sucralfate enemas beat oral sulfasalazine plus rectal steroids on clinical response at 4 weeks in radiation proctosigmoiditis, N = 37
cards.people: 37 consecutive patients with radiation-induced proctosigmoiditis randomised to 3.0 g oral sulfasalazine plus twice-daily 20 mg rectal prednisolone enemas (n=18) or 2.0 g twice-daily rectal sucralfate enemas plus oral placebo (n=19) for 4 weeks, double-blind; 32 completed the trial.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly on clinical and endoscopic measures. Sucralfate enemas gave a significantly better clinical response than the sulfasalazine/steroid combination (p<0.05), although the endoscopic response did not differ significantly between groups. The authors judged sucralfate better tolerated and cheaper.
cards.watchOut: Very small (37 randomised, 32 completing) and only 4 weeks long — a short-term clinical-response result, with the endoscopic endpoint itself not significantly different.
cards.source: Kochhar R et al. Radiation-induced proctosigmoiditis. Prospective, randomized, double-blind controlled trial of oral sulfasalazine plus rectal steroids versus rectal sucralfate. cards.headline: Kochhar 1999: topical sucralfate suspension stopped or greatly reduced bleeding in 92.3% by 16 weeks in a single-arm series, N = 26 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.summary: Kochhar 1999: topical sucralfate suspension stopped or greatly reduced bleeding in 92.3% by 16 weeks in a single-arm series, N = 26 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.type: Single-arm treatment series (observational — labelled as such) (Kochhar 1999)
cards.people: 26 patients with radiation proctosigmoiditis (10 with moderate and 16 with severe rectal bleeding) treated with 20 mL of 10% rectal sucralfate suspension enemas twice daily until bleeding ceased or therapy was judged to have failed; median follow-up 45.5 months after bleeding stopped.
cards.result: A good response (bleeding severity improved by two grades) was seen in 76.9% at 4 weeks, 84.6% at 8 weeks and 92.3% at 16 weeks; 2 patients required surgery for poor response. Of responders, 70.8% had no further bleeding over follow-up and all recurrences responded to a further short course. No treatment-related complications were observed.
cards.watchOut: No comparator: radiation proctopathy bleeding can settle spontaneously, so a 92% response in an uncontrolled series cannot be read as the drug's effect size — it supports feasibility and durability only, alongside the small randomised trial.
cards.source: Kochhar R et al. Natural history of late radiation proctosigmoiditis treated with topical sucralfate suspension. Digestive Diseases and Sciences. 1999. PMID: 10235606. cards.headline: Synthesis: hyperbaric oxygen helps refractory proctitis in one crossover RCT but not broader bowel dysfunction in HOT2; sucralfate enemas rest on one very small RCT plus uncontrolled series; formalin and argon plasma coagulation have no carded randomised evidence here
cards.summary: Synthesis: hyperbaric oxygen helps refractory proctitis in one crossover RCT but not broader bowel dysfunction in HOT2; sucralfate enemas rest on one very small RCT plus uncontrolled series; formalin and argon plasma coagulation have no carded randomised evidence here
cards.people: Carded evidence: two double-blind hyperbaric oxygen RCTs (150 entered; 84 randomised), one small sucralfate RCT (37) and one sucralfate series (26). RICH-ART is a radiation cystitis trial, not proctopathy, and is not carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Clarke 2008 found an absolute responder advantage of 32% for hyperbaric oxygen in refractory proctitis; HOT2 2016 found no difference (the treatment made no difference) on bowel or bleeding scores in the broader bowel-dysfunction population. Sucralfate enemas were clinically superior to sulfasalazine plus rectal steroids in a 37-patient RCT and produced durable responses in an uncontrolled series. No randomised comparison of formalin application or argon plasma coagulation was carded — their place rests on non-randomised practice literature outside this shelf's cards. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the split in the stamp.
cards.watchOut: This is a comparative-treatment shelf built from a patchwork — per-intervention sections must not be pooled into one verdict, and the hyperbaric oxygen answer depends on which population (refractory proctitis vs general bowel dysfunction) is meant.
cards.source: Synthesis of Clarke RE et al. 2008 (PMID: 18342453); Glover M et al. 2016 (PMID: 26703894); Kochhar R et al. 1991 (PMID: 1670631); Kochhar R et al. 1999 (PMID: 10235606).

shelves.title: Treatment of bile acid diarrhoea: colesevelam beats placebo short-term, liraglutide beat colesevelam in one small head-to-head trial, and colestyramine intolerance drives sequestrant failure
shelves.question: In adults with bile acid diarrhoea, do bile-acid sequestrants (colesevelam, cholestyramine) or liraglutide versus placebo or each other reduce stool frequency?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Bile Acids and Salts · Colesevelam Hydrochloride · Diarrhea · Abdominal Pain · Nausea · Taurocholic Acid
shelves.balance: This shelf asks the TREATMENT question only. The diagnostic question — whether to test for bile acid diarrhoea before rifaximin in IBS-D — is homed on Shelf #5678, which is cross-pointed here in prose; none of its references are carded here. On treatment: the SINBAD phase 4 trial (Borup 2023) randomised 168 patients and, in its C4-diagnosed primary population, colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo over 12 days (adjusted odds ratio 9.1, a relative measure, with a very wide confidence interval). Kårhus 2022 (n=52) found liraglutide superior to colesevelam, the standard sequestrant, on a ≥25% stool-frequency reduction (77% vs 50% at 6 weeks) in a trial designed for non-inferiority. Practice data (Orekoya 2015, observational, labelled) show ~63% respond to a first sequestrant, colestyramine failure is often intolerance (45% of failures), and colesevelam rescues about half of colestyramine failures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction, small and short trials.

cards.headline: Borup 2023 (SINBAD): colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo in C4-diagnosed bile acid diarrhoea (adjusted OR 9.1 — a relative measure), N = 168 randomised
cards.summary: Borup 2023 (SINBAD): colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo in C4-diagnosed bile acid diarrhoea (adjusted OR 9.1 — a relative measure), N = 168 randomised
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 4 trial (SINBAD, Borup 2023)
cards.people: 168 adults attending SeHCAT testing for suspected bile acid diarrhoea at four Danish centres, randomised 1:1 to colesevelam (625 mg tablets, titrated over 5 days) or placebo for 12 days; the primary outcome population was the 41 patients with bile acid diarrhoea diagnosed by plasma C4 above 46 ng/mL, with a SeHCAT-defined secondary population of 75 patients.
cards.result: In the C4-defined primary population, remission (neither daily-mean stool criterion met on days 6–12) occurred in 14 of 22 (64%) on colesevelam vs 3 of 19 (16%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 9.1, 95% CI 1.9–62.8, p=0.011 — an odds ratio is a relative measure; the absolute rates are 64% vs 16%). In the SeHCAT-defined population, remission was 59% vs 13% (adjusted OR 11.1, 95% CI 3.4–45.6). No serious adverse events; transient abdominal pain, bloating and nausea were the common events.
cards.watchOut: Treatment lasted only 12 days and the primary (C4-defined) population was 41 of the 168 randomised — the confidence interval on the odds ratio is very wide (1.9–62.8); the result shows short-term remission induction, not long-term control.
cards.source: Borup C et al. Efficacy and safety of colesevelam for the treatment of bile acid diarrhoea: a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 4 clinical trial. The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2023. PMID: 36758570. Registry ID: NCT03876717. cards.headline: Kårhus 2022: liraglutide beat colesevelam head-to-head — ≥25% stool-frequency reduction in 77% vs 50%, N = 52
cards.summary: Kårhus 2022: liraglutide beat colesevelam head-to-head — ≥25% stool-frequency reduction in 77% vs 50%, N = 52
cards.people: 52 adults aged 18–75 with SeHCAT-verified moderate-to-severe primary bile acid diarrhoea at a Copenhagen centre, randomised double-blind, double-dummy to daily subcutaneous liraglutide (uptitrated 0.6–1.8 mg over 3 weeks) or colesevelam 625 mg three capsules twice daily (standard of care) for 6 weeks after a 1-week run-in; designed as a non-inferiority trial with a 15% margin.
cards.result: 20 of 26 (77%) on liraglutide and 13 of 26 (50%) on colesevelam achieved a ≥25% reduction in daily stool frequency — a risk difference of 27 percentage points in favour of liraglutide, meeting non-inferiority and, on the authors' analysis, superiority. Mild nausea lasting 10–21 days occurred in 6 liraglutide patients vs 1 on colesevelam; no other adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: N = 52 at a single centre over 6 weeks, designed for non-inferiority — the superiority reading is real but fragile at this size, and the authors themselves call for larger confirmatory trials powered for superiority. Liraglutide for this indication is off-label.
cards.source: Kårhus ML et al. cards.headline: Orekoya 2015: in routine practice 63% of bile acid malabsorption patients responded to a sequestrant; colestyramine failed in 44% (45% of failures from intolerance) while colesevelam rescued 47% of colestyramine failures, N = 264 records (observational — labelled as such)
cards.summary: Orekoya 2015: in routine practice 63% of bile acid malabsorption patients responded to a sequestrant; colestyramine failed in 44% (45% of failures from intolerance) while colesevelam rescued 47% of colestyramine failures, N = 264 records (observational — labelled as such)
cards.people: Retrospective review of 264 SeHCAT-tested patient records at a UK centre, recording bile acid malabsorption subtype and severity, sequestrant use and response, and colonic histology; 53% of those tested had bile acid malabsorption.
cards.result: 63% of patients with bile acid malabsorption had a successful sequestrant response, with a trend to lower response at lower severity. Colestyramine was unsuccessful in 38 of 87 (44%), and 17 of those 38 failures (45%) were medication intolerance; 7 of 15 colestyramine failures (47%) then responded to colesevelam, and no patient reported colesevelam intolerance. Colonic histology did not predict response.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, uncontrolled and from tested (already-suspected) patients — response rates here describe practice, not efficacy; the randomised efficacy evidence is the Borup and Kårhus cards. Note the older literature's spelling 'colestyramine' is the same drug as cholestyramine.
cards.source: Orekoya O et al. Quantifying bile acid malabsorption helps predict response and tailor sequestrant therapy. Clinical Medicine (London). 2015. PMID: 26031975. cards.headline: Synthesis: colesevelam works against placebo in a 12-day phase 4 trial, liraglutide outperformed colesevelam in one small head-to-head trial, and practice data show colestyramine intolerance is the commonest reason sequestrant therapy fails
cards.summary: Synthesis: colesevelam works against placebo in a 12-day phase 4 trial, liraglutide outperformed colesevelam in one small head-to-head trial, and practice data show colestyramine intolerance is the commonest reason sequestrant therapy fails
cards.people: Carded evidence: two Danish RCTs (168 randomised, primary population 41; and 52) and one UK retrospective series (264 records). The diagnostic question — testing for bile acid diarrhoea before rifaximin in IBS-D — is homed on Shelf #5678 and is not re-asked here; none of that shelf's references are carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo in C4-diagnosed disease over 12 days (Borup 2023), and liraglutide achieved a ≥25% stool-frequency reduction in 77% vs 50% against colesevelam over 6 weeks (Kårhus 2022). In practice, about two-thirds respond to a first sequestrant, colestyramine intolerance drives much of the failure, and colesevelam rescues about half of colestyramine failures (Orekoya 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent across two small randomised trials, but no trial is large or long.
cards.watchOut: All randomised evidence is Danish and short (12 days to 6 weeks); durability, adherence over years, and liraglutide's place relative to simply switching sequestrants are untested in trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Borup C et al. 2023 (PMID: 36758570); Kårhus ML et al. 2022 (PMID: 35868334); Orekoya O et al. 2015 (PMID: 26031975).

shelves.title: ESD versus EMR for early GI neoplasia: ESD wins en-bloc and R0 resection and recurrence at every site, and loses on perforation and time — on mostly non-randomised evidence
shelves.question: In adults with early gastrointestinal neoplasia (Barrett's, gastric, colorectal), does endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection achieve higher en-bloc and R0 resection and lower recurrence, at what cost in perforation and procedure time?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Aged · Barrett Esophagus · Carcinoma in Situ · Endoscopic Mucosal Resection · Esophageal Neoplasms · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf: the comparative base is predominantly non-randomised, and the site strata are kept separate rather than pooled. Gastric (Tao 2019, 18 studies, 6,723 patients): en-bloc odds ratio 9.00 and recurrence odds ratio 0.18 favouring ESD, perforation odds ratio 2.55 against it — all relative measures from mostly retrospective data. Colorectal laterally spreading tumours (Zhao 2020, 3,062 lesions): en-bloc 95% vs 42.8%, recurrence 0.5% vs 15.9%, perforation 2.4% vs 1.8%. Barrett's (Terheggen 2017, the only RCT, n=40): R0 10/17 vs 2/17 for ESD, yet complete remission at 3 months was 15/16 vs 16/17 — the resection-quality win did not change the clinical outcome at this lesion size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational basis stated on the face.

cards.headline: Terheggen 2017 RCT (Barrett's): ESD achieved R0 resection in 10/17 vs 2/17 with EMR (p=0.01), but complete remission at 3 months was identical (15/16 vs 16/17) — the only randomised trial, N = 40
cards.summary: Terheggen 2017 RCT (Barrett's): ESD achieved R0 resection in 10/17 vs 2/17 with EMR (p=0.01), but complete remission at 3 months was identical (15/16 vs 16/17) — the only randomised trial, N = 40
cards.people: 40 patients with neoplastic Barrett's oesophagus (focal high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia or early adenocarcinoma 3 cm or smaller) randomised to endoscopic submucosal dissection (n=20) or endoscopic mucosal resection (n=20).
cards.result: R0 resection (margins free of neoplasia) was achieved more often with ESD (10/17 vs 2/17, p=0.01), but complete remission from neoplasia at 3 months did not differ (ESD 15/16 vs EMR 16/17, p=1.0), nor did need for elective surgery (4 vs 3) over a mean 23 months of follow-up; one recurrent cancer occurred, in the ESD group. Two severe adverse events were recorded for ESD and none for EMR (p=0.49), and ESD was more time-consuming.
cards.watchOut: N = 40, and the headline R0 denominators are 17 per arm — the trial shows the R0 advantage did not translate into better remission, recurrence or surgery outcomes in Barrett's lesions of this size; do not generalise it to large gastric or colorectal lesions.
cards.source: Terheggen G et al. A randomised trial of endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for early Barrett's neoplasia. Gut. 2017. PMID: 26801885. randomised controlled trial (terheggen 2017) 40 patients with neoplastic barrett's oesophagus (focal high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia or early adenocarcinoma 3 cm or smaller) randomised to endoscopic submucosal dissection (n=20) or endoscopic mucosal resection (n=20). r0 resection (margins free of neoplasia) was achieved more often with esd (10/17 vs 2/17, p=0.01), but complete remission from neoplasia at 3 months did not differ (esd 15/16 vs emr 16/17, p=1.0), nor did need for elective surgery (4 vs 3) over a mean 23 months of follow-up; one recurrent cancer occurred, in the esd group. two severe adverse events were recorded for esd and none for emr (p=0.49), and esd was more time-consuming. n = 40, and the headline r0 denominators are 17 per arm — the trial shows the r0 advantage did not translate into better remission, recurrence or surgery outcomes in barrett's lesions of this size; do not generalise it to large gastric or colorectal lesions. terheggen g et al. a randomised trial of endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for early barrett's neoplasia. gut. 2017. pmid: 26801885. registry id: nct01871636. mesh: adenocarcinoma · aged · barrett esophagus · carcinoma in situ · endoscopic mucosal resection · esophageal neoplasms · esophagectomy · female · follow-up studies · humans · male · margins of excision · middle aged · neoplasm recurrence, local · neoplasm, residual · prospective studies · reoperation

cards.summary: Tao 2019 meta-analysis (gastric): ESD raised en-bloc resection (OR 9.00 — a relative measure) and cut local recurrence (OR 0.18), at the cost of more perforation (OR 2.55) and longer procedures — 18 studies, 6,723 patients, predominantly non-randomised
cards.type: Meta-analysis of predominantly non-randomised comparative studies (Tao 2019)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 18 studies comprising 6,723 patients with early gastric cancer comparing endoscopic submucosal dissection with endoscopic mucosal resection, searched to January 2018.
cards.result: ESD was associated with higher en-bloc resection (odds ratio 9.00, 95% CI 6.66–12.17), complete resection (OR 8.43, 95% CI 5.04–14.09) and curative resection (OR 2.92, 95% CI 1.85–4.61), and lower local recurrence (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.09–0.34) — all relative measures. Bleeding did not differ (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.88–1.80, p=0.203), but perforation was higher with ESD (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.48–4.39) and operation time longer.
cards.watchOut: Almost entirely retrospective comparisons: larger, harder lesions are channelled to ESD and expert centres report both techniques — odds ratios this large from non-randomised data overstate what a randomised comparison would show. Gastric stratum only; do not merge with the Barrett's or colorectal cards.
cards.source: Tao M et al. Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for patients with early gastric cancer: a meta-analysis. BMJ Open. 2019. PMID: 31874864. cards.headline: Zhao 2020 meta-analysis (colorectal laterally spreading tumours): en-bloc resection 95% with ESD vs 42.8% with EMR, recurrence 0.5% vs 15.9%, perforation 2.4% vs 1.8% — 12 studies, 3,062 lesions, non-randomised
cards.summary: Zhao 2020 meta-analysis (colorectal laterally spreading tumours): en-bloc resection 95% with ESD vs 42.8% with EMR, recurrence 0.5% vs 15.9%, perforation 2.4% vs 1.8% — 12 studies, 3,062 lesions, non-randomised
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 12 studies of colorectal laterally spreading tumours, totalling 3,062 lesions (1,906 treated by endoscopic mucosal resection, 1,156 by endoscopic submucosal dissection).
cards.result: En-bloc resection was 95% (1,098/1,156) with ESD vs 42.8% (815/1,906) with EMR, and complete resection 93.2% vs 71.9% in the subsets reporting it. Recurrence was 0.5% after ESD vs 15.9% after EMR. Bleeding did not differ (3.5% vs 4.2%), but perforation was higher with ESD (2.4% vs 1.8%, p=0.04). Reported odds ratios in the paper are relative measures and are oriented EMR-versus-ESD; the absolute rates above are the carded figures.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective lesion-level data: piecemeal EMR of large laterally spreading tumours is expected to recur more, and recurrence after EMR is usually re-treatable endoscopically — the recurrence gap is not the same as a cancer-outcome gap. Colorectal stratum only.
cards.source: Zhao HJ et al. Endoscopic mucosal resection versus endoscopic submucosal dissection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors: a meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: across all three sites ESD wins on en-bloc and R0 resection and on recurrence, and loses on perforation and procedure time — but only the small Barrett's comparison is randomised, and there the R0 win changed no clinical outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: across all three sites ESD wins on en-bloc and R0 resection and on recurrence, and loses on perforation and procedure time — but only the small Barrett's comparison is randomised, and there the R0 win changed no clinical outcome
cards.people: Carded evidence: one RCT (Barrett's, 40 patients) and two meta-analyses of predominantly non-randomised comparisons (gastric, 6,723 patients; colorectal laterally spreading tumours, 3,062 lesions). Site strata are kept separate on this shelf, per the slate instruction.
cards.result: ESD's resection-quality advantage is consistent in direction at every site (en-bloc odds ratio 9.00 in gastric cancer; en-bloc 95% vs 42.8% in colorectal laterally spreading tumours; R0 10/17 vs 2/17 in the Barrett's RCT) and recurrence is consistently lower, while perforation is consistently higher (gastric OR 2.55; colorectal 2.4% vs 1.8%) and procedures take longer. The one randomised trial found no difference in remission, recurrence or surgery despite the R0 gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence labelled as such: the trade-off is real, its size is not randomised-trial-grade.
cards.watchOut: Lesion size and morphology drive technique choice in practice; these comparisons do not answer which technique a given lesion should get, only what each achieves in the lesions it was used on.
cards.source: Synthesis of Terheggen G et al. 2017 (PMID: 26801885); Tao M et al. 2019 (PMID: 31874864); Zhao HJ et al. 2020 (PMID: 33207885).

shelves.title: EUS-guided biliary drainage versus ERCP first-line for malignant distal biliary obstruction: equal drainage success, less pancreatitis and stent dysfunction with the EUS route
shelves.question: In adults with malignant distal biliary obstruction, does first-line EUS-guided biliary drainage versus ERCP achieve comparable technical and clinical success with less post-procedure pancreatitis and stent dysfunction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bile Duct Neoplasms · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde · Cholestasis · Drainage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stents · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: The randomised base is FIRST-LINE drainage (the slate row was reframed on verification): three carded RCTs (Paik 2018, n=125; DRA-MBO/Teoh 2023, n=155; Bang 2018, n=67) and their meta-analysis (Miller 2019). Success is a tie everywhere: technical 93.8% vs 90.2% (Paik), 96.2% vs 76.3% (DRA-MBO, against an unusually low ERCP rate), 90.9% vs 94.1% (Bang); clinical success 90–97% in all arms. The differences are in harms and durability: pancreatitis 0% vs 14.8% in Paik and pooled risk ratio 0.12 (a relative measure) against ERCP; stent dysfunction requiring reintervention pooled RR 0.41; reintervention 15.6% vs 42.6% in Paik — though DRA-MBO found equal 1-year patency (91.1% vs 88.1%) and Bang found no significant difference in anything. The after-failed-ERCP comparison (EUS-guided vs percutaneous drainage) is a thinner limb, labelled as such on the meta-analysis card and not part of this shelf's claim. Device note (clarification exception): DRA-MBO used a lumen-apposing metal stent for choledochoduodenostomy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), expert-centre caveat on the face.

cards.headline: Paik 2018 RCT: EUS-guided drainage matched ERCP on success (technical 93.8% vs 90.2%; clinical 90.0% vs 94.5%) with no pancreatitis (0% vs 14.8%), fewer adverse events (6.3% vs 19.7%) and far less reintervention (15.6% vs 42.6%), N = 125
cards.summary: Paik 2018 RCT: EUS-guided drainage matched ERCP on success (technical 93.8% vs 90.2%; clinical 90.0% vs 94.5%) with no pancreatitis (0% vs 14.8%), fewer adverse events (6.3% vs 19.7%) and far less reintervention (15.6% vs 42.6%), N = 125
cards.people: 125 patients with unresectable malignant distal biliary obstruction at four South Korean tertiary centres, randomised to first-line EUS-guided biliary drainage (n=64) or ERCP transpapillary stenting (n=61).
cards.result: Technical success was 93.8% (60/64) with EUS-guided drainage vs 90.2% (55/61) with ERCP (non-inferior within a 10% margin); clinical success 90.0% vs 94.5% (p=0.49). Overall adverse events were lower with EUS-guided drainage (6.3% vs 19.7%, p=0.03), including post-procedure pancreatitis in 0 vs 14.8%, reintervention was lower (15.6% vs 42.6%), stent patency higher (85.1% vs 48.9%), and quality of life better preserved at 12 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Expert Korean tertiary centres and a mixed EUS-drainage technique set — the zero pancreatitis rate reflects bypassing the papilla, but the patency and reintervention gaps are larger than other trials found and may not transfer to lower-volume practice.
cards.source: Paik WH et al. EUS-Guided Biliary Drainage Versus ERCP for the Primary Palliation of Malignant Biliary Obstruction: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29961772. Registry ID: KCT0001396 (CRIS), as reported in the record. cards.headline: Teoh 2023 (DRA-MBO): EUS-guided choledochoduodenostomy with a lumen-apposing metal stent had higher technical success than ERCP (96.2% vs 76.3%) and half the procedure time, with equal 1-year stent patency (91.1% vs 88.1%), N = 155
cards.summary: Teoh 2023 (DRA-MBO): EUS-guided choledochoduodenostomy with a lumen-apposing metal stent had higher technical success than ERCP (96.2% vs 76.3%) and half the procedure time, with equal 1-year stent patency (91.1% vs 88.1%), N = 155
cards.people: 155 patients with obstructive jaundice from unresectable malignant distal biliary obstruction at international centres, randomised to EUS-guided choledochoduodenostomy using a lumen-apposing metal stent (the named tested device class; clarification exception) (n=79) or ERCP with covered metal stents (n=76). Primary outcome: 1-year stent patency.
cards.result: One-year stent patency did not differ (91.1% vs 88.1%, p=0.52) and clinical success was similar (93.7% vs 90.8%), but technical success was higher with EUS-guided drainage (96.2% vs 76.3%, p<0.001) and median procedure time much shorter (10 vs 25 minutes, p<0.001). Thirty-day adverse events and mortality were similar.
cards.watchOut: The unusually low ERCP technical success (76.3%) drives the headline difference — in centres where ERCP cannulation succeeds more often, the technical-success gap narrows; stent misdeployment is the EUS-specific failure mode (about 7% in the combined-trials analysis).

cards.headline: Bang 2018 RCT (pancreatic cancer): adverse events and success were statistically indistinguishable between EUS-guided drainage and ERCP (adverse events 21.2% vs 14.7%, p=0.49), N = 67
cards.summary: Bang 2018 RCT (pancreatic cancer): adverse events and success were statistically indistinguishable between EUS-guided drainage and ERCP (adverse events 21.2% vs 14.7%, p=0.49), N = 67
cards.people: 67 patients with distal biliary obstruction from pancreatic cancer at a single US centre, randomised single-blind to EUS-guided transmural biliary drainage (n=33) or ERCP (n=34) as primary treatment, followed to death or at least 6 months.
cards.result: Adverse events were 21.2% with EUS-guided drainage vs 14.7% with ERCP (risk ratio 0.69 as reported, 95% CI 0.24–1.97, p=0.49 — a relative measure), with no procedure-related deaths. Technical success (90.9% vs 94.1%), treatment success (97% vs 91.2%) and reinterventions (3.0% vs 2.9%) did not differ significantly, and neither approach impeded later pancreaticoduodenectomy (about 15% in each arm).
cards.watchOut: The discordant card on this shelf: in this pancreatic-cancer-only, single-centre trial the adverse-event advantage seen in Paik did not appear (numerically more events with EUS-guided drainage, not significant) — small numbers (67) mean it neither confirms nor refutes the pooled result.
cards.source: Bang JY et al. Stent placement by EUS or ERCP for primary biliary decompression in pancreatic cancer: a randomized trial. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2018. PMID: 29574126. cards.headline: Miller 2019 meta-analysis of RCTs: against ERCP, EUS-guided drainage cut stent dysfunction requiring reintervention (RR 0.41 — a relative measure) and post-procedure pancreatitis (RR 0.12), with no difference in technical or clinical success — 3 first-line trials, 222 patients
cards.summary: Miller 2019 meta-analysis of RCTs: against ERCP, EUS-guided drainage cut stent dysfunction requiring reintervention (RR 0.41 — a relative measure) and post-procedure pancreatitis (RR 0.12), with no difference in technical or clinical success — 3 first-line trials, 222 patients
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of EUS-guided biliary drainage for distal malignant obstruction: six trials in total, of which three (222 patients) compared EUS-guided drainage with ERCP as first-line therapy and three (132 patients) compared it with percutaneous drainage after failed ERCP.
cards.result: EUS-guided drainage was associated with less stent/catheter dysfunction overall (risk ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.27–0.57) and against ERCP specifically (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.23–0.74), and with less post-procedure pancreatitis than ERCP (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01–0.97) — risk ratios are relative measures. Technical and clinical success did not differ. The after-failed-ERCP comparison (against percutaneous drainage, RR 0.37 for dysfunction) is a separate, thinner limb and is reported here as such, not merged with the first-line result.
cards.watchOut: Only three first-line trials (222 patients) underlie the ERCP comparison, and the pancreatitis confidence interval (0.01–0.97) nearly reaches 1 — the pooled direction is consistent with the individual trials carded here, but the randomised base remains small and expert-centre.
