meta-analysis of randomised trials (miller 2019) systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of eus-guided biliary drainage for distal malignant obstruction: six trials in total, of which three (222 patients) compared eus-guided drainage with ercp as first-line therapy and three (132 patients) compared it with percutaneous drainage after failed ercp. eus-guided drainage was associated with less stent/catheter dysfunction overall (risk ratio 0.39, 95% ci 0.27–0.57) and against ercp specifically (rr 0.41, 95% ci 0.23–0.74), and with less post-procedure pancreatitis than ercp (rr 0.12, 95% ci 0.01–0.97) — risk ratios are relative measures. technical and clinical success did not differ. the after-failed-ercp comparison (against percutaneous drainage, rr 0.37 for dysfunction) is a separate, thinner limb and is reported here as such, not merged with the first-line result. only three first-line trials (222 patients) underlie the ercp comparison, and the pancreatitis confidence interval (0.01–0.97) nearly reaches 1 — the pooled direction is consistent with the individual trials carded here, but the randomised base remains small and expert-centre. miller cs et al. endoscopic ultrasound-guided biliary drainage for distal malignant obstruction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials. endoscopy international open. 2019. pmid: 31723579. registry id: none in the record. mesh: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: first-line EUS-guided drainage drains as reliably as ERCP and, across trials, causes less pancreatitis and less stent dysfunction — the honest claim is equivalence on success with a safety/patency edge, from expert centres
cards.summary: Synthesis: first-line EUS-guided drainage drains as reliably as ERCP and, across trials, causes less pancreatitis and less stent dysfunction — the honest claim is equivalence on success with a safety/patency edge, from expert centres
cards.people: Carded evidence: three first-line RCTs (125, 155 and 67 patients) and one meta-analysis of the randomised literature (3 first-line trials, 222 patients, overlapping the carded trials). The after-failed-ERCP question (EUS-guided vs percutaneous drainage) is a separate limb with thinner evidence and is not this shelf's claim.
cards.result: Technical and clinical success were comparable in every carded trial; pancreatitis was 0% vs 14.8% in Paik and pooled RR 0.12 against ERCP in Miller; stent dysfunction/reintervention favoured EUS-guided drainage in Paik (15.6% vs 42.6%) and in the pooled analysis (RR 0.41), while DRA-MBO found equal 1-year patency and Bang found no significant differences at all. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): multiple concordant RCTs plus their meta-analysis support comparable success with fewer papilla-related harms — with the expert-centre caveat on the face.
cards.watchOut: All trials come from centres expert in both techniques; the shelf does not establish that EUS-first is safer where EUS-guided drainage experience is limited, and device-specific failures (lumen-apposing stent misdeployment) are the counterweight harm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Paik WH et al. 2018 (PMID: 29961772); Teoh AYB et al. 2023 (PMID: 37121331); Bang JY et al. 2018 (PMID: 29574126); Miller CS et al. 2019 (PMID: 31723579).

shelves.title: Endoscopic treatment of Zenker's diverticulum: Z-POEM, flexible and rigid septotomy all succeed in about 9 of 10 patients — no randomised trials, and the techniques separate on adverse events, not success
shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic Zenker's diverticulum, how do Z-POEM, flexible endoscopic septotomy and rigid septotomy compare on clinical success, adverse events and recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Esophagoscopy · Female · Humans · Male · Myotomy · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Zenker Diverticulum
shelves.balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf: there are no randomised trials of Zenker's diverticulum treatment — every card is retrospective, and that is stated on the face. The largest comparison (Al Ghamdi 2022, 245 patients, 12 centres) found clinical success statistically indistinguishable (Z-POEM 92.7%, rigid 89.2%, flexible 86.7%; p=0.26) and recurrence similar, but adverse events clearly graded (rigid 30.0%, Z-POEM 16.8%, flexible 2.3%). A meta-analysis of seven non-randomised studies (Singh 2025, 580 patients) gives Z-POEM a clinical-success edge over flexible septotomy (risk ratio 1.11, a relative measure) with equal technical success, recurrence and adverse events — a point estimate the largest cohort does not confirm, so it is not upgraded here. Sarkis 2025 (60 patients) likewise found equal success with more and worse adverse events after needle-knife septotomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, observational basis stated.

cards.headline: Al Ghamdi 2022: clinical success was statistically indistinguishable across Z-POEM (92.7%), rigid septotomy (89.2%) and flexible septotomy (86.7%), p=0.26 — but adverse events were 30.0% rigid vs 16.8% Z-POEM vs 2.3% flexible, N = 245 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.summary: Al Ghamdi 2022: clinical success was statistically indistinguishable across Z-POEM (92.7%), rigid septotomy (89.2%) and flexible septotomy (86.7%), p=0.26 — but adverse events were 30.0% rigid vs 16.8% Z-POEM vs 2.3% flexible, N = 245 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.type: Multicentre retrospective cohort (observational — labelled as such) (Al Ghamdi 2022)
cards.people: 245 consecutive patients (mean age 72.6 years) treated at 12 centres between 2016 and 2019 for Zenker's diverticulum with Z-POEM (n=119), flexible endoscopic septotomy (n=86) or rigid endoscopic septotomy (n=40); clinical success was a Dakkak and Bennett dysphagia score of 1 or less. Multicentre retrospective comparison.
cards.result: Clinical success did not differ significantly (92.7% Z-POEM, 89.2% rigid, 86.7% flexible; p=0.26), and recurrence did not differ either (24 patients in total; p=0.47). Adverse events differed significantly: 30.0% with rigid septotomy, 16.8% with Z-POEM and 2.3% with flexible septotomy (p<0.05) — flexible septotomy appeared the safest and rigid the most complication-prone.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: technique choice followed centre practice and anatomy, follow-up was short and uneven (mean about 282 days in the Z-POEM arm), and the adverse-event gradient may reflect case mix as much as technique.
cards.source: Al Ghamdi SS et al. Zenker's peroral endoscopic myotomy, or flexible or rigid septotomy for Zenker's diverticulum: a multicenter retrospective comparison. Endoscopy. 2022. cards.headline: Singh 2025 meta-analysis: Z-POEM had higher clinical success than flexible septotomy (RR 1.11 — a relative measure) with equal technical success, recurrence and adverse events — 7 comparative studies, 580 patients, all non-randomised
cards.summary: Singh 2025 meta-analysis: Z-POEM had higher clinical success than flexible septotomy (RR 1.11 — a relative measure) with equal technical success, recurrence and adverse events — 7 comparative studies, 580 patients, all non-randomised
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of non-randomised comparative studies (Singh 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of seven comparative studies (searched to September 2024) totalling 580 patients with symptomatic Zenker's diverticulum treated with Z-POEM (n=274) or flexible endoscopic septotomy (n=306); mean ages 68.9–74.9 years.
cards.result: Technical success was similar (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.96–1.02). Clinical success was higher with Z-POEM (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04–1.18, p=0.001 — a relative measure; against flexible septotomy's roughly 87% success in the largest cohort this is a single-digit absolute difference). Recurrence, adverse events, hospital stay and procedure time did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The RR 1.11 point estimate must not be read as proven superiority: every pooled study is retrospective, the largest single cohort (Al Ghamdi, carded here) found no significant difference, and publication bias favours the newer technique.
cards.source: Singh S et al. Peroral endoscopic myotomy (Z-POEM) versus flexible endoscopic septotomy (FES) for treatment of Zenker's diverticulum: a systematic review and meta-analysis of outcomes. Annals of Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 39802284. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Sarkis 2025: Z-POEM and flexible needle-knife septotomy had similar clinical success at 6, 12 and 24 months, but septotomy caused more and worse adverse events (29% vs 5%) and more hospitalisation (71% vs 33%), N = 60 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.summary: Sarkis 2025: Z-POEM and flexible needle-knife septotomy had similar clinical success at 6, 12 and 24 months, but septotomy caused more and worse adverse events (29% vs 5%) and more hospitalisation (71% vs 33%), N = 60 (observational — labelled as such)
cards.type: Single-centre retrospective comparison (observational — labelled as such) (Sarkis 2025)
cards.people: 60 consecutive patients (mean age 72 years) treated at a single US institution between 2016 and 2023 with flexible endoscopic needle-knife septotomy (n=21) or Z-POEM (n=39) for symptomatic Zenker's diverticulum; adverse events graded by the AGREE classification, with Dakkak and Bennett scores at 6, 12 and 24 months.
cards.result: Overall technical success was 98.3% and clinical success (dysphagia score 1 or less) was similar between techniques at every time point, by both per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses. Adverse events were more prevalent (29% vs 5%, p=0.018) and more severe (p=0.032) after needle-knife septotomy, which also led to more post-procedure hospitalisation (71% vs 33%, p=0.007). Reintervention was needed in 5 patients (about 10% in each group) over a median 18 months.
cards.watchOut: Small (60 patients, only 21 septotomy) and single-centre; the hospitalisation difference may reflect era and local practice (septotomy cases cluster earlier in the series) rather than the techniques themselves.
cards.source: Sarkis Y et al. Comparison of flexible endoscopic needle-knife septotomy and peroral endoscopic myotomy for treatment of Zenker's diverticulum. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2025. PMID: 39218270. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: all endoscopic techniques succeed in roughly 87–93% of patients; no randomised trial exists, the largest cohort finds no efficacy difference, and the real separation is in adverse events — highest with rigid septotomy, lowest with flexible septotomy
cards.summary: Synthesis: all endoscopic techniques succeed in roughly 87–93% of patients; no randomised trial exists, the largest cohort finds no efficacy difference, and the real separation is in adverse events — highest with rigid septotomy, lowest with flexible septotomy
cards.people: Carded evidence: one multicentre retrospective comparison (245 patients), one meta-analysis of seven non-randomised comparative studies (580 patients, overlapping the cohorts) and one single-centre retrospective comparison (60 patients). No randomised trial of any Zenker's technique exists.
cards.result: Clinical success clusters at 86.7–92.7% across Z-POEM, rigid and flexible septotomy in the largest cohort (p=0.26); the meta-analysis favours Z-POEM over flexible septotomy on clinical success (RR 1.11, relative) while finding technical success, recurrence and adverse events equal. Adverse events are where the cohorts separate: 30.0% rigid, 16.8% Z-POEM, 2.3% flexible in Al Ghamdi; 29% vs 5% against needle-knife septotomy in Sarkis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational evidence only, labelled: high success for all techniques, no proven efficacy winner.
cards.watchOut: GAP-E framing: with zero randomised trials, every number on this shelf is vulnerable to selection by anatomy, diverticulum size and operator — the shelf compares reported series, not assigned treatments.
cards.source: Synthesis of Al Ghamdi SS et al. 2022 (PMID: 34198355); Singh S et al. 2025 (PMID: 39802284); Sarkis Y et al. 2025 (PMID: 39218270).

shelves.title: Alfapump for refractory ascites: paracentesis falls to near zero in every report including one small RCT — at the cost of serious adverse events, reinterventions and explants
shelves.question: In adults with cirrhosis and refractory ascites, does an implanted alfapump (automated low-flow ascites pump) versus standard serial large-volume paracentesis reduce paracentesis requirements, and at what cost in adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Ascites · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Paracentesis · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate row stated all alfapump evidence is single-arm; verification this session found a multicentre randomised trial (Bureau 2017, n=60, NCT01528410) — it is carded first, and the GAP-E framing is retained because the randomised base remains one small trial. Device naming (clarification exception): alfapump® (Sequana Medical). The pattern is unusually consistent: paracentesis falls from ~2–3.4 to ~0.2 sessions per month in the RCT, the POSEIDON pivotal cohort (n=40; 77% with ≥50% reduction) and both European cohorts; quality of life improves; survival does not change. The harms are equally consistent: serious adverse events 85.2% vs 45.2% in the RCT, early acute kidney injury, catheter blockage, reinterventions in about a third, explants 15% by 6 months (POSEIDON) and 48% over longer follow-up in a TIPS-ineligible cohort. The EASL 2026 recompensation post-hoc analysis is congress/press only and is fenced, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Bureau 2017 RCT: alfapump versus large-volume paracentesis — median time to first paracentesis not reached at 6 months vs 15 days (HR 0.13, a relative measure), quality of life better, but serious adverse events 85.2% vs 45.2% — N = 60
cards.summary: Bureau 2017 RCT: alfapump versus large-volume paracentesis — median time to first paracentesis not reached at 6 months vs 15 days (HR 0.13, a relative measure), quality of life better, but serious adverse events 85.2% vs 45.2% — N = 60
cards.people: 60 adults with cirrhosis and refractory ascites randomised at seven centres to the alfapump system (alfapump®, Sequana Medical — the named tested device; clarification exception) (n=27 analysed) or standard-of-care large-volume paracentesis (n=31 analysed), observed for 6 months; mean MELD 11.7. A nutrition/haemodynamics sub-study included 18 patients.
cards.result: Median time to first large-volume paracentesis was not reached at 6 months in the pump group vs 15.0 days with standard care (hazard ratio 0.13, p<0.001 — a relative measure), and Chronic Liver Disease Questionnaire scores improved significantly more with the pump. Adverse events were more frequent with the pump (96.3% vs 77.4%) and serious adverse events significantly more so (85.2% vs 45.2%, p=0.002), predominantly early acute kidney injury and pump-related reinterventions, mostly treatable; survival was similar.
cards.watchOut: PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate row, which stated all alfapump evidence is single-arm: this randomised trial exists and is carded first. It is still small (60 patients, 58 analysed), unblinded by necessity, and the serious-adverse-event excess is the price of the paracentesis reduction.
cards.source: Bureau C et al. Alfapump® system vs. large volume paracentesis for refractory ascites: A multicenter randomized controlled trial. Journal of Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 28645737. Registry ID: NCT01528410. cards.headline: POSEIDON 2025 (North America): therapeutic paracentesis fell from 3.2 to 0.2 sessions per month at 6 months, 77% achieving at least a 50% reduction; 15% of pumps explanted for device-related events within 6 months — N = 40, single-arm
cards.summary: POSEIDON 2025 (North America): therapeutic paracentesis fell from 3.2 to 0.2 sessions per month at 6 months, 77% achieving at least a 50% reduction; 15% of pumps explanted for device-related events within 6 months — N = 40, single-arm
cards.people: 40 patients with cirrhosis and refractory ascites requiring at least two therapeutic paracenteses in the prior 30 days (mean MELD-sodium 15) implanted with the alfapump system (Sequana Medical) and followed for up to 24 months; primary efficacy endpoint was paracentesis reduction at 6 months.
cards.result: Therapeutic paracentesis fell from 3.2 ± 1.5 to 0.2 ± 0.6 sessions per month at 6 months (p<0.001), with 77% of patients achieving a reduction of at least 50%. Six pumps (15%) were explanted within 6 months for device-related adverse events (3 for pump-site skin erosion, 3 for bladder discomfort); 24 renal events occurred in months 0–6, 16 of them readily reversible stage 1 acute kidney injury. Ascites symptom scores and the physical (not mental) component of the SF-36 improved; five deaths within 6 months were judged unrelated to the device.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the pre/post paracentesis comparison has no concurrent control, and patients were selected as suitable for implantation — the 0.2/month figure describes what happened after implant in selected patients, not a randomised effect.
cards.source: Wong F et al. The Effects of Alfapump on Ascites Control and Quality of Life in Patients With Cirrhosis and Recurrent or Refractory Ascites. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 39760647. Registry ID: NCT03973866. cards.headline: Bellot 2013 (PIONEER-era multicentre cohort): the pump removed 90% of ascites and cut median large-volume paracentesis from 3.4 to 0.2 per month over 6 months — N = 40, single-arm
cards.summary: Bellot 2013 (PIONEER-era multicentre cohort): the pump removed 90% of ascites and cut median large-volume paracentesis from 3.4 to 0.2 per month over 6 months — N = 40, single-arm
cards.people: 40 patients with refractory ascites at nine European centres (2010–2011) receiving the implanted automated low-flow pump moving ascites from the peritoneal cavity to the bladder, followed for 6 months; primary outcome was safety, in a multicentre non-randomised trial.
cards.result: The pump removed 90% of the ascites and reduced median large-volume paracentesis from 3.4 (range 1–6) to 0.2 (range 0–4) per month (p<0.01). Surgical complications occurred early in the study and became less frequent with experience; cirrhosis-related adverse events decreased along follow-up. The authors judged safety still moderate and noted a randomised trial against paracentesis was underway (the Bureau 2017 trial carded on this shelf).
cards.watchOut: First-generation experience with an explicit learning curve — early surgical complications improved as technique developed, so this cohort's safety figures are a floor-era estimate, in both directions.
cards.source: Bellot P et al. Automated low flow pump system for the treatment of refractory ascites: a multi-center safety and efficacy study. Journal of Hepatology. 2013. PMID: 23318604. cards.headline: Stirnimann 2017: median paracentesis fell from 2.17 to 0.17 per month, but the pump was explanted in 48% and 23 pump-related reinterventions were needed over up to 24 months — N = 56, single-arm
cards.summary: Stirnimann 2017: median paracentesis fell from 2.17 to 0.17 per month, but the pump was explanted in 48% and 23 pump-related reinterventions were needed over up to 24 months — N = 56, single-arm
cards.people: 56 patients (mean age 62) with cirrhosis and refractory ascites and a contraindication to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, treated with the alfapump system (Sequana Medical AG, Zurich, Switzerland, as named in the record) at centres in Germany, Switzerland, the UK and Spain, followed for up to 24 months.
cards.result: Median paracentesis frequency fell from 2.17 to 0.17 per month. The commonest technical complication was peritoneal catheter blockage; 23 pump-related reinterventions (17 patients) and 12 pump exchanges (11 patients) were required. The pump was explanted in 48% of patients (17 for serious adverse events, 9 at liver transplantation, 1 for recovery from refractory ascites); 23 patients died and 9 were transplanted during follow-up. The authors conclude technical and procedural improvements are required to reduce adverse events and reinterventions.
cards.watchOut: A TIPS-ineligible, sicker population than the trial cohorts — the 48% explant rate and the mortality reflect that case mix as well as the device; read alongside, not against, the randomised card.
cards.source: Stirnimann G et al. Treatment of refractory ascites with an automated low-flow ascites pump in patients with cirrhosis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2017. PMID: 28940225. cards.headline: MOSAIC 2020: interventional-radiology implantation was technically successful in 29/29, with a 31% adverse-event incidence, 2 explants and 4 reinterventions by 3 months — N = 29, single-arm feasibility
cards.summary: MOSAIC 2020: interventional-radiology implantation was technically successful in 29/29, with a 31% adverse-event incidence, 2 explants and 4 reinterventions by 3 months — N = 29, single-arm feasibility
cards.people: 29 patients (mean age 60) with cirrhotic refractory ascites in the multicentre open-label MOSAIC study receiving the alfapump system implanted by interventional radiology under ultrasound guidance (pump in a subcutaneous abdominal pocket; catheters to peritoneum and bladder).
cards.result: Technical success was 100% (29/29). By 3 months, three possibly procedure-related serious adverse events had occurred (ascites leakage, bacterial peritonitis, postoperative bleeding), with two explantations (6.8%; cellulitis, pump-pocket infection) and four reinterventions (pump or catheter replacement) — an adverse-event incidence of 9/29 (31.0%). Five patients required deviation from the instructions for use.
cards.watchOut: An implantation-technique study, not an efficacy study — it answers 'can IR implant it safely enough', and its 3-month window cannot speak to the longer-term explant and reintervention burden the other cards show.
cards.source: Bendel EC et al. Feasibility and Procedural Safety of alfapump System Implantation by IR: Experience from the MOSAIC Study. Journal of Vascular and Interventional Radiology. 2020. PMID: 32654961. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the alfapump reliably cuts paracentesis to near zero in every report — one small RCT included — and reliably costs reinterventions, kidney injury and explants; survival is unchanged where measured
cards.summary: Synthesis: the alfapump reliably cuts paracentesis to near zero in every report — one small RCT included — and reliably costs reinterventions, kidney injury and explants; survival is unchanged where measured
cards.people: Carded evidence: one multicentre RCT (60 randomised), the North American pivotal cohort (40), two European cohorts (40 and 56) and an implantation-feasibility study (29). Device naming (clarification exception): the alfapump® system (Sequana Medical) is the tested product throughout. The EASL 2026 recompensation post-hoc analysis is congress/press only and is not carded.
cards.result: Paracentesis frequency fell by roughly 90% or more in every report (3.2→0.2 and 3.4→0.2 and 2.17→0.17 sessions per month), quality of life improved in the RCT and the pivotal cohort, and survival did not differ in the RCT. Against that: serious adverse events 85.2% vs 45.2% in the RCT, explants 15% within 6 months in POSEIDON and 48% over longer follow-up in the TIPS-ineligible cohort, and a steady reintervention burden everywhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): large, consistent effect on the burden outcome, real device harms, one small RCT.
cards.watchOut: GAP-E framing retained from the slate, corrected on one point: the evidence is not all single-arm — Bureau 2017 is randomised — but it remains one small RCT plus selected single-arm cohorts, in patients chosen as implantable.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bureau C et al. 2017 (PMID: 28645737); Wong F et al. 2025 (PMID: 39760647); Bellot P et al. 2013 (PMID: 23318604); Stirnimann G et al. 2017 (PMID: 28940225); Bendel EC et al. 2020 (PMID: 32654961).

shelves.title: L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine for hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia and psychometric scores improve in every small trial — surrogates only, dominated by one research group, no clinical-outcome endpoint
shelves.question: In adults with hepatic encephalopathy, does L-carnitine or acetyl-L-carnitine versus placebo improve ammonia levels, psychometric performance and encephalopathy grade?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ammonia · Carnitine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychological Tests
shelves.balance: The evidence base is dominated by a single research group (Malaguarnera and colleagues, Catania) — printed here as the slate requires. Their two double-blind RCTs (n=150 in 2005; n=120 in 2003, grades 1–2) found significant ammonia reductions and psychometric gains on L-carnitine 2 g twice daily; a third, smaller open-control trial (Cecere 2002, 27 completers, 6 g/day) found ammonia normalised in 14 of 16 treated patients. The Cochrane review of the sister compound acetyl-L-carnitine (five RCTs, 398 participants) found all trials single-team, high risk of bias and underpowered, with none reporting mortality, serious adverse events or hospitalisation. Outcomes throughout are surrogates (ammonia, psychometric tests); no mortality endpoint exists. Supplement note (clarification exception): preparations differ by maker and no commercial brand is named in the publications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with those limits on the face.

cards.headline: Malaguarnera 2005: L-carnitine 2 g twice daily for 90 days significantly lowered fasting ammonia and improved psychometric tests versus placebo in hepatic encephalopathy — N = 150
cards.summary: Malaguarnera 2005: L-carnitine 2 g twice daily for 90 days significantly lowered fasting ammonia and improved psychometric tests versus placebo in hepatic encephalopathy — N = 150
cards.people: 150 patients with hepatic encephalopathy (aetiologies: hepatitis C 78, hepatitis B 41, cryptogenic cirrhosis 21, alcohol 10) randomised double-blind to L-carnitine 2 g twice daily or placebo for 90 days, from the Catania research group.
cards.result: At the end of treatment, fasting serum ammonia fell significantly in the L-carnitine group (p<0.05), and significant differences favouring L-carnitine were found on the symbol digit modalities test and block design psychometric measures. The authors conclude L-carnitine has a protective effect against ammonia-precipitated encephalopathy in cirrhotic patients. The record reports significance levels rather than full effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Abstract-level reporting gives p-values without the ammonia values or test scores themselves, so the size of the effect cannot be judged from the record — and this is one of several positive trials from the same single research group (see balance).
cards.source: Malaguarnera M et al. Effects of L-carnitine in patients with hepatic encephalopathy. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2005. PMID: 16437672. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Malaguarnera 2003: L-carnitine for 60 days reduced ammonia at days 30 and 60 and improved the number-connection test in grade 1–2 encephalopathy versus placebo — N = 120
cards.summary: Malaguarnera 2003: L-carnitine for 60 days reduced ammonia at days 30 and 60 and improved the number-connection test in grade 1–2 encephalopathy versus placebo — N = 120
cards.people: 120 patients with mild or moderate (grade 1 or 2) hepatic encephalopathy randomised double-blind to L-carnitine 2 g twice daily or placebo for 60 days, from the same Catania group.
cards.result: Ammonia fell significantly with L-carnitine at day 30 and more markedly at day 60 in both grade 1 and grade 2 patients, and a significant therapeutic effect was observed on the NCT-A (number connection test A), an accepted psychometric test in cirrhotic patients with encephalopathy. As with the group's 2005 trial, the record reports significance rather than full numerical effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Same group, same dose, same surrogate outcomes as the 2005 card — two trials from one centre are not independent replication, and neither reports encephalopathy episodes, hospitalisation or mortality.

cards.headline: Cecere 2002: L-carnitine 6 g/day for 4 weeks normalised ammonia in 14 of 16 treated patients (mean reduction 60.1 vs 1.4 µmol/L in controls) with net psychometric improvement — N = 31 enrolled, 27 completing
cards.summary: Cecere 2002: L-carnitine 6 g/day for 4 weeks normalised ammonia in 14 of 16 treated patients (mean reduction 60.1 vs 1.4 µmol/L in controls) with net psychometric improvement — N = 31 enrolled, 27 completing
cards.type: Small randomised controlled trial, open control (Cecere 2002)
cards.people: 31 patients with hepatic cirrhosis and subclinical hepatic encephalopathy (diagnosed by Wechsler and Halstead-Reitan psychometric subtests) randomised to oral L-carnitine 6 g/day in two divided doses for 4 weeks (16 completers) or no treatment (11 completers); ammonia measured weekly.
cards.result: L-carnitine produced rapid, sustained ammonia reductions (mean reduction 60.1 vs 1.4 µmol/L in controls), with normal ammonia attained in 14 of 16 treated patients, and a net overall improvement in psychometric test results versus controls. No clinically significant adverse events were reported. Note the control group received no treatment rather than a matched placebo.
cards.watchOut: Tiny (27 completers), 4 weeks, unblinded control, and subclinical encephalopathy only — the ammonia effect is large on its face but the design cannot exclude expectation and practice effects on the psychometric outcomes.
cards.source: Cecere A et al. Efficacy of L-carnitine in reducing hyperammonaemia and improving neuropsychological test performance in patients with hepatic cirrhosis: results of a randomised trial. Clinical Drug Investigation. 2002. PMID: 23315430. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Cochrane 2019 (acetyl-L-carnitine): five RCTs, 398 participants — all from a single Italian team, all at high risk of bias and underpowered; none reported mortality, serious adverse events or hospitalisation
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019 (acetyl-L-carnitine): five RCTs, 398 participants — all from a single Italian team, all at high risk of bias and underpowered; none reported mortality, serious adverse events or hospitalisation
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of acetyl-L-carnitine plus standard care versus placebo or no acetyl-L-carnitine plus standard care in people with hepatic encephalopathy (covert or overt, all with cirrhosis), searched to September 2018; five trials, 398 participants, all conducted in Italy by a single team.
cards.result: None of the five trials reported all-cause mortality, serious adverse events or days of hospitalisation; only one (67 participants) assessed quality of life. The review's framing is that acetyl-L-carnitine may reduce ammonia toxicity, but the trial base is uniformly high risk of bias and underpowered — the record's abstract is truncated in this session's fetch before its pooled effect estimates, so no pooled number is carded here.
cards.watchOut: This card covers the acetyl-L-carnitine limb specifically; its verdict on evidence quality (single team, high bias risk, underpowered) applies with equal force to the L-carnitine trials carded above, which come from the same research environment.

cards.headline: Synthesis: L-carnitine lowers ammonia and improves psychometric scores in every small trial — all surrogates, mostly one research group, with no mortality, episode or hospitalisation endpoint anywhere in the base
cards.summary: Synthesis: L-carnitine lowers ammonia and improves psychometric scores in every small trial — all surrogates, mostly one research group, with no mortality, episode or hospitalisation endpoint anywhere in the base
cards.people: Carded evidence: three small RCTs of L-carnitine (150, 120 and 31 patients) and a Cochrane review of five acetyl-L-carnitine RCTs (398 participants). Supplement note (clarification exception): L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine are supplement products whose preparations differ by maker; the carded trials used pharmaceutical-grade material at 4–6 g/day, and the publications do not name a commercial brand — current retail products may differ in content and effect.
cards.result: Ammonia fell significantly in all three L-carnitine trials and psychometric performance improved; the Cochrane review of the sister compound found the same direction in a base it judged entirely high risk of bias, single-team and underpowered, with no trial reporting mortality, serious adverse events or hospitalisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — surrogate outcomes only, single-group dominance stated on the face.
cards.watchOut: No carded study tests carnitine against or added to standard encephalopathy therapy (lactulose, rifaximin) on clinical episodes — the shelf answers the ammonia/psychometric question only.

shelves.title: Baveno non-invasive criteria to spare screening endoscopy: the VI rule safely spares about a third of endoscopies (pooled missed varices-needing-treatment 0.3%); the expanded rule spares 40% at a 1.6% missed rate
shelves.question: In adults with compensated advanced chronic liver disease, do the Baveno VI/VII non-invasive criteria (platelet count plus liver stiffness measurement) safely identify patients who can avoid screening endoscopy without missing varices needing treatment?
shelves.mesh: Elasticity Imaging Techniques · Endoscopy · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis
shelves.balance: PARTIAL build, synthesis-only per the miner: Shelf #6727 is the HVPG PHYSIOLOGY home (what the gradient measures; the 10/12/16/20 mmHg ladder) — Baveno appears there only in aliases, and the validation question is not asked there. This shelf asks only the validation question and cards none of #6727's references; the two shelves are cross-pointed in prose. The safety crux leads, ahead of the spared counts: pooled missed varices-needing-treatment is 0.3% for the original Baveno VI criteria (Szakács 2019, 13 studies, 4,464 patients), with about a third of endoscopies spared; the original validation cohort (Maurice 2016) had a 0.98 negative predictive value but still held 13% of its (few) high-risk varices inside the spared group. The expanded criteria (Augustin 2017, 925 patients) spare 40% at a 1.6% missed rate within the spared group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-accuracy framing throughout.

cards.headline: Maurice 2016: Baveno VI criteria spared 33% of endoscopies with a 98% negative predictive value — but 2% of patients meeting the criteria had high-risk varices, 13% of all high-risk varices in the cohort, N = 310
cards.summary: Maurice 2016: Baveno VI criteria spared 33% of endoscopies with a 98% negative predictive value — but 2% of patients meeting the criteria had high-risk varices, 13% of all high-risk varices in the cohort, N = 310
cards.people: 310 patients with compensated chronic liver disease (liver stiffness at least 10 kPa and an upper GI endoscopy within 12 months) from two institutions, 2006–2015; 55% hepatitis C, 89% Child-Pugh A. Varices were graded low-risk (grade under 2) or high-risk (grade 2 or above). The Baveno VI rule tested: liver stiffness under 20 kPa plus platelet count over 150,000/µL.
cards.result: Varices were present in 23% and high-risk varices in 5%. Overall 102/310 (33%) met the Baveno VI criteria; within that group 11% had varices and 2% had high-risk varices — 2 of the 15 patients (13%) with high-risk varices overall. The criteria gave sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.34, positive predictive value 0.06 and negative predictive value 0.98 for high-risk varices; the authors conclude the criteria correctly identified 98% of patients who could safely avoid endoscopy.
cards.watchOut: The safety figure cuts both ways: a 0.98 negative predictive value in a cohort with only 5% high-risk-varices prevalence still meant 13% of all high-risk varices sat inside the 'spare endoscopy' group — prevalence in the reader's own population moves that number.
cards.source: Maurice JB et al. Validation of the Baveno VI criteria to identify low risk cirrhotic patients not requiring endoscopic surveillance for varices. Journal of Hepatology. 2016. PMID: 27388923. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Elasticity Imaging Techniques · Endoscopy · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Varicose Veins

cards.headline: Augustin 2017: expanded criteria (platelets over 110 × 10⁹/L plus stiffness under 25 kPa) spared 40% of endoscopies vs 21% for original Baveno VI, with missed varices-needing-treatment of 1.6% within the spared group — N = 925 across three cohorts
cards.summary: Augustin 2017: expanded criteria (platelets over 110 × 10⁹/L plus stiffness under 25 kPa) spared 40% of endoscopies vs 21% for original Baveno VI, with missed varices-needing-treatment of 1.6% within the spared group — N = 925 across three cohorts
cards.people: Patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease: the ANTICIPATE derivation cohort (499 patients, mixed aetiologies) plus validation cohorts from London (309) and Barcelona (117) — 925 patients in total. The outcome was varices needing treatment (VNT).
cards.result: The best expanded rule was platelet count over 110 × 10⁹/L with liver stiffness under 25 kPa. Applied across the cohorts, the expanded criteria would spare 367 (40%) of endoscopies versus 21% with the original Baveno VI criteria, with a risk of missing VNT of 1.6% (95% CI 0.7%–3.5%) among patients meeting the criteria and 0.6% (95% CI 0.3%–1.4%) in the overall population. Performance held in hepatitis C, alcoholic and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis aetiologies.
cards.watchOut: The expanded rule trades safety margin for yield: 1.6% missed VNT within the spared group sits above the original criteria's pooled missed rate (see the meta-analysis card) and close to the 5% ceiling the Baveno framework itself set — the two rules are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Augustin S et al. Expanding the Baveno VI criteria for the screening of varices in patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease. Hepatology. 2017. PMID: 28696510. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Szakács 2019 diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis: pooled missed varices-needing-treatment rate 0.3% with 32.8% of endoscopies spared — 13 studies, 4,464 patients with suspected compensated advanced chronic liver disease
cards.summary: Szakács 2019 diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis: pooled missed varices-needing-treatment rate 0.3% with 32.8% of endoscopies spared — 13 studies, 4,464 patients with suspected compensated advanced chronic liver disease
cards.people: Systematic review and diagnostic-test-accuracy meta-analysis of studies testing the Baveno VI criteria (liver stiffness by transient elastography under 20 kPa plus platelet count over 150 × 10⁹/L) against screening endoscopy; 13 studies including 4,464 patients with suspected compensated advanced chronic liver disease (stiffness over 10 kPa), with an expanded analysis of 27 studies and 7,534 patients in broader compensated chronic liver disease.
cards.result: In suspected compensated advanced chronic liver disease, the pooled missed VNT rate was 0.3% (95% CI 0.1%–0.6%) and the pooled spared-endoscopy rate 32.8% (24.8%–41.4%), with sensitivity 97%, specificity 41% and area under the curve 96%. Missed VNT rates by aetiology were 0.0% (hepatitis C), 1.2% (hepatitis B), 0.0% (fatty liver disease) and 0.0% (alcohol). In the broader chronic-liver-disease population the missed rate was 0.2% with 30.5% of endoscopies spared. Heterogeneity in spared-endoscopy rates was very high (I² = 97%).
cards.watchOut: The pooled 0.3% missed rate coexists with individual cohorts (Maurice, carded here) missing a visibly larger share of high-risk varices — outcome definitions differ (varices needing treatment vs grade ≥2 varices), and the spared-rate heterogeneity (I² 97%) means local yield varies widely.
cards.source: Szakács Z et al. Baveno Criteria Safely Identify Patients With Compensated Advanced Chronic Liver Disease Who Can Avoid Variceal Screening Endoscopy: A Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in Physiology. 2019. PMID: 31481896. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Quantitative liver-clearance tests: ICG disappearance runs ~23%/min in health and galactose elimination capacity falls with age and liver failure
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what do the quantitative liver-clearance tests measure — indocyanine green disappearance rate and galactose elimination capacity in health, how do they fall with age and liver blood flow, and how were their normal ranges established?
shelves.mesh: Indocyanine Green · Galactose · Liver Function Tests · Liver Circulation · Aging
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for what these two tests measure and their healthy ranges, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on hepatic clearance: indocyanine green (ICG) is removed almost exclusively by the liver, so its plasma disappearance is a flow-and-uptake-limited clearance signal, while galactose elimination capacity (GEC) at saturating dose is a capacity-limited measure of functional hepatocyte mass. The carded human data: in 41 adults without liver disease, noninvasive ICG plasma disappearance rate averaged 23.1 ± 7.9%/min but ranged 9.7–43.2%/min — wide enough that the commonly cited 18%/min 'liver failure' cutoff sits inside the healthy range (Reekers 2010). Ageing shrinks the signal: in 65 healthy subjects aged 24–91, liver volume, ICG-derived apparent liver blood flow and flow per unit liver volume all fell significantly with age (Wynne 1989). For galactose, GEC per kg is highest in young children and falls to the adult level by about age 16, and is lower in chronic liver disease at every age (Lange 2011, 10 healthy + 30 diseased children); in 781 newly diagnosed cirrhosis patients the normal-range threshold was ≥1.75 mmol/min, and below it each 0.5 mmol/min higher GEC carried a relative hazard of death of 0.64 after adjustment (Jepsen 2009). REFUSAL: the classic Caesar-era ICG anchor (Caesar et al., Clin Sci 1961) was refused — its PubMed record carries no abstract, so nothing from it is carded or quoted; the same applies to Tygstrup's original galactose-elimination reports, which no fetched record verifies. This shelf is about clearance-test physiology, not about the urea-synthesis (functional hepatic nitrogen clearance) question shelved elsewhere in the library.

cards.headline: Wynne 1989: in 65 healthy people aged 24–91, liver volume and ICG-derived apparent liver blood flow fell significantly with age
cards.summary: Wynne 1989: in 65 healthy people aged 24–91, liver volume and ICG-derived apparent liver blood flow fell significantly with age
cards.type: Human clearance/ultrasound study (ICG plasma clearance in healthy ageing), Hepatology 1989
cards.people: Sixty-five healthy subjects between 24 and 91 years of age; liver volume by grey-scale B-mode ultrasound, and apparent liver blood flow from the plasma clearance of indocyanine green, on the stated assumption that hepatic extraction of the dye does not change with age.
cards.result: Age correlated negatively and significantly with liver volume and with apparent liver blood flow (P < 0.001), whether expressed in absolute terms or per unit body weight, and with liver blood flow per unit liver volume — liver perfusion (P < 0.005). The authors' reading: the shrinking liver and its falling perfusion at least partly explain why clearance of many liver-metabolised drugs declines with age. The record prints correlations and significance, not the absolute flow values, and this card claims no more than that.
cards.watchOut: 'Apparent' flow is the record's own word: it assumes constant dye extraction with age, so any true extraction fall would be folded into the flow estimate.
cards.source: Wynne HA, Cope LH, Mutch E, Rawlins MD, et al.. The effect of age upon liver volume and apparent liver blood flow in healthy man. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1989. PMID: 2643548. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reekers 2010: ICG plasma disappearance rate in 41 patients without liver disease averaged 23.1 ± 7.9%/min — but ranged 9.7–43.2%/min, straddling the 18%/min 'failure' cutoff
cards.summary: Reekers 2010: ICG plasma disappearance rate in 41 patients without liver disease averaged 23.1 ± 7.9%/min — but ranged 9.7–43.2%/min, straddling the 18%/min 'failure' cutoff
cards.type: Human methods/normative study (ICG-PDR by pulse dye densitometry), Anesth Analg 2010
cards.people: Forty-one ASA physical status I–II patients without signs of liver disease, scheduled for elective nonhepatic surgery; 10 mg indocyanine green intravenously, disappearance measured noninvasively by pulse dye densitometry (finger probe in 33, nose probe in 8), with arterial-blood comparison in a subset.
cards.result: Mean noninvasive ICG-PDR was 23.1 ± 7.9%/min (n = 41), range 9.7–43.2%/min — values in people without liver failure fell well below the 18%/min figure generally cited as the hepatic-failure cutoff, so the authors conclude that cutoff needs reconsideration. Against arterial-blood measurement, finger-probe bias was 1.6%/min (limits of agreement −5.2 to 8.3%/min) and nose-probe bias −6.0%/min (−15.5 to 3.4%/min): the finger measurement is adequate, the nose measurement is not interchangeable.
cards.watchOut: Surgical patients under anaesthesia care pathways, not resting volunteers — the 'healthy range' is a perioperative one, and its width is itself the finding.
cards.source: Reekers M, Simon MJ, Boer F, Mooren RA, et al.. Pulse dye densitometry and indocyanine green plasma disappearance in ASA physical status I-II patients. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2010. PMID: 20081133. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lange 2011: galactose elimination capacity per kg is highest in the youngest children, reaches the adult level by ~16 years, and runs lower in chronic liver disease (10 healthy + 30 diseased children)
cards.summary: Lange 2011: galactose elimination capacity per kg is highest in the youngest children, reaches the adult level by ~16 years, and runs lower in chronic liver disease (10 healthy + 30 diseased children)
cards.type: Human clearance study (galactose elimination capacity across childhood), Scand J Gastroenterol 2011
cards.people: Ten healthy children (median age 10.7 years, range 7 months–16 years) and 30 children with chronic liver disease (median 8.6 years, range 3 months–16 years); GEC estimated from the linear fall in galactose concentration in arterialised capillary blood after intravenous galactose infusion. Small healthy group — N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: In both groups GEC (µmol/min/kg body weight) was highest in the youngest children and decreased with age, at a significantly lower level in the liver-disease group (P = 0.05). Healthy children's GEC was significantly higher than healthy adults', diminishing to the adult level by age 16. So the 'normal' GEC is an age-moving target in childhood, and the test separates diseased from healthy children as it does adults.
cards.watchOut: Healthy N = 10, printed on the face; the adult comparison is to previously published adult values, not a concurrently studied adult group in this record.
cards.source: Lange A, Grønbæk H, Vilstrup H, Keiding S. Age-dependency of galactose elimination capacity in healthy children and children with chronic liver disease. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21034348. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jepsen 2009: in 781 newly diagnosed cirrhosis patients, a GEC below the normal range (≥1.75 mmol/min) strongly predicted death — relative hazard 0.64 per 0.5 mmol/min higher GEC after adjustment
cards.summary: Jepsen 2009: in 781 newly diagnosed cirrhosis patients, a GEC below the normal range (≥1.75 mmol/min) strongly predicted death — relative hazard 0.64 per 0.5 mmol/min higher GEC after adjustment
cards.type: Human registry cohort (GEC at cirrhosis diagnosis and mortality), BMC Gastroenterol 2009
cards.people: Seven hundred and eighty-one Danish patients with newly diagnosed cirrhosis who had a galactose elimination capacity test at diagnosis (1992–2005), linked to healthcare registries; 454 (58%) died over 2,617 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Seventy-five per cent had a decreased GEC (<1.75 mmol/min); in that group GEC strongly predicted 30-day, 1-year and 5-year mortality — crude relative hazard ratio 0.74 (95% CI 0.59–0.92) and adjusted relative hazard ratio 0.64 (95% CI 0.51–0.81) per 0.5 mmol/min increase in GEC (hazard ratios are relative measures; the absolute backdrop is 58% overall mortality in the cohort). The association held for alcoholic and non-alcoholic cirrhosis and predicted cirrhosis-related, not unrelated, mortality. In the 25% with GEC in the normal range (≥1.75 mmol/min) the association was weak (adjusted relative HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.60–1.08). The 1.75 mmol/min line is this record's normal-range threshold for the test.
cards.watchOut: A disease-prognosis cohort, carded for what it establishes about the test's scale and normal threshold — not a healthy-volunteer normative study.
cards.source: Jepsen P, Vilstrup H, Ott P, Keiding S, et al.. The galactose elimination capacity and mortality in 781 Danish patients with newly-diagnosed liver cirrhosis: a cohort study. BMC gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19566919. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ICG disappearance tracks hepatic flow and uptake (~23%/min in health, falling with age); galactose elimination tracks functional capacity (normal ≥1.75 mmol/min in adults, higher per kg in children)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ICG disappearance tracks hepatic flow and uptake (~23%/min in health, falling with age); galactose elimination tracks functional capacity (normal ≥1.75 mmol/min in adults, higher per kg in children)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Wynne 1989; Reekers 2010; Lange 2011; Jepsen 2009), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account of hepatic clearance — flow-limited versus capacity-limited elimination — as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: Two different quantities hide under 'liver function test'. ICG disappearance is a clearance signal: mean 23.1%/min by pulse densitometry in patients without liver disease, but with a healthy range (9.7–43.2%/min) so wide that a single cutoff misclassifies, and the underlying apparent liver blood flow falls with age alongside liver volume. Galactose elimination at saturating dose is a capacity signal: highest per kg in infancy, adult-level by ~16 years, and in adults the normal range begins at ≥1.75 mmol/min, below which the value grades mortality risk in cirrhosis. REFUSALS, stated plainly: the classic Caesar et al. 1961 ICG paper and Tygstrup's original galactose-elimination-capacity reports were NOT carded — their PubMed records carry no abstract (Caesar) or were not verifiable in any record fetched this session (Tygstrup), so no number on this shelf rests on them; every value above comes from a fetched record. Nothing here duplicates the library's urea-synthesis shelf — nitrogen clearance is a different hepatic quantity.
cards.watchOut: ICG values are method- and setting-dependent (invasive vs finger vs nose probe; anaesthetised vs resting). GEC is reported in mmol/min (a rate), not a concentration, so no mg/dL conversion applies.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 2643548, 20081133, 21034348, 19566919), with textbook framing as cited. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Small-intestinal permeability in health: lactulose leaks through at ~0.3% of dose against ~30% for mannitol — and NSAIDs open the barrier within months
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how permeable is the small intestine on sugar-probe testing — urinary lactulose/mannitol (and lactulose/rhamnose) recovery ratios in health, how do NSAIDs and coeliac disease move them, and how reproducible are the ratios within a person?
shelves.mesh: Lactulose · Mannitol · Rhamnose · Permeability · Intestinal Mucosa
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the sugar-probe measurement and its healthy behaviour, framed by Boron & Boulpaep on the intestinal barrier and paracellular transport. The principle, from the carded human studies: a disaccharide (lactulose) crosses mainly paracellularly and barely at all in health, while a monosaccharide (mannitol or rhamnose) crosses freely, so the urinary recovery ratio corrects for transit, dilution and renal handling. In the modern standardised measurement in 60 healthy adults, median 24-hour urinary recovery was ~30% of dose for 13C-mannitol and ~15% for rhamnose against only 0.32% for lactulose (Khoshbin 2021) — a roughly hundredfold separation — but between-person variation is large (median interindividual coefficient of variation 76.5%). Timing is not a detail: in 12 healthy volunteers the lactulose/mannitol ratio in 0–2 h urine was 0.08 against 0.32 in 8–24 h urine, because liquid reaches the colon within 2 hours in most people, so early urine mixes small-bowel and colonic signals (Camilleri 2010). The barrier is drug-sensitive: permeability was normal in untreated rheumatoid arthritis but almost invariably abnormal on NSAIDs (Bjarnason 1984), and in long-term NSAID users small-intestinal inflammation was present in 54–72% across conventional NSAIDs, developing in 9 of 13 followed patients by 6 months (Sigthorsson 1998). In coeliac disease the lactulose/rhamnose ratio and 51Cr-EDTA both rise while polyethylene glycol permeation falls — markers travel by different routes and are not interchangeable (Bjarnason 1994). This is the paracellular-leak question; the library's transcellular sugar-absorption shelf asks a different quantity and is cross-pointed, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Bjarnason 1984: intestinal permeability was normal in untreated rheumatoid arthritis but almost invariably abnormal on NSAIDs — 24 patients excreted significantly more 51Cr-EDTA than 34 controls
cards.summary: Bjarnason 1984: intestinal permeability was normal in untreated rheumatoid arthritis but almost invariably abnormal on NSAIDs — 24 patients excreted significantly more 51Cr-EDTA than 34 controls
cards.type: Human permeability study (51Cr-EDTA absorption, NSAID effect), Lancet 1984
cards.people: Twenty-four patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 34 controls, tested with the 51Cr-EDTA absorption test; osteoarthritis patients were studied to localise the NSAID effect, and indium-111-labelled leucocyte scans looked for intestinal inflammation (positive ileocaecal scans in 6 of 9 patients on or recently on NSAIDs).
cards.result: The rheumatoid patients excreted significantly more 51Cr-EDTA than controls — but permeability was normal in untreated patients and almost invariably abnormal in those treated with NSAIDs. The osteoarthritis studies showed the abnormality was an NSAID effect on both proximal and distal intestine, systemically mediated, with ileocaecal inflammation on leucocyte scans. The founding observation of the NSAID-enteropathy literature: the drug, not the disease, opens the barrier.
cards.watchOut: 51Cr-EDTA is a whole-gut probe, not the small-bowel-specific sugar ratio; carded as the classic NSAID-permeability anchor, with the sugar-probe cards carrying the quantitative ratios.
cards.source: Bjarnason I, Williams P, So A, Zanelli GD, et al.. Intestinal permeability and inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis: effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Lancet (London, England). 1984. PMID: 6150232. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bjarnason 1994: the four markers do not measure the same thing — after intravenous dosing, 24-h urinary recovery was 40% (PEG 400), 72% (rhamnose), 93% (lactulose) and 97% (51Cr-EDTA); in coeliac disease the lactulose/rhamnose ratio rose while PEG permeation fell
cards.summary: Bjarnason 1994: the four markers do not measure the same thing — after intravenous dosing, 24-h urinary recovery was 40% (PEG 400), 72% (rhamnose), 93% (lactulose) and 97% (51Cr-EDTA); in coeliac disease the lactulose/rhamnose ratio rose while PEG permeation fell
cards.type: Human probe-comparison study (four permeability markers, controls and coeliac disease), Scand J Gastroenterol 1994
cards.people: Control subjects and patients with coeliac disease (numbers not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such) given polyethylene glycol 400, L-rhamnose, lactulose and 51Cr-EDTA simultaneously, intravenously and orally, in iso- and hyperosmolar test solutions.
cards.result: The intravenous limb validates the probes' renal handling: nearly all absorbed lactulose and 51Cr-EDTA appears in urine, less rhamnose, and only 40% of PEG 400. Orally, lactulose showed an osmotic retention effect in hyperosmolar solution, and hyperosmolar glycerol increased permeation of every marker except L-rhamnose — test-dose osmolarity changes the answer. The lactulose/L-rhamnose urine ratio discriminated coeliac disease from controls about as sensitively as 51Cr-EDTA alone; both rose in coeliac disease while PEG permeation fell, and no marker correlated significantly with jejunal histology. Conclusion on the face: the markers permeate by different routes, affected differently by disease.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face. Osmolarity of the test drink is a confounder the field still standardises poorly.
cards.source: Bjarnason I, Maxton D, Reynolds AP, Catt S, et al.. Comparison of four markers of intestinal permeability in control subjects and patients with coeliac disease. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1994. PMID: 7939400. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sigthorsson 1998: in long-term NSAID users, permeability changes depended on test-dose osmolarity, and small-intestinal inflammation affected 54–72% across conventional NSAIDs — 9 of 13 followed patients had developed it by 6 months
cards.summary: Sigthorsson 1998: in long-term NSAID users, permeability changes depended on test-dose osmolarity, and small-intestinal inflammation affected 54–72% across conventional NSAIDs — 9 of 13 followed patients had developed it by 6 months
cards.type: Human permeability/inflammation cohort (long-term NSAID users), Gut 1998
cards.people: Sixty-eight patients on six different NSAIDs for over six months, given combined absorption–permeability tests at three test-dose osmolarities (iso-, hypo- and hyperosmolar); 286 patients on 12 NSAIDs assessed for intestinal inflammation by indium-111 white-cell faecal excretion, with a sequential subgroup followed from treatment start.
cards.result: Iso- and hyperosmolar tests showed significant malabsorption of 3-O-methyl-D-glucose, D-xylose and L-rhamnose; permeability changes were significantly more pronounced and frequent with hypo- and hyperosmolar than iso-osmolar test doses. In the sequential study, 4 of 13 patients had developed intestinal inflammation by 3 months and 9 of 13 by 6 months of NSAID treatment. Prevalence across the 286 patients was 54–72% for the conventional NSAIDs, with no significant difference by drug, dose, age, sex or disease duration — except aspirin and nabumetone, which showed no evidence of intestinal inflammation.
cards.watchOut: Patients with arthritis, not healthy volunteers — carded for the NSAID limb of the question; the healthy ranges rest on the Camilleri and Khoshbin cards.
cards.source: Sigthorsson G, Tibble J, Hayllar J, Menzies I, et al.. Intestinal permeability and inflammation in patients on NSAIDs. Gut. 1998. PMID: 9824578. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Camilleri 2010: in 12 healthy volunteers the lactulose/mannitol ratio was 0.08 in 0–2 h urine but 0.32 in 8–24 h urine — because liquid reaches the colon within 2 hours, early urine is not a pure small-bowel signal
cards.summary: Camilleri 2010: in 12 healthy volunteers the lactulose/mannitol ratio was 0.08 in 0–2 h urine but 0.32 in 8–24 h urine — because liquid reaches the colon within 2 hours, early urine is not a pure small-bowel signal
cards.type: Human methods study (two-sugar excretion timing in healthy volunteers), Neurogastroenterol Motil 2010
cards.people: Twelve healthy volunteers in a crossover study comparing urinary lactulose/mannitol ratios after the sugars in liquid formulation versus delayed-release methacrylate-coated capsules, both radiolabelled, with urine collected 0–2, 2–8 and 8–24 h and scintigraphic tracking of the dose.
cards.result: Two hours after the liquid dose, gastric residual was 15.9 ± 6.2% and 49.6 ± 7.8% of the dose was already in the colon — liquid had entered the colon in 11 of 12 participants; capsules arrived in the colon at 5.16 ± 0.46 h on average. Mannitol was extensively absorbed in the first 8 h, lactulose absorption stayed low throughout 24 h. The lactulose/mannitol ratio (geometric mean) was 0.08 (95% CI 0.05–0.11) in 0–2 h urine versus 0.32 (0.16–0.46) in 8–24 h urine (P < 0.05). The authors' caution, carried on the face: the higher late ratio does not mean the colon is more permeable than the small intestine — collection windows measure different segments.
cards.watchOut: N = 12, printed on the face. Ratios from different collection windows or formulations are not comparable — the central reproducibility lesson of this shelf.

cards.headline: Khoshbin 2021: the standardised healthy reference — median 24-h urinary recovery ~30% of dose for 13C-mannitol, ~15% rhamnose, 0.32% lactulose and 2.3% sucralose in 60 healthy adults, with wide between-person variation (median CV 76.5%)
cards.summary: Khoshbin 2021: the standardised healthy reference — median 24-h urinary recovery ~30% of dose for 13C-mannitol, ~15% rhamnose, 0.32% lactulose and 2.3% sucralose in 60 healthy adults, with wide between-person variation (median CV 76.5%)
cards.type: Human validation study (multi-sugar permeability test in healthy adults), Gastroenterology 2021
cards.people: Sixty healthy adults aged 18–70 in three randomised studies on standardised diets (16.25 g fibre in two studies, 32.5 g in one), ingesting 12C- and 13C-mannitol, rhamnose, sucralose and lactulose with urine collected 0–2, 2–8 and 8–24 h and sugars measured by HPLC–tandem mass spectrometry; 18 IBS-D patients provided pilot comparison data.
cards.result: Median 24-h excretions (percentage of administered dose) were approximately 30% for 13C-mannitol, 15% for rhamnose, 0.32% for lactulose and 2.3% for sucralose; 13C-mannitol and rhamnose reflected mainly small-intestinal permeability. Within-person excretions were consistent between repeat tests, with only minor differences between the two fibre intakes, but the median interindividual coefficient of variation was 76.5% (10–90th percentile 34.6–111.0). No significant effects of sex, age or BMI. A practical trap the record documents: baseline 12C-mannitol (from diet) was detectable in every participant, which precludes its use — 13C-mannitol is the preferred small-bowel probe.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are medians ('approximately' in the record) on this protocol's doses and diet; they are protocol-specific reference values, not universal cutoffs.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in health the small bowel passes ~30% of a mannitol dose and ~0.3% of a lactulose dose into urine; the ratio is a timing- and osmolarity-sensitive instrument, and NSAIDs measurably open the barrier
cards.summary: Synthesis: in health the small bowel passes ~30% of a mannitol dose and ~0.3% of a lactulose dose into urine; the ratio is a timing- and osmolarity-sensitive instrument, and NSAIDs measurably open the barrier
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human studies above (Bjarnason 1984; Bjarnason 1994; Sigthorsson 1998; Camilleri 2010; Khoshbin 2021), framed by the Boron & Boulpaep account of the intestinal barrier and paracellular transport as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The healthy small intestine is a selective sieve, and the sugar probes quantify the selectivity: free passage for monosaccharides (~30% of mannitol, ~15% of rhamnose recovered in 24 h) against near-exclusion of the disaccharide lactulose (~0.32%). Three discipline points the records force: (1) the ratio depends on when you collect — 0.08 early versus 0.32 late in the same healthy people — and on the drink's osmolarity; (2) between-person spread is wide (CV ~76%) even when within-person repeatability is good, so single values grade groups better than individuals; (3) the barrier is pharmacologically fragile — NSAIDs made permeability abnormal in almost every treated patient in the classic study and produced small-bowel inflammation in most long-term users within 6 months, aspirin and nabumetone excepted in that cohort. Coeliac disease raises the lactulose-based ratios, as the question requires, but marker choice matters because probes travel by different routes. Cross-point, not duplicated: the library's transcellular sugar-absorption shelf measures carrier uptake, a different quantity from this paracellular leak.
cards.watchOut: No animal permeability data are carded. 'Leaky gut' as a clinical syndrome claim goes beyond anything these measurement studies establish — this shelf is about the measurement and its healthy behaviour.

shelves.title: Selonsertib in MASH: a failed programme — STELLAR-3 and STELLAR-4 both missed their primary endpoint (fibrosis improvement 10–14% vs 13% on placebo)
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and bridging fibrosis (F3) or compensated cirrhosis (F4), does selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) versus placebo improve liver fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis?
shelves.mesh: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Liver Cirrhosis · MAP Kinase Kinase Kinase 5 · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): a failed programme, with the failure on the face. STELLAR-3 (F3, n=802) and STELLAR-4 (F4, n=877) both missed their primary endpoint — fibrosis improvement without worsening of steatohepatitis was 10–14% on selonsertib versus 13% on placebo (the treatment made no difference) — with no effect on biochemistry, non-invasive tests, progression or clinical events despite target engagement. The earlier promise rested on one open-label, placebo-free phase 2 trial of 72 patients and two analyses of the same population.

cards.headline: STELLAR-3 and STELLAR-4 (2020): both phase 3 trials missed their primary endpoint — fibrosis improvement was 10–12% on selonsertib versus 13% on placebo in F3, and 13–14% versus 13% in F4 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: STELLAR-3 and STELLAR-4 (2020): both phase 3 trials missed their primary endpoint — fibrosis improvement was 10–12% on selonsertib versus 13% on placebo in F3, and 13–14% versus 13% in F4 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trials in one publication (STELLAR-3/-4), J Hepatol 2020
cards.people: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) once daily for 48 weeks in MASH (NASH): STELLAR-3 in bridging fibrosis (F3; selonsertib 18 mg n=322, 6 mg n=321, placebo n=159) and STELLAR-4 in compensated cirrhosis (F4; 18 mg n=354, 6 mg n=351, placebo n=172), randomised 2:2:1, with biopsies at screening and week 48.
cards.result: Neither trial met the primary endpoint (at least 1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH at week 48). In STELLAR-3 the endpoint was reached by 10% (31/322) on 18 mg (P=0.49 versus placebo), 12% (39/321) on 6 mg (P=0.93) and 13% (21/159) on placebo. In STELLAR-4: 14% (51/354, P=0.56), 13% (45/351, P=0.93) and 13% (22/172). Despite dose-dependent reductions in hepatic phospho-p38 (target engagement), there was no significant effect on liver biochemistry, non-invasive fibrosis tests, progression to cirrhosis or clinical events; adverse events were similar across groups. The failure is printed on the face of this shelf, as commissioned.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication count as one publication toward this shelf's floor, per the standing convention; the floor is met by the phase 2 reports below. Response rates at or below placebo in both trials leave no dose or stage subgroup to rescue.
cards.source: Harrison SA, Wong VW, Okanoue T, et al. Selonsertib for patients with bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis due to NASH: results from randomized placebo-controlled phase III trials. Journal of Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 32147362. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03053050; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03053063. cards.headline: Phase 2 trial 2018: the open-label signal that launched the programme — fibrosis improvement in 43% (18 mg) and 30% (6 mg) versus 20% on simtuzumab alone, in 72 patients with no placebo arm
cards.summary: Phase 2 trial 2018: the open-label signal that launched the programme — fibrosis improvement in 43% (18 mg) and 30% (6 mg) versus 20% on simtuzumab alone, in 72 patients with no placebo arm
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label randomised trial (no placebo arm), Hepatology 2018
cards.people: 72 patients with NASH and stage 2–3 fibrosis randomised to 24 weeks of open-label selonsertib 6 or 18 mg daily, with or without weekly simtuzumab injections, or simtuzumab alone; because simtuzumab showed no histological effect, selonsertib groups were pooled across it (18 mg n=30, 6 mg n=27, simtuzumab alone n=10 analysed for the fibrosis endpoint), with paired biopsies, MR elastography and MRI fat fraction.
cards.result: One-or-more-stage fibrosis reduction occurred in 13 of 30 (43%, 95% CI 26–63) on selonsertib 18 mg, 8 of 27 (30%, 14–50) on 6 mg and 2 of 10 (20%, 3–56) on simtuzumab alone; improvement tracked with falls in liver stiffness, collagen content and lobular inflammation. There were no significant differences in adverse events between groups. The authors' own wording was that selonsertib 'may' reduce fibrosis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, no placebo, 72 patients and a comparator (simtuzumab alone, n=10) that was itself an inactive drug — the classic set-up for a phase 2 signal that a blinded phase 3 then refutes, which is exactly what STELLAR did.
cards.source: Loomba R, Lawitz E, Mantry PS, et al. The ASK1 inhibitor selonsertib in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a randomized, phase 2 trial. Hepatology. 2018. PMID: 28892558. cards.headline: Phase 2 imaging–histology report 2019: MR elastography predicted fibrosis improvement only weakly (AUROC 0.62) and MRI fat fraction predicted steatosis response modestly (AUROC 0.70)
cards.summary: Phase 2 imaging–histology report 2019: MR elastography predicted fibrosis improvement only weakly (AUROC 0.62) and MRI fat fraction predicted steatosis response modestly (AUROC 0.70)
cards.type: Imaging–histology correlation analysis of a phase 2 trial, J Hepatol 2019
cards.people: Patients with NASH and stage 2–3 fibrosis from the phase 2 selonsertib study with paired MR elastography, MRI proton-density fat fraction and centrally read biopsies at baseline and week 24: 54 patients in the elastography analysis and 65 in the fat-fraction analysis.
cards.result: Fibrosis improved (at least 1 stage) in 18 of 54 (33%); the AUROC of MR-elastography stiffness for predicting that improvement was 0.62 (95% CI 0.46–0.78), with 67% sensitivity and 64% specificity at the optimal threshold (any relative reduction). Steatosis improved by at least 1 grade in 18 of 65 (28%); MRI fat fraction AUROC was 0.70 (0.57–0.83), with 89% sensitivity but 47% specificity. The authors call the data preliminary support for further evaluation of the imaging tools.
cards.watchOut: A methods report about monitoring tools, drawn from the same 72-patient phase 2 population — it is not treatment evidence and is carded only as the programme's imaging limb, labelled as such.
cards.source: Jayakumar S, Middleton MS, Lawitz EJ, et al. Longitudinal correlations between MRE, MRI-PDFF, and liver histology in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. cards.headline: Phase 2 patient-reported-outcomes report 2018: no consistent quality-of-life difference between regimens; patients whose histology improved reported better outcomes
cards.summary: Phase 2 patient-reported-outcomes report 2018: no consistent quality-of-life difference between regimens; patients whose histology improved reported better outcomes
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes analysis of a phase 2 trial, Liver Int 2018
cards.people: The same 72 phase 2 patients (mean age 54, 31% male, 65% stage 3 fibrosis, 71% with diabetes) receiving selonsertib 6 or 18 mg alone or with simtuzumab, or simtuzumab alone, for 24 weeks, with SF-36, chronic-liver-disease and work-productivity questionnaires and paired biopsies.
cards.result: There were no consistent differences in treatment-emergent patient-reported-outcome changes between regimens (P>0.05 throughout). Patients who achieved at least a 2-point fall in NAFLD activity score or at least 1-stage fibrosis reduction reported significant improvements (up to +15.5% of a scale range), and those with at least a 50% relative fall in collagen improved by up to +21.5%, while those whose collagen rose by more than 17% worsened (up to −13.9%). Baseline CK-18, IL-6 and CRP correlated with baseline scores.
cards.watchOut: Responder analyses ('people who improved felt better') cannot attribute benefit to the drug — and the between-regimen comparison, the only randomised read, was null; the same phase 2 population as the two cards above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme, stated plainly — an unblinded 72-patient phase 2 signal, then two blinded phase 3 trials (1,679 patients) at or below placebo on every endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme, stated plainly — an unblinded 72-patient phase 2 signal, then two blinded phase 3 trials (1,679 patients) at or below placebo on every endpoint
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above (STELLAR-3/-4, 2020; phase 2 trial, 2018; imaging report, 2019; outcomes report, 2018).
cards.result: Selonsertib does not improve liver fibrosis in MASH: the two phase 3 trials randomised 802 (F3) and 877 (F4) patients and found primary-endpoint rates of 10–14% on drug versus 13% on placebo, with no effect on biochemistry, non-invasive tests, progression to cirrhosis or clinical events, despite demonstrated target engagement (phospho-p38 reduction). The phase 2 reports — one small open-label trial and two analyses of the same 72 patients — are carded so the record shows where the programme's promise came from and why it did not survive blinding. Fibrosis endpoints throughout are biopsy surrogates. Cross-point: the library's MASH shelf (live #323) covers the agents with positive phase 3 data; selonsertib is not among them and is not carded there.
cards.watchOut: A completeness shelf for a failed phase 3 programme: the verdict is negative, and the phase 2 cards must never be quoted without the STELLAR card beside them.

shelves.title: Emricasan in MASH cirrhosis: a failed programme — portal pressure, decompensation and fibrosis endpoints all null across four trials
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) cirrhosis — including decompensated cirrhosis and cirrhosis with severe portal hypertension — does emricasan (pan-caspase inhibitor) versus placebo reduce portal pressure, prevent decompensation, or improve fibrosis?
shelves.mesh: Liver Cirrhosis · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Caspase Inhibitors · Hypertension, Portal · Portal Pressure
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): a failed programme, with the failure on the face. Emricasan (pan-caspase inhibitor) missed every primary endpoint in four randomised trials: portal pressure did not fall in NASH cirrhosis with severe portal hypertension (ENCORE-PH, n=263), death/new decompensation was not prevented in decompensated cirrhosis (n=217; hazard ratios 1.02 and 1.28), fibrosis improvement in F1–F3 NASH was numerically below placebo (11–12% versus 19%; ENCORE-NF, n=318), and post-transplant fibrosis was unchanged (n=64). Target engagement without clinical effect, consistently.

cards.headline: ENCORE-PH 2020: emricasan did not lower portal pressure — HVPG changes were −0.21, −0.45 and −0.58 mmHg across the three doses versus placebo in 263 patients with NASH cirrhosis and severe portal hypertension (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: ENCORE-PH 2020: emricasan did not lower portal pressure — HVPG changes were −0.21, −0.45 and −0.58 mmHg across the three doses versus placebo in 263 patients with NASH cirrhosis and severe portal hypertension (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ENCORE-PH), J Hepatol 2020
cards.people: 263 patients with NASH-related cirrhosis and baseline hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) of at least 12 mmHg, randomised double-blind 1:1:1:1 to emricasan 5, 25 or 50 mg twice daily or placebo for up to 48 weeks; 201 (76%) had compensated cirrhosis. The primary endpoint was HVPG change at week 24 — a surrogate, labelled as such.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in HVPG change for any emricasan dose versus placebo (−0.21, −0.45 and −0.58 mmHg for 5, 25 and 50 mg, adjusted for baseline HVPG, compensation status and beta-blocker use). Compensated patients tended to a greater HVPG fall on emricasan (P=0.06), larger at higher baseline HVPG, with a significant baseline-HVPG-by-treatment interaction — a subgroup pattern, not the primary result. Biomarkers (aminotransferases, caspases, cytokeratins) fell by week 24 but returned to baseline by week 48. Decompensating events (~10% over a median 337 days), MELD and Child-Pugh progression and adverse events were similar across groups; the drug appeared safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: HVPG is a surrogate endpoint; even on the surrogate the trial was null, and the compensated/high-baseline-HVPG pattern is interaction-driven subgroup colour that no card here upgrades.
cards.source: Garcia-Tsao G, Bosch J, Kayali Z, et al. Randomized placebo-controlled trial of emricasan for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis-related cirrhosis with severe portal hypertension. Journal of Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 31870950. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02960204.
