cards.headline: Decompensated cirrhosis trial 2021: emricasan did not prevent death or new decompensation — hazard ratios 1.02 (5 mg) and 1.28 (25 mg) versus placebo in 217 patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Decompensated cirrhosis trial 2021: emricasan did not prevent death or new decompensation — hazard ratios 1.02 (5 mg) and 1.28 (25 mg) versus placebo in 217 patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, J Hepatol 2021
cards.people: 217 individuals with decompensated NASH cirrhosis, randomised double-blind 1:1:1 to emricasan 5 mg, emricasan 25 mg or placebo twice daily, stratified by decompensation status and baseline MELD-Na; the primary endpoint combined all-cause mortality, a new decompensation event (variceal haemorrhage, new ascites needing diuretics, hepatic encephalopathy grade 2 or more, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) or a MELD-Na rise of at least 4 points.
cards.result: Event rates did not differ between either emricasan dose and placebo: hazard ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.59–1.77, P=0.94) for 5 mg and 1.28 (0.75–2.21, P=0.37) for 25 mg — point estimates at or above 1, the 25 mg estimate numerically favouring placebo. MELD-Na progression was the commonest outcome. There was no significant effect on MELD-Na, INR, bilirubin, albumin or Child-Pugh score. Emricasan was generally safe and well tolerated; the authors' conclusion is that it was safe but ineffective.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's hardest clinical endpoint — death and decompensation, not a surrogate — and it is unambiguously null; the failure belongs on the face of the shelf and is printed here.
cards.source: Frenette C, Kayali Z, Mena E, et al. Emricasan to prevent new decompensation in patients with NASH-related decompensated cirrhosis. Journal of Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 33038432. cards.headline: ENCORE-NF 2020: in 318 patients with NASH and F1–F3 fibrosis, fibrosis improvement was lower on emricasan (11.2% and 12.3%) than on placebo (19.0%) over 72 weeks (the treatment made no difference — numerically worse)
cards.summary: ENCORE-NF 2020: in 318 patients with NASH and F1–F3 fibrosis, fibrosis improvement was lower on emricasan (11.2% and 12.3%) than on placebo (19.0%) over 72 weeks (the treatment made no difference — numerically worse)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ENCORE-NF), J Hepatol 2020
cards.people: 318 patients with definite NASH and fibrosis stage F1–F3 on a centrally read biopsy within 6 months, randomised double-blind 1:1:1 to emricasan 5 mg or 50 mg twice daily or placebo for 72 weeks; primary objective was fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH, with NASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis as the secondary objective — both biopsy surrogates.
cards.result: The primary objective was not achieved: fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH occurred in 11.2% on emricasan 5 mg and 12.3% on 50 mg versus 19.0% on placebo (odds ratios 0.530 and 0.588; P=0.972 for both as printed in the record). NASH resolution was likewise lower on drug (3.7% and 6.6% versus 10.5%). The authors state emricasan did not improve liver histology despite target engagement and may have worsened fibrosis and ballooning, possibly by diverting cells to alternative death pathways; serum ALT fell in the short term only.
cards.watchOut: Numerically worse than placebo on both histological objectives: this card is the clearest single refutation of the programme's premise in pre-cirrhotic disease, and its harm hypothesis (alternative cell-death pathways) is the authors', printed as theirs.
cards.source: Harrison SA, Goodman Z, Jabbar A, et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of emricasan in patients with NASH and F1-F3 fibrosis. Journal of Hepatology. 2020. PMID: 31887369. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02686762. cards.headline: Transplant-recipient trial 2021: in 64 hepatitis-C-cured liver transplant recipients, fibrosis stability/improvement was 77.1% on emricasan versus 74.1% on placebo over 24 months (the treatment made no difference overall)
cards.summary: Transplant-recipient trial 2021: in 64 hepatitis-C-cured liver transplant recipients, fibrosis stability/improvement was 77.1% on emricasan versus 74.1% on placebo over 24 months (the treatment made no difference overall)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Liver Transpl 2021
cards.people: 64 liver transplant recipients with residual fibrosis or cirrhosis after sustained virological response to hepatitis C therapy, randomised double-blind 2:1 to emricasan 25 mg twice daily (n=41) or placebo (n=23) for 24 months; 32 emricasan (78.0%) and 19 placebo (82.6%) participants completed the study. A different population from the MASH cards — carded as a limb, not as support for the cirrhosis claim, as commissioned.
cards.result: There was no difference in the primary endpoint (fibrosis improvement or stability by Ishak stage): 77.1% on emricasan versus 74.1% on placebo (P=NS), and no difference in fibrosis improvement alone (54.5% versus 60.7%). In the pre-specified F3–F5 subgroup, stability or improvement was higher on emricasan (95.2% versus 54.6%, P=0.01). Tolerability and safety profiles were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: 64 patients in a post-transplant, post-SVR population — it cannot rehabilitate the MASH programme, and its one positive read is a subgroup of an already small trial; both cautions are on the face of the card.
cards.source: Weinberg EM, Curry MP, Frenette CT, et al. Multicenter, double-blind, randomized trial of emricasan in hepatitis C-treated liver transplant recipients with residual fibrosis. Liver Transplantation. 2021. PMID: 33164276. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme across every population tested — portal pressure, decompensation, fibrosis histology and post-transplant fibrosis all null, one trial numerically worse than placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme across every population tested — portal pressure, decompensation, fibrosis histology and post-transplant fibrosis all null, one trial numerically worse than placebo
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded trials above (ENCORE-PH, n=263; decompensated cirrhosis trial, n=217; ENCORE-NF, n=318; transplant-recipient trial, n=64).
cards.result: Emricasan, an oral pan-caspase inhibitor, engaged its target (caspase and aminotransferase biomarkers fell transiently) and changed no outcome that matters: HVPG did not fall in severe portal hypertension, death and decompensation were not prevented in decompensated cirrhosis (hazard ratios 1.02 and 1.28), fibrosis histology in F1–F3 NASH was numerically worse than placebo, and post-transplant fibrosis was unchanged overall. The residual favourable patterns — a compensated-subgroup HVPG interaction, an F3–F5 transplant subgroup — are subgroup reads inside null trials and are graded as such. HVPG and biopsy endpoints are surrogates and are labelled so throughout. The failure is printed on the face of this shelf, as commissioned. Cross-point: the library's MASH shelf (live #323) covers agents with positive data; emricasan is not carded there.
cards.watchOut: Four randomised trials, four null primaries, ~860 patients: there is no population left in this programme where a benefit claim can honestly be made.

shelves.title: Oral vancomycin in primary sclerosing cholangitis: the 2026 placebo-controlled trial found no liver benefit — the claimed benefit is bowel, and observational only
shelves.question: In adults (and, in the earlier literature, children) with primary sclerosing cholangitis, with or without inflammatory bowel disease, does oral vancomycin versus placebo or metronidazole improve liver biochemistry and liver-related endpoints?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bilirubin · Biomarkers · Cholangitis, Sclerosing/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Vancomycin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised and observational limbs point different ways, and the randomised limb governs the liver question. The 2026 Mayo phase 3 placebo-controlled trial (82 randomised adults, 18 months) found alkaline phosphatase normalisation in 5% on placebo vs 6.7% on oral vancomycin (the treatment made no difference), with no difference in Mayo PSC risk score or liver stiffness, although the fall in alkaline phosphatase was larger on vancomycin (-21.9% vs +1.2%). The small 2013 pilot randomised trial (35 patients, 12 weeks) had found alkaline phosphatase falls of about 40-43% on vancomycin, reaching its primary endpoint — a short, small, surrogate-only signal the larger trial did not confirm on liver-related endpoints. The observational limb answers a different question: in a 90-patient retrospective PSC-IBD cohort, vancomycin was associated with bowel improvement (clinical improvement 50%, endoscopic inactivity rising from 18.8% to 60.3%) while the median alkaline phosphatase change was not significant (-48.5 U/L, P=0.57). So: no demonstrated liver benefit in the only large randomised trial; a possible bowel benefit in PSC-IBD that rests on uncontrolled data. The Italian VanC-IT trial is protocol-only and is not carded.

cards.headline: Mayo 2026 phase 3 RCT: oral vancomycin did not normalise alkaline phosphatase (6.7% vs 5% on placebo) and made no difference to Mayo risk score or liver stiffness over 18 months (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Mayo 2026 phase 3 RCT: oral vancomycin did not normalise alkaline phosphatase (6.7% vs 5% on placebo) and made no difference to Mayo risk score or liver stiffness over 18 months (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 82 adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis and serum alkaline phosphatase above 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, randomised to placebo or oral vancomycin 125-375 mg four times daily (dose by biochemical response) for 18 months; 73 had at least one outcome assessment.
cards.result: Alkaline phosphatase normalisation was 5% on placebo vs 6.7% on vancomycin (P=1.00). The percentage fall in alkaline phosphatase was larger on vancomycin (-21.9% vs +1.2%, P=0.03), but there were no differences in change in Mayo PSC risk score (-0.1 vs -0.1) or liver stiffness (+0.1 kPa placebo vs -4.0 kPa vancomycin, P=0.15). Teeth and tongue discoloration was the commonest side effect (17.5%). The authors concluded vancomycin was not associated with clinically significant reductions in markers of PSC disease severity.
cards.watchOut: Nine of 82 randomised patients had no outcome assessment, and early withdrawers rated their baseline health worse — attrition could bias either way; alkaline phosphatase is a surrogate, and even its larger percentage fall did not translate into risk-score or stiffness benefit.
cards.source: Mayo Clinic investigators. cards.headline: Tabibian 2013 pilot RCT: vancomycin lowered alkaline phosphatase by 40-43% at 12 weeks and reached the primary endpoint, where metronidazole did not
cards.summary: Tabibian 2013 pilot RCT: vancomycin lowered alkaline phosphatase by 40-43% at 12 weeks and reached the primary endpoint, where metronidazole did not
cards.type: Pilot double-blind randomised trial (four dose arms, no placebo arm)
cards.people: 35 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis randomised double-blind to vancomycin 125 mg or 250 mg four times daily, or metronidazole 250 mg or 500 mg three times daily, for 12 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (decrease in alkaline phosphatase at 12 weeks) was reached in the low-dose (-43%, P=0.03) and high-dose (-40%, P=0.02) vancomycin groups, with alkaline phosphatase normalisation in two low-dose patients. Mayo PSC risk score fell significantly in the low-dose vancomycin group (-0.55, P=0.02). Adverse events led to discontinuation in six patients, four of them on metronidazole.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-five patients split across four arms, 12 weeks, no placebo group and a biochemical surrogate only — exactly the profile that the 2026 placebo-controlled trial was designed to test, and on liver endpoints it did not confirm the pilot.

cards.headline: PSC-IBD cohort 2026: vancomycin was associated with bowel improvement (endoscopic inactivity 18.8% to 60.3%) but the alkaline phosphatase change was not significant — an observational limb, labelled as such
cards.summary: PSC-IBD cohort 2026: vancomycin was associated with bowel improvement (endoscopic inactivity 18.8% to 60.3%) but the alkaline phosphatase change was not significant — an observational limb, labelled as such
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre cohort (observational — no concurrent control)
cards.people: 90 adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease (80% ulcerative colitis; median age at PSC diagnosis 17.4 years) treated with oral vancomycin at one centre, 1992-2024, studied retrospectively; low dose was 500 mg/day or less, high dose above 500 mg/day.
cards.result: Clinical improvement in intestinal inflammation occurred in 50% and remission in 12.2%. Endoscopic inactivity rose from 18.8% to 60.3% and histologic inactivity or mild disease from 57.7% to 86.2%; median faecal calprotectin fell from 485 to 67.7 micrograms/g. The median change in serum alkaline phosphatase was -48.5 U/L and was not significant (P=0.57). Improvements were seen in both dose groups.
cards.watchOut: No control group, three decades of changing background care, and treatment given to selected patients: the bowel signal is hypothesis-grade, and this cohort's own liver-biochemistry result was null, so it does not soften the randomised trial's liver verdict.
cards.source: Oral Vancomycin Is an Effective Therapy in Adult Patients With Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis. Gastro Hep Advances. 2026. PMID: 42006187. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — no liver benefit in the large randomised trial; the bowel-benefit claim in PSC-IBD rests on uncontrolled cohort data only
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — no liver benefit in the large randomised trial; the bowel-benefit claim in PSC-IBD rests on uncontrolled cohort data only
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one phase 3 placebo-controlled trial (82 randomised), one pilot randomised trial (35 patients) and one retrospective cohort (90 patients).
cards.result: For liver endpoints the best evidence is negative: normalisation 6.7% vs 5% (the treatment made no difference), with no risk-score or stiffness benefit. The pilot's 12-week alkaline phosphatase falls were real but surrogate and unconfirmed at scale. For the bowel in PSC-IBD, cohort data suggest benefit, graded observational. A clinician asked 'does vancomycin help the liver in PSC?' should answer: not on current randomised evidence; asked about colitis symptoms in PSC-IBD, the honest answer is 'possibly, unproven'.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the cohort limb outvote the randomised limb; paediatric vancomycin reports in PSC are small and are not carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 42489629, 23384404, 42006187). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Fenofibrate add-on in primary biliary cholangitis with incomplete UDCA response: liver tests improve in randomised and cohort data — clinical outcomes unproven
shelves.question: In adults with primary biliary cholangitis and an incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid, does adding fenofibrate versus continued UDCA alone improve alkaline phosphatase and biochemical response?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Fenofibrate/therapeutic use · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary/drug therapy · Cholagogues and Choleretics/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ursodeoxycholic Acid/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Adult · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase/metabolism · Bilirubin/metabolism · Cholagogues and Choleretics/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Female · Fenofibrate/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Retrospective Studies · Ursodeoxycholic Acid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Alkaline Phosphatase
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — concordant biochemical benefit across two randomised trials and comparative cohorts, but the evidence is surrogate-led and the hard-outcome signal is observational. Premise resolved on the face: the slate's PICO asks about UDCA incomplete responders, and that population does have its own randomised trial (48 patients: complete normalisation of alkaline phosphatase, gamma-GT and bilirubin in 20.8% on fenofibrate add-on vs 0% on UDCA alone; normal alkaline phosphatase 54.2% vs 4.2%) — the 2023 trial the miner verified (117 patients, biochemical response 81.4% vs 64.3% by the Barcelona criterion) was in treatment-naive patients and is carded as that separate, earlier-treatment slice, not as evidence about incomplete responders. Cohorts in incomplete responders, including a cirrhotic cohort (alkaline phosphatase normalisation 37% vs 11%), point the same way, and one propensity-adjusted cohort associated fenofibrate with better transplant-free survival — observational and labelled as such. Harms: early creatinine and transaminase rises that settled in the trial; about 22% discontinued for adverse events in one cohort, and bilirubin rose faster in cirrhotic patients in that cohort, so cirrhosis needs monitoring. Bezafibrate evidence (a different fibrate, with its own home in the PPAR family) is not imported here. Stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY: no randomised trial is powered on clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: Randomised trial in UDCA incomplete responders (2022): adding fenofibrate normalised alkaline phosphatase in 54.2% vs 4.2% on UDCA alone at 12 months
cards.summary: Randomised trial in UDCA incomplete responders (2022): adding fenofibrate normalised alkaline phosphatase in 54.2% vs 4.2% on UDCA alone at 12 months
cards.people: 48 patients with primary biliary cholangitis and incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid, randomised to UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day plus fenofibrate 200 mg/day (24 patients) or continued UDCA alone (24 patients), followed at least 12 months.
cards.result: All three of alkaline phosphatase, gamma-GT and total bilirubin normalised in 20.8% of the fenofibrate group vs 0% of controls (difference 20.8 percentage points, 95% CI 4.6 to 37.0). Normal alkaline phosphatase alone: 54.2% vs 4.2% (difference 50 percentage points, 95% CI 28.5 to 71.5). Alkaline phosphatase and IgG improved more with fenofibrate (P<0.001 and P=0.026).
cards.watchOut: Small (48 patients), single-centre and biochemical endpoints only — it establishes the add-on's effect on liver tests in exactly the PICO population, not an effect on transplant or death.

cards.headline: Treatment-naive RCT 2023: fenofibrate plus UDCA from the start gave a higher biochemical response than UDCA alone (81.4% vs 64.3%, Barcelona criterion) — a different, earlier-treatment slice
cards.summary: Treatment-naive RCT 2023: fenofibrate plus UDCA from the start gave a higher biochemical response than UDCA alone (81.4% vs 64.3%, Barcelona criterion) — a different, earlier-treatment slice
cards.type: Randomised, parallel, open-label trial in treatment-naive patients
cards.people: 117 treatment-naive patients with primary biliary cholangitis at one hospital, randomised open-label for 12 months to standard-dose UDCA alone or UDCA plus fenofibrate 200 mg daily.
cards.result: Biochemical response by the Barcelona criterion at 12 months was 81.4% (95% CI 69.9 to 92.9) with the combination vs 64.3% (51.9 to 76.8) with UDCA alone (P=0.048). There was no difference in non-invasive fibrosis measures or in biochemical markers other than alkaline phosphatase. Creatinine and transaminases rose in the first month in the combination group, then returned to normal and stayed stable, including in patients with cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: This trial does NOT enrol the incomplete-responder population of the shelf question — it is carded to keep the two slices distinct, and its borderline P value (0.048) and open-label design counsel against upgrading the stamp on its account.

cards.headline: Comparative cohort in incomplete responders (2016, observational): fenofibrate was associated with biochemical response in 41% vs 7% and with better transplant-free survival — labelled observational
cards.summary: Comparative cohort in incomplete responders (2016, observational): fenofibrate was associated with biochemical response in 41% vs 7% and with better transplant-free survival — labelled observational
cards.type: Retrospective comparative cohort with propensity adjustment (observational)
cards.people: 120 patients with primary biliary cholangitis and incomplete response to UDCA at a tertiary centre: 46 treated with fenofibrate plus UDCA (median 11 months) and 74 with UDCA alone, compared retrospectively with propensity-score adjustment.
cards.result: Toronto-criterion biochemical response (alkaline phosphatase at or below 1.67 times the upper limit of normal) occurred in 41% vs 7% (P=0.0001). Fenofibrate was associated with improved decompensation-free and transplant-free survival (hazard ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.32 in the unadjusted comparison; fenofibrate use remained independently associated on multivariable analysis, HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.93). Twenty-two percent discontinued fenofibrate for adverse events (mainly abdominal pain and myalgias); in cirrhotic patients bilirubin rose more rapidly in the fenofibrate group (P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and propensity-adjusted only: the survival association is hypothesis-grade, the unadjusted hazard ratio of 0.09 is implausibly large for a fibrate, and the cirrhosis bilirubin signal cuts the other way.
cards.source: Combined ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and fenofibrate in primary biliary cholangitis patients with incomplete UDCA response may improve outcomes. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2016. cards.headline: Cirrhotic PBC cohort (2022, observational): fenofibrate add-on normalised alkaline phosphatase in 37% vs 11% with UDCA alone, without a hepatic-deterioration excess
cards.summary: Cirrhotic PBC cohort (2022, observational): fenofibrate add-on normalised alkaline phosphatase in 37% vs 11% with UDCA alone, without a hepatic-deterioration excess
cards.type: Retrospective comparative cohort in cirrhotic PBC (observational)
cards.people: 59 patients with PBC-related cirrhosis and incomplete response to UDCA: 32 received UDCA plus fenofibrate and 27 continued UDCA alone, compared retrospectively.
cards.result: Alkaline phosphatase normalisation was 37% with fenofibrate vs 11% without (P=0.020); add-on fenofibrate was independently associated with normalisation (hazard ratio 7.68, 95% CI 2.06 to 28.63). Hepatic deterioration occurred in 40% vs 48% (P=0.562) and liver-related death or transplantation in 11% vs 37% (P=0.111). After 12 months of add-on therapy, median alkaline phosphatase had fallen by a relative 35% and the UK-PBC risk score by a relative 52%. No significant adverse effects were attributed in this cohort.
cards.watchOut: Small, retrospective and non-randomised; the death/transplant difference was not significant, and the other cohort on this shelf saw faster bilirubin rise in cirrhotic fenofibrate patients — cirrhosis is a monitor-closely subgroup, not a settled one.
cards.source: Efficacy and safety of fenofibrate addition therapy in patients with cirrhotic primary biliary cholangitis with incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid. Hepatol Commun. 2022. cards.headline: Synthesis: fenofibrate add-on improves liver biochemistry in UDCA incomplete responders — POSSIBLE, surrogate-led, with the survival claim observational only
cards.summary: Synthesis: fenofibrate add-on improves liver biochemistry in UDCA incomplete responders — POSSIBLE, surrogate-led, with the survival claim observational only
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two randomised trials (48 incomplete responders; 117 treatment-naive) and two comparative cohorts (120 incomplete responders; 59 with cirrhosis).
cards.result: Every limb agrees on biochemistry: normal alkaline phosphatase in roughly half of incomplete responders on add-on fenofibrate vs under 5% on UDCA alone in the randomised comparison. No randomised evidence addresses transplant or death; the survival association comes from one retrospective cohort. That pattern — concordant surrogates, observational outcomes — is a POSSIBLE. The FLOOR-FLAG stop-condition was checked and passed: the 2023 randomised trial plus two comparative cohorts with at least 10 patients per arm were each verified from their own PubMed records this session, and a further randomised trial in the exact incomplete-responder population was found and carded first.

shelves.title: Liver abscess: catheter drainage beats needle aspiration on success and speed of recovery, with no added complications — aspiration remains the fallback for small, liquefied abscesses
shelves.question: In adults with liver abscess (pyogenic or amoebic) large enough to drain, does percutaneous catheter drainage versus percutaneous needle aspiration achieve higher success rates with fewer repeat interventions?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aftercare · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Catheters/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data · Drainage/methods · Female · Humans · India/epidemiology · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Liver Abscess/drug therapy,microbiology,pathology,surgery · Male · Needles/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data · Paracentesis/methods,trends · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography, Interventional/instrumentation · Catheters · Drainage · India · Liver Abscess/diagnostic imaging,therapy · Drainage/methods,adverse effects,instrumentation · Liver Abscess/therapy,diagnosis · Catheterization/adverse effects,methods,instrumentation · Risk Factors · Odds Ratio · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY — percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD) beats percutaneous needle aspiration (PNA) on treatment success across multiple independent randomised trials and three successive meta-analyses, with no complication penalty. The largest single randomised comparison on this shelf (543 patients) and two smaller ones (190 and 60 patients) all found faster clinical improvement and faster halving of the cavity with a catheter; pooled across 15 randomised trials (1,626 patients) the success-rate risk ratio was 1.21 favouring PCD with less recurrence at 6 months (relative risk 0.41), and the 2026 synthesis of 12 trials (1,425 patients) found higher success (odds ratio 4.12) with complication rates the same (odds ratio 1.02, the treatment made no difference to complications). Stratification the shelf must keep: the catheter advantage is clearest in larger, partially liquefied or thick-pus abscesses; aspiration remains a reasonable, simpler option for smaller, fully liquefied abscesses and where catheter care is unavailable, accepting more repeat procedures. Amoebic and pyogenic abscesses are pooled in most trials — a limitation printed on the cards. The trials are small, single-centre and mostly South Asian, which is why the stamp rests on concordance across trials and syntheses rather than on any one study.

cards.headline: Randomised trial 2019 (190 patients): catheter drainage improved patients faster (4.2 vs 7.0 days) and halved the cavity faster (4.4 vs 7.1 days) than needle aspiration
cards.summary: Randomised trial 2019 (190 patients): catheter drainage improved patients faster (4.2 vs 7.0 days) and halved the cavity faster (4.4 vs 7.1 days) than needle aspiration
cards.people: 190 patients with liver abscess at one Indian hospital (2015-2017), randomised to ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration (95 patients) or pigtail catheter drainage (95 patients), both with systemic antibiotics.
cards.result: Mean time to clinical improvement was 4.22 ± 1.25 days with catheter drainage vs 6.96 ± 1.33 days with aspiration; time to 50% reduction in cavity size 4.43 ± 1.27 vs 7.05 ± 1.25 days; hospital stay 11.44 ± 4.15 vs 12.9 ± 4.02 days. The authors concluded catheter drainage is the better modality, especially in larger, partially liquefied abscesses.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre; the abstract does not report the headline success rate or abscess-size strata, so the size claim rests on the authors' conclusion and the wider pooled record.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2023 (15 RCTs, 1,626 patients): catheter drainage raised success (relative risk 1.21) and cut 6-month recurrence (relative risk 0.41), with no difference in adverse events
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2023 (15 RCTs, 1,626 patients): catheter drainage raised success (relative risk 1.21) and cut 6-month recurrence (relative risk 0.41), with no difference in adverse events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing percutaneous catheter drainage with needle aspiration for liver abscess, searched to July 2022; 15 trials, 1,626 patients.
cards.result: Pooled success favoured catheter drainage (risk ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.31) — a relative measure; recurrence at 6 months was lower (risk ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.79, relative). Catheter drainage was faster to clinical improvement (mean difference -1.78 days), to 50% cavity reduction (-2.83 days) and needed fewer antibiotic days (-2.13 days). Adverse events did not differ (risk ratio 2.2, 95% CI 0.51 to 9.54) and hospital stay did not differ significantly. Continuous outcomes were heterogeneous.
cards.watchOut: Pools small single-centre trials with heterogeneous continuous outcomes; the adverse-event confidence interval is wide (0.51 to 9.54), so 'no difference shown' is not 'no difference exists'.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2026 (12 RCTs, 1,425 patients): catheter drainage had higher treatment success (odds ratio 4.12) with complication rates the same as aspiration, consistent across size and aetiology subgroups
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2026 (12 RCTs, 1,425 patients): catheter drainage had higher treatment success (odds ratio 4.12) with complication rates the same as aspiration, consistent across size and aetiology subgroups
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (most recent synthesis)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials directly comparing catheter drainage with needle aspiration in adults with liver abscess; 12 trials, 1,425 patients, random-effects pooling.
cards.result: Treatment success was higher with catheter drainage (odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.01 to 8.45; P<0.001; I-squared 56%) — an odds ratio, which overstates the relative benefit when success is common; the 2023 synthesis's risk ratio of 1.21 is the more conservative relative measure. Overall complications did not differ (odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.30 to 3.50). Subgroup analyses by abscess size and aetiology were consistent with the main result.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios flatter the winner for common outcomes; read the benefit through the risk-ratio synthesis. Trials rarely separated amoebic from pyogenic abscesses, so aetiology-specific claims stay modest.

shelves.title: Glepaglutide in short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure: twice-weekly dosing cut parenteral-support volume by 5.13 versus 2.85 L/week on placebo in the phase 3 trial; once-weekly dosing did not beat placebo
shelves.question: In adults with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure dependent on parenteral support, does glepaglutide (long-acting GLP-2 analogue, twice-weekly or once-weekly) versus placebo reduce parenteral-support volume over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Short Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy/therapy/physiopathology/diagnosis · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Glucagon-Like Peptide 2/adverse effects/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Parenteral Nutrition · Drug Administration Schedule · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme from a single sponsor (Zealand Pharma, named here for clarification because glepaglutide is its specific long-acting GLP-2 analogue product), and the shelf says so. The established GLP-2 home in this library is teduglutide, a different drug with daily dosing, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. In the phase 3 EASE-1 trial (106 patients with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure on parenteral support at least 3 days a week), glepaglutide 10 mg twice weekly reduced weekly parenteral-support volume by 5.13 L/week versus 2.85 L/week on placebo at 24 weeks (P=.0039); clinical response (at least 20% reduction) was 65.7% versus 38.9%, at least one day per week off parenteral support was gained by 51.4% versus 19.4%, and 5 patients (14%) on twice-weekly dosing weaned off parenteral support completely versus none on placebo. Once-weekly dosing did NOT differ significantly from placebo on the primary or key secondary endpoints — the dose schedule is part of the answer. The supporting reports are thinner than the report count suggests: the phase 2 trial (18 patients) and its morphology companion come from one small single-centre Copenhagen cohort family, and the phase 3b absorption study enrolled exactly 10 patients (N=10, printed on its card). Parenteral-support volume is a clinical-use endpoint, not a mortality endpoint: no survival or intestinal-transplant claim is made anywhere in this evidence.

cards.headline: EASE-1 phase 3 (Jeppesen 2025): parenteral-support volume fell 5.13 L/week on twice-weekly glepaglutide versus 2.85 on placebo (P=.0039); 14% weaned off support completely versus 0%; once-weekly dosing was not significant
cards.summary: EASE-1 phase 3 (Jeppesen 2025): parenteral-support volume fell 5.13 L/week on twice-weekly glepaglutide versus 2.85 on placebo (P=.0039); 14% weaned off support completely versus 0%; once-weekly dosing was not significant
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, international trial (EASE-1)
cards.people: 106 patients with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure requiring parenteral support at least 3 days per week were randomised 1:1:1 to 24 weeks of glepaglutide 10 mg twice weekly, glepaglutide 10 mg once weekly, or placebo. Parenteral-support volume counted as reduced only if 48-hour urine volume exceeded baseline by more than 10%.
cards.result: Twice-weekly glepaglutide significantly reduced weekly parenteral-support volume from baseline to week 24 versus placebo (mean change -5.13 versus -2.85 L/week; P=.0039, the primary endpoint), with similar results across major anatomic subgroups. Key secondary endpoints also favoured twice-weekly dosing: clinical response (at least 20% volume reduction at weeks 20 and 24) in 65.7% versus 38.9% (P=.0243); a reduction of at least 1 day per week on parenteral support in 51.4% versus 19.4% (P=.0043); and complete weaning ('enteral autonomy') in 5 patients (14%) versus 0 on placebo. Patient Global Impression of Change also favoured glepaglutide. No statistically significant differences were found for once-weekly glepaglutide versus placebo on the primary or key secondary endpoints. Glepaglutide was assessed as safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group also reduced its volume by 2.85 L/week, so the drug-attributable gain is the 2.28 L/week difference, not the full 5.13. The positive result belongs to the twice-weekly schedule only, and 24 weeks in 106 patients cannot speak to durability, survival or transplant avoidance.

cards.headline: Phase 2 crossover trial (Naimi 2019): faecal output fell 592 g/day on 1 mg and 833 g/day on 10 mg daily glepaglutide; no change on 0.1 mg — a dose response in 18 patients
cards.summary: Phase 2 crossover trial (Naimi 2019): faecal output fell 592 g/day on 1 mg and 833 g/day on 10 mg daily glepaglutide; no change on 0.1 mg — a dose response in 18 patients
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, crossover, single-centre trial
cards.people: 18 adults with short bowel syndrome and faecal wet weight output of at least 1500 g/day (of 22 screened) were randomised to one of six dose sequences, receiving daily subcutaneous glepaglutide at two of the doses 10 mg, 1 mg and 0.1 mg for 3 weeks each, separated by a 4–8 week washout; 16 completed. Primary endpoint: absolute change in faecal wet weight output by metabolic balance study. Funded by Zealand Pharma.
cards.result: Adjusted mean faecal output changed by -592 g/day (95% CI -913 to -272; P=0.002) on 1 mg and -833 g/day (95% CI -1152 to -515; P=0.0002) on 10 mg versus baseline; no change was seen with 0.1 mg. Common treatment-related adverse events were stoma complications (13 patients, 72%), injection site reactions (11, 61%), peripheral oedema (10, 56%), nausea and abdominal pain (8 each, 44%); related serious events (abdominal pain, stoma obstruction, catheter-related sepsis, infection of unknown origin) occurred in two patients in the 0.1 mg and two in the 10 mg periods. No patient died.
cards.watchOut: Eighteen patients, 3-week periods, and a faecal-output endpoint measured against baseline rather than a parallel placebo — this is dose-finding physiology, and its cohort is the same small Copenhagen population that the morphology card below re-reports.

cards.headline: Phase 3b absorption study (Pinar 2025): N=10 exactly — wet-weight absorption rose 398 g/day (P=0.0585) and energy absorption 1038 kJ/day (P=0.0215) at 24 weeks; parenteral volume fell 800 mL/day by week 52
cards.summary: Phase 3b absorption study (Pinar 2025): N=10 exactly — wet-weight absorption rose 398 g/day (P=0.0585) and energy absorption 1038 kJ/day (P=0.0215) at 24 weeks; parenteral volume fell 800 mL/day by week 52
cards.type: Phase 3b, single-centre, open-label study — N=10, at the evidence floor exactly; printed on the face as required
cards.people: 10 patients with short bowel syndrome — 8 with intestinal failure and 2 with intestinal insufficiency — received glepaglutide 10 mg once weekly subcutaneously. Intestinal absorption was measured by metabolic balance studies; the primary endpoint was absolute change in intestinal wet weight absorption at 24 weeks, with parenteral-support use and body composition followed to 52 weeks.
cards.result: At week 24, mean intestinal wet weight absorption rose numerically by 398 g/day (P=0.0585, not significant) and mean energy absorption by 1038 kJ/day (P=0.0215); electrolyte and macronutrient absorption also improved. At week 52, mean parenteral-support volume was reduced by 800 mL/day (P=0.0106) and its energy content by 866 kJ/day (P=0.0103). Body composition and weight remained stable, and the safety profile was manageable.
cards.watchOut: N=10, open-label, no comparator, and the once-weekly schedule that did not beat placebo in the phase 3 trial — this card is mechanistic support for absorption, nothing more. Its wet-weight primary endpoint missed significance (P=0.0585).
cards.source: Pinar I et al. Outcomes of glepaglutide on intestinal absorption and parenteral support in patients with short bowel syndrome. Clin Nutr ESPEN. 2025. PMID: 40774623. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04991311 and EudraCT 2020-005194-27, named in the record's abstract (no databank entry). cards.headline: Phase 2 morphology report (Naimi 2023): plasma citrulline rose 15.3–15.6 micromol/L on 1 mg and 10 mg in the same 18-patient cohort; villus and crypt trends rose, perfusion did not change
cards.summary: Phase 2 morphology report (Naimi 2023): plasma citrulline rose 15.3–15.6 micromol/L on 1 mg and 10 mg in the same 18-patient cohort; villus and crypt trends rose, perfusion did not change
cards.type: Secondary/exploratory morphology and perfusion report of the phase 2 crossover trial — same 18 patients as the phase 2 card, not an independent population
cards.people: The same 18 patients with short bowel syndrome from the randomised crossover dose-finding phase 2 trial, assessed before and after 3 weeks of glepaglutide with plasma citrulline, mucosal biopsies (morphology and gene expression) and stoma perfusion imaging (laser speckle contrast and indocyanine green fluorescence angiography).
cards.result: Glepaglutide significantly increased plasma citrulline by 15.3 micromol/L (P=0.001) in the 1 mg group and 15.6 micromol/L (P=0.001) in the 10 mg group, with trends toward increased villus height, crypt depth and epithelium height in the same groups. No significant changes were seen in absorption/proliferation/tight-junction gene expression or in intestinal perfusion.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker (citrulline) and biopsy trends from the identical small cohort as the phase 2 card — it deepens the mechanism story but adds no independent patients, and the perfusion hypothesis it tested came back null at 3 weeks.
cards.source: Naimi RM et al. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 2023. PMID: 35511704. Registry ID: none in the record (parent phase 2 trial as on the phase 2 card). cards.headline: Synthesis: twice-weekly glepaglutide reduces parenteral support in one positive phase 3 trial, on a thin supporting base — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: twice-weekly glepaglutide reduces parenteral support in one positive phase 3 trial, on a thin supporting base — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: the EASE-1 phase 3 trial (106 patients), one phase 2 crossover cohort (18 patients, reported twice) and one open-label phase 3b study (10 patients) — a single sponsor programme whose independent populations number three, two of them very small.
cards.result: Twice-weekly glepaglutide beat placebo on parenteral-support volume (-5.13 versus -2.85 L/week), response rate (65.7% versus 38.9%), days off support and complete weaning (14% versus 0%); once-weekly dosing did not. Phase 2 data show a dose-ordered fall in faecal output and a citrulline rise consistent with mucosal growth.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE, not higher: one programme, one positive phase 3 trial at one dose schedule, and no mortality, transplant or long-term durability data. Regulatory status should be re-checked before any clinical use is contemplated; the teduglutide shelf is the separate home for the established GLP-2 comparison.

shelves.title: Aramchol in MASH (NASH): the one placebo-controlled MASH trial (ARREST, 247 patients) missed its primary liver-fat endpoint (P=0.066); the supporting reports are a small NAFLD trial and an uncontrolled open-label biopsy cohort of 51 patients
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and fibrosis, does aramchol (fatty-acid–bile-acid conjugate, SCD1 modulator) versus placebo reduce liver fat and improve fibrosis?
shelves.mesh: Alanine Transaminase · Biopsy · Cholic Acids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver/drug effects/metabolism/pathology · Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/drug therapy/genetics/pathology · Stearoyl-CoA Desaturase/genetics · Triglycerides/metabolism
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — read the structure before the signals. The floor for this shelf is met by REPORT count, not by three independent controlled populations, and the face says so: (1) a 60-patient phase 2 trial in fatty liver disease (only 6 of its 60 patients had steatohepatitis) showed a dose-dependent fall in liver fat at the 300 mg dose; (2) ARREST, the one placebo-controlled trial in MASH (247 patients), MISSED its primary endpoint — the placebo-corrected fall in liver triglycerides on 600 mg was -3.1 (95% CI -6.4 to 0.2; P=0.066), which precluded further formal statistical testing, leaving the histology numbers (steatohepatitis resolution 16.7% versus 5%; fibrosis improvement 29.5% versus 17.5%, both with wide confidence intervals crossing no-effect) as unconfirmed signals; (3) the third report is NOT a controlled trial at all: it is an open-label, single-arm cohort of 51 patients from the ARMOR study given aramchol 300 mg twice daily, whose paired biopsies improved by 31% on conventional staging and more often on a continuous digital-pathology score — with no placebo group, some or all of that improvement may be natural history, regression to the mean, or biopsy sampling. The phase 3 ARMOR randomised trial has no published report; no phase 3 evidence exists and none is implied. Liver fat and biopsy fibrosis are surrogate endpoints throughout. Aramchol (the tested product was made by Trima Israel Pharmaceutical Products Ltd, named in the phase 2 record — named here for clarification) remains investigational.

cards.headline: Phase 2 NAFLD trial (Safadi 2014): liver fat fell 12.57% on aramchol 300 mg over 3 months while rising 6.39% on placebo (P=.02); the 100 mg change was not significant — a dose response in 60 patients, only 6 with steatohepatitis
cards.summary: Phase 2 NAFLD trial (Safadi 2014): liver fat fell 12.57% on aramchol 300 mg over 3 months while rising 6.39% on placebo (P=.02); the 100 mg change was not significant — a dose response in 60 patients, only 6 with steatohepatitis
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (10 centres, Israel)
cards.people: 60 patients with biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (6 with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis) randomised to aramchol 100 mg, aramchol 300 mg or placebo once daily for 3 months (n=20 per group); 58 completed. Main endpoint: between-group difference in change in liver fat content by magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The tested product was Aramchol from Trima Israel Pharmaceutical Products Ltd, as named in the record.
cards.result: Over 3 months, liver fat content decreased by 12.57% (SD 22.14) on 300 mg/day aramchol and increased by 6.39% (SD 36.27) on placebo (P=.02 for the adjusted between-group difference). The 100 mg group decreased by 2.89% (SD 28.22), not significant (P=.35), giving a dose-response trend (P for trend=.01). Changes in endothelial function, alanine aminotransferase and adiponectin were nonsignificant, and insulin-resistance scores did not change. No serious or drug-related adverse events were observed in the 58 completers.
cards.watchOut: A fatty-liver population, not a MASH-with-fibrosis population — only 6 of 60 patients had steatohepatitis, none of the endpoints is histology, and 3 months of a fat-content surrogate in 60 patients is the weakest limb of this shelf.
cards.source: Safadi R et al. The fatty acid-bile acid conjugate Aramchol reduces liver fat content in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2014. PMID: 24815326. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01094158, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ARREST phase 2b (Ratziu 2021): primary endpoint missed — placebo-corrected liver triglyceride change -3.1 (95% CI -6.4 to 0.2; P=0.066) on 600 mg; histology signals (resolution 16.7% versus 5%; fibrosis improvement 29.5% versus 17.5%) left formally untestable
cards.summary: ARREST phase 2b (Ratziu 2021): primary endpoint missed — placebo-corrected liver triglyceride change -3.1 (95% CI -6.4 to 0.2; P=0.066) on 600 mg; histology signals (resolution 16.7% versus 5%; fibrosis improvement 29.5% versus 17.5%) left formally untestable
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ARREST) — the programme's only placebo-controlled MASH trial
cards.people: 247 patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis randomised to aramchol 400 mg (n=101), aramchol 600 mg (n=98) or placebo (n=48) for 52 weeks. Primary endpoint: decrease in hepatic triglycerides by magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 52 weeks on 600 mg. Key secondary endpoints: liver histology and alanine aminotransferase. Histology denominators are the patients with paired biopsies (78 on 600 mg, 40 on placebo).
cards.result: Aramchol 600 mg produced a placebo-corrected decrease in liver triglycerides that did not meet prespecified significance (-3.1, 95% CI -6.4 to 0.2; P=0.066), precluding further formal statistical analysis. Steatohepatitis resolution without worsening fibrosis occurred in 16.7% (13 of 78) on 600 mg versus 5% (2 of 40) on placebo (odds ratio 4.74, 95% CI 0.99 to 22.7 — a relative measure whose interval includes no effect) and fibrosis improvement by at least 1 stage without worsening steatohepatitis in 29.5% versus 17.5% (odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 0.7 to 5.0). The placebo-corrected alanine aminotransferase change on 600 mg was -29.1 IU/L (95% CI -41.6 to -16.5). Early termination for adverse events was under 5%, with no imbalance in serious or severe events.
cards.watchOut: Because the primary endpoint missed, the histology percentages — the numbers most likely to be quoted for this drug — were never formally tested and rest on 78 versus 40 biopsied patients; the resolution odds ratio's confidence interval starts at 0.99. Treat them as hypothesis-generating, exactly as the trial's own analysis plan requires.
cards.source: Ratziu V et al. Aramchol in patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial. Nat Med. 2021. PMID: 34621052. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02279524, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ARMOR open-label biopsy cohort (Ratziu 2025): 51 patients, no placebo group — fibrosis improved in 31% by conventional staging and 74.5% by any digital-pathology score reduction on aramchol 300 mg twice daily
cards.summary: ARMOR open-label biopsy cohort (Ratziu 2025): 51 patients, no placebo group — fibrosis improved in 31% by conventional staging and 74.5% by any digital-pathology score reduction on aramchol 300 mg twice daily
cards.type: Open-label, single-arm cohort report (open-label part of the ARMOR study) with paired biopsies — uncontrolled; NOT a re-read of ARREST material and NOT a randomised trial
cards.people: 51 patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis enrolled in the open-label part of the ARMOR study received aramchol 300 mg twice daily and had paired pre- and post-treatment liver biopsies, scored by consensus of 3 hepatopathologists and separately by a digital image analysis platform (PharmaNest) generating a continuous Fibrosis Composite Severity score. Every patient received the drug; there is no comparator group.
cards.result: Fibrosis improved in 31% of patients by conventional NASH-CRN staging (at least 1 stage reduction), 51% by ranked pair assessment, 74.5% by any digital-score reduction (at least 0.3 absolute) and 41% by a substantial digital-score reduction (at least 25% relative — a relative threshold, as reported). Improvement increased with treatment duration (conventional staging: 25% under 48 weeks versus 39% at 48 weeks or more). Most patients scored 'stable' conventionally still showed a digital-score reduction. Liver stiffness, Pro-C3 and enhanced liver fibrosis scores also fell, and digital-score changes correlated positively with liver stiffness changes.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled: without a placebo arm, biopsy improvement rates cannot be attributed to the drug — MASH biopsies improve spontaneously and sampling variation alone moves stage in a sizeable minority. The digital score is more sensitive by construction (it counts any 0.3-point fall as improvement), so the 74.5% figure and the 31% conventional figure describe the same biopsies with different rulers. This report's 51-patient population is at the floor in size but contributes no controlled evidence.
cards.source: Ratziu V et al. Aramchol improves hepatic fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: Results of multimodality assessment using both conventional and digital pathology. Hepatology. 2025. PMID: 38916482. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04104321 and EudraCT 2019-002073-56, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: signals without a confirmed controlled win — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: signals without a confirmed controlled win — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: a 60-patient NAFLD phase 2 trial, the 247-patient placebo-controlled ARREST trial in MASH, and a 51-patient open-label ARMOR cohort — three reports, but only one controlled trial in the asked population, and it missed its primary endpoint.
cards.result: Liver fat fell dose-dependently in phase 2 and nearly significantly in ARREST (-3.1, P=0.066); ARREST histology and the uncontrolled ARMOR biopsies lean favourable. No report shows a formally confirmed benefit on any prespecified primary endpoint in MASH, and no phase 3 report exists.
cards.watchOut: The floor here is a report-count floor. Anyone citing the ARMOR percentages or the ARREST histology without their structures — open-label/single-arm, and secondary-after-a-missed-primary — is overstating this evidence. Biopsy and liver-fat endpoints are surrogates throughout.

shelves.title: Pegbelfermin in MASH with bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis: a failed programme — FALCON 1 missed its biopsy primary endpoint (24–31% versus 14%, P=.134) and FALCON 2 responses ran below placebo (24–28% versus 31%, P=.361)
shelves.question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and stage 3 (bridging) fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis, does pegbelfermin (pegylated FGF21 analogue) versus placebo improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/complications/drug therapy/pathology · Liver/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Polyethylene Glycols/adverse effects · Liver Cirrhosis/complications/drug therapy/pathology · Inflammation/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Fibroblast Growth Factors/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — present the failure on the face: pegbelfermin is a FAILED programme. Both of its phase 2b trials missed their primary biopsy endpoints, and the shelf reports the two fibrosis stages as two separate limbs, never pooled. In FALCON 1 (stage 3 bridging fibrosis, 197 patients), the week-24 primary endpoint — at least a 1-point fibrosis improvement without steatohepatitis worsening, or steatohepatitis improvement without fibrosis worsening — was met by 14% on placebo versus 24–31% across the pegbelfermin dose arms, but the prespecified dose-response test was not significant (P=.134), so the endpoint was not met: the treatment made no difference that the trial could confirm. In FALCON 2 (compensated cirrhosis, stage 4; 155 patients), week-48 fibrosis improvement without worsening was 24–28% on pegbelfermin versus 31% on placebo (P=.361) — numerically favouring placebo. What did move were surrogates around the biopsy: liver fat fraction, elastography stiffness, collagen propeptide and liver enzymes improved on pegbelfermin in FALCON 1, and a biomarker report from that trial found significant improvements in composite fibrosis scores (ELF, FIB-4, APRI), fibrogenesis markers and all four blood protein signatures — while its own concordance analysis showed biomarker 'responses' exceeding and sometimes disagreeing with biopsy responses. Biopsy endpoints are themselves surrogates for clinical outcomes; here even the surrogates disagreed with each other. The FGF21-class homes for other drugs in earlier fibrosis stages are separate shelves and are not evidence for this drug in F3/F4 disease.

cards.headline: FALCON 1, stage 3 fibrosis (Loomba 2024): primary biopsy endpoint not met — 24–31% across dose arms versus 14% on placebo with no dose response (P=.134); liver fat and stiffness measures improved
cards.summary: FALCON 1, stage 3 fibrosis (Loomba 2024): primary biopsy endpoint not met — 24–31% across dose arms versus 14% on placebo with no dose response (P=.134); liver fat and stiffness measures improved
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised (1:1:1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (FALCON 1) — bridging fibrosis limb
cards.people: 197 patients with biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and stage 3 (bridging) fibrosis received weekly subcutaneous pegbelfermin 10, 20 or 40 mg or placebo for 48 weeks. The week-24 primary endpoint was a composite biopsy outcome (at least a 1-point fibrosis decrease without steatohepatitis worsening, or steatohepatitis improvement without fibrosis worsening), tested by a Cochran-Armitage dose-response trend test.
cards.result: At week 24 the primary endpoint was met by 14% (placebo) versus 24–31% (pegbelfermin arms), but statistical significance was not reached because there was no pegbelfermin dose response (P=.134) — the trial did not meet its primary endpoint. At weeks 24 and 48, more pegbelfermin patients achieved at least 30% relative reductions in hepatic fat fraction on MRI than placebo patients (relative reductions, as reported; no difference reached significance). Magnetic resonance elastography stiffness, N-terminal type III collagen propeptide, alanine and aspartate aminotransferases improved versus placebo. Adverse events occurred at similar frequencies across arms, with no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A numerically favourable but formally failed primary: without a dose response, the 24–31% versus 14% gap is compatible with chance and with biopsy sampling noise, which is exactly why the prespecified trend test governs the verdict. The imaging and enzyme improvements are secondary surrogates.
cards.source: Loomba R et al. Pegbelfermin in Patients With Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis and Stage 3 Fibrosis (FALCON 1): A Randomized Phase 2b Study. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024. PMID: 37088457. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03486899, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: FALCON 2, compensated cirrhosis (Abdelmalek 2024): primary biopsy endpoint not met — fibrosis improvement 24–28% on pegbelfermin versus 31% on placebo at week 48 (P=.361)
cards.summary: FALCON 2, compensated cirrhosis (Abdelmalek 2024): primary biopsy endpoint not met — fibrosis improvement 24–28% on pegbelfermin versus 31% on placebo at week 48 (P=.361)
cards.type: Phase 2b, randomised (1:1:1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (FALCON 2) — cirrhosis limb, reported separately from FALCON 1
cards.people: 155 patients with biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and stage 4 fibrosis (compensated cirrhosis) were randomised (154 treated) to weekly subcutaneous pegbelfermin 10, 20 or 40 mg or placebo. Primary endpoint: at least 1 stage of fibrosis improvement without steatohepatitis worsening at week 48, tested by dose-response trend.
cards.result: At week 48, 24% to 28% of the pegbelfermin arms met the primary endpoint versus 31% of the placebo arm (P=.361) — the trial did not meet its primary endpoint, and the point estimates favoured placebo. Steatohepatitis activity-score improvements were more frequent with pegbelfermin, driven mainly by reduced lobular inflammation. Liver stiffness and steatosis improvements were numerically more frequent on pegbelfermin but not statistically significant; collagen propeptide and liver enzymes were numerically lower on the 20 and 40 mg arms. Serious adverse events were more frequent with pegbelfermin than placebo, though none were judged treatment-related; one patient (40 mg) stopped for worsening ascites.
cards.watchOut: A 31% placebo 'response' rate on biopsy in cirrhosis shows how much of any single-arm improvement rate is sampling and reading variation — the essential context for uncontrolled MASH biopsy claims generally. Cirrhosis (F4) is a different limb from FALCON 1's bridging fibrosis (F3); the two must not be pooled.
cards.source: Abdelmalek MF et al. Pegbelfermin in Patients With Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis and Compensated Cirrhosis (FALCON 2): A Randomized Phase 2b Study. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024. PMID: 37088458. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03486912, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: FALCON 1 biomarker report (Brown 2023): pegbelfermin significantly improved ELF, FIB-4, APRI, PRO-C3, adiponectin, CK-18, MRI liver fat and all four SomaSignal signatures at week 24 — while biomarker and biopsy responses were partly discordant
cards.summary: FALCON 1 biomarker report (Brown 2023): pegbelfermin significantly improved ELF, FIB-4, APRI, PRO-C3, adiponectin, CK-18, MRI liver fat and all four SomaSignal signatures at week 24 — while biomarker and biopsy responses were partly discordant
cards.type: Post hoc biomarker–histology correlation analysis of the FALCON 1 trial — same patients as the FALCON 1 card, not an independent trial
cards.people: FALCON 1 patients with available data (stage 3 fibrosis, pegbelfermin versus placebo) through week 24; blood-based composite fibrosis scores, individual biomarkers, imaging measures and blood protein signatures (SomaSignal) were modelled against treatment and correlated with the week-24 biopsy primary endpoint.
cards.result: At week 24, pegbelfermin significantly improved blood-based composite fibrosis scores (ELF, FIB-4, APRI), fibrogenesis biomarkers (PRO-C3 and PC3X), adiponectin, CK-18, hepatic fat fraction by MRI-proton density fat fraction, and all four SomaSignal steatohepatitis component tests (steatosis, inflammation, ballooning, fibrosis). Correlations grouped into steatosis/metabolism, tissue injury, fibrosis and biopsy-based categories; concordant and discordant effects versus the biopsy endpoint were both observed, with the clearest concordant effects on liver steatosis and metabolism measures.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and multiplicity-heavy: when the prespecified biopsy endpoint fails, a sweep of significant biomarkers is the expected pattern under selective emphasis — and the authors' own concordance analysis shows non-invasive 'response' can exceed and disagree with biopsy response. This card explains the programme's rationale, not a rescued efficacy claim.
cards.source: Brown EA et al. Effect of pegbelfermin on NASH and fibrosis-related biomarkers and correlation with histological response in the FALCON 1 trial. JHEP Rep. 2023. PMID: 36866389. cards.headline: Synthesis: two biopsy trials, two misses — biomarkers moved, histology did not — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two biopsy trials, two misses — biomarkers moved, histology did not — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: FALCON 1 (197 patients, stage 3 fibrosis), FALCON 2 (155 patients, compensated cirrhosis) and a post hoc biomarker analysis of FALCON 1's patients. The F3 and F4 limbs are reported separately throughout.
cards.result: Neither trial met its primary biopsy endpoint (FALCON 1 trend P=.134; FALCON 2 responses 24–28% versus 31% on placebo, P=.361) — on the endpoints the programme staked itself on, the treatment made no difference. Liver fat, stiffness, enzyme and blood-biomarker measures improved, most consistently for steatosis.
cards.watchOut: A failed programme: development on this evidence did not proceed to an approved treatment. Do not let the biomarker card rehabilitate the biopsy verdict, and do not pool F3 with F4 — the cirrhosis limb is, if anything, the weaker of the two. All endpoints here are surrogates for clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Loomba R et al. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024 (PMID: 37088457), Abdelmalek MF et al. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024 (PMID: 37088458), Brown EA et al. JHEP Rep. 2023 (PMID: 36866389). Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03486899, NCT03486912.

shelves.title: Natalizumab in Crohn's disease: induction results split (ENACT-1 missed, ENCORE met in patients with raised CRP), maintenance in responders was clearly positive (sustained response 61% versus 28%) — and the indication was abandoned over progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
shelves.question: In adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does natalizumab (anti-alpha4-integrin monoclonal antibody) versus placebo induce response/remission and maintain remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Cell Adhesion Molecules/antagonists & inhibitors · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Integrin alpha Chains/antagonists & inhibitors · JC Virus · Leukoencephalopathy, Progressive Multifocal/chemically induced · Male · Natalizumab · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and the safety fact comes first on this shelf: natalizumab's Crohn's disease use was abandoned because of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), the JC-virus brain infection that killed a patient in this programme's open-label extension. This is a historical/completeness shelf for a withdrawn indication, not a live treatment option; the gut-selective integrin drug vedolizumab is a different agent with its own homes in this library and is not evidence here. The efficacy record itself splits. Induction: the large ENACT-1 trial (905 patients) missed its primary contrasts — response 56% versus 49% (P=0.05) and remission 37% versus 30% (P=0.12) at week 10, small and nonsignificant — while ENCORE (509 patients selected for raised C-reactive protein) met its primary endpoint clearly (sustained response 48% versus 32%, P<.001; sustained remission 26% versus 16%, P=.002), and the earlier dose-ranging trial (248 patients) missed its week-6 remission primary at the 6 mg/kg dose while showing higher response rates. Maintenance is the strong limb, with a design caveat printed on its card: ENACT-2 re-randomised only the 339 patients who had already responded to natalizumab, and in that responder-enriched population continuing the drug beat switching to placebo decisively (sustained response 61% versus 28%, P<.001; remission 44% versus 26%, P=0.003). Serious adverse events were similar between arms in the controlled trials (about 7–10%); the PML death occurred in open-label extension use, which is where rare catastrophic harm characteristically appears.

cards.headline: Ghosh 2003 dose-ranging trial: week-6 remission primary missed at 6 mg/kg, but two-infusion groups beat placebo on remission at multiple time points; highest response rate 71% and remission 44% (3 mg/kg, week 6)
cards.summary: Ghosh 2003 dose-ranging trial: week-6 remission primary missed at 6 mg/kg, but two-infusion groups beat placebo on remission at multiple time points; highest response rate 71% and remission 44% (3 mg/kg, week 6)
cards.people: 248 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease randomised to four groups: two placebo infusions; one infusion of natalizumab 3 mg/kg then placebo; two infusions of 3 mg/kg; or two infusions of 6 mg/kg, given 4 weeks apart. Outcomes: Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) change, remission (CDAI under 150), response (fall of at least 70 points), quality of life and C-reactive protein.
cards.result: The 6 mg/kg two-infusion group did not have a significantly higher remission rate than placebo at week 6 — the prospectively defined primary endpoint of the efficacy analysis. Both two-infusion groups nonetheless had higher remission rates than placebo at multiple time points, response rates were significantly improved, and the highest remission (44%) and response (71%) rates occurred at week 6 in the 3 mg/kg two-infusion group. Quality of life improved in all natalizumab groups and C-reactive protein improved in the two-infusion groups. Adverse event rates were similar across all four groups.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary with favourable secondary time points, across three dose arms and many comparisons — the pattern that later trials had to confirm. Dosing here is weight-based (mg/kg); the later programme used a fixed 300 mg dose, so the arms are not directly interchangeable.
cards.source: Ghosh S et al. Natalizumab for active Crohn's disease. N Engl J Med. 2003. PMID: 12510039. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial 248 patients with moderate-to-severe crohn's disease randomised to four groups: two placebo infusions; one infusion of natalizumab 3 mg/kg then placebo; two infusions of 3 mg/kg; or two infusions of 6 mg/kg, given 4 weeks apart. outcomes: crohn's disease activity index (cdai) change, remission (cdai under 150), response (fall of at least 70 points), quality of life and c-reactive protein. the 6 mg/kg two-infusion group did not have a significantly higher remission rate than placebo at week 6 — the prospectively defined primary endpoint of the efficacy analysis. both two-infusion groups nonetheless had higher remission rates than placebo at multiple time points, response rates were significantly improved, and the highest remission (44%) and response (71%) rates occurred at week 6 in the 3 mg/kg two-infusion group. quality of life improved in all natalizumab groups and c-reactive protein improved in the two-infusion groups. adverse event rates were similar across all four groups. a missed primary with favourable secondary time points, across three dose arms and many comparisons — the pattern that later trials had to confirm. dosing here is weight-based (mg/kg); the later programme used a fixed 300 mg dose, so the arms are not directly interchangeable. ghosh s et al. natalizumab for active crohn's disease. n engl j med. 2003. pmid: 12510039. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · antibodies, monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized · c-reactive protein/analysis/drug effects · crohn disease/drug therapy · double-blind method · female · humans · infusions, intravenous · male · middle aged · natalizumab · quality of life · remission induction/methods

cards.headline: ENACT-1 and ENACT-2 (Sandborn 2005): induction missed (response 56% versus 49%, P=0.05; remission 37% versus 30%, P=0.12), but continuing natalizumab in responders gave sustained response 61% versus 28% (P<0.001) — and a patient died of PML in the extension
cards.summary: ENACT-1 and ENACT-2 (Sandborn 2005): induction missed (response 56% versus 49%, P=0.05; remission 37% versus 30%, P=0.12), but continuing natalizumab in responders gave sustained response 61% versus 28% (P<0.001) — and a patient died of PML in the extension
cards.type: Two randomised controlled trials reported together: induction (ENACT-1) and responder-re-randomised maintenance (ENACT-2)
cards.people: ENACT-1: 905 patients with active Crohn's disease randomised to natalizumab 300 mg or placebo at weeks 0, 4 and 8; primary outcome response (CDAI fall of at least 70 points) at week 10. ENACT-2: 339 patients who had responded to natalizumab in ENACT-1 were re-randomised to natalizumab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks through week 56; primary outcome sustained response through week 36.
cards.result: In ENACT-1, response (56% versus 49%; P=0.05) and remission (37% versus 30%; P=0.12) at week 10 were similar between groups — small, nonsignificant improvements. In ENACT-2, continuing natalizumab produced higher sustained response (61% versus 28%; P<0.001) and remission (44% versus 26%; P=0.003) through week 36 than switching to placebo. Serious adverse events occurred in 7% of each ENACT-1 group and in 8% (natalizumab) versus 10% (placebo) in ENACT-2. In the open-label extension study, a natalizumab-treated patient died from progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy associated with JC virus.
cards.watchOut: ENACT-2's maintenance numbers apply only to patients who already responded to the drug — a responder-enriched design that cannot be read as the effect of starting natalizumab in unselected patients. The PML death, in uncontrolled extension use, is the event that defines this drug's Crohn's history and outweighs the controlled trials' reassuring short-term safety counts.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Natalizumab induction and maintenance therapy for Crohn's disease. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID: 16267322. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00032786 and NCT00032799, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ENCORE (Targan 2007): in patients with raised CRP, sustained response 48% versus 32% (P<.001) and sustained remission 26% versus 16% (P=.002) — the induction win ENACT-1 did not produce
cards.summary: ENCORE (Targan 2007): in patients with raised CRP, sustained response 48% versus 32% (P<.001) and sustained remission 26% versus 16% (P=.002) — the induction win ENACT-1 did not produce
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled induction trial (ENCORE) in an inflammation-selected population
cards.people: 509 patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease and active inflammation shown by elevated C-reactive protein concentrations, randomised 1:1 to natalizumab 300 mg or placebo intravenously at weeks 0, 4 and 8. Primary endpoint: response (CDAI fall of at least 70 points) at week 8 sustained through week 12.
cards.result: Response at week 8 sustained through week 12 occurred in 48% of natalizumab patients versus 32% on placebo (P<.001), and sustained remission in 26% versus 16% (P=.002). Week-4 response was 51% versus 37% (P=.001), and response and remission rates remained significantly higher at weeks 4, 8 and 12 (remission P at most .009). The frequency and types of adverse events were similar between treatment groups.
cards.watchOut: ENCORE's population was selected for elevated CRP — objective inflammation — which is the most plausible explanation of why it succeeded where unselected ENACT-1 did not; its percentages should not be quoted for Crohn's patients without that selection. Sixteen- and ten-percentage-point absolute gains also mean most treated patients did not achieve the sustained endpoints.
cards.source: Targan SR et al. Natalizumab for the treatment of active Crohn's disease: results of the ENCORE Trial. Gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 17484865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gordon 2001 pilot: a single 3 mg/kg infusion cut CDAI by 45 points versus 11 on placebo at week 2; remission 39% versus 8% — in 30 patients
cards.summary: Gordon 2001 pilot: a single 3 mg/kg infusion cut CDAI by 45 points versus 11 on placebo at week 2; remission 39% versus 8% — in 30 patients
cards.people: 30 patients with mild to moderately active Crohn's disease (CDAI 151 to 450) randomised to a single infusion of natalizumab 3 mg/kg (n=18) or placebo (n=12). Primary endpoint: change in CDAI at week 2.
cards.result: At week 2, CDAI fell by a mean of 45 points after natalizumab versus 11 points on placebo (significant versus baseline for natalizumab only). Seven natalizumab patients (39%) achieved remission at week 2 versus 1 (8%) on placebo; rescue medication by week 2 was required by 2 (11%) natalizumab versus 4 (33%) placebo patients. Circulating B and T lymphocytes rose significantly only after natalizumab, consistent with interrupted lymphocyte trafficking. Common adverse events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients and a 2-week endpoint — a proof-of-mechanism pilot, carded as the programme's first report, not as efficacy evidence of weight. The authors themselves note the single dose may have been suboptimal.
cards.source: Gordon FH et al. A randomized placebo-controlled trial of a humanized monoclonal antibody to alpha4 integrin in active Crohn's disease. Gastroenterology. 2001. PMID: 11487536. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: real but split efficacy, ended by PML — SPLIT, and a closed indication
cards.summary: Synthesis: real but split efficacy, ended by PML — SPLIT, and a closed indication
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: four randomised trials (248, 905 with 339 re-randomised responders, 509 and 30 patients) of natalizumab versus placebo in active Crohn's disease, plus the open-label extension in which the PML death occurred.
cards.result: Induction split: ENACT-1 and the Ghosh dose-ranging primary missed; ENCORE, in CRP-elevated patients, met its endpoints with absolute gains of 16 (response) and 10 (remission) percentage points. Maintenance in prior responders was strongly positive (sustained response 61% versus 28%). Against all of this stands one extension death from progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, the risk that ended the indication.
cards.watchOut: SPLIT names the induction split; it is not a balanced live choice. Natalizumab for Crohn's disease is a withdrawn indication — this shelf exists so the record, including why it ended, is findable. Do not transfer these results to the gut-selective integrin agent, which has separate shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghosh S et al. N Engl J Med. 2003 (PMID: 12510039), Sandborn WJ et al. N Engl J Med. 2005 (PMID: 16267322), Targan SR et al.
