shelves.title: Filgotinib in Crohn's disease: a failed phase 3 — FITZROY phase 2 remission was 47% versus 23%, but DIVERSITY missed its week-10 co-primary endpoints in both induction studies (endoscopic response difference 5.5% and 0.1%, both not significant)
shelves.question: In adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does filgotinib (JAK1 inhibitor) versus placebo induce and maintain clinical remission and endoscopic response?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Pyridines/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Young Adult · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Triazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Adolescent · Remission Induction · Induction Chemotherapy · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Patient Reported Outcome Measures
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — present the failure on the face: filgotinib in Crohn's disease is a FAILED phase 3 programme. The floor rests on two trials plus a post hoc report of one of them, and the shelf says so. FITZROY, the phase 2 trial (174 patients), was positive: clinical remission at week 10 in 47% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 23% on placebo (difference 24 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 39; P=0.0077). Its 2025 post hoc analysis asked whether ileal disease responds differently from colonic disease and, after adjusting for baseline activity and within-patient clustering, found no significant difference — a methods report of the same trial, adding no patients. DIVERSITY, the phase 3 programme (induction studies A and B, 707 and 665 patients; maintenance 481), then missed its week-10 co-primary endpoints: PRO2 clinical remission on 200 mg reached significance in study B (29.7% versus 17.9%; P=0.0039) but not study A (32.9% versus 25.7%; P=0.0963), and endoscopic response was not significant in either (differences 5.5 and 0.1 percentage points); the 100 mg dose met no co-primary endpoint anywhere. At week 58, among patients re-randomised after responding during induction, filgotinib 200 mg did meet both co-primary endpoints versus withdrawal to placebo (PRO2 remission 43.8% versus 26.4%; endoscopic response 30.4% versus 9.4%) — a responder-enriched maintenance result that does not rescue the failed induction. Filgotinib's ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis questions are homed on separate shelves; nothing here transfers to them.

cards.headline: FITZROY phase 2 (Vermeire 2017): clinical remission at week 10 in 47% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 23% on placebo (difference 24 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 39; P=0.0077)
cards.summary: FITZROY phase 2 (Vermeire 2017): clinical remission at week 10 in 47% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 23% on placebo (difference 24 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 39; P=0.0077)
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (FITZROY; 52 centres, nine European countries)
cards.people: 174 patients aged 18–75 with ileal, colonic or ileocolonic Crohn's disease of at least 3 months (centrally read endoscopy; CDAI 220–450) were randomised 3:1 to filgotinib 200 mg once daily (130 enrolled; 128 in the intention-to-treat analysis) or placebo (44) for 10 weeks, stratified by prior anti-TNF exposure, screening C-reactive protein and corticosteroid use; responders then entered a further 10-week observational period on assigned doses. Funded by Galapagos.
cards.result: Clinical remission (CDAI under 150) at week 10 was achieved by 60 (47%) of 128 patients on filgotinib 200 mg versus 10 (23%) of 44 on placebo (difference 24 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 39; P=0.0077). Across all filgotinib and placebo exposure periods over 20 weeks, serious treatment-emergent adverse effects were reported in 14 (9%) of 152 filgotinib-exposed patients and 3 (4%) of 67 placebo-exposed patients. The authors judged the safety profile acceptable.
cards.watchOut: A 3:1 randomisation leaves only 44 placebo patients, so the 23% placebo rate — and therefore the 24-point difference — is imprecisely estimated; and a CDAI-based remission endpoint in phase 2 is exactly what the phase 3 programme, with stricter patient-reported and endoscopic co-primaries, then failed to reproduce.
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. Clinical remission in patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease treated with filgotinib (the FITZROY study): results from a phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 27988142. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02048618, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: FITZROY ileal-versus-colonic post hoc (Ma 2025): unadjusted remission favoured colonic disease (75.9% versus 41.6%), but after adjustment there was no significant difference by disease location (P=0.85 for CDAI; P=0.48 for endoscopic score)
cards.summary: FITZROY ileal-versus-colonic post hoc (Ma 2025): unadjusted remission favoured colonic disease (75.9% versus 41.6%), but after adjustment there was no significant difference by disease location (P=0.85 for CDAI; P=0.48 for endoscopic score)
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of the FITZROY phase 2 trial — same trial and same patients as the FITZROY card, not an independent trial
cards.people: The FITZROY patients with ileal-dominant versus isolated colonic Crohn's disease treated with 10 weeks of filgotinib 200 mg daily or placebo; changes in CDAI and in the Simple Endoscopic Score for Crohn's Disease (SES-CD) were compared using a mixed effects model with a treatment-by-location interaction, adjusting for baseline disease activity by location and within-patient clustering.
cards.result: Numerically, greater proportions of patients with isolated colonic disease than ileal-dominant disease achieved clinical remission (CDAI under 150: 75.9% versus 41.6%) and endoscopic response (SES-CD reduction of at least 50%: 52.5% versus 15.5%) at week 10. After adjustment, however, there was no significant difference in treatment response by disease location: mean difference in CDAI change between ileal-dominant and isolated colonic disease +9.24 (95% CI -87.19 to +105.67; P=0.85) and in SES-CD change -1.93 (95% CI -7.03 to +3.44; P=0.48). The authors conclude filgotinib showed similar efficacy by location once baseline activity and clustering were handled appropriately.
cards.watchOut: This report's lesson is methodological: the striking unadjusted gap (75.9% versus 41.6%) dissolves under adjustment, so neither figure should be quoted alone. It adds no patients and no new efficacy evidence to the shelf — the floor counts it as a report of FITZROY, not a third trial.
cards.source: Ma C et al. Re-evaluating Methods for Assessing Differences in Response in Ileal vs Colonic Crohn's Disease: A Post-hoc Analysis of the FITZROY Trial. J Crohns Colitis. 2025. PMID: 39030919. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02048618, named in the record's abstract (parent FITZROY trial). p=0.85) and in ses-cd change -1.93 (95% ci -7.03 to +3.44; p=0.48). the authors conclude filgotinib showed similar efficacy by location once baseline activity and clustering were handled appropriately. this report's lesson is methodological: the striking unadjusted gap (75.9% versus 41.6%) dissolves under adjustment, so neither figure should be quoted alone. it adds no patients and no new efficacy evidence to the shelf — the floor counts it as a report of fitzroy, not a third trial. ma c et al. re-evaluating methods for assessing differences in response in ileal vs colonic crohn's disease: a post-hoc analysis of the fitzroy trial. j crohns colitis. 2025. pmid: 39030919. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct02048618, named in the record's abstract (parent fitzroy trial). mesh: adult · female · humans · male · middle aged · colon/pathology · crohn disease/drug therapy/pathology · ileum/pathology · janus kinase inhibitors/therapeutic use · pyridines/therapeutic use · remission induction · severity of illness index · treatment outcome · triazoles/therapeutic use

cards.headline: DIVERSITY phase 3 (Vermeire 2025): co-primary endpoints missed at week 10 in both induction studies — endoscopic response differences 5.5% (P=0.1365) and 0.1% (P=0.9797); week-58 maintenance co-primaries met only in re-randomised responders on 200 mg
cards.summary: DIVERSITY phase 3 (Vermeire 2025): co-primary endpoints missed at week 10 in both induction studies — endoscopic response differences 5.5% (P=0.1365) and 0.1% (P=0.9797); week-58 maintenance co-primaries met only in re-randomised responders on 200 mg
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled programme (DIVERSITY): two induction studies and one responder-re-randomised maintenance study (371 centres, 39 countries)
cards.people: 1372 patients aged 18–75 with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease were enrolled: induction study A (n=707; biologic-naive and later biologic-experienced patients) and induction study B (n=665; biologic-experienced), randomised 1:1:1 to filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg or placebo once daily for 11 weeks. Patients on filgotinib who reached PRO2 clinical remission or an endoscopic response at week 10 were re-randomised (2:1) to continue their dose or switch to placebo to week 58 (maintenance n=481). Co-primary endpoints: PRO2 clinical remission and endoscopic response (at least 50% SES-CD reduction) at weeks 10 and 58.
cards.result: At week 10 on filgotinib 200 mg, PRO2 clinical remission was significantly higher than placebo in induction study B (29.7% versus 17.9%; difference 11.9 percentage points, 95% CI 3.7 to 20.2; P=0.0039) but not in study A (32.9% versus 25.7%; difference 6.9, 95% CI -1.4 to 15.2; P=0.0963), and endoscopic response did not differ significantly in either study (A: 23.9% versus 18.1%; difference 5.5, 95% CI -2.0 to 12.9; P=0.1365. B: 11.9% versus 11.4%; difference 0.1, 95% CI -6.5 to 6.6; P=0.9797). Co-primary endpoints were not met for filgotinib 100 mg in any study, so the induction co-primaries failed overall. At week 58, in the re-randomised responder population, filgotinib 200 mg met both co-primaries versus withdrawal (PRO2 remission 43.8% versus 26.4%; difference 16.8, 95% CI 2.0 to 31.6; P=0.0382. Endoscopic response 30.4% versus 9.4%; difference 20.6, 95% CI 8.2 to 33.1; P=0.0038). No deaths occurred; serious treatment-emergent events ran 6–16% across induction groups and 5–13% in maintenance groups.
cards.watchOut: One publication reporting two induction studies plus a maintenance study: the maintenance 'win' is conditioned on having already responded during induction (a responder-enriched withdrawal design) and cannot offset the failed induction co-primaries — most patients starting the drug are in the induction population, where the programme's own success criteria were not met.
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. Efficacy and safety of filgotinib as induction and maintenance therapy for Crohn's disease (DIVERSITY): a phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2025. PMID: 39637881. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02914561, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: phase 2 promise, phase 3 induction failure — MAYBE (weak evidence) for a failed programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 2 promise, phase 3 induction failure — MAYBE (weak evidence) for a failed programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: FITZROY phase 2 (174 patients) and its post hoc location analysis (same patients), and the DIVERSITY phase 3 programme (1372 patients across two induction studies; 481 re-randomised responders in maintenance). Two trials and one same-trial report — the floor's structure, stated plainly.
cards.result: FITZROY showed a 24-percentage-point remission advantage on a symptom-score endpoint; DIVERSITY, ten times larger with patient-reported plus endoscopic co-primaries, missed those co-primaries at induction in both studies (endoscopic differences 5.5 and 0.1 points), with benefit confined to continued treatment of induction responders at week 58.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence), not a balanced split: when a large phase 3 programme fails its prespecified co-primary endpoints, the earlier small positive trial does not hold the scale level. This shelf records the programme's failure so the phase 2 result is not quoted without it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vermeire S et al. Lancet. 2017 (PMID: 27988142), Ma C et al. J Crohns Colitis. 2025 (PMID: 39030919), Vermeire S et al. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2025 (PMID: 39637881). Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02048618, NCT02914561.

shelves.title: Mepolizumab in eosinophilic oesophagitis: oesophageal eosinophils fall sharply, but dysphagia does not improve more than with placebo — a histology–symptom split
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, does mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) versus placebo reduce oesophageal eosinophilia and improve dysphagia symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Eosinophilic Esophagitis/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Deglutition Disorders/drug therapy · Eosinophils/pathology · Interleukin-5
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is between tissue and symptoms, and it is the recurring anti-IL-5 pattern in eosinophilic oesophagitis (the same lesson as the benralizumab MESSINA shelf, pack #3613). On histology, mepolizumab works in every report: in the largest randomised trial (Dellon 2023, n=66) peak eosinophil counts fell from 113 to 36 per high-power field against a rise on placebo, with histologic responses (<15 eos/hpf) in 42% versus 3%; the paediatric dose-ranging trial (Assa'ad 2011, n=59, no placebo arm) and the small adult pilot (Straumann 2010, N = 11, printed on the face) point the same way. On symptoms, the largest trial missed its primary endpoint: dysphagia scores improved no more than with placebo at 3 months (p=0.14 — the treatment made no difference to dysphagia), and longer treatment to 6 months added nothing. A shelf that converted the histology win into a symptom claim would misstate this evidence. The paediatric programme's post-hoc analysis (Wong 2023) is a report of the Assa'ad trial, not an independent population, and is labelled as such. A 2006 four-patient report is sub-floor and is not carded. Stamp: SPLIT, naming the split.

cards.headline: Dellon 2023: mepolizumab 300 mg monthly in 66 adolescents/adults — eosinophil counts and histologic response improve sharply, but the primary dysphagia endpoint is missed (p=0.14; the treatment made no difference to dysphagia)
cards.summary: Dellon 2023: mepolizumab 300 mg monthly in 66 adolescents/adults — eosinophil counts and histologic response improve sharply, but the primary dysphagia endpoint is missed (p=0.14; the treatment made no difference to dysphagia)
cards.people: Sixty-six patients aged 16–75 with eosinophilic oesophagitis and dysphagia symptoms (EoE Symptom Activity Index), randomised 1:1 to mepolizumab 300 mg monthly or placebo for 3 months (64 completed month 3); in part 2 the mepolizumab group continued 300 mg monthly and the placebo group switched to mepolizumab 100 mg monthly for 3 further months (56 completed month 6). Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled.
cards.result: At month 3 the primary outcome — change in dysphagia symptom score — fell 15.4 ± 18.1 points on mepolizumab versus 8.3 ± 18.0 on placebo (p=0.14; the treatment made no difference to dysphagia). Peak eosinophil counts fell from 113 ± 77 to 36 ± 43 on mepolizumab versus 146 ± 94 to 160 ± 133 on placebo (p<0.001); histologic responses were achieved by 42% versus 3% at <15 eos/hpf and 34% versus 3% at ≤6 eos/hpf. Endoscopic severity also improved more with mepolizumab. At month 6, symptom scores had fallen similarly in both sequences (18.3 vs 18.6 points, p=0.85) — longer treatment yielded no additional improvement. Injection-site reactions were the most common adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The symptom–histology dissociation is the finding: do not read the eosinophil fall as evidence patients swallow better. Part 2 had no placebo arm, so month-6 symptom changes are uncontrolled.
cards.source: Dellon ES, Peterson KA, Mitlyng BL et al. Mepolizumab for treatment of adolescents and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Gut. 2023. PMID: 37423717. Registry ID: NCT03656380. cards.headline: Assa'ad 2011: paediatric dose-ranging trial (n=59, no placebo) — mean oesophageal eosinophil counts fall from 39.1 to 9.3 per hpf across all three mepolizumab doses, with no dose separation
cards.summary: Assa'ad 2011: paediatric dose-ranging trial (n=59, no placebo) — mean oesophageal eosinophil counts fall from 39.1 to 9.3 per hpf across all three mepolizumab doses, with no dose separation
cards.type: Randomised dose-ranging trial without placebo, Gastroenterology 2011
cards.people: Fifty-nine children with eosinophilic oesophagitis (baseline peak intraepithelial eosinophils ≥20/hpf) in an international multicentre double-blind randomised study; three infusions every 4 weeks of mepolizumab 0.55, 2.5 or 10 mg/kg. No placebo group was used; 57 children were evaluated 4 weeks after the third infusion.
cards.result: Peak eosinophil counts fell below 5/hpf in 5 of 57 children (8.8%), with no differences among the three dose groups. Mean counts fell from 39.1 ± 3.63 to 9.3 ± 1.25 per hpf and peak counts from 122.5 ± 8.78 to 40.2 ± 5.17 per hpf (both p<0.0001 versus baseline); peak counts <20/hpf were reached by 31.6% and mean counts <20/hpf by 89.5%. A higher baseline mean eosinophil count predicted a greater reduction.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm — the eosinophil fall is a within-group change and cannot separate drug effect from natural fluctuation or regression to the mean; symptom outcomes were not the focus of this report.
cards.source: Assa'ad AH, Gupta SK, Collins MH et al. An antibody against IL-5 reduces numbers of esophageal intraepithelial eosinophils in children with eosinophilic esophagitis. Gastroenterology. 2011. PMID: 21835135. Registry ID: NCT00358449. cards.headline: Straumann 2010: adult pilot (N = 11) — mepolizumab cuts mean oesophageal eosinophilia by 54% versus 5% on placebo at 4 weeks, with only limited symptom improvement
cards.summary: Straumann 2010: adult pilot (N = 11) — mepolizumab cuts mean oesophageal eosinophilia by 54% versus 5% on placebo at 4 weeks, with only limited symptom improvement
cards.type: Small randomised placebo-controlled pilot trial, Gut 2010
cards.people: Eleven adults with active eosinophilic oesophagitis (>20 peak eosinophils/hpf and dysphagia), randomised to mepolizumab 750 mg (n=5) or placebo (n=6), two intravenous infusions 1 week apart, with two further doses (1500 mg or placebo) at weeks 8–12 for those not in complete remission. N = 11 printed on the face.
cards.result: Mean oesophageal eosinophilia fell 54% on mepolizumab versus 5% on placebo at 4 weeks (p=0.03), with no further reduction after the additional infusions. Expression of the remodelling markers tenascin C (p=0.033) and transforming growth factor beta1 (p=0.05) fell in the oesophageal epithelium by week 13. Clinically, only limited symptom improvement was seen, with a trend between weeks 4 and 13. Mepolizumab was well tolerated, including at the 1500 mg dose.
cards.watchOut: N = 11 — a pharmacodynamic pilot, not an efficacy estimate; doses (750–1500 mg intravenous) far exceed the doses used in later trials, so its tolerability read does not transfer directly.
cards.source: Straumann A, Conus S, Grzonka P et al. Anti-interleukin-5 antibody treatment (mepolizumab) in active eosinophilic oesophagitis: a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Gut. 2010. PMID: 19828470. Registry ID: NCT00274703. cards.headline: Wong 2023: post-hoc predictors analysis of the SAME paediatric trial — higher BMI and endoscopic exudate plaques predict histologic response (companion report, not an independent population)
cards.summary: Wong 2023: post-hoc predictors analysis of the SAME paediatric trial — higher BMI and endoscopic exudate plaques predict histologic response (companion report, not an independent population)
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the Assa'ad 2011 trial (one programme), Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the multicentre paediatric mepolizumab trial reported by Assa'ad 2011 (same programme, NCT00358449); histologic response at week 12 was defined two ways — <15 eosinophils/hpf, or a ≥50% reduction in peak eosinophil counts — and predictors were tested in multivariable logistic models.
cards.result: Higher BMI predicted histologic response under both definitions (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.07–1.60 for the <15/hpf definition; adjusted odds ratio 1.70, 95% CI 1.06–2.74 for the ≥50%-reduction definition — adjusted odds ratios are relative measures). Endoscopic exudate plaques strongly predicted the ≥50%-reduction response (adjusted odds ratio 18.30, 95% CI 2.11–158.53, a relative measure with a very wide interval). The authors call for validation in further studies.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial population as the Assa'ad card — it adds predictor information, not independent efficacy evidence, and must not be counted as a fourth trial. The exudate-plaque odds ratio rests on few events (CI 2.11–158.53).
cards.source: Wong ECL, Gleave AL, Marshall JK et al. Predictors of histologic response to mepolizumab in pediatric eosinophilic esophagitis. European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology. 2023. PMID: 37577798. Registry ID: NCT00358449. cards.headline: Synthesis: anti-IL-5 therapy reliably clears oesophageal eosinophils in EoE but has not been shown to relieve dysphagia better than placebo — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: anti-IL-5 therapy reliably clears oesophageal eosinophils in EoE but has not been shown to relieve dysphagia better than placebo — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: two placebo-controlled randomised trials (Dellon 2023, n=66; Straumann 2010, N = 11), one paediatric dose-ranging trial without placebo (Assa'ad 2011, n=59) and its post-hoc predictors report (Wong 2023, same programme).
cards.result: Across children and adults, mepolizumab reduces oesophageal eosinophil counts by roughly half or more and produces histologic responses in about a third to two-fifths of patients versus ~3% on placebo. The one trial powered on symptoms missed its primary dysphagia endpoint (the treatment made no difference to dysphagia, p=0.14), the pilot saw only limited symptom improvement, and extending treatment to 6 months added nothing. The honest shelf claim is therefore split: a real histologic and endoscopic effect, an unproven symptom effect. Sibling EoE biologic questions live elsewhere — dupilumab (pack #5881), benralizumab (pack #3613) and cendakimab (pack #6863) are different drugs and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial shows a patient-important symptom benefit; any future phase 3 symptom-positive report would change this stamp and should be checked at re-verification.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 37423717, 21835135, 19828470, 37577798). Registry ID: NCT03656380, NCT00358449, NCT00274703 as carded. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Octreotide for angiodysplasia bleeding: the OCEAN randomised trial cut transfusion needs by about 10 units a year versus standard care, concordant with the earlier pooled patient-level data
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent or transfusion-dependent bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasias, does octreotide (long-acting release) versus standard care reduce transfusion requirements and rebleeding?
shelves.mesh: Angiodysplasia/complications/drug therapy · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/drug therapy/etiology · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Erythrocyte Transfusion
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised-era limbs and one large pooled analysis agree on direction and rough size. The OCEAN trial (2024, n=62, open-label against standard care that included endoscopic therapy) found about 10 fewer transfusion units over a year with octreotide long-acting release (11.0 vs 21.2 units). The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the pre-OCEAN literature (212 patients; one randomised trial and ten cohort studies, the cohort limb graded low-certainty and kept visibly separate here) found transfusions falling from a mean 12.8 units at baseline to 2.3 on treatment, with 83% good responders. The oldest limb (Junquera 2007) compared an octreotide cohort with an external placebo control group from a concurrent trial — an external-control design, labelled as such, not a within-study randomisation. Transfusion need and rebleeding are the outcomes; no mortality claim is made. For the overlapping population treated with a different drug, see the sibling shelf on thalidomide for recurrent small-intestinal angiodysplasia bleeding (#7113) — a distinct evidence base, cross-pointed here in prose and not re-carded.

cards.headline: OCEAN 2024: octreotide LAR versus standard care in 62 transfusion-dependent patients — 11.0 versus 21.2 transfusion units over a year (mean reduction 10.2 units, p=.012)
cards.summary: OCEAN 2024: octreotide LAR versus standard care in 62 transfusion-dependent patients — 11.0 versus 21.2 transfusion units over a year (mean reduction 10.2 units, p=.012)
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised controlled trial (OCEAN), Gastroenterology 2024
cards.people: Sixty-two patients (mean age 72; 32 men) with angiodysplasia-related anaemia at 17 Dutch hospitals, each having required at least 4 red-cell units or parenteral iron infusions in the preceding year (mean 20.3 transfusion units and 2.4 endoscopic procedures), randomised 1:1 to octreotide long-acting release 40 mg intramuscularly every 28 days (n=31) or standard care including endoscopic therapy (n=31) for 1 year. Open-label, multicentre randomised trial.
cards.result: Total transfusions (red cells plus parenteral iron) were lower with octreotide: 11.0 units (95% CI 5.5–16.5) versus 21.2 (95% CI 15.7–26.7) — an adjusted mean reduction of 10.2 units (95% CI 2.4–18.1; p=.012). Octreotide also reduced the annual number of endoscopic procedures by 0.9 (95% CI 0.3–1.5).
cards.watchOut: Open-label against standard care — patients and clinicians knew the allocation, though transfusion counts are a hard outcome. The population was heavily transfusion-dependent at entry (mean ~20 units in the prior year), so the absolute saving applies to that stratum.
cards.source: Goltstein LCMJ, Grooteman KV, Bernts LHP et al. Standard of Care Versus Octreotide in Angiodysplasia-Related Bleeding (the OCEAN Study): A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2024. PMID: 38158089. Registry ID: NCT02384122. cards.headline: Junquera 2007: octreotide cohort versus external placebo controls — treatment failure 23% versus 48%, rebleed-free at 2 years 68% versus 36% (external-control design, labelled)
cards.summary: Junquera 2007: octreotide cohort versus external placebo controls — treatment failure 23% versus 48%, rebleed-free at 2 years 68% versus 36% (external-control design, labelled)
cards.type: Prospective octreotide cohort with external placebo controls, Am J Gastroenterol 2007
cards.people: A cohort of 32 patients with bleeding gastrointestinal angiodysplasia treated with octreotide 50 µg subcutaneously twice daily for 1–2 years (30 analysed after 2 losses), compared with an external control group of 38 patients who had received placebo (1 tablet/day) in a concurrent randomised trial (35 analysed after 3 early dropouts). This is a cohort-versus-external-control comparison, not a within-study randomisation.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 7 of 30 (23%) on octreotide versus 17 of 35 (48%) on placebo (p=0.043). The actuarial probability of remaining free of rebleeding was 77% versus 55% at 1 year and 68% versus 36% at 2 years (log rank p=0.030). Iron requirements were lower with octreotide (p<0.001); bleeding-episode counts and transfusion requirements did not differ significantly between groups, and major adverse events (1 vs 1) and mortality (0 vs 1) were similar.
cards.watchOut: External controls invite selection and era bias — this limb supports, and cannot substitute for, the randomised OCEAN comparison. The subcutaneous twice-daily regimen also differs from the monthly long-acting-release regimen tested in OCEAN.
cards.source: Junquera F, Saperas E, Videla S et al. Long-term efficacy of octreotide in the prevention of recurrent bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasia. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 17311647. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: IPD meta-analysis 2021: 212 patients pooled from 1 randomised trial and 10 cohort studies — transfusions fall from a mean 12.8 to 2.3 units on somatostatin analogues (relative IRR 0.18), 83% good responders
cards.summary: IPD meta-analysis 2021: 212 patients pooled from 1 randomised trial and 10 cohort studies — transfusions fall from a mean 12.8 to 2.3 units on somatostatin analogues (relative IRR 0.18), 83% good responders
cards.type: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021
cards.people: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis of somatostatin analogue therapy (octreotide or lanreotide) in gastrointestinal angiodysplasia: 11 eligible studies (one randomised controlled trial, ten cohort studies), individual data obtained or extracted for 212 patients with red-cell transfusion-dependent anaemia; median treatment and follow-up 12 months. The cohort limb is observational and is graded low-certainty by the authors.
cards.result: Somatostatin analogues reduced red-cell transfusions with a relative incidence rate ratio of 0.18 (95% CI 0.14–0.24; p<0.0001) — alongside the relative measure, the absolute mean fell from 12.8 units (95% CI 10.4–15.8) at baseline to 2.3 (1.9–2.9) on treatment, an absolute decrease of 10.5 units. A good response (≥50% reduction) occurred in 177 of 212 patients (83%). Response was worse for gastric angiodysplasias and better with octreotide than lanreotide (interaction analyses). Adverse events occurred in 18% and 5% discontinued for them; the commonest were loose stools, gallstones, flatulence and injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: Ten of the eleven pooled studies are cohorts comparing on-treatment with the same patients' baseline — a design that flatters the drug (regression to the mean after a bad bleeding year); the randomised OCEAN card above is the bias-controlled limb, and this pooled estimate should be read as its upper-bound companion.
cards.source: Goltstein LCMJ, Grooteman KV, Rocco A et al. Effectiveness and predictors of response to somatostatin analogues in patients with gastrointestinal angiodysplasias: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2021. PMID: 34508668. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42020213985. cards.headline: Synthesis: octreotide reduces transfusion requirements in angiodysplasia bleeding — randomised and pooled evidence agree; the sibling thalidomide shelf (#7113) covers a different drug for an overlapping population
cards.summary: Synthesis: octreotide reduces transfusion requirements in angiodysplasia bleeding — randomised and pooled evidence agree; the sibling thalidomide shelf (#7113) covers a different drug for an overlapping population
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above: the OCEAN randomised trial (n=62), the Junquera external-control comparison (70 patients enrolled) and the individual-patient-data meta-analysis (212 patients, mostly observational).
cards.result: The bias-controlled estimate is OCEAN's: about 10 fewer transfusion units over a year and about one fewer endoscopic procedure, in patients who entered heavily transfusion-dependent. The pooled and external-control limbs point the same way with larger apparent effects, as their designs would predict. No carded report establishes a mortality benefit. Cross-point in prose: thalidomide for recurrent bleeding from small-intestinal angiodysplasia is a separate drug question with its own randomised evidence, homed at shelf #7113 — the two shelves share a population, not an evidence base, and neither re-cards the other's trials.
cards.watchOut: OCEAN was open-label and Dutch; lanreotide's pooled performance was weaker than octreotide's, so the stamp belongs to octreotide, not automatically to the whole somatostatin-analogue class.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 38158089, 17311647, 34508668). Registry ID: NCT02384122; PROSPERO CRD42020213985 as carded. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Thalidomide for recurrent small-intestinal angiodysplasia bleeding: a 150-patient placebo-controlled trial found effective responses in 68.6% (100 mg) and 51.0% (50 mg) versus 16.0% on placebo
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent bleeding from small-intestinal angiodysplasia, does thalidomide (100 mg or 50 mg daily for four months) versus placebo reduce bleeding episodes over the following year?
shelves.mesh: Angiodysplasia/complications/drug therapy · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/drug therapy/etiology · Thalidomide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intestine, Small/blood supply · Recurrence
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one large, well-conducted placebo-controlled trial dominates and the syntheses agree with it. In the Chen 2023 multicentre trial (n=150; four months of treatment, at least a year of follow-up), an effective response — at least a 50% reduction in bleeding episodes in the year after treatment versus the year before — occurred in 68.6% on thalidomide 100 mg and 51.0% on 50 mg versus 16.0% on placebo. A meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis of the three randomised trials (279 patients, 87.1% small-intestinal) found the cumulative evidence already exceeded the required information size, and a 2026 systematic review of six studies (265 patients) reports the same direction, including the earlier iron-controlled randomised trial (response 71.4% vs 3.7%). The harm face is mandatory: thalidomide is teratogenic — pregnancy prevention is an absolute condition of use — and the trial's common adverse events were constipation, somnolence, limb numbness, peripheral oedema, dizziness and raised liver enzymes, with peripheral neuropathy the standing long-term concern. Cross-point in prose: octreotide (somatostatin analogues) for gastrointestinal angiodysplasia bleeding is the sibling drug question, homed at shelf #7112 with a distinct evidence base; neither shelf re-cards the other's trials.

cards.headline: Chen 2023: thalidomide versus placebo in 150 patients — effective response 68.6% (100 mg) and 51.0% (50 mg) versus 16.0% on placebo over the year after a 4-month course
cards.summary: Chen 2023: thalidomide versus placebo in 150 patients — effective response 68.6% (100 mg) and 51.0% (50 mg) versus 16.0% on placebo over the year after a 4-month course
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: One hundred and fifty patients with recurrent bleeding due to small-intestinal angiodysplasia (at least four bleeding episodes in the previous year), randomised in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial in China to thalidomide 100 mg daily (n=51), thalidomide 50 mg daily (n=49) or placebo (n=50) for 4 months, then followed for at least 1 year after treatment ended.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — effective response, a reduction of at least 50% in bleeding episodes during the year after treatment compared with the year before — occurred in 68.6% (100 mg), 51.0% (50 mg) and 16.0% (placebo) (p<0.001 for the three-group comparison). Secondary endpoints (cessation of bleeding without rebleeding, transfusion, hospitalisation for bleeding, bleeding duration, haemoglobin) supported the primary result. Adverse events were more common on thalidomide: constipation, somnolence, limb numbness, peripheral oedema, dizziness and elevated liver-enzyme levels.
cards.watchOut: Thalidomide is teratogenic — use requires strict pregnancy prevention — and causes cumulative peripheral neuropathy (limb numbness was among the trial's common events); the trial's 4-month course and 1-year follow-up do not define the safety of repeated or longer courses.
cards.source: Chen H, Wu S, Tang M et al. Thalidomide for Recurrent Bleeding Due to Small-Intestinal Angiodysplasia. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 37913505. Registry ID: NCT02707484. cards.headline: Song 2024: meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis of 3 randomised trials (279 patients) — thalidomide improves haemoglobin and response outcomes, and the cumulative evidence already exceeds the required information size
cards.summary: Song 2024: meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis of 3 randomised trials (279 patients) — thalidomide improves haemoglobin and response outcomes, and the cumulative evidence already exceeds the required information size
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis, Ther Adv Gastroenterol 2024
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of thalidomide in gastrointestinal angiodysplasias (searching CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and Chinese databases), with trial-sequential analysis and GRADE assessment: 3 randomised trials, 279 patients, of whom 87.1% had small-intestinal angiodysplasia. The Chen 2023 trial is the largest component — this synthesis overlaps it and is not an independent population.
cards.result: Thalidomide improved the mean change in haemoglobin (mean difference 3.06, 95% CI 2.66–3.46, as reported) without severe adverse effects occurring, and the effective response rate, cessation of bleeding, hospitalisation for bleeding, hospital-stay duration, transfused red-cell requirements and overall adverse-effect outcomes all favoured thalidomide over control. Trial-sequential analysis exceeded the required information sizes for all outcomes, with cumulative Z-curves crossing the monitoring boundaries; the authors grade almost all evidence moderate quality and recommend large real-world studies over further identical trials.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three pooled trials are small, so the pooled precision is largely the Chen trial restated; trial-sequential sufficiency applies to the tested comparison and population, not to rarer harms such as neuropathy.
cards.source: Song K, He K, Yan X et al. Efficacy and safety of thalidomide in gastrointestinal angiodysplasias: systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Khan 2026: systematic review of 6 studies (265 patients) — response rates consistently favour thalidomide, including 71.4% versus 3.7% in the earlier iron-controlled randomised trial, with neuropathy among the reported harms
cards.summary: Khan 2026: systematic review of 6 studies (265 patients) — response rates consistently favour thalidomide, including 71.4% versus 3.7% in the earlier iron-controlled randomised trial, with neuropathy among the reported harms
cards.people: Systematic review (1994 to February 2024) of clinical trials and case series with at least five adults treated with thalidomide for angiodysplasia-related gastrointestinal bleeding: six studies (two randomised trials, one retrospective observational study, three case series), 265 patients, median age 63.5 years, 37% male; angiodysplasia diagnosed by endoscopy, colonoscopy or push enteroscopy.
cards.result: Outcomes consistently favoured thalidomide: the Chen randomised trial's response gradient (68.6% at 100 mg, 51% at 50 mg) is restated, and the earlier Ge randomised trial found a response rate of 71.4% (20/28) on thalidomide versus 3.7% (1/27) on iron (risk difference 67.7%, 95% CI 51.1–84.2); one series reported an 84% response rate by haemoglobin improvement. Common adverse effects were constipation, dizziness, fatigue, limb numbness and peripheral neuropathy. The authors stress heterogeneity in dosing, outcome definitions and safety reporting.
cards.watchOut: Half the included studies are case series without controls, and the review's randomised content overlaps the Chen card — it corroborates direction, it does not multiply the independent evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a 4-month thalidomide course roughly triples-to-quadruples the chance of halving bleeding episodes versus placebo — benefit is LIKELY, and teratogenicity plus neuropathy bound its use; octreotide (#7112) is the sibling shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 4-month thalidomide course roughly triples-to-quadruples the chance of halving bleeding episodes versus placebo — benefit is LIKELY, and teratogenicity plus neuropathy bound its use; octreotide (#7112) is the sibling shelf
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above: the Chen 2023 placebo-controlled trial (n=150) and two syntheses (3 randomised trials, 279 patients; 6 studies, 265 patients) that substantially overlap it.
cards.result: The evidence structure is one large rigorous trial plus smaller concordant randomised data: absolute effective-response rates of 68.6% (100 mg) and 51.0% (50 mg) against 16.0% on placebo are the numbers to quote, with secondary outcomes (transfusion, hospitalisation, haemoglobin) aligned. That concordance supports LIKELY despite the single dominant trial. Cross-point in prose: for the same bleeding population treated with somatostatin analogues, see the octreotide shelf (#7112) — a different drug and a distinct evidence base; the choice between the two is not settled by any head-to-head trial in either shelf.
cards.watchOut: All randomised evidence is from China and from short (4-month) courses; long-term neuropathy risk and performance in other populations rest on the much weaker case-series limb.

shelves.title: Endoscopic versus surgical drainage of pancreatic pseudocyst: success is equivalent in the small randomised trials — endoscopy wins on hospital stay (2 vs 6 days) and cost, not on cure
shelves.question: In adults with a symptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst suitable for either approach, does endoscopic (including EUS-guided) cystogastrostomy/drainage versus surgical cystogastrostomy achieve equivalent success with shorter stay and lower cost?
shelves.mesh: Pancreatic Pseudocyst/surgery · Drainage/methods · Endoscopy, Digestive System/methods · Endosonography · Laparoscopy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a procedure-strategy (GAP-E) shelf, confined to pseudocyst (no or minimal solid debris); walled-off necrosis is a different collection with its own step-up shelves and is not re-carded here. The randomised trials are small and single-centre, so equivalence claims are necessarily soft: in the one head-to-head trial of endoscopic versus open surgical cystogastrostomy (Varadarajulu 2013, n=40), recurrence, success, complications and re-interventions did not differ (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes), while stay (median 2 vs 6 days) and cost ($7,011 vs $15,052) favoured endoscopy. The endoscopic-versus-laparoscopic trial (Garg 2020, n=60) mixed pseudocyst with walled-off necrosis and is carded as a mixed-population limb, not pure pseudocyst evidence. A third randomised trial answers the within-endoscopy question (EUS-guided versus conventional transmural drainage, Park 2009), and a systematic review of ten comparative studies — most of them cohort comparisons, labelled observational — reaches the same shape of conclusion. Technique has moved since the earliest trial (lumen-apposing metal stents postdate much of this record), so the evidence is dated on its face. Observational and small-trial structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Varadarajulu 2013: endoscopic versus surgical cystogastrostomy in 40 patients — no recurrence on endoscopy versus 1 on surgery, no difference in success or complications (the treatment made no difference), but stay 2 versus 6 days and cost $7,011 versus $15,052
cards.summary: Varadarajulu 2013: endoscopic versus surgical cystogastrostomy in 40 patients — no recurrence on endoscopy versus 1 on surgery, no difference in success or complications (the treatment made no difference), but stay 2 versus 6 days and cost $7,011 versus $15,052
cards.people: Forty patients with pancreatic pseudocysts at a single centre, randomised open-label to endoscopic cystogastrostomy (n=20) or surgical cystogastrostomy (n=20); primary endpoint pseudocyst recurrence over 24 months of follow-up, with treatment success/failure, complications, re-interventions, hospital stay, health scores and total costs as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: No endoscopy patient had a recurrence versus one surgical patient; there were no differences in treatment success, complications or re-interventions between the groups (the treatment made no difference on efficacy outcomes). Hospital stay was shorter with endoscopy (median 2 vs 6 days, p<0.001), physical and mental health component scores improved more over follow-up (p=.019 and p=.025), and mean total cost was lower ($7,011 vs $15,052, p=.003).
cards.watchOut: N = 40 at one centre — far too small to prove equivalence for uncommon harms, and the endoscopic technique of 2013 (plastic stents era) predates lumen-apposing metal stents; the cost figures are single-centre US dollars of that period.
cards.source: Varadarajulu S, Bang JY, Sutton BS et al. Equal efficacy of endoscopic and surgical cystogastrostomy for pancreatic pseudocyst drainage in a randomized trial. Gastroenterology. 2013. PMID: 23732774. Registry ID: NCT00826501. cards.headline: Park 2009: EUS-guided versus conventional transmural endoscopic drainage in 60 patients — technical success 94% versus 72%, with all 8 conventional failures rescued by EUS; resolution rates do not differ
cards.summary: Park 2009: EUS-guided versus conventional transmural endoscopic drainage in 60 patients — technical success 94% versus 72%, with all 8 conventional failures rescued by EUS; resolution rates do not differ
cards.type: Prospective randomised technique trial (EUS-guided vs conventional endoscopic), Endoscopy 2009
cards.people: Sixty consecutive patients with pancreatic pseudocysts randomised prospectively to EUS-guided transmural drainage (n=31) or conventional transmural drainage (n=29); technical success, complications and short- and long-term resolution were assessed prospectively. This card answers the within-endoscopy technique question, not endoscopy versus surgery.
cards.result: Technical success was higher with EUS guidance: 94% (29/31) versus 72% (21/29) (p=0.039, intention-to-treat). All 8 conventional failures — nonbulging pseudocysts — crossed over to EUS-guided drainage successfully. Complications were 7% versus 10% (p=0.67). Short-term resolution was 97% (28/29) versus 91% (19/21) (p=0.565) and long-term per-protocol success 89% (33/37) versus 86% (18/21) (p=0.696) — no difference in clinical resolution. The authors conclude both are first-line for bulging pseudocysts, with EUS preferred for nonbulging ones.
cards.watchOut: Long-term denominators are per-protocol and include crossover patients (33/37 in the EUS group), so the long-term comparison is no longer a pure randomised contrast; the trial predates modern EUS stent practice.
cards.source: Park DH, Lee SS, Moon SH et al. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided versus conventional transmural drainage for pancreatic pseudocysts: a prospective randomized trial. Endoscopy. 2009. PMID: 19798610. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garg 2020: endoscopic versus laparoscopic drainage in 60 patients with pseudocyst OR walled-off necrosis (mixed population, labelled) — overall success 90% versus 93.3%, but post-procedure infection higher with endoscopy (19 vs 9 events)
cards.summary: Garg 2020: endoscopic versus laparoscopic drainage in 60 patients with pseudocyst OR walled-off necrosis (mixed population, labelled) — overall success 90% versus 93.3%, but post-procedure infection higher with endoscopy (19 vs 9 events)
cards.type: Randomised trial in a mixed pseudocyst/walled-off-necrosis population, Surg Endosc 2020
cards.people: Sixty patients with symptomatic pseudocysts or walled-off necrosis after acute pancreatitis, suitable for either approach, randomised to endoscopic transmural cystogastrostomy (n=30, with lavage/necrosectomy step-up for infected collections) or laparoscopic cystogastrostomy (n=30); collections had <30% debris. Mixed-population limb — not pure pseudocyst evidence.
cards.result: Initial success was 76.6% endoscopic versus 83.3% laparoscopic (p=0.7) and overall success 90% (27/30) versus 93.3% (28/30) (p=1.0) — no difference in resolution (the treatment made no difference on success). Two patients in each group crossed to the other modality for persistent collections. Post-procedure infection was higher in the endoscopic group (19 vs 9 events, p=0.01), requiring endoscopic re-intervention. The authors conclude the choice should rest on expertise and patient preference.
cards.watchOut: Walled-off necrosis is biologically different from pseudocyst (solid debris, infection risk) — pooling it here dilutes the pseudocyst-specific read, which is why this shelf keeps the Varadarajulu pure-pseudocyst trial as its head-to-head anchor.
cards.source: Garg PK, Meena D, Babu D et al. Endoscopic versus laparoscopic drainage of pseudocyst and walled-off necrosis following acute pancreatitis: a randomized trial. Surgical endoscopy. 2020. PMID: 31140002. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Teoh 2016 systematic review: 10 comparative studies (3 randomised, the rest cohort comparisons — observational) — endoscopic and surgical success and adverse events comparable, with stay, cost and quality of life favouring EUS-guided drainage
cards.summary: Teoh 2016 systematic review: 10 comparative studies (3 randomised, the rest cohort comparisons — observational) — endoscopic and surgical success and adverse events comparable, with stay, cost and quality of life favouring EUS-guided drainage
cards.type: Systematic review of comparative (mostly cohort) studies, World J Gastrointest Endosc 2016
cards.people: Systematic review of comparative studies of pancreatic pseudocyst drainage published 1980–May 2014: ten studies, of which three were randomised trials and the remainder cohort comparisons (observational evidence, labelled as such) — four comparing percutaneous versus surgical drainage, three EUS-guided endoscopic versus surgical drainage, and three EUS versus conventional endoscopic drainage. No pooled patient count is stated in the record.
cards.result: For EUS-guided versus surgical drainage, clinical success and adverse-event rates appeared comparable, while the EUS approach reduced hospital stay and cost and improved quality of life. For percutaneous versus surgical drainage, a large national study found surgery associated with lower mortality and adverse events than the percutaneous approach. EUS-guided drainage had better success than conventional endoscopic drainage for nonbulging cysts. The authors call for large randomised studies with current pseudocyst definitions and longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative review without pooled effect sizes, resting mostly on cohort comparisons subject to selection bias (sicker or anatomically unfavourable patients are channelled to surgery or percutaneous routes); it corroborates, and cannot upgrade, the small randomised limbs.
cards.source: Teoh AY, Dhir V, Jin ZD et al. Systematic review comparing endoscopic, percutaneous and surgical pancreatic pseudocyst drainage. World journal of gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2016. PMID: 27014427. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: for a pseudocyst suitable for either route, drainage success is equivalent and endoscopy's advantages are stay, cost and recovery — POSSIBLE, on small dated trials plus observational comparisons
cards.summary: Synthesis: for a pseudocyst suitable for either route, drainage success is equivalent and endoscopy's advantages are stay, cost and recovery — POSSIBLE, on small dated trials plus observational comparisons
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: two small single-centre randomised trials of endoscopic versus surgical drainage (one pure pseudocyst, n=40; one mixed with walled-off necrosis, n=60), one randomised endoscopic-technique trial (n=60), and one systematic review of ten comparative studies.
cards.result: No carded evidence shows surgery draining pseudocysts more successfully than endoscopy (the treatment made no difference on success or recurrence in the head-to-head trial); endoscopy's demonstrated advantages are a median 4-day shorter stay, roughly half the cost in the US single-centre trial, and better recovery scores. Within endoscopy, EUS guidance raises technical success, decisively for nonbulging cysts. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE: the trials are small, single-centre and predate lumen-apposing metal stents, and the supporting comparative literature is observational.
cards.watchOut: Collections with substantial solid debris (walled-off necrosis) follow a different, step-up evidence base homed elsewhere; this shelf's equivalence claim must not be extended to them.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 23732774, 19798610, 31140002, 27014427). Registry ID: NCT00826501 as carded. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.question: In healthy general-population adults, what is normal bowel habit — defecation frequency per week, usual timing and stool form — and how wide is the range (the 'three times a day to three times a week' rule) by sex and population?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 63-64 (GI motility/defecation reflexes); Boron & Boulpaep (GI motility); colonic transit — the mechanism under the habit — is homed on pack #6439. The prospective East Bristol study (838 men, 1,059 women) found the textbook picture wrong in detail: once daily was a minority habit, a regular 24-hour cycle appeared in only 40% of men and 33% of women, a third of women defecated less often than daily and 1% once a week or less, and symptom-free stool types were only 56-61% of all stools (Heaton 1992). A south-western Nigerian community sample (N = 506) sits at the frequent end: 97.2% defecate at least daily (Jemilohun 2021). Symptom criteria cut across frequency: 24.5% of Dutch adults (N = 1,259) meet Rome III constipation criteria and 7.9% faecal-incontinence criteria, while about half of each group call their own habit good (Meinds 2017). The 'three a day to three a week' rule is the envelope of these distributions, not their centre. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: East Bristol prospective study (838 men + 1,059 women): once daily is a minority habit — a regular 24-hour cycle in only 40% of men and 33% of women; 1% of women defecate once a week or less (Heaton 1992)
cards.summary: East Bristol prospective study (838 men + 1,059 women): once daily is a minority habit — a regular 24-hour cycle in only 40% of men and 33% of women; 1% of women defecate once a week or less (Heaton 1992)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prospective general-population bowel habit and stool form)
cards.people: 838 men and 1,059 women, 72.2% of a random stratified sample of the East Bristol general population; questionnaire plus prospective records of three consecutive defecations with stool form on a validated six-point scale from hard round lumps to mushy.
cards.result: Although once daily was the most common single habit, it was a minority practice in both sexes: a regular 24-hour cycle was apparent in only 40% of men and 33% of women, and a further 7% of men and 4% of women had a regular twice- or thrice-daily habit — most people had irregular bowels. A third of women defecated less often than daily and 1% once a week or less. Stools at the constipated end of the scale were passed more often by women than men; women of childbearing age were shifted toward constipation and irregularity compared with older women. 'Normal' stool types (least likely to evoke symptoms) accounted for only 56% of stools in women and 61% in men. Most defecations occurred in the early morning, earlier in men than women. Age otherwise had little effect.
cards.watchOut: A 1992 UK population on its era's diet, using a six-point stool scale that predates the seven-point Bristol scale: the frequency distribution and the irregularity finding are the durable content.
cards.source: Heaton KW et al. Gut. 1992. PMID: 1624166. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Defecation/physiology · Feces · Female · Gastrointestinal Transit/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Sex Factors · Time Factors

cards.headline: South-western Nigerian community study (N = 506, ages 18-70): 97.2% defecate at least daily — 70.8% once, 21.9% twice, 4.5% more than twice daily (Jemilohun 2021)
cards.summary: South-western Nigerian community study (N = 506, ages 18-70): 97.2% defecate at least daily — 70.8% once, 21.9% twice, 4.5% more than twice daily (Jemilohun 2021)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (community bowel habits, Bristol scale and Rome IV)
cards.people: 506 adults aged 18-70 years in a community-based cross-sectional survey in south-western Nigeria; bowel habits by questionnaire with the Bristol Stool Scale shown to each respondent, plus Rome IV bowel-disorder questions.
cards.result: 492 participants (97.2%) had at least one bowel motion per day: 358 (70.8%) once daily, 111 (21.9%) twice daily and 23 (4.5%) more than twice daily; 9 (1.8%) defecated once in two days and 5 (1.0%) once in three or more days. Bowel-movement frequency showed no significant relationship with age or gender. Among bowel-movement disorders present at least 30% of the time over 3 months, hard stools were commonest (13.0%) and fewer than three motions per week least frequent (5.3%). The authors attribute the generally low disorder frequencies in part to a fibre-rich African diet.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported habit in one Nigerian region: the near-universal daily motion contrasts with Bristol's irregular majority — diet, reporting method and culture all sit inside that contrast, so neither distribution is a universal norm.
cards.source: Jemilohun AC et al. West African journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34174181. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Constipation · Cross-Sectional Studies · Habits · Humans · Movement Disorders · Nigeria

cards.headline: Dutch general-population study (N = 1,259): by Rome III criteria 24.5% are constipated and 7.9% faecally incontinent — yet about half of each group call their own bowel habit 'good' or 'very good' (Meinds 2017)
cards.summary: Dutch general-population study (N = 1,259): by Rome III criteria 24.5% are constipated and 7.9% faecally incontinent — yet about half of each group call their own bowel habit 'good' or 'very good' (Meinds 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population prevalence of constipation and FI by Rome III)
cards.people: 1,259 respondents, a cross-section of the Dutch general population, completing the Groningen Defecation & Fecal Continence checklist; constipation and faecal incontinence (FI) defined by Rome III criteria.
cards.result: Constipation prevalence was 24.5% (95% CI 22.1-26.8), FI 7.9% (95% CI 6.4-9.4), and both together 3.5% (95% CI 2.5-4.5); constipated respondents were 2.7 times more likely to have FI (95% CI 1.8-4.0). Yet 48.7% of constipated respondents, 35.0% with FI and 38.6% with both rated their bowel habits 'good' or 'very good', and about half of each group had never discussed the complaints with anyone — symptom-criteria prevalence and self-judged 'normal habit' are different quantities.
cards.watchOut: Criteria-based prevalence, not a frequency distribution: this card bounds how much of a general population falls outside 'normal habit' by symptom criteria, complementing the frequency studies.
cards.source: Meinds RJ et al. International journal of colorectal disease. 2017. PMID: 27913883. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 'normal' bowel habit spans roughly three motions a day to three a week — but the centre of the distribution is population-specific: irregular and often less-than-daily in Bristol, at-least-daily in 97% in Nigeria, and criteria-constipated in a quarter of Dutch adults
cards.summary: Synthesis: 'normal' bowel habit spans roughly three motions a day to three a week — but the centre of the distribution is population-specific: irregular and often less-than-daily in Bristol, at-least-daily in 97% in Nigeria, and criteria-constipated in a quarter of Dutch adults
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (ch. 63-64, gastrointestinal motility and defecation reflexes) and Boron & Boulpaep (GI motility); the transit mechanism underneath the habit is homed on the colonic transit time shelf (pack #6439), cross-pointed in prose. The classic prospective data (Heaton 1992; 1,897 adults) demolish the tidy textbook picture: once daily is a minority habit, only 40% of men and 33% of women keep a regular 24-hour cycle, a third of women defecate less often than daily and 1% once a week or less, with early-morning predominance. A Nigerian community sample sits at the other end — 97.2% defecate at least daily (Jemilohun 2021) — showing the distribution moves with population and diet. Symptom criteria cut across both: 24.5% of Dutch adults meet Rome III constipation criteria while half of them rate their habit good (Meinds 2017). The folk rule 'three times a day to three times a week' survives as the outer envelope of these distributions, not as a description of any one population's centre. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Frequency alone does not define normality: stool form, regularity and symptoms separate the distributions' healthy bulk from their tails, and each population study's diet and method are part of its numbers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heaton KW et al. Gut. 1992 (PMID: 1624166); Jemilohun AC et al. West African journal of medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34174181); Meinds RJ et al. shelves.title: Golimumab in ulcerative colitis (PURSUIT): induction response 51-55% vs 30% on placebo; maintained response in responders 47-50% vs 31% through week 54
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis naive to TNF antagonists, does subcutaneous golimumab induce clinical response/remission and maintain response versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Adult · Aminosalicylic Acids/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Azathioprine/therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Mercaptopurine/therapeutic use · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Remission Induction/methods · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit, from a single programme (PURSUIT). Induction (774 patients in the phase 3 portion): week-6 clinical response 51.0% (200/100 mg) and 54.9% (400/200 mg) versus 30.3% on placebo. Maintenance (464 induction responders re-randomised — a responder-enriched design): response maintained through week 54 in 47.0% (50 mg) and 49.7% (100 mg) versus 31.2% on placebo. The third card is a pharmacokinetic/exposure-response report of the same programme, not a separate trial. Harms include serious infection and tuberculosis, as with other TNF antagonists.

cards.headline: PURSUIT-SC induction (Sandborn 2014): golimumab 200/100 mg and 400/200 mg gave week-6 clinical response in 51.0% and 54.9% versus 30.3% on placebo in TNF-antagonist-naive ulcerative colitis
cards.summary: PURSUIT-SC induction (Sandborn 2014): golimumab 200/100 mg and 400/200 mg gave week-6 clinical response in 51.0% and 54.9% versus 30.3% on placebo in TNF-antagonist-naive ulcerative colitis
cards.type: Phase 2/3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled induction trial (PURSUIT-SC), golimumab vs placebo
cards.people: Integrated phase 2 dose-finding and phase 3 dose-confirmation programme in 1,064 adults with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (Mayo score 6-12, endoscopic subscore ≥2) naive to TNF antagonists despite conventional treatment; 774 patients were in the phase 3 portion. Golimumab was given subcutaneously at weeks 0 and 2 (100/50 mg phase 2 only, 200/100 mg, or 400/200 mg).
cards.result: In phase 3, week-6 clinical response was 51.0% (200/100 mg) and 54.9% (400/200 mg) versus 30.3% on placebo (both P≤.0001) — absolute gains of about 21 and 25 percentage points. Clinical remission, mucosal healing and IBDQ score changes were also significantly greater with golimumab (P≤.0014). Serious adverse events were 3.0% in the golimumab groups versus 6.1% on placebo, and serious infections 0.5% versus 1.8%; one patient in the 400/200 mg group died from surgical complications of an ischiorectal abscess.
cards.watchOut: One programme (PURSUIT), not two independent programmes — the induction, maintenance and pharmacokinetic reports on this shelf are reports of the same programme. The phase 2 and phase 3 portions were integrated in this single report.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Subcutaneous golimumab induces clinical response and remission in patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 23735746. Registry ID: NCT00487539. cards.headline: PURSUIT-M maintenance (Sandborn 2014): among induction responders, clinical response was maintained through week 54 in 47.0% (50 mg) and 49.7% (100 mg) versus 31.2% on placebo
cards.summary: PURSUIT-M maintenance (Sandborn 2014): among induction responders, clinical response was maintained through week 54 in 47.0% (50 mg) and 49.7% (100 mg) versus 31.2% on placebo
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind maintenance trial (PURSUIT-M), golimumab 50/100 mg every 4 weeks vs placebo, in induction responders only
cards.people: 464 adults who had responded to golimumab induction in the PURSUIT programme, re-randomised to placebo or golimumab 50 mg or 100 mg every 4 weeks through week 52 (responder-enriched maintenance design). Patients who had responded to placebo induction continued placebo; induction nonresponders received 100 mg golimumab and were not part of this randomised comparison.
cards.result: Clinical response was maintained through week 54 in 47.0% on 50 mg and 49.7% on 100 mg versus 31.2% on placebo (P=.010 and P<.001) — absolute gains of about 16 and 19 percentage points. At weeks 30 and 54, clinical remission and mucosal healing on 100 mg were 27.8% and 42.4% versus 15.6% and 26.6% on placebo (P=.004 and P=.002). Serious adverse events were 7.7% (placebo), 8.4% (50 mg) and 14.3% (100 mg); serious infections 1.9%, 3.2% and 3.2%. Among all patients given golimumab in the study, 3 died (sepsis, tuberculosis, cardiac failure — all on 100 mg) and 4 developed active tuberculosis.
cards.watchOut: Responder-enriched design: only patients who already responded to golimumab induction were re-randomised, so these maintenance rates do not apply to an unselected starting population. Same PURSUIT programme as the induction card.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Subcutaneous golimumab maintains clinical response in patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 23770005. Registry ID: NCT00488631. cards.headline: PURSUIT pharmacokinetics / exposure-response (Adedokun 2017): higher serum golimumab concentrations were associated with higher response rates; proposed target concentrations 2.5 µg/ml at induction week 6 and 1.4 µg/ml trough in maintenance (programme report, not a new trial)
cards.summary: PURSUIT pharmacokinetics / exposure-response (Adedokun 2017): higher serum golimumab concentrations were associated with higher response rates; proposed target concentrations 2.5 µg/ml at induction week 6 and 1.4 µg/ml trough in maintenance (programme report, not a new trial)
cards.type: Programme report: pharmacokinetic and exposure-response analysis of the PURSUIT induction and maintenance studies (same programme — not independent efficacy evidence)
cards.people: Patients from the PURSUIT induction (N=1,064) and maintenance (N=464) studies with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis — the same patients as the two cards above.
cards.result: Serum golimumab concentrations were approximately dose-proportional: week-6 median concentrations were 0.78, 1.78 and 4.01 µg/ml after 100/50 mg, 200/100 mg and 400/200 mg induction. Maintenance trough medians ranged 0.69-0.83 µg/ml (50 mg) and 1.33-1.58 µg/ml (100 mg). Higher concentrations were associated with higher efficacy response rates in both phases. Body weight, antibody-to-golimumab status, serum albumin, alkaline phosphatase, faecal markers, C-reactive protein and pancolitis were associated with exposure. The authors proposed target concentrations of 2.5 µg/ml (induction week 6) and 1.4 µg/ml (maintenance trough), requiring prospective validation.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic programme report of the same PURSUIT patients, not a third trial. The proposed target concentrations are derived, not prospectively validated. A paediatric PURSUIT-2 report exists but was not carded: its design was not verified as randomised for this shelf.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme (PURSUIT) — induction response 51-55% versus 30% on placebo at week 6, and, in induction responders only, maintained response 47-50% versus 31% through week 54
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Subcutaneous golimumab induced clinical response in about half of TNF-antagonist-naive patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (51.0% and 54.9% for the two phase 3 dose regimens versus 30.3% on placebo at week 6), and maintained response through week 54 in 47.0-49.7% of induction responders versus 31.2% on placebo. The third card is a pharmacokinetic report of the same programme, not independent evidence. Harms were those of TNF antagonism, including serious infection and, in the maintenance study, tuberculosis cases and three deaths among golimumab-treated patients (all on 100 mg).

shelves.title: Certolizumab pegol in Crohn's disease (PRECISE): modest response gain, no remission difference in PRECISE 1; maintained response 63% vs 36% in responders in PRECISE 2
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, does certolizumab pegol (400 mg subcutaneous) versus placebo induce response and maintain response/remission, including after prior loss of response to infliximab?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Antibodies · Antibodies, Antinuclear · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Certolizumab Pegol · Crohn Disease/classification/drug therapy/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin Fab Fragments/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Remission Induction · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit — modest in unselected patients, clearer in responders. PRECISE 1 (662 randomised): response 35% vs 27% at week 6 and 23% vs 16% at weeks 6 and 26, with NO significant remission difference. PRECISE 2 (428 of 668 induction patients who responded, re-randomised — responder-enriched): maintained response 63% vs 36% and remission 48% vs 29% through week 26. WELCOME (infliximab-experienced; dose-interval comparison, no placebo) showed quality-of-life gains, and PRECISE 4 showed uncontrolled recapture after relapse. Certolizumab's Crohn's licence is US-only (never EU-approved for Crohn's).

cards.headline: PRECISE 1 (Sandborn 2007): certolizumab pegol 400 mg gave a modest response gain — 35% vs 27% at week 6 in the overall population — with NO significant difference in remission
cards.summary: PRECISE 1 (Sandborn 2007): certolizumab pegol 400 mg gave a modest response gain — 35% vs 27% at week 6 in the overall population — with NO significant difference in remission
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PRECISE 1), certolizumab pegol 400 mg vs placebo, induction and continued treatment to week 26
cards.people: 662 adults with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, randomised to certolizumab pegol 400 mg or placebo subcutaneously at weeks 0, 2 and 4 and then every 4 weeks, stratified by baseline C-reactive protein (CRP).
cards.result: In patients with baseline CRP ≥10 mg/L, response at week 6 was 37% versus 26% (P=0.04), and response at both weeks 6 and 26 was 22% versus 12% (P=0.05). In the overall population, response at week 6 was 35% versus 27% (P=0.02) and at both weeks 6 and 26, 23% versus 16% (P=0.02) — absolute gains of 7-11 percentage points. Remission rates at weeks 6 and 26 did NOT differ significantly (P=0.17). Serious adverse events: 10% versus 7%; serious infections 2% versus <1%. Antibodies to the drug developed in 8% and antinuclear antibodies in 2% of the certolizumab group.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is a response benefit, not a remission benefit: remission did not differ significantly in this trial. Absolute response gains were modest (7-11 percentage points).
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Certolizumab pegol for the treatment of Crohn's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17634458. Registry ID: NCT00152490. cards.headline: PRECISE 2 (Schreiber 2007): in week-6 responders, continued certolizumab maintained response through week 26 in 63% vs 36% on placebo, and remission in 48% vs 29%
cards.summary: PRECISE 2 (Schreiber 2007): in week-6 responders, continued certolizumab maintained response through week 26 in 63% vs 36% on placebo, and remission in 48% vs 29%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind maintenance trial (PRECISE 2), certolizumab pegol 400 mg every 4 weeks vs placebo, in induction responders only
cards.people: 668 adults received open-label certolizumab pegol 400 mg induction at weeks 0, 2 and 4; the 428 (64%) with a clinical response at week 6 were re-randomised to certolizumab pegol 400 mg or placebo every 4 weeks through week 24, with follow-up to week 26 (responder-enriched maintenance design).
cards.result: Among responders with baseline CRP ≥10 mg/L (the primary endpoint population), response was maintained through week 26 in 62% on certolizumab versus 34% on placebo (P<0.001); in the intention-to-treat responder population, 63% versus 36% (P<0.001). Remission at week 26 among responders was 48% versus 29% (P<0.001). Efficacy was also shown in patients previously treated with infliximab and in those who had not been. Infectious serious adverse events (including one case of pulmonary tuberculosis) occurred in 3% versus <1%. Antinuclear antibodies developed in 8% and antibodies against certolizumab pegol in 9% of patients who entered induction.
cards.watchOut: Responder-enriched: only the 64% who responded to open-label induction were randomised, so these rates do not describe an unselected starting population. Same PRECISE programme family as PRECISE 1, in a separate population.
cards.source: Schreiber S et al. Maintenance therapy with certolizumab pegol for Crohn's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17634459. Registry ID: NCT00152425. cards.headline: WELCOME (Feagan 2011): in patients who had lost response to or could not tolerate infliximab, certolizumab every 2 or every 4 weeks improved work productivity, daily activity and quality of life through week 26 — a health-outcomes report of the WELCOME trial
cards.summary: WELCOME (Feagan 2011): in patients who had lost response to or could not tolerate infliximab, certolizumab every 2 or every 4 weeks improved work productivity, daily activity and quality of life through week 26 — a health-outcomes report of the WELCOME trial
cards.type: Randomised double-blind dose-interval trial (WELCOME), certolizumab pegol 400 mg every 2 weeks vs every 4 weeks after open-label induction, in infliximab-experienced patients — health-outcomes report
cards.people: Patients with active Crohn's disease who had previously responded to infliximab but lost response or could not tolerate it; they received open-label certolizumab pegol induction and were randomised to double-blind maintenance with certolizumab pegol 400 mg every 2 weeks or every 4 weeks through week 24, evaluated at week 26. The fetched abstract record does not state the total number randomised.
cards.result: Baseline quality-of-life burden was representative of moderately to severely active Crohn's disease. Health-related quality of life (Inflammatory Bowel Disease Questionnaire), daily activity and work productivity (Work Productivity and Activity Impairment: CD questionnaire) improved in both dosing groups as early as week 6 and were maintained through week 26, with similar benefits for every-2-week and every-4-week dosing. This report presents health-outcome endpoints; it has no placebo arm — both randomised groups received certolizumab.
cards.watchOut: A different population (infliximab-experienced) and a different comparison (dose interval, no placebo): do not pool this with the PRECISE placebo-controlled limbs. The abstract record does not state the randomised N, and none is printed here rather than guessed.
cards.source: Feagan BG et al. Randomised clinical trial: improvement in health outcomes with certolizumab pegol in patients with active Crohn's disease with prior loss of response to infliximab.
