cards.headline: PRECISE 4 (Sandborn 2010): after relapse, reinduction (after drug interruption) or one extra dose (on continuous therapy) recaptured response in 63-65% at week 4, maintained in 55-59% of responders to week 52 — open-label, no control group
cards.summary: PRECISE 4 (Sandborn 2010): after relapse, reinduction (after drug interruption) or one extra dose (on continuous therapy) recaptured response in 63-65% at week 4, maintained in 55-59% of responders to week 52 — open-label, no control group
cards.type: Open-label extension study (PRECISE 4) of PRECISE 2 relapsers — reinduction / extra-dose recapture, uncontrolled
cards.people: 124 patients who had responded to certolizumab induction in PRECISE 2 and then relapsed before week 26 — 49 who had been on continuous certolizumab therapy and 75 whose therapy had been interrupted (placebo in PRECISE 2) — entered this open-label extension.
cards.result: At week 4 of PRECISE 4, response (Harvey-Bradshaw Index) was 63% in patients who relapsed on continuous therapy (treated with a single extra 400 mg dose) and 65% after drug interruption (treated with reinduction at weeks 0, 2 and 4, then maintenance every 4 weeks). Response was maintained in 55% and 59% of these responders, respectively, through week 52.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, in a selected relapser population from PRECISE 2: recapture percentages have no comparator and cannot be read as placebo-controlled efficacy. A programme report of the PRECISE family, not an independent trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: certolizumab gives a modest response benefit — PRECISE 1 response +7 to +11 percentage points with no significant remission difference; PRECISE 2, in responders only, maintained response 63% vs 36% and remission 48% vs 29% at week 26
cards.summary: Synthesis: certolizumab gives a modest response benefit — PRECISE 1 response +7 to +11 percentage points with no significant remission difference; PRECISE 2, in responders only, maintained response 63% vs 36% and remission 48% vs 29% at week 26
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the PRECISE programme, certolizumab pegol 400 mg produced modest response gains over placebo in unselected patients (PRECISE 1: 35% vs 27% at week 6; 23% vs 16% at weeks 6 and 26) without a significant remission difference in that trial, while in the responder-enriched PRECISE 2 maintenance trial continued treatment maintained response (63% vs 36%) and remission (48% vs 29%) through week 26. WELCOME adds quality-of-life and work-productivity improvements in infliximab-experienced patients (no placebo arm), and PRECISE 4 shows uncontrolled recapture after relapse. Certolizumab's Crohn's licence is US-only — it was never approved for Crohn's disease in the EU.

shelves.title: Mongersen in Crohn's disease: a failed programme — phase 2 remission 55-65% vs 10% was not reproduced in phase 3 (22.8% vs 25% on placebo); batch controversy on the face
shelves.question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does mongersen (GED-0301, oral SMAD7 antisense oligonucleotide) versus placebo induce clinical remission?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Oligonucleotides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Oligonucleotides, Antisense/therapeutic use · Remission Induction · Smad7 Protein/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme, presented as failed. The phase 2 trial reported striking day-15 remission after only 2 weeks of treatment (55% at 40 mg, 65% at 160 mg, versus 10% on placebo), but the phase 3 trial (701 randomised, terminated for futility) found week-12 remission of 22.8% on mongersen versus 25% on placebo, with placebo ahead on endoscopic response. A later report raised the possibility that the phase 2 result depended on a pharmacologically active batch — two batches used in the phase 3 programme did not inhibit SMAD7 in vitro — and that controversy is on the face of this shelf, not smoothed over.

cards.headline: Phase 2 (Monteleone 2015): 2 weeks of mongersen 40 mg and 160 mg gave day-15 remission in 55% and 65% versus 10% on placebo — the striking result the phase 3 trial later failed to reproduce
cards.summary: Phase 2 (Monteleone 2015): 2 weeks of mongersen 40 mg and 160 mg gave day-15 remission in 55% and 65% versus 10% on placebo — the striking result the phase 3 trial later failed to reproduce
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, mongersen 10/40/160 mg daily for 2 weeks vs placebo
cards.people: Adults with active, steroid-dependent/resistant Crohn's disease, randomised to mongersen 10, 40 or 160 mg daily or placebo for only 2 weeks. The fetched abstract record does not state the total number randomised, and no total N is printed here rather than guessed from outside the record.
cards.result: Clinical remission at day 15 (Crohn's Disease Activity Index <150, maintained at least 2 weeks) was reached by 55% on 40 mg and 65% on 160 mg versus 10% on placebo (P<0.001); the 10 mg group (12%) did not differ from placebo. Clinical response at day 28 was 37% (10 mg), 58% (40 mg) and 72% (160 mg) versus 17% on placebo. Most adverse events were complications and symptoms of Crohn's disease itself.
cards.watchOut: Treatment lasted only 2 weeks and the primary endpoint was day-15 remission — this is not durable disease control. Read this card together with the phase 3 failure and the batch-controversy card below: the phase 2 result was not reproduced.

cards.headline: Phase 2 post-hoc report (Monteleone 2016): remission advantages for 40 mg and 160 mg appeared across disease-duration and CRP subgroups, and were clearest at lower baseline CDAI — a post-hoc analysis of the same phase 2 trial, not a new trial
cards.summary: Phase 2 post-hoc report (Monteleone 2016): remission advantages for 40 mg and 160 mg appeared across disease-duration and CRP subgroups, and were clearest at lower baseline CDAI — a post-hoc analysis of the same phase 2 trial, not a new trial
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of the phase 2 mongersen trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same phase 2 trial population as the card above (steroid-dependent/resistant active Crohn's disease; mongersen 10/40/160 mg or placebo for 2 weeks, followed for 10 weeks), analysed post hoc by disease duration (<5 / ≥5 years), hsCRP (<3 / ≥3 mg/L) and baseline CDAI (≤260 / >260).
cards.result: Remission and response rates were significantly higher on mongersen 40 and 160 mg (not 10 mg) than placebo, independent of disease duration and hsCRP. Patients with baseline CDAI ≤260 had significantly higher remission on both higher doses; with CDAI >260, remission was statistically greater on 160 mg and numerically better on 40 mg. Adverse event rates were similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of a single small phase 2 trial whose headline result the phase 3 trial did not reproduce. Subgroup consistency cannot rescue a result that failed confirmatory testing.

cards.headline: Phase 3 (Sands 2020): mongersen did NOT work — week-12 remission 22.8% on GED-0301 versus 25% on placebo (P=0.62), with placebo ahead on endoscopic response and clinical response; the programme was terminated early for futility
cards.summary: Phase 3 (Sands 2020): mongersen did NOT work — week-12 remission 22.8% on GED-0301 versus 25% on placebo (P=0.62), with placebo ahead on endoscopic response and clinical response; the programme was terminated early for futility
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, mongersen (GED-0301) regimens vs placebo — terminated prematurely for futility
cards.people: 701 patients with active Crohn's disease randomised (1:1:1:1) to placebo or one of three once-daily oral GED-0301 (mongersen) regimens built around 160 mg for 12 weeks then 40 mg continuously or alternating schedules, through week 52. The study was terminated prematurely; 78.6% (551/701) completed week 12 and only 5.8% (41/701) completed week 52.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — clinical remission (CDAI <150) at week 12 — was attained by 22.8% on GED-0301 versus 25% on placebo (P=0.6210), i.e. the treatment made no difference. Placebo was ahead on week-12 endoscopic response (>50% decrease in endoscopic score: 18.1% vs 10.1%) and clinical response (44.4% vs 33.3%); week-52 outcomes were similar between groups. Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal and related to active Crohn's disease. Two deaths occurred in the GED-0301 group (small intestinal obstruction and pneumonia), neither judged treatment-related by the investigator. The authors concluded GED-0301 did not demonstrate efficacy versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Premature termination means week-52 data rest on only 41 completers; the week-12 primary endpoint, on 701 randomised patients, is the load-bearing result, and it is null.

cards.headline: Batch controversy (Marafini 2021): an open-label study of 18 patients reported remission again — and showed in vitro that the mongersen batch used in it inhibited SMAD7 while two batches used in the phase 3 programme did not
cards.summary: Batch controversy (Marafini 2021): an open-label study of 18 patients reported remission again — and showed in vitro that the mongersen batch used in it inhibited SMAD7 while two batches used in the phase 3 programme did not
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label uncontrolled study (n=18) with in-vitro batch-comparison experiments
cards.people: 18 patients with active Crohn's disease (CDAI >220 with endoscopic lesions) received open-label mongersen 160 mg/day for 12 weeks; in parallel, different mongersen batches from the development programme were tested for SMAD7 inhibition in HCT-116 cells in vitro.
cards.result: Clinical remission was 38.9%, 55.6% and 50.0% at weeks 4, 8 and 12, and clinical response 72.2%, 77.8% and 77.8% (open-label, no comparator). Mongersen reduced circulating CCR9-expressing CD45+ cells. Critically, the batch used in this study inhibited SMAD7 expression in HCT-116 cells, but two batches used in the phase 3 study did NOT — raising the possibility that the phase 2 result depended on a pharmacologically active batch and that inactive batches contributed to the phase 3 failure. This controversy is part of the evidence record and is flagged on the face of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, uncontrolled and small (n=18): its remission percentages cannot be compared with placebo-controlled rates. Its load-bearing content is the batch finding — batches differed in SMAD7 inhibition — which is a hypothesis about why the programme failed, not proof that any batch works in patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme — the phase 3 trial (701 randomised) found remission 22.8% on mongersen versus 25% on placebo, contradicting the small phase 2 trial's 55-65% remission; a later report raised the possibility that the phase 2 result depended on a pharmacologically active batch
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme — the phase 3 trial (701 randomised) found remission 22.8% on mongersen versus 25% on placebo, contradicting the small phase 2 trial's 55-65% remission; a later report raised the possibility that the phase 2 result depended on a pharmacologically active batch
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Mongersen's record is a phase 2 result (2 weeks of treatment; day-15 remission 55% at 40 mg and 65% at 160 mg versus 10% on placebo) that the adequately sized phase 3 trial did not reproduce: week-12 remission 22.8% versus 25% on placebo (P=0.62), with placebo ahead on endoscopic and clinical response, and the programme terminated for futility. The post-hoc phase 2 report adds no independent evidence. The 2021 batch report (open-label, n=18) showed that batches used in the phase 3 programme failed to inhibit SMAD7 in vitro while the batch used in that small study did — a possible explanation for the discrepancy, flagged on the face, but not evidence of patient benefit. The programme is presented here as failed.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Budesonide MMX in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis: remission 17.9% and 17.4% vs 7.4% and 4.5% on placebo — a real benefit, but absolute remission under 18%
shelves.question: In adults with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, does once-daily budesonide MMX 9 mg versus placebo induce combined clinical and endoscopic remission at 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Budesonide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy/pathology · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Mesalamine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit, but small in absolute terms — stated plainly. CORE I: week-8 remission 17.9% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 7.4% on placebo. CORE II: combined clinical and endoscopic remission 17.4% versus 4.5% (pooled: 17.7% vs 6.2%). Absolute remission on the effective dose is under 18% in both trials, so most patients do not reach remission; the 6 mg dose did not separate from placebo. Induction only; the tested product is the MMX colonic-release formulation, distinct from ileal-release budesonide (CORE II's reference arm).

cards.headline: CORE I (Sandborn 2012): budesonide MMX 9 mg induced week-8 remission in 17.9% versus 7.4% on placebo — a real but small absolute benefit; remission stayed under 18%
cards.summary: CORE I (Sandborn 2012): budesonide MMX 9 mg induced week-8 remission in 17.9% versus 7.4% on placebo — a real but small absolute benefit; remission stayed under 18%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy placebo-controlled trial (CORE I), budesonide MMX 9/6 mg vs mesalamine reference vs placebo, 8 weeks
cards.people: 509 patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, randomised to budesonide MMX 9 mg or 6 mg once daily, mesalamine 2.4 g (reference arm) or placebo for 8 weeks. Budesonide MMX is the multi-matrix (MMX) colonic-release formulation — a different tested product from ileal-release budesonide.
cards.result: Week-8 remission was 17.9% on budesonide MMX 9 mg, 13.2% on 6 mg and 12.1% on mesalamine, versus 7.4% on placebo (P=.0143 for 9 mg; the 6 mg and mesalamine comparisons were not significant) — an absolute gain of 10.5 percentage points for the 9 mg dose. Clinical improvement was 33.3% (9 mg) versus 24.8% on placebo (not significant); symptom resolution 28.5% versus 16.5% (P=.0258). Adverse events occurred at similar frequencies across groups. The absolute remission rate on the effective dose was under 18% — most patients did not reach remission.
cards.watchOut: The mesalamine arm was a reference arm, not a powered head-to-head comparison. This is an induction question only — no maintenance claim. Absolute remission rates are low and are printed plainly on this shelf.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Once-daily budesonide MMX® extended-release tablets induce remission in patients with mild to moderate ulcerative colitis: results from the CORE I study. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22892337. Registry ID: NCT00679432. cards.headline: CORE II (Travis 2014): combined clinical and endoscopic remission 17.4% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 4.5% on placebo (odds ratio 4.49, a relative measure) — again, under 18% absolute remission
cards.summary: CORE II (Travis 2014): combined clinical and endoscopic remission 17.4% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 4.5% on placebo (odds ratio 4.49, a relative measure) — again, under 18% absolute remission
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CORE II), budesonide MMX 9/6 mg vs Entocort EC reference vs placebo, 8 weeks
cards.people: 410 patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis evaluated for efficacy, randomised 1:1:1:1 to budesonide MMX 9 mg or 6 mg, Entocort EC 9 mg (ileal-release budesonide; reference arm) or placebo once daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Combined clinical and endoscopic remission was 17.4% on budesonide MMX 9 mg, 8.3% on 6 mg, 12.6% on Entocort EC and 4.5% on placebo; the 9 mg versus placebo difference was significant (OR 4.49; 95% CI 1.47 to 13.72; P=0.0047 — an odds ratio, a relative measure; the absolute rates are 17.4% versus 4.5%, a gain of 12.9 percentage points). Histological healing was 16.5% versus 6.7% (P=0.0361) and symptom resolution 23.9% versus 11.2% (P=0.0220) for 9 mg versus placebo. Adverse event profiles were similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: The reference arm was Entocort EC (ileal-release budesonide), a different formulation — it is not a second MMX trial and is not counted as independent MMX evidence. Absolute remission on 9 mg was 17.4%: more than 8 in 10 patients did not reach combined remission.

cards.headline: Pooled CORE I + II analysis (Sandborn 2015): combined clinical and colonoscopic remission 17.7% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 6.2% on placebo (P=0.0002); the 6 mg dose (10.9%) was not significantly better than placebo
cards.summary: Pooled CORE I + II analysis (Sandborn 2015): combined clinical and colonoscopic remission 17.7% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 6.2% on placebo (P=0.0002); the 6 mg dose (10.9%) was not significantly better than placebo
cards.type: Pooled analysis of the CORE I and CORE II phase 3 trials (same trials as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: Pooled modified intent-to-treat population of the two CORE trials (patients with histological evidence of baseline inflammation): 232 on budesonide MMX 9 mg, 230 on 6 mg and 210 on placebo.
cards.result: Combined clinical and colonoscopic remission was 17.7% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 6.2% on placebo (P=0.0002) — an absolute gain of 11.5 percentage points — but only 10.9% on the 6 mg dose, which was not significantly greater than placebo. The 9 mg primary-endpoint advantage held in most subgroups analysed. Symptom resolution and colonoscopic improvement rates were also significantly greater with 9 mg. Budesonide MMX was described as safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of the same two trials carded above, not a third trial. It confirms the dose pattern (9 mg works, 6 mg does not separate from placebo) but adds no new patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: budesonide MMX 9 mg beats placebo in both CORE trials, but absolute remission is low — 17.9% and 17.4% versus 7.4% and 4.5% on placebo; the 6 mg dose does not work

cards.result: Two randomised trials agree: once-daily budesonide MMX 9 mg for 8 weeks induced remission in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis in 17.9% (CORE I) and 17.4% (CORE II) of patients versus 7.4% and 4.5% on placebo — absolute gains of about 10-13 percentage points, with the pooled rate 17.7% versus 6.2%. The benefit is real but small in absolute terms: more than 8 in 10 treated patients did not reach remission. The 6 mg dose did not separate from placebo. This shelf answers an induction question only; the tested product is the MMX colonic-release formulation, not ileal-release budesonide.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Omega-3 for Crohn's maintenance: positive in the small 1996 trial (relapse 28% vs 69%), negative in the large EPIC trials — the split that decides the shelf
shelves.question: In patients with Crohn's disease in remission at high risk of relapse, does enteric-coated omega-3 free fatty acid / fish-oil supplementation versus placebo prolong remission?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on the large trials, with a visible era split. The small 1996 trial of enteric-coated fish oil (n=78) was strongly positive (1-year relapse 28% vs 69% on placebo), but the two large EPIC trials (363 and 375 patients, one publication) found no benefit (relapse 31.6% vs 35.7% and 47.8% vs 48.8%), and the Cochrane review's analysis restricted to those two low-bias trials was null (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05). The split by era and formulation is presented plainly and not pooled away. Tested preparations (enteric-coated fish oil; omega-3 free fatty acids, Epanova) differ from generic retail fish oil.

cards.headline: Belluzzi 1996: enteric-coated fish oil cut 1-year relapse to 28% versus 69% on placebo in 78 patients at high risk of relapse — the small, positive, older trial
cards.summary: Belluzzi 1996: enteric-coated fish oil cut 1-year relapse to 28% versus 69% on placebo in 78 patients at high risk of relapse — the small, positive, older trial
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, enteric-coated fish oil vs placebo, 1 year (n=78)
cards.people: 78 patients with Crohn's disease in remission but at high risk of relapse, randomised to nine enteric-coated fish-oil capsules daily (2.7 g/day of n-3 fatty acids) or nine placebo capsules for one year (39 per group). The tested product was a specific enteric-coated fish-oil preparation, named here under the clarification exception because preparations differ by maker.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 11 of 39 (28%) on fish oil versus 27 of 39 (69%) on placebo — an absolute difference of 41 percentage points (95% CI 21 to 61; P<0.001). After one year, 59% on fish oil remained in remission versus 26% on placebo (P=0.003). The odds ratio for relapse, placebo versus fish oil, was 4.2 (95% CI 1.6 to 10.7) — a relative measure, with the absolute rates printed above. Four patients on fish oil dropped out because of diarrhoea versus one on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=78), single-era and single-preparation: its large effect was not reproduced by the much larger EPIC trials below. The era and formulation split is the balance of this shelf and is kept visible, not pooled away.

cards.headline: EPIC-1 and EPIC-2 (Feagan 2008, two trials in one publication): omega-3 free fatty acids 4 g/day did NOT prevent relapse — 1-year relapse 31.6% vs 35.7% (EPIC-1) and 47.8% vs 48.8% (EPIC-2)
cards.summary: EPIC-1 and EPIC-2 (Feagan 2008, two trials in one publication): omega-3 free fatty acids 4 g/day did NOT prevent relapse — 1-year relapse 31.6% vs 35.7% (EPIC-1) and 47.8% vs 48.8% (EPIC-2)
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (EPIC-1 and EPIC-2) reported in one publication, omega-3 free fatty acids 4 g/day vs placebo, up to 58 weeks
cards.people: Patients with quiescent Crohn's disease (CDAI <150), evaluated in two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials at 98 centres: EPIC-1, 363 patients evaluated, and EPIC-2, 375 patients evaluated. Treatment was omega-3 free fatty acids 4 g/day (the Epanova preparation) or placebo for up to 58 weeks; no other Crohn's treatments were permitted. EPIC-1 and EPIC-2 are two trials reported in ONE publication, counted here as one report.
cards.result: Relapse at 1 year in EPIC-1 was 31.6% on omega-3 versus 35.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.51 to 1.19; P=.30 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). In EPIC-2, relapse was 47.8% versus 48.8% (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.21; P=.48). Neither trial showed a benefit. Serious adverse events were uncommon and mostly related to Crohn's disease. The authors concluded omega-3 free fatty acids were not effective for prevention of relapse in Crohn's disease.
cards.watchOut: MeSH line note: the registry IDs in the record are NCT00613197 (EPIC-1) and NCT00074542 (EPIC-2) as listed in the abstract text. Together the EPIC trials evaluated 738 patients — nearly ten times the 1996 trial — and both were negative.
cards.source: Feagan BG et al. Omega-3 free fatty acids for the maintenance of remission in Crohn disease: the EPIC Randomized Controlled Trials. JAMA. 2008. PMID: 18398081. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Lev-Tzion 2014): pooling all 6 trials suggested a marginal benefit, but restricting to the two large low-bias trials (738 patients) the benefit disappeared — relative risk of relapse 0.88 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.05), a relative measure
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Lev-Tzion 2014): pooling all 6 trials suggested a marginal benefit, but restricting to the two large low-bias trials (738 patients) the benefit disappeared — relative risk of relapse 0.88 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.05), a relative measure
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials of omega-3 / fish oil for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease
cards.people: Six randomised placebo-controlled trials with 1,039 patients in remission at recruitment, followed at least six months; the two largest studies (the EPIC trials, 738 patients) were rated low risk of bias on all items, while four studies were unclear or high risk of bias on several items.
cards.result: Across all six studies, 39% on n-3 relapsed at 12 months versus 47% on placebo (relative risk 0.77; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.98 — a relative measure), but GRADE rated this evidence very low (unexplained heterogeneity I²=58%, publication bias, bias concerns). When only the two large low-risk-of-bias studies were pooled, relapse was 37% versus 42% (relative risk 0.88; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05) — not statistically significant, moderate-quality evidence. No serious adverse events were recorded, but diarrhoea (relative risk 1.36) and upper gastrointestinal symptoms (relative risk 1.65) were more frequent on n-3. The review concluded evidence from two large high-quality studies suggests omega-3 fatty acids are probably ineffective for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease.
cards.watchOut: The headline pooled estimate mixes the small positive older trials with EPIC; the review's own low-bias-restricted analysis is the more trustworthy limb and it is null. Preparations differed across trials (enteric-coated fish oil in 1996; omega-3 free fatty acids, Epanova, in EPIC) and differ from generic retail fish oil — current products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Lev-Tzion R et al. Omega 3 fatty acids (fish oil) for maintenance of remission in Crohn's disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24585498. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Belluzzi 1996 (n=78) found relapse in 28% on enteric-coated fish oil versus 69% on placebo. EPIC-1 and EPIC-2 (363 and 375 patients evaluated; one publication) found 1-year relapse of 31.6% versus 35.7% and 47.8% versus 48.8% on omega-3 free fatty acids 4 g/day versus placebo — no benefit in either. The Cochrane review's all-trials pool was marginally positive on very-low-quality evidence, but its restriction to the two large low-risk-of-bias trials gave a relative risk of relapse of 0.88 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.05), not significant. The weight of the large, rigorous trials is that omega-3 does not maintain remission in Crohn's disease; the 1996 result stands unreconciled and unreplicated, and the preparations tested differ from generic retail fish oil.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Latiglutenase in coeliac disease: challenge trials suggest mucosal protection, but the 494-patient symptomatic trial was negative — a split record
shelves.question: In adults with coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet, does latiglutenase (ALV003 / IMGX003, oral mixture of two recombinant gluten-specific proteases) versus placebo protect against gluten-induced mucosal injury and symptoms — during controlled gluten challenge, and in symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Autoantibodies/blood · Biomarkers/blood · Biopsy · Celiac Disease/diagnosis/drug therapy/enzymology/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Duodenum/drug effects/enzymology/immunology/pathology · Female · Finland · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Glutens/adverse effects/metabolism · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa/drug effects/enzymology/immunology/pathology · Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Peptide Hydrolases/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The two gluten-challenge trials (n=41 and n=50; 2 g/day gluten, 6 weeks) show mucosal-protection signals on the surrogate villus-height/crypt-depth endpoint — clear in 2014, with the 2022 trial's primary endpoint at P=.057. The one large real-world trial — 494 symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet — was NEGATIVE on its primary histology endpoint, with no symptom advantage either. The seropositive-subgroup symptom report is a post-hoc analysis of that negative trial and is labelled as such. ALV003 and IMGX003 are the same enzyme mixture under successive names.

cards.headline: Gluten-challenge trial (Lähdeaho 2014): ALV003 prevented gluten-induced mucosal injury — placebo villus height:crypt depth fell 2.8 to 2.0 on 2 g/day gluten while the ALV003 group showed no significant deterioration (a surrogate histology endpoint)
cards.summary: Gluten-challenge trial (Lähdeaho 2014): ALV003 prevented gluten-induced mucosal injury — placebo villus height:crypt depth fell 2.8 to 2.0 on 2 g/day gluten while the ALV003 group showed no significant deterioration (a surrogate histology endpoint)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled gluten-challenge trial, ALV003 vs placebo with 2 g/day gluten for 6 weeks
cards.people: Adults with biopsy-proven coeliac disease randomised to ALV003 (latiglutenase; n=20) or placebo (n=21) with a daily gluten challenge for 6 weeks, after a dose-finding phase selected 2 g/day gluten; 16 on ALV003 and 18 on placebo were eligible for efficacy evaluation.
cards.result: On placebo, mucosal injury appeared: mean villus height to crypt depth ratio changed from 2.8 before challenge to 2.0 afterward (P=.0007) and CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocyte density rose from 61 to 91 cells/mm (P=.0003). No significant mucosal deterioration was observed on ALV003, and between-group differences in morphologic change and lymphocyte counts were significant (P=.0133 and P=.0123). There were no statistically significant differences in symptoms between groups. Villus height:crypt depth is a surrogate histological endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Small (41 randomised, 34 efficacy-evaluable) and a controlled-challenge design with a surrogate histology endpoint — not a trial of ordinary life on a gluten-free diet. ALV003 and IMGX003 are the same enzyme mixture under successive development names.
cards.source: Lähdeaho ML et al. Glutenase ALV003 attenuates gluten-induced mucosal injury in patients with celiac disease. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24583059. cards.headline: Symptomatic-patient trial (Murray 2017): latiglutenase did NOT beat placebo on its primary histology endpoint in 494 symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet — no difference in villous atrophy, lymphocytes, serology or symptoms
cards.summary: Symptomatic-patient trial (Murray 2017): latiglutenase did NOT beat placebo on its primary histology endpoint in 494 symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet — no difference in villous atrophy, lymphocytes, serology or symptoms
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, latiglutenase 100-900 mg vs placebo, 12-24 weeks, in symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet
cards.people: 494 patients with coeliac disease in North America and Europe, on a gluten-free diet for at least 1 year, with moderate or severe symptoms and villous atrophy (villus height:crypt depth ≤2.0), randomised to placebo or latiglutenase 100, 300, 450, 600 or 900 mg daily for 12 or 24 weeks.
cards.result: In the modified intent-to-treat population there were NO differences between latiglutenase and placebo in change in villus height:crypt depth ratio (the primary endpoint), intraepithelial lymphocyte numbers, or serologic markers. All groups — including placebo — had significant improvements in histologic and symptom scores. The authors concluded latiglutenase did not improve histologic or symptom scores compared with placebo in symptomatic coeliac disease.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest trial on the shelf and the only one testing the real-world question (symptomatic patients eating a gluten-free diet, no deliberate challenge) — and it is negative on its primary endpoint. The challenge-trial cards answer a different sub-question and must not be pooled with it.
cards.source: Murray JA et al. No Difference Between Latiglutenase and Placebo in Reducing Villous Atrophy or Improving Symptoms in Patients With Symptomatic Celiac Disease. Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 27864127. Registry ID: NCT01917630. cards.headline: Post-hoc seropositive-subgroup report (Syage 2017): in the 173 seropositive patients from the negative 494-patient trial, symptom severity fell dose-dependently — abdominal pain severity 58% lower and bloating 44% lower at 900 mg versus placebo (percentages as reported; post-hoc, hypothesis-generating only)
cards.summary: Post-hoc seropositive-subgroup report (Syage 2017): in the 173 seropositive patients from the negative 494-patient trial, symptom severity fell dose-dependently — abdominal pain severity 58% lower and bloating 44% lower at 900 mg versus placebo (percentages as reported; post-hoc, hypothesis-generating only)
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis (seropositive patients) of the randomised trial carded above — not an independent trial
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the trial carded above: of 398 completers, 173 (43%) were seropositive at baseline; the highest-dose subgroup was small (900 mg, n=14, versus placebo n=54 in the comparison reported).
cards.result: A statistically significant, dose-dependent reduction in symptom severity and frequency was detected in seropositive but not seronegative patients: abdominal pain severity was reduced by 58% and bloating by 44% at the highest dose (900 mg) relative to placebo, as reported, with improvement increasing from week 6 to week 12 and a trend to greater improvement with greater baseline severity. The parent trial's primary histology endpoint was not met.
cards.watchOut: POST-HOC: a subgroup analysis of a trial that was negative on its primary endpoint, with a very small highest-dose subgroup (n=14). It is labelled post-hoc on this shelf and is never upgraded into a positive trial.
cards.source: Syage JA et al. Latiglutenase Improves Symptoms in Seropositive Celiac Disease Patients While on a Gluten-Free Diet. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2017. PMID: 28755266. Registry ID: NCT01917630. cards.headline: IMGX003 gluten-challenge trial (Murray 2022): 1,200 mg attenuated gluten-induced mucosal damage — villus height:crypt depth change -0.04 vs -0.35 on placebo (P=.057, not significant) with a significant lymphocyte difference (P=.018)
cards.summary: IMGX003 gluten-challenge trial (Murray 2022): 1,200 mg attenuated gluten-induced mucosal damage — villus height:crypt depth change -0.04 vs -0.35 on placebo (P=.057, not significant) with a significant lymphocyte difference (P=.018)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled gluten-challenge trial, IMGX003 1,200 mg vs placebo with 2 g/day gluten for 6 weeks
cards.people: 50 patients with coeliac disease randomised to IMGX003 (latiglutenase) 1,200 mg or placebo with 2 g/day gluten for 6 weeks; 43 completed (IMGX003 n=21, placebo n=22).
cards.result: Mean change in villus height:crypt depth (primary endpoint) was -0.04 on IMGX003 versus -0.35 on placebo (P=.057 — not statistically significant). Mean change in intraepithelial lymphocyte density was 9.8 versus 24.8 cells/mm epithelium (P=.018). Symptom worsening was numerically less on IMGX003 (abdominal pain change 0.22 vs 1.63 relative units, P=.231; bloating 0.96 vs 3.29, P=.204; tiredness 0.02 vs 3.20, P=.113), with significant 3×2-week trend lines for all three symptoms (P=.014, .030 and .002). The authors concluded IMGX003 reduced gluten-induced mucosal damage and symptom severity.
cards.watchOut: Small (50 randomised) challenge trial whose primary endpoint narrowly missed significance (P=.057); histology is a surrogate endpoint. IMGX003 is the same enzyme mixture as ALV003 under its later development name.
cards.source: Murray JA et al. Latiglutenase Protects the Mucosa and Attenuates Symptom Severity in Patients With Celiac Disease Exposed to a Gluten Challenge. Gastroenterology. 2022. PMID: 35931103. Registry ID: NCT03585478. MeSH: Humans · Glutens/adverse effects · Celiac Disease/diagnosis/drug therapy · Peptide Hydrolases · Intestinal Mucosa

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the two small gluten-challenge trials show mucosal-protection signals on a surrogate endpoint, while the one large real-world trial in symptomatic patients (n=494) was negative on its primary endpoint; the seropositive symptom signal is post-hoc
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the two small gluten-challenge trials show mucosal-protection signals on a surrogate endpoint, while the one large real-world trial in symptomatic patients (n=494) was negative on its primary endpoint; the seropositive symptom signal is post-hoc
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The challenge trials (n=41 and n=50, 2 g/day gluten for 6 weeks) found latiglutenase attenuated gluten-induced mucosal injury, though the 2022 trial's primary endpoint missed significance (P=.057). The 494-patient trial in symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet — the real-world question — found no difference from placebo on histology, serology or symptoms. The seropositive symptom improvement comes from a post-hoc subgroup of that negative trial (highest-dose n=14) and is hypothesis-generating only. Villus height:crypt depth is a surrogate endpoint throughout.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Growth hormone in short bowel syndrome: small trials (n=41, 12, 10) show short-term PN and absorption gains — Cochrane calls the evidence inconclusive
shelves.question: In adults with short bowel syndrome dependent on parenteral nutrition, does recombinant human growth hormone — alone, or combined with glutamine and a high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet — versus placebo increase intestinal absorption and reduce parenteral-nutrition requirements?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Combined Modality Therapy · Diet · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glutamine/administration & dosage · Human Growth Hormone/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Requirements · Nutritional Status · Parenteral Nutrition/statistics & numerical data · Probability · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Short Bowel Syndrome/diagnosis/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Small trials throughout — every N printed on the face: Byrne 2005 (n=41) found GH-containing regimens reduced PN volume more than glutamine + diet at 4 weeks, with only GH + glutamine + diet holding the gain at 3 months, and its design cannot separate GH from glutamine/diet in the combination arm; Séguy 2003 (n=12, crossover) found absorption gains; Ellegård 1997 (n=10, at the floor exactly) found body-composition gains but null absorption endpoints; a sub-floor n=8 crossover is carded as a labelled limb only, never load-bearing. The Cochrane review calls the evidence inconclusive, with effects short-lived after treatment stops. Endpoints are short-term (3-8 weeks); no long-term PN-independence or survival claim.

cards.headline: Byrne 2005 (n=41): growth hormone + diet cut parenteral nutrition volume by 5.9 L/week versus 3.8 L/week on glutamine + diet; only growth hormone + glutamine + diet (7.7 L/week) held the gain at 3 months
cards.summary: Byrne 2005 (n=41): growth hormone + diet cut parenteral nutrition volume by 5.9 L/week versus 3.8 L/week on glutamine + diet; only growth hormone + glutamine + diet (7.7 L/week) held the gain at 3 months
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=41), GH alone vs glutamine alone vs GH + glutamine, all with optimised diet
cards.people: 41 adults with short bowel syndrome dependent on parenteral nutrition (PN), randomised after 2 weeks of stabilisation and dietary optimisation to oral glutamine 30 g/day + growth hormone (GH) placebo (control, n=9), GH 0.1 mg/kg/day + glutamine placebo (n=16), or GH + glutamine (n=16); all on an optimised diet, treated 4 weeks in-house and followed 3 months. The tested GH product for this indication was marketed as Zorbtive (somatropin) — named under the clarification exception where the programme used it.
cards.result: After 4 weeks, PN volume reduction was 5.9 ± 3.8 L/week on GH + diet versus 3.8 ± 2.4 L/week on glutamine + diet (P<0.05), with PN calorie reductions of 4,338 versus 2,633 calories/week and infusion reductions of 3 versus 2 per week. GH + glutamine + diet gave the greatest reductions (7.7 ± 3.2 L/week; 5,751 calories/week; 4 infusions/week; P<0.001 versus control). At 3-month follow-up, only the GH + glutamine + diet group maintained significant PN reductions (P<0.005).
cards.watchOut: The design cannot separate the growth-hormone effect from glutamine and diet optimisation in the combination arm — the control itself was an active glutamine + optimised-diet regimen, and every arm reduced PN. Endpoints are short-term PN volume/calories, not long-term PN independence or survival. Print the Ns: the control arm had only 9 patients.
cards.source: Byrne TA et al. Growth hormone, glutamine, and an optimal diet reduces parenteral nutrition in patients with short bowel syndrome: a prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial. Annals of surgery. 2005. PMID: 16244538. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Séguy 2003 (n=12): low-dose growth hormone (0.05 mg/kg/day, 3 weeks) increased intestinal energy absorption by 15% and nitrogen absorption by 14% in a double-blind crossover — a small, short, absorption-endpoint study
cards.summary: Séguy 2003 (n=12): low-dose growth hormone (0.05 mg/kg/day, 3 weeks) increased intestinal energy absorption by 15% and nitrogen absorption by 14% in a double-blind crossover — a small, short, absorption-endpoint study
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, low-dose GH vs placebo, 3-week periods (n=12)
cards.people: 12 adult home-PN-dependent patients with short bowel syndrome (mean remnant small bowel 48 ± 11 cm; HPN duration 7 ± 1 years) on an unrestricted hyperphagic diet, randomised in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover to low-dose GH and placebo for two 3-week periods separated by a 1-week washout. N=12 — printed on the face, near the floor.
cards.result: GH increased intestinal absorption of energy by 15% ± 5% (P<0.002), nitrogen by 14% ± 6% (P<0.04), carbohydrate by 10% ± 4% (P<0.04) and fat by 12% ± 8% (not significant); the increased food absorption represented 37% ± 16% of total parenteral energy delivery. Body weight, lean body mass, D-xylose absorption, IGF-1 and IGF binding protein 3 all increased, without any major adverse effect.
cards.watchOut: N=12 and 3-week treatment periods: absorption is a short-term surrogate for PN independence, and crossover effects in 12 patients cannot support a durable-benefit claim.
cards.source: Seguy D et al. Low-dose growth hormone in adult home parenteral nutrition-dependent short bowel syndrome patients: a positive study. Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 12557135. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ellegård 1997 (n=10, exactly at the floor): low-dose rhGH for 8 weeks increased body weight and lean body mass by about 5% and fat-free mass by 6%, but did NOT significantly change absorptive capacity for water, energy or protein
cards.summary: Ellegård 1997 (n=10, exactly at the floor): low-dose rhGH for 8 weeks increased body weight and lean body mass by about 5% and fat-free mass by 6%, but did NOT significantly change absorptive capacity for water, energy or protein
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, low-dose rhGH vs placebo, 8-week periods (n=10, at the floor exactly)
cards.people: 10 patients with short bowel syndrome from Crohn's disease, treated with daily subcutaneous low-dose recombinant human growth hormone (0.024 mg/kg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover with at least 12 weeks' washout. N=10 — at the floor exactly, printed on the face.
cards.result: Low-dose rhGH doubled serum IGF-1 and increased body weight, lean body mass and total body potassium by 5% (P<0.05), and fat-free mass and total body water by 6% (P=0.008); increases in IGF-1 correlated with increases in fat-free mass (r=0.77, P<0.02). No significant changes in absorptive capacity of water, energy or protein were detected — the body-composition effect did not come with measured absorption gains in this trial.
cards.watchOut: N=10, at the floor exactly, and its absorption endpoints were null — this trial supports at most a body-composition signal, not improved absorption. Crossover design with metabolic-ward measurements.
cards.source: Ellegård L et al. Low-dose recombinant human growth hormone increases body weight and lean body mass in patients with short bowel syndrome. Annals of surgery. 1997. PMID: 8998124. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Wales 2010): growth hormone with or without glutamine increased weight, lean body mass and energy/nitrogen absorption across 5 studies, but effects were short-lived — 'the evidence is inconclusive to recommend this therapy'

cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of growth hormone with or without glutamine in short bowel syndrome (5 studies)
cards.people: Five randomised trials of human growth hormone with or without glutamine in (mainly adult) short bowel syndrome, including the trials carded above — a small total evidence base, with crossover designs prominent.
cards.result: Growth hormone with or without glutamine was associated with increased weight (mean difference 1.66 kg; 95% CI 0.69 to 2.63), lean body mass (mean difference 1.93 kg; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.90) and energy and nitrogen absorption; the single trial focused on PN requirements found decreased PN volume, calories and infusions, with only the GH + glutamine group maintaining significant reductions at 3 months. The reviewers stressed that in most trials effects were short-lived, returning to baseline shortly after treatment stopped, called the clinical utility into question, and concluded the evidence is inconclusive to recommend the therapy.
cards.watchOut: The review pools the same small trials carded above — it is a synthesis of this shelf's base, not independent patients. Its own verdict is inconclusive, and durability after stopping treatment is the central weakness.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Growth hormone — alone or with glutamine and an optimised diet — reduced parenteral nutrition requirements in the one parallel-group trial (n=41; only the GH + glutamine + diet arm held its gain at 3 months) and increased absorption or body composition in two small crossovers (n=12; n=10, at the floor exactly, whose absorption endpoints were null). The sub-floor n=8 crossover is carded as a labelled limb only. The Cochrane review of 5 studies found weight, lean-mass and absorption gains but judged the evidence inconclusive to recommend therapy, because effects are mostly short-lived. No trial shows long-term PN independence or a survival benefit. Cross-point: the GLP-2 analogue questions (teduglutide, glepaglutide, apraglutide) are different drugs, homed elsewhere — apraglutide is shelf #7219.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Sphincterotomy for sphincter of Oddi dysfunction: benefit only in manometry-verified stenosis in small older trials; EPISOD found sham better in unselected patients
shelves.question: In adults with biliary-type pain after cholecystectomy attributed to sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, does endoscopic sphincterotomy versus sham sphincterotomy reduce pain and pain-related disability — and does sphincter manometry predict who benefits?
shelves.mesh: Ampulla of Vater/surgery · Cholangiopancreatography, Endoscopic Retrograde · Cholecystectomy · Clinical Trials as Topic · Common Bile Duct Diseases/physiopathology/surgery · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Manometry · Middle Aged · Pain · Prospective Studies · Random Allocation · Sphincter of Oddi/physiopathology/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by era and population, and that split is the answer. The 1989 and 2000 trials randomised manometry-characterised patients and found benefit only with elevated basal pressure / manometric stenosis (small subgroups: 10/11 vs 3/12; 11/13 vs 5/13), and none at normal pressure. EPISOD (2014, n=214) randomised unselected suspected type III dysfunction irrespective of manometry and found sphincterotomy WORSE than sham (success 23% vs 37%) with no predictive value for manometry. The 2024 Cochrane review (4 trials, 433 participants) rates all outcomes very low certainty. ERCP/sphincterotomy carries a real pancreatitis risk (11-15% in EPISOD, both arms).

cards.headline: Geenen 1989 (n=47): sphincterotomy helped only patients with elevated sphincter pressure — pain improved in 10 of 11 with elevated pressure versus 3 of 12 on sham; with normal pressure, sphincterotomy was no better than sham
cards.summary: Geenen 1989 (n=47): sphincterotomy helped only patients with elevated sphincter pressure — pain improved in 10 of 11 with elevated pressure versus 3 of 12 on sham; with normal pressure, sphincterotomy was no better than sham
cards.type: Randomised double-blind sham-controlled trial, endoscopic sphincterotomy vs sham, randomisation before manometry (n=47)
cards.people: 47 patients with biliary-type pain after cholecystectomy and clinical features suggesting biliary obstruction, randomised (23 sphincterotomy, 24 sham) BEFORE manometric examination of the sphincter of Oddi — so treatment groups were later read against measured basal sphincter pressure.
cards.result: At one year, pain scores improved in 10 of 11 patients with elevated sphincter pressure who had sphincterotomy, versus only 3 of 12 with elevated pressure who had sham. In patients with normal sphincter pressure, pain scores were similar regardless of treatment. Forty patients were followed for four years: of 23 with increased sphincter pressure, 17 of 18 who ultimately underwent sphincterotomy (initially or after sham) benefited and remained virtually free of pain. The authors concluded sphincterotomy offers long-term relief in manometry-verified sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, and no benefit at normal pressure.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=47) and from the manometry-selected era of the diagnosis: the benefit claim applies only to the elevated-pressure subgroup (11 versus 12 patients in the key comparison). ERCP and sphincterotomy carry a real pancreatitis risk — see the EPISOD card (11-15% post-procedure pancreatitis).
cards.source: Geenen JE et al. The efficacy of endoscopic sphincterotomy after cholecystectomy in patients with sphincter-of-Oddi dysfunction. The New England journal of medicine. 1989. PMID: 2643038. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Toouli 2000 (n=81): in manometric sphincter-of-Oddi stenosis, symptoms improved in 11 of 13 after sphincterotomy versus 5 of 13 after sham (P=0.041); in dyskinesia or normal manometry, sphincterotomy and sham did not differ
cards.summary: Toouli 2000 (n=81): in manometric sphincter-of-Oddi stenosis, symptoms improved in 11 of 13 after sphincterotomy versus 5 of 13 after sham (P=0.041); in dyskinesia or normal manometry, sphincterotomy and sham did not differ
cards.type: Randomised double-blind sham-controlled trial stratified by manometry category, endoscopic sphincterotomy vs sham (n=81)
cards.people: 81 patients with biliary-type pain after cholecystectomy (with a dilated bile duct, transient liver-enzyme rises after pain, or a positive morphine/neostigmine challenge) who underwent endoscopic biliary manometry and were randomised within each manometric category — stenosis, dyskinesia or normal — to sphincterotomy or sham, followed 24 months.
cards.result: In the stenosis group, symptoms improved in 11 of 13 sphincterotomy patients versus 5 of 13 sham patients (P=0.041). When manometry showed dyskinesia or was normal, results from sphincterotomy and sham did not differ. Complications were uncommon but included mild pancreatitis in seven patients (14 episodes) and a right-upper-quadrant collection, presumably from a minor perforation. At three months the incision was extended in 19 patients because manometry showed incomplete sphincter division.
cards.watchOut: The positive comparison rests on 13 versus 13 patients in the stenosis category. Like Geenen, this trial randomised manometry-characterised patients — a different population from EPISOD's unselected suspected type III dysfunction, below. Present the era/population change, not three votes on one claim.
cards.source: Toouli J et al. Manometry based randomised trial of endoscopic sphincterotomy for sphincter of Oddi dysfunction. Gut. 2000. PMID: 10601063. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EPISOD (Cotton 2014, n=214): in unselected post-cholecystectomy pain, sphincterotomy was WORSE than sham — treatment success 23% versus 37% (adjusted risk difference -15.6%) — and manometry did not predict who benefited
cards.summary: EPISOD (Cotton 2014, n=214): in unselected post-cholecystectomy pain, sphincterotomy was WORSE than sham — treatment success 23% versus 37% (adjusted risk difference -15.6%) — and manometry did not predict who benefited
cards.type: Multicentre randomised sham-controlled trial (EPISOD), endoscopic sphincterotomy vs sham irrespective of manometry (n=214)
cards.people: 214 patients with pain after cholecystectomy, no significant imaging or laboratory abnormalities, and no prior sphincter treatment or pancreatitis, randomised 2:1 after ERCP to sphincterotomy (n=141) or sham (n=73) IRRESPECTIVE of manometry findings, at 7 US referral centres; patients with elevated pancreatic sphincter pressure assigned to sphincterotomy were re-randomised to biliary or dual sphincterotomy. A further 72 patients entered a parallel observational study.
cards.result: Treatment success (fewer than 6 days of pain disability in the prior 90 days at both months 9 and 12, no narcotics, no further sphincter intervention) was achieved by 23% on sphincterotomy versus 37% on sham — adjusted risk difference -15.6% (95% CI -28.0 to -3.3; P=.01), favouring sham. Among patients with pancreatic sphincter hypertension, success was 30% with dual sphincterotomy and 20% with biliary sphincterotomy alone. Manometry results were not associated with outcome, and no clinical subgroup benefited more. Pancreatitis occurred in 15 patients (11%) after primary sphincterotomy and 11 (15%) in the sham group (who also underwent ERCP with manometry). The authors concluded the findings do not support ERCP and sphincterotomy for these patients.
cards.watchOut: EPISOD's population — suspected (largely type III) dysfunction without objective abnormalities — is not the manometry-verified stenosis population of the older trials; the trials disagree partly because the diagnosis itself changed. Post-ERCP pancreatitis was frequent in both arms (11% and 15%), a real harm of the ERCP pathway.
cards.source: Cotton PB et al. Effect of endoscopic sphincterotomy for suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction on pain-related disability following cholecystectomy: the EPISOD randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 24867013. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Naing 2024): across 4 trials and 433 participants, sphincterotomy versus sham may have little to no effect on treatment success (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.66 — a relative measure) on VERY LOW-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Naing 2024): across 4 trials and 433 participants, sphincterotomy versus sham may have little to no effect on treatment success (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.66 — a relative measure) on VERY LOW-certainty evidence
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of endoscopic sphincterotomy for biliary sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (4 trials, 433 participants)
cards.people: Four randomised trials (1989-2015), 433 participants with sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (trial sizes 47 to 214, median 86; median age 45 years), comparing endoscopic sphincterotomy with sham, with endoscopic papillary balloon dilation, or with dual sphincterotomy.
cards.result: For sphincterotomy versus sham, the review found it may have little to no effect on treatment success (relative risk 1.05; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.66; 3 trials, 340 participants), serious adverse events (relative risk 0.71; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.46; 1 trial, 214 participants), health-related quality of life (mean differences -1.00 on physical and mental scales) and liver-function improvement — but the evidence is very uncertain for every outcome. Comparisons with balloon dilation and with dual sphincterotomy were likewise very uncertain. All four trials were underpowered, and the review concluded we do not know whether sphincterotomy increases, reduces or makes no difference to treatment success.
cards.watchOut: The pooled relative risk averages trials from different diagnostic eras and populations — exactly the split this shelf keeps visible. The review's fourth trial (a balloon-dilation comparison) is not carded separately here; the sham-controlled trials are the three cards above.
cards.source: Naing C et al. Endoscopic sphincterotomy for adults with biliary sphincter of Oddi dysfunction. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024. PMID: 38517086. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by era and population — benefit confined to manometry-verified stenosis in two small older trials (n=47; n=81), no benefit and a sham advantage in EPISOD's unselected population (n=214), and a very-low-certainty null pool in Cochrane
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by era and population — benefit confined to manometry-verified stenosis in two small older trials (n=47; n=81), no benefit and a sham advantage in EPISOD's unselected population (n=214), and a very-low-certainty null pool in Cochrane
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Geenen 1989 and Toouli 2000 randomised manometry-characterised patients and found sphincterotomy helpful only where basal pressure was elevated / manometry showed stenosis (key subgroups of 11-13 patients per arm), with no benefit at normal pressure or in dyskinesia. EPISOD 2014 randomised 214 unselected patients with suspected dysfunction irrespective of manometry and found success in 23% on sphincterotomy versus 37% on sham, with manometry not predictive. The Cochrane review pools these eras to a null, very-low-certainty estimate. This is a change in the question's population across eras, not three votes on one claim — and the ERCP pathway carries an 11-15% pancreatitis risk in EPISOD.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ramosetron in IBS-D: stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men (5 µg), global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women (2.5 µg) — sex-specific dosing, PARTIAL to pack #2772
shelves.question: In adults with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does ramosetron (5 µg daily in men; 2.5 µg daily in women) versus placebo improve stool consistency and global IBS symptoms?

shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit in the populations tested — PARTIAL shelf (home for the class question: pack #2772). Men's phase 3 (n=296, 5 µg): improved stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% on placebo (relative risk 2.57, labelled relative). Women's phase 3 (n=576, 2.5 µg): global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% (relative risk 1.58). The women's dose-finding trial (n=409) is why dosing is sex-specific: 2.5 µg, not 5 µg, was effective and least harmful in women. A ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (4 RCTs, 1,623 participants) pools relative risks of 1.41-1.72 across outcomes. Pack #2772 (ondansetron in IBS-D) cards a class-level 5-HT3 meta-analysis with ramosetron as a pooled limb — cross-pointed here, NOT re-carded. All primary trials are Japanese, 12-week, Rome III; constipation is the main harm, and the alosetron class history (ischaemic colitis) is context, not ramosetron evidence.

cards.headline: Men's phase 3 trial (Fukudo 2014, n=296): ramosetron 5 µg daily improved stool consistency in 50.3% versus 19.6% on placebo in the first month (relative risk 2.57, a relative measure; NNT 3.25)
cards.summary: Men's phase 3 trial (Fukudo 2014, n=296): ramosetron 5 µg daily improved stool consistency in 50.3% versus 19.6% on placebo in the first month (relative risk 2.57, a relative measure; NNT 3.25)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ramosetron 5 µg daily vs placebo, 12 weeks, in men with IBS-D (Japan)
cards.people: 296 male outpatients with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) at 52 centres in Japan, randomised to oral ramosetron 5 µg once daily (n=147) or placebo (n=149) for 12 weeks after a 1-week baseline period.
cards.result: Improved stool consistency in the first month (primary endpoint) was reported by 50.3% on ramosetron versus 19.6% on placebo (P<.001) — an absolute gain of 30.7 percentage points; the relative risk was 2.57 (95% CI 1.79 to 3.70) and the number needed to treat 3.25 (95% CI 2.44 to 4.89). Monthly rates of relief of overall IBS symptoms and IBS-related quality of life were also significantly higher on ramosetron. The authors identified improved stool consistency as the best endpoint for ramosetron studies in IBS-D.
cards.watchOut: Japanese, 12-week, Rome III population — generalisability beyond that setting is untested. The licensed male dose (5 µg) is twice the women's dose (2.5 µg); the dose history is part of this shelf's answer (see the dose-finding card). Cross-point: the class-level 5-HT3 antagonist question and ondansetron in IBS-D are homed at pack #2772 — its class meta-analysis is NOT re-carded here.
cards.source: Fukudo S et al. Effect of ramosetron on stool consistency in male patients with irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea. cards.headline: Women's phase 3 trial (Fukudo 2016, n=576): ramosetron 2.5 µg daily gave global improvement in 50.7% versus 32.0% on placebo (relative risk 1.58, a relative measure; NNT 6), with constipation in 11.0%
cards.summary: Women's phase 3 trial (Fukudo 2016, n=576): ramosetron 2.5 µg daily gave global improvement in 50.7% versus 32.0% on placebo (relative risk 1.58, a relative measure; NNT 6), with constipation in 11.0%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial, ramosetron 2.5 µg daily vs placebo, 12 weeks, in women with IBS-D (Japan)
cards.people: 576 female outpatients with IBS-D (Rome III criteria) at 70 academic gastroenterology departments in Japan, randomised to ramosetron 2.5 µg once daily (n=292) or placebo (n=284) for 12 weeks after a 1-week baseline period.
cards.result: Global improvement at the last evaluation point was reported by 50.7% on ramosetron versus 32.0% on placebo — an absolute difference of 18.6 percentage points (95% CI 10.7 to 26.5; P<.001); the relative risk was 1.58 (95% CI 1.29 to 1.94) and the number needed to treat 6 (95% CI 4 to 10). Increased stool consistency was 40.8% versus 24.3% (difference 16.5 points; P<.001). Abdominal pain/discomfort was significantly reduced (P=.001) and quality of life improved (P=.002). Ramosetron induced constipation in 11.0% of patients.
cards.watchOut: The women's licensed dose is 2.5 µg — half the men's — because the higher dose was not the effective/safe choice in women (see the dose-finding card). Japanese, 12-week, Rome III population. Class context, not ramosetron evidence: the related 5-HT3 antagonist alosetron was withdrawn/restricted over ischaemic colitis; no ischaemic colitis was reported in the ramosetron trials carded here.

cards.headline: Women's phase 2 dose-finding trial (Fukudo 2017, n=409): 2.5 µg was the effective dose — 5 µg was NOT the best option in women — establishing the sex-specific dosing (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women)
cards.summary: Women's phase 2 dose-finding trial (Fukudo 2017, n=409): 2.5 µg was the effective dose — 5 µg was NOT the best option in women — establishing the sex-specific dosing (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding trial, ramosetron 1.25/2.5/5 µg vs placebo, 12 weeks, in women with IBS-D (Japan)
cards.people: 409 female outpatients with IBS-D in Japan, randomised to placebo (n=102) or ramosetron 1.25 µg (n=104), 2.5 µg (n=104) or 5 µg (n=99) once daily for 12 weeks after a 1-week baseline period.
cards.result: The middle dose, 2.5 µg, significantly improved abdominal pain/discomfort at month 2 (62.5%, P=.002), month 3 (60.6%, P=.005) and the last evaluation point (63.5%, P=.002), and improved weekly Bristol Stool Form Scale scores at most weeks, versus placebo; quality of life did not change. Ramosetron induced more constipation than placebo. The authors concluded 2.5 µg is the most effective and least harmful option for women with IBS-D — the basis for sex-specific dosing.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding trial: its role on this shelf is the dose history (why women are dosed at 2.5 µg and men at 5 µg), not a second efficacy proof at the licensed women's dose. Primary-endpoint detail for month 1 is reported in the abstract mainly through the pain/discomfort results quoted here.

cards.headline: Ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (Qi 2018): across 4 RCTs and 1,623 participants, ramosetron beat placebo on overall relief (relative risk 1.70), pain relief (relative risk 1.41), bowel-habit improvement (relative risk 1.72) and stool consistency (relative risk 1.71) — all relative measures — with more hard stool and constipation and no serious adverse events reported
cards.summary: Ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (Qi 2018): across 4 RCTs and 1,623 participants, ramosetron beat placebo on overall relief (relative risk 1.70), pain relief (relative risk 1.41), bowel-habit improvement (relative risk 1.72) and stool consistency (relative risk 1.71) — all relative measures — with more hard stool and constipation and no serious adverse events reported
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ramosetron randomised trials in IBS-D (4 RCTs, 1,623 participants) — ramosetron-specific, distinct from the class meta-analysis at pack #2772
cards.people: Four randomised controlled trials of ramosetron versus placebo in IBS-D, 1,623 participants in total — the ramosetron-specific synthesis named in the commissioning row. (The class-level 5-HT3 meta-analysis carded at pack #2772, in which ramosetron trials are one pooled limb, is a different synthesis and is NOT re-carded here.)
cards.result: Versus placebo, ramosetron gave relief of overall IBS symptoms (relative risk 1.70; 95% CI 1.48 to 1.95), relief of abdominal discomfort/pain (relative risk 1.41; 95% CI 1.24 to 1.59), improvement in abnormal bowel habits (relative risk 1.72; 95% CI 1.50 to 1.98) and improvement in stool consistency (relative risk 1.71; 95% CI 1.40 to 2.08) — all relative risks, labelled relative. Benefit appeared in both sexes (relative risk 1.94 in men; 1.49 in women). Reported adverse events overall: relative risk 1.10 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.26); hard stool (relative risk 4.74) and constipation (relative risk 2.53) were more frequent on ramosetron. No serious adverse events (e.g. ischaemic colitis) were reported.
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis pools the primary trials carded above (plus one further RCT) — it is a synthesis of this shelf's base, not independent patients. All pooled effects are relative risks; the primary-trial cards carry the absolute rates.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ramosetron at sex-specific doses (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women) consistently beats placebo in Japanese IBS-D trials — stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men, global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women — with constipation the main price; this shelf is PARTIAL to pack #2772's class question
cards.summary: Synthesis: ramosetron at sex-specific doses (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women) consistently beats placebo in Japanese IBS-D trials — stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men, global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women — with constipation the main price; this shelf is PARTIAL to pack #2772's class question
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three Japanese randomised trials and a ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (4 RCTs, 1,623 participants) agree: ramosetron improves stool consistency, global symptoms, pain/discomfort and quality of life in IBS-D, at 5 µg daily in men and 2.5 µg daily in women — the sex-specific doses set by the women's dose-finding trial, in which 2.5 µg, not 5 µg, was the effective and least harmful dose. Constipation and hard stool are the consistent harms; no ischaemic colitis was reported in these trials, though the class history of alosetron (withdrawal/restricted access over ischaemic colitis) is relevant context for any 5-HT3 shelf. PARTIAL home note: pack #2772 asks the ondansetron question in IBS-D and cards a class-level 5-HT3 meta-analysis in which ramosetron trials are a pooled limb; that class synthesis is cross-pointed here in prose and is NOT re-carded on this shelf, and no ramosetron primary trial is carded at #2772. All primary trials are Japanese, 12-week, Rome III populations.

cards.search: synthesis: ramosetron at sex-specific doses (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women) consistently beats placebo in japanese ibs-d trials — stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men, global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women — with constipation the main price; this shelf is partial to pack #2772's class question synthesis: ramosetron at sex-specific doses (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women) consistently beats placebo in japanese ibs-d trials — stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men, global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women — with constipation the main price; this shelf is partial to pack #2772's class question in adults with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does ramosetron (5 µg daily in men; 2.5 µg daily in women) versus placebo improve stool consistency and global ibs symptoms? synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. three japanese randomised trials and a ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (4 rcts, 1,623 participants) agree: ramosetron improves stool consistency, global symptoms, pain/discomfort and quality of life in ibs-d, at 5 µg daily in men and 2.5 µg daily in women — the sex-specific doses set by the women's dose-finding trial, in which 2.5 µg, not 5 µg, was the effective and least harmful dose. constipation and hard stool are the consistent harms; no ischaemic colitis was reported in these trials, though the class history of alosetron (withdrawal/restricted access over ischaemic colitis) is relevant context for any 5-ht3 shelf. partial home note: pack #2772 asks the ondansetron question in ibs-d and cards a class-level 5-ht3 meta-analysis in which ramosetron trials are a pooled limb; that class synthesis is cross-pointed here in prose and is not re-carded on this shelf, and no ramosetron primary trial is carded at #2772. all primary trials are japanese, 12-week, rome iii populations. see the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Apraglutide in short bowel syndrome-intestinal failure (STARS, n=163): parenteral-support volume -25.5% vs -12.5% relative change — FLOOR-RISK, all supporting reports n≤9
shelves.question: In adults with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure dependent on parenteral support, does once-weekly apraglutide (long-acting GLP-2 analogue) versus placebo reduce parenteral-support volume?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Short Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Colon/drug effects · Intestinal Failure/drug therapy · Intestinal Absorption/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit — FLOOR-RISK, on the binding condition in the commissioning row. Only ONE report meets the floor: STARS phase 3 (n=163), where once-weekly apraglutide gave a mean relative change in weekly parenteral-support volume of -25.5% versus -12.5% on placebo at week 24 (P=.001), with the stoma subgroup at -25.6% versus -7.8% and ≥1 day/week off PS in 43.0% versus 27.5%; week-48 colon-in-continuity secondary endpoints were not significant. Every supporting report is sub-floor — n=8 (randomised crossover), n=8 (metabolic-balance), n=9 (colon-in-continuity cohort) — with those Ns printed on the face of each card and in the stamp. Built on the report-count rule (≥3 cardable reports, sub-floor labelled); if the developer requires ≥3 at-floor reports, this shelf demotes to Audit B. Parenteral-support volume is the endpoint; no mortality or enteral-autonomy claim beyond STARS' (non-significant) secondary results.

cards.headline: STARS phase 3 (Joly 2026, n=163 — the shelf's ONE at-floor report): once-weekly apraglutide reduced weekly parenteral-support volume by a mean relative change of -25.5% versus -12.5% on placebo at week 24 (P=.001)
cards.summary: STARS phase 3 (Joly 2026, n=163 — the shelf's ONE at-floor report): once-weekly apraglutide reduced weekly parenteral-support volume by a mean relative change of -25.5% versus -12.5% on placebo at week 24 (P=.001)
cards.type: Phase 3 global randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (STARS), once-weekly apraglutide vs placebo (n=163 — the shelf's one at-floor report)
cards.people: 163 patients with short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure (SBS-IF) dependent on parenteral support (80 with stoma, 83 with colon-in-continuity), randomised 2:1 to once-weekly subcutaneous apraglutide or placebo, stratified by remnant anatomy. This is the only report on this shelf at or above the 10-patient floor by a wide margin — every supporting report below is sub-floor (n=8, n=8, n=9), printed on each card's face.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — relative change from baseline in weekly parenteral-support (PS) volume at week 24 (a relative measure, labelled as such) — was -25.5% on apraglutide versus -12.5% on placebo (P=.001) in the overall population, and -25.6% versus -7.8% (P<.001) in the stoma subgroup. A reduction of ≥1 day/week of PS at week 24 was achieved by 43.0% versus 27.5% (P=.040). At week 48 in the colon-in-continuity subgroup, ≥1 day/week reduction was 51.8% versus 44.4% (P=.348) and enteral autonomy 12.5% versus 7.4% (nominal P=.387) — neither significant. Apraglutide was described as well tolerated with a favourable safety profile. PS volume is a clinical-use endpoint, not mortality; no enteral-autonomy claim beyond these secondary results is made.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK shelf: this single phase 3 trial is the only at-floor report; all supporting reports are sub-floor (n=8, n=8, n=9) and are labelled as such on their cards and in the stamp. The week-48 colon-in-continuity secondary endpoints were not significant.

cards.headline: Sub-floor limb (n=8, labelled, not load-bearing): phase 2 randomised crossover — apraglutide 5 mg and 10 mg once weekly increased urine volume output by 714 and 795 ml/day versus placebo, indicating increased intestinal fluid absorption
cards.summary: Sub-floor limb (n=8, labelled, not load-bearing): phase 2 randomised crossover — apraglutide 5 mg and 10 mg once weekly increased urine volume output by 714 and 795 ml/day versus placebo, indicating increased intestinal fluid absorption
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=8 — SUB-FLOOR, labelled, not load-bearing)
cards.people: 8 adults with SBS-IF — SUB-FLOOR (n=8, below the 10-patient floor), printed on the face — treated in a placebo-controlled double-blind randomised crossover with once-weekly apraglutide 5 mg for 4 weeks and 10 mg for 4 weeks, with 6-10-week washout between treatments.
cards.result: Safety was the primary endpoint: common treatment-related adverse events were mild to moderate (polyuria, decreased stoma output, stoma complications, decreased thirst, oedema); no serious adverse events were judged related to apraglutide. Urine volume output increased by an adjusted mean of 714 ml/day (95% CI 490 to 939) on 5 mg and 795 ml/day (95% CI 195 to 1,394) on 10 mg versus placebo (both P<.05), with no significant difference between doses — evidence of increased intestinal fluid absorption in 8 patients.
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: n=8. A safety-primary crossover in 8 patients; its absorption signal supports, but cannot carry, this shelf. The phase 3 STARS card is the load-bearing evidence.
