cards.headline: Sub-floor limb (n=8, labelled, not load-bearing): phase 1/2 metabolic-balance trial — 4 weeks of apraglutide 5 mg increased wet-weight absorption by 741 g/day and energy absorption by 1,095 kJ/day in 8 patients (4 SBS-II, 4 SBS-IF)
cards.summary: Sub-floor limb (n=8, labelled, not load-bearing): phase 1/2 metabolic-balance trial — 4 weeks of apraglutide 5 mg increased wet-weight absorption by 741 g/day and energy absorption by 1,095 kJ/day in 8 patients (4 SBS-II, 4 SBS-IF)
cards.type: Open-label phase 1/2 metabolic-balance trial (n=8 — SUB-FLOOR, labelled, not load-bearing)
cards.people: 8 adult patients — SUB-FLOOR (n=8, below the 10-patient floor), printed on the face — 4 with short bowel syndrome with intestinal insufficiency (SBS-II) and 4 with intestinal failure (SBS-IF), all with faecal output ≥1,500 g/day, receiving once-weekly subcutaneous apraglutide 5 mg for 4 weeks in an open-label metabolic-balance study.
cards.result: Safety was the primary endpoint: common treatment-related adverse events included decreased stoma output (n=6), stoma complications (n=6 and n=5 across categories), nausea (n=5), flatulence (n=4) and polyuria (n=3); the only treatment-related serious adverse event was abdominal pain in one patient. Wet-weight absorption increased by an adjusted mean of 741 g/day (95% CI 194 to 1,287; P=0.015) and energy absorption by 1,095 kJ/day (95% CI 196 to 1,994; P=0.024); sodium absorption rose by 38 mmol/day and potassium by 18 mmol/day. (Absorption units here are grams and kilojoules per day; the mmol/day electrolyte figures are amounts absorbed, not concentrations, so no mg/dL conversion applies.)
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: n=8, open-label, 4 weeks, safety-primary. Mixed SBS-II and SBS-IF population. Supports the absorption mechanism only; it carries no conclusion on this shelf.

cards.headline: Sub-floor limb (n=9, labelled, not load-bearing): colon-in-continuity phase 2 cohort — over 52 weeks, parenteral-support volume fell by 4,702 ml/week (-52% relative change, as reported) and 7 of 9 patients achieved ≥1 day off PS
cards.summary: Sub-floor limb (n=9, labelled, not load-bearing): colon-in-continuity phase 2 cohort — over 52 weeks, parenteral-support volume fell by 4,702 ml/week (-52% relative change, as reported) and 7 of 9 patients achieved ≥1 day off PS
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre open-label metabolic-balance study in colon-in-continuity SBS-IF (n=9 — SUB-FLOOR, labelled, not load-bearing)
cards.people: 9 adult patients with SBS-IF and colon-in-continuity — SUB-FLOOR (n=9, below the 10-patient floor), printed on the face — in a multicentre open-label 52-week metabolic-balance study of once-weekly subcutaneous apraglutide, with a 48-week PS-adjustment period.
cards.result: PS volume decreased by 4,702 ml/week at week 52 (a -52% relative change, as reported; P<0.001) and 7 patients (78%) achieved ≥1 day off PS. At 4 weeks faecal output fell by 253 g/day (P=0.013); at 48 weeks wet-weight absorption rose by 316 g/day (P=0.039), energy absorption by 1,134 kJ/day (P=0.041) and carbohydrate absorption by 56.1 g/day (P=0.024). Measured small-bowel length increased from 29.7 to 40.7 cm (P=0.012) and duodenal wall thickness by 0.8 mm (P=0.02). A total of 127 adverse events was reported, mostly mild to moderate. Open-label, no comparator — these within-patient changes cannot be read against placebo.
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: n=9, open-label and uncontrolled over 52 weeks. Its 2026 microbiota report (PMID 41903849) studies this same 9-patient cohort and is not carded separately — it would add no new patients. Cross-point: teduglutide (live shelf) and glepaglutide are different GLP-2 analogues, homed elsewhere.
cards.source: Verbiest A et al. Efficacy and safety of apraglutide in short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure and colon-in-continuity: A multicenter, open-label, metabolic balance study. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2024. PMID: 39461299. Registry ID: NCT04964986. cards.result: Once-weekly apraglutide reduced parenteral-support volume in the STARS phase 3 trial (163 randomised): mean relative change -25.5% versus -12.5% on placebo at week 24 (P=.001), with 43.0% versus 27.5% achieving ≥1 day/week off PS; week-48 colon-in-continuity secondary endpoints (days off PS, enteral autonomy) were not significant. Every other report is sub-floor — a randomised crossover in 8 patients, a metabolic-balance trial in 8 patients, and an open-label colon-in-continuity cohort of 9 (whose microbiota report adds no patients) — and each is labelled sub-floor on its face and carries no conclusion. This shelf therefore rests on a single at-floor trial: if the developer's floor reading requires ≥3 at-floor reports, this shelf demotes to Audit B, as the commissioning row binds. No mortality claim is made; PS volume is the endpoint, and relative changes are labelled relative.

shelves.title: Gastric-emptying 'normal' is per-meal: solid half-time median 68.7 min on a rice meal, liquid 10–60 min — women slower for solids, slowest in the luteal phase (PARTIAL slice of #6154)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for gastric-emptying scintigraphy — percentage retention at 1, 2 and 4 hours and half-emptying time for standard solid and liquid test meals — by sex and meal type, and how much do camera view and analysis method move them?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Gastric Emptying/physiology · Gastrointestinal Motility/physiology · Humans · Indium Radioisotopes · Male · Pentetic Acid · Pyloric Antrum/diagnostic imaging,physiology · Radionuclide Imaging · Radiopharmaceuticals · Reference Values · Sex Characteristics · Technetium Tc 99m Sulfur Colloid
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 63–64 (gastrointestinal motility); Boron & Boulpaep, GI motility. PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #6154: #6154 asks what SETS the rate of gastric emptying and how fat and acid slow it — a regulation/mechanism question; it does not give scintigraphic reference values, which are this shelf's question alone. One normative dataset (the Nottingham test-meal reference intervals) is already carded inside #6154 and is NOT re-carded here. The free normative programme: a multicentre rice-meal study (189 completers) gives median half-time 68.7 minutes with 4-hour retention 1.1% (Vasavid 2014); a vegetarian-meal study (N = 36) gives a half-time reference range of 23–109 minutes (Saifi 2022); a liquid-meal study (N = 35) gives a half-time range of 10–60 minutes (Dhukia 2024); and a compartmental study (20 women, 31 men) shows solid emptying far slower in women (half-time 86.2 vs 52.2 minutes) with no liquid sex difference (Bennink 1998). Meal composition is destiny in this measurement — values are carded per-meal, never pooled — and the small Ns on three anchors are printed on their faces. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Multicentre Asian rice-meal scintigraphy (189 completers, 7 centres): median half-time 68.7 min, retention 16.3% at 2 h and 1.1% at 4 h — women slower than men, slowest in the luteal phase (Vasavid 2014)
cards.summary: Multicentre Asian rice-meal scintigraphy (189 completers, 7 centres): median half-time 68.7 min, retention 16.3% at 2 h and 1.1% at 4 h — women slower than men, slowest in the luteal phase (Vasavid 2014)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre normal solid gastric-emptying values, Asian rice meal)
cards.people: 192 healthy volunteers enrolled at seven tertiary centres in Thailand; 189 completed (99 women; age 43 ± 14 years). Scintigraphy in the 45-degree left anterior oblique view after a 267-kcal steamed-rice meal with technetium-99m-labelled microwaved egg and 100 mL water, imaged for up to 4 hours.
cards.result: Medians (5th–95th percentiles) for all volunteers: lag time 18.6 min (0.5–39.1), gastric-emptying half-time 68.7 min (45.1–107.8), retention 16.3% (2.7–49.8) at 2 hours and 1.1% (0.2–8.8) at 4 hours. Women emptied significantly more slowly than men (half-time 74 [48–115] vs 63 [41–96] min; P < 0.05), and women in the luteal phase more slowly than in the follicular phase or after menopause (85 [66–102] vs 69 [50–120] or 72 [47–109] min; P < 0.05). Smoking men emptied faster than non-smoking men (56 [44–80] vs 67 [44–100] min; P < 0.05). Age, BMI and alcohol habits did not affect the values. The meal was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: These are rice-meal, single-view (left anterior oblique) values: the 2-hour retention median of 16.3% belongs to this meal and view and must not be applied to an egg-sandwich geometric-mean protocol. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Standard vegetarian-meal reference values (N = 36): half-time reference range 23–109 min; delayed emptying defined as retention >40% at 2 h and >5% at 4 h by the geometric-mean method (Saifi 2022)
cards.summary: Standard vegetarian-meal reference values (N = 36): half-time reference range 23–109 min; delayed emptying defined as retention >40% at 2 h and >5% at 4 h by the geometric-mean method (Saifi 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (global and regional gastric-emptying reference values, vegetarian meal, camera-view comparison)
cards.people: 36 consecutive healthy subjects aged 18 years or older undergoing gastric-emptying scintigraphy with a standard vegetarian meal acceptable to the Indian population; anterior, posterior and left anterior oblique views acquired, with global and regional parameters derived by single-view and geometric-mean methods. N = 36 printed on the face.
cards.result: The reference range for gastric-emptying half-time was 23–109 minutes. By the geometric-mean method, rapid emptying was defined as retention <20% at 1 hour and delayed emptying as retention >40% at 2 hours and >5% at 4 hours. The reference value for intragastric meal distribution at time zero was >64%, and the retention-index reference range was 0.7–1.3. Parameter distributions differed statistically between camera-view methods (P reported as < 1.00 in the record), but the differences in derived reference values were small and judged clinically insignificant; the authors recommend the geometric-mean method, with a single left-anterior-oblique view as an acceptable alternative.
cards.watchOut: N = 36, printed on the face: percentile reference ranges from 36 subjects are wide and fragile at the tails — the 23–109-minute half-time range is this meal's range in this sample, not a universal solid-meal range. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Liquid gastric-emptying norms (N = 35): half-time reference range 10–60 min; delayed defined as retention >33% at 1 h, >20% at 2 h and >4% at 4 h by geometric mean — no sex or age effect for liquid (Dhukia 2024)
cards.summary: Liquid gastric-emptying norms (N = 35): half-time reference range 10–60 min; delayed defined as retention >33% at 1 h, >20% at 2 h and >4% at 4 h by geometric mean — no sex or age effect for liquid (Dhukia 2024)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative liquid gastric-emptying and small-bowel transit values)
cards.people: 35 consecutive healthy participants (28 women, 7 men; mean age 42 ± 11 years, range 23–65) undergoing liquid gastric-emptying scintigraphy at 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 hours (optional 24-hour imaging), with small-bowel transit also assessed. N = 35 printed on the face.
cards.result: By the geometric-mean method, rapid liquid emptying was defined as retention <8% at 30 minutes and delayed emptying as retention >33% at 1 hour, >20% at 2 hours and >4% at 4 hours; the half-time reference range was 10–60 minutes. The small-bowel transit reference was an index >30% at 4 hours, with rapid transit defined as caecal activity within 1 hour. Anterior-view parameters ran higher than geometric-mean values (P ≤ 0.019, except 2-hour retention, P = 0.510) without changing the reference values enough to matter clinically. Sex had no effect on liquid emptying or transit (P ≥ 0.173) and age showed no moderate or strong correlation — in contrast to the solid-meal sex difference on the other cards.
cards.watchOut: N = 35 with only 7 men, printed on the face: the 'no sex effect' for liquid rests on a small male cell, and liquid values must never be read across to solids — the same laboratory tradition gives solid half-times several-fold longer. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Compartmental scintigraphy in 20 women and 31 men: solid half-emptying 86.2 min in women vs 52.2 min in men — a prolonged lag and slower terminal slope, with more early proximal retention; no sex difference for liquid (Bennink 1998)
cards.summary: Compartmental scintigraphy in 20 women and 31 men: solid half-emptying 86.2 min in women vs 52.2 min in men — a prolonged lag and slower terminal slope, with more early proximal retention; no sex difference for liquid (Bennink 1998)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (total and compartmental gastric emptying and antral motility, men vs women)
cards.people: 20 healthy women (studied in the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle) and 31 healthy age-matched men; a standard gastric-emptying test with additional compartmental (proximal vs distal) evaluation and dynamic antral imaging, for both solid and liquid test meals. Ns printed on the face.
cards.result: Women had a significantly longer solid half-emptying time than men (86.2 ± 5.1 vs 52.2 ± 2.9 min; P < 0.05), accounted for by a significantly prolonged lag phase and a significantly decreased terminal slope; dynamic antral scintigraphy showed no significant sex difference, so antral motility alone does not explain it. Women showed more early proximal retention of the meal, and the distal stomach's terminal slope was significantly lower in women. There was no significant sex difference in liquid emptying. The authors conclude that separate normal values for men and women are required in gastric-emptying scintigraphy, for clinical and research use.
cards.watchOut: Women were studied in the follicular window (first 10 days) by design — the Vasavid card shows the luteal phase empties slower still, so this 86.2-minute figure is a follicular-phase solid value, not a cycle-averaged female norm.
cards.source: Bennink R et al. Comparison of total and compartmental gastric emptying and antral motility between healthy men and women. European journal of nuclear medicine. 1998. PMID: 9724379. cards.people: Synthesis of the four normative datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall, ch. 63–64, and Boron & Boulpaep (GI motility). PARTIAL slice of home pack #6154 (what sets the emptying rate; fat and acid braking): the mechanism is #6154's question, the reference values are this shelf's, no study is shared, and the Nottingham test-meal dataset already carded inside #6154 is not re-carded here. Across the free normative programme the ordering is stable: liquids empty far faster than solids (half-time reference 10–60 min, Dhukia 2024, N = 35); solids centre near a median 68.7 min on a multicentre rice meal (Vasavid 2014, N = 189) within a vegetarian-meal reference range of 23–109 min (Saifi 2022, N = 36); and the sex difference for solids is the most replicated finding — women slower in the multicentre data (74 vs 63 min), in the compartmental data (86.2 vs 52.2 min, Bennink 1998), and slower still in the luteal phase — while liquid emptying shows no sex difference in either dataset that tests it. Camera view and analysis method move values statistically (anterior > geometric mean for liquids) but, in both method-comparison datasets, not enough to change the reference ranges' clinical use; the geometric-mean method is the recommended default. These are the thresholds the gastroparesis treatment shelves' 'delayed emptying' labels presuppose (packs #2037, #2770, #2882, #5630, #5642 — cross-point only). PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Never pool meals: a rice meal, a vegetarian meal and an egg-sandwich meal have different normal values by design, and a retention percentage quoted without its meal, view and method is uninterpretable.

shelves.title: Sargramostim in Crohn's disease: a failed programme — NEJM phase 2 missed its primary endpoint (54% vs 44%, P=0.28) and the Cochrane pool (537 patients) was not significant for remission
shelves.question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active Crohn's disease, does daily subcutaneous sargramostim (6 µg/kg for 56 days) versus placebo induce clinical response or remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibody Formation · Crohn Disease · Female · Granulocyte-Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa · Lymphocyte Count · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Recombinant Proteins · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A FAILED PROGRAMME, stated plainly. The phase 2 NEJM trial (124 patients, sargramostim 6 µg/kg/day for 56 days) MISSED its primary endpoint: clinical response (at least a 70-point CDAI decrease at day 57) was 54% versus 44% on placebo (P=0.28). Its secondary endpoints were positive — 100-point response 48% versus 26% (P=0.01) and remission 40% versus 19% (P=0.01) — but the Cochrane review pooling the randomised base (3 studies, 537 patients, one in abstract form only) found no significant difference for remission (25.3% vs 17.5%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) or 100-point response (relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.97), and graded the evidence low quality. The small Japanese phase 1–2 study (11 patients total, open-label) is carded as a programme limb and is never load-bearing. No phase 3 programme confirmed the phase 2 signal and development stopped. Endpoints throughout are clinical (CDAI-based); no endoscopic-outcome trial exists.

cards.headline: Korzenik 2005 (NEJM phase 2): sargramostim MISSED its primary endpoint — 70-point CDAI response 54% vs 44% (P=0.28) — while secondary endpoints (100-point response 48% vs 26%; remission 40% vs 19%) were positive; 124 patients
cards.summary: Korzenik 2005 (NEJM phase 2): sargramostim MISSED its primary endpoint — 70-point CDAI response 54% vs 44% (P=0.28) — while secondary endpoints (100-point response 48% vs 26%; remission 40% vs 19%) were positive; 124 patients
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, daily subcutaneous sargramostim vs placebo for 56 days
cards.people: 124 patients with moderate-to-severe active Crohn's disease randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous sargramostim 6 µg/kg/day or placebo for 56 days; antibiotics and aminosalicylates were allowed, immunosuppressants and glucocorticoids prohibited. Primary endpoint: clinical response, defined as a decrease of at least 70 points in the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) at the end of treatment (day 57).
cards.result: There was no significant difference on the primary endpoint: 70-point CDAI response on day 57 was 54% on sargramostim versus 44% on placebo (P=0.28). Secondary endpoints favoured sargramostim: 100-point CDAI response 48% versus 26% (P=0.01) and remission (CDAI 150 or less) 40% versus 19% (P=0.01) on day 57, with response and remission rates also significantly higher on day 29 and 30 days after treatment, and significant quality-of-life improvement. Mild-to-moderate injection-site reactions and bone pain were more common on sargramostim, and three patients in that group had serious adverse events possibly or probably related to treatment. The authors state the study was negative for its primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: A primary-endpoint-negative trial whose positive secondary endpoints were never confirmed in a phase 3 programme — the classic failed-programme pattern. Presenting only the secondary endpoints would misrepresent this trial.
cards.source: Korzenik JR et al. Sargramostim for active Crohn's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 15917384. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Takazoe 2009 (Japanese phase 1–2, N=11 total): open-label dose study — clinical response in 1 of 6 in the step-1 extension and 0 of 5 in step 2; remission in 1 patient in each step
cards.summary: Takazoe 2009 (Japanese phase 1–2, N=11 total): open-label dose study — clinical response in 1 of 6 in the step-1 extension and 0 of 5 in step 2; remission in 1 patient in each step
cards.type: Open-label phase 1–2 dose / pharmacokinetic study (programme limb, N=11)
cards.people: Japanese patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease: step 1, an open-label phase 1 study of sargramostim 2 µg/kg/day subcutaneously for 4 weeks with an optional 8-week extension at 6 µg/kg/day (6 patients); step 2, an open-label phase 1–2 study of 6 µg/kg/day over 4 weeks with 8-week efficacy and safety assessment (5 patients). Total N=11 across both steps — printed on the face; this card is a programme limb, never load-bearing.
cards.result: Serum sargramostim concentrations peaked within 1 hour, mean terminal half-life was 2 hours, maximal concentrations increased with dose, and there was no accumulation with repeated daily dosing. One of the six patients in the step-1 extension and none of the five in step 2 achieved a clinical response (at least a 100-point CDAI decrease); clinical remission (CDAI 150 or less) was reported in one patient in each step. Median CDAI scores decreased notably in the extension and step 2. Drug-related adverse events included injection-site reaction, pyrexia, back pain and bone pain.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, uncontrolled and tiny (6 + 5 patients): it can describe tolerability and pharmacokinetics only. Any efficacy reading from 1–2 responders among 11 patients would be noise, and this card carries no weight in the stamp.
cards.source: Takazoe M et al. Sargramostim in patients with Crohn's disease: results of a phase 1-2 study. Journal of gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19352588. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Roth 2011 (Cochrane review): pooling 3 studies (537 patients), sargramostim did NOT significantly improve remission (25.3% vs 17.5%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) or 100-point response — evidence graded low quality
cards.summary: Roth 2011 (Cochrane review): pooling 3 studies (537 patients), sargramostim did NOT significantly improve remission (25.3% vs 17.5%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) or 100-point response — evidence graded low quality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials for induction of remission in Crohn's disease
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials of sargramostim for induction of remission in clinically active Crohn's disease (searches to April 2011, including trial registries and conference abstracts): 3 studies identified (2 published as full papers, 1 in abstract form only), 537 patients in total. Primary outcome: clinical remission (CDAI under 150) at end of treatment.
cards.result: No statistically significant difference for clinical remission: 25.3% on sargramostim versus 17.5% on placebo (relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50; P=0.17; 3 studies, 537 patients — a relative measure whose confidence interval includes no effect; absolute rates as printed). No significant difference for 100-point clinical response (38.3% vs 24.8%; relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.97; P=0.06) or 70-point response (54.3% vs 44.2%; relative risk 1.23, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.82; P=0.30; 1 study, 124 patients). Adverse events overall (95.8% vs 89.3%) and serious adverse events (12.0% vs 4.8%) did not differ significantly; bone pain, musculoskeletal chest pain and dyspnoea were more frequent on sargramostim. GRADE quality for the primary and secondary outcomes was low. The authors conclude sargramostim does not appear more effective than placebo for induction of remission or clinical improvement.
cards.watchOut: One of the three pooled studies exists in abstract form only, heterogeneity was high, and GRADE was low — the pooled null is the best summary available, not a precise proof of zero effect. It nonetheless removes any basis for claiming the NEJM secondary endpoints as established benefit.
cards.source: Roth L et al. Sargramostim (GM-CSF) for induction of remission in Crohn's disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2011. PMID: 22071853. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme — the one adequate trial missed its primary endpoint, the pooled randomised base is not significant for remission, and no phase 3 confirmation ever followed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme — the one adequate trial missed its primary endpoint, the pooled randomised base is not significant for remission, and no phase 3 confirmation ever followed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (phase 2 RCT 124 patients; phase 1–2 limb N=11; Cochrane pool 537 patients across 3 studies).
cards.result: Sargramostim for active Crohn's disease rests on a single phase 2 trial that was negative on its prespecified primary endpoint (54% vs 44%, P=0.28), with positive secondary endpoints that the Cochrane pooled analysis (remission relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) could not confirm as significant, on low-quality evidence. Development stopped without a phase 3 programme. This shelf is the record of that complete, failed evidence base.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each study's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Satavaptan for ascites in cirrhosis: a failed programme — 1,200-patient long-term programme failed every primary endpoint despite short-term weight and sodium effects; never marketed
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and ascites — with or without hyponatraemia, and after large-volume paracentesis — does satavaptan added to diuretic therapy improve ascites control and delay recurrence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Ascites · Diuretics · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines · Proportional Hazards Models · Secondary Prevention · Spiro Compounds · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A FAILED PROGRAMME, stated plainly. Short-term phase 2 trials showed real pharmacology: in hyponatraemic patients (110) satavaptan reduced body weight dose-dependently and raised serum sodium, and in patients without hyponatraemia (148) it reduced weight by about 2.1–2.5 kg versus 0.36 kg on placebo over 14 days; after large-volume paracentesis (151 patients) it reduced paracentesis frequency. But the definitive long-term programme — three randomised trials, 1,200 patients across the spectrum of ascites severity — failed every primary endpoint (worsening of ascites; cumulative large-volume paracenteses over 12 weeks), showed only slight secondary-endpoint advantages, did not reduce hepatic encephalopathy (395 episodes pooled), and in one trial mortality was higher on satavaptan (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.15). Satavaptan was never marketed for ascites and development was abandoned: this shelf is the record of a complete randomised evidence base for a drug patients cannot be prescribed. Ascites endpoints are weight, volume and recurrence measures, not survival. Cross-point: tolvaptan in cirrhotic ascites (pack #7291) is the same class with a different drug and a different evidence fate — the shelves are not merged.

cards.headline: Wong 2012 (three-trial long-term programme, 1,200 patients): satavaptan was NOT more effective than placebo on ANY primary ascites endpoint, and mortality was higher on satavaptan in study 2 (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.15)
cards.summary: Wong 2012 (three-trial long-term programme, 1,200 patients): satavaptan was NOT more effective than placebo on ANY primary ascites endpoint, and mortality was higher on satavaptan in study 2 (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.15)
cards.type: Three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials reported in one publication (long-term satavaptan programme, 1,200 patients)
cards.people: 1,200 patients with cirrhosis and ascites in three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies: study 1, uncomplicated ascites (463 patients); studies 2 and 3, difficult-to-treat ascites with and without concomitant diuretic treatment (497 and 240 patients). Primary efficacy endpoints: worsening of ascites (study 1) and cumulative number of large-volume paracenteses during 12 weeks (studies 2 and 3).
cards.result: Satavaptan was not more effective than placebo in the control of ascites in any of the three populations on the primary endpoints. Some secondary endpoints related to ascites were met in all three studies, suggesting a slight advantage in delaying ascites formation, and satavaptan improved serum sodium in patients with hyponatraemia. Major complications of cirrhosis did not differ significantly between groups. Treatment-related adverse events, serious treatment-related events and discontinuations did not differ significantly overall — however, in study 2 mortality was higher on satavaptan than placebo (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.15 — a relative measure; absolute mortality rates are not printed in the record), with no significant mortality difference in the other two studies and no specific cause identified; most deaths were associated with known complications of cirrhosis. The authors conclude satavaptan, alone or with diuretics, is not clinically beneficial in the long-term management of ascites in cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: This is the definitive evidence on this question and it is negative on every primary endpoint, with a mortality harm signal in one of the three trials. The short-term positive trials carded below do not outweigh it — they explain why the programme was pursued, not why it should be used.
cards.source: Wong F et al. Satavaptan for the management of ascites in cirrhosis: efficacy and safety across the spectrum of ascites severity. Gut. 2012. PMID: 21836029. Registry ID: NCT00358878; NCT00359437; NCT00366795. cards.headline: Ginès 2008 (hyponatraemia trial, 110 patients): satavaptan improved ascites control and raised serum sodium over 14 days — weight −1.59 and −1.68 kg at 12.5 and 25 mg versus +0.49 kg on placebo
cards.summary: Ginès 2008 (hyponatraemia trial, 110 patients): satavaptan improved ascites control and raised serum sodium over 14 days — weight −1.59 and −1.68 kg at 12.5 and 25 mg versus +0.49 kg on placebo
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised dose-ranging trial, satavaptan vs placebo in cirrhosis with hyponatraemia (14 days)
cards.people: 110 patients with cirrhosis, ascites and hyponatraemia (serum sodium 130 mmol/L (≈299 mg/dL) or less) in a multicentre double-blind randomised trial of satavaptan 5 mg, 12.5 mg or 25 mg once daily versus placebo for 14 days; all patients received spironolactone 100 mg/day.
cards.result: Satavaptan improved ascites control: mean body-weight change at day 14 was +0.49 kg (±4.99) on placebo versus +0.15 kg (±4.23), −1.59 kg (±4.60) and −1.68 kg (±4.98) on satavaptan 5, 12.5 and 25 mg (P=0.05 for a dose-effect relationship), with a parallel reduction in abdominal girth. Serum sodium improved dose-dependently: mean change to day 5 was 1.3 mmol/L (≈3.0 mg/dL) (±4.2) on placebo versus 4.5 mmol/L (≈10.4 mg/dL) (±3.5), 4.5 mmol/L (≈10.4 mg/dL) (±4.8) and 6.6 mmol/L (≈15.2 mg/dL) (±4.3) on the three satavaptan doses (P<0.01 for all versus placebo). Thirst was significantly more common on satavaptan; other adverse events were similar.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen days, weight and sodium endpoints only: a short-term pharmacological effect that the 1,200-patient long-term programme (card above) did not convert into ascites control. Do not read this card as evidence for long-term use.
cards.source: Ginès P et al. Effects of satavaptan, a selective vasopressin V(2) receptor antagonist, on ascites and serum sodium in cirrhosis with hyponatremia: a randomized trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2008. PMID: 18508290. Registry ID: NCT00501722. cards.headline: Wong 2010 (post-paracentesis recurrence, 151 patients): satavaptan significantly reduced paracentesis frequency over 12 weeks, but time to first paracentesis and ascites accumulation rate were not significantly different
cards.summary: Wong 2010 (post-paracentesis recurrence, 151 patients): satavaptan significantly reduced paracentesis frequency over 12 weeks, but time to first paracentesis and ascites accumulation rate were not significantly different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, satavaptan after large-volume paracentesis (12 weeks)
cards.people: 151 cirrhotic patients with recurrent ascites, with or without hyponatraemia and with normal to mildly abnormal renal function, randomised double-blind after a large-volume paracentesis to satavaptan 5 mg (39), 12.5 mg (36) or 25 mg (40) or placebo (36) for 12 weeks, added to spironolactone 100 mg. Child-Pugh scores were about 8.7–9.2 across groups.
cards.result: Median time to first paracentesis was 23, 26 and 17 days on satavaptan 5, 12.5 and 25 mg versus 14 days on placebo (not significant for any dose). The frequency of paracenteses was decreased significantly (P<0.05) in all satavaptan groups versus placebo. Mean ascites accumulation was 2.82 ± 0.48 L/week on placebo versus 2.12 ± 0.40, 2.14 ± 0.33 and 2.06 ± 0.40 L/week on the three doses (not significant for any dose). Major adverse events were similar across groups; increases in serum creatinine, orthostatic systolic pressure changes and thirst were more common on satavaptan. The authors conclude satavaptan has the potential to reduce ascites recurrence after large-volume paracentesis.
cards.watchOut: A mixed result within one trial: the significant endpoint is paracentesis frequency, while time to first paracentesis and the ascites accumulation rate were not significant. Superseded for practice by the negative long-term programme carded above.
cards.source: Wong F et al. Effects of a selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, satavaptan, on ascites recurrence after paracentesis in patients with cirrhosis. Journal of hepatology. 2010. PMID: 20541828. Registry ID: NCT00501384. cards.headline: Ginès 2010 (short-term combination trial, 148 patients without hyponatraemia): satavaptan added to diuretics reduced body weight by about 2.1–2.5 kg versus 0.36 kg on placebo over 14 days
cards.summary: Ginès 2010 (short-term combination trial, 148 patients without hyponatraemia): satavaptan added to diuretics reduced body weight by about 2.1–2.5 kg versus 0.36 kg on placebo over 14 days
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, satavaptan plus diuretics vs diuretics alone (14 days)
cards.people: 148 patients with cirrhosis, ascites and serum sodium above 130 mmol/L (≈299 mg/dL) in a multicentre double-blind randomised trial of satavaptan 5 mg, 12.5 mg or 25 mg once daily versus placebo for 14 days; all patients received spironolactone 100 mg/day plus furosemide 20–25 mg/day. Average MELD scores were 12.3–13.8 across groups.
cards.result: Satavaptan was associated with a decrease in ascites: mean body-weight change was −0.36 kg (±3.03) on placebo versus −2.46 kg (±3.11), −2.08 kg (±4.17) and −2.28 kg (±3.24) on satavaptan 5, 12.5 and 25 mg/day (P=0.036, P=0.041 and P=0.036 respectively versus placebo). Thirst and slight increases in serum sodium were more common on satavaptan, while other adverse events were similar. The authors conclude 14 days of satavaptan reduces ascites in moderately severe cirrhosis without hyponatraemia under diuretic treatment.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen days and a weight endpoint: the largest short-term weight effect in the programme, and still only a surrogate for ascites control. The long-term programme failed its primary endpoints — this card is programme history, not a treatment recommendation.
cards.source: Ginès P et al. multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, satavaptan plus diuretics vs diuretics alone (14 days) 148 patients with cirrhosis, ascites and serum sodium above 130 mmol/l (≈299 mg/dl) in a multicentre double-blind randomised trial of satavaptan 5 mg, 12.5 mg or 25 mg once daily versus placebo for 14 days; all patients received spironolactone 100 mg/day plus furosemide 20–25 mg/day. average meld scores were 12.3–13.8 across groups. satavaptan was associated with a decrease in ascites: mean body-weight change was −0.36 kg (±3.03) on placebo versus −2.46 kg (±3.11), −2.08 kg (±4.17) and −2.28 kg (±3.24) on satavaptan 5, 12.5 and 25 mg/day (p=0.036, p=0.041 and p=0.036 respectively versus placebo). thirst and slight increases in serum sodium were more common on satavaptan, while other adverse events were similar. the authors conclude 14 days of satavaptan reduces ascites in moderately severe cirrhosis without hyponatraemia under diuretic treatment. fourteen days and a weight endpoint: the largest short-term weight effect in the programme, and still only a surrogate for ascites control. the long-term programme failed its primary endpoints — this card is programme history, not a treatment recommendation. ginès p et al. clinical trial: short-term effects of combination of satavaptan, a selective vasopressin v2 receptor antagonist, and diuretics on ascites in patients with cirrhosis without hyponatraemia--a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2010. pmid: 20102356. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · antidiuretic hormone receptor antagonists · ascites · body weight · diuretics · double-blind method · drug combinations · female · humans · liver cirrhosis · male · middle aged · morpholines · prospective studies · spiro compounds · spironolactone · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Watson 2013 (meta-analysis of the long-term programme): satavaptan did NOT reduce hepatic encephalopathy — 395 episodes recorded across the three trials (1,200 patients), no reduction in any study or pooled
cards.summary: Watson 2013 (meta-analysis of the long-term programme): satavaptan did NOT reduce hepatic encephalopathy — 395 episodes recorded across the three trials (1,200 patients), no reduction in any study or pooled
cards.type: Meta-analysis of the three long-term randomised satavaptan trials, hepatic encephalopathy outcome
cards.people: Meta-analysis of the three randomised double-blind long-term studies of satavaptan (5–10 mg/day) versus placebo over a one-year treatment period in 1,200 patients with cirrhosis and uncomplicated ascites, analysing incidence of hepatic encephalopathy episodes in the individual-study and pooled databases, adjusted for hyponatraemia and previous encephalopathy episodes.
cards.result: Hyponatraemia was improved by satavaptan, but 395 hepatic encephalopathy episodes were recorded and the risk of an episode and the mean number of episodes were not reduced by satavaptan in any of the three studies, in the overall population or in patients hyponatraemic on entry; the pooled analysis confirmed this. The authors conclude satavaptan did not reduce the frequency of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis and ascites, despite correcting the hyponatraemia associated with encephalopathy risk.
cards.watchOut: A programme meta-analysis by programme investigators of a single outcome (encephalopathy) across the same three trials carded above — not independent evidence, and not a synthesis of ascites efficacy. Its value is closing the 'correcting sodium prevents encephalopathy' hypothesis for this drug.
cards.source: Watson H et al. Satavaptan treatment for ascites in patients with cirrhosis: a meta-analysis of effect on hepatic encephalopathy development. Metabolic brain disease. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme — real short-term weight and sodium effects that did not convert into long-term ascites control in 1,200 randomised patients, with a mortality signal in one trial and no encephalopathy benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme — real short-term weight and sodium effects that did not convert into long-term ascites control in 1,200 randomised patients, with a mortality signal in one trial and no encephalopathy benefit
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (long-term programme 1,200 patients; short-term trials 110, 151 and 148 patients; programme encephalopathy meta-analysis).
cards.result: Satavaptan reliably aquareses: over 14 days it reduced weight by roughly 2 kg more than placebo and raised serum sodium dose-dependently, and after paracentesis it reduced paracentesis frequency. Over 12 weeks to a year, in the three-trial 1,200-patient programme, it failed every primary ascites endpoint, did not reduce hepatic encephalopathy, and was associated with higher mortality in one trial (hazard ratio 1.47). Development was abandoned and the drug was never marketed for ascites. The shelf stands as the complete record of that evidence base.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Tolvaptan for diuretic-resistant cirrhotic ascites: short-term weight and ascites-volume reductions in a Japanese 7-day programme (3.21 vs 1.75 kg vs added furosemide, 56 patients); hard outcomes untested
shelves.question: In patients with liver cirrhosis and ascites/hepatic oedema responding insufficiently to conventional diuretics, does adding tolvaptan (3.75–7.5 mg daily) versus placebo or diuretic adjustment improve body weight, ascites volume and oedema?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antidiuretic Hormone Receptor Antagonists · Ascites · Benzazepines · Diuretics · Double-Blind Method · Electrolytes · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Tolvaptan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for short-term weight and oedema only. The entire programme is Japanese and short (7 days of randomised treatment in both double-blind reports): a dose-finding trial found tolvaptan 7.5–30 mg/day reduced body weight and abdominal circumference versus placebo, with 7.5 mg/day giving the maximum change with preferable tolerability; a phase 3 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study found dose-dependent decreases in body weight and ascites volume and increased urine output at 3.75 and 7.5 mg/day. Neither double-blind record prints its participant count or numeric effect sizes — both cards say so on their faces ('N not documented' in the record). The one fully quantified randomised comparison is small and open-label (56 patients): adding tolvaptan 7.5 mg lost 3.21 kg versus 1.75 kg with added furosemide over 7 days (P=0.0412 between groups). No trial tests decompensation, transplant or survival, and none should be implied. Tolvaptan's hepatic-oedema licence is Japan-specific; in the US the drug carries a liver-injury warning from the ADPKD programme — that tension is part of the face. Cross-points: satavaptan in ascites (pack #7290, same class, failed programme) and the refractory-ascites shelves are different questions.

cards.headline: Okita 2014 (dose-finding trial): tolvaptan 7.5–30 mg/day reduced body weight and abdominal circumference versus placebo over 7 days; 7.5 mg/day was judged the optimal dose — N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Okita 2014 (dose-finding trial): tolvaptan 7.5–30 mg/day reduced body weight and abdominal circumference versus placebo over 7 days; 7.5 mg/day was judged the optimal dose — N not documented in the record
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding trial, tolvaptan add-on vs placebo (7 days)
cards.people: Patients with liver cirrhosis and hepatic oedema (including ascites) showing inadequate response to conventional diuretic therapy, in a 7-day multicentre double-blind trial randomised to tolvaptan 7.5, 15 or 30 mg/day or placebo, once daily as an add-on to conventional diuretics. The number of participants is not documented in the fetched record — this card prints that rather than a number.
cards.result: Tolvaptan at 7.5–30 mg/day reduced body weight and abdominal circumference compared with placebo (the fetched record reports the direction without printing the numeric changes). Serum sodium concentrations remained within the normal range in all tolvaptan groups. No serious adverse events were observed, and the most common adverse event was thirst. Tolvaptan 7.5 mg/day showed the maximum change in body weight and abdominal circumference together with preferable tolerability, and was considered the optimal dose in cirrhosis patients with hepatic oedema inadequately responsive to conventional diuretics.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record and no numeric effect sizes are printed in it — this card supports direction and dose selection only, and carries correspondingly limited weight. Seven days of treatment; weight and circumference endpoints only.

cards.headline: Sakaida 2012 (phase 3 PK/PD study): tolvaptan 3.75 and 7.5 mg/day gave dose-dependent decreases in body weight and ascites volume and increased urine output over 7 days — N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Sakaida 2012 (phase 3 PK/PD study): tolvaptan 3.75 and 7.5 mg/day gave dose-dependent decreases in body weight and ascites volume and increased urine output over 7 days — N not documented in the record
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind parallel-group phase 3 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study, tolvaptan 3.75 vs 7.5 mg/day (7 days)
cards.people: Patients with liver cirrhosis-associated ascites and insufficient response to conventional diuretic treatment, in a multicentre double-blind parallel-group phase 3 study allocated to oral tolvaptan 3.75 or 7.5 mg/day once daily for 7 days, measuring pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and efficacy variables. The number of participants is not documented in the fetched record — this card prints that rather than a number.
cards.result: Tolvaptan showed high plasma concentrations and prolonged maximum-concentration time and half-life in these patients with impaired hepatic function. It produced dose-dependent decreases in body weight and ascites volume and increases in urine output (the fetched record reports these directions without printing the numeric changes), with no effects on urinary or serum electrolytes. Tolvaptan was well tolerated with a good safety profile. The authors conclude 3.75 mg/day exerts some effect through its pharmacokinetic profile in cirrhosis, and 7.5 mg/day is a clinically useful option for patients responding poorly to conventional diuretics.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm is described in the record (a two-dose comparison), N is not documented in the record, and no numeric efficacy values are printed in it — a dose/pharmacology card, not a quantified efficacy estimate. Seven days only.

cards.headline: Uojima 2017 (randomised combination study, 56 patients): adding tolvaptan 7.5 mg lost more weight than adding furosemide 40 mg over 7 days (−3.21 vs −1.75 kg; between-group P=0.0412)
cards.summary: Uojima 2017 (randomised combination study, 56 patients): adding tolvaptan 7.5 mg lost more weight than adding furosemide 40 mg over 7 days (−3.21 vs −1.75 kg; between-group P=0.0412)
cards.type: Two-centre randomised open-label prospective study, tolvaptan add-on vs furosemide add-on (7 days)
cards.people: 56 Japanese patients with cirrhotic ascites at two centres, randomised open-label to a combination group (tolvaptan 7.5 mg added, 28 patients) or a conventional group (furosemide 40 mg added, 28 patients) for 7 days, in addition to the natriuretic drug used before enrolment. Primary endpoint: change in body weight from baseline.
cards.result: Average decrease in body weight on the final dosing day was 3.21 ± 3.17 kg in the tolvaptan combination group (P<0.0001 versus baseline) and 1.75 ± 2.36 kg in the conventional furosemide group (P=0.0006 versus baseline); after 1 week the reduction was significantly greater with the tolvaptan combination than with conventional therapy (P=0.0412). The authors conclude that combining a natriuretic with an aquaretic drug (tolvaptan) is more effective for cirrhotic ascites than natriuretic therapy alone, on this weight endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 56 patients, 7 days, and the comparator is an added furosemide dose rather than placebo — the only quantified randomised card on this shelf, and a small one. Weight at 7 days is not decompensation, transplant or survival.
cards.source: Uojima H et al. Efficacy of combination therapy with natriuretic and aquaretic drugs in cirrhotic ascites patients: A randomized study. World journal of gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 29259382. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Flumazenil in overt hepatic encephalopathy: brief improvement in a subset (17.5% vs 3.8% neurological improvement in grade III, 527-patient crossover trial), no mortality effect — a probe, not a treatment strategy
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and grade III–IV hepatic encephalopathy, does intravenous flumazenil versus placebo produce short-term clinical improvement in encephalopathy grade or consciousness?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Benzodiazepines · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Flumazenil · GABA Modulators · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Italy · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Nervous System · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for TRANSIENT improvement only, with the Ns printed. One large trial carries the base: the Italian multicentre crossover study (527 cirrhotic patients with grade III–IVa encephalopathy) found neurological-score improvement in 17.5% of grade III and 14.7% of grade IVa patients on flumazenil versus 3.8% and 2.7% on placebo, with EEG improvement in 27.8% and 21.5% versus 5% and 3.3%. Everything else is small and old: the pragmatic trial behind it is 14 patients contributing 18 episodes. The Cochrane review (14 trials, 867 participants; analyses on 842) found a beneficial effect on hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.80, as reported) but NO effect on all-cause mortality (7.4% vs 9.3%; relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.16), on low-quality evidence with most trials at high risk of bias and follow-up under one day in the majority. Flumazenil is therefore framed as a short-acting diagnostic/therapeutic probe that can briefly lighten encephalopathy in a subset of patients — not a treatment strategy, and not episode prevention. The duplicate 2017 Cochrane record (the same review under a second record) is deliberately not carded; one review, one card.

cards.headline: Barbaro 1998 (Italian multicentre crossover, 527 patients): flumazenil improved the neurological score in 17.5% (grade III) and 14.7% (grade IVa) versus 3.8% and 2.7% on placebo; EEG improved in 27.8% and 21.5% versus 5% and 3.3%
cards.summary: Barbaro 1998 (Italian multicentre crossover, 527 patients): flumazenil improved the neurological score in 17.5% (grade III) and 14.7% (grade IVa) versus 3.8% and 2.7% on placebo; EEG improved in 27.8% and 21.5% versus 5% and 3.3%
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, intravenous flumazenil vs placebo in grade III–IVa hepatic encephalopathy
cards.people: 527 cirrhotic patients with hepatic encephalopathy grade III (132 in the flumazenil sequence) and IVa (133) admitted to intensive care units over 5 years, in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial: 265 patients received flumazenil and 262 received placebo in the compared periods (130 grade III and 132 grade IVa on placebo). Treatment began within 15 minutes of randomisation; response was assessed by neurological score and continuous EEG recordings.
cards.result: Improvement of the neurological score was documented in 17.5% of grade III patients treated with flumazenil and 14.7% of grade IVa patients, compared with 3.8% and 2.7% respectively on placebo. EEG tracing improvements were observed in 27.8% of grade III and 21.5% of grade IVa patients on flumazenil, versus 5% and 3.3% on placebo. Benzodiazepines were detected in the serum of only 10 patients (4 grade III, 6 grade IVa). The authors conclude flumazenil is beneficial only in a selected subset of cirrhotic patients with severe hepatic encephalopathy, and that applicability to unselected patients remains to be determined.
cards.watchOut: Even in this, the one large trial, only about 1 in 6 patients improved neurologically — a subset effect, measured over minutes to hours. A crossover design in an ICU population with a short-acting drug: it tests transient reversal, not recovery, survival or recurrence.
cards.source: Barbaro G et al. Flumazenil for hepatic encephalopathy grade III and IVa in patients with cirrhosis: an Italian multicenter double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over study. cards.headline: Cadranel 1995 (pragmatic trial, N=14 patients, 18 episodes): flumazenil improved the EEG within minutes in 66% of episodes versus 0% on placebo (P<0.01), with modest delayed clinical improvement
cards.summary: Cadranel 1995 (pragmatic trial, N=14 patients, 18 episodes): flumazenil improved the EEG within minutes in 66% of episodes versus 0% on placebo (P<0.01), with modest delayed clinical improvement
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled pragmatic trial (14 patients, 18 episodes)
cards.people: 14 patients with cirrhosis (median age 54 years, range 41–73; 10 men, 4 women) enrolled during 18 episodes of hepatic encephalopathy in a liver intensive care unit over 2 years, in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled study: flumazenil 1 mg infused at 0.1 mg/min (average amount infused 0.7 mg, range 0.4–1 mg) or placebo in coded vials. Encephalopathy was graded clinically and by EEG. N=14 patients — printed on the face; this card is a small-trial limb, never load-bearing on its own.
cards.result: In the 8 episodes where placebo was infused first, no improvement occurred (0%). During the 12 episodes in which flumazenil was administered, the EEG recording improved within 7 minutes (range 4–47 minutes) — reported as 12 out of 18 cases, 66% versus 0% for flumazenil versus placebo (P<0.01) — and a modest clinical improvement in encephalopathy grade was observed within 83 minutes (range 30–340 minutes). The authors describe a modest but rapid EEG improvement and a moderate but delayed clinical improvement.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen patients and 18 episodes, with episodes (not patients) as the unit in parts of the analysis — hypothesis-confirming at best alongside the large crossover trial. The record's own wording mixes episode denominators; the percentages carded are exactly as printed in the record.

cards.headline: Goh 2017 (Cochrane review): 14 trials, 867 participants — flumazenil improved hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.80) but did NOT reduce all-cause mortality (7.4% vs 9.3%; relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.16); evidence low quality
cards.summary: Goh 2017 (Cochrane review): 14 trials, 867 participants — flumazenil improved hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.80) but did NOT reduce all-cause mortality (7.4% vs 9.3%; relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.16); evidence low quality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, flumazenil vs placebo or no intervention in cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised clinical trials of flumazenil versus placebo or no intervention in cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy (searches to May 2017): 14 eligible trials with 867 participants, the majority with an acute episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy; outcome data could not be gathered from 2 trials (25 participants), so analyses include 842 participants from 12 trials. One trial was at low risk of bias overall; the remaining trials were at high risk of bias. Follow-up ranged from a few minutes to two weeks and was under one day in the majority of trials.
cards.result: All-cause mortality: 32/433 (7.4%) on flumazenil versus 38/409 (9.3%) on placebo died (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.16; 11 trials; low-quality evidence) — no beneficial or harmful effect on mortality, confirmed by trial sequential analysis and by the one low-risk-of-bias trial (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.53; that trial is the 527-patient crossover carded above). Hepatic encephalopathy: flumazenil was associated with a beneficial effect when all trials were included (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.80; 824 participants, 9 trials, as reported by the review) and in the low-risk-of-bias trial alone (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.84; 527 participants), supported by trial sequential analysis. The trials reported little on causes of death and non-fatal serious adverse events. The authors conclude there is low-quality evidence of a short-term beneficial effect on hepatic encephalopathy and no evidence of an effect on mortality, and that large high-quality trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: The pooled base is one large trial plus many small, old, high-risk-of-bias trials with follow-up often under a day, and encephalopathy was measured on several different scales across trials. The review exists in two 2017 records for the same review — only this one is carded, per the one-home rule.

cards.headline: Synthesis: flumazenil can briefly lighten overt hepatic encephalopathy in a subset of patients — about 1 in 6 in the one large trial — with no mortality effect and no evidence beyond hours
cards.summary: Synthesis: flumazenil can briefly lighten overt hepatic encephalopathy in a subset of patients — about 1 in 6 in the one large trial — with no mortality effect and no evidence beyond hours
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (crossover trial 527 patients; pragmatic trial 14 patients / 18 episodes; Cochrane pool 867 participants across 14 trials).
cards.result: The evidence supports a short-term effect on encephalopathy grade and EEG: neurological improvement 17.5%/14.7% versus 3.8%/2.7% in grade III/IVa in the large crossover trial, and a pooled beneficial effect in the Cochrane review — alongside a clear absence of mortality benefit (7.4% vs 9.3%, confidence interval including no effect) and follow-up measured in minutes to hours in most trials. Nothing here supports flumazenil as ongoing therapy or prophylaxis; its role on this evidence is a brief diagnostic/therapeutic probe in severe overt encephalopathy.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Lexipafant in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: a failed programme — small trials improved organ-failure scores, but the phase 3 trial (n=290) found no prevention of organ failure (57% vs 58%) and no mortality benefit
shelves.question: In patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, does lexipafant (a platelet-activating-factor antagonist) versus placebo prevent organ failure and reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Biomarkers · Double-Blind Method · E-Selectin · Female · Humans · Imidazoles · Interleukin-8 · Length of Stay · Leucine · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Organ Failure · Pancreatitis · Placebos · Platelet Activating Factor · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme, stated plainly. Two small early trials (n=83 and n=50) reported reduced organ-failure scores with the platelet-activating-factor antagonist lexipafant, but the adequately powered phase 3 trial (n=290) found no effect on new organ failure (organ failure in 57% on lexipafant versus 58% on placebo) and no significant mortality difference, and the Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions found no evidence that any drug, lexipafant included, reduces short-term mortality in acute pancreatitis. Lexipafant was never licensed. Severity prediction used 1990s criteria (APACHE II / Glasgow), which dates the context.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Kingsnorth 1995): lexipafant 60 mg for 3 days reduced organ failure at 72 hours in 83 patients with acute pancreatitis — the early signal the programme was built on
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Kingsnorth 1995): lexipafant 60 mg for 3 days reduced organ failure at 72 hours in 83 patients with acute pancreatitis — the early signal the programme was built on
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, lexipafant 60 mg IV for 3 days vs placebo
cards.people: 83 patients with acute pancreatitis randomised to lexipafant 60 mg intravenously for 3 days (n=42) or placebo (n=41); 29 patients had severe disease (APACHE II score 8 or more). Groups were matched at entry for age, sex, aetiology, APACHE II score and organ failure score.
cards.result: There was a significant reduction in the incidence of organ failure (P=0.041) and in total organ failure score (P=0.048) at the end of medication (72 hours). Among patients with severe pancreatitis, 7 of 12 on lexipafant recovered from an organ failure, versus 2 of 11 on placebo, with 2 others on placebo developing new organ failure. Serum interleukin-8 fell significantly (P=0.038) and interleukin-6 declined on day 1; there was no effect on C-reactive protein.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=83) and short: the endpoint was organ-failure score at 72 hours, not mortality, and only 29 patients had severe disease — a physiological signal, not a clinical-outcome verdict.
cards.source: Kingsnorth AN et al. Randomized, double-blind phase II trial of Lexipafant, a platelet-activating factor antagonist, in human acute pancreatitis. The British journal of surgery. 1995. cards.headline: Multicentre RCT (McKay 1997): lexipafant infusion produced a greater fall in organ failure score over 7 days in 50 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, with only trends on mortality
cards.summary: Multicentre RCT (McKay 1997): lexipafant infusion produced a greater fall in organ failure score over 7 days in 50 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, with only trends on mortality
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial, lexipafant 100 mg/day infusion for up to 7 days vs placebo
cards.people: 50 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, selected from 188 screened over 14 months in 11 hospitals in the West of Scotland, randomised to lexipafant 100 mg/day by continuous intravenous infusion for up to 7 days or placebo.
cards.result: The fall in organ failure score over the 7 study days was significantly greater on lexipafant: mean change −1.42 (median −1) versus mean change 0.17 (median 0) on placebo (P=0.003). This was associated with trends towards reduced mortality and a reduced incidence of systemic complications — the abstract reports no significant mortality result and gives no mortality counts.
cards.watchOut: Only 50 patients from 188 screened, and the significant result is a score change, not a patient outcome; the mortality and complication findings were trends only.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT (Johnson 2001): in 290 patients, lexipafant did NOT prevent new organ failure (57% vs 58% developed organ failure) and deaths did not differ significantly — the programme's definitive, negative trial
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT (Johnson 2001): in 290 patients, lexipafant did NOT prevent new organ failure (57% vs 58% developed organ failure) and deaths did not differ significantly — the programme's definitive, negative trial
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, lexipafant 100 mg/day for 7 days vs placebo
cards.people: 290 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis (APACHE II score >6) in a multicentre trial, randomised to lexipafant 100 mg/24 hours intravenously for 7 days, started within 72 hours of symptom onset (n=148 analysed), or placebo (n=138 analysed).
cards.result: Overall, 85 of 148 (57%) on lexipafant and 80 of 138 (58%) on placebo developed one or more organ failures. The primary hypothesis was undermined because 44% of patients already had organ failure on entry and only 39 patients (14%) developed new organ failure; lexipafant had no effect on new organ failure during treatment. Organ failure scores were reduced on lexipafant only on day 3 (median change −1 versus 0; P=0.04). Systemic sepsis affected fewer patients on lexipafant (4 of 148 versus 13 of 138; P=0.023) and pseudocysts were fewer (5% versus 14%; P=0.025), but local complications overall did not reach significance (20% versus 30%; P=0.065) and deaths attributable to acute pancreatitis were not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own lesson: most organ failure was already present within 72 hours of symptom onset, so a drug started in that window could not 'prevent' it — the early small trials' score improvements did not translate into prevented organ failure or saved lives.
cards.source: Johnson CD et al. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Moggia 2017) — lexipafant limb only: no mortality benefit for any pharmacological intervention; the lexipafant limb rests on the single phase 3 trial (N=290, very low-quality evidence)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Moggia 2017) — lexipafant limb only: no mortality benefit for any pharmacological intervention; the lexipafant limb rests on the single phase 3 trial (N=290, very low-quality evidence)
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane) of pharmacological interventions for acute pancreatitis — lexipafant limb extracted
cards.people: The review included 84 randomised trials with 8,234 participants across all pharmacological interventions for acute pancreatitis; the lexipafant comparisons rest on the trials carded above, with the mortality and serious-event estimates drawn from the single 290-patient phase 3 trial.
cards.result: There was no evidence of a difference in short-term mortality in any comparison in the review (very low-quality evidence). For lexipafant specifically, the number of serious adverse events was lower than control (rate ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.96 — a relative measure; N=290, 1 study, very low-quality evidence) and the proportion with sepsis was lower (odds ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.83 — a relative measure; N=290, 1 study, very low-quality evidence). This card extracts the lexipafant limb only; the review as a whole covers many other drugs and is not a lexipafant-only synthesis.
cards.watchOut: Very low-quality evidence throughout the review, and the lexipafant event estimates come from one trial — they do not add an independent confirmation beyond the phase 3 card above.

systematic review (cochrane) of pharmacological interventions for acute pancreatitis — lexipafant limb extracted the review included 84 randomised trials with 8,234 participants across all pharmacological interventions for acute pancreatitis; the lexipafant comparisons rest on the trials carded above, with the mortality and serious-event estimates drawn from the single 290-patient phase 3 trial. there was no evidence of a difference in short-term mortality in any comparison in the review (very low-quality evidence). for lexipafant specifically, the number of serious adverse events was lower than control (rate ratio 0.67, 95% ci 0.46 to 0.96 — a relative measure; n=290, 1 study, very low-quality evidence) and the proportion with sepsis was lower (odds ratio 0.26, 95% ci 0.08 to 0.83 — a relative measure; n=290, 1 study, very low-quality evidence). this card extracts the lexipafant limb only; the review as a whole covers many other drugs and is not a lexipafant-only synthesis. very low-quality evidence throughout the review, and the lexipafant event estimates come from one trial — they do not add an independent confirmation beyond the phase 3 card above. moggia e et al. pharmacological interventions for acute pancreatitis. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. pmid: 28431202. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acute disease · anti-bacterial agents · antioxidants · confidence intervals · gastrointestinal agents · humans · pancreatitis · pancreatitis, acute necrotizing · probiotics · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme — two small trials improved organ-failure scores, the 290-patient phase 3 trial found no prevention of organ failure and no mortality benefit, and lexipafant was never licensed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme — two small trials improved organ-failure scores, the 290-patient phase 3 trial found no prevention of organ failure and no mortality benefit, and lexipafant was never licensed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The randomised record is three lexipafant trials plus the Cochrane lexipafant limb. Kingsnorth 1995 (n=83) and McKay 1997 (n=50) showed better organ-failure scores over 3–7 days. Johnson 2001 (n=290), the only adequately powered trial, found organ failure in 57% on lexipafant versus 58% on placebo, no effect on new organ failure, and no significant difference in deaths. The Cochrane review found no mortality benefit for any pharmacological intervention in acute pancreatitis. Treatment of severe acute pancreatitis remains supportive care; lexipafant is a historical, unlicensed programme.

shelves.title: Clevudine in chronic hepatitis B: potent 12–24-week suppression in three placebo trials (59–92% undetectable, ALT normalisation 68–75%) — and myopathy in 3.9% on longer exposure, the cost that halted development outside South Korea
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative), does the nucleoside analogue clevudine, compared with placebo or adefovir, suppress HBV DNA and normalise ALT — and what is its myopathy cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Alanine Transaminase · Antiviral Agents · Arabinofuranosyluracil · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis B · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Muscular Diseases · Republic of Korea
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term viral suppression — on three Korean placebo-controlled randomised trials (n = 243, 98 and 86) in which 12–24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg daily cut median HBV DNA by about 4.3–5.1 log10 copies/mL against about 0.2–0.5 on placebo, normalised ALT in 68–75% versus 18–33%, and left durable off-therapy suppression. THE MYOPATHY COST STAYS ON THE FACE: clevudine is a single-region programme (developed and marketed in South Korea as Levovir; never FDA-approved), its development elsewhere was halted over myopathy on longer exposure, and in a 102-patient Korean series on treatment beyond 6 months, myopathy developed in 3.9% (reversible on stopping) and resistance reached 11% by 60 weeks. The trials carded here ran only 12–24 weeks — too short to show that harm. The emtricitabine-plus-clevudine combination trial is a different question and is not counted or carded here.

cards.headline: Phase III, HBeAg-positive (Yoo 2007): 243 randomised — 24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg cut median HBV DNA by 5.10 log10 copies/mL vs 0.27 on placebo, with undetectable DNA in 59.0% and ALT normalisation in 68.2% vs 17.5%; suppression persisted off therapy
cards.summary: Phase III, HBeAg-positive (Yoo 2007): 243 randomised — 24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg cut median HBV DNA by 5.10 log10 copies/mL vs 0.27 on placebo, with undetectable DNA in 59.0% and ALT normalisation in 68.2% vs 17.5%; suppression persisted off therapy
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (clevudine 24 weeks, HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B)
cards.people: 243 hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg)-positive patients with chronic hepatitis B randomised 3:1 to clevudine 30 mg once daily (n = 182) or placebo (n = 61) for 24 weeks, then followed for a further 24 weeks off therapy (South Korean programme).
cards.result: Median serum HBV DNA reductions from baseline at week 24 were 5.10 and 0.27 log10 copies/mL in the clevudine and placebo groups respectively (P < 0.0001). Suppression was sustained off therapy, with 3.73 log10 reduction at week 34 and 2.02 log10 reduction at week 48. At week 24, 59.0% of the clevudine group had undetectable serum HBV DNA by Amplicor PCR (less than 300 copies/mL). ALT normalisation was 68.2% on clevudine versus 17.5% on placebo at week 24 (P < 0.0001) and was maintained off treatment. Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups and no resistance was detected during the 24 weeks of dosing.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks of dosing with 24 weeks of follow-up cannot see the myopathy that appears on longer exposure (see the Jang card): 'no resistance and similar adverse events' is a statement about this short window only.

cards.headline: 12-week trial, HBeAg-positive (Lee 2006): 98 randomised to placebo, clevudine 30 mg or 50 mg — median HBV DNA reductions at week 12 of 0.20, 4.49 and 4.45 log10 copies/mL, with suppression and ALT normalisation sustained through 24 weeks off therapy
cards.summary: 12-week trial, HBeAg-positive (Lee 2006): 98 randomised to placebo, clevudine 30 mg or 50 mg — median HBV DNA reductions at week 12 of 0.20, 4.49 and 4.45 log10 copies/mL, with suppression and ALT normalisation sustained through 24 weeks off therapy
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (clevudine 12 weeks, two doses, HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B)
cards.people: 98 patients with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B randomised to placebo (n = 32), clevudine 30 mg (n = 32) or clevudine 50 mg (n = 34) once daily for 12 weeks, then followed off therapy for a further 24 weeks.
cards.result: Median serum HBV DNA reductions at week 12 were 0.20 (placebo), 4.49 (30 mg) and 4.45 (50 mg) log10 copies/mL (P < .0001) — no added antiviral effect from the 50 mg dose. Post-treatment activity was sustained, with 3.32 and 2.99 log10 reductions at 12 weeks off therapy and 2.28 and 1.40 log10 reductions at 24 weeks off therapy in the 30 mg and 50 mg groups. Median ALT decreased markedly during treatment and stayed below the upper limit of normal throughout the 24 off-therapy weeks in both clevudine groups. Adverse events and grade 3/4 laboratory abnormalities were similar across the three groups.
cards.watchOut: The shortest trial on this shelf (12 weeks): its durability claim rests on off-therapy follow-up of a brief course, and it predates the longer-exposure safety record entirely.

cards.headline: HBeAg-negative trial (Yoo 2007): 86 randomised — 24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg cut median HBV DNA by 4.25 log10 copies/mL vs 0.48 on placebo, with undetectable DNA in 92.1% at week 24 and ALT normalisation in 74.6% vs 33.3%
cards.summary: HBeAg-negative trial (Yoo 2007): 86 randomised — 24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg cut median HBV DNA by 4.25 log10 copies/mL vs 0.48 on placebo, with undetectable DNA in 92.1% at week 24 and ALT normalisation in 74.6% vs 33.3%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (clevudine 24 weeks, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B)
cards.people: 86 patients with hepatitis B e antigen-negative chronic hepatitis B randomised 3:1 to clevudine 30 mg daily (n = 63) or placebo (n = 23) for 24 weeks, then followed for an additional 24 weeks after withdrawal of treatment.
cards.result: Median HBV DNA changes from baseline at week 24 were −4.25 (clevudine) and −0.48 (placebo) log10 copies/mL (P < 0.0001); suppression was sustained after withdrawal, with a 3.11 log10 reduction at week 48. At week 24 and week 48, 92.1% and 16.4% of the clevudine group had undetectable serum HBV DNA by Amplicor PCR (less than 300 copies/mL) — the week-48 figure showing most patients relapsing virologically off therapy despite the sustained median reduction. ALT normalisation at week 24 was 74.6% on clevudine versus 33.3% on placebo (P = 0.0006) and was well maintained off treatment. Adverse events were similar in the two groups and no resistance was detected during treatment; the authors state treatment longer than 24 weeks would be needed for durable remission.
cards.watchOut: Read the two undetectable-DNA figures together: 92.1% on treatment falling to 16.4% at week 48 off treatment — 'durable suppression' in the title describes the median, not most individual patients, and the authors themselves call for longer treatment, which is where the myopathy risk lives.
cards.source: Yoo BC et al. Clevudine is highly efficacious in hepatitis B e antigen-negative chronic hepatitis B with durable off-therapy viral suppression. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2007. cards.headline: The harm limb — longer-exposure series (Jang 2011): 102 nucleoside-naïve patients treated more than 6 months (median 53 weeks) — cumulative virological response 81% at 48 weeks, but clevudine resistance 11% at 60 weeks and myopathy in 3.9%, reversible after discontinuation
cards.summary: The harm limb — longer-exposure series (Jang 2011): 102 nucleoside-naïve patients treated more than 6 months (median 53 weeks) — cumulative virological response 81% at 48 weeks, but clevudine resistance 11% at 60 weeks and myopathy in 3.9%, reversible after discontinuation
cards.type: Retrospective observational series (clevudine longer-exposure efficacy, resistance and myopathy) — programme support for the harm limb, not a trial anchor
cards.people: 102 nucleoside-naïve patients with chronic hepatitis B in South Korea who had received clevudine for more than 6 months with good compliance (median treatment duration 53 weeks, range 25–90 weeks); retrospective analysis of medical records. Observational programme support for the harm side — not a randomised anchor, and labelled as such.
cards.result: The cumulative rate of virological response (HBV DNA below 2,000 copies/mL) at 48 weeks was 81%, and the cumulative rate of clevudine resistance was 11% at 60 weeks of treatment. Independent predictors of virological response were HBeAg negativity and rapid early viral-load decrease. Clevudine-related myopathy developed in 3.9% of patients and was reversible after discontinuation of clevudine. The authors conclude long-term therapy beyond 1 year produced considerable resistance and myopathy, and alternative agents should be considered if either develops.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-country, no comparator: the 3.9% myopathy figure is a floor estimate from records of compliant patients, and mitochondrial-toxicity reports on longer exposure sit behind the halted development programme — the face of this shelf keeps that cost in view.
cards.source: Jang JH et al. Clevudine for chronic hepatitis B: antiviral response, predictors of response, and development of myopathy. Journal of viral hepatitis. 2011. PMID: 20196804.
