cards.headline: Synthesis: clevudine suppresses HBV potently for 12–24 weeks in both HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative disease (about 4.3–5.1 log10 vs about 0.2–0.5 on placebo, ALT normalisation 68–75%) — and its longer-exposure record is resistance in 11% by 60 weeks and reversible myopathy in 3.9%, the harm that halted development outside South Korea
cards.summary: Synthesis: clevudine suppresses HBV potently for 12–24 weeks in both HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative disease (about 4.3–5.1 log10 vs about 0.2–0.5 on placebo, ALT normalisation 68–75%) — and its longer-exposure record is resistance in 11% by 60 weeks and reversible myopathy in 3.9%, the harm that halted development outside South Korea
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three Korean placebo-controlled trials (Yoo 2007, n = 243, HBeAg-positive, 24 weeks; Lee 2006, n = 98, HBeAg-positive, 12 weeks, NCT00305019; Yoo 2007, n = 86, HBeAg-negative, 24 weeks, NCT00313274) agree on potent, partly off-therapy-sustained HBV DNA suppression and ALT normalisation, with no resistance detected within their short dosing windows. The longer-exposure series (Jang 2011, n = 102, median 53 weeks, observational) supplies the other half of the balance: 81% cumulative virological response at 48 weeks alongside 11% resistance at 60 weeks and myopathy in 3.9%, reversible on stopping. LIKELY (benefit) for short-term viral suppression, as the balance states — a single-region programme (Levovir in South Korea, never FDA-approved) whose development elsewhere was halted over myopathy, so the stamp answers the suppression question, not a recommendation to use clevudine where modern first-line agents are available. The emtricitabine-plus-clevudine combination trial was not counted or carded: it asks a different question.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the trials' clean 12–24-week safety lines stand for the drug's safety: the harm emerged on the longer exposure that durable remission would require.

shelves.title: Entecavir + adefovir rescue in lamivudine-resistant HBV: 29% vs 4% below 60 IU/mL at 52 weeks vs continuing lamivudine + adefovir, rising to 42% by 104 weeks — a historical-era answer on one randomised programme
shelves.question: In adults with lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B (including suboptimal responders to lamivudine plus adefovir and multiple-drug-refractory infection), does entecavir plus adefovir combination rescue therapy, compared with lamivudine plus adefovir or adefovir-based strategies, achieve virological response?
shelves.mesh: Adenine · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · Drug Resistance, Viral · Female · Guanine · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Lamivudine · Male · Middle Aged · Organophosphonates · Young Adult · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hepatitis B virus · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a historical-era question, printed on the face: lamivudine resistance is now uncommon where entecavir / tenofovir are first-line, and this shelf answers the rescue question as it stood in that era, in small single-region trials (Korea / China lineage). One randomised programme (Lim: 90 patients who had suboptimal response to lamivudine plus adefovir) found entecavir plus adefovir clearly superior to continuing lamivudine plus adefovir at 52 weeks — virological response 29% vs 4%, mean HBV DNA reduction −2.2 vs −0.6 log10 IU/mL, new resistance mutations 0% vs 15% — and its 104-week extension (the same trial, labelled as such, not a second trial) showed progressive response once both arms received the combination. A three-way comparison (91 patients) points the same way. One commissioned anchor was REFUSED: the Heo 2014 randomised trial (PMID 25587617) has an empty abstract in its PubMed record, so no numbers could be verified from the record this session and it is not carded — the refusal is stated on the Synthesis card. The ACE study (add adefovir vs switch to entecavir, PMID 23295056) asks a different strategy question and is cross-pointed, not carded.

cards.headline: Randomised rescue trial (Lim 2012): 90 patients with lamivudine-resistant HBV and suboptimal response to lamivudine plus adefovir — switching to entecavir plus adefovir gave HBV DNA below 60 IU/mL in 29% vs 4% at 52 weeks, with mean reduction −2.2 vs −0.6 log10 IU/mL and no new resistance vs 15%
cards.summary: Randomised rescue trial (Lim 2012): 90 patients with lamivudine-resistant HBV and suboptimal response to lamivudine plus adefovir — switching to entecavir plus adefovir gave HBV DNA below 60 IU/mL in 29% vs 4% at 52 weeks, with mean reduction −2.2 vs −0.6 log10 IU/mL and no new resistance vs 15%
cards.type: Randomised active-control trial (entecavir plus adefovir vs continued lamivudine plus adefovir, lamivudine-resistant HBV with suboptimal response)
cards.people: 90 adults with lamivudine-resistant hepatitis B virus whose serum HBV DNA remained above 2,000 IU/mL after at least 24 weeks of lamivudine plus adefovir rescue therapy (mean baseline HBV DNA 4.60 log10 IU/mL, SD 1.03), randomised to entecavir plus adefovir (n = 45) or continuation of lamivudine plus adefovir (n = 45) for 52 weeks; all 90 completed treatment.
cards.result: At week 52 the primary endpoint — serum HBV DNA below 60 IU/mL — was reached by 29% (13 of 45) on entecavir plus adefovir versus 4% (2 of 45) on continued lamivudine plus adefovir (P = 0.004) — an absolute difference of about 25 percentage points. The mean reduction in HBV DNA was −2.2 versus −0.6 log10 IU/mL (P < 0.001). Additional mutations causing resistance to adefovir or entecavir were detected in none of the entecavir-plus-adefovir group but in 15% of the lamivudine-plus-adefovir group (P = 0.018). Safety and adverse-event profiles were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Even the winning arm suppressed only 29% below 60 IU/mL at 52 weeks: 'superior rescue' in this era still left most patients viraemic — the comparison is against a failing regimen, not against modern first-line therapy.
cards.source: Lim YS et al. Randomized trial of entecavir plus adefovir in patients with lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B who show suboptimal response to lamivudine plus adefovir. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2012. PMID: 22430972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Extension of the SAME trial (Lim 2013): 89 of the 90 patients continued on entecavir plus adefovir for a second year — virological response at week 104 was 42.2% in those randomised to it from the start and 34.1% in those switched to it, with pre-existing resistant mutants falling in both groups
cards.summary: Extension of the SAME trial (Lim 2013): 89 of the 90 patients continued on entecavir plus adefovir for a second year — virological response at week 104 was 42.2% in those randomised to it from the start and 34.1% in those switched to it, with pre-existing resistant mutants falling in both groups
cards.type: Extension report of the Lim randomised trial (up to 104 weeks of entecavir plus adefovir, multiple-drug-refractory HBV) — same programme as the card above, not an independent trial
cards.people: 89 of the 90 patients who completed the 52-week Lim randomised trial (card above) enrolled in this extension: the 45 originally randomised to entecavir plus adefovir (EA-EA) and 44 of those originally on lamivudine plus adefovir (LA-EA) all received entecavir plus adefovir for an additional 52 weeks. This is the same trial programme reported at a later time point — labelled as an extension, not counted as an independent trial.
cards.result: Proportions with virological response (HBV DNA below 60 IU/mL) increased gradually in both groups and were comparable at week 104: 42.2% (EA-EA) versus 34.1% (LA-EA) (P = 0.51). Mean HBV DNA reductions from the original baseline were identical (−2.8 and −2.8 log10 IU/mL; P = 0.87). Patients retaining pre-existing HBV mutants resistant to adefovir or entecavir decreased from 8 to 2 (EA-EA) and from 15 to 6 (LA-EA) (P = 0.27), with no selection of additional resistance mutants and favourable safety in both groups.
cards.watchOut: After week 52 there is no untreated comparator left — both arms are on the combination — so the week-104 figures show accumulation over time, not a randomised contrast; the randomised evidence on this shelf is the 52-week card.

cards.headline: Three-way rescue comparison (Ha 2012): 91 lamivudine-resistant (YMDD) patients treated at least 24 months — adefovir plus entecavir gave the deepest suppression (−5.58 log10 IU/mL at 24 months), 78.1% undetectable at 6 months, and no viral breakthrough or genotypic resistance, vs breakthrough in 27.6% on adefovir alone and 13.3% on adefovir plus lamivudine
cards.summary: Three-way rescue comparison (Ha 2012): 91 lamivudine-resistant (YMDD) patients treated at least 24 months — adefovir plus entecavir gave the deepest suppression (−5.58 log10 IU/mL at 24 months), 78.1% undetectable at 6 months, and no viral breakthrough or genotypic resistance, vs breakthrough in 27.6% on adefovir alone and 13.3% on adefovir plus lamivudine
cards.type: Three-way rescue comparison (adefovir alone vs adefovir plus lamivudine vs adefovir plus entecavir, lamivudine-resistant HBV) — programme support
cards.people: 91 adults with chronic hepatitis B and lamivudine-resistance (YMDD) mutations, treated for at least 24 months with adefovir monotherapy (n = 29), adefovir plus lamivudine (n = 30) or adefovir plus entecavir (n = 32). PubMed types this report as a randomised controlled trial; its abstract describes the three treated groups, and it is carded as programme support for the Lim programme, as commissioned.
cards.result: Mean serum HBV DNA decreases in the adefovir-plus-entecavir group were −3.23, −4.41, −5.32 and −5.58 log10 IU/mL at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months — the most significant among the three groups (P < 0.01). HBV DNA undetectability (below 60 IU/mL) at 6 months in the adefovir-plus-entecavir group was 78.1%, also the most significant (P = 0.024). Viral breakthrough and genotypic mutations were detected in 8 patients (27.6%) on adefovir monotherapy and 4 (13.3%) on adefovir plus lamivudine, whereas no case was detected in the adefovir-plus-entecavir group after 24 months (P < 0.05). The authors conclude the entecavir combination was superior for initial response and long-term suppression and best prevented cross-resistance to all three agents.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (29–32 per arm) from a single centre's lamivudine-resistant population, with very deep mean suppression that sits oddly beside the Lim trial's 29% response rate — different populations and response definitions; the two are concordant in direction, not interchangeable in magnitude.
cards.source: Ha M et al. Rescue therapy for lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B: adefovir monotherapy, adefovir plus lamivudine or entecavir combination therapy. Internal medicine (Tokyo, Japan). 2012. PMID: 22728482. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: entecavir plus adefovir beat continuing lamivudine plus adefovir in the one randomised rescue programme (29% vs 4% below 60 IU/mL at 52 weeks), with progressive response to 104 weeks and a concordant three-way comparison — a historical-era answer, on a small single-region base. REFUSAL, stated here as required: the Heo 2014 randomised trial of entecavir plus adefovir versus adefovir plus lamivudine in HBeAg-positive lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B (PMID 25587617) was NOT carded because its PubMed record carries an empty abstract — no numbers could be verified from the record this session, and this shelf cards no number it cannot fetch
cards.summary: Synthesis: entecavir plus adefovir beat continuing lamivudine plus adefovir in the one randomised rescue programme (29% vs 4% below 60 IU/mL at 52 weeks), with progressive response to 104 weeks and a concordant three-way comparison — a historical-era answer, on a small single-region base. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The randomised evidence is one programme: Lim 2012 (90 patients, suboptimal responders to lamivudine plus adefovir) — virological response 29% vs 4% at 52 weeks (absolute difference about 25 percentage points), mean reduction −2.2 vs −0.6 log10 IU/mL, new resistance 0% vs 15% — plus its own 104-week extension (Lim 2013, NCT01023217; 89 of the same 90 patients, response rising to 42.2% and 34.1% once both arms received the combination), labelled an extension and not a second trial. The three-way comparison (Ha 2012; 91 patients) is concordant: deepest suppression and no breakthrough on adefovir plus entecavir. POSSIBLE (benefit): one randomised programme plus one supporting comparison, in small single-region (Korea / China) samples, answering a historical-era question — lamivudine resistance is now uncommon where entecavir / tenofovir are first-line. The ACE study (PMID 23295056; adding adefovir versus switching to entecavir) asks a different strategy question and is cross-pointed here, not carded. Refused for an empty abstract record: Heo 2014, PMID 25587617 — see this card's headline; a full-text pull could restore it at a refresh.
cards.watchOut: Era and base are printed on the face for a reason: do not present a 29% 52-week response against a failing regimen as evidence about entecavir-plus-adefovir's place in current practice, where tenofovir-based rescue has superseded this question.

shelves.title: Lamivudine as treatment for chronic hepatitis B — a superseded first-line agent (YMDD resistance): NEJM trials showed HBV DNA suppression (44% vs 16% sustained), ALT normalisation and histologic improvement over placebo
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive initial treatment; advanced liver disease; and children), does lamivudine, compared with placebo or interferon-era controls, suppress HBV DNA, normalise ALT and slow liver-disease progression — and at what resistance cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Alanine Transaminase · Antiviral Agents · Chronic Disease · DNA, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis B · Hepatitis B virus · Humans · Lamivudine · Male · Middle Aged · Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors · Zalcitabine
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) in its era, on three placebo-controlled NEJM trials — and a historical-foundation shelf: lamivudine is a SUPERSEDED first-line agent because viral resistance (YMDD) emerges on continued therapy, and that history leads this face. Dienstag 1995 (preliminary, 32 patients): 100 mg and 300 mg doses made HBV DNA undetectable in 100% of patients during 12 weeks, but DNA reappeared in most after stopping. Dienstag 1999 (US initial treatment, 143 randomised, 52 weeks): histologic response 52% vs 23% on placebo, sustained HBV DNA suppression 44% vs 16%, ALT normalisation 41% vs 7%. Jonas 2002 (children, 288 randomised): virologic response 23% vs 13%. The fetched trial reports do not print a resistance rate, so none is printed here; the resistance cost is stated qualitatively, as the commissioning row records it. The advanced-liver-disease NEJM trial of lamivudine is carded in the live library and is cross-pointed in the synthesis only — it is NOT carded on this shelf (gate discipline). Lamivudine's HIV and chemotherapy-prophylaxis questions live on other shelves and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Preliminary RCT (Dienstag 1995): 12 weeks of lamivudine made HBV DNA undetectable in 100% of patients on 100 mg or 300 mg daily — but DNA reappeared in most after treatment stopped
cards.summary: Preliminary RCT (Dienstag 1995): 12 weeks of lamivudine made HBV DNA undetectable in 100% of patients on 100 mg or 300 mg daily — but DNA reappeared in most after treatment stopped
cards.type: Preliminary randomised double-blind dose-ranging trial, lamivudine 25/100/300 mg vs each other (no placebo arm), 12 weeks' treatment
cards.people: 32 patients with chronic hepatitis B (all with hepatitis B antigen in serum; 17 had not responded to earlier interferon), randomly assigned to oral lamivudine 25 mg, 100 mg or 300 mg daily for 12 weeks, then followed for 24 weeks.
cards.result: HBV DNA became undetectable (≤1.5 pg/mL) in 70% of patients on 25 mg and 100% of those on 100 mg or 300 mg. In most patients HBV DNA reappeared after therapy ended; however, 6 patients (19%), including 5 prior interferon non-responders, had sustained HBV DNA suppression with normalisation of alanine aminotransferase, and hepatitis B e antigen disappeared in 4 of these 6 (12% of all patients). Alanine aminotransferase levels at least doubled during or after therapy in 5 patients (50%) on 25 mg and 8 (36%) on the higher doses. Minor adverse events were not dose-related; transient asymptomatic amylase, lipase and creatine kinase elevations occurred.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=32) and short (12 weeks), with no placebo arm — a dose-finding preliminary trial, carded as the programme's first report and not load-bearing alone; its central lesson is relapse after stopping, not durable cure.
cards.source: Dienstag JL et al. A preliminary trial of lamivudine for chronic hepatitis B infection. The New England journal of medicine. 1995. PMID: 7477217. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: US initial-treatment RCT (Dienstag 1999): one year of lamivudine 100 mg beat placebo on histology (52% vs 23%), HBV DNA suppression (44% vs 16%) and ALT normalisation (41% vs 7%)
cards.summary: US initial-treatment RCT (Dienstag 1999): one year of lamivudine 100 mg beat placebo on histology (52% vs 23%), HBV DNA suppression (44% vs 16%) and ALT normalisation (41% vs 7%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, lamivudine 100 mg daily for 52 weeks as initial treatment
cards.people: 143 previously untreated US patients with chronic hepatitis B randomly assigned to lamivudine 100 mg or placebo daily for 52 weeks, then followed 16 weeks; 137 were included in the efficacy analysis (66 lamivudine, 71 placebo). The primary endpoint was a reduction of at least 2 points in the Histologic Activity Index.
cards.result: After 52 weeks, lamivudine recipients were more likely than placebo recipients to have a histologic response (52% vs 23%, P<0.001), loss of hepatitis B e antigen (32% vs 11%, P=0.003), sustained suppression of serum HBV DNA to undetectable levels (44% vs 16%, P<0.001) and sustained ALT normalisation (41% vs 7%, P<0.001), and were less likely to have increased hepatic fibrosis (5% vs 20%, P=0.01). HBeAg seroconversion occurred in 17% vs 6% (P=0.04) and persisted in most patients 16 weeks after stopping. Lamivudine was well tolerated; self-limited post-treatment ALT elevations (≥3 times baseline) were more common on lamivudine (25% vs 8%, P=0.01), with all patients' clinical condition remaining stable.
cards.watchOut: A one-year, interferon-era trial: its endpoints are histologic, virologic and biochemical, not clinical outcomes, and its record does not quantify the YMDD resistance that later ended lamivudine's first-line era — that cost is stated qualitatively on this shelf's face, not given a number the record does not contain.
cards.source: Dienstag JL et al. Lamivudine as initial treatment for chronic hepatitis B in the United States. The New England journal of medicine. 1999. PMID: 10528035. multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, lamivudine 100 mg daily for 52 weeks as initial treatment 143 previously untreated us patients with chronic hepatitis b randomly assigned to lamivudine 100 mg or placebo daily for 52 weeks, then followed 16 weeks; 137 were included in the efficacy analysis (66 lamivudine, 71 placebo). the primary endpoint was a reduction of at least 2 points in the histologic activity index. after 52 weeks, lamivudine recipients were more likely than placebo recipients to have a histologic response (52% vs 23%, p<0.001), loss of hepatitis b e antigen (32% vs 11%, p=0.003), sustained suppression of serum hbv dna to undetectable levels (44% vs 16%, p<0.001) and sustained alt normalisation (41% vs 7%, p<0.001), and were less likely to have increased hepatic fibrosis (5% vs 20%, p=0.01). hbeag seroconversion occurred in 17% vs 6% (p=0.04) and persisted in most patients 16 weeks after stopping. lamivudine was well tolerated; self-limited post-treatment alt elevations (≥3 times baseline) were more common on lamivudine (25% vs 8%, p=0.01), with all patients' clinical condition remaining stable. a one-year, interferon-era trial: its endpoints are histologic, virologic and biochemical, not clinical outcomes, and its record does not quantify the ymdd resistance that later ended lamivudine's first-line era — that cost is stated qualitatively on this shelf's face, not given a number the record does not contain. dienstag jl et al. lamivudine as initial treatment for chronic hepatitis b in the united states. the new england journal of medicine. 1999. pmid: 10528035. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · alanine transaminase · dna, viral · double-blind method · female · hepatitis b e antigens · hepatitis b virus · hepatitis b, chronic · humans · lamivudine · liver · male · middle aged · mutation · prospective studies · reverse transcriptase inhibitors · united states

cards.headline: Children's RCT (Jonas 2002): lamivudine for 52 weeks gave a higher virologic response than placebo in children with chronic hepatitis B (23% vs 13%)
cards.summary: Children's RCT (Jonas 2002): lamivudine for 52 weeks gave a higher virologic response than placebo in children with chronic hepatitis B (23% vs 13%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in children, lamivudine weight-based dosing for 52 weeks
cards.people: Children with chronic hepatitis B randomly assigned 2:1 to oral lamivudine (3 mg/kg, maximum 100 mg) once daily (n=191) or placebo (n=97) for 52 weeks, from 403 children screened. The primary endpoint was virologic response (absence of serum hepatitis B e antigen and serum HBV DNA) at week 52.
cards.result: The virologic response rate at week 52 was higher on lamivudine than placebo (23% vs 13%, P=0.04). Lamivudine was well tolerated and was also associated with higher rates of HBeAg-to-antibody seroconversion, ALT normalisation and HBV DNA suppression (the report's abstract states these directions without printing the rates).
cards.watchOut: The absolute virologic-response gain in children was modest (23% vs 13%), and this is a paediatric population — its result should not be read across to adults beyond showing the same direction of effect.
cards.source: Jonas MM et al. Clinical trial of lamivudine in children with chronic hepatitis B. The New England journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 12037150. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three placebo-era NEJM trials agree lamivudine suppresses HBV and improves histology and ALT — and the drug was still superseded, because resistance (YMDD) accumulates on continued therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: three placebo-era NEJM trials agree lamivudine suppresses HBV and improves histology and ALT — and the drug was still superseded, because resistance (YMDD) accumulates on continued therapy
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (Dienstag 1995, n=32; Dienstag 1999, n=143; Jonas 2002, n=288 randomised).
cards.result: Across the preliminary dose-ranging trial, the US initial-treatment trial and the children's trial, lamivudine consistently suppressed HBV DNA, normalised ALT more often and improved liver histology versus placebo, with responses partly sustained after stopping in the adult initial-treatment trial. Two limits frame the shelf. First, durability: HBV DNA reappeared in most patients after the 12-week preliminary course. Second, resistance: lamivudine's first-line era ended because YMDD resistance emerges on continued therapy — the fetched reports carded here do not print a resistance rate, so this shelf prints none and states the cost qualitatively. Separately, the randomised trial of lamivudine in advanced liver disease is carded in the live library and is cross-pointed here only; it is not re-carded on this shelf. Modern first-line hepatitis B therapy (entecavir, tenofovir) is homed on its own shelves.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Adefovir dipivoxil in chronic hepatitis B — a superseded agent: histologic improvement 53–64% vs 25–33% on placebo and HBV DNA suppression in both NEJM trials; stopping lost the benefit, resistance reached 5.9% by 144 weeks
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative), does adefovir dipivoxil, compared with placebo, suppress HBV DNA and improve liver histology?
shelves.mesh: Adenine · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Alanine Transaminase · Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Liver · Male · Middle Aged · Organophosphonates
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) in its era, on two NEJM placebo-controlled trials plus the HBeAg-negative programme's long-term extension report (labelled as extension lineage on its card) — and a historical shelf: adefovir is a SUPERSEDED agent (nephrotoxicity at higher doses; resistance emerging on long therapy), printed here on the face. Marcellin 2003 (HBeAg-positive, 515 randomised): histologic improvement 53% on adefovir 10 mg vs 25% on placebo, with HBV DNA undetectable in 21% vs 0%. Hadziyannis 2003 (HBeAg-negative, 185 randomised): histologic improvement 64% vs 33%, HBV DNA below 400 copies/mL in 51% vs 0%, ALT normalisation 72% vs 29%. The 2005 long-term report (the same HBeAg-negative programme, continued): benefit was maintained to 144 weeks on continued therapy (HBV DNA <1,000 copies/mL in 79%) and lost in most patients switched to placebo; resistance mutations (rtN236T, rtA181V) had emerged in 5.9% by 144 weeks. At the licensed 10 mg dose the 48-week safety profile resembled placebo; the 30 mg dose produced more adverse events and renal laboratory abnormalities. Tenofovir-versus-adefovir is a tenofovir question, cross-pointed in the synthesis, not carded here.

cards.headline: HBeAg-positive RCT (Marcellin 2003): adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg improved liver histology in 53% vs 25% on placebo and made HBV DNA undetectable in 21% vs 0% at 48 weeks
cards.summary: HBeAg-positive RCT (Marcellin 2003): adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg improved liver histology in 53% vs 25% on placebo and made HBV DNA undetectable in 21% vs 0% at 48 weeks
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg or 30 mg daily for 48 weeks
cards.people: 515 patients with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B randomly assigned to adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg (n=172), 30 mg (n=173) or placebo (n=170) daily for 48 weeks. The primary endpoint was histologic improvement in the 10 mg group versus placebo.
cards.result: At 48 weeks, histologic improvement occurred in 53% (10 mg, P<0.001), 59% (30 mg, P<0.001) and 25% (placebo). Median serum HBV DNA reductions were 3.52, 4.76 and 0.55 log copies/mL respectively; undetectable HBV DNA (<400 copies/mL) in 21%, 39% and 0%; ALT normalisation in 48%, 55% and 16%; HBeAg seroconversion in 12% (P=0.049), 14% (P=0.01) and 6%. No adefovir-associated resistance mutations were identified. The 10 mg dose's safety profile was similar to placebo; the 30 mg group had more adverse events and renal laboratory abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: The 30 mg dose was more potent virologically but is not the licensed hepatitis B dose — its renal laboratory signal is why the 10 mg dose carries the favourable risk-benefit statement; endpoints are histologic/virologic, not clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Marcellin P et al. Adefovir dipivoxil for the treatment of hepatitis B e antigen-positive chronic hepatitis B. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 12606735. cards.headline: HBeAg-negative RCT (Hadziyannis 2003): adefovir 10 mg improved histology in 64% vs 33% on placebo, with HBV DNA below 400 copies/mL in 51% vs 0% at 48 weeks
cards.summary: HBeAg-negative RCT (Hadziyannis 2003): adefovir 10 mg improved histology in 64% vs 33% on placebo, with HBV DNA below 400 copies/mL in 51% vs 0% at 48 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg daily for 48 weeks in HBeAg-negative disease
cards.people: 185 patients with HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B randomly assigned 2:1, double-blind, to adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg or placebo once daily for 48 weeks. The primary endpoint was histologic improvement.
cards.result: At week 48, histologic improvement occurred in 64% of the adefovir group (77 of 121 with baseline biopsy specimens) versus 33% on placebo (19 of 57, P<0.001). Serum HBV DNA fell below 400 copies/mL in 51% (63 of 123) versus 0% (0 of 61, P<0.001); the median decrease in log HBV DNA was 3.91 vs 1.35 log copies/mL (P<0.001). ALT had normalised in 72% (84 of 116) versus 29% (17 of 59, P<0.001). No HBV polymerase mutations associated with adefovir resistance were identified, and the safety profile was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: This trial is the parent study of the long-term report carded next — the two cards are one programme's lineage, not two independent trials; histologic denominators are the patients with baseline biopsy specimens, as printed.
cards.source: Hadziyannis SJ et al. Adefovir dipivoxil for the treatment of hepatitis B e antigen-negative chronic hepatitis B. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 12606734. cards.headline: Long-term extension report (Hadziyannis 2005) — the HBeAg-negative programme continued: benefit was maintained to 144 weeks on continued adefovir and lost after switching to placebo; resistance mutations reached 5.9% by week 144
cards.summary: Long-term extension report (Hadziyannis 2005) — the HBeAg-negative programme continued: benefit was maintained to 144 weeks on continued adefovir and lost after switching to placebo; resistance mutations reached 5.9% by week 144
cards.type: Long-term continuation / re-randomisation report of the HBeAg-negative trial programme (extension lineage of the Hadziyannis 2003 card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same 185 HBeAg-negative patients as the 2003 trial above (extension lineage, labelled as such): after 48 weeks, patients on adefovir were re-randomised to a further 48 weeks of adefovir or to placebo; patients originally on placebo switched to adefovir; continued therapy was then offered to week 144 and beyond.
cards.result: On continued adefovir, the median decrease in serum HBV DNA was 3.47 log copies/mL at week 96 and 3.63 log copies/mL at week 144, with HBV DNA below 1,000 copies/mL in 71% at week 96 and 79% at week 144. In most patients switched from adefovir to placebo the benefit was lost (median HBV DNA change −1.09 log copies/mL; only 8% below 1,000 copies/mL at week 96). Side effects in weeks 49–144 resembled the first 48 weeks. Resistance mutations rtN236T and rtA181V were identified in 5.9% of patients after 144 weeks.
cards.watchOut: An extension report of one programme: it answers the continuation-versus-stopping question for that programme only, and its 5.9% resistance figure at 144 weeks is the shelf's quantified resistance cost — resistance was absent at 48 weeks in both parent trials.
cards.source: Hadziyannis SJ et al. Long-term therapy with adefovir dipivoxil for HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 15987916. cards.headline: Synthesis: adefovir 10 mg improved histology, HBV DNA and ALT in both HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative disease; continuing maintained the benefit, stopping lost it, and resistance and dose-related renal effects mark its superseded status
cards.summary: Synthesis: adefovir 10 mg improved histology, HBV DNA and ALT in both HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative disease; continuing maintained the benefit, stopping lost it, and resistance and dose-related renal effects mark its superseded status
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (Marcellin 2003, n=515; Hadziyannis 2003, n=185; Hadziyannis 2005, the same HBeAg-negative programme's extension).
cards.result: Two independent NEJM trials — one HBeAg-positive, one HBeAg-negative — found the same pattern at 48 weeks on adefovir 10 mg: roughly double the histologic improvement of placebo, HBV DNA suppression in about half of HBeAg-negative patients (51% vs 0% below 400 copies/mL), and ALT normalisation in 48–72%. The extension report adds the duration lesson: benefit persisted to 144 weeks on continued therapy and was lost in most patients switched to placebo, while resistance mutations emerged in 5.9% by week 144. Adefovir is nonetheless a superseded agent — the 30 mg dose showed renal laboratory abnormalities, and more potent, higher-barrier successors (entecavir, tenofovir) are homed on their own shelves; the tenofovir-versus-adefovir trial is a tenofovir question and is cross-pointed here, not carded.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Telbivudine vs lamivudine in chronic hepatitis B — ONE PROGRAMME ONLY (GLOBE): superior therapeutic response and DNA suppression at 1 and 2 years, more creatine-kinase elevation; withdrawn from the US market in 2016
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B, does telbivudine, compared with lamivudine, achieve greater HBV DNA suppression and therapeutic response (GLOBE programme) — and at what cost in creatine-kinase elevation, myopathy and peripheral neuropathy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · DNA, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Viral · Female · Genotype · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Lamivudine · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Nucleosides · Pyrimidinones · Telbivudine · Thymidine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus lamivudine — ONE-PROGRAMME flag, printed on the face: every report carded here comes from the single GLOBE trial programme (its 1-year primary, its 2-year report, and a programme renal-function secondary analysis, labelled as such), so there is no independent replication. Within GLOBE, telbivudine was superior to lamivudine: therapeutic response at 1 year in HBeAg-positive patients 75.3% vs 67.0%, and at 2 years 63% vs 48% (HBeAg-positive) and 78% vs 66% (HBeAg-negative), with deeper HBV DNA suppression and less viral resistance (2-year resistance 25.1% vs 39.5% in HBeAg-positive patients). The cost was muscle: grade 3/4 creatine-kinase elevations were more common on telbivudine (12.9% vs 4.1% at 2 years). Telbivudine was withdrawn from the US market in 2016 (commercial withdrawal) and carries a boxed-warning history for myopathy and peripheral neuropathy, especially with interferon — printed here as the commissioning row records it. The renal report's eGFR improvement is a secondary analysis of programme data, not an independent renal trial.

cards.headline: GLOBE 1-year primary (Lai 2007): telbivudine beat lamivudine on therapeutic response in HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (75.3% vs 67.0%) with greater HBV DNA suppression and less resistance
cards.summary: GLOBE 1-year primary (Lai 2007): telbivudine beat lamivudine on therapeutic response in HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (75.3% vs 67.0%) with greater HBV DNA suppression and less resistance
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (GLOBE, 1-year primary report), telbivudine 600 mg vs lamivudine 100 mg
cards.people: 1,370 patients with chronic hepatitis B randomly assigned, double-blind, to telbivudine 600 mg or lamivudine 100 mg once daily. The primary endpoint was therapeutic response (HBV DNA below 5 log10 copies/mL plus HBeAg loss or ALT normalisation); the trial was designed for noninferiority with superiority testing.
cards.result: At week 52, a significantly higher proportion of HBeAg-positive patients on telbivudine than lamivudine had a therapeutic response (75.3% vs 67.0%, P=0.005) or a histologic response (64.7% vs 56.3%, P=0.01); telbivudine was also not inferior in HBeAg-negative patients. In both HBeAg groups telbivudine was superior on mean HBV DNA reduction, the proportion with PCR-undetectable HBV DNA, and development of resistance. Elevated creatine kinase levels were more common on telbivudine; elevated ALT and AST were more common on lamivudine.
cards.watchOut: One programme only (see the face): this is the GLOBE trial's primary report, and the two cards that follow are reports of the same programme — the trial base of this shelf is a single trial, however large.

cards.headline: GLOBE 2-year report (Liaw 2009): telbivudine's superiority persisted at 104 weeks (therapeutic response 63% vs 48% HBeAg-positive; 78% vs 66% HBeAg-negative), with grade 3/4 creatine-kinase elevations in 12.9% vs 4.1%
cards.summary: GLOBE 2-year report (Liaw 2009): telbivudine's superiority persisted at 104 weeks (therapeutic response 63% vs 48% HBeAg-positive; 78% vs 66% HBeAg-negative), with grade 3/4 creatine-kinase elevations in 12.9% vs 4.1%
cards.type: Two-year results report of the same GLOBE randomised trial (programme lineage of the Lai 2007 card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The GLOBE population over 2 years: HBeAg-positive (n=921) and HBeAg-negative (n=446) patients receiving telbivudine or lamivudine once daily for 104 weeks; primary outcome therapeutic response (HBV DNA <5 log10 copies/mL plus HBeAg loss or ALT normalisation), intent-to-treat.
cards.result: Therapeutic response favoured telbivudine in HBeAg-positive (63% vs 48%, P<.001) and HBeAg-negative (78% vs 66%, P=.007) patients. HBeAg-positive patients on telbivudine had more nondetectable viraemia (<300 copies/mL; 55.6% vs 38.5%, P<.001), more HBeAg loss (35.2% vs 29.2%, P=.056) and less viral resistance (25.1% vs 39.5%, P<.001); HBeAg seroconversion was 29.6% vs 24.7% (P=.095), and 36% vs 27% (P=.022) in patients with baseline ALT at least twice normal. HBeAg-negative patients on telbivudine had more nondetectable viraemia (82.0% vs 56.7%, P<.001) and less resistance (10.8% vs 25.9%, P<.001). Adverse events occurred with similar frequency overall, but grade 3/4 creatine-kinase increases were more common on telbivudine (12.9% vs 4.1%, P<.001).
cards.watchOut: A later report of the same single trial: it extends follow-up, it does not replicate. Note the comparator is lamivudine, itself a superseded agent — superiority over lamivudine is not superiority over modern first-line therapy.
cards.source: Liaw YF et al. 2-Year GLOBE trial results: telbivudine Is superior to lamivudine in patients with chronic hepatitis B. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19027013. cards.headline: Programme secondary analysis — renal function (Gane 2014): eGFR rose on telbivudine during GLOBE (+8.5% by MDRD over 2 years) and the gain was maintained in extension studies — a secondary analysis of programme data, NOT an independent trial
cards.summary: Programme secondary analysis — renal function (Gane 2014): eGFR rose on telbivudine during GLOBE (+8.5% by MDRD over 2 years) and the gain was maintained in extension studies — a secondary analysis of programme data, NOT an independent trial
cards.type: Programme secondary analysis pooling GLOBE with its extension studies and a decompensated-cirrhosis study (labelled secondary analysis — not an independent randomised renal trial)
cards.people: Adults with chronic HBV and compensated liver disease in the GLOBE study (telbivudine 600 mg vs lamivudine 100 mg for 2 years) and in long-term extension studies (4–6 years), plus patients with decompensated cirrhosis treated for 2 years; renal function estimated from serum creatinine by Cockcroft-Gault, MDRD and CKD-EPI equations.
cards.result: The three eGFR equations were concordant: renal function improved on telbivudine during the 2-year GLOBE study (an 8.5% increase in mean eGFR by the MDRD equation) and the improvement was maintained for 4–6 years. Gains were larger in patients at increased renal risk: baseline eGFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² (+17.2%), age over 50 years (+11.4%), and Ishak fibrosis score 5–6 (+7.2%); in decompensated patients eGFR also improved (+2.0%). The authors state the mechanism of this apparent renal protective effect remains to be determined.
cards.watchOut: A pooled secondary analysis across programme studies with no randomised renal endpoint: the eGFR signal is hypothesis-generating, is not load-bearing for this shelf's stamp, and must not be quoted as a proven renal benefit.
cards.source: Gane EJ et al. Telbivudine improves renal function in patients with chronic hepatitis B. Gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24067879. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: within its single GLOBE programme, telbivudine suppressed HBV more deeply and with less resistance than lamivudine over 2 years, at the cost of more creatine-kinase elevation — one programme, a superseded comparator, and a withdrawn product
cards.summary: Synthesis: within its single GLOBE programme, telbivudine suppressed HBV more deeply and with less resistance than lamivudine over 2 years, at the cost of more creatine-kinase elevation — one programme, a superseded comparator, and a withdrawn product
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf — all from the single GLOBE programme (1-year primary, n=1,370; 2-year report; renal secondary analysis).
cards.result: GLOBE's 1-year and 2-year reports agree: telbivudine produced higher therapeutic-response rates, deeper HBV DNA suppression and less viral resistance than lamivudine in both HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B. The consistent harm was muscle enzyme elevation (grade 3/4 creatine-kinase increases 12.9% vs 4.1% at 2 years), in keeping with telbivudine's myopathy and peripheral-neuropathy warning history. Three framings govern any reading: the base is ONE programme (no independent trial exists on this shelf); the comparator, lamivudine, is itself superseded; and telbivudine was withdrawn from the US market in 2016. The renal-function report is a labelled secondary analysis and adds no independent weight.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Levosulpiride in functional dyspepsia: two small placebo trials positive on symptoms and gastric emptying; at least as effective as cisapride in a 140-patient pilot — old, short evidence, D2-antagonist harms, not licensed in the US/UK
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia (dysmotility-like / postprandial distress, with or without delayed gastric emptying), does levosulpiride versus placebo — or versus cisapride — improve dyspeptic symptoms and gastric emptying?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia · Female · Gastric Emptying · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Sulpiride
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a small, old base. Two small double-blind placebo trials (42 patients with delayed gastric emptying, 1998; 30 patients, 1994) found levosulpiride improved dyspeptic symptoms more than placebo and accelerated gastric (and gall-bladder) emptying. A larger exploratory pilot trial (140 patients, 2004) found levosulpiride at least as effective as the active comparator cisapride (total symptom score fell 79.9% versus 71.3%; P=0.07), with medication-related adverse effects in 18.8% versus 11.3%. There is no modern Rome-IV-era trial. Levosulpiride is a dopamine D2 antagonist — hyperprolactinaemia and extrapyramidal effects are part of the real-world answer — and it is not licensed in the US/UK.

cards.headline: Placebo RCT in delayed gastric emptying (Song 1998): levosulpiride improved symptom scores more than placebo (P<0.05) and shortened gastric emptying time, with improvement correlating with emptying (r=0.47)
cards.summary: Placebo RCT in delayed gastric emptying (Song 1998): levosulpiride improved symptom scores more than placebo (P<0.05) and shortened gastric emptying time, with improvement correlating with emptying (r=0.47)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, levosulpiride 25 mg three times daily for 3 weeks
cards.people: 42 patients with functional dyspepsia showing delayed gastric emptying entered a 3-week double-blind randomised comparison of levosulpiride 25 mg three times daily or placebo; symptoms and gastric scintigraphy were assessed before and after treatment.
cards.result: Symptom-score improvement was higher on levosulpiride than placebo (P<0.05). Global efficacy on levosulpiride was rated excellent in 1 (6%), good in 11 (65%), fair in 4 (24%) and nil in 1 (6%), versus fair in 9 (60%), nil in 5 (33%) and poor in 1 (6%) on placebo. Benefit was clearest in the dysmotility-like (P<0.05) and nonspecific (P<0.05) subgroups. The reduction in gastric emptying time was greater on levosulpiride (P<0.05), and change in symptom score correlated with change in emptying time (r=0.47, P=0.01). No serious adverse effects were reported; two patients reported mild somnolence on levosulpiride.
cards.watchOut: Only 42 patients entered and the global-efficacy percentages imply fewer were assessed at the end; a 3-week symptom trial from 1998, in patients selected for delayed gastric emptying — not a general functional-dyspepsia population.
cards.source: Song CW et al. Effects of levosulpiride in patients with functional dyspepsia accompanied by delayed gastric emptying. The Korean journal of internal medicine. 1998. PMID: 9538626. cards.headline: Emptying and symptom RCT (Arienti 1994): levosulpiride 75 mg/day for 20 days accelerated gastric and gall-bladder emptying and reduced symptom index and intensity versus placebo — n=30 printed here
cards.summary: Emptying and symptom RCT (Arienti 1994): levosulpiride 75 mg/day for 20 days accelerated gastric and gall-bladder emptying and reduced symptom index and intensity versus placebo — n=30 printed here
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=30), levosulpiride 75 mg/day for 20 days
cards.people: 30 adults with functional dyspepsia in a randomised double-blind study of levosulpiride (75 mg/day) or placebo for 20 days; gastric emptying by epigastric impedance (liquid meal) and gall-bladder emptying by real-time ultrasonography (mixed meal).
cards.result: Levosulpiride, compared with placebo, accelerated mean gastric half-emptying time of liquids (P<0.05), gastric emptying (P<0.001 at 180 min; P<0.05 at 240 min) and gall-bladder emptying (P<0.05 at 60 and 120 min). Both the mean cumulative symptom index (P<0.05) and overall symptom intensity (P<0.025) fell significantly more on levosulpiride.
cards.watchOut: 30 patients and 20 days, with physiological emptying endpoints alongside symptoms; the abstract gives P values without the underlying emptying times or symptom scores.

cards.headline: Levosulpiride versus cisapride pilot RCT (Mearin 2004): no significant difference — total symptom score fell 79.9% on levosulpiride versus 71.3% on cisapride (P=0.07); adverse effects 18.8% versus 11.3%
cards.summary: Levosulpiride versus cisapride pilot RCT (Mearin 2004): no significant difference — total symptom score fell 79.9% on levosulpiride versus 71.3% on cisapride (P=0.07); adverse effects 18.8% versus 11.3%
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-masked exploratory pilot trial, levosulpiride vs cisapride (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 140 patients with dysmotility-like functional dyspepsia in a multicentre randomised double-masked exploratory pilot trial: levosulpiride 25 mg three times daily (n=69) or cisapride 10 mg three times daily (n=71) for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Both treatments improved individual symptoms, global symptom score and health-related quality of life, with no change in anxiety. Total symptom score fell 79.9% on levosulpiride and 71.3% on cisapride, with no significant between-treatment difference (P=0.07 for total symptom score). Medication-related adverse effects occurred in 13 of 69 patients (18.8%) on levosulpiride and 8 of 71 (11.3%) on cisapride; significantly more cisapride patients abandoned the trial because of side effects (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: An exploratory pilot with an active comparator and no placebo arm: similarity to cisapride cannot by itself prove efficacy, and cisapride was itself later restricted for cardiac harm — the comparison is historical.
cards.source: Mearin F et al. Levosulpiride and cisapride in the treatment of dysmotility-like functional dyspepsia: a randomized, double-masked trial. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology. 2004. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small placebo trials (n=42 and n=30) were positive on symptoms and gastric emptying, and a 140-patient pilot found levosulpiride at least as effective as cisapride — a POSSIBLE benefit from small, old, short trials only
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small placebo trials (n=42 and n=30) were positive on symptoms and gastric emptying, and a 140-patient pilot found levosulpiride at least as effective as cisapride — a POSSIBLE benefit from small, old, short trials only
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The placebo-controlled record is two trials totalling 72 entered patients, both positive on symptom scores and on gastric-emptying measures, with only mild somnolence reported in the 1998 trial. The 2004 pilot (n=140) adds an active-comparator limb, not placebo evidence. No trial is modern, large, or long, and none used Rome IV definitions. Levosulpiride is a dopamine D2 antagonist, so hyperprolactinaemia and extrapyramidal effects belong in any real-world assessment, and the drug is not licensed in the US/UK.

shelves.title: Mosapride in functional dyspepsia: largest placebo trial and overall meta-analysis negative (the treatment made no difference vs placebo); later trials match nortriptyline and acotiamide but have no placebo arm
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does mosapride (including controlled-release) versus placebo — or versus acotiamide or nortriptyline strategies — improve postprandial distress and global dyspeptic symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzamides · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). The placebo-controlled record is negative overall: the largest dose-finding trial (566 patients evaluated, 2002) found mosapride made no difference versus placebo at any dose, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,091 mosapride-treated and 1,129 control patients) found an overall relative risk of 0.999 for global efficacy, with a positive signal only in a high-quality-trials sensitivity analysis and none in Rome III studies. Two later trials compare mosapride with active treatments — nortriptyline (2024) and acotiamide (2021) — and found similar improvement in both arms, but with no placebo arm they cannot separate drug effect from placebo response and natural course. The acotiamide question itself is homed elsewhere (pack #2767); this shelf cards that trial only as a mosapride comparator limb.

cards.headline: Dose-finding placebo RCT (Hallerbäck 2002): mosapride was NOT superior to placebo at any dose — symptom-score changes −0.88 to −0.94 across all arms including placebo; 59–61% felt better in every group (n=566 evaluated)
cards.summary: Dose-finding placebo RCT (Hallerbäck 2002): mosapride was NOT superior to placebo at any dose — symptom-score changes −0.88 to −0.94 across all arms including placebo; 59–61% felt better in every group (n=566 evaluated)
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding randomised trial (566 patients evaluated)
cards.people: Patients with functional dyspepsia in a double-blind multicentre multinational trial, randomised to placebo (n=141 evaluated) or mosapride 5 mg twice daily (n=140), 10 mg twice daily (n=143) or 7.5 mg three times daily (n=142); the primary measure was change in symptom severity score from an untreated baseline week to week 6.
cards.result: Mean changes in the overall dyspeptic symptom score were −0.90 (placebo), −0.94, −0.88 and −0.89 across the three mosapride regimens, and the proportions feeling better at the end of treatment were 60%, 59%, 59% and 61% respectively. No statistically significant difference was seen: treatment of functional dyspepsia with mosapride was not superior to placebo — the treatment made no difference in this trial.
cards.watchOut: The largest and cleanest placebo test of mosapride in functional dyspepsia — and it is negative at three doses; later positive-looking reports must be read against this trial.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Bang 2015): 13 RCTs — overall relative risk 0.999 (the treatment made no difference); a positive signal only in the high-quality sensitivity analysis (relative risk 1.114), and none in Rome III studies (relative risk 0.906)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Bang 2015): 13 RCTs — overall relative risk 0.999 (the treatment made no difference); a positive signal only in the high-quality sensitivity analysis (relative risk 1.114), and none in Rome III studies (relative risk 0.906)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials, mosapride vs placebo or other drugs
cards.people: 13 randomised trials of mosapride for functional dyspepsia (2002–2013), including 1,091 mosapride-treated patients and 1,129 control patients (placebo or other drugs); symptom response rates analysed as risk ratios (relative measures) under a random-effects model.
cards.result: Overall, mosapride showed a relative risk of 0.999 (95% CI 0.869 to 1.150; P=0.992) for improving global efficacy or symptom-based scores — no effect. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to high-quality trials the relative risk was 1.114 (95% CI 1.011 to 1.227; P=0.029), but in studies using Rome III diagnostic criteria it was 0.906 (95% CI 0.807 to 1.016; P=0.092), and funded studies were positive (relative risk 1.131) while unfunded studies were not (0.966). Publication bias was not detected. The authors concluded they could not find a significant effect of mosapride on functional dyspepsia. Absolute response rates are not given in the abstract, so the relative measures stand as reported.
cards.watchOut: The control group mixes placebo and other drugs, diagnostic criteria and outcome measures were heterogeneous, and the positive signal depends on which subset of trials is chosen — the overall pooled result is null.
cards.source: Bang CS et al. Mosapride treatment for functional dyspepsia: a meta-analysis. Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2015. PMID: 25041564. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mosapride controlled-release versus nortriptyline RCT (Tae 2024): overall improvement 53.7% versus 54.0% — similar efficacy, but no placebo arm
cards.summary: Mosapride controlled-release versus nortriptyline RCT (Tae 2024): overall improvement 53.7% versus 54.0% — similar efficacy, but no placebo arm
cards.type: Multicentre double-placebo double-blind randomised trial, mosapride controlled-release vs nortriptyline (no placebo-only arm)
cards.people: 109 participants with functional dyspepsia were recruited; 54 in the mosapride controlled-release group (mosapride CR 15 mg plus nortriptyline placebo) and 50 in the nortriptyline group (mosapride CR placebo plus nortriptyline 10 mg) were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis of this multicentre double-placebo, double-blind randomised trial; treatment lasted 4 weeks.
cards.result: The rate of overall dyspepsia improvement was similar between groups (53.7% mosapride CR versus 54.0% nortriptyline; P=0.976), with no difference in any subtype (postprandial distress 59.3% versus 52.5%; epigastric pain 44.4% versus 40.0%; overlap 50.0% versus 59.1%). Both treatments significantly improved anxiety, depression and quality of life from baseline.
cards.watchOut: Extract the mosapride limb carefully: this trial tests two active strategies against each other, so the ~54% improvement in both arms includes placebo response and natural course — it does not show mosapride beats no treatment.

cards.headline: Acotiamide versus mosapride phase 3 RCT (Sinha 2021): responder rates 98% versus 93.27% per-protocol (95.15% versus 89.81% intention-to-treat) at 4 weeks — a comparator limb for mosapride, with no placebo arm (n=220)
cards.summary: Acotiamide versus mosapride phase 3 RCT (Sinha 2021): responder rates 98% versus 93.27% per-protocol (95.15% versus 89.81% intention-to-treat) at 4 weeks — a comparator limb for mosapride, with no placebo arm (n=220)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised active-comparator trial, acotiamide vs mosapride (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 220 patients (aged 18–64) with functional dyspepsia–postprandial distress syndrome, centrally randomised 1:1 to acotiamide 100 mg three times daily or mosapride 5 mg three times daily for 4 weeks; the primary endpoint was the responder rate for overall treatment effect.
cards.result: At 4 weeks, overall-treatment-effect responders were 98% on acotiamide versus 93.27% on mosapride in the per-protocol population, and 95.15% versus 89.81% in the intention-to-treat population. The authors reported acotiamide significantly improved postprandial fullness, upper abdominal bloating, early satiation and quality of life, with efficacy and safety profiles similar to mosapride. Carded here only as the mosapride comparator limb; the acotiamide question is homed at pack #2767.
cards.watchOut: Responder rates above 89% in both arms over 4 weeks, with no placebo group, are compatible with a large non-specific response; this trial cannot establish that mosapride itself works.

shelves.title: Gabexate mesilate in acute pancreatitis: large German trial negative on mortality and complications; meta-analysis — no mortality effect but fewer complications; small severe-disease trial claimed a survival benefit
shelves.question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (including severe pancreatitis with organ dysfunction), does intravenous gabexate mesilate versus placebo/no treatment — or versus aprotinin — reduce mortality and complications?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gabexate · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis · Placebos
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The large German Pancreatitis Study Group trial (223 patients with moderate/severe pancreatitis, 1993) found gabexate made no difference to mortality or complications versus placebo. A 1995 meta-analysis of five randomised trials agreed on mortality (no effect at 90 days, P=0.27) but found fewer complications overall (odds ratio 0.69 — a relative measure) and fewer complications requiring surgery (odds ratio 0.61 — relative). Against that, a small severe-disease trial (52 patients, 26 treated, 2000) reported significantly reduced 7- and 90-day mortality, and the GA.ME.P.A. trial found gabexate more efficacious than aprotinin on early complications of necrotising pancreatitis. This is the treatment question only: gabexate for post-ERCP prophylaxis is a separate question, homed elsewhere, and the 2017 Cochrane pharmacological-interventions review is not carded here (it is a limb of the lexipafant shelf).

cards.headline: German Pancreatitis Study Group RCT (Büchler 1993): gabexate made NO difference to mortality or complications in 223 patients with moderate/severe acute pancreatitis
cards.summary: German Pancreatitis Study Group RCT (Büchler 1993): gabexate made NO difference to mortality or complications in 223 patients with moderate/severe acute pancreatitis
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=223), gabexate 4 g/day for 7 days
cards.people: 223 patients with moderate or severe acute pancreatitis (mild pancreatitis excluded by strict criteria) from 29 hospitals, randomised double-blind to placebo or gabexate mesilate 4 g/day intravenously for 7 days, followed for 90 days; the analysis covered 14 complications including death.
cards.result: There was no statistical difference in either mortality or complications associated with acute pancreatitis between the placebo and gabexate groups. The authors concluded gabexate mesilate was not effective in preventing complications and mortality in acute pancreatitis — the treatment made no difference in this, the programme's largest trial.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the negative result without the mortality or complication rates themselves; the trial excluded mild pancreatitis, so its verdict covers moderate/severe disease.

cards.summary: GA.ME.P.A. trial (Pederzoli 1993): gabexate was more efficacious than aprotinin in reducing early complications of necrotising acute pancreatitis when given within 72 hours (patient number not stated in the fetched abstract)
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind multicentre trial, gabexate vs aprotinin (active comparator, no placebo)
cards.people: Patients with acute pancreatitis in a prospective randomised double-blind multicentre study of gabexate mesilate versus aprotinin; the endpoints were the early systemic complications of pancreatitis. cards.result: The authors concluded that gabexate mesilate is more efficacious than aprotinin in reducing the early complications of necrotizing acute pancreatitis, if administered within 72 h of onset of symptoms, and that its good tolerability means it can be used safely even at the dose of 3 g/24 h. The abstract gives no event rates or P values, so the claim is carded as the authors' conclusion only.

cards.summary: Severe pancreatitis with organ dysfunction RCT (Chen 2000): gabexate improved coagulopathy, ileus and pain and significantly reduced 7- and 90-day mortality — 52 patients enrolled, 26 treated (N printed here)
cards.type: Prospective randomised study in severe acute pancreatitis with organ dysfunction (n=52; 26 treated)
cards.people: 52 patients with acute pancreatitis and organ dysfunction were enrolled; the treatment group of 26 patients received intravenous gabexate mesilate 100 mg/hour for 7 days, with intensive monitoring of APACHE-II score and clinical and biochemical parameters.
cards.result: Coagulopathy, ileus and abdominal pain were significantly improved with gabexate mesilate, which also reduced the necessity for surgical intervention and peritoneal lavage. The 7-day mortality and 90-day mortality rates were also significantly reduced with gabexate therapy, per the authors. The abstract reports significance without giving the mortality rates or event counts, so no rates are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (26 treated patients) claiming a mortality benefit that the 223-patient placebo trial did not find; its abstract gives no rates, so the size of the claimed effect cannot be checked from the record.

cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Messori 1995): five randomised trials — no effect on 90-day mortality (P=0.27), but fewer complications (odds ratio 0.69, relative) and fewer complications requiring surgery (odds ratio 0.61, relative)
cards.people: Five randomised trials of gabexate mesilate in acute pancreatitis identified by literature search; endpoints were mortality, complications, and complications requiring surgery.
cards.result: Treatment with gabexate mesilate did not affect mortality at 90 days (P=0.27), but significantly reduced complications requiring surgery (odds ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.89; P<0.05) and complications in general (odds ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; P<0.05) — both are relative measures, and absolute rates are not given in the abstract. The authors judged the clinical impact small, because the drug benefits only a low proportion of treated patients, and noted a pharmacoeconomic evaluation showing a very high cost per complication prevented if given to all patients.
cards.watchOut: A 1995 pooling of an early, small trial base; its complication benefit is a relative odds reduction with no absolute rates in the abstract, and its mortality verdict agrees with the large German trial — no mortality benefit.

shelves.title: Ulinastatin in acute pancreatitis: two placebo trials suggest less death and organ dysfunction in severe disease; 2025 meta-analysis agrees — small single-region (Asia-only licensing) base, and one named anchor refused as a protocol with no results
shelves.question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (mild or severe), does intravenous ulinastatin added to standard supportive care versus placebo/standard care reduce complications, organ failure and mortality?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycoproteins · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis · Trypsin Inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit in severe disease, on a small single-region base — with the builder position stated plainly: this shelf rests on two placebo-controlled randomised trials (India, n=135 randomised; China, n=181) plus a 2025 meta-analysis of seven studies. The third anchor named at mining, Yao & Li 2019 (PMID 31651883), was checked at build and is a systematic-review PROTOCOL (PROSPERO CRD42019149566) with no results — it is refused and not carded as evidence. The 2025 meta-analysis pools ulinastatin given alone or in combination with other agents, so it must not be read as ulinastatin-alone evidence; the surrounding combination literature (ulinastatin plus somatostatin/octreotide) is likewise not presented here as ulinastatin-alone evidence. Ulinastatin is licensed in parts of Asia only. The post-ERCP prophylaxis question is separate and not folded in.

cards.headline: Multicentre placebo RCT (Abraham 2013): in severe pancreatitis, death 1 on ulinastatin versus 6 on placebo (P=0.048) and new organ dysfunction 12 versus 29 (P=0.0026); no such differences in mild disease
cards.summary: Multicentre placebo RCT (Abraham 2013): in severe pancreatitis, death 1 on ulinastatin versus 6 on placebo (P=0.048) and new organ dysfunction 12 versus 29 (P=0.0026); no such differences in mild disease
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (n=135 randomised), ulinastatin added to standard care
cards.people: 135 subjects aged 18–70 with acute pancreatitis and elevated C-reactive protein were randomised across 15 centres in India to intravenous ulinastatin 200,000 IU or placebo every 12 hours for 5 days, both with standard care; 129 completed the study (62 mild, 67 severe by APACHE II). Pancreatitis was alcohol-related in 81%. Efficacy was evaluated in subjects who received at least 3 days (6 doses).
cards.result: In severe pancreatitis, one subject in the ulinastatin group versus six in the placebo group died (P=0.048) — counts as reported; the abstract does not give the efficacy-subset denominators, so no percentages are printed. New organ dysfunction in severe disease developed in 12 ulinastatin versus 29 placebo subjects (P=0.0026), versus 5 versus 4 (P=0.744) in mild disease. Adverse events were significantly lower with ulinastatin in severe pancreatitis (P=0.00001, as reported). C-reactive protein reduction did not differ, median hospitalisation was one day shorter on ulinastatin (not significant), and there were no infusion-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The mortality result rests on 1 versus 6 deaths in an efficacy subset whose denominators the abstract does not state — a fragile count; the population was 81% alcohol-related pancreatitis in Indian centres.
cards.source: Abraham P et al. Efficacy and safety of intravenous ulinastatin versus placebo along with standard supportive care in subjects with mild or severe acute pancreatitis. cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial in severe acute pancreatitis (n=181), ulinastatin vs placebo
cards.people: 181 patients hospitalised in intensive care units with severe acute pancreatitis, allocated by computer-based random sequencing 1:1 to ulinastatin 400,000 IU (n=91) or placebo (n=90); outcomes included 7-day mortality, clinical efficacy, inflammatory response, coagulation, infection, liver and renal function, and adverse effects.
cards.result: The authors report that 7-day mortality and clinical efficacy in the ulinastatin group were remarkably improved compared with placebo, that ulinastatin protected against hyperinflammation and improved coagulation dysfunction, infection, liver function and renal function, and that hospital stays and costs were markedly decreased, with fewer adverse reactions. The fetched abstract gives no mortality counts, rates or P values for these claims, so none are printed here — the size of the effect cannot be verified from the record.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, and its abstract asserts benefit without numbers: this card supports the direction of the Indian trial but cannot be checked quantitatively from the published record fetched here.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Bandyopadhyay 2025): seven studies in severe acute pancreatitis — a significant pooled reduction in mortality risk (95% CI 0.20 to 0.65 for the risk ratio, as printed), no significant effect on hospital stay or APACHE-II; pools ulinastatin alone AND in combination
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Bandyopadhyay 2025): seven studies in severe acute pancreatitis — a significant pooled reduction in mortality risk (95% CI 0.20 to 0.65 for the risk ratio, as printed), no significant effect on hospital stay or APACHE-II; pools ulinastatin alone AND in combination
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (seven studies pooled for mortality), ulinastatin alone or in combination
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020) of prospective and retrospective studies of ulinastatin in adults with severe acute pancreatitis; seven studies entered the pooled mortality analysis. Outcomes included mortality, hospitalisation duration, APACHE-II score, white cell count, C-reactive protein, TNF-α, IL-6 and time to disappearance of abdominal pain.
cards.result: The pooled analysis of seven studies found a significant reduction in mortality risk with ulinastatin (the abstract prints the risk-ratio 95% CI as 0.20 to 0.65, I²=53%, without a point estimate in the text fetched). There were no significant reductions in hospitalisation duration or APACHE-II score (mean difference −0.11, 95% CI −1.48 to 1.26; I²=97%). White cell count, C-reactive protein, time to abdominal-pain disappearance, TNF-α and IL-6 improved significantly. The authors state ulinastatin was administered either alone or in combination with other therapeutic agents — so this pooling is not ulinastatin-alone evidence.
cards.watchOut: Mixes prospective and retrospective studies and alone-versus-combination use, with very high heterogeneity on secondary outcomes (I² up to 98%); it corroborates the two placebo trials' direction but is not an independent ulinastatin-alone test.
cards.source: Bandyopadhyay S et al. Ulinastatin for the treatment of severe acute pancreatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 40890662. shelves.title: Metadoxine in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis: two open-label RCTs from one Mexican programme (n=70, n=135) found large survival gains, echoed by a 2026 synthesis limb — unreplicated elsewhere
shelves.question: In patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, does adding metadoxine to standard care (with or without corticosteroids) improve short- and medium-term survival versus standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alcohol Deterrents · Antioxidants · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Esophageal and Gastric Varices · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Glucocorticoids · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Hepatitis, Alcoholic · Hepatorenal Syndrome · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone · Pyridoxine · Pyrrolidonecarboxylic Acid · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, with the base stated on the face: this shelf rests on TWO randomised trials from a single Mexican programme (n=70 in 2014; n=135 in 2015), both open-label, plus the metadoxine limb of a 2026 systematic review — that limb was verified at build and is extractable (28-day mortality relative risk 0.47 for metadoxine plus corticosteroids versus corticosteroids alone). Both trials found large survival differences (90-day survival 68.6% versus 20.0% in 2014; 3-month survival 68.6% versus 20% for prednisone plus metadoxine versus prednisone in 2015), and the 2015 trial also found patients on metadoxine maintained abstinence more often (74.5% versus 59.4%) — itself a survival factor, and a confounder of the drug claim. There is no replication outside this one programme, and nothing here extends to non-severe disease.

cards.headline: RCT (Higuera-de la Tijera 2014): adding metadoxine to prednisone raised 30-day survival to 74.3% versus 45.7% and 90-day survival to 68.6% versus 20.0% in severe alcoholic hepatitis (n=70)
cards.summary: RCT (Higuera-de la Tijera 2014): adding metadoxine to prednisone raised 30-day survival to 74.3% versus 45.7% and 90-day survival to 68.6% versus 20.0% in severe alcoholic hepatitis (n=70)
cards.type: Randomised open-label trial (n=70), prednisone plus metadoxine vs prednisone alone
cards.people: 70 patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis randomised at Mexico's General Hospital to prednisone 40 mg/day, or prednisone 40 mg/day plus metadoxine 500 mg three times daily, for 30 days; survival at 30 and 90 days, complications, adverse events and Lille-model response were assessed.
cards.result: Survival was higher with metadoxine at 30 days (74.3% versus 45.7%; P=0.02) and at 90 days (68.6% versus 20.0%; P=0.0001). Encephalopathy developed or progressed less often (28.6% versus 60.0%; P=0.008), as did hepatorenal syndrome (31.4% versus 54.3%; P=0.05), and Lille-model response was better (0.38 versus 0.63; P=0.001). There were no differences in variceal haemorrhage or infection, and adverse events (mainly gastrointestinal) were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, 70 patients — and a 90-day control-group survival of only 20% makes the absolute difference unusually large; an effect of this size from one small open-label trial needs independent replication.
cards.source: Higuera-de la Tijera F et al. Treatment with metadoxine and its impact on early mortality in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Annals of hepatology. 2014. PMID: 24756009. Registry ID: Registry Key DIC/10/107/03/043 (as given in the record). cards.summary: Four-arm RCT (Higuera-de la Tijera 2015): metadoxine improved 3- and 6-month survival whether added to prednisone or to pentoxifylline (n=135) — and patients on metadoxine stayed abstinent more often
cards.type: Randomised open-label four-arm trial (n=135), metadoxine added to prednisone or pentoxifylline
cards.people: 135 patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis randomised at the Hospital General de México to prednisone 40 mg/day (n=35), prednisone plus metadoxine 500 mg three times daily (n=35), pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily (n=33), or pentoxifylline plus metadoxine (n=32); treatment lasted 30 days, with survival assessed at 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: Survival at 3 months was higher with metadoxine in both backbones: prednisone plus metadoxine 68.6% versus prednisone 20% (P=0.0001), and pentoxifylline plus metadoxine 59.4% versus pentoxifylline 33.3% (P=0.04). At 6 months: 48.6% versus 20% (P=0.003) and 50% versus 18.2% (P=0.01) respectively. Relapse in alcohol intake was the primary independent factor predicting mortality at 6 months, and patients receiving metadoxine maintained greater abstinence (74.5% versus 59.4%; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Same programme and hospital as the 2014 trial — not independent replication. The abstinence difference (74.5% versus 59.4%) is part of the survival story: metadoxine may work partly by keeping patients off alcohol, which the design cannot separate from a direct liver effect.
cards.source: Higuera-de la Tijera F et al. Metadoxine improves the three- and six-month survival rates in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. World journal of gastroenterology. 2015. PMID: 25945012. Registry ID: NCT02161653. cards.headline: Synthesis limb (Islam 2026): in a 52-trial systematic review of severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, metadoxine plus corticosteroids reduced 28-day mortality versus corticosteroids alone (relative risk 0.47) and versus pentoxifylline (relative risk 0.50)
cards.summary: Synthesis limb (Islam 2026): in a 52-trial systematic review of severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, metadoxine plus corticosteroids reduced 28-day mortality versus corticosteroids alone (relative risk 0.47) and versus pentoxifylline (relative risk 0.50)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (52 RCTs overall) — metadoxine limb only, as the commissioning row directs
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 52 randomised trials (5,121 participants) of pharmacological therapy for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, searched to 16 February 2025; the primary outcome was 28-day mortality, with GRADE certainty assessed. This card covers only its metadoxine limb, verified at build from the fetched record.
cards.result: A survival benefit at 28 days was observed for metadoxine combined with corticosteroids over corticosteroids alone (relative risk 0.47, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.90 — a relative measure) and over pentoxifylline (relative risk 0.50, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.96 — relative). For context within the same review, corticosteroids beat placebo (relative risk 0.62) and corticosteroids plus N-acetylcysteine beat corticosteroids alone (relative risk 0.35). Certainty of evidence across the review ranged from very low to moderate, and the authors state further studies are needed to confirm these benefits. Absolute mortality rates for the metadoxine limb are not given in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: The metadoxine limb of this review rests on the same Mexican programme carded above — it is a synthesis of that programme, not new patients; the whole review's other limbs (steroids, N-acetylcysteine, G-CSF) belong to their own shelves and are not re-carded here.

The 2015 four-arm trial: the same pattern against both prednisone and pentoxifylline backbones at 3 and 6 months, with better abstinence on metadoxine (74.5% versus 59.4%) — a plausible mediator the trials cannot separate from a direct effect. The 2026 systematic review's metadoxine limb gives a 28-day mortality relative risk of 0.47 versus corticosteroids alone.
