shelves.title: Propylthiouracil in alcohol-associated liver disease: long-term trial halved mortality in compliant patients (0.13 vs 0.25), but severe-hepatitis trial negative and Cochrane pooling of 710 patients found no benefit — a historical, unconfirmed programme
shelves.question: In patients with alcoholic liver disease / alcoholic hepatitis, does propylthiouracil versus placebo improve short-term and long-term mortality?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Drug Evaluation · Fatty Liver, Alcoholic · Hepatitis, Alcoholic · Humans · Liver · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic · Liver Diseases, Alcoholic · Liver Function Tests · Placebos · Propylthiouracil · Prothrombin Time · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a historical programme with an unconfirmed signal. The programme's long-term trial (Orrego 1987, 310 compliant patients, up to two years) found cumulative mortality of 0.13 on propylthiouracil versus 0.25 on placebo, with a hazards ratio of 0.38 (a relative measure). But the short-term severe-hepatitis trial (Hallé 1982, n=67) found the treatment made no difference (deaths 7 of 31 versus 7 of 36), the 1979 short-term trial improved a composite clinical-laboratory index without assessing mortality, and the Cochrane review (2005 version carded here — ONE version only, per the flumazenil precedent) pooling six trials and 710 patients found no significant effect on all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.93), liver-related mortality, complications or histology. No modern trial has confirmed the long-term signal, and current alcohol-hepatitis reviews largely omit this programme. The tension belongs on the face: propylthiouracil carries a severe-hepatotoxicity warning from its thyroid use, yet was tested as a liver treatment.

cards.headline: Short-term RCT (Orrego 1979): propylthiouracil improved a composite clinical-laboratory index in alcoholic hepatitis (normalisation rate 43.6 versus 19.8; P<0.001) — a severity-index result, not mortality (n=133)
cards.summary: Short-term RCT (Orrego 1979): propylthiouracil improved a composite clinical-laboratory index in alcoholic hepatitis (normalisation rate 43.6 versus 19.8; P<0.001) — a severity-index result, not mortality (n=133)
cards.type: Short-term randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=133), composite severity index endpoint
cards.people: 133 patients with alcoholic liver disease in a short-term randomised double-blind trial of propylthiouracil 300 mg/day versus placebo; disease severity was scored by a composite clinical and laboratory index (CCLI), and a normalisation rate (NR) of improvement in that index was calculated.
cards.result: Patients with alcoholic hepatitis, with and without cirrhosis, had a significantly higher normalisation rate on propylthiouracil (43.6 ± 4.6) than on placebo (19.8 ± 3.3; P<0.001); a similar effect was seen in patients with abnormal prothrombin without biopsy (32.9 ± 6.9 versus 2.6 ± 3.7; P<0.005). Split by severity, propylthiouracil had a significant effect only in the more severely ill half (NR 41.4 ± 3.8 versus 22.5 ± 4.2; P<0.005), and it was ineffective in inactive cirrhosis. Mortality was not the endpoint of this short-term trial.
cards.watchOut: An index-improvement result from 1979: the composite score can improve without any survival benefit, which is exactly what the later pooled analysis found — do not read this card as efficacy on outcomes that matter.
cards.source: Orrego H et al. Effect of short-term therapy with propylthiouracil in patients with alcoholic liver disease. Gastroenterology. 1979. PMID: 758131. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Severe acute alcoholic hepatitis RCT (Hallé 1982): propylthiouracil made NO difference — deaths 7 of 31 (23%) versus 7 of 36 (19%) on placebo over 6 weeks, and it induced hypothyroidism in 4 patients (n=67)
cards.summary: Severe acute alcoholic hepatitis RCT (Hallé 1982): propylthiouracil made NO difference — deaths 7 of 31 (23%) versus 7 of 36 (19%) on placebo over 6 weeks, and it induced hypothyroidism in 4 patients (n=67)
cards.type: Double-blind controlled randomised trial in severe acute alcoholic hepatitis (n=67)
cards.people: 67 patients with severe acute alcoholic hepatitis entered a double-blind controlled trial of propylthiouracil versus placebo over 6 weeks; morbidity, mortality, complications and hepatic biochemical tests were evaluated.
cards.result: Twenty-three percent (7 of 31) given propylthiouracil and 19% (7 of 36) given placebo died during the 6-week study. Propylthiouracil did not reduce the frequency or incidence of complications and produced no beneficial effect on any hepatic biochemical test, but it induced hypothyroidism in 4 patients. The authors were unable to show any beneficial effect on morbidity or mortality — the treatment made no difference in severe acute disease.
cards.watchOut: Small and short (6 weeks), but it is the direct test in severe acute alcoholic hepatitis — and it is negative, with a real harm (induced hypothyroidism) on the propylthiouracil side.
cards.source: Hallé P et al. Double-blind, controlled trial of propylthiouracil in patients with severe acute alcoholic hepatitis. Gastroenterology. 1982. PMID: 7037524. cards.headline: Long-term RCT (Orrego 1987, NEJM): two years of propylthiouracil halved cumulative mortality in compliant patients — 0.13 versus 0.25 overall, hazards ratio 0.38 (relative); in the severely ill subgroup 0.25 versus 0.55 (n=310 compliant)
cards.summary: Long-term RCT (Orrego 1987, NEJM): two years of propylthiouracil halved cumulative mortality in compliant patients — 0.13 versus 0.25 overall, hazards ratio 0.38 (relative); in the severely ill subgroup 0.25 versus 0.55 (n=310 compliant)
cards.type: Long-term (up to 2 years) double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, analysis in 310 compliant patients
cards.people: 310 compliant patients with alcoholic liver disease in a long-term double-blind randomised trial of propylthiouracil 300 mg/day (n=157) or placebo (n=153) for a maximum of two years; the groups did not differ in demographics, clinical characteristics, biopsy-confirmed diagnoses at randomisation, or daily urinary alcohol levels during the study.
cards.result: Cumulative mortality was 0.13 on propylthiouracil versus 0.25 on placebo (P<0.05) in the total sample, and 0.25 versus 0.55 (P<0.03) in a severely ill subgroup (n=56 versus n=41). The hazards ratio indicated mortality on propylthiouracil was 0.38 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83) of that on placebo — a relative measure, with the absolute cumulative rates given above. Protection was not observed in patients with high morning urinary alcohol levels. The cumulative two-year dropout rate was high in both groups (0.68 versus 0.60, not significantly different). No clinically important side effects were observed at the dose used.
cards.watchOut: The analysis population is 'compliant patients' and two-year dropout was ~60–68% — a long-term mortality signal from a selected, adherent subset of a 1980s programme, never re-tested in a modern trial; this is the signal the Cochrane pooling could not confirm.
cards.source: Orrego H et al. Long-term treatment of alcoholic liver disease with propylthiouracil. The New England journal of medicine. 1987. PMID: 3317042. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane review, 2005 version — the ONE version carded (Rambaldi & Gluud): six trials, 710 patients — no significant effect on all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.93), liver-related mortality, complications or histology
cards.summary: Cochrane review, 2005 version — the ONE version carded (Rambaldi & Gluud): six trials, 710 patients — no significant effect on all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.93), liver-related mortality, complications or histology
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (2005 version only), six randomised trials, 710 patients
cards.people: Six randomised clinical trials including 710 patients with alcoholic steatosis, fibrosis, hepatitis and/or cirrhosis, comparing propylthiouracil at any dose versus placebo or no intervention; analyses were by intention-to-treat. This shelf cards the 2005 version only; the 2011 update (PMID 21678335) is deliberately not carded, per the one-version rule.
cards.result: Combining the six trials demonstrated no significant effects of propylthiouracil versus placebo on all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.30 — a relative measure), liver-related mortality (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.29), complications of the liver disease, or liver histology. Propylthiouracil was associated with a non-significant increased risk of non-serious adverse events and with the seldom occurrence of serious adverse events (leukopenia). The authors concluded there is no evidence for using propylthiouracil for alcoholic liver disease outside randomised clinical trials, noting the confidence intervals were wide.
cards.watchOut: The pooled verdict is 'no demonstrated benefit' with wide confidence intervals — it does not prove the long-term Orrego signal false, but it means the programme as a whole does not support use; adverse events, including leukopenia, sit on the propylthiouracil side.
cards.source: Rambaldi A et al. Propylthiouracil for alcoholic liver disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2005. PMID: 16235302. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — one long-term trial from the Orrego programme found mortality halved (relative hazards ratio 0.38; absolute 0.13 versus 0.25 in compliant patients), while the severe-hepatitis trial was negative and the Cochrane pooling of all six trials (710 patients) found no significant benefit on any outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — one long-term trial from the Orrego programme found mortality halved (relative hazards ratio 0.38; absolute 0.13 versus 0.25 in compliant patients), while the severe-hepatitis trial was negative and the Cochrane pooling of all six trials (710 patients) found no significant benefit on any outcome
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Short-term: index improvement only (1979, n=133); severe acute hepatitis: no difference, 7/31 versus 7/36 deaths (1982, n=67). Long-term: a mortality signal in compliant patients over two years (1987, n=310). Pooled: relative risk 0.93 for all-cause mortality, no significant effect on liver-related mortality, complications or histology (Cochrane 2005, the one version carded). This is a historical 1970s–80s programme whose signal was never confirmed in a modern trial; it is presented as that record, not as a treatment option — and propylthiouracil's own severe-hepatotoxicity warning from thyroid use is part of why the programme reads as a cautionary one for a liver disease.

shelves.title: Nicotine in active ulcerative colitis: patches beat placebo for induction (remission 19/71 vs 9/70) but not standard therapy, with heavy side effects; enemas negative — a programme abandoned in practice
shelves.question: In adults with active ulcerative colitis, does transdermal nicotine — or nicotine enemas — added to standard therapy versus placebo/standard therapy induce clinical improvement or remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adult · Affect · Colitis, Ulcerative · Cotinine · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nicotine · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by route and by comparator. Transdermal nicotine beat placebo for induction in the pooled placebo trials carded by the 2004 Cochrane review (remission 19 of 71 versus 9 of 70; odds ratio 2.56 — a relative measure), and the founding NEJM trial (Pullan 1994, n=72) found complete remission in 17 of 35 on nicotine versus 9 of 37 on placebo — but with far more side effects (23 versus 11 patients). Against standard therapy (prednisone or mesalamine) the same Cochrane review found no advantage for nicotine, and across all five studies the pooled result was not significant. Nicotine enemas (Ingram 2005, n=104) made no difference versus placebo enemas (remission 27% versus 33%). This is an induction-only, 1990s programme that was never adopted in practice — nicotine-naïve patients had substantial nausea, light-headedness, headache and sleep disturbance, and adverse-event withdrawals were much commoner on nicotine. The trials, not the smoking epidemiology, are this shelf.

cards.headline: NEJM RCT (Pullan 1994): transdermal nicotine added to mesalamine gave complete remission in 17 of 35 versus 9 of 37 on placebo (P=0.03) at 6 weeks — with side effects in 23 versus 11 patients (n=72)
cards.summary: NEJM RCT (Pullan 1994): transdermal nicotine added to mesalamine gave complete remission in 17 of 35 versus 9 of 37 on placebo (P=0.03) at 6 weeks — with side effects in 23 versus 11 patients (n=72)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=72), transdermal nicotine as add-on therapy for 6 weeks
cards.people: 72 patients with active ulcerative colitis treated with transdermal nicotine patches or placebo patches for 6 weeks in a randomised double-blind study; most tolerated nicotine doses of 15 to 25 mg per 24 hours. All patients had been taking mesalamine and 12 were receiving low-dose glucocorticoids, continued unchanged.
cards.result: Seventeen of 35 patients in the nicotine group had complete remissions, compared with 9 of 37 in the placebo group (P=0.03). The nicotine group had greater improvement in the global clinical grade (P<0.001) and histologic grade (P=0.03), lower stool frequency (a difference of 1.6 stools daily; P=0.008), less abdominal pain (P=0.05) and less fecal urgency (P=0.009). More patients in the nicotine group had side effects (23 versus 11; P=0.002) — most commonly nausea, lightheadedness, headache and sleep disturbance. Withdrawals due to ineffective therapy were more common on placebo (8 versus 3; P=0.12).
cards.watchOut: 72 patients, 6 weeks, add-on to mesalamine (and steroids in 12) — a real but small induction signal bought with side effects in two-thirds of the nicotine group; it says nothing about maintenance, which the follow-on literature found negative.
cards.source: Pullan RD et al. Transdermal nicotine for active ulcerative colitis. The New England journal of medicine. 1994. PMID: 8114833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane review (McGrath 2004): transdermal nicotine beat placebo for remission (19/71 versus 9/70; odds ratio 2.56, relative) but NOT standard therapy (odds ratio 0.77), and adverse-event withdrawals were far commoner (odds ratio 5.82, relative)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (McGrath 2004): transdermal nicotine beat placebo for remission (19/71 versus 9/70; odds ratio 2.56, relative) but NOT standard therapy (odds ratio 0.77), and adverse-event withdrawals were far commoner (odds ratio 5.82, relative)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, five randomised trials (two placebo-controlled)
cards.people: Five randomised trials met the inclusion criteria (of seven identified), in active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, comparing transdermal nicotine 15 to 25 mg/day with placebo or standard treatment (corticosteroids or mesalamine); the primary outcome was clinical or sigmoidoscopic remission by intention-to-treat.
cards.result: In the two placebo trials (71 nicotine, 70 placebo patients), clinical remission at 4–6 weeks occurred in 19 of 71 on nicotine versus 9 of 70 on placebo (odds ratio 2.56, 95% CI 1.02 to 6.45 — a relative measure), and improvement or remission in 29 of 71 versus 14 of 70 (odds ratio 2.72, 95% CI 1.28 to 5.81). Against standard medical therapy there was no significant benefit (remission 33 of 66 on nicotine versus 34 of 63 on standard therapy; odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.60), and pooling all five studies (137 nicotine, 133 control) gave no significant benefit (odds ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.14). Patients on nicotine were significantly more likely to withdraw because of adverse events (odds ratio 5.82, 95% CI 1.66 to 20.47) and to suffer an adverse event (odds ratio 3.54, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.08) — both relative measures, with the absolute remission counts given above.
cards.watchOut: The placebo pool is only 141 patients and includes the Pullan trial carded above — the review is a synthesis of that small base, not independent evidence; its own all-studies pooling is null, and its harm signals are the strongest findings in it.
cards.source: McGrath J et al. Transdermal nicotine for induction of remission in ulcerative colitis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2004. PMID: 15495126. cards.headline: Nicotine enema RCT (Ingram 2005): 6 mg nicotine enemas made NO difference — clinical remission 14 of 52 (27%) on active treatment versus 14 of 43 (33%) on placebo (P=0.55); well tolerated (n=104)
cards.summary: Nicotine enema RCT (Ingram 2005): 6 mg nicotine enemas made NO difference — clinical remission 14 of 52 (27%) on active treatment versus 14 of 43 (33%) on placebo (P=0.55); well tolerated (n=104)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=104), nicotine enemas as add-on therapy for 6 weeks
cards.people: 104 patients with active ulcerative colitis treated with 6 mg nicotine enemas or placebo enemas for 6 weeks in a randomised double-blind study, as supplemental treatment; patients continued oral therapy if any (68 taking mesalamine, 15 prednisolone, 12 thiopurines). The primary endpoint was induction of clinical remission, also measured by the ulcerative colitis disease activity index.
cards.result: Clinical remission was achieved in 14 of 52 (27%) patients on active treatment and 14 of 43 (33%) on placebo (P=0.55), as reported. The disease activity index improved by 1.45 points in the active group and 1.65 points on placebo (P=0.88). Only one patient discontinued because of an adverse event (abdominal pain). In the 47 patients taking mesalamine only, remission occurred in 9 of 25 on active therapy versus 4 of 21 on placebo (P=0.20) — a non-significant subgroup difference. The authors concluded 6 mg nicotine enemas were well tolerated but not efficacious for active ulcerative colitis — the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: The enema route solved the tolerability problem and lost the effect: remission was numerically commoner on placebo. Denominators for the remission analysis (52 versus 43) are as printed in the abstract.
cards.source: Ingram JR et al. A randomized trial of nicotine enemas for active ulcerative colitis. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology. 2005. PMID: 16271342. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: Induction, patches: Pullan 1994 (17/35 versus 9/37 complete remission) and the Cochrane placebo pooling agree on a benefit over placebo; the Cochrane all-studies pooling (odds ratio 1.23) and the standard-therapy comparison (odds ratio 0.77) do not show an advantage over treatment patients would actually receive. Induction, enemas: no difference (27% versus 33% remission). Harms: side effects in 23 versus 11 patients in Pullan, and a relative odds of 5.82 for adverse-event withdrawal in the review. Maintenance is outside this shelf's question, and the programme was never adopted — the shelf is the trial record of why.

shelves.title: Olsalazine in ulcerative colitis: modest benefit in small 1980s trials (Ns printed — 60+40, 105, 66), clearest in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients; dose-limiting secretory diarrhoea
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis — including patients intolerant of sulfasalazine — does olsalazine versus placebo induce and maintain remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aminosalicylic Acids · Clinical Trials as Topic · Colitis, Ulcerative · Enema · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Random Allocation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on small, old evidence — the Ns are printed on the face of every card: 60 randomised to enemas plus a separate 40-patient oral trial in one 1985 paper; 105 patients in the 1989 Gut trial; 66 sulfasalazine-intolerant patients in the 1987 dose-ranging trial. The consistent findings are modest: significant endoscopic improvement in the rectum in 1989 (with most symptom measures not significantly different), significant clinical and sigmoidoscopic improvement for oral olsalazine in the small 1985 oral trial, and a dose-response pattern in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients (improvement in 16% on placebo rising to 50% at 3 g/day). Olsalazine's dose-limiting secretory diarrhoea is the clinically decisive harm — it caused premature termination in the 1989 trial and a withdrawal in 1987. Olsalazine is a distinct azo-bonded 5-ASA dimer with its own trial base; the mesalamine dose/route shelves (packs #6087–#6089) and the balsalazide shelf (#7361) are separate questions, and no one of them is a class verdict.

cards.headline: Two trials in one paper (Selby 1985): olsalazine ENEMA — clinical improvement 19 of 29 (66%) versus 12 of 28 (43%) on placebo, not significant; oral olsalazine 2 g/day — significant clinical and sigmoidoscopic improvement (Ns printed: 60 and 40 randomised)
cards.summary: Two trials in one paper (Selby 1985): olsalazine ENEMA — clinical improvement 19 of 29 (66%) versus 12 of 28 (43%) on placebo, not significant; oral olsalazine 2 g/day — significant clinical and sigmoidoscopic improvement (Ns printed: 60 and 40 randomised)
cards.type: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials reported in one publication (enema, 60 randomised; oral, 40 randomised)
cards.people: First trial: 60 patients with mildly active distal ulcerative colitis randomly allocated to olsalazine 1 g or placebo as a nightly retention enema for 2 weeks (results reported for 29 olsalazine and 28 control patients). Second trial: 40 patients randomised to oral olsalazine 2 g daily or placebo capsules for 2 weeks.
cards.result: Enema trial: clinical improvement in 19 (66%) and sigmoidoscopic improvement in 17 (59%) of the 29 patients receiving olsalazine, compared with 12 (43%) and 11 (39%) of the 28 in the control group — these differences were not significant. Oral trial: significant clinical and sigmoidoscopic improvement was seen in patients receiving oral olsalazine compared with placebo (the abstract gives no counts for this second trial). The authors concluded oral olsalazine may be valuable in mildly active ulcerative colitis, with its role in maintaining remission yet to be determined.
cards.watchOut: Two very small 2-week trials in one paper: the enema comparison is formally negative and the oral comparison's significance comes without published counts in the abstract — 1985 evidence, printed with its Ns as required.
cards.source: Selby WS et al. Olsalazine in active ulcerative colitis. British medical journal (Clinical research ed.). 1985. PMID: 3933675. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gut RCT (Feurle 1989): olsalazine 2 g/day for 4 weeks — significant improvement in rectal endoscopic findings, a positive trend for mucus and blood, and NO significant difference in stool frequency, pain or biopsy; diarrhoea stopped treatment in 3 patients (n=105 printed)
cards.summary: Gut RCT (Feurle 1989): olsalazine 2 g/day for 4 weeks — significant improvement in rectal endoscopic findings, a positive trend for mucus and blood, and NO significant difference in stool frequency, pain or biopsy; diarrhoea stopped treatment in 3 patients (n=105 printed)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=105), olsalazine 2 g/day for 4 weeks
cards.people: 105 patients with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis in a randomised double-blind trial of olsalazine 2 g daily (n=52) versus placebo (n=53) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: After 4 weeks there was a statistically significant improvement in the endoscopic findings in the rectum and a positive trend in reduction of rectal mucus and blood discharge on olsalazine. No statistically significant difference was found for stool frequency, consistency, urge to defecate, abdominal pain or biopsy findings. Within-group comparison showed significant improvement in six of ten parameters on olsalazine and two of ten on placebo. Treatment was terminated prematurely because of untoward effects of olsalazine (mainly diarrhoea) in three patients, and for treatment failure (increased rectal bleeding) in four patients (one olsalazine, three placebo). The authors concluded 2 g olsalazine was slightly superior to placebo and suggested 3 or 4 g/day might show a more definite effect.
cards.watchOut: The win is endoscopic and rectal; the symptom measures patients feel were mostly not significantly different, and olsalazine's own diarrhoea — indistinguishable from a colitis symptom — already appears as the dose-limiting harm.
cards.source: Feurle GE et al. Olsalazine versus placebo in the treatment of mild to moderate ulcerative colitis: a randomised double blind trial. Gut. 1989. PMID: 2684804. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sulfasalazine-intolerant patients RCT (Meyers 1987): clinical improvement 35% on olsalazine versus 16% on placebo, with a dose-response pattern — 16% (placebo), 29% (0.75 g), 27% (1.5 g), 50% (3 g); P=0.04 (n=66 printed)
cards.summary: Sulfasalazine-intolerant patients RCT (Meyers 1987): clinical improvement 35% on olsalazine versus 16% on placebo, with a dose-response pattern — 16% (placebo), 29% (0.75 g), 27% (1.5 g), 50% (3 g); P=0.04 (n=66 printed)
cards.type: Prospective randomised placebo-controlled double-blind dose-ranging trial (n=66) in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients
cards.people: 66 outpatients with active ulcerative colitis who were intolerant of sulfasalazine, in a prospective randomised placebo-controlled double-blind dose-ranging trial of olsalazine sodium 0.75, 1.5 or 3 g daily, or placebo.
cards.result: Overall, 35% of patients receiving olsalazine improved clinically, compared with 16% on placebo. Comparing colitis activity at entry with completion, significant or nearly significant improvement was shown within the combined olsalazine group (P=0.01) and within the 1.5 g (P=0.04) and 3 g (P=0.055) groups. The proportions improved were 16%, 29%, 27% and 50% in the placebo and 0.75 g, 1.5 g and 3 g groups respectively (P=0.04) — a suggested dose-response. A similar pattern was seen sigmoidoscopically, without a demonstrated dose-response. Four patients were withdrawn for adverse reactions: two developed skin rash on olsalazine, and two had diarrhoea (one on olsalazine, one on placebo). The authors concluded olsalazine is effective and well tolerated in patients intolerant to sulfasalazine.
cards.watchOut: 66 patients split across four arms — each dose group is very small, so the dose-response percentages rest on handfuls of patients; the population (sulfasalazine-intolerant) is the niche where olsalazine's value was clearest.
cards.source: Meyers S et al. Olsalazine sodium in the treatment of ulcerative colitis among patients intolerant of sulfasalazine. shelves.title: Balsalazide in ulcerative colitis: dose-response and faster onset than mesalamine — but all comparators are low-dose mesalamine (1.2–2.4 g/day), no placebo arm, and 12-month remission was equal (58% both)
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, does balsalazide versus mesalazine/mesalamine induce remission faster, and does it maintain remission as well or better?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit — with the comparator warning on the face: every comparison here is against LOW-DOSE mesalamine by modern standards (2.4 g/day in the induction trial; 1.5 g/day and 1.2 g/day in the maintenance trials), there is no placebo arm anywhere, and these results must not be read as superiority over modern-dose mesalamine. Within those limits: the dose-response trial (n=154) found balsalazide 6.75 g/day significantly better than balsalazide 2.25 g/day on bleeding, stool frequency, sigmoidoscopy and global assessment, and faster in onset than mesalamine 2.4 g/day; the maintenance trial (n=133) found high-dose balsalazide (3 g twice daily) superior to low-dose balsalazide and to mesalazine 1.5 g/day in maintaining remission (77.5% versus 43.8% and 56.8%); and ABACUS (n=99) found equal 12-month remission (58% both) with fewer early relapses and better nocturnal symptom control on balsalazide 3 g/day versus mesalazine 1.2 g/day. cards.headline: Dose-response induction RCT (Levine 2002): balsalazide 6.75 g/day beat balsalazide 2.25 g/day on rectal bleeding (64.7% versus 32.4%), stool frequency, sigmoidoscopic score and global assessment, and acted faster than mesalamine 2.4 g/day (n=154)
cards.summary: Dose-response induction RCT (Levine 2002): balsalazide 6.75 g/day beat balsalazide 2.25 g/day on rectal bleeding (64.7% versus 32.4%), stool frequency, sigmoidoscopic score and global assessment, and acted faster than mesalamine 2.4 g/day (n=154)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind dose-response active-comparator trial (n=154), 8 weeks
cards.people: 154 patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis (verified by sigmoidoscopy) in a multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy dose-response trial of balsalazide 6.75 g daily, balsalazide 2.25 g daily, or mesalamine (pH-dependent delayed-release) 2.4 g daily, for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Balsalazide 6.75 g daily gave significantly greater improvement than 2.25 g daily in rectal bleeding (64.7% versus 32.4%; P<0.006), stool frequency (58.8% versus 29.4%; P<0.006), sigmoidoscopic score (78.9% versus 52.5%; P<0.015) and Physician's Global Assessment (73.7% versus 51.3%; P<0.03). Against mesalamine 2.4 g daily, balsalazide 6.75 g had a significantly more rapid onset (2-week sigmoidoscopic improvement 54.7% versus 29.4%; P=0.006) with numerically greater improvement at 8 weeks in five of seven measured signs and symptoms. Balsalazide was well tolerated, with no significant safety differences between groups.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm, endpoints are improvement in signs and symptoms (not remission counts), and the mesalamine comparator is 2.4 g/day — a low dose by modern standards, flagged on the face as the commissioning row requires.
cards.source: Levine DS et al. A randomized, double blind, dose-response comparison of balsalazide (6.75 g), balsalazide (2.25 g), and mesalamine (2.4 g) in the treatment of active, mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2002. PMID: 12094857. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Maintenance RCT (Kruis 2001): high-dose balsalazide (3 g twice daily) maintained remission in 77.5% versus 43.8% on low-dose balsalazide and 56.8% on mesalazine 0.5 g three times daily (P=0.006) over 26 weeks (n=133)
cards.summary: Maintenance RCT (Kruis 2001): high-dose balsalazide (3 g twice daily) maintained remission in 77.5% versus 43.8% on low-dose balsalazide and 56.8% on mesalazine 0.5 g three times daily (P=0.006) over 26 weeks (n=133)
cards.type: Double-blind multicentre randomised maintenance trial (n=133), 26 weeks
cards.people: 133 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission in a double-blind multicentre randomised trial: balsalazide 1.5 g twice daily (n=49), balsalazide 3.0 g twice daily (n=40), or mesalazine 0.5 g three times daily (n=44), for 26 weeks; efficacy by clinical activity index, endoscopic and histological scores.
cards.result: Balsalazide 3.0 g twice daily gave a significantly higher clinical remission rate (77.5%) than balsalazide 1.5 g twice daily (43.8%) and mesalazine 0.5 g three times daily (56.8%) (P=0.006). Times to relapse were 161 days, 131 days (P=0.003 versus high-dose balsalazide) and 144 days (not significant) respectively. The final endoscopic score differed significantly between the two balsalazide groups (P=0.005) but not between either balsalazide group and mesalazine. Nine patients discontinued for adverse effects (three low-dose balsalazide, two high-dose, four mesalazine), with no clinically important new safety findings.
cards.watchOut: The mesalazine comparator totals 1.5 g/day — low-dose by modern standards — so 'superior to mesalazine' here means superior to 1.5 g/day; the cleanest finding is the internal balsalazide dose-response (77.5% versus 43.8%).
cards.source: Kruis W et al. cards.headline: ABACUS maintenance RCT (Green 1998): balsalazide 3 g/day versus mesalazine 1.2 g/day over 12 months — remission 58% in BOTH groups, but fewer relapses by 3 months on balsalazide (10% versus 28%; P=0.0354) and better nocturnal symptom control (n=99; 95 evaluable)
cards.summary: ABACUS maintenance RCT (Green 1998): balsalazide 3 g/day versus mesalazine 1.2 g/day over 12 months — remission 58% in BOTH groups, but fewer relapses by 3 months on balsalazide (10% versus 28%; P=0.0354) and better nocturnal symptom control (n=99; 95 evaluable)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind maintenance comparison (n=99), balsalazide 3 g/day vs mesalazine 1.2 g/day, 12 months
cards.people: 99 patients (95 evaluable) with ulcerative colitis in remission in a randomised double-blind comparison of balsalazide 3 g daily (delivering 1.04 g 5-ASA) versus mesalazine 1.2 g daily for 12 months.
cards.result: Remission at 12 months was 58% in both groups. Balsalazide patients relapsed less within 3 months (10% versus 28%; P=0.0354) and, during the first 3 months, experienced more asymptomatic nights (90% versus 77%; P=0.0011), more symptom-free nights per week (6.4 ± 1.7 versus 4.7 ± 2.8; P=0.0006) and fewer nights with blood, mucus or sleep disturbance (each P<0.05); asymptomatic days did not differ significantly (58% versus 50%). Similar proportions reported adverse events (61% balsalazide versus 65% mesalazine); there were five serious adverse events (two balsalazide, three mesalazine) and four withdrawals for unacceptable adverse events (three balsalazide, one mesalazine).
cards.watchOut: The mesalazine comparator is 1.2 g/day — the lowest dose in this shelf — and the headline 12-month result is equality (58% both); the balsalazide advantages are early relapse and night-time symptoms, not overall remission.
cards.source: Green JR et al. Maintenance of remission of ulcerative colitis: a comparison between balsalazide 3 g daily and mesalazine 1.2 g daily over 12 months. ABACUS Investigator group. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 1998. PMID: 9882028. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Aldafermin (FGF19 analogue) in MASH — FAILED programme: ALPINE 2/3 missed its primary fibrosis endpoint and development was discontinued; liver fat fell in phase 2, and a later cirrhosis trial improved a biomarker score only
shelves.question: In adults with MASH and stage 2–3 fibrosis — or compensated cirrhosis — does aldafermin versus placebo improve liver fat, fibrosis or MASH resolution?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factors · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: FAILED PROGRAMME — stated plainly. Aldafermin, an engineered FGF19 analogue, reduced liver fat in its phase 2 trial (78 patients) but did NOT significantly improve fibrosis or resolve MASH there (38% versus 18% fibrosis improvement, P=0.10; 24% versus 9% MASH resolution, P=0.20). The phase 2b ALPINE 2/3 trial (171 randomised) MISSED its primary endpoint — no significant dose response for fibrosis improvement of at least one stage with no worsening of MASH (placebo 19%; aldafermin 0.3 mg 31%, 1.0 mg 15%, 3.0 mg 30%; dose-response P=0.55) — and development of aldafermin for MASH was discontinued. A later, separate trial in compensated cirrhosis (160 patients, 48 weeks) found a significant reduction in the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis score at 3 mg (least-squares mean difference −0.5) with fibrosis improvement in 23% versus 15% — a biomarker-led result in a different population, which must not be pooled with the F2–F3 question as if confirmatory. LDL-cholesterol elevation is the FGF19 class effect and belongs on the face (it was managed with statins in the trials; the fetched abstracts give no LDL numbers). This shelf is the FGF19 limb only — efruxifermin (live #1710) and pegbelfermin (pack #7108) are FGF21 analogues and different questions.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Harrison 2021): aldafermin 1 mg reduced liver fat significantly (reduction 7.7% versus 2.7% on placebo; P=0.002) but fibrosis improvement (38% versus 18%; P=0.10) and MASH resolution (24% versus 9%; P=0.20) were NOT significant (n=78)
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Harrison 2021): aldafermin 1 mg reduced liver fat significantly (reduction 7.7% versus 2.7% on placebo; P=0.002) but fibrosis improvement (38% versus 18%; P=0.10) and MASH resolution (24% versus 9%; P=0.20) were NOT significant (n=78)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=78), aldafermin 1 mg for 24 weeks
cards.people: 78 patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, NAFLD Activity Score ≥4, stage 2 or 3 fibrosis and absolute liver fat ≥8% by MRI proton density fat fraction, at 9 US centres, randomised 1:2 to subcutaneous placebo (n=25) or aldafermin 1 mg daily (n=53) for 24 weeks, with serial liver biopsies; the primary outcome was change in absolute liver fat content at week 24.
cards.result: At week 24 the aldafermin group had a significant reduction in absolute liver fat (reduction 7.7%) compared with placebo (reduction 2.7%; difference 5.0%, 95% CI reduction 8.0% to 1.9%; P=0.002). Aldafermin also produced significantly greater decreases in 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one, bile acids, alanine and aspartate aminotransferases and Pro-C3. Fibrosis improvement (≥1 stage) with no worsening of NASH was achieved in 38% on aldafermin versus 18% on placebo (P=0.10), and NASH resolution with no worsening of fibrosis in 24% versus 9% (P=0.20) — neither significant. No aldafermin patient discontinued for adverse events, versus 4% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was liver fat, a surrogate — the histology endpoints that decide MASH programmes were trends only in 78 patients; this trial is the promise the phase 2b trial then failed to confirm.
cards.source: Harrison SA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Aldafermin, an Engineered FGF19 Analog, in a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Patients With Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis. cards.headline: ALPINE 2/3 phase 2b RCT (Harrison 2022): PRIMARY ENDPOINT MISSED — fibrosis improvement with no worsening of MASH in 19% on placebo versus 31% (0.3 mg), 15% (1.0 mg) and 30% (3.0 mg) on aldafermin, with no dose response (P=0.55); development for MASH was discontinued (171 randomised; 786 screened)
cards.summary: ALPINE 2/3 phase 2b RCT (Harrison 2022): PRIMARY ENDPOINT MISSED — fibrosis improvement with no worsening of MASH in 19% on placebo versus 31% (0.3 mg), 15% (1.0 mg) and 30% (3.0 mg) on aldafermin, with no dose response (P=0.55); development for MASH was discontinued (171 randomised; 786 screened)
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ALPINE 2/3, n=171 randomised), three aldafermin doses for 24 weeks
cards.people: Patients with biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and stage 2 or 3 fibrosis at 30 US sites, randomised 1:1:1:1 (stratified by fibrosis stage) to placebo (n=43), aldafermin 0.3 mg (n=43), 1.0 mg (n=42) or 3.0 mg (n=43) once daily for 24 weeks; 786 patients were screened and 171 randomised and included in the intention-to-treat population, of whom 145 (85%) completed treatment. The primary endpoint was improvement in liver fibrosis of at least one stage with no worsening of NASH at week 24.
cards.result: Among patients with biopsies at baseline and week 24, the primary endpoint was met by 7 (19%) of 36 on placebo, 11 (31%) of 36 on aldafermin 0.3 mg (difference 12%, 90% CI −9 to 33; P=0.11), 5 (15%) of 34 on 1.0 mg (difference −5%, 90% CI −24 to 13; P=0.80) and 11 (30%) of 37 on 3.0 mg (difference 10%, 90% CI −9 to 30; P=0.12) — without meeting the prespecified significance for dose response (P=0.55): the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint. Adverse events were mostly mild or moderate; diarrhoea occurred in 14% on placebo, 7% (0.3 mg), 12% (1.0 mg) and 23% (3.0 mg). Serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar between groups. The authors concluded aldafermin did not produce a significant dose response on fibrosis improvement despite positive effects on a number of secondary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme-deciding trial and it failed on its prespecified primary analysis — secondary-endpoint movement does not rescue it. LDL-cholesterol elevation, the FGF19 class effect managed with statins in the trials, is not quantified in the fetched abstract, so no LDL numbers are printed.

cards.headline: Compensated cirrhosis RCT (Rinella 2024): aldafermin 3 mg significantly reduced the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis score versus placebo (least-squares mean difference −0.5; P=0.0003) at 48 weeks, with fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage in 23% versus 15% — a separate, later population, NOT a rescue of ALPINE 2/3 (n=160)
cards.summary: Compensated cirrhosis RCT (Rinella 2024): aldafermin 3 mg significantly reduced the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis score versus placebo (least-squares mean difference −0.5; P=0.0003) at 48 weeks, with fibrosis improvement ≥1 stage in 23% versus 15% — a separate, later population, NOT a rescue of ALPINE 2/3 (n=160)
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in compensated cirrhosis (n=160), 48 weeks — separate population from ALPINE 2/3
cards.people: 160 patients with compensated NASH cirrhosis in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b trial, randomised to aldafermin 0.3 mg (n=7), 1 mg (n=42), 3 mg (n=55) or placebo (n=56) for 48 weeks; the 0.3 mg group was discontinued to limit exposure to suboptimal doses. The primary endpoint was change in Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score from baseline to week 48, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: At week 48, the least-squares mean difference in change in ELF was −0.5 (95% CI −0.7 to −0.2; P=0.0003) between the 3 mg group and placebo. Fibrosis improvement of at least one stage occurred in 15% (placebo), 21% (1 mg) and 23% (3 mg), and fibrosis improvement without NASH worsening in 13%, 16% and 20% respectively (no P values given in the abstract for these proportions). Alanine and aspartate aminotransferases, Pro-C3 and liver stiffness favoured aldafermin. Diarrhoea occurred in 26% (1 mg) and 40% (3 mg) versus 18% on placebo, and discontinuations for treatment-related adverse events were 0% (placebo), 2% (1 mg) and 9% (3 mg).
cards.watchOut: A different question (cirrhosis, ELF-score primary endpoint) reported after the F2–F3 programme had failed: a significant biomarker change with modest, untested histology proportions must not be pooled with ALPINE 2/3 as if it confirmed the original programme.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a FAILED programme — liver fat and biomarkers moved, the deciding phase 2b trial missed its primary fibrosis endpoint (dose-response P=0.55) and MASH development was discontinued; the later cirrhosis trial's ELF-score result is a separate population and does not rescue it
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Harrison 2021 (n=78, F2–F3): significant liver-fat reduction, non-significant fibrosis and resolution trends. ALPINE 2/3 (n=171, F2–F3): primary endpoint missed at all three doses (19% placebo versus 31%, 15%, 30%), no dose response — development of aldafermin for MASH was discontinued. Rinella 2024 (n=160, compensated cirrhosis): significant ELF-score reduction at 3 mg (−0.5) with fibrosis improvement in 23% versus 15%, diarrhoea in up to 40% and treatment-related discontinuations in 9% at 3 mg. LDL-cholesterol elevation (the FGF19 class effect, managed with statins in the trials) belongs on the face of any account of this programme. FGF21 analogues (efruxifermin, pegbelfermin) are different molecules with their own shelves and are not evidence for or against aldafermin.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Besifovir in chronic hepatitis B (all evidence South Korean): noninferior HBV suppression to entecavir and tenofovir, with preserved bone and kidney measures — and carnitine depletion
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B, does besifovir dipivoxil maleate, compared with entecavir or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, suppress HBV DNA with less kidney and bone toxicity? (All trial evidence is from South Korea, where besifovir is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents · Bone Density · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Guanine · Hepatitis B virus · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organophosphonates · Republic of Korea · Tenofovir · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-region (South Korea) programme. Besifovir dipivoxil maleate suppressed HBV DNA to the same degree as entecavir over 96 weeks in a phase 2 trial (undetectable HBV DNA in about 80% on each drug) and was noninferior to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in the phase 3 programme: virological response was 87.7% versus 92.1% at 144 weeks and 92.5% versus 93.1% at 192 weeks for continuing besifovir versus switching from TDF, with no drug-resistant mutations detected. A separate randomised switch trial (n=153) found 100.0% versus 98.5% maintained HBV DNA <20 IU/mL after switching from long-term TDF to besifovir versus staying on TDF. The distinguishing claim is safety: bone mineral density and renal function were preserved on besifovir and improved after switching from TDF. The offsetting harm is carnitine depletion — carnitine supplements were prescribed to 83.9% (90 mg) and 100% (150 mg) of besifovir patients with a low carnitine level in the phase 2 trial. All trials were conducted in South Korea, where besifovir is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. The phase 3 efficacy reads after week 48 come from open-label extensions, not continued blinded comparison.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Yuen 2015): two-year besifovir versus entecavir — mean HBV DNA decline 5.29 and 5.15 log IU/mL (besifovir 90 mg and 150 mg) versus 5.67 log IU/mL (entecavir); undetectable HBV DNA in 80.7%, 78.6% and 80%
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Yuen 2015): two-year besifovir versus entecavir — mean HBV DNA decline 5.29 and 5.15 log IU/mL (besifovir 90 mg and 150 mg) versus 5.67 log IU/mL (entecavir); undetectable HBV DNA in 80.7%, 78.6% and 80%
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised trial, besifovir 90 mg or 150 mg vs entecavir 0.5 mg, 96 weeks
cards.people: 89 treatment-naive patients with chronic hepatitis B in a multicentre randomised trial: besifovir 90 mg (n=31), besifovir 150 mg (n=28) or entecavir 0.5 mg (n=30), monitored for 96 weeks.
cards.result: Mean decline in HBV DNA from baseline to week 96 was 5.29, 5.15 and 5.67 log IU/mL for besifovir 90 mg, besifovir 150 mg and entecavir respectively (P>0.05). Undetectable HBV DNA (<20 IU/mL) was achieved in 80.7%, 78.6% and 80%; ALT normalisation in 90.3%, 78.6% and 93.3%; and loss of HBeAg in 20%, 21.4% and 22.2% (all P>0.05). One patient on besifovir 90 mg had a virological breakthrough attributed to non-compliance; no patient developed drug-resistance mutations. Ten patients had serious adverse events, none related to the study medications. The most common besifovir-related side effect was carnitine depletion: carnitine supplements were prescribed to 83.9% and 100% of patients who had a low carnitine level at any time on besifovir 90 mg and 150 mg respectively. No patient had a creatinine increase >0.5 mg/dL from baseline.
cards.watchOut: Small phase 2 trial (89 patients across three arms) conducted in a single region (South Korea programme); it establishes comparable viral suppression, not superiority, and the carnitine-depletion signal required supplementation in most besifovir patients with a low level.
cards.source: Yuen MF et al. Two-year treatment outcome of chronic hepatitis B infection treated with besifovir vs. entecavir: results from a multicentre study. Journal of hepatology. 2015. cards.headline: Phase 3 programme, 144-week open-label extension (Yim 2020): virological response 87.7% continuing besifovir versus 92.1% after switching from tenofovir (P=0.36); bone and renal measures preserved on besifovir and improved after switching
cards.summary: Phase 3 programme, 144-week open-label extension (Yim 2020): virological response 87.7% continuing besifovir versus 92.1% after switching from tenofovir (P=0.36); bone and renal measures preserved on besifovir and improved after switching
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the phase 3 besifovir vs tenofovir trial (same programme as the 192-week card below — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 197 treatment-naive patients with chronic hepatitis B randomised in the phase 3 double-blind comparison of besifovir versus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for 48 weeks; 170 entered the second-year and 158 the third-year open-label besifovir extension, and 153 completed 144 weeks (continuing besifovir, BSV-BSV, versus TDF for 48 weeks then besifovir, TDF-BSV).
cards.result: The primary endpoint was virological response (HBV DNA <69 IU/mL). Over 144 weeks the virological response rate was 87.7% in the BSV-BSV group and 92.1% in the TDF-BSV group (P=0.36). ALT normalisation and HBeAg seroconversion rates were similar between the groups, and no drug-resistant mutations to besifovir were noted. Bone mineral density and renal function were well preserved in the BSV-BSV group and were significantly improved after switching therapy in the TDF-BSV patients.
cards.watchOut: Programme lineage: after the 48-week double-blind phase, everyone received open-label besifovir, so the 144-week comparison is continuing-versus-switched, not besifovir versus continued tenofovir; attrition from 197 randomised to 153 completing also applies.
cards.source: Yim HJ et al. Besifovir Dipivoxil Maleate 144-Week Treatment of Chronic Hepatitis B: An Open-Label Extensional Study of a Phase 3 Trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2020. PMID: 32355123. Registry ID: NCT01937806. cards.headline: Phase 3 programme, 192-week report (Song 2021): virological response 92.50% continuing besifovir versus 93.06% after switching from tenofovir (P=0.90); no resistance; bone and renal measures recovered after the switch
cards.summary: Phase 3 programme, 192-week report (Song 2021): virological response 92.50% continuing besifovir versus 93.06% after switching from tenofovir (P=0.90); no resistance; bone and renal measures recovered after the switch
cards.type: 192-week extension report of the phase 3 besifovir vs tenofovir trial (same programme as the 144-week card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same phase 3 programme: of 197 randomised patients, 170 (86%) entered the open-label phase and 152 (77%) entered the 192-week extension (continuing besifovir, BSV-BSV, versus tenofovir for 48 weeks then besifovir, TDF-BSV).
cards.result: Virological response rates over 192 weeks were 92.50% (BSV-BSV) and 93.06% (TDF-BSV) (P=0.90). HBeAg seroconversion and ALT normalisation rates were similar between the groups (P=0.75 and P=0.36 respectively). There were no drug-resistant mutations to besifovir. Bone mineral density and renal function were well preserved in the BSV-BSV group, whereas in the TDF-BSV group they initially worsened on tenofovir and then recovered after switching to besifovir.
cards.watchOut: Same single phase 3 programme as the 144-week report — the two extension reports are one trial's lineage, not two trials. Long-term reads are open-label and completer-based (152 of 197 randomised entered this extension).

cards.headline: Randomised switch trial (Yim 2025): switching from long-term tenofovir to besifovir was noninferior — HBV DNA <20 IU/mL in 100.0% versus 98.5% at 48 weeks — with improved bone turnover markers and bone density
cards.summary: Randomised switch trial (Yim 2025): switching from long-term tenofovir to besifovir was noninferior — HBV DNA <20 IU/mL in 100.0% versus 98.5% at 48 weeks — with improved bone turnover markers and bone density
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority switch trial, besifovir vs continued tenofovir, 48 weeks
cards.people: 153 patients with chronic hepatitis B treated with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for at least 48 weeks with HBV DNA <20 IU/mL (median prior TDF duration 4.14 years), randomised to besifovir 150 mg or continued TDF 300 mg for 48 weeks; the per-protocol analysis included 130 patients (64 besifovir, 66 TDF).
cards.result: After 48 weeks, 100.0% of the besifovir group and 98.5% of the TDF group met the primary endpoint (HBV DNA <20 IU/mL), demonstrating noninferior antiviral efficacy (95% CI for the difference −0.01 to 0.04; P>0.999; predefined margin −0.18). Mean percentage change in estimated glomerular filtration rate was slightly better with besifovir (+1.67 ± 11.73%) than with TDF (−1.24 ± 11.02%). The besifovir group showed significant improvement in bone turnover biomarkers compared with TDF, and hip and spine bone mineral density increased in the besifovir group.
cards.watchOut: A switch trial in patients already fully suppressed on tenofovir — it answers whether suppression is maintained after switching, not whether besifovir works as initial therapy; the primary analysis is per-protocol (130 of 153 randomised).

cards.headline: Synthesis: one Korean programme — besifovir matches entecavir and tenofovir for HBV DNA suppression across a phase 2 trial, one phase 3 programme (48-week blinded comparison plus 144- and 192-week open-label extensions) and a randomised switch trial, with preserved bone and renal measures and a carnitine-depletion cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: one Korean programme — besifovir matches entecavir and tenofovir for HBV DNA suppression across a phase 2 trial, one phase 3 programme (48-week blinded comparison plus 144- and 192-week open-label extensions) and a randomised switch trial, with preserved bone and renal measures and a carnitine-depletion cost
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No report shows besifovir superior for viral suppression: the reads are equivalence/noninferiority reads throughout (undetectable HBV DNA about 80% versus entecavir at 96 weeks; virological response 92.5% versus 93.1% at 192 weeks in the phase 3 lineage; 100.0% versus 98.5% maintained suppression in the switch trial), with no drug resistance detected. The consistent secondary finding is bone and renal preservation on besifovir, with improvement after switching from tenofovir. Carnitine depletion, requiring supplementation in most affected patients, is the programme's characteristic harm. The entire evidence base is South Korean; besifovir is approved there and is not FDA- or EMA-approved, so generalisation beyond that setting is untested.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Granulocyte/monocyte apheresis (Adacolumn) in ulcerative colitis: a sham-negative programme — 17% vs 11% remission against sham, with positive reads only from open-label trials
shelves.question: In adults with active moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, does granulocyte/monocyte adsorptive apheresis (the Adacolumn Apheresis System) versus sham apheresis induce remission or response — and can it maintain remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Colitis, Ulcerative · Colonoscopy · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Granulocytes · Humans · Japan · Leukapheresis · Male · Middle Aged · Monocytes · North America · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) on the blinded evidence — a sham-negative programme. The only large sham-controlled induction trial (Sands 2008, pivotal n=168) found clinical remission in 17% on granulocyte/monocyte apheresis (the Adacolumn Apheresis System) versus 11% on sham (P=.361), with response 44% versus 39% (P=.620); the companion study and pooled data were the same. A small double-blind sham-controlled maintenance trial (n=33) also found no significant difference overall. The more positive reads come from designs without a sham control: the open-label maintenance trial (n=164) missed its primary endpoint (cumulative clinical remission 46.6% versus 36.4%, P=0.1621) though endoscopic remission was higher (42.5% versus 25.9%, P=0.0480), and adding apheresis to prednisone in steroid-dependent disease did not increase steroid-free remission (13% versus 7%, P=0.11). The 2010 systematic review states the split plainly: remission rates looked higher against medical therapy but NOT against sham. That blinded-negative versus open-positive design split is this shelf's central fact and is not pooled away.

cards.headline: Sham-controlled induction RCT (Sands 2008): remission 17% on apheresis versus 11% on sham (P=.361) and response 44% versus 39% (P=.620) — the pivotal trial was negative
cards.summary: Sham-controlled induction RCT (Sands 2008): remission 17% on apheresis versus 11% on sham (P=.361) and response 44% versus 39% (P=.620) — the pivotal trial was negative
cards.type: Randomised double-blind sham-controlled trial (pivotal study plus identical-design companion study), Adacolumn apheresis vs sham, induction
cards.people: Patients with active moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (Mayo score 6–11) at community and tertiary centres: a North American pivotal study (N=168; apheresis n=112, sham n=56, randomised 2:1) and a smaller companion study of identical design in Europe and Japan (N=47). Treatment was 9 weeks of granulocyte/monocyte apheresis with the Adacolumn Apheresis System (JIMRO, Ltd, Takasaki, Japan) or sham apheresis.
cards.result: In the pivotal study, clinical remission rates (Mayo score 0–2, with 0 on rectal bleeding and 0 or 1 on endoscopic examination) were 17% for apheresis and 11% for sham (P=.361). Clinical response (Mayo reduction of 3 or more points) was 44% versus 39% (P=.620). Endoscopic remission and response, and changes in Mayo and quality-of-life scores, were similar between groups. The companion study and the pooled data from both studies yielded similar results. Apheresis was well tolerated but did not demonstrate efficacy for induction of clinical remission or response.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's only large blinded test and it is negative; the positive reputation of apheresis in ulcerative colitis rests on open-label experience, which this trial's sham arm shows can produce an 11% remission and 39% response rate without the column.
cards.source: Sands BE et al. A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study of granulocyte/monocyte apheresis for active ulcerative colitis. Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18602921. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Open-label maintenance RCT (Naganuma 2020): cumulative clinical remission at 12 months 46.6% with apheresis versus 36.4% without (P=0.1621) — primary endpoint not met; endoscopic remission 42.5% versus 25.9% (P=0.0480)
cards.summary: Open-label maintenance RCT (Naganuma 2020): cumulative clinical remission at 12 months 46.6% with apheresis versus 36.4% without (P=0.1621) — primary endpoint not met; endoscopic remission 42.5% versus 25.9% (P=0.0480)
cards.type: Open-label prospective multicentre randomised trial, maintenance apheresis vs no apheresis, 12 months
cards.people: 164 patients with ulcerative colitis in remission induced by granulocyte/monocyte adsorption apheresis or leukocytapheresis (enrolled 2013–2017), randomised 1:1 to maintenance apheresis twice per month for 12 months or to no apheresis.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, cumulative clinical remission (Mayo score 2 or less) at 12 months, was 46.6% in the apheresis group and 36.4% in the control group (P=0.1621) — not significant. Endoscopic remission at 12 months was significantly higher with apheresis (42.5% vs 25.9%; P=0.0480). Clinical remission (47.5% vs 32.1%; P=0.0540) and complete endoscopic remission (33.8% vs 19.8%; P=0.0513) tended to be higher with apheresis but were not significant. No severe adverse events were observed in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no sham control — the design the sham-controlled trial warns against — and its primary endpoint was not met; the significant endoscopic-remission result is a secondary endpoint among several.
cards.source: Naganuma M et al. Efficacy of apheresis as maintenance therapy for patients with ulcerative colitis in an open-label prospective multicenter randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Small double-blind sham-controlled maintenance trial (Fukunaga 2012): avoiding-relapse rates at 48 weeks 40.0% monthly apheresis versus 9.1% sham versus 18.2% no intervention — no significant difference among the three arms (n=33)
cards.summary: Small double-blind sham-controlled maintenance trial (Fukunaga 2012): avoiding-relapse rates at 48 weeks 40.0% monthly apheresis versus 9.1% sham versus 18.2% no intervention — no significant difference among the three arms (n=33)
cards.type: Small randomised double-blind sham-controlled maintenance trial (n=33), monthly apheresis vs sham vs no intervention
cards.people: 33 corticosteroid-refractory patients with active ulcerative colitis who first received 10 weekly granulocyte/monocyte adsorption sessions as remission induction, then were randomised to one apheresis session every 4 weeks (n=11), extracorporeal circulation without the column (sham, n=11), or no additional intervention (n=11) for 48 weeks.
cards.result: At week 48, the rates of avoiding relapse were 40.0% (true apheresis), 9.1% (sham) and 18.2% (control). All patients were steroid-free, but no statistically significant difference was seen among the three arms. In the subgroup who could taper prednisolone to under 20 mg/day during induction, avoiding relapse was better in the true-apheresis group than in the sham (P<0.03) or control (P<0.05) groups.
cards.watchOut: Very small — 11 patients per arm — so the numerical gap (40.0% versus 9.1%) is compatible with chance, as the non-significant overall test shows; the significant result is a subgroup read. It is carded as the second blinded test, not as positive evidence.
cards.source: Fukunaga K et al. cards.headline: Apheresis added to prednisone in steroid-dependent UC (Domenech 2018): steroid-free remission at week 24 in 13% versus 7% (P=0.11) — no increase, though relapse was delayed and steroid adverse events were fewer
cards.summary: Apheresis added to prednisone in steroid-dependent UC (Domenech 2018): steroid-free remission at week 24 in 13% versus 7% (P=0.11) — no increase, though relapse was delayed and steroid adverse events were fewer
cards.type: Randomised multicentre open trial, apheresis + prednisone vs prednisone alone, steroid-dependent ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 123 patients (the report also states 63 in the apheresis group and 62 on prednisone alone) with active steroid-dependent ulcerative colitis (Mayo score 4–10), randomised to 7 weekly granulocyte/monocyte apheresis sessions plus oral prednisone (40 mg/day with a 9-week taper) or prednisone alone, stratified by thiopurine use.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, steroid-free remission at week 24 (total Mayo score 2 or less with no subscore above 1, without re-introducing corticosteroids) was achieved in 13% (95% CI 6 to 24) with apheresis plus prednisone and 7% (95% CI 2 to 16) with prednisone alone (P=0.11). Time to relapse was significantly longer with apheresis (hazard ratio 1.7 [95% CI 1.16 to 2.48] as reported for the comparison, P=0.005 — a relative measure) and steroid-related adverse events were significantly lower (6% vs 20%; P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Open trial (no sham) whose primary endpoint was not met; the delayed-relapse and fewer-steroid-events findings are secondary. The report's own numbers are internally inconsistent (123 included; arms of 63 and 62) — the figures are printed as reported.
cards.source: Domènech E et al. Addition of Granulocyte/Monocyte Apheresis to Oral Prednisone for Steroid-dependent Ulcerative Colitis: A Randomized Multicentre Clinical Trial. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2018. PMID: 29490024. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review (Thanaraj 2010): 10 RCTs — remission rates generally higher against medical therapy, NOT significantly higher against sham; only 2 of 10 trials at low risk of bias
cards.summary: Systematic review (Thanaraj 2010): 10 RCTs — remission rates generally higher against medical therapy, NOT significantly higher against sham; only 2 of 10 trials at low risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review of 10 RCTs of granulocyte/monocyte adsorptive apheresis in ulcerative colitis (no meta-analysis performed)
cards.people: Ten randomised controlled trials of granulocyte/monocyte adsorptive apheresis in adults with ulcerative colitis (chronically active despite 5-aminosalicylates or immunomodulators, or corticosteroid-dependent), comparing apheresis with conventional medical therapy, with sham procedure, or intensive versus conventional apheresis regimens; six trials were conducted in Japanese patients.
cards.result: Formal meta-analysis was not undertaken because of concerns about the methodological quality of the identified studies. Compared with medical therapy, remission rates with apheresis were generally higher and corticosteroid-sparing effects were observed. Compared with sham procedure, apheresis did not achieve significantly higher remission rates. Intensive regimens generally showed higher remission rates and shorter time to remission than conventional regimens. Only two RCTs were at low risk of bias. The authors concluded that high-quality RCTs against medical therapy or sham in Western populations, with endoscopically confirmed disease activity, are required.
cards.watchOut: A 2010 review whose included trials overlap the primary reports carded here — it is carded for its sham-versus-medical-therapy contrast, not as independent evidence, and it predates the 2018 and 2020 trials carded above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: every blinded test of granulocyte/monocyte apheresis in ulcerative colitis is negative — sham-controlled induction (17% vs 11% remission) and the small sham-controlled maintenance trial both missed — while the positive signals come only from open-label designs whose primary endpoints also missed

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The programme's central fact is a design split. Blinded: Sands 2008 induction, remission 17% versus 11% on sham (P=.361); Fukunaga 2012 maintenance, no significant difference among apheresis, sham and control arms. Open-label: Naganuma 2020 maintenance missed its primary endpoint (46.6% vs 36.4%, P=0.1621) with a significant secondary endoscopic result, and Domenech 2018 missed its primary endpoint (steroid-free remission 13% vs 7%, P=0.11) with delayed relapse. The 2010 systematic review found the same pattern across 10 RCTs. Apheresis was well tolerated in every report — the question is efficacy, and against sham it has not been shown.

shelves.title: Tradipitant in gastroparesis — 2 randomised reports only: phase 2 reduced nausea, but the phase 3 trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.741); programme presented as failed at phase 3
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic or idiopathic gastroparesis, does tradipitant (a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist) versus placebo reduce nausea and overall gastroparesis symptoms? (Evidence base: exactly 2 randomised reports — phase 2, n=152; phase 3, n=201.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Diabetes Complications · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastroparesis · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Neurokinin-1 Receptor Antagonists · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on exactly 2 randomised reports (phase 2, n=152; phase 3, n=201) — the base is printed here because it is the whole evidence. The phase 2 trial (4 weeks) was positive: nausea score fell by 1.2 on tradipitant versus 0.7 on placebo (P=.0099), with more nausea-free days (28.8% versus 15.0% increase; P=.0160). The larger, longer phase 3 trial (12 weeks) FAILED its prespecified primary endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (difference in nausea severity change, P=.741) and its prespecified secondary endpoints; its supportive findings are post hoc (patients with high tradipitant blood levels, and sensitivity analyses adjusting for rescue medication and baseline severity inflation). Per the commissioning row's builder condition, the programme is therefore presented as failed at phase 3 on the face of this shelf: a positive small phase 2 that the definitive trial did not confirm. A healthy-volunteer mechanistic study (n=24) is carded, clearly labelled, only to record that tradipitant did not retard gastric emptying; it is not efficacy evidence and does not count toward the base.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Carlin 2021): nausea score fell 1.2 on tradipitant versus 0.7 on placebo at 4 weeks (P=.0099); nausea-free days increased 28.8% versus 15.0% (P=.0160)
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Carlin 2021): nausea score fell 1.2 on tradipitant versus 0.7 on placebo at 4 weeks (P=.0099); nausea-free days increased 28.8% versus 15.0% (P=.0160)
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, tradipitant 85 mg twice daily, 4 weeks (n=152)
cards.people: 152 adults with diabetic or idiopathic gastroparesis at 47 US sites (2016–2018), randomised to oral tradipitant 85 mg twice daily (n=77) or placebo (n=75) for 4 weeks. Symptoms were assessed by a daily symptom diary, Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index scores and other patient-reported questionnaires; the primary outcome was change to week 4 in average nausea severity on the Gastroparesis Core Symptom Daily Diary.
cards.result: Nausea score decreased by 1.2 on tradipitant versus 0.7 on placebo at week 4 (P=.0099). Nausea-free days increased by 28.8% on tradipitant versus 15.0% on placebo (P=.0160). In patients with nausea and vomiting at baseline (n=101), the nausea decrease was 1.4 versus 0.4 (P<.0001) and nausea-free days improved 32.3% versus 7.6% (P=.0003). An average nausea score of 1 or less at week 4 was reached by 32.9% on tradipitant versus 11.8% on placebo (P=.0013), and a greater-than-1-point improvement in Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index score by 46.6% versus 23.5% (P=.0053).
cards.watchOut: A short (4-week), 152-patient phase 2 trial — the programme's only positive randomised report, and the result the phase 3 trial was designed to confirm and did not (see next card).

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT (Carlin 2024): the prespecified primary endpoint was NOT met — nausea severity change versus placebo at week 12, P=.741; supportive findings are post hoc exposure and sensitivity analyses only
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT (Carlin 2024): the prespecified primary endpoint was NOT met — nausea severity change versus placebo at week 12, P=.741; supportive findings are post hoc exposure and sensitivity analyses only
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial, tradipitant 85 mg twice daily, 12 weeks (n=201) — primary endpoint negative
cards.people: 201 adults with diabetic or idiopathic gastroparesis, randomised to oral tradipitant 85 mg twice daily (n=102) or placebo (n=99) for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was change from baseline to week 12 in average nausea severity by daily symptom diary; blood levels were monitored for an exposure-response analysis.
cards.result: The intention-to-treat population did not meet the prespecified primary endpoint at week 12 (difference in nausea severity change, drug versus placebo; P=.741) or the prespecified secondary endpoints. Post hoc analyses were performed to control for drug exposure, rescue medications and baseline severity inflation: subjects with high blood levels of tradipitant significantly improved average nausea severity from early time points (weeks 2–4), and post hoc sensitivity analyses showed statistically significant improvements in nausea at week 12. The authors concluded the findings suggest tradipitant has potential for the symptom of nausea in gastroparesis — a conclusion resting on the post hoc analyses, not on the trial's prespecified test.
cards.watchOut: The definitive trial failed its prespecified primary and secondary endpoints; every positive read in this report is post hoc (high-exposure subgroup, rescue-medication and baseline-inflation adjustments) and cannot carry an efficacy claim. This card is why the shelf presents the programme as failed at phase 3.

cards.headline: Mechanistic study in healthy volunteers (Khanna 2022) — NOT efficacy evidence: tradipitant for 9 days did not significantly affect gastric emptying, gastric volumes or satiation, and did not retard gastric emptying (n=24)
cards.summary: Mechanistic study in healthy volunteers (Khanna 2022) — NOT efficacy evidence: tradipitant for 9 days did not significantly affect gastric emptying, gastric volumes or satiation, and did not retard gastric emptying (n=24)
cards.type: Mechanistic randomised study in healthy volunteers (n=24) — carded as mechanism/safety context only; NOT gastroparesis efficacy evidence and NOT part of the 2-report efficacy base
cards.people: 24 healthy volunteers in a single-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of tradipitant 85 mg twice daily or matching placebo for 9 consecutive days, with scintigraphic gastric-emptying measurement, SPECT gastric volumes and a nutrient-drink satiation test on the last 2 days.
cards.result: There were no significant effects of tradipitant versus placebo on gastric emptying, gastric volumes, satiation, or symptoms 30 minutes after the maximum tolerated volume. Blood levels of tradipitant showed nonsignificant positive correlations with accommodation gastric volume and gastric emptying at 4 hours. The authors concluded tradipitant does not significantly affect gastric motor functions and, importantly for gastroparesis use, did not retard gastric emptying.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, 9 days, n=24: this study cannot support or refute symptom efficacy in gastroparesis. It is carded, labelled, solely because the commissioning row records it as seen-but-not-counted; the shelf's efficacy base remains exactly 2 randomised reports.

shelves.title: Liver-panel reference intervals: sex/age partitioning required; metabolically verified ALT upper limits 34 U/L (men) and 22 U/L (women) sit below historically printed limits
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the liver panel — alanine and aspartate aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase and bilirubin — by sex, age and ancestry, and how far do metabolically defined 'healthy' upper limits for ALT sit below the limits laboratories have historically printed?
shelves.mesh: Liver Function Tests/standards · Reference Values · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Bilirubin/blood · Female · Humans · Male · Adult · Middle Aged · Sex Factors · Age Factors · Asian People
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, liver / gastrointestinal physiology chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three primary datasets: a Chinese multicentre study (3,210 healthy adults aged 20-79 across six regions, seven analytes on three analytical systems, validated in 21 hospitals) which found the intervals then in use were no longer applicable — under the old intervals, 15.2% of results for total bilirubin fell outside on one side against a nominal 2.5%; a metabolically and histologically verified Korean living-liver-donor analysis (5,455 screened; 1,553 with no steatosis who met Prati metabolic criteria) setting the ALT upper reference limit at 34 U/L for men and 22 U/L for women — well below historically printed laboratory limits; and CARDIA (over 5,000 young US adults), in which values for six liver-associated tests differed significantly by race and sex and at least one test was out of range in 38% of men and 19% of women using common intervals. The contested number is the ALT upper limit, and the population-definition rule (which metabolic exclusions were applied) moves it more than the assay does — that rule is printed beside the interval on its card. Values are in U/L; no fetched record on this shelf prints bilirubin in mmol/L, and where bilirubin appears it is handled in mg/dL terms only as the records allow (none prints a numeric bilirubin interval, and none is claimed). The stamp is graded down: only three datasets, from three different population-definition traditions, and the ALT limit is definition-dependent. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Chinese multicentre reference intervals (Mu 2013): 3,210 healthy adults, seven liver tests — sex partitioned ALT, GGT and total bilirubin; age partitioned ALP and albumin; the intervals then in use no longer fitted the population
cards.summary: Chinese multicentre reference intervals (Mu 2013): 3,210 healthy adults, seven liver tests — sex partitioned ALT, GGT and total bilirubin; age partitioned ALP and albumin; the intervals then in use no longer fitted the population
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre liver-panel reference intervals, Chinese adults)
cards.people: 3,210 individuals aged 20-79 years enrolled in six representative geographical regions of China; alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), total protein, albumin and total bilirubin were measured on the three analytical systems mainly used in China, and the new intervals were validated in 21 large hospitals nationwide (1,220 validation results).
cards.result: Common reference intervals for the seven liver function tests were established for the Chinese adult population. Partitioning was required by sex for ALT, GGT and total bilirubin, by age for ALP and albumin, and by region for total protein. More than 86% of the 21 laboratories passed validation in every subgroup, and 95.3% to 98.8% of validation results fell within the new intervals. Against the intervals previously recommended in China, the one-sided out-of-range proportions deviated significantly from the nominal 2.5% — for example total bilirubin 15.2%, ALP 0.2% and albumin 0.0% — and most intervals differed obviously from those of other populations. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval tables, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Population-specific by design (Chinese adults, three named analytical systems): the finding that intervals differ by population is the content — these intervals must not be exported as universal liver-panel limits.
cards.source: Mu R et al. First definition of reference intervals of liver function tests in China: a large-population-based multi-center study about healthy adults. PloS one. 2013. PMID: 24058449.
