cards.headline: Metabolically verified ALT limits (Choi 2024): in 1,553 liver donors with no steatosis meeting Prati criteria, the ALT upper reference limit was 34 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women — below conventionally accepted values
cards.summary: Metabolically verified ALT limits (Choi 2024): in 1,553 liver donors with no steatosis meeting Prati criteria, the ALT upper reference limit was 34 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women — below conventionally accepted values
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (histologically and metabolically defined ALT reference interval, Asian liver donors)
cards.people: 5,455 potential Asian living liver donors (2005-2019; median age 30 years; 66.2% men) screened for hepatitis B and C, HIV and alcohol use, with liver histology. Of these, 3,162 (58.0%) had no hepatic steatosis, and 1,553 (49.1% of those) also met the Prati criteria for metabolic health: body mass index below 23 kg/m2, triglycerides at most 200 mg/dL, fasting glucose at most 105 mg/dL and total cholesterol at most 220 mg/dL.
cards.result: The updated upper reference limit for ALT, taken as the 95th percentile among participants without steatosis who met the Prati criteria, was 34 U/L for males and 22 U/L for females — significantly lower than conventionally accepted values. Using this revised limit, 72.8% of males with ALT at or above 34 U/L and 55.0% of females at or above 22 U/L showed signs of steatosis, whereas 32.7% of males and 22.2% of females met criteria for metabolic syndrome.
cards.watchOut: The low limits are a product of the strict population definition (histologically steatosis-free AND metabolically screened, young donors, median age 30): applying 34/22 U/L to an unscreened general population reclassifies many people as abnormal — the definition rule, printed on this card, is inseparable from the numbers.
cards.source: Choi J et al. Updated Reference Intervals for Alanine Aminotransferase in a Metabolically and Histologically Normal Population. cards.summary: CARDIA (Manolio 1992): over 5,000 young US adults — AST, GGT, ALP, total bilirubin, total protein and albumin all differed significantly by race and sex; at least one test was out of range in 38% of men and 19% of women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (liver-associated chemistry distributions by sex and race, CARDIA young adults)
cards.people: More than 5,000 Black and white men and women in the CARDIA study (young adults), with simultaneous multiple automated analyses of liver-associated serum chemistry tests, examined by race and sex with adjustment for age, body mass, reported ethanol intake, smoking and oral contraceptive use.
cards.result: Serum values of aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, total protein and albumin showed clinically and statistically significant differences by race and sex, not explained by differences in age, body mass, ethanol intake, smoking or oral contraceptive use. Results for at least one of the six tests were out of range in 38% of the men and 19% of the women under the intervals then applied. The authors recommend sex- and race-specific reference intervals to reduce values reported as abnormal in otherwise healthy young adults. The fetched record does not print the numeric intervals, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Young adults only, and a differences study rather than a formal interval-establishment study: it shows why single intervals misclassify, but supplies no replacement interval table on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: liver-panel intervals are population- and definition-bound — and the ALT upper limit is the contested number: 34 U/L (men) and 22 U/L (women) when 'healthy' means steatosis-free and metabolically screened
cards.summary: Synthesis: liver-panel intervals are population- and definition-bound — and the ALT upper limit is the contested number: 34 U/L (men) and 22 U/L (women) when 'healthy' means steatosis-free and metabolically screened
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (liver / gastrointestinal physiology; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature). The Chinese multicentre study (3,210 adults) establishes that intervals must be partitioned by sex (ALT, GGT, bilirubin), age (ALP, albumin) and even region (total protein), and that inherited intervals misclassify badly (15.2% one-sided out-of-range for total bilirubin against a nominal 2.5%). CARDIA (over 5,000 young adults) shows the same lesson in a US population: six analytes differ by race and sex, with at least one out-of-range result in 38% of men and 19% of women. Choi 2024 then shows what the ALT controversy is made of: the upper limit is 34 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women only under a histologically and metabolically screened definition of healthy (Prati criteria, printed on its card). Downgrade reason, on the face: three datasets from three population-definition traditions, with numeric tables printed in the fetched records only for ALT — hence EMERGING. Cross-point: the full-blood-count interval shelf is the haematology panel; this is the chemistry panel's liver limb, and hepatitis / drug-induced-liver-injury treatment shelves presuppose these intervals rather than re-carding them.
cards.watchOut: Never quote an ALT upper limit without its population-definition rule, and never apply one population's intervals to another population's patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Octreotide in acute pancreatitis: no benefit in the 302-patient double-blind trial or the 720-patient meta-analysis — the small positive reports are design-flagged
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe or severe acute pancreatitis, does octreotide versus placebo or conservative care reduce mortality, complications and hospital stay?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide · Pancreatitis · Severity of Illness Index · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — the two reports that can carry weight agree. The large randomised double-blind multicentre trial (n=302, 32 hospitals) found no significant difference in mortality (16% placebo vs 15% and 12% on octreotide 100 and 200 µg three times daily), complications, pain duration, surgery or hospital stay. The agent-specific meta-analysis (11 randomised trials, 720 participants) found mortality relative risk 0.88 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.45) and complications relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.26) — relative measures, neither significant. Against that stand two small positive reports with their design flags on the face: a severe-pancreatitis study analysing 50 of 60 entered patients whose record describes its design inconsistently (case-control indexing over a prospective randomised description), and a 43-patient sequentially allocated (quasi-randomised) high-dose study with 48-hour biochemical endpoints and one death in each group. The 2017 Cochrane pharmacological-interventions review (PMID 28431202) is fenced to the lexipafant build at pack #7293 and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Multicentre RCT (Uhl 1999): octreotide 100 or 200 µg three times daily for 7 days gave NO benefit in moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis — mortality 16% on placebo vs 15% and 12% on octreotide, with no significant differences in complications, pain duration, surgery or hospital stay (n=302)
cards.summary: Multicentre RCT (Uhl 1999): octreotide 100 or 200 µg three times daily for 7 days gave NO benefit in moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis — mortality 16% on placebo vs 15% and 12% on octreotide, with no significant differences in complications, pain duration, surgery or hospital stay (n=302)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind multicentre placebo-controlled trial, octreotide 100/200 µg three times daily, 7 days (n=302)
cards.people: 302 patients from 32 hospitals fulfilling criteria for moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis within 96 hours of symptom onset, randomly assigned to placebo (n=103), octreotide 100 µg (n=98) or octreotide 200 µg (n=101) by subcutaneous injection three times daily for seven days. The primary outcome was a score composed of mortality and 15 typical complications of acute pancreatitis.
cards.result: An intention-to-treat analysis of all 302 patients revealed no significant differences among treatment groups with respect to mortality (placebo 16%; octreotide 100 µg 15%; octreotide 200 µg 12%), the rate of newly developed complications, the duration of pain, surgical interventions, or the length of hospital stay. A valid-for-efficacy analysis of 251 patients also revealed no significant differences. The authors concluded the trial shows no benefit of octreotide in the treatment of acute pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: The largest and best-designed trial on this shelf, and it is null on every component of its composite — the two smaller positive reports below have to be read against it, not beside it as equals.
cards.source: Uhl W et al. A randomised, double blind, multicentre trial of octreotide in moderate to severe acute pancreatitis. Gut. 1999. PMID: 10369711. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Severe pancreatitis study (Paran 2000): octreotide 0.1 mg three times daily was associated with less sepsis (24% vs 76%, P=0.0002), less ARDS (28% vs 56%, P=0.04), shorter hospital stay (20.6 vs 33.1 days) and fewer deaths (2 vs 8, P<0.019) — in 50 patients analysed of 60 entered, with the record's own design wording inconsistent
cards.summary: Severe pancreatitis study (Paran 2000): octreotide 0.1 mg three times daily was associated with less sepsis (24% vs 76%, P=0.0002), less ARDS (28% vs 56%, P=0.04), shorter hospital stay (20.6 vs 33.1 days) and fewer deaths (2 vs 8, P<0.019) — in 50 patients analysed of 60 entered, with the record's own design wording inconsistent
cards.type: Prospective randomised study in severe acute pancreatitis as described in the abstract text, indexed in the record as a case-control study (n=50 analysed of 60 entered)
cards.people: Patients with severe acute pancreatitis (three or more Ranson prognostic signs and CT findings of severe pancreatitis) in three hospitals in Israel; 60 patients entered between 1992 and 1996 and 50 were analysed (25 octreotide, 25 conservative treatment only) after 10 were excluded for failing entry criteria, incomplete data or incorrect diagnosis.
cards.result: The complication rate was lower in the treatment group for sepsis (24% vs 76%, P=0.0002) and ARDS (28% vs 56%, P=0.04). Hospital stay was shorter on octreotide (20.6 vs 33.1 days, P=0.04). Two patients died in the treatment group and eight in the control group (P<0.019). The authors suggest octreotide may have a beneficial effect in severe acute pancreatitis.
cards.watchOut: Design flag, printed as the commissioning row requires: the abstract calls this a prospective randomised study in its text while the record indexes it as a case-control study, and 10 of 60 entered patients were excluded before analysis — so the very large differences (sepsis 24% vs 76%) come from a small, inconsistently described, post-exclusion analysis, and are contradicted by the 302-patient double-blind trial above.
cards.source: Paran H et al. Octreotide treatment in patients with severe acute pancreatitis. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2000. PMID: 11215748. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: High-dose octreotide study (Karakoyunlar 1999): sequentially allocated (quasi-randomised) — no significant difference in biochemical or physiological prognostic criteria at 48 hours, though amylase fell more, pancreatic oedema was less frequent and oral intake resumed sooner (n=43)
cards.summary: High-dose octreotide study (Karakoyunlar 1999): sequentially allocated (quasi-randomised) — no significant difference in biochemical or physiological prognostic criteria at 48 hours, though amylase fell more, pancreatic oedema was less frequent and oral intake resumed sooner (n=43)
cards.type: Prospective controlled study with sequential allocation (quasi-randomised), high-dose IV octreotide infusion, 48-hour endpoints (n=43)
cards.people: 43 patients with acute pancreatitis (acute abdominal pain and serum amylase >1000 IU/L) between 1995 and 1997, sequentially allocated to high-dose octreotide 0.5 µg/kg/hour by continuous intravenous infusion (n=22) or control (n=21), with other treatment similar in both groups.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the groups on admission in Ranson criteria (P=0.13), and no significant difference at admission or at 48 hours in fasting blood glucose, albumin, calcium, haemoglobin, haematocrit, white cell count, LDH, AST, urea, blood pressure, heart rate or fever — but serum amylase changes were significantly different (P=0.000). Pancreatic oedema at 48 hours was more frequent in the control group (52.4% vs 13.6%, P=0.022); pleural effusion was more frequent on octreotide (22.7% vs 9.5%, not significant). One death occurred in each group. Patients on octreotide tolerated oral intake sooner (3.76 vs 4.9 days, P=0.041).
cards.watchOut: Sequential allocation is not randomisation — allocation was predictable — and the endpoints are 48-hour biochemical and radiological criteria, with one death in each group. This report cannot carry a mortality or complications claim.
cards.source: Karakoyunlar O et al. High dose octreotide in the management of acute pancreatitis. Hepato-gastroenterology. 1999. PMID: 10430379. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Agent-specific meta-analysis (Xu 2013): 11 randomised trials, 720 participants — mortality relative risk 0.88 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.45) and complications relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.26), neither significant; only two of the 11 trials were of high quality

cards.type: Agent-specific meta-analysis of randomised trials of octreotide in moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis (11 trials, 720 participants)
cards.people: 11 randomised clinical trials with 720 participants in primary moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis, identified from CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, the Science Citation Index Expanded and the Chinese Biomedicine Database (searched September 2011); major outcomes were mortality, complication incidence, surgical intervention rate and length of hospital stay.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk of mortality was 0.88 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.45) and of complication incidence 1.08 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.26), neither statistically significant; the other two outcomes could not be combined for lack of data. Only two of the 11 included trials had high study quality and were combined in the meta-analysis. The authors concluded that present evidence does not support octreotide's benefit in the major outcomes of moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis and that further large, high-quality randomised trials are required. Both relative risks are relative measures: the mortality estimate is compatible with anything from a 47% relative reduction to a 45% relative increase, and no pooled absolute rates are given in the record.
cards.watchOut: Only two of the 11 pooled trials were rated high quality, so the pool is mostly small low-quality trials — its null result agrees with the one large double-blind trial, which is why the shelf rests on those two together.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the large double-blind multicentre trial (n=302) found no benefit on mortality, complications, pain, surgery or hospital stay, and the agent-specific meta-analysis (11 trials, 720 participants) found mortality relative risk 0.88 and complications relative risk 1.08, both non-significant — the two small positive reports are a 50-patient study with inconsistent design wording and post-entry exclusions, and a 43-patient sequentially allocated study with 48-hour surrogate endpoints

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: This shelf cards the primary trials and the 2013 agent-specific meta-analysis only. The 2017 Cochrane pharmacological-interventions review for acute pancreatitis (PMID 28431202) is deliberately NOT carded here: it is homed as a limb of the lexipafant build at pack #7293, and under the one-home rule it is cross-pointed, not re-carded. shelves.title: Mesalamine in Crohn's disease: no induction benefit (CDAI -18 points, not remission) but fewer symptomatic recurrences after surgery (31% vs 41%) — two limbs, never pooled
shelves.question: In adults with mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease, does oral mesalamine versus placebo induce remission or response — and, in the separate postoperative limb, after surgical resection does it prevent recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Aminosalicylic Acids · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Budesonide · Crohn Disease · Delayed-Action Preparations · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy · Mesalamine · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sulfasalazine
shelves.balance: SPLIT — two limbs, labelled, never pooled. INDUCTION limb: mesalamine does not induce remission in mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease — the Cochrane review (20 studies, 2,367 patients) found high-dose controlled-release mesalamine 4 g/day not superior to placebo (CDAI mean difference -19.8 points, 95% CI -46.2 to 6.7) and low-dose mesalamine not superior either, while the meta-analysis of the three Pentasa 4 g/day trials (304 vs 311 patients) found a net CDAI difference of -18 points (P=0.04) whose clinical significance its own authors call unclear. POSTOPERATIVE limb: mesalamine 3 g/day after resection reduced symptomatic recurrence versus placebo in one trial (31% vs 41%; relative risk 0.628, 90% CI 0.40 to 0.97; n=163), and in a two-year three-arm trial (n=131) clinical recurrence was 58% on mesalamine versus 77% on placebo and 50% on 6-mercaptopurine — mesalamine the middle arm — while endoscopic recurrence was 63% on mesalamine versus 64% on placebo. Pre-biologic-era evidence throughout.

cards.headline: INDUCTION LIMB — Cochrane review (Lim 2016): 20 studies, 2,367 patients — high-dose controlled-release mesalamine 4 g/day was NOT superior to placebo for remission, producing a clinically non-significant CDAI reduction (mean difference -19.8 points, 95% CI -46.2 to 6.7; 3 studies, 615 patients), and low-dose mesalamine was not superior either
cards.summary: INDUCTION LIMB — Cochrane review (Lim 2016): 20 studies, 2,367 patients — high-dose controlled-release mesalamine 4 g/day was NOT superior to placebo for remission, producing a clinically non-significant CDAI reduction (mean difference -19.8 points, 95% CI -46.2 to 6.7; 3 studies, 615 patients), and low-dose mesalamine was not superior either
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review — INDUCTION limb: aminosalicylates for induction of remission/response in mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease (20 studies, 2,367 patients)
cards.people: 20 randomised studies with 2,367 patients with mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease, evaluating sulfasalazine or mesalamine against placebo, corticosteroids or other aminosalicylates for induction of remission or response (searches to June 2015). This card is the INDUCTION limb only; the postoperative limb is carded separately below and the two are never pooled.
cards.result: Low-dose mesalamine (1 to 2 g/day) was not superior to placebo for induction of remission: 23% (43/185) entered remission at week 6 versus 15% (18/117) on placebo (risk ratio 1.46, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.40; n=302; GRADE low). High-dose controlled-release mesalamine (4 g/day) was not superior to placebo, inducing a clinically non-significant reduction in CDAI (mean difference -19.8 points, 95% CI -46.2 to 6.7; 3 studies, 615 patients), and was inferior to budesonide (risk ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.78; 1 study, 182 patients; GRADE low). High-dose delayed-release mesalamine (3 to 4.5 g/day) was not superior to placebo for remission (risk ratio 2.02, 95% CI 0.75 to 5.45; 1 study, 38 patients; GRADE very low). Sulfasalazine — a different aminosalicylate, carded here only as part of this review's framing — showed a non-significant trend over placebo confined mainly to Crohn's colitis and was inferior to corticosteroids. Commonly reported adverse events were headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Eight studies were at high risk of bias for incomplete outcome data and potential selective reporting, and two for lack of blinding. All risk ratios are relative measures, printed with the absolute remission rates beside them where the review gives them.
cards.watchOut: This review also covers sulfasalazine and olsalazine, which are not this shelf's drug — only its mesalamine limbs are used here, and its induction question must not be merged with the postoperative prophylaxis trials below.

cards.headline: INDUCTION LIMB — Pentasa meta-analysis (Hanauer 2004): across the three double-blind placebo-controlled trials of slow-release mesalamine (Pentasa) 4 g/day, the net CDAI difference versus placebo was -18 points (P=0.04) — statistically significant, of unclear clinical significance
cards.summary: INDUCTION LIMB — Pentasa meta-analysis (Hanauer 2004): across the three double-blind placebo-controlled trials of slow-release mesalamine (Pentasa) 4 g/day, the net CDAI difference versus placebo was -18 points (P=0.04) — statistically significant, of unclear clinical significance
cards.type: Meta-analysis of three double-blind placebo-controlled trials — INDUCTION limb: slow-release mesalamine (Pentasa) 4 g/day in active Crohn's disease (615 patients)
cards.people: Three double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised multicentre trials in adult patients with mild-to-moderate active Crohn's disease treated with Pentasa 4 g/day for 16 weeks: 304 patients in the Pentasa groups and 311 in the placebo groups. The primary efficacy variable was the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI). This card is the INDUCTION limb only.
cards.result: For intention-to-treat patients on Pentasa, the overall mean reduction in CDAI from baseline to the final visit was -63 points; the corresponding change on placebo was -45 points, a net difference of -18 points, statistically significant (P=0.04). Restricted to protocol-correct patients the effect was more pronounced (overall mean reduction -83 CDAI points; P=0.02 versus placebo). Trial-specific CDAI reductions on placebo differed significantly between the trials. The authors state that Pentasa 4 g/day is superior to placebo in reducing the CDAI but that the clinical significance of the magnitude of this difference is not clear. Product naming under the clarification exception: the induction trials tested one named slow-release product, Pentasa, at 4 g/day, named here as the publications name it.
cards.watchOut: A CDAI difference of -18 points is the whole induction effect, and the review above reads the same trials as not superior for remission — the two cards agree that whatever induction effect exists is small; the disagreement is over a continuous activity score versus a remission endpoint.
cards.source: Hanauer SB et al. Oral Pentasa in the treatment of active Crohn's disease: A meta-analysis of double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. cards.headline: POSTOPERATIVE LIMB — prophylaxis RCT (McLeod 1995): mesalamine 3 g/day after surgical resection reduced symptomatic recurrence versus placebo (31% vs 41%; relative risk 0.628, 90% CI 0.40 to 0.97) over up to 72 months (n=163)
cards.summary: POSTOPERATIVE LIMB — prophylaxis RCT (McLeod 1995): mesalamine 3 g/day after surgical resection reduced symptomatic recurrence versus placebo (31% vs 41%; relative risk 0.628, 90% CI 0.40 to 0.97) over up to 72 months (n=163)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — POSTOPERATIVE limb: mesalamine 3 g/day vs placebo after surgical resection (n=163)
cards.people: 163 patients who had undergone surgical resection for Crohn's disease with no evidence of residual disease, randomised within 8 weeks of surgery to mesalamine 1.5 g twice daily (n=87) or placebo (n=76), followed for a maximum of 72 months. This card is the POSTOPERATIVE limb only — a different question from induction in active disease.
cards.result: The symptomatic recurrence rate (symptoms plus endoscopic and/or radiological confirmation) was 31% (27/87) on mesalamine versus 41% (31/76) on placebo (P=0.031) — an absolute difference of 10 percentage points. The relative risk of developing recurrent disease was 0.628 (90% CI 0.40 to 0.97) on intention-to-treat analysis (P=0.039, one-tail test) and 0.532 (90% CI 0.32 to 0.87) on efficacy analysis — relative measures, printed with the absolute rates beside them. Endoscopic and radiological recurrence was also significantly decreased (relative risks 0.654 and 0.635). There was one serious side effect (pancreatitis) in the treatment group.
cards.watchOut: The headline analysis uses a one-tailed test and 90% confidence intervals, both more permissive than convention, and the absolute symptomatic gain is 10 percentage points over a follow-up of up to six years.
cards.source: McLeod RS et al. Prophylactic mesalamine treatment decreases postoperative recurrence of Crohn's disease. Gastroenterology. 1995. PMID: 7615189. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: POSTOPERATIVE LIMB — two-year three-arm RCT (Hanauer 2004): clinical recurrence by life-table analysis was 58% on mesalamine 3 g/day versus 77% on placebo and 50% on 6-mercaptopurine, but endoscopic recurrence was essentially identical on mesalamine and placebo (63% vs 64%) (n=131)
cards.summary: POSTOPERATIVE LIMB — two-year three-arm RCT (Hanauer 2004): clinical recurrence by life-table analysis was 58% on mesalamine 3 g/day versus 77% on placebo and 50% on 6-mercaptopurine, but endoscopic recurrence was essentially identical on mesalamine and placebo (63% vs 64%) (n=131)
cards.type: Two-year double-blind double-dummy three-arm trial — POSTOPERATIVE limb: 6-mercaptopurine vs mesalamine vs placebo after ileocolic resection (n=131)
cards.people: 131 patients randomised at five centres after resection and ileocolic anastomosis to 6-mercaptopurine 50 mg, mesalamine 3 g or placebo daily in a double-blind, double-dummy trial, with clinical assessments every 3 months, colonoscopy at 6, 12 and 24 months and small bowel series at 12 and 24 months. This card is the POSTOPERATIVE limb only.
cards.result: Clinical recurrence rates (intention-to-treat) by life-table analysis at 24 months were 50% (95% CI 34% to 68%) on 6-mercaptopurine, 58% (95% CI 41% to 75%) on mesalamine and 77% (95% CI 61% to 91%) on placebo. Endoscopic recurrence rates were 43% (95% CI 28% to 63%), 63% (95% CI 47% to 79%) and 64% (95% CI 46% to 81%), and radiographic recurrence rates 33%, 46% and 49% respectively. Only 6-mercaptopurine was more effective than placebo (P<0.05) at preventing clinical and endoscopic recurrence; mesalamine was the middle arm throughout. Withdrawals left 69% of the study population evaluable for the clinical recurrence endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Mesalamine's clinical-recurrence advantage here is a life-table estimate with wide, overlapping confidence intervals and 31% of patients not evaluable for that endpoint, while its endoscopic recurrence rate (63%) is the same as placebo's (64%) — the two postoperative trials do not tell one clean story.
cards.source: Hanauer SB et al. Postoperative maintenance of Crohn's disease remission with 6-mercaptopurine, mesalamine, or placebo: a 2-year trial. Gastroenterology. 2004. PMID: 15362027. shelves.title: Rifaximin in Crohn's disease: 800 mg twice daily induced remission (62% vs 43%) in the large trial — but the maintenance report's 100% remission rate is implausibly complete and is flagged
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderately active Crohn's disease, does rifaximin versus placebo induce remission — and, in the separate maintenance limb, after steroid-induced remission does it maintain remission?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · C-Reactive Protein · Chi-Square Distribution · Crohn Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Rifamycins · Rifaximin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for induction at 800 mg twice daily, on two multicentre placebo-controlled trials: remission 52% versus 33% on placebo in 83 patients (not statistically significant overall; significant in the elevated-CRP subgroup, with treatment failures 4% vs 33%, P=0.010), and 62% (61/98) versus 43% (43/101) (P=0.005) in 402 patients with the extended-intestinal-release formulation, maintained through follow-up (45% vs 29%). There is no dose-response — the 400 mg and 1,200 mg doses and once-daily dosing all failed against placebo. The MAINTENANCE limb is flagged on the face and does not carry this shelf: the single 2014 report (n=168) reports 100% (83/83) remission at 12 weeks on rifaximin and 78% versus 41% maintained at 24 weeks, an implausibly complete result for this disease from a small single-programme report.

cards.headline: Induction RCT (Prantera 2006): rifaximin 800 mg twice daily gave remission in 52% versus 33% on placebo at 12 weeks, a difference that was NOT statistically significant overall — the significant separation was in the elevated-CRP subgroup, and treatment failures were significantly fewer (4% vs 33%, P=0.010) (n=83)

cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled induction trial, rifaximin 800 mg once or twice daily, 12 weeks (n=83)
cards.people: 83 patients with mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease randomised to three treatments for 12 weeks: rifaximin 800 mg once daily plus placebo, rifaximin 800 mg twice daily, or placebo twice daily.
cards.result: Clinical remission was achieved by 52% of the twice-daily group, 32% of the once-daily group and 33% of the placebo group; clinical response was seen in 67%, 48% and 41% respectively, without reaching a statistically significant difference. Treatment failures were 4% (twice daily), 12% (once daily) and 33% (placebo) (P=0.010). Remission and response rates on rifaximin 800 mg twice daily were significantly higher than those on placebo and on rifaximin 800 mg once daily in patients with elevated C-reactive protein values (P<0.05). The authors state that rifaximin 800 mg twice daily was superior to placebo in inducing remission although this difference was not statistically significant, while the number of failures on placebo was significantly higher.
cards.watchOut: The headline remission difference (52% vs 33%) is not statistically significant in a trial of 83 patients split three ways — the significant findings are a subgroup (elevated CRP) and the treatment-failure count, so this trial supports rather than establishes the induction claim.
cards.source: Prantera C et al. Antibiotic treatment of Crohn's disease: results of a multicentre, double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial with rifaximin. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2006. PMID: 16611272. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Induction phase 2 RCT (Prantera 2012): rifaximin extended-intestinal-release 800 mg twice daily induced remission in 62% (61/98) versus 43% (43/101) on placebo at 12 weeks (P=0.005), maintained through 12 weeks of follow-up (45% vs 29%, P=0.02) — but the 400 mg and 1,200 mg doses did NOT differ from placebo (n=402)
cards.summary: Induction phase 2 RCT (Prantera 2012): rifaximin extended-intestinal-release 800 mg twice daily induced remission in 62% (61/98) versus 43% (43/101) on placebo at 12 weeks (P=0.005), maintained through 12 weeks of follow-up (45% vs 29%, P=0.02) — but the 400 mg and 1,200 mg doses did NOT differ from placebo (n=402)
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled induction trial, rifaximin extended-intestinal-release 400/800/1,200 mg twice daily (n=402)
cards.people: 402 patients with moderately active Crohn's disease in a multicentre randomised double-blind trial of rifaximin extended-intestinal-release (a gastroresistant formulation) 400, 800 or 1,200 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, compared with placebo, with a further 12-week follow-up. The primary endpoint was remission (Crohn's Disease Activity Index <150) at the end of treatment.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, 62% of patients on rifaximin-EIR 800 mg twice daily (61/98) were in remission versus 43% on placebo (43/101) (P=0.005) — an absolute difference of 19 percentage points. The difference was maintained through the 12-week follow-up (45% [40/89] vs 29% [28/98]; P=0.02). Remission was achieved by 54% (56/104) on 400 mg and 47% (47/99) on 1,200 mg, neither differing from placebo. Withdrawal because of adverse events was low on the 400 mg and 800 mg doses and significantly higher on 1,200 mg (16% [16/99]). Product naming under the clarification exception: this trial tested a named gastroresistant formulation, rifaximin extended-intestinal-release, named as the publication names it.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is confined to the middle dose with no dose-response — 400 mg and 1,200 mg both failed against placebo — which weakens a straightforward causal reading, and the tested product is a specific gastroresistant formulation, not rifaximin generally.
cards.source: Prantera C et al. Rifaximin-extended intestinal release induces remission in patients with moderately active Crohn's disease. Gastroenterology. 2012. PMID: 22155172. cards.headline: MAINTENANCE report (Jigaranu 2014) — FLAGGED ON THE FACE: remission maintained at 24 weeks in 78% (65/83) on rifaximin versus 41% (34/83) on placebo, after a reported 100% (83/83) remission rate at 12 weeks on rifaximin — an implausibly complete result from a small single-programme report, which does not carry this shelf (n=168)
cards.summary: MAINTENANCE report (Jigaranu 2014) — FLAGGED ON THE FACE: remission maintained at 24 weeks in 78% (65/83) on rifaximin versus 41% (34/83) on placebo, after a reported 100% (83/83) remission rate at 12 weeks on rifaximin — an implausibly complete result from a small single-programme report, which does not carry this shelf (n=168)
cards.type: Maintenance report: blinded randomised trial of rifaximin 800 mg twice daily vs placebo after steroid-induced remission (n=168) — flagged, not load-bearing
cards.people: 168 patients with a previous history of moderately active Crohn's disease who had previously achieved remission with standard therapy (prednisone/budesonide), in a blinded randomised trial conducted December 2011 to December 2012: rifaximin 800 mg twice daily for 12 weeks (83 patients) versus placebo (83 patients), with follow-up to 48 weeks. The primary endpoint was maintaining remission during follow-up.
cards.result: As reported: all patients (100%; 83/83) on rifaximin 800 mg were in remission after 12 weeks of treatment, compared with 84% (70/83) on placebo. The difference persisted at the 24-week follow-up (78% [65/83] vs 41% [34/83]). At 48 weeks, disease activity was present in 45% (38/83) of the rifaximin group versus 75% (63/83) of the placebo group. The authors conclude that remission previously obtained with standard treatment can be sustained after administration of rifaximin 800 mg.
cards.watchOut: Credibility flag, as the commissioning row requires: a 100% remission rate at 12 weeks (83 of 83 patients) is implausibly complete for Crohn's disease, the placebo arm's remission rate falls from 84% at 12 weeks to 41% at 24 weeks, and this is a small single-programme report with no registry ID in the record. Its numbers are printed exactly as published, but the maintenance claim rests on this report alone and must not carry the shelf.

Rifaximin's hepatic encephalopathy, IBS-D and travellers' diarrhoea shelves are different questions. Dose matters throughout this shelf: once-daily dosing and both the lower and higher twice-daily extended-release doses failed against placebo, so no class-wide or any-dose claim is made.

shelves.title: Tacrolimus for steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis: response 50% vs 13% and mucosal healing 44% vs 13% at 2 weeks — small Japanese trials, low-certainty Cochrane support, remission unproven
shelves.question: In patients with corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis, does oral tacrolimus versus placebo induce clinical response, mucosal healing and remission?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Beclomethasone · Colitis, Ulcerative · Cyclosporine · Humans · Proctitis · Remission Induction · Suppositories · Tacrolimus
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for short-term clinical response and mucosal healing, at low certainty. The Cochrane review (5 RCTs, 347 participants) found tacrolimus may be superior to placebo for clinical remission (14/87 vs 1/61; risk ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.73 — a relative measure; absolute rates 16% vs 2%) and clinical improvement (45/87 vs 7/61; risk ratio 4.47, 95% CI 2.15 to 9.29), both rated LOW certainty, and its authors state no clinical practice conclusions can be made. The two primaries are small, Japanese and short: a trough-target dose-finding trial (n=63) with DAI improvement in 68.4% at a 10-15 ng/mL trough versus 10.0% on placebo at 2 weeks, and a hospitalised steroid-refractory trial (n=62) with response 50.0% versus 13.3% and mucosal healing 43.8% versus 13.3% at 2 weeks, but remission 9.4% versus 0.0% and not significant. Tacrolimus nephrotoxicity, tremor and glucose effects, and the need for trough monitoring, belong on the face.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Gordon 2022): five RCTs, 347 participants — tacrolimus may be superior to placebo for clinical remission (14/87 vs 1/61; risk ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.73) and clinical improvement (45/87 vs 7/61; risk ratio 4.47, 95% CI 2.15 to 9.29), both LOW certainty
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Gordon 2022): five RCTs, 347 participants — tacrolimus may be superior to placebo for clinical remission (14/87 vs 1/61; risk ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.73) and clinical improvement (45/87 vs 7/61; risk ratio 4.47, 95% CI 2.15 to 9.29), both LOW certainty
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (2022; the 2008 version, PMID 18646177, is not carded — one version only), tacrolimus for induction in corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis (5 RCTs, 347 participants)
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials with 347 participants with active ulcerative colitis or ulcerative proctitis, with intervention durations of two to eight weeks. The placebo comparison covers oral and rectal tacrolimus (3 studies); separate single studies compared oral tacrolimus with intravenous ciclosporin (113 participants) and tacrolimus suppositories with beclometasone suppositories (88 participants).
cards.result: Tacrolimus (oral and rectal) may be superior to placebo for clinical remission (14/87 on tacrolimus vs 1/61 on placebo; risk ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.73; 3 studies) and for clinical improvement (45/87 vs 7/61; risk ratio 4.47, 95% CI 2.15 to 9.29; 3 studies) — relative measures, printed with the absolute rates beside them: remission 16% versus 2%, improvement 52% versus 11%. Both results are of low certainty due to imprecision and risk of bias. The evidence is very uncertain for serious adverse events versus placebo (2/87 vs 0/61; risk ratio 2.44, 95% CI 0.12 to 48.77). Versus ciclosporin the evidence is very uncertain (remission risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 0.92 to 2.50), and versus beclometasone suppositories there may be little to no difference (remission risk ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.88). The reviewers conclude that no clinical practice conclusions can be made, that the cohorts were small with short follow-up, and that further adequately powered research is needed.
cards.watchOut: Low and very-low certainty throughout, on 347 participants in total across five trials mixing oral and rectal routes and three different comparators — the pooled placebo risk ratios rest on 15 remission events in total (14 vs 1).

cards.headline: Trough-target dose-finding RCT (Ogata 2006): DAI improvement in 68.4% on high-trough tacrolimus (10-15 ng/mL) versus 10.0% on placebo (P<0.001) at 2 weeks, with mucosal healing in 78.9% and clinical remission in 20.0% (n=63 randomised)
cards.summary: Trough-target dose-finding RCT (Ogata 2006): DAI improvement in 68.4% on high-trough tacrolimus (10-15 ng/mL) versus 10.0% on placebo (P<0.001) at 2 weeks, with mucosal healing in 78.9% and clinical remission in 20.0% (n=63 randomised)
cards.type: Randomised dose-finding (trough-target) double-blind placebo-controlled trial, oral tacrolimus in refractory ulcerative colitis (n=63)
cards.people: 63 patients with refractory active ulcerative colitis randomly assigned to a high trough concentration group (10-15 ng/mL; n=21), a low trough concentration group (5-10 ng/mL; n=22) or placebo (n=20), receiving oral tacrolimus starting at 0.025 mg/kg twice daily or placebo; efficacy was evaluated in 60 patients on the disease activity index (DAI), and 58 patients went into a 10-week open-label extension.
cards.result: An improvement in DAI score (at least 4 points, all categories improved) was observed in 68.4% of the high-trough group compared with 10.0% on placebo (P<0.001). In the high-trough group 20.0% of patients had clinical remission and 78.9% had mucosal healing. In the open-label extension 55.2% of all patients had an improved DAI score at week 10, and mean prednisolone dose fell from 19.7 mg/day at entry to 7.8 mg/day at week 10. The incidence of side effects in the high-trough group was significantly higher than on placebo (P=0.043); the most common event was mild finger tremor. The authors conclude the optimal target range appears to be 10-15 ng/mL for two-week therapy.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding design whose comparative value comes from its placebo arm, with the benefit concentrated in the high-trough arm of about 21 patients over two weeks — and side effects significantly more frequent in that arm. Trough monitoring is intrinsic to the intervention, not an optional extra.
cards.source: Ogata H et al. A randomised dose finding study of oral tacrolimus (FK506) therapy in refractory ulcerative colitis. Gut. 2006. PMID: 16484504. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hospitalised steroid-refractory RCT (Ogata 2012): clinical response at 2 weeks in 50.0% (16/32) on oral tacrolimus versus 13.3% (4/30) on placebo (P=0.003), and mucosal healing in 43.8% versus 13.3% (P=0.012) — but clinical remission did not differ significantly (9.4% vs 0.0%, P=0.238) (n=62)
cards.summary: Hospitalised steroid-refractory RCT (Ogata 2012): clinical response at 2 weeks in 50.0% (16/32) on oral tacrolimus versus 13.3% (4/30) on placebo (P=0.003), and mucosal healing in 43.8% versus 13.3% (P=0.012) — but clinical remission did not differ significantly (9.4% vs 0.0%, P=0.238) (n=62)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial, oral tacrolimus in hospitalised steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis, 2 weeks (n=62)
cards.people: 62 hospitalised patients with steroid-refractory, moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (total disease activity index 6 or more, with a mucosal appearance subscore of 2 or 3), randomised double-blind to oral tacrolimus or placebo for 2 weeks. Mean total DAI at entry was 9.8 ± 1.61 in the tacrolimus group and 9.1 ± 1.05 on placebo.
cards.result: At week 2 the clinical response rate (improvement in all DAI subscores) was 50.0% (16/32) on tacrolimus versus 13.3% (4/30) on placebo (P=0.003) — an absolute difference of 37 percentage points. Mucosal healing (mucosal appearance subscore 0 or 1) was 43.8% (14/32) versus 13.3% (4/30) (P=0.012). Clinical remission (total DAI 2 or less with individual subscores of 0 or 1) was 9.4% (3/32) versus 0.0% (0/30) (P=0.238), not significant. The therapies were well tolerated, with only minor side effects reported in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks is the whole horizon, and the endpoint that separated was response, not remission: only 3 of 32 patients on tacrolimus reached remission. 'Only minor side effects' in 62 patients over 2 weeks cannot characterise tacrolimus's renal and metabolic toxicity.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two small Japanese placebo-controlled trials (n=63 trough-target; n=62 hospitalised) both show substantially more clinical response and mucosal healing on oral tacrolimus at 2 weeks (68.4% vs 10.0% DAI improvement at high trough; 50.0% vs 13.3% response, 43.8% vs 13.3% mucosal healing), and the Cochrane pool reads the same way at low certainty — but remission is far less secure (9.4% vs 0.0%, not significant, in the hospitalised trial) and no trial runs beyond a short induction horizon
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small Japanese placebo-controlled trials (n=63 trough-target; n=62 hospitalised) both show substantially more clinical response and mucosal healing on oral tacrolimus at 2 weeks (68.4% vs 10.0% DAI improvement at high trough; 50.0% vs 13.3% response, 43.8% vs 13.3% mucosal healing), and the Cochrane pool reads the same way at low certainty — but remission is far less secure (9.4% vs 0.0%, not significant, in the hospitalised trial) and no trial runs beyond a short induction horizon

cards.result: Japanese programme predominance: both primaries and most of the pooled evidence come from one country's programme, in steroid-refractory patients. Tacrolimus requires trough monitoring (the dose-finding trial's benefit sat in the 10-15 ng/mL arm, which also had significantly more side effects, chiefly tremor), and its nephrotoxicity, tremor and glucose effects belong on the face of any use of this shelf — the trials carded here are too small and too short to quantify them. Ciclosporin in severe ulcerative colitis is a different drug and a different shelf; it is cross-pointed, not merged.

shelves.title: Cisapride in functional dyspepsia (WITHDRAWN drug): no significant benefit over placebo in three trials — therapeutic gain 0.1% in the largest — and withdrawn for QT/torsades risk
shelves.question: In adults with functional (non-organic) dyspepsia, does cisapride versus placebo improve dyspeptic symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Cisapride · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nizatidine · Piperidines · Predictive Value of Tests · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for any benefit — and the drug was withdrawn. Cisapride was withdrawn/restricted because of QT prolongation and torsades risk, and this shelf is the historical record of its functional-dyspepsia programme, not a treatment option. Of the three placebo-controlled trials carded, two found no significant advantage over placebo on global symptom outcomes (overall response 63% vs 44%, not significant, in general practice; therapeutic gain 0.1% [95% CI −14% to 14%] in the 330-patient primary-care trial), and the third found total symptom scores fell similarly on cisapride and placebo. Cisapride's gastroparesis trials are NOT folded in here — they are limbs of the prokinetic network home at shelf #3601. The Cochrane prokinetics-for-functional-dyspepsia class review is a cross-point only and is not carded.

cards.headline: General-practice RCT (de Groot 1997): cisapride 10 mg three times daily — overall response 63% vs 44% on placebo, NOT statistically significant
cards.summary: General-practice RCT (de Groot 1997): cisapride 10 mg three times daily — overall response 63% vs 44% on placebo, NOT statistically significant
cards.type: Placebo-controlled randomised double-blind trial in general practice, cisapride vs placebo
cards.people: 121 patients with functional dyspepsia entered in general practice (61 cisapride, 60 placebo); 113 were available for the efficacy analysis after referral to exclude ulcers, oesophagitis, pancreatitis and gallstones.
cards.result: After 4 weeks a statistically significant reduction in symptoms was found, but it was similar in the two groups. The difference in overall response (63% on cisapride vs 44% on placebo) did not reach statistical significance, and there was no significant difference between placebo and cisapride overall. Helicobacter pylori-positive patients showed neither specific symptoms nor a different response to cisapride.
cards.watchOut: A non-significant trend on a subjective overall-response measure in 121 entered patients; symptom reduction occurred in both arms, which is the recurring pattern of this programme.
cards.source: de Groot GH et al. Cisapride in functional dyspepsia in general practice. A placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind study. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1997. cards.headline: Placebo-run-in RCT (Kellow 1995): total symptom score fell similarly on cisapride and placebo (8.9→5.8 vs 9.7→5.5) — no major difference shown
cards.summary: Placebo-run-in RCT (Kellow 1995): total symptom score fell similarly on cisapride and placebo (8.9→5.8 vs 9.7→5.5) — no major difference shown
cards.type: Placebo-controlled randomised double-blind trial after placebo run-in, cisapride vs placebo
cards.people: 74 patients entered a 2-week placebo run-in; 61 were eligible for the 4-week double-blind phase of cisapride 10 mg or placebo three times daily, stratified by Helicobacter pylori gastritis and classified retrospectively as reflux-like (n=29) or motility-like (n=32) dyspepsia; gastric emptying was assessed scintigraphically.
cards.result: At the end of treatment there was a similar significant (P<0.001) reduction in total symptom score from baseline in both groups (cisapride 8.9 to 5.8; placebo 9.7 to 5.5). Scores for heartburn and continual bloating fell significantly on cisapride but not placebo, with improvement attributable to patients with normal rather than delayed gastric emptying. Global improvement rates by investigator and patient did not differ significantly between groups. The authors were unable to show major differences in short-term efficacy between cisapride and placebo.
cards.watchOut: Only 61 patients in the double-blind phase, and the positive signals are subgroup findings (normal gastric emptying; reflux-like dyspepsia) inside an overall negative trial — hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
cards.source: Kellow JE et al. Efficacy of cisapride therapy in functional dyspepsia. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 1995. PMID: 7605855. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary-care RCT (Hansen 1998): symptomatic response 62% on cisapride — therapeutic gain over placebo 0.1% (95% CI −14% to 14%); NOT superior to placebo
cards.summary: Primary-care RCT (Hansen 1998): symptomatic response 62% on cisapride — therapeutic gain over placebo 0.1% (95% CI −14% to 14%); NOT superior to placebo
cards.type: Placebo-controlled randomised double-blind three-arm trial in primary care, cisapride vs nizatidine vs placebo
cards.people: 330 patients with minor or no abnormalities at endoscopy, recruited directly from primary care, randomised double-blind to cisapride 10 mg three times daily, nizatidine 300 mg at night, or placebo for 2 weeks.
cards.result: A symptomatic response was found in 62% of patients on cisapride, a therapeutic gain over placebo of 0.1% (95% CI −14% to 14%); nizatidine's gain was −8% (95% CI −22% to 7%). Response was independent of symptom classification (reflux-like, dysmotility-like, ulcer-like or unclassifiable). Neither cisapride nor nizatidine was superior to placebo over 2 weeks in unselected primary-care dyspepsia.
cards.watchOut: The largest and least selected of the three trials, and the most clearly negative: the confidence interval for the therapeutic gain is centred on zero. The treatment course was only 2 weeks.

cards.result: The functional-dyspepsia record for cisapride is negative-to-mixed: the 330-patient primary-care trial found a therapeutic gain of 0.1% over placebo, the general-practice trial's 63% vs 44% overall response did not reach significance, and the run-in trial found symptom scores falling equally on drug and placebo, with positive signals only in subgroups. No carded trial measured cardiac outcomes; the withdrawal/restriction of cisapride for QT prolongation and torsades risk is the reason the drug is unavailable, and it leads this shelf's framing. Cisapride's gastroparesis trials belong to the prokinetic network home at shelf #3601 and are not carded here.

shelves.title: Dexlansoprazole in erosive oesophagitis: healing non-inferior to lansoprazole (92–95% vs 86–92%); maintenance 75–87% vs 26–27% on placebo (3 publications, 4 trials)
shelves.question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does dexlansoprazole MR (dual delayed-release) heal oesophagitis versus lansoprazole, and does it maintain healing and heartburn relief versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: 2-Pyridinylmethylsulfinylbenzimidazoles · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dexlansoprazole · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Esophagitis · Female · Humans · Lansoprazole · Male · Middle Aged · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), on three publications covering four trials. On the STRATOS convention stated on the face of this shelf, the two identical healing trials count as ONE publication: the floor rests on three reports covering four trials. Healing: in two identical randomised trials reported together (4,092 patients), dexlansoprazole MR 60/90 mg healed 92–95% by week 8 by life-table versus 86–92% on lansoprazole 30 mg — non-inferior, with the life-table differences not statistically significant (crude-rate analyses favoured the 90 mg dose). Maintenance: in two separate trials in already-healed patients, 6-month maintenance of healing was 87%/82% (60/90 mg) and 75%/83% (30/60 mg) versus 26% and 27% on placebo by life-table — a large, consistent placebo-controlled benefit. Healing comparisons are against an active comparator (lansoprazole), maintenance comparisons against placebo; the non-erosive reflux disease reports are a separate slice and are not folded in.

cards.headline: Two identical healing RCTs in ONE publication (Sharma 2009; STRATOS convention — counts as one report): week-8 healing 92–95% on dexlansoprazole MR vs 86–92% on lansoprazole by life-table — non-inferior, differences not significant
cards.summary: Two identical healing RCTs in ONE publication (Sharma 2009; STRATOS convention — counts as one report): week-8 healing 92–95% on dexlansoprazole MR vs 86–92% on lansoprazole by life-table — non-inferior, differences not significant
cards.type: Two identical double-blind randomised trials reported in one publication (counts as one report — STRATOS convention), dexlansoprazole MR vs lansoprazole
cards.people: 4,092 patients with erosive oesophagitis across two identical double-blind randomised trials, receiving dexlansoprazole MR 60 mg or 90 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg once daily; week-8 healing was tested first for non-inferiority, then superiority, against lansoprazole.
cards.result: Dexlansoprazole MR achieved non-inferiority to lansoprazole. By life-table analysis it healed 92–95% of patients in the individual studies versus 86–92% for lansoprazole, and those differences were not statistically significant (P>0.025). By crude-rate analysis, dexlansoprazole MR 90 mg was superior to lansoprazole in both studies and 60 mg was superior in one study. Week-4 healing exceeded 64% with all treatments in both studies. In an integrated analysis of moderate-to-severe (Los Angeles grades C and D) disease, dexlansoprazole MR 90 mg was superior to lansoprazole at 8 weeks. All treatments relieved symptoms and were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Two trials, one publication — do not count this card as two reports. The comparator is lansoprazole 30 mg (active treatment, not placebo), and the headline life-table healing differences were not statistically significant; superiority claims rest on crude-rate and moderate-to-severe subgroup analyses.
cards.source: Sharma P et al. Clinical trials: healing of erosive oesophagitis with dexlansoprazole MR, a proton pump inhibitor with a novel dual delayed-release formulation--results from two randomized controlled studies. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19183157. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Maintenance RCT, 60/90 mg (Howden 2009): 6-month maintenance of healing 87% and 82% vs 26% on placebo by life-table
cards.summary: Maintenance RCT, 60/90 mg (Howden 2009): 6-month maintenance of healing 87% and 82% vs 26% on placebo by life-table
cards.type: Double-blind randomised maintenance trial, dexlansoprazole MR 60/90 mg vs placebo in healed erosive oesophagitis
cards.people: 451 patients whose erosive oesophagitis had healed in one of the two dexlansoprazole MR healing trials, randomised double-blind to dexlansoprazole MR 60 mg, 90 mg or placebo once daily for 6 months.
cards.result: Both doses were superior to placebo for maintaining healing (P<0.0025). Maintenance rates by life-table were 87% (60 mg) and 82% (90 mg) versus 26% on placebo; by crude rate, 66% and 65% versus 14%. Both doses were also superior for heartburn-free days (96% and 94% vs 19% of 24-hour days) and nights (98%, 97% and 50%). Diarrhoea, flatulence, gastritis symptoms and abdominal pain occurred more frequently on dexlansoprazole MR than placebo but were not dose-related.
cards.watchOut: A maintenance trial in patients already healed on dexlansoprazole — the placebo arm's 26% maintenance rate describes relapse after healing, not untreated disease; life-table rates are higher than the crude rates (66%/65% vs 14%), and both are printed.
cards.source: Howden CW et al. Clinical trial: efficacy and safety of dexlansoprazole MR 60 and 90 mg in healed erosive oesophagitis - maintenance of healing and symptom relief. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19681809. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Maintenance RCT, 30/60 mg (Metz 2009): 6-month maintenance of healing 75% and 83% vs 27% on placebo by life-table
cards.summary: Maintenance RCT, 30/60 mg (Metz 2009): 6-month maintenance of healing 75% and 83% vs 27% on placebo by life-table
cards.type: Double-blind randomised maintenance trial, dexlansoprazole MR 30/60 mg vs placebo in healed erosive oesophagitis
cards.people: 445 patients with healed erosive oesophagitis, randomised double-blind to dexlansoprazole MR 30 mg, 60 mg or placebo once daily for 6 months; the primary endpoint was maintenance of endoscopic healing.
cards.result: Both doses were superior to placebo (P<0.0025). By life-table analysis, maintenance rates were 75% (30 mg), 83% (60 mg) and 27% (placebo); crude maintenance rates were 66% for both dexlansoprazole doses and 14% for placebo. Dexlansoprazole controlled heartburn (medians of 91–96% heartburn-free 24-hour days and 96–99% heartburn-free nights). The only adverse event significantly more common on dexlansoprazole per patient-month of exposure was upper respiratory tract infection.
cards.watchOut: Same design caveat as the companion maintenance trial: an already-healed population randomised to continue drug or switch to placebo, so the contrast measures relapse prevention, not initial healing.

cards.headline: Synthesis: healing non-inferior to lansoprazole (92–95% vs 86–92% at week 8, life-table, not significant) and maintenance clearly superior to placebo in two trials — three publications covering four trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: healing non-inferior to lansoprazole (92–95% vs 86–92% at week 8, life-table, not significant) and maintenance clearly superior to placebo in two trials — three publications covering four trials
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Counted on the STRATOS convention, this shelf rests on three publications covering four trials: one publication reporting two identical healing trials (4,092 patients; non-inferior to lansoprazole 30 mg, life-table differences not significant) and two maintenance trials (451 and 445 already-healed patients) in which 6-month maintenance of healing was 87%/82% and 75%/83% on dexlansoprazole MR versus 26% and 27% on placebo by life-table. The benefit claim is strongest for maintenance of healing; for initial healing the honest claim is non-inferiority to an active PPI comparator with possible advantages in moderate-to-severe disease. Non-erosive reflux disease reports are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Colchicine in primary biliary cholangitis: biochemistry improved, survival and histology did not — Cochrane pool of 11 trials (716 patients) found no mortality benefit, and UDCA beat it head-to-head
shelves.question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does colchicine versus placebo (or added to ursodeoxycholic acid) improve liver biochemistry, histology and survival?
shelves.mesh: Cholagogues and Choleretics · Colchicine · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary · Liver Transplantation · Methotrexate · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Ursodeoxycholic Acid
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the classic older-programme pattern. Colchicine consistently improved liver biochemistry (albumin, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol and aminotransferases in the 1986 NEJM trial; alkaline phosphatase fell from 281 to 112 IU/L over 4 years in the 1988 trial), but no trial showed a symptom or histology benefit, the 1995 head-to-head trial found colchicine only modest while ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) improved liver tests significantly, and the Cochrane pool of 11 trials (716 patients) found no significant difference in deaths (relative risk 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06) or death/transplantation — with a worst-best-case sensitivity analysis suggesting possible detriment. These trials predate modern UDCA-standard care (the 1995 trial is the transition point). This is one of three separate pre-UDCA-era PBC drug questions — see also methotrexate (shelf #7426) and D-penicillamine (shelf #7427); they are not merged into a class verdict. Colchicine's gastrointestinal and neuromuscular toxicity in liver disease belongs on the face alongside the diarrhoea reported in the trials.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Gong 2004): 11 trials, 716 patients — no significant difference in deaths (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06) or death/transplantation; evidence neither supports nor refutes colchicine
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Gong 2004): 11 trials, 716 patients — no significant difference in deaths (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06) or death/transplantation; evidence neither supports nor refutes colchicine
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, colchicine vs placebo/no intervention or other control
cards.people: 11 randomised clinical trials involving 716 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis, comparing colchicine with placebo/no intervention or other control therapy; primary outcomes were deaths, and deaths and/or liver transplantation.
cards.result: No significant differences were detected between colchicine and control on deaths (relative risk 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06 — a relative measure), deaths and/or transplantation (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.49), liver complications, liver biochemical variables, liver histological measurements, or adverse events. A best-worst-case analysis showed no significant mortality effect (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.15), while a worst-best-case analysis showed a significant detrimental effect (RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.17 to 4.44). Colchicine did reduce the number of patients without improvement of pruritus (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.87), based on only 156 patients from three trials. Trial methodology was generally low with some high drop-out rates. The reviewers found no evidence either to support or refute colchicine and suggested it be used only in randomised trials. Only this Cochrane version is carded; the journal version of the same review is not carded separately.
cards.watchOut: The pooled biochemical outcomes were not significant in this review even though individual trials reported improvements — the split between single-trial biochemistry and the pooled hard-outcome record is the shelf's central fact. Sensitivity analyses swing the mortality estimate in both directions because of drop-outs.
cards.source: Gong Y et al. Colchicine for primary biliary cirrhosis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2004. PMID: 15106254. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: NEJM RCT (Kaplan 1986): biochemical improvement over 2 years but NO symptom or histology benefit; cumulative liver-disease mortality at 4 years 21% vs 47% (P=0.05)
cards.summary: NEJM RCT (Kaplan 1986): biochemical improvement over 2 years but NO symptom or histology benefit; cumulative liver-disease mortality at 4 years 21% vs 47% (P=0.05)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (NEJM 1986), colchicine vs placebo
cards.people: 60 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (30 early-stage, 30 advanced) in a double-blind randomised trial of colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily versus placebo; patients remaining in the blind phase at 2 years had repeat liver biopsy and then open-label colchicine.
cards.result: Over 2 years the colchicine group, compared with placebo, improved in serum albumin, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol and aminotransferases. There was no such improvement in the severity of symptoms or physical findings, and no significant difference in histologic changes at liver biopsy. At 4 years after entry, cumulative mortality from liver disease was 21% on colchicine versus 47% on placebo (P=0.05). The only side effect noted was diarrhoea, in three patients. The authors concluded colchicine may provide some long-term benefit, while its failure to reduce hepatic inflammation and fibrosis left the long-term effect uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The 4-year mortality comparison (21% vs 47%) comes after the blind phase ended at 2 years and patients crossed to open-label colchicine, in only 60 patients — it is not confirmed by the Cochrane pool and must not be read as a proven survival benefit.
cards.source: Kaplan MM et al. A prospective trial of colchicine for primary biliary cirrhosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1986. PMID: 3537784. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Four-year double-blind RCT (Bodenheimer 1988): alkaline phosphatase fell 281→112 IU/L on colchicine (P<0.01 vs control) and bilirubin stabilised — but NO difference in histologic progression
cards.summary: Four-year double-blind RCT (Bodenheimer 1988): alkaline phosphatase fell 281→112 IU/L on colchicine (P<0.01 vs control) and bilirubin stabilised — but NO difference in histologic progression
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial over 4 years, colchicine vs placebo
cards.people: 57 patients with biopsy-proven primary biliary cirrhosis randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or identical placebo, with clinical and laboratory evaluation every 3 months and liver biopsy annually for 4 years.
cards.result: Differences in mean alkaline phosphatase and alanine aminotransferase between colchicine and placebo were statistically significant at 4 years: mean alkaline phosphatase fell from 281 to 112 IU/L on colchicine (P<0.01 versus controls) and mean alanine aminotransferase from 129 to 86 IU/L (P<0.05). Bilirubin and immunoglobulin M were lower on colchicine without reaching significance; bilirubin remained stable on colchicine, even when initially elevated, whereas it nearly doubled on placebo. No difference in histologic progression was detected between the groups.
cards.watchOut: A 57-patient trial whose positive outcomes are laboratory values; the histology endpoint — the outcome closest to disease modification — was negative.
cards.source: Bodenheimer H et al. Evaluation of colchicine therapy in primary biliary cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 1988. PMID: 3286360. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Head-to-head RCT (Vuoristo 1995): colchicine improved liver tests only modestly while UDCA improved them significantly — the transition to UDCA-standard care
cards.summary: Head-to-head RCT (Vuoristo 1995): colchicine improved liver tests only modestly while UDCA improved them significantly — the transition to UDCA-standard care
cards.type: Placebo-controlled randomised trial, colchicine vs ursodeoxycholic acid vs placebo
cards.people: 90 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis in a 2-year placebo-controlled trial comparing colchicine and ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), with clinical events, laboratory tests and liver histology recorded at the start and end.
cards.result: Pruritus was reduced by both active drugs, and there were significantly fewer dropouts for hepatic reasons on UDCA than placebo. Colchicine improved liver function tests only modestly, whereas UDCA significantly decreased aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase compared with both colchicine and placebo; total bilirubin fell only on UDCA. Both drugs reduced serum cholesterol; UDCA also reduced immunoglobulin M and G and significantly decreased ductular proliferation compared with colchicine or placebo.
cards.watchOut: This trial is the era's transition point: read against UDCA, colchicine was the weaker drug on almost every measure, which is why colchicine did not become standard PBC care.
cards.source: Vuoristo M et al. A placebo-controlled trial of primary biliary cirrhosis treatment with colchicine and ursodeoxycholic acid. Gastroenterology. 1995. PMID: 7729640. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent biochemical improvement, no demonstrated survival or histology benefit in the pooled record, and UDCA beat colchicine head-to-head — a pre-UDCA-era programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent biochemical improvement, no demonstrated survival or histology benefit in the pooled record, and UDCA beat colchicine head-to-head — a pre-UDCA-era programme
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across 11 pooled trials (716 patients) colchicine showed no significant effect on deaths (relative risk 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06) or death/transplantation, and no histology benefit in any carded trial, despite reproducible improvements in alkaline phosphatase, aminotransferases and other liver tests in the individual trials. The one favourable mortality signal (21% vs 47% at 4 years in the 60-patient NEJM trial) was generated after the blind phase ended and is not confirmed by the pool. In the 1995 head-to-head trial UDCA was superior to colchicine on liver tests and histology-related measures. shelves.title: Methotrexate in primary biliary cholangitis: the mortality concern leads — PUMPS (n=265) stopped for futility, long-term trial showed a 2.9-fold higher death/transplant rate, no benefit shown
shelves.question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does methotrexate — alone versus placebo, or added to ursodeoxycholic acid — improve disease course, and what is its mortality signal?
shelves.mesh: Colchicine · Folic Acid Antagonists · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary · Liver Transplantation · Methotrexate · Pruritus · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: The pooled mortality concern leads. Methotrexate improved some biochemistry in PBC trials, but the long-term placebo-controlled trial found a 2.9-fold (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25) higher rate of death or liver transplantation on methotrexate alongside rising bilirubin and Mayo score with time, the Cochrane record carries the 2005 version's finding that methotrexate seemed to significantly increase mortality (the 2010 update's pooled estimate is relative risk 1.32, 95% CI 0.66 to 2.64, not significant), and the large PUMPS trial (265 patients, median 7.6 years) found adding methotrexate to UDCA had no effect on the course of PBC and was stopped early for futility. Methotrexate is not presented here as a PBC treatment option. Its hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity on a liver-disease shelf belong on the face. Cross-points: colchicine in PBC (shelf #7425) and D-penicillamine in PBC (shelf #7427) are separate drug questions from the same pre-UDCA era.

cards.headline: Cochrane review, 2010 update (Giljaca 2010): pooled mortality RR 1.32 (95% CI 0.66 to 2.64), not significant — but the 2005 version had found methotrexate seemed to significantly increase mortality
cards.summary: Cochrane review, 2010 update (Giljaca 2010): pooled mortality RR 1.32 (95% CI 0.66 to 2.64), not significant — but the 2005 version had found methotrexate seemed to significantly increase mortality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, 2010 update, methotrexate vs placebo/no intervention or colchicine
cards.people: Five randomised trials: four trials with 370 patients comparing methotrexate with placebo or no intervention (three adding an equal dose of ursodeoxycholic acid to both groups), and one trial with 85 patients comparing methotrexate with colchicine. Only this 2010 update is carded; the 2005 version is not carded separately.
cards.result: The 2010 update found no statistically significant effect of methotrexate on mortality (relative risk 1.32, 95% CI 0.66 to 2.64 — a relative measure), mortality or liver transplantation combined, pruritus (as a dichotomous outcome), fatigue, liver complications, liver biochemistry, liver histology, or adverse events; the background records that the 2005 version of this review found methotrexate seemed to significantly increase mortality. The pruritus score was significantly lower on methotrexate (mean difference −0.17, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.09), and prothrombin time was significantly worsened (mean difference 1.60 s, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.02). Against colchicine, methotrexate improved pruritus score, alkaline phosphatase and immunoglobulin M without significant differences in mortality or adverse events. The reviewers concluded there is no sufficient evidence to support methotrexate for primary biliary cirrhosis. The bias risk of the placebo-controlled trials was high.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mortality estimate is imprecise and not significant in the update, but its direction is adverse and it sits beside a significant worsening of prothrombin time — the review is a harm-concern record, not a reassurance.
cards.source: Giljaca V et al. Methotrexate for primary biliary cirrhosis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20464729. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Long-term placebo-controlled RCT (Hendrickse 1999): biochemical improvement but a 2.9-fold higher rate of death or transplantation on methotrexate (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25; P=0.09)
cards.summary: Long-term placebo-controlled RCT (Hendrickse 1999): biochemical improvement but a 2.9-fold higher rate of death or transplantation on methotrexate (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25; P=0.09)
cards.type: Single-centre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial over up to 6 years, low-dose methotrexate vs placebo
cards.people: 60 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis in a single-centre double-blind randomised trial of methotrexate 7.5 mg/week (n=30) versus placebo (n=30) for up to 6 years, with 3-monthly symptoms and liver tests and biopsy and gastroscopy at baseline, 2 years and 4–6 years.
cards.result: On methotrexate, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, immunoglobulin M and G, and (after 24 months) aminotransferases were significantly lower than on placebo, with a non-significant trend to lower pruritus scores and similar inflammatory scores on biopsy. Against that, bilirubin and Mayo score rose more with time on methotrexate (both significant after 5 years), and the rate of death or liver transplantation from liver disease was 2.9-fold higher on methotrexate (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25; P=0.09) in Cox multivariate analysis. The authors concluded the results do not support the clinical use of low-dose methotrexate in PBC.
cards.watchOut: Only 60 patients, so the 2.9-fold mortality/transplant estimate is very imprecise and not conventionally significant — but it is a harm signal in the direction of the pooled concern, generated by the longest placebo-controlled exposure in the programme.
cards.source: Hendrickse MT et al. Low-dose methotrexate is ineffective in primary biliary cirrhosis: long-term results of a placebo-controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 1999. PMID: 10419922. cards.headline: PUMPS RCT (Combes 2005): methotrexate added to UDCA for a median 7.6 years had NO effect on the course of PBC — stopped early for futility
cards.summary: PUMPS RCT (Combes 2005): methotrexate added to UDCA for a median 7.6 years had NO effect on the course of PBC — stopped early for futility
cards.type: Multicentre placebo-controlled randomised trial (PUMPS), methotrexate + UDCA vs UDCA alone
cards.people: 265 antimitochondrial-antibody-positive patients without ascites, variceal bleeding or encephalopathy, with serum bilirubin less than 3 mg/dL and albumin 3 g/dL or greater, who had taken UDCA 15 mg/kg daily for at least 6 months; randomised to methotrexate 15 mg/m² (maximum 20 mg) once weekly plus UDCA versus UDCA alone, stratified by Ludwig histological stage. Median follow-up 7.6 years (range 4.6–8.8).
cards.result: There were no significant differences between UDCA plus methotrexate and UDCA alone in treatment-failure outcomes (death without transplantation; transplantation; variceal bleeding; ascites, encephalopathy or varices; bilirubin doubling to 2.5 mg/dL or greater; albumin falling to 2.5 g/dL or less; histological progression) or in time to treatment failure. The trial was stopped early by the National Institutes of Health on Data Safety Monitoring Board advice for futility. The authors concluded methotrexate added to UDCA had no effect on the course of PBC treated with UDCA alone.
cards.watchOut: The largest and longest trial in the programme and a clean null on the add-on question — so the biochemical improvements seen in the smaller trials did not translate into any change in disease course when methotrexate was added to standard UDCA.
cards.source: Combes B et al. Methotrexate (MTX) plus ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in the treatment of primary biliary cirrhosis. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2005. PMID: 16250039. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no benefit in the largest trial, a mortality concern in the pooled and long-term records — methotrexate in PBC is a harm-led historical programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: no benefit in the largest trial, a mortality concern in the pooled and long-term records — methotrexate in PBC is a harm-led historical programme
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The three carded reports agree on the absence of a usable benefit: PUMPS (265 patients, median 7.6 years) found no effect of adding methotrexate to UDCA and was stopped for futility; the Cochrane pool found no significant effect on mortality, transplantation, histology or complications; and the harm side of the record — a 2.9-fold (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25) higher death/transplant rate in the 6-year placebo-controlled trial, the 2005 Cochrane version's significant mortality increase, and significantly worsened prothrombin time in the update — is why this shelf leads with the mortality concern rather than the biochemical improvements. Cross-points: colchicine (shelf #7425) and D-penicillamine (shelf #7427) in PBC are separate questions from the same era.
