shelves.title: D-penicillamine in primary biliary cholangitis: two negative NEJM trials, no efficacy, major side effects in 22–31% — a failed copper-chelation programme
shelves.question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does D-penicillamine versus placebo improve survival, symptoms, biochemistry and histology?
shelves.mesh: Chelating Agents · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary · Penicillamine · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: A negative, toxic programme — the failure is on the face. Two NEJM randomised trials found no benefit: in advanced disease (227 patients) penicillamine did not improve survival, symptoms, laboratory values or histology, and major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22% of patients on the drug; in the earlier prospective trial (52 patients) there was no improvement in survival or symptoms after 28 months, with major side effects in 31% and less serious side effects in a further 46%. The Cochrane pool of seven trials (706 patients) found D-penicillamine tended to increase mortality (relative risk 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64 by fixed-effect; 1.46, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.50 by random-effects, with substantial heterogeneity) and significantly increased adverse events (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.33 to 4.16, fixed-effect), and its authors do not support its use. This shelf is the historical record of the copper-chelation era of PBC care, not a treatment option. Cross-points: colchicine (shelf #7425) and methotrexate (shelf #7426) in PBC are separate drug questions from the same era.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Gong 2004): seven trials, 706 patients — adverse events significantly increased (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.33 to 4.16) and mortality tended to increase; use not supported
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Gong 2004): seven trials, 706 patients — adverse events significantly increased (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.33 to 4.16) and mortality tended to increase; use not supported
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, D-penicillamine vs placebo/no intervention or other control
cards.people: Seven randomised trials randomising 706 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis, comparing D-penicillamine with placebo/no intervention or other control; primary outcomes were mortality and the combination of death or liver transplantation. Only this Cochrane version is carded; the journal version of the same review is not carded separately.
cards.result: D-penicillamine tended to increase mortality (relative risk 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64 by fixed-effect; RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.50 by random-effects — relative measures, with substantial heterogeneity). No significant differences were found for mortality or liver transplantation combined, pruritus, liver complications, progression of histological stage, or liver biochemical variables (except alanine aminotransferase). D-penicillamine significantly increased the risk of adverse events (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.33 to 4.16, fixed-effect; RR 4.18, 95% CI 1.38 to 12.69, random-effects). The reviewers concluded D-penicillamine did not appear to reduce mortality but significantly increased adverse events, and did not support its use in primary biliary cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: The mortality estimate differs by model (significant by fixed-effect, not by random-effects) with substantial heterogeneity — printed both ways here; the adverse-event increase is consistent and large under both models.

cards.headline: NEJM RCT in advanced disease (Dickson 1985): NO survival improvement on penicillamine 1 g/day — and major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22%
cards.summary: NEJM RCT in advanced disease (Dickson 1985): NO survival improvement on penicillamine 1 g/day — and major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22%
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (NEJM 1985) in advanced disease, penicillamine vs placebo
cards.people: 227 patients with histologically advanced primary biliary cirrhosis in a double-blind randomised controlled trial (111 penicillamine 1 g/day, 116 placebo), highly comparable at entry on clinical, biochemical and histologic features; the trial continued in early-stage patients after this report.
cards.result: Penicillamine did not result in an overall improvement in survival compared with placebo. Clinical symptoms and serial hepatic laboratory values reflected progressive disease and were similar in both groups, and there were no substantial differences in the morphologic features of sequential biopsy specimens. The development of major side effects led to permanent discontinuation of penicillamine in 22% of patients taking the drug. The authors concluded penicillamine is not useful for patients with histologically advanced primary biliary cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: An advanced-disease population with a poor prognosis; the null result here is a null in the patients with most to gain, and roughly one in five patients on the drug had to stop it permanently for major side effects.
cards.source: Dickson ER et al. Trial of penicillamine in advanced primary biliary cirrhosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1985. PMID: 3885033. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: NEJM prospective RCT (Matloff 1982): no improvement in survival or symptoms after 28 months — major side effects in 31%, minor side effects in a further 46%
cards.summary: NEJM prospective RCT (Matloff 1982): no improvement in survival or symptoms after 28 months — major side effects in 31%, minor side effects in a further 46%
cards.type: Prospective double-blind randomised trial (NEJM 1982), D-penicillamine vs placebo
cards.people: 52 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis in a prospective double-blind trial (26 D-penicillamine 250 mg four times daily, 26 identical placebo), followed for 28 months.
cards.result: Although the desired urinary copper excretion was achieved on D-penicillamine, there was no improvement in survival or symptoms after 28 months. Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase increased equally in both groups; alanine and aspartate aminotransferases were lower on D-penicillamine but serum albumin was also lower; liver histology worsened equally in both groups. Major side effects, some appearing more than 24 months after starting treatment, occurred in 31% of patients receiving D-penicillamine, and less serious side effects in an additional 46%. The authors concluded D-penicillamine at this dosage is not effective in primary biliary cirrhosis and is associated with a high incidence of serious side effects.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (52 patients), but its toxicity record is the point: over three-quarters of patients on the drug had major or minor side effects, some major effects appearing after 2 years of treatment.
cards.source: Matloff DS et al. A prospective trial of D-penicillamine in primary biliary cirrhosis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1982. PMID: 7033789. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two negative NEJM trials and a pooled record of more adverse events with a mortality trend the wrong way — the copper-chelation era's failure, recorded plainly
cards.summary: Synthesis: two negative NEJM trials and a pooled record of more adverse events with a mortality trend the wrong way — the copper-chelation era's failure, recorded plainly
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No carded report shows D-penicillamine improving survival, symptoms or histology in primary biliary cirrhosis: the 227-patient NEJM trial in advanced disease and the 52-patient NEJM trial were both negative, and the Cochrane pool of seven trials (706 patients) found significantly more adverse events (relative risk 3.11) with mortality tending to increase. Major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22% in one trial and occurred in 31% in the other. This is a failed programme from the copper-chelation era, not a treatment option. Cross-points: colchicine (shelf #7425) and methotrexate (shelf #7426) in PBC are separate questions from the same era.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Impedance–pH normal values are population-specific: median total reflux episodes 20.5 in Argentina, 40 in China, 49 in rural South Africa — 95th percentiles from 50 to 97
shelves.question: In healthy asymptomatic adults, what are the normal values for 24-hour ambulatory oesophageal multichannel intraluminal impedance–pH monitoring — total, acid, weakly acid and weakly alkaline reflux episode counts (median and 95th percentile), bolus exposure and acid exposure time — and how much do population and diet move the upper limits used to define abnormal reflux?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Electric Impedance · Esophageal pH Monitoring · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux/diagnosis · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Healthy Volunteers
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, gastrointestinal physiology chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative monitoring literature, and says so. Four independent healthy-volunteer populations give four different 'normal' pictures, and that spread is the finding: multicentre 2004 (60 volunteers — reflux common upright, median 27 episodes, rare recumbent, median 1); Chinese 2009 (70 volunteers — median total 40 episodes, 95th percentile 75); rural South African 2016 (median total 49, 95th percentile 97 — roughly double the Chinese 95th percentile); Argentine 2022 (median total 20.5, 95th percentile 50 — the lowest reported). No single normal episode count may be printed without its population. The Lyon-consensus thresholds are clinical decision limits derived partly from these data, not a fifth dataset, and are not carded as one. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, because the upper limits are population-bound and no universal limit survives the four datasets.

cards.headline: Multicentre normal values (Shay 2004): 60 healthy volunteers — reflux was common upright (median 27 episodes) and rare recumbent (median 1); a median 34% of upright reflux reached the proximal oesophagus
cards.summary: Multicentre normal values (Shay 2004): 60 healthy volunteers — reflux was common upright (median 27 episodes) and rare recumbent (median 1); a median 34% of upright reflux reached the proximal oesophagus
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre impedance–pH normal values)
cards.people: 60 normal volunteers without reflux symptoms undergoing 24-hour ambulatory simultaneous impedance and pH monitoring, with impedance at six sites (3, 5, 7, 9, 15 and 17 cm above the lower oesophageal sphincter) and pH at 5 cm above the sphincter; reflux episodes were characterised by the pH probe as acid, weakly acidic, nonacid or superimposed acid.
cards.result: Reflux frequency was common upright (median 27; 25th-75th quartiles 16, 42) but rare recumbent (median 1; 0, 4). A median of 34% (14%, 49%) of upright reflux reached the proximal oesophagus. Mixed liquid+gas composition accounted for 49% of episodes and liquid-only for 51%. Acid reflux was two-fold more common than weakly acidic reflux (p<0.001); superimposed acid and nonacid reflux were rare. Acid neutralisation to pH 4 took twice as long as volume clearance measured by impedance.
cards.watchOut: The first normative dataset (2004) and a posture-split picture: upright and recumbent counts differ by an order of magnitude, so any total-episode figure from later cards must be read against its own posture and meal-period handling.
cards.source: Shay S et al. Twenty-four hour ambulatory simultaneous impedance and pH monitoring: a multicenter report of normal values from 60 healthy volunteers. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2004. PMID: 15180722. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chinese normal values (Xiao 2009): 70 healthy volunteers — median total reflux episodes 40, 95th percentile 75 (acid 22/54, weakly acidic 16/40, weakly alkaline 0/4)
cards.summary: Chinese normal values (Xiao 2009): 70 healthy volunteers — median total reflux episodes 40, 95th percentile 75 (acid 22/54, weakly acidic 16/40, weakly alkaline 0/4)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Chinese impedance–pH normal values)
cards.people: 70 healthy volunteers (33 men, 37 women) in a Chinese population undergoing 24-hour ambulatory combined multichannel intraluminal impedance and pH monitoring; episodes characterised by pH (acidic, weakly acidic, weakly alkaline) and composition (liquid, mixed, gas).
cards.result: The median and 95th-percentile total reflux episodes over 24 hours were 40 and 75; for acidic episodes 22 and 54, weakly acidic 16 and 40, and weakly alkaline 0 and 4. Of all episodes, 53.3% were acidic, 44.7% weakly acidic and 2% weakly alkaline; 52.4% were mixed composition, 37.2% liquid and 10.4% gas. 26.6% of episodes reached 15 cm above the lower oesophageal sphincter. Male sex was associated with more acid, liquid, mixed and proximal episodes (p<0.05). The authors concluded the number of reflux episodes in the Chinese population was similar to the Western population.
cards.watchOut: Sex moves the counts (men higher on several episode types), so a pooled 95th percentile overstates the female limit and understates the male one; catheter system and meal handling are this study's own, as published.
cards.source: Xiao YL et al. Normal values of 24-hour combined esophageal multichannel intraluminal impedance and pH monitoring in the Chinese population. Digestion. 2009. PMID: 19295211. cards.headline: Rural South African normal values (Ndebia 2016): median total reflux episodes 49, 95th percentile 97 — the highest upper limit of the four populations; 95th-percentile acid exposure time 8.6% of 24 hours as published
cards.summary: Rural South African normal values (Ndebia 2016): median total reflux episodes 49, 95th percentile 97 — the highest upper limit of the four populations; 95th-percentile acid exposure time 8.6% of 24 hours as published
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (rural South African impedance–pH normal values)
cards.people: Healthy rural South African participants undergoing 24 hours of oesophageal impedance and pH monitoring (the participant number is not printed in the fetched abstract); median and 95th-percentile values are reported for total and subtype episodes, bolus clearance and exposure, and proximal extent.
cards.result: Median and 95th-percentile total reflux episodes were 49 and 97; acidic 15 and 55, weakly acidic 17 and 51, and weakly alkaline 8 and 36. Composition medians/95th percentiles were 5 and 21 for liquid, 27 and 72 for mixed, and 10 and 39 for gas reflux. Median bolus clearance was 18 seconds and median bolus exposure 14 minutes per 24 hours; proximal extent was 6%. The 95th-percentile time of oesophageal exposure to acid was 8.6 (units as published in the record). Female and overweight participants had more reflux events. The authors noted more reflux episodes, and more weakly alkaline episodes, than in previous similar studies.
cards.watchOut: The 95th percentile for total episodes (97) is roughly double the Argentine figure and well above the Chinese 75 — population and diet move the upper limit, which is why this shelf prints no universal count. The cohort N is not printed in the fetched abstract and none is claimed.
cards.source: Ndebia EJ et al. Normal values of 24-hour ambulatory esophageal impedance-pH monitoring in a rural South African cohort of healthy participants. cards.headline: Synthesis: impedance–pH 'normal' is population-specific — median total episodes run from 20.5 (Argentina) to 49 (rural South Africa) and 95th percentiles from 50 to 97, so the upper limit used to call reflux abnormal must carry its population with it
cards.summary: Synthesis: impedance–pH 'normal' is population-specific — median total episodes run from 20.5 (Argentina) to 49 (rural South Africa) and 95th percentiles from 50 to 97, so the upper limit used to call reflux abnormal must carry its population with it
cards.people: Synthesis of the four population datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall gastrointestinal physiology (framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative monitoring literature). The multicentre 2004 dataset (60 volunteers) established the method's normal picture — reflux common upright (median 27), rare recumbent (median 1), acid episodes twice weakly acidic. The Chinese dataset (70 volunteers) gives median total 40, 95th percentile 75. The rural South African dataset gives median 49, 95th percentile 97, with more weakly alkaline episodes than earlier studies. The Argentine dataset gives median 20.5, 95th percentile 50, the lowest reported. Gastric-emptying norms and bowel-habit physiology are different measurements, homed elsewhere and not re-carded. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: four genuine datasets, but their upper limits differ roughly two-fold by population, so no single normal episode count exists to be established.
cards.watchOut: Catheter system, meal-period handling and population diet differ by study and are printed per card; never quote a 95th percentile without naming the population it came from.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Tegoprazan in erosive oesophagitis: healing matched esomeprazole (98.9% vs 98.9%) and maintenance matched lansoprazole (90.6% vs 89.5%) — the patient trials pack #5882 does not card
shelves.question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does tegoprazan heal oesophagitis versus esomeprazole or lansoprazole, and does it maintain healing versus lansoprazole?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Benzene Derivatives · Double-Blind Method · Esomeprazole · Esophagitis · Female · Humans · Imidazoles · Male · Middle Aged · Potassium · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — on four patient trials, none carded at pack #5882. Healing: tegoprazan matched esomeprazole at week 8 in Korea (98.9% vs 98.9%, n=302) and in China as LXI-15028 (91.1% vs 92.8%, n=261), and beat lansoprazole numerically to week 4 in a phase 4 trial (95.2% vs 86.2%, n=218; non-inferior, superior on that trial's own analysis, which its authors say needs confirmation in severe disease). Maintenance: 24-week remission 90.6% vs 89.5% on lansoprazole (n=351), in mostly mild (LA A/B) healed disease. PARTIAL against pack #5882, which cards tegoprazan only as healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic limbs for the severe-disease/night-time question — those limbs are not re-carded here; cross-point #5882. Korean and Chinese programmes only.

cards.headline: Phase 3 healing trial vs esomeprazole (Lee 2019): week-8 cumulative healing 98.9% on tegoprazan 50 mg, 98.9% on 100 mg and 98.9% on esomeprazole — non-inferior
cards.summary: Phase 3 healing trial vs esomeprazole (Lee 2019): week-8 cumulative healing 98.9% on tegoprazan 50 mg, 98.9% on 100 mg and 98.9% on esomeprazole — non-inferior
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind trial, tegoprazan 50/100 mg vs esomeprazole 40 mg (healing limb)
cards.people: 302 Korean patients with endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis (Los Angeles grades A–D) randomised to tegoprazan 50 mg, tegoprazan 100 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg for 4 or 8 weeks.
cards.result: Cumulative healing at week 8 was 98.9% (91/92) on tegoprazan 50 mg, 98.9% (90/91) on tegoprazan 100 mg and 98.9% (87/88) on esomeprazole 40 mg; both tegoprazan doses were non-inferior to esomeprazole. Adverse-event incidence was comparable among the groups and tegoprazan was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority design against an active PPI, Korean patients, all LA grades pooled — it does not show superiority over a PPI, and it is not the severe-disease slice homed at pack #5882.

cards.headline: Phase 4 healing trial vs lansoprazole (Shin 2025): cumulative healing to week 4 was 95.2% on tegoprazan vs 86.2% on lansoprazole — non-inferior, and superior on this trial's own analysis
cards.summary: Phase 4 healing trial vs lansoprazole (Shin 2025): cumulative healing to week 4 was 95.2% on tegoprazan vs 86.2% on lansoprazole — non-inferior, and superior on this trial's own analysis
cards.type: Phase 4 multicentre randomised double-blind active-comparator trial, tegoprazan 50 mg vs lansoprazole 30 mg (healing limb)
cards.people: 218 patients with endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis (LA grades A–D) randomised to tegoprazan 50 mg or lansoprazole 30 mg; full-analysis set 103 tegoprazan and 109 lansoprazole participants.
cards.result: Cumulative healing up to week 4 was 95.2% (98/103) on tegoprazan versus 86.2% (94/109) on lansoprazole (difference 8.91 percentage points, 95% CI 1.22 to 16.59; P<0.0001 for non-inferiority and P=0.0266 for superiority); week-2 healing was 88.4% (91/103) versus 82.6% (90/109). Healing on tegoprazan was consistent regardless of CYP2C19 genotype.
cards.watchOut: The one superiority reading in this programme — a phase 4 trial whose own authors state that further studies are necessary to confirm the findings and clarify superiority, especially in severe erosive oesophagitis; do not carry it into severe disease, which is pack #5882's slice.

cards.headline: Chinese phase 3 healing trial, tegoprazan as LXI-15028, vs esomeprazole (Zhu 2025): week-8 healing 91.1% vs 92.8% — non-inferior
cards.summary: Chinese phase 3 healing trial, tegoprazan as LXI-15028, vs esomeprazole (Zhu 2025): week-8 healing 91.1% vs 92.8% — non-inferior
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial, tegoprazan (LXI-15028) 50 mg vs esomeprazole 40 mg (healing limb, Chinese programme)
cards.people: 261 patients with erosive oesophagitis randomised 1:1 (132 tegoprazan, 129 esomeprazole) at 32 sites in China to tegoprazan 50 mg/day or esomeprazole 40 mg/day; the publication gives tegoprazan's code name as LXI-15028.
cards.result: Cumulative endoscopic healing at week 8 was 91.1% on tegoprazan versus 92.8% on esomeprazole (difference −1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −8.5 to 5.0; P=0.008 for non-inferiority). Reflux questionnaire and quality-of-life changes and symptom-free days did not differ significantly between groups. Adverse events were reported by 71.5% (93/130) on tegoprazan versus 61.7% (79/128) on esomeprazole, with serious adverse events in 2.3% versus none.
cards.watchOut: Chinese programme, non-inferiority design; LXI-15028 is tegoprazan as the publication names it — the code name is not a different drug.

cards.headline: Maintenance trial vs lansoprazole (Cho 2023): 24-week endoscopic remission 90.6% on tegoprazan 25 mg vs 89.5% on lansoprazole 15 mg — non-inferior, in mostly mild healed disease
cards.summary: Maintenance trial vs lansoprazole (Cho 2023): 24-week endoscopic remission 90.6% on tegoprazan 25 mg vs 89.5% on lansoprazole 15 mg — non-inferior, in mostly mild healed disease
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind multicentre maintenance trial, tegoprazan 25 mg vs lansoprazole 15 mg (maintenance limb)
cards.people: 351 patients with endoscopically confirmed healed erosive oesophagitis randomised 1:1 to tegoprazan 25 mg (n=174) or lansoprazole 15 mg (n=177) once daily for up to 24 weeks; most had mild disease (LA grade A 57.3%, grade B 37.3%).
cards.result: Endoscopic remission after 24 weeks was 90.6% on tegoprazan versus 89.5% on lansoprazole; tegoprazan was non-inferior at both 24 and 12 weeks, with no significant difference by LA grade and a consistent effect in CYP2C19 extensive metabolisers. Increases in serum gastrin were not higher on tegoprazan than on lansoprazole, and the safety profile was similar.
cards.watchOut: The enrolled disease was mostly mild (LA A/B) healed oesophagitis — these remission rates must not be carried into severe disease. (The drug name is tegoprazan throughout this shelf; the trial tested the 25 mg maintenance dose.)
cards.source: Cho YK et al. Randomised clinical trial: comparison of tegoprazan and lansoprazole as maintenance therapy for healed mild erosive oesophagitis. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2023. PMID: 36314172. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Lansoprazole · Gastrins

cards.headline: Synthesis: tegoprazan healed erosive oesophagitis at rates matching esomeprazole and lansoprazole in three healing trials (week-8/4 healing 91–99%) and maintained healing non-inferiorly over 24 weeks — a patient-trial shelf that cross-points, and does not re-card, pack #5882's healthy-volunteer limbs
cards.summary: Synthesis: tegoprazan healed erosive oesophagitis at rates matching esomeprazole and lansoprazole in three healing trials (week-8/4 healing 91–99%) and maintained healing non-inferiorly over 24 weeks — a patient-trial shelf that cross-points, and does not re-card, pack #5882's healthy-volunteer limbs
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three healing trials (n=302, n=218, n=261) and one maintenance trial (n=351), all against active PPIs, from Korean and Chinese programmes.
cards.result: Healing: 98.9% versus 98.9% against esomeprazole at week 8 (Lee 2019); 95.2% versus 86.2% against lansoprazole to week 4, non-inferior and superior on that phase 4 trial's own analysis (Shin 2025); 91.1% versus 92.8% against esomeprazole at week 8 in China (Zhu 2025). Maintenance: 24-week remission 90.6% versus 89.5% against lansoprazole in mostly mild healed disease (Cho 2023). PARTIAL against pack #5882: #5882 asks the PCAB-class question for severe (LA C/D) oesophagitis with night-time breakthrough and cards tegoprazan only as healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic limbs — those limbs are NOT re-carded here; this shelf is only the unasked agent-specific patient healing and maintenance slice, and cross-points #5882.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Korean/Chinese) programmes and non-inferiority designs predominate; the maintenance base is mostly mild disease. See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Fexuprazan in erosive oesophagitis: healing matched esomeprazole in two trials and did not depend on meal timing — one retracted phase III report fenced, never carded
shelves.question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does fexuprazan 40 mg heal oesophagitis versus esomeprazole 40 mg, and does healing differ by dosing timing relative to meals?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Amines · Double-Blind Method · Esomeprazole · Esophagitis, Peptic · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Peptic Ulcer · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Pyrroles · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — fexuprazan 40 mg healed erosive oesophagitis non-inferiorly to esomeprazole 40 mg in two trials (week-8: 88.5% vs 89.0% full-analysis, 97.3% vs 97.9% per-protocol, n=332 in the full set; 99.1% vs 99.1% per-protocol, 263 randomised), and a third trial (n=175) found after-meal dosing non-inferior to before-meal dosing (100.00% vs 98.77% at week 4) — a timing limb with no PPI comparator, not a third healing trial. FENCED: the retracted phase III report PMID 38892973 is never carded and the count of 3 stands without it (named on the Synthesis card). Korean programme; non-inferiority designs throughout. Cross-point #5882 and #7473 without merging agents into a class verdict.

cards.headline: Phase III trial vs esomeprazole (Zhuang 2024): week-8 healing 88.5% vs 89.0% in the full analysis set and 97.3% vs 97.9% per-protocol — non-inferior
cards.summary: Phase III trial vs esomeprazole (Zhuang 2024): week-8 healing 88.5% vs 89.0% in the full analysis set and 97.3% vs 97.9% per-protocol — non-inferior
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind multicentre trial, fexuprazan 40 mg vs esomeprazole 40 mg (healing limb)
cards.people: 332 subjects in the full analysis set (311 per-protocol) with endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis, randomised to fexuprazan 40 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg once daily for 4–8 weeks.
cards.result: Healing at 8 weeks was 88.5% (146/165) on fexuprazan versus 89.0% (145/163) on esomeprazole in the full analysis set, and 97.3% (145/149) versus 97.9% (143/146) per-protocol; non-inferiority was demonstrated in both analyses. Healing at 4 weeks, symptom responses and quality-of-life changes did not differ significantly. Drug-related adverse events: 19.4% (32/165) versus 19.6% (32/163).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority design against an active PPI; the full-analysis and per-protocol healing rates differ by about 9 points, so quote the set you mean.

cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, fexuprazan 40 mg vs esomeprazole 40 mg (healing limb, Korean programme)
cards.people: 263 Korean adults with endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis randomised 1:1 to fexuprazan 40 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg once daily for 8 weeks; 218 completed per protocol (107 fexuprazan, 111 esomeprazole).
cards.result: Week-8 healing was 99.1% (106/107) on fexuprazan versus 99.1% (110/111) on esomeprazole per protocol — non-inferior. cards.watchOut: The headline 99.1% rates are per-protocol (218 of 263 randomised); non-inferiority against an active PPI, not superiority and not a placebo comparison.

cards.headline: Dosing-timing trial (Lee 2025): fexuprazan after meals healed 100.00% vs 98.77% before meals at week 4 — after-meal dosing non-inferior (no PPI comparator; the timing limb)
cards.summary: Dosing-timing trial (Lee 2025): fexuprazan after meals healed 100.00% vs 98.77% before meals at week 4 — after-meal dosing non-inferior (no PPI comparator; the timing limb)
cards.type: Multicentre open-label non-inferiority trial, fexuprazan before vs after meals (dosing-timing limb — both arms fexuprazan)
cards.people: 175 patients with typical reflux symptoms and endoscopically confirmed erosive oesophagitis randomised 1:1 to fexuprazan 40 mg daily 30 minutes before a meal (n=89) or after a meal (n=86); treatment ended at 2 or 4 weeks when healing was confirmed.
cards.result: Healing up to week 4 was 98.77% before meals versus 100.00% after meals (difference 0.01%, 95% CI −0.01% to 0.04%); week-2 healing was 95.77% versus 97.14%. Treatment-emergent adverse events were 9.78% and 8.70% in the before-meal and after-meal groups respectively. After-meal dosing was non-inferior to before-meal dosing.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received fexuprazan: this is a timing limb with a 2–4-week horizon, not a third healing-versus-PPI trial, and it must not be counted as one.
cards.source: Lee SP et al. Randomized Multicenter Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Fexuprazan According to the Timing of Dosing in Patients With Erosive Esophagitis. shelves.title: Ilaprazole: duodenal-ulcer healing matched other PPIs (relative risk 1.02; 89.7% vs 87.0%) and reflux-oesophagitis healing matched esomeprazole (83.54% vs 82.79%) — two limbs, never pooled
shelves.question: In adults with active duodenal ulcer, does ilaprazole heal ulcers versus omeprazole or rabeprazole — and in reflux oesophagitis, does it heal versus esomeprazole?
shelves.mesh: 2-Pyridinylmethylsulfinylbenzimidazoles · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Aryl Hydrocarbon Hydroxylases · Benzimidazoles · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Double-Blind Method · Duodenal Ulcer · Female · Genotype · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Omeprazole · Polymorphism, Genetic · Sulfoxides · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — in two limbs that are labelled and never pooled. Duodenal ulcer: week-4 healing 93.0% vs 90.8% on omeprazole (494 in efficacy analyses), 77.86%/83.72% on ilaprazole 5/10 mg vs 75.38% on rabeprazole (390 completed), and a meta-analysis of 5 articles (1,481 patients) giving a week-4 healing relative risk of 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.06) with absolute rates 89.7% vs 87.0%. Reflux oesophagitis: week-8 healing 83.54% vs 82.79% on esomeprazole (537 randomised) in the trial published under the spelling 'Ilaparazole'. All comparators are active PPIs — no placebo-controlled healing trial exists in either limb. Chinese/Korean programme.

cards.headline: Duodenal-ulcer limb — phase III vs omeprazole (Wang 2012): week-4 healing 93.0% on ilaprazole 10 mg vs 90.8% on omeprazole 20 mg
cards.summary: Duodenal-ulcer limb — phase III vs omeprazole (Wang 2012): week-4 healing 93.0% on ilaprazole 10 mg vs 90.8% on omeprazole 20 mg
cards.type: Phase III multicentre randomised double-blind controlled trial, ilaprazole 10 mg vs omeprazole 20 mg (DUODENAL ULCER limb)
cards.people: 494 patients in the efficacy analyses with at least one endoscopically diagnosed active duodenal ulcer, randomised 2:1 to ilaprazole 10 mg/day or omeprazole 20 mg/day for 4 weeks.
cards.result: Ulcer healing at week 4 was 93.0% on ilaprazole versus 90.8% on omeprazole (rate difference 2.2 percentage points, 95% CI −2.8 to 7.2). More than 80% of patients became asymptomatic. Adverse drug reactions were similar (8.5% vs 11.5%), and healing on ilaprazole did not vary obviously by CYP2C19 genotype.
cards.watchOut: Active-comparator trial with no placebo arm; the 2.2-point difference's confidence interval includes no difference — read as equivalence, not superiority.

cards.headline: Duodenal-ulcer limb — dose comparison vs rabeprazole (Fan 2019): week-4 healing 75.38% on rabeprazole 10 mg, 77.86% on ilaprazole 5 mg and 83.72% on ilaprazole 10 mg
cards.summary: Duodenal-ulcer limb — dose comparison vs rabeprazole (Fan 2019): week-4 healing 75.38% on rabeprazole 10 mg, 77.86% on ilaprazole 5 mg and 83.72% on ilaprazole 10 mg
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-controlled multicentre dose-comparison trial (DUODENAL ULCER limb)
cards.people: 390 patients who completed the study, aged over 18 with at least one endoscopically confirmed active non-malignant duodenal ulcer, treated for 4 weeks with rabeprazole 10 mg, ilaprazole 5 mg or ilaprazole 10 mg.
cards.result: Healing at 4 weeks was 75.38% on rabeprazole 10 mg, 77.86% on ilaprazole 5 mg and 83.72% on ilaprazole 10 mg; the ilaprazole 5 mg versus rabeprazole difference was 2.48 percentage points (95% CI −7.79 to 12.74), meeting the non-inferiority hypothesis. Ilaprazole 10 mg was superior to ilaprazole 5 mg at week 2 on logistic regression (odds ratio 1.92, 95% CI 1.02 to 3.59; P=0.04 — a relative measure). About 80% of patients became asymptomatic, and safety profiles were similar across the three groups.
cards.watchOut: Completion-based numbers (390 completed) and a lower absolute healing range than the omeprazole trial — the two duodenal-ulcer trials used different comparators and populations and are labelled, not pooled.
cards.source: Fan L et al. Ilaprazole Compared With Rabeprazole in the Treatment of Duodenal Ulcer: A Randomized, Double-blind, Active-controlled, Multicenter Study. cards.people: 537 patients diagnosed with reflux oesophagitis by gastroscopy randomised to ilaprazole 10 mg once daily (n=322) or esomeprazole 40 mg once daily (n=215) for 8 weeks; 471 completed treatment.
cards.result: After 8 weeks, healing in the full-analysis set was 83.54% on ilaprazole versus 82.79% on esomeprazole (rate difference 0.75 percentage points, 95% CI −5.72 to 7.22; per-protocol 92.50% vs 94.94%). cards.headline: Duodenal-ulcer limb — meta-analysis (Ji 2014): week-4 healing relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.06) vs other PPIs, absolute rates 89.7% vs 87.0%
cards.summary: Duodenal-ulcer limb — meta-analysis (Ji 2014): week-4 healing relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.06) vs other PPIs, absolute rates 89.7% vs 87.0%
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials (DUODENAL ULCER limb only)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of ilaprazole versus other proton pump inhibitors in duodenal ulcer: 5 articles, 1,481 patients (searches to July 2013).
cards.result: There was no difference in the 4-week healing rate between ilaprazole and other PPIs: 89.7% versus 87.0%, relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.06; P=0.32) — a relative measure, with the absolute rates printed beside it. Adverse-effect rates were 9.7% versus 13.0% (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.07; P=0.14), also not significant, and sensitivity analyses did not change the results.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools the duodenal-ulcer trials (including programmes overlapping the primaries carded above), so it corroborates rather than adds independent patients; it says nothing about oesophagitis.

shelves.title: Rebamipide in functional dyspepsia: both placebo-controlled primaries negative on overall symptoms — a meta-analytic signal on one metric only
shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does rebamipide versus placebo improve dyspeptic symptoms and quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adult · Alanine · Antacids · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Double-Blind Method · Dyspepsia · Eructation · Female · Helicobacter Infections · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quinolones · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the negative primaries lead. Both named placebo-controlled primaries failed on their overall symptom outcomes: the two multicentre studies in one publication (272 randomised across the two studies) found rebamipide not superior to placebo on individual symptom scores at end of treatment, and the Japanese trial (81 recruited) found no significant difference in overall symptom change at 4 weeks, with three individual items favouring rebamipide. The meta-analysis (17 publications, 2,170 subjects) found a functional-dyspepsia signal on the standardised mean difference only (SMD −0.62, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.08) and none on the risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.45). Report-count convention: the 2001 publication contains two studies — three reports covering three trials plus the meta-analysis. Japanese programme predominance.

cards.headline: Two multicentre placebo-controlled studies in one publication (Talley 2001): rebamipide was NOT superior to placebo on individual symptom scores at end of treatment — 272 randomised across the two studies
cards.summary: Two multicentre placebo-controlled studies in one publication (Talley 2001): rebamipide was NOT superior to placebo on individual symptom scores at end of treatment — 272 randomised across the two studies
cards.type: Two multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled studies reported in one publication, rebamipide 100/200 mg three times daily vs placebo
cards.people: 557 patients with functional dyspepsia were divided a priori into two studies by Helicobacter pylori status; after a 2-week baseline period, 99 H. pylori-positive and 173 H. pylori-negative patients still having at least moderate upper abdominal pain or discomfort were randomised to rebamipide 100 mg, rebamipide 200 mg or placebo three times daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Individual symptom scores improved from baseline in all treatment arms, but no significant improvement of individual symptom scores was observed in either rebamipide group at the end of the studies compared with placebo; the belching score was significantly reduced on both rebamipide doses at week 2 only (P=0.017 and P=0.012) in H. pylori-positive patients. Among H. pylori-positive patients, the proportion who requested the study medication again was 85% (100 mg) and 96% (200 mg; P=0.020) versus 72% on placebo. There were no serious study-medication-related adverse events. The authors' conclusion: rebamipide was not superior to placebo in terms of individual symptoms at the end of treatment.
cards.watchOut: Report-count convention on the face: this is ONE publication containing TWO studies — the shelf's floor rests on three reports covering three trials plus a meta-analysis, and this card must not be counted as two publications.
cards.source: Talley NJ et al. Double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre studies of rebamipide, a gastroprotective drug, in the treatment of functional dyspepsia with or without Helicobacter pylori infection. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2001. PMID: 11564000. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Japanese placebo-controlled trial (Miwa 2006): overall symptom change did NOT differ significantly from placebo at 4 weeks — three individual items favoured rebamipide
cards.summary: Japanese placebo-controlled trial (Miwa 2006): overall symptom change did NOT differ significantly from placebo at 4 weeks — three individual items favoured rebamipide
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled single-centre trial, rebamipide 100 mg three times daily vs placebo
cards.people: 81 Japanese patients with functional dyspepsia recruited at a single centre and treated with rebamipide 100 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks; symptom data were analysed for 38 rebamipide and 33 placebo patients.
cards.result: Overall symptoms improved significantly from the untreated baseline in both groups, and the mean changes in overall symptoms were not significantly different between rebamipide and placebo. Improvement was significantly greater on rebamipide for three items — bloating, belching, and pain or discomfort relieved after a meal. In per-protocol quality-of-life analysis, social restriction (P=0.048) and pain intensity (P=0.031) improved significantly more on rebamipide.
cards.watchOut: Small (81 recruited, 71 analysed), single-centre, 4 weeks; the positive findings are individual items and a per-protocol quality-of-life subset, against a negative overall-symptom primary comparison.
cards.source: Miwa H et al. Effect of a gastro-protective agent, rebamipide, on symptom improvement in patients with functional dyspepsia: a double-blind placebo-controlled study in Japan. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jaafar 2018): in the functional-dyspepsia limb, symptom improvement appeared on the standardised mean difference (SMD −0.62) but NOT on the risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01)
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jaafar 2018): in the functional-dyspepsia limb, symptom improvement appeared on the standardised mean difference (SMD −0.62) but NOT on the risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (functional-dyspepsia limb reported separately)
cards.people: 17 randomised controlled trial publications, 2,170 subjects (1,224 rebamipide, 946 placebo/control) across organic and functional dyspepsia; five of the trials were in functional dyspepsia and twelve in organic dyspepsia.
cards.result: Overall, dyspepsia symptom improvement favoured rebamipide (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.93 for the dichotomous outcome as printed; standardised mean difference −0.46, 95% CI −0.83 to −0.09 — relative/standardised measures). In organic dyspepsia both metrics favoured rebamipide (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.86; SMD −0.23, 95% CI −0.40 to −0.07). In functional dyspepsia, symptom improvement was observed on the pooled SMD (SMD −0.62, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.08) but not on the risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.45). The authors concluded rebamipide is effective in organic dyspepsia and may improve symptoms in functional dyspepsia.
cards.watchOut: Most of the pooled base (12 of 17 publications) is organic dyspepsia, a different question; only the functional-dyspepsia limb belongs on this shelf, and within that limb the two metrics disagree.
cards.source: Jaafar MH et al. Efficacy of Rebamipide in Organic and Functional Dyspepsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Digestive diseases and sciences. 2018. PMID: 29192375. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: one publication containing two multicentre studies (272 randomised), one Japanese trial (81 recruited), and one systematic review/meta-analysis whose functional-dyspepsia limb covers five trials within 17 publications (2,170 subjects overall).
cards.result: Talley 2001 (two studies): rebamipide was not superior to placebo on individual symptom scores at end of treatment. The healthy-volunteer NSAID small-bowel crossover study retrieved in mining (n=10) is not folded in.

shelves.title: Somatostatin in acute pancreatitis: signals on markers, CT evolution and surgery in three old small trials (one unblinded, n=50) — no mortality effect shown
shelves.question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (including severe disease), does intravenous somatostatin versus control/standard care reduce complications, need for surgery, hospital stay and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Clinical Trials as Topic · Female · Humans · L-Lactate Dehydrogenase · Leukocyte Count · Male · Middle Aged · Pancreatitis · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Random Allocation · Somatostatin · Urea
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on an old, small, mostly unblinded primary-trial programme, carded as the slice slate-13's octreotide row (S13-2-06) expressly did not fold in; cross-point that row, never a merged analogue verdict. Signals: day-2 laboratory markers and a trend to fewer local complications (n=71, 1989); CT evolution and hospital stay significantly favouring somatostatin (n=100, 1994); and, in severe disease, fewer surgical interventions (45.8% vs 86.4%, P=0.005) in a prospective randomised UNBLINDED trial of 50 patients (1998), with no difference in stay or ICU mortality. No trial was powered for mortality. The gated 2017 Cochrane review (PMID 28431202, pack #7293) is NOT carded — primaries only. Dosing differed (100 vs 250 micrograms/h after a 250 microgram bolus).

cards.headline: Prospective randomised trial (Choi 1989): white-cell count, LDH and urea significantly lower at day 2 on somatostatin, with a trend to fewer, especially local, complications — mortality low in both arms
cards.summary: Prospective randomised trial (Choi 1989): white-cell count, LDH and urea significantly lower at day 2 on somatostatin, with a trend to fewer, especially local, complications — mortality low in both arms
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial, somatostatin 100 micrograms/h after 250 microgram bolus vs control
cards.people: 71 patients with acute pancreatitis randomised to control (n=36) or somatostatin (n=35), given as 100 micrograms/h after a 250 microgram bolus for the first two days.
cards.result: Of nine laboratory tests compared, white blood cell count, lactate dehydrogenase and urea concentrations were significantly lower in the somatostatin group two days after admission. Severity of pancreatitis increased after hospitalisation in fewer somatostatin patients (not significant). There was a trend toward fewer complications, especially local, in the somatostatin group, and mortality in both groups was low. The authors concluded somatostatin appeared to reduce local complications and that a larger trial was necessary to show a beneficial effect conclusively.
cards.watchOut: 1989 trial, n=71, surrogate laboratory endpoints at day 2 and a non-significant complication trend; no trial in this programme was powered for mortality.
cards.source: Choi TK et al. Somatostatin in the treatment of acute pancreatitis: a prospective randomised controlled trial. Gut. 1989. PMID: 2564834. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Prospective randomised study (Luengo 1994): CT evolution of pancreatic lesions and hospital stay significantly favoured somatostatin
cards.summary: Prospective randomised study (Luengo 1994): CT evolution of pancreatic lesions and hospital stay significantly favoured somatostatin
cards.type: Prospective controlled randomised study, somatostatin 250 micrograms/h for 48 h after bolus vs control
cards.people: 100 patients with acute pancreatitis randomly divided into a control group (n=50) and a somatostatin group (n=50), somatostatin given at 250 micrograms/h for 48 hours following a 250 microgram bolus; groups were homogeneous in age, sex, aetiology and severity on admission.
cards.result: CT evolution of pancreatic lesions and length of hospital stay differed significantly in favour of somatostatin. The authors state another study using a larger sample would be required to evaluate the remaining parameters (need for surgery and mortality).
cards.watchOut: The record reports the CT and stay findings as significant without printing the underlying numbers, so no effect size can be stated from this record; dosing (250 micrograms/h) differed from the 1989 trial (100 micrograms/h) — regimens are stated as published on each card.

cards.headline: Severe-pancreatitis randomised study, UNBLINDED (Planas 1998): overall surgical interventions 45.8% on somatostatin vs 86.4% on control (P=0.005) — no difference in hospital stay or ICU mortality; N = 50
cards.summary: Severe-pancreatitis randomised study, UNBLINDED (Planas 1998): overall surgical interventions 45.8% on somatostatin vs 86.4% on control (P=0.005) — no difference in hospital stay or ICU mortality; N = 50
cards.type: Prospective randomised UNBLINDED study in severe acute pancreatitis, somatostatin plus conventional treatment vs conventional treatment (design flag on the face)
cards.people: 50 patients with severe acute pancreatitis in a general ICU at a university hospital, classified severe by APACHE II score, Ranson's criteria and CT Balthazar classification; all received conventional treatment, and the study group received somatostatin in addition over a 10-day period.
cards.result: The study group required fewer overall surgical interventions than the control group (45.8% vs 86.4%; P=0.005). Late surgical procedures related to pancreatic necrosis were more common in controls (63.6% vs 37.5%; P=0.07). No differences in length of hospital stay or ICU mortality were observed. The authors describe the only advantage as a slight reduction in the need for surgery due to local complications.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, n=50, single ICU, 1998 — the surgical-intervention contrast is the programme's largest effect and its least protected against bias; biliary aetiology differed between groups (63.6% control vs 37.5% study; not significant).
cards.source: Planas M et al. Severe acute pancreatitis: treatment with somatostatin. Intensive care medicine. 1998. PMID: 9503220. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Glycyrrhizin in chronic hepatitis C: ALT fell (phase III ≥50% reduction 28.7–29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo) but viraemia did not — a biochemical, interferon-era benefit
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C who were ineligible for, or non-responders to, interferon therapy, does intravenous glycyrrhizin versus placebo (or across dose frequencies) reduce ALT and improve liver histology — and does it affect viraemia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycyrrhizic Acid · Hepatitis C, Chronic · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Liver Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — biochemical only, ALT not viraemia) — across four randomised reports in interferon-ineligible/non-responder chronic hepatitis C: mean ALT fell 26% vs 6% on placebo at 4 weeks with no viral clearance and no significant HCV-RNA effect (n=57); mean ALT fell 26% (three-times-weekly) and 47% (six-times-weekly) vs no significant placebo change, disappearing after cessation (72 treatment courses); ALT response was maintained by dose frequency at 26 weeks (60%/24%/9%, P<0.001) with NO significant histological improvement (121 entered, 72 responders randomised); and the phase III trial (379 patients) found at least 50% ALT reduction in 28.7%/29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo at 12 weeks (P<0.0001), with necro-inflammation improvement in about 45–46% at 52 weeks in an uncontrolled open phase. Interferon-era evidence — not against the direct-acting-antiviral standard. Mineralocorticoid-type harms are homed at pack #3467; cross-point it.

cards.headline: Phase I/II placebo-controlled trial (van Rossum 1999): mean ALT fell 26% on glycyrrhizin vs 6% on placebo at 4 weeks — with NO viral clearance and no significant HCV-RNA effect (the ALT-not-viraemia split, on the face)
cards.summary: Phase I/II placebo-controlled trial (van Rossum 1999): mean ALT fell 26% on glycyrrhizin vs 6% on placebo at 4 weeks — with NO viral clearance and no significant HCV-RNA effect (the ALT-not-viraemia split, on the face)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled phase I/II trial, intravenous glycyrrhizin three times weekly for 4 weeks
cards.people: 57 European patients with chronic hepatitis C who were non-responders to, or unlikely to respond to, interferon therapy (genotype 1/cirrhosis), randomised to glycyrrhizin 240, 160 or 80 mg or placebo, given intravenously three times weekly for 4 weeks, with 4 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: Mean ALT decrease at the end of active treatment was 26% on glycyrrhizin versus 6% on placebo (mean percentage decreases from baseline, as printed); within 2 days ALT had dropped 15% below baseline in the dose groups (P<0.02), with no clear dose-response (29%, 26% and 23% for 240, 160 and 80 mg). ALT normalised in 10% (4 of 41). The ALT effect disappeared after cessation. Viral clearance was NOT observed: the mean decrease in plasma HCV-RNA was 4.1 x 10(6) genome equivalents/mL (95% CI 0 to 8.2 x 10(6); P>0.1) — not significant. No major side-effects were noted and no patient withdrew for intolerance.

cards.type: Randomised trial of intravenous glycyrrhizin three vs six times weekly vs placebo, 4 weeks
cards.people: European patients with chronic hepatitis C who were nonresponders to, or unlikely to respond to, interferon therapy; 72 treatment courses of intravenous glycyrrhizin three or six times weekly (or placebo) for 4 weeks, with 4 weeks of follow-up; 69 of 72 courses were completed per protocol, and the placebo group numbered 13.
cards.result: There was no significant ALT change on placebo. No major side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The unit is treatment courses (72), and the placebo group is small (n=13); a 4-week biochemical effect that vanishes on stopping is not disease modification. The publication does not name a branded product in this record.

cards.headline: 26-week randomised continuation trial (Orlent 2006): ALT response maintained in 60% on six-times-weekly, 24% on three-times-weekly and 9% on once-weekly continuation (P<0.001) — with NO significant histological improvement
cards.summary: 26-week randomised continuation trial (Orlent 2006): ALT response maintained in 60% on six-times-weekly, 24% on three-times-weekly and 9% on once-weekly continuation (P<0.001) — with NO significant histological improvement
cards.type: Randomised phase II continuation trial (responders randomised to dose frequency), 26 weeks total
cards.people: 121 patients with chronic hepatitis C (HCV-RNA-positive, elevated ALT, marked fibrosis or necro-inflammation, not eligible for interferon therapy) entered a 4-week induction of six glycyrrhizin infusions weekly; the 72 responders (60%) were randomised to continue for 22 weeks at six-times, three-times or once-weekly frequency.
cards.result: At the end of treatment the ALT response was maintained in 60%, 24% and 9% of patients in the six-times, three-times and once-weekly groups respectively (P<0.001). In ALT responders the necro-inflammation score improved non-significantly compared with ALT non-responders, and the authors conclude the ALT response did not translate into a significant histological improvement after 6 months. Quality of life (SF-36) increased on study drug, unrelated to ALT response.
cards.watchOut: Only the 72 of 121 entrants who responded to induction were randomised — a responder-enriched design; the histology result at 26 weeks is negative and is printed here, not buried.

cards.headline: Phase III placebo-controlled trial (Manns 2012): at least 50% ALT reduction at 12 weeks in 28.7% (five-times-weekly) and 29.0% (three-times-weekly) vs 7.0% on placebo (P<0.0001), with necro-inflammation improvement in about 45–46% at 52 weeks
cards.summary: Phase III placebo-controlled trial (Manns 2012): at least 50% ALT reduction at 12 weeks in 28.7% (five-times-weekly) and 29.0% (three-times-weekly) vs 7.0% on placebo (P<0.0001), with necro-inflammation improvement in about 45–46% at 52 weeks
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (12 weeks) plus randomised open continuation (40 weeks), in interferon non-responders
cards.people: 379 patients with chronic hepatitis C who had failed previous interferon-alpha-based (interferon plus ribavirin) therapy, randomised in a double-blind phase to intravenous glycyrrhizin five-times or three-times weekly or five-times-weekly placebo for 12 weeks, followed by a randomised open phase of glycyrrhizin five-times versus three-times weekly for 40 weeks.
cards.result: The proportion with at least 50% ALT reduction after 12 weeks was 28.7% on five-times-weekly (P<0.0001 vs placebo) and 29.0% on three-times-weekly glycyrrhizin (P<0.0001), versus 7.0% on placebo. The proportion with improvement in necro-inflammation after 52 weeks was 44.9% (five-times-weekly) and 46.0% (three-times-weekly); the authors also report improvement of necro-inflammation and fibrosis after 52 weeks. Treatment was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The 52-week histology phase was open and had no placebo arm, so the necro-inflammation figures are uncontrolled; the placebo-controlled evidence is the 12-week ALT endpoint. Interferon-era population — not a comparison with direct-acting antiviral therapy. The publication does not name a branded product in this record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the ALT-not-viraemia split leads — glycyrrhizin lowered ALT consistently across four randomised reports (phase III: at least 50% ALT reduction 28.7–29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo) while HCV viraemia did not change; histology improved only in the uncontrolled 52-week phase III limb and not at 26 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: the ALT-not-viraemia split leads — glycyrrhizin lowered ALT consistently across four randomised reports (phase III: at least 50% ALT reduction 28.7–29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo) while HCV viraemia did not change; histology improved only in the uncontrolled 52-week phase III limb and not at 26 weeks
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: four randomised reports (n=57; 72 treatment courses; 121 entered/72 responders randomised; n=379), all in interferon-ineligible or interferon-non-responder chronic hepatitis C. This shelf corrects the slate-13 count: two further glycyrrhizin-alone randomised reports (PMIDs 16905220 and 22762137) take the count from 2 to 4.
cards.result: ALT: mean decrease 26% versus 6% on placebo at 4 weeks with no viral clearance and no significant HCV-RNA effect (van Rossum 1999); 26% and 47% mean decreases on three- and six-times-weekly dosing versus no significant placebo change, disappearing after cessation (van Rossum 2001); response maintained in 60%/24%/9% by continuation frequency with no significant histological improvement at 26 weeks (Orlent 2006); at least 50% ALT reduction in 28.7%/29.0% versus 7.0% on placebo at 12 weeks (P<0.0001), with necro-inflammation improvement in 44.9%/46.0% at 52 weeks in the open phase (Manns 2012). Combination reports (glycyrrhizin plus ursodeoxycholic acid; interferon plus glycyrrhizin) are different questions and are not folded in. Glycyrrhizin's mineralocorticoid-type harms (hypokalaemia, hypertension) are the subject of pack #3467 — cross-point #3467.
cards.watchOut: Interferon-era evidence in patients who could not take or had failed interferon; it must not be presented against the direct-acting-antiviral standard of care, and never as an antiviral claim. The tested preparation is the intravenous glycyrrhizin formulation used in these trials (the Japanese glycyrrhizin preparation, Stronger Neo-Minophagen C, where the publications name it); none of the four records carded here names a branded product in its record, and that is stated plainly on each card. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Teprenone for gastric mucosal protection (one drug, three names — teprenone = geranylgeranylacetone = tetraprenylacetone): less NSAID/aspirin mucosal injury and fewer recurrences as an adjunct; endoscopic endpoints only
shelves.question: In adults with gastric mucosal injury — NSAID- or low-dose-aspirin-associated injury, active gastric ulcer, gastritis with erosions, and healed ulcer at risk of recurrence — does teprenone, alone or added to acid suppression, versus control improve endoscopic injury, ulcer healing and recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Anti-Ulcer Agents · Beijing · Diterpenes · Drug Administration Schedule · Dyspepsia · Female · Gastric Mucosa · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — endoscopic endpoints only), on an adjunct-and-prevention programme whose limbs are labelled and never pooled. IDENTITY, stated on the face: teprenone, geranylgeranylacetone (GGA) and tetraprenylacetone (TAP) are the SAME drug under three names in these publications — the five reports are not three drugs. No report tests teprenone as sole ulcer therapy against placebo. The prevention limbs: in long-term NSAID users (158 randomised), Lanza scores and dyspeptic symptom scores fell on teprenone and rose on control over 12 weeks; in low-dose-aspirin prevention (130 patients), gastric mucosal injury occurred in 13.38% on teprenone versus 40.0% on placebo — with NO ulcers in either arm, so that trial's endpoint is mucosal injury, not ulcer. The adjunct limbs: added to cimetidine, 4-week ulcer healing was 72.4% versus 52.1% (converging by 8 weeks); added to omeprazole, 12-week healing was similar but recurrence within 12 months was significantly less frequent; and as a sole-agent comparison in gastritis, geranylgeranylacetone beat cimetidine on endoscopic improvement (86.0% versus 64.8%). Endoscopic surrogate endpoints throughout; no bleeding or perforation outcome trial. An East Asian programme (China and Japan, with the aspirin trial from the same regional literature) — single-region flag on the face; the 1996 healing report is in a Chinese-language journal with an English abstract.

cards.headline: NSAID prevention trial (Gong 2019): in 158 randomised long-term NSAID users, Lanza scores and dyspeptic symptom scores FELL on teprenone and ROSE on NSAID alone over 12 weeks
cards.summary: NSAID prevention trial (Gong 2019): in 158 randomised long-term NSAID users, Lanza scores and dyspeptic symptom scores FELL on teprenone and ROSE on NSAID alone over 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised trial, teprenone + NSAID vs NSAID alone, endoscopic (Lanza score) prevention limb, 12 weeks
cards.people: 369 patients taking NSAIDs for at least 12 weeks were endoscopically screened; patients without gastroduodenal ulcer and without Helicobacter pylori infection were randomised to NSAID plus teprenone 150 mg/day (n=74) or NSAID only (n=84) for 12 weeks; 71 and 79 patients respectively were analysed. The study was conducted in Beijing, China (per the record's MeSH).
cards.result: After treatment, Lanza scores and dyspeptic symptom scores decreased significantly in the teprenone group while they increased in the control group (P<0.05), and the changes in both scores were greater in the teprenone group than in the control group (P<0.05). In subgroup analysis, the improvement was significant both in patients on long-term low-dose aspirin and in patients on other NSAIDs (P<0.05). The fetched abstract prints no numeric Lanza score values and none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Prevention limb with an endoscopic surrogate (Lanza score) and symptom scores — no ulcer, bleeding or perforation outcomes. Of 369 screened patients only 158 were randomised (those without ulcer or H. pylori at baseline), so this is a selected low-risk population.

cards.headline: Low-dose-aspirin prevention trial (Chitapanarux 2019): gastric mucosal injury in 13.38% on teprenone versus 40.0% on placebo at 12 weeks — with NO ulcers in either arm
cards.summary: Low-dose-aspirin prevention trial (Chitapanarux 2019): gastric mucosal injury in 13.38% on teprenone versus 40.0% on placebo at 12 weeks — with NO ulcers in either arm
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, teprenone vs placebo for prevention of low-dose-aspirin mucosal injury, 12 weeks
cards.people: 130 aspirin-naïve patients who required aspirin 100 mg/day for vascular protection, without gastroduodenal ulcer and without Helicobacter pylori infection, randomised double-blind to teprenone 150 mg/day (n=64) or placebo (n=66) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: There was no incidence of ulcer after 12 weeks in either group. The incidence of gastric mucosal injury was 13.38% on teprenone versus 40.0% on placebo (P=0.039). Mean change in modified Lanza score was 0.271 on teprenone versus 0.767 on placebo (P=0.003). Mucosal oedema, hyperaemia and haemorrhage scores and the change in gastrointestinal symptom rating scale did not differ between groups. There were no treatment-related adverse events. The authors conclude teprenone prevents gastric mucosal injury on low-dose aspirin, and that preventive effects on ulcers require further investigation.
cards.watchOut: The ulcer endpoint was zero in BOTH arms — this trial shows prevention of endoscopic mucosal injury, not of ulcers, and must not be quoted as ulcer prevention. H. pylori-negative, ulcer-free patients only.

cards.headline: Ulcer-healing adjunct trial (Hu 1996): cimetidine + teprenone healed 72.4% at 4 weeks versus 52.1% on cimetidine alone, converging by 8 weeks (93.1% vs 89.6%) — an add-on limb, in a Chinese-language journal
cards.summary: Ulcer-healing adjunct trial (Hu 1996): cimetidine + teprenone healed 72.4% at 4 weeks versus 52.1% on cimetidine alone, converging by 8 weeks (93.1% vs 89.6%) — an add-on limb, in a Chinese-language journal
cards.type: Randomised trial, cimetidine + teprenone vs cimetidine alone for active gastric ulcer healing (adjunct limb)
cards.people: 106 patients with active gastric ulcer proven by endoscopy, randomly allocated to cimetidine 800 mg at bedtime plus teprenone 50 mg three times daily (n=58) or cimetidine 800 mg at bedtime alone (n=48), with healing and quality of healing assessed at 4 and 8 weeks. The report is in a Chinese-language journal (Zhonghua nei ke za zhi) with an English abstract, from which these numbers are taken.
cards.result: At 4 weeks, 72.4% (42/58) on the combination versus 52.1% (25/48) on cimetidine alone had healed — a significant difference, indicating faster healing with the combination; by 8 weeks the rates had converged (93.1% [54/58] versus 89.6% [43/48]). Quality-of-healing (stage S2) rates were 34.5% versus 10.4% at 4 weeks and 50.0% versus 20.8% at 8 weeks (both P<0.05). Gastric mucosal hexosamine levels rose significantly after treatment in the combination group, which the authors link to stimulated mucosal glycoprotein synthesis.
cards.watchOut: Adjunct limb: teprenone was added to cimetidine, an H2-blocker-era regimen — this is not evidence for teprenone as sole ulcer therapy, and the 4-week advantage had converged by 8 weeks. Chinese-language journal with an English abstract, as stated on the card.

cards.headline: Ulcer-recurrence adjunct trial (Nagasawa 1998): omeprazole + tetraprenylacetone (the same drug as teprenone) — 12-week healing similar, but recurrence within 12 months significantly less frequent
cards.summary: Ulcer-recurrence adjunct trial (Nagasawa 1998): omeprazole + tetraprenylacetone (the same drug as teprenone) — 12-week healing similar, but recurrence within 12 months significantly less frequent
cards.type: Randomised trial, omeprazole + tetraprenylacetone vs omeprazole alone, healing and 12-month recurrence (adjunct limb)
cards.people: 95 patients with H. pylori-positive gastric ulcer were studied; 90 were randomised in the treatment comparison — omeprazole 20 mg alone (44 patients) or omeprazole 20 mg plus tetraprenylacetone (TAP) 150 mg (46 patients). Ulcer healing was assessed endoscopically at 12 weeks, and patients with healed ulcers were followed for a further 12 months without further therapy.
cards.result: The rate of ulcer healing at week 12 was similar with and without TAP. However, within 12 months of follow-up, ulcers recurred significantly less frequently in patients treated with omeprazole plus TAP than with omeprazole alone; the fetched abstract prints no recurrence percentages and none are claimed here. Alkaline-phosphatase staining showed the mucosal microvascular architecture of healed ulcers improved significantly more frequently with the combination. The authors conclude TAP plus omeprazole decreases ulcer recurrence through improved mucosal restoration.
cards.watchOut: Adjunct limb, and an identity point: tetraprenylacetone (TAP) is the same drug as teprenone/geranylgeranylacetone — do not read this as a second agent. The recurrence percentages are not printed in the fetched abstract and are not claimed; the healing limb itself was negative (similar rates).
cards.source: Nagasawa Y et al. Prevention of gastric ulcer recurrence with tetraprenylacetone. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 1998. PMID: 9489907. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gastritis trial (Sakamoto 2007): geranylgeranylacetone (the same drug as teprenone) versus cimetidine — endoscopic improvement 86.0% versus 64.8% and cure 80.0% versus 55.6%, but symptom disappearance NOT significant
cards.summary: Gastritis trial (Sakamoto 2007): geranylgeranylacetone (the same drug as teprenone) versus cimetidine — endoscopic improvement 86.0% versus 64.8% and cure 80.0% versus 55.6%, but symptom disappearance NOT significant
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind trial, geranylgeranylacetone vs cimetidine in gastritis with erosions (sole-agent comparison limb)
cards.people: 128 H. pylori-positive gastritis patients with dyspeptic symptoms and mucosal erosions and/or petechial haemorrhage, randomised double-blind in Japan to geranylgeranylacetone (GGA) 150 mg three times daily or cimetidine 400 mg twice daily for 2 weeks; 104 patients were analysed (50 GGA, 54 cimetidine).
cards.result: Endoscopic improvement rates were significantly higher on GGA (86.0% versus 64.8%; P=0.014), as were endoscopic cure rates (80.0% versus 55.6%; P=0.012). Symptom disappearance rates were 52.0% on GGA versus 42.6% on cimetidine, a difference that was not significant, and there was no significant difference in mucosal neutrophil infiltration. The authors conclude GGA appears more effective than cimetidine for chronic gastritis-associated erosion and petechial haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: Identity point: geranylgeranylacetone (GGA) is the same drug as teprenone. Two weeks only, endoscopic endpoints, and the patient-relevant endpoint (symptom disappearance) was not significant — the endoscopic win must be read with that. 128 randomised but only 104 analysed.
cards.source: Sakamoto C et al. Comparison of the effectiveness of geranylgeranylacetone with cimetidine in gastritis patients with dyspeptic symptoms and gastric lesions: a randomized, double-blind trial in Japan. Digestion. 2007. PMID: 17971666. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one drug under three names (teprenone = geranylgeranylacetone = tetraprenylacetone) — an adjunct-and-prevention programme with endoscopic benefits and no clinical-outcome trial; limbs labelled, never pooled
cards.summary: Synthesis: one drug under three names (teprenone = geranylgeranylacetone = tetraprenylacetone) — an adjunct-and-prevention programme with endoscopic benefits and no clinical-outcome trial; limbs labelled, never pooled
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the five carded reports, teprenone reduced endoscopic mucosal injury in NSAID users (Lanza and symptom scores falling on teprenone, rising on control) and in low-dose-aspirin users (mucosal injury 13.38% versus 40.0%, with no ulcers in either arm — an injury endpoint, not ulcer prevention). As an adjunct it sped early ulcer healing on cimetidine (72.4% versus 52.1% at 4 weeks, converged by 8 weeks) and reduced 12-month recurrence on omeprazole without changing 12-week healing; as a sole agent in gastritis it beat cimetidine endoscopically (86.0% versus 64.8%) without a significant symptom advantage. No report tests teprenone alone against placebo for ulcer healing, and no trial reports bleeding or perforation outcomes. The programme is East Asian (China and Japan reports carded, with the aspirin trial from the same regional literature); the 1996 report is in a Chinese-language journal with an English abstract. The rebamipide and sucralfate/misoprostol mucosal-protectant questions are homed on their own shelves and are not re-carded here (one-home rule).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Polaprezinc in gastric ulcer: spontaneous-ulcer trial NOT significant vs rebamipide (81.5% vs 74.3%); post-ESD, added to a PPI it cut ulcer-base protrusion (1.3% vs 20.7%) — two limbs, never pooled
shelves.question: In adults with gastric ulcer, does polaprezinc (zinc-L-carnosine) heal spontaneous ulcers versus rebamipide, and — added to a proton pump inhibitor after endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) — does it improve healing of the artificial ulcer versus PPI alone or versus rebamipide + PPI?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Anti-Ulcer Agents/therapeutic use · Carnosine/therapeutic use,analogs & derivatives · Gastroscopy · Stomach Ulcer/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Organometallic Compounds/therapeutic use · Zinc Compounds/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two limbs point differently and are never pooled. Spontaneous gastric ulcer: one double-blind trial (224 patients) found polaprezinc's 8-week endoscopic effective rate 81.48% versus 74.31% on rebamipide, NOT significant (P=0.1557). Post-ESD artificial ulcer: two trials — lansoprazole + polaprezinc cut ulcer-base protrusion versus lansoprazole alone (1.3% [1/77] vs 20.7% [16/77], P=0.0001, with better healing), and polaprezinc + pantoprazole was non-inferior to rebamipide + pantoprazole for 4-week healing (90.3% vs 91.4%). No placebo-controlled healing trial exists; the programme is Japanese/Chinese (single-region flag). Polaprezinc is the zinc-L-carnosine chelate as the publications name it.

cards.headline: SPONTANEOUS-ULCER LIMB — Shen 2022: polaprezinc vs rebamipide in spontaneous gastric ulcer — 8-week endoscopic effective rate 81.48% vs 74.31%, NOT significant (P=0.1557)
cards.summary: SPONTANEOUS-ULCER LIMB — Shen 2022: polaprezinc vs rebamipide in spontaneous gastric ulcer — 8-week endoscopic effective rate 81.48% vs 74.31%, NOT significant (P=0.1557)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy active-comparator trial — SPONTANEOUS gastric ulcer limb (polaprezinc vs rebamipide)
cards.people: 224 patients with gastric ulcer at 10 clinical centres in China, randomised to polaprezinc (111) or rebamipide tablets (113); the primary endpoint was the gastroscopy-confirmed effective treatment rate after 8 weeks.
cards.result: The 8-week endoscopic effective rate was 81.48% on polaprezinc versus 74.31% on rebamipide (P=0.1557 — not significant). Gastrointestinal symptom improvement was comparable at 4 weeks (44.44% vs 39.45%, P=0.4559) and 8 weeks (81.48% vs 77.06%, P=0.4223), and adverse events and drug reactions were similar in the two groups. The authors concluded efficacy and safety were similar to rebamipide — an active-comparator similarity reading, not a placebo-controlled healing result.
cards.watchOut: The spontaneous-ulcer limb rests on this single trial, against an active comparator, with a non-significant primary difference; there is no placebo-controlled healing trial of polaprezinc. It must not be pooled with the post-ESD limb below — different ulcer, different question.
cards.source: Shen W et al. Efficacy and safety of polaprezinc in the treatment of gastric ulcer: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, positive-controlled clinical trial. Medical engineering & physics. 2022. PMID: 35999163. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: POST-ESD LIMB — Inaba 2010: lansoprazole + polaprezinc vs lansoprazole alone after ESD — ulcer-base protrusion 1.3% (1/77) vs 20.7% (16/77), P=0.0001, with better healing
cards.summary: POST-ESD LIMB — Inaba 2010: lansoprazole + polaprezinc vs lansoprazole alone after ESD — ulcer-base protrusion 1.3% (1/77) vs 20.7% (16/77), P=0.0001, with better healing
cards.type: Randomised trial — POST-ESD artificial ulcer limb (lansoprazole + polaprezinc vs lansoprazole alone)
cards.people: 163 patients who underwent endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), randomly allocated to lansoprazole 30 mg/day alone or lansoprazole 30 mg/day plus polaprezinc 150 mg/day for the ESD-induced ulcer; 154 patients (77 per group) were assessed, with the ulcer condition blindly assessed two months after ESD.
cards.result: Ulcer-base protrusion — a healing-quality endpoint — occurred in 1.3% (1/77) with lansoprazole plus polaprezinc versus 20.7% (16/77) on lansoprazole alone (P=0.0001), and ulcer healing was significantly better with the combination (P<0.0001). Polaprezinc was the only significant factor differentiating patients with protrusion (n=17) from those without (n=137).
cards.watchOut: The winning endpoint is ulcer-base protrusion, a healing-quality measure, not a bleeding, perforation or complete-healing outcome; 163 were randomised but the protrusion analysis covers 154 assessed patients. Post-ESD artificial ulcers are not spontaneous ulcers — this limb is labelled and never pooled with the limb above.
cards.source: Inaba T et al. Basal protrusion of ulcers induced by endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) during treatment with proton pump inhibitors, and the suppressive effects of polaprezinc. Hepato-gastroenterology. 2010. PMID: 20698249. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: POST-ESD LIMB — Jung 2021: polaprezinc + pantoprazole vs rebamipide + pantoprazole after ESD — 4-week healing 90.3% vs 91.4% intention-to-treat, non-inferior
cards.summary: POST-ESD LIMB — Jung 2021: polaprezinc + pantoprazole vs rebamipide + pantoprazole after ESD — 4-week healing 90.3% vs 91.4% intention-to-treat, non-inferior
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial — POST-ESD artificial ulcer limb (polaprezinc + PPI vs rebamipide + PPI)
cards.people: 210 patients with ESD-induced ulcers, randomly allocated to polaprezinc 150 mg/day plus pantoprazole 40 mg/day or rebamipide 300 mg/day plus pantoprazole 40 mg/day; ulcer healing rate and ulcer condition were evaluated 4 weeks after dissection.
cards.result: Four-week ulcer healing was not inferior with polaprezinc plus pantoprazole versus rebamipide plus pantoprazole: 90.3% versus 91.4% in the intention-to-treat analysis (P=0.523) and 89.9% versus 91.1% per protocol (P=0.531). A short procedure time was an independent predictive factor for a high healing rate (odds ratio 0.975, 95% CI 0.958 to 0.993, P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority reading against another mucosal protectant added to the same PPI — it shows polaprezinc + PPI is no worse than rebamipide + PPI at 4 weeks, not that either beats PPI alone on healing rate; the PPI-alone comparison lives only in the Inaba 2010 card, on its protrusion endpoint.
