cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Two limbs, never pooled. Spontaneous gastric ulcer (one trial, 224 patients): polaprezinc's 8-week endoscopic effective rate was 81.48% versus 74.31% on rebamipide — not significant (P=0.1557), with similar symptoms and adverse events. Post-ESD artificial ulcer (two trials): added to a PPI, polaprezinc sharply reduced ulcer-base protrusion versus PPI alone (1.3% vs 20.7%) and was non-inferior to rebamipide + PPI for 4-week healing (90.3% vs 91.4%). No placebo-controlled healing trial exists in either limb, and the programme is Japanese/Chinese (single-region). Polaprezinc is the zinc-L-carnosine chelate compound as the publications name it. Cross-point: shelf S15-2-03 (teprenone) is the same mucosal-protectant family but a different drug — no class verdict is made here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Thymosin alpha-1 in chronic hepatitis B: the phase III double-blind trial was NEGATIVE (14% vs 4%, P=0.084) — positive readings come only from an untreated-control trial and an uncontrolled dose comparison
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B, does thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) versus placebo, no treatment or a lower dose improve HBV-DNA and HBeAg clearance, ALT normalisation and histology?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/therapeutic use · Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · DNA, Viral/blood · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis B e Antigens/blood · Hepatitis B virus/isolation & purification,physiology · Hepatitis B, Chronic/drug therapy,virology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Thymalfasin · Thymosin/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the failure leads: the programme's one phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial (97 patients) did NOT confirm efficacy (complete response 14% vs 4% on placebo, P=0.084; 25% vs 13% including delayed responses, P<0.11). The positive readings come from an untreated-control trial (98 patients; complete virological response 40.6% [26 weeks] and 26.5% [52 weeks] vs 9.4% at 18 months, separating only after treatment ended) and a 316-patient dose comparison with no untreated control arm. A 12-patient mixed-preparation pilot is labelled sub-floor and never load-bearing. Pre-nucleos(t)ide-era evidence (1991–2005) — not a comparison against entecavir/tenofovir.

cards.headline: THE FAILURE LEADS — Mutchnick 1999 phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial: complete response 14% on thymosin alpha-1 vs 4% on placebo, P=0.084 — the programme's largest blinded trial did NOT confirm efficacy
cards.summary: THE FAILURE LEADS — Mutchnick 1999 phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial: complete response 14% on thymosin alpha-1 vs 4% on placebo, P=0.084 — the programme's largest blinded trial did NOT confirm efficacy
cards.type: Phase III multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (thymosin alpha-1 / thymalfasin vs placebo)
cards.people: 97 patients with serum HBV-DNA- and HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg-positive for at least 12 months), randomised to thymosin alpha-1 1.6 mg (49) or placebo (48), twice weekly for 6 months, with 6 further months of follow-up; groups were comparable for age, sex, histological grading, aminotransferases and HBV-DNA at entry.
cards.result: Complete response — sustained HBV-DNA negativity during the 12-month study with negative HBV DNA and HBeAg at month 12 — occurred in 7 patients (14%) on thymosin alpha-1 versus 2 (4%) on placebo (P=0.084, not significant). Including delayed responses after the study period, sustained HBV-DNA loss with HBeAg negativity totalled 12 (25%) versus 6 (13%) (P<0.11, also not significant). The authors stated plainly: 'These results do not confirm observations of treatment efficacy reported in other clinical studies.'
cards.watchOut: This is the only double-blind placebo-controlled phase III trial in the programme and it missed its endpoint — it leads this shelf by design. The delayed-response totals are post-treatment constructions (responses accruing after treatment ended) and are labelled as such wherever they are quoted.
cards.source: Mutchnick MG et al. Thymosin alpha1 treatment of chronic hepatitis B: results of a phase III multicentre, randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled study. Journal of viral hepatitis. 1999. PMID: 10607256. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chien 1998: thymosin alpha-1 vs UNTREATED control — complete virological response at 18 months 40.6% (26 weeks) and 26.5% (52 weeks) vs 9.4% on control
cards.summary: Chien 1998: thymosin alpha-1 vs UNTREATED control — complete virological response at 18 months 40.6% (26 weeks) and 26.5% (52 weeks) vs 9.4% on control
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial vs untreated (no-treatment) control — NOT placebo-controlled or blinded treatment
cards.people: 98 patients with clinicopathologically proven chronic hepatitis B, randomly allocated to 26 weeks of thymosin alpha-1 1.6 mg subcutaneously twice weekly, the same regimen extended to 52 weeks, or an untreated control group followed for 18 months; groups were comparable in clinicopathological features at entry.
cards.result: At 18 months, complete virological response (clearance of serum HBV DNA and HBeAg) was 40.6% after 26 weeks of thymosin alpha-1 and 26.5% after 52 weeks, versus 9.4% in the untreated control group (26-week vs control P=.004; 52-week vs control P=.068). Complete response rates were similar across groups when first assessed at the end of therapy — responses accumulated after treatment ended. Blinded histological assessment showed significant improvement in treated patients, particularly lobular necroinflammation; no patient lost HBsAg, and no significant side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is no treatment, not placebo, and the separation appears only at 18 months — after therapy ended — so this positive reading rests on delayed, post-treatment response accrual in an unblinded comparison. It does not outweigh the negative double-blind phase III trial carded above.
cards.source: Chien RN et al. Efficacy of thymosin alpha1 in patients with chronic hepatitis B: a randomized, controlled trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1998. PMID: 9581695. cards.headline: Iino 2005: Japanese dose-comparison with NO untreated control — 0.8 mg vs 1.6 mg thymosin alpha-1; at 72 weeks, 1.6-mg group ALT normalisation 36.4%, HBV-DNA clearance 30%, HBeAg clearance 22.8%
cards.summary: Iino 2005: Japanese dose-comparison with NO untreated control — 0.8 mg vs 1.6 mg thymosin alpha-1; at 72 weeks, 1.6-mg group ALT normalisation 36.4%, HBV-DNA clearance 30%, HBeAg clearance 22.8%
cards.type: Randomised dose-comparison trial (0.8 mg vs 1.6 mg) — NO untreated or placebo control arm
cards.people: 316 Japanese patients with chronic hepatitis B, positive HBV DNA and abnormally high ALT, randomised to thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) 0.8 mg or 1.6 mg monotherapy for 24 weeks, with observation to 72 weeks (12 months after treatment ended). There was no placebo or untreated arm.
cards.result: At 72 weeks in the 1.6-mg group, ALT normalisation was 36.4%, HBV-DNA clearance 30% by branched-DNA assay (15% by transcription-mediated amplification) and HBeAg clearance 22.8%; the 0.8-mg group achieved similar efficacy rates overall, with a significantly better response to 1.6 mg in patients with advanced fibrosis (intragroup analysis; patients were not stratified by biopsy). All adverse drug reactions were mild, mostly liver-enzyme fluctuation, and adverse-event incidence was similar between doses.
cards.watchOut: With no untreated control, the 72-week clearance rates cannot be separated from the natural history of chronic hepatitis B — this card describes dose and safety, it is not efficacy evidence against a comparator, and it is never load-bearing for a benefit claim.
cards.source: Iino S et al. The efficacy and safety of thymosin alpha-1 in Japanese patients with chronic hepatitis B; results from a randomized clinical trial. Journal of viral hepatitis. 2005. cards.headline: SUB-FLOOR PILOT, labelled, never load-bearing — Mutchnick 1991: 12 patients only, MIXED thymosin preparations (fraction 5 or alpha-1) — HBV-DNA clearance 86% (6/7) vs 20% (1/5) on placebo
cards.summary: SUB-FLOOR PILOT, labelled, never load-bearing — Mutchnick 1991: 12 patients only, MIXED thymosin preparations (fraction 5 or alpha-1) — HBV-DNA clearance 86% (6/7) vs 20% (1/5) on placebo
cards.type: Placebo-controlled pilot trial — SUB-FLOOR (n=12, mixed thymosin fraction 5 / alpha-1 preparations), labelled, never load-bearing
cards.people: 12 patients with chronic hepatitis B (histological and biochemical active liver disease for at least 6 months, serum HBV-DNA- and HBsAg-positive): 7 received thymosin fraction 5 OR thymosin alpha-1 and 5 received placebo, twice weekly for 6 months, with assessment at 1 year. N=12 — printed on the face; this pilot is below the programme's reference floor in size and is never load-bearing.
cards.result: Serum aminotransferases improved significantly in thymosin-treated patients but not on placebo; 6 of 7 thymosin-treated patients (86%) versus 1 of 5 placebo patients (20%) cleared HBV DNA from serum (P<0.04, Fisher's exact test), and replicative HBV-DNA forms persisted in liver specimens of 4 of 5 placebo patients versus 1 of 7 thymosin patients. No significant side effects were seen, and responders' improvement was sustained over 26 ± 3 months of follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Twelve patients, and the treatment arm mixes two different preparations (thymosin fraction 5 and thymosin alpha-1), so even its striking percentages are not alpha-1-specific evidence. Carded only to complete the programme record, exactly as the commissioning row directs.
cards.source: Mutchnick MG et al. Thymosin treatment of chronic hepatitis B: a placebo-controlled pilot trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 1991. PMID: 1874487. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: A programme whose best trial was negative. The phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial (97 patients) missed its endpoint: complete response 14% versus 4% (P=0.084), and 25% versus 13% even after delayed post-treatment responses were counted (P<0.11). The positive readings come from weaker designs: an untreated-control trial (98 patients; 40.6% and 26.5% vs 9.4% at 18 months, separation only after treatment ended) and a 316-patient dose comparison with no untreated arm at all. The 12-patient mixed-preparation pilot is sub-floor and never load-bearing. All of this is pre-nucleos(t)ide-era evidence (1991–2005) and must not be read against the entecavir/tenofovir standard of care. A 2026 Cochrane review of thymosin alpha-1 in chronic hepatitis B (PMID 42713852, fetched this session, not carded — it pools combination-therapy trials that are different questions) likewise rated the certainty of evidence very low for nearly every outcome. Thymalfasin is thymosin alpha-1 as the publications give it.

cards.search: synthesis synthesis in patients with chronic hepatitis b, does thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) versus placebo, no treatment or a lower dose improve hbv-dna and hbeag clearance, alt normalisation and histology? synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. a programme whose best trial was negative. the phase iii double-blind placebo-controlled trial (97 patients) missed its endpoint: complete response 14% versus 4% (p=0.084), and 25% versus 13% even after delayed post-treatment responses were counted (p<0.11). the positive readings come from weaker designs: an untreated-control trial (98 patients; 40.6% and 26.5% vs 9.4% at 18 months, separation only after treatment ended) and a 316-patient dose comparison with no untreated arm at all. the 12-patient mixed-preparation pilot is sub-floor and never load-bearing. all of this is pre-nucleos(t)ide-era evidence (1991–2005) and must not be read against the entecavir/tenofovir standard of care. a 2026 cochrane review of thymosin alpha-1 in chronic hepatitis b (pmid 42713852, fetched this session, not carded — it pools combination-therapy trials that are different questions) likewise rated the certainty of evidence very low for nearly every outcome. thymalfasin is thymosin alpha-1 as the publications give it. see the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Normal liver stiffness by transient elastography: screened-healthy ranges 2.3–5.9 kPa (Hong Kong) and 3.9–5.3 kPa (Korean donors) vs 3.2–8.5 kPa in a free-living population
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal values for liver stiffness measured by transient elastography (FibroScan) — mean, spread and 5th–95th percentile range in kilopascals — by sex, body-mass index and metabolic status, and how far do screened-healthy reference ranges sit below general-population values that include people with the metabolic syndrome?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Body Mass Index · Elasticity · Female · Humans · Liver · Male · Metabolic Syndrome · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Reference Values · Risk Factors · Sex Factors · Ultrasonography · Adolescent · Asian People · Elasticity Imaging Techniques · Hong Kong · Living Donors · Republic of Korea · Tissue Donors · Young Adult · Case-Control Studies · Developing Countries · India · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Diseases · Obesity · ROC Curve
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, gastrointestinal / hepatic sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary elastography reference literature, and says so. Four independent populations, and the reference-population definition moves the upper limit more than the device does. Screened-healthy ranges are tight: 2.3–5.9 kPa in 530 rigorously screened Hong Kong Chinese volunteers (mean 4.1 kPa) and a 5th–95th percentile range of 3.9–5.3 kPa in 69 healthy Korean living donors (mean 4.6 kPa). Less-screened general populations run higher and wider: mean 5.49 kPa in 429 French check-up attendees, with metabolic syndrome at 6.51 kPa after adjustment; and a 5th–95th percentile range of 3.2–8.5 kPa in 437 healthy Indian adults, in whom both lean and obese subjects were stiffer than normal-BMI subjects. The screened Hong Kong ceiling (5.9 kPa) and the unscreened Indian ceiling (8.5 kPa) are different kinds of 'normal' and are never merged on this shelf. All values are transient-elastography (FibroScan) values in kilopascals — not interchangeable with MR-elastography or shear-wave values — and measurement failure rises steeply with BMI (4.6% overall, 88% at BMI >40 in the French cohort). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: General-population check-up cohort (Roulot 2008): mean liver stiffness 5.49 ± 1.59 kPa in 429 apparently healthy adults — men 5.81 vs women 5.23 kPa; metabolic syndrome 6.51 vs 5.33 kPa after adjustment; measurement failure 88% at BMI >40
cards.summary: General-population check-up cohort (Roulot 2008): mean liver stiffness 5.49 ± 1.59 kPa in 429 apparently healthy adults — men 5.81 vs women 5.23 kPa; metabolic syndrome 6.51 vs 5.33 kPa after adjustment; measurement failure 88% at BMI >40
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transient-elastography liver stiffness, general-population check-up cohort)
cards.people: 429 consecutive apparently healthy adults with no overt cause of liver disease and normal liver enzymes, undergoing a free medical check-up (prospective study); liver stiffness measured by transient elastography. The metabolic syndrome was present in 59 subjects (13.7%).
cards.result: Mean liver stiffness was 5.49 ± 1.59 kPa. Values were higher in men than women (5.81 ± 1.54 vs 5.23 ± 1.59 kPa, P = 0.0002) and in subjects with BMI >30 kg/m² (6.26 ± 1.89 vs 5.37 ± 1.51 kPa, P = 0.0003). After adjustment for sex and BMI, stiffness was higher with the metabolic syndrome than without (6.51 ± 1.64 vs 5.33 ± 1.51 kPa, P < 0.0001). Transient elastography failed in 4.6% of cases overall, and the failure rate rose with BMI, reaching 88% above 40 kg/m².
cards.watchOut: 'Apparently healthy' check-up attendees, not a rigorously screened reference population — 13.7% had the metabolic syndrome, which is exactly why this cohort's values sit above the screened cohorts below; its failure rate at high BMI is part of the number.
cards.source: Roulot D et al. Liver stiffness values in apparently healthy subjects: influence of gender and metabolic syndrome. Journal of hepatology. 2008. PMID: 18222014. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rigorously screened Hong Kong cohort (Fung 2013): reference range 2.3–5.9 kPa (mean 4.1 ± 0.89) in the 530 volunteers retained from 2,528 after exclusions; median stiffness fell with age, 4.2 kPa under 25 years to 3.4 kPa over 55
cards.summary: Rigorously screened Hong Kong cohort (Fung 2013): reference range 2.3–5.9 kPa (mean 4.1 ± 0.89) in the 530 volunteers retained from 2,528 after exclusions; median stiffness fell with age, 4.2 kPa under 25 years to 3.4 kPa over 55
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transient-elastography liver stiffness, rigorously screened healthy volunteers)
cards.people: 2,528 healthy volunteers recruited from the general population and the Red Cross Transfusion Center in Hong Kong, all with questionnaire, anthropometry, fasting blood tests, abdominal ultrasound and transient elastography; 1,998 were excluded (abnormal ultrasound, chronic medical conditions, abnormal blood tests, high BMI, high blood pressure or invalid scans), leaving 530 without known liver disease.
cards.result: The reference range in the 530 retained subjects was 2.3 to 5.9 kPa (mean 4.1, SD 0.89). Median stiffness was higher in men than women (4.3 vs 4.0 kPa, P < 0.001) and declined with age, from a median of 4.2 kPa in those under 25 years to 3.4 kPa in those over 55 years (P = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The tightest ceiling on this shelf (5.9 kPa) is a product of the screening: four of five recruited volunteers were excluded. It is a screened-healthy range, not a general-population range, and must not be applied to unscreened patients.
cards.source: Fung J et al. Defining normal liver stiffness range in a normal healthy Chinese population without liver disease. PloS one. 2013. PMID: 24386446. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy living donors, South Korea (Kim 2010): mean 4.6 ± 0.5 kPa with a 5th–95th percentile normal range of 3.9–5.3 kPa in 69 donors — no age or sex effect
cards.summary: Healthy living donors, South Korea (Kim 2010): mean 4.6 ± 0.5 kPa with a 5th–95th percentile normal range of 3.9–5.3 kPa in 69 donors — no age or sex effect
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transient-elastography liver stiffness, healthy living donors)
cards.people: 69 healthy living liver and kidney donors in South Korea (mean age 38.9 ± 11.9 years; 35 men, 34 women), none with diabetes, hypertension, hepatitis B or C, heart dysfunction, liver dysfunction or the metabolic syndrome; liver histology was available in 12 liver donors (8 normal, 4 with steatosis under 5%). Measurement failure rate 2.7%.
cards.result: Mean liver stiffness was 4.6 ± 0.5 kPa (range 3.3–5.6 kPa). Values did not differ significantly between men (4.6 ± 0.6 kPa) and women (4.5 ± 0.5 kPa, P = 0.636), nor by age (P = 0.851). The normal range, from the 5th and 95th percentiles, was 3.9 to 5.3 kPa — the narrowest range on this shelf, from its smallest and most selected population.
cards.watchOut: Only 69 donors — transplant-selected, metabolically clean volunteers; the absence of a sex effect here, against clear sex effects in the larger cohorts, is most plausibly a small-sample finding, and the 3.9–5.3 kPa range should not displace the larger cohorts' ranges.
cards.source: Kim SU et al. What are 'true normal' liver stiffness values using FibroScan?: a prospective study in healthy living liver and kidney donors in South Korea. Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver. 2010. PMID: 19929903. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Free-living Indian population cohort (Das 2012): 5th–95th percentile range 3.2–8.5 kPa in 437 healthy adults — both lean (BMI <18.5) and obese healthy subjects were stiffer than normal-BMI subjects
cards.summary: Free-living Indian population cohort (Das 2012): 5th–95th percentile range 3.2–8.5 kPa in 437 healthy adults — both lean (BMI <18.5) and obese healthy subjects were stiffer than normal-BMI subjects
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transient-elastography liver stiffness, free-living population cohort)
cards.people: 437 healthy subjects with normal alanine aminotransferase recruited from a free-living population project (the Birbhum Population Project, a health and demographic surveillance system in India); liver stiffness measured by transient elastography (FibroScan). A separate liver-disease clinic group in the same report is not part of this reference card.
cards.result: In healthy subjects, the 5th and 95th percentile values — the study's normal range — were 3.2 and 8.5 kPa. Healthy subjects with a BMI below 18.5 kg/m² had higher stiffness than normal-BMI subjects, comparable to obese subjects (6.05 ± 1.78 vs 5.51 ± 1.59 and 6.60 ± 1.21 kPa respectively). Mean stiffness in the healthy group overall was 5.63 ± 1.64 kPa.
cards.watchOut: The widest 'normal' range on this shelf (to 8.5 kPa) comes from the least-screened population: it describes a free-living population including lean, undernourished subjects, and is a different kind of normal from the screened Hong Kong and donor ranges — never merged with them.
cards.source: Das K et al. "Normal" liver stiffness measure (LSM) values are higher in both lean and obese individuals: a population-based study from a developing country. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2012. PMID: 21952989. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: screened-healthy transient-elastography ranges sit at 2.3–5.9 kPa (Hong Kong) and 3.9–5.3 kPa (Korean donors), while general-population values run higher and wider (mean 5.49 kPa in France; 3.2–8.5 kPa in India) — the population screened defines the 'normal'
cards.summary: Synthesis: screened-healthy transient-elastography ranges sit at 2.3–5.9 kPa (Hong Kong) and 3.9–5.3 kPa (Korean donors), while general-population values run higher and wider (mean 5.49 kPa in France; 3.2–8.5 kPa in India) — the population screened defines the 'normal'
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep (gastrointestinal / hepatic sections; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary elastography reference literature). Across four independent populations the pattern is consistent: rigorous screening produces low, tight ranges (Fung 2013: 2.3–5.9 kPa, mean 4.1; Kim 2010: 3.9–5.3 kPa, mean 4.6), while check-up and free-living populations produce higher means and higher ceilings (Roulot 2008: mean 5.49 kPa, metabolic syndrome 6.51 kPa after adjustment; Das 2012: 3.2–8.5 kPa). Sex (men stiffer in the two large cohorts), BMI at both extremes, and the metabolic syndrome all shift values; measurement failure rises steeply with BMI. All values are FibroScan transient-elastography kilopascals. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: four independent datasets agree on the structure — a screened-healthy centre near 4–5 kPa with population definition, sex and metabolic status as the movers — while each population's exact limits stay its own.
cards.watchOut: Never print one population's upper limit as the universal normal ceiling: 5.9 kPa (screened) and 8.5 kPa (free-living) answer different questions, and neither transfers to MR elastography or shear-wave elastography.

shelves.title: Biofeedback for faecal incontinence: the largest trial found no benefit over standard care with advice (53% vs 54% improved); a smaller trial beat exercises alone
shelves.question: In adults with faecal incontinence, does biofeedback-based sphincter training — versus standard care/advice, versus pelvic floor exercises alone, and in home versus office delivery — reduce incontinence episodes and severity and improve quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anal Canal/physiopathology · Biofeedback, Psychology · Counseling · Defecation · Depression/etiology,/psychology · Electromyography · Exercise Therapy · Fecal Incontinence/physiopathology,/psychology,/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pressure · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and the largest trial is negative, printed first. The 171-patient four-arm trial found biofeedback yielded no greater benefit than standard care with advice (53% improved on hospital biofeedback vs 54% on advice alone), while every group improved on episodes, continence score and quality of life. Against a narrower comparator the picture differs: after a medication/education run-in, biofeedback plus exercises beat exercises alone on adequate relief at 3 months (76% vs 41%). The remaining limbs answer different questions and are never pooled: two biofeedback exercise regimens did not differ (72 participants), and home biofeedback was non-inferior to office biofeedback in 30 patients. The base supports 'structured conservative therapy helps; the biofeedback component's added value over good standard care is unproven.' All trials are unblinded behavioural interventions with subjective endpoints. The tested programmes are named as the publications give them (computer-assisted sphincter pressure biofeedback; manometric biofeedback) under the programme-naming exception. Cross-points, not folded in: sacral nerve stimulation (pack #2659) and anal bulking injections (pack #5318); biofeedback for dyssynergic defecation is a different, opposite-physiology question (pack #2517).

cards.headline: Largest trial (Norton 2003): biofeedback yielded NO greater benefit than standard care with advice — 53% improved on hospital biofeedback versus 54% on advice alone (171 patients, four arms)
cards.summary: Largest trial (Norton 2003): biofeedback yielded NO greater benefit than standard care with advice — 53% improved on hospital biofeedback versus 54% on advice alone (171 patients, four arms)
cards.type: Four-arm randomised controlled trial of biofeedback vs standard care/advice and exercises in faecal incontinence
cards.people: 171 patients with faecal incontinence randomised to one of four groups: (1) standard care (advice); (2) advice plus instruction on sphincter exercises; (3) hospital-based computer-assisted sphincter pressure biofeedback; or (4) hospital biofeedback plus use of a home electromyogram biofeedback device, with outcomes including diaries, symptom questionnaires, continence score, patient rating of change, quality of life, psychological status and anal manometry.
cards.result: Biofeedback yielded no greater benefit than standard care with advice (53% improved in group 3 vs 54% in group 1), and there was no difference between the groups on any measure — while all groups improved: incontinence episodes fell from a median of 2 to 0 per week (P < 0.001), continence score (worst = 20) fell from a median of 11 to 8 (P < 0.001), disease-specific and general quality of life and psychological scores improved, and resting, squeeze and sustained squeeze pressures all rose (all P < 0.002). Improvements were largely maintained 1 year after finishing treatment. The authors concluded that conservative therapy improves continence and quality of life, but neither pelvic floor exercises nor biofeedback was superior to standard care supplemented by advice and education.
cards.watchOut: This is the load-bearing trial of the shelf — the largest, and the only one testing biofeedback against full standard care — and it is negative for the biofeedback component. Everyone got better; biofeedback was not the reason they got better more.
cards.source: Norton C et al. Randomized controlled trial of biofeedback for fecal incontinence. Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 14598248. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Heymen 2009: after a run-in that had already treated 21% adequately, manometric biofeedback plus exercises beat exercises alone — adequate relief 76% vs 41% at 3 months (108 patients)
cards.summary: Heymen 2009: after a run-in that had already treated 21% adequately, manometric biofeedback plus exercises beat exercises alone — adequate relief 76% vs 41% at 3 months (108 patients)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of manometric biofeedback plus pelvic floor exercises vs pelvic floor exercises alone, after a conservative-management run-in
cards.people: 108 patients (83 women; average age 59.6 years) with faecal incontinence who remained symptomatic after a run-in of medication, education and behavioural strategies — a run-in that adequately treated 21% of those who entered it — randomised to pelvic floor exercises alone (63 patients) or manometric biofeedback plus pelvic floor exercises (45 patients); both groups were taught behavioural strategies to avoid incontinence.
cards.result: At 3 months, biofeedback patients had significantly greater reductions in the Fecal Incontinence Severity Index (P=0.01) and fewer days with faecal incontinence (P=0.083); biofeedback increased anal canal squeeze pressure more than exercises alone (P=0.014) with less abdominal tension during squeeze (P=0.001). Adequate relief was reported by 76% of biofeedback patients versus 41% on exercises alone (P < 0.001). At 12 months the severity-index advantage persisted (P=0.03), with more biofeedback patients continuing to report adequate relief (P=0.056). The authors concluded the investigation provides definitive support for the efficacy of biofeedback.
cards.watchOut: A positive trial, but read its comparator and its funnel: it tests biofeedback as an add-on to exercises alone (not against the full advice-and-education standard care of the Norton trial), in patients pre-selected by failing a run-in that had already treated a fifth of entrants adequately. It does not overturn the larger negative trial.
cards.source: Heymen S et al. Randomized controlled trial shows biofeedback to be superior to pelvic floor exercises for fecal incontinence. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2009. PMID: 19966605. cards.headline: Bartlett 2011: two biofeedback exercise regimens did not differ — severity fell from 11.5/20 to 5.0/20 in both groups combined (72 participants); compliance, not regimen, predicted outcome
cards.summary: Bartlett 2011: two biofeedback exercise regimens did not differ — severity fell from 11.5/20 to 5.0/20 in both groups combined (72 participants); compliance, not regimen, predicted outcome
cards.type: Randomised comparison of two biofeedback exercise regimens (standard vs rapid-squeeze) in faecal incontinence — a regimen limb, not an efficacy-versus-care trial
cards.people: 72 participants (19 men; mean age 62.1 years) with faecal incontinence at an anorectal physiology clinic in Townsville, Australia, randomised to the standard clinical protocol (sustained submaximal anal and pelvic floor exercises; 37 patients) or an alternative regimen adding rapid squeezes (35 patients), over 5 clinic sessions with home practice and a postal survey 2 years later; 69 completed treatment.
cards.result: No significant differences were found between the two exercise groups at the beginning or end of the study, or as a result of treatment, in objective, quality-of-life or severity measures. Across both groups, faecal incontinence severity decreased significantly (11.5/20 to 5.0/20; P < 0.001), 86% (59/69) of participants reported improved continence, and quality of life improved significantly (all P < 0.001), sustained 2 years later. Patients who practised at least the prescribed number of exercises had better outcomes than those who practised fewer.
cards.watchOut: There is no non-biofeedback control group: this trial cannot say whether biofeedback works, only that adding rapid squeezes to the regimen changed nothing. The within-group improvement mirrors the Norton trial's pattern — structured programmes improve symptoms regardless of the specific component tested.
cards.source: Bartlett L et al. Biofeedback for fecal incontinence: a randomized study comparing exercise regimens. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2011. PMID: 21654252. cards.headline: Xiang 2021: home biofeedback was non-inferior to office biofeedback — weekly episodes fell significantly in both arms (30 patients)
cards.summary: Xiang 2021: home biofeedback was non-inferior to office biofeedback — weekly episodes fell significantly in both arms (30 patients)
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial of home vs office biofeedback delivery in faecal incontinence — a delivery-setting limb, n=30
cards.people: 30 patients with faecal incontinence (at least 1 episode per week; 26 women, 4 men) randomised to home biofeedback therapy (20 patients) using a novel device providing resistance training and electrical stimulation with voice-guided instructions, performed daily, or office biofeedback therapy (10 patients) in six weekly sessions, for 6 weeks; both methods involved anal strength, endurance and coordination training.
cards.result: Weekly faecal incontinence episodes decreased significantly after home therapy (change 4.7 ± 1.8, 95% CI as reported; P=0.003 versus baseline) and after office therapy (3.7 ± 1.6; P=0.0003), and home therapy was non-inferior to office therapy (P=0.2). Severity scores improved significantly in the home group (P < 0.02), bowel pattern, bowel control and quality-of-life domains improved significantly in the home arm (P < 0.023), and resting and maximum squeeze pressures improved in both groups without group differences. The authors concluded home biofeedback is safe, effective and could improve access.
cards.watchOut: A 30-patient delivery comparison with unequal arms (20 vs 10): it addresses where biofeedback can be given, not whether it beats standard care, and its non-inferiority read rests on very small numbers. Labelled a delivery limb, never load-bearing for efficacy.
cards.source: Xiang X et al. Randomized controlled trial of home biofeedback therapy versus office biofeedback therapy for fecal incontinence. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The limbs must not be pooled. Efficacy versus care is two trials and they split by comparator: the largest trial (n=171) found biofeedback no better than standard care with advice (53% vs 54% improved), while a 108-patient trial found biofeedback plus exercises superior to exercises alone (adequate relief 76% vs 41%) in patients who had already failed a conservative run-in. The regimen limb (n=72) found no difference between two biofeedback programmes, and the delivery limb (n=30) found home treatment non-inferior to office treatment. Two further retrieved reports (an acupuncture-versus-biofeedback trial, 2024, and a 2026 home-based trial) were retrieved at summary level only in the mining session and are not carded here. What the base supports is structured conservative therapy with advice and education; whether the biofeedback component itself adds benefit over that standard remains unproven.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Rikkunshito for functional dyspepsia: the largest trial missed its primary endpoint (P=0.09); DREAM was positive in a placebo-run-in-enriched population
shelves.question: In patients with functional dyspepsia, does rikkunshito (TJ-43) versus placebo (or versus a prokinetic) improve global dyspepsia response, epigastric pain and postprandial fullness?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Drugs, Chinese Herbal/therapeutic use · Dyspepsia/blood,/drug therapy · Female · Ghrelin/blood · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the negative primary leads. The largest trial (247 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled) missed its primary endpoint: global-assessment responders were 33.6% on rikkunshito versus 23.8% on placebo at 8 weeks, P=0.09 — not significant — although epigastric pain improved significantly (P=0.04). The DREAM study was positive on its overall-treatment-efficacy endpoint (P=.019), but it randomised only the 128 of 192 enrolled patients who remained symptomatic after a single-blind placebo run-in — an enriched population, labelled as such. The two remaining limbs are small and never load-bearing: a Belgian crossover mechanistic trial (23 completers) found no significant change in gastric accommodation or intragastric pressure, with high placebo responses on symptom diaries; and a domperidone-comparator trial (27 patients) found symptom improvement in both groups. PRODUCT NAMING (herb rule): the tested preparation is rikkunshito (TJ-43), as the programme's publications name the product; where a carded publication's fetched record names no product code or company, its card says so plainly, and other preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. A Japanese programme with one small Belgian limb — region flag on the face. The chemotherapy-induced-nausea rikkunshito trials ask a different question and are not folded in; STW 5, a different herbal product, stays at pack #4235.

cards.headline: Largest trial (Suzuki 2014): rikkunshito MISSED its primary endpoint — global responders 33.6% vs 23.8% on placebo at 8 weeks, P=0.09 (247 randomised); epigastric pain did improve (P=0.04)
cards.summary: Largest trial (Suzuki 2014): rikkunshito MISSED its primary endpoint — global responders 33.6% vs 23.8% on placebo at 8 weeks, P=0.09 (247 randomised); epigastric pain did improve (P=0.04)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of rikkunshito in functional dyspepsia, 8 weeks
cards.people: 247 patients with functional dyspepsia in a Japanese multicentre trial, randomly assigned to rikkunshito 2.5 g or placebo three times daily for 8 weeks; the primary endpoint was the proportion of responders at 8 weeks by global patient assessment, with a four-symptom severity scale and plasma ghrelin levels also assessed.
cards.result: At week 8 the rikkunshito group had more global-assessment responders than placebo (33.6% vs 23.8%), but this did not reach statistical significance (P=0.09) — the primary endpoint was not met. Epigastric pain improved significantly (P=0.04) and postprandial fullness tended to improve (P=0.06). Rikkunshito was relatively more effective among Helicobacter pylori-infected participants (40.0% vs 20.5%; P=0.07) and seemed less effective among uninfected participants (29.3% vs 25.6%; P=0.72); among H. pylori-positive individuals, acyl ghrelin levels improved only in the rikkunshito group. There were no severe adverse events in either group.
cards.watchOut: The load-bearing trial of this shelf, and its headline is a missed primary endpoint: the significant epigastric-pain result is one symptom among several tested, in a trial whose global endpoint failed. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation as rikkunshito, 'a standardized Japanese herbal medicine', with its dose; it names no TJ-43 code and no company.
cards.source: Suzuki H et al. Randomized clinical trial: rikkunshito in the treatment of functional dyspepsia--a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2014. PMID: 24766295. Registry ID: UMIN000003954. cards.headline: DREAM study (Tominaga 2018): overall treatment efficacy was higher on rikkunshito at 8 weeks (P=.019) — in the 128 of 192 patients still symptomatic after a placebo run-in (an enriched population)
cards.summary: DREAM study (Tominaga 2018): overall treatment efficacy was higher on rikkunshito at 8 weeks (P=.019) — in the 128 of 192 patients still symptomatic after a placebo run-in (an enriched population)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (DREAM) of rikkunshito in functional dyspepsia after a single-blind placebo run-in, 8 weeks
cards.people: 192 patients with functional dyspepsia meeting Rome III criteria, without Helicobacter pylori infection, predominant heartburn or depression, enrolled at 56 hospitals in Japan; after 2 weeks of single-blind placebo treatment, the 128 patients with continuous symptoms were randomly assigned to 8 weeks of rikkunshito (64 patients) or placebo (61 patients) in a double-blind trial — the randomised arms as printed total 125 of the 128 randomised.
cards.result: Rikkunshito increased the primary endpoint, global assessment of overall treatment efficacy, compared with placebo at 8 weeks (P=.019). Upper gastrointestinal symptoms improved on the PAGI-SYM, Global Overall Symptom and modified reflux-symptom scales at 8 weeks, especially postprandial fullness/early satiety (P=.015 and P=.001) and bloating (P=.007 and P=.002) subscales at 4 and 8 weeks. Anxiety/depression scores (HADS) improved at 8 weeks (P=.027) and the improvement correlated with symptom improvement. The authors concluded rikkunshito may simultaneously treat gastrointestinal and psychological symptoms in functional dyspepsia.
cards.watchOut: A positive trial in an enriched population: a third of enrolled patients (64 of 192) left the trial before randomisation because the placebo run-in had already settled their symptoms, so DREAM's result describes placebo-run-in non-responders with H. pylori-negative Rome III dyspepsia — not functional dyspepsia generally, and not a contradiction of the larger trial's missed primary. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as rikkunshito, a Japanese herbal medicine; it names no product code and no company.
cards.source: Tominaga K et al. Rikkunshito simultaneously improves dyspepsia correlated with anxiety in patients with functional dyspepsia: A randomized clinical trial (the DREAM study). Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2018. PMID: 29498457. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Belgian crossover mechanistic trial (Masuy 2020): rikkunshito did NOT significantly change intragastric pressure or gastric accommodation; diary symptoms improved on rikkunshito and on placebo alike (23 completers)
cards.summary: Belgian crossover mechanistic trial (Masuy 2020): rikkunshito did NOT significantly change intragastric pressure or gastric accommodation; diary symptoms improved on rikkunshito and on placebo alike (23 completers)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover mechanistic trial of rikkunshito in Belgian functional dyspepsia (postprandial distress syndrome)
cards.people: 23 patients with functional dyspepsia (postprandial distress syndrome) in Belgium who completed a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover: after a 2-week run-in, rikkunshito or matching placebo 2.5 g three times daily for 4 weeks, separated by a 4-week washout; intragastric pressure was measured to evaluate gastric accommodation and motility, with symptom diaries and validated questionnaires throughout.
cards.result: Intragastric pressure was numerically but not significantly lower after rikkunshito compared with baseline and placebo (P=.14), and no differences were found in gastric accommodation, nutrient volume tolerance, or symptoms assessed during the pressure measurements. Early satiation and postprandial fullness on the daily diary decreased after rikkunshito compared with baseline (P < 0.041 for both), but placebo also improved most other symptoms assessed, with similarly high placebo effects on the symptom diary and questionnaires. No significant changes occurred in visceral-sensitivity scores and no adverse reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: A small physiology limb (23 completers), labelled and never load-bearing: its mechanistic endpoints were null and its symptom readings are inseparable from the large placebo responses the authors themselves report. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as rikkunshito, a traditional Kampo medicine, with its dose; it names no product code and no company.
cards.source: Masuy I et al. The effect of rikkunshito on gastrointestinal symptoms and gastric motor function: The first study in a Belgian functional dyspepsia population. Neurogastroenterology and motility. 2020. PMID: 31608532. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Domperidone-comparator trial (Arai 2012): dyspeptic symptoms improved in BOTH groups over 4 weeks; plasma acylated ghrelin rose on rikkunshito (27 patients — an active-comparator limb)
cards.summary: Domperidone-comparator trial (Arai 2012): dyspeptic symptoms improved in BOTH groups over 4 weeks; plasma acylated ghrelin rose on rikkunshito (27 patients — an active-comparator limb)
cards.type: Parallel randomised controlled trial of rikkunshito vs domperidone in functional dyspepsia, 4 weeks — active-comparator limb
cards.people: 27 patients with functional dyspepsia in Japan, in a parallel randomised controlled trial of rikkunshito or domperidone for 4 weeks; the overall change in dyspeptic symptoms was evaluated by the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS), and plasma acylated ghrelin levels were measured.
cards.result: There was a significant improvement in dyspeptic symptoms in both groups on the GSRS score, with no between-group superiority result reported in the fetched record. Acylated ghrelin levels increased significantly in plasma in the rikkunshito group at 2 weeks (P < 0.05), and improvements in reflux (r=−0.73, P=0.04) and indigestion (r=−0.76, P=0.03) symptoms in the rikkunshito group correlated with the increase in acylated ghrelin. The authors concluded rikkunshito improves upper gastrointestinal symptoms in functional dyspepsia, accompanied by increased acylated ghrelin.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-seven patients, no placebo arm, and improvement in both groups: this limb can show rikkunshito performed alongside an established prokinetic, not that it beats anything. Its ghrelin findings are mechanistic. Never load-bearing. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as rikkunshito, a traditional Japanese medicine; it names no product code and no company.

cards.result: A split programme whose largest and cleanest test failed its primary endpoint. Suzuki 2014 (n=247) found global responders 33.6% versus 23.8% on placebo, P=0.09 — not significant — with a significant epigastric-pain improvement as a secondary reading. DREAM (128 randomised of 192 enrolled, after a placebo run-in removed run-in responders) found overall treatment efficacy higher on rikkunshito, P=.019, in H. pylori-negative patients. The Belgian crossover (23 completers) found no motility mechanism and placebo-sized symptom effects; the domperidone limb (27 patients) improved on both drugs. The preparation tested is rikkunshito (TJ-43) as the programme's publications name the product; the standing herb-rule statement applies — other preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness, and current products are not shown equivalent to the tested preparation by anything on this shelf.

shelves.title: Racecadotril for acute diarrhoea in adults: one small positive placebo trial; as effective as loperamide in larger comparisons, with less rebound constipation
shelves.question: In adults with acute (watery) diarrhoea, does racecadotril versus placebo reduce stool output and duration, and how does it compare with loperamide on duration and rebound constipation?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Antidiarrheals/therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neprilysin/antagonists & inhibitors · Protease Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Thiorphan/adverse effects,/analogs & derivatives,/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as effective as loperamide, with less rebound constipation; not shown superior to it, and the placebo base is thin. This shelf cards the adult slice only: the children's question is homed at live #1361, and the one adult racecadotril-versus-loperamide limb carded inside the loperamide shelf (Vetel 1999, pack #2478) stays homed there and is cross-pointed, never re-carded here. The placebo evidence is a single small trial (70 adults): stool weight on day 1 was significantly lower on racecadotril (P=0.025), with fewer diarrhoeic stools after 1 day (P=0.027) and less post-treatment abdominal distension (5.6% vs 18.2%). The comparative base shows equivalence, not superiority: in 945 outpatients diarrhoea resolved in 55.0 hours in both groups, with significantly less constipation on racecadotril (16% vs 25%); in 62 outpatients clinical success was 95.7% versus 92.0%, with median duration numerically longer on racecadotril (19.5 vs 13 hours) and more reactive constipation on loperamide (29.0% vs 12.9%). Two of the three carded trials are single-blind. Era flag: a 1999–2005 programme, largely pre-dating current oral-rehydration-era adult diarrhoea guidance.

cards.headline: Placebo trial (Hamza 1999): racecadotril significantly reduced day-1 stool weight (P=0.025) and diarrhoeic stools after 1 day (P=0.027) in 70 adults — the programme's only placebo test
cards.summary: Placebo trial (Hamza 1999): racecadotril significantly reduced day-1 stool weight (P=0.025) and diarrhoeic stools after 1 day (P=0.027) in 70 adults — the programme's only placebo test
cards.type: Two-centre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of racecadotril in adults with acute diarrhoea
cards.people: 70 adult patients with acute diarrhoea in a two-centre, double-blind, parallel-group randomised study of racecadotril 100 mg three times daily versus placebo; the objective criterion of antisecretory activity was stool weight.
cards.result: Racecadotril produced a significant (P=0.025) decrease in stool weight during the first day of treatment compared with placebo, and was associated with significantly fewer diarrhoeic stools than placebo after 1 day of treatment (P=0.027). Racecadotril and placebo were equally well tolerated, with a similar frequency of symptoms and signs after 4 days; fewer patients on racecadotril suffered abdominal distension following treatment (5.6% vs 18.2% on placebo). The authors concluded racecadotril acts rapidly to resolve acute diarrhoea with an adverse-event incidence similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: One small placebo trial carries the entire efficacy-versus-no-treatment claim for adults, on a day-1 stool-weight endpoint: it shows antisecretory activity, not fewer complications, admissions or deaths. Everything else on this shelf is a comparison with loperamide.

cards.headline: Multinational loperamide comparison (Prado 2002): diarrhoea resolved in 55.0 hours in BOTH groups (945 outpatients, single-blind); abdominal symptoms resolved faster and constipation was less frequent on racecadotril (16% vs 25%)
cards.summary: Multinational loperamide comparison (Prado 2002): diarrhoea resolved in 55.0 hours in BOTH groups (945 outpatients, single-blind); abdominal symptoms resolved faster and constipation was less frequent on racecadotril (16% vs 25%)
cards.type: Multinational single-blind randomised comparison of racecadotril vs loperamide in adults with acute watery diarrhoea
cards.people: 945 outpatients from 21 centres in 14 countries with acute watery diarrhoea of less than 5 days' duration, receiving racecadotril 100 mg or loperamide 2 mg three times daily in a single-blind study; duration of diarrhoea was the primary measure, with abdominal pain and distension, other associated symptoms, constipation and adverse events also assessed.
cards.result: Diarrhoea resolved rapidly with both treatments (55.0 h in both groups), with 92% of patients on racecadotril and 93% on loperamide being treatment successes — equivalence on duration, not superiority. Racecadotril produced a significantly greater reduction in abdominal pain and distension than loperamide (P=0.024 and P=0.03), the duration of abdominal distension was significantly shorter (5.4 vs 24.4 h; P=0.0001), and constipation was significantly less frequent (16% vs 25%; P=0.001). One hundred and eighty patients (19%) experienced one or more adverse events: 14.2% in the racecadotril group versus 23.9% in the loperamide group (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, and its primary result is identical durations (55.0 h in both arms): the trial supports 'as effective as loperamide, gentler on the bowel afterwards', not greater efficacy. The fourth adult comparison — Vetel 1999 (157 adults; duration 14.9 vs 13.7 hours, more rebound constipation on loperamide) — stays homed inside the loperamide shelf, pack #2478, and is cross-pointed there, not re-carded here.
cards.source: Prado D. A multinational comparison of racecadotril and loperamide in the treatment of acute watery diarrhoea in adults. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2002. PMID: 12126242. cards.headline: Two-centre loperamide comparison (Wang 2005): clinical success 95.7% vs 92.0%, median duration 19.5 h on racecadotril vs 13 h on loperamide, reactive constipation 12.9% vs 29.0% (62 outpatients, single-blind)
cards.summary: Two-centre loperamide comparison (Wang 2005): clinical success 95.7% vs 92.0%, median duration 19.5 h on racecadotril vs 13 h on loperamide, reactive constipation 12.9% vs 29.0% (62 outpatients, single-blind)
cards.type: Two-centre single-blind randomised comparison of racecadotril vs loperamide in adult outpatients with acute diarrhoea
cards.people: 62 adult outpatients with acute diarrhoea in a two-centre, randomised, parallel-group, single-blind study of racecadotril 100 mg three times daily versus loperamide; the main efficacy criterion was duration of diarrhoea after beginning treatment, with other signs, symptoms and adverse events evaluated.
cards.result: Clinical success rates were 95.7% for racecadotril and 92.0% for loperamide. Median duration of diarrhoea was 19.5 hours on racecadotril compared with 13 hours on loperamide — numerically favouring loperamide, with the authors concluding the two are rapid, equally effective treatments. Rapid improvement in anal burn and nausea was found for each drug. More patients on loperamide suffered reactive constipation (29.0% vs 12.9%), while itching was notably higher in the racecadotril group (28.6% vs 0%); other adverse events and concomitant medication use were similar.
cards.watchOut: A small single-blind trial whose duration point estimate actually favours loperamide: carded because it is part of the honest comparative base, and it reinforces equivalence-plus-less-constipation rather than any superiority claim. The itching signal on racecadotril (28.6% vs 0%) is part of that base too.

cards.result: The adult racecadotril record is one small placebo trial plus equivalence trials. Against placebo (n=70), racecadotril reduced day-1 stool weight and stool counts — antisecretory activity in adults, on a surrogate-style endpoint. Against loperamide, in 945 + 62 carded outpatients (plus the 157-patient Vetel limb homed at pack #2478), duration and success rates were the same or numerically favoured loperamide, while rebound/reactive constipation was consistently commoner on loperamide (25% vs 16%; 29.0% vs 12.9%; and 18.7% vs 9.8% in the homed Vetel limb) and abdominal distension resolved faster on racecadotril. The fair claim is 'as effective as loperamide, with less rebound constipation', in a 1999–2005 evidence base; the children's question, where the placebo evidence is stronger, stays at live #1361.

shelves.title: Colchicine in non-PBC cirrhosis: the 1988 trial's dramatic survival benefit (11 vs 3.5 years) was never reproduced — the 549-patient VA trial was null
shelves.question: In patients with established cirrhosis (alcoholic, posthepatitic or hepatitis-B-related — the non-PBC programme), does long-term colchicine versus placebo improve survival and reverse fibrosis histologically?
shelves.mesh: Colchicine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver/drug effects,/pathology · Liver Cirrhosis, Alcoholic/drug therapy,/epidemiology,/mortality,/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Morbidity · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — the programme's arc is one striking positive followed by larger negatives, presented in that order of weight. A single-centre Mexican double-blind trial (NEJM 1988, 100 patients with mixed alcoholic and posthepatitic cirrhosis) reported median survival of 11 years on colchicine versus 3.5 years on placebo (P<0.001), with 5-year survival 75% versus 34% and histological improvement in 9 of 30 re-biopsied colchicine patients. That result was not reproduced: the VA cooperative trial in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis (549 patients, Pugh B/C, treated 2–6 years) found all-cause mortality 49% on colchicine versus 45% on placebo (P=.371), and an HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis trial (100 patients) found no improvement in biochemistry, histology or hepatic pressure gradient and no significant survival difference (P=0.8). The earliest double-blind trial (43 patients) was also non-significant. The Cochrane synthesis of 15 trials (1,714 patients, excluding primary biliary cholangitis) found no significant effect on mortality (relative risk 1.00) and a significantly increased risk of adverse events (relative risk 4.35). Populations differ by limb and are never pooled into one survival number. Era flag: pre-antiviral, pre-transplant-era cirrhosis care; the HBV limb's patients received no nucleos(t)ide therapy, so it does not bear on modern treated HBV cirrhosis. Colchicine in primary biliary cholangitis is a different disease question, homed at pack #7425, and no PBC trial is re-carded here.

cards.headline: Mexican NEJM trial (Kershenobich 1988): median survival 11 years on colchicine versus 3.5 years on placebo (P<0.001); 5-year survival 75% vs 34% — the programme's striking, unreplicated positive (100 patients)
cards.summary: Mexican NEJM trial (Kershenobich 1988): median survival 11 years on colchicine versus 3.5 years on placebo (P<0.001); 5-year survival 75% vs 34% — the programme's striking, unreplicated positive (100 patients)
cards.type: Single-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of long-term colchicine in mixed-aetiology cirrhosis
cards.people: 100 patients with cirrhosis of the liver followed for up to 14 years in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of colchicine 1 mg per day, five days per week: 45 had alcoholic cirrhosis, 41 posthepatitic cirrhosis and 14 cirrhosis of other causes; histology was available for 92%; 73 patients were Child-Turcotte class A, 26 class B and 1 class C; 54 received colchicine and 46 placebo.
cards.result: Overall survival was markedly better on colchicine: median survival 11 years versus 3.5 years on placebo (P<0.001); cumulative 5-year survival was 75% versus 34%, and 10-year survival 56% versus 20% — absolute survival rates as printed in the record. Among the 30 colchicine patients who underwent repeated liver biopsies, histologic improvement was seen in 9 (the liver appeared normal in 2 and 7 had minimal portal fibrosis); no histologic improvement was observed in the 14 placebo patients with two or more biopsies. Few side effects were observed in either group.
cards.watchOut: A remarkable result from 100 patients at one centre, in mostly Child-Turcotte class A disease — and the outlier of this programme: the 549-patient VA trial and the HBV trial that followed (next cards) found no benefit at all. It is presented as the unreplicated result it proved to be, never averaged into a benefit claim.

cards.headline: VA cooperative trial (Morgan 2005): in 549 patients with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis, all-cause mortality was 49% on colchicine versus 45% on placebo (P=.371) — no benefit, and the authors recommended against colchicine
cards.summary: VA cooperative trial (Morgan 2005): in 549 patients with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis, all-cause mortality was 49% on colchicine versus 45% on placebo (P=.371) — no benefit, and the authors recommended against colchicine
cards.type: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled VA cooperative trial of long-term colchicine in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis, 2–6 years
cards.people: 549 patients with advanced (Pugh B or C) alcoholic cirrhosis randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily (274 patients) or placebo (275 patients), treated for 2 to 6 years in a multicentre VA cooperative trial; the primary outcome was all-cause mortality, with liver-related morbidity and mortality secondary, and liver biopsy requested before entry and after 24 months; alcohol intake was less than 1 drink per day in 69% of patients, and attendance and adherence were similar between groups.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, all-cause mortality was similar: 49% on colchicine versus 45% on placebo (P=.371). Mortality attributed to liver disease was 32% versus 28% (P=.337). Fewer colchicine patients developed hepatorenal syndrome. In 54 patients with repeat biopsies after 24 or more months, cirrhosis improved to septal fibrosis in 7 patients (3 colchicine, 4 placebo) and to portal fibrosis in 1 (colchicine) — histological improvement at similar rates on placebo. The authors concluded colchicine does not reduce overall or liver-specific mortality and is not recommended for patients with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: The definitive limb: five times the size of the 1988 trial, in sicker (Pugh B/C) patients, and null on every mortality measure — including a placebo-group histological improvement rate that undercuts the antifibrotic reading of the earlier trial's biopsies. Population differs from the 1988 trial (advanced alcoholic vs mostly class A mixed), and the limbs are labelled, not pooled.

cards.headline: HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis trial (Wang 1994): no improvement in biochemistry, histology or hepatic pressure gradient on colchicine, and cumulative survival not significantly different (P=0.8) (100 patients)
cards.summary: HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis trial (Wang 1994): no improvement in biochemistry, histology or hepatic pressure gradient on colchicine, and cumulative survival not significantly different (P=0.8) (100 patients)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial of colchicine in HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis
cards.people: 100 patients with hepatitis B virus-related postnecrotic cirrhosis (94 men, 6 women, aged 32–80; 70% with histological proof of cirrhosis; 80 in Child-Pugh class A, 19 in class B, 1 in class C), assigned to colchicine 1 mg daily or identical placebo, followed for 15 to 51 months (median 26 months) in a prospective double-blind controlled trial; this report presents the preliminary results.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, there was no improvement in the colchicine group after 24 months in any biochemistry measure (serum albumin, alkaline phosphatase, alanine and aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, prothrombin time). The difference in cumulative survival rates at 51 months did not reach statistical significance (P=0.8). There was no histological improvement in the 30 patients who underwent repeated biopsies, and no trend toward improvement of the hepatic venous pressure gradient. Neither clinical deterioration nor death was prevented by colchicine, and the authors concluded colchicine has no effect in the treatment of HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: A pre-antiviral-era trial: these HBV patients received no nucleos(t)ide therapy, so this null result describes untreated HBV cirrhosis of the 1990s and does not bear on modern treated HBV cirrhosis. Reported by its authors as preliminary results, with a median follow-up of 26 months — shorter than the survival horizons of the 1988 trial.

cards.headline: Early double-blind trial (Kershenobich 1979): liver-related deaths 4 on colchicine versus 8 on placebo in 43 patients — not statistically significant
cards.summary: Early double-blind trial (Kershenobich 1979): liver-related deaths 4 on colchicine versus 8 on placebo in 43 patients — not statistically significant
cards.type: Early double-blind randomised trial of colchicine in cirrhosis (same Mexican programme as the 1988 trial)
cards.people: 43 patients with cirrhosis in a double-blind randomised controlled trial, assigned to colchicine 1 mg daily, five days a week (23 patients) or indistinguishable placebo (20 patients); the time between diagnosis and inclusion was about 14 months in both groups.
cards.result: Mortality related to liver disease occurred in 4 patients on colchicine and 8 on placebo; the probability of surviving was greater in the colchicine group, but the difference did not reach statistically significant levels. In three colchicine-treated patients a remarkable decrease in liver fibrosis was observed on serial biopsies; in two other patients, carcinoma of the liver developed. Six survivors on colchicine improved clinically (disappearance of ascites and edema, decrease in spleen size), while all survivors on placebo continued to show clinical deterioration, and serum albumin rose and was maintained on colchicine in contrast to the usual drop. The authors concluded that liver fibrosis could in some cases be modified by antifibrotic drugs, and that colchicine use should remain within controlled studies.
cards.watchOut: The programme's first trial: 43 patients, a non-significant mortality difference, and hypothesis-generating biopsy and albumin observations — the seed of the 1988 trial, from the same investigators, not an independent replication of it.
cards.source: Kershenobich D et al. Treatment of cirrhosis with colchicine. A double-blind randomized trial. Gastroenterology. 1979. PMID: 378754. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Rambaldi 2005): across 15 randomised trials (1,714 patients, excluding primary biliary cirrhosis), colchicine had no significant effect on mortality (relative risk 1.00) and significantly increased adverse events (relative risk 4.35)
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Rambaldi 2005): across 15 randomised trials (1,714 patients, excluding primary biliary cirrhosis), colchicine had no significant effect on mortality (relative risk 1.00) and significantly increased adverse events (relative risk 4.35)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of colchicine for alcoholic and non-alcoholic liver fibrosis and cirrhosis (15 RCTs)
cards.people: Systematic review of 15 randomised clinical trials in which 1,714 patients with alcoholic or non-alcoholic liver fibrosis or cirrhosis (induced by alcohol, virus or unknown cause; primary biliary cirrhosis excluded) were randomised to oral colchicine versus placebo or no intervention, irrespective of blinding, language or publication status (searches to September 2004).
cards.result: No significant effects of colchicine were found on mortality (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.16), liver-related mortality (relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.33), complications (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.38), liver biochemistry, liver histology or alcohol consumption (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.39) — all relative measures. Colchicine was associated with a significantly increased risk of adverse events (relative risk 4.35, 95% CI 2.16 to 8.77). The reviewers concluded colchicine should not be used for alcoholic, viral or cryptogenic liver fibrosis or cirrhosis outside randomised clinical trials.
cards.watchOut: The synthesis pools smaller and older trials of varying quality alongside the carded trials, and its search closed in September 2004, before the VA trial's 2005 publication was incorporated — but its null mortality estimate and its adverse-event signal point the same way as the large trial. The 1996 trial of colchicine to prevent cirrhosis in chronic hepatitis B asks a prevention question in patients without cirrhosis and is not folded in here.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One programme, one arc: an early small trial (n=43, non-significant) generated the hypothesis; a striking single-centre result (n=100; median survival 11 vs 3.5 years) made the claim; and the two subsequent 100- and 549-patient double-blind trials — in HBV postnecrotic cirrhosis and in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis — found no survival, biochemical or histological benefit, with the Cochrane pool of 15 trials (1,714 patients) estimating mortality at relative risk 1.00 and adverse events significantly increased (relative risk 4.35). The 1988 result stands on this shelf as what it proved to be: an unreplicated outlier, not a benefit to be averaged. No established benefit of colchicine exists in non-PBC cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline in NASH: four small trials totalling 135 patients — one positive histology trial (n=55), three without between-group separation
shelves.question: In adults with biopsy-proven (or imaging/enzyme-defined) non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, does pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day versus placebo improve histological activity (NAS), steatosis and liver enzymes over 3–12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adiponectin/blood · Adult · Alanine Transaminase/metabolism · Apoptosis/drug effects · Aspartate Aminotransferases/metabolism · Biopsy · Fatty Liver/drug therapy,/pathology · Female · Humans · Insulin Resistance · Liver/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease · Pentoxifylline/administration & dosage,/adverse effects · Placebos · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage,/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/blood
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a small-trial programme, with its numbers printed: four randomised trials totalling 135 patients (55, 30, 30 and 20). Only the largest, a 55-patient US trial in biopsy-confirmed NASH, has a positive between-group histological primary: NAS fall of at least 2 points in 38.5% on pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day versus 13.8% on placebo at 1 year (P=0.036). The other three rest on weaker readings: a 30-patient biopsy-proven trial found aminotransferases and some histology improved within the pentoxifylline arm but between-group comparisons were non-significant; a 30-patient Iranian trial in ultrasound/enzyme-defined NASH found aminotransferases fell in both groups (attributed by its authors to diet and exercise) with no between-group difference; and a 20-patient pilot with diet-and-exercise co-intervention in both arms found a greater AST reduction on pentoxifylline (P=0.038). Definitions differ by limb (biopsy-proven in three trials as the records describe them, ultrasound/enzymes in one) and are labelled per card. There are no fibrosis-regression-at-scale, clinical-outcome or long-term safety data. Era flag: pre-resmetirom, pre-GLP-1-era MASH care — this shelf must not be read against the current treatment landscape. Pentoxifylline in alcohol-associated hepatitis and diabetic kidney disease are different questions, homed elsewhere and not folded in.

cards.headline: US trial (Zein 2011): pentoxifylline improved NASH histology — NAS fall ≥2 points in 38.5% vs 13.8% on placebo at 1 year (P=0.036); mean NAS change −1.6 vs −0.1 (55 adults, biopsy-confirmed)
cards.summary: US trial (Zein 2011): pentoxifylline improved NASH histology — NAS fall ≥2 points in 38.5% vs 13.8% on placebo at 1 year (P=0.036); mean NAS change −1.6 vs −0.1 (55 adults, biopsy-confirmed)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial of pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day in biopsy-confirmed NASH, 1 year
cards.people: 55 adults with biopsy-confirmed non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, randomised to pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily (26 patients) or placebo (29 patients) over 1 year; the primary endpoint was improvement in histological features reflected by a decrease of at least 2 points in the NAFLD activity score (NAS).
cards.result: By intention-to-treat, a decrease of at least 2 points in NAS occurred in 38.5% of pentoxifylline patients versus 13.8% on placebo (P=0.036); per protocol the figures were 50% versus 15.4% (P=0.01). Mean NAS change was −1.6 on pentoxifylline versus −0.1 on placebo (P < 0.001). Pentoxifylline significantly improved steatosis (mean change −0.9 vs −0.04; P < 0.001) and lobular inflammation (median change −1 vs 0; P=0.02), with no significant effect on hepatocellular ballooning; fibrosis score changed by −0.2 versus +0.4 (P=0.038), although the proportion improving in fibrosis (35% vs 15%) was not statistically significant (P=0.17). Adverse effects were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The programme's one positive between-group histological result — and it rests on 55 patients, with the fibrosis-proportion reading non-significant. Its mechanistic secondary report (oxidised lipid products) is a report of this same trial, not a fifth trial, and is not carded separately.

cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day in biopsy-proven NASH, 12 months
cards.people: 30 patients with biopsy-proven NASH, randomised 2:1 to pentoxifylline 1,200 mg/day or placebo for 12 months in a double-blind trial; metabolic parameters, aminotransferases, liver histology and hepatic gene expression were compared.
cards.result: After 12 months, ALT fell from 92 ± 12 IU/L to 67 ± 13 IU/L and AST from 67 ± 6 IU/L to 47 ± 6 IU/L within the pentoxifylline group (P < 0.05), with no significant effect seen on placebo; steatosis and cellular ballooning improved in the pentoxifylline group (P < 0.05), whereas no histological feature improved on placebo. However — the abstract's own framing — between-group comparisons of both biochemical and histological features were non-significant, pentoxifylline failed to reduce transaminases compared with placebo, and no metabolic marker improved. Adverse events were mild (most frequently headache and abdominal cramps) and did not differ between groups. The authors concluded pentoxifylline is safe and well tolerated but that translating it into clinical practice may prove challenging.
cards.watchOut: Within-arm improvement is not a treatment effect: with 30 patients split 2:1, the trial could not separate pentoxifylline from placebo on any measure. Carded with its authors' own caution, as a non-confirmatory limb.
cards.source: Van Wagner LB et al. Pentoxifylline for the treatment of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis: a randomized controlled trial. Annals of hepatology. 2011. PMID: 21677329. Registry ID: NCT00267670. cards.headline: Iranian trial (Baniasadi 2015): aminotransferases fell in BOTH groups with no between-group difference; TNF-α was lower on pentoxifylline at 6 months (30 patients, ultrasound/enzyme-defined NASH)
cards.summary: Iranian trial (Baniasadi 2015): aminotransferases fell in BOTH groups with no between-group difference; TNF-α was lower on pentoxifylline at 6 months (30 patients, ultrasound/enzyme-defined NASH)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day in ultrasound/enzyme-defined NASH, 6 months
cards.people: 30 patients with NASH defined by ultrasonography and a 1.5-fold mean change from baseline in serum liver aminotransferases, randomised to pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day or placebo for 6 months in a double-blind trial in Iran; serum aminotransferases and cytokines (interleukin 6, TNF-α, interleukin 8) were compared between groups at various time points.
cards.result: Serum aminotransferases fell significantly at 3 and 6 months versus baseline in both groups, and interleukin 6 fell in both groups at 6 months. Compared with placebo, serum TNF-α was significantly decreased in the pentoxifylline group at 6 months, while interleukin 8 rose in both groups without reaching clinical significance. There was no significant difference in serum aminotransferases or cytokines between the intervention and placebo groups overall, and the authors attributed the decreases in both groups to low-calorie diets and exercise rather than to pentoxifylline.
cards.watchOut: No biopsy confirmation (ultrasound and enzymes defined the disease), no between-group enzyme benefit, and a single cytokine difference: a surrogate limb whose own authors credit diet and exercise for the improvements seen. Never load-bearing.
cards.source: Baniasadi N et al. Effects of Pentoxifylline on Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial in Iran. Hepatitis monthly. 2015. PMID: 26834792. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Pilot trial (Lee 2008): with diet and exercise in BOTH arms, AST fell significantly more on pentoxifylline (P=0.038) over 3 months (20 randomised — a pilot limb)
cards.summary: Pilot trial (Lee 2008): with diet and exercise in BOTH arms, AST fell significantly more on pentoxifylline (P=0.038) over 3 months (20 randomised — a pilot limb)
cards.type: Randomised controlled pilot trial of pentoxifylline plus diet/exercise vs placebo plus diet/exercise in biopsy-proven NASH, 3 months
cards.people: 20 patients with biopsy-proven NASH and persistently elevated alanine aminotransferase (greater than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal), randomised to pentoxifylline (11 patients) or placebo (9 patients) for 3 months, with a step 1 American Heart Association diet and daily exercise in both groups; liver function tests, lipids, TNF-α, interleukin 6 and plasma hyaluronic acid were measured at baseline and weeks 6 and 12.
cards.result: After 3 months, body mass index, ALT and AST decreased significantly in both groups. There was no difference between groups in BMI reduction (P=0.897). The reduction in AST was significantly greater in the pentoxifylline group (P=0.038), with a trend toward lower ALT (P=0.065). TNF-α and interleukin 6 decreased significantly in both groups, with no significant difference between groups. The authors concluded that 3 months of pentoxifylline with diet and exercise gave a significantly greater AST reduction than diet and exercise with placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 20-patient, 3-month pilot whose one significant result is an AST difference against a background of improvement in both arms from the shared diet-and-exercise co-intervention: hypothesis-generating only, and labelled a pilot on its face.
cards.source: Lee YM et al. A randomized controlled pilot study of Pentoxifylline in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Hepatology international. 2008. PMID: 19669304. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record
