cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Four trials, 135 patients in total, one positive primary. Zein 2011 (n=55, biopsy-confirmed) found a histological NAS benefit for pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day over 1 year (≥2-point fall in 38.5% vs 13.8%). Van Wagner 2011 (n=30, biopsy-proven) found within-arm improvements but no significant between-group separation. Baniasadi 2015 (n=30, ultrasound/enzyme-defined) found enzymes fell in both groups, credited by its authors to diet and exercise. Lee 2008 (n=20, pilot) found a greater AST fall with diet and exercise in both arms. No trial measured fibrosis regression at scale, clinical outcomes or long-term safety, and all predate the resmetirom/GLP-1 era of MASH care. That is a MAYBE (weak evidence) base: a real histological signal in one small trial, unconfirmed by the three smaller ones.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 crossover reports, 45 adults, all favouring rifampicin for short-term itch relief (n=9 limb sub-floor)
shelves.question: In adults with cholestatic pruritus (chiefly primary biliary cholangitis/cirrhosis), does rifampicin (rifampin) versus placebo or phenobarbitone relieve itch — the unasked slice beside the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head homed at pack #3618?
shelves.mesh: Antipyrine/pharmacokinetics · Bile Acids and Salts/metabolism · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary/complications,metabolism · Middle Aged · Placebos · Pruritus/drug therapy · Random Allocation · Rifampin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 45. FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: the complete adult randomised base for rifampicin's own efficacy in cholestatic pruritus is 3 crossover reports totalling 45 adults (1988–1991), each limb ≤14 days. All three favoured rifampicin — 8 of 9 preferred it to placebo (Ghent, n=9, SUB-FLOOR and never load-bearing alone); itch improved in 19 vs 8 patients against phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 (Bachs, n=22); itch disappeared in 11 of 14 on rifampin vs partial response in 2 on placebo (Podesta, n=14). PARTIAL: the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head is homed at pack #3618 and is not re-carded; this shelf is only the unasked slice — rifampicin versus placebo/phenobarbitone. Harms belong on the face: one withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure, drug-induced hepatitis risk in cholestatic patients (the reason monitoring is mandatory), and potent enzyme induction with wide drug interactions. Short-term itch relief only; no long-term randomised safety base.

cards.headline: Ghent 1988 double-blind crossover (n=9, SUB-FLOOR, labelled — never load-bearing alone): 8 of 9 patients preferred rifampin to placebo (P=0.03), with visual-analogue itch scores significantly reduced (P<0.002)
cards.summary: Ghent 1988 double-blind crossover (n=9, SUB-FLOOR, labelled — never load-bearing alone): 8 of 9 patients preferred rifampin to placebo (P=0.03), with visual-analogue itch scores significantly reduced (P<0.002)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised crossover trial, rifampin vs placebo (n=9 — sub-floor, labelled)
cards.people: 9 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis and pruritus received rifampin 300–450 mg/day and placebo sequentially in random order, each for 14 days with a 14-day washout between treatments (double-blind crossover).
cards.result: All 9 completed the trial and 8 preferred rifampin to placebo (P=0.03). Visual-analogue pruritus scores showed a highly significant reduction on rifampin (P<0.002), evident within the first week, with no significant placebo response. Rifampin produced a 33% reduction in antipyrine plasma half-life and no change in fasting total serum bile acids; cholestyramine use did not change significantly. No adverse reactions were reported in this small trial.
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: only 9 patients — below the ~10-human reference floor. Labelled on the face and never load-bearing on its own; it is one limb of an exactly-counted 3-report, 45-patient base.
cards.source: Ghent CN et al. Treatment of pruritus in primary biliary cirrhosis with rifampin. Results of a double-blind, crossover, randomized trial. Gastroenterology. 1988. PMID: 3275568. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bachs 1989 crossover vs phenobarbitone (n=22): itch improved in 19 patients on rifampicin vs 8 on phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 on rifampicin; one rifampicin withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure
cards.summary: Bachs 1989 crossover vs phenobarbitone (n=22): itch improved in 19 patients on rifampicin vs 8 on phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 on rifampicin; one rifampicin withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial, rifampicin vs phenobarbitone (n=22)
cards.people: 22 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis received rifampicin 10 mg/kg and phenobarbitone 3 mg/kg in a crossover randomised trial, each agent for 14 days with a 30-day washout between treatments.
cards.result: 21 patients completed rifampicin and 18 completed phenobarbitone. Rifampicin was withdrawn in 1 patient when anaemia and renal failure developed; 3 patients stopped phenobarbitone because of a rash and a fourth refused it. Itch improved in 19 patients on rifampicin versus 8 on phenobarbitone, with a greater degree of improvement on rifampicin, and pruritus disappeared in 9 patients on rifampicin (3 of them remained itch-free on switching to phenobarbitone). Both drugs induced hepatic microsomal function equally; rifampicin additionally reduced cholestasis.
cards.watchOut: Crossover limbs were only 14 days each (1989). The anaemia and renal-failure withdrawal on rifampicin is printed here because rifampicin's harms — including drug-induced hepatitis risk in cholestatic patients and potent enzyme induction with wide drug interactions — belong on this shelf's face.
cards.source: Bachs L et al. Comparison of rifampicin with phenobarbitone for treatment of pruritus in biliary cirrhosis. Lancet (London, England). 1989. PMID: 2564110. cards.headline: Podesta 1991 randomised crossover (n=14): pruritus disappeared in 11 patients and partially improved in 3 on rifampin vs partial response in only 2 on placebo (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Podesta 1991 randomised crossover (n=14): pruritus disappeared in 11 patients and partially improved in 3 on rifampin vs partial response in only 2 on placebo (P<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial, rifampin vs placebo (n=14), with an 8-month open extension in the same report
cards.people: 14 patients with primary biliary cirrhosis and pruritus, in a randomised crossover study: after a 15-day washout, patients received rifampin 600 mg/day or placebo in week 1 and week 3, with no treatment in week 2; pruritus was scored subjectively on a 0–100 scale.
cards.result: On rifampin, pruritus disappeared in 11 patients and partially improved in 3; on placebo, only 2 patients had a partial response (P<0.001). Six patients with a prior poor or no response to cholestyramine improved on rifampin. No biochemical changes or side effects were observed during the randomised period. In an 8-month open extension in the same report, relief was maintained and one individual developed an allergic reaction.
cards.watchOut: One-week randomised limbs and a subjective itch score; the 8-month open extension is uncontrolled and is not counted as randomised evidence. Short-term relief only — there is no long-term randomised safety base.
cards.source: Podesta A et al. Treatment of pruritus of primary biliary cirrhosis with rifampin. Digestive diseases and sciences. 1991. PMID: 1988266. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 crossover reports, 45 adults in total (n=9 + 22 + 14), all from 1988–1991, all pointing the same way: rifampicin relieves cholestatic itch short-term versus placebo and versus phenobarbitone
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 crossover reports, 45 adults in total (n=9 + 22 + 14), all from 1988–1991, all pointing the same way: rifampicin relieves cholestatic itch short-term versus placebo and versus phenobarbitone
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: 45 adults with primary biliary cirrhosis / cholestatic pruritus across three crossover trials.
cards.result: Every report favoured rifampicin: 8 of 9 preferred it to placebo (Ghent, sub-floor n=9); itch improved in 19 vs 8 against phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 (Bachs, n=22); and itch disappeared in 11 of 14 on rifampin versus partial response in 2 on placebo (Podesta). No report had a limb longer than 14 days of randomised treatment, so this is a short-term itch-relief record only. PARTIAL position: the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head (n=36) is homed at pack #3618 and is NOT re-carded here — this shelf cards only rifampicin's own placebo/active-comparator base, which #3618 does not ask. Harms on the face: one withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure (Bachs), one allergic reaction in open long-term use (Podesta), and rifampicin's known drug-induced hepatitis risk in cholestatic patients plus potent enzyme induction — monitoring is mandatory in practice, and no long-term randomised safety base exists (the 1992 long-term administration report is not a randomised trial and is not counted).
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base stated exactly: 3 reports, 45 adults, every limb a short crossover; the n=9 limb is sub-floor and never load-bearing. See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

synthesis all reports carded on this shelf: 45 adults with primary biliary cirrhosis / cholestatic pruritus across three crossover trials. every report favoured rifampicin: 8 of 9 preferred it to placebo (ghent, sub-floor n=9); itch improved in 19 vs 8 against phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 (bachs, n=22); and itch disappeared in 11 of 14 on rifampin versus partial response in 2 on placebo (podesta). no report had a limb longer than 14 days of randomised treatment, so this is a short-term itch-relief record only. partial position: the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head (n=36) is homed at pack #3618 and is not re-carded here — this shelf cards only rifampicin's own placebo/active-comparator base, which #3618 does not ask. harms on the face: one withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure (bachs), one allergic reaction in open long-term use (podesta), and rifampicin's known drug-induced hepatitis risk in cholestatic patients plus potent enzyme induction — monitoring is mandatory in practice, and no long-term randomised safety base exists (the 1992 long-term administration report is not a randomised trial and is not counted). floor-risk base stated exactly: 3 reports, 45 adults, every limb a short crossover; the n=9 limb is sub-floor and never load-bearing. see the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Gatifloxacin for uncomplicated enteric fever: SPLIT — matched most comparators, beat cefixime, failed once high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged (Nepal–Vietnam programme)
shelves.question: In children and adults with uncomplicated enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever, does 7 days of oral gatifloxacin versus chloramphenicol, cefixime, ofloxacin, azithromycin or intravenous ceftriaxone achieve faster fever clearance and less treatment failure and relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Chloramphenicol/administration & dosage · Feces/microbiology · Fluoroquinolones/administration & dosage · Gatifloxacin · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Nepal · Proportional Hazards Models · Salmonella enterica/drug effects,isolation & purification · Time Factors · Treatment Failure · Typhoid Fever/blood,drug therapy,microbiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by comparator and by resistance era. In five open-label Nepal–Vietnam trials, 7 days of oral gatifloxacin matched chloramphenicol (failure 12 vs 14 in 352 culture-confirmed), azithromycin (failure 9% vs 9.3%; fever clearance 106 hours in both arms) and ofloxacin (failure 5/87 vs 6/83 in nalidixic-acid-resistant isolates) on treatment failure, and beat cefixime clearly (failure 3.5% vs 37.6%) in a trial stopped early on DSMB advice. Against intravenous ceftriaxone the overall result was null (15% vs 16%), but culture-confirmed patients failed more on gatifloxacin (26% vs 7%) and that trial was stopped early because high-level fluoroquinolone resistance had emerged. Resistance-era flag (load-bearing): these trials were run where nalidixic-acid resistance was common; their results do not transfer to today's extensively drug-resistant S. Typhi settings. Safety flag: gatifloxacin was withdrawn from many markets over dysglycaemia — this shelf is a record of a completed programme, not a prescribing recommendation. Two of five trials stopped early; both stop reasons are on the cards.

cards.headline: Arjyal 2011 vs chloramphenicol (352 culture-confirmed within 844 randomised): treatment failure 12 on gatifloxacin vs 14 on chloramphenicol (hazard ratio 0.86 — no difference); fever clearance ~3.9 days in both arms; adverse events 14% vs 24%
cards.summary: Arjyal 2011 vs chloramphenicol (352 culture-confirmed within 844 randomised): treatment failure 12 on gatifloxacin vs 14 on chloramphenicol (hazard ratio 0.86 — no difference); fever clearance ~3.9 days in both arms; adverse events 14% vs 24%
cards.type: Open-label randomised superiority trial, gatifloxacin vs chloramphenicol (Nepal)
cards.people: 844 children and adults clinically diagnosed with enteric fever at Patan Hospital, Kathmandu, Nepal (median age 16 years), randomised to gatifloxacin 10 mg/kg once daily for 7 days or chloramphenicol 75 mg/kg/day in four divided doses for 14 days; 352 had blood-culture-confirmed enteric fever (177 gatifloxacin, 175 chloramphenicol). Open-label superiority trial; primary outcome was a composite treatment failure.
cards.result: In culture-confirmed patients, treatment failure occurred in 12 on gatifloxacin versus 14 on chloramphenicol (hazard ratio for time to failure 0.86, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.86; P=0.70 — a relative measure, with the absolute counts beside it). Median fever clearance was 3.90 days on gatifloxacin versus 3.95 days on chloramphenicol. Late relapses: 2 of 177 versus 3 of 175. Adverse events occurred in 59 patients (14%) on gatifloxacin versus 99 (24%) on chloramphenicol. The authors preferred gatifloxacin for its shorter course and fewer adverse events, not greater efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Open-label; the efficacy population is the 352 culture-confirmed patients within the 844 randomised. Run in the nalidixic-acid-resistance era — see the shelf balance on transfer to today's extensively drug-resistant settings.
cards.source: Arjyal A et al. Gatifloxacin versus chloramphenicol for uncomplicated enteric fever: an open-label, randomised, controlled trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2011. PMID: 21531174. Registry ID: ISRCTN53258327. cards.headline: Pandit 2007 vs cefixime (390 randomised; enrolment SUSPENDED EARLY on DSMB advice): fever clearance 92 vs 138 hours; overall treatment failure 3.5% on gatifloxacin vs 37.6% on cefixime
cards.summary: Pandit 2007 vs cefixime (390 randomised; enrolment SUSPENDED EARLY on DSMB advice): fever clearance 92 vs 138 hours; overall treatment failure 3.5% on gatifloxacin vs 37.6% on cefixime
cards.type: Open-label randomised trial, gatifloxacin vs cefixime (Nepal) — STOPPED EARLY
cards.people: 390 patients with clinically diagnosed uncomplicated enteric fever at Patan Hospital, Nepal, randomised to gatifloxacin 10 mg/kg once daily for 7 days or cefixime 20 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 7 days; the primary outcome was fever clearance time in culture-positive enteric fever.
cards.result: Enrolment was suspended early on the advice of the independent data safety monitoring board because significant differences in both primary and secondary outcomes had emerged and a priori endpoints were attained — an early stop, which inflates apparent effects. Median fever clearance was 92 hours on gatifloxacin versus 138 hours on cefixime (hazard ratio 2.171, 95% CI 1.545 to 3.051; P<0.0001 — a relative measure). Among patients completing the 7-day trial, acute clinical failure was 1 of 88 (1%) on gatifloxacin versus 19 of 70 (27%) on cefixime. Overall treatment failure was 3.5% versus 37.6% (hazard ratio 0.084, 95% CI 0.025 to 0.280; P<0.0001 — relative, absolute rates beside it). There was one death, in the cefixime group.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for emerging differences — early stops exaggerate effects, and the very large failure contrast (3.5% vs 37.6%) should be read with that caution. Open-label.
cards.source: Pandit A et al. An open randomized comparison of gatifloxacin versus cefixime for the treatment of uncomplicated enteric fever. PloS one. 2007. PMID: 17593957. Registry ID: ISRCTN75784880. cards.headline: Arjyal 2016 vs intravenous ceftriaxone (239 in the modified intention-to-treat population; STOPPED EARLY by the DSMB): overall failure 15% vs 16%, but in culture-confirmed patients failure was 26% on gatifloxacin vs 7% on ceftriaxone as high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged
cards.summary: Arjyal 2016 vs intravenous ceftriaxone (239 in the modified intention-to-treat population; STOPPED EARLY by the DSMB): overall failure 15% vs 16%, but in culture-confirmed patients failure was 26% on gatifloxacin vs 7% on ceftriaxone as high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged
cards.type: Open-label two-centre randomised superiority trial, gatifloxacin vs intravenous ceftriaxone (Nepal) — STOPPED EARLY
cards.people: Children aged 2–13 years and adults aged 14–45 years with suspected enteric fever at two hospitals in the Kathmandu valley, Nepal, randomised to 7 days of oral gatifloxacin 10 mg/kg/day or intravenous ceftriaxone (60 mg/kg up to 2 g/day in children; 2 g/day in those ≥14 years); 725 were screened and 239 formed the modified intention-to-treat population (120 gatifloxacin, 119 ceftriaxone).
cards.result: The trial was stopped early by the data safety and monitoring board on July 14, 2014 because S. Typhi strains with high-level resistance to ciprofloxacin and gatifloxacin had emerged. Overall treatment failure was 18 of 120 (15%) on gatifloxacin versus 19 of 119 (16%) on ceftriaxone (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.98; P=0.91 — relative, absolutes beside it). In the culture-confirmed subpopulation, failure was 16 of 62 (26%) on gatifloxacin versus 4 of 54 (7%) on ceftriaxone (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.73; P=0.01, printed as reported for ceftriaxone versus gatifloxacin); in culture-negative patients the direction reversed (2 of 58 [3%] vs 15 of 65 [23%]). A similar number of non-serious adverse events occurred in each group and no serious events were reported. The authors concluded fluoroquinolones should no longer be used for enteric fever in Nepal.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for an external reason — the emergence of high-level fluoroquinolone resistance — not for an efficacy boundary; the culture-confirmed and culture-negative subgroups point in opposite directions, so neither subgroup result should be read alone.
cards.source: Arjyal A et al. Gatifloxacin versus ceftriaxone for uncomplicated enteric fever in Nepal: an open-label, two-centre, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2016. PMID: 26809813. Registry ID: NCT01421693. cards.headline: Dolecek 2008 vs azithromycin in Vietnam (358 enrolled; 287 culture-confirmed): median fever clearance 106 hours in BOTH arms; treatment failure 9% vs 9.3% — no difference; 96% of isolates were nalidixic-acid-resistant
cards.summary: Dolecek 2008 vs azithromycin in Vietnam (358 enrolled; 287 culture-confirmed): median fever clearance 106 hours in BOTH arms; treatment failure 9% vs 9.3% — no difference; 96% of isolates were nalidixic-acid-resistant
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised trial, gatifloxacin vs azithromycin (Vietnam)
cards.people: 358 children and adults with suspected typhoid fever enrolled in a multicentre open-label trial in Vietnam; 287 had blood-culture-confirmed typhoid (145 gatifloxacin, 142 azithromycin), treated with gatifloxacin 10 mg/kg/day or azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day, each once daily for 7 days. Primary outcome was fever clearance time.
cards.result: There were no deaths. Median fever clearance was 106 hours in both arms (hazard ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.26; P=0.984 — relative, with identical absolute medians beside it). Overall treatment failure was 13 of 145 (9%) on gatifloxacin versus 13 of 140 (9.3%) on azithromycin. Of the S. Typhi isolates, 96% (254/263) were nalidixic-acid-resistant and 58% (153/263) multidrug-resistant. Both drugs showed excellent efficacy and safety in this setting; a 7-day gatifloxacin course cost about one third of azithromycin in Vietnam at the time.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in a population where 96% of isolates were already nalidixic-acid-resistant — efficacy here does not transfer to settings with high-level fluoroquinolone resistance of the kind that stopped the 2016 Nepal trial.
cards.source: Dolecek C et al. A multi-center randomised controlled trial of gatifloxacin versus azithromycin for the treatment of uncomplicated typhoid fever in children and adults in Vietnam. PloS one. 2008. PMID: 18493312. Registry ID: ISRCTN67946944. cards.headline: Koirala 2013 vs ofloxacin (627 randomised; 170 with nalidixic-acid-resistant isolates): treatment failure in the resistant subset 5/87 on gatifloxacin vs 6/83 on ofloxacin — no difference in failure; fever cleared faster on gatifloxacin (3.31 vs 4.70 days)
cards.summary: Koirala 2013 vs ofloxacin (627 randomised; 170 with nalidixic-acid-resistant isolates): treatment failure in the resistant subset 5/87 on gatifloxacin vs 6/83 on ofloxacin — no difference in failure; fever cleared faster on gatifloxacin (3.31 vs 4.70 days)
cards.type: Open-label randomised trial, gatifloxacin vs ofloxacin (Nepal)
cards.people: 627 children and adults clinically diagnosed with uncomplicated enteric fever in Nepal (median age 17 years), randomised to gatifloxacin 10 mg/kg/day in a single dose or ofloxacin 20 mg/kg/day in two divided doses, each for 7 days, with 6 months of follow-up; 218 had culture-confirmed enteric fever, of whom 170 had nalidixic-acid-resistant isolates. The primary outcome was treatment failure in the resistant subset.
cards.result: In the nalidixic-acid-resistant subset, treatment failure was 5 of 87 on gatifloxacin versus 6 of 83 on ofloxacin (hazard ratio for time to failure 0.81, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.65; P=0.73 — relative, absolutes beside it). Median fever clearance was faster on gatifloxacin: 3.31 days versus 4.70 days (hazard ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.18; P=0.004). Results in all culture-confirmed patients and all randomised patients were comparable.
cards.watchOut: Open-label; the primary (failure in the resistant subset) was null — the fever-clearance advantage is a secondary outcome and should not be upgraded into a superiority claim.
cards.source: Koirala S et al. Gatifloxacin versus ofloxacin for the treatment of uncomplicated enteric fever in Nepal: an open-label, randomized, controlled trial. PLoS neglected tropical diseases. 2013. PMID: 24282626. Registry ID: ISRCTN63006567. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by comparator and by resistance era — gatifloxacin matched chloramphenicol, azithromycin and ofloxacin on failure, beat cefixime clearly in an early-stopped trial, and failed culture-confirmed patients once high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged in Nepal
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by comparator and by resistance era — gatifloxacin matched chloramphenicol, azithromycin and ofloxacin on failure, beat cefixime clearly in an early-stopped trial, and failed culture-confirmed patients once high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged in Nepal
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: five open-label Nepal–Vietnam trials (844, 390, 239 modified-ITT, 358 and 627 patients enrolled/randomised as each trial reports them; culture-confirmed subsets stated per card, never pooled).
cards.result: Against chloramphenicol, azithromycin and ofloxacin, gatifloxacin showed no difference in treatment failure (12 vs 14; 9% vs 9.3%; 5/87 vs 6/83 in the resistant subset), with faster fever clearance than ofloxacin only. Against cefixime it was markedly better (failure 3.5% vs 37.6%), in a trial stopped early on DSMB advice — a design that inflates apparent effects. Against ceftriaxone the overall result was null (15% vs 16%), but in culture-confirmed patients gatifloxacin failed more (26% vs 7%), and that trial was stopped early because high-level ciprofloxacin/gatifloxacin resistance had emerged. Two of the five trials stopped early; the stop reason for each is printed on its card. This shelf is a record of a completed programme, not a prescribing recommendation: gatifloxacin was withdrawn from many markets over dysglycaemia, and these nalidixic-acid-resistance-era results do not transfer to today's extensively drug-resistant S. Typhi settings. Cross-point: pack #2973 (azithromycin vs ceftriaxone in children) is a different enteric-fever question and its trial is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: All five trials were open-label and mixed children and adults as each enrolled them (age ranges per card). See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Tribendimidine for Opisthorchis viverrini: highly active in one Lao phase 2 programme (3 publications / 4 trials) — but non-inferiority to praziquantel on cure was not shown
shelves.question: In children and adults infected with Opisthorchis viverrini, does single-dose tribendimidine, at what dose, achieve cure and egg reduction comparable with praziquantel, the only established treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Animals · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Loa · Male · Middle Aged · Opisthorchiasis/diagnosis,drug therapy,parasitology · Opisthorchis/drug effects,isolation & purification · Parasite Egg Count · Phenylenediamines/administration & dosage · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-region, single-programme phase 2 record, counted exactly: 3 publications reporting 4 trials, all in Laos from one collaboration. Tribendimidine is clearly active against Opisthorchis viverrini: dose-ranging cure rose to 91.5% at 400 mg in adolescents/adults with egg reduction ~99% at ≥100 mg, and in the head-to-head trial single-dose tribendimidine cured 93.6% versus 97.3% on two-dose praziquantel with 99.9% egg reduction in both groups and fewer adverse events on tribendimidine. But non-inferiority on cure was NOT shown (difference −3.8 percentage points; lower confidence limit −7.1 exceeded the pre-specified −3 margin) — that failure is on the face, not buried. The exploratory trial's tribendimidine limb (27 children, one of five arms) is labelled and never load-bearing. Endpoints are parasitological only; no phase 3, no approval, and tribendimidine (Chinese-developed) is not US/EU-marketed.

cards.headline: Sayasone 2016 dose-ranging phase 2 — TWO trials reported together in one publication (labelled): cure rose with dose to 91.5% at 400 mg in adolescents/adults and 98.9% at 100 mg in children, with egg reduction ~99% at ≥100 mg
cards.summary: Sayasone 2016 dose-ranging phase 2 — TWO trials reported together in one publication (labelled): cure rose with dose to 91.5% at 400 mg in adolescents/adults and 98.9% at 100 mg in children, with egg reduction ~99% at ≥100 mg
cards.type: Two randomised single-blind dose-ranging phase 2 trials reported together in one publication (one programme — labelled)
cards.people: Two randomised, parallel-group, single-blind dose-ranging phase 2 trials in Champasack province, southern Laos, reported in this single publication: 318 adolescents and adults (≥15 years) randomised across tribendimidine doses of 25–600 mg, and 128 children (8–14 years) randomised to 100, 200 or 400 mg (plus one non-randomised group of 39 children given 50 mg in the second study). Primary endpoints were cure rate (no eggs in stool) and egg reduction rate.
cards.result: In adolescents and adults, cure increased with dose up to 100 mg: 25.6% (10/39) at 25 mg, 42.6% (20/47) at 50 mg and 77.3% (34/44) at 100 mg, with geometric mean egg reduction of 86.9%, 95.9% and 99.1% respectively; at 400 mg, cure was 91.5% (43/47) and at 600 mg 80.0% (36/45). In children, 100 mg cured 40 of 44 (printed as 98.9%, 95% CI 78.3 to 97.5) with egg reduction 99.7%, and higher doses added nothing; 50 mg cured 16 of 39 children (41.0%). Adverse events were mostly mild — vertigo (11%), headache, nausea and fatigue in adolescents/adults — with no serious events.
cards.watchOut: This publication reports two of the programme's four trials — it is one publication, not two independent programmes. Participants had mainly low-intensity infection; efficacy in moderate/high-intensity infection was not assessed. The cure percentage for children at 100 mg is printed exactly as the record gives it.
cards.source: Sayasone S et al. Efficacy and safety of tribendimidine against Opisthorchis viverrini: two randomised, parallel-group, single-blind, dose-ranging, phase 2 trials. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2016. PMID: 27472949. Registry ID: ISRCTN96948551. cards.headline: Sayasone 2018 non-inferiority phase 2 vs praziquantel (607 assigned): cure 93.6% on single-dose tribendimidine vs 97.3% on two-dose praziquantel — non-inferiority NOT shown (difference −3.8 percentage points; lower confidence limit −7.1 exceeded the −3 margin); egg reduction 99.9% in both groups; fewer adverse events on tribendimidine
cards.summary: Sayasone 2018 non-inferiority phase 2 vs praziquantel (607 assigned): cure 93.6% on single-dose tribendimidine vs 97.3% on two-dose praziquantel — non-inferiority NOT shown (difference −3.8 percentage points; lower confidence limit −7.1 exceeded the −3 margin); egg reduction 99.9% in both groups; fewer adverse events on tribendimidine
cards.type: Open-label randomised non-inferiority phase 2 trial, tribendimidine vs praziquantel
cards.people: 607 children (8–14 years) and adolescents/adults (≥15 years) with confirmed O. viverrini infection in Champasack province, Laos, randomised to a single oral dose of tribendimidine (200 mg children; 400 mg older participants) or two oral doses of praziquantel (50 mg/kg then 25 mg/kg, 6 hours apart); 596 provided stool at 3 weeks and formed the available-case analysis (295 tribendimidine, 301 praziquantel). Open-label randomised non-inferiority phase 2 trial; the pre-specified non-inferiority margin for cure-rate difference was −3 percentage points.
cards.result: Cure was 276 of 295 (93.6%) on tribendimidine versus 293 of 301 (97.3%) on praziquantel — a difference of −3.8 percentage points (95% CI −7.1 to −0.4), so the lower confidence limit exceeded the non-inferiority margin and non-inferiority was NOT shown. Egg reduction was 99.9% in both groups. Adverse events were mild/moderate and more frequent on praziquantel (odds ratio 4.5, 95% CI 3.2 to 6.3; P<0.0001 — a relative measure); the most frequent were headache, vertigo, nausea and fatigue.
cards.watchOut: The honest headline is the failed non-inferiority test, not the high absolute cure rates: tribendimidine cured slightly fewer patients than praziquantel by more than the pre-specified margin allowed. Open-label (tablet differences made masking impractical).
cards.source: Sayasone S et al. Efficacy and safety of tribendimidine versus praziquantel against Opisthorchis viverrini in Laos: an open-label, randomised, non-inferiority, phase 2 trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2018. PMID: 29153938. Registry ID: ISRCTN96948551. cards.headline: Soukhathammavong 2011 exploratory five-arm phase 2 (125 school children; the tribendimidine arm is ONE limb of five — labelled, never load-bearing): 19 cured on tribendimidine vs 14 on praziquantel in the intention-to-treat analysis, egg reduction 99.3% vs 98.4%; mefloquine and artesunate arms essentially failed
cards.summary: Soukhathammavong 2011 exploratory five-arm phase 2 (125 school children; the tribendimidine arm is ONE limb of five — labelled, never load-bearing): 19 cured on tribendimidine vs 14 on praziquantel in the intention-to-treat analysis, egg reduction 99.3% vs 98.4%; mefloquine and artesunate arms essentially failed
cards.type: Exploratory five-arm open-label randomised phase 2 trial — tribendimidine is one arm of five (labelled)
cards.people: 125 school children aged 10–15 years with O. viverrini infection in Attapeu Province, Laos, randomised across five arms: mefloquine (25), artesunate (24), mefloquine–artesunate (24), tribendimidine (27) and praziquantel (25); 19 patients were lost to follow-up. Randomised, exploratory, open-label phase 2 trial.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 19 patients on tribendimidine were cured versus 14 on praziquantel (odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 0.60 to 5.85 — a relative measure, absolute counts beside it), versus none on mefloquine and one each on artesunate and mefloquine–artesunate. Egg reduction was 99.3% for tribendimidine and 98.4% for praziquantel, versus 30.2% (mefloquine), 31.5% (artesunate) and 41.3% (combination). Most adverse events were mild/moderate; serious events (vertigo, nausea, vomiting, anxiety) occurred only with mefloquine or mefloquine–artesunate.
cards.watchOut: The tribendimidine limb is 27 children in an exploratory five-arm trial — labelled here and never load-bearing. Its role is early signal within one programme, not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Soukhathammavong P et al. Efficacy and safety of mefloquine, artesunate, mefloquine-artesunate, tribendimidine, and praziquantel in patients with Opisthorchis viverrini: a randomised, exploratory, open-label, phase 2 trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: one Lao phase 2 programme — 3 publications reporting 4 trials (labelled) — shows tribendimidine is highly active against O. viverrini (cure ~94% at the chosen doses, egg reduction 99.9%), but it did NOT prove non-inferior to praziquantel on cure
cards.summary: Synthesis: one Lao phase 2 programme — 3 publications reporting 4 trials (labelled) — shows tribendimidine is highly active against O. viverrini (cure ~94% at the chosen doses, egg reduction 99.9%), but it did NOT prove non-inferior to praziquantel on cure
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: 3 publications reporting 4 phase 2 trials from one research collaboration (Swiss TPH / Lao programme) in Laos — the 2016 publication reports two dose-ranging trials; the 2018 publication reports the non-inferiority trial; the 2011 publication reports the exploratory five-arm trial.
cards.result: Dose-ranging established ≥100 mg as the active range (cure up to 91.5% at 400 mg in older participants; 99% range egg reduction). Head-to-head, single-dose tribendimidine cured 93.6% versus 97.3% on two-dose praziquantel and egg reduction was 99.9% in both groups, but non-inferiority on cure was not shown (difference −3.8 points; lower limit −7.1 vs the −3 margin), with fewer adverse events on tribendimidine. Endpoints throughout are parasitological (cure = no eggs in stool; egg reduction) — no trial measures biliary or cancer outcomes, although O. viverrini's cholangiocarcinoma risk is the disease rationale. There is no phase 3 trial and no approval: this is a phase 2, single-region, single-programme record. Product naming (clarification exception): tribendimidine is a Chinese-developed anthelmintic as the publications describe it; it is not marketed in the US/EU, so current products elsewhere may differ. The hookworm/soil-transmitted-helminth and Clonorchis sinensis tribendimidine questions are different parasite questions and are not folded in.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, one region, one programme — the count is stated exactly (3 publications / 4 trials) so the base is not mistaken for independent replication. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Needle aspiration in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess: no benefit over metronidazole alone in three small trials (PARTIAL beside pack #7009's drainage-technique shelf)
shelves.question: In adults with uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, does ultrasound-guided needle aspiration added to metronidazole, versus metronidazole alone, speed resolution of pain, fever and the abscess cavity? (The drainage-technique question — catheter versus needle — is homed at pack #7009 and is not re-carded here.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Case-Control Studies · Female · Humans · Liver Abscess, Amebic/therapy · Male · Metronidazole/therapeutic use · Random Allocation · Suction/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — PARTIAL beside pack #7009: #7009 asks catheter drainage versus needle aspiration (which technique, presupposing drainage) and its trials are not re-carded; this shelf asks the prior, unasked question — whether to aspirate at all in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess. Three small randomised trials (n=39, 39, 57) over 24 years consistently found metronidazole alone sufficient: clinical improvement, laboratory normalisation and cavity healing similar in both groups (1989); only liver tenderness improved faster, over the first 3 days, in one trial (2003); earlier pain/fever resolution was not significant in the third (2013; P=0.16, P=0.48), with no deaths, failures or ruptures in any arm. The Cochrane synthesis (7 trials, 310 patients) could neither support nor refute aspiration. Size limbs are labelled per trial and the answer does not extend to >10 cm, left-lobe, ruptured or impending-rupture abscesses. All trials predate routine E. histolytica antigen/PCR confirmation in their settings.

cards.headline: Sharma 1989 randomised trial (39 patients, 37 completed, ≥1-year follow-up): clinical improvement, laboratory normalisation and cavity healing were SIMILAR in both groups — aspiration added nothing to metronidazole
cards.summary: Sharma 1989 randomised trial (39 patients, 37 completed, ≥1-year follow-up): clinical improvement, laboratory normalisation and cavity healing were SIMILAR in both groups — aspiration added nothing to metronidazole
cards.type: Randomised trial, metronidazole + needle aspiration vs metronidazole alone (n=39)
cards.people: 39 consecutive patients with amoebic liver abscess in the right lobe at a referral gastroenterology clinic, of whom 37 completed the study; all received metronidazole 2.4 g/day for 10 days, and 19 additionally had needle aspiration of the abscess on the day of admission. Randomised case-control design with a minimum 1-year follow-up; pain, fever, anorexia and hepatomegaly plus blood tests were measured.
cards.result: Clinical improvement was similar in both groups, as were improvement in haematological and biochemical variables and rates of healing of the abscess cavities. The authors concluded that chemotherapy with a potent tissue amoebicidal drug such as metronidazole is optimally effective in amoebic liver abscess and that, in uncomplicated cases, routine aspiration is not required.

cards.headline: Blessmann 2003 randomised trial in Huế, Vietnam (39 patients, right-lobe abscesses 6–10 cm): liver tenderness improved significantly faster with aspiration over the first 3 days (P<0.001), with NO difference in any other parameter
cards.summary: Blessmann 2003 randomised trial in Huế, Vietnam (39 patients, right-lobe abscesses 6–10 cm): liver tenderness improved significantly faster with aspiration over the first 3 days (P<0.001), with NO difference in any other parameter
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial, metronidazole + ultrasound-guided needle aspiration vs metronidazole alone (n=39, abscesses 6–10 cm)
cards.people: 39 adult patients with amoebic liver abscess in the right liver lobe, 6–10 cm in diameter, at the Central Hospital of Huế, Vietnam; bacterial abscesses were excluded microbiologically in all patients. Nineteen received metronidazole for 10 days alone and 20 additionally had ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of the abscess fluid. Symptoms, laboratory parameters and abscess size were followed for 38 days.
cards.result: Improvement in liver tenderness was significantly faster in the aspiration group during the first 3 days (P<0.001); fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, white blood cells, haemoglobin, C-reactive protein and abscess size showed no differences between the groups. The authors judged this minor benefit insufficient to justify routine needle aspiration and advocated drug treatment alone for uncomplicated amoebic liver abscesses up to 10 cm in the right lobe.
cards.watchOut: The single positive finding is faster tenderness relief in the first 3 days only — every other measured parameter was null. Size limb 6–10 cm, right lobe only; the result does not extend to larger, left-lobe or complicated abscesses.

cards.headline: Bammigatti 2013 randomised trial (57 patients, abscesses 5–10 cm): pain and fever resolved earlier with aspiration but NOT significantly (P=0.16 and P=0.48); no deaths, failures or ruptures in either arm
cards.summary: Bammigatti 2013 randomised trial (57 patients, abscesses 5–10 cm): pain and fever resolved earlier with aspiration but NOT significantly (P=0.16 and P=0.48); no deaths, failures or ruptures in either arm
cards.type: Randomised trial, metronidazole + ultrasound-guided needle aspiration vs metronidazole alone (n=57, abscesses 5–10 cm)
cards.people: 57 patients with a solitary, right-lobe, uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess of 5–10 cm, randomised to metronidazole alone (29) or ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration plus metronidazole (28).
cards.result: Resolution of pain occurred at 27 hours in the aspiration group versus 48 hours on metronidazole alone, and fever at 17 versus 30 hours — earlier, but not statistically significant (P=0.16 and P=0.48 respectively). There were no deaths during the study; treatment failure, complications (rupture of abscess), days to normalisation of leukocytosis and duration of hospitalisation were similar in both groups. The authors concluded aspiration plus metronidazole was no better than metronidazole alone for uncomplicated, solitary, right-lobe abscesses of 5–10 cm.
cards.watchOut: Non-significant differences in a 57-patient trial are compatible with a small real benefit or none — the card prints the P values rather than calling the earlier resolution a gain. Size limb 5–10 cm, solitary right-lobe only.
cards.source: Bammigatti C et al. Percutaneous needle aspiration in uncomplicated amebic liver abscess: a randomized trial. Tropical doctor. 2013. PMID: 23550199. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Chavez-Tapia 2009) — the builder's synthesis cross-point, not a fourth trial: 7 low-quality randomised trials, 310 patients; needle aspiration did NOT significantly increase fever resolution (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.61) and the reviewers concluded benefit could be neither supported nor refuted
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Chavez-Tapia 2009) — the builder's synthesis cross-point, not a fourth trial: 7 low-quality randomised trials, 310 patients; needle aspiration did NOT significantly increase fever resolution (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.61) and the reviewers concluded benefit could be neither supported nor refuted
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (synthesis cross-point — includes the era's trials, not independent of them)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised or quasi-randomised trials of image-guided percutaneous procedure plus metronidazole versus metronidazole alone in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, searched to 2007; 7 low-quality trials including a total of 310 patients, with fewer patients analysable for several outcomes because of selective outcome reporting.
cards.result: Pooled analysis of three homogeneous trials showed needle aspiration did not significantly increase the proportion of patients with fever resolution (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.61 — a relative measure, printed with its wide interval). Benefits in days to resolution of pain (mean difference −1.59 days), abdominal tenderness (−1.70 days) and hospitalisation (−1.31 days) were observed in the aspiration group only in heterogeneous trial subsets. The reviewers concluded that adjunctive therapeutic aspiration cannot be supported or refuted on the present evidence, and that the trials lack methodological rigour and adequate sample size.
cards.watchOut: The review's trials overlap the primary reports carded above and add other small trials — it is carded as the synthesis cross-point the row directs, not as independent evidence, and its own verdict is 'cannot be supported or refuted', weaker than any single-trial reading.
cards.source: Chavez-Tapia NC et al. Image-guided percutaneous procedure plus metronidazole versus metronidazole alone for uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2009. PMID: 19160244. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistently negative answer, presented as one — three small trials (n=39, 39, 57) over 24 years all found metronidazole alone sufficient in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, with at most faster tenderness relief in the first 3 days in one trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistently negative answer, presented as one — three small trials (n=39, 39, 57) over 24 years all found metronidazole alone sufficient in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, with at most faster tenderness relief in the first 3 days in one trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three randomised trials totalling 135 patients, plus the Cochrane synthesis cross-point (7 trials, 310 patients). PARTIAL position: pack #7009 asks catheter drainage versus needle aspiration for large liver abscesses — a technique-versus-technique question that presupposes drainage; its drainage-technique trials are NOT re-carded here. This shelf asks only the unasked prior question: whether to aspirate at all.
cards.result: Sharma 1989 found clinical improvement, laboratory normalisation and cavity healing similar with and without aspiration. Blessmann 2003 found only faster liver-tenderness relief in the first 3 days (P<0.001), with no difference in any other parameter. Bammigatti 2013 found earlier pain and fever resolution that was not significant (P=0.16, P=0.48), with no deaths, failures or ruptures in either arm. The Cochrane synthesis could neither support nor refute adjunctive aspiration. The answer must not be extended beyond the trials: abscess-size limbs differ per trial (right-lobe unselected; 6–10 cm; 5–10 cm) and nothing here applies to large (>10 cm), left-lobe, ruptured or impending-rupture abscesses, where drainage practice differs. All trials predate routine Entamoeba histolytica antigen/PCR confirmation in their settings — a diagnostic-certainty flag on the face.
cards.watchOut: Three small trials over 24 years, none individually definitive; the stamp rests on their concordance plus the Cochrane verdict. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Stretta radiofrequency for GERD: symptoms move, acid exposure doesn't — and the PPI-refractory heartburn trial was flatly negative
shelves.question: In adults with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — including PPI-responsive disease and PPI-refractory heartburn — does endoluminal radiofrequency energy delivery (the Stretta procedure) to the gastro-oesophageal junction versus a sham procedure improve heartburn, reflux quality of life, acid exposure and medication use?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Radio Waves · Radiofrequency Therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — symptoms move, reflux does not. In the early sham-controlled trials, heartburn and reflux quality-of-life scores improved more on active radiofrequency (Stretta) than on sham, while oesophageal acid exposure and medication use did not differ in the first trial and did not change in the mechanistic crossover trial. The three-arm dose trial's improvements are within-group readings against baseline, labelled as such. The programme's most rigorous trial — in PPI-refractory heartburn, the population most often offered the procedure — was flatly negative: its primary endpoint was reached by 3.4% on radiofrequency versus 15.1% on sham. Every trial is small (n=22-64) with subjective primary endpoints, so expectation effects are the standing alternative explanation. The tested procedure is the Stretta radiofrequency system as the publications name it (clarification exception); results do not transfer to other endoluminal devices.

cards.headline: First sham-controlled RCT (Corley 2003): heartburn and quality of life improved on radiofrequency (61% vs 33% without daily heartburn) — but acid exposure and medication use did not differ
cards.summary: First sham-controlled RCT (Corley 2003): heartburn and quality of life improved on radiofrequency (61% vs 33% without daily heartburn) — but acid exposure and medication use did not differ
cards.type: Randomised sham-controlled trial (Stretta procedure), radiofrequency energy delivery vs sham, GERD
cards.people: 64 patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease randomised to radiofrequency energy delivery to the gastro-oesophageal junction (35 patients) or a sham procedure (29 patients), with principal outcomes of reflux symptoms and quality of life at 6 months; interested sham patients then crossed over to active treatment.
cards.result: At 6 months, more active than sham patients were without daily heartburn (19 [61%] versus 7 [33%], P=0.05) and more had a >50% improvement in reflux quality-of-life score (19 [61%] versus 6 [30%], P=0.03); symptom improvements persisted at 12 months. There were NO differences in daily medication use after a withdrawal protocol (17 [55%] versus 14 [61%], P=0.67) or in oesophageal acid exposure times. There were no perforations or deaths.
cards.watchOut: The split is the finding: subjective symptom and quality-of-life endpoints improved while the objective reflux measures (acid exposure, medication use) did not. Small trial (n=64) with subjective primary endpoints — expectation effects are the standing alternative explanation.
cards.source: Corley DA et al. Improvement of gastroesophageal reflux symptoms after radiofrequency energy: a randomized, sham-controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 12949712. cards.headline: Three-arm dose RCT (Aziz 2010): single and repeat Stretta sessions improved quality of life, sphincter pressure, acid exposure and PPI dose versus baseline at 12 months — within-group readings, labelled as such
cards.summary: Three-arm dose RCT (Aziz 2010): single and repeat Stretta sessions improved quality of life, sphincter pressure, acid exposure and PPI dose versus baseline at 12 months — within-group readings, labelled as such
cards.type: Prospective three-arm randomised trial, sham vs single-session vs repeat-session Stretta, GERD (12 months)
cards.people: 36 patients with GERD randomised to sham (12), a single Stretta session (12), or a single session with a repeat session if quality of life had not improved 75% by 4 months (12); 56 radiofrequency lesions were created per session.
cards.result: At 12 months, in both Stretta groups the mean quality-of-life scores of those off medications, lower oesophageal sphincter basal pressure, 24-hour pH scores and daily PPI dose were significantly improved FROM BASELINE (P<0.01) — within-group readings, not sham-adjusted differences. The double session was numerically but not significantly better than the single session on most parameters, though more double-session patients normalised their quality-of-life score (7 versus 2, P=0.035). Sham patients also had small significant decreases in daily PPI dose and quality-of-life scores. No serious complications occurred, but two patients had significant delayed gastric emptying after the second Stretta treatment.
cards.watchOut: The headline improvements are changes from baseline within the active groups, and the sham group also improved significantly on two measures — this card must not be read as a sham-controlled win on acid exposure. Twelve patients per arm.
cards.source: Aziz AM et al. A prospective randomized trial of sham, single-dose Stretta, and double-dose Stretta for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Surgical Endoscopy. 2010. PMID: 19730952. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mechanistic crossover RCT (Arts 2012): symptoms improved and gastro-oesophageal-junction compliance fell after Stretta — with no change in acid exposure or sphincter pressure
cards.summary: Mechanistic crossover RCT (Arts 2012): symptoms improved and gastro-oesophageal-junction compliance fell after Stretta — with no change in acid exposure or sphincter pressure
cards.type: Double-blind sham-controlled crossover mechanistic trial, Stretta vs sham, GERD (n=22)
cards.people: 22 patients with GERD (17 women, mean age 47 years) in a double-blind randomised crossover study at a tertiary care centre: two endoscopies 3 months apart, with active or sham Stretta in randomised order, and assessment by symptoms, endoscopy, manometry, 24-hour pH monitoring and a barostat distensibility test.
cards.result: Initial sham treatment did not affect any parameter studied. Three months after the initial Stretta procedure, oesophageal acid exposure and lower oesophageal sphincter pressure were unchanged, while the symptom score improved significantly and gastro-oesophageal-junction compliance decreased significantly. Sildenafil, an oesophageal smooth-muscle relaxant, normalised the compliance change back to the pre-Stretta level — arguing against gastro-oesophageal-junction fibrosis as the mechanism, and suggesting altered sphincter neuromuscular function instead.
cards.watchOut: The smallest trial in the base (n=22) and a mechanistic study: it reproduces the symptom-without-acid-exposure split and offers a compliance mechanism, but it is not powered to settle clinical benefit. Reflux evaluation did not include impedance monitoring.
cards.source: Arts J et al. A double-blind sham-controlled study of the effect of radiofrequency energy on symptoms and distensibility of the gastro-esophageal junction in GERD. cards.headline: PPI-refractory heartburn RCT (Zerbib 2020): radiofrequency was FLATLY NEGATIVE — primary endpoint reached by 3.4% on radiofrequency versus 15.1% on sham
cards.summary: PPI-refractory heartburn RCT (Zerbib 2020): radiofrequency was FLATLY NEGATIVE — primary endpoint reached by 3.4% on radiofrequency versus 15.1% on sham
cards.type: Randomised double-blind sham-controlled multicentre trial, oesophageal radiofrequency (Stretta) vs sham, PPI-refractory heartburn
cards.people: 62 patients with moderate-to-severe heartburn at least 3 times a week not improved by continuous PPI treatment, randomised double-blind in a multicentre study to oesophageal radiofrequency (29) or sham (33); the primary endpoint was clinical success at week 24 (fewer than 7 PPI doses in the preceding 2 weeks plus adequate symptom control as judged by the patient).
cards.result: The primary endpoint was reached by 1/29 (3.4%) on radiofrequency versus 5/33 (15.1%) on sham — not significant, and numerically in favour of sham. There was no significant difference in days without heartburn, days with PPI consumption in the last 2 weeks, or patients not taking PPIs, and no pH-impedance parameter was associated with clinical response. Adverse events were similar in both groups. The authors concluded the study did not demonstrate any efficacy of oesophageal radiofrequency for PPI-refractory heartburn.
cards.watchOut: On the face, as the row directs: the programme's most rigorous trial, in exactly the population most often offered the procedure, found the sham arm numerically ahead on its primary endpoint. Any shelf-level symptom claim from the earlier trials must be read against this result.
cards.source: Zerbib F et al. Randomised clinical trial: oesophageal radiofrequency energy delivery versus sham for PPI-refractory heartburn. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2020. cards.result: The Stretta record splits by endpoint type: subjective symptom and quality-of-life measures moved in the 2003, 2010 and 2012 trials (the 2010 improvements being within-group readings), objective acid exposure did not separate in the sham-controlled comparisons, and the 2020 trial in PPI-refractory heartburn showed no efficacy on symptoms or PPI consumption at all. shelves.title: Torasemide vs furosemide in cirrhotic ascites: 6 small reports (1988-1997, documented N=87 + one N not documented) — more natriuresis short-term, surrogates only
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and ascites — including diuretic-resistant ascites — does torasemide versus furosemide (each on a background of an aldosterone antagonist) produce greater natriuresis, diuresis and weight loss?
shelves.mesh: Ascites · Diuretics · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Furosemide · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Spironolactone · Sulfonamides · Torsemide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base stated exactly: 6 randomised reports, all from 1988-1997, with documented N=87 plus one report whose abstract states no N (printed as N not documented). Every trial is small (n=7-28 where stated), short (single dose to 70 days), and powered only on surrogate endpoints — urine sodium, urine volume and weight over hours to days. Torasemide produced greater natriuresis or diuresis in most of the short trials, while the one long-term (70-day) trial found similar weight, urinary volume and sodium effects with less electrolyte excretion on torasemide. No trial measures ascites resolution, hospitalisation, renal failure or survival. All trials gave an aldosterone antagonist to both arms — this is loop-diuretic choice on top of spironolactone/canrenoate, not torasemide monotherapy — and the equipotency doses were set from healthy-volunteer data. One retrieved record (a xipamide trial with an open torasemide series appended) is fenced out of this count and is not carded.

cards.headline: Double-blind 3-day RCT (Laffi 1991): torasemide produced significantly greater natriuresis than furosemide on all 3 days in non-azotaemic cirrhosis — N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Double-blind 3-day RCT (Laffi 1991): torasemide produced significantly greater natriuresis than furosemide on all 3 days in non-azotaemic cirrhosis — N not documented in the record
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, torasemide vs furosemide (both with potassium canrenoate), non-azotaemic cirrhosis with ascites (3 days) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Patients with non-azotaemic cirrhosis and ascites in a randomised double-blind trial of torasemide 10 mg/day versus furosemide 25 mg/day (doses shown equipotent in healthy subjects), both with potassium canrenoate 200 mg/day, over 3 days. The record states no participant count — N not documented.
cards.result: Torasemide induced significantly greater natriuresis than furosemide (P<0.02), with a twofold greater percentage increase over basal values (day 1: 130% versus 50%; day 2: 104% versus 42%; day 3: 65% versus 26% — relative increases, as reported). Body weight loss was significantly greater during torasemide (P<0.02); diuresis was also higher but not significantly (P=0.08). Kaliuresis was almost identical despite the natriuresis difference, and effects on plasma electrolytes, creatinine clearance, blood urea nitrogen, mean arterial pressure, heart rate and plasma arginine vasopressin were similar.
cards.watchOut: N not documented: the fetched record states no participant count, and none is claimed. A 3-day pharmacodynamic trial — urine sodium and weight only, no clinical outcomes. FLOOR-RISK base: one of exactly 6 reports.
cards.source: Laffi G et al. Comparison of the effects of torasemide and furosemide in nonazotemic cirrhotic patients with ascites: a randomized, double-blind study. Hepatology. 1991. PMID: 2050329. cards.headline: Double-blind crossover RCT (Gerbes 1993): single-dose torasemide gave greater 24-hour diuresis than furosemide (2863 vs 2111 mL), driven by the 6-24-hour window and by furosemide weak-responders
cards.summary: Double-blind crossover RCT (Gerbes 1993): single-dose torasemide gave greater 24-hour diuresis than furosemide (2863 vs 2111 mL), driven by the 6-24-hour window and by furosemide weak-responders
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial, single-dose torasemide vs furosemide, cirrhosis with ascites (n=14)
cards.people: 14 patients with cirrhosis and ascites, after a 4-day equilibration period without diuretics, given single oral doses of torasemide 20 mg and furosemide 80 mg (equipotent in healthy subjects) in randomised double-blind crossover order with at least 2 days' washout.
cards.result: Cumulative 24-hour diuresis was greater on torasemide (2863 +/- 343 versus 2111 +/- 184 mL, P<0.01). Cumulative 0-6-hour sodium excretion did not differ (96 +/- 17 versus 92 +/- 23 mmol), but 6-24-hour natriuresis was more pronounced on torasemide (38 +/- 11 versus 17 +/- 4 mmol, P<0.05). The five patients with a weak response to furosemide showed significantly higher natriuresis and diuresis after torasemide. No significant haemodynamic, renal or hormonal changes and no adverse effects were noted with either drug.
cards.watchOut: Single-dose pharmacodynamics in 14 patients. The advantage sits in the later (6-24-hour) window and in furosemide weak-responders — a subgroup reading within a very small crossover trial.
cards.source: Gerbes AL et al. Advantages of the new loop diuretic torasemide over furosemide in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. A randomized, double blind cross-over trial. Journal of Hepatology. 1993. PMID: 8315263. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Long-term double-blind RCT (Fiaccadori 1993): over 70 days, torasemide and furosemide had similar weight, urine volume and sodium effects — torasemide spared potassium, calcium, phosphate and magnesium
cards.summary: Long-term double-blind RCT (Fiaccadori 1993): over 70 days, torasemide and furosemide had similar weight, urine volume and sodium effects — torasemide spared potassium, calcium, phosphate and magnesium
cards.type: Long-term randomised double-blind trial, torasemide vs furosemide (both with spironolactone), cirrhosis with controlled ascites (70 days, n=28)
cards.people: 28 non-azotaemic cirrhotic patients with controlled ascites, randomised double-blind to torasemide 20 mg/day or furosemide 50 mg/day, both with spironolactone 200 mg/day, for 70 days — the longest trial in this base.
cards.result: The treatments did not modify creatinine clearance and had a similar effect on body weight, urinary volume and fractional excretion of uric acid, sodium and chloride. Torasemide's effect on fractional potassium excretion was lower than furosemide's, and torasemide spared calcium, inorganic phosphate and magnesium excretion more, with a stronger action on free water clearance. No serum parameter changes were induced by either treatment; two episodes of hepatic encephalopathy occurred in the torasemide group.
cards.watchOut: The only trial longer than a few days found NO natriuresis or weight advantage — the short-trial advantages did not persist as differences at 70 days; the separation was in electrolyte handling. Two encephalopathy episodes occurred on torasemide.
cards.source: Fiaccadori F et al. Torasemide versus furosemide in cirrhosis: a long-term, double-blind, randomized clinical study. The Clinical Investigator. 1993. PMID: 8374255. cards.headline: Crossover RCT in tense ascites (Gentilini 1993): torasemide gave markedly higher natriuresis (120 vs 33 mmol/day) and diuresis than furosemide — SUB-FLOOR-SIZED report (n=7), never load-bearing
cards.summary: Crossover RCT in tense ascites (Gentilini 1993): torasemide gave markedly higher natriuresis (120 vs 33 mmol/day) and diuresis than furosemide — SUB-FLOOR-SIZED report (n=7), never load-bearing
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial, torasemide vs furosemide (both with potassium canrenoate), tense ascites (n=7 — sub-floor in size, labelled, never load-bearing)
cards.people: 7 patients with cirrhosis and tense ascites, in a randomised crossover study of torasemide 20 mg/day versus furosemide 50 mg/day, each over 4 days, on a low-sodium diet (40 mmol/day) with potassium canrenoate 100 mg twice daily. This report's n=7 is below the library's 10-human reference floor and is labelled as such.
cards.result: Torasemide induced a higher natriuretic effect (120 +/- 15 versus 33 +/- 6 mmol/day, P<0.02) and diuretic effect (1450 +/- 63 versus 900 +/- 58 mL, P<0.005) than furosemide, and body weight loss was significantly higher (P<0.01). Kaliuresis was similar despite the natriuresis difference, and neither drug significantly changed serum electrolytes, creatinine or ammonia.
cards.watchOut: Seven patients: the largest natriuresis ratio in the base comes from its smallest report. Carded to complete the exact 6-report count; it carries no weight of its own.
cards.source: Gentilini P et al. Torasemide in the treatment of patients with cirrhosis and ascites. Cardiovascular Drugs and Therapy. 1993. PMID: 8435382. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Single-dose PK/PD RCT in diuretic-resistant ascites (Gentilini 1996): torasemide's advantage was confined to the first hour, and both drugs' natriuretic potency was markedly reduced in this population
cards.summary: Single-dose PK/PD RCT in diuretic-resistant ascites (Gentilini 1996): torasemide's advantage was confined to the first hour, and both drugs' natriuretic potency was markedly reduced in this population
cards.type: Randomised pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic trial, single IV dose torasemide vs furosemide, diuretic-resistant ascites (n=18)
cards.people: 18 patients with cirrhosis and diuretic-resistant ascites, randomly allocated to a single intravenous dose of torasemide 40 mg or furosemide 80 mg, with renal response, plasma and urinary drug concentrations measured over 24 hours.
cards.result: Torasemide induced significantly greater diuretic and natriuretic effects than furosemide in the first hour after administration; no other significant differences in renal response were observed. Both drugs showed reduced renal and non-renal elimination and a longer half-life than in healthy subjects, and the natriuretic potency of BOTH drugs was markedly reduced in these patients — the equipotency assumption imported from healthy-volunteer data does not hold in diuretic-resistant cirrhosis.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic study whose clinical reading is a warning: in the population where a stronger loop diuretic is most wanted, both drugs lose potency and the torasemide advantage lasts one hour.
cards.source: Gentilini P et al. Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of torasemide and furosemide in patients with diuretic resistant ascites. Journal of Hepatology. 1996. PMID: 8912147. cards.headline: Parallel-group RCT (Marelli 1997): natriuretic, diuretic and weight effects were significantly better on torasemide over 8 days
cards.summary: Parallel-group RCT (Marelli 1997): natriuretic, diuretic and weight effects were significantly better on torasemide over 8 days
cards.type: Randomised parallel-group trial, torasemide vs furosemide (both with potassium canrenoate), cirrhotic ascites (n=20)
cards.people: 20 patients with cirrhosis and ascites, randomly divided to torasemide 20 mg/day or furosemide 50 mg/day, all also receiving potassium canrenoate 200 mg/day; the furosemide group later crossed to torasemide, and the torasemide group continued for 8 days.
cards.result: Natriuretic and diuretic effects and consequent weight loss were significantly better in the torasemide group; potassium loss and the urinary sodium/potassium ratio were not significantly higher. No change was observed in blood pressure, pulse, plasma electrolytes, azotaemia, creatininaemia or serum albumin. Diuresis increased significantly from the fourth day when the furosemide group was switched to torasemide, and the torasemide group maintained efficient diuresis over 8 days with no side effects.
cards.watchOut: The last report in the base (1997) and one of the smallest parallel trials; the switch-over limb is uncontrolled. Surrogate endpoints only, like every report on this shelf.
cards.source: Marelli A et al. [Comparison between torasemide and furosemide in the treatment of ascites in cirrhotic patients]. Minerva Medica. 1997. PMID: 9148226. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: exactly 6 randomised reports (1988-1997), documented N=87 plus one N-not-documented — short-term natriuresis favours torasemide, the 70-day trial found no sodium or weight difference, and no trial measured a clinical outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: exactly 6 randomised reports (1988-1997), documented N=87 plus one N-not-documented — short-term natriuresis favours torasemide, the 70-day trial found no sodium or weight difference, and no trial measured a clinical outcome
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Torasemide beat furosemide on urine sodium, urine volume or weight in the 3-day, single-dose, tense-ascites and 8-day reports, matched it on sodium and weight over 70 days with better electrolyte sparing, and beat it only in the first hour in diuretic-resistant ascites. The whole base is a pharmacodynamic programme that was never taken to outcomes: no ascites resolution, hospitalisation, renal failure or survival data exist, and nothing postdates 1997.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. A further retrieved record (PMID 7954550) is a xipamide-versus-spironolactone/furosemide trial with an open torasemide series appended — it is not a torasemide randomised report, is fenced out of the count of 6, and is not carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Losartan for portal hypertension: a non-randomised ~45% HVPG fall never replicated — four small randomised trials (n=136) split, the largest negative with a renal harm limb
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, does losartan versus propranolol (or versus untreated control) reduce hepatic venous pressure gradient, and at what cost to arterial pressure and renal function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Blood Urea Nitrogen · Creatinine · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypertension, Portal · Liver Circulation · Liver Cirrhosis · Losartan · Male · Middle Aged · Propranolol · Splanchnic Circulation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — an unreplicated dramatic start, then small split trials. The programme's originating controlled study (1999, NOT randomised, labelled programme support) reported a ~45% relative fall in hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) on losartan — a result no later trial approached. The four randomised trials (n=27-40, total 136) split: two report responder-rate or within-group HVPG advantages for losartan, while the largest and longest — in patients treated after variceal bleeding — found losartan did not reduce HVPG at all (-2% versus -10% on propranolol) and concluded losartan is not an alternative to propranolol. Every endpoint is the HVPG surrogate over 2-12 weeks; no trial measures variceal bleeding or death. The harm limb is on the face: arterial pressure fell in most reports, and glomerular filtration rate fell in Child-Pugh B patients in the 2001 trial. Populations differ (post-bleeding, compensated, decompensated) and are never pooled.

cards.headline: Randomised post-bleeding RCT (Gonzalez-Abraldes 2001): losartan did NOT reduce HVPG (-2%, NS) while propranolol did (-10%, P=0.003) — and losartan reduced GFR in Child-Pugh B patients
cards.summary: Randomised post-bleeding RCT (Gonzalez-Abraldes 2001): losartan did NOT reduce HVPG (-2%, NS) while propranolol did (-10%, P=0.003) — and losartan reduced GFR in Child-Pugh B patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, long-term losartan vs propranolol after variceal bleeding (6 weeks, n=40)
cards.people: 40 patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension treated endoscopically after a variceal bleeding episode, randomised to losartan (n=25) or propranolol (n=15) for 6 weeks, with HVPG, systemic haemodynamics, renal function and vasoactive factors measured before and at 6 weeks.
cards.result: Losartan did not reduce HVPG (-2% +/- 12%, not significant — a relative change) but significantly decreased mean arterial pressure (-8% +/- 10%, P=0.001). Propranolol significantly reduced HVPG (-10% +/- 11%, P=0.003) and cardiac output (-16% +/- 12%, P=0.001) without modifying mean arterial pressure. Losartan increased angiotensin II levels, reduced aldosterone, and decreased glomerular filtration rate in Child-Pugh B patients; propranolol did not modify renal function. Adverse events were mild and similar. The authors concluded losartan is not an alternative to propranolol in preventing variceal rebleeding.
cards.watchOut: The largest and longest randomised trial in the base, in the highest-stakes population (post-bleeding), is the negative one — and it carries the renal harm limb (GFR fall in Child-Pugh B). HVPG is a surrogate; rebleeding itself was not measured.
cards.source: González-Abraldes J et al. Randomized comparison of long-term losartan versus propranolol in lowering portal pressure in cirrhosis. Gastroenterology. 2001. PMID: 11487547. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Randomised 14-day RCT (De 2003): more HVPG responders on losartan (15/19, 79%) than propranolol (9/20, 45%), though the mean percentage HVPG fall did not differ significantly
cards.summary: Randomised 14-day RCT (De 2003): more HVPG responders on losartan (15/19, 79%) than propranolol (9/20, 45%), though the mean percentage HVPG fall did not differ significantly
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, losartan vs propranolol (14 days, n=39)
cards.people: 39 patients with cirrhosis randomised to losartan (n=19) or propranolol (n=20) for 14 days, with HVPG measured at baseline and day 14; responders were defined as an HVPG reduction of at least 20% of baseline. Patients were not receiving diuretics.
cards.result: Responders numbered 15/19 (79%) on losartan versus 9/20 (45%) on propranolol (P<0.05). The mean percentage HVPG reduction was higher on losartan (26.74 +/- 21.7% relative) than propranolol (14.52 +/- 32% relative) but the difference was not significant. The losartan fall was driven mainly by a significant drop in wedged hepatic venous pressure (32.42 to 28.31 mmHg, P<0.05). Among alcohol-abusing patients, responders were 81.8% on losartan versus 27.2% on propranolol (P<0.05), and all seven non-ascitic losartan patients responded. No significant side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The positive reading is a responder-rate (threshold) analysis over 14 days; the continuous between-group comparison — mean percentage HVPG fall — was not significant. Subgroup readings (alcohol use, non-ascitic) are small and labelled as such.
cards.source: De BK et al. Portal pressure response to losartan compared with propranolol in patients with cirrhosis. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2003. PMID: 12818283. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Randomised 12-week RCT in compensated cirrhosis (Castano 2003): HVPG fell on losartan from 15.6 to 11.8 mmHg (P=0.002), driven by reduced portal resistance
cards.summary: Randomised 12-week RCT in compensated cirrhosis (Castano 2003): HVPG fell on losartan from 15.6 to 11.8 mmHg (P=0.002), driven by reduced portal resistance
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, losartan vs propranolol in compensated cirrhosis (12 weeks, n=27)
cards.people: 27 compensated cirrhotic patients randomised to losartan 25 mg/day (n=17) or propranolol (n=10) for 12 weeks, with HVPG, portal blood flow (Doppler) and systemic haemodynamics measured at baseline and after treatment; portal resistance was calculated as HVPG/portal blood flow.
cards.result: Losartan decreased HVPG from 15.6 (+/- 4.2) to 11.8 (+/- 3.5) mmHg (P=0.002), without changes in portal blood flow or systemic haemodynamics; changes in HVPG correlated with variations in portal resistance (r=0.88, P<0.0001). On losartan, 5/17 patients had an HVPG reduction of 10-19% and 8/17 a reduction of 20% or more, with responders concentrated in severe portal hypertension (baseline HVPG at least 16 mmHg). Propranolol reduced cardiac output and heart rate, and HVPG fell from 16.4 to 13.1 mmHg (P=0.07), with six responders.
cards.watchOut: The losartan result is a within-group change in 17 patients; propranolol's own HVPG fall in this trial was itself borderline (P=0.07) with only 10 patients. Compensated cirrhosis only — the result does not extend to the post-bleeding or decompensated limbs.
cards.source: Castaño G et al. A randomized study of losartan vs propranolol: Effects on hepatic and systemic hemodynamics in cirrhotic patients. Annals of Hepatology. 2003. PMID: 15094704. Registry ID: none in the record.
