cards.headline: Randomised RCT in decompensated disease (Agasti 2013): equal responders on losartan and propranolol (6/15 in each group), with greater but non-significant falls in wedged pressure and HVPG on losartan
cards.summary: Randomised RCT in decompensated disease (Agasti 2013): equal responders on losartan and propranolol (6/15 in each group), with greater but non-significant falls in wedged pressure and HVPG on losartan
cards.type: Randomised comparative trial, losartan vs propranolol in decompensated Child-Pugh B cirrhosis (4 weeks, n=30)
cards.people: 30 patients with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis and large varices, with no prior therapy for portal hypertension, randomised to losartan (n=15) or propranolol (n=15) for 4 weeks, with HVPG, wedged and free hepatic venous pressures and mean arterial pressure measured at baseline and after therapy; responders were defined here as HVPG below 12 mmHg.
cards.result: An equal number of responders was seen in both groups (6/15, 40.0%). The reduction in wedged hepatic venous pressure and HVPG was greater on losartan than propranolol, but no significant differences between groups were found. Heart rate decreased more on propranolol (P<0.01) without correlating with HVPG reduction. The fall in mean arterial pressure was greater with losartan, again not significantly. One losartan responder had a gastrointestinal bleed 2 months after administration, from small varices, not requiring definitive therapy.
cards.watchOut: Responder definitions differ across this shelf's trials (a 20% fall in De 2003; HVPG below 12 mmHg here) — responder rates must not be compared across cards. Decompensated Child-Pugh B is the population where the 2001 trial's GFR harm limb appeared.
cards.source: Agasti AK et al. Comparative randomized study on efficacy of losartan versus propranolol in lowering portal pressure in decompensated chronic liver disease. Journal of Digestive Diseases. 2013. PMID: 23280243. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme support — originating controlled study (Schneider 1999, NOT randomised): losartan was associated with a ~45% relative fall in HVPG over 1 week — the dramatic result the randomised trials never reproduced
cards.summary: Programme support — originating controlled study (Schneider 1999, NOT randomised): losartan was associated with a ~45% relative fall in HVPG over 1 week — the dramatic result the randomised trials never reproduced
cards.type: Programme support: controlled clinical trial (not randomised), losartan vs untreated controls (1 week, n=70) — never counted among the randomised trials
cards.people: 70 patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension: 45 treated with losartan 25 mg once daily for 1 week (30 with severe portal hypertension, HVPG at least 20 mmHg; 15 with moderate, HVPG below 20 mmHg) and 25 untreated cirrhotic controls (15 severe, 10 moderate). Typed a Controlled Clinical Trial — not randomised; labelled programme support and never counted as a randomised trial.
cards.result: Losartan was associated with a significant fall in HVPG in severe portal hypertension (-46.8% +/- 15.5% relative, P<0.001) and moderate portal hypertension (-44.1% +/- 14.7% relative, P<0.001), with no significant change in the controls. Losartan caused a slight but significant fall in mean arterial blood pressure, and one patient had a short symptomatic hypotensive reaction after the first dose that did not recur. No deterioration of liver or kidney function was observed over the week.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised, 1 week, untreated controls: this is the programme's origin story, carded and labelled as programme support only. Its ~45% relative HVPG fall was never approached by any of the four randomised trials carded above — that gap is the shelf's central fact. Candesartan and irbesartan reports are different agents and are cross-points only, not anchors.
cards.source: Schneider AW et al. Effect of losartan, an angiotensin II receptor antagonist, on portal pressure in cirrhosis. Hepatology. 1999. PMID: 9918907. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four small randomised trials (total n=136) split on the HVPG surrogate — two favourable readings, the largest post-bleeding trial negative with a renal harm limb — after a non-randomised ~45% relative fall that was never replicated
cards.summary: Synthesis: four small randomised trials (total n=136) split on the HVPG surrogate — two favourable readings, the largest post-bleeding trial negative with a renal harm limb — after a non-randomised ~45% relative fall that was never replicated
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Losartan's portal-pressure record is an arc: a dramatic non-randomised 1999 result, then randomised trials that found responder-rate or within-group HVPG advantages (De 2003; Castano 2003), equivalence on responder counts in decompensated disease (Agasti 2013), and no HVPG effect at all after variceal bleeding, with reduced GFR in Child-Pugh B patients (Gonzalez-Abraldes 2001). No trial measured variceal bleeding or death, so no bleeding-prevention claim can be made from this base.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: UDCA in NASH/MASH: histology negative at both doses (n=166 and n=185) — the positive trial measured ALT, not the disease
shelves.question: In adults with biopsy-proven non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH/MASH), does ursodeoxycholic acid — at conventional dose, at high dose, or combined with vitamin E — versus placebo improve liver histology and liver enzymes over 12-24 months?
shelves.mesh: Alanine Transaminase · Aspartate Aminotransferases · Cholagogues and Choleretics · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Liver · Fibrosis · Humans · Liver · Necrosis · Ursodeoxycholic Acid
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) on histology — the disease answer is negative at both doses, and it is printed on the face. The two trials with histological primary endpoints (n=166 at conventional dose over 2 years; n=185 at high dose over 18 months) found no benefit over placebo in steatosis, necroinflammation, fibrosis or overall histology. The positive trial (n=126) had a biochemical primary endpoint: ALT fell 28.3% relative on high-dose UDCA versus 1.6% on placebo, and ALT normalised in 24.5% versus 4.8% — an enzyme answer, not a disease answer, in a programme where liver biochemistries also improved on placebo in the 2004 trial. The combination limb (UDCA plus vitamin E, n=48) improved enzymes and steatosis-driven activity but cannot attribute its signal to UDCA rather than vitamin E, and UDCA alone in that same trial did not separate histologically. Era flag: pre-resmetirom, pre-GLP-1-era MASH care in biopsy-defined NASH populations — a closed question, not a treatment option. Norursodeoxycholic acid is a different drug; its NAFLD trial is never counted here.

cards.headline: US RCT (Lindor 2004): conventional-dose UDCA for 2 years was NOT better than placebo on liver histology in NASH — biochemistries improved in both groups
cards.summary: US RCT (Lindor 2004): conventional-dose UDCA for 2 years was NOT better than placebo on liver histology in NASH — biochemistries improved in both groups
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, UDCA 13-15 mg/kg/day vs placebo, biopsy-proven NASH (2 years, n=166)
cards.people: 166 patients with liver-biopsy-proven non-alcoholic steatohepatitis randomised to ursodeoxycholic acid 13-15 mg/kg/day or placebo for 2 years; 126 patients completed 2 years of therapy and paired pre- and post-treatment biopsies were available in 107.
cards.result: Serum liver biochemistries were stable or improved in BOTH the UDCA and placebo groups. Changes in the degree of steatosis, necroinflammation or fibrosis over therapy were not significantly different between UDCA and placebo. UDCA was well tolerated and body weight was stable. The authors concluded that 2 years of UDCA at 13-15 mg/kg/day, although safe and well tolerated, is not better than placebo for patients with NASH.
cards.watchOut: A histology-primary trial and a negative one — the conventional-dose question is answered. Note the both-arms enzyme improvement: it is the standing warning against reading ALT falls as drug effects in this disease.
cards.source: Lindor KD et al. Ursodeoxycholic acid for treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: results of a randomized trial. Hepatology. 2004. PMID: 14999696. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: German high-dose RCT (Leuschner 2010): high-dose UDCA also failed on histology — no significant difference by Brunt score (P=0.881) or NAS (P=0.355); only lobular inflammation improved, fibrosis unchanged
cards.summary: German high-dose RCT (Leuschner 2010): high-dose UDCA also failed on histology — no significant difference by Brunt score (P=0.881) or NAS (P=0.355); only lobular inflammation improved, fibrosis unchanged
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, high-dose UDCA 23-28 mg/kg/day vs placebo, histologically proven NASH (18 months, n=185)
cards.people: 185 patients with histologically proven NASH randomised (intention-to-treat) to high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid 23-28 mg/kg/day or placebo for 18 months; 147 were treated per protocol and a second biopsy was obtained from 139 of 185 (107 of the 137 NAS-confirmed NASH patients).
cards.result: Significant differences in overall histology could not be detected between the groups with the modified Brunt score (P=0.881) or the NAFLD activity score (P=0.355). Only lobular inflammation improved significantly (P=0.011 by Brunt; P=0.005 by NAS), including in subgroup analyses. The fibrosis score did not change (P=0.133 intention-to-treat; P=0.140 per protocol). With the exception of gamma-glutamyl transferase, UDCA did not improve laboratory data. The authors concluded high-dose UDCA failed to improve overall histology in NASH versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: The second histology-primary trial, at roughly double the conventional dose, is also negative — dose escalation does not rescue the histology claim. The lobular-inflammation component and the subgroup readings are secondary findings inside a negative trial.
cards.source: Leuschner UF et al. High-dose ursodeoxycholic acid therapy for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Hepatology. 2010. PMID: 20683947. cards.headline: French high-dose RCT (Ratziu 2011): high-dose UDCA cut ALT by 28.3% relative versus 1.6% on placebo and normalised ALT in 24.5% vs 4.8% — a biochemical primary endpoint, with no histological primary
cards.summary: French high-dose RCT (Ratziu 2011): high-dose UDCA cut ALT by 28.3% relative versus 1.6% on placebo and normalised ALT in 24.5% vs 4.8% — a biochemical primary endpoint, with no histological primary
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, high-dose UDCA 28-35 mg/kg/day vs placebo, biopsy-proven NASH (12 months, n=126) — biochemical primary endpoint
cards.people: 126 patients with biopsy-proven NASH and elevated ALT randomised double-blind to high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid 28-35 mg/kg/day or placebo for 12 months across multiple centres; the primary endpoint was reduction in ALT levels.
cards.result: Mean ALT fell by -28.3% relative to baseline on high-dose UDCA versus -1.6% on placebo (P<0.001), and ALT normalised (35 IU/L or below) in 24.5% versus 4.8% (P=0.003); neither result was accounted for by weight change. The FibroTest serum fibrosis marker fell significantly versus placebo (P<0.001), and markers of glycaemic control and insulin resistance improved. There were no safety issues. The authors themselves called for studies with histological endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The programme's only positive primary is an enzyme (surrogate) endpoint. In the 2004 trial, enzymes improved on placebo too, and both histology-primary trials at both doses were negative — this card cannot carry a disease-modification claim. Note the title's spelling 'ursodesoxycholic' is the publication's own.
cards.source: Ratziu V et al. A randomized controlled trial of high-dose ursodesoxycholic acid for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Journal of Hepatology. 2011. PMID: 21145828. cards.headline: Three-arm combination RCT (Dufour 2006): UDCA plus vitamin E improved enzymes and the steatosis-driven activity index over 2 years — UDCA alone did not separate histologically; the combination limb, labelled as such
cards.summary: Three-arm combination RCT (Dufour 2006): UDCA plus vitamin E improved enzymes and the steatosis-driven activity index over 2 years — UDCA alone did not separate histologically; the combination limb, labelled as such
cards.type: Three-arm randomised placebo-controlled trial, UDCA + vitamin E vs UDCA alone vs double placebo, biopsy-proven NASH (2 years, n=48) — combination limb, labelled
cards.people: 48 patients with elevated aminotransferases, alcohol intake under 40 g/week and biopsy-proven NASH, randomised to UDCA 12-15 mg/kg/day plus vitamin E 400 IU twice daily (n=15), UDCA plus placebo (n=18), or double placebo (n=15) for 2 years, with a second biopsy scored blinded by a single pathologist; 8 patients dropped out, none because of side effects.
cards.result: AST and ALT diminished significantly only in the UDCA/vitamin E group; in the UDCA-alone group only ALT improved, and neither enzyme improved on double placebo. Histologically, the activity index was unchanged in the double-placebo and UDCA-alone groups but significantly better in the combination group, mostly as a result of regression of steatosis. Body mass index was unchanged during the study.
cards.watchOut: A combination limb: its signal cannot be attributed to UDCA rather than vitamin E, and the trial's own UDCA-alone arm did not separate histologically — consistent with the two larger negative histology trials. Never load-bearing for a UDCA claim.
cards.source: Dufour JF et al. Randomized placebo-controlled trial of ursodeoxycholic acid with vitamin e in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2006. cards.result: Ursodeoxycholic acid does not improve liver histology in NASH at 13-15 mg/kg/day over 2 years or at 23-28 mg/kg/day over 18 months. High-dose UDCA does lower ALT (28.3% relative versus 1.6% on placebo) and a serum fibrosis marker, and UDCA plus vitamin E improved enzymes and steatosis-driven activity in a 48-patient trial — but enzymes improved on placebo in the 2004 trial, and no carded trial shows a histological benefit attributable to UDCA. shelves.title: Nitazoxanide in HCV genotype 4: one positive programme trial (SVR 79% vs 50%), then two larger independent negatives — an interferon-era record
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4, does nitazoxanide — as monotherapy, or added to peginterferon + ribavirin (with a nitazoxanide lead-in) — versus placebo or standard peginterferon + ribavirin increase rapid and sustained virological response?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiparasitic Agents · Antiviral Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Genotype · Hepacivirus · Hepatitis C, Chronic · Humans · Interferon alpha-2 · Interferon-alpha · Male · Middle Aged · Nitro Compounds · Polyethylene Glycols · Recombinant Proteins · Ribavirin · Thiazoles · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) as an adjunct — and the interferon-era flag leads: every trial here is peginterferon-era, genotype 4, Egyptian, and the question is closed by the direct-acting-antiviral era; this shelf is a record of a tested-and-failed adjunct, never an option against current standard care. One positive programme trial (2009, from the developer-linked Egyptian programme) reported sustained virological response of 79% with nitazoxanide triple therapy versus 50% on standard care. Two larger independent trials then failed to reproduce it: SVR 50% versus 48% (n=100, open-label) and 58.2% versus 60.8% (n=195 evaluated, double-blind placebo-controlled) — differences of 2 and -2.6 percentage points. The earlier monotherapy signal (undetectable HCV RNA in 30.4% versus 0%) was confined to patients with low baseline viral load, a subgroup reading. Nitazoxanide is a licensed antiparasitic used off-label here, stated plainly.

cards.headline: Monotherapy RCT (Rossignol 2008): nitazoxanide alone produced undetectable HCV RNA in 7/23 (30.4%) versus 0/24 on placebo — all responders had low baseline viral load
cards.summary: Monotherapy RCT (Rossignol 2008): nitazoxanide alone produced undetectable HCV RNA in 7/23 (30.4%) versus 0/24 on placebo — all responders had low baseline viral load
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, nitazoxanide monotherapy vs placebo, HCV genotype 4 (24 weeks)
cards.people: 50 adult patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4 at three Egyptian centres, randomised double-blind to nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 24 weeks, with 24 weeks of follow-up after therapy (23 and 24 patients in the analysed groups as reported).
cards.result: Seven of 23 patients (30.4%) on nitazoxanide achieved undetectable serum HCV RNA during therapy versus 0 of 24 on placebo (P=0.004). Every one of the seven responders had a baseline HCV RNA of 400,000 IU/mL or below — the signal is confined to the low-baseline-viral-load subgroup, labelled as such. Six of the seven responders were followed for 24 weeks after treatment, and four (17.4% of the 23 treated) had a sustained virological response. Adverse events were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A small monotherapy signal in a subgroup (low baseline viral load) — hypothesis-generating only. Interferon-era, genotype-4, Egyptian population; monotherapy has no place in any era's standard HCV care.
cards.source: Rossignol JF et al. Clinical trial: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of nitazoxanide monotherapy for the treatment of patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2008. PMID: 18616643. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme combination RCT (Rossignol 2009): nitazoxanide + peginterferon + ribavirin gave SVR 79% versus 50% on standard care (P=0.023) — the programme's positive trial
cards.summary: Programme combination RCT (Rossignol 2009): nitazoxanide + peginterferon + ribavirin gave SVR 79% versus 50% on standard care (P=0.023) — the programme's positive trial
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (programme trial), nitazoxanide lead-in + triple therapy vs standard peginterferon/ribavirin, HCV genotype 4 (n=96)
cards.people: 96 previously untreated patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4 at two Egyptian centres, randomised to standard care (peginterferon alfa-2a plus ribavirin for 48 weeks, n=40), nitazoxanide monotherapy lead-in then nitazoxanide plus peginterferon (n=28), or nitazoxanide lead-in then nitazoxanide plus peginterferon plus ribavirin (n=28).
cards.result: Sustained virological response was 79% on the nitazoxanide triple therapy versus 50% on standard care (P=0.023), with rapid virological response 64% versus 38% (P=0.048). The nitazoxanide plus peginterferon (no ribavirin) arm was intermediate (SVR 61%, RVR 54%). Adverse events were similar across groups except for higher anaemia rates in the ribavirin-containing groups.
cards.watchOut: The positive result came from the developer-linked programme that originated the hypothesis. It was the result the two independent trials carded below set out to confirm — and did not. Read this card together with them, never alone.
cards.source: Rossignol JF et al. Improved virologic response in chronic hepatitis C genotype 4 treated with nitazoxanide, peginterferon, and ribavirin. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19135998. cards.type: Independent open-label randomised controlled trial, nitazoxanide lead-in + triple therapy vs standard care, HCV genotype 4 (n=100)
cards.people: 100 treatment-naive patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4, in an independent open-label randomised trial: standard pegylated interferon plus weight-based ribavirin for 48 weeks (n=50) versus 4 weeks of nitazoxanide alone followed by 48 weeks of nitazoxanide triple therapy (n=50). Baseline characteristics were similar except higher BMI in the standard group (28.5 versus 26.5, P=0.01).
cards.result: Sustained virological response was 24/50 (48%) on standard care versus 25/50 (50%) with nitazoxanide (P=0.84). Rapid, complete early and end-of-treatment response rates were also similar, as was biochemical response at week 12. Complications were similar except more dyspepsia on nitazoxanide (32% versus 14%, P=0.03). The authors concluded adding nitazoxanide does not improve virological or biochemical response rates in genotype 4.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, but larger than the positive programme trial and independent of it — and flatly null on every response measure. This is one of the two negatives that decide the balance.

cards.people: 200 patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4 enrolled and randomised 1:1 to placebo or nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily as add-on therapy to pegylated interferon alfa-2a plus ribavirin after a 12-week lead-in phase; 195 were evaluated (97 placebo add-on, 98 nitazoxanide add-on).
cards.result: Sustained virological response was achieved by 59/97 (60.8%) on placebo add-on versus 57/98 (58.2%) on nitazoxanide add-on (P=0.70) — a difference of -2.6 percentage points, not significant. The authors concluded their data did not show any significant impact of nitazoxanide on SVR.
cards.watchOut: The largest and most rigorous trial in the base — double-blind and placebo-controlled — and the point estimate favours placebo. Together with Shehab 2014 it outweighs the single smaller programme positive.

cards.headline: Cross-point synthesis (Cochrane 2014): across 7 randomised trials (538 participants, genotypes 1 and 4), nitazoxanide reduced failure to achieve SVR (relative risk 0.85) — but every trial was at high risk of bias and evidence on clinical outcomes was very low quality or absent
cards.summary: Cross-point synthesis (Cochrane 2014): across 7 randomised trials (538 participants, genotypes 1 and 4), nitazoxanide reduced failure to achieve SVR (relative risk 0.85) — but every trial was at high risk of bias and evidence on clinical outcomes was very low quality or absent
cards.type: Cross-point: Cochrane systematic review of nitazoxanide for chronic hepatitis C (genotypes 1 and 4) — synthesis cross-point only, not an additional genotype-4 trial
cards.people: 538 participants aged 18 or older with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 or 4 in seven randomised trials comparing nitazoxanide with placebo or no intervention, six with antiviral co-interventions given equally to all groups. This synthesis covers genotypes 1 and 4 together — it is a cross-point, not a genotype-4-only report, and is not counted in this shelf's genotype-4 trial base.
cards.result: Nitazoxanide decreased the risk of failure to achieve sustained virological response versus placebo or no intervention (159/290 (55%) versus 133/208 (64%); relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.97 — a relative measure), a result supported by trial sequential analysis; the end-of-treatment response result was not so supported and might be a random error. The relative effect on adverse events was uncertain (relative risk 1.10, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.71). Only one trial reported mortality (no deaths in either group), none assessed morbidity or quality of life, and all trials were at high risk of bias. The reviewers concluded the SVR signal might be real but could be influenced by systematic error, and that more low-bias-risk trials were needed.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane pool mixes genotypes and is dominated by the programme trials at high risk of bias; its cautious SVR signal predates the 2016 double-blind negative carded above and does not overturn the two independent genotype-4 negatives.
cards.source: Nikolova K et al. Nitazoxanide for chronic hepatitis C. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24706397. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive programme trial (SVR 79% vs 50%), then two larger independent negatives (50% vs 48%; 58.2% vs 60.8%) — the negatives decide the balance in a closed, interferon-era question

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Nitazoxanide monotherapy showed a small signal confined to low-baseline-viral-load patients, and the developer-linked programme's triple-therapy trial reported a large SVR advantage. Both subsequent independent randomised trials — one open-label (n=100) and one double-blind (195 evaluated) — found SVR differences of 2 and -2.6 percentage points. The Cochrane synthesis, pooling genotypes 1 and 4 at high risk of bias, could not settle clinical outcomes. All of this is peginterferon-era evidence, superseded by direct-acting antivirals.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Emodepside for intestinal nematodes: one programme, 4 trials — cure 96.6% vs 81.2% on albendazole for hookworm, 85% predicted vs 17% for whipworm, matching ivermectin for Strongyloides in a dose-finding design
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults infected with hookworm, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) or Strongyloides stercoralis, does a single oral dose of emodepside (5-30 mg) versus albendazole, ivermectin or placebo achieve parasitological cure 14-21 days after treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Animals · Humans · Albendazole · Feces · Hookworm Infections · Soil · Trichuriasis · Trichuris · Depsipeptides · Antinematodal Agents · Young Adult · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one development programme, 3 publications reporting 4 randomised trials, labelled as one programme with species limbs never pooled. Against whipworm (Trichuris), predicted cure at emodepside 5 mg was 85% versus 10% on placebo and an observed 17% on albendazole; against hookworm, cure rose dose-dependently from 32% at 5 mg to 95% at 30 mg in the phase 2a trials, and in the phase 2b superiority trial cure was 96.6% on emodepside 30 mg versus 81.2% on albendazole; against Strongyloides, predicted cure plateaued at 89.1% at 15 mg versus an observed 88.0% on ivermectin in a dose-ranging (not powered head-to-head) design and 0% on placebo. The endpoint throughout is parasitological cure at 14-21 days — no trial measures anaemia, growth, transmission or clinical outcomes. Harms belong on the face: transient visual blurring, headache, dizziness and somnolence in roughly a third of recipients at higher doses, predominantly mild, with no serious adverse events. Emodepside is a veterinary anthelmintic repurposed for human use and is not licensed for human use; veterinary preparations are not the tested product. There is no independent replication outside this programme.

cards.headline: Phase 2a dose-ranging trials in ONE report (Mrimi 2023): emodepside against whipworm — predicted cure 85% at 5 mg vs 10% placebo and 17% observed on albendazole; against hookworm — cure rose from 32% at 5 mg to 95% at 30 mg
cards.summary: Phase 2a dose-ranging trials in ONE report (Mrimi 2023): emodepside against whipworm — predicted cure 85% at 5 mg vs 10% placebo and 17% observed on albendazole; against hookworm — cure rose from 32% at 5 mg to 95% at 30 mg
cards.type: Phase 2a dose-ranging randomised controlled trials (two trials — whipworm and hookworm — in one report), single-dose emodepside vs albendazole and placebo
cards.people: Two phase 2a dose-ranging randomised controlled trials in adults 18-45 years with Trichuris trichiura or hookworm eggs in stool (Tanzanian field programme): 266 persons enrolled in the whipworm trial and 176 in the hookworm trial, assigned to single oral emodepside 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 mg, albendazole 400 mg, or placebo. Primary outcome was cure rate 14-21 days after treatment by Kato-Katz thick smear.
cards.result: Whipworm: the predicted cure rate in the emodepside 5 mg group was 85% (95% CI 69 to 93; 25 of 30 participants), higher than the predicted placebo cure rate of 10% (95% CI 3 to 26; 3 of 31) and the observed albendazole cure rate of 17% (95% CI 6 to 35; 5 of 30). Hookworm: the observed cure rate was dose-dependent — 32% (95% CI 13 to 57; 6 of 19) at emodepside 5 mg and 95% (95% CI 74 to 99.9; 18 of 19) at 30 mg, versus 14% (3 of 21) on placebo and 70% (14 of 20) on albendazole. Headache, blurred vision and dizziness were the most common adverse events at 3 and 24 hours, generally increasing dose-dependently; most were mild and self-limited, there were few moderate events and no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One report containing two dose-ranging trials, with dose arms as small as 19-31 participants; cure is a parasitological endpoint at 14-21 days, not a clinical, anaemia or transmission outcome. This is a limb of a single development programme — see the synthesis.

cards.headline: Phase 2b hookworm superiority trial (Taylor 2024): emodepside 30 mg cured 96.6% vs 81.2% on albendazole (odds ratio 0.14, p=0.0001) — with visual blurring in 39% at 3 hours
cards.summary: Phase 2b hookworm superiority trial (Taylor 2024): emodepside 30 mg cured 96.6% vs 81.2% on albendazole (odds ratio 0.14, p=0.0001) — with visual blurring in 39% at 3 hours
cards.type: Phase 2b double-blind superiority randomised controlled trial, emodepside 30 mg vs albendazole 400 mg, hookworm
cards.people: 293 adolescents and adults aged 12-60 years with hookworm infection on Pemba Island, Tanzania, treated in a double-blind superiority phase 2b randomised trial: 146 received emodepside 30 mg (six 5 mg tablets) and 147 received albendazole 400 mg. Efficacy was cure rate (hookworm-positive becoming hookworm-negative) at 14-21 days.
cards.result: Emodepside demonstrated superiority: observed cure rate 96.6% versus 81.2% on albendazole (odds ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.04-0.35; p=0.0001). The most common adverse event on emodepside was vision blur at 3 hours (57 of 146, 39%), vision blur at 24 hours (55, 38%), headache at 3 hours (55, 38%) and dizziness at 3 hours (43, 30%); 298 (93%) of 319 adverse events on emodepside were mild, and no serious adverse events were reported. On albendazole the commonest events were headache (27 of 147, 18%) and dizziness (14, 10%) at 3 hours.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2b superiority trial from the same single programme and region as the phase 2a trials — not independent replication. The efficacy advantage comes with transient visual symptoms in about two in five recipients.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: 266 + 176 participants in the two phase 2a trials of the 2023 report, 293 treated in the phase 2b hookworm trial, and 202 randomised in the Strongyloides dose-ranging trial — all from a single European Research Council-funded development programme at Tanzanian and Laotian field sites.

shelves.title: Enteral nutrition as induction in adult Crohn's disease: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 trials, N=150 — the multicentre trial found it inferior to steroids (53% vs 79% remission); two small trials read positive
shelves.question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does enteral nutrition as sole therapy (elemental or oligopeptide diet) versus corticosteroid-based drug treatment induce clinical remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Crohn Disease · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enteral Nutrition · Female · Food, Formulated · Humans · Male · Methylprednisolone · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfasalazine · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 randomised reports totalling 150 patients (1984-1997), stated on the face, with the largest and only multicentre trial negative. ECCS IV (107 randomised): remission within 6 weeks in 29 of 55 on enteral nutrition versus 41 of 52 on methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine (p<0.01), with median time to remission 30.7 versus 8.2 days — enteral nutrition was less effective than drug treatment. The two small trials point the other way: O'Morain 1984 (21 patients) found an elemental diet improved patients as much as, and by some criteria more than, prednisolone over 4 weeks; the Italian trial (22 enrolled, 20 analysed, 2 weeks) found significant activity-index and nutritional improvements on an oral elemental diet and concluded short-term equivalence on activity with better nutritional recovery. The small positive readings cannot carry the balance against the multicentre result. Era flag, load-bearing: every comparator is a steroid-era regimen — no trial compares enteral induction with any modern therapy, so this shelf is a record of a closed question, not an induction option. The separate maintenance question (one trial) is not folded in. Tested feeds are named as the publications give them (Vivonex; Peptamen, Clintec), with the standing statement that current products may differ.

cards.headline: ECCS IV (Lochs 1991, 107 randomised, multicentre): enteral nutrition was LESS effective than drug treatment — remission 29/55 (53%) vs 41/52 (79%) within 6 weeks, and remission took 30.7 vs 8.2 days
cards.summary: ECCS IV (Lochs 1991, 107 randomised, multicentre): enteral nutrition was LESS effective than drug treatment — remission 29/55 (53%) vs 41/52 (79%) within 6 weeks, and remission took 30.7 vs 8.2 days
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (European Cooperative Crohn's Disease Study IV), enteral oligopeptide diet vs methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine
cards.people: 107 patients with active Crohn's disease (Crohn's Disease Activity Index >200) randomised in the multicentre European Cooperative Crohn's Disease Study IV to enteral nutrition with a liquid oligopeptide diet as sole therapy (55) or 6-methylprednisolone 48 mg daily tapered plus sulfasalazine 3 g daily (52). Remission was a fall in the activity index by 40% or at least 100 points.
cards.result: Twenty-nine patients in the diet group and 41 in the drug group reached remission within 6 weeks (p<0.01). Median time to remission was 30.7 days on enteral nutrition versus 8.2 days on drug treatment (p<0.01). No influence of initial disease activity or disease location on the effect of either treatment was shown. The authors conclude enteral nutrition is less effective than the combination of 6-methylprednisolone and sulfasalazine in treating active Crohn's disease.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial on this shelf and the only multicentre one — and it is the negative one. Its comparator (methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine) is a steroid-era regimen; the trial says nothing about enteral nutrition versus modern therapy.
cards.source: Lochs H et al. Comparison of enteral nutrition and drug treatment in active Crohn's disease. Results of the European Cooperative Crohn's Disease Study. IV. Gastroenterology. 1991. cards.headline: Italian oral elemental diet trial (Zoli 1997, 22 enrolled, 20 analysed, 2 weeks): significant activity-index and nutritional improvements on the elemental diet; authors concluded short-term equivalence to steroids on activity with better nutritional recovery
cards.summary: Italian oral elemental diet trial (Zoli 1997, 22 enrolled, 20 analysed, 2 weeks): significant activity-index and nutritional improvements on the elemental diet; authors concluded short-term equivalence to steroids on activity with better nutritional recovery
cards.type: Randomised controlled study, oral elemental diet (Peptamen, Clintec — named as the publication gives it) vs corticosteroids, 2 weeks
cards.people: 22 patients (ages 18-60) with moderately active Crohn's disease enrolled in a randomised study of an oral elemental diet (Peptamen, Clintec, USA; 10 patients) versus high-dose corticosteroids (10 patients analysed), each for 2 weeks. Disease activity, nutritional status, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, interleukin-6, intestinal permeability and other measures were assessed before and after treatment.
cards.result: After 2 weeks there were significant improvements in the simple Crohn's disease activity index, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, permeability index, body mass index, prealbumin, retinol binding protein and multiskin test in the elemental diet group; in the corticosteroid group there were significant improvements in the activity index and fat-free mass. The authors suggest an oral elemental diet is, in the short term, at least as effective as steroids in inducing remission of mild-to-moderately active Crohn's disease and may be more effective in improving nutritional status, probably through more rapid restoration of normal intestinal permeability.
cards.watchOut: A 2-week trial with 20 analysed patients and within-group significance readings — an equivalence conclusion from a trial far too small to establish equivalence. Tested product named under the clarification exception; current products may differ.

cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 reports, total N=150, none after 1997: the multicentre trial (n=107) found enteral induction clearly inferior and slower; the two small trials (n=21; n=20 analysed) read positive or equivalent
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: ECCS IV (107 randomised), O'Morain 1984 (21 randomised) and Zoli 1997 (22 enrolled, 20 analysed) — 150 randomised patients in total.
cards.result: Remission within 6 weeks was 53% on enteral nutrition versus 79% on methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine in the only multicentre trial, with remission taking nearly four times as long (30.7 versus 8.2 days). The balance rests on the multicentre result: enteral nutrition as sole induction therapy was less effective than steroid-era drug treatment. The elemental-versus-polymeric feed-comparison trials ask which feed, not whether feeding beats drugs, and are not counted; the maintenance question rests on a single separate trial and is not folded into this shelf.

shelves.title: Plasma exchange in acute-on-chronic liver failure: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, both 2026 — short-term survival benefit (28-day mortality 44.3% vs 63.9%), no 90-day benefit in the larger trial, prior randomised pooling null
shelves.question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), does therapeutic plasma exchange added to standard medical therapy versus standard medical therapy alone improve short-term (28-30-day) survival?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure · Plasma Exchange · Adult · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 modern randomised reports, both 2026, both single-centre and open-label, stated on the face. The Indian trial (194 randomised, EASL-CLIF grades 1-3b): 28-day mortality 44.3% on therapeutic plasma exchange plus standard therapy versus 63.9% on standard therapy alone (p=0.006; absolute reduction 19.6 percentage points) — but 90-day mortality did NOT differ, and only 57.7% of the exchange group completed all 5 planned sessions, haemodynamic instability the leading cause of discontinuation. The alcohol-related ACLF trial (100 randomised, up to 3 sessions): in-hospital mortality 24% versus 52% (p=0.007) and 30-day survival 72% versus 36% (p<0.001; adjusted hazard ratio for mortality 0.43, a relative measure). Against these stands the pre-2026 randomised record: the 2024 systematic review's randomised-trial subgroup analysis in ACLF found NO survival difference between plasma exchange and standard therapy. The shelf's answer is that tension, printed whole: two positive 2026 single-centre trials against a pooled randomised null, with the larger trial's benefit not persisting to 90 days. Population limbs are labelled and never pooled. Cross-point: albumin dialysis (MARS) and fractionated plasma separation (Prometheus) are a different modality, homed at pack #6540 — RELIEF and HELIOS are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Indian RCT (Swaroop 2026, 194 randomised): plasma exchange cut 28-day mortality to 44.3% vs 63.9% (p=0.006; absolute reduction 19.6 points) — but 90-day mortality did NOT differ, and only 57.7% completed all 5 sessions
cards.summary: Indian RCT (Swaroop 2026, 194 randomised): plasma exchange cut 28-day mortality to 44.3% vs 63.9% (p=0.006; absolute reduction 19.6 points) — but 90-day mortality did NOT differ, and only 57.7% completed all 5 sessions
cards.type: Single-centre open-label randomised controlled trial, therapeutic plasma exchange (5 sessions) plus standard therapy vs standard therapy alone, ACLF
cards.people: 194 adults aged 18-60 years with acute-on-chronic liver failure (EASL-CLIF grades 1-3b) randomised (1:1) at a single centre (2022-2025), open-label, to standard medical therapy plus 5 sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange (97) or standard therapy alone (97). Primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 28 days.
cards.result: 28-day mortality was significantly lower with plasma exchange: 43 patients (44.3%, 95% CI 34.2%-54.8%) versus 62 (63.9%, 95% CI 53.5%-73.4%), p=0.006; absolute risk reduction 19.6% (95% CI 5.8%-33.3%). Ninety-day mortality was similar between groups — the benefit did not persist. Plasma exchange produced greater reductions in ammonia and higher rates of resolution of hepatic and coagulation failure by day 7. Only 56 patients (57.7%) received all 5 sessions (74.2% completed 3); haemodynamic instability was the leading cause of discontinuation (18 of 41 discontinuations, 43.9%). Dyselectrolytemia and shivering were the most common complications.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and open-label, and over 40% of the exchange group did not complete the planned sessions — feasibility in the sickest patients is part of the question. The 90-day null is on the face, beside the 28-day benefit. One of exactly 2 modern randomised reports on this shelf.

cards.headline: Alcohol-related ACLF RCT (Sareen 2026, 100 randomised): in-hospital mortality 24% vs 52% (p=0.007) and 30-day survival 72% vs 36% (p<0.001; adjusted hazard ratio for mortality 0.43, relative)
cards.summary: Alcohol-related ACLF RCT (Sareen 2026, 100 randomised): in-hospital mortality 24% vs 52% (p=0.007) and 30-day survival 72% vs 36% (p<0.001; adjusted hazard ratio for mortality 0.43, relative)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, plasma exchange (up to 3 sessions) plus standard therapy vs standard therapy alone, alcohol-related ACLF
cards.people: 100 patients with alcohol-related acute-on-chronic liver failure randomised (1:1) to plasma exchange (up to 3 sessions) plus standard medical therapy (50) or standard therapy alone (50). Coprimary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and 30-day survival; all 100 patients completed follow-up.
cards.result: In-hospital mortality was lower with plasma exchange (24% versus 52%, p=0.007), an absolute risk reduction of 28% (number needed to treat 3.6). Thirty-day survival was higher with plasma exchange (72% versus 36%, p<0.001), with an adjusted hazard ratio for mortality of 0.43 (p=0.003 — a relative measure, with the absolute survival rates beside it). Disease-severity scores (MELD-sodium, AARC and Child-Turcotte-Pugh) and several laboratory measures improved more with exchange, hospital stay was shorter (19 versus 24 days, p=0.023), and no major plasma-exchange-related adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: An alcohol-related ACLF population only, with up to 3 sessions — a different limb from the mixed-aetiology, 5-session trial above; the two are never pooled. One of exactly 2 modern randomised reports on this shelf.
cards.source: Sareen M et al. Therapeutic plasma exchange improves survival in alcohol-related acute-on-chronic liver failure: a randomized controlled trial. European journal of gastroenterology & hepatology. 2026. PMID: 42992479. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Prior randomised record (Beran 2024 systematic review): in the randomised-trial subgroup analysis in ACLF, plasma exchange showed NO survival difference versus standard therapy — the pooled null the 2026 trials must be read against

cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2024) — the pre-2026 synthesis cross-point for this shelf, not a third randomised report
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies comparing plasma exchange versus standard medical therapy in adults with acute liver failure and acute-on-chronic liver failure: 20 ACLF studies including 5,705 patients (2,856 plasma exchange versus 2,849 standard therapy) and 5 acute-liver-failure studies including 343 patients.
cards.result: Across all ACLF studies, plasma exchange was associated with higher 30-day survival (risk ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.22-1.52 — a relative measure) and 90-day survival (risk ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.10-1.34). But on subgroup analysis of randomised controlled trials, results remained unchanged in acute liver failure while NO differences in survival were found between plasma exchange and standard therapy in ACLF. The authors conclude plasma exchange is associated with improved survival in acute liver failure and could improve survival in ACLF, and that further randomised trials are needed to confirm a survival benefit in ACLF.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis, not a trial: its overall ACLF pooling mixes study designs, and its randomised-only subgroup — the reading that matters for this shelf — is null. The DPMAS-plus-low-volume-exchange combination trials and the standard-versus-high-volume exchange trial ask different questions and are not counted.
cards.source: Beran A et al. Plasma exchange for acute and acute-on-chronic liver failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 modern randomised reports (both 2026, both single-centre and open-label, n=194 and n=100), both positive at 28-30 days, against a pre-2026 randomised pooling that was null and a 90-day result that was null in the larger trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 modern randomised reports (both 2026, both single-centre and open-label, n=194 and n=100), both positive at 28-30 days, against a pre-2026 randomised pooling that was null and a 90-day result that was null in the larger trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the two 2026 randomised trials (294 randomised in total across two different ACLF populations, never pooled), plus the 2024 systematic review carded as the prior-record cross-point.
cards.result: At 28-30 days both trials favour plasma exchange: 28-day mortality 44.3% versus 63.9% (absolute reduction 19.6 points) in mixed-aetiology EASL-CLIF ACLF, and 30-day survival 72% versus 36% in alcohol-related ACLF. Neither trial is blinded or multicentre; in the larger trial the benefit did not persist to 90 days and over 40% of patients did not complete the planned sessions; and the 2024 review's randomised-trial subgroup in ACLF found no survival difference. Short-term benefit is possible on this base; a durable survival benefit is not demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK stated exactly: 2 randomised reports. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data. Albumin dialysis / fractionated plasma separation (pack #6540) is a different modality and is not carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Trichuris suis ova for IBD: a small positive UC index trial (n=54, null on remission), then two large null trials — Crohn's n=252 and UC PROCTO n=119 (remission 30% vs 34% on placebo)
shelves.question: In patients with active ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, do orally administered embryonated Trichuris suis ova (2,500–7,500 ova every 2 weeks) versus placebo improve disease activity or induce clinical remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Animals · Colitis, Ulcerative · Double-Blind Method · Female · Host-Parasite Interactions · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ovum · Severity of Illness Index · Swine · Treatment Outcome · Trichuriasis · Trichuris
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit), on a four-report randomised base (461 randomised in total) whose limbs must never be pooled. ULCERATIVE COLITIS limb: the small 2005 Iowa trial (n=54) was positive on an improvement index (43.3% vs 16.7%) but NOT on remission, and the larger 2024 PROCTO trial (n=119) found clinical remission at or below placebo (30% vs 34%; risk ratio 0.89, a relative measure). CROHN'S DISEASE limb: the only efficacy trial (n=252, three doses) found no dose beating placebo on remission, response, inflammatory markers or mucosal healing; the remaining Crohn's report (n=36) is a single-dose SAFETY trial only. The arc is a tested-and-failed hypothesis: a small positive index trial followed by two adequately sized null trials. The tested preparation — embryonated Trichuris suis ova produced for clinical use — is an investigational biological product, not a supplement, and preparations differ by maker.

cards.headline: UC limb — Iowa RCT (Summers 2005): TSO improved the Disease Activity Index (13/30, 43.3% vs 4/24, 16.7%; P=.04) but the proportion reaching an index of 0–1 (remission) was NOT significantly different
cards.summary: UC limb — Iowa RCT (Summers 2005): TSO improved the Disease Activity Index (13/30, 43.3% vs 4/24, 16.7%; P=.04) but the proportion reaching an index of 0–1 (remission) was NOT significantly different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ulcerative colitis limb, repeated-dose TSO vs placebo
cards.people: 54 patients with active ulcerative colitis (Ulcerative Colitis Disease Activity Index ≥4) at the University of Iowa and select private practices, randomised to 2,500 Trichuris suis ova (ova obtained from the US Department of Agriculture) or placebo orally every 2 weeks for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Improvement in the Disease Activity Index (the primary variable) occurred in 13 of 30 patients (43.3%) on ova versus 4 of 24 (16.7%) on placebo (P=.04), with improvement also on the Simple Index by week 6. The difference in the proportion achieving a Disease Activity Index of 0–1 — remission — was not significant. Treatment induced no side effects.
cards.watchOut: The smallest efficacy trial on this shelf (n=54) and the only positive one — and even it was null on its remission reading. Its positive improvement index must not be read over the two larger null trials carded below.
cards.source: Summers RW et al. Trichuris suis therapy for active ulcerative colitis: a randomized controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2005. PMID: 15825065. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Crohn's limb — SAFETY report only (Sandborn 2013): a single dose of TSO (500 / 2,500 / 7,500 ova) was well tolerated — gastrointestinal events in 25.9% on TSO vs 33.3% on placebo, no dose-dependent signal (a safety report, never an efficacy anchor)
cards.summary: Crohn's limb — SAFETY report only (Sandborn 2013): a single dose of TSO (500 / 2,500 / 7,500 ova) was well tolerated — gastrointestinal events in 25.9% on TSO vs 33.3% on placebo, no dose-dependent signal (a safety report, never an efficacy anchor)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled sequential dose-escalation SAFETY trial, Crohn's disease limb, single-dose TSO
cards.people: 36 patients with Crohn's disease (18 men, 18 women, aged 20–54 years) randomised in three sequential dose-escalation cohorts of 12 (500, 2,500 or 7,500 viable embryonated TSO as a single oral dose, or placebo), assessed to 6 months.
cards.result: All patients were dosed and completed the initial 2-month follow-up. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent events: 7 of 27 TSO-treated patients (25.9%) versus 3 of 9 placebo patients (33.3%), with no dose-dependent relationship (33.3% placebo; 44.4% TSO 500; 0% TSO 2,500; 33.3% TSO 7,500 experiencing at least one GI event) and no clinically meaningful changes in GI signs and symptoms. The authors concluded a single dose up to 7,500 ova was well tolerated with no short- or long-term treatment-related side effects.
cards.watchOut: Safety and tolerability were this trial's question — it carries no efficacy information and is never counted as an efficacy report. Single dose only; it says nothing about repeated dosing.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Randomised clinical trial: the safety and tolerability of Trichuris suis ova in patients with Crohn's disease. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2013. cards.headline: Crohn's limb — efficacy RCT (Schölmerich 2017): NO TSO dose beat placebo — clinical remission 38.5% / 35.2% / 47.2% across 250 / 2,500 / 7,500 ova vs 42.9% on placebo, with no advantage on response, inflammatory markers or mucosal healing
cards.summary: Crohn's limb — efficacy RCT (Schölmerich 2017): NO TSO dose beat placebo — clinical remission 38.5% / 35.2% / 47.2% across 250 / 2,500 / 7,500 ova vs 42.9% on placebo, with no advantage on response, inflammatory markers or mucosal healing
cards.type: Multicentre phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging efficacy trial, Crohn's disease limb
cards.people: 252 adults with mildly-to-moderately active ileocolonic, uncomplicated Crohn's disease, randomised double-blind to six fortnightly doses of 250, 2,500 or 7,500 embryonated viable Trichuris suis ova or placebo, with 4 weeks' follow-up; primary endpoint clinical remission (CDAI <150) at week 12.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 38.5% (TSO 250), 35.2% (TSO 2,500) and 47.2% (TSO 7,500) versus 42.9% on placebo — no dose showed a clinically relevant effect over placebo on remission or response. TSO induced a dose-dependent immunological response, but there was no response in laboratory markers of inflammation and no advantage on other secondary efficacy variables. No serious adverse drug reaction occurred and no safety concern was identified.
cards.watchOut: The definitive Crohn's efficacy test: an immunological response to the ova did not translate into any clinical, inflammatory or mucosal benefit. Placebo remission (42.9%) exceeded two of the three dose arms.
cards.source: Schölmerich J et al. A Randomised, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Trial of Trichuris suis ova in Active Crohn's Disease. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2017. PMID: 27707789. cards.headline: UC limb — PROCTO RCT (Prosberg 2024): clinical remission at week 24 in 30% on TSO vs 34% on placebo (risk ratio 0.89 — a relative measure; P=0.80); only a temporary week-12 symptomatic signal, in the subgroup not receiving corticosteroids
cards.summary: UC limb — PROCTO RCT (Prosberg 2024): clinical remission at week 24 in 30% on TSO vs 34% on placebo (risk ratio 0.89 — a relative measure; P=0.80); only a temporary week-12 symptomatic signal, in the subgroup not receiving corticosteroids
cards.type: Single-centre phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PROCTO), ulcerative colitis limb
cards.people: 119 patients with moderate ulcerative colitis (Mayo score 6–10) at a single centre, randomised to 7,500 Trichuris suis ova (n=60) or placebo (n=59) every 2 weeks for 24 weeks; primary outcome clinical remission at week 24.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 24 was achieved in 30% on TSO versus 34% on placebo (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.50; P=0.80, intention to treat). No difference was found in clinical response in any subgroup, nor in complete corticosteroid-free clinical remission or endoscopic remission. In patients who did not need corticosteroids during the trial, a temporary effect appeared in symptomatic remission at week 12 (P=0.01) and partial Mayo score at weeks 14 and 18 — a subgroup reading, labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: The week-12 symptomatic signal is a temporary subgroup finding inside an otherwise null trial — never a headline. Single-centre, moderate UC only.

cards.summary: Synthesis: four randomised reports, 461 patients — a small positive UC index trial (n=54, null on remission) and a Crohn's safety trial (n=36), then two adequately sized null efficacy trials (Crohn's n=252; UC n=119): helminth-ova therapy is a tested-and-failed hypothesis in IBD
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No randomised trial has shown Trichuris suis ova to induce remission in ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. The UC limb rests on n=54 (positive on improvement, null on remission) and n=119 (remission 30% vs 34% on placebo); the Crohn's efficacy limb rests on n=252 (no dose above placebo on any clinical, inflammatory or mucosal outcome), with the n=36 report safety-only. The ova were consistently well tolerated — the failure is one of efficacy, not safety. The 2005 open-label uncontrolled Crohn's series is not carded as evidence, per the row's fence. The tested preparation is an investigational biological product (embryonated T. suis ova produced for clinical use); it is not a supplement and preparations differ by maker.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Disease limbs are labelled throughout and never pooled.

shelves.title: Cannabis/CBD for active Crohn's disease: symptoms and quality of life improved in 2 of 3 tiny trials (total N=97), but no endoscopic or inflammatory change — and low-dose CBD was null
shelves.question: In adults with active Crohn's disease not responding to standard therapy, does a cannabis preparation (smoked THC-rich cannabis, oral cannabidiol, or CBD-rich cannabis oil) versus placebo induce remission or improve disease activity over 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cannabinoids · Crohn Disease · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, symptoms only) — based on a very small randomised base of 3 trials totalling 97 patients. The symptom–inflammation split is the answer: every positive reading is a symptom or quality-of-life index (the Crohn's Disease Activity Index is symptom-weighted), while the one trial that scoped patients found NO endoscopic change and inflammatory markers never moved. The smoked-cannabis trial MISSED its primary remission endpoint (45% vs 10%, P=.43); the purified low-dose CBD trial was outright null; the CBD-rich oil trial improved CDAI and quality of life but not endoscopic scores (SES-CD), C-reactive protein or calprotectin. Nothing here is disease modification. The three tested preparations are DIFFERENT products — THC-rich smoked cannabis, purified low-dose oral CBD (10 mg twice daily), and a CBD-rich oil with THC (160/40 mg/mL) — named exactly as published; current commercial cannabis/CBD products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness and were not what was tested. All three trials are from Israel and all lasted 8 weeks; smoked THC is effectively unblindable by subjective effect, and the symptom endpoints are the ones most exposed to that bias.

cards.headline: Smoked THC-rich cannabis (Naftali 2013): primary remission endpoint NOT met (complete remission 5/11, 45% vs 1/10, 10%; P=.43), though clinical response was more frequent (10/11 vs 4/10; P=.028) and appetite and sleep improved
cards.summary: Smoked THC-rich cannabis (Naftali 2013): primary remission endpoint NOT met (complete remission 5/11, 45% vs 1/10, 10%; P=.43), though clinical response was more frequent (10/11 vs 4/10; P=.028) and appetite and sleep improved
cards.type: Prospective randomised placebo-controlled trial, smoked THC-rich cannabis vs placebo cigarettes, 8 weeks (Israel)
cards.people: 21 patients with active Crohn's disease (CDAI >200) not responding to steroids, immunomodulators or anti-TNF therapy, randomised to cannabis cigarettes containing 115 mg THC twice daily (n=11) or placebo cigarettes (cannabis flowers with THC extracted, n=10) for 8 weeks, with 2 weeks' follow-up.
cards.result: Complete remission (CDAI <150) — the primary endpoint — was achieved by 5 of 11 (45%) on cannabis versus 1 of 10 (10%) on placebo (P=.43): not significant. A clinical response (>100-point CDAI fall) occurred in 10 of 11 versus 4 of 10 (P=.028); CDAI fell from 330 ± 105 to 152 ± 109 on cannabis versus 373 ± 94 to 306 ± 143 on placebo. Three cannabis patients were weaned from steroid dependency, and patients reported improved appetite and sleep with no significant side effects.
cards.watchOut: n=21, and the primary endpoint was missed — the response reading is secondary. Smoked THC is effectively unblindable by subjective effect, and CDAI is a symptom-weighted index: exactly the endpoints most exposed to that bias.
cards.source: Naftali T et al. Cannabis induces a clinical response in patients with Crohn's disease: a prospective placebo-controlled study. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2013. PMID: 23648372. Registry ID: NCT01040910. cards.headline: Purified low-dose oral CBD (Naftali 2017): NO beneficial effect — CDAI fell similarly on CBD (≈337→220) and placebo (≈308→216) over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Purified low-dose oral CBD (Naftali 2017): NO beneficial effect — CDAI fell similarly on CBD (≈337→220) and placebo (≈308→216) over 8 weeks
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, purified oral cannabidiol 10 mg twice daily vs placebo, 8 weeks (Israel)
cards.people: 20 patients aged 18–75 with moderately active Crohn's disease (CDAI >200) not responding to standard treatment (steroids, thiopurines or TNF antagonists), randomised to oral cannabidiol 10 mg twice daily or placebo for 8 weeks, other treatment unchanged; 19 completed.
cards.result: Average CDAI before treatment was 337 ± 108 on CBD and 308 ± 96 on placebo; after 8 weeks it was 220 ± 122 and 216 ± 121 respectively (P=NS) — cannabidiol was safe but had no beneficial effect. Haemoglobin, albumin and kidney and liver function tests remained unchanged and no side effects were observed. The authors' own caveats are printed: the null could reflect the small CBD dose, the small number of patients, or a lack of synergy with other cannabinoids.
cards.watchOut: n=20 and a low dose (10 mg twice daily) — this null rules out benefit for THIS preparation at THIS dose, not for every cannabinoid preparation; the three preparations on this shelf are different products and are never pooled.

cards.headline: CBD-rich cannabis oil (Naftali 2021): CDAI and quality of life improved more on oil, but endoscopic scores (SES-CD) and inflammatory markers (CRP, calprotectin) did NOT change
cards.summary: CBD-rich cannabis oil (Naftali 2021): CDAI and quality of life improved more on oil, but endoscopic scores (SES-CD) and inflammatory markers (CRP, calprotectin) did NOT change
cards.type: Single-centre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, CBD-rich cannabis oil 160/40 mg/mL CBD/THC vs placebo, 8 weeks (Israel)
cards.people: 56 patients with Crohn's disease (30 cannabis oil, 26 placebo; mean age 34.5 years) in a single-centre double-blind randomised trial of oral cannabis oil containing 160/40 mg/mL cannabidiol/tetrahydrocannabinol (CBD/THC) versus placebo for 8 weeks; CDAI and the simple endoscopic score for Crohn's disease (SES-CD) assessed before and after treatment.
cards.result: CDAI fell from a median 282 to 166 on oil versus 264 to 237 on placebo (P<0.05), and median quality-of-life score improved from 74 in both groups to 91 on oil versus 75 on placebo (P=0.004). But SES-CD was unchanged (cannabis 10→7; placebo 11→8; P=0.75) and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, calprotectin) remained unchanged. The extract was well absorbed; the authors concluded cannabis in Crohn's should be used only in clinical trials until further studies are available.
cards.watchOut: The largest of the three trials (n=56) and the only one with endoscopy — its dissociation (symptoms better, mucosa and markers unchanged) is the shelf's central finding. Single centre, 8 weeks.
cards.source: Naftali T et al. Oral CBD-rich Cannabis Induces Clinical but Not Endoscopic Response in Patients with Crohn's Disease, a Randomised Controlled Trial. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2021. shelves.title: Low-dose naltrexone for Crohn's induction: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (N=81) directly split — 2011 positive (n=40) vs 2026 futility-stopped, remission favouring placebo (n=41)
shelves.question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily versus placebo induce clinical and endoscopic remission over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Colonoscopy · Crohn Disease · Fatigue · Female · Humans · Intestinal Mucosa · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone · Narcotic Antagonists · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 adult randomised trials exist, totalling 81 patients, and they split completely. The 2011 single-centre trial (n=40; entry by clinical activity, CDAI 220–450) reported striking benefit: ≥70-point CDAI decline in 88% vs 40% (P=0.009) and endoscopic response in 78% vs 28% (P=0.008). The 2026 Dutch multicentre trial (n=41; entry REQUIRED mucosal ulcers on endoscopy, SES-CD 3–15) was STOPPED EARLY FOR FUTILITY, with endoscopic remission 5.6% vs 18.8% (P=0.233) and clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0% (P=0.037 — favouring placebo). The populations differ — clinically active versus endoscopically confirmed, milder disease — which is part of why the readings may differ, and both entry rules are stated rather than the trials being averaged. The 2026 trial's only positive reading was a fatigue score, a lone secondary outcome in a futility-stopped trial — never a headline. No serious adverse events occurred in either trial.

cards.headline: Smith 2011 RCT (n=40): low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg — ≥70-point CDAI decline in 88% vs 40% on placebo (P=0.009); endoscopic response 78% vs 28% (P=0.008); endoscopic remission 33% vs 8%
cards.summary: Smith 2011 RCT (n=40): low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg — ≥70-point CDAI decline in 88% vs 40% on placebo (P=0.009); endoscopic response 78% vs 28% (P=0.008); endoscopic remission 33% vs 8%
cards.type: Single-centre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily vs placebo, 12 weeks
cards.people: 40 adults with active (moderate to severe) Crohn's disease in a single-centre randomised double-blind trial of oral naltrexone 4.5 mg daily versus placebo for 12 weeks; primary outcome a 70-point decline in Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI); mucosal healing assessed by colonoscopy (CDEIS) and histology.
cards.result: Eighty-eight percent of naltrexone-treated patients had at least a 70-point CDAI decline versus 40% on placebo (P=0.009). After 12 weeks, 78% on naltrexone showed an endoscopic response (≥5-point CDEIS decline) versus 28% on placebo (P=0.008), and 33% achieved endoscopic remission (CDEIS <6) versus 8% on placebo. Fatigue was the only side effect reported significantly more often — in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: n=40, single centre, entry by clinical activity — the largest endoscopic-response gap in this programme comes from its smallest, least endoscopically-selected trial. Its readings are printed with their N and are directly contradicted by the multicentre trial below.

cards.headline: Dutch multicentre RCT 2026 (n=41): STOPPED EARLY FOR FUTILITY — endoscopic remission 5.6% on LDN vs 18.8% on placebo (P=0.233) and clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0% (P=0.037, favouring placebo); only the fatigue score favoured LDN
cards.summary: Dutch multicentre RCT 2026 (n=41): STOPPED EARLY FOR FUTILITY — endoscopic remission 5.6% on LDN vs 18.8% on placebo (P=0.233) and clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0% (P=0.037, favouring placebo); only the fatigue score favoured LDN
cards.type: Multicentre (7-hospital) randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, prematurely terminated for futility, low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily vs placebo, 12 weeks
cards.people: 41 adults with mild-to-moderate active Crohn's disease — entry required mucosal ulcers on endoscopy (Simple Endoscopic Score for Crohn's Disease 3–15) — randomised 1:1 in 7 Dutch hospitals to low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks; primary endpoint endoscopic remission at week 12. The trial was stopped early due to futility.
cards.result: Endoscopic remission occurred in 1 patient (5.6%) on LDN versus 3 (18.8%) on placebo (P=0.233), and clinical remission in 22.2% on LDN versus 70.0% on placebo (P=0.037) — both favouring placebo. No serious adverse events were reported. The only positive reading was fatigue: the FACIT-Fatigue median difference after 12 weeks was 2.5 (IQR 0–7) on LDN versus −3 (IQR −7 to 2) on placebo (P=0.012), a secondary patient-reported outcome; other patient-reported outcomes did not differ. The authors concluded LDN was not effective for inducing remission in Crohn's disease.
cards.watchOut: Futility-stopped at n=41, so its estimates are imprecise — but its direction (remission favouring placebo) is the opposite of the 2011 trial, in a population with endoscopically confirmed activity. The fatigue signal is a lone secondary outcome against a null primary in a stopped trial — never a headline.

multicentre (7-hospital) randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, prematurely terminated for futility, low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily vs placebo, 12 weeks 41 adults with mild-to-moderate active crohn's disease — entry required mucosal ulcers on endoscopy (simple endoscopic score for crohn's disease 3–15) — randomised 1:1 in 7 dutch hospitals to low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks; primary endpoint endoscopic remission at week 12. the trial was stopped early due to futility. endoscopic remission occurred in 1 patient (5.6%) on ldn versus 3 (18.8%) on placebo (p=0.233), and clinical remission in 22.2% on ldn versus 70.0% on placebo (p=0.037) — both favouring placebo. no serious adverse events were reported. the only positive reading was fatigue: the facit-fatigue median difference after 12 weeks was 2.5 (iqr 0–7) on ldn versus −3 (iqr −7 to 2) on placebo (p=0.012), a secondary patient-reported outcome; other patient-reported outcomes did not differ. the authors concluded ldn was not effective for inducing remission in crohn's disease. futility-stopped at n=41, so its estimates are imprecise — but its direction (remission favouring placebo) is the opposite of the 2011 trial, in a population with endoscopically confirmed activity. the fatigue signal is a lone secondary outcome against a null primary in a stopped trial — never a headline. van de pol n et al. low-dose naltrexone in crohn's disease: a prematurely terminated randomized trial showing reduced fatigue without clinical or endoscopic benefit. digestive diseases and sciences. 2026. pmid: 42701992. registry id: none in the record. mesh: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 adult RCTs, N=81, directly split: a small positive 2011 trial (endoscopic response 78% vs 28%) and a 2026 multicentre trial stopped for futility with remission favouring placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 adult RCTs, N=81, directly split: a small positive 2011 trial (endoscopic response 78% vs 28%) and a 2026 multicentre trial stopped for futility with remission favouring placebo
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily for Crohn's induction rests on two 12-week trials of about 40 patients each pointing in opposite directions. The 2011 trial's clinical and endoscopic readings were strongly positive; the 2026 trial, which required endoscopic activity at entry, stopped for futility with endoscopic remission 5.6% vs 18.8% and clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0%, both favouring placebo, and only a secondary fatigue score favouring naltrexone. On this base no efficacy claim in either direction is secure — the honest stamp is a split, floor-risk record. The uncontrolled pilots of the programme are not carded as evidence.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Mesenchymal stem cells for decompensated cirrhosis: SPLIT — the only placebo-controlled trial (n=27) was negative; the largest open-label trial (n=219, umbilical-cord MSCs) reported higher survival; products differ by trial
shelves.question: In patients with decompensated cirrhosis, does mesenchymal stem cell therapy (autologous bone-marrow-derived, or allogeneic umbilical-cord-derived) added to standard care versus standard care or placebo improve liver function, fibrosis, or survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bilirubin · Bone Marrow Cells · Creatinine · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Function Tests · Male · Mesenchymal Stem Cell Transplantation · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Prothrombin Time · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the only placebo-controlled trial is negative and the largest trial is open-label and positive, and the four trials do not test the same treatment. Products, named exactly as published (clarification exception — these are investigational manufactured cell products and no marketed equivalent was tested): autologous bone-marrow MSCs by peripheral-vein infusion (Iran, n=27 — NEGATIVE: no difference in Child, MELD, albumin, INR, transaminases or liver volumes at 12 months, with 3 deaths in the MSC arm, all in patients with significantly higher baseline MELD); autologous bone-marrow MSC transplantation on entecavir (China, HBV cirrhosis, 56 enrolled / 39 completed — liver function improved further, framed mechanistically via Treg/Th17 shifts); autologous bone-marrow MSCs by hepatic-artery injection, one or two doses (Korea, abstinent alcoholic cirrhosis, n=72 — histological fibrosis fell WITHIN the treated groups, 25% and 37% relative reductions, a within-group before–after reading, and Child-Pugh improved; two injections were not superior to one); and allogeneic umbilical-cord MSCs, three infusions, plus conventional therapy (China, HBV decompensated cirrhosis, n=219 — overall survival significantly higher over follow-up to 75 months, HCC-free survival not different, liver-function indices improved over 48 weeks). Four countries (Iran, China, Korea, China), 2013–2021, standard care of their eras. Never an averaged 'stem cells improve cirrhosis' headline.

cards.headline: Iranian placebo-controlled RCT (Mohamadnejad 2013): autologous bone-marrow MSC infusion probably has NO beneficial effect — Child, MELD, albumin, INR, transaminases and liver volumes did not differ at 12 months; 3 deaths in the MSC group, all with higher baseline MELD
cards.summary: Iranian placebo-controlled RCT (Mohamadnejad 2013): autologous bone-marrow MSC infusion probably has NO beneficial effect — Child, MELD, albumin, INR, transaminases and liver volumes did not differ at 12 months; 3 deaths in the MSC group, all with higher baseline MELD
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, autologous bone-marrow MSCs by peripheral-vein infusion vs placebo (Iran)
cards.people: 27 patients with decompensated cirrhosis randomised to autologous bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cell infusion (15 patients; a median of 195 million cultured MSCs, range 120–295 million, through a peripheral vein) or placebo infusion (12 patients); primary outcome absolute change in MELD score at 12 months.
cards.result: One patient in each group was lost to follow-up. Three patients in the MSC group died of liver failure (at 3 months, one; at 5 months, two) after infusion; the deceased patients' baseline MELD scores were significantly higher than those of patients who remained alive in either group (20.0 vs 15.1; P=0.02). Absolute changes in Child scores, MELD scores, serum albumin, INR, serum transaminases and liver volumes did not differ significantly between the MSC and placebo groups at 12 months. The authors concluded autologous bone marrow MSC transplantation through a peripheral vein probably has no beneficial effect in cirrhotic patients.
cards.watchOut: n=27 — the smallest trial here, but the ONLY placebo-controlled one, and it is negative. The 3 treated-arm deaths occurred in patients with significantly higher baseline MELD (a baseline imbalance, printed as the trial reports it) — neither a proven harm nor dismissible.
cards.source: Mohamadnejad M et al. Randomized placebo-controlled trial of mesenchymal stem cell transplantation in decompensated cirrhosis. cards.headline: HBV-cirrhosis RCT (Xu 2014): autologous bone-marrow MSC transplantation on entecavir improved liver function further than control, alongside Treg/Th17 shifts — but only 39 of 56 enrolled patients completed the study
cards.summary: HBV-cirrhosis RCT (Xu 2014): autologous bone-marrow MSC transplantation on entecavir improved liver function further than control, alongside Treg/Th17 shifts — but only 39 of 56 enrolled patients completed the study
cards.type: Randomised trial, autologous bone-marrow MSC transplantation vs control, both on entecavir, HBV cirrhosis (China)
cards.people: 56 patients with hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis enrolled and randomly assigned to autologous bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (ABMSC) transplantation or control, both groups receiving entecavir; after 24 weeks' follow-up, 39 patients completed the study (20 transplantation, 19 control). MELD scores, liver function and Treg/Th17 measures were assessed.
cards.result: Patients in both groups improved significantly on entecavir; ABMSC transplantation further improved liver function. Treg cells increased significantly and Th17 cells decreased markedly in the transplantation group versus control, raising the Treg/Th17 ratio, with concordant changes in Foxp3 and RORγt mRNA and in serum TGF-β (higher early) and interleukin-17, TNF-α and interleukin-6 (lower). The authors framed the benefit as mediated at least in part through regulation of the Treg/Th17 balance.
cards.watchOut: A 30% non-completion rate (39 of 56) and a mechanistic-immunology framing: the efficacy reading rests on liver-function indices in completers, with no survival endpoint. Both flags are load-bearing.
cards.source: Xu L et al. Randomized trial of autologous bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells transplantation for hepatitis B virus cirrhosis: regulation of Treg/Th17 cells. Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2014. PMID: 24942592. Registry ID: none in the record.
