cards.headline: Korean alcoholic-cirrhosis phase 2 RCT (Suk 2016): histological fibrosis fell WITHIN the MSC groups (25% and 37% relative reductions — within-group before–after readings, not placebo-controlled differences) and Child-Pugh improved; two injections were not superior to one
cards.summary: Korean alcoholic-cirrhosis phase 2 RCT (Suk 2016): histological fibrosis fell WITHIN the MSC groups (25% and 37% relative reductions — within-group before–after readings, not placebo-controlled differences) and Child-Pugh improved; two injections were not superior to one
cards.type: Multicentre randomised open-label phase 2 trial, autologous bone-marrow MSCs via hepatic artery (one vs two injections) vs control, alcoholic cirrhosis (Korea)
cards.people: 72 patients with biopsy-proven alcoholic cirrhosis, alcohol-abstinent for more than 6 months, in a multicentre randomised open-label phase 2 trial: control, or one or two hepatic-artery injections of 5 × 10^7 autologous bone marrow-derived MSCs 30 days after bone-marrow aspiration; follow-up biopsy at 6 months; outcomes analysed per protocol. Primary endpoint improvement in fibrosis quantification (picrosirius red staining).
cards.result: Fibrosis quantification fell within the one-injection group by 25% (19.5 ± 9.5% to 14.5 ± 7.1%) and within the two-injection group by 37% (21.1 ± 8.9% to 13.2 ± 6.7%) (both P<0.001, before versus after) — relative reductions and within-group readings, labelled as such. Two injections were not superior to one on fibrosis quantification (P>0.05). Child-Pugh scores also improved significantly in both MSC groups (one-time 7.6 ± 1.0 to 6.3 ± 1.3; two-time 7.8 ± 1.2 to 6.8 ± 1.6; P<0.05). The proportion of patients with adverse events did not differ among the three groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with per-protocol analysis, and the fibrosis claim — this shelf's surrogate-endpoint flag — rests on within-group histology, not on a blinded between-group difference. Abstinent alcoholic cirrhosis only.
cards.source: Suk KT et al. Transplantation with autologous bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells for alcoholic cirrhosis: Phase 2 trial. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2016. PMID: 27339398. cards.headline: Chinese UC-MSC RCT (Shi 2021): the largest trial (n=219) — overall survival significantly higher with three umbilical-cord MSC infusions plus conventional therapy over follow-up to 75 months; HCC-free survival did not differ
cards.summary: Chinese UC-MSC RCT (Shi 2021): the largest trial (n=219) — overall survival significantly higher with three umbilical-cord MSC infusions plus conventional therapy over follow-up to 75 months; HCC-free survival did not differ
cards.type: Prospective open-label randomised controlled trial, allogeneic umbilical-cord MSCs (three infusions) + conventional therapy vs conventional therapy alone, HBV decompensated cirrhosis (China)
cards.people: 219 patients with HBV-related decompensated liver cirrhosis in a prospective open-label randomised trial: umbilical cord-derived MSC (UC-MSC) treatment (n=108; three infusions at 4-week intervals) plus conventional treatment, versus conventional treatment alone (n=111), enrolled 2010–2017 with follow-up from 13 to 75 months. Primary endpoints overall and HCC-free survival.
cards.result: Over the 13- to 75-month follow-up, overall survival was significantly higher in the UC-MSC group than in controls (the abstract reports this comparison qualitatively, without survival percentages), while hepatocellular carcinoma event-free survival did not differ between groups. UC-MSC treatment markedly improved liver function — serum albumin, prothrombin activity, cholinesterase and total bilirubin — over 48 weeks of follow-up. No significant side effects or treatment-related complications were observed in the UC-MSC group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, HBV-only — and the survival claim, the strongest on this shelf, comes from its least blinded design, while the only placebo-controlled trial (card 1) is negative. No survival percentages are printed in the abstract; none are invented here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a split record across four different products — the only placebo-controlled trial (n=27) is negative, the largest trial (n=219, open-label) is positive on survival, and the fibrosis claim rests on within-group histology: product heterogeneity is the finding, not a nuisance
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split record across four different products — the only placebo-controlled trial (n=27) is negative, the largest trial (n=219, open-label) is positive on survival, and the fibrosis claim rests on within-group histology: product heterogeneity is the finding, not a nuisance
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The four trials test three different products (autologous bone-marrow MSCs intravenously; autologous bone-marrow MSCs via the hepatic artery; allogeneic umbilical-cord MSCs intravenously ×3) in different aetiologies (mixed decompensated; HBV on entecavir; abstinent alcoholic; HBV) with four different primary readouts (MELD/Child change; liver function plus immunology; histological fibrosis; survival) — they are limbs, never pooled. The 2026 real-world matched cohort of this programme is observational and is not counted, per the row's fence; the acute-on-chronic liver failure MSC literature asks a different syndrome's question and is cross-pointed, not folded in. These are investigational manufactured cell products, named exactly as each publication describes them; no marketed equivalent was tested.

shelves.title: Lactitol vs lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy: never shown different in 3 trials totalling only 89 patients (one a 9-patient crossover) — equivalence by underpowering, with a tolerability signal from the smallest trial
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and acute or chronic hepatic (portal-systemic) encephalopathy, does oral lactitol versus lactulose improve encephalopathy grade, psychometric performance and ammonia, and how do the two non-absorbable disaccharides compare on tolerability?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Bacterial Infections · Disaccharides · Electroencephalography · Female · Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Lactulose · Liver Cirrhosis · Male · Middle Aged · Sugar Alcohols
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 89. Three randomised trials (1987–1991) compared lactitol with lactulose in acute PSE (n=40), chronic HE (n=9 crossover, sub-floor, labelled and never load-bearing alone) and maintenance PSE (n=40). None showed a difference, none prespecified a non-inferiority margin, and the labelled meta-analysis gives a pooled odds ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.82). Lactitol was never shown different from lactulose in trials too small to show a difference; a tolerability signal favouring lactitol on flatulence/diarrhoea comes from the 9-patient crossover, while the 1991 study found crystalline lactulose better accepted.

cards.headline: Acute PSE trial (Heredia 1987): complete resolution in 11 of 20 patients on EACH sugar over 5 days — a flat equivalence reading in a 40-patient trial
cards.summary: Acute PSE trial (Heredia 1987): complete resolution in 11 of 20 patients on EACH sugar over 5 days — a flat equivalence reading in a 40-patient trial
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, lactitol vs lactulose in acute portal-systemic encephalopathy, 5 days
cards.people: 40 cirrhotic patients with an acute episode of portal-systemic encephalopathy (PSE), randomised 20 to lactulose (30 ml every 6 hours) and 20 to lactitol (12 g every 6 hours), doses adjusted daily to two bowel movements per day for 5 days. Limb: acute PSE.
cards.result: Complete clinical resolution of PSE occurred in 11 patients in each group; moderate improvement in 5 on lactulose and 6 on lactitol; non-response in 4 on lactulose and 3 on lactitol. No side effects attributable to therapy were observed in either group. The authors concluded lactitol is as effective as lactulose in acute PSE — from 20 patients per arm, with no prespecified non-inferiority margin.
cards.watchOut: Small and short: 'as effective as' here means no difference was detected in a trial too small to detect one. Endpoints were clinical examination, EEG and number-connection testing; no mortality or hospitalisation outcomes.
cards.source: Heredia D et al. Lactitol versus lactulose in the treatment of acute portal systemic encephalopathy (PSE). A controlled trial. Journal of hepatology. 1987. PMID: 3598162. cards.headline: Chronic HE crossover trial (Morgan 1987): 9 patients (sub-floor N=9 — labelled, never load-bearing alone) — both sugars equally effective over 3 months each; flatulence in 5 and diarrhoea in 8 patients on lactulose vs 2 and 4 on lactitol
cards.summary: Chronic HE crossover trial (Morgan 1987): 9 patients (sub-floor N=9 — labelled, never load-bearing alone) — both sugars equally effective over 3 months each; flatulence in 5 and diarrhoea in 8 patients on lactulose vs 2 and 4 on lactitol
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial (N=9, sub-floor), lactitol vs lactulose in chronic hepatic encephalopathy, 3 months per period
cards.people: 9 cirrhotic patients in a randomised double-blind crossover comparison, treated for 3 months with each sugar in solutions identical in taste and appearance (initial dose 0.75 ml/kg, adjusted to two semi-soft stools daily). Limb: chronic hepatic encephalopathy. N=9 is below the ~10-human reference floor on its own and is printed on the face for that reason.
cards.result: Adequate catharsis was achieved at mean daily doses of 31.9 g lactitol or 32.9 ml (21.9 g) lactulose syrup. Both sugars were equally effective on the clinical, psychometric and laboratory variables monitored. Side effects were more frequent on lactulose: excessive flatulence in 5 patients and diarrhoea in 8 on lactulose, versus 2 and 4 respectively on lactitol; events likely to cause decompensation arose in 5 patients during lactitol periods and 1 during lactulose periods.
cards.watchOut: SUB-FLOOR: 9 patients. This crossover carries the programme's tolerability signal and nothing more — it is never load-bearing alone, and a crossover in 9 patients cannot establish equivalence.
cards.source: Morgan MY et al. Lactitol versus lactulose in the treatment of chronic hepatic encephalopathy. A double-blind, randomised, cross-over study. Journal of hepatology. 1987. PMID: 3295020. cards.type: Comparative study (double-blind per the record's MeSH), crystalline pure lactulose vs lactitol powder in maintenance PSE therapy — English abstract only
cards.people: 40 patients with liver cirrhosis treated for associated portal-systemic encephalopathy (PSE), comparing crystalline pure lactulose (Laevolac Cristalli) with lactitol powder. Limb: maintenance therapy of PSE. This is an English-abstract-only report of an Italian-language paper, labelled as such.
cards.result: Both disaccharides proved effective in the maintenance therapy of PSE. The crystalline lactulose formulation had a significantly lower incidence of side effects than the previous lactulose formulation and, showing similar efficacy and side-effect rise to lactitol, proved better accepted by the subjects of this study.
cards.watchOut: English-abstract-only report: the abstract prints no per-arm outcome numbers, so none are claimed. Its acceptance reading (favouring crystalline lactulose) runs against the crossover's tolerability reading (favouring lactitol) — both are printed, neither is promoted.

cards.type: Support only: meta-analysis of lactitol RCTs in chronic hepatic encephalopathy — labelled support, never counted as a trial on this shelf
cards.people: Meta-analysis of published randomised trials of lactitol in chronic hepatic encephalopathy: 4 eligible RCTs — three against lactulose and one against lactose in lactase-deficient patients (that lactose-comparator trial could not be retrieved as a separate indexed report and is never counted as a primary here).
cards.result: Lactitol was as effective as the other disaccharides: pooled odds ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.82) for freedom from encephalopathy — an odds ratio, a relative measure, whose confidence interval spans from substantial benefit to substantial harm. Patients experienced fewer side effects on lactitol, but that pooled odds ratio was not statistically significant; lactitol was considered more palatable in all studies.
cards.watchOut: A 1993 meta-analysis of the same small trial base carded above (plus one lactose-comparator trial): it adds a pooled estimate, not new patients, and its confidence interval is wide enough to include meaningful effects in both directions.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 randomised trials totalling 89 patients (40 + 9 + 40), all from 1987–1991 — lactitol was never shown different from lactulose, in trials too small to show a difference; the 9-patient crossover (sub-floor) carries a tolerability signal favouring lactitol that the 1991 maintenance study's acceptance reading does not confirm

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three trials (total N=89) plus one labelled meta-analysis as support.
cards.result: No trial prespecified a non-inferiority margin, and none measured mortality or hospitalisation. The honest summary is equivalence-by-underpowering: identical complete-resolution counts in the acute trial (11 of 20 each), equal effectiveness readings in the crossover and maintenance studies, and a pooled odds ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.82) that excludes nothing clinically important. Era flag: all three trials predate rifaximin-era standard care and used PSE-index / EEG-era endpoints.

shelves.title: Ornithine phenylacetate for overt hepatic encephalopathy: exactly 2 trials (N=279) — the one adequately sized trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.129); the oral trial is a 5-day ammonia study its authors call hypothesis-generating
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis and overt hepatic encephalopathy (or a history of overt episodes), does ornithine phenylacetate — intravenous in hospitalised acute episodes, or oral in stable outpatients — versus placebo (or rifaximin) speed clinical improvement or lower ammonia?
shelves.mesh: Hepatic Encephalopathy · Humans · Lactulose · Liver Cirrhosis · Ornithine · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised trials, total N=279, one programme. STOP-HE (intravenous, n=231) missed its primary endpoint (P=.129); its median-21-hours-sooner reading is a central-laboratory subset analysis. The oral YAQ007 phase 2a trial (n=48) measured plasma ammonia over 5 days, not clinical outcomes, and its authors call it exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The PK/PD paper (PMID 35238476) is a secondary report of STOP-HE itself (shared NCT01966419) and is never counted as a second intravenous trial. The two formulation limbs are labelled and never pooled.

cards.headline: STOP-HE phase 2b RCT (Rahimi 2021): the primary endpoint MISSED — time to confirmed clinical response did not differ on the local-laboratory intention-to-treat analysis (P=.129); a median 21 hours sooner in the central-laboratory-confirmed subset (n=201), a subset analysis of a primary-null trial
cards.summary: STOP-HE phase 2b RCT (Rahimi 2021): the primary endpoint MISSED — time to confirmed clinical response did not differ on the local-laboratory intention-to-treat analysis (P=.129); a median 21 hours sooner in the central-laboratory-confirmed subset (n=201), a subset analysis of a primary-null trial
cards.type: Phase 2b multicentre double-blind randomised trial (STOP-HE), intravenous ornithine phenylacetate vs placebo, both plus standard care, in overt hepatic encephalopathy
cards.people: 231 hospitalised patients with cirrhosis, increased ammonia at screening and acute/overt hepatic encephalopathy, randomised to intravenous ornithine phenylacetate (10, 15 or 20 g/day by severity of liver disease) plus standard care or placebo plus standard care, at sites in North America, Europe, Israel and Australia (2014–2016).
cards.result: Median times to clinical improvement did not differ significantly between ornithine phenylacetate and placebo on the primary (local-laboratory) analysis (P=.129). In the central-laboratory-confirmed hyperammonaemia subset (n=201), clinical improvement came a median 21 hours sooner on ornithine phenylacetate. Serious adverse events occurred in 25% on ornithine phenylacetate vs 29% on placebo (P=.552), and no specific adverse event differed significantly.
cards.watchOut: PRIMARY-NULL: the positive reading lives in a laboratory-defined subset analysis and must never be printed as the headline. This is one of exactly two trials in the programme — see the count fence on the synthesis card.

cards.headline: Labelled secondary report of STOP-HE (Safadi 2022): pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of the SAME trial (shared registry NCT01966419) — ammonia fell faster on ornithine phenylacetate; NOT a second intravenous trial
cards.summary: Labelled secondary report of STOP-HE (Safadi 2022): pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of the SAME trial (shared registry NCT01966419) — ammonia fell faster on ornithine phenylacetate; NOT a second intravenous trial
cards.type: Secondary report (pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic) OF the STOP-HE trial — same programme, same registry NCT01966419, not an independent trial
cards.people: The STOP-HE population: adults hospitalised with an overt HE episode, cirrhosis and plasma ammonia above the upper limit of normal who had failed to improve after 48 hours of standard care, randomised to continuous intravenous ornithine phenylacetate (10, 15 or 20 g/day by Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) or placebo for 5 days. This report shares registry number NCT01966419 with the STOP-HE efficacy report above — it is the same trial.
cards.result: Phenylacetic acid showed dose-dependent pharmacokinetics; urinary phenylacetylglutamine excretion represented about 50–60% of administered phenylacetic acid across doses. Mean reduction in plasma ammonia at 3 hours post-infusion was significantly greater on ornithine phenylacetate than placebo (P=0.014), time to ammonia at or below the upper limit of normal was significantly shorter (P=0.028), and achieving a clinical response was associated with a greater reduction in mean plasma ammonia (P=0.009).
cards.watchOut: MISCOUNT FENCE: this paper and the STOP-HE efficacy paper are ONE trial. Anyone counting them as two intravenous trials doubles the programme's apparent base; the programme's genuine second trial is the oral study below.

cards.headline: Oral YAQ007 phase 2a RCT (Ballester 2026): 48 patients, 5 inpatient days — ammonia fell by day 5 in the two higher-dose YAQ007 groups (within-group P=0.009 and P=0.002); the authors' own conclusion is exploratory and hypothesis-generating
cards.summary: Oral YAQ007 phase 2a RCT (Ballester 2026): 48 patients, 5 inpatient days — ammonia fell by day 5 in the two higher-dose YAQ007 groups (within-group P=0.009 and P=0.002); the authors' own conclusion is exploratory and hypothesis-generating
cards.type: Phase 2a randomised open-label trial, oral YAQ007 (L-ornithine phenylacetate) vs rifaximin, 5 days, pharmacodynamic ammonia endpoint
cards.people: 48 patients with cirrhosis and a history of overt hepatic encephalopathy (28 men, mean age 57.2 years, mean Child-Pugh 8, MELD 10), randomised 1:1:1:1 to one of three oral YAQ007 regimens (2 g three times daily; 4 g twice daily; 4 g three times daily — 36 patients in total) or rifaximin 550 mg twice daily (12 patients), for 5 days under inpatient conditions.
cards.result: A decrease in ammonia at day 5 was observed in the 4 g three-times-daily group (P=0.009) and the 4 g twice-daily group (P=0.002) — within-group readings, printed as such. After multivariable adjustment, the 4 g twice-daily group vs rifaximin, bilirubin, INR and sodium remained significant factors for absolute ammonia reduction. Urinary phenylacetylglutamine excretion increased on day 5 vs day 1 across all YAQ007 dose groups (P<0.001); no clear dose-response was demonstrated. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 20 of 36 (55.6%) on YAQ007 and 5 of 12 (41.7%) on rifaximin, mainly mild gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. The authors conclude the findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is plasma ammonia over 5 days — a pharmacodynamic surrogate, not a clinical outcome — in stable patients with a HISTORY of overt HE, not patients in an acute episode. YAQ007 is the oral formulation of L-ornithine phenylacetate as the publication names it, an investigational product. This molecule must never be conflated with L-ornithine L-aspartate or with glycerol phenylbutyrate — different molecules, different evidence bases.

cards.result: The efficacy headline is null: the only adequately sized trial missed its primary endpoint, and its positive reading is a laboratory-defined subset. The oral trial shows short-term ammonia lowering the authors themselves call hypothesis-generating. Ammonia lowering is mechanistically coherent (the PK/PD report ties ammonia reduction to clinical response within STOP-HE), but no trial has yet shown ornithine phenylacetate to improve a clinical outcome on its primary analysis.

shelves.title: Cobitolimod for ulcerative colitis: COLLECT's primary endpoint missed (remission 44.4% vs 46.5% on placebo) and CONDUCT was positive in only 1 of 4 dose arms, on an 80% CI with a one-sided p-value
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe left-sided (COLLECT: refractory) ulcerative colitis, do rectally administered cobitolimod enemas (two to four doses over 3–4 weeks) versus placebo induce clinical or symptomatic remission?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Colitis, Ulcerative · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oligodeoxyribonucleotides · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Two trials: COLLECT missed its primary endpoint outright, with week-12 clinical remission numerically below placebo (44.4% vs 46.5%); CONDUCT met its week-6 remission endpoint in only the 2 × 250 mg arm (21% vs 7%; odds ratio 3.8, 80% CI 1.5 to 9.5; one-sided P=0.025), with the other three dose arms null and no dose-response. The two further reports carded are labelled reports of the same programme (a COLLECT post-hoc analysis and a biomarker study), not independent trials.

cards.headline: COLLECT RCT (Atreya 2016): primary endpoint MISSED — clinical remission at week 12 was 44.4% on cobitolimod vs 46.5% on placebo, numerically BELOW placebo; symptomatic remission at week 4 (32.1% vs 14.0%, P=0.020) and histological improvement are secondary readings
cards.summary: COLLECT RCT (Atreya 2016): primary endpoint MISSED — clinical remission at week 12 was 44.4% on cobitolimod vs 46.5% on placebo, numerically BELOW placebo; symptomatic remission at week 4 (32.1% vs 14.0%, P=0.020) and histological improvement are secondary readings
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (COLLECT), topical DIMS0150/cobitolimod at colonoscopy vs placebo, in standard-therapy-refractory UC
cards.people: 131 patients with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis refractory to standard therapy, randomised to two single 30 mg doses of DIMS0150 (cobitolimod) or placebo, administered topically during lower gastrointestinal endoscopy at baseline and week 4.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary endpoint, clinical remission (Clinical Activity Index ≤4) at week 12: 44.4% on cobitolimod vs 46.5% on placebo. Secondary readings favoured cobitolimod: symptomatic remission 32.1% vs 14.0% at week 4 (P=0.020) and 44.4% vs 27.9% at week 8 (P=0.061); histological improvement (Geboes) 30.9% vs 9.3% at week 4 (P=0.0073); mucosal healing 34.6% vs 18.6% (P=0.09); clinical remission with mucosal healing at week 4, 21% vs 4.7% (P=0.02). Cobitolimod was well tolerated with no safety signals vs placebo.
cards.watchOut: A primary-null trial whose remission rate was numerically below placebo: every positive number on this card is a secondary endpoint, labelled as such. Delivery was at colonoscopy in a refractory population — a different limb from CONDUCT's enema delivery.
cards.source: Atreya R et al. Clinical Effects of a Topically Applied Toll-like Receptor 9 Agonist in Active Moderate-to-Severe Ulcerative Colitis. Journal of Crohn's & colitis. 2016. PMID: 27208386. cards.headline: CONDUCT phase 2b RCT (Atreya 2020): clinical remission at week 6 met ONLY in the 2 × 250 mg arm — 21% vs 7% on placebo (odds ratio 3.8, 80% CI 1.5 to 9.5; one-sided P=0.025); the other three dose arms did not differ from placebo and there is no dose-response
cards.summary: CONDUCT phase 2b RCT (Atreya 2020): clinical remission at week 6 met ONLY in the 2 × 250 mg arm — 21% vs 7% on placebo (odds ratio 3.8, 80% CI 1.5 to 9.5; one-sided P=0.025); the other three dose arms did not differ from placebo and there is no dose-response
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (CONDUCT), cobitolimod enema vs placebo in left-sided UC
cards.people: 213 patients randomised (211 treated) with moderate-to-severe left-sided ulcerative colitis and inadequate response to conventional or biological therapy, at 91 sites in 12 European countries, to rectal enemas of cobitolimod 2 × 31 mg (n=40 treated), 2 × 125 mg (n=43), 4 × 125 mg (n=42), 2 × 250 mg (n=42), or placebo (n=44), dosed at weeks 0 and 3 (the 4 × 125 mg arm weekly for 4 weeks).
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 6: 2 × 250 mg, 9 of 42 (21%) vs 3 of 44 (7%) on placebo — odds ratio 3.8 (80% CI 1.5 to 9.5), one-sided P=0.025, an odds ratio (a relative measure) reported with an 80% confidence interval and a one-sided p-value, exactly as the trial reports them; the trial prespecified one-sided tests with P<0.10 as significant and no multiplicity adjustment. The other arms did not differ from placebo: 2 × 31 mg 13% (P=0.18), 2 × 125 mg 5% (P=0.66), 4 × 125 mg 10% (P=0.33). Severe adverse events occurred in 8 of 211 patients (4%); one placebo patient died after colectomy for disease worsening.
cards.watchOut: The single positive arm rests on an 80% CI and a one-sided p-value at the highest of four dose regimens, with no dose-response across the other three arms. '21% vs 7%' must never be printed without those facts beside it.

cards.headline: Labelled post-hoc report of COLLECT (Atreya 2018): patient-reported-outcome analysis of the COLLECT data (e-diary subset n=104) — symptomatic remission at week 12 in 38.6% vs 17.6% (P=0.04); NOT a third trial
cards.summary: Labelled post-hoc report of COLLECT (Atreya 2018): patient-reported-outcome analysis of the COLLECT data (e-diary subset n=104) — symptomatic remission at week 12 in 38.6% vs 17.6% (P=0.04); NOT a third trial
cards.type: Programme report: post-hoc patient-reported-outcome analysis OF the COLLECT trial — same programme, not an independent trial
cards.people: 104 patients from the COLLECT trial with e-diary records — a post-hoc subset of the 131-patient COLLECT population carded above, analysed with patient-reported-outcome-defined endpoints (absence of blood in stool and mean daily stool frequency <4).
cards.result: Symptomatic remission was achieved at week 4 in 17.1% on cobitolimod vs 5.9% on placebo (P=0.13), at week 8 in 35.7% vs 17.6% (P=0.07), and at week 12 in 38.6% vs 17.6% (P=0.04). Effects were smaller in anti-TNF-experienced patients with a broadly similar relative effect size, and efficacy was higher in moderate than severe disease.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, in a subset (104 of 131), using redefined endpoints, of a trial whose prespecified primary endpoint missed. It is carded, labelled, only to complete the programme record.

cards.type: Support only: randomised biomarker / steroid-sensitivity study of DIMS0150 — mechanistic support for the cobitolimod programme, never counted as an efficacy trial
cards.people: 34 subjects with active steroid-dependent or steroid-resistant ulcerative colitis on concomitant steroid therapy, randomised to a single rectal administration of DIMS0150 30 mg or placebo, with blood-derived cells assayed for steroid-response biomarkers (EudraCT 2006-001846-15); a preceding non-interventional pilot compared steroid-refractory patients with healthy volunteers.
cards.result: Three candidate biomarkers (CD163, TSP-1 and IL-1RII) showed steroid responses significantly enhanced when DIMS0150 was applied, and on unblinding the biomarker assay had correctly predicted clinical response in over 90% of patients, by the authors' report. The study's purpose was identifying likely responders, not estimating a treatment effect.
cards.watchOut: 34 patients, a single dose, and a biomarker primary endpoint: this report cannot carry an efficacy claim and is never counted in the programme's trial base.

cards.result: The primary-endpoint record is the face of this shelf: one outright miss and one single-arm-of-four positive under exploratory statistics. Cobitolimod (development names DIMS0150 / Kappaproct in the earlier reports) is an investigational DNA-based oligonucleotide that activates Toll-like receptor 9; it is not a marketed product, and current products, if any emerge, may differ. Delivery limbs differ — colonoscopy dosing in refractory disease (COLLECT) vs enema dosing in left-sided disease (CONDUCT) — and are not pooled.

shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Three randomised trials, three labelled limbs: in therapy-refractory disease (n=329) no dose of recombinant human IL-10 beat placebo on remission; in mild-to-moderate disease (n=95) a single mid-dose cell (5 µg/kg, 23.5% vs 0%) combined remission with endoscopic improvement in a safety-first dose-ranging trial and higher doses were less effective; after resection (n=65) endoscopic recurrence was 46% on Tenovil vs 52% on placebo. Dose-dependent reversible anaemia and thrombocytopenia recurred. A tested-and-failed anti-inflammatory-cytokine hypothesis, presented as such.

cards.headline: Mild-to-moderate Crohn's trial (Fedorak 2000): 95 patients — clinical remission with endoscopic improvement in 23.5% at 5 µg/kg vs 0% on placebo at day 29, with higher doses LESS effective; a bell-shaped dose response in a small dose-ranging trial whose primary objective was safety
cards.summary: Mild-to-moderate Crohn's trial (Fedorak 2000): 95 patients — clinical remission with endoscopic improvement in 23.5% at 5 µg/kg vs 0% on placebo at day 29, with higher doses LESS effective; a bell-shaped dose response in a small dose-ranging trial whose primary objective was safety
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled sequential dose-escalation trial, rhuIL-10 in mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease (safety primary, efficacy secondary)
cards.people: 95 patients with mild to moderately active Crohn's disease (CDAI 200–350), not on corticosteroids, mesalamine or immunosuppressives, randomised to subcutaneous recombinant human interleukin-10 (1, 5, 10 or 20 µg/kg) or placebo once daily for 28 days, then followed for 20 weeks. Limb: mild-to-moderate active disease.
cards.result: At day 29, 23.5% (95% CI 6.8% to 49.9%) of patients on 5 µg/kg experienced clinical remission and endoscopic improvement, vs 0% (95% CI 0% to 14.8%) on placebo. Higher doses were less effective than 5 µg/kg. Adverse effects were dose-related, mild-to-moderate and reversible; asymptomatic reversible anaemia and thrombocytopenia occurred at higher doses; no IL-10 accumulation or anti-IL-10 antibodies were detected.
cards.watchOut: The positive cell combines clinical remission WITH endoscopic improvement at the single best of four doses — a multiplicity-exposed reading in 95 patients, from a trial designed primarily for safety. This is the programme's only positive efficacy reading, and the larger trial below did not confirm it.
cards.source: Fedorak RN et al. Recombinant human interleukin 10 in the treatment of patients with mild to moderately active Crohn's disease. The Interleukin 10 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Cooperative Study Group. Gastroenterology. 2000. PMID: 11113068. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Therapy-refractory Crohn's trial (Schreiber 2000): 329 patients — NO dose beat placebo on remission (18% / 20% / 20% / 28% across doses vs 18% on placebo); clinical improvement at 8 µg/kg (46% vs 27%) was presented by the authors as a tendency
cards.summary: Therapy-refractory Crohn's trial (Schreiber 2000): 329 patients — NO dose beat placebo on remission (18% / 20% / 20% / 28% across doses vs 18% on placebo); clinical improvement at 8 µg/kg (46% vs 27%) was presented by the authors as a tendency
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial, rhuIL-10 in therapy-refractory Crohn's disease
cards.people: 329 therapy-refractory patients with Crohn's disease, randomised to subcutaneous recombinant human interleukin-10 (1, 4, 8 or 20 µg/kg) or placebo daily for 28 days, in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled study. Limb: therapy-refractory active disease.
cards.result: Remission (CDAI <150) rates were 18% (1 µg/kg), 20% (4 µg/kg), 20% (8 µg/kg) and 28% (20 µg/kg) vs 18% on placebo — no dose separated from placebo on remission. Clinical improvement (≥100-point CDAI fall) occurred in 46% at 8 µg/kg vs 27% on placebo, described by the authors as a tendency toward clinical improvement but not remission. Treatment produced a fully reversible, dose-dependent decrease in haemoglobin and platelet (thrombocyte) counts, with no clinically significant side effects reported.
cards.watchOut: The programme's largest and most decisive trial is null on its remission endpoint. The 46% vs 27% improvement figure is a secondary reading the authors themselves called a tendency — it must not be upgraded into an efficacy claim.
cards.source: Schreiber S et al. Safety and efficacy of recombinant human interleukin 10 in chronic active Crohn's disease. Crohn's Disease IL-10 Cooperative Study Group. Gastroenterology. 2000. PMID: 11113067. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Postoperative prevention trial (Colombel 2001): 65 patients — endoscopic recurrence at 12 weeks in 46% on pooled Tenovil vs 52% on placebo (not significant); severe recurrence 9% in both groups — a null prevention reading
cards.summary: Postoperative prevention trial (Colombel 2001): 65 patients — endoscopic recurrence at 12 weeks in 46% on pooled Tenovil vs 52% on placebo (not significant); severe recurrence 9% in both groups — a null prevention reading
cards.type: Double-blind controlled trial, Tenovil (rhuIL-10) for prevention of postoperative endoscopic recurrence in Crohn's disease
cards.people: 65 patients randomised within 2 weeks of curative ileal or ileocolonic resection for Crohn's disease to subcutaneous Tenovil (recombinant human interleukin-10) 4 µg/kg once daily (n=22), 8 µg/kg twice weekly (n=21), or placebo (n=22), for 12 weeks; 37 Tenovil and 21 placebo patients were evaluable by endoscopy. Limb: postoperative recurrence prevention — a different question from treating active disease.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, recurrent lesions were present in 17 of 37 patients (46%) in the pooled Tenovil group vs 11 of 21 (52%) on placebo (not significant); severe endoscopic recurrence was 9% in both groups. Adverse events were mostly mild or moderate and equally distributed. The authors concluded there was no evidence that Tenovil prevented endoscopic recurrence.
cards.watchOut: A null prevention trial in a third, distinct limb. The evaluable denominators (37 and 21) are smaller than the randomised numbers — attrition is part of the reading.
cards.source: Colombel JF et al. Interleukin 10 (Tenovil) in the prevention of postoperative recurrence of Crohn's disease. Gut. 2001. PMID: 11413109. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 randomised trials, one programme, and the arc is the answer — a 95-patient dose-ranging trial with a single mid-dose signal was followed by a 329-patient trial in which no dose beat placebo on remission and a 65-patient postoperative trial with no prevention of recurrence; recombinant human IL-10 was tested and failed in Crohn's disease

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: mild-to-moderate active disease (n=95), therapy-refractory active disease (n=329) and postoperative prevention (n=65) — three limbs, labelled and never pooled.
cards.result: Dose-dependent reversible falls in haemoglobin and platelet counts recurred across the programme. The tested product is recombinant human interleukin-10 (development name Tenovil in the postoperative trial), an investigational biological that was never marketed. These are pre-biologic-era (2000–2001) trials with CDAI-era endpoints.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Alicaforsen enema for left-sided ulcerative colitis: week-6 primaries null against both placebo and mesalazine in the two larger trials — only post-treatment durability signals remain, as secondary readings
shelves.question: In patients with mild-to-moderate active left-sided / distal ulcerative colitis, does a nightly alicaforsen enema (120–240 mg, or 0.1–4 mg/mL dose cohorts) for 4–6 weeks versus placebo — or versus mesalazine enema — improve disease activity, and does any response last longer after treatment stops?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Colitis, Ulcerative · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Enema · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oligodeoxyribonucleotides, Antisense · Phosphorothioate Oligonucleotides · Rectum · Recurrence · Thionucleotides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for durability only, not for acute effect. In the two adequately sized trials the week-6 primary endpoint did not separate alicaforsen enema from placebo (n=112) or from mesalazine enema (n=159). The positive material is the 40-patient dose-escalation study (2-patient placebo cells per cohort) and secondary post-treatment durability readings (DAI reduction persisting to week 30; median response duration 128–146 days vs 54 days on mesalazine), which are hypothesis-level and carry selective-emphasis risk.

cards.headline: Dose-escalation trial (van Deventer 2004): 40 patients in four cohorts of 10 (8 active / 2 placebo each — 2-patient placebo cells, printed with the design) — dose-dependent DAI improvement (overall P=0.003); 4 mg/mL improved DAI by 70% vs 28% on placebo at day 29
cards.summary: Dose-escalation trial (van Deventer 2004): 40 patients in four cohorts of 10 (8 active / 2 placebo each — 2-patient placebo cells, printed with the design) — dose-dependent DAI improvement (overall P=0.003); 4 mg/mL improved DAI by 70% vs 28% on placebo at day 29
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled escalating-dose trial, alicaforsen enema in distal UC — dose-finding, not confirmatory
cards.people: 40 patients with mild to moderately active distal ulcerative colitis (Disease Activity Index 4–10), assigned to four dosing cohorts of 10 (8 active, 2 placebo per cohort), receiving 60 ml alicaforsen enema (0.1, 0.5, 2 or 4 mg/mL) or placebo once daily for 28 days, with follow-up to 6 months.
cards.result: At day 29, DAI improvement was dose-dependent (overall P=0.003): the 4 mg/mL cohort improved DAI by 70% vs a placebo response of 28% (P=0.004). At month 3, the 2 and 4 mg/mL cohorts had improved DAI by 72% and 68% vs 11.5% on placebo (P=0.016 and P=0.021). No patient in the 4 mg/mL group, vs 4 of 8 placebo patients, required additional medical or surgical intervention over the 6 months. The safety profile was favourable.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient dose-finding study whose placebo comparison rests on 2-patient cells within each cohort (8 placebo patients in total). Its positive reading is hypothesis-generating only — the two larger trials below are the confirmatory test, and both missed their primaries.
cards.source: van Deventer SJ et al. A randomised, controlled, double blind, escalating dose study of alicaforsen enema in active ulcerative colitis. Gut. 2004. PMID: 15479686. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 2 placebo-controlled trial (van Deventer 2006): 112 subjects — NO significant difference on the primary endpoint (DAI at week 6); a prolonged DAI reduction in the daily 240 mg arm from week 18 (51% vs 18%, P=0.04) to week 30 (50% vs 11%, P=0.03) is a post-treatment durability reading after a null primary

cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, alicaforsen enema in left-sided UC
cards.people: 112 subjects with an acute exacerbation of mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis, equally randomised to one of four alicaforsen enema regimens or placebo, daily for 6 weeks, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: No significant difference was observed between the treatment arms and placebo on the primary endpoint, Disease Activity Index at week 6. A prolonged reduction in mean percentage DAI relative to baseline was observed in the daily 240 mg arm vs placebo from week 18 (51% vs 18%, P=0.04) to week 30 (50% vs 11%, P=0.03). Alicaforsen enema was safe and well tolerated at all doses; the authors suggested the durability might indicate a disease-modifying effect.
cards.watchOut: NULL PRIMARY: everything positive in this trial happens 12–24 weeks AFTER the 6-week primary endpoint failed, off treatment — selective-emphasis risk is stated on the face, and the durability reading must never be promoted to a headline finding.
cards.source: van Deventer SJ et al. A phase II dose ranging, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of alicaforsen enema in subjects with acute exacerbation of mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2006. PMID: 16669956. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Active-controlled trial (Miner 2006): 159 subjects — NO significant difference on the primary endpoint (DAI at week 6) vs mesalazine enema either; median duration of response 128 and 146 days on alicaforsen vs 54 days on mesalazine is a secondary durability reading; complete mucosal healing 24% (240 mg) vs 17%
cards.summary: Active-controlled trial (Miner 2006): 159 subjects — NO significant difference on the primary endpoint (DAI at week 6) vs mesalazine enema either; median duration of response 128 and 146 days on alicaforsen vs 54 days on mesalazine is a secondary durability reading; complete mucosal healing 24% (240 mg) vs 17%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-controlled trial, alicaforsen enema vs mesalazine enema in left-sided UC
cards.people: 159 subjects with mild to moderate active left-sided ulcerative colitis, randomised to nightly enema for 6 weeks with alicaforsen 120 mg (n=55), alicaforsen 240 mg (n=50) or mesalazine 4 g (n=54), followed by 24 weeks of monitoring.
cards.result: No significant difference was observed between the treatment arms on the primary endpoint, Disease Activity Index at week 6. The median duration of response was 128 days (120 mg) and 146 days (240 mg) on alicaforsen vs 54 days on mesalazine — a secondary durability reading, labelled as such. Complete mucosal healing occurred in 24% of the 240 mg alicaforsen group vs 17% on mesalazine. The authors concluded alicaforsen's acute response and safety resembled mesalazine's, differentiated by a more durable response.
cards.watchOut: NULL PRIMARY against an active comparator as well as against placebo (in the trial above): alicaforsen showed no acute advantage over standard mesalazine enema. The duration-of-response contrast is secondary and hypothesis-level.
cards.source: Miner PB et al. Safety and efficacy of two dose formulations of alicaforsen enema compared with mesalazine enema for treatment of mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis: a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2006. PMID: 16669955. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Normal bile and pancreatic duct diameters: MRCP limits 8 mm (<65) / 11 mm (≥65) and 3 / 4 mm — ultrasound means ~2.5–2.8 mm, with the two ultrasound series disagreeing (7 mm vs 10 mm)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the normal diameters of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct — by imaging modality (ultrasound vs MRCP) and age — how steeply does duct diameter rise with age, and how many healthy people exceed the conventional upper limits (about 6–7 mm for the bile duct) that trigger further investigation?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, on three independent populations in two modalities, carded separately and never merged. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, hepatobiliary sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. On MRCP (Pomerania, 938 / 774 healthy individuals) the age-dependent 95th-percentile upper limits are 8 mm (<65 years) and 11 mm (≥65 years) for the common bile duct and 3 mm and 4 mm for the pancreatic duct, and 10.9% / 18.2% of healthy people exceed the conventional limits. On ultrasound the means are far smaller (2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis, 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point in 830 donors, none above 7 mm), while a whole-duct-visualisation series reports up to 10 mm — the two ultrasound series disagree, and that disagreement is content, preserved on the face.

cards.headline: Population MRCP (Beyer 2023): age-dependent 95th-percentile upper limits are 8 mm (<65 years) and 11 mm (≥65 years) for the common bile duct and 3 mm and 4 mm for the pancreatic duct — 10.9% of healthy people exceeded the conventional bile-duct limit and 18.2% the pancreatic-duct limit
cards.summary: Population MRCP (Beyer 2023): age-dependent 95th-percentile upper limits are 8 mm (<65 years) and 11 mm (≥65 years) for the common bile duct and 3 mm and 4 mm for the pancreatic duct — 10.9% of healthy people exceeded the conventional bile-duct limit and 18.2% the pancreatic-duct limit
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based MRCP reference derivation, Study of Health in Pomerania)
cards.people: 938 healthy individuals with common bile duct diameters and 774 with pancreatic duct diameters on MRCP, from the population-based Study of Health in Pomerania whole-body MRI cohort, after excluding pre-existing pancreaticobiliary conditions.
cards.result: Duct diameters increased significantly with age (P < 0.0001). Age-dependent upper reference limits, defined as the 95th percentile, were up to 8 mm in subjects <65 years and up to 11 mm in subjects ≥65 years for the common bile duct, and up to 3 mm (<65 years) and up to 4 mm (≥65 years) for the pancreatic duct. The conventional upper reference limits were exceeded in 10.9% (bile duct) and 18.2% (pancreatic duct) of healthy individuals. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, hepatobiliary sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so.
cards.watchOut: MRCP diameters run larger than ultrasound diameters (cards below) and the two modalities' limits are carded separately and never merged; these are 95th-percentile limits from one German population cohort.

cards.headline: Ultrasound in 830 healthy blood donors (Niederau 1983): mean bile-duct diameter 2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis and 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point; no healthy subject above 7 mm at any site and 95% below 4 mm at both sites
cards.summary: Ultrasound in 830 healthy blood donors (Niederau 1983): mean bile-duct diameter 2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis and 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point; no healthy subject above 7 mm at any site and 95% below 4 mm at both sites
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prospective ultrasound derivation in healthy blood donors)
cards.people: 830 healthy blood donors examined prospectively by ultrasound; measurement site (porta hepatis vs widest point) is printed on this card, as it must be on every card on this shelf. The same paper's cholelithiasis and post-cholecystectomy patient groups are not healthy-population data and are not carded as norms here.
cards.result: Mean diameter was 2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis and 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point (correlation between the two sites r = 0.84). None of the healthy subjects had a diameter larger than 7 mm at any site, and in 95% the diameters were less than 4 mm at both sites. Diameters correlated significantly with age (r = 0.16) and weight (r = 0.11), but not with sex, height or body surface area.
cards.watchOut: A donor population, not a general-population sample, and a 1983 ultrasound technique: its 'none above 7 mm' finding disagrees with the 1984 series below — a technique / visualisation difference that is content, not an error to be averaged away.
cards.source: Niederau C et al. Extrahepatic bile ducts in healthy subjects, in patients with cholelithiasis, and in postcholecystectomy patients: a prospective ultrasonic study. cards.headline: Ultrasound of the whole extrahepatic duct (Wu 1984): inner diameter ranged 1–10 mm and was age-dependent (r = 0.60) — up to 10 mm in a series mixing healthy subjects with patients free of hepatobiliary disease
cards.summary: Ultrasound of the whole extrahepatic duct (Wu 1984): inner diameter ranged 1–10 mm and was age-dependent (r = 0.60) — up to 10 mm in a series mixing healthy subjects with patients free of hepatobiliary disease
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (real-time ultrasound, whole-duct visualisation)
cards.people: 256 healthy subjects and patients without hepatobiliary disease — that mixed composition is printed on the face of this card; the full extrahepatic duct was visualised in 203, using a high-resolution real-time scanner with multiple longitudinal oblique approaches.
cards.result: The inner diameter of the widest point of the duct varied from 1 mm to 10 mm and was age-dependent (r = 0.60, P < 0.001). The authors conclude that, based on visualisation of the entire extrahepatic duct, the normal inner diameter of the common bile duct can be up to 10 mm, with a mild change of duct size with age.
cards.watchOut: This series' 10 mm upper range directly disagrees with the 830-donor series above (none above 7 mm): the disagreement is a technique / visualisation difference and is never averaged into a single 'normal range'; the population is also mixed (healthy subjects plus patients without hepatobiliary disease), stated above.
cards.source: Wu CC et al. Effect of aging on common bile duct diameter: a real-time ultrasonographic study. Journal of clinical ultrasound : JCU. 1984. PMID: 6436325. cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, hepatobiliary sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three independent populations, two modalities, are carded and never merged: the Pomerania MRCP cohort (938 bile-duct / 774 pancreatic-duct healthy individuals; 95th-percentile bile-duct limits 8 mm under 65 and 11 mm at 65 and over, pancreatic-duct limits 3 and 4 mm; 10.9% and 18.2% of healthy individuals above the conventional limits), the 830-donor ultrasound series (means 2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis and 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point; none above 7 mm; 95% below 4 mm; age correlation r = 0.16) and the 256-person whole-duct ultrasound series (range 1–10 mm; age correlation r = 0.60; mixed healthy / no-hepatobiliary-disease composition). Measurement site prints on every card. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the age gradient is consistent across all three datasets, but no single upper limit is universal — it is a property of modality, measurement site, age band and visualisation technique.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: never print a single bile-duct 'normal range' without its modality, site and age band; the two 1980s ultrasound series disagree with each other (7 mm vs 10 mm upper range) and that disagreement is preserved, not resolved, on this shelf.

shelves.title: Somatostatin analogues for polycystic liver volume (3 randomised primaries, total N = 144): liver volume fell roughly 3–5% over 6–12 months on imaging — a surrogate endpoint only — and pasireotide caused new diabetes in 59% vs 7%
shelves.question: In patients with polycystic liver disease (autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease or autosomal-dominant polycystic liver disease, including severe liver involvement), does a somatostatin analogue versus placebo reduce total liver volume over 6–12 months, and at what metabolic cost?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Cysts/drug therapy/etiology/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Liver Diseases/drug therapy/etiology/pathology · Liver Function Tests · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Size · Peptides, Cyclic/therapeutic use · Polycystic Kidney, Autosomal Dominant/complications/drug therapy/pathology · Quality of Life · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — on imaging liver volume only). Three randomised primaries, three different molecules, total N = 144: lanreotide −2.9% vs +1.6% on placebo (p < .01), octreotide −4.95% vs +0.92% (p = 0.048) and pasireotide −3% vs +6% (p < 0.001) in height-adjusted total liver volume over 6–12 months. SURROGATE-ENDPOINT FLAG: every primary is imaging volume; whether shrinking a polycystic liver by roughly 3–5% over a year helps patients is untested. HARM ASYMMETRY: the pasireotide limb's glycaemic harm — hyperglycaemia 79% vs 27%, and new diabetes in 59% vs 7% of patients without diabetes at baseline — is far larger than any harm signal in the other two limbs and is never averaged away in this balance.

cards.headline: Lanreotide trial (van Keimpema 2009): 54 patients randomised — liver volume −2.9% on lanreotide vs +1.6% on placebo over 24 weeks (P < .01), an imaging-volume endpoint
cards.summary: Lanreotide trial (van Keimpema 2009): 54 patients randomised — liver volume −2.9% on lanreotide vs +1.6% on placebo over 24 weeks (P < .01), an imaging-volume endpoint
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, lanreotide vs placebo in polycystic liver disease (ADPKD or PCLD)
cards.people: 54 patients with polycystic liver because of autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) or autosomal-dominant polycystic liver disease (PCLD), randomised to lanreotide 120 mg or placebo, administered every 28 days for 24 weeks, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in two tertiary referral centres; analyses were intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Mean liver volume decreased 2.9%, from 4606 mL to 4471 mL, in patients given lanreotide, and increased 1.6%, from 4689 mL to 4895 mL, in the placebo group (P < .01), measured by computed tomography at weeks 0 and 24. Post hoc stratification for ADPKD or PCLD showed similar changes, with statistically significant differences in patients given lanreotide (P < .01 for both diseases). Baseline characteristics were comparable except that more patients with ADPKD were assigned to placebo (P = .03).
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE-ENDPOINT FLAG (load-bearing): every primary endpoint in this base is imaging liver volume over 6–12 months. No trial shows benefit on symptoms patients feel, on liver-related complications, or on transplantation.
cards.source: van Keimpema L et al. Lanreotide reduces the volume of polycystic liver: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19646443. cards.summary: Octreotide trial (Hogan 2010): 42 patients randomised — liver volume −4.95% vs +0.92% on placebo over 1 year (P = 0.048), an imaging-volume endpoint; improved perception of bodily pain was a secondary readout
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, octreotide long-acting release vs placebo in severe polycystic liver disease
cards.people: 42 patients with severe polycystic liver disease resulting from ADPKD (34 patients) or autosomal-dominant polycystic liver disease (8 patients), randomly assigned 2:1 to octreotide long-acting release depot (up to 40 mg every 28 ± 5 days) or placebo for 1 year, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Liver volume decreased by 4.95% ± 6.77% in the octreotide group but remained practically unchanged (+0.92% ± 8.33%) in the placebo group (P = 0.048), measured by MRI. Among patients with ADPKD, total kidney volume remained practically unchanged (+0.25% ± 7.53%) on octreotide but increased by 8.61% ± 10.07% on placebo (P = 0.045) — a secondary kidney-volume readout of this liver trial, labelled as such. Changes in GFR were similar in both groups. Octreotide was well tolerated; treated individuals reported an improved perception of bodily pain and physical activity.
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE-ENDPOINT FLAG (load-bearing): every primary endpoint in this base is imaging liver volume over 6–12 months. No trial shows benefit on symptoms patients feel, on liver-related complications, or on transplantation. The bodily-pain improvement is a secondary quality-of-life readout, not a symptom primary endpoint.

cards.headline: Pasireotide trial (Hogan 2020): 48 patients randomised — height-adjusted total liver volume −3% vs +6% on placebo (P < 0.001), BUT hyperglycaemia in 79% vs 27% and new diabetes in 59% vs 7% of patients without diabetes at baseline: the harm limb is load-bearing
cards.summary: Pasireotide trial (Hogan 2020): 48 patients randomised — height-adjusted total liver volume −3% vs +6% on placebo (P < 0.001), BUT hyperglycaemia in 79% vs 27% and new diabetes in 59% vs 7% of patients without diabetes at baseline: the harm limb is load-bearing
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, pasireotide long-acting release vs placebo in severe polycystic liver disease
cards.people: 48 individuals with severe polycystic liver disease (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney or liver disease with severe liver involvement), assigned 2:1 in a 1-year double-blind randomised trial to pasireotide long-acting release or placebo; 41 completed total liver volume measurements (29 pasireotide, 12 placebo).
cards.result: Annualised change in height-adjusted total liver volume was −3% ± 7% on pasireotide long-acting release compared with +6% ± 7% on placebo (P < 0.001 for both the absolute and percentage changes). Total kidney volumes decreased by −1% ± 4% on pasireotide compared with a 4% ± 5% increase on placebo (P = 0.05). Changes in eGFR were similar between groups. Among the 48 randomised, hyperglycaemia occurred in 26 of 33 (79%) on pasireotide versus 4 of 15 (27%) on placebo (P < 0.001), and among the 47 without diabetes at baseline, 19 of 32 (59%) on pasireotide versus 1 of 15 (7%) on placebo developed diabetes (P = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The glycaemic harm on this card is never averaged away against the other two molecules: new diabetes in over half of non-diabetic recipients is a harm of a different order from anything in the lanreotide or octreotide limbs. SURROGATE-ENDPOINT FLAG (load-bearing): every primary endpoint in this base is imaging liver volume over 6–12 months. No trial shows benefit on symptoms patients feel, on liver-related complications, or on transplantation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 randomised primaries, 3 different molecules, total N = 144 — somatostatin analogues shrink polycystic livers by roughly 3–5% over a year on imaging; whether that helps patients is untested, and pasireotide carries a large glycaemic harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: 3 randomised primaries, 3 different molecules, total N = 144 — somatostatin analogues shrink polycystic livers by roughly 3–5% over a year on imaging; whether that helps patients is untested, and pasireotide carries a large glycaemic harm
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: lanreotide (n = 54), octreotide (n = 42) and pasireotide (n = 48) — three randomised primaries totalling 144 randomised patients, in mixed ADPKD/PCLD populations with severe liver involvement in all three, most explicitly in the second and third.
cards.result: Not counted as primaries: the DIPAK-1 liver subanalysis and the 12-patient crossover post-hoc liver analysis are liver readouts of kidney-question trials whose question is homed at pack #3195 (somatostatin analogues for kidney growth in ADPKD — a different organ question), and the pooled quality-of-life analysis of the two earlier trials is a secondary analysis, never a fourth trial; they are cross-points only. Pasireotide's endocrine homes (acromegaly/Cushing's questions) share no anchor with this shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Fontolizumab (anti-interferon-gamma antibody, never marketed) in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease: 3 randomised reports, total N = 379 — both larger trials missed their primary endpoints while CRP and endoscopic measures moved
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 250–450), does fontolizumab versus placebo induce clinical response or remission, and does any clinical effect track the drug's clear biological (C-reactive protein / endoscopic) activity?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Infusions, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Severity of Illness Index · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a tested-and-failed interferon-gamma hypothesis: the biology engaged without clinical benefit at the tested doses/schedules. Three randomised reports, total N = 379. Both adequately sized trials missed their primary clinical endpoints (day-29 response 31–38% across all groups including placebo in the 201-patient trial; the single-dose primary did not differ in the 133-patient trial), while C-reactive protein and endoscopic measures moved. Every positive clinical reading is a later-timepoint or two-dose-subgroup analysis after a null primary, stated on the face. Era: 2006–2010, CDAI-era endpoints. Fontolizumab is an investigational humanised antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly.

cards.headline: Phase 2 multiple-dose trial (Reinisch 2010): 201 patients randomised — the primary endpoint, day-29 clinical response, did not differ (31–38% across all groups including placebo); later timepoints favoured the 1.0/1.0 mg/kg regimen and all fontolizumab groups significantly improved CRP — secondary readings of a primary-null trial
cards.summary: Phase 2 multiple-dose trial (Reinisch 2010): 201 patients randomised — the primary endpoint, day-29 clinical response, did not differ (31–38% across all groups including placebo); later timepoints favoured the 1.0/1.0 mg/kg regimen and all fontolizumab groups significantly improved CRP — secondary readings of a primary-null trial
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multiple-dose trial, fontolizumab vs placebo in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 201 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 250–450), randomised to an initial intravenous dose of fontolizumab 1.0 or 4.0 mg/kg or placebo, followed by up to 3 subcutaneous doses of 0.1 or 1.0 mg/kg fontolizumab or placebo every 4 weeks; 135 patients (67%) completed the study.
cards.result: Day 29 response rates — the primary efficacy endpoint, a decrease in CDAI of at least 100 points — were similar in all treatment groups (31%–38%). At subsequent timepoints a significantly greater proportion of patients in the 1.0 mg/kg intravenous / 1.0 mg/kg subcutaneous group had clinical response and significantly greater improvement in CDAI compared with placebo. All fontolizumab groups had significant improvement in C-reactive protein levels. The overall frequency of adverse events was similar in all groups (58%–75%), most related to exacerbation of Crohn's disease; neutralising antibodies to fontolizumab occurred in 5.2%.
cards.watchOut: Primary-null trial: the positive clinical readings are later-timepoint analyses after the missed day-29 primary, and the CRP improvement is a biological signal, not a clinical benefit. Fontolizumab is an investigational humanised anti-interferon-gamma antibody that was never marketed.
cards.source: Reinisch W et al. Fontolizumab in moderate to severe Crohn's disease: a phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple-dose study. Inflammatory bowel diseases. 2010. PMID: 19637334. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 2006 Gut trial (Hommes 2006): 133 patients randomised — the single-dose primary endpoint did not differ; in the two-dose subgroup, day-56 response was 69% (4 mg/kg) and 67% (10 mg/kg) vs 32% on placebo (p = 0.02 and p = 0.03), a dose-subgroup reading after a null primary
cards.summary: 2006 Gut trial (Hommes 2006): 133 patients randomised — the single-dose primary endpoint did not differ; in the two-dose subgroup, day-56 response was 69% (4 mg/kg) and 67% (10 mg/kg) vs 32% on placebo (p = 0.02 and p = 0.03), a dose-subgroup reading after a null primary
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, fontolizumab (one or two doses) vs placebo in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 133 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 250–450 inclusive), randomised to placebo or fontolizumab 4 or 10 mg/kg; 42 patients received one dose and 91 patients received two doses on days 0 and 28, double-blind.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in the primary endpoint (clinical response, a decrease in CDAI of 100 points or more) between the fontolizumab and placebo groups after a single dose at day 28. Patients receiving two doses demonstrated a doubling in response rate at day 56 compared with placebo: 69% (22/32, p = 0.02) at 4 mg/kg and 67% (21/31, p = 0.03) at 10 mg/kg versus 32% (9/28) on placebo. Stratification by elevated baseline C-reactive protein decreased the placebo response and produced more pronounced differences. Two grade 3 adverse events were considered related to Crohn's disease; one death (during sleep) and one serious adverse event (an elective hospitalisation) were considered unrelated.
cards.watchOut: The day-56 figures are a two-dose-subgroup reading after a null single-dose primary — multiplicity-exposed and labelled as such, never a headline confirmation. Fontolizumab was never marketed.
cards.source: Hommes DW et al. Fontolizumab, a humanised anti-interferon gamma antibody, demonstrates safety and clinical activity in patients with moderate to severe Crohn's disease. Gut. 2006. PMID: 16507585. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dose-escalation safety trial (Reinisch 2006): 45 patients randomised — primary objectives safety/tolerability; no difference in clinical activity (placebo response 60%), with greater falls in endoscopic severity index (p = 0.02) and CRP (p < 0.001) at 4.0 mg/kg: a biological-activity signal in a safety trial, never an efficacy confirmation
cards.summary: Dose-escalation safety trial (Reinisch 2006): 45 patients randomised — primary objectives safety/tolerability; no difference in clinical activity (placebo response 60%), with greater falls in endoscopic severity index (p = 0.02) and CRP (p < 0.001) at 4.0 mg/kg: a biological-activity signal in a safety trial, never an efficacy confirmation
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-escalation safety/tolerability trial, fontolizumab in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 45 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 250–450), randomised double-blind in dose-escalating fashion to single doses of fontolizumab 0.1, 1.0 or 4.0 mg/kg or placebo; by day 29, patients with clinical response were re-randomised to three additional doses of half their initial fontolizumab dose or placebo at four-weekly intervals.
cards.result: Treatment was generally well tolerated, with slightly more reports of chills, flu-like syndrome, asthenia, nausea and vomiting in the 1.0 and 4.0 mg/kg cohorts; two serious adverse events rated as worsening of Crohn's disease occurred under fontolizumab, and antibodies to fontolizumab were confirmed in one patient. No differences in clinical activity parameters were noted between any active treatment group and placebo, with the placebo group having a particularly favourable outcome (60% response and 40% remission). By day 29, a more enhanced decrease in median Crohn's disease endoscopic index of severity (p = 0.02) and serum C-reactive protein (p < 0.001) was observed in the 4.0 mg/kg cohort (n = 14) compared with placebo (n = 10).
cards.watchOut: A safety trial by design: its endoscopic and CRP falls are pharmacodynamic signals in 14 vs 10 patients, never an efficacy confirmation — and its placebo group outperformed every active group clinically.

by day 29, patients with clinical response were re-randomised to three additional doses of half their initial fontolizumab dose or placebo at four-weekly intervals. treatment was generally well tolerated, with slightly more reports of chills, flu-like syndrome, asthenia, nausea and vomiting in the 1.0 and 4.0 mg/kg cohorts; two serious adverse events rated as worsening of crohn's disease occurred under fontolizumab, and antibodies to fontolizumab were confirmed in one patient. no differences in clinical activity parameters were noted between any active treatment group and placebo, with the placebo group having a particularly favourable outcome (60% response and 40% remission). by day 29, a more enhanced decrease in median crohn's disease endoscopic index of severity (p = 0.02) and serum c-reactive protein (p < 0.001) was observed in the 4.0 mg/kg cohort (n = 14) compared with placebo (n = 10). a safety trial by design: its endoscopic and crp falls are pharmacodynamic signals in 14 vs 10 patients, never an efficacy confirmation — and its placebo group outperformed every active group clinically. reinisch w et al. a dose escalating, placebo controlled, double blind, single dose and multidose, safety and tolerability study of fontolizumab, a humanised anti-interferon gamma antibody, in patients with moderate to severe crohn's disease. gut. 2006. pmid: 16492717. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · antibodies/blood · antibodies, monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized · c-reactive protein/metabolism · crohn disease/drug therapy/immunology · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · drug administration schedule · female · gastrointestinal agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · hla-dr antigens/metabolism · humans · interferon-gamma/antagonists & inhibitors · male · middle aged · severity of illness index · treatment outcome

shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis — or, as a labelled second limb, moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease — does ontamalimab versus placebo induce and maintain clinical remission?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — by disease, and the limbs are never pooled. Ulcerative colitis limb: positive across phase 2 (TURANDOT week-12 remission 11.3% / 16.7% / 15.5% / 5.7% across dose groups vs 2.7% on placebo, significant in three of four dose groups, with no benefit at the highest dose and one-sided multiplicity-adjusted p-values, printed as reported) and phase 3 (two induction studies and a re-randomised maintenance study; 75 mg week-12 remission 29.8% vs 15.8% and 29.5% vs 12.5%; week-52 maintenance remission 53.5% at 25 mg and 40.2% at 75 mg vs 8.2% and 12.8% on placebo). Crohn's limb: the phase 2 primary (CDAI-70 response at week 8 or 12) was missed, and the Crohn's phase 3 results exist only in the phase 3 publication's supplementary data. The programme was discontinued in 2020 for reasons unrelated to drug safety or efficacy, as its publication states — a commercial discontinuation, stated plainly. Ontamalimab (PF-00547659) is an investigational antibody that was never marketed.

cards.headline: TURANDOT, UC phase 2 (Vermeire 2017): 357 patients randomised — week-12 remission 11.3% / 16.7% / 15.5% / 5.7% across the dose groups vs 2.7% on placebo, significantly greater in three of four dose groups, with no benefit at the highest dose; all p-values are one-sided and multiplicity-adjusted, printed as reported
cards.summary: TURANDOT, UC phase 2 (Vermeire 2017): 357 patients randomised — week-12 remission 11.3% / 16.7% / 15.5% / 5.7% across the dose groups vs 2.7% on placebo, significantly greater in three of four dose groups, with no benefit at the highest dose; all p-values are one-sided and multiplicity-adjusted, printed as reported
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (TURANDOT), ontamalimab (PF-00547659) in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 357 patients aged 18–65 years with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (total Mayo score ≥6, Mayo endoscopic subscore ≥2, disease extending more than 15 cm beyond the anal verge) who had failed or were intolerant to at least one conventional therapy, randomised to subcutaneous ontamalimab (PF-00547659) 7.5 mg (n = 71), 22.5 mg (n = 72), 75 mg (n = 71) or 225 mg (n = 70) or placebo (n = 73) every 4 weeks, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial stratified by previous anti-TNFα treatment.
cards.result: Remission rates at week 12 were 11.3% (8/71) at 7.5 mg, 16.7% (12/72) at 22.5 mg, 15.5% (11/71) at 75 mg and 5.7% (4/70) at 225 mg versus 2.7% (2/73) on placebo — significantly greater in three of four dose groups, with no benefit at the highest dose. The stratum-adjusted risk differences versus placebo were 8.0% for 7.5 mg (90% CI 1.9 to 14, p = 0.0425), 12.8% for 22.5 mg (5.6 to 19.9, p = 0.0099), 11.8% for 75 mg (4.8 to 18.8, p = 0.0119) and 2.6% for 225 mg (−1.2 to 6.4, p = 0.1803). All p values were one-sided and multiplicity-adjusted, as reported. No safety signal was observed for the study drug.
cards.watchOut: ONE-SIDED P-VALUE FLAG: TURANDOT's p-values are one-sided by design and multiplicity-adjusted — printed as reported, never read as two-sided. The dose pattern is non-monotonic: the highest dose (225 mg) showed no benefit. Ontamalimab is an investigational antibody that was never marketed.
cards.source: Vermeire S et al. Anti-MAdCAM antibody (PF-00547659) for ulcerative colitis (TURANDOT): a phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28527704. Registry ID: NCT01620255. cards.headline: OPERA, Crohn's phase 2 (Sandborn 2018): 265 patients randomised — the primary endpoint, CDAI-70 response at week 8 or 12, did not differ significantly from placebo, while soluble MAdCAM fell dose-dependently: pharmacological activity without a clinical primary
cards.summary: OPERA, Crohn's phase 2 (Sandborn 2018): 265 patients randomised — the primary endpoint, CDAI-70 response at week 8 or 12, did not differ significantly from placebo, while soluble MAdCAM fell dose-dependently: pharmacological activity without a clinical primary
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (OPERA), ontamalimab (PF-00547659) in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 265 adults aged 18–75 years with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 220–450), a history of failure or intolerance to anti-tumour necrosis factor and/or immunosuppressive agents, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein >3.0 mg/L and ulcers on colonoscopy, randomised to ontamalimab (PF-00547659) 22.5 mg, 75 mg or 225 mg or placebo, in a phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: CDAI-70 response — the primary endpoint — was not significantly different with placebo versus ontamalimab treatment at weeks 8 or 12. Soluble MAdCAM decreased significantly from baseline to week 2 in a dose-related manner and remained low during the study in ontamalimab-treated patients, and circulating β7+ CD4+ central memory T-lymphocytes increased at weeks 8 and 12 — pharmacological activity without a clinical primary. No safety signal was seen.
cards.watchOut: The Crohn's limb missed its phase 2 primary — it is never pooled with the positive ulcerative colitis limb. The remission-rate observation in patients with higher baseline C-reactive protein is a subgroup reading of a primary-null trial, not a headline.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. Phase II evaluation of anti-MAdCAM antibody PF-00547659 in the treatment of Crohn's disease: report of the OPERA study. Gut. 2018. PMID: 28982740.
