cards.headline: Phase 3 programme report (Vermeire 2024): six phase 3 trials in ONE publication — UC induction studies randomised 659 patients and the UC maintenance study 366; week-12 remission on 75 mg was 29.8% vs 15.8% (p = 0.018) and 29.5% vs 12.5% (p = 0.014), and week-52 maintenance remission was 53.5% (25 mg) and 40.2% (75 mg) vs 8.2% and 12.8% on placebo (p < 0.001); the Crohn's phase 3 results appear only in the supplementary data; the programme was discontinued in 2020 for reasons unrelated to drug safety or efficacy
cards.summary: Phase 3 programme report (Vermeire 2024): six phase 3 trials in ONE publication — UC induction studies randomised 659 patients and the UC maintenance study 366; week-12 remission on 75 mg was 29.8% vs 15.8% (p = 0.018) and 29.5% vs 12.5% (p = 0.014), and week-52 maintenance remission was 53.5% (25 mg) and 40.2% (75 mg) vs 8.2% and 12.8% on placebo (p < 0.001); the Crohn's phase 3 results appear only in the supplementary data; the programme was discontinued in 2020 for reasons unrelated to drug safety or efficacy
cards.type: Phase 3 programme report (six trials in one publication: two induction + one maintenance study per disease), ontamalimab in ulcerative colitis (main text) and Crohn's disease (supplementary data only)
cards.people: Six phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — two induction studies and one re-randomised maintenance study per disease — comparing ontamalimab 25 mg and 75 mg once every 4 weeks with placebo in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. The ulcerative colitis induction studies included 659 randomised patients and the ulcerative colitis maintenance study 366.
cards.result: In the ulcerative colitis induction studies, more patients on ontamalimab than placebo achieved clinical remission at week 12 (25 mg: 18.5% vs 15.8%, p = 0.617, and 27.0% vs 12.5%, p = 0.027; 75 mg: 29.8% vs 15.8%, p = 0.018, and 29.5% vs 12.5%, p = 0.014). In the maintenance study, significantly more patients on ontamalimab achieved week-52 clinical remission (25 mg: 53.5% vs 8.2%, p < 0.001; 75 mg: 40.2% vs 12.8%, p < 0.001). Endoscopic improvement was generally significantly different versus placebo. Adverse event rates were similar between ontamalimab and placebo groups. The Crohn's disease studies are described only in the publication's supplementary data. The programme was discontinued in 2020 for reasons unrelated to drug safety/efficacy, as the publication states.
cards.watchOut: One publication covering six trials — never counted as six reports. The Crohn's phase 3 data exist only as supplementary material and are labelled as such; the 25 mg dose was null in one of the two UC induction studies (p = 0.617), printed on this card. Discontinuation was commercial, not for safety or efficacy — this shelf is neither a failed drug nor an available therapy.

shelves.title: Interleukin-17 blockade in Crohn's disease (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, total N = 189; both harmful/null): secukinumab's analysis favoured placebo and brodalumab was stopped early for worsening disease
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, does blocking interleukin-17 signalling — secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) or brodalumab (anti-IL-17 receptor) — versus placebo improve disease activity, or does it worsen Crohn's disease?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 trials, 2 molecules, 1 pathway, 189 randomised patients, and the harm direction is the content. The secukinumab proof-of-concept trial's Bayesian primary analysis estimated a <0.1% probability that secukinumab reduces CDAI by ≥50 points more than placebo, and its secondary area-under-curve analysis differed in favour of placebo (mean ΔCDAI 49 [95% CI 2 to 96], p = 0.043), with 20 infections including four local fungal infections on secukinumab vs none on placebo. The brodalumab phase 2 trial was terminated early because of an imbalance in worsening Crohn's disease in the active groups, with no meaningful efficacy. This is a 'do not extrapolate the psoriasis result to Crohn's' shelf: its balance leads with worsening, not with the single 15% mid-dose remission cell (no dose-response; the 700 mg arm read 9% and the 210 mg arm 3%).

cards.headline: Secukinumab proof-of-concept trial (Hueber 2012): 59 patients randomised — the Bayesian primary analysis estimated a <0.1% probability that secukinumab reduces CDAI by ≥50 points more than placebo, and the secondary area-under-curve analysis differed in favour of placebo (mean ΔCDAI 49 [95% CI 2 to 96], p = 0.043); 20 infections including four local fungal infections on secukinumab vs none on placebo
cards.summary: Secukinumab proof-of-concept trial (Hueber 2012): 59 patients randomised — the Bayesian primary analysis estimated a <0.1% probability that secukinumab reduces CDAI by ≥50 points more than placebo, and the secondary area-under-curve analysis differed in favour of placebo (mean ΔCDAI 49 [95% CI 2 to 96], p = 0.043); 20 infections including four local fungal infections on secukinumab vs none on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled proof-of-concept trial, secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 59 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI ≥220 to ≤450), assigned 2:1 to intravenous secukinumab 2 × 10 mg/kg (n = 39) or placebo (n = 20) in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled proof-of-concept study; mean baseline CDAI was 307 and 301 respectively, and 18 of 59 patients (31%) discontinued prematurely.
cards.result: The primary endpoint analysis — Bayesian statistics augmented with historical placebo information — estimated a <0.1% probability that secukinumab reduces the CDAI by ≥50 points more than placebo at week 6. The secondary area-under-the-curve analysis (weeks 4–10) showed a significant difference (mean ΔCDAI = 49; 95% CI 2 to 96; p = 0.043) in favour of placebo. Fourteen serious adverse events occurred in 10 patients (seven secukinumab, three placebo); 20 infections, including four local fungal infections, were seen on secukinumab versus none on placebo. A post hoc subgroup analysis suggested unfavourable responses on secukinumab were driven by patients with elevated inflammatory markers (CRP ≥10 mg/L and/or faecal calprotectin ≥200 ng/mL) — a subgroup observation, labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — this is one of exactly two trials on this shelf (total N = 189). The harm reading rests on a Bayesian primary that excluded benefit and a secondary analysis favouring placebo; the inflammatory-marker subgroup is post hoc and never a headline.

cards.headline: Brodalumab phase 2 trial (Targan 2016): 130 patients randomised — the study was terminated early because of an imbalance in worsening Crohn's disease in the active groups; week-6 remission 3% / 15% / 9% vs 3% on placebo, with no dose pattern and no meaningful efficacy
cards.summary: Brodalumab phase 2 trial (Targan 2016): 130 patients randomised — the study was terminated early because of an imbalance in worsening Crohn's disease in the active groups; week-6 remission 3% / 15% / 9% vs 3% on placebo, with no dose pattern and no meaningful efficacy
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (terminated early), brodalumab (anti-IL-17 receptor) in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease
cards.people: 130 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease and evidence of active inflammation, randomised 1:1:1:1 to brodalumab 210, 350 or 700 mg (at baseline and week 4) or placebo in a phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, at the time the study was terminated early.
cards.result: At week 6, remission rates (CDAI ≤150, the primary endpoint) were 3% (210 mg), 15% (350 mg), 9% (700 mg) and 3% (placebo), and CDAI response occurred in 16%, 27%, 15% and 13% respectively. Mean change in CDAI at week 6 was −8.7 (210 mg), −35.4 (350 mg), −0.6 (700 mg) and −28.2 (placebo). Besides worsening of Crohn's disease — the imbalance that terminated the study — overall incidences of adverse events were similar across treatment groups. The authors concluded that brodalumab resulted in a disproportionate number of cases of worsening Crohn's disease and no evidence of meaningful efficacy.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — the second of exactly two trials on this shelf (total N = 189). The single 15% mid-dose remission cell has no dose pattern around it (210 mg 3%, 700 mg 9%, placebo 3%) and is never the headline; the headline is early termination for worsening disease on treatment.

The American journal of gastroenterology. 2016. PMID: 27481309. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cross-report reading of the same two trials (not a third trial): one trial's analysis favoured placebo outright and the other was stopped for worsening disease on treatment — the complete randomised base for IL-17 blockade in Crohn's disease is exactly these 2 trials, N = 189
cards.summary: Cross-report reading of the same two trials (not a third trial): one trial's analysis favoured placebo outright and the other was stopped for worsening disease on treatment — the complete randomised base for IL-17 blockade in Crohn's disease is exactly these 2 trials, N = 189
cards.type: Cross-report summary of the two carded trials — not an additional trial
cards.people: The complete randomised base: secukinumab proof-of-concept trial (2012, n = 59) and brodalumab phase 2 trial (2016, n = 130) — the same two trials carded above, read together. No other randomised report is counted on this shelf.
cards.result: Read together: blocking IL-17A (secukinumab) gave a <0.1% Bayesian probability of the target CDAI advantage and a secondary analysis significantly favouring placebo, with an infection excess; blocking the IL-17 receptor (brodalumab) was stopped early for an imbalance in worsening Crohn's disease, with week-6 remission of 3% / 15% / 9% vs 3% on placebo and no dose pattern. Two molecules, one pathway, the same direction: ineffective, with worsening on treatment.
cards.watchOut: This card adds no new source — it is a cross-report summary of the two trials above, labelled as such so the count is never inflated. Both trials enrolled patients with objective inflammatory activity. The IL-17 inhibitors' psoriasis and arthritis shelves ask different-disease questions; their benefit there is exactly what makes this Crohn's harm shelf clinically worth having.

shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis despite conventional therapy, does subcutaneous abrilumab versus placebo induce clinical remission at week 8?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 trials totalling 399 patients, one programme, both phase 2, both 8-week induction reads; no maintenance trial was ever reported and the programme did not proceed. In the global phase 2b trial, week-8 remission was 13.3% on 70 mg and 12.7% on 210 mg vs 4.3% on placebo (p < .05 for both), with odds ratios 3.35 and 3.33 carrying 90% (not 95%) confidence intervals, printed as reported. In the Japanese phase 2 trial, week-8 remission was 12.9% across the abrilumab groups vs 0 of 13 on placebo, in per-dose cells of 1–2 patients. No progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and no deaths in either trial. Abrilumab (development name AMG 181) is an investigational antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly. The base is ulcerative-colitis-only: no abrilumab Crohn's trial report exists.

cards.headline: Global phase 2b trial (Sandborn 2019): 354 patients dosed — week-8 remission 13.3% on 70 mg and 12.7% on 210 mg vs 4.3% on placebo (P < .05 for both); odds ratios 3.35 (90% CI 1.41–7.95) and 3.33 (90% CI 1.34–8.26), with 90% confidence intervals printed as reported
cards.summary: Global phase 2b trial (Sandborn 2019): 354 patients dosed — week-8 remission 13.3% on 70 mg and 12.7% on 210 mg vs 4.3% on placebo (P < .05 for both); odds ratios 3.35 (90% CI 1.41–7.95) and 3.33 (90% CI 1.34–8.26), with 90% confidence intervals printed as reported
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b double-blind placebo-controlled trial, abrilumab (anti-α4β7 integrin antibody, AMG 181) in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 354 patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (total Mayo Score 6–12, recto-sigmoidoscopy score ≥2) despite conventional therapies, who received ≥1 dose of investigational product: placebo (n = 116) or subcutaneous abrilumab 7 mg (n = 21), 21 mg (n = 40), 70 mg (n = 98) or 210 mg (n = 79), in a randomised phase 2b double-blind placebo-controlled study; the primary endpoint was remission for the two highest dosages at week 8.
cards.result: Non-adjusted remission rates at week 8 were 4.3% on placebo, 13.3% on abrilumab 70 mg and 12.7% on abrilumab 210 mg (P < .05 for 70 and 210 mg vs placebo). The odds of achieving remission were significantly greater with abrilumab 70 mg (odds ratio 3.35; 90% CI 1.41–7.95; P = .021) and 210 mg (odds ratio 3.33; 90% CI 1.34–8.26; P = .030) than with placebo — odds ratios are relative measures, printed beside their absolute remission rates above, and their confidence intervals are 90%, as reported. Response and mucosal healing rates with these dosages were also significantly greater than with placebo. There were no cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or deaths.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — one of exactly 2 trials on this shelf (total N = 399). PRECISION FLAG: the headline odds ratios carry 90% (not 95%) confidence intervals, printed as reported and never silently widened or narrowed. An 8-week induction read only; abrilumab was never marketed.

cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial, abrilumab in Japanese patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 45 Japanese patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis despite conventional treatments, randomised to subcutaneous abrilumab 21 mg (n = 11), 70 mg (n = 12) or 210 mg (n = 9) or placebo (n = 13) for 12 weeks, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase II study, followed by a 36-week open-label period and a 28-week safety follow-up.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 8 (the primary efficacy variable) was 4 out of 31 (12.9%) overall in the abrilumab groups versus 0 out of 13 in the placebo group: abrilumab 21 mg 1/10 (10.0%), 70 mg 2/12 (16.7%) and 210 mg 1/9 (11.1%), as reported. In both the double-blind and open-label periods, fewer patients in the abrilumab groups experienced ≥1 adverse event compared with the placebo group. There were no cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and no deaths. The authors read the 70 mg and 210 mg results as numerically better than placebo, with the 210 mg dose showing more consistent treatment effects.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — the second of exactly 2 trials on this shelf (total N = 399). The remission cells are 1–2 patients per dose; a single patient moving cells would change every percentage on this card. This record carries no MeSH terms, and its source line says so.

randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase ii trial, abrilumab in japanese patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis 45 japanese patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis despite conventional treatments, randomised to subcutaneous abrilumab 21 mg (n = 11), 70 mg (n = 12) or 210 mg (n = 9) or placebo (n = 13) for 12 weeks, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase ii study, followed by a 36-week open-label period and a 28-week safety follow-up. clinical remission at week 8 (the primary efficacy variable) was 4 out of 31 (12.9%) overall in the abrilumab groups versus 0 out of 13 in the placebo group: abrilumab 21 mg 1/10 (10.0%), 70 mg 2/12 (16.7%) and 210 mg 1/9 (11.1%), as reported. in both the double-blind and open-label periods, fewer patients in the abrilumab groups experienced ≥1 adverse event compared with the placebo group. there were no cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and no deaths. the authors read the 70 mg and 210 mg results as numerically better than placebo, with the 210 mg dose showing more consistent treatment effects. floor-risk base — the second of exactly 2 trials on this shelf (total n = 399). the remission cells are 1–2 patients per dose; a single patient moving cells would change every percentage on this card. this record carries no mesh terms, and its source line says so. hibi t et al. efficacy and safety of abrilumab, an α4β7 integrin inhibitor, in japanese patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis: a phase ii study. intestinal research. 2019. pmid: 30739435. registry id: none in the record. mesh: none in the record.

cards.people: The complete randomised base: the global phase 2b trial (354 patients dosed) and the Japanese phase 2 trial (45 patients randomised) — the same two trials carded above, read together, totalling 399 patients. No other randomised report is counted on this shelf.
cards.result: Read together: week-8 remission favoured abrilumab 70 mg and 210 mg in the global trial (13.3% and 12.7% vs 4.3%; odds ratios 3.35 and 3.33 with 90% confidence intervals) and was numerically higher on abrilumab in the Japanese trial (12.9% overall vs 0/13 on placebo, in 1–2-patient cells). The programme did not proceed: no maintenance trial was ever reported, and no Crohn's disease trial report exists — the base is ulcerative-colitis-only.

shelves.title: Visilizumab (anti-CD3 antibody, never marketed) in severe corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, only one placebo-controlled): the controlled trial was null on every endpoint, with colectomy 18% vs 7%
shelves.question: In patients with severely active ulcerative colitis despite at least 5 days of intravenous corticosteroids, does visilizumab (two daily intravenous doses) versus placebo — or across dose levels — induce response or remission without unacceptable harm?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit — with a harm shadow). FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 randomised reports, total treated N ≈ 231 across the two studies, and only one of them has a placebo arm. The placebo-controlled trial is null on every efficacy endpoint — day-45 response 55% vs 47% (p = 0.475), remission 8% vs 9%, mucosal healing 29% vs 26% — with numerically more colectomies on visilizumab (18% vs 7%, p = 0.130) and more cardiac and vascular disorders. The dose-escalation report's uncontrolled symptomatic response rates (50–71%) are never printed without that controlled null beside them. The honest summary: visilizumab did not work in the population that most needed rescue therapy, and carried a safety shadow. Era: 2010-era severe-UC rescue landscape, before modern rescue sequencing. Visilizumab is an investigational antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly.

cards.headline: Placebo-controlled trial (Sandborn 2010): 127 patients randomised — null on every efficacy endpoint (day-45 response 55% vs 47%, p = 0.475; remission 8% vs 9%; mucosal healing 29% vs 26%), with colectomy 18% on visilizumab vs 7% on placebo (p = 0.130) and cardiac and vascular disorders more frequent on visilizumab: harm leads
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled trial (Sandborn 2010): 127 patients randomised — null on every efficacy endpoint (day-45 response 55% vs 47%, p = 0.475; remission 8% vs 9%; mucosal healing 29% vs 26%), with colectomy 18% on visilizumab vs 7% on placebo (p = 0.130) and cardiac and vascular disorders more frequent on visilizumab: harm leads
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, visilizumab (anti-CD3 antibody) in severe intravenous corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 127 patients with severely active ulcerative colitis despite treatment with ≥5 days of intravenous corticosteroids, randomised double-blind to visilizumab 5 µg/kg or placebo intravenously on days 1 and 2, with corticosteroids tapered according to disease activity and follow-up for 90 days.
cards.result: Response at day 45 (the primary endpoint) occurred in 55% of patients receiving visilizumab compared with 47% on placebo (p = 0.475). Remission at day 45 occurred in 8% versus 9% (p = 0.704) and mucosal healing in 29% versus 26% (p = 0.799); symptomatic response at day 15 occurred in 82% versus 74% (p = 0.244). Colectomy was performed in 18% of patients receiving visilizumab compared with 7% on placebo (p = 0.130). Cardiac disorders and vascular disorders occurred more frequently in the patients who received visilizumab. The authors concluded that visilizumab at 5 µg/kg for two consecutive days was not effective for severe, corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis and was associated with increased cardiac and vascular adverse events.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — one of exactly 2 randomised reports on this shelf, and the only one with a placebo arm. The colectomy and cardiac/vascular excesses are numerical, not significant (p = 0.130 for colectomy) — printed with their p-values, as a safety shadow beside a complete efficacy null, never as proven harm. Visilizumab was never marketed.

cards.headline: Phase I/II dose-escalation trial (Baumgart 2010): 104 patients treated as reported, NO placebo arm — symptomatic response at day 15 was 71% / 70% / 50% / 61% across the ascending doses in stage I and 54% in stage II, an inverse-looking dose pattern in an uncontrolled comparison; serious adverse events included atrial fibrillation, cytomegalovirus infection and oesophageal candidiasis
cards.summary: Phase I/II dose-escalation trial (Baumgart 2010): 104 patients treated as reported, NO placebo arm — symptomatic response at day 15 was 71% / 70% / 50% / 61% across the ascending doses in stage I and 54% in stage II, an inverse-looking dose pattern in an uncontrolled comparison; serious adverse events included atrial fibrillation, cytomegalovirus infection and oesophageal candidiasis
cards.type: Prospective randomised open-label multicentre phase I/II dose-escalation trial (no placebo arm), visilizumab (HuM291) in severe steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis
cards.people: 104 patients treated as reported, with severe intravenous steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis: in stage I, 73 patients were randomly assigned across four visilizumab dose levels (5, 7.5, 10 or 12.5 µg/kg/day for 2 consecutive days); in stage II, 33 patients received visilizumab at the selected 5 µg/kg/day dose for 2 days. Open-label, multicentre, with no placebo arm in either stage.
cards.result: Symptomatic response rates at day 15 in the 5, 7.5, 10 and 12.5 µg/kg dose groups were 71%, 70%, 50% and 61% respectively in stage I, and 54% in stage II; symptomatic remission rates were 35%, 5%, 22% and 11% in stage I and 18% in stage II. Clinical response rates at day 30 were 71%, 65%, 50% and 67% in stage I and 55% in stage II, with clinical remission rates of 6%, 5%, 0% and 11% and 6%. All patients experienced adverse events; serious adverse events included abdominal abscess, cytomegalovirus infection, atrial fibrillation, herpes zoster and oesophageal candidiasis. Results with 5 µg/kg/day were similar to those with higher doses.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — the second of exactly 2 randomised reports, and it has no placebo arm: its 50–71% response rates are uncontrolled and must never be printed without the controlled trial's null (card above) beside them. The dose pattern is inverse-looking (the lowest dose read highest), which is what uncontrolled dose comparisons in a fluctuating disease look like.

cards.result: Read together: without a control arm, visilizumab looked active (symptomatic response 50–71% across doses); with one, it did nothing (response 55% vs 47%, remission 8% vs 9%, mucosal healing 29% vs 26%) and carried numerically more colectomies and more cardiac and vascular events. That contrast — not the uncontrolled rates — is the shelf's answer for severe corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis.

shelves.title: Nitazoxanide for rotavirus diarrhoea in children: 3 small single-centre randomised trials (total N = 175) all found diarrhoea roughly 24–44 hours shorter on a 3-day course, with a mixed-virus adult trial as labelled support
shelves.question: In children hospitalised with rotavirus diarrhoea, does a 3-day course of oral nitazoxanide versus placebo (or versus probiotics / rehydration alone) shorten the duration of diarrhoea and hospitalisation?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Infective Agents/therapeutic use · Cell Survival/drug effects · Cells, Cultured · Child · Child, Preschool · Diarrhea/drug therapy/virology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastroenteritis/drug therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Infant · Male · Nitro Compounds · Rotavirus Infections/drug therapy · Thiazoles/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small single-centre paediatric trials, all pointing the same way on the same endpoint: diarrhoea duration roughly 24–44 hours shorter on a 3-day course of nitazoxanide (median time to resolution 31 h vs 75 h in the 2006 Lancet trial's analysis set of 38 of 50 enrolled children; median diarrhoea duration 54 h vs 79 h and hospitalisation 81 h vs 108 h in the Bolivian trial; 54 h vs 80 h and 68 h vs 90 h in the Indian trial), with no significant adverse events reported. The limits are size and setting: each trial is single-centre (Cairo, Bolivia, India) and under 80 patients, no trial followed children beyond the hospital stay, and the rotavirus epidemiology in these trials predates today's vaccine coverage in most settings. A mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial is carded as labelled support only, never counted as a paediatric rotavirus primary.

cards.headline: Severe-rotavirus trial (Rossignol 2006): 50 children enrolled, 38 analysed with rotavirus as the sole pathogen — median time to resolution of illness 31 h on nitazoxanide vs 75 h on placebo (p = 0.0137)
cards.summary: Severe-rotavirus trial (Rossignol 2006): 50 children enrolled, 38 analysed with rotavirus as the sole pathogen — median time to resolution of illness 31 h on nitazoxanide vs 75 h on placebo (p = 0.0137)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, nitazoxanide in hospitalised children with severe rotavirus diarrhoea
cards.people: Children admitted to Cairo University Children's Hospital with severe rotavirus diarrhoea: 50 children were enrolled in the randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, and 38 children aged 5 months to 7 years (median age 11 months) with rotavirus as the sole identified cause of gastroenteritis formed the analysis set, randomly assigned to nitazoxanide oral suspension 7.5 mg/kg or placebo twice a day for 3 days, remaining in hospital for 7 days after the start of treatment.
cards.result: Survival analysis showed the median time to resolution of illness was 31 h (IQR 22–73) for the nitazoxanide-treated group compared with 75 h (51–124) for the placebo group (p = 0.0137), by modified intention-to-treat analysis of the primary endpoint. No significant adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The analysis set is 38 of 50 enrolled children (rotavirus as the sole pathogen) — printed on the face, never rounded up to the enrolled number. Single-centre (Cairo), 2005 enrolment, pre-dating today's rotavirus vaccine coverage in most settings.

cards.headline: Bolivian trial (Teran 2009): 75 children randomised, single-blind — median diarrhoea duration 54 h on nitazoxanide vs 79 h on control (p = 0.009) and median hospitalisation 81 h vs 108 h (p = 0.017); probiotics performed similarly
cards.summary: Bolivian trial (Teran 2009): 75 children randomised, single-blind — median diarrhoea duration 54 h on nitazoxanide vs 79 h on control (p = 0.009) and median hospitalisation 81 h vs 108 h (p = 0.017); probiotics performed similarly
cards.type: Randomised single-blind controlled trial, nitazoxanide vs probiotics vs rehydration alone in Bolivian children with acute rotavirus diarrhoea
cards.people: 75 children aged 28 days to 24 months with rotavirus diarrhoea, randomly assigned in a randomised single-blind controlled trial to oral nitazoxanide 15 mg/kg/day twice a day for 3 days, a combination of oral probiotics 1 g twice a day for 5 days, or oral or systemic rehydration solutions alone; duration of diarrhoea and of hospitalisation were the primary outcome measures.
cards.result: The median duration of diarrhoea was significantly reduced (p = 0.009) in children who received nitazoxanide (54 h) and probiotics (48 h) compared with the control group (79 h). The median duration of hospitalisation was significantly shorter (p = 0.017) in patients who received nitazoxanide (81 h) and probiotics (72 h) compared with rehydration alone (108 h). Small differences in favour of nitazoxanide were found in comparison with probiotics, as the authors report.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (not double-blind), single-centre, and the control is rehydration alone rather than placebo; the probiotic arm performed about as well as nitazoxanide, so this trial supports 'better than rehydration alone' rather than any nitazoxanide-specific advantage.
cards.source: Teran CG et al. Nitazoxanide vs. probiotics for the treatment of acute rotavirus diarrhea in children: a randomized, single-blind, controlled trial in Bolivian children. cards.headline: Indian trial (Mahapatro 2017): 50 rotavirus-positive children randomised from 174 screened — median diarrhoea duration 54 h vs 80 h and hospitalisation 68 h vs 90 h on nitazoxanide vs placebo
cards.summary: Indian trial (Mahapatro 2017): 50 rotavirus-positive children randomised from 174 screened — median diarrhoea duration 54 h vs 80 h and hospitalisation 68 h vs 90 h on nitazoxanide vs placebo
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial, nitazoxanide in Indian children with acute rotavirus diarrhoea
cards.people: 50 rotavirus-positive children randomised from 174 children aged 12 months to 5 years screened with acute diarrhoea, in a double-blind randomised trial; the intervention group received syrup nitazoxanide twice daily (100 mg at 12–47 months, 200 mg at ≥4 years) for 3 days along with standard treatment of diarrhoea, and duration of diarrhoea was the primary outcome measure.
cards.result: The median duration of diarrhoea (54 versus 80 hours) and of hospitalisation (68 versus 90 hours) was significantly shorter in the nitazoxanide group, as reported with 95% confidence intervals for the differences. No significant difference was seen in the median duration of fever or vomiting or in the proportion of children requiring parenteral rehydration. There was no report of any adverse events.
cards.watchOut: 50 randomised children from 174 screened, single-centre; this record carries no MeSH terms, and its source line says so. The registry reference is printed as the record gives it (CTRI REF/2016/10/012507).

cards.headline: LABELLED SUPPORT — mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial (Rossignol 2006): 50 out-patients aged ≥12 years enrolled, 45 analysed — median time to symptom resolution 1.5 days vs 2.5 days (P < 0.0001), with rotavirus and norovirus subsets both significant; never counted as a paediatric rotavirus primary
cards.summary: LABELLED SUPPORT — mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial (Rossignol 2006): 50 out-patients aged ≥12 years enrolled, 45 analysed — median time to symptom resolution 1.5 days vs 2.5 days (P < 0.0001), with rotavirus and norovirus subsets both significant; never counted as a paediatric rotavirus primary
cards.type: LABELLED SUPPORT (mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial) — nitazoxanide in viral gastroenteritis; never counted as a paediatric rotavirus primary
cards.people: 50 out-patients at least 12 years of age (mean 33.5 years) presenting with diarrhoea and stool-positive for norovirus, rotavirus or adenovirus, enrolled in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial and randomly assigned to nitazoxanide 500 mg or placebo twice daily for 3 days; the modified intent-to-treat analysis covered 45 patients, excluding five with other identified enteropathogens at baseline.
cards.result: The median time from first dose to resolution of symptoms was 1.5 days (IQR 0.5–2.5) for nitazoxanide-treated patients and 2.5 days (IQR 1.5–4.5) for the placebo group. Significant reductions were observed for all patients analysed (P < 0.0001) and for the subsets of patients with rotavirus (P = 0.0052) and norovirus (P = 0.0295); the number of patients with adenovirus (n = 5) was too small to draw any conclusion. No significant adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Labelled support only: a mixed-virus (norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus) trial in adults and adolescents, not a paediatric rotavirus trial — its rotavirus subset is a subset, never a fourth paediatric primary.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 randomised paediatric reports, total N = 175 randomised — all three point the same way (diarrhoea roughly 24–44 hours shorter on a 3-day course), in small single-centre trials from the pre-vaccine-coverage era, with no follow-up beyond the hospital stay

cards.people: All paediatric reports carded on this shelf: the severe-rotavirus trial (50 enrolled, 38 analysed), the Bolivian trial (75 randomised) and the Indian trial (50 randomised) — three randomised paediatric reports totalling 175 randomised children. The mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial (50 enrolled, 45 analysed) is labelled support only.
cards.result: Consistency, stated plainly: all three paediatric trials agree in direction on the same endpoint, with no significant adverse events reported — and all three are single-centre and under 80 patients. Neighbouring homes are the rotavirus vaccine shelf, racecadotril for acute watery diarrhoea, and the nitazoxanide giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis and chronic hepatitis C slices — different questions, sharing no anchor. Era flag: these trials predate today's rotavirus vaccine coverage in most settings, which bears on the question's current applicability, not on what the trials found.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Vebicorvir added to nucleos(t)ide therapy for chronic hepatitis B: deeper DNA suppression but null antigen primaries — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, N = 98 as reported
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B — virologically suppressed on nucleos(t)ide therapy, or treatment-naïve starting entecavir — does adding the core inhibitor vebicorvir 300 mg daily versus placebo deepen viral suppression (HBV DNA / pregenomic RNA) or reduce viral antigens (HBsAg / HBeAg) over 24 weeks? (FLOOR-RISK on the face: exactly 2 randomised trials, total N = 98 as reported; the open-label extension is never counted. Name-collision fence: vebicorvir is not bersacapavir.)
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/adverse effects · DNA, Viral · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B e Antigens · Hepatitis B virus/genetics · Hepatitis B, Chronic · Humans
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK — exact base on the face: exactly 2 randomised trials, total N = 98 as reported (73 enrolled in the suppressed-patient trial; 25 completing as reported in the treatment-naïve trial — 13 vebicorvir, 12 placebo). The programme's long-term open-label extension is NOT counted as a report: 92 patients entered it, 43 met stopping criteria and no patient achieved its off-treatment primary endpoint (HBV DNA <20 IU/mL at 24 weeks off treatment) — that outcome belongs on the face as the programme's outcome, never as a third report. Surrogate flag (load-bearing): every endpoint in this base is virologic (HBV DNA, pregenomic RNA, HBsAg/HBeAg change over 24 weeks); the antigen primaries were null in both trials and no functional-cure outcome was shown. Population flag: both trials excluded cirrhosis; the naïve trial is HBeAg-positive only and very small. Name-collision fence: vebicorvir (a core inhibitor, development code ABI-H0731) is NOT bersacapavir — bersacapavir is a different capsid assembly modulator whose reports sit inside a different shelf's home; the two are never merged or cross-carded here. Product naming under the clarification exception: vebicorvir is an investigational drug that was never marketed — stated plainly.

cards.headline: Report 1 of exactly 2 — suppressed-patient trial (2022, N = 73 enrolled), labelled slice A, the antigen primary: no differences in change from baseline at week 24 for HBsAg or HBeAg in either the HBeAg-positive (47 patients) or HBeAg-negative (26 patients) stratum — the antigen primary was null

cards.type: Primary report — phase 2 randomised trial in nucleos(t)ide-suppressed patients, slice A of 2 labelled slices of this one report (FLOOR-RISK base: exactly 2 trials, N = 98 as reported)
cards.people: 73 non-cirrhotic, nucleos(t)ide-suppressed patients with chronic hepatitis B randomised to vebicorvir 300 mg once daily or matching placebo for 24 weeks, stratified by HBeAg status (47 positive, 26 negative); the primary endpoint was change from baseline in serum HBeAg or HBsAg at week 24.
cards.result: In HBeAg-positive and -negative patients there were no differences in the change from baseline at week 24 for HBsAg or HBeAg. Treatment-emergent adverse events on vebicorvir plus nucleos(t)ide included upper respiratory tract infection, nausea and pruritus; no serious adverse events, grade 4 events or deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: One report, presented in two labelled slices (cards 1 and 2) to meet format without inflating the count — this is still exactly one of only two randomised trials in the entire base. Its primary endpoint — viral antigens — was null.

cards.headline: Report 1 of exactly 2 — suppressed-patient trial (2022, N = 73 enrolled), labelled slice B, the virologic signal: on a high-sensitivity assay, a greater proportion of vebicorvir patients with detectable baseline HBV DNA achieved undetectable DNA at week 24, and pregenomic RNA fell more in HBeAg-positive patients — virologic-signal readings beside a null antigen primary, labelled as such
cards.summary: Report 1 of exactly 2 — suppressed-patient trial (2022, N = 73 enrolled), labelled slice B, the virologic signal: on a high-sensitivity assay, a greater proportion of vebicorvir patients with detectable baseline HBV DNA achieved undetectable DNA at week 24, and pregenomic RNA fell more in HBeAg-positive patients — virologic-signal readings beside a null antigen primary, labelled as such
cards.type: Primary report — phase 2 randomised trial in nucleos(t)ide-suppressed patients, slice B of 2 labelled slices of this one report (FLOOR-RISK base: exactly 2 trials, N = 98 as reported)
cards.people: The same 73-patient suppressed-patient trial as card 1 (one report, second labelled slice): virologic endpoints beyond the antigen primary, including HBV DNA on a novel high-sensitivity assay and HBV pregenomic RNA.
cards.result: Using the high-sensitivity assay, a greater proportion of patients with detectable HBV DNA at baseline achieved undetectable HBV DNA at week 24 in the vebicorvir plus nucleos(t)ide group versus placebo plus nucleos(t)ide. In HBeAg-positive patients, a greater change from baseline in HBV pregenomic RNA was observed at week 24 with vebicorvir. The authors concluded that, while there were no significant changes in viral antigen levels, enhanced viral suppression was demonstrated by greater changes in DNA and pregenomic RNA.

cards.headline: Report 2 of exactly 2 — treatment-naïve trial (2022, 25 patients completed as reported: 13 vebicorvir, 12 placebo): mean HBV DNA reduction at week 24 was −5.33 log10 IU/mL on vebicorvir + entecavir vs −4.20 on placebo + entecavir (p = 0.0084), with greater pregenomic-RNA reductions (p < 0.0001) and similar changes in viral antigens; all treatment-emergent adverse events were grade 1/2
cards.summary: Report 2 of exactly 2 — treatment-naïve trial (2022, 25 patients completed as reported: 13 vebicorvir, 12 placebo): mean HBV DNA reduction at week 24 was −5.33 log10 IU/mL on vebicorvir + entecavir vs −4.20 on placebo + entecavir (p = 0.0084), with greater pregenomic-RNA reductions (p < 0.0001) and similar changes in viral antigens; all treatment-emergent adverse events were grade 1/2
cards.type: Primary report — phase 2 randomised double-blind trial in treatment-naïve patients (FLOOR-RISK base: exactly 2 trials, N = 98 as reported)
cards.people: HBeAg-positive, non-cirrhotic, treatment-naïve patients with chronic hepatitis B randomised 1:1 double-blind to vebicorvir 300 mg + entecavir 0.5 mg or placebo + entecavir 0.5 mg once daily for 24 weeks; the primary endpoint was change in mean log10 HBV DNA from baseline to weeks 12 and 24. All patients in both groups (13/13 and 12/12) completed the study, as reported.
cards.result: At week 12 the mean HBV DNA reduction was −4.45 (SD 1.03) versus −3.30 (SD 1.18) log10 IU/mL (p = 0.0077); at week 24, −5.33 (SD 1.59) versus −4.20 (SD 0.98) (p = 0.0084). Greater mean reductions in pregenomic RNA were observed at weeks 12 and 24 (both p < 0.0001). Changes in viral antigens were similar in both groups. Two patients had HBV DNA rebound on treatment with no resistance breakthrough; no drug interaction with entecavir was observed, and there were no deaths, serious adverse events or drug-induced liver injury.
cards.watchOut: 25 completing patients is a very small base for a −1.13 log10 DNA difference, and the antigen changes — the outcome that would matter for cure strategies — were similar between groups. HBeAg-positive, non-cirrhotic patients only.

cards.people: All randomised reports carded on this shelf: the suppressed-patient trial (N = 73 enrolled, presented in two labelled slices) and the treatment-naïve trial (25 completing as reported). The open-label extension is described in prose only, as the programme's outcome, and is never counted.
cards.result: The honest summary of this base is: deeper nucleic-acid suppression, null antigen primaries in both trials, no functional-cure outcome, and an extension in which no patient met the off-treatment endpoint. Bersacapavir is a different molecule and appears nowhere in this base.

shelves.title: CDP571 for Crohn's disease — the founding anti-TNF programme (5 randomised reports, 1997–2006): short-term response signals, both steroid-sparing primaries missed at their prespecified timepoints
shelves.question: In patients with Crohn's disease — moderately active disease, or corticosteroid-dependent disease — does intravenous CDP571 versus placebo induce clinical response or remission, and can it spare corticosteroids without disease flare?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies/therapeutic use · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Crohn Disease/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Glycoproteins/blood · Humans · Middle Aged · Placebos · Remission Induction · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/immunology · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Infliximab · Male · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Crohn Disease/blood/drug therapy · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors/immunology · Antibodies, Anti-Idiotypic/blood · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Crohn Disease/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Steroids/administration & dosage · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Budesonide/administration & dosage · Crohn Disease/drug therapy/pathology · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: The arc is the answer: CDP571, the engineered humanised anti-TNF antibody that preceded certolizumab pegol, produced a real short-term response signal (week-2 response 45% vs 27%, p = 0.023, in 169 patients; median CDAI 263→167 after a single infusion in 31 patients) that did not hold — the only long-term active-disease primary (week 28, 396 patients) was null (30.4% vs 23.5%, p = 0.102) outside a post-hoc CRP subgroup, and both steroid-sparing trials missed their prespecified primaries (week 36: 29.3% vs 36.7%, p = 0.24, numerically favouring placebo; week 10: p = 0.452, with a secondary week-16 reading). One steroid-sparing report's abstract prints mutually inconsistent Ns (71 treated; arms 39+42; a percentage implying n = 32) — printed unresolved on its card rather than resolved by choice. Era flag: 1997–2006, every endpoint CDAI-based. CDP571 was never marketed.

cards.headline: Stack 1997 — the founding trial: a SINGLE infusion in 31 patients with a 2-week endpoint; median CDAI fell 263 to 167 on CDP571 (p = 0.0003) with no significant change on placebo
cards.summary: Stack 1997 — the founding trial: a SINGLE infusion in 31 patients with a 2-week endpoint; median CDAI fell 263 to 167 on CDP571 (p = 0.0003) with no significant change on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled single-infusion proof-of-concept trial (Stack 1997) — active-disease report 1 of 3
cards.people: 31 patients with moderately active Crohn's disease randomly assigned to a single infusion of CDP571 5 mg/kg (n = 21) or placebo (n = 10); the primary endpoint was change in Crohn's Disease Activity Index 2 weeks after the infusion. One treated patient with no follow-up was excluded from the analyses.
cards.result: Median CDAI fell from 263 to 167 at 2 weeks on CDP571 (p = 0.0003); the placebo change (253 to 247) was not significant. Six patients achieved remission (CDAI ≤150). Harvey-Bradshaw score, key symptom score, alpha-1 glycoprotein and ESR also improved significantly; CRP fell non-significantly (p = 0.067).
cards.watchOut: A single dose, a 2-week endpoint and 31 patients: this p-value must never be printed without its design beside it. It proved the TNF hypothesis in Crohn's disease; it did not establish a treatment.
cards.source: Stack WA et al. Randomised controlled trial of CDP571 antibody to tumour necrosis factor-alpha in Crohn's disease. Lancet. 1997. PMID: 9048788. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sandborn 2001 — 24-week dose/interval trial: clinical response at week 2 in 45% on CDP571 vs 27% on placebo (p = 0.023); retreatment benefit suggested but secondary endpoints not consistently significant
cards.summary: Sandborn 2001 — 24-week dose/interval trial: clinical response at week 2 in 45% on CDP571 vs 27% on placebo (p = 0.023); retreatment benefit suggested but secondary endpoints not consistently significant
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose/interval trial (Sandborn 2001) — active-disease report 2 of 3
cards.people: 169 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease randomised to a single dose of CDP571 10 or 20 mg/kg or placebo, then retreated with 10 mg/kg every 8 or 12 weeks over 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was clinical response (CDAI fall ≥70 points) at week 2.
cards.result: Clinical response at week 2 occurred in 45% of CDP571-treated patients vs 27% on placebo (P = 0.023). Patients appeared to benefit from retreatment over 24 weeks, but not all secondary-endpoint results were statistically significant. Severe or serious adverse-event frequency was similar among groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is again a week-2 reading. The 24-week retreatment story rests on secondary endpoints that were, in the authors' own words, not consistently significant.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. An engineered human antibody to TNF (CDP571) for active Crohn's disease: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2001. PMID: 11313302. cards.headline: Sandborn 2004 — 28-week trial: the long-term primary was NULL (response 30.4% vs 23.5%, p = 0.102); the significant week-28 CRP-subgroup reading is post-hoc and is labelled as such
cards.summary: Sandborn 2004 — 28-week trial: the long-term primary was NULL (response 30.4% vs 23.5%, p = 0.102); the significant week-28 CRP-subgroup reading is post-hoc and is labelled as such
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 28-week trial (Sandborn 2004) — active-disease report 3 of 3
cards.people: 396 patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease randomised to intravenous CDP571 10 mg/kg (n = 263) or placebo (n = 132) every 8 weeks to week 24; the primary outcome was clinical response at week 28.
cards.result: Clinical response at week 28 occurred in 80/263 (30.4%) on CDP571 vs 31/132 (23.5%) on placebo (p = 0.102) — the long-term primary was null. Week-2 response was 34.2% vs 21.2% (p = 0.011). In a post-hoc exploratory subgroup of 159 patients with baseline CRP ≥10 mg/L, response differed significantly at weeks 2 (49.5% vs 15.5%, p < 0.001) and 28 (28.7% vs 12.1%, p = 0.018) — a post-hoc subgroup, labelled as such. Adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The only long-term active-disease primary in the programme missed. The CRP ≥10 mg/L subgroup was defined after the data were seen and cannot carry a week-28 efficacy claim.
cards.source: Sandborn WJ et al. CDP571, a humanised monoclonal antibody to tumour necrosis factor alpha, for moderate to severe Crohn's disease: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial. Gut. 2004. PMID: 15361500. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Feagan 2006 — steroid-dependent slice, 36-week phase 3: steroid-sparing NULL, with the point estimate favouring placebo (29.3% on CDP571 vs 36.7% on placebo, p = 0.24)
cards.summary: Feagan 2006 — steroid-dependent slice, 36-week phase 3: steroid-sparing NULL, with the point estimate favouring placebo (29.3% on CDP571 vs 36.7% on placebo, p = 0.24)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 steroid-sparing trial (Feagan 2006) — steroid-dependent report 1 of 2, a separate slice from the active-disease reports
cards.people: 271 patients with steroid-dependent Crohn's disease (CDAI ≤150 on prednisolone/prednisone 15–40 mg/day or budesonide 9 mg/day, with a previously failed taper attempt) randomised to intravenous CDP571 10 mg/kg (n = 181) or placebo (n = 90) every 8 weeks to week 32, with a defined steroid taper. The primary endpoint was steroid-sparing — discontinuation of steroids without disease flare — at week 36. This is a different question from the active-disease cards above and is not merged into their count.
cards.result: Steroid-sparing occurred in 53/181 (29.3%) on CDP571 vs 33/90 (36.7%) on placebo (P = 0.24) — null, with the point estimate favouring placebo. Adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A prespecified primary missed in the direction of placebo. No reading of this trial supports a steroid-sparing claim at any dose or duration tested in the phase 3.

cards.headline: Feagan 2005 — steroid-dependent slice, 16-week trial: the week-10 primary was NULL (p = 0.452); the week-16 reading (p = 0.032) is a secondary timepoint after a missed primary — and this report's abstract prints mutually inconsistent Ns, printed here unresolved rather than resolved by choice
cards.summary: Feagan 2005 — steroid-dependent slice, 16-week trial: the week-10 primary was NULL (p = 0.452); the week-16 reading (p = 0.032) is a secondary timepoint after a missed primary — and this report's abstract prints mutually inconsistent Ns, printed here unresolved rather than resolved by choice
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 16-week steroid-sparing trial (Feagan 2005) — steroid-dependent report 2 of 2, a separate slice; abstract denominators internally inconsistent, printed unresolved
cards.people: Patients with corticosteroid-dependent Crohn's disease (CDAI ≤150) received intravenous CDP571 (20 mg/kg at week 0, 10 mg/kg at week 8) or placebo, with a predefined steroid taper; the primary endpoint was corticosteroid-sparing at week 10 and the major secondary endpoint corticosteroid-sparing at week 16. DENOMINATOR INCONSISTENCY, printed unresolved: the fetched abstract states 'seventy-one patients received treatment', yet prints week-10 arm sizes of 39 (CDP571) and 42 (placebo) — summing to 81 — and a week-10 placebo percentage of 40.6% that arithmetically implies a denominator of 32, the denominator it prints at week 16. The denominators could not be verified against the journal full text at build, so no single N is chosen on this card.
cards.result: As printed in the abstract: corticosteroid-sparing at week 10 in 19/39 (48.7%) on CDP571 vs 13 printed with denominator 42 (40.6%) on placebo (P = 0.452) — the week-10 primary was null; and at week 16 in 18/39 (46.2%) vs 7/32 (21.9%) (P = 0.032) — a secondary timepoint after a missed primary, labelled as such. CDP571 was well tolerated and serious adverse-event incidence was similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote any arm size or total N from this report without the inconsistency note: 71 treated, arms of 39 + 42, and a percentage implying 32 cannot all be true. The week-16 p-value follows a missed prespecified primary and is hypothesis-generating only.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 5 randomised reports, 1997–2006, in two labelled slices: active disease (31, 169 and 396 patients) and steroid-dependent disease (271 patients, and one report whose abstract denominators are internally inconsistent and printed unresolved). Every endpoint in this programme is CDAI-based — the era flag is load-bearing: the programme predates treat-to-target, endoscopic primary endpoints and therapeutic drug monitoring. CDP571 was never marketed and development was discontinued; it is a distinct molecule from certolizumab pegol, its Fab′ successor, and is not merged with that home.
cards.result: The arc is the answer: a real short-term response signal (week 2 in two trials) that did not hold — the only long-term active-disease primary (week 28) was null outside a post-hoc CRP subgroup, and both steroid-sparing trials missed their prespecified primary timepoints (one numerically favouring placebo). The programme proved the TNF hypothesis in Crohn's disease while failing as a product.
cards.watchOut: Era flag: 1997–2006 CDAI endpoints throughout. The founding trial's design (single infusion, 31 patients, 2 weeks) must travel with its p-value wherever it is quoted.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Saroglitazar for MASLD/MASH — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 abstract-verified reports (N = 281): ALT and imaging-fat improvements on surrogate endpoints only, over 16–24 weeks
shelves.question: In adults with NAFLD/MASH, does saroglitazar 4 mg daily versus placebo — or versus vitamin E or no treatment — improve alanine aminotransferase, liver fat (MRI-PDFF / controlled attenuation parameter) and liver stiffness over 16–24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue/diagnostic imaging · Adult · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Aspartate Aminotransferases/blood · Cholesterol/blood · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Cholesterol, VLDL/blood · Double-Blind Method · Elasticity Imaging Techniques · Female · Humans · Insulin Resistance · Liver/diagnostic imaging · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease/blood/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · PPAR alpha/agonists · PPAR gamma/agonists · Phenylpropionates/therapeutic use · Pyrroles/therapeutic use · Triglycerides/blood · gamma-Glutamyltransferase/blood
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 abstract-verified randomised reports, total N = 281 — the phase 2 placebo-controlled trial (Gawrieh 2021, N = 106, 16 weeks: ALT −45.8% on 4 mg vs +3.4% on placebo, P < 0.001; MRI-PDFF liver fat −19.7% vs +4.1%) and the open four-arm SVIN trial (Mir 2024, N = 175, 24 weeks, no placebo arm: ALT and CAP improved vs untreated control; liver stiffness improved only in the combination arm). The summary-level proof-of-concept report and the pooled analysis are never counted. Surrogate flag (load-bearing): every endpoint is ALT, imaging fat or elastography stiffness — no verified report has a histologic primary with results in its abstract, and no clinical-outcome data exist. Both verified trials are Indian-population studies of a drug approved in India and not FDA-approved; the diabetes/hypertriglyceridaemia question is homed at pack #6666 (diagnosis-first, cross-point only).

cards.headline: Gawrieh 2021 — labelled slice 1 of 2 (primary endpoint) of FLOOR-RISK report 1 of exactly 2: ALT fell 45.8% on saroglitazar 4 mg vs a 3.4% rise on placebo at 16 weeks (P < 0.001) — a surrogate-endpoint trial with no histology primary
cards.summary: Gawrieh 2021 — labelled slice 1 of 2 (primary endpoint) of FLOOR-RISK report 1 of exactly 2: ALT fell 45.8% on saroglitazar 4 mg vs a 3.4% rise on placebo at 16 weeks (P < 0.001) — a surrogate-endpoint trial with no histology primary
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Gawrieh 2021) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (ALT primary) of report 1 of exactly 2 abstract-verified reports, total N = 281
cards.people: 106 patients with NAFLD/NASH, ALT ≥50 U/L and BMI ≥25 kg/m², randomised 1:1:1:1 to placebo or saroglitazar 1, 2 or 4 mg for 16 weeks in a randomised controlled double-blind phase 2 trial. The primary efficacy endpoint was percentage change in ALT at week 16. This card and the next are two labelled slices of this ONE report — the base of this shelf is exactly 2 reports, and slices are never counted as reports.
cards.result: Least-squares mean percentage change in ALT at week 16 was −25.5% (1 mg), −27.7% (2 mg) and −45.8% (4 mg) vs +3.4% on placebo (P < 0.001 for all doses) — percentage changes as reported in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: ALT is a surrogate. No verified report in this base has a histologic (biopsy) primary with results in its abstract, and no clinical-outcome data exist — an ALT fall is not a MASH-resolution claim.
cards.source: Gawrieh S et al. Saroglitazar, a PPAR-α/γ Agonist, for Treatment of NAFLD: A Randomized Controlled Double-Blind Phase 2 Trial. Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 33811367. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03061721. cards.headline: Gawrieh 2021 — labelled slice 2 of 2 (imaging fat and metabolic measures) of FLOOR-RISK report 1 of exactly 2: liver fat by MRI-PDFF improved on 4 mg (−19.7% vs +4.1%); mean weight gain was 1.5 kg vs 0.3 kg (p = 0.27)
cards.summary: Gawrieh 2021 — labelled slice 2 of 2 (imaging fat and metabolic measures) of FLOOR-RISK report 1 of exactly 2: liver fat by MRI-PDFF improved on 4 mg (−19.7% vs +4.1%); mean weight gain was 1.5 kg vs 0.3 kg (p = 0.27)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Gawrieh 2021) — labelled slice 2 of 2 (MRI-PDFF fat and metabolic measures) of report 1 of exactly 2 abstract-verified reports, total N = 281
cards.people: The same 106 patients as the slice above (saroglitazar 1/2/4 mg or placebo, 16 weeks); liver fat content was assessed by MRI proton density fat fraction. This is the second labelled slice of the same single report, not a further report.
cards.result: On 4 mg vs placebo, liver fat content improved (−19.7% vs +4.1% as printed), as did adiponectin, HOMA-IR and triglycerides (−68.7 vs −5.3 mg/dL) (P < 0.05 for all). Saroglitazar was well tolerated; mean weight gain was 1.5 kg on 4 mg vs 0.3 kg on placebo (P = 0.27).
cards.watchOut: Imaging fat and insulin-resistance measures are surrogates over 16 weeks. The weight-gain direction (1.5 kg on the effective dose) is part of this drug's profile and belongs beside the metabolic gains.

cards.headline: Mir 2024 (SVIN) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (design, ALT and CAP) of FLOOR-RISK report 2 of exactly 2: ALT fell significantly vs untreated control on saroglitazar (p = 0.002) in an open four-arm trial with NO placebo arm
cards.summary: Mir 2024 (SVIN) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (design, ALT and CAP) of FLOOR-RISK report 2 of exactly 2: ALT fell significantly vs untreated control on saroglitazar (p = 0.002) in an open four-arm trial with NO placebo arm
cards.type: Prospective randomised four-arm comparative trial, SVIN (Mir 2024) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (design, ALT, CAP) of report 2 of exactly 2 abstract-verified reports, total N = 281
cards.people: 175 NAFLD patients prospectively randomised to saroglitazar 4 mg alone (n = 44), vitamin E 800 IU alone (n = 41), the combination (n = 47) or control (n = 43) for 24 weeks. The design is open with an untreated control arm — no placebo arm, and no blinding is stated in the abstract. This card and the next are two labelled slices of this ONE report.
cards.result: Compared with control, the decrease in ALT was significant on saroglitazar (95% CI 6.27–28.25, P = 0.002), on vitamin E (P = 0.047) and on the combination (P = 0.001). Controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) fell significantly on saroglitazar (P = 0.015) and the combination (P = 0.026).
cards.watchOut: An untreated control is not a placebo: expectation and co-intervention effects are uncontrolled, and ALT/CAP are surrogates. This report's record carries no MeSH terms — its source line says so rather than borrowing another report's.
cards.source: Mir BA et al. A Prospective Randomised Comparative Four-arm Intervention Study of Efficacy and Safety of Saroglitazar and Vitamin E in Patients With Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)/Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)-SVIN TRIAL. cards.headline: Mir 2024 (SVIN) — labelled slice 2 of 2 (stiffness and metabolic measures) of FLOOR-RISK report 2 of exactly 2: ONLY the combination arm reduced liver stiffness significantly (p = 0.001) — the saroglitazar-alone stiffness claim must not be printed
cards.summary: Mir 2024 (SVIN) — labelled slice 2 of 2 (stiffness and metabolic measures) of FLOOR-RISK report 2 of exactly 2: ONLY the combination arm reduced liver stiffness significantly (p = 0.001) — the saroglitazar-alone stiffness claim must not be printed
cards.type: Prospective randomised four-arm comparative trial, SVIN (Mir 2024) — labelled slice 2 of 2 (stiffness, glycaemic and lipid measures) of report 2 of exactly 2 abstract-verified reports, total N = 281
cards.people: The same 175 patients as the slice above (saroglitazar alone, vitamin E alone, combination, or control, 24 weeks), with liver stiffness measurement and CAP recorded at baseline and reassessment. This is the second labelled slice of the same single report, not a further report.
cards.result: Only combination therapy significantly reduced liver stiffness (95% CI 0.41–1.68, P = 0.001). Saroglitazar alone and the combination significantly improved HbA1c (P = 0.001 and P = 0.015); saroglitazar alone significantly reduced triglycerides (P = 0.038) and LDL (P = 0.018).
cards.watchOut: The stiffness benefit belongs to the combination arm only. Printing it as a saroglitazar effect would misattribute the one structural measure in this base to the wrong arm.

cards.people: FLOOR-RISK base, stated exactly: exactly 2 abstract-verified randomised reports, total N = 281 (106 + 175), carded as four labelled slices — two slices per report, never counted as four reports. Both verified trials are Indian-population studies. Saroglitazar is a named product marketed in India (by Zydus, as the publications give it) and is not FDA-approved — named under the clarification exception, for clarification, not promotion.
cards.result: Every endpoint in the verifiable base is a surrogate — ALT, MRI-PDFF/CAP fat and elastography stiffness over 16–24 weeks; no verified report has a histologic primary with results in its abstract, and no clinical-outcome data exist. The Western-population biopsy proof-of-concept report is summary-level only (its abstract states no participant count and no results) and is never counted; the pooled lipid analysis of other trials is likewise never counted as a report. The saroglitazar-alone stiffness claim does not exist in this base — stiffness improved only in the combination arm of SVIN.

shelves.title: Anakinra-based combinations vs corticosteroids for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (N = 251): the combinations differ and the readings conflict; the larger, later trial found its combination significantly worse than prednisone
shelves.question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (MELD >20), does a combination built on the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist anakinra — with zinc, or with pentoxifylline plus zinc — versus corticosteroids improve survival at 90–180 days?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Prednisone/adverse effects · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein/adverse effects · Zinc/therapeutic use · Hepatitis, Alcoholic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Acute Kidney Injury/chemically induced/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · End Stage Liver Disease/drug therapy · Female · Hepatitis, Alcoholic/diagnosis · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein/therapeutic use · Male · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Pentoxifylline/therapeutic use · Receptors, Interleukin-1/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 randomised trials, total 251 participants randomised as reported. Both readings are printed and they conflict: COMB (Szabo 2022, N = 104; anakinra + pentoxifylline + zinc vs methylprednisolone) gave a non-significant 180-day survival trend favouring the combination (67.9% vs 56%, HR 0.69, p = 0.3001), while DASH (Gawrieh 2024, N = 147; anakinra + zinc vs prednisone) was stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis because prednisone was superior — 90-day survival 90% vs 70% (HR for death 0.34 [0.14–0.83], p = 0.018) with more acute kidney injury on the combination (45% vs 22%, p = 0.001). The combinations differ and are never averaged into a class claim. Neighbouring severe-AH homes (G-CSF #6539, FMT #6548, larsucosterol #6724) ask different questions and share no anchors.

cards.headline: Gawrieh 2024 (DASH) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of FLOOR-RISK trial 1 of exactly 2: STOPPED EARLY because prednisone was superior — 90-day survival 90% on prednisone vs 70% on anakinra + zinc (HR for death 0.34 [0.14–0.83], p = 0.018)
cards.summary: Gawrieh 2024 (DASH) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of FLOOR-RISK trial 1 of exactly 2: STOPPED EARLY because prednisone was superior — 90-day survival 90% on prednisone vs 70% on anakinra + zinc (HR for death 0.34 [0.14–0.83], p = 0.018)
cards.type: Phase IIb double-blind randomised trial stopped early at interim analysis, DASH (Gawrieh 2024) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of trial 1 of exactly 2 trials, total N = 251
cards.people: 147 participants randomised (74 anakinra + zinc, 73 prednisone) with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis and MELD 20–35, in a phase IIb double-blind trial: anakinra 100 mg daily for 14 days plus zinc sulfate 220 mg daily for 90 days vs prednisone 40 mg daily for 30 days, both under a day-7 Lille stopping rule. The trial was stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis. This card and the next are two labelled slices of this ONE trial — the base is exactly 2 trials.
cards.result: 90-day overall survival was 90% on prednisone vs 70% on anakinra + zinc (hazard ratio for death 0.34 [95% CI 0.14–0.83], p = 0.018) and transplant-free survival 88% vs 64% (HR 0.30 [0.13–0.69], p = 0.004) — the combination was significantly worse than standard care on the primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: A stopped-early trial showing harm relative to standard care is the strongest evidence on this shelf and leads it. The hazard ratios favour prednisone; reading them in the other direction would invert the trial's result.

cards.result: Acute kidney injury occurred in 45% on anakinra + zinc vs 22% on prednisone (p = 0.001). Infection rates were similar (31% vs 27%, p = 0.389). All study drugs were stopped for uncontrolled infection or a ≥5-point MELD increase, per protocol.

cards.headline: Szabo 2022 (COMB) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of FLOOR-RISK trial 2 of exactly 2: 180-day survival 67.9% on the triple combination vs 56% on methylprednisolone (HR 0.69, p = 0.3001) — NOT significant, and the combination differs from DASH's
cards.summary: Szabo 2022 (COMB) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of FLOOR-RISK trial 2 of exactly 2: 180-day survival 67.9% on the triple combination vs 56% on methylprednisolone (HR 0.69, p = 0.3001) — NOT significant, and the combination differs from DASH's
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, COMB (Szabo 2022) — labelled slice 1 of 2 (survival) of trial 2 of exactly 2 trials, total N = 251
cards.people: 104 subjects randomised (53 combination, 50 methylprednisolone, 1 dropped out before randomization, as the abstract reports it (the abstract's own wording; its arm counts of 53 + 50 plus that 1 make up the 104)) with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (MELD >20, Maddrey discriminant function >32): anakinra 14 days plus pentoxifylline 28 days plus zinc 180 days vs methylprednisolone 28 days. This combination includes pentoxifylline, which DASH's combination does not — the two trials test different combinations and are never averaged. This card and the next are two labelled slices of this ONE trial.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier survival at 180 days was 67.9% on the combination vs 56% on methylprednisolone (HR 0.69, p = 0.3001) — not significant. Survival at 28 days was similar (83.4% vs 81.2%). The survival curves separated by 90 days (69.8% vs 58.0%, HR 0.69, p = 0.28), also non-significant.
cards.watchOut: A non-significant trend in 104 patients (p = 0.3001) is not a benefit finding, and it cannot be pooled with DASH: different combination, different corticosteroid comparator, opposite direction of reading.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: FLOOR-RISK base, stated exactly: exactly 2 randomised trials, total N = 251 randomised as reported (147 + 104), carded as four labelled slices — two slices per trial, never counted as four trials. Both trials enrolled MELD >20 severe alcohol-associated hepatitis in US centres; neither supports use outside that severity band. Zinc appears in both combinations as a co-intervention — this is not a zinc shelf (zinc in hepatic encephalopathy is homed at pack #6102, a different question, untouched). All components are generic; no clarification exception applies.
cards.result: The two trials must never be averaged into a class claim: the combinations differ (pentoxifylline present in COMB, absent in DASH), the comparators differ (methylprednisolone vs prednisone), and the readings conflict — a non-significant survival trend favouring the triple combination in 104 patients (2022) versus a stopped-early trial showing significantly worse 90-day survival and more acute kidney injury on the double combination in 147 patients (2024). The honest summary is that the larger, later trial found the strategy inferior to prednisone. This shelf presents a tested-and-failed immunomodulatory strategy, with the earlier null trial beside it for completeness.
cards.watchOut: Failed verification would have stopped this build; verification did not fail — both trials were fetched this session with non-empty abstracts and the exact count (2 trials, N = 251) verified. The DASH design papers and its AKI secondary analysis are not trials and are not counted.

shelves.title: Alisporivir for chronic hepatitis C — one programme, 3 randomised reports (N = 1,880): higher SVR than peginterferon/ribavirin in every trial, in a programme halted by a regulatory clinical hold and never resumed
shelves.question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C — genotype 1 treatment-naïve, genotype 1 prior non-responders/relapsers, or genotype 2/3 treatment-naïve — does alisporivir (400 mg twice daily or 600–1,000 mg daily) added to peginterferon-α/ribavirin, or given interferon-free with ribavirin, improve sustained virological response versus peginterferon/ribavirin alone?

shelves.balance: One programme, counted exactly: 3 publications covering 3 trials, N = 1,880. Alisporivir raised SVR over peginterferon/ribavirin in every population tested — SVR12 69% vs 53% in treatment-naïve genotype 1 (ESSENTIAL II, phase 3), superior early response and SVR12 in prior non-responders/relapsers (FUNDAMENTAL), and SVR24 80–85% vs 58% including interferon-free arms in genotype 2/3 (VITAL-1). Two load-bearing flags frame all of it: the era flag — every comparator is the obsolete peginterferon/ribavirin standard — and the hold flag — an FDA partial clinical hold over pancreatitis cases truncated dosing in both genotype 1 trials, the programme was never resumed, and alisporivir (DEB025) was never marketed. The 90% and 92% subset figures in this base are duration-/response-selected readings, never headline rates.

cards.summary: Zeuzem 2015 (ESSENTIAL II) — phase 3: SVR12 was 69% across alisporivir groups vs 53% on peginterferon/ribavirin alone; an FDA partial clinical hold stopped alisporivir dosing mid-trial
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ESSENTIAL II (Zeuzem 2015) — report 1 of 3 in one programme, N = 1,880 across the programme
cards.people: 1,081 patients randomised with treatment-naïve chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 infection (12% cirrhosis) to alisporivir 600 mg daily (response-guided or fixed 48 weeks) or 400 mg twice daily plus peginterferon/ribavirin, vs peginterferon/ribavirin alone. Following the FDA partial clinical hold, alisporivir/placebo was discontinued and patients completed peginterferon/ribavirin only; at that point 87% had received ≥12 weeks and 20% ≥24 weeks of triple therapy.
cards.result: Sustained virological response at 12 weeks (SVR12, the primary endpoint) was 69% in all alisporivir groups vs 53% on control. The highest SVR12 (90%) was in patients who received >24 weeks of the 400 mg twice-daily triple regimen — a duration-selected subgroup reading, labelled as such, never a headline rate.
cards.watchOut: Every SVR contrast here is against peginterferon/ribavirin — an obsolete comparator — and the exposure itself was truncated by a regulatory hold. The 90% figure describes patients selected by how long they stayed on the regimen, not the randomised effect.
cards.source: Zeuzem S et al. Randomised clinical trial: alisporivir combined with peginterferon and ribavirin in treatment-naïve patients with chronic HCV genotype 1 infection (ESSENTIAL II). Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2015. PMID: 26238707. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ESSENTIAL II (Zeuzem 2015) — labelled harms-and-hold slice of report 1 of 3 in one programme
cards.people: The same 1,081 randomised patients as the card above. This is a labelled slice of that ONE report (its safety and programme-fate findings), not a further report — the programme count stays 3 reports.
cards.result: Seven cases of pancreatitis were reported, with similar frequency between alisporivir/peginterferon/ribavirin and control (0.6% vs 0.8%). Adverse events more frequent on alisporivir were anaemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinaemia and hypertension. The FDA partial clinical hold that truncated this trial arose from pancreatitis cases across the global programme; the programme was never resumed and alisporivir was never marketed for hepatitis C.
cards.watchOut: Pancreatitis frequency was similar between arms in this trial — the hold was a programme-level regulatory decision, and printing the 0.6% vs 0.8% without the hold beside it would misstate the drug's fate.

cards.headline: Buti 2015 (FUNDAMENTAL) — phase 2 in prior non-responders/relapsers: complete early virological response was superior on every alisporivir arm (highest 74% vs 36%, p < 0.0001); the clinical hold truncated dosing here too
cards.summary: Buti 2015 (FUNDAMENTAL) — phase 2 in prior non-responders/relapsers: complete early virological response was superior on every alisporivir arm (highest 74% vs 36%, p < 0.0001); the clinical hold truncated dosing here too
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, FUNDAMENTAL (Buti 2015) — report 2 of 3 in one programme, N = 1,880 across the programme
cards.people: 459 patients randomised with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 infection in whom prior peginterferon/ribavirin had failed (43% relapsers, 34% null responders, 23% partial responders) to alisporivir 600 or 800 mg daily or 400 mg twice daily plus peginterferon/ribavirin, vs placebo plus peginterferon/ribavirin for 48 weeks. When the global programme was put on clinical hold, all patients had received ≥31 weeks of randomised treatment and completed 48 weeks on peginterferon/ribavirin alone.
cards.result: Complete early virological response (the primary endpoint) was superior on every alisporivir arm (P ≤ 0.0131), highest at 74% vs 36% on the twice-daily arm (P < 0.0001). SVR12 rates on the programme ranged 63–68% vs 3–26% on control across prior-response strata as reported. One case of pancreatitis (fully recovered) occurred on alisporivir; hypertension was infrequent but more common on alisporivir.
cards.watchOut: Prior-failure strata (relapsers vs null responders) have very different prognoses — the stratum-specific SVR12 ranges must not be collapsed into a single rate. Dosing was again truncated by the programme hold.
cards.source: Buti M et al. Alisporivir with peginterferon/ribavirin in patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 infection who failed to respond to or relapsed after prior interferon-based therapy: FUNDAMENTAL, a Phase II trial. Journal of Viral Hepatitis. 2015. PMID: 25412795. Registry ID: none in the record.
